- [fact] Ordinary fingerprints identify little without a comparison sample. When: a print is found on a dramatic object. Why: a print means nothing until it is matched to a known source.
- [fact] Ambiguous physical evidence often admits several explanations, and each must be weighed against what the witnesses say.
- [fact] Prints found on different objects can be compared, and a match ties both objects to one person. When: Linking physical objects to a suspect. Why: Matching traces create a physical connection between separate items.
- [fact] Prints can overlap and be superimposed, but a sufficiently distinct set may still be identified. When: Several people handled the same object. Why: Superimposition blurs impressions without erasing them entirely.
- [fact] Thinning oil paint with turpentine or another flatting agent makes it dry within about an hour, but the finish is dull rather than glossy.
- [fact] With a stiff arm and raised shoulder, the height of an aimed weapon tracks the shooter's height closely, so weapon height gives a usable estimate.
- [fact] A typed note's typeface, faded ribbon and fold pattern can link it to a particular machine and a route of delivery. Why: typewriter and paper traces are physical signatures.
- [fact] Some executions are recorded as probably resting on confession, though the basis was assumed rather than documented.
- [fact] Small objects can be identified at a distance through glass by their shape and color.
- [fact] An empty hiding place proves only that the object has moved, not that it has left the area. When: A concealment has been searched and found empty. Why: The object may have been relocated within the same space.
- [fact] A draught that carries a smell upstairs shows an opening existed while the event occurred.
- [fact] Dust or grime on glass can block what a view shows, forcing the scene to be read from another light source.
- [fact] A physical trace such as a fingerprint can be copied so closely that inspection of the copy reveals no difference from the original.
- [fact] A forger needs access to a genuine sample to copy it, so access to the source is a precondition for forgery.
- [fact] Fine airborne dust that settles into cloth can record where an object has hung over a long period.
- [fact] Rough or rusty surfaces do not take fingerprints, so a blank surface of that kind carries no information about handling.
- [fact] Control of a key, including one worn on the person, limits access to its holder and anyone they gave it to. Tracing key movements is needed to establish who could enter. When: When a locked room's key is central to who could enter. Why: Access to a key defines the set of people who could have opened the door.
- [fact] The time a message is sent and the time it is delivered can differ by a large margin, and that gap can decide who could have acted. When: When a message's timing matters to an alibi. Why: Delivery delay creates an unobserved window.
- [fact] Ordinary household habits, such as a window left open or a door left unbolted, can provide routes into a room that appear locked.
- [fact] Former homesteads often survive as cellar hollows, stone heaps or scattered bricks, which can corroborate written records.
- [fact] People with plain voices and ordinary builds offer few distinguishing features, so many suspects remain unidentified.
- [fact] A physical trace such as a fingerprint or bloodstain is one fact among others. Its evidential value depends on how it came to be where it was found.
- [fact] Trifles that can form a circumstantial chain include a scrap of paper, a torn garment shred, a coat button, an incautious word, a letter fragment, a door's sound, a shadow on a blind, and a precisely timed moment. When: Assembling a case from small clues. Why: Each item is minor alone but can link into a chain.
- [fact] Physical traces require a surface that records marks; hard or dry surfaces that keep no impressions offer little evidence.
- [fact] Fused wiring and burned insulation point to a high-energy event rather than impact damage alone.
- [fact] Faint trickles of water in sand can show a body was carried in or moved by a current. When: Examining wet ground near a body. Why: Water flow leaves marks that record movement.
- [fact] Sympathetic ink stays invisible until heated, so applying heat to a surface can expose hidden writing in a single action. When: A document with hidden text. Why: Heat changes the ink's visibility, so a simple action exposes text that looked blank.

## witness testimony reliability
- [model] Witnesses' confident accounts can supply a false culprit; a mystery can use their testimony as the misdirect and reread the scene to expose it. When: A crime where several observers describe an intruder. Why: Confident group testimony is accepted as evidence, so the false culprit persists until the setting is reinterpreted.
- [definition] A hidden witness is someone present in a scene who knows what was said but goes unnoticed by the people being observed.
- [mechanism] Each retelling reshapes an account: tellers pick what to repeat, links drop details or qualifiers like 'I think', listeners embellish; trace accounts to their source. When: information passes through several people before reaching the investigator. Why: Every link filters and reshapes the account, and each depends on the one before, so later versions can outgrow the original. (x2)
- [mechanism] NPC answers can depend on whether a cover story is believed, so each persona needs a backstory that holds under light townsfolk questioning. When: Designing disguises, infiltrator NPCs, or a false persona or pretext. Why: Light questioning is how players are most likely to probe a cover.
- [mechanism] A witness's reputation changes how much weight a listener gives their word, so a discredited witness may be dismissed whatever the truth of the account.
- [mechanism] A hypnotised subject can only reflect what the operator already believes, so apparent insight traces back to the operator.
- [mechanism] Evidence relayed through several people is filtered at each step, so its reliability depends on who speaks, who translates and who has a stake. When: An account reaches the player through intermediaries. Why: Each relay can lose core facts or add bias.
- [mechanism] NPC dialogue can let enemies discredit witnesses in advance, so the player must find evidence that cannot be explained away.
- [mechanism] When one impression lies over another, the mark on top was made later, so overlapping marks reveal the order of events. When: When soft ground records impressions that overlap. Why: Physical layering preserves temporal order.
- [mechanism] Pressure on an emotional NPC can make its dialogue volatile and reveal hidden knowledge, while calmer tone options keep the conversation on track.
- [mechanism] Multiple NPCs giving slightly different versions of an event let the player cross-check and rank their accounts. When: designing an event witnessed by several NPCs. Why: variation gives the player material to test and compare.
- [mechanism] If NPC decision-makers weigh different factors, such as manner, physical proof or grudges, identical evidence can produce different verdicts. When: Designing a tribunal or jury system in a game.
- [mechanism] NPC witnesses can carry confidence levels, so 'I think it was him' sounds different from 'I saw his face.' When: designing NPC testimony. Why: graded confidence tells the player how much weight to give a claim.
- [mechanism] A timed answer system that causes details to be forgotten under pressure models hurried recall and rewards slower, careful questioning.
- [mechanism] A witness hidden behind a locked door who overhears an interview reframes earlier pressure as a setup when revealed at the end.
- [mechanism] A single rumour can gain a new name with each retelling, until a whole faction turns against one character.
- [mechanism] Reporting a remark to rivals can change factional trust and set a conflict in motion between the speaker and the reporter's opponents. When: When a character passes a private remark to an opposing group. Why: Rivals react to the content, altering alliances.
- [mechanism] When a claim says an unseen agent acted regardless of location, no alibi, distance or good character can rebut it. When: A witness reports harm by an agent only the accuser perceives. Why: The claim is defined so that no ordinary evidence can contradict it.
- [mechanism] A vendor can recognise an NPC face shown from a portrait or poster, so a canvassing mechanic can link a purchased object to a character. When: When designing a canvass or shop-inquiry mechanic. Why: Vendors remember customers' faces, letting players connect objects to people.
- [mechanism] Each false statement adds a new fact that must be defended, so a lie made to explain one anomaly increases the chances of exposure. When: A person maintains a deception to cover an anomaly. Why: Every added claim creates another point at which the story can be contradicted.
- [mechanism] A witness afraid of trouble may change their story, so their account must be weighed against their motive to protect themselves. When: When a witness faces possible consequences. Why: Self-protection motivates altered testimony.
- [mechanism] Players who cross-check NPC accounts against each other and against their own observations can reach conclusions the game never states directly. When: When a game presents several conflicting NPC accounts. Why: Comparison across sources yields inferences that no single source provides.
- [mechanism] An echo copies the listener's own rhythm, so footsteps that pause or change tempo independently argue against a simple echo. When: Judging whether a sound is an echo. Why: An echo can only reproduce what was made, so independent timing reveals another source.
- [mechanism] A claim resting only on a dead person's word cannot be checked, so it stays weak evidence even when stated with certainty. When: Evaluating a testimony whose only source is unavailable. Why: Without a living or recorded source, the claim has nothing to be tested against.
- [mechanism] When testimony is too vague to link a suspect to the event, the investigation can end without a finding of responsibility. When: when the available accounts cannot connect a person to the act. Why: Without a link between person and act, the case cannot reach a conclusion.
- [mechanism] A dying character's ambiguous late remark can reopen an answer the player believed settled, adding doubt without new proof. When: when a settled answer needs a late jolt. Why: ambiguity invites reinterpretation of earlier evidence.
- [behavior] Witnesses who hear the outcome may sincerely reinterpret earlier sensory details as linked to it, so compare later accounts with the original record. When: witness hears news after the event. Why: new information reshapes memory of earlier sensory details. (x2)
- [behavior] Witnesses with a stake, grudge, hostility toward one party, a wish to promote another, or a strong moral or religious framework bias reports, fusing checkable facts with judgments. When: a witness has a personal stake, grudge, or strong moral or religious framework. Why: Bias colours perception and reporting, so factual claims and verdicts arrive fused together.
- [behavior] Wary informants clam up when their information seems important or no assurance has been given; pressing early yields silence, while those feeling heard under protest may give more. When: questioning a wary or reluctant informant before any assurance has been given. Why: Perceived importance and fear of exposure make witnesses guard what they know.
- [behavior] An excited or elated witness mixes their own feelings into the facts, so the listener must separate what is felt from what is known. When: A witness is biased, emotional or distracted. Why: Strong emotion colours how the witness reports events.
- [behavior] Excited observers inflate what they saw, reporting impressions of closeness or detail as if they were measurements. When: A striking event is observed by an excited group. Why: Emotion turns impressions into confident claims.
- [behavior] A sincere young witness may report accurate concrete details while drawing sweeping, emotional conclusions from them. When: a child reports events they witnessed. Why: Feelings and loyalties shape interpretation.
- [behavior] A child's vivid testimony can seem supernatural because of the child's age, which makes it harder to dismiss.
- [behavior] Rising agitation in a witness signals that the testimony is coloured by emotion and should be checked against other evidence. When: A witness's account becomes more anxious or emotional as it proceeds. Why: Anxiety distorts perception and recall, making the account less reliable.
- [behavior] A partner whose trust wavers may be steadied by receiving full written detail of each step, which also creates a shared record. When: Trust between conspirators is shaken. Why: Complete disclosure reduces suspicion and ties both parties to one account.
- [behavior] A witness's temper and the questioner's manner both shape how the witness's answers are heard and interpreted. When: a witness is questioned under pressure.
- [behavior] A witness pressed to explain herself by an accusatory questioner answers briefly and turns away to signal objection. When: An interrogator shifts from enquiry to accusation. Why: Insistent demands turn the exchange into an accusation, so the witness protects herself through minimal replies.
- [behavior] A correct detail from an unreliable witness can be coincidence, so it needs independent checking before it is trusted. When: When a drunk, hostile or self-interested witness gives one checkable detail. Why: Partial accuracy from an unreliable source does not establish the rest of its account.
- [behavior] People assume a familiar routine held to the end, so a person's unusual final hours often go unchecked by others. When: when someone describes a routine they follow daily. Why: others assume the usual pattern without checking it.
- [behavior] A brief glimpse under shock can feel certain yet be wrong, and memory of the period after a shock is often unreliable. When: When a witness reports a vivid memory formed under stress. Why: Shock impairs perception and memory, producing confident but inaccurate recall.
- [behavior] An agitated witness may volunteer useful detail but may also drift off topic. When: a witness is emotionally charged during questioning. Why: emotion loosens recall and focus at the same time.
- [behavior] Accounts taken soon after an event, from a household or crowd that is agitated and gossiping, tend to be muddied as recollections blend together. When: when early accounts are collected from an unsettled group. Why: Shared talk and emotion blend individual memories.
- [behavior] A witness's story can shift step by step under precise questioning, such as moving from one location to another, and each shift is a signal to check against other evidence. When: When a witness is questioned closely about a timeline or location.
- [behavior] Witnesses recall routine events poorly, and their memory of which day it happened fades further as questioning is delayed. When: asked about a repeated daily event. Why: a routine occurrence blends into others, so single days are hard to separate.
- [behavior] A confessor may swear an oath without understanding what it means, so a sworn statement is not automatically informed. When: judging a sworn confession. Why: the oath may have been taken without understanding its weight.
- [behavior] An instinctive physical withdrawal can signal unease the person cannot justify, and the other party may read it as a slight.
- [behavior] Distracted observers often fail to notice a small deliberate action performed in front of them and treat it as incidental. When: attention is pulled elsewhere during the action. Why: unattended actions are not registered.
- [behavior] Bystanders filter testimony through their assumptions, dismissing a speaker as mad and missing content that may matter. When: a witness speaks in an emotional state. Why: prior assumptions shape what is heard.
- [behavior] A distant observer who cannot hear an exchange must infer its meaning from gestures, which can be staged or misread. When: Judging a conclusion drawn from a watcher far from the event. Why: Gestures are visible but ambiguous, and they cannot reveal the words spoken.
- [behavior] People who are not careful distinguish observed traces from suppositions tend to accept every detail as certain once a theory is presented to them. When: Presenting a theory to a sceptic or a listener. Why: Without marking which links are supported, all links feel equally proven.
- [behavior] A fixed date gives memory a starting point, so witnesses supply more detail than they do from vague recollection. When: recalling events without a fixed reference point. Why: fixed anchors cue memory.
- [behavior] A minor witness may confirm a basic event but give no name or direction; when follow-up answers stay empty, the investigator should accept the limit and move on. When: Minor witness is the only source for a basic event. Why: Such witnesses often lack identifying detail, so pressing further yields nothing.
- [behavior] Players and observers notice hidden things through reflections or partly blocked views, so information visible only indirectly still registers as a clue. When: The relevant object or person is out of direct line of sight. Why: Indirect views reveal what direct views hide, and players can be trained to look for them.
- [behavior] Memory of minor details, such as the position of a fixture, degrades after repairs or distress, so such details deserve less trust. When: when a witness recalls small physical details after a change or upsetting event. Why: Changes and distress disrupt memory of incidental features.
- [behavior] Witnesses who see the same shadowy shape describe it differently, filling gaps with their own expectations and fear. When: When several witnesses report on one brief or poorly lit sighting. Why: Observers complete ambiguous shapes with what they expect or fear.
- [behavior] Light, teasing exchanges can calm a witness and loosen their account, so they begin to speak more freely. When: when a guarded witness has stopped offering detail. Why: relaxed rapport lowers defensiveness and encourages disclosure.
- [behavior] A witness may leave a stop out of a summary and admit it only when asked directly, so an account that seems complete can still be incomplete. When: a witness narrates a journey in brisk summary. Why: Summaries compress the route and omit legs the speaker does not volunteer.
- [behavior] A figure that boards unseen and leaves at the last moment is identified only when two observers recognise it together. When: when a single observer might miss a fleeting figure. Why: independent confirmation raises confidence in a brief sighting.
- [behavior] A plausible wrong answer is attractive because it fits what the audience already expects. When: The audience holds a prior expectation about the solution. Why: Fit with expectations hides the error.
- [behavior] A witness questioned repeatedly may adopt a feature they were led to notice, and retract it only when pressed again. When: a witness faces leading questions. Why: a suggested detail can come to feel like something seen.
- [behavior] A witness who knows about a reconstruction may act differently, so the test can be compromised. When: a witness learns the purpose of a replay. Why: awareness changes behavior.
- [behavior] Witness descriptions of a person in a role shrink to generic traits such as rough height, clean-shaven face and ordinary clothes. When: A witness recalls someone seen briefly in a familiar role.
- [behavior] An eager informant who is keen on their own theory can push an inquiry forward without checking the source, leading to costly action. When: A witness proposes a suggestion and presses to act on it quickly. Why: Enthusiasm and pride can override verification.
- [behavior] Discovering a discrepancy in presented evidence can reverse a witness's trust in the investigator who presented it. Why: the witness reads the difference as a trap.
- [behavior] A witness who was asleep, drowsy or distracted may have registered a sound or sight without noticing it at the time. Why: attention is reduced, so perception is weak but not absent.
- [behavior] A witness who answers only exactly what is asked volunteers little, leaving the investigator with little to work with. When: when interviewing a reserved or literal witness.
- [behavior] Distinctive costume items are easier to recall than faces, so they work well as search keys for finding an unknown person. When: searching for someone seen only in passing. Why: unusual visual elements stand out in memory.
- [behavior] A concealed listener who gathers information may keep returning and improve their position for further listening, showing that eavesdropping is itself rewarding to them. When: Designing a concealed observer character. Why: Listening yields both knowledge and enjoyment, which encourages repeat visits.
- [behavior] An emotional witness may confirm an identity too readily, so the examiner must press for firm, definite answers. When: A grieving or distressed witness is confirming identity. Why: Emotional state can push a witness toward quick agreement.
- [behavior] When others present deny a witness's perceived event, the witness's account is often not withdrawn.
- [behavior] A witness with a motive may describe a subject in vivid terms that reveal the witness's own feelings more than the subject's character. When: when testimony comes from someone with a stake. Why: motive shapes what the witness notices.
- [behavior] A highly impressionable observer at close range may feel a crowd as a pull, while observers behind cover see only the disturbance, not its cause. When: A concealed observer watches a crowd up close. Why: Limited vantage shows effects without their sources.
- [behavior] A witness approached unexpectedly may be badly startled and fail to recognize a familiar person until reminded of an earlier contact. When: when an investigator approaches a witness from behind. Why: Surprise impairs immediate recognition.
- [behavior] Stunned witnesses in a shocking event give fragmentary, weak accounts, and repeating a single phrase is not a reliable identification. When: Witnesses describe an event in high-emotion, chaotic conditions. Why: Shock narrows what a witness can recall and say clearly.
- [behavior] Hope for an outcome or admiration for the person seen can colour recollection, shifting reports toward the wish or favourable detail rather than what the witness knew. When: when a witness has an emotional stake in the result or admires the person described. Why: Emotional response shapes memory and reporting.
- [behavior] Dramatic or erratic conduct alone does not show falsehood, since performance and clear thinking coexist; yet a convincing performance is not proof of sincerity either. When: A witness shows extreme or theatrical behavior, or delivers a performance. Why: Performance and clear thinking can occur together in one person, and emotional convincingness distorts evidence as much as dismissal does.
- [behavior] A frightened or angry witness may be sincere yet wrong; suspicions colored by fear are persuasive but unverified and must be tested before they shape the case. When: A witness is driven by fear, distrust or grief. Why: Strong emotion shapes what is perceived and reported, so fear-colored suspicions are not established facts.
- [behavior] A witness who seems certain may hedge or retract when frightened, so record the hedge as a sign of weak evidence. When: A witness is pressed under pressure. Why: Fear can weaken a stated certainty.
- [behavior] When many observers praise the same person in identical terms, the praise may reflect what observers want to see rather than what the person did. When: A character's reputation rests on many similar accounts. Why: Shared expectations shape how observers describe someone.
- [behavior] Local oral tradition can explain a present event through a causal account, but its claims are hard to verify, so the investigator must often rely on the teller's word alone. When: A setting has a long oral history but the physical proof has decayed. Why: Inherited memory supplies explanations and past procedures, yet no independent check is available.
- [behavior] A teller may move his own situation to another place or period, telling his account at a safe distance. When: A suspect tells a story whose setting differs from his real situation. Why: Distance from the real events lowers the teller's perceived risk of exposure.
- [behavior] Laughter, a darkening face, stillness or sudden distrust signal where a witness's concealed knowledge lies. When: Questioning a reluctant witness on a sensitive subject. Why: Involuntary reactions betray emotional stakes that answers may hide.
- [behavior] A witness's interpretation of events, such as a belief in a conspiracy, can be wrong while the observed facts remain accurate. When: When a witness reports strange or frightening conclusions. Why: Emotional or confused witnesses often mix accurate observation with unreliable explanation.
- [behavior] Witnesses often confuse what they heard reported at an inquest with what they personally saw. When: Taking testimony from a witness after a public proceeding. Why: Repeated information blends into memory and feels like firsthand experience.
- [behavior] A precise, sequential account with checkable facts feels more credible to listeners, who use it to test against what they already know. When: when a witness gives a detailed, ordered account. Why: Specific details give the listener something to verify.
- [behavior] Witnesses often believe they watched continuously when they were in fact away from the key sightline during a blind interval. When: A witness reports an unbroken view of a door or route. Why: Attention and movement take witnesses out of the critical sightline without their noticing.
- [behavior] A witness may state a negative fact with firm certainty while having never checked it, reasoning that they would have noticed if it were present. When: A witness's denial is the main support for a conclusion. Why: Certainty can rest on an assumed observation rather than an actual one.
- [behavior] Players accept an eyewitness account as proof of guilt until a new explanation reframes what the witness saw. When: A witness reports a suspect's act with confidence. Why: A direct report feels like firm evidence, so it stays settled until another reading challenges it.
- [rule] Do not equate a motivated witness with a liar, or discard their account for bias alone; corroborate it against independent evidence before weighing it. When: a witness is prejudiced or has a stake in the outcome. Why: A biased source can still report true facts, and dismissing them loses evidence. (x2)
- [rule] Tag NPC testimony with a visible stake or grudge, so players must weigh it against inspectable traces and other clues before accepting it. When: designing an in-game witness whose account may be self-serving. Why: Visible bias lets players judge a claim instead of accepting it as fact. (x2)
- [rule] Do not accuse a person on an overheard keyword or lone testimony; require confirmation from a second source, such as a records terminal, first. When: narrowing down speakers of an overheard clue before accusing anyone. Why: A single hearing cannot establish who spoke. (x2)
- [rule] Keep reported speech, such as what another person said, separate from the speaker's own words, and note when the speaker confirms a statement. When: A witness quotes someone else, or statements are recorded in a case file or dialogue log. Why: Mixing the two blurs who said what; confirmed speech is stronger evidence than secondhand report. (x2)
- [rule] Give each witness one precise, checkable detail, such as a ring or a clock chime, that can be matched against other clues. Why: A distinctive detail becomes a usable identifier or timing anchor.
- [rule] Give witness NPCs an age, a role and a list of acts they can attest to, so players can weigh each account. When: when creating NPC witnesses. Why: shared attributes make accounts comparable.
- [rule] Have NPC reports state their basis (saw, heard, or deduced) so players can weigh each claim. When: designing NPC testimony. Why: Stated sources let players judge reliability.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses a bias value that shifts with their relationship to the player and their emotional state, so their statements vary. When: designing NPC testimony.
- [rule] Check whether anything observed about a person contradicts their claimed routine or availability.
- [rule] Do not rely on a shaken or frightened witness's account; distress, fear, shielding someone or betraying a confidence can distort what they say even when sincere.
- [rule] Track NPC reputation separately from claim accuracy, so the player can see when trust is doing the work instead of evidence.
- [rule] Do not treat answers from an impaired or altered-state witness as verified fact; hold them until independent checks confirm them and note the limit in the record. When: A witness's recall or judgment is impaired by altered state or a possible physical cause. Why: Such answers reflect the witness's view, can be shaped by questioning, and cannot confirm or rule out events.
- [rule] Do not rely on a witness's account or its specific details until they are checked against independent accounts or physical evidence. When: Testimony is the main basis for a conclusion, or one witness supplies a specific fact that will drive the investigation. Why: Testimony can be incomplete, biased or misremembered and needs corroboration.
- [rule] Treat facts that a suspect or NPC volunteers, or supplies as the only source, as unverified until an outside source confirms them, and weigh why the source offered them. When: A suspect or NPC volunteers unrequested information, or is the only source for a fact. Why: Accepting offered facts at face value can send the investigator down the wrong path.
- [rule] Show a narrator's blind spots openly, and include later corrections that reveal what an earlier account shielded, so readers can weigh the witness against the investigator's reading. When: A narrator reports a scene the investigator reads differently, or a narrator's statement is partial. Why: Otherwise readers may doubt the investigator rather than the witness, and later corrections let them verify claims.
- [rule] Question even helpful witnesses about unobserved gaps, checking the timing of sightings as well as the count, since a few seconds is enough to slip away and rejoin. When: Testing who could have moved unseen between two points. Why: Cooperation does not remove unobserved gaps, and counts alone miss short windows.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses varying reliability through conditions or bias, such as drowsy, drunk, frightened, prejudiced or a confident noble, so players must cross-check their statements. When: Designing NPC testimony. Why: A conditioned or biased witness is less reliable and should not be taken at face value.
- [rule] Make some NPC witnesses unreliable or only partly accurate, giving partial or conflicting details that players must cross-check or confirm before acting. When: Authoring NPC testimony for a mystery. Why: Partial reliability makes verification a required step.
- [rule] Limit each NPC's account to its own vantage point, giving partial or conflicting information, so players must assemble the truth from several partial logs. When: Designing several NPCs who saw the same event. Why: Vantage-based variation makes cross-checking necessary.
- [rule] For an event that will be publicly doubted, choose witnesses with standing and wait for them to be present before acting. When: An event's account will face public disbelief. Why: Credible witnesses give the account weight.
- [rule] Question a child carefully, since leading questions can draw out details but can also shape the answer. When: interviewing a minor.
- [rule] Do not accept an unnamed or unlocated witness as proof; rate their account with low credibility. When: a sighting cannot be traced to a named person. Why: An untraceable source cannot be checked.
- [rule] Take a cooperative witness's full account at the first meeting, while they are willing, rather than planning to return for the rest. When: the witness is cooperative and holds partial knowledge. Why: Willingness can end, and a return visit may yield much less.
- [rule] Vary a gatekeeper NPC's refusal wording so it reflects the reason behind the refusal, rather than repeating identical lines. When: A gatekeeper NPC refuses the player more than once. Why: Varied wording gives the player a signal about the underlying motive.
- [rule] Store each NPC's exact words and what it actually saw, so later contradictions can be checked against the record. When: Designing NPC testimony in a game.
- [rule] Do not rely on a witness who only repeats one explanation; move on to someone who engages with details. Why: Repeated explanations add no new information.
- [rule] Keep atmospheric description purposeful; each detail should carry information or tension, since long passages slow the scene. When: When writing scene descriptions.
- [rule] Offer a feigned-disinterest dialogue option that unlocks more detail from talkative NPCs.
- [rule] Compare accounts from several witnesses; when they describe the same strange effect in similar terms, a common cause is likely. When: Several accounts cover the same event. Why: Shared descriptions point to one source.
- [rule] Let NPC witnesses state a confidence level with a reason, and let the player's follow-up question change what they say. When: designing NPC testimony in dialogue. Why: confidence and reasons make testimony feel earned and revisable.
- [rule] Check each witness answer against the question actually asked, since witnesses sometimes answer a different question. When: Interviews about access or timing. Why: An answer to an unasked question can seem relevant while leaving the real question open.
- [rule] Place a witness in hiding beside the action, so the audience learns events through a limited, close view. When: When a scene needs tension and must be seen through one character's limited view. Why: A close, restricted view keeps the audience uncertain.
- [rule] Give an NPC who offers a theory a motive for steering the player, so players learn to question sources. When: Writing NPCs who suggest explanations. Why: Players must weigh a suggestion by its origin.
- [rule] Let an NPC's stated opinion be wrong, and reward the player for checking it against other evidence. When: When an NPC gives a verdict or interpretation of events. Why: Checking opinion against observation teaches the player to separate conclusions from facts.
- [rule] Ask every witness the same yes-or-no question and compare answers, giving no visible reaction to any reply.
- [rule] Observe a group from a concealed recess with a view of its entrance and stairs, learning its structure without entering the room. When: You need to learn who meets and how members are admitted without contact. Why: Watching arrivals reveals structure without risking exposure through entry.
- [rule] Give guard or townsfolk NPCs a memory of a player or suspect, tied to a world event the player also witnessed.
- [rule] Vary NPC witness descriptions by lighting, distance and observation time so the player must weigh each account. When: designing witness dialogue. Why: Differing conditions make accounts differ in detail and trust.
- [rule] Start questioning from what the witness actually perceived, separating features they saw, such as clothing and build, from features they never saw, such as the face. When: the witness had a partial view. Why: Claims should match the observation actually made.
- [rule] Let a pressured or bargaining NPC give the player's next clue, and show the reason for their cooperation in the dialogue. When: designing NPCs who reveal information under pressure. Why: A visible motive makes the disclosure believable.
- [rule] Unlock an NPC's recall of a fact only after a prompt, to model delayed memory. When: Designing NPC memory in a mystery game. Why: Gated recall mirrors how real memory surfaces under prompting.
- [rule] Give each witness request a different category of witness, so the player must decide which channels are worth their time.
- [rule] Do not rely on an exact-detail comparison when the original is remembered only in general terms. Why: vague memory cannot reveal small differences.
- [rule] Give NPCs memories that cover only regulars, so a stranger is noticed only when the player asks in the right way. When: When designing NPC knowledge of the people in their environment. Why: Selective memory makes investigation depend on precise questioning rather than general queries.
- [rule] Generate a mix of true alibis, false but checkable alibis, and alibis resting on one witness with a motive to lie. When: When designing a set of NPC alibis for a mystery. Why: Mixed reliability keeps the player verifying claims rather than trusting them all equally.
- [rule] Assign each witness NPC a reliability score and a set of statements, and flag any statement that conflicts with physical state for the player. When: designing an NPC witness system. Why: explicit reliability lets players weigh testimony against the world.
- [rule] Admit uncertainty openly and do not present a provisional premise as proven. When: When presenting a deduction. Why: Keeps the reasoning honest and checkable.
- [rule] Keep the identifying photograph hidden from other observers during a witness check so that official presence does not influence the witnesses' answers. When: Running an identification with witnesses in the presence of other people. Why: Visible photos or observers' reactions can steer what witnesses report.
- [rule] Let an NPC's account be checked against its earlier retellings, and let consistency across retellings raise the player's trust. When: An NPC repeats information to the player over time. Why: Stable retellings signal reliability and can be compared against the record.
- [rule] Do not end questioning when a witness becomes difficult, since that removes the chance to test their story. When: A witness's account changes or they become uncooperative.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses a reputation score, so honest, consistent witnesses are trusted even when they testify against the player.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses varying reliability, so their statements about a door or object may be wrong or self-serving.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses sight and hearing limits so players must cross-check what each one could actually perceive.
- [rule] Let NPC dialogue sound threatening or mocking when it is routine, and reveal its real meaning later through another NPC or an object.
- [rule] Check claims made during fits or claims to see hidden things before relying on them.
- [rule] Assign reports a confidence value that drops for sightings made at range or relayed through rumour, and let it govern how much the report counts. When: When the game models NPC or player witness reports.
- [rule] Show players the last-seen times of NPCs so they can compare them against a process clock. When: Designing investigation clues that depend on timing. Why: Players need the last-seen data to apply the process clock.
- [rule] An NPC's response to a planted item can vary with its motive and knowledge, so quests should account for different responses. When: Designing a quest where an NPC reacts to a planted item. Why: Motive and knowledge drive different reactions.
- [rule] Let players catch NPCs in contradictions by comparing dialogue choices against items and other NPCs' statements, with lower reliability for impaired speakers. When: designing NPC dialogue and clues. Why: cross-checking statements rewards careful players.
- [rule] Let lights, silhouettes and routines act as sightings that players interpret, with explicit rules stating when a sighting counts as identification. When: when designing observation-based clues. Why: Players can reason from sightings only when identification rules are clear.
- [rule] Design an NPC's claimed shared past so a document or another NPC can confirm or contradict it. When: an NPC claims a personal history with another character. Why: Outside checks let players test the claim.
- [rule] Let a character pause while memory catches up instead of forcing an early identification. When: recognition is partial and the character is still searching. Why: A premature answer can lock in a wrong identity.
- [rule] Give an impaired or tired NPC witness vague timings and uncorroborated sightings, and provide a physical trace the player can use to check them.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses a reliability score and known biases, and mark each of their claims as first-hand or rumour.
- [rule] Place a silent NPC at a hidden exit so it records the player's return and can use that knowledge later.
- [rule] Count two witnesses as corroboration only if they saw the same thing from the same place without collusion; crowd agreement that is only shared belief is not independent evidence. When: When assessing whether two witnesses or a crowd support each other. Why: Shared motive, coordination or belief makes agreement worthless as corroboration.
- [rule] Do not treat a witness's agreement as independent confirmation when they are simply accepting what they are told. When: Evaluating a witness who responds with 'if you say so' or similar deference. Why: Deferential agreement reflects the questioner's prompt, not the witness's memory.
- [rule] Make two in-world reports agree on mundane facts but differ on uncanny ones, so the designer controls how far the player can trust each. When: Designing competing in-world reports. Why: Agreement on ordinary facts grounds trust, and disagreement on the uncanny tests it.
- [rule] Let one NPC discredit another so the player must weigh competing accounts. When: Designing conflicting testimony in a mystery. Why: Conflict forces the player to evaluate sources rather than accept the first one.
- [rule] Trust the facts of strained testimony while discounting its tone, since distress changes how a witness speaks without changing what they saw.
- [rule] Do not rely on one witness's sense of gender or identity when physical evidence contradicts it; weigh it against other evidence. When: Witnesses disagree about a suspect's identity characteristics. Why: Perception of identity under stress is unreliable.
- [rule] Do not accept a single informant's explanation of a hidden event until its claims about dates, people and places are checked against independent records. When: A single informant is the only source of an account.
- [rule] When the protagonist's own memory is unreliable, source the decisive proof from an external record or witness rather than from their recollection. When: The solver's memory conflicts with the truth. Why: A mistaken memory cannot prove what happened, but an independent record can.
- [heuristic] A routine settles within days so can anchor inferences, but visitors and disturbances can change it; witnesses may describe ideal practice, so verify actual routine first. When: When deciding whether a character's usual schedule or routine can anchor an inference. Why: Schedules become stable quickly, yet unexpected events can break them, and ideal routines often differ from actual practice. (x2)
- [heuristic] Character can be checked through public records, but good standing does not prove testimony; relatives' or associates' character testimony may be partial and needs independent knowledge. When: Witness reliability is attacked. Why: Character and content are separate matters. (x2)
- [heuristic] Testimony from intoxicated, frightened or retelling witnesses is weak; separate what was seen from details added later, and check the most confident details, which may exceed the facts. When: Weighing gossip, a drunk's recollection or a story retold through several people. (x2)
- [heuristic] Give two sources conflicting accounts, such as a messenger versus a sender or a protective lie, and let physical evidence or a record decide which holds. When: Designing a conflict between witnesses or an intermediary NPC. Why: Conflict forces the player to weigh evidence; physical evidence or a record gives a neutral way to settle the clash. (x2)
- [heuristic] Let witness NPCs describe a room correctly in one respect and wrongly in another, so players test every statement; a witness wrong about everything undermines all clues.
- [heuristic] Compare a witness's first account with later ones; changes after pressure or new facts reveal errors or concealment and are warning signs. When: a witness's account changes over repeated questioning or after new evidence emerges. Why: pressure and new facts expose inconsistencies that first accounts conceal.
- [heuristic] Witnesses who deny knowing each other, or omit a prior link they consider irrelevant, may still be acquainted; ask directly and check hidden connections. When: witnesses give matching denials or are interviewed about people involved in an incident. Why: Denials are easy to make and hard to verify, and participants omit links they judge irrelevant until asked directly.
- [heuristic] A late witness can overturn or reframe the theory; keep theories open until late evidence is checked, since a witness held back can supply the missing motive and sequence. When: late in the inquiry when key facts are still unknown. Why: Late firsthand accounts fill gaps that physical clues alone cannot explain.
- [heuristic] Never treat a later account as equal to contemporary records; check its author's position before use, since long-after writing may inflate tradition and temperament; its praise and claims need caution.
- [heuristic] Disagreement about what an image or perception shows hints at hidden content; an NPC who perceives something others don't can signal a hidden event without revealing it. When: characters disagree about what an image depicts, or an NPC's perception conflicts with others'. Why: The disagreement signals that something hidden is happening without revealing it.
- [heuristic] When accounts conflict, a trait they all share may be a more telling pattern than any single description, and it may form the reliable core; disputed traits mark uncertainty. When: accounts conflict and none settles the matter.
- [heuristic] Read an honest gap in recall as possibly a trauma effect, not deceit, and test where recall ends; admitting inability to identify people keeps the account credible. When: a witness cannot account for a period or describe a person. Why: Trauma can erase recall without intent to mislead, and an honest gap is more believable than a full description.
- [heuristic] Volunteered detail growing under pressure may be invented, and precise detail about a briefly seen stranger may be unreliable; vagueness can be honest. When: a witness's account grows more detailed under pressure, or describes a briefly seen stranger.
- [heuristic] Judge reliability per claim: a witness can be accurate on one point and wrong on another, or hide a lie or relationship among many accurate details to protect someone. When: a witness's account is checked and is mostly accurate. Why: Errors and accuracy occur independently across details; accurate details make a false one look reliable.
- [heuristic] A witness who is frightened or stunned gives a less reliable account, so weigh their testimony accordingly unless another check exists. Why: fear distorts observation and memory.
- [heuristic] A late witness can reshape a timeline, and holding the strongest testimony for last can sway a judge who is already wavering.
- [heuristic] Narrow questions about a person's routine habits can expose unusual nervousness or inconsistency with their normal behaviour.
- [heuristic] Let witness NPCs be accurate on some fields and vague on others, such as an emblem seen clearly while the face stays hidden.
- [heuristic] Differing serial numbers across items in one outfit suggest it was assembled from different sources.
- [heuristic] Gather pieces of the story from several people who each saw only part of it, rather than relying on one witness who knows the whole picture. When: Reconstructing a past event from accounts. Why: Each partial witness contributes a fragment, and their independent accounts can be compared for consistency.
- [heuristic] Make some rumours true and some false, and let players verify them against records, so gossip is useful but not trusted blindly.
- [heuristic] Grade a witness by listing what they can fix, such as events, sights and sounds, and what they cannot, such as exact dates or intervals. When: Assessing how far to trust a witness's account.
- [heuristic] Learning a suspect's routine, such as where they work, can answer a question about a missing item without asking them directly. When: An item is missing and the suspect would not answer directly.
- [heuristic] A close associate of a victim often supplies more useful names, habits and rivalries than a casual witness does.
- [heuristic] Give NPC testimony as raw observations, letting the player supply interpretations and test them against other clues.
- [heuristic] Use a witness's detail as a lead when it can be checked against the physical setting, such as a window's height or the presence of a ladder.
- [heuristic] An alibi holds best when strangers with no stake in the outcome remember the suspect being present, not just when the suspect claims it.
- [heuristic] Do not read evasion into a statement reported second-hand until you have checked that the wording was not paraphrased. When: A statement reaches the investigator through other people. Why: Paraphrase can change the meaning of a narrow answer.
- [heuristic] Check whether a disappearance has a known routine explanation, such as habitual short-notice departures, before reading the absence as guilt. When: A person vanishes without warning. Why: A familiar pattern can explain the absence without any crime.
- [heuristic] Check each suspect's statements against outside records. A claim that records contradict, such as a denied sum later found elsewhere, is evidence to pursue. When: a suspect's account can be compared with financial or other records.
- [heuristic] Give suspect characters varied reactions to pressure, so the player must read behaviour rather than assume guilt from demeanour. Why: uniform reactions let players shortcut to a verdict.
- [heuristic] A routine, neutral observer carries more weight than the investigator who arranged the observation. Why: Independence from the investigation makes the testimony more credible.
- [heuristic] A local observer with no stake in the matter can supply a dated sequence of arrivals, departures and occupancy at an empty site. When: A site is found empty and its occupancy history is needed. Why: A disinterested witness reports without bias.
- [heuristic] When a location is closed, nearby passersby may be the only source of information, so ask them for leads.
- [heuristic] A reported sighting in a distant place or at a given hour may be mistaken or used to escape notice; check it against independent sources or records.
- [heuristic] A sighting at a distance, through a window, in poor light or as a brief glimpse is weak evidence of identity; state the conclusion as tentative. When: when judging an identification made from far away, in low light or from a brief glimpse. Why: Reduced detail makes recognition unreliable.
- [heuristic] An admitted lie neither proves nor disproves later claims; admitted trivia can buy credibility, so weigh each claim on its own evidence and track unresolved key gaps. When: when a witness has admitted a lie or confesses small falsehoods. Why: Candour about trivia can distract from unresolved key facts.
- [heuristic] Give disguises or suspects a visible tell, such as a mask seam, mismatched detail, bandage, stain or glove, that a careful player can check with an examine action. When: Designing clues on a suspect character or disguise. Why: A visible tell gives the player a concrete test without needing dialogue.
- [heuristic] Keep routine steps brief and vary sources during long waits: repeated steps and time stamps drag and dull a final disclosure, while new sources keep attention on the stakes. When: when a wait extends over a long period or routine testimony runs long. Why: New sources keep attention on the stakes, and brief routine keeps the final disclosure impactful.
- [heuristic] A well-known person meets only a small share of a city, so someone walking many routes can pass unrecognized; overestimating recognition leads to false claims that a movement was seen.
- [heuristic] Before accepting a claim, trace it to its origin and ask whether the accuser saw it directly; second-hand claims from friends or motivated sources, unchecked against records, are weak. When: when a claim rests on a single relayed source. Why: Relayed claims lose verification and motivated sources bias what is passed on.
- [heuristic] Honest failure to notice under heavy workload differs from a wish to conceal; the investigator must distinguish the two before judging a witness. When: when a busy staff member cannot recall a visitor.
- [heuristic] Unqualified confidence in a witness's account is a warning sign, while honest hedges should be recorded as meaningful.
- [heuristic] A respondent who offers no proof of identity deserves suspicion, since an impostor sent by the suspect would normally arrive carrying proof.
- [heuristic] An NPC who saw the player can be asked open questions first, then shown a sketch, with answers graded by specificity and hedging. When: designing an identification by an NPC witness. Why: graded answers reward careful questioning.
- [heuristic] Rank witnesses by how certain they are, how closely they saw the subject, and whether other witnesses agree before accepting a claim. When: several witnesses give overlapping accounts. Why: each factor independently affects how much a claim can be trusted.
- [heuristic] Evidence gained by watching or listening unseen can confirm a suspicion that a direct question would alert the target to. When: a target would react to being asked. Why: Concealment keeps the target's behavior natural.
- [heuristic] Do not dismiss a late account as false merely because it came late. Why: Delay alone does not show deception.
- [heuristic] Treat a statement cut off before its key point as an open question to return to, not as a closed fact.
- [heuristic] The person who knows the suspect best may be first to see through a display of feeling, so track their reactions.
- [heuristic] Let an unreliable witness contradict themselves later, so attentive players can detect the problem by comparing statements. When: Designing a witness whose reliability should be discoverable.
- [heuristic] Keep a witness's report in reserve as intelligence to use later when it becomes relevant. When: A report is incomplete or does not yet bear on the case. Why: Early reports can gain value as other facts emerge.
- [heuristic] A damaged document can make one answer unreadable, leaving the player to infer it from context and other testimony. When: designing partially legible evidence. Why: Inference rewards cross-referencing sources.
- [heuristic] Use distance from neighbours and public roads as a parameter for how likely a crime in the world is to be noticed. When: When generating locations where crimes or hidden events may occur. Why: Proximity to witnesses and authority controls detection likelihood.
- [heuristic] A witness NPC present during dialogue can act as a verifier whose confirmation unlocks a claim the player cannot confirm alone.
- [heuristic] Tie a witness's reluctance to a specific stake, such as a job or debt, that a later player choice can remove.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC react visibly to an unseen threat before players learn its source, so the threat is felt before it is shown. When: When a threat will be revealed later in the level. Why: Visible reactions create dread without explanation.
- [heuristic] Give characters a sore-spot trait that determines which accusation provokes anger, so the same claim lands differently on each NPC.
- [heuristic] Tie any lie-detection cue to checkable world state rather than NPC animation or voice tone, which players can learn to exploit. When: Designing a lie-detection mechanic. Why: Demeanour cues are easy to exploit.
- [heuristic] Before assigning an order to a suspect, check who could have heard it, since a witness's expected reaction can rule them out. Why: Someone who heard an order would have reacted to it.
- [heuristic] Seek a second witness who reports the same fact from a different angle, and note what that witness did not say. When: Verifying a witness statement. Why: Independent angles and omissions reveal more than repetition.
- [heuristic] A complete account that stays the same across retellings is treated as a sign of truthfulness, even when the teller's motive is doubted. When: Judging a witness or suspect's account. Why: Consistency is hard to fake across repeated tellings.
- [heuristic] Keep an event log with timestamps from different NPCs so players can spot where two accounts of the same events disagree. When: Designing NPC accounts of shared events.
- [heuristic] Two characters who repeat each other can be built as a trap when they share a motive, so the player must check whether their accounts are linked. When: Designing paired NPC witnesses. Why: Apparent corroboration hides a common interest that the player must uncover.
- [heuristic] Ask a concealing witness what they fear and address any fear of retaliation before asking for cooperation, since fear often explains refusal. When: A witness's cooperation becomes selective. Why: Fear makes witnesses hesitant to testify and often explains the refusal.
- [heuristic] Attach a reliability value to each NPC's information and let players check it against a second source before acting on it.
- [heuristic] Give each NPC statement a reliability level; intoxicated or frightened NPCs give vague or contradictory directions while sober ones are precise, so let statements conflict for cross-checking. When: Designing NPC dialogue for investigation or directions. Why: Witness state changes the precision and consistency of what they report; cross-checking against physical clues tests conflicting statements.
- [heuristic] Separate a witness's firsthand observations from impressions and feelings about a person; trust concrete, testable facts such as clothing or arrival time over sympathetic opinions. When: When a witness is emotional, gives opinions, or is invested in the person described. Why: Sincere emotion can distort details; emotional investment makes descriptions more favorable than the evidence supports.
- [heuristic] Weigh a sighting by the witness's prior familiarity with the person; a witness who never knew them gives weak identification and should not anchor a timeline. When: A key identification or last-seen timeline depends on a witness who may not have known the person. Why: Without prior knowledge, the witness cannot distinguish the person from look-alikes, so an unfamiliar witness may misidentify them.
- [heuristic] A hostile dismissal of a frightened witness can make her seem more sincere to the audience, since her fear is visibly real. When: Writing a suspect who shuts down a witness. Why: Audiences read hostility toward a weak accuser as a sign that the accuser may be right.
- [heuristic] Let NPCs give conflicting accounts of one figure, each shaped by their own interests or vantage point. When: Designing a mystery around a disputed figure. Why: Conflicting accounts push the player to weigh sources.
- [heuristic] A witness can be friendly and detailed yet still know nothing past a certain date, so check each account's coverage window before relying on it. When: Interviewing a witness who knew the subject only for part of their history. Why: Detail and friendliness do not extend knowledge beyond the time the witness actually had contact.
- [heuristic] Treat an exaggerating witness's claims as unverified until corroborated, even if the room accepts them as entertainment. When: A witness boasts or exaggerates in front of others. Why: Exaggeration makes testimony unreliable though it may hide real clues.
- [heuristic] Test a source's claim of insider knowledge by weighing what only insiders could know, such as a private confidence or a spouse's jealousy. When: when a masked or anonymous speaker claims special knowledge. Why: Private details are hard to fake and reveal whether the claim is credible.
- [heuristic] Show each rival expert's reasoning so a dispute reads as a genuine disagreement rather than simple ridicule. When: Two experts disagree on a cause. Why: Visible reasoning lets the audience judge each expert's trustworthiness.
- [heuristic] Make an informant useful but self-interested, so that their testimony is shaped by a secret they are protecting and must be checked against documents. When: Designing witnesses who hold partial truths. Why: A biased source gives real information while keeping the player doubting its completeness.
- [heuristic] Vivid observations are hard to fake but still subjective, so they support a claim without proving it.
- [heuristic] A witness can be accurate about some details and wrong about others, so judge each claim separately rather than discarding or accepting the whole account. When: Evaluating a witness whose testimony mixes reliable and unreliable claims. Why: Reliability varies across different parts of an account.
- [heuristic] A witness's own slip, such as glancing toward a family, can draw suspicion onto that family, so the slip should be noticed and its effect weighed. When: When a witness's unguarded movement is seen by an audience. Why: Observers attach significance to small involuntary actions.
- [heuristic] Place a watcher with a non-committal expression in the crowd to hint that they know more than they show. When: Staging a reveal where an informed character should be signalled without being exposed. Why: A subtle cue invites the player to suspect the watcher without confirming it.
- [heuristic] Do not treat a witness's claim as proof until a physical record confirms it, such as a sketch or journal that shows only scribbles. When: A character's account rests on a record that proves less than claimed. Why: Subjective impressions can exceed what the physical record supports.
- [heuristic] Reliability rests on consistency of central facts and on the witness's manner, not on polish. Peripheral details may shift across retellings while the core stays stable. When: Weighing a witness whose retellings vary. Why: Stable central memory is a better reliability sign than uniform wording.
- [heuristic] Let a disguised character act as a witness, and reveal the impersonation later as a second-phase confrontation with the culprit. When: a key witness is missing or unreliable. Why: A later reveal recasts earlier testimony and raises the stakes of the final confrontation.
- [heuristic] Test a witness's professed neutrality against what they gain from each outcome, since a neutral stance can hide a lean toward one side. When: A witness claims impartiality while an undisclosed gain depends on the outcome. Why: Financial or other interest can shape influence even when the stated stance sounds reasonable.
- [heuristic] Read a witness's physical signs, such as tiredness, colouring or steady eyes, as clues to their state, but treat them as support for judgement, not as facts about events. When: when assessing an upset or exhausted witness. Why: Body signals reflect condition but do not confirm what happened.
- [heuristic] Stage a reproduction in front of sceptical witnesses so its outcome cannot be dismissed as luck or staging. When: A test is meant to prove a hidden mechanism. Why: A sceptic's presence makes success harder to explain away.
- [heuristic] Let a dying witness speak the largest secret, so a single scene delivers a major reveal.
- [heuristic] Let a witness's mistaken sighting count as a clue that is dismissed at first and later proves to be a key fact. When: A witness reports something the characters initially reject. Why: Dismissed testimony stays in the reader's memory and gains weight when the reveal returns to it.
- [heuristic] Explain a fabricated name or detail with a real object in the world, such as a printed title or label, so the discovery feels earned. Why: The reveal then feels grounded rather than arbitrary.
- [heuristic] Discredit the witness before the reveal, so the audience is unsure whose account to trust when the testimony arrives.
- [heuristic] Let a character's vision or testimony be accurate but leave its source unexplained, so the player must weigh its reliability. When: A character reports something the player cannot verify. Why: Unverified but accurate testimony keeps the player uncertain about the character's sanity or insight.
- [procedure] 1) Pick a concrete, checkable detail in the account, such as a garment or a number. 2) Find an independent object from the same period. 3) Compare the detail with the object. When: a witness gives a specific detail and an object survives.
- [procedure] 1) Open with yes-or-no prompts to settle the witness. 2) Ask open questions about the event. 3) Have key terms defined in the witness's own words. 4) Repeat any surprising question to check the answer. 5) Record pauses, tone and phrasing changes. When: Interviewing a witness whose recall is impaired by a trance, fever or similar state. Why: Staged prompts reduce confusion and make replies comparable across attempts.
- [procedure] 1) Record each witness's account as points: what they saw, when, what they did, and what they could not swear to. 2) Keep the firm claims and the uncertain claims in separate lists.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a hiding spot with sightlines over the likely return point, ideally covering two approaches. 2) Stay hidden and wait until the subject arrives. 3) Approach the subject by a route they can see. When: when a person is likely to return to a place to finish an action.
- [procedure] 1) Repeat the witness's own phrases back to them. 2) Pose a hypothetical about their intent instead of naming a crime. 3) Reverse a sentence's form to test for automatic agreement. 4) Add one unexpected provocation to test the reaction. 5) Stay quiet and still so they keep talking. When: Witness is intoxicated, drowsy, evasive or hard to reach, and the questioner can stay with them over time.
- [procedure] 1) Predict a suspect's behaviour from observed habits. 2) Ask an independent witness. 3) Compare the answer with the suspect's claim.
- [procedure] 1) Restore the witness's composure before questioning. 2) Ask for the account as an ordered sequence, without interruption. 3) Ask targeted questions only after the narrative is complete. When: when the witness is agitated and an ordered account is needed. Why: A calmer witness gives a clearer timeline, and the investigator keeps details that interruption would lose.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the specific loss the witness fears. 2) Find who can waive it. 3) Obtain a signed guarantee against that loss. 4) Present it and state your belief in the witness's innocence. When: a witness's silence rests on fear of a specific loss. Why: a guarantee that removes the fear can make the witness speak.
- [procedure] 1) Split the witness statement into separate claims such as names, appearance, times and actions. 2) Check each claim against independent evidence. 3) Accept or reject each claim on its own result. When: a witness gives several details of different kinds. Why: claims of different kinds can have different reliability.
- [procedure] 1) Hold back specific facts. 2) Ask broad questions first. 3) Narrow them to times, places and objects. 4) Have the suspect commit to exact claims. 5) Check each claim against evidence. When: when a suspect's account can be tested. Why: committed specific claims can be proven false later.
- [procedure] 1) Identify a distinguishing physical feature the witness noticed. 2) Ask the witness to specify it exactly. 3) Have the witness commit to that specific answer. When: When a witness's identification must be precise. Why: Forcing a precise answer exposes vague or invented claims.
- [procedure] 1) List the physical traces the claimed event should leave. 2) Work out where each would land from the actor's position. 3) Inspect those spots. 4) Schedule any check that needs time. When: A witness describes physical events that leave traces. Why: Physical traces can confirm or contradict a witness's account.
- [procedure] 1) Restate a vague answer as a specific figure, such as a distance or time. 2) Ask the witness to confirm or correct it. 3) Note any claim that cannot be checked. When: questioning a witness who answers loosely. Why: Specific figures expose inconsistencies that vague answers hide.
- [procedure] 1) Collect time-stamped reports from each observer. 2) Lay them on one timeline, interval by interval. 3) Mark who was out of sight at the critical moment. When: The crime window is narrow and observers cover overlapping views. Why: Overlaying reports shows who could not have seen the event.
- [procedure] 1) Establish a witness's regular pattern, such as meetings or visits, as a baseline. 2) Ask independent witnesses to confirm each element of it. 3) Compare the accounts for agreement. When: when a witness describes a regular routine. Why: independent confirmation tests a single account.
- [procedure] 1) Ask direct questions about the witness's relationship to the victim and about the critical time. 2) Accept the first account only as a hypothesis. 3) Check specific details independently. 4) Record which claims are verified. When: A witness gives a timeline covering the critical window. Why: Initial belief must be tested before it is relied on.
- [procedure] 1) Check the witness's claims against other evidence and records. 2) Note the witness's stake, bias and reasons to justify themselves. 3) Test the wording for a contradiction hidden inside a passage. When: A witness's account is self-justifying, the witness had something to gain, or a private account conflicts with public records. Why: Self-interest and loose wording can make an account look reliable when it is not.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each earlier written or recorded statement by the suspect. 2) Compare them with later statements. 3) Reuse them only as recorded, and flag any contradictions. When: when a suspect's account changes across sessions. Why: earlier statements can be reused in later sessions, so their accuracy matters.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the time a witness claims. 2) Reproduce the event under the same conditions. 3) Check whether the witness could have heard or seen it from where they were. When: a witness's account of time conflicts with the physical setting. Why: the setting limits what can be perceived from a given place.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the alibi's sole link, usually one witness's statement. 2) Re-question that witness, possibly with a different investigator. 3) Apply pressure or a counter-threat. 4) Check whether the testimony changes. When: When a suspect's alibi rests on one witness who may have a reason to lie. Why: Pressure on a weak link can produce a changed account that exposes a false alibi.
- [procedure] 1) Record every account and what each witness saw or did not see. 2) Compare accounts and note contradictions and their reasons. 3) Note what a witness chose not to report and why. 4) Test each account against physical traces. 5) Ask neutral follow-up questions checking accounts against evidence. When: Several people share one event and their accounts must be reconciled. Why: Comparison separates reliable details from errors, distortion or influence; physical evidence and probing questions separate accurate reports from mistaken ones.
- [procedure] 1) Remove unnecessary people from the room. 2) Limit listeners to those whose presence serves the goal. 3) Speak with the informant alone when they will reveal more without others present. When: When an investigator needs a candid account from a witness. Why: Controlling the room controls who the witness will speak to freely.
- [procedure] 1) Stage an ordinary-looking role, such as a disguise, that asks the suspect for a short written reply. 2) Collect the reply. 3) Compare it with the original document's distinctive features. 4) Accept the link only if several features agree. When: A suspect's written link to a document must be verified without alerting them. Why: A controlled test produces comparable evidence while staying inconspicuous.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each firsthand account. 2) Collect secondhand accounts of the same person. 3) Compare each against the firsthand record and against each other. When: Several witnesses describe the same person or event. Why: Secondhand reports can carry the observer's guesses rather than the subject's facts.
- [procedure] 1) Ask about details that are hard to fake and rarely noticed. 2) Compare the witness's answers with what was actually observed. 3) Note the gap between confident claims and detailed recall. When: Testing whether a confident identification rests on real observation. Why: Unnoticed details expose assumptions that the witness did not actually check.
- [procedure] 1) Treat each statement as a claim. 2) Check it against documents, physical traces, and other witnesses. 3) Accept it only if it survives the cross-check; reconcile any contradictions before relying on it. When: Weighing statements that may conflict or come from people with a motive. Why: Statements that have not been tested against independent sources can be wrong or self-serving.
- [tradeoff] Show NPC reliability as a visible rating with factors like distance, light, motive or intoxication, or only via state like fright; ratings ease checking, state requires inference. When: Designing NPC witness reliability. Why: Visible factors let the player judge trust; hidden state requires inference.
- [tradeoff] Hiding a body's face prevents identification but invites suspicion about why it was hidden, so concealment can backfire. Why: Deliberate concealment reads as a sign of intent.
- [pitfall] Extraordinary claims from respectable, conventional, calm, sincere or distressed witnesses get trusted over their content; check every unverifiable claim against facts, not manner, deference or standing. When: weighing a witness whose status or demeanour looks reassuring. Why: appearance and standing trigger trust before content is checked. (x2)
- [pitfall] Agreement is not corroboration when witnesses share a vantage, expectation, fear, grievance or source; they may echo one assumption, motive or told story, even the same wrong time. When: when several witnesses give the same time estimate or account. Why: social pressure, shared assumptions and common motives align their errors; repeated testimony may trace to one story. (x2)
- [pitfall] Cooperative subjects may guess what the questioner wants and confirm it; eager agreement or cued reactions can reflect politeness rather than real memory, and they may accept suggested identifications. When: interpreting reactions to cues, or a witness seems eager to help or agrees after being shown material. Why: People respond to perceived expectations and want to please questioners, not only to memory.
- [pitfall] Accepting a witness's moral judgments as facts, or ignoring an inconvenient account because its source is biased, both corrupt the evidence base. Why: Verdicts are opinion, and discarding inconvenient testimony hides real evidence.
- [pitfall] Sustained pressure or a tense questioner pushes witnesses toward answers that end questioning or please the questioner, making their statements unreliable. When: under sustained pressure or when pressing a witness for specific answers. Why: distress favours quick answers, and pressure pushes witnesses toward what the questioner wants to hear.
- [pitfall] Sincerity does not establish accuracy: honest witnesses can be wrong or partial, and an honest-looking account can still hide a puzzle. When: evaluating any testimony. Why: Sincerity and accuracy are separate properties.
- [pitfall] Confident judgement from a witness outside their competence, such as physical ability or a non-expert's opinion, is a guess to check, not evidence. Why: Confidence does not turn a guess into evidence.
- [pitfall] Speech recalled from a stressful moment or an overheard confession is only as reliable as the witness's exact memory; a key phrase may be misremembered. When: Relying on an overheard admission as evidence. Why: Memory of spoken words is imperfect and can be disputed.
- [pitfall] Confirmations extracted after a fact is stated, or accounts shaped for a witness, may be repeated unchecked; treat them as leads to check against independent evidence. Why: Witnesses may agree to end pressure, and shaped accounts replace observation.
- [pitfall] A mismatch does not prove fakery: an honest witness whose account conflicts with a suspect's can be suspected, and honest interests can look like camouflage. When: when accounts are compared. Why: Suspicion spreads to whoever does not fit, and a mismatch alone does not prove one fact is fake.
- [pitfall] Rewards or pardons offered for testimony can shape accounts toward the incentive and encourage invented detail; tag such testimony as motivated. When: a witness gains from testifying. Why: incentives distort recall and reporting.
- [pitfall] A witness who is overwhelmed or unwilling can leave the room, creating gaps in the record that later testimony cannot fill.
- [pitfall] A witness who carried out instructions faithfully can be honest and still wrong about what those instructions actually did.
- [pitfall] A witness drawn in by a wager can be overconfident, so every fact he states should be checked against the records.
- [pitfall] A witness recovering from stupor or shock may give no usable timeline at first, so their sense of time should not be trusted early.
- [pitfall] Routine checks can confirm the wrong story when each source is asked only about its own record.
- [pitfall] A witness with a motive to hurt the accused is easy to dismiss, which can hide real facts within their account.
- [pitfall] An identification made under pressure or suggestion can be wrong, so a later denial should not be dismissed merely because it came later. When: Assessing a witness who has identified or refused to identify a suspect. Why: Suggestion and pressure distort memory, so either the identification or its denial may be unreliable.
- [pitfall] Cross-examination can shift a witness's timeline, such as a medical estimate of time of death, creating doubt without any new fact. When: when questioning focuses on exact times or details. Why: pressure on details can produce apparent inconsistency.
- [pitfall] Counting everyone who saw a routine as a suspect, without evidence that they acted on it, inflates the suspect list.
- [pitfall] Relying on a routine examination to rule out a hidden cause, or treating a natural death as settled before checking small signs, misses concealed causes.
