- [pitfall] Witnesses who testify in a hurry tend to tangle their accounts further, adding conflicts rather than clarity. When: A witness is rushed or pressed to answer quickly.
- [pitfall] A concealed witness may be the culprit, so readers may suspect the helper too late for a reversal to land.
- [pitfall] Stating a claim with more precision than the evidence supports can reveal the investigator's mistake to the suspect. Why: A suspect may recognize an overly specific claim as wrong.
- [pitfall] Interrogating an innocent but uninformed witness for information can mislead, since they can only offer inference. When: when a witness lacks direct knowledge. Why: their answers reflect guesswork.
- [pitfall] Dramatic retellings tend to grow in the telling, so compare them against what the teller could actually have seen. Why: Each retelling adds detail the original source never had.
- [pitfall] Witnesses can differ in how much of a condition they really observed, so confirm each person's view separately. When: Several witnesses describe the same object. Why: Confident accounts may rest on partial observation.
- [pitfall] A plausible identification, such as matching a figure to a known person, can take an investigator far from the truth if unchecked. When: An identification rests on a partial view or resemblance. Why: Investigators tend to stop testing a conclusion once it seems to fit.
- [pitfall] Trusting a first-person account written after the fact is risky, because its author controls which events appear. Why: Selection by the author can remove key events without any false statement.
- [pitfall] A guarded witness may withhold the core fact at first, so early accounts are partial and should not be treated as complete. When: Initial questioning of a guarded witness. Why: Core facts are often hidden until trust develops.
- [pitfall] A confirmed return time does not prove the earlier part of the account, which needs its own checks.
- [pitfall] Impressions formed after the fact are unreliable, so observer agreement should be checked before it carries weight.
- [pitfall] An account repeated to others before it is tested hardens into apparent fact, making later verification harder. When: A witness shares an unverified claim with people who will repeat it. Why: Repetition gives an untested claim the look of corroboration.
- [pitfall] Pressing too hard can close a witness down, leaving answers at blanket denials until questions reach a painful subject. When: An investigator keeps pushing a defensive witness on the same line. Why: Sustained pressure raises defensiveness, so the witness stops offering anything new.
- [pitfall] Overstating a trivial remark before corroboration can mislead the reader or investigator into a false conclusion.
- [pitfall] Vague times and generic descriptions from one witness, such as shortish or a mustache, cannot identify anyone alone and need a second source.
- [pitfall] Attacking minor points can look like quibbling and distract from the central claim, which is the one that needs testing.
- [pitfall] Do not assume a witness's account is spontaneous or truthful when the witness was chosen and briefed by someone with an interest in the outcome. Why: A chosen witness can serve the briefing party's timeline rather than the truth.
- [pitfall] Do not treat a confession as settled when the speaker is feverish, exhausted, or defending a theory of their own.
- [pitfall] A witness who is both pitiable and unreliable can make the audience trust emotion over verifiable facts; keep the two apart.
- [pitfall] An adult's casual dismissal of a witness's report can close a question prematurely, so the report should be weighed on its own terms.
- [pitfall] A secondhand report written years later may describe a different place or time than the event it claims to describe.
- [pitfall] Testimony given under fear or relief may be incomplete, skewed and dramatised, so it should be checked against other evidence. Why: Strong emotion distorts memory and attention and shapes how the witness tells the account.
- [pitfall] Quantity of detail is not proof of accuracy; rehearsed or fluent accounts can be highly detailed without firsthand knowledge or checking. When: A witness gives a long, elaborate, confident account. Why: Detail reflects rehearsal as well as genuine observation, and volume and fluency feel like reliability.
- [pitfall] Testimony from a witness loyal to a suspect, such as a close associate or trusted manager, is hard to assess and may be coloured by that loyalty. When: When a witness has a clear interest in protecting a suspect. Why: Loyalty and interest distort judgment and can lead an investigator to discount conflicting evidence.
- [pitfall] Drunk or agitated witnesses often misremember distances and durations, and alcohol distorts both speech and recall, so timing claims need checking. When: When a witness is drunk, agitated or talking over drink. Why: Intoxication lowers the reliability of both speech and memory.
- [pitfall] Children's testimony against a family member, given under pressure, is unreliable evidence and should be weighed with great caution. When: When children are questioned in a charged case against a parent. Why: Pressure can shape what children say.
- [pitfall] Motive claims often arrive with reliability attacks in the same breath, so test each claim separately rather than letting one carry the other.
- [pitfall] A sincere alibi can still be wrong, and trust in the source is not evidence of the fact. When: When evaluating an alibi from a trusted or sincere witness. Why: Belief reflects the witness's confidence, not the event itself.
- [pitfall] Pious or formal phrasing can make a troubling conclusion sound acceptable, so look past the wording to the claim it carries. Why: Tone can disguise an idea that would be questioned if stated plainly.
- [pitfall] Treating an angry or distressed remark as a confession without knowing the question that prompted it. When: A remark is made during questioning or after a dispute. Why: The prompt often determines what the words mean.
- [pitfall] Remarks recalled after an event can be reshaped to fit it, so they are weak evidence of prior intent.
- [pitfall] A writer who admits bias can still steer an account through what they choose to stress.
- [pitfall] Agreement among accusers who describe the same vision can come from shared fear or shared expectation, so it must be checked rather than read as independence.
- [pitfall] Elimination reasoning fails if the starting state is misremembered, because the excluded agents depend on an accurate baseline. When: Reasoning from a remembered earlier state. Why: A wrong baseline breaks the chain of exclusions.
- [pitfall] A witness's sincere belief that no one could have guessed a secret does not rule out a leak.
- [pitfall] A test seems valid when it sometimes gives the expected result, but occasional agreement does not establish that it is reliable. When: when evaluating a test or puzzle mechanic.
- [pitfall] Crowded scenes with weeping, knocked-over furniture and fleeing people distort observation and make accurate recording harder.
- [pitfall] A character's known habits often come from other people's accounts rather than measurement, so a baseline built on testimony is only as reliable as those accounts. Why: habit claims are themselves unverified.
- [pitfall] Confident recognition can be wrong, especially when suspicion colours the memory. When: A person believes they recognise someone and suspects them. Why: Suspicion biases memory toward confirming the suspicion.
- [pitfall] Discarding a whole account after one falsehood can throw away its true parts. Check each part separately before deciding what to keep. When: A single claim in an account is shown to be false. Why: One false claim does not make every claim false.
- [pitfall] A witness's guess about nationality or language, drawn from accent, should not be treated as fact. When: A witness infers a person's origin from speech. Why: Accent-based inference is unreliable and easily wrong.
- [pitfall] A witness who swears that an event was impossible is making an inference, not reporting an observation, and the inference needs checking.
- [pitfall] A witness who says they just got an impression may be right, or may be recalling what they expected to hear.
- [pitfall] An NPC witness can report an event at the wrong hour or from the wrong door, so the player must reconcile its report with other sources. When: an NPC reports events it observed. Why: NPC perception and recall can be incomplete or wrong.
- [pitfall] Treating a delirious accusation as fact, or dismissing a witness as simply mad, misreads what the words show; judge the content over the label. When: Weighing testimony from a feverish or disturbed character. Why: Such speech shows inner fear, so it is neither proof of events nor noise; dismissing it can hide real information.
- [pitfall] A witness who glimpsed someone in passing may be wrong about the person or the day. When: The identification rests on a brief or incidental sighting. Why: Brief observation gives little opportunity to confirm identity or date.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a witness's account too quickly can hide the real physical evidence. When: Investigators weigh a witness's testimony against other explanations. Why: Premature dismissal stops the search for corroborating traces.
- [pitfall] A witness may be sure a route was clear only because nothing happened in front of them; test such claims against timing.
- [pitfall] Telling a witness they are wrong can talk them out of a correct observation. When: A witness has just made a valid identification. Why: Discouragement can override a sound memory.
- [pitfall] An unclear sighting in fog can be dismissed as imagination without a record, so the observation is lost. When: Encountering an ambiguous visual event. Why: Without a written note, the unclear observation cannot be compared with later evidence.
- [pitfall] Accepting a witness's claim of prior ignorance without checking can mislead, since people may not recognize their own exposure to a subject.
- [pitfall] A confident witness can be certain of a wrong detail, so confidence is not evidence of accuracy. When: when assessing a witness's firmly stated claim. Why: Certainty reflects the witness's manner, not whether the observation was correct.
- [pitfall] Verified details lend credibility to unverified claims only by association, and the investigator must note this. When: Some of a witness's claims are confirmed and others are not. Why: Confirmed facts can make unconfirmed claims seem reliable without justification.
- [pitfall] A witness left uncross-examined is not thereby believed; silence may reflect a tactical choice rather than acceptance. When: When evaluating testimony that went unquestioned. Why: Lack of challenge may be strategic and does not confirm the account.
- [pitfall] A confident explainer who claims to know the victim's inner thoughts may be trusted too easily, even when nothing is corroborated. When: Someone offers an explanation with unusual certainty about another person's mind. Why: Apparent insight into a person's thoughts is mistaken for reliability.
- [pitfall] A frank, practised performance can read as honest at first and then as deceptive once contradictions appear, so players may swing their trust sharply. When: a suspect's story is delivered with confidence. Why: Confident delivery is ambiguous, and each contradiction flips the reading of earlier statements.
- [pitfall] A claim that cannot be checked is treated as unreliable by default, so the audience may dismiss it unless concrete details are given. When: A story depends on an unverifiable source to move the plot. Why: Without testable details the audience has no basis to trust the source.
- [fact] A witness can confirm one part of a story and not another, such as a man's presence without being able to describe a masked companion.
- [fact] Signs such as stiffening vary widely between individuals, so they give limited precision on when death occurred.
- [fact] Even a genuine report may be compromised, since observers and detectives can be bribed.
- [fact] When a person dies without a written will, survivors' accounts of his spoken wishes become the main evidence of what he intended. When: a death occurs with no written will. Why: No document remains to record his decisions.
- [fact] Routine signed entries, such as payment receipts, create many known samples of a person's hand that can be compared later. When: a record book is kept over a long period.
- [fact] A witness who gave harmful testimony can carry lasting personal cost, shown in later decline.
- [fact] A witness with no knowledge of the matter can still be questioned, and their ignorance is itself evidence about how reliable their confident claims are. When: A witness gives a confident answer on a subject they could not have observed.
- [fact] A witness's assurance about someone's character reflects the witness's belief, not proof of what that person did. When: When weighing a character judgment about a suspect. Why: Belief about character is not evidence of specific conduct.
- [fact] An account that reports another person's words passes that person's version on only secondhand, through the narrator's own framing.
- [fact] A witness who avoids news and conversation may lack key facts, such as a victim's identity or an innocent party's arrest. When: A witness's knowledge is compared with what happened in the wider world. Why: Isolation limits what a person knows about the events they describe.

## decoy design
- [model] A lure has four parts: a trusted-seeming intermediary, a false professional role, a decoy stop, and a delivered message that draws the victim away. When: Planning a ruse or reconstructing how a person was lured away.
- [model] Misdirection takes three forms: plausible theories, dramatic spectacle, and unexamined assumptions about a clue.
- [model] A decoy trap works when the target believes the bait is the prey while the trapper watches unseen from a concealed observation post. When: the target monitors a location and reacts to visible activity.
- [definition] Misdirection is a planted false or incomplete trail, often via an unchecked assumption, that points an investigation at the wrong person or answer; audiences must see through it.
- [definition] Misdirection draws attention onto a seemingly significant figure, theory or false explanation, such as the supernatural or a convenient outsider, so the real trail goes unnoticed. Why: it pulls attention onto a plausible wrong conclusion.
- [definition] Misdirection leads an investigator toward a wrong reading through a false explanation, a harmless fact, or a detail that seems to settle the question.
- [definition] Misdirection steers the investigator and reader toward a suspect through appearance, prejudice and physical traces that look damning but have innocent explanations.
- [definition] Misdirection keeps a key fact hidden while the audience or investigator pursues other leads.
- [definition] Modus operandi is the characteristic method a person uses to commit an offence, and it is the basis for judging whether two crimes match. When: comparing a past offence with a new one. Why: method is more telling than the category of wrongdoing.
- [definition] A decoy is a false lead meant to draw attention away from the real target or to buy time.
- [definition] Two ways to mislead an audience with true words: implying something false, and withholding a truth that matters.
- [definition] A diversion holds one party in polite conversation while another opens a door or container, so timing and small details reveal the purpose.
- [mechanism] A fake lead that draws an NPC or victim away opens a window of reduced vigilance in which the player or offender can act elsewhere. When: Designing NPC diversion events or a decoy event that draws attention. Why: Distraction creates a window of reduced vigilance. (x2)
- [mechanism] Misdirection works best when its false explanation fits what the audience expects or appears to resolve the evidence, so it is accepted without testing. When: When designing a false explanation for a mystery. Why: A familiar explanation is accepted without testing.
- [mechanism] A stolen item can route the player through a chain of NPCs, each giving one step toward the next. When: designing a stolen-item quest.
- [mechanism] A crime staged to look like another crime uses a plausible cover story, so hosts and victims accept it and the investigation follows a false trail.
- [mechanism] A decoy's hold on a target lasts only as long as the decoy's own performance keeps the target engaged.
- [mechanism] A misdirection can escape its author's control, so the framed person may suffer harm the culprit did not intend.
- [mechanism] A staged event such as a fake haunting can serve a concealed motive, like clearing people away while a search goes on. Why: The decoy hides the real goal behind a convincing backdrop.
- [mechanism] A prize that seemed valuable but proves counterfeit turns an apparent success into a failure, reversing the audience's view of the theft.
- [mechanism] Misdirection works by offering explanations that fit part of the evidence while pointing elsewhere. Competing theories that each rest on a different kind of evidence must each be tested against physical facts. When: several explanations compete and each rests on a different kind of evidence. Why: Plausible-looking theories steer attention, so only physical checks separate the true one from decoys.
- [mechanism] A decoy object that looks valuable draws observers' attention away from the real find.
- [mechanism] A distant decoy lead can hold attention away from a nearby danger, so the investigator overlooks the real suspect close to home. Why: Attention goes to the far lead, leaving the nearby suspect unexamined.
- [mechanism] A decoy that draws a pursuer away lets the real threat act unobserved. When: A decoy NPC or false trail is in play.
- [mechanism] A prominent lead pursued before it is tested absorbs investigative effort, since it is followed until checked against the rest of the evidence.
- [mechanism] An open call for information acts as a lure, and each reply becomes a potential source of evidence.
- [mechanism] A decoy object placed far from the scene can divert investigators, but moving it creates a trail that can expose the scheme.
- [mechanism] A staged public rumour can make an unrelated financial move look like insider knowledge, drawing suspicion away from the real act.
- [mechanism] Circulating rumour can redirect suspicion toward other people and offer alternative explanations for a death. When: a community discusses an unresolved death. Why: rumour changes who seems plausibly responsible.
- [mechanism] Matching motif clues spread across several rooms raise a player's confidence in a hidden culprit with each additional match. When: clues sharing a recognisable pattern are placed in separate locations. Why: the player connects the clues into a pattern that points to one person.
- [mechanism] A theory that gives a rival a strong motive can draw attention away from the real suspect. Why: a sympathetic motive makes the rival a more attractive target.
- [mechanism] A documented similar incident, such as a report of a series of break-ins, explains disorder at a scene and makes a staged intrusion more credible.
- [mechanism] An antagonist whose worldview filters perception produces systematic misreadings of events, and these misreadings can become puzzles the player solves by checking evidence. When: An antagonist with a fixed belief system, such as a faith that sees omens everywhere. Why: The belief system causes errors the player can detect.
- [mechanism] A fake signal tied to what a guard protects, or a visible decoy event such as a noise or removed guard, can draw patrols away and open a route to a captive. When: Stealth situations with patrolling or guarding watchers.
- [mechanism] A misleading lead can be paired with a hidden trigger or second NPC that tracks the culprit, so the culprit's reaction becomes observable evidence the player can use. When: Designing deceptive investigation sections or NPC-driven deception. Why: The trigger rewards reading the reaction, not only the clue.
- [mechanism] A mismatch between a method and the scene, such as a tool that cannot open a container, can be a deliberate clue that players interpret. Why: An ill-fitting method invites the player to ask why the actor chose it.
- [mechanism] A crime scene can hold planted items that contradict the framed NPC's habits, so observant players can notice the mismatch. When: When generating a scene that frames a specific NPC. Why: Habit mismatches give players a discoverable way to spot the staging.
- [mechanism] A clue conclusive to one faction and meaningless to another teaches the player that proof depends on the frame in which it is judged. When: when placing clues in a multi-faction world. Why: the same evidence yields different verdicts under different beliefs.
- [mechanism] A decoy that must be unwrapped or untied forces a struggle, buying a timed moment of distraction before the real danger is revealed. When: A target must be delayed at a set point. Why: Each step of undoing the decoy takes time the target cannot skip.
- [mechanism] A near-miss, where the player learns the target left just before they arrived, reveals the timeline and can sustain pursuit. When: Designing a chase or search where the target moves ahead of the player. Why: The player gets evidence of both the target's movement and their own lateness.
- [mechanism] A thief who uses a message drawing the owner away reveals knowledge of the owner's affairs and habits, which can be a sharper clue than the lock itself. When: A break-in involves a lure or deception aimed at the owner. Why: Knowing personal details is harder to fake than entry methods.
- [mechanism] A false clue placed in public information can change a suspect's behaviour if he believes it and concludes he is safe to act. When: When the suspect reads the channel where the clue is placed and has no reason to doubt it. Why: People act on information they believe is accurate, including when it is false.
- [mechanism] A lifelike decoy can make a hostile character act, and the act itself serves as evidence of intent. When: An investigator wants a suspect to reveal intent through action. Why: The suspect acts on the decoy's apparent identity, exposing their purpose.
- [mechanism] A tracker following a strong planted odour on an object will follow the scent rather than the person who carried it. When: a tracking enemy encounters a scented decoy. Why: trackers follow the strongest matching trail.
- [mechanism] When observers' attention is fixed on a dramatic moment, a covert act needs only one instant to go unseen, not a long unobserved stretch. When: a loud, climactic or scripted event holds the attention of nearby actors. Why: people watching a climax do not look elsewhere.
- [mechanism] A decoy taken into custody can hold pursuers for a period, buying the real escaper time to move. When: A substitute can be captured in view of pursuers. Why: Pursuers must deal with the decoy before resuming the search.
- [mechanism] A decoy figure simulating occupancy makes a checking target see what it expects, so the watcher's presence stays concealed. Why: checks rely on expected appearance.
- [mechanism] A decoy with a human silhouette, built from simple props under blankets, satisfies a quick glance in dim light but not a touch or closer inspection. When: when an observer checks occupancy visually. Why: A glance judges outline and shape, not detail.
- [behavior] Targets accept a false offer readily when it matches a reward they want; strong interest overrides caution and lowers scrutiny of its terms. When: a plausible offer promises a wanted reward, or the target has a single strong weakness. Why: the wanted reward reduces motivation to question terms; the strong interest overrides caution.
- [behavior] A suspect who fears attention may still answer a notice offering valued property back, especially when short of money. When: a notice offers recovery of something the suspect values. Why: the appeal of recovery can outweigh the fear of exposure.
- [behavior] Investigators tend to accept the most obvious name on an access list when it fits existing household beliefs, skipping routes they have not considered. When: A small group with known access is questioned. Why: Fit with existing belief makes the familiar suspect feel certain.
- [behavior] Each step of a lure looks ordinary to the victim, and trust in a shared secret becomes the lever that moves them. When: A target is being manipulated through a trusted contact. Why: Routine-looking steps lower suspicion, so the victim does not resist.
- [behavior] A character who loudly names every known exposure method makes listeners feel the trick is covered, so they accept her proposed controls without scrutiny. When: A character sets the conditions of a test while claiming expertise. Why: Stated expertise signals rigour, lowering the audience's guard.
- [behavior] A specific place and a short deadline tend to draw a target alone to a site chosen by someone else, which is a lure pattern. When: an unexpected summons arrives. Why: the deadline discourages checking and isolates the target.
- [behavior] A distracted witness keeps pursuing a promised lead, so a plausible false promise can hold them away until a set time passes. When: A witness is about to disrupt a scene and a plausible lead is available. Why: The witness wants the promised lead, so attention stays on it.
- [behavior] Pursuers who find bait may react visibly, such as going pale, swearing or leaving without waiting for change, and the alarm shows how much they stake on it. When: a planted lure is discovered. Why: strong reactions reveal who is watching and what they fear.
- [behavior] A brief deliberate exposure to one pursuer spreads word along a search line, so the group turns toward the apparent route and follows a false trail. When: searchers hear a reported sighting and terrain hides the real route. Why: pursuers react to shared reports and commit to the first apparent trail.
- [behavior] A decoy lure does not need real value to work. It only needs to interest the watcher enough to draw it toward the chosen location. When: Creating a fake item, notice or reward to attract an agent. Why: The agent responds to perceived interest, not to the object's substance.
- [rule] Use a false in-world report or visible monument, such as a newspaper, guard notice or faction marker, that players must weigh against their own evidence or documents. When: When designing a prominent marker or an in-world report. Why: Visible official sources invite trust, so players need a reason to verify them. (x2)
- [rule] Place a misleading object near a suspect NPC or space to invite false accusation, and let a later discovery correct the mistaken reading. When: designing red herrings in a level or near a suspect.
- [rule] Make an inference checkable yet misleadable: a naive reading of a clue should point to a plausible wrong culprit that a closer look corrects. When: designing clues that support deduction. Why: players should be able to revise wrong conclusions.
- [rule] Make decoy loot look like the real treasure, so players must inspect items closely to tell the two apart. When: Designing loot where the valuable item is among lookalikes.
- [rule] Give each NPC one true fact, like a sighting chain where each reveals one route fragment, so no single NPC holds the answer and the player must combine them. When: Designing witness dialogue or character-driven investigation.
- [rule] A decoy NPC matching the real suspect's appearance seems plausible and can lead the player to follow the wrong character until a later clue exposes the mistake.
- [rule] Make a false lead checkable through a fair counter-clue, counterevidence, or a second sign or clearer view in better conditions; an untestable decoy feels arbitrary or unfair. When: When designing false leads, red herrings or misleading clues. Why: A fair counter-clue lets careful players avoid the trap; untestable decoys feel arbitrary or unfair.
- [rule] Resolve every red herring later with a clue or recorded innocent explanation from facts the audience already has; unresolved misdirection feels like cheating. When: When planting false leads, red herrings or hidden reasoning in a mystery. Why: Audiences accept deception only when the truth explains it; untested decoys read as cheats.
- [rule] Keep a decoy plausible enough to hold briefly but disprovable under scrutiny; too weak is dismissed at once, too strong cannot be disproved; don't rely on a frame alone. Why: A clever defence can dismantle a case built on weak planted items.
- [rule] Place decoys near a rival suspect while a purchase or delivery trail leads to the true planner; players check placement and trails to separate decoy from lead. When: Designing a mystery with a false suspect, where a decoy should mislead but stay fair. Why: A traceable trail lets careful players separate the decoy from the real culprit.
- [rule] Let NPC rumors or bulletins reinforce a decoy, such as a false lead a rival NPC acts on, so the player's belief forms in-world and can be discovered as false. When: When designing information flow among NPCs in a mystery. Why: NPCs reacting to false information create consequences the player can trace.
- [rule] Let public channels or decoy quests repeat the decoy while true clues sit in quieter, private places or side conversations, and keep the decoy checkable.
- [rule] Hide the key item among decoys, such as a decoy chest in the expected spot, and let players deduce its real location or sale and transfer history from NPC dialogue. When: When designing hidden loot or a key item with a false lead.
- [rule] Route a lead through an NPC, possibly a second one, that may be misdirection, so the player must judge the source's reliability or verify it elsewhere. When: When designing a deception the player can detect, or NPC dialogue that gives hints. Why: A relayed report adds a source the player must evaluate; a hinted lead may be misdirection to verify.
- [rule] Give a fake job or offered found object a checkable in-world detail, such as a mismatch with search results, so players can test whether it is genuine. When: When a quest-giver posts a job, or a helpful character offers a found object, that could be a lure. Why: Players can only doubt an offer they have a way to check.
- [rule] Keep a lure or NPC hint to what the speaker actually knows, since revealing real knowledge lets wrong readers learn it and warns the target. When: When designing a lure or an NPC hint about a trap. Why: Leaked solutions expose the trap and warn the target.
- [rule] Use a lure only when the target's motive and attachments are known and strong, and the target can be assumed not to see the trap. When: Choosing a trap approach. Why: A lure fails if the target suspects a setup; the method depends on knowing what it values most.
- [rule] Build bait around the target's motive, such as greed, money or fear, so it is believable; a faked wound can draw an enemy into a prepared room. When: Designing an enemy or NPC that can be baited. Why: Predictable motives make the enemy walk into the trap.
- [rule] Do not release a false lure where it could harm innocent people or spread uncontrollably; a frightened suspect may turn on a bystander. When: When considering a planted false report or a decoy that would point at an uninvolved real person. Why: Uncontrolled or harmful rumors hurt people who did nothing; a false lead can make a stranger the target of a frightened suspect.
- [rule] Make a trace or decoy explanation misleading or partly matching when read alone, so the player must test it against remaining traces before acting. Why: Forces comparison rather than reaction to a single clue.
- [rule] Give items a consistent material, stamp or small flaw, such as a brand mark or rare ingredient, that players can match to an NPC, workshop or genuine sample found elsewhere. When: When items are forged, counterfeit or made by specific creators. Why: Distinctive marks let players trace an item's origin or spot a fake.
- [rule] Give a room's state, such as a flood, collapse or trap, a misleading apparent cause that redirects exploration until a contradicting clue, such as a smear or moved object, appears. Why: A plausible but wrong cause redirects exploration until evidence overturns it.
- [rule] Make an obvious injury or debris suggesting violence a decoy, and place a subtler sign such as residue, foam or missing blood that reveals the true cause. When: When designing a death or scene puzzle with a misleading cause. Why: Players who stop at the obvious injury or debris miss the real solution; attentive players can find the subtler sign.
- [rule] Build scene arrangements whose obvious reading, such as a monster or trap causing it, is wrong; reward players who inspect object positions and rebuild the event order. Why: An earlier actor may have set up the scene, so players must rebuild the event order.
- [rule] Place a decoy event or object, such as an alarm, loud scene or misleading item, in one area so attention goes there while the real evidence stays in another.
- [rule] Place a mismatched item, such as a wrong colour, initial, cover, label or prop, that an observant player must notice and explain to reconstruct a hidden trigger.
- [rule] Use a distraction, such as a social scene, mini-game or unrelated topic, to draw focus from a clue or from being watched, and keep the clue available for careful return. When: Designing a distraction around a hidden clue. Why: Players who return to the clue reward attention and avoid losing it permanently.
- [rule] Give a decoy or innocent NPC coherent, checkable evidence, such as a lab, purchase record, trip, motive or absence, that deeper investigation can expose while the real culprit stays hidden. When: Placing red herrings in a generated case. Why: Coherent false evidence rewards players who dig deeper.
- [rule] Plant decoy motives, such as a rival faction or a debt, while keeping one hard clue that every theory must fit. Why: Players must test each motive against the one fixed clue.
- [rule] Have an NPC hint at a past event the player missed, so the player knows when to turn back to it.
- [rule] Record exactly where a kept detail can be found again, since an unlabelled kept item loses its value.
- [rule] Use a decoy only with a clear purpose, such as protecting one specific person.
- [rule] Do not rely on a lure when the suspect may be armed or the room is not prepared for force.
- [rule] Treat a note that gives a person but no time or place as a lead to trace, not a conclusion.
- [rule] Plant a visible suspect with motive and contact, and hide the true culprit inside a routine part of the world. When: Designing a mystery where the player must look past the obvious answer. Why: A routine presence is easy to overlook when attention is held by a conspicuous suspect.
- [rule] Reuse a motif in an unrelated context, such as an item name, so the player must decide whether the two connect.
- [rule] Include a readable script item that may contain claims its speaker does not actually know, so the player can test those claims.
- [rule] Plant a decoy suspect whose visible traits invert the culprit's, so a careful player can learn to recognise the staging. When: Designing suspects for a mystery.
- [rule] An NPC's gut-feeling hint should be backed by world evidence the player can inspect, not left as an unsupported suspicion.
- [rule] Give a suspicious NPC a non-murder secret, so the player spends effort on a false suspect until the secret is revealed. When: Designing a suspicious NPC who is not the culprit. Why: A separate secret explains suspicion without solving the crime.
- [rule] Use decoy clues, such as a forged note or planted item, that a later discovery disproves. When: designing a mystery with false leads. Why: Decoys reward players who keep testing their assumptions.
- [rule] Place a false clue that points to a wrong suspect, and include a later check that reveals its flaw.
- [rule] Every element of a lure, including materials and handwriting, must pass the target's own scrutiny, since one false detail exposes the trap. When: Building a forged lure or document. Why: A target who recognizes the ruse will not act.
- [rule] Build NPC hints as deliberate pointers that the player must interpret, rather than as explicit instructions.
- [rule] Do not assume a wrong location was given deliberately until other evidence supports that reading. When: A witness gives a location that does not match.
- [rule] Let an early item circulate through NPC dialogue, with each NPC offering a different reading of its meaning.
- [rule] Use captions that mislead slightly, so players must check the image or a second source.
- [rule] Reveal hidden decoy quests in a closing sequence that explains why the earlier misdirection happened. When: Ending a game with a deceptive side thread. Why: A closing explanation resolves the purpose of the misdirection.
- [rule] A message system can carry deliberately misleading reports, each with a tell such as an odd detail that rewards careful players.
- [rule] Make a true but misleading clue available so the player must decide whether to act on it. When: When designing mysteries with red herrings. Why: A true clue that points the wrong way tests the player's reasoning rather than only their recall.
- [rule] Generate decoy traces matching an item's size or type, then let the player discover that the item has a second, hidden history. When: designing layered clues around a single object. Why: A decoy that matches an item invites investigation into the item's deeper history.
- [rule] Record an NPC's death as the failure mechanism while leaving the triggering event undetermined, so players can discover what pushed the character over the edge. When: An NPC dies from a chronic condition. Why: Keeping the trigger open gives the player an investigable cause.
- [rule] Give non-player characters partial overheard fragments so players assemble a motive from pieces, with a second character able to change its meaning. When: Designing motive reveals in dialogue. Why: Assembling and reframing fragments makes the motive a player-built deduction.
- [rule] Leave a clue meant to mislead and reward players who question why it survived. When: Designing red herrings or misdirection in a mystery. Why: Questioning survival rewards careful reasoning over surface reading.
- [rule] Let an NPC's expression or line hint that they already know a secret, so the player can infer it before the formal reveal. When: Scripting a secret that an NPC holds. Why: Inference from behaviour rewards attention more than a direct statement does.
- [rule] Place a decoy so that a reaction test identifies no one, pushing players to look for other clues.
- [rule] Let factions plant false clues for their own motives, and make those motives visible so the player can detect a misleading NPC. When: Designing rival factions that interfere with the player's investigation. Why: Visible motives give players a way to discount deliberately misleading clues.
- [rule] A note or journal entry can carry a name or seal the player reasonably links to a known character, with the real author revealed only at a meeting. When: designing a mystery sender in dungeon or quest content.
- [rule] Have an NPC give a plausible reason for entering a room, and let the player verify it against where the stated item actually is. When: designing NPC behavior that hides intent. Why: a checkable errand turns a suspicious visit into a clue.
- [rule] Let a player use a dummy figure or a bundle under blankets to fool a patrolling guard's glance. When: Designing a stealth dungeon.
- [rule] Plant a visibly hostile NPC whose motive does not fit the crime, rewarding players who check logic rather than following mood.
- [rule] Let a random event redirect the plot, and treat the mistake that caused it as a clue the player can follow.
- [rule] Have the player lure a guard away with a forged order before searching a locked room, and give them a signal when the decoy fails. When: Designing a heist or investigation mission with a timing puzzle. Why: A recoverable signal keeps the timing puzzle playable after the decoy fails.
- [rule] Use an item or NPC as a decoy that steers the player's route toward a false suspect.
- [rule] Make loot look valuable but be counterfeit, with the real reward being information or access that an NPC reveals afterward.
- [rule] Give containers weight or sound cues so a fake one feels suspicious to a player who inspects it, such as a chest that is too light. When: when designing containers players can inspect.
- [rule] Be ready to drop the most striking theory when the facts disagree with it. When: A dramatic or eccentric suspect attracts attention. Why: Striking suspects are often decoys.
- [rule] Place tracks or clues deliberately, and decide in advance who could have made each one, so players can test the trace against the event. When: Designing clues for a deduction puzzle. Why: Predetermined makers make traces fair and testable.
- [rule] Make decoy clues, such as fresh tracks or a suspicious person, look decisive at first and resolve on closer inspection.
- [rule] Place a suspicious object or NPC with a believable motive as a decoy, and resolve it later with a clue. When: when designing a misleading lead. Why: A resolved decoy keeps the mystery fair.
- [rule] Place decoy corpses or too-convenient keys whose placement betrays the antagonist's plan, rewarding players who examine the setup.
- [rule] Place a decoy hazard that players must rule out before they can find the real one. When: A level contains a real hazard that must be identified.
- [rule] Place a decoy quest-giver or locked room that pulls suspicion away from the true culprit, while keeping the real route fair. When: designing a mystery in a level.
- [rule] Place a visible guide that leads toward a dead end, and reward players who cross-check it against the terrain.
- [rule] A puzzle can include decoy key items that look like the solution but tie to a framing plot revealed later.
- [rule] Use a cloaked figure in a dim corridor as a deliberate misidentification trap, revealing its identity only when it speaks. When: when staging an ambiguous encounter. Why: Delayed identification creates surprise and tension.
- [rule] Place decoy scent sources, such as a spilled reagent in a storage yard, so tracking skill branches, and give the player a route back to the fork. When: Designing tracking puzzles. Why: Branches reward careful tracking without stranding players.
- [rule] Lure the player into a room with an apparent safe objective, lock the exit behind them, and trigger the ambush only once they are committed. When: Designing a trap encounter in a puzzle room. Why: Committing the player first removes their escape option and heightens tension.
- [rule] Build a lure quest with bait at a set location and hour, isolated buildings and a timed arrival of reinforcements. When: Designing an encounter where the player sets a trap for an NPC. Why: Fixed timing and isolation control when and where the confrontation happens.
- [rule] Use a memorial or grave site as a return-to-scene trigger where an NPC appears, and require the player to test the reason the NPC gives. When: when designing NPC encounters at significant locations. Why: Revisited places give NPCs a reason to appear while keeping their claims checkable.
- [rule] Place the lure trigger in the world, such as a bell, message or ringing device, so the player can discover it by observation.
- [rule] Let NPCs offer rumors naming other characters, and track whether each rumor matches what that NPC could know. When: When designing NPC rumor systems. Why: Tracking knowledge lets rumors be consistent with NPC access, making deception checkable.
- [rule] Place a decoy clue along the route players expect the culprit to take, such as a discarded weapon near an exit. When: Designing misleading evidence for a mystery scene.
- [rule] Design a faction that looks like the obvious culprit as a red herring that players investigate before the real threat appears. When: When a level needs misdirection through a visible group. Why: Players committed to a plausible suspect delay discovering the true threat.
- [rule] Design rooms or shops that require a player action to enter as traps that cost time and reveal the player. When: Placing venues that trap a stealthy player. Why: Required actions hold the player in place, creating a costly risk.
- [rule] Design a clue that points the wrong way until a later interview supplies its explanation.
- [rule] Do not treat a missing object as proof of guilt; it may be an accident of household cleaning or another innocent cause. When: when a key item is unaccounted for. Why: A disappearance alone is ambiguous and can mislead the investigation.
- [rule] Plant a grim motif that players first read as theme, then let a later clue contradict the staging so the motif misleads only at first.
- [rule] Design an NPC's report of a lost key as wrong, with the key in a container beyond the spots the player checks first. When: A quest depends on the player finding an item the NPC misplaced. Why: The player must test the claim and search beyond the obvious places.
- [rule] Plant a fake note or map in an NPC's space, then record which guards react and where they go. When: designing stealth or detective gameplay.
- [rule] Have guards follow a decoy route, letting players lose them by doubling back through a crowded area.
- [rule] Show the decisive clue or device early as ordinary scenery, so the audience files it away and recognises it when it pays off. When: Designing a fair-play reveal. Why: A clue in plain view is accepted as furniture, so its later use surprises without cheating.
- [rule] Do not use a lure that would alarm the people you are protecting. Check that the bait does not disturb those it is meant to guard. When: Choosing a lure in a space shared with non-target characters.
- [rule] Design a stalking NPC to dismiss a transport or change direction, so the player must track the real route rather than the apparent one. When: designing a pursuit or stealth encounter. Why: the visible route then misleads the observer.
- [rule] Offer a plausible false suspect whose apparent motive matches a known grudge, so the misdirection fits what the player already believes. When: Designing misdirection in a mystery. Why: Red herrings work best when they fit a motive the investigator already holds.
- [heuristic] Test a decoy by asking what its planner needed to make it convincing, like a matching second item; an isolated item is random unless an independent trace contradicts its story. When: A decoy or planted item is being judged for plausibility.
- [heuristic] Conveniently visible objects are often placed rather than dropped, and a very clear print can be a decoy; verify its owner before taking it as evidence. When: an object is conveniently visible or a striking print appears at a scene. Why: convenient placement and deliberately conspicuous tracks can signal planting or misdirection.
- [heuristic] Decoy routes, NPCs walking a different path, or disguised items can draw pursuing tails or patrols away from the real target, especially when it is alert to followers. When: a target is alert to followers or pursued by patrols.
- [heuristic] A decoy hiding real contents in a worthless-looking shell works best when its outer appearance matches the target's expectations; a mismatch is seen through immediately.
- [heuristic] Lures succeed when hard to check on the spot; requiring verification through a second trusted NPC or route before acting makes deception harder to sustain. When: the target must be absent from their post, or a quest message may be a trap. Why: verification through a trusted second source removes the uncertainty the lure depends on.
- [heuristic] Place a false-confession NPC mid-quest with a checkable motive, so players must check the claim against physical evidence before acting on it. When: designing a case with a false suspect who has reason to confess. Why: a checkable motive turns the confession into a question.
- [heuristic] Use showy ornament or a flaunted item on an NPC to distract from the object the player should inspect, hiding the ordinary secret elsewhere.
- [heuristic] Place a plausible but harmless or irrelevant object, or a wrong gaze, near a key clue so players spend time on it before the true meaning is revealed. When: when the reader should misread a scene briefly. Why: the decoy delays the correct interpretation.
- [heuristic] Use a plausible, visible second suspect with a complete-looking motive to draw suspicion from the real culprit, hiding an alternate planner behind them for players to uncover. When: the audience would otherwise identify the culprit early.
- [heuristic] When a scene contains many odd events, sort each by who benefits from it and what it requires. When: Many odd events appear in one case. Why: Staged events often serve a hidden motive.
- [heuristic] Use misdirection only when clues stay fair and traceable, and avoid framing stories with internal gaps an audience can easily find. When: Designing a red-herring suspect. Why: Fair clues let careful readers separate framing from fact.
- [heuristic] Use decoy clues that fit the scene but contradict one detail, giving the player a fair way to reject them. When: Designing misleading evidence in a game scene. Why: A single checkable contradiction lets careful players dismiss the decoy.
- [heuristic] Judge a lure as probable rather than certain, and plan for the target not arriving. Why: a lure can fail even when the target is likely to respond.
- [heuristic] A wrong inference does little harm when used deliberately as a lure, because it still steers attention.
- [heuristic] Have a turned insider plant a false clue, so the pursuer reaches the wrong conclusion through their own reasoning. When: when a pursuer must be steered to the wrong place.
- [heuristic] An NPC under influence can reveal a clue when the player asks hypothetical questions and repeats key phrases; build dialogue options that echo the NPC's own words.
- [heuristic] An NPC expert can give a confident but incorrect account of a crime's aftermath, creating a misdirection the player can test.
- [heuristic] Build expectation about a character through third-party rumour before showing their abilities, so the first demonstration lands with more weight. When: Introducing a mysterious or highly capable character. Why: Prior rumour primes the player to read the demonstration as significant.
- [heuristic] An object's weight can falsely suggest value when it comes from construction rather than contents; explaining the construction later keeps the misdirection fair. When: Using weight as a cue to valuable contents. Why: Weight is read as a sign of what is inside.
- [heuristic] Pressure for a quick result and a claim that the case is simple encourage investigators to settle on the wrong suspect. When: when a case is under public or official time pressure. Why: urgency discourages testing contrary evidence.
- [heuristic] Send observers on a harmless errand with a clear instruction but no reason, so they cannot interfere with the real watch.
- [heuristic] A decoy works best when it rests on a real item whose meaning is open to dispute. When: when designing a misleading clue. Why: a genuine item gives the wrong reading credibility.
- [heuristic] Ask why something is hidden and why it is hidden in this particular way; this separates decoy concealment from genuine concealment.
- [heuristic] A red herring works best when it is more absorbing than the plain facts, such as a dramatic supernatural lure, so it draws attention away from the simple truth. When: When designing a decoy explanation. Why: Vivid explanations hold attention more strongly than mundane ones.
- [heuristic] An apparently dead NPC can act as a decoy; add a second clue, such as a booking or rumour, that reopens the question. When: when a character seems eliminated from the story. Why: a fresh clue restores uncertainty and sustains investigation.
- [heuristic] Use an ambiguous initial as deliberate misdirection that a later clue resolves, so the player's first reading is plausible but wrong. When: When designing a mystery's red herrings. Why: A plausible wrong reading rewards players who revise it when evidence changes.
- [heuristic] Make a suspect's background a misdirection the player must see through, and pair the noisy accusation with a checkable fact the player can test. When: designing a crowd accusation scene. Why: a determined player can ignore the mob and verify the claim.
- [heuristic] Use an in-world rumour as a red herring, but leave a logged clue showing who benefits from spreading it. When: when designing a supernatural rumour that hides a human culprit.
- [heuristic] In a staged scene, the most obvious suspect deserves the closest test, because the arrangement may be designed to deflect suspicion from the real culprit. When: when the scene looks arranged.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC or faction a decoy incident that explains the first one, and let the player find the inconsistency between them.
- [heuristic] A rumour system can steer players toward a red-herring suspect, with clues in one location that point to a false culprit. When: when designing rumour-based mysteries. Why: Rumour sets priorities and can lock players onto a wrong answer.
- [heuristic] Let the player's first assumption of robbery be wrong, and reveal the true goal through which containers were opened and which were ignored, placing valuables that contradict the theft reading. When: When designing a scene that should prompt the player to revise a motive. Why: Visible evidence that conflicts with the first theory forces a revision.
- [heuristic] Give a detective or quest-giver NPC a manner that can mislead, such as an encouraging tone or a leading question, that the player must check against evidence. When: Designing quest-giver or detective NPCs. Why: Misleading manner tests the player's judgment without lying outright.
- [heuristic] Build a late reveal around a small mismatch, such as wrong footwear, that the player can notice and check. When: When designing the reveal of a false account. Why: Visible small mismatches reward attention without new information.
- [heuristic] Give the mystery a visible culprit whose misdeeds are real but unrelated to the main plot, so players who test the story against timelines and resources are rewarded. Why: Obvious answers should be checkable and not always correct.
- [heuristic] Keep a decoy explanation partly true, and place a later contradiction the player can find, so trusting the decoy has a reason but fails a physical check. When: Designing a misleading journal entry or NPC explanation. Why: Partial truth makes the wrong part credible, while a checkable contradiction rewards careful testing.
- [heuristic] A decoy figure can draw targets' attention while a hidden listener moves into position unseen.
- [heuristic] A puzzle can present genuine and decoy clues to be sorted, rewarding a correct sort, with decoys built so a wrong sort looks obvious. When: designing a sorting or identification puzzle. Why: Gives players a clear, testable challenge.
- [heuristic] Use a forged or misleading message that requires insider knowledge, so players must weigh who could have written it. When: Designing a lure or deception clue. Why: Message content can narrow suspects by what the writer knew.
- [heuristic] Place a fake quest letter from a trusted NPC that leads into danger, and let the player later find the real sender to expose the trick. When: Designing a deceptive quest hook in a dungeon or level. Why: Players trust NPC letters, and the later reveal rewards investigation.
- [heuristic] Add weight to a decoy so the target does not notice it is fake during the first moment of handling. When: A substitute object is handed to a target. Why: Expected weight makes the substitute feel like the real item at first touch.
- [heuristic] Build a lure from an NPC's known vanity or need to draw the player into a hidden chamber. When: Designing a route into a concealed area. Why: A motivated NPC gives a believable reason for the player to follow.
- [heuristic] Escape routes through crowded streets or busy venues feel plausible to players and can serve as misdirection away from the true path. When: designing escape routes for a fleeing culprit.
- [heuristic] A costly-to-open chest that holds nothing can redirect players toward the real reward elsewhere. When: Designing a locked container as a misdirection. Why: Players invest effort before they learn it is empty.
- [heuristic] When decoy objects are scattered, make sure the key clue can be recovered by reasoning rather than luck. When: Designing a clue-based investigation with distractors. Why: Players who cannot distinguish the key clue from noise will be stuck through no fault of their reasoning.
- [heuristic] A decoy must look convincing from the observer's distance and angle, for example through silhouette and costume, so the illusion holds from the street-level viewpoint.
- [heuristic] Leave a tampered lock or entry in place and set a concealed watch rather than alerting the intruder, since an easy entry warns a cautious visitor. When: Expecting a suspect to return to retrieve an object they failed to take. Why: Visible changes to the scene would make a careful intruder abandon the approach.
- [heuristic] Visible open movement can draw attention away from the real observation post, masking where the watch is actually kept. When: A hidden watch must avoid notice. Why: Attention follows the visible movement rather than the concealed position.
- [heuristic] Pair a damning object found in a suspect's space with a second clue showing someone else arranged it, so the player must weigh both. When: A suspect's room holds incriminating evidence.
- [heuristic] Place a distinctive object in an early area and let it reappear later with a different meaning, while official NPCs dismiss its importance to create a red herring. When: when designing a multi-area clue chain. Why: dismissed clues delay the player's connection until enough evidence accumulates.
- [heuristic] Let a player's first guess be partly right so a later clue can widen the search without making the first answer useless.
- [heuristic] A decoy piece matching a hiding spot makes the real one look like part of a pair and less conspicuous.
- [heuristic] Give decoy characters plausible but checkable alibis, so players are pulled away from the culprit and can return when the alibi fails. When: Designing suspects in a mystery. Why: Checkable alibis let players correct a wrong lead.
- [heuristic] A misfit, such as a dark seam where a panel does not sit flush with its frame, is a tell that a concealed compartment lies behind it.
- [heuristic] Make a decoy detectable in hindsight so the player can reason afterward that the pursuers were tricked. When: Designing a trick that the player can later recognize. Why: Retrospective clarity rewards attention without spoiling the moment.
- [heuristic] Let players stash a key item and give inspectors set procedures, so a visible decoy can succeed where a hidden item might fail. When: when designing searches in a game. Why: procedural inspectors may miss visible decoys.
- [heuristic] A decoy has no value unless an opponent actually watches or follows it; if pursuers ignore the bait or do not return, it gains nothing.
- [heuristic] Use a planted decoy the suspect will find as a probe, logging how the suspect reacts, so the reaction tests a hypothesis without committing early. When: When a suspect's reaction is the only way to test a hypothesis.
- [heuristic] A door sealed from inside can misdirect players when the real entry is a hidden hatch, such as a roof trap-door reached by a rope. When: Designing a sealed-room reveal. Why: A sealed door suggests there is no other route.
- [heuristic] Use a lure when the culprit is among a known group and will respond to a believable pretext. When: the culprit belongs to a known group.
- [heuristic] Time a false focus to a known absence of the target, so the gained time is spent on the real line of inquiry. When: the target is temporarily away or unable to act. Why: Time bought during the target's absence is not lost.
- [heuristic] A believed false lead slows pursuers or rivals while hiding the true path; notices can carry false leads that players must read between the lines. When: When designing in-world information channels or NPCs that should delay or mislead a rival. Why: Believed false leads slow pursuers and reward careful reading.
- [heuristic] A visible crime may be the first stage or a smaller act hiding a larger planned one; do not close the case when the solved act seems to explain everything. When: A theft or attack seems to be the whole plan, or the first solved crime leaves a gap. Why: The obvious motive absorbs attention, and the discovered act draws it away from the source of the larger plan.
- [heuristic] A visible-guilt suspect, especially a stereotyped public one, can absorb suspicion and end the search while the real motive lies elsewhere; verify the obvious suspect. When: A suspect looks guilty early, or the audience already expects a particular culprit. Why: Visible guilt ends the search; public stereotypes make a decoy seem obvious.
- [heuristic] Make an outside threat the obvious suspect, then eliminate it early with a hard alibi so attention turns to the inner circle. When: Designing a locked-room or closed-circle mystery that begins with an external threat. Why: A firm alibi removes the easy answer; late clues planted early make the insider's guilt feel fair in retrospect.
- [heuristic] A red herring must be disconnected from the solution but still useful to the culprit. Otherwise it is only decoration. When: Designing a decoy event for a mystery. Why: A decoy earns its place only by serving the real plan.
- [heuristic] The most convincing suspect should be wrong for a reason the player can recheck, so the solution is fair when the evidence is revisited. When: When designing a strong false suspect in a mystery. Why: A recheckable flaw lets a careful player reach the truth before the reveal.
- [heuristic] Design bait so the suspect's expected response follows from their known habits, such as reading the press and preparing for a predicted event.
- [procedure] 1) Send messages under a cover identity to each member of a known group, requesting arrival at a set time. 2) Meet candidates one at a time in a prepared room. 3) Dismiss non-suspects with a small payment and hold them apart. 4) Ask for something only the culprit would answer to.
- [procedure] 1) Estimate the target's role and habits. 2) Identify where the target would read or hear a notice. 3) Place the notice where that audience reads. 4) Prepare the meeting before the target arrives. When: target's likely location and motives are known well enough. Why: a notice only reaches targets who are likely to see it.
- [procedure] 1) Write a counterfeit reply that copies the genuine message's structure and figures but changes its meaning. 2) Deliver it through a channel the suspect trusts and that you control. 3) Observe the first reactions: gaze, hesitation before touching, expression, and how it is opened. 4) Compare the reaction with that of a recipient who was not expecting a message. When: The suspect is likely to communicate through an intermediary and the channel can be controlled. Why: Reactions to the decoy reveal what the suspect knows and whether he trusts the channel.
- [procedure] 1) Post a short notice in widely read places. 2) Include where the item was found, the item itself, and a specific time and address to claim it. 3) Keep a second method ready if the first fails. When: When the owner of a found object is unknown and direct return is impractical. Why: A public, specific notice reaches the true owner and lets the finder verify them.
- [procedure] 1) Act against someone who is not the real target. 2) Let the true suspect believe attention has moved on. 3) Post an observer to follow the expected move. 4) Use that move to reach the key witness. When: the true suspect is watching the investigators. Why: a feeling of safety draws out the suspect's move.
- [procedure] 1) Write from the target's own correspondence, taking up the open business. 2) Give a reason for needing more payment or detail. 3) Set precise conditions: payment form, place and hour. 4) Explain why the sender cannot come to the target. 5) Predict the response and be ready at the set place. When: when the suspect is identified and in active contact with a known party. Why: A specific, plausible lure draws the target to a place the investigator controls.
- [procedure] 1) Learn the suspect's fixed routine and timing. 2) Choose a point on that route where the suspect will pass alone and be able to see the plant. 3) Place the item there so the suspect will certainly find it. 4) Ensure a witness does not pick it up first. When: Planting an item to draw suspicion onto a person with a predictable route. Why: Predictable routines let the planner control when and where the suspect meets the plant.
- [procedure] 1) Make a duplicate of the valuable object. 2) Move the real object by a separate route. 3) Leave a visible false trail that pursuers will follow. When: the real object must move unseen while pursuers need a misleading path. Why: Pursuers follow visible cues, so a convincing decoy diverts attention from the real item.
- [procedure] 1) Use the demanded meeting time and place. 2) Require the courier to carry a visible signal object. 3) Place the watcher so the signal is lit and the watcher stays in shadow. 4) Approach the carrier by name at handover. When: an unknown party sets the time and place of a payment.
- [procedure] 1) Invent a false target the suspect is likely to chase. 2) Observe how the suspect reacts. 3) Treat defensive or panicked reactions as evidence of what they are hiding. When: A witness's account of an unseen person keeps dissolving under questioning and cannot be checked directly. Why: A hidden party that fears identification tends to react to a dangled lead in revealing ways.
- [procedure] 1) Give the target a believable reason to leave, such as a lead they can check themselves. 2) Note how long they will be absent. 3) Search during that window. When: when a small object must be found while a suspect is away. Why: a convincing errand keeps the suspect occupied for a known period.
- [procedure] 1) Read the initials on the monogram. 2) Use them as the search target. 3) Match candidates against other clues before concluding. When: A found item carries initials.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a suspect NPC. 2) Plant items where that NPC would not normally keep them. 3) Include one detail a careful player can use to see the setup, such as a missing normal wear mark. When: Designing a frame-up puzzle in a dungeon or town. Why: A fair detail lets careful players detect the frame-up.
- [procedure] 1) Have an NPC place a key item on another character during a friendly exchange. 2) Trigger a forced search later. 3) Give a second NPC a sightline on the handoff so it can be exposed. When: Building a false-clue puzzle for the player.
- [procedure] 1) Pick one simple invariant, such as two roles sharing a visual trait. 2) Add decoys around it. 3) Confirm the player can solve the puzzle by stripping away the decoys to reach the invariant. When: when designing a puzzle.
- [procedure] 1) Create a decoy item that seems significant. 2) Give it an innocent origin. 3) Make that origin discoverable by the player. Why: decoys stay fair when they pay off.
- [procedure] 1) Create a hazard that draws all watchers to one point. 2) Use a condition, such as a falling tide, that keeps the hazard in place for hours. 3) Leave by another route while attention is fixed on the hazard.
- [procedure] 1) Place a rigged object that makes noise where pursuers will investigate. 2) Wait out of sight nearby. 3) Trigger the noise at the right moment. 4) Leave by another route while pursuers head to the sound. When: when being pursued by searchers.
- [procedure] 1) Cut or scrape a hidden area of the object, such as its base. 2) Inspect the material exposed beneath the outer finish. 3) Judge authenticity from the colour and sheen of that material. When: when an object's authenticity is in doubt. Why: the material beneath a coating can differ from the genuine article.
- [procedure] 1) Pick information the target believes is private. 2) Place a lure based on it. 3) Predict the target's response from their motive. 4) Prepare the setting so the target is caught when they come. When: Targeting a culprit with a strong motive who does not suspect a trap. Why: Psychological prediction turns a lure into a capture.
- [procedure] 1) Pick a concealed observation point with a clear view of the decoy. 2) Make the decoy convincing from the target's viewing angle. 3) Move it at regular intervals, about every fifteen minutes, out of the target's sight. 4) Wait in concealment for the target to act.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the target's strongest attachment. 2) Find a channel the target uses to contact the outside. 3) Confirm the channel exists in an ordinary record. 4) Send a plausible emergency at a set time and move in while the target is away. When: when ordinary approach cannot reach the target. Why: the target leaves its guarded position on schedule.
- [procedure] 1) Set up the decoy before the check begins. 2) Complete any changes of appearance beforehand. 3) Leave before the check arrives, so no time-consuming changes are needed under observation. Why: Time-consuming changes under observation risk exposure.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the belief the trap relies on. 2) Build a lure the watcher will find attractive. 3) Post observers only at the entry that belief predicts. 4) Check whether the watcher actually approaches. When: Luring an observing agent into a chosen space.
- [tradeoff] An obviously false decoy is seen through quickly and can expose its planner, while a conspicuous fake can deliberately test whether players check evidence first. When: When a forged clue is cheaply made, or when designing a deliberately obvious forgery as a player test. Why: Investigators test suspicious items and find the fabrication; a conspicuous fake tests whether players check evidence before acting.
- [tradeoff] An obvious decoy gets investigated; a subtle one may go unnoticed. Make it look like a lead yet easy to dismiss, so the watcher dismisses it and stops looking.
- [tradeoff] Feeding a decoy to a witness can protect an operation, but may cost that witness's trust later.
- [tradeoff] Convicting an innocent person and freeing a guilty one are both serious errors; a verdict system should weigh both costs rather than favour one.
- [tradeoff] Hiding a stash to fake a prop gives the player a ready cover, but costs them if the lie is discovered. When: Designing a cover mechanic for players.
- [tradeoff] A decoy sighting buys time on broken ground with cover, but fails on bare slopes where any figure is visible far off, forcing the fugitive to rely on speed. When: deciding whether to use a deliberate exposure. Why: cover determines whether a sighting can be hidden from the rest of the pursuit.
- [pitfall] Looking only at the most obvious loser, or skipping each party's share of gain or loss, leads to wrong conclusions about motive.
- [pitfall] An NPC's accusation driven by personal grudge can serve as a red herring that the player must test against physical facts. When: designing misleading NPC dialogue. Why: Biased testimony creates a meaningful test of evidence-based reasoning.
- [pitfall] Decoys depend on the assumptions victims and the public make about who would commit such a crime.
- [pitfall] A decoy lacking real circumstantial features, or conflicting with physical facts, is seen through at once and defeats its purpose. When: Designing false clues or trails. Why: Players test decoys against the scene's logic and reject inconsistent ones.
- [pitfall] Mistaking a decoy for the central fact, or letting it look like the central mystery, holds attention from the real goal and sends the investigation the wrong way.
- [pitfall] An obvious motive, fact or explanation can conceal a different answer; check other possibilities, since accepting it early stops the search before the distinguishing clue appears. When: A case or motive seems settled or obvious early. Why: The distinguishing clue is missed if the search stops early; a motive can mislead if the method points elsewhere.
- [pitfall] The most obvious rivalry or simplest match, such as a name seeming to name the culprit, can be a decoy hiding a larger design; test it against the evidence.
- [pitfall] The most visible feature, such as an injury, safeguard or main door, absorbs attention; checking only it leaves subtler signs, hidden routes or the true cause unexamined. When: Investigating a suspect with a visible safeguard, or forming a conclusion from the first striking finding. Why: Visible protections and striking findings pull attention away from hidden access or subtler evidence.
- [pitfall] Decoys buy time, not safety: a pursuer can strike at any stop along the route, and one who knows the land can anticipate the fugitive's circuit. Why: Local knowledge lets searchers anticipate the flanking route.
- [pitfall] Decoys work only while believed; they collapse when someone recalls a detail, or when a searcher opens them and finds only substitutes or no real value. When: When a character must be moved away from a location, or a searcher may open the decoy. Why: A decoy works only while its target believes it; inspection reveals that the decoy contains no real value.
- [pitfall] Staging visible from some angles, such as an open curtain or gap, can reveal a decoy or the watcher's position to a sharp observer. When: A decoy or disguise is used to deceive an enemy or observer. Why: Staging visible from some angles breaks the illusion, since the decoy depends on the target's assumptions.
- [pitfall] A lure or distraction that looks unusual or staged alerts the target to a trap, so it must read as an ordinary notice or have a believable cause.
- [pitfall] Misdirection fails if its correct reading is never shown, is too obscure, or rests on a fact the audience never sees; players need an accessible route to the truth. When: Designing a misleading clue.
- [pitfall] A physical mark or a displayed body part pointing to a conclusion may be a deliberate decoy or a careless gesture; corroborate before assuming either. When: When a physical mark points to a conclusion, or a suspect offers a display of a marked body part. Why: The same action can have two causes, and the choice needs corroboration.
- [pitfall] A wrong prediction or inferred hidden motive can send the search the wrong way and distort the whole investigation, so hold working hypotheses loosely.
- [pitfall] A key-text code yields nothing from the wrong edition, and a wrong key can produce plausible-looking words; confirm the exact copy and check decoded text for meaning. Why: Plausible-looking words can come from a mismatched text.
- [pitfall] Do not assume the target will come in person; an accomplice, proxy or diversion may respond, so a trap can catch someone other than the intended culprit. When: Planning a lure or trap that yields an arrival. Why: The actual responder may differ from the expected target, and arrivals may be diversions.
- [pitfall] Keeping teammates uninformed about a provocative bait or plan can alarm them, make them judge the method dishonest, and damage trust in the person acting. When: Using a provocative tactic within an investigation team. Why: Colleagues who do not understand the bait may judge the method as dishonest.
- [pitfall] Staging a decoy to bait a hostile character can provoke violence or endanger people nearby, so be ready to intervene and control timing. When: A decoy is placed to bait a hostile character. Why: Hostile reactions can escalate quickly and put others at risk.
- [pitfall] A decoy that is too obviously a decoy reads as bravado, and the audience then discounts it.
- [pitfall] A decoy must be ready before the scheduled delivery because the window for delivery is short. When: Preparing a planted message for a timed exchange. Why: A late or unprepared decoy misses the moment and wastes the test.
- [pitfall] A probe may seem to succeed by chance, since a reaction can be misread as confirmation of a guess.
- [pitfall] A wrong motive can make an innocent witness look guilty, so a calm, unembarrassed reaction is evidence against that motive. When: An investigator fixes on a motive without testing it. Why: Innocent witnesses can seem guilty under an untested theory, and their calm reactions expose the error.
- [pitfall] If the charming character is also the obvious suspect, misdirection fails; apparent helpfulness must be separated from apparent motive. When: Designing a charming character who is a suspect. Why: Audiences connect charm with guilt when both are visible together.
- [pitfall] An obviously guilty culprit ruins a mystery, and the problem often appears only on a full reread.
- [pitfall] An observer who misreads what they see can serve as a red herring, even when their account still matches other evidence.
- [pitfall] A lure fails if a close witness reads the performance as false, so the closest witnesses must stay convinced. When: A false condition is staged in front of people who know the victim. Why: Those witnesses have the most knowledge and the most reason to notice wrongness.
- [pitfall] A lure that relies on greed or urgency fails with a cautious target, who may refuse the meeting.
- [pitfall] Early theories about what is valuable can mislead. A clever cover story can also make the real target, such as a secret or history, seem less important than it is.
- [pitfall] Clearing a decoy too quickly collapses the misdirection and exposes the real offender too early.
- [pitfall] A plausible outside suspect may be offered by someone with their own interest, so treat it as a lead to check, not an answer.
- [pitfall] Expectation-based misdirection collapses once an observer tests the assumption, so one open doubt can end the whole plan.
- [pitfall] Fragments from two objects can be mixed and create a false match; sort foreign pieces before fitting.
- [pitfall] A detailed account can be wrong in one place; the listener's correction shows which parts are accurate.
- [pitfall] The most obvious accomplice may be a red herring; one person can often do all the work a plot seems to need.
- [pitfall] Piling on exotic details until a decoy reads as the author's own fancy rather than a planted lead weakens it. When: When constructing a false explanation. Why: Excess invention makes the decoy visible as artifice.
