- [pitfall] A published record that seems to settle a question may be wrong or incomplete, so it should be checked against other evidence. When: when a document appears to clear or implicate a suspect. Why: records can contain errors or omit relevant information.
- [pitfall] The suspect with the most visible quarrel attracts suspicion first, which can hide the real culprit behind a red herring. When: When one person has a documented threat against the victim. Why: Visible motive is easy to accept and so is rarely questioned.
- [pitfall] Accepting the most obvious reading of a fragment, such as a number taken as an address, without checking it. Why: The obvious reading may be a coincidence or a wrong interpretation.
- [pitfall] A decoy can cast suspicion on an innocent party, so the investigation must clear that person as well as identify the planner.
- [pitfall] A public line can also mislead the investigators who hear it, since the words alone do not reveal whether they are sincere.
- [pitfall] A decoy that draws attention to a real suspect creates new evidence about that suspect, which can cut against the planner. When: A planted clue points at an actual person. Why: Investigating the decoy yields facts that can implicate the planner.
- [pitfall] A dramatic deadline can act as a decoy that draws attention to one date while the real danger develops elsewhere. When: A scripted threat includes a fixed deadline. Why: Focus on the deadline leaves the actual threat unobserved.
- [pitfall] Experienced pursuers who expect to be noticed will see through a naive decoy, so a false trail must survive their questioning. When: A decoy is used against a skilled tail. Why: Skilled trackers verify claims, and a staged story that fails questioning collapses.
- [pitfall] A feigned distraction can mislead teammates as much as the subject, so keep notes on what each answer may mean.
- [pitfall] Redirecting a watcher can expose the decoy to the same danger the watcher posed to the original target.
- [pitfall] A false summons can separate a character from an ally, and guilt about abandoning the ally makes the lure effective.
- [pitfall] Confidence in the bait can make the investigator miss a second observer nearby.
- [pitfall] A fire or other diversion can pull guards away from the point they protect, so defences must assume decoys that may be recognised only late.
- [pitfall] A second, nearby source of smoke can hide the real origin of a fire, so each apparent source must be checked. When: A fire has more than one plausible source nearby.
- [pitfall] A decoy can be built from true facts, such as a real access route or view, that prove only possibility and point away from the real trail. When: When evaluating a suspect or route that appears to explain an event. Why: True but partial facts can seem conclusive while leaving the actual cause untested.
- [pitfall] Planted information can spread past its intended reader, so check who else will see it before releasing it.
- [pitfall] A decoy works only if the evidence that clears it arrives in time; without elimination, the scapegoat stands. When: Using a scapegoat as misdirection.
- [fact] NPC rumour can work as a decoy: it is recorded as a lead, then later contradicts itself and sends the player back.
- [fact] A single story can contain both a red herring and the true clue, so each part of a digression should be checked.
- [fact] Misleading leads and accusations can divert attention from the true path.

## timeline reconstruction
- [model] A timeline built from clock times, dates and events shows the order in which people were where, which is the basis for checking claims. When: reconstructing who was present at what moment. Why: Ordering events exposes contradictions that isolated accounts hide.
- [model] A scene reveals how a body or visitor arrived through five trace types: disturbed ground, broken growth, wheel marks, left objects, and food provenance. Why: Each trace type records a different part of the arrival or departure sequence.
- [definition] Establishing when an event could have happened means testing the time window, verifying alibi documents, and asking whether a person could realistically have been seen.
- [definition] Trace inference runs backward from a mark or residue on a surface or object to the body or item that produced it.
- [definition] Timeline reconstruction builds an ordered sequence of events from a witness's approximate durations, order of actions and the gaps between them. When: a witness saw events only in pieces. Why: an ordered account is needed for the investigation.
- [definition] A reconstructed timeline is a sequence of dated events and fixed checkpoints, with undated actions placed between them.
- [definition] A locked-room puzzle can be solved by asking when a closure was made, not only how an opening was sealed or forced. When: A room seems closed and rules out an outside intruder.
- [mechanism] Scheduled events such as appointments, patrols, train arrivals or NPC routines can serve as fixed points from which a player reconstructs a timeline. When: designing timeline-based puzzles. Why: Fixed events give the player reference points to order other events.
- [mechanism] A timeline view logging timed departures, arrivals, shots and each character's claim lets players cross-check accounts against each other and scene evidence; short blocking intervals can create or break an alibi. When: players must verify NPC whereabouts or accounts. Why: Checking claims against a shared timeline turns testimony into a puzzle.
- [mechanism] Store each game event with its game time, location and presence list, including room entries, trap triggers and sightings, so designer and player can rebuild an intrusion and see who is excluded. Why: Players can check which characters are excluded from each event.
- [mechanism] Travel times between locations set timing constraints: an arrival message or lead calculation shows how soon a character can reach a place, defining the window in which to act. When: designing timed NPC movement or player action windows. Why: Travel time bounds what is possible.
- [mechanism] A timed weather event gives a time boundary: marks made after a snowfall began date to the interval since then, and tracks lying on fresh snow were made after it stopped. When: using a timed weather event as evidence of when movement happened. Why: A known start point lets traces be dated relative to it.
- [mechanism] Travel times between areas can be tuned so that a player who stops to listen or carry a burden runs out of time before a scheduled event. When: When designing timed sequences in a game. Why: Movement costs and pauses change how much time remains, creating tension.
- [mechanism] A plot built on a precise schedule fails when one fixed date falls out of order, because later steps cannot undo an event already fixed earlier in the sequence. When: A scheme depends on a strict chain of dated steps, such as substitutions or false identities. Why: Each step assumes the prior date held, so a single conflicting date can collapse the whole arrangement.
- [mechanism] A fixed deadline makes each lost day shrink the characters' options; a flexible deadline loses tension. When: the deadline is firm and cannot be delayed.
- [mechanism] Fixed mechanical records, such as a timed device that logs an event, can pin down the moment something happened. When: When a crime or event must be dated. Why: Automatic recorders give times independent of witness memory.
- [mechanism] When each backstory event triggers the next, the timeline carries a motive's logic and reveals it in order.
- [mechanism] A timeline puzzle that gives timestamps, travel durations and messages lets the player work backward to when an event occurred. When: Designing a time-based deduction puzzle. Why: Known durations constrain the possible time of the event.
- [mechanism] A second timer can trigger a routine at regular intervals, such as renewing air roughly every forty minutes, so recurring actions happen without a person present. When: an action must recur while the character is unobserved. Why: the second timer schedules the routine.
- [mechanism] An object shown to have moved after an event the audience thought was earlier overturns prior assumptions and changes which characters are suspected. When: when the reveal depends on the order of events. Why: reversing the sequence reinterprets every earlier clue at once.
- [behavior] An unexplained absence or undisclosed visitor leaves a gap that observers fill with guesses, keeping the question alive. When: the source of a gap is hidden. Why: people prefer a guess to an open question.
- [behavior] A person who does not know they are watched shows conduct they would otherwise hide, so a hidden observer can capture it. When: an observer stays out of the target's view. Why: concealing the watch keeps behaviour natural.
- [behavior] A long wait builds tension but can dull watchers' attention, as companions grow restless and fidget.
- [behavior] People often underweight a soft deadline and keep searching past the point where they should leave. When: a deadline is flexible rather than fixed. Why: A deadline that seems negotiable loses its urgency.
- [behavior] Felt time in a tense wait can far exceed real time; a few minutes of watching a risky object can seem like an hour. When: A watcher waits with attention fixed on a risky object or sound. Why: Attention to each small change stretches perceived duration.
- [behavior] At peak suspense a character can forget their next plan, leaving them stuck between options.
- [rule] Give suspects and NPCs timestamped movement and transport records so players can check alibis against a schedule. When: when designing alibi or movement puzzles. Why: A timestamped schedule gives a concrete, checkable basis for accepting or rejecting an alibi. (x2)
- [rule] Use timetables, drifting or misset clocks, ticket records, transport logs, servant testimony and NPC schedules that players must order and reconcile to notice disagreements. When: when designing a timeline or movement-based mystery. Why: Requiring players to order and reconcile records makes the puzzle depend on reasoning rather than a single clue. (x2)
- [rule] Treat a reenactment as evidence of what is possible, not proof of what happened; urgency and vivid performance can make a plan feel more convincing than the evidence supports. When: A theory has been tested by reenactment under time pressure, or a reconstructed sequence is offered as an explanation of events. Why: A plausible route does not establish that the suspect took it; vivid performance feels like confirmation even when it only shows what is possible.
- [rule] Every step and witness time must agree with the rest, since one conflicting window or time can shift or break the whole timeline. When: Several witnesses give times for the same events. Why: Inconsistent times can shift the whole timeline.
- [rule] Record each time's source and reliability: discount times recalled from memory and trust times tied to something the witness saw or heard; ask how they know a time. When: when a witness gives a time. Why: Approximate or memory-based times can shift an apparent sequence; the basis of a time shows its reliability.
- [rule] Do not rest a timeline on one interested or single witness; require independent corroboration from clocks, objects or other people, since one mistaken or biased witness can distort the sequence. When: when a key sequence depends on a single account. Why: Without a second source, one mistaken or biased witness can distort the whole sequence.
- [rule] Let players fill a timeline board from partial clue cards, checking placements against in-game schedules and checkpoints drawn from watches or schedules.
- [rule] Let players rebuild events from scattered or timestamped receipts, travel records and witness sightings; a late-discovered record can re-date the plot, forcing revised theories. When: when designing deduction puzzles. Why: Re-dating makes earlier conclusions revisable and rewards careful reconstruction.
- [rule] Merge NPC accounts into one timeline and show gaps between confirmed events, highlighting where an NPC could have acted unseen. When: when building a mystery with multiple NPC witnesses or player-facing investigation tools. Why: Gaps in shared knowledge create investigation targets.
- [rule] Give NPCs timestamped schedules and logged sightings; players build a clock from statements and cross-check each against another NPC's schedule to find the one who could not have been present. When: when designing a mystery with multiple suspects. Why: Consistent, time-stamped data lets players test contradictions and verify a reasoning path.
- [rule] Model travel distances and fixed travel times between map locations, with dated messages from distant NPCs, so players can test whether a claimed route or alibi is physically possible. When: when designing movement or NPC alibis between locations. Why: Impossible travel exposes false alibis; known travel times make a claimed movement checkable.
- [rule] Do not treat the order of any stretch a witness cannot recall as certain; record the witness's inability to fix a time as information. When: when a witness reports an unrecalled gap.
- [rule] Attach to each timeline step its named time source and supporting proof, such as documents or notes, so every interval can be checked on its own. When: when reconstructing a sequence of past events. Why: An interval with no stated reference cannot be checked by anyone; attached proof lets each link be checked rather than trusted as a whole story.
- [rule] Store each timeline event with its source tag and reliability, so first-hand reports, relayed reports and physical traces are weighed separately rather than treated as equally trustworthy. When: when witnesses are scarce or their accounts overlap only partly. Why: Sources differ in how directly they observed events, so their reliability differs.
- [rule] Store event time ranges and flag conflicting times, such as two NPC witnesses' accounts, as a visible puzzle the player must resolve with another source. When: when two NPCs give conflicting times. Why: An unresolved conflict drives the player to seek more evidence.
- [rule] Ask for exact times: when an event ended, how long a person was away, and whether they had returned before the next event began. When: When an alibi depends on intervals. Why: Precise intervals are needed to measure whether a trip fits.
- [rule] Keep the seal and the crime separate in time; a seal applied afterwards can be an afterthought that does not reflect the event.
- [rule] In a timed travel system, record each leg and place an NPC witness at each stop who can confirm that leg.
- [rule] When a predicted time and a recorded time disagree, look for a source of error before trusting either figure.
- [rule] Provide a field-notes journal that logs observations as facts and a timeline of movements, so the player can check who was where and when. When: Designing a game where the player gathers and interprets observations. Why: Separating logged facts from interpretation lets the player build their own conclusions.
- [rule] State a concrete deadline early and repeat it, so every later delay carries a cost. When: an action or investigation must feel urgent. Why: Repetition keeps the clock visible throughout the story.
- [rule] Record your own path before examining tracks, so your disturbances are not mistaken for evidence. When: Investigating a scene with soft ground. Why: Own movement can overwrite or add prints.
- [rule] After a clock correction removes a contradiction, re-test the corrected timeline against the other facts rather than treating it as proof of the favoured explanation. Why: a resolved conflict does not confirm the investigator's preferred story.
- [rule] Delay sensitive reveals, such as an accusation, until the required evidence is in the player's log. When: when a reveal would be unfair if made early. Why: Evidence should precede the accusation so the player can verify it.
- [rule] Author the event timeline so that every trace is explicable by some sequence of actions. When: Designing a crime with physical evidence. Why: Unexplained traces make the solution feel unfair.
- [rule] Test a disputed movement by reenacting it with a person of similar height and weight over the same ground. When: The physical feasibility of a movement is contested. Why: A reenactment shows whether the movement is actually possible.
- [rule] Do not treat the authority that orders an action, such as issuing a warrant, as the same authority that decides on it, such as judging the case. Why: Different roles in one process carry different responsibility for a failure.
- [rule] Generate timing coincidences as background noise, so players learn that a single timing match does not prove intent. Why: noise teaches players to weigh coincidence correctly.
- [rule] Make the date of a watched event visible to the player so they can plan around it.
- [rule] For a puzzle that asks players to reconstruct events, let them replay a suspect's path and have the game check whether the timing fits. When: when designing a deduction puzzle with a timed sequence. Why: timed replay turns the player's theory into a testable check.
- [rule] Let a clock, timer or valve in a level show a state the player must explain, such as stopped while still holding stored run. When: designing an environmental clue.
- [rule] Encode a timeline in physical state: soot, a burnt-down candle, a bullet hole, a casing and footprints each reveal a different time or position. Why: Each prop then gives the player a separate clue to the sequence.
- [rule] Let NPC witnesses supply timing details, so players verify a document's date by questioning them rather than being told by a narrator.
- [rule] Use stopped clocks, NPC routines and staged scenes to create a timeline the player must reconstruct from clues. When: designing timed investigation content. Why: Players then build the sequence of events themselves.
- [rule] Store each stage of a faction's history as a timeline event so players can rebuild the causal order from in-game records. When: generating or authoring faction histories.
- [rule] Ask players to order a set of events and identify the single event that changes the plan. When: Designing a puzzle or challenge built on a sequence of events. Why: Ordering requires players to reason about cause, sequence and consequence.
- [rule] Design a reclassification step in which secondary traces, such as residue or lock marks, reverse the first reading of a scene. When: a scene looks like one kind of event. Why: contradicting traces should overturn a surface reading.
- [rule] Give time-of-death estimates as ranges rather than exact times, so the timeline remains a problem the player must solve. When: when a game reports a death time to the player. Why: Exact times would remove the deduction work.
- [rule] Make an unexplained interval in a level's timeline a lead that players can investigate in the world. When: designing movement or timeline puzzles. Why: Players can pursue gaps through locations and encounters.
- [rule] Design timestamp puzzles in which door logs, patrol routes or burn times must be reconciled, and each claimed action must fit the available minutes. When: Designing a time-based deduction puzzle. Why: Players can then catch impossible accounts through arithmetic.
- [rule] If in-world clocks drift, give players a calibration method such as a watch or sundial before timestamps on notes or witness statements can be trusted. When: Designing time-based clues in a world with unreliable clocks. Why: Players need a reference to correct timestamps.
- [rule] Give the world a clock and log each NPC's position against it, and make physical states such as a warm corpse or a dry puddle readable clocks the player can inspect. When: designing evidence the player uses to infer time. Why: readable physical state lets the player bound events without witnesses.
- [rule] Build a fair timeline puzzle from a table of timestamped events that the player compares against witnesses' differing clocks.
- [rule] Show two characters at different times, and reward a player who notices they were never present together. When: designing a character who may be one person in disguise.
- [heuristic] Let players log timed sightings or note timestamps and sort them into a timeline to reconstruct routes, alibis or suspects, making the timeline itself a puzzle. When: designing deduction puzzles from in-world records. Why: Sorting timed entries reveals sequences players must reason about, showing who could have seen what. (x2)
- [heuristic] Fix each recurring event's timestamp on a timeline so gaps, returns and sequences show whether events are connected or a natural cause explains them. When: when events recur irregularly, or any clue is built from repeated small events. Why: Dates expose patterns that memory blurs; timing and recurrence separate a pattern from chance. (x2)
- [heuristic] Treat witness time estimates as approximate and provisional; cross-check them against other sources or a public clock before relying on them. When: a timeline depends on witness statements or estimated absence durations. Why: Human time estimates drift and are often imprecise; an independent clock gives the firmer fix.
- [heuristic] Events with a known clock time, such as a striking clock or gunshot, serve as fixed anchors; anchor each witness's report to them so accounts can be sequenced. When: several witnesses describe the same short event. Why: A shared time reference lets accounts be compared and sequenced.
- [heuristic] Before rejecting a theory over conflicting witness times, identify each clock's reference; a fixed offset is corrected by subtraction, so fifteen minutes fast turns twenty past into five past. When: witness times from different locations or sources appear inconsistent. Why: A hidden fixed offset between clocks can make a contradiction vanish.
- [heuristic] Check whether each event could occur before the events that depend on it; an effect appearing before its cause signals a broken order.
- [heuristic] Objects left in their final state, such as a half-played board or lights still burning, can serve as time markers.
- [heuristic] Use a timing cue such as weather or a dried puddle to date an event for the player without any NPC stating it.
- [heuristic] Combine time sources that are vague or disagree into the narrowest window that all of them allow. When: Several time sources disagree or are vague. Why: The overlap of independent estimates is tighter than any one of them.
- [heuristic] Place events relative to a fixed, timed object with a known installation time; this is more robust than an unanchored estimate. When: when the question is when something happened.
- [heuristic] A wind-up mechanism that runs about fourteen to fifteen hours shows, when stopped, the time it was last wound or touched, if its start time is known. When: A scene contains a timed object whose running state can be read. Why: Its running time is predictable, so its stopped position fixes when someone interacted with it.
- [heuristic] A timeline gives an interrogator a structure for questions, since each timed step is a point where the suspect's account must fit. When: When questioning a suspect about their whereabouts. Why: Each checkpoint forces a specific, testable answer.
- [heuristic] Combine separate approaches by the same person into one timeline, which can show that preparation came before the key event.
- [heuristic] Leave a margin for error when planning a route so that one party arrives before a set hour and another is in position before a later one. When: Planning a timed sequence of movements. Why: Uncertain travel time makes a zero-margin plan fragile.
- [heuristic] Work backwards from the critical window to test whether a suspect could have been in two places at once.
- [heuristic] An event during a pending transaction, such as the death of the party who must honour it, makes failure likely. Why: The transaction cannot settle once the required party is gone.
- [heuristic] If an occupant's first outing comes right after moving in, the person who arrived may not be the person who later returns. When: comparing an occupant's arrival and departures. Why: a sudden change in routine can mark a substitution.
- [heuristic] A witness may know that someone was present without knowing when they arrived or left, so test witness times against each other. When: Reconstructing a timeline from witness accounts. Why: Partial knowledge yields gaps in the timeline.
- [heuristic] Set a specific time for a reveal, which makes the wait concrete and public and turns impatience into anticipation. When: A reveal is deliberately delayed. Why: A named moment gives the audience a fixed endpoint to wait toward.
- [heuristic] Before counting a disordered detail as a sign of haste, check whether ordinary sequence explains it, such as outer clothing being put on last. When: when a detail seems out of place. Why: routine order of actions often explains apparent disorder.
- [heuristic] Check event order: if an early stimulus would have produced a reaction, any later feigned response must begin after that stimulus.
- [heuristic] Compare a witness's account against an outside fixed point, such as a dated message, to check whether the sequence of events holds together.
- [heuristic] An alibi that shifts under questioning and has no fixed anchors is weak. Test it against fixed points such as transport records or timed events. When: When the account changes on repeated questioning.
- [heuristic] Choose which witnesses to visit first by the specific hour each one can cover.
- [heuristic] Shadow a suspect toward the likely hiding place rather than confronting him early. When: a suspect may hold the object somewhere not yet known. Why: early confrontation alerts the suspect and can end the trail.
- [heuristic] Judge what an absence implies by trip length: someone leaving a base takes different things than someone away for a weekend. When: interpreting missing belongings. Why: the items needed depend on how long the person expects to be away.
- [heuristic] When one link in a chain is missing, work from the known parts and ask what must have been true for the rest to fit.
- [heuristic] A known period when a character is away from their post fixes the window in which another party's visit or action can occur.
- [heuristic] Demonstrate a suspected position with your own body so others can test and accept a reconstruction.
- [heuristic] An independent witness's sighting, including confirmation that no one passed, can fix a scene at a particular time.
- [heuristic] Break an accusation into ordered steps, each tied to a named person, so every step can be checked on its own. When: when reconstructing a disputed incident. Why: a single unified claim hides which step can be verified.
- [heuristic] A step that appears out of sequence, or a required step that is missing, can expose a disputed or irregular action worth investigating.
- [heuristic] Check whether key evidence arrived after decision-makers had formed their view, since the weight of late evidence depends on that timing.
- [heuristic] Let the player disprove a frame by finding a timing or motive gap in the accusation. When: Designing a murder mystery with a framed suspect. Why: Discoverable gaps give players a route to clear the innocent and find the culprit.
- [heuristic] Use travel time between locations as a pacing tool, with brief waits that let players review their clues. Why: Pauses restore attention before the next step.
- [heuristic] Make a timeline puzzle require the player to track when each character could reach a location. When: Designing a time-based deduction challenge. Why: Reachability over time turns alibis into a checkable puzzle.
- [heuristic] Reward players who work out which production method produced a forged item, not only those who notice that it looks wrong. When: When a forgery puzzle has more than one solution path. Why: Reasoning about method tests deeper understanding than surface inspection.
- [heuristic] Backward timeline planning should be used only when timings are known; with guessed timings it produces false precision. When: when the durations are estimates. Why: exact-looking results rest on unverified numbers.
- [heuristic] A scene-reconstruction system can require the player to check a claimed action against the traces the true event would leave, such as disturbed objects or reacting NPCs.
- [heuristic] Require players to test a reconstructed story against dated events before a final accusation unlocks.
- [heuristic] Reconstruct a timeline only when several actions depend on timed conditions; without fixed points, there is nothing to anchor it. When: deciding whether timeline analysis applies. Why: fixed points supply the anchors that windows are measured from.
- [heuristic] Narrow the window of tampering by timing, placing it after the event and before the scene is formally examined. When: Evidence of tampering must be dated. Why: Timing bounds which people could have had access.
- [heuristic] Leave a watch post before staying becomes conspicuous to staff and customers, since familiar faces may begin to notice or question you. When: Maintaining a long stakeout in a public place. Why: Repeated presence draws attention and undermines cover.
- [heuristic] A trace that places a suspect at a different time can eliminate that suspect from the event being investigated. When: Comparing a suspect's confirmed movements against the time of the event. Why: A person cannot be present at two places at once, so a timing mismatch rules them out.
- [heuristic] A person's movements can be rebuilt from hotel registers, telephone logs, mail and staff recollections, and no single source needs to be complete. When: The person has left a trail of institutional records.
- [heuristic] Store a disputed mechanism, such as a dragged body, as a reenactment puzzle that resolves only when the correct movement is replicated. Why: Requiring the right action makes the mechanism a skill-based challenge.
- [heuristic] A stopped in-game clock can hint that a power cut or tampering happened. When: when designing environmental clues.
- [heuristic] A timeline that rests on witnesses who may misjudge the hour or place is weak and should not be trusted alone. When: Witness accounts are the only source for event timing.
- [heuristic] Ask witnesses for an orderly, lucid account, since the order of their statements exposes gaps.
- [heuristic] A timed observation fixes that a person was present at one moment only, so it narrows the window but does not prove presence later. When: when a witness reports someone at a specific time. Why: A single sighting is a snapshot, not continuous proof.
- [heuristic] A stand-in's timing can give the trick away, for example by leaving late when the house is quiet. When: Testing whether a visible presence was the person it appeared to be. Why: Unusual timing contradicts the expected behavior of the person being impersonated.
- [heuristic] Deliver a new piece of information when the protagonist's resolve is weakest, so tension restarts. When: A protagonist is wavering or close to giving up. Why: Fresh information at a low point reignites conflict.
- [heuristic] Give a timing clue an early, dismissible explanation, then bring it back with a stronger witness so the player is taught to discount it before it matters. When: A clock or timer clue is central to an alibi or timeline. Why: A clue dismissed early and reraised later with better testimony pays off without feeling sudden.
- [heuristic] Timelines are weak when all times are estimates with no fixed events to anchor them. When: Reconstructing events from witness estimates only. Why: Without anchors, errors in each estimate accumulate unchecked.
- [heuristic] Start a disappearance timeline at the last moment the missing person was reliably seen, not at a later rumour or sighting. When: A disappearance is being investigated and its start is disputed. Why: A convenient later start date can hide the true window of opportunity.
- [heuristic] A discovery that coincides with a party beginning a legal or financial action is suspicious timing that can point toward whoever controlled the discovery.
- [heuristic] Place dated records of orders, deliveries and events side by side, so timing can be checked against each suspect's access. When: a case depends on when means were obtained relative to when effects began. Why: Matching dates across separate records can confirm or break a suspect's link to the cause.
- [heuristic] Resolve an impossible state by reordering events already shown, not by adding new ones; the reveal feels fair because the timing was set out early. When: when a sealed or impossible scene needs an explanation. Why: the audience already holds every piece, so the solution feels earned.
- [heuristic] Use a timed event, such as a stop that reopens an alibi, as the hinge of the case, forcing the reader to decide which witness to believe about it. When: Constructing an alibi that seems closed but may be reopened. Why: A time window converts a settled alibi into a live question without new characters.
- [procedure] 1) Record each suspect's arrivals, departures and returns with times. 2) Compare these with the offence time and any sightings. 3) Flag each claimed alibi or location that conflicts with the record. When: testing alibis or whereabouts. Why: A shared frame exposes alibis that do not fit the timing; contradictions with the record are the basis for challenging an alibi. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Gather dated entries from depositions, warrants, letters and later memoirs. 2) Date each source and note each author's motive. 3) Reconcile conflicting figures. 4) Sort all entries and build the full timeline before concluding intent or plans. When: several documents disagree or mention events. Why: Dating and motive-weighing show which conflicts matter and which can be resolved. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) List each person's stated movements with times and locations. 2) Compare them with what independent witnesses observed. 3) Map distances and check each leg against the time it takes. 4) Chain events in order. 5) Mark gaps and implausible speeds as weak points. When: several accounts must fit together within time windows, or whether a sequence was physically possible is being tested. Why: Stories fail where stated times conflict with observations or physical limits; timed legs and distances expose impossible sequences. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Collect arrival and departure times and stated times from every account. 2) Lay all events on one timeline. 3) Check whether overlapping accounts can both be true. 4) Mark which claims are independent and which rest on one witness; cross-check disputed vehicles or times before accepting them. When: when several accounts give times for the same event or witnesses report movements around one event. Why: Overlapping events on one timeline expose contradictions that single accounts hide; the timeline shows which statements corroborate each other. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Collect every account. 2) Sort all events by time into one sequence per person, covering every party. 3) Look for long empty stretches. 4) Test the sequence against physical limits such as travel distance and speed; test each alibi against it, not on its face. When: when several accounts conflict, one date decides whether a person could have been at a scene, or several suspects claim locations around a crime. Why: A single ordered schedule covering all parties exposes gaps and impossible movements. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Fix the last moment the victim is known alive. 2) Anchor the timeline on objective clocks or markers. 3) Convert each witness claim into a window. 4) Compare windows for gaps and overlaps. 5) Test every suspect's movements against that moment. When: Several witnesses give differing times, or a timeline for a death is being built. Why: Events cannot be placed without a known starting point; fixed references and windows reveal who could have acted when.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each witness's timed statements, such as a departure, a sighting or a late check. 2) Attach a source to each point and anchor it to events others heard or saw. 3) Lay the points in one sequence. 4) Examine the gaps between points, where the open questions lie. When: Several partial accounts or witness times must be joined into one ordered sequence.
- [procedure] 1) Date each event from documents or witnesses, such as letters, a rupture, a visit or the crime. 2) Order all events by date. 3) Test each claim against the sequence and mark the gaps between consecutive events. When: reconstructing a sequence of events. Why: Gaps show where time is unaccounted for.
- [procedure] 1) Verify each date against a reliable record. 2) Lay out the events in order. 3) Test whether the sequence explains the motive and the awkward timings. When: events are spread over years and their order is the key clue. Why: Verified dates make the chain trustworthy; testing against awkward timings exposes gaps.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness recount their day step by step in fixed order, from first contact through each later event. 2) Check each small decision against independent sources. 3) Repeat the account and compare each repetition with notes. When: A witness's day must be fixed in time, such as at the start of an interview. Why: Ordered recording with repetition exposes shifts and contradictions.
- [procedure] 1) Write a clear history of the event and state each claimed time or event. 2) For each claim, ask how it is known and name an independent witness who could confirm it. 3) Accept a time as strong only when an independent source confirms it. 4) Test whether stated durations are plausible. When: reconstructing a timeline from witness accounts or testimony. Why: Speakers may not be telling the truth, so each claim needs an independent check.
- [procedure] 1) Record each person's movements in time order, such as departures, appointments, returns and visits, with location and time. 2) Attach a witness to each leg. 3) Compare records, marking gaps where no one is accounted for and overlaps where two conflict. When: several people's movements must be reconciled or who was where during a time window must be reconstructed. Why: Gaps and overlaps reveal windows of opportunity and false alibis; ordered, witnessed legs expose gaps that scattered statements hide.
- [procedure] 1) Collect movement reports of the same person over the same hours from several staff or witnesses. 2) Anchor each report to appointments or schedules and place events in order. 3) Test each entry against the others, records, physical facts and stated plans, noting gaps. When: several people report the same person's movements, or alibis must be tested. Why: Several independent reports anchored to schedules are harder to distort than one account.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the time and place of each event in order, listing each person's movements with times. 2) Anchor the list to the estimated event time, even when times are approximate. 3) For each moment, mark who could have been at that place and compare each position with the timing of the threat. When: several events must be placed in order and the question is who could reach a place at a given time. Why: A shared time anchor brackets the event and shows who had access to it.
- [procedure] 1) Have an unremarked observer follow the suspect, close enough not to lose them but far enough to avoid notice. 2) Log each stop and meeting in order. 3) Check each stop against known facts. 4) Read gestures when words cannot be heard; leave blank stretches empty. When: a suspect's movements over hours must be tracked, or the subject may move or meet others.
- [procedure] 1) Store each witness time estimate as a range. 2) Collect the last confirmed events, such as a door fastened at a known hour, and add the medical window. 3) Add each range as a boundary. 4) Narrow the overlap to the smallest shared window. When: several sources give overlapping or differing times. Why: Overlapping ranges bound the true interval better than any single estimate.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor timed sightings, such as arrival, an overheard exchange, movement, entry and any later call, to clock times. 2) Order unclocked events using sounds such as locks, shots or calls for help. 3) Write each step in clock order and check each movement against the time it requires. When: multiple witnesses describe the sequence of an event. Why: Clocks and sounds give fixed points, and travel checks expose accounts that move faster than possible.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the present result or surviving physical evidence. 2) Ask which earlier event or act would produce it. 3) Link each earlier stage to the next by evidence such as a sale, visit, letter or death. 4) Repeat until the chain reaches the root cause, checking each step against independent facts. When: Tracing a present crime or situation back through its background, or the cause is hidden by later damage or change. Why: Working backward keeps each step tied to what it explains; surviving traces constrain what could have happened and expose gaps.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor the timeline to one reliable time reference or known event. 2) Work outward, estimating when other events happened from witnesses' sense of time, treating each event as its own link. 3) Mark each person's position at each moment and note gaps. When: Several accounts overlap in time and must be ordered, or when events happened is being reconstructed. Why: A fixed anchor lets uncertain times be placed relative to each other.
- [procedure] 1) Record each person's evening and morning as timed events, collecting each witness's times for the night. 2) Anchor them to fixed times and order arrivals and departures on one timeline. 3) Test overlaps: who saw whom in the same room at the same time. 4) Find gaps where a suspect is unaccounted for and check each time against an independent source. When: several people claim to have been somewhere at a particular hour or give times for the same night.
- [procedure] Have a witness narrate their actions in sequence, anchoring each step to the event, to place them in time.
- [procedure] 1) List each timed event a witness reports. 2) Record each time from an independent source, such as separate watches. 3) Compare the sources and mark disagreements. 4) Accept only events whose times agree. When: when a witness's timeline depends on clock readings. Why: independent sources expose errors that one clock hides.
- [procedure] 1) Fix a known starting event and its time. 2) Add each leg's duration in order: departure, travel, waiting, walking. 3) Sum to predict the arrival time. 4) Compare it with the recorded time. When: Checking whether a suspect's claimed movements fit a tight timeline.
- [procedure] 1) Record the time each event starts and ends. 2) Find scheduled fixed points such as transport arrivals. 3) Subtract the time needed for movement and actions to find the window available. 4) Check whether the plan fits within that window. When: When checking whether a person could have been at a place and acted within known times. Why: Fixed times define the window in which the events must have occurred.
- [procedure] 1) Fix anchor times, such as the last sighting and the discovery. 2) Compute the gap between them. 3) Compare the gap with how long a natural process takes. When: when a case hinges on whether a timeline is physically possible.
- [procedure] 1) List each dated interval, such as time held before burial or time since a space was last disturbed. 2) Treat each interval as a checkable claim. 3) Compare each claim against remains and reports. When: rebuilding when events happened.
- [procedure] 1) Assign a named watcher to the suspect. 2) Instruct the watcher to stay unseen and say nothing. 3) Also watch any companion who may carry the object or plan. 4) If the subject travels, place a hidden observer in the same transport.
- [procedure] 1) Fix a bounded interval from one witness's time. 2) Narrow it with a second witness's upper or lower limit. 3) Check each window against the witness's routine and what they could perceive. When: when accounts must be fitted together and the order of events is uncertain. Why: Overlapping bounded windows fix the sequence of events more reliably than any single account.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct a suspect's movements step by step using transport and sightings. 2) Turn each gap in the timeline into a question. 3) Answer each question with evidence. When: A suspect's movements must be verified. Why: Gaps in the timeline are the weak points that an investigator must close.
- [procedure] 1) Rebuild each suspect's known movements as a timeline. 2) Mark the gaps. 3) Look for a gap in which an unseen round trip could fit. When: When several suspects' movements are uncertain. Why: Unexplained gaps are where a hidden trip would have to occur.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the time with a reliable instrument reading. 2) Fix the position with a second reading. 3) Inventory equipment and supplies. 4) Separate what is intact from what is missing. 5) Record each result when it is found. When: reconstructing what happened after a disruption. Why: a recorded sequence of readings keeps later reconstruction reliable.
- [procedure] 1) Record when each absence begins. 2) Record when it ends. 3) Treat the two dates as the window in which the relevant event must fall. When: a person is away from the scene. Why: Absence dates fix when that person could not have acted.
- [procedure] 1) Take a fragment of the victim's words. 2) Infer the secret it implies. 3) Infer who had reason to hide it. 4) Turn each guess into a testable hypothesis. When: when the victim's last words are among the few clues.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness narrate one stage at a time: each place, action, meal or drink. 2) Record estimated durations and place events on a clock. 3) Mark blank periods explicitly. 4) Anchor each gap with outside points. When: a witness was impaired and the order of events determines who was where. Why: Fragmentary memory can still yield an ordered account if gaps are marked and anchored.
- [procedure] 1) List dated events in order. 2) List every treatment or action given, with its time. 3) Compare each witness account against both lists. 4) Flag each mismatch for investigation. When: the answer depends on order and timing. Why: Timing claims can only be checked against records.
- [procedure] 1) Establish whether the marked item exists. 2) Identify whose item it is. 3) Ask its owner to account for their whereabouts during the time window. When: A physical trace links an item to a suspect and the time of an event. Why: Each answer narrows the next question, so the inquiry stays on course.
- [procedure] 1) List each event with the time it occurred. 2) Order the events relative to one another. 3) Mark events that fall within the same short window. When: Several actors acted within a short period and their actions might be related. Why: Ordering events exposes overlaps and sequences that scattered accounts hide.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the earliest event that gave the plotters a chance to act. 2) Step forward, noting what information each step needed. 3) Check each step against what they could obtain. When: Explaining a plot or a criminal's sequence of actions. Why: Ordering the plan reveals which information each step depended on.
- [procedure] 1) Establish what the culprit wanted. 2) Read the setting for materials and ignition sources. 3) Order the events from the traces. 4) Weigh each alternative by probability and by the culprit's expectations. 5) Label the result as a theory. When: physical traces and a known motive together suggest a sequence of events.
- [procedure] 1) List every fixed date in the timeline. 2) Compare each against records from separate sources. 3) Find the entry that conflicts. 4) Treat that single conflict as the key clue. When: The mystery depends on who was where and when. Why: A single conflicting date often exposes the whole plan, while one isolated error may be only clerical.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor the sequence on checkable facts such as delays, arrival hours or missed connections. 2) Record durations as well as clock times. 3) Note who was awake or present to witness each event. 4) Fix a later known time to anchor the next sequence. When: A witness's account of timing must be checked against independent facts. Why: Checkable facts and durations create a sequence that can be tested against other accounts.
- [procedure] 1) Fix each event to a time source that others can confirm. 2) Lay out each person's day in order, including idle periods. 3) Check the stretch between each pair of anchors for gaps. 4) Compare each alibi with an independent account. When: the central question is who was where and when. Why: gaps and contradictions only show once every stretch is timed.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor the timeline to a known event. 2) Ask whether an interval exceeded a set duration. 3) Repeat with a larger duration to shrink the window. 4) Test each bracket against the next question. When: a suspect's presence during a crime window must be established. Why: each answer either survives or fails under the next question.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm the person's real identity through a search. 2) Match a date to a transport or passenger record. 3) Check photographs with people who dealt with them. 4) Assess background traits to judge motive. When: the case depends on identity or a past connection held only in records. Why: each record narrows identity, timing or motive.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the known start point of a transaction. 2) Count the procedural waiting days. 3) Estimate its status on a given day. 4) Compare it with other events during the waiting period. When: A suspect's financial or administrative action leaves a trail with known waiting times. Why: Counting from a known start yields a checkable timeline.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the last firm account, such as a departure time or stated plan. 2) Infer the likely next event. 3) Check it against independent witnesses. 4) Repeat until the sequence is complete. When: A suspect's movements are disputed and independent witnesses exist. Why: Turns intuition into a checkable sequence of times, places and people.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the timeline of the event. 2) Check whether the suspect had time to take the clue. 3) If not, look for another person present who could have taken it. When: When a clue seems to point at one suspect.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the timeline of the hours before the event. 2) Identify the window that matters most. 3) Test each candidate theory against that window. 4) Keep the theories that survive. When: When a hostile or emotional exchange was heard but not fully understood. Why: Timeline checks remove theories that conflict with known movements.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the routine that sets the window of opportunity. 2) Estimate time from physical signs. 3) Compare with known patterns. 4) Check each witness account against the routine. When: A case depends on who could be present at a specific hour. Why: Routines and physical signs constrain when events could have happened.
- [procedure] 1) Date each event from records or timestamps. 2) Infer elapsed time from physical signs of change. 3) Order events in sequence. 4) Check each interval against witnesses. When: when events, witnesses and physical signs must be placed in sequence. Why: Combining dated events with physical change gives a sequence no single source provides.
- [procedure] 1) List each account's stated times. 2) Overlay the accounts on one timeline. 3) Check whether each witness was placed to hear or see the event. 4) Mark which accounts conflict. When: several accounts must fit one clock.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each witness's remembered sounds and their approximate times. 2) Test what could be heard from each location with doors open or shut. 3) Move the event time to the sound that matches what was audible. 4) Check the witness's hearing before relying on her account. When: Witnesses give approximate times and a remembered sound might be the crime. Why: Audibility tests can show that a recalled sound was the event, not a later one.
- [procedure] 1) Record each event with its time and source. 2) Attach a margin to each approximate time. 3) Compare gaps and conflicts between events. 4) Check unusual timings against known routines. 5) Keep the timeline provisional and revise it as facts arrive. When: Several witnesses give times and events must be put in order. Why: Anchoring events and testing conflicts narrows the window for the act.
- [procedure] 1) Start from an undeniable physical fact. 2) Reason backward to the causes that could produce it. 3) Reason forward from motive. 4) Treat the point where both chains meet as the likely truth. When: The outcome is fixed but its cause is uncertain. Why: Agreement between a physical chain and a motive chain narrows the answer.
- [procedure] 1) Check each source's own record 2) Confirm that each person did what the cover story claims 3) Seek formal authority only after the checks are complete. When: an investigator must clear several sources before acting.
- [procedure] 1) Timestamp every event: letter posting, message relayed, instructions given, warning delivered. 2) Compare the gaps between events. 3) Use the speed of each hop to narrow who could have relayed information. When: A leak is suspected and events have clock times or dates. Why: Gaps between events reveal how information traveled and who had a direct channel.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the ordinary routine as a baseline. 2) Anchor events to shared time markers that others can check. 3) Record each attempt or event with its time. 4) Cross-check times against a second source. When: a suspect's account depends on times or relative positions. Why: deviations only mean something against a baseline and checked times.
- [procedure] 1) Collect times from everyone who handled the subject. 2) Mark each time as a last or first sighting. 3) Test the sequence for gaps and contradictions. When: Establishing when a person was last seen and where they went next. Why: Separate witnesses fix times more firmly than a single source.
- [procedure] Recount the whole account in order, fact by fact, to expose weak points in the reasoning. When: before presenting a solution.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the witness's last known contact to build a timeline. 2) Check each answer against earlier ones. 3) Ask what the witness expected when they claim ignorance. 4) Press on hesitations before moving on. When: interviewing a witness who may conceal information. Why: A structured timeline exposes gaps and contradictions.
- [procedure] 1) List each event with its time or duration. 2) Mark uncertain times as approximate. 3) Note what the witness could not see. 4) Order the events to rule sequences in or out. 5) Add the elapsed time since the event. When: building a timeline from witness accounts. Why: each step keeps the account accurate and bounded.
- [procedure] 1) Derive the shot's direction from the wound path. 2) Match that angle to a position in the layout that gives the needed height. 3) Test the resulting position against witness timing.
- [procedure] 1) Ask each witness who saw whom. 2) Ask what was said. 3) Ask how long it lasted. 4) Ask what happened next. 5) Test each answer against facts already known.
- [procedure] 1) Record the state of each observable object at every visit. 2) Compare consecutive states to find what changed. 3) Order the changes, anchoring them to any timed event heard. When: a witness returns to the same place at intervals. Why: changes between visits reveal when events happened.
- [procedure] 1) Start at the beginning of the case. 2) Present each clue in the order it was found. 3) Label conjectures as conjectures. 4) Confirm or drop each one with later facts. 5) Explain hidden details once their supporting facts are shown. When: The player has seen the clues and needs them connected.
- [procedure] 1) Record each trace's position and flow direction. 2) Use gravity to infer the orientation when each formed. 3) Order traces by which overlays which. 4) Check the sequence obeys physical rules. When: reconstructing what happened to a body. Why: traces give a timeline only once ordered and checked.
- [procedure] 1) Place each known event, including estimated times, on a timeline. 2) Check whether events line up in sequence. 3) Group facts under a plausible motive. 4) Record each reasoning step so it can be tested against each fact. When: When there are several dated facts and a suspected motive. Why: A timeline and motive organise facts into a testable explanation.
- [procedure] 1) List each observed trace. 2) Compare it with the person's usual routine. 3) Record contradictions without forcing a single story. 4) Delay conclusions until enough of the scene is examined. When: when several traces must be sorted against a known baseline. Why: a baseline shows which changes are meaningful.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness for exact times, the sequence of events and who said what. 2) Place each item on a timeline. 3) Anchor each item to a clock time and to independent physical facts. 4) Mark gaps and fill them from other sources.
- [procedure] 1) Lay the chart out as a shared reference and trace the claimed route on it. 2) Order dated records into a timeline. 3) Inventory physical traces left behind. 4) Check each trace and environmental variables such as tide against the sequence. When: when rebuilding a complex, spatial, time-dependent event. Why: combining map, dates and damage tests a claimed sequence from several sides.
- [procedure] 1) Write each step of a witness account in order with its time. 2) Check every step against the others for consistency. 3) Flag steps that rest on only one source. When: Reconstructing what happened from one or more accounts. Why: Each step can be tested against the rest, exposing gaps or contradictions.
- [procedure] 1) List ordinary records such as logbooks, consumed supplies and deliveries. 2) Date each record. 3) Cross-check each against the others and the witness accounts. 4) Note what the timeline does not prove. When: a case depends on where people were and when. Why: independent routine records corroborate or contradict witness accounts.
- [procedure] 1) Find an object or mark that does not fit the expected scene. 2) Match it to a likely source. 3) Rebuild the sequence step by step, checking that each action explains the next trace. When: Reconstructing events from small remnants. Why: Each step must be consistent with the physical record.
- [procedure] 1) Establish when writing or tearing happened. 2) Establish when cleaning happened. 3) Establish when scraps were disposed of. 4) Confirm the order with a witness account. When: Reconstructing what was discarded from a tidied scene.
- [procedure] 1) List each dated event with its source. 2) Anchor the sequence on fixed checkpoints such as a stopped watch, a departure time or a medical window. 3) Place each undated event in the only interval consistent with all constraints. 4) Test the derived sequence for contradictions. When: several events carry times from different sources that must be reconciled. Why: checkpoints give a fixed frame, and a derived time is credible only if it fits everything else.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the victim, household, evening, doctor's visit, morning discovery and inquest, in that order. 2) Note the gaps where the order breaks down. When: building a case from witness accounts.
- [procedure] 1) List every fixed point the timeline assumes. 2) Ask which one could be wrong. 3) Propose an alternative window that fits both accounts. 4) Check that window against witnesses before discarding the original timeline. When: Two testimonies seem to conflict about when an event happened.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the last firm sighting of each person. 2) Check each clock and routine against it. 3) Place medical and physical findings within the resulting window. When: the order of events matters and clocks disagree. Why: A fixed reference point anchors the rest.
- [procedure] 1) Fix an exact time for the key meeting. 2) Place each person's route around that time. 3) Check that each stage can be confirmed by someone. When: several people claim to be in different places. Why: A fixed time and a documented route make claims testable.
- [procedure] 1) Collect time-stamped statements from independent witnesses. 2) Convert medical estimates into time windows. 3) Check which events fit inside the windows. 4) Flag any event that fits none as unexplained and explain it separately. Why: Events that fit no window must not be forced into the timeline.
- [procedure] 1) Pin down the key time points: when a sound was heard, when the body was found, when death was estimated. 2) Mark the gaps between them. 3) Test each account against those gaps. When: Several accounts of who was where conflict. Why: Ordering events exposes which alibis clash and which can be set aside.
- [procedure] 1) Collect dated objects and records. 2) Set each event's possible window. 3) Compare expert estimates with the dates. 4) List rival explanations side by side against the timeline. When: several events must be placed in order. Why: the combined timeline tests which explanations fit.
- [procedure] 1) Let each witness give their account in their own words first. 2) Compare accounts covering the same movements. 3) Anchor memories to datable events. 4) Narrow a time window using several estimates. 5) Mark agreements, conflicts and silences. When: When a single witness's time is vague or several sources must form one sequence. Why: Unprompted accounts avoid shaping, and comparison exposes what is reliable.
- [procedure] 1) List every handoff of the item in order. 2) Time how long each holder had it alone. 3) Identify each person who could see each handoff. 4) Check each observer's sightline against the room layout. When: Investigating who could have tampered with an item or dose. Why: Summaries of access can hide short or wider windows, so each handoff must be timed and each observer identified.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor the timeline to the most regular daily events, such as meals and departures. 2) Have the witness recount the day in order without skipping stretches. 3) Mark the last confirmed sighting. 4) Mark the first unexplained gap. 5) Record each time as a range, not a single point. When: Reconstructing when a person left, where they went, and when they were due back. Why: Routine events give reliable timestamps, and ranges absorb recall drift.
- [procedure] 1) Track each NPC's location and actions over time. 2) Let the player compare claimed movements against that record. 3) Use mismatches to expose opportunity. When: Designing an investigation where a character's opportunity is tested. Why: Players can only check alibis if the world records where characters were.
- [procedure] 1) Identify each time's source and known error. 2) Correct each reading by its offset. 3) Anchor the sequence to a fixed reference time. 4) Check adjusted times against independent sightings. 5) Record every correction. When: several sources give disagreeing times, or cause and effect order matters. Why: Corrected, cross-checked times let someone else verify the chain.
- [procedure] 1) Attach a witness's vague date to a fixed public event. 2) Ask whether they accept that anchor as close enough. 3) Use the anchored date to order other events. When: The witness needs to place an event in time and the event is recent enough for a public anchor to exist. Why: Fixed events give vague memories a reference point that can be checked.
- [procedure] 1) Record each known event with its time. 2) Note which periods each observer covered. 3) Narrow the window to uncovered intervals. 4) Mark hours without cover for evidence from elsewhere. When: several people had chances to act at different times. Why: Coverage rules out action during watched periods, leaving a smaller window.
- [procedure] 1) Collect a record of each movement, such as tickets, luggage labels, routine patterns, and transport bookings. 2) Order the movements by time. 3) Check each time reading against the clock or source that produced it. 4) Build the sequence only from readings that pass the check. When: When a case depends on the order and timing of movements. Why: A sequence built on a single unverified time reading can point to a false conclusion.
- [procedure] 1) Build a timeline of events and object states. 2) Record each state change. 3) Design each false testimony detail as a visible inconsistency against the timeline. When: Authoring a mystery with testimony that players can check. Why: A timeline gives players a fixed reference to catch false details.
- [procedure] 1) List every timed event from testimony in order. 2) Overlay the events to narrow the window of the crime. 3) Use fixed departure or arrival times as boundaries. 4) Eliminate routes that conflict with the timeline. When: A time of death or crime is disputed and testimony gives times.
- [procedure] 1) Map each witness's position. 2) Check what that position could hear, given distance, stairs and closed doors. 3) Place each sound in sequence against the others. 4) Explain any unexpected silence. When: the sequence of events depends on what people heard. Why: Positions limit what each witness could have perceived.
- [procedure] 1) Mark known gaps and environmental conditions as fixed boundaries. 2) Place each act inside the window those boundaries allow. 3) Test each act against all windows in sequence, not from a preferred conclusion. When: several acts depend on timed conditions. Why: placing acts without testing them can hide conflicts between windows.
- [procedure] Build the timeline from fixed household routines, such as a set breakfast hour, a daily wake-up call, or a habitual walk, to serve as reference points. When: People follow predictable daily habits. Why: Routines give checkable times against which claims can be measured.
- [procedure] 1) Record and order by time every timed event, including handovers, notes, arrivals and independent arrival and departure records. 2) Mark each person's movements on the timeline. 3) Find unwatched windows, such as a visitor no one can place in a crowd. 4) For each window, list who could have been present and who has no confirmed location. When: when several people have overlapping, unverified movements, or when reconstructing who was where during an incident. Why: Unwatched windows are where an alibi or act can hide, so mapping them focuses the investigation; independent records anchor the timeline so gaps stand out.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the deadline or anchor time, such as a departure. 2) Estimate each leg's minimum duration, including any required wait, and set a maximum for each travel duration. 3) Subtract the legs from the deadline to find the latest start. 4) Subtract every delay from the remaining margin. When: when an event is tied to a fixed time and place, or several events must line up around a fixed time such as a train or rendezvous. Why: Counting backward reveals whether the plan is feasible and how much margin remains for delays.
- [procedure] 1) Recreate the original conditions: exact positions and props, temperature, locks, latches, who is present or asleep, and what could be heard. 2) Act out the disputed steps. 3) Time each step. When: when a claim about access, timing or audibility is disputed. Why: Reenactment is valid only when conditions match; small changes in positions or props can alter what is heard or seen.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor each witness account to an approximate time or nearby identifiable event, such as a noise, departure or arrival. 2) Place the accounts in order. 3) Check each against the others to test alibis and sightings. When: when a witness cannot state the exact time, or witness times are approximate and must be compared. Why: Relative order can be fixed from anchored events, and ordered anchors reveal which accounts agree and which conflict.
- [procedure] 1) Take the witness's account of activities. 2) Tie each activity to a set hour. 3) Test each timed point against an independent source. When: A witness gives a sequence of activities. Why: Anchoring each activity to a time makes gaps and contradictions visible.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the stages of an event in order. 2) Place each witness's claimed actions within those stages. 3) Compare the placements for gaps or mismatches. When: when several witnesses describe one evening or event. Why: Order exposes an account that does not fit.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the order of events, such as the crime first and the cleanup after. 2) Note which cleanup method was chosen at each step. 3) Use each step to narrow the set of possible culprits.
- [procedure] 1) List each person involved. 2) Fix each person's time and place using calls, memos, or guard logs as time-stamped witnesses. 3) Cross-check each claim against a first-hand source. When: A case depends on who was where between two known times. Why: Time-stamped records make alibis checkable.
- [procedure] 1) Log each event with its time. 2) Require the player to place events in order. 3) Accept an alibi as confirmed only after the order holds. When: Designing a timeline-based puzzle. Why: Ordering checks make alibis testable.
- [procedure] 1) Note the time of waking. 2) Estimate time lost to sleep. 3) Cross-check against routine events, such as a recurring noise at a fixed hour, to bound the sequence. When: reconstructing when events occurred during the night. Why: routine markers give independent anchors for uncertain time.
- [procedure] 1) Separate what the witness saw from what they heard reported. 2) Cross-check the fragments against other witnesses and dated records. 3) Order the events using outside references. When: Rebuilding a sequence of events from a partial witness account. Why: Independent references keep a timeline from relying on one unreliable memory.
- [procedure] 1) Record the time of each event from a clock or in-game timestamp. 2) Place each claimed urgency on that timeline. 3) Note any gap between claimed urgency and elapsed time. When: Testing a witness's sequence of events or claim of urgency. Why: A gap between a claimed emergency and the clock is a signal worth noting.
- [procedure] 1) Fix a clock time for each event. 2) Measure the intervals between events. 3) Compare each person's claimed whereabouts against the timeline. 4) Re-check the account wherever an interval is tight. When: Several statements about the same period must be checked against one another. Why: Short intervals often decide whether an alibi holds.
- [procedure] 1) Mark statements that lack dates. 2) Order them using other dated records. 3) Compare each witness's earlier and later accounts to find when and how they changed. When: undated testimony.
- [procedure] 1) Fix each dated entry as a point on the timeline. 2) Pair parallel records from different offices to see both sides of a dispute. 3) Check names against original documents for clerk errors. 4) Mark outcomes missing from the record. 5) Use a later account only after checking its author's position. When: a key outcome is missing from official records. Why: Dated fragments from several sources can be ordered into a sequence even when one outcome is unknown.
- [procedure] 1) List every accusation with its date. 2) Record its target and order. 3) Compare the sequence against who gained from each step. 4) Judge whether the pattern suggests planning. When: Testing whether accusers acted in concert. Why: Ordered timelines reveal planning that single events hide.
- [procedure] 1) Date the earlier connection. 2) Link it to the later outcome. 3) Note each figure's official position. 4) Note new authorities' arrival and first impressions. 5) Date the setup and start of any institution. 6) Record its proceedings and any later suppression. 7) Compare key figures' later views with earlier conduct. When: an outcome may have roots in earlier events. Why: ordering the stages shows how one stage enabled the next.
- [procedure] 1) Record a witness's claim with its time before any confirmation arrives. 2) Wait for independent news of the event. 3) Compare the claimed time with the confirmed event time. When: testing a witness's account of a distant or hidden event. Why: Early written records prevent a match being fitted after the fact.
- [procedure] 1) Record each threat, later harm and recovery with its date. 2) Order the events. 3) Check whether each recovery lines up with an event or with a natural cause. When: when reconstructing a sequence from testimony with uncertain dates. Why: Ordering events makes it possible to test which cause fits the timing.
- [procedure] 1) Measure how much flows in a set time. 2) Adjust the flow restriction until the target duration matches. 3) Repeat calibration before relying on the device. When: a timer depends on a fixed flow rate. Why: the flow must match the intended duration.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the source of the materials. 2) Infer the tools from the cut and residue marks. 3) Note any gaps where the maker resorted to a fallback. 4) Read placement and disguise to infer state of mind. 5) Record null results. 6) Weigh competing readings by likelihood. When: A physical artifact is the main clue and its making can be reconstructed. Why: Working backward from the object to its production yields evidence about the maker, their tools and their conditions.
- [procedure] 1) List the chain of events that had to follow the event in question. 2) Note each delay between them. 3) Subtract the delays backward from the moment of the later event. 4) Use the result to fix when the event occurred. When: Establishing the time of an event from later records. Why: Each required step bounds how early the event could have happened.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor each event to a shared public clock reference, such as a striking clock. 2) Place events relative to the last recognised strike. 3) Order arrivals and departures from those fixed points. When: when witness times are vague and a shared public clock is available. Why: Shared references let separate accounts be combined into one sequence.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the record the claim implies, such as a payment date tied to a scheduled event. 2) Check the date against that record. 3) Confirm with a source separate from the claimant. When: when a suspect or witness gives a timed account. Why: Records the claimant does not control give an independent test of the claim.
- [procedure] 1) Record when each character was known to be in each place. 2) Check whether each event was possible given those positions. 3) Note which knowledge each character had at each time. When: Testing who could have been present at an event. Why: Timelines built on incomplete knowledge of movements can mislead.
- [procedure] 1) List each outflow with its recipient and amount. 2) Sum the list. 3) Compare the total with cash still held. 4) Use any difference to check or infer missing payments. When: A timeline depends on many small transactions that are easy to forget one by one. Why: Summing recalled payments against remaining cash gives a rough cross-check on memory.
- [procedure] 1) List departure and arrival times for each leg of the journey. 2) Note every stop and its time. 3) Estimate the arrival at the final location. 4) Confirm the hour with an independent source. When: when reconstructing a person's movements or an alibi. Why: Chained times expose impossibilities, and an independent source confirms the reconstruction.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the central date from an external record. 2) Link any false statement to that date to test whether it was prepared in advance. 3) Use a stated hour and place to narrow the window. 4) Treat absence of later sightings as evidence. 5) Label the working conclusion as belief until proven. When: Several dated facts can be checked against each other. Why: Records outside any one memory make a timeline testable and resistant to a single witness's errors.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor each event to a routine such as meals, shift changes or timetables. 2) Check any clock that may be unreliable before use. 3) Mark spans with no sighting as windows to explain. 4) Check each source against the others before accepting it. When: A claim about the time of an event is needed to test an alibi or movement. Why: Routines give more trustworthy anchors than estimated hours, and unreliable clocks can mislead the whole reconstruction.
- [procedure] 1) Log each dated, specific sighting. 2) Look for a repeated pattern. 3) Form a candidate explanation that fits the pattern. When: Investigators must reconstruct an unexplained behaviour. Why: Dated repetition turns scattered observations into evidence.
- [procedure] 1) List the stated schedule. 2) Gather independent facts such as letters, sightings and hiding places. 3) Order them to reveal the hidden sequence. 4) Check each step against a witness or trace. When: Reconstructing a suspect's true whereabouts. Why: Independent facts reveal gaps that a stated schedule conceals.
- [procedure] 1) Fix anchor times from each account. 2) Record observation conditions such as light and distance. 3) Compare routes and streets. 4) Check whether the parties saw each other. 5) Test each admission for new timeline gaps.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor events to marked times. 2) Fix each person's state, awake or asleep, and location. 3) Compare witnesses' accounts for conflicts. 4) Discount sensory reports made in fear, fatigue or poor visibility. When: when several people were present at different points in a night. Why: Timed anchors and fixed positions make alibis checkable.
- [procedure] 1) Fix when each person arrived, was last seen, and was heard. 2) Identify the last confirmed presence of the victim. 3) Check each account against independent facts. 4) Note gaps where attention was distracted. When: Multi-witness cases with a time-bounded window. Why: A timeline anchored to fixed points lets each account be tested.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor the timeline with fixed events such as telegrams, departures, deaths, and clock times. 2) Measure distances and travel times between places. 3) Compare arrival and departure times across the whole route. When: Several people give times for overlapping events. Why: Fixed events and measured travel make claimed presence testable.
- [procedure] 1) Note timed events such as clock strikes and recurring sounds. 2) Check physical markers, such as seals, each morning. 3) Compare markers across rooms to see whether a disturbance stayed in one place. 4) Check the timeline against the markers before trusting any account, including your own. When: Deciding whether an intruder was human. Why: Physical markers that persist provide an objective check on recollection.
- [procedure] 1) Start with the earliest documented event. 2) Add each dated item in order, recording its author, date and claim. 3) Note the gaps between items, since short and long intervals show urgency and hesitation. 4) Test later claims against the line. 5) Mark missing dates rather than filling them with assumptions.
