When: when a case depends on who knew what and when. Why: A single ordered line exposes contradictions and gaps that scattered records hide.
- [procedure] 1) Record each person's movements as times and places. 2) Overlay them on the moment of the event. 3) Mark the windows when each person could have reached the object or room. When: Several people claim different whereabouts and the event depends on who could reach a place. Why: A time-ordered record exposes who could have acted and when an object could have been moved.
- [procedure] 1) Normalize all event dates to one calendar, adjusting for time-zone or date-line offsets. 2) Place events from separate sources on one timeline. 3) Look for several independent matches within a window. When: When clues from several locations must be compared by date. Why: A date recorded on different sides of a date line can be a day off, so unnormalized dates create or hide coincidences.
- [procedure] 1) Fix a few checkable clock times for key events, such as arrival, departure, a celestial cue and a deadline. 2) Leave other times vague. 3) Use the anchors to verify the sequence of events. When: Timed ordeal or investigation where an alibi window or deadline matters. Why: Few firm times keep the sequence verifiable without dulling the scene.
- [metric] Fix a narrow event window from two bounds: a physical estimate of when the event happened, and the last confirmed sighting of the person alive. When: early in an investigation. Why: Two bounds turn vague timing into a testable interval.
- [tradeoff] Official or public records, such as a published timetable, can fix the timeline accounts must match, yet official times can be hasty, so check them against physical signs. When: accounts disagree about timing, or when reviewing an official report. Why: Public records are independent of witnesses, but official conclusions may not match physical evidence.
- [tradeoff] If the item was already owned, tracing it to its owner is less likely; if the method came first, the item must be sought and the search leaves traces.
- [pitfall] A timeline built on one party's account, whether suspect's or accuser's, distorts events or can be wrong; each step needs corroboration from witnesses who can confirm it. Why: Other accounts can contradict or confirm that party's version.
- [pitfall] A timeline resting on one disputed or unconfirmed hour or date fails, since every event placed relative to it inherits the error; ask how a claimed hour was established. Why: All other placements inherit the error; unverified numbers can lock an argument onto a false time.
- [pitfall] A timeline is only as good as its dates: check every date against its source, and treat a mismatch as an argument, not proof, until confirmed. When: using a date mismatch to challenge a story. Why: Calendar dates are often misremembered, and unverified dates can be disputed.
- [pitfall] A witness can be accurate about events yet wrong about intervals and finish times, so confirm start and end points with observers before using a time reckoning. When: a timeline relies on witness recollection of durations. Why: Recalled events are often correct while recalled gaps and finish times are not.
- [pitfall] Confusing the order of events can make chance overlap look like cause. Why: a cause must precede its effect, so a wrong order creates false links.
- [pitfall] A timeline built on one household's account inherits every gap in that household's knowledge, so it needs outside corroboration. When: Building a timeline from one group's testimony. Why: One source carries its own blind spots.
- [pitfall] A witness's sense of time can be shifted by clocks, a late bell or a suggested remark, so timed alibis based on memory are weak.
- [pitfall] A witness who knows that times matter to investigators may shape their time reports rather than give them neutrally.
- [pitfall] Calculating backwards from remembered intervals fails when those intervals were never logged, and one missed entry can break an otherwise sound chain. When: Reconstructing dates from memory or sparse logs. Why: Unrecorded intervals have no reliable value to calculate from.
- [pitfall] Fragments taken out of order can support several readings, so a partial exchange can be misinterpreted. When: a listener assembles partial dialogue. Why: sequence is needed to fix meaning.
- [pitfall] A witness's time estimate loses weight when conditions such as fog are admitted to have allowed faster travel than claimed.
- [pitfall] Adding approximate durations together accumulates error, so the total can drift far from the true span. When: summing several estimated intervals. Why: each approximation carries its own error.
- [pitfall] Reading intent backward from the outcome can make coincidences look like a deliberate plan.
- [pitfall] Assuming that an arrest or other event caused a recovery, without testing other causes, can attribute healing to the wrong factor. When: when suffering stops around the time of a notable event. Why: Recoveries often coincide with events for reasons unrelated to them.
- [pitfall] Timeline puzzles where the player aligns ages, intervals and places from several testimonies should be solvable, with one contradiction that the player can find. When: When designing investigative puzzles from multiple testimonies. Why: A puzzle with no findable contradiction, or with several, gives the player no clear path to a solution.
- [pitfall] A single transit record shows only a route someone travelled, and can push a search toward the wrong place. When: when a record is used to locate someone.
- [pitfall] Events following each other show only time order, not cause; a threat followed by harm needs checks of what else happened in that period.
- [pitfall] A character's stated timing can be wrong, and a mismatch against a clock or log becomes a checkable clue rather than a plot error. When: when an alibi or timing claim is given. Why: Stated times can be checked against recorded events.
- [pitfall] A person woken from sleep has an unreliable sense of timing, and sounds seem louder or closer than they were. When: when a witness was asleep before the event. Why: Sleep disrupts time perception and sound localization.
- [pitfall] Time estimates made under stress are unreliable, even when counted with a steady rhythm. When: when a person is frightened or under strain. Why: stress distorts perceived elapsed time.
- [pitfall] A reconstruction can only approximate original conditions, so its results carry some uncertainty. When: when a scene cannot be fully recreated. Why: small differences in conditions can change timing results.
- [pitfall] A timeline is only as reliable as its inputs; if clocks cannot be read in the dark, the plan's timings become unusable. When: Time readings depend on poor light.
- [pitfall] Uncertainty about the hour of death can itself be exploited by a defence to challenge the timeline. When: When the time of death is only approximately known. Why: A wide window gives an opponent room to dispute the prosecution's timeline.
- [pitfall] A timeline built on one record can break if that record is incomplete or partly preserved. When: The central date rests on one document or one witness's word. Why: A single source has no check if it is damaged or misremembered.
- [pitfall] A timeline built from one account can look exact while resting on guesses. Why: Precise times in one telling hide the approximation underneath.
- [pitfall] A walk or car journey can take far longer than expected, so claimed travel times must be checked against realistic durations. When: A suspect's account relies on a quick journey. Why: Travel delays are easy to underestimate.
- [fact] A time-of-death estimate is a range, not a precise moment, so it should be treated as a window and not as an exact time. When: using an examiner's or any time-of-death estimate. Why: Post-mortem timing depends on conditions, so it has limits.
- [fact] A timeline removes hiding places but alone forces no confession and settles no guilt, since the same timeline can support opposite prosecution and defence conclusions. When: relying on a timeline to extract a confession or prove guilt. Why: Pressure from facts does not compel admission of guilt.
- [fact] A reliable timeline combines the sequence of events, sounds, movements and physical remains.
- [fact] A case story can open with the commission before the crime's facts, so the audience meets the frame before the details.
- [fact] Where an object is found and where it is later delivered are fixed points that constrain the timeline and must both be checked.
- [fact] Timeline reasoning about messages weakens when messages can travel by unrecorded means. When: Messages may be sent by unrecorded means.
- [fact] Time of death is hard to fix when a body is found after prolonged exposure, such as cold, and the medical estimate may span many hours. When: When a body is found long after death or in harsh conditions. Why: Environmental effects alter decay, so the estimated window can be wide.
- [fact] A reconstructed timeline shows what was possible, not what happened, so physical evidence is still needed to confirm it.

## alibi definition and design
- [model] A reconstructed absence, such as a disguise followed by an exit and a false alibi, can be set out as a chain of linked facts. When: when a disguised or staged absence can be listed as ordered actions. Why: Ordering the actions makes each dependency between steps visible.
- [model] Prepared answers can be modelled as dialogue branches where questions outside the script receive deflecting responses, letting a clever player test the performer. When: When designing dialogue for a deceptive NPC. Why: Off-script questions expose the limits of prepared content.
- [model] Grade each alibi into one of four tiers: witnessed with a specific time, witnessed but vague, self-reported only, or purely negative with no one seeing the suspect. When: deciding whether a suspect stays in the case. Why: corroboration varies in strength.
- [definition] An alibi places a suspect elsewhere at the critical time; it excludes only if timed overlapping accounts cover that moment and a third party or record confirms them. When: A suspect's movements at the critical hour are disputed. (x2)
- [definition] An alibi is a claim about where a person was at a given time, and it needs independent proof to carry weight.
- [definition] An alibi places a suspect elsewhere at the critical time, and can be broken by showing that someone else could have occupied that place.
- [definition] An alibi is a claim that a person was elsewhere during a window of time, and it must be judged against how long the act takes.
- [definition] A companionship alibi is a claim that a witness stayed with the suspect throughout a period. It rules the suspect out only for events that fall within that exact period. When: a single companion vouches for a suspect.
- [definition] An opportunity window is the span of seconds during which one person is alone with an item and could tamper with it, measured between handoffs.
- [definition] An alibi is an account placing a suspect elsewhere during a critical time window; it is only as strong as its corroboration and must be checked before counting as evidence.
- [mechanism] Vouching passes trust from a trusted local to a newcomer without proof, forming a chain the player can trace to its source to judge reliability. When: A stranger's cover is backed by someone locals trust, or characters who have not met need trust built. Why: Trust passes from the vouching person to the newcomer; traceable vouching lets the player judge reliability.
- [mechanism] Official obstacles such as hearings, bail and a magistrate extend the wait and keep the character from acting. When: A reveal must be delayed.
- [mechanism] An NPC's refusal can be a state that other actions change, and an unprompted remark can open a new lead.
- [mechanism] A continuous alibi removes its suspect and any theory requiring their presence, closing the line of inquiry that pointed to them. When: An alibi is verified by independent sources. Why: A proven position in the crime window rules out the act within that window.
- [mechanism] One person can pose as two witnesses who are never seen together, each seeming to vouch for the other's absence, so non-overlapping sightings hide a single actor. When: A suspect's alibi depends on sightings that never overlap. Why: Non-overlapping sightings hide a single actor.
- [mechanism] Model witness NPCs to give partial, hedged statements with gaps the player fills from world state, so inconsistencies become discoverable and the player must weigh what they hear.
- [mechanism] If an observer is alert, a suspect's movement out of a single-exit room is limited; if the observer is inattentive, the alibi collapses. When: When an alibi depends on a guard stationed at a room's only door. Why: The observer's attention is the only barrier to leaving.
- [mechanism] When several independent informants describe the same routine, confidence in that routine rises.
- [mechanism] An arranged alibi works as insurance: if the act goes wrong, the culprit can answer any accusation with a powerful witness. Why: the witness's standing serves as the defence.
- [mechanism] Fog and slow signals make positions hard to confirm, so a person can move between hidden sections of a journey unseen and a claimed route can conceal a different one. Why: poor visibility weakens the link between a stated position and actual movement.
- [mechanism] An NPC's claim such as hearing nothing can be tied to a bell or door the player can test, making dialogue checkable against the world. When: When designing NPC dialogue that players should verify.
- [mechanism] Incapacitating a guard removes the one observer of a route, opening a path that was previously watched. When: A guarded passage whose watcher is drugged, distracted or absent. Why: Without a watcher, the route's only check is gone.
- [mechanism] An accuser who claims the accused acted through an invisible agent makes the alibi irrelevant, since no record of absence can refute the claim. When: A suspect has a strong alibi. Why: An unobservable method cannot be disproved by location evidence.
- [mechanism] Praise for a witness's honesty from an opposing party adds weight beyond the witness's own words. When: A dispute involves a record of the witness's honesty. Why: Such praise is costly to give against one's own interest, so it signals credibility.
- [mechanism] NPC schedules and night logs let players assemble a timeline from witness entries and find where the entries break.
- [mechanism] An NPC claiming an official role can be checked by a second NPC or an in-game record; a mismatch can trigger a hostile reveal. When: Designing NPCs whose claims the player may test. Why: Cross-checking exposes the lie and changes the NPC's behaviour.
- [mechanism] Let an NPC's written report be contradicted by the player's own memory log, so the player must decide whom to believe. When: Designing conflicting testimony between an NPC report and player knowledge. Why: Conflicts force the player to weigh sources rather than accept one passively.
- [mechanism] An alibi resting on people who did not notice the suspect is hard to disprove, but becomes fragile once someone starts searching for the suspect.
- [mechanism] Let companion characters unintentionally reveal clues about other NPCs' motives and temperament through idle chatter, opening paths the player can exploit.
- [mechanism] An alibi can be a recorded sound played by a timed device, such as a voice or scream, that a witness takes for a living person's presence. Why: Witnesses trust what they hear, so an audio trick can fake a person.
- [behavior] A suspect who refuses a private interview and insists on witnesses limits the questioner's pressure, because others present make direct pressing costly. When: when a suspect controls the setting. Why: observers constrain what the questioner can press.
- [behavior] A witness who depends on a party for position or income tends to shape testimony in that party's favour. When: Weighing a witness's evidence. Why: Dependence gives a reason to be careful with the truth.
- [behavior] A timing that does not match expectation may be dismissed without comment, which signals that it did not fit the theory. When: A reenactment's measured time conflicts with the working theory. Why: Investigators often set aside results that do not support their view.
- [behavior] Colleagues may accept a confident but unproven claim provisionally because they trust its source. When: An investigator asserts a conclusion before proof is found. Why: Trust in the speaker lowers the demand for evidence.
- [behavior] A player with no prepared lines for a cover stalls at the first question, which exposes the pretext. When: improvising a pretext. Why: no rehearsed lines exist to answer the first challenge.
- [behavior] A reply showing the witness already checked for a possibility is a tell that they had considered it before the question was asked. When: A witness answers a question about a possibility they should not yet have considered.
- [behavior] A suspect who explains a visitor before being asked is perceived as anticipating suspicion and trying to pre-empt it. When: A suspect volunteers an explanation no one requested. Why: An unprompted account signals the suspect saw a risk of being suspected.
- [behavior] After disturbed sleep, people cannot always separate what their imagination produced from what they actually observed. When: a witness recalls events after disturbed sleep or strong fear. Why: Dream images can blend into waking memory.
- [behavior] Prisoners' statements can shift to match what questioners already expect to hear, so the examiners' hypothesis shapes the testimony they produce. When: questioning follows a hypothesis set by the investigators.
- [behavior] When a jury cannot agree, the accused may be held in custody and the jurors kept ready, pending further direction from a higher authority. When: when a jury deadlocks on a capital case. Why: a hung verdict cannot be entered, so the case is held open for a higher decision.
- [behavior] A suspect with excuses prepared in advance meets each accusation with a ready defence, so direct challenges lose force.
- [behavior] Players catch an unreliable claimant when the claimant's behavior contradicts the story, such as never acting on a supposed reward. When: A source claims value or action that its conduct does not reflect. Why: Inconsistency between words and deeds signals doubtful testimony.
- [behavior] People misjudge elapsed time and distance, often underestimating or overestimating how long an action took, so recalled timelines are unreliable. When: witnesses recall time after a social event or walk. Why: memory of duration is distorted.
- [behavior] A culprit can stage sightings of the victim at a late hour to place death after the suspect was already elsewhere, and can have witnesses confirm a fabricated timeline. When: When a suspect's alibi depends on witnesses placing the victim alive later. Why: Witness testimony can be shaped to build a false timeline that clears the suspect.
- [behavior] An absence on a key night looks suspicious to observers even when it has no link to the event. When: a character is missing at a moment the audience expects them. Why: absence on a critical moment is read as meaningful.
- [behavior] Witnesses often forget brief separations from a group, so a short gap can vanish from memory unless checked against other sources. When: Reconstructing group movements from recollection. Why: Short absences do not seem significant when remembered.
- [rule] Check an NPC's alibi against a second NPC's independent statement, and show both to the player so discrepancies point toward the true source before judgement. When: Designing witness-checking gameplay or NPC testimony. Why: Two sources let the player judge. (x2)
- [rule] Do not accept an alibi resting only on the suspect's word, or on relatives' or a spouse's or close associate's testimony; seek a second, independent source.
- [rule] Treat the whole chain as sound only when every link holds; one unverified step leaves the whole reconstruction open. When: when judging a reconstructed alibi. Why: A chain holds only as strongly as its weakest link.
- [rule] Weight a vouching witness's alibi by their own reliability and independence from the suspect; a spouse's vouching counts for less than an independent witness, so confirmation needs a second source. When: when one witness vouches for another's whereabouts, or when designing alibi characters. Why: A vouching witness can share the same interest or bias, so their support adds limited weight.
- [rule] Check times recalled from memory against dated or logged records before relying on them, since a witness's sense of elapsed time can be badly wrong. When: a timeline relies on remembered times. Why: Memory of clock times is error-prone and drifts.
- [rule] An alibi resting on one person's word stays unproven, especially if that witness has a motive or could be removed. Seek an independent record before accepting it. When: an alibi depends on a single account. Why: Accepting an unverified alibi leaves the case open to a false claim; a compromised witness cannot anchor an alibi.
- [rule] Accept an alibi provisionally and mark a weak one unverified rather than discarding it, testing it against an independent source before relying on it. When: an alibi lacks independent confirmation.
- [rule] Corroborate an alibi with two or more independent sources, such as a guard log, door state, footprint or staff member, not the alibi holder's own account. When: when verifying a whereabouts claim. Why: One source can be wrong or controlled, and independent confirmation can refute a story that fits what listeners want to hear.
- [rule] Write NPC dialogue claims about times, places and objects that players can check against inventory items, records or room state, so contradictions become discoveries. When: when writing NPC or witness dialogue in a mystery. Why: Checkable claims reward attentive players and let them catch contradictions between witnesses.
- [rule] Give NPC alibis concrete, checkable details such as which hand was used, work in progress, a meal, weather or passing train that players can cross-check against other records. When: when writing an NPC's account of their whereabouts. Why: Checkable details let players test claims instead of simply accepting them.
- [rule] A usable NPC alibi names a specific time and place and has at least one independent source, from someone present, that can confirm or contradict it. When: when judging or authoring an NPC's whereabouts claim. Why: Vague claims give no timeline and are easily broken; checkable times let players test claims.
- [rule] Build NPC alibis from in-world records or world conditions the player must find and check, such as tickets, guard logs, storm logs, closed gates or patrol schedules, not dialogue alone. When: when designing alibi puzzles.
- [rule] Schedule NPC routines with hourly locations and travel times so players can test alibis against the in-game clock and find the gap in a suspect's route. When: when designing NPC routines or timed alibis for a mystery. Why: Schedules give the player a clock to check claims against; a gap in one path can point to the true culprit.
- [rule] Use travel times between map areas to set how much time a suspect actually has, so whether they could reach the scene in time can be checked. When: when designing movement and alibi windows. Why: Travel durations convert stated times into a measurable window of opportunity.
- [rule] Do not build a case on a single timing inference or small detail; confirm it with other corroborating evidence first. When: an interval is central to a case, or a small detail is used as a clue.
- [rule] A suspect's concealment or refusal to account for their time does not prove guilt, but the gap stays open until explained or verified. When: a suspect hides where they were or declines to say how time was spent. Why: Concealment damages credibility without establishing the crime.
- [rule] Give each NPC informant or witness a reliability value tied to motive, since one with reason to hide their own part or exaggerate is less reliable. When: NPCs supply information or testimony to the player. Why: Motive affects whether an account is complete and honest.
- [rule] Make each NPC explanation, including false ones, checkable against a second or physical source so players can tell a true recollection from a convenient one. When: when NPCs explain events.
- [rule] Place alibi witnesses in the world and let players check a claim by visiting them in turn, showing any gap no one can explain. When: designing alibi checks or verification in a game. Why: Verification becomes an active player task.
- [rule] Give an NPC's alibi or claim to have heard, or heard nothing, a positional basis the player can verify, such as distance, walls, doors or sound propagation. When: when an NPC offers an alibi or says they heard, or heard nothing. Why: The player needs a checkable sightline or earshot to judge the claim.
- [rule] Model alibis as traversable routes with real geometry, including exits like balconies, so players can test whether a sleeping or stationary suspect could have left unseen. When: when a character's whereabouts are disputed or claimed asleep or stationary. Why: Players can only check an alibi if the layout and paths exist; unobserved exits make stationary claims unverifiable.
- [rule] When a companion or NPC offers an alibi, make the player verify it against the named witness or a transport or door-log record before it counts as established. When: designing an NPC-provided alibi. Why: A checkable alibi gives the player a verifiable way to test it.
- [rule] Give an NPC who matches a rumored description and sits near the crime a checkable alibi.
- [rule] Plant two NPC accounts of one event that conflict on a name, direction or time the player can verify elsewhere. When: Designing contradictory testimony for players to resolve. Why: Checkable mismatches let players detect the liar through evidence.
- [rule] A companion can change a line of dialogue to hint at knowledge before the full information is available to the player.
- [rule] A companion can withhold a location or event until a trigger, using dialogue lines that carry two meanings depending on what the player later learns.
- [rule] Before a risky meeting, check a third party who may share the key fact, since a secret known only to two people is hard to confirm. When: before confronting a person who holds a key fact.
- [rule] Treat pursuers' and witnesses' descriptions as provisional, since they may be wrong and are often corrected in conversation. When: Relying on a description to identify someone. Why: Observers can be mistaken.
- [rule] Let a player's alibi check rest on dated records they can rebuild, leaving one gap that a single witness can fill.
- [rule] Give each NPC time-stamped statements covering different windows, so the player must find the moment where no statement overlaps the critical event. When: designing a timeline puzzle. Why: An uncovered gap becomes the clue the player has to locate.
- [rule] When a private clock is disputed, establish when it was last set, since a recent reset limits how far it could have drifted. When: a witness's timing depends on a private clock.
- [rule] Let a suspect narrate the crime in dialogue while the player verifies each claim against objects collected earlier in the game.
- [rule] Let a companion character give incomplete reports, so the player discovers what was missed by examining the scene and comparing it with the companion's account. When: when designing companion dialogue in a game investigation. Why: the gap gives the player a reason to examine the environment.
- [rule] An alibi that survives a timing check is stronger than one that was never tested.
- [rule] Leave part of the evidence for official investigators to find and keep part for one's own analysis. When: Collecting evidence that others will also examine. Why: Shared discovery supports the official record while retained material allows independent checking.
- [rule] A person proven elsewhere during the crime window could not have carried out the act then, but knowledge or access may still link them. When: when testing an alibi.
- [rule] Make an NPC's cover story checkable against records the player can search, such as shop logs, journals or book collections. When: designing NPC alibis or explanations.
- [rule] When a pretext is weak, invent a plausible reason for unusual behaviour, such as slow progress or frequent stops, before it is questioned.
- [rule] Let a companion keep a secret that is revealed only when the player's trust reaches a set threshold.
- [rule] Do not rely on a silhouette alibi where a clear view of the face is possible, and state the similar profile to the player before any reveal. When: Designing a witness-based alibi or disguise reveal. Why: A visible face defeats the substitution, and an unstated profile makes the reveal feel unfair.
- [rule] Make a physical mark, such as a scar or tattoo, a checkable identity feature that players must confirm before trusting an NPC.
- [rule] Keep a character-based conclusion provisional until the question of who acted has been answered by evidence.
- [rule] Treat the moment a poison is given, the moment it takes effect and the moment of death as three separate events, each opening a different window of suspects. When: when establishing when a poisoning could have happened. Why: Assuming they coincide leads to wrong suspect windows.
- [rule] Let a companion character reach the solution from the same material, giving the player a fair chance to match it. When: A companion accompanies the player through an investigation. Why: Shared material lets the player verify the companion's conclusion.
- [rule] Do not treat an alibi as broken when independent physical evidence already fixes the time of the event. When: When physical evidence and an alibi conflict. Why: Fixed physical evidence can outweigh an uncertain witness account.
- [rule] Check whether a document places the suspect himself, or only a vehicle, a driver or paperwork; a document may prove one without the others. When: Evaluating a documented alibi.
- [rule] Build a timeline table for a level with each NPC's movements and sounds, and mark the alibi windows the player can check. When: designing a multi-NPC mystery. Why: visible time windows let players reason about who could have acted.
- [rule] Check for a mechanical cause before reading a habit into a placement; a catch that snags fabric can force one orientation.
- [rule] An alibi exculpates only if the facts it relies on come before the disputed act; a cover that falls after the event does not help. When: Evaluating a suspect's cover story for a specific act. Why: Presence after the act says nothing about presence during it.
- [rule] Do not accept an alibi because the person is respectable or high-ranking; social status does not verify a claim. When: Assessing an alibi from a trusted or prominent person. Why: Reputation is not evidence of where someone was.
- [rule] Let players build an alibi timeline from scheduled NPC routines, and flag any claimed emergency that does not match the in-game clock. When: Designing alibi and timeline puzzles.
- [rule] Include a suspect's physical capacity in the timeline, since an injury or lack of transport can make reaching a distant scene impossible regardless of intent. When: when a suspect is accused of travelling to a scene. Why: presence requires the ability to get there.
- [rule] Make alibis depend on physical access, such as locked doors and window size, rather than on claims alone. When: designing alibi checks in a game. Why: physical constraints can be tested while claims cannot.
- [rule] Log timed events and NPC movements so the player can reconstruct who was where, and record a player's detour as a stall that can change what guards know. When: a world tracks player movements over time. Why: logged history supports reconstruction and consequences.
- [rule] Give NPC statements a reliability value that drops when the NPC is impaired or coached, so the player must cross-check those claims against scene evidence. When: when designing NPCs who may give partial or misleading answers. Why: it lets the player treat impaired testimony as leads.
- [rule] Attach a clear gain or loss to each suspect so players can test motive rather than react to mood.
- [rule] Generate murderers with explicit financial motives, such as an inheritance, an insurance payout or a debt that changes on death, so players can verify them.
- [rule] Use burning candles, half-melted torches, drying puddles and settled dust as ambient clocks so players can judge how long an NPC has been present. When: Designing rooms where NPC timelines matter.
- [rule] Split a backstory clue across two documents, such as a letter and an obscure journal, so the player must combine them and check dates to solve it. When: designing a hidden backstory revealed through documents. Why: Combining sources and checking dates is what turns a puzzling phrase into a resolved fact.
- [rule] Place a deed in one location and its counter-deed in another, so players must visit both to learn the real terms. When: designing a land or ownership dispute in a game world. Why: The true terms appear only when both documents are found.
- [rule] Have a companion question an NPC's vagueness and respond to it in dialogue, so the evasion is visible to the player.
- [rule] Let the player unlock pre-written excuses as they gather evidence, so cover stories grow with the investigation.
- [rule] Use a victim's hidden favours and past dealings to seed extra motives and widen the suspect pool. When: generating a murder scenario. Why: the victim's history creates new interested parties.
- [rule] Track two evidence tiers per suspect, suspicion from circumstance and proof from direct observation, and gate arrest or accusation on the proof tier.
- [rule] Build a suspect web listing each NPC's room access and how long each has known the target, so the player can see which questions to ask. When: Designing a mystery with several NPCs who had access. Why: Access and familiarity guide which accounts the player can test.
- [rule] Let an NPC's alibi be an absence from a location, which the player can verify by checking that location's logs.
- [rule] Score each alibi by its number of independent witnesses and timestamps, and reveal partial results rather than a clean yes or no. Why: graded results match partial evidence.
- [rule] In a torn-document puzzle, use the gap size as a constraint on the missing text so the answer stays bounded. When: when designing a fragment-based clue. Why: Constraints make the puzzle solvable and checkable.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses schedules and departure dates, so the player must reach them before they leave the map.
- [rule] Build a verification path where the decoy's alibi can be tested, so it clears them only when the player goes looking.
- [rule] Define several opportunity windows across the in-game day so that players must identify which window fits the event. When: when designing a case with multiple possible times. Why: Multiple windows turn timing into a deduction task rather than a single obvious answer.
- [rule] An NPC-set time limit can serve as a timed mechanic the player must respect or exploit, and each timed event should have a witness NPC who can confirm or contradict it. When: designing timed events in investigation. Why: the player must build timelines from several sources.
- [rule] Give shops, guards and offices fixed opening and closing times, so the player must plan routes around them and deadlines create real pressure on choices. When: designing a town with time-restricted locations. Why: fixed hours turn movement into scheduling.
- [rule] Rule out a route when earlier walkers would have passed the spot, since they would have noticed anyone there. When: When a location was recently traversed by known observers. Why: Prior traffic through a spot makes concealment there unlikely.
- [rule] Explain an apparent timing discrepancy with a specific, checkable cause, and verify that cause with an independent witness. When: A person's movements seem to conflict with the timeline. Why: Vague excuses cannot be tested, while specific causes can be confirmed or refuted.
- [rule] Show a timed escape or guard schedule through ambient cues such as bells or footsteps, so the player feels the clock. When: when designing timed sequences in a level.
- [rule] Scatter traces such as blood, tracks or dropped items so their order implies events, letting players assemble a timeline in a journal.
- [rule] Give a level a clock puzzle: the player aligns a timed event such as a bell, rainfall, or locking door with an NPC's claimed schedule to expose a lie.
- [rule] Let a companion NPC carry a task list the player assigns and return results on a timer. When: Designing companion-driven investigation tasks. Why: A timed, prioritized task keeps the player's investigation moving.
- [rule] Build rescue or alarm systems whose timing can be checked, so that a late response becomes evidence a player can use. Why: Measurable response times turn delays into readable clues.
- [rule] Give staff or guard testimony small timing facts, such as who left last, that the player can check against the level layout.
- [rule] Empty an area of potential witnesses on a schedule to define the window in which a character has an alibi.
- [rule] Give an alibi puzzle a timestamped token, such as a gate log, that places a suspect while leaving identity open for a second clue.
- [rule] Give an NPC an alibi of illness for a span of in-game days, and provide a witness or record that contradicts it for the player to find. When: designing NPC alibis.
- [rule] Give NPC investigators a stock explanation that the player can test and find lacking. When: designing NPC investigators who offer a theory.
- [rule] Encode whether an NPC's omission is an oversight or deliberate in its behaviour, letting players infer intent from what it leaves out.
- [rule] Store each NPC's statements so the game can flag contradictions between them, such as conflicting durations or sources. When: when NPCs make checkable claims. Why: contradictions expose lies.
- [rule] Build an alibi from many small, checkable claims that each pass on first check, so the player trusts the whole account. When: when writing a false alibi. Why: Each passed check adds to trust in the full account.
- [heuristic] A claim of sleeping through an event may be a lie or unreliable perception, so test it against the scene and ask how many distinct sounds were heard. When: a witness says they slept through or heard nothing of an event. Why: People vary widely in what wakes them, and waking perception separates distinct sounds that sleep would blur.
- [heuristic] An alibi is weak when witnesses share the suspect's loyalties or interests, or were not truly at the claimed place; checking records against timed events tests it. When: Testing a suspect's alibi. Why: Witnesses bound to the suspect may lie, so their independence sets the alibi's strength.
- [heuristic] Alibis need confirmation by another person at each stage, not only being seen elsewhere; unwitnessed intervals, such as time alone in a room, stay open. When: when evaluating an alibi. Why: Only independent confirmation closes an unverified interval.
- [heuristic] An alibi holds when several independent witnesses place the suspect at a known location at the critical moment, with each time source checked; lone proximity without vouching is weak. When: Comparing alibis for a time-bound event, where testimony about time is the only way to exclude a suspect. Why: One witness can be mistaken, so independent corroboration is much stronger; independent witnesses confirm position at the moment that matters.
- [heuristic] A detail confirmed by a second, independently positioned witness is stronger than a single account; for arrival or departure times, several independent staff agreeing on the hour is most reliable. When: weighing a witness's claim, or fixing when a person arrived or left. Why: Independent agreement reduces the chance of a single error.
- [heuristic] Signs of preparation before a break-in, such as an unlatched window or bound guard, suggest knowledge of the routine or inside help, but not proof; check access records. When: A break-in looks too precise for an outsider, or an insider is inferred from signs of planning. Why: Preparation usually requires access to the place, yet outsiders can also prepare and records show who truly had access.
- [heuristic] Model each suspect's alternative or arranged story as a hypothesis with explicit, checkable requirements, tested against new facts rather than treated as settled. When: Handling multiple suspect accounts or a suspected arranged alibi. Why: Explicit requirements make accounts testable.
- [heuristic] Second-hand accounts of when someone was last seen need checking, since absent witnesses may repeat what they were told, sincerely; another witness must verify them. When: A timeline depends on second-hand accounts, or an alibi rests on what someone else told the witness. Why: Those absent can only repeat what they were told, and sincerity does not make it accurate.
- [heuristic] Accept a provisional point and return to it later rather than resolving all at once; a claim lacking a motive stays provisional, not proven. When: a serious claim lacks a complete motive. Why: A missing motive is not a reason to halt investigation, yet acceptance must stay provisional.
- [heuristic] Define the crime window from the gap between last sighting and discovery, then check which alibis within it have an independent witness; a bounded gap gives a clear question. When: Designing a deduction question about a victim's death window, or a suspect claims to be at home or asleep over a long period. Why: A bounded gap gives players a clear question to resolve.
- [heuristic] Describe a clue's distinctive features before the object appears, so the audience can recognize it when it returns.
- [heuristic] A suspect who stages a visible quarrel or refusal may be building a later claim of innocence, so ask whether the account was prepared in advance. When: when a suspect's defence depends on a witnessed dispute. Why: A staged scene can make a later claim look credible.
- [heuristic] An actor's movements over several days form their own timeline, which can be checked against deadlines and other events. Why: Movements recorded in sequence reveal preparation and timing.
- [heuristic] Confirm a reaction across more than one moment, since a single observation can overturn a settled belief.
- [heuristic] A plausible excuse given right after a slip suggests it was prepared in advance; check it against what information was available at the time. When: When a suspect explains knowledge they should not have.
- [heuristic] Infer an adult's character from the behaviour of children or dependants in their care, treating it as grounds for suspicion rather than proof. When: An adult's behaviour is hard to read directly. Why: A dependant's behaviour can reveal household tensions.
- [heuristic] Split a large search area so each searcher covers one side of it.
- [heuristic] A respectable role can hide a personal interest; let that interest stay concealed behind the role until a clue exposes it.
- [heuristic] An actor who wants to secure an object tends to act early, before the loss is noticed. When: when estimating when a theft most likely occurred within a window. Why: Early action reduces the chance of discovery.
- [heuristic] Evidence that a party tried to prevent the harm can complicate a simple motive reading.
- [heuristic] Wait until an impaired suspect recovers before questioning, but words spoken while impaired can still be used as leverage.
- [heuristic] A timed decision, such as a choice made after an interruption, can be confirmed by asking the person who relayed the message. When: A witness's timing depends on an event that others observed. Why: A relay witness can corroborate when the decision was made.
- [heuristic] Route marks and purchases show opportunity and preparation, but rarely prove an alibi false on their own. When: Evaluating physical or behavioural evidence against a stated alibi. Why: Each item fits many innocent explanations until combined with timing and testimony.
- [heuristic] When witness times are unreliable or absent, use objective measures such as fuel use and mileage to reconstruct when events happened. When: no reliable witness time exists. Why: objective measures do not depend on memory.
- [heuristic] A suspect far from the scene can be cleared by distance, but the times of their arrivals and departures must still be checked. When: a suspect's location at the scene matters. Why: Distance clears a suspect only if their movement timing also fits.
- [heuristic] Whoever knows what a suspect is doing can get in front of them; one who only guesses at it must keep behind.
- [heuristic] Compare an estimated dose with the quantity of medicine dispensed and remaining; if the amount cannot account for it, accidental overdose is excluded.
- [heuristic] An observed onset far later than a substance's known onset is a mismatch to investigate, not proof of any particular cause.
- [heuristic] The posting or delivery time of a document can be evidence when reconstructing an event. When: a document arrives close to a key moment. Why: timing links the document to what could have been known.
- [heuristic] Prepare verifiable proof before a confrontation, since an alert opponent can infer hidden preparation.
- [heuristic] Have an NPC who believes a false cause state it with real certainty, so players must test the claim before accepting it.
- [heuristic] Ask about details the subject could not have prepared for, since accurate answers to those reveal real knowledge. When: testing whether a subject's account is genuine. Why: A rehearsed story rarely covers unexpected specifics.
- [heuristic] An unusual choice, such as a later train over an earlier one, is a point to probe.
- [heuristic] A companion's testimony that leans toward a suspect should be checkable against other sources, so the player can detect the lean. When: designing a companion who testifies. Why: checkable testimony keeps bias from going unnoticed.
- [heuristic] Occupancy and rough timing can be established from traces even when no clue to the occupant's identity exists.
- [heuristic] Test the weakest alibi first, since breaking it earns the cooperation needed to test the stronger one.
- [heuristic] A witness's claimed timing can be tested against a public schedule that no one present controls. If the claimed hour conflicts with it, the alibi fails without a second witness. When: A witness's timing is tied to a public event with a known schedule. Why: A fixed public schedule is an independent anchor the witness cannot alter.
- [heuristic] Whoever prepared a masking agent probably also added the harmful agent. Check who had access to both the preparation and the dose. When: when a harmful agent was hidden in a prepared item. Why: The same person often handles both steps, linking the preparer to the harm.
- [heuristic] Dialogue systems that let players ask NPCs about routines and times make contradictions checkable.
- [heuristic] Weigh a claimed absence against how long the trip would take; a short errand covers a gap only if its timing fits within that gap. When: A suspect says they briefly left and returned. Why: A trip that cannot fit the gap cannot cover it.
- [heuristic] A single motive label can hide two emotions aimed at two different people, so split it when new facts reveal this. When: when a crime involves several interested parties.
- [heuristic] Unfinished obligations due soon after a disappearance suggest a sudden break rather than a planned departure. When: when judging whether an absence was planned. Why: someone preparing to leave usually settles pending deals first.
- [heuristic] A plausible physical excuse such as fever is often accepted too easily, so the designer must decide whether the NPC believes it.
- [heuristic] Agreement between companions proves less when they shared the same expectations.
- [heuristic] Partial reports from several witnesses of one event corroborate the story where they overlap. When: When multiple people saw different parts of one incident. Why: Independent partial views that agree support one another.
- [heuristic] Treat a physical absence as a clue that needs interpretation, not as proof on its own. When: A search finds only a missing part or an empty space. Why: One absence can be read in several ways.
- [heuristic] Judge a person's character from surface behavior only provisionally, since hidden inner states are not a reliable basis for accusation. When: Assessing a suspect whose motives are not visible.
- [heuristic] Leave some links in a generated history unverified, so the chain has honest gaps that players can choose to investigate. When: Designing a discoverable backstory. Why: Unresolved gaps give players something to pursue and avoid presenting a suspiciously complete history.
- [heuristic] Filter suspects by hard-to-fake attributes, removing easily disguised features from the comparison so that the remaining traits decide who matches. When: Generating or resolving a set of possible culprits. Why: Easily faked features cannot reliably separate suspects.
- [heuristic] Make some alibi witnesses members of the suspect's faction so the player must weigh their testimony against other evidence.
- [heuristic] Keep an unidentified victim a mystery until players gather identity clues that unlock the case.
- [heuristic] Have a guard or innkeeper claim a room is full while an unlocked empty room is nearby, so the player exposes the lie by looking. When: Designing NPC dialogue that the player can verify in the level. Why: Letting players test claims turns dialogue into discoverable clues.
- [heuristic] A warning that arrives late is worth less than one that arrives early, and delaying a response gives the enemy the advantage.
- [heuristic] Timing that breaks the expected order of events, such as an item collected before it could have been needed, can itself become a clue.
- [heuristic] Deduction from a timeline works best when a plan is bounded by a physical clock such as tide, schedule or fuel. When: A suspect's route depends on a limiting physical factor. Why: Fixed limits turn a vague plan into testable time windows.
- [heuristic] A gap in a sequence is meaningful when the missing value has a reason, such as a non-working day, rather than being accidental.
- [heuristic] Test a witness's account by asking whether their route and timing make sense given what they knew at each moment; an odd path choice is a clue to conduct or intent. When: When a witness includes an action that seems unnecessary or contrary to their stated purpose. Why: Actions that contradict the stated goal often reveal knowledge, intent, or concealment.
- [heuristic] Reward specific, checkable information more than pleading, so players learn to test claims instead of accepting emotional appeals. When: when designing NPC dialogue rewards. Why: Rewards shape what players learn to trust.
- [heuristic] Give a clue object such as a pocket watch a fixed game-time value, so players can rebuild event order from known schedules like guard rotations.
- [heuristic] Model an alibi as a timetable the player checks against timed events, and place one contradiction in an unrelated object found while searching for something else. When: designing a mystery with a claimed alibi. Why: a checkable schedule gives a fair test and an incidental clue rewards thorough searching.
- [heuristic] Record when the last known baseline was taken, since every change must fall after that moment. When: dating a discovered change. Why: Anything earlier is already reflected in the baseline.
- [heuristic] NPCs who believe culprits must be clever will read an alibi gap differently from those who do not; let the player judge which NPC reasons sensibly. When: NPCs comment on a suspect's lack of alibi. Why: Beliefs about cleverness shape interpretation of the same fact.
- [heuristic] An NPC can bluff by behaving as though the player's case is complete, prompting a culprit to act and reveal themselves. When: designing a culprit's reaction to pressure. Why: Feigned certainty triggers a response the culprit would otherwise hold back.
- [heuristic] A timetable can make an alibi seem objective; a staged or misleading timeline can make a suspect appear cleared, so check the timeline the alibi depends on. When: A suspect's innocence rests on a sequence of times or events. Why: A designed timeline can look innocent while hiding the actual sequence.
- [heuristic] Check a witness's time claim against a neutral, independent source, such as another witness whose own timing is fixed, since witnesses share clocks and memories that may be wrong. When: A witness states when they saw someone or when an event happened, from testimony alone.
- [heuristic] When several parties move to the same place within a short window, they probably had a planned meeting rather than a chance encounter. When: movement times and destinations line up closely. Why: Matching schedules are unlikely to occur by coincidence.
- [heuristic] Split a covert meeting into separate roles so that no single observer can prove the whole arrangement. When: a group must meet discreetly under possible surveillance. Why: Each observer sees only a fragment and cannot connect the parts.
- [heuristic] Give each alibi a player-performable check, such as a cell record or time-stamped movement log, stored in the game so the claim can be tested. When: designing alibis for suspects in a mystery. Why: Movement records give the player an independent source to test a claim against.
- [heuristic] A candle that has not guttered shows an opening was open only briefly, which narrows the window of access.
- [procedure] 1) Place each person's statement on one timeline and compare accounts of the same event to locate conflicts. 2) Ask which claims someone other than the speaker can confirm; treat a claim as supported only if independent witnesses agree. 3) Check records such as registers or manifests. When: Several people claim to have last seen the victim or left a place at different times, or to have been somewhere at the same time. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Use a message's dated write and receipt times to fix the sequence of events. 2) Note who knew what and when. 3) Check the sequence before questioning other witnesses. When: A written message is near an event in time, or a dated written statement frames the sequence. Why: Timing of communication can establish that an event followed or preceded it; the fixed sequence frames later questioning.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the source of an alibi document or counter-alibi. 2) Verify the source independently. 3) Accept it only if the source is confirmed; never take a documented alibi at face value. When: A witness or suspect offers a document as proof of location, or a counter-alibi is offered. Why: Unverified documents can be false or misattributed.
- [procedure] 1) Split the alibi into time and place claims and the witnesses who confirm them. 2) Separate claims resting only on the subject's word. 3) Test verifiable claims first against independent sources. 4) Ask each witness how they know the hour. Breaking the alibi into parts exposes points of failure. When: A suspect presents a neat or airtight alibi, a complete timeline, or a time-and-place defence. Why: Each part can be tested separately.
- [procedure] 1) Record each person's claimed location, span and activity per time slot, noting who confirms it. 2) Find an independent source for each point. 3) Mark unsupported points as weak or open. 4) Re-examine weak entries first. When: An alibi or event timing is in question, or several people give overlapping accounts of the same hours.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the crime window and order independent timed sightings or records around it. 2) Ask where the suspect was during each part and mark gaps between consecutive fixed points. 3) Check whether travel, walks and calls fit each gap. 4) Treat the alibi as broken if any leg cannot be covered in time. When: A suspect's whereabouts during a crime window are disputed, or they could be in two places within the window. Why: Physical travel time decides whether a claimed alibi is possible.
- [procedure] 1) Estimate earliest possible departure from realistic travel speed. 2) Add time for each small delay, such as dressing or starting a vehicle, and weigh reasons for any delay. 3) Compare the result with the stated arrival. 4) Check fixed times and side evidence against independent records or witnesses. When: A suspect's whereabouts are claimed for a specific window, or a reconstruction depends on journey times, opening hours or call logs. Why: Timing shows whether the alibi is physically possible, and small delays can decide whether a timing holds.
- [procedure] 1) List each claimed action and its time. 2) Estimate the minimum time each takes and compare the total with the available window. 3) Name who confirms each claim and whether they are independent of the suspect. 4) Note steps no witness could confirm. When: Checking a suspect's account of a period, especially one that depends on one person or a tight schedule. Why: Shows whether the schedule is physically possible and where it depends on unverified or non-independent claims.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor each timeline to fixed independent events, such as recorded times, medical estimates, a phone call or other observers' schedules. 2) Ask each person where they were in the window. 3) Check claims against records and room layout, and whether timing permits later events. 4) Mark gaps and contradictions. When: The crime time is narrow and several people claim alibis, or several independent clocks or observers are available.
- [procedure] 1) Have each person state their claimed time and position in their own words, pinning vague answers with specific questions. 2) Record clock times for movements, checkpoints, absences and returns. 3) Compare each claim against a physical record such as tickets or logs, and test other witnesses against it. 4) Compare movements across people to see who could have acted. When: Several people's movements or overlapping claims must be compared. Why: Matching recorded times shows who was in position to act; building the timeline from the suspect's own words makes any later contradiction clear and fair.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the window in which the act could have happened. 2) List everyone who could have been near the victim, not only obvious suspects. 3) Check each claimed location against that window and verify it independently. 4) Test whether a substitute could have occupied the suspect's place. When: Assessing a suspect's alibi when the crime time is narrow and several people had access to the victim. Why: A claimed location counts only if it fits the minutes the act could have occurred; a wide list prevents tunnel vision and independent verification prevents accepting a firmly stated alibi.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the exact time of the act and the clock times each alibi witness gives, aligning the clocks they came from. 2) Line up each alibi window with the crime window. 3) Measure the gap between them. 4) Reject the alibi if the margin is too small to be credible. When: An alibi depends on a short time window, or a suspect's exact location at a precise time is contested. Why: Times must be checked against a clock, since a loose estimate leaves little room for error.
- [procedure] 1) Agree rules in advance. 2) Stagger each person's movements. 3) Stage a brief quarrel loud enough to be heard. 4) Give each accomplice one task so no one performs the whole act and no single person is seen doing it.
- [procedure] 1) Describe the act in physical terms, such as lifting a weight or crossing a difficult route. 2) Compare those demands with the suspect's age, health and mobility. 3) Note any mismatch; a claimed action may be impossible for that person. When: Deciding whether a suspect could physically perform an act, or a claimed action involves a physical skill. Why: Tests capability directly against the requirements of the act.
- [procedure] 1) Ask for exact times and places rather than general accounts. 2) Pin each stage to a location. 3) Check each fixed point against other evidence. 4) Note every interval the witness cannot account for. When: when a suspect's account places them near a crime. Why: specific claims can be tested against the clock and other evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Record each party's departure time and destination from witnesses. 2) Note any arrival times. 3) Align all times on one clock. 4) Look for overlaps that reveal a shared destination. When: witnesses can give times and destinations, even roughly. Why: Aligned times show which parties were heading to the same place.
- [procedure] 1) Ask indirect questions about the suspect's movements during the crime window, not whether they have an alibi. 2) Keep your reactions neutral. 3) Build a timeline of the suspect's arrival, departure and destinations. When: a close companion of the suspect is available to question. Why: Indirect questions let the witness volunteer details freely.
- [procedure] 1) List everyone who could have learned the secret. 2) Record where each person was at the relevant time. 3) Keep those with access and opportunity as possible actors. When: An event's cause depends on who knew of a hidden object or secret. Why: Presence at a place and time determines which actors are possible.
- [procedure] 1) Note the reason given for a sudden departure. 2) Check it against an independent record such as a telegram, ticket or travel log. 3) Weigh it against known facts about the people involved. When: a suspect or witness leaves at an awkward moment with a stated reason.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the known times: calls, appointments, arrivals, departures and the discovery time. 2) Ask who can confirm each step. 3) Check the route taken. 4) Measure the unwitnessed gap between the last contact and the death. When: Testing a suspect's claimed movements before a crime. Why: Fixed times and witnessed steps show where an account is unverified.
- [procedure] 1) Establish when the dose was delivered and when it was consumed. 2) Look up the known onset time of the substance. 3) Compare the observed onset with the expected onset. 4) Weigh each alternative explanation by the size of the gap.
- [procedure] 1) Make a room look used, such as a rumpled bed. 2) Use a known harmless habit as cover, such as a long bath. 3) Keep the noise long enough for listeners to settle, then reduce it. 4) Arrange lights and doors to suggest someone is home. 5) Set up a prior excuse for absence. When: when someone must appear present to a witness checking at a given hour. Why: Staged signs of routine make an absent person seem present, and the cover depends on the household's habits.
- [procedure] 1) Establish a person's fixed hours and day off. 2) Identify the free periods in which they could have been elsewhere. 3) Check those periods against the event window. When: testing whether a person could have been at a location. Why: routine fixes the times they were unaccounted for.
- [procedure] 1) Take the last time the victim was seen alive. 2) Take the time the body was found. 3) Check whether the suspect had access to the agent during that span.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor the timeline to a witness-recorded time. 2) Establish the suspect's known movements. 3) Work out whether the suspect could travel and act within the gap. 4) Add corroborating times. 5) Check the suspect's belongings and state against the timeline. When: When a suspect claims to be elsewhere or a witness gives a time. Why: A claimed alibi can only be judged against checkable times and travel possibilities.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the object and when it was unguarded. 2) Identify who could reach it during that interval. 3) Check whether the interval fits the act's duration. When: when a poisoning, trap or theft must be timed. Why: Comparing the window to the act shows whether a suspect could have done it.
- [procedure] When a witness's timing seems off, press for the exact hour; a firm answer shows whether the discrepancy is real.
- [procedure] 1) Take one witness aside for a private talk. 2) Have a partner search the rest of the scene while the talk continues. When: when two parties must be occupied at once. Why: Separation creates time and space for a search.
- [procedure] 1) Get each companion's own account of the same event. 2) Compare what each perceived. 3) Note what each expected beforehand. 4) Treat differences as clues. When: two or more people shared an experience.
- [procedure] 1) Separate the time a message was sent from the time it was delivered. 2) Compare each time with where the suspect was seen. 3) Estimate the travel time for the key journey. 4) Count the free minutes left to the suspect. 5) Check who handled the message and whether a copy exists. 6) Test the suspect's likely next move against the schedule. When: When a claimed alibi depends on stated times that others can verify. Why: Converting suspicion into a checkable schedule reveals whether the suspect had the opportunity to act.
- [procedure] 1) List every possible route into or out of a place. 2) Check each route for the marks it would leave. 3) Exclude routes whose expected marks are absent. 4) Test remaining marks against known sources. When: Deciding how someone reached or left a place. Why: Systematic exclusion narrows the route to the one that matches the evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Find physical traces of passage, such as torn cloth or a fresh gap in a barrier. 2) Measure the height needed to reach the gap. 3) Test the route physically to confirm the traced trait. When: Reconstructing how a person moved through a barrier. Why: Testing the route checks measurements that can be wrong on paper.
- [tradeoff] A flawless alibi often rests on arranged details, like a convenient clock or witnesses who never lost sight, though true ones can look staged; weigh objective evidence. When: Judging an alibi that looks flawless or unusually complete. Why: Arranged details are the usual weak points, yet appearance alone can mislead in both directions.
- [tradeoff] An alibi from witnesses related to the suspect, or from witnesses who saw the suspect only briefly, is less conclusive than one from independent, sustained observation. When: when weighing alibi evidence.
- [tradeoff] Verifying a method that needs specific conditions, such as a stopped vehicle, makes the plan depend on chance. When: The method works only under transient conditions. Why: If the condition never occurs, the method cannot be tested or used.
- [tradeoff] Passing evidence to a trusted companion moves it out of your hands, but its safety then depends on that person's loyalty. When: Concealing proof from searchers. Why: Control transfers to another person.
- [pitfall] A witness's silence does not prove nothing happened, since sleep depth and window position limit what they could hear, so a lodger's claim depends on their alertness. When: when assessing whether a witness's silence is meaningful, such as a lodger vouching for a sleeping suspect. Why: Hearing a movement depends on the listener being awake and attentive. (x2)
- [pitfall] Respectable conduct or good humour does not prove innocence: it can conceal forgery, and letting reputation settle the question lets social impression override evidence. (x2)
- [pitfall] An alibi can be a constructed story designed to place the accused elsewhere, so it is not automatically a true record of movements.
- [pitfall] An alibi or reconstruction fails if its assumed time is wrong, such as a presumed time of death resting only on identification, or a time of tearing or writing. Why: The alibi depends entirely on the fixed time it is measured against.
- [pitfall] Splitting attention or a watch between two people leaves each exposed: a target may move unexpectedly, or coverage is lost if one is reassigned without notice.
- [pitfall] An alibi with gaps can look solid while every link depends on the person who gave it or on their own account rather than independent records.
- [pitfall] An alibi supported by a companion or witness who cannot be questioned loses its support and stays unverified.
- [pitfall] Consistent or coordinated accounts do not clear anyone: mutual vouching can be circular, especially with a shared interest, since agreement shows fit, not absence of opportunity. When: Several suspects share the same window and their accounts interlock.
- [pitfall] A check made at one time, such as a morning lock inspection, says nothing about events in the earlier hours. When: a status is confirmed only at a later time. Why: the check did not observe the intervening period.
- [pitfall] An alibi based on a door being locked fails if the door was never secured, so check the lock before trusting the alibi.
- [pitfall] Forgetting that a dependant can raise an alarm leaves a plan exposed, so every person able to alert others must be accounted for. When: a plan focuses on the main target and ignores others present. Why: Any person who can call for help can ruin a timed action.
- [pitfall] Letting a suspect's household open the door before investigators are inside gives the suspect time to flee.
- [pitfall] A respectable or saintly reputation does not remove a beneficiary from suspicion, and motive may exist that the records do not show. When: clearing a beneficiary on character or on the records alone. Why: Motive is defined by legal stake and personal knowledge, not reputation.
- [pitfall] A planted item is only as strong as its stated reason; a weak cover story leads the audience to question the item. When: the explanation for an item is thin. Why: audiences test explanations and find gaps.
- [pitfall] A witness who answers 'I am not sure' marks a gap rather than a guilty answer, and a witness who was away gives an absent alibi, not a confirmed one. When: Interpreting uncertain or absent alibi testimony. Why: Uncertainty and absence are unconfirmed positions, not proof of innocence or guilt.
- [pitfall] Assuming a suspect will remain in place while a game or scene continues is risky, since a deadline can end the wait early. When: the suspect is free to leave. Why: suspects act when the scene's pace changes.
- [pitfall] Companions who withhold their own findings create a false sense of progress. When: when several characters share investigative work. Why: Hidden findings look like advancement while no shared picture forms.
- [pitfall] An alibi that cannot be verified can make an innocent person look guilty, because the gap invites the worst reading. When: when a witness's whereabouts cannot be confirmed. Why: Unexplained time is readily read as concealment.
- [pitfall] A departure time given by a servant may be imprecise. Note the imprecision before relying on it to build a timeline.
- [pitfall] A witness who was off duty cannot confirm a routine on the critical day. When: Relying on staff testimony about a specific day. Why: Absence means no observation of that day.
- [pitfall] A suspect with a prepared medical explanation can use it to account for physical traces, so the explanation must be tested before it is accepted. When: A suspect offers a health-based explanation for physical evidence. Why: A ready story can cover real traces and delay scrutiny.
- [pitfall] A corroborated cover story can still be false, because a plan can hide behind a believable research explanation.
- [pitfall] A scheme that depends on a stranger's unseen cooperation has many points of failure.
- [pitfall] Reading packing as a getaway can be wrong: the same preparation may come from a suspect who plans to surrender. When: When a suspect's preparations suggest flight.
- [pitfall] An alibi strong for one event can be weak for another, so test each suspect against the same moment. When: Several events with different suspects' alibis. Why: Coverage of one time does not extend to others.
- [pitfall] Treating a claim of sleep as proof of innocence ignores the chance that the claim is false. Why: sleep cannot be verified by the investigator.
- [pitfall] An alibi relies on witnesses failing to connect the victim's summons to the danger, so witnesses who are calm while the victim is sent to harm give the alibi its force. Why: The alibi works only while the witnesses do not connect the events.
- [pitfall] Using the time help was summoned as the time of an event's onset can misplace the events, since discovery may lag the event by a substantial interval. When: Building a timeline of a sudden event such as a collapse. Why: Summoning help is a later event than the thing it responds to, so treating the two as one shifts the whole sequence.
- [pitfall] A witness who was in company may pass over a gap in the timeline as if it were spent at home. When: Evaluating an account given by someone who was with others. Why: Shared company can make unaccounted time seem accounted for.
- [pitfall] Unplanned participants can change a timed plan without warning, so model their likely arrival as a risk. When: a plan relies on a fixed sequence of events. Why: extra actors alter timing and outcomes.
- [pitfall] A late arrival in a usually punctual routine can force a rushed plan with almost no margin, so timed plans need slack. When: The plan depends on a single scheduled event.
- [pitfall] Assuming people who met at a station went to the same destination afterward is an error; a missing shared destination proves little.
- [pitfall] An absence used as an alibi needs checking for when it started and ended, and whether the absent person could still act through others.
- [pitfall] Trusting an alibi because it is stated firmly leads to missed contradictions; a confident claim is not verification. When: When a suspect delivers a confident alibi. Why: Confidence of delivery is not evidence that the events occurred.
- [fact] Concrete details of a journey and a third party's confirmation at the destination both corroborate a traveller's account.
- [fact] Provisional bookings on several vessels can explain why a traveller's name appears on a list while the traveller's actual movements remain uncertain. When: when a passenger list is used as evidence. Why: a name on a list does not prove the person boarded it.
- [fact] A second identity is far easier to sustain when built over years in advance than invented at the last moment.
- [fact] Four methods used on suspected witches to extract confessions were pricking, waking, watching and testing.
- [fact] An alibi can be genuine yet carry little weight if it cannot be supported against the prosecution's case.
- [fact] If death followed an act within minutes, the act likely happened in the presence of the victim. Short onset narrows who could have performed it. When: When a medical estimate gives a short time between an act and death. Why: A fast-acting effect requires the perpetrator to be close to the victim when the act occurs.
- [fact] An empty seat at a stated time shows that its holder had not yet arrived, which can date arrival. When: Attendance at a fixed event is observed at a known time. Why: Occupancy at a specific moment bounds when a person could have come in.
- [fact] A ticket holder may sit somewhere other than the assigned seat, so the seat alone does not prove where a person was. When: Location is inferred from a ticket's assigned seat. Why: People can move or swap seats, so assigned seats are weak proof of actual position.

## interrogation and questioning
- [model] Interrogators unsettle a suspect with three tools: an accusing timeline, a bluff, and a fixed steady stare.
- [definition] Interrogation confronts a suspect with specific facts in a planned sequence under pressure, noting concessions; the questioner controls which facts surface and when. When: during a suspect questioning scene.
- [definition] Witnesses who hold a post or keep a watch define who could have entered a place and when, which gives a fixed frame of times and places.
- [definition] Psychological pressure applies delay, feigned friendliness and tone shifts to a suspect's nerves instead of hard evidence, aiming to make him talk or reveal himself under strain.
- [mechanism] Interrogation dialogue can branch on evidence the player presents, unlocking options or a confession only when claims are backed by a full set of supporting clues. When: Designing NPC interrogation or dialogue that rewards deduction. Why: Gating ties the option to demonstrated reasoning rather than chance.
- [mechanism] An NPC interrogation logs every stated fact and flags conflicts with earlier statements or world records, unlocking new questions and reveals. When: Designing NPC interrogation in a game. Why: Logged statements make conflicts detectable.
- [mechanism] An interrogation can branch on questions about routines, associates and recorded events, revealing what the character knows and changing the available dialogue. When: When designing NPC dialogue in a mystery or dungeon-style game. Why: Different questions open different information paths, so the player's choices shape what is learned.
- [mechanism] A dialogue option whose reply varies with an NPC's knowledge lets players extract hidden information through the form of the answer.
- [mechanism] In a stimulating drug phase, the most vivid recent worry can harden into a fixed idea that overrides judgment and drives purposeful action. When: A person is in the stimulating phase of a drug. Why: The stimulated state narrows attention onto one dominant concern.
- [mechanism] A questioner can extract information indirectly by letting a second person supply the answers, and a witness who notices this can limit what she gives away. When: Someone questions a witness while an ally or third party steers the exchange. Why: Helpful-seeming suggestions and interruptions redirect the witness, and a pressing follow-up can make her disclose more than intended.
- [mechanism] Timing answers that narrow as the player supplies more events reward systematic questioning over guessing. When: an NPC answers questions about when events occurred. Why: each new anchor shrinks the possible window.
- [mechanism] Naming a consequence for silence makes a partially cooperative NPC more likely to yield further detail.
- [mechanism] A suspect character can carry timed watch states that log messages and calls, which the player can intercept or overhear. When: In games where an NPC's communications should be trackable.
- [mechanism] A dialogue system can gate information behind keywords, so a player who uses the right term, such as a place name or repeated phrase, unlocks the next line.
- [mechanism] An interrogation system can lock NPCs in separate rooms and sequence them, letting the player revisit lines in a fixed order.
