- [rule] Tie a witness's memory to a physical object that can be shown again, so the claim can be checked rather than merely believed. When: when a witness recalls an item or document. Why: presentable objects allow verification.
- [rule] Treat a written memory aid, such as a list of positions, as a clue to how a combination is meant to be operated. When: A note lists symbols or positions. Why: It records the operating sequence.
- [rule] Do not press a witness in shock for a full account; schedule fuller questioning for when she is stronger. When: witness is still in shock.
- [rule] Stop witnesses who volunteer theories or conclusions and keep them to what they observed. When: A witness moves from observation to speculation. Why: Theories from witnesses can replace evidence and mislead the record.
- [rule] Let a recall bring a suspect back once new evidence is found, and let a closing summary list the verdict options. When: designing investigation mechanics.
- [rule] Give each witness one memorable event so that their recall feels specific and plausible. When: When writing witness dialogue for a deduction scene. Why: A single vivid anchor makes testimony feel credible.
- [rule] Recheck a witness's claim by searching the area they described, such as a stairway they said was guarded.
- [rule] Let an NPC's forgotten detail return through a journal, another witness or a physical item, so the player reconstructs it instead of hearing it repeated. When: designing an NPC who loses a quest detail. Why: reconstruction turns a lost memory into a discovery.
- [rule] Let a drunk or concussed NPC recall the night as shuffled fragments that the player must sort into order. When: Designing an NPC whose memory of an event is impaired. Why: Sorting fragments turns recall into a puzzle the player solves.
- [rule] Track each witness's position, line of sight and distance; limit reports to what they could perceive, e.g. a figure seen from behind gives height and clothing, not a face. When: designing NPC perception and witness reports, or an NPC has partial information about an event. Why: keeps testimony consistent with what the NPC could perceive.
- [rule] Log which NPCs were in each location at each time so that detailed knowledge can be traced to a witness. When: building an NPC location and knowledge system.
- [rule] Tag NPC recollections made long after an event with a decay marker, prompting players to verify them against a second source.
- [rule] Make the path to a hidden name run through an informant with a tie to the record-keeper, so the player must earn it through trade or favours. When: A key identity is locked behind a non-player intermediary. Why: Earned access gives the player a reason to invest in relationships.
- [rule] Add an informant NPC with a grudge who reveals a hidden detail, rewarding players who talk to disgruntled characters. Why: Grudges make NPCs willing to disclose secrets.
- [rule] Let information travel only through defined channels such as letters, staff and rumours, so the player can trace any leak back to its source.
- [rule] Give an in-world expert's claim a visible basis, so the player can judge whether that expert's authority applies to the clue at hand. When: when generating expert NPCs who vouch for clues. Why: players need grounds to weigh authority against evidence.
- [rule] Test whether a witness was awake and positioned to perceive an event, and do not assume that a sound heard by one person was heard by all nearby. When: Comparing accounts of who heard or saw something. Why: Perception depends on location, sleep and attention.
- [rule] Place each observer at a fixed vantage point hidden from the subject, with a retreat position nearby in case the subject looks back. When: the subject might turn and notice an observer. Why: a noticed observer changes what the subject does.
- [rule] Position light sources so their glare does not hit the subject's eyes, and move or extinguish a light at the key moment to keep observers concealed. When: observing during a staged or timed moment. Why: light can expose observers or dazzle the subject.
- [rule] Enforce observer silence with agreed hand signals and quiet footwear, so observers can follow the subject without being heard.
- [rule] Check a chance remark that links to an existing lead before weighing it, since coincidences are common. Why: An unchecked remark can look meaningful while being pure coincidence.
- [rule] Let a stealth NPC believe the player has been fooled while the player prepares an ambush.
- [rule] A voice disguise mechanic should let guards who have heard the NPC up close recognise the difference.
- [rule] Track which claims the player volunteered, so later NPCs react to what was already admitted. When: when multiple NPCs question the player. Why: NPCs should not ignore disclosures made earlier.
- [rule] Two crimes with the same design and execution suggest the same mind is behind both. When: a new case resembles an older one. Why: a repeated signature is harder to attribute to coincidence.
- [rule] Store each NPC's reactions to named people as relationship data that dialogue and behaviour can draw on.
- [rule] Let a player place a fuzzy NPC memory on a known game event, such as a bell ringing or a guard shift change. Why: Shared anchors make vague testimony usable.
- [heuristic] An honest witness can still be wrong, and a memory lapse, possibly from illness or exhaustion, is a limit of observation, not proof of lying. When: a witness fails to recall a detail or shows confusion after sleep or sickness. Why: Fever and fatigue genuinely impair recall, and a gap in memory is not proof of deception.
- [heuristic] Anchor witness times to fixed or scheduled events, such as lamps being lit, a shop closing or a timed climax, so approximate recollections can be checked against the clock. When: witnesses recall times loosely or place an event relative to a scheduled cue. Why: A shared or independent reference point gives memory something to be checked against.
- [heuristic] Reveal witness memory in fragments that players must assemble, rather than a complete memory at once, keeping them reasoning toward the full picture. When: designing memory reveals or traumatic, confused witness scenes. Why: Fragments keep the player actively reasoning toward the full picture.
- [heuristic] Limit NPC witnesses' perception, such as by a wall, deafness or partial vision, so testimony covers only part of the scene and players must work out what each could know. When: designing witness NPCs for an investigation. Why: Limits make testimony a puzzle rather than a fixed fact source.
- [heuristic] Treat a witness's lost stretch of memory as possible evidence that someone deliberately arranged it. When: a witness cannot recall a period of time.
- [heuristic] A witness who cannot recall events is evidence about the witness's condition, not proof that nothing happened, and should prompt a check of what the witness consumed. When: Witnesses have gaps in memory after a shared drink or meal. Why: A common substance can explain memory loss and point to a tampering route.
- [heuristic] Recalling a planted detail at the point it becomes important reminds the reader of it. When: a clue's meaning is about to be revealed. Why: The reminder links the early detail to the moment of payoff.
- [heuristic] A witness's recollections can show that documents said more than a narrow reading allowed, so memory should be checked against the record.
- [heuristic] Use short prompts that extend the witness's own recollection, such as asking whether they knew someone before a certain date. When: A witness is recalling past events. Why: Small prompts let the witness lead and carry the memory forward.
- [heuristic] An alibi or sightline is only as strong as the witness's position, attention and record; check where each witness stood and what they were doing.
- [heuristic] Recall-probing questions check what a witness observed, not what they intended, so they cannot establish motive.
- [heuristic] A habit of attention, such as methodical detail-by-detail scrutiny, can hint at a person's training or background. When: when forming early hypotheses about a person with few hard facts. Why: how someone attends to the world reflects their past.
- [heuristic] Witnesses often forget names and minor details, so accepting a gap can be better than pressing for it. When: when a witness cannot recall specifics.
- [heuristic] Verifying a witness's claim about where someone is staying can reveal that another person has been asking about the same target. When: A witness's account of a location cannot be confirmed.
- [heuristic] Read a witness's evasions, mood and stake in the outcome alongside their words, since each affects how far the account can be trusted. When: assessing any witness. Why: The shape of an answer carries information the content does not.
- [heuristic] A partial view can confirm a general impression, such as a person's presence, but not a specific identity.
- [heuristic] Recall a witness after other evidence has come in when their account conflicts with what was later revealed. When: a witness's account conflicts with later evidence.
- [heuristic] A small detail recalled late, such as part of a number, can be checked quickly and may yield either a confirmation or a new lead.
- [heuristic] Whether the watched person saw the witness reveals the witness's own risk, which raises the urgency of protecting them.
- [heuristic] Distance and poor conditions limit what a witness can reliably report, so a lead should stop where the observation actually ends.
- [heuristic] When a witness's account has a gap, test it against another person's record of the same events before trusting or dismissing it. When: the missing detail matters to the case. Why: a lapse can be genuine or convenient, and only corroboration tells them apart.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's new recall by specificity, consistency and checkability. Details that grow vaguer or harder to verify deserve less weight. When: A witness's memory changes over time.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC witness's memory improve with dialogue progress, but tier each new detail and make it checkable against world state. When: Designing NPC memory that unlocks through conversation.
- [heuristic] A guard who saw someone leave but dismissed it can hide a clue, giving the player reason to question the testimony. When: designing unreliable witnesses. Why: expectations hide what the witness saw.
- [heuristic] Offer players the choice between accepting a suspect's reaction at face value and testing it against other evidence. When: designing accusation scenes. Why: choice makes evidence checking a deliberate act.
- [heuristic] A harmless-looking NPC can carry hidden knowledge; an offhand remark by another NPC hinting the cover is false lets players catch it. When: When designing a low-status NPC who holds important information. Why: Hints make the mismatch discoverable.
- [heuristic] Place an incidental remark that reads innocently at first and gains meaning once the player's assumption is overturned. When: Scripting dialogue meant to pay off after a reveal. Why: A remark that is reinterpreted later rewards attentive players without signposting the answer.
- [heuristic] Counting containers and their marks can show how many people were present, and a discrepancy in the count can overturn a theory. When: Reconstructing who took part in a gathering. Why: Each person leaves traces such as wet rings or used glasses, so a mismatch shows an absent or extra person.
- [heuristic] Recalling a suspect while their emotions are still raw may prompt a confession sought as relief, though a calm suspect may still refuse. When: right after an emotionally charged scene. Why: the suspect may want to relieve distress.
- [heuristic] Treat witness approximations, such as 'about' times or 'four or five days', as ranges, not exact values, and distrust a sudden precise clock time from someone vague elsewhere. When: Reconstructing events from witness accounts. Why: Approximate estimates are common and witnesses often cannot recall exact numbers or times; a sudden precise figure may be unreliable.
- [heuristic] A witness's impression of a person's mood can count against a reading that implies deliberate harm, so compare it with the physical evidence. When: When a witness describes a victim's state of mind before an event. Why: An unsuspecting mood argues against a deliberate act.
- [heuristic] Readings of involuntary cues depend on background knowledge of the subject, so an observer without that history should treat a confident reading as unreliable. When: When interpreting a subject's cues without knowing their history. Why: Each link in a cue chain relies on known background.
- [heuristic] Trust a sensory report according to what that sense can reliably tell, so a firm sound from a known direction outweighs a cry of uncertain source. When: when judging a witness who heard something without seeing it. Why: Senses differ in localization and identification accuracy.
- [heuristic] Preserve or restate a clue in persistent written form so players can work it out at their own pace. When: When a puzzle needs sustained thought rather than a quick reaction. Why: Players solving over time need the clue available again without relying on memory.
- [heuristic] Collect independent reports from several observers before revealing your own conclusion, then compare them to expose disagreements.
- [heuristic] Choose a reconstruction timing window when observers are distracted, since people absorbed elsewhere notice little. When: Testing whether an act could go unseen. Why: Distraction determines whether a sequence could have passed unobserved.
- [heuristic] Compare who wrote each account, what access the writer had, and what the writer stood to gain before relying on it. When: When the primary record is lost or the writer had a stake in the outcome. Why: Access shows what a writer could know, and interest shows what they might distort.
- [heuristic] Assume a trained agent memorised a document after a brief look, rather than assuming it was carried away. When: when judging what a trained agent has learned from papers. Why: trained agents memorise closely.
- [heuristic] Give each NPC's knowledge a confidence value, and have the player cross-check two or three NPCs before acting on a clue. When: Designing NPCs with partial or uncertain knowledge. Why: Confidence values and cross-checks keep unreliable clues from being trusted alone.
- [heuristic] Treat details outside a witness's attention focus as unrecorded: the most vivid memory marks where attention was fixed, and divided attention may leave a detail never recorded. When: when weighing a witness's memory of a brief, fast or chaotic event.
- [heuristic] A witness's account is more reliable when backed by notes written at the time, with dates and hours. Why: Notes made close to the event resist later distortion.
- [heuristic] A witness who knows the household's routines and the person's appearance well carries more weight as an identifier. When: when weighing a close associate's identification. Why: Intimate knowledge makes recognition more reliable.
- [heuristic] Plant a precise number in an offhand witness memory, so the audience can re-read it later as evidence. When: a witness gives a casual account. Why: A detail recorded as trivial becomes decisive once its exact value is checked.
- [procedure] 1) Note visible cues in sequence, such as shifts in mood, gesture, gaze or expression, rather than waiting for words. 2) Tie each cue to the thought or need it implies. 3) Adjust your behavior to what they seem to need. 4) Test each reading against other sources or the subject's own account. When: When a witness's account is partial or impaired, or when inferring a subject's train of thought from observed cues. Why: Silent or impaired people signal through behavior, and single readings can mislead; linking each cue to a thought makes the reading testable. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) List each event with its source. 2) Mark which times are firm, from logs, and which are recollections or estimates, so players know which entries to doubt. 3) Leave gaps unfilled rather than assuming what happened in them. When: Several witnesses give partial times for the same events.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a free-recall prompt and let the subject narrate as far back as they can; the sequence should come from them, not your questions. 2) Note gaps, hedges and self-protective remarks. 3) Branch to narrower questions based on what they said. 4) Re-ask key points later. When: At a first interview or NPC dialogue before anything is checked. Why: Unprompted narration reveals what the subject chooses to include and omit.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the dated claim in a recollection. 2) Anchor it to an independent dated record, such as a journal, note or receipt. 3) Accept only the dates that match. When: A witness cannot recall when something happened or needs a memory of dates or times. Why: Recollection drifts, but independent dated records fix it.
- [procedure] 1) Record vague descriptors such as height, age and dress. 2) Compare them against physical evidence. 3) Narrow the suspect pool, then confirm with a physical or documentary source. When: A witness describes a person who is not known to the investigator. Why: Witness descriptions are imprecise, so they only narrow the field until corroborated.
- [procedure] 1) Assign one person to record events in real time. 2) Take notes of everything observed. 3) Build the account from those notes, either condensed or verbatim. When: Testimony will need to be checked or retold later.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness write what was worn or carried. 2) Compare that list with what is actually missing. 3) Name a specific omitted detail and ask again, waiting for recall. When: A witness can recall events but not every item.
- [procedure] 1) Ask about the most recent entry the witness is sure of. 2) Ask what came before it. 3) Use the layout of the record to fix position. 4) Bring in other people as anchors. 5) Confirm each inference, moving from general points to particular ones. When: When a witness cannot give a free account of a past day but can recall specific fixed points. Why: Each confirmed fixed point cues the next, rebuilding the sequence step by step.
- [procedure] 1) Ask when the witness first remembered a fact. 2) If memory appeared only after prompting, weigh the recollection as weaker. When: A witness suddenly recalls a fact useful to the case. Why: Recall triggered by a prompt may reflect suggestion rather than observation.
- [procedure] 1) Establish where the witness was posted. 2) Establish what they were busy with. 3) Ask what they could not see. 4) Identify every entry and exit they were meant to watch. When: When an alibi rests on a single observation point. Why: Blind spots define where unseen movement could happen.
- [procedure] Name a specific occasion, such as a particular day, to anchor a witness's memory, then ask who else was present.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the same question again later. 2) Ask what happened just before the event. 3) Compare the answers with independent records. When: a witness claims not to remember. Why: repeated and sideways questions reveal whether a blank is real or convenient.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the clue's symbol system. 2) Link its imagery to a known lore reference. 3) Form a reading. 4) Test the reading against later events or actions. When: A clue is written in a language, code, or symbol system the player or investigator does not know. Why: A reading validated by consequences is more reliable than one based on a single matching symbol.
- [procedure] 1) Choose cues with a known link to the matter. 2) Present them one at a time. 3) Watch for recognition or unthinking reactions. 4) Record partial recall and how quickly it fades. When: A subject's memory is in question. Why: Deliberate cues can bring up memory the subject cannot report on demand.
- [procedure] 1) Invite the witness to a discussion. 2) Present several facts at once. 3) Ask about specific familiar objects in a comfortable setting, which may trigger recall. When: when a witness's knowledge is essential but not surfacing.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm the witness's identity and route. 2) Ask for specifics such as names, places and mood. 3) Test the stated timing against an independent source such as a phone call. 4) Compare with physical traces. When: A single witness's account needs corroboration. Why: Specific, independently checked details separate reliable accounts from vague ones.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the vantage point, such as a hill, where the event could be seen. 2) Estimate how many people could fit within clear view. 3) Use that number to judge the scale of the event. When: When estimating how many witnesses an event could have had. Why: Visibility limits the audience, which constrains the event's likely size.
- [procedure] 1) Separate the advice a document gives from the outcome it endorses. 2) Check clauses that grant grounds for action against those that restrain it. 3) Compare the document with the later record of what was actually done. When: Evaluating a formal or hedged source whose conclusion matters. Why: Advice, permissions and actual outcomes can diverge.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness for a description of the person or event. 2) Note how vivid and specific the answer is. 3) Treat a vague answer as a weak link. When: When a witness claims to remember a person or event. Why: A description reveals how much the witness actually observed, and vague memory limits what can be built on.
- [tradeoff] Verbatim repetition shows retention of wording, but reconstruction under pressure can keep the memory while the wording drifts, so the test is less reliable then. When: A witness is asked to reconstruct a statement under pressure. Why: Stress can change phrasing even when the underlying memory is intact.
- [pitfall] Overheard words gain meaning once a witness learns of an event; a warning reported after the harm may be recalled afterwards, so it is not proof of prediction. When: a witness recalls overheard words or a warning after learning of an event. Why: Later knowledge reshapes memory and can add significance that was not there. (x2)
- [pitfall] Recollections formed later are shaped by suspicion or a prior favourable view of one side, so they may differ from what was said and are weak evidence. When: When testimony rests on an old recollection the witness admits is uncertain, or a witness holds a view of one side. Why: Later suspicion or prior opinion can reshape what was remembered. (x2)
- [pitfall] Approximate ages and appearance estimates vary with the witness and year, so they should narrow the suspect pool and be checked against a register, not identify one person precisely. (x2)
- [pitfall] A detail planted too far before its payoff may be forgotten entirely, so the payoff must come within reach of the player's memory.
- [pitfall] Leading questions and emphasis can plant false memories, so agreement with a supplied detail proves little; the witness may agree with the questioner instead of recalling. When: When a questioner supplies or stresses a detail the witness should confirm. Why: Suggestion can replace recall.
- [pitfall] Witnesses fill gaps in later recall with assumptions or expectations held at the time, so observed facts must be recorded apart from inferences.
- [pitfall] Identifications from partial views or incomplete recall can be wrong despite confidence, as similar coats or builds produce the same recognition; corroborate uncertain matches with a second source.
- [pitfall] Frightened or motivated witnesses' firm answers, and confident recalled dates or exact times, can be wrong; keep time windows open until independently confirmed before timelines count as proof. When: Relying on a witness's confident directions, recalled dates or timelines. Why: Confidence in delivery or recall does not guarantee accuracy.
- [pitfall] Recalled speech and letters are reconstructions, so exact wording is approximate; check quoted letters against originals, and write down statements when heard, since no other listener can verify private talk. When: When a witness recalls or reads aloud speech, a private conversation, or a letter. Why: Recall of wording degrades, and exact-wording memory depends on listener memory and attention.
- [pitfall] Recaps repeat old errors or add new ones and spread hearsay; each retold item should add a correction or new link, since repetition delays the answer without adding information.
- [pitfall] Single observers see only part of a scene and tend to overstate partial glimpses, so ask what they did not see and check their account against other accounts and traces. When: When a single observer describes a scene or a partial glimpse. Why: A glimpse such as a few lines read from a distance is easy to overstate.
- [pitfall] Old memories of events decades past are reconstructed and blurred, so sworn testimony about them, including childhood memories, can sound more certain than it is. When: When a witness recounts events long past, such as early life or decades-old events. Why: The oath does not fix the facts; reconstruction can feel more certain than it is.
- [pitfall] Observers who break agreed protocol or report different kinds of result make the group's record incomparable and unreliable; a record is comparable only when everyone follows the same protocol. When: When several observers or investigators report one event or progress.
- [pitfall] Sensory impressions such as drafts, smells or sounds are easily misremembered, and a recalled sound may not be the one that matters, so they should not carry a claim alone. Why: Witnesses may also misremember times or sounds.
- [pitfall] A witness who suddenly recalls more, or recalls a sound after the fact, may assign it to a convenient person without evidence, shifting blame. When: When a witness suddenly names a person or recalls a sound, especially after a threat or deadline.
- [pitfall] Absorbed observers drift from their posts, and eager ones who move or peer around cover give themselves away to the subject, so undisciplined watchers cannot be trusted.
- [pitfall] Routine records such as laundry days are easy to misremember under stress, so they need checking against other sources. When: Relying on a witness's recall of household routines. Why: Stress degrades memory of ordinary events.
- [pitfall] A single witness's recollection can miss the decisive fact, and gossip channels often carry it, so ignoring servants and tradespeople is a mistake. When: Investigating how information spread. Why: Lower-status channels move news between households and often hold the key detail.
- [pitfall] A deadline mentioned once and then dropped loses its pressure, so later scenes no longer feel like a race.
- [pitfall] Approximate times and descriptions can be wrong without any intent to deceive, so error and lying must be told apart.
- [pitfall] A link that exists only in memory may be coincidence or a recall error; re-check the original wording before relying on it.
- [pitfall] Relying on a witness's memory that items were unchanged is only as strong as that witness's reliability. When: When the argument depends on a witness recalling the state of a place or object. Why: Unchanged-item testimony can be wrong or misremembered.
- [pitfall] A deliberate habit such as keeping a clock fast can be forgotten when a witness reconstructs an event later, shifting their reported times. When: Reconstructing times from memory. Why: The bias may not be in the witness's mind when they recall the event.
- [pitfall] A witness's inventory count can be wrong or self-serving, so the inference from a mismatch depends on the count being accurate. When: When relying on a witness's account of possessions. Why: Witnesses may misremember or misreport, which can create a false mismatch.
- [pitfall] Staff recollections are approximate and may conflict, so they should be cross-checked against records.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a report because the accused cannot remember the event is a mistake, since memory failure does not disprove the report. When: Evaluating a report against a suspect's claimed lack of memory. Why: Forgetting is not evidence that the event did not occur.
- [pitfall] An examiner who misreports another witness's words to the accused can mislead them into admissions.
- [pitfall] A key fact can be missed when it is buried under filler, and a deviation can be mistaken for noise because the witness shrugs it off. When: When a witness delivers a long account with several details. Why: The witness's casual tone can hide the significance of a detail the investigator needs.
- [pitfall] Revealing a fact in a way that lets the suspect trace it can expose the source to retaliation, so the source must be protected. When: The disclosed fact came from a named or identifiable source. Why: A suspect who turns blame onto the informant can damage a useful contact.
- [pitfall] A distressed client may withhold the real reason for a request and give less precise answers, while sympathy can lead the investigator to accept the account too quickly. When: Interviewing an emotionally distressed client. Why: Distress reduces precision and sympathy lowers scrutiny.
- [pitfall] Treating a later summary as an eyewitness record overstates its reliability. When: When a secondary account is cited as if it came from a witness. Why: Summaries pass through another writer's selection and memory.
- [pitfall] A verbal credential that is never verified lets a false claim pass as true at a checkpoint.
- [pitfall] Small details recalled from memory, such as an accessory or whether something was left in place, are often wrong unless closely noticed; check the object itself. When: when witnesses are asked about personal accessories or small details. Why: unnoticed details are rarely remembered accurately, and the object itself is more reliable than recall.
- [pitfall] A witness's confident time estimate may be inaccurate, and a rambling answer can hide that the witness did not notice the time. When: Relying on a witness's stated duration. Why: Certainty and detail feel reliable but do not measure elapsed time.
- [pitfall] Witnesses record details that seem unimportant to them, such as whether a house was dark, and forget details the inquiry needs. When: Collecting witness testimony for an investigation. Why: Witnesses judge relevance by their own experience, not by the inquiry's needs.
- [pitfall] A witness who recalls a detail only after reflection may have that memory shaped by later thinking, so early and late accounts should be compared. When: when a witness remembers a detail after a delay. Why: Reflection can reconstruct or alter what was originally perceived.
- [pitfall] Timelines built from memory are unreliable and should be anchored to records where possible. When: When reconstructing an event sequence from witness recall. Why: Memory drifts, so records give firmer anchors.
- [fact] A witness reports only what angle, distance, light, attention and memory let them perceive; a brief glance in poor light yields a sparse, shaky picture of features. When: a witness had a brief or poor view. Why: Limited light, time, angle and attention restrict what is actually perceived.
- [fact] Identification from memory is weaker than a receipt or record and must be checked against it, since partial impressions are fallible. When: a witness's recollection conflicts with a documented sale or record. Why: Memory is fallible in ways written records are not.
- [fact] A detailed witness description can still be partial: height, age or dress may be recalled while other traits, like eye colour, are not.
- [fact] A witness's memory of writing seen in unusual conditions, such as floating in air, may be unreliable for judging gender or style. When: Relying on a witness to identify a writer. Why: Unusual viewing conditions limit what can be reliably observed.
- [fact] Witnesses often cannot confirm whether a specific bolt was engaged, even when they know a related door was usually locked. When: when questioning witnesses about door states at night. Why: routine knowledge of one door does not transfer to others.
- [fact] Witnesses to a document signing often see the manner of the process rather than the contents, so their reports describe behaviour, not text.
- [fact] A witness's remembered details, such as a distinctive physical feature, are only as reliable as the memory behind them. When: A witness supplies specific remembered details, especially under duress. Why: Memory can be incomplete or mistaken even for vivid details.
- [fact] A clue's physical size does not determine its value; a large object can be overlooked while investigators search for small traces. When: Judging the importance of physical evidence. Why: Size is a poor proxy for evidential relevance.
- [fact] Identifying someone by voice through a wall is only as strong as the voice's distinctiveness and the listener's attention, and distinctive voices are often easy to imitate. When: when a single auditory witness is the only evidence someone was present. Why: The trait that makes a voice memorable also makes it easy to mimic.

## reasoning bias
- [definition] A belief frame is a shared doctrine that fixes in advance who is suspect, what counts as the offence, and what proof of it looks like.
- [definition] A guess is a specific, definite conclusion drawn from facts that justify only a general, indefinite one.
- [mechanism] Model an early biased report that later evidence gradually corrects, giving players a slow reversal of belief. When: designing a story where a reputation must be overturned. Why: gradual correction feels earned.
- [mechanism] An observer who accepts an early explanation reads later anomalies as confirmation, so a confident unproven theory can end inquiry before it is proven. When: observer has accepted a neat explanation, or an investigator holds an unproven theory and collects new clues. Why: A fitting frame makes new facts look like support; early hypotheses shape how later details are read.
- [mechanism] When reader and character share the same wrong assumption, the error stays hidden until a face-to-face meeting forces a check. When: a story uses a misleading sender or identity. Why: the meeting tests the assumption directly.
- [mechanism] A player's assumptions from earlier encounters bias how they read later evidence, which designers can use for fair misdirection.
- [mechanism] Two characters who share one trait the player has not compared give a link that is discoverable only when the player looks for it. When: Designing connections between NPCs. Why: Unlinked traits stay hidden until the player compares them.
- [mechanism] When many judges, clergy and scholars endorse one belief, its apparent breadth can look like independent proof, even when all draw on the same underlying authority. When: A belief appears to be supported by many respected figures. Why: Repeated endorsement from connected sources creates the appearance of separate confirmation.
- [mechanism] A person caught near a crime scene is not necessarily the culprit; they may be a decoy or simply in the wrong place, so proximity alone should not settle guilt. When: A suspect is found near the scene but has no clear link to the stolen goods. Why: Physical presence at a scene is weak evidence of responsibility.
- [behavior] Repetition makes a claim feel confirmed, even when it rests on one unverified root; repetition is not verification, and a planned deception gains strength from being repeated. When: a claim must seem believable to several observers. Why: Independent-seeming confirmation raises trust in a claim. (x2)
- [behavior] Emotional closeness, attraction or sympathy toward a suspect or witness colours how cues and later facts are read, even when the investigator tries to dismiss the thought. When: suspicion falls on a person the investigator knows well, or an interviewer is emotionally involved with a witness. Why: emotional closeness biases interpretation of new evidence.
- [behavior] Players accept an object's look as its label, or a barrier's look as security, ignoring contradicting physical evidence like unexpected weight until testing overturns it. When: an object's visible identity conflicts with how it feels, or a locked barrier is presented as impassable. Why: Visual appearance substitutes for testing; a familiar identity removes the question the anomaly raises.
- [behavior] Several independent confirmations make an investigator feel the account is solid, even when the key question remains unanswered. When: when multiple checks agree on secondary points.
- [behavior] A witness's prior opinion of a person shapes how they interpret and report that person's behaviour. When: when a witness has an existing view of the person.
- [behavior] A person who walks straight to the correct door and office shows prior familiarity with a place, which can expose a claim of being a stranger. When: A suspect claims never to have been in a location. Why: Unprompted navigation reveals learned routes.
- [behavior] Believing a person to be a seer gives followers a new purpose and binds them together. When: Followers hold a belief about a mystical figure among them.
- [behavior] A suspect who names a fact before anyone has announced it reveals that they already knew it. When: When news is shared in a group scene. Why: Early mention of unannounced information shows prior knowledge.
- [behavior] Frequent daily contact with someone does not protect others from being fooled by an imitation of that person's voice.
- [behavior] Listeners who owe the accuser a favor are more willing to hear an extraordinary claim out. When: When a claim challenges what the listener believes. Why: Past goodwill lowers the resistance that disbelief would otherwise create.
- [behavior] Investigators may feel sick about a close that leaves questions open, even when the legal outcome is settled. When: when a case ends with unresolved questions. Why: Moral questions can remain after the legal decision.
- [behavior] A witness who hoped to share in the prestige of an event may shape their account to fit that wish, colouring how they speak. When: when a witness had a stake in being connected to an event. Why: A desire for reflected status biases recall and tone.
- [behavior] A crime staged to echo a familiar story gives observers a ready script they recognize at once, before its details are checked. When: a scene repeats a known story, rhyme or name. Why: recognition of a known script happens instantly.
- [behavior] Courts and crowds can credit vivid unverifiable testimony even when the accused know it to be false. When: Dramatic testimony is delivered before an audience. Why: Vivid accounts carry authority independent of their truth.
- [behavior] A witness whose belief changes during a case may reshape the account to fit the outcome they now expect. When: a witness changes their view mid-case. Why: recollection is adjusted to match new belief.
- [behavior] A listener who openly dismisses a legend can still react to an ordinary sound the legend predicts, showing belief that persists below conscious rejection. When: a legend links an ordinary sign to a curse. Why: long-held belief lingers beneath stated disbelief.
- [behavior] Once an unexplained object's purpose is revealed, the solution seems obvious in hindsight, though it was not obvious before. When: after a puzzle is solved. Why: Revealed facts make the answer appear self-evident.
- [behavior] People who do not know a language judge it by intonation alone and still sound confident, so their certainty does not reflect competence. When: when hearing speech in an unfamiliar language. Why: they lack the words and grammar to judge accurately.
- [behavior] A suspect's suspicious reaction, such as fainting, may have an innocent cause that must be weighed against guilt. When: a suspect shows distress or odd behaviour during an investigation. Why: emotional shock can mimic guilt.
- [behavior] When sound cannot be heard at a distance, suspicion grows from what is seen and what is missing, not from confirmed facts. When: when observing from far away. Why: the observer lacks confirmed information.
- [behavior] Investigators tend to dismiss a repeated token as a prank or coincidence when each incident, taken alone, looks like an accident. When: each incident has already been ruled accidental. Why: no single event looks suspicious, so the shared mark is not connected to the others.
- [behavior] Players and investigators tend to accept the first complete explanation offered by a trusted source, even when it leaves a key detail unexplained. When: A tidy solution from an authority or press account arrives early. Why: A complete-seeming story relieves the need to keep searching.
- [behavior] Suspicion of a stranger is raised more by others' reactions to him than by his own behaviour. When: introducing an unknown character. Why: Observers read threat from how a group responds.
- [behavior] Opposing parties press the same timing data toward their own theories, so one set of facts can support both. When: when a case has rival narratives. Why: a range allows either side to pick the end that suits it.
- [behavior] A target who believes he is being followed is unlikely to lead his pursuers to contacts or hidden goods. When: A released suspect may notice surveillance. Why: Awareness of pursuit changes the target's behavior and ends the expected trail.
- [behavior] An investigator's assumption about a suspect's position can make the correct conclusion seem impossible and hide the answer already in view. When: The likely answer conflicts with a player's assumptions about a character. Why: Preconceived views about who could act filter out contradicting evidence.
- [behavior] People look for a difference when they expect one and for a match when they expect a match. When: comparing two faces, records or accounts. Why: the expectation directs what the comparison searches for.
- [behavior] A confident denial of danger from an authority can make the audience question the denial itself, since its certainty draws scrutiny. When: a character insists a dangerous route is perfectly safe. Why: overconfidence reads as a cue to test the claim.
- [behavior] A witness absorbed in other business may not register a substitution at all, since attention is limited. When: when a witness is occupied during the event. Why: attention is limited and goes to what seems important.
- [behavior] A person who offers an alternative theory may gain from steering attention elsewhere. When: Someone proposes an explanation that benefits them. Why: Their stake shapes what they suggest.
- [behavior] Witnesses judge strangers by appearance and status, so a recognized face may be misfiled at first.
- [behavior] Audiences fixate on facts that are emphasised and miss facts presented as background, so a key clue can sit in plain view unnoticed. When: a key fact is stated as ordinary scene detail. Why: background details seem unimportant and are skipped.
- [behavior] An offhand remark, once repeated by a character, can grow into a full theory the character then acts on. When: a casual remark is repeated and elaborated. Why: repetition makes a loose hint feel like evidence.
- [behavior] Observers hold stereotyped expectations of how sincere and calculating people look, and they treat a match with that stereotype as confirmation. When: An observer judges a person's intentions from manner. Why: Confirmation of a stereotype feels like evidence, even when it is not.
- [behavior] A second, more damaging version of the same secret shifts suspicion onto the person already suspected, even when a third party only asserts it. When: A rumour reframes a known secret more harshly. Why: Each new teller adds an interpretation.
- [behavior] Opponents often underestimate a character they dismiss as foolish, but that advantage ends once they learn the character's true purpose.
- [behavior] When each linked identity is examined alone, the investigator may never compare them directly, so a shared link can stay hidden for a long time. When: Investigating several related records one at a time. Why: Separate examination frames the subjects as unrelated.
- [behavior] When every character is listed as a possible suspect, players spread attention thinly and miss the few people with both motive and access. When: when a large suspect pool is presented without filtering. Why: Broad suspicion dilutes focus across too many leads.
- [behavior] Players judge who could act from how other characters describe one another, so those descriptions shape suspicion as much as the facts do. When: Characters describe the people around a victim.
- [behavior] A character who judges another by an assumed type will shape what they tell that person and what they withhold. When: one character forms a quick opinion of another. Why: The judgment, not the facts, guides the interaction.
- [behavior] People accept offers from a host who controls every step of a familiar routine, such as pouring and toasting, which makes a trap possible. When: when an offer follows a social ritual. Why: guests trust routine hospitality.
- [behavior] Conspicuous behaviour such as stopping to dispose of something in a busy place looks suspicious to passers-by. When: A concealer acts in view of others. Why: Unusual actions draw attention even when the object is hidden.
- [behavior] A target who cannot explain a discovered item sounds less credible when denying it, even if innocent, because the item looks more convincing than the denial. When: A planted item is found and the target has no memory of it. Why: Having no account of the item weakens the denial.
- [behavior] Suspicion settles more readily on people already disliked, poor, or isolated than on fresh evidence. When: a community is looking for someone to blame. Why: few are positioned to speak for them.
- [behavior] A private channel of influence is assumed to serve personal interests, even when its holder intends to help. When: Decisions are made privately and their basis is hidden. Why: Secrecy makes benevolent and self-serving motives indistinguishable from outside.
- [behavior] One event, such as a sudden change of fortune, can be read as luck or as providence, so it supports opposing interpretations. When: Observers react to a sudden change in a family's fortune. Why: Interpretation depends on the observer's framework, not on the event itself.
- [behavior] Distrust and attachment can coexist; an observer may suspect someone while remaining reluctant to lose sight of them.
- [behavior] Suspicion of a character shifts as new reactions and grudges appear, so earlier judgments of that character should be revisited. Why: New behaviour and disputes change how earlier actions read.
- [behavior] An investigator's cheerful or evasive manner can conceal progress and lead others to misjudge what is known. When: A character hides their findings behind a light manner. Why: Demeanour is read as a sign of state of knowledge.
- [rule] Before accepting a single witness at face value, check for a prior dispute, such as a recent quarrel, between accuser and accused.
- [rule] A reflex shows that a mark exists but is not proof of guilt; combine it with other facts before drawing a conclusion. When: a physical test produces a reaction. Why: A reaction confirms a physical fact, not the motive or the act.
- [rule] Use an NPC's stated beliefs or habits as a suspect filter, and let players test the filter with a search or check. When: Designing suspect logic in a mystery.
- [rule] Do not rely on shorthand alone when a wrong reading would send someone to the wrong place.
- [rule] Let a suggested reading settle for a pause before pressing for an answer. When: a witness is considering a proposed explanation. Why: A hurried witness gives a less considered response.
- [rule] Ask an expert for the basis of each estimate, and treat hedged estimates as ranges rather than fixed facts. When: Medical or forensic evidence is central to a claim. Why: Estimates depend on assumptions, and the basis shows how much confidence they deserve.
- [rule] Before judging a missing item, establish whether its earlier state is known, because an absence cannot be measured against an unrecorded state. When: assessing a clue that has disappeared. Why: Without a recorded prior state, no comparison is possible.
- [rule] If a target was already being watched or threatened, treat an unexpected summons with extra suspicion.
- [rule] Ask witnesses when they arrived and what they knew of the victim, which tests prior acquaintance and timing and can reopen earlier conversations.
- [rule] Gather a subject's medical history before reading a physical sign, since a long-standing condition can explain a mark that examiners would otherwise read as significant. When: when examining a person for signs of a condition. Why: context from family or records can account for the sign.
- [heuristic] Check whether the same behaviour was seen or recorded before: a repeated pattern suggests routine, makes an account more credible, and quickly tests whether a story fits. When: judging whether an odd behaviour is significant or an NPC's account needs quick verification.
- [heuristic] Do not assume a biased witness is lying or treat deception as mere bias; they look alike but need different responses, and a disclosed bias can be corrected for. When: assessing a witness with a personal stake, such as affection for a suspect. Why: Disclosed bias can be corrected for rather than discarded; bias and deception produce similar surface behavior.
- [heuristic] An investigator should set aside personal distress to examine and record marks accurately. When: when documenting a painful case. Why: Distress can make the record less accurate.
- [heuristic] Early, when evidence is thin, list several plausible explanations and treat each as a testable theory. When: Evidence is thin and the investigation has just begun. Why: Several testable explanations give the investigation direction without committing to one.
- [heuristic] Trust a long, close acquaintance with someone's normal condition over descriptions of that person in an unusual or disturbed state. When: judging a claim about a person's behavior at a particular time. Why: long familiarity gives a stable baseline.
- [heuristic] A feature shared by two suspects can read as a pairing rather than as evidence, so check it on its own terms.
- [heuristic] Two matching shared past events make a stronger identification than appearance alone. Why: Shared history is harder to fake than a face.
- [heuristic] A beneficiary told of a gift in advance has a different relationship to the death than one who was surprised, so note foreknowledge when weighing motive. When: assessing beneficiaries. Why: Foreknowledge changes how a beneficiary relates to the outcome.
- [heuristic] Rivals are sensitive to shared credit; a clear account of who did what avoids later friction.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC confirm a plausible but wrong theory, then supply the contradicting clue at a later stage so players must revise it.
- [heuristic] Test a supernatural explanation by asking who gains from the belief, instead of ruling it in or out in advance. When: when a set of events invites a supernatural explanation. Why: a belief that serves a person may be planted rather than real.
- [heuristic] Treat a witness's favourite explanation as information about the witness as well as about the crime.
- [heuristic] Cryptic notes written in a shorthand players learn over time reward familiarity, since decoding gets easier with each exposure.
- [heuristic] A victim's report of feeling unwell before leaving can rule out a dose taken after leaving, if the symptom came from the poison. When: A victim describes early symptoms before a departure. Why: Early symptoms place the dose before the departure.
- [heuristic] Doubt any theory that requires a person to act against deeply held principles, even if the theory is logically possible. When: a suspect's behaviour depends on a change of character or belief. Why: character constrains what a person would realistically do.
- [heuristic] Treat a convenient outside-intruder explanation as a hypothesis. Drop it when the evidence fits it poorly, even if it fits the first clues. When: when the crime seems to point to an outsider. Why: Early evidence can make a stranger look plausible while later traces contradict the theory.
- [heuristic] Treat an investigator's personal tie to the victim as a possible motive, and test it rather than dismissing it quickly. When: the investigator knew the victim closely. Why: a quick dismissal of one's own motive can hide a real suspect.
- [heuristic] Agreement among authorities is not a reason to discount a well-informed view that is backed by data. When: A dissenting view is supported by evidence. Why: Popularity does not determine correctness; evidence does.
- [heuristic] Do not assume bias without evidence; establish it from documented actions and writings. When: suspecting an official of partiality.
- [heuristic] Use ordeal verdicts when a setting's justice rests on divine or natural judgment, and make clear the result is a matter of belief rather than fact-finding.
- [heuristic] Reward early hunches with progress, but keep the final accusation gated behind conclusive clues. When: designing an investigation with several clues.
- [heuristic] When evidence is incomplete, weigh competing presumptions against each other, and when the balance lies with the accused, favor the accused. When: evidence is incomplete. Why: charity to the accused guards against wrongful verdicts.
- [heuristic] An early sense that two handwritings match is often overconfident and should be retested on closer study.
- [heuristic] Life cues around a body, such as clothing, food set out, and a used dish, make observers assume the person is merely asleep. When: When a still person sits in a room showing ordinary activity. Why: Signs of routine life suggest the occupant is only resting.
- [heuristic] Track the player's personal bias toward particular NPCs, since bias can steer which suspects the player pursues.
- [heuristic] A group that matches a public stereotype is easily accepted as a false lead, because stereotypes fill gaps in evidence and make innocent people look guilty. When: When a suspect fits an expected profile too neatly. Why: Shared stereotypes substitute for individual evidence.
- [heuristic] When a questioner shows doubt, push back against the doubt itself rather than defending the name. When: when a questioner begins to disbelieve the cover. Why: defending the name invites a closer check.
- [heuristic] Judgment of people improves when a natural instinct is made systematic through study of psychology.
- [heuristic] A theory explaining every clue at once feels more certain than it is; treat it with extra suspicion and test it as rigorously as any rival. When: a combined theory appears to resolve every clue. Why: Persuasive completeness hides flaws; explaining every clue is not proof.
- [heuristic] Trusting a source because it is emotional or vivid, rather than because it is first-hand, leads to error. When: Choosing which account to believe. Why: Vividness can substitute for direct knowledge.
- [heuristic] Principled belief or disbelief, like 'people do not do such things', should be a prior lowering likelihood, not a verdict; keep the test open since rare acts happen.
- [tradeoff] Vivid, personal events anchor timelines because witnesses date them consistently, yet vivid, confident accounts can still be wrong about order and dates; verify them. When: Ordering events from memory. Why: Vivid events are encoded more strongly, so dates are more stable across witnesses, but confidence does not ensure accuracy.
- [tradeoff] Acting on a false claim costs one thing and ignoring a true claim costs another, so uncertain claims can remain unresolved. When: Deciding whether to act on an unverified claim.
- [tradeoff] A wrong but believable public theory builds pressure on a suspect, but it muddies the record of what is actually known. When: when pressure on a suspect is the goal.
- [pitfall] Vivid, memorable or unfalsifiable details feel reliable but are weak support, not proof, leading to untestable conclusions; prefer plain, checkable details with independent corroboration. Why: A detail that stands out is not thereby verified. (x2)
- [pitfall] Once a suspect is labelled guilty, audiences and interrogators read denials as evasion, silence as confirmation, and new facts as support, so contrary evidence is ignored. When: an accuser or interrogator holds a fixed suspicion. Why: the accusation becomes the frame for interpreting new facts. (x2)
- [pitfall] A listener's jealousy or an observer's irritation can shape how a stated-versus-real mismatch or partial view is read as motive; such readings need more evidence. (x2)
- [pitfall] Suspicion, fear or unease can make innocent details and objects look guilty or sinister, so record such feelings as feelings, not proof. When: an observer holds a belief or is under suspicion. Why: Fear can mimic evidence; suspicion colours how ordinary things are read. (x2)
- [pitfall] Once suspicion settles on one person, later evidence and mishaps are read as fitting that accusation and alternatives go untested; the reading darkens with each added fact. When: an investigator holds an early theory of who is responsible, a case builds against one person, or a suspect has been named. Why: Fixation makes weak or unrelated facts look like support; each fact is read through the first theory. (x2)
- [pitfall] A vivid, specific account can make a biased, gossipy or aggrieved witness seem more reliable, since the most vivid record may be the most biased. Why: Detail makes a witness feel credible regardless of bias. (x2)
- [pitfall] Relief or a wished-for outcome, such as finding a guilty person, can decide which facts seem related or justify weaker proof; the desire must not override the standard of proof. When: pressure to reach a verdict is high, or relief or a preferred outcome shapes reading. (x2)
- [pitfall] Once a theory forms early, contrary facts are reinterpreted as support or dismissed as noise, while new clues are fitted to it, keeping the real culprit out of view. When: an investigator commits early to a single theory or suspect. Why: confirmation bias protects a settled conclusion.
- [pitfall] A private suspicion makes neutral replies, remarks or wording read as confirmation, so ordinary phrases start to feel like warnings or proof of guilt. When: an investigator or reader already holds a prior suspicion or senses a concealed motive. Why: Confirmation bias turns neutral remarks into apparent support.
- [pitfall] Once a theory of guilt is held, tailing a suspect or existing expectations make each new act, even ambiguous laughter, be fitted to the theory. When: a single theory of the suspect's guilt is already held. Why: Investigators tend to see confirmation in what they already expect.
- [pitfall] Feelings about a case, or attachment to a theory because it is coherent and exciting, make a plausible story seem certain before its links are tested. When: forming a preferred theory during an investigation. Why: Feelings about a case can tilt weighing of the same facts.
- [pitfall] Clinging to one favoured theory as settled blinds the investigator to better hypotheses and filters contrary evidence; keep several explanations open until facts close them. When: one explanation feels most likely early on. Why: attachment to a theory filters out contrary evidence.
- [pitfall] Vivid, eye-catching clues are often overweighted, though the least damaging item may be the most striking one.
- [pitfall] Vivid reconstruction can outrun the evidence, so flag uncertain details such as the presence of objects or people.
- [pitfall] An investigator with a personal stake may read a sequence of actions as proof of intent, so the observer's own bias must be checked too.
- [pitfall] An investigator who already suspects a person may read that person's probing question as proof of guilt rather than as a check on the claim. When: The investigator formed the belief before the test. Why: Prior belief shapes how the same question is interpreted.
- [pitfall] Personal stake or sympathy, such as rivalry, grief, anger or liking a suspect, can skew evidence and motive readings, persist against contrary clues, and hide clues otherwise noticed. When: investigator has a personal link to a suspect, victim or witness, holds rivalry, grief or anger, or favours a character. Why: Feelings shape what a person attends to and how evidence is weighed.
- [pitfall] Affection, attachment, charm or social standing toward a witness, or personal unease, can bend an investigator's judgement of their account; feeling is not evidence of reliability. When: weighing a trusted acquaintance's, charming or prominent witness's account, or contact goes beyond the professional. Why: Emotion colours self-assessment, so the bias may go unnoticed.
- [pitfall] Reading each new fact in a favoured theory's favour means it is never really tested; test a favoured theory as hard as its rivals, since one's own hypothesis can mislead.
- [pitfall] A settled early view resists later evidence, and a motive-driven theory can be shaped by the investigator's prejudice as well as the suspect's apparent motive. Why: A settled conclusion filters how later evidence is weighed.
- [pitfall] Reading a room or alarming fragment to confirm a theory yields findings fitting the theory, not the evidence; a fixed view of a suspect makes observers record matching details. When: observers hold a fixed view of a suspect, interpret incomplete evidence under suspicion, or read a room to confirm a theory. Why: Expectation shapes perception so unrelated facts look like support.
- [pitfall] An early unverified assumption about who, when or what the case concerns steers every later inference and search; test it against data and revise when contradicted. When: framing an investigation around an unconfirmed suspicion or assumption.
- [pitfall] Witness or group agreement can reflect shared expectations, a staff roster, a common story or cultural belief rather than independent observation; list shared assumptions before trusting it. When: several witnesses or a group agree on a detail, account or explanation. Why: Shared sources make agreement look stronger than it is.
- [pitfall] A tidy, convenient or settled explanation discourages testing: convenience replaces evidence, other causes go unsearched, contrary clues are missed, and unchecked accounts get built upon. When: a scene looks too tidy, a clue conveniently implicates one suspect, or an explanation is accepted as settled. Why: A satisfying story reduces the felt need to check contradictions.
- [pitfall] Vivid memory of a person, especially under stress, is not proof of identity or whereabouts; detail makes someone memorable without making them traceable or certain. When: a witness describes someone in rich detail or relies on a vivid, shocked recollection. Why: Memorable description supplies no verifiable identifiers; stress can make a chance resemblance seem certain.
- [pitfall] Vivid, specific testimony can be sincere yet wrong, reconstructed later or uncorroborated, especially when it fits expectations; richness is not verification, so check physical facts or other witnesses. When: a witness gives vivid, specific detail such as dates, escapes or personal objects, especially when it fits expectations. Why: Concrete texture feels like proof even when no one has verified it.
- [pitfall] Vivid, emotional accusations can pass as fact or silence a skeptic, and old phrases from angry speakers can sound like evidence; check physical support and origin before accepting the reading. Why: Drama and emotion make claims feel true; emotion gives hearsay the sound of proof.
- [pitfall] Vivid phrasing or lively narration can replace the precise observation and blur what was seen with what was guessed; check the observation itself. When: a witness uses colourful, emotive or lively narration. Why: Memorable phrasing replaces precise detail and carries assumptions.
- [pitfall] A vivid detail or explanation can pull attention from physical contradictions, seem central when it is not, and make a weak lead look stronger than the evidence supports. Why: Vividness captures attention before physical facts are checked.
- [pitfall] A neat reversal, or a single confession that explains everything or adds unseen facts, can feel contrived to an audience, especially when introduced for convenience rather than planted earlier. When: writing a final explanation of a mystery. Why: Audiences resist explanations that look introduced for convenience.
- [pitfall] Observers read a look or flush through their own bias; attractiveness or sympathy can pass for innocence and nervousness for guilt. When: interpreting a character one finds appealing or unsettling, or a bodily reaction. Why: Appearance and emotion distort how signs are read.
- [pitfall] Attraction, greed or personal interest in an item or person can distort judgement; not every examined object is evidence, so irrelevant objects get overvalued.
- [pitfall] Rumours about someone one likes or distrusts are weighed through pride, sympathy or prior suspicion; accepting one that fits a held suspicion leads to false conclusions. When: assessing a rumour about a person one already likes or distrusts. Why: Personal feelings distort the weighing of probability against character.
- [pitfall] Once a reading, match or suspect is adopted, people seek confirming evidence, overrate a second match, and ignore counterexamples; test a pattern against cases that do not fit. When: a new reading of a clue is adopted, a match is found, or suspicion attaches to one person. Why: People favour evidence that confirms a hunch.
- [pitfall] Clinging to a convenient accident explanation, such as a body knocked about by natural forces, can hide a wound made during life until physical evidence forces revision. When: an injury could be explained by accidental movement.
- [pitfall] A clue matching an expected suspect profile or confirming an assumption, or one that looks deliberately placed, may be exactly what the offender intended. When: an investigator's prior belief makes a clue seem to fit, or a placement looks deliberate. Why: Preconceptions make planted evidence convincing; deliberate placement attracts suspicion.
- [pitfall] The first plausible reading, often a habit of thought, may fit one detail yet fail the remaining facts; test it against all facts before accepting it. When: decoding a fragment with several candidate readings. Why: Early plausibility does not survive checks against the full evidence.
- [pitfall] Treating an intuitive guess or chain of plausible guesses as established fact lets deduction outrun evidence; mark which steps remain unproven.
- [pitfall] An investigator's own impressions of a witness can be as unreliable as the witness's impressions of the suspect. When: When forming judgments about people from limited acquaintance. Why: Limited acquaintance lets feelings shape the judgment.
- [pitfall] Reasoning from similar past cases helps, but it can push a deduction toward a familiar pattern and away from the evidence at hand. Why: past experience creates expectations that can override new facts.
- [pitfall] Settling on an unseen suspect's name early can end further inquiry, because the player stops looking for evidence that could contradict it. Why: A settled label feels like an answer.
- [pitfall] A witness's bias can colour a conclusion even when their facts are accurate. Separate what they observed from what they concluded. When: when a witness has a personal stake in the outcome. Why: Accurate observations can be paired with biased inferences.
- [pitfall] Visible frustration in an investigator gives the suspect an opening and can reveal the investigator's theory.
- [pitfall] Players may treat a confirmed prediction as proof of guilt when it only confirms a fact, so the payoff should be scoped to what it actually shows. When: A verified clue points toward a suspect or conclusion. Why: Confirmation of one fact is often mistaken for confirmation of a broader conclusion.
- [pitfall] A child's account can be vivid yet incomplete, with the observer's own idle time filling much of the report.
- [pitfall] A witness who denies everything by reflex gives a record that changes with each question.
- [pitfall] A reading shaped by suspicion can mislead, because traces that show some people were present cannot prove that others were absent. When: Interpreting tracks while already suspecting a particular account. Why: Absence of a trace is not evidence of absence of a person.
- [pitfall] Accepting a witness's vivid impression over the limits they admit about what they could perceive.
- [pitfall] An accused who claims to have been tricked may be believed by listeners unless the trap's logic is clear and recorded.
- [pitfall] Treating the early favourite as the answer, or assuming proof against one suspect eliminates the others. When: An investigation has settled on one person. Why: Other suspects are never tested once the favourite seems confirmed.
- [pitfall] A thorough earlier search can wrongly convince investigators that a hidden object is gone, when it lies in a spot searchers never tested. When: Reviewing what previous searchers covered. Why: A search covers only the places its method reaches.
- [pitfall] Identity judged from height, build or clothing fails when a body part has been replaced or altered after death. When: Identifying a badly damaged or altered body. Why: Whole-body impressions can be deliberately arranged.
- [pitfall] A vivid story about the means can hide a missing reason, so the motive should be checked separately.
- [pitfall] Making a withheld fact too blatant makes the reveal feel obvious, so omissions should be subtle yet fair.
- [pitfall] Reading a biased witness's omissions as silence misjudges them, because a witness with a stake may leave things out on purpose.
- [pitfall] An investigator's own secrecy and control over a group can make the investigator a target of suspicion.
- [pitfall] A suspect's character or ideology can make a theory seem likelier than the evidence supports. When: Judging a suspect by unpopular beliefs. Why: Disliked views bias judgment toward guilt.
- [pitfall] Several sources confirming a suspect's story can be mistaken for proof of innocence, while the central question may still be open.
- [pitfall] Building a motive first and then searching for evidence biases the search toward confirming that motive and overlooks evidence that contradicts it. When: When a suspect or motive is chosen before the evidence is examined. Why: Searchers look for what fits the chosen explanation and discount what does not.
- [pitfall] An investigator's impatience can close off useful testimony.
- [pitfall] A time limit on early questioning can force a superficial first interview, so initial statements should be treated as provisional until later cross-checked. When: Questioning must happen under a strict deadline. Why: Rushed first statements omit details that later examination would surface.
- [pitfall] A bystander who moves evidence as a precaution can destroy clues, because moving an item removes the traces it carried. When: evidence is handled before investigators arrive. Why: Good intentions can erase the physical record.
- [pitfall] A new detail that fits the theory is the most dangerous kind of testimony; test it against physical facts first. Why: A detail that confirms expectations is easy to accept without checking.
- [pitfall] A uniform habit may belong to several people, so do not assign it to one person without checking who shares it.
- [pitfall] An investigator's own temperament can decide which facts seem important; a reading based on atmosphere rather than evidence is unreliable.
- [pitfall] Early theories that match a bias can close off other leads.
- [pitfall] A visitor who has already searched or intruded may be lying about the reason for the visit.
- [pitfall] Bias can pass for ordinary procedure when irregularities of every kind are allowed and no one checks the process.
- [pitfall] Shared vocabulary shows that influence existed but does not identify who carried it; the carrier must be established separately.
- [pitfall] A conclusion held in advance can blind a reasoner to the meaning of their own statements. Why: Prior commitment filters out evidence that cuts against the conclusion.
- [pitfall] Citing a past minor offence can lend weight to a new charge without showing that the new act was committed. When: A defendant's record is used to support a new accusation. Why: Past conduct is not proof of the present act.
- [pitfall] When belief fixes an ordeal's result, no evidence can exonerate anyone, since any outcome confirms the accusation.
- [pitfall] Choosing the version that fits your own theory of the case is a common error when accounts conflict.
- [pitfall] Confusing a vivid likeness with a fact about conduct; an image shows appearance, not what someone did. When: When a striking image is taken as proof of guilt or behavior. Why: Visual impressions feel conclusive but do not establish actions.
- [pitfall] When observers choose which movements count and the subject can see the test, the pattern may reflect what the observers expected rather than a real link. When: A test is run by people who already suspect the subject. Why: Observer selection and visible testing bias results.
- [pitfall] Vivid, repeated examples can replace a checkable tally of cases, so count outcomes against records rather than relying on memorable instances.
- [pitfall] Prior-act evidence can build a character rather than prove the charge; keep it separate so players can tell proof from colour.
- [pitfall] Looking only at the first available option can hide a better connection that costs less time or risk. When: when choosing a transfer or route. Why: the first option is not always the best.
- [pitfall] A visible correlation, such as damaged versus undamaged, may hide the real variable, such as entry time, so players can settle on the wrong cause. Why: Surface differences are easier to notice than underlying causes.
- [pitfall] Rivalry within an investigation team spreads doubt about a theory, and hierarchy or jealousy can decide which theory is pursued. When: A sceptical colleague or superior dismisses the investigator's theory. Why: Personal and status pressures bias what gets followed up.
- [pitfall] Untested impressions, including intuition about people, can harden into certainty; check them against facts, since trained judgment is not infallible. When: A conclusion rests on impressions rather than verified facts. Why: Untested impressions are easily mistaken for established truth.
- [pitfall] An interviewer's suspicions or private doubts about a subject leak through tone and questions, biasing recorded answers; the suspect may sense them. When: When an investigator has already favoured one suspect or privately doubts a subject. Why: Bias leaks through demeanour unnoticed by the one holding it.
- [pitfall] Surface respectability, courtesy, or silence does not prove innocence, since a disguised or guilty person can display them too. Why: Those cues fit guilty knowledge as well as innocence, so they let disguised people pass unchallenged.
- [pitfall] Searching only for confirming facts once an identity is assumed, and never testing the reverse hypothesis that the body is someone else. When: When investigators settle on an identity for a body or remains. Why: Looking only for confirmation leaves alternative identities untested.
- [pitfall] Strong reactions can come from unrelated grudges, so a reaction to a trigger is not proof of guilt until checked against the reactor's other motives. When: Interpreting an angry or hostile reaction from a suspect. Why: Personal hostility produces the same visible signs as guilty knowledge.
- [pitfall] Mistaking suspicion for proof, or treating any one confirmatory item as conclusive, leads to wrong or premature conclusions. When: Evaluating a case built on partial evidence. Why: Strength of feeling and single items can look decisive without converging support.
- [pitfall] Bystanders may judge an investigator's questions as pointless until their purpose is revealed, so a sound method can look inadequate.
- [pitfall] Underrating a person because they seem simple is a mistake; a plain person can be more subtle than others assume.
- [pitfall] Letting a witness's moral verdicts shape how you read other people's actions carries the witness's bias into your interpretation. When: A witness judges the character of people involved. Why: Verdicts frame facts before the investigator has assessed them.
- [pitfall] Relying on a witness's view of another person's mental state without checking it turns impressions into apparent facts. When: A witness describes someone's inner state, such as fear or confusion. Why: Mental states are seldom observed directly, so the witness's reading may be wrong.
- [pitfall] Revealing your suspicions tells the witness which answers matter, letting them shape answers around what you want to hear. When: When interviewing a witness who may be hiding something. Why: A witness who knows which details matter can tailor the account to them.
- [pitfall] A proven lie about activity does not prove guilt of a crime; the contradiction shows the account is wrong, not why it is wrong. When: Concluding guilt from a contradicted account. Why: A false statement can have innocent motives, so moving to guilt is a risky leap.
- [pitfall] A satisfying story can hide the real culprit, so a case that feels complete should still be checked against evidence. When: when a suspect's guilt seems narratively satisfying. Why: Narrative appeal substitutes for proof.
- [pitfall] Do not treat a performance as sincere merely because many observers watched it, since crowds are often equally deceived. When: Assessing whether a witness's symptoms are genuine. Why: Shared observation does not reveal a skilled performance, so consensus can be wrong.
- [pitfall] An investigator's own bias colours their reading of rivals, making their account of others' motives partisan.
- [pitfall] A single vivid detail, such as a cry, can pull a timeline toward a conclusion before the time windows are checked. When: when reconstructing a sequence from testimony. Why: Vivid details attract attention and anchor judgment.
- [pitfall] Assuming every changed mood conceals a plan is a mistake; a listener may imagine inattention that has no hidden cause.
- [pitfall] Judging guilt only as premeditated overlooks wrongs that grow from small, thoughtless acts into a steady course of misconduct. When: When assessing a pattern of wrongdoing rather than a single act. Why: Gradual wrongs arise from accumulated choices, not one decision, so they fail a test that looks only for a plan.
- [fact] A broad belief framework shaping speech, drama, tales and public ritual sets what a population finds plausible, and circulates before any accusation, making charges easier to accept.
