When: assessing when a belief entered a community or what a population finds plausible. Why: A prepared framework makes accusations easier to accept.
- [fact] Evidence of an interest formed before an event supports both innocent research and early planning, so it does not settle intent. When: a subject interest is used to justify an act.
- [fact] Sincere decision-makers can be misled by admitted evidence and only later recognise their error.

## interview and questioning technique
- [definition] Cross-examination tests a witness by putting pointed propositions one after another, forcing a choice between admission and denial, and looking for conflicts with the known record.
- [mechanism] Closed questions that fix one fact at a time narrow what can have happened, since each negative answer eliminates a possibility from the timeline. When: confirming a timeline before confronting a suspect.
- [mechanism] Each unanswered question can point to another person to check, so an open-question list tends to grow in several directions at once.
- [mechanism] Give NPCs secrets that players can pry loose by confronting them with a verified fact.
- [mechanism] An NPC who feels unthreatened by the player gives more information, so the player's choice of tone changes how much is revealed. When: Designing dialogue where the player questions a suspect. Why: Lower perceived threat reduces guardedness, so disclosure rises with a relaxed approach.
- [mechanism] When dialogue options differ in phrasing, neutral questions can return a fuller NPC description than leading ones, so phrasing changes the information received. When: Designing dialogue options.
- [mechanism] A reveal can be triggered by asking the right question at the right moment rather than by a fixed dialogue option. When: Designing interrogation-driven discovery. Why: Context-sensitive triggers reward good questioning.
- [mechanism] A comic beat after a tense peak releases built-up pressure and resets tension before the next section. When: a scene has reached a peak. Why: humour breaks the pressure.
- [mechanism] An authority that refuses joint meetings and sees people one at a time forces each witness into a separate account, which lets players gather corroboration.
- [behavior] A suspect who first denies everything may break down and confess when confronted with a checkable fact, or abandon denial once investigators visibly know more than expected. When: the evidence is real and cannot be dismissed easily, or the suspect sees investigators' knowledge exceeds expectations. Why: A precise, verifiable fact removes room to deny; visible knowledge removes hope of concealment.
- [behavior] A casual or idle-seeming question does not trigger defensiveness, so a witness who cannot see the questioner's aim may reveal facts they would hide under direct questioning. When: a direct question would alert the subject, or a guarded witness is questioned about a sensitive subject in a casual setting. Why: Casual framing hides the purpose and lowers the listener's guard.
- [behavior] Reminding a suspect that his own conduct will shape the outcome tends to lower his confidence.
- [behavior] Asking how an offence happened, rather than whether it happened, moves a witness from flat denial toward explanation. When: the investigator already believes an act occurred. Why: presupposing the act removes the easy option of denial.
- [behavior] Cross-examination can unsettle a witness until they withdraw even a claim of recognition. When: A witness is questioned repeatedly or aggressively. Why: Pressure erodes confidence in uncertain memories.
- [behavior] People questioned about a private matter often show hesitation and embarrassment, which can mark a topic the family would rather not discuss. When: investigators press on a victim's personal life. Why: the subject exposes private matters.
- [behavior] A suspect may surrender to shift suspicion onto a lesser charge. When: A suspect faces a serious accusation.
- [behavior] Re-examining an object after a new idea arises often reveals changes the first look missed. When: when a new question prompts a review of earlier observations. Why: The first look was not framed by the new question.
- [behavior] Readers file an object introduced for a joke as comic detail, not clue, so its later reinterpretation as evidence can surprise them. When: A prop appears in a light, comedic scene. Why: A humorous tone lowers attention to the object's details.
- [behavior] A short written refusal carries weight when the writer's character is known, since brevity itself signals resolve. When: A person known to the investigator refuses in writing with few words. Why: Brevity from a known character reads as deliberate and firm.
- [behavior] An ambush question placed before a hostile audience can turn sympathy toward the witness and against the questioner. When: Confronting a witness in front of an unfriendly group. Why: Audiences react to perceived unfairness, weakening the questioner's position.
- [behavior] A witness who challenges a claim by demanding proof invites the investigator to produce documents, so the challenge can be answered with evidence. When: the investigator holds documents supporting the claim. Why: A demand for proof gives the investigator a reason to present evidence.
- [behavior] Asking who gains from an event, or floating an impersonation, provokes a reaction the questioner can read.
- [behavior] A listener who sees that advice would isolate them from rivals may read it as a trap rather than sincere counsel. When: When advice would alter a listener's alliances. Why: Awareness of the consequence reveals the hidden intent.
- [behavior] A witness asked about surrounding events rather than the target often gives answers that reveal more to the investigator than to themselves, because they do not know what matters. When: a witness does not know the significance of what they know, or direct questions would alert a suspect. Why: Indirect questions avoid triggering guarded answers, so the investigator learns facts the witness does not realise are relevant.
- [behavior] A suspect who asks to hear the investigator's method before giving an account reverses the usual questioning order and shifts control of the interview to the suspect. When: A prepared suspect opens negotiations before any statement is given. Why: The suspect has anticipated the inquiry and wants to set the frame first.
- [rule] Do not press a witness who is distressed, likely to shut down, or hesitating; change subject instead. Avoid pressing when the investigator is angry and may lose control. When: a witness hesitates, grows evasive, or is distressed, or the investigator is angry. Why: pressure at that moment raises guardedness. (x2)
- [rule] Question witnesses privately, dismissing other staff or keeping only a reliable witness present, so no one overhears. Others present make witnesses close up and raise the cost of honest answers. When: a witness is reluctant to answer in front of others, or sensitive relationship questions are asked. Why: Witnesses close up when observed by colleagues or subordinates.
- [rule] Ask how a witness knows a claim and what evidence supports it; accept the claim only with a stated source.
- [rule] Let the player choose an interview venue, private or public, since each choice changes what NPCs say and who overhears.
- [rule] Do not use a cruel or harmful disclosure as a test of reaction, even when it might reveal the truth.
- [rule] Use a public disruption, such as a performance breaking down, to open a private dialogue option with a second NPC. When: a scripted scene can be interrupted by one character's distress. Why: The disruption creates a moment where a bystander can speak privately.
- [rule] Take a statement only once the witness can give it clearly; interviewing too early can lose the evidence.
- [rule] Use interviews for motive and context, and keep physical traces as the evidence the player must find.
- [rule] Question a match before accepting it as a conclusion, and ask what further evidence it needs.
- [rule] Ask what was said and who said it, rather than whether the statement is true, when assessing a witness's testimony. When: Evaluating a statement from a witness. Why: Attribution and wording reveal the speaker's position and hidden views, which a bare truth check misses.
- [rule] Ask whether anything else weighed on a person's mind, and accept a flat denial as the answer rather than pressing it further.
- [rule] Make a sudden request, such as borrowing money, a quest trigger that players can trace back to its cause.
- [rule] Use a shared signal, such as a familiar whistled tune, to open a contact so both parties recognise each other and build rapport. Why: a shared cue creates a sense of belonging between strangers.
- [rule] Question witnesses about all visitors, not just those they consider expected or important.
- [rule] Keep questioning on points relevant to the case, since off-topic questions weaken the examination. When: when examining a witness. Why: Irrelevant lines waste time and give the witness cover.
- [rule] Ask for physical proof of claims, and when none can be produced, record that the claim cannot be checked.
- [rule] Offer interview options such as a legal warning, a personal appeal and a precise follow-up question, each producing a different witness response. When: designing witness dialogue.
- [rule] Stop pressing when continued questions would make a bystander's position worse, even if more information is still available.
- [rule] In a death inquiry, ask a witness directly whether any suicidal remarks were made, and record the answer even when it is negative. When: the cause of a death is uncertain. Why: A recorded negative answer is still evidence that the question was asked.
- [rule] Let a yes-or-no oracle NPC or device narrow a name, location or code, so players reach the answer through structured questions.
- [rule] Explain at the start that withholding information is risky and that what is said will be kept confidential. When: when opening an interview. Why: sets expectations for a full account.
- [rule] Use a direct question when the witness is likely to answer honestly, and reserve indirect probes for partly cooperative witnesses. Why: Indirect probes are less efficient than direct questions.
- [rule] Track each suspect's concessions as state, since pressure can lower trust or open a false-confession branch. When: designing NPC questioning.
- [rule] Do not use indirect probing on a target who already recognises it; they will read the method as an accusation.
- [rule] Ask a witness a closed question about one physical object's state at one fixed moment, and require a positive answer rather than a general account. When: a witness's general account is clear but a specific physical state is needed.
- [rule] Separate an interview phase from a formal hearing; an NPC who denies attending the hearing leaves the interview open as a question for the player to probe. When: designing an investigation with several stages.
- [rule] When records are silent, infer an event from surviving documents and physical traces rather than stating it as recorded. When: A historical event has no direct documentation. Why: A silent record supports inference, not a stated fact.
- [rule] Let an NPC ask probing questions and react to the player's answers, so the player's reactions become information. When: when designing NPC dialogue that tests the player.
- [rule] Prompt a character with an object rather than a direct question, so they reveal what they recall without being forced to testify. When: Eliciting information from a reluctant or confused character. Why: Indirect cues lower pressure, so the response shows genuine recall.
- [heuristic] Draw out guarded, reserved or hostile sources through casual conversation, shared meals, neutral subjects and tactful indirect questions, since blunt questions make them defensive. When: A source is guarded, emotional, hostile or reserved. Why: Direct questions trigger guardedness and close the channel.
- [heuristic] Question a suspect unexpectedly and early, before a cover story is settled, since warning or delay gives time to build a false account that cannot be checked. When: A suspect is likely to prepare answers if warned, or their account is not yet fixed. Why: Time to reflect lets the suspect prepare a false, uncheckable account.
- [heuristic] Question the person whose duties cover a given detail, since they are most likely to have noticed it. When: Seeking information about a specific detail. Why: Routine responsibility gives the most reliable knowledge of that detail.
- [heuristic] A suspect questioned early, when woken, hungry and half awake, is less guarded than one questioned at midday. When: choosing when to confront a suspect. Why: fatigue and hunger lower defences.
- [heuristic] Hold a strange remark open, since it may show knowledge or merely seek attention, until more evidence arrives. When: a witness says something ambiguous. Why: one remark cannot tell knowledge from attention-seeking.
- [heuristic] Arranging facts in order of occurrence can reveal links between events that seemed unrelated when reported out of sequence.
- [heuristic] A hidden state can be inferred from what a correspondent avoids saying, such as repeated direct questions that receive no direct answer. When: The reader must infer a state from a correspondent who will not state it. Why: Persistent evasion on a specific point signals something being withheld.
- [heuristic] When a witness knows a detail not in the record, ask directly where it came from before assuming a secret, since simple misremembering also explains it. When: a witness appears to know something unpublished. Why: witnesses may simply misremember a source.
- [heuristic] When a skeptic objects that the target seems unrelated, ask what the sender gained and what they wanted the recipient to know. When: Judging a motive is unclear. Why: Purpose often explains a message even when the target looks unconnected.
- [heuristic] An interview may need only to see the witness and their setting to build a clear picture, not to extract a full statement.
- [heuristic] A visitor who asks more about consequences than about the facts needed reveals priorities worth testing.
- [heuristic] Frame recall questions open-endedly so the witness answers from memory, not from the interviewer's own theory.
- [heuristic] Re-examine physical details that witnesses remember poorly, since such details are easy to misstate.
- [heuristic] Ask about habits and locations, such as where an item was kept, before testing a suspect's claim.
- [heuristic] Unusual precautions taken by a witness, such as bolting a door or borrowing a weapon, should be questioned for their reason. When: A witness reports a precaution out of the ordinary. Why: Unusual precautions can signal prior knowledge or fear that bears on the case.
- [heuristic] Let an evasive person describe events in their own words rather than leading with direct questions, which can draw out more voluntary disclosure.
- [heuristic] Ask specific closed questions about when, where and purpose; their answers can be checked against other evidence. When: interviewing a witness about events. Why: specific answers can be verified, unlike vague ones.
- [heuristic] A question that seems to ask about distance may really test what a suspect possesses. Ask what each question is meant to reveal. When: Interviewing a suspect whose answers may conceal planning. Why: Innocent-sounding questions can expose preparation the suspect did not intend to reveal.
- [heuristic] In a fixed, fully known population, a single unexpected person stands out at once, because routine makes any deviation visible. When: the suspect pool is small and fixed. Why: Known routines make a stranger's presence conspicuous.
- [heuristic] Probe what a sincere but confused witness cannot describe; the gaps reveal how little their claim actually rests on.
- [heuristic] Confront a witness with a document or record when they have a motive to distort it and the record must be explained. When: a witness has a motive and a record needs explaining.
- [heuristic] When a target may conceal identity, ask about descriptions and dates, not only names. When: when a target may use an assumed name.
- [heuristic] If an adversary acted on information only later, someone must have passed it on. Ask when the adversary learned a fact to infer who their source was. When: Tracing how sensitive information spread. Why: The timing of knowledge reveals the chain of communication.
- [heuristic] Turn a question back on the questioner to avoid revealing your own view.
- [heuristic] Ask what happened after each step, and look for the one unexplained move in an otherwise tidy chain.
- [heuristic] An engaging NPC who asks questions about a location can be designed so that the questions reveal what the player is really seeking.
- [heuristic] Open questioning with irrelevant small talk, then strike with a pointed question, so the suspect lowers his guard before the key point arrives. When: the pointed question is the real goal. Why: a relaxed suspect is less prepared to deflect.
- [heuristic] When a volunteered account seems loosely connected to the case, press for exact times, outcomes and departures to test whether it fits the rest of the evidence. When: When a witness offers a detail that seems convenient or peripheral. Why: Specific, checkable details are harder to fabricate consistently than vague accounts.
- [heuristic] When a witness says something happened 'at the time', ask for the exact time to force a precise sequence and expose hidden contradictions. When: a witness gives a vague time reference. Why: vague timing hides gaps in the sequence of events.
- [heuristic] Open a conversation by praising a witness's work or interest, then listen; private worries and relationships tend to surface while they talk about it. When: witness is talkative or trusting. Why: people share more when they do not realise their words are being weighed.
- [heuristic] Ask indirect questions, such as who the witness remembers visiting, to draw out details that a direct question about a named suspect may not reach. When: Witness will not share directly.
- [heuristic] Ask the person who made a stain before relying on a laboratory, since their account may be faster and sufficient.
- [heuristic] Let co-interviewers signal each other privately, so questioning keeps its rhythm and the witness does not notice the interruption. When: when two people question one witness.
- [heuristic] Pressing a suspect to speak works best when the suspect's account can clear an innocent person and the key facts are already largely established. When: Deciding whether to press a suspect for a full account. Why: Known facts let the suspect's account be checked and make the cost of silence concrete.
- [heuristic] Ask direct questions about the suspect's known secrets, such as an unexplained payment or an item found in their property.
- [heuristic] Hint at the truth through facts and suggestions rather than an outright accusation, so the other party reaches the conclusion alone.
- [heuristic] Ask witnesses directly about prior acquaintances, since a hidden link may only emerge when someone asks the right question. When: Interviewing witnesses in an investigation. Why: Unprompted accounts omit links that the witness considers unimportant.
- [heuristic] Probing for hidden motive matters less when the visitor openly explains the request.
- [heuristic] Open with a sound, object or short reply that signals a death or major event before any name is given.
- [heuristic] Brief, closed questions get terse answers, which questioners tend to accept as clear, so the pace of the exchange controls what gets heard.
- [heuristic] A claim of a hidden ability can be tested by varying conditions and asking for tasks that a true possessor could pass but a performer could not. When: A claim depends on a hidden ability or reaction, and conditions can be varied. Why: Varied conditions separate a real ability from a performance that only fits the examiner's expectations.
- [heuristic] An NPC who bans public talk to prevent unrest can serve as a suppression obstacle that players must overcome. When: When designing authority figures who restrict information. Why: Restriction creates a barrier for the player to break.
- [heuristic] Ask what a request for documents aims to achieve; records requested to answer critics may serve as a defense rather than neutral record. When: Documents are requested or circulated during a dispute. Why: Stated purpose can differ from recorded purpose.
- [heuristic] A direct, plain question often provokes a flustered denial that exposes an evasion more readily than an indirect approach. When: When a witness appears to be concealing an intent or fact. Why: Direct questions leave less room for a prepared, smooth answer.
- [heuristic] Avoid open identification demands when a witness has already refused to name a candidate, since they tend to backfire. When: A witness has resisted naming a suspect. Why: Direct pressure can harden refusal and undermine the witness's later cooperation.
- [heuristic] Ask background questions about a witness's reading or past to check whether their knowledge came from an outside source. When: when a witness shows unusual knowledge of a subject. Why: Outside exposure can explain knowledge a witness attributes to experience.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a vague remark that invites others to speak. 2) Let them volunteer what they know before questioning directly. 3) Pin down who made each specific claim. When: interviewing witnesses, especially when the community talks freely. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Re-ask the detail in neutral wording or a different form, avoiding hints of the answer. 2) Compare it with the verbatim earlier record. 3) Note any change and ask why it happened. When: a witness or suspect's account of a key fact may be inconsistent. Why: Leading questions shape answers; rephrasing shows whether an answer is stable or invented.
- [procedure] 1) Ask one short, narrow factual question at a time. 2) Have the witness answer only what was asked, steering rambling replies back. 3) Ask for the witness's own impression separately from what they claim to know. Why: Keeps the account clean and checkable.
- [procedure] 1) Record the witness's firm claim and ask for exact times, names and actions. 2) Ask about conditions of observation and what was seen directly versus inferred. 3) Ask about incidental details and how sure they are. 4) Offer a plausible alternative. 5) Keep the claim only at the level answers support. When: A witness is certain but the view was brief, partial or poor, or an identification is being tested. Why: Certainty about minor details often exceeds what was observed; confidence does not guarantee accurate details.
- [procedure] 1) State a fact or inference aloud, real or pretended. 2) Watch for denial, evasion, sudden admission or visible fear. 3) Offer a second hypothesis and note which answer is guarded. 4) Use the visible fear to draw out the missing detail. When: when testing a specific point in a suspect's account or a suspect is withholding a detail. Why: Reactions show which point the suspect protects; naming the inference makes fear visible.
- [procedure] 1) Ask about a specific detail, such as colour, count, or who handed over an object. 2) Record the answer. 3) Ask a follow-up that the answer must match. 4) Compare the answers for consistency. When: Questioning a witness whose account cannot be checked directly. Why: Each specific detail creates a point that a later answer can contradict.
- [procedure] 1) Repeat key questions in different wording and watch for hesitation or pallor. 2) Narrow to specific dates, places and reasons. 3) Check answers against records the witness cannot easily change. When: a witness gives a partial story and may be concealing part of it.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness to begin well before the event of interest. 2) Move forward point by point in sequence until reaching the event. When: the witness is not a practised narrator and sequence matters. Why: Starting early and advancing in order produces a plain account without gaps.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a plain question about enemies or who benefits. 2) Hold the witness's gaze. 3) Record any hesitation or vague answer. 4) Repeat back a recalled remark exactly, including its pronouns. When: When a polished witness might reveal knowledge through one phrase. Why: Exact repetition and attention to hesitation expose what the words meant.
- [procedure] 1) Learn the household through casual sources such as neighbours, tradespeople and servants before any formal interview. 2) Use a pretext and small courtesies to open conversation. 3) Clarify your purpose so gatekeepers admit you. When: Gathering information before a formal interview. Why: Informal sources often know more than formal witnesses and are easier to approach.
- [procedure] 1) Adopt a persona or disguise that allows indirect speech. 2) Tell a story that hints at the secret. 3) Watch the target's reactions in order. 4) Weigh the reactions as evidence against innocent explanations. When: when a target has motive but is unlikely to admit it.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm the inquiry's official progress. 2) Set a trap that tests the suspect. 3) Question each key party in turn. 4) Examine documents such as receipts. 5) Raise public stakes last. When: when a witness is hiding knowledge. Why: each question narrows the field of possible answers.
- [procedure] 1) Open with neutral or general topics far from the subject. 2) Build rapport through flattery and shared sympathy. 3) Ask many small indirect questions. 4) Note which answer lands. When: When a direct question would be refused or met with silence. Why: Lowering the witness's guard brings out facts a direct question would not reach.
- [procedure] 1) Have the suggestible subject focus on a fixed stimulus. 2) Ask questions in a fixed order, moving from route to possession to timing. 3) Note any pause before each answer. When: When questioning a compliant or suggestible informant. Why: A fixed order can draw out knowledge of plans.
- [procedure] 1) Ask for exact words, order and setting. 2) Ask directly what was left out. 3) Check the answers for gaps. When: interviewing a witness through a relay. Why: Specific detail and direct omission questions expose gaps.
- [procedure] 1) Ask numbered questions one at a time. 2) Hold each answer before moving on. 3) Note each refusal or evasion for later. 4) Use the answers to decide the next terms. When: A bargaining scene where one side controls the setting. Why: Each answer reveals what the other side knows and how much leverage remains.
- [procedure] 1) Address the source with deference and praise their judgement. 2) Ask guessing questions that let them confirm or correct your guess. 3) Ask open questions about their interests. 4) Ask one targeted case question. 5) Keep your own statements short and vague so the source does most of the talking. When: Source is talkative and vain; guarded sources will not respond the same way.
- [procedure] 1) Open on a neighbouring subject. 2) Watch for involuntary signs. 3) Ask a follow-up question to test any sign. 4) Ask the subject to justify why you asked. 5) Ask agreeable questions to fix their stated terms. When: A direct question would make the subject guarded and you need their own framing of their stake.
- [procedure] 1) Prepare a checklist of topics. 2) Open with small, checkable questions. 3) Raise sensitive topics later. 4) Strike off each topic when covered. 5) Restate answers for confirmation. When: Running a formal interview where terms must be confirmed. Why: A checklist keeps coverage complete and the record clear.
- [procedure] 1) State the suspect's position as an impartial observer would. 2) Ask narrow questions about the unexplained item. 3) Separate admissions from refusals and treat each answer as narrowing the field. When: The suspect refuses to explain a possession and has limited information to offer. Why: Framing the case calmly and asking narrow questions can draw partial admissions.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a broad request. 2) Build background about who the person is and where they came from. 3) Ask the critical question directly. 4) Pull drifting answers back by matching reported words to facts already known. When: When a witness holds partial, second-hand knowledge that comes out in pieces. Why: Background builds rapport, and direct questions prevent a frightened witness from shutting down.
- [procedure] 1) Break the account into small steps: timing, door state, objects present and order of events. 2) Ask about small physical details the witness may not have rehearsed or noticed. 3) Compare each answer with known facts about the place or object. When: a witness's account is smooth, may be assembled from a story, or may have missed details. Why: Fabricated accounts and missed details tend to fail on small points the witness did not prepare or notice.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a broad question about who else was present. 2) Only then name the person sought. 3) Show a photograph and ask for confirmation. When: a witness saw a stranger earlier. Why: naming the target early can seed the witness's memory; a plain who-else-was-present question can move a witness from denial toward confession.
- [procedure] 1) State the events in order. 2) Establish a fixed routine as the baseline. 3) Fix the times of each event. 4) Cross-check times against each other. 5) Theorise about causes last. When: a case needs a clear account of what happened and when, before explaining why. Why: A fixed sequence of events prevents explanations from distorting the facts.
- [procedure] 1) Make a specific false claim about a shared past, such as meeting at an event. 2) Observe whether the witness denies it. 3) Treat a firm denial of a detail as informative, without accusing them directly. When: a witness may know more than they say. Why: a witness who knows the truth will tend to deny a false detail.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whether a crime occurred. 2) If so, ask what it was and how it was done. Use both questions to set the scope before analysis. When: at the start of any case.
- [procedure] 1) Give an ordered, precise account of the suspect's actions. 2) Present physical evidence they cannot easily refute. 3) Offer protective terms if they cooperate. When: suspect is present, evidence is specific, and a private resolution is possible. Why: Specificity makes denial hard, and protection gives the suspect a reason to confess.
- [procedure] 1) Ask leading questions about the stranger's purpose and past. 2) Note any trouble or violence he admits to. 3) Observe his temper when warned. 4) Compare his answers with what others report. When: A stranger's background is unknown. Why: Answers, conduct and reputation together give evidence about who he is.
- [procedure] Ask who else knew of the meeting, whether valuables are kept, whether theft is feared, and how long the witness has lived there, then compare answers with other evidence. When: questioning a witness about a planned meeting or property. Why: these questions narrow the list of people with knowledge and motive.
- [procedure] 1) Ask short closed questions to fix the witness's exact claim. 2) Return the witness's own words to expose an assumption. 3) Ask them to explain a mechanism to test plausibility. 4) Bank admissions for later argument. When: Questioning a witness who is precise.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whether the event was recorded at the time. 2) Ask how the date was fixed. 3) Ask what written record exists. 4) Press each answer with narrow follow-up questions. When: a witness is certain of an identification. Why: certainty can outrun documentation.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the first fact the audience knows. 2) State the motive, then the link to the suspect, then the means. 3) Eliminate alternatives in turn. 4) Answer the questions left open. When: at the reveal of a mystery solution. Why: each inference rests on facts already shown, so the answer feels earned.
- [procedure] Accept a witness's account as partial, then ask why each action was taken, since the reason is often withheld until pressed.
- [procedure] Test an apparently sealed barrier with a probe or push before accepting it; a probe through a keyhole can show whether a key sits in the lock from the other side. When: Investigating a room that appears locked. Why: A locked state can be weaker than it appears.
- [procedure] 1) Ask an open question so the witness recalls freely. 2) Record that free account before adding your own frame. 3) Narrow with specific questions, noting which details came from you. When: questioning a witness whose memory could be shaped. Why: the witness's own memory is captured before the investigator's framing is introduced.
- [procedure] 1) Make a small, harmless change in the suspect's surroundings. 2) Observe whether the reaction is immediate, absent or unusually quiet. 3) Weigh the reaction against the wider pattern.
- [procedure] 1) Begin with a broad request for everything observed. 2) Interrupt if the witness jumps to a conclusion, and return to the order of events. 3) After the full account, ask directly about any odd point. 4) Shape each next question around the last telling answer.
- [procedure] 1) Ask neutral questions about a place or event. 2) Record each answer. 3) Compare answers across suspects and note contradictions with earlier statements. When: when a suspect cannot be pressed directly.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a claim the witness would find hard to defend. 2) Use an earlier fact the witness remembers to test memory. 3) State each accusation as a proposition. 4) Record every denial. 5) Cover alternative explanations in turn.
- [procedure] 1) Watch for pauses, blushes or sudden topic changes when a witness answers. 2) Ask a narrow question about one specific object or fact. 3) Let the narrowness make a simple denial hard. When: a witness is partly truthful and one precise fact is being withheld. Why: a narrow question leaves little room for evasion and exposes the withheld fact.
- [procedure] 1) Ask for an exact moment of an event. 2) Ask who left first. 3) Repeat for each step of the meeting, so every step is pinned down. When: when a suspect's timing forms a gap. Why: Exact sequence questions expose inconsistencies that vague answers hide.
- [procedure] 1) Use a cover story that grants access. 2) Drop a small test remark. 3) Watch who reacts and how. 4) Discard answers that do not bear on the case. When: a target is guarded and a direct question would alert them. Why: Indirect tests reveal reactions without tipping off the target.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a neutral shared interest, such as a local activity. 2) Let the talk drift to related people and places. 3) Turn to the people or events under investigation. When: when an informant is reluctant or guarded. Why: a neutral start lowers resistance.
- [procedure] 1) Ask yes-or-no questions that narrow the field. 2) Use each answer to eliminate options and choose the next question. 3) For spelled-out answers, confirm each uncertain letter before moving on. 4) Repeat and confirm slow or ambiguous signals. When: The subject can answer only briefly, or one fact is needed at a time. Why: Accuracy depends on confirming each step.
- [procedure] 1) Get a formal denial on record before the subject narrates. 2) Let the subject give a complete account in chronological order. 3) Review the notes and ask pointed follow-up questions. 4) Ask for exact counts, durations and times. 5) Ask for a witness to each movement; log unnamed gaps as open tasks. When: when interviewing a suspect for a full account.
- [procedure] 1) List every known event with its date or time. 2) Order events by when they happened, not when they were learned. 3) Put undated facts in a separate list. 4) Scan the sequence for patterns and gaps. When: evidence arrives piecemeal from several sources. Why: Discovery order can scramble the real sequence and hide patterns.
- [procedure] 1) Open by stating the known case against the suspect and advising that candor serves their interest. 2) Cover topics in order: acquaintance, disputed possessions, timeline, finances. 3) Return to any point the suspect avoided. When: A suspect holds information and a non-coercive approach may still work.
- [procedure] 1) Open with an apology and a framing remark to lower the suspect's guard. 2) Ask about the past relationship in an incurious tone. 3) Put the sensitive question directly and note the reply. When: Suspect has an obvious reason to deny. Why: A lowered guard makes later denials easier to read.
- [procedure] Question peripheral witnesses first and compare their timing and sound accounts before questioning the central witness. Why: earlier interviews fix the baseline that later ones are checked against.
- [procedure] Open with establishing questions about location, hearing and sight, then narrow to doors, locks, light and movement.
- [procedure] 1) Note any detail a witness volunteers before being told it. 2) Ask where they heard it. 3) Name a key person or fact to test their reaction. 4) Watch for changes in posture and speech.
- [procedure] 1) Let the suspect give their own account first. 2) Quote the disputed words exactly. 3) Ask what the words meant, not for a yes or no. When: when a statement has two plausible readings.
- [procedure] 1) Restore order with a firm rebuke when a suspect loses control. 2) Return to a calm, ordinary question.
- [procedure] 1) Ask general questions about the household or group. 2) Move to the people most closely involved. 3) Keep the most sensitive questions for later, once witnesses are at ease. When: A case involves many relationships and motive is unclear. Why: Starting broad lets witnesses speak with less embarrassment.
- [procedure] 1) Declare the category of crime at once so everyone understands the stakes. 2) Assign searches to named helpers in advance. 3) Question witnesses one at a time, pinning each to a specific fact. 4) Record exact words. 5) Use scene watchers to fix the timeline and cross-check. When: At first arrival at a scene while witnesses are still present. Why: Accounts are fresher and not yet shaped by one another.
- [procedure] 1) Lay out the physical evidence first. 2) Ask the suspect to explain it. 3) Test each explanation against an independent source. 4) Press on the motive until the suspect explains. When: a suspect offers an explanation that may be true but is unverified. Why: evidence fixes the facts before the suspect's account is judged.
- [procedure] 1) Frame a personal question as an impersonal or literary point. 2) Invite the suspect to recognise himself in a category. 3) Treat refusal or defiance as evidence. When: Probing a suspect whose writings or beliefs may reveal motive, and who would refuse a direct question. Why: An indirect frame makes the suspect react, and the reaction becomes the clue.
- [procedure] 1) Keep the target talking through small talk and silences. 2) Drop a specific known detail. 3) Watch the reaction. 4) Shift topic suddenly. 5) Compare answers with known facts. When: there is no decisive proof and the aim is to see how a suspect handles pressure. Why: reactions and fit with known facts reveal knowledge without an accusation.
- [procedure] 1) Ask rapid, direct questions about who, what and when. 2) If answers stay thin, drop that line rather than force it.
- [procedure] 1) Begin with an opening ritual. 2) Question the accused in sequence. 3) Read witness statements aloud. 4) Let witnesses contradict the accused. 5) Record each answer.
- [procedure] 1) Make a suspect believe a key matter is important to them. 2) Leave them unobserved for a set period. 3) Check for a physical change that reveals their action. When: When a suspect is likely to act to protect their position and the action leaves a trace. Why: Perceived freedom to act makes the suspect more likely to reveal themselves through a checkable change.
- [procedure] 1) Check the pretext's basis by asking others whether the item belongs to them. 2) If the target offers no opening, create one with a plausible excuse. 3) Ask a question that invites advice. 4) Use the target's own suggestion to extend the contact. When: The target will not invite contact or sits alone.
- [procedure] 1) Raise one implausible point lightly. 2) Accept the defensive reply and note each new detail it adds. 3) Ask about motive or access without accusing. 4) Mark checkable details as leads for later. When: A witness's story is plausible but has one weak point. Why: Each defence adds verifiable facts without provoking the witness into closing up.
- [procedure] 1) Agree a time limit openly with the suspect before the interview begins. 2) Have an officer record the statement. 3) Let the suspect speak at length, noting the sequence of events and the gaps. 4) End the interview when the agreed time expires. When: A suspect is willing to talk but controls the pace. Why: Open terms and a recorded statement keep the interview constrained and usable as evidence.
- [tradeoff] Chronological retelling from before the key moment suits non-practised narrators and lets order emerge; some ask every witness, yet it adds little for crisp accounts or single facts. Why: Sequence matters only when the account must be built step by step.
- [tradeoff] Probing questions gather evidence but can expose the investigator's interest, and a neutral inquiry can quickly turn personal. Holding back preserves secrecy at the cost of detail. When: the investigator is hidden and the suspect is unaware. Why: each option trades information against exposure.
- [tradeoff] Closed questions reliably pin down specific facts or a precise witness but limit what is volunteered. Open questions yield fuller accounts at the cost of precision and risk losing control of a confused witness. When: choosing a questioning style.
- [tradeoff] Asking openly for an item reveals your role, while taking it covertly avoids that but risks discovery and delays awareness of any reaction. When: when an item would be refused if requested openly.
- [tradeoff] Open inquiry preserves social trust but cannot reach what covert methods uncover; splitting the work between two investigators covers both at the cost of coordination. When: Dividing investigation methods between characters. Why: Each approach has reach and cost that the other lacks.
- [tradeoff] Naming a key subject early can expose a guarded witness, but it also alerts them, so later questions lose their element of surprise. When: a probe is used on a subject who is already guarded. Why: the witness adjusts their guard after the first reaction.
- [tradeoff] Indirect questioning through a witness's interests works with talkative or trusting witnesses but yields little from guarded ones who recognise the questions. When: choosing an interview approach. Why: guarded witnesses notice what is being asked.
- [tradeoff] Direct questions gather facts quickly but may close a witness; indirect casual conversation reveals behavior more slowly but yields more candid answers. When: when deciding how to question a witness or household. Why: direct pressure can make people withhold information they would otherwise share.
- [tradeoff] Voicing an unusual theory risks being thought absurd, while holding it back risks losing a lead. When: a witness holds a theory the inquiry did not ask about. Why: fear of ridicule versus loss of evidence.
- [tradeoff] A direct accusation reveals a reaction quickly but can end the exchange; a softer probe keeps talk going but reveals less.
- [pitfall] A question that reveals what the investigator knows, through its content or its order, tips off the witness and invites a prepared answer.
- [pitfall] Asking a witness about details outside their knowledge yields unreliable answers. When: Choosing whom to question. Why: Guessing replaces knowledge when a witness has no real basis.
- [pitfall] Losing temper hands the other party an advantage and makes the interviewer appear the aggressor. When: An interviewer faces repeated evasion. Why: Visible anger shifts sympathy to the evader and weakens the interviewer's position.
- [pitfall] A comforter's follow-up questions can shape the account a witness gives, so the exact wording of questions should be recorded with the answers. When: a witness is questioned after an emotional moment. Why: Questions frame what the witness recalls and how they describe it.
- [pitfall] An interviewer's own visible embarrassment at a name can alert the source and reverse the balance of the exchange. When: when questioning someone who reads emotional cues. Why: Reactions signal which facts matter.
- [pitfall] Thorough questioning is not the same as checking; pressing a witness hard without testing answers against the clock leaves contradictions unexposed.
- [pitfall] A threatened suspect may shift blame onto others to save themselves.
- [pitfall] Questions that depend on one another can loop back to the start, so the list makes no progress without new evidence.
- [pitfall] Overusing sudden threats dulls tension.
- [pitfall] Reassuring a witness with promises that cannot be guaranteed turns comfort into deception.
- [pitfall] A witness with privileged access to the scene may frame the story to suit themselves.
- [pitfall] Warmth in an interview can disarm the interviewer as much as the witness, causing the interviewer to miss gaps. When: when an interview becomes friendly. Why: rapport lowers the interviewer's guard against inconsistencies.
- [pitfall] A probe can backfire: an accepted cover story invites further testing, so each new claim adds to the risk.
- [pitfall] Rephrasing the same question often only reconfirms the same answer; switch to a new angle such as finances or contacts.
- [pitfall] Asking an acquaintance to pass on what they heard can apply pressure rather than gather neutral facts. When: Seeking information through an intermediary who knows the subject. Why: The intermediary is shaped by their relationship to the subject.
- [pitfall] Marking every helpful character as a suspect destroys the signal, so suspicion stops distinguishing the guilty from everyone else.
- [pitfall] Reading meaning into a silent person's signals invites projection from the reader's own feelings, and the impaired person may also read the reader as a symbol. Why: Interpretation runs in both directions and distorts both readings.
- [pitfall] Baiting a suspect can make later answers more guarded, and a reaction indicates concern rather than guilt. When: Using a bait fact to test a suspect. Why: Suspects who sense a test grow careful, and worry has many causes besides guilt.
- [pitfall] Relentless pressure can make a witness faint or break down, ending the examination before the account is complete; get key facts on record first.
- [fact] A line of inquiry closes when the people who could confirm it are gone, so the investigator must turn to other sources.
- [fact] A third party may arrive mid-interview and cut it short, so interviews can end before the questioner gets the full account.
- [fact] Partial disclosure of suspicions or withheld evidence gives the witness leverage to judge how much to trust the questioner and how much to reveal. When: When an investigator discloses some suspicions but withholds other evidence. Why: The witness uses what she knows about the investigator's position to decide what to say.

## witness credibility
- [model] A witness's reliability depends on position to observe, attention or hearing, memory, and honesty or motive; a weakness in any one can make the account unreliable. When: when weighing a witness account.
- [model] Judge a witness by four things: why they were present, their habits, their tools such as clocks, and whether other accounts contradict them.
- [model] Testimony is weighed on three factors: corroboration by other observers, the witness's reliability, and counter-claims made against the accuser. When: judging a disputed accusation.
- [mechanism] Give NPC witnesses a reliability rating based on distance, training, grudges or fear, since frightened witnesses give vaguer descriptions, so players weigh their accounts differently. When: designing NPC witnesses. Why: visible reliability shapes how players use testimony.
- [mechanism] A testimony's reliability should rise only when an independent second clue supports it, so a single NPC's account cannot solve a case. When: when designing NPC testimony in a game.
- [mechanism] A witness's account is limited by what they could perceive, whether they had reason to shade the truth, and how well it fits other testimony. When: Weighing overlapping testimonies. Why: Sincerity does not guarantee accuracy when perception or motive is limited.
- [mechanism] A witness's standing can be a stored value that changes how other characters weight that witness's testimony, independent of what was observed.
- [mechanism] A rule that counts several accusers as one person reduces corroboration, so their joint account carries less weight.
- [mechanism] When one witness discredits another, the competing accounts must both be weighed, changing how each is trusted. When: A witness is warned against another witness. Why: Pressure on one account reshapes trust in the other.
- [mechanism] A later judgment can discredit a witness's supernatural testimony after the verdict, citing possible fraud or outside influence, which weakens the verdict it supported. When: a conviction that rests on a witness whose status is reassessed. Why: the verdict depended on that witness's credibility.
- [behavior] A witness with a stake in the outcome filters what they report through their interests, feelings and self-image, so the same event can be told in a self-serving way. When: the witness has a personal stake or strong moral views about the matter. Why: Interests and self-image determine which details are emphasised and how they are framed.
- [behavior] A verdict reached early by intuition, especially one tied to the judge's self-image, resists revision and treats contradiction as a personal attack. When: the witness has a prior personal investment in the opinion. Why: defending the opinion protects the judge's sense of self.
- [behavior] A questioner may avoid pressing details, so vague questioning is safe for the witness. When: when the questioner has not yet formed a suspicion. Why: close probing could reveal the questioner's own suspicion.
- [behavior] A shift from firm knowledge to hesitation, such as 'let me think', signals weakening certainty and is worth recording. When: witness is questioned about a specific detail. Why: hesitation can mark the edge of what the witness actually knows.
- [behavior] Witnesses often avoid a concrete event with a vague word such as things, and a gentle follow-up on that word can open the matter. When: A question touches a specific event. Why: Vague words let witnesses avoid committing to details.
- [behavior] An unsure witness tends to adopt the first plausible option the questioner offers, then describes it with growing confidence. When: Witness is uncertain and eager to help, and options are offered. Why: Agreeing pleases the questioner and relieves uncertainty.
- [behavior] A witness whose testimony proves useful may be released, which suggests usefulness rather than innocence drove the release. When: a witness is freed after giving key testimony. Why: release can serve the accuser's aims.
- [behavior] Speaking up for someone at personal risk, such as during dangerous times, signals sincerity and gives the testimony added credibility. When: Speaking for an accused person is dangerous. Why: Costly action is hard to fake, so observers read it as sincere.
- [behavior] A party criticized in a published account may annotate its copy, which signals that the account was being read and taken seriously. When: a published account attacks a named person.
- [behavior] Telling a resisting suspect that another witness has already spoken tends to make them stop resisting and speak. When: a suspect is withholding information. Why: Corroboration removes the point of continued resistance.
- [behavior] Only a newcomer lacking background has no preset reading of a scene, so their first interpretation is free of expectation. When: a witness joins without prior accusation. Why: background knowledge sets expectations.
- [behavior] An accused person whose argument is undercut by a trusted witness may be left speechless, since the blow is emotional as well as logical. When: the witness was trusted and did not expect to speak against the accused. Why: the reversal hits both reasoning and feeling.
- [behavior] A witness who is pressed may give a self-protective account and stop at the point where it becomes dangerous, cutting the story short at a convenient spot. When: A witness's account is shaped by self-interest and is being questioned. Why: Self-protection makes the witness avoid the most incriminating part of the story.
- [behavior] A suspect cannot tell whether a stranger who accuses them saw the crime or is only trying to frighten them. When: When a stranger silently follows a suspect and accuses them. Why: The stranger's knowledge, motive and reliability are all unknown.
- [behavior] A vivid or emotionally certain account tends to be accepted, even though certainty does not make it accurate. When: when a witness speaks with conviction. Why: emotional force is mistaken for evidence.
- [rule] Give in-game witnesses an explicit stake, such as a cause to defend, so players must weigh and check their testimony against a conflicting source. (x2)
- [rule] Do not dismiss a witness merely for motive, ridicule or name change; discrediting the teller does not impeach testimony, so test the claims on their own grounds. When: a witness's motive or background is in question. Why: An accusation of motive is an attack, not proof that testimony is false. (x2)
- [rule] Label each reported fact as seen directly, heard secondhand, inferred or rumor, and weigh each category differently. When: presenting witness accounts or designing in-game testimony. Why: Mixing sight with rumour and guesswork hides how much each claim is worth; source type determines evidential weight. (x2)
- [rule] Weigh each witness by sleep, fear, drink, drowsiness, sobriety, distance, light, duration and attention; brief, distant or poorly lit sightings carry little weight. When: evaluating any eyewitness testimony. Why: Impaired perception and poor viewing conditions distort what a witness reports, so the same account can carry very different weight.
- [rule] Keep a witness's stated doubt attached to the statements it qualifies, naming which claims are shaky, so the audience can weigh the weakest parts. When: the witness admits being unsure what they perceived. Why: Unnamed doubt cannot be checked; marking it shows the least reliable parts.
- [rule] Track each witness's reliability and motive as a visible stat, since a dramatic witness may add a sighting the player must verify. When: designing multi-source testimony or witnesses whose statements the player evaluates. Why: Visible reliability tells the player which accounts need checking rather than accepting them as fact.
- [rule] When a witness is a participant or beneficiary, accept only the parts corroborated by other evidence, and weigh each claim separately. When: the witness gains money, status or protection from their account. Why: A stake can colour the whole account.
- [rule] Check an alibi witness's reliability before accepting it, including any record or habit that could discredit their testimony. When: Relying on an alibi from a witness. Why: An alibi is only as strong as its witness.
- [rule] Tie a trace to a specific craft or class so players can narrow suspects without receiving a direct answer.
- [rule] Give the player a clue that contradicts the crowd's account of a suspect, so the community verdict can be tested. When: villagers push a convenient suspect. Why: a contradiction lets the player question the consensus.
- [rule] Tag each testimony with a confidence level and a verification status that the player can update as new evidence arrives. When: designing player-facing clue systems.
- [rule] Tell a witness that the whole truth is wanted, so they feel free to include details they might otherwise skip. When: opening an interview.
- [rule] Use a drug- or state-driven amnesia to explain an out-of-character act only when a plausible trigger and a known state are present. When: Explaining an act by someone who cannot remember it. Why: Without a trigger and known state, the explanation is an unfalsifiable excuse.
- [rule] Mark an unreliable guide with visible cues, such as drunkenness or self-absorption, so players know to weigh their hints. When: a guide gives useful but suspect hints. Why: the player can judge how far to trust them.
- [rule] Threaten only with consequences you can actually carry out, since a failed bluff ends cooperation.
- [rule] Test a witness's assumptions, such as believing an illness is a known recurrence, before treating their account as fact. When: a family member explains a medical or personal event. Why: A belief can replace the investigation that would confirm it.
- [rule] Do not accept a story merely because it is consistent with known facts; consistency can be engineered. When: when an account fits the physical evidence. Why: A coordinated story can be built to match known facts.
- [rule] Record testimony the game cannot confirm and leave the player to judge which governing rule applies.
- [rule] Make an in-world pamphlet credible by naming its author, letting copies circulate, and allowing rival NPCs to contradict its claims. When: designing a document players should be able to trust or doubt.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses slightly different versions of one event, so the player must find the consistent core that all versions share. When: Designing an event that players reconstruct from witness accounts. Why: Variation forces players to compare accounts and identify what is reliable.
- [rule] Do not rely on a single witness's description of a person's class or height. When: A single witness estimates a person's social class or stature. Why: Such estimates are easily wrong and need corroboration.
- [rule] Judge a witness's coverage of the time window rather than attacking their character, since a truthful witness can still have a narrow view. When: a witness seems respectable and honest. Why: A credible witness gives an accurate but partial window that must be measured.
- [rule] Do not assume a witness is unreliable merely because their story sounds odd. When: when weighing an unusual testimony.
- [heuristic] A witness's account depends on their opportunity to observe, condition at observation, interest in the outcome, and whether others or independent records confirm it. When: weighing any witness account. Why: Opportunity, condition and corroboration determine how far a report can be trusted. (x2)
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's admitted doubt about their perception, and doubt reports from drowsy or just-woken witnesses, since fatigue or haste can distort what was seen or heard. When: A witness raises uncertainty about their own observation, or is drowsy or has just woken. Why: Impaired or hurried perception can distort what was seen. (x2)
- [heuristic] Verify dramatic or self-centred accounts, and check whether fear or dream produced an impossible, emotionally charged detail, since strong emotion or embellishment can add false detail. When: A witness delivers an account with strong embellishment or a personal stake; evaluating a report with a prior motive. Why: Dramatic framing can add or inflate details, so checking is needed; vivid false detail can come from emotion. (x2)
- [heuristic] Judge a writer by what they state, not by spelling, grammar or craft quality, which say little about intelligence, honesty or motive. When: assessing a writer's competence or reliability. Why: Poor technique may reflect lack of training rather than a sign of guilt. (x2)
- [heuristic] Weigh testimony by who speaks, how they speak, what they omit or gain or lose, and whether neutral observers can confirm it. When: testimony rests on a single source or a source with a stake, or conflicting accounts. Why: stake and corroboration shape how far an account can be trusted. (x2)
- [heuristic] A witness can be accurate on one point and self-serving or wrong on another; judge each claim separately rather than the teller as a whole. When: the witness has a stake in the outcome, or reliability is mixed. Why: Motive biases some claims but not all; the teller of a claim is not the claim itself. (x2)
- [heuristic] Rank testimony by directness: seen directly outweighs heard directly, which outweighs heard secondhand; a claim passed through two or three people ranks lowest. When: deciding how far to trust a witness report. Why: direct access reduces distortion.
- [heuristic] Weigh each witness by state (grief, drink, emotion), closeness to events, motives and reticence, and whether independent checks confirm; a sober eyewitness outweighs a grieving or drunk one. When: Several witnesses with different access to events, or interviews with several witnesses. Why: Emotion, drink, grief and access to events each distort what is reported; accounts vary in reliability and motive.
- [heuristic] Check a witness's stake (financial, legal, social, or a theory protecting them) before accepting their claim; never treat their word as settled, and lower weight for prior history. When: A witness benefits or risks from the result, or has a prior history or personal stake. Why: A stake gives a reason to shape testimony; bias from history or investment distorts reports.
- [heuristic] A witness's weight depends on what they could have known and on what might have constrained them from speaking plainly. When: Weighing a witness's testimony. Why: Access to events and social restraint both affect how reliable and how candid an account is.
- [heuristic] Testimony is strongest when many independent people agree on the same action, and weaker when a witness was present but did not notice the detail in question. When: Weighing several witnesses to one event. Why: Independent agreement is hard to fake, while inattentive presence gives no real evidence on the disputed detail.
- [heuristic] Before trusting a witness, check who saw, from what distance and position, and how the account reached you. When: weighing testimony from hidden or distant observers.
- [heuristic] A witness's account is credible only if they were positioned to perceive what they claim, so test the basis of an alibi, not just the claim itself. When: when a witness offers an alibi or clearing testimony. Why: a claim can be sincere yet rest on a vantage point that could not have supplied it.
- [heuristic] Judge a witness's report by how well they had access to the event and whether they have a motive to shape what they say. When: evaluating any testimony in a story. Why: Access limits what was observed, and motive biases what gets reported.
- [heuristic] Weigh testimony by the witness's motive, senses and standing, not only by what they say. When: When a case rests on what someone heard, saw or said about a person. Why: Content alone can hide bias, perceptual limits or social pressure.
- [heuristic] A witness's account can be bent by emotion, self-interest and selective sharing, so weigh it against documents and other statements. Why: Testimony filtered through feeling or motive can drift from what actually happened.
- [heuristic] Weigh each witness by what they gain or lose: grief, grudge, loyalty or rivalry can shape what someone says and what they leave out. When: witnesses give conflicting accounts of a person's motives or behaviour. Why: Personal interest distorts reporting.
- [heuristic] Weigh each witness's account by their position, attention, motives and habits, rather than accepting or dismissing it wholesale. When: when several witnesses give partial or unhelpful accounts.
- [heuristic] Test a new accusation against what you already know of the accuser's behavior, asking why they waited or never asked earlier. When: A claim comes from someone whose past conduct is known. Why: Gaps in behavior make a claim look improbable.
- [heuristic] Consistency checks lose force when a claim rests on a physical object or document the target cannot dismiss.
- [heuristic] Judge testimony by its source, its consistency with other accounts, and whether it covers the period that matters. When: weighing any witness claim. Why: Each factor exposes a different way an account can mislead.
- [heuristic] A witness who states the basis of a belief and admits faults on their own side is usually more credible, but the concession must be genuine. When: Challenged about bias or motive.
- [heuristic] A witness NPC with a stated stake, such as a payment or debt, can be probed by asking for the basis of their testimony.
- [heuristic] A person asked to report a traveller's progress to someone else becomes a witness to that journey.
- [heuristic] Avoid writing witnesses as simply truthful or simply false; give each a limit or motive so judgment is required. When: when writing witness characters. Why: flat reliability removes the need for careful evaluation.
- [heuristic] A witness whose presence at the time has a plausible, independent explanation is more credible.
- [heuristic] Judge testimony by the witness's position, bias and evasions as well as by the words used, since each shapes what the words are worth.
- [heuristic] Test an offhand comment against concrete facts; it matters only when it conflicts with something physical.
- [heuristic] Openly clearing one suspect can make the rest of an investigator's case more credible, if the method behind the clearing is shown to be sound.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's account against their stake in the outcome; someone who owns the weapon used has a motive to protect themselves. When: a witness has a personal interest in the event. Why: Self-interest can shape how an account is told, including what is stressed or left out.
- [heuristic] Weigh testimony against motives such as resentment or trust, since a personal accusation or a vouching may not reflect the facts. When: ranking witness statements. Why: Motives color testimony, and vouching is not proof.
- [heuristic] A witness's assurance of having no personal stake cannot be taken as certain, since witnesses are not always impartial about their own feelings. Why: People are poor judges of their own bias, especially when emotionally involved.
- [heuristic] Avoid treating a suspect's appearance or reputation as proof of guilt or innocence. When: weighing a suspect against the evidence. Why: Appearance and reputation are not evidence of the act itself.
- [heuristic] Explain away each anomaly in a witness's account on its own terms, but do not dismiss core observations that resist explanation. When: a witness reports alarming or unusual events. Why: dramatic accounts may be exaggerated yet still contain real observations.
- [heuristic] Errors that all fall on the same specific true points suggest the writer knew those facts well, whereas random falsehoods scatter across unrelated details. When: assessing whether a document's inaccuracies are chance. Why: a person lying by chance gets some facts right and misses others at random.
- [heuristic] Vagueness about amounts or dates is a reason to check the account, not to accept it, and gaps should not be filled by the investigator's own assumptions. When: When a witness is vague on key facts.
- [heuristic] When probing a suspect, make only truthful but vague statements, so nothing checkable is given away while the other side fills the gaps.
- [heuristic] Treat an oddly vague phrase as a clue, since a speaker who meant a specific person would usually have named them plainly.
- [heuristic] Judge a witness's account by their position, attention and certainty. A witness can be sure of one fact and only guess at another. When: Weighing any witness testimony. Why: Each part of an account depends on what the witness could actually perceive.
- [heuristic] A motive becomes credible when the prize is stated in concrete terms, such as commercial value or the interest of rival powers.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's account by how much the witness gains from one version of events, and whether an impartial observer saw the same thing. When: Several accounts conflict and one speaker controlled evidence or benefited from its outcome. Why: A witness who gains from an outcome may shape the account toward it.
- [heuristic] Opponents may attack both a witness's perception and their motives or sobriety; assess each attack separately. When: when a witness's rival disputes their account. Why: character and perception are separate questions.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's statement only as far as the witness is reliable, disinterested, and believed by the audience; do not treat a denial as proof when the witness has a personal stake. When: Deciding how much a witness's statement can support a conclusion. Why: Personal stakes, grudges, loyalty or kindness can bias testimony as much as malice.
- [heuristic] Judge witness accounts by the speaker's name, age, role and the specific acts they can attest to. When: when a witness account is central to a case. Why: concrete identity and acts make claims checkable against the speaker's position.
- [heuristic] A checkable detail makes a weak test when it is common or easily guessed, because a lucky guess can match it by chance. When: Choosing which detail a witness must get right. Why: Common details give correct answers by coincidence, so passing them proves little.
- [heuristic] When a motivated source's story stays consistent across its core details, treat that core as credible even while doubting its emphasis or framing. When: a source with a stake gives an account.
- [heuristic] When a group assures that a practice rarely endangers the innocent, test that assurance against actual cases rather than treating it as settling objections. When: a group defends a practice by claiming it rarely harms innocents.
- [heuristic] A witness's own standing and a large petition from long-known neighbors add weight to character evidence.
- [heuristic] Vague answers such as 'I do not know' or 'about' give nothing to test; press with precise questions on distance, direction, time, names or places, or seek a second source. When: a witness gives non-specific replies. Why: Vague answers cannot be tested against other sources.
- [heuristic] Test what each state of a witness knows, rather than dismissing the witness as unreliable altogether.
- [heuristic] Weigh testimony from a source with a record of dishonesty as weak evidence, and test its claims against physical facts. When: A witness has a criminal or dishonest record. Why: Such testimony is often self-serving and unreliable.
- [heuristic] Count a secondhand report as credible only when a named, reliable witness vouches for it, and mark the rest as uncertain.
- [heuristic] Rumor and folk legend carry little weight until traced to firm sources, though they can point investigators toward a suspect.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness by motive, character, corroboration, and whether they admit their own wrongdoing; an admission of wrongdoing strengthens testimony because it is costly to make. When: When testimonies conflict or the only witness is compromised. Why: Each factor shows whether the witness gains from lying and whether the account is likely to be true.
- [heuristic] Let players check a witness's report against conditions like distance, distraction or fatigue. When: When designing testimony the player must weigh. Why: Checkable conditions let players judge reliability themselves.
- [heuristic] Judge a witness's reliability by reputation, by others' opinions, and by how the record was made, and check secondhand warnings against the testimony itself. When: Deciding whether a source is trustworthy or whether a record may have been altered. Why: Reputation and transcripts each give partial, sometimes misleading evidence.
- [heuristic] Do not treat a witness's confidence about a brief look in poor light as proof of identity. When: A witness claims to recognize someone from a short or dim observation. Why: Confidence does not guarantee accuracy under poor viewing conditions.
- [procedure] 1) Check the basis of the witness's knowledge. 2) Corroborate with independent sources; a single account is easily wrong or biased. 3) Compare with other accounts. 4) Look for bias and motive. 5) Track changes under repeated questioning. 6) Test claims against physical facts. When: a single testimony would decide a verdict or a claim is important. Why: Single accounts are easily wrong or biased. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Tag each claim as directly seen, heard, inferred or admitted. 2) Note the witness's known bias for each claim. 3) Check each claim against other evidence before relying on it. When: a witness is credible on some points and suspect on others. Why: Sorting claims by source shows which parts can carry weight.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether the source's manner, such as unusual precision, fits how real witnesses speak. 2) Check whether the claimant's actions match the claim. 3) Check the text's form for signs of a private draft. When: A claim's authority depends on who published it, or a document seems unintended for publication. Why: Credibility can be judged from the text before its facts are weighed.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the same short question at intervals. 2) Wait through silences instead of filling them. 3) Record each answer exactly, including contradictions. 4) Follow up with consistency probes. When: Questioning a weak or confused witness whose replies come slowly. Why: Short repetition reduces confusion, and exact records preserve evidence of contradiction.
- [procedure] Test a suspect's story for consistency with physical details, such as a claimed residence abroad or the condition of their hands, and ask them to explain any mismatch. When: A suspect tells a detailed personal story. Why: Physical details can contradict claimed experiences.
- [procedure] 1) Trace the claim to its source. 2) Ask whether a true knower would have given specifics, since silence about details suggests partial knowledge. 3) Note whether the witness's condition could make the claim less reliable. 4) Check the claim against independent facts.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness for the exact words used. 2) Record them verbatim, including every claimed link and claim about others. 3) Mark which names and places remain unknown. 4) Search independent records for mention of them. When: A witness's account is the main evidence and must be tested. Why: Exact wording lets the listener judge what was actually said and gives a fixed basis for checking.
- [procedure] 1) Note the witness's state, such as fear, intoxication or distance from the event. 2) Note whether the witness knows the source direction of a sound or event. 3) Separate what the witness saw from what they believed or were told. When: Assessing a witness's account. Why: Emotional state, perception and inference each affect accuracy.
- [procedure] 1) Check the witness's condition, such as drink or fatigue. 2) Check distance and light. 3) Check the date of the sighting against the event. 4) Use the account only if all pass. When: a witness's account is the only source for a time or identity. Why: each factor distorts perception.
- [procedure] 1) Ask about the witness's stake and feelings toward those involved. 2) Separate observed facts from interpretation. 3) Compare answers over time and flag changes. 4) Check key claims against physical traces. 5) Record half-remembered details as uncertain.
- [procedure] 1) Check what the witness could actually have observed. 2) Rate how sure they are. 3) Look for embellishment or self-interest. 4) Weigh the account accordingly. When: Assessing a witness's account. Why: Access, confidence and embellishment each affect reliability.
- [procedure] 1) Check the witness's name and qualifications. 2) Confirm membership in a relevant professional body. 3) Vet the witness before trusting them, since enemies can send a false witness. When: a witness supplies key evidence. Why: enemies may plant false witnesses.
- [procedure] 1) Check the conditions of perception and the witness's state. 2) Seek corroboration from others or from evidence. 3) Check named details against known places and timing. When: a claim rests only on what one witness perceived.
- [procedure] 1) Check how precise the witness's times and details are. 2) Verify what they could physically see or hear from their position. 3) Fix timing with device logs. 4) Probe for personal bias. 5) Cross-check with other witnesses. When: a case depends on who passed a single choke point. Why: each check tests a different way a confident witness can still be wrong.
- [procedure] 1) Tell the witness and any attending party the time limit, and keep within it. 2) Open with a short, reassuring statement of who is asking and why. 3) Ask one question at a time. 4) Use gentle, repeated prompts to recover a fact the witness has lost track of. When: The witness is the only source for a fact and cannot be interviewed at length.
- [procedure] 1) Trace who told whom along the chain. 2) Separate first-hand reports from second-hand ones. 3) Look for agreement among independent accounts. 4) Reconcile differences with a plausible scenario. 5) State what remains unknown. When: when no document names a place but people's accounts of it survive. Why: Oral accounts gain weight only when their transmission and independence are established.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a precise question whose answer can be checked against the physical scene. 2) Compare the answer with the evidence. 3) If it conflicts, re-run the same procedure with one controlled change. 4) Keep instructions identical across trials so differences come from the change. When: A witness's directions or memory must be turned into a physical action that can be verified. Why: Identical repetition isolates the variable responsible for any difference in outcome.
- [procedure] 1) Let a long-talking witness speak without interruption. 2) Filter out digression. 3) Record material facts about routine, deviations and people. 4) Note the witness's conclusions separately as opinion. When: When interviewing a witness who speaks at length and knows a routine. Why: Material facts are often buried under filler, and conclusions can be wrong even when observations are accurate.
- [procedure] 1) Ask about a specific person at a specific time. 2) Let the witness volunteer contrasts with other people. 3) Use volunteered contrasts to identify the person sought. When: When a witness is unlikely to recall a person from general questioning. Why: Specific questions and volunteered contrasts reach memories that broad questions miss.
- [tradeoff] Past similar deceptions make a new false story more believable, but when reputation is contested, judge by consistency, candour and conduct, not standing or past accusations. When: A suspect has a history of deception, or a witness's reputation is disputed without direct evidence.
