- [pitfall] A story or view repeated without retraction, even word-for-word as if memorized, shows persistence, not accuracy; repeated questioning validates flimsy accounts as readily as honest ones. Why: stability under pressure is not the same as accuracy. (x2)
- [pitfall] Vagueness, especially about dates, is mistaken for evasion or lying though it often reflects honest memory gaps; dismissing such a witness discards accurate testimony. Why: Imprecision is read as motive rather than memory limits.
- [pitfall] Treating one sworn, vague or partisan statement as settled proof is a mistake, whichever way it points; the public often assumes the defence will never answer it.
- [pitfall] Accepting a witness's credibility from social standing alone lets an arranged alibi pass unexamined.
- [pitfall] Vague witnesses can be wrongly taken as hiding something, so each claim needs its own source before it is trusted.
- [pitfall] Treating a vague recollection as confirmation of a claim leads to false certainty. Why: A vague memory cannot confirm specifics.
- [pitfall] Accepting an emotionally invested account without checking it against neutral sources hides the observer's slant. Why: Bias goes unnoticed without independent comparison.
- [pitfall] A witness's grievances and self-interest colour part of the account, so their statements need checking.
- [pitfall] A consistent story can still be partial, so consistency alone does not establish the whole truth.
- [pitfall] An account can be internally consistent yet still mislead, and a theory that fits its own facts can fail against the physical scene.
- [pitfall] A rough sketch may read as a gag, leading viewers to write off a real clue as sloppy art.
- [pitfall] A listener's promise to keep a secret does not limit what they do with the information next.
- [pitfall] Assuming a witness cannot speak to a topic narrows an inquiry and can send questions to the wrong people. When: Planning which questions to ask whom.
- [pitfall] A vague question such as did she look strange invites agreement; narrow questions give the witness less room to shape answers. Why: open wording lets the witness mirror the questioner.
- [pitfall] A witness who made an earlier mistake, or whose time depends on an unchecked clock, is a weaker source even when delivering a firm figure. When: Assessing a time or figure from a witness. Why: Prior errors and unverified instruments undermine precision.
- [pitfall] If the antagonist's shock at the reveal is not credible, the reversal feels staged and loses its impact.
- [pitfall] Knowledge learned for one occasion covers only what was studied and tends to break under unexpected questions. When: Testing whether someone's expertise is genuine. Why: Surface knowledge lacks the depth to answer unplanned questions.
- [pitfall] A witness's embarrassment can lead them to undervalue accurate details they did notice.
- [pitfall] A weak-sounding excuse is not proof of guilt, and a dismissive judgment about it must still be tested against records.
- [pitfall] Once a clue is destroyed, the case rests on testimony about it and on who had access, so those witnesses must be credible. Why: weak witnesses cannot carry the case once the physical evidence is gone.
- [pitfall] Reading a vague phrase as a list of suspects can mislead the investigation.
- [pitfall] Assuming a witness would notice a substitution is an error when their contact with the real person was only momentary and their impression is weak.
- [pitfall] If a witness's reason for staying silent is weak, the omission reads as contrivance rather than character.
- [pitfall] Attacking a witness's character can make the witness shut down and stop sharing information.
- [pitfall] Confidence does not reflect precision; test a witness's certainty against what they could observe, and record exactly what each saw and for how long. Why: Confidence does not reflect precision.
- [pitfall] Loyalty or kindness can make a witness knowingly lie, such as repeating a false time for a partner; lower their credibility, including corrected accounts, when allegiance is disclosed. When: a witness knows a fact that would harm someone they care about, or allegiance is disclosed. Why: Loyalty can outweigh accuracy; protective motives produce knowing false testimony even when no rule excludes the witness.
- [pitfall] Attacking a witness's character does not prove the accused innocent or answer the evidence; it removes one support, so other evidence must still be examined.
- [pitfall] Witnesses can be wrong about the hour, the person involved or what they checked; ask each whether an identity or date error is possible, and test the account against other records and witnesses. When: a case depends on who was where and when. Why: Observation and memory are fallible and can conflict.
- [pitfall] Sympathy, distress or charm lowers scrutiny; accepting a sympathetic or pleasant speaker's account unchecked leads to false conclusions and missed withheld facts. Why: Emotional appeal lowers scrutiny.
- [pitfall] Fully believed or fully dismissed witnesses remove the need for deduction, and heavy unreliability signals make audiences distrust everything; balance credibility and keep verifiable anchor facts. When: writing NPC reports the player must evaluate. Why: Balanced credibility keeps the player reasoning about evidence.
- [pitfall] Witnesses under pressure or eager to please may confirm a suggested identity; ask them to confirm only when fully sure, since the answer may mirror the questioner's expectation. When: a witness is asked to confirm identity. Why: Pressure and suggestion can override uncertain memory; willingness to please makes identification reflect expectation rather than what was seen.
- [pitfall] A stated reason that sounds weak may still be the true one, so an inferred hidden motive needs confirmation before it is treated as fact.
- [pitfall] Interviewers who move quickly, pass over weak or unexpected answers, and repeat the question to another witness steer the collective result.
- [pitfall] Judgments of whether a witness is credible or an act is beyond human strength depend on what the judge already believes is possible. When: Weighing extraordinary testimony. Why: Prior beliefs decide what counts as impossible, so the same account can be accepted or rejected.
- [pitfall] Reading too much into a witness's words can invent meaning; confirm the intended sense with the witness where possible. When: Interpreting a witness's phrasing or tone. Why: Wording and memory can differ from what the investigator infers.
- [pitfall] Eliminating a route on the word of a single witness is fragile, since that witness may be mistaken or the account may itself be disputed. When: When ruling out an access route based on one person's observation. Why: Unverified testimony can wrongly close a route that was actually open.
- [pitfall] Relying on a single witness for a destroyed document leaves the only record as that witness's account, which may be unreliable. When: When a key document was destroyed and only one person saw it. Why: Without a second source the account cannot be verified.
- [pitfall] Affection or sympathy for a witness can bias how their behaviour is read, so an investigator should check for it. When: when a witness is personally liked or close. Why: sympathy shapes interpretation of ambiguous signs.
- [pitfall] A witness who clings to a theory despite contrary facts is not automatically guilty; loyalty or fear can drive the stubbornness.
- [pitfall] Guards who testify about each other's sleep are not independent witnesses, so their accounts need an outside check such as a third party who was awake. When: when guards vouch for each other's whereabouts. Why: Mutual testimony shares the same bias and gap.
- [pitfall] A witness's reliability can be challenged on grounds such as fatigue, so testimony needs corroboration. When: When a witness contradicts a suspect. Why: Fatigue or other conditions can make a witness's account unreliable.
- [pitfall] Discounting a witness because they are fearful of the supernatural or hysterical does not establish that they are wrong, and such a witness may have seen something real. When: When a witness's temperament is used to dismiss their account. Why: Emotional state affects delivery, not necessarily the accuracy of the observation.
- [fact] A witness is reliable only for what they directly perceived; a narrator who never heard a sound cannot describe it, and a signed record verifies nothing beyond observation. Why: Testimony covers observation, not identity or unobserved links. (x2)
- [fact] Witness testimony does not substitute for documents or physical evidence that can be examined directly.
- [fact] A witness's value depends on how precisely events are recorded, how checkable the account is, and whether the sighting is physically possible.
- [fact] A witness's confidence in what they heard does not establish that the account is accurate.
- [fact] A signer may not know witnesses are watching, yet the formality is still met. Witnesses can later swear the signing was properly done.

## alibi verification and testing
- [model] Model NPC verification in three tiers: some never check, some check one record, and some check everything. When: designing NPC checks on player identity.
- [mechanism] Timed records (a driver's trip, a performance, a train departure, a published timetable) fix a person to a place and hour, confirming or breaking alibis against witness times. When: Designing alibi or transit-based investigation, including NPC alibis players can check. Why: Matching times across independent sources exposes contradictions.
- [mechanism] A timed absence can give a suspect an opportunity to act, and the resulting changes become evidence for the player to find. When: When designing timed or absence-based investigation mechanics. Why: Removing observation creates a window in which hidden actions occur and leave traces.
- [mechanism] A letter from a trusted intermediary vouching for a bearer lets an unknown stranger be accepted when combined with the token. When: A stranger is introduced to a contact they do not know. Why: Endorsement from a trusted party carries weight with the person approached.
- [mechanism] An alibi covering a gap can be exposed by asking whether the claimed hours could physically hold the claimed actions, given the true timeline. When: A suspect's account relies on undocumented events filling a time gap. Why: Invented events must fit the physical constraints of the time window to hold up.
- [mechanism] An alibi is contradicted when a measurable interval between known points is much longer than the travel time between them, leaving an unexplained gap that may cover the crime. When: When a suspect's account of a short interval can be measured against travel times. Why: The unexplained surplus of time is the window in which the suspect could have acted.
- [mechanism] Guard patrol schedules define alibi windows, so a player who checks the rounds can find the gap in which a theft was possible. When: Designing alibis or timing puzzles around guard routes. Why: Patrol gaps create opportunity windows that players can reconstruct.
- [mechanism] A solid alibi keeps suspicion from settling on a suspect until new evidence breaks the alibi.
- [mechanism] An alibi made of many small claims can pass each check alone yet collapse when the claims are linked, so the lie appears only when checks are combined. When: when a suspect's alibi is tested. Why: Each claim looks independent, so its failure is hidden until the claims are compared.
- [behavior] Testimony from brief, dim, crowded or shocked sightings, including of disguised people, yields only general impressions and must be tested before trust. When: poor lighting, distance, crowding, disguise, brief glimpses or shock. Why: Recall depends on what observers could see and what they were attending to.
- [behavior] Sleep is a weak alibi: a sleeper cannot vouch for their own timing, so the claim is unverifiable and the timeline must rely on other evidence. When: When an alibi rests on being asleep, or a timeline is built from testimony during a night event. Why: Unconscious time is unobserved and unverifiable; sleep disrupts awareness of time.
- [rule] Keep timestamped logs and telemetry, such as power or water use, of NPC movements and events, linking each whereabouts claim to them so players can rebuild order and find contradictions. When: When designing a mystery or witness system where timing or whereabouts matter. Why: Ordered, recorded entries let players check consistency; contradictions become discoverable by comparison. (x2)
- [rule] Test an alibi against the household routine, which must itself be verified; a claimed location conflicting with usual pattern, like a room found empty when occupied, exposes it. When: A witness claims to have been somewhere during a routine period, or when evaluating a character's whereabouts against a routine. Why: Deviations from habit are hard to explain away; a routine never observed is only a claim. (x2)
- [rule] Verify an alibi through a source the suspect does not control, such as a third party's call or an employer's shift log, rather than the suspect's own word. When: When checking a suspect's stated whereabouts. Why: A source the suspect controls can confirm a false story; a bare statement clears no one until verified.
- [rule] Accept an alibi only when independent, disinterested witnesses confirm the exact time window that matters; discount confirmation from someone with a stake, such as a spouse. When: Assessing an alibi that rests on witnesses. Why: A confirmer with a personal interest has reason to shade the account; disinterested witnesses are less likely to.
- [rule] Check a mutual alibi against a separate independent source, and whether the two vouchers were ever observed in the same place at the same moment. When: Two witnesses vouch for each other.
- [rule] Let the player confirm an NPC's alibi with a second NPC; a mismatch exposes the lie, so record each NPC's reliability in its character data. When: Designing alibis in a game, when an NPC gives a claimed whereabouts. Why: Independent accounts can conflict.
- [rule] Give each NPC a schedule players can verify through clocks, bells, guard rotations or travel times, plus an alibi checker comparing NPC statements against them, letting characters contradict one another. When: Designing a game with NPC alibis. Why: Travel-time checks make alibis testable through play.
- [rule] Every leg of a claimed schedule needs an independent witness, such as a clerk, conductor or companion, who saw the person at that place and time; unwitnessed legs stay unverified. When: A suspect offers a detailed schedule. Why: Unwitnessed legs cannot be verified.
- [rule] Do not accept a schedule-based alibi or timestamped purchase until the crime time is confirmed by an independent source or fixed in the game state. Why: The alibi holds only if the time it rests on is genuine; it can only be checked against a known event time.
- [rule] Treat an alibi as something to actively disprove, tested by investigators against physical and timing evidence; the suspect need not prove it. Why: Checking is the investigator's job.
- [rule] Test a stated alibi against a source the suspect does not control, and check whether the claimed place and time were physically possible. When: A suspect gives a specific time and place. Why: Proof supplied by the suspect can be fabricated; only an outside source can confirm it.
- [rule] Treat an alibi as unconfirmed when its owner refuses to say where they were, since silence cannot verify absence.
- [rule] Undated or estimated times cannot support a timeline check, so mark them as unverifiable rather than as established. When: a witness gives vague times. Why: Vague timing cannot confirm or refute presence.
- [rule] Check an alibi against how the person would plausibly have behaved, since a claimed alibi can fail on behavioral grounds alone.
- [rule] Design alibi documents with a detectable mismatch so the player must spot the inconsistency before an NPC is cleared.
- [rule] Verify a claimant's description of the item against the item itself before handing it over. When: When a person comes forward to claim a found object. Why: A claim that matches the item is far more likely to be genuine than one that does not.
- [rule] Test a claim of continuous presence against a machine record, and discount any log kept by the person whose claim is being tested. When: when a witness claims to have been present throughout. Why: a self-kept log is not independent.
- [rule] Contact a person named on a found item directly, such as through a listed number, and ask them to attend before trusting the link. When: A found item names a person. Why: A direct check reveals whether the name belongs to the case.
- [rule] Clearing one party of a link to a crime does not clear another suspect; assess each suspect's evidence separately. When: a finding absolves one person linked to the case. Why: a partial clearance does not transfer to other suspects.
- [rule] Test each alibi with an independent witness, ideally at a separate location, who recalls the suspect at a stated time.
- [rule] Build alibis that hold in some NPC accounts but not others, so players must check public activity to find the truth.
- [rule] When several alibis rest on the same witness, test each against the corrected timeline, since one timing error affects all of them. When: Multiple alibis come from one witness. Why: A shared source spreads its timing error across each claim.
- [rule] Judge each suspect by whether they could independently have acted, not by how well their accounts fit together. Why: a shared alibi can look convincing while proving nothing.
- [rule] Use alibi witnesses who can state where the suspect stayed up to a stated hour, and check that their account covers the whole window rather than one moment.
- [rule] Attack an alibi by naming the exact time in question and pressing it with independent written evidence rather than another person's word. When: a suspect claims to have been elsewhere.
- [rule] Check each alibi against independent records, such as staff-confirmed room occupancy, and flag it when the claimant's own description contradicts those records. Why: Records made by others are harder to bend than the claimant's account.
- [rule] Give each NPC alibi a checkable record, such as a ticket, call log or timestamped message, that a neutral NPC can confirm or refute. When: Designing alibi puzzles. Why: Players verify claims rather than accept them.
- [rule] Accept an alibi only when the timeline and the people vouching for it line up with each other. Why: An alibi that conflicts with the timeline or its witnesses is not reliable.
- [rule] Design alibi puzzles where the player compares each character's claimed actions with task durations and with what could be heard. When: Building a deduction puzzle around schedules. Why: Gives the player concrete values to test claims against.
- [rule] Do not split a line of inquiry that depends on one witness who must be seen first; keep that line sequential.
- [rule] Before accepting an accusation, check whether the accused could physically perform the act given strength, reach and timing. When: evaluating a suspect's confession or accusation. Why: a claim the body cannot support is unreliable.
- [rule] Use patrol routes, shift logs and door logs as alibi evidence, since they reveal who was absent at a critical time. Why: Logged movement from other areas can confirm or break a claimed location.
- [rule] Use published notices or posted schedules as independent sources that can contradict an NPC's stated alibi. When: Designing a mystery where an NPC's account can be checked. Why: Independent sources let the player test claims without relying on the NPC.
- [rule] Test a suspect's stated location independently, since an alibi can misplace where the suspect was even when the account is confident.
- [rule] Make an impostor's identity checkable against a witness list so the player can verify the alibi independently. When: Writing a disguise or false-identity twist. Why: Checkable alibis let players test the solution against the evidence rather than accept it on authority.
- [rule] Plant an alibi's witness in the first act, but delay testing the alibi until suspicion has been spent on other suspects. Why: A late test then reads as a reversal rather than a repeat of earlier doubts.
- [heuristic] Dated documents such as letters, receipts or absence records can support an alibi, verified against an independent travel or movement log or by others' confirmation. Why: Cross-checking independent dated sources tests a claimed whereabouts. (x2)
- [heuristic] An alibi or quarrel account is only as strong as the independent witnesses who saw events; named witnesses who cannot be found or whose roles do not fit are fragile. (x2)
- [heuristic] Ask where unstated time went and check the edges and exceptions of long or fixed alibis, since short absences and unobserved gaps may hide there. When: A timeline has silent periods, an alibi covers a long span, or a schedule seems fixed. Why: Silent windows and window edges can hide movements the account omits.
- [heuristic] An alibi resting on one uncertain sighting, or on a sighting covering only part of the required interval, is partial and should not clear a suspect. When: when the witness admits the sighting may be mistaken, or covers only part of the span. Why: Sightings can cover only part of an interval, so partial or uncertain coverage cannot clear the whole window.
- [heuristic] An untested alibi or unrecorded gap should stay open and be reopened when new evidence fills or changes it, since a claim is not verified until checked.
- [heuristic] Check an alibi through independent accounts covering each hour in question; detailed, corroborated records can clear a suspect despite an early failure to account for time. When: verifying a suspect's movements. Why: independent coverage of each window tests the claim.
- [heuristic] Check a detained person's identity before treating them as the target, since a plausible arrival can be the wrong person.
- [heuristic] Let NPCs accept a cover identity only when they lack a verifying contact, so a player who learns the network can expose the impostor. When: Designing NPC trust in an impostor plot. Why: Gating acceptance on verification gives players a route to expose the lie.
- [heuristic] Combine a process-based time window with each person's last-seen time to narrow who could have acted. Why: Intersecting two independent time constraints eliminates candidates.
- [heuristic] Use a third party's sighting to test a claimed alibi when that party was positioned to see the departure. When: Checking whether someone was where they claimed. Why: A positioned observer can confirm or break a claimed location.
- [heuristic] Before trusting a report of hearing nothing, ask what the observer's own noise and attention were at the time. When: a witness says they heard nothing. Why: The observer's conditions may have masked what others could hear.
- [heuristic] Tie an alibi to other characters' sightings and a travel time, so the claim can be checked against the distance involved. When: when building a character's alibi. Why: checkable claims make deception testable.
- [heuristic] An alibi based on being elsewhere can be arranged to avoid a suspected item, so verify the absence itself. When: a suspect's alibi is an absence.
- [heuristic] Corroboration from a suspect's own companion carries little weight, since that witness shares the suspect's interest. When: when assessing an alibi supported only by a companion. Why: A companion may be unable or unwilling to contradict the suspect.
- [heuristic] Check a suspect's claimed history of odd episodes against the timing of the suspicious act and against other witness statements before accepting it as the innocent explanation. When: A suspect's past episodes are offered to explain suspicious conduct. Why: A convenient explanation may be invented or misdated, so it needs independent checking.
- [heuristic] A leg that the first object cannot explain can reveal a second object or a hidden handover between parties.
- [heuristic] Record when a clue was removed and when it returned. The gaps between these times show when the room was empty and when someone could have handled the clue. When: A physical clue moves within a room whose occupancy you can track. Why: Movement timing reveals the handler's routine.
- [heuristic] Give several NPCs overlapping schedules, each with a plausible alibi, so players must test opportunity rather than consistency. When: designing suspect sets. Why: alibis that look consistent force players to check access instead.
- [heuristic] When a group of related items is missing, check that group's records instead of dropping the gap, since clustered absences can share a cause. When: Several linked items have no recovered record. Why: Clustered absences can point to a shared event.
- [heuristic] A verified location at the time of an alleged act contradicts the claim and suggests the account was fabricated. When: when the time and place of the act are reasonably reliable.
- [heuristic] Several broken routines together are stronger evidence than one missed routine, which alone proves little.
- [heuristic] Letting a sceptic check a detail personally turns doubt into belief more effectively than assertion. When: Persuading a doubter of a physical claim. Why: Being able to verify a detail removes the need to trust the presenter.
- [heuristic] Build a cover story from real, checkable particulars, because mixing true details makes the lie easier to hold. When: when a cover story must survive checks. Why: true details are consistent with what the questioner can observe.
- [heuristic] An arrival that no one witnessed, when a normal means of transport would have brought the person to the door, is a gap to investigate. When: A suspect's return home is unobserved. Why: Unobserved movement can hide a swap of identities.
- [heuristic] Build a timeline by lining up dated events, witness ages and intervals from several testimonies; a timeline that fits all of them is more credible than one that fits only some. When: When reconstructing events from partial records. Why: Independent dates and ages can be cross-checked against each other to expose errors.
- [heuristic] An absent principal with an alibi can be used to avoid suspicion, so the player must find the party who actually acted. When: Designing a mystery where the planner is away. Why: Distance from the crime protects the planner and shifts investigation.
- [heuristic] When an alibi cannot be checked, it is not decisive, so weigh it against the other available evidence. When: When an alibi has no independent check.
- [heuristic] A sighting placed around midnight is only as reliable as its time, so find a source that can fix the hour. Why: approximate times weaken a sighting.
- [heuristic] Design NPC alibi statements that can be checked against other clocks, since a claimed location cuts down the possible window. When: when designing suspect statements in a mystery level. Why: Checkable claims let players narrow the timeline and test the suspect.
- [heuristic] A stated schedule can be false, so check an alibi against independent sightings and physical evidence. When: Evaluating a suspect's claimed whereabouts. Why: A written or reported schedule can be fabricated.
- [heuristic] A fact that seems to clear a suspect should be checked for who could have produced it, since a planner can stage an alibi.
- [heuristic] An alibi given by an associate of a suspect is weak support, and it can keep that suspect in the frame.
- [procedure] 1) List each sighting of the suspect's two identities. 2) Check whether any moment shows both together; a missing joint sighting is an easily overlooked gap. 3) Look for arrivals or departures no one saw. 4) Test whether the absence matters before concluding impersonation. When: A suspect's whereabouts rest on sightings of separate identities, or people described as separate may be one person. Why: Gaps in witnessed overlap reveal possible impersonation. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Take the last sighting alive as earliest bound and discovery time as latest. 2) Narrow the range with maximum survival time after a known poisoning. 3) List each witness's position and view. 4) Check whether each suspect was covered in the window. When: Testing whether a suspect could have been present when the time of death is uncertain but independent times exist. Why: Two bounds plus a known duration limit the window; an alibi is only as strong as the timeline and witness coverage. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Record where each witness was and measure the distance to the place described. 2) Stand there and look along the claimed line of sight. 3) Reject observations from places the witness could not have reached or seen from. When: Testing a witness's claim to have seen an event. Why: A claim requires physical presence and a clear line of sight. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) State the claimed location, time and companion. 2) Find an independent record, such as a doorman's log or establishment time-clock, that the claimant does not control. 3) Confirm whether the claimed event occurred there; accept the alibi only if the record supports it. When: when an alibi rests on an arrival, appointment or presence claim. Why: Only evidence the witness did not control confirms a claimed hour, place or companion; the suspect's own account alone is weak support.
- [procedure] 1) Bound a person's movements with timestamps from their last sighting and report. 2) Test the alibi against several independent witnesses at different times and points. 3) Weigh whether coincidental sightings are linked or unrelated. When: when verifying a suspect's account against a timeline or when an alibi rests on sightings. Why: Several independent sources make an alibi more reliable; one vague witness can be mistaken or lying, and independent observers at different points make movement hard to fake.
- [procedure] 1) Record every event time against one shared reference clock. 2) Log later checks at fixed times. 3) Test each reported time against those recorded points. When: Alibis or movements depend on times within a building, or several alibis fall within one window. Why: Shared clocks prevent inconsistent memories from distorting comparison; reconciling reported times with clocks actually read prevents memory errors.
- [procedure] 1) State the claimed identity, title or document. 2) Find an independent record, such as an authoritative reference, handwriting sample, laundry mark, directory or insurer's registration, that can confirm or exclude it. 3) Check the record against the claim. 4) Note what the record cannot show. When: when an identity, title or document must be confirmed before it is accepted. Why: Independent records test a claim, while a claim with no independent check rests on assumption.
- [procedure] 1) Record each event with its time. 2) Compare event times with witness-stated times and activity durations. 3) Test whether each claimed movement fits the gaps between events. When: a suspect's movements are in doubt, witnesses give different times, or events are reconstructed from observations. Why: Repeated time-ordered records let investigators rebuild where a vessel or person moved and rule possibilities in or out, showing whether a claimed position was physically possible.
- [procedure] 1) Note the time and place of the claimed engagement. 2) Send a note to the named other party through a third person. 3) Use the reply to confirm or contradict the claim. A dead party cannot confirm it, so the appointment stays unverified. When: a suspect names a specific appointment, or a witness claims an arrangement with someone who has died. Why: Only the other party can confirm the arrangement, and an independent party can verify the claim.
- [procedure] 1) Split the suspect's account into separate, checkable movements, with times, places and sums. 2) Find an independent source for each, such as staff accounts, purchase logs, shipping manifests, telegrams or people with no stake. 3) Mark unconfirmed or contradicted steps and weigh them rather than dismissing them. When: a suspect or witness claims a place and time, or gives a timed account with several checkable steps. Why: Each movement must stand on its own evidence; a precise, checkable account is harder to fake than a vague one.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the witness's position. 2) Determine what could physically be seen from it. 3) Separate what was observed from what was assumed, and check the observation is possible. When: when judging any eyewitness account or claim to have seen something from a position. Why: Physical visibility can rule out an observation regardless of the witness's sincerity.
- [procedure] 1) Fix each claimed time from a witness. 2) Estimate travel time between claimed positions, to the scene and back. 3) Check whether the gap allows the claimed location to be reached and returned from in time. When: testing whether a suspect could reach the scene or a claimed location.
- [procedure] 1) Write the claimed route with its times. 2) Check whether visibility and timing allow unseen positions along it. 3) Test secondary records such as tickets, timepieces and dated vouchers against the route, since checking only the headline misses cover-ups. When: checking whether a claimed alibi holds. Why: Secondary records can contradict a claim that looks correct at first.
- [procedure] 1) Identify who vouches for the suspect and when each saw them, or the exact time and place of a specific sighting. 2) Check that the witness's coverage spans that time and place. 3) Rule the suspect out only if the window covers the crime moment. When: a suspect claims to have been elsewhere during a narrow window, or a specific sighting contradicts or supports presence. Why: An alibi clears a suspect only if its window overlaps the crime; a broad alibi can fail to cover a narrow sighting.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the alibi's claim and its vague points. 2) Note where timing or location is uncertain. 3) Test the weakest point first against the suspect's behaviour, seeking direct confirmation from the source rather than a written summary. When: checking a suspect's alibi, especially one reported second-hand. Why: Vague alibis hide weak points, summaries drop details that expose them, and a suspect's later response can reveal them.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a second NPC about the same person, or ask the speaker to repeat a detail. 2) Check every newly named person against other witnesses. 3) Accept identity only when the checks agree. When: when a player must verify who is speaking or who has been named. Why: Independent checks turn a cue into confirmation.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who could have been elsewhere at the time. 2) Identify independent witnesses who could confirm the claimed whereabouts. 3) Check the distance and travel time between places against the claim. When: when testing whether a suspect was elsewhere. Why: independent confirmation and travel feasibility decide whether the alibi holds.
- [procedure] 1) Verify the alibi documents. 2) If they hold, drop the suspect. 3) If they are false, keep the suspect in play. When: before clearing any suspect.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the timeline with exact times for each event. 2) List the physical traces the account implies. 3) Search for marks that differ by direction of movement. 4) Recover any objects said to have changed hands. 5) Use a plausible pretext for inspection. When: when a suspect's alibi rests on a private meeting no one else can confirm. Why: Physical traces and fixed times test whether the account is consistent with the scene.
- [procedure] 1) Note the unknown sighting. 2) List every household member. 3) Place each one at the relevant time by direct observation or report. 4) Rule out those placed elsewhere. 5) Keep narrowing until the gap is small. When: when a sighting or noise must be placed among known people.
- [procedure] 1) Choose the time of an event. 2) Look up where each suspect was at that time. 3) Flag any conflict between a suspect's location and the event as a clue. When: when the player checks suspects against an event. Why: Conflicts in location and time become discoverable evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Record the exact detail of the alibi document, such as seat, row and date. 2) Compare it with an independent record. 3) Treat a mismatch as a contradiction of the alibi. When: a suspect's alibi rests on a ticket or similar document. Why: independent records are harder to alter than a suspect's account.
- [procedure] 1) Identify people with no stake in the outcome who were near the place. 2) Ask each specific questions about the suspect's presence during the window. 3) Record which claims each one confirms. When: when a suspect's presence at a place and time is central.
- [procedure] 1) Map the claimed location and the route to it. 2) Look for physical traces of a route out and back. 3) Time the trip against the critical window. 4) Check the suspect's recent purchases for preparation. When: A suspect claims to have been elsewhere and the layout of the location may decide whether that is possible. Why: Geometry, timing and possession together show opportunity and planning that a bare claim does not.
- [procedure] 1) Record the suspect's claimed location and time. 2) Gather accounts from people with no stake in the claim. 3) Find accounts that place the suspect elsewhere during the same window. 4) Attack the single conflict rather than the whole story. When: a suspect's account depends on being somewhere else. Why: One independent contradiction can break an otherwise coherent alibi.
- [procedure] 1) Build a timeline of the suspect's stated movements. 2) Confirm each step through sources the suspect does not control. 3) Request replies quickly so they can shape the next step. 4) Compare travel distance with the time window. When: When testing whether a suspect could have been present at a crime. Why: Independent records are harder to fake than a suspect's own account.
- [procedure] 1) Pin down the exact date by asking the witness directly. 2) Ask whether a specific person was involved before accepting any description. 3) Test the record against other facts before building a timeline on it. When: a minor official recorded who passed and when.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the alibi-giver. 2) Ask whether the alibi-giver would swear to the account under legal scrutiny. 3) Check the account against transport or witness records. When: An alibi depends on one person's word. Why: A sworn account exposes weak or false claims to challenge.
- [procedure] 1) List the claimed times: departure, arrival, and activity between. 2) Identify who can confirm each step. 3) Note weak links. 4) Corroborate each step with independent records or witnesses. 5) Keep a separate timeline per person and compare them. When: when a suspect offers a timed account of their movements. Why: An alibi is strong only if each of its times can be checked independently.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the suspect's location with witnesses at the trigger time. 2) Have the victim move to the danger zone at a chosen moment. 3) Keep witnesses' attention away from the danger. When: a suspect must appear innocent while the crime is timed by them. Why: Combining a witnessed location with a victim's timed movement breaks the link between suspect and crime.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the departure time and the announced route. 2) Estimate expected arrival from usual travel time and the shortest route. 3) Contact the expected destination to learn whether the party has arrived. 4) Choose how fast to act from the lead. When: a witness's account of movements can be checked at a fixed point. Why: a check at a point someone else controls turns an estimate into a verified fact.
- [procedure] 1) Have the suspect confirm the exact time of the claimed event. 2) Establish whereabouts across the whole crime window. 3) Compare the claimed behavior with the person's known routine. 4) Note hesitations or self-corrections. When: an alibi depends on a claimed time or place. Why: a claim is only as strong as its time and location.
- [procedure] 1) Pin the suspect to a location at the exact hour of the crime. 2) Question everyone present where the suspect claims to have been. 3) Canvass the route between that location and the crime scene. 4) Seek one reliable witness who places the suspect near the scene in the window. When: a suspect has a claimed alibi that can be checked. Why: one reliable sighting turns an alibi into circumstantial evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the suspect's claimed time and place. 2) Ask the people who were with them then. 3) Cross-check each account against other reports for shared contacts or conflicts.
- [procedure] 1) Start from an unaccounted group of seats or tickets. 2) Get the specific seat numbers. 3) Check them against unsold-ticket stock and issuing records. When: a group of tickets or seats is unaccounted for, or attendance contradicts the normal pattern.
- [procedure] 1) Mark fixed event cues on a shared timeline. 2) Mark when each person had to be present. 3) Find the gap that would let an absent person leave and return unnoticed. When: An alibi depends on minutes within a scheduled event. Why: A timeline anchored to fixed cues exposes the windows where a person could act unseen.
- [procedure] 1) Record each suspect claim about movements, possessions or state. 2) Link each claim to a named witness or dated record. 3) Mark which claims others confirm or contradict. When: a suspect's whereabouts are the central question. Why: each claim can then be tested against independent sources.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the independent witnesses who can confirm an alibi. 2) Check the alibi against each witness's account. 3) Treat an unverified alibi as unproven, not cleared; an alibi resting only on the suspect's word is weak. When: A suspect offers an alibi. Why: Independent confirmation is needed; a given alibi may be weak or stronger than believed.
- [procedure] 1) Pin the alibi to an exact time. 2) Check the physical route between the claimed place and the scene. 3) Look for a third party's timestamp that fixes the suspect's movements. 4) Measure travel time against the gap. When: Testing whether a claimed whereabouts can be true. Why: A time-bound claim checked against routes and independent records can be confirmed or broken.
- [procedure] 1) Fix each person's arrival, location and last sighting of the victim. 2) Treat each claimed meeting as a hypothesis. 3) Test it against independent witnesses, records and physical traces. 4) Record who gave each statement and when. When: A suspect's presence depends on memory or a single uncorroborated account. Why: Independent checks separate verified facts from unsupported claims.
- [procedure] 1) Record the time and place the suspect names. 2) Compare them with the timeline of the act. 3) Look for a witness who can confirm the location. When: A suspect offers an alibi against a specific charge. Why: A time alone, without a witness, is hard to prove.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the traces that must exist if the account is true. 2) Check the site for each one. 3) Note which traces are absent or contradicted before accepting the claim. When: A witness describes entry or exit through a closed space. Why: Physical traces test whether an impossible route really happened.
- [procedure] Place each suspect's location at relevant hours, and confirm what each person could have known, such as whether the owner knew the contents of a secured place. When: Establishing who could have acted during a time window. Why: Locations and knowledge at specific hours separate possible actors from impossible ones.
- [procedure] 1) Pin down the time span when the offence was possible. 2) Test other plausible time spans. 3) Compare the suspect's known activities against sightings in each span. 4) Ask who could have taken the suspect's place. When: a suspect's whereabouts at a precise hour decide the case. Why: an alibi holds only if it fits the window the evidence supports.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the time gap the alibi must cover. 2) Establish what was physically possible in that window. 3) Anchor the timeline to independent dated events. 4) Verify claimed communications with the source system, not the recipient. When: Testing a suspect's alibi against other evidence. Why: Recipients can confirm a message arrived while the system record shows it never happened.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the timeline of the evening with known times. 2) Measure the intervals between known points, starting with the most measurable one. 3) Use the measured travel time to test each explanation the suspect offers. 4) Press on duration when the suspect says time simply passed. When: When testing a suspect's alibi against a crime time. Why: Measurable intervals give a fixed reference that vague explanations cannot easily cover.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the chain of people the lead passed through. 2) Discount the teller's emotion and prejudice. 3) Test the named person against an independent record. 4) If no match, try other records or regions before deciding. 5) Make further discreet inquiries rather than accepting or dismissing the claim. When: Information arrives through several relays, especially from a biased teller. Why: Each relay adds distance from the original event, and a failed match in one register does not prove a claim false.
- [procedure] 1) State a prediction with an exact time and place. 2) Synchronize all clocks beforehand. 3) Place the observer where they cannot be seen, with a plan for afterward. 4) Watch and record the outcome, including if nothing happens. When: when a theory depends on a person's routine or on something being perceived. Why: shared time and hidden position make the observed result trustworthy.
- [procedure] 1) Revisit the scene to test its layout, sightlines and exit routes. 2) Question each witness about timing. 3) Test the times against each other. 4) Note every vehicle or visitor present. When: Timing and positions at a scene are unclear. Why: Witnesses often know parts of a sequence but not all of it.
- [procedure] 1) Record every stated time. 2) Compute the intervals between them. 3) Check whether each movement fits its gap. 4) Mark unaccounted windows. 5) Treat estimates such as about or nearly as ranges. When: Reconstructing a sequence of events from a confession or witness account. Why: Laying out intervals shows what was physically possible and where the account fails.
- [procedure] 1) Follow a subject with a tail. 2) Have the tail report each sighting with its time and place. 3) Link sightings into a route. When: A subject's movements must be tracked across a location. Why: Timed, located reports build a route that can be checked.
- [procedure] 1) Collect dated church votes, diary entries and wills. 2) Order them by date. 3) Cross-check each date against a second source where possible. 4) Use the ordered list as the timeline. When: When building a town or institution's history from documents. Why: Dated documents give fixed points, and cross-checking catches conflicting dates.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the time window a suspect's account fixes. 2) Find a physical trace that could test that window, such as weather marks or dust disturbance. 3) Confirm the environmental fact from an independent source before drawing a conclusion. When: When a suspect's account fixes a time window that a physical trace can test. Why: Independent confirmation prevents an innocent cause from being mistaken for guilt.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the NPC who arrived when and by which route. 2) Compare the account with recorded arrivals. 3) Confirming or contradicting the account unlocks the next line of questioning. When: Building alibi checks in an investigation game. Why: Arrival records give a checkable structure for testing NPC accounts.
- [procedure] 1) Ask how long the witness believes an event lasted. 2) Compare that against dated, independent records such as registers or logs. 3) Check any physical trace that fixes when the event ended. When: when a witness's timing is central to an alibi or to a claim that events lasted longer than records show. Why: Independent records are not shaped by the witness's memory.
- [procedure] 1) Time the alibi and identify the window in which an absence could occur. 2) Identify each confirming source. 3) Ask whether each source had a stake in the outcome. 4) Seek independent support for interested sources. When: Assessing an alibi confirmed by family or associates. Why: Interested witnesses may shade their account, so independent support is needed.
- [procedure] 1) Place each event on a shared timeline. 2) Test each alibi against the recorded times. 3) Check each claimed location against the travel routes of the people involved. When: Several people claim to be elsewhere.
- [procedure] 1) Write down every day and place named in each statement. 2) Compare each claimed location against an independent source such as a schedule or log. 3) Note the day where a record contradicts a claim. 4) Compare each person's claimed visits against the record. When: Two accounts of the same time conflict, or a record can confirm or refute a claim. Why: Independent records expose contradictions that the accounts themselves conceal.
- [tradeoff] Clearing a suspect with several independent checks makes exoneration credible and gives separate steps; one concrete physical detail is quicker and more convincing. When: When exonerating a suspect seen near the scene or in a mystery. Why: Several checks add verifiable steps, while a single specific detail is faster to state. (x2)
- [tradeoff] A narrow crime window makes alibi checks useful, while a wide window or a suspect-only source of movement data makes them less informative. When: When deciding how much an alibi check can reveal. Why: A narrow window constrains which claims matter; a wide one lets many claims fit.
- [pitfall] An alibi is a dead end if its witness cannot be named or questioned, and weak when no one can confirm the suspect's location or the alibi witness is unreliable. (x2)
- [pitfall] An alibi or timeline resting on a single source, such as one person's word, one watch reading or one police check, is unverified and needs independent corroboration. When: A schedule or alibi depends on one source or one outside check. Why: A single source can be wrong, incomplete or influenced, and unchecked claims cannot be confirmed against independent facts.
- [pitfall] Accepting an alibi or a witness's explanation of presence without checking its exact hours, or timings never checked against each other, lets a suspect pass with a gap.
- [pitfall] Relative phrases such as 'about thirteen years ago', and dates taken from secondary accounts, must be checked against other dates or primary records, since errors shift the timeline. Why: Relative phrases drift and can point to the wrong year; a secondary account's error spreads through everything built on it and can move a case to the wrong decade.
- [pitfall] Trusting a device's reading without asking whether it runs true lets an uncorrected offset silently distort the whole timeline.
- [pitfall] Counting repeated events such as laps or rounds without a record produces vague estimates of how many occurred.
- [pitfall] A first check on an alibi can be too thin to catch a lie, so follow up with deeper verification. When: When an alibi has been checked only once. Why: Shallow verification misses fabrications that deeper testing would expose.
- [pitfall] Vague dates with no in-character reason for the vagueness feel like authorial convenience rather than character. Why: Readers accept vagueness only when it has a cause.
- [pitfall] Accepting an alibi without checking its timeline for gaps, or keeping a theory after the suspect is cleared, leads to wrong arrests and wasted investigation.
- [pitfall] Confirming one link of an alibi does not confirm the whole chain, and a partly true story can hide the time that matters. When: when evaluating an alibi with several steps. Why: Each link must hold on its own for the chain to hold.
- [pitfall] Fixing the suspect window on the moment of collapse ignores earlier dosing and can clear the real culprit.
- [pitfall] Assuming an object's place of origin equals the place of the crime ignores its transit history, since items can be moved, re-addressed or reused to mislead. When: when an object's origin is used to locate an event. Why: Objects travel through several places, and their labels or wrappers may not reflect where they were last used.
- [pitfall] A witness who offers a useful accusation may still be lying about their own movements, so check both.
- [pitfall] A distance or alibi test works only when each witness's location is recorded in the sources.
- [pitfall] A theory that fits the timing of deposits may still be wrong, so hold it as provisional until a second source confirms it. When: Adopting a leading theory from financial records. Why: Timing agreement is one signal and does not establish cause.
- [pitfall] A sleeping witness cannot confirm his own activity, so an alibi resting only on his presence proves little. When: when an alibi depends on the alibi holder's own presence or activity. Why: The witness cannot observe the claimed activity while asleep.
- [pitfall] Self-reported durations can hide errors, since people often estimate how long an activity lasted from their own sense of it. When: A witness gives the length of a noise or activity without a clock. Why: Subjective time perception is unreliable.
- [pitfall] An unexplained delay in an account, such as a short errand taking long, is itself worth examining. When: A witness's stated duration for a simple task seems too long. Why: The gap may hide the actual activity.
- [pitfall] An absent alibi is not proof of guilt; an unconfirmed alibi is an open checklist question, not evidence against the person. Why: Two innocent and guilty readings of the same gap are both possible.
- [pitfall] A suspect's irregular habits make an alibi from a household member weak. When: when a household member vouches for a suspect's movements. Why: Erratic routines are hard for others to track reliably.
- [pitfall] Dropping alibi checks once a case feels settled lets an apparent solution hide the real lead. When: A case appears resolved early. Why: Settled-feeling cases stop being tested.
- [pitfall] A self-reported alibi should not be treated as settled; check it against other events and records. When: Assessing a suspect's claimed whereabouts. Why: Self-reports can be wrong or deliberately false and need independent corroboration.
- [fact] Callers' visits and calls can serve as a second record of who was present in a place and at what time. When: When corroborating a household or location timeline with outside observations. Why: Independent witnesses to presence cross-check the routine.
- [fact] Several independent alibis from separate sources count for more than one unverified claim, since each source can be checked on its own. When: Ranking suspects by alibi strength. Why: Independent sources do not share the same error or motive.
- [fact] Household records of times out and in confirm departure and return but say nothing about what happened in between. When: when using door or entry records to check a suspect's timeline. Why: Entry times bracket a period without showing activity within it.
- [fact] A fixed timeline can look trustworthy at first, then be exposed by checking it against a second clock source that reveals the timings were staged. When: Designing a mystery where a character's alibi relies on a timetable or clock. Why: A second independent time source can contradict an apparently solid timeline and expose the deception.
- [fact] Playing the reproduced sound can serve as its own proof of an audio alibi, so no witness is needed to establish the trick. Why: The sound itself matches the claimed alibi.

## deduction
- [model] A detective combines three faculties with logic: close observation of details, knowledge of how people think, and insight into motive and feeling. When: Designing an investigator character or deduction system. Why: Each faculty supplies a different kind of input, and reasoning joins them into conclusions.
- [model] A solution is a chain of inferences where each link depends on the one before; one wrong link, such as a single wrong date, invalidates the whole conclusion.
- [definition] Evidence that only one person can perceive, such as an apparition, cannot be checked by others and so cannot be tested against the world.
- [mechanism] When each dead end gives a clear, checkable result, the pattern of falsehood itself becomes information that points toward the truth. When: When a chain of false leads is followed in order. Why: Repeated failures of a similar kind reveal a deliberate design behind them.
- [mechanism] One sound inference tends to suggest others, so a single absence can open a chain of further reasoning. Why: Each conclusion creates new expectations that can be tested.
- [mechanism] Equally strong evidence against two suspects leaves an audience with no clear answer about which one is guilty.
- [mechanism] Each new fact, such as a destroyed document or a jammed key, shrinks the pool of people who could have entered.
- [mechanism] Unforeseen events chained together can push a concealed plan into the open, even when each event alone is minor.
- [mechanism] An ambiguous clue carrying two meanings stays open until one discovered object resolves which meaning holds, so the player reasons toward a single answer. Why: A single decisive object closes the question that ambiguity left open.
- [mechanism] Forensic reports can give a time range rather than a single time, and different examiner NPCs can give different ranges with stated reasoning for the player to compare. When: When designing forensic evidence in a game. Why: Ranges and disagreements make the player weigh reliability rather than accept one answer.
- [behavior] The same facts can support opposite conclusions; readers adopt the conclusion their assumptions favor, and observers sharing evidence differ by frame of mind. When: when a fact must be interpreted or a group shares the same evidence. Why: Expectations and habits of mind, not evidence alone, shape how ambiguous evidence is read.
- [behavior] Commitment to a favored suspect, or a wish to benefit someone, makes reasoners overstate deductions and harden weak suspicion into belief. When: when a favored suspect is pushed or a suspect's guilt would serve a personal wish. Why: Commitment and desire bend how strongly evidence is weighed.
- [behavior] Deduction looks remarkable to audiences who missed the small observable fact that makes it simple, while experts find the same inference routine. When: when a solution is revealed or a player watches an expert reason from minor clues. Why: Expertise makes familiar inference feel effortless to its practitioner.
- [behavior] A suspect may argue that the evidence can be read two ways, leaving physical facts ambiguous rather than conclusive.
- [behavior] Authorities admitted evidence no one could sense directly when they believed the crime could not otherwise be uncovered. When: a hidden crime with no other route to proof. Why: they believed no other method could expose the crime.
- [behavior] An observer may first read an event as ordinary and only later recognise it as meaningful, so early reports can be reinterpreted. When: the event seemed harmless when first reported. Why: Significance often becomes clear only with later information.
- [behavior] Who discovers a scene first, and what they already believe, shapes their report, and a culprit can arrange this order. When: when witnesses arrive at a scene they expect to be a crime. Why: prior belief shapes what is seen and reported.
- [behavior] A commonplace act looks suspicious when unusual circumstances, such as an odd hour or unusual care to avoid noise, surround it. When: an ordinary action happens under unusual conditions. Why: the surrounding circumstances change how the act reads.
- [behavior] When characters disagree about a fact, the disagreement itself often reveals how each reads the case. When: Two investigators or witnesses dispute the existence or role of a person or fact. Why: Each side's assumptions show through what they are willing to accept.
- [behavior] Connections between clues usually form during slow reflection and comparison, not on first hearing. When: player encounters a clue that may relate to an earlier one. Why: linking is an act of reflection.
- [behavior] A mismatch between spoken and written accounts is treated as significant even when both versions could be true. When: Evaluating two accounts from the same source. Why: Any difference warrants checking, regardless of innocent explanations.
- [rule] Label each conclusion as record, physical evidence, inference, or tradition, and store recorded words separately from inferred links. When: writing up a reconstruction. Why: Readers see how strongly each claim is supported, and inferred links are not mistaken for fact. (x2)
- [rule] Check each premise or link in a chain separately before accepting its conclusion; a chain is only as sound as its weakest link, and gaps can hide unshown steps. When: Validating a reconstructed sequence of events or any chain of premises. Why: One false premise can make correct reasoning give a wrong answer, and a chain may look continuous while resting on unsupported connections.
- [rule] Store case facts as a graph and show a conclusion only when every fact fits; check chain completeness before allowing an arrest. When: Designing a deduction system or generating mystery content with linked clues. Why: A graph lets the game verify that each link is present and lets players check their reasoning.
- [rule] Give every apparently supernatural or ambiguous event a rational explanation players can find, since an unexplained impression reads as a cheat. When: Designing mysterious events in a game.
- [rule] Present a deduction as a short chain of facts, each resting on the one before, and list the queries or inquiries that would test each step. When: Presenting a deduction.
- [rule] Present competing readings or conflicting sources side by side and let the reader weigh them, rather than forcing one story. When: A document, remark or record supports opposite conclusions. Why: Openly stated readings keep the evidence weighable and the reader engaged.
- [rule] Deliberately discount your own expectations when weighing evidence, because they shape what you notice and how you read silence.
- [rule] Do not confuse an unusual case with an unsolvable one; the oddities of a case often point toward its answer. When: when official explanations have stalled.
- [rule] When a theft or fraud affects several parties, check whether each loses the same amount rather than assuming the largest loser is the only interested party.
- [rule] Do not claim certainty about a sample that was never tested; state the gap openly rather than filling it with guesswork.
- [rule] When a companion character withholds a hint, reveal a checkable basis for it later in the game. When: an NPC guide keeps a deduction back. Why: a hidden basis that never appears feels like teasing.
- [rule] When evaluating an argument, ask what facts were left out, and check the connection between each piece of evidence and the conclusion. When: A case is presented persuasively. Why: Persuasive presentation can hide missing links.
- [rule] Let players combine a deed, a handwriting sample and a map location to deduce who wrote an anonymous note. When: designing a detective mode. Why: matching several evidence types gives a stronger deduction.
- [rule] Resolve a contradictory testimony with a test, such as moving the suspect into full light, rather than explaining it away in dialogue.
- [rule] Begin an inquiry with independent evidence rather than the accusers' claims, so accusations do not set the agenda of the proceedings. When: When running a hearing based partly on accusations. Why: Starting with accusations lets them frame what counts as evidence.
- [rule] Do not conclude a witness is lying from a timing discrepancy alone, since memory and wording can produce it. When: A witness's account conflicts with another clue. Why: Discrepancies have innocent causes as well as deceptive ones.
- [rule] Keep personal interpretations out of the factual record so the notes can be checked later.
- [rule] Track which hypothesis the player holds so later clues can be written to fit both readings of an ambiguous sound or sight. When: When a level contains an ambiguous event two characters could have caused. Why: Clues matched to both readings keep the mystery open for longer.
- [rule] Let a forensic minigame require sorting samples under magnification, and let a residue tied to a trade narrow the list of NPC suspects. When: Designing a forensic investigation minigame. Why: Trade-linked residue gives the player a concrete way to filter suspects.
- [rule] Let each damaged object record whether its damage happened during the event or afterward, so staged scenes can be exposed by inconsistent timing. When: building a damage system for a scene. Why: Timing of damage is a checkable clue that separates genuine events from staged ones.
- [rule] Design a code whose rule, such as interval, weekday or letter match, a careful player can infer from several observations, rather than a random lookup. When: Creating puzzle codes or hidden schedules in generated content. Why: A rule-based code rewards deduction while a random lookup only rewards memorization.
- [rule] Let players test a hypothesis at a search point, such as searching a location where a trace would be if the hypothesis holds. Why: Testing a route hypothesis gives a clear yes or no result.
- [rule] Let players confirm a document fragment against an in-world record, such as a harbor log, to unlock the next location. When: when designing a fragment-based clue. Why: Confirmation against a second source rewards careful matching.
- [rule] Build the case from several confirmatory items that converge, rather than relying on a single decisive proof. When: No single item is conclusive but each supports the same conclusion. Why: Individually weak clues become strong when they point to the same suspect together.
- [rule] Do not conclude from style alone; each feature inferred from writing needs corroboration from other evidence. When: when drawing conclusions from a document's style. Why: Style reflects habits and hostility as much as intent.
- [rule] Present physical evidence rather than describing it, because a bare claim invites the question of where the evidence is. When: Arguing a conclusion before a sceptic or authority. Why: Shown evidence can be checked, while a described clue depends on trust.
- [rule] Check whether a simple, obtainable test, such as comparing a known handwriting sample, was ever requested before concluding a question is unanswerable. When: A question about a document or item seems unresolved. Why: A cheap test can settle a question that reasoning alone cannot.
- [rule] Admit sensory reports as evidence only after checking them against a firmly held reasoned premise, never letting raw perception override logic. When: Sensory reports conflict or are heavily emotional. Why: Senses are unreliable alone and must serve reasoning to be trusted.
- [rule] Do not treat an immediate reaction to a touch or a glance as proof of a person's guilt or power. When: when a reaction is the only evidence offered. Why: reactions have other causes, including fear and expectation.
- [rule] Build a tally-based clue with one deliberately uncertain figure, so players must reason from the range to locate a character's whereabouts. When: Designing a clue puzzle from payments or purchases. Why: A range keeps the answer deducible without making every figure exact.
- [rule] Show how the player reached a conclusion as a flourish, rewarding attention without forcing an accusation. When: Presenting a deduction to the player. Why: Visible reasoning rewards observation while letting the player keep control of the confrontation.
- [rule] Make the reveal a conclusion drawn from records the audience already saw, rather than a confession, so the scene rewards reasoning. When: designing the moment a hidden identity or swap is exposed. Why: Deduction from known evidence feels earned, while a confession only delivers information.
- [heuristic] Each resolved answer or constraint narrows the next, since constraints interact, keeping a single-trace inquiry focused and reducing directions to check. When: when reasoning through a mystery's facts or an investigation has a single trace with several linked questions. Why: One resolved fact points to further conclusions.
- [heuristic] Puzzles and journal entries should match clues found earlier, so the player's prior knowledge confirms the answer rather than introducing it. When: designing investigation puzzles. Why: Matching rewards the player's prior knowledge.
- [heuristic] Set explicit evidence tiers, such as lead, supporting and proof, and make the game enforce the difference between them. When: Designing investigation or accusation systems. Why: Explicit tiers stop a lead from being treated as a verdict.
- [heuristic] Track confidence in each deduction separately, distinguishing suspected from proven, so players can act on a suspicion before it is proven. When: when designing a deduction or journal system. Why: Players reach suspicion well before proof, and labelling the difference keeps their reasoning honest.
- [heuristic] Players read a crooked chain of cause and effect as a sign of a human plan, so a convoluted puzzle reads as deliberate rather than supernatural. When: when a puzzle's mechanics involve several indirect steps. Why: Winding, traceable paths communicate intent to the player.
- [heuristic] The more exact a parallel between two cases, the more likely it is a coincidence rather than a rule; use it to suggest questions, not to settle answers. When: using a previous case to reason about a new one. Why: a striking match is often accidental.
- [heuristic] A partial, unfinished change shows both what was done and that someone may return to complete it.
- [heuristic] When a decision arrives through a chain of replies, each document can be checked against the others to make the order of decisions visible. When: Several letters or messages each prompt the next. Why: Each link is a separate document, so the sequence of decisions can be verified link by link.
- [heuristic] If a task is too heavy for one person, assume a helper was present, and that the helper had to be close enough to avoid detection. When: A physical task exceeds one person's strength. Why: Physical limits constrain how many people were involved.
- [heuristic] Ask who a person was waiting for, and why they waited at that particular place rather than at home, to infer their intent. When: a person is seen lingering somewhere unusual. Why: The choice of location reveals an expected meeting or departure.
- [heuristic] A document can confirm one fact while leaving the key question open; note what each clue establishes and what it does not.
- [heuristic] Argue from checkable detail rather than claimed witness, so the detail carries the argument and not the speaker's authority.
- [heuristic] Leave the purpose of an antagonist's arrangements unstated, so the eventual reveal remains open. When: when showing a schemer's actions before the reveal. Why: an unexplained purpose keeps the reveal available for later.
- [heuristic] When a physical estimate contradicts a timeline built from other clues, treat the conflict as a lead to resolve rather than something to ignore. When: a timeline and a physical estimate disagree. Why: one source must be wrong, or the event happened earlier than assumed.
- [heuristic] A substance used to make a mechanism run silently suggests its user wanted silence, which narrows the list of people who needed quiet. When: the residue has a known purpose.
- [heuristic] Before relying on an unusual physical action in a reconstruction, test whether it is feasible and whether anyone would have noticed it. When: when a reconstruction depends on an action few people would perform.
- [heuristic] Build a chain of small checkable facts toward a conclusion, verifying each before using the next. When: Assembling a case from many minor findings. Why: Each verified link supports the next and limits error.
- [heuristic] A match between a trace and a suspect shows presence, not purpose, so ask what the person intended as well as who made the mark. When: A physical match links a suspect to a scene. Why: Motive and method can differ from what the traces alone suggest.
- [heuristic] Rank candidate explanations by how probable each is given how a person of that character would realistically behave, not by whether it is merely possible. When: several explanations are offered and one must be chosen. Why: many explanations are possible, but few are probable.
- [heuristic] Physical constraints such as layout, sightlines and access points can rule out most candidate methods quickly.
- [heuristic] A link to the crime that cannot be traced to any one suspect usually signals a missing fact, not proof of guilt. When: a connection exists but points to no specific person. Why: The unresolved link often reflects an unknown fact.
- [heuristic] A crowd that agrees quickly has often been shaped by a few voices, so quick agreement is not proof. When: when judging whether public consensus is genuine.
- [heuristic] Rank dated records above self-reported figures and oral tradition, and check any one person's claim, such as a count of descendants, against independent records. When: sources disagree about a family's history or numbers. Why: A self-report is one person's claim, and tradition is weaker than a dated entry.
- [heuristic] Require stronger evidence at each escalating stage, so detention and especially conviction need more than a claim of a supernatural sighting.
- [heuristic] A puzzle can ask the player to reassemble a torn map or ledger, using edges and margins as matching hints. When: Designing document-based puzzles in generated levels. Why: Matching fragments rewards observation and gives a clear solution path.
- [heuristic] Gate hidden information behind dialogue that requires the player to reconstruct the suspect's actions exactly, unlocking secrets only after an accurate account. When: When designing interrogation or confrontation dialogue. Why: Requiring an accurate reconstruction rewards careful reasoning over guessing.
- [heuristic] Let geometric clues such as wound angle, trajectory or footprint direction eliminate some suspects but not all, so the player checks the remaining options against room positions. When: building a deduction puzzle around a physical clue. Why: keeping several options open leaves the final choice to the player.
- [heuristic] Let a body's injuries contradict a staged scene so a careful player notices the mismatch.
- [heuristic] Link dying-word fragments to locations or characters players have already met, so they know where to follow each fragment. When: When placing hint fragments across the level. Why: Familiar anchors tell players where to go.
- [heuristic] Rules valid for physical quantities hold only within their domain and may not transfer to motives, social behavior or psychological evidence. When: Applying a quantitative rule to human choices or motives. Why: Parts do not always add up to the whole outside their domain.
- [heuristic] Clients often mix what they know with what they assume; separate the two and check each against independent sources before accepting them. When: Taking a client's account at the first interview. Why: Assumptions presented as facts can mislead the investigation.
- [procedure] 1) List every plausible explanation, such as accident, illness, flight, arrest, suicide and murder, or state the contradiction precisely. 2) Test each against known facts. 3) Discard contradicted explanations, keeping untested ones open. 4) Gather new facts when none survive. When: Early in a case with scattered facts, or when facts seem to contradict one another. Why: Testing rival explanations narrows the field without fixing on a first guess and exposes the assumption to drop.
- [procedure] 1) List each known fact as a numbered point. 2) State what each point implies. 3) Test each conclusion against the others. 4) Revise the list when a new fact changes the picture. When: several facts must be weighed together.
- [procedure] 1) State what each small fact implies. 2) Link the implications into a single hypothesis. 3) Test the hypothesis against a witness or record before accepting it. When: several small observations may share a common cause. Why: loosely related facts can point to one answer.
- [procedure] 1) Lay out a reconstructed sequence of events in order. 2) Ask the suspect to confirm, deny or correct each step. 3) Revise the sequence using every correction. When: the investigator has partial knowledge and needs confirmation.
- [procedure] 1) Start from one simple visible sign. 2) Reason one step at a time to a next inference. 3) State each step separately so it can be checked. When: Evidence is sparse and only small signs are available. Why: Stated links can each be tested, so errors are found.
- [procedure] 1) Derive physical or temporal constraints from the clue. 2) Obtain a complete candidate list from an authoritative source. 3) Filter candidates by constraints. 4) Check the remainder through reconnaissance and records. When: a clue constrains the search space and candidates can be listed. Why: Constraints cut a large field to a checkable short list.
- [procedure] 1) Ask why the lead was offered, not only whether it is true. 2) Check it against facts the speaker should not know. 3) Verify it independently, such as by searching the named person's location. When: When a suspect volunteers a rival culprit. Why: A volunteered lead may be honest help or a diversion that shifts blame.
- [procedure] 1) Check where each relevant object was at the time. 2) Check who could physically reach it. 3) Check whether the timing allows the act. 4) Check what the method required and whether that was available. When: when testing an accusation.
- [procedure] 1) Link the item to the act. 2) Link the act to a physical trait, such as the hand that held the weapon. 3) Link the trait to a suspect. Test each link. When: a physical clue is used to point at a suspect. Why: Each step is an assumption until it is verified.
- [procedure] 1) Arrange physical proofs in order, such as photographs, samples and clues. 2) Confront the suspect with them. 3) Reveal that an earlier decoy was invented. 4) Check the suspect's detailed admissions against the assembled traces. When: When the suspect has been misled and the evidence is concrete. Why: Ordered, physical proof lets the suspect's account be tested step by step.
