- [procedure] 1) Separate what is known from what is inferred. 2) Walk through the chain of inference step by step, linking each step to an earlier clue. 3) Keep the recap short and specific, adding no new facts. 4) Reveal the motive as the final link. When: Closing a mystery to show how the solution follows from clues. Why: Traceable steps make the solution feel earned rather than conjured.
- [tradeoff] A suspect's silence alone is only a suggestion that must be backed by evidence; combined with known contact with the victim, it can justify holding them until they explain. When: Silence is used as evidence; holding is justified only when known victim contact is also present. Why: Silence has many possible causes and does not prove guilt, but it gains weight when linked to a known connection.
- [tradeoff] A piece of evidence can support both a suspect and an alternative; an item that suggests a marked assailant may also count against the apparent suspect. When: Evidence seems to implicate one person. Why: Physical details must match the suspect as well as the theory.
- [pitfall] One detail or set of facts can support opposing theories or blame readings, so weigh it against other evidence; records may never settle responsibility. (x2)
- [pitfall] Connections feel significant to investigators, so pattern-building treats coincidence as evidence; coincidences are common, and attributing every event to one hidden hand overfits, with that figure's identity only guessable. (x2)
- [pitfall] A story fitting every fact can be wrong if its key link is untested; neat logic can convince people of undeserved guilt, and theories should be judged by field observation. (x2)
- [pitfall] Argument from silence overreaches and assumes rational behavior under pressure, which people often depart from; mark such inference as inference and treat it as one input. When: A conclusion rests on what a source fails to mention. Why: Silence is ambiguous, and human behavior often departs from incentives. (x2)
- [pitfall] Accepting a confession without testing its details against physical traces lets false or incomplete admissions pass.
- [pitfall] Deductions must rest on facts shown to the audience; a clue held privately or a reveal built on unseen facts cannot be weighed and reads as a cheat. When: Writing a reveal that depends on information the player has not seen. Why: Players cannot reproduce a conclusion built on hidden facts.
- [pitfall] A single indicator, such as a pulse or a shift in language under pressure, has several possible causes and is weak evidence that must not be overread. When: when one sign or reaction is used to judge a condition. Why: Different causes can produce the same sign, and the reaction may have innocent causes.
- [pitfall] Accepting an explanation for a trace without identifying the person who gave it leaves the link unverified, and any third party it names still needs identifying. Why: The explanation may be invented to cover the link.
- [pitfall] One wrong or newly discovered fact can undermine a whole reconstruction, letting the suspect dismiss it and forcing the theory to be rebuilt from scratch; overstating costs credibility. Why: Overstating a deduction costs the investigator credibility.
- [pitfall] Verify assumed facts first: an unverified anchor, personal detail or link passes its error to every later inference, even where later details seem confirmed. When: when a conclusion depends on one assumed fact about a suspect. Why: A knowledge-based deduction inherits the uncertainty of its premises.
- [pitfall] Confidence does not track accuracy in poor light, weather, crowds or strong emotion; observers give conflicting directions or confident identifications, and excitement can inflate impressions. When: when evaluating a witness report, locating a sound or event, or spreading a sighting. Why: Each observer fills the gap with a different guess, and confidence and emotion inflate impressions beyond the observation.
- [pitfall] Confidence in one explanation or one reading of a tell, even an expert's, can close off other leads and make the real suspect easy to miss. Why: Certainty closes off other leads.
- [pitfall] Reading 'consistent with' as 'proves' leads players and reviewers to accept a conclusion that only one reading supports. When: Evaluating evidence that fits a claim without excluding alternatives. Why: Consistency with a claim does not rule out other explanations.
- [pitfall] Dismissing an objection without testing it can hide a real gap in the reconstruction.
- [pitfall] Accepting a convenient reinterpretation without testing it is a mistake, even when it dissolves the contradiction.
- [pitfall] Keeping the anchor fact broad, such as naming a culprit, lets one dispute collapse the whole chain; a narrow time-bound fact is safer. When: Stating the basis of a deduction. Why: A broad claim invites challenge, while a narrow one survives scrutiny.
- [pitfall] An inference built from a visit, a letter and a manner of speech can feel like proof while each link is unverified, and one new fact can collapse it.
- [pitfall] Inference chains can seem far-fetched to listeners until their basis is stated, even when each conclusion is correct. When: a conclusion is shared without its evidence. Why: listeners cannot judge a leap they cannot follow.
- [pitfall] A witness who claims honesty too often invites suspicion; such claims should appear only where the character would plausibly make them. Why: Repeated protestations read as performance.
- [pitfall] Treating a witness's clenched hand or nervousness as proof of a lie leads an investigator to conclude guilt from a subjective impression alone. When: An investigator is certain of a witness's dishonesty based only on body language. Why: Body language is ambiguous and the investigator's impression is not verifiable evidence.
- [pitfall] A summary that lays out a chain of beliefs and events but leaves the conclusion unstated shifts the burden of testing onto the listener. Why: The listener must then test the chain personally rather than hear a finished argument.
- [pitfall] A staged meeting only works if the target is confident enough to attend; a wary target will not walk in, so the trap fails before it can close. Why: The plan depends on the target's own expectations, not on the investigator's control.
- [pitfall] A stated reason for a choice that others cannot reproduce cannot be checked, which weakens any account built on it.
- [pitfall] A claim repeated by several people is not the same as a checked record, so each link in a custody chain must be confirmed independently. When: Tracing an item through several hands. Why: Repetition can make a weak link look strong and hide the link that matters most.
- [pitfall] A test that depends on an unverified handoff proves little either way, whether it passes or fails.
- [pitfall] If a captive can answer freely, the reply constraint loses its meaning; keep the limit in place and its reason clear to the player.
- [pitfall] Accepting an official's quick categorisation of an event, such as calling it mischief, without checking the facts can miss a deliberate act.
- [pitfall] An overly literal reading of a clue can exclude the correct answer.
- [pitfall] Over-eager helpers can reveal an investigator's presence and turn a quiet signal into an alarm. When: Relying on third parties to pass on or respond to a signal. Why: Excess activity draws the attention of watchers.
- [pitfall] Treating every possibility as equally likely leaves an investigation stuck in an endless might-have-been stage with no progress.
- [pitfall] Claims about evidence that has been destroyed cannot be checked, so they should not be relied on without independent support. When: When a witness says a document or item existed but no longer exists.
- [pitfall] A verification answer from an unknown party does not prove who is speaking, and a plausible reply can still be false.
- [pitfall] An overlong or pedantic expert account can seem more authoritative than it is; judge it by the evidence it actually gives. When: An expert gives a long, detailed explanation. Why: Length and detail can be mistaken for certainty.
- [pitfall] Estimates offered as guesswork are easy to over-trust, and a witness's own timing also depends on fallible memory.
- [pitfall] A random-killer or copycat explanation fits any crime without naming anyone, so it narrows nothing and can serve as a red herring.
- [pitfall] Answers obtained under a false identity or an overstated threat are not clean evidence and should be checked against independent sources. Why: the method itself may have shaped what the witness said.
- [pitfall] Building a theory on the everyday meaning of a technical term can mislead, because specialist vocabulary often means something different. When: a clue is a title, term, or jargon.
- [pitfall] Admitting a statement is not the same as weighing it; decision-makers may accept accusers while setting character evidence aside.
- [pitfall] An honorific can attach to a deputy acting in an absent officeholder's place, so check who was acting before naming the holder. When: The office holder was away when the document was produced. Why: Titles can outlast the actual holder's presence.
- [pitfall] Once an unverifiable kind of evidence is admitted in any form, it can control every case and make corroboration add little. Why: Admission gives the evidence power that other evidence cannot match.
- [pitfall] Judges without legal training may lean heavily on counsel from a single source, which narrows the range of views the verdict reflects. When: when a court has no legal expertise among its members. Why: without independent expertise, the judges depend on the advice they receive.
- [pitfall] A chain of misfortunes can look like a pattern when each link rests on a single neighbour's report. When: when a series of harms is attributed to one person on one witness's word. Why: a linked sequence feels convincing even when each link is unverified.
- [pitfall] Finders tend to assume more meaning than partly legible writing supports; read damaged evidence carefully before drawing conclusions. When: when a clue is partly illegible. Why: gaps invite overinterpretation.
- [pitfall] Some supposed proofs, such as ordeal-style tests, are themselves unsound and can introduce error rather than provide evidence.
- [pitfall] Once a hidden deduction is explained, it can seem absurdly simple, which undercuts the player's sense of achievement.
- [pitfall] Confidence in a first theory makes contrary facts look like errors, so people discard evidence that should prompt revision. When: when players or characters hold a settled theory. Why: Commitment to an explanation filters out opposing data.
- [pitfall] Settling a method on the claim that a victim could not have been woken is fragile; if that claim is wrong, the whole chain fails, and alternatives need direct checks. When: A reconstruction depends on a victim's sleep or incapacity. Why: A single unverified assumption can break an otherwise consistent theory.
- [pitfall] Reasoning that only adds the most obvious next step, such as another exit, is shallow and can overlook the real explanation. When: Proposing explanations for a puzzle. Why: The obvious continuation is often the first thing considered and may miss the actual cause.
- [pitfall] Treating a routine household sound as proof of a particular person's presence is an error, since many people can produce the same sound. When: A witness links a common sound to a specific individual. Why: Routine sounds are shared by everyone in the household.
- [pitfall] Vague labels make later comparison impossible; each label must describe exactly what was tested. When: Recording physical samples. Why: Unclear provenance cannot be compared later.
- [pitfall] A claim that nothing could pass through an opening is only as reliable as the inspection behind it, and unchecked openings invalidate it. When: Ruling out entry through windows or doors. Why: Each untested opening, such as rear windows or interior doors, can still provide a route.
- [fact] Credit between rivals with different strengths alternates, since each side's method wins some rounds and the other's wins others. When: Two investigators with contrasting methods share a case.
- [fact] Evidence that helps one suspect often also gives that suspect a motive, so each fact must be weighed against everyone involved. When: Several suspects share a set of facts. Why: A fact favouring one person may incriminate them.
- [fact] An unverifiable account shows only that it cannot yet be checked; it establishes neither innocence nor guilt.
- [fact] Publicly known crimes are skewed toward detected failures, because successful crimes are never reported, so the visible record does not represent all crimes committed. When: Learning from famous or documented cases. Why: Only discovered cases enter the public record, and discovery usually follows a mistake.
- [fact] Most people reason forwards from events to results, and few can reconstruct the path back from a given end.

## claim verification
- [model] A dialogue system can store an NPC's earlier answers and flag contradictions when the player returns to the topic. When: Designing NPC dialogue that must stay consistent. Why: Stored answers let the system detect and surface contradictions.
- [mechanism] An NPC's report of a sound, missing item or routine, or what a servant or object shows, can contradict a suspect's stated movements, creating a clue the player must reconcile. When: Designing NPC testimony in a game.
- [mechanism] An NPC formally questioned may later give a changed version, which the player can detect by comparing its statements against earlier ones. Why: A formal statement creates a record that later accounts can be checked against.
- [rule] Let players test an NPC's claim against a second source or a checkable action, such as opening a locked item or visiting a place; raise trust only after the check passes. When: when designing verifiable in-world claims. Why: A claim that survives an attempted contradiction earns trust. (x2)
- [rule] Mix checkable claims with deliberate lies or contradictions in NPC testimony about sightings, injuries, routes or times; each fails a specific test against world records or objects. When: Designing NPC dialogue, testimony or backstory delivery. Why: Rewards players who check claims against evidence. (x2)
- [rule] Tie each clue and claim to a checkable source, such as a device, dated document, travel record, clinic ledger, ship manifest or sworn statement; unsupported assertions cannot be confirmed. When: Designing clues or forensic evidence. Why: A clue can only be tested against a known source; concrete records let players test claims. (x2)
- [rule] Classify witness statements and mark each claim unverified until a physical trace or independent source confirms it, especially a claim only one NPC perceived. When: Handling witness statements, including dungeon generation with NPC witnesses. (x2)
- [rule] Verify dates and implied days against a calendar before building a timeline from undated, conflicting or altered documents; a plausible mapping can be false. When: Using undated, conflicting or altered documents as evidence. Why: A wrong date can reverse the apparent order of events. (x2)
- [rule] Tag each NPC claim as seen, heard from another character, or guessed, and note any interest that may bias what that NPC reveals, so players can judge reliability. When: when writing NPC dialogue that reports events in a mystery. Why: Tags make the epistemic status of each claim visible.
- [rule] Verify a witness's central or checkable location claim immediately, before building on it; keep trust partial until the check passes and state the cost of a false claim.
- [rule] State the limits of a reasoning method, such as secondhand reports or the point where the signs stop, rather than implying certainty beyond the evidence. When: when a deduction reaches the edge of what the signs or access allow. Why: Explicit limits keep the reasoning credible.
- [rule] State key constraints and premises plainly, such as no key on the body or an object's starting state, before the conclusion so the audience reasons from the same facts. When: when writing a locked-room puzzle or presenting a deduction. Why: Shared premises let the audience check the reasoning.
- [rule] Store each NPC or suspect claim with time, place and verification status so players can check it against other NPCs, ledgers or world records; testimony becomes checkable evidence. When: when designing NPC dialogue or an investigation system. Why: Checkable claims turn dialogue into gameplay evidence.
- [rule] Compare each NPC claim with stored records and observed behaviour, flagging conflicts and any claim that exceeds what that NPC could have known.
- [rule] Let players cross-check NPC statements and reconstruct sequences from fragments, deducing who saw what and from where; fragments form a sequence only when compared.
- [rule] Make an unverifiable note or document a claim that players must corroborate before relying on it.
- [rule] Tag clues as misleading, suggestive or conclusive, so players learn which kinds of evidence to trust before naming a culprit. When: when designing a deduction puzzle with several clue types. Why: Explicit reliability tags teach players how to weigh evidence.
- [rule] Let an NPC state a small fact, such as which item was used, that one found clue contradicts; make that clue decisive so the NPC cannot explain it away. When: Designing a puzzle where the player catches an NPC lying. Why: A single decisive contradiction gives the player a clear, fair way to expose the lie.
- [rule] Do not accept a pattern-based motive or dismiss a suspicious clue as a blind until the victim's background or a confession or record confirms it. When: Interpreting a suspicious clue or inferred motive at a crime scene. Why: Background facts can override a misleading pattern and fix the real motive.
- [rule] Treat a neat deduction as a conjecture and require a verification step, such as a search, so correct answers are confirmed by observation and wrong ones are exposed. When: Designing a deduction puzzle, including one whose solution is inferred from constraints. Why: Observed confirmation makes the answer feel earned and prevents lucky guesses; tidy reasoning can still be wrong.
- [rule] Offer a plausible but wrong explanation players can verify, and treat a leading explanation as a starting point to verify before committing resources. When: Designing a puzzle, or before committing resources to one line of inquiry. Why: A careful player who verifies still reaches the real answer, since the obvious reading is not automatically correct.
- [rule] Let the player check an NPC's account, especially one that cannot recall events, against objects the player can examine.
- [rule] Give NPCs sincere but wrong causal explanations, so players must test them against items and locations before accepting them. Why: a confident wrong explanation rewards checking rather than trust.
- [rule] Check your own figures as carefully as the suspect's, since a corrected number can change the case.
- [rule] Verify explanations such as a loan or sale against records rather than dismissing them.
- [rule] Let a suspect make a public statement the player can check against evidence, so the claim can be tested. When: When designing suspect dialogue.
- [rule] Keep each discrepancy checkable by the player so that noticing it is rewarded. When: when designing clues.
- [rule] Give an NPC who claims to know the dungeon a boast that the player can check against the map or a rival's account.
- [rule] When a witness claims to see inside a closed space, check the claim against the sightline through its openings, such as windows, gaps or doors. When: when a witness describes the interior of a room they could not enter. Why: openings define what can physically be seen.
- [rule] Do not treat a firm statement as settled until its basis, including distance, light, sobriety and the source of any time given, is known. When: A case rests on a witness's firm claim. Why: A confident account may rest on weak conditions.
- [rule] Make a dialogue confrontation require a verified detail, so the suspect's account unlocks evidence and changes later options. When: designing suspect dialogue. Why: the player's earlier work gates the new information.
- [rule] Each criminal act needs its own evidence; a person's record should not be treated as one bundle that proves every offence. When: assigning guilt for multiple offences. Why: offences differ in method and proof.
- [rule] Do not drop a suspect on the strength of one document; seek partial or independent answers from multiple sources. When: when a single record seems to clear a suspect. Why: one source may be incomplete or misleading.
- [rule] Let an NPC accept a player's cover story, then create later conflicts that expose its flaws so the player must manage the lie. When: designing deception-driven quests.
- [rule] Script two NPC experts to disagree about one piece of evidence, and provide a verifiable third source the player can consult to settle it.
- [rule] Challenge a claim with a pointed question to test whether the other party concedes what they do not know.
- [rule] Identify and state the limit of an alibi, naming which parts no one could observe. When: Summarising how well an alibi is supported. Why: Makes clear what remains unverified.
- [rule] Give an NPC story many details the player can check against records, other NPCs and the world map, while leaving one core claim open for later. When: when writing an NPC's account. Why: Verifiable details build trust, and the open core keeps the mystery going.
- [rule] Flag contradictions between an NPC's established personality and the evidence against them, so the player can weigh the mismatch. When: When generated evidence conflicts with an NPC's traits. Why: Showing the mismatch invites the player to reason about it.
- [rule] Check for innocent explanations before treating a gap as proof of a crime, since a gap alone does not establish one.
- [rule] Create a timed clue from contradictions between two NPCs who both protect a third, so the player must resolve the conflict to fix a time.
- [rule] Check the alibi of every named person, not only the main suspects, since a minor name can prove decisive.
- [rule] Check every possible exit, not only the obvious one, before accepting that a place was sealed. When: Assessing a locked or guarded location. Why: An unguarded route can make a seemingly sealed location passable.
- [rule] Give an NPC a gap between its stated attitude and its actual schedule, so an observant player can detect the contradiction.
- [rule] Give an NPC an innocent explanation for an incriminating item, and let players check it against records or ownership marks.
- [rule] Judge a character's claims by their checkable content, separately from the manner of delivery such as tears, kneeling or pleading. Why: Manner does not establish whether a statement is true.
- [rule] Require a verifying find, such as a document in a hidden place, before a case can be marked closed.
- [rule] Gate a final accusation behind a checklist of verified links, so the player must confirm each one before the reveal.
- [rule] Treat an anomaly as a clue only after it is verified, and test it rather than assume an innocent or sinister cause. When: An unexpected object or mark conflicts with the apparent story. Why: Unverified anomalies can have innocent explanations that mislead.
- [rule] Do not rely on evidence whose original form was never examined, such as a postal envelope that was never seen. When: when evidence depends on a document or package that was not inspected directly. Why: Without examining the original, its postal or transit details cannot be trusted.
- [rule] Place checkable clues earlier in the level rather than revealing the answer only in a final cutscene.
- [rule] Make clue wording matter, so near-synonymous descriptions lead to different solutions and players must read carefully. When: Writing text-based clues for puzzles. Why: Precise wording rewards close reading.
- [rule] Make an accident verdict checkable by requiring players to find the object the verdict assumed was used, or to notice that it is missing. When: designing a crime scene with an official accident verdict. Why: a checkable verdict rewards careful inspection.
- [rule] Give the player a case journal that automatically lists found clues, so overlooked items become visible. When: Designing investigation-based gameplay. Why: An automatic list reduces the chance a clue is forgotten.
- [rule] Separate checkable details from hearsay, and verify the checkable parts directly rather than accept the relayed claim. When: Weighing a secondhand account. Why: Only verified details can support a conclusion.
- [rule] Let a culprit's borrowed justification be checkable at its source, since the culprit may have avoided checking it. When: A culprit cites a precedent or authority. Why: Exposing the source can undermine the rationalization on which the wrong rests.
- [rule] Check a claimed family relationship or identity against an independent verifiable fact, such as the claimed person's physical condition at the time. When: A caller or visitor claims a relationship to someone. Why: A checkable fact can prove a claimed identity false.
- [heuristic] Check a claim from an interested or boastful claimant through a second source, and confirm that source is independent, since the claimant may have chosen it. When: When a lead comes from a claimant who benefits from its acceptance. Why: Confidence and personal interest can make an unreliable claim seem credible. (x2)
- [heuristic] Give two NPCs slightly different versions of one event or explanation; players compare dialogue to find the discrepancy, and the difference points to the liar. When: when designing a mystery with unreliable witnesses or two characters describing the same event. Why: Conflicting versions create a choice that rewards careful comparison.
- [heuristic] Log each NPC's claimed whereabouts with a time window and an independent verifier; check claimed travel against map distances and surface mismatches as follow-up clues. When: Designing alibis for characters in an investigation game. Why: Independent verifiers and time windows make claims testable by the player.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC a believable cover story or lie with a checkable contradiction in a reachable object, room or physical evidence, so the player can expose it. When: When designing an NPC who hides a secret or makes self-serving claims. Why: The player can expose the cover story by investigating what is reachable.
- [heuristic] Make clues specific and testable, with names, places or predicted object locations an independent source can check; vague hints fit any outcome and prove nothing. When: Writing clues or NPC claims meant to pay off later. Why: Specific, checkable details can be confirmed or refuted.
- [heuristic] Test physical assumptions directly on site, such as a restraint's position relative to a hazard or whether a path exists, before committing to a plan built on them.
- [heuristic] Judge a suspect's account mainly by how much of its checkable parts outside witnesses, records and observations confirm, and weigh demeanour only as a minor factor. When: when a story contains many checkable claims alongside a key claim that cannot yet be checked. Why: Instinct about manner can err, while independent confirmation is more reliable.
- [heuristic] Tag information gathered from NPCs as unverified so the player can choose whether to trust it. When: Designing NPC dialogue that offers schedules or habits. Why: Marking uncertainty lets players weigh the risk of acting on it.
- [heuristic] Two NPCs describing the same event with different detail corroborate it, and their disagreements can be designed as leads for players.
- [heuristic] An NPC's claimed relationship can be checked by a second character who should know the real person, with that character's reaction serving as a cue. When: Designing a dialogue where an NPC's identity is in doubt.
- [heuristic] A false claim is easiest to catch when the listener already knows the true fact, such as having seen the speaker's real ability.
- [heuristic] Check a claimed injury against who visits, who speaks for the person, and whether they act like someone in pain. When: a medical excuse covers a long absence.
- [heuristic] Check a sensational report against behaviour the player has already seen before the report is accepted. When: An NPC delivers a dramatic accusation or diagnosis.
- [heuristic] After probing a witness's view of a person's mood or behaviour, ask for objective evidence such as copies, drafts or old papers to test it. Why: subjective impressions are weaker than documents.
- [heuristic] Test a new reading of a scene against other witnesses' times before accepting it. When: A reinterpretation changes the timeline of a scene. Why: A reading that fits one account may conflict with others.
- [heuristic] Make each contradiction a checkable item, such as a missing garment or an untouched item, that falsifies a theory when inspected. When: Designing evidence that disproves a theory. Why: Concrete items can be verified.
- [heuristic] Make a false identity or mix-up follow from a visible, checkable step, not from luck alone. When: When designing a plausible deception or belonging swap. Why: Audiences and players can later trace the error back to something they saw.
- [heuristic] Let NPCs give different accounts of the same location depending on who asks, rewarding the player for cross-checking.
- [heuristic] An apparent large conspiracy may be a fabricated setup, so verify its scale before reacting to it. When: When a threat seems much bigger than its visible evidence. Why: Constructed hoaxes can make minor sources look like organized plots.
- [heuristic] Test a claimed timeline by asking about a related, hard-to-invent detail such as a meal or weather. Rehearsed accounts often omit such specifics. When: When a timeline rests on a single witness.
- [heuristic] A recorded statement is only as reliable as the checks made on it afterwards.
- [heuristic] Partial checks give partial confidence, so record the remaining doubt explicitly and decide whether it is acceptable to proceed. When: verification is incomplete. Why: unrecorded doubt is easily forgotten and distorts later decisions.
- [heuristic] Verifying existing alibis tends to eliminate suspects rather than produce new leads, so it should be paired with questions that open new lines. When: Investigating with little new evidence. Why: Checking confirms or refutes existing claims but does not generate new ones.
- [heuristic] Narrow factual questions that can be checked against dates and records break evasion better than general accusations. When: A witness gives vague answers about a past event. Why: Specific answers can be verified, which makes evasion costly and gives the witness less room to deflect.
- [heuristic] A fixed-point check is unhelpful when the expected destination cannot be reached or the schedule itself is unknown.
- [heuristic] Check the timing of a side detail before trusting it, since a real detail can still be a dead end.
- [heuristic] Let confirmation rest on a document the other party can read, not on the investigator's word alone. When: Presenting a deduction to others.
- [heuristic] Test a claim of unusual strength against the claimant's known training or physical history before treating it as a supernatural effect.
- [heuristic] Claims about when a specific route was abandoned should follow the surviving record, since no fixed rule dates such changes.
- [heuristic] A false claim can be exposed by asking for a detail that only a real witness could know, and whose answer can be confirmed apart from the witness's word. When: A witness claims to have observed something that others can check. Why: A checkable answer exists independently of the witness, so it can confirm or refute the claim.
- [heuristic] A statement written to defend a person or group often shifts emphasis toward that party's favored framing compared with earlier accounts of the same events. When: a later account is written or circulated to protect a reputation. Why: a defensive purpose changes what gets stressed or omitted.
- [heuristic] An account with concrete, checkable specifics gains trust when no one challenged them, because a false specific would likely have been refuted. When: an account names times, places or words. Why: false details are easy targets for rebuttal.
- [heuristic] Test an explanation by restoring the lost item: if that ends the trouble, the ordinary explanation is at least as strong. When: Choosing between an ordinary and a supernatural cause of loss. Why: Ending the trouble by ordinary means points to an ordinary cause.
- [heuristic] When a witness's stated belief shifts, examine how the question was framed before accepting the statement.
- [heuristic] Give players a test kit with a clear detection threshold, so a clue's type is verified before it is trusted.
- [heuristic] Let a fragile rope be upgraded to a sturdier cable as a progression step, so the player's channel becomes more dependable over time. When: Designing gradual progression through a traversal or communication system. Why: Visible upgrades communicate growth and reduce the risk of losing a route.
- [heuristic] Give each source trace an unrepeatable feature so that only a careful check exposes a copy. When: Designing traces that can be forged. Why: Unrepeatable features keep copies imperfect and reward thorough inspection.
- [heuristic] When no independent source exists for a claim, judge it on other grounds rather than treating it as verified.
- [heuristic] A puzzle to tell whether an NPC is dead or unconscious can use checks with clear, distinct results, such as a pulse, a mirror or a responding limb.
- [heuristic] Use a checkable marker such as a plate or inscription so players can confirm an identity they must verify. When: crypt or graveyard levels.
- [heuristic] Rank clues by how tightly they bind to one place: common clutter should count for less than rare, localised traces. When: when weighting clues.
- [heuristic] Place low-value props that carry checkable data, so thorough players are rewarded while the main path does not depend on them. When: When designing optional detail in a level. Why: Optional depth rewards exploration without blocking progress.
- [heuristic] Make variables such as tide, time of day or weather checkable, so players can test whether a claimed sequence was physically possible. When: when designing a past-event puzzle. Why: checkable constraints let players verify the reconstruction.
- [heuristic] Make records such as a roster or ledger checkable, so players can confirm or disprove a claim by visiting a second location.
- [heuristic] Separate a claim that a place holds a supernatural trace from evidence that a human act occurred there, and test the claim before accepting it. When: When an atmosphere or local legend is offered as explanation for an event. Why: Ordinary houses can conceal crimes without leaving visible traces, so setting alone proves nothing.
- [heuristic] Casual remarks give hints rather than proof, so confirm an offhand connection with a second independent source before relying on it. When: Using gossip or chance remarks to advance an investigation. Why: A listener can misread a remark, and hints alone do not establish facts.
- [heuristic] Treat claims of a perfect record, such as many cases without failure, as unverified when no checkable detail about those cases is given.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC state a negative confidently, then offer a follow-up question that exposes what they did not check, so the player must verify it. When: Designing an NPC testimony that can be challenged. Why: A follow-up question turns an assumed claim into a checkable one.
- [heuristic] Introduce a late counter-objection that breaks a neat solution, forcing players to recompute the timeline rather than accept the first answer. When: The mystery is approaching its apparent solution around the late middle or final stretch. Why: A last-minute challenge keeps players reasoning instead of settling early.
- [procedure] 1) List each factual claim in the statement. 2) Compare each claim with facts you already hold, such as a price. 3) Record wrong claims and the correct version; a mismatch shows the story cannot be complete. When: a statement describes events you can check. Why: Claims are tested against known evidence, not tone.
- [procedure] 1) Note the suspect's claimed skill or background. 2) Ask for a demonstration of that skill. 3) Repeat the demonstration in any other languages or forms claimed. 4) Treat a mismatch as a flag for a false identity. When: A suspect claims a skill or background that can be shown on request. Why: A live demonstration tests claims that a story alone cannot confirm.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether the claim would be valid under the stated rules if its facts hold. 2) For each factual element, ask what source could show it. 3) Check whether each source still survives. 4) Note what support remains. When: a claim rests on a formal or legal conclusion.
- [procedure] 1) Identify a claim checkable against records held by others. 2) Run a cheap test. 3) Let the result confirm or rule out the lead. When: A claim or location can be checked independently. Why: Independent records give cheap, decisive checks.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the stated times with other timed events. 2) Compare stated positions with where objects or people were found. 3) Record each mismatch. When: a witness's story can be checked against objects, positions or times.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the exact arrangement shown in the scene. 2) Take test prints of the same digits in that arrangement. 3) Compare the test prints with the scene under matching conditions. When: when a claimed pose seems physically impossible. Why: a fair comparison needs the same conditions as the scene.
- [procedure] 1) Store each NPC claim as a record with a time and place. 2) Let the player choose which record to present against a suspect. 3) Compare the chosen record with the NPC's answer. When: when building an interrogation system in a game. Why: structured claim records make contradictions checkable by the player.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness to look again without naming the feature. 2) Record whether they still report it unprompted. 3) Discount any detail that appears only after a suggestion. When: a claimed detail came after a suggestion. Why: Suggested details often disappear when retested.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the statement with what other people report seeing. 2) Compare it with the physical record. 3) Note any period or contact the statement leaves out. Why: Independent sources reveal omissions that a consistent account hides.
- [procedure] 1) Record each verified event with its time. 2) Order the events chronologically. 3) Link consecutive events by the travel or interval between them. When: Building a timeline from verified times. Why: A chain of confirmed times reveals where each person could have been.
- [procedure] 1) Form a conclusion from the pattern. 2) List each supporting fact. 3) Confirm each fact separately using a record or a targeted question. 4) Reveal the conclusion only after every link is confirmed. When: a conclusion is clear but unconfirmed. Why: each link is weaker than the conclusion until checked.
- [procedure] 1) Take a stakeholder's events one at a time. 2) For each, ask where, when, why and how it happened. 3) Settle that event before opening the next. 4) Check it against physical traces and other accounts. When: Checking an account from a witness or suspect.
- [procedure] 1) Find a complete copy of the source if one survives. 2) Compare its omitted passages with the quoted ones. 3) Note which omissions change the conclusion.
- [procedure] 1) Find a small object near the crime. 2) Test it against its most likely match, such as fitting a key to a damaged lock. 3) Treat a successful fit as confirmation of the link.
- [procedure] 1) Let the subject approach far enough for a clear view of the face. 2) Keep the observer in a dark spot. 3) Confirm identity at close range before the subject escapes. When: A suspect must be identified at close range before escape. Why: Close, unhurried viewing gives a reliable identification while the observer stays concealed.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain a baseline from someone who knows the space, including recent movements. 2) List every item that should be present. 3) Check each listed item for absence. 4) Treat any unexpected object as a change made after the baseline. When: a space should match a known state and changes must be found. Why: Comparing against an explicit list and a known baseline reveals what was added, moved, or removed.
- [procedure] 1) Treat a damaging, unverified claim as a lead rather than a verified fact. 2) Seek independent confirmation before acting on it. When: An informant brings a claim that would harm the target if believed. Why: Unverified accusations can mislead and cause harm if acted upon.
- [procedure] 1) Note a witness's claim. 2) Compare it against what other people or records show. 3) Use any mismatch to decide where to press further. When: A witness makes a claim that cannot yet be verified. Why: Mismatches identify weak points to investigate, without being proof on their own.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the NPC's motive for the account. 2) Find a second source that can confirm or contradict a key claim. 3) Act on the claim only after the second source is checked. When: When designing a dialogue system in which an NPC offers a self-serving account. Why: A second source lets the player test an interested party's claim before acting on it.
- [tradeoff] A challenge-countersign check tests knowledge, not identity, so anyone who overhears the exchange can pass as a legitimate visitor. When: Relying on a password to admit visitors. Why: Knowledge of the phrase can be obtained by eavesdropping.
- [pitfall] Persuasive stories, sympathetic or dramatic witnesses, emotional appeals and confident explanations are not proof; weigh them only after checking against corroboration and known facts. (x2)
- [pitfall] Accepting a verified detail as proof of the whole account is a mistake, even if framing is doubtful; each claim in a timeline or chain needs its own check.
- [pitfall] Each elimination filter, plan or route deduction rests on assumptions, such as a sound's source; verify them, since a contradicting result collapses every branch built on them.
- [pitfall] Treat an inferred entry route or location from residue as a hypothesis until logs, witnesses or on-site checks confirm it, since inference chains can hide fallacies. When: when reasoning about how someone got into a location or from residue to location. Why: Inferred routes can be wrong without corroboration.
- [pitfall] A theory may fit most clues or one clue yet contradict or miss another, such as a shot time or body position; test every condition before trusting a confident solution. When: Evaluating a theory against the full set of evidence. Why: An unexplained detail can overturn an otherwise convincing answer.
- [pitfall] Accepting a sealed-room or constant-presence statement without asking when it was true or cross-checking it creates false impossibilities or false eliminations.
- [pitfall] Confirming harmless details in a document can make its accusations seem proven, even though accuracy on minor points says nothing about the central claim. Why: Correct description proves familiarity, not guilt.
- [pitfall] A clear, persuasive argument can blind a listener to its own weakness, especially when the weak point wounds their pride.
- [pitfall] A reproduction test is only as strong as its match to the original conditions. Loosely matched conditions can make a result look like confirmation when it is not. When: Interpreting the result of a reconstruction test. Why: Differences in weight or position can produce a trace that the original did not.
- [pitfall] A verified detail is true but not necessarily meaningful; confirming a fact does not show what it means or who is responsible.
- [pitfall] Saying that a check was already made can stop others from repeating it, even when its result is unknown to them. When: Reporting that a forensic or other check has been done. Why: Listeners assume the matter is covered and do not pursue it.
- [pitfall] Claiming superior hidden means of verification without carrying out the checks signals skipped verification and leaves the case unsupported.
- [pitfall] A persuasive connection that goes nowhere can consume time that belongs to new evidence. When: a connection seems meaningful but cannot be followed. Why: Attention spent on a dead end delays productive lines of inquiry.
- [pitfall] Repeating a staged test for an audience rewards the performer and adds no evidence, since the same reaction is simply shown again. When: A test is staged and repeated for observers rather than varied. Why: Repetition for onlookers gives the performer more stage time, not new information about the claim.
- [pitfall] Relying on a single lie to hold fails when the claimed absence can be verified. When: when an alibi or excuse can be checked.
- [pitfall] Accepting a physical trace as proof that a person was somewhere, without asking who else could have moved it, leads to wrong conclusions.
- [pitfall] A player theory that rests on a mistaken assumption can be exposed by a cheap verification step such as a ledger or record check. When: Designing a deduction puzzle where players reason from assumed facts. Why: Cheap checks let bad deductions be caught rather than rewarded.
- [pitfall] Confirm a check's coverage before ruling out a room, feature or item, or calling a search thorough or a container empty; limited checks miss items among ordinary contents. When: Deciding whether an object, feature or room has been found, is absent or can be eliminated. Why: Limited surveys can miss features or items that exist; unchecked eliminations can hide the real route.
- [pitfall] A claim nobody can check leaves the story stalled; the player needs a path to corroboration.
- [fact] A test that worked once may fail when repeated, so past success is no guarantee that the same result will follow.
- [fact] Unsupported written assertions can be used as evidence against the person who made them, since their unproven claims can be read against them. When: A written statement is read in court or to an audience. Why: Assertions without support can be turned by the other side.

## disguise and impersonation
- [model] A disguise can combine a grown beard, eyeglasses, speech mannerisms borrowed from the impersonated person, clothing bought elsewhere and a documented persona.
- [definition] A double identity: one person keeps two identities in one community, each covering the other; the second life, with one confidant, explains absences and lets an apparent victim vanish. When: a character must be unrecognisable to people who see them daily.
- [mechanism] Altered features, changed clothes and a new haircut let one person pass as a different person, so appearance serves as cover for identity.
- [mechanism] An impostor can swap costume items such as cloaks, cards and wigs; checks against a register, a witness or unchangeable traits expose it better than appearance. When: Designing an NPC that impersonates another character. Why: Verification methods determine success, and changeable items are defeated by unchangeable traits.
- [mechanism] A visible impersonation at a remote place makes the act seem to occur elsewhere, so the impersonation itself becomes the cover for the crime. Why: observers take the visible presence as proof of location.
- [mechanism] A disguised person who changes appearance gradually, copying another's build, hair colour and dress, may pass unnoticed by people who see them daily. When: A character must pass as another person without being detected by close acquaintances. Why: Slow change avoids the sudden contrast that would alert observers.
- [mechanism] A culprit who surveys a location under a disguise, such as a delivery role, learns its layout without being recognized and can plan the crime accordingly.
- [mechanism] A clue given an ordinary, reasonable-sounding explanation draws attention away from its real meaning, so the explanation ends further questioning. When: a clue has an innocent-looking explanation offered. Why: the explanation sounds natural and satisfies the need for an answer.
- [mechanism] An NPC's written description of a missing person can be compared against items the player has found, turning dialogue output into a checkable clue.
- [mechanism] Presenting a story as a true account with disguised names gives its invented documents the weight of real evidence rather than a fictional device. When: when a fictional document must feel credible. Why: the framing lends authenticity to the device.
- [mechanism] Pre-answering each likely question leaves an official little to probe, so the inquiry closes early and controls what authorities hear. When: a party wants an inquiry to end quickly. Why: ready answers remove openings for follow-up.
- [mechanism] Discovering a substitution changes who could have acted, and can show that a plausible plan was pre-empted by someone else. Why: The swap alters the facts that earlier testimony depended on.
- [mechanism] A ticket for one destination can disguise the real route, making an event appear to follow a later journey from a different place. When: a document points to a false travel path. Why: the document supports a misleading timeline.
- [mechanism] A disguised character is exposed when their claimed location, behavior or known details contradict facts the player can observe and check. When: designing an impersonator or disguised NPC. Why: Contradictions between the disguise and checkable facts give players a way to detect the deception.
- [mechanism] Information from a deceiver is worthless even when partly true, since mixing truths with lies makes the lies believed.
- [mechanism] A guard who logs visitors can build a trail: a permit issued under one name but used by someone with different features lets players deduce the impostor. When: Designing an access-log puzzle. Why: A mismatch between recorded and observed features reveals the impostor.
- [mechanism] A guard animal that reacts differently to a disguised player exposes an impostor without dialogue, when its reaction is readable at a predictable moment. When: Designing a disguise or impostor encounter. Why: Animal recognition gives a non-verbal test the player can set up and read.
- [mechanism] An identity-swap mechanic lets the player replace one corpse with another, and inconsistencies in the swapped features create detectable clues for NPC investigators. When: When designing corpse-based puzzles in a game. Why: Checks against recorded features expose mismatches the player must avoid.
- [mechanism] A disguise mechanic with a removal moment lets the player use a disguise, and the removal changes the situation. When: a stealth or infiltration mechanic.
- [mechanism] NPCs recognise a disguised player only after a trigger, such as a repeated gesture or a particular conversation topic.
- [mechanism] A disguise system can let player clue-hunting reveal the real identity behind an altered look, turning recognition into a deduction task. When: when a disguise mechanic is part of play.
- [mechanism] A person can appear to be somewhere they are not by sending a stand-in of similar build in their clothes, supported by a written token that explains the absence. When: A character needs to fake presence elsewhere. Why: Observers who see clothing and a note assume the person is present.
- [mechanism] When a player stages a disguise to test a guard's story, dialogue can branch on whether the claim survives the test. When: A player tests an NPC's claim through a disguise. Why: Claim outcomes depend on whether the story holds up under the test.
- [mechanism] Impersonation can break an alibi: each sighting is genuine but attaches to the wrong identity. When: Witnesses place one person in two places at once. Why: Genuine sightings misattributed to different identities create an apparent contradiction without any false statement.
- [mechanism] One person can cover several identities with few accomplices, so three characters can be played by two people. When: A household or group is suspected of using disguises. Why: Shared roles let a small group produce many apparent witnesses.
- [mechanism] A cover role such as a posed professional can grant access to a suspect who would refuse an open investigator, letting them speak in a relaxed way. When: The suspect would refuse an open inquiry. Why: The cover lowers the suspect's guard.
- [mechanism] A supernatural frame, such as a hooded or masked figure, keeps observers from looking closely at the person beneath. When: when a disguised or hidden person must avoid scrutiny. Why: the frame discourages close inspection and invites belief instead.
- [behavior] A planner who expects scrutiny may build an alibi beforehand by being seen in public places where others will remember them. When: when the planner expects an investigation. Why: later witnesses can confirm their presence.
- [behavior] A striking, memorable feature draws observers' attention so strongly that they fail to notice the face beneath a disguise. When: a disguise includes a conspicuous scar, lip, or hair colour. Why: observers fixate on the most distinctive feature rather than the underlying person.
- [behavior] A disguise lets an investigator move among servants and tradespeople unnoticed, so they can approach households and their contacts without drawing attention. When: Investigating a closed household or group. Why: Low-visibility cover opens access that open questioning would not.
- [behavior] A party with something to hide may confess selected faults to key listeners in its own framing, presenting itself as a victim and warning that accusers are malicious. Why: Prior framing makes later accusations sound like attacks from known enemies.
- [behavior] A message sent in another person's name can pass unnoticed by a recipient who barely knows that person's voice, so the recipient may not question it. When: the recipient has little contact with the supposed sender. Why: unfamiliar voices are hard to recognise.
- [behavior] A striking act reported publicly can be imitated by others, so the behavior spreads through a group like a rumor. When: the act is dramatic and widely reported. Why: people copy visible, reported behavior.
- [behavior] A small item hidden among many similar-looking objects is hard to notice as missing, because it blends into the crowd. When: Items of similar appearance are scattered or stored together. Why: Visual similarity removes the cue to check for a specific item.
- [behavior] A few visible traits, such as height, a beard or a steep forehead, can name a figure only tentatively when the view is brief. When: when observation is partial, brief or distant. Why: incomplete features leave the match uncertain.
- [behavior] A passing sight can supply a later false identity: a remembered detail, such as a book title, can be reattached to a remark and mistaken for a clue. When: A player or witness links an incidental detail to a claim. Why: Incidental details are easily recalled and reinterpreted.
- [behavior] Rehearsed forms of deference can gradually become sincere, so a pretended role can turn into real attitude. When: A character repeatedly performs a role they do not hold. Why: Habitual performance shapes the performer's actual feelings over time.
- [rule] Change appearance and adopt a false identity when known faces would be recognised, since recognition makes sources refuse to talk or ends an infiltration at its first step. When: sources or watched people would recognise the investigator's known face. Why: recognition makes sources refuse to talk and would end the infiltration. (x2)
- [rule] Tie every disguise to the plot as a mechanic that stages late reveal scenes, since a costume that links to nothing leaves readers feeling cheated. When: when a mystery relies on a character concealing identity. Why: mechanical use of disguise creates the reveal scenes that drive the resolution. (x2)
- [rule] Tie guards', merchants' or staff's identity to a name, badge, invitation or item check, so players judging by role-typical looks are not misled. When: NPCs can be disguised by swapping outfits; designing identity checks in a game. Why: A checkable credential lets the player catch impostors.
- [rule] Keep a disguise consistent in manner, objects, voice, appearance, gait and invented ailments; otherwise acquaintances who know the real habits will expose any mismatch under scrutiny. When: Acting a disguise before people who know the real person. Why: Mannerisms are harder to fake than looks; habits betray a disguise that looks sound.
- [rule] Choose a substitute body of similar height, build and hair colour, dressed in the target's clothes, rings and personal items, so a casual viewer accepts it. When: when a fugitive needs a death accepted as their own, or a body is too damaged for face identification. Why: Items and shared features are easier to fake than unalterable traits.
- [rule] Do not rely on costume alone where people who know the person, such as guards familiar with regular staff, would see their face at close range. When: when judging whether a disguise will hold. Why: close familiarity uses facial cues that costume cannot fake.
- [rule] Give each NPC fixed outfits and body sizes, and let outfits decide who can pass guards, so clothing and fit checks rule suspects in or out. When: designing a suspect-elimination or stolen-item puzzle with guards. Why: fixed attributes make eliminations checkable; outfits constrain who can plausibly carry the item.
- [rule] Gate a player disguise behind acquired skills or profession facts, so NPCs accept the persona only after the player has learned the required knowledge. When: designing player disguises or cover-identity mechanics. Why: the persona is credible only to someone who earned it.
- [rule] Documents and clothing can be copied, so confirm identity through a physical trace or behavior discrepancy the impostor cannot match. When: designing identity mysteries or a disguised NPC could be mistaken for a wanted figure. Why: paper passes but behavior and physical traces are much harder to fake.
- [rule] Let a disguise or forged permit grant restricted-area entry, with checks that expose false pretexts and NPC reactions to a test item revealing what they hide. When: a game has guarded or restricted areas or when designing stealth. Why: a pretext system gives a non-combat way in; disguise and tests turn stealth into information gathering.
- [rule] Make every visible detail match the persona, since one prop signalling a different origin or class can expose a disguise that observers inspect up close. When: when observers will inspect the disguised person up close. Why: a single inconsistent detail can expose the whole disguise; observers examine details rather than glancing at the face.
- [rule] An investigator's disguise must suit the setting, match a common local role, and hold up through extended conversation. Why: a costume that fits the local type is accepted without scrutiny.
- [rule] Use a disguise only when the disguised person has a plausible reason to be in place. When: when a character adopts a false identity.
- [rule] Make a helper NPC the disguised antagonist, planting an odd habit or item early so the later reveal reframes it.
- [rule] Design a minor NPC as a hidden antagonist, using its ordinariness as deliberate disguise.
- [rule] Give concealment a plausible motive such as protection, so the audience is unsure whether it is kind or sinister. When: A plot depends on one character's knowledge being kept back.
- [rule] Model a voice impersonation as a timed action that leaves a sound event on the world timeline, so later checks can use it.
- [rule] Track every claim made under a cover story, since any witness who remembers it could later expose the cover.
- [rule] Make a disguised character's tell noticeable but not conclusive, and give it a fixed pattern that a careful player can catch. Why: the player must corroborate it.
- [rule] Track NPC identity across scenes so that a former servant or guard who reappears in a new location is recognisable.
- [rule] Give an impersonator a plausible routine, and place one environmental slip that corrects it. When: designing a disguise puzzle. Why: A single slip lets a careful player detect the substitution.
- [rule] Trace every planted link, such as an order, a delivery address or a collected parcel, since each can lead back to whoever arranged it.
- [rule] Give each watcher a plausible cover role, such as a vendor, a worker or an acquaintance, so their presence in the area needs no explanation. When: watchers must stay near a location without drawing attention. Why: an ordinary role explains presence and is seldom questioned.
- [rule] A substitution theory needs independent confirmation of the trip before it is treated as proven.
- [rule] Link NPCs by marriage and property so rivalries can be found by reading records rather than stumbled upon. When: designing NPC relationships for a game.
- [rule] Vary an NPC's name spelling across in-world documents so that a player who links the variants must solve an identity puzzle. When: designing document-based clues.
- [rule] Cross-check NPC ages against a parish register, so a claimed age that does not fit the record becomes a clue.
- [rule] Give NPC judges, guards and witnesses an allegiance attribute; when one faction staffs a tribunal, players should read its verdicts differently. When: designing a tribunal or court in a game.
- [rule] Place discarded clothing or items in rooms as physical traces that show a character changed identity. When: Populating rooms with evidence.
- [rule] Let the player check credentials or membership in an in-game database to detect impostors.
- [rule] Let players pass guards by changing costume, and base recognition checks on outfit and behavior, not only identity. When: Designing guard or NPC recognition systems. Why: Outfit and conduct are the cues a real observer would use.
- [rule] Give NPCs several visible tags, such as clothing, gait and voice, so a witness's description can be matched to one NPC. Why: a description can then single out one character.
- [rule] Let players copy an NPC's action, such as raising a lantern, to trigger a hidden response elsewhere in the level.
- [rule] Make a trap or weapon look like a harmless accessory, so the player finds it by examining NPC belongings or testing the gesture that delivers it.
- [rule] A disguise mechanic can let a character pass as someone else for a limited time, with a visible tell such as a changed feature. When: when designing identity mechanics.
- [heuristic] Let observers misidentify a disguised character in low light or brief sight, then let the player exploit that mistake later as a clue. When: designing a mistaken-identity encounter. Why: low visibility makes misidentification plausible and creates a clue. (x2)
- [heuristic] A strong smell or sudden scent change may hide another odor; ask what the masking covers and why it is so strong. When: A room has an odd smell or new finish, or a suspect's scent is unusually strong or changes after an event. Why: Concealment often leaves a suspicious surplus of one cover scent; a strong masking odor can hide the original trace.
- [heuristic] When a bitter or unexpected taste appears, ask what strong-tasting or effervescent agent could mask it, and test the drink for taste before accepting that. When: when a substance may be concealed in food or drink. Why: Masking covers taste, so a clear taste test separates masked from unmasked cases.
- [heuristic] Give disguised NPCs a consistent tell, such as a scar, accent, ring, gait, habit, repeated gesture, dropped item or careless remark, so an attentive player can unmask them. When: when an NPC changes appearance with a hood, mask, hair or disguise. Why: Description checks fail once appearance changes, and a tell gives attentive players a checkable clue.
- [heuristic] Plant a disguised character's trait or belonging, such as an accent, repeated gesture, story mismatch or knowledge a stranger should not have, early so the later reveal feels earned. When: Designing a character who will later reveal a disguise. Why: Prior clues let the audience accept the reveal instead of feeling cheated.
- [heuristic] Let a disguised NPC hide identity during a scene while leaving a recognizable detail, such as clothing or voice, for later recovery. When: Generating masked or hooded characters. Why: Players can later connect the hidden figure to a known person.
- [heuristic] Do not assume the deeper the inquiry, the closer the truth; in important matters the answer often lies close to the surface. When: an investigator digs ever deeper without progress. Why: searching harder in one place can miss what is obvious nearby.
- [heuristic] A clue that the victim did not react suggests the attacker was trusted, which can steer the player's suspicion toward known characters. When: when designing a murder with a known killer. Why: lack of reaction implies familiarity.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs visible signs such as tan lines, worn uniforms or tattoos so players can infer their past, and let a later character confirm it. When: Authoring NPC backstory that should be discoverable through play. Why: Readable signs reward observation, and confirmation makes the inference feel earned.
- [heuristic] A double identity is weak when one observer knows the face and habits well, or when the disguise leaves traces a search can reveal.
- [heuristic] A disguise can explain why a witness was frightened without revealing who was present; identify the person separately from the reason for the scare. When: a witness reports a phantom or unidentifiable figure. Why: the scare and the identity have different causes.
- [heuristic] Coats and similar identity items are easily swapped; confirm which garment is genuinely linked to which person before relying on it.
- [heuristic] A companion with a transparent manner reveals private suspicions through behavior, so withholding a theory from them keeps the test honest. When: when a theory is kept from someone who could betray it. Why: a transparent manner leaks suspicion.
- [heuristic] An NPC's quest can match identities by description and known aliases, so a player who asks the wrong question is not dead-ended.
- [heuristic] Use a cover story that is plausible for the searcher, so the people questioned have no reason to suspect a real inquiry. When: When gathering information from people who might be alarmed by a real inquiry.
- [heuristic] A person who tries to obtain a substitute key, such as by impersonating its owner on a call, needs access they lack.
- [heuristic] When a document shows one traveller but a second person was expected, consider that someone else was used in the person's place. When: A register or bill covers fewer people than the case implies. Why: A stand-in can carry the documented identity.
- [heuristic] The person chosen for impersonation reveals what the manipulator knew about the target, so the choice of impostor is itself a clue. When: a message was faked in someone's name. Why: the choice reflects the manipulator's knowledge.
- [heuristic] Compare a speaker's exact wording against earlier statements, since a changed qualifier or stressed detail can reveal concealment. When: The speaker's earlier statements are available for comparison.
- [heuristic] Track whom an NPC hires, invites or sends for; these readable signals let players infer allegiance without confession. Why: Visible associations convey alliances without explicit dialogue.
- [heuristic] Separate the two impostor roles so each guards the other from exposure, and let the player connect them through one unchanged detail. When: designing a quest where two characters share a false identity. Why: Keeping roles apart limits what one discovery reveals, and a shared detail rewards careful observation.
- [heuristic] Encode a character's identity across many small props, such as trade-specific items and habit traces, so a careful player can assemble a profile. When: A hidden culprit must be discoverable from the scene. Why: Players reward attention when clues from several props converge on one identity.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs a hidden true-identity field, revealed through an earlier detectable inconsistency that players can notice. When: Generating NPCs with secret identities. Why: Players need a fair chance to spot the inconsistency.
- [heuristic] Give two characters a similar build or coat so a witness misidentifies one, creating a false identification the player must correct.
- [heuristic] Give a disguised NPC partial cues, such as a gait or voice line, that the player must match later, and let each cue carry some uncertainty. When: Designing a disguised character for identification. Why: Uncertain partial cues make the later match a reasoned judgement, not a lookup.
- [heuristic] Do not make a disguise the only route to a solution, since that route depends on the audience accepting the reveal. When: Designing a solution path that depends on a disguise. Why: A single route fails if the reveal does not land.
- [heuristic] A lookalike decoy wearing the same outfit lets the player eliminate suspects by checking a distinctive trait.
- [heuristic] Let a disguise mechanic open access to guarded NPC groups, with each cover story unlocking different dialogue and information. When: Designing stealth or social infiltration.
- [heuristic] Check each disguise prop against what an observer would expect, and raise suspicion per mismatch rather than for the disguise as a whole. When: when designing a stealth disguise system. Why: per-detail checks show the player which element failed.
- [heuristic] Tie recognition to outfit: a player in other garb may pass unnoticed, while the same player in a known outfit is spotted. When: when designing a disguise recognition system. Why: observers match the outfit as well as the face.
- [heuristic] Decoys can nest, with a container meant to fool a thief holding a second decoy inside it, multiplying the layers of deception. When: when designing hidden loot in a dungeon.
- [heuristic] A disguise need not be perfect; a plausible setting does most of the work in passing an impostor. When: when planning a substitution. Why: observers judge the setting before the person.
- [heuristic] When a target uses an alias, match descriptions, appearance, or possessions rather than names, and offer an alternative route such as a witness who knows the face. When: Designing a search for a wanted NPC under a false name. Why: Names fail for an alias, while physical traits remain identifiable.
- [heuristic] Let one character appear as two separate people, betrayed by a distinctive physical trait that a careful observer notices. When: designing an impostor reveal. Why: Players can connect the trait only if they examine people closely.
- [procedure] 1) Prepare a duplicate in advance. 2) Create a pretext that brings the valuable within reach. 3) Take the real item while the owner is expected not to notice quickly. When: reconstructing how a theft was planned.
- [procedure] 1) List every appearance of the suspect. 2) Sort the features by how easily each can be altered. 3) Build a profile from the hardest-to-change traits. 4) Generate candidates matching the profile and eliminate them using checks until few remain. When: One person appears under several disguises. Why: Hard-to-change traits survive disguise and make the candidate pool small.
- [procedure] 1) Identify where the scene's object is sold locally. 2) Visit each shop and show a photograph of the suspect. 3) Record the time and any clothing descriptions the shopkeeper gives. 4) Report findings so their weight can be assessed. When: When the object is sold commercially and sales are not logged. Why: Shopkeepers may recognise a face and link it to a known time and place.
- [procedure] 1) Note what the outline alone shows. 2) Identify a physical attribute the outline cannot settle. 3) Test that attribute directly at closer range. When: When an outline is ambiguous and the identity matters. Why: A direct physical test resolves what appearance from afar cannot.
- [procedure] 1) Show the image to several people, not one. 2) Ask the witness to fix the time of the sighting. 3) Collect concrete descriptors such as height, clothing and speech. 4) Separate direct observation from inference. When: Testing a witness's recognition of a person from a photograph. Why: Several viewers reveal whether recognition is reliable, and concrete details can be checked.
- [procedure] 1) Study the target group's current slang and manner. 2) Adopt a cover identity that uses them consistently. 3) Build trust through in-character behaviour. 4) Confirm any partner knows and plays their assigned role. When: An investigator must gain trust from a suspicious group. Why: A convincing, consistent cover draws out information while avoiding exposure.
- [metric] Disguise preparation can be cheap and quick: a card printed on demand, a second-hand uniform, and a beard and wig from a costumier are enough for a convincing impersonation. When: Estimating how hard a disguise is to obtain in a game world. Why: Cheap materials make impersonation a realistic option for characters.
- [pitfall] True facts, such as debt, can seem to confirm a theory they do not support; a lead built on them can close a question too early and needs separate testing. When: A widely accepted story seems complete. Why: Correct facts can support a false conclusion when combined with a plausible but wrong interpretation. (x2)
- [pitfall] Changing only surface details, such as clothing, is quickly seen through; matching appearance without matching behaviour, name or details, also fails under scrutiny. Why: Gait and manner are strong recognition cues that clothing does not hide.
- [pitfall] A witness's later identification can rest on inference; separate cues actually seen, like voice or gait, from assumed ones and from conclusions reached by later reasoning. When: A suspect was disguised during the observed event, or a witness names someone after reflecting on it. Why: Witnesses fill gaps with inference, and later reasoning can reconstruct an identity never seen.
- [pitfall] A disguise is only as good as the target's experience; someone who has practised deception may recognise the costume.
- [pitfall] Overconfidence in one's disguise, driven by pride, misjudges a skilled observer and invites exposure.
- [pitfall] A disguise can defeat assumptions about age or gait, so one observation should not settle a suspect's identity. When: when judging a disguised person's identity from appearance. Why: Disguises alter the visible cues people rely on.
- [pitfall] Accepting an identity based only on voice or sound as certain, when it is an impression rather than proof. When: A witness identifies someone without seeing them. Why: Sound cues are ambiguous and can be mistaken.
- [pitfall] Assuming a disguise must be elaborate, or trusting a uniform, title or card without checking it, leaves investigators open to con artists. When: Evaluating whether a claimed identity is genuine. Why: Small, well-timed changes can be enough to deceive.
- [pitfall] A substitute body depends on passing as genuine, so a witness who knows the person can expose the substitution. When: a body is presented as a known individual. Why: someone familiar with the person can spot the mismatch.
- [pitfall] A plausible reason for knowledge, such as a newspaper report, can cover a real slip, so check the claimed source against what was actually published. When: a suspect explains away what they know. Why: a convincing cover can hide genuine insider knowledge.
- [pitfall] Forgetting a drink's own strong taste, such as coffee's bitterness, can wrongly exclude a candidate, because that taste may hide the poison.
- [pitfall] A disguise that build and bearing give away conceals little; judge whether the disguise hides identity before relying on it.
- [pitfall] A substitute identity is convincing only if the features others check are the ones altered. Changing unchecked features does not protect the disguise. When: When faking the identity of a body. Why: Investigators verify specific identifiers, so alterations elsewhere are irrelevant.
- [pitfall] Do not accept a double identity on one trait; check complementary features against independent records. Why: a single shared feature can be coincidence.
- [pitfall] A hint can arrive disguised as a question about a hobby or entertainment, so it is easily missed.
- [pitfall] A visual disguise can cover the face while a small trace, such as an ink mark, remains on the hands, so a check limited to appearance can miss it. When: When verifying a suspect's identity or activity. Why: Searchers who focus on the face overlook evidence elsewhere on the body.
- [pitfall] If a roster is the only place a character is described, later clues about that character are easy for the player to miss.
- [pitfall] A name that fails to match one register does not prove it false, because other registers or regions may hold the record. When: Checking a name against a single reference source. Why: Records are incomplete and spelled or filed differently across sources.
- [pitfall] A disguise that works only at distance or in poor light will be dismissed as implausible by the audience.
- [pitfall] A visitor's apparent frailty can be a disguise or a tactic to gain time, so physical signs alone should not be trusted as evidence of honesty. When: Assessing a stranger's account. Why: Sympathetic appearance can lower an interrogator's guard.
- [fact] A disguise works mainly through role and manner, a performance a culprit can put on and off; a cover persona may hide a trained performer.
- [fact] A disguise often betrays itself through a thin visible seam, such as a pale line at the hairline, where an artificial layer meets real skin or hair. When: A character's appearance relies on layered parts such as a wig, beard, or stained complexion. Why: Attachments and cosmetics leave edges that a careful observer can notice.
- [fact] A beard or dark clothing can hide a protector's identity from the person they guard.
- [fact] A substitute body may come from an institutional source, such as a dissection supply, that is unlikely to be questioned. When: a false death requires a body to pass as the subject. Why: an unquestioned source avoids scrutiny of the body's origin.
- [fact] A disguise can hide a threat behind a mask of concern, such as a guardian enforcing a rule under an outside identity.
- [fact] Small changes such as an altered brow line, a hairpiece, hidden shoe lifts, and a cap and apron can disguise a person from people who know them. When: A person must avoid recognition by acquaintances. Why: Recognition depends heavily on familiar features and silhouette, which these changes alter.
