- [fact] A disguise prepared in advance, with a false identity and supporting paperwork, can look ordinary to routine checks.
- [fact] Grease paint around the eyes is enough to change how observers read a face.
- [fact] A disguise changes hair, clothes, face and manner, but usually leaves habits, expressions and physical traces such as fingerprints unchanged.
- [fact] Footwear and posture can add a little height, and a small feature can be built up, but a large feature cannot be reduced quickly by disguise. When: Judging which traits a disguise can change. Why: Disguise methods add material or alter posture but cannot easily remove bulk.
- [fact] A substitute who matches the suspect in height, voice, gait, dress or disguise can make a false alibi appear to hold. When: when a suspect's alibi rests on being seen elsewhere.

## evidence custody and provenance
- [model] A case can be built as a chain of linked facts in which each fact confirms the one before, and the final link connects to the suspect. When: When assembling an accusation from several facts. Why: Linked facts show how each element supports the next.
- [model] A land record chain logs each grant with its date, each sale with its buyer, and owners at a later date, linking people across holdings. When: tracing who was connected to whom through property.
- [mechanism] Confronting a suspect with an item can branch their replies and open new lines; an item contradicting a denial can trigger the next interrogation step. When: designing an interview system with evidence items.
- [mechanism] A trail that weather or chance can erase rewards quick pursuit, and any delay in following it can lose the case. When: tracking a fragile trail. Why: traces are lost to events that accumulate over time.
- [mechanism] If a test works regardless of trace age, better tools gain value. Freshness-dependent methods lose value as in-game time passes. When: Evidence decays over in-game time.
- [mechanism] Make some evidence destructible, so that cleanup by a culprit leaves fragments players must reconstruct. When: Designing evidence that can be destroyed. Why: Partial remains keep the investigation alive.
- [mechanism] Evidence a suspect discards in an ordinary place can be recovered when a witness with a hidden sightline sees the disposal and keeps the item, though luck, not method, decides whether this happens. When: A suspect disposes of evidence in an outdoor or public container. Why: Witness sightlines and retained items create recovery chances, but unplanned keeping is unreliable.
- [mechanism] Requiring a second clue before an accusation counts as solved, with different proof levels producing different outcomes, rewards thorough investigation over guessing. When: A player makes an accusation in a mystery game. Why: Multiple proof tiers make weak accusations fail and strong ones succeed.
- [mechanism] Moving an item changes which clues remain in the scene, so player actions on evidence should have consequences. When: designing interactable evidence. Why: Irreversible handling makes player choices meaningful.
- [mechanism] Each handover of a valuable object between locations creates a window in which it can be seen or taken.
- [mechanism] Accumulating small independent findings progressively narrows the set of plausible explanations, until the remaining candidates share a common origin. When: When several minor clues are collected over time. Why: Each finding eliminates alternatives that are inconsistent with it.
- [mechanism] A missing item, such as a disposed key, becomes a clue in its own right, since its absence is a gap in the record. When: An expected object cannot be found at a scene. Why: Absence of an expected item breaks the chain of evidence.
- [behavior] Reading a source only as far as suits the speaker, or cutting the clause that carries its warning, changes the conclusion drawn from it.
- [behavior] Memory of an ordinary day fades quickly when nothing distinguished it from others, so witnesses are often unsure of the specific day. When: when a witness is asked about a routine day. Why: Without a distinguishing event, days blend together in memory.
- [rule] Tag each claim by source and confidence (direct observation, opinion, first-hand, repeated, gossip, third-party hearsay, suspect's report) so players can trace it and weigh each class differently. When: when designing witness dialogue or evaluating a chain of testimony. Why: Visible sources let the player judge how reliable each claim is; secondhand claims depend on their informant. (x2)
- [rule] Give each in-world document visible provenance (author or holder, date, bias, whether its container is present) so players can judge reliability and cross-check accounts of the same event. When: When authoring in-game documents as clues or recording one event from different sides. Why: Visible provenance lets players assess a document's reliability instead of guessing. (x2)
- [rule] Give items a provenance log of owners, sales, locations and confirmers so players can verify claimed owners, argue from it, trace stolen items and flag wrong-person or mismatched-inscription finds. When: Designing evidence items, clues tied to objects, or a stolen-item mechanic. Why: Recorded owners and locations make the item's history checkable and give players a traceable path.
- [rule] Check a claim resting on one author's reading against the sources that author cites; a citation alone confirms nothing until its source actually supports the claim. When: when a claim about the past depends on one author's reading.
- [rule] Make key items leave a record, such as a log entry or an NPC who saw it, so they cannot be removed or denied without a trace. When: before a key item is formally secured. Why: A routine observer's account is hard to dismiss.
- [rule] Take discovered evidence to one authority and examine it in their presence, keeping a documented chain of custody from discovery onward to prevent disputes over where it was found. When: when physical evidence is found during an investigation. Why: A documented chain protects the evidence from dispute.
- [rule] Let items show history through physical state, such as a scuffed grip, a strap worn to one size or an unexplained detail no NPC understands, so players infer earlier holders. When: when designing items with a history or environmental storytelling through objects. Why: Physical state can communicate history without dialogue.
- [rule] Test a written statement against the physical form: an unusual cut, an incomplete page or a handwriting mismatch undermines its claimed origin. When: Examining a document presented as testimony. Why: Physical inconsistencies reveal forgery or staging.
- [rule] A lock, ID, or trace that appears to prove identity should require a second independent check, such as a matching key or alibi record, before being accepted as proof. When: Designing a clue that the game treats as conclusive. Why: Independent checks prevent a single clue from closing the mystery too early.
- [rule] Let looted items carry wear and marks that players learn to read as backstory; repairing or cleaning an item erases that evidence, which is a deliberate design choice. When: when designing item histories. Why: wear makes objects narrative and cleaning becomes a meaningful choice.
- [rule] Give items recorded origin tags, such as a shop mark, guard post, chest or workshop, so players can trace each item to its source and the NPCs with access. When: designing item provenance or generated items that serve as trace clues. Why: Origin tags link items to characters.
- [rule] Track each evidence item's custody and owner history so players can ask and trace who handled or held it and when. When: designing items that move between characters or clue items for investigation. Why: A recorded chain of handlers makes item provenance a usable clue, and ownership makes an item's meaning depend on who handled it.
- [rule] Give objects persistent states such as indentations, stains, fresh residue, broken, wet or scorched, encoding time and cause so players can compare them with a claimed timeline. When: designing environmental storytelling. Why: States act as readable evidence of past events and of recent use or movement.
- [rule] Keep physical-possibility clues (time, means) separate from psychological-fit clues (character); a suspect may pass one and fail the other, and opportunity alone does not establish guilt. When: designing suspect clues or narrowing suspects in a mystery. Why: Opportunity alone does not establish that a suspect is the culprit.
- [rule] Give found items provenance: who gave them, where they came from and who sold them, so each object can open a new line of questioning.
- [rule] Collect every scrap of evidence, but read it without a fixed preconception, since gathering alone does not prevent distorted interpretation.
- [rule] Give each evidence item several possible owners but design the correct one to match properties the player can inspect, such as colour or length. When: Designing evidence that can be attributed to more than one character. Why: Inspectable properties let careful players rule out rival owners.
- [rule] Track each key item's ownership and location history, so routine NPC tasks such as laundry or delivery create checkable evidence. When: Designing items that move between characters in a generated world. Why: Movement history turns routine activity into testable clues.
- [rule] Check a document's claims against other clues so it works as evidence to weigh rather than as a plain answer.
- [rule] When a formal document decides who has a claim, check its exact wording before deciding who must be told. When: Disclosure would harm a third party, or a document governs inheritance.
- [rule] Record what was left behind as well as what was taken, since remaining items show what was not needed and can reveal which exit was used. When: Investigating a departure or disappearance. Why: What remains in place narrows the possible exit and time of departure.
- [rule] Track which character holds a key item, so progress requires delivering it to the correct authority.
- [rule] Establish an object's earlier location or ownership before treating it as evidence; a found item proves little on its own. When: an item is found at a scene. Why: its significance depends on when it arrived and who owned it.
- [rule] Examine each fact before dismissing it, because its evidential value is unknown until it has been examined. When: Early in an investigation, when evidence is thin and many facts look equally unimportant. Why: A trivial-looking object can become key evidence once its properties are checked.
- [rule] Show the initial meeting or event openly, so later clues can be traced back to what the audience has already seen. When: Planting clues that should pay off later. Why: Clues linked to earlier shown events feel fair and rewarding when they return.
- [rule] Check each claim against the means the witness says they had of knowing it, such as seeing, hearing or inferring.
- [rule] Scale a clue's reliability rating by how close the listener stood and whether the listener was interrupted. When: Assigning a confidence level to overheard clues. Why: Proximity and clean hearing make the captured words more trustworthy.
- [rule] Make booking clerks NPCs who remember names and dates, so a player who asks the right questions can recover an alias. When: designing service NPCs. Why: Remembered details reward careful questioning.
- [rule] Give a clue an identifying name or mark that reveals its owner simply by being seen.
- [rule] Mark each clue as material (timeline, records) or inferential (behaviour, tells), so players know which kind of evidence they hold. When: when designing investigation clues.
- [rule] Attach a grudge to a specific item in game lore so a non-player character's behaviour toward that item becomes a motive hook the player can uncover. When: writing character history for a game. Why: A visible symbol makes hidden motives discoverable.
- [rule] Use a clerk's sworn statement that an entry was written in his presence as a provenance check.
- [rule] Scatter partial archives across a generated world, with a missing page the player must infer from surviving series.
- [rule] Let an in-game pamphlet or sermon label a faction, and reveal the motive behind the label so players can judge it.
- [rule] Order testimony so the final witness carries extra weight, and make that ordering visible so the player understands it matters.
- [rule] Log an item's contents and any return condition at each transfer, so the player can later verify claims about its ownership. When: In item-transfer systems that carry conditions. Why: A stored record lets the player check what an NPC or item history says.
- [rule] Keep an access log showing which NPCs handled food, so players can eliminate suspects by opportunity. When: when generating poisoning mysteries. Why: Opportunity records give players a checkable basis for elimination.
- [rule] Give crates, keys or letters a movement log, so that a leg that does not match the record can expose a second item.
- [rule] Encode inheritance rules as data so each heir's share recalculates when an NPC dies, letting the player see shifting stakes. When: when building a game with inherited wealth or property. Why: recalculated shares make the consequences of each death visible.
- [rule] When a player destroys a document, keep its authors and witnesses reachable and let them be re-interviewed, so the loss does not feel complete. When: Designing evidence that players can collect or destroy. Why: Removing only the paper leaves sources who can still testify.
- [rule] Log which character handled each object during a set-piece, so a later puzzle can reconstruct who moved what.
- [rule] Give each key or relic a logged history of holders and locations, so players can reconstruct who could have opened a given door.
- [rule] Use object states such as a hung cloak or an open door as timestamps when no NPC was watching. When: Designing environmental clues for a time-based puzzle. Why: Environmental state can record events without any witness.
- [rule] Let volatile clues such as smells or residues decay on a timer, rewarding players who examine a scene early. When: Designing evidence that changes over time. Why: Time pressure gives examination a reason to happen promptly.
- [rule] Design partial-state clues, such as a half-cleaned statue or moved object, that imply an NPC will return so players can wait and watch.
- [rule] Make each seal's state observable, such as a raised bridge, lit lamp or drawn curtain, so players can reason about entry periods.
- [rule] Compare claimed possessions with physical proof; a stated large sum with no trace of the goods is a warning sign. When: A party claims to hold valuables or funds. Why: Unverified claims can be fabricated to support a scheme.
- [rule] Do not count evidence awaiting confirmation, such as a pending expert report, as proven. When: when reviewing a case before an arrest or theory is committed.
- [rule] Before shipping, confirm that every clue needed to reach the solution is placed and reachable. When: when validating a mystery level.
- [rule] Record each clue's source and timing, so designers can see which explanations depend on unverified assumptions. When: When building a mystery or evidence system that must be checked for consistency. Why: Provenance and timing make contradictions and unverified assumptions visible before the content ships.
- [rule] Rank clues by how usefully they trace to a person: location clues like postmarks are useful, while mass-produced items cannot identify a buyer and should be deprioritised. When: Choosing which clues to pursue in an investigation. Why: Pursuing untraceable clues wastes time.
- [rule] Once an envelope is opened or a paper is handled, it no longer proves who sealed it, so its trustworthiness should be lowered accordingly. When: Judging the reliability of a sealed document. Why: Breaking a seal or handling a paper removes the guarantee of origin.
- [rule] Preserve and record a bite impression before confronting the suspect, or the impression can be lost.
- [rule] Confirm a container was not reopened after packing before trusting what it shows.
- [heuristic] Treat a clue confirming a direction, or a reproduced match, as a lead or plausibility, not proof; probable clues may be accidental, so be wary if the holder is evasive. When: when a reconstruction matches the original mark.
- [heuristic] Give each evidence item a log in the player's record of who examined or handed it over, when, and what was found, with a signature or stamp at each handover. When: Designing evidence tracking in a game. Why: A structured, timestamped log lets players compare findings and supports later checks.
- [heuristic] Before treating a piece of evidence as proof, check who produced it and which part of it actually carries the claim. When: a note, signature or object seems to prove guilt directly. Why: strong-looking evidence can carry little information when it rests on an unexamined assumption.
- [heuristic] Test each suspect against several independent observations. One matching detail may be chance, but a set of matching details is strong evidence. When: a hidden agent has left traces across different sources. Why: Coincidence can explain a single match, but not many independent matches.
- [heuristic] Tag each clue with its real origin, so a knife or note can belong to another character and let players reject a false link. When: authoring clues in a mystery. Why: clear origin enables correct rejection of false links.
- [heuristic] Expensive, stiff paper suggests a writer of means, so the medium itself can narrow the field of possible writers.
- [heuristic] Record who gave each personal item, since a gift traces back to a relationship that can reveal a connection and a possible motive.
- [heuristic] Ask whether an item was worn openly or hidden under clothing, because visibility limits who could have seen it and recognized the wearer. When: testing who could have known the wearer from an item.
- [heuristic] A damaged or partial document, or one carried by someone, can be read as significant or innocent; keep both readings open until other evidence settles it.
- [heuristic] Plant a strong-looking clue that points at the wrong character, and make it resolvable by a second check the player can perform. When: Designing misdirection in a mystery. Why: A resolvable red herring is fair and rewards careful play.
- [heuristic] Checking which hand an item is made for can narrow suspects by a physical trait such as handedness. When: a worn or held item fits only one hand.
- [heuristic] Judge whether a found item was delivered deliberately, and who presents it, before accepting it at face value. When: An object is handed over or turns up at a convenient moment. Why: A planted object can steer an inquiry toward a chosen suspect.
- [heuristic] Record who knew an object existed; wide knowledge of an item widens the set of people who could have moved it. When: an item has disappeared. Why: Knowledge of an object is not limited to its owner.
- [heuristic] When a document's key term carries an argument, compare its rendering with the original wording before accepting it. When: the term may have been chosen to suit a patron or theory. Why: renderings can be shaped to fit a theory.
- [heuristic] A writer who revisits a document at different moments may cite different sections, so date each citation before reading it as the writer's settled view. When: The same author quotes a document at more than one time. Why: Stakes and opinion shift, changing what is cited.
- [heuristic] Do not treat a suspect's manner alone as evidence of guilt; check the account against documented records.
- [heuristic] Items passed between NPCs can carry a custody history, so a puzzle can reveal whether a clue was altered along the way.
- [heuristic] Place discarded disguise items as findable clues in a drain, river or bin, so disposal leaves a trail rather than a clean escape.
- [heuristic] A matching item in one location can link two places, letting a found item connect the player to a shop or room.
- [heuristic] Check a trivial detail against physical inventories: a missing or matching item can link a gossip thread to a physical clue. When: when a peripheral fact may connect to an object.
- [heuristic] Rank clues by reliability and spend effort on the strongest first; keep weak clues as long shots that matter mainly alongside a stronger one. When: Multiple clues differ in strength and effort is limited. Why: Weak clues rarely succeed alone but can confirm stronger leads.
- [heuristic] Let players sample a clue with a tool, seal it, and receive lab results after a delay, making evidence handling a playable step.
- [heuristic] Give each scene object a plausible role, such as a ladder, a removed plank or a cut, so the player forms and tests a hypothesis. When: designing a crime scene. Why: plausible roles let players reason about how the act was done.
- [heuristic] An object's position shows where a person had to stand to use it, so players can infer where someone was. When: A functional object such as a bell rope or lever is placed in a room. Why: Use requires physical presence at a specific spot.
- [heuristic] A permanent change to a character or item, like a scar or breakage, can serve as a fixed check that it could not have been somewhere else. When: when designing identity or location checks.
- [heuristic] Check any object out of its usual alignment, since it may hide something beneath it.
- [heuristic] Movable props such as lamps or fires make a room feel alive and can set up later reveals. When: designing a room for atmosphere and later payoff. Why: interactable objects invite attention.
- [heuristic] When tracing many items, divide them into categories, assign each category to a different searcher, and let item quality suggest where to search. When: when tracing a large set of items.
- [heuristic] Form a provisional interpretation of a clue quickly, then revise it as later evidence arrives. When: Early evidence is ambiguous. Why: Fast provisional readings let the player act and later correct wrong guesses.
- [heuristic] Item size or wear can encode ownership, letting players match items to NPC profiles.
- [heuristic] Use a physical substitute to break a chain of custody, so the apparent captive is not the real threat. When: a trial or capture scene. Why: Substitution invalidates the assumption that custody guarantees containment.
- [procedure] 1) When transcriptions conflict or are hard to read, re-examine the originals. 2) Check dates, gaps and page placement against the original, not a certified copy. 3) Treat earlier compilations as secondary until checked against them. When: when a copy, summary or earlier transcription of court or archive papers is offered as proof. Why: Mismatches in placement can reveal forgery that a copy hides; transcription errors propagate through later accounts. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Identify the item and the shared space it passed through. 2) List each person who held or was near it. 3) Mark who had access, who was positively excluded, and follow the chain back to its owner. When: when an item may have been handled by several people or may link a person to a place or event.
- [procedure] 1) Establish how many identical copies were produced. 2) Account for each copy's known holder. 3) Attribute any unaccounted copy to a hidden holder, likely the commissioner; a single recovered copy does not prove the case, since a second identical item may exist elsewhere. When: when a weapon or token exists in several identical copies. Why: Counting reveals possessions no witness mentioned.
- [procedure] 1) Label each item separately as collected, with description, date and source. 2) Record who handled it. 3) Obtain signed statements for identity, sampling and analysis. 4) Lock and log storage. 5) Hand to analyst with a written request. When: Any sample may be needed later in court or comparison. Why: A signed chain keeps results usable even when inconclusive.
- [procedure] 1) Find the full original source. 2) Compare the excerpt against it, noting unmarked omissions, especially cuts that remove material undercutting the claim. 3) Check disputed words against standard definitions. 4) Check claims of non-reading against cited sources. 5) Note what was removed and why. When: when a claim depends on one quoted passage. Why: Cuts can silently remove the evidence that weakens the claim.
- [procedure] 1) Gather corroborating letters and documents. 2) Interview the people who can confirm or contradict the account. 3) Arrest only once the evidence is sufficient. When: when a suspect's guilt rests on presumption. Why: Corroboration prevents an early strike from failing and damaging trust in justice.
- [procedure] 1) Pull out each specific, checkable claim in the document. 2) Compare each one with known facts. 3) Record which claims hold, and keep those results separate from the accusations. When: A single unsigned document is the only lead and it contains checkable facts. Why: Verified details show familiarity with the subject, not that the accusations are true.
- [procedure] 1) Let the player collect each clue. 2) Have the player present the chain of evidence to a group of NPCs. 3) Make the NPCs respond to the chain. When: for a final reveal in a game. Why: presenting evidence to NPCs turns collected clues into a scene with consequences.
- [procedure] 1) Compare each printed entry with independent accounts from family or witnesses. 2) Note any conflict in names or dates. 3) Record verified names and dates in your notes.
- [procedure] 1) Empty each container of evidence. 2) Sort contents into groups by type, such as papers, coins and keys. 3) Record every item before bagging, so nothing is lost or confused. When: When collecting items from pockets, bags or other containers. Why: Logging keeps each item traceable.
- [procedure] 1) Name who recognised the item. 2) Name who confirmed ownership. 3) Note how that confirmation was obtained. 4) Judge the clue's weight from these answers. When: Assessing an object offered as evidence. Why: Provenance shows whether a clue's link to a person is independent or shaky.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the entry's date with the events it describes. 2) Note hedged wording that avoids admitting fault. 3) Check the setting where the act took place. 4) Test whether the claimed event could have happened as described. 5) Read who was present or absent as a sign of intent. When: an official record conflicts with other sources about who acted and why. Why: Each check exposes a different way that a record can soften, omit or invent events.
- [procedure] 1) Count how often each writer cites each source. 2) Trace the common root of the citations. 3) Treat agreement between writers as corroboration only after steps 1 and 2. When: a long chain of writers seems to confirm one view. Why: a shared origin makes apparent agreement weaker than it looks.
- [procedure] 1) Record the witness who sees the disposal. 2) Record who keeps the item. 3) Obtain the lawful access permission or key. 4) Recover the item. 5) Pass it to the analyst with custody documented. When: Designing or tracing a recovered physical clue. Why: An explicit chain keeps the evidence admissible and the discovery fair.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the maker's mark on each object. 2) Check the maker's customer records for duplicate or matching items. 3) Use the maker's profile of customers to judge how likely a matching purchase is. When: Objects carry manufacturer marks and records of sales are available. Why: Records link an item to a buyer and show whether a match is expected.
- [procedure] 1) Write every gathered clue in one list. 2) Mark which clues have been followed. 3) Check the list for omissions. 4) Prune leads as dead ends appear. When: Many clues are gathered and the central clue is not yet clear. Why: A complete list exposes overlooked items and limits wasted effort on dead ends.
- [procedure] 1) Test every arrangement and discard impossible ones, or 2) hold all elements in view until a combination appears. 3) Test the sudden combination against the facts before trusting it. When: Scattered clues need to be linked into one explanation. Why: Systematic elimination and holistic recognition are both routes to a solution, but insight needs checking.
- [procedure] 1) Label each exhibit at collection. 2) Record where and from whom it was taken. 3) Keep items separate to prevent mix-ups. When: Collecting physical evidence during an investigation. Why: Clear provenance prevents confusion between items and supports later proof.
- [tradeoff] Hiding a clue in plain view conceals it from players who expect hiding, but makes it easy to miss entirely; a must-find clue needs a more reliable placement. When: The clue must be reliably found for progression. Why: Obvious objects can be overlooked even when visible.
- [tradeoff] Cutting an object reveals its internal mechanism but destroys evidence that must stay intact. Cut only when preservation is not required. When: when the object may be needed in court.
- [pitfall] Identifying someone by a ring, clothing, record, interested party's claim or family recognition is weak until independently compared; items swap and records match substitutes. When: when establishing who a body or person is. Why: Items can be swapped or planted and records can be matched by a substitute.
- [pitfall] A matching item in a suspect's room or a paper trace shows access or location, not who wore, wrote or caused the event on a given night. When: when a suspect's item is found at a scene. Why: Objects can pass through many hands before and after an event.
- [pitfall] Handling evidence destroys or contaminates traces like stains, alignment or prints; touching adds new prints. Examine before repeated handling, since early contact removes traces tests need. When: when handling evidence before examination, such as for a fingerprint check. Why: Early contact removes or alters traces, and added prints confuse the original trace.
- [pitfall] Handling evidence before its meaning is understood can delay or lose its value.
- [pitfall] Clerks may refuse information out of professional discretion or annoyance, which can cut off a trail.
- [pitfall] Public suspicion can rest on partial knowledge, since the detailed terms of a private agreement are often unknown to the community.
- [pitfall] A clerk's added comments can tilt a deposition toward guilt, so additions must be read separately from the witness's words. When: When a record contains marginal or appended notes. Why: Annotators may bring their own views into the account.
- [pitfall] A medical or natural verdict offered before access is resolved closes the question too early.
- [pitfall] A plausible sequence built from guesswork can fit the facts without being true, and unexplained facts such as an unrecorded visit must be addressed or the theory looks weak. When: when assembling an alternative explanation. Why: Fit alone does not establish truth, and unexplained facts expose the gaps.
- [pitfall] A fixture that looks newer than the rest of the room may mark a deliberate change rather than a repair. Why: Recent-looking additions can be intentional.
- [pitfall] Withholding findings from those who must act on them can be read as insubordination and breeds mistrust.
- [pitfall] A trace that was not anticipated, such as a small personal object, can still connect the scene to the offender. When: An offender cleans up but misses an item. Why: Removal efforts focus on expected traces and miss others.
- [pitfall] Handling a trace object early, especially in front of others, can contaminate or confuse it, and a quick deduction from it can be wrong until a second source confirms it. When: Examining a small object at the start of an inquiry. Why: Careless handling can destroy the trace and tempt an unconfirmed conclusion.
- [pitfall] Inspecting a physical object late in the investigation can lose context and cause important evidence to be overlooked. Why: Details noticed early are tied to the scene and people present at the time.
- [pitfall] Treating a coincidence in time, such as a storm at the same hour as an execution, as a cause or sign of guilt is an error. When: When two events occur together and one is read as explaining the other. Why: Simultaneity does not establish causation.
- [pitfall] A state that ends on its own may be mistaken for the effect of an intervention performed just before it.
- [pitfall] A mark placed on an item other than the one that was moved proves nothing about the item that mattered. When: When applying custody marks to evidence. Why: Only the mark on the actually moved object records its absence.
- [fact] A document cannot predate the machine used to produce it, so its equipment can contradict a date the document claims. When: checking a document's claimed date. Why: A machine's manufacture date sets the earliest possible date for its output.
- [fact] Yellowed edges and an old erasure suggest a sheet was kept for years, and an erasure can preserve faint earlier writing that is still readable.
- [fact] Parish membership and rate lists follow residence on land, recording legal membership rather than friendship or private loyalty.
- [fact] Church and baptismal records establish a person's standing and family links.
- [fact] A sworn statement that is dated, taken before a court and closed by a named clerk can have its origin and authority checked. When: when judging how much weight a written account deserves. Why: a named recorder and date make the record traceable.
- [fact] Names in old court records may contain clerical errors that complicate later reconstruction of who was accused. When: reconstructing cases from historical records. Why: Scribes can misrecord names.
- [fact] A prosecution case built on one trace is prima facie, meaning it is an apparent case that still needs testing. It is not a conviction.
- [fact] Mirror placement affects both what can be seen and where light reflects, so mirror positions must be recorded room by room.

## cover stories
- [model] A hidden second identity is supported by a separate residence, separate money, a forged signature and staff briefed in advance, so the public party keeps a clean alibi. When: when a character must act covertly while keeping a public alibi. Why: Layered separation keeps the second identity from being linked to the first.
- [definition] A cover story is a plausible explanation for odd behavior or an activity that hides the real purpose and discourages checking, steering observers wrong.
- [definition] A cover name is an alias two correspondents adopt, so their letters are addressed to a false identity and remain private. When: when a hidden correspondence channel is needed. Why: The false identity hides who is actually writing.
- [mechanism] Suspects mix a convenient lie with accurate details or silence on the key point, then may admit a lie and concede some truth, shaping the listener's conclusion. When: A suspect must look cooperative while concealing a key fact; when questioned about a detailed story. Why: A single false claim, surrounded by truth, shapes the listener's conclusion.
- [mechanism] A cover story holds when observers are incurious and records are hard to check, and fails once claims can be verified. Why: Distance and lack of curiosity protect the story.
- [mechanism] An invented disappearance or crime can explain both a missing person and missing assets, so one fabricated event covers two losses. When: When a missing person and missing money appear together. Why: A single story that accounts for both losses is more convincing than two separate explanations.
- [mechanism] A motive can be hidden by staging a cover story, such as making a killing look like an unrelated crime so suspicion does not fall on the real beneficiary. When: A culprit wants to deflect suspicion from a clear motive. Why: An unrelated explanation draws the investigation away from the person who gains.
- [mechanism] A cover story collapses once the questioner already knows the real identity, however convincing the details are. When: when the questioner holds the real name and face. Why: a known identity makes the cover's claims false.
- [mechanism] Mood, family history and dark backstory can pull player attention away from concrete clues toward emotional leads that cannot be checked physically. When: when a mystery surrounds the crime with atmosphere. Why: Emotional content is vivid and easy to follow, so it competes with less memorable physical traces.
- [mechanism] A group story holds only while every party repeats the same line; one party breaking ranks, or physical evidence contradicting it, causes it to collapse. When: Multiple parties coordinate a shared account. Why: Coordinated stories depend on unanimous repetition and consistency with physical facts.
- [behavior] A pleasing, courteous, or attractive suspect can lower an observer's or official's guard, so charm may be mistaken for innocence and hide motive. When: A suspect is polished, respectable, courteous, attractive or charming. Why: Impression and attraction shape judgment, and pleasant conduct draws attention away from purpose.
- [behavior] A conspicuous cover draws attention to the secret it claims to hide, so observers fixate on that claim while the real secret goes unexamined. When: a visibly displayed concealment. Why: visible concealment invites the question of what it protects, and the answer offered is accepted.
- [behavior] People explain a short absence with ready-made reasons such as nerves or a clothing problem, and these reasons lose credibility as the absence lengthens. When: a person leaves a social scene briefly.
- [behavior] A witness facing a contradictory sworn statement may claim confusion or a disturbed state of mind to explain it away. When: a witness is confronted with an earlier statement. Why: A claimed mental state offers a ready explanation for the contradiction.
- [behavior] A detail framed as a joke is rarely treated as a clue, so players notice its significance only in hindsight.
- [behavior] A sudden show of pleasantness from a suspect after a threat appears can be read by an observant audience as a warning rather than reassurance. When: A suspect becomes unusually polite or attentive after a visit or threat. Why: Players who know something is hidden interpret friendliness as a cover.
- [behavior] An investigator who looks at objects rather than the person addressed hides what he has noticed, and observers struggle to read his thoughts. When: An interrogator wants to keep suspicions from a suspect. Why: Eye contact is a channel for revealing attention, and averting it withholds that signal.
- [behavior] A weapon that a stranger shows briefly and then hides invites suspicion from observers. When: A stranger reveals and conceals a weapon.
- [behavior] A caught suspect often claims he was lured, showing he is already building a counter-story. When: A suspect is caught in a trap. Why: Self-defence leads the suspect to blame the trap's setter.
- [behavior] A plausible cover story can make a source speak freely, even when the cover story is false. When: when a source is given a believable reason for being questioned. Why: plausibility lowers suspicion.
- [behavior] When someone erases marks, the erasure itself shows care and expectations about what investigators would find. When: Some marks are missing or clearly removed while others remain. Why: Erasing selectively implies the actor anticipated scrutiny of certain traces.
- [behavior] A bluff is reinterpreted afterwards once the listener knows the pressure was staged. When: a listener learns that a deadline or message was fake. Why: knowing the staging changes how the pressure is understood.
- [behavior] A witness's certainty can shift after speaking with a third party, so a changed account should be treated as a new statement to test. When: when a witness changes account after talking to someone else.
- [behavior] A suspect may avoid a particular change if they fear the investigator has already seen it, choosing caution over a clear commitment. When: When a suspect has partial knowledge of what the investigator has observed. Why: Avoiding a detectable commitment protects them if the trap is already known.
- [behavior] Eager or careless speech often reveals information the speaker did not mean to share, such as a plan not yet announced. When: in casual conversation.
- [behavior] A person hiding their inquiries about a sensitive matter may seek advice from strangers under another name, leaving few direct traces. When: Investigating whether a suspect sought advice about a sensitive matter. Why: Using an alias avoids involving trusted advisers who might grow suspicious.
- [behavior] A witness who claims not to remember a particular topic may be concealing something, and the questioner must decide whether to press. When: A witness avoids or disclaims a specific topic. Why: Selective forgetting can be a way to withhold information.
- [behavior] A person who hides an embarrassing but true fact, such as paying a blackmailer, can look guilty even when innocent. When: When a witness denies a meeting or payment. Why: Concealing shame is read as concealing a crime.
- [behavior] Demanding one specific falsehood from a written claim shifts the burden of proof, and disputants often reject the whole document instead. When: A long written accusation is contested. Why: Locating one error is harder than rejecting everything at once.
- [behavior] A concealer keeps re-checking the hiding place for signs of disturbance, so a concealment is never fully trusted. When: A character has hidden something and remains nearby. Why: Doubt about whether the hiding will hold drives repeated checks.
- [behavior] Others read a conspicuous silence on a topic everyone else avoids as a sign that the silent person suspects something. When: a person never asks about a subject others steer around. Why: the absence of a question is noticed and interpreted as evidence.
- [behavior] Visible props, such as spare clothing packed for show, make a hasty departure look ordinary and support a cover story. When: Someone must leave quickly without drawing notice. Why: Plausible surface evidence hides the real motive.
- [behavior] Authorities may adopt a convenient public theory that excuses their failure, presenting selected evidence while leaving contrary evidence unmentioned. When: when an official explanation protects the force from blame. Why: Protecting reputation makes a convenient explanation more attractive than an accurate one.
- [behavior] A suspect asked about an odd appearance or absence often gives a plausible reason, and several such reasons may conflict with each other or with what others saw. When: when questioned about a conspicuous detail or unexplained absence. Why: People improvise explanations under questioning, and the improvised reasons often do not fit together.
- [behavior] A culprit who rehearses a deception until it becomes automatic is more convincing under questioning, and a rehearsed cover can be tested against the investigator before acting. When: a planned deception must survive an inspection. Why: Practice removes hesitation, and a test lets the culprit decide whether the investigator is a threat.
- [rule] Treat a suspect's specific excuse as a checkable statement, and test a narrow excuse offered under pressure against the wider record. When: A suspect offers a specific prior engagement or narrow excuse under pressure. Why: Excuses can be tested against other sources and the wider record. (x2)
- [rule] A cover story must match every earlier statement and everyone who might hear it, and be backed by documents establishing the claimed identity; one inconsistency exposes it. When: A character maintains a false account across several witnesses. Why: Cross-checking exposes contradictions in a scripted lie. (x2)
- [rule] Avoid vague bluffs; back a cover with a plausible, checkable backstory, since suspicious people can test its details and a single slip exposes it. When: Maintaining an alias during questioning; using a pretext to gain access. Why: Checkable details give a suspicious observer a way to expose the cover. (x2)
- [rule] Keep a cover story simple, repeatable and matching visible facts, such as a name on clothing that others can read and repeat. Why: Visible facts are checked first and must agree, and visible details reinforce the cover through repetition.
- [rule] Give a disguise an ordinary routine, such as an activity that explains repeated presence, so observation of suspects does not raise alarm. When: A disguised character must observe others over time. Why: A plausible routine supplies a reason to be present.
- [rule] Claim only beliefs you can defend. A target who tests a claim will catch any mismatch.
- [rule] Check a cover story against direct observation, and drop it once observation contradicts it. When: When a suspect offers an easy explanation for odd behaviour. Why: Direct observation is more reliable than a convenient account.
- [rule] A cover story or reveal must account for physical traces such as clothing or body positioning, since any contradicting trace exposes the lie or gets the reveal rejected. When: someone offers an explanation for an act; solving a staged crime. Why: Physical details are the evidence a staged plan must account for.
- [rule] Make each alibi checkable through a witness, receipt, logged route or environmental clue, such as a sound trigger or arrival time, that the player can reach and test. When: designing NPC alibis. Why: A checkable alibi turns testimony into a puzzle the player can solve.
- [rule] Avoid a cover story whose claims touch records, witnesses or accents that will be consulted, such as a stranger checked against records or a native speaker catching an accent.
- [rule] Script half-confessions with missing words recoverable from other clues; a gap is a clue only when the investigator notices it and asks. When: designing NPC confessions in a mystery.
- [rule] Agree a common account with a companion before being seen together, since a shared story is harder to break than a single one.
- [rule] Control people close to a secret by restricting their movements and binding them to silence.
- [rule] Use a false cover when a subject would refuse to speak to an official, and avoid it when the subject has seen the investigator before or may recognize the cover. When: Choosing between official and undercover approaches. Why: Recognition ends the cover and the access it provided.
- [rule] A cover story must explain the secrecy, the odd hours and the hidden workplace together, surviving a glance while failing a closer look. When: a world needs a reason for hidden activity.
- [rule] Correct wrong conclusions openly, since a mistaken reading can still show where the truth lies. When: when an investigator's earlier deduction proves partly wrong.
- [rule] Make rumours of supernatural events partly true but misattributed, so players must check which witness actually saw what. When: designing rumour-based clues. Why: Partial truth rewards verification of the source rather than the claim.
- [rule] Use specific details in an alibi reply, such as arrival time, meals and departures, as checkable points, and check whether a booking reported as made actually led to travel. When: When evaluating a reply from a distant source. Why: Concrete details can be verified and expose false stories.
- [rule] Use a cover only with a background that can be checked, since an employer may test the applicant with background questions and a named reference. When: Entering a household or job under a false identity. Why: Reference checks expose any claim that cannot be verified.
- [rule] Offer interview dialogue a partial truth with a stated consequence, letting the player choose between pressing for detail and offering discretion. When: Writing confrontation dialogue for a guarded character. Why: Offering a choice with a clear cost makes the interview an informed decision.
- [rule] Send a cover witness ahead of the main investigator so that arrivals look unrelated and the coordination goes unnoticed.
- [rule] Offer a cover-story dialogue option that unlocks access or new branches, with consequences for the NPC's trust. When: designing player deception options.
- [rule] Record an NPC's agreement to a cover arrangement as a game flag, so a restricted area opens only when that flag is set. When: when designing access to a restricted area.
- [rule] In a deduction puzzle, hide an item where the placing character's limits (keys, ownership, time) allow it, so players can narrow the candidate locations. When: Designing a hidden item or body for players to find. Why: Known limits reduce the search space and make the puzzle solvable by reasoning.
- [rule] Trace the source of any written argument a suspect presents, and check it against known works in the world before accepting it as the suspect's own reasoning. When: A character submits a written defence or document. Why: A borrowed argument shows dishonesty about its origin even when its content is sound.
- [rule] Build a cover story so a contradicting independent witness can expose it, and let the player compare repeated wording against another source. When: designing an antagonist's false explanation in a game. Why: exposure requires an independent check.
- [heuristic] Distrust fluent answers that fit every trap, since rehearsed replies fit any follow-up; a clever liar may overplay wit or seem too composed, so waiting often exposes the slip. When: A suspect is skilled at controlled speech, or a witness's answers are prompt and seamless. Why: Over-control and rehearsed polish are unnatural, so fluency alone does not show truth. (x2)
- [heuristic] Base a cover story on real events or profession with a few details changed; true details are harder to expose and easier to maintain under questioning. When: when building a false pretext or a character must mislead a listener. Why: True details lend credibility and survive casual questioning.
- [heuristic] Make NPC testimony partly true, such as a reported movement later confirmed by a find, so players learn selective trust and explore without the answer being given away.
- [heuristic] A cover must hold under direct testing: a thin one fails after a few questions, so learn the target's domain facts first, or the interview ends.
- [heuristic] Judge an account by consistency of voice, gesture and detail; a confident delivery can still betray a lie through changed voice or avoided eye contact, and such judgment can err.
- [heuristic] A cover story built on one true, checkable detail is hard to break, though it can still hide a lie about the purpose of contact.
- [heuristic] Build a false identity on a core of truth, so the cover can explain any slip in speech or manner. When: An investigator must pass as someone else in conversation. Why: Facts from one's real life are easier to recall consistently under questioning.
- [heuristic] Choose a cover that gives a natural reason to ask questions, such as a purchase or a trade. When: Planning an investigator's false role. Why: A plausible reason makes questions feel ordinary to the subject.
- [heuristic] Use a plausible cover story, such as a reserved seat or a stated decision, to justify presence, and ask for discretion so it stays quiet. When: when an investigator needs a reason to be somewhere. Why: A believable cover is accepted and keeps the real purpose hidden.
- [heuristic] Give each cover identity a reason to exist in the world, such as merchant, pilgrim or tax collector, so each disguise opens specific dialogue. When: Designing player or NPC disguises. Why: A grounded role gives the disguise dialogue options that fit it.
- [heuristic] Use the target's own interests as an entry point, since showing knowledge of their subject builds trust quickly. When: the target shares a belief or interest you can match.
- [heuristic] Arguments aimed at one conclusion show their weakness in what they omit.
- [heuristic] A cover story about a third party can carry a real truth, because listeners see their own situation in it and react to that recognition. When: An investigator uses a fabricated tale to prompt a confession. Why: Listeners project their own circumstances onto a parallel story.
- [heuristic] A suspect's generous offer may aim to close a matter rather than confess; ask whether it exposes the culprit, protects the victim, or buys silence. When: A suspect's cooperation seems too convenient.
- [heuristic] Conspicuous courtesy can coincide with a covert purpose, but not every courtesy is sinister; suspicion shapes how it is read. When: A suspect's courtesy overlaps with unexplained absences. Why: Observers primed by suspicion over-read ordinary behavior.
- [heuristic] Test a stranger's cover story and stated address by checking whether the place it names matches the claim.
- [heuristic] Townsfolk who repeat the same cover story can be marked as sharing one origin, so their agreement counts as one source.
- [heuristic] Give a planted item a plausible cover story that explains its presence as ordinary character detail. When: an item is introduced for a later reveal. Why: a believable reason keeps the item from looking like setup.
- [heuristic] When a contact cannot check a stranger's face or papers, a shared phrase or gesture can verify the bearer's identity. When: A contact and a stranger share a secret in advance.
- [heuristic] Give each audience a different version of the cover story or decoy, designed around what that recipient needs to believe.
- [heuristic] Use a cover story when the real purpose would alarm others; use a decoy when you want a target to focus somewhere else.
- [heuristic] Anticipate the obvious objection a listener will raise and answer it within the replay.
- [heuristic] An account that fits the schedule is not proven by fitting it; a consistent timeline only shows the claim is possible. Why: Many false accounts can also match the timeline.
- [heuristic] A minor witness's simple, checkable answer about where someone was on given days can corroborate another person's account.
- [heuristic] Confirm a half-remembered line with a document found elsewhere, so the hint is checked rather than taken at face value.
- [heuristic] Let the official reason be partly true, so a careful player can separate it from the hidden cause. When: Designing a faction-driven town where a public crime covers a private struggle. Why: A partly true reason gives players a fair route to see through the cover story.
- [heuristic] If an item needed only to be destroyed, elaborate precautions would be unnecessary, so elaborate care in handling an item usually points to concealment or retrieval. When: Judging why someone took special care with an object. Why: Destruction needs no means of recovery, while hiding does.
- [heuristic] A cover story's absurdity can make it harder to disprove, since few would invent something so ridiculous to hide a crime. When: Judging a suspiciously silly explanation. Why: People assume no one would fabricate something so unlikely.
- [heuristic] A half-truth linking an innocent person to the crime can mislead more effectively than an outright lie.
- [heuristic] Do not accept a plausible explanation merely because it is offered first or with confidence. When: Weighing competing explanations for an event. Why: Order and confidence of delivery do not establish truth.
- [heuristic] Keep an assumed identity consistent once adopted, since switching names invites contradictions in the story. When: A stranger is using a false name.
- [heuristic] Act out the cover persona's habits, speech and manners fully, not only its surface look. When: when maintaining a cover under questioning. Why: behaviour that fits the persona is harder to doubt.
- [heuristic] A suspect's behaviour can change when a new servant appears, so the player must keep the cover story consistent. When: when a disguise or cover requires NPC substitution. Why: Inconsistent cover details alert observers and break the plan.
- [heuristic] Ground a cover-up in a routine the audience already knows, such as a bath or a hospital delivery, so the cover story feels ordinary. When: designing a mechanism of concealment. Why: Familiar routines seem innocent, so the audience does not question the cover story.
- [procedure] 1) List every plausible explanation for the odd act, including one not yet named. 2) Keep the list open rather than settling on an authority's preferred one. 3) Test each separately until one survives. When: An unexplained act has several candidate causes, or early evidence fits several explanations. Why: A closed or early explanation can omit the true cause.
- [procedure] 1) Identify evidence the witness cannot account for. 2) Offer a neutral, innocent explanation that fits the facts, not an accusation. 3) Watch whether the witness adopts it, and how. When: a witness cannot account for evidence and a neutral explanation exists. Why: A calm, fitting explanation is less likely to provoke defence than an accusation.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the suspicious features of the explanation, such as false names or repeated acts. 2) Find sources the suspect does not control. 3) Check whether those sources support or contradict the explanation. When: a suspect offers an innocent explanation for suspicious acts. Why: independent records are harder to bias than the suspect's own account.
- [procedure] 1) State the coherent theory against a suspect. 2) List every objection the theory cannot answer. 3) Check each objection against evidence to keep or drop the theory. When: A convincing suspect appears early. Why: Explicit objections turn elimination into a testable task rather than an instinct.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the staff who clear the location or hold lost property whether the claimed item was found. 2) Treat a missing record as evidence against the claim. When: When a witness claims they lost an item at a location. Why: Records kept by staff provide an independent check on the claim.
- [procedure] 1) Offer a plausible cover explanation for a sensitive topic. 2) Refuse to discuss it on a stated grounds. 3) Let a later clue expose the cover as false. When: Designing dialogue where an NPC hides the truth. Why: A plausible cover misleads on first pass, and the later clue rewards careful players.
- [tradeoff] Verifiable cover details build credibility, but one easily checked claim exposes the persona; when a questioner can verify facts, stay vague on testable points. When: a follower must explain their presence and a questioner can verify facts. Why: Verifiable claims are tested by the target; a verifiable invented claim exposes the persona.
- [tradeoff] Describing a source through a cover account protects a person's relationship or position, but risks distrust if the true route to the evidence comes out. When: Evidence was obtained in a way that could embarrass a person or strain a relationship.
- [tradeoff] Cutting and burning, burying, dumping in a well, or shipping out each have physical or practical costs; the choice depends on which risk is least acceptable. When: Selecting a method to dispose of a hidden object. Why: Each method exposes the culprit to different detection risks.
- [tradeoff] Use an ordinary cover story only as far as needed; a more elaborate cover risks exposing the inquiry, so keep the purpose hidden without adding unnecessary detail. When: When a questioner needs a pretext to ask about something without revealing the inquiry. Why: A simple cover keeps the inquiry discreet, while excessive detail draws attention.
- [tradeoff] A bluff that lands can be misread as real knowledge, so the questioner may not understand why the witness reacted. When: A questioner states a guess meant to force a denial. Why: A strong reaction to a guess looks the same as a reaction to proof.
- [pitfall] Partly verified details from an informant or witness create unwarranted confidence, and blended fabrications survive; check each detail separately. When: An informant's or witness's claims are partly confirmed. Why: One verified detail does not validate the unverified rest. (x2)
- [pitfall] A simple, tidy explanation from a suspect or official can close inquiry and hide the single lead that counts. When: when a suspect offers an account of a death or an authority offers a sensible reason for a witness's account. Why: A reasonable theory satisfies listeners and ends inquiry.
- [pitfall] A cover story used to gain entry can leave an impression on those inside, and one too convenient makes a doorman or porter question the visitor. When: using a cover story for entry. Why: suspicion rises when a story seems too neat.
- [pitfall] A cover explanation for one detail can deflect attention from a more significant item it mentions, so check what the explanation draws attention away from.
- [pitfall] A cover story that is only partly true can cost trust, and the questioner may have to correct it before the witness will continue. When: An investigator explains their stake to a guarded witness. Why: Partial truths get exposed and make the witness withdraw cooperation.
- [pitfall] A partly true story can unravel from one inconsistency, especially when an ally can check its details against facts they know.
- [pitfall] A suspect who knows the consequences may give a half-truth or a false denial rather than a full confession.
- [pitfall] Speaking too freely in a bluff reveals the limits of what you know. When: Maintaining a bluff under questioning. Why: Every extra detail gives the listener something to check and test.
- [pitfall] Overplaying a bluff makes the suspect cautious rather than frightened, which defeats its purpose. When: a bluff is performed with too much force. Why: a cautious suspect hides more carefully.
- [pitfall] A plausible reason can be a cover story. An audience that accepts it unchecked lets the suspect control the narrative.
- [pitfall] Discarding a whole account because one part is false is an error, since even a fully false account still leaves gaps to examine.
- [pitfall] An account partly true in spirit but false in detail is hard to separate, and one early lie can colour later trust in every source. When: a source has mixed accuracy. Why: errors spread into judgment of the whole account.
- [pitfall] A casually stated reason can read either as a cover story or as ordinary character, so players may misjudge which it is.
- [pitfall] An alibi given by a close associate is open to challenge, especially if the associate has little contact with the person they vouch for. When: Evaluating an alibi from a companion. Why: Limited acquaintance makes the claim hard to verify and easy to dispute.
- [pitfall] Relying on an account that suits everyone who hears it, since such accounts are easily shaped to fit.
- [pitfall] An offer shows what the sender believes, not what is true; a suspect's guess about the sender's knowledge may be wrong and must be checked. When: A suspect interprets a bribe as proof of guilt or knowledge. Why: Reasoning from an offer is inference, and inference can fail.
- [pitfall] A visible alibi can be an artifice, so confirm the movement between the two points, not just the appearance.
- [pitfall] Overplaying a character's harmless cover can turn them into a joke that never recovers, weakening the later reveal. When: When a persona is played for comedy over a long stretch. Why: Audiences stop taking the character seriously.
- [pitfall] Plans stated as future events in testimony can be overtaken by later changes, so the sequence needs revising whenever new facts appear.
- [pitfall] A target who sees through a bluff can call it, so a bluff needs displayed evidence that looks convincing.
- [pitfall] Pretending to know a witness's secret can make them reveal more, but the pressure coerces rather than establishes the truth. Why: Fear produces disclosure whether or not the claim is accurate.
- [pitfall] Viewers who share a protagonist's bias may read a cover action as a personal slight and miss its covering function. When: a distraction is seen through a biased viewpoint. Why: the emotional reading takes precedence over the plot function.
- [pitfall] Signs of wealth or novelty, such as new clothing, can betray a cover and expose the investigator. When: Maintaining a disguise among people who know each other's routines. Why: Unfamiliar or new items stand out against the community's established appearance.
- [pitfall] Maintaining a deceptive persona can cause inner conflict and guilt, which may degrade the performance of the person wearing it. When: a long-running deceptive cover. Why: moral cost weighs on the player.
- [pitfall] Tidiness proves neither truth nor falsehood: a complete story can be persuasive yet wrong, and rejecting a plausible ending only for being tidy can hide the real answer. Why: Coherence is easy to build from partial evidence.
- [pitfall] A plausible excuse can conceal the real reason for an arrangement, so excuses should be weighed against what they hide.
- [pitfall] A cover story that depends on a partner who does not know their role adds risk of exposure. When: Staging a cover involving more than one person. Why: Uninformed partners can contradict the cover at the wrong moment.
- [pitfall] A decoy lure is only as good as its cover story, and a fabricated report can be traced back to its source. When: Planting a false report to draw someone out. Why: If the fabrication is traceable, the lure can backfire on its author.
- [pitfall] A person who acts to create a belief in their own death bears the consequences of that belief. When: When a presumption arises from someone's own conduct. Why: The law holds people responsible for beliefs they deliberately produce.
- [pitfall] A cover story never revisited can leave the misled person confused about what was actually done.
- [fact] Confusion during an event can shield a prominent participant from later scrutiny.
- [fact] Surviving records often cannot separate a witness's honest hallucination from deliberate fabrication.
- [fact] Hiding a body is easier to conceal when the site is unexamined, and removal is too risky when neighbors may notice. When: Choosing between disposal options. Why: Visibility and exposure shape which concealment method is viable.
- [fact] A witness opens up more when the questioner's cover story flatters her importance, so acknowledging a witness's standing can increase cooperation. When: When a witness is reluctant and the questioner uses a cover identity. Why: Feeling important lowers a witness's guard and increases willingness to share.
- [fact] A cover identity can build trust yet not fully remove suspicion, so the investigator may still be questioned about who they are. When: Relying on a persona to resolve a suspect's doubts. Why: Trust built by a persona is partial and can be re-examined.

## documents and records
- [definition] Internal evidence is information a text supplies about what its writer expected to happen, revealed by the terms it contains. When: Analysing a written document such as a will or contract. Why: The writer's assumptions show through the wording.
- [mechanism] Worn or missing words force players to infer gaps from what remains; a wrong reading can send them chasing a red herring. (x2)
- [mechanism] A copied or translated in-world record can diverge from its original, so comparing versions can expose an altered clue.
- [mechanism] An in-world quoted decree that silently drops a clause becomes a discovery when players compare it with a full copy found elsewhere in the game world. When: In-world documents exist in partial and complete versions. Why: Comparison reveals hidden omissions.
- [mechanism] Placing the explanation in an embedded document a character reads aloud delays the reveal and sets the document's origin before its contents. When: when the solution depends on events the investigator did not see. Why: The source and framing shape how the contents are received.
- [mechanism] Official doubt about an object can delay the connection between that object and the solution, acting as misdirection. When: when authority figures dismiss a clue. Why: the dismissal removes the obvious link until the player assembles the evidence.
- [mechanism] Official responses such as gathering people in a shelter or sending reinforcements make a rumor seem more serious, which raises fear further. When: a rumor prompts visible authority action. Why: official action is read as confirmation of the threat.
- [mechanism] A council convened with a majority chosen by one party can turn public opinion toward the party it targets. When: a dispute is settled by a council. Why: visible unfairness shifts sympathy.
- [mechanism] A faction that enters its own account into an official record can recast a rival's intervention as an accusation against that rival. When: two factions contest authority over the same case. Why: Official records carry legitimacy, so the account written into them gains weight with observers.
- [mechanism] An official act such as a seal or closed gate can reveal who held authority at a given hour, so players can infer control from visible acts. When: Authority changes over the course of the game world. Why: Official acts are observable evidence of who is in charge.
- [mechanism] An NPC's official status can differ from the player's knowledge, such as a wanted figure marked presumed dead, so the game world tracks a record that the player may see differently. When: A character's status is uncertain and the official record is updated separately from the truth. Why: Records are changed by procedures and authorities, which may lag behind or contradict what actually happened.
- [mechanism] A player can take a suspect's physical records, such as prints, and compare them with scene clues, so the match or mismatch changes which suspects remain in play. When: When a game offers forensic comparison as a mechanic. Why: Comparison turns physical evidence into a decision that narrows the suspect pool.
- [mechanism] A puzzle can hide a deliberate discrepancy that the player detects by comparing a record, such as a receipt, with the current state. When: Designing an inventory or evidence puzzle.
- [mechanism] When the audience knows a hidden relation the characters do not, ordinary acts such as punishment or appeals for help acquire tension, since the characters misread them. When: The story depends on what characters will misjudge. Why: Audience knowledge turns the characters' misreadings into visible stakes.
- [behavior] A recognition by a former authority figure carries more weight than local rumour, and changes how others treat the person once confirmed. When: An official with past experience identifies a person from a record. Why: Specific, documented confirmation is more credible and status-changing than general talk.
- [behavior] An official statement made right after a harsh act often aims to stop public sympathy from forming.
- [behavior] Judges and jurors bound by statutes in force apply them even when doing so risks serious personal consequences. When: when the law in force is harsh. Why: They are expected to apply the law as written, and refusal is not reasonably expected.
- [rule] Log every money transfer and place receipts, inventories and payment logs in-world so players reconstruct who paid for what and why; unrecorded deals become clues. When: when designing NPC transactions. (x2)
- [rule] Do not treat a record as independent when its controller is the person being checked; a single party-held record can be incomplete or altered and needs verification. When: choosing records for corroboration, or when the only record of a visit or event is controlled by one person. Why: Controlled records can be arranged to match the claim, and gaps or changes can hide a contradiction or make a false claim look true. (x2)
- [rule] Present in-world archive documents, such as letters, earlier verdicts and jury notes, in full with their provenance so players can cross-check them against present testimony. When: designing an in-game archive.
- [rule] Give in-game documents distinct authors, handwriting and attestation details so players can judge each source's reliability and compare them. When: when designing in-game documents. Why: Players weigh sources by their provenance.
- [rule] Treat an official's confident conclusion or closed verdict as a claim to test, separating forecasts drawn from reputation from demonstrated proof. When: when an authority figure declares a suspect guilty or a case is closed. Why: Confidence and proof are different things; official verdicts can be confident and still wrong.
- [rule] Locate and record where a document is hidden, such as a locked or secret drawer, before relying on its contents.
- [rule] Write in-world journals, letters and diaries as partial testimony with deliberate omissions that players can notice. When: when designing documents for players to find in the world.
- [rule] Provide an in-world ledger of entries and appointments that players can consult on demand as a reference record.
- [rule] Place a removed page in a ledger or shop book so the player can find a hidden payment by reading its last entries first. When: designing a record-based clue.
- [rule] Give in-world documents period-appropriate spelling, paper and script, and plant a near-correct forgery so an observant player can catch it. When: Authoring letters, maps or ledgers for a game world. Why: Players who know period conventions can judge authenticity and gain clues about the forger.
- [rule] Give in-world letters and notices regional wording or spelling that signals their true author, and let players compare terms against an NPC's stated background. When: Designing in-world documents that serve as clues. Why: Players can detect a false origin by comparing the language with what they know.
- [rule] Use a suspect's past offences to narrow the search only when the method of the past crime closely matches the new one. When: deciding whether a criminal record is relevant. Why: matching method gives real evidence.
- [rule] Send a sensitive written message by a courier instructed to hand it to the addressee personally, so it cannot be lost or opened by others. When: when the message must reach one specific person intact. Why: Personal delivery prevents interception and keeps control of the document's contents.
- [rule] Design in-world newspapers or bulletins with errors the player can correct using other evidence, so the document is a source to test rather than a fact. When: When an in-world document conveys story information. Why: Players then learn to cross-check sources instead of accepting printed claims.
- [rule] Give an in-game letter or journal a later-added line in a different ink tone or smudge, so a careful player can infer an edit. When: designing document clues. Why: physical cues reward close inspection without hiding any text.
- [rule] In-game newspapers and letters can serve as dated lore, and a collection can hide one entry the player must find.
- [rule] In a forensic game, withhold the method behind an expert's report and let the player reconstruct it from other clues, or leave gaps they can infer.
- [rule] Place wills and inventories in the world as documents that reveal ownership and which rooms were restricted.
- [rule] Record the scene at discovery with a photograph or snapshot before others arrive, fixing evidence that later clues can be checked against.
- [rule] Write journal entries that players can re-read after a reveal, so earlier notes take on the new meaning.
- [rule] Build a missing-person quest as a chain of records, such as a receipt, ledger entry or station register, each naming the next location. Why: Chained records give players a traceable path.
- [rule] Design broken floors or scorch marks with readable edges that reveal whether a collapse was forced or staged. When: generating environmental damage as evidence. Why: damage should carry checkable information.
- [rule] Link a physical clue to a document clue, such as a receipt or delivery log, so finding an object leads the player to a record. When: when designing clue chains.
- [rule] Make destroyed documents recoverable, by keeping a copy elsewhere or scattering pieces to reassemble, so players can compare a witnessed account with the record or race to rebuild it. When: a plot document is destroyed, torn up or lost. Why: Copies let players check testimony against the record, and recovery turns destruction into a playable challenge.
- [rule] Give in-world documents a provenance tag, date and drafting history; mark undated or omitted material, and let later editions correct earlier ones with their own timestamp. When: presenting letters, depositions, reports or case files as evidence; designing contracts, wills or maps as clues. Why: Readers need to judge a source's reliability and completeness, and provenance, dating and metadata let players weigh sources and test whether later events fit by design.
- [rule] Give in-world letters a readable aim, such as a threat or a demand, so the player learns to read the sender's motive.
- [rule] Give shops ledgers of pledged items, so player-owned objects become traces that an investigator can check.
- [rule] Model legal documents as game state: a filed document with the right authority changes inheritance, so players must learn that rule before using it. When: a game includes deeds, wills or similar papers.
- [rule] Tie each document to its finding location, since where a document was found changes what it means.
- [rule] Have an examine action log counted, verifiable details, such as the number of steps or the marks on an object, so the player can reach the same inference. When: Clues are physical objects in the game. Why: Verifiable details let the player reason rather than guess.
- [rule] Build document checks into the inventory, such as a ledger or receipt that confirms or refutes a claim, so players can test NPC statements. When: when designing verifiable clues. Why: Physical documents give players a way to check claims.
- [rule] Design multi-step delivery puzzles so each handoff is recorded, letting the player see where the item went.
- [rule] Include every person who matters to the solution in the roster; any omitted person forces the player to guess. Why: An omitted person breaks the fair-play contract.
- [rule] Give each rare item to only a few characters so that matching an item to its carrier is meaningful. When: designing item ownership for dungeon or level content. Why: Widely held items cannot identify a single owner.
- [rule] Record cryptic NPC lines in the player's journal so they can be recalled and linked when the related event occurs. When: Designing hints that pay off later in a game. Why: Players forget ambiguous lines unless a record preserves them.
- [rule] Keep alternative motives open when interpreting a clue, and do not treat a hint as proof. When: Reasoning about a clue that suggests one suspect. Why: Overreading a hint can mislead investigators toward a wrong conclusion.
- [heuristic] Use a searchable in-world case file accepted as precedent as a source of false belief whose cover story contradicts later facts; let the player correct it with new evidence.
