When: when designing world history that shapes current beliefs. Why: Precedent carries errors forward until someone tests them. (x2)
- [heuristic] A shop, tailor or economy that logs every sale, pickup and transfer of a unique item lets the player trace its path and learn who bought it. When: Designing a trace that leads from an item to a buyer, or unique items the player can track. Why: Complete transaction logs make item provenance recoverable; records connect objects to people through a verifiable source.
- [heuristic] Hide a key item or document in an unexpected location or among routine papers, so thorough search or patient reading reveals the motive. When: Designing motive discovery in a level or a social-stealth puzzle. Why: Unexpected placement rewards thorough search without being unfair; patient readers find what quick ones miss.
- [heuristic] Read a strange message as possibly hiding a second text, such as one readable by every third word or every second letter. When: When a document seems innocent but its context suggests a hidden meaning.
- [heuristic] Test official or first-responder reports against physical facts before acting; a hasty first reading or standard-phrased announcement can hide a false lead others will act on. When: reports from officials or first responders; reading police or authority reports. Why: Others may act on the early reading and delay the correct response; public statements may conceal a false lead.
- [heuristic] Compare units produced with units recovered; a gap signals a hidden possession, but only when the owner can state how many units should be present. Why: Every produced copy must be somewhere; without an expected number there is no baseline to compare against.
- [heuristic] A case that looks insoluble to officials may be solvable, since their confusion often reflects their method rather than the case itself.
- [heuristic] When case files lack a motive, published records such as biographical dictionaries and family histories can supply one. When: A conflict between people with unknown histories, or behavior that suggests a private grudge.
- [heuristic] Rank an official record above an informal statement, since a spoken proof can be fabricated or improvised. When: Sources disagree on a checkable fact. Why: Records are harder to improvise than a witness's word.
- [heuristic] A detective game can gate a clue behind archive work, such as photographs, passenger lists and a timeline the player assembles.
- [heuristic] A partly recovered message can still steer the next objective if the surviving words name a danger or an ally. When: only fragments of text survive. Why: fragments carry enough meaning to direct action.
- [heuristic] Officials usually refuse direct requests for another person's records, so access often needs a formal authority or a plausible pretext. When: When a record is held by an official who has no reason to share it. Why: Officials protect records from unauthorised disclosure.
- [heuristic] A retailer's pay records give the last date a person was paid, which can be compared with a sale date to place that person in time. When: when dated payment or sales records are available for a suspect's workplace. Why: Dated payments link a person to a place and period.
- [heuristic] In-world bulletins or news tickers can carry a faked status, adding suspense about what the rival believes.
- [heuristic] A dispute resting on an old or unusual record is worth investigating, since its outcome is uncertain.
- [heuristic] Keep the most personal record on your person, where it never leaves you. When: when a search may take items. Why: it cannot be seized from a hiding place.
- [heuristic] Record loyalty, resentment, fear and past history early, since they shape what each witness will admit.
- [heuristic] Notes, journals and letters can carry clues through style, smudges and crossings-out that hint at the writer's condition; keep inferences open so players must confirm them elsewhere. When: when designing readable documents as clues. Why: Open-ended inference makes players verify rather than accept the clue.
- [heuristic] A document lacking a clerk's signature or proper legal notice carries less authority, so lower its weight in case reasoning. When: Judging the reliability of a recorded decision. Why: Missing formalities weaken the record's legal standing.
- [heuristic] When testimony claims knowledge no one can verify, check whether the procedure can separate truth from delusion before accepting it. When: when a claim rests on supernatural or unobservable sources. Why: a test that cannot tell truth from delusion gives no support.
- [heuristic] An in-world note can sound protective while its instructions still grant access. Build such notes so attentive players who read the full text catch the mismatch. When: Designing written in-world notes, such as a warden's memo with conditional warnings. Why: Players who read past the opening reassurance can detect the contradiction.
- [heuristic] A forged note misleads a player only if its details are plausible given what the player already knows.
- [heuristic] Give each suspect a timeline of signed records such as ticket stubs or guard logs, and let the player find the entry that breaks the chain. When: when designing an alibi-breaking puzzle. Why: Locating the one inconsistent record rewards careful reading of timelines.
- [heuristic] Tickets, badges and tags generated with serial numbers or torn-stub patterns let the player cross-match them to expose a timeline problem. When: Designing collectible items that players cross-check. Why: Matching serials or tear patterns give players a verifiable clue.
- [heuristic] Show the player only discovered incidents and keep some unnoticed ones hidden, so the player's model of the world stays biased toward what was noticed. When: designing a detective or crime-tracking system. Why: Players reason from what the system reveals.
- [heuristic] Document each entry into a controlled stock with its source and authorization, so that unauthorized entries stand out. When: items arrive through a controlled supply. Why: Known sources make anything outside them conspicuous.
- [heuristic] Keep a partial observation open by listing who belongs in the scene and who the observed figure could not be, instead of filling in the missing identity. When: An investigator has one incomplete sighting. Why: A guessed identity from partial evidence is often wrong and closes off other explanations.
- [heuristic] Use historical records to fix time, place and fate of a figure, such as crimes, dates and former locations. When: Building a backstory for an identified figure. Why: Dated, located records make a reveal concrete and checkable.
- [heuristic] An accusation system can show a suspect with motive and no alibi, while a planted document later invalidates the motive. When: when designing a suspect that the player may wrongly accuse. Why: A later document lets the player correct an early error.
- [heuristic] An ironic final image that echoes an earlier clue ties the ending back to the mystery.
- [heuristic] Hand over the solution through an in-world document instead of an investigation scene, so the explanation comes in the character's own voice.
- [procedure] 1) Look up each principal's name in reference works. 2) Read the family's record, not only the individual's. 3) Follow each record to its consequences. 4) Read later generations' entries for inherited grudges. When: A case has an unexplained conflict between people with unknown histories.
- [procedure] 1) Search old records for events similar to the current case. 2) Check whether an earlier unresolved case shares motive and method. 3) Verify the pattern against the present details before applying it. When: A current case may echo an earlier one. Why: Past patterns can explain present events but may be misapplied.
- [procedure] 1) Collect every notice from the open channel. 2) Order the messages by content, since dates may be missing. 3) Record the medium's details, such as column and position. 4) Match the channel to other evidence to identify the sender. When: Secret messages are passed through a public medium. Why: A rebuilt sequence and a traced channel can reveal who is communicating.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the disputed sheet's watermark with known stationery to find its source. 2) Compare the handwriting with a sample the suspect is known to have written. 3) Re-examine the first impression closely. 4) Send both documents for specialist comparison and record remaining uncertainty. When: Authorship of a letter or order is in question and a reliable known sample exists. Why: Watermarks and first impressions can each mislead, so a layered check is needed.
- [procedure] 1) Note the document's date and production time to set its earliest appearance. 2) Count copies and assign each to a recipient or file. 3) Record the last time the document was seen on its usual surface. 4) Treat a copy found somewhere illogical as evidence of someone else's handling. When: A written record serves as a link in a timeline. Why: Accounting for every copy shows whether a document was moved and when.
- [procedure] 1) Extend the sequence beyond its last known item using the same interval and rule. 2) State the predicted position as a testable hypothesis. 3) Link the predicted position to a known event. 4) Treat the prediction as a lead, not as proof. When: A strong pattern across several records suggests a missing member. Why: A prediction gives a date and a reason to search, without assuming the item exists.
- [procedure] 1) Write the letter to name specific checkable leads, such as witnesses and locations. 2) Ensure those leads can be reached from other sources. 3) Let a suspect destroy the letter while the leads stay available to the player. When: Designing a document that points toward the truth but can be destroyed. Why: Destruction removes one copy, and leads elsewhere keep the mystery solvable.
- [tradeoff] An in-game archive with missing records or incidental receipts forces the player to combine documents to reconstruct events, and a historian NPC can offer partial records the player must judge. When: When designing an in-game archive or case file. Why: Incomplete evidence makes the player reason across sources rather than read a single answer.
- [tradeoff] A letter is testimony that cannot answer questions, so its claims should be checked against observed facts and cannot replace questioning. When: Documents or letters are used as evidence. Why: A document cannot be cross-examined, and its author may have written it with an agenda.
- [pitfall] Old records may be incomplete, memory fades and accounts reflect writers' purposes, so check each source's reliability; narrators should acknowledge gaps. When: Using a recording narrator to report investigative detail. Why: Admitted gaps mark where the record is firm and where it may drift. (x2)
- [pitfall] Official reports and verdicts can skip the small detail that matters or miss a trace only a close observer saw; check the raw evidence yourself. When: when relying on an official finding.
- [pitfall] Officials trust what they saw directly and may accept a plausible cover story, while flaws stay visible to a closer observer; subtler inferences lose out. When: When authorities investigate a staged disappearance. Why: Official investigators may not test the internal consistency of a plausible account.
- [pitfall] Plausible but unverified figures can grow into strong suspicion; verify them before acting on them. When: financial or gossip information seems to fit a theory. Why: plausibility feels like confirmation.
- [pitfall] Partial reports from witnesses can mislead an arriving character, so the audience should be told how little that character knows. When: A character arrives after events and relies on fragments.
- [pitfall] A partial reproduction gives a weaker conclusion, since missing conditions such as mood or state of mind can change the result. When: Recreating an original act with some conditions unmatched. Why: Unreproduced factors can alter the outcome, so a match is less conclusive.
- [pitfall] Omitted passages can hide information needed to check a timeline, and a narrator's stated limit does not guarantee completeness. When: Verifying a sequence of events from an edited account. Why: Edits can remove facts needed for verification.
- [pitfall] A large archive of familiar cases can make ordinary incidents feel dull to the investigator.
- [pitfall] Partial overheard words invite confirmation bias, so a name heard in fragments may point to the wrong person. When: When a single name or word is the only clue from overheard speech. Why: Incomplete information is easily fitted to a preferred suspect.
- [pitfall] A hurried reading can invert a note's instruction, so reread a message before acting on it. When: Acting on a short or urgent note. Why: Brief wording is easy to misread, especially under pressure.
- [pitfall] Official-looking paperwork is not proof, since a neat, authoritative document can be forged.
- [pitfall] Assuming a single shipment when paperwork may hide a second, similar one can mislead the reconstruction.
- [pitfall] Following a recorded address without checking it wastes effort, and the trail goes cold when the address was invented.
- [pitfall] Visitors with official standing may go unlogged and unquestioned, letting unrecorded access pass as legitimate.
- [pitfall] Named sources and titles alone do not establish a claim's truth; citations without checking give false confidence. When: Evaluating a story that relies on references. Why: Listeners may act on the appearance of documentation rather than its substance.
- [pitfall] Early surveys made by walking or rough measurement were often poor, so grants overlapped and maps seem more precise than the original surveys justify. Why: Rough measurement cannot support the precision a drawn map suggests.
- [pitfall] Paper records are partial, and a lost or missing deed can start a real dispute, so a gap in the record can itself matter.
- [pitfall] A reversal or remedy limited to those who petitioned leaves unnamed victims unrestored.
- [pitfall] An editor's correction can itself be an error, so corrections should be checked against the source where possible. When: when relying on an edited or annotated transcription. Why: Editors work from the same imperfect records and can introduce mistakes.
- [pitfall] Totals counted from a partial list can mislead, because the final count depends on which cases are included.
- [pitfall] Dramatic irony is flat if the audience has no reason to care about the hidden truth. When: Creating a secret the audience knows. Why: Irony needs stakes to produce tension.
- [pitfall] Approximate or inconsistent dates produce illusory patterns, so a timeline must be reliable before matches are trusted. When: When event dates come from sources of uneven accuracy. Why: Noise in dates gives the appearance of correlation where none exists.
- [fact] An inquest gathers witness accounts early, before police work is advanced, and can surface facts that no one has yet connected. Why: Memories are fresh and the facts have not been linked yet.
- [fact] A claim that a document was destroyed cannot be verified directly and can only be reconstructed indirectly from surrounding evidence. Why: The destruction itself leaves no content to examine.
- [fact] Phone calls record who spoke to whom and when, so the phone itself becomes a timeline record.
- [fact] Phone calls can establish a person's whereabouts and state of mind, but the listener's account of a call is often partial.
- [fact] Hotel registration records typically show arrival date, city of origin, baggage and calls charged to the room.
- [fact] In many past periods a stepparent was commonly called by a parent's title, so an odd family label may reflect custom rather than error. When: interpreting old records that name family relations. Why: Customs of the period shape how relationships are worded.
- [fact] A deed takes effect during the giver's lifetime, whereas a will takes effect only at death. When: choosing how to transfer property or honour a promise. Why: The timing of effect differs between the two instruments.
- [fact] What looks like ignorance may have been the accepted learned philosophy of the period, taught in universities and applied in law and medicine.
- [fact] Official parish records typically list votes and proceedings of legally called meetings and omit outside events.
- [fact] Grammar norms of earlier periods differed from modern rules, for example singular verbs often followed plural subjects, so modern grammar is a poor test of a writer.
- [fact] One official's hand recurring across many records reveals who drove the procedure and who wrote most of its examinations.
- [fact] When oral tradition is thin, deed and will registers are often the main source for locating past events and people.
- [fact] Petitions record who survived and who pressed a claim, so they show who could seek relief.
- [fact] Spelling in original records is often inconsistent, even within a single document.
- [fact] An official arriving later may inherit many reported victims and prior arrests, so early reports can set the agenda before facts are examined. When: When a new authority takes over an ongoing accusation case. Why: Inherited records frame the official's first decisions.
- [fact] Official records can be lost or withheld for decades, so early accounts built on incomplete material may later need revision. Why: Access to primary records can arrive long after events.
- [fact] Periodical collections can mix original papers, letters, diaries, biographical notices, proceedings, notes and queries, reprints of rare tracts and miscellany, each attributed to named contributors.
- [fact] Early legal codes protected testimony and courts through harsh penalties for witness intimidation, false testimony and judicial tampering, and they relied on written records.

## staged reveal sequencing
- [definition] A reveal assembles suspects and witnesses, lays out the reasoning step by step, and ends in a confrontation where the guilty party is compelled to reveal themselves.
- [definition] A staged reveal holds a crucial fact back and releases it in parts, so the audience reaches the answer through a sequence of clues.
- [mechanism] Disclosing a secret or motive, even a sympathetic one, gives the listener knowledge they can act on, and can make them reassess your intentions or turn it against you. When: a character reveals a secret to someone with a stake in it, or while negotiating with a party who controls the setting. Why: The listener gains information they can act on; a revealed motive lets the other side reassess your intentions.
- [mechanism] Creaking furniture, cracking railings, passing shadows and lamps carried near a hidden listener raise the risk of discovery and build tension.
- [mechanism] A staged news event in dialogue can change what an NPC is willing to reveal afterward.
- [mechanism] Confronting a disguised person in front of others removes their ability to keep up the pretence.
- [mechanism] Information delivered in parts and from several sources keeps suspense alive, since each report adds to the picture while leaving gaps. When: The protagonist is away from the scene. Why: Partial reports sustain curiosity.
- [mechanism] Adding a missing fact can make a pattern look clearer before it explains anything. Players may feel progress while the explanation is still missing. When: when a key fact arrives without a clear connection. Why: Completing a table of facts gives a sense of resolution that outruns understanding.
- [mechanism] A fair-play reveal narrows suspects in layers, each stage removing a group, and ends with one trait only one suspect has, after every clue has already been shown to the reader. Why: Readers can track survivors and judge the solution themselves, which makes the ending feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [mechanism] When facts are released in stages, each new fact reframes the earlier ones, so a late fact can change how the whole earlier sequence is read. When: Structuring a mystery or quest with a central revelation. Why: The audience reinterprets prior facts once the final link is known.
- [mechanism] Delivering a key fact over several steps, such as a rumor, then a headline, then a full report, lets each piece register instead of being absorbed at once. When: when the information is important and would be missed if given in one block. Why: information delivered all at once is absorbed too quickly to register.
- [behavior] Surprise has several causes: at an unexpected figure it can signal missing information and a lead; at a stated deduction, being found out or embarrassment. When: observing a character's reaction to a figure or to a deduction put to them. Why: The same visible reaction can have different causes, so an observer must not read it in isolation.
- [behavior] Learning who now benefits from a discovery can lead an investigator to keep it secret when speaking would help no one. When: deciding whether to disclose a discovery. Why: The value of disclosure depends on who would gain from it.
- [behavior] Revealing a danger after it has passed, such as a projectile found later, makes the audience realize how close it came. When: when a threat missed the characters during action. Why: Hindsight shows the danger the characters never registered at the time.
- [behavior] A witness with reasons to limit their account may release information in stages, often framing a disclosure as protecting someone's feelings or reputation. When: When a witness fears embarrassment, professional exposure, or public questioning. Why: Controlling the timing and framing of information lets the witness manage the consequences.
- [behavior] A speaker who stresses one word so it reaches a listener while blurring the rest makes the fragment look staged, which signals intent.
- [rule] Release an NPC's information in stages: each follow-up question unlocks the next line, and only the final stage names the key fact, so answers cannot be tailored. When: designing dialogue for an NPC or informant who holds information the player must earn; NPC is weak, fading or guarded. Why: Staged release controls pacing and access, and stops the source tailoring answers to facts already disclosed.
- [rule] Introduce no new facts or evidence at the reveal; every clue the solution uses must already have been shown to the audience, or it reads as a cheat. When: writing the final explanation or solution of a mystery or puzzle. Why: Players cannot reason toward an answer built on facts they never saw; late evidence undermines trust in the investigator.
- [rule] In a staged performance between accomplices, include a small slip, such as a shared glance, so an attentive observer has a fair chance to catch it. When: designing a fake quarrel or misdirection. Why: without a visible seam the player cannot catch the fake.
- [rule] Reveal a staged scene's arrangement afterward with its discovery order and timings, so the audience can verify the logic.
- [rule] Do not withhold knowledge when doing so would endanger others or breach a duty of disclosure.
- [rule] Introduce a relevant habit or fact casually early, then make it the basis of a later plan or trap. When: Designing scripted events that depend on earlier information. Why: A casual mention reads as background, so the later use feels fair and surprising.
- [rule] Deliver the solution in a formal setting, such as a trial or accusation, that forces it to be heard. When: The answer must be heard by everyone involved.
- [rule] Gate a reveal behind a delivery mechanic such as a messenger, a witness present, or a timed arrival, so the response is staged rather than instant. When: when designing an in-game interrogation or message exchange. Why: A delivery condition lets the sender release partial information on a controlled schedule.
- [rule] Hold the culprit's identity back, revealing parts of their past first, then unmask them late before a witness whose viewpoint the audience shared. When: culprit or masked leader whose identity has a past that must be disclosed.
- [rule] Stage a scene detail so it supports one story until a second detail reveals a different cause, shifting the player's reading.
- [rule] Control the order of revelation by asking for the facts before the full account, so a speaker cannot jump ahead to the conclusion. When: interrogation or testimony scenes. Why: the sequence determines what the listener learns first.
- [rule] Hold back a motive for a late reveal while showing the means early, so suspicion grows in step with the evidence.
- [rule] Structure a reveal by planting small details early and letting them gain meaning once the key fact is given.
- [rule] Every planted instruction, such as a recipient, signal or deadline, must pay off later; an unresolved setup reads as noise.
- [rule] Structure NPC dialogue with a neutral opener, then sharper branches that unlock only after evasive answers.
- [rule] Do not dismiss every mysterious event as staged; keep open the possibility that a real unexplained cause exists.
- [rule] Design reveals where the player re-examines a known object after new information arrives, rather than finding a new item.
- [rule] Record whether each clue was disclosed early or late, so other characters react to the player's timing. When: designing clue-tracking state in a game. Why: Disclosure timing is a meaningful signal for other characters.
- [rule] Reveal evidence in order, record each denial, and unlock new names only after earlier answers are logged. When: when designing an interrogation sequence.
- [rule] Disclose information to others in steps, according to their trust, and keep back a client's identity until the investigator has spoken to the client. When: Managing who learns what and when. Why: Controlled disclosure protects the client and keeps leverage over what others know.
- [rule] Place a disclaimer about a witness's reliability before the event it qualifies, not after. When: A witness's observations are compromised by a known condition. Why: Readers should know the reliability limits before they encounter the observations.
- [rule] Reveal a forged item and then the genuine item in separate steps so that each reveal changes the player's belief. Why: A combined reveal shifts the player's belief only once.
- [heuristic] Release key information in stages, each adding a new sight or sound, so the audience stays uncertain and gathers pieces before the full explanation arrives.
- [heuristic] Reveal hidden evidence by pointing investigators to a specific container, or breaking it open, in front of witnesses; a visible payoff is more convincing than a general search. When: ending an investigation whose answer is hidden inside an object. Why: A tangible reveal makes the earlier effort feel rewarded.
- [heuristic] Introduce a companion or object early so the audience cares about it, then let its later loss or threat carry emotional weight.
- [heuristic] Show near-misses instead of announcing each intent to confess, since tension comes from the narrow escape.
- [heuristic] Identity based on appearance can be tested by removing a disguise in stages, outermost layer first, rather than all at once. When: Identity depends on appearance and the disguise has several layers. Why: Each stage can show a different reaction or trace that confirms or contradicts the suspicion.
- [heuristic] Hold back information from fragile or anxious witnesses when early disclosure could alarm them or let them change their account. When: Deciding when to tell a witness what you know. Why: Premature disclosure can distort later testimony.
- [heuristic] Present major revelations first and hold smaller details for later reference, so they can pay off once context arrives.
- [heuristic] Reveal a motive only as far as the case needs it, so an irrelevant secret does not complicate the presentation.
- [heuristic] Reveal a villain's motive in stages through letters, ledgers or diaries, so each document adds one more piece. When: Designing how a hidden motive is discovered.
- [heuristic] Reveal a solution in stages, first the decision, then the reconstruction, then the written record, with breaks between stages to build suspense.
- [heuristic] Store the full cause-and-effect chain of events, so a late explanation can reconstruct every earlier hint.
- [heuristic] A reveal can end with a staged escape, giving a cinematic close without making the player re-learn the solution.
- [heuristic] A room transition can end on a character's reaction to an unseen area, holding the reveal for the next room. When: pacing an area change that hides what lies beyond. Why: withholding the view builds anticipation.
- [heuristic] Release a central secret in stages, with early hints the protagonist cannot yet use, so suspense builds until the teller speaks. When: the audience needs a reason to keep going.
- [heuristic] Follow a success with a discovery that undoes it, undercutting confidence and raising pressure.
- [heuristic] When a trail ends at an unexpected name, that surprise should redirect the inquiry. When: A trail resolves to someone not suspected. Why: The unexpected name may reveal a different line of action.
- [heuristic] Use a pause or interruption before the accusation so the accused can react, and use visible audience reactions to signal how strongly the reveal lands. When: Scripting a confrontation or accusation scene. Why: Reactions from characters and observers make the emotional weight of the reveal legible.
- [heuristic] Release information about a death in stages, holding back explanation so that questions drive the reader forward. When: the opening must raise questions before answers arrive. Why: Withheld detail sustains suspense.
- [heuristic] Place the reveal of a major loss in a crowded, festive setting, so the news lands amid noise and distraction.
- [heuristic] Choose a structure that suits the material: keep threads that happen together in one timeline, and split only content that stands alone without losing its effect. When: Deciding how to divide a narrative. Why: Forced division damages material that depends on continuity.
- [heuristic] Release a major reveal in stages of questions and answers or extended description, each raising stakes and lengthening anticipation before the key fact. When: Delivering a major revelation across a scene; when the answer is close and should be held back. Why: Incremental pressure builds anticipation before the key fact.
- [heuristic] A set-piece confrontation can reveal evidence in a fixed order, escalating pressure toward a confession. When: Designing a scripted confrontation scene. Why: Fixed escalation gives players a clear structure to follow.
- [procedure] 1) Play a sound cue or let touch establish the scene before anything is seen. 2) Add a short pause or a closed door. 3) Show a partial image first. 4) Reveal the full scene. When: dark or low-visibility scenes, or when a discovery should land with force. Why: Staged information keeps the audience engaged; each stage prepares the next so the full reveal hits harder.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the culprit's plan and motive, in order, from their accumulated pressures or emotional state. 2) Tie each planted clue to one step. 3) Explain the staging. 4) Answer each loose end, or state the outcome for surviving characters. When: ending a mystery where all clues should point to one explanation. Why: An ordered reveal makes every clue's role clear and the solution feel earned.
- [procedure] 1) Split unwelcome or checkable facts into separate claims. 2) Pause after each claim. 3) Record the listener's physical and vocal reactions. 4) Deliver the next claim only after reading the reaction. When: the listener has a stake in the news, or the interrogator holds specific evidence the suspect cannot easily check. Why: Each reaction shows what the listener feels before more is revealed; each verifiable fact removes a denial, so defensive options shrink as the list grows.
- [procedure] 1) Present the solution in chronological order covering movements, confrontation, concealment and flight. 2) Explain each misleading clue and its ordinary cause. 3) Leave one thread open about another person's involvement. When: the final explanation must account for many earlier clues.
- [procedure] 1) Apply initial heat to strengthen the main outline. 2) Apply further exposure to bring out finer figures and text. 3) Repeat as needed until the full message appears. When: a clue must be physically hidden in a surface and revealed through a specific act of investigation.
- [procedure] 1) Decide who may hear the findings. 2) Hold private conversations with key witnesses before the formal report. 3) Report first to the authority who commissioned the work. 4) Let that authority decide whether the inquiry continues.
- [procedure] 1) Show a presence before showing its source, such as sounds of approach. 2) Show a figure at a distance with its identity hidden. 3) Reveal identities one at a time. 4) End the scene on the moment of recognition. When: a structural turning point where expectation can be overturned.
- [procedure] 1) State the aims plainly. 2) Give the account. 3) Show the documents. 4) Bring in other people's testimony. When: the audience must be persuaded and the evidence is complex. Why: a clear order lets the audience check each claim in turn.
- [procedure] 1) Assemble a case from real and invented details. 2) State it aloud as a finished conclusion. 3) Watch each listener's reaction, noting who answers, hesitates or gives themselves away. When: evidence is circumstantial and a guilty party is likely to react to a direct accusation. Why: a guilty person under a direct claim is pushed to respond and may reveal knowledge.
- [procedure] 1) Arrange a meeting the target expects to be safe. 2) Prepare evidence and authorisation in advance. 3) Keep the pursuer hidden until needed. 4) Close the exit quietly while the target is engaged. 5) Reveal physical evidence at the moment of confrontation. When: The target is overconfident and will come to the meeting voluntarily. Why: A controlled room with the target already inside removes escape options before the confrontation begins.
- [procedure] 1) Deliver the culprit's motive account first. 2) Lay out the chain of clues in order, linking each to the conclusion. 3) Show public reaction, which may distort the truth. When: The solution depends on a chain of observations. Why: Staged delivery builds suspense and lets the reader check reasoning.
- [procedure] 1) Withhold the solution until the trap is ready. 2) Keep the suspect occupied with a harmless task. 3) Close the trap. 4) Name the culprit before witnesses. When: when a suspect would flee if warned early. Why: A prepared trap prevents escape and makes the reveal public.
- [procedure] 1) Hold back a stated conclusion. 2) Wait for a physical result that can confirm it. 3) Reveal the conclusion when the evidence arrives. When: The conclusion can be verified by a later discovery. Why: A confirmed deduction is more satisfying than one stated without support.
- [procedure] 1) Arrange the meeting in a controlled place. 2) Have a witness present. 3) Ask the witness to stay as a check on the record. 4) After the reveal, walk through each stage so each clue's link is clear. When: a reveal must be credible to all parties. Why: a witness and a recap make the record reliable and the logic followable.
- [procedure] 1) State the event the hypothesis predicts. 2) Create conditions that provoke it. 3) Place observers where the event is visible. 4) Keep observers hidden and still until the event occurs. When: A hypothesis predicts an event that can be provoked and watched. Why: Provoking the predicted event turns a suspicion into an observable test.
- [procedure] 1) Hold back the conclusion while the audience collects clues. 2) Fill the interval with travel, waiting and errands. 3) Deliver the answer at a dramatic moment, such as a sudden entrance. When: the solution depends on information the audience has not yet seen. Why: A delayed, staged answer makes the reveal land with more impact.
- [procedure] 1) Let the first sign be a sound. 2) Follow with a forced door. 3) Then show a scene the audience did not expect. When: when revealing a concealed person.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the event in order: entry, actions and escape. 2) State openly what piece is still missing. 3) Reveal the hidden fact physically, such as pointing to a concealed space or having the hidden person step out. When: At the end of an investigation, once the reconstruction is complete and every link is checked. Why: Physical staging turns a theory into a visible fact the audience can accept.
- [procedure] 1) Present the investigator's reasoning first 2) Stage a confrontation where the suspect's own account completes the picture. When: the audience must feel the stakes before the answer arrives. Why: Reasoning followed by a confession keeps the answer earned and tense.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who gains from the discovery. 2) Check whether its timing fits a plausible culprit plan. 3) Check where the find came from and who could have placed it. When: a single discovery conveniently fits one suspect. Why: staged finds are placed to point at someone.
- [procedure] 1) Put the same matter to two connected people in different terms. 2) Attribute an unverified statement to one while questioning the other. 3) Compare answers for conflict or confirmation. When: Two suspects share knowledge and one answer can be checked against the other. Why: Conflicting or confirming answers expose false accounts.
- [procedure] 1) Show the reasoning behind the solution. 2) Name the gaps the audience must fill. 3) Ask the audience to confirm or correct the reasoning. 4) Deliver the withheld fact. When: when a solution depends on one fact. Why: the solution feels earned.
- [procedure] 1) Gather all suspects in one room and bar exits until the reveal ends. 2) Present evidence from strongest direct to weakest indirect. 3) State each suspect's motive and means. 4) Narrow to the culprit and invite confession. When: evidence has narrowed the field to a few suspects who know one another. Why: Keeping suspects present makes their reactions visible.
- [procedure] 1) Present the solution before the people most affected, so they cannot avoid it. 2) Verify the physical claim quickly while the room waits. 3) Close with a question aimed at the one person connected to the crime.
- [procedure] 1) Publish a partial account of the events. 2) Follow with a later correction that revises it and names what is still missing. 3) Keep the open questions for the next installment.
- [procedure] 1) Sound a warning that brings rescue nearer. 2) Let the victim attempt to act, with the attempt blocked. 3) Stop the rescue at the last moment, so hope is withdrawn. 4) Show the antagonists' relief, raising stakes for the next move. When: When building climactic tension where options are narrowing. Why: Raising then removing hope deepens threat more than a simple delay.
- [procedure] 1) Describe the people and their motives first. 2) Tell the story of the event. 3) Give the solution's mechanics last, answering held questions as the account reaches them. Why: the human story can hold attention more than the puzzle itself.
- [procedure] 1) Give partial evidence first. 2) Escalate to a more disturbing discovery. 3) Hold the full horror back until a later stage, so each step raises the stakes. When: Pacing a sequence of discoveries. Why: Escalating stages keep the audience anticipating what comes next.
- [procedure] 1) State the intent to present events in order. 2) Give facts step by step. 3) Hold the headline conclusion for the end. 4) End each segment on an unresolved hook. When: When a conclusion would spoil the story if stated early. Why: Readers meet the evidence before the verdict and stay engaged between segments.
- [procedure] 1) List the staged actions in order, such as disguise, exit and false alibi. 2) Link each step to a clue. 3) Let the player verify each link against that clue before the solution is revealed. When: when building a staged-death or locked-room puzzle.
- [procedure] 1) Let the audience perceive an effect such as a sound, glimpse or image. 2) Hold back its cause. 3) Explain the cause later through dialogue or a log entry. When: scripted reveals in a game. Why: perceiving the effect first builds the question the explanation then answers.
- [procedure] 1) Gather suspects in a bounded space under a harmless pretext. 2) Let them relax and talk. 3) Change the lighting to show details hidden before. 4) Add time pressure. 5) Signal prepared help and cut the lights to seize. When: a suspect will not confess and the investigator has a confirmed tell. Why: relaxed talk, better light and deadlines expose unguarded reactions.
- [procedure] 1) Assemble every involved party in a single space and assign each a seat. 2) Walk through the case in stages: setting, physical traces, timeline, then motive. 3) Hold back the decisive proof until the chain of events is complete, then present it as the final link. 4) Confront the culprit. Why: Seating everyone keeps all parties observed, and a held-back proof lets the audience follow the chain.
- [procedure] 1) Control lighting so every suspect is visible. 2) Read out the list of suspects. 3) Build a sense of a closing trap before the final moment.
- [procedure] 1) Gather all suspects together. 2) Address the suspect pool directly, with an apparent deadline for disclosure. 3) Present a prop, such as a message, suggesting new evidence has arrived. 4) Shift tone sharply to signal danger. When: the investigator suspects someone but lacks proof for arrest. Why: pressure can provoke the guilty party into revealing themselves.
- [procedure] 1) Cut the victim off so only sound reveals their position. 2) Give the rescuer a physical tool, such as a pole or string, to locate the victim by touch. 3) Bring extra help and gear in stages. 4) Keep the outcome uncertain until the victim is freed. When: a rescue from a hazard the rescuer cannot see into. Why: Staging keeps the threat active across several beats.
- [procedure] 1) Clear the surrounding material. 2) State the suspicion quietly. 3) Lift the key item slowly rather than all at once. When: When revealing a key item to build tension.
- [procedure] 1) Seat the suspect directly across from the questioner. 2) Place officers beside the suspect to cover any move. 3) Agree on a signal before questioning begins so the arrest happens at the right moment. When: A suspect is likely to hold back but has been confronted with physical evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Name the decisive evidence first. 2) Let the suspect acknowledge that the case is closed. 3) Have the confession supply motive, movements, any second death and timing. 4) Check each detail against earlier clues. When: All clues have been presented and only explanation remains. Why: Each claim in the confession can then be verified against the record.
- [procedure] 1) Lay out each piece of evidence with a label. 2) Seat suspects in a fixed order. 3) Wait until the room is silent. 4) Present the reasoning, naming each item as its label does. When: the solution depends on many objects. Why: the audience can track each item.
- [procedure] 1) Present the motive first. 2) Present the physical evidence. 3) Assemble the proof chain. 4) Name the culprit last, after the reasoning is complete. When: Structuring an accusation scene or final reveal. Why: Ordered parts let the audience follow each inference, so the name lands as a conclusion rather than a guess.
- [procedure] 1) Hold back the strongest evidence until the suspect has committed to an account 2) Reveal motive, alibi break, witness and any second-hand account in stages. When: the questioner holds more evidence than the suspect knows.
- [procedure] 1) Give a partial fact early. 2) Give a later fact that reframes the first. 3) Hold the decisive fact until the player has the tools to use it. When: Pacing a mystery across a sequence of revelations. Why: Each stage changes how earlier facts are understood.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a dated contradiction to the suspect's earlier account. 2) Name a specific time and place. 3) Pause after each claim to read the reaction. 4) Reveal only part of the evidence, holding the rest back. When: confronting a suspect whose story is contradicted by dated records or documents. Why: Staged disclosure builds pressure gradually and lets the investigator judge each reaction before committing further.
- [procedure] 1) Hold the eerie frame in place. 2) Introduce concrete physical facts. 3) Let those facts overturn the supernatural reading. When: When structuring a reveal in a haunted or eerie scene. Why: Keeping the frame until facts arrive lets the reader move from ghost to living person.
- [procedure] 1) Hint at a secret. 2) Ask a related question. 3) Ask a closer question. 4) Present the physical object that proves the fact. When: Revealing a key fact to an audience or player. Why: Each step moves nearer the answer, so tension builds before the proof lands.
- [procedure] 1) Introduce the key object in an ordinary context early on. 2) Plant the fact that later explains it. 3) Gather the suspects and witnesses. 4) Produce the object to show the solution. 5) Observe reactions to confirm it. When: The solution can be shown physically and the clues are already in the scene. Why: Shared, previously seen evidence makes the reveal convincing to the audience.
- [procedure] 1) Gather evidence through a staged procedure in front of a witness who can later confirm it. 2) Show the physical findings to witnesses one at a time. 3) Reveal the identity only after the findings are shown. When: A reveal must be credible to others. Why: Each step can be checked, so the disclosure is earned rather than asserted.
- [procedure] 1) Gather all suspects, their advisers, and a record-keeper in one room. 2) Seat opposing parties apart, each near their own adviser. 3) Give formal warnings that statements may be used. 4) Present evidence in order: substance, supply, method, motive, sequence of events. 5) Use recorded words and a hidden device to reveal the culprit before any arrest. When: A suspect's own words are the strongest evidence and the case is plausible but incomplete. Why: Ordered presentation and seating limit coordination and build pressure.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the suspected mechanism with a stand-in object. 2) Show it working in front of a witness. 3) Obtain the witness's confirmation of the culprit's behaviour. 4) Support it with measurable or photographic proof. When: As the final step of a mystery, instead of a confession. Why: A demonstration lets the audience verify the mechanism themselves.
- [procedure] 1) State an idea drawn from a known rule and the observed clues. 2) Test the idea with a controlled action, stating the reasoning first. 3) Show the observed result. When: Revealing a hidden mechanism to the audience. Why: Stages let the audience reason forward and give a clear payoff.
- [procedure] 1) Summon suspects separately. 2) Report a false accusation to one of them. 3) Watch which suspect reacts. 4) Let the guilty party reveal themselves. When: Forcing a culprit to act instead of relying on deduction alone. Why: A staged trap makes the guilty party's reaction an observable clue.
- [tradeoff] Staged reveals build suspense, but a fact the player needs immediately to continue frustrates when delayed; quick delivery trades tension for speed. Stage only information not yet needed. When: Use staging for information the player does not yet need to move forward.
- [tradeoff] Staging evidence persuades better in complex cases with a chain of clues and keeps secrets in reserve; a single-stage reveal suits cases with fewer clues.
- [tradeoff] Disclose facts that add weight to suspicion, since silence misleads; but withhold a fact when disclosing it could alert a suspect or compromise a source. Why: Silence can mislead as much as a false statement.
- [tradeoff] Concealing evidence usually harms the suspect more than disclosure does, and involving a spouse in concealment makes the harm worse. When: Someone urges another to hide or destroy evidence. Why: Concealment escalates exposure and draws in more people.
- [tradeoff] Resolving a mystery without a trial leaves no legal proof, so the conclusion rests entirely on the detective's reasoning. When: When the ending skips legal confirmation. Why: Readers must accept the deduction as the only evidence.
- [pitfall] A demonstration staged with controlled objects, or in front of the claimant, can confirm the claimant's own premise; observers who miss the preparation take it as proof. When: a reveal or demonstration in front of witnesses who do not control the props or timing. Why: Observers cannot see who arranged the objects and timing, so the performance looks convincing.
- [pitfall] A twist or unmasking with no earlier setup feels arbitrary or confusing rather than surprising; plant it with earlier masked appearances and repeated signals. Why: Unprepared reveals lose impact and read as a cheat.
- [pitfall] Attributing a story's turning point to luck feels arbitrary if nothing earlier prepares for it.
- [pitfall] A staged performance can look like a genuine quarrel, so gestures alone are weak evidence. When: Interpreting visible behaviour between people. Why: Performed actions imitate real emotion convincingly at a distance.
- [pitfall] Quietly dropping a discovery on the spot leaves its trace unexplained, which frustrates players unless it is resolved later.
- [pitfall] A sudden dramatic reveal can make a suspect collapse, and an unconscious person cannot give a statement.
- [pitfall] Overstating the detective's own cleverness in the reveal can make the solution feel self-congratulatory rather than earned. When: Writing the detective's commentary on the solution. Why: Emphasis on the investigator's brilliance distracts from the evidence.
- [pitfall] If a worthless prize is not hinted early through the victims' finances, the reversal feels like a cheat.
- [pitfall] A partly correct explanation can sit very near the truth yet still be wrong, so accepting it early ends the inquiry prematurely.
- [pitfall] A staged demand that reveals facts alarming the people meant to pay works against its own aim, because the alarm may prompt rescue instead of payment.
- [pitfall] A solution so neat that it reads like a story rather than a deduction weakens the sense that the audience could have solved it.
- [pitfall] Theatrical delivery can distract from weak evidence, so listeners respond to the performance rather than the argument. When: A reveal delivered with heavy drama. Why: Audiences judge spectacle by emotional impact, which can mask gaps in the logic.
- [pitfall] Constant escalation with no quiet stretches leaves no room for tension to build. Why: Tension depends on contrast; without low points there is no rise.
- [fact] Information disclosed to one party, such as the police, is effectively disclosed to everyone; an early reveal can reach the opponent and change other suspects' behaviour. When: a result implicates one person while others remain under suspicion. Why: Public knowledge changes how each suspect behaves and is treated, so disclosure timing matters.
- [fact] A summary by a hostile or sympathetic reporter, or a historian's account, is an argument that changes meaning through chosen evidence, not the speaker's own words.

## corroboration
- [model] A case is built as a chain of links, and tracking which link is still missing shows what must be proven next. When: when organising evidence toward a conclusion. Why: Each link must hold for the chain to stand, so the gap is visible at the weakest link.
- [definition] Testing a claim's origin means classifying it as original, suggested by someone else, or revised later under pressure. When: When an accusation may come from another person's suggestion or a witness changes their story. Why: It shows whether the claim came from direct knowledge or from outside influence.
- [mechanism] Lighting, distance and fear shape how many details a witness can report, so poor conditions yield vague or uncertain accounts. When: Evaluating eyewitnesses at a scene. Why: Weak perception reduces what can be sworn to, even when witnesses are sure of the event.
- [mechanism] When the same phrase appears in a second independent source, it connects two separate events that the first source alone did not link.
- [mechanism] Physical traces such as wasted muscle or wear on an object can test an NPC's claim about its past condition, giving the player a way to check a story. When: Designing an NPC whose backstory can be verified. Why: Physical evidence lets the player test a story rather than simply accept it.
- [mechanism] An accuser's account gains strength when a named bystander who was present is asked to confirm what they saw. When: when a case rests on one person's word. Why: a third party who saw events can confirm or contradict.
- [mechanism] A busy public location where an NPC handles steady trade acts as an observation post; its traffic and transaction records yield a timeline of who was present and when. When: Designing a shop, tavern or market as a source of witnesses and movement records. Why: Regular, continuous traffic creates a sequence of observable events the player can reconstruct.
- [rule] Corroborate a witness's account with a second independent source before it supports a charge or key claim, and show any dissenting view. When: A testimony claim is checkable against records or other people, such as a child's age or a contact's letter. Why: A single account can be mistaken or biased, and single-witness claims can be wrong; independent checks reveal errors. Two agreeing observers carry more weight than one. (x2)
- [rule] Corroborate a confident report or family retelling against independent records before relying on it; confidence does not guarantee accuracy, and retellings can hide errors and bias. When: a witness's confident account of the past shapes the next lead.
- [rule] Separate what a witness observed from how they report it: a stake or pride can bend the report even when the observation was accurate. When: judging a relayed account. Why: Heavy stress on certain words often reflects pride rather than fact; the report can bend toward a purpose while perception stays correct.
- [rule] Let a second, independent clue test an item's owner rather than simply telling the player; a single clue is easy to dismiss, while two can cross-check each other. When: revealing the owner of a found item or designing an object-based clue. Why: A player who tests the identity earns the conclusion.
- [rule] Do not rely on one witness when physical traces can check the account; test a stated time against a clock, a log or a door's state. When: A key account rests on one person. Why: Physical traces do not depend on memory or mood.
- [rule] Check claims against independent sources before building a theory or case, especially claims only one or two people can confirm; do not build a theory on a single odd remark.
- [rule] Do not treat a single trace as proof; each detail needs a second independent trace before it anchors a theory, especially when several explanations fit. When: Evaluating a single physical clue. Why: One trace can be misleading on its own.
- [rule] Cross-check each testimony against other accounts of the same moment and independent observers; a claim conflicting with a reliable observation must be questioned.
- [rule] Offer cross-checks for each claim from a biased source: bias can make a true claim look false and a biased witness can report wrongly; judge each on its own evidence. When: When a witness shows clear bias.
- [rule] Compare a character's earlier spoken account with a later written or physical record; a mismatch is a lead even when the speaker seems honest. When: the claim can be checked against an object or place the speaker could not easily alter. Why: Contradictions can expose hidden facts that sincerity does not rule out.
- [rule] Require a second independent clue before the player's character can make an arrest or accusation. When: when designing accusation rules in a mystery game. Why: A single weak lead should not be enough to act on.
- [rule] Let an NPC's statement look consistent with the chart on the surface, so the player must check details to find the lie.
- [rule] Offer the sources behind a claim for direct inspection, so others can verify them instead of trusting the reporter.
- [rule] Let players bring a second NPC who holds a separate view, creating a meaningful verification step in the scene. Why: An independent view makes verification a real choice.
- [rule] Do not rely on a single barrier; an impossibility is credible only when several independent checks agree.
- [rule] Test a witness's account by checking whether each described physical action is possible given the scene's geometry and objects. When: When a witness describes reaching, climbing, tying or moving something. Why: An impossible action shows the account is wrong or staged.
- [rule] Require formal follow-up on a witness who offers a sworn statement, or the alibi stays unconfirmed on the record.
- [rule] Do not rely on a handwriting match alone; treat it as one clue that needs corroboration. When: Using writing comparison as proof. Why: Matching handwriting can be coincidental or imitated.
- [rule] Do not treat a single overheard phrase as proof of motive; require independent corroboration before drawing that conclusion. When: a motive is inferred from one overheard line. Why: a fragment can be misread, so it needs support.
- [rule] Keep corroborating evidence in the world for true testimony, so a player who believes an honest NPC can still prove it.
- [rule] Independent checks complement direct questioning of everyone present; they do not replace it.
- [rule] Separate a statement's source from its claim. A statement may reach you through an intermediary, so it counts as that intermediary's testimony, not the original speaker's. When: When a key claim is relayed rather than heard directly. Why: Relayed claims can be altered or invented without the original speaker's knowledge.
- [rule] Do not rely on a one-sided record, or one assembled by someone with an agenda, without independent corroboration.
- [rule] Treat testimony as a lead, not proof; a witness's trust in someone reveals the witness's state of mind, not the facts of the event.
- [rule] Verify a privately disclosed account through separate sources. A confidence given in return for discretion does not establish that the account is true. When: When a witness's private disclosure is relied upon for the case. Why: The witness's motive to shape the account is unchanged by the promise of privacy.
- [rule] Watch one suspect through several channels at once: follow them in person, listen in on their calls, and intercept their written notes. When: When a suspect's contacts and intent cannot be learned from a single source.
- [rule] Track which witnesses share a grievance so the game can flag testimonies that are not independent of each other.
- [rule] Make a witness NPC's expected mention of an event a testable gap, so that skipping it gives players a clue.
- [rule] Check an anchor's installation time against a second source before building a timeline on it, since second-hand timing is weak alone.
- [rule] Make stated amounts such as rewards match or conflict with actual loot, so a mismatch becomes a clue. When: Designing bounty or reward text. Why: Conflicts give investigators a lead.
- [rule] Give players a case log of stored statements that they can reread at any time, so claims remain available as a record. When: when a mystery spans many NPC conversations. Why: a persistent record lets players compare claims over time.
- [rule] Tag each witness NPC with a reliability value and a motive, and let players cross-check reports against neutral NPCs who were present. When: when designing witness networks. Why: explicit bias makes reports checkable.
- [rule] Do not accept a rational explanation when an independent observer reports the same event in a place the proposed mechanism could not reach. When: Evaluating an explanation against witness reports. Why: An explanation that cannot reach the reported location does not account for the event.
- [heuristic] Several independent observers or sources who describe the same events consistently strengthen a claim more than a single account, and a repeated telling by the same person adds nothing. When: when weighing character evidence, witness accounts or rumours. Why: Independent confirmation makes claims checkable and reduces shared error; a single record can be forged or misremembered. (x2)
- [heuristic] Two independent sources that agree beat either alone, and a mismatch points to a lead; e.g., a suspect's admission and an independent source, or local knowledge and a physical survey. When: A single account is contested or hard to verify, or a deduction needs confirming. Why: Independent agreement makes it unlikely either account was shaped to match the other; two unrelated sources make the conclusion more convincing, so the match feels earned. (x2)
- [heuristic] Matching witness accounts strengthen a claim only if witnesses did not hear it from each other or coordinate on the point, since shared sources or coordination can produce agreement. When: multiple witnesses give matching accounts, or a second witness matches on a point the first had no reason to coordinate. Why: Uncoordinated agreement is less likely to be shared invention; shared belief can also produce agreement without observation.
- [heuristic] Back a single witness's identification with an independent observation, such as a separate description or a second witness recognising the same detail, which strengthens it more than either alone. When: identifying a person from a witness's description, when an identification rests on one witness. Why: Independent agreement reduces the chance of error.
- [heuristic] Check testimony against physical traces or objects and locations whenever both exist; treat it as established only after corroboration. When: a story covers actions that left traces, testimony is central, a witness describes how an object was handled, or a witness and an object point in different directions. Why: Physical facts confirm or contradict claims independent of the speaker; each source can mislead, so agreement between them is stronger than either alone.
- [heuristic] Traces confirm or contradict only parts of an account, so check each part of a doubtful account against physical traces rather than treating a trace as proof of the whole. When: a witness account is unreliable or lacks direct verification. Why: Traces support parts of a story without confirming the whole; a trace can confirm the part that happened even when the rest is doubtful.
- [heuristic] Let players test an NPC's travel, purchase or history claim against an independent transport log, ledger, archive, letter, register, timetable or ticket record. When: an NPC makes a claim about travel or purchases, and the player holds data the NPC cannot control. Why: Records from separate game systems are independent of the NPC's story, so a false account can be exposed; independent logs let players test claims directly.
- [heuristic] Check a disputed recollection against dated records and schedules rather than trusting how someone looked; a matching entry turns the memory into corroborated evidence. When: the outcome depends on exact wording or dates.
- [heuristic] When a primary witness cannot confirm a date or event, a second independent record, such as a transport order-book, can add facts no one else recorded and extend the timeline. When: the primary witness cannot confirm a date or event. Why: A backup record keeps the timeline provable.
- [heuristic] When one clue or symptom fits several causes, test each explanation against an independent trace or fact, such as a second sense, since a matching feature fits all equally. When: one observation supports two readings, a single physical clue has several possible causes, or a visual clue seems significant. Why: An independent trace can separate the possible causes.
- [heuristic] Witnesses who share a suspect's group, interests or ties, were chosen by one party, or can be bribed form one echo, not independent confirmation; check before accepting corroboration. When: a witness supports an alibi or corroborates a story, or judging how strongly a corroborating source supports it. Why: Shared loyalties or sympathy can bend an account, so an outside party's record weighs more than friends' support.
- [heuristic] Settle a person's status or identity on several features that agree, not on a single feature such as a shoe or a gesture.
- [heuristic] Do not treat a single trace as proof; build the inference from several traces that agree with one another. When: when concluding a suspect's size, gait, equipment or injury. Why: one trace can be coincidental or misread.
- [heuristic] Confirm a measured value against an external record, such as a seller's stock, rather than relying on the subject's own word. When: A subject claims a size, identity or origin. Why: An outside source cannot be shaped by the subject's claim.
- [heuristic] Settle a disputed fact against official records, which can resolve it even when an admitted fault is also on file. When: a disputed fact can be checked against records.
- [heuristic] A witness report can justify action, but a claim of awareness or movement stays unverified until physical evidence corroborates it.
- [heuristic] To test a claim quickly, find an independent witness who could have observed the same visitor, such as household staff. When: when a claim about a visit cannot be checked directly. Why: observers without a stake provide a separate check.
- [heuristic] When a lead moves to a new place, shift the inquiry there rather than continuing at the old location.
- [heuristic] Have an NPC confirm the details of a recovered note, such as age, clothing or direction, before a new quest branch opens. When: gating a quest branch on evidence. Why: checking details verifies the player's findings.
- [heuristic] Test a lead's importance before spending more time on it, but do not drop it merely because it is inconvenient to follow.
- [heuristic] Have two observers count the same signal independently and compare results, which catches counting mistakes that one observer would miss.
- [heuristic] A physical trace already on record, such as a footprint outline, can support an eyewitness sighting and strengthen a weak description.
- [heuristic] A detail offered late, such as a half-seen movement, is hard to verify and should be treated as a lead rather than an established fact.
- [heuristic] Check an unfamiliar term or name against an independent reference, such as a manual or blotter, before relying on it. When: A term or name found in evidence is unfamiliar. Why: An independent source confirms or corrects the reading.
- [heuristic] Witnesses who disagree about whether others were present open gaps that an opposing side can exploit.
- [heuristic] An alibi is strongest when several unconnected people confirm the same minute.
- [heuristic] A pickup-point NPC who records each claimant creates a chain of witnesses the player can question one by one.
- [heuristic] Test one witness's account against another's by setting the statements against each other until one side must concede. When: two parties give conflicting accounts. Why: Direct contradiction forces a check against independent facts.
- [heuristic] Inspect physical objects before recollection and rumour, since objects stay put while accounts drift. When: early in an investigation. Why: memory and testimony change over time.
- [heuristic] A separate contact that points to a broader interest can strengthen a motive hypothesis, though it does not prove it.
- [heuristic] Favour a witness whose account links to independent records, such as who admitted a visitor, over one whose account stands alone.
- [heuristic] Corroborate a lead with a separate record, such as a news item placing an event at the same location during the subject's stay.
- [heuristic] Treat a witness's certainty about an object's identity with caution when they saw it briefly or in poor conditions. When: brief or poor-condition viewing. Why: Certainty does not guarantee that the object was the genuine one.
- [heuristic] An account of someone's movements that depends on a watcher reveals a source; ask who supplied the information.
- [heuristic] Corroborate a compromised witness with an independent account of the same state or scene before relying on their memory.
- [heuristic] Accounts that agree on small details, such as menu items and preparation, strengthen each other. When: Comparing several witness accounts. Why: Matching specifics are harder to coincide by chance.
- [heuristic] Do not conclude from one shared feature; several independent features should agree before a document is linked to a common source. Why: a few defects can overstate a match.
- [heuristic] Rank competing leads by how likely each is to yield a motive or suspect, and pursue the one with concrete next steps first. When: Several investigation leads compete for attention. Why: Concrete next steps show quickly whether a lead is productive.
- [heuristic] Physical evidence such as forged documents or traces carries stronger reasoning than motive alone, so build deduction on the physical trail. When: When structuring an investigation's reasoning. Why: Physical traces can be tested; motives are only backgrounds.
- [heuristic] Corroborate private remarks from an insider by checking them against external facts before relying on them. When: Information comes from a servant or other insider with access to private matters. Why: Insider access makes information revealing, but it still needs independent confirmation.
- [heuristic] Anchor a timeline with physical traces such as impact position and freshness, since they can rule out explanations that relayed statements cannot. When: When a case includes objects, marks or damage that can be dated or placed. Why: A trace records an event directly, so it constrains the story more reliably than hearsay.
- [heuristic] Let a crowd repeat the first claim it hears, so the player must find a second, independent source to correct it. When: Designing crowd dialogue that carries misinformation.
- [heuristic] Separate what is observed from what is told when using objects and places as evidence. When: Reading a scene that combines physical traces with stories. Why: Legends can attach to objects and look like proof.
- [heuristic] Use a written report as corroboration when a suspect's memory is unreliable or self-serving. When: A suspect denies or fails to recall the event. Why: Corroboration from a second source compensates for the suspect's unreliable account.
- [heuristic] When witnesses conflict, corroboration from those with extended, direct observation can outweigh a weaker, shorter account.
- [heuristic] Repeat a physical examination with a different examiner. Disagreement between reports suggests the first examiner may have been biased. When: When a single examiner's finding is decisive. Why: Independent observers reduce the effect of one person's expectations.
- [heuristic] Trust a second-hand account less than one backed by physical traces; corroboration by records or objects matters more than who told the story. When: when an account arrives second-hand.
- [heuristic] Use logs, rosters or visitor books as search filters, so the player narrows locations by elimination. When: Designing a location search in a game. Why: Elimination through records turns investigation into a readable process.
- [heuristic] A single fact rarely proves a conclusion on its own, so it should be corroborated by independent evidence before being relied on. When: A clue appears to decide a case alone. Why: One premise cannot establish a conclusion without support from other facts.
- [heuristic] Two absences that point the same way, such as a missing item and a missing record, strengthen the conclusion that the item was taken.
- [heuristic] When several independent witnesses report the same pattern or thing across separate inquiries, a conclusion gains credibility and a simple imagined explanation becomes less likely. When: A mystery must be made to feel established; judging whether a reported sighting is real. Why: Independent agreement reduces the chance that one observer's error stands alone and reduces the chance of shared illusion.
- [heuristic] Count sources by independence of origin, not number: sources drawing on one authority are not independent, and two accounts count only if from different first-hand sources. When: Weighing agreement among multiple sources, or two witnesses reporting the same claim. Why: Repetition of a single origin inflates apparent support; two people repeating one source add no independent confirmation.
- [heuristic] Let earlier environment or NPC details gain meaning when a later reveal or new document changes the motive or beneficiary; re-run the case file so clues are reinterpreted. When: A new discovery changes the likely motive or beneficiary in a generated mystery. Why: Reinterpreting existing clues keeps the mystery coherent and rewarding.
- [heuristic] Build a case in layers: each independent confirmation adds weight before the conclusion is stated.
- [heuristic] Claims about one event that appear in several accounts, such as an agreed meal, may be reliable while disputed details such as money or objects need separate testing. When: Witnesses agree on some points and disagree on others. Why: Agreement on incidental facts does not confirm the contested ones.
- [heuristic] Identity is stronger when several traces, such as a fragment and a location, are gathered together and point the same way. When: Weighing evidence that links a person to a place or event. Why: Converging independent traces are harder to explain away as coincidence or planting.
- [heuristic] Use two independent witnesses to reinforce a false time, so the error appears verified and the player stops questioning it.
- [procedure] 1) Separate what a witness saw directly from what they were told, including reports by others on a record. 2) Mark each claim as first-hand or hearsay. 3) Weigh each source on its own. When: Evaluating testimony or a record that mixes observation and report. Why: Witnesses often present hearsay as if it were observed. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Assign one watcher per target. 2) Give each watcher a separate reporting channel. 3) Obtain records at their source and cross-check the reports against each other. When: When suspects move apart and one observer cannot cover them all. Why: Separate channels and cross-checking keep multiple observers reliable and independent.
- [procedure] 1) Record the disputed account in writing. 2) Gather independent sources such as diaries, letters, official records and other witnesses. 3) Check each source against the others. 4) Form a judgement only afterwards. When: A single account conflicts with the record.
- [procedure] 1) Collect details that condemn and details that favour the accused. 2) Take the accused's account as a working hypothesis. 3) Follow where it leads and test it against each witness's stated limits. When: Testimony contains both incriminating and exculpatory details. Why: Selective reading of witness details distorts the case.
- [procedure] 1) List the physical traces the described event should leave, such as powder marks, footprints or impact range. 2) Compare each trace with the account. 3) Doubt the account where traces contradict it, even if witnesses agree. When: a witness gives a detailed account of a fast event.
- [procedure] 1) Find people who knew the person involved. 2) Look for letters or records. 3) Compare them with the witness account before accepting it. When: when a single account is the only source for a fact.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the official account with personal first-hand observation. 2) Ask the witness for the private facts behind it. 3) Check the record against physical evidence. 4) Note which observations were made before the scene was disturbed. When: when an official finding seems to close a case too quickly.
- [procedure] 1) Name the source of the lead. 2) Check whether that source actually holds the item or fact. 3) If every source is negative, close the branch and return to other evidence. When: A lead is taking time without yielding results. Why: Closing an empty branch frees effort for leads that can move the case forward.
- [procedure] 1) Compare each witness statement with physical facts such as the body, the doors and the keys. 2) Mark each conflict. 3) Keep the testimony provisional until the conflicts are resolved.
- [procedure] 1) List each claim in the testimony. 2) Match each claim to a physical item or record. 3) Re-ask the questions and note which answers change. When: Assessing a witness or suspect's account. Why: Physical checks reveal contradictions, and shifting answers reveal weak claims.
- [procedure] 1) Take the witness's account of an event. 2) Check it against other facts and reports. 3) Look for a physical trace confirming it. 4) Compare timing with separate accounts. 5) Check that the witness had access and time to plant the object. When: a witness's account links a person to an object or place.
- [procedure] 1) Ask each witness for times and locations. 2) Link each account to the next. 3) Test the linked accounts against physical evidence. When: when several witnesses give partial accounts.
- [procedure] 1) List each incident with its source. 2) Mark which incidents are independently verified and which rest on one informant. 3) Count only independent links toward a pattern. 4) Keep the pattern provisional while sources are second-hand. When: Building a case from reports and accounts. Why: Only independent evidence can make a chain of events trustworthy.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the person who actually saw the event. 2) List every person who repeated the account. 3) Mark which parts are first-hand, reported, or the teller's guess. 4) Check each link against an eyewitness. When: Presenting or auditing a clue delivered through hearsay. Why: Explicit chains let the audience judge reliability link by link.
- [procedure] 1) Identify which accounts copy or borrow from others. 2) Trace each copy back to its original witness. 3) Count independent witnesses only. 4) Check claims against any direct chain of evidence. When: Sources quote or borrow from each other. Why: Copies add no independent confirmation.
- [procedure] 1) Record the exact kind of object found at a scene. 2) Trace its source by inquiry. 3) Search other scenes for the same kind. 4) Confirm by physical comparison where possible.
- [procedure] 1) Count the events the scene implies. 2) Match each event to a physical mark it left. 3) Investigate any event with no matching mark, or any mark with no matching event. When: when a scene's physical record seems inconsistent.
