- [pitfall] Witnesses who share a grudge, rely on each other, or repeat one source add no independent weight; matching accounts can share the same error and need independent testing. When: Multiple witnesses agree on the same accusation, or several people report one account from one source. Why: Shared motive or shared source makes agreement a single voice; shared origin is not independent confirmation. (x2)
- [pitfall] Accounts of a dispute often come from one side only, and a record written by one side is not impartial; the full facts may never be recoverable. When: when reconstructing a dispute from testimony or a published account. Why: The party who tells the story has a stake in its version; a published account can shape opinion before anyone tests it.
- [pitfall] Agreement is not independent confirmation when witnesses share expectations or agree with a detail offered to them, since they may all be wrong in the same direction. When: many people agree an object is familiar, or a witness confirms a detail that was offered. Why: Shared expectations or offers produce agreement without evidence; agreement and recollection look the same in the record.
- [pitfall] A wrong time in a public notice can mislead the whole timeline, so official documents must be checked against what witnesses actually observed. When: a published document sets a time or fact.
- [pitfall] A witness's statement that they were never alone with an item is unreliable unless timing and sightline are documented, because the real access window is often wider.
- [pitfall] Anyone who heard the original conversation could have written a letter, including the apparent recipient, so keep authorship open.
- [pitfall] If the audience cannot tell which speakers are drunk, biased or passing on gossip, every statement feels equally reliable and the mystery loses its texture.
- [pitfall] A record that quotes one side's report can be contradicted by the full examination, so compare the two before accepting either. When: when working from a summary or secondhand account.
- [pitfall] Physical traces such as marks or objects can look objective, yet they may be matched to the accusers' own claims and so prove little.
- [pitfall] A group that agrees together can look like independent corroboration when its agreement is only deference to a leader.
- [pitfall] A second anchor that depends on the same unverified source is not independent, so it does not confirm the first line of inquiry. When: An investigator treats two leads as corroborating each other. Why: Shared origin means both leads inherit the same error.
- [fact] Examination rules that bind only the accused make the accused's compliance look like proof, while the accusers' conduct goes unchecked.

## identity recognition
- [mechanism] Remarks made within hearing of accusers can suggest names, and those suggested names are then acted on.
- [mechanism] A player-mentioned name can set a hidden flag when an NPC hesitates, letting later dialogue react to the NPC's unease. When: Designing NPC reactions to named characters. Why: Hesitation is a detectable signal that can change the NPC's future responses.
- [mechanism] A recognition trigger, such as a particular word or symbol, can unlock a memory of an earlier encounter. When: a character must reconnect to a past event. Why: the trigger reactivates the associated memory.
- [mechanism] Recognition cues such as a garment, hat or posture can stand in for a face, so an impersonator needs to copy only those cues.
- [mechanism] A recognisable outline, such as a silhouette, or a deliberate cue, such as a loud song, lets a watching contact identify a person without names. When: A contact must recognise an investigator who cannot be openly identified. Why: Distinct visual or audible signals convey identity to someone who knows what to look for.
- [mechanism] Giving each persona a small habit fingerprint, such as a brand of product, lets players link two characters when the fingerprints match. When: Designing NPC identities that can be linked. Why: A shared private habit is harder to fake than public identity.
- [mechanism] Each named person, place or transport gives a detail that can later be confirmed or contradicted by other evidence. When: a witness gives an account with specific names.
- [mechanism] Documents with deliberate name variants or errors force the player to reconcile them with a second document, turning each conflict into a cross-check puzzle. When: when in-game letters, ledgers or depositions are generated with inconsistencies. Why: Conflicting records require comparison to resolve, which makes the discrepancy the challenge.
- [behavior] Witnesses who omit or withhold a detail may recall or confirm it once a specific named item or guess is offered; general questions miss it. When: Asking about a detail the witness left out or seems to withhold. Why: Specific cues retrieve memories general questions miss, and a concrete proposal is easier to confirm than an open question.
- [behavior] A suspect asked to list people present gives names reluctantly, and recalls a forgotten person only when the interviewer offers a name already known. When: when a suspect is asked to list people present. Why: recall is cued by a specific name rather than generated freely.
- [behavior] A close relative's recognition of a personal item tends to be emotional and is often accepted as the strongest confirmation. When: a relative of a missing person sees a possession. Why: personal attachment makes the relative's identification feel certain.
- [behavior] A witness who cannot recall a person's face may still recall their name when it matches something already known to them. When: when a witness cannot describe a face clearly. Why: A shared detail anchors recall.
- [behavior] A character recognises a distinctive object only if they saw it before, so recognition depends on earlier exposure. When: A worn or distinctive object reappears later in a story. Why: Recognition requires having seen the object earlier.
- [behavior] A recognized personal item can show that someone knew the wearer even though the wearer did not know them in return. When: an onlooker recognizes a marked item on a person. Why: the mark reveals the wearer's identity to the viewer.
- [behavior] A witness may be sure of a face yet unable to recall a name, so an identification of a face does not establish a correct identity. When: When a witness claims to recognize someone but cannot give a full identity. Why: Face memory and name memory are separate, and confidence attaches to the face.
- [behavior] A witness may reverse an identification made in a charged moment once she recognises someone close to the accused, and then decline to prosecute. When: when the identified person is known to the witness. Why: Personal relationships change the stakes of testimony.
- [behavior] Observers recognise a distant figure by build and gait before seeing the face; this can beat a close view of a disguised face. When: identifying someone at a distance or behind a disguise. Why: silhouette and movement are harder to alter than facial features.
- [behavior] A witness who saw only part of a figure, such as its back or a voice, forms an identity from cues and expectations, so a missing face goes unnoticed. When: the witness saw only part of a person and expects someone familiar to be present. Why: expectation fills the unseen parts of the perception.
- [behavior] A witness who sees only part of a person, such as gait, build and a distinctive coat, can recognize them with confidence, though less surely than from a clear face. When: the view is partial, such as from behind or at a distance. Why: Recognition combines partly seen and partly remembered features.
- [behavior] Offering a list of names can reveal a witness's knowledge: a witness who denies knowing one name may still name someone else from the same situation. When: When a witness conceals knowledge of people connected to a case. Why: Witnesses concentrate on the names they fear and can slip on the rest.
- [behavior] Witnesses can recognise a person from small habits the witness never consciously noticed, such as a repetitive fidget at the table. When: a witness has observed the person at close range. Why: habits are registered without conscious attention.
- [rule] Plant a distinctive, persistent cue the player sees early, such as a tool, cord or remembered item, so a disguised or masked figure is recognised fairly at the reveal. When: A recognition beat depends on noticing a clue; a confrontation at a deadline in a crowded location; a character's identity was hinted at earlier. Why: A visible constant cue makes recognition fair and solvable, letting players resolve confrontations quickly and feel the reveal is earned. (x2)
- [rule] Require two or more independent identifiers or sources before accepting an identity, so one compromised or unreliable witness cannot close the case alone. When: Designing quest or case completion in a game; a body's or person's identity rests on a single compromised source. Why: One unreliable witness can mislead the conclusion; a single source may be wrong, shaken or biased.
- [rule] Verify an identity link before relying on dependent clues; an identity inferred from a single report can be wrong and silently invalidates every clue that follows. When: A clue chain depends on who a person is. Why: A plausible chain can look complete yet rest on one false premise.
- [rule] Record a witness's identification confidence separately from its accuracy; confidence can rest on a partial view, like a lit face through a window, and still be wrong. When: Photo or lineup identification. Why: A sure witness can still be wrong.
- [rule] Test claimed identity with hard-to-disguise marks or routine behaviour an impostor fails; use marks only alongside other evidence, since they can be altered or engineered.
- [rule] Recognition depends on attention and motive, such as vanity or gain; don't accept a recognition claim alone, check it against the witness's motives and opportunities. When: A witness identifies someone at a distance, after a long gap, or in changed circumstances.
- [rule] When a witness omits a step, name that step explicitly and state they have not told everything; the gap exposes a flaw and invites further questions. When: When listening to a witness's narration or when a witness's account seems incomplete. Why: Naming the gap signals that the story is not accepted and invites more detail.
- [rule] Establish a person's identity from official letters, licences and lodging addresses, and record letters as evidence once read. When: A person's background is unclear.
- [rule] Use wanted posters, prison records and newspaper notices as in-world sources that can either hide or reveal a character's identity. When: Worlds where characters have pasts that players can uncover. Why: Ordinary public records give players diegetic ways to discover identities.
- [rule] Matching a physical feature requires expertise in that feature; without it, the comparison is only a guess.
- [rule] Make an NPC's recognition question change how the NPC treats the player, so a wrong answer alters the NPC's willingness to help. When: designing NPC contacts who verify identity. Why: a visible consequence makes the challenge meaningful.
- [rule] Make identity cues in NPC dialogue something players must verify; a voice heard through a wall should not confirm identity automatically. When: when designing identity clues. Why: Unverified cues can mislead players.
- [rule] Let vendors or passersby describe the expected pattern so players can detect a missing element without being told directly.
- [rule] Ask what a witness could actually know before weighing their testimony, since recognition depends on prior acquaintance. When: When a witness's account would rule out a suspect. Why: A witness cannot recognize someone they never knew.
- [heuristic] Feeling certain does not guarantee an accurate identification; a confident memory of a face is a claim to test against the person actually in view. When: A sighting or memory of a face is the basis for identifying or linking a person. Why: Identification depends on memory, condition and confidence.
- [heuristic] An engraved or monogrammed item can link an unidentified body or injured person to its named owner when papers are missing, but its presence alone does not prove identity. When: A body or injured person has no papers but keeps personal items. Why: An object can be worn or passed on by others.
- [heuristic] A failed identification still narrows possibilities without eliminating the suspect; it does not prove innocence until the witness's view, limited by lighting and distance, is known. When: A witness is shown a lineup or a person and cannot confirm them. Why: Lighting and distance limit what a witness can see, so a near miss may be a poor view.
- [heuristic] A partial identifier, such as a vehicle plate from a particular region or its first digits, narrows a search without solving it, since it shrinks candidates rather than isolating one. When: A full identifier is not available. Why: Partial information shrinks the candidate set but rarely isolates one answer.
- [heuristic] A remark revealing knowledge the speaker could not have had should be challenged, since it can betray involvement; asking whether an item was returned implies they could not check. When: A speaker says something showing what they knew, or a suspect speaks of details only the culprit could know. Why: Offhand remarks often expose information the speaker did not intend to share.
- [heuristic] Vague descriptions widen the suspect pool while precise ones narrow it; test how many people a description fits, since one matching a large share identifies no one. When: Identifying a suspect from testimony. Why: A description identifies someone only when few people fit it.
- [heuristic] Record people through what they repeatedly do, such as watching or drinking, rather than only through labels, since habits reveal more than descriptions.
- [heuristic] Name the specific people who use a place and why, which turns a general claim about traffic into one that can be checked.
- [heuristic] A distinctive personal item can stand in for a person's face when the owner was never seen clearly, linking an unexplained event to that person. When: a figure was seen at a distance or cannot be named. Why: an item unique to a person can carry identity where a face cannot.
- [heuristic] Naming specific verified facts, such as a known meeting or offer, can push a guarded suspect toward confession.
- [heuristic] Before trusting a conversation, consider whether a listener behind a door is an ally or a rival. When: a private exchange may be overheard. Why: Listeners carry different loyalties and can change what is said.
- [heuristic] Choose a time and lighting in which the target has the least reason to recognise you, such as after seeing you only in darkness. When: planning a covert approach. Why: recognition depends on conditions as well as appearance.
- [heuristic] A culprit who wants a body unidentified tends to strip its most recognisable items. Identifiable items found apart from the body suggest the discard was deliberate. When: Interpreting where identifying belongings were left after a death.
- [heuristic] Check objects against the identity they claim; a detail such as clothing sized wrong for its owner can expose deliberate misdirection. When: an object seems to belong to someone it does not fit. Why: Misdirection often leaves a small inconsistency on close inspection.
- [heuristic] Naming the consequences of continued silence before leaving can prompt a fuller account.
- [heuristic] A distinctive mark such as a brand on the forearm identifies a body once clothing slips and exposes it.
- [heuristic] When a face is hidden by a mask, veil or covered hair, identification depends on whatever partial features were actually seen. When: A victim or suspect was disguised. Why: Concealment limits identification to visible traits.
- [heuristic] Test a claimed identity by introducing the claimant to someone who knows the real person; a failure of recognition exposes the false claim. When: A claimed identity is doubtful and a related person may be hiding behind it. Why: Someone who knows the real person can recognize an impostor.
- [heuristic] A substitute chosen for partial resemblance makes each outside check confirm something true, strengthening the deception. When: Choosing a double. Why: Matching facts pass verification.
- [heuristic] Close scrutiny of a stranger's face and clothing can defeat a disguise, since a careful observer registers details that a costume leaves unchanged. When: a disguised suspect is in view. Why: Detailed observation exposes features a disguise cannot fully hide.
- [heuristic] A witness who names the giver of an object, retracts, then restates the claim is showing unreliable memory or concealment.
- [heuristic] An identification based on a known habit depends on that habit, not on the object's own features, and should be weighed as such.
- [heuristic] Do not treat a face or outline as identification without checking for disguise. When: a witness saw a person only briefly.
- [heuristic] A half-formed recognition of a voice is weak evidence and should not count as identification until it is tested. When: when a witness recognizes a voice only partly. Why: Partial recall is easily mistaken.
- [heuristic] When a body's face is destroyed by burns, identity becomes a legitimate doubt that a test can confirm or rule out. When: A victim cannot be recognised visually. Why: Visual identification is unavailable, so other evidence must decide.
- [heuristic] A single meeting is weak evidence of identity; repeated meetings need checking before they support a link between people. When: Connecting a person seen in passing to a suspect or name. Why: One sighting can be mistaken, while repeated sightings can be tested.
- [heuristic] Verify identities in records before trusting counts, since two people with the same name can make totals unreliable.
- [heuristic] Match characters on traits that survive wear and change, such as expression, because they still show through decay and ageing. When: A person's appearance has changed since the earlier image. Why: Surface details fade over time while core features endure.
- [heuristic] A physical description that matches a suspect is only a starting point, because broad descriptions fit many people and need corroboration. When: Matching a suspect to a witness or record description. Why: Common physical traits are shared by many individuals.
- [heuristic] Verify a stranger with a shared sign or challenge, like a known alias; a bluffer fails, but a real contact may lapse, so one miss is weak evidence. When: Checking whether a stranger belongs to a group; a contact must verify identity without revealing much. Why: Only someone who knows the sign can answer it correctly; memory lapses happen even for real contacts.
- [heuristic] A buyer who gives no address can still be identified by a detail such as appearance or payment habit that picks them out from a crowd. When: Tracing a customer who left few personal records. Why: Distinctive traits can single out a person even without contact details.
- [procedure] 1) Drop or ask about a name or visitor the witness should or should not know. 2) Observe stammering, denial, blushing, embarrassment, sudden anger, colour change or asking who talked. 3) Treat reactions as leads to test, not proof of guilt. When: Testing whether a witness knows a particular person, or a suspect holds information you need. Why: Recognition or unease is revealed more reliably by reaction than by spoken answers; an unexpected name triggers fear of exposure.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the features the disguise hides or alters. 2) Obtain one hard-to-change feature, such as a scar, from a witness who saw the person closely, and examine permanent marks up close. 3) Compare marks with records of past injury or background. 4) Match each mark against candidate identities. When: A suspect's name or papers may be false, or a disguised person is suspected. Why: Disguises rarely alter physical marks.
- [procedure] 1) List each claim the stated identity makes, such as name and address. 2) Check each claim against independent records, such as criminal records, property histories and physical descriptions. 3) Flag mismatches; record each match as a link between person, place and victim. When: A stated identity may be false and independent records about people, places or crimes exist. Why: Independent records expose inconsistent claims, and independent matches build a chain harder to fake than a single claim.
- [procedure] 1) Start from a past fact the suspect once revealed. 2) Trace the records of that past role. 3) Match descriptions, names and corroborating details from several sources. 4) Accept the identification only when independent sources agree. When: A suspect has changed name or appearance but left a traceable past; the record may use a different name. Why: A name can change while descriptions and records persist, so a match may rest on descriptions rather than the name.
- [procedure] 1) Collect every name variant and title. 2) Link variants to one identity using family ties, residence and repeated sworn testimony. 3) Accept a link only when it rests on more than the name. When: Before comparing dates, places or alibis across documents. Why: A name alone cannot confirm identity, so context must support each link.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a witness for the unseen person's build, complexion and whiskers. 2) Verify any rough description before acting on it. When: a witness can describe a third party.
- [procedure] 1) Collect a physical description, such as height and build. 2) Fix the time of the event. 3) Note what each observer did. 4) Match the description and timing to the most probable person.
- [procedure] 1) Gather people who knew the person's appearance. 2) Check a physical marker, such as an engraved item. 3) Combine their evidence with the discovered facts. 4) Test the doubted claim against that combined result.
- [procedure] 1) Ask an open identity question. 2) Ask a follow-up about shared context. 3) Offer a familiar everyday cue. 4) Accept the identity only after two shared facts match. When: a character must confirm who another is from memory.
- [procedure] 1) Estimate when an absence would first cause concern. 2) Estimate when that concern leads to a published notice. 3) Search the press around that date. 4) Match identifying marks, such as initials, against the notice. When: identifying an unknown victim through the press.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the partial identifier, such as initials. 2) Test it against local knowledge and records. 3) Accept a match only when several corroborating local facts support it. When: A witness or document gives only a partial identifier. Why: A single initial match is weak and can mislead.
- [procedure] 1) Note the first identification and its emotional weight. 2) Check features not yet examined, such as a beard, scar or tattoo. 3) Link borrowed or traced items to their source. 4) Revise the whole reading of the event. When: when a first identification may be wrong.
- [procedure] 1) Pick a predictable moment when the suspect must slow down. 2) Station a hidden observer. 3) Release a familiar animal at that moment. 4) Read its reaction as evidence of identity. When: A person's identity or a substitution is in doubt and a familiar animal is available. Why: The animal's recognition is hard for an impostor to fake.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whether the witness would pick the person out of a group later. 2) Test the answer with a lineup that includes similar people. 3) Accept the identification only if it holds. When: A key identification rests on a witness's memory of a common-looking person. Why: Recognition among similar people is weak, so a lineup tests whether the memory can actually single out the person.
- [procedure] 1) Record the lighting, distance, duration of view and any face-obscuring items. 2) Weigh the identification against those conditions. 3) Treat a poorly lit, brief or obscured view as weak evidence. When: Assessing how far an eyewitness identification can be trusted. Why: Each limiting condition reduces what the witness could actually perceive, so the identification carries less weight.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the identifying witness whether the suspect is the person. 2) Record a denial and any alternative description given. 3) Compare the alternative description against the suspect's actual features. When: A witness is asked to identify a suspect and may deny the identification. Why: A denial and a differing description can cast doubt on the original identification.
- [procedure] 1) Adopt a plausible official role. 2) Ask a neutral question, such as about household members. 3) Confirm or discard the identity from the answer, without revealing interest. When: checking whether a named person is at an address. Why: a neutral question avoids alerting the subject.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness examine the body or image long and carefully. 2) Ask whether they are sure. 3) Ask which specific marks the identification rests on. When: a witness gives an identification from partial evidence. Why: Confirms the basis is specific marks rather than a general impression.
- [procedure] 1) Note features that survive disguise, such as build, height, beard, bodily marks, voice, accent, and speech habits. 2) Track each unidentified person under a stable label. 3) Check each feature for reliability. When: a witness sees only parts of several people. Why: Disguises hide the face but not every trait, so some features remain usable.
- [procedure] 1) Note the familiar face and the feeling that it is known. 2) Place it in the earlier context where it was seen. 3) Confirm the identity with a direct question.
- [procedure] 1) State the investigation goals before questioning anyone. 2) Review physical and medical facts, such as cause and approximate time of death. 3) Filter a records list by sex, age, area and description. 4) Confirm each candidate with a non-physical detail, such as clothing or possessions. When: a victim is unidentified and a records list exists. Why: Filtering narrows candidates, and a non-physical detail can confirm or eliminate them.
- [procedure] 1) List the habits and possessions each persona is known to use. 2) Compare the lists for overlap. 3) Check where the shared items were, and whether they disappeared when one persona vanished. When: Linking two identities by evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Raise the name the witness currently uses. 2) If they deny a connection, press on the name. 3) Once they show distress, reassure them to draw out an admission. When: When a witness is hiding a family tie. Why: Name challenges unsettle concealment and reassurance encourages honesty.
- [procedure] 1) Name a witness to the suspect without revealing more. 2) Observe whether the suspect mentions, avoids or contacts that witness. 3) Record the reply as an inference, since the witness may now be prepared. When: A suspect has omitted a witness who logically should have been mentioned.
- [procedure] To test identification, have the witness view the body or item and confirm the person who did the action.
- [procedure] 1) List the features in the description. 2) Approach the candidate under similar viewing conditions. 3) Check each listed feature against the person before accepting the match.
- [procedure] 1) Match names, dates and places across sources. 2) Label each identity as stated, inferred or assumed. 3) Use only the stated and inferred identities as a basis for conclusions, and flag the assumed ones. When: When cases rest on fragmentary, undated or annotated records. Why: Explicit labels stop an assumption from being mistaken for a documented fact.
- [procedure] 1) Approach the subject while they are visible. 2) Ask them to show their face. 3) Tell them recognition is intended. 4) Fix the image in memory for later identification. When: when a face must be recognised later and the subject can be approached. Why: A deliberate look at a face produces a more reliable memory than a passing glimpse.
- [tradeoff] A close associate may miss a disguised person when key cues like look or manner changed, since appearance overrides memory; yet a spouse often recognises the face through long familiarity. When: A disguised person meets someone who knew them well or is in close contact; recognition by a spouse or long-time associate holds when familiarity is long. Why: Appearance and manner can override memory, while long familiarity gives recognition cues others lack.
- [tradeoff] Naming a witness to a suspect can yield information, but it may let the witness be coached, destroying the independent check that witness could have provided. When: Only one independent source of verification exists.
- [tradeoff] When documents fail to prove identity, a rival's recognition of a personal tell can serve as proof; documents are stronger evidence but slower to establish. When: a reveal depends on identifying a disguised character. Why: Recognition resolves the question in a single scene, at the cost of being less legally rigorous.
- [pitfall] Identical-looking items defeat tracing and can mislead reconstruction when assumed to be one object or several without checking distinguishing features recorded when placed.
- [pitfall] A reaction to a named person shows familiarity or unease, not its content or guilt; it justifies further investigation, not a conclusion. When: A name probe produces a visible reaction. Why: Unease has many causes, and a reaction confirms familiarity but not what the knowledge is.
- [pitfall] Naming people during questioning can plant those names in the witness's mind and make later answers unreliable. When: When testing a witness with names of possible suspects. Why: A witness may adopt a name suggested by the questioner rather than recall it independently.
- [pitfall] Linking two people as one because their descriptions overlap is unsound; a description match alone does not establish that they are the same person.
- [pitfall] A partial match on a shared model can be coincidence, since many copies of a product share the same features.
- [pitfall] Fixating on a minor name in a file can absorb attention while the central question stays unanswered.
- [pitfall] Recognition after a long gap can be mistaken, so a remembered identification should be checked against earlier sightings. When: A witness identifies someone seen only once, long before. Why: Memory of appearance fades and can drift over time.
- [pitfall] Naming one's own bias does not remove it; a witness may admit prejudice and still have answers coloured by it.
- [pitfall] A fragment that names a person without implying a stake carries little weight.
- [pitfall] Identifying a person or object under public pressure, in poor light and with a crowd watching, is fragile and often unreliable. When: A character is asked to identify something quickly in a tense setting. Why: Pressure and poor visibility reduce accuracy.
- [pitfall] A description alone is weak where the target can blend into a large city.
- [pitfall] A correct match showing whose trace it is does not show when the trace was made. A planted mark can match the right person perfectly. When: When evaluating a trace that identifies a suspect. Why: Identity and timing are separate facts that a single comparison does not establish.
- [pitfall] Assuming the person who arrived is the same as the person who left is a common error that hides an occupant substitution.
- [pitfall] Assuming a body's identity is certain can hide a staged death.
- [pitfall] Relabelling a character after the fact can mislead audiences about who is present and what role they play. When: When editing a story's labels or framing late in production. Why: Audiences build their model of the cast from the labels they are given.
- [pitfall] A sign of identity can be recognised by the wrong people as well as the right ones.
- [pitfall] A direct question about a name fails if the target uses an alias, producing a false negative that looks like a dead end.
- [pitfall] A caller who quotes another person's name does not thereby become that person; a name in a message is not proof of who is speaking. When: when a message names a speaker. Why: A name can be borrowed or false.
- [pitfall] Handling a sheet by its face can destroy fingerprints or other marks the investigator wants to keep. When: Collecting loose paper as evidence. Why: Contact with the surface disturbs traces.
- [pitfall] Treating a face as a mirror of the soul traps a reader or investigator once later events overturn the first impression.
- [pitfall] A description that fits a real person's appearance looks like corroboration but does not prove the perceived event occurred.
- [pitfall] Assuming a repeat visitor is a stranger ignores visible traces that link the two visits.
- [fact] A single witness identification placing a suspect at a site and time can justify arrest, though it is a fragile basis for the case.
- [fact] A witness identification informs a case, but the decision to charge depends on whether the whole case holds together.
- [fact] Establishing identity between close lookalikes, especially from personal recognition alone, is among the hardest questions to settle. When: a claim depends on who someone is. Why: resemblance undermines recognition.
- [fact] A person can be linked to an identity through marked objects, physical descriptions, or third-party references, and each method needs its own check before it is trusted. Why: Each link method can mislead in a different way.
- [fact] Recognition is often partial: a witness may know a voice without recognising the face, and may confirm only height and general look. When: identifying a person from voice or appearance.
- [fact] An identification method works only if someone is known to keep the records it needs, such as dental records kept over years.

## red herrings and misdirection
- [model] A conspicuous, valuable lure draws attention away from a small, unremarkable item that carries the real meaning, which is hidden beneath or within the lure. When: Designing a clue that should be seen but missed on first pass. Why: Attention goes to the valuable object, so the true clue is overlooked.
- [model] An expected outsider can serve as cover for an insider culprit, because the foreign or unusual figure draws attention away from the household. When: when a mystery has a conspicuous outside figure. Why: the audience's suspicion settles on the most memorable stranger.
- [model] Mystery solutions can stack several false theories, each anchored in a document or witness, which the investigator peels back one at a time.
- [definition] A clue points toward the truth; a red herring is a plausible, misleading lead built from true facts that mean something different in context, drawing attention toward an innocent party.
- [definition] A red herring is a harmless or distracting detail with an innocent cause that draws suspicion and speculation away from the real evidence, which remains elsewhere in the story.
- [mechanism] A decoy resembling the real item, once accepted at face value, ends the search: the true item or offender stays hidden and players stop further checking. Why: Accepting the apparent answer stops further search.
- [mechanism] A sinister-looking suspect draws attention away from others, so players who fixate on that person stop examining the rest of the cast. When: when a character is styled as an obvious villain. Why: Visible menace gives a quick answer that discourages further checking.
- [mechanism] A suspect's unpopular beliefs can serve as a false lead, provided the real clue points elsewhere. When: Designing decoy suspects. Why: Prejudice-based suspicion can mislead, but the true clue must still be discoverable.
- [mechanism] A torn map or note on an enemy can point players to a hidden piece held by a specific NPC or stored in a specific container.
- [mechanism] A suspect's helpful remark can steer attention toward another person while hiding the suspect's own suspicion. When: a suspect offers hints about a poison, a cause or another person. Why: the remark's effect on the investigator differs from its motive.
- [mechanism] A plausible staged event, such as a relocation, can explain away a hidden loss, so the audience first accepts the cover story before discovering the concealment. When: The audience should accept a plausible explanation and later learn it was constructed. Why: The mundane cover story absorbs the audience's attention and suspicion.
- [mechanism] A widely discussed, separate crime draws attention and provides cover for the real offence, even when the two are unconnected. When: A second plausible event coincides with the real crime. Why: Attention and expectation are directed toward the decoy.
- [mechanism] An authority figure's false explanation steers the audience toward a wrong culprit, so the audience stops weighing clues that point elsewhere. When: when a mystery needs the audience to commit to a wrong suspect before the reversal. Why: the audience trusts the authority figure's account and treats it as settled.
- [behavior] A supernatural explanation can divert attention from a human with access, because it removes any human actor from consideration. When: When an unseen or supernatural agent seems to explain an event. Why: An explanation that excludes humans makes the human suspects easy to overlook.
- [behavior] A culprit hinted at midway but overshadowed by other suspects reads as a fresh reversal when finally tested. When: the hinted suspect is tested late. Why: Earlier suspicion has been spent on other characters, so the late test feels new.
- [rule] Place incomplete text, such as a torn note with blanks, offering several valid completions so players must test which fits the torn edge. When: Designing written clues in a mystery. Why: Players must assemble meaning from fragments and test fit rather than accept the first reading.
- [rule] Resolve every red herring and decoy explicitly before the story ends, accounting for each one introduced; unresolved misdirection reads as cheating or error and undermines trust. Why: Readers and players expect misdirection to be explained.
- [rule] Make each decoy testable against evidence the player already has, dismissed through a fact it cannot explain rather than declared false. When: When a decoy is planted or offered to the player. Why: A decoy no later evidence can resolve reads as cheating; a testable decoy rewards careful reasoning.
- [rule] Design clues with two valid readings, such as torn cloth suggesting a brawl or a tumble, then add a later clue that flips or settles the reading.
- [rule] Give each clue an ordinary early reading and a later one appearing after a key discovery, reusing planted items so the reveal reframes known evidence. When: Designing clues in a level, puzzle chain or mystery twist. Why: An item gains meaning once the player makes a key discovery; reframing familiar evidence rewards earlier observation.
- [rule] Tag decisive-looking evidence as possibly coincidental, then build red-herring suspects from it, so players are misled by a fair case rather than by design cheating.
- [rule] Include decoy events, such as fake sounds, alarms or staged monsters, that draw players or guards away; record time cost in world state and offer an in-game test exposing them. When: Designing a generated dungeon.
- [rule] Design each obvious answer to fail on one checkable observable, such as a monster's supposed route blocked by a locked door, so players can test and reject it. When: designing a misleading but solvable explanation. Why: Rewards careful players who test before concluding.
- [rule] A decoy item, such as a second set of tracks or a spare key, must carry enough detail for the player to test it against the layout.
- [rule] Place the critical fact in a passage that reads as backstory, not as a direct answer to the obvious question. When: writing NPC dialogue with clues. Why: Players who keep listening find it; players who only ask direct questions miss it.
- [rule] Leave a lure unresolved, so the player has a reason to return to that NPC later. When: Designing NPC side leads.
- [rule] Avoid accidental red herrings that cluster on one NPC unless the cluster is meant to resolve to a single schedule or item.
- [rule] Vary decoy clues in position and detail so they do not repeat exactly, since identical generated decoys give players a tell. When: Generating decoy clues from a template. Why: Exact repetition reveals the generator, letting players separate decoys from real clues.
- [rule] Plant a plausible false location for a stolen item, so players who assume the obvious answer find their assumption unsupported. When: designing a mystery's solution path. Why: Tests whether players check premises.
- [rule] Place decoy objects that look valuable but lead nowhere as red herrings within clutter.
- [rule] Test a suspicious link before acting on it, since a shadowing figure may be unconnected to the case. When: A figure appears linked to the case but the link is unproven. Why: Unverified links lead to wrong confrontations.
- [rule] Give a red herring suspect a strong motive and a mock verdict to mislead players before the real culprit is exposed. Why: a convincing false verdict delays the true answer.
- [rule] A red-herring NPC can carry a secret that forms a side quest rather than part of the central mystery. When: designing suspicious characters that are not central to the plot. Why: Separate secrets reward exploration without confusing the main investigation.
- [rule] Place irregular spacing at phrase boundaries in an inscription as a fair hint, leaving room for the player to test each possible split. When: Designing a coded document or wall inscription. Why: Players notice the crowding and can use it to divide the message.
- [rule] Place signs of disturbance, such as a broken container or displaced object, that imply an event, with an innocent explanation players must rule out.
- [rule] Hold a major connection back until a region ends, and plant hints the player recognizes only in hindsight. When: quest chains spanning regions.
- [rule] Add a suspicious side encounter that resolves to nothing, teaching players to verify leads instead of pursuing every anomaly.
- [rule] Make the clues on the true path at least as easy to find as those on the false path.
- [rule] Let an apparent culprit with a motive prove innocent, and place the true clue in a quieter room.
- [rule] Give a silent NPC a surface excuse first and a deeper hidden reason later, with the reason findable through other characters as players gather clues.
- [rule] Let a locked NPC hint that a secret exists without revealing its content, so the player's need to know drives exploration.
- [rule] Leave the true route as the last unexcluded option and place a physical clue for it, such as a hook, a rope or worn ledges. When: Designing a locked-room solution. Why: The surviving option should be clearly supported.
- [rule] Build clue chains of two or three links, so each discovery points clearly to the next location or item. When: when structuring a sequence of environmental clues. Why: short chains keep the player's path clear while still rewarding reasoning.
- [rule] Build an event that has two plausible explanations, so the player must choose a test that separates them. When: when designing a mystery scene with a deduction goal. Why: a discriminating test turns ambiguity into a decision.
- [rule] Build conflicting NPC descriptions on purpose, so players must check physical evidence to decide which is true. When: When designing witness conflicts as puzzles. Why: Physical evidence gives players a way to resolve contradictions.
- [rule] Add idiosyncratic features to important items so that their provenance can be checked by the player. When: Designing clues whose origin matters to the plot. Why: Unique physical features let the player match a copy to its source.
- [rule] Give concealed items a telegraph such as a bulge, clink or unnatural gait so careful players can infer hidden loot or enemies.
- [rule] Make a cover-up ambiguous by offering a guilty reading and a protective reading, and define the possible causes of an incident in advance with the behaviour each predicts. When: When designing suspect concealment in a game mystery. Why: Players must test which reading the other clues support.
- [rule] Do not accept a neat invented mechanism, such as secret stairs or hidden panels, until you confirm the real construction allows it. When: a proposed solution relies on hidden structure.
- [rule] Give look-alike NPCs a visible costume or prop change, plus a record such as a portrait or marked token, so careful players can resolve the confusion.
- [rule] Place objects that look identical but differ in weight or material, so players must test them to find the altered or trapped one. When: Designing a puzzle with apparent duplicates. Why: Testing reveals differences that inspection cannot.
- [rule] Hide a clue in a name, sign or inscription whose letters only make sense when compared with another location's text.
- [rule] Place objects that are ambiguous alone and only resolve in combination with other clues, so the player must connect them. When: designing clue placement in rooms.
- [rule] Offer a tidy false ending that resolves the visible threat while leaving a hidden thread for players who check details.
- [rule] Do not rely on an inventory comparison when the baseline is uncertain, because a poor memory of the original state gives poor results. When: the original state of a space is poorly remembered. Why: A comparison is only as reliable as its reference state.
- [rule] Give a suspicious discovery an innocent-sounding cause, and leave a clue elsewhere that contradicts it. When: Designing a body, stash or other suspicious find. Why: The contradiction rewards attentive players.
- [rule] Let an ally NPC offer a benign explanation for a suspicious event as a red herring that the player must test before accepting. When: When an ally NPC explains away a suspicious event. Why: Testing the benign reading keeps the player engaged rather than settled early.
- [rule] Build a red-herring outcome where the strongest reaction points to the less guilty suspect, forcing the player to re-check. When: designing a confrontation scene with two suspects. Why: a misleading strongest signal makes the player re-examine the evidence.
- [rule] Use a misdirect that is literally true, so the clue supports the eventual reveal rather than contradicting it when the truth comes out. When: Building a false suspicion that will later be explained. Why: A clue that is true but misread keeps trust in the story, because the audience can recall it as fair once the reveal lands.
- [rule] Give a misleading clue two competing readings in the same scene, and have the investigator correct one immediately so the error is visible. Why: the player sees how the error arose.
- [heuristic] Make hidden text react to a specific tool or environmental element, such as a torch or brazier, since players otherwise dismiss blank items as worthless. When: Designing secret messages or hidden information in a level. Why: Tool-triggered reveals reward experimentation and inventory use.
- [heuristic] An accurate observation or background lore can still support the wrong conclusion; check whether it actually shows what it is claimed to show against specific evidence.
- [heuristic] A suspicious-seeming tool or action, such as hiding an item, can have a harmless explanation; test it before treating it as incriminating. When: designing a misleading action that players will investigate. Why: A benign reveal rewards closer inspection and prevents players from accepting first impressions.
- [heuristic] An in-world newspaper or bulletin can present an obvious motive as fact, or credit an NPC with the player's deductions, rewarding players who check alternative explanations.
- [heuristic] Plant a decoy suspect with surface traits that look guilty, and provide a quick test that clears them. When: Designing a mystery with multiple suspects. Why: A fair test lets players eliminate the decoy through reasoning.
- [heuristic] Design a red-herring suspect whose motive and route are discoverable, so the plausible sequence collapses when the player tests one required condition. When: when designing suspects for a mystery. Why: The player reconstructs the same case and the failing condition exposes the red herring.
- [heuristic] Examine seemingly absurd possibilities rather than dismissing them, since preconceived ideas can hide the true answer. When: an investigator's expectations rule out an unusual explanation. Why: preconceptions narrow the search.
- [heuristic] The most incriminating detail may support innocence under another reading, so check each damning fact against alternative explanations. When: Evidence appears to point strongly at one person. Why: Each fact can fit more than one story.
- [heuristic] A theory may explain some evidence yet fail on one critical detail; name that detail to test the theory. When: A plausible theory is offered for the case. Why: One unexplained key fact can overturn an otherwise coherent explanation.
- [heuristic] End each scene with an open question that the next scene in another thread partly answers, keeping the story moving between threads. When: Structuring a story that alternates between investigators or locations. Why: Partial answers sustain interest and carry the audience forward.
- [heuristic] Check absorbent surfaces near a written document for a reversed impression, since it can survive after the original is removed. When: The original document is not in hand.
- [heuristic] When a clue seems impossible on its own, look for a second, outside source that supplies the missing link, then check that link against the dates. When: a statement in one source seems to contradict the other known facts. Why: A connecting fact often sits in a source about a different subject, outside the usual archive.
- [heuristic] A ransacked room can hold a mismatched inventory whose real purpose is to hide the one object the raider sought, prompting players to question the cover story. When: When designing ransacked or looted locations. Why: Odd loot patterns invite players to look for a motive behind the obvious culprit.
- [heuristic] Plant decoy items that support one theory while weakening another, so the player must weigh them. When: Designing clues for a mystery. Why: Ambiguous items force comparison between theories.
- [heuristic] Place missing objects deliberately, such as a weapon never found, as the open question the player must resolve. When: when designing a mystery with a central unknown. Why: an absence gives the player a clear target for investigation.
- [heuristic] Give a room a decoy item that looks like evidence for one suspect but is common in the item pool, and place a matching twin elsewhere. When: when designing a suspect and item misdirection. Why: the player must decide which item truly belongs to the scene.
- [heuristic] Plant a clue that frames a scapegoat NPC and can be disproved by a measured comparison with a known fact.
- [heuristic] A written measurement may hold only for one part of a chamber, so a careful player can catch the error by checking the level's geometry.
- [heuristic] Design inconsistent NPC actions, such as a debtor who keeps spending, as clues that, linked together, reveal a hidden employer. When: Building a mystery with a concealed patron. Why: Players who connect contradictions reach a motive they can confront.
- [heuristic] Place a room whose contents its occupant's role cannot afford, so the player is prompted to look for hidden income or a secret stash. When: Designing a suspect's home or workplace. Why: A mismatch between role and possessions gives the player a reason to search.
- [heuristic] Let each accusation rest on several independent clues, and expose one weak link as a late twist.
- [heuristic] An object with a known theft history can serve as a built-in motive or target, because the history sets up its role before any theft occurs. When: designing a heist-style objective or target object. Why: A known history gives players a reason to expect the object to be taken, shaping their expectations.
- [heuristic] Leave the owner of a planted item ambiguous until a later scene, so the player must keep the item and revisit it.
- [heuristic] Build a puzzle on a regular, learnable cycle, such as water levels or door states, and expect players to infer the hidden state from observable signs.
- [heuristic] Give containers and labels mismatched details, such as weight, finish or handwriting, that a careful player can compare against each other.
- [heuristic] Give each scene several alternative readings so the player must choose the one that fits the other clues. When: when designing ambiguous scenes for deduction. Why: Multiple readings make the player test hypotheses rather than accept one story.
- [heuristic] Design visual cues such as lit windows or moving shadows so they can be wrong, letting players test their assumptions. When: Signalling occupancy or activity in a level. Why: A cue that can mislead rewards checking rather than blind trust.
- [heuristic] Make a vivid rumour a red herring whose only flaw is one fact the player can test.
- [heuristic] Use plausible non-criminal explanations, such as a financial motive or an unusual hidden cause, as red herrings that absorb attention. When: building misdirection into a mystery. Why: reasonable alternatives are accepted without further checking.
- [heuristic] Resolve each red herring by closing its link to the real plot, after leaving that link open long enough to feel fair; an unresolved lead reads as a design error. When: When a decoy suspect or misleading clue is planted. Why: An unresolved decoy makes the mystery feel unfair, and players treat an unexplained lead as a mistake in the design.
- [heuristic] A suspicious NPC can be explained by a harmless cause, such as a patrol or a debt collector, with the true cause revealed later. When: Designing NPC behaviour that looks suspicious. Why: Harmless explanations keep the player engaged until the real cause is shown.
- [heuristic] A believable second culprit diverts suspicion from the true one, and the existence of that suspect makes the real culprit harder to see. When: a mystery needs a misdirect that holds until late in the story. Why: Players accept a plausible alternative and stop searching for the true answer.
- [heuristic] Plant the innocent cause of a red herring earlier in the story, so the explanation does not feel like a cheat when it arrives. When: Resolving a suspicious detail that was innocent all along. Why: Readers feel cheated when the explanation appears only at the end without earlier setup.
- [heuristic] Red herrings work best when each one explains some of the observed facts, so they remain plausible until tested. When: Designing misleading suspects in a mystery. Why: A decoy that explains nothing is quickly dismissed.
- [heuristic] Misdirection works best when the wrong theory is coherent and backed by plausible evidence, such as shared secrets and an engagement that serves one party's interest. When: Designing a false theory the player should adopt for a time. Why: Coherence and supporting evidence make the wrong theory hard to reject.
- [heuristic] Let an investigator's staged display mislead other characters, so the reader does not have to do all the misdirection work alone. When: Steering a character toward a false suspect in front of the audience. Why: A visible staged act gives the false lead a concrete, believable basis.
- [heuristic] Place a detail that undercuts the main accusation in a passing aside, where the player is likely to move past it quickly. When: Writing testimony or dialogue that should later be re-read as contradictory. Why: Players skim asides, so the detail survives unnoticed on first pass and rewards attentive re-reading.
- [procedure] 1) For each indication, state the innocent route by which it could have arrived. 2) Rank it by how specifically it ties to one person. 3) Judge whether it would hold up as evidence. When: when several partial clues point the same way.
- [procedure] 1) Build a claimant or rival faction that looks central to the mystery. 2) Let players invest effort in it. 3) Reveal a fact that disqualifies it. 4) Let players re-evaluate the remaining leads. When: when designing a misleading lead. Why: a disqualifying fact forces players to re-evaluate their assumptions.
- [procedure] 1) Show a clue. 2) Show a critique of the official reading. 3) Show the full reconstructed sequence. When: for puzzle or story reveals. Why: each stage deepens the reading.
- [procedure] 1) Give the player a convincing wrong explanation early, such as a rival faction or prankster. 2) Place a later clue that contradicts it. 3) Prompt the player to re-evaluate rather than silently accepting the old theory. When: When structuring misdirection in a mystery. Why: A staged contradiction turns the false lead into a test the player must actively resolve.
- [tradeoff] A countdown alone clarifies timing but not the real threat; pairing it with a misleading false target hides danger at the cost of making the eventual reveal feel unfair if clues were never planted. When: Designing a timed reveal with a hidden threat. Why: Suspense depends on the reader knowing when, while misdirection depends on the reader not knowing what.
- [pitfall] Filling every gap with a sinister explanation misleads investigators; the simplest explanation is often true, so include clues pointing to ordinary motives rather than one grand conspiracy. When: Designing mystery plot structure. Why: Ordinary motives keep the mystery grounded and believable.
- [pitfall] A sudden reversal of opinion about a character is credible only if the audience has already seen supporting evidence; without earlier setup it reads as a cheat and damages trust.
- [pitfall] Reading an unexplained absence as sinister when an innocent explanation exists, such as a person simply unseen for a while, misleads the investigation. When: A household member goes unseen.
- [pitfall] A plausible story can absorb contrary details if they are not checked one by one, and an explanation that sounds complete can end the search for alternatives. When: Accepting an explanation because it sounds convincing. Why: Narrative coherence lowers the perceived need to test each detail.
- [pitfall] A witness can give a correct count of visible figures while being wrong about what those figures are, so the number is accurate but its implication misleads. When: a testimony rests on a headcount. Why: Counting observed objects does not reveal their true status, such as a dead person among the living.
- [pitfall] A clue can be read to fit a popular theory instead of being tested against it, so the same fact seems to confirm a conclusion reached earlier. When: an explanation has become fashionable. Why: fashion lets the theory absorb evidence without proof.
- [pitfall] Do not accept a demonstration as proof when one side controls both the props and the timing of the reactions. When: Evaluating a demonstration offered as evidence. Why: Control over props and timing lets one side produce any reaction it wants.
- [pitfall] A single search that finds no hole does not solve a sealed-room problem, and earlier searchers may have disturbed the scene. When: Investigating a locked room after others have already searched. Why: One check is incomplete and prior disturbance can hide or fake evidence.
- [pitfall] Reading a sealed space too literally makes the player never consider what has been moved across its boundary.
- [pitfall] Trusting a marker without checking it against terrain or prior knowledge walks players into a trap, and poor lighting makes such markers harder to catch.
- [pitfall] Tidying a moved object can set off a trap, so the object should be examined for danger before anyone touches it.
- [pitfall] Each lock or light has a plausible innocent explanation, so the puzzle lies in their combination rather than in any single clue. When: Interpreting a single door or light state. Why: A single state alone rarely proves wrongdoing; the combination carries the evidence.
- [pitfall] Revealing a red herring's weakness too early removes the misdirection and makes the real mystery feel like an afterthought; keep the true cause unexplained after the decoy is exposed. When: When pacing the reveal of a decoy suspect's weakness. Why: The decoy must stay credible until the player has been misled long enough, and a resolved-looking case closes the player's curiosity.
- [pitfall] A striking detail, such as a loud object or animal, can pull attention away from the scene that matters. When: when a dramatic side event occurs during a crime. Why: Vivid events dominate attention and divert it from the key evidence.
- [pitfall] A suspect who points at another person may be offering a red herring or an honest correction, so both possibilities must be tested before trusting the lead. When: A suspect shifts blame onto someone else. Why: Redirection can look convincing whether it is deceptive or accurate.
- [pitfall] A red herring can be a real person with a genuine motive who is still not the culprit, so a suspect's guilt in one matter does not prove guilt in another. When: When an early arrest or suspect seems to fit the case. Why: A real offender may be unrelated to the central crime, misleading the investigation.
- [pitfall] A red herring can pass as a central clue, or a real clue can be dismissed as a red herring; each detail should be tested against the whole scene. When: When designing or reading a mystery with misleading details. Why: Misjudging which details matter can send the solver down the wrong path.
- [pitfall] Explaining away one strange event while leaving another unaccounted for makes the whole explanation look selective and unconvincing. Why: Partial coverage invites the audience to doubt the entire explanation.
- [fact] Accumulated coincidence can build a strong case against an innocent suspect, leaving the real culprits unseen.
- [fact] A substance that has barely spread from its injection site has not yet acted on the body, so it cannot explain a death that follows soon after. When: When a body shows the substance has not spread. Why: Effects depend on how far the substance has reached the body.
- [fact] Evidence can point strongly at the wrong person and still survive a convincing demonstration pointing elsewhere.
- [fact] A reflected image can make a person appear to stand where no one is, and a mirror at a corridor's end can make someone far off look like they came from inside. When: A reflective surface is present in a scene. Why: Reflection places images at positions that differ from the real figures.

## emotion and fear in testimony
- [mechanism] Fear and an instruction to stay still can fix attention on one spot, so ambiguous shapes such as a fold of cloth are perceived as a threatening figure. When: A person is frightened and told to remain still while in an unfamiliar or dark space. Why: Focused attention plus fear makes ambiguous stimuli read as threats.
- [mechanism] Fear of convicting an innocent person raises the proof threshold, so doubtful reviewers tend toward acquittal. When: reviewers face an uncertain case. Why: the cost of error makes them demand more.
- [mechanism] A scene of fear can freeze pursuers, giving the attacker time to escape. When: an attack is staged amid fear. Why: Fear paralyses pursuit.
- [mechanism] After a hidden event, a witness's fear shifts to the practical problem of escape, with time pressure set by others' movements. When: After a concealed witness has observed an event. Why: Practical urgency replaces fear and keeps tension.
- [mechanism] A character who can only wait under a deadline feels intensified pressure, because the lack of control adds to the time threat. When: when the character cannot act on the deadline. Why: loss of control compounds the time threat.
- [mechanism] A witness's fear of consequences is the lever that draws out a concealed connection; visible panic signals that the witness is ready to talk. When: A witness is caught hiding a connection that matters. Why: Fear makes the cost of silence feel greater than the cost of speaking.
- [mechanism] Strong emotional shock changes what people reveal and how clearly they recall events, so reports taken during distress are less reliable. When: when a witness is interviewed right after a frightening or distressing event. Why: Intense feeling disrupts memory encoding and willingness to disclose.
- [behavior] Fear and expectation inflate confidence in brief or partial sightings, so frightened observers may report imagined threats, such as faces in windows, as clear proof. When: a witness is under fear, or an area is already alarming. Why: Fear fills gaps in partial views, making accounts more vivid than accurate. (x2)
- [behavior] Fear of a feared or criminal group, or of informers, may silence witnesses until the threat is exposed or removed, so silence can reflect fear rather than ignorance. When: witnesses decline to speak about a feared group or secret organisation. Why: Fear of retaliation or informers suppresses testimony independently of what the witness knows.
- [behavior] Fear, illness or strong expectation shapes what is heard, so sounds are recalled as more than was perceived and ordinary noise is read as threat. When: a witness is agitated, already expects something, or hears sounds after a frightening event. Why: Emotional and bodily states and prior expectation colour what is heard and remembered.
- [behavior] Flush, pallor, trembling or sudden tone change is a sign to note, not proof of deception; innocent fear or embarrassment can cause it. When: a witness or suspect reacts strongly to questioning or shown evidence. Why: Emotion has many causes, including fear, embarrassment or protecting someone.
- [behavior] Awkward manner, avoidance, tears or reticence often come from embarrassment, fatigue or a wish to bury a matter, as well as guilt. When: a witness avoids a painful subject or seems awkward. Why: Embarrassment and fatigue look like guilt from outside.
- [behavior] A frightened or guilty listener may mishear speech and fill in missing words, so their account of what was said can be wrong. When: a witness recounts a conversation or sound under fear or guilt. Why: fear and guilt shape what a person perceives and recalls.
- [behavior] A frightened or grieving witness may fit an ambiguous word to a familiar idea, so their interpretation of it needs checking.
- [behavior] Anxiety and fear of appearing weak can push an investigator to settle on a theory before the facts are gathered.
- [behavior] A witness speaking in anger or grief describes a suspect's character in detail, often revealing traits and motives without meaning to. When: Interviewing an emotionally involved witness. Why: Strong feelings loosen restraint and invite characterization.
- [behavior] A witness who fears for their life may shade or withhold what they say, so the account can be less complete or less accurate than their knowledge allows. When: when a witness is threatened or frightened. Why: fear changes what the witness is willing to reveal.
- [behavior] Posture and facial tension before a person speaks can signal fear, and an investigator can use that reading to choose how to approach them. When: a person arrives visibly distressed. Why: body language shows emotion before any words.
- [behavior] A guarded witness may suddenly become warm or genial when offered a tempting claim, revealing an interest they had been hiding. When: the witness is offered something they want. Why: the reaction shows what the words conceal.
- [behavior] People may delay approaching a feared person or scene, so discovery can come hours after an event and stretch the timeline. When: a discovery is delayed. Why: fear of the person or scene.
- [behavior] A suspect subjected to a pointed test may hold back anger and comply, and the restraint itself becomes evidence of how they respond to pressure. When: A suspect is challenged in private. Why: Controlled reaction under suspicion reveals character as much as the test result.
- [behavior] Words heard during an emotional moment stay vivid in memory, making the witness feel their meaning is reliable even when the interpretation is wrong. When: a witness recalls words spoken in a charged moment. Why: emotional tone strengthens memory of the words but not of their meaning.
- [behavior] Fear, tears and confusion make witnesses poor judges of what their words might damage, so their statements can harm or help a party unintentionally. When: when a witness is distressed. Why: Strong emotion impairs judgment about consequences.
- [behavior] A person who fears assassination may suspect even trusted employees, so a victim's fears can point suspicion toward insiders. When: a victim expressed fear of being killed. Why: fear extends to people close by.
- [behavior] A strong fear or feeling is not evidence, but it is a useful cue to search the place it points at. When: when a character feels a strong unexplained fear. Why: Fear can point to a real hiding place even when it proves nothing.
- [behavior] A suspect who asks how much you know reveals their own fear; vague answers grow that uncertainty.
- [behavior] A suspect may pause before answering a question about a fact already stated, and the pause can signal concealment. When: when asked to repeat or confirm an account already given. Why: a false version must be recalled and defended, which causes delay.
- [behavior] A person who fears detection may remove one piece of evidence and forget that an existing precaution already protected it. When: A suspect removes an object from a scene after a crime. Why: Fear of one trace can override knowledge of other protections.
- [behavior] Servants or staff who fear blame may deny involvement, so their denial is weak evidence of innocence. When: staff are questioned after an incident. Why: Fear of consequences motivates denial regardless of guilt.
- [behavior] A witness who fears being blamed adds self-justifying asides and makes sudden topic changes, which colour what they say. When: when a witness is under suspicion. Why: Fear of blame shapes what the witness chooses to emphasise.
- [behavior] A witness who fears losing their job may be guarded and glance at a supervisor, which can shape what they admit. When: when a witness is watched by an employer. Why: Fear of losing a job affects admissions.
- [behavior] A sudden revelation of a secret provokes a reaction that shows whether the witness already knew it and whether others shared that knowledge. When: A witness knows a sensitive fact and will not state it directly. Why: A strong reaction or a question about how it was learned betrays prior knowledge.
- [behavior] A person may use grief, tears, affection or a sudden accusation to steer an interview or to test the listener's reaction. When: when an interview turns emotional. Why: a display can serve a goal even when it looks sincere.
- [behavior] A grieving person's accusation can shape suspicion even when it rests on emotional state rather than evidence. When: when a bereaved relative accuses an investigator. Why: Emotional certainty is persuasive to observers.
- [behavior] Fear and a wish to appear respectable make a witness's account hurried and incoherent, lowering how far it can be trusted. When: when a witness is frightened or concerned for reputation. Why: emotion and self-presentation colour what is reported.
- [behavior] A known threat or grudge can shape the images a witness later recalls, so a dread can reappear as a detail of a supposed event. When: the witness had an earlier fear of or dispute with someone. Why: Prior fear primes the imagination.
- [behavior] A sudden change from warmth to a cold, fixed look can reveal the real mood beneath a performance.
- [behavior] When respected members of a community are jailed, every household feels exposed, and fear spreads well beyond the accused. When: prominent members are arrested during a campaign. Why: Anyone in the same community can plausibly be next.
- [behavior] Strong dread combined with light falling on a face can leave a viewer unable to decide whether the face matches what they expect. When: Close examination under emotional stress. Why: Emotion and light both alter what is perceived at close range.
- [behavior] Fear slows a person's understanding of a sudden threat, so their reactions and comprehension lag behind events. When: A sudden danger unfolds around the person. Why: Fright delays processing of what is happening.
- [behavior] An uncanny image seen from a distance draws attention and frames a place as threatening until later evidence explains it innocently. When: a frightening detail appears before its cause is known. Why: Players attend to threat cues and let them set the explanation.
- [behavior] Hurried or barely legible handwriting can indicate that the writer was frightened when writing. When: messages written under threat. Why: Stress disrupts careful writing.
- [behavior] A frightened witness may invent supernatural or unlikely details to cover a real absence. When: A witness under pressure offers fanciful explanations. Why: Fear pushes people toward inventions that deflect suspicion.
- [behavior] Fear and the sense that help is close shape choices, so a frightened character may avoid calling a guard who is only feet away. When: tense scenes with an ally nearby.
- [behavior] A witness who shuts their eyes in fright observes poorly, so a description given in fear is weaker evidence. When: the witness was frightened during the event. Why: fear impairs what is seen.
- [behavior] Emotionally involved discoverers can hold a wrong idea about a victim's identity, and that idea can persist and resist correction.
- [behavior] A lie about one's whereabouts can come from fear rather than guilt, so a false statement does not prove culpability. When: A suspect is caught in an inaccurate account. Why: People lie to avoid suspicion for reasons unrelated to the crime.
- [behavior] Fear can recast an unexplained extra figure as a supernatural presence, so belief shapes how an observed count is interpreted. When: an unexplained figure appears in a tense situation. Why: Emotional state pushes observers toward supernatural explanations for anomalies.
- [behavior] Jealousy, resentment or fear can bend how an investigator reads a clue, shaping their interpretation of another person's motive. When: An investigator has a personal stake in the people involved. Why: Strong feelings shift attention and reasoning toward conclusions that match the feeling.
- [behavior] A character's own question about whether they would be silenced if discovered reveals inner fear and makes the threat feel personal. When: A character is in danger of being discovered. Why: Internal doubt shows the stakes from the inside.
- [behavior] People spread fear faster than facts, often assuming the worst, such as a dangerous weapon, before anything has been confirmed. When: when a frightening event is reported second-hand. Why: Alarm moves through rumour faster than verification.
- [behavior] A person who fears being seen avoids actions that expose them, so a choice that risks exposure suggests the person did not fear discovery. When: Deciding whether an action was accidental or deliberate. Why: People weigh exposure risk when they act, so risky choices reveal intent.
- [behavior] Emotional drama draws attention away from a quiet object lying on the floor. When: a tense or tearful scene is unfolding. Why: Strong emotion captures attention and hides small details.
- [behavior] A fear of public shame can drive a character's money and relationship decisions as well as their social choices. Why: the same underlying fear shapes several parts of life.
- [behavior] Fear can attach significance to ordinary things, making a guilty person treat even trivial objects as possible witnesses. When: a person is afraid of being discovered. Why: fear inflates the meaning of small details.
- [behavior] Peripheral witnesses who believe they are under suspicion grow frightened and deny knowledge before real questions are asked, making their later answers less reliable. When: A witness is peripheral and their status is unclear, or they expect to be blamed. Why: Fear and fatigue make people defensive, and prolonged waiting or heavy questioning increases anxiety.
- [behavior] A decision-maker afraid of error may stop weighing doubtful evidence and defer to an expert instead, letting the expert's view replace their own judgment. When: when a judge doubts the case but fears being wrong. Why: fear of error discourages a full, independent summing-up.
- [behavior] In a fearful community, the same figure can appear in many people's dreams, so contagion reinforces testimony.
- [behavior] Frightened, overwhelmed people treat trifles as strong confirmation, which makes a weak corroboration standard effectively empty. When: Under fear or pressure. Why: Heightened alarm lowers the bar for what counts as evidence.
- [behavior] After one member recoils, a group tends to draw near together, so the discovery becomes a shared first account.
- [behavior] An alarm that rings on every entry unsettles whoever is inside, so the sound itself adds tension to each arrival. When: when an entry alert sounds in an occupied space. Why: each ring announces an unexpected visitor.
- [behavior] A witness under emotional strain may project meaning onto moving light and water, then report that meaning as something actually seen. When: when a character is frightened or distressed. Why: Mood shapes perception, and imagination fills in shapes.
- [behavior] Some people faint or react strongly at harmless objects, so a fit triggered by a look or object does not by itself show that any harmful cause is present. When: when a strong reaction follows a sight that seems to prove a cause. Why: a phobic response can mimic a real effect.
- [rule] Cross-check a frightened NPC's sighting of a monster or ghost against other witnesses, since it may be a disguised ally. When: designing fear-driven testimony.
- [rule] Give suspects behavioural tells, such as an odd refusal or offer, that the solver must explain; a solution that ignores them should be flagged as weak. When: when designing a mystery's suspects.
- [rule] Treat enthusiasm for a topic as weak evidence of cover, since people often simply care about what they are talking about.
- [heuristic] Separate a witness's feelings and judgments from their factual claims; emotion distorts interpretation more than recalled facts, so concrete timings and signals can stay reliable. When: A witness speaks with strong feeling, such as bitterness, intoxication or emotional investment, about events. Why: Strong feeling colours interpretation and reporting. (x2)
