- [heuristic] A respectable person may commit a crime to protect standing, since losing reputation is the most serious loss to them. When: when a suspect has a reputation to protect. Why: threats to standing motivate people who have little else to lose.
- [heuristic] Leave a character's motive unexplained when the story does not need it, so an unresolved flight or escape adds tension. When: A secondary character's motive is not central to the reveal. Why: An open question keeps the audience engaged after the main twist.
- [procedure] 1) List each party's debts and financial stake. 2) List legal stakes: inheritance position, any marriage settlement, pending divorce. 3) Ask who gains from the death and whether that gain is documented. When: building suspect motives after a death. Why: Written financial positions and legal stakes can be checked against records, while rumoured motives cannot.
- [procedure] 1) List every party with an interest in the death. 2) Eliminate each by a distinct argument, such as their physical state, their character, or whether the plot suits them. 3) Widen the search to the victim's past dealings. When: ranking suspects by motive. Why: listing every interested party avoids stopping at the first.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who wanted the victim dead. 2) List motive lines: business enemies, including anyone whose fortune the victim may have ruined; romance rivals; jilted suitors; former partners of rivals. 3) Answer every question each line raises before reporting. When: starting a case with several possible motives. Why: it organizes the search into separate lines.
- [procedure] 1) List the outcomes a character gains from an act. 2) Propose a motive that produces them. 3) Test the motive against further evidence, including the character's own account. 4) Keep the conclusion provisional until it survives testing. When: inferring why a character acted. Why: explicit steps expose assumptions before they harden into conclusions.
- [procedure] 1) List who dies and in what order. 2) Note what each death yields and to whom. 3) Use the chain as a lead to be tied to means and opportunity. When: Building a motive chain for several linked events. Why: A written chain shows how sequence shifts rewards, and a motive is only a lead until tied to means and opportunity.
- [procedure] 1) List what the crime did not take or gain. 2) Rule out motives the evidence contradicts. 3) Take the remaining motive and find people with a grudge or gain from it. 4) Test each candidate by character and self-interest. When: When the purpose of a crime is unclear and suspects must be narrowed. Why: Eliminating contradicted motives leaves a smaller field of plausible explanations.
- [procedure] 1) List the apparent motives for the event. 2) Test each against the facts. 3) Remove suspects whose motive makes no sense given those facts. When: When many people are connected to an event and several motives seem possible. Why: Testing motives against facts removes suspects without a plausible reason to act.
- [procedure] When ordinary motives all fail, consider less obvious motives, such as protecting a reputation or hiding a loss or fault. When: When the usual motives do not fit the facts. Why: Hidden motives often explain actions that obvious motives cannot.
- [procedure] 1) Where the surface shows no grievance, trace the suspect's past relationships. 2) Interview people who saw the relationship from different angles. 3) Follow the history through the places it unfolded. 4) Link the grievance to a specific need or object. When: When a case has no obvious motive on its surface. Why: A motive built from documented history is easier to connect to the crime than one assumed from appearances.
- [tradeoff] Leaving a late-revealed culprit's motive unstated can weaken the reveal, but a one-word motive such as 'spite' lets players fill the gap so the reveal lands on their own assumptions. When: revealing a culprit's motive late; an unstated motive weakens the reveal, while a minimal motive works when players can supply the reason. Why: Players may notice an unexplained gap after exposure, whereas a minimal motive is completed by the player. (x2)
- [tradeoff] An NPC's journal or confession can state its own motives, and the player can compare those claims against the scene's setup to test them. When: When designing NPC testimony that the player must verify. Why: Stated motives become checkable against physical evidence, so the player weighs claims instead of accepting them.
- [pitfall] Inferring a witness's motive without independent facts is guesswork; a stake does not prove a statement false, only that it needs independent support. When: when a witness has a stake. Why: stake raises doubt but does not establish error. (x2)
- [pitfall] Motive shows who benefits or has reason to act, not that they acted; pair it with opportunity before implicating anyone. When: concluding guilt from benefit, or evidence establishes a motive only. Why: Gain shows incentive, not action; wanting something is not proof of doing it.
- [pitfall] Motive alone does not prove guilt: innocent people can look guilty when a motive is visible, and sincere anger may never be acted upon. When: a suspect has a visible reason to act, or had a reason to kill but no proven act. Why: Motive is compatible with innocence.
- [pitfall] Motive can be supplied by imagination; gaps filled this way should be treated as provisional until the facts are checked. When: A motive is accepted without supporting evidence. Why: Imagined links feel convincing but may not match what happened.
- [pitfall] Assigning intent from a single remark or a single gap risks error; rule out an innocent explanation before settling on a motive. Why: one cue rarely supports a motive without alternatives being excluded.
- [pitfall] Reading motive into an emotion that has another cause, or mistaking coincidence for sabotage, leads to wrong conclusions.
- [pitfall] A relationship detail creates only a possible reason and is not an accusation, so it needs evidence before it is treated as guilt. When: Presenting a relationship detail during an investigation. Why: A possible motive can be mistaken for proof if not checked.
- [pitfall] A rival's motive is not evidence that the rival was present at the scene.
- [pitfall] Building a motive on past resentment alone, without evidence that the benefit was actually at stake, is a common error.
- [pitfall] A stated motive or a chain of links built by one interested party can look like proof when it is only a story. When: an accusation rests on one party's account of another's reasons. Why: The party presenting the chain has a stake in its conclusion.
- [pitfall] Attacking a witness's motive shifts the debate from the content of the evidence to the witness's character.
- [pitfall] A written motive can support two readings depending on who wrote it and whom they feared. When: Interpreting a motive stated in a personal record. Why: Authorship and fear shape what a text really means.
- [pitfall] Framing the motive question too narrowly can point the investigation at the wrong target.
- [pitfall] Seeming inadequate is not evidence of innocence.
- [pitfall] A motive can remain real even after the person who held it has died, so do not dismiss it for that reason alone.
- [pitfall] Assuming every missing record is a cover-up overlooks loss through neglect, such as records never kept or not preserved.
- [pitfall] Envy often presents itself as public concern, which hides a personal motive behind a moral framing.
- [pitfall] Judging a possible accomplice only by financial self-interest can miss non-financial motives such as fear or loyalty that would make joining rational.
- [pitfall] Motives built on hidden secrets are hard to check and can be invented to fit a theory.
- [pitfall] Letting a motive stand alone without checking the alibi or the physical evidence leads to an unsupported accusation. When: when building an accusation from motive. Why: A motive does not establish that a person acted.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a motive because a suspect looks well off misses hidden debts and private money needs, which often surface only later. When: When a suspect appears prosperous. Why: Visible wealth hides financial strain.
- [pitfall] A strong motive can fill gaps in weak evidence and make the case feel conclusive when it is not. When: A suspect has a compelling motive but thin physical or testimonial evidence. Why: Motive is persuasive, so it can mask missing proof.
- [fact] Many people could name someone they wish dead, so starting an investigation from motive narrows little and can point at several people, including associates. When: judging a suspect by motive, starting an investigation from motive rather than evidence, or using motive to choose a suspect. Why: Wanting harm is common, so motive does not discriminate between people.
- [fact] Mistaking the motive is the greatest obstacle to solving a crime, so motive and search pattern should be kept distinct when reasoning. When: When investigating any crime with an unclear purpose. Why: Conflating the two hides the true aim.
- [fact] Murder motives fall into three broad kinds: material gain, a passionate crime, and a killing for an idea that suggests mental derangement.
- [fact] Confessed motives often arise from social pressure such as poverty, fear of poverty, or the wish for better social standing, and are presented by the teller as self-justification. When: A character explains a past act. Why: Social pressure supplies motive, while the teller frames it to justify the act.
- [fact] Past marriages, rivalries, business disputes and romantic competition can each give several people a motive at the same time.
- [fact] A motive can arise from a long-standing legal restriction and an inherited grievance rather than from a single event. When: Investigating property, inheritance or shared-resource disputes. Why: A standing agreement can be the real source of conflict between parties.

## accusation
- [model] A suspect's capacity for a violent act has three separate parts: physical ability, moral acceptance, and nervous capacity for violence. When: testing whether a theory fits a suspect. Why: each part can fail independently.
- [definition] A charge withdrawn with no evidence offered clears the accused differently from an acquittal on the merits.
- [mechanism] Untested suspicion of a person spreads as gossip among neighbours and within a community, hardening into accepted fact or a formal accusation before anyone checks it. When: when a person is publicly suspected before any charge is made. Why: Talk among neighbours reinforces suspicion until it is formalised.
- [mechanism] Public accusation or examination can cost the accused their reputation, support and livelihood before any finding, even if the accusation later fails.
- [mechanism] Acting on incomplete evidence can alert suspects, letting them move assets, destroy proof or prepare alibis before the case is ready. When: Evidence is incomplete and suspects can flee or destroy proof. Why: A warning reaches the target before the investigator can secure the full case.
- [mechanism] A culprit who tightens a frame against a target can expose their own trick, so a visible overreach is a satisfying way to undo them. When: Designing how a villain is caught. Why: Excess effort to incriminate leaves a trace that contradicts the original deception.
- [mechanism] A confrontation overheard in a public place spreads through a town, so a stranger becomes known there before his claims are verified. When: A stranger clashes with officials in public. Why: Public exchanges are repeated, which builds a reputation regardless of accuracy.
- [mechanism] Arrests made on thin grounds tend to collapse once movements are documented, so detainees with no case against them get released.
- [mechanism] Publicly asking a witness whether they noticed a sign forces them to agree or appear foolish, which pushes the group toward the investigator's finding. When: An investigator confronts an expert or official in front of others. Why: Refusing to agree in public risks looking incompetent.
- [mechanism] A vague but heavy warning about a powerful antagonist raises dread without spelling out the consequence.
- [mechanism] Acting on an insufficient accusation can bring consequences from authority figures, such as a reprimand, so procedural error carries its own cost.
- [mechanism] Accusations move from vague descriptions to named people, and first names are drawn from those the public already distrusts.
- [mechanism] Competing claims to the same ground can build lasting hostility between families and neighbours, supplying a motive that later shapes who gets suspected. When: two parties hold overlapping rights to one plot. Why: Contested ground keeps rivalry active across years.
- [mechanism] A scripted accusation can prompt a guilty NPC to act, and the reaction itself can expose a clue the player can notice. When: the NPC is designed to be guilty and the trigger is a stated claim. Why: a direct claim provokes a response the script can use.
- [behavior] Flight, shrieking or collapse by a confronted person can look like guilt, but fear, shame or an innocent explanation can produce the same behaviour. When: when an accused person reacts to the supposed victim or a suspect's behaviour appears to indicate guilt. Why: Fear and shame produce dramatic reactions regardless of responsibility; surface behaviour is ambiguous and the true reason can be benign. (x2)
- [behavior] A distressed witness shows tells such as fidgeting with nearby objects, glancing around the room, flushing, or pulling a hand away. When: A witness is avoiding or struggling with a topic. Why: Discomfort leaks through small bodily movements.
- [behavior] Strong involuntary signs such as clenched hands, trembling lips, or a hateful stare can signal that a person is feeling strong emotion about a trigger. When: A person reacts sharply to a stimulus connected to a concealed matter. Why: Strong feeling about a secret shows in the body before the person speaks.
- [behavior] A witness who feels guilt or fear may confess with a motive that shapes what they stress and what they leave out. When: A witness with a personal stake in the events. Why: Guilt or superstition gives them reasons to speak beyond what they saw.
- [behavior] A guilty suspect may react to an accusation against a loved one with an outburst that reveals guilt, even while insisting the charge is false. When: A suspect hears an accusation against someone they care about. Why: Strong feeling can expose a concealed involvement through an involuntary response.
- [behavior] Accusing a suspect in a populated scene exposes each listener's stake, because everyone reacts at once and their reactions are visible to the others. When: a disclosure is made in front of a group. Why: Listeners have their own interests, so their reactions reveal loyalty and knowledge.
- [behavior] When the culprit is a trusted friend, the audience feels the unmasking emotionally as well as logically, because trust raises what the revelation costs. When: when the culprit is a character the audience has trusted.
- [behavior] A guilty party may reveal themselves after hearing an unverified report that someone else has confessed. When: a suspect is pressed and then hears of another's confession. Why: fear of exposure can push a guilty person to act.
- [behavior] A suspected affair that a household never discusses openly can still create lasting strain that acts as a motive. When: A relationship is suspected but not confronted. Why: Unspoken suspicion builds emotional pressure without resolution.
- [behavior] Apparent willingness to take guilt on oneself can earn leniency from judges, even when the motive offered is weak. When: a culprit appears to exaggerate his own guilt. Why: contrition is read as a mitigating sign.
- [behavior] Officials record a suspect's pallor, stammering and near-collapse as observations, so physical distress becomes part of what they believe about him. When: a suspect is visibly distressed during questioning. Why: questioners interpret physical signs as evidence about the person.
- [behavior] A target who trusts and loves the requester, and who feels guilt, may yield to a request framed as saving the requester's life. When: when the target cannot easily verify the threat. Why: guilt and tenderness override refusal.
- [behavior] An openly violent character draws suspicion as the obvious danger, pulling attention from a hidden threat.
- [behavior] The most visible person with obvious motive and contact tends to become the focus of attention, even without stronger evidence. When: An investigation has one person with a conspicuous link to the victim. Why: Visible motive substitutes for checked evidence and is easy to act on.
- [behavior] A warning that silence may cause suspicion can be heard as a threat, even when the speaker denies any threatening intent. When: a witness with a stake in the outcome hears a caution. Why: The listener interprets the consequence as coercion regardless of intent.
- [behavior] A guilty person who feels exposed often takes unnecessary steps to cover traces, and these steps can draw attention and reveal them. When: a suspect feels threatened by an inquiry. Why: Fear of exposure pushes them to over-act.
- [behavior] A suspect may confess and give a full account when loved ones are present to press them. When: confronting a suspect with family present. Why: pressure from people close to the suspect weakens resistance.
- [behavior] An unwelcome visitor is read as a threat, which raises suspicion among the people already present. When: a newcomer is unwanted by the people in the room.
- [behavior] A guilty person checks every hiding place and detail with dread, fearing a single overlooked trace could become decisive. When: a person has hidden something incriminating. Why: fear makes ordinary traces seem dangerous.
- [behavior] A guilty person may treat a stranger as a witness even when the stranger knows nothing, so fear itself becomes part of the evidence.
- [behavior] A visible, emotional motive such as jealousy can draw investigators toward a false cause while the real concern stays hidden. When: when an obvious emotional motive fits the situation. Why: A plausible surface motive is accepted before its fit with all facts is tested.
- [rule] Shock, grief, fear, worry or illness produce signs like guilt, so never read distress as proof of guilt or knowledge; check it against other evidence first. When: when judging a suspect or witness by emotional or body signs. Why: distress has many causes besides guilt.
- [rule] Unverifiable testimony or accusation can justify opening an inquiry but must never alone settle a person's identity or guilt, since it can implicate innocent people. Why: Prompting investigation and proving guilt are different functions of evidence.
- [rule] Make threats and accusations in scripted scenes checkable against other NPCs' claims and scene objects, so players can expose lies through facts rather than the designer's word. When: when writing NPC accusations, threats or timelines. Why: Checkable claims reward investigation and let players test the accuser instead of simply trusting or distrusting them.
- [rule] Let a suspect's reaction reveal something but keep it ambiguous, so it is never proof on its own.
- [rule] When a suspicion cannot be confirmed, keep distance from the suspect anyway. When: strong suspicion remains without a verdict. Why: avoiding the suspect limits risk while the question stays open.
- [rule] Record vague plans and unverified suspicions as vague or unverified, not as settled fact. When: a witness mentions a plan without details, or a suspicion is presented. Why: Loose talk of a project is not evidence of a decided course of action.
- [rule] Present an identification with independent pieces of evidence, such as a photograph and several witness descriptions, and check whether doubt remains. When: Concluding an identification in front of others. Why: Independent sources make an identification more persuasive than a single claim.
- [rule] Offer a present-evidence dialogue option that changes NPC behaviour, such as hesitation, shifted posture or a slipped name, so the player can read those tells. When: designing NPC confrontation dialogue. Why: Visible reactions give the player a checkable reading of the NPC.
- [rule] When designing a guilty NPC's path, list every action it requires and check each against its motive and risk.
- [rule] Score each non-player character by motive, access to the scene and ability to act, and flag any who hide or alter evidence. When: Building a guilt-tracking system for NPCs in a mystery. Why: Structured scoring makes suspicion trackable and consistent.
- [rule] Design interrogation dialogue so a player can see when a question presupposes guilt. When: designing interrogation dialogue.
- [rule] Track which NPCs believe which accuser and why, so the player must examine the motive as well as the claim.
- [rule] Make the scene of the crime a place the culprit is drawn back to, so the player can catch the culprit returning.
- [heuristic] Hold quietly gathered findings and the decisive accusation until the end of an exchange, so they carry more weight and tension builds across it. Why: Delayed presentation can make evidence more persuasive.
- [heuristic] A promised reward must have a source, so the person who made the promise is the one to find. When: evidence suggests someone was paid to act or stay silent.
- [heuristic] The order in which evidence is presented can differ from the order of events, so the audience meets clues in a constructed sequence.
- [heuristic] Move from a physical trace to the writer's intention: a later line may have been added to produce a particular effect on the reader. Why: the sequence of writing reveals a deliberate choice.
- [heuristic] Treat a name for a figure known only through reports as a working label, not a conclusion, until other evidence confirms the identity. When: A suspect is discussed but never seen clearly. Why: Reports can be wrong, and an early label shapes all later reasoning.
- [heuristic] A mismatch between refined presentation and neglected habits can be the clue itself, because the contrast points to an inconsistent person. When: When a person's appearance and habits seem to belong to different backgrounds. Why: Real people rarely have uniform traces across every area of life.
- [heuristic] Credit rivals for correct observations even when their conclusions were wrong, so every contributor stays inside the shared work. Why: the reveal then completes common work rather than defeating opponents.
- [heuristic] Weigh a claim of a hidden bargain more lightly when it offers nothing that could be checked, and prefer a rebuttal backed by inspectable evidence. When: when comparing an accusation with a rebuttal. Why: unverifiable claims cannot be tested against physical facts.
- [heuristic] A public, costly confession by someone who helped cause a wrong can reverse how the whole story is read, while a free or unwitnessed confession has little effect. When: a character must admit an earlier role in harming another. Why: Witnessed cost gives the admission weight, and the reversal depends on that weight.
- [heuristic] Guilty people often reveal themselves through other behavior and traces, so look for independent signs beyond the accusation itself. When: when an accusation lacks other support.
- [heuristic] Hedging phrases such as reluctant qualifiers often come just before an admission, and signal that a follow-up question is worth asking. When: A witness hesitates or qualifies a statement. Why: Hedges mark the boundary between a denial and a partial admission.
- [heuristic] A witness who watched the street through a crime window clears the street but not the household, so it narrows only the external route. When: using a watcher's report to exclude outsiders. Why: Street observation rules out passage outside but not inside the house.
- [heuristic] Do not sum motive or evidence weights naively; the combined effect of two motives can differ from the sum of their separate strengths. When: A suspect-scoring or decision system combines several factors. Why: Motives and evidence can interact in ways a simple total misses.
- [heuristic] An accuser who presses hard for one conclusion may be signalling confidence or a stake, so examine why they press before accepting it. When: A prosecutor or accuser is insistent. Why: Eagerness can reveal grounds or interest that bear on the case.
- [procedure] 1) Collect physical proofs for each required category. 2) Explain or remove every unexplained gap. 3) Condense the evidence so the accusation arrives backed by proofs. When: preparing an accusation for a sceptical reviewer. Why: unsupported links invite rejection.
- [procedure] 1) List evidence that could vanish, such as witnesses who may die or lose their faculties. 2) List the readings still open. 3) Accuse only after testing the perishable claims. When: before a formal accusation.
- [procedure] 1) Give the subject assurances of safety first. 2) Unveil the object slowly, under good light. 3) Link its history to the crime. 4) Watch for changes in expression and speech. When: confronting a suspect with an object. Why: lowering the subject's guard first makes reactions easier to read.
- [procedure] 1) Identify who benefits from the death, such as through a will. 2) Identify who controlled access to the victim. 3) Ask who arranged each change in personnel or affairs. When: When a death follows unusual statements, staff changes or legal arrangements.
- [procedure] 1) Lay out the sequence of actions as a numbered, precise account. 2) Name the witnesses. 3) Recall small details to show nothing was overlooked. 4) Offer closure if the suspect confesses before others. 5) Warn of harsher measures if refused. 6) If denied, turn the factual question into a moral one, such as ingratitude. When: a suspect must be pressed publicly. Why: detail and witnesses make the accusation credible, and the offer makes confession the price of closure.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the history of disputes, marriages, refused dowries and business ties among the parties. 2) Date each episode from testimony. 3) Treat the present accusation as the latest step in that history. When: building a motive for an accusation. Why: Motive is usually traced through a long history of relations rather than the single event under dispute.
- [procedure] 1) Record each loss or harm in a community. 2) Link it to any earlier recorded dispute with the blamed person. 3) Show the player how the accusation formed from that link. When: when designing an in-world accusation the player must trace. Why: Visible causal links let players reconstruct how suspicion grew.
- [procedure] 1) Accept the test's rule as the accuser states it. 2) Apply the same test to the accuser under the same conditions. 3) Check whether the accuser passes or fails by that rule. When: a case rests on a test whose validity has been accepted without checking. Why: A rule the accuser cannot pass exposes inconsistency in the accuser's own standards.
- [procedure] 1) State the conclusion first. 2) Name the sources of the facts. 3) Accuse plainly. 4) Offer a bargain for a confession. 5) State the consequence if the confession is refused. When: when silence is driven by shame or social standing and partial evidence needs a confession to complete it. Why: Naming sources shows the case rests on testimony, and an explicit consequence makes the choice concrete.
- [tradeoff] An open unresolved suspicion keeps the true cause hidden, but feels like cheating if never settled, so firm information must arrive in time. When: a suspected crime is used to hide the real cause. Why: unfinished theories erode trust in the story.
- [tradeoff] A public confession ends the matter, while denial keeps the accusation open and invites harsher measures; the audience raises the social cost of denying. When: the player should choose between confessing and denying.
- [tradeoff] An accusation resting on unverifiable testimony builds tension, but gives the player no fair test to disprove it. When: Designing a story accusation the player cannot check.
- [pitfall] A witness's guilt, shock or fear can distort what they perceive and hear, so their certainty or claim may reflect their fears rather than the events.
- [pitfall] Fixing on an early suspect before evidence is fully examined makes investigators gather only incriminating evidence, ignore contrary traces and clearing checks, and stop seeking other culprits. When: An early favourite emerges in an investigation. Why: Commitment to one explanation filters what counts as relevant evidence.
- [pitfall] Confronting or accusing someone in public warns the culprit and associates, giving them time to act and ending any chance of watching them quietly.
- [pitfall] Accusing or acting before evidence supports it outruns proof, risking a wrong arrest or exposing the wrong person.
- [pitfall] Judging people by visible company or affiliations, such as kinship, service or friendship with a convicted person, widens suspicion beyond evidence. When: when a community meets a newcomer whose visitors or affiliations are visible. Why: Associations are easy to see and offer a ready explanation where direct knowledge is missing.
- [pitfall] Vague warnings, notices or planted motives feel like padding, draw irrelevant replies or get discounted; tie each to specific names, dates, places or details. When: when writing public notices, warnings or motive clues. Why: generic gossip carries little weight as evidence.
- [pitfall] An untested suspicion kept private or left as a loose thread is never confirmed or dismissed, hiding the truth; track such suspicions for pursuit or dismissal. When: when someone has a suspicion but doubts it, or a suspicion is raised in dialogue. Why: Untested suspicions cannot be confirmed or dismissed, so the truth stays hidden.
- [pitfall] An accusation made in distress can be undermined when the accuser later calms down and denies it. Why: Emotional state can distort what a witness reports.
- [pitfall] Confronting a witness too early reveals what you already know and lets them adjust their story.
- [pitfall] Announcing an accusation too early ends the interview and removes the chance to observe the suspect's reactions. When: when running an interrogation scene. Why: Early accusation makes the suspect guarded and transparent.
- [pitfall] Confronting a suspect before the physical test is complete weakens the case, because the match is not yet confirmed.
- [pitfall] Challenging a suspect too early can provoke a physical response that overpowers the investigator. When: confronting a suspect before gathering enough evidence. Why: Premature confrontation gives the suspect a chance to act while the investigator is unprepared.
- [pitfall] Vivid impressions of guilt, such as a shifty look, are weak evidence and can mislead as much as they point toward the truth. Why: A striking appearance attaches suspicion to a person without supporting evidence.
- [pitfall] A vague label for an impulse can stand in for a verified cause and hide the real motive from the audience.
- [pitfall] Reading a suspect's distress at arrest as a confession ignores that a clever suspect could explain the same reaction another way.
- [pitfall] Sales records may state only a vague purpose, such as general medicinal use, which tells the investigator little about the buyer's intent.
- [pitfall] Assigning a trait to one parent without evidence, when the behaviour could come from either, misleads the reader. When: Inferring a trait from a child's conduct. Why: The child's conduct alone cannot identify which adult caused it.
- [pitfall] A public confrontation gives a suspect an audience and sympathy, and onlookers can turn against the person doing the confronting. When: when an arrest or accusation is made in front of a crowd. Why: onlookers side with the person being pressed.
- [pitfall] Treating every normal routine as suspicious is an error, because ordinary households are usually ordinary and an innocent surface is not evidence of guilt. Why: suspicion must be targeted to inconsistencies, not to all normality.
- [pitfall] Vague official causes of death, such as heart failure after shock, are hard to test and can close an inquiry without settling it.
- [pitfall] Treating every silence as proof of guilt leads to false conclusions; a withheld topic is an inference to be tested, not a confirmed fact. When: Silence has an obvious innocent cause or no link to the crime. Why: Silence can come from many motives unrelated to the crime.
- [pitfall] A joke about guilt left unaddressed can later be taken seriously, so the writer must track such remarks to avoid an unresolved loose thread. When: A suspicion remark is dismissed as a joke and not followed up. Why: Dropped remarks read as careless when the story later depends on them.
- [pitfall] An overheard threat can be misjudged by the listener, and the speaker's explanation may be impossible to test. When: when a threat is heard from another room.
- [pitfall] Inferring a culprit's great skill from one neat arrangement overrates them, since a neat setup may be the product of a simple plan. When: Assessing a suspect's capability from staged evidence. Why: Tidy evidence can look sophisticated without reflecting real ability.
- [pitfall] A suspect who looks guilty may still be guilty; clearing them by constraint works only if the facts behind the constraint hold. When: when clearing a suspect on physical grounds. Why: An unreliable premise can clear the wrong person.
- [pitfall] A suspect who is ill, poor or upset can look guilty through erratic behaviour alone, and interrupting him blocks the explanation that could clear him.
- [pitfall] Accusers who keep naming ever more respected people overreach, and a trusted target's innocence can expose the whole accusation. Why: Doubt spreads once a trusted name is hit.
- [pitfall] A vague charge such as works beyond nature can cover almost any misfortune and needs no clear link between act and harm. When: A charge names no specific act or victim. Why: Nothing in the charge can be tested.
- [pitfall] A speaker who reports talk rather than facts often stays vague on purpose, which makes rumor hard to check.
- [pitfall] Hope that a favoured suspect is guilty makes an investigator want a match, so the measurable test must still be run. When: A suspect fits the investigator's theory emotionally. Why: Desire for a conclusion biases how the evidence is weighed.
- [pitfall] Pallor and silence on recognition can signal fear of the investigator, grief or guilt, so the reaction alone does not decide which. When: when a witness reacts strongly to being recognized. Why: Several emotions produce the same visible reaction.
- [pitfall] Relying on folk beliefs that guilty people always give themselves away or return to the scene can lead to wrong conclusions, since most killers escape detection. When: Reasoning about who committed a crime from assumptions about guilty behaviour. Why: Such beliefs are not supported by evidence and mislead the investigator.
- [pitfall] Accusing someone without showing evidence invites a firmer denial and fills the silence with unprompted details and protests. When: Confronting a suspect with a claim alone. Why: Without proof the suspect has nothing to retract and every incentive to push back.
- [pitfall] Blaming the tracker before checking the environment for other sources of the same smell misreads a fault that lies in the scene. When: A tracker goes wrong. Why: Other sources can explain the error.
- [fact] A grand jury presentment rests on general reputation and formally delivered testimony, refers suspects to a higher court for custody and further proceedings, and states suspicion without proving it.
- [fact] Innocent people sometimes enter a guilty plea as a tactic, so a guilty plea does not reliably show actual guilt.
- [fact] Objects show how they were used, not the intention behind it, so motive must come from other evidence. When: reconstructing a scene from traces alone.
- [fact] A weak motive does not exclude a suspect, since motives for serious acts are sometimes weak, and careful planning can indicate a motive strong enough for deliberate action. When: Judging whether a proposed motive is sufficient. Why: Motive strength is not the same as proof of action.

## hearsay and secondhand testimony
- [definition] Hearsay is a claim relayed from someone else, such as a dying person's words, and it is harder to verify than a witness's own observation. When: when a key account comes secondhand. Why: The reporter may not know the points relayed, and the original speaker is unavailable to confirm them.
- [definition] Second-order knowledge is what one party knows about another party's knowledge, such as a holder knowing that the victim knows the holder has a secret.
- [definition] Hearsay is a witness repeating what others said, while direct observation is what the witness perceived personally.
- [mechanism] Each person who relays a claim adds distance from the original observation, may embellish or misremember it, and loses precision, so reliability drops with every link. When: a claim reaches a listener through intermediaries. Why: each relay adds distance from the original fact.
- [mechanism] Each extra teller in a chain of sources adds framing and distance, so the audience must judge how far the account can be trusted. When: A story or clue reaches the audience through intermediaries. Why: Every relay can reshape the account, and its origin becomes harder to verify.
- [mechanism] Evidence relayed through several retellings loses reliability at each link, so the chain of who saw what and who repeated it should stay visible to the audience. When: A case depends on what one person says another person saw. Why: Each retelling adds distortion, and the audience must judge every link to weigh the account.
- [mechanism] Information passed through several speakers shifts in wording and meaning, so it must be checked against the original speaker. When: When testimony reaches the investigator secondhand. Why: Each relay adds a paraphrase and the relayer's colouring.
- [mechanism] Testimony relayed through another person is filtered twice: by the original witness's memory and again by the teller's retelling. Why: Each retelling adds room for gaps and error.
- [mechanism] A simple prearranged signal, such as a light in a window meaning the coast is clear, can be read by a relay who does not know the full plan. When: an accomplice must pass status without knowing the purpose. Why: the reader needs only the part of the meaning that concerns them.
- [mechanism] A person who relays a suspicion while disliking the suspect can carry that hostility into the rumour, making it sound more certain than the evidence supports.
- [mechanism] Each relay in a gossip chain can add, drop or distort details, so information passed through servants or several people loses precision and gains exaggeration. When: Information reaches a character through several people. Why: Each retelling reshapes details; each intermediary can misremember, mishear or reinterpret them.
- [behavior] Hearsay drifts and grows with each retelling as listeners add or alter detail, so the most elaborate version is often least reliable and far from its origin. When: a secret or story passes by word of mouth through several people before reaching an investigator. Why: each retelling adds material and loses the original source.
- [behavior] A witness's report reaches a listener already shaped by the witness's wording, emphasis and wish to look competent. When: a character passes on information they did not see firsthand. Why: Speakers select and stress details to protect their own standing.
- [behavior] Hearsay about hidden secrets and family history suggests intrigue, and witnesses weigh such surmise differently, so each source's reliability varies. When: Witnesses repeat rumours about a person's past. Why: Surmise is offered without evidence.
- [behavior] A go-between relaying a story may betray their own doubts through hedged tone. When: when a third party carries another person's account. Why: The go-between may privately doubt what they carry.
- [rule] Trace relayed claims to a first-hand witness; treat the chain as a lead, not proof, and rely on neither version when gossip conflicts with an official account. When: A clue or claim reaches the investigator only through intermediaries. Why: Secondhand versions drift from the original event; relayed claims can be distorted at any link. (x2)
- [rule] Mark hearsay as hearsay; do not treat a relayed or final rumour, or a precise time no witness observed, as firsthand, even when the relay claims exact knowledge. When: When a witness repeats or describes events they did not observe. Why: Hearsay can be presented as firsthand knowledge. (x2)
- [rule] Label rumour and hearsay with its source and confidence, distinguishing it from firsthand reports so players know what is unverified; keep it for later even if unhelpful now. When: When gathering history from hearsay or presenting rumour in a journal or dialogue. Why: Hearsay may be wrong; heat or indignation in gossip does not indicate knowledge of events. (x2)
- [rule] Treat secondhand testimony relayed through intermediaries as weaker than direct observation, since each relay can shift meaning and lose tone and context. When: when knowledge passes through several people. Why: every intermediary can distort the picture.
- [rule] Separate firsthand observations from relayed accounts and tag each testimony or detail as firsthand, hearsay, or read in a document, so readers can weigh each claim by source. When: when assessing any witness account. Why: second-hand details can be repeated with the same confidence as firsthand memory.
- [rule] Treat an account relayed through another person as unverified and record who passed it on, since a repeater adds no observation and must be checked against the original source. Why: relayed details can distort or lose context.
- [rule] Treat hearsay, rumour, gossip and relayed observations as unconfirmed leads that direct inquiry, not timeline facts or findings, until direct evidence checks them. Why: relays lose precision, and the original observer's viewpoint may have limited what was seen.
- [rule] Second-hand alibis and claims about what another person did need separate confirmation rather than acceptance from the witness who reports them, since they are weaker than direct observation.
- [rule] Make relayed clues, including a quest-giver's rumour, verifiable: they keep the core claim but lose specifics, so give players a way to check or contradict them before acting. When: designing secondhand information. Why: relayed claims need a route to checking.
- [rule] Limit each narrator to what they personally saw and heard, naming the source when relaying others, so readers can assemble the truth from overlapping firsthand accounts. When: when a story depends on several people's testimony or viewpoints. Why: readers can weigh each claim only when they know who observed it.
- [rule] Separate relayed observations from the conclusions drawn from them, and check each conclusion before relying on it. When: several people relay the same event.
- [rule] Separate dramatic detail and personal commentary from the observed facts before weighing a witness's account. When: when a witness's account is vivid or emotionally charged. Why: embellishment can make weak observations seem stronger.
- [rule] Record hearsay with its source, and treat it as evidence of motive only after the original report is confirmed accurate. When: when a witness repeats what someone else said. Why: Hearsay is only as reliable as its original source.
- [rule] Separate reported times and facts from a publication's editorial speculation before using them.
- [rule] Do not rule out a suspect on a third-party description alone; confirm the relevant trait directly, since gossip about age or health can be wrong. When: Relying on gossip or hearsay about a suspect. Why: Secondhand claims are often inaccurate.
- [rule] Do not treat relayed information as confirmed until a second, independent source checks it. When: a fact arrives through an intermediary. Why: relayed accounts can carry distortion.
- [rule] Trace a go-between's message to its original sender, since the messenger may distort it, add content, pursue their own motive, or not share the sender's purpose. When: A key message reaches the investigator through a go-between. Why: The messenger may not know or share the sender's true purpose.
- [rule] Do not rely on eavesdropped or relayed testimony for precise facts without a firsthand source or corroboration. When: when a fact rests on overheard or relayed speech.
- [rule] Trust a message passed through an intermediary only when it carries a credential the recipient can recognise, such as a name or code phrase. When: When a message arrives via a third party. Why: A credential lets the recipient verify the sender.
- [rule] Add a dialogue option where the player relays a cryptic line, and let the NPC's next line depend on whether they understand it.
- [rule] Use remembered secondhand accounts for description, and mark any inference drawn from them, such as materials guessed from how objects were disposed of.
- [rule] Give the player two linked rumours, one blatantly false, that together lure them toward a trap location. When: when designing quest hooks or lures.
- [heuristic] Separate what a person saw directly from what they heard, and record who told each claim, since each retelling loses detail, adds guesses, and lets assumptions pass unnoticed. When: a clue reaches you through other people. (x2)
- [heuristic] Judge a relayed report by each link's access to events, how it was known, honesty and motive; note who first observed each step. When: evaluating testimony passed along by others. Why: access to events determines how reliable a report is.
- [heuristic] Attach a confidence value that drops at each relay step, so an NPC's claim passed through another NPC is weaker than a direct one, modelling unreliable hearsay. When: generating NPC testimony about events. Why: each translation step can lose or distort the core fact.
- [heuristic] Second-hand reports of a dying person's words are open to several readings and cannot settle a matter alone.
- [heuristic] Second-hand testimony needs its own reliability check, since the original source may be wrong or self-interested. When: A person is known only through what another person reported. Why: Each retelling adds a layer of possible distortion.
- [heuristic] Secondhand accounts relay what others saw; weigh them by who told them and how they came to know it.
- [heuristic] A witness who relays the questions they were asked reveals what the questioner was probing for.
- [heuristic] A first-person account gives the absent party's own testimony rather than observers' guesses, but it still needs checking.
- [heuristic] NPC dialogue that relays events secondhand can contain deliberate gaps that players must close with follow-up questions.
- [heuristic] Information overheard or relayed by another person is secondhand, and should be weighed as weaker than direct observation, although a matching physical detail can still strengthen it. When: When a witness reports what they heard through a door or from someone else. Why: Secondhand accounts can be incomplete or mistaken, but independent matches add credibility.
- [heuristic] Rumoured sightings relayed secondhand have weak reliability and should be weighted lower than direct observation. When: a supernatural claim rests on rumour. Why: Each relay adds distortion and no direct check.
- [heuristic] Ask how a second-hand reporter knows a fact, and whether its details match what is already known. A detail that changes between tellings is a warning sign. When: When a rumour or reported fact contains a decisive detail.
- [heuristic] Weigh a report from a hired observer, telegram or distant letter against physical facts and the observer's own reliability, even when it looks authoritative. When: when an absent party's movements rest on secondhand messages.
- [heuristic] A fact passed on secondhand is still usable, but its reliability must be judged separately from its usefulness.
- [heuristic] A motive can be inferred from a third party's report of a document the investigator has not read firsthand; treat the report as a lead to test. When: a document's content is only reported. Why: Secondhand reports can carry motive but may be inaccurate.
- [heuristic] Ask how the same phrasing would be judged coming from a friend, to separate what is said from who said it.
- [heuristic] If a speaker confidently describes evidence never reported in writing, he probably heard it in person, since hearsay usually produces hedged language. When: a speaker claims detailed knowledge of unpublished proceedings.
- [heuristic] Second-hand accounts carry the relayer's own opinions, so check them against what can be observed about the person described.
- [heuristic] Mark entries that rely on secondhand reports as unconfirmed, and weaken any timeline that depends on them. When: A movement is reported by someone who did not witness it. Why: Second-hand accounts can be wrong and should not carry the same weight as direct observation.
- [heuristic] Separate a witness's quoted words from their commentary on those words, since admiration or disgust can colour the commentary while the quoted words remain usable.
- [heuristic] Corroborate a rumor from a second, independent source before acting on it, especially for exact amounts or dates. When: A secondhand report is about to drive a decision. Why: A single relay may carry noise.
- [heuristic] Treat secondhand accounts as incomplete, but still extract the facts they reliably state, such as dates, places and listed items. When: When only press reports or hearsay are available. Why: Reports often omit essential facts yet keep dependable details.
- [procedure] 1) Ask each witness who said what to whom and mark each statement as direct or relayed. 2) Trace each relayed step back to its first-hand source, counting retellings. 3) Weigh each account by its distance from observation. When: A case or story depends on hearsay passed through several people. Why: each retelling is a step away from the original event and can alter it. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Separate what the witness personally saw, heard and inferred. 2) Ask explicitly for the personal part. 3) Weigh each as distinct evidence and record heard or inferred parts as hearsay or opinion, since inference mixed with perception overstates what was known and can distort the timeline. When: when weighing any witness account, especially one that seems to settle a scene's reconstruction. Why: firsthand knowledge carries more weight than relayed or inferred claims.
- [procedure] 1) Trace the chain of people back to the first holder of a suspicion. 2) Record who knew what and when. 3) Note who failed to report it in time. When: An investigation begins from relayed suspicion rather than a formal accusation. Why: Relays change detail and can delay evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the key facts in a witness account. 2) Separate them from irrelevant digressions. 3) Check only the key facts against other evidence. When: A witness mixes relevant facts with digressions. Why: Digressions can bury the facts the audience needs.
- [procedure] 1) Separate what each person saw firsthand from what was reported secondhand. 2) Record who saw what. 3) Reconcile conflicts only after the sources are clear. When: Witness accounts conflict. Why: Mixing direct observation with hearsay makes conflicts impossible to assess.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the damaging claim and its source. 2) Test whether the claim is true. 3) Test where it came from. 4) Weigh which is more probable: the accused acted as reported, or the informant is wrong. 5) Judge against the accused's known character. When: A damaging claim about a person arrives second-hand and cannot be checked directly. Why: Separating the claim from its source and weighing both by probability avoids accepting a rumour on trust.
- [tradeoff] Relayed lore adds distance and uncertainty that can enrich a story, but each extra layer adds reading load that is wasted if the source's reliability does not matter. When: Deciding whether a clue should pass through an intermediary. Why: Layers add atmosphere but also cost the player attention.
- [tradeoff] A reconstructed account keeps the event offstage, but an audience that needs direct evidence to believe the central mystery will reject it. When: the central mystery is at stake.
- [pitfall] Second-hand or relayed reports have limited reliability; verify them with the original observer or an independent source before relying on them, since each relay adds a distortion layer. Why: Distance from the original source removes direct confirmation. (x2)
- [pitfall] Each relay adds the teller's interpretation, emotion, gossip or slant, so an account may be overstated, lose detail, or gain unintended meaning, though useful detail often survives. When: accounts or clues pass through several people before reaching the investigator. Why: every retelling is an interpretation.
- [pitfall] Second-hand news and vivid hearsay can be mistaken for firsthand observation, so note whether each report is firsthand or secondhand and check it against its source. Why: vivid detail sounds like something the listener saw.
- [pitfall] Building motive on a friend's gossip about rivalry or romance treats hearsay as fact; hearsay about character can suggest motive but cannot establish facts. When: when a third party supplies motive information.
- [pitfall] A reaction reported second-hand, whether by another person or through a letter, is already filtered by the reporter's memory and attention, so its details may be incomplete. When: when a reaction is relayed by another person or a letter.
- [pitfall] A messenger's bias, competitive spirit, dislike or stake can shade or misreport relayed words and tone, corrupting a message or a probe's result. When: when a character relays an authority's words or a probe is relayed through a messenger. Why: the messenger's own opinions or stake colour the retelling.
- [pitfall] Relayed testimony can lose its exact wording, so accepting the first natural reading without checking the original words can lock in a wrong interpretation.
- [pitfall] Witnesses often rely on others for key events; a central event no reporter saw directly is the weakest link, since each retelling adds error or shading. When: the central event was witnessed by someone other than the reporter. Why: direct access to key events is often limited.
- [pitfall] A relayed account can distort both what was asked and why, since the relayer shapes it with their own ideas.
- [pitfall] A message passed through intermediaries, such as a secretary, becomes a chain of hearsay that can distort its meaning, so trace it back to its originator. Why: Each relay can alter, shorten or obscure the content.
- [pitfall] A secondhand report depends on the reporter's notes and memory, and may drift from the original account. When: A timeline is based on a report passed along by another person. Why: Each retelling can change details without the teller noticing.
- [pitfall] Each handoff can drop or shade details, so an early relayed report should not be treated as final.
- [pitfall] Claims about staged events that rest on people who did not see everything are weak evidence and should be checked.
- [pitfall] A track account that comes from a family story is secondhand. Confirm the snow record itself before treating it as proof. When: a track claim comes from a witness account.
- [pitfall] Confident testimony can rest on second-hand sources, so the chain of transmission must be checked before relying on it.
- [pitfall] A sincere but second-hand account accepted to keep rapport can be wrong, so it must be verified later. When: A witness reports something they did not witness directly. Why: Sincerity does not make secondhand information accurate.
- [pitfall] Secondhand retellings distort facts, and a garbled or exaggerated version can spread and fuel disbelief in the original event.
- [pitfall] A relayed written account filters both words and tone, so the reader cannot judge the original speaker's manner or sincerity. When: evidence reaches the player second-hand in writing. Why: Only the relayer's wording survives.
- [pitfall] Predictions reported secondhand are only as reliable as the person who relays them. When: a prediction about future events comes through another party. Why: Each relay adds a chance of error or distortion.
- [pitfall] Others' reports of a suspect's absence can shape the investigator's view before the suspect is questioned directly.
- [pitfall] A chain of hearsay can carry an identification that no one has checked, so its reliability is uncertain. When: When an identification reaches the investigator through intermediaries. Why: Each relay can distort or omit the original verification.
- [pitfall] A story relayed by a third party carries that party's stake in it, and the relayer may have arranged the account with the suspect. When: when a suspect's story reaches you through another person. Why: The relayer may share an interest in the same account.
- [pitfall] Treating a secondhand published accusation as a verdict on a person's character, without hearing the original act, lets reputation replace evidence.
- [pitfall] Trusting a respected name or a striking anecdote without having seen the event itself makes a claim unverifiable. When: when relying on reports rather than direct observation. Why: Reputation and vivid stories can stand in for checked facts.
- [pitfall] Hearsay from drunk or frightened sources can compress or stretch time, so each stated interval should keep its source label.
- [pitfall] Names relayed by accusers through intermediaries and written into a complaint without checking can point to the wrong person, especially when names are common. When: When a complaint names someone from another person's report. Why: Unverified intermediaries can mistake which person was meant.
- [pitfall] Curiosity, affection, gossip, and old resentment can all color a secondhand account before it reaches the listener.
- [pitfall] Accounts relayed through several tellers, or told long after events, can carry the teller's assumptions, so the original facts may be lost.
- [pitfall] Secondhand press accounts are often incomplete or wrong. Do not treat them as full records of an event.
- [pitfall] A secondhand report can itself be wrong, so a small checkable detail in it should be verified before relying on the testimony it supports. When: relying on a report passed through another person. Why: A wrong detail in a relayed account weakens everything built on it.
- [pitfall] Repeating hearsay as fact, or letting a relayer's disgust or prejudice shape what you take from the report. When: Using secondhand information as a basis for conclusions. Why: Hearsay carries the teller's bias and unverified claims.
- [pitfall] A relayed opinion can look like a relayed fact, so separate what was said from what the speaker thought it meant. When: A reported statement mixes report with judgment. Why: Interpretation blended into quoted words can be mistaken for objective content.
- [pitfall] Treating an unverified second-hand report as proof of a shared past or hidden link, without checking it, builds a conclusion on hearsay.
- [pitfall] Debts and conflicts reported by servants are hearsay until verified against records or other witnesses. When: When household gossip is the source of a motive. Why: Secondhand reports can be wrong.
- [pitfall] Relying on second-hand reports of an offer's terms without checking the exact wording can miss the clause that carries the clue. When: When evaluating a deal or bargain. Why: Paraphrases drop the conditions that reveal intent.
- [pitfall] Hearsay can omit the one fact that changes the answer, so do not rule out a possibility based on an omitted detail until it is verified. When: When relying on incomplete accounts. Why: Absence from a report is not evidence the event did not happen.
- [pitfall] Information passed on verbally, such as an address, can be misheard or misunderstood, so it should be tested against the world before being trusted. When: A player or character receives a location or instruction through dialogue. Why: Spoken details are easily garbled and may not match physical reality.
- [fact] Second-hand statements by a person who cannot be questioned are often inadmissible as proof, even when they contradict a suspect. When: in legal settings. Why: such statements cannot be tested by cross-examination.
- [fact] A key event can be relayed through an absent witness, so the audience must reconstruct it from a report they cannot question directly. When: a central witness never sees the event.
- [fact] Reports relayed by others are secondhand and shaped by the teller, while physical traces must be examined before they are read.
- [fact] A conclusion relayed from another person, such as a diagnosis, is a judgment built on a few observations, not a raw fact. When: when someone repeats an expert's opinion.
- [fact] A witness who knows an event only through rumour or sounds heard from afar gives second-hand testimony with limited evidential weight. When: A witness did not observe the event directly. Why: Rumour and distant sounds convey incomplete and possibly distorted information.
- [fact] A published report may be a corrected, amplified or annotated version of a shorthand record, so its claims pass through several editing layers. When: Evaluating a document that reports events witnessed by others. Why: Each editing layer can change what the reader sees.
- [fact] Information relayed through intermediaries, such as over a phone call, tends to be partial and garbled, so it carries less weight than firsthand accounts. Why: each relay step can drop or distort details.

## confession
- [mechanism] A confession can close a case when the culprit reconstructs events step by step, so the audience can check each claim against known facts.
- [mechanism] Applying pursuit or pressure makes a stressed NPC choose between silence and speech, which can reveal what it knows. When: Designing a pursuit sequence where an NPC holds hidden knowledge. Why: Stress reduces the NPC's control over what it discloses.
- [mechanism] A character's false denial can be exposed when a player later finds a journal entry, map note or log that contradicts it.
- [mechanism] A symptom reported by one witness can be explained by another character's later confession, so a clue resolves through cross-referencing sources. When: Two sources describe the same odd behaviour. Why: The confession supplies the cause the witness could not know.
- [mechanism] A late confession can reframe the reader's view of earlier clues, reversing how those clues seem. Why: The reversal only holds up if the earlier clues were placed fairly.
- [mechanism] A confession obtained after a trap closes can clear a previously suspected person and flip the player's assumptions. When: a late reveal changes who is suspected. Why: new testimony overturns earlier conclusions.
- [mechanism] A confession mechanic can release information in stages, where each stage depends on which listener the player chooses. When: Designing a confession with several possible listeners. Why: Different listeners draw out different levels of disclosure.
- [mechanism] A false confession by a wrong suspect can muddle a case so the real culprit stops being suspected, even though no proof points at him. When: no independent proof exists against the true culprit. Why: investigators without proof may let the matter rest on the confession.
- [mechanism] A false confession arriving mid-interview shocks the scene and forces the investigator to test whether the account is genuine.
- [mechanism] Confessions can expand a conspiracy's apparent scope, naming office-holders and a planned hierarchy of leaders.
- [mechanism] A confession made after a death sentence is signed can delay the outcome, opening a window before it is fixed. When: a sentence has been signed but not carried out. Why: the outcome is paused while the new statement is examined.
- [mechanism] A recantation mechanic that is unlikely to be believed mirrors how retractions were overridden, making the cost of telling the truth part of the story.
- [mechanism] A confession can unlock a hidden location, turning a narrative payoff into newly reachable space.
- [mechanism] A false confession can serve as a quest twist, where players are rewarded for noticing inconsistencies rather than accepting the surface. When: Designing a narrative where a confession turns out to be false. Why: Rewarding scrutiny makes the false confession a meaningful discovery.
- [behavior] Under long questioning or threats, confessions grow longer and more detailed as resistance wears down, whether or not the added detail is accurate; repetition can also adopt ungrounded statements. When: prolonged questioning under threat or repeated pressure. Why: Resistance wears down over time, and repeated pressure can make a witness adopt a pushed confession. (x2)
- [behavior] A person with temperament, religious conviction or a wish to suffer for another may falsely confess; probing details only the real culprit would know exposes it. When: a confession conflicts with other evidence, or an NPC confesses to a crime. Why: The desire to suffer can motivate an invented guilt.
- [behavior] Witnesses who see accusers collapse or regret their accusations may confess to harm they believe they caused, even offering their own punishment as atonement. When: accusations are made in a distressing setting, or a confessor regrets earlier accusations. Why: Fear of causing suffering and guilt over accusations shape what they say.
- [behavior] A self-blaming witness tends to reveal his most damaging detail last, often only after being pressed. When: interviewing a witness who blames himself for a lapse. Why: Self-blame makes the witness shade admissions or hold back the worst detail.
- [behavior] People choose meeting places out of earshot of the household, so a confession or claim can be made without witnesses. When: a sensitive disclosure must happen. Why: others who can overhear may influence or expose the speaker.
- [behavior] An adversary who never mentions a central item may know more than they say, so the omission is itself evidence.
- [behavior] A witness who volunteers an alibi only after coming under suspicion may be motivated to clear themselves, which warrants closer testing of that alibi. When: when the alibi appears only after the witness's own name or a related person is under suspicion. Why: the timing suggests a motive to deflect rather than a recollection.
- [behavior] Under pressure, a witness may break down and make emotional admissions that show genuine distress, though these do not prove the account is complete.
- [behavior] A suspect pressed on a specific fact may admit a partial truth, revealing the outline of a secret before its details. When: when a suspect is confronted with a precise fact.
- [behavior] A confession can be rejected and reattempted at a later session when its wording is judged evasive.
- [behavior] Sustained public pressure can move an accused person from denial to full compliance, so the resulting statement reflects pressure rather than truth.
- [behavior] Sustained pressure often brings out a second secret the questioner did not ask about at first. When: a suspect is worn down by repeated questioning. Why: Fear and fatigue loosen what the suspect was holding back.
- [rule] Accept a confession only when its embarrassing details match traces the player already found, so it rewards investigation rather than replacing it. When: designing NPC or late confessions. Why: Matching details earn trust, and confirmation rewards earlier effort.
- [rule] Offer a false-confession branch, such as an NPC confession conflicting with a verifiable schedule or world state, that players can expose by checking the scene. When: designing false confessions in a game. Why: A checkable conflict turns the false confession into a puzzle.
- [rule] Do not accuse from avoidance alone; avoiding a task or showing nervousness has many causes unrelated to the matter under investigation. When: a character refuses or shuns a duty. Why: Unease about the duty may have nothing to do with the matter under investigation.
- [rule] Build contradictions between NPC accounts of the same event, so players must decide which to believe, letting physical evidence arbitrate. When: investigation where witnesses disagree. Why: Letting physical evidence arbitrate turns conflicting testimony into a reasoning task.
- [rule] Make NPC confessions partly unreliable, marking some details unverified until the player verifies them with evidence such as a bottle, record or other clue. Why: A partial confession invites checking and avoids presenting coerced speech as fully reliable.
- [rule] Tie a criminal NPC's hostility to a hidden past or secret the player unlocks through records, dossiers or old associates, so the trigger and motive are traceable. When: narrative quests built around a character's secret. Why: Unlocking a concealed past rewards investigation and explains the character's conflicts.
- [rule] Hold a major accusation for a late cutscene or prompt, delivered after players have gathered the supporting clues.
- [rule] Have a quest-giver promise a revelation after a condition is met, with the answer or reward placed at the end.
- [rule] Do not accuse a witness outright; a direct, factual challenge is more likely to draw out the rest of the account.
- [rule] Structure dialogue so the NPC commits to an account before the player receives confirmation of the facts. When: Writing an interrogation or confession exchange. Why: Committed statements are more meaningful when later checked.
- [rule] Let an NPC accuse the player of setting the trap, so the dialogue reveals the NPC's own guilt.
- [rule] Be ready to prevent self-harm before pressing a suspect who may carry a concealed means of escape.
- [rule] Give a guilty NPC a dialogue option to speak first before the player presents evidence, rewarding careful questioning. When: when designing a confrontation scene. Why: letting the NPC volunteer a confession rewards questioning.
- [rule] Let a friendly NPC offer a false confession, with clues that reveal the sacrifice to a careful player. When: Designing a sympathetic NPC who hides the true culprit.
- [rule] Hold back the identity of a threat until peak danger, revealing it through a change in a speaker's face or manner. When: Building suspense toward a reveal. Why: A late reveal concentrates the audience's tension at the moment it matters most.
- [rule] Offer a confession option that reveals a motive but comes with a mutual alibi, forcing the player to check the alibi through another source. When: designing NPC confessions in a game.
- [rule] Model a confession as an item that one NPC writes and another NPC witnesses, with the player delivering it to the proper authority. When: Designing a confession mechanic in a game. Why: A witnessed document is a concrete, transferable piece of quest progress.
- [rule] Avoid public appeals when the suspect may read them and take precautions; use a private, targeted mailing instead. When: the suspect may be watching public notices. Why: public appeals warn the suspect.
- [rule] Give similar-looking items one distinctive property, so players must find it to identify the true owner.
- [rule] Offer eavesdropping as a mechanic that yields partial information, which the player must confirm through other means. When: designing stealth-based listening.
- [rule] Give letters, notes and maps physical traits such as smudges, ink differences or sealed flaps, so players can judge their origin. When: Designing in-world documents as clues. Why: Physical detail gives players grounds to assess authenticity.
- [rule] Give the character who discovers a body a checkable account of their actions so players can test it against the scene.
- [rule] Give important non-player characters one distinguishing trait the player can recall, such as a scar or a voice, and make crowd members look alike. When: Designing characters that the player must later identify. Why: A single memorable trait lets the player recall and match a character, while similar crowd members test that recall.
- [rule] Attach a confidence level to each NPC claim in a timeline, rating heard events below seen events. When: A game tracks what NPCs report about night-time events. Why: Players need to judge which testimony to rely on.
- [rule] Present an obvious suspect early so players must test that suspect's evidence against the level's mechanics before accepting the accusation.
- [rule] Make a crime's style point to a class of suspects rather than one, leaving players to narrow the class with further evidence.
- [rule] Make a witness's detail accurate only under certain conditions, such as daylight, so the player must recreate those conditions to verify it.
- [rule] Let a relative or child NPC reveal a location in casual dialogue, so the player learns an address through conversation.
- [rule] Let players name a culprit only when the level provides documented clues from human sources, not revelations from a magical or unexplained source. When: when designing the final accusation in a mystery level. Why: The player's verdict must rest on evidence they could examine and check.
- [rule] Design a confession so that it requires a matching physical trace in the world, mirroring the pairing of confession and deed. When: when a suspect's confession is a clue in a level. Why: A confession corroborated by the world is more convincing than one standing alone.
- [rule] Build a confessing or gloating character's account to be partly true and partly self-serving, so the player must test it against evidence. When: Writing a suspect's self-justifying account. Why: Partial truth makes the account checkable rather than simply accepted.
- [rule] Let a confession supply proof the protagonist cannot stage on screen, then have the protagonist reconstruct the event afterwards.
- [rule] Resolve a hidden-boss reveal through a confession under threat, so the villain's own speech delivers the layered information in one scene. When: the antagonist is cornered. Why: A cornered villain has reason to explain, and explanation carries the backstory.
- [heuristic] A confession alone gives closure without verification; plant evidence earlier and add a follow-up check so the emotional reveal confirms rather than settles the question. When: a mystery ends with a confession or an emotional reveal scene. Why: Emotion and the culprit's word alone should not settle the question; the audience needs independent support.
- [heuristic] Use a self-accusing witness when the audience should doubt the account while still hearing it clearly. When: A confession or accusation should be both believable and suspect. Why: The audience hears the claim directly and can judge it against what it knows.
- [heuristic] An accomplice NPC can give a false confession naming an innocent partner to shift blame. When: Designing an accomplice who turns on the group. Why: A confession carries weight and redirects investigation.
- [heuristic] A culprit's first-person confession can reveal the mechanics of the deed while still concealing motive, method, or earlier falsehoods. When: when the solution should come from the culprit's side. Why: The narrator controls which facts are disclosed.
- [heuristic] Do not expect a full confession from a partial account; a suspect who admits a lie has often kept the most important part hidden.
- [heuristic] A freely made confession containing details the accused could not otherwise know carries more weight than one that only echoes known facts. When: judging a confession as evidence.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC be innocent yet unable to prove their whereabouts, so players must find a second witness rather than simply arrest someone.
- [heuristic] Give damning-looking items, such as a weapon or stained cloth, innocent causes the player must consider before accepting guilt. When: Placing incriminating evidence in generated scenarios. Why: Players then need to test interpretations rather than accept surface appearance.
- [heuristic] Give a misleading accuser NPC a visible grudge and a stated source the player can check, so the accusation can be tested. When: Generating a murder-mystery or investigation quest. Why: A testable claim rewards player reasoning and avoids an unfair dead end.
- [heuristic] An angry or hurt NPC can reveal character traits and hidden motives in dialogue, opening new lines of questioning for the player. When: Designing NPC dialogue for investigation. Why: Emotional speakers disclose more than neutral ones.
- [heuristic] Staging a dialogue room through light, seating and distance shapes how the player and NPC interact. When: Designing a space for a conversation with a sensitive character. Why: Physical arrangement sets the emotional tone and who holds control.
- [heuristic] A friendly NPC can cue a hidden action, such as switching off a light or slipping an object, that surveillance does not catch. When: Designing covert cooperation between captive and ally NPCs. Why: Surveillance misses actions that are hidden in darkness or out of sight.
- [heuristic] A dialogue option about a third party can expose an NPC's own abilities, unlocking a skill check or path that depends on that knowledge. When: when designing dialogue-gated progression. Why: Answers about others unintentionally reveal the speaker's own knowledge.
- [heuristic] Testimony admitting the speaker's own wrongdoing, such as opening a drawer they had no right to open, is more credible than flattering or accusation-only testimony, since admitting it costs them. When: Assessing a self-damaging statement. Why: Admitted faults suggest the account is not shaped to flatter the teller, and a liar is unlikely to invent an accusation that includes themselves.
- [heuristic] An admission that damages the speaker's own position, made to an accuser, is hard to believe and should be treated as a clue.
- [heuristic] A boast, slip or unprompted action can expose a guilty character more reliably than outside deduction. When: the reveal depends on the culprit's own conduct.
- [heuristic] Let a confession carry the emotional payoff of a case, so the culprit's account resolves the sympathy built during the mystery.
- [heuristic] Let the culprit's confession carry the backstory, explaining earlier objects and events without extra exposition.
- [heuristic] Use extracted confessions later recanted as a source of doubt, letting the designer plant suspicion without stating it. When: a story where testimony is contested. Why: Recanted confessions give players reason to doubt without a direct claim.
- [heuristic] Place a retraction in the same record as the confession so the reversal reads as a plot beat rather than a cheat.
