- [procedure] 1) Assemble the case first. 2) Deliver the solution as the culprit's own written account. 3) Have a character read it aloud so the audience hears it alongside the events. When: Revealing a solved mystery. Why: Explains the whole plot in one place while the audience is already informed.
- [procedure] 1) Give each NPC witness specific features they can recognise in a document. 2) Make their recognition vague at first. 3) Let the player press them for the basis of the claim. When: Designing witnesses who authenticate or dispute a document. Why: Pressing vague recognition exposes weak evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Present the solver's evidence chain as an ordered sequence of inferences. 2) Let the culprit's confession confirm the inferred details. 3) Keep the confession from introducing facts the audience could not have known. When: When ending a mystery whose answer depends on a chain of inferences. Why: An ordered chain lets the audience check the confession rather than accept it on trust.
- [tradeoff] A late culprit account can fill gaps in motive, movement and timing, but should add only what earlier clues implied, since unverifiable facts make the reveal feel unfair. When: writing a culprit's admission in a final act. Why: Gap-filling confirms the reveal, while facts the player could not check undermine its fairness.
- [tradeoff] Self-revealing follow-up questions can expose hidden knowledge, but are unreliable when the suspect can simply avoid the topic without arousing suspicion. When: a person is asked how they know something, or a suspect can deflect a question. Why: A question can disclose what the person knows, but evasion leaves no revealing phrasing to observe.
- [tradeoff] A dated written confession can fix a timeline and carry strong credibility, but the writer's motives shape its content, so it should not be relied on alone. When: One document must carry both a timeline and a motive. Why: Admitting one's own wrongdoing lends credibility, yet self-interest and emotional state can distort facts.
- [pitfall] Pressured confessions may be false, partial or regretted, may echo the interviewer's wishes, and hesitation is not proof; test them against other evidence, especially when they fit the preferred theory. When: a confession or account is obtained under interview pressure, threat or leverage. Why: Pressure can extract untrue or distorted statements as easily as true ones.
- [pitfall] Self-analysis, self-criticism and confessions are not proof: they can shift blame, minimise one's role, deny intent or pre-empt doubt, so test them against the record. Why: Self-justification shapes an account, and self-criticism can disarm scrutiny.
- [pitfall] Sympathy or a wish for forgiveness shapes confessions; read self-justification, such as stated motives or claims of facing facts, as framing, and check against physical evidence or the record. When: reviewing a confession or admission. Why: Emotional confessions can distort or simplify the true sequence of events.
- [pitfall] A retraction may stop a case, but it often arrives after harm is done and cannot undo a verdict or punishment already in effect. When: a case where an accuser reverses. Why: Accusations act before any retraction is heard.
- [pitfall] Partial confessions can hide worse acts or the key part behind a plausible reason, and can look complete; verify each detail and check which parts were held back. When: a confession is given in carefully chosen parts. Why: Gaps in an admission are easy to miss when the spoken parts are convincing.
- [pitfall] Sympathetic pressure can produce false confessions or invented details, so treat new admissions as claims to verify.
- [pitfall] A confession made under pressure may be partial, leaving some claims unverified and needing separate checks. When: After a witness confesses under interview pressure. Why: Witnesses admit what they must and keep back what they fear would cost them more.
- [pitfall] A confession that only lists facts without changing what the listener believes produces no dramatic effect. When: when writing a confession or exposition scene. Why: Information lands only when it reshapes the listener's understanding.
- [pitfall] A speaker's partial admissions can be used against them by a questioner, so each concession should be weighed before it is given.
- [pitfall] A confession can be partial, and a flippant or cheerful manner of telling can color how the audience judges its truth. When: when a suspect confesses. Why: Tone shapes judgment independently of what is actually confirmed.
- [pitfall] A self-incriminating account can be false and still be believed, and innocent people may be harmed as a result.
- [pitfall] A culprit who writes down dangerous plans out of a need for self-expression creates evidence that can later convict him.
- [pitfall] A confession may cover only a small secret, and its stated reasons may not explain the concealment, so check whether it covers the whole matter.
- [pitfall] A mentally unwell person can confess to a crime that never happened, so a signed confession is not proof of the act.
- [pitfall] Recognizing a trap only after entering the room is too late to avoid it.
- [pitfall] Doubt about one's own senses can be sincere, or it can be a convenient way to deflect blame, and the two look alike. When: A witness questions whether their own perception was accurate.
- [pitfall] Treating a coerced confession as self-proving ignores the method that produced it and hides the pressure behind it.
- [pitfall] Confessions given under condemnation or fear can name others and multiply the case rather than resolve it. When: A confession is made under threat of death or fear. Why: The confessor may name others, expanding the accusations.
- [pitfall] People discontented or in despair may falsely accuse themselves, and a recantation at the moment of punishment can reveal that the confession was false. When: A confession is made in distress or near execution. Why: Despair and abandonment can drive false self-accusation.
- [pitfall] Schedule entries marked as conditional, such as weather-dependent stops, describe possibilities rather than certainties and should be checked before use.
- [pitfall] Pressure or a dramatic interrogation setting can produce admissions reflecting the questioner's expectations or social atmosphere, and threatened witnesses may fill gaps to satisfy the pressing questioner. When: Evaluating a confession obtained under pressure or in a dramatic setting. Why: Social pressure and atmosphere push people toward admission rather than evidence.
- [pitfall] A confession obtained through promises or threats can be sincere and still be unusable as proof. When: an NPC or suspect confesses after being offered protection or threatened. Why: inducements weaken the statement's evidential value.
- [fact] A culprit's confession can explain motive, method, and the purpose of earlier incidental details, recasting them as deliberate.
- [fact] A confession is often the only route to facts held by one person alone, such as where a body lies or what happened in a private moment. When: No physical or witness evidence exists for a private fact. Why: Only the participant holds that knowledge.
- [fact] Without an eyewitness and with evidence pointing at one person, a confession from the actual offender is the main route to proof. When: A case has no eyewitness and only circumstantial evidence. Why: Only the offender can directly confirm the act.

## rival explanations
- [mechanism] A plausible alternative explanation for a fact creates reasonable doubt, even when no direct evidence contradicts the prosecution's account.
- [mechanism] Parallel cases competing for the same authority's attention slow an investigation, since limited attention is split. When: several cases share one decision-maker. Why: Divided attention reduces progress on each.
- [mechanism] Each theory generates predictions; checking them by measurement or search tests whether the theory holds.
- [behavior] When an ambiguous message is read aloud, a character who tests several readings before the facts arrive keeps the audience weighing competing explanations. When: an ambiguous hint is received before evidence.
- [behavior] Rival theories can read the same object in opposite ways, so each reading must be tested against the full set of evidence, not a single item.
- [behavior] Rivals informally test ideas with each other, and both gain, because a theory challenged by a rival is improved or dropped sooner.
- [behavior] When many similar traces in a scene differ in condition, players compare them to infer timing or order of events, turning scattered clues into a hypothesis. When: A scene holds many similar objects with varied damage or position. Why: Comparison reveals which differences track when or how each object was involved.
- [rule] Before accepting a supernatural or occult reading, test ordinary human explanations such as motive, secret or circumstance; keep the supernatural open only while they fail. When: A mysterious cause is claimed or an occult hint has a possible human cause. Why: Ordinary causes often explain outcomes attributed to unusual ones; testing them keeps the story fair. (x2)
- [rule] Hold several explanations open at once, each accounting for all known facts, and keep each provisional until evidence separates them; dropping or committing to one early hides the right answer. When: Early in an inquiry while facts are thin, or when several explanations fit the same events.
- [rule] Keep a merely possible rival provisional and test it before accepting it; present any conclusion as probable, not settled, until tests support it, since possibility alone does not establish truth. When: A rival explanation is proposed or a conclusion is being formed.
- [rule] Offer two or three plausible explanations for one puzzling clue, such as a folk reading and a mundane one, each backed by different clues, so only one survives all tests. When: Designing a mystery or puzzling physical clue with a single true cause. Why: Players must test explanations to find the one consistent with all evidence.
- [rule] Let a community or rumour system keep rival explanations of one event alive, each with some support (personal killing, a fight, deliberate disappearance), so players must weigh them.
- [rule] For an unexplained disappearance, keep rival explanations open and test each, such as death, imprisonment, extracting information, wagering on outcomes or demanding ransom. When: An unexplained disappearance occurs.
- [rule] Before committing to a theory, list every competing explanation it must beat, keep a record of each alternative, and weigh each against the evidence.
- [rule] Before reading silence as evidence, check whether an innocent cause such as fear or distance fits the timing; a fear that did not yet exist cannot explain it. Why: silence has many causes, and only a cause present at the right time can account for it.
- [rule] Include a rival NPC who reaches a confident early conclusion, so the player sees the cost of acting on partial proof.
- [rule] Test a hostile witness's account against a neutral witness when the two share a household and may have rivalries.
- [rule] Keep rival explanations open when judging odd behaviour, and do not settle unresolved questions by assumption. When: Interpreting a suspect's or witness's unexplained actions. Why: Assumed answers hide alternatives that may be true.
- [rule] Test a comforting explanation against facts before accepting it; do not present an argued theory as tested when it has not been checked. When: a theory offers relief from a painful outcome. Why: comfort is not evidence.
- [rule] Test each plausible explanation against a specific observed detail, and reject it when that detail contradicts it, not merely because it seems unlikely. When: A plausible theory is offered and an observation can test it.
- [rule] A plausible but unproven alternative does not disprove a case; test each link of the main case independently.
- [rule] Give rival NPC investigators preconceived theories that the player must expose by finding contradicting evidence. When: Designing competing investigators in a mystery. Why: Players then engage in reasoning by testing rather than accepting the first answer.
- [rule] Test every theory, including elegant and complete ones, against physical constraints such as strength, reach, and distance before accepting it. When: several explanations are on the table. Why: An elegant, complete theory can still be wrong, and physical constraints are what rule out impossible acts.
- [rule] A theory that clears a suspect of the worst charge must be tested against the evidence like any other theory.
- [rule] Give rival readings of a document to different NPCs so the player must judge which interpretation is trustworthy. When: Designing competing interpretations in a mystery. Why: Conflicting authorities make the player weigh credibility.
- [rule] Before building a theory on an odd detail, test each rival explanation for it, such as the person fled versus was never there. When: when a single unusual detail is central to a theory.
- [rule] Put rival hypotheses to an expert so they must commit to one or back away, exposing the limits of their opinion.
- [rule] Let two NPCs describe the same evening with matching outlines but different details, so the player must compare them.
- [rule] List each clue with its plausible innocent alternatives so the reader or player can weigh them instead of accepting the intended reading. When: Designing evidence in an investigation story or game. Why: Unmentioned alternatives make weak evidence look conclusive.
- [rule] Let a suspect finish personal explanations before judging him, since background such as motive often explains erratic behaviour.
- [rule] Test a companion's ready explanation of odd behaviour before accepting it, because accepting it lets the explainer control the story. When: someone offers an explanation before examining the behaviour. Why: an unexamined explanation can close inquiry prematurely.
- [rule] Keep a second solution path open so a player who discards a red herring can still reach the answer.
- [rule] Stage scenes with props suggesting a struggle or gang attack so players form a false theory that they must test. When: Designing crime scenes for investigation.
- [rule] Test a theory's logic with a hypothetical method; a joke about method is not evidence but can expose a flaw in the theory. When: Evaluating an elaborate suspect theory. Why: Pushing a theory to an absurd case reveals whether its logic holds.
- [rule] Give every explanation a credible rival so the player keeps a theory but never a certainty. When: Misdirected investigation stage. Why: Competing readings sustain doubt.
- [heuristic] Test simpler explanations first, such as a spare item, and prefer the simpler human one when it fits; set aside elaborate mechanisms the evidence does not need. When: Choosing between explanations for an apparently impossible or elaborate action. Why: Testing simpler causes first avoids unjustified complex conclusions.
- [heuristic] Offer rival motives for an unexplained act, such as bribery, a promised payment, romantic interest, attention-seeking or embarrassment, and test each against the other evidence. When: A person's cooperation or conduct has several plausible motives. Why: The same act can have different causes, so each motive must be checked.
- [heuristic] A rival who suspects another character can serve as a red herring, so players should check opportunity before accepting motive as the answer. When: A rival's suspicion points toward an innocent character.
- [heuristic] Make a rival NPC who gains from a false accusation a natural red herring, and give the player a way to check that rival's motive. When: designing mystery suspects in a game. Why: A checkable motive makes the red herring fair.
- [heuristic] Alternate viewpoints so each step toward the answer is paired with another character's fear.
- [heuristic] Compare the chosen location with nearby alternatives to see which one satisfies the actor's needs. When: explaining why an act took place at a specific spot.
- [heuristic] Deductive reasoning is only as reliable as its list of alternatives, so an omitted explanation can make the correct one look impossible.
- [heuristic] Build a detailed alternative explanation that fits the same facts, and keep it open until a fact contradicts it. When: The official case rests on items that each have innocent explanations. Why: Tested rivals expose weak links that a single account hides.
- [heuristic] Judge any explanation by whether it accounts for all the evidence, not only the part it was built to cover.
- [heuristic] A competing explanation, such as food slowing absorption, must be weighed against how large the gap actually is before it is accepted.
- [heuristic] Avoid claiming much knowledge; a boast invites checks, while modest claims keep the other side guessing.
- [heuristic] Keep a rival explanation open, such as a real criminal framing an innocent person, until evidence rules it out.
- [heuristic] When a physical object matches a claim, weigh rival explanations of how it came to be that way before accepting the claim. When: when a found object seems to confirm a testimony. Why: the same object may fit a different account of events.
- [heuristic] Use the situation's goals, such as speed and secrecy, to narrow candidates by distance and destination. When: when candidates differ in distance or destination. Why: the goals of the situation favour some candidates over others.
- [heuristic] Ask whether the proposed theory is consistent with the charge being made; a mismatch exposes a gap in the reasoning. When: A theory is offered to explain a specific accusation. Why: Inconsistency between theory and charge reveals unsupported links.
- [heuristic] Identify the evidence each hypothesis depends on, since the same evidence, such as regular large payments, can fit opposite stories. When: A single piece of evidence supports more than one explanation. Why: Shared evidence cannot decide between explanations on its own.
- [heuristic] Test each innocent explanation a suspect offers for a trace rather than accepting it, since each trace can be given a harmless source.
- [heuristic] Test every leading theory, simple or convenient, against the evidence before accepting or rejecting it. Why: A theory that fits the investigator's hopes can warp how facts are read.
- [heuristic] Include a checkable rival explanation, such as an accident, so the player's first theory can prove wrong. When: Designing a mystery with a tempting first solution. Why: A live alternative keeps the investigation from closing too early.
- [heuristic] Reasoning that starts from one favoured explanation may overlook the others, so keep several explanations open until facts separate them. When: when an investigator has a favourite explanation early. Why: a favoured explanation can filter out evidence for alternatives.
- [heuristic] Offer a competing mechanism late in the mystery so players can test their reconstruction against it before the true method is revealed.
- [procedure] 1) List each reading the evidence allows. 2) Name a test that confirms or rules out each. 3) Keep rivals open and test each against every new fact. 4) Run tests before settling; discard any the facts break, since a single fitting fact rarely separates rivals. When: Evidence fits several explanations and facts are incomplete. Why: Keeping rivals open prevents premature conclusions; a fixed first answer can fit part of the evidence while being wrong.
- [procedure] 1) State each alternative as a separate theory. 2) List the physical traces or records it predicts. 3) Check them against the scene, records and expert knowledge. 4) Keep theories whose traces match; drop any a test removes. Plausibility or mood alone establishes nothing. When: Several explanations fit early clues or a plausible explanation is not yet verified. Why: Explanations that fit mood but not traces should not survive testing.
- [procedure] 1) Recreate the suspected cause, such as a trap or animal, under the original conditions. 2) Compare its damage pattern or effect with the observed one. 3) Reject the hypothesis if the effects differ.
- [procedure] 1) Accept a new hypothesis for argument. 2) Derive what it implies about other parts of the case, such as an act that must have been done in parts. 3) Check whether the earlier theory survives, and reject any hypothesis whose implications do not fit. When: Two or more explanations fit the same facts. Why: Consequences expose contradictions that a theory alone hides.
- [procedure] 1) Name the innocent or familiar explanation. 2) List what it cannot explain, such as why a target was chosen when more valuable items were left. 3) Check each physical detail against what it would produce. 4) Adopt it as a working presumption only if it fails. When: An obvious convenient theory rests on a common category and has not been checked against physical details. Why: A plausible explanation can leave real evidence unexplained; unexplained details can reveal a different motive.
- [procedure] 1) Name each rival explanation, such as accident, suicide or murder. 2) Test each against specific clues. 3) Count the coincidences each requires as costs. 4) Drop any hypothesis a single clear clue contradicts. Keep separate questions apart so one does not block the others. When: A case or trace has more than one plausible explanation. Why: Systematic exclusion is more reliable than favouring one explanation early.
- [procedure] 1) List the supernatural explanation alongside every plausible human one, such as a prank, a concealment or a precedent. 2) Test each against the physical traces. 3) Keep open any the facts do not yet rule out. When: An odd or apparently impossible event invites a supernatural reading but evidence is limited. Why: Physical checks separate plausible explanations from unfounded ones.
- [procedure] 1) Name the explanation offered for a sound or trace. 2) Ask whether the suspect would have produced that sound or trace. 3) If not, weaken or drop the explanation. When: a sound or trace is explained away as harmless.
- [procedure] 1) List candidate explanations for an act. 2) Ask a witness who saw the actor about alertness, gaze and gait. 3) Discard explanations those answers contradict. When: one witness observed the actor's condition closely. Why: Testimony about physical and mental state can rule out explanations.
- [procedure] 1) When one testimony or trace fits two sources, assign each reading to a different tester. 2) Have each test every new fact against their reading. 3) Compare which reading accumulates contradictions. When: When evidence supports two explanations equally well. Why: Parallel testing against the same facts exposes which reading fails.
- [procedure] 1) Test the new theory against all the facts the old theory used. 2) Check whether any expected reaction, such as a silence, fails to appear under the new theory. 3) Revise until every trace is explained. When: Re-examining a case after a reversal. Why: A reversal that leaves facts unexplained will not hold.
- [procedure] 1) State each motive hypothesis. 2) Note the kind of victim and planner each implies. 3) Find one check whose result separates the hypotheses. When: Several motives fit a case. Why: A distinguishing test lets the investigator choose between hypotheses instead of holding them all.
- [procedure] 1) Ask which facts the rival theory leaves untouched 2) Note each concrete contradiction 3) Seek evidence that resolves each contradiction. When: a neat explanation fits the main fact but must be checked. Why: A theory can fit its central fact yet fail on details.
- [procedure] 1) Keep the accurate observation. 2) Set aside the supernatural or improbable explanation. 3) Ask which ordinary act would produce the same appearance, then test it against all other details. When: A striking observation has an improbable cause and an ordinary cause could produce the same appearance. Why: Keeping the observation avoids discarding real evidence with the false explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each account of the same behaviour. 2) Read the rival account aloud so each speaker can answer it. 3) Test both against known facts and choose the account that fits best. When: Two people explain the same observed act differently. Why: Setting accounts against each other and facts exposes which claims hold up.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the single strong fact. 2) Ask who else could have produced it and when. 3) Build a rival explanation that accounts for the same fact. 4) Test it against known facts. 5) Look for corroboration. When: one fact points one way and no rival explanation exists.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the proposed explanation with the victim's character and routine. 2) Check the physical setting for fit. 3) Check the suspect's account against the other people's positions. When: A death is presented as self-inflicted or accidental. Why: Each check can expose a staged explanation.
- [procedure] 1) List every account the evidence allows of how a death occurred. 2) Add hypotheses such as a third party being shielded. 3) For each account, state the conduct it would predict. 4) Test each against observed behaviour before settling. When: When the cause of a death is contested. Why: Different accounts predict different behaviour, so testing separates them.
- [procedure] 1) List each explanation that fits the body. 2) For each, state which trace it predicts. 3) Note which traces contradict each explanation. 4) Keep both open until the traces decide between them. When: when a death could be self-inflicted or caused by another person. Why: each trace narrows the field only if its prediction is explicit.
- [procedure] 1) List every explanation that fits the locked state. 2) Identify the physical change each explanation requires. 3) Test each change against the scene. 4) Discard explanations the evidence contradicts. When: when a locked state has been broken or disturbed.
- [procedure] 1) List each competing reading of an event. 2) For each, state the traces a true version would leave. 3) Check the scene for those traces. 4) Treat an expected trace that is missing as evidence against that reading. When: when an account could be a real act or a staged one.
- [procedure] 1) State each candidate explanation for the anomaly. 2) Test each against the timeline. 3) Reject any explanation that fits one fact but fails the timing. When: When several explanations fit the observed mismatch. Why: An explanation must fit all facts, not just one.
- [procedure] 1) List each competing explanation for an event. 2) Work out what behaviour each would predict afterwards. 3) Compare each prediction with what was observed and drop explanations that conflict. When: Two or more explanations compete. Why: Each explanation implies different behaviour afterwards.
- [procedure] Give NPCs competing goals and plan culprit actions under time limits, then check whether the traces left are consistent with that plan. When: When generating or designing a murder mystery. Why: Time-constrained plans leave checkable traces, letting players choose among plausible reconstructions.
- [procedure] 1) List each candidate explanation. 2) Mark each part that lacks a supporting trace or witness. 3) Test each part against physical evidence and the timeline. 4) Drop any explanation that the evidence contradicts. When: Several explanations compete for the same evidence. Why: Testing each part separately exposes weak links that a tidy whole story hides.
- [procedure] 1) Note where the object was found. 2) Note what it was used for. 3) Test the suspect's innocent explanation against both before accepting it. When: A common object appears at a scene where harm was attempted. Why: Context can reveal an innocent story to be incomplete.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the object or act the official account requires. 2) Perform or imagine that act. 3) Check whether the object would have been needed and whether it was present. When: an accepted explanation rests on a single object or inference. Why: a required object that is absent counts against the account.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the observation conditions: distance, light, weather and wind direction. 2) Propose a known mechanism. 3) Check whether it reproduces each reported detail, including timing and how the sight faded.
- [procedure] 1) Fix a timeline from known dates. 2) Use it to limit when each suspect could have acted. 3) For each rival, request an independent record. 4) Keep the rival until confirmed or ruled out. 5) Combine timeline and records to narrow the search. When: multiple explanations fit the known facts and each can be checked against records.
- [procedure] 1) State the hypothesis as an untested supposition. 2) Build its strongest case: motive, means to conceal, a substitute, and a disposal site. 3) Ask how each fact bears on it. 4) Invite a challenger to question each step. When: an investigator needs to test a damaging theory before believing it. Why: explicit testing exposes weak links that a confident argument hides.
- [procedure] 1) Infer who used a place from small objects and worn paths. 2) Write the theory as numbered points. 3) List the facts it leaves unexplained. 4) Weigh each anomaly by how much it damages the theory. 5) Judge the theory by how many anomalies it covers. When: a theory explains most facts and needs a checklist of its gaps. Why: listing anomalies shows what the theory must still account for.
- [procedure] 1) Test each explanation against all the circumstances. 2) Group small, individually weak facts that point the same way. 3) Judge each explanation by how well it covers them. 4) Compare with alternatives that may be just as strange. When: Choosing among several candidate explanations. Why: Weak facts gain force when they converge, and alternatives must be judged on equal terms.
- [procedure] 1) Offer an alternative source for a damaging trace. 2) Compare the trace's properties, such as colour, length and condition, with that source. 3) Reject the alternative if any property does not fit. When: A physical trace is assigned to a suspect by rival explanations. Why: Property mismatch disproves an alternative owner.
- [procedure] 1) Give each suspect a visible motive. 2) Supply a second, equally plausible explanation for the event. 3) Test each explanation separately against the evidence. When: Investigating an event with several suspects or possible causes. Why: Testing alternatives separately prevents a single visible motive from settling the case.
- [procedure] 1) List ordinary explanations: conspiracy, disordered mind, illness, shadow, misremembered sight, coincidence. 2) Test each against all the evidence. 3) Consider a supernatural cause only after ordinary ones fail. When: unexplained events occur. Why: ordinary causes are checked first so a strange cause is not accepted by default.
- [procedure] 1) Name each candidate explanation for a strange event. 2) For each, list the facts it explains and the facts it leaves unexplained, testing against the whole pattern. 3) Keep the best-fitting explanation as the working answer until it fails. When: when a strange event could have a supernatural or human cause and several candidate explanations are available. Why: No single candidate accounts for every occurrence, so only testing against the full pattern shows which explanation survives and where the residue lies.
- [procedure] 1) List all plausible explanations for the event, making sure none is omitted. 2) Test each against known motives, opportunities and behaviour. 3) Eliminate an option only when the evidence is decisive. 4) Accept the remaining option only after confirming the list of alternatives is complete. When: A player or investigator must choose among rival explanations, or elimination has left a single explanation standing. Why: An incomplete list makes the remaining option look inevitable when it may not be, and a missing alternative makes an elimination-based conclusion unsound.
- [procedure] 1) When a new story fits the known facts, list each link of the existing chain. 2) Test each link against the rival story. 3) Keep links the rival does not explain. 4) Re-judge the verdict from the surviving links. When: A credible rival explanation appears against a circumstantial case. Why: Rejecting the whole chain discards links that may still hold.
- [procedure] 1) List the human explanations for each strand: fabrication, coincidence, error, malice. 2) Test each against the evidence. 3) Note which strands resist every human explanation. When: When a mystery has both a rational path and an apparently supernatural cause. Why: Systematically failing human explanations lets the player see when the uncanny is the only fit.
- [procedure] 1) Separate what is known from what is merely asserted. 2) Weigh the source's knowledge and motives. 3) Check the timeline the explanation depends on. 4) Test each layer of the account separately. When: A second party offers an explanation for a hidden event. Why: Confident explainers can be wrong or self-interested.
- [pitfall] Mixing rival theories, or a single story explaining every fact, yields a conclusion that fits everything, explains nothing, cannot be tested, and hides alternatives fitting the same evidence. When: Combining explanations of the same evidence, or accepting a single story that explains every fact.
- [pitfall] Two incompatible explanations can fit the same residues, so residues alone rarely settle who acted or how.
- [pitfall] An appealing alternative theory can replace the evidence if the investigator stops checking it against facts.
- [pitfall] Do not treat the most detailed version of an account as the most accurate.
- [pitfall] A theory that fits one suspect while leaving the others unexamined is incomplete; test every candidate against it.
- [pitfall] Fixating on one clue blinds the investigator to the rest of the evidence, so the whole picture is lost. When: Many clues conflict and attention narrows to one. Why: Overweighting a single item hides how the others fit together.
- [pitfall] An explanation that fits the narrator's own framework can make every outcome seem to confirm the theory, while remaining untestable against the scene.
- [pitfall] A supernatural explanation can be a cover story, so check whether it explains the traces better than a human agent does. When: A supernatural explanation is offered for physical traces. Why: A human agent may be hiding behind the appearance of the supernatural.
- [pitfall] A narrator with partial information can form a confident wrong theory, and acting on it can lead to an unjust accusation. When: When an observer sees only part of events. Why: Missing facts can look like complete ones.
- [pitfall] Treating an outsider theory and an insider theory as mutually exclusive can hide a lead, since both can be tested.
- [pitfall] Confirming a rival narrative, such as blaming an outside group, while the simpler explanation goes untested, leads the investigation to the wrong conclusion. When: Several stories compete to explain an event. Why: A dramatic rival explanation attracts attention and can displace testing of ordinary causes.
- [fact] Two appeals to a person's character, one from pattern and one from personal knowledge, can compete without either settling the question.

## witness evasion and withholding
- [mechanism] A witness withholding out of care for someone may reveal the fact only after repeated contact, trust or the right evidence; a single appeal to confidentiality does not compel disclosure. When: A witness protects someone they care about, or an NPC withholds a fact for an understandable reason. Why: Motive to conceal outweighs a single request, so repeated contact or evidence is needed to change the position.
- [mechanism] A witness NPC's choice to reveal or withhold a fact can change how other characters judge the suspect. When: a witness holds a fact that bears on a suspect. Why: Other characters weigh the suspect according to what they are told.
- [mechanism] Tie a secret to a trust or reputation value, so revealing it changes how other characters respond to the player or NPC.
- [mechanism] Revealing a secret that the other person finds shameful can turn an outwardly steady relationship into hostility.
- [mechanism] Prolonged questioning through standing, sleep loss, and repeated urging by several questioners in turn wears prisoners down until they agree to nearly anything. When: An interrogation is long and rotates through multiple questioners. Why: Exhaustion and repetition erode resistance and blur memory.
- [behavior] Hedged or technically true wording, declining to speculate, or stated motives for silence can hide how a speaker knew something or intended, signalling a self-serving or incomplete account. When: A statement is smooth but its source or purpose is unclear, or a witness narrates events with qualifiers or a reason to conceal. Why: Careful phrasing avoids admitting hearsay, self-interest or a hidden plan; committing to claims exposes the witness to contradiction; speakers soften claims they are unsure of. (x2)
- [behavior] Witnesses often give vague phrases and admit key facts only when pressed, so a brief answer signals reticence; the admission can reframe earlier events they reported. When: Questioning a witness who may have something to hide, or whose account seems incomplete. Why: Fear of consequences keeps witnesses silent.
- [behavior] Under direct questioning, evasion shows as sharp refusals, claimed forgetting, sudden subject changes, flat replies, comfort or lies, and reluctance to discuss a hobby. When: A suspect is questioned directly about a sensitive matter. Why: Fear, pride, indifference or self-protection can each produce evasion that hides the truth.
- [behavior] A subject who changes the topic or answers a key point with irrelevant questions is stalling; note the redirection and return to it later, as evasion marks a sensitive area. When: A subject steers away from a topic, or is questioned about a key point. Why: Avoidance points to a matter worth revisiting; the redirection itself draws suspicion.
- [behavior] Evasive witnesses show hesitation, delayed replies, folded arms, hands working together, shrugging, nervousness, blame-redirection or a watchful manner replacing a warm greeting. When: During questioning, especially when hesitation or body language conflicts with a flat denial. Why: Such signs are leads to follow up, not proof of guilt; discomfort or shock can produce them innocently, so weigh unprompted disclosures above answers given only when asked.
- [behavior] Hospitality, small talk and flattery build rapport and make a guarded witness talk more freely, especially one short of money. When: A witness is unhelpful at first or in financial need.
- [behavior] Calm, gentle questioning, or warm talk about a topic a person enjoys, makes a guarded witness share more fluently than direct questions do. When: A witness answers in short or guarded replies to direct questions. Why: A relaxed interviewer or conversation lowers the witness's guard.
- [behavior] Framing questioning as help, and stating openly that full candor serves the witness, can make a reluctant witness accept and tell everything. When: A witness holds back information but needs help.
- [behavior] Careful characters avoid writing anything that could later be used against them, and word notes so only the intended reader grasps their purpose. When: a message could incriminate its sender. Why: written words become evidence that outsiders can use.
- [behavior] A witness with failing memory may hide the lapse and recall a point only when a specific cue, such as a named event, prompts it. When: questioning someone whose memory is impaired. Why: People conceal lapses to protect their standing, so recall may appear only when a precise cue is offered.
- [behavior] A witness who refuses to become complicit and asks how silence can be secured reveals their own stake, which is itself evidence. When: a witness is asked to keep quiet. Why: Reasons for silence show what the witness fears.
- [behavior] An evasive witness answers a direct question with mockery, compliments and topic changes rather than a direct reply. When: A witness is pressed on a point she wants to avoid. Why: Deflection keeps control of the exchange and avoids the substance of the question.
- [behavior] A witness with a grudge against a target tends to color statements about that target, even when the details they give sound precise. When: the witness holds open hostility toward the subject. Why: a motive to harm shapes what they emphasize or invent.
- [behavior] A person who knows the attackers but will not name them, or who overstates a vague danger, is likely hiding a personal secret. When: An attacked person is evasive about who attacked them. Why: Refusal to answer and overstated fear signal where the real stakes lie.
- [behavior] A witness bound by silence may speak once a serious charge threatens someone who cannot speak for themselves. When: a secret is held and an absent person is accused. Why: the reason for speaking limits how far the account can be trusted.
- [behavior] A witness who initially hides what they know may have been pressed for silence by the subject, so the reluctance is itself evidence. When: A witness had direct contact with an unknown subject. Why: Pressure to stay quiet shows in the witness's hesitation.
- [behavior] Answers under questioning can be evasive; vague replies, such as excuses about poor visibility, should be recorded and tested rather than accepted. When: a witness gives vague answers about conditions. Why: vagueness can hide the true vantage or motive.
- [behavior] A character may bind others to secrecy and still refuse to explain why, so the reason stays hidden even after the secret is shared.
- [behavior] A guarded suspect often probes with questions about the topic at hand, so the pattern of those questions reveals what they care about. When: a suspect is questioning the investigator.
- [behavior] Several suspects who each hide a private engagement look alike, which can disperse suspicion across the group. When: Multiple suspects conceal similar private activities. Why: Shared secrecy makes innocent and guilty concealments hard to tell apart.
- [behavior] A witness who speaks around a subject, or fixates on an unrelated detail, may be passing on a suggestion without stating it outright. When: speech is circumlocutory, reluctant or oddly fixated. Why: the witness avoids stating the fact directly.
- [behavior] A witness who keeps avoiding a specific object, or sounds strained when it is mentioned, may know more about it than they say. When: Behavior contradicts their words in a narrow, specific way. Why: Awareness of the object can cause avoidance.
- [behavior] Hostility toward a group can grow without any open act, from resentment of its rise or of its separate standing in the community. When: a family or group stands apart from the wider community. Why: resentment and suspicion can spread without a specific offense.
- [behavior] In a divided community, ordinary acts are read as hostile, and evidence is gathered to fit each camp's position. When: a community split into rival parties. Why: Existing hostility shapes how each side interprets events.
- [behavior] A creature guarding something valuable shows it through altered posture, head movement and repeated inspection of one spot. When: a creature has hidden or protects an item. Why: Guarding changes the creature's ordinary conduct.
- [behavior] When neither side makes careless errors, the winner is the player who anticipates the opponent's likely mistakes and exploits them. When: a reduced endgame where both players play carefully. Why: small, predictable mistakes decide the result.
- [behavior] When two parties sense a trap, they test each other with indirect questions and answer carefully, each reading the other as calculating. When: mutual suspicion in a conversation. Why: each side fears the other is steering the exchange.
- [behavior] A pretender who answers probing questions with indignant refusal rather than answers tends to be read as evasive and suspicious. When: A claimed expert is pressed with specialist questions. Why: Anger in place of answers gives the test away and invites suspicion.
- [behavior] A witness who answers indirectly can be pressed with a sequence of narrow, direct questions, and bystanders often judge the resulting account to be untrue when it is evasive. When: A witness refuses or deflects direct questions about money, relationships or motive. Why: Narrow questions remove room for vague answers, and evasion under pressure reads as deception to observers.
- [behavior] A guarded professional's refusal or rebuff to questions signals that they know something relevant, and their suspicion of the questioner's motives often reveals this. When: An NPC refuses to answer or reacts with suspicion. Why: Withholding information is a sign of knowledge or concern.
- [behavior] A guarded character may defend a claim with a plausible explanation, then retreat when asked a specific follow-up about its practical details. When: A character's explanation is pressed with a concrete follow-up question. Why: A prepared surface story often lacks the details needed to answer follow-ups.
- [behavior] Characters often withhold information by default, so trust between them is partial on all sides.
- [behavior] A witness who is evasive or strained, or repeats a last-seen account word for word and denies too quickly, may be guarded; this warrants more questions, not proof of guilt. When: When a witness shows discomfort or reluctance during questioning. Why: Strain and quick denials can come from concealment, or from ignorance, fear or innocence.
- [behavior] A pressed witness often answers with a rejoinder that deflects suspicion without adding information. When: When a witness is questioned on a point they would prefer to avoid. Why: Deflection protects the witness while appearing responsive.
- [behavior] A witness who repeats an answer rather than adding detail, or refuses to commit when asked who had access to a suspected substance, may be protecting someone.
- [rule] Make an NPC's account incomplete or omit one important fact, so a later clue or second source exposes what was left out. When: Designing NPC statements that change over the game. Why: Delayed exposure rewards players who keep and compare clues. (x2)
- [rule] Make an evasive or off-topic answer a cue that prompts the player to follow up. When: Designing NPC dialogue that hides knowledge.
- [rule] Have NPCs withhold information by default so players must cross-check claims rather than trust a single source.
- [rule] Let a friendly NPC whose kind conduct conflicts with other clues hide a hostile objective that the player uncovers later.
- [rule] Keep an investigator's answers neutral and unconcerned when a suspect is listening, so the suspect gains nothing to read. When: when a suspect may be probing what the investigators know. Why: revealed reactions let the suspect adjust.
- [rule] A performer's rules can protect the deception by treating refusal to answer as acceptable while forbidding admission of ignorance, so silence becomes a non-answer. When: When a performer is questioned about something it cannot answer. Why: Refusal preserves the illusion, while admitting ignorance would expose it.
- [rule] Let a hostile reply end the conversation or open a different route, rather than simply failing the player.
- [rule] Do not treat a pleasant or hospitable manner as proof of innocence; judge by behaviour rather than courtesy.
- [rule] Give a secret-holding NPC a trust flag that the player's promise sets, controlling which other characters may learn the information. When: Designing NPCs who share information conditionally. Why: Conditional disclosure makes the player's promises matter.
- [rule] Give dialogue trees evasion flags, with I don't remember options that unlock or lock later questions.
- [rule] Remove a witness from the scene with a plausible errand for a set time so the rest of the scene can be searched unobserved. When: when a search must happen without a witness watching. Why: The witness is absent while the errand lasts.
- [heuristic] Evasion, refusal or curt reply signals concealment, not proof of guilt, innocence or a specific fact; record and test it against other evidence, since fear or caution may cause it. When: A witness refuses, postpones or curtly answers a direct question, even with other details offered, avoids eye contact, over-protests, turns hostile, or is asked about a claim they may have reason to hide. Why: Refusal can reflect fear, principle, irrelevance or caution rather than concealment of fact; a lost trail alone should not confirm wrongdoing; a witness may deny doubt while still evasive. (x2)
- [heuristic] Insider knowledge spreads widely, so a narrow circle of knowers is a hypothesis to test; knowledge many share, like a weapon's location, narrows suspects only slightly. When: Narrowing suspects by what they knew. Why: Routines, schedules and leaks can give outsiders the same facts.
- [heuristic] When a witness says 'I don't know' to a point they plainly can answer, name that directly and re-ask from a different angle or in plainer words. When: A witness repeatedly declines or says 'I don't know' to a specific question. Why: They may be guarded rather than ignorant; reframing can reach information withheld without the witness knowing it.
- [heuristic] A witness who lies about several unrelated details, or takes the blame, may be shielding another person, so look for a motive to protect someone else.
- [heuristic] Mention a guessed name or relationship as already known, then read the witness's reaction, which confirms the link more reliably than a verbal answer and exposes anxiety. When: A witness may confirm a suspect's identity, or an interviewer wants a guarded witness to reveal anxiety. Why: Witnesses react to perceived knowledge held by the questioner.
- [heuristic] Make threats a player option with consequences, such as a witness who turns hostile and refuses further talk.
- [heuristic] When two people share the same hesitation and avoid the same subject, infer that a secret is being kept from the investigator and others. When: Witnesses withhold the same topic.
- [heuristic] Read a hostile or biased source against its grain; its false claims can reveal what its writer wants to hide. When: A source is malicious or self-interested.
- [heuristic] Give NPC dialogue a false justification that the player must test against a clue, such as a note or letter.
- [heuristic] A suspect's weak point can be found in a secret that gives leverage, and the conspirator with a separate personal motive is the one to pressure when another will stay silent. When: One conspirator is unlikely to talk. Why: A second, personal motive offers a lever the silent party lacks.
- [heuristic] Establish a person's usual behaviour first, so that a departure from it stands out as meaningful. When: when watching a suspect's reactions. Why: Change is only visible against a known pattern.
- [heuristic] A refusal to give a name or identity is not evidence in itself, but it signals that the claim needs independent checking.
- [heuristic] An NPC who holds a damaging secret can serve as an early warning, because the culprit may target that NPC. When: Designing an NPC whose secret drives a later threat.
- [heuristic] Answer a direct question evasively to keep it open and build suspense. When: a character is asked a question they are not ready to answer. Why: an unresolved question keeps the audience pressing for the answer.
- [heuristic] Keep an unidentified figure as a default suspect, which prevents the search from closing on the first plausible culprit. When: a mystery has several viable suspects. Why: an open unknown keeps the search from closing early.
- [heuristic] Ambiguous, guarded parting lines leave a character unsettled and keep tension open between scenes.
- [heuristic] Treat each hostile act, such as a bribe, threat or staged fight, as evidence of the opponent's plan.
- [heuristic] Holding back indications that are not yet confirmed keeps an inquiry open and prevents premature conclusions.
- [heuristic] A minimised claim about one's own timing, such as being a few minutes late, should be checked against external records because it can conflict with what actually happened. When: a witness reports their own arrival or movements. Why: self-reports tend to soften timing.
- [heuristic] A stranger who offers a drink at once while watching the target's reaction is giving a second warning sign of an ambush.
- [heuristic] Do not assume every reported remark is strategic, since ordinary candour can explain advice as well. When: When judging the motive behind a piece of counsel. Why: Sincere advice is also common.
- [heuristic] Record what a source withholds as well as what it gives, since omissions can be informative. When: interviewing a guarded witness. Why: refusals can point to hidden facts.
- [heuristic] A contact that someone omits from their account is a fact to check, because the silence can be an inconsistency. When: Comparing a character's account against records. Why: Omissions can conceal relevant connections.
- [heuristic] Hold a key alibi witness back behind fear or confrontation, so the witness gives their account only after the player resolves a related threat. When: designing a critical witness who will not speak freely. Why: Earned testimony carries more weight and ties the witness to the story's stakes.
- [procedure] 1) Match the hostile witness's tone so she does not dismiss you. 2) Reveal your purpose only after she accepts you and presses for it. 3) Press one precise point repeatedly without pause. 4) Record unguarded remarks and watch behaviour after the exchange. When: Interrogating a guarded witness with a hidden tie to a suspect. Why: Rapport lowers defences, precise triggers provoke reactions that broad questions do not, and rapid repetition leaves no time to compose a reply.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the topic the NPC avoids. 2) Assign the NPC a motive to shield another, such as loyalty or fear. 3) Unlock the motive when the player asks the correct follow-up. When: Authoring a guarded NPC whose secret involves another character. Why: A stated motive gives the player a concrete path to the hidden truth.
- [procedure] 1) Appraise the witness before pressing. 2) Adopt a relaxed, sympathetic manner. 3) Accept a stated point, even a doubted one, to keep the witness talking. 4) Verify accepted points later. When: A witness is guarded and a direct question would simply be denied. Why: Lowering the guard keeps the witness talking, but accepted points may be unreliable.
- [tradeoff] Sharing enough evidence wins cooperation, but revealing the core theory can warn the suspect; share evidence and hold the theory back. When: When questioning a cooperative suspect.
- [tradeoff] Guarding answers strongly to a curious stranger protects secrets but can cost goodwill with a contact who may later prove useful.
- [tradeoff] Keeping plans to oneself limits leaks, but it leaves allies guessing and unable to act on accurate information.
- [tradeoff] Locking a secret clue to one character until a later choice creates a real dilemma between sharing it and keeping it private. When: When designing information gating in a mystery. Why: Withholding carries risk, so the player must weigh the cost.
- [tradeoff] Revealing a backup witness early proves a point at once, while holding them back keeps evidence in reserve for use only if the main evidence is challenged. When: Deciding when to disclose a second witness. Why: Early disclosure gives up the option to use the witness as a fallback.
- [tradeoff] A sudden hostile exchange releases built-up tension but closes off the lines of inquiry that were open.
- [pitfall] Failing to defend oneself or reacting with anger toward accusers is an interpretation and weak evidence, not proof of guilt or innocence. When: An accused person fails to defend themselves or confronts or drives off accusers. Why: Anger under accusation can arise from injustice as easily as from guilt. (x2)
- [pitfall] Harsh pressing, mockery or provocation can make a witness refuse cooperation, give contradictory or false information, hide the key detail, and turn into an enemy. When: Pressing a witness who is already defensive or frightened. Why: Pressure triggers defensiveness, lowering account quality and making later checking harder.
- [pitfall] Stalling an answer without new clues frustrates characters and players, reads as evasion rather than suspense, and worsens the longer it lasts. When: The investigator must wait for information, or a central answer is delayed over many scenes. Why: Anticipation needs visible progress to stay engaging; players may stop caring about the answer.
- [pitfall] Withholding a fact without a visible motive shifts audience sympathy away from the holder and frustrates players, so the holder needs a clear reason. When: Writing secrecy into a character's actions. Why: Unexplained concealment seems unfair to the audience.
- [pitfall] Withheld information is not proof of guilt: witnesses may conceal from fear of suspicion, to shield another, or to keep a private matter or innocent errand hidden. When: A suspect or witness keeps a secret. Why: A suspect who keeps a secret can look guilty though innocent.
- [pitfall] Asking a witness to keep a secret can compromise their neutrality later.
- [pitfall] A staged confrontation fails once suspects compare notes, because the separation that makes the test work is lost. When: Running a separated-suspect reaction test. Why: The test relies on suspects not knowing about each other's summons.
- [pitfall] Assuming a secret is a loan or financial transaction by default causes investigators to miss the real nature of the hidden item. When: A hidden object or payment is found without its contents being checked. Why: A familiar explanation is accepted before the evidence is examined.
- [pitfall] Withholding an outcome without sensory clues leaves the scene unclear and the audience unable to follow it.
- [pitfall] Guarding against one risk can create another, such as an escape route that implicates a third party.
- [pitfall] A guarded answer is not always a lie; a witness may speak only about what she was permitted to see.
- [pitfall] A witness who feels confided in may overshare or say what the listener wants to hear, so a single conversation can distort testimony. When: when a witness has been drawn into a sympathetic exchange. Why: Sympathy and flattery bias what a witness reports.
- [pitfall] A host who steers the talk toward personal matters may be shaping the interview, so keep returning to the investigative question.
- [pitfall] A guard's account of who passed is only as reliable as his attention during the watch. When: a guard is the only source of who used an exit.
- [pitfall] A leading hypothetical read as a trap hardens the suspect's defences, so the probe gains little. When: The suspect suspects the frame is a trap. Why: Once the frame is seen, the suspect refuses to engage.
- [pitfall] Confessions that repeat the accusers' described acts may reflect shared sources rather than independent fact.
- [pitfall] Accepting the first tidy answer without asking what it fails to explain is a common investigative error.
- [pitfall] Sharing a theory with a single official can expose the trap to rivals or the press.
- [pitfall] Refusing to hear a witness can lose evidence, since a witness who insists on telling their story may hold what the investigator needs. When: When an investigator wants to avoid a witness's account. Why: Declining to listen discards testimony the witness is willing to give.
- [pitfall] A witness who refuses to confront a supposed source may be hiding a human cause, so the refusal itself deserves scrutiny. When: A witness avoids investigating a claimed threat. Why: Avoidance can protect a concealed mundane explanation.
- [pitfall] A forgetfulness explanation can cover a timeline mismatch, so it should be treated as a claim to test rather than a fact. When: When an anomaly is explained by a person's lapse of memory. Why: Memory-based explanations are easy to accept without verification.
- [fact] A secret can be priced in money, and the person holding it may raise their demands over time. When: when a secret is used as leverage.
- [fact] In a small community where watchers exchange tales, secrets are hard to keep because observations spread from person to person.
- [fact] Everyone inside a guarded, sealed room is a witness for everyone else during the seal, but only for the period the seal lasted.

## records and documents
- [mechanism] Third-party logs, such as exchange records of long-distance calls from a house or postal delivery, link a clue or claimed call to a specific person and can expose a pretence. When: when a suspect claims to have made a call at a set time. Why: Third-party logs exist independently of the suspect.
- [mechanism] Incriminating letters bind the partner who holds them and also expose the writer, so written evidence used as leverage cuts both ways. When: Accomplices have written proof of each other's part in a crime. Why: Written evidence creates shared exposure, not one-sided control.
- [mechanism] A signed or filed document changes recorded ownership, and that record, not physical reality, determines inheritance and tax outcomes. When: ownership or inheritance is disputed.
- [mechanism] A slowly growing material records past exposure: a substance absorbed at the root moves outward with growth, so its position along the strand shows when exposure occurred. When: a material grows steadily and keeps a trace. Why: Growth carries the trace away from its origin over time.
- [mechanism] An abridged version can remain the standard reference long after a full text is available, so the distortion keeps shaping belief. Why: Familiar summaries are reused more than full originals.
- [mechanism] When one side refuses to meet and reconcile accounts, the signed contemporaneous record becomes the only fixed reference point for the disputed events. When: Parties refuse a meeting to resolve a dispute. Why: Without agreement, the earlier written record stands alone.
- [mechanism] A journal entry can cross-reference a clipping from an earlier location, linking two independent sources for the player to find.
- [behavior] Sequentially numbered items were likely issued together, to one recipient, at about the same time. When: When a set of numbered items shares consecutive serial numbers. Why: Sequential issue batches are typically handed out as a unit.
- [behavior] Discarded drafts show hesitation, so a polished letter reflects deliberate effort rather than spontaneous feeling. When: A letter appears to be carefully composed. Why: Each rewrite reflects a choice about tone or content.
- [behavior] In a dispute with signed petitions, people who sign neither side's paper are read as sympathetic to the opposing side. When: both sides circulate signed papers.
- [rule] Write in-world records and NPC reports with observable events, actions and timestamps, leaving feelings and intent for the player to infer. When: Writing in-world records or reports. Why: Facts keep the record reliable while inferred intent adds mystery; feelings and guesses introduce doubt.
- [rule] Give each in-world document a date so players can order documents into a timeline and spot any that refer to events after their own timestamp. When: Writing in-world documents or players collect them. Why: Ordering documents rewards careful reading.
- [rule] Provide checkable records such as ledgers, ferry manifests, registers or NPC schedules so players can confirm or break an alibi rather than simply accept it. When: when designing alibi checks or alibi-based mysteries. Why: Verifiable records turn an alibi into a puzzle the player can solve.
- [rule] Store shared affiliations, such as a dentist or clinic, as records that link two people and can reveal a hidden relationship. Why: A shared record links two people through a common entry.
- [rule] Give NPCs inspectable records such as registers and ledgers, so handwriting or ink details can be checked. When: designing NPC-held evidence.
- [rule] Tie each NPC's stake in a title or inheritance to in-world documents, so the player can see who gains if a ruling goes one way.
- [rule] Match an in-game document's register to its author's intent, so players can read from the wording whether the author is official, threatening or friendly. When: when writing NPC letters or documents. Why: Register conveys the author's stance without explicit description.
- [rule] Build NPC profiles from overheard anecdotes, such as tournaments, pranks and grudges, rather than from a single description.
- [rule] Record which characters were together at past events so later dialogue can reference that shared history. When: Designing social systems for a cast.
- [rule] In an interrogation system, record answers so players can contest the wording, since the transcript should not be the only version of what was said.
- [rule] Keep a dated event log for each NPC so the player can reconstruct who could reach a given location on a given day. When: Designing a mystery world with characters who move between places. Why: A log lets players test alibis against travel and timing.
- [rule] Use signed bonds and official returns as hard evidence, since they record what was done and resist dismissal as hearsay.
- [rule] Use access records for a captive or locked store as a puzzle, showing which NPC could have acted. When: Designing an investigation of a leak or sabotage in a game. Why: Access lists narrow the suspect pool with checkable facts.
- [rule] Make in-world paperwork such as certificates or receipts correct in every line, yet pointing to a false conclusion when combined. Why: Players learn to read records as a whole, not line by line.
- [rule] Place a torn, half-burned note in a searchable grate, with cut edges and a seal impression that point to a specific item or NPC. Why: Partial destruction makes evidence discovery a rewarding search.
- [rule] Let an anonymous note found in the level match a character's handwriting in another document, so the player makes a deduction. Why: Gives players a clear inference step.
- [rule] Make an in-world forged document checkable against a reference the player finds elsewhere, so the forgery is detectable. When: Designing forged documents. Why: Detection needs an independent source.
- [rule] Record which generated clues are planted and which are genuine, so a puzzle can reward players who spot the staging.
- [rule] Build a victim's history as discoverable records, letters and witness recollections so the player can rank suspects by motive. When: When generating background content for a murder-style mystery. Why: Ranking suspects requires evidence the player can gather.
- [rule] Plant deliberate gaps in a document so careful readers notice the omission and follow it to another room or object.
- [rule] Leave a trace of any altered ruling in the court record, so the player can find the original sealed verdict and compare the two. When: when generating in-world court records.
- [rule] Check when and by whom a record was written before trusting it, since existence alone does not establish accuracy. When: Using a diary, ledger or log as evidence. Why: A record made later or by a biased author can be inaccurate.
- [rule] Record exactly what was offered in return for a confession, and mark the confession as conditional so the player must decide whether to trust it. When: a game lets an NPC confess under a deal. Why: the terms of the deal affect how far the confession can be trusted.
- [rule] Keep facts that seem unconnected to the central matter in the record under a formal heading, since later events may reveal links to them. Why: a fact that looks irrelevant early can connect to the main issue later.
- [rule] Record every promise or reward made to a witness, and check whether their later testimony changes afterward. When: Evaluating testimony from a witness who has received a benefit. Why: A stake in the outcome lowers reliability, and changes after a reward can reveal hidden influence.
- [rule] Arrange records so a chosen person's name appears on them, keeping another's out, when the written trail matters later. When: Records whose names will matter to a later reveal. Why: Names on documents become evidence.
- [rule] A recording shows that a physical event occurred, not who caused it; identifying the person needs further evidence. When: Interpreting an instrumental record of an event. Why: A trace establishes occurrence, not agency.
- [rule] A summarized secondhand record must still give enough concrete detail for the player to check it. When: When a reveal is delivered through a summary rather than the full source. Why: Vague summaries cannot be verified, so they feel like assertion rather than evidence.
- [heuristic] A statement or letter gains weight when independent records, such as venue lists, visit logs or contemporaneous diaries, confirm its names, dates and places, or independent sources agree. When: Verifying a witness statement or letter. Why: Independent records test a claim without relying on the source's word; contemporaneous records reduce reliance on later memory. (x2)
- [heuristic] A dated record that contradicts a claimed timeline, or is dated after the event it describes, shows later writing or alteration and undermines every claim it supports. When: when testimony depends on dates. Why: Dating exposes fabrication that the record's content alone hides. (x2)
- [heuristic] A burnt or torn document can still yield a lead: surviving words may point to intent or destination without proving authorship, so combine them with other records to reconstruct meaning. When: A document is burnt, torn or otherwise incomplete. Why: Surviving content can point to intent or destination without proving authorship. (x2)
- [heuristic] Show a comparable earlier event as precedent so an unusual mechanism or action seems plausible, then verify the same conditions existed in the present case. When: a current contradiction or unusual action resembles a documented earlier event. Why: A known precedent shows a mechanism is possible, but it must still be checked against present facts; shared practice lowers implausibility. (x2)
- [heuristic] A dated document signed by several participants gains weight; record each signatory in the game so players can trace and question every person named to check it. When: Verifying what was said at a past event. Why: Multiple signers allow the account to be cross-checked against living witnesses.
- [heuristic] Record small or odd details, such as where a screen stands or which light is off, since they can later serve as reference points or prove significant. When: a scene will be revisited later, or a detail seems trivial. Why: Fixed details give later events a comparison point; trivial anomalies can later prove significant.
- [heuristic] Treat press reports as data to compare with each other and with physical records; repetition in a published account can make an unverified claim look settled. Why: Repetition in a report can hide that no one actually observed the claimed fact.
- [heuristic] Let NPCs hold letters as key items, and let the player obtain them through a cover story the NPC offers.
- [heuristic] Documents help answer questions about ownership, inheritance or the intent behind an act.
- [heuristic] A late letter from a distant NPC can confirm where a stolen item went, leaving a loose thread for a sequel. When: A stolen item must be traced to a remote location late in play. Why: A distant witness can supply confirmation without resolving the whole case.
- [heuristic] Do not assume a notice came from the person it names; check the details it contains against known facts. Why: A notice's named sender can be a cover for another writer.
- [heuristic] Separate conversations in which each NPC reacts differently to the same item let the player identify which one is lying. When: when the player can question several NPCs about one object. Why: inconsistent reactions expose the liar.
- [heuristic] Keep a factual written record of case events that stays separate from the recorder's own role in them.
- [heuristic] Give unidentified NPCs a dossier of blank fields that the player fills through conversation, documents and records, and track which fields remain empty. When: Designing investigation-driven NPCs. Why: Gradual field filling gives players a clear sense of progress.
- [heuristic] Use separate notices for the body and for individual garments, so that each lead can be followed on its own.
- [heuristic] Repeat a witness's testimony at different times and favor the sober version when the player holds a verifying record. When: designing repeated testimony.
- [heuristic] Accommodating a neighbor's boundary claim, even with a small concession, tends to prevent later lawsuits that would otherwise harden into long feuds. When: when a minor boundary quarrel arises between neighbors. Why: early concessions keep a quarrel from becoming an entrenched legal record.
- [heuristic] Deeds and wills record transactions, not feelings, so a stated affection in a document does not prove the real closeness of the parties.
- [heuristic] A lore codex can hold an abridged letter whose full original, kept in another archive, contains an omitted line that changes the reading. When: designing lore documents with hidden context. Why: Players who find the full text reinterpret the summary.
- [heuristic] Note how an entry was squeezed or slanted into place when comparing hands, since layout can reveal how the writing was made. When: comparing handwriting across entries.
- [heuristic] Administrative bills for lodging and transport show which venues were used for an event and how heavily each was employed. When: reconstructing where official proceedings took place.
- [heuristic] A person named in a later account but absent from contemporary petitions or certificates weakens the claim of their role.
- [heuristic] Let in-world ledgers or deed books hold several small transfers so the player must compile them to see that one party gains control of a district. When: Designing investigation content in a generated world. Why: Compiling scattered records rewards the player with a discovered pattern.
- [heuristic] A clue journal can use one tab per suspect plus a general tab, and flag when two accounts disagree. When: designing an in-game clue log. Why: Makes conflicts visible side by side.
- [heuristic] A character who records details carefully signals that the record will matter later, so the note works as a clue flag. When: a character writes down dates or details. Why: careful record keeping implies future use.
- [heuristic] A letter written for private reasons can later serve as evidence, because affectionate or detailed description may record facts the author never intended to preserve. When: A personal letter is later used by an investigator. Why: The author wrote for emotional purposes, so specific details are incidental and can be checked.
- [heuristic] Record a stated explanation alongside the physical evidence so the player can compare them, rather than being told the answer. When: Designing a clue that tests a claim. Why: Side-by-side comparison lets the player reach the conclusion.
- [heuristic] A found document gains credibility when it states who wrote it, how it was recovered, and what was left out. When: when a story relies on a recovered record. Why: Provenance lets the reader weigh the evidence before trusting the content.
- [heuristic] Dialogue choices that record promises let later NPCs check whether the player kept them, creating consequences. When: when designing branching dialogue with promises. Why: Tracked commitments turn choices into later consequences.
- [heuristic] Fresh mud prints found after a dry week were made that day, and their presence in one place can show which entrance was used.
- [heuristic] Read a record for repeated annotations and gaps, since a recurring mark may look significant without context and a sudden stop often signals a change in routine. When: Interpreting a diary, log or dated record found in the world. Why: Patterns and gaps point to events, but the meaning of a repeated mark stays uncertain until connected to other evidence.
- [heuristic] Record unexplained anomalies as open rather than forcing a verdict when the evidence for and against a human cause is balanced.
- [heuristic] Make the proof a records trail, such as an order or registry entry, that can be checked within the story world. When: providing evidence for a late-stage reveal. Why: Checkable records make the solution verifiable rather than a bare accusation.
- [procedure] 1) State the suspect's false claim. 2) Refute it with authenticated records. 3) Present a parallel case showing how such an impostor could be built. 4) Link the suspect to the impostor identity. When: when a suspect has built a false identity.
- [procedure] 1) Record each exhibit at handover. 2) Note who handed it over and who received it. 3) Link the exhibit to its role in the case.
- [procedure] 1) List every known fact as a short numbered entry. 2) Group entries by event. 3) Record who was or could have been present at each event. 4) Read all entries together to find connections between them. When: many facts seem to conflict and no unifying idea has emerged.
- [procedure] 1) Check the document for formal defects such as a missing witness. 2) Trace any appeal to the highest authority that rules on it. 3) Compare the disputed document with later documents. 4) Decide the outcome from the formal result, not from intent alone. When: A claim depends on a disputed will or similar instrument. Why: Formal requirements decide validity, and later documents can override earlier ones.
- [procedure] 1) Collect constable returns and warrants with dates. 2) Order them chronologically. 3) Read the sequence of pursuit and arrest to place each person's movements at each date. When: reconstructing a series of arrests or pursuits.
- [procedure] 1) Write minutes of the event the same evening. 2) Have present witnesses sign to confirm them under oath. 3) Share the record with the opposing party. 4) Invite specific corrections. 5) Answer each objection on its merits. When: An event will later be disputed and memories must be fixed while fresh. Why: Early, witnessed records resist later reconstruction.
- [procedure] 1) Write a vague statement that hints at a breakthrough and implies a motive without naming anyone. 2) Release it through a channel the target reads daily. 3) Prepare the next move before release, so the reaction can be met. When: The suspect follows the public record and will react to it. Why: A prepared follow-up turns the target's reaction into a useful encounter.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each official or local record connected to the case. 2) Trace every entry. 3) Discard entries unrelated to the scene. 4) Test each remaining record against the others to find a link or dead end.
