When: The suspect pool is scattered across several sources. Why: Records confirm or drop suspects.
- [tradeoff] A factual record is reliable and checkable but can leave readers cold and hide what matters most to the people reading it. When: Choosing between a bare record and an emotional account. Why: Removing interpretation also removes the meaning readers care about.
- [tradeoff] Clue documents can carry dates, scribes and handwriting, with a later hand altering a clue so the player must work out which version is original. When: When designing in-game documents as puzzle clues. Why: Provenance details give the player a way to verify evidence rather than accept it at face value.
- [pitfall] A consistent record shows the story is consistent, not that it is true; the item may have passed through hands unnoticed.
- [pitfall] A fully executed document is hard to undo, so errors in its wording are costly once it has been signed. When: drafting a binding agreement.
- [pitfall] A person asked to sign a partly hidden document cannot know what she attests, so she cannot judge the commitment she makes. When: A contract or pledge is shown only in part.
- [pitfall] An exhibit linked to a suspect may prove presence or contact only, not the act itself; test what it actually shows.
- [pitfall] A code known to only one person loses its security when that person is captured.
- [pitfall] A shared record proves a common connection but not necessarily a significant one, so weigh it before drawing conclusions.
- [pitfall] A dated record reflects only what was recorded at that instant, so a claim must be checked against entries both before and after the event.
- [pitfall] An excerpt that reads smoothly is not thereby complete; smooth prose can hide cuts that only a comparison with the full text reveals.
- [pitfall] Absence of a recorded inquiry is not proof that no inquiry took place.
- [pitfall] A record kept by a distracted or inexperienced clerk can be corrupted by mixed-up goods, change and entries, making the total uncertain and misleading. When: Planting ledgers or tallies as in-game evidence. Why: Confused record-keeping can mislead as much as having no record at all.
- [pitfall] Identity evidence depends on accurate records; a match is only possible if the original distinctive features were recorded. When: Using records to match physical traces. Why: Without a recorded baseline, the match cannot be made.
- [pitfall] Personal writings reflect the writer's self-image and mood as much as events, so their damaging lines may be read as moods rather than plans. When: A diary or journal is offered as evidence. Why: Writers often exaggerate or express feelings in low spirits.
- [pitfall] A reference record with a wrong name or date produces false matches or mismatches, so the provenance of every record must be verified. When: When relying on an archive of identifiers for identification. Why: Errors in labels propagate into every comparison made against them.
- [pitfall] A humble record such as a plain headstone can carry more intimate evidence than a grand monument, so humble records should not be dismissed. When: Weighing the evidential value of different kinds of records. Why: Plain records often reflect personal, individual detail rather than public display.
- [fact] Destroying a document does not remove the people who wrote, signed or witnessed it; their testimony and memories remain available to questioning.
- [fact] A solitary record fails to convince others for three reasons: its circumstances lie outside ordinary experience, it embodies the recorder's own theory, and only the recorder vouches for it.
- [fact] A witness who heard a dying person's words may be the only record of them, so that account carries special weight.
- [fact] Outgoing letters placed in a shared collection bag leave no trace for the household, limiting what anyone can learn about one person's correspondence. Why: Once collected, the letter's contents are no longer accessible to those in the home.
- [fact] Serial-numbered physical currency can be traced through the issuing institution, linking each holder to a place and time along its path.
- [fact] A separate account under a second name keeps that identity's money away from the bank where the person is known.
- [fact] A written document can carry evidence through its phrasing and omissions as well as through its stated facts.
- [fact] Authority to dispose of land can pass from a central body to local towns, so a later grant must be checked against the body that actually issued it. When: records that span a change in who controlled land disposal.
- [fact] Collecting case reports from many correspondents and printing their replies creates a shared reference set that other communities can read and copy. When: When case accounts are gathered and published. Why: Printed collections make one case's details available elsewhere.
- [fact] Authors rearrange real details to suit their purposes, so documents supply raw material rather than a finished account. When: Interpreting a work that draws on historical records. Why: Creators select and reshape evidence to serve the story they want to tell.
- [fact] A printed date on a document can fix when the material it contains was obtained. When: when dating physical records.

## trace evidence analysis
- [definition] Material facts such as times, distances and records differ from inferences drawn from a suspect's character or behaviour.
- [definition] Trace evidence is faint physical residue, such as a shallow floor depression or spilled particles, that shows where an object once stood or what was moved.
- [mechanism] Physical traces that look incriminating, shown before the innocent explanation is available, lead the audience to settle on a wrong suspicion.
- [mechanism] Overlapping marks on one object can form a puzzle in which the player separates two sets of traces and attributes each to a person.
- [mechanism] Offenders remove traces by wearing gloves, brushing or drying mud and clothing, disposing of tools or keys, and altering a victim's hair or face. When: An offender tries to hide their presence. Why: Each method targets a different kind of trace.
- [mechanism] A physical trace identifies a person only by matching a stored record, such as a fingerprint file; without that record the trace proves little. When: a trace may link to a known record. Why: identification depends on a database entry to compare against.
- [behavior] A trace's description can shift as an observer looks closer, moving from a vague label to a specific and more serious one. Why: Close inspection changes what the observer sees and names.
- [behavior] Dust, mould and mud record shapes; a mark that looks like a shapeless smudge can hold a clear pattern when examined closely under magnification. When: when a trace first looks uninformative. Why: fine detail survives in soft deposits and is missed at a glance.
- [rule] A trace proves identity only with independent confirmation, such as weather, a garment's cut or a disinterested witness; trace inference alone is not proof. (x2)
- [rule] Before treating a trace as proof, check it fits the injury's location, direction and finality; a trace that does not fit the wound proves little and can support rival readings. When: When traces seem to support a theory or evidence is weighed against an injury. Why: Odd traces are easy to over-read, and mismatched traces can support rival readings.
- [rule] A trace becomes evidence only when matched to a second object or record that could have made it and to a record of who held it. When: when a physical trace is used as a clue. Why: A trace without a comparison cannot link to a source.
- [rule] Match footwear found at the scene to the prints by fitting pattern and wear, and treat an identifying mark such as a worn heel as a unique identifier. When: when a suspected shoe is recovered. Why: Specific wear patterns can tie a print to one item.
- [rule] Compare suspect fingerprints with case prints only when a clean, reliable record exists; without one, a match cannot be confirmed. When: When using fingerprints to link or exclude a suspect. Why: Poor or incomplete records prevent a reliable identification.
- [rule] A matching trace shows a link, not a sole explanation; weigh each object against the rest of the evidence. When: when a trace matches a suspect.
- [rule] Avoid placing traces whose meaning is never tied to any character or event, since players cannot use them.
- [rule] Examine a document's material properties, such as paper stock, printed marks and envelope, as well as its words. When: A document lacks a name or signature. Why: Physical traits can reveal origin and handling.
- [rule] When a clue depends on a matched pair and the expected partner is missing from its usual place or found elsewhere, the theory built on that clue must change. When: a clue relies on an item having a matching partner. Why: the pair no longer fits the theory.
- [rule] Do not settle a cause of death from physical traces alone; read them together with motive and timing. When: Choosing between accident, suicide and murder. Why: Traces are ambiguous and gain weight only when combined with other evidence.
- [rule] Every physical trace and dated record must fit the proposed sequence of events; a sequence that fails any one trace is rejected. When: when evaluating a reconstructed sequence. Why: each trace is independent evidence of how the event happened.
- [rule] Keep a master key in the calculation unless its guarding is strict enough to rule out its use. When: A master key exists and is guarded.
- [rule] Use wear and material on a gate or post as a dating clue for a room's history. When: Designing a space with a layered history. Why: Physical wear reveals approximate age and changes over time.
- [rule] Turn small material disputes into motive records so players can identify which rival holds the strongest grievance.
- [rule] Cover remaining fragile traces with boxes or boards so they survive until they can be recorded. When: Traces cannot be captured immediately. Why: Physical covers slow the damage from thaw or weather.
- [rule] Distinguish a faint trace from an identifiable impression, and do not treat an ambiguous mark as a print until other evidence supports it. When: Interpreting a faint mark at a scene. Why: Hopeful investigators can read ambiguous marks as definite prints.
- [rule] Make the final proof multi-part and physical, combining items such as document fragments, a lab extract and a found object. When: Assembling the evidence for a mystery's climax. Why: Several physical pieces together are harder to dismiss than a single claim and give the reveal weight.
- [heuristic] A trace proves contact, not guilt; treat a trace link as a lead, not a verdict, since innocent contact and trades can produce the same trace. When: Interpreting a trace as evidence against a person or linking a trace substance to a suspect's item. Why: Contact is common and does not establish intent.
- [heuristic] Match small traces such as soil or grit to the places where that material occurs, comparing them with comparable samples, to narrow where a person recently went. When: when a person's movements are unknown. Why: A distinctive material links the trace to a location.
- [heuristic] Read wear, stains and odd or repetitive marks as records of a person's habits, methods and activities; untrained observers see only appearance. When: examining people or objects for evidence; a trace is odd or repetitive and its purpose is unclear. Why: Traces record repeated behaviour.
- [heuristic] A match on an unusual detail, such as a paper watermark, rare tobacco blend or unusual match type, ties a common object to one owner; a common detail is weak. When: asking who made, owned or used a common object.
- [heuristic] Residue that looks uniform to the naked eye can break into recognisable fragments under magnification, so examine samples under a microscope. When: when analysing dust or residue. Why: fragments identify the substances and sources.
- [heuristic] A physical trace can have several possible makers, so do not identify a person from it until you have considered who else could produce it. When: A trace could have been made by more than one person. Why: Shoes, sizes and borrowed items let different people leave the same mark.
- [heuristic] A trace is strong evidence when its location matches where the event should have occurred. When: Checking a stain or mark against a hypothesised event.
- [heuristic] Note precisely where a trace sits: a deposit in one narrow spot is stronger evidence than a diffuse smear.
- [heuristic] Compare scene fragments side by side with items from a suspect's rooms, matching by material, colour and damage. When: when two locations may share a trace.
- [heuristic] Physical traces that match an account test its consistency, not its truth, because a planned alibi can also fit the physical evidence. When: when a detailed account matches the scene. Why: A carefully prepared story can account for every visible trace.
- [heuristic] Materials and craftsmanship reveal an owner's care and class, and can rule out a careless owner.
- [heuristic] Compare a fragment's material, not only its shape, since a matching outline can come from a different cloth. When: matching a found piece to its claimed source. Why: shape alone can match by chance.
- [heuristic] Choose a trace that splits the suspects, so a trait carried by few candidates narrows the field at once. When: Selecting a clue for an elimination test.
- [heuristic] Do not force a closed door when the traces show no danger; the traces should decide whether to act. When: Deciding whether to open a closed space.
- [heuristic] Treat a reading of a trace as a hypothesis to test; it may show staging without explaining how the event itself happened. When: interpreting a suspicious physical detail. Why: a staged detail is evidence about behaviour, not the mechanism of the act.
- [heuristic] Read a physical trace against each competing hypothesis, because one mark can support two opposite accounts of the same death. When: Cause of death is disputed between accident, suicide and murder. Why: Scratches and marks have several possible causes, so the same trace can fit different stories.
- [heuristic] Check each physical trace against other known facts before trusting it, and build conclusions only from several small facts that can be checked separately.
- [heuristic] Matching prints across several objects link one person to all of them, but the timing of each print must still be established.
- [heuristic] Compare dirt or soot on a floor with material from outside the location. Similar residue suggests the same route was taken. When: when a trace is found inside and the route is unknown. Why: Matching materials links an interior trace to an exterior path.
- [heuristic] Match bruise patterns to the places where fabric is torn to infer how a person was gripped. When: Grip-like marks and torn fabric are both present. Why: Marks at matching locations point to a shared cause.
- [heuristic] Game maps can carry trace evidence such as disturbed soil, cut vegetation or boat marks, letting players reconstruct events by asking what the terrain would have allowed. Why: Physical traces make past events discoverable without direct testimony.
- [heuristic] Particles found across an entire item suggest the air of where it habitually hangs, while particles on one side suggest traces picked up along the way. When: when comparing particle distribution across an item.
- [heuristic] A combination of particle types found in only one district can narrow the locality when checked against a directory of local trades. When: when particle types indicate local industries. Why: unusual combinations tie to few places.
- [heuristic] Missing dirt can be as informative as present dirt: if a claimed route should have left sand, gravel or earth on shoes, its absence contradicts the claim. When: a claimed route crosses a surface that leaves traces. Why: the route would have deposited that material on footwear.
- [heuristic] Estimate a document's age by comparing it side by side with a newer sample, since visible wear such as yellowing and thickness differences reveal age. When: A clue depends on when a material was produced. Why: Side-by-side comparison exposes differences that are hard to judge from one sample alone.
- [heuristic] Collect and label small trace objects such as cigarette ends before any testing; an unlabeled or mixed trace cannot be reliably linked to its source. When: A small object might connect a person to a scene. Why: Preserving the link between trace and source is what makes the trace usable as evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Find the physical trace. 2) Find candidate objects that could have made it. 3) Accept a match only when the object fits exactly. 4) Only then link the mark to that person. When: when a trace could belong to several people. Why: an unmatched print proves nothing about who made it.
- [procedure] 1) List every physical trace in the scene. 2) For each trace, list people who could have made it and test their capacity for that act. 3) Keep only suspects consistent with all traces. Why: Isolated traces mislead; matching each one to possible makers turns it into evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Treat each trace as a question, since it usually supports several explanations. 2) Record it and state its probable meaning. 3) State at least one alternative reading. 4) Withhold judgement until both readings are tested. When: Interpreting physical evidence at a scene, early before further tests return. Why: Logging before judging keeps an early theory from dismissing traces that fit another reading.
- [procedure] 1) Count the links between you and the account. 2) Trace each link back to its speaker to find the first witness. 3) Check which relays were actually verified. 4) Treat repeated phrasing as a possible sign of a single origin. When: Several people or agencies seem to confirm the same account. Why: Repetition can hide a single original report.
- [procedure] 1) Examine soles and garments with a lens and naked eye, and inspect seams under magnification. 2) Lift fibres or particles with tweezers, not fingers. 3) Seal each sample at once in a labelled envelope, noting its source. 4) Wrap the item in clean paper and keep it for later analysis. When: Trace material is small enough to be lost. Why: Fingers and loose handling contaminate or lose fine traces.
- [procedure] 1) Record each sample's exact location on the object and when it was collected; undocumented samples weaken evidence. 2) Seal each in its own labelled container so materials do not mix. 3) Keep records for later comparison. When: When collecting small, easily overlooked or easily destroyed trace samples for analysis. Why: Exact location and time allow later comparison; separate containers prevent cross-contamination.
- [procedure] 1) Record the unknown trace's shape and features. 2) Create or obtain a known reference of a candidate source. 3) Place the reference beside the unknown trace. 4) Note which features match and which differ. When: when an unknown mark must be attributed to a source. Why: a side-by-side comparison exposes differences a lone trace hides.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the object's outline with the trace on the body 2) Check whether a fixed part, such as a buckle prong, fits the most-worn position. When: a body trace may belong to a seized object.
- [procedure] Collect trace evidence with care, such as fibres under a victim's nails or cloth cut from where a weapon was wiped, before the scene is disturbed. When: processing a crime scene. Why: traces are small and easily lost.
- [procedure] 1) Collect loose material from the suspect, such as dust from their feet. 2) Collect a matching sample from the place in question. 3) Compare the two samples side by side. 4) Seal and preserve each item until trial. When: A suspect denies presence at a place and a trace from that place is available. Why: A match between suspect and scene material tests the denial, and sealing preserves the chain of custody.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the paper colour of the two sheets side by side. 2) Hold both to light and compare their appearance. 3) Align the edges and check whether ruling lines match. 4) Note distinctive defects that recur across consecutive sheets. When: A document's paper can be compared with a known stock. Why: Shared physical features across sheets point to a common source.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain a known sample from the item's original source. 2) Compare its traits, such as colour and thickness, with the found item. 3) If they match, conclude the found item came from that source and that someone else had access to it. When: an item is found in a place where it should not be. Why: a verified match turns an odd find into evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Examine the sample under low magnification. 2) Sort visible particles by type, such as fibres, dust, skin and residue. 3) Identify the residue substance. 4) Link the substance to a trade or activity. When: An object carries residue or debris that may tie it to a person or trade. Why: Sorting particles by type and identifying the substance gives a traceable lead.
- [procedure] 1) Cut a small sample from the stained area. 2) Mount it in a fluid reagent on a slide. 3) Examine individual cell or fibre shapes under magnification. 4) Compare them with a labelled reference collection to identify the source. When: When a stain or small object could link a suspect to a place, animal or setting. Why: Microscopic structure distinguishes sources that look alike to the naked eye.
- [procedure] 1) Judge the trace's freshness to tie it to a time. 2) Check where the item is sold. 3) Rule out household members who use it. 4) Compare the trace with the suspect's own possessions.
- [procedure] 1) Record a physical trace immediately, with its time. 2) Compare it against the suspect's known profile. 3) Store the match result in the case file. When: investigating a physical trace such as a bite or mark. Why: Immediate recording prevents loss of the trace and keeps the comparison checkable.
- [procedure] 1) Collect traces from the body and its footwear. 2) Identify each trace's material under magnification. 3) Compare the materials with candidate locations. 4) Exclude traces the investigators carried in themselves.
- [procedure] 1) Collect trace material onto a clean surface in the suspect's presence. 2) Divide it, giving the suspect's custodian a portion to seal. 3) Seal the portion in front of the suspect. 4) Record the custody chain. When: A trace must later be matched to a location and the suspect might dispute it. Why: Sealing in the suspect's presence prevents a later claim that the sample was switched.
- [procedure] 1) Discard trampled central paths. 2) Inspect the edges and surroundings of the path where impressions remain distinct. 3) Note marks that differ in walking pattern. 4) Read overlapping prints so the later step cuts into the earlier one. 5) Follow each trail to its endpoints and look for turns, doubling back or struggle. When: Interpreting footprint evidence in a scene. Why: Contaminated paths mislead and overlaps and endpoints show order and cause.
- [procedure] 1) Fire test projectiles through the same cloth and layers as the suspect garment. 2) Compare their marks with the recovered projectile under matching conditions. 3) Treat a partial impression judged by eye alone as weak evidence. When: A recovered projectile must be linked to a garment.
- [metric] A cigarette lit with matches typically uses about three matches, so a count of spent matches estimates how many cigarettes were lit. When: matches are the only available measure of smoking. Why: each light consumes a roughly fixed number of matches.
- [tradeoff] Fine, stretchable threads give more reliable traces than adhesive glue, because they are nearly invisible and do not give a false disturbance. When: When choosing a material for a trap or trace that must not be noticed. Why: A material that is hard to see and sensitive to contact records movement more reliably.
- [pitfall] Over-reading a trace common to many occupations or a widely owned object convicts the wrong person; it does not prove who owned or used a particular item. When: Linking a common trace substance or widely owned object to a suspect. Why: A widely shared substance or item cannot single out one person.
- [pitfall] Assuming a trace belongs to the culprit can wrongly implicate an innocent visitor or a household member.
- [pitfall] Physical traces can be misread, and a timing inference drawn from one, such as a liquid level, is a guess that may not match the true time.
- [pitfall] Reading a surface detail as old without checking its freshness can lead to a wrong conclusion, so judge freshness before drawing inferences. When: when interpreting labels or marks. Why: A new label can look like an old one.
- [pitfall] Weather, light and handling degrade traces, and a suspect can exploit these conditions to cast doubt on physical evidence. When: When a trace is collected under poor or changing conditions. Why: Degraded conditions give a suspect grounds to dispute the trace.
- [pitfall] A small print can be misread as belonging to a child or a small person; only comparison with a reference reveals its true type. When: when interpreting a print's size or owner. Why: a single trace gives an unreliable first impression.
- [pitfall] A physical trace that contradicts a witness may expose either the witness or a second party, so check the trace before trusting either. When: Physical evidence disagrees with a testimony. Why: Either account may be wrong, and the trace may reveal a hidden actor.
- [pitfall] Assuming a sequence from one trace, or overlooking small ones such as a towel or knuckle marks, produces a wrong reconstruction.
- [pitfall] A dull, patchy surface is easily taken for simple shabbiness, and its meaning is missed unless someone reads the pattern.
- [pitfall] A mark that looks intentional may come from natural forces, and a mark that looks natural may be deliberate, so each mark's physical logic must be tested.
- [pitfall] Linking two cases through a shared trace is often an assumption rather than a finding, especially when the investigators already know each other. Why: Acquaintance does not establish that one actor left both traces.
- [pitfall] An investigator's own lapse, such as an unlocked door, can become the decisive gap, so record exact times of each opening and closing. Why: undocumented times make one's own mistake indistinguishable from a culprit's.
- [pitfall] Faint or smeared marks can make layering ambiguous, so a confident reading of their order may be wrong. When: Marks are faint, smeared or partly covered. Why: Unclear edges make the overlap order uncertain.
- [pitfall] A trace placed where a casual visitor will meet it may be disturbed, but one placed where a visitor avoids it will record nothing. When: When positioning a trace or trap. Why: Placement determines whether the expected visitor interacts with it.
- [fact] A physical trace shows that movement, entry or an object's presence occurred, not who caused it or handled it; treating it as proof of who moved something is a mistake. When: When a trace is used as evidence. Why: The trace records the disturbance, not the identity of the one who caused it.
- [fact] Fingerprints, mud, hair, fibres, dust, debris and small clothing damage record where a person has been and what they did. When: When a person's whereabouts are in question or a scene is examined for presence. Why: Each object carries physical traces of contact.
- [fact] When material facts seem to exclude a suspect favored by character tests, the conflict stays unresolved until a method is found.
- [fact] Under magnification, the shape of hairs and fibres identifies their material or source, so a small trace can point to a particular animal or material.
- [fact] Matching initials or markings can link two people to one object, and testing true ownership can reverse a conclusion.
- [fact] A matching object shows two items are alike, not who owned them or why they were there.
- [fact] Hair torn out with tissue still on its roots indicates that the pulling force was great. When: reading force from a physical trace. Why: tissue tearing with the hair shows strong pulling.
- [fact] A message built from cut-out printed words carries evidence in its paper, typeface and fragments, which can reveal where it came from.
- [fact] A smear or stain can place an object at a location, and a name written on it can tie the object to its owner.
- [fact] Certain materials, such as tarred twine, are associated with particular trades, so the material can suggest a sender's occupation or environment. When: When identifying the origin of a packaged object. Why: Materials tend to be tied to specific workplaces and crafts.
- [fact] A trace that connects two separated places can show that an event happened even when no witness saw it.

## delayed and retrospective reveals
- [definition] Dramatic irony is the gap between what an audience knows and what characters understand, so the audience sees more than the speakers do.
- [definition] A delayed reveal withholds the full explanation of an event until after it happens, then reconstructs the plan in a debrief.
- [definition] Delayed disclosure is a message held by a third party and released only after the sender's death or on a set date.
- [definition] Delayed reveal withholds a central fact across repeated pauses, so the audience waits for it while the pauses build suspense.
- [mechanism] Faint, seemingly arbitrary details gain meaning only after a reveal; withholding their purpose rewards careful notice without signalling importance when they appear. When: The solution depends on details that look arbitrary when first encountered. Why: The later explanation reframes the earlier details. (x2)
- [mechanism] A sealed item or packet with a stated release condition defers its content while staying visible, and can give a second, personal account; the wait builds interest rather than confusion. When: Designing a clue that pays off after a set condition, or when the answer should arrive in stages. Why: Withholding content defers the payoff while keeping the item visible; the reader waits for a condition they can follow. (x2)
- [mechanism] Giving the audience a fact characters do not weigh creates dramatic irony: the audience sees the plan or danger a character walks toward, making each decision feel fraught. When: when the audience has information a character lacks.
- [mechanism] Holding back a key fact or source and delaying its reveal raises expectation, so each delay makes the eventual reveal carry more weight, especially when it reinterprets earlier events. When: the reveal reinterprets earlier events, or a long investigation promises a next source. Why: A late reinterpretation lands harder than information given up front.
- [mechanism] A notice sent by post or carried by a courier can sit undelivered, so the recipient learns of an arrival only when the visitor appears; reveal the missed delivery later. When: plot depends on information reaching a character late. Why: An undelivered message removes the recipient's warning.
- [mechanism] An earlier clue gains meaning only when a later revelation links it to a name or fact, so unexplained clues should be kept on record until then. When: Clue is planted long before its explanation. Why: The link is recalled only when the late fact arrives.
- [mechanism] Postponing a key witness while a deadline stays fixed extends the unresolved wait and raises tension. Why: Each postponement adds time in which the stakes remain undecided.
- [mechanism] A requested delay combined with a pending action, such as an arrest, raises tension because the audience cannot know whether the action will happen in the meantime. When: a reveal is postponed while a threatened step is pending. Why: uncertainty about the outcome raises the stakes.
- [mechanism] Holding back a confession just before it is spoken builds suspense, and each postponement raises the stakes. When: a reveal depends on a delayed decision. Why: anticipation grows with each delay.
- [mechanism] Delivery routes and day schedules constrain when a sent item can arrive, so arrival timing can serve as a clue pointing to a later event.
- [mechanism] Delaying the alarm lets the body cool and stiffen, which blurs any later estimate of when death occurred. When: when the discovery of a body is delayed. Why: post-mortem changes alter the evidence over time.
- [mechanism] A hidden witness who cannot leave without revealing their presence is forced to wait, and that waiting builds suspense. When: When a character is concealed near an event and must stay put. Why: Inability to act while close to danger raises tension.
- [mechanism] Showing the reader the crime and the culprit's identity before the investigators learn them creates dramatic irony and suspense, while clues remain fair because the reader has witnessed them directly. When: Designing stories where audience knowledge should drive tension. Why: The audience holds information the characters lack, so each character action carries suspense.
- [mechanism] Delaying disclosure builds tension, which is released when a full reconstruction makes the solution verifiable.
- [mechanism] A blocked route can delay a hearing and let whichever party is present act first, creating an organic deadline that shifts control to another faction. When: a legal or political process depends on travel or timing. Why: Delay changes who is able to act before others.
- [mechanism] Delay can be used to hold an outcome back, such as a confirmation left pending for long periods or a meeting postponed.
- [mechanism] Dramatic irony arises when the audience sees the gap between an outsider's reading of a group and what the group actually means.
- [mechanism] Withholding the culprit's identity until the supporting proof is laid out builds suspense, and a pause before the accusation lets the accused react and extends tension. When: A climactic reveal where the audience should be able to follow the reasoning. Why: Delay raises anticipation, and an ordered presentation of the case lets listeners verify each step before the payoff.
- [mechanism] Withholding what is happening and giving a single partial clue sustains tension and drives characters to act before the full picture is known.
- [mechanism] A delayed-onset effect keeps open only those earlier stages that could still have acted before symptoms began, so onset time narrows the window. When: a harmful effect takes time to appear. Why: A stage cannot cause symptoms that appear before it could have acted.
- [mechanism] Holding the full backstory until it is complete makes the later reveal more meaningful, but long withholding costs audience engagement as attention wanders. When: Choosing when to release backstory. Why: Delay increases impact but risks losing the audience.
- [mechanism] Revealing an inheritance chain link by link forces the player to establish each relation before the motive becomes clear. When: a motive is spread across several documents. Why: Sequential revelation makes the player check each step rather than jump to a conclusion.
- [behavior] A painful disclosure that is put off repeatedly is rarely made; concealment grows by inertia rather than by a decision. When: a character holds a secret that causes guilt. Why: Each deferral lowers the odds of ever speaking.
- [behavior] Each retelling of a rumour adds vivid physical details, while the cause of the event shrinks to a few words. When: Event relayed through several people. Why: The most dramatic version tends to travel fastest.
- [behavior] When the audience knows a scheme that the target does not, the target's calm moments become tense, because each ordinary action is read against the threat. When: when building suspense before a confrontation. Why: knowledge of the hidden plan changes how the audience reads ordinary moments.
- [rule] Each step of a repeated or delayed reveal must add a new fact; repeats without new information dull tension and cause frustration. When: a disclosure is built up for suspense.
- [rule] Declare each delayed effect as a testable rule, not a generic excuse; if observed timing diverges from the expected delay, suspect another source or an interfering factor.
- [rule] Do not treat a dramatic lead or result as proof, since it can hide weak reasoning; check it against physical evidence before acting on it. When: a striking message or claim draws attention. Why: Attention is not proof.
- [rule] Place a physical sign, such as a mismatched ticket half, that stays inert until a later explanation reframes it, and show the concealed action in the scene itself. When: When designing a clue.
- [rule] A later reveal, such as dialogue, can recast an earlier event or completed quest, so design outcomes to read differently once new information arrives. When: Designing a late plot revelation. Why: New information changes the meaning of details already seen.
- [rule] Note an unexplained word or claim and hold it for later follow-up rather than pressing on it now. When: A suspect uses a term or claim that is not yet explained. Why: Deferred questions preserve a lead without tipping the suspect off.
- [rule] Delay revealing the cause of a character's reaction, letting it stand unexplained for a while before the reason is shown. When: a character's knowledge is suspected but not stated.
- [rule] After a confession, re-tag earlier objects and events with their true purpose, so replaying the game reveals new meaning from the same content. When: when a reveal recasts earlier content. Why: Objects gain significance once their purpose is known.
- [rule] Use delayed reveals at a climax, where partial information raises stakes, and end the scene before the full picture is shown. When: at a climax.
- [rule] If a substance could not have acted by the stated hour, that hour is ruled out as a time of effect. When: Testing a claimed dosing time. Why: Physical timing rules out impossible claims.
- [rule] Give each listener a distinct reaction, such as shock, cold distance, declared loyalty or collapse, so each reaction reveals where that person stands. When: writing a group reveal.
- [rule] Leave the physical or mental cause of a sealed room's mystery open until enough clues have accumulated to support one. Why: Premature answers close the puzzle before the evidence is gathered.
- [rule] Delay revealing a character's identity until a set point, such as a doorway or ladder, to build suspense without cheating the audience. When: Introducing a character whose identity should be revealed gradually. Why: Withholding the face or identity briefly builds tension, while withholding it too long feels like a trick.
- [rule] Delay a key reveal by interrupting the speaker or withholding the explanation until others have acted on the evidence. When: A character holds knowledge the audience needs later. Why: Postponing the explanation keeps the question open and the tension high.
- [rule] Hold back an NPC's secret until repeated questioning or a later event, so the reveal works as a payoff.
- [rule] Decide the feeling the player should have first, then make every element serve that effect, with no detail left idle. When: Designing a mystery or puzzle experience. Why: Working from the effect keeps all parts pointed toward one centre.
- [heuristic] Reveal a hidden fact or threat late, after suspicion has built, since showing it early would resolve the tension that depends on uncertainty. When: a fact would resolve tension too early if shown sooner. Why: The reveal lands harder once expectations are built, and suspense depends on uncertainty.
- [heuristic] Leave a damning clue unexplained and name the witness, step, or journal entry that will explain it later, so players can check their own deduction.
- [heuristic] Frame a request for delay as a condition of the inquiry, or as a branching choice that changes what the player learns next, to secure time from a reluctant witness.
- [heuristic] Do not press a hinting witness at once; reopen the topic at a later pretextual meeting, or wait until your position lets you press without losing access. When: A witness has hinted but not disclosed, or the investigator is a guest or otherwise restricted. Why: Early pressure makes the witness guarded and closes off information.
- [heuristic] Mark a costly choice with a retrospective narrator line or journal hint, so the player later links the choice to its lasting consequences. When: Designing a decision whose consequences appear after the choice. Why: Hindsight hints darken what came before; a later reflection links the choice to its outcome.
- [heuristic] Explain a dangerous action or withheld reasoning only after its danger has been felt; the explanation then follows the tension and lets the earlier scene reread as a clue.
- [heuristic] Defer the core reveal to the final moment so that the audience's curiosity stays unsatisfied until the end.
- [heuristic] Delay explaining how an impressive feat is achieved, and reveal the method later in the playthrough, so the mystery sustains engagement. When: A character performs a feat whose mechanism would spoil tension if shown immediately. Why: Withholding the method keeps the mystery alive while the player still has motive to pursue it.
- [heuristic] Hold back the full explanation until records and evidence align, so the reveal rests on corroboration rather than assertion. When: revealing a solved mystery. Why: corroborated reveals are more convincing.
- [heuristic] Deliver the most damaging point deliberately, since a shocking fact forces the witness to respond and reveals how they react to the truth. When: the interviewer has a decisive fact. Why: A shock produces a visible reaction that can be read.
- [heuristic] Withholding the explanation until after the events lets the audience's expectations be challenged alongside those of the characters. When: designing a mystery where the audience follows the investigator's wrong view. Why: Delay keeps the audience inside the misdirection until the reveal.
- [heuristic] A retrospective account can list the disguised person's movements that earlier scenes only hinted at, completing the reveal.
- [heuristic] Design an NPC who refuses to account for themselves so that a later clue, rather than the refusal, reveals where they were.
- [heuristic] A brief pause before a key line marks emotion and builds suspense, but frequent pauses drain tension rather than build it.
- [heuristic] Announce a delayed decisive element publicly so the audience knows an outcome is pending, turning the wait into suspense rather than confusion. When: The outcome depends on a witness or item that can plausibly be delayed. Why: Advance notice sets expectations and makes the eventual arrival feel earned.
- [heuristic] A narrator can frame a chance delay as decisive in hindsight, building suspense and signalling stakes before the disruption is explained. When: Building anticipation before a disruption. Why: Hindsight claims make the audience expect consequences.
- [heuristic] Time a delivery to a target's known daily routine so it arrives when the target is present.
- [heuristic] A single pointing gesture naming the accused can serve as the climax of an accusation scene. When: the reveal is staged before a group. Why: a clear gesture focuses attention on one person.
- [heuristic] A delay before an admission builds tension when it shows the gap between the speaker's inner resolve and outward hesitation. When: The climax of a scene is a confession. Why: The audience feels the cost of saying the words through the visible struggle.
- [heuristic] Promising a full reveal later builds suspense, and the wait for it, rather than the disclosure itself, drives most of the tension. When: A secret must be held back for dramatic effect. Why: Anticipation sustains attention longer than the fact does.
- [heuristic] Delaying the opening of news and withholding its details builds suspense, because the audience anticipates the answer before it arrives. When: Pacing a moment where a key fact is about to be revealed.
- [heuristic] The time between an event and a later reference to it can measure how little progress followed. When: When a later document recalls an earlier proclamation or act. Why: Long gaps show the issue stayed unresolved.
- [heuristic] Delay revealing a plan to build tension, provided the player has enough information to avoid unfair losses.
- [heuristic] Keep the real purpose concealed until the last possible moment, so the cover stays intact for as long as it matters.
- [heuristic] Reveal an ally's debts and principles in a later scene, so the player reinterprets his earlier dialogue in light of the new motive. Why: A late motive gives earlier lines a second meaning.
- [heuristic] Place the motive in a document the player reads early but cannot interpret until a legal rule changes its meaning.
- [procedure] 1) Replay the chain of inference in the order evidence was weighed. 2) Tie each conclusion to an observation shown earlier. 3) Mark which steps the player found and which were only confessed. 4) Keep the replay short, as a checklist rather than a second plot. When: Ending a mystery where clues were encountered earlier, so the player can verify the solution's fairness. Why: Showing the logic and re-presenting clues makes the solution feel earned and reachable rather than arbitrary.
- [procedure] 1) Withhold the hidden identity until the climax. 2) Pause the action with a stretch of silence. 3) Speak the identity aloud. 4) Recap hidden earlier acts so they read as managed events rather than misfortune. When: Structuring a mystery whose antagonist is concealed until the end. Why: A timed reveal and retrospective recap make earlier events reinterpreted as clues.
- [procedure] 1) Show the reaction first. 2) Withhold its cause. 3) Deliver the reason through a secondary source, such as a lore book, after the reaction is registered. When: a clue's meaning should follow a surprise. Why: the audience forms an expectation before learning the explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Note the delay as a gap in the timeline. 2) List known constraints such as surveillance or routine. 3) Propose an explanation that fits them. 4) Test it with an independent check. When: a message or report arrives much later than expected. Why: constraints narrow the explanation and an independent check tests it.
- [procedure] 1) Keep the narrator or guide ignorant of the plan. 2) Show each needed clue early in a neutral form. 3) Stage the event. 4) Reconstruct the sequence in a debrief that links each clue to its meaning.
- [procedure] 1) Pause the present-day case. 2) Deliver the motive through a self-contained embedded story. 3) Return to the present case with the motive now known to the audience. When: The motive for a crime depends on events that happened long before the present investigation. Why: Giving history separately keeps the audience informed without losing the thread of the active case.
- [tradeoff] Delayed clues reward recall but can frustrate players if the payoff comes too late; an obvious clue avoids that frustration.
- [tradeoff] Delaying a reveal builds suspense and lets the audience watch reactions to each step, but it gives the suspect time to escape.
- [pitfall] Testimony given at a dramatic moment may be shaped by surrounding events, and dramatic reports mix real events with imagination; check for that influence and separate the two before concluding.
- [pitfall] Later confessions and reflections can shift blame and simplify a messy process, so they must be dated and checked against events recorded at the time.
- [pitfall] Withholding the explanation too long after the reveal can make the solution feel like a trick rather than earned. When: Deferring a solution until after a reward is shown. Why: A delayed explanation loses its link to the reward and reads as artificial.
- [pitfall] Withholding a hidden identity or map area too long feels like withholding; reveal it once the escape has begun, so the reveal feels earned. When: a restricted section ends and the player exits. Why: a reveal tied to the escape feels earned rather than arbitrary.
- [pitfall] A dramatic reversal, such as returned stolen goods or a motive explanation, can pull attention away from how the culprit got in. When: Investigating a crime with a striking twist. Why: Stakes and motive compete with the method question.
- [pitfall] Attention fixes on dramatic changes and misses ordinary habits that continued, weakening the reading of the scene.
- [pitfall] Delay can make a timeline harder to rebuild, because witnesses' memories fade while the investigator travels.
- [pitfall] Long environmental surveys before a reveal slow pacing and can drain tension from the discovery that follows. When: a discovery is close. Why: description delays the payoff.
- [pitfall] A delayed reveal is believable only when the character has already shown careful reasoning in the open. When: A character announces a hidden answer. Why: Audiences trust a withheld answer only after seeing the character reason well.
- [pitfall] Delaying disclosure of a clue the investigator already holds can look like concealment and undermines fair play.
- [pitfall] A delayed response can be innocent, so check the times before assuming the delay was designed. Why: Delays often have ordinary causes such as distance or confusion.
- [pitfall] A plan with a narrow timing window and long transit leaves no slack, so any delay can cause the whole operation to fail. When: when travel or preparation is long. Why: no margin remains once the window is set.
- [pitfall] A recipient may read a delayed instruction as sentiment; the message should state plainly that it is part of a plan.
- [pitfall] Waiting for public demand before correcting a verdict can leave the record uncorrected for years.
- [pitfall] A delayed trigger's timing is hard to predict, so an early or late activation can expose the plan. When: the trigger depends on an estimated rate of change. Why: the actual rate depends on conditions the actor can only guess.
- [pitfall] Delaying the reveal too long drains the tension it was meant to build.
- [fact] News can reach a character days late, so knowledge lags events; a delay, such as a misdelivered letter, changes what each party could know and when. When: Modelling what characters know at a given time. Why: Information travels with delay, creating gaps between events and awareness.
- [fact] A substance's effects can change with dose and stage, so assuming one simple effect can mislead a timeline. When: Reasoning about when a substance acted. Why: Effects vary over time and quantity.

## rumour and gossip
- [mechanism] Gossip can supply a motive and make a suspect seem guilty before any act or evidence appears, redirecting the inquiry and pressuring the player to clear or convict. When: early in an investigation, when a community forms opinion about a suspect or suspicion forms before any specific act is documented. Why: A motive narrative directs attention; social expectation of a motive makes the accusation seem plausible in advance. (x2)
- [mechanism] When facts are withheld, audiences fill the gap with invented news; rumour gathers around the unknown into a fanciful account that explains everything without hard evidence. When: when key information is delayed or withheld and people fill the gap with rumour. Why: Invention resolves uncertainty, and a dramatic story feels complete without evidence.
- [mechanism] Bad weather, low traffic or non-market days delay rumours and news, so people in some areas lack information others already have. When: when rain, wind or a non-market day reduces travel along a route, or rumour spread is tied to travel or weather. Why: Fewer travellers means fewer carriers of news; delayed travel delays the information carried with it.
- [mechanism] Withholding facts from one person does not stop news; it travels through staff, servants and tradespeople, who pass on partial information to the wrong people.
- [mechanism] A rumour that is partly right and partly unverifiable can be confirmed or contradicted later by inspection.
- [mechanism] Hearings held before a packed crowd let the crowd's outrage feed back into officials' conduct. When: when officials hold public hearings amid strong feeling. Why: officials respond to the pressure in the room.
- [mechanism] Overheard rumours and crowd reactions keep observers uncertain, sustaining tension while the decision is pending. When: A waiting audience hears partial information. Why: Partial, unconfirmed news prevents the tension from resolving.
- [mechanism] A suspense timer built on an unconfirmed rumour lets the player wait, check and decide while the threat stays uncertain.
- [mechanism] In a crowded, noisy gathering, important remarks are lost among overlapping conversations.
- [mechanism] Gossip in a shared space such as a tavern spreads information, letting the player test who heard what and when. When: When designing social spaces where NPCs exchange news. Why: Shared channels spread details between NPCs.
- [mechanism] Gossip that spreads findings can warn culprit NPCs, so a discretion rule can gate how far a discovery propagates.
- [mechanism] Third-party gossip can reveal motive by naming who gains and who loses from a death, such as inheritance or will terms, while sounding like idle talk. When: a character speaks about a third party's wealth. Why: concrete beneficiary facts connect a person to a motive.
- [mechanism] An investigation can grow from a few visible disturbances into a community-wide hunt, with public demand deciding which names get offered. When: when a mystery depends on public suspicion.
- [mechanism] Early accusations can trigger guards, arrests and public notices, and each step makes the next accusation more credible to other characters. When: When a local rumour gains official force. Why: Each official action serves as apparent confirmation for later claims.
- [mechanism] Mass accusation can fill prisons, halt business and drive people to flee, as fear replaces normal economic and social life. When: when accusations spread widely through a community. Why: Fear disrupts trade, work and households at once.
- [mechanism] Passion in one person can set off the same feeling across a crowd, and the force of the spread grows with the zeal of those affected.
- [mechanism] A rumor spread by an NPC after a confrontation can damage the player's credibility, making later quests or requests harder for others to accept. When: after the player confronts an NPC with accusations. Why: Reputation damage carries forward, so later interactions start from a lower trust level.
- [mechanism] Trust relationships between NPCs can carry a rumor to a respected figure first, so the player must repair that standing to restore trust. When: when NPCs have tracked trust ties. Why: Rumors travel along trust links, so the most trusted listener shapes how the player is perceived.
- [mechanism] Theories built from partial observation diverge widely, so each NPC's rumor reflects only what they personally saw. When: NPCs who witnessed fragments of an event. Why: Incomplete information produces competing guesses.
- [mechanism] Public theories spread faster than evidence and can settle on a suspect from sympathy alone, ignoring an alibi the evidence supports. When: A popular theory forms about a suspect before the facts are established. Why: Sympathy and narrative appeal move through a public faster than verification.
- [behavior] Partial information spreads faster than it is verified, so a group may learn a threat exists before learning its identity, breeding suspicion. When: A group receives an incomplete message. Why: Rumor outpaces checking.
- [behavior] Unverified rumour can outrun fact and trigger panic within minutes, and its origin may remain unclear. When: when a whispered or unchecked story reaches a crowd. Why: Rumour travels faster than verification, so people react before facts are known.
- [behavior] An unverified claim gains force as it passes from person to person, and in a charged moment few stop to test it before acting. When: during tense or emotional events. Why: momentum carries the story into action.
- [behavior] A crowd tends to echo the first confident version of an event, so a group's agreement can make a claim seem settled. When: Several bystanders describe the same incident together. Why: Social agreement lends a claim false credibility.
- [behavior] A single definitive statement about a closed house shapes a crowd's suspicion toward the people inside, even before it is tested. When: When a group hears a categorical claim about who could have acted. Why: Definitive statements anchor group judgment.
- [behavior] Speakers often deliver claims with more confidence than they have earned, which makes rumour sound like fact.
- [behavior] Curious onlookers often give empty or contradictory accounts, while a few witnesses give precise details. When: many people gather after a public event. Why: Curiosity draws in people who have little to report.
- [behavior] Rumour offers rival motives for an act, and audiences may accept the loudest one without evidence.
- [behavior] A witness who has heard public talk may reshape an account from rumour rather than memory, so later statements can reflect talk. When: rumour about the case is circulating.
- [behavior] Whom a community chooses, invites or consults as arbiter can reveal what it believed about a person's allegiances, even without direct testimony. When: Direct statements are missing and group belief must be inferred from actions. Why: Selection choices reflect collective judgment about trust and sympathy.
- [behavior] A listener eager for adventure accepts an unusual story quickly, especially when it offers danger and excitement. When: the listener is primed for adventure. Why: appetite for the unusual lowers scrutiny of claims.
- [behavior] Onlookers' reactions, such as screams or a stampede, are witness material and should be recorded as data about who saw what.
- [behavior] Once a verdict is voiced publicly, a crowd hardens it quickly, and reversing it costs the speaker face, so people keep defending it. When: a noisy group reacts to an accusation. Why: public commitment raises the social cost of changing one's mind.
- [behavior] A suspect who learns a witness was present reconstructs what the investigator now knows from what could have been overheard. When: When a hidden witness is revealed after an interview. Why: Hearing the exchange lets the suspect infer what was asked and admitted.
- [behavior] When opposing a prevailing belief is dangerous, doubters may stay silent, so the record looks more unanimous than the community actually was. When: Dissent is punished, whether as heresy or as a crime. Why: Silencing doubters removes visible disagreement and makes the consensus appear complete.
- [behavior] A bewildered group that wants a verdict can overlook contradictions, letting a caught liar escape exposure. When: group is confused and seeks a resolution.
- [behavior] Publicized claims draw curious visitors, and the expectation that a respected figure will attend can draw larger crowds. When: When news of an unusual event spreads locally. Why: Curiosity and anticipation of authority bring people to witness it.
- [behavior] Neighbourhood whispers can influence a formal proceeding even before any charge is laid, because the court may weigh the community's talk. When: Rumour circulates about a person before a trial begins.
- [behavior] Gossip driven by rivalry tends to exaggerate or contradict, as speakers compete to score points. When: when speakers are rivals. Why: competition rewards contradiction.
- [behavior] A suspect with a position of trust can spread a counter-accusation through a trusting listener, who may repeat it without testing it. When: when the investigator is isolated or acting alone. Why: Trust makes the listener an effective channel, so a claim can reach others before the investigator responds.
- [behavior] A group awaiting a stranger grows more excited as news and a shared letter are passed along and re-read. When: characters or players are waiting for an announced newcomer. Why: Each retelling adds attention and speculation, so expectation builds before the newcomer is seen.
- [rule] Community opinion, public condemnation or neighbourhood consensus naming a suspect is not evidence of their actions; hostility can make an innocent person look guilty. When: when a community names, condemns or judges a suspect by reputation or local opinion. Why: Opinion reflects reputation, hostility and prejudice, not conduct; a prejudiced audience can make a later verdict look predetermined. (x2)
- [rule] Treat gossip as a lead to check, not as proof, and note the speaker's motive; keep a sourceless rumour unconfirmed until its source is traced. When: when the rumour is repeated without a source.
- [rule] Let unproven rumours change NPC prices or trust before the truth is shown, so false stories carry in-game cost, such as spoiled goods cutting trade.
- [rule] Tie rumor and news-style reports to facts the game currently knows, so they stay consistent with player progress. When: a game system generates in-world news or rumor. Why: Reports that match known facts build trust.
- [rule] Generate journals and NPC gossip as partial secondhand accounts with omitted details, so players must cross-check other sources. When: Designing quest text and rumors in games. Why: Makes players verify information rather than accept it at face value.
- [rule] Give rumoured names and histories small conflicts, so the player must verify them before trusting any single account. When: when writing NPC rumours about people or places. Why: Small inconsistencies make checking necessary and prevent accepting rumour at face value.
- [heuristic] Make NPC rumours and post-quest gossip partly true and partly false, rewarding players who verify before acting on them. When: when writing NPC gossip, tips or post-quest gossip. Why: Mixed accuracy rewards checking and prevents players from trusting every tip blindly. (x2)
- [heuristic] Rumour changes with each relay, sounding certain while contradicting itself on details; verify information passed through several people before acting. When: when information passes through multiple people. Why: Each retelling adds, alters or loses details, and every retelling can add distortion or lose the original detail.
- [heuristic] Give rumour-spreading NPCs a visible bias so players learn to discount their claims; let gossip repeat a suspect's reputation so players test it against facts. When: when designing gossip characters or a suspect's public image in a mystery. Why: A known bias lets players correct for the source and separate reputation from evidence.
- [heuristic] Give some sources a bias or motive and make a source that refuses to explain itself a suspicious clue. When: Designing lore sources for a mystery. Why: Biased sources add ambiguity and reward critical reading.
- [heuristic] Do not discard a biased source outright, since its bias may itself be the clue.
- [heuristic] Overheard hearsay in a crowd, such as bystanders describing a body, can supply the first decisive lead.
- [heuristic] A social acquaintance can supply a quick profile of a target, such as their standing and habits, without revealing why the questioner wants it.
- [heuristic] Seed a runaway NPC with a debt, a routine and an unfinished deal so the player can rule out explanations by checking the same records. When: when designing a missing-person or runaway quest. Why: elimination gives the player a reasoning path.
- [heuristic] Use rumours to add atmosphere and alternative suspicion; do not use them for clues a player must reliably deduce from.
- [procedure] 1) Plant a false rumour on an in-world notice board. 2) Track which characters change behaviour. 3) Unlock a confession dialogue once the player supplies a checkable fact. When: Designing a suspect who reacts to rumour. Why: Behaviour changes reveal who is concealing and gate a confession behind player evidence.
- [tradeoff] Gossip-driven motives can be plausible red herrings, but they must stay unproven, or they stop distracting and start resolving the case. When: a rumor is used as a motive. Why: plausible but unverified gossip misleads without closing the case.
- [tradeoff] Community memory fills gaps that records leave, but it is biased and adds little once complete documents exist. When: when choosing between local testimony and written records.
- [pitfall] Repeated claims sharing one origin look like independent corroboration, though none has been checked and each repeat merely echoes the first. When: when a claim appears in many accounts, such as neighbourhood gossip, that share a single origin. Why: Repetition along a chain is mistaken for corroboration; agreement reflects spread rather than verification. (x3)
- [pitfall] Public agreement, crowd size or social standing is not proof that a claim is true; it must be tested against the evidence. When: when a claim is judged by how many people believe it or several people repeat the same belief. Why: Numbers and status measure belief and influence, not accuracy; a shared error can look like consensus. (x2)
- [pitfall] Family gossip about a quarrel is background context, not proof of motive; a real grudge can exist without being the cause of the accusation. (x2)
- [pitfall] Vivid, sensational or often-repeated rumour is not necessarily the likeliest truth; repetition makes unverified theories seem established before they are checked. When: when a dramatic event is covered by media or gossip. Why: Striking explanations are more memorable and widely shared than cautious ones. (x2)
- [pitfall] Relayers color speech with their own opinion, praise, disapproval and irrelevant speculation, so relayed speech is not neutral. When: when information passes through a helper or relayer who has opinions about the subject. Why: Relayers color reports with their own attitudes, which do not bear on the facts that matter. (x2)
- [pitfall] Public gossip and opinion can steer an investigation toward the wrong suspect; most loose suspicions are red herrings that connect to a claim without establishing it. When: when a name is raised in gossip or a disputed document circulates among the public. Why: Crowd belief can substitute for evidence and pull attention before facts support it.
- [pitfall] Witnesses often repeat rumour as confirmed fact and blur dates and causes; separate what they saw from what they heard, and ask what the speaker actually witnessed. When: when a witness states a claim confidently or testimony is gathered from locals or secondhand sources. Why: Confidence and repetition make hearsay sound firsthand, and repetition mixes observation with hearsay.
- [pitfall] Ignoring who supplied information is a mistake: a source may have a motive to mislead, favour one side or exaggerate, so check biased claims independently. When: when gossip comes from a staff member, a rival or another biased source. Why: A supplier's motive can distort the picture, so biased claims need independent checking.
- [pitfall] A discovery witnessed by many can still be misremembered, shaped by who arrived first and who was afraid.
- [pitfall] A shared fear can make a crowd settle on one story that no member individually witnessed. When: Many observers saw a frightening event. Why: Fear and group agreement override individual perception.
- [pitfall] A witness who gossips tends to overstate what they heard, so treat their account of others' words with caution. When: The witness is known to repeat rumour. Why: Habitual repetition inflates partial hearing into confident quotation.
- [pitfall] A reputable informant can still repeat a claim they did not witness, and a good reputation alone does not confirm the claim.
- [pitfall] Asking a witness to pick from a crowd can mislead when the description is vague, because several people may fit.
- [pitfall] When accusers ask strangers in a crowd for their names, identical or similar names can lead to the wrong person being recorded and detained. When: Shared or similar names exist in one community. Why: Identification by name alone is unreliable in a crowd.
- [pitfall] A community verdict built on one incident and gossip is not independent corroboration. Why: its sources reduce to the same single event.
- [pitfall] Trusting a story because several people repeat it consistently. Identical details from an interested circle may reflect coordination rather than fact. When: When several witnesses from one interested group give matching accounts. Why: Agreement among parties who share a stake is not independent corroboration.
- [pitfall] Gossip volunteers much irrelevant material; without a clear question, the investigator must sit through unrelated detail to find what matters. When: Interviewing gossipy informants.
- [pitfall] A thief who heads straight for the expected hiding place may have heard household gossip, so the choice reveals a source rather than a real hiding place.
- [pitfall] Relayed news is partial: an absent character only learns what the sender wrote down, so unreported actions stay hidden. When: Information passes through a messenger or report. Why: The receiver knows only what was transmitted.
- [pitfall] Judging how often crimes are solved from reported cases alone overstates success, because unreported and never-found cases are never observed. When: forming beliefs from reported or discovered incidents. Why: The observed sample is filtered by what gets noticed.
- [pitfall] Secondhand routines from insiders can be stale, exaggerated or wrong, so they should be verified before a plan commits to them. When: Relying on rumour or household gossip about a target's habits. Why: Hearsay is not observed evidence of actual movement.
- [pitfall] In crowds, a person not seen is not proof of absence, because movement through dense crowds hides people. When: Assessing whether someone was present in a crowded space such as during an interval. Why: Crowds obscure people from observers.
- [pitfall] Acting on unverified hearsay can make the investigator look as unreliable as the people they distrust.
- [pitfall] One person changing their belief does not automatically change the beliefs of others who share the same framework.
- [pitfall] A leaked report can be exaggerated, and it may create panic rather than useful information. When: Outside rumor or press reaches the investigation. Why: Partial and inflated accounts spread faster than accurate ones.
- [pitfall] A jest or teasing remark is not proof; it only opens a line of inquiry that later evidence must confirm. When: When a remark seems to implicate someone. Why: Words said in banter can be exaggerated or meaningless.
- [pitfall] Shared talk about a decoy can make witnesses assume a link to the real crime that does not exist. When: A decoy is widely discussed in a community. Why: Common talk creates expectations of connection.
- [fact] A person may know that a secret exists and who it touches while knowing none of its particulars.
- [fact] Grudges within a community often trace to disputes over money, housing and voting rights, which are the concrete stakes people contest.
- [fact] A dated newspaper notice can carry news across a distance, so anyone who reads it can learn of events they did not witness. When: Information must travel between distant places in a story. Why: Printed notices reach readers far from the event.

## combining and linking evidence
- [mechanism] Several modest or explainable incidents sharing one person, place or grievance can jointly imply motive, since the linked sequence gives weight that no single event has. When: a suspicion depends on observations meaningful only in combination. Why: A repeated thread makes coincidence look like cause. (x2)
- [mechanism] Facts fitting one hypothesis gain cumulative force, though one fit is insufficient; interlocking hypotheses reinforce each other, making each part seem more believable than it is alone.
- [mechanism] Each clue in a sequence should raise stakes and point to the next, such as a sample decoding earlier clues or a small object leading to a larger hidden one. When: designing a series of cryptic messages or hiding-place finds. Why: Later items provide the reference or location needed for the next step.
- [mechanism] Each added piece of circumstantial evidence against an innocent suspect raises suspicion, even when each piece is coincidental, so the false lead persists. Why: Accumulated weak clues feel like a pattern.
- [mechanism] Changing perspective can show circumstantial evidence pointing to a different person, so the same details may support the accused. When: Reviewing evidence against a suspect. Why: Incriminating details often admit an innocent reading.
- [mechanism] A maker's mark on an object can lead to a shop, and the shop's sales record plus the seller's description can link a purchase to a person and a time. When: an object found at a scene carries a maker's mark or retailer stamp. Why: each record narrows the field from object to shop, then to buyer and moment.
- [mechanism] Matching physical evidence, such as the same weapon used on two victims, can tie a crime to a chosen suspect. When: when a frame needs support from forensic evidence. Why: a match makes the suspect appear to be the one responsible.
- [behavior] An interpretive question about a sensory detail draws a fuller answer and can relax the room.
- [behavior] Powerful connections can change a legal outcome, as a letter from an influential relative can lead to release. When: when an accused person has influential kin or patrons. Why: influence can override the usual course of a case.
- [rule] Design clues needed together not one key item: pair small clues such as a refusal and an unusual grip, each answering a separate question; together they prove one link. When: building a deduction puzzle or a reveal that needs two pieces of evidence. Why: Combined partial clues keep players engaged; pointing to the suspect only together feels earned. (x2)
- [rule] Make traces such as a boot print, rope blood smear and spilled chemical, or flow direction and bruising, agree so players can deduce one profile or order of events. When: designing evidence for a suspect. Why: consistent evidence supports a single deduction.
- [rule] Weigh motive, opportunity and interested testimony together rather than assessing each one alone. When: building a case against a suspect.
- [rule] Make npc schedules show consistent travel times so players can detect an alibi that cannot be physically true. When: when designing npc alibis. Why: Visible travel times let players check plausibility.
- [rule] Keep route and clock data consistent across the world so that contradictions are real and findable, not accidental. Why: Accidental mismatches would mislead players.
- [rule] Pair a recalled clue with an independent physical trace so the solution forms a chain of evidence, not one lucky guess. Why: Independent clues corroborate each other.
- [rule] Let an NPC recognise a person through a sequence of clues, with the player supplying an item or a shared memory. When: designing a dialogue or quest identity check.
- [rule] Combine several facts that point the same way, such as a weapon's state, the victim's position, and room access, rather than resting on one. When: When building a circumstantial case. Why: Converging facts are harder to explain away than a single clue.
- [rule] Interpret ambiguous words by their form and delivery, not by the answer one hopes for.
- [rule] Use the interval between a recorded opening and a recorded closing to bound when a departure could have happened.
- [rule] Plant a trace that is useless alone but gains meaning when combined with a later clue.
- [rule] Design a staged clue so it is consistent with a hidden action, such as a muffling door, giving careful players a way to see through the deception. When: When designing a false-exit or staged-trace puzzle. Why: A detectable inconsistency rewards observation and keeps the puzzle fair.
- [rule] NPC answers to repeated questions should stay consistent unless a change in the NPC's knowledge or motive is shown, so players can test their reliability. When: designing dialogue that players can re-ask. Why: Players detect contradictions only when repeated answers are comparable.
- [rule] Do not accept an accumulation of oddities as proof until a single explanation connects the items. Why: separate items with innocent answers remain separate without a link.
- [rule] Do not act on a strong but single clue; require a confirming circumstantial thread first. Why: a single indication can often be explained away.
- [rule] Let players rebuild a crime's sequence from discovered clues, with each clue unlocking one step of the chain. Why: the player assembles the plan through evidence rather than being told it.
- [rule] Open sealed evidence in a controlled setting, such as a station, so the handling of the object stays recorded.
- [rule] Give unexplained local customs, such as tipping an innkeeper or a guard's greeting, a consistent meaning the player can work out.
- [rule] Give a seal or handwriting only one partial clue so the player must combine it with other finds to identify its author. When: When designing identifying evidence in a game world. Why: Partial clues reward players who collect and connect multiple sources.
- [heuristic] Accept a conclusion only after combining several weak physical signs, since any single sign can have many causes and no single object settles the matter. When: building a suspect profile from physical traces. Why: converging weak signs raise confidence where a single sign cannot.
- [heuristic] Compare separate witness reports; distinctive details such as clothing, haste, carried objects or payment method recurring across independent reports identify a person more reliably than general descriptions. When: matching witness reports to one suspect. Why: Specific details that repeat across observers are hard to produce by chance.
- [heuristic] Objects that change hands, such as a forgotten coat, carry evidence of who controlled them, and when two suspects' stories do not overlap, a shared object physically links them. When: two suspects' stories do not overlap. Why: a shared object is evidence of contact.
- [heuristic] Agreement among several sources that do not borrow from one another, or among several independent clue types, is the strongest support; no single source must carry the conclusion. When: multiple sources point to the same connection. Why: Independent convergence is hard to explain by copying.
- [heuristic] Interpret clues as a set: unrelated weak facts pointing one way, such as an unfinished activity, a habit or an owner-traceable item, together outweigh any one and each adds weight. Why: Each fact adds weight even when none is conclusive alone.
- [heuristic] Build a circumstantial case from linked facts such as motive, means, opportunity, scene access, knowledge of absences, unexplained silence and odd conduct, then test it against physical facts.
