When: no direct evidence or witness exists. Why: Several weak links together form a plausible case that still needs verification; each linked fact is individually uncertain.
- [heuristic] Two independent descriptions, such as a witness's account and a physical trait of a victim, that converge strengthen a link between scenes. When: When a suspect's identity is not directly known. Why: Independent sources agreeing reduces the chance of coincidence.
- [heuristic] Judge a condition from several signs together rather than from one, since any single sign can be produced by an unusual but living state.
- [heuristic] Individually weak physical traces, such as a scent, wood shavings or a misplaced key, can jointly link a person to a place and time; no single trace should be treated as conclusive. Why: Several small links that agree can carry an accusation even though each is uncertain.
- [heuristic] Several independent traces tying a suspect to a scene can together form a stronger case than any single trace.
- [heuristic] Combine several traces into one pattern rather than judging each alone, since each single inference about the number of actors is weaker than the combined reading. When: Reasoning about the number of actors from scene evidence. Why: Independent traces that agree strengthen the conclusion more than any one trace.
- [heuristic] Treat a suspect's refusal to name anyone as a signal to interpret beside other evidence, not as a neutral result. When: a suspect refuses to answer or name an accomplice.
- [heuristic] A link to a suspect often lies outside the scene: in an envelope's address, a postal record, or a distant contact's report.
- [heuristic] Chain each clue into one account so every detail explains part of the final result, rather than standing as an isolated fact. When: a case has several scattered clues. Why: a linked account shows how the clues jointly produce the outcome.
- [heuristic] Overlapping time windows from independent sources can be intersected to narrow a probable range. When: when several sources give estimates of the same event. Why: agreement between independent estimates narrows the plausible span.
- [heuristic] Do not discard a suspect merely because the evidence against them is circumstantial. When: Evidence is indirect but consistent with involvement. Why: Circumstantial evidence can be strong when several pieces align.
- [heuristic] Small facts gathered from casual talk, such as a construction date or a distance, can be combined into one route conclusion.
- [heuristic] Independent injury signs that agree, such as a head wound plus signs of suffocation, support one sequence of events more strongly than any single sign.
- [heuristic] Pairing an anomaly with an inventory of losses makes a stronger case than either evidence alone.
- [heuristic] A physical trace from a concealed mechanism can link it to the event and to the witness's position.
- [heuristic] An inference resting on widely shared knowledge is a valid basis for reasoning, so check it against general experience rather than dismissing it.
- [heuristic] Read small physical traces one by one, then combine them, since no single detail is conclusive about a person's origin or affiliation.
- [heuristic] An object's reading and a written clue from the same time may point the same way, so check whether they corroborate before weighting either. When: an object and a message both bear on one time.
- [heuristic] Before accepting a tidy conclusion, ask who benefits from that appearance and look for evidence that does not fit it. When: A case rests on few clues that fit together too neatly. Why: A staged or convenient case can look more certain than the evidence supports.
- [heuristic] Compare physical traces, such as prints lifted from different objects, to show that two apparently separate identities belong to one person. When: when a suspect has adopted a second name. Why: traces outlast a disguise.
- [heuristic] Connect separate objects, such as a prize and a group photo, to reveal links like a family's ties to an institution. When: reconstructing history from several items. Why: combined items support conclusions that single items cannot.
- [heuristic] Several items that each break the same common custom are strong together, though any single item is weak alone.
- [heuristic] A single mismatch rarely settles a location, but several independent mismatches together can reject the obvious scene. When: Each mismatch has been confirmed on its own. Why: Independent weak points reinforce each other when they agree.
- [heuristic] Assemble the truth from several partial sources, since no single witness can provide the full picture. When: reconstructing events from accounts. Why: each source knows only part of the story.
- [heuristic] An evidence board can require the player to link several weak clues, such as a sighting, a weapon and a motive, before an accusation unlocks. When: when designing an accusation mechanic in a mystery game. Why: Requiring multiple linked clues rewards reasoning over single-clue guessing.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each witness's partial view of a suspect. 2) Cross-check the parts for consistency. 3) Build the identity only from parts that agree, since unchecked assumptions can join two half-views into a whole fitting no one. When: no single witness saw the suspect fully; assembling identity from partial sightings. Why: Unchecked assumptions join parts that do not belong to the same person.
- [procedure] 1) Collect small, seemingly trivial facts. 2) Check each is independent of the others. 3) Test how they combine. 4) Treat their combined weight as proof only when they converge on one explanation. When: no single clue is conclusive. Why: Converging minor facts can give stronger proof than any one clue; no single weak clue is enough.
- [procedure] 1) Record where the object was found and its make. 2) Infer the likely origin, such as a nearby town. 3) Show it to local businesses that could identify it. 4) Cross-check the names and details they give. When: An unidentified object must be traced to its owner. Why: Each small fact narrows the search, so a chain of checks identifies the owner.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the object by its description, fittings or registration number. 2) Trace that identifier to a registered owner. 3) Compare the owner's account with where the object was found. When: When a found object may link a person to a place.
- [procedure] 1) Start with one hard fact from an outside source. 2) Add a dated fact that fits it. 3) Add physical resemblance. 4) Add a character trait. 5) Check each link against the previous one. 6) Confirm the chain with an independent document. When: No single clue is decisive but several independent clues point the same way. Why: Each independent fact reinforces the chain.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the most concrete physical object. 2) Ask what kind of person would use or carry it. 3) Trace its custody forward and backward. 4) Test each link against independent facts. When: Building a case from many small clues. Why: Each link is only as strong as its tests, and concrete objects are easier to trace than reputations or impressions.
- [procedure] 1) Trace the object's chain of handling back to the victim. 2) Find where a foreign substance could enter unseen. 3) Check its weight, solubility and settling. 4) Test the method in practice. 5) Note who selected or handled the object. 6) Consider how traces could be removed. When: Victim's food or drink passed through a vessel or shell that could have been opened. Why: Each step turns a vague suspicion into a checkable route.
- [procedure] 1) Decide whether two incidents are one mystery or two by locating a figure who stands between both. 2) Describe each end by what it lacks. 3) Check the link beyond proximity using motive, access and knowledge. 4) Set out the chain in order, admitting its gaps. 5) List and answer each objection separately. When: Two apparently separate events may share a cause. Why: A shared figure with the right motive, access and knowledge is stronger evidence than mere presence.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the detail across the incidents. 2) Check the match directly against the physical evidence. 3) Confirm the link through independent facts before treating incidents as one series. When: When a shared detail suggests incidents may be connected. Why: A link resting on one remark is fragile; direct comparison and independent confirmation turn coincidence into evidence.
- [tradeoff] Consistent circumstantial clues can support a firm verdict when no direct proof exists; yet alone they are insufficient, since inferred links have other explanations, and a confession is decisive. When: weighing case strength: clues align without direct proof, or a confession exists. Why: Independent clues that agree reinforce each other; inferred links always admit another explanation.
- [pitfall] Check every interval, not just the main event: an error in one interval carries into every bound derived from it, and small gaps can change what seems possible.
- [pitfall] Shared items, such as rings or widely sold designs, belong to many people, so a match narrows little; a habit or ownership claim must be specific to one owner. When: using a shared object or material as a clue to identity or ownership. Why: Common designs can belong to many people.
- [pitfall] Several weak matches combined into near-certainty can mislead when none has been tied independently to the suspect, since each match may be coincidence. Why: common items and shared features make chance matches likely.
- [pitfall] Matching a trace to an object does not prove who used it; access and elimination of other people must also be established. When: when moving from an object found to a suspect.
- [pitfall] Circumstantial links, such as a shared business or an unexplained absence, can look stronger in public reporting than the evidence supports. When: public reports link a suspect to a crime. Why: reporting tends to amplify suggestive connections.
- [pitfall] A common event, such as a vehicle slowing and driving on, is weak evidence on its own.
- [pitfall] Accepting an argument whose premise already assumes its conclusion, a circular argument, lets an investigation rest on nothing.
- [pitfall] Circumstantial evidence can all point one way while still leaving a gap, so a neat set of facts is not automatically complete. When: When circumstantial facts converge on one suspect. Why: Convergence can hide an unexplained link.
- [pitfall] Asking someone to interpret a document they have not read yields opinion rather than evidence.
- [pitfall] When both refusal and confession are read as guilt, the reading of a suspect's behavior becomes circular.
- [pitfall] A community's choice shows what people believed, not what happened, so it cannot establish guilt. Why: Local tension can drive selections as easily as evidence can.
- [pitfall] Judging each circumstantial fact in isolation misses the force of their combination, which is what gives a chain its weight. When: Evaluating a set of circumstantial clues. Why: A link's weight depends on the others it connects to.
- [fact] Objects record unseen events through changed state, such as liquid levels, floor marks, misplaced clothing or missing items; tie each record to a person and route before it counts. When: reconstructing events from a scene; objects moved or carried through a scene. Why: Traces prove events only when tied to an actor and path; objects change state from actions taken on them.
- [fact] Physical items carry information that words cannot, such as folded paper, sealed keys or pencilled cards, and can serve as keys to a code or show how they were handled.
- [fact] A timed unobserved interval reveals that something happened but not what, so the result requires interpretation. When: reading evidence from an unobserved test. Why: Timing shows occurrence, not content.
- [fact] Two observers can read the same room differently, because interpretation depends on each reader's assumptions.
- [fact] Direct evidence of a crime is rarely available, so circumstantial evidence is often the strongest proof an investigator has. Why: crimes are usually committed without witnesses or recordings.

## witness testimony
- [mechanism] Follow-up questions, especially about date or hour, pin a witness to narrower details than a vague first account and can change the meaning of what was seen. When: when a witness gives a vague first account. Why: Precise prompts force the witness to commit to details they might otherwise leave out. (x2)
- [mechanism] A brief partial view, limited by distance, obstruction, light or reflection, raises a question without settling it; reflections distort and occlusions hide detail, so assuming clarity misleads. When: An observer sees something out of place, or relies on a reflection or obstructed view for key information. Why: Missing detail leaves the identity open. (x2)
- [mechanism] When a culprit stages a non-player witness to observe an event, the account that witness later gives the player carries that staging and can be checked against other accounts. When: a non-player character reports an event the culprit arranged. Why: staged observations leave traces that differ from honest ones.
- [mechanism] Record whether a witness was pressured during an interview, so later dialogue reflects the change in their attitude.
- [mechanism] Placing a witness to see an object or person creates a memory link, and later questioning can steer that recollection toward a chosen target. When: suspicion may later fall on the intended target. Why: recollection of a link is open to suggestion once the witness is asked about it.
- [mechanism] A guard's logged observation with time and description gives players a time window and object to match against suspects' records, narrowing suspects without a full identity. When: Designing clue logs for an investigation puzzle. Why: Partial, timed observations let players eliminate suspects without a full identity.
- [mechanism] A watch whose effectiveness drops the longer it runs can model player boredom and fatigue during long stakeouts.
- [mechanism] When a character doubts their own perception, such as whether a sound was real, the audience is pulled to question what they know. When: when a narrator's senses are unreliable under stress. Why: Making perception itself uncertain raises doubt about what is true.
- [behavior] A witness's first account may be incomplete rather than false, and later answers can change under pressure to include omitted activity. When: A witness claims to have stayed at a post or location. Why: People often leave out uncomfortable details until pressed.
- [behavior] Under repeated questioning, a witness's account may change in stages, with each admission arriving later and vaguer than the one before. When: A witness is pressed over several sessions. Why: Fear of consequences and pressure from questioning.
- [behavior] An observer with a personal stake reads events through that stake, so feelings can impair judgement about the people involved. When: the observer has a relationship with those involved. Why: Emotional investment colours perception of others' behaviour.
- [behavior] Actions taken in one drug state may be recalled when the same state returns. When: A character has lost memory of an act done under a drug. Why: Memory can be linked to the state in which it was formed.
- [behavior] Observers trained to read signs draw more precise inferences from the same brief glimpse than untrained observers do. When: when judging a stranger from a brief observation. Why: Reading signs is a learned skill that sharpens with practice.
- [behavior] A witness close to events but bound by family ties may speak indirectly, so the wording of their account becomes evidence. When: A witness has close access to events but a loyalty that limits what they can say. Why: Ties of loyalty restrain direct statement, so the witness signals meaning through phrasing.
- [behavior] A witness who flinches under a direct question has shown they understood it before denying knowledge, which is evidence worth noting. When: A direct question touches a sensitive fact. Why: A reaction can reveal knowledge that a denial conceals.
- [behavior] Witnesses often volunteer useful details as the questioner leaves, such as an unprompted remark about an injury. When: When an interview is ending and the witness has relaxed. Why: Relief and the lessening of pressure loosen the witness's control over what they reveal.
- [behavior] Witnesses who saw only hands, a sleeve or a back give little identifying help, and such partial sightings narrow the suspect pool only slightly. When: Evaluating witness reports of a disguised person. Why: Fragmentary details are shared by many people.
- [behavior] A witness who saw only part of a person, such as a chin under a large hat, may still feel sure they would recognise the item again. When: when a witness recalls a distinctive but partly seen item. Why: Confidence about recognition can exceed what the partial view actually recorded.
- [rule] Voice can identify a hidden face, but never treat sincere certainty as proof; verify with a second sense or source, since mimicry and honest error look alike. When: when the face is hidden or a witness identifies a character only by sound. Why: An honest mistake looks the same as a deliberate lie, and a stranger or accomplice can imitate the voice.
- [rule] Vary the expected responses so that a refusal is informative but not automatically damning. When: scripting NPC reactions to requests. Why: Players should not treat every refusal as proof of guilt.
- [rule] Unlock interrogation options only after the player presents a specific document or object that justifies them. When: designing NPC questioning in a game.
- [rule] State how information was obtained, since testimony from a hidden or unverified source can be dismissed later. Why: The source determines how much weight the reader gives the testimony.
- [rule] Keep witnesses apart so their accounts stay independent and cannot be shaped by one another. When: Several witnesses must be questioned about the same event. Why: Overheard answers let a witness adjust their story to match others.
- [rule] Weigh a statement that earns release with the same suspicion applied to other coerced statements, since the reward gives the speaker a motive to say what is wanted. When: A statement is offered in exchange for release or leniency. Why: An inducement creates an incentive to tell the questioner what they want to hear.
- [rule] Weigh independent testimony from fellow prisoners or witnesses against a witness's later statements rather than letting the later statement override it. When: A witness recants earlier claims. Why: Earlier independent accounts can contradict a later turn.
- [rule] A signaler must watch the observer's reaction and change the act immediately if the observer seems to notice it. When: when a covert signal is in progress. Why: An irritated remark shows the signal was registered as noise.
- [rule] Notice when a question's framing points toward one reading of the evidence, since it steers how the evidence is weighed. When: Posing a question about ambiguous evidence to a judge or player. Why: Framing shapes which interpretation seems natural.
- [rule] Track a witness NPC's knowledge as game state, so their removal changes which alibis remain checkable. Log guard patrols, door openings and cart movements so players can test whether a suspect's route was possible. When: designing NPC knowledge and environmental logs. Why: State and logs let consequences of removing witnesses be felt and tested.
- [rule] Give little weight to testimony hedged with phrases like 'I think' or 'it might have been' when it concerns dates. When: when judging a witness's answer about a date. Why: Hedged answers do not fix a specific date.
- [rule] Use an NPC guard or doorman as an alibi witness, letting the player ask about times and routes. When: When designing a location with a stationed NPC. Why: A stationed witness gives the player a source to question.
- [rule] Add a witness-log record, such as a taxi entry or guard roster, that confirms or contradicts claimed alibis. When: Designing alibi checks in a game. Why: A neutral log gives the player a source independent of the suspect.
- [rule] Model interrogation pressure as escalation steps such as repetition, rephrasing and language switch, each raising the chance that a scripted answer cracks. When: Building an interrogation minigame. Why: Graduated steps give the player meaningful choices about how hard to press.
- [rule] Track interviewed NPCs, and when every lead loops back to the same people, prompt the player to reassess their line of inquiry. When: Designing investigation progression. Why: Looping leads signal a stalled line.
- [rule] Make testimony count only when a second witness is present, so players must find a second witness before the gate opens. When: a puzzle or quest needs corroboration.
- [rule] Let witness-only claims raise suspicion without granting conviction, and require the player to find physical traces before a verdict is possible. When: when designing accusation mechanics around unseen or private perceptions. Why: Private claims can be false, so they should guide inquiry, not settle the outcome.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses partial, emotionally coloured testimony, and let the player cross-check positions and times to resolve it. When: Designing NPC witness accounts.
- [rule] Do not discard a distorted witness entirely; they may still hold one true detail worth cross-checking. When: A witness is unreliable but may have seen something real.
- [rule] Make NPC knowledge partial so players must choose which questions to ask and which answers to trust. When: An NPC holds information relevant to a mystery. Why: Incomplete knowledge makes the player's choices matter.
- [rule] Plant character clues in dialogue, such as who refuses a test or arrives for a specific reason, so the player can recall them later. When: Writing dialogue for witnesses or suspects. Why: Small, memorable details in conversation become useful evidence when the player connects them later.
- [heuristic] Record when and by whom each trace or object was seen; an object recognised by several independent observers links to a person more strongly than any single recognition. When: When physical traces or objects are used as evidence. Why: Dated, multiply seen traces can be rechecked; agreement across separate observers reduces the chance of a single mistake. (x2)
- [heuristic] Independent witnesses who give the same description or answer at different points strengthen each other's reliability, since separate confirmation reduces the chance one observer is mistaken. When: When weighing the reliability of a sighting or answer. Why: Independent confirmation reduces the chance that one observer is mistaken.
- [heuristic] NPC dialogue can be a tree where information unlocks only through precise questions, or the right keyword or topic, rather than a verbose release. When: Designing NPC dialogue or conversation systems for an investigation.
- [heuristic] Independent observers who track a party's movements can expose an assembled or staged accusation. When: group testimony appears to support one account. Why: group testimony can be built to back a single story.
- [heuristic] Two witnesses who recall the same sound corroborate each other even if neither knows its source.
- [heuristic] Treat an unexpected NPC reaction as a clue with several possible readings rather than as a failure state.
- [heuristic] Each new independent witness adds detail that narrows the suspect pool.
- [heuristic] Adjust manner to each witness: deferential with long-serving staff, careful and guarded with one who resists.
- [heuristic] Check a character's account of their own movements against an independent sensory cue, such as a sound or footstep. When: a character's whereabouts are disputed. Why: Sensory cues are harder to shape than a spoken account.
- [heuristic] Do not accept a confident recollection as accurate when the witness admits large gaps in memory. When: Assessing a witness's account of an event. Why: Confidence does not repair missing memory.
- [heuristic] Two credible witnesses who are present and give sworn accounts of the same physical act carry strong weight, while a single account carries little. When: A claim involves an act that ordinary means cannot explain. Why: Independent corroboration reduces the chance that one person's error or invention alone decides the outcome.
- [heuristic] Test a claim that nobody passed by asking whose role was excluded from the count, since a person seen but not recorded may still have passed. When: A witness statement rules out all movement. Why: People are counted by their expected roles, so an unexpected role can pass unrecorded.
- [heuristic] A detail that feels familiar but cannot be placed should be held open, since recall of its source may come later and make it significant. When: A detail is noticed but its source is unknown. Why: A stray observation can gain meaning once a related fact surfaces.
- [heuristic] A hidden witness the culprit does not know about can defeat an apparently safe barrier, so a locked hiding place should not be treated as guaranteed to conceal the act. When: designing a scene where a character might observe a crime from concealment. Why: Physical barriers can hide the act from the culprit's view while leaving an observer inside.
- [heuristic] An interrogation mini-game can log each answer and flag variations, so the player sees a contradiction build over repeated questions. When: designing a questioning mechanic. Why: Visible logs make inconsistency a playable clue.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC's testimony carry withheld details that unlock after trust or corroboration, and mark omissions in logs so players know the record is partial. When: designing NPC dialogue and journals. Why: Players learn what is missing and earn the rest.
- [heuristic] The person at the centre of a case can fill gaps that intermediaries could not see, making their own account the strongest confirmation. When: Resolving disputed events in a case.
- [heuristic] Accept hesitant, partial answers and let the witness reach the conclusion themselves rather than stating it for them.
- [heuristic] A single reinterpretation of one timestamp can recolour all earlier testimony that relied on it, so earlier scenes change meaning without being altered.
- [procedure] 1) Speak loudly to one person so a nearby listener hears. 2) Act as if unaware of that listener. 3) Aim the words at a known emotional weak spot. 4) Read the listener's reactions as evidence. 5) Repeat the point if interrupted.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the person's last known record. 2) Send inquiries to registries in other places. 3) Publish rewards and appeals. 4) Watch the likely return point. 5) Filter incoming leads before acting.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the original source of a claim. 2) Check whether that source can be reached directly. 3) Note each intermediary and what they might gain from relaying it. When: Assessing information that arrived secondhand.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm the detail is unusual. 2) Show it circulated before the later accounts. 3) Identify a plausible carrier. 4) State any remaining gap in the chain. When: testing whether separate accounts are independent or copied.
- [procedure] 1) List each public note's details. 2) Order the act, the time gap and the note's appearance. 3) Infer which observers could have seen the act and passed it on. When: Working out who witnessed a private act from unsigned public messages. Why: Timing and content narrow the set of possible watchers.
- [procedure] 1) Avoid asking the hidden question directly. 2) Raise a related side topic. 3) Wait for the target to volunteer the desired name or detail. When: When a hostile or guarded character shuts down direct questions. Why: Direct pressure can harden resistance, while a side approach lets the answer surface on its own.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness to describe the person they saw. 2) Record the description. 3) Match it later against suspects. When: when a witness saw an unidentified person. Why: A recorded description allows a later match.
- [procedure] 1) Take each household member's account separately. 2) Record their routines and sleep times. 3) Check reported sounds and their timing against claimed movements. 4) Check missing items against each report. 5) Search every space large enough to hold the object in question. When: The household was active during the relevant time and staff can describe it. Why: Separate accounts with timings expose gaps that a single neat story hides.
- [procedure] 1) Open with reassurance and a reward, making clear the witness is not the main target. 2) Bluff about what you already know. 3) Watch for flinches under direct questions. 4) Apply a visible time limit. 5) State the stakes, including legal consequences. 6) Move to a private room once the witness starts talking. 7) Remove other interviewers so the witness does not feel watched. When: The witness has a clear fear that the interviewer can address. Why: Each step lowers the witness's fear or raises the cost of silence.
- [procedure] 1) Run standard screens for all common agents first. 2) If nothing matches, suspect an unfamiliar substance. 3) Identify it by weighing its properties together, not one at a time. When: Cause of death is clear, the agent is unknown, and standard tests return nothing useful. Why: Common agents must be excluded before rarer ones are considered.
- [tradeoff] Physical traces show what moved, was hidden or was altered, but testimony is needed to explain how the trace came to be there. When: the case depends on a moved, hidden or altered object.
- [pitfall] Recalled details can be mistaken, so confirm them against the physical scene before acting on them, since a recalled answer is only as reliable as the memory behind it. When: when a player relies on a recalled detail to draw a conclusion. Why: Recall reconstructs the scene and can introduce errors. (x2)
- [pitfall] A witness or subject knows only what they saw and may give an incomplete account, so every statement must be checked against other evidence rather than accepted for its detail.
- [pitfall] Damaging hearsay often comes from someone with a stake in the outcome, and that stake should lower its weight.
- [pitfall] Judging a witness only by whether the statement contains false facts misses accounts that are accurate yet hide the decisive event. Why: A fully accurate account can still omit the most important fact.
- [pitfall] Vague recollections of an earlier meeting leave gaps that must be filled from records or other sources rather than trusted alone. When: Relying on a witness's memory of a past meeting. Why: Memory of an event years old is unreliable.
- [pitfall] Trusting direct observation is not enough, since even what one sees can mislead when read without checking.
- [pitfall] A story that depends on the audience's indifference fails once they become curious.
- [pitfall] A character's stated temperament is useful evidence, but it can be misread and should be weighed with other facts. When: Judging whether a victim would have acted in a certain way.
- [pitfall] A routine described by staff may not match what happened on the critical occasion, since memory tends to reflect general practice. When: when testing an access claim against a stated routine. Why: people describe usual practice rather than a specific event.
- [pitfall] A witness questioned informally may give a first version later discounted as a lie, which damages the record.
- [pitfall] Trusting a witness's conclusion over their observations is a mistake, since the conclusion may be an interpretation that outruns the evidence.
- [pitfall] A witness list built at the scene can be incomplete, since people in a crowd may go unnoticed until later.
- [pitfall] Treating a true detail supplied by a spirit as proof that the accused is guilty confuses an accurate fact with a guilty identity.
- [pitfall] An eavesdropper who hears only part of a conversation may misjudge the whole, because she hears one side of a judgment without its reasons. When: A character acts on fragments of an overheard talk. Why: Missing reasoning makes a partial hearing misleading.
- [fact] Accounts of overheard speech often break off just before the words that matter, leaving the critical content missing. When: when a witness reports overheard speech.
- [fact] A document that promises a fuller account later signals that it is withholding facts.

## final resolution
- [definition] A fair-play reveal delays the answer, then shows the specific clues that made it possible, tracing each event to a means already available to the audience.
- [mechanism] A late reveal is fair when its cause was set up openly earlier and reframes clues already shown, explaining each earlier fact without contradicting it or adding unseen facts. When: when planning a late reveal or confession near the end of a story. Why: Recalling known clues rewards attention, while new facts at the end feel like a cheat; a reveal works only when earlier clues allow reinterpretation without contradiction.
- [mechanism] A late fact or reversal after the solution seems complete overturns the accepted theory, forcing reassessment of earlier confession and evidence and keeping the audience uncertain until the last step. When: when the mystery appears solved or the working answer appears complete before the final turn. Why: Audience trust in the answer is what the late information undermines; the last check tests a key assumption.
- [mechanism] A motive revealed late can recast earlier facts and shift suspicion onto characters who looked clear before.
- [mechanism] Late-arriving evidence from outside the current scene can flip the balance between theories and reopen a closed case. When: New information arrives after a theory has been accepted. Why: Fresh facts can change which explanation fits the full set of evidence.
- [mechanism] A late explanation that unifies several earlier anomalies recasts each one, giving every earlier oddity a new meaning. When: several unexplained events share one hidden cause.
- [mechanism] A late reveal of a disguised identity reframes earlier scenes, so the audience must reread them with the true identity in mind.
- [mechanism] A late reveal that shifts the balance of power between two characters makes earlier scenes read differently and carries suspense forward. When: ending a chapter or act. Why: Hindsight changes how earlier details are read.
- [behavior] Officials and the public readily accept a tidy closure, which lowers scrutiny of the explanation. When: a case is resolved quickly. Why: relief at a closed case reduces the urge to check details.
- [behavior] What people do after an event, such as refusing a particular officiant or leaving a settlement, reveals what they knew and whom they trusted or blamed. When: the motive for a later act is unclear. Why: Post-event choices reflect beliefs formed during the event.
- [behavior] Officials rarely question the basis of a legal process until doubts about its evidence grow, and then they may pull back. Why: Doubt about evidence quality triggers the reversal.
- [behavior] Players who gain background later reinterpret earlier small details as clues, so early planting rewards recall. When: when the solution depends on knowledge the player lacks at first. Why: Background gives an earlier detail its meaning.
- [rule] Every fact a reveal needs, especially the decisive one, must be shown early in plain view so the audience can verify the solution and it feels earned, not arbitrary. When: when building a mystery, puzzle or reveal, especially one that withholds the solution until the end and must be solvable from the text or game world alone. Why: Reveals relying on unseen facts feel like a cheat and undermine trust; players can only trace a deduction from facts visible to them.
- [rule] A deduction reveal screen should reconstruct the clue chain in order with collected clues highlighted, so the player verifies a solution built from clues they already hold, not new facts. When: when designing the answer, confession or end-of-case reveal screen of a deduction game. Why: Reframing already-collected clues rewards earlier observations and keeps the solution checkable.
- [rule] Place every clue needed to reconstruct a reversal earlier, visible to the player, so the audience recognises the truth on reflection and it feels fair, not arbitrary. When: planning a late twist, reversal or reveal. Why: A reversal with no earlier trace feels unfair or arbitrary.
- [rule] Show the disguise cue and identifying evidence before the reveal, so the earlier mistake is one a careful observer could have avoided.
- [rule] In a fair-play reveal, every point in the recap should map to a clue the player already had access to. Why: the reveal must add no facts the player could not have gathered.
- [rule] A late reveal is fair when every element it uses, including motive, opportunity, means and earlier misleading observations, was planted before the reveal. When: Writing a closed puzzle that ends with a full reconstruction. Why: New facts introduced only at the reveal feel unfair to the audience.
- [rule] Every clue used in a late reveal must be shown to the audience before the reveal, or the solution feels unearned. When: story uses a reversal of suspicion. Why: the audience must be able to check the explanation against earlier evidence.
- [rule] A confession resolves a mystery fairly only when every fact it reveals has already been shown to the audience in the story. When: when a culprit explains the solution. Why: Facts introduced only in the confession feel like a cheat.
- [rule] A confession should explain events the audience has already seen and answer questions raised earlier, not introduce new evidence. Why: Otherwise the solution feels unearned.
- [rule] Stage a reversal where a late-revealed record reframes earlier clues, and make the reveal depend on evidence players already found. When: Designing the final act of a mystery. Why: Earlier clues gain new meaning and the player feels the solution was fair.
- [rule] Place reveal items late in a level so they explain events the player has already witnessed. When: Designing the solution to a mystery in a level. Why: Lets the player connect the reveal to what they saw.
- [rule] Present an accusation alongside its supporting clues, with each clue linked to a scene or moment the player actually witnessed. When: when designing a deduction or accusation screen.
- [rule] A final chamber can hold physical evidence that recontextualises earlier clues, such as a lure quest or misleading document. When: Designing the last reveal of a mystery. Why: Physical evidence confirms the solution and gives earlier clues a new meaning.
- [rule] A case-notes or solution screen can reveal the method first and keep the suspect's identity locked until a condition is met.
- [rule] Gate a reconstruction screen behind key evidence recorded in the player's journal.
- [rule] Leave one or two details unresolved before the final confession, so the confession adds information rather than repeating what the player already knows. When: when designing a game investigation's clue structure.
- [rule] A detective's claim to predict an outcome is fair only if the clues supporting it were visible to the audience.
- [rule] A reversal of an earlier claim feels fair only when the earlier fact is shown to have been ambiguous, not when it simply changes.
- [rule] Match time of day, light and door states when replaying an event, so the comparison is fair. Why: Unmatched conditions make the comparison unreliable.
- [rule] Let players present accumulated clues in a final confrontation, with NPC admissions unlocked only by correct evidence. When: Designing the climax of an investigation. Why: Tying admissions to evidence rewards the player's reasoning.
- [rule] Let a late-arriving clue invalidate an earlier elimination, so players must revisit their notes. When: designing deduction puzzles. Why: Revisiting notes keeps the investigation open.
- [rule] Use a late-game reveal in which two NPCs with separate records share one underlying identity, deducible from complementary traits.
- [rule] A fair-play reveal lands when clues planted earlier pointed to the revealed person, even if the player did not expect that identity.
- [rule] Have the investigator admit their own missed signs, so the audience can see what should have been noticed earlier. When: writing a solution reveal. Why: Admitted blind spots keep the reveal honest and fair.
- [rule] Use NPC names or UI labels to frame how the player expects a character to behave, and treat that framing as a possible planted misdirection. When: When naming characters or labelling interface elements. Why: Players form expectations from labels before they observe behavior.
- [rule] Make a document's full text readable only after interaction, so the first glance creates suspicion that the full reading then resolves.
- [rule] Leave the last decision to the player after the proof is delivered, rather than resolving the outcome by script.
- [rule] Make exposing the truth carry a cost beyond the reveal itself, such as a loss of reward or a failure of justice, so solving the mystery does not end the story cleanly. When: designing the aftermath of a twist or the resolution of a mission. Why: A reveal that restores everything leaves no lasting weight, while withheld victory keeps the consequences felt.
- [heuristic] A retelling can carry the solution if every fact it needs has already appeared earlier, so attentive audiences can assemble the answer themselves. When: the answer depends on facts shown early and recontextualised later. Why: recognised facts let the audience rebuild the solution.
- [heuristic] A fair reveal depends on clues the audience has already seen but not connected, so the answer feels earned. When: Designing a mystery's solution.
- [heuristic] Give the player the object early and its explanation late, so the eventual reveal feels fair rather than arbitrary. When: when a reveal depends on an earlier clue. Why: the player had the information but lacked the interpretation.
- [heuristic] A late reveal lands best when small details already seen, such as a grudge or an object, fit the new history. When: a hidden past is revealed late.
- [heuristic] Keep innocent-seeming characters in the suspect pool, so a late reveal can recast a trusted character as a suspect. When: when planning a late twist.
- [heuristic] Leave unresolved gaps open rather than forcing a theory to fit, because a story that explains everything may be hiding an unverified link. When: Building an explanation that must account for all facts. Why: A theory that appears complete can conceal weak or unsupported connections.
- [heuristic] Physical details a witness gives about a closure, such as a loud door or a watched exit, can be checked to test a closed-circle claim. When: When a witness claims no one could have left unseen. Why: Verifiable details turn a general claim into testable facts.
- [heuristic] End an interview by framing the danger the witness has escaped, which makes further cooperation the sensible choice. When: closing an interview with a witness who has been compromised. Why: Recognising a near-miss makes cooperating feel like self-protection.
- [heuristic] Include one link that appears solid but is unconfirmed, and reveal its status late in the sequence. When: when designing a multi-step reconstruction puzzle. Why: A plausible but unverified step can keep the player's conclusion provisional until later.
- [heuristic] An exit shut before the crime forces the actor to have remained inside, so closing times fix when escape was possible. When: Recorded closing times exist for the exits. Why: An exit that was closed cannot have been used afterward.
- [heuristic] Build a late reveal in which an accuser recants after the player has acted, making the consequence irreversible and raising the stakes of an early choice. When: Designing a story twist about a false accusation. Why: A reversal that comes too late makes the player's earlier decision matter more.
- [heuristic] Reveal a case one layer at a time, such as suspect alone then with accomplice, so the player sees how each new clue changes the picture. When: building a quest or investigation interface. Why: incremental reveal shows the effect of each clue.
- [heuristic] Order facts impartially when the audience must reach a decision. When: The audience must decide an outcome from the presented information. Why: An impartial order avoids steering the decision.
- [heuristic] A final boss's or NPC's dying statement can explain several earlier hints, such as a noise, a missing item and an odd door, if each is planted first.
- [heuristic] Let characters' aftermath states reflect how the resolution changed their situations. When: Writing post-resolution states for characters. Why: Consequences that track the verdict make the ending feel coherent.
- [heuristic] Use a late confrontation to convert a solved mechanism into a human resolution, with a document or proof resolving the dispute. When: Closing a mystery where the mechanism is already exposed. Why: A human confrontation gives the solved case an emotional ending.
- [heuristic] Vary the justice at the end of each case, using unpunished culprits and ironic deaths, so a collection does not become a predictable formula. When: writing a multi-case mystery collection.
- [heuristic] Allow a non-legal resolution, such as returning a stolen item without charges, so the audience can choose how justice is done.
- [heuristic] Keep a final claim as a reasoned inference voiced by a rival character, so the designer can later decide whether to confirm it. When: the last link of a mystery must stay open. Why: A rival's inference leaves the conclusion open for a sequel or later confirmation without contradicting the story.
- [heuristic] End with the investigator's credit diminished, so the aftermath keeps an edge rather than offering a clean triumph. When: the closing act of a mystery.
- [heuristic] Leave one character's fate unresolved after a mystery closes, which suggests a continuing world beyond the scene. When: closing a mystery. Why: An open thread invites the player to imagine events beyond the last scene.
- [heuristic] Let the final confrontation trigger a violent reversal from the antagonist when exposed, raising the stakes of the reveal.
- [heuristic] Close a mystery with a record of later ownership or consequences, settling loose ends without restating the solution.
- [heuristic] Leave the wider consequence of a reveal unresolved, with no formal verdict, so the discovery exposes the truth without restoring order. Why: An open social outcome keeps the reveal from closing the story too neatly.
- [procedure] 1) Reveal the result, or let the culprit narrate the scheme from trigger to execution. 2) Retrace the reasoning in order, first action to last, marking which deductions were correct. 3) Tie each step to a fact the audience already saw. 4) Name the technique or source behind each inference so others can verify it. When: Ending a mystery or presenting a solved case whose solution depends on reinterpreting facts already shown. Why: Reconstruction from earlier facts makes the ending feel earned; sequence and sourcing let the audience check the reasoning; clues planted in plain sight make the answer fair and recognisable in hindsight.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm the solution through physical evidence at the final beat. 2) List each main party and state their outcome. 3) Describe what has changed in each location the player searched. 4) Let the world keep some traces of the solved crime. 5) Optionally leave one thread open for later. When: ending a case in a game or story, once the mystery is ending and the solution must be made clear. Why: Players need to see consequences for each party and place; evidence grounds the resolution rather than leaving it to assertion; an open thread keeps the ending from feeling forced.
- [procedure] 1) Present all clues before the conclusion. 2) Hold back the full explanation until the right moment. 3) Reconstruct the act in order: plan, preparation, action, outcome. 4) Explain each earlier oddity. When: ending an investigation once clues have been shown. Why: A sequenced reconstruction lets the audience connect every clue to a stated explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Attach an inheritance to a condition. 2) Make the condition a task the player must complete. 3) Let completing it unlock the legacy. When: when building a quest around an inheritance. Why: The reward is tied to the investigative theme.
- [procedure] 1) Release the character's history in fragments. 2) Begin with the most open wound. 3) Add later losses one at a time. 4) Let each fragment change how the player reads his conduct. When: When a character's past should be learned gradually through play. Why: Gradual disclosure keeps the player interested and lets each piece reframe earlier behaviour.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm every clue used in the solution appears before the reveal. 2) List each clue needed for the solution. 3) Check that none is introduced for the first time at the end. When: Designing a mystery whose solution must feel earned. Why: Introducing new facts at the reveal makes the solution feel invented.
- [procedure] 1) Release partial answers first, such as how an action was done. 2) Give the final answer only after trust is built. 3) Tie the final answer to a checkable item. When: A conclusion must land with the audience's trust intact. Why: Partial proof earns belief before the full claim is made.
- [procedure] 1) List the known facts in numbered order. 2) Show how a minor fact was examined and gained importance. 3) Connect each later step to earlier clues. 4) End with the general principle the case illustrates. When: At the end of a mystery, to close the logic and make the solution verifiable. Why: A stated chain lets the audience confirm every step was available before the reveal.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the anomaly that first drew attention. 2) Address doubt about identity. 3) Lay out the timeline and method. 4) Explain how the parts of the motive chain depended on each other. When: when writing the solution of a mystery. Why: ordering the reveal from the anomaly outward makes the logic easy to follow.
- [procedure] 1) Present the evidence the player has collected. 2) Let the player assemble the planner's motive and method from it. 3) Show the single physical link that connects planner to method. When: for a final-deduction screen in a game.
- [procedure] 1) State the standard of proof first. 2) Restate the facts in time order. 3) Repeat key dates. 4) Mark which details are uncertain and which are settled. 5) Set competing readings side by side, with what was not proved. 6) End with the questions to be decided. When: A long, complicated set of facts must be presented to non-specialists. Why: A fixed order helps a lay audience follow and decide.
- [procedure] 1) Bring all suspects into one room. 2) Recap the facts and the proof of cause before naming the means. 3) Demonstrate the effect visibly to the group. 4) Name the culprit and let reactions be read as admissions. When: A final act, once the evidence is complete enough to name the means and the person. Why: Staging and a fair-play recap make the reveal feel earned.
- [procedure] 1) Gather physical proof visibly, including tests and recovered documents. 2) Lay out the case to the culprit privately. 3) Use a bluff with a plausible fake piece of evidence so the culprit's reaction exposes them. When: closing a mystery with a confrontation. Why: Visible proof makes the bluff credible, and the reaction confirms the answer.
- [tradeoff] A culprit's death before trial closes the case without formal judgement, but leaves the investigator to weigh the ethics of the outcome alone. When: Culprit dies before trial.
- [pitfall] A reveal or confession that introduces evidence or events only at the end, or only in a summary, feels arbitrary or like a cheat, since the audience never saw them. When: when resolving a mystery or designing a confession. Why: Audience cannot recall or connect clues never shown in their original context; the explanation works only when its facts were given fairly earlier.
- [pitfall] A reveal delayed too long weakens the tension that the withholding built.
- [pitfall] Even a careful summary can tilt the audience, and the presenter's tone can be read as hostile. Why: Word choice and emphasis shape how neutral the presentation seems.
- [fact] A final event can confirm a reversal without re-explaining it in detail, leaving the reader to link it to earlier clues.
- [fact] When all named beneficiaries are gone, a fallback recipient such as a state or third party often takes the estate, which can make the chain of deaths matter. When: when reading the final-case clause of an inheritance. Why: the fallback determines who gains once no named heir remains.

## testing a theory
- [mechanism] Small differences between cases compound through repeated steps, much as a small early error grows larger with each later step. When: reasoning from a close match through a long chain of inference. Why: each step carries the early difference forward and enlarges it.
- [mechanism] If a case rests on one category of unverifiable testimony, a single ruling excluding that category can leave the proceeding with no working basis. When: a case's evidence depends on one testimony type.
- [rule] Make a mystery's explanation testable, and make each competing explanation predict something checkable so the player can rule options out. When: when designing a mystery's explanation or competing explanations. Why: untestable answers give no route to the truth. (x2)
- [rule] Treat a conjecture or a cause reached by elimination as a theory: test it against all known facts, and do not treat it as certain while its grounds allow challenge. When: forming a conclusion from partial evidence. Why: a conjecture that fits some facts may fail others, and unverified grounds leave the conclusion open.
- [rule] Test each candidate theory against every known clue and physical fact, listing unexplained clues, and drop any explanation that requires what the evidence rules out. When: choosing between competing explanations of a mystery. Why: a theory must fit all clues, not only the one that makes it seem convincing; one explaining only some is incomplete.
- [rule] Do not treat a complete-looking chain as proof until its premise and each link are tested; solid-looking facts can build a convincing case against an innocent. When: evaluating a prosecution-style case or a player's accusation.
- [rule] Withhold unverified theories, whether assumed motives or gossip, from the wider group until checked, since they can steer an investigation without evidence.
- [rule] Do not build a theory or reversal on a single name, silence or fact, since disproving that one premise collapses the whole reconstruction. When: evaluating a theory or a bold reinterpretation of a case. Why: a theory built on one premise is fragile.
- [rule] Before using an expert's or witness's theory as evidence, test it against exact physical evidence, samples and testimony, however authoritative its source; drop it when a detail contradicts it.
- [rule] To test a witness's vague judgment about someone, ask for specific words, actions and dates that support it. When: when a witness says someone never seemed worried or was always something. Why: specifics can be checked, while generalities cannot.
- [rule] Test the first hypothesis against other possible motives before accepting it, especially when it looks too neat.
- [rule] A theory that fits the known facts may still be wrong, so test it before accepting it, and keep it separate from the true solution. When: Several theories fit the facts.
- [rule] Let the player present a deduction to an NPC who raises objections, and win the NPC over only with answers backed by evidence. When: Designing a theory-presentation mechanic. Why: Requiring evidence rewards linking clues rather than guessing.
- [rule] Reject a colleague's theory only on evidence, not on a hunch about a suspect's nature; find evidence that supports or refutes it. When: when weighing competing explanations.
- [rule] Plan safety for anyone placed at risk in a test, and arrange a fallback such as moving them to a safe place afterwards. When: A test exposes a person to danger. Why: Testing a theory carries a moral and practical cost.
- [rule] When a subject's reaction could come from knowing about a test, rerun the test with the trigger hidden from the subject. When: A test result depends on what the subject could see or guess. Why: Hidden triggers separate real reactions from reactions to knowledge.
- [rule] Adopt an unfamiliar test only after checking established reference guidance, and avoid any test whose lawfulness or validity is disputed among practitioners.
- [heuristic] Test any offered explanation against the timeline; do not fill an unknown interval with an unverified event to fit a preferred suspect. When: when a discovery contradicts an earlier account, or a timeline has a gap. Why: timing reveals gaps an explanation may hide, and assumed events hide the true alternatives. (x2)
- [heuristic] Test a neat, emotionally complete explanation at its weakest checkable point until it fails or survives, rather than judging it by coherence. When: when an early account explains everything through one motive, before its facts are checked. Why: a satisfying story can stop checking.
- [heuristic] A theory that explains a motive but not how the act was done, or how access or location was gained, is incomplete; revise or reject it. When: evaluating competing explanations. Why: a theory must account for the method as well as the motive.
- [heuristic] A single reading or physical trial can be wrong or prove little; test each early conclusion against a second observation or repeated trial. Why: a first reading of evidence can be wrong.
- [heuristic] Confirm a route or trace only when several traces agree; one comparison, odd detail, or single match can be coincidence. When: verifying a route or a scene's objects as the main record of events. Why: multiple independent traces are harder to explain away; a trace matching only one hypothesis is not proof.
- [heuristic] Lay out the chain of reasoning aloud and let a skeptical listener, including the person it concerns, challenge each link before trusting a hunch. When: when a provisional conclusion about a person rests on inference and emotion. Why: challenge reveals gaps, and a chain that cannot be explained to others may rest on fixation.
- [heuristic] Treat an explanation that cannot be checked, such as an unknown intermediary, as a weak point to press rather than a settled answer.
- [heuristic] Some phrases in a prearranged code cannot be deduced, so test a pattern before assuming arbitrary wording is meaningful.
- [heuristic] Test a proposed explanation by reproducing its mechanism under the same conditions; a matching result gives the explanation real support. When: checking a solution to a puzzle or mystery. Why: reproduction turns a plausible story into a tested one.
- [heuristic] Before accepting a deduction, check whether it tests a claim against new evidence or only restates the claim in other words. When: evaluating an argument or in-world inference. Why: A restated claim looks like proof but adds no support.
- [heuristic] Present a stated theory to a reluctant witness as a test, since the response to it reveals more than a direct question. When: When a witness will not answer a direct question. Why: Accepting, rejecting, or challenging a theory shows what the witness knows and fears.
- [procedure] 1) List each premise a conclusion or explanation requires. 2) Test each premise against evidence. 3) Judge by whether the premises hold, not how neat it sounds; check whether it survives if any link fails. When: when a conclusion depends on several assumed links, or a suspect offers a neat explanation for an odd act. Why: a chain fails if any one premise is false; an explanation is only as strong as its premises. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Hold the current theory as provisional and use it to direct inquiry. 2) Identify the most unexplained fact. 3) Test whether the theory accounts for it. 4) Revise the theory if it does not. When: pursuing a working theory, especially when a neat theory leaves a key behaviour unexplained. Why: facts it cannot explain show it covers only part of the evidence and can expose a red herring. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) State the theory as a story accounting for the facts. 2) List each fact it must explain and check it against the evidence. 3) Mark facts it cannot explain as weak spots. 4) Drop or revise it when a contradiction holds. When: when a plausible explanation is proposed and must be checked before anyone acts on it. Why: listing facts exposes where an explanation breaks; a theory fitting some facts can still be wrong.
- [procedure] 1) State the key premise plainly. 2) Present each inference to a sceptical colleague, who challenges each link. 3) Answer each objection with a new fact or reason. 4) Drop, revise or rebuild any link that fails. When: testing a deduction or a complicated theory before relying on it. Why: objections expose weak links that stay hidden while the theory is held only in the mind.
- [procedure] 1) State a provisional theory covering all current facts. 2) Name what else must be true, or predictions that would confirm or break it. 3) Check those consequences against new facts. 4) Drop or revise it if one fails. When: deciding whether a suspect theory deserves pursuit, or evidence is incomplete and action is needed before certainty. Why: accepting a theory without testing its consequences lets weak explanations survive; predictions make a hypothesis testable.
- [procedure] 1) Build a reconstruction from the object's features and location, labelled provisional. 2) Choose two checks, such as revisiting the scene for a predicted physical trace, that would confirm or refute it. 3) Run them with knowledgeable people before acting on it. When: an object found at a scene is used to explain an event. Why: stating observable predictions lets a reconstruction be refuted, so it is tested rather than assumed.
- [procedure] 1) State the theory. 2) List the strongest objections, including motive and contrary evidence. 3) Answer each objection with a specific explanation. 4) Check whether all answers rest on one assumption. When: Before acting on a theory. Why: Forcing rebuttals exposes weak links that a neat story can hide.
- [procedure] 1) Consider an unwelcome theory seriously. 2) Examine it from every side. 3) Act on it only after that full review.
- [procedure] 1) List each physical trace and each witness observation. 2) For each, ask whether the hypothesis predicts it. 3) Keep the theory open for any trace it cannot explain. When: A working theory depends on where an object was found or on a partial witness account. Why: A theory that fits the main facts can still fail on small details it does not explain.
- [procedure] 1) Summarise the plot from the clues already found. 2) Compare the summary with the late witness's account. 3) Deduce what remains, then confirm it against facts. When: When a late witness account is available to check a theory. Why: A reconstruction is only trustworthy once it matches independent testimony.
- [procedure] 1) Build a full story from known facts. 2) Test each element against facts. 3) Keep the parts that survive and discard those contradicted. When: Roles or relationships in a story are unclear. Why: Plausible theories can contain errors that only testing reveals.
- [procedure] 1) List every act a theory requires of the culprit. 2) For each, ask whether a sensible offender with goals such as silence and escape would perform it. 3) Rank theories by how plausible their acts are. When: Several explanations fit the physical facts. Why: Checking each act against a rational actor ranks theories by how plausibly the culprit would have acted.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a cheap test whose outcome depends on whether the theory is true. 2) Perform it. 3) Read the reaction to decide whether the theory holds. When: A trace suggests a theory and a cheap test is available. Why: A test whose result depends on the theory discriminates it from alternatives better than assertion.
- [procedure] 1) State the hypothesis as depending on one checkable fact. 2) Ask a precise question whose answer confirms or defeats it. 3) Seek a second independent source for that fact. When: A working theory must be tested against the record. Why: A single precise fact gives a clear test, and a second source reduces error.
- [procedure] 1) State the conclusion as a hypothesis with a stated likelihood. 2) List the other explanations that could produce each matching fact. 3) Narrow the location in stages, from wide to specific. 4) Check the narrowed location physically. When: When a few indirect clues point to a small set of places and a cheap check can confirm or refute the claim. Why: Staged narrowing keeps checks cheap and makes the hypothesis testable.
- [procedure] 1) List every oddity in the scene. 2) Propose a hypothesis. 3) Check it against each item. 4) Reject any hypothesis that leaves an item unexplained. When: a set of oddities resists a single account.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the central claim the solution depends on. 2) Ask for checkable specifics only the presenter could know, such as names, descriptions and dates. 3) Press the central claim before any minor points. When: the solution rests on identifications or documents not yet shown to the group. Why: a claim that cannot be checked, or that resists pressure, is the likely weak point.
- [procedure] 1) Note the missing detail. 2) Check whether the account is false on that point. 3) Look for a simple cause, such as the person never having looked. When: A gap in a suspect's account seems suspicious.
- [procedure] 1) Form a hypothesis from observed differences. 2) Predict the outcome of the next case before it occurs. 3) Compare the prediction to the result. 4) Revise the hypothesis when predictions fail. When: Checking whether a pattern in game evidence or design holds. Why: Predictions made in advance test a hypothesis; recalling outcomes afterward does not.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the points where the theory needs knowledge or actions it cannot explain. 2) For each gap, test whether a proposed explanation closes it against independent facts. 3) Check who knew what and when in each explanation. 4) Reject the theory if gaps remain unanswered. When: When a theory has been built and needs vetting before it is acted on. Why: A theory can look sound while resting on untested assumptions or ad hoc patches.
- [procedure] 1) Match the scene to documented precedent cases with the same method. 2) Verify background facts in primary records. 3) Let each new fact confirm or reject the working theory. When: when the crime follows a known pattern and reliable records exist. Why: Two independent checks, method and history, confirm or reject the theory.
- [procedure] 1) Form a theory, accepting it may be guesswork. 2) List facts that must hold if it is right. 3) Assign each check to a separate party, splitting queries so no one learns the purpose. 4) Treat the theory as proven only if all predictions are independently confirmed. When: Verifying a theory the investigator cannot check alone. Why: Independent checks test the theory without revealing it to checkers.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whether anything was taken. 2) Check whether the witness still has valuables. 3) Look for physical disturbances such as a missing key or displaced furniture. 4) Test whether the cause fits a human search. When: A witness reports a strange event. Why: Physical facts can discriminate between human and supernatural causes.
- [procedure] 1) State the theory. 2) Ask what it predicts that an alternative would not. 3) Check each contradicting detail against it. 4) Drop the theory if a detail it cannot explain is physically or testimonially confirmed. When: when a tidy explanation is being accepted for an event. Why: A theory must survive checks against details, not merely fit the overall story.
- [procedure] 1) Note a character's sudden reaction to a stimulus, such as a flinch or flight, and keep it as a clue. 2) Later, use that same stimulus deliberately while testing a hypothesis about the character. 3) Read the reaction as evidence only after its meaning is understood. When: When a hidden trait would appear only under pressure. Why: A deliberate stimulus chosen for a reason exposes a trait, and the earlier reaction gives the result its meaning.
- [procedure] 1) Form several candidate explanations for a person from their surroundings. 2) Treat each as an open option to test. 3) Keep the one that survives further evidence. When: Forming a first judgment about a person from their environment. Why: First impressions from surroundings alone are often wrong, so they should be held open.
- [procedure] 1) Identify an improbable pattern and treat it as a suspicion, not proof. 2) Test it with controlled trials while a helper records observations independently. 3) Use an instrument that reacts to the hidden cause. 4) Reveal the physical evidence first, then explain the mechanism. When: A pattern could be chance or deliberate control and you can test which. Why: Layered revelation with independent corroboration makes the conclusion checkable.
- [procedure] 1) Test the explanation against the facts it must explain. 2) Test it against other cases it should also fit. 3) Check whether the speaker could actually have observed what they claim. When: A confident explanation is about to close a case.
- [procedure] 1) Check the location for signs of the suspected act. 2) Test the theory rather than assuming it. 3) If the suspect is caught doing something suspicious, check what they actually did before accepting the theory. When: When a motive-rich suspect appears to explain an event. Why: Confirming a suspect's presence does not confirm they caused the whole event.
- [procedure] 1) List reasons a suspect might want the victim gone. 2) Separate wish from resolve. 3) For each element, name the fact that would confirm or drop it. 4) Check that fact and update. When: Building a suspect case before physical proof exists. Why: Each element becomes testable instead of a general suspicion.
- [tradeoff] Following one essential clue is faster, while following all clues in full is slower but catches leads that would otherwise be missed. When: Choosing how to investigate with several open leads. Why: Speed and completeness pull in opposite directions.
- [tradeoff] A test that reproduces the effect supports a natural explanation, while a test that fails narrows the field without proving an unexplained cause. When: Interpreting the outcome of a source test. Why: Failure to reproduce a sound rules out one cause but does not establish another.
- [pitfall] An untestable mood-based explanation, which assumes anything may mean something, lets any fact fit and makes every outcome look like support. When: when a theory rests on mood rather than specific evidence. Why: a theory that explains everything cannot be checked against facts. (x2)
- [pitfall] Supernatural claims about invisible agents cannot be sworn or checked and absorb attention without producing evidence; weigh them skeptically. When: when central evidence is a claim no one can check or a theory cannot be tested practically. Why: an untestable explanation lures investigators away from the facts. (x2)
- [pitfall] An elegant or internally consistent theory can seem proven to its proposer yet be wrong; test it against physical facts before committing. When: when a theory explains everything heard so far or feels elegant. Why: consistency with testimony does not confirm the theory. (x2)
- [pitfall] Untestable explanations such as blood in the ears or agitation can dismiss a detail without checking the scene or other witnesses; prefer testable answers. When: when a witness reports a sound or event, or a detail is explained away. Why: such explanations are easy to offer and hard to check.
- [pitfall] A solution that works in outline but lacks checkable data, or rests on evidence the audience never sees, cannot be tested and fails under scrutiny. Why: the audience cannot test a claim whose supporting data is missing or hidden.
- [pitfall] A vivid, far-fetched idea matching one clue, or a single matching word, can seem convincing while other evidence contradicts it; check every clue. When: when evaluating a compelling hypothesis that has not been checked. Why: vivid ideas and striking details draw attention before they are tested.
- [pitfall] Observers' expectations, including a reader's belief in guilt, shape how results are read, so a single success or repeated test is not established without separating results from expectations.
- [pitfall] A smooth story built from correct facts can hide unsupported links and be false; test the whole story and mark each link with its evidence. Why: fluent narration makes gaps harder to notice.
- [pitfall] An accused claim can be shielded by an excuse that resists checking, which ends the test without settling the claim. Why: An untestable excuse leaves the examiner no way to confirm or refute the claim.
- [pitfall] Endless untestable theories cloud judgement and produce nothing that can be checked.
- [pitfall] Building an entry or exit theory on one missing trace is risky; check the surrounding evidence first.
- [pitfall] Without weather records and witness statements, a physical trace proves little because it cannot be dated. When: Relying on a physical mark as evidence. Why: Undated traces cannot place events in time.
- [pitfall] Treating a frightened tipster's account as the full story is risky. A single explanation, such as guilty conscience, may be incomplete.
- [pitfall] A correct prediction can still fail if the response is too slow to act on it before the moment passes. When: acting on a timed prediction. Why: Scheduled events do not wait for investigators.
- [pitfall] Overconfidence in a character's plan makes a reversal sharper, but it feels contrived when no earlier setup supports that confidence.
- [pitfall] A theory that fits one hiding place may collapse when another candidate is tested, so every candidate must be checked in turn. When: Building a deduction around a concealment. Why: Fit with one location does not establish fit with others.
- [pitfall] A gut conviction without a specific flaw can persuade characters but not readers or players.
- [pitfall] A single-object explanation fails if the physics cannot explain how the tainted item stayed separate from the rest of the contents. Why: Physical properties like settling can contradict a theory.
- [pitfall] Speculating that a professional burglar was involved, based only on gloves or a forcing tool and without supporting evidence, misleads the investigation.
- [pitfall] Assuming a single cause for a missing item can hide an accomplice who took it. When: An item's absence seems explained by one actor. Why: Other people may have been involved.
- [pitfall] Letting an untestable source decide something that affects a person's life causes real harm.
- [pitfall] A test can alert the person being watched, and an unknown timing makes the test impossible to schedule, so check both before acting. When: when setting up a timed observation.
- [fact] Untestable clues invite folk remedies, and a remedy that brings brief relief before relapse can seem to work and give false confidence. Why: temporary improvement looks like a cure.

## financial motive
- [mechanism] Mounting debt narrows a character's options, raising willingness to accept a deal they would refuse; track what they own, owe and have sold, since each debt adds pressure. When: when a character is under financial pressure or is designed with a financial motive. Why: Fewer alternatives make the bargain more attractive; each debt adds pressure and narrows choices.
- [mechanism] Once an accusation exists, minor earlier quarrels are reread as evidence of harm, so a rival's frightening encounter is presented as proof of guilt. When: a new accusation is made against someone with a past quarrel, or an earlier dispute resurfaces during an accusation. Why: Accusers and audiences reinterpret prior events to fit the new charge; earlier conflict already gives a motive to read into events.
- [mechanism] A debt with a fixed due date creates urgency that can push a person toward risky choices. When: when a character owes money on a set date.
- [mechanism] Dated property transfers can explain later meetings held on that land, since groups often gather where a sympathetic member controls the space.
- [mechanism] Concrete property such as land, a house or a salary turns personal feuds into formal legal action.
- [mechanism] A deed or old grant can give one family a motive against a rival, and the player can find it in an archive. When: Designing faction motives tied to land or property.
- [mechanism] An accusation that reaches a patron's own family can cost the patron the support they had given the prosecution.
- [mechanism] Motive can be read from who gains or loses money or status, and the same facts can be argued to support opposite conclusions. When: Assessing whether a suspect gained from a death. Why: A loss to one party can be presented as a gain to another, so the reading depends on who is counted.
- [mechanism] A staged theft of a replica, insured at full value, can disguise a loan, turning the insured value into cash for the owner. Why: The insurance payout converts a hidden asset into money without an apparent sale.
- [behavior] A past dispute over money can make a person's honour seem doubtful to an accuser, so earlier quarrels shape how later claims are judged. When: an accuser weighs someone's reputation. Why: Earlier conflict colours present suspicion.
- [behavior] A suspect whose clear motive is stated openly is easy to blame, because the motive needs no digging to be stated. When: a motive is strong and visible. Why: Investigators can name a visible motive at once.
- [behavior] In a new fight, an unresolved old debt or grievance is often voiced as justification, showing that the confrontation has a longer history. When: a fight appears to have sprung from a single incident. Why: Unsettled grievances carry over into later confrontations.
- [behavior] A person under financial threat may read pressure from dependents as a threat to expose their secret, and anger toward them can reveal underlying fear. When: when a suspect is being pressed for money by someone who knows a secret. Why: Fear of exposure drives hostile reactions that can expose the suspect's concerns.
- [rule] Tie a suspect's motive to a traceable resource (key, debt, safe, inheritance) with an explicit link to a specific actor so players can reason to the culprit.
