When: designing a motive that players must trace through the game or uncover. Why: Players can only reason to a culprit if the motive is traceable to a specific person. (x2)
- [rule] Do not use financial beneficiary analysis as the only motive test, since a beneficiary who gains nothing may still have a non-financial motive. When: Confirming or dismissing a motive for a death. Why: Financial gain is one motive among several.
- [rule] Express a suspect's motive through observable signs, such as debts in a ledger or nervous habits, for the player to interpret. Why: Visible signs let players infer motive rather than be told it.
- [rule] Give characters a believable reason for omitting a fact, so hidden presence can be explained once it is discovered.
- [rule] In an in-game property ledger, give each building a sequence of owners, and make a missing transfer a clue the player can reconstruct. When: Designing property history for a game world. Why: A gap in the sequence prompts players to infer the missing transfer.
- [rule] Let property change hands after an accusation, so the motive becomes visible in the world state.
- [heuristic] Infer motive by asking who gains from a death or crime, who bears its cost, and who is under pressure the gain would relieve. When: investigating a suspect's motive, especially when several people had access or the gains are concrete. Why: Gain and pressure together explain why a person might act, narrowing the suspects; gain is a common reason to act. (x2)
- [heuristic] Financial pressure (debt, large unexplained payments, speculative losses) can explain why a suspect might act, but alone does not link them to a specific act or prove intent. When: when financial motive is the only link to a crime. Why: Debt is common without criminal action; money alone does not prove intent. (x2)
- [heuristic] Financial trouble, such as a closed bank or missing securities, can motivate flight or disappearance, but motive alone does not prove the act or any foul play. When: when assessing a disappearance or flight with a financial angle. Why: A person may leave voluntarily for money reasons, so motive is not proof of harm. (x2)
- [heuristic] Show a death's financial gain through wills, debts, policies and transfers, tracing the estate's legal path to the true beneficiary rather than assuming motive from wealth or the obvious heir. When: when a death or disappearance has a financial benefit or a suspect's benefit is in question. Why: Motive often lies in who gains from the estate, not in the obvious heir; wealth alone does not show who benefits or how.
- [heuristic] When motive is hidden, financial records such as lender and trader figures on debts and spending often reveal more than testimony, exposing pressure that suggests motive. When: when a suspect's account is in doubt or a suspect's motive is unclear. Why: Financial records can expose pressure that testimony leaves out.
- [heuristic] Objects and signs of strain, such as pawn tickets, repaired worn clothing or footwear, reveal financial pressure a person has not mentioned and bear on motive.
- [heuristic] A witness with a debt, pledge or payment at stake may shape the story; a promised payment shows willingness to deal but does not guarantee the information is true. When: when a witness has a debt, pledge or payment at stake, or information is offered for money. Why: Interest can bend what is told; motive to be paid can encourage a witness to say what is wanted.
- [heuristic] Check actual holdings before accepting a money motive: a verifiable financial position weakens a theft motive, since someone who can raise funds quickly has less reason to steal. When: when a suspect's motive rests on money or theft. Why: Assumed wealth can be wrong, and the motive disappears once real holdings are known.
- [heuristic] Treat a debt as motive only after checking who else had reason to act.
- [heuristic] Judge whether an accused person had reason to act by checking their finances, character and the value of what was taken; a theft with no apparent gain looks unlikely. When: when weighing a suspect. Why: Without a gain, the act has no evident purpose.
- [heuristic] Combine a gap in a record with the timing of a visit and the demand made before inferring a payment motive.
- [heuristic] A personal object such as a photograph can reveal a link between two people and so carry a motive. When: When a found item suggests a relationship between suspects.
- [heuristic] When a scheme looks absurd, infer its purpose from the costs and fixed routines it demands, then ask which single purpose would justify them. When: An investigator must find the function of a bizarre plot. Why: Costs and schedules reveal what the scheme must achieve.
- [heuristic] Examine who controls the money and who would benefit from an inheritance or trust, since financial control often reveals motive. When: a case involves an inheritance, trust or income. Why: Those who control or draw on funds may have reasons to act.
- [heuristic] Rank suspects by motive, starting with who urgently needed a large sum of money. When: suspects may have a financial motive.
- [heuristic] A suspicious figure such as a large recent cash withdrawal is a lead to carry forward, not proof of guilt.
- [heuristic] Large payments to a person suggest a financial tie, but do not prove that person holds the key secret; test that assumption separately.
- [heuristic] A fact left unmentioned may still matter, and silence about it can have a deliberate motive behind it.
- [heuristic] A large policy taken shortly before a death, combined with financial ruin, is a motive signal worth checking.
- [heuristic] Heavy reworking of a piece that departs from copied styles elsewhere can signal personal purpose behind it.
- [heuristic] Link motive to financial records: a debt or cash need that the victim could resolve gives a concrete reason for the act.
- [heuristic] A person in financial trouble who courts someone with an expected inheritance has a money-based motive worth checking. When: Someone's finances are strained and an inheritance is expected. Why: The inheritance would relieve the financial problem.
- [heuristic] Infer a suspect's motive from who had access and who gains, then confirm or refute it with a later clue.
- [heuristic] Follow prices, partial payments and mortgages as evidence of a party's finances; a debt cleared years later marks the point where its plan succeeded. When: a party's economic situation or plan is unclear from narrative alone. Why: Money trails track how finances changed over time.
- [heuristic] Ask who gains from each accusation to uncover the real motive behind suspicion. When: designing faction rivalries that drive accusations. Why: Beneficiaries are the likeliest source of the accusation.
- [heuristic] When testimony is disputed, use financial records to infer the attitudes of those who ran a process, not to establish a person's guilt. When: testimony is disputed and a financial or physical record exists.
- [heuristic] Use tax and rent records to estimate who had the most to lose from a dispute, and whether a landholder was newly exposed by a transfer.
- [heuristic] Trace a building or burial ground through marriages, sales and descendants to see which families held it and whether they still do. When: linking a physical site to named people. Why: ownership records connect a place to a lineage.
- [heuristic] Compare payments across cases; unequal allocations, especially to witnesses with influence, can reveal favoritism or a patron's sway.
- [heuristic] Compare each payment against its case's outcome; a payment to a pardoned party far above one to an executed party's family signals unjust distribution.
- [heuristic] Trace who held property and office before and after removals, since changes in ownership reveal what was at stake. When: Investigating whether an expulsion or punishment served economic or political interests. Why: Ownership and office changes show who gained from the outcome.
- [heuristic] A small first exchange can be framed as the first real result of a plan, marking a turning point in the situation.
- [heuristic] A large unexplained payment to a victim's family can suggest blackmail, giving a second motive to check. When: a payment is linked to a secret or a signed document.
- [heuristic] Institutional records, such as bank accounts, can reveal assets a suspect holds that the physical scene does not show.
- [heuristic] Ask who gains from the uncertainty itself, not only from the death, when a disappearance affects inheritance or payments. When: When investigating a disappearance tied to a legal or financial outcome. Why: A party that profits from an unresolved state may prefer the state persist.
- [heuristic] Trace a suspect's motive to a specific pressure, such as debt, and check whether the act would bring the gain they need. When: when a stated reason for a crime seems vague or grand. Why: Concrete financial pressure usually explains actions more reliably than broad claims.
- [procedure] 1) Read the seller's name from the item's label. 2) Visit the seller and find its sales register. 3) Narrow to entries near the probable date of the event. 4) Read the buyer and witness names from the matching entry.
- [procedure] 1) List each beneficiary of a death or event. 2) Record the amount each receives. 3) Note the legal terms governing it. 4) Ask whether each beneficiary knew of the gain beforehand. When: a death or threat might be financially motivated. Why: Sorting beneficiaries by stake and knowledge shows who had a motive.
- [procedure] 1) Trace the suspect's business connections. 2) List recent large sums they received, and check the source of each. When: a financial motive has been identified. Why: hidden income can supply both motive and funds.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the most recent document. 2) Check whether a marriage or later act revoked earlier ones. 3) Find the beneficiaries under the valid document. 4) Treat their gains as candidate motives. When: when a death may bring inheritance gain.
- [procedure] 1) Map the inheritance chain across generations. 2) Identify who was passed over. 3) Identify who gains from a death. 4) Check each claimed motive against records before accepting it. When: when a death or disappearance may relate to property.
- [procedure] 1) Establish whether a will exists and compare all versions. 2) Trace money flows such as royalties and copyright to named beneficiaries. 3) Check for insurance and who held an insurable interest. 4) Examine debts that may shrink the estate. 5) Separate those who profit from the death from those who profit from its publicity. When: Testing whether a death served someone's financial interest. Why: Financial gain is traced through documents and flows, and publicity gains can mimic motive.
- [procedure] 1) Trace each transfer forward through successive deeds. 2) Identify the earliest owner and how they acquired the property. 3) Test an uncertain link against a related document. 4) Use lawsuits to show possession where title is unclear. 5) Keep proven and conjectured links separate. When: A claim of ownership or inheritance must be checked, or one missing transfer is central. Why: A structured chain shows where ownership is documented and where it is only inferred.
- [tradeoff] Paying a witness loosens their tongue but sets expectations of judgment; paying in front of others can make them greedy or distrustful and alter what they say next. When: when offering incentives to an informant or paying a witness. Why: Payment alters the witness's incentives during the exchange.
- [tradeoff] A financial motive is practical and clear when its figures are stated, but it adds nothing unless the figures connect to the plot's choices. When: choosing a motive for a character.
- [tradeoff] Financial motive has three forms, robbery, insurance and inheritance, and each requires a different method and a different holder of interest. When: Sorting money-based motives in a case. Why: Each form implies different actors and different evidence to check.
- [pitfall] Money is rarely the only driver: jealousy, revenge, relationships, secrets, or quarrels over manners and records often operate alongside it, so do not let financial motive stand alone. When: when a financial motive is found early or appears to explain a suspect's act. Why: Investigators stop searching once a plausible explanation is found; money explains who benefits but rarely all reasons, and several motives often operate together. (x3)
- [pitfall] Financial motive can be real yet not the actual reason; debts can mask an unrelated cause, so check it against other evidence before concluding money was the reason. When: when money pressure seems to explain a suspect's actions. Why: Financial pressure is visible and can mask a different cause. (x2)
- [pitfall] Financial gain establishes motive, not action, and is only as strong as each link in the chain; the beneficiary may have a clean explanation for the missing link. When: when a suspect profits from a death or disappearance and the motive is used as evidence. Why: Motive is circumstantial and does not prove that a person acted.
- [pitfall] Paying a dependent for silence invites repeated demands; each payment shows silence can be bought and each new demand raises its price, so look for the next pressure point. When: when a secret is bought, as in a blackmail or hush-money situation. Why: Demands continue as long as the secret remains valuable to the holder.
- [pitfall] A large sum shows that money moved, not who received it or why; the recipient and purpose still need separate evidence.
- [pitfall] A financial match shows that a link exists, not why it exists.
- [pitfall] A map of property motive is weak when accusers have no material stake, and seeing property motive everywhere can hide sincere belief.
- [pitfall] Accepting a livestock or crop loss as proof of a supernatural cause skips the ordinary explanations that must be ruled out first.
- [fact] A death can end a suspect's income, such as a paid case or engagement, so that person may appear to have no motive.
- [fact] Past divorce and custody arrangements can shape present relationships, so trace them as background before judging current ties. When: A family's history includes separation.
- [fact] Financial motives can be documented through three records: a will favouring a beneficiary, a life insurance policy, and a mortgage that ends on death.
- [fact] When householders are made responsible for funding a shared office, the right to decide its pay and property becomes the basis of local power and dispute. When: a community must fund a shared office such as a minister. Why: Payment duties determine who holds a vote on money and property.
- [fact] Property disputes between factions can remain unresolved in court for years.
- [fact] Investments made by guardians or trustees with another's money leave deed and transfer records that can reveal actions the trustee never announced.
- [fact] A will refused probate has no legal effect, so a legacy clause in it cannot be carried out.
- [fact] Gambling losses raise the general risk of embezzlement. They are a general risk to weigh, not proof that a particular theft or killing occurred. Why: Risk patterns describe populations; individual guilt needs direct evidence.
- [fact] Sabotage can be motivated by money: betting that a stock will fall lets a saboteur profit if a disaster drops its price. Why: A financial stake can hide behind a political or accidental appearance.

## sightings and witness reliability
- [mechanism] Repeated sightings, especially by several witnesses who build on earlier reports, reinforce a legend and make mundane explanations less likely until the whole community shares the alarm. When: a rumour is repeatedly confirmed by witnesses, especially several people. Why: Accumulated, mutually reinforcing reports shift belief toward the supernatural. (x2)
- [mechanism] Repeated pressure on one surface leaves a mark at a consistent position. That position can reveal the person's occupation or habit. Why: the same motion recurs in the same place.
- [mechanism] Each link in a sighting chain gives the next investigator a place and time to check, so the chain advances forward in time.
- [behavior] Recognition, such as hearing a familiar name or seeing a known person, can trigger an involuntary reaction like pallor or a sudden movement. When: Confronting a suspect with a familiar name or person, or a disguised person is in the presence of someone who knows them. Why: Physical reactions are harder to control than spoken words; recognition triggers an unconscious physical response.
- [behavior] A person who sees someone often over a long period may still fail to recognize them later. When: a witness has had frequent contact with a person over time. Why: recognition depends on attention, not exposure alone.
- [behavior] People who pass a familiar place daily often see it without observing it, so they cannot count or describe its specific details. When: Someone has passed a place many times without attention. Why: Passive seeing does not record countable facts.
- [behavior] People are seen far less often in empty settings, such as quiet Sunday mornings when most people are indoors, so sightings depend on the hour. When: when judging whether a witness could have seen someone. Why: few people are out to observe.
- [behavior] A suspect's habitual action, such as a repeated song at a set time, can be a signal to outsiders. When: A routine action recurs at a fixed time. Why: Habits can carry hidden communication.
- [behavior] People trying to match a changed face to a remembered one may fail on overall appearance yet accept one stable feature as enough to settle identity. When: Someone must identify a person altered by time, disguise or illness. Why: A constant feature can anchor recognition even when most other traits have changed.
- [behavior] A person who seats themselves with light behind them makes their face hard to read, which may be deliberate. When: A person chooses a seat facing a window. Why: Shadow hides expression from the observer.
- [behavior] People who benefit from a visible pattern may hear the warning, accept the facts, and still refuse to draw the conclusion. When: A recognised pattern threatens a group's interests. Why: Those who gain from the status quo resist its implications.
- [behavior] Observers unaware of a concealed mirror can misread its reflection as a separate, possibly distorted figure, especially in silhouette. When: when a reflective surface lies outside the observer's view. Why: the observer cannot see the mirror.
- [behavior] A suspicious sighting explained at once with a simple, plausible reason closes the lead for the audience. When: a suspicious sighting is given an easy explanation. Why: a plausible explanation ends the need for further thought.
- [behavior] A familiar, old exchange device, such as a returned dropped item, can act as a signal that an observant person recognises as a hidden link. When: Two parties exchange an ordinary-looking object. Why: Observers who know the convention read the exchange, while others see only the object.
- [behavior] A repeated chance encounter turns a coincidence into unease, and people read repeats either as design or as fate. When: The same person is met by chance more than once. Why: Repetition suggests a pattern, which invites an explanation beyond chance.
- [behavior] When a witness recognises the key figure at a reveal, the mood shifts from searching to shock. When: At the climax of a staged reveal. Why: Recognition makes the discovery personal.
- [behavior] Asking a witness whether they are entirely certain of a speaker's identity can make them reconsider and reverse an earlier assumption, reordering other facts. When: when a witness has identified someone from a voice or call. Why: a suggested alternative reopens doubt.
- [rule] Do not accept a sighting or let a single unverifiable report carry a verdict until a second independent witness confirms it, since one report cannot separate truth from error. When: Evidence rests on a single unverifiable report. Why: One mistaken witness cannot decide the case; a report cannot separate truth from error. (x2)
- [rule] When a night has no witnesses, offer other ways to resolve it, such as footprints, receipts or a stranger's description, rather than making the gap decisive. When: designing an unwitnessed period. Why: A single gap should not settle the question alone.
- [rule] Do not use a fevered or half-conscious witness's vivid impressions as evidence. When: the witness is in a fevered or half-waking state.
- [rule] Repeat an observation before trusting it, because a single look can be misread. When: verifying a suspicious act. Why: a second look checks perception.
- [rule] Recount any bundle whose count surprises you before drawing conclusions, since a first miscount can look like a discovery. Why: Counting errors are common, and a wrong count can mislead an investigation.
- [rule] A sighting from a different night bears only on that night and cannot settle the time of a separate event.
- [rule] Test a claimed observation against conditions such as darkness and weather; a face seen through glass in rain and dark would require contact with the pane. Why: Physical conditions limit what can be seen.
- [rule] Design an apparent victim with a hidden plan to vanish, revealed through a ledger or letters the player finds.
- [rule] When a character seems to vanish, ask who holds a key or knows a route, and do not assume a secret passage without evidence of a key or door. When: investigating an apparent disappearance. Why: keys and known doors are the usual explanation.
- [rule] Treat each sighting as a boundary on time, not as a precise point in time. When: Converting witness sightings into a time estimate. Why: A sighting shows only that something was true before or after a moment.
- [rule] Use an unresolved suspicious figure as a plausible false lead, but do not use it where a clue must be clean and unambiguous. When: Designing misdirection in a mystery. Why: A lead the player cannot resolve keeps suspicion alive without confirming guilt.
- [rule] If a witness saw an object at one point, account for the time it was out of sight before assuming it is still there. When: when an object's location is reported at an earlier time. Why: the object could have been moved during the unobserved interval.
- [rule] Treat an unwitnessed claimed activity, such as walking the streets, as an unverified gap rather than as an alibi. Why: Without a witness or record, the claim cannot confirm where the person was.
- [rule] Design clues where the pattern of a repeated action, not any single action, reveals the culprit's purpose.
- [heuristic] A vanished suspect or missing item invites a conclusion of flight or supernatural cause, so test several innocent or misleading explanations before accepting either. When: a suspect, NPC or item vanishes or goes missing. Why: Disappearance is ambiguous and can mislead; absence should not automatically point to a supernatural cause. (x2)
- [heuristic] Treat a sighting that is the only link between a person and a place or time as tentative until it is checked. When: A single witness sighting is the main evidence.
- [heuristic] Treat a brief flicker of recognition as data, recording its strength and how quickly it fades. When: Observing a subject during cued recall. Why: Partial and fading recall shows the shape of a memory.
- [heuristic] A witness with repeated direct contact with a subject, such as a driver who often carries the same person, is a reliable source of routine facts. Why: Repeated first-hand contact gives direct knowledge.
- [heuristic] Learning a target's new lodging quickly suggests the target has been followed since arrival. When: when a target reaches a new location soon after being seen.
- [heuristic] Record how often an observer watched, since the number of sightings depends on how much time they spent watching. When: when weighing a count of repeated sightings. Why: A count means little without the watch frequency behind it.
- [heuristic] A visitor who enters and leaves by the same route repeatedly without hindrance suggests familiarity with that route.
- [heuristic] Log NPC sightings with game time so players can rebuild an event by cross-referencing them.
- [heuristic] Investigators weigh whether a revealed fact can support the case, and withhold testimony that would hurt an innocent party without helping the case. When: When deciding how to use a witness's disclosure.
- [heuristic] An unwitnessed claim can gain support by preserving any document it refers to, which serves as corroboration. When: when a claim has no witness.
- [heuristic] Two different callers asking about the same valuable item on the same day is a warning sign, especially if one caller's name matches a known alias. Why: Coordinated or repeated interest in one item suggests a threat.
- [heuristic] A repeated object detail may be explained by an origin the story has not yet mentioned, so check for unseen history before reading the detail as a clue.
- [heuristic] A small, harmless errand, such as returning a dropped item, gives a reason to revisit the same spot repeatedly. When: when watching a location over time without drawing attention.
- [heuristic] A subtle tell, such as an NPC repeatedly looking at one object, can point to a hidden link without any dialogue.
- [heuristic] A witness who cannot follow the question gives answers that carry no information and should not be weighed as evidence.
- [heuristic] A flawed or unreliable witness can still reveal part of the truth, so do not dismiss them entirely. When: When a source's reliability is in doubt.
- [heuristic] Two documents sharing an impossible date suggest a systematic pattern rather than a single clerical error. When: when a record's dates fail a check.
- [heuristic] Make an object's testimony repeatable, so a second copy or second examination yields the same contradiction, which strengthens its reliability. When: When an artifact is meant to serve as evidence. Why: Consistent results across attempts reduce the chance of a fluke.
- [heuristic] A sighting is weak when the witness's times are approximate or the lighting was poor.
- [procedure] 1) Ask how the witness perceived the event, including distance, cover and light. 2) Ask what else the observed person carried and whether they saw the witness. 3) Test whether each person involved can be identified. 4) Check whether minor errors undermine the core claim. 5) Judge whether the report rests on perception or imagination. When: A witness's account depends on sight, hearing, distance or memory, especially at night, briefly or in fright. Why: Perceptual limits can undermine identification even when core words are recalled; each question separates observed detail from imagined detail. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Note the time and place of the reported sighting. 2) Establish the suspect's verified location at that time. 3) If verifiably elsewhere, treat the sighting as false. 4) Otherwise check whether the person could physically have reached that place then. When: a witness places a suspect at a scene. Why: A person cannot be in two places at once, and physical reach limits where they could have been.
- [procedure] 1) Check overhead openings such as skylights first. 2) Check roofs and the eaves for ladders or external objects. 3) Check any overlooked routes before accepting a sealed-room explanation. When: When a sealed room's occupant has vanished. Why: Vertical and overlooked routes are often missed when attention is fixed on doors and walls.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the last verified trace, such as a messenger, luggage or ticket. 2) Test each link in turn. 3) Follow unanswered letters or wires as further traces. When: A suspect disappears. Why: Each verified link narrows where the person went.
- [procedure] 1) Steer repeatedly to named people and specific points. 2) Note the few concrete details. 3) Set aside opinion and digression. 4) Return to any point met with hesitation. When: A verbose witness knows a social circle and facts are buried in digressions.
- [procedure] 1) Reassure the witness 2) Present the contradicting fact 3) Ask about one small detail and note whether the account holds. When: a witness's account depends on a fleeting view. Why: gentle steps reveal whether the detail survives challenge.
- [procedure] 1) List every plausible approach to a spot. 2) For each, ask whether a watcher with a clear view would have seen it and was facing that way. 3) Remove failing routes; the remainder points to a hidden route. When: When several watchers report a sudden appearance or disappearance. Why: Visibility and attention together determine which routes could have gone unnoticed.
- [metric] A recognition flicker in the eyes lasts only a fraction of a second, making it hard to fake and easy to miss.
- [metric] Shopkeeper identification made near closing time, under pressure, should be weighted against time of day and customer volume. When: When a shopkeeper identifies a buyer during a busy or closing period. Why: Pressure and crowding reduce the accuracy of recognition.
- [tradeoff] Recognition may rely mainly on the first-seen setting, so a changed setting can hide a known person; yet habits or expressions can reveal a disguised person in a new setting. When: A pursuer has seen the suspect only in another setting; a known person reappears in a new setting. Why: Setting cues can dominate recognition, while habits and expressions survive a change of appearance.
- [pitfall] Identifications from a single or brief view, such as a momentary voice, glimpsed figure or partial silhouette, are unreliable; witnesses may say only that a person resembles them. When: a witness saw the person once or identifies someone from fleeting cues. Why: Brief exposure limits recall, and witnesses fill gaps by inference, so a confident identification is unreliable. (x2)
- [pitfall] Viewing from afar or in weak light gives shadowy figures little detail, and witnesses fill gaps with expectation; assuming a fleeting distant shape matches someone known misidentifies them. When: a sighting is made from far away or under weak light. Why: Limited line of sight and light force the mind to supply missing features from prior belief. (x2)
- [pitfall] Fluent, smooth or detailed speech is weak evidence: it can pass checks while hiding gaps, rehearsal, guesswork or motive; gaps surface only under direct demand. When: a witness's story sounds complete, consistent, fluent or detailed. Why: Smooth or detailed talk feels trustworthy and can mask lapses the speaker is unaware of or wants to conceal.
- [pitfall] Once a theory forms, the investigator may fit vague reports to it, and witnesses who share information may look independent when they are not. When: When a suspect theory is already formed and witness reports arrive. Why: Confirmation bias and shared gossip make weak evidence look strong.
- [pitfall] A witness description that matches a record may still be false; compare the witness account with the official record, not with the first person named. When: When identifying a person from a witness description and a record. Why: Matching to the first name on a record ignores that the record may name the wrong person.
- [pitfall] A disturbance can hide an act from observers but not necessarily their report, so a witness may still log the sighting even if no one can act on it. When: An escape is partly masked by noise or confusion. Why: Observers may still record what they saw, even when the noise prevents an immediate alarm.
- [pitfall] A sighting with no conversation confirms that a person was present, but not their state of mind or intent.
- [pitfall] Witnesses may misplace a sighting in the wrong room or compartment, so its location must be checked against other evidence.
- [pitfall] A narrator close to the detective may flatter him, so audiences should weigh praise separately from evidence. When: Presenting an investigator through a loyal narrator. Why: Admiration can colour the reported reasoning.
- [pitfall] A person who handled an object once may have handled it again in an unmapped window, so each access period must be tracked. When: when reconstructing who touched an object. Why: single known access is not the full access history.
- [pitfall] A dramatic reveal loses force when repeated, so later reveals must add new information.
- [pitfall] A sighting that dissolves when approached cannot be verified and makes poor evidence; record who saw it and from where.
- [pitfall] A fabricated sighting can hold up if its travel and timing seem plausible, so each detail needs independent checking. When: When accepting a claimed later sighting. Why: Surface plausibility does not establish that the sighting occurred.
- [fact] A silhouette or backlit outline confirms presence and shape but not identity or activity, because interior detail is lost. When: a suspect's location matters with only partial evidence, or a figure is backlit or seen from a distance in a dark space. Why: Light behind a subject removes the surface detail needed for recognition.
- [fact] Bystander sightings give a direction of travel but not an exact position, so they should not be relied on alone for tracking. When: Tracking a fugitive through a crowd or street. Why: Direction from several witnesses narrows the search area without fixing where the person is.
- [fact] A report attributed to an eyewitness cannot be verified from the text alone; the reader needs independent corroboration.
- [fact] Common objects with angular outlines, such as a hat with corners, can distort a silhouette so that it looks inhuman.
- [fact] An empty room after a sighting does not disprove the sighting, since the observed figure may already have moved away. When: When a search finds nothing after a reported sighting. Why: A search that occurs later may miss a person who has left.

## legal process and procedure
- [model] An indictment has four parts: the accused, a place and trade, the act, and the statutory consequence.
- [definition] An intent-based offence is defined by a malicious intention or an allegiance, so guilt can rest on proving that link without showing any harmful act.
- [mechanism] Each arrest or unresolved hearing produces new accusers, so a single entry point can escalate within days into dozens of arrests.
- [mechanism] Procedures with built-in waiting times, such as clearing a cheque between banks, delay outcomes, so a pending status can be inferred from when the process began. Why: The waiting period means the result is not yet settled at the time of the action.
- [mechanism] A framer who aims for arrest rather than conviction expects a weak trial to leave the suspect exposed and easier to pressure. When: A frame is designed to be used after a failed case. Why: A flawed case still weakens the suspect's position.
- [mechanism] A procedural delay before a reveal builds tension only when it is tied to the stakes; otherwise it deflates tension.
- [mechanism] A legal rule about inheritance or residence can turn a grievance into a practical plan by deciding who gains and who must stay. When: when a motive depends on property or living arrangements. Why: Rules set the conditions under which a resentment becomes an actionable option.
- [mechanism] A procedural motion can defer a question for a set period, so the matter is neither closed nor pursued. Why: the deferral suspends the issue without resolving it.
- [mechanism] A decree that favors one group over an earlier settlement can seed a grudge that outlasts the lawsuits and resurfaces in later disputes. When: when an authority reassigns land already settled by others. Why: the displaced party keeps the unresolved loss in memory.
- [mechanism] When power shifts between factions, members of the losing side may be endangered, exiled or ruined.
- [mechanism] A new decree that redefines a crime can reverse which characters count as guilty, so players must notice and track the change.
- [mechanism] Rebuking juries that depart from public mood pushes verdicts toward crowd opinion rather than the evidence.
- [mechanism] When accused people must pay board, jailer's fees and court costs before release, the process gives officials and creditors financial stakes in seizing property.
- [mechanism] A procedural condition, such as a witness being unable to testify in the accused's presence, can control how fast a proceeding moves.
- [behavior] A prosecutor who values a clean record will drop a doubtful case rather than risk losing it, and will accept one conviction over a tangled multi-defendant trial. When: when deciding whether to pursue a messy case. Why: clean outcomes protect the record.
- [behavior] Official proceedings can omit the investigator's evidence, so the player's knowledge may outpace the court's. When: when designing an official resolution. Why: Institutional limits can leave the truth known to the player but unresolved in the world.
- [rule] A capital prisoner's jury must be the jury that decides; a verdict reached after the panel is replaced or re-polled can be challenged as unlawful. When: a juror is absent or replaced, or a deadlocked group is replaced or re-polled, before a verdict is returned. Why: changing the panel breaks due form of law and undermines the verdict; legitimacy depends on who made the decision.
- [rule] Let trial systems route uncertain cases to a higher court, since its outcome can differ from the local one, including full acquittal. When: when the local authority is uncertain.
- [rule] Before any irreversible decision, establish the matter as true and certain through diligent search, and never rest it on bare presumptions alone. When: a capital or otherwise irreversible decision rests on contested evidence.
- [rule] Let quests shift a power balance by returning or replacing a secret item rather than by combat, so the change comes from knowledge rather than force. When: Designing blackmail, faction intrigue or secret-based quests.
- [rule] Do not let a personally aggrieved official hold exceptional power over a detained person; resentment can turn that power into harm. When: someone with a grudge controls a prisoner's custody or treatment. Why: private resentment can drive actions outside procedure.
- [rule] When reassuring someone bound by a pledge, do not shrink the difficulty; measure the commitment against the longer, harder struggle. When: a person is asked to keep a promise under emotional strain. Why: understated stakes make the promise fragile.
- [rule] When a suspect is cleared, keep looking for positive evidence of the real culprit.
- [rule] Charge only offences the evidence can support, even when a theory about other crimes is firmly believed. When: when framing a case for legal proceedings. Why: Belief alone cannot secure a conviction.
- [rule] Make an arrest only after the object's location is linked to the suspect, not before. Why: an early arrest can lose the link that the rest of the case needs.
- [rule] Let a private intervention by the player skip the public stage of a hearing. When: a private act can settle the matter.
- [rule] Use unverifiable testimony to open an inquiry, never as sufficient grounds for condemnation. When: A case rests on claims no one can confirm. Why: An inquiry is a lead, not a verdict.
- [rule] Ask whether a claimed objection appears in any document; a witness who never objects in writing cannot be read as having objected. When: A witness claims to have protested or opposed something. Why: An undocumented protest is weak evidence of opposition.
- [rule] Penalize an official who alters a sealed verdict heavily, remove them from the bench, and bar them from hearing that case again. When: when a game's court system needs checks on rulings. Why: This blocks officials from quietly changing outcomes.
- [rule] When a scenario builds a conflict of interest into an investigator character, offer the player a recusal or reassignment option. When: a conflict of interest is part of a case. Why: it gives the player a way to respond to bias.
- [rule] Give restraint of a character, such as locking a door on a suspect, a consequence like escape or a legal penalty. When: Game state lets the player hold an NPC. Why: Consequences keep restraint from being a free action.
- [rule] Make an arrest a scripted sequence with a clear signal, so the player understands the moment of commitment.
- [rule] Require the player to restrain an enemy's hands before opening a pocket, so searching carries a hidden-weapon risk. When: Designing search interactions with armed enemies. Why: The risk makes the search a meaningful decision rather than a free action.
- [rule] A new procedural route needs its own proof and cannot simply reuse the reasoning of the earlier verdict. When: Reopening a closed verdict through a different channel. Why: Each procedure requires evidence that satisfies its own standards.
- [rule] In a formal hearing, raise only what can be shown on record; an unproven inference will be dismissed as conjecture. When: a hearing that accepts only evidence.
- [heuristic] Ask who actually sent an inquiry, not just who it was attributed to, since a rival usually sends their own agents. When: an inquiry has been traced to a feared person. Why: the sender may be someone else.
- [heuristic] Infer how an item was processed by reasoning about normal handling, such as whether a laundry would starch it, to judge its origin. When: An ordinary item is found in an unusual state. Why: Normal treatment practices show whether the item came from a usual source.
- [heuristic] An arrest dialogue can record the player's exact words so they have consequences later.
- [heuristic] Opposition to a faction that has long dominated a community adds a political motive to accusations against its opponents.
- [heuristic] Check whether a tribunal was formed through normal legal channels, since a special body set up without usual representation may lack lawful authority. When: a special court handles a case.
- [heuristic] Separate condemning unjust statutes from blaming officials who were bound to apply them. When: assessing officials who enforced harsh laws.
- [heuristic] Test an explanation by asking whether it would change if the accused were innocent; if not, it cannot be checked. When: Evaluating an accusation or deduction. Why: An explanation that stays the same either way gives no evidence.
- [heuristic] Build a kangaroo-court encounter where one NPC is judge, prosecutor and jailer, so players must find an outside authority to get a hearing. When: Designing corrupt legal encounters. Why: Concentrated roles force players to seek an external check.
- [heuristic] Pair an intent-only law with a clue showing the intent was never real, so players can challenge the verdict. When: Designing in-world law for a game.
- [heuristic] Weigh irreversible penalties more cautiously: a guilty person left alive can be judged later, while an executed innocent person cannot be restored. When: when a verdict cannot be reversed. Why: errors that cannot be corrected justify more caution.
- [procedure] 1) Start with routine facts such as identification and timeline. 2) Present technical findings. 3) Follow with emotional personal testimony. 4) Add minor witnesses. 5) Deliver the central disclosure late. 6) Close with a verdict. Why: each step prepares the next.
- [procedure] 1) List the next lines of inquiry as a short set. 2) Give each line a clear test that can confirm or rule it out.
- [procedure] 1) Comfort the witness first. 2) Then collect facts: when things began, who knew, and what was said. 3) Assemble them into a timeline of relationships, quarrels and motives. When: A witness has made an emotional confession. Why: Comfort restores trust, and the timeline later supports reasoning about motive.
- [tradeoff] Intent-only liability can punish acts that could never cause harm, but proof rests on testimony about the accused's mind or associations, which invites bias. When: A law punishes intent to harm.
- [tradeoff] Strict legal order can slow action when speed matters most, yet after a confrontation the formal process should be kept intact rather than shortcut.
- [tradeoff] A warrant or formal action cannot be undone once issued, so it should be weighed before a bluff is made. When: threatening formal action. Why: a bluff that must be carried out binds the investigator.
- [tradeoff] Offering a choice between arrest and restitution gives the player a trade-off, with each option leading to a different ending. When: A dialogue choice resolves a crime. Why: Competing outcomes make the decision meaningful.
- [tradeoff] Following disclosure procedure promptly protects a suspect, while postponing it for personal feeling weakens the appearance of good faith even when intentions are sincere.
- [pitfall] Estimating a natural process's duration from general experience can mislead when local conditions differ from the usual case.
- [pitfall] Repeated withholding with no payoff frustrates the audience, so deferred questions must eventually be resolved. When: Pacing a long mystery with multiple deferrals. Why: Endless postponement reads as a broken promise.
- [pitfall] A legal framing can hide the human stakes of an outcome, and the author's own bias toward a drafted settlement can color the account. When: A rule-based explanation covers personal consequences. Why: Technical language shifts attention from who is harmed.
- [pitfall] A single preparation, such as a repeated outfit or a common object, can have an innocent explanation and should not be treated as proof of planning.
- [pitfall] Arresting a convenient suspect can close a case too early, creating an appearance of progress while the real culprit remains free. When: A case has a suspect who is easy to arrest but weakly linked. Why: Arrests give an impression of progress that can mislead the inquiry.
- [pitfall] Promising authorities a result before the evidence is in hand creates pressure the investigator may not be able to meet.
- [pitfall] A defendant's use of procedural rights, such as challenging jurors, does not by itself protect against a biased verdict. When: when a fair trial is assumed from its forms.
- [pitfall] A council hears only the evidence put before it, so its ruling is shaped by what the parties supply.
- [pitfall] A confession taken after arrest, in a hostile setting, can be the least reliable part of a case. When: A confession is taken from a detained suspect. Why: Hostile settings add pressure that distorts statements.
- [pitfall] Procedural stages can turn on decision-makers' private doubts rather than a clear legal standard, making the outcome hard to predict.
- [pitfall] Arresting someone on suspicious silence alone can hide the truth and make real witnesses less willing to speak.
- [pitfall] A defense may attack procedure, such as the handling of evidence, instead of the facts, even when the underlying fact is established. When: Evidence handling is challenged in court or inquiry. Why: Technical objections can cloud a fact that stands on its own.
- [pitfall] A procedural argument that reverses guilt feels like a cheat if the governing rule was never established earlier in the story. When: A verdict changes on a procedural point the audience never saw. Why: Players cannot anticipate a rule they were never shown, so the twist reads as arbitrary.
- [fact] An insufficient-proof or reasonable-doubt acquittal frees the accused without clearing their name; a defamation verdict likewise leaves suspicion, and both verdict and doubt can be recorded. Why: Doubt about guilt is weaker than a finding of innocence. (x2)
- [fact] A pledged object usually carries a set term after which its owner may redeem it, creating a predictable date.
- [fact] A person can be legally accountable for a loss, such as missing property, while not being morally responsible for it.
- [fact] An inquest can return an accident verdict, a self-infliction verdict, a deliberate homicide verdict, or an open verdict when the evidence is insufficient. When: When a death inquiry must record a finding. Why: Verdict categories let the inquest distinguish cause from proof of means.
- [fact] Related legal acts, such as a power of attorney and a will, differ in meaning, so confusing them changes what a visit implies.
- [fact] A correct clue can appear wrong when it omits a procedural detail, such as the direction to turn a dial first. When: An attempt based on a partial instruction fails. Why: The missing step makes a valid sequence look invalid.
- [fact] A formal inquest asks narrow questions and rarely invites a witness's own theories about the cause.
- [fact] Disputes that run through formal rules over testimony and convening can be decided by procedure, not only by which side holds the stronger position. When: a conflict is governed by formal rules on who may testify or convene. Why: rule compliance can outweigh a weaker side's position.
- [fact] A rule that a harmful agent may appear in an innocent person's shape removes innocence as a defense. Why: Appearance becomes evidence the accused cannot disprove.
- [fact] A defendant who pleads not guilty puts themselves on trial, so the case moves toward a verdict.
- [fact] A rule can make a case legally valid without establishing the underlying fact that the act could cause the harm alleged.

## assumptions
- [model] Investigation divides into gathering facts from physical traces and interpreting them through method, sequence and psychology, which are separate tasks. Why: traces supply facts, but meaning requires reasoning about intent.
- [mechanism] Once sedation takes hold, the actor becomes inert and sleeps, and on waking has no memory of what was done during the night. When: A person passes from a stimulated state into deep sedation. Why: The sedative phase blocks the formation of memory.
- [mechanism] Seating placement determines who sits near whom, and this proximity shapes which conversations happen at a table.
- [behavior] One confirmed fact can suddenly re-sort many small earlier oddities into a single pattern, making them feel connected.
- [behavior] Audiences assume the poorer party in a secret relationship is the one under threat, and they accept that reading until something contradicts it. When: A hidden relationship with an expected victim-and-aggressor dynamic. Why: Stereotyped expectations about wealth and power shape the first theory readers form.
- [rule] Record each fact's origin (rumour, document or place) with a reliability tag, marking rumours unverified and separate from firsthand observations so players can weigh each. When: when recording witness information or presenting clues in a journal. Why: Players cannot judge trust without knowing the source type. (x2)
- [rule] Log observations and inferences as separate journal entries, marked suspected or proven, so players see which conclusions need verification and revisions don't alter what was seen. When: when a journal or case log records clues or witness statements. Why: Inferences are often revised as new evidence arrives, so separation lets players revisit conclusions.
- [rule] Before using an account, separate firm observations from guesses and assumptions, for witnesses and investigators alike, such as a shocked witness's belief an object was gone or window open.
- [rule] Keep independent confirmations of each minute, and who could confirm it, separate from the suspect's own account, and check any published report against them.
- [rule] When explaining a solution, open with facts found yourself and label each revealed fact as confessed or deduced; presenting confession facts as deductions breaks fair play. When: when reconstructing or explaining how a solution was reached.
- [rule] Separate observed facts from interpretations such as motive or character, and record each with its own confidence level. When: when a witness mixes what they saw with what they believe about it. Why: interpretations can be wrong even when observations are right.
- [rule] Keep a clue's raw fact apart from the interpretation attached to it, such as where an object was found versus who is guilty. When: Evaluating any physical clue. Why: The same fact supports different conclusions depending on the account placed around it.
- [rule] Separate established facts from hypotheses and hold both to the same standard of proof.
- [rule] Let players mark a theory as a guess until they have checked it against the physical evidence. When: players form hypotheses from physical clues. Why: marking guesses separates untested theories from confirmed conclusions.
- [rule] Separate 'seen' and 'inferred' entries in a clue journal so players can test an NPC's account against other evidence.
- [rule] Tag each witness statement as seen, heard or inferred, so players can weigh how much each line is worth.
- [rule] Separate a witness saying they saw something from being able to identify it; a sincere witness with conflicting details is still weak evidence. When: Judging how much a sighting can support a conclusion. Why: Sincerity does not make a detail reliable.
- [rule] Set explicit evidence thresholds and show the gap between accusation and proof in the game's journal. Why: players can see how far they are from a conclusion.
- [rule] Keep uncertain identifications separate from confirmed ones, so weaker evidence does not inflate the strength of the case. When: Compiling a list of evidence. Why: Mixing confidence levels overstates what is actually known.
- [rule] Keep evidence separate from the conclusions others draw from it, and keep testing alternative explanations until the evidence settles them.
- [rule] Separate a biased witness's factual claims from their judgments and opinions, keeping the facts and discounting the judgments. When: When a witness is biased but may still be a source of reliable facts. Why: Biased people can still report accurate events.
- [rule] Discard speculation about a suspect's race or nationality, since it is unsupported by evidence and misleads the investigation.
- [rule] Separate what records document from what is inferred, such as motives, when identifying a figure from household records. Why: identifications built on inference are weaker than documented ones.
- [rule] Let players hold two conflicting readings of one note and resolve them only after finding physical evidence.
- [rule] Make the victim's rank a variable in investigation depth, so a high-status death triggers a fuller inquiry and the player can see the difference. When: Designing how thoroughly a death is investigated.
- [rule] Let players collect accurate clues that point to the wrong suspect, then reward the clue that breaks the chain.
- [rule] Show confirmed links with check marks in a deduction interface, so the player sees each fact established.
- [rule] Keep emotional scenes that raise NPC trust separate from evidence flags, so players do not confuse emotional rapport with proof. When: Tracking NPC relationships and case evidence. Why: Trust and evidence are different states and should not be merged.
- [rule] Log which lines the player has heard, and surface them when matching evidence appears, so delayed recall feels earned.
- [rule] Let a clue journal retag earlier entries with new meaning when a key revelation fires, so players see links they had missed.
- [rule] Keep retracted NPC accusations in the dialogue log as valid clues the player can revisit. When: an NPC withdraws a claim during dialogue. Why: Withdrawn claims can still carry usable information.
- [rule] Let players tag which collected NPC statements they trust, then check those tags against later evidence. When: players gather testimony in a journal or dialogue log. Why: tagging makes the player's judgements visible and testable.
- [rule] Tag dialogue lines that matter so the game can guide the player's attention without a direct hint.
- [rule] Store second-hand facts, such as an NPC's claimed hour, as uncertain so a later discovery can correct them.
- [heuristic] Local talk is often affectionate or hostile, so separate what people remember from what they merely assume. When: when collecting community accounts.
- [heuristic] A guess thrown out to unsettle a witness may draw admissions, but a lucky hit does not prove the guess. When: An investigator uses a speculative accusation to provoke a reaction. Why: Reactions to a guess can be coincidental or caused by pressure.
- [heuristic] Facts that affected parties never disputed at the time and that were never later refuted can be treated as settled. When: Reconstructing a past event where contemporary parties were in a position to challenge claims. Why: Lack of contemporary or later challenge is weak but real evidence of accuracy.
- [heuristic] Set a counter-argument against an observation and treat the observation as suggestive rather than proof when the counter-argument has strong grounds. When: Reasoning from observation that conflicts with a theory. Why: Observations can be misleading, so they should not be treated as settled.
- [heuristic] Adopt a working premise, such as the subject's innocence, before weighing evidence. The premise determines which evidence is sought and which lines of inquiry are pursued. When: when deciding what evidence to pursue.
- [heuristic] Check a fresh theory against the clue it accounts for least well, since a theory that fits that clue poorly is weak. When: a new theory competes with an existing one.
- [heuristic] When several predicted facts all hold, the chance of that happening by coincidence is low, supporting the theory. When: Several independent predictions are confirmed. Why: Joint coincidence is unlikely if the theory is wrong.
- [heuristic] Separate confirmed facts from inferences in the case file, and let players run experiments such as a climb or a cut to verify a route. When: building an investigation journal. Why: players need to know which claims are verified.
- [procedure] 1) Build a base layer of facts that no one could reasonably deny. 2) Keep interpretations and rumours apart from it. 3) Test each interpretation against the base layer. When: Many accounts conflict and the investigator must decide what is established. Why: A clean fact base keeps theories from being mistaken for evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Write down what is established. 2) Name each assumption and the facts it rests on. 3) Find an alternative that fits the same facts. 4) Decide what evidence would separate the two. 5) Test the most fragile assumption first. When: When a theory depends on an assumed route, timing or method.
- [tradeoff] Let players choose between watching a suspect and acting on them, with a visible cost for waiting.
- [pitfall] An attractive theory feels settled when stated in orderly steps or when other links are plausible; each link still needs its own evidence. When: when assembling a case from several partly supported facts. Why: Plausibility elsewhere does not verify a specific link. (x2)
- [pitfall] Do not trust a routine or social norm about what someone does without checking when circumstances, such as weather, could have broken it. When: When inferring behavior from routine or social expectation. Why: Circumstances can override habits that people usually follow. (x2)
- [pitfall] Explanations accepted unchallenged, such as an object's first plausible reading or a settled claim from an official-sounding source, can yield a confident but mistaken reading; test them.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a detail as trivial, or because its theory is weak, can hide a real clue resolving a contradiction; check it against physical evidence. When: when judging whether a detail matters. Why: A weak theory does not make every related detail false.
- [pitfall] A conclusion built on an unexamined premise can make an investigator overlook the evidence that would refute it.
- [pitfall] A theory that rests on an unproven assumption is weaker than one that explains each fact; check whether key evidence is assumed rather than shown. Why: An assumed premise can carry a whole explanation without support.
- [pitfall] A place that looks secluded is often busy in practice, so its seclusion should be verified rather than assumed.
- [pitfall] Treating an attractive hypothesis as settled before testing it lets unrelated events appear to confirm it. When: a case dominates the investigator's thinking. Why: fixation makes coincidences look confirming.
- [pitfall] Assuming others are ignorant of a matter without checking is risky, since a wrong guess changes what should be done. When: Deciding who knows what.
- [pitfall] Taking the list of stolen items at face value sends the investigation after a generic thief instead of the actual motive behind the crime. When: When a theft's loot list looks like ordinary opportunism. Why: The cover story hides the real aim until the motive is found.
- [pitfall] A least-observation conclusion depends on assumptions such as no accomplice and no silence by witnesses; each assumption must be stated and tested. Why: Hidden assumptions can make a plausible timeline wrong.
- [pitfall] Confusing a fact with its interpretation, or treating the obvious solution as proven, produces a conclusion the evidence does not support.
- [pitfall] Plausible but unsupported claims, such as an unnamed party's warnings, should be marked unresolved until evidence arrives. When: a theory depends on an unseen actor. Why: plausibility alone does not establish a fact.
- [pitfall] A bluff that the target sees through weakens the interrogator's position.
- [pitfall] Assuming a source's motive is obvious without testing it can lead the investigator to misjudge both the source and the claim.
- [pitfall] Treating a rule drawn from finite cases as absolute leads to dismissing exceptions that should be considered. Why: Absolute assumptions block consideration of counterexamples.
- [pitfall] Matching one shared trait to one category commits the undistributed middle error, treating a common trait as identifying a single category.
- [pitfall] Treating an accurate forensic match as final proof ends the inquiry too early. Popular belief overrates the evidential value of prints. When: when a single match seems to settle a case.
- [pitfall] Reading a deviation as meaningful without knowing the normal routine leads to false conclusions. When: Interpreting a change in a setting's behaviour. Why: A change is only evidence relative to a known baseline.
- [pitfall] An explanation that accounts for every observation can still be impossible to prove, so it needs a test that could fail.
- [pitfall] Clearing one suspect can cause tunnel vision toward the remaining suspect, so re-check the rest of the field.
- [pitfall] Assuming a crime was unplanned because it looks violent can mislead, since that reasoning rests on habit and character rather than evidence.
- [pitfall] A demonstration that answers one objection can leave another open, so each separate objection needs its own test. When: a reconstruction addresses one doubt but others remain. Why: One successful test does not settle questions about other actors or sequence.
- [pitfall] Frustration can make a line of questioning look pointless to teammates, causing it to be dropped before its value shows. When: A line of questioning yields little at first. Why: Impatience hides slow-building evidence from the people judging the work.
- [pitfall] Concluding that there is no reason for a suspicious act, such as an alias, because no motive has been found is an assumption, not a finding. When: When an investigator explains away an anomaly for lack of a discovered motive. Why: Failing to find a motive does not establish that none exists.
- [pitfall] Assuming the window was the only exit from a room can mislead, since other routes may remain open. When: when deducing how an intruder entered or left. Why: Overlooking an alternative route leads to a wrong conclusion.
- [pitfall] Inferring the perpetrator's skill from one feature can mislead, since different backgrounds can produce the same result. When: A profile of a culprit rests on a single technical feature. Why: Several kinds of training can produce identical physical outcomes.
- [pitfall] An unexamined assumption about what a witness knows can invalidate an elimination. When: When excluding a suspect based on a witness's recognition. Why: The witness's knowledge is often assumed rather than established.
- [fact] Raw facts gain meaning only through inference; gathering facts without organising and interpreting them leaves a case unexplained. When: An investigator relies only on collected facts. Why: Facts do not explain themselves.
- [fact] A witness who listened without looking has only sound-based evidence, which supports weaker claims about what happened than sight does. When: when a witness reports events only through sound. Why: sound conveys less specific information than sight.

## alibi presence and opportunity timing
- [definition] An opportunity window is the interval in which an object is unguarded and a person can reach it, measured by duration and by who has access. Only people present during it could have acted. When: when assessing who could have moved, taken or acted on an object. Why: Opportunity links a person to the act through timing and access.
- [definition] Opportunity and mechanism show how an act could happen, while motive shows why someone would do it; the two must not be confused.
- [mechanism] Culprits faking time often assume all timers stop alike and miss the one still running; a timepiece set by hand to a false hour keeps working, exposing the tampering. When: when staging a false timeline, or a timing claim rests on a damaged or staged timepiece. Why: Hands moved by hand leave the mechanism working while the setting is false.
- [mechanism] An NPC's routine, such as locking up or watching a window, can serve as an alibi the player must test against what they observe. When: When an NPC's routine is used as evidence in a level. Why: Routines create expectations that the player can check for gaps.
- [mechanism] Schedule-based alibis let a player verify NPC locations through independent NPC or log records. When: When designing NPC movement and alibi checks. Why: Scheduled positions create records that can confirm or refute claims.
- [mechanism] A suspect who believes he is cleared may act on his own, producing new movements and disclosures the questioner can observe. When: when the questioner withholds a contradiction. Why: confidence leads the suspect to take steps he would avoid if alarmed.
- [mechanism] Presence can serve as a shield: a guilty person may be absent while an innocent person is present, and a crime can be carried out at a distance through an agent on the scene. When: Investigating who was present at a crime or where the culprit went. Why: Physical presence and absence can both disguise the actual perpetrator.
- [mechanism] Flagging which NPC claims conflict and letting the player choose which to verify turns contradictions into investigation targets. When: When NPC schedules overlap in a shared space.
- [mechanism] Showing the stolen item at the right moment can break an insider's composure or alibi, so the confrontation should be timed around revealing the object. When: Confronting a suspect who denies knowledge.
- [rule] Vague times leave room for doubt; reject an estimate or alibi that fixes only a general period, press for an exact time, and treat its absence as a weak point.
- [rule] Release clues through an in-world bulletin or news system on a schedule the designer controls, so information arrives in stages. When: when designing a case that unfolds over time. Why: Controlled timing paces discovery and prevents early disclosure.
- [rule] Do not assume who was present; check the assumption against the witness's own description before acting on it. When: Investigator holds a working hypothesis about a visitor. Why: A hypothesis can make the investigator hear the expected answer.
- [rule] Tie an NPC routine to a fixed day or hour, so the window in which the player must act is set by the routine. When: a visit or action is allowed only at certain times. Why: a time-limited routine creates a deadline.
- [rule] Use schedules such as patrols, shop hours and collections to set time windows that the player must reconcile with other evidence. When: Designing time-based clues in a world. Why: Schedules give players a concrete timeline to check against other clues.
- [rule] Time an accuser's relief to the suspect's restraint as a red flag the player is meant to notice. When: when designing a false-accusation scene.
- [rule] Generate physical limits such as injury or a locked stable as constraints that rule a suspect out of a scene. When: when designing suspects for a mystery. Why: constraints let the player eliminate suspects through world state.
- [rule] Give an absence an ordinary cause, such as a meeting or a delivery, so players accept the wait before they learn it was suspicious. When: when building delay into a timeline. Why: An ordinary explanation makes the delay look harmless.
- [rule] Keep one alibi link that depends on a fact outside the alibi's own frame, such as a boat's sailing time or a switchboard record. Why: An outside fact can break a claim the suspect controls.
- [heuristic] A vague alibi lacking names, times or places, such as not remembering clearly, is not an alibi; it leaves a gap to test, not proof of guilt. When: an alibi lacks names, times or places.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs fixed daily schedules with clear time windows so players can infer who had opportunity at a given time, and let a break in routine become a detectable change. When: When designing NPC schedules for a mystery or investigation. Why: Players can only reason about opportunity and anomalies if the baseline is explicit.
- [heuristic] A route shown to be feasible is not thereby proven; feasibility only means the act could have happened that way. When: testing an inferred route. Why: possibility differs from evidence that it happened.
- [heuristic] Test a route's feasibility against observer timing, such as patrol passes and quiet hours, to see whether an approach could go unseen. When: an act could have been done unobserved. Why: observer schedules determine exposure.
- [heuristic] When a remark implies knowledge of an act, infer the act happened at the first opportunity rather than later. When: A remark suggests someone knew an event had occurred. Why: The earliest window of opportunity is where the act most likely took place.
- [heuristic] A single fragile link can be gnawed or snapped, so a hidden channel needs a backup or a sturdier material. When: Relying on a thin link to carry messages. Why: Losing contact removes the only route of communication.
- [heuristic] A perpetrator avoids notice by acting at low-traffic hours and wearing clothing that does not draw attention. When: Assessing how a culprit moved unseen. Why: Empty corridors and plain dress reduce witnesses.
- [heuristic] Check first any alibi that depends on a single witness or a single record, since one failure removes the whole claim. When: when a suspect's alibi rests on one source. Why: a single source has no backup if it is wrong.
- [heuristic] A false alibi is fragile, and a detective who suspects it will attack its weakest link, such as the timing of transport. When: An alibi is suspected to be false. Why: Weak links in a fabricated timeline are easier to break than the whole story.
- [heuristic] Assume that any information shared with several people may leak, and plan for it.
- [heuristic] Ask whether a claimed action is practical under the conditions the suspect describes; an account that is hard to carry out may have been built to be believed. When: A suspect's account involves an unusual or difficult action. Why: Constructed stories often favor plausibility on the surface over practical feasibility.
- [heuristic] A staged scene can present a false cause of death; the player finds a missing object and works out how it left the scene. When: designing a misleading death scene. Why: Recovering the object's route exposes the staging.
- [heuristic] Treat vague quantities such as 'about' a given acreage as ranges, since they can support both sides and must be checked against the physical record. When: a grant or deed gives approximate measures. Why: Approximate wording invites competing readings.
- [heuristic] A stealth level can use a guard or merchant's schedule as a timing puzzle, with a window of a few hours for the player to act and a clear closing signal when it ends. When: Designing a stealth or infiltration puzzle. Why: A readable schedule lets the player plan around it, and a closing signal makes the deadline fair.
- [heuristic] Design NPC alibis around scheduled public events, and record which witnesses saw the NPC there.
- [heuristic] Include a later timestamped sighting that breaks a presumed death time, so players must revise their timeline.
- [heuristic] Place a timetable or schedule in an NPC's room with marked entries that indicate a route, letting players predict the next move. When: designing clues for NPC movement. Why: Players can act on a readable schedule to intercept the NPC.
- [heuristic] Show each NPC's schedule on a timeline panel, so the player can align sightings and locate the gap where a suspect could be elsewhere. When: Designing an investigation interface with NPC movement. Why: Aligned schedules expose the windows in which an account can be false.
- [heuristic] Use quest timers, NPC daily schedules and routine events such as meal service to test which NPC could have been at a given place and time.
- [heuristic] A scene-investigation system can use decay timers: weather erases traces, and NPC memories fade after a set number of in-game hours. When: when designing investigation mechanics with time pressure. Why: Decay makes the timing of player action matter.
- [heuristic] Treat a shared room as only a partial alibi, and check who was awake and whether an open door limited what each could see. When: Two people sleep in the same or adjoining room. Why: Proximity gives partial cover, but an open door limits what each could observe.
- [heuristic] Clear the leading suspect with a documented alibi at the midpoint so the investigation must find a new suspect. When: Structuring a whodunit around a strong early suspect. Why: A verified alibi removes the leading suspect and forces a fresh line of inquiry.
- [heuristic] Compare a principal's known absence dates with any act credited to them, since an act performed during their absence points to a deputy. When: A title or act is ascribed to a senior figure who was away. Why: Only someone present could have performed the act, so timing exposes the real actor.
- [procedure] 1) State the physical access the act required. 2) List who was present and could reach that place at that moment, given access controls, such as staff and guests. 3) Note when the victim would have been unguarded. 4) Review each candidate on that shortlist. When: a crime requires access that only some people had, or when assessing whether a suspect could have acted. Why: Access and timing limit who could physically commit the act, so the shortlist rests on opportunity.
- [procedure] 1) Fix a clock time for each event. 2) Compute travel time from distance and vehicle performance for each pair of places. 3) Compare gaps and overlaps with the account. 4) Check each link against independent facts. 5) Identify the weakest link and seek an explanation before accepting the account. When: When an alibi depends on movement across distance and a fixed schedule, or a suspect lacks an alibi and event times are known. Why: A sound-looking chain can hide one assumed step; gaps and overlaps show whether a person could have reached a scene in time.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a broad question about where the suspect was. 2) Narrow to destination, departure time, transport, companions and arrival time. 3) Ask for names of people, venues and transport. When: an alibi is a sketch with blanks where names and times should be. Why: Specific details can later be confirmed or contradicted.
- [procedure] 1) Record fixed times and when the house or place is empty. 2) Note known absences that open a window for entry. 3) Use routines and ordinary pretexts that allow access. 4) Count elapsed time since the last confirmed sighting. 5) Verify whether the clock itself is reliable. When: Opportunity or an alibi depends on timing. Why: Knowing when a person could act requires both who was absent and whether the timekeeping can be trusted.
- [metric] A large dose of a fast-acting poison should act within roughly an hour, so a long delay between dose and collapse counts against the simple theory. When: when testing a poisoning theory against the clock.
- [tradeoff] Vague time intervals suit natural storytelling but frustrate players who need exact times to check an alibi; exact times allow checking. When: when choosing how a timeline is presented to players.
- [tradeoff] Chronological ordering helps most when evidence arrives piecemeal, and adds little when every event is witnessed and precisely timed. When: deciding whether to build a full timeline. Why: Precise timing already gives the order, so the extra work yields little.
- [pitfall] A chain of times or sources breaks if any one link is wrong; check each link, since one wrong time breaks every later inference. When: a chain of events relies on several sources. Why: One weak link undermines the whole sequence.
- [pitfall] Character is an assumption about behaviour, and strong emotion can make people act out of character, so do not rule out a suspect on temperament alone. When: A suspect has been cleared only by temperament. Why: Emotion and pressure can override usual behaviour.
- [pitfall] Reading imprecise witness times as evasion ignores that stress weakens time sense and short-interval memory is unreliable; check remembered durations against physical signs. When: a witness gives imprecise times about a tense event, or a timeline depends on remembered durations. Why: Stress weakens time estimation, and memory of short intervals is unreliable.
- [pitfall] Assumed waiting, travel or lead times can be wrong; a procedure may run faster or the adversary may be further ahead, so check assumptions and recompute when new evidence arrives. Why: Unverified assumptions carry into the conclusion and can understate how much time is lost.
- [pitfall] Accepting a single vague time as an exact fact distorts the timeline. Why: approximate times carry a margin of error.
- [pitfall] Timelines built from vague periods such as a month or five weeks are hard to reconcile; make dates firm wherever a later test depends on them.
- [pitfall] A schedule with vague durations cannot reveal a gap, so the timeline cannot be reconstructed from it. When: When writing or auditing a timed schedule meant to expose deviations. Why: Without numbers there is no baseline to compare against.
- [pitfall] A vague claim such as 'I was out that night' gives no timeline and can be broken by any single counter-witness.
- [pitfall] Inferring the number of culprits assumes the group behaves rationally, so careless groups can produce traces that mislead the reasoning. When: Inferring a group size from traces. Why: Groups can act carelessly, which the inference does not account for.
