- [pitfall] Dismissing a suspect because a plot seems unwise assumes a rational culprit, yet hired killers can themselves be dangerous. When: a suspect is cleared on the basis of plot sense. Why: the culprit may act irrationally or hire a risky accomplice.
- [pitfall] A deadline that is vague or never felt by the audience does not create tension.
- [pitfall] A witness who seems insensible may still be listening, so the questioner should not assume they have stopped attending.
- [pitfall] Assuming a sleeper would wake from any disturbance is a mistake; check how loud the disturbance would actually be first. When: a claim says someone nearby heard nothing. Why: Many actions are too quiet to wake a sleeper, but others are not.
- [pitfall] An account of whereabouts with no names, places, or titles cannot be checked, yet it may be accepted because it sounds like work. When: when a suspect explains an absence in general terms. Why: vague specifics sound credible.
- [pitfall] Assuming everyone present in a scene was active can hide a silent or already incapacitated participant. When: A witness describes several people in the same place. Why: Presence and activity are different and are easy to conflate.
- [pitfall] Assuming an offender always acts in character can be exploited by one who deliberately changes methods. When: Predicting a known offender's next move.
- [pitfall] A time window built on an assumption can make a valid alibi look false, or a false alibi look valid.
- [pitfall] A witness who assumes a benign cause for a missed routine event may delay raising an alarm. When: A regular event such as a meal is missed. Why: The witness explains the absence with an expected reason and waits too long.
- [pitfall] Naming a character type from clothing and manner builds a label on assumption rather than evidence.
- [pitfall] Assuming a seated person was present throughout an event. Absences during long thinking go unnoticed unless the timing record is checked.
- [pitfall] Assuming an actor always acts sensibly makes the inference unreliable; it holds only when the actor's goal is understood. When: Reasoning backward from an odd action. Why: Without the goal, the act's purpose cannot be reconstructed.
- [pitfall] An alibi that depends on a third party's silence or ignorance is fragile; travel records and direct inquiry can expose it.
- [pitfall] A shared boundary or old feud shows that someone could make an accusation, not that the accused actually caused harm. Why: Opportunity and motive do not establish that an act took place.
- [pitfall] Losing track of a person who leaves the group breaks the alibi chain and hides their movements.
- [fact] A locked, scheduled collection system, such as a sealed box emptied at a fixed time, produces a known sequence of records.
- [fact] Opportunity and presence can be manufactured or shielded, so they cannot by themselves settle guilt. When: When a suspect's presence or access is established. Why: Presence can be arranged or concealed.

## tool marks
- [definition] A strong physical trace links a body, object or location to a place that the accepted account rules out.
- [mechanism] A physical trace, such as a fragment caught in a bolt, can reveal a passage route that a sealed door appears to rule out.
- [mechanism] A torn or partial document can leave one detail for the player to find while the rest of its content is revealed. When: Designing a reveal that should hold back a single fact. Why: The missing detail becomes a final objective.
- [mechanism] When a clue's location and presence change over time and are saved, players can deduce hidden NPC activity from the record of removals and returns. When: Designing items that change state during play. Why: Recorded state lets players reconstruct an unseen actor's behavior.
- [mechanism] Scatter several traces, like footprints, a glove and a torn map piece, each linked to one NPC, so players must work out which belongs to whom.
- [mechanism] A supernatural-looking event can be explained or excluded by the absence of expected traces, so a no-trace check lets players rule out a cause.
- [mechanism] A lock that has been taken apart and reassembled shows that someone had access to the door. When: When investigating whether a locked space was entered. Why: Disassembly and reassembly leave a physical record of access.
- [behavior] Silence can be read as honour or as evasion, and which reading prevails often depends on who speaks for it.
- [behavior] A physical mark's color, size and shape may be redescribed as time passes, so later descriptions are less reliable than first observations. When: When a mark is recorded days or weeks after it was first seen. Why: Memory and suggestion reshape descriptions as the mark changes or is discussed.
- [behavior] An expert can identify a tool by a peculiar nick in its blade and its dimensions, linking it to earlier crimes with the same tool. When: A tool mark at a scene is compared with marks from other scenes. Why: Distinctive wear on a tool leaves a repeatable signature in the marks it makes.
- [rule] Do not read a physical mark as a sign of a specific cause until ordinary explanations are ruled out, since innocent events and many people can leave the same mark. When: When a physical mark is found on an object or surface and used to attribute a cause. Why: Many common marks have ordinary explanations that look identical to the sought sign. (x2)
- [rule] Mark uncertain items and object-based inferences as guesses, such as with a question mark, and list those needing outside confirmation before treating them as fact. When: When recording notes or drawing conclusions from room evidence.
- [rule] Store footprints, mud, dust and traces left by vehicles and NPCs as persistent world state so players can reconstruct who passed through, when, and their route. When: Designing environmental storytelling in a game world. Why: Persistent traces let players infer past events.
- [rule] Before accepting a tool, check it could survive the force needed on the material; one that would break or bend is ruled out, since fitting a mark is not proof. When: A proposed tool fits or fails to match the damage.
- [rule] Treat a distinctive mark seen in passing as a lead needing corroboration, since another person may share the same feature. When: linking a person to an earlier sighting by one visible feature. Why: Common features can match several people, so uniqueness must be checked.
- [rule] Mark an unknown interval as unknown rather than filling it with assumption.
- [rule] Flag secondhand, exaggerated, or paraphrased material as such, and state where the account is still vouched for, so readers can calibrate trust per claim. When: when a text mixes sources of different reliability. Why: readers need per-claim trust signals.
- [rule] Mark withheld information as withheld so the player knows there is more to learn. When: Designing a reveal that is intentionally postponed. Why: Explicit withholding keeps curiosity active rather than causing confusion.
- [rule] A partial wall inscription placed low on the floor can point the player toward the culprit or a hidden item. When: Designing a victim-message clue.
- [rule] Read a mark's position together with timing evidence before drawing conclusions, rather than dismissing a mark because others were nearby. When: When a mark's location seems to conflict with the timeline. Why: Position and timing must be read together.
- [rule] Reuse the same phrasing or images for key facts, so the audience recognises each fact when it returns later. When: a fact will matter again in a later reveal. Why: repeated wording makes the fact easy to recall.
- [rule] Mark each informant's interest in the outcome so players know how far to discount what that informant says.
- [rule] Let a relic taken from a hidden event persist as physical evidence after the event ends, so the player can revisit and examine it.
- [rule] Mark each gap where a chain of ownership breaks, and label any link that depends on guesswork. When: Records of ownership are incomplete. Why: Unmarked guesses can be mistaken for documented transfers.
- [rule] Mark which observations are unreliable and why, so the player can check them rather than having a real clue silently discarded. When: Writing reports or sightings that a player must weigh.
- [rule] Mark a character's wishful theories as hope rather than fact, so readers do not mistake them for established knowledge. When: Writing a character who holds an unverified belief. Why: Readers accept stated beliefs as truth unless the text signals otherwise.
- [rule] A moved movable object should leave a misaligned footprint; a player who checks alignment can detect tampering. When: A level has rugs, shelves or similar movable objects.
- [rule] Use a worn or partly hidden maker's mark as a lead to a second location, rewarding close inspection. When: When designing hidden clues on items. Why: Inspection-rewarding clues make careful players feel rewarded.
- [rule] Confirm a mark is recent by checking the scene against its earlier recorded state.
- [rule] Let environment states, such as an unfastened latch or a burned document, record past events so players can rebuild the sequence from them. When: In mystery or puzzle spaces meant to be reasoned out.
- [rule] Plant mud-over-print layering on an object so that careful inspection of the object rewards the player with a sequence of events. When: Designing an environmental clue on an object. Why: Layer order turns an object into a readable event record.
- [heuristic] Count a gap as meaningful only if the record was meant to hold that entry. When: A record is incomplete and the missing part might matter. Why: Ordinary gaps are otherwise mistaken for deliberate concealment.
- [heuristic] Look for struggle signs such as trampled earth, broken bushes and torn fabric, and for dragging signs such as displaced fences, to reconstruct how a body moved.
- [heuristic] Treat a bruise from a grip as a record of force, not only as a sign of pain. When: when assessing physical marks as evidence. Why: Marks show how an action was done, which can matter for judgement.
- [heuristic] A rough, uneven cut on an object's end suggests a blunt tool rather than teeth or a sharp blade. When: An object's end shows a cut. Why: Tool edges leave characteristic marks.
- [heuristic] Physical traces such as mud or marks can anchor a sequence of events to a specific place and moment. When: ordering events at a location.
- [heuristic] Any tool or method that touches a scene leaves residue, such as fibers, scorch marks or scratches, that can be traced back to the tool. When: when designing or reading a scene where something had to be handled. Why: physical contact transfers material between objects.
- [heuristic] A personal trace such as a hair can connect a person to a room, so collect and keep it for comparison with suspects.
- [heuristic] Examine small fragments under magnification for material and curvature; a fragment of different glass with a different curve may come from another object.
- [heuristic] If a person bears a mark but no wound, look for an injury on the other party, such as cut knuckles, that could have caused it. When: a mark has no obvious source. Why: an injury on the attacker can leave a mark on the victim.
- [heuristic] Traces that survive a heavily disturbed scene are worth checking, since they may still carry usable time signatures. When: A scene has been trampled or handled by many people. Why: Disturbance removes many traces but not all.
- [heuristic] Partly erased shoe prints can still reveal who moved a body.
- [heuristic] Hiders often mark a hidden spot with an object chosen for private amusement, so an odd, personally meaningful object can point investigators toward the concealment. When: when investigating a hiding place. Why: Hiders tend to express their own humour or habits in how they mark things.
- [heuristic] Persistent personal marks, such as carved initials, can identify a character across time and remain as traces after they leave. When: Designing environmental clues tied to a character's past. Why: Physical marks survive the character's presence and link them to places.
- [heuristic] Scrapes on a chest or disturbed floor tiles can encode what action happened and how hurried it was. When: designing environmental clues.
- [heuristic] Persistent ground marks such as footprints or flattened grass give players a route-checking puzzle they can solve by reading the scene.
- [procedure] 1) Record the regular pattern of the impression. 2) Infer the tool shape that could leave it. 3) Collect each candidate object, such as a boot or horseshoe. 4) Compare each directly against the impression. 5) Confirm or exclude each, linking a match to a specific item and owner. When: When an impression or indentation may identify a tool, object or person. Why: Matching a pattern to a source converts an unexplained mark into evidence. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Examine the mark under magnification rather than judging its general look. 2) Look for variation in intensity within it. 3) Propose concrete candidate instruments. 4) Test each against the observed pattern. 5) Keep the interpretation open. When: the mark is the main physical trace and its cause is disputed.
- [procedure] 1) Create a pretext for the suspect to show their hands or body. 2) Watch the reaction as they comply. 3) Note any hidden mark, wound or stain revealed. When: The crime may have left marks on the attacker. Why: A pretext that asks for the body lets the investigator observe the result and the reaction together.
- [procedure] 1) Prepare an object that records handling. 2) Show it to each suspect separately. 3) Compare their answers for consistency. 4) Examine what they discarded afterwards. When: when the question is whether a suspect has seen or handled a specific object. Why: separate questioning keeps witnesses from coordinating answers.
- [procedure] 1) Note the mark, such as a scratch or notch. 2) Ask what action could have produced it. 3) Reproduce the mark with the suspected tool. 4) Check that the tool is strong enough for the job. When: A trace could have been made by more than one action. Why: A reproduced mark tests the link between tool and trace rather than assuming it.
- [procedure] 1) Subdue the suspect with a minimal, controlled hold. 2) Let one officer focus on handcuffing while another keeps watch. When: A suspect has been subdued after an outburst.
- [procedure] 1) Attach a speaker to each line of a rumour. 2) Keep the line order. 3) Let the player compare adjacent lines to find which link added a new detail. When: when a rumour is shown to the player as a chain of statements. Why: Speaker attribution lets players locate where the change entered.
- [pitfall] Not every absence is meaningful: items can simply be lost and indifference explains much neglect, so corroborate a gap or silence before reading it as a clue. When: An item is missing without a pattern, or a character fails to mention something. Why: Ordinary loss and simple indifference produce the same gap or silence as concealment.
- [pitfall] A partial match on one letter form is not proof of authorship and should be treated only as a lead. When: Attributing handwriting to a suspect. Why: Letter forms can be similar across writers, and one match is weak evidence.
- [pitfall] Reading a mark as proof of identity alone misleads, because it shows what the culprit wanted others to believe; check it against physical facts. When: Interpreting a message left at a scene. Why: Signatures can be staged.
- [pitfall] A trace surviving a fire may be partial or misleading, so record both what survives and what is missing. When: Physical evidence has been damaged. Why: Missing parts can change the reading of the rest.
- [pitfall] Removing one trace does not remove others, such as a message's content or the sender's habits, which can still reveal origin. When: A culprit hides a trail by erasing marks. Why: Other traces remain behind.
- [pitfall] Two accounts of one meeting can agree on words but differ in meaning, so compare interpretation as well as wording. When: Comparing witness accounts of the same exchange. Why: Identical words can carry different intent depending on the listener.
- [pitfall] Scratches on a tool or catch have many causes, and others may own similar tools; a tool-to-mark match is an inference, not a certainty. Why: Similar marks and objects can come from different sources.
- [pitfall] Marks left by a previous reader, such as pencilled lines and queries, can link an object to a case but do not reveal what a message means.
- [pitfall] Traces cut both ways: a player may only notice their own traces later, so check your own trail as well.
- [fact] A specialist can infer the instrument that made a mark, and the skill behind it, from the shape and placement of the damage.
- [fact] A soft surface such as snow keeps a record of movement, including who passed, in what order, how fast and where people hesitated. When: The ground holds fresh soft impressions. Why: Soft materials deform under weight, preserving traces of passage.
- [fact] A mark pressed into a surface can identify the object that made it, such as a cap's peak impressed in brushed snow.
- [fact] Dry, hard ground often fails to hold tyre impressions, so tracks cannot be read there. When: Reading vehicle tracks across a surface.
- [fact] Marks left on an object can show it was opened with an improvised tool rather than the one a witness would expect. When: when a witness describes how an object was opened. Why: Tool marks carry evidence of method that witnesses may not have observed.
- [fact] Magnification reveals structure only when the observer knows which features separate one candidate cause from another.
- [fact] A crossed-out entry can be the only trace of a fact, and the struck line can reveal what an official tried to correct or hide.
- [fact] Walls, gates, wells, trees and roads keep traces of old boundaries, which can be compared with deed descriptions. When: Deed bounds must be checked against the ground. Why: Physical features can preserve the location of boundaries recorded in old documents.
- [fact] Physical marks on a surface, such as a blade scrape on a door panel, are concrete evidence, while stories about the place are legend.
- [fact] Odours and residues persist in rooms and on clothing, so they mark where a person has been.
- [fact] Objects keep impressions, stains and fresh marks that can show posture, recent handling and what happened in a room.
- [fact] Reversed impressions left on absorbent blotting paper can be read in a mirror, revealing writing from a sheet that was pressed against it.

## evidence and proof
- [behavior] Accusers find inspectable objects harder to dismiss than verbal assurances, so an accused person who shows the means of an outcome can rebut a hidden-cause charge. When: when an accusation rests on a cause no one can see. Why: objects can be examined by accusers, unlike claims about hidden causes.
- [behavior] A suspect's excuse relayed by a third party, with no reason given for it, can be mistaken for evidence. When: A third party repeats a suspect's explanation. Why: Stated explanations sound credible without support.
- [behavior] Evidence only one person can observe, such as a vision, is hard to check and tends to be weighed by whether it can secure a conviction. Why: No one else can test the claim against the world.
- [rule] Prove the culprit with the stolen item and the trace of its movement; without physical proof an evidence chain is only testimony that can be rationalised away. Why: Physical proof is harder to dispute than the word of others. (x2)
- [rule] Separate inference from proof: a converging-clue conclusion is plain inference, not settled, until a witness, document or decisive source confirms the link.
- [rule] Label a conclusion drawn from circumstance or timeline as inference built on the evidence, not proof, until confirmed.
- [rule] Check an inference from a physical sign against a second independent sign or direct question; do not rest it on one observation or tone alone. When: A sign could be explained by more than one cause, or an inference rests on a single observation or tone. Why: A single sign often has several plausible causes, and one can mislead.
- [rule] Do not dismiss inconvenient evidence, even a small fact; test each explanation against the facts it cannot explain, since a small fact may matter later. When: several explanations fit the first observation. Why: Choosing between explanations depends on what each fails to explain.
- [rule] Treat a motive inferred from an unexpected choice, or an intention known only from an uncorroborated remark, as speculation until a separate record confirms it. Why: An inference is only as strong as the facts known about the actor; no one else can confirm the remark.
- [rule] Explain a conclusion step by step with the evidence shown, so the audience can verify it; an unexplained accusation or twist feels arbitrary. When: when an expert presents a conclusion from a physical object, or when delivering a solution to a suspect or audience. Why: Visible reasoning builds trust and makes the twist feel earned without requiring acceptance of the expert's word alone.
- [rule] Let a rumor-based clue be real but weak, with a physical check such as a test or trace that can confirm or refute it. When: Designing a clue that rests on rumor. Why: A checkable physical test lets players resolve a weak clue rather than guess.
- [rule] Let an object's meaning depend on a second clue, so players must check their reading against other evidence.
- [rule] Present a circumstantial inference as an inference, not as proof, and be ready to show the link when it is challenged. When: When communicating a conclusion drawn from indirect evidence. Why: Overstated certainty invites rejection when an alternative appears.
- [rule] Do not accept a conclusion that outruns the visible signs; a chain of inference that goes beyond its evidence should be questioned.
- [rule] Draw conclusions only as far as the evidence supports, and do not theorize beyond the data. When: deducing from physical traces. Why: unsupported leaps make reasoning wrong.
- [rule] Keep gaps in a log visibly empty so players must infer rather than receive false certainty. When: When designing timeline clues.
- [rule] Show players a visible list of open questions and the clues each competing theory fails to explain. When: Designing a mystery that players must solve by reasoning. Why: A visible gap list directs players toward what remains unresolved.
- [rule] Design confrontation options so that an accusation's reaction exposes hidden knowledge, and reward the player for it. When: When designing confrontation or dialogue mechanics in a game. Why: Reactions that reveal knowledge let players advance by reasoning rather than guessing.
- [rule] Do not accuse anyone on a name alone; treat the inference as a hypothesis until other evidence supports it.
- [rule] Ask a witness how they know a claim, since an impression can be thin support for a conclusion. When: A witness states an inference about another person's state of mind. Why: A conclusion resting on impression rather than observation is weakly supported.
- [rule] Hold paper to the light to check for a watermark; a matching watermark links two notes to the same paper stock. When: when linking an unsigned document to a sender or to other documents.
- [rule] Treat an inference drawn from a trace as a hypothesis and check it against other evidence before relying on it. Why: Cluttered scenes produce false traces.
- [rule] Present a conclusion about intent as an inference, and keep it open to revision if the missing item later turns up. When: Concluding from an absence. Why: Inference from absence is weaker than direct proof.
- [rule] A warrant listing several sentences cannot be dated earlier than the last of those sentences; the latest referenced event sets the earliest possible date.
- [rule] Keep observed facts separate from inferences, so a wrong inference can be found and dropped without losing the evidence. Why: mixing them hides which conclusions are weak.
- [rule] Keep a deduction's conclusion to what the facts warrant, stating only the general category they support rather than a specific name. When: A clue points to a set of possible causes. Why: Narrowing to a category is justified; naming one member needs more independent evidence.
- [rule] An outside examiner should work only within the permissions officials grant, and stay inside a partial grant rather than exceeding it. When: when an outsider must work alongside officials who control access. Why: officials' authority limits what can be examined or done.
- [rule] A method of crime narrows the likely motives but is not proof of emotion or intent.
- [rule] Accept a hidden code only if it holds across every item, not from one coincidental match.
- [heuristic] Test a frightening or confidently told account against independent checks before accepting it; vivid, emotional detail can make a sinister reading seem proven. Why: A sinister reading may rest on a wrong premise, and emotionally loaded accounts lead to false threat assessment. (x2)
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's inferences, including beliefs from out of earshot or sight, below direct observations, especially where hedges such as I think or I can't tell mark them. When: when testimony mixes seen events with reasoning, or the witness was out of earshot or sight. Why: Inferences are less reliable than directly perceived events; secondhand knowledge is inference.
- [heuristic] Visible evidence endorsed by experienced staff tends to outweigh a theory built on subtle inference from one remark.
- [heuristic] Witnesses rarely give major revelations, but one faint clue can matter, so collect even weak leads.
- [heuristic] An inference drawn from a purchase needs an independent check before it is treated as proof.
- [heuristic] Build a conclusion about a hidden action from several small facts together, such as an adversary's sudden change, rather than from one observation. When: an adversary's behaviour changes suddenly and the reason is hidden.
- [heuristic] Give a sympathetic NPC a visible injury that contradicts their cover story, so a player who looks closely can catch the discrepancy. When: Designing character clues.
- [heuristic] A single small mismatch is weak evidence; it gains weight only when combined with an independent fact that could explain it.
- [heuristic] Keep an inferred reading of a witness's evasion separate from what the witness has actually stated. Why: evasion suggests but does not prove.
- [heuristic] Physical evidence that fits a gap, such as cut pages matching pasted words, can outweigh moral argument or testimony. When: testimony conflicts with a physical object.
- [heuristic] A tentative match from partial traces is worth using to direct the next inquiry, provided it is not treated as confirmed identity. When: only partial or low-quality traces exist. Why: A tentative lead focuses effort without overstating the evidence.
- [heuristic] Narrow means by asking who could obtain the specific substance or tool without difficulty, such as a prescriber or a person with ready access. When: The method requires a specific substance or tool. Why: Limiting access to the method narrows the suspect pool.
- [heuristic] The weapon or method of a killing can indicate how much forethought the killer had; a brutal improvised method suggests an unplanned act, while a prepared weapon suggests planning. When: The weapon or lack of one is known. Why: Prepared weapons imply planning, while improvised violence suggests a sudden impulse.
- [heuristic] Resolve a reversal by letting documents carry the proof rather than staging a confession scene, so the player assembles the chain of evidence. Why: Assembled evidence feels earned and avoids a single convenient admission.
- [procedure] 1) Establish what was bought and from where. 2) Infer the item's purpose from its type and quantity. 3) Check whether the time available could produce it. 4) Link the purchase to a missing or altered item. 5) Note what remains unexplained. When: when a purchase or supply record may match a missing or altered item.
- [procedure] 1) List each separate fact. 2) For each fact, remove the candidates it rules out. 3) Check that the remaining candidate agrees with every fact. When: when no single clue is conclusive. Why: each independent fact narrows the candidates, so the conclusion rests on several.
- [procedure] 1) Build the accusation from motive, opportunity and means. 2) Question the suspect about a specific physical detail of the scene. 3) Note whether the suspect reveals knowledge that was not public. When: After evidence has narrowed the field of suspects.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the constraints on the people involved, such as secrecy, poverty, tenancy and timing. 2) Consider what a secret or hurried act would require. 3) Check opportunity and legal title. 4) Combine the constraints to narrow the options. 5) State confidence, and raise it only when independent evidence agrees. When: No witness or document records an act, but motive and means can be constrained. Why: Constraints can point to the most probable outcome when direct records are absent.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the expected sound or event. 2) Check the listener's distance, hearing and sleep habits. 3) Only then weigh its absence as evidence. 4) Confirm the inferred route with physical traces. When: When drawing a conclusion from an absent sound, sight or movement. Why: Unverified silence can support a false route.
- [tradeoff] A longer chain of inferences reveals more about a person but adds doubt at each step, so keep each link checkable. When: an object supports several inference steps. Why: each added step can be wrong, weakening the whole conclusion.
- [tradeoff] Responding visibly to a suspected leak alerts the culprit and may forfeit the advantage, while changing a carefully made plan is costly and some changes may be impossible. When: choosing between responses to a leak.
- [pitfall] Witnesses often present an inference from an indirect cue, such as loudness, marks or earlier statements, as if they observed the act. When: when a witness names or describes someone or an event they did not clearly see or hear. Why: Witnesses often do not distinguish their conclusions from their perceptions; indirect cues mislead when treated as observation.
- [pitfall] An observer who forms a theory early, or delivers it confidently, may report the conclusion as something actually seen. When: when an observer forms a theory before examining the evidence, or delivers an inference confidently. Why: Expectation and confident delivery override raw input when reporting.
- [pitfall] Accusations are not proof of guilt: they follow proximity and rivalry, and many accusers without added verification establish nothing. When: when judging whether accused people are guilty. Why: Accusations follow proximity and rivalry as much as conduct; volume adds no proof.
- [pitfall] A well-argued supposition, or treating an accusation as a game, can pass for proven fact; label hypotheses clearly so argument polish is not mistaken for evidence. When: a hypothesis is presented with a strong, detailed case. Why: Coherence of reasoning is easily confused with proof; persuasive performance is not demonstrated fact.
- [pitfall] An untestable claim is not evidence merely because it cannot be disproved, nor proof of a lie; demanding doubters disprove it shifts the burden; physical checks need a verifiable trace. When: only someone's word is available about events that left no trace. Why: Absence of a check leaves the claim unresolved, not false.
- [pitfall] A vivid story that fills evidence gaps, or a lead made significant only by vivid or repeated telling, can be mistaken for proof. When: when reconstructing an unseen person or event from a few traces, or when a lead is vivid or repeated. Why: Narrative detail and repetition feel convincing even when the supporting traces are few or the lead is untrue.
- [pitfall] A partly visible or poorly reproduced detail, such as a cut-off inscription, supports an inference rather than a fact and should be weighed, not treated as proof. Why: A poor reproduction can hide the features needed for identification.
- [pitfall] A perfect match does not prove identity: a forged trace may be copied from the suspect, or one trace copied from the other. When: when a trace seems to match exactly. Why: A perfect match can equally mean one trace was copied from the other.
- [pitfall] Treating an observer's inference from a signal, such as a light or moving shadow, as a direct sighting of the event itself. Why: A signal suggests an event but does not record it.
- [pitfall] Meaning inferred from partly understood speech, such as one repeated word, is provisional and can mislead. When: Speech heard in a language only partly followed.
- [pitfall] Several conclusions may rest only on inference, such as a death by fright or a creature heard but not seen, and they remain unproven without direct evidence. When: when a case depends on unseen causes or unobserved actors.
- [pitfall] A poorly linked cue reveals nothing, so cues must be chosen for a clear connection to the matter being tested. When: Selecting cues for recall tests. Why: Without a meaningful link, the subject has no reason to react.
- [pitfall] Treating an inference as a fact inside a list carries the error forward into every later step that depends on it.
- [pitfall] Linking a sudden new document to a quarrel is an inference, not proof, even when motive and timing line up.
- [pitfall] An anomaly can have an innocent cause not yet discovered, so it must not be read as proof of guilt. When: A physical sign is out of pattern. Why: Unexplained is not the same as culpable.
- [pitfall] A shared meal is weak evidence of intimacy on its own; stronger proof comes from records of private use.
- [pitfall] An accusation made in anger does not count as evidence, and should not stand in for proof of what happened. When: A claim about a weapon or a poisoning is made emotionally without support.
- [pitfall] When authorities assume witnesses are honest, the burden shifts to the accused to explain the witnesses' behavior.
- [pitfall] A procedure can be bent to exclude someone without any explicit vote against them. When: reviewing how a body made a decision.
- [pitfall] Observations that are not truly independent of one another add little confirmation, so the chain should be checked for overlap. When: Several clues are presented as confirmation of one conclusion. Why: Overlapping evidence looks like more support than it actually provides.
- [pitfall] Narrowing suspects by a shared trait, such as formal dress, does not identify the culprit and may still leave many candidates.
- [fact] The prosecution, not the accused, must prove guilt, so an accused can insist that the burden stays with the prosecution.
- [fact] The arrangement test is weaker when experts dispute the physical evidence itself.

## dating evidence
- [behavior] A day-by-day ledger of an NPC's movements makes unexplained gaps visible, letting players notice what the NPC did not account for. When: players review an NPC's recorded movements. Why: Gaps stand out when events are laid out in sequence with their times.
- [behavior] People struggle to fix a past date without a written note, and alarming events further blur the timing. When: a witness is asked when something happened. Why: Without records, memory of dates degrades.
- [behavior] People dismiss a time reading they believe is inaccurate, such as a bell that seems wrong, even when other sources agree with it. When: time sources conflict. Why: a prior belief about one clock overrides the other evidence.
- [rule] Store dated in-world documents, portraits, letters and deeds as quest-log entries so players order them, spot turning points, gaps and contradictions between official and travel records. When: Designing mysteries or investigative quests built from dated records. Why: Visible ordering lets players find contradictions, turning points and gaps themselves. (x2)
- [rule] Store NPC letters and statements as dated versions so players can spot contradictions between letters or with later statements, and detect revisions and retractions as clues. When: Designing NPC dialogue memory or narrative clues where an NPC can change or retract a statement. Why: Dated records make change over time detectable. (x2)
- [rule] Confirm recalled and single-source dates against a second independent record before building a timeline; one error can break every dependent link. When: Building a timeline from recalled or single-source dates. Why: Memory of dates is unreliable, and one record can be mistaken or incomplete. (x2)
- [rule] Log dated household events such as repairs or faults so players can order them, use them as fixed timeline points, and test alibis; such events may later prove decisive. When: Building a timeline the player can inspect. Why: Dated events give players fixed points to reason from; a minor event can anchor the order of other events.
- [rule] Stamp world items with dated, location-based records such as receipts or ledgers, so players can check NPC dialogue against them.
- [rule] Keep dated records in the game world so players can check when a claimed piece of knowledge could have reached a character.
- [rule] Let players assemble dated official returns into a timeline of who was where, supporting alibi checks.
- [rule] Record each statement with its date and attach it to the case file so later readers can see who said what and when. When: When collecting formal testimony. Why: A dated, attached record makes the sequence of statements checkable.
- [rule] Shift NPC dialogue or routine after a key event so players can date when the NPC's attitude turned.
- [rule] Give an elder's account of an old event a date, an age at the time and a stated uncertainty, so the player can weigh it. When: designing NPC testimony about past events. Why: Memories of old events drift, and the player needs cues to judge reliability.
- [rule] Give players a dated case file with entries from several offices, and leave one outcome for a later document they must find.
- [rule] Use dated reversals, such as a town revising its verdict years later, as late-game revelation beats. When: When planning story twists in a long-running timeline. Why: Delayed reversals pay off earlier events.
- [rule] Log threats with dates so players can check whether the misfortune actually followed them. Why: Dated records let players test the sequence instead of accepting it.
- [heuristic] Dated records fix event order, show who was present and who had motive, and can reveal a writer's unstated intentions. When: Investigating presence, opportunity, motive, or a diary or log. Why: Dates create a cross-checkable sequence; entries reveal intentions. (x2)
- [heuristic] Date each in-world journal or diary entry and show its heading, so players can order events and place entries against the events they describe. When: Presenting a story or writing in-world documents through dated records. Why: Dates and headings give context that shapes how the text is read. (x2)
- [heuristic] Compare dates across documents to expose impossible sequences, such as a person shown alive or travelling when a record says otherwise; one inconsistent date marks a cover story's weak point. When: A claim about death, whereabouts, travel or a cover story depends on dates.
- [heuristic] Fix an undated or uncertain recollection by linking it to a memorable event, such as a public holiday or a fault costing a day's trade; confirm with a second witness. When: A witness gives an undated or unsure recollection of a day. Why: Tying a date to a notable event makes recall more reliable.
- [heuristic] Estimate how long an object has been in place from its condition, such as mildew, matting or overgrowth, by comparing it with known growth or decay rates. When: An object is found away from the main scene, or a physical condition is used to date an event. Why: Weathering accumulates over time; a known rate converts condition into elapsed time.
- [heuristic] Estimate unused time from dust depth or decay such as mould: dust builds at a steady rate, so heavy layers mean long neglect, light layers or none mean recent use. When: Estimating how long an object has been unused or unattended. Why: Decay and dust accumulate at roughly known rates, so their state tracks elapsed time.
- [heuristic] Dated repeated incidents can reveal a recurring interval no single event shows; trust the cycle only once exceptions are explained, since an unexplained one may mean the model is wrong. When: A series of incidents may share a hidden schedule. Why: Single events look random; their dates together expose the cycle.
- [heuristic] A date of death earlier than an event can remove a person from consideration as a claimant or heir. When: when ruling out candidates by timeline.
- [heuristic] A dated item written on a day its supposed author was away on public business deserves a second look before that author is credited. When: Candidate author's travel or duties are recorded. Why: The author could not have been present to write or seal it.
- [heuristic] Prefer day-by-day dated records when reconstructing a sequence of events, since undated accounts cannot establish order.
- [heuristic] Later actions reveal earlier knowledge: a group that changes plans before dawn must have learned of the problem during the night.
- [heuristic] When a person claims knowledge of an event, check when that knowledge was first voiced, since it may show whether they could have known it beforehand. When: when a witness's knowledge of a night's event is in question. Why: Knowledge that appears only after the event may have been learned from others.
- [heuristic] Date an object from the condition of what it touched; a snapped but still living stem suggests the object landed recently. When: estimating when an item was placed. Why: living surroundings show little time has passed.
- [heuristic] Date a change in a person's behaviour or mood to when it began, since that onset fixes a point in the timeline; household members often notice it first. When: building a timeline of a suspect's conduct. Why: A change with a known start is an anchor for other events.
- [heuristic] Use a dated sequence of movements to test whether a witness could have been present at a given time. When: checking an alibi or presence claim. Why: Dates make presence testable.
- [heuristic] Verify a stated timeline against independent official records before trusting it, since the claimant's dates may be false. When: A character presents a schedule as fully controlled. Why: Official records register events on their actual dates and can contradict a self-serving account.
- [heuristic] Date a found object from its context, such as the coins it contains or the rulers named in the text. When: when identifying an object from clues alone. Why: Known historical sequences narrow down when an object belongs.
- [heuristic] Judge how recent a scratch or cut is by contrast: fresh damage shows bright, unoxidised material, while old damage has dulled to match the surrounding surface. When: When deciding whether damage happened before or during the current scene. Why: Exposed material darkens and dulls with time and exposure.
- [heuristic] Dated in-game documents can establish a deadline, so a player who notes the cut-off can see why one NPC benefits from an event before it.
- [heuristic] A dated object bounds events: it cannot have reached a place before its date, and its travel time limits when it could have been brought there. When: placing events on a timeline using dated items. Why: physical objects move at limited speeds and cannot predate their date.
- [heuristic] Attach a confidence level to each dated entry, so approximate dates count for less than firm ones. When: building a timeline from uncertain records.
- [heuristic] Contemporaneous letters fix a person's intentions and mood at specific dates, and later statements can be checked against them. When: a victim's own writing is the main record of their state of mind. Why: Writing made at the time records circumstances before any later change.
- [heuristic] A dated item left in a room, such as a tear-off calendar showing a given day, can fix the day a person left.
- [heuristic] Date and identify a building from its construction traces and surveyed plans, ranking specific evidence above local tradition. When: Confirming a surviving structure's age or original occupant. Why: Physical and documentary evidence can be checked; oral stories often cannot.
- [heuristic] Date an undated document by reasoning from where its examination took place and who in the surrounding area is named.
- [heuristic] Ordering dated depositions, votes and orders shows what was owed and known at each moment, and can expose an action as breaking an earlier agreement. When: Checking claims about who owed what, and when.
- [heuristic] Compare a person's stated role against behaviour recorded on the same day, since a claimed role can contradict a dated record. When: a person's public image conflicts with a diary entry.
- [heuristic] Disputed dates can be argued from the season a given month falls in and from the dating conventions of the period. When: Two sources give conflicting dates for an event. Why: Seasonal and period conventions limit which dates are plausible.
- [heuristic] A dated record that matches an undated entry by name, place or event can fix the identity and date of the undated one. When: When a dated primary record exists alongside an undated fragment. Why: Matching shared details links the two entries to the same event.
- [heuristic] Log a faction dispute as dated in-world entries, so contradictions between entries and later claims become clues the player can check. When: designing a readable document trail for a quest. Why: Dates let players sequence events and test claims.
- [heuristic] Dates tied to personal events such as a birthday, a journey, or a death are sturdier in memory than bare numbers. When: When reconstructing dates from recollection. Why: Personal events are more memorable and more likely to be recalled accurately than abstract dates.
- [heuristic] Undisturbed dust on a surface can date marks: marks with no dust over them are recent, because dust had not yet settled on them. When: When the object's history of being undisturbed is known. Why: Dust accumulates over time, so its absence on a mark indicates recency.
- [heuristic] Use a contemporaneous diary or log as the primary source for exact dates wherever one exists. Why: Written records made at the time are more precise than recollection.
- [procedure] 1) Collect every dated entry on the subject. 2) Order them chronologically. 3) Check each against the others for conflicts. 4) Mark gaps and overlaps. 5) Decide which matter for the question. When: Sources are partial or unevenly dated, or claims and alibis are checked against dated entries. Why: Sequence exposes contradictions, gaps and overlaps, showing what was possible and what was disputed.
- [procedure] 1) List each event with its date. 2) Add purchases, absences and arrivals. 3) Check the order of events. 4) Test each claimed cause against the sequence before accepting it. When: a witness reports a cause that must be checked. Why: a sequence shows whether a supposed cause came before or after the effect it explains.
- [procedure] 1) Examine period-specific letterforms and conventions before reading the content. 2) Estimate an age range, ideally within about a decade. 3) Compare the estimate with any date written on the page. 4) Record any gap as a finding. When: A document's age or authenticity matters and a period reference is available. Why: Physical conventions change over time, and reading content first can bias the dating.
- [procedure] 1) Recall the scene's state at the last check. 2) Compare it with the current state. 3) Treat any object that has appeared since then as recent. When: the timing of an object is the key question.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the date a letter was written with its arrival date. 2) Estimate transit delay from its routing. 3) Check the writer's stated expectations against that timeline. When: Using dated documents to fix a sequence of events. Why: Indirect routing can make arrival far later than sending.
- [procedure] 1) Name the witnesses to the document's creation. 2) Ask each for the time. 3) Offer a candidate time and see whether witnesses confirm or correct it. 4) Narrow the date to the window all accounts support. When: when a document's date is uncertain.
- [procedure] 1) Collect dated records such as orders, dispatches and appointments. 2) Order them by date. 3) Check whether preparation predates the event an alibi covers. 4) Treat earlier preparation as evidence the alibi was arranged. When: an alibi covers a journey or event. Why: Dated paper trails can show that a plan began before the apparent alibi.
- [procedure] 1) Date the record. 2) Match its date to the moment of a key event. 3) Use it to establish what a person was reading or knew at that time. 4) Check the content against an intact copy. When: A dated document links to a key moment. Why: Dates tie documents to events and reveal what people knew.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the witness's account as a sequence of dated facts. 2) Restate the whole account in order. 3) Let listeners check the restated order against the facts.
- [procedure] 1) List each dated act or statement. 2) Note its speaker. 3) Mark which voices or parties are absent at each point. When: When several dated documents must show how opinion changed. Why: Ordering the record reveals trends and silences.
- [procedure] 1) Record the date each document can support. 2) Order events so no document precedes an event it refers to. 3) Check each date against an independent record. 4) Use a third party's diary to fix contested days. When: Dates on letters, diaries, warrants and reprieves are the main clues. Why: Ordered dates expose impossible sequences.
- [procedure] 1) Collect indirect signs of time, such as temperature, unlit fires and completed or unfinished tasks. 2) Compare them against the routine of the person. 3) Estimate the death window from the mismatch. When: When rebuilding when a death occurred without a firm medical time. Why: Indirect environmental and routine signs can bound the hour when direct evidence is weak.
- [tradeoff] Dated sequences can reveal a rival's escalation campaign that single incidents hide, yet ordering events can make a trend look inevitable when it was not. When: Attributing rival hostility favours the sequence view; presenting a chronology as progression calls for caution. Why: Sequence turns scattered events into a pattern, but also suggests direction and causation that may not exist. (x2)
- [pitfall] Establish a baseline before dating marks or dust: misreading old dust as recent, or recent handling as old, misleads conclusions about who entered. When: Interpreting footprints, marks, dust or disturbed ground. Why: Mark age decides which event produced them; dust baselines must be known before disturbances can be dated.
- [pitfall] A narrator's dates may be accurate while the account of intent is not, so dated facts and claimed motives should be assessed separately. When: Evaluating a first-person account. Why: Accurate timing does not guarantee accurate reasons.
- [pitfall] An estimate off by more than a decade signals either a flawed method or a different document than assumed. When: Comparing a dating estimate with a stated date. Why: Large gaps indicate a problem in the method or in the document's identity.
- [pitfall] A date error may be innocent, so verify it with another source before reading guilt into it.
- [pitfall] A dating conclusion depends on the assumed growth rate and on the trace moving at a steady pace; check both before trusting it.
- [pitfall] A date alone does not confirm content, so check the wording against how the event must have worked.
- [pitfall] Keeping a position number in memory while counting is fragile; record positions with physical markers instead.
- [fact] A dated message fixes a person's travel and timeline, giving a checkable point in a sequence of events.
- [fact] A dated, step-by-step record shows who was summoned, what they were asked, when they replied, and how they answered. When: reconstructing a community dispute from documents. Why: Sequence and dates make each step checkable.
- [fact] Without a clock, a steady bodily rhythm such as pulse can be counted to estimate elapsed minutes. When: when no clock is at hand.

## forgery and tampering
- [definition] A witnessed transfer is an exchange of an object before a third party, whose presence creates a record independent of either principal's account. Why: A third-party record can settle later disputes about who held the object and on what terms.
- [mechanism] Residues such as mud or puddles that dry over time let the game estimate when an action happened; decay states show how long an object stayed in place, revealing staging. When: When a game records residue or props whose state changes over time. Why: The rate of change gives a time reference for the event; condition reveals how long an object was there.
- [mechanism] A copy of a person's trace can be made from an impression taken earlier, such as a seal pressed into soft material, and later transferred to a scene. When: When a trace matches a suspect too neatly. Why: A stored impression lets someone reproduce the trace at a time they choose.
- [mechanism] A forgery mechanic can let a player copy a seal, key impression, or handprint from a source item, with the copy passing inspection unless a hidden deviation exists. When: Designing forgery or counterfeiting mechanics. Why: Hidden deviations give careful inspection a payoff without making copies obvious.
- [mechanism] A forged document delivered through a trusted person can establish a false identity, because the target accepts it through a channel they already trust and cannot check it independently. When: A false identity must enter a household or group. Why: Trusted delivery and lack of an independent check let the claim pass.
- [mechanism] Destroying a document in front of witnesses makes the act public and removes the paper as a later source of evidence, while witnesses can later vouch for its loss. When: a party wants a document gone and controls how its story is told.
- [mechanism] A weakened heart makes a dose of an anaesthetic more likely to be fatal, which explains an outcome without proving who administered it. When: When a medical cause of death is consistent with an agent but the agent's administrator is unknown. Why: Pre-existing weakness changes the lethal threshold, so the cause of death can be explained without identifying the person responsible.
- [mechanism] A pencil with broken shavings and a worn tip shows hurried work and the need to repair the tool mid-task.
- [mechanism] A forged record can be made by changing a few words that pass a quick reading, and the forgery often leaves a trace in another witness's account. When: when a document passes through a suspect or third party. Why: Small edits escape casual checking, but other accounts may not match.
- [mechanism] A forged message signed with a trusted name can lure a target to a chosen place, and its success depends more on the forger knowing who is trusted than on the message's wording. When: The target must be moved quickly to a specific location. Why: People act on urgent messages from names they trust without checking them.
- [mechanism] Volatile substances evaporate, so a long delay before examination can erase the trace, and a small dose may leave no detectable sign.
- [mechanism] Attempts to buy a valuable object make its worth known, which can prompt a forger to make a copy. When: when a buyer or rival shows interest in a treasure. Why: public valuation signals a market for copies.
- [mechanism] Discovering a forgery can overturn the group's assumptions and expose a party they trusted as the source of the copy. When: when a treasure is revealed to be fake.
- [mechanism] A threat against a witness should flag the case and make the threatening character a suspect in the investigation. When: when a game has witnesses and intimidation events.
- [mechanism] A poorly concealed trace such as a scorch mark or blood trail can carry information about who tried to remove it and with what tools. When: Designing hidden-cover-up clues in a game world. Why: Imperfect concealment leaves readable traces of the actor's method.
- [mechanism] Attaching a timing window to tampering evidence lets the player narrow down when the tampering happened. When: Designing investigation puzzles with time-based evidence. Why: A time bound lets players eliminate suspects by alibi.
- [behavior] A forger may produce a clumsy, easily detected forgery so that it is discarded and an earlier valid document stands. When: A forged document appears alongside an earlier genuine one. Why: Exposure of the forgery removes it, which can leave the earlier document as the controlling version.
- [rule] Tag in-world documents with source and editing, and store them as dated objects with occasional conflicts, so players judge reliability and build a timeline by cross-checking claims. When: Designing in-world documents or a mystery-driven quest. Why: Source tags let players weigh claims; cross-checking makes the player an active reader of evidence. (x2)
- [rule] Give forged or swapped items a precise original state with detectable differences, so players who compare them with the original can spot the substitution. When: Designing a substitution or trap quest. Why: Detectable forgeries reward attention.
- [rule] Give forged documents physical details, such as mismatched stock, typeface, print, letterhead or trimmed edges, that point to a visitable source device or place, so checks narrow suspects. When: A document is the main lead in an investigation or quest. Why: Physical traces link the document to its production source, so checking them shrinks the candidate pool.
- [rule] Make a broken or damaged unique item a lock-and-key clue: players search the level for its missing piece or match its damage to a door or suspect's knowledge. When: Designing physical clues that connect to locations or characters. Why: Matching a distinctive feature to its source is a satisfying deduction.
- [rule] Mark which in-world documents each report draws on, and count reports that share one origin as a single witness when players weigh evidence. When: building a case file of in-game reports.
- [rule] Let a forged quest note be contradicted by an offhand remark from a background NPC, opening a new branch. When: when designing forged or altered quest material. Why: Background detail gives players a way to detect the forgery.
- [rule] Place in-world reference books, chronicles or family registers that the player can read to uncover a historical grudge behind an NPC. When: Designing clue content that explains NPC motives.
- [rule] Let an inn register record every traveller's name so players who check it for a false alias can find a suspect who used a different identity in each town. When: Designing traveller records in a game world. Why: Registers give players a searchable trail across locations.
- [rule] Let characters leave fibres of a set colour on objects they snag, so the player can match an item to a suspect.
- [rule] Record change dates in an inheritance or contract system so the player can check whether a change came before or after a crime. When: Designing a documentary inheritance or ownership mechanic. Why: Timing lets players test whether a change could be a motive.
- [rule] Give the game an official summary of an event that omits one detail, so players who visit the scene can find the missing trace and correct the record. When: when designing in-world records or reports.
- [rule] Let environmental clues decay over time, rewarding players who investigate quickly. Why: Time pressure makes early investigation valuable.
- [rule] Let abandoned routes leave the playable map but persist as plowed boundaries, fence lines or old labels that players can rediscover.
- [rule] Offer a quest with a possible feigned death, leaving the player to decide whether the witness is genuine.
- [heuristic] Documents dated after the event they order or report expose later insertions or forgery; papers were sometimes procured later to support a verdict, and readers consulting them miss this. When: Accepting a complete-looking archive as a whole, or checking a suspect document.
- [heuristic] Give authoritative-looking forged letters checkable errors, such as a postmark or seal conflicting with the date, route, named place, handwriting, signature, paper or form, so observant players can catch them. When: Designing a forged document clue. Why: Verifiable details reward careful players and keep the puzzle fair.
- [heuristic] Plant a gap or discrepancy in a document timeline, such as a blank day or one guest where two were expected, so players must find the missing record elsewhere. When: Designing a readable document as a clue source.
- [heuristic] Give forged notes a recurring habitual quirk, such as a letter form or machine trace, that players match against known samples, since disguises hide obvious traits but rarely habits. When: Designing a forgery reveal or a puzzle around a forged document. Why: Repeated habits give players a checkable pattern.
- [heuristic] A clause written in smaller hand and fainter ink than the surrounding text may be a later addition, so check ink and hand.
- [heuristic] Traces seen by many observers at once are more credible than traces seen by a single party. When: weighing physical evidence in a case. Why: Shared observation is harder to fabricate or misremember than individual observation.
- [heuristic] Stationery such as a letterhead ties an object to a past source, and that old relationship can explain how a person came to hold it. When: the paper bears a firm's or source's marks. Why: past dealings can explain possession long after the link ended.
- [heuristic] Give forged documents plausible sources, dates, names and an intermediary, so players must judge the chain of trust against other evidence.
- [heuristic] A body that is wrapped or tied suggests it was carried from elsewhere rather than harmed at the spot where it lies. When: a body is found bundled or bound. Why: bundling is a sign of transport.
- [heuristic] Letterhead details such as a crest, place of writing and date can indicate a writer's rank, location and time. When: A letter carries printed or written header details. Why: Stationery reflects the writer's status and circumstances.
- [heuristic] Two drinking vessels set out for a guest, with none of the host's drink present, point to a visitor rather than a resident. When: reading drinking vessels in a room. Why: set-out vessels show who was expected.
- [heuristic] Tracks showing no wear on heels or soles, or new-looking heels, are unlikely to come from independent walkers and may signal staging.
- [heuristic] An item that routine staff checks would have caught or handled differently can indicate it was planted to mislead. When: an item's presence does not fit normal practice. Why: fabricated evidence often ignores routine procedure.
- [heuristic] A forger NPC behind a copy can serve as a later reveal that changes the quest's objective. When: when designing a quest around a valuable object. Why: a discovered forger reframes the goal.
- [heuristic] Give each NPC a writing sample so players can match an anonymous note to its writer through in-game comparison. When: Generating written clues. Why: Comparison turns a note into a deduction task.
- [heuristic] Track which characters walk where so their footwear carries plausible traces that point players toward the route they took.
- [heuristic] A journal item can carry a culprit's plans and misjudgments about other NPCs, letting players verify a reveal from a primary source.
- [heuristic] A forgery or crafting mechanic can require a reference record and a specific tool, with a chain of steps such as photograph, copy, and press. When: When designing a crafted-forgery system. Why: A multi-step chain gives the player a meaningful process to solve.
- [heuristic] Let a player frame an NPC, and make the frame hold only if the NPC's authority incentives and a physical match the player can test both support it. When: when designing a framing mechanic. Why: the frame then depends on checkable conditions.
- [heuristic] Compare the layers of a forged item; a detail missing from one layer but present in another can expose the forger.
- [procedure] 1) Establish who had seen the true handwriting sample. 2) Examine the forgery for details only a non-viewer would get wrong, such as a misspelled signature; forgers copy visible script but often miss spelling. 3) Match the error to that list. When: when a written clue could have been produced by more than one person.
- [procedure] 1) Check each visible feature, such as a stamp or postmark. 2) Cross-check the dates and routes they imply. 3) Compare handwriting against an available specimen. Forgers who anticipate single checks are caught only by linked checks. When: Verifying a document that claims a distant origin or specific author, or rests on one visible proof. Why: Each faked feature answers one check, so only cross-checking the chain behind them exposes the forgery.
- [procedure] 1) Compare entry dates and density across the document. 2) Check for missing leaves and frayed or pruned edges. 3) Check whether a stretch shares one uniform style, suggesting a single writing session. When: when a written record may have been altered. Why: edits leave gaps in dates, physical damage, and uniform writing.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the expected source of the trace. 2) Check whether that source is absent. 3) See whether the pattern varies as one source's movement would. 4) Check for a means of imitation, such as freshly altered objects. When: A trace looks ordinary but may be fabricated. Why: A missing source plus a source-like pattern points to imitation.
- [procedure] 1) State what a display or arrangement should contain. 2) Compare the actual contents with that expectation. 3) For any gap, inspect its fixing for signs of hasty removal. 4) Ask why that specific item would be taken. When: when a display, inventory or regular arrangement should be complete. Why: a gap in an expected arrangement can be evidence.
- [procedure] Reconstruct a tampering sequence in order: select the items, open an entry point, remove the original contents, insert the substance, refill, reseal, and restore the packaging. When: physical evidence suggests an item was altered after it was sealed. Why: ordering the steps shows how the act could have been carried out.
- [tradeoff] A feigned harmless, flustered or weaker persona makes targets underestimate visitors, reveal more and speak freely, but an overplayed act can be noticed. When: An investigator or character hides capability or adopts a gentle, scattered manner around a suspect. Why: People relax around someone who seems unthreatening or unobservant.
- [tradeoff] Adopt a false role when officialdom is blocked or targets would refuse an identified officer, but avoid it where it exposes the investigator to legal or ethical risk. When: When the official approach is blocked or a false identity could expose the investigator to legal or ethical risk.
- [pitfall] Detecting a forgery does not identify its author or beneficiary, so combine it with evidence of motive or a second clue. When: Investigating who produced a forged document. Why: Knowing a document is false does not identify its author or beneficiary; detection and attribution are separate steps.
- [pitfall] A forged message or document is exposed by a simple check at its claimed source, since forgers rely on no one consulting the original; plans must allow verification. When: A decoy message is used to move a character, or a forged document is circulated. Why: Easy verification undoes the deception.
- [pitfall] A message that appears to confirm a threat can be fabricated even when its details are accurate, so a convincing message is not proof of genuineness. When: a single message drives a serious decision. Why: a forger may have researched accurate details.
- [pitfall] Assuming a forgery requires the original object is wrong, since a copy can be produced from a printed record. Why: Access to a record can be enough to fake a trace.
- [pitfall] A stamp or mark identifies a location, not a person, so it must be linked to someone before it is treated as a lead.
- [pitfall] Handwriting and enclosed objects can be forged or taken from someone else, so a physical document alone cannot prove its source. When: Relying on a document or enclosed item as proof. Why: Imitation and theft break the link between the physical item and its true author.
- [pitfall] Washing or disturbing a surface can erase or mislead traces, so a clean area may hide where someone walked. When: When a scene has been cleaned or handled after an event. Why: Cleaning removes the impressions that would otherwise record movement.
- [pitfall] Packaging shows where the wrapping material came from, not who wrapped the goods or when, and a discarded item may have been passed on.
- [pitfall] A matching print can produce a false match that appears to implicate someone the investigator wants to trust, so matches need independent confirmation. When: A print match points toward a favored suspect. Why: Investigator bias can make a weak match seem decisive.
- [pitfall] A fingerprint impossible to produce by pressing all digits at once suggests forgery, since a forger may press each finger separately to match a record. When: when examining a print matched to a suspect. Why: Simultaneous impression mechanics expose a print assembled from separate pressings.
- [fact] A calling card taken from a real person can be used to implicate that person further, since it links the impersonator's actions to a real identity. When: An impersonation plot needs to shift suspicion onto a real individual. Why: Authentic-looking props make a false trail more convincing.
- [fact] A well-made forgery can be so exact that its maker cannot tell it from the original, even when they are placed side by side. Why: Appearance alone cannot prove a trace is genuine.
- [fact] A document written on a standard printed form is easier to forge quickly, since the template is widely available. When: Assessing how hard a document is to forge. Why: Common templates reduce the effort required.

## lies and deception
- [model] Model interrogation as gated questions, where some answers unlock only after a fact is established elsewhere.
- [mechanism] Offering a fair hearing, protection or immunity to a candid suspect or witness facing consequences draws out motives and accounts they would otherwise withhold. Why: Fear of consequences makes full disclosure risky until terms are offered; those who expect fair treatment volunteer reasons they would hide.
- [mechanism] Literally accurate statements, such as a bare phrase about nothing left undone, can conceal a key action and leave a false overall impression when read in context.
- [mechanism] In an interrogation mini-game, the NPC's response can depend on which evidence the player presents, and its denials can reveal what it knows.
- [mechanism] A partner's own exposure can serve as leverage, since someone who would be exposed by speaking has reason to stay silent.
- [mechanism] Let players expose a propaganda document by comparing it with an original record or the scene it describes.
- [mechanism] When a found material does not match what a person claims to have used, the item likely came from another source, possibly another person. When: a claimed use is compared with residue found on the item.
- [mechanism] A confess-for-leniency branch changes a suspect's later behaviour and the case outcome, so the choice should carry lasting consequences.
- [mechanism] Witness dialogue can be made fallible, so an NPC misremembers a detail such as a room unless the player passes a perception check.
- [mechanism] NPC dialogue can carry an explanation that a later observation contradicts, letting the player catch a lie without a direct accusation. When: when a stated explanation can be checked against a later event. Why: Letting the player spot the contradiction rewards attention without requiring an explicit accusation.
- [behavior] When an offer is questioned, a suspect who shifts to a new offer shows that the plan is being improvised. When: A suspect is pressed on a gesture.
- [behavior] A suspect who knows he is exposed will watch the people who threaten him, check their outgoing messages, and destroy evidence. When: The suspect has learned that someone is closing in. Why: Exposure gives the suspect a reason to protect himself.
- [behavior] A guilty party may reframe the act with softer, mitigating language, insisting on terms that cast it as justified. When: a suspect confesses but resists the word for the act.
- [behavior] Witnesses answer the sense they infer from a question rather than its literal wording, so a truthful denial can still hide a fact. When: when an NPC denies something that physical evidence contradicts. Why: People filter questions through what they think the asker wants.
- [behavior] Loose talk in a casual setting often reveals rivals, disputes and habits beyond the topic that was asked about. When: a suspect or acquaintance talks freely over a meal or drink.
- [behavior] A confession made in mockery is often retracted at once, so it needs support from other clues to hold weight. When: A speaker admits something and then laughs it off. Why: Retreating into jest lets the speaker deny the admission.
- [behavior] People whose knowledge others cannot follow are often suspected of sorcery, because their skill looks unexplained. When: a learned person's methods are hidden from the community. Why: Opacity invites supernatural explanation.
- [behavior] When questioned about a visitor's absence, a guilty party offers a false explanation, such as a departure aboard a passing vessel. When: when questioned about someone who has gone missing. Why: to account for the absence without admitting involvement.
- [behavior] Captors who cannot verify a concealed threat tend to comply when a visible cue makes the threat appear real. When: When a captive makes a threat that cannot be checked. Why: An unverifiable threat backed by a visible cue is treated as genuine.
- [rule] Do not treat a detected lie as proof of guilt; treat it as a lead needing corroboration, and weigh innocent explanations such as fear first. When: a statement is contradicted by evidence. Why: Contradictions can have innocent explanations; fear and embarrassment produce lies without guilt.
- [rule] Make NPC claims checkable against neutral scene evidence, such as scorch marks, mud prints, weapon range, inventory items or records, so players can separate fact from bias and catch lies. When: designing NPC testimony or dialogue with factual statements. Why: Verifiable claims let players weigh accounts against evidence; neutral evidence separates fact from bias.
- [rule] Do not accept a confession alone; verify it against objects, records, map and other witnesses, and author confessions with checkable details so players earn the truth. When: Designing an NPC confession in a game. Why: Checkable claims make the player's verification the path to the truth.
- [rule] Flag testimony from a witness or accuser with a personal stake, since anger or reputation distorts it, and require an independent source before acting on it. When: a witness or accuser has a personal stake in the outcome, or an NPC's claim benefits them. Why: Emotion and reputation distort what is reported.
- [rule] Keep sensitive material and trap staging out of observable channels and openings, since outsiders who see contents or setup expose the plan before it is sprung. When: A prepared ambush room has openings to the outside. Why: Observation along the way exposes contents; visible preparation exposes the plan before it is sprung.
- [rule] Let the player bluff a suspect with a note showing knowledge, unlocking a confession branch in dialogue. When: Designing dialogue puzzles where the player holds hidden knowledge. Why: Showing knowledge rewards investigation and opens new dialogue paths.
- [rule] Use overheard monologue as a dialogue trigger, letting the player collect fragments that combine into a theory.
- [rule] Design dialogue so a lie-detecting pretext triggers a different response, rather than a plain refusal. Why: A changed response keeps the conversation useful.
- [rule] Let NPCs answer literally so that players must ask precise questions to get information.
- [rule] Let an NPC admit one lie while insisting on a core truth, and let players check each detail against world records. When: when designing a suspect's story.
- [rule] Give a faction NPC a fixed premise, and let the player expose it by finding a fact the premise cannot explain. When: designing a cult or faction with a belief that drives its actions. Why: Players can defeat a closed belief system only with evidence it cannot absorb.
- [rule] Let a false informer be exposed later, with consequences for the NPCs they falsely named.
- [rule] Keep a cover story consistent with earlier statements, so it fits what the opponent has already heard.
- [rule] Let in-world judges sometimes ignore contradicting evidence, so players learn the system is biased and must seek independent proof. When: when designing a judgment system in a mystery. Why: ignored evidence teaches players to verify independently.
- [rule] Feign distress or an ailment only when the performance can be made convincing to those watching. When: Using a staged illness to gain access. Why: A weak performance draws suspicion rather than cover.
- [rule] An NPC can withhold information until the player meets a trust or favor condition, and the refusal can be logged.
- [rule] Store partial confessions as flags so that a later denial can be checked against them automatically. When: when an NPC makes a partial admission. Why: stored flags expose inconsistent later denials.
- [heuristic] Mix opinion with fact, or one true and one false fact, in dialogue so players must cross-check claims against other evidence. When: designing dialogue for a deceptive or unreliable character. Why: Sorting mixed statements becomes a rewarding task. (x2)
- [heuristic] Ask why a witness misleads: a false account where refusal was possible signals concealment; a lie about one fact often protects someone present, so ask who it shields. When: a witness gives a false account instead of declining, or misstates one fact about a visit or event. Why: People lie most readily about facts that would expose someone they want to protect.
- [heuristic] Gate information behind a bluff or implied threat, and let a failed bluff trigger a clear consequence such as a cooperation penalty, locked door or guard response.
