When: Designing a dialogue system with pressure options. Why: A penalty for failed bluffs makes the choice a risk, not a free reveal; the outcome feels earned.
- [heuristic] Concede a smaller, defensible fact so an opponent believes they have seen the whole picture, while the real line of inquiry stays hidden. When: when the opponent has something to lose from exposure and will accept a plausible explanation. Why: a satisfied opponent may stop probing.
- [heuristic] A competitor who lets the opponent win early and then wins quickly lowers the opponent's guard and gains the advantage. When: Designing an opponent in a game of skill. Why: A feigned concession relaxes the opponent before the decisive move.
- [heuristic] When a suspect denies knowing a fact that the displayed evidence implies, treat the denial as a sign they do know it.
- [heuristic] Model a suspect's lie as an attempt to avoid a larger danger, so a player who finds the lie can also find its reason. Why: A motivated lie gives the player a path from contradiction to motive.
- [heuristic] A plan that requires many exposed steps with no clear gain is suspicious and deserves closer scrutiny. When: an account requires a long, risky sequence of actions. Why: Each exposed step is another chance to be noticed, so the sequence is hard to justify.
- [heuristic] Challenge a witness's lie by reasoning about who else could have acted; the logic can expose the lie even without direct proof. When: the witness's account depends on who else was present.
- [heuristic] Expose a concealed truth when a false account would wrongly blame an innocent person by name in lasting form; stay silent when the falsehood only praises the dead. When: Deciding whether to reveal a memorialised falsehood. Why: Harm to the innocent outweighs harm to a reputation.
- [heuristic] A habitual liar's additional falsehood reveals little, so the lie-as-tell signal works only against a clear honesty baseline. When: when a character often lies. Why: without a baseline, one more lie breaks no pattern.
- [heuristic] When a suspect is caught in one false detail, re-examine every other statement they gave, since a lie about one detail weakens the rest. When: A suspect's account contains a proven falsehood. Why: A fabricated detail suggests the other claims may also be constructed.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC's theory be wrong in a checkable way so the player can disprove it with a found item.
- [heuristic] Test whether a claim survives its strongest alternative explanation before treating it as established. When: Weighing an inference drawn from physical or testimonial evidence. Why: An inference that an alternative undermines is weakened, as with wound placement that a second cause can produce.
- [heuristic] Offer a clear-the-room dialogue option that removes bystanders before a sensitive exchange, and let persistent questions resist topic changes so NPCs cannot dodge them. When: Designing dialogue for sensitive conversations. Why: Removing observers and persisting questions preserve the focus of the exchange.
- [heuristic] Dialogue can branch on reaction tags such as pale or halting speech, not only on yes or no answers, and a tag can be tied to a secondary fear the player must verify. When: Designing dialogue that reads NPC emotional state. Why: Richer tags let the player interpret NPC behaviour and avoid acting on a single misleading signal.
- [procedure] 1) Identify each odd event. 2) Ask what it requires and who gains from it. 3) Run a test that exposes whether the event is staged. When: A case contains several staged or misleading events.
- [procedure] 1) Show the suspect proof that you know their past. 2) Lay out the evidence you hold. 3) Ask for the one missing fact. 4) State the deal and its alternative plainly. When: the suspect knows a needed fact and the evidence against them is strong.
- [procedure] 1) Identify checkable figures, dates and claims in a witness's account. 2) Compare each with sources the witness does not control. 3) Flag disagreements for follow-up. When: a witness's account includes verifiable details. Why: Independent sources expose claims the witness may have invented.
- [tradeoff] An open accusation warns a suspect and may force early action, while feigned ignorance lets them act on a false belief but risks surprise and exposure. When: A direct accusation would warn the suspect before evidence is secured.
- [tradeoff] A long closing speech adds moral and emotional weight but slows pacing and can dull the final beat.
- [pitfall] A bluff holds only until tested: an unexecuted threat or a single check by the opponent exposes it and reveals the questioner's limits.
- [pitfall] An exposed bluff or easily checked pretext makes the suspect more guarded for the rest of questioning, so avoid cover stories the subject can verify. When: the subject has ready access to verify the claim. Why: exposure gives the suspect a reason to resist and conceal.
- [pitfall] Accusations and pressed testimony often mix true and invented details; label and check each claim piece by piece, since speakers and listeners can lose track of what is real. Why: The lure can confuse its own user as well as its target; stress blends accurate details with self-serving claims.
- [pitfall] Emotionally loaded framing or hypotheticals can make a witness defensive and end answers, or push them toward the investigator's theory so it confirms a guess rather than reveals truth.
- [pitfall] A bluff about knowledge can be exposed, and a suspect who sees through it may then answer falsely to avoid trouble.
- [pitfall] A bluff about authority can be exposed later, and the cooperation it earned is then lost along with the investigator's credibility. Why: the witness learns the claim was false.
- [pitfall] A withheld plan can leave a subordinate exposed to suspicion if he is followed.
- [pitfall] A partial claim that is false and easy to expose will be called a bluff, so the interviewer must be ready for correction. When: Making a partial claim that the other party can check.
- [pitfall] Reading stated affection literally misses a letter's real purpose, which may be financial or manipulative. When: A warm letter seems to express friendship. Why: Affection is often used as a means to a practical end.
- [pitfall] A failed trap can expose its planner, so a prepared fallback explanation is often needed for a plan that might not work. When: when a hidden plan depends on a device working correctly. Why: failure leaves evidence that points back to the planner.
- [pitfall] Stating the pressure method openly lets a sharp suspect recognise it and refuse to react.
- [pitfall] People who seem clear and open can be deceptive in depth, so an observer's confidence in reading them is itself a warning sign.
- [pitfall] A lie can be a cover for an innocent reason, so a detected falsehood does not by itself reveal the motive behind it. Why: a lie signals concealment, not its purpose.
- [fact] Marks in exposed places, such as sand, damp ground and fallen leaves, are erased by wind, rain and tidal action.
- [fact] A failed physical check does not prove a witness lied; it shows only that the sign is weak evidence.

## theories and conclusions
- [mechanism] Each new conviction or arrest adds names to the list of suspects, so an accusation process can feed on itself and widen steadily. When: when accused people are asked to name accomplices. Why: Each verdict supplies new names that prompt further charges.
- [mechanism] When a character's own careless act triggers the worst threat, stakes rise because the danger traces back to a choice the character made. When: a character's imprudent action drives a crisis.
- [mechanism] A correction written later than the date of the page it sits on shows that the record was revised after the events it describes. When: checking whether a compiled record is contemporaneous. Why: Later insertions can carry earlier page dates.
- [mechanism] Model a confession as a revisable statement, so a later retraction changes game state instead of deleting the earlier line. When: Implementing confessions that can be withdrawn. Why: Keeping both versions preserves the history of the case.
- [behavior] A reasoner with a firm conclusion tends to examine new contrary evidence closely before reversing their view. When: a new document contradicts a strong prior belief. Why: certainty raises the bar for revision.
- [behavior] Stating that one fact may overturn a theory keeps suspects and readers guessing, since the theory is presented as provisional. When: an investigator holds a theory openly. Why: a provisional theory keeps others uncertain.
- [behavior] A witness who begins a question, stops and corrects it may reveal knowledge they have not admitted, and the gap can be completed to expose it.
- [behavior] A witness first confronted with a physical object often revises an earlier account. When: a witness is shown an object that ties to their story. Why: Denial becomes harder when the object contradicts the first version.
- [behavior] Conflicting public theories of a theft each act as a lead, and only the one that fits the physical record survives checking. When: Several competing explanations circulate about one event. Why: False leads are cheap to produce, but physical evidence constrains which story can be true.
- [rule] Revise or drop a working explanation once a new clue or account contradicts it, rather than defending it against later evidence. When: when a new clue or account does not fit the current explanation. Why: Facts outrank the theory built before them; a theory built on early clues can fail the next one, and clinging to it misleads the investigator.
- [rule] Treat a timeline as a provisional hypothesis: it may fit while resting on unverified steps, so revise it when new evidence arrives or awkward timings remain unexplained. When: when reconstructing events from records. Why: New evidence can overturn an order that looked settled.
- [rule] Mark motive-based conclusions provisional until questioning or evidence confirms them, since a motive is not proof; a delegated brief is not established fact. Why: A motive is not proof.
- [rule] Let expert NPC opinions be revised after the player challenges them with new evidence. When: when an expert NPC states a firm conclusion. Why: Revisable opinions reward players for pressing with evidence.
- [rule] Offer the player a way to revise a conclusion, such as a second witness or an object to inspect, so that an early judgment can be corrected. When: Designing a case the player can reopen. Why: Allowing correction keeps the investigation open and rewards further checking.
- [rule] Keep a hypothesis open to revision, since a new fact such as a stain or a message can overturn a theory built on older facts.
- [rule] Treat each theory as provisional until it has been tested against evidence. When: Forming an investigative conclusion. Why: Untested theories can be wrong.
- [rule] Treat an inference from a clue as a lead that may point somewhere, not as proof, and confirm it with a separate test before acting on it. When: A deduction rests on a single clue or a single witness. Why: A plausible inference can be wrong, and a second check guards against acting on it.
- [rule] Keep working assumptions about identity or motive provisional, and do not treat them as settled before confirmation, since that prejudices the inquiry.
- [rule] Do not treat an exclusion as final until the access evidence behind it has been checked.
- [rule] Do not treat a neat alibi as proof of innocence until its travel and timing facts have been checked against independent sources.
- [rule] When new evidence contradicts a character's hypothesized role, reassign the role, such as puppet, accomplice or mastermind, rather than keeping the original assignment. When: Tracking suspects' roles in a mystery. Why: Roles are hypotheses, and contradicting evidence shows the earlier role does not fit.
- [rule] Carry out the critical checks yourself rather than delegating them, since the conclusion is only as strong as the checks behind it.
- [rule] When a contradiction persists, revise the theory or add an outside agent that explains it, rather than discarding the observed fact. When: A reconstruction cannot explain a fact without extra factors. Why: Keeping the fact and changing the story preserves the evidence.
- [rule] Make an NPC's arrest or suspicion provisional, so a player-supplied alibi can clear them and release them. Why: A wrongly held suspect should be releasable once the alibi appears.
- [rule] Hold a witness's own theory as provisional, since it may serve that witness's interests.
- [rule] Let a motive label be revised as understanding grows, updating the player's view without contradicting earlier clues.
- [rule] Do not adopt a neat theory until evidence supports each link; keep several explanations open until evidence narrows them. When: Several suspects or explanations remain possible.
- [heuristic] A theory that fits neatly, or appears to prove itself, still needs each assumption and piece of evidence checked; a sense of fit is not confirmation.
- [heuristic] Revise an official's conclusion when a later physical report arrives, since new evidence can overturn an early, comfortable reading.
- [heuristic] New evidence, such as spare plain clothing, should revise a working theory rather than simply confirm it.
- [heuristic] When a found object contradicts the working explanation, revise the explanation rather than forcing the evidence to fit it. When: a scene object does not match the expected story. Why: a contradicting object often reveals a second story.
- [heuristic] Ask questions that let the witness name their own wishes or choices, rather than leading them to a predetermined answer. When: Eliciting an opinion or intention from a witness. Why: Self-stated answers are more reliable than answers the questioner suggested.
- [heuristic] Entertain a suspect's rival explanation provisionally, without endorsing it, to lower their guard.
- [heuristic] An act that works against the culprit's own aims, such as a noisy weapon for a silent escape, lowers a theory's standing without disproving it. Why: Real offenders sometimes act oddly, so implausibility weakens a theory without ruling it out.
- [heuristic] Let a late reversal reduce certainty without fully closing doubt, so the ending stays open to checking. When: the reversal overturns the answer but cannot yet be confirmed.
- [heuristic] Hold a provisional hypothesis to give the inquiry direction, and replace it as soon as later facts require. When: early in an investigation.
- [heuristic] Keep a private inference provisional until a comparison can show it to others; a hunch is not confirmation. Why: Premature conclusions can be wrong.
- [heuristic] Do not convict or clear a suspect on bodily timing alone; weigh it against routine and other evidence. Why: bodily signs give only rough estimates.
- [heuristic] Revise a first explanation of an odd action once a stated reason is known, since the reason can change how the whole act is read.
- [heuristic] Test a self-inflicted explanation by asking what purpose it would serve once the attacker's goal has already been achieved. When: when a victim's condition could be self-inflicted or imposed.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC's odd behavior more than one possible explanation, and tie each explanation to a check the player can run.
- [heuristic] A solution that explains a crime's mechanics but conflicts with the characters or their behaviour is not yet trustworthy, even if it closes every gap. When: when judging a complete explanation of a mystery. Why: Mechanism alone does not account for how people actually act.
- [heuristic] Check whether an injury could have been made by the victim's own hand; if it could not, self-infliction is ruled out. When: Deciding whether injuries were self-inflicted. Why: Physical reach limits what a person can do to themselves.
- [heuristic] Hold suspicion as a score that is revised as each new fact arrives, rather than locking it when a suspect is accused. When: Tracking suspicion during an investigation.
- [heuristic] Plant a later correction on a page that predates it, so a player who checks dates can detect that the record was altered. When: designing a document that hides a later edit. Why: Date mismatches reward careful readers.
- [heuristic] Dialogue that contradicts itself within one exchange can serve as a fair-play clue that rewards close reading. When: Designing clues in character dialogue. Why: Players who read carefully can catch the inconsistency and gain information.
- [heuristic] Use the self-growing hearing pattern when a public proceeding should expand by itself; not every accusation spreads this way.
- [heuristic] An object or statement that fits the expected story too neatly deserves scrutiny before it is accepted.
- [heuristic] A fixed belief must give way when a new witness detail contradicts it.
- [heuristic] Treat an inference about hidden feelings as provisional until a second independent fact confirms it.
- [procedure] 1) State the current hypothesis or reconstruction from the facts available. 2) Compare each new fact, recollection or witness detail with it. 3) Revise it whenever a new detail contradicts or adds to it, rather than keeping the earlier view.
- [procedure] 1) Name the feeling toward the suspect. 2) Reflect on whether it persists when calm. 3) If it persists, treat it as a conflict and recuse; if it fades, continue with explicit checks. When: an investigator notices strong anger or affection toward a case figure. Why: passing emotions can be separated from lasting bias.
- [procedure] 1) Replay the whole observation afterward. 2) Test each inference against what was seen and said. 3) Discard or flag any inference that fails. When: after an interview or tail. Why: errors often survive until checked again.
- [procedure] 1) Ask about a third party's ability in a way that requires a direct answer. 2) Listen for phrasing that reveals the respondent's own knowledge. 3) Treat a refusal to answer as informative. When: when the suspect is likely to answer with habitual or instinctive language. Why: A reply about someone else can expose the respondent's own skill or access.
- [procedure] 1) Collect small objects and habits that fit together, such as a key matching a hidden door. 2) Link them into one theory. 3) Test the theory before having proof, using knowledge of the person's character. When: Circumstantial evidence accumulates without a clear proof. Why: Small connecting items can form a coherent theory that a test can confirm or refute.
- [pitfall] An unverifiable accusation can sustain itself with no new facts, since each reaction and each reported harm reinforces the next accusation and appears to confirm it.
- [pitfall] Neatness alone does not prove staging; test a suspected arrangement against the physics of the claimed event before concluding anything. Why: orderly scenes can occur naturally.
- [pitfall] A frame that is too neat can make the investigator suspect the planted object itself.
- [pitfall] A neat collection of evidence can persuade observers to stop looking for whoever arranged it.
- [pitfall] A rival theory checked only by the investigator's own reasoning can survive by default, so independent sources are needed to confirm or break it.
- [pitfall] Trusting a neat tip over the physical evidence that accompanies it can mislead an investigator.
- [pitfall] An account can be internally consistent yet contradict external records, so consistency alone does not establish truth. When: evaluating a polished witness story. Why: a story can be coherent while still being wrong.
- [pitfall] A reconstruction that fits neatly can still be a story built around a preferred suspect rather than the facts.
- [pitfall] A reply that is too neat makes a clue look like the answer rather than an open question for the player to weigh.
- [pitfall] A theory can undermine itself: if a supposed ally inflicts the harm, the alliance it claims becomes contradictory.
- [pitfall] Once a suspect is named, every harm can be attributed to the suspect, so alternative natural causes are overlooked. When: when an accusation has been made against a specific person. Why: the accusation becomes the lens through which later events are read.
- [pitfall] Confessors may name innocent people to shield themselves, so accomplice names from a confession are not reliable without verification. When: A confessor names others. Why: Naming others can reduce a confessor's own blame.
- [pitfall] A theory with a missing link fails even when every other fact supports it. When: Assessing a theory built from many supporting facts. Why: Knowledge of a possibility is not proof of the specific intent the theory requires.
- [pitfall] An explanation that fits a favored theory elegantly can still be wrong; test it against independent sources.
- [pitfall] A plausible picture of a suspect's mind remains a guess until physical evidence agrees with it. When: when a suspect fits a motive profile. Why: character fit alone can mislead without corroboration.
- [fact] Correcting a widely circulated text after the fact is slow and incomplete, so earlier errors persist, even after their author changes view.
- [fact] A verdict reached on present evidence is provisional and may be revised when further evidence appears.

## witness testimony accounts
- [mechanism] Give each NPC claim a source, and make recall reliability depend on conditions such as lighting, distance, time of day or setting; quiet places retain memories, busy hubs do not. When: designing witness NPCs whose accounts vary by conditions. Why: Conditional reliability forces players to judge sources.
- [mechanism] An NPC can describe a figure or object accurately while wrongly assuming its identity, so players must separate the reliable detail from the unreliable claim.
- [mechanism] When an NPC's testimony conflicts with the timeline, the player must reconcile the two.
- [mechanism] Incomplete recall of a door or object can be built into an NPC, so players must work around it with other evidence.
- [behavior] Witnesses close to a suspect or victim give partial accounts covering different windows, and may disagree about a key event. When: statements come from family or close associates. Why: Personal feeling shapes what they recall and what they emphasise.
- [behavior] Persistent, sincere requests lead residents to give cooperation and information about the building and its residents. When: when a canvasser keeps returning with a sincere manner. Why: Persistence and sincerity build willingness to help.
- [behavior] A suspect asked to recount events in their own words cannot prepare answers for questions they have not yet been asked. When: Before direct questions are put to the suspect. Why: Direct questions allow prepared answers, whereas open narratives expose the suspect's unprepared account.
- [behavior] A formal questioner usually opens gently with fact-gathering questions, then escalates to firm, direct questions on the point that matters most. When: Formal questioning of a witness.
- [rule] Tag each NPC testimony with its basis (saw, heard, inferred or assumed) and the speaker's bias; verify biased rumours against physical items before relying on them. When: designing NPC dialogue or knowledge systems that report events. Why: Players weigh testimony differently once its source is visible, and tags show which claims can be verified physically.
- [rule] Give each NPC statement separate, checkable claims, such as a timestamp, ledger, guest book or shift roster entry, matching logged world records, a clock or other NPCs' accounts. When: when designing NPC testimony or interrogation dialogue. Why: Separate claims let players verify one at a time and reward comparing accounts.
- [rule] Log NPC timed statements, leaving approximate times and unconfirmed intervals, such as an unexplained long wait, so players build the timeline from several sources and question the gaps. When: when designing NPC alibis or timelines. Why: Unconfirmed intervals create investigable gaps.
- [rule] Ask a witness for the whole account, word for word, even when it seems to harm the accused, since an answer's bearing cannot be judged in advance. Why: A clear standard for testimony keeps the full record available.
- [rule] Give several NPCs partial, inconsistent accounts of one sound, creature or item, so their shared trait or mismatch becomes a puzzle clue the player resolves.
- [rule] Treat poor-visibility witness detail, such as a sound or brief glimpse, as true but partial, probabilistic clues the player must interpret rather than firm identification. When: witnesses saw a person briefly, at a distance, in disguise or in poor light.
- [rule] Present an NPC's stated theory as a hypothesis the player can disprove, not as a fact the game asserts. When: when an NPC explains an event. Why: keeps player reasoning active and avoids handing out settled answers.
- [rule] Deliver a charge in a formal set phrase to mark the move from suspicion to action and show that the scene has escalated.
- [rule] Let an NPC who warns and then retracts leave a verifiable hint, so a player who returns to the question is rewarded. When: designing NPC warnings. Why: A retraction that leaves evidence keeps the warning useful.
- [rule] Treat a frightened witness's partial, emotional first account as a statement to be checked against facts, not as a complete record.
- [rule] Treat a witness report that gives a time and an object but no person as a usable lead, and test it against other accounts before relying on it. When: A witness gives a time and object but cannot identify a person. Why: A partial sighting can narrow a timeline, but untested it remains unreliable.
- [rule] Treat an NPC's remark about the player's state as a witness statement that the player can later challenge or explain.
- [rule] Trigger NPC reports when a player or suspect revisits a changed location and asks the wrong questions.
- [rule] A formal defect, such as a missing witness, can invalidate a document regardless of what its author intended. When: A document is disputed on grounds of form. Why: Legal validity depends on meeting formal requirements, not on the author's wishes.
- [rule] Design odd NPC behaviour so two motives fit the early acts, and only the true motive explains the later ones. When: Designing an NPC whose behaviour the player must interpret. Why: Staged evidence lets the player discriminate between motives over time.
- [rule] Make an NPC's costly choice a visible tell, and give players a record that lets them check the motive they infer from it.
- [rule] Let NPCs make specific, checkable claims that players can verify in the world, and reward players who record them with a later payoff. When: Designing NPC dialogue or notes that feed later encounters. Why: Verifiable claims let players feel their notes matter.
- [rule] Give a witness NPC only a general direction, so the player must follow up at a later location to narrow it down. When: Generating NPC information in a dungeon or level. Why: Partial hints create a reason to explore and link locations.
- [rule] Let careful inspection reveal a reversal through several features, such as a scar or tattoo, so players who examine the full body find the truth. When: when designing a mistaken-identity twist.
- [rule] Build NPC dialogue where the player presents a claim and the NPC checks it against facts the player gathered earlier.
- [rule] Give an NPC a prepared cover story using one true detail, so the player exposes the contradiction only by bringing a second source.
- [rule] Record each NPC's claimed location at each time, and let players find witnesses who confirm or break those claims.
- [rule] Let a character with a stake in a theory push that explanation, giving players a biased source to weigh.
- [rule] Let an NPC give information only when the player claims a role; record the claim and let the NPC retract the information if the claim proves false.
- [rule] Provide an authority NPC, such as a lawyer or constable, who can confirm or refute a rumour, rewarding a visit to the right place.
- [rule] Let non-player witnesses identify a face from a photograph, and give them a hidden incentive that explains their cooperation.
- [rule] Give a comic or minor NPC a real motive or action that is later explained, and let the player test that NPC before discarding them. When: building a suspect NPC for a mystery. Why: A testable suspect makes the dismissal a player choice rather than an arbitrary cut.
- [rule] Flag an NPC's claim that conflicts with an event the player witnessed, so careful play is rewarded.
- [rule] Let an NPC withhold a fact it dislikes sharing, and let the player recover it by cross-checking with a second NPC.
- [rule] Let an interrogated NPC keep consistent rebuttals under pressure, so the player can test contradictions against its earlier answers. When: when designing an interrogation mechanic.
- [rule] Log minor disputes as timestamped world events, so a later accusation can recast an ordinary quarrel as motive.
- [rule] Let NPCs' later choices, such as refusing a marriage or leaving a village, serve as clues to what they know.
- [rule] Let child NPCs give partial or false clues, with adults having reasons to dismiss them; a child's warning can be a valid hint for the player to check. When: when designing NPC hints.
- [heuristic] Give NPC witnesses partial, uncertain details, such as a random subset of traits, height, clothing, an accessory or direction, so players must combine several witnesses to identify a suspect. When: designing NPC witnesses for identification puzzles. Why: Partial information keeps players inferring, and combining partial views rewards careful comparison.
- [heuristic] An NPC's stated theory may contain deliberate errors or explain only some clues, such as not the placement of key items, so players should check each claim against objects and testimony. When: a case is delivered through an NPC's account. Why: Unchecked claims can mislead the player in a designed way.
- [heuristic] Give a reticent NPC a trust value: pressing too early lowers trust, while a non-committal answer unlocks a narrower follow-up question. When: Designing dialogue for NPCs who withhold information. Why: Trust gates what the player can learn and keeps interrogation meaningful.
- [heuristic] Program an NPC who refuses to discuss a topic to reveal information only after the player meets a condition or presses for a set number of answers. When: Designing NPC dialogue gated by conditions. Why: Gated disclosure makes persistence a meaningful player choice.
- [heuristic] Recover items under formal authority with a documented search, so the trace is recorded rather than merely noticed.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC witness's retraction depend on whether the threatening faction member is present, so separating them preserves testimony. When: designing NPC witnesses linked to a faction.
- [heuristic] NPC witnesses should report only what they observed, while the player decides which inferences to voice. When: Designing inquiry scenes with NPC testimony. Why: Separating observation from inference leaves the reasoning to the player.
- [heuristic] Open a confrontation with a frank statement of what is known, including the witness's withheld link to the event. When: the interviewer has established facts about the witness. Why: Plain disclosure signals that the investigator knows enough to continue.
- [heuristic] An NPC can recall a detail the player has not yet linked, letting the player make the connection through a new conversation.
- [heuristic] Give NPC witnesses partial, slightly wrong knowledge, such as an almost-right name, so the player must cross-check them against other evidence. Why: a witness who is nearly right forces verification instead of acceptance.
- [heuristic] Re-questioning only helps with a new angle; repeating the same questions mostly yields the same answers. When: questioning a witness a second time. Why: without new framing, the session produces repetition rather than new facts.
- [heuristic] Partial witness detail is weaker than a full description. A witness who recalls nothing specific about a person supports nothing about that person's identity. When: Assessing a witness who saw someone but cannot describe them. Why: Identity needs distinguishing features, which partial recall lacks.
- [heuristic] Non-player characters can answer vaguely unless the player asks precise, neutral questions, and their answers can be marked as suggestible when the player offered a suggestion. When: Designing NPC dialogue that tracks question framing. Why: Tracking suggestion lowers the reliability of replies and rewards careful questioning.
- [heuristic] Put a family lead, such as a relative's trade or service, into an NPC's chatter, and place visitors and money trails that point to a hidden past, so the player reconstructs the motive. When: When generating NPC dialogue and environmental clues for a mystery. Why: Scattered small leads let the player assemble a motive without a direct explanation.
- [heuristic] An NPC interview tree can ask background and routine questions first, unlocking pointed questions only after baseline facts are gathered. When: designing NPC dialogue trees. Why: baseline facts make pointed questions meaningful.
- [heuristic] Release a late witness only after players hold enough evidence to judge whether that testimony fits.
- [heuristic] An NPC can answer some questions and refuse others, signalling which topics are protected. When: Designing NPC dialogue for an investigation. Why: Selective refusal tells the player where the secret lies.
- [heuristic] An NPC can report a true observation while omitting context, so players should cross-check it against other NPCs' accounts. When: Designing NPC testimony in a mystery or dungeon. Why: A single account can be accurate yet incomplete.
- [heuristic] Give witnesses conflicting accounts of the same presence. Their disagreement becomes a clue that points to one staged source the player must reconcile. When: When a supernatural presence is the central mystery.
- [procedure] 1) Give the witness a formal warning that the statement may be used against them. 2) Record the statement in writing afterward so it becomes an official record. When: when the witness could become a suspect. Why: A formal warning changes the legal weight of the statement and creates a record that later accounts can be checked against.
- [tradeoff] Witnesses should report all relevant facts, since each fact's value depends on the others; a shortened account can suit a puzzle when the full version is available from other sources.
- [tradeoff] Informal talk over tea can yield more detail than formal questioning, but it mixes fact with rumour and spreads quickly. When: When gathering accounts from a household.
- [tradeoff] A confession explaining everything can read like a lecture, while ending it abruptly leaves a gap the audience must accept rather than resolve. When: Deciding how completely to explain a solution. Why: Full explanation risks tedium, and a break risks an unresolved detail.
- [pitfall] A witness who speaks only to protect one side can be attacked as partial, which weakens the whole record. Why: Visible bias lets opponents discredit the testimony as a whole.
- [pitfall] A respected witness can be accurate for one time window and silent about another, so trustworthiness does not extend their account to every period. When: a witness covers only part of the night or day. Why: observation is limited to where the witness was.
- [pitfall] Facts relayed quickly under time pressure, such as by telephone, are incomplete and should not be treated as the full picture.
- [pitfall] Assuming a sworn, signed, written report is objective because it is formal ignores the examiner's beliefs and the guide they used.
- [pitfall] Treating a formal apology as closing a dispute, without watching for later misconduct, leads to wrongly judging the matter resolved.
- [pitfall] A witness may deny that a trait is conclusive while admitting it matches; record the denial and the admission separately. When: When taking testimony on a physical comparison. Why: Merging the two loses the witness's real assessment.
- [fact] Each witness observes a different slice of events, so no single account gives the complete sequence.
- [fact] Witnesses can agree on a general impression while none can name the specific feature responsible. When: when several witnesses describe the same person. Why: General impressions can align without identifying specifics.

## premature conclusions and closure
- [mechanism] The earliest vivid account can shape public belief for years, and later corrections may take a long time to displace it. Why: first impressions anchor belief.
- [mechanism] A known medical history can supply an easy natural explanation, so a death may be certified without inquest and the case closes early. Why: The ready explanation discourages further examination.
- [behavior] Listeners who hear a neat, plausible explanation accept it fully without independent check and stop asking questions. When: A second-hand account offers a clear cause, or a trace is explained right after discovery. Why: Plausibility makes listeners stop asking. (x2)
- [behavior] An investigator with an early neat theory reinterprets or dismisses contrary facts, treating nervous behaviour as evidence, and steers toward a favoured suspect. When: when an official or rival investigator holds a convenient suspect. Why: a plausible chain of common sense makes disconfirming facts seem explainable away.
- [behavior] A preferred theory, whether one's own or an authority's, directs attention toward confirming evidence and leads investigators to dismiss contradicting evidence. When: when an authority or respected figure favours one theory. Why: pride and preference for one's own view; the preferred theory directs attention toward confirming evidence.
- [behavior] A person who has been fully won over may accept any further conjecture, even conjecture resting on thin evidence. When: A listener has just become convinced of a theory. Why: Belief once gained stops being checked, so weak extensions pass unexamined.
- [behavior] Investigators, like other people, prefer a clean explanation, and that wish for a neat answer can colour how they weigh evidence. When: Competing explanations exist and one offers a simpler resolution. Why: A desire for closure biases judgement toward the tidier case.
- [behavior] People who already hold opinions tend to settle on the easiest solution and stop searching once it appears to have no visible flaw. When: When a group has reached a quick conclusion about a case or problem. Why: A solution without visible gaps removes the incentive to look further, so confirmation replaces testing.
- [behavior] A witness who has settled on an explanation may stop noticing details that contradict it. Why: A confident explanation replaces continued observation.
- [behavior] Players often miss correct signs in early evidence when more prominent details overlay them, so early theories can be wrong even when the answer was present.
- [behavior] After an alarming event, people instinctively close and fasten windows and doors, so a seal often dates from after the event. When: A sealed room is reported right after a shocking incident. Why: People instinctively secure a space once they feel threatened.
- [behavior] People reach for the most familiar or dramatic explanation of an event, such as a romance or a rival faction, even when that explanation fits the shape people expect rather than the facts. When: Witnesses or NPCs explain an unexplained event. Why: Familiar narratives feel satisfying and close the question, hiding the actual cause.
- [rule] Do not name a culprit or share a conclusion until proof is complete, the group is ready, or the inquiry is finished; early answers mislead. When: The true explanation depends on evidence not yet gathered. Why: An early conclusion can send the audience or group toward a wrong answer.
- [heuristic] Treat a self-inflicted or accidental reading of a death as a trap: check tools, marks and residue against physical facts, since earlier threats or nearby self-harm can end search early. When: a death first looks self-inflicted or accidental. Why: Players accept the easy explanation unless the evidence contradicts it. (x2)
- [heuristic] Bring in an outside investigator early, before anyone disturbs evidence or handles the body, while the setting remains intact. When: when foul play is possible. Why: Untouched evidence remains usable for the investigation.
- [procedure] Mark the suspects who need the closest study as a separate priority group within the working roster. When: when the roster is too large to study equally.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the audience's guessed answers. 2) Eliminate each guess through plot changes. 3) Repeat until common guesses fail before the reveal. Why: Revision prevents the puzzle from being solved early by accident.
- [tradeoff] Confronting a suspect early can force a confession, but dismissal or departure may remove the only source of information. When: when deciding whether to press a source now or later. Why: Pressure can end access to a witness who could have supplied more.
- [tradeoff] Confronting a suspect with thin evidence risks a flat denial and a more guarded suspect. When: when deciding when to confront a suspect. Why: confrontation timing shapes the suspect's response.
- [tradeoff] Arresting a suspect early may steady him or end the chance to gather more evidence; delaying keeps evidence coming but leaves the suspect free to act. When: the case still needs more proof.
- [pitfall] A case or confirmation that feels complete ends inquiry early, so investigators stop checking, untested gaps stay hidden and missed evidence slips through. When: A single explanation is accepted, or a circumstantial case appears convincing. (x2)
- [pitfall] A satisfactory account or convincing demonstration can close an inquiry before an available direct check or other causes are tested. When: An account is declared satisfactory, or a defence is being evaluated. (x2)
- [pitfall] Conclusions stated before their evidence is shown get rejected as guesses or mistaken for proof; untested hunches should stay labelled until verification confirms them. When: when an investigator presents a fast answer in a formal inquiry, or when briefing someone who has a prior belief. Why: formal inquiries need proof, not guesses; a bare conclusion gives the listener nothing to weigh, so they defend their existing view. (x2)
- [pitfall] Seeking direct confirmation or confronting a suspect too early alerts the culprit, letting them adjust, destroying evidence and exposing the witness who revealed a discrepancy. When: Investigating an ongoing scheme, or confronting a suspect with a discrepancy. (x2)
- [pitfall] An official or familiar-category explanation, such as mistaken identity or a fitting motive, closes inquiry before the motive is examined and hides facts that do not fit. When: An official gives a quick explanation, or a suspect matches a familiar motive category. Why: A familiar story is accepted before its details are tested; fitting one category feels like a complete answer. (x2)
- [pitfall] A neat, harmless explanation or plausible generalisation ends the question early and stops the search for a deeper cause; treat it as probable until an independent check supports it. When: An ordinary cause or generalisation is offered for an eerie, suspicious or contradictory event. Why: A ready explanation satisfies curiosity before the evidence is checked.
- [pitfall] Accepting a plausible explanation early, such as a faint or a warning, closes the question and stops the search for alternatives, possibly burying a clue whose meaning is unchecked. When: An explanation appears plausible early, especially an innocent one. Why: Early acceptance stops the search for alternatives.
- [pitfall] A plausible explanation covering only part of the evidence can hide a real threat or remaining facts, so weigh all evidence before accepting it. When: An investigator has a theory or first natural explanation that fits part of the evidence. Why: Partial fit feels like proof, so contradicting facts are ignored until the theory breaks down.
- [pitfall] Committing to a theory built from partial facts before witnesses are cross-checked hardens it, so later evidence is fitted to the theory rather than tested and misread.
- [pitfall] Deciding guilt, or hardening a theory into a formal charge, before evidence is checked locks in an unverified conclusion and risks a mistaken arrest. When: Early theories are acted on before verification. Why: Commitment to a first theory discourages later checking.
- [pitfall] Clearing a suspect on partial proof, or on a judgment about their cover, is as hasty as accusing early; test that hypothesis before clearing them.
- [pitfall] Treating a probable reading, a striking clue, or a dramatic headline as settled closes rival explanations; keep them open until alibis and other evidence are checked. When: An investigation is under public or internal pressure, or a striking find appears. Why: Vivid clues feel decisive and create a sense of resolution that discourages further checking.
- [pitfall] Reading a key document dramatically, or through someone's summary, settles a case early; check the source text and its stated times against other evidence first. When: Reading a key document in a case. Why: Dramatic framing and secondhand summaries replace checking the source text.
- [pitfall] Labelling an anomalous act accidental, or an anomaly forgetfulness or a mistake, closes the question and hides the clue that would disprove a weak theory. When: A missing detail or anomalous act is explained away without evidence. Why: An accident label closes the question before any alternative has been tested.
- [pitfall] Explaining away a witness's report, or a quick label for a suspect's odd conduct, such as overtired, overexcited or mad, closes inquiry before the claim is checked. When: A group explains away a witness's report, or a neighbour or biased informant offers a quick label for unusual conduct. Why: Attributing the report to the witness's state replaces checking the claim; a dismissive label ends investigation before the behaviour is understood.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a lead or an improbable account before verifying the fact that closes it, or testing its details, can discard a real line of inquiry or a true report.
- [pitfall] Assuming the subjects outmanoeuvred the searchers, or abandoning after repeated empty results, ends the search before untested leads are tried. When: A trail goes cold after exhausting known sources, or many checks return nothing. Why: Assuming defeat stops the search before untested leads are checked; repetition creates fatigue and false closure.
- [pitfall] Declaring a crime or method impossible before listing when each barrier was in place, and checking each step it requires, hides the window or explanation that allowed it.
- [pitfall] Abandoning an explanation or timing mismatch for a new theory before checking the old one against expert evidence leaves unverified conclusions and the anomaly unexplained.
- [pitfall] Naming a suspect without evidence for a withheld cause, or assigning ownership of a found object too quickly, can point at the wrong culprit. When: A cause is withheld, or a found object is first attributed.
- [pitfall] Accepting a neat clue sequence or one strong physical clue, and stopping once it seems complete, lets a wrong suspect or answer settle the case. Why: A single clue can mislead, and the first theory is often the least tested.
- [pitfall] Early impressions from physical signs, or formed in darkness or confusion, are often wrong; treat them as provisional until checked against a reliable cue. When: Bystanders interpret a body or scene before experts examine it, or impressions form in darkness or while confused. Why: Initial readings are made without full evidence, so they can mislead later investigation.
- [pitfall] A theory defended by patches for each contradiction, or built from one plausible mechanism, must have each patch or mechanism tested independently against alternatives. When: A theory is defended by successive explanations, or developed from a plausible mechanism. Why: Individually plausible patches can hide that the overall structure rests on unverified assumptions; confidence can hide untested alternatives.
- [pitfall] Accepting a witness's account without independent confirmation early in a case can delay the investigation for a long time.
- [pitfall] An investigator convinced of the culprit can stop testing other readings while the evidence still allows them. When: before the suspect is questioned. Why: certainty ends further testing.
- [pitfall] Clearing the wrong person too early, or with an unsound method, can make the public distrust the whole investigation.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a character's claims too early can make a later reversal feel unearned. Why: players who ignored the claim cannot see why it was later vindicated.
- [pitfall] Acting on an unchecked label can produce a decision that later looks wrong, and doubts that arrive afterwards do not undo it.
- [pitfall] A sorted list of clues is still a hypothesis; conclusions drawn too quickly should be re-tested against the facts. Why: Quick sorting can produce confident but wrong chains of reasoning.
- [pitfall] Forgiving a revealed motive can end the inquiry early and leave other threads untested, so do not accept a late confession as complete. When: a confession resolves part of a mystery. Why: Unexplained facts may remain.
- [pitfall] Closing off every safe option too early leaves the protagonist's remaining risk looking arbitrary rather than chosen.
- [pitfall] A rare explanation can be accepted too early; common explanations should be rejected first, with evidence.
- [pitfall] A first-thought theory can survive only as narrowed by new evidence. Keep other candidate explanations open after a timing clue eliminates some of them. Why: Early favorites tend to persist even when the evidence only partly supports them.
- [pitfall] Dismissing an unusual explanation early, based on a quick check of precedent, can close off the real answer; treat such checks as tests, not verdicts. When: an event seems to fit no ordinary explanation. Why: precedent can be incomplete, so early verdicts hide valid options.
- [pitfall] A clue can be dismissed on first reading and regain meaning only after a later event, so keep early clues on file for reexamination.
- [pitfall] A firm witness claim may be a deliberate lie; accepting it early keeps the investigator treating a room as sealed when it is not.
- [pitfall] Publishing a clue before it is understood can send a whole community down the same wrong path.
- [pitfall] Early judgments drawn from appearance can close an investigation before the decisive question is asked. When: An official reaches a conclusion before establishing the key facts.
- [pitfall] Resolving a threat too early leaves a later reversal with no weight, because the audience no longer fears the outcome the reversal would overturn.
- [pitfall] Accepting a plausible decoy early ends the search for the fact that contradicts it, so the case stays closed on a false answer.
- [pitfall] Public demand can push for disclosure before the solution is ready, so the reveal may be rushed. When: Under public pressure before a solution is complete. Why: Audiences want answers and may press for them before the evidence is in place.
- [pitfall] Abandoning a sound theory after one disappointing scene is overreaction, while explaining every anomaly as cover is underreaction; both stop the theory from being revised correctly. When: when evidence contradicts a theory once or repeatedly. Why: a theory should change in proportion to the weight of evidence.
- [pitfall] A failed public appeal can reflect a flaw in the method rather than an absence of witnesses, so check why it produced nothing.
- [pitfall] Closing the supernatural question early on a mundane cause that fits only one observation leads to a wrong conclusion. When: When an eerie event has a plausible natural explanation. Why: Partial fit is mistaken for full explanation.
- [pitfall] Overusing official sign-offs can make a case feel closed too early and reduce suspense. When: Writing investigation resolutions. Why: Verified-seeming outcomes leave nothing to uncover.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a fated or supernatural explanation too quickly can hide a real human cause, so still check the arrangement of facts.
- [pitfall] A neat match between a weapon and a fragment can close a case too quickly, before other evidence has been weighed. When: A physical match appears to resolve the question. Why: A single convincing link can hide competing explanations.
- [pitfall] Treating a lost stretch of time as supernatural before the dates have been checked jumps to a conclusion the records may explain.
- [pitfall] Jumping to cause before establishing identity leaves every later inference without an anchor, and speculation treated as a finding weakens the case when contradicted. When: Building or solving mystery narratives. Why: Unsupported inferences collapse when new evidence arrives.
- [pitfall] Closing the case once the visible culprit is found can miss the planner behind the scene. When: A minor culprit has been caught. Why: The visible act is not always the main one.

## scene and event reconstruction
- [definition] Reconstructing events from a scene's leftovers, marks and arrangements lets an investigator infer who was present and what happened, without any witness. When: a scene has no witnesses.
- [mechanism] An entry added to the original after a copy was made appears only in the original, so its absence from the copy marks when it was added.
- [mechanism] An explanation after a reveal can recast a feared group as amateurs who chose dramatic trappings yet faced real danger.
- [mechanism] Royalty and copyright value can rise sharply after a death through renewed sales, so the financial stake can grow after the event. When: Estimating the value of a legacy after a death. Why: Renewed attention increases sales of the deceased's work.
- [mechanism] A projectile in an unexpected spot that conflicts with the intended story prompts the player to search more deeply. When: Designing a mystery that should reward closer inspection. Why: Contradictions with the expected story create curiosity and a reason to continue searching.
- [behavior] Occupants who want no identifying trace may wear gloves and rubber soles, leaving only indirect marks behind.
- [behavior] A character's posture or line delivery that changes after an emotional scene gives players a readable cue about that character's state. Why: Visible shifts in demeanour signal how the scene affected the character.
- [behavior] After an outcome, characters summarise events through their own bias, such as romantic, legal, social or club concerns, so their conclusions differ. When: When characters discuss a resolved case. Why: Each speaker's personal interest shapes what they take from the same facts.
- [behavior] A sudden event tends to generate rumours with specific physical details, and these can outlast the facts behind them.
- [rule] A trial run must use the real steps, strength, timing and attention of a realistic performer; timing only the fastest version of an act misstates feasibility. When: Setting up a timed re-enactment of a suspect's action. Why: An ordinary person acting under stress differs from a trained or unhurried performer, so unrealistic conditions produce a misleading result.
- [rule] A reenactment must match the original conditions in angle, height, and sequence; small differences can make the test prove nothing. When: running a physical reconstruction to test a claim. Why: The result is only valid if the test reproduces the conditions it claims to verify.
- [rule] To understand an actor's conduct, reconstruct what people of the time accepted as true and as evidence, rather than judging by later knowledge.
- [rule] Give a generated map shifting place names and dated land records, so players must reconcile old and new labels to locate a site. When: designing a world with renamed locations.
- [rule] When a scene has been altered, reconstruct its original positions from witnesses rather than the current layout, unless the changes were recorded. When: furniture or objects were moved before examination. Why: the current layout no longer reflects the event.
- [heuristic] End a case with a reconstruction screen replaying the player's deductions in order, labeling each theory and the clue that revised it, so the player sees how clues connect. When: Concluding an investigation sequence, such as a dungeon's solution summary. Why: A summary links clues to the outcome.
- [heuristic] When the culprit is unknown and has no record, work from the crime and the traces it leaves, studied closely. When: no records or informers apply. Why: The scene itself is then the only material available.
- [heuristic] Present a reconstruction of events one claim at a time and watch the suspect's reaction to each claim.
- [heuristic] Reconstruct the crime as a plausible, step-by-step story, including how the act was carried out, so the suspect can see how the evidence fits together. When: the evidence supports each step.
- [heuristic] Let players assemble a reconstruction of events from physical traces, such as blood, weight or displacement, found among scene objects.
- [heuristic] A game can reconstruct a past event for the player from a map, timestamps and damage to an in-world object. When: when the player must learn what happened before the scene. Why: the player can infer the sequence from consistent traces.
- [heuristic] Scene traces can reveal how many people were involved: one person's methods, such as a single drag trail or an improvised carrying device, differ from what a group would need. When: Deciding whether a crime at a scene was committed by one person or several. Why: A group could lift and carry directly, while a lone actor needs aids and may return for items.
- [heuristic] Check the trim and cut edges of a sheet, since cutting can remove the marks that would link it to its source. When: A sheet's origin matters and its edges have been altered. Why: Trimming erases the evidence that connects a sheet to a stack or bundle.
- [heuristic] In dialogue, let the player present collected events and let the NPC confirm, deny or correct each one, with each reply opening a new branch. When: designing a dialogue tree for investigation.
- [heuristic] Delivering a reversal in conversation after the event reveals facts without interrupting the scene itself.
- [heuristic] Use sequence reconstruction when a witness account and the physical record disagree. When: Testimony and physical evidence conflict. Why: Reconstruction can reconcile the two sources.
- [heuristic] A matched trace, such as a hair, places a person at a location but does not by itself show who else was present. Why: Traces establish presence at a place, not the full set of people there.
- [heuristic] Test whether a scene supports a theory by checking whether its traces fit the proposed action. When: A theory about an event is being evaluated against the scene. Why: Traces inconsistent with the proposed action count against the theory.
- [heuristic] Rehearse the actual steps of a plan instead of trusting reasoning alone, since untested steps hide failure points. When: Before committing to a multi-step plan.
- [procedure] 1) Gather every surviving source: court papers, diaries, letters, minutes, itineraries, later official reports, and site visits. 2) Date each one. 3) Check each claim against an independent dated source. 4) Do not rely on one partisan account when others exist. When: Later reconstruction of a disputed event documented only in fragments, with some records lost or withheld. Why: Independent dated sources can check a partisan narrative and confirm or refute individual claims.
- [procedure] 1) Sort surviving documents, family memory and local tradition by date and provenance, and check the sites and remains they mention. 2) Match each source against the others. 3) Distinguish details the sources support from details invented to fit. 4) Note how well each part is supported. When: Rebuilding an old incident or incomplete record from partial sources of differing reliability. Why: Combining sources of different kinds exposes gaps and can corroborate or contradict a written account, keeping the account honest.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the original conditions: room state, objects, people, routine (walk and meal timing) and subject's mental state. 2) Restore each condition, refurnishing the room exactly as before. 3) Repeat the act and record the outcome. 4) Count a mismatch against the theory; a repeated result supports it. When: A theory of how an act happened depends on conditions that can be restored, such as room state or the subject's routine. Why: Reproduction can confirm or weaken the theory; matching the original setting and the subject's condition keeps other variables from distorting the comparison.
- [procedure] 1) Form the timing hypothesis and identify every step the act requires. 2) Perform each step in order at realistic pace, timing the whole run. 3) Compare total time with the available window or the witness's account. 4) If it fits, the claim is possible; if not, it is ruled out. When: A suspect's alibi, access or disputed timing depends on a short absence or fixed time window. Why: Measured durations tested against the real steps of an act reveal feasibility better than guesses.
- [procedure] 1) Separate traces by who left them. 2) Identify the traces that belong to the event. 3) Read each mark for the action that made it. 4) Order the actions into a sequence. 5) Combine several traces before concluding. When: a scene can be read from traces of movement.
- [procedure] 1) List each physical trace and the person's condition. 2) For each, ask who could have produced it and in what state. 3) Combine them into one story. 4) Test that story against what nearby people do next. When: a scene holds several small traces that together imply a sequence.
- [procedure] 1) Build one ordered chain of who, when, what and why from partial accounts. 2) Check that every observed detail fits the chain. 3) Disclose the chain step by step so each conclusion follows from evidence already shown. When: Concluding an investigation where the solver must justify the answer to the audience. Why: A reveal feels credible when each step follows from evidence and no link is covered by assertion.
- [procedure] 1) Build a motive-based account of the crime. 2) Test it against facts the audience has already seen. 3) Confirm it explains every earlier oddity. 4) Deliver it as a reconstruction. When: when the reveal should be earned through facts shown earlier. Why: a reconstruction built only on shown facts feels fair and satisfying.
- [procedure] 1) Recount the case from the point the investigator entered it. 2) Label each early impression. 3) Name the clue that revised each impression. 4) End with the complete chain and final reversal. When: Closing a mystery with a fair-play reveal. Why: The reader can check each step against facts already shown.
- [procedure] 1) Replay events in order from first act to last. 2) Explain how each act was set up. 3) Reinterpret earlier oddities as clues now that the solution is known. When: all clues have been collected and the reveal should reward re-examination. Why: Hindsight shows how earlier details fit the solution.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the old sources: letters, court records and witness memory. 2) Test the present claim against each source. 3) Note which accounts agree and which conflict. When: A present accusation depends on events from long ago. Why: Independent sources can confirm or break a claim that no single source can settle.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the scene under the original conditions, including the same door, bolt and observers. 2) Use only improvised tools that were plausibly available. 3) Perform the mechanism step by step with witnesses present. 4) Let skeptics test the result directly before accepting it. When: testing whether a locked-room claim depends on a physical mechanism others doubt. Why: A reenactment turns an abstract theory into something observers can check for themselves.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the final remark or conclusion. 2) Work backward through the chain of associations. 3) Check each link against an observed act. 4) Treat any link lacking an observed act as a guess. When: inferring what someone thought but did not say. Why: backward tracing exposes a chain that looks incoherent forward.
- [procedure] 1) Estimate the offender's intelligence and assume the simplest effective method. 2) Identify the physical constraints of the task. 3) Infer the number of people and their positions. 4) Look for marks the proposed sequence should leave. 5) Check the scene's disorder against the sequence. When: A hidden event must be rebuilt from physical traces. Why: A capable offender tends to choose the simplest workable route, and the method leaves checkable marks.
- [procedure] 1) Note where the body lies relative to the access routes to infer how it arrived. 2) Record absent traces, such as missing blood or items. 3) Match trace positions against the setting's physical mechanics. 4) Test each fact against one unified hypothesis, and check it against the known schedule. When: Cause and place of a death are in doubt and the physical layout can be checked. Why: Physical position and absences constrain how the event could have happened.
- [procedure] 1) Describe the scene step by step from each participant's viewpoint, including non-human ones. 2) Check each step for plausibility. 3) Build one account covering every observed fact. When: A closed scene with an unusual mechanism needs a full explanation. Why: Viewpoint steps expose actions that cannot physically happen as described.
- [procedure] 1) Document the scene and body positions before anything is moved. 2) Check each exit separately. 3) Search every plausible hiding place for the weapon. 4) Note untouched valuables. 5) Exclude each explanation that needs an exit, step by step. When: a death occurs in an apparently sealed space.
- [procedure] 1) Inspect the arrangement of objects, openings and the culprit's own records. 2) Infer the sequence of actions these arrangements imply. 3) Check whether that sequence explains every trace. When: when a scene offers no witness or confession. Why: Arrangements and records hold traces that show how an act was done.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each trace found at the scene. 2) Record which person each trace fits. 3) Give no decisive weight to a trace until its owner is established. When: a scene holds several traces whose owners are unknown.
- [procedure] 1) Walk the approach and note side entrances. 2) Trace paths hidden behind cover to the body's position. 3) Search the ground closely over a wide area. 4) Ask what could be seen from outside. 5) Sketch the room and inventory its contents. When: Surveying a crime scene. Why: Each step reveals a different kind of information about access, concealment and disturbance.
- [procedure] 1) Reproduce the scene with the same people, positions and props. 2) Speak the lines as originally spoken. 3) Test whether sound or line of sight from the disputed spot matches the witness's account. When: a witness describes an action that can be physically replayed. Why: a replay tests the account against physical conditions.
- [procedure] 1) Describe the pose and fall direction a claimed wound would normally produce. 2) Compare the body's pose and the positions of its belongings with that description. 3) Note each mismatch for follow-up. When: The stated cause of death and the body's posture or belongings seem inconsistent. Why: A wound produces a predictable fall, so departures from it reveal a different sequence of events.
- [procedure] 1) Record where the witness was and what that position allowed them to hear. 2) Identify speakers by voice traits. 3) Order the heard events into a sequence. 4) Check each step against physical evidence. 5) Mark which steps are inference. When: witness heard but did not see the event. Why: a sequence built from sound must be tested against the room to be trusted.
- [procedure] 1) Note damage to objects, such as a torn fence or broken railing. 2) Infer the victim's position from it. 3) Use scorch patterns to estimate range. 4) Check the ground for tracks to infer routes.
- [procedure] 1) Collect dated grants and later deeds for the site. 2) Note the natural features each cites as boundary points. 3) Compare neighboring records that cite the same features. 4) Track renamed landmarks across periods. 5) Check which authority issued each record. 6) Converge on the most consistent line. When: a site's boundaries survive only in documents that use changing names and perishable markers. Why: no original survey of the markers survives.
- [procedure] 1) Note what the official record omits and test any claimed event against it. 2) Date each document against the events it supposedly relates to. 3) Track participant attendance to find when a view changed. 4) Match that change with the arrival of a key document to infer cause. When: A narrative's sequence conflicts with dated records and attendance data exists. Why: Dates and attendance reveal decisions that no record states outright.
- [procedure] 1) Identify each source and whether its writer witnessed the events. 2) Mark direct testimony apart from summaries. 3) State where the record ends and what is missing. 4) Say whether chosen examples illustrate a pattern or count all cases. When: building an account from records you did not witness. Why: readers can judge reliability and avoid overreading selected cases.
- [procedure] 1) Read prints and ash against each other. 2) Note the order of marks. 3) Infer what was carried and where the boots went from missing steps. When: Reconstructing a sequence of actions from physical traces. Why: Comparing marks and their order reveals carried objects and removed footwear.
- [procedure] 1) Log timestamped player actions during play. 2) Reconstruct the sequence afterward. 3) Use it to test an alibi or to check which event happened first. When: Designing mysteries where players must verify alibis or event order. Why: A reconstructable log lets designers and the game check consistency.
- [procedure] 1) Mark the seated victim's position, the firing spot and the wall impact point. 2) Join them with a straight line. 3) Use the line to determine which side of the victim the shot came from. When: A shot's origin and direction must be tested against who could have stood where. Why: A straight line from impact back to source fixes the shooter's side and approximate position.
- [procedure] 1) Record each damaged item's force direction and posture of the victim. 2) Test whether the damage matches the victim's own movements or an attacker's. 3) Test whether each item was damaged before or after the event. 4) Accept the explanation that fits all force directions. When: injuries and damage seem to conflict with the stated sequence. Why: Force direction and object position reveal the order of events.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the door state. 2) Build the timeline from sound and light. 3) Mark objects that moved. 4) Note physical traces. 5) Check the order in which people entered. When: a closed room holds a body or disturbance. Why: each witness sees only part of the event, so the sequence must be rebuilt from each vantage point.
- [tradeoff] Assembling a full reconstruction is useful after facts are gathered, but early on gathering facts matters more than building a theory.
- [pitfall] Accounts recorded after events, including memories formed after reading press coverage, are not independent evidence and make matches with reported facts look stronger than they are. When: A witness reports a recollection after reading a public account of the event, or any account is recorded after the event. Why: The later account may be shaped by what was read. (x2)
- [pitfall] Neither disorder nor tidiness proves innocence or guilt; disorder may result from one event rather than a struggle, so establish its cause before inferring a fight. When: Investigating a disturbed room. Why: Assuming a struggle can point the investigation at the wrong people. (x2)
- [pitfall] Trampling by many people blurs or erases overlapping prints, so the order of events becomes unreadable; keep observers still and away from the scene. When: Several people cross a surface holding footprints or evidence before it is examined. Why: Foot traffic overwrites the impressions being studied.
- [pitfall] Small unrecorded details, such as misplaced props or loose litter, can break a faithful reconstruction of an earlier scene. When: A scene is rebuilt from memory or an incomplete record. Why: Minor changes alter the conditions in ways the test does not account for.
- [pitfall] Reproduction tests are weak when the scene has already been disturbed, because they then recreate a changed situation rather than the original event.
- [pitfall] Revealing the answer before the audience has the clues to reach it, or covering a gap in the chain with assertion instead of evidence, breaks the sense of fair play. When: Writing a mystery or puzzle reveal. Why: The audience cannot verify or reproduce a conclusion whose supporting clues were withheld.
- [pitfall] A body may be moved and its limbs arranged before the investigator arrives, so the original position of the body is lost.
- [fact] An object found at a scene does not show who left it or when; physical traces such as a fresh stain may be the only timing clue.
- [fact] A reenactment shows only that a mechanism could have been used, not that it was used; the demonstration does not prove the act happened. When: interpreting a reconstruction of an impossible exit. Why: Possibility and actual occurrence are different claims.

## conflicting accounts
- [mechanism] Tracking what each witness saw and assumed lets inconsistent accounts generate new questions the player must resolve.
- [rule] Conflicting accounts do not prove a lie: memory failure and differing vantage points, roles or attention can cause them, so weigh each source on its own record. When: When several people describe one incident or accounts of one event disagree. Why: Disagreement can come from different vantage points, not deceit; vantage point, role and attention differ across observers. (x2)
- [rule] Drop an explanation that physical evidence contradicts, rather than adjusting evidence or excusing contradictions by an outside cause, which hides flaws in testimony. When: When accusers and confessors disagree or physical evidence contradicts a theory. Why: Reshaping evidence to save a theory corrupts the reasoning. (x2)
- [rule] Conflicting descriptions may mean a disguise, a different person, or an innocent cause, so treat the mismatch as a possibility to test, not proof of identity. When: Several witnesses describe the same person differently. Why: Descriptions can be wrong, and mismatches have innocent causes.
- [rule] Let an NPC's stated plan or claimed departure be contradicted by a later clue, such as their movements or an item they would not have left behind. When: When designing NPC dialogue or a missing-character quest. Why: A checkable contradiction rewards attention to behavior.
- [rule] Let NPC factions or sources pass rumours of differing accuracy, so the player weighs each against the scene and what they know and reconciles conflicting figures. When: When designing gossip or rumours about a shared event in a game world. Why: Reconciling competing sources turns hearsay into a reasoning task.
- [rule] Record conflicting witness answers or perception logs on the same point and leave the disagreement open for the player to weigh, rather than resolving it automatically.
- [rule] Let several NPCs who share knowledge of an event give partial, conflicting accounts, reconcilable through physical evidence such as footprints, broken locks, wounds, dropped items, ammunition or keys. When: When designing contradictory testimony or branching investigation dialogue. Why: Resolving conflicts through evidence makes the player's deduction the source of truth.
- [rule] Have NPCs describe the same sighting or exchange differently, including those kept in the dark, so the player must reconcile the accounts rather than trust one. When: When designing witness testimony in a mystery. Why: Conflicting accounts require the player to weigh evidence.
- [rule] Make NPC tells and claims conflict with each other or with scene evidence, so the player must weigh them rather than accept one clear signal or speaker. When: When designing clue sets or an NPC's account of events. Why: Forces players to judge reliability rather than trust the speaker.
- [rule] Mark the time each witness gives for the same event side by side; conflicting times and routes show which accounts need checking.
- [rule] Build a contradiction into two NPC accounts so the player must find a third source to decide which account is accurate. When: when designing witness dialogue.
- [rule] Let a puzzle NPC mix truth and falsehood in directions, and track contradictions across conversations so the player can detect them. When: Designing a helpful but unreliable NPC. Why: Tracking contradictions rewards careful listening.
- [rule] Compare a witness's retellings for constant facts and for changes in details, not for changes in manner. When: a witness has told the story more than once. Why: Tone changes easily, while factual inconsistencies reveal problems.
- [rule] Break a claimed alibi with one reliable sighting that contradicts it; that single contradiction can overturn the claimed location.
- [rule] When a story is split among several narrators, compare their overlapping events to check each account against the others.
- [rule] Have several NPCs agree on a character's key features but vary on minor ones, so players can assemble a composite description.
- [rule] Do not treat one observer's reading as the truth. Compare it with another observer's account, since interpretation bias can change what is reported.
- [rule] Give NPCs statements that can contradict one another, so the player must compare sources and find the account that was prompted by someone else. When: in designed witness or dialogue scenes. Why: Contradictions give the player a reason to cross-check.
- [rule] Give a claim one confirming witness and one contradicting witness, so the player must decide which witness to question first. When: when designing npc dialogue around a disputed claim.
- [rule] Build a landmark whose layout contradicts an NPC's story about it, so the player can test the tale against what they see. When: Designing NPC stories about landmarks.
- [rule] Have two NPC authors publish conflicting views, so the player must reconcile them.
