- [rule] Testimony rejected as unreliable in one kind of case, such as from a distracted or possessed person, must be rejected in every similar case. When: when judging witnesses across different charges. Why: Applying different reliability rules to the same kind of witness is inconsistent.
- [rule] Place conflicting NPC testimony in different rooms so players must decide which witness to trust. When: When designing witness NPCs whose accounts conflict. Why: Spatial separation makes players weigh sources instead of receiving a single answer.
- [heuristic] Make an NPC's flat denial a branch that a later sighting or discovery contradicts, so the player must choose between exposing a lie and embarrassment. (x2)
- [heuristic] Witnesses may give opposite accounts, and confident claims may rest on partial knowledge, so compare conflicting versions, each from a different source, rather than accept the most confident one. When: When two witnesses describe one event differently. (x2)
- [heuristic] Give witnesses timing claims that conflict with each other or with another clue, so the player must work out which account is reliable and build a coherent timeline. When: Designing testimony or investigative narrative with multiple witnesses. Why: Conflicting testimony makes the player weigh evidence instead of accepting a single source. (x2)
- [heuristic] Weigh conflicting witnesses by observing conditions such as position and noise, giving more weight to the account made under better conditions rather than a trust ranking. When: When two witnesses' accounts conflict. Why: Conditions explain disagreement better than a trust ranking; better conditions give more reliable perception.
- [heuristic] When two statements, such as two NPCs' accounts, cannot both be true, their contradiction is itself a clue marking where the facts must be tested. When: When two witnesses describe the same event differently. Why: The conflict marks where the facts must be tested.
- [heuristic] When witnesses disagree about an agreement's terms, lay each account beside the dates of the offers and votes it describes. Why: Matching accounts to dates shows which version fits the record.
- [heuristic] Let witness details conflict in small ways so the player resolves each conflict using other evidence. Why: conflicts teach the player to test sources rather than trust them whole.
- [heuristic] Read contradictory replies with care, since distress affects speech as much as it affects the facts being reported. When: A witness gives inconsistent answers while in distress. Why: Confusion can produce contradictions without any change in the underlying facts.
- [heuristic] When an object's location contradicts an owner's account, treat the contradiction as a lead to press, not as proof of guilt. When: When a found object places its owner somewhere they denied being.
- [heuristic] Compare reactions across people: both surprise and its absence are signals, so note who shows none when others do.
- [heuristic] Withhold news from a suspect, then compare how each person responds; differences in concern are harder to fake than direct answers. When: the suspect does not already know the event. Why: reactions to identical news are harder to fabricate than direct answers.
- [heuristic] Contradictions inside one witness account, such as denying a problem while describing it as severe, mark exactly the claims that need checking. Why: inconsistent statements show where the account is unreliable.
- [heuristic] Reports that contradict the expected route may point to a second person or a false trail and should be recorded, not discarded. When: When sightings do not fit the route being tested. Why: Contradictions can reveal an accomplice or a misdirection.
- [heuristic] A detail that conflicts with what people have said about themselves or each other is worth recording as a clue. When: when a remark does not fit the expected pattern. Why: Mismatches between statements can point toward concealment or error.
- [heuristic] Any statement made under any circumstances can be contested, so the goal is to judge which way the probabilities lean rather than to reach certainty.
- [heuristic] Compare accounts of the same event point by point, looking for differences in emphasis or detail. When: Accounts of one event conflict.
- [heuristic] A muted reaction to a fact can give way to strong shock when the real news arrives; compare the two responses to judge what was expected.
- [heuristic] Compare testimonies from multiple witnesses; a contradiction between two accounts can force a fuller account from the one who lied. When: Two witnesses give accounts that cannot both be true. Why: Confronting one account with another exposes the weaker claim.
- [heuristic] When two testimonies conflict, offering a plausible innocent alternative keeps the choice genuinely open for the player. When: when two accounts contradict each other. Why: a credible alternative prevents the obvious answer from being automatic.
- [heuristic] Give companions conflicting reasons to blame each other, so the player must weigh each accusation against the timing data. When: Designing suspect dialogue in a mystery. Why: Conflicting accusations make the player check evidence instead of accepting claims.
- [heuristic] A witness detail that seems to weaken a theory may strengthen it; ask what the theory predicts before dismissing the detail. When: the theory predicts unusual behaviour the detail could show. Why: Predicted unusual behaviour can look like a contradiction.
- [heuristic] Agreement among several witnesses on raw observed facts carries weight even when their interpretations differ. When: Judging whether multiple testimonies establish a fact. Why: Independent agreement on what was seen is harder to produce by chance than shared interpretation.
- [heuristic] Discount witness descriptions of a person's mood or sanity when those descriptions are themselves disputed, since they cannot settle a timeline. When: witnesses disagree about a suspect's mental state. Why: subjective impressions are weak evidence for factual timing.
- [heuristic] Judge testimony by consistency and tone; plain, steady accounts that do not reveal partisanship deserve more weight.
- [heuristic] Compare a reported remark with the speaker's own account, since the reporter's bias may shape how it was passed on. When: When evaluating a secondhand quotation. Why: Relaying introduces the reporter's slant.
- [heuristic] Let NPC reports conflict with what the player observed, and let the player choose which witness to trust. When: when designing testimony in a mystery. Why: Choosing a source makes the player responsible for the conclusion.
- [heuristic] Let at least one identity proof conflict with the true answer, so the leading theory is tested rather than simply confirmed. Why: A clue that resists the answer keeps the player's belief in the solution under genuine test.
- [procedure] 1) Record each claim from every statement separately. 2) Line up spoken and written versions claim by claim. 3) Note which details change and who gains from each version. When: A witness gives a spoken account and a written one, or two accounts at different times. Why: Discrepancies between accounts are the first lead in identifying inconsistencies.
- [procedure] 1) Record each statement in the order it was given. 2) Mark firsthand details separately from told or read details. 3) Compare prepared answers with recalled answers. 4) Flag any version that changed after a prompt or document.
- [procedure] 1) Record each version and who received it. 2) Ask what each witness could physically perceive. 3) Test whether each version fits the timeline and public records. When: when two parties describe one event differently. Why: the discrepancy is evaluated against each witness's access.
- [procedure] 1) Present disagreeing accounts side by side. 2) Let the player see which claims conflict. 3) Ensure at least one verifiable detail can settle each conflict. When: designing a mystery where witnesses disagree. Why: The player must decide which facts can be verified, so each contradiction needs a checkable resolution.
- [procedure] 1) List every statement with its date and speaker. 2) Mark who first introduced the claim. 3) Weigh earlier recorded accounts above later revised ones. When: When a witness's story has changed or a claim may have been suggested. Why: Earlier accounts are less shaped by later pressure or retraction.
- [procedure] 1) Find the original file behind a published account. 2) Check each cited document's date and whether it was presented at the proceeding. 3) Note exculpatory material the account omits. 4) Judge whether the writer knew of it. When: A published account and an original file both exist. Why: Exclusions and misdated evidence are visible only in the original.
- [procedure] 1) Date each statement by one source. 2) Note its intended audience. 3) Note its purpose. 4) Decide which version to trust using those three facts. When: two statements by one source disagree. Why: date, audience and purpose reveal the pressures that shaped each version.
- [procedure] 1) Let the player interview several NPCs who claim to have been present. 2) Collect their versions, which may contradict each other. 3) Treat the chain of who told whom as the puzzle to solve. When: when designing an event witnessed in fragments by several NPCs. Why: Contradictions require the player to reconstruct the sequence.
- [procedure] 1) Compare reports from two observers standing at the same spot. 2) Check light, angle and position at that moment. 3) Accept the alarming report only if the physical conditions support it. When: when two observers of the same spot report different things. Why: A second viewpoint can expose an ordinary cause.
- [procedure] 1) Compare competing accounts of the same events. 2) Weigh each by detail, caution and inclusion of key documents. 3) Note what is missing. 4) Trace the status of any lost source through correspondence about it. When: Testimony about one case exists in more than one version, or a source is lost. Why: Comparing accounts and tracing provenance reveals which record is most reliable even when the best source is gone.
- [procedure] 1) Place each witness's interpretation beside rival interpretations. 2) Identify what each witness gains from a particular reading. 3) Weigh the accounts against independent evidence before settling on one. When: Two or more witnesses offer conflicting explanations of the same event. Why: Motive and partial knowledge can bias each account, so none should be accepted alone.
- [pitfall] Witnesses who disagree on a person's description or a key object weaken any identification built on it, since inconsistent details cannot merge into one reliable image. When: When several witnesses describe the same person or object differently. Why: Inconsistent details do not combine into a single trustworthy likeness; disagreement undermines the shared basis for identification.
- [pitfall] A mismatch between traces, such as a lens fitted to an older person than the body, is a reason to look closer, not a conclusion.
- [pitfall] A precise threshold invites narrow, contested testimony, so every witness account may be treated as suspect when stakes are clear. When: Witnesses must fix an exact time that decides an outcome. Why: Interested parties have reason to shade precise timing claims.
- [pitfall] Speaking freely in a contested forum can hand the opposing side a formal charge, so statements should use exact, defensible wording. When: a statement is made where it can be formally tested. Why: loose words can become legal grounds against the speaker.
- [pitfall] Recording a claim beside facts that contradict it, with neither tested, gives the claim standing it has not earned.
- [pitfall] When a tenant and an owner both claim the land, the question of who may speak for it is itself contested. When: Tenant and owner both assert a claim to the same property. Why: Competing claims make authority over the land part of the dispute.

## grudges and feuds
- [model] Model property and inheritance records as a searchable motive system, letting players trace deeds and probate documents to find who gained, lost or was trusted.
- [definition] A grievance plot is driven by a rising run of small humiliations and quarrels, and its central question is who is deceiving whom, not a single whodunit.
- [mechanism] Grudges outlive their holder: resentment over a lost inheritance passes to heirs, and faction resentment spreads house to house, keeping hostility toward later leaders. When: a family member lost money through a passed-over inheritance. Why: a grudge can outlive the person who first felt it. (x2)
- [mechanism] A quarrel over a boundary, shared property or livestock plants a grudge that resurfaces as a formal accusation and can draw in a wider circle of people. When: after a dispute between neighbours over a boundary or livestock. Why: unresolved grievances persist and get reused when a new accusation is needed.
- [mechanism] A private dispute can draw in neighbors through testimony and gossip, so people with no stake in it still take sides. When: a dispute is discussed publicly or given as evidence. Why: testimony and talk spread involvement beyond the parties.
- [mechanism] Accomplice NPCs with grudges can leak information when offered protection, so distrust can be modelled as a stat that changes what each NPC reveals. When: When designing NPCs whose willingness to share depends on relationships. Why: Grudges lower loyalty, making protection a lever that opens disclosure.
- [mechanism] A change made in many small steps can pass every single check, so only the trend across checks reveals it. When: Appearance or identity changes over time. Why: No single check sees a break.
- [mechanism] A grudge can pass through family ties: a refused match between two households can later reach a third person through a marriage link. Why: Kinship links carry old disputes into new accusations.
- [mechanism] A prolonged estate dispute can strain a whole household and may contribute to later distress in one of its members. Why: The strain is a plausible contributing cause, not a proven one.
- [mechanism] Encode NPC relationships as a graph of marriages, inheritances and alliances, and let grudges propagate along those edges to new NPCs. When: when designing NPC relationships in a game.
- [mechanism] Repeated land lawsuits keep contested claims in public view and sustain feuds between neighbours over many years. Why: Each new filing reopens the dispute in front of the community.
- [mechanism] A boundary defined by a particular house can turn a small dispute into a dispute over the whole community.
- [mechanism] A map layer of land claims and parish lines defines which NPCs side with which faction, so a boundary change creates new suspects.
- [mechanism] A relationship or grudge flag that changes how later clues are read lets a past dispute distort the player's interpretation of evidence, and each rumour's source should be visible.
- [mechanism] An NPC's acceptance of a player's accusation can depend on the strength of the evidence and the NPC's standing with other characters. When: In quest and faction design. Why: Credibility is shaped by both proof and social standing.
- [mechanism] Track rumours along NPC relationships, so a grudge between two NPCs raises the chance that one accuses the other, and the player can trace who started the story.
- [behavior] Misfortunes, such as illness after a rival's visit or a run of mishaps after a dispute, get blamed on the feud, since an existing quarrel supplies a ready cause. When: harm follows soon after a visit or confrontation with a rival, or a run of misfortunes follows a dispute. Why: the existing grudge or quarrel supplies a ready cause.
- [behavior] A judgment of a new person can rest on earlier grief or resentment toward someone similar, so the verdict reflects the past more than the present. When: a character judges a person resembling a lost or disliked one. Why: prior loss shapes present perception.
- [behavior] A witness report can be honest and still unreliable, because grief and anger fill in what was not observed. When: A witness who suffered loss reports events. Why: Strong emotion supplies the missing details.
- [behavior] A grieving or horrified witness describes the victim's body in emotional terms, and the first impression is dominated by the body rather than by the surroundings. When: when a witness first encounters a death scene. Why: strong emotion takes over attention, so the room is recorded later.
- [behavior] A witness with a grudge may volunteer complaints about a third party that a neutral witness would keep back. When: a witness has a personal grievance.
- [behavior] A witness's grief at seeing evidence can show that the working theory is wrong, so the investigator should revise it rather than defend it.
- [behavior] Suspicion often follows existing quarrels, property disputes and family tensions more than fresh evidence. When: when a new accusation targets someone already in conflict. Why: people reach for a known grievance to explain events.
- [behavior] When a legal dispute stalls, disputants often move the contest onto the ground, such as by felling a disputed tree or mustering crews. When: when a land dispute fails in court. Why: physical contest continues where legal channels have failed.
- [behavior] Grief over a death can push a person to blame a nearby figure for it, so emotional strain can act as a hidden motive for an accusation. When: an accuser has recently lost someone close. Why: Blaming someone gives the loss a target. This is a hypothesis to test, not a fact.
- [behavior] A pending land lawsuit can make a rival a source of sworn accusations, and the accused may still never be tried.
- [behavior] Communities tend to treat whoever clears and fences land as its rightful owner, since labor is seen as adding most of its value. When: land is cleared and improved by a settler. Why: labor is seen as the main source of land value.
- [behavior] An accusation from a witness with a long-held grudge is easy to dismiss, because the listener sees the accuser's bias and stops there. When: the accuser has a long-standing grievance. Why: bias is visible and tempting to treat as the answer.
- [behavior] Boundary controversies between neighbors can later aggravate larger feuds that surface under pressure, even when each quarrel was handled courteously at the time. When: when a land quarrel between households precedes a larger conflict. Why: earlier disputes leave a ledger of grievance that later conflicts draw on.
- [rule] Record disputes such as boundaries, debts or broken promises as discoverable motives, and let a rival's accusation point to an older grudge revealed through household or property records. When: when building a motive for an NPC-driven crime or designing accusation quests. Why: Discoverable motives let players judge plausibility.
- [rule] Let an NPC's old grudge or minor insult become a rumour that grows as characters repeat it, each repetition tied to a named accuser. When: designing village rumour systems.
- [rule] Plant an NPC with a grudge against another as a red herring, and reward the player for recognizing the grudge as the motive behind the accusation.
- [rule] Use a grudge as motive only when a source ties it to the act itself, not merely to the suspect's character or past quarrels. When: when a grudge is offered as the motive for an accusation. Why: an older quarrel does not establish that the suspect committed a new act.
- [rule] A witness's quarrel with the accused explains why they may speak, but does not by itself show that their account is false. When: When judging a witness with a known dispute. Why: A motive makes an account suspect, not wrong; its content must be checked separately.
- [rule] Give each suspect a motive the player can rate, and let a weak motive still matter when combined with other clues. When: Designing suspect motives in a generated mystery. Why: Players weigh motives, and weak ones gain value through combination.
- [rule] Design NPC motives so one motive explains two roles, and let the player find the link through evidence. When: When designing linked NPCs in a mystery. Why: One motive connecting two roles rewards deduction.
- [rule] Model property boundaries and shared fences as triggers for disputes, and track each NPC's grudges over time so they can later become accusations. When: when generating neighbouring households or villages. Why: boundary disputes give durable, traceable motives.
- [rule] Store grudges with timestamps and let them fade, so an NPC acts on an old feud only while the grudge is still held. When: NPCs carry memories of past incidents. Why: Stale grudges create false motives.
- [heuristic] A grudge shows who had a reason to act, not who did, so check opportunity and whether the money would have passed to them anyway. (x2)
- [heuristic] Treat an accusation from someone with a grievance against the accused as a lead to test, not a finding, because a grudge can steer testimony. When: a suspect is named by a person with a personal grudge, or a witness points at a household member. Why: a grudge can steer testimony.
- [heuristic] Before accepting an accusation that matches a grudge, ask who supplied it, who quarrelled with whom, and who gains from the outcome, since the grudge may have produced it.
- [heuristic] A dispute record can supply a suspect's motive without revealing who acted, so players can use it as a lead rather than a verdict. When: Designing a motive for a suspect in an investigation. Why: Shared motive narrows suspicion but does not identify the actor.
- [heuristic] Informants with grievances, such as dismissed servants, can reveal internal household secrets but may exaggerate, so their claims need corroboration. Why: Grievance motivates disclosure and also distorts it.
- [heuristic] Judge a bereaved person's emotional demeanour against their relationship history and known character, not against a stock script of how grief should look. When: A witness's reaction after a death seems odd or muted. Why: People express loss differently, and relationship history often explains a reaction that a generic script would misread.
- [heuristic] A past partnership that ended in threats is worth testing as a motive, because the reason for violence is already on record. When: When a past dispute has been documented. Why: A recorded conflict gives a concrete reason rather than speculation.
- [heuristic] Resolve a feud gradually, removing root causes in well-timed steps, rather than relying on one decisive act. When: mediating a long-running conflict. Why: Root causes return if only the surface is addressed.
- [heuristic] When accused families hold land that rivals claim, old land grievances often overlap with the accusations.
- [heuristic] Map property stakes and grudges when several accusations come from one circle, since accusers may gain from the accused's seizure. When: several accusations come from the same circle.
- [heuristic] Let a rival NPC voice a suspicion so the player must test it rather than being told the answer.
- [heuristic] Allow small or personal motives, such as revenge or minor gain, to drive NPC plot events.
- [heuristic] Limit how many parallel secrets exist in one area so the mystery stays readable. When: Populating an area with side mysteries. Why: Too many simultaneous threads overwhelm the player.
- [heuristic] A grudge or a wish to protect one's position can colour every detail of an account, so each detail needs independent checking.
- [procedure] 1) Record which families sit on each committee or seat. 2) Trace recurring family names across years to follow a grudge over time. When: a community has long-kept records. Why: Recurring names expose enduring rivalries that single events hide.
- [pitfall] Accounts from someone holding a grudge are shaped by spite, so discount their harsh claims; a speaker's grudge or an observer's disapproval colours what gets reported. When: a witness has a visible grudge against the subject of their testimony. Why: Hostility shapes what a speaker emphasizes and how they describe others. (x2)
- [pitfall] Trusting a witness who holds a grudge, or an accusation it drives, can fix an investigation on the wrong person and waste the search for the real culprit.
- [pitfall] A document that records a family grievance creates a possible motive without proving the grievance led to an act. When: Evaluating a bitter document as motive. Why: Resentment recorded in writing is not the same as action taken on it.
- [pitfall] Witnesses may downplay a relationship or claim slight acquaintance, so casually described ties need corroboration from others.
- [pitfall] Mistaking a suspect's real grief or sincerity for proof of innocence, or accepting a folk ordeal as a valid test. When: Judging a suspect after an emotional scene. Why: Emotional sincerity and superstition do not establish facts.
- [pitfall] Taking a stated grievance at face value, without comparing it to what was already agreed, misreads the dispute.
- [pitfall] Buying unrelated goods to justify your presence costs time and money and can still fail if the subject leaves while you wait. Why: The cover consumes resources without guaranteeing the trail.
- [pitfall] Treating neighbours' quarrels and livestock losses as proof of guilt is fragile: an accuser acting from spite can break the whole chain. When: evidence is built from social grievances. Why: Small grievances can motivate the accuser, so the chain is only as reliable as its motives.
- [fact] A motive can originate in events long before the crime, such as a secret past that threatens a person's reputation or legitimacy. When: A crime is tied to a hidden history rather than a recent event.
- [fact] A witness who only fixes when they parted from a suspect sets a timeline boundary but does not prove where the suspect was during the crime.
- [fact] Disputes that move through petitions, town votes and higher approval leave a dated paper trail that shows how tension escalated.
- [fact] Creditors may pursue a deceased person's estate, or even the body, over debts, so grievances can continue after death through legal channels.
- [fact] Land disputes produce sworn depositions, lawsuits and lasting rivalries that record who had a stake in a boundary. When: Assessing who had an interest in a piece of land. Why: Disputes make the stakeholders and their claims visible in formal records.
- [fact] Legal fees and imprisonment costs can be paid by seizing a household's goods, so a lawsuit can fall on property itself. When: A family faces legal action and penalties. Why: Fees and costs may be recovered directly from movable possessions.
- [fact] Local sayings about a feud show that a community has already framed the grievance as a motive.

## absence as evidence
- [mechanism] A deliberate absence of a tell can itself signal that a character is hiding something.
- [mechanism] An unexplained absence following an unexplained scene can become the clue itself, holding the audience's question open until the cause is revealed. When: a figure vanishes without explanation. Why: the missing figure invites inference.
- [behavior] Once expected people are missing, others treat their absence as meaningful, so an absent person quickly becomes a default suspect.
- [behavior] People who stay away from public gatherings get marked as suspect once the crowd has committed to a cause. When: when a community is mobilised against suspects. Why: absence reads as disagreement with the group.
- [behavior] A key figure who is absent, glimpsed or only reported second-hand builds anticipation, so the audience expects the encounter before it arrives. When: setting up a major character or confrontation. Why: withheld presence keeps the audience waiting for the figure.
- [behavior] A host tends to read an absent invitee as a deliberate insult, though absences often have innocent causes.
- [behavior] An offender who shows no remorse may be isolated by others, who distrust him and give reasons that differ from the real ones. When: a character's lack of regret becomes known. Why: peers judge the person by visible guilt rather than the act alone.
- [behavior] A stated, ordinary plan, such as a visit to a relative with a planned pickup, explains a long absence and keeps it from looking suspicious. When: when someone is unseen for a long stretch. Why: an ordinary explanation accounts for the gap.
- [behavior] Observers treat absent signs, such as missing breath or no movement, as evidence, so silence itself comes to carry meaning.
- [rule] Absence alone is not proof of guilt; keep innocent causes like illness or servants' routes open, and do not accept a routine explanation until confirmed. When: A person is missing, unaccounted for, or absence is used as evidence of avoidance or guilt. Why: Absence has many innocent causes, and both guilt and innocence need evidence beyond the absence itself. (x2)
- [rule] Present an NPC's convenient absence or travel as a time window the player can plan around; it also constrains when the culprit can time a crime. When: Designing NPC travel or timing in a mystery. Why: Windows let the player plan and let the culprit time actions.
- [rule] Give an absent NPC a motive trail built from documents such as a map, letter or diary so the player can reconstruct the crime. When: when designing a crime in the player's past. Why: documents let the player reason backward to the motive.
- [rule] Record where blood is absent as well as where it is present, since missing blood on a hand or floor constrains how an act could have occurred. When: when documenting a scene with a wound. Why: Absences limit the possible sequence of actions.
- [rule] Check for expected traces that are missing, since their absence shows what probably did not happen.
- [rule] Check a reported absence, departure or illness by contacting the place the person should be, and do not accept the claim unconfirmed. When: A second party reports that someone left or is unavailable. Why: Reported absences are claims that need independent confirmation.
- [rule] Let gaps in the records be real, so the player infers events from surviving documents and places rather than finding a complete record. When: Designing the information available in a mystery. Why: Incomplete records make inference a real part of play.
- [rule] In an inventory system, the lack of expected accessories or duplicates can signal that a character never carried them, letting players deduce it. When: When designing character inventories that players can inspect. Why: Absence of expected items is readable as information.
- [rule] Before dismissing a missing item as unimportant, check whether it was actually expected at that location. When: an item's absence seems to have no obvious cause. Why: Assuming no one expected it skips the check that could reveal a meaningful gap.
- [rule] Use absence as storytelling: tracks with no livestock, or a patrol route with no guard, can signal that a disguise is in use.
- [rule] Place an absent object, such as a missing lamp, as a clue the player must notice and reason about.
- [rule] Design a timeline puzzle by giving each character an absence window so that exactly one window fits the event, and players must find it.
- [heuristic] A missing expected reaction, such as grief, pain, tears or a fit, is weak evidence of guilt, since age, illness, fear, pride or habitual silence can suppress it. When: A test relies on an expected bodily or emotional reaction. Why: Many innocent conditions suppress the reaction, and the same outward appearance can arise from different causes. (x2)
- [heuristic] A missing expected person or object is a clue only when an established routine or habitual baseline makes it expected; without a known baseline, do not over-read the gap. When: Someone or something is expected in a location and does not appear, or a gap is judged for meaning. Why: Breaking an established pattern makes a missing element significant; without a known baseline, a gap may be ordinary. (x2)
- [heuristic] A missing expected trace, like hoof marks, should be checked at the site before accepting a supernatural reading, since it counts against the claim that would have produced it. When: Testimony conflicts or a reported trace is missing or moved. Why: Absence is easy to over-interpret when the expected trace is not found. (x2)
- [heuristic] A missing expected item or presence, in a scene, body or routine, is as revealing as an unexpected one that turns up, and should prompt an explanation. When: When examining a scene, body, routine or belongings for clues. Why: An expected thing that is absent signals a change in events; checking absences against what is normally there reveals removal or hidden events.
- [heuristic] A missing valued or concealed item narrows suspects: its taker must have known it existed and had access, and the reason for taking it points to who wanted it. When: A private, concealed or valued item is absent from where it should be. Why: Taking an item requires knowing about it, and the reason for an absence points to who had access and what they wanted.
- [heuristic] A character absent from a key scene is evidence of a gap to investigate, not a neutral fact.
- [heuristic] Notice when a person who should have been present is missing, since that absence can be the result of a deliberate act. When: A scene lacks someone who normally or expectedly would be there. Why: Engineered absence removes a witness and can hide a second actor.
- [heuristic] A missing action that an innocent person would normally take can be evidence, because its absence points toward knowledge or guilt. When: a key person fails to do what they would be expected to do. Why: innocent people usually act to clear themselves, so their silence is informative.
- [heuristic] Ask whether an absence fits the other known facts; if it needs its own separate explanation, the inference drawn from it is weaker.
- [heuristic] When someone fails to know a widely reported event, treat that gap as a clue about where they were.
- [heuristic] Note what reports leave out. Gaps mark where to seek details from the people directly involved. When: public records give few details. Why: the missing parts need primary sources.
- [heuristic] A missing part of a matched pair suggests the item was disposed of nearby, so start an investigation from what is absent.
- [heuristic] Treat missing traces, such as absent blood or a missing ticket, as evidence that points to where an event happened.
- [heuristic] A scene can be read by what it lacks, such as missing stuffed gaps or an unblocked transom, to narrow the possible routes.
- [heuristic] A theory that depends on an absence, such as no wound, can be exposed by a single later test of that absence. When: Checking a theory that assumes something did not happen. Why: One test can falsify a claim that rests on something missing.
- [heuristic] Build a payoff where the expected target is absent and a different one takes its place, with earlier hints the player could have caught.
- [heuristic] A deleted line, blank stretch or sudden silence in a written account can indicate what the writer avoided, and should be weighed as a possible signal. When: Reading a written account or witness testimony for clues. Why: Writers often leave out what they did not want revealed.
- [heuristic] Treat an expected event or object that is missing as evidence in itself. Ask what should have happened and did not, and require any theory to explain that gap. When: A theory feels complete but has not been checked against what did not happen. Why: Missing expected details reveal intent, pace or care that present details alone do not show.
- [heuristic] An expected item that is missing from a person's usual state, such as jewellery a visitor would normally wear, can serve as a clue to an earlier event. When: A person's appearance does not match their usual habits. Why: Absences from normal patterns are informative when the pattern is well established.
- [heuristic] An abandoned location can carry a timeline the player reconstructs from an NPC's account and traces such as moved furniture or a dropped key.
- [heuristic] An empty space can be evidence: a vacant spot marks where an object used to be and can be read like a present object.
- [heuristic] An absence of footprints on a surface below an entry point can indicate that no one landed there, which the player must reason about. When: when examining the ground beneath a window or drop. Why: Missing traces constrain how an intruder could have entered or left.
- [heuristic] An absent item is not proof of wrongdoing, since it may have been moved legitimately.
- [heuristic] Do not treat a missing sign as proof alone; it gains weight only when a later test confirms a second cause. When: when using an absent or contrary result as an investigative clue. Why: An anomaly without confirmation can mislead the investigator.
- [procedure] 1) Model the person's habits and the items they imply. 2) List what they usually owned, bought or carried. 3) Compare recovered items against that list; treat each unaccounted item as an open question. 4) Search the most likely storage places thoroughly. 5) If none are found, conclude it was probably never present, provisionally; revise if it turns up. When: An expected item cannot be found or a scene is checked for gaps. Why: A gap is visible only against a known baseline, and a thorough search makes the absence conclusion trustworthy.
- [procedure] 1) List what was removed. 2) List what was left. 3) Find the element common to the removed items. 4) Use that element as the motive clue. When: when damage or loss looks organized.
- [tradeoff] Lack of sightings can be informative when nearby people are busy, but silence means little when witnesses were not positioned or expected to observe or report. When: When asking witnesses whether they saw someone leave or return, or inferring from absence of reports. Why: Busy observers miss unnoticed departures, so silence reflects attention and position rather than absence. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Absent marks suggest no passage only where the surface would record it, like soft ground after rain showing only investigators' prints; on surfaces that hold no traces, absence proves nothing. When: When reading a scene for entry, exit or route evidence. Why: Passage leaves marks only on surfaces that record it, so a clean surface shows nobody else passed only in that case.
- [tradeoff] Absent residue on expected surfaces can rule out a mechanism, but a missing weapon, cloth or trace cannot prove no method was used; absence settles only what tests could detect. When: When using missing residue or traces to rule a method in or out; choose which tests are worth running.
- [pitfall] Silence in a report or record does not prove an event or claim never happened; it may fall in a blind spot, so treat the gap as a question. Why: A report may omit a fact because it was never recorded, and some families had disappeared or received no notice. (x3)
- [pitfall] Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; a missing witness does not prove no one was present, so inference from what is missing stays provisional.
- [pitfall] Absence-based deductions, like no footprints or dry clothing, are weak unless the search covered where a rival would leave traces and the evidence should have appeared. When: A search finds nothing or a deduction relies on something missing. Why: Silence supports a theory only when the search could have detected the rival's traces.
- [pitfall] An absence can support almost any theory, so a missing-item investigation can end in dead ends.
- [pitfall] Nobody having suspected anything is not evidence that nothing happened; an error can stay hidden until a sealed space is opened years later.
- [pitfall] A conviction obtained in default rests on the accused's absence and says nothing about guilt in itself. When: Interpreting a verdict reached without the accused present. Why: The verdict reflects procedure and absence, not an evaluation of the evidence against the person.
- [pitfall] An expected person's absence is easy to overlook as routine, though it can contradict a stated plan. When: Reviewing a timeline for missing people. Why: Absences look normal unless compared against the plan.
- [pitfall] Absence and a shared common object are not proof of guilt, yet they can build a convincing false lead. When: a suspect is absent and matches a common clue. Why: many people share the same trait or circumstance.
- [pitfall] Lack of rebuttal may reflect limited access rather than truth, so establish whether rivals could actually read and answer the account before inferring its accuracy.
- [pitfall] A departed visitor is not evidence of who the visitor was; treating an absence as proof of identity is an unsupported inference.
- [pitfall] A clean-looking cloth does not prove a stain was absent, because what the cloth shows depends on how it was handled. Why: handling can remove or hide a stain.
- [pitfall] Assuming an item was burned or destroyed ends the search too early; partial survival such as a half-burnt item may still be enough.
- [pitfall] Sending away the only witness can itself draw notice, because an unusual absence of staff becomes a pattern that others can observe. When: A suspect removes servants or observers to cover a movement. Why: Unusual absences are noticeable in their own right.
- [pitfall] Silence in response to an appeal can be read as refusal or death, but it may simply reflect an unrecognised name. Why: Non-response has several causes that the notice itself cannot distinguish.
- [pitfall] Indirect answers can carry no information when the witness lacks the relevant knowledge, so a null answer should not be read as evidence of absence. When: an investigator interprets an answer that avoids the target subject. Why: A witness who knows nothing relevant gives an answer that looks informative but tells nothing.
- [fact] A person who is missing and whose body is not found does not automatically count as dead, because no positive proof of death exists. When: A character's status is uncertain and no body or direct evidence is available. Why: Lack of a body leaves death unproven, so a formal finding of death requires more than absence.
- [fact] Absence of fingerprints does not show the offender feared prints, since gloves explain it equally well. When: when interpreting a clean scene. Why: a gloved offender leaves no prints without any deliberate wiping.

## physical evidence and traces
- [definition] Circumstantial evidence links modest facts through time, place and records, without an eyewitness; none proves the act alone, but together they can implicate even the least likely person. When: No direct proof or witness exists and the case must be built from documents and dates. Why: Convergence of connected circumstances can establish a conclusion that no single fact shows.
- [mechanism] When a character removes or lures a nearby observer, the set of characters able to witness other actions changes, altering what the world notices. When: A player or NPC sends away, distracts or lures a guard or witness. Why: Observation depends on who is present, so removing one observer opens unwatched space.
- [mechanism] The route to a protected suspect can itself reveal evidence, and a disorienting route prevents the investigator from later reconstructing how they arrived. When: A suspect is reached through a long, dim or shifting route. Why: Disorientation erases the investigator's memory of the path while the setting still tells something about the person.
- [mechanism] Linking two locations through one shared object gives the investigator a route between them and a second place to search.
- [mechanism] A group's verdict on a speaker, once settled, persists and gets reinforced by later discussion, outliving the remark that caused it. When: A reputation has formed in a group. Why: People interpret new evidence to fit the existing verdict.
- [mechanism] Limited light radius leaves the upper part of a room in darkness, which can make the space seem taller than it is. When: An observer relies on lamplight in a dim room. Why: Unlit regions are lost from view, so the perceived dimensions drift from the actual ones.
- [mechanism] A mundane cause can explain early anomalies, then a later clue the cause cannot explain reveals a deeper source. When: when structuring a mystery over time. Why: The unexplained residue appears only after the mundane answer has been accepted.
- [mechanism] Being the last person seen with a victim places that person at the centre of the timeline, making their account decisive. When: when reconstructing the final movements of a victim. Why: The last contact is the reference point for everything that follows.
- [mechanism] Open safes, ransacked boxes and stripped fittings can contradict a suicide story and point to a slow, deliberate robbery.
- [mechanism] Physical traces such as trampled ground, drag marks, and a repurposed cloth can show that one actor did the work, undermining a group theory.
- [mechanism] Pair a mechanical clue with a human motive, so one device explains both the original death and a later death. Why: A device linked to a motive explains more than one event.
- [behavior] Involuntary reactions escape control: a brief change in expression can expose known hidden information, and a flinch when a covered area is touched can reveal a concealed mark. When: A suspect sees unexpected evidence, or a concealed bodily mark is suspected; provoke the reaction rather than asking directly. Why: Reactions escape control for a moment and are harder to control than spoken answers.
- [behavior] Household members notice distress signs, such as red eyes after lawyer visits or long closed-door talks, which signal conflict before any proof exists. When: When a conflict is developing privately. Why: Visible changes in habit reveal tension early.
- [behavior] A careful hoaxer can restore disturbed objects, but traces such as wet prints and displaced items can remain. When: When checking a staged event for evidence of tampering. Why: Restoration hides some traces but rarely removes all of them.
- [rule] Plant a small voice or phrase clue, and log every detail the player sees, so an idle-seeming detail returns as proof in the reveal. When: Authoring clues in a mystery scene. Why: Rereading or a returning detail turns an overlooked item into proof once the truth is known, rewarding attention. (x2)
- [rule] Design a chain of independent physical traces, such as ash, wax, an unlit grate or a ledger entry, linking across rooms and NPCs to a culprit or mechanism. When: Designing a mystery with physical evidence. Why: Linked traces reward observation, and several unrelated matches are harder to dismiss than a single clue.
- [rule] Give each found or staged object a precise, checkable physical detail, such as a time, engraving, length or placement, so players can test a theory or confession. When: Writing or introducing a physical clue meant to support a theory or a staged tool. Why: A checkable detail can be compared against other facts, turning acceptance into testing.
- [rule] Use a depiction as an impression that raises suspicion, not as proof, when a portrait or document image is evidence about a person. When: A portrait or document image is part of the evidence.
- [rule] Use a physical comparison between a trace and a known reference, so the player's deduction can be checked rather than guessed.
- [rule] Do not release a lure where a false alarm would cost the investigation its credibility.
- [rule] Ask what was not searched as well as what was; log every container and piece of furniture checked and leave gaps to be revisited. When: A search for a person or object in a room is being assessed. Why: A search carried out to find a person, rather than to check every hiding place, can miss the person hidden there.
- [rule] Design a household that maintains a pretence to reveal its real beliefs under pressure or through small slips. When: Building characters who hide beliefs behind a shared fiction. Why: Pressure and slips expose beliefs that the fiction conceals.
- [heuristic] Check every link in a circumstantial chain: one missing or unprovable link weakens the whole inference and can free a suspect. When: Building a case from several modest linked clues, where no single fact is decisive. Why: Each inference depends on the one before, so chains are only as strong as their weakest link.
- [heuristic] Answer a prosecution chain of inferences one link at a time rather than only rebutting the overall story. When: When a case is built from a sequence of linked claims. Why: A weak link can break the chain even when the overall story sounds plausible.
- [heuristic] Listeners often read an ironic remark literally and reason from that reading as if it were a serious argument, which can seal a damaging label. When: A character's remark has two possible readings. Why: Literal interpretation is the default when the irony is not signaled.
- [heuristic] Match a bite by its gaps and irregularities, such as a missing tooth in each jaw, rather than overall shape; a person with a full, regular set cannot have made it.
- [heuristic] Separation by pulling and separation by a blade leave different marks; the absence of blade marks suggests the bones were pulled apart. When: Determining how bones were separated from one another. Why: Cutting and pulling produce distinct traces on bone surfaces.
- [heuristic] A closing explanation can resolve the main question and leave minor details open, which makes the world feel larger than the player's knowledge. When: The main mystery is solved but the setting should feel deeper. Why: Some open detail signals a world beyond what the player has learned.
- [heuristic] When a standing restriction lapses or an owner dies, ask who gains control and who is affected, to find the parties with a stake. When: A restriction, charter or shared right changes hands. Why: A lapse shifts who can act, so it reveals who benefits.
- [heuristic] Test a claimed account against where an object was found; if the claimed actor could not have reached that spot, the account conflicts with the evidence. When: A reported self-inflicted or staged account is given.
- [heuristic] Hesitation, such as hanging back before one person goes to a target, is a behavioural clue worth recording.
- [heuristic] Physical trace reading is less useful when the scene has been cleared or the setup happened elsewhere.
- [heuristic] A planted item made from a traceable source can betray its maker, since its fit with another fragment shows a shared origin.
- [heuristic] Demonstrate the investigator's method in an unrelated scene before the crime is described, so the reader trusts the later reading.
- [heuristic] Use a lure built from the villain's own medium, such as a note in the code they use, to force contact.
- [heuristic] Let an ambiguous household trace, such as extra food or ash, carry the proof, provided it is backed by physical evidence.
- [heuristic] Use an injury, such as a sprained ankle or a stocking-clad foot, as physical evidence that points at the wrong person, making the reader's suspicion feel earned. When: a suspect's body shows a clue that resembles the culprit's. Why: A bodily sign is persuasive, so the false lead convinces the reader before it is overturned.
- [heuristic] Explain the mechanism of a trap or clue by demonstrating it to a character who witnesses it, so the explanation is shown rather than only told. When: Resolving a clue whose logic the player must understand. Why: A demonstration makes the solution vivid and verifiable.
- [procedure] 1) Publish a notice in a public channel that names the target's known connection, such as a ship, place or guild. 2) Promise secrecy and a private meeting time. 3) Wait for the target to respond. When: The target is known to be connected to a specific name or place. Why: A notice tied to a known connection draws out the intended person through their recognition of it.
- [procedure] 1) Revisit the scene and compare it with the written account. 2) Note what is missing, out of place or discarded. 3) Walk any claimed route to test whether it is possible. When: a scene can still be examined.
- [procedure] 1) Record the scene, including labels, bottles and loose papers, before anyone tidies it. 2) Only then allow clearing and handling. When: a death scene is being investigated.
- [procedure] 1) Hide the identity of each sample from the examiner. 2) Mix the suspect's sample among known control samples. 3) Record the examiner's identifications and compare them against the true sources. When: When an identification must be defensible and chance could explain a correct match. Why: Hiding identities prevents the examiner's expectations from influencing the match.
- [procedure] 1) Oil the object to protect it. 2) Cast the clearest impression in quick-setting plaster. 3) Fit the object back onto the mold to see whether the projections fill a suspect's teeth gaps. 4) Make a second mold from the same object and compare the two. When: When a bite or patterned mark is left on an object that can be preserved and cast. Why: Casting captures the impression, and fitting tests whether a suspect's teeth match.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain a map of the scene 2) check spatial relations between places 3) test whether a witness's route or distance is physically possible. When: when a case depends on where things happened.
- [procedure] 1) Watch the suspect's residence to learn their routine. 2) Create a moment when they believe they are alone. 3) Give them a reason to retrieve the hidden item. 4) Observe or swap the item before they can check it. When: when a suspect is known to hide an item and return to check it. Why: A suspect who believes they are unobserved is likely to reveal their interest.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the bones with possible sources. 2) Note that graveyard bones are usually weathered and incomplete. 3) Note that dealer and dissecting-room bones often carry drilled holes or red-lead marks. 4) Choose the source that fits the traces. When: Identifying where a set of bones probably came from. Why: Each source leaves characteristic marks that distinguish it from others.
- [procedure] 1) Record the claimed event with an instrument the believers do not control. 2) Place the recorder while the believer is absent, and remove any sign of setup. 3) Review the trace for the pattern of events. 4) Locate the source by testing surfaces for matching sounds. When: An effect is claimed to be non-physical and can be measured. Why: An independent record separates the event from the witness's account.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether the dispute assumes only two states and look for a third condition. 2) Focus on the disputed object and how it behaves under real conditions. 3) Test the candidate mechanism against the recorded facts, including environment and equipment state. 4) Use any independent technical check to confirm whether the mechanism was altered. When: Two sworn accounts clash and the disputed physical object is central. Why: A mechanism that makes both accounts true can resolve a contradiction without a liar.
- [procedure] 1) List every way the suspect could have carried out the harm. 2) Record where the suspect was at that time. 3) Keep only methods the suspect could physically have used. When: when assessing whether a suspect could have caused an incident. Why: A plausible method is worthless without access and opportunity at the moment it mattered.
- [procedure] 1) Post a lure that draws the real culprit to a set place. 2) Lock the exit behind them. 3) Reveal a weapon to force a confession.
- [procedure] 1) Gather traces the player can collect, such as possessions and skill marks. 2) Infer the culprit's profile from them. 3) Bait a trap that draws a matching person to a chosen room. Why: the lure becomes an earned step rather than a guess.
- [tradeoff] Reconstructing the physical scene can reveal a hidden mechanism without witnesses, yet physical traces can suggest a false cause that testimony must correct. When: When a case rests on physical clues: reconstruct to show the mechanism, and check each inference against testimony when no eyewitness confirms it. Why: Scenes can show mechanisms directly, while witnesses can correct traces that suggest false causes. (x2)
- [tradeoff] An unauthorised search risks an investigator's career even when it succeeds, so searching requires proper authority. When: Considering a search without formal permission. Why: Acting outside authority exposes the investigator to dismissal regardless of outcome.
- [pitfall] Labelling an act as 'mad' replaces the question of what can be proven and closes investigation early; keep the diagnosis and the evidence separate. When: Explaining an odd event or behaviour with a diagnosis or label. Why: Labels stop investigation before the evidence is examined and hide the purpose of the act.
- [pitfall] A single physical mark does not prove guilt, since it may have another cause and an observer can misread its color or age. When: Drawing conclusions from one physical trace. Why: Alternative causes and reading error are both possible.
- [pitfall] Hindsight makes a chain of events look inevitable, though the path to a discovery was often fragile and accidental. When: When explaining or evaluating how a discovery was reached. Why: After the fact, minor accidents are reinterpreted as deliberate steps.
- [pitfall] Clues written as ordinary words or phrases can hide their meaning; a reader who takes the wording at face value misses the reference. When: clue text that uses a local term or place name. Why: readers assume ordinary meaning unless prompted otherwise.
- [pitfall] A lure frightens innocent people as well as guilty ones, so a reaction does not by itself prove guilt.
- [pitfall] Overlooking the object that explains how a victim was incapacitated can stall an investigation.
- [pitfall] Finding an object at a place shows that a visit happened there, but not when it happened. When: An item is discovered at a location during a timeline reconstruction. Why: Presence at a place does not fix the time of the visit.
- [fact] A witness who cannot read cannot check a written record put to them, so their answers rest on memory alone. When: questioning a witness about documents. Why: reading is needed to verify written content.
- [fact] The arrangement of teeth in a bite can be distinctive enough to help identify its maker, much as a thumbprint or signature does.
- [fact] A stopped clock or other striking detail can draw remark while proving nothing about the event. When: When a conspicuous object seems to offer a clue. Why: Vivid details attract attention regardless of their evidential value.
- [fact] Ordinary arrangements such as furniture set for an absent person or doors held open can serve as traces pointing to a second party.
- [fact] A sealed container can be imaged with X-ray to reveal its contents without opening it. When: Contents must be known without destroying the container. Why: Imaging shows internal contents while leaving the container intact.
- [fact] A rough surface produces an irregular spot border regardless of drop height, so surface texture must be considered before reading height.
- [fact] Routine chores such as dusting leave traces of who opened a container, even when the container was never locked. Why: Dust on ledges shows that drawers had to be opened to be cleaned.

## pressing and confronting suspects
- [mechanism] A confession can be obtained by confronting one NPC's testimony with another's contradicting account. When: Designing interrogation mechanics with multiple witnesses. Why: Presenting a contradiction forces the witness to revise or admit the truth.
- [mechanism] A false claim by a witness or staff member can point the player toward the wrong suspect until a physical object contradicts it. When: claim conflicts with an object found on the premises.
- [behavior] A detail that witnesses disagree on, such as a closed window, often surfaces only under repeated questioning, and each disagreement becomes a lead. When: Multiple witnesses describe the same physical detail differently. Why: Pressing for detail exposes conflicts that a single account hides.
- [behavior] A witness confronted with the exact words of a quarrel may admit the quarrel but refuse to state its subject. When: when a quoted phrase exposes a partial account. Why: admitting the event is easier than naming its cause.
- [behavior] Pressing an evasive speaker can make the questioner look rude, so a deflection works socially even when it answers nothing.
- [rule] Confront a suspect only when the proof is complete and each link can be stated clearly, since any gap lets the suspect deny or counter and destroy evidence. When: Choosing when to confront a suspect. Why: An incomplete confrontation warns the suspect and lets evidence be destroyed; premature confrontation gives openings to deny. (x2)
- [rule] Confront only with solid dated evidence, and ease pressure on sick, distressed, dying or fragile witnesses, since forced answers may be unreliable and excess pressure can cause collapse or self-harm. When: Questioning a frail, distressed or frightened witness. Why: Fear makes witnesses withdraw or reshape answers; excess pressure can cause harm and produce no useful admission. (x2)
- [rule] Gate a confrontation on the player holding a proven fact or enough collected contradictions, so it has a checkable basis and is not run without evidence. When: Gating NPC confrontations or scheduling a confrontation scene. Why: A confrontation without proof can fail with nothing learned or test nothing.
- [rule] Confront a bluffing suspect by opening with undeniable concrete items, naming corroborating witnesses, showing physical evidence, and laying out each detail rather than one accusation. When: The suspect tries to deny or bluster during a confrontation with real evidence. Why: Undeniable, complete specifics are harder to deflect and establish credibility before harder claims are made.
- [rule] Test a strong motive by asking whether it explains the act itself, not only why the suspect is blamed. When: a suspect has a clear motive.
- [rule] Before accepting a grudge as the explanation for an accusation, test the actual claim, since a motive explanation can be plausible yet untested. When: deciding whether a grudge explains an accusation away.
- [rule] Fire the confrontation event at the moment the player presents the final piece of proof, not earlier in the sequence.
- [rule] Confront a suspect publicly only when the evidence is strong enough that onlookers' reactions cannot stop the confrontation from succeeding. When: when planning an accusation in a crowded setting. Why: a weak case collapses under crowd pressure.
- [rule] Do not confront a suspect when the account could be overheard or key facts remain unverified, since an interruption can derail the decisive moment.
- [rule] Build a suspect's case from several weak clues, but include a contradiction the player can find, so a neat case is not automatically correct. When: Designing a suspect the player can build a case against. Why: A findable contradiction rewards checking instead of accepting the first tidy theory.
- [rule] Model a confrontation as a question sequence in which each answer unlocks the next fact the player can use.
- [rule] Do not accept a witness's first refusal as final; press for the account, since reluctance often reflects loyalty rather than falsehood. When: A witness declines to share what they heard. Why: Initial refusal is common and can be overcome by persistence.
- [heuristic] Test each link of an accusation chain separately, including awkward ones, since a suspect may steer attention toward a rival and an avoided question stays unresolved. When: a suspect points suspicion at another party. Why: A single persuasive chain can hide a weak or missing link.
- [heuristic] Press hardest on the points a witness hesitates over, such as who suggested an action or who forbade an appointment. When: during an interview where a witness pauses. Why: Hesitation marks where the withheld information lies.
- [heuristic] Test a proposed purpose for a victim against their clothing or state; attire that contradicts the purpose makes it unlikely. When: a victim's reason for leaving or acting is proposed.
- [heuristic] Avoid heavy pressure on a witness whose cooperation you still need, since pressure can produce a prepared answer.
- [heuristic] When a community turns against a successful member with no verifiable facts, test the claim against physical or documentary evidence wherever it exists. When: an accusation rests only on rumor. Why: Unverifiable claims cannot be settled by reputation.
- [heuristic] Build suspense in a confrontation with silences, repeated actions and objects knocked over during the conversation.
- [procedure] 1) Get the suspect to commit to a specific claim with a time and place. 2) Check it against an independent sighting or record they do not control. 3) Put any contradiction to them and note the answer or change. When: A statement conflicts with another witness or can be checked against an independent record. Why: A commitment makes the contradiction harder to escape; a verified contradiction tests the account directly. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Pick a specific fact you already hold that the suspect believes you know. 2) Confront them with it without revealing its source. 3) Note the details they give next. When: A witness refuses to answer or has given an incomplete account. Why: Naming a fact they think you hold prompts them to fill in details without exposing the source. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Obtain a third party's account of the suspect's whereabouts. 2) Confront the suspect with its specific claim rather than accepting or rejecting it outright. 3) Compare the two accounts detail by detail. When: a suspect's account conflicts with or supplements another witness. Why: Specific comparison reveals agreement and gaps.
- [procedure] 1) Hold the confrontation back until the audience has context. 2) Lengthen the approach with dim light, weather and a glimpsed figure. 3) Pause before entry, using a plea to add hesitation. 4) Close with a quiet remark looking back. When: building tension toward a key confrontation. Why: withholding and delaying the final step raises the weight of the moment.
- [procedure] 1) List every way in and out of the location. 2) Test the suspect theory against each route. 3) If the theory fails every route, discard it and check the remaining mechanisms. When: a convenient culprit is proposed for a locked or sealed scene.
- [procedure] 1) Check the scene geometry: exits, sightlines and who watches them. 2) Check the victim's known habits. 3) Check the logistics the theory needs. 4) If the theory fails, clear the suspect and shift to whoever has access, motive and means. When: when a dramatic suspect's route to the crime seems too easy. Why: Physical constraints can rule out an obvious culprit.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the accuser how they know the claim. 2) Check whether the timing fits the known events. 3) Check whether the accuser's motive fits. 4) Compare the claim with facts already established. When: A character points suspicion at another person. Why: A claim that fails these checks may be a red herring or deliberate misdirection.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the broad motive pool for all suspects. 2) Ask the accuser for specifics. 3) Test those specifics against scene facts, such as how each victim was struck. 4) Reject claims needing impossible sequences or two culprits. When: when one witness directly accuses another with little independent support. Why: Motivated accusations must be checked against facts before they are accepted.
- [procedure] 1) Identify what the act was meant to achieve. 2) Check whether that aim fits the suspect's temperament and goals. 3) If it does not fit, consider a different actor or motive. When: A crime detail is hard to explain. Why: Working from purpose narrows the explanations for an unusual act.
- [procedure] 1) Find when the alleged grudge began. 2) Compare that date with the date of the event. 3) If the relationship started after the event, reject the grudge as an explanation for the testimony. When: A witness is accused of acting from a prior quarrel. Why: A grudge cannot cause testimony that predates it.
- [procedure] 1) State the accusation plainly. 2) Watch for fear and loss of composure. 3) Threaten exposure to what the suspect values most. 4) Note any shift from defiance to bargaining. When: evidence is secure enough to accuse. Why: reactions and demands reveal what is at stake.
- [procedure] 1) State the claim's checkable prediction. 2) Search the most obvious place. 3) If it is empty, search a second place. 4) Rule out each rival explanation one at a time.
- [procedure] 1) State the suspicion. 2) Check it against the known routine and access rules. 3) Discard it if the routine makes it impossible. When: A witness offers an unfounded opinion. Why: Routine checks expose suspicions that rest on no basis.
- [procedure] 1) State the benefit given up. 2) List every rival explanation for giving it up. 3) Rule out those that fail. 4) Keep the remaining explanation provisional until an independent check confirms it.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whether one event could have caused the other. 2) Check what each person knew at that time. 3) Reject the link if either check fails. When: A suspected causal link between two events in a timeline.
- [procedure] 1) Name a plausible motive that the evidence suggests. 2) Offer an alternative explanation for it. 3) Watch the witness's response for shame or confusion. 4) If she shows neither, drop the motive and seek a different cause. When: A motive looks plausible but is unconfirmed. Why: A calm, unembarrassed reaction to the alternative rules out the suspected motive, forcing the investigator to find another explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Accept the witness's denial at first. 2) Arrange a second view where the suspect's full face is visible to the witness. 3) Point the suspect out again and watch for colour change or stillness. 4) Redirect the witness's gaze and watch whether the suspect relaxes. When: a witness's denial and a suspect's behaviour may disagree. Why: a visible reaction can contradict a verbal denial.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whether the suspicion comes mainly from personal dislike. 2) Test the suspect's motive. 3) Compare stated aims with conduct. 4) Weigh claimed sacrifices against known character. 5) Decide. When: a suspicion rests mainly on feeling and must be checked before acting or accusing. Why: feeling alone can mislead, so motive, statements and conduct give a firmer basis.
- [procedure] 1) Refuse to excuse a reluctant witness when you have the authority to insist. 2) Press persistently until the withheld answer is given. 3) Weigh the disclosure, since the witness may be shielding someone or hiding their own part. When: A witness's reluctance is itself a clue and the questioner can insist on an answer. Why: Persistent pressure can force disclosure of a third party's name.
- [procedure] 1) Rebuild the motive as a causal chain of steps. 2) Present the chain aloud to the suspect. 3) Invite correction. 4) Watch the suspect's response for signs of admission. When: Evidence supports a motive but not yet a confession. Why: A coherent chain that cannot be disputed can force an admission.
- [procedure] 1) Show the suspect that the evidence is complete and escape is impossible. 2) Reconstruct the crime step by step from known facts. 3) Watch the reaction. 4) Ask for the true account of the missing act. When: the facts are assembled and the suspect's own account is the missing piece. Why: reconstruction removes the suspect's grounds for denial.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the terms of the reward or agreement first. 2) State the accusation plainly, naming the responsible party. 3) Verify an outside fact before confronting. 4) Press for full detail until the account is complete. When: Revealing that a powerful or trusted figure is responsible. Why: Settled terms and verified facts prevent denial and make the confrontation effective.
- [procedure] 1) Check the outsider claim against physical traces, such as footmarks along the border. 2) Check it against conditions such as weather and lighting. When: when a single explanation depends on an unseen visitor. Why: Physical and environmental facts often contradict an unseen intruder.
- [procedure] 1) Gain access with a brief, pointed message. 2) Confront the suspect with knowledge that makes denial costly. 3) Let the suspect speak, then test each claim against facts. 4) Set terms using the threat of consequences. When: A suspect is guarded and holds information the investigator needs. Why: Known evidence makes denial costly and draws out a fuller account.
- [procedure] 1) Hear the witness's simple account. 2) Test it against independent physical traces such as a route or timing. 3) When the account conflicts with the traces, recite the full checked route. 4) Press with a direct accusation to force the witness to respond. When: A witness's account includes a route or timing that physical evidence can check. Why: Presenting a verified sequence leaves the witness no room to dispute details.
- [procedure] 1) Weigh how unlikely the match is, and check whether the matching item is common. 2) Test each profile trait separately: means, knowledge, skill, access. 3) Widen the pool to everyone with the same access. 4) Weigh motive and relationship. 5) Check whether the suspect could have learned the knowledge innocently. When: a clue appears to name a particular person. Why: Keeps a match a hypothesis until independent evidence supports it.
- [procedure] 1) Narrate the full sequence with times and each person's moves, including disposal of evidence. 2) Ask the listener to check each step. 3) Note what they correct, since corrections reveal what they most want to protect. When: the suspect has already been placed at the location by evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the claim the sworn alibi cannot explain. 2) Name the specific lie, not the broader crime. 3) Apply pressure through what the suspect stands to lose. 4) Obtain a detailed admission. 5) Check one detail against independent facts before accepting it. When: a sworn account conflicts with other testimony. Why: a specific lie is easier to address than a general accusation.
- [procedure] 1) Gather facts about the witness's past before the interview. 2) Put them one at a time in rapid succession, so each question names a real event. 3) Watch for the witness's physical reaction. When: when a witness may hide a past. Why: Specific, prepared facts make evasion harder.
- [procedure] 1) State the wrongdoing plainly and say the truth is wanted. 2) Ask one narrow question that is hard to dodge. 3) Give the witness a reason to talk. 4) Follow up on a related point. When: questioning a frightened witness with a clear self-interest. Why: A narrow question and a clear reason to cooperate lead a reluctant witness to fill in details.
- [procedure] 1) Present the evidence to the suspect face to face. 2) Ask a pointed question about who would gain from the suspect's death or disgrace. 3) Observe the answer and any secondary reactions. 4) Decide whether to withdraw or press further. When: When the suspect's reaction is itself informative and a formal charge is premature. Why: The reaction to direct evidence reveals more than a formal accusation would.
- [procedure] 1) Open with familiar small talk to keep the relationship. 2) Cut the preliminaries with rapid, short questions. 3) Ask directly for the result until it is given. When: A contact is reluctant to give information. Why: Pressing briefly keeps the relationship intact.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a narrow question that pins down a claimed item or detail. 2) Repeat the question when the answer conflicts with earlier statements. 3) Request a demonstration that tests the claim directly.
- [procedure] 1) Name the motive and the suspect's inner conflict first. 2) Recap the chain of events in order. 3) State the terms plainly. Use a one-way channel so the suspect cannot interrupt. When: the evidence is complete enough that denial would be pointless. Why: an ordered recap and a controlled channel let the investigator control the telling.
- [procedure] 1) Make a neutral request for information and wait. 2) If the suspect deflects, press in steps. 3) Raise the stakes with a formal consequence, then offer a choice between two formal options. When: Suspect has a known relationship to the victim but says little. Why: Escalating stakes gives continued silence a cost.
- [procedure] 1) Separate the verifiable fact in an accusation from its emotional charge. 2) Test that fact on its own. 3) Ask follow-up questions and watch whether the accused's answers grow vaguer. When: a witness accuses another person. Why: isolating the fact keeps the emotional charge from deciding the question.
- [procedure] 1) Stage a confrontation in front of the group. 2) Use a prompt that makes the guilty person act. 3) Let a sudden movement or reaction expose them. 4) Confirm the summary with a co-conspirator's confession. When: When the reveal should be dramatized rather than explained. Why: A reaction under pressure makes the trait visible in the moment.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a direct question. 2) Allow a pause. 3) Note whether the answer deflects, contradicts, or fits the facts. 4) Judge each reply against the situation. When: Questioning a suspect or NPC under pressure. Why: The pattern of response shows where the answer is hidden without relying on one reply.
- [procedure] 1) Tell the accused that accusations are being made against them. 2) Let them hear who the accusers are. 3) Have each accuser name the accused in turn. 4) Ask the accused to explain why they were named.
- [procedure] 1) Move the conversation to a private room and close the door before speaking. 2) Ask about a named person and their history, not general matters. 3) Describe the suspicion without naming a source, saying others share it. 4) State the fallback route you will take if the witness refuses. When: A witness is reluctant to answer.
- [pitfall] Confronting a suspect with a full accusation before controlling the exits or securing the case can warn them, letting them flee or coordinate their story before investigators test it. When: The suspect is confronted before the investigator controls the exits or the rest of the case is secured. Why: Pressure drives a guilty suspect to escape, and a warned suspect can align accounts with others.
- [pitfall] Pressing a reluctant, protective or gatekeeping witness too hard, abruptly, after refusal, or by demanding memory proof, can make them withdraw and close off later cooperation. When: Interviewing a reluctant or protective witness. Why: Pressure raises fear, and being asked to prove recall reads as an accusation, so the witness protects themselves.
- [pitfall] Pressuring a loved one to extract a confession can damage the relationship and undermine the case.
