- [pitfall] Pressuring a witness over the phone can cost their cooperation, so the cost should be weighed before pushing a reluctant witness. When: Witness is reluctant to talk.

## withholding
- [mechanism] Withholding strong contrary evidence while a belief hardens makes the eventual reversal more striking, since the prior conviction is stronger. When: a character holds a firm conclusion that new evidence will overturn.
- [mechanism] Withholding an early suspicion from those who could act loses evidence that would otherwise have been available at the time. When: A witness notices something but does not report it. Why: Delay lets evidence degrade or disappear.
- [mechanism] When feuding families withhold their payments, the official who depends on them goes unsupported, which deepens community turmoil.
- [mechanism] Withholding is staged disclosure: the holder controls what is seen and when, and reveal timing drives suspense. When: When a character controls access to information. Why: Paced reveals keep the investigator uncertain and engaged.
- [behavior] Witnesses may withhold evidence or suspicions for honest reasons such as personal reticence, avoiding endorsement of a superstition, or protecting property value, not guilt. When: A witness has something relevant but does not mention it, or gives a partial account. Why: Silence can come from temperament or social or reputational motives rather than guilt.
- [behavior] A witness with direct access may hold back the decisive fact out of fear of blame, loyalty, shame or embarrassment or a promise, while truthfully telling everything else. When: A witness has relevant knowledge or a legitimate reason to stay silent. Why: Self-protection and loyalty suppress disclosure.
- [behavior] Witnesses withhold what they judge unimportant or unrecognized, or out of delicacy, pride or feeling, and may recall it only when asked a precise question or after reflection. When: A witness is questioned about a sensitive event or the night of a crime. Why: Witnesses judge relevance from their own view, assuming authorities would ask if it mattered; feelings and reputation shape disclosure.
- [behavior] A short, unusually light message that gives no cause but a new address leaves the reader to supply the danger. When: Delivering a warning that must be delayed or hidden. Why: A missing cause invites the audience to imagine the threat.
- [behavior] A character may offer a plausible alternative route while holding stronger suspicions in private, leaving others unsure what the character actually believes. When: a character proposes a theory that differs from their own.
- [behavior] When an ally shares a plan but refuses to discuss the personal reason, listeners expect a confidence that never comes, and their expectations shift. When: an ally discloses a goal and withholds the personal side. Why: withheld information changes what the listener expects.
- [behavior] Characters often keep unconfirmed discoveries private, and the audience sees the reservation only later.
- [behavior] Withholding the source of a document can prompt the suspect to accept questioning, since the questioner appears to know more than they reveal. When: Questioning a suspect about a document whose origin is undisclosed. Why: Unknown knowledge on the questioner's side creates implied pressure, encouraging cooperation.
- [behavior] A questioner who demands information while hiding their own knowledge can make the other party refuse to continue. Why: the other party sees the exchange as unfair.
- [behavior] A stoic character may hold back information for a stated reason that the player learns only after earning trust. When: A reserved NPC conceals knowledge. Why: Trust unlocks the true motive behind the silence.
- [behavior] A character may deliberately refuse to learn facts in order to avoid a duty or to protect someone, and this refusal shapes what the story can reveal. When: when a powerful witness would be harmed by knowing a crime. Why: Choosing not to know spares the character a painful burden or a dangerous obligation.
- [rule] Withhold the decisive fact or solution while investigators keep asking questions and stay active, so tension and anticipation persist until the next clue. When: A story needs sustained tension before the next clue. Why: Repeated questions signal that an answer exists, creating anticipation. (x2)
- [rule] Do not withhold information the audience needs to reason toward the answer; give the decisive clue before the tests begin, not at the final moment. When: Building suspense through concealment or designing a mystery reveal. Why: Unfair concealment prevents reasoning toward the answer; players need the means to deduce it. (x2)
- [rule] Give each withholding character a believable motive; if they could simply speak, unexplained silence reads as arbitrary, contrived or lazy plotting, breaking trust and suspense. When: Deciding whether a character should delay disclosure. Why: Audiences tolerate delay when the silence seems motivated. (x2)
- [rule] When a narrator or reveal omits steps or knowledge, state the omission openly and keep the basis of reasoning visible; unstated gaps look like missing evidence. When: A reveal depends on reasoning the reader cannot see, or a narrator chooses not to reveal everything. Why: Unstated omissions look like gaps in evidence rather than deliberate choices.
- [rule] Do not withhold a fact the audience needs to follow the next scene or keep the goal in view; a missing fact breaks comprehension rather than building suspense. When: The next scene depends on that fact.
- [rule] Withhold your knowledge, a document's source, a find's origin or a check's method when disclosure would let a suspect tailor their account, warn them, or ruin a trap. When: During questioning or when sharing case details. Why: Revealing the source or method lets the suspect adjust their account or conceal evidence, and preserves leverage.
- [rule] Let an NPC withhold information until a condition such as player goodwill is met, giving a timed, specific account players can check against map locations and other NPC accounts. When: Designing an NPC who controls access to information. Why: Tying disclosure to goodwill makes social actions affect information flow.
- [rule] Keep a finding from the public when publishing it could alert suspects. When: publicity would warn culprits.
- [rule] Let the game hide some evidence from the player while keeping the deduction chain checkable from clues the player has already seen.
- [rule] When a character who holds information leaves or is removed, make that information available from another source so the player is not blocked. When: when an information-holding NPC can exit the game state.
- [rule] Hold back a key object and tease its owner before linking the two, so the player connects them only at the reveal.
- [rule] Withhold the conclusion until the evidence has been shown; signal only the next questions so the player assembles the pieces. When: when designing a reveal that depends on player deduction. Why: Players who build the answer themselves value the reveal more.
- [rule] Withhold key clues during the first part of a mystery and release them in clusters before each reveal, so the player's reading of the case is only overturned at the right time. When: Pacing clue release in a short mystery. Why: Early disclosure of reasoning removes suspense, while clustered release lets the reveal recontextualise several clues together.
- [rule] Let a helper character withhold a key timeline fact, with a clear tell, so the cost of withholding drives the mystery's core.
- [heuristic] Hold the decisive revelation, witness line or central name that flips the hypothesis back until pressure has built, approaching it indirectly first; early disclosure drains suspense. When: A scene's reversal, culprit identity or quest hypothesis depends on one revelation. Why: Delay concentrates the audience's attention on the reveal. (x2)
- [heuristic] Withhold the cause of a disturbance or visual evidence so characters speculate; speculation sustains tension, but concrete facts released early end it. When: The audience must feel pressure but does not yet need facts to act on. Why: Withheld visual evidence leaves partial descriptions that keep speculation open.
- [heuristic] Keep part of your knowledge in reserve when questioning a witness who may hide facts, revealing it only to get confirmation; early full disclosure makes hostile witnesses close down. When: Questioning a witness who may hide facts. Why: Hostile witnesses close down under direct probing.
- [heuristic] A witness may confirm a decision yet withhold its reason, and the gap between the two is where the hidden motive usually sits. When: A witness acknowledges an action but refuses to explain it. Why: The unexplained reason often concerns something the witness wants kept private.
- [heuristic] Keep a key NPC out of reach until late, so their account reframes the clues the player has already gathered. When: When designing a narrative twist. Why: Late testimony gains weight when earlier clues have built up unresolved questions.
- [heuristic] An official's refusal to show a document can itself be a clue, since the refusal may protect the official's own position.
- [heuristic] Holding back part of a payment and naming a smaller figure can draw a witness's interest without revealing the full value of the offer. When: Negotiating a bribe or payment for information. Why: Partial withholding keeps the witness engaged while preserving leverage.
- [heuristic] Withhold a procedural hint only when a second clue exists that corrects the first failed attempt. When: Designing a puzzle that requires a specific procedure. Why: Without a correcting clue, players cannot recover from a wrong attempt.
- [heuristic] Do not hold back evidence that helps the accused if the opponent can recover it quickly on its own. Why: Concealment is exposed when the other side finds the item anyway.
- [heuristic] Let NPCs give partial answers and reward players who ask the correct follow-up question. When: Designing dialogue that hides part of its information. Why: Partial answers keep the player engaged and reward precise questioning.
- [procedure] 1) Hold one specific clue back from a suspect or companion. 2) Watch whether they repeat or reference it later. 3) Treat any repetition as evidence of their knowledge. When: when testing a theory without alerting others.
- [tradeoff] Withholding a central fact builds suspense, but holding it too long loses the audience. A character may keep a theory private without lying, limiting talk to public facts. When: When staging the disclosure of a central fact, or when a character holds a private theory while others seek answers. Why: Suspense depends on the listener having context to judge what is withheld; delay past a point costs clarity. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Withholding a suspect's name guards people and serves legal caution and drama, but leaves a listener with authority unable to verify or act on the claim. When: When the listener has authority or a personal stake and could alert the suspects. Why: Partial disclosure guards people at the cost of the listener's ability to check the account. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Withholding a find or suspicion protects leverage, but colleagues or allies lose information and may act on an incomplete picture; weigh the cost of silence.
- [tradeoff] Withholding a theory or key fact from a partner keeps control and misdirects them, but leaves their theory incomplete and risks strain, humiliation on discovery, or failure if circumstances change.
- [tradeoff] Keeping partners uninformed protects the lead from interference but costs trust, and can turn cooperation into rivalry or leave sent-away partners angry and suspicious.
- [tradeoff] Withholding decisive evidence or the answer builds dread and engagement, but withholding too much makes the reveal feel withheld rather than earned, frustrating a reader who cannot reach it. When: Deciding how much of the answer or a delayed reveal to hold back, including through secondhand sources. Why: Withholding creates engagement but risks frustration if clues do not reach a reachable conclusion.
- [tradeoff] Keeping a state ambiguous builds suspense, but if it stays unresolved when players need clarity, it becomes frustrating. When: when a character's condition must stay uncertain.
- [tradeoff] Withholding the answer from an accused person keeps the reveal intact but costs them the chance to respond, while telling them gives hope but risks spoiling the reveal. When: Deciding how much an accused person should know before a set reveal. Why: Information given early can help the accused but weakens the surprise.
- [tradeoff] Keeping back a discovery protects a rival advantage but weakens shared evidence and slows progress for both sides.
- [tradeoff] Withholding facts keeps leverage and lets a questioner reveal them at the right moment, but too much secrecy can make the questioner seem arbitrary and stall progress. When: A character knows facts the player or party does not and should reveal them selectively. Why: Revealing too early warns the other party; revealing nothing leaves them stuck.
- [tradeoff] Withholding a true clue can prevent authorities from reading it as support for a mistaken explanation, but it can also distort the case and leave a private reading unchecked. When: When a true clue would reinforce a false impression if disclosed. Why: Selective disclosure protects against misreading but risks the investigator's own judgement being wrong.
- [tradeoff] Withholding a solution gives a stronger proof but can prolong suspense for others, which may be regretted later. When: Deciding how long to keep a conclusion private. Why: Delay protects the case while imposing emotional costs on people kept in the dark.
- [pitfall] Concealing a discovery or hypothesis too long makes it look like deception once revealed, making innocent later statements seem suspect and damaging trust. When: When an investigator keeps a theory or discovery from partners for an extended period. Why: Delayed disclosure reads as hidden intent once the reasoning emerges. (x2)
- [pitfall] Withholding evidence, a sealed document or an answer too long frustrates and feels cheated; once revealed it must pay off quickly, or it reads as a dead end. When: A mystery holds back key evidence, a sealed document or an explanation. Why: Players tolerate suspense only while they expect the answer to arrive. (x2)
- [pitfall] Prolonged stasis drains tension: a long wait without a turn, peril without change, or a hesitating speaker. Recovering attention needs a sudden shift in action.
- [pitfall] A participant who keeps part of their knowledge back leaves the shared picture incomplete, misdirecting helpers or theories built on it. When: Pooling information across several parties, or a helper acts on partial information.
- [pitfall] Evidence a witness withholds to protect someone can mislead the investigator later, even when the motive is kind. When: a witness keeps back an item to spare an ally. Why: The omission hides facts the investigator needs.
- [pitfall] Withholding information can conceal truths that matter to other people who are entitled to them. When: Keeping an investigation private.
- [pitfall] Withholding findings from a client can cost goodwill and trust, even when the withholding is strategically sound. When: When an investigator keeps key findings from the party who hired them. Why: Clients expect information and may judge the investigator negatively for silence.
- [pitfall] Holding evidence back from authorities lets an investigator steer the case, often in directions nobody planned.
- [pitfall] Keeping a finding from a companion can leave them confused and suspicious, weakening the working relationship. When: When an investigator withholds a discovery from a partner. Why: Partial information breeds distrust.
- [pitfall] A bluff can appear to fail for a long time, so observers may grow frustrated before its payoff arrives. When: a misdirection is running. Why: The payoff is delayed by design, and impatience can undermine it.
- [pitfall] Refusing to name the source of a trace breaks its chain of custody, so the trace stays unlinked to anyone.
- [pitfall] Withholding can frustrate the audience if they have no reason to keep following the investigator.
- [pitfall] A recipient who hesitates to share an anonymous letter may hide its real impact, which can delay the investigation. When: When a recipient is reluctant to show a threatening message. Why: Embarrassment or fear can make the recipient withhold the most important detail.
- [pitfall] Holding back a theory can let a wrong verdict stand and leave a dangerous person free.
- [pitfall] A cut-off line of inquiry can leave the audience believing a hidden answer exists, which raises suspicion of the authorities who blocked it. When: when a question is blocked without explanation. Why: people infer concealment from unanswered questions.

## self-serving and interested testimony
- [definition] A witness counts as interested if they have a stake in the outcome, including an investigator who found the key object.
- [mechanism] Evidence that reads as proof to an in-world authority can read as malice to the player, because the player sees the motive behind the testimony. When: Testimony is presented to a court, jury, or other in-world judge. Why: The player has access to context that the authority lacks, so the same statement carries a different meaning.
- [behavior] A participant's written account often justifies their motives, casting accusers as the real slanderers, and mixes admissions of fear and confusion with claims of entitlement. When: A participant writes or tells a statement about their own role, especially when a campaign faces later scrutiny. Why: Self-protection against reprisal shapes the framing; they have a stake in how they are judged and how the record reads. (x2)
- [behavior] Witnesses who fear consequences or gain from an account shape it to protect themselves: pushing blame onto others, stressing helpful facts, or relying on people who cannot be checked. When: A witness is involved in or near an incident with possible consequences, or has reason to move suspicion away from themselves. Why: Self-interest bends recollection and biases which facts are volunteered.
- [behavior] When a large reward and a pardon are offered to members of a group, one member tends to betray the others early. When: a group of accomplices faces pressure or an offer of clemency. Why: the incentive to talk outweighs loyalty for the individual.
- [behavior] A narrator personally affected by events filters what he reports toward his own comfort and irritation, dismissing others' concerns and misjudging people he dislikes. When: A participant with a personal stake narrates events the player must interpret. Why: Personal stakes shape attention and judgment, so details that matter to him dominate while others are waved away.
- [behavior] A person's offered help often carries expectations of gratitude or obedience, and their motive shows in how they picture their own standing. When: a character gives help, money or a proposal. Why: people value what makes them feel equal or superior to others.
- [behavior] A person who deceives others can come to half-believe their own claim and act on it, so a human scheme can produce results nobody planned. When: A character runs a deception that depends on a shared belief. Why: Self-deception makes the schemer's actions sincere but still produce unintended outcomes.
- [behavior] A witness who benefits from the story may let personal satisfaction color their account. When: When a witness reports an outcome that reflects well on them. Why: Self-interest shapes what is remembered and emphasized.
- [rule] Testimony from a witness who wants an outcome or protects a reputation carries less weight alone; check details favouring the teller, like insisting on a key action, against independent accounts. When: A witness has a stake in the outcome or protects a reputation. Why: Self-interest shapes what is reported and how firmly it is held. (x2)
- [rule] Check the account of a witness who is implicated, controls the scene, or gains or loses from the outcome against physical traces and other statements before trusting it. When: A witness is implicated in the events, under suspicion, or has a stake in the outcome. Why: A personal stake gives reason to shape the account; people shade accounts to protect themselves.
- [rule] Interest is a reason to check an account, not to reject it; test a self-interested claim or corroborated alibi against facts rather than dismissing it. When: Evaluating testimony from a motivated witness, or an alibi backed by a close witness. Why: Self-interest explains why someone may lie, but truth depends on evidence.
- [rule] Treat a suspect's account of motives, past or sequence of events as a lead revealing motive and method, accepting only parts confirmed by other witnesses and records. When: A suspect volunteers an account or confession. Why: A self-written account is not final proof; the speaker benefits from how it is received.
- [rule] Give an NPC a self-serving retelling with visible motive, and let the player check its claims against documents or other NPCs. When: Writing a character who withholds or distorts information. Why: Visible motives teach players to question claims rather than accept them.
- [rule] A witness who admits wrongdoing loses some trust but may have reason to avoid trouble, so weigh both the lost credibility and the motive. When: the only witness has a self-interested record. Why: an admission lowers trust while revealing a motive to speak.
- [rule] Treat each witness as having a stake, and check their claims against physical evidence before accepting them. When: A witness also controls the scene or answers for an event. Why: Self-interest can shape what a witness reports about the scene.
- [rule] Test a suspect's self-description against facts, such as what support was actually provided, before accepting a claimed grievance. When: when a suspect claims neglect or suffering. Why: a claimed grievance may not match the record.
- [heuristic] Lower the weight of a statement from someone who gains from the outcome, such as a paid or rewarded witness, since personal gain biases what they choose to say. When: A witness was paid or otherwise rewarded. Why: People who profit from a conviction tend to speak first, and their interest may selectively shape the account. (x2)
- [heuristic] A statement against the speaker's own interest carries more weight than one serving it; do not accept a self-protective denial at face value, especially when safety is at stake. When: When judging whether a denial or admission is credible. Why: A speaker gains little by inventing a claim that hurts them; self-interest shapes what a speaker admits. (x2)
- [heuristic] Claims about another's wealth or one's own ruin, from a party who stands to gain or lose, are self-serving; discount them and verify against records outside the party's account. When: A character makes financial claims, or a source has a financial or reputational stake. Why: Claimants benefit from how their money story is told. (x2)
- [heuristic] Know who holds an interest before trusting testimony or verdicts; interest shapes who testifies and how an ambiguous sign is read as evidence, through the lens of those who benefit. When: Weighing testimony or a verdict from a party with a stake, or an ambiguous sign used to support a verdict.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC informant tell a full story with a hidden motive, flagging self-serving parts in dialogue or with an interest tag so players can separate them from confirmable facts. When: Designing informant dialogue or witness records.
- [heuristic] Weigh an informant's or witness's account against what they gain, lose or fear, since a stake may shape the story, especially when they are the only source for key events. When: The informant or witness has something to gain or lose, such as a career, reputation or grievance at stake.
- [heuristic] When a person's acts work against their own interest, look for a hidden controller who gains from them, and compare acts and statements for the pattern. When: A suspect's behavior makes no sense for their own benefit. Why: Actions that hurt the actor often serve someone else's stake.
- [heuristic] A character with a stake who declares that no proof exists is making a one-sided claim, which the audience can test against the people involved. When: A character claims evidence has been fully destroyed. Why: Self-interested reassurance is incomplete while witnesses still exist.
- [heuristic] Evidence handed over by people who benefit from the outcome arrives already sorted, so check what was kept, returned or removed before trusting it. Why: the handler can shape what the audience sees.
- [heuristic] A speaker who asks to be judged fairly in advance is presenting their own case, so that framing should be noted. When: a speaker pleads for a fair hearing before giving an account. Why: The request shapes how the listener is expected to receive the claims.
- [heuristic] A mark repeated across incidents may signal a group rather than one person, which changes the pool of likely suspects. When: the same initials or token recurs across several events. Why: a shared sign can belong to an organisation, not a single individual.
- [heuristic] Several witnesses giving the same account usually outweigh a single voice, and a clear timeline backed by them can outweigh a weak identification.
- [heuristic] Expect that many self-described witnesses will stretch facts to be helpful, and weigh each account by the witness's position and motive.
- [heuristic] Treat information offered in exchange for a favour as possibly self-interested, since the informant expects something back.
- [heuristic] An alibi from someone who fears scandal or has their own name at stake should be weighed as shaped by that interest. When: the witness is protecting a partner or their own reputation. Why: the witness has a motive to make the account favour the protected person.
- [heuristic] An account that turns toward self-pity and requests for sympathy suggests the speaker is shaping the story for their own benefit. When: when a witness asks for sympathy. Why: sympathy-seeking reveals a motive for shaping the account.
- [heuristic] A writer who claims to have doubted events should be checked against their other writings from the same period. Why: Self-defense can contradict earlier public statements.
- [heuristic] Accept an account from someone with a stake in the outcome provisionally, then test it for what it leaves out. When: The witness has motive to shape the story and the official version rests on it. Why: Plausibility is not truth, and interested witnesses smooth over disputes or motives.
- [heuristic] A witness who undercuts her own accusation in the same passage invites the audience to weigh the claim as weak.
- [procedure] 1) Gather suspects, witnesses and officials in the scene room and treat them alike. 2) Have people re-establish object and personal positions on site. 3) Let them discuss freely. 4) Record each claim that conflicts with the physical layout. When: Individual interviews have stalled and the scene can be reconstructed; suspects and witnesses replay it together. Why: Physical positions force people to commit to specifics that separate interviews may let them avoid, so contradictions surface.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the group to mentally return to the moment of the event. 2) Invite each to report any impression, however trivial. 3) Narrow volunteers' accounts with follow-up questions on time, appearance and clothing. 4) Question each person separately, out of earshot of others. 5) Schedule a second interview, since forgotten details can return later. When: group shared one viewpoint and memories are still fresh. Why: Group settings suppress shy witnesses, and private questioning prevents copying or revision of answers.
- [procedure] 1) Announce a general claim that everyone present is hiding something. 2) Watch who looks away or over-explains. 3) Approach each person in turn and note who reacts most. When: Several suspects share a secret and none has volunteered it privately.
- [procedure] 1) Question the group in a fixed order 2) Record each member's answer on a key event 3) Compare the answers for agreement and conflict. When: a household or group shares one event. Why: a fixed order keeps answers comparable.
- [pitfall] Treating a self-serving statement or self-defense as neutral history or established fact gives the writer's agenda unexamined authority; test its claims against other sources. (x2)
- [pitfall] Relatives, acquaintances or grieving parties who defend their interests or speak for each other give partial testimony on a victim's relationships, motive or state; weigh it as biased. When: Gathering accounts from family members or others about a victim. Why: Shared interest colours what is reported. (x2)
- [pitfall] Advice or an offer to drop the matter from someone close to the case may protect the giver's interest in keeping the truth out of reach rather than the truth. When: Receiving a warning or offer from someone close to the case. Why: Protective motives and self-interest can overlap in the same message. (x2)
- [pitfall] A witness with a stake, or who wants to avoid blame, frames events in their own favour; accepting that self-serving framing at face value yields a skewed picture. When: A witness tells their own part in events, or testimony about a disputed event is weighed. Why: Self-interest biases the account. (x2)
- [pitfall] Records made by someone with a stake in the dispute may be biased or wrong on particular points; check them before trusting and invite correction. When: A record's author gains from its contents. Why: Stakes can bias what is written. (x2)
- [pitfall] Corroboration from stakeholders, whether a self-interested endorsement or interested parties signing each other's accounts, only repeats their own position and is not independent. When: A writer or party with a stake vouches for their own record, or interested parties sign each other's accounts. Why: A stakeholder's praise confirms their claims, not the facts. (x2)
- [pitfall] A self-authored account is shaped by a writer who protects their own position and chooses what to reveal and how to present themselves; check its claims against other records.
- [pitfall] A self-serving narrator who tells events from their own viewpoint, flattering themselves or minimising or overstating guilt, is a biased source; check the timeline against other sources.
- [pitfall] A motive offered by an interested party, such as a threat-maker, may be leverage or sympathy; check it against their own gain, and treat appeals to honesty as persuasion. When: Evaluating a confession, explanation or motive from a party pursuing their own aim. Why: The teller may shape the account to gain sympathy; the source may use the claim for leverage rather than to reveal the truth.
- [pitfall] Questioning witnesses in front of others or signalling suspicion to a whole group contaminates answers; they may close ranks or invent accounts to escape scrutiny. When: Questioning a group of witnesses together. Why: Collective fear encourages coordination or fabrication to avoid blame.
- [pitfall] A single witness whose account serves their interests produces a misleading picture, and a lone corroborating witness is insufficient if they could share the suspect's interest.
- [pitfall] A witness with a personal stake may frame events to protect his standing; separate his feelings from the verifiable facts. When: interviewing a client who has a stake in the outcome.
- [pitfall] A timeline built from a suspect's own account is easy to bend, so it must be cross-checked against objects and other witnesses.
- [pitfall] A dying suspect's account can be self-serving, so verify it against other evidence before relying on it.
- [pitfall] Pressing a suspect for more details can produce self-serving versions of events that favour the suspect.
- [pitfall] Theories offered by people with a stake in the outcome steer the investigation toward their preferred answer. When: a character advances a theory that favours a particular suspect. Why: Interested parties shape what others look for, so their theories need independent verification.
- [pitfall] A cover built on an interest backfires if the target knows more about that interest than the persona does.
- [pitfall] An interested witness may supply a motive that strengthens a case while also biasing the account they give. Why: personal stake shapes what is reported.
- [pitfall] Vague, self-serving accounts often reveal the witness's bias more than the truth.
- [pitfall] Accepting one faction's account of its own fairness is unreliable, because the faction benefits from that account. When: a faction describes its own proceedings.
- [pitfall] A witness who says they always opposed a practice may have supported it, so their claim of objection needs checking against the record. Why: Self-justifying accounts shape how the witness describes their own past conduct.
- [pitfall] Officials who profit from an accusation process have an incentive to keep it going. When: when officials gain fees, property or status from convictions. Why: Personal gain from the process rewards its continuation.
- [pitfall] A long monologue can slow the reveal, and the teller's partial, self-serving account should be tested against other evidence. When: A character gives an extended explanation. Why: Length and self-interest both reduce reliability.
- [pitfall] A victim's or employer's own timeline can be wrong or self-serving, and confidence in a person's honesty does not establish the facts. When: When an account comes from someone with a stake in the outcome or a trusted reputation. Why: Trust and personal interest bias recollection and reporting.
- [pitfall] A motive reported by an interested party may be coloured by jealousy or grievance.
- [fact] A suspect's own recorded words about the sequence of events can serve as proof of their role in that sequence.

## suspect profiles and motive
- [model] A compartmented plan can use four roles: a naval liaison, a construction supervisor, a local labour and pilot organiser, and a promoter who supplies information and guides the expedition. When: when organising a multi-part covert operation. Why: each role covers a separate function.
- [mechanism] Attaching small traits to NPC bodies or rooms, such as stains, ash or nail marks, lets a suspect's profile narrow as the player gathers clues. When: Designing environmental evidence that identifies a suspect. Why: Each trait removes candidates, so the profile converges as evidence accumulates.
- [mechanism] Inheritance can set the suspect list, since each heir has a motive tied to the estate. When: A death or crime concerns property that passes between relatives.
- [mechanism] A sighting that contradicts a locked door, held privately by observers, keeps a puzzle open until an ordinary, checkable explanation appears. When: when planting an apparently impossible entry or exit. Why: Unresolved contradictions drive players to keep reasoning.
- [mechanism] Confrontation can require the player to show a physical item, such as a bottle or stub, before a suspect's claim changes.
- [behavior] When a topic is raised indirectly, the subject may step into the frame and place themselves at its centre before anyone names them.
- [behavior] A culprit who believes the investigator lacks key knowledge tends to fortify a position and commit to it, giving the investigator time to find a clue. When: The investigator waits quietly rather than confronting the culprit. Why: Committed positions are harder to abandon, and the commitment exposes more evidence over time.
- [behavior] Repeatedly using a diminished or altered name for a person can shape how readers perceive them. When: A writer refers to an accused person in demeaning terms. Why: Repeated naming frames the reader's view.
- [rule] Give each suspect a distinct personality and motive profile, such as debt, reputation or need for an item, checked against their character and the value of any stolen object. When: Designing suspects for a theft or a deduction puzzle. Why: Distinct profiles let players match behaviour and motive to evidence.
- [rule] Gate the final accusation until all statements and clues are gathered and earlier reveals logged, each unlocked from collected clues; optional timers or guard actions add pressure. When: The game has a final accusation step. Why: Gating holds the reveal until the evidence is complete.
- [rule] Change appearance fully when re-entering a scene where a suspect has already seen you, so that person does not recognize you. When: Returning to a scene with a previously observed suspect. Why: A full change is what made the disguised figure unrecognizable to a prior observer.
- [rule] Name a suspect only after checking who could plausibly have made the change, given their recent capability.
- [rule] Learn which hand an item suits by trying it on a person, rather than asking anyone directly about their hand use. When: a suspect might deny or hide a physical trait. Why: A fitting test reveals the trait without the question being asked.
- [rule] Let a character's changed employment open new questions, such as when and why they left their previous post.
- [rule] Attach strength or mobility values to each suspect and check them against the physical demands of the scene, such as moving a heavy object. When: Building suspects whose capability matters to the crime. Why: Lets the player test whether a suspect could have acted.
- [rule] When an answer does not come out whole, suspect your own working before blaming the evidence. When: a theory leaves loose ends.
- [rule] Let the public story stand while investigators keep their real suspicions hidden, so the culprit does not realise they are suspected. When: Investigators are setting a trap for a culprit.
- [rule] Let a hung jury delay a case rather than resolve it, so the case remains open for later stages.
- [rule] Research the background of everyone connected to a case for past scandal that could reveal a motive. When: Building a suspect list.
- [heuristic] A departure from known routine is evidence: a change in a familiar pattern or a new object in an empty place is often the first sign something happened. When: Judging an actor's likely action or identity, or when an observer knows a place or household's normal state well. Why: Routine gives a baseline against which anomalies stand out, making deviations both noticeable and credible.
- [heuristic] A public image of cheerfulness or respectability may conceal private pressure, so question the surface of a case when a respected figure is involved. When: a public figure's image may hide private strain. Why: Public presentation and private circumstances often diverge, and the gap can supply motive.
- [heuristic] Public causes or respectable activities may be a front for a private link that actually explains the gathering.
- [heuristic] A pin or badge paired with a habit can indicate membership of a fraternal group. When: a person wears a group emblem and shows matching habits. Why: paired signs make membership more likely than a single sign.
- [heuristic] Keep investigative actions separate from raw facts so the chain of reasoning stays transparent. When: A case is being documented or reviewed. Why: Mixing actions with facts hides which conclusions rest on which evidence.
- [heuristic] An agent's choice of action reveals what they believed; ask what they would have known to explain it.
- [heuristic] A former admirer or rival of the victim should be treated as a suspect to be cleared or confirmed. When: Asking about a victim's other admirers or romantic history. Why: Past rivalries can supply motive that current relations hide.
- [heuristic] A recent change in a person's plans, such as a withdrawn commitment, can reveal a motive worth probing even when the stated reason seems weak. When: motive is unclear and the victim's personal life offers a lead.
- [heuristic] A sequence of actions shows what was done but not why; the same actions can fit several motives, which must be assessed as a separate question. When: when a reconstruction establishes what happened. Why: Actions are observable, while motives must be inferred from other evidence.
- [heuristic] Judge a suspect's apparent folly against the likely intelligence of the culprit. A clever culprit would not act so openly, so the folly may show the plan was not the suspect's. When: when a suspect behaves in a way that seems out of character. Why: Someone else may have arranged the damaging actions.
- [heuristic] Flag implausible details in a witness's description, such as a disguise that seems false, and note them for checking later.
- [heuristic] Track a suspect's motive, access and behaviour as separate entries, so the player must combine them before making an accusation. When: designing a suspect board for players. Why: separate entries force the player to link evidence rather than match a single clue.
- [heuristic] An actor's need to avoid suspicion explains why some traces were wiped and others left behind. When: Accounting for uneven traces in a scene. Why: Concealment is selective, so the wiped and missed traces reflect what the actor feared being caught doing.
- [heuristic] Character profiles can narrow a suspect field but cannot identify one culprit alone, since many people may fit the same profile. When: ranking suspects when alibi evidence is incomplete. Why: Personality fit is weaker evidence than physical or alibi facts.
- [heuristic] Ask what subject was discussed at a past meeting, since a shared subject can link that meeting to evidence found later.
- [heuristic] Reasoning about what an actor would prefer, such as avoiding a patrolled room, is the weakest location evidence and should carry the least weight. When: Location is argued from the killer's habits rather than physical traces. Why: Preferences are guesses; physical and timing facts can be checked.
- [heuristic] Judge individuals rather than groups; a person's role alone does not reveal their intentions.
- [heuristic] Show who was positioned to influence each decision, so readers can see how one stage made the next possible. When: explaining a chain of decisions.
- [heuristic] A portrait may look unfriendly because its subject dislikes being seen, so the witness may be distorted by the subject's own behavior. When: When judging a likeness that seems to contradict a reputation. Why: The subject's reluctance can alter the recorded appearance.
- [heuristic] Keep a contract's cost unknown until revealed, and give players an informed NPC or a search to read the full terms. When: Designing a sign-or-refuse choice. Why: Players can then decide with information they earned.
- [heuristic] The strongest item often completes a case that other items have already built.
- [heuristic] Begin an investigation by treating every suspect as possible, then narrow the list as facts arrive, to avoid committing early. When: when several people could plausibly be responsible. Why: early commitment can lock in a wrong suspect.
- [procedure] 1) Start from a response that seems wrong for the stated reason. 2) Replay the scene: who was present, what could be said openly, and what each person did next. 3) Ask which motive makes each act natural, and test rival motives against the same acts. When: A person's conduct contradicts the reason they give for it. Why: Acts reveal relationships that spoken accounts conceal.
- [procedure] Build a full roster covering household members, neighbours, tradespeople, professionals and acquaintances who could affect the case. When: when the cast is still unknown. Why: A missed suspect is costly early on.
- [procedure] 1) Compare two observations of the same person. 2) Find the recorded event between them. 3) Test whether a witness could perceive that event from their position. 4) Link the event to a motive. When: two accounts of one person's behavior differ with no stated reason.
- [procedure] 1) For each suspect, list what they want, what they fear, and whom they fear most. 2) Use these to explain why they hide, refuse or invent. 3) Test the motive against their behavior and the physical evidence. When: the investigation depends on predicting a suspect's next move.
- [procedure] For each suspect, build one sequence: who wanted money, who learned of the will, and who had access to the means. When: Assessing motive and opportunity across suspects. Why: A single chain shows whether each suspect could have acted.
- [procedure] 1) Check ordinary outgoings against receipts to find discrepancies. 2) Isolate regular unexplained payments. 3) Chart income by period. 4) Match income timing against spending changes. When: Reconstructing a person's finances from records. Why: Separating explained from unexplained flows exposes the hidden transactions.
- [procedure] 1) Map each person's sums owed and interest rates. 2) Note whether debts were rolled into principal. 3) Record stated figures to check later contradictions. 4) Verify figures with a second source. When: A death or disappearance changes someone's financial position. Why: Debts and stakes show motive, but figures are often hidden or overstated.
- [pitfall] An elimination conclusion is only as good as its candidate list; a missing agent, route or location carries its gap into the verdict, so a certain-seeming answer may be provisional. When: Using elimination to explain an effect. Why: Unlisted causes cannot be excluded, and the remaining answer depends on the list being complete.
- [pitfall] Warning or alarming a suspect before others are questioned lets them coordinate answers or coach witnesses, weakening later checks.
- [pitfall] Choosing suspects for surface traits such as name, habit, timing, poverty, past failure or social standing, rather than evidence, shows only thin evidence and does not establish guilt. When: A suspect is picked for superficial reasons, or a theory rests on reputation. Why: Surface traits and social judgment substitute for proof.
- [pitfall] Investigators may fix on one suspect because evidence against that person is easiest to gather, narrowing attention before alternatives are weighed. When: several people have motives and opportunities. Why: convenient evidence draws attention away from stronger but harder leads.
- [pitfall] Offering too many alternative explanations stalls the investigation and makes the audience lose interest.
- [pitfall] Treating visible agitation as proof of guilt misreads grief, since grief and anger can look identical. When: Judging a suspect by how upset or agitated they appear.
- [pitfall] A stated reason may be an afterthought, so it should be weighed as a claim rather than accepted as the true motive.
- [pitfall] A theory whose named suspect would have no reason to perform the action it describes explains its clue only loosely.
- [pitfall] Assuming a companion was present, based on a single object, can mislead the investigation. When: inferring who was with a person from one clue. Why: one object rarely proves who was present.
- [pitfall] A conclusion that the real document differs from the displayed one is a working hypothesis, not proof, until the real document is found. Why: Behaviour around a document is suggestive but not conclusive.
- [pitfall] A subject who quietly fills an interviewer's slip with a near match can make a false account look consistent.
- [pitfall] Stacking too many grudges makes none of them stand out, so each suspect's motive loses weight.
- [pitfall] Legal title and physical occupancy can point to different people, so the visible defender of a plot may not be its legal owner. Why: Each party's stake depends on the kind of claim it holds.
- [pitfall] Choosing a more favorable court can be procedural pressure that hides weak evidence behind a convenient verdict.
- [pitfall] Counting only helps when the production record is complete, so the investigator must verify records directly with the maker. Why: missing records make the count unreliable.
- [pitfall] Investigators often record a statement and forget the behaviour that contradicts it.
- [fact] A testator who revises a will often makes a sudden new beneficiary, even an outsider, less surprising to those who handled the estate.
- [fact] A suspect's admission of intent, such as an offer of money or a readiness to do anything, states a motive that investigators can test.

## stated intent and motive
- [mechanism] Stating the penalty an attacker would face can make a reluctant witness weigh the cost of silence against the cost of speaking. When: witness refuses to name a suspect. Why: a stated cost changes the balance between speaking and staying silent.
- [mechanism] Plans that rely on routine sequences fail where the planner assumed something would stay fixed; a single cancelled event can break the whole chain of dependent steps. When: A plan depends on a sequence of routine events the planner cannot fully control. Why: Each assumed fixed event is a link; if one changes, every later step that relied on it breaks.
- [behavior] A witness can recall a planned action as one that actually happened, so intention and event blur together in memory. When: A witness describes an action they only intended or prepared. Why: Memory may record the plan as the event.
- [behavior] A wound to pride outlasts brute jealousy and can keep driving action long after the original humiliation. When: when judging whether a grievance is a plausible motive. Why: pride wounds persist while jealousy tends to fade.
- [behavior] A rare method implies its user looked up specialised knowledge, so the knowledge itself becomes a clue to who acted. When: The method is known only to specialists or through reference works. Why: Obtaining rare knowledge requires deliberate effort, which leaves a trace.
- [behavior] A delayed account may be driven by a hidden personal reason that shapes what the witness reveals. When: a witness's account is late or incomplete. Why: Concealed motives such as protecting a private relationship distort disclosure.
- [behavior] A visitor who gives a plausible reason for a visit may be hiding a different purpose, especially when he repeatedly mentions a plan without naming it. When: a character's stated reason does not fully explain their behaviour. Why: a stated motive can cover a concealed one.
- [rule] Treat a narrator's claims about their own intentions and good faith as unverifiable; a claim of good intentions does not prove the account is accurate. (x2)
- [rule] Compare a suspect's stated plan or reason with actual conduct; the gap often holds the real motive, so ask which explanation the conduct fits better. When: a stated plan or explanation conflicts with actions, or an absence needs explaining. Why: conduct that contradicts a plan reveals the real intent; behaviour reveals what words conceal.
- [rule] Give each non-player character a hidden financial stake, such as inheritance or debt, that surfaces only through certain dialogue choices or questions on adjacent topics. When: writing suspect dialogue. Why: hidden pressure rewards questioning and keeps early suspicion open.
- [rule] Separate intent from action: documents that show a plan do not prove it was carried out.
- [rule] Compare an object's stated purpose with how well it actually serves that purpose; if another use fits better, the stated purpose may be false.
- [rule] When a document is destroyed, give a stated motive, because destruction without a reason reads as a plot convenience.
- [rule] Design an NPC whose hidden motive turns the player's first reading of a threat into a second reading of protection once the motive is unlocked. When: designing NPC secrets. Why: Reinterpretation rewards exploration.
- [rule] Check a witness's stated reason for being present against the calendar before accepting it. When: when a witness explains their presence at a place tied to the case. Why: A plausible reason can be false when the date does not fit.
- [rule] Measure a beneficiary's gain against the prior state, not against a disputed document; the wrong baseline can reverse who appears to gain. When: inheritance or ownership is contested. Why: a disputed document may itself be false.
- [rule] Give a victim character a hidden financial motive that the player can uncover through documents or records. When: Designing a character whose motives are not obvious. Why: Discoverable motives reward investigation and make the character's conduct intelligible.
- [rule] Check any testimony given after a payment or reward for influence, because an inducement can shape what the witness says.
- [rule] Separate what a character intended from what their actions caused. Someone may produce an outcome without knowing it, so do not infer conspiracy from consequences alone.
- [rule] Place a closing question that reaches a suspect's hidden motive to open a confrontation or a new objective.
- [rule] Model a quest giver who offers a large reward for an item and refuses to name its owner as a hidden-motive NPC.
- [rule] Do not rely on intent-reading when a document is formally valid and clearly worded. When: A document meets formal requirements and its terms are plain. Why: Clear wording makes inference about intent unnecessary.
- [rule] Heated insults such as calling a witness a liar carry no evidential weight unless specific statements are shown to be false.
- [rule] Track a suspect's purchases and errands, so that items bought together can reveal a plan the player must assemble.
- [rule] Compare a person's stated reason for going somewhere with the first questions they ask there; a mismatch exposes a false explanation. When: when a character gives a reason for an action that others can observe. Why: Actions that do not serve the stated purpose reveal the real intent.
- [heuristic] Do not treat a death's financial gain as proof of motive or action; gain shows who benefits, not why, so separate gain from personal motive. When: ranking suspects by what they stand to gain. Why: financial benefit can be a contributing factor while the true motive is personal; no evidence of intent. (x2)
- [heuristic] Attach a visible stated reason and a concealed personal reason, such as a grudge, to each accusation, so players must trace relationship history to find the hidden one. When: designing a character's motive in a mystery. Why: A visible reason with a concealed one rewards investigation.
- [heuristic] Do not assume a suspect's stated plan or agreement will hold, since feelings and circumstances change; verify plans such as a lease or schedule with a third party. When: relying on a suspect's stated future location, plans or agreements. Why: stated plans can change.
- [heuristic] Reconstructing an author's intent from wording, later deeds and conduct is speculative, and the planned change may never have been carried out. When: A court or reader must infer intent from a formally defective document. Why: Unrealized plans leave no formal trace, so intent is an inference rather than a fact.
- [heuristic] Judge a stated motive against the record of actions. The order of events is itself evidence, and a motive that does not fit the sequence needs checking. When: Evaluating a confession or self-explanation. Why: Actions are harder to shape than a speaker's account of their own feelings.
- [heuristic] The method of a killing can hint at the killer's standing, such as whether they acted personally or hired someone, though this is only a hint. Why: people of different rank tend to act differently.
- [heuristic] Build hidden motives as findable items such as letters or plans, so a player who finds them can reinterpret earlier scenes. When: designing a concealed motive. Why: discovered items let players recast prior evidence.
- [heuristic] Use hidden motives where a concealed reason explains a suspicious-looking act, and not when all relevant facts are already in view.
- [heuristic] A suspect who pushes for a loud, visible explanation when a quiet one would serve them better is acting oddly if concealing a crime. When: comparing a suspect's stated aim with what they actually push for. Why: concealment normally prefers the less visible outcome.
- [heuristic] Telling the audience the likely outcome early shifts attention from what will happen to how it will happen. When: The outcome is predictable but the path to it is not. Why: With the result known, interest moves to the process of reaching it.
- [heuristic] Motive often lies in a hidden quarrel rather than a stated fact, so reveal it through a conflict scene or dialogue event.
- [heuristic] Valuables left unclaimed in a disturbed space suggest the intruder was not a common thief or was interrupted before taking them.
- [heuristic] A claim that someone acted on purpose goes beyond the observed position and is an interpretation, not an observation. When: a relayed report attributes intent to a person.
- [heuristic] Attach a motive tag to a witness's claim so players must weigh an accusation against why that witness might make it.
- [heuristic] A stated purpose for a journey must fit the story, since locals will question its details and invite follow-up questions. When: when questioned by locals or officials.
- [heuristic] Give a plausible, stated reason for asking about history, so the witness understands why outsiders want background. When: when asking about family or community history.
- [heuristic] Scene details showing preparation or a wish for company can distinguish a deliberate act from an accident or a solitary choice. When: deciding whether an event was intended. Why: preparation and social signals point to intent in ways accidents do not.
- [heuristic] When a witness lies about a motive, check whether it hides a stronger second motive and press on that.
- [heuristic] When a character's gain matches an earlier quarrel or insult, the motive can be provisionally accepted while still being an interpretation. When: an accusation follows an earlier dispute. Why: a matching history makes the motive plausible.
- [heuristic] Check a public act of kindness against who benefits from it, though a kind act may still be genuinely kind. When: Judging a character's motive from a generous gesture.
- [heuristic] A sharp change in a witness's manner around one topic or person, such as blushing, blinking, or blocking a passage, can signal a hidden motive. When: A witness's manner shifts sharply around one subject or person. Why: Emotional reactions can leak concealed reasons, but they are signs to test, not conclusions.
- [heuristic] When a character's stated reason can be measured, compare its cost or scale with the act it explains. A reason too small to justify the act points to a hidden motive. When: A character gives a reason for an action that can be checked against a sum, count or other fact. Why: A mismatch between claimed purpose and measurable scale signals the real want.
- [heuristic] A victim's earlier threat of self-harm makes a suicide reading plausible, but it explains the scene only if the physical evidence agrees with it. When: A victim has voiced suicidal intent before dying.
- [heuristic] Events close together in date can link a motive to an action, which is a hypothesis to test rather than proof of guilt.
- [heuristic] A gap between a person's claim of not desiring an office and their recorded actions is evidence of motive. When: a candidate disclaims interest in a contested post.
- [heuristic] Judge culpability by both inward intent and outward act, since a minimal physical act can carry grave intent. When: Assessing a character's responsibility for a past death.
- [heuristic] Decide the next investigative step before a trail goes cold, such as checking a witness's account of the time. When: During a surveillance or tracking sequence. Why: A ready next step keeps momentum when the target's trail is lost.
- [pitfall] Assuming the claimant's gain is obvious while the holder has no reason to act misses other suspects.
- [pitfall] A pretext that insults a suspect can damage the investigator's standing with allies who witness it. When: Using a provocative test on a suspect in front of others. Why: Observers may side with the suspect when the test seems unfair.
- [pitfall] Matching an object's kind is not matching its source. A widely sold item fits many possible owners, so the match only supports a line of inquiry.
- [pitfall] Accepting a clean physical match while the motive stays unexplained leaves the case open, since the act may not serve the suspect's apparent goal. When: A violent act does not fit the suspect's apparent purpose. Why: A mismatch between act and goal suggests the motive is incomplete.
- [pitfall] A clean motive picture can hide a deliberate reset, where the person later reappears under a new name with a new family. When: when an absence seems to have no motive.
- [pitfall] Accepting the first stated motive, such as a bad temper, without checking records like wills and estates can miss documents that contradict it. Why: Records often show circumstances that contradict the common story.
- [pitfall] Reading an owner's intention into an object from its storage place alone, without other evidence, is unsupported.
- [fact] The person who actually commits a killing often gains little beyond portable valuables, so beneficiaries and perpetrators need not coincide. When: judging a suspect by apparent gain. Why: gain from a death is not the same as the act of killing.
- [fact] A motive can lie hidden behind a long, outwardly calm relationship and surface only through a change in behaviour or a revealed secret.
- [fact] Disappearances fall into three kinds, and voluntary disappearance is the most common.
- [fact] An insult, even a documented one, does not by itself establish a motive to kill. When: Judging whether a grievance explains a violent act. Why: Grievance and violence are separated by the question of gain.
- [fact] The reason a party formally records for an action can differ from the pressure that actually drove it, so an official reason may be accurate yet incomplete. When: a formal demand or decision is given with stated grounds.
- [fact] Financial records show what was paid and when, but not why, so they support a theory without establishing its motive. When: Using ledgers or bank records as evidence. Why: Records log transactions, not intent.

## dialogue design
- [mechanism] A false persona or assumed role, such as a nurse or relative's agent, unlocks access or disclosures, including indirect accusations, that the true identity would be refused. When: an investigator must enter a home or restricted place, or access depends on a role. Why: Access is granted to the believed identity, not the true one; roles carry consequences that change what NPCs reveal. (x2)
- [mechanism] Broad questions return generic or vague answers that unlock narrower questions once a related clue is held; hedged answers can be flagged low-confidence. When: designing an NPC conversation with a sequence of questions. Why: Gating keeps the conversation following the order in which evidence is found.
- [mechanism] In dialogue, an NPC's guard can drop when a sensitive topic is raised, unlocking lines that are otherwise hidden from the player. When: A dialogue system ties hidden lines to an emotional topic. Why: Raising a sensitive subject reduces the NPC's defences and reveals more.
- [mechanism] A dialogue system can let an NPC decline a topic in a way that reveals a concern, and the player can learn more by trying related topics. When: when designing NPC dialogue. Why: Declined topics become an inference puzzle rather than a dead end.
- [mechanism] An NPC suspect's cover explanation can be tracked against whether the player accepts it, challenges it, or reveals knowledge, changing what that NPC believes the player knows. When: when designing a suspect NPC at a crime scene.
- [mechanism] Let an NPC revise its answer after another NPC reminds it of an event, and tag which details are firsthand and which are reconstructed. Why: Lets the player trace how the memory changed.
- [mechanism] An NPC interrogation can be staged in phases: a hostile opening, a run of narrow factual prompts, then a reassurance node that unlocks the confession. When: Designing a dialogue sequence that extracts a secret from an NPC. Why: Each phase changes the NPC's state, so the confession follows from the earlier phases.
- [mechanism] An NPC's first answer can be deliberately wrong, with the corrected answer unlocked only after the player shows a matching object or logged event.
- [behavior] A respected member's action can make others follow: handing over keys speeds compliance during group searches, and objecting to an unjust case makes others defer. When: during group searches, or when a dispute involves an unjust action. Why: Others follow or defer to the respected figure's standing and judgment. (x2)
- [behavior] A character who is not the main offender may answer a notice, because avoiding it gives them little reason. When: character is a partial participant, not the principal culprit. Why: fewer reasons to hide reduce the urge to avoid exposure.
- [behavior] A witness who refuses to accept a correction to a recalled remark may reveal what the original words meant to them. When: When an interviewer corrects a witness's recalled phrase. Why: Holding to wording often signals private knowledge.
- [behavior] A suspect who asks that an overheard exchange be kept from authorities reveals that they fear its content more than the investigation.
- [behavior] A witness's wording that names a source, such as having been told something, reveals how the knowledge was acquired.
- [behavior] Extreme personal reserve can unsettle others and be read as suspicious, yet it suggests a motive without proving one.
- [behavior] A partly true threat of legal consequence can turn a hostile gatekeeper cooperative. When: the threat has some basis in fact. Why: a credible threat raises the cost of continued refusal.
- [behavior] A subject who knows the examiner's dislikes tends to shape answers toward what the examiner wants, so the answers mirror the examiner's beliefs. When: The subject can learn the examiner's known prejudices during the test. Why: A performer reads the audience and gives expected answers rather than true ones.
- [behavior] Saying one will forgive and wait can make a pressing aim look patient rather than urgent.
- [rule] Let answers vary with question phrasing, and make checkable details reachable only through precise, verifiable questions, rewarding precision as a skill. When: designing dialogue for hypnotized, delirious or altered characters, or for checkable details. Why: Rewarding precision gives players a reason to refine questions and makes answers testable. (x2)
- [rule] Let weakened NPCs (injured, sick, exhausted, or rescued) give partial answers first; repeated prompts, rest or later progress unlock fuller testimony. When: designing dialogue for an injured, sick, exhausted or rescued character. Why: Staged disclosure rewards persistence without giving everything at once.
- [rule] Let an NPC summarise a route or events while omitting a key stop or scene, which follow-up questions, a later conversation or a found letter reveal.
- [rule] In dialogue trees, let neutral or sympathetic player prompts unlock more NPC disclosure, and track which claims the player has already heard. When: when authoring branching NPC conversations. Why: Sympathetic prompts make NPCs talk more freely.
- [rule] Do not repeat a bluff that has already failed to move the suspect.
- [rule] Let an NPC argue against the player's theory using stakes the player has not considered, so the theory must be retested rather than accepted. When: Writing dialogue that challenges a player's deduction. Why: New stakes reveal gaps in the player's reasoning.
- [rule] In a dialogue system, force the player to ask questions in an order that narrows the NPC's options, and track each answer for consistency.
- [rule] Let NPCs keep talking by offering follow-up topics tied to what the player has just learned, instead of ending on one fixed line. Why: Linked topics reward the player's recent discoveries.
- [rule] Give an NPC a dilemma the player can discuss; the NPC's response reveals a choice that can unlock a hidden location or item. When: designing NPC dialogue that hides optional content.
- [rule] In a dialogue tree, let an NPC volunteer a motive when asked about their last contact, and unlock a hidden line through a follow-up question. When: When designing NPC conversation branches for investigation. Why: Layered questioning rewards players who probe rather than accept the first answer.
- [rule] Build dialogue options that are true but unhelpful, so the player can deflect without giving new information. When: Designing evasive dialogue choices. Why: Deflection options let players protect information without lying.
- [rule] Offer dialogue options with different wording, such as stranger, visitor, or anyone carrying cargo, so the choice of framing becomes a fair-play puzzle. When: when a question's wording changes the answer. Why: Precise framing exposes answers that broad framing hides.
- [rule] Make NPC dialogue literally true yet misleading when the player's knowledge is incomplete, and let later evidence revise earlier statements in the player's notes. When: When designing NPC testimony in a game. Why: Lets players discover that accurate words can still hide the truth.
- [rule] Open a new NPC question only after the player has overheard and recorded an exact phrase from another character, rewarding careful listening. When: designing dialogue progression. Why: quotations link conversations and reward attention.
- [rule] Build reticent dialogue options that signal hesitation without stating the secret, so the player senses something is held back. When: Designing dialogue for a character who knows more than they say.
- [rule] After an NPC reacts strongly, offer a later return point, since forcing dialogue then can shut it down. When: An upset NPC ends or refuses conversation. Why: Pressing an agitated character closes off further dialogue.
- [rule] Model NPC interviews as dialogue options for sympathy, pressure and bribery, each changing what the NPC reveals and how reliable it is. When: designing NPC interrogation.
- [rule] Write witness dialogue with perspective bias so players can compare two accounts and spot the distortions.
- [rule] A dialogue system can offer an honest option that an NPC reads as a joke or lie, with the reading depending on the NPC's traits. When: When designing dialogue choices that depend on NPC personality. Why: NPC traits change how the same truthful statement is interpreted.
- [rule] Write NPC dialogue with filler and a few key facts, so the player must sort useful lines from noise. When: When writing long NPC monologues. Why: Filler makes the key facts a test of attention, giving the player an active role.
- [rule] Design NPC dialogue to open with fixed low-stakes questions that record a baseline, then branch on the reply to a pointed question.
- [rule] Let an NPC answer aggressive dialogue options with silence, while a respectful or culturally specific option unlocks a structured account.
- [rule] Let players receive partial payment first and the rest after proof, so the mechanic tests NPC sincerity.
- [rule] Let NPCs sign public statements of good character that the player can collect as a counter-case.
- [rule] Let a boastful NPC mention a location or name in passing, so the player's deduction, not the NPC's intent, delivers the clue. When: designing NPC dialogue.
- [heuristic] Order NPC conversation from background to events to opinions, and let an NPC tell its full story before handing out clues, so players gather facts before theories. When: designing dialogue that carries clues. Why: Complete context lets the player interpret each clue correctly.
- [heuristic] Ask witnesses about peripheral details they may have seen unnoticed; answers reveal whether the account was observed. A prompt asking if an NPC noticed a detail unlocks otherwise hidden observations.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs unprompted plausible explanations for traces, and let each cover story hold until the player finds a conflicting fact, turning the explanation into a test. When: designing NPC dialogue that hides a truth. Why: Delayed contradiction turns a stated explanation into a puzzle the player can test against evidence.
- [heuristic] In dialogue, give a key word two valid meanings tied to different items or places, so the player must test each reading. When: designing clue dialogue. Why: the player must weigh alternatives rather than accept one.
- [heuristic] Structure quest-giver dialogue as a checklist of topics the player must cover before the NPC reveals a key fact. When: Designing gated dialogue.
- [heuristic] Test an NPC's claimed identity with a dialogue branch that offers a choice and a warning, showing a visible behavior change if the claim is false. When: Designing a dialogue where an NPC's identity can be challenged.
- [heuristic] Offer a dialogue option that lets the player threaten to reveal a secret, with the NPC responding differently depending on trust and evidence collected. When: when designing NPC interrogation. Why: leverage gives the player agency and makes NPC responses depend on prior play.
- [heuristic] Asking what someone said as they departed can expose their intent, since farewell remarks often carry it.
- [heuristic] Patience and small personal rapport keep a suspect talking better than force does, while the core secret stays protected. When: when a suspect guards a central secret. Why: rapport keeps the subject talking.
- [heuristic] A suspect who asks to postpone questions while promising a full account later is making a telling move worth noting. When: a suspect reacts with a request to defer questioning. Why: deferral often signals something being held back.
- [heuristic] When a suspect's performed image conflicts with a genuine emotional reaction, the mismatch is a clue that can expose the performance. When: a single event reveals the suspect's true reaction. Why: People performing a role tend to show the emotions that fit the role, so a genuine reaction breaks the pattern.
- [heuristic] Script an informant NPC with a grudge to reveal a location or object when the player gives a partial answer, and include self-justifying lines that the player must weigh. When: Designing an NPC informant in a dialogue-driven game. Why: Partial answers and biased framing make the reveal feel earned and keep reliability uncertain.
- [heuristic] Use a pause once, and use a physical prop to focus attention on the key evidence; repeated pauses dull the effect. When: Staging a reveal's climax. Why: A single well-placed pause and a visible prop direct attention without fatigue.
- [procedure] 1) Tell the other party you already know part of the matter. 2) Ask them to supply what is missing. 3) Note which parts they correct or react to. When: Interviewing someone who would refuse a direct question.
- [procedure] 1) Gather concrete points of evidence. 2) Secure endorsement from independent authorities. 3) Make the accusation only after that support is in place. When: When an extraordinary claim meets resistant listeners. Why: Independent endorsement counters the suspicion that the accuser is unbalanced.
- [pitfall] A suspect who suspects a trap may perform innocence, so the observer's reading of the reaction can be misleading. When: A decoy test is used on a suspect who may be alert. Why: A deliberate act can imitate the reaction of an innocent recipient.
- [pitfall] Staying passive while detained lets the opponent act freely; relying only on your own standing can fail when you are a stranger.
- [pitfall] A restated answer can be taken as a commitment the subject never made, so restatements should be checked with the subject.
- [pitfall] When the exchange turns personal, the interview can end early and the questioner loses control of it.
- [pitfall] Gathering all parties into one room reveals motives, but witnesses may then perform for the room rather than report honestly. When: A group confrontation is staged. Why: People adjust their statements when others are watching.
- [pitfall] Sincere penitence does not prove the earlier testimony was true.
- [fact] Accused people in such records respond in three ways: they confess, they refuse to plead, or they confess and later withdraw the confession.

## handwriting analysis
- [mechanism] Offer two plausible writing orders for a document and let the game check which one matches the item's recorded history. When: designing document puzzles.
- [behavior] An unfamiliar handwriting on a known person's document often looks like a forgery, until a physical condition such as an injury explains a slow, cramped or awkward script. When: A known person's writing looks unfamiliar. Why: Players and characters assume forgery before considering physical causes.
- [rule] Handwriting conclusions need known comparison samples from the suspect or a second source; testimony about the writing is not proof, so do not authenticate an unfamiliar hand without them. Why: Without comparison material, conclusions are easily overclaimed and rest only on whoever holds the papers. (x2)
- [rule] Model handwriting or prints as puzzle mechanics: give players a suspect's known sample to compare against a forged or altered note; comparison is a concrete, checkable method. When: Designing document-based deduction puzzles or forgery clues. Why: Comparison lets players test authorship themselves. (x2)
- [rule] Separate the words actually spoken from the meaning later attributed to them; knowing vocabulary does not mean knowing the sense, so each can be disputed alone. When: A remark is later interpreted as a serious claim, or a fragment is heard. Why: An ambiguous remark can be read as stronger than what was said.
- [rule] Keep an independent duplicate of an in-game record out of the forger's reach, and make forged entries complete but in another hand, so players detect them by comparison. When: Designing alterable documents such as ledgers or shrine records, or placing in-world records. Why: A second source exposes the forgery.
- [rule] Record a witness's account in their own words, so nuances an interpreter might flatten are preserved. When: taking statements that will later be interpreted.
- [rule] Do not present a witness's words as proof of a fact the witness did not assert. When: Using testimony to support a claim.
- [rule] Compare a written instruction against another copy, since a single dropped word can change where the search should go. When: when a riddle or document exists in more than one version. Why: Copying errors can alter the meaning of a direction.
- [rule] Make a written description complete, since it may later be circulated for identification and every omission weakens it. When: A witness's description will be used to identify a missing person or item. Why: Gaps reduce the description's usefulness.
