- [rule] Give NPC ledgers or receipts a deliberate anomaly so a player who questions it uncovers a hidden transaction. When: When designing NPC-owned records for a mystery. Why: Questioning an anomaly rewards observation and drives discovery.
- [rule] Write found letters so their meaning shifts with what the player has already learned, rather than fixing a single reading.
- [rule] Give documents fixed entry slots so that a deleted entry shows as a gap, letting players detect tampering from layout alone. When: Designing in-game records meant to be checked.
- [rule] Use an introduction letter from a trusted NPC as an item that gates access to a faction or location.
- [rule] Hide information on a document's reverse side, and let an object's scene location carry part of the story. When: designing clues that reward close inspection. Why: Hidden layers and placement add meaning beyond the visible text or item.
- [rule] Let a note's handwriting or wording carry clues about the writer's physical condition, such as a cramped script or a left-handed slant. When: Designing written clues in a game. Why: Physical details in writing give players a testable link to a character's state.
- [rule] Give an NPC a distinctive written trait, such as a letterform or phrasing, so players can match it against a note found elsewhere. When: Designing written clues that link to a character. Why: A matchable trait lets players connect documents to characters.
- [rule] Record which features were compared when an expert judges handwriting, rather than letting a quick verdict settle the matter. When: when relying on an expert's opinion on authorship. Why: Unrecorded reasoning cannot be checked or challenged.
- [heuristic] Compare anonymous writing with known signed samples and interlineations of similar length and type; a match ties the writer, but may point to more than one writer. When: Attributing anonymous writing to a person, especially when a name or seal cannot be trusted alone. Why: Samples of similar form make the comparison meaningful. (x2)
- [heuristic] Phrasing and structure of an unsigned letter can hint at the writer's sex or background, weighed against other evidence; incoherent writing can raise doubts about state of mind.
- [heuristic] Unusual word choice, word order or sentence structure can point to a writer's native language or origin, letting the player narrow the writer down to one region.
- [heuristic] Ink stains on a writer's fingers, especially on the outer edge with the pen type, can link a suspect to a writing act; check hands as well as face. When: Investigating a suspect connected to written messages, or a writer's hand bears ink marks. Why: Small traces remain on the body after the act; writing habits leave consistent marks.
- [heuristic] Handwriting matches are strong only with distinctive features; generic script proves little, and several agreeing distinctive letterforms together are stronger than one, since one may match by chance. When: Comparing a handwriting sample with a suspect's writing. Why: Shared generic features occur across many writers, while rare features point to one person.
- [heuristic] Two distinct handwriting styles on one document indicate that different people wrote it. Why: Hands differ in pressure and letter form.
- [heuristic] Compare stroke strength, such as the crossing of t's, across words to attribute each word to one writer.
- [heuristic] A difference in ink shade between two parts of a writing can imply a pause, suggesting the writer stopped to look something up and was unfamiliar with the content. When: Judging a written note's composition from its appearance. Why: Ink dries and fades over time, so a shade change marks a break in writing.
- [heuristic] Compare the tone of different lines; a dark and a pale ink in one document suggest separate moments of writing. When: a document's wording or hand seems to change partway through. Why: separate writing moments leave marks of different freshness.
- [heuristic] Handwriting that differs from a person's usual hand suggests disguise or that the writer is not who is assumed.
- [heuristic] Combine material clues with a messenger's description to infer the social circle of the document's writer. When: A document's writer is unknown but a messenger was seen.
- [heuristic] Straggling letters, a broad pen with poor ink, and a corrected spelling together suggest a writer of limited education who is unfamiliar with the place named. When: When assessing a writer's background from handwriting and spelling. Why: Multiple small writing signs reinforce one another.
- [heuristic] When one writer leaves blanks that a second writer must fill, the writer who left the gaps wrote first and planned the text.
- [heuristic] Read the steadiness of a rushed record as evidence of conditions: neat writing suggests stillness, shaky writing suggests movement, and the worst writing suggests a bumpy or jolting ride. When: When a written record was made under physical conditions that are unknown. Why: Writing quality changes with the motion or stress of the writer.
- [heuristic] Compare handwriting by letter forms, stroke length and line steadiness; disguised writing often shows an uneven upstroke or letters that straggle as if the hand shook.
- [heuristic] A pseudonym or wordplay signature may be a deliberate choice meant to be noticed, but should not be read as a confession. Why: signatures can signal intent without admitting guilt.
- [heuristic] Minor wording variation is normal, so ask whether a variation changes substance before treating it as a contradiction. When: Comparing two accounts of the same event. Why: Most differences are phrasing, and only substantive ones undermine a claim.
- [heuristic] A dead NPC's letter hidden in a mailbox or journal can carry times, names and objects that the player must cross-check against other clues.
- [heuristic] A print with an identifiable scar can be matched to a known person, while smudges repeated over several surfaces can suggest gloves.
- [heuristic] Use handwriting features such as letter size, irregularity and underlining to infer something about the writer, with emphasis marking deliberate stress. When: A written document has distinctive handwriting or marked words. Why: Writing habits reveal education level, intent and sometimes identity.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain known samples of the writer's hand and signature. 2) Judge the disputed writing on its own, then place it beside them, reproduced at the same scale. 3) Compare letter forms line by line, noting shared forms that differ in slope or detail. 4) Judge authenticity or single authorship only from that comparison. When: A document's authenticity or author is central to a claim or in doubt. Why: Authenticity can only be assessed against known samples; step-by-step comparison exposes resemblance and difference rather than a quick verdict. (x3)
- [procedure] 1) Obtain two independent records of the same event. 2) List the details each keeps and drops. 3) Treat differences as evidence of the recorder's choices, not of what happened; they show which points each emphasized.
- [procedure] 1) Compare a handwritten item's signature with a signed sample from a known source. 2) Flag a likely match for formal laboratory confirmation. When: when the authenticity of handwriting matters.
- [procedure] 1) List recurring letter forms across the disguised samples. 2) Check whether the same forms recur in each sample. 3) Compare them with a known hand to confirm or rule out a match. When: Two writings may share an author. Why: Habitual letter forms are hard to disguise consistently.
- [procedure] 1) Identify distinctive letter forms in the disputed sample. 2) Compare those same forms in a known sample. 3) Record the result as full, partial, or no match. When: Checking whether a disputed writing belongs to a known person. Why: Focusing on distinctive forms gives a more reliable comparison than general impressions.
- [procedure] 1) Note the audible fragment of a word. 2) Match the fragment against a map or list of names, allowing for the hidden letters. 3) Check each candidate against independent background facts. When: a dying utterance or partial word is heard. Why: a fragment can be completed by matching it against a known list.
- [procedure] 1) List the visible fragments. 2) Propose several candidate readings. 3) Match each candidate to the surviving marks and discard those that fit poorly. 4) Test survivors against the likely author and context. When: A partial or damaged document is the only source of a fact. Why: Testing candidates against marks and authorship filters out plausible but wrong readings.
- [procedure] 1) Collect a known sample of the suspect's writing and the paper it is on. 2) Compare both with the note. 3) Compare with a second person's writing to rule out a match. When: A note must be tied to a writer. Why: Matching paper and hand together is stronger than either alone, and a control shows discrimination.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain known exemplars from the suspected machine. 2) Examine the questioned item and exemplar closely before consulting others. 3) Compare them side by side at the same scale. 4) Identify several shared flaws. 5) Have others check the comparison. When: matching a questioned document to a machine. Why: independent examination first limits outside influence, and several shared flaws are needed for a sound match.
- [procedure] 1) Notice the visible marker. 2) Apply the fixed selection rule, such as taking every nth word. 3) Read the resulting words. 4) Interpret them as coordinates, times or instructions. When: When a short text carries a hidden message. Why: A fixed rule plus a marker turns innocent-looking text into a decodable message.
- [metric] Handwriting can estimate age within about a decade: steady bold hand suggests youth, broken declining hand suggests age, but illness or weakness can make it look older.
- [pitfall] Handwriting resemblance is not identity: carelessness, disguise or gloves can change a hand; report attribution hedged, open to more than one reading, never as proof or from handwriting alone. Why: Handwriting alone has limited reliability. (x2)
- [pitfall] Handwriting is weak evidence and experts may disagree, even on disguise; relying on an expert without noting limits invites being overturned under challenge. When: Handwriting is offered as proof of authorship, or expert readings of a damaged document are used as evidence. Why: Expert opinions have bounded confidence that opposing sides can attack; disguised script gives too little to conclude reliably. (x2)
- [pitfall] A handwriting match alone is weak since any hand can be imitated; weigh it alongside other evidence and confirm with a second independent source. Why: Forgers can copy a writing style; handwriting rarely settles who wrote a document on its own.
- [pitfall] Paper stock and colour are common across households, so a bare match proves little; a match needs distinctive features such as defects or matching ruling, combined with other traits. Why: Widely shared materials produce matches by chance.
- [pitfall] A later narrator or listener can change exact wording, turning a loose account into apparent proof, so compare original phrasing with retellings. When: A story is retold across records or time, or a private remark is reported by a second person. Why: Memory and interpretation alter exact words, so the original claim may never be fully settled.
- [pitfall] Relying on handwriting alone works only once the list of who had seen the true sample has been established.
- [pitfall] A case sheet that fills every heading can still be wrong, and circumstantial evidence can be stacked against an innocent person. When: When a case looks complete on paper. Why: Filled headings reflect assembly, not proof.
- [pitfall] Assuming record writers shared a reader's values misreads routine entries, which may reflect norms different from the reader's own.
- [fact] Handwriting can improve with practice; hurried or shaky script can reflect the writer's agitation and focus, and imitation leaves its own traces. Why: Writing quality reflects state of mind.
- [fact] Handwriting in an unsigned document usually reveals little beyond a rough education level, since a faint or blotted hand gives few clues to identity.
- [fact] Pen and pencil leave different impressions on lower layers, so the writing tool affects what can be recovered.
- [fact] A short handwritten note can compress a whole plan into routes, times, places and open questions, so it carries much in few words.
- [fact] Witness signatures show that others were prepared to swear to a record, but they do not by themselves prove that its contents are accurate.
- [fact] Edges worn beyond normal and creases matching old folds show a sheet was refolded and resealed, which a careful player can read as tamper evidence.
- [fact] Writing signed in gloves under a false name can produce unusual handwriting that resembles a disguised hand. When: A suspect signs a register while trying to hide identity. Why: Gloves and deliberate writing change letterforms, creating an atypical signature.

## contradiction detection
- [mechanism] Store contradictions between statements or facts; each unlocks follow-up questions on a single detail, including flagged evasive answers, so the player can press for resolution. When: when designing interrogation dialogue or NPC testimony. Why: Contradictions create a new goal, pushing the player to investigate further. (x2)
- [mechanism] Design clues with a known comparison source, such as mud matched to a room floor, or a ledger or NPC record, so players can test statements. When: Designing physical or environmental clues. Why: A known source gives players a concrete test to apply.
- [mechanism] A conversation system can compare an NPC's spoken claims against stored verbatim records or recorded facts, flagging conflicts the player exposes through questioning. When: when the game stores a witness's words or facts that NPCs may contradict. Why: Verbatim records make earlier statements retrievable and comparable, so the contradiction becomes detectable through the player's questions.
- [mechanism] A clue that conflicts with the known timeline or working theory, such as an obedient servant, forces the player to revise who could be present or the whole account. When: when designing a mystery puzzle or a mystery where the player holds a working theory. Why: The conflict forces reassessment of an assumption.
- [mechanism] Minor out-of-place details each mean little alone, but together they reveal one actor's deliberate pattern once the player collects enough of them. When: when a hidden actor leaves small anomalies across several locations. Why: A pattern only becomes visible when several anomalies are compared.
- [mechanism] A measured discrepancy between a room's dimensions and its plan can be placed as a clue that reveals a hidden room, and the reveal should stay visible to the player. When: Designing a level with concealed rooms. Why: The player who noticed the mismatch earns the payoff when the room is revealed.
- [rule] Record every NPC statement and build contradictions into witness accounts that players can expose by comparing statements, rewarding those who spot them rather than excusing them. When: when writing multiple NPC statements. Why: exposed contradictions reward careful comparison. (x2)
- [rule] Design contradictions visible only when two answers or records are compared, so players must cross-check; reward those who note days and times. When: when writing interrogation dialogue or clues that depend on cross-referencing. Why: Hidden contradictions reward careful note-taking and make the solution feel earned. (x2)
- [rule] When a fact contradicts a theory or deduction, doubt the premise behind it rather than bending or discarding the fact.
- [rule] Have two or more NPCs give conflicting accounts of the same event or third person, so players must weigh sources and check which matches physical evidence.
- [rule] Give two NPC experts conflicting readings of one object, such as a diagnosis or poison, and let the player settle it with the right follow-up question or verification. When: Designing identification puzzles.
- [rule] Log or file contradicting answers for later review rather than smoothing or discarding them, since a later player may need the conflict to resolve the case.
- [rule] Reveal or resolve a withheld purpose later; otherwise the ominous action feels arbitrary.
- [rule] Let players keep a contradiction list on a mystery board, where each missing or conflicting detail is resolved by later evidence. When: designing a mystery that players solve through evidence.
- [rule] Accept an explanation for a document contradiction only when it fits the physical evidence; then the document can be returned safely.
- [rule] When an object contradicts a witness's claim, verify both the claim and the object's context before accepting either. When: When testimony and physical evidence conflict. Why: Either may be mistaken or false.
- [rule] Give observers biased theories so their notes need cross-checking before the player trusts them. When: when designing observer NPCs.
- [rule] An NPC whose behaviour contradicts their stated reason can form a deduction puzzle in which the player assembles who was present, what was said, and what the NPC does next. When: Designing an NPC whose stated reason conflicts with observed conduct. Why: Contradiction invites the player to reconstruct the scene.
- [rule] Reward players for checking a written clue against independent sources, so that accurate details build trust in the note and accusations need separate proof.
- [rule] Attach small, unreliable witness details to the case file as corroboration rather than proof. When: Populating a generated case file with witness information. Why: Partial details accumulate into a stronger case without a single decisive clue.
- [rule] Tag each story claim as core, affecting the solution, or flavour, never checked, so the player is not required to verify decorative details.
- [rule] Give a legend or in-world history several contradictory versions, then let the player check each against a physical record to find the reliable one. When: when generating lore or documents.
- [rule] In pursuit encounters, let NPCs give conflicting descriptions that are corrected mid-exchange, so players must reconcile them. When: Designing NPC dialogue during a chase.
- [rule] Plant a blank or altered document in an NPC's possession, and offer the dismissal as a dialogue option that a later reveal can reopen. When: Designing NPC-held clues.
- [rule] Design a clue to point one way while surrounding context points another, so the player must weigh both before deciding. When: designing clue sets. Why: conflicting signals make deduction meaningful.
- [rule] Give players an item whose state contradicts the expected story, such as a costume on a body that its owner would not wear, and let the answer come from a second item elsewhere. When: Designing physical clues for a mystery. Why: Contradictions invite inquiry, and a second location forces the player to connect separate clues.
- [heuristic] Check each account against other accounts and observed details; a single contradiction, such as a conflicting remark or denied knock, opens a line of inquiry, especially who-where-when disagreements. When: when witness accounts disagree with each other or with observed details, or when choosing which answers to challenge. Why: Conflicts point to the account that is false or incomplete, and timing and location conflicts are where accounts can be tested. (x2)
- [heuristic] Let a cover story vary between repetitions, since inconsistent versions can reveal the truth to a careful listener who compares them.
- [heuristic] Place objects or later clues that contradict an NPC's stated habits or public image, such as a feeding dish with no listed pet, so players must ask or compare sources. When: when designing NPC rooms with stated habits or public images hiding a different truth. Why: the mismatch prompts inference; comparing sources rewards careful players.
- [heuristic] Test NPC and witness claims against checkable world state, such as timestamps, positions, locked doors, logs or a second witness, treating each account as true until contradicted. When: when designing witness statements, NPC testimony or alibis. Why: Checkable contradictions give players a fair way to find inconsistencies.
- [heuristic] Present contradicting or ambiguous clues that a later clue, such as a map or receipt, resolves, so players reason through competing evidence instead of receiving one answer. When: when a clue has two valid readings or investigation design needs competing evidence. Why: A corroborating clue narrows the readings without removing the puzzle.
- [heuristic] Use several converging traits, each eliminating candidate origins, and confirm the surviving match with a later physical find; a lone mark proves little. When: when authoring physical evidence or a clue database for a mystery. Why: Only converging marks make the inference reliable; layered elimination lets players reason to an answer.
- [heuristic] Make ambiguous NPC phrases resolvable only by checking the room, not by dialogue alone.
- [heuristic] A flawed line of inquiry can still lead to the truth, so keep checking other leads instead of abandoning the investigation.
- [heuristic] When a client's stated view contradicts their request, treat the mixed signal as something to clarify before proceeding. When: when a client both disbelieves and fears an explanation.
- [heuristic] When a witness's account contradicts a known fact, the contradiction shifts doubt onto whoever produced the conflicting event. When: a claim about a detail conflicts with verified evidence. Why: The conflict shows which account fails to fit the record, pointing scrutiny at the party it implicates.
- [heuristic] When a fact contradicts a theory, look for one plan that explains both, then test each hypothesis that results.
- [heuristic] Test a witness's account against a physical item or verifiable record the witness did not expect the investigator to have. When: A witness's account is rehearsed or plausible. Why: Prepared stories hold against expected questions but not against unanticipated evidence.
- [heuristic] When two accounts of one event conflict and both parties are present, comparing them against the original document exposes contradictions. When: Two parties give conflicting accounts of the same event. Why: The original text is the only fixed reference both sides must accept.
- [heuristic] When two records disagree, weigh the keeper's motive, check what each omits, and use the richer source where the other is silent.
- [heuristic] When sources disagree on identity, prefer the account closer to the event, but check how each document was made before trusting either. When: A first-hand letter conflicts with a formal record. Why: A formal record may rest on second-hand answers.
- [heuristic] A writer's contradictions and hedges may hide unfairness, so check whether they blur facts or shift blame. When: A writer's logic does not follow consistently. Why: Confusing logic can conceal partiality.
- [heuristic] Make the weak reason behind an NPC's claim discoverable so a careful player can catch the gap. When: when designing NPC testimony that may be wrong or self-serving. Why: discovery rewards careful checking and makes the reasoning feel fair.
- [heuristic] Phrase a prediction as a checkable statement, such as a departure in N minutes, so the player can confirm it against an in-game schedule. When: writing clue text. Why: A verifiable claim rewards careful checking and builds trust in the clue.
- [heuristic] Give a test result that contradicts an NPC's claim, forcing the player to revise the plan.
- [heuristic] Give a speaker a plausible reason to deny an overheard remark, so the player must cross-check with another witness. When: Designing overheard NPC lines that serve as clues. Why: A deniable line forces the player to gather corroboration.
- [heuristic] When some traits of a substance match a known compound and others do not, expect the identification to need extra analysis to resolve the conflict.
- [heuristic] Attack a consensus point by point, pairing each claim with a counter-clue, rather than rejecting it wholesale.
- [heuristic] Let a culprit's own statements contradict each other so the player can catch them out. When: when writing a suspect's testimony. Why: Contradictions give the player a way to expose a lie without a confession.
- [procedure] 1) List each unresolved thread. 2) Assign each a concrete outcome, such as money, income or management of assets. 3) Resolve the last emotional thread.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the conflicting detail between accounts. 2) Return to the witness with a specific question about that detail. 3) Accept the account that holds under that question. When: When two descriptions of the same person or event disagree. Why: A specific question tests which account is accurate.
- [procedure] 1) List the innocent explanation, such as a memory error. 2) List the deliberate explanation, such as withheld information. 3) Test each with a separate check. When: A witness's account contradicts what was found.
- [procedure] 1) Identify which referent the witness had in mind. 2) Check whether the witness can recall the date. 3) Test whether that reading explains the conflict without requiring forgery.
- [procedure] 1) State the statement that existing facts seem to contradict. 2) Search outside sources for a connecting fact. 3) Read the wording by the customs of its period. 4) Test the proposed answer against dates. 5) Check whether it explains other odd facts.
- [procedure] 1) Record each conflicting statement with its timestamp. 2) Lay the statements on one timeline. 3) Find the point where two accounts cannot both be true. 4) Test the claims on each side of that point separately. When: Several accounts of one period conflict. Why: A shared timeline exposes the exact contradiction that needs resolving.
- [tradeoff] Resolving a recurring figure later pays off the setup. Leaving him a red herring tests the player's judgement but risks the thread feeling unfinished. When: Designing a figure who appears across several scenes.
- [pitfall] A contradiction can arise from honest error, confusion, fatigue or forgetfulness as easily as deceit, so treat it as an error to check, not automatically a lie. When: when a witness's account conflicts with known facts. Why: Honest memory errors also produce contradictions.
- [pitfall] Investigators tend to inflate a minor oddity, such as one open window, into a conspiracy, giving it disproportionate weight; look for other evidence before building a plot around it. When: when a minor object or fact conflicts with the expected picture. Why: Anomalies stand out against the expected pattern and accumulate in attention.
- [pitfall] An investigator who warns about hearing errors must apply the same caution to their own inferences. When: when an investigator critiques others' testimony. Why: Self-made inferences are also prone to error.
- [pitfall] Describing the same trace differently in different scenes confuses the reader unless the change is clearly marked.
- [pitfall] A time reported by a witness may not match the moment of the act, so timelines should allow for delay between event and report.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a contradiction between two witnesses instead of asking what each could hear hides the explanation. When: two accounts of sound disagree. Why: Positional differences often explain the conflict.
- [pitfall] A statement can reject one thing and accept it in the next clause, so a contradiction may sit inside a single passage. Why: Close reading is needed to catch a reversal hidden within one sentence.

## faction politics
- [model] A hidden organizer directs crime through layers of expendable agents who carry out the physical acts, keeping the planner out of sight.
- [model] A faction model can split roles into those who order an action and those who decide on it, so players can trace which authority shielded whom. When: designing faction or political systems. Why: Separated roles make the chain of responsibility visible to the player.
- [mechanism] Once an adversary's plan is exposed or it learns the player knows it, it changes timing or switches to a fallback route, so predictions based on the old plan lapse. When: after the adversary's plan is exposed or it learns the player knows it. Why: a known plan can be countered, and the player must keep that knowledge hidden.
- [mechanism] A visible mark on the body lets members recognise one another on sight, so a stranger can be identified without questioning. When: designing faction membership. Why: Recognition on sight is quicker than verbal checks.
- [mechanism] A hidden occupant can be served through a fixed routine, such as a tray left out and collected later, so that no one sees them. When: someone must be sustained while kept out of view. Why: a predictable exchange avoids direct contact.
- [mechanism] A faction that loses members one by one can have survivors' dialogue hint at a traitor, so players sense the betrayal. When: designing faction storylines.
- [mechanism] When a faction leader dies, its remaining members can flee or lose control, leaving documents the player can collect.
- [mechanism] An influential faction can be won over through a sequence of corroborating witnesses, each adding support to the claim.
- [mechanism] Removing a faction's members from a body can sharply weaken its hold, opening a window for rivals to act. When: an election or vote changes a body's membership.
- [mechanism] NPCs can judge the player by allies or factions the player is visibly associated with, so a visible affiliation changes how a town treats them. When: The player is seen with a group the town distrusts. Why: Groups stand in for individual knowledge of the player.
- [mechanism] Raising a faction's threat level lowers the chance that witnesses talk, so the player must reduce that threat before testimony becomes available. When: Faction-controlled districts in a game. Why: Fear suppresses cooperation, so threat should directly cut witness willingness.
- [mechanism] A reputation value that rises when accusations are backed by evidence and falls when they are not gives players a reason to gather proof first.
- [mechanism] A faction's shared belief can be modelled as a mechanic that changes its members' actions, even when the belief is false.
- [mechanism] Model an opposing faction's reaction to a public notice as a timed consequence, such as moving a hostage once the notice appears. When: Levels or quests where a public action triggers enemy responses. Why: A timed reaction makes the player's public move carry a cost that can be seen and planned against.
- [mechanism] When a captor's goal is met or appears lost, the captive's value falls and the danger to the captive rises. Finding or destroying the wanted object can trigger escalation.
- [mechanism] A body or object modeled as a state machine makes deviation from expected states a clue that prompts the player to ask who interfered. When: Designing physical states in a game world. Why: The game rules define what is expected, so departures are detectable.
- [mechanism] NPCs that react to events after a delay reveal when they learned of them, letting the player rebuild the information timeline.
- [behavior] In a watched group, private meetings are reported quickly, so members should expect their contacts to be known to superiors. When: when a group monitors its members. Why: surveillance spreads news of meetings fast.
- [behavior] A group with a shared interest in conviction can keep pressing a case after individual members have begun to doubt it. When: when a faction has invested in an outcome. Why: group identity and shared stakes outlast private doubts.
- [behavior] Factional loyalty can lead a witness to defend or attack a suspect regardless of what they actually saw. When: when a witness belongs to a rival or allied group of the suspect. Why: group loyalty shapes testimony more than direct observation does.
- [rule] Record NPC land and fence disputes as sworn statements in a relationship ledger, keeping settled quarrels on record so players can compare accounts and see past motives. When: designing faction-driven motives or generating NPC relationships. Why: Recorded disputes generate motive and let players compare competing accounts, and past settled conflicts still shape present motives.
- [rule] Give each faction its own accepted theories, so the same clue or sudden event carries different meanings for each group, feeding reputation or suspicion. When: when designing factions in a game world.
- [rule] Have a faction state its stake in plain terms so the player's choice between a rival's gain and their own losses is clear.
- [rule] Plant small odd details, such as a stamp or seal on a letter, that suggest a hidden faction, and let the player choose which explanation to test. When: designing hidden factions. Why: players enjoy testing their own reading.
- [rule] Give a faction a cover-up history shown through monuments or signs that repeat a false account, which players can uncover by comparing them with physical evidence. When: Designing hidden history in a game world.
- [rule] Let factions share some clues and withhold others under a written rule set, so trades are predictable enough for the player to anticipate.
- [rule] Give hidden factions anonymous identities and let players learn their true names through separate clues. When: designing factions whose members conceal who they are. Why: Separate clues spread the reveal across the game and keep identities mysterious.
- [rule] Create a self-appointed faction that escalates suspicion, arrests suspects and pressures official leaders, so official process is not the only source of pressure. When: when designing a town's power structure.
- [rule] A hearing mechanic can let a rival faction discount the character witnesses a player collects. When: designing hearing or trial mechanics.
- [rule] Let a fight over one plot change a whole faction's reputation, using rules for gossip and witness statements.
- [rule] Give a faction a mission that makes its members read ordinary crimes as parts of a larger plot, and state that mission in documents the player can find.
- [rule] Escalate a local investigation by moving it to a higher court or faction with new rules, a larger audience and new NPCs, signalled by who arranged the transfer.
- [rule] Treat faction membership as a record the player can check, such as a rate roll, rather than a fact an NPC simply states.
- [rule] Make a succession a visible prize with recorded votes and abstentions, so players can trace who was excluded and why. When: designing a faction succession plot.
- [rule] Give a council a faction-controlled nominal lord; a player tracing appointments can discover that the real authority is an advisor. When: designing a faction-run government in a game.
- [rule] Lay out a faction's history as a dated chain of events, such as a grudge, an appointment and an accusation, so a mystery's motive emerges as a traceable sequence. When: designing a faction backstory for a mystery.
- [rule] Tie faction and grudge flags to NPC reactions and to suspect assignment, and show the reputation effect in dialogue. When: Designing a system where reputation shapes who is blamed.
- [rule] Let accusations spread from one faction to others, each tied to a property or rivalry interest the player can investigate. When: town-scale mystery design.
- [rule] Let a hostile NPC's exit close one line of player inquiry while opening another. When: a confrontation ends with the NPC leaving.
- [rule] Define crimes by a faction's doctrine, such as heresy defined by belief rather than deed, and let the game's evidence rules follow that worldview. When: when generating laws and evidence for a faction. Why: what counts as proof depends on how the faction defines the offence.
- [rule] Store a territory dispute as landmarks that drift over time, so players who track them get different answers depending on when they check. When: when generating land disputes with physical markers. Why: drifting markers make the boundary itself a clue to reconstruct.
- [rule] Map factions by their land claims, and let players uncover a grudge behind a fight through an old debt entry or lawsuit record.
- [rule] Tie how much a rival faction shares with the player to reputation, so cooperation changes with the player's standing.
- [rule] Give AI enemies believable goals such as silence and escape; a pointless action will read as a clue and can make the player distrust the scene.
- [heuristic] Use oblique in-world phrases or faction idioms for hidden objectives or threats, letting players misread them until later context reveals meaning. (x2)
- [heuristic] Give a faction's officials a stated bias that the player can recognise and test against the evidence.
- [heuristic] Identify a source's grudge, such as envy, ambition or vanity toward a rival, and use it as a lever to win cooperation. When: When a witness or colleague is driven by resentment or pride. Why: A personal grudge makes the source willing to talk.
- [heuristic] Give each faction or NPC a plausible gain from a stolen item so players can reason about who would act.
- [heuristic] Give a helper a specific job, such as watching roads and reporting back, to keep them busy and away from the real work. When: an ally is helping with a hidden purpose. Why: an occupied helper is less likely to discover the true activity.
- [heuristic] Give each faction or character a different goal, such as conviction or a scapegoat, so players must weigh their claims.
- [heuristic] Make land, tithes or office a visible stake in each faction's quarrel so players can predict who will accuse whom. When: designing faction conflicts for a game. Why: Visible stakes make accusation patterns predictable.
- [heuristic] An executive act such as a reprieve shows who held office when it was performed, even when the document names only the office. When: A document records an act that only an office holder could perform. Why: The act implies who held the power then.
- [heuristic] Compare who is named in a list of trusted or signed figures with who is absent. An absence can be evidence of allegiance, but party rivalry may explain it instead. When: A case has factions and lists of signatories or invitees survive. Why: Lists reflect alignments, but rivalry can account for a name being left off.
- [heuristic] Make factions protect some NPCs and expose others, so inconsistent enforcement is visible and players question the motives behind it. When: Designing faction-driven justice in a game world. Why: Visible inconsistency prompts players to investigate.
- [heuristic] Environmental objects can carry faction, class or occupation cues such as worn leather or cheap cloth, letting players infer who was present. When: Designing scenes that should imply who was there. Why: Players read visual markers as evidence of identity and status.
- [heuristic] Give each suspect a plausible rival explanation that the timeline can later disprove, so players test theories rather than accept the first one. When: when designing competing suspect theories. Why: checkable rivals make reasoning active.
- [heuristic] When a faction leader accuses another of a crime, let players inspect the records that would confirm or refute the claim, and give the accuser a motive and source they can trace. When: when designing faction accusations in generated content. Why: Traceable sources and checkable records let players judge the claim instead of accepting it.
- [heuristic] Give a skilled enemy a cleanup routine that removes most traces but leaves a few mistakes the player can discover. When: when designing an antagonist that covers its actions. Why: Imperfect cleanup keeps discovery possible without making the enemy look careless.
- [heuristic] Give enemy factions distinct procedures, such as fixed patrols, personal courier meetings or memorised codes, so players can predict and exploit them. When: when designing enemy factions. Why: distinct procedures give players readable patterns.
- [heuristic] Have ambient NPCs react to behaviour, such as a wrong name or a stale detail, rather than only to appearance.
- [heuristic] Give a faction or NPC two options with reputational stakes, so the player forces a choice rather than a fight.
- [heuristic] Give each faction a grievance that seeds its own suspect, so suspicion rotates among factions and the whole system breaks when an accusation hits a respected figure.
- [procedure] 1) Give each NPC property, pay and committee seats. 2) When a faction gains power, activate its grudge list so hostility shifts to the people previously marked. When: designing faction-driven NPC behavior. Why: Shifting power should redirect hostility toward existing targets.

## reaction as evidence
- [definition] A character's sudden shift in posture, voice or gaze, triggered by one detail, can serve as a clue in itself, signalling knowledge the character has not stated.
- [mechanism] A reaction system showing which fact or option an NPC reacts to most strongly, or a mismatch with an unpleasant option's class, points the player to what the NPC hides.
- [mechanism] When accusers' reactions track a suspect's movements and are accepted as proof, the reactions themselves become the evidence, untested for whether they are staged. When: accusers react to the suspect during an examination. Why: Reactions that match the accusation seem to confirm it.
- [mechanism] A startled reaction or a concealed object can be read as guilt, but that reading stays a suspicion until a second source tests it. When: A character's reaction or hidden item suggests guilt while an innocent cause is also possible. Why: Reactions and concealment are ambiguous signals, so they support several explanations.
- [mechanism] A blocked question, together with a witness's visible agitation, can signal that the answer matters and that the witness should be revisited. When: A question is stopped or a witness reacts strongly to it. Why: Obstruction and agitation hint at a sensitive answer.
- [behavior] An angry reaction to an innocent question often betrays a real concern; a strong anger when caught in a restricted area reveals more than spoken words. When: an innocent question is asked, or a person is caught in a restricted area. Why: the reaction exposes what the person wants to conceal.
- [behavior] Alarm at an object found somewhere it should not be signals a link to known evidence; a surprised subject may freeze, drop what they hold and leave hurriedly. When: an object turns up somewhere it should not be, or a subject unexpectedly sees a damning object. Why: surprise and alarm betray knowledge of the object's significance and disrupt normal behaviour.
- [behavior] A sudden, specific question or meeting a witness's eyes can cause colour change, rigidity or dilated pupils even when spoken answers stay smooth, signalling a hidden connection. When: a subject gives smooth answers that leave something out, or a suspect meets a witness's eyes. Why: fear and concealed recognition show involuntarily when a hidden fact is touched or exposed.
- [behavior] A person's manner when an object is raised can reveal more than their words, so investigators watch the reaction closely.
- [behavior] A sudden change of tone after learning a secret can betray a person's real concern, such as a cool manner that turns into relief. When: a character learns a fact that touches their interests. Why: the shift reveals what they value.
- [behavior] A person who pretends an identity can betray it through an involuntary reaction when addressed in the language they actually know. When: checking whether a claimed identity or disguise holds. Why: An unexpected trigger produces a reaction the pretence cannot control.
- [behavior] A request for proof can be read as suspicion, so the person asked may react visibly even while denying distrust. When: A character is asked to prove a claim. Why: Being asked to verify implies doubt, which causes discomfort.
- [behavior] A suspect who collapses or begs after a step-by-step reconstruction shows that the reconstruction has struck home. When: a reconstruction of the crime is presented. Why: the suspect recognises the facts against them.
- [behavior] Mentioning a name the suspect cannot explain can unsettle them, and their reaction can show whom they fear most. When: Probing a suspect with information they did not expect you to have. Why: A guilty or threatened person reacts strongly to a name tied to danger.
- [behavior] A person with nothing to hide tends to object at once to a small unexpected change, while one hiding something may stay silent. When: testing a suspect with a harmless provocation. Why: concealment makes a person prefer going unnoticed.
- [behavior] When an interrogator stresses a single word, the witness often reacts visibly and reframes how they present the account. When: an interrogator emphasises a word the witness used. Why: the stress signals doubt about the claim.
- [behavior] A sudden accusation made before others can provoke the guilty party into an outburst or rash move before they have time to prepare a denial. When: when the culprit is confronted with evidence in front of a group. Why: Lacking time to prepare a denial, the guilty party's reaction exposes them.
- [behavior] A witness confronted with a true fact may show visible physical distress, though such a reaction alone does not establish guilt. When: when a true accusation is put to a witness. Why: Pressure produces involuntary signs.
- [behavior] A suspect's physical reaction to an offered test, such as a tightened grip or a fixed gaze, is a readable signal. When: a test is offered during questioning.
- [behavior] A witness's manner can shift from defiant to frightened when told of a death, after which answers begin to come more readily. When: A witness learns of a serious event tied to them. Why: Fear can overcome resistance and open cooperation.
- [behavior] Showing a person where a found object was located can provoke a strong reaction, which may reveal a connection or be caused by shock alone. When: when an object found on a body is returned to its owner. Why: Both guilt and shock produce strong, similar reactions.
- [behavior] Characters tied to an exposed past often feel shame and resentment and try to limit the damage to their family's name. When: a hidden history touches a character's family.
- [behavior] Witnesses' reactions can track testimony: they grow quiet when an account is accepted and distressed when it is denied. When: group testimony is given in front of an audience. Why: reactions respond to the account rather than to an independent event.
- [behavior] Without sound, observers read meaning from body language such as trembling, turning away, and repeated leaving and returning. When: observing a scene through glass or at a distance. Why: sound is lost, so gestures become the only channel of meaning.
- [behavior] A suspect who refuses a question with a crude, fierce reaction reveals more than a calm answer would, so design confrontations where refusal is itself informative. When: a character is asked a question they do not want to answer. Why: strong refusals expose temperament and stakes.
- [behavior] A suspect whose face changes or who fails to deny a claim has shown a reaction the investigator can take as information. When: A direct claim is made that the suspect cannot easily check. Why: Involuntary reactions and silence can betray what a suspect knows.
- [behavior] A shared glance between people in a tense group can signal strain between them, not proof of guilt.
- [behavior] A character's fearful reaction to a sign can show they know of a group but not its role in the crime, helping judge whom to believe. When: A character reacts to a symbol or sign. Why: Reactions reveal how much a person knows, which may differ from what they say.
- [behavior] A suspect confronted with an unanswerable claim often shows a visible reaction and then changes account.
- [behavior] A person intolerant of opposition on a side issue may be sensitive there while open-minded in their main work. When: when a person's reactions seem inconsistent across topics. Why: vanity can concentrate on one particular subject.
- [behavior] A violent reaction to a question about a partner can itself reveal jealousy or control, which becomes evidence about the person.
- [behavior] A quick return to playful indifference after a reaction shows control, and that control is itself information about the subject.
- [behavior] People's reactions to a missing item, whether joking it off or showing fear, reveal how each person relates to that item. When: a gap is noticed among a group. Why: Each person's stake in the object shapes the reaction.
- [behavior] Observers read a listener's sudden reaction, such as drawing back or glancing toward an exit, as a sign of fear or concealment. When: A named person or place provokes an unexpected response. Why: Involuntary body language signals hidden knowledge to those watching.
- [behavior] A character's unusually strong reaction to news can signal a belief they have not voiced, though the same reaction may also come from simple distress. When: A character reacts strongly to a news item or found object without stating a belief. Why: Strong reactions are observable signals, but their cause is ambiguous and must be interpreted.
- [behavior] A long, silent look followed by calm speech after a hesitation can signal a shift in control of the exchange that alarms the questioner. When: A questioner falters and the witness responds with a prolonged silent look. Why: Sudden stillness and composure change the balance of the encounter.
- [rule] Log NPC tells, such as silence, pacing, a flush, a pale face, an angry whistle, pauses or sudden interest, as readable concealment signals the player learns to interpret. When: NPCs react to a tense interaction, or an NPC is questioned about a sensitive claim. Why: recorded tells let players infer hidden states and how much an interviewee has to conceal, without explicit exposition.
- [rule] In accusation or confession scenes, let the guilty NPC's dialogue visibly change, or send a message implying the player knows more, and treat the reaction as a new clue. When: scripting an NPC confession or accusation scene, or designing an accusation scene. Why: a visible change in dialogue lets the player notice the guilty reaction; the reaction reveals guilt or innocence through behaviour.
- [rule] Reaction branches can be keyed to vulnerabilities the player learned about earlier in the game.
- [rule] Follow a reveal with a brief reaction from a minor character to show how the solution is received. When: Closing a revealed mystery. Why: Shows the consequences of the revelation without more exposition.
- [rule] Validate any reaction-based identification with a control: a decoy who should not trigger the reaction, and an observer who does not know which person is the suspect. When: a suspect is identified by a physical or visible reaction.
- [heuristic] Watch a suspect's pauses, tone changes and body changes alongside the words after each claim, since reactions and aborted answers can reveal what landed or knowledge they should not have. When: interrogating a suspect who may be composed, or a witness who may conceal knowledge. Why: involuntary reactions can reveal information that spoken answers hide. (x2)
- [heuristic] Watch a listener's reaction, such as hostility, fear, a flash of anger, a pause or a follow-up question, to a name as evidence of hidden history and stakes. When: a name or topic is raised in company, or touches a source's concerns. Why: involuntary reaction can reveal past connections and expose hidden stakes.
- [heuristic] A character's visible reaction conveys a threat's stakes, a loss, or the importance of a trivial signal or item before details are explained, guiding attention. When: a threat or death is revealed before explanation, a mysterious first signal is introduced, or an item matters to the plot. Why: reactions tell the audience danger is coming and emotion conveys blows faster than facts; observed alarm lends a signal meaning it lacks alone.
- [heuristic] Treat a reaction as one signal, not proof; corroborate it with other evidence before acting, since fear, grief or guilt can each cause it. When: interpreting a suspect's emotional response, or a reaction to a named clue or remark. Why: the same reaction has several emotional causes beyond guilt.
- [heuristic] Treat a visible reaction to a remark or fact as a signal to investigate further, not a confession; a witness may be affected yet stay silent. When: a suspect reacts strongly to a cryptic phrase, or a witness responds to a confronting fact. Why: reactions can come from other causes such as fear of exposure; emotion shows engagement but not guilt or full knowledge.
- [heuristic] Record a witness's or listener's reaction before interpreting it and alongside what they say; check it against the character's other known traits, since a reaction has several readings.
- [heuristic] Read a listener's face and demeanour, which can betray knowledge before words: missing surprise at startling news signals prior knowledge; going pale or starting can outweigh answers. When: observing a group react to new information, or a confrontation where one party may already know a secret. Why: expressions betray what a listener already understands.
- [heuristic] Reactions to a search, such as objection, refusal or fainting, are behavior clues about who may have something to hide, not proof of guilt. When: Observing a group during a search. Why: Stress reactions vary, and the reaction itself is weaker evidence than the search result.
- [heuristic] A suspect's unguarded reaction, such as a flare of pride, can confirm identity more strongly than an alibi. When: deciding how to judge a suspect at the reveal. Why: involuntary reactions are harder to fake than stated accounts.
- [heuristic] Show a physical item to a suspect when evidence is strong but the link to them is open, then watch their reaction as well as their answer. When: evidence strong, link to person unproven. Why: Reactions can reveal knowledge that spoken answers conceal.
- [heuristic] A reaction to a staged test is a lead, not proof; confirm it through searches and outside records before relying on it.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a sharp follow-up question naming the specific source of a key fact. 2) Watch for pallor, hesitation, halting speech or evasion. 3) Check each tell against secondary fears before concluding knowledge. When: a suspect appears to hold information and a general question gives no clear reaction. Why: naming the source sharpens the reaction, but physical signs can come from fear rather than knowledge.
- [procedure] 1) Question the parties separately and alternate attention between them. 2) State the implication plainly and watch each person's reaction. 3) Confirm the suspicion without accusing directly, then require proof. When: When a suspect is protected by status and cannot be pressed directly. Why: Reactions to a stated fact can expose hidden intent that direct accusation would not reach.
- [procedure] 1) Seat the subject comfortably. 2) Present a list of words from an unrelated topic. 3) Insert the crime-related word among them so it sits naturally. 4) Record physical response and manner at each word. When: using a physiological test as a prompt for questioning. Why: a response tied to one word may reveal recognition.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a neutral, open question about a sensitive event. 2) Watch for a sharp reaction or sudden change of tone. 3) Mark that subject for follow-up questions. When: when a guarded witness gives polished answers. Why: Unplanned reactions reveal where the witness is sensitive.
- [tradeoff] A listener's pallor, stepping back, lowered voice or changed subject may show recognition, but reactions to a hypothetical also show only attitude, not guilt; weigh them with other evidence. When: a listener responds to a hypothetical confession or scenario. Why: physical shifts can signal recognition, but reactions are open to interpretation and not proof alone.
- [tradeoff] A sudden flash of interest after a pointed hint can be a stronger tell than a flat denial, yet puzzlement at a cryptic message also occurs in innocent people. When: after a suspect hears a hint only an insider would grasp, or receives a cryptic probe. Why: a person who recognises the hidden meaning attends more closely, but real confusion and curiosity show the same signs.
- [pitfall] A single reaction, such as pallor or surprise, is not proof of knowledge or guilt: fear, distress or a startled innocent person can show the same signs. When: drawing a conclusion from a single tell, or reading surprise or pallor during questioning. Why: fear of being suspected produces the same signs as knowing the answer; distress and suspicion look alike. (x2)
- [pitfall] Reading a pale face, nervous laughter or hesitation as proof of guilt is a mistake: the guilty may seem calm and the innocent nervous, since reactions have many causes. When: treating a listener's reaction as proof, or evaluating a suspect's or NPC's demeanour or hesitation during questioning. Why: reactions have several causes besides guilt, and each is only one data point needing corroboration.
- [pitfall] Treating an emotional or sudden reaction as conclusive proof of guilt or a hidden motive overreaches; it only justifies asking what the person knows or testing a hypothesis. When: judging a witness's response without checking records, or interpreting a sudden or emotional reaction. Why: the same reaction, such as jealousy, can explain behaviour without any wrongdoing.
- [pitfall] Answering a counter-accusation in kind can make the accuser look as culpable as the accused to outside observers.
- [fact] A concrete reaction from a person can refute a favoured idea when that reaction contradicts it. Why: observed behaviour is evidence that can overturn a preference.

## confession verification
- [mechanism] A confession shaped by fear, promised release, exhaustion, taunt, threat or crisis is weak evidence to discount, even as the only proof, and needs independent corroboration. When: A confession is the sole or main evidence, was obtained under pressure, or a story resolves through an interrogation confession. Why: Pressure and inducements can produce false self-accusations, so the statement reflects the pressure rather than the facts. (x3)
- [mechanism] A candid confession can retroactively explain earlier traces, such as cut ropes and planted lies, tying loose clues into one account. When: a case has several unexplained physical traces. Why: one account links separate clues.
- [mechanism] Prolonged isolation and repetition can blur memory until a confessor partly believes their own statements. When: A person is held in isolation and repeatedly questioned over months. Why: Repetition and loss of outside reference points make invented accounts feel remembered.
- [mechanism] A confession that names others can make the confessor instantly credible to authorities, and further warrants can follow the next day. Why: Authorities act on the confessor's testimony before checking it.
- [behavior] Visible candour, such as admitting small faults or not justifying oneself, makes listeners believe the rest of the account and can move them toward leniency. When: a speaker confesses minor flaws while defending themselves, or a defendant speaks before judgment without justifying themselves. Why: Listeners read candour about small faults, or apparent candour, as sincerity overall.
- [behavior] Abruptly leaving an interview or shutting a door on the questioner signals refusal to answer, ending questioning as effectively as words would.
- [behavior] A false confessor gives plausible answers on some points but loses the thread on others, revealing what they do not actually know. When: when questioning a confessor.
- [behavior] Withdrawing from communal worship while a disruption continues is read as a sign of distance from the disrupting party. When: a community is disrupted by accusers. Why: Absence from shared events signals which side a person stands with.
- [behavior] Targets speak more freely when they believe a listener cannot hear them, such as when an audible distraction makes the listener seem absent. When: a target is talking with others while a listener is nearby. Why: Targets assume they are out of earshot.
- [behavior] A rescued captive may distrust rescuers, cling to a familiar person, and reveal captivity details gradually as strength and trust return. When: a witness has just been freed from captivity. Why: fear and exhaustion limit recall and trust.
- [behavior] Accomplices threatened with arrest may revise their account, and reassurance after the change can keep them cooperating. When: when a minor witness faces charges as an accomplice. Why: Fear of legal consequences pushes witnesses to change what they say.
- [behavior] When damaging an object would cost the actor, they move cautiously and slowly. When: Handling a fragile or valuable object under time pressure. Why: The risk of breaking it keeps the actor careful.
- [behavior] A fact stated plainly can be disbelieved, because listeners may assume the speaker is joking, sarcastic, or lying. When: When a true statement is delivered in a casual or direct manner. Why: Listeners who expect concealment or humor discount literal statements.
- [behavior] An apology made under pressure often does not change the behaviour that prompted it, so later conduct is a better indicator of sincerity than the apology itself. When: Someone apologises after being ordered or pressured to do so. Why: Compliance addresses the demand for an apology without changing underlying intentions.
- [rule] Require the player to verify a confession against independent in-world evidence, such as physical findings or the victim's family, before it unlocks progress or closes the case. When: a suspect offers an admission or confession branch in a game, or explains motive after capture or confrontation. Why: A confession alone does not close the case; corroborated confessions carry more weight, and verification should be visible to the player. (x3)
- [rule] Treat a confession as a claim or lead to verify against independent evidence, not as proof or substitute for it; confessors may shape it for gain or to shield another. When: A suspect's admission is the main result of an interrogation, or a confession is the main link to a suspect. Why: Confessions can be false or given for reasons unrelated to guilt; rewards, relief from torment, coercion or defence give confessors motives to shape accounts. (x2)
- [rule] When a confession shifts or is retracted, keep both versions, reexamine the earlier one, and compare them side by side; the correction itself can reveal the suspect. When: A suspect withdraws or changes an earlier confession, or a record holds both a confession and its retraction. Why: Both versions can carry information; each reflects different pressures, and the contrast shows what changed. (x2)
- [rule] Require a confession and a matching deed together: a confession alone may be delusion or a sincere but wrong admission, and a deed alone may be accident. When: when a verdict rests on a confession or physical act, or a confession describes an act that may not have occurred. Why: Each on its own can be explained by something other than guilt; confession and physical fact can diverge in either direction. (x2)
- [rule] Treat claims about who knew what, including a witness's exclusive-knowledge claim or your own guess, as hypotheses to test against other witnesses or the source. When: a witness asserts exclusive knowledge or professes ignorance of someone, or you guess what a source knows. Why: Sincere witnesses can still be wrong about who knew; claimed ignorance is a checkable statement.
- [rule] Treat a confession as a claim checked against physical traces such as hidden objects, routes and timings; reject one they contradict, whatever its sincerity or emotional tone. When: after physical evidence has narrowed the suspect, a confession is central to resolving the case, or a suspect's answers show a pattern that needs a second look. Why: Physical traces expose self-serving or false accounts, so the record outweighs sincerity.
- [rule] Accept a confession as grounds for judgment only if it is voluntary, made after examination, and given by someone of sound mind, and treat extracted confessions as weaker. When: A suspect's confession is used to decide a case. Why: Coercion and impaired mental state undermine the confession's reliability.
- [rule] An informant who admits their own role may earn player trust, but their claims should still be checkable against world records.
- [rule] A jailed NPC who offers a confession can be rewarded for confessing and penalized for recanting.
- [rule] Receive confessions with great caution, especially when they match accusations already made by others.
- [rule] Let a confession, not scene evidence alone, establish who authored a forged clue.
- [rule] Test both a confession and a verified alibi before accepting either, since each can be staged to cover a culprit. Why: Either can look settled while concealing the real actor.
- [heuristic] Test a confession, especially one shaped by safety incentives, against details only the true culprit could know, such as hidden objects or return visits; false confessors fail those. When: a confession may be false. Why: a false confessor does not know what the culprit would know. (x2)
- [heuristic] A withdrawn, sudden or recanted confession is a claim to check, proving neither guilt nor innocence until its motive is checked.
- [heuristic] Ask questions that test what the other party knows and when, rather than revealing your own knowledge first, since revealing it tells the suspect what to conceal or act on. When: Cross-examining a suspect who may conceal facts, or running a test that shows your knowledge. Why: Revealing what you know tells the suspect what to conceal, and a visible test can prompt them to act.
- [heuristic] A confession is more credible when its awkward, self-damaging details are hard for a careless or foolish teller to have invented. When: a suspect's account is the main direct evidence. Why: Embarrassing details are unlikely to be fabricated casually.
- [heuristic] Admissions of error that blame others or one's own heart need as much scrutiny as boasts, and the few that matter often sit inside long self-praise.
- [heuristic] A written message can forbid explanation and promise full understanding later, so the character and the audience wait together.
- [heuristic] Set a confirmed admission aside as a fact to check against other evidence later, rather than resolving it at once or treating it as corroboration.
- [heuristic] A partial admission is most likely when witnesses already hold the fact the earlier lie tried to hide. When: A suspect is confronted with proof of a lie. Why: Once the fact is known, admitting part of it looks more honest than further denial.
- [heuristic] Accept a firm immediate denial as the answer for now, but test it against other evidence later. When: A witness denies recognizing a person in a recognition question. Why: A quick denial may be sincere or may hide knowledge, so it needs checking.
- [heuristic] Before treating a confession as proof, check how many sessions it took and who supplied its details. When: Judging the weight of a confession. Why: Many sessions and examiner-supplied details signal coaching rather than independent knowledge.
- [heuristic] Do not treat kindness as proof of innocence, nor suspicion as proof of guilt.
- [heuristic] Close a reveal with a confession, backed by a separate document that corroborates a different fact than the method.
- [heuristic] Keep an investigator's doubts about a confession visible but unresolved until a later reversal. When: A case appears closed on weak evidence. Why: Visible doubt keeps the reader skeptical and sets up the reversal.
- [procedure] 1) List each concrete, dated detail in the confession. 2) Match it against physical evidence, documents or deadlines. 3) Check the timeline against known events. 4) Accept the account only where its details agree with independent facts. When: confirming a confession. Why: Independent facts test what the teller alone cannot prove; the account is weighed by its matches.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the confessor's behaviour and wording with what a guilty person would show, and examine the form for signs of invention. 2) List reasons an innocent person might confess, including shielding another. 3) Check the confession against physical facts and outside evidence before accepting it. 4) Hold off on closure until these checks are done. When: A confession arrives before charges, indictment or publicity, or a suspect admits guilt quickly. Why: A convenient confession can mislead, and early closure can lock in a wrong answer; admissions must be verified, not accepted on their face.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a question whose answer you already know. 2) Compare the reply with the truth. 3) Note what the reply reveals about what the other person does not know. When: you need to gauge someone's knowledge without seeming to test them. Why: answers to known questions expose gaps, so knowledge can be tracked through natural dialogue.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether the confession explains every trace at the scene. 2) Compare its details with what the scene shows. 3) Test it against independent evidence such as tracks or other witnesses. 4) Record it verbatim so changes can be compared later. When: a confession arrives early or conveniently, or conflicts with traces.
- [procedure] 1) Build a reconstruction of events from the evidence. 2) Compare the culprit's confession with it stage by stage. 3) Mark each part as confirmed, corrected or newly revealed. When: when a culprit confesses at the end of an investigation. Why: the confession acts as a second source for testing the reconstruction.
- [procedure] 1) Confront the suspect with the record of motive and pressure. 2) Obtain a full account. 3) Ask the suspect to correct false impressions about others. 4) Give a formal warning that the statement may be used. When: a confession is needed to clear or convict. Why: a complete, corrected and formally cautioned statement is more usable.
- [procedure] 1) Lay out the known facts in order. 2) Show the suspect that investigators know more than expected. 3) Separate the crimes and seek the lesser admission first. 4) Offer a conditional lighter penalty or reparation. 5) Have the suspect write the statement. When: after the suspect is confronted with strong evidence. Why: denial becomes pointless once the investigators' knowledge is shown.
- [procedure] 1) Note where the speaker's confidence ends and reservation begins. 2) Ask directly about the gap. 3) Press until the missing part is given or the refusal is noted. When: Interrogating a speaker who gives partial information. Why: The boundary between confidence and reservation marks what is being hidden.
- [tradeoff] Free confessions suffice for conviction generally, but in murder cases independent evidence must support them; indirect or contested evidence needs a stricter standard. When: when deciding whether a confession alone can support a conviction. (x2)
- [tradeoff] A confession is strong evidence when freely given, but weak when it follows coercive questioning, so its weight depends on how it was obtained. When: when deciding how much weight a confession deserves. Why: the method of obtaining a confession determines whether it reflects the facts.
- [tradeoff] A confession that matches the evidence is worth checking but should not be settled, since it may be correct for the wrong reasons. When: A confession appears consistent with known facts. Why: Consistency with evidence does not reveal the confessor's real motive.
- [pitfall] Do not treat a confession as final: confessions and denials can change during trial, and a later retraction can reopen a case the confession seemed to close.
- [pitfall] A character who keeps quiet out of kindness and one who keeps quiet out of guilt look the same on the surface, so motives must be shown.
- [pitfall] A confessor's account is not neutral, since they frame events to their own advantage and often present themselves as the wronged party.
- [pitfall] Assuming a confession will follow a bluff is a mistake, since the guilty party may find another way out. When: expecting a bluff to produce a confession. Why: the suspect may take a different course of action.
- [pitfall] An admission that explains known sightings does not explain the central act; test the admitted detail against the physical evidence. When: A suspect's admission accounts for what witnesses saw. Why: Explaining presence does not establish innocence of the main crime.
- [pitfall] An ambiguous remark can be read as an admission against the accused when it is ambiguous, inflating the apparent strength of the case. When: when a suspect's remark can be read in more than one way. Why: investigators tend to read ambiguous statements in the direction of their existing suspicion.
- [pitfall] Promising a disclosure and then withdrawing it without later consequence is a pitfall.
- [pitfall] Participants invited under pressure may feel coerced, which can distort their behaviour and can make the investigator's invitation hard to justify. When: running a social test with invited participants. Why: Perceived obligation changes how people act and how they can be judged.
- [pitfall] A suspect's emotional breakdown under pressure is not a confession. Treat it as a change in state that still requires further proof. Why: Distress shows that pressure is working, not that the suspect is guilty.
- [pitfall] A confession offered for mercy may still need checking against physical evidence before it is trusted.
- [pitfall] Confessions extracted under torment and later recanted at execution are unreliable proof of guilt. When: a verdict rests on a confession obtained under pressure. Why: Pressure can produce false admissions, and recantation exposes them.
- [fact] A confession is an admission that a formal decision-maker must still weigh and test; it is not a verdict in itself.

## silence and refusal as evidence
- [mechanism] Refusing a proposed condition makes the refuser look suspicious, so a stated safeguard can become a trap the target cannot safely decline. When: A condition is framed as a reasonable safeguard in front of an audience. Why: Declining signals guilt to observers.
- [mechanism] A refusal that comes with a stated threat spells out the stakes within the exchange itself, so both sides understand what is at risk. When: A proposal is rejected by a party with leverage. Why: Explicit consequences make the refusal a message that can be acted on.
- [mechanism] An official who stops acting on accusations can become a target, and refusal can draw accusation onto their own family.
- [mechanism] Silence can be designed so its meaning depends on the institution interpreting it.
- [behavior] A silent occupant of a locked room may be asleep, drunk, ignoring noise or incapacitated, so silence alone shows neither unawareness nor refusal. When: an occupant does not reply after being warned at a locked room, or a lack of reaction to a sound inside a locked room. Why: Silence has multiple causes, and an investigator should not assume refusal; several states produce the same lack of response. (x2)
- [behavior] A refusal marks its subject as sensitive, such as a weapon or wound, and the shape and conditions of the refusal reveal where hidden material lies. When: a witness declines to answer about a sensitive detail, or a character withholds answers during questioning. Why: Refusal often signals the detail is secret or important; refusals and conditional offers signal concealment, so listeners draw conclusions from them. (x2)
- [behavior] A silent accused, often read as weak, or a witness refusing to explain, looks as though hiding something; an unanswered charge before an audience weighs heavily. When: a charge is made in front of an audience. Why: Silence is taken as a sign the charge cannot be refuted.
- [behavior] A questioner's pause or minimal prompt after an answer or contradiction pressures people to fill the silence with more detail, confidences or concessions. When: interviewing a motivated source, in a one-sided quiet conversation, after an answer, or after a specific contradiction is put to a witness hiding something. Why: People feel pressure to fill silence and elaborate, so a quiet listener often gathers more than an active questioner, and a partial liar may volunteer more.
- [behavior] After a disclosure, silence signals the other party's turn; pausing before disclosing a fact invites the listener to fill the silence, revealing what they know. When: a conversation pauses after one party reveals something; the listener may hold relevant knowledge. Why: People read silence as an open turn and feel pressure to fill it, and tend to fill silence with talk.
- [behavior] A refusal to answer may mean guilt or protection of someone who holds the secret; a suspect under direct pressure may accept loss of position rather than name them. When: a witness or suspect is pressed on a sensitive point or refuses a direct question. Why: Loyalty to a confederate can outweigh the suspect's own interests, so refusal has more than one meaning.
- [behavior] Refusal and stalling end or delay the exchange, but they still reveal what is being withheld, so the questioner can infer from what is left unsaid.
- [behavior] Holding back after stating a goal, and watching the listener's reaction, can make a witness fill the silence and volunteer information they meant to hide. When: When a witness seems to know more than they are saying. Why: People feel pressure to fill silence, and unguarded remarks can slip out before they are asked about the topic.
- [behavior] A witness who refuses to name the cause of tension may be protecting someone, and the refusal itself is information to record. When: A witness declines to explain a strained relationship. Why: Protecting others can produce refusal without guilt.
- [behavior] A silent suspect cannot be cleared, and an audience may read the silence as guilt. When: a suspect refuses to explain a key time window. Why: without an account, an open gap looks like concealment.
- [behavior] When a person reveals nothing of her past, neighbours know little about her history, and that absence can itself be information, though it may also be deliberate concealment. When: When witnesses cannot describe a victim's background. Why: Those with secrets may hide their past on purpose, so silence does not mean no connections.
- [behavior] Absence of expected follow-up can be read as proof of a convenient explanation rather than as evidence. When: Expected contact stops after an anomaly.
