- [behavior] Silence or turning away from a question can itself be a tell, since the absence of speech carries the signal. When: a person is pressed on a topic.
- [behavior] An offerer may recast a refusal as a wrong done to them, shifting blame and claiming the moral high ground.
- [behavior] A reluctant answer from a witness may be the most important one, and the witness controls what they choose to reveal. When: A witness withholds details out of delicacy or self-interest. Why: Withholding signals content worth checking.
- [behavior] A suspect who refuses to speak appears guilty, but silence can also protect innocent people from making errors, so it leaves investigators with no information either way. When: A suspect declines to answer questions during an investigation. Why: Silence is ambiguous and yields no new evidence.
- [behavior] Silence in news or reports can be read as a sign of further events, even when nothing is confirmed. When: A story is missing expected coverage. Why: Absence of information invites speculation.
- [rule] Do not treat a refusal as proof of guilt; record it as a clue needing explanation, weigh it with other evidence, and move on if nothing else supports it. When: a witness or suspect refuses a reasonable request or to answer questions. Why: Silence has many causes, including hidden personal matters unrelated to the crime, and one reaction rarely settles a question.
- [rule] Record refusals and withheld answers alongside what was said, as facts that shape later suspicion, since what a subject avoids is evidence.
- [rule] Set a dialogue flag on a refusal, not only a plain 'no', so it unlocks or blocks later branches and an objective, and repeated questioning opens further branches. When: designing NPC dialogue trees or systems; a silent or defiant NPC, or a tense scene staged around a sensitive subject. Why: Refusal then has consequences instead of dead-ending, and refusals can reveal that a hidden matter exists.
- [rule] Do not infer an outcome from silence in a record. An unrecorded verdict or fate is unknown, not implied. When: When a case ends without a documented result. Why: Records can be incomplete for many reasons unrelated to the outcome.
- [rule] Let a witness refuse or shorten answers when a pressing question seems to expose a secret, and treat the refusal as a clue. When: A question touches a concealed matter. Why: A refusal signals that the question hit something real, which the player can use.
- [rule] A claimant who refuses to explain their past should fail a verification check, unless the examiner accepts a partial answer.
- [rule] Do not treat an empty search as clearance for someone who refused to be searched. When: A person refused a search and the search found nothing. Why: Refusal leaves the person unverified, so an empty result proves nothing about them.
- [heuristic] Silence about an event a person would certainly learn of or a witness would normally report is evidence, such as unmentioned widely reported news or a requested visit. When: only where the event would be widely reported, or a witness fails to mention something memorable such as a requested visit. Why: A living person would normally respond to such news; a witness would normally report it, so omission suggests reluctance or refusal. (x2)
- [heuristic] A refusal to explain how an item came to be somewhere, or to name its true owner, is a clue to weigh for hidden motive.
- [heuristic] A missing reaction counts as evidence only against a clear expectation. A guard animal that stays quiet for a visitor suggests the visitor was known to it. When: A known reaction should occur for an arrival and does not. Why: Silence means something only when the reaction is normal and reliable for that animal or person.
- [heuristic] When an expected consequence of a crime fails to appear, such as a sale or report, its absence is evidence about what happened. When: an expected timeline of reactions is reliable. Why: without a reliable expected timeline, silence means nothing.
- [heuristic] When a suspect stays silent, look for a motive and outside support, such as who would be paid to keep quiet. When: a suspect's silence is unexplained. Why: Silence that persists needs a reason.
- [heuristic] Treat a group's silence as a statement, since saying nothing about an event shapes how others' accounts are received. When: Witnesses saw an event but say nothing about it.
- [heuristic] Treat a refusal or a short reply such as 'I do not know' as information: it means the captive is either ignorant or resisting.
- [heuristic] Test a witness's claim to have heard nothing against what would normally have been audible; an accepted explanation for silence can hide a contradiction. When: witness says they heard nothing.
- [heuristic] When a person refuses entry to a place, consider whether they are avoiding being seen there. When: a household member blocks access to a room.
- [heuristic] A silence in the record, such as no one seeing a person leave a place, is a gap worth treating as the next question. When: Reviewing an assembled timeline. Why: Unexplained gaps point to unexamined movements.
- [heuristic] A pause after an emotional admission can act as an assurance, since both sides expect the next words to be truthful. When: A witness has just confessed a feeling or strong statement. Why: A quiet pause signals that the next answer will be sincere.
- [heuristic] A party who stays silent while others speak in a dispute is a clue, since their absence in a timeline can signal reluctance. When: When a timeline shows some parties acknowledging an issue and others not. Why: Absence within a dated sequence can mark avoidance.
- [heuristic] Repeated polite non-answers suggest the matter concerns private feeling rather than public fact. When: A witness evades many questions with courteous but empty replies. Why: Courtesy paired with silence signals a personal reason for withholding information.
- [heuristic] People who meet danger tend to cry out, so an absent cry where a sound could carry suggests the person met someone they did not fear. When: When a person vanished in a place where a cry would have been heard. Why: Fear usually produces an audible reaction, so its absence points to a calm encounter.
- [procedure] Treat a refusal as information: record it, then re-ask a narrower question with the refusal in view.
- [tradeoff] Refusing to answer can be read as complicity and draw formal threats, while answering gives up information; the questioner must weigh both costs. When: when a suspect is pressed to talk.
- [pitfall] Do not treat a suspect's silence or reaction as an admission unless no other explanation exists and fact-based confirmation supports it. When: A suspect remains silent under accusation; a witness gives no spoken answer but reacts visibly to a question. Why: Silence and reactions are ambiguous; a fair question must be answerable in fact before evasion carries evidential weight. (x2)
- [pitfall] Silence has many causes, such as distance, fear, a sleeping household or illness, so an absence of sound supports a conclusion only after other causes are considered. When: when reasoning from a lack of noise. Why: Several unrelated conditions can produce the same quiet.
- [pitfall] A witness's failure to hear does not prove an event such as a struggle did not occur; inferring no struggle assumes what the witness could hear. When: when a witness reports not hearing something. Why: Hearing depends on distance, sleep and attention, so absence of report is weak evidence.
- [pitfall] Do not conclude an event did not occur because a record is silent; records are often incomplete or lost, so compare against surviving series first. When: concluding that nothing happened because no record exists. Why: Records are often incomplete or lost.
- [pitfall] Reading an accused's refusal to plead or confess as further guilt, especially after the institution has decided, makes denials impossible to disprove. When: an institution has already decided, or an accused is pressed to confess or affirm a claim. Why: Silence is misread when the institution has already decided.
- [pitfall] Silence that is advised or a deliberate legal tactic, such as a suspect's or witness's, is no testimony and not evidence of guilt.
- [pitfall] Taking a silent or uninformed witness as proof that nothing happened is a mistake.
- [pitfall] Reading silence as sleep or refusal without testing the assumption leads to wrong conclusions about a person's state.
- [pitfall] Reading a refusal through an existing belief lets it confirm a theory already formed, so the test becomes circular. When: the tester already holds a theory. Why: Interpretation is shaped by prior belief.
- [pitfall] A witness's silence is not an alibi, and readers or investigators can misread it.
- [pitfall] A silent wait that adds no new information drags and loses the audience's attention. When: A scene is held in silence for a long stretch. Why: Tension needs new input to keep growing; without it, waiting becomes boredom.
- [pitfall] A refusal to speak ill of the dead may be sincere, so it alone is not evidence of guilt. When: A witness declines to criticize the victim. Why: Respect for the dead is a common reason to refuse.
- [pitfall] A writer's silence about a rival does not prove that the writer worked independently; check the citations themselves.
- [pitfall] Refusing to continue an accusatory process can itself be read as guilt, turning accusers against anyone who hesitates.
- [pitfall] Treating a suspect's refusal to account for their whereabouts as proof of guilt is a mistake, since the silence may hide something unrelated. When: when a suspect will not give an alibi. Why: concealment can have many causes.
- [pitfall] A witness's first answers can be vague or evasive, and a point may be admitted only after pressing.
- [pitfall] Treating a refusal as a denial is a mistake; the listener often reads it as confirmation that something is being hidden. When: A character declines to answer a question. Why: A refusal carries implied information that a flat denial would not.
- [fact] Silence on one topic may come from loyalty or shame rather than guilt.

## verifying witness accounts
- [model] Witness accounts are weighed against three things: one another, the timeline, and the witness's manner.
- [mechanism] A clue system can let players test a suspect's claimed movements against other NPCs' logs, doors and timestamps, rewarding cross-checks. When: designing evidence-based investigation.
- [rule] Check any claimed time or movement against independent records, other witnesses or events, such as a receipt, a schedule, a light seen or help called, rather than the witness's word. When: A witness offers a claimed time or movement that other records or events can check. Why: Independent confirmation exposes errors in a single witness's timing. (x2)
- [rule] Check a witness's event sequence or details against independent physical evidence, such as access controls, keys or guards posted outside, especially when memory may be confused. Matches raise trust. (x2)
- [rule] Testimony from a drugged, coached, exhausted or frightened witness needs independent verification or measurement before being treated as fact; checked sequence information can still be useful. When: A witness was impaired or prompted before speaking. Why: Impairment and coaching can distort or omit details; perception may be distorted yet sequence remains useful when corroborated. (x2)
- [rule] Separate what a witness saw from the conclusions, interpretation and emotion added, testing each part before accepting; vivid accounts can still be biased, and crowds blend seen with invented. When: Any account, especially vivid, grief-laden or crowd-witnessed ones. Why: Vivid or grief-laden retellings mix observation with inference, and crowd accounts blend what was seen with what was added.
- [rule] Treat a witness's bare facts and any stated fact as unestablished until checked against the written record or source it names, not the teller's word.
- [rule] Sort each account into what was seen, heard and inferred, record only observations, label inferences from others' behaviour, and weigh each category separately. When: Taking testimony from several witnesses, especially partial views such as silhouettes without faces. Why: Inference can pass as observation if it is not labelled.
- [rule] Compare statements of household members and stakeholders about the same fact, such as a widow's remarks about family members, since they may confirm, contradict or correct one another. When: Several people describe the same person or event.
- [rule] Check physical claims, such as marks, stains or damage, against the scene and verify any claimed origin, since witnesses may name different origins for the same mark.
- [rule] Check a confession, slanted journal entry or biased NPC dialogue against physical evidence the player can find elsewhere in the level. When: A source is subjective or of uncertain reliability. Why: So that false or biased information can be tested.
- [rule] Let players cross-check one NPC's account against another's, rewarding a matching detail or unlocking a second independent witness to question.
- [rule] Make an NPC's claims about places, times or people checkable through a second witness or record, so players can test them before the game rewards trust. When: Designing an NPC account, especially a self-justifying one. Why: A checkable claim turns the account into a puzzle rather than a fact.
- [rule] Verify each sighting link with its observer and other evidence before it fixes a person's position, since missing people are often reported in several places at once.
- [rule] Verify a claimed supporter, alibi or listed record witness with that person, confirming the claim and that they were informed; the witness may already be under suspicion. When: A suspect cites someone as a witness or supporter, or a record lists one. Why: Unverified claims of support are a common gap in an investigation.
- [rule] Limit a witness's account to what they observed, given partial view or stake; ask the same question of several people and let no single account settle a question. When: Assessing witness statements, especially with a partial view or personal stake. Why: Single accounts can be confused or wrong, and a witness cannot establish facts they could not observe.
- [rule] Count a physical reaction as a clue only if it can be reproduced under controlled conditions with someone other than the accuser watching.
- [rule] Test a nervous pause against other evidence before reading it as guilt, since anxiety can look like guilty awareness. When: when a suspect hesitates or looks around. Why: nervousness mimics guilt.
- [rule] Verify that a guard or observer was awake and watching before treating their post as a barrier. When: When relying on a guard's watch to limit movement. Why: Observer attention is testimony and can be mistaken.
- [rule] Treat a strong claim offered as proof, such as a message said to show someone is alive, as something to check rather than accept.
- [rule] Confirm that a claimed purchase or trip actually produced its stated result, such as fuel being brought back, before accepting the claim. When: when an action is claimed as an alibi.
- [rule] A witness who hides one fact often hides others, so verify each statement separately rather than trusting the whole account.
- [rule] Check a worker's claimed skill with a practical test, since a written credential can be false. When: A character's stated expertise matters to the plot or to a decision.
- [rule] Let an NPC with a grudge give accurate sightings mixed with self-serving claims, so the player must cross-check them with another NPC. When: designing NPC testimony. Why: Mixed reliability rewards verification.
- [rule] Treat a witness's claim to have thought they heard someone as something to verify, not as a fact. When: A witness reports hearing or seeing with uncertainty. Why: Hedged perception is weak evidence until checked.
- [rule] Write witness dialogue so players can verify its details, since an NPC may be right about an event and wrong about its cause. When: an NPC reports a sighting.
- [rule] Keep an accusation checkable through physical evidence, so a rumour about the accuser's reliability cannot fully replace testing the original claim. When: Designing a discredited witness or rival rumour. Why: Verifiable evidence lets the player separate the claim from the attack on the accuser.
- [heuristic] Treat witness, official, victim or principal statements as leads to test against independent sources and physical facts, not settled proof; standing or kindness does not establish accuracy. When: Deciding weight to give a witness, especially an account fixing a time or place that matters to the case. Why: Personal qualities and official status do not establish facts; accounts are limited by what the speaker could observe and by their interests. (x2)
- [heuristic] Use a second independent witness to confirm or refute a key claim or fact; agreement between separate accounts is stronger evidence than a single voice. When: A key claim or fact rests on one interested witness or account. Why: Independent agreement reduces dependence on a single self-interested account and the chance that one error or bias carries the fact.
- [heuristic] Test witness statements and timelines against each other and against records; a statement conflicting with an earlier one, such as about what she could do, reveals a gap worth probing. When: When an account changes or conflicts with a record. Why: Contradictions with earlier statements or records are evidence to weigh.
- [heuristic] A vague or doubted testimony becomes checkable when tied to a physical trace; examine the mark before accepting or rejecting the claim, since a trace can confirm or refute it. When: A witness describes a bodily or physical event, or the group doubts the report. Why: A matchable trace gives a concrete, checkable detail independent of who made the claim.
- [heuristic] Prefer a direct, verifiable witness account over emotional or fragmentary testimony when both are available.
- [heuristic] Once a witness makes an admission, check it against another witness's account to confirm the timing. When: When a witness finally admits to being present somewhere. Why: Independent accounts confirm or refute the admission.
- [heuristic] A witness's proposed cause of death is a hypothesis to be tested, not a fixed answer, even when the witness is a medical professional. When: A witness suggests a cause for an unusual body. Why: An observation can point to a cause without confirming it.
- [heuristic] Check a witness's account of a person's mood against that person's known behavior; a conflict marks the account as unreliable. Why: Statements about a person can be wrong and contradicted by consistent behavior.
- [heuristic] Rival theories usually point to different witnesses, so ask which witness could settle which key assumption before choosing whom to question. When: rival explanations each suggest a witness. Why: witnesses differ in what they can confirm.
- [heuristic] Cross-check each witness against other sources, asking about the suspect's friends and acquaintances to see how much the witness actually knows. When: a witness claims close knowledge of a suspect. Why: knowledge that does not hold up under questions is weak evidence.
- [heuristic] Test a revised account by putting it back to its source and noting anger, refusal or evasion as signals of what is being protected.
- [heuristic] Verify a watcher's report before acting on it, since a watcher can misidentify a figure in poor light. When: a watcher reports a suspect. Why: Poor visibility and bias both distort observation.
- [heuristic] Interview witnesses separately: mismatched details become clues to investigate, while details that match across separate accounts raise confidence in them. When: when players question several witnesses.
- [heuristic] Doubtful testimony can be useful once independently checked against other sources. When: When testimony is weak or unclear. Why: Verification can recover value from unreliable accounts.
- [procedure] 1) Ask each witness how they know, splitting firsthand facts from hearsay or opinion. 2) Check each firsthand detail against independent records and other witnesses. 3) Corroborate key claims with present witnesses, not secondhand ones. 4) Use confirmed details to limit who had access. When: Gathering testimony about one event, especially specific physical or positional details, or before acting on a key claim. Why: Independent checks separate reliable detail from error or emotion, and only firsthand witnesses can confirm what happened. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Ask several witnesses about the same event and record each answer. 2) Relay one statement to another and ask whether it matches their own observation. 3) Compare accounts, noting agreement, contradiction and gaps; conflicts need examination. 4) Check them against outside facts, such as bank entries, and note vague or unconfirmed points. When: Two or more witnesses or accounts describe the same event. Why: Contradictions expose weak testimony and gaps that a single witness would hide.
- [procedure] 1) List each account's claims with times, places, objects and events. 2) Align overlapping claims by time and who was present. 3) Mark conflicts in outline, timing and detail separately. 4) Test claims against known facts, noting hesitation before confirming. When: Two or more accounts overlap in time, place or describe the same events. Why: Contradictions show up only when claims are set side by side.
- [procedure] 1) Check the subject's state with several independent observable signs. 2) Repeat each check. 3) Have other observers examine the subject and confirm the result. When: The subject's condition is unclear and the stakes depend on it.
- [procedure] 1) Lift the eyelid of the person in a claimed faint. 2) Feel the pulse. 3) Judge genuineness from these physical signs, not from the performance. When: claimed collapse or distress.
- [procedure] 1) Isolate the witness's specific claim. 2) Find an independent record, such as a registration, that can confirm or refute it. 3) Compare the record with the claim. When: A witness's claim can be checked against records.
- [procedure] 1) List the dates and places for each person involved. 2) Check which pairs could have met. 3) Confirm or reject the relationship from the reconstructed timeline, not from impression. When: a claimed relationship is disputed. Why: Impressions are unreliable; dated records can settle the question.
- [procedure] 1) Stay with the target until the action completes. 2) Confirm the movement you saw. 3) Only then draw a conclusion from it. Why: unconfirmed movement is easily misread.
- [procedure] 1) Note the informant's motive to please, mislead or evade. 2) Split claims into checkable facts. 3) Verify each against independent sources. 4) Weight each claim by the strength of the motive. Why: specific detail from a paid or biased witness is not proof of accuracy.
- [procedure] 1) Identify a fact the public record lacks. 2) Ask the witness how she learned it. 3) Test the stated source for plausibility. 4) Check public sources to rule out the press. When: a witness states a detail that is not in the public record.
- [procedure] 1) Separate what the witness saw from what they assumed. 2) Check the conditions of observation. 3) Identify distinctive, checkable details. 4) Match timing anchors against other evidence. When: A single witness is the only source of a description. Why: Each point is only as reliable as what the witness could actually perceive.
- [procedure] 1) List the identifying details a witness gives, such as names, employers and addresses. 2) Note which are missing. 3) Search records that could confirm the rest, such as postal, transport or company logs. When: a witness is sincere but offers details that cannot yet be checked. Why: Independent records can confirm or refute claims the witness cannot back up.
- [procedure] 1) Record the witness's account in full. 2) Compare each claim with physical traces at the scene. 3) Flag claims the traces contradict. 4) Question the witness on the flagged points. Why: physical traces are harder to bend than statements.
- [procedure] 1) Test each claim against physical evidence, such as whether an item matches. 2) Check it against the timeline. 3) Compare it with other witnesses to find where an account was shaped. When: several people share knowledge and give partial, conflicting accounts.
- [procedure] 1) Gather fragments from separate sources, such as official records, informant reports, personal diaries and memoirs. 2) Weigh each source's reliability. 3) Ask who saw the object in each state. 4) Compare the accounts for consistency. When: Assembling the truth from scattered lore or witness accounts. Why: Independent sources expose errors that a single source hides.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a narrow, checkable question about a specific detail or time. 2) Have the witness walk the route, tying each step to a place. 3) Secure the factual account. 4) Only then probe for motive or resentment.
- [procedure] 1) Restate the witness's claim. 2) Reproduce the event under the same conditions from the claimed position. 3) Check whether the expected sound or sight occurs. 4) Reject the claim if it does not. When: when a witness claims to have sensed an event from a distance.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each witness's account of the same interval. 2) Place all accounts on one shared timeline anchored to fixed events. 3) Flag any interval where a person's whereabouts are unaccounted for. Why: Unaccounted intervals are where suspects can hide.
- [procedure] 1) Have the NPC claim to have seen something. 2) Tie the claim to a detail the player can inspect or change. 3) Repeat the test with a changed detail to expose any evasion. When: Designing a deduction puzzle around a witness NPC. Why: Changing the detail retests the claim, and an evasive NPC falls back on excuses that cannot be checked.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness what kind of detail they observed. 2) Restate the question to see whether the answer changes. 3) Check whether the witness had the opportunity to observe the detail at all. When: Assessing how reliable a witness's confident claim is. Why: Shifting or vague answers reveal that the detail was assumed rather than seen.
- [pitfall] Cutting a witness short loses detail that may become important later. When: During an interview or testimony. Why: Interruption interrupts the flow and removes details that were not yet recognised as relevant.

## gated clue and dialogue release
- [model] Model clues as a graph where a physical item links two or more characters, and lock dependent clues until the identity node is confirmed. When: Generating interlinked investigation content. Why: Gating prevents players from building conclusions on an unverified identity.
- [mechanism] A later event that matches an earlier joking remark turns it into a confirmed prediction, shifting listeners from doubt to belief.
- [mechanism] Small items such as a button, a torn wrapper or a stain can persist in the world and be found later, letting the player rebuild a sequence of events. When: designing a clue system. Why: the items keep their state until discovered.
- [mechanism] A delayed discovery sets the time window for a crime in a level timeline, since the event could have occurred any time before discovery.
- [mechanism] Treating each clue as a filter condition and counting NPCs that satisfy all of them lets a generator tune how hard a deduction is. When: Generating clue sets for a deduction puzzle. Why: Each added condition narrows the candidate set.
- [mechanism] Evidence can be revealed in tiers: each accepted clue unlocks the next line of testimony, so progress is gated by the proof the player presents. When: when designing an interrogation scene that the player drives with evidence. Why: Gating testimony behind clues rewards careful evidence use over guessing.
- [mechanism] A non-player investigator holding a private theory reveals it only when the player supplies matching evidence, which paces disclosure. When: when designing an NPC who knows more than they say. Why: gated disclosure ties information release to player progress.
- [mechanism] Social events such as dinners or festivals can open conversations that remain locked outside them, rewarding patient play. When: Designing gated NPC dialogue. Why: Shared hospitality lowers guard and creates natural openings.
- [rule] Gate a sensitive detail or evidence behind a rapport or trust meter, an earned trust cue, or a set game point, so players build a relationship before it is revealed. When: designing NPC dialogue that hides key information. (x2)
- [rule] Start dialogue with low-stakes topics; unlock pointed or sensitive questions only after rapport, supporting evidence or a trigger, since pressing too early closes later options. When: designing a dialogue system with sensitive subjects. Why: Early trust makes sensitive topics less likely to shut the conversation down. (x2)
- [rule] Promise a payoff for every open question or promised reveal and never leave threads permanently unresolved, since an unpaid question frustrates the audience and erodes trust. Why: An unpaid question frustrates the audience.
- [rule] Unlock dialogue bluff or sharper follow-up options only when the player holds a matching clue; store an omitted detail as a hidden flag that only that follow-up reveals. When: designing interrogation or NPC dialogue that withholds information. Why: Bluffs should rest on something the player actually has.
- [rule] Gate a motive reveal or character-related reward behind a second independent NPC who confirms the claim, so corroborated claims unlock more than single-source ones. When: designing reveals. Why: Corroboration makes the reveal credible.
- [rule] Gate a level's key reveal behind a sequence of scenes or locations, each ending on an unanswered question that the next partly resolves, so anticipation accumulates. When: designing multi-location investigations or sequencing reveals across levels. Why: Sequenced gating paces the reveal and keeps the player moving.
- [rule] Open on a mystery only when the question will be paid off later; an opening puzzle should not be left hanging. When: Planning an opening image with a hidden cause. Why: Players expect opening puzzles to pay off.
- [rule] An NPC gatekeeper can withhold a clue until the player meets a condition or gives a reason for asking. When: Designing an NPC who guards information. Why: Conditioned release makes the clue feel earned and ties it to the player's reasons.
- [rule] Let a confidential NPC reveal background only when the player asks the right question, which can open a new investigation branch.
- [rule] A payoff should follow from a detail introduced earlier, never appear for the first time at the reveal.
- [rule] Unlock each next quest question only after the previous fact is confirmed, so the quest log follows the chain. When: designing quest logic.
- [rule] Gate a key reveal on the player's own committed conclusion, so its arrival tests and rewards revising that theory.
- [rule] Let an NPC share a secret only after the player brings a proof-of-goodwill item. When: designing dialogue that withholds information. Why: the item signals trust and unlocks cooperation.
- [rule] When a second entry route is raised, pay it off later, since a route never mentioned again leaves the audience feeling cheated.
- [rule] Gate the reveal of a distinguishing trait behind a skill check or a dialogue with the right character, so the player must earn the identification. When: when the trait is a key clue for a puzzle or quest.
- [rule] Gate finer readings of physical traces behind a specialist NPC who can interpret them precisely. When: designing layered clue reading. Why: Specialist access gives players a reason to seek out NPCs.
- [rule] Let an NPC accept a pretext only after the player has asked the right other characters first.
- [rule] Gate a key NPC clue behind earlier dialogue answers, and let the NPC's reaction vary with which clue is shown first, so question order matters. When: When designing dialogue that reveals evidence. Why: Rewards careful sequencing.
- [rule] Let the player propose a theory, list its implications, and mark which implications the game's known facts contradict. When: Designing a deduction interface for players. Why: Making implications explicit lets players test theories against evidence.
- [rule] Reward players who ask what a large object was for, not only those who search for small items. When: Designing clue discovery paths. Why: Rewarding functional reasoning supports varied investigation styles.
- [rule] Give each generated clue a strength rating and a list of innocent explanations, and require a corroborating clue before an accusation unlocks; tag clues sharing a source as correlated. When: when building a case-file system. Why: keeps players from over-trusting clues that come from one NPC.
- [rule] Use a cancelled appointment in a character's schedule as a hook that leads the player to a second character.
- [rule] Tag each clue item as traceable, untraceable or contextual so the generator and the player know which clues can identify a person. When: Building a clue system for a generated case. Why: Explicit tags keep clues from failing silently.
- [rule] Use a closed counter or locked door as a constraint that eliminates an option, and present it to the player as a clue. When: Designing access constraints in a level or investigation. Why: Eliminating options through visible facts makes deduction satisfying.
- [rule] Require proof before a character concedes a point, so the concession becomes a gated objective the player must earn. When: When designing quest progression involving a stubborn NPC. Why: Conditional concessions turn persuasion into a clear task with a defined reward.
- [rule] Make destructive actions such as cutting or breaking available only after gentler checks have been tried, then reveal hidden contents.
- [rule] Make a ledger or inventory record accessible only after an NPC grants permission, with the NPC's willingness as the unlock condition. When: Designing gated information in a game. Why: Conditional access ties information reveal to relationship and trust.
- [rule] Let an NPC give partial information with tells such as hesitation or evasive phrasing, so players can detect omissions and press to unlock the rest. When: Designing dialogue that reveals information gradually. Why: Visible tells reward attentive questioning.
- [rule] Let a non-player character reveal a secret only after the player mentions an item, name or event they have already found. When: Designing dialogue that gates information.
- [rule] Reveal a checkable NPC detail only after the player has separated the claim from the evidence. When: Sequencing NPC information reveals. Why: Gating detail behind sorting rewards careful reasoning over passive listening.
- [rule] Gate NPC information behind trust and tag sensitive topics, so a keyword that triggers a visible reaction shows the player where to press. When: Designing dialogue that reveals secrets. Why: Visible reactions guide players toward the lines of questioning that matter.
- [rule] Offer questions that do not name the target, but surface a clue only when the NPC holds the relevant fact, so information is gained by inquiry rather than by name. When: designing dialogue options that reveal a hidden subject. Why: Indirect questioning keeps the suspect unaware, and it rewards players who ask the right general questions.
- [heuristic] Plant a passing remark that pays off later, even one a speaker laughs off; have the reveal explicitly recall it, since casual lines are easily overlooked. When: when planting information for a late reveal or constructing clues for a mystery. Why: casual mention is easily forgotten and feels fair when recalled.
- [heuristic] Hide a key document or locked compartment in a hidden drawer or passage, signal its existence elsewhere, and make it a reward giving a reason to return.
- [heuristic] Show a threat or trace only in part, holding back its full meaning so the audience supplies the rest and connects it to later evidence. When: building suspense before a reveal or when a trace will matter later in the story. Why: partial views activate the imagination.
- [heuristic] A passing remark by a tavern or casino NPC can gain weight once a later room or item is discovered. When: placing dialogue early in a game. Why: a remark that seems idle becomes meaningful with later discovery.
- [heuristic] Tell the audience what to compare before the reveal, so the recognition has context to land. Why: a clue needs a reference point to be recognised.
- [heuristic] A detail a speaker mentions in passing, such as an unusual pay arrangement, is worth a short confirming question before moving on. Why: Incidental details often expose inconsistencies or motives.
- [heuristic] Design some NPCs to reveal information only when no other NPC is present, so the player must separate characters to learn it.
- [heuristic] Weigh what each possible actor gains from a hidden outcome; a motive is more plausible when disclosure would publish damaging facts. When: choosing suspects from a set of possible actors.
- [heuristic] Divide clues into those that point toward a suspect and those that prove guilt, so suggestive evidence cannot unlock the final accusation. When: designing an investigation with several clues.
- [heuristic] Use delayed news such as a notice or rumour to pace a mystery, so the player waits between revelations. When: Pacing a mystery across a generated level or quest. Why: Spacing revelations creates anticipation between discoveries.
- [heuristic] A constraint, such as needing a second person, can point the player toward where a helper is hidden. When: Designing NPC locations for a puzzle. Why: The constraint narrows the search space for the player.
- [heuristic] Present conflicting clues first and let the planted order emerge only as the player assembles them, rewarding players who keep unexplained facts.
- [heuristic] A confidant who holds a secret can serve as a gated information source that the player must earn.
- [heuristic] A quest can end a scene on uncertainty, such as a sound behind a door, so the player must continue to learn the cause. When: when designing a quest scene ending. Why: unresolved cues motivate the next step.
- [heuristic] Let a secret held by one NPC be leaked when a second NPC applies pressure, and make the leak a trigger for the next quest stage. When: Designing progression through NPC secrets. Why: The leak connects two characters and advances the plot.
- [heuristic] An NPC offering several opening lines can unlock a hidden topic, with the player's tone or choices determining whether the NPC reveals it. When: when a clue is hidden behind a reluctant character. Why: Multiple entry points let different approaches reach the same secret.
- [procedure] 1) Write each deduction as a separate claim. 2) Grade it as established, probable or speculative. 3) List the events that support it. When: building a conclusion from many events.
- [procedure] 1) Begin with a slow approach. 2) Add a detour that delays arrival. 3) Give a last chance to leave. 4) Present the player's choice to confess or flee. When: Staging a climactic confrontation before a key choice. Why: Each gate adds pressure before the decision, making the choice weightier.
- [procedure] 1) List every clue placed in the content. 2) Check that each clue appears in at least one step of the replayed sequence. 3) Flag any clue that no step uses. When: generating a case that must be solvable. Why: A clue no step uses is either noise or a broken chain.
- [pitfall] A list makes weak points look as strong as firm ones unless each item is graded by how well it is supported.
- [pitfall] A partly visible clue may read as a smudge and be missed by the searcher.

## innocent explanations
- [mechanism] Giving an innocent NPC a plausible motive forces the player to test their theory against physical evidence instead of accepting it on motive alone. Why: Motive creates a convincing but false suspicion that only evidence can resolve.
- [mechanism] A new fact that shifts who gains most from a death reframes the earlier evidence, so the most likely culprit changes. When: A new fact changes the likely beneficiary of a crime. Why: The benefit-based theory of who committed the crime depends on who gains, so reassigning gain reassigns suspicion.
- [mechanism] Once the means behind an effect is identified, the supernatural cover is removed and the staged elements of the scene become legible. Why: identified causes turn mysterious effects into understood ones.
- [behavior] Victims are drawn into a trap by innocent-seeming lures, such as a letter in an unfamiliar hand or a polite encounter.
- [behavior] Details of habits and travel times can pass through innocent conversation, so a suspect may know them without intent. When: a suspect appears to have insider knowledge. Why: Casual talk spreads private routines.
- [behavior] A suspect seen by a witness may already have an innocent reason for being there, so a firm sighting is not automatically damning.
- [behavior] Innocent people may refuse a search out of embarrassment or privacy, so a refusal is ambiguous evidence. When: the request touches private belongings. Why: Refusal has motives other than guilt.
- [rule] Give each suspicious clue an innocent explanation via an NPC or document, such as a weak seal, offered before the darker one; players must weigh both. When: designing a red herring suspect or ambiguous clues. Why: keeps the player from assuming guilt; ruling out innocent causes makes the eventual payoff stronger.
- [rule] Benefit from an event establishes a reason, not a deed; when several parties gain, it narrows suspects without naming a culprit. When: several heirs or interested parties gain from a death. Why: Several people may have reasons, so motive alone does not settle who acted.
- [rule] A mundane crime should carry more distinguishing clues per suspect, because many motives seem plausible on their face. When: designing a routine crime with several suspects. Why: without distinguishing clues, every suspect looks equally likely.
- [rule] Exhaust ordinary explanations before accepting an unusual one. Give supernatural claims a fair hearing, but test them last. When: when an unusual explanation is offered. Why: Accepting an uncanny explanation early can end the investigation before ordinary evidence is gathered.
- [rule] Ask where an object would naturally fail or wear, then check whether the actual break or damage is at that point. When: When an object's condition may have been arranged to look accidental. Why: A break at an unnatural point is a sign that someone interfered.
- [rule] Use an innocent-looking setting as a deliberate red herring, and reward players who keep their suspicion alive by finding the one wrong detail. When: designing a hideout or suspect location. Why: rewarding persistence keeps the deception meaningful.
- [rule] Accept a natural explanation only where it can be demonstrated, not merely described, since an incomplete visible explanation can still leave the real cause unexplained. When: when judging a claimed natural cause. Why: demonstration tests the explanation; description does not.
- [heuristic] Explain odd sensations, sounds, knocks or ambiguous signs with ordinary causes, such as a respiratory complaint, before concluding a scene is staged, sinister or supernatural. When: a witness reports unusual sensory details or an odd sound has a plausible ordinary source. Why: Ordinary objects frequently account for strange impressions. (x2)
- [heuristic] Test physical traces for mundane causes, such as evaporation for an empty lamp, and check evidence rules them out before concluding an event occurred; weigh against other traces. When: A trace fits a dramatic explanation and also a common one. Why: Common actions can leave the same marks as unusual ones. (x2)
- [heuristic] Test each link in an accusation chain for an innocent explanation, such as an ordinary cause for a vehicle fault; one plausible alternative can dissolve the whole pattern. When: building or checking an accusation; a link has a plausible ordinary explanation. Why: a chain is only as strong as its weakest link; ignoring innocent explanations inflates apparent strength. (x2)
- [heuristic] When a detail contradicts an account or stated habit, look for an innocent explanation, such as a round trip, and check rather than accuse. When: a physical detail seems to contradict an account. Why: an innocent cause can explain the detail without refuting the account.
- [heuristic] A damning-looking fact often has a mundane innocent explanation, but a plausible one is not shown innocent; check it against evidence rather than stopping there. When: A suspicious fact has a plausible harmless explanation. Why: A plausible explanation lowers suspicion, so investigators often look no deeper until new evidence forces a second reading.
- [heuristic] Concealment or evasion may be innocent, such as protecting someone else; check for an innocent cause before treating a revealed omission or evasion as evidence of guilt. When: a suspect conceals or refuses to explain their actions. Why: Many motives for evasion are unrelated to the crime.
- [heuristic] A death that looks natural is not closed: ask what routine checks would miss and what evidence the culprit would lose, rather than dismissing a motive. When: analysing an apparently natural death, or medical opinion says the death was natural. Why: Points to the concealed cause and the evidence to look for.
- [heuristic] Check whether a mark has a mundane mechanical cause, such as friction from a pulled chain, before treating it as a separate attack. When: A mark lies in the area of a struggle. Why: Ordinary mechanics can produce marks that look like wounds.
- [heuristic] Check plausible natural causes before a deliberate one for a physical trace, since warm places can attract insects or similar traces. When: A trace could be innocent or planted. Why: Natural causes are often overlooked when a culprit is suspected.
- [heuristic] When a death is attributed to natural causes and occurs close in time to another violent event, check whether the two are linked before accepting the verdict. When: A natural-causes verdict and a nearby violent death appear together. Why: A deliberate trigger can act on a body that an illness has already weakened.
- [heuristic] An innocent explanation for an object does not prove it irrelevant; test that explanation before accepting it. When: An object has a harmless purpose that also fits the scene. Why: The explanation may account for the object without ruling out its role in the crime.
- [heuristic] Do not assume every innocent-seeming story is a red herring; some stories are true, so test each one rather than dismissing it.
- [heuristic] Place the party who benefits from the confusion among the helpful onlookers, so their interest stays hidden while they watch the suspect closely.
- [heuristic] Someone may benefit from an object being destroyed by accident, not only from selling or using it, so include them among suspects.
- [heuristic] A rival who gains from a failed arrest may quietly encourage it, so ask who benefits before acting. When: when a confrontation could collapse. Why: a failed arrest can free a competitor to act.
- [heuristic] Before accepting an apparent second attack, test mundane causes such as a nightmare, a fall, or an accidental discharge.
- [heuristic] Choose clue objects with a plausible everyday purpose so each reads as harmless when first mentioned. When: planting an object meant to matter later. Why: an innocent purpose keeps the object from drawing suspicion early.
- [heuristic] An innocent history for how an object was acquired does not explain why it is arranged the way it is.
- [heuristic] Before reading a timeline gap as sinister, list innocent explanations for it, since many gaps come from ordinary errands. When: a suspect's timeline has a gap. Why: Ordinary activity often fills gaps that look suspicious.
- [heuristic] When an item goes missing, first test a harmless cause, such as it was moved for safety, by questioning those who handled it. When: when an item is missing from its expected place.
- [heuristic] A plausible record can look like evidence of a plan until an ordinary error, such as a clerk's mistake, explains it.
- [heuristic] A repeated remark is often an innocent disclosure, not a leak; check the reason for repeating it before treating it as a breach.
- [heuristic] Innocent suspects can usually show where they were, so a suspect with no way to confirm their whereabouts deserves closer scrutiny.
- [heuristic] Plant clues that each have an innocent explanation and reveal the true cause later, so players must test the pattern rather than accept it. When: designing mystery clue sets. Why: players learn to question coincidence.
- [heuristic] Give an innocent character an odd routine that a search would expose, and make the item that clears them findable in their own space. When: Designing a suspect who looks guilty but is innocent. Why: A visible oddity invites suspicion, and a findable clearing item lets players resolve it.
- [heuristic] Give an early suspect an innocent-seeming remark that a later solution reframes as a meaningful clue. When: planting clues in a suspect's dialogue. Why: Readers reread the remark once the reframing exposes its relevance.
- [heuristic] Keep one or two clues with an innocent explanation until the late convergence, so they can be reread as evidence when the case closes.
- [heuristic] An innocent character can look guilty through her own visible actions, such as making a call or tending a suspicious process, because those actions are read as evidence. Why: Visible actions are read as evidence even when their purpose is innocent.
- [procedure] 1) List everyone who gains, linking each to a visible benefit such as a vacancy, promotion or rival's removal. 2) Note who does not gain; absence can be a clue. 3) Verify each gainer's movements, removing those whose alibi holds and keeping unverified alibis open. 4) Use the remaining list to narrow suspects, without naming a culprit from benefit alone. When: Investigating an event with unclear cause or purpose, early in the investigation. Why: Beneficiary checks remove suspects cheaply; visible gains give a concrete basis for motive. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Name the innocent explanation for a trace. 2) Compare it with the known routine habits of the person who could have caused it. 3) Keep or drop the explanation on that basis. When: an innocent explanation must be excluded before accepting a conclusion. Why: Routine habits show whether an explanation is plausible.
- [pitfall] An absence can have a mundane cause, such as an item moved, lost or stored elsewhere; check that assumption, and keep the gap open until the item is located. When: Reasoning rests on an item having been taken.
- [pitfall] A shared or disputed trait is weak evidence until innocent sources, such as an old machine in common office use or many small causes, are ruled out. Why: Suspects can offer benign explanations; many small causes can explain one object's stability.
- [pitfall] A found object can have an innocent explanation; check for one before treating it as incriminating, since a plausible explanation leaves no firm proof linking it to the crime. When: When a found object seems to link a person to a crime.
- [pitfall] Drinking, nerves and restlessness have innocent causes and can mislead an audience about guilt.
- [pitfall] Silence or absence can have innocent causes such as travel, so it should not be read as guilt on its own.
- [pitfall] Treating a bloodstain as proof of violence ignores innocent transfer, such as blood from carrying a body by the shoulders. When: Interpreting stains or residues on a suspect. Why: Helping move a victim transfers blood without any involvement in the act.
- [pitfall] An innocent motive for one suspicious act does not prove innocence of the central crime, so the suspect must still be tested separately. When: A suspect is cleared of a side issue. Why: Clearing one suspicious act leaves other links to the crime unexamined.
- [pitfall] An innocent person can be detained on weak evidence, so a false lead must be tested quickly before the cost grows.
- [pitfall] A small difference between two versions of an item may be innocent, such as a second version taken in the same session.
- [pitfall] Unwitting participants in an arranged plan can be wrongly treated as conspirators, so each person's knowledge should be established before accusing them. Why: innocent go-betweens may only have carried a message.
- [pitfall] A discarded document may have been thrown away for innocent reasons, and interpretation such as assuming interest in a target can outrun the evidence. When: when reading meaning into discarded papers. Why: Innocent explanations are often overlooked.
- [pitfall] A clean surface or missing item can have an innocent cause, such as routine cleaning, so each trace must be weighed against ordinary explanations. When: When interpreting cleanliness or absence as evidence of intrusion. Why: Routine activity produces the same traces as an intrusion.
- [pitfall] A frightened witness may offer a false but plausible explanation for their fear, which should be checked against other evidence. When: When a witness explains a reaction in a way that deflects attention. Why: People often invent innocent-sounding reasons to hide their real concern.
- [fact] A natural cause, such as a physical predisposition triggered by emotional crisis, can make a suspicious death look ordinary to observers.
- [fact] Ordinary objects can carry clues, such as a dropped key, a clock stopped at a set time, a partly drunk glass, or a footmark on a chair.
- [fact] A witness can be innocent of the crime under investigation and still guilty of a lesser secret. When: when a witness's past is uncovered. Why: Hidden lesser faults can be exposed without solving the crime.
- [fact] Holding a belief, even one that accepted decisive evidence of its day, does not by itself show malice; a person can be judged free of vindictiveness.

## staged clue tests
- [mechanism] A staged crime or attack, a blind, fake vehicles or fake officers give investigators a plausible false trail, so the real method, motive or route looks normal. When: A real cause, motive or route must stay hidden. Why: A plausible explanation ends the search for alternatives; a false trail misdirects the search.
- [mechanism] A staged false rumour can provoke a reaction that exposes the true antagonist, because the antagonist acts on information they believe is real. When: the true antagonist is hidden from the player.
- [mechanism] A staged clue that copies a known pattern can mislead people who have not seen the precedent, but an investigator who checks the precedent sees through it. When: A scene looks arranged, too tidy or copied from elsewhere. Why: The copied pattern reveals its artificiality to anyone who knows the original.
- [mechanism] A killing staged as an open, formal contest looks fairer than a hidden attack, so the death draws less suspicion and attention shifts to the spectacle. When: A planner wants a murder to pass as a legitimate fight. Why: Observers judge public, rule-bound conflict as acceptable.
- [mechanism] A staged sound or movement triggered by the player can mislead other characters into a false conclusion. When: Designing a trick that other characters observe. Why: Observers reason from the effect they perceive and may reach a wrong conclusion.
- [mechanism] Observers' reactions can be staged on cue, so apparent symptoms seem to confirm the examiners' claims. When: an examination relies on displays by accusers. Why: Performed symptoms look like independent proof.
- [behavior] Culprits plant clues such as a card, moved object, forced entry or false footprints to imply an outsider or false motive; test each apparent clue separately. When: A scene's items suggest a stranger acted, its evidence fits too neatly with one suspect or contradicts the entry point, or a clue conveniently implicates an outsider or a single date. Why: Investigators who accept a clue at face value follow the path the planner intended while the real plan proceeds elsewhere; staging makes evidence seem to support a conclusion the act does not.
- [rule] Test a proposed explanation against conditions it cannot easily explain, such as undressing in deep cold beside an open window.
- [rule] When an NPC stages evidence, ask who benefits from what remains, since the staging usually serves a particular person's interest. When: When an NPC could be framing another character. Why: Staged evidence is built to favour one conclusion over others.
- [rule] Ask who could have placed an item, why, and whether its owner genuinely used it, rather than accepting a name or mark as proof. When: Evaluating a clue that points to a particular person. Why: Names and marks can be copied or stamped, so they are weak proof of ownership or use.
- [rule] Make scent clues testable by letting the player compare items that were in contact, so the player can see which one carried the odour.
- [rule] When placing a staged item to implicate a non-player character, give it a true owner that the player can discover, so the decoy can be exposed. When: Designing a red herring built on a planted object. Why: A discoverable owner lets players test the clue instead of accepting it at face value.
- [rule] Each new device invented to save a theory from a contradiction must come with its own test that could prove it wrong.
- [rule] Turn a witness's claim into a testable one by tying it to a physical fact, such as a bell or door that would have sounded. When: When a witness says they heard or saw nothing.
- [rule] Tie accuser reactions to the suspect's movements so the player can test whether a reaction is real or staged.
- [heuristic] Evidence that is too neat, complete or pointed at one person may be arranged; real evidence is vague. Judge planted items by whether their placement is natural for the owner. When: A case looks too clean against one suspect, or an item is found where its owner would not normally keep it. Why: A frame-up is built to point one way, unlike messy real traces; staged placements show unnatural order or convenience.
- [heuristic] A staged loss fools only those who do not look closely; an outcome that is too tidy is the usual giveaway.
- [heuristic] An item that looks stolen but still holds valuables may be a decoy, so test whether the robbery was staged. When: when a scene suggests a robbery.
- [heuristic] Test signs of a multi-person attack for staging before accepting them, and do not accept a suspect as framed merely because a relative or gang is named. Why: Naming a plausible culprit does not prove the plant.
- [heuristic] Test a claim that a suspect could not have reached a remote scene by asking whether they would have been seen in a busy area nearby. Why: a known person's presence in a busy place can be checked.
- [heuristic] Test an apparent conclusion against every detail; one anomaly is enough to reopen a case that otherwise looks settled. When: a scene's reading seems complete. Why: Each detail must agree with the conclusion for it to hold.
- [heuristic] Treat a detail that overdoes its own style as possibly a staged imitation, since a genuine author rarely performs the style so exaggeratedly. When: when a detail is too neat or theatrical. Why: Imitators tend to exaggerate the expected signs.
- [heuristic] Stage an alarm to find a hidden object only if the owner's priorities are predictable; avoid it if the target lacks attachment or would spot the staging. When: the object's location is unknown but its owner's priorities are predictable.
- [heuristic] When opponents watch, make a visible move that looks genuine while the real move happens elsewhere, unnoticed. When: When the opposition is known to observe and follow. Why: Watchers act on what they see, so the staged move draws them away.
- [heuristic] A show of searching for a document, or a readily handed-over suspect copy, can signal a decoy meant to make the document seem to have existed earlier. When: a person's theatrics around a document seem out of proportion to its importance. Why: Staging can manufacture an impression of an earlier record.
- [heuristic] A claimed locked state can be tested directly; a lock that opens at a touch contradicts the claim and the account behind it. When: a suspect describes a secured object or fastening.
- [heuristic] Assume anything visible was seen by the culprit too; a clue in an unusual place, given the victim's normal habits, may have been arranged to mislead. When: A clue seems too neat or placed oddly. Why: A clever offender can anticipate what the investigator will notice.
- [heuristic] A sudden staged outburst shows whether a person is rattled, since a rattled person reacts visibly.
- [heuristic] Fabricated traces and invented similar incidents can shift suspicion away from the person who made the marks. When: A disturbed scene needs an innocent explanation.
- [heuristic] Compare recovered remains with witness descriptions of age, height and missing teeth to test a claim. When: a grave or body is found and the records describe the person. Why: physical evidence can confirm or contradict testimony.
- [procedure] 1) Know how the material actually fails. 2) Check whether the reported result fits that failure pattern. 3) Check whether the required forces and edge conditions can really occur. When: when a physical damage claim is central to a case.
- [procedure] 1) Predict how an honest person of the claimed class would react. 2) Apply a controlled stimulus. 3) Compare the actual reaction with the prediction. 4) Treat a mismatch as a clue. When: A suspect's class or background is in doubt and the stimulus can be controlled.
- [procedure] 1) Present a plausible cover story to the suspect. 2) Arrange a moment where they must react to it. 3) Observe their unscripted reaction, which reveals more than their words. When: a true motive must stay hidden, or a suspect's reaction is needed to test them.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whose item the trace belongs to. 2) Ask how its owner accounts for being present. 3) Establish the time window in which the mark could have occurred. 4) Test the inference against other facts. When: a physical trace seems conclusive.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whether the claimed act would have been audible. 2) Check any mechanism involved, such as a lock. 3) Attempt the act or an equivalent. 4) List each required step and judge its credibility. 5) Ask the witness to explain each detail. When: a claim depends on sound, strength or how an object or lock works. Why: Physical checks expose claims that cannot happen as described.
- [procedure] 1) State each inference from a specific sign. 2) List the alternative causes that would produce the same sign. 3) Eliminate alternatives the sign contradicts. 4) Hold remaining inferences loosely. When: When an object's signs have several plausible causes. Why: A sign may fit more than one cause and must be checked before it is trusted.
- [procedure] 1) Let the opposing side believe the investigator has left. 2) Route that news through a channel the investigator controls. 3) Return and act when the suspects have dropped their guard. When: the suspect watches the investigator and would be alerted by knowledge of the investigation. Why: A false belief of absence removes suspicion, letting the investigator act unseen.
- [procedure] 1) List each clue that points to an outside agent. 2) Test each against physical evidence, such as whether a trace matches a suspect's object. 3) Note any mismatch between clues. 4) Accept the outside explanation only if the tests hold. When: A scene's clues point neatly to an outsider, especially early and conveniently. Why: Staged traces can mislead; testing against physical evidence separates real clues from planted ones.
- [procedure] 1) Ask which body part was affected. 2) Ask whether another part could have done the task. 3) Ask whether the claimant could perform the task at all. When: when a witness claims a physical reason for being unable to act. Why: Specific, checkable questions expose excuses that cannot hold.
- [procedure] 1) Measure or describe the suspicious item precisely. 2) Compare it with the suspect's known possessions or marks. 3) Note whether the match is exact or only similar. 4) Discount items that contradict measured facts. When: an item seems to point at one person. Why: Measured comparison separates real matches from convenient resemblance.
- [procedure] 1) List the possible answers to a question the object could settle. 2) Note that every answer is itself a usable fact. 3) Run the test and use whatever result it gives. When: When an object seems unimportant but a test could resolve an open question about it. Why: Each outcome gives information, so the test is worth running whatever it shows.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether the object's type is widely owned. 2) Check whether a matching object belonged to someone else. 3) Note whether it lies in an obvious place. 4) Match it to physical evidence. 5) Test rival explanations against the timeline. When: when a striking object seems to point to one person. Why: a single-owner inference needs the object to be rare and placed by its owner.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who benefits from the suspicion. 2) Check whether the suspect was already an easy target. 3) Test each neat fact for a contradiction, such as an alibi that breaks it. When: when evidence points too directly at one person. Why: A frame-up needs a convenient scapegoat and tangible proof, so it can be checked on both.
- [procedure] 1) Treat a blank page as possibly hiding text. 2) Consider and reject simpler explanations, such as a decoy or nothing being there. 3) Test the page with a suspected reagent or heat source. When: A recovered document appears blank. Why: Invisible writing is revealed only by a specific action, so blank pages must be tested before being discarded.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the route the apparent effect uses. 2) Secure that route, such as locking a door. 3) Observe whether the effect still occurs; if it does, that route was not its cause. When: a door or object appears to move on its own. Why: a physical effect depends on access that the test removes.
- [procedure] 1) Check whose object it really is, using markings or initials. 2) Test whether the attached explanation is plausible. 3) Check whether any witness account changed after talking to someone else. When: when an object or statement fits the expected story too neatly.
- [procedure] 1) Note the marked or unusual object. 2) Ask whether it could be a deliberate message or pure chance. 3) Check its meaning against a second, independent source. 4) Discard it if no source confirms it. When: when an object seems to carry a message.
- [procedure] 1) Place the key object where the subject will see it 2) Keep its significance unannounced 3) Arrange a predictable reason for the subject to enter 4) Observe from concealment 5) Define beforehand which reactions count. When: testing whether a subject knows about an object. Why: a prepared setup makes reactions interpretable.
- [procedure] 1) Note where the clue sits and what is normal for that object or person. 2) Propose an innocent explanation for its placement. 3) Propose a staged explanation. 4) Choose the explanation that a habit or placement rule can test. When: Judging whether a clue is genuine or planted. Why: An innocent and a staged explanation must be tested against a fact the player can check.
- [procedure] 1) Establish a person's habits through people who know them well. 2) Compare each planted item with those habits. 3) Note how each item breaks a habit, such as how it is stored or used. 4) Count how many items break the same habit. When: A scene looks arranged to implicate someone.
- [procedure] 1) Describe what the site would have looked like and how hard it was to reach. 2) State what the claimed procedure would demand. 3) Compare that picture with the claim and with surviving traces. When: A site or procedure is part of the evidence for a claim. Why: Physical constraints can confirm or contradict a claim about how an event happened.
- [procedure] 1) Offer the tester a substitute object or method chosen by the other side. 2) Watch whether they accept it. 3) Treat refusal to use a neutral substitute as evidence that the test is rigged. When: when a test's result depends on an object or method controlled by the tester. Why: A fair test should give the same result with any neutral substitute.
- [procedure] 1) Show the physical clue early with no explained meaning. 2) Let suspicion attach to a wrong suspect. 3) Demonstrate the clue's mechanism. 4) Link the mechanism to a social leak that reveals who acted. When: Revealing how a locked or hidden mechanism worked in an investigation. Why: Separating the object, the demonstration and the social chain keeps the mystery moving while the method is confirmed.
- [pitfall] A test that seems to confirm guilt can be staged or flawed (blindfolds, cued reactions, pins readied in advance); its flaws may be discoverable, so it is not independent proof.
- [pitfall] A dramatic or sensational detail can absorb attention and hide the rational plan behind a case.
- [pitfall] A made-up badge shown to a child can spread the story further than intended, exposing the cover to people who talk. When: Using a false credential to win an insider's trust. Why: Children and casual listeners repeat what they see and hear.
- [pitfall] A staged scene can produce a reaction that is not a confession; the real admission may come later, after the moment, not during it.
- [pitfall] A displayed object can be staged for the occasion, so confirm it was actually in use when the outcome occurred before treating it as an explanation. When: when a suspect presents tools or items as proof of innocence. Why: items displayed later may not reflect the earlier reality.
- [fact] Dents on the nose from spectacles indicate regular wear, and they can suggest a visual condition.
- [fact] Planted evidence can serve as a red herring that the player must test against independent facts. When: designing misleading evidence. Why: Tested red herrings reward careful players.

## covert operations
- [model] A sting lures a guilty party with a paired reward: one for the object and one for the person, so anyone bringing the object in is caught holding both. When: Target is motivated by money and must pass through a predictable channel such as pawnbrokers. Why: The bait exploits greed and the assumption that a thief will sell the stolen item through known channels.
- [definition] A bait is a message written to provoke a specific reaction from a suspect and placed where the target will see it. The investigator watches for the predicted reaction.
- [definition] Covert inquiry gathers information without alerting the suspect, using a hidden investigator identity, a stated pretext and a paid lure so the witness answers freely.
- [mechanism] Bait works best when the target believes they are gaining something they want, so a tempting offer can draw out a cautious person. When: Designing a lure to draw a specific target. Why: Desire can outweigh suspicion, and a target who suspects a trap may still check it.
- [mechanism] Covert dialogue options that require special knowledge can pass unnoticed by NPCs, letting players probe without alerting them.
- [rule] Let players write a reply in the open channel that sets a meeting place, time and payment, and see whether the hidden NPC arrives. When: The player must reach a hidden contact through an open medium. Why: The contact expects replies through the watched channel, and player-set terms give agency and test understanding of NPC motives.
- [rule] In a game, a posted notice can act as bait that triggers a hidden NPC's reaction. Script the expected reaction and a visible follow-up to reward the player's prediction. When: designing antagonist reactions. Why: Rewards player deduction with a visible consequence.
- [rule] Keep the real deadline hidden from the suspect, because the trap depends on the hider acting before it.
- [rule] Collect suspect evidence in secret, since discovery would alert the suspect. When: when gathering reference samples from a suspect.
- [rule] Keep identifying details out of bait messages, so the recipient cannot trace the bait back to its sender. Why: Traceable bait gives away the test.
- [rule] Avoid covert placement when it could expose the investigator or harm the people involved. When: Considering placing an agent in a target's workplace or home. Why: Exposure and harm outweigh the information gained.
- [rule] Avoid covert inquiry when the witness is likely to repeat the conversation to the suspect, unless the questions are carefully controlled.
- [rule] Enter a room on a harmless pretext to observe the objects people use there without arousing suspicion.
- [rule] Do not treat a confirmed presence at a scene as proof of the act; being there and committing the crime are different claims.
- [rule] Design the agreed recording cue so it looks like ordinary behaviour, because a signal the subject notices alerts him. When: Setting up a covert recording cue. Why: A conspicuous signal reveals the observation to the suspect.
- [rule] Hide wires along floor seams and room edges, and cover them, then check the concealment more than once. When: Running wires for a concealed device. Why: A visible wire alerts the people being watched and ends the advantage.
- [heuristic] Use an advertised item, quest hook or harmless planted note as bait, and track which NPC or faction responds so the player can trace the responder. When: Designing a lure or faction/NPC tracking within a game world. Why: Tracking responders turns the bait into an investigation thread.
- [heuristic] An NPC may act differently when believing they are alone, so a hidden observer or a scene where they think no one watches can reveal the truth. When: Designing an interrogation or a suspect's private moment. Why: Unobserved behavior shows what the character hides in public.
- [heuristic] Following a suspect unnoticed gathers more information than confronting them, because the target keeps behaving naturally. When: gathering evidence before acting. Why: a confrontation changes the behaviour being observed.
- [heuristic] Ask about an acquaintance under cover of an ordinary question to get informal confirmation without revealing your purpose.
- [heuristic] A message may be planted by an opponent as bait, so solvers should consider who wrote it and why before acting on it.
- [heuristic] A prized missing item can be a bluff: the culprit may want it searched for, so its apparent importance should be treated with suspicion. When: A missing object appears to be the key to a case. Why: A search for the object can serve the culprit's diversion.
- [heuristic] A public offer of something the suspect values, such as return of lost property, can draw the suspect out into the open. When: When the suspect has a clear want that a notice can address without revealing the investigation. Why: People respond to offers that touch a want, which exposes them to observation.
- [heuristic] A locked-room impossibility can rest on observers' assumptions about a barrier's condition rather than on a true physical impossibility. When: a sealed space seems impossible to enter or leave.
- [heuristic] Hide an unusual activity inside an existing routine that nobody questions, so it looks like normal activity. Why: The cover only holds if the routine already exists and is accepted as ordinary.
- [heuristic] A pretext check can be a mini-game with a fail state, where a poor cover is exposed by one odd remark.
- [heuristic] Offer players a controlled test, such as a lure they set, and require a blind rerun before a suspect is confirmed. When: Designing investigation puzzles.
- [heuristic] Design stealth or dialogue sequences where an NPC observer records what is said on an in-game cue, and let the player review the transcript later as evidence. When: Designing stealth or dialogue sequences. Why: A reviewable record turns overheard talk into usable evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Predict the suspect's likely reaction. 2) Place the bait on a channel the suspect monitors. 3) Watch for the predicted reaction. 4) Use the reaction as evidence. When: the suspect is likely to act on information. Why: A bait turns a prediction into an observable test.
- [procedure] 1) Send a bland message with no meaningful content to the suspect's channel. 2) Observe the reply or any follow-up. 3) Use the response to identify who is watching or passing messages. When: When a suspect is hiding behind an intermediary. Why: Only the watcher reacts to content that means nothing to others.
- [procedure] 1) Hide your real identity behind an alias, including bookings and advertisements. 2) Adopt a plausible pretext that gives the witness a reason to talk. 3) Offer modest payment and ask for secrecy. 4) Question the witness on details only the true source would know. When: when a direct approach would warn a suspect who could destroy evidence or coach witnesses. Why: the suspect cannot link the inquiry to the investigator if the alias stays hidden.
- [procedure] 1) Name a specific item the suspect wants back. 2) Offer its recovery through a reward in a notice. 3) Require claimants to describe the item, which filters out people who do not know it. When: luring a suspect who avoids attention. Why: the tempting recovery draws the suspect out while the identifying test screens false claimants.
- [procedure] 1) Publish a notice naming the missing people and offering a reward for information. 2) Give a code number to route replies privately. 3) Treat each reply as a lead to verify. When: People with knowledge are unknown but likely to read a public notice. Why: A reward gives a reason to respond, and a code keeps the investigation hidden.
- [procedure] 1) Open with innocent questions. 2) Watch whether listeners react; silence suggests they do not understand. 3) If there is no reaction, escalate to riskier questions within the same exchange. When: When others may overhear but cannot understand the language, and the questioner has that advantage.
- [procedure] 1) Test the suspicion quietly first. 2) Restore the original situation. 3) Announce a false plan that threatens the hidden item. 4) Watch who acts before the stated deadline. When: when a hidden item must be flushed out.
- [procedure] 1) Wait for darkness and watch the building. 2) Approach quietly, stopping to listen at each movement. 3) Look through gaps before entering. 4) Secure the exits. 5) Check rooms from the ground floor up, noting objects in each. When: A team raids a suspected hideout where the number and position of suspects is uncertain. Why: Watching first and moving in a fixed order limits the suspects' warning and gives a clear picture of the interior.
