- [procedure] 1) Create bait, such as a withheld or sealed document, expected to draw out the hidden leader. 2) Treat the bait as working only once the adversary's response confirms it. When: Trying to expose a concealed leader who controls an organisation. Why: Responses confirm whether the adversary took the bait, avoiding reliance on untested assumptions.
- [procedure] 1) Position out of sight near the people talking. 2) Listen without being seen. 3) Note any motive or pressure the talk reveals. 4) Approach the person using that knowledge. When: A meeting between a suspect and another person can be watched unnoticed.
- [procedure] 1) Invent a plausible reason for being at the place. 2) Adjust the helper's appearance and props to match that role. 3) Plan views from fixed viewpoints in advance. 4) Set the camera so fine detail is captured. 5) Keep the investigator apart from the helper. When: When a scene must be documented without alerting people who may be involved. Why: A believable cover and planned views avoid suspicion and produce usable records.
- [procedure] 1) Soften the gummed flap over steam. 2) Slip a thin blade under it. 3) Lift the flap cleanly without tearing. 4) Read the contents, holding the flap folded back. 5) Dry the flap, re-gum it and press it down. When: A gummed envelope is the only barrier and the contents must stay undetected. Why: The method restores the seal to its prior state.
- [procedure] 1) Create a plausible vacancy in the target office. 2) Place a trusted agent into it. 3) Give clear instructions on what to listen for and how to act unobtrusively. 4) Have the agent report back regularly. When: Direct questioning of the target would be refused. Why: A placed insider hears staff talk that outsiders cannot access.
- [procedure] 1) Write a message in a trusted person's name and voice. 2) Post it from a distant point. 3) Give the target an exact place, time and recognition signs. 4) Keep the real associate under watch. 5) Hide officers near the meeting spot and close in from both ends at once. When: Luring a suspect into a controlled arrest when a meeting can be set. Why: A trusted-seeming message gets the target to the spot, and simultaneous approach limits escape.
- [procedure] 1) Approach a nervous informant away from others and speak quietly. 2) Pass written instructions discreetly so only the two of you see them. 3) Assign the follow-up to a trusted subordinate. 4) Plan a fallback, since the errand may fail. When: official search would draw attention or a suspect might be tipped off. Why: Discretion prevents tipping off suspects; informants may be fearful or unreliable.
- [procedure] 1) Watch a suspect's routine until a repeated action recurs at a fixed interval. 2) Obtain a duplicate that matches visible markings and placement. 3) Swap the duplicate in while keeping the item count unchanged. 4) Study the original at a safe place. When: When an object is in a suspect's routine and cannot be kept in place. Why: A matched duplicate lets the investigator study the object without the owner noticing.
- [procedure] 1) Keep the subject on the topic where he is most likely to betray himself. 2) Let him speak freely and use tact to decide when to encourage a line of talk. 3) Seat the hidden observer out of the subject's sight but within the questioner's view. 4) Agree start and stop signals beforehand. 5) Have the observer record passively without hinting or commenting. When: Interviewing a suspect who would alarm easily at open note-taking. Why: A covert observer captures statements without disturbing the subject's behavior.
- [tradeoff] Covert methods gain information but carry ethical cost; one proposed limit is to use improperly gained information only when it reveals criminal activity. When: When deciding whether to use information from questionable surveillance.
- [tradeoff] Leaving the room to let suspects speak freely gives access to private talk, but the device must stay undiscovered until the chosen moment. When: Planning a covert listening operation. Why: Early discovery of the device ends the advantage.
- [pitfall] A lure can alert the target, closing other leads and causing behaviour change before the test completes, so use it only when that cost is acceptable. When: When the bait is public and the suspect can see or hear about it. Why: The same notice that invites a response also signals that someone is investigating.
- [pitfall] A false threat or bait fails if the target doubts it, consults another person, checks identity independently, or an authority calls the plan impossible. When: A scheme depends on a target not verifying information. Why: Independent contact exposes the decoy.
- [pitfall] A cautious target who recognises bait as a trap may send a proxy in their place, so the lure reveals an intermediary rather than the target. When: Designing a lure against a suspicious target. Why: Suspicion lets the target avoid exposure by delegating the risk.
- [pitfall] A bait notice can attract the wrong party as well as the right one, so every visitor must still be checked. When: When a lure is used to draw out the true claimant. Why: Anyone interested in the item can respond to the notice.
- [pitfall] Baiting a suspect whose intent is unknown can turn dangerous, so the bait should be controlled and the suspect's possible violence planned for. When: the suspect's motives or mercy cannot be trusted. Why: a bait that succeeds can still provoke a violent response.
- [pitfall] A bait can reach and endanger people who are not the suspect, and can provoke an outcome worse than the one investigated. Weigh these costs before using it.
- [pitfall] Steam, blades and re-gumming can leave traces that a careful owner might notice, so covert opening carries detection risk. When: Opening a sealed item without the owner's knowledge. Why: Tampering methods leave physical evidence.
- [pitfall] A courier who stops or wanders can alter the evidence, so the handoff to the lab must be direct and unaltered.
- [pitfall] A reluctant observer who skips parts of the conversation leaves gaps in the record. When: Relying on a hidden recorder. Why: An unwilling recorder does not follow the agreed plan.
- [pitfall] A sting is only as good as its premise; if the lured object was never stolen or never existed, the trap catches nothing. When: The lure depends on an unverified object. Why: No culprit will come forward for an item that is not in play.
- [pitfall] A sting that runs too long, or an alert outsider studying its structure, can expose it to the target or to gossip. When: A trap stays open over an extended period. Why: Time and outside reasoning let the target recognize the scheme's shape.
- [fact] A physical act can demand knowledge of a site, a suitable build, care with gloves, strength to lower a weight, and composure when handling a body.

## dismissed clues and traces
- [mechanism] A link dismissed as coincidence delays the real connection, and the dismissal is later shown to be wrong. When: when a character explains away an early clue. Why: the rejected link is the one the story needs to reach the answer.
- [behavior] A clue that seems trivial, fits a held theory, or lies outside the current objective is often dismissed and understood only later. When: an offhand remark does not match the current theory, or concerns a topic outside the current objective. Why: commitment to a theory, a sense of triviality, or attention filtering out off-task information hides its meaning.
- [behavior] Peers and listeners may wave off a subtle inference or visible hesitation as imagined or high-sounding talk when they want the conclusion to hold; test it rather than argue. When: the group is invested in accepting the solution. Why: doubts that threaten a wanted conclusion are easy to discount.
- [behavior] Investigators often ignore an unexplained clue until someone forces it into view, after a theory has been accepted. When: A favored theory has already been adopted. Why: Commitment to a theory reduces attention to the facts that contradict it.
- [behavior] A recipient may wave away an anomaly that someone else reports, and may deny having noticed it, avoiding investigation. When: An outside party reports a suspicious detail to someone involved. Why: Reporting through another party lets the recipient deny awareness.
- [behavior] Household members may dismiss an outside investigator's foul-play theory as a specialist's private obsession, so resistance should be expected. When: when an outside investigator proposes that a death was a crime.
- [behavior] An assumption that a case is trivial lowers the investigator's guard, so the clue that matters is dismissed before its significance appears. When: A case looks harmless with a small apparent loss. Why: Expectations of low stakes reduce attention to details that could signal serious offence.
- [behavior] Reasoning that others dismiss as not really evidence can still shape a group's vote.
- [behavior] Audiences who saw a warning dismissed as fancy recall it when danger escalates, so cashing in a dismissed clue feels satisfying. When: a warning was described and then explained away. Why: They registered the clue as description, so it reads as earned when it returns.
- [rule] Before dismissing a frightened witness's sighting as nerves, inspect the physical scene for traces that would confirm or refute it. Why: A dramatic sighting can rest on something real.
- [rule] Discount an individual mark when it could have been made after the event or when no one saw it before the event.
- [heuristic] Press witnesses and suspects on small incidents or details they wave off as unimportant, since dismissed details often prove central to the case. When: when a witness or suspect waves away a specific detail. Why: Dismissing a detail under pressure is often a sign that it touches the truth. (x2)
- [heuristic] Place the clue in plain sight within a dismissed conversation or physical scene so the player sees it without registering it until the late reveal. When: hiding the solution in plain sight. Why: a dismissed detail is recalled differently once revealed.
- [heuristic] Dismiss an early clue, such as burnt paper, in a neutral voice so players treat it as irrelevant, then reopen it when a later test or reveal makes it key. When: planting a clue whose function is revealed later in the scenario or at the climax. Why: A dismissed clue is easily forgotten, and its return rewards attentive players and makes the solution feel inevitable.
- [heuristic] Plant early clues, including the true explanation, that an authority figure dismisses, so attentive players can later reinterpret them to overturn the accusation. When: opening a mystery with an official dismissal. Why: Players who recall the dismissed clue gain a sense of insight when it is later vindicated.
- [heuristic] Dismissing an obvious question quickly can make the audience stop asking it, which can be used deliberately to steer attention.
- [heuristic] Plant a vivid but ambiguous observation early, dismissed at the time, so its meaning becomes clear when later facts arrive. When: a clue must be understood only later. Why: delayed recognition makes the clue feel earned.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a small or mundane detail as accidental or trivial, without evidence, can hide the real clue; routine marks may be decisive when read with timing and sources. When: Reviewing ordinary-looking evidence. Why: Minor details may prove relevant, and routine marks may carry the decisive information.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a small mark or detail as unimportant can lose the case-resolving clue; apparent importance is unreliable, and trivial details gain meaning when linked to other facts. When: A small mark or detail seems too trivial to test. Why: Apparent importance is not a reliable guide to relevance.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a trace because it does not fit the favoured theory discards evidence that may later prove relevant; a fixed theory leads investigators to treat conflicting clues as unimportant.
- [pitfall] Ignoring contrary evidence, including residue that does not fit the theory, lets a wrong explanation stand unchallenged; contrary traces must be explained before a conclusion is accepted.
- [pitfall] Dismissing evidence as planted or deceptive without testing it is as unsound as trusting it blindly; each item still needs its own test.
- [pitfall] Ignoring a retraction made after the pressure ended discards the accused's correction and evidence of how the confession was obtained; a false confession may stand. When: A confession is later withdrawn. Why: The retraction is evidence about how the original statement was obtained.
- [pitfall] A half-remembered resemblance dismissed as a side effect of repetition is effectively lost, so the clue must be made recognizable on its own. When: when a clue sits in a confusing or repetitive scene. Why: repetition overloads memory.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a tell because it was brief causes an observer to lose evidence that could be recalled and checked again.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a clue because its meaning is unclear when first noticed can lose the detail that the solution later needs.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a clue because its reference is unrecognised can discard the key evidence; the investigator's ignorance is itself a risk.
- [pitfall] Missing a small moved object that others dismissed as unimportant can hide the key trace. When: A minor detail is set aside by others. Why: Small disturbances often carry the decisive evidence.
- [pitfall] Players and investigators often drop small oddities as trivial, though the smallest detail may reveal how an act was done. Why: Minor-looking details are easily filtered out as noise.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a small loss or detail as harmless can leave a trace that others later connect to the act.
- [pitfall] A small delay or odd address on a sent item can be the key clue; dismissing it as unimportant can lose the lead.
- [pitfall] A clue dismissed as trivial can misdirect an inquiry for a long time, because the dismissal shapes everyone's later reasoning.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a small mark as trivial, without checking when its material was wet, can assign it a wrong and ordinary cause.
- [pitfall] A clue dismissed early and never revisited becomes noise, so the contradicting detail must be kept alive for later return. When: writing or designing a mystery. Why: An unresolved detail loses its meaning when forgotten.
- [pitfall] Dismissing an inconvenient object as coincidence can hide the truth, and investigators who do so leave the strongest clue unexamined. When: A physical clue conflicts with the favoured theory. Why: Waving away the clue removes the test that could expose the error.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a sound or clue because it seems unlikely for the culprit to produce it can cause the investigator to overlook the culprit's real choices. When: An investigator judges a clue against an assumption about how the culprit would act. Why: The assumption about method may be wrong, so the discarded clue may be the true evidence.
- [pitfall] Dismissing an odd detail without conviction can leave a real threat unexamined.
- [pitfall] Ignoring the direction a trace runs makes any inference drawn from it unreliable.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a small trace as trivial can delay an inquiry, because seemingly irrelevant details such as diet can later prove meaningful. When: When a small residue seems unimportant to the case. Why: Minor traces can connect to places or people not yet known.
- [pitfall] Overlooking a trivial remark or minor detail can miss the clue that reopens a timeline, since idle talk often points back to an absence. Why: Casual comments can carry facts that matter once a sequence is checked.
- [pitfall] A tiny trace is easily dismissed as debris; the investigator must ask why it is there.
- [pitfall] Clumsy-looking incidents are easily dismissed as unimportant, so a plan can go unnoticed until the full chain is read. When: when investigating a crime with many small events. Why: each event seems harmless when viewed alone.
- [pitfall] Assuming a sound is harmless because nothing visible is present is a mistake, since the sound may still signal a real threat. When: Deciding how seriously to treat an unexplained noise. Why: Absence of visible evidence does not rule out a hidden presence.
- [pitfall] Dismissing an answer that contradicts a favoured theory, before asking what that theory predicts, discards possible evidence.
- [pitfall] Ignoring traces of a second person because a confession names only one actor leaves the case incomplete.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a witness's description of a suspect's temper or speech can hide an early clue that only makes sense later. When: when a witness offers a passing remark about a character. Why: Trivial-seeming remarks can gain meaning once background is known.
- [pitfall] Dismissing an offhand remark as unimportant can delay the lead it points to, until it is recorded in full and tested. When: Reviewing a passing comment in testimony. Why: Remarks that seem trivial may later prove to be the key lead.
- [pitfall] A single lit detail can be dismissed as imagination, so an observer's doubt may be the only thing stopping it from being acted on. When: a brief sighting of one detail. Why: one brief detail is easy to doubt.
- [pitfall] Ignoring a contradiction because it seems minor can delay the answer for days.
- [pitfall] Dropping a lead because it seems absurd or comic can cause the investigator to miss the real clue it contains.
- [pitfall] Ignoring the accuser's grievance, property or income when weighing testimony is a common mistake.
- [pitfall] Answering a counterargument by calling it emotion dismisses it without addressing the question it raises.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a theory only for being improbable can be as careless as accepting it only for being neat. When: Evaluating competing explanations. Why: Both shortcuts skip checking the premises against evidence.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a small measured difference is a mistake, since a very small discrepancy can be decisive. When: Evaluating a forgery with minor measured variation. Why: Forgeries are often exposed by differences too small to notice without measurement.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a clue through a character's stupidity makes the reveal feel cheap. Why: The reveal depends on the character's error rather than on the player's reasoning.
- [pitfall] A detail offered casually at the end of an interview can be dismissed as trivial when it may be significant. When: When a late remark does not fit the main line of inquiry. Why: Incidental remarks can carry clues that the questioner has not yet connected.
- [pitfall] An interviewer who dismisses trivial details discards the very details that carry the timeline. When: Questioning a witness whose account is built from everyday routines. Why: Mundane details serve as cues for the sequence of events.
- [pitfall] Ordinary details are dismissed as coincidence until the investigator has a reason to notice them. When: A small detail seems too mundane to matter. Why: Without a link to the timeline or people, the detail looks harmless.
- [fact] A group can keep members ignorant of a crime so they have nothing to testify to and cannot be forced to speak.

## fragment matching
- [mechanism] A line cut through a surface that deepens toward a door shows the direction the object was pulled.
- [mechanism] A physical marking too subtle to see can reveal itself through differing effects in use, so testing an item can expose what inspection misses.
- [behavior] A listener who hears only fragments fills the gaps with their own fears, expectations or distrust, so the fragment is evidence about the listener too. When: when overhearing a partial conversation or when the audience receives partial information. Why: Missing words invite the listener's assumptions; people fill missing parts with what they expect or want.
- [behavior] Hosts extend hospitality, such as clothing and a bath, to a guest vouched for by a trusted sponsor, without knowing the guest's name or checking identity. When: a sponsor's word is offered for a guest. Why: trust transfers through the sponsor rather than through direct verification.
- [rule] A fragment that matches a known item or gap, such as a garment, ties its owner or origin to the place where it was found. When: A torn or broken fragment is found in a room or at a scene. Why: A matching source connects its owner or origin to the location. (x2)
- [rule] Partial fragments often cannot be reconstructed reliably; state any inferred reading as an inference and do not complete it with more meaning than the trace supports. When: clues are damaged or incomplete. Why: missing parts cannot be recovered with confidence.
- [rule] Never let a single fragment or mark carry a conclusion alone; building a large theory on it inflates weak evidence until other evidence corroborates it. When: a clue or lone physical trace is the only support for a conclusion. Why: A fragment alone offers no way to verify it.
- [rule] Confirm a partial text or impression's source against a known sample, such as handwriting, and recover its full text rather than inferring contents from the fragment. Why: A partial impression can be misread, and a fragment cannot establish contents.
- [rule] When a story has passed through several hands, go back to the original place or witness, or question the first informant directly, to check the details. When: A reconstruction depends on accounts that passed through several reporters.
- [rule] Assemble partial documents from several locations so the player must collect each fragment to reconstruct the whole. When: Designing a letter or record split across the world.
- [rule] Confirm a dying message fragment with other evidence before committing to a course of action based on it. When: a partial message would drive a major decision such as an accusation or pursuit. Why: Fragments are partial and can be misread, so unconfirmed meaning may mislead.
- [rule] Do not name a culprit on the strength of a dying fragment alone. When: a dying message is the only evidence against a suspect. Why: A few incomplete words cannot establish guilt.
- [rule] Match a torn fragment to a known item by close examination of its fibres, such as a fringe, against a known sample. When: a fragment is found at a scene and the owner's garment is known.
- [rule] Track which message fragments the player has heard, so earlier words gain meaning when a later fragment arrives. When: a game lets players collect message fragments over time. Why: Fragments only gain meaning when linked, so the game must remember what was heard.
- [rule] Verify a claimed source by asking details that only the true source would know.
- [rule] Reveal a non-verbal character's past only in fragments that the player must assemble. When: designing non-verbal companion NPCs.
- [rule] Mark which conclusions a player can prove and which remain suspicions, so the game clearly separates belief from evidence. When: Designing an investigation where the player forms theories. Why: Players can misread suspicion as fact unless the game distinguishes them.
- [rule] Sort overlapping prints and smudges by source before concluding that they came from one person. Why: Superimposed marks can look like a single source.
- [rule] Hide clues in burned or torn remnants that the player must combine, as in an inspection or crafting puzzle.
- [rule] Match the full sequence of marks, including the gaps, rather than relying on a single distinctive mark. When: Comparing a partial trace with a candidate.
- [heuristic] Dismissing a fragment as meaningless or over-reading it both mislead; test it against all known facts, and treat any pieced-together meaning as a lead until checked. When: a dying phrase, odd note or pieced-together fragments are interpreted. Why: Fragments can seem trivial yet matter, or create a false pattern when over-read.
- [heuristic] A fragment may seem meaningless or unimportant until a later fragment links to it or to earlier clues, so compare separated parts before judging its meaning. When: A late fragment refers to earlier clues, or a character hears a place name or phrase without grasping its importance. Why: Meaning depends on links found later; connections to earlier material make the story cohere.
- [heuristic] At each link in a chain of testimony, ask whether the speaker saw the event or was only told about it. When: Testimony reaches you through other people. Why: Second-hand reports can look like first-hand ones.
- [heuristic] Write a dying character's lines as fragments whose neighbours constrain the missing words, so players assemble the meaning themselves. When: for dialogue meant to be pieced together by the player. Why: Constraints from surrounding words let players infer meaning without it being stated.
- [heuristic] A clue that names a person and implies a stake, without explaining the matter, tells the audience someone holds a key without revealing its purpose. When: when introducing a clue ahead of its meaning. Why: Partial information creates a question the audience wants answered.
- [heuristic] Place dialogue fragments mentioning an NPC's name or a quest item so the player must connect them, leaving room for a misreading. When: designing partial dialogue for discovery. Why: connection effort makes discovery feel earned.
- [heuristic] A cut cord with an intact knot shows how a parcel was opened and suggests the knot itself carries meaning worth examining. When: When reconstructing how a sealed package was handled. Why: The manner of cutting or untying reveals both handling and significance.
- [heuristic] Consider who made a claim, who was present, and what they gain from the suggestion. When: when a single explanation rests on one source's word. Why: A source with a stake in the outcome may mislead.
- [heuristic] The shape of a cut can match a particular tool, so repeated curved cuts suggest a tool with a bent blade. Why: Blade geometry leaves a characteristic mark.
- [heuristic] Check whether a witness's stated source fits her confidence; a claim to know only a dead man's past yet speak surely about his death is suspect. When: A witness's certainty seems greater than her stated access to information. Why: Confidence beyond the source suggests inference or invention.
- [heuristic] Keep any fragments found stuck together by accident, since they can be the most valuable clues. When: When searching a fragmented clue site. Why: Pre-joined pieces preserve context that scattered pieces lose.
- [heuristic] A small fragment can prompt a hypothesis about a larger missing part, and a search guided by that hypothesis may locate the rest. When: A small piece of evidence suggests a larger missing object or body part. Why: A fragment identifies the structure it belongs to, pointing the search.
- [heuristic] Clue-matching puzzles can present a sequence with deliberate gaps that the player must align against the evidence. When: Designing matching puzzles.
- [procedure] 1) Read only the words that survive. 2) Set aside weak fragments at first. 3) Keep partial observations on record and reread after new facts arrive. 4) Use the result as a lead to test, not a final answer. When: interpreting a partly legible document. Why: New context can change what surviving words mean; a fragment can later become evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Learn the shorthand conventions, such as underlines, dashes and short phrases. 2) Link key words into a coherent story. 3) Test the story against dates. 4) Note the gaps the story leaves unexplained. When: a community or habit gives the shorthand shared meaning. Why: Shared conventions give fragments a common meaning.
- [procedure] 1) Collect every fragment, including small ones. 2) Fit them together. 3) Count missing or surplus pieces. 4) A complete set means breakage at the find site; many missing pieces mean the rest lie elsewhere, while surplus or shortfall suggests another place or cause. When: investigating a broken object.
- [procedure] 1) Identify an unusual, specific feature of the object. 2) Compare it, with its type, edge wear and discolouring, against the suspect's or source's possessions. 3) Confirm with a second, independent feature that only one source could match. 4) Check that source's remaining stock for matching items. When: a found item may come from a suspect's possessions or a household or workplace inventory.
- [procedure] 1) Give a dying character a partial message. 2) Scatter the remaining parts across locations. 3) Make each fragment point to a place the player can reach. When: designing a quest hook built from a dying character's words. Why: The player must be able to complete the message by visiting the places the fragments name.
- [procedure] 1) Bring the two torn pieces together. 2) Try each orientation: front to front, back to back, and back to front. 3) Accept a match only if the torn edges coincide in one orientation. When: Two physical fragments look alike or must be matched.
- [procedure] 1) Check the page number; a high number implies many missing pages around it. 2) Count the gap to the surrounding pages. 3) Look for shifts in narrative voice or point of view. 4) Note handwriting and provenance that tie it to a household. When: a document fragment is the only surviving evidence.
- [procedure] 1) List the objects that could have made the mark. 2) Recreate the mark with each candidate. 3) Compare each result with the original. 4) Keep the candidates that match and narrow the suspects. When: a specific mark is found and the set of possible tools is known.
- [procedure] 1) Name each mark and the question it answers. 2) Measure overall size, span and proportions, recording them apart from the visual impression. 3) Eliminate candidates with clear mismatch. 4) Report any match as tentative. When: only fragments of a trace survive. Why: Measured records and explicit tentativeness keep conclusions from outrunning faint evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Record the damage and infer the tool's shape from its marks. 2) Locate candidate tools. 3) Compare each candidate's marks with the damaged surface. 4) Measure and sketch each tool so the comparison can be repeated. 5) Test the fit with the actual tool. When: damage suggests a specific tool was used. Why: A repeatable, measured comparison is more reliable than judging fit by eye.
- [procedure] 1) Sort each fragment into a flat container in the order found. 2) Find a pre-joined clump and use it as the central anchor. 3) Build outward from the anchor. 4) Mark any filled-in gaps as inferred. When: When reassembling a torn or fragmented document. Why: A stable central piece gives a reliable starting point and keeps each addition traceable.
- [procedure] Split a fragment that carries writing on both sides to create a blank backing before reassembling it. When: When reconstructing double-sided paper fragments. Why: A blank backing lets the piece join without covering one side's text.
- [procedure] 1) Sort fragments by edge: straight edges with text starting at them mark an opening. 2) Join pieces by overlapping torn words. 3) Check each join against edges and neighbouring words. 4) Keep alternative readings open until another clue decides. When: A document has been torn and its fragments are available to align. Why: Edge shape and overlapping text constrain which pieces fit together.
- [procedure] 1) Take the broken fragment found on the body. 2) Pass it with the second fragment found elsewhere to the decision group. 3) Let each member check whether the ends fit. 4) Confirm the match is clean before accepting it. When: Proving that two broken pieces of an object belong together before a group. Why: Letting several people check the fit independently makes the match more credible.
- [pitfall] A fragment supports several readings, so without its surrounding words or fit with the rest of the record it leads to conjecture; keep context and check consistency before trusting it. When: using an incomplete, garbled or partial fragment as evidence. Why: Partial text supports many readings, so only context or consistency with other evidence makes its meaning reliable. (x2)
- [pitfall] Taking an overheard fragment as the whole statement, or a relayed phrase as verbatim, misstates what was said. When: when using eavesdropped or relayed speech. Why: Fragments and relays lose content.
- [pitfall] Treating words from a speaker in shock as a complete statement, when they may be only the end of a longer thought. When: The speaker was in shock or delirious. Why: Shock fragments omit context that the full thought would supply.
- [pitfall] An accurate fragment can distort a motive when read alone; another witness's added context can change its meaning entirely. When: Interpreting a partial overheard statement. Why: Missing context shifts how a fragment reads.
- [pitfall] Forcing a fragment to fit when its edges do not match, or missing that a document runs across several pages, produces a wrong reconstruction. When: Assembling torn or burned documents. Why: Edge evidence must agree before pieces are joined, and multi-page documents can hide pieces.
- [pitfall] Constant cutaways fragment attention when no thread is resolved, leaving the audience without a clear sense of progress. When: Many threads run in parallel without resolution. Why: Too many open threads dilute focus.
- [pitfall] A dedication, reprint, or later notice shows someone was alive at one moment, not where they went afterwards.
- [pitfall] Identical colour and printing do not show that two pieces came from the same source; only the fit of the torn edge settles it. When: Pieces match visually but have not been fitted. Why: Many items share colour and print.
- [pitfall] Joining fragments by assumption can yield a fluent but false phrase; fit must be verified against the physical edges. When: Piecing together torn text without clear edge matches. Why: Plausible wording can hide an incorrect join.
- [fact] Partial damage can destroy a name while a surviving fragment, such as a printed corner or a postscript recovered from ash, still identifies the document's source or writer. When: A burnt or torn document is examined. Why: Partial survival can still identify its writer.
- [fact] Surviving archives are often scattered, damaged and partly abstracted, with only a few items reaching repositories by chance.
- [fact] An entry with no name, sex or date cannot establish who was involved on its own and must be matched against other sources before it supports any conclusion. When: When a record mentions a person without identifying details.

## informant handling
- [model] A feud can be modeled as a rising tension meter: each dispute raises tension, and clear triggers push it toward a public accusation. When: designing community conflict systems. Why: Visible escalation lets players anticipate crises.
- [mechanism] Offering a witness control over whether a secret is published or suppressed, or dropping a charge, for a full account prompts fuller, candid answers than formal questioning. When: A witness has a reason to hide a relationship or the whole truth, and a credible reason to speak. Why: The witness weighs the consequences of disclosure.
- [mechanism] Leverage from a held secret lasts only while the item stays hidden and unused; using or revealing it ends the power over the victim. When: A character holds damaging information over another. Why: The power depends on the threat being unspent and the victim knowing of it.
- [mechanism] An informant's answer can disclose a fact the questioner could not check otherwise, which makes the exchange valuable.
- [mechanism] A credibility value on each informant, lowered when that informant is exposed, cascades to every clue they supplied, reducing the weight those clues carry. When: Designing NPC informants in dungeon or narrative generation.
- [mechanism] In an information-trade mechanic, the NPC's reaction to an offered item signals how much it has to hide.
- [mechanism] A player-controlled network of informants, each placed in a different location, can supply gossip and clues across the map. When: A game world spans several locations. Why: Distributed sources report on places the player cannot watch directly.
- [mechanism] A social-network view that records relationships learned from gossip lets the player map a community as they learn more about it.
- [mechanism] A found item that contradicts an NPC's story can trigger a confrontation, turning a clue into a dialogue encounter. When: In investigation games with NPC testimony.
- [mechanism] Informant NPCs who can be bribed or threatened into a covert task should carry real risk and a chance of failure, and a failed errand can branch the mystery rather than close it.
- [mechanism] When suspicion is high, NPCs refuse to trade or help, which hides clues and narrows the player's options. When: when a game uses community suspicion as a mechanic. Why: Refusals block access to information and resources.
- [mechanism] An informant's account often has three layers: what they saw, what they heard from others, and what they conclude from both. When: Evaluating a claim from an informant who followed or observed a target. Why: Separating layers shows which parts are direct observation and which are inference.
- [behavior] Unwitting bystanders, such as fellow travellers, can repeat what they heard without grasping its significance, so their reports carry information they do not understand. When: A target's movements are being traced after the fact. Why: Casual conversation reveals details the speaker does not recognise as significant.
- [behavior] An informant's cooperation can depend on payment, and once paid, the informant may give help and leave without further commitment. When: A street informant is offered money. Why: Reward, not loyalty, drives the exchange.
- [behavior] An informant with a stake may try to steer the investigator's suspicions toward another person before those suspicions form. When: The informant fears suspicion falling on someone they protect. Why: Shaping the imagination first can steer conclusions.
- [rule] Give informants a visible price, bias or stated stake, such as payment or grudge, plus a real chance of false names, so players must weigh their reliability before acting. When: Designing informant characters, especially NPCs who trade information for leniency. Why: Reliability becomes a meaningful choice. (x2)
- [rule] Attach a reliability value to informant answers that depends on the informant's current condition, such as fatigue or confusion, which can also end a session early. When: When designing informant answers.
- [rule] Keep rumours as unverified leads: weigh them against evidence rather than dismissing them as improbable, and do not treat them as clues until checked. When: A rumour contains improbable details. Why: A rumour may still hold a true detail; treating gossip as a clue chases noise.
- [rule] Give some NPCs stock answers and others richer, linked knowledge, so players learn which informants to trust. Why: Depth contrast teaches players to judge sources.
- [rule] Give an informant NPC hurried or illegible notes written under pressure, as a reliability cue the player can read. When: designing informant characters.
- [rule] In a leverage mechanic, give the NPC a deadline and a required action, with options to threaten or to bargain.
- [rule] Test an informant's claims against dated, independent facts such as letters, reports and the timing of earlier events. When: an informant gives an account. Why: dated records can confirm or contradict the claims.
- [rule] Give a trusted local a specific watch brief, such as reporting motors or aircraft, to turn them into a reliable informant. When: monitoring a region for pursuers. Why: a narrow task gets clearer reports than a general request.
- [rule] Give an informant NPC a sample collection quest with ordered steps the player must follow exactly, such as sealed kit, timing and delivery. When: designing NPC-driven investigation tasks.
- [rule] Plant a paid-but-never-used lead that players can verify against venue records.
- [rule] Make an informant reachable only through a specific intermediary or channel, so players must plan how and when to make contact. When: when designing hidden informants.
- [rule] Trigger an NPC reaction, such as an attack or flight, when the player shows the correct item at the right moment.
- [heuristic] Judge a paid or interested source by testing checkable claims against independent records, since verified claims lend credibility to unverified ones; payment gives reason to shape the story. When: The only available witness is paid or has a stake in the outcome. Why: Checkable claims give an independent measure of the source's accuracy. (x2)
- [heuristic] When paid seats go unused after sales errors are ruled out, the non-use is likely deliberate; check records rather than accepting a witness's claim of non-use. When: A witness claims a paid seat or channel went unused.
- [heuristic] Treat information bought for money with caution, especially cryptic warnings that are hard to test.
- [heuristic] Gather information from nearby bystanders by questioning them rather than approaching the subject, and keep one's own purpose hidden. When: Learning about a target without alerting them. Why: Questioning others keeps the target unaware.
- [heuristic] Unusual limits on contact, such as allowing only untraceable correspondence, are a signal worth noticing and investigating. When: someone arranges communication in an unusual, hard-to-trace way. Why: Restricting traceable contact can hide a person's identity or whereabouts.
- [heuristic] Use an unexplained cryptic message to test whether a suspect knows a specific fact without asking directly.
- [heuristic] Explain how a suspect learned of an opportunity through overheard or indirect knowledge.
- [heuristic] Check whether an accuser is paid per accusation, since that income gives reason to keep finding targets.
- [heuristic] Let NPC gossip carry concrete physical details marked as unverified, so players can check the world state and see whether the rumour holds.
- [heuristic] Give a late arriving character a risk, such as forcing the player to expose a secret they hold, so the choice changes later encounters. Why: A costly choice makes the arrival meaningful rather than a passive event.
- [heuristic] Release a dying or fearful NPC's information in steps: a hint, a related question, then a physical object that proves the point. When: An NPC holds key information in a game. Why: Staged disclosure keeps the player engaged and lets the proof carry the final weight.
- [heuristic] A servant or informant who knows secrets can gate late-game information, with their trust earned through earlier tasks. When: When designing an NPC who holds hidden knowledge. Why: Earned trust makes the reveal feel earned rather than handed over.
- [procedure] 1) Ask how the informant learned the fact. 2) Check claims for self-consistency and directions against landmarks. 3) Note what reward the informant wants and what they gain. 4) Verify key claims against independent accounts before acting on them. When: Assessing any informant, especially when the informant is the only route to a fact or place. Why: Informants can contradict themselves, mislead and act for pay.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the source's grudge. 2) Offer small courtesies that signal respect. 3) Let the source talk first. 4) Reveal only what is needed to steer the conversation. When: When questioning a witness or informant who is reluctant to share.
- [procedure] 1) State what you already know, so lying clearly costs more than the truth. 2) Reveal hidden dealings to show concealment has failed. 3) Name the motive. 4) Show a real pending consequence. 5) Demand one specific act in return. When: Real leverage over a suspect exists and can be shown.
- [procedure] 1) Use short neutral prompts that invite elaboration. 2) Show insight into the source to unsettle them. 3) Offer a small payment. 4) Press for precise details. When: a source is motivated by money or vanity.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the fact you need. 2) Have a trusted contact fetch it without revealing why it matters. 3) Deliver the result to the subject and watch their reaction. When: A direct question would alert the subject.
- [procedure] 1) Approach the source through a mutual acquaintance in an informal setting. 2) Start from the source's own interests. 3) Introduce the real subject only after rapport is established. 4) Record the exchange as dialogue, noting evasions and omissions. When: The source talks freely informally and would close up under direct questioning. Why: Informal rapport loosens speech, and recorded dialogue reveals pressure points.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm there are no signs of forced entry, such as a picked lock, forced bolt or marked panel. 2) Conclude that an accomplice admitted the culprit. 3) Rank occupants by how much access each had.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the stranger's identity and set the conditions for sharing news. 2) Probe who is involved and how the informant learned it. 3) Test the claim against a fact already known. 4) Ask for a verifiable anchor, such as a location and return meeting, to hold the claim to account. 5) Note the subject's physical bearing. When: A witness offers a serious, checkable claim. Why: Sequencing identity, sources, verification and anchors exposes unsupported claims before action is taken.
- [tradeoff] Paying or flattering a witness secures cooperation and can yield more detail, but the incentive can lead them to invent, exaggerate or shape the account; cooperation never establishes accuracy. When: A witness is offered money or favours. Why: Payment changes the witness's incentive to please the questioner.
- [tradeoff] A paid informant can reach places and routines the investigator cannot, but each claim they sell is shaped by payment and must be verified. When: the investigator lacks access and can later check the claims. Why: the informant's money motive can bias what they volunteer.
- [tradeoff] Pressuring an informant with a dependence you hold can yield the name, but the information gained this way is tainted by the abuse of position that produced it. When: A trail depends on a reluctant intermediary who relies on the investigator. Why: Coerced information is less trustworthy and costs the investigator moral standing.
- [tradeoff] A reluctant witness can be moved by a threat, a favour or money, and the interrogator should choose the lever that fits the witness's motive. When: A witness has a clear motive to trade information. Why: Each lever suits a different motive, and a mismatch makes the offer fail.
- [pitfall] An unrecorded handoff can be overlooked by both the investigator and the audience if it is never written down or shown. When: a key transfer happens off the page or off screen. Why: nothing in the record points to it.
- [pitfall] A message repeated from memory can differ from the original, so check its wording against the account's other claims before trusting it.
- [pitfall] An informant's stiff, flat delivery can make a scene feel colder than the news itself.
- [pitfall] A false summons only becomes evidence once the claimed sender is shown not to have sent it. When: A message claims to come from a particular person who was absent. Why: Until the claimed source is checked, the message can be taken as genuine.
- [pitfall] An overly eager informant or an implausible cover story can alarm the community and end the inquiry.
- [pitfall] An ally who blurts out the investigator's true knowledge can ruin a bluff, so control what each party knows. When: When other people are present during a bluff. Why: Revealed knowledge tells the suspect the claim is false.

## npc knowledge
- [mechanism] A minor NPC who observes a destroyed note can later report it, letting the player reconstruct a missing clue. When: When designing evidence that is destroyed in-game. Why: Witnesses to destruction preserve the content indirectly.
- [mechanism] An NPC with memory loss answers only about events after a set trigger, so the player learns the boundary of what can be asked. When: Designing an NPC with amnesia. Why: A defined boundary makes the limit legible rather than arbitrary.
- [mechanism] NPCs can be built so that two identities are never on screen together, and the player must catch the moment they overlap to reveal the deception. When: Designing a double-identity mystery. Why: Overlap detection rewards careful observation of timing.
- [behavior] A bribed insider's loyalty depends on how much they stand to lose if caught. When: when a bribed insider must keep a secret. Why: A person weighs exposure risk against payment.
- [behavior] Insiders' remarks that sound like praise or warning can be taken literally by outsiders, when they are actually routine or teasing.
- [rule] Limit NPC witnesses' perception by light levels, distance and sensory range (what they could hear or smell from their position), flagging low-light identifications as partial so players weigh testimony. When: When designing NPC witnesses or their reports. Why: Perception limits make witness reports realistic and create partial clues. (x2)
- [rule] Limit an NPC's knowledge to their post, and let recall of past events depend on matching keywords or precise questions, fading if the player presses too hard. When: When designing NPC dialogue that holds clues. Why: Gating recall behind keywords or precise questions rewards inquiry over repetition. (x2)
- [rule] Track what each NPC knows and could have learned separately, so dialogue reacts correctly to concealment and flags any reference to a secret the NPC had no route to. When: when NPCs may or may not learn facts the player has. Why: Per-character knowledge state lets dialogue respond accurately to concealment. (x2)
- [rule] Model each NPC's line of sight through windows, gaps and light levels, so players check sightlines against geometry; a reflection or candle can make a claim plausible or impossible. When: When an NPC's claimed sightline or witness account must be checkable against the environment. Why: Physical constraints and geometry let players test claims against the world.
- [rule] Make overheard NPC conversations at doors or vents partial, so players infer context, may guess wrong, and combine fragments with other sources to uncover hidden factions. When: When designing overheard dialogue as a clue. Why: Incomplete context creates inference the player must test; overheard fragments hint at hidden factions without a direct scene.
- [rule] Keep a turned insider inside their normal role so they keep the appearance of innocence and can keep helping. When: when the insider's cover is needed for later actions. Why: Visible involvement exposes the insider.
- [rule] Store observer notes as a log the player can review later, with each detail tagged for its later relevance. When: when designing observer records.
- [rule] Stage a lineup where an NPC notices one candidate among several placed unannounced, so the player sees a spontaneous reaction rather than a prompted answer. When: when designing an NPC identification moment. Why: unprompted reactions carry more information than answers given after prompting.
- [rule] Track what each NPC saw separately from what they heard, so the player can weigh the two kinds of evidence differently. When: when logging NPC knowledge of events. Why: sight and sound differ in reliability and detail.
- [rule] Give each NPC witness a knowledge limit, such as illiteracy or fear, that changes how they respond to a note or question. When: when designing NPCs who can testify or be influenced. Why: limits make responses believable and varied.
- [rule] Let players probe an NPC on a side topic to reach the desired information, and give the NPC motives that colour how they interpret the player's questions. When: When designing dialogue for a guarded or hostile NPC. Why: Indirect approaches and motive-coloured answers make the same question yield different responses from different NPCs.
- [rule] Let a quest-giving character react differently when questioned alone versus in front of others, so the player can infer which of their claims is false. When: When designing NPC dialogue that depends on social context. Why: Changing reactions by context gives the player a way to test claims.
- [rule] Give an informant NPC in a heightened mood partial reports with gaps, and let the player fill them by checking a document or another NPC. Why: Rewards careful cross-checking.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses traits such as heavy sleep or a faulty clock that players must factor into how much they trust each testimony.
- [rule] Model NPC recognition so a witness can identify the wrong person, and let the player pick a suspect from descriptions in a line-up. When: Designing identification mechanics for suspects in a game. Why: Wrong identifications create tension and force the player to test descriptions against evidence.
- [rule] Build each motive around a specific non-player character so players can test it. When: Designing motives for a murder-mystery scenario. Why: A motive tied to a concrete character can be checked by the player.
- [rule] Let a witness NPC recognize a player character while misremembering a name or place, and require the player to cross-check the claim against an in-world record. When: When designing recognition scenarios. Why: Misremembered details force verification through records.
- [rule] Let an NPC witness an argument and report its tone but not its content, leaving the player to find the subject elsewhere. When: Designing a witnessed event that carries a hidden subject. Why: Partial testimony prompts the player to investigate further.
- [rule] Place an NPC conversation the player can overhear from cover, and let its content change how the player approaches a later encounter.
- [rule] Move NPC dialogue through stages (guarded, pressured, conceding), unlocking information through raised stakes or by the player presenting a document. When: Designing NPC interrogation dialogue.
- [rule] Give NPC sightings time windows rather than exact times; overlapping windows create real alibi questions the player must resolve. When: when designing npc movement and alibis. Why: Overlap produces genuine ambiguity.
- [rule] Track what each NPC believes against the true world state, so that reassurances and claims can be checked by the player. When: an NPC's dialogue may be wrong or incomplete. Why: Comparing belief to truth turns NPC statements into testable information.
- [rule] Let an NPC voice certainty about what investigators can find, so the player can later contradict that statement. When: Writing NPC dialogue about detection. Why: A confident claim becomes a checkable statement that the player's findings can refute.
- [rule] Split an NPC's knowledge across several conversations, releasing the decisive fact only after the earlier clues have been collected.
- [rule] Let the player's questions about how an NPC knew something change what the player can deduce about that NPC's knowledge. When: When an NPC holds information that the player must trace. Why: The source of knowledge is itself evidence about the NPC's role.
- [rule] Attach knowledge flags to witnesses, such as knows the victim or has seen the face, that determine whether their testimony can rule out a suspect. When: Implementing witness systems in games. Why: Keeps testimony logic tied to what each character could plausibly know.
- [heuristic] Treat an insider's reports as leads, weighing them against loyalty, fear and resentment, since bribery, persuasion or spite can bias what they say. When: When relying on reports or gossip from an insider or servant. Why: Insider motives can bias what is reported; informants' claims are often partly motivated by spite.
- [heuristic] An anonymous threat citing private details few people knew, especially one sent before officers arrive, implies inside knowledge and foreknowledge, pointing toward the sender's identity. When: writing or analysing an anonymous threat. Why: Only someone close to the target could know those details; private details imply access and timing.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs conflicting accounts and tag testimony with its bias, so players weigh each speaker's access and motive; a grieving or hostile speaker's account is marked partly unreliable. When: Designing interview, investigation or NPC statement content. Why: Weighing sources turns dialogue into a reasoning task; visible bias lets players discount partial accounts.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC a confident claim that is wrong or only partly right, so the player must test it against other evidence and is rewarded for checking. When: Writing dialogue where an NPC's explanation or secret knowledge is wrong or partly right. Why: A believable but mistaken account turns the player into an investigator rather than a passive reader.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs timed routines and timestamped sightings the player can cross-check across witnesses, building an alibi window and clearing a suspect whose account holds across several NPCs. When: when designing NPC schedules for a mystery. Why: Cross-checked timestamps make elimination fair and checkable.
- [heuristic] An insider's notes can be valuable as a factual record while their judgment is unreliable, if the insider was carried away by the same belief. When: reconstructing events from one participant's account. Why: Participation biases interpretation even when observations are accurate.
- [heuristic] When a lock is opened without forced entry, suspect an insider with legitimate access rather than a burglar. When: When a secured container is opened with no sign of damage. Why: An unbroken lock suggests the opener had the proper credentials.
- [heuristic] Quoting a phrase that only someone with the relevant knowledge would use can make a clerk cooperate. When: When a gatekeeper controls access and the player can learn an insider phrase. Why: Recognising insider knowledge reduces the clerk's suspicion of the requester.
- [heuristic] A friendly NPC who volunteers damaging information about another character adds tension and reshapes how their group is understood.
- [heuristic] A narrator who experienced the events and draws on that experience gives a reveal authority, because the audience can check the account against facts they have seen. When: when a reveal depends on one character's knowledge. Why: checkable firsthand detail builds trust in the solution.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC know something about an object before the player mentions it, so that knowledge becomes a lead for the player.
- [heuristic] Place a chain of guards, ferrymen or innkeepers who each log a fleeing enemy's clothing, pace or possessions, and use distinctive details such as a paid toll or dropped bag to make the trail checkable. When: When designing a pursuit or tracking sequence without a map marker. Why: Distinct details let the player reconstruct the route from dialogue alone.
- [heuristic] Gate some clues by language or background so only certain characters can understand them, turning the difference into a deduction. When: Designing NPC dialogue or glyph clues. Why: Knowledge gaps give players an inference to make.
- [heuristic] Pair a limited light source with a short fuel timer, so brief flashes reveal the room layout in intervals. When: designing dark exploration areas. Why: Timed light forces the player to build a mental map from partial views.
- [heuristic] Lighting, weather and sound can amplify a reveal, such as opening a hidden chamber during a storm at night. When: Placing a hidden area or secret reveal in generated content. Why: Environmental conditions heighten the emotional impact of the discovery.
- [heuristic] A non-player character who starts a sentence and stops can mark a hidden room, item or fact that a later event reveals. When: Placing secrets for players to discover. Why: Interrupted dialogue signals hidden content without giving it away.
- [heuristic] Record which non-player characters know about a hidden treasure, so the player's suspect list is limited to those who know. When: Designing a mystery where the treasure's location is secret. Why: Knowledge tracking narrows the suspect pool.
- [heuristic] Let dialogue overheard during ordinary movement carry a hint whose meaning resolves only after a later event tests it.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC approximate, somewhat generic details, and let a second source narrow them down to a specific identity.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs small tells, such as a glance toward a companion, and time reactions to a known figure's arrival, so players can detect suspicion without dialogue. When: designing non-verbal cues for suspicion. Why: visual tells reward players who watch characters rather than objects.
- [procedure] 1) Estimate the risk the insider takes. 2) Offer compensation matched to that risk. 3) Give a written guarantee of safety and protection. 4) Schedule contact around the target's routine, away from observation. When: when you need an insider to control access or a record. Why: Money, guarantees and safety address the insider's personal risk.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a question only an insider would know. 2) Withhold the expected answer. 3) Reveal it and watch for a reaction that betrays prior knowledge. When: Checking whether an evasive suspect actually has insider knowledge.
- [pitfall] Suspecting insiders with access to a captive or record on presentiment alone, without proof, misdirects inquiry, diverting effort and weakening colleagues' trust in the investigation. When: A leak or sabotage is suspected inside an investigating organisation, or an investigation turns toward internal suspects without proof. Why: Rivalry and access create plausible motive that pulls attention from evidence; unverified accusations divert effort and weaken confidence.
- [pitfall] Trusting an insider's account as neutral observation is a mistake when the account is itself part of the campaign it describes.
- [pitfall] An insider premise can exclude outsiders too early and shape every later question, so keep an outside accomplice open as a possibility.
- [pitfall] A naive map overcounts witnesses; foliage or other obstructions can leave only one window with a usable view.

## concealment as guilt
- [mechanism] A hidden occupant can persist when part of a building is rarely visited, few staff remain, and one keyholder controls access. When: A hidden person or item is kept in a sealed area. Why: Absence of witnesses removes the chance of discovery.
- [mechanism] Each concealment limits the information available to the character kept out, and the pattern of hidden facts creates suspicion.
- [mechanism] A planted clue can expose the plant itself: a second observer who saw the handoff can later reveal the frame, giving the player a path to the truth. When: A false clue must eventually lead to the true culprit. Why: The witness's knowledge of the handoff is a checkable trail back to the planter.
- [mechanism] Hiding the real victim inside an ordinary-looking object, while staging a separate false victim, misdirects investigators toward the wrong suspects. When: when a story needs a concealment that looks like a different crime. Why: the false victim points to a suspect the truth does not implicate.
- [behavior] Characters withhold news from someone when they judge it would distress or endanger that person, and this concealment shapes what that person can know and do. When: The news would cause distress or put the person at risk, or a character's health or safety is cited as the reason for hiding information. Why: Protection is the usual motive for keeping someone uninformed, which makes concealment look kind.
- [behavior] A witness protecting someone may speak of them in general terms, omit how the witness was affected, or give misleading details without intent to deceive. When: A witness's account is smooth but a physical sign suggests another story, or a witness describes a scene involving someone they wish to shield. Why: Protective motives lead witnesses to soften, omit or distort facts.
- [behavior] A suspect who covers for or withholds from someone may be shielding another person, and that protective behaviour can reveal who is being shielded. When: A suspect acts to cover for someone or withholds a secret. Why: Protection reveals a relationship or secret.
- [behavior] Witnesses may agree to withhold information about someone they judge already in trouble, sparing that person further harm. Why: they believe the person is already in enough trouble.
- [behavior] A witness may lie about one fact to protect someone they care about while telling the truth about everything else. When: the witness has a close tie to the person being shielded. Why: loyalty can outweigh the wish to be fully candid.
- [behavior] A witness may withhold what they know to protect another person, showing hesitation, a shift in attitude when that person is named, and resistance to questions about them alone. When: A witness cooperates generally but resists questioning about one specific target. Why: Fear for another person drives the refusal, not necessarily involvement in the event.
- [behavior] A clumsy concealment, such as an obviously missing leaf, can reveal the concealer's unease as much as the gap itself. When: when someone alters a record carelessly. Why: crude edits are easy to notice and expose anxiety.
- [behavior] A person hiding their presence tends to avoid others by leaving late and returning quickly, so timing details can reveal concealment. When: a suspect avoids contact with the victim. Why: Avoiding contact favours late departure and quick return.
- [behavior] Destroying or hiding an object is itself evidence, because it signals a deliberate effort to conceal something. When: A suspect disposes of an item such as clothing. Why: Concealment acts are deliberate and so reveal intent.
- [rule] Show key facts fairly and do not hide them so long that the audience loses trust; a delayed reveal otherwise reads as concealment rather than suspense.
- [rule] Hide a finding from suspects only until it can be tested; evidence others must verify should stay open. Why: Openly shown evidence can be checked by everyone.
- [rule] Design a non-player character's protective secret so it unlocks only when the player presents a specific piece of evidence. When: Building a game where an NPC withholds information. Why: Gating the reveal on evidence rewards investigation over questioning alone.
- [rule] Let written notes and letters from NPCs be deceptive, and reward players who test them against in-person behaviour. When: when designing NPC documents as clues. Why: Written text can mislead, so checking it against observed behaviour gives players a meaningful test.
- [heuristic] Characters may withhold a secret to protect third parties, and the suppression reads as fair when they agree on it and state their reasons.
- [heuristic] Ground every hidden-reveal method in the game's fiction; a reveal left unexplained erodes player trust.
- [heuristic] A person planning to return tends to avoid arrangements, such as a check-in call, that would expose their absence. When: a person is hiding a temporary absence. Why: such arrangements would reveal the lie.
- [heuristic] An item kept out of its normal place, such as clothing hidden between trunks rather than hung up, suggests concealment.
- [heuristic] Judge a captor's deception separately from any ill-treatment of the captive, because the two may not go together. When: Assessing a concealing keeper's conduct. Why: Hiding someone does not prove harm was done to them.
- [heuristic] A speaker who risks a lie that is easily disproven may be protecting someone.
- [heuristic] A staged incident that looks clumsy and does little damage may be an attempt to place a weapon within reach. When: when an incident seems unimportant. Why: the apparent failure may hide an intention to prepare the scene.
- [heuristic] When physical evidence is ambiguous, decide which account is false by weighing every witness account against the others.
- [heuristic] Test whether a claimed deception is needed for the act it supposedly explains; if a simpler statement would have sufficed, the deception does not explain the act.
- [heuristic] A request that is urgent, routine-looking and hurried can signal that something is being hidden.
- [heuristic] Even when an account is disproved, ask whether the suspect still has something to conceal before closing the line of inquiry.
- [heuristic] Treat every statement from someone intent on deception as something to check, since such a person may tell far more falsehoods than truths. When: a suspect is actively lying. Why: lies are mixed into accounts and cannot be assumed from tone.
- [heuristic] Tie a false confession to a protective motive so the confessor can become an ally who helps the player uncover the truth later. When: designing non-player character confessions. Why: Protective motives make a false statement sympathetic rather than merely deceptive.
- [heuristic] A small flat object can be concealed in a container's lining, but a bulky solid object cannot, so concealment capacity narrows the candidates. When: Judging what a container could have held. Why: Physical size and shape limit what fits.
- [heuristic] A remote, shut-in site makes little sense for public display, while a bare, elevated site fits display; the terrain suggests the intent behind a site's use. When: Inferring why a site was chosen for an event. Why: Concealment and display call for different landscapes.
- [heuristic] When a culprit seems clumsy and the evidence looks damning, investigators should be most on guard against error.
- [heuristic] Features that look like hiding places or escape routes may not function as such; test whether a spot has an exit before reading it as concealment. When: A location seems suited to hiding or escape. Why: A spot with no exit cannot serve as a route for someone leaving.
- [procedure] 1) Release a provocative or false item to a group. 2) Observe who reacts. 3) Note who shows no expected reaction. 4) Follow up with the reacting and non-reacting parties. When: A guarded party may conceal a fact touched by the item. Why: Concealing parties tend to react to a lure that threatens their secret.
- [procedure] 1) List each candidate hiding place. 2) Check whether the act could physically happen there. 3) Check who had sightlines to it. 4) Check when traffic was low. 5) Discard candidates that fail any check. When: When a body or object must have moved through an observed space and observers' schedules are known. Why: Each candidate must be tested against physical, visual and timing constraints to find which account remains possible.
- [tradeoff] A false cover story gains access and information, while an honest approach keeps the target's trust; the lie carries a moral cost. When: choosing how to approach a suspect.
- [pitfall] Concealment is a reason for suspicion, not proof of guilt; innocent motives such as loyalty, fear of exposure or of a worse outcome, or shielding someone also produce it. When: A witness or suspect hides information or disguises actions. Why: Protective silence and guilty silence look alike, and cover-ups can protect the innocent as well as the guilty.
- [pitfall] Do not assume a staged scene is clumsy or that every culprit hides clues shrewdly; a careful hand may arrange a scene, and real concealers may act carelessly. When: Predicting how a culprit hid a clue or judging whether a staged scene is clumsy. Why: Careful staging and careless concealment both occur, and real concealers may act on different assumptions.
- [pitfall] A witness who hides facts out of kindness can look like a suspect, so the motive for concealment must stay visible to the player.
- [pitfall] Treating a staged absence as proof of the act it conceals confuses concealment with the act itself. When: when a disguise or false alibi is found. Why: Concealing an event does not establish what the event was.
- [pitfall] Deception used to extract information can damage trust if it is discovered later.
- [pitfall] A deceiver's remorse can return mid-scene and make the staged performance falter.
- [pitfall] Framing an act as protecting someone's reputation can disarm questions about why it was done, so trusting listeners may accept it unexamined.
- [pitfall] Helpers who seem trustworthy may be the culprits, so their accounts should be checked against other evidence.
- [pitfall] A locked door, a dropped object, or a single passing witness can undo a concealment scheme. When: Relying on hidden evidence to avoid discovery. Why: Concealment depends on chance factors outside the culprit's control.
- [pitfall] Deliberate concealment can be mistaken for ordinary eccentricity when the evidence is not weighed carefully.
- [pitfall] Overheard plans may include deliberate false leads aimed at investigators, so verify them before acting on them.
- [pitfall] Discarding a credible witness to protect a theory is a common mistake; the error often lies in the model the theory was built on.
- [pitfall] A staged scene reads as a deliberate story, so a doubtful investigator can find the detail that is too neat and reopen the case.
- [pitfall] A natural-looking pose may be arranged, so appearance alone does not settle whether a scene is genuine. When: A scene looks ordinary or relaxed. Why: Staging can imitate normal appearance.
- [pitfall] A confession that protects another person can look credible because it sounds noble, which can mislead investigators. When: A confessor appears to sacrifice themselves for someone else. Why: Selfless framing makes the confession seem more trustworthy.
- [pitfall] Naming a clue can warn the culprit that investigators are closer, so weigh the risk to any witness before revealing it.
- [fact] A poison delivered by needle leaves only a small puncture, which a routine post-mortem may not notice.
- [fact] Gloves, cloth and felt are the usual ways to avoid leaving fingerprints at a scene.

## expert authority
- [definition] A qualified denial answers only the literal question asked, so it can be true while still leaving a false impression. When: A suspect's statement is narrow or carefully worded. Why: Literal truth and misleading implication can coexist when the question is narrow.
- [mechanism] An adviser who repeatedly tells a witness they need not answer takes over the pace of the exchange and blocks further questioning.
- [mechanism] Advice given to a subject can directly change her next action, so an answer to a hypothetical question can trigger the behavior the questioner then observes.
- [mechanism] A game can represent symptoms and time of death as ranges, so the player learns to reason from uncertainty. When: Designing a forensic or medical clue. Why: Ranges reflect real uncertainty and reward careful reasoning over guessing.
- [mechanism] A mystery's misdirect can be placed in an expert's own explanation, so the audience's trust in the expert becomes the obstacle to the truth. When: Designing a misleading explanation in a mystery. Why: Expert credibility makes the mathematical or technical explanation feel conclusive.
- [behavior] Listeners who accept a confident expert's theory become less likely to question it, so a wrong theory can hold a whole group's attention. When: an authority presents a plausible but untested account. Why: trust in expertise lowers scrutiny.
- [behavior] A player who knows how a craft is normally done can spot a prop that contradicts a character's stated activity, rewarding expertise. When: a player has domain knowledge of the activity. Why: recognising the normal way exposes the wrong detail.
- [behavior] Formal procedure, such as assigned roles and a majority vote, can lend a weak accusation credibility it has not earned. When: a red herring is presented in a structured forum. Why: the form of a trial signals rigour regardless of the case's quality.
- [behavior] Judges and audiences often defer to a prestigious expert's word on a disputed matter, so the expert's reputation can settle a verdict without adding evidence about the case. When: when an expert testifies to facts in dispute. Why: status is mistaken for proof of the particular claim.
- [behavior] A belief endorsed by judges and learned figures as well as ordinary people is hard for any single observer to question. When: when a doctrine has institutional and popular support. Why: broad sanction makes dissent appear unreasonable.
- [behavior] A confident interpretation from a respected authority can end an investigation early, so people stop testing a sighting once it is declared a message. When: A public figure endorses a supernatural reading of an event. Why: Trust in the authority replaces further checking.
- [behavior] Experts' confident identifications can be wrong, and their doubtful picks may lean the same wrong way, so confidence does not guarantee accuracy. When: experts identify genuine versus counterfeit items. Why: Observed in a controlled sorting trial.
- [rule] Require a second, independent source before adopting one expert's conclusion or approval; expert opinion alone may fail to secure a verdict and enthusiasm can override judgment. When: When expert opinion is offered as the main support for a case. Why: Expert testimony may not outweigh the rest of the proceeding; enthusiasm can override careful judgment. (x2)
- [rule] Do not treat an expert's confident conclusion on timing or cause as proof; test it against the timeline and the evidence it rests on, since confidence is separate from accuracy. When: When an expert gives a firm opinion on timing or cause, or when an expert's timeline supports a conclusion. Why: Confidence does not establish the facts, and experts can be confidently wrong.
- [rule] Use a specialist's findings to test your theory rather than replace it; test a preliminary expert account of cause, shot count, weapon or time window against your own observations first. Why: Preliminary accounts can be incomplete or wrong.
- [rule] Let an expert's questions follow physical evidence, asking about approach, speed and origin rather than repeating the witness's account; questioning the wrong witnesses misses key facts. When: When judging an expert's investigation or framing its questions.
- [rule] State the margin of error when reporting an expert's estimate, since such estimates are often given with more confidence than they deserve. When: reporting expert reconstructions. Why: Overconfident estimates can mislead later reasoning.
- [rule] Do not let an expert's verdict settle a dispute unless the reasoning behind it is shown. When: Accepting a specialist's conclusion. Why: An unexplained verdict can hide errors.
- [rule] Have a person who knows an object identify it, and record the confidence of each identification. When: An object must be tied to a person or place. Why: Familiarity makes identification more reliable, and confidence shows how much weight it deserves.
- [rule] Tag qualifying phrases in dialogue as clue flags that link to another character's statement, and trigger a follow-up when the player notices a mismatch. When: Designing dialogue systems that carry implicit information. Why: Linking hedges to other statements lets the player discover implications through comparison.
