- [procedure] 1) Write a few plain sentences of what is known. 2) Ask what was actually seen and heard. 3) Turn that into one concrete question to pursue next. When: when theories multiply without evidence. Why: plain statements restore a practical view.
- [procedure] 1) List each timed event with its source. 2) Check each clock's reliability. 3) Anchor on the most precise time. 4) Test other events against it. 5) Confirm the full sequence fits one consistent order. When: when several witnesses and devices give times.
- [procedure] 1) List who was present at each time. 2) Match each claim to that timeline. 3) Weigh a secondhand repetition below a first-hand account unless it is independently confirmed. When: when one claim is repeated secondhand and conflicts with a first-hand account.
- [procedure] 1) Pair former rivals in shared tasks. 2) Formally revoke verdicts that still stand in the official books. 3) Prepare the group before the vote. 4) Lead the question rather than waiting for public pressure. When: a group must keep working together after a bitter internal conflict. Why: Shared work builds cooperation, and formal revocation corrects the record that outlasts the conflict.
- [tradeoff] Checking every factor thoroughly costs time that could go to the central question, so weigh each check against its likely value. When: Deciding how far to verify minor facts. Why: Investigative time is limited.
- [pitfall] A single slip or contradiction is a lead to test, not proof: it can point at the wrong person, and reading too much into one word sends investigations astray. When: When a witness's phrasing seems to betray knowledge. Why: One word rarely carries enough weight to establish guilt or knowledge.
- [pitfall] Assuming a culprit must be clever enough to prepare cover can lead investigators to read an honest person's gap as innocence or dismiss it entirely. When: judging a suspect with no alibi. Why: The assumption about cleverness drives the reading of the gap.
- [pitfall] A frame can be undone by one detail the planner did not foresee. Small overlooked items often expose the staging. Why: a planner cannot control every detail the accused might carry.
- [pitfall] The same checklist can fit more than one person, so a fully matched list alone does not single out a suspect. When: When several people share similar circumstances. Why: Shared opportunity and motive can fill the same entries.
- [pitfall] Two sincere witnesses can disagree about the same conversation, and choosing the version that fits a theory can distort the record. When: when witness accounts of one event conflict. Why: sincerity does not guarantee accurate recall, and selection bias can enter the evidence.
- [fact] A game can seed an improbable lead that pays off as side information, rewarding players who try unusual routes. When: Designing optional clues or routes in a game. Why: Unusual routes that yield information reward exploration.

## identity claims
- [model] A manufactured-identity mystery chains identity proofs, each partly wrong; the answer emerges only when the proofs are reconciled and their conflicts explained. When: designing a mystery whose hidden character must be identified from clues. Why: Single proofs mislead, so the solution depends on how the whole chain fits together.
- [mechanism] Visible sentiment toward one person can mask a concealed purpose aimed at another person.
- [mechanism] An identification puzzle can use several NPCs who partly match a description, with a distinctive mark as the decisive clue. When: designing a character-identification puzzle. Why: partial matches create ambiguity that a single clue resolves.
- [behavior] A character who jokes about being suspected can make suspicion seem harmless, and the joke draws attention away from the real trail until evidence arrives. When: A character volunteers a damning-seeming motive or suspicion early in a mystery. Why: A light tone lowers the audience's guard against a remark that may later be taken seriously.
- [rule] Do not accept an alibi resting only on the suspect's own word, servants or fellow group members, since they may be complicit; track which parts independent others corroborate. When: Evaluating a suspect's whereabouts or alibi. Why: Self-report and interested parties are not independent verification.
- [rule] Hide an identifying mark under clothing so the player must expose it, for example by rolling up a sleeve, to verify identity.
- [rule] Mark one visual feature on a hostile figure so that a later encounter can be matched to an earlier sighting.
- [rule] Do not decide whether a person is alive or dead from appearance alone, since deep sleep and death can look alike. When: When a person is motionless and still. Why: Visual signs overlap between unconsciousness and death.
- [rule] Build identification puzzles so the player must consider the alternative hypothesis, that two appearances are the same person, before the trick becomes visible. When: designing a puzzle that hinges on recognizing someone. Why: the player must weigh both possibilities before the answer is clear.
- [rule] Answer whether two traces share a source separately from whether two cases are linked. Why: A matching pair of traces can settle one question while leaving the other open.
- [rule] Let item details such as monograms, shades and key types encode an owner's name and habits, so players can deduce identity and eliminate non-matching suspects. When: Designing mystery-item puzzles.
- [heuristic] When a witness disclaims their own accuracy, weigh each detail separately: they may be right on key points, while blamed conditions can hide gaps or be self-serving evasions. When: A witness's account matters for later reasoning and the witness has disclaimed their own accuracy. Why: Explicit disclaimers signal observations made in a compromised state; self-disclaimers can be partial truths or evasions.
- [heuristic] Appearance-based first impressions are only hints to test against later facts; they distort judgment, especially when signs contradict each other.
- [heuristic] When appearance conflicts with behavior or a stated claim, weigh both signals and record the conflict; neither alone decides, and the conflict is itself informative. When: A suspect's look conflicts with their behavior or what they say about themselves. Why: Either signal alone can mislead, and their conflict is itself informative.
- [heuristic] Appearance, clothing, footwear and manner poorly indicate guilt or social rank; respectable, pious people have committed murders, and observers may misread who holds authority. When: When judging suspects or ranks by how they look or act. Why: Culprits who seem ordinary force players to rely on clues rather than instinct.
- [heuristic] Appearance reveals recent activity: loosened clothing or ongoing activity suggests how long someone has been in a place, while clean, mud-free clothing suggests they stayed indoors. When: Inferring a person's recent movements or time in a place. Why: Dirt and wear accumulate from outdoor activity.
- [heuristic] Treat a character's claim of skill, past events or relationships as untested until it is checked against something observable. When: the claim matters to the plot. Why: self-reported accounts may be biased or mistaken.
- [heuristic] If a supposed force would act the same way elsewhere, a limit tied to one location is a weak point in the claim. When: when evaluating a supernatural claim.
- [heuristic] A physical trace, such as a ticket stub, that does not fit the described appearance of the occupant points to a different person.
- [heuristic] Each check confirms that someone did what a story claims, not that the central subject is who they seem to be.
- [heuristic] A harmonious portrait can hide one jarring detail, which may be the thread worth examining. When: A victim or subject is described as uniformly admirable.
- [heuristic] A colour mismatch can look like a dead end; inspect the disguised area up close, because older marks may show faintly through the new layer. When: a disguise seems to fail at first glance. Why: thin or uneven coats let earlier layers show through.
- [heuristic] A neat, self-supplied alibi can be deliberate: a careful culprit planning for safety would arrange exactly that kind of paperwork.
- [heuristic] Show a witness's own disclaimer in dialogue to warn the player that the testimony is incomplete. When: An NPC witness has a known condition affecting their testimony. Why: Transparent warnings give the player fair notice of unreliability.
- [heuristic] An item chosen to match a target's known preference suggests the actor knew that target's habits.
- [procedure] 1) Plant an object suggesting a habit. 2) Add a second object that confirms or refutes it. 3) Require that verification before the player names a suspect; checkable habits, such as never wearing a ring, can rule an NPC out. Why: Keeps player inference checkable.
- [procedure] 1) Check the history of any named reference person. 2) Query contacts abroad where the claim places the subject. 3) Circulate the subject's photograph to many authorities. When: a suspect's claimed identity cannot be confirmed directly.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the cryptic signature or alias. 2) List sources the suspect may have read, such as plays, histories or cultural texts. 3) Search them for the term. 4) Keep a match only if it ties to the people and facts. When: a signature or alias has several possible meanings. Why: a source the culprit drew on can narrow the meaning.
- [procedure] 1) List identifiers to collect: name, address, occupation, marital status, family, and links to third parties. 2) Collect physical description and habits from witnesses. 3) Check each candidate against records. 4) Reconstruct meetings using event records like guest lists. When: The only known link to a suspect is a face, voice or name. Why: Memory alone is vague, and records fill the gaps.
- [procedure] 1) Compare shared generic traits such as hair, skin and build first. 2) Compare distinctive marks such as scars against the body. 3) Compare objects that touch the body, such as rings and locket hair. 4) Compare the same fingers and marks in both cases. When: When matching a body to a missing person. Why: Shared traits carry little weight alone, while distinctive marks and objects carry more.
- [tradeoff] Claiming authority you do not hold can win cooperation, but if the witness checks the claim, it can backfire and damage the case. When: when a volatile witness may refuse or retract.
- [tradeoff] A council chosen by one party rules only on the evidence that party supplies, whereas a jointly accepted body can issue a verdict both sides must respect.
- [pitfall] A suspect's self-description or bold self-declaration is not evidence: a profile built from their own opinions restates them, self-assessment echoes praise, and admiration does not confirm the claim. (x2)
- [pitfall] A witness's claim of sanity or wellness does not prove accurate perception, and may make them least reliable about own actions; impairment can affect one task while another seems fine. (x2)
- [pitfall] A witness's or narrator's claim of candour or fairness is an assertion to test against conduct; volunteering damaging facts can be impression management, not proof of sincerity. Why: Stated fairness is easy to assert and can earn undeserved trust; confession alone does not establish sincerity.
- [pitfall] Judging a witness's credibility by clothing, status, accent or nervousness biases the account's reception; appearance should not decide truth, and sympathetic readings stay unverified until checked. When: Assessing a witness's credibility, especially a low-status witness giving an account to an official or court. Why: Appearance is judged before the account is heard.
- [pitfall] Records under another person's name mislead investigators who check only the suspect's name; a name missing from one record but present in a related one may reveal an alias. When: A suspect may travel or register under an alias. Why: The person may have used another name in that record.
- [pitfall] A search can find nothing and still be incomplete. A scene can look clean to the person who made it, so a concealer's confidence is not evidence.
- [pitfall] Do not treat a name or origin given at registration as verified; it may be false and may give no address.
- [pitfall] Judging a stain by appearance alone can mislead; confirm what a fluid is with microscopic or chemical testing.
- [pitfall] A witness who admits their own anger may still be shielding someone, so the bystanders' accounts must be checked against theirs. When: when a witness is a participant in a quarrel. Why: self-criticism can make an account more credible while still concealing facts.
- [pitfall] Judging age by appearance alone can be wrong by years, so check the estimate against other dated facts.
- [pitfall] A false name can be exposed when it is linked to the investigator's real business or address, so the alias must be kept apart from those links.
- [pitfall] A confessed bad motive, such as being blackmailed, can redirect suspicion onto others, so it should be weighed carefully. When: Suspect admits a motive while denying the act. Why: An admitted motive shifts blame elsewhere.
- [pitfall] A self-declared expert whose accusations keep multiplying can damage a whole region until exposed as a fraud.
- [pitfall] Naming the attacker from the side of a wound alone is a mistake, because the same wound angle can fit more than one person. Why: position narrows suspects but does not single one out.
- [pitfall] Identifying a substance does not prove who used it or when. A separate step is needed to establish administration. When: a test confirms what something is. Why: a positive test shows possession, not the act or its timing.
- [fact] A changed appearance, such as a new shave or disguise, cannot confirm identity, and a sighting proves nothing when an unseen agent could copy that appearance. (x2)
- [fact] Changing visible appearance, such as clothing or footwear, hides a traveler from pursuers who identify people by face or dress.
- [fact] Physical strength and appearance can diverge, so delicate build or movement does not reliably show weakness.
- [fact] Different records may give one building different names, including a common term for dwellings of the period, so a differing name does not necessarily mean a different place. When: Matching records about a building. Why: Naming conventions vary across records.

## legend and rumour
- [mechanism] Legends spread through talk among neighbors and grow with each telling, so the most repeated version often drifts from the original.
- [mechanism] A folk legend or natural cause can hide a human agent by placing a death outside human hands, such as blaming fright or a weak heart. When: a death is attributed to a supernatural or natural cause. Why: A cause beyond human reach discourages further investigation.
- [mechanism] A culprit who learns a local legend can stage a death to match it, so the crime looks supernatural and investigators are steered away from a human agent. When: a local legend is known to the culprit. Why: A supernatural frame directs suspicion away from people.
- [mechanism] A local ghost legend can absorb unexplained events, so a household ready to blame the uncanny stops looking for physical causes. When: unexplained events occur in a place with a ghost legend. Why: the legend supplies a ready explanation that ends investigation.
- [mechanism] Model a rumour as a message that gains or loses detail as NPCs repeat it, letting the player trace its origin.
- [behavior] Ambiguous remains found in a secluded place can prompt townsfolk to form a foul-play theory that is repeated as hearsay without proof. When: remains are partial and mixed with unrelated debris. Why: partial evidence invites a dramatic story that gossip spreads without checking.
- [behavior] Rumour about an investigator's competence shapes how everyone reads the evidence, so the investigator's reputation can become the weakest point of the case. When: Rumours question an investigator's judgment. Why: Colleagues interpret evidence through their view of the investigator.
- [behavior] People may reject a legend's literal claims yet privately accept its moral, such as crime bringing its own punishment. When: when a folk story offers a moral explanation. Why: a moral frame can feel satisfying without evidence.
- [rule] Let players check a retold rumour against a physical or primary record that confirms or contradicts it. When: when designing NPC gossip and clues. Why: Retellings can mutate as they pass between people. (x2)
- [rule] Tag each rumour retelling, and claims from unreliable NPCs, with a confidence level so players weigh them before other evidence confirms them. When: when designing rumour propagation. (x2)
- [rule] Present rumours as partial observations from several tellers who each add opinion, so players compare accounts and sort fact from framing. When: Designing rumours in narrative or dungeon generation, or news passing between residents of a small community. Why: Each teller frames the story with personal views. (x2)
- [rule] Label secondhand NPC reports as rumour, opinion or verified fact, keeping direct witness testimony distinct, since rumour lacks direct basis and can mislead the timeline. When: designing dialogue about a suspect, or gathering witness accounts. Why: Labels let players judge reliability without a separate check.
- [rule] Use a rumour to open a lead on where to search or whom to question, but resolve it only with a verifiable clue, never as grounds for an accusation. Why: Rumors start inquiries, while verifiable clues close them.
- [rule] Let a legend be partly true and partly embellished, with relayed details shifted, so players must check each retelling against physical evidence in the world. When: Designing a rumour or legend within a game world; designing npc gossip. Why: A mixed legend rewards checking claims against evidence rather than accepting or rejecting it outright.
- [rule] Label journal entries as rumour or fact so players know which leads still need verifying. When: designing player journals or logs. Why: Clear labels keep unverified information from being treated as settled.
- [rule] Let an unreliable NPC reveal a real fact in distorted form, so players must cross-check the claim against the environment.
- [rule] Let a legend predict signs that vanish under close inspection, rewarding players who check facts over folklore.
- [rule] Test a supposed supernatural threat with a physical test, such as wounding it, that shows whether it is mortal and therefore an ordinary creature. When: a supernatural explanation is proposed. Why: A mortal result removes the supernatural premise.
- [rule] Take an unusual witness report seriously, but look for the mechanism that could produce it before accepting the supernatural explanation. When: When a witness reports an apparently impossible event. Why: Most unusual reports have a physical cause that can be identified.
- [rule] Give a haunted sound a findable physical cause and a documented source, so the legend stays testable hearsay rather than unexplained lore. When: Designing a local supernatural legend. Why: Players can then check the claim against the location.
- [heuristic] Treat rumour as testimony with a source: ask who repeats it and weigh each strand by its source, keeping physical traces separate from sighting claims. (x2)
- [heuristic] Treat a local legend as framing rather than fact; a legend tied to an object adds weight without proving it, so check claims against records. When: when a folk story is tied to a case. (x2)
- [heuristic] Let the player correct a rumour by reaching the first-hand witness, who holds the original version of events.
- [heuristic] Tie a rumour's reliability to the speaker's relationship with its subject, so biased speakers yield less reliable information. When: Designing or evaluating rumours in a game. Why: A speaker with a stake distorts what they pass on.
- [heuristic] Check a witness NPC's account against a time-stamped log so players can catch a rumour that contradicts an eyewitness.
- [heuristic] Test a legend's internal logic against the setting, such as whether a claimed haunting fits the place where the claimed crime happened.
- [heuristic] Test an inherited explanation against the physical form of the site it describes; layers, sizes, and positions that contradict it weaken the explanation. When: A received account conflicts with what can be seen of a site or object. Why: Physical arrangement is evidence about how a site was made.
- [heuristic] Require a rumour to be confirmed by two sources before it is trusted, so players cross-check claims rather than accepting one. When: Designing rumour systems.
- [heuristic] When separate accounts do not fit together in sequence, assume the joints were distorted, with each person telling either less or more than they know. When: Several people give separate chronological accounts. Why: Mismatched sequences more often signal selective telling than simple confusion.
- [heuristic] Separate rumour and suspicion from positive evidence when judging a case, since many facts can be read in two ways.
- [heuristic] Trace whether a legend has a documented origin or only repeated tellings before accepting its supernatural claim. When: A local tradition claims a supernatural witness.
- [heuristic] Later embellishments of a story are weaker evidence than the core elements that every retelling keeps.
- [heuristic] A local legend can encode a rule about what a sign means before the event occurs, so it should be checked rather than dismissed. When: When a folk tale describes a signal or trap behavior. Why: Legends often carry usable information about how a phenomenon works.
- [procedure] 1) Record the original witness of an event. 2) Log each person who relays it and count the hops. 3) Note the details each hop added or removed. When: Designing or tracking a gossip or rumour system.
- [procedure] 1) List each claim with its source. 2) Separate physical traces from sightings. 3) Check each trace against the record and the actual scene. 4) Tag each claim by how well it is supported. When: when rumours must be tested before they are used. Why: Vivid rumours can pass as fact without checking.
- [pitfall] Rumour repeated in talk or print passes as fact; accept it as evidence only after weighing it, since dismissing it outright loses partial truths.
- [pitfall] Hearsay built on unverifiable perception, or early rumour, is no independent check on later testimony; stacked reports look like more evidence, and stages may be driven by fear or grudge.
- [pitfall] Eager witnesses and well-meaning gossips, wanting to help or love talk, may add detail never observed, so each report needs checking. Why: Desire to help can produce invented detail.
- [pitfall] Local legends may be exaggerated or distorted in retelling, so their details can mislead.
- [pitfall] A bystander's remark is not itself a timeline and needs checking against fixed times before it can support a conclusion. When: A witness offers an informal observation as evidence of timing. Why: Remarks lack fixed reference points and can be wrong.
- [pitfall] Treating a rumour as proof, or assuming a secret is unknown because the people involved never spoke of it, leads to false conclusions.
- [pitfall] A vivid, detailed description can make a rumor feel verified when later tellers added the detail.
- [pitfall] A legend offers a ready explanation that can stand in for evidence, and a frame that explains everything blocks testing of ordinary causes.
- [pitfall] Public accounts can credit the wrong people and misstate motives, so how a case is perceived can matter as much as what was done.
- [pitfall] Rumour can misdirect an audience and make it reject correct evidence, so it should create tension rather than settle the story's logic. When: Designing public opinion or gossip within a mystery. Why: Rumour is persuasive but unsupported, so it can outweigh facts that point the other way.
- [pitfall] Searching for hidden passages because of old stories wastes effort when the building has none. When: Investigating a sealed room. Why: Folklore replaces evidence about the building.
- [pitfall] A sign that matches a legend exactly is suspicious when the legend may have been constructed from the sign, so check which came first. When: a symbol seems to confirm a legend. Why: Stories are often shaped to fit existing signs, reversing the apparent evidence.
- [pitfall] Mixing legend and documented fact in the final account corrupts the conclusion.
- [pitfall] Calling a legend proven while presenting it as a theory that explains a pattern overstates what the evidence shows.
- [fact] Local legends can present unverifiable witness reports as proof of supernatural events, and such stories persist through repetition.
- [fact] A family belief in a curse may have grown out of a documented prophecy, and a later fictional curse may echo that belief, so cause and effect can run either way. When: Tracing how a legend and a recorded event relate. Why: Legends and records feed each other, so the order of influence is often unclear.

## reversal design
- [model] A reveal can overturn a prevailing belief with dated documents; it lands best when the contradicting texts are already in the reader's hands, needing only comparison. When: Designing a mystery where the truth is found in records rather than announced. Why: Documents let the reader reassess a settled belief without confrontation; self-discovery by comparison makes the reversal feel earned.
- [model] A reversal mystery leads the audience to a false solution, then exposes the true one through a physical fact that the false solution cannot satisfy. Pages to avoid this: the true culprit is hidden in plain sight as the apparent victim.
- [model] A polemical argument can work like a mystery: each rebuttal turns on documents whose dates, omissions and attributions reshape what the reader believes.
- [mechanism] A reveal that re-reads evidence already present, e.g. attacks recast as harm prevention or theft as planned fraud, makes every clue fit one consistent logic and feels always there. When: Evidence is already on the table and read one way, or a final explanation reinterprets a prior clue. Why: Reinterpretation changes the meaning of evidence the player has already seen. (x2)
- [mechanism] Reversing apparent culprit and victim, with the investigator as culprit, recasts earlier clues against a new suspect; a blackmailer-victim swap turns expected motive into its opposite. (x2)
- [mechanism] A late reveal that the apparent evidence was manufactured or the suspect was a scapegoat reverses earlier clues, recasting the accused as innocent and the scheme as deliberate. When: Fair-play structure has planted the clues the reversal depends on; apparent evidence is later shown manufactured. Why: Reinterpreting planted clues recasts the accused as innocent and the scheme as deliberate.
- [mechanism] A firm inference or witness's certain account can be overturned by an objective record or expert physical examination, forcing a fresh reading of earlier events. When: A witness account seemed certain, or an apparent cause is accepted. Why: An objective record or examination can outweigh a recollection.
- [mechanism] When a reveal clears the wrongly accused and exposes the real culprit, earlier suspicions are recast as errors and the investigator's trust in appearances breaks. When: at the close of a mystery. Why: Reversing the target of suspicion gives the ending lasting weight.
- [mechanism] A sudden reversal, such as a surprise visit or news item, can turn a stalled situation into a plan and shift the mood at once. When: when a quiet investigation has stalled. Why: Unexpected information breaks the waiting and gives characters a direction.
- [mechanism] A safeguard a character trusts can be reversed later, so the same condition that protected him removes his means of calling for help. When: a reversal turns an earlier reassurance into the cause of harm. Why: the condition that reassured also isolates the character.
- [mechanism] A second discovery that contradicts the working theory forces a reassessment and raises suspense.
- [mechanism] Reversing apparent roles, so those who seemed criminal prove to be agents, reframes the whole situation for the audience.
- [mechanism] A minor background character dismissed early can be revealed as a wanted culprit later, provided the early dismissal is shown as a judgment the player can revise. When: Planting a key suspect in a mystery. Why: A fair reveal depends on the earlier judgment being visible and open to revision.
- [mechanism] A case that first points toward the occult, then reverses that belief through a late cluster of physical evidence, keeps the player's assumptions active until the turn.
- [mechanism] One overlooked qualifying word in a settled document can reverse a claim the reader already accepted, once the document is checked against its exact wording. When: A property, ownership or rights claim has been treated as settled. Why: Readers trust a settled claim and rarely recheck its exact terms.
- [behavior] A suspect who turns questions back on the questioner may be deflecting rather than admitting anything.
- [behavior] After an apparent unmasking, continued threats show that the first explanation was incomplete and re-read earlier events. When: A threat seems resolved but signals continue. Why: The first explanation covered only part of the cause.
- [rule] Reverse a wrongful accusation at the end with a specific new clue proving innocence, using it to open a second suspect thread and close the innocent party's arc. When: Ending a story that clears a falsely accused character. Why: An evidenced clearing is credible and keeps the story moving. (x2)
- [rule] A late reversal is fair and credible only when its overturning clue appears earlier and explains, rather than replaces, clues already shown; unplanted reversals feel arbitrary and break trust. When: Planning a late twist or a turn to break a stalled investigation. Why: Readers accept only reversals they could have checked against earlier evidence.
- [rule] Plant setup before an empty reveal, such as misleading weight, a lost key or a forced lid, so the audience reads the emptiness as meaningful. When: Building a reversal. Why: Without setup the reversal has no weight.
- [rule] Plant the clue that supports a late reversal in the earlier narrative, and make the related character's absence visible, so the audience can recognise its significance. Why: a reversal relying on information the audience never had feels like a cheat.
- [rule] Recognizable enemy groups can be used for misdirection if their reveal is later reversed. When: When planning a late twist on a known enemy type. Why: Players trust familiar groups, so reversing them creates surprise.
- [rule] Reveal a wrongdoer's error late, since revealing it early removes the suspense the later reversal depends on.
- [rule] Reverse the perceived victim and culprit within one visual scene, so the audience's belief changes in a single moment. When: Staging a late twist that overturns the assumed threat. Why: One scene carrying both the body and the empty room forces an immediate re-reading of the whole situation.
- [rule] Stack two twists so the player resolves one belief and then discovers a second, more mundane belief underneath it.
- [rule] Build the reveal so it reverses the premise object, such as showing it never moved, so the search must look inward rather than outward.
- [heuristic] Treat a reversed order as a hypothesis to test: damage may follow its event, a method may follow an owned item; let it reorder which records to check first. When: Physical damage is read as evidence of how an entry happened, or an assumed sequence of decisions is taken for granted. Why: Damage can be produced either before or after the action, so the apparent order can be reversed.
- [heuristic] When one reading is plausible, check whether the reverse reading fits equally well; if a fragment's reverse holds only unrelated content, rule that side out. When: When one reading of an identity is plausible, or a fragment is printed on both sides. Why: Quickly rules out a candidate reading or source.
- [heuristic] After a reversal exposes a false accusation following an irreversible act, show its cost via petitions, compensation or public confession; the act cannot be undone. When: A reversal is revealed after the verdict is carried out. Why: Consequences make a reversal emotionally weighty rather than only informative; irreversibility increases the stakes of the lie.
- [heuristic] A sympathetic first impression can be reversed by a later, independent source, provided earlier cues such as fear and secrecy fit the new explanation. When: a character was presented as a victim. Why: Consistent early cues make a reversal feel earned rather than unfair.
- [heuristic] If access is unclear, check whether the victim was watched more closely than they watched others, which can reveal hidden access. When: when a locked or closed space has no obvious means of entry.
- [heuristic] A line near the reveal that hints at the reversal signals it to the audience without spelling it out in full.
- [heuristic] A reversal lands only if the audience still remembers the earlier facts, so plant them early enough to be recalled. When: designing a late reversal. Why: recontextualising needs the original fact to be remembered.
- [heuristic] Instead of asking who wanted a clue read a certain way, ask what the victim could have intended by the object's state. When: a staged clue points at a convenient time or suspect. Why: the victim may have left the sign themselves.
- [heuristic] Place a reversal at the end of a chapter to give it strong emphasis.
- [heuristic] Let a decisive reveal arrive after the audience believes the situation is lost, since a reversal at that point carries the most momentum. Why: Apparent defeat raises stakes, so a sudden turn feels stronger.
- [heuristic] A theory that looks impossible can still be the one to pursue if it explains the facts better than the ordinary explanation.
- [heuristic] When evidence fits two candidate targets, test the assumed intended victim, because a plan that seemed to misfire may have succeeded against someone else. When: A reconstruction where every inquiry points one way but the planned outcome is unverified. Why: A flawed premise about the target can make every new fact fit a wrong reading.
- [heuristic] A character who seemed unable to act can later perform the key act, and this reversal increases the impact of the admission. When: A passive character is positioned to make the final statement. Why: The contrast with earlier passivity makes the act more striking.
- [heuristic] A trusted character can be the culprit as a reversal, provided the proof is delivered in order.
- [heuristic] A reversal at a moment of apparent defeat works when the protagonist's plan was signalled earlier, so the audience accepts the twist in hindsight. When: The protagonist seems trapped and the audience expects rescue or disaster. Why: Planted signs make the twist feel earned rather than convenient.
- [heuristic] Reuse one twist shape, such as impersonation, across a collection so players learn to expect it and the next reversal feels both fair and surprising. When: writing a multi-case mystery collection.
- [heuristic] A reversal that shows an apparently voluntary event was forced can reframe the apparent schemer as a manipulator who offered a misleading account.
- [procedure] 1) State the events in their true chronological order. 2) Link them with dated records. 3) List unresolved possibilities and note whether they change the outcome. 4) Stage the final proof as a visible demonstration. When: Presenting a solved case whose events were discovered backward. Why: Discovery order differs from true order; the explicit timeline lets the audience follow the logic.
- [procedure] 1) State the assumed order of events. 2) Trace each object's custody chain. 3) Test whether reversing the order fits the custody facts. 4) Adopt the order that the custody evidence supports. When: A timeline built on assumed sequence conflicts with object custody. Why: Custody facts can overturn an intuitive order of events.
- [procedure] 1) Re-read every object under the reversed purpose. 2) Rebuild the events as an ordered timeline. 3) Check that each clue planted earlier explains its place in the timeline.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the outcome. 2) Read the earlier events backward. 3) Ask how each event led to the next. 4) Treat an event as part of the plan only if it links to the chain. When: after a crime, to test whether it was prepared. Why: reading backward shows how ordinary events connect to the result.
- [pitfall] Treating a reversal as a resolution is a mistake; a reversal reframes the case, and closure needs further steps.
- [pitfall] A physical reveal that can be undone or reversed leaves the evidence unrecorded or incomplete.
- [pitfall] A verdict reversed by a higher court can conceal a flawed first stage, so the whole case path should be reviewed, not only the result.
- [pitfall] A reversal that depends on a convenient rescue, or contradicts the protagonist's established capability, weakens the character and makes the audience feel cheated. When: Resolving a tense scene with a turn of events. Why: Rescues the protagonist did not cause undercut their established competence.

## bluff and deception tactics
- [model] A rigged examination can set seating, restraint, required gaze, a recited prayer, a touch test, staged cures, and limits on contact, each step able to turn compliance into guilt. When: analyzing or designing an ordeal. Why: Each procedural rule can be bent toward a predetermined result.
- [mechanism] A bluff about information the target lacks reveals its reaction, but works only while the target believes it, and its force comes from the target's own fear. When: The bluff depends on information the target lacks, or the questioner claims evidence it cannot produce. Why: A bluff relies on the other side not knowing the truth; belief, not proof, gives the threat its effect. (x2)
- [mechanism] Naming a detail the suspect hides, like a second name or a visitor they met, makes them believe you know more, so they may confirm or supply it. When: When a suspect is frightened and may reveal more if they think you know. Why: A suspect who believes you know a hidden detail may confirm it, and a third party may supply it.
- [mechanism] A suspect who stages a test visit to read the investigator's reaction treats a lack of reaction as proof of safety, even though the investigator may be concealing knowledge. When: a suspect has one investigator they fear and can arrange an inspection. Why: Silence is ambiguous, so a suspect who reads it as safety can be misled by an investigator who does not show what they know.
- [mechanism] A bluff offered to a suspect, such as a claimed poison on a harmless item, exposes the suspect when their reaction contradicts what they should know. When: when a confession is absent. Why: A guilty suspect's reaction reveals knowledge they should not have.
- [behavior] Mocking a subject keeps listeners from asking what a procedure is really for, so they focus on the claim rather than the method. When: A character dismisses a practice with ridicule while controlling it. Why: Derision discourages scrutiny of intent.
- [behavior] A witness may reveal a hidden connection when offered a choice between two candidates, because a pause, flinch or unusually quick denial signals a link. When: Questioning a witness who withholds a secret that direct questions will not reach. Why: Reactions to a concrete pair of options expose what words conceal.
- [rule] Offer a bluff dialogue option that changes the NPC's response, and record that reaction as a clue so the player can read hidden knowledge from it. When: Designing dialogue that can expose a character's secret, where the game tracks reactions. Why: Players can use reactions as evidence when the game tracks them.
- [rule] Give NPC bluff checks where confronting with an item reveals a clue if correct and a harmless denial if wrong; add a reassurance option unlocking further dialogue. When: Designing NPC dialogue that hides information. Why: Both outcomes keep the player engaged without punishing a guess.
- [rule] Back any bluff with real evidence the other party can check, and state it openly with supporting facts attached, since unbacked claims are exposed when tested. When: When confronting a suspect with a reconstruction or partial proof. Why: A bluff built on guesses fails under challenge and destroys credibility.
- [rule] Do not use a staged bluff that could endanger an innocent person or the investigator, or push an innocent person into a false confession. When: Considering a bluff against a suspect. Why: The bluff may provoke a second crime.
- [rule] Do not bluff with challenges that depend on details the suspect could check, unless independent evidence exists. When: when no independent evidence supports the accusation. Why: a bluff collapses once the suspect can verify the detail.
- [rule] If a player falsely accuses, track the consequence of the accusation, not only the reveal. When: a player makes an accusation that proves wrong. Why: consequences give the accusation meaning in the game world.
- [rule] Let the player choose between a bluff and a promise of protection, with each choice changing what the witness will reveal.
- [rule] Do not use a bluff as a substitute for evidence where a legal or formal standard must be met. When: the outcome requires proof for a court or formal inquiry. Why: A bluff creates pressure, not admissible proof.
- [rule] Let the player watch a suspect stage a test visit to check the detective's reaction, so the player sees the suspect's reasoning and the risk it carries. When: designing a scene where a suspect probes an investigator. Why: Showing the test lets the player judge whether the suspect's conclusion is justified.
- [heuristic] Bluff a calm, guarded suspect by claiming you hold more than you reveal, without naming a source, and watch his reaction. When: The suspect has already made a statement that can be checked.
- [heuristic] Use a bluff when the suspect is anxious, time is short and a credible threat exists; avoid it when the claim is easy to check.
- [heuristic] Prepare a list of key people and memorised notes before a bluff, so the pressure is consistent and well informed. When: planning a confrontation built on partial evidence. Why: Inconsistent claims under pressure are easy to expose.
- [heuristic] Openly name a suspect's stance as a bluff, then see whether the suspect's answers hold up against the facts.
- [heuristic] A bluff that the case is complete works only while suspects believe it; revealing the trap early ends its effect. When: Using a feigned exit or feigned weakness to make suspects speak freely. Why: Suspects speak candidly only when they think the pressure is gone.
- [procedure] 1) Offer the suspect something that seems to invite checking, such as a key. 2) Watch answer timing and reactions. 3) Physically verify the offer before trusting it. When: The suspect is confident and a direct question would be deflected. Why: A generous-seeming offer draws out a reaction, and verification exposes an empty offer.
- [procedure] 1) Claim knowledge you cannot yet prove. 2) Watch the listener's reaction for hesitation or a pointed reply. 3) Press the advantage where they seem unsure. 4) Break off as if you revealed too much, so the slip reads as confirmation. When: The other side's knowledge is uncertain and there is time to probe. Why: Reactions expose what the listener does and does not know.
- [procedure] 1) Let the suspect believe you hold proof they cannot dispute. 2) Keep the real evidence hidden from them. 3) Keep allies unaware of your true knowledge. 4) Observe the suspect's action on the false belief. When: When a suspect will deny an act unless convinced you hold proof. Why: A false belief removes the suspect's chance to deny, so their own move can reveal the truth.
- [procedure] 1) Plant a false report whose details matter only to the person you want to draw out. 2) Watch whether that person reacts. 3) Verify the reaction before trusting it. When: Someone is hiding and has a strong personal stake in a particular detail. Why: A false detail that only the target cares about flushes them into view.
- [procedure] 1) Present a worthless object as valuable. 2) Watch whether the suspect shows strong interest or agitation. 3) Treat that reaction as evidence of knowledge. 4) Reveal the object's real value in front of the suspect. When: A suspect has a visible interest in a specific object and the evidence is circumstantial. Why: A desperate interest in a worthless object exposes knowledge the suspect should not need to show.
- [procedure] 1) Lay out the crime sequence in order: arrival, method, the victim's state, result. 2) Make a bold claim about a hidden object to test the reaction. 3) When the suspect breaks, offer secrecy or protection for the full account. When: You hold partial proof and the suspect is emotionally strained. Why: Each detail acts as a hook, and an assurance lowers the guard.
- [tradeoff] Pressing a convincing but unproven theory early can force a guilty party to act, but may reveal how little evidence is held and warn them investigators are guessing. When: Choosing when to press a suspect on a convincing but unproven theory. Why: Pressure can force a guilty party to act and reveal themselves; early pressure exposes how thin the evidence is.
- [tradeoff] A bluff of partial knowledge can shake a guilty party, but exposure ends cooperation and destroys trust; a promise of protection keeps cooperation possible. When: Choosing whether to bluff or how to press a witness.
- [tradeoff] A bluff tests a suspect but tips them off if the claim is wrong; a direct question alerts no one yet is easily deflected.
- [tradeoff] A bluff can force a guilty party to act, but the action may endanger others, so the risk must be weighed against the gain. When: deciding whether to use pressure on a suspect. Why: provocation can produce a new crime.
- [tradeoff] A bluff mechanic lets the player claim evidence they lack, where later matching clues reward the gamble and failed bluffs cost trust. When: Designing a player-facing bluff or pressure option in a dialogue system. Why: Rewarding successful bluffs and penalising failed ones makes the gamble a meaningful risk.
- [tradeoff] A bluff can extract reactions, but it proves nothing alone and can make the investigator seem unreliable to people he needs. When: An investigator considers feigning knowledge or withholding facts. Why: Reactions are suggestive evidence, and a deceptive investigator loses trust.
- [tradeoff] A bluff can backfire if the suspect can check the object's value before the reveal, so the bait must survive independent checking. When: Using a worthless object as bait. Why: A verifiable bluff exposes the investigator instead of the suspect.
- [pitfall] A bluff about evidence collapses once the other side can check it, so avoid bluffs where checking is simple; rely only on claims unverifiable on the spot. When: The other party has access to a means of verification. Why: Unsupported claims cannot survive an independent check; verification exposes the false claim and removes its leverage, and a checkable false claim destroys credibility and control. (x2)
- [pitfall] A bluffed claim about nonexistent evidence or knowledge is likely to be tested and exposed, ending trust and cooperation for the rest of the exchange. When: Claiming evidence or knowledge the questioner does not have. Why: A suspect or witness who can check a specific claim will often do so, and a disproved claim weakens the whole approach. (x2)
- [pitfall] A bluff can backfire if the witness sees through it, feels threatened into silence, or concludes its knowledge is worthless and stops talking. When: Using an implied threat or bluffed claim of knowledge to pressure or test a witness. Why: A witness who detects the bluff may withdraw or resist when threatened; one who feels dismissed may withdraw. (x2)
- [pitfall] A bluff or accusation can provoke a revealing reaction, but fright or innocence can mimic guilt and leading questions can elicit expected answers; treat reactions as leads, not proof. When: Using a bluffed claim or accusation to test a witness. Why: Shock and guilt can produce similar reactions, and a reaction shows concern that may have innocent or guilty causes.
- [pitfall] A bluff or accusation without real evidence held fails or backfires if wrong: it yields no useful reaction, lets the witness discredit the investigator, and ends any chance of confession. When: Deciding whether to challenge a witness's account or accuse a suspect. Why: A suspect who sees the claim is unfounded keeps denying; an unsupported accusation lets the witness discredit the investigator.
- [pitfall] Stating an unverified fact as if it were known risks exposure, since the witness may check it and reveal the bluff. When: When pressing a witness with an unconfirmed claim.
- [pitfall] A bluff can produce an object that proves less than hoped, so an extracted item should be checked before it is treated as decisive.
- [pitfall] A rigid script can make the interviewer miss answers that fall outside the prepared topics.
- [pitfall] An improbable method still needs a physical test. Assuming it works without checking timing and distance is an error. When: A surprising method is proposed for a crime. Why: Plausibility on paper does not confirm that the method works in practice.
- [pitfall] Trusting a trap's result before its sample is analysed risks a false conclusion; the reading should rest on the sample and the reaction together.
- [pitfall] A feint that no one tests feels too convenient to believe, so a visible test or plausible cause is needed to make it credible.
- [pitfall] A bluff built on a weak explanation exposes the investigator when the suspect's reaction shows the explanation has gaps. When: the explanation behind the pressure is unsound. Why: Pressure only holds up when the reasoning behind it is sound.
- [pitfall] A reveal based only on inference can feel unfair if the earlier action was never shown to the audience. When: when a twist depends on unseen actions. Why: the audience cannot check the inference.
- [pitfall] A test whose result always confirms the examiner's belief is not evidence; it is a rigged clue that can never disprove the accused. When: Assessing a test used to establish guilt. Why: Outcomes fixed in advance carry no information.
- [pitfall] An earlier lie gives the other side leverage, so a bluff in one direction makes the liar vulnerable. When: when a character has told a lie. Why: A false statement can be exposed or used as a threat later.
- [pitfall] Bluffing without a plan for the suspect's likely reaction, such as running for the door, can leave the investigator with no control.

## object provenance tracing
- [model] Inscriptions from successive owners, each adding a link such as a gift or transfer, trace an object's chain of ownership, linking present owner to past one. When: An object carries inscriptions from several owners over time. Why: Successive hands document the object's chain of custody. (x2)
- [mechanism] A lock that needs two separate secrets held by different people narrows suspects to those who hold both, and a strong lock shifts the question to who held its credentials. When: When a container is protected by a key and a secret, held by different people. Why: Opening requires legitimate access to both credentials, so the question becomes who had them.
- [mechanism] An item left at one scene and carried to another location acts as a traceable record of who was where. When: a personal object moves between places during an event. Why: The object carries a person's presence from one location to another.
- [mechanism] A single person linked to several unrelated objects creates a web that an investigator can trace back to that person.
- [rule] Trace an object's handling route and timeline, with witness accounts, before treating it as proof; owning an object does not establish that its owner used it. When: An object is linked to a person through a place, visit or unusual position. Why: Objects are often carried or handed over by ordinary actions, so an object alone can be explained innocently.
- [rule] Give weapons provenance records, such as owner's name or loaded count, so a found blade reveals its holders and the player can verify claims about it. When: Designing weapons that serve as clues.
- [rule] Test an unusual physical object, such as a small scrap of paper, by asking each involved person whether they recognise its origin. When: when an unidentified object turns up in an investigation.
- [rule] Stamp found items with a maker's mark and a shop, so a player can trace each item to a merchant NPC who keeps a sales record. When: designing clue items for a mystery or investigation. Why: the mark gives the player a route from object to person.
- [rule] Attach a traceable item, such as a cap with a maker's mark, to an NPC, and let its trace fade on dry ground. When: Designing a clue that links an NPC to a scene.
- [rule] Track where keys were lost, claimed or returned, since those intervals are when keys can be copied. When: Determining how a locked space was reached. Why: Custody gaps are the moments of possible duplication.
- [rule] Check a character's stated origin for an object against the object's marks before accepting it. Why: marks can reveal a different source than the one claimed.
- [rule] Give objects or secrets an explicit in-world value so players understand why factions compete for them.
- [rule] Place an accidentally dropped object in a crowded setting as a traceable trail the player can follow. When: Designing a clue that moves through the world. Why: The object's journey gives the player a path to follow.
- [rule] Give each in-world typewriter or printing press a distinctive fault so the player can match a forged note to its source. When: designing forged documents in a game. Why: Matching faults let the player trace an item to its origin.
- [rule] Flag which NPCs handled an object, so their recollections become usable clues. When: An item passes through several characters before reaching the target. Why: Handlers can recall details that the player can check.
- [rule] Give items traits tied to one handler, so a document or item traces back to a single source and sets a concrete exploration goal. When: When designing clue objects in a game.
- [rule] Decide which items carry traceable marks, since this sets which leads the player can follow. When: When designing items that players may trace. Why: Marked and unmarked items determine whether a trail exists at all.
- [rule] Mark original objects with a distinguishing label and wrap them for transport so they remain identifiable.
- [heuristic] Speech accent, cap insignia, dress, grooming, inscriptions, vessel names or a small object's brand, type or habit can reveal a region, affiliation or owner; identify origin before concluding.
- [heuristic] Initials, monograms, brands, shades, tools, rust specks or storage location can point to an owner and narrow suspects; each inference stays a guess until confirmed. When: An object is found without a clear owner. Why: Distinctive features narrow which owner and storage place the object came from.
- [heuristic] A message that refers to the recipient's past, such as an old identifier, narrows the list of possible senders. When: a sender is unknown but the message reveals shared history. Why: few people share that history with the recipient.
- [heuristic] An unaddressed item carrying an identifying line can link a found object to its sender.
- [heuristic] A worse tool is chosen only when the best option is unavailable, so an improvised object at a scene dates the moment the better option was lost. When: a fallback object appears where a better one would be expected. Why: the choice reveals the actor's constraints at that point.
- [heuristic] A careful actor discards a weapon out of sight, so a weapon left in a convenient place suggests haste or framing rather than a coolly planned act.
- [heuristic] Improvised repairs such as knots carry the habits of whoever made them, so they can help identify a person.
- [heuristic] An item's origin can be traced to a known place, which links the item to a specific location and person. When: an object is found at a scene and its source may be known. Why: A traceable origin connects the object to a location and can narrow the suspect pool.
- [heuristic] An item prepared in view of witnesses and never sent out of their sight has a fully traceable path, so its contact with the victim can be checked. When: An item is made at the table and shared. Why: Its handling is observed from start to finish.
- [heuristic] Town NPCs such as clerks or porters can hold trace data that the player must earn or buy to rebuild a suspect's route. When: Designing a town with investigation content.
- [heuristic] Let a clue object show its own history, such as repairs or handling marks, as part of the evidence.
- [heuristic] A concealed object that pairs with an earlier object can link a present event to a past tragedy. When: When designing clues that connect the present to backstory. Why: A household item with a known partner ties two events together.
- [heuristic] Trace an object's history of owners and givers, since a recognised object can link a crime to a known circle of people. When: an object is found at a scene.
- [procedure] 1) List every stage the object passed through. 2) Mark stages where no one observed it. 3) For each unobserved gap, compare its length with the time the suspected change would need. 4) Confirm identity at each stage using weight, fittings, contents or other physical features. When: An object must have stayed intact along a chain of handoffs between NPCs or rooms. Why: Testing gaps against required time shows whether a change was possible, and physical traits persist through handoffs.
- [procedure] 1) Note where the object sits at each scene. 2) Record each handover or hiding and who did it, including when it entered and left each location. 3) Arrange these into a custody timeline showing who controlled it when. When: When an object's location or ownership matters to the question. Why: Ordered records make transfers of control visible.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the object's current location or from the first record naming a handler, such as a supplier, employee or address. 2) Check each recorded destination against reality. 3) Trace each prior handler, confirming every link by record or questioning, until reaching the origin or crime. When: An object has changed hands and each handler left written records or can be questioned. Why: Each confirmed link supports the next, and each record names the next handler, so the chain depends on every link.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the item's origin. 2) At each stage obtain the seller's sales records listing every buyer of the item. 3) Treat each buyer as a possible holder and narrow to a short named list. When: Tracing a physical object that carries a label, licence or signed record through a chain of trade records. Why: Each record stage shrinks the set of possible holders.
- [procedure] 1) Record the object's history from owner to finding place, including its route. 2) Take the object to its maker and compare the maker's order and dispatch records with the account given by the person who moved it. 3) Explain every discrepancy before accepting either account. When: An object links a person to a scene and its ownership or history must be documented back to its source. Why: The maker's records may contradict the suspect's version.
- [procedure] 1) Identify who could recognize the object. 2) Reconstruct its custody chain through each place it was moved. 3) Check for missing parts and their causes. 4) Note expected publicity that did not occur. When: an object at a scene links a suspect to a place or time. Why: each step tests whether the object's movement and the owner's knowledge fit together.
- [procedure] 1) Check the owner's sale catalogue. 2) If a notable item is absent, assume it was given or sold earlier. 3) Identify the most likely recipient, such as a close friend. 4) Work outward from that circle of people. When: an object has passed through several hands and its owner's records are incomplete. Why: An absent item points to a transfer that happened before the sale.
- [procedure] 1) Trace the item's movement through the suspect's belongings. 2) Check what was bought, destroyed or moved. 3) Rebuild the sequence from hiding to later movement. When: a suspect is linked to a stolen or hidden item.
- [procedure] 1) Gather every plausible candidate object. 2) Test each against the trace. 3) Keep the candidates that fit and rule out the rest by their measurable features. When: a trace is left in soft ground and candidate objects are finite. Why: physical testing narrows possibilities to the true source.
- [procedure] 1) Assess the object's condition, such as whether it looks new. 2) Ask staff who know the container's normal contents when it was acquired. 3) Match residual traces, like cut hairs, to a suspect.
- [procedure] Ask where an object was bought, and for whom, to connect it to a relationship rather than to the scene where it was found. When: An object's link to a person is unclear. Why: A history can place the object within a personal connection that explains its presence.
- [procedure] 1) Identify where the object was last seen. 2) Find the staff who handled that place. 3) Question them under a simple pretext about the object's whereabouts. When: a lost object was last seen in a staffed place.
- [procedure] 1) Examine the packaging as well as the object. 2) Identify each mark, such as punctures, folds or print marks. 3) Match the mark to a candidate source location. 4) Check each candidate source directly. 5) Keep or eliminate each lead based on what is found. When: An object's location of origin is uncertain but its packaging carries marks. Why: Physical marks on wrapping can link an object to a specific place, and checking sources confirms or closes each lead.
- [procedure] 1) Record each weapon's owner and its history. 2) List who had access to it and when. 3) Compare each party's account against the weapon's physical state. When: A dispute arises over who owned or used a weapon.
- [procedure] 1) Describe the stolen item to museums, collectors and dealers, including those abroad. 2) Treat any offer or sale as a traceable lead. When: When a stolen item is distinctive enough to recognize. Why: Circulating the item turns loot into a trackable object.
- [procedure] 1) Ask one narrow, specific question at each source, such as whether a particular item was made there for a customer. 2) Repeat across sources until one answers yes. When: Tracing an object back to its maker or buyer. Why: A precise question gets a clear answer from makers who recognise the item.
- [tradeoff] Tracing an item to its maker or shop narrows possible owners, but depends on records that may be incomplete. When: When an item's origin is used to identify its owner. Why: Origin links are useful but limited by what the records capture.
- [fact] Stains found on a weapon can reveal its earlier history rather than the identity of the current attacker. When: Forensic analysis of an object used in a crime. Why: Analysis answers the question it is asked, and the object may carry traces of unrelated events.
- [fact] An item sent through a trackable channel, such as mail, leaves a timed trace that may lead to a holding location without naming the recipient.

## sincerity and accuracy
- [model] An agent who feeds false information while believing it serves a cause can drift into a confused, double position between truth and deception. When: when judging a character who seems to act a part.
- [mechanism] Once a corrected sequence shows two events were nearly simultaneous, a person's belief about their own chances of success can change. When: A reconstructed timeline contradicts what the person assumed. Why: The revealed order changes which actions were possible, altering their sense of control.
- [behavior] A guarded party who hears a partly wrong accusation often corrects the wrong half, which reveals what they already knew. When: Confronting someone with a partial and partly wrong claim. Why: They assume the interviewer already knows the other half.
- [behavior] A person may lie to avoid being linked to a crime they fear being blamed for, even when the lie hides an innocent act. When: A suspect had been near a crime scene. Why: Fear of being blamed makes an innocent act look suspicious, so people conceal it.
- [rule] A witness's sincere belief, including a claimed persecution, does not confirm the reported event occurred; sincerity reflects belief, not evidence. Why: Sincerity reflects belief, not evidence. (x2)
- [rule] Vividness, detail, confidence or sincerity does not establish accuracy; a witness's interpretation must not replace observable facts. Check accounts against independent evidence. When: weighing any account, memory or testimony. Why: Vividness and certainty do not establish accuracy. (x2)
- [rule] Judge a witness's sincerity separately from their account's truth; tone and sincerity are not tests of truth, since sincere-sounding accounts can be wrong or false. When: when weighing testimony. Why: Sincerity and accuracy are independent.
- [rule] A single confession, even freely given, is not proof; without independent checks it remains one party's version, since sincerity does not establish accuracy. When: A confession is the only source offered for a motive, or a witness volunteers history unprompted. Why: A self-serving speaker shapes the record, and honest delivery can rest on wrong memory or motive.
- [rule] Ask what was actually done or said by the original source rather than relying on a summary given by someone in between.
- [rule] Unrefuted does not mean true in every detail; separate an account's core claim from its exact wording before trusting either.
- [rule] A red herring must be correctable by evidence the player can later find, because an uncorrected false lead leaves players feeling cheated. When: Designing a misleading clue or suspect in a mystery. Why: Players accept misdirection only when it is later explained and resolved.
- [rule] Correct imprecise wording in testimony, separating what was seen from what was identified, because loose phrasing can mislead later.
- [rule] Use transcription errors or damaged records as in-world clues, such as a misnumbered page that conceals a timeline.
- [heuristic] Distinguish original editions from later reprints, and note which originals have become rare, when judging a source's reliability.
- [heuristic] A witness can be accurate on key facts while padding the account with irrelevant detail, so separate the core facts from the embellishment. When: when a testimony is long and digressive. Why: Accurate core facts can make irrelevant or wrong padding seem credible.
- [heuristic] Judge a participant's sincerity separately from whether their conduct was mistaken, since both can be true at once.
- [heuristic] When a character's grievance sits beside professed devotion, the audience must judge where sincere feeling ends and a hidden motive begins. When: A character claims affection while resenting obligations. Why: Mixed signals keep the question open.
- [heuristic] A victim's correspondence or relationship log can carry motive hints that players piece together over time.
- [heuristic] Separate characters who sincerely act on false information from those who hold the facts, since their demeanour may differ.
- [heuristic] When a witness adds a step to explain an earlier point, the new step may clash with another part of the account. When: A witness corrects or extends an earlier statement under questioning. Why: Each added detail creates new claims that can conflict.
- [heuristic] Treat a witness's honesty and the certainty of what was decided as separate questions; an honest witness can still be wrong about the decision. When: a witness is trusted but reports only what was said. Why: Sincerity concerns the speaker, while certainty concerns the decision.
- [heuristic] When a questioner remarks on a disguise detail, fold the remark into a plausible explanation that the persona could give. When: when a questioner comments on a prop or detail.
- [procedure] 1) Record the original's details precisely. 2) Compare the item presented as found against that record. 3) Note any difference in detail. When: provenance of an item is disputed and an exact original exists. Why: precise originals expose swaps.
- [procedure] 1) Accept a partial payment first. 2) Raise the offered amount. 3) Watch how the client responds to judge seriousness.
- [tradeoff] Witnesses may be sincere yet mistaken, so their honesty should not be taken as proof that their account is accurate. When: when assessing a witness whose belief drives their account. Why: sincere belief can distort perception as much as deliberate lying distorts testimony.
- [pitfall] Sincerity does not guarantee accuracy: an honest witness can omit, misremember or misperceive details, so check their account against other facts. Why: Honesty and accuracy must be assessed separately; sincere witnesses can omit or misremember details. (x2)
- [pitfall] A quoted fragment without its surroundings can mislead readers into a meaning the speaker never intended, so check dates and surrounding text before accepting it. Why: Missing context invites wrong interpretation; isolated quotations can imply a sequence the surrounding text contradicts. (x2)
- [pitfall] Confidence and visible distress are not verification; sincerity does not establish what a witness perceived, and a private sworn observation stays uncorroborated.
- [pitfall] A suspect's frankness, tears or sincere-sounding confession can be a performance shaped by self-interest; judge the explanation by its content, not apparent sincerity. When: when weighing a suspect's account or confession. Why: Sincerity of tone does not guarantee an accurate account of motive.
- [pitfall] Sincerity measures conviction, not correctness: a sincere person may hold false beliefs, flawed reasoning or be a poor judge of what they report, yet act with integrity. When: when judging a character or witness who believes something false. Why: Honest belief can coexist with flawed reasoning.
- [pitfall] A party can take a witness's remark out of context and use it to back a claim the witness never made. When: Hearing a witness quoted in a dispute.
- [pitfall] A public apology may be sincere or self-serving, and the two are hard to tell apart.
- [pitfall] Emotional hints from a witness may be sincere or self-protective, so they need checking before they shape an investigator's theory. Why: the motives behind a hint are often mixed.
- [pitfall] Believing a witness from intuition is not evidence; a sense that someone is sincere must be tested against proof.
- [pitfall] A witness who talks freely is not necessarily accurate; the account may be vague, repetitive or distorted.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a route because it was absent at an earlier check. The scene may have changed since, so recheck. When: When a route was checked at an earlier time. Why: Someone may have altered the scene after the first check.
- [pitfall] Information about a room's layout from one person's memory may be outdated, especially if it is more than a year old, so verify before relying on it.
- [pitfall] Treating a sincere witness as accurate ignores physical limits such as distance or walls that restrict what they could have perceived. When: A witness is sincere but positioned poorly. Why: Honest testimony still fails when the witness lacked access to the event.
- [pitfall] Older textbook rules for cooling and rigidity can mislead an expert, so estimates should not lean on them uncritically. Why: rules of thumb may not fit the case.
- [pitfall] Confidence about an object's origin from general knowledge is not a confirmed link to a particular person.
- [pitfall] An old photograph may not show a subject's current appearance, so it can mislead identification.
- [pitfall] Guessing a person's appearance from cosmetic shades is weak inference and should be treated as opinion.
- [pitfall] Clues that depend on one habit or one witness are not independent, so counting them separately creates false confidence.
- [pitfall] Assuming an accusation is sincere ignores the accuser's motive when a land or family dispute gives them one.
- [pitfall] An old title can outlast the office that gave it, so a title can mislead about current authority or real wealth.
- [pitfall] A clause removed from a later revision can still be quoted as if it remained in the newer version. When: The source exists in several editions or revisions. Why: Earlier wording looks current when revision history is ignored.
- [pitfall] Confidence drawn from one's own inspection is not a test; an untested conclusion can be wrong. When: Assessing whether a concealment succeeded. Why: Self-assessment lacks an independent check.
- [pitfall] Reading too much into omissions, or confusing a writer's habits with their intent, is a common error, especially when the reader is hostile to the writer. When: when interpreting a writer's omissions or habits. Why: The reader's feelings shape what they notice and how they interpret it.
- [pitfall] A sincere believer may notice contrary facts less, not more, because the belief already explains them away. When: a person's conviction is strong and shared. Why: A fixed premise filters out evidence it cannot explain.
- [fact] Finding an ordinary source for a claim does not prove the witness is lying; it only shows the knowledge did not require a supernatural explanation.

## explanation and inference chains
- [definition] An inference reveal overturns a belief by combining evidence from several source kinds, such as tradition, testimony, records and comparison, rather than a confession or found artifact. When: a truth must be deduced because no single item shows it.
- [mechanism] Once a community accepts an expert's verdict of an outside cause, other lines of inquiry are closed off. When: when an authority offers a ready explanation. Why: the accepted explanation leaves no reason to look elsewhere.
- [mechanism] Conclusions often form by linking small visible signs into a chain of inference, frequently so fast the reasoner does not notice each intermediate step. When: A player must reach a conclusion from several observable details. Why: Each sign narrows the possibilities, and the chain can feel instantaneous even when it is long.
- [behavior] Investigators keep a favoured theory despite counter-evidence, or after its supporting physical evidence weakens, especially when a key fact stays unexplained or a vivid fact anchors belief. When: a favoured theory faces contrary evidence, or its supporting evidence is lost or cleared. Why: Attachment, trust in a companion, and a vivid fact anchoring belief more firmly than its later support can outweigh contrary evidence.
- [behavior] Advocates may keep a favoured theory after admitting the central question is unsolved, so the theory persists without new evidence. When: repeated searches have failed to confirm the theory. Why: Commitment to an idea can outlast the evidence for it.
- [behavior] Investigators who accept correction without argument when shown an error avoid compounding that error. When: A colleague shows a flaw in an investigator's reasoning. Why: Defending a mistake keeps the wrong theory in place.
- [behavior] Players and investigators readily adopt a plausible alternative theory as their working explanation, especially when an authority figure endorses it. When: When a credible substitute explanation is presented. Why: A plausible decoy gives a ready answer, so it is accepted without testing.
- [behavior] A suspect offered money tends to infer the offerer's hidden knowledge from the offer itself, reasoning that a sensible person does not pay without cause. When: A suspect receives an unexplained payment proposal. Why: People read motive backward from unusual behaviour, which can be right or wrong.
- [behavior] A widely held assumption about a kind of person can steer inquiry toward the expected suspect and away from others.
- [behavior] A witness who hears an alarming sound may explain it away with a benign assumption and not investigate, and may later regret that choice. When: A witness hears a disturbing sound and leaves the scene. Why: An assumption formed at the time can replace checking what happened.
- [behavior] A theory linking many facts to a larger hidden network attracts belief because it explains everything at once, even when it is only conjecture. Why: explanatory breadth feels like confirmation.
- [behavior] Witnesses treat a coincidental effect as confirmation when it matches the accusers' story, such as fits stopping at a touch.
- [behavior] Several weak clues, each modest alone, joined into one sequence can look unbroken and persuasive, even though no single link is strong. When: several small incriminating facts point the same way. Why: Joined links appear complete, so the sequence feels proven.
- [rule] Explain surprising observations and each deduction step from known principles, not bare assertion, so listeners can verify the conclusion. When: Presenting a conclusion drawn from physical traces or a surprising observation. Why: Listeners cannot accept or verify a leap they cannot follow.
- [rule] Test each explanation of a suspicious fact against verifiable records, such as bank deposits or ledgers, before accepting it.
- [rule] Refuse to witness or sign a document until its terms have been explained, and say so openly. When: Pressed to commit under time pressure. Why: Understanding is needed before commitment.
- [rule] Store whether an NPC accepted the player's explanation of a clue as checkable state, so later questions can depend on whether the player pressed the point.
- [heuristic] An explanation accounting for every known fact, including rarity and secrecy, outranks one accounting for most, and is stronger than one fitting only the fact supporting it. When: Comparing rival explanations of a clue. Why: A theory that leaves facts unexplained is easier to undermine.
- [heuristic] Test each premise of a tidy chain separately; each step feeling convincing lets a single weak link pass unnoticed and carry a wrong conclusion. When: An explanation or suspect assessment is built from several steps or smaller clues. Why: Logical neatness and apparent support between steps do not show that each premise matches the facts.
- [heuristic] Trace one established fact back to its causes and forward to its likely results, building the chain from that single link. When: a reasoner has one reliable fact. Why: a known link constrains what came before and what follows.
