- [heuristic] Lay the facts out in order so their relative importance and their links to each other become visible. When: A set of established facts must be reasoned about. Why: Order reveals which facts bear on the conclusion.
- [heuristic] Explaining too little is better than explaining too much, so leave some details unexplained rather than forcing every object into the solution.
- [heuristic] An explanation that accounts for symptoms can itself raise a new question about access to its source; check that before accepting it.
- [heuristic] Judge an explanation by how well it fits the surrounding circumstances, not by a single fact taken alone. When: When several explanations fit one event.
- [heuristic] A planted-object explanation holds only until a forensic or ownership check disproves it.
- [heuristic] Check a volunteered explanation against the speaker's own earlier statements and memory, since a conflicting recollection exposes the cover story.
- [heuristic] Separate misleading evidence caused by bad luck from errors caused by poor method, and judge each on its own cause. When: An investigation yields a misleading trace. Why: Misattributing the cause of error leads to wrong fixes.
- [heuristic] An explanation that works only if a character was feigning turns their behavior into an unverified performance, so test it closely.
- [heuristic] A test with a visible result, such as a colour change, bubbling or smoke, can support a rational explanation of an impossible effect.
- [heuristic] Distinguish a state, such as sleepwalking, from the cause of an event, since a state explains behaviour without proving a supernatural source. When: when a character's unusual action is explained by a condition. Why: Conflating a condition with its cause hides the actual mechanism.
- [heuristic] Let the detective reach the answer through a single theory that links separate pieces of evidence, rather than through isolated facts. When: writing the climax of a deduction-based mystery. Why: A unifying theory explains why the clues fit together and makes the breakthrough feel earned.
- [procedure] 1) List each reported detail of the event. 2) Propose one physical mechanism for each detail. 3) Accept only the mechanism explaining every detail; a plausible ordinary cause alone does not close a strange event. When: when a witness describes an event that seems to break physical rules. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Take each apparent impossibility in turn. 2) Identify the mundane means that could produce it and how it was physically made. 3) Check that chain against the physical facts of the setting and link it to an earlier planted clue. When: a striking trace or mystery effect looks supernatural. Why: Ordinary causes are testable before any supernatural reading is accepted.
- [procedure] 1) List each step of the inference. 2) State the assumption behind each step, such as an object's height or the tool used. 3) Treat early findings as provisional until confirmed. When: deducing a person's traits from physical traces. Why: Explicit assumptions show where an error would enter the chain.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the witness's full account before judging any fact. 2) Arrange the facts in order and check that each links to the next. 3) Mark every missing link as a significant gap.
- [procedure] 1) List every plausible explanation, such as accident, error or deliberate act. 2) For each, state the consequences it would produce. 3) Seek evidence that separates the explanations. When: Direct evidence is missing or several explanations fit.
- [pitfall] Explaining anomalies one by one protects the first theory while hiding what it cannot explain; each added rescue seems ingenious yet adds no evidence and more risk of error. When: an investigator faces contrary facts. Why: Rescue explanations make a theory look more persuasive without supplying evidence.
- [pitfall] Explaining away the first tell generously can make later reactions look innocent too, so each tell needs its own check.
- [pitfall] Trivial details are easily explained away as accidents; require a second explanation before dismissing a clue.
- [pitfall] Inventing a fact to explain away a conflicting description replaces assessing how reliable the witness was.
- [pitfall] A tidy explanation of a sound can leave the essential question open, since it does not settle who was present afterwards.
- [pitfall] An explanation that fits one detail can contradict another, so every proposed explanation must be checked against all the details.
- [pitfall] A plausible chain of inferences can lead away from the truth, and a single purchase is not proof of intent. When: Building a theory from a suspect's purchases and possessions. Why: Each link may seem reasonable while the overall conclusion is wrong.
- [pitfall] A clear, plausible motive can make a theory feel certain before the physical facts are checked. When: Forming a theory from motive alone. Why: Narrative coherence is mistaken for evidence.
- [pitfall] A bound person may be free, so restraints should be tested rather than trusted to hold. When: When evaluating whether a restrained character is still constrained. Why: Restraints the bound person tied can be loosened by that person.
- [pitfall] A watcher often assumes the target is unaware because nothing overt happens, which can lead to a poor plan. When: A target shows no visible reaction. Why: Absence of overt action is mistaken for absence of awareness.
- [pitfall] Assuming the records are complete is an error; a count that does not reconcile signals missing entries. When: Totals from records do not match the known number of items. Why: Unrecorded transactions leave a gap that only the count reveals.
- [pitfall] A plausible explanation that is convenient for the speaker and accounts for an earlier lie should not end the inquiry. Why: Convenience and a prior lie are reasons to doubt the explanation.
- [fact] An investigator explains the reveal in dialogue, while a narrator often confesses under pressure to an unseen or unwilling listener.

## lost evidence and record gaps
- [definition] Grounds for strict examination of a suspect, such as notoriety, a co-accused's naming, or unexplained harm, are not sufficient for conviction on their own. When: when deciding whether a clue justifies questioning. Why: suspicion can open an inquiry but cannot by itself establish guilt.
- [mechanism] A missing document needed to make a plan work is itself a clue pointing to who must explain the gap.
- [mechanism] Internal gaps make a story look disconnected, and a target may come to suspect a fabrication designed to frighten.
- [mechanism] Details lost from memory stay unrecovered without new evidence, so the trail goes cold. Why: Memory cannot regenerate specifics that were never retained.
- [mechanism] When supporting records are lost, a claim falls back on the claimant's sworn word, which a contradicting sworn witness can overturn.
- [mechanism] Evidence written off as lost can later arrive through an unexpected outside channel, which can reopen an investigation.
- [mechanism] When key physical evidence such as a grave is lost over time, the investigator is left with testimony and no object to examine, and the missing evidence drives the search. When: A key site has been removed or no living person can locate it. Why: Without the physical object, the investigator cannot confirm the story.
- [rule] Mark which records survived and which are lost, and build an in-world archive with lost, partial and undated records, so players must piece together the timeline themselves. (x2)
- [rule] A missing lot in a record is evidence of absence, not proof of innocence. When: A record shows no trace of an item or transaction. Why: Absence may reflect concealment or lost records equally.
- [rule] Count a lost record as evidence neither for nor against a claim.
- [rule] Record a broken item's missing piece together with the owner's account of it, since the gap itself can be a clue.
- [rule] Hours without coverage must be filled with evidence from outside the window, such as companions' accounts of where a person was. When: a suspect was unobserved for a stretch of time. Why: Unobserved time cannot be cleared by coverage alone.
- [rule] Turn missing pages into a deliberate investigation hook, with a surviving copy held by an NPC who may or may not share it. When: Designing a clue trail built around a partly lost document.
- [rule] Let a missing register entry or an inscription that avoids a claim matter to a later puzzle. When: Designing a puzzle that depends on an absent or non-committal record. Why: Gaps in records give players a clue to pursue.
- [heuristic] Ask what a record leaves out: one unlisted fact can reconcile contradictions and reveal a pattern's structure; a missing consequence shows what a complete account must contain. When: when known facts do not form a coherent reading, or an account is detailed but skips a logical consequence. Why: The missing item often explains contradictions that look unrelated. (x2)
- [heuristic] A missing part or original may have an innocent explanation; test that explanation rather than accepting or dismissing it at once, and ask for the original rather than a summary. When: a part or source document is absent from its expected place. Why: The original's wording can be compared against a summary.
- [heuristic] A single gap in an otherwise maintained set is a trace; compare it with untouched matching items nearby to see whether it was singled out. When: a set of objects is normally kept in order by someone. Why: Deviation from a consistent standard suggests a different handler or a disruption; the maintainer would not normally allow it.
- [heuristic] Treat gaps in a witness's account, such as a blank stretch or unnamed employer, address or identifier, as signs to examine, though some omissions are trivial. When: when an account is internally consistent but skips a period or contact, or a witness cannot name an employer, address or other identifier. Why: Some omissions hide significant events while others are trivial; missing identifiers can point to concealment or an unverifiable story.
- [heuristic] When an action leaves one part behind, like a spilled match or torn document, search pockets and nearby belongings for the missing counterpart. When: when a partial record or item is found on a body or at a scene. Why: The missing half is likely kept close at hand by whoever took it.
- [heuristic] A missing document is evidence: reason about what the lost set would have proved, and treat the gap as something the story must explain. When: A key document is absent from a case.
- [heuristic] Check unexplained gaps in time against known cycles or schedules, since a gap matching a schedule suggests an interruption rather than a break. When: a long unexplained interval appears. Why: schedules can account for gaps that otherwise look like abandonment.
- [heuristic] When a lead dismisses a case as routine, the gap this leaves lets a junior actor investigate without formal approval of the theory.
- [heuristic] The intervals between dated events, such as a reversal within a day or a slow worsening over days, show how a situation shifted. Why: Change in a situation appears in the spacing and direction of dated events.
- [heuristic] A missing public report that should exist, such as news of a death, is evidence that the matter is being concealed.
- [heuristic] Reward players who find gaps or conflicts between witness statements that questioning has not yet closed. Why: discovering contradictions is the act that moves the investigation forward.
- [heuristic] Local memory can lose a site's history; land records can recover who owned or used a place earlier.
- [heuristic] Note missing closing records, such as formal releases or farewell letters, as explicit gaps in the trail. When: Reconstructing a departure with no final document.
- [procedure] Read each gap in an event sequence as a question about who had opportunity during that interval, and ask what the unseen party did there, since unexplained time is where unseen actions hide. When: when an interval between two events is unaccounted for. Why: A gap only matters if someone was present to act within it; unexplained time is where unseen actions can hide.
- [metric] The blank space left by a removed section, divided by line spacing, estimates how many entries were removed. When: when a torn document has a missing section above surviving text. Why: Gap size bounds the amount of missing text.
- [pitfall] A gap in an archival record is not proof that nothing happened; missing entries say nothing about omitted events, and an argument from absence needs independent support. When: When inferring intent from a gap in documents. Why: Gaps can result from archival loss.
- [pitfall] A timeline gap or inconsistency is not proof of guilt or falsity; treat it as a question to test, since a claim with gaps can still be true. Why: A gap has many innocent explanations until it is checked; inconsistency gives grounds for doubt, not a verdict.
- [pitfall] Without an established normal pattern, a later spike or deviation gives the observer nothing to compare against, so it goes unnoticed. When: Designing a pattern meant to reveal an anomaly. Why: An anomaly is detectable only relative to a known baseline.
- [pitfall] Losing or failing to date a document can remove the evidence that would have settled the question. When: Handling written evidence.
- [pitfall] A missing letter removes the means of knowing the lure, so gaps in evidence need other routes to recover them.
- [pitfall] Skipped diary entries and late-arriving letters change what each character knows at a given point, and missing records invite readers to fill holes wrongly. When: Reconstructing a timeline from incomplete records. Why: Gaps alter what characters could know, and readers tend to guess at what is missing.
- [pitfall] A missing spare key is suggestive of a hidden copy but does not prove one exists; it should be treated as a lead rather than conclusive evidence. Why: Absence of a duplicate may reflect incomplete searching rather than its non-existence.
- [pitfall] The most important link often sits inside an unexplained gap, so a chain with gaps must not be treated as complete.
- [pitfall] Missing a will made casually or stored outside official papers can hide the real motive from the start of an investigation. When: Searching for a beneficiary. Why: Informal documents are often filed away from official records.
- [pitfall] Keeping notes only of conclusions loses the facts that support them, making later checking impossible. Why: without the underlying facts, conclusions cannot be tested.
- [pitfall] Ideas stated in writing may be misread or exaggerated by others, so an author's position should be checked before it is used as a motive. When: Using a character's written ideology as evidence. Why: Readers and critics can distort a text's meaning.
- [pitfall] Not every gap in a text is meaningful; some come from damage, padding or later editing, so treat readings of gaps as interpretations. When: Interpreting erasures or missing stretches as clues. Why: Gaps have many causes, and reading one as meaningful can mislead.
- [pitfall] A gap in the record may come from exclusion of the defence rather than from the absence of a defence, so do not conclude that no answer existed. When: Reading a trial record with little or no defence testimony. Why: Exculpatory evidence can be blocked from reaching decision-makers, leaving no trace in the outcome.
- [pitfall] A missing entry can make an event look as if it never happened, and an extra entry can do the reverse, so first check whether the record should contain it.
- [pitfall] Losing track of who held an object and where it was kept breaks the logic of a locked-room event, since the custody record is what makes the impossibility checkable. When: An object moves between locked or guarded places. Why: Custody gaps let the player doubt the event instead of testing it.
- [pitfall] Citation markers placed inconsistently, before or after the claim, can attach a reference to the wrong statement.
- [pitfall] Failing to record an appearance, through no photograph or few meetings, leaves a search dependent on fragile memory. When: when a suspect's appearance is not documented. Why: Without a stored record, recognition depends on individual recall.
- [fact] Gaps in a split account show events no narrator witnessed, which a reader must treat as unknown rather than as nothing happening.
- [fact] A gap in a diary may mean nothing happened or that the entry was never written, so a blank day cannot be read without further evidence. When: When an expected entry is absent from a personal record. Why: Absence is ambiguous between no event and no record.
- [fact] Many original records are removed, transferred to other archives, lost, or held privately, so copies can lack pages or sources.

## object ownership evidence
- [mechanism] Pledge records and queryable registries of an item, showing owner and location history, link its owner to a place and time, letting investigators trace the person. When: Investigation games with trackable objects, or items pledged to third parties.
- [mechanism] An object left by an absent owner can reveal an unfinished plan the owner meant to carry out. Why: The owner's death or absence interrupted the plan.
- [mechanism] Object state such as plant growth or residue type can encode elapsed time and identity, letting players date events and identify habits. When: Designing world objects that record history. Why: Physical change accumulates over time.
- [mechanism] An object that is normal in its usual place becomes evidence when found in a crime setting, because its owner's habits link it to that person. When: A familiar item turns up somewhere unexpected. Why: Its owner's known routine ties the item to the owner's presence.
- [rule] Ownership shows who owns an object, not who used it; track owner and user as separate facts, and establish access separately. When: Linking an object found at a scene to a person, or when its registered owner may not be its user. Why: Ownership and use are different facts, and access connects the two.
- [rule] Track who held each evidential object and when, since each handler can alter, remove or reinterpret it and a label alone can be altered. When: Designing or investigating scenes where several characters touch evidence, or using a labeled object as identity evidence. Why: Each handler can alter, remove or reinterpret what is left; without a custody record, a label can be altered or misattributed.
- [rule] Examine a body for the marks it should have, including injuries under a bandage, not only for what is visibly present. Why: Coverings can conceal the injury a story depends on, so the check must look beneath them.
- [rule] Have someone who knows an object confirm its identity, tying it to a specific place. Why: Confirmed identity links physical evidence to a location.
- [rule] Make props offered as proof, such as tickets or receipts, checkable against a world-state record so they can be confirmed or exposed. When: When designing evidence items.
- [rule] Do not conclude a trace was planted until the owner's possessions have been checked. When: A clue seems to implicate a specific person. Why: Checking inventory tests whether the trace fits what the person actually had.
- [rule] Make written inventories that can be checked against physical items, so the player can detect a missing or misreported object.
- [rule] Do not treat an object found in a place shared by many people as proof of its owner's intent unless its custody is traced. Why: Anyone with access could have placed it there.
- [rule] Let an object's history, such as being stolen or moved, serve as the player's time anchor, but allow that anchor to be wrong. Why: a plausible anchor that can mislead rewards checking other evidence.
- [rule] Ask the owner whether the item was ever missing and when the loss was first noticed. When: Investigating a suspected stock loss. Why: The owner's answers date the loss and may reveal an earlier shortage that went unexamined.
- [rule] Track each item's owner and history so the player can trace a weapon or key back to the person who gave it.
- [rule] Let the obvious suspect hold the murder weapon, and reveal that another character had access to it. When: authoring a mystery where the weapon points to a wrong suspect. Why: Shifting from ownership to access reframes the weapon as evidence against someone else.
- [heuristic] Read every physical trace through its owner's routine; an unusual movement or object is more informative than a usual one. Why: Routine sets a baseline against which the unusual stands out.
- [heuristic] Read an object's wear against its owner's known habits; a deviation from those habits gives the wear its meaning as a clue. When: The owner's habits are established, so a deviation stands out. Why: Wear alone is ambiguous; only contrast with normal treatment shows it is out of place.
- [heuristic] Test a colour difference that nobody has noticed by asking the owner when they last saw the object. When: a replaced part looks new or different. Why: The owner's memory of the earlier appearance can confirm the change.
- [heuristic] Recognising an object as belonging to a particular person is often the decisive step that ties a trace to an identity.
- [heuristic] A matching object proves nothing unless its owner can be tied to the scene, so an object should be linked to a person before it counts as evidence.
- [heuristic] If an owner knows an object's location without public reports explaining it, that knowledge needs its own explanation; the owner is not automatically the offender.
- [heuristic] Possessions, clothing and purchases can reveal spending beyond known means and suggest motive, even without direct proof of wrongdoing. When: When assessing a suspect's motive from their lifestyle. Why: Visible spending can contrast with stated income and point to a need for money.
- [heuristic] An absent owner's habits can be inferred from wear, repairs, cost and damage on an object they handled daily, with each inference resting on a specific, checkable sign. When: When the owner is absent but left a habitually used object behind. Why: Daily handling leaves consistent traces of habit and means.
- [heuristic] Checking found garments and items against a record of who used them narrows the question of ownership and can contradict a claimed owner. When: Several items are found and their owners are disputed. Why: A record of use is independent of the witness's account.
- [heuristic] Use readable deeds, wills and registry entries as props with dated terms, so the player must order ownership changes to understand the situation. When: designing document-based puzzles. Why: Dated transfers force sequencing.
- [heuristic] A marked item in an NPC's inventory can link the player to a hidden character, so the hidden identity can be deduced from the object. When: Designing an alias reveal.
- [heuristic] An object's size and weight suggest the kind of work it was used for, and so narrow its likely owner, such as a tool kit item rather than a personal item. When: Linking a found weapon or tool to a person. Why: Physical properties reflect the tasks an object was made for.
- [heuristic] Use the investigation's own tools as clues: equipment only an insider could access points to the culprit without a separate accusation. When: A forensic or investigative tool leaves traces at the scene. Why: Access to specialized tools narrows the suspect pool more reliably than a motive alone.
- [procedure] 1) Measure the object tied to a person. 2) Compare the measurement with each candidate owner's known habits. 3) Note which owner the measurement fits. When: an object is found with a person and its owner is assumed rather than established.
- [procedure] 1) List every item a person carries. 2) Mark items that are out of character for them. 3) Test each marked item against an independent source before drawing conclusions. When: a person's belongings include an item that seems out of character. Why: Ordinary possessions reveal a hidden life only when one item does not fit.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether the object's design is exclusive to one owner. 2) Check how the identification was made. 3) Weigh a suspect's denial against the link. When: One object is claimed to tie a suspect to a scene. Why: Ownership claims are only as strong as their exclusivity and method.
- [procedure] 1) Open a hidden cache carefully. 2) Inventory its contents item by item against the owner's list. 3) Note every listed item that is absent. When: a cache is found and the owner's list exists. Why: the missing items reveal what the owner or thief took.
- [procedure] 1) Present an object bearing a marker, such as an initial, as if found in a shared space. 2) Ask whether it belongs to a named person. 3) Record the immediate reaction. 4) Compare the answer with other facts. When: A suspect may deny a link to a place or person. Why: An object with a marker can test a connection without revealing the true purpose of the question.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness describe the marks before showing the object. 2) Compare fresh samples under magnification with the original evidence. 3) Confirm that the shapes and alignment agree. When: When identity rests on a mass-produced product. Why: An independent description checks the match.
- [procedure] 1) Identify physical objects linked to the method or scene, such as rope. 2) Trace each object to its owner and time of use. 3) Check whether the owner's account fits the trace. When: When a physical object is connected to a death or attack. Why: Ownership and timing link physical evidence to people.
- [pitfall] Ownership marks such as stamps, monograms or shared identifiers can be duplicated or made by many owners, so they prove nothing until the owner and context are confirmed. When: Using a manufactured, copied or personal object as proof of identity. Why: Stamps are easy to duplicate; multiple people may own identical items, weakening a claimed link. (x2)
- [pitfall] Accepting an owner's claim that a key never left their hands misleads when others also held it; treat the claim as testimony to check against other facts.
- [pitfall] Assuming an owner would notice a change they never examined closely is an error. When: relying on the owner to report a change. Why: Unnoticed changes stay unreported.
- [pitfall] Assuming an object's owner from its position alone can mislead until witness accounts are heard.
- [pitfall] An inference chain can break at the ownership step, since an object may have been picked up from someone else by mistake.
- [pitfall] Similar-looking damaged items may not be the same object, so confirm that a mark is unique before linking two scenes.
- [pitfall] A change of owner does not by itself prove why a use stopped; an inferred abandonment is probable, not confirmed. When: ownership changes are the only evidence of a stopped use.
- [pitfall] Many signatures can make a claim look firmer without making it more verifiable.
- [pitfall] Treating an identification as settled when the reference record may be unreliable or outdated leads to false conclusions. When: when matching against stored records.
- [pitfall] Assume an object's owner is not necessarily the person who hid something in it. When: Attributing a concealed item to a character. Why: Items change hands, and ownership alone does not establish who placed a hidden object.
- [pitfall] A dated inscription can belong to an earlier owner, so it can mislead about current possession. Why: Items change hands, and the writing records only the past.
- [fact] Possessions can be read as proof of theft, so a witness who owns visible luxuries may be suspected because of what they own. When: A theft investigation involves valuable possessions. Why: Inventories of wealth invite inference of guilt.
- [fact] An ordinary object can carry both the method of a crime and the proof of it, with its danger hidden in its mechanism. When: A crime uses a concealed device. Why: The device that harms also records how the harm was done.

## moved and missing objects
- [mechanism] A missing object, such as a weapon absent near a body, becomes the question an investigation must resolve; each interview returns to it, prompting denial, admission or explanation of access. When: when an unaccounted-for item is central to an investigation. Why: an expected missing item changes what the scene implies, and the object becomes a thread every interview returns to.
- [mechanism] A single missing link found later can turn weak circumstances into conviction, whichever party it actually implicates. When: a set of weak circumstances awaits one decisive discovery. Why: The late piece reorganises the whole body of evidence around it.
- [mechanism] A single missing item can drive both a motive for conflict and an investigation to recover it. When: A dispute or case turns on one item that cannot be found. Why: The absence gives one party a stake and gives others a reason to search.
- [mechanism] A missing object that should be present, such as a key that is not on a body, can be flagged by the game as an anomaly so the player works out the inference from the level's facts. When: Designing puzzles where absence is the clue. Why: Flagging the gap directs attention while leaving the reasoning to the player.
- [behavior] An actor may move evidence to a new place to delay discovery, which shows the actor needed time before a known deadline. When: Leaving the evidence where it was would reveal the act soon. Why: Relocating it buys time at the cost of extra exposure.
- [rule] Treat a missing object as evidence only once its absence is shown to matter to the explanation under test, since the act may have been done another way. When: when using an absent object to challenge a verdict or explanation. Why: absence proves little unless the object was needed for the explanation.
- [rule] A missing item, such as a tool that damage implies, is still evidence: record its absence and order a search rather than assume it is gone. When: when a key piece of evidence or a tool implied by damage is absent. Why: the missing tool may still be hidden or carried away, and finding it confirms the theory.
- [rule] Plant a moved object as a clue players may dismiss, and record it so later confirmation rewards attention.
- [rule] Make a missing piece of a standard item, such as a letter or ticket, a gameplay clue, and size it so it can hold only a few characters to narrow deduction. When: designing an item set with a discoverable gap. Why: A size limit makes the missing content deducible rather than arbitrary.
- [rule] Place a missing item in a plausible hiding spot so players must reason about where discarded objects end up. When: designing a clue around a missing object. Why: Players then use real-world logic about disposal to find it.
- [rule] Keep a lost-and-found system that logs every item found on a route so players can check claims against the records. When: When designing item-tracking systems for a world with routes or transit. Why: A logged record lets the player verify or refute a claim independently.
- [rule] Make a missing instrument the next quest goal, so the unfilled element drives the player's progress. When: When a case is blocked by a missing item. Why: A clear missing element gives the player a concrete objective.
- [heuristic] If a witness expects an absent item, ask where it was normally kept and who could have taken it; it may simply have been left behind. When: when questioning a witness about a person's belongings or an item the witness expects to be present. Why: people often leave behind items they would otherwise carry.
- [heuristic] Treat an expected object's absence, from a scene, usual spot or complete set, as evidence: record it like a present one and search for where it went. When: when something expected is absent from a scene, usual spot or complete set. Why: absence records that something was taken or moved and can point to who took it.
- [heuristic] An item missing from an otherwise complete inventory, or removed after an event, suggests a second person acted on the scene, possibly whoever first reached the body. When: when comparing a victim's belongings with what is expected. Why: missing items often indicate deliberate removal.
- [heuristic] A missing object can have several explanations, so a second clue is needed to choose; until found, it can keep two theories open. When: an object is missing and its fate is unknown. Why: absence alone does not show what happened.
- [heuristic] A missing item is evidence only when its usual carry pattern is known; a secure item absent from a person's belongings was probably carried and then lost. When: when comparing a person's belongings with what is expected.
- [heuristic] A moved or missing tool, such as a ladder found in the wrong place, can reveal how an entry was made and who had recent access.
- [heuristic] An item missing from a shared place implies its taker is still on the premises or used a known route, which narrows the escape options.
- [heuristic] A witness's report of a lost object can be checked by matching it against the object found, which may show it was moved.
- [heuristic] Note missing identifying marks on a container, since they can break the trail to where its contents came from.
- [heuristic] An expected object or action that is absent can reveal how an event really happened, such as a message passed where no device existed. When: a detail contradicts the apparent explanation. Why: absence rules out the stated method and points to another.
- [heuristic] An item stored outside its owner's usual place suggests a hurried change or an altered routine. Why: People keep to habitual storage, so a misplaced item breaks the expected pattern.
- [heuristic] A moved or missing object is itself a clue, so an offender's accident can become the investigator's lead. When: An object is out of place after an accident. Why: Its displacement records where the offender's action went.
- [heuristic] A small item that a person normally carries but is absent on a significant date can expose whether a stated sequence of events is credible. When: Testing a witness's or suspect's account of a day. Why: Routine habits are hard to fake consistently.
- [heuristic] When a planned action lacks its usual preparations, such as packed necessities, question whether it was really planned. When: when a planned departure or task seems incomplete.
- [heuristic] Compare the items a room should hold against what remains; missing toiletries or personal items can show how someone left. When: a room is a candidate for a timeline and the departure is disputed. Why: expected items that are gone reveal what was taken.
- [heuristic] Consider ordinary misplacement before reading an absence as theft; infer theft only when ordinary causes are less likely.
- [heuristic] An item absent from its usual place can be evidence that someone took or moved it, so check each place it is normally kept before concluding it is lost. When: An item has a known routine location and its absence matters. Why: Absence from a routine spot points to recent access by someone.
- [heuristic] A missing key can point to a framing plan, so test that hypothesis before presenting it in a reveal. Why: an absent item may be deliberately removed to mislead.
- [heuristic] When a key item is missing, ask two questions: was the item incriminating in itself, or did it hold something the taker wanted? When: A key object has vanished from a scene. Why: The answer shows whether the item or its contents mattered.
- [heuristic] A personal item the victim should have carried but lacked can point to another place linked to that item. When: A usual possession is absent from the body or the scene. Why: People normally keep such items on them.
- [heuristic] A fixture such as a gate or bar that now stands on a different side of a wall can show that the dividing line has moved. When: A feature's position differs from its position in an older description. Why: The shifted fixture reveals that the boundary changed over time.
- [heuristic] Food packaging or containers left at a scene suggest the victim was not alone.
- [heuristic] A small loss becomes decisive once it is linked to a suspect's access, especially a recent visit that explains how they could take it. When: A shortage is found after a suspect visited the storage. Why: Access explains the loss, so the small shortage points to a person.
- [heuristic] If someone's belongings appear where that person could not have been, someone else probably wore, carried or placed them.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the belongings or found set against its expected composition or equipment. 2) Re-check the absence before concluding it is real. 3) Ask where it could have been taken, not whether it was ever present. 4) Search likely locations and infer its place from nearby context. When: an alibi depends on equipment, or a found set has known composition. Why: an absent item may have been removed after use.
- [procedure] 1) List objects missing from where they should be. 2) Fix one defensible premise, such as that the object has left the area. 3) Work out how and when each could have left, testing each route against physical logic and what each possible carrier was visibly wearing. When: a scene has absent objects and observed constraints limit the possible routes. Why: A workable exit route can expose a staged removal; routes failing visible constraints can be eliminated.
- [tradeoff] Reasoning from one missing item stays tractable, but when many items vanish at once, the constraints multiply and the chain of inference becomes hard to follow. When: Several items are missing together. Why: Each missing item adds constraints that must be checked.
- [pitfall] Moving or tidying a body, objects or scenery erases posture or original-position evidence and can mislead about where and when objects were used; examine and record in place first. When: when a body or scenery is rearranged before examination. Why: the original arrangement may be needed for the clue.
- [pitfall] Landmarks and boundaries can shift or be redrawn, and names attached to them may be recent, so an old name or boundary may not match the current one. When: when relying on a named landmark, dividing wall or bound tree from old records. Why: features shift, decay or get redrawn, and labels can be added later.
- [pitfall] Exclusion fails if one option is left off the list; an overlooked gap can be the true answer.
- [pitfall] Assuming an expected object was never present, when it was removed afterwards, overlooks the simplest explanation. When: an expected object is missing from belongings. Why: removal leaves the same absence as non-existence.
- [pitfall] Without elimination prints from household staff and family, innocent people's prints look like those of an unknown party. When: Analysing prints on objects handled by many people. Why: Unidentified prints get mistaken for an outsider's.
- [pitfall] Items missed by a thorough search can turn up later, so scenes and clothing already searched should be rechecked as the theory develops. Why: A search can miss objects hidden in pockets or out of the obvious path.
- [fact] A moved object returned to its place shows that someone handled the room after the event, but the move alone does not reveal who did it. When: An object is found displaced and later restored. Why: The disturbance proves handling without identifying the handler.
- [fact] Objects that are moved, scattered or hidden leave traces that a stated account may not explain. Why: Concealment requires physical actions that leave evidence.
- [fact] A moved object leaves a record at each handler, so following records from one handler to the next leads to the object.

## character evidence and reputation
- [model] Strong character evidence combines five kinds of source: the accused's written plea, a spouse's statement, a clergyman's oath, magistrates' affirmations, and a neighbors' petition.
- [definition] Character evidence describes a person's habits and disposition. It argues that a charge clashes with known conduct but does not disprove a specific event.
- [definition] A character certificate is a signed statement from people who knew the accused for years, attesting to good conduct.
- [mechanism] Attacking a witness's character targets the reliability of the accuser rather than the event being described. When: when a witness's account is challenged.
- [mechanism] Cross-examining a witness about a person's conduct and manners can build a counter-impression that makes a motive seem implausible. When: A prosecution rests on a motive of temper or jealousy. Why: A witness's picture of the person shapes how the jury judges whether that person would act.
- [behavior] Knowing a person's self-destructive tendencies makes a self-inflicted explanation a live hypothesis, so disposition can make one explanation more plausible than another. When: weighing theories about how a death occurred. Why: Known dispositions raise the likelihood of some explanations.
- [behavior] A witness who speaks freely about a side topic may reveal their attitudes, such as contempt for a group, without any direct accusation.
- [rule] Use established character to narrow suspects, treating the judgement as support, not proof; confirm with physical facts, since character cannot show how the act was done. When: when ruling a suspect in or out by traits, or when a motive reading points at one suspect. Why: a plausible character can still be wrong without physical evidence. (x2)
- [rule] Treat a mismatch between a suspect's known character and the act as a flag to investigate; excluding or accusing on that basis without a physical check risks wrongly clearing or implicating them. When: when the suspect's known behavior does not match the crime. Why: a mismatch may point to error or concealment rather than innocence.
- [rule] Make traits testable by showing the NPC acting against them, and tie each inferred trait to an independent clue, such as a physical or timeline fact. When: when designing NPC traits as puzzle clues, or before clearing or condemning a suspect. Why: character alone is a soft clue and cannot settle guilt; a second clue lets the player confirm a guess.
- [rule] A character who withholds a fact must have a believable in-world reason for doing so. Why: Unexplained silence reads as authorial convenience rather than character.
- [rule] Give an NPC an odd prejudice or rule that drives the quest's central choice. When: Designing a character whose attitude shapes the plot. Why: An irrational-seeming attitude can force decisions and create conflict.
- [rule] Record a suspect's past outbursts as character evidence that the player weighs as a reliability factor, not as proof.
- [rule] Give important NPCs an unusual, visible trait, such as a deformed hand or missing finger, so that a damaged or hidden body can still be matched to them. When: when a character's identity may need confirming later in the game.
- [rule] Record each character's weaknesses, hobbies and follies beside their official facts, so a motive can be matched to the right suspect. When: tracking many suspects or NPCs.
- [rule] Reject a theory that requires a character to act far outside their established temperament and habits. When: testing a suspect against a theory.
- [rule] Check each suspect motive against the NPC's established traits, and narrow the clue chain until only one solution fits that character. When: designing or solving motive and clue sets. Why: a solution consistent with character is the most probable one.
- [rule] Separate a person's character or status from the evidence; lack of success does not establish guilt. When: judging a suspect. Why: Status is not a finding.
- [rule] Accept character evidence only from someone who knew the accused well over a long period. When: when weighing a character witness.
- [heuristic] Habit testimony can weigh against violence, but clearing a suspect on temperament alone is unreliable, since a quiet nature can hide dangerous potential. When: when assessing a suspect's likelihood of violence. Why: character evidence lowers suspicion but does not prove innocence.
- [heuristic] Use a suspect's character and motive to rank suspects for checking, not to convict them, since character arguments are weak proof. When: Deciding who to investigate first. Why: Character inferences can mislead.
- [heuristic] A witness account that conflicts with what is known of the subject's character should be doubted until confirmed independently.
- [heuristic] When several people's complaints about one person contradict each other, each complaint weakens the others and the reputation becomes unreliable evidence. When: assessing a person's reputation from others' accounts. Why: conflicting claims cancel out.
- [heuristic] Character readings from letter shapes are interpretive and weaker than matching recurring forms, and observers may disagree about them. When: Judging a writer's temperament from a sample. Why: Shape readings depend on the reader.
- [heuristic] Distinguish controlled from open emotion; a speaker's restrained agitation can be stronger than another's loud distress.
- [heuristic] Check whether a suspect's reputation fits their account, and treat a convenient detail, such as a spouse's refusal, as a point to test. When: a suspect supplies a convenient explanation. Why: details that suit the suspect may be invented.
- [heuristic] A character's temperament can rule out a deliberate, elaborate plan, though it cannot rule out a sudden act of passion. When: An elaborate method suggests a calculating planner. Why: Impulsive anger produces spontaneous acts, not long-prepared schemes.
- [heuristic] Center the inquiry on one figure whose access and interest connect to the event, then check that figure's conduct closely. Why: A single connecting figure keeps the search focused.
- [heuristic] Judge whether a prime suspect's known character fits the crime separately from whether the evidence points at them. A fraud may still be unlikely to commit violence. When: When the suspect fits the motive but not the temperament.
- [heuristic] Consistent statements by the accused over time are harder to fake than a single outburst, so they count as character evidence.
- [heuristic] Use witness descriptions of a person's character to judge whether a document's unusual terms fit the person who wrote them. When: When a document contains odd or unexpected terms. Why: A known trait such as stubbornness can explain otherwise puzzling content.
- [procedure] 1) Hear an outside warning about your involvement. 2) Examine your own feelings honestly. 3) Set explicit rules that keep dealings strictly professional. 4) Let duty to the case outrank the attachment. 5) Check any exceptions made for favoured people. When: An investigator notices personal interest or affection for a witness, which can make a reading lenient or harsh. Why: Self-judgement is coloured by the same emotion, so outside views and fixed rules add checks; the evidence alone does not justify such leniency or harshness.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a companion to describe the person without polite restraint. 2) Ask for recent episodes such as quarrels and plans. 3) Note habits, grudges and how the person took offence. 4) Note the person's mood just before the event. When: Profiling a suspect through a companion's talk.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the costume and other fixed visible traits against the earlier image. 2) Check persistent features such as the face. 3) Offer an object that triggers memory. 4) Ask indirectly and read the response. When: A character cannot reliably state who they are and must be identified through objects and senses. Why: Recognition is a chain of matching steps, so confidence builds from several checks rather than one leap.
- [pitfall] A character argument or remark that someone is incapable of a deed is opinion, not evidence; with no link to physical evidence it can be dismissed as speculation.
- [pitfall] A reading of character can silently replace a reading of the facts and colour judgment of a person without establishing anything about the event.
- [pitfall] Judging a story true from the teller's foolishness, or an account true from its extraordinary people, substitutes character for evidence; suspicion from character or shock is insufficient for accusing. When: accepting a story on the teller's personality, or naming a culprit after a shocking event. Why: a clever liar could produce the same details; character and feeling cannot establish what happened.
- [pitfall] Appeals to the unknowability of a person's character can end an investigation too early, before motive or physical evidence is tested.
- [pitfall] A source's characterization of other people is not independent evidence about them.
- [pitfall] Building a theory on an assumed character type is speculation unless evidence shows the emotional tie existed.
- [pitfall] Character testimony can excuse as well as condemn, so keep the uses for mitigation and for establishing guilt separate.
- [pitfall] A summary calling a document full of a theme can be false when the quoted entries show no such content. When: Judging a secondary summary of a primary document. Why: Summaries can assert tone the actual text does not support.
- [pitfall] A plea of good character set against testimony, without fresh evidence, leaves the verdict in the accusers' favour. When: when the defence offers only reputation.
- [pitfall] Character testimony describes a person's general nature but does not prove a specific act, so it cannot settle a case alone. When: Testimony is offered to vouch for an accused person. Why: Judgment built on long acquaintance rests on observation, not on proof of the act.
- [pitfall] Judging a witness only by reputation discards useful content, while judging only by the transcript misses how the testimony was delivered. When: Assessing a witness's trustworthiness. Why: Both reputation and transcript give incomplete evidence.
- [fact] Character evidence cannot disprove a claim that the court refuses to examine.

## escalating threats
- [mechanism] Announcing a final threat in advance builds suspense toward a later confrontation. When: A boss or major threat is scheduled. Why: Anticipation raises tension before the threat arrives.
- [mechanism] Moving an inquiry to a higher body changes its authority, audience and stakes, so the transfer can shape the outcome more than the local events do. When: a case moves from local officials to a higher body.
- [mechanism] When a local jury refuses to convict, accusers may move the case to a higher tribunal with broader reach. When: a first venue fails to deliver the desired verdict. Why: Venue choice can decide an outcome that the evidence alone would not.
- [mechanism] Layering dangers of increasing severity, each followed by short relief, keeps tension climbing across an extended sequence without needing one big climax. When: danger must build gradually across an extended sequence.
- [mechanism] When an investigator lacks decisive proof, announcing the suspicions to an interested party can force a guilty person to confess, because the disclosure pressures them. When: Physical proof is absent, a deadline looms, and the suspects' loyalties, fears and self-interest can be judged. Why: Confession from an involved party is the only remaining source of the missing proof.
- [mechanism] An unexpected incident that repeats an earlier threat's symptoms with a new victim raises stakes and drives the audience toward the answer. Why: Repetition signals that the threat is ongoing and growing.
- [mechanism] Escalating warnings, each more direct than the last, raise stakes while leaving the target free to choose a response. When: An antagonist warns a target before acting. Why: Growing directness increases pressure without forcing the target's decision.
- [mechanism] A planned action that never happened, such as a planned change to a will, can still supply motive if its outcome would have helped or hurt someone.
- [mechanism] Remarks egged on by others escalate tension in a crowded scene, and the rising tension can be used to pace a reveal.
- [mechanism] When an accuser's account conflicts with the accused's denial, pressing the accuser for a more specific charge escalates the conflict instead of resolving it.
- [mechanism] Once accusers gain attention and public confidence, they have no safe way to retreat, so their motives shift and the affair escalates.
- [mechanism] A claimed threat from a jailed person increases restraint: if spirits could roam from jail, heavier chains were ordered whenever one was claimed. Why: each claimed threat justified stronger measures.
- [mechanism] Worsening conditions such as bad air or heat act as a timer: the longer a trapped character stays, the weaker they become and the greater the danger. When: A character is confined in a space with a rising hazard.
- [behavior] A searcher who fails to find the target tends to destroy more of the room as the search goes on, so the wreckage records the growing panic. When: a search repeatedly fails to find its target. Why: frustration grows with each failed attempt.
- [behavior] An interrogator whose answer disappoints tends to escalate pressure, such as tearing up a reply and threatening the captive, which signals desperation. When: a captive's answer disappoints the interrogator.
- [behavior] A threat the audience already expects still shocks when it arrives, so foreshadowing does not remove the impact of the event. When: a horror event has been announced or foreshadowed in advance. Why: dread about how the event will land persists after it is anticipated.
- [rule] Explicitly promise a later payoff to sustain expectation without revealing the answer, and deliver it at a known, reachable point. When: Holding an answer back for later in a story. Why: A stated promise keeps the question open, but only delivery justifies it.
- [rule] Have the NPC carry out a conditional threat when the player breaks the condition, because untested threats lose force on later encounters.
- [rule] Stage a puzzle as escalating contingency behaviours, such as escape routes and disguise attempts, that the player can follow to the culprit.
- [rule] Show a hazard openly before the player commits to the area, so it cannot be dismissed as an unfair trap. When: a room or path has a dangerous feature. Why: prior visibility makes the hazard a fair choice.
- [rule] Attach sound triggers or expected alarms to routine events, so the player can notice when a reaction that should happen does not. When: Stealth or investigation levels. Why: A missing reaction is only noticed when the player has a clear expectation of it.
- [rule] A glowing light in a dark area can act as a moving enemy's tell, rewarding players who stay still and read the signal.
- [rule] Make the antagonist's counterattack credible, such as threats or a claim that the investigator is unreliable, so it becomes a second conflict.
- [heuristic] State a specific prediction, such as when a key event will happen, to set a clear expectation that the next scene can pay off. When: Building anticipation toward a scene that will confirm or defeat the prediction. Why: A concrete expectation gives the audience something to watch for.
- [heuristic] A threat made publicly in anger is strong motive evidence, especially when the threatened act later occurs. When: Building a case around a suspect's stated grudge.
- [heuristic] Announce an expected visit in front of several characters, so their knowledge of the meeting is fixed before the crime occurs. When: A crime depends on who knew of a visitor and when.
- [heuristic] If someone announces in advance that they will reveal a particular culprit, treat the accusation as produced by the announcer rather than discovered. When: When an accuser promises to name a specific person before any evidence is shown. Why: A stated plan to name a target signals the accusation was intended, not observed.
- [heuristic] End an area on a half-seen threat so the player keeps moving toward it. When: an area should lead onward. Why: an unresolved threat pulls the player forward.
- [heuristic] Time a rising storm or other hazard to build as an investigation or boss approach nears, so the hazard acts as a visual tension meter.
- [heuristic] Hazards such as rotten boards and unstable stairs test a visitor's nerve, and each step should add tension. When: When designing a hazardous passage.
- [heuristic] Infer intent from a chain of escalating demands rather than a single outburst. When: When judging whether a grievance amounts to a motive. Why: A documented series of pressures shows purpose more convincingly than one emotional moment.
- [heuristic] Escalate hints from vague to specific across a story, so each step raises stakes before the explanation arrives. When: Building anticipation before a mystery's answer. Why: Gradual escalation keeps the audience engaged without giving the answer early.
- [procedure] 1) Claim evidence and watch the reaction. 2) If the suspect keeps refusing, threaten a formal search. 3) Keep courteous pressure until the suspect hands over the object. When: a suspect resists a bluff.
- [procedure] 1) Begin with a small, ambiguous threat. 2) Place each new threat closer to the target. 3) Increase its severity with each step. 4) Space the steps with gaps for reflection and evidence gathering. 5) End with a clear deadline. When: A threat must grow steadily and the audience needs time between escalations. Why: Rising intimacy and severity build dread while the gaps let the player gather clues.
- [procedure] 1) Shift the surface from chop to a directed current. 2) Make the water go still. 3) Raise a copper-colored cloud fast on the horizon. 4) Overcast the sky within two minutes. When: building a learnable warning sequence. Why: a fixed order lets players learn to read the warning.
- [procedure] 1) Name the leverage. 2) Refuse a small payment. 3) Demand a humiliating concession. 4) Set a short deadline. Each step weakens the suspect's resistance. When: a suspect is holding back a secret. Why: Escalation wears down resistance until a confession comes.
- [tradeoff] Announcing suspicions can harm an innocent person and warn the guilty, who may hide evidence or flee; the method rests on a fallible prediction of character. When: Using a disclosure as a last-resort pressure tactic. Why: The disclosure is public and cannot be withdrawn, and character predictions can be wrong.
- [tradeoff] A staged ambush can invert a suspect's identity rather than only add danger, but it reveals the hidden figure's role and may collapse the suspect list at once. When: Choosing how a hidden-character encounter should advance the mystery. Why: Using an ambush for identity reversal adds information, while using it only for danger adds tension without narrowing suspects.
- [pitfall] If gaps between escalating events are too long, tension sags or a wait with no incident frustrates; if events are too similar, they stop feeling new. When: Pacing an escalating sequence of threats. Why: Tension depends on both interval length and variation between steps.
- [pitfall] Promises the investigator cannot keep, including protection, undermine the case and end informant cooperation; a false promise leaves a grievance that can bring the witness back. When: Negotiating with a suspect or informant, or offering assurance to an informant. Why: A broken promise ends cooperation.
- [pitfall] Threats or warnings that are never followed up make the threat feel empty and waste audience trust, so every announced threat must be paid off. When: a warning or threat is introduced. Why: Empty threats reduce belief in later warnings.
- [pitfall] A promised reveal or announced solution that never arrives makes earlier delays read as padding and frustrates the audience. Why: The promised answer goes unsupported.
- [pitfall] When escalation outruns the available clues, players lose the thread; each new event should connect to the previous one. When: Designing a multi-step mystery with escalating events. Why: Players need a link between steps to keep tracking the threat.
- [pitfall] A flood of retroactive meaning can make earlier scenes seem more sinister than they actually were.
- [pitfall] An expected threat may never arrive, so a rumoured deadline can mislead a player as much as it creates tension.
- [pitfall] When examiners announce an outcome, observers' own perceptions can be overridden by the announcement. Why: Authority pronouncement outweighs direct observation.

## rumour reliability and verification
- [mechanism] A faction or NPC that disbelieves the player can be shown wrong through evidence the player gathers, proving the player's minority conclusion later. When: Designing NPCs who doubt the player's findings. Why: Gathered evidence turns a disputed conclusion into a verified one.
- [mechanism] NPC social routines such as gossip exchanges or community meetings can serve as channels through which the player earns introductions to target characters. When: Designing an insular community with social networks. Why: Routine social interactions naturally provide reasons and openings to meet targets.
- [behavior] A vain source may first mock or withhold information to enjoy the other's discomfort, then release it as a favour. When: Dealing with a status-conscious source who holds information. Why: Vanity makes the source enjoy displaying power over the questioner.
- [behavior] Hearsay gains the appearance of fact when it is repeated and when the speaker personally checks it, even if the original source is anonymous. When: Rumors circulate in a shared workplace or community. Why: Repetition and apparent verification lend credibility to unverified claims.
- [rule] Neighbourhood gossip about a person's strength or habits is hearsay, not proof; require physical evidence to corroborate it first. When: Evidence rests on reputation or talk rather than direct observation. Why: Secondhand talk cannot confirm what the speaker did not see. (x2)
- [rule] Do not treat gossip or an unverified report as evidence or verdict; treat it as a lead to test, since any link in the passing-on chain may be wrong. When: Early information is hearsay. Why: relayed claims lose accuracy as they pass between people. (x2)
- [rule] Treat gossip about relationships as a lead, not fact, until its source is verified; use it to choose what to check next, not as the basis for an arrest. When: Using acquaintance testimony about a suspect. Why: Gossip can be inaccurate or biased. (x2)
- [rule] Do not accept a source's claim on its word; have an independent observer check it in person or find an independent link to confirm or contradict it. When: a secondhand report affects a decision.
- [rule] Let NPC gossip or an insisting NPC present a wrong theory, and give players evidence to weigh so their findings decide which explanation holds.
- [rule] Give witness NPCs reliability values that drop with intoxication, fear, distance, poor lighting or date mismatch, so players must cross-check their statements.
- [rule] Give each NPC witness a reliability tag or level, such as sobriety or honesty, that raises or lowers how much testimony counts; players learn over time which to trust.
- [rule] Let NPC rumours spread through chains of NPCs, adding a slight distortion at each hop, so players must trace a claim back to its origin before relying on it. When: when generating an NPC gossip system. Why: distortion makes unverified claims unreliable.
- [rule] Record informal talk with its source, verify it independently against a record before relying on it, and weigh disclosure consequences; servants may repeat or exaggerate rumour. When: Information comes from informal talk. Why: Unverified gossip can be inaccurate or self-serving.
- [rule] Separate reported gossip from confirmed fact, and require corroboration before counting a rumored affair or debt as motive. When: A witness offers rumor about relationships or money. Why: Rumor can be false or exaggerated.
- [rule] Verify claims repeated in press reports, such as a stated family relationship, against independent sources.
- [rule] Confirming that a story's names, dates and sources are sound does not establish that the story itself is true. Why: Accurate details can sit inside a false or unproven account.
- [rule] Let NPCs protect or obstruct the player, so testimony must be weighed by the speaker's interest. When: Designing NPC dialogue that carries clues. Why: Interested testimony teaches players to weigh sources critically.
- [rule] NPC rumors can carry accurate facts, so give players world-state checks such as a stopped clock or a cold stove. When: when designing NPC testimony.
- [rule] Keep an NPC's reported interpretation separate from its raw observations, so players can reach a different conclusion from the same evidence.
- [rule] A trustworthy NPC gives specific details the player can check; an evasive NPC contradicts an earlier line.
- [rule] Model witness credibility through bystander NPC reactions that laugh at or dismiss a speaker, signalling how much to trust them.
- [rule] Track quarrels between NPCs in a reputation system, and flag a new accusation that falls near an old feud as suspicious to the player. When: when a game world contains NPC conflicts. Why: a link to an old feud gives the player a lead.
- [rule] Give each rumor a way for the player to test it, and store competing rumors in a log so the player can compare claims against physical evidence. When: Designing rumors that circulate in a town or household. Why: Testing lets the player separate rumor from fact.
- [heuristic] Let a paid informant sell partial or mixed true and false details; the player must verify a few before acting on the rest. When: Designing an NPC who sells information. Why: Partial verification lets the player estimate the reliability of unverified claims.
- [heuristic] Neighbours' gossip about lovers and bad character may be prejudiced or malicious, and can be used to cover other facts, so it must be checked. When: When rumour is the main source about a victim's conduct. Why: Gossip reflects social bias and can distract from real connections.
- [heuristic] Check whether a witness verified the source their claim relies on, such as a postmark or record, before accepting the claim. When: when a claim rests on a document or mark. Why: Witnesses often pass on claims they never checked.
- [heuristic] Use a family member's knowledge, such as the institutions they have used, as a starting point for narrowing where to check. When: when searching for a concealed person. Why: Close relations know habits and places.
- [heuristic] Treat a relayed witness report as a lead to verify rather than a fixed fact, especially when the teller admits uncertainty.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC a personal history the player learns in fragments, and let its resentments bias how the NPC treats suspects, so the player checks his account against the scene. When: When generating a dialogue-driven NPC who gives the player information. Why: A biased source forces the player to verify claims instead of accepting them.
- [heuristic] When told a person is somewhere, go and check the place yourself rather than accepting the claim. When: A claim about someone's location comes from an interested party. Why: Secondhand statements can be false.
- [heuristic] Test a claim against people who would have known the fact, rather than accepting it because someone reports it.
- [heuristic] A hearsay report with an unreliable tone can still contain a useful lead, such as an agitated visitor's enquiries. When: Evaluating gossip whose tone is biased. Why: Concrete actions and details can be accurate even when framing is not.
- [heuristic] A witness whose key claim rests on rumor is weakened once they must concede the rumor was only rumor. When: Cross-examining a witness whose key claim came from hearsay. Why: Admitting the source was rumor removes the claim's basis.
- [heuristic] Weigh vague gossip by the credibility of its speaker; a suggestive hint from an unreliable source should direct further questions, not establish a motive. When: when a rumour suggests a hidden relationship or motive. Why: Vague hints are easily misread and mislead if treated as established fact.
- [heuristic] Test a supernatural rumour first by asking whether the story matches how real people behave, before accepting any uncanny explanation. When: when a place or person is surrounded by lurid rumour. Why: rumours that no one who has been inside can confirm are often unfounded.
- [procedure] 1) Contact the place through a separate channel. 2) Confirm whether the named person is absent and who is in charge. 3) Record what remains unverified before acting. When: a tip names a place and a person. Why: an independent channel reduces the chance the sender controls the check.
- [procedure] 1) State the suspicion. 2) Find an independent reference that can confirm or deny it. 3) Build on the suspicion only if the reference confirms it. When: A suspicion comes from memory or intuition. Why: An unverified hunch can be wrong.
- [pitfall] Gossip can be wrong, garbled or incomplete, with similar names or places easily confused; its accuracy may only be confirmed after events.
- [pitfall] Gossip can spread faster than verified information, so a reputation built in one public setting may not reflect the facts.
- [pitfall] Gossip errs both ways: a true document can be rejected for bad reasons, and a false one can pass on the word of a sworn witness.
- [pitfall] Gossip about a suspect's temper can colour how others see him and bias the investigation. When: Witnesses repeat reputations rather than observed facts.
- [pitfall] Vague or amused witnesses add colour that may be unreliable, so useful details must be separated from embellishment.
- [pitfall] A vague excuse for knowing a restricted fact is not proof of guilt, since it may be innocent gossip.
- [pitfall] Gossip repeated as fact by one speaker can mislead, and a contested denial shows the rumor is disputed rather than proven.
- [pitfall] Attributing knowledge to a vague source such as the town names no channel and does not explain how the fact spread.
- [pitfall] A date taken from a single second-hand source can be wrong, so check it against another source before building a timeline on it.

## changing accounts
- [mechanism] One admitted fact can expose a related fact the witness did not intend to reveal, so each admission opens the next line of questioning. Why: facts in a case are connected, so confirming one narrows the others.
- [behavior] A stated reason often shifts over time; the first explanation is often incomplete, and a move from not knowing to a simpler reason suggests improvisation. When: A listener asks for the basis of a claim about motive. Why: The teller may have no real basis and improvises. (x2)
- [behavior] An answer that changes under repeated or small follow-up questions signals uncertainty, a bent fact, or an account fitted to a story. When: a witness is pressed on the same point more than once, or a small follow-up changes details. Why: A speaker who is unsure or hiding something revises the answer under pressure.
- [behavior] A coached witness repeats a fixed answer smoothly under gentle questions but breaks under sharp repetition, a change of language, or separate questioning, where co-witnesses contradict. When: a witness has been told what to say, or several witnesses were given the same script. Why: A memorized line is comfortable only while the question stays familiar; it breaks under follow-up questions.
- [behavior] Bystanders tend to accept an official's confident pronouncements without challenge, so the confidence goes unexamined within the scene. When: an official speaks with confidence in a group. Why: social deference discourages questioning.
- [behavior] Defenders often rely on character testimony describing a long, known way of life when no accuser or evidence is named, since reputation becomes the remaining counterweight. When: when an accused has no physical defense and accusers are unnamed. Why: a respected record of conduct is the only evidence left to offer.
- [rule] Do not build a reconstruction on unchecked second-hand claims; hearsay gains authority through repetition, especially when it points an investigation one way. When: when rumours from servants or bystanders circulate. Why: unverified claims gain authority through repetition. (x2)
- [rule] Present an NPC's unverified feeling or report as a weak lead the player must corroborate with a second clue before it becomes fact; it may be wrong until checked. When: When an NPC reports a feeling or impression no other evidence supports, or supplies information about a suspect. Why: Uncorroborated impressions are not hard evidence and can mislead the player; checking makes the report a lead rather than a fact.
- [rule] Do not rely on a companion's account when they are likely coached or protecting the suspect, since it may be a constructed alibi. When: a witness has motive to shield the suspect. Why: Protective accounts can be fabricated.
- [rule] Design informant interrogations so each answer unlocks the next question and points to a new lead. When: When designing an informant scene.
- [rule] Flag a witness who recites details already circulated as coached, so players can detect planted testimony.
- [rule] Flag a witness NPC's account that depends on a vision as uncorroborated, and withhold any verdict until a physical trace supports it. When: Designing a witness whose claim only they could perceive. Why: Players accept a verdict only when evidence they can check supports it.
- [rule] A source that cannot be questioned or held to account must not be accepted as a witness, even if it offers an oath. When: when deciding whether to accept testimony from a supernatural or hidden source. Why: An oath has weight only when the one swearing can be examined and judged.
- [rule] Do not accept a candid partisan's conclusions because his details feel vivid and honest; judge the conclusions separately from the details they report. When: the only surviving source comes from one side of a dispute. Why: Vivid detail can carry a conclusion the evidence does not support.
- [rule] Let a culprit NPC's dialogue shift as cover becomes belief, giving the player an account that changes over time to compare. When: Writing a culprit NPC whose attitude evolves. Why: A changing account lets the player detect the gap between performance and belief.
- [heuristic] Record each revision a speaker gives under pressure, including shifting motive, such as account, then denial, then partial admission; check each against others and physical facts before accepting the last. When: questioning presses a suspect or witness repeatedly. Why: Pressure produces successive versions; shifts between them are worth comparing. (x2)
- [heuristic] Ask whether an independent fact confirms an account; unconfirmed testimony stays a loose lead, not a finding, especially from witnesses with partial knowledge or a stake in the outcome. When: a claim cannot be checked against other evidence. Why: partial knowledge and personal stakes can bias the account.
- [heuristic] Give testimony concrete, locatable details or figures, such as an amount of money, which can be checked against physical evidence; vague claims cannot be tested. When: a witness gives concrete, locatable details, or when designing testimony players should test. Why: Specific details make false accounts easier to expose; a stated number can be confirmed or refuted.
- [heuristic] When a witness revises a time or gives a second account of the same evening, compare versions and record the change; a correction can hide an earlier statement. When: A witness gives a second statement that differs from the first. Why: Memory and motive can shift timing details between tellings.
- [heuristic] Secure a witness's signed statement while they are still committed, since a witness who has signed finds withdrawal harder. When: when a witness may change their mind. Why: Commitment makes retraction costly.
- [heuristic] A lead can be built from a chain of brief, partial sightings by different witnesses, each adding one fact, weighted by how well each could observe. When: The case depends on strangers who saw something briefly.
- [heuristic] A plan changed at the last moment often reveals the planner's reasoning, so note which flaw forced the revision. When: the culprit's plan was altered shortly before the act. Why: the revision exposes what the planner feared would fail.
- [heuristic] Treat a witness whose judgments of others reverse within hours as unreliable about character.
- [heuristic] When a witness claims a larger role in the events than before, treat that change as a point to examine rather than accept it. When: A witness's described role in events shifts.
- [procedure] 1) Hold an independent timeline. 2) Note slips such as shifting pronouns or compressed stretches. 3) Ask one clear question at a time about each omitted leg. When: a witness summarises events and the listener has a separate timeline to compare against. Why: Summaries hide gaps, and a direct question about a skipped stretch is what brings them out.
- [procedure] 1) Repeat the question in a firmer, more detached voice. 2) Rephrase it or switch to the witness's own language. 3) Ask who told the witness the answer and when. 4) Calm the witness before asking more. 5) Show knowledge of the core truth. When: A witness repeats a fixed phrase that seems rehearsed. Why: Each step removes comfort from the scripted answer and invites the real memory.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the recantation's wording with the accounts of the people it harmed. 2) Note whether it blames an outside cause. 3) Note whether it admits faults in the witness's own statements. When: a witness recants earlier testimony.
- [pitfall] Shifting testimony is weak evidence of guilt, not proof; nervousness, confusion or better recall can cause it. Check when each version was made and what the speaker then believed. When: a witness's statement changes or answers contradict under questioning. Why: Innocent people also produce changes and contradictions, possibly from an honest shift in belief about timing. (x2)
- [pitfall] An unchallenged account is not verified: silence may be strategic, and an unchallenged witness can still be wrong, so test it against the facts. When: a party leaves a witness account unchallenged. Why: Silence reflects no judgment on accuracy; lack of objection is not verification. (x2)
- [pitfall] An uncorroborated account, whether a suspect's bare denial or an honest witness's true testimony, can be dismissed just as easily, so a plea alone rarely settles where someone was. When: when a suspect offers only a bare denial or a witness's account lacks corroboration. (x2)
- [pitfall] Accepting a suspect's explanation or a witness's word as proof, without an independent check, closes the inquiry before the claim is tested; a common error.
