- [pitfall] Accepting a suspect's or household member's statement before checking it against the scene can build a case on claims that do not hold. When: a suspect's or household member's statement is accepted without checking. Why: unchallenged testimony can shape the official record.
- [pitfall] Accepting an event sequence or a conceded fact without checking its timing and surrounding steps against other evidence leaves the story only partly verified. When: when a suspect concedes one fact, or a witness gives a sequence of events. Why: surrounding steps and timing can still be false.
- [pitfall] Reading a person's state or temperament from appearance, expression or posture is a hypothesis needing corroboration; a confident detail given in haste from a dim encounter may need revision. When: a clue about inner state rests only on outward signs, or a first description comes from a brief or dim encounter. Why: Expression and posture are ambiguous and can mislead; hasty recall of minor details is unreliable.
- [pitfall] A claimed vision cannot be cross-examined, so its contradictions are easy to dismiss and its weight tracks audience trust and staging rather than facts. When: testimony that only one witness can perceive. Why: no one else can contradict it.
- [pitfall] A confession matching the accusers' claims is not independent corroboration, since questioners supply the content; where one group interrogates and applies force, no one can test it. When: A confession agrees with the accusation, or one group both interrogates and applies force. Why: the match may come from coaching; nobody is positioned to test the confession.
- [pitfall] A witness may reverse a story once they realise its danger, so record their first account before they learn why it matters. When: a witness's account could implicate the suspect. Why: Realising the stakes can change what they say.
- [pitfall] Obvious narrator unreliability with no later check reads as lazy writing; the contradiction must be something the player can actually test. When: Designing a narrator whose account is meant to be doubted. Why: Untestable contradictions give the player no way to confirm the gap, and unchallenged self-exculpation loses the fair-play signal.
- [pitfall] Accepting an answer without asking how it is known, or letting emotion or digression replace the answer, weakens the interview.
- [pitfall] A partial account later revised can leave the audience with a wrong picture of what happened.
- [pitfall] Trusting an account of a past case without checking its record can import false facts into the present investigation.
- [pitfall] Failing to ask a witness about every person they noticed leaves a gap that one simple follow-up question could have closed.
- [fact] Character testimony establishes habits, character and motive, not how an act was done or whether it occurred; once the act is established, it shapes how intent and punishment are weighed.
- [fact] An uncorroborated statement from a dying person is open to challenge, and its weight depends on a second witness.
- [fact] An accused person connected to respected families often gains neighbors and clergy who speak for their character. When: When a family with social standing is accused. Why: Social ties mobilize defenders.

## misdirection types
- [mechanism] Reversing who threatens and who is threatened hides the motive: a character who seems to threaten the protagonist is revealed as the victim. When: when the audience holds a strong expectation about a relationship or a late reveal reverses perceived danger. Why: A coherent wrong theory is accepted in place of checking hidden dynamics, and earlier choices are recast once the threat is reversed. (x2)
- [mechanism] A sudden movement or noise in the dark reveals the observer's position, so the intruder may flee before being seen.
- [mechanism] A sound such as a cart heard at speed makes a household look outward, away from the house where the real act occurs. When: An ambiguous noise occurs near the scene. Why: People interpret sounds through the context already in their minds.
- [mechanism] A culprit may spread suspicion across several people, so investigators holding conflicting evidence split their attention away from the real actor. When: Several suspects have plausible but conflicting evidence against them. Why: Equal weight on many suspects dilutes focus on the one who actually acted.
- [mechanism] A secondary mystery can absorb the audience's attention, and reframing it midway shifts the focus onto the real answer. When: layering two linked mysteries in one story. Why: The audience invests in the first question, so reversing it redirects belief toward the hidden truth.
- [behavior] Audiences weigh conspicuous facts, such as a payment, showy accessory or boastful talk, over quieter clues like an object's construction; look beneath them. When: a conspicuous fact is presented early or a character volunteers attention-grabbing details about an item. Why: Striking facts draw attention away from the underlying cause and decisive link, so attention fixes on apparent meaning rather than function. (x2)
- [behavior] Plausible false targets, such as a familiar cause or an early living suspect, absorb attention and worry, so the real danger goes unexamined and arrives unexpectedly. When: A real threat is present but a more familiar cause or an early living suspect is available. Why: Plausible false targets absorb worry and attention that the true source of danger needed.
- [behavior] Readers accept a claimed security guarantee and dismiss a watching character when a confident expert declares the system impregnable, so clues placed there are easily overlooked. When: clues are planted early and a character dismisses them. Why: confident dismissal by an authority lowers the reader's suspicion of what is dismissed.
- [rule] Withhold the solution or a fact only if every clue needed to deduce it is shown on the page or in the game. When: when delaying a mystery's answer or designing a twist or hidden solution. Why: Hidden clues make the answer unfair and unreachable; a missing fact must be given first.
- [rule] Show a deduction's reasoning clearly enough to be checked; withhold reasoning only if the detective's full explanation is given later. When: revealing a solution to a mystery or a deduction is kept back. Why: Unexplained leaps make the solver appear to have supernatural insight, and an unexplained deduction feels like a cheat if never revealed.
- [rule] Use a supernatural explanation as a red herring, but keep visible physical traces pointing to a human actor so the eventual reveal feels earned, not a trick. When: when a level or mystery offers a supernatural explanation for events. Why: Traces that contradict the supernatural reading reward close looking, and a visible physical clue makes the natural solution feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [rule] Let a supernatural or unverifiable clue, such as a dream or ghost's word, open inquiry, but require a second observer or physical trace before accusation. When: Designing investigation or accusation systems. Why: Physical traces or independent witnesses keep unverifiable clues from ending an investigation alone.
- [rule] Pair an ambiguous gaze or object-focused hint with a second, checkable clue so players are not misled. When: Designing NPC hints that players must interpret. Why: A lone ambiguous tell can send players down false paths.
- [rule] Every superstitious explanation an NPC offers should come with a fair check the player can run. When: Designing NPCs who suggest supernatural causes. Why: Misdirection stays fair only if it can be tested.
- [rule] Strangeness becomes a problem only when nothing independent supports the claim; judge the support, not the oddness alone. When: when assessing an unusual witness account.
- [rule] Do not use darkness to hide clues the reader needs to test fairly; keep needed evidence visible enough to check. When: mystery scenes. Why: hidden evidence cannot be tested.
- [rule] A sympathetic NPC who misleads is designed misdirection; reward players for testing claims rather than trusting character warmth.
- [rule] Frame physical clues inside a supernatural premise so they read as part of the mystery rather than as its solution. When: when designing a mystery where the player might otherwise solve the case early. Why: The supernatural frame makes physical evidence look like atmosphere, so players underweight it.
- [rule] Hide the decisive clue inside a conversation or joke so the audience hears it without weighing it. When: when a clue must be present but not yet recognized as important. Why: attention is spent on the banter, so the clue passes unexamined.
- [heuristic] Check physical origins and possibilities before accepting a supernatural cause for a striking object, sealed scene, or loss; people otherwise skip ordinary inquiry. When: a scene appears sealed or a loss or damage has no obvious cause. Why: A mundane path is easily overlooked when a dramatic cause is assumed first. (x2)
- [heuristic] Ground each misdirect in a real fact, such as a visit or borrowed item, so the false alternative is credible; weak alternatives deceive no one. When: when designing a misleading explanation or red herring. Why: Players weigh only credible alternatives, and misdirects grounded in true facts reward careful reading when overturned. (x2)
- [heuristic] Before accepting a plausible explanation or single-clue reading, ask what it accounts for and leaves unexplained, and check it against other evidence. When: a conclusion rests mainly on appearances or a single clue suggests a tidy explanation. Why: Plausible stories can point investigators at the wrong explanation; surface resemblance does not confirm it, and the gaps reveal red herrings.
- [heuristic] Seed a plausible wrong theory early, before the solution, and label it as misdirection so players cannot tell whether it is true. When: planning the reveal of a mystery. Why: This gives the design a fair-play structure; an unresolved alternative keeps the player uncertain until the reversal.
- [heuristic] Front-load a misdirect, amplifying evidence against the false suspect openly, while planting the culprit's clues early in passing and holding the decisive physical trace until mid-case. When: Structuring clue distribution across the acts of a mystery. Why: Casually presented clues are discounted, while prominently displayed clues dominate the reader's suspicion.
- [heuristic] A surface explanation for a death can be presented as a verdict the player is invited to test.
- [heuristic] Hold a striking coincidence as an open lead rather than dismissing it or treating it as proof. When: an unexplained coincidence links to a theory. Why: it may be meaningful or merely chance.
- [heuristic] A scene's surface can support a neat, socially expected conclusion that is wrong, so look for a detail that fails to fit. When: a scene suggests a simple explanation matching the people's class or occupation.
- [heuristic] Include some strange details in a mystery, since ordinary crimes offer few distinctive features to deduce from, while unusual details narrow the possible explanations. When: when designing a mystery's clue set. Why: Each unusual detail carries information that filters suspects.
- [heuristic] A surface's drying or wear pattern can expose a recent repaint and older marks beneath it, so read the pattern, not just the colour. When: a surface looks freshly altered or mismatched. Why: the pattern records how the layers were applied.
- [heuristic] Check a summons from someone linked to the target, since it may be a diversion that pulls watchers out of position.
- [heuristic] A blind, such as a visible line that appears to end elsewhere, misleads only observers who look at the wrong end. When: Concealing the true path of an operation. Why: Misdirection works only when observers attend to the decoy.
- [heuristic] Let a mundane explanation carry the misdirect, so the audience accepts it before the physical proof is shown.
- [heuristic] A character's stated fear can point the reader toward the wrong suspect, so the stated cause should be checked against other evidence. When: A character confides a fear about another person.
- [heuristic] Give an innocent suspect a prior criminal record, which makes their guilt look plausible and pulls the player's first suspicion onto them.
- [heuristic] Name plausible outside beneficiaries, such as rivals or foreign powers, to draw suspicion away from trusted insiders.
- [procedure] 1) Plant a misleading fact early. 2) Have a trusted witness fix it. 3) Let an authority dismiss a contrary clue. 4) Reopen that clue later through a lower-status witness. 5) Confirm with testimony and physical evidence.
- [tradeoff] Answers built from shown details are recognizable on reflection, while reveals that introduce unseen information surprise but cheat the audience.
- [pitfall] A supernatural explanation can lead players to dismiss a clue with a plain physical cause; keep the physical reading checkable. When: an unexplained sound is blamed on the supernatural. Why: Players may accept the ghostly reading without checking the sound's ordinary cause.
- [pitfall] A striking supernatural explanation distracts from and ends the search for a mundane one, so it should not be a last resort or be taken as proof. When: designing a mystery's resolution for a sealed-room puzzle. Why: A supernatural answer removes the need to reason about evidence, leaving the real answer undiscovered.
- [pitfall] Dismissing an object because its surface meaning seems obvious, such as treating a stained item as plain evidence against its owner, hides its real value. Why: The surface meaning is assumed rather than tested.
- [pitfall] Attributing harm to an unseen cause removes from view the human agents who relied on the claim. Why: The unseen cause draws attention away from the people who acted on it.
- [pitfall] Declaring an event supernatural to avoid explaining it costs the reader's trust, especially if the claim has no checks the reader can apply. When: Resolving a mystery with an impossible element. Why: Readers trust a puzzle more when its impossibility can be tested against evidence.
- [pitfall] A narrator's emphasis on one detail can be misdirection rather than a signpost, so the player must judge which it is. When: a detail is stressed. Why: emphasis looks the same in both cases.
- [pitfall] Strong insistence on one person's innocence steers attention away from other suspects and can serve as misdirection. When: a character is defended repeatedly. Why: repeated defence draws attention away from others.
- [pitfall] A simultaneous disturbance, such as a light going out during a sound, can cover someone's movement.

## travel and arrival timing
- [model] An arrival has five ordered parts: vehicle stops, passenger steps down, luggage left, knock, vehicle leaves. A witness can rebuild them as a timeline.
- [mechanism] Tracking whether a player keeps a promised meeting arranged through a public channel lets the game respond to that choice. When: A promised meeting is set through a public channel.
- [mechanism] An arrival made too early or too late can alter the target's behaviour, and the target may leave before the party arrives, defeating the plan. Why: The plan assumes the target stays put until the chosen moment.
- [mechanism] A fixed departure time forces a scene to end early, so a fixed schedule acts as a ticking clock that shapes how characters behave.
- [mechanism] Environmental states like weather gate when an action is possible, and can hide or expose objects.
- [rule] Within a gap between two confirmed events, measure walking time between the locations; travel time limits what a person could do and can rule a route in or out. When: Judging whether a person could act or travel during a gap between two fixed times at different places. Why: Travel time limits what movement is physically possible within the gap. (x2)
- [rule] Check the route length between the suspect's location and the scene, since a short side exit can make a trip feasible within a small window. When: When a trip must fit a short window. Why: Shorter routes make brief absences plausible.
- [rule] Plan a witness's arrival from published schedules rather than guessing, so the meeting time is known in advance. When: A witness is travelling to meet an investigator. Why: Calculated arrivals allow the investigator to prepare the meeting without waiting.
- [rule] Log every quest-relevant transaction with a timestamp so players can rebuild what was owed or promised on any given day.
- [rule] Let a note arrive through a messenger the player never clearly sees, so attribution rests on the note's content. When: Designing anonymous delivery.
- [rule] Gate puzzle solutions by in-world travel time, so an NPC cannot be in two places within the game clock and players can test accusations against it.
- [heuristic] A traffic-based check can show a hiding claim is implausible, but it cannot prove when an object was placed.
- [heuristic] A trace found by tracking can explain an otherwise unaccounted movement, such as a return made by an indirect route.
- [heuristic] Compare a suspect trace with a record of the scene from before the event. A mark absent from the earlier record must have been added afterward. When: When a trace is suspiciously convenient or a pre-event scene state is available. Why: A mark absent before the event cannot have been made by the event itself.
- [heuristic] Station a watcher at a transit point to log arrivals and departures, and place the watcher where travellers actually pass. When: tracking who comes and goes.
- [heuristic] Delay explaining a twist until players hold the same clues as the protagonist, keeping the reveal fair.
- [heuristic] The gap between a call and an arrival bounds how long a witness could have spent elsewhere. When: checking an alibi against response times. Why: the time gap limits the window in which the witness could have acted.
- [heuristic] Compare a player's stated route or time against logged events, so an NPC's question can hinge on a fact only that player could know.
- [heuristic] Include routes the investigators themselves used earlier; these are easy to overlook yet can be the real access path. When: a death or disappearance has no obvious access point. Why: familiarity makes a used route seem already ruled out.
- [heuristic] Wheel marks and trampled ground around a spot show that a vehicle was backed up to it.
- [heuristic] Travel times, such as a walk plus a scheduled train, fix when a person could have departed or arrived. When: A movement must be placed within a time window. Why: Scheduled transport gives a hard constraint on movement.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the times the suspect was known to be elsewhere and note the claimed departure place and time. 2) Estimate walk or travel time for each leg to the next claimed place. 3) Add the legs and any meeting length. 4) Compare the total with the time elapsed or gap available, checking whether the claimed arrival is physically possible. When: Testing whether a suspect's claimed route or timed alibi fits the available window.
- [procedure] 1) Stage a transfer with an insecurely locked van door, or offer a timed opening in a transport section. 2) Track the prisoner's response and choices as clues to intent. 3) Accept the risk of a real escape chance. When: A prisoner's response to an opening is informative and the transfer or section can be staged safely. Why: Timed openings let player and NPC choices reveal intent; a suspect who takes the chance may reveal a plan.
- [procedure] 1) Measure the total gap between two known times. 2) Subtract fixed intervals such as intermissions. 3) The remainder is the time available for the trip and any act. When: When checking whether a suspect could leave and return during an event. Why: Fixed intervals reduce the free time a movement must fit into.
- [procedure] 1) Transfer the captive to another prison before release. 2) This cuts off warnings from outside friends. When: Preparing a controlled release. Why: Distance from allies prevents warnings during surveillance.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each character's sightings and sounds. 2) Order them in time. 3) Check whether any character could have been in two places at once. When: testing alibis.
- [procedure] 1) Name the trace that seems to prove something. 2) Ask whether it was left before, during or after the event. 3) Write what each timing predicts for other traces. 4) Keep the timing that other traces support.
- [procedure] 1) List each specific physical detail a witness gives about a route. 2) Walk the route yourself. 3) At each named point, search for the predicted objects or marks. 4) Note the order in which they appear. When: a witness describes a location and an event that can leave traces. Why: checking predicted marks tests the account against the ground.
- [procedure] 1) Time the real trip between the two locations. 2) Compare the measured time with the claimed window. 3) Conclude only that the movement was feasible, not that it happened. When: A suspect's movements depend on travel time. Why: A timed route shows possibility, not use.
- [procedure] 1) List every role a person holds across the case. 2) Order those roles by stage. 3) Check for a shift from witness to accused and trace the path to the outcome.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the procedure that filled the post. 2) List each candidate and how each was declined or passed over. 3) Note who was excluded at each stage. When: analysing a contested appointment.
- [metric] A stated arrival is possible only if verified distance divided by realistic walking or running pace, lowered by fatigue, fits the time available. When: Testing whether someone could reach a place in time. Why: Independent travel records set a hard bound on movement.
- [metric] A claimed meeting is impossible if the travel time exceeds the window; a fifteen to twenty minute trip cannot fit a ten-minute window. When: Checking a timed alibi. Why: Physical travel time bounds what a witness could have done.
- [metric] Estimate travel time between two known points to infer where a person could have spent an unexplained interval. When: A person is missing for a stretch and the window of possible locations is needed. Why: Known travel times bound the places reachable within the gap.
- [tradeoff] A taxi leaves a traceable record while a bus or underground leaves less, so a careful suspect prefers the less traceable option. When: when a suspect chooses how to travel during a crime.
- [pitfall] Travel-time timeline tests depend on assumed mode and speed; establish how the person moved first, or present results as probabilities, not proof. Why: Travel time estimates depend entirely on the mode and speed of movement, and the method does not establish vessel type.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a route as impassable or merely unlikely, without checking the map, can eliminate the true answer or leave the real access path unexamined. When: Constraints are assumed rather than checked against the map. Why: Players and designers who skip verification lose valid candidates.
- [pitfall] Each stage of a concealment plan carries its own exposure, and moving a body is often the riskiest stage. When: When planning a multi-step cover-up. Why: Physical movement risks discovery by people who would otherwise not notice anything.
- [pitfall] Trusting the first recorded destination of an object can hide its real movement.
- [pitfall] An old name such as a simple track label can understate how developed a route became, and a newer name can hide an older track.
- [pitfall] A route dismissed without checking its timing makes the final solution look like cheating to the player.
- [pitfall] Travel estimates vary, so allow a few minutes more or less before calling a timeline gap suspicious. When: When judging whether a travel-time gap is suspicious. Why: Small variations in travel time are normal and would falsely flag innocent accounts.
- [fact] Prisoner transport is guarded by mounted escorts, warders in the van's passage and on the driver's box, and a holding cell at the courthouse.
- [fact] A person's movements across places, recorded in travel or passenger lists, can serve as timeline clues in an investigation.
- [fact] A stop during a timed trip leaves a window in which someone could slip in or out unseen, even if the driver noticed nothing.

## ambiguity in clues
- [model] An incident can be split into a real first phase and a later phase that was staged or misread. Witnesses may hear the second phase without seeing it.
- [mechanism] A single physical object, such as a footprint, can support two opposing readings, and the reading shifts as later objects are found. When: Writing evidence that must be re-interpreted during an investigation. Why: Holding the mismatch detail visible from the start lets the eventual reversal feel earned.
- [behavior] The same fact can support opposing conclusions depending on framing, so a clue tied to two places cannot single out either one. When: A clue points at a suspect and also at other possibilities. Why: Shared relevance to several candidates dilutes the inference toward any one of them.
- [rule] Leave a deliberate gap, such as a question an official never asks, that a second, more specific conversation or later quest can close. When: Designing an unresolved thread for later payoff.
- [rule] Leave one clue element unexplained, such as ink with no visible pen, until a later location, document or character resolves it, so the gap drives the player forward. When: Designing multi-location clue chains or pacing a mystery's reveals. Why: An open question sustains curiosity until a later location answers it.
- [rule] Treat a blotted, missing record or envelope as a designed gap the player must fill from another source, such as another NPC, object or records office. When: A key detail is missing from a written record. Why: Gaps force players to seek corroboration elsewhere.
- [rule] Plant an accident that can be either a trap or bad luck, and give both readings some visible support so the player must weigh them.
- [rule] Place a visible but misleading clue, and give the player a test that corrects the path, so the red herring teaches rather than wastes time. When: when designing a mystery.
- [rule] Let an NPC detail that seems to clear a suspect also fit a disguised culprit, so the player can work out the second reading. When: designing witness clues. Why: Ambiguity rewards careful reasoning.
- [rule] When two explanations fit the facts equally well, test which is true rather than adopting the first plausible one. When: A clue has two plausible readings. Why: A single wrong choice can send the whole investigation the wrong way.
- [rule] Ambiguity should come from the text itself, not from a character refusing to explain, and should be used only where the clue is meant to be unclear. When: Deciding how to make a clue uncertain. Why: Ambiguity from evasion feels like withholding, while textual ambiguity invites reasoning.
- [rule] Show unknown intervals in a game's record, such as a missing witness or unreachable log, so the player has a concrete gap to pursue. When: When designing mystery or investigation content. Why: A visible gap gives the player a next step, while a hidden gap gives none.
- [rule] Leave one ownership link deliberately unexplained, and let the player infer it from a related document. When: Designing a document-based puzzle. Why: Inference from a related record rewards players who connect documents.
- [rule] Have an NPC describe an item or room almost correctly, then let the player confirm it by finding the real item, rewarding cross-checking.
- [rule] A word an NPC emphasises on purpose can be a designed signal that the player is meant to notice.
- [rule] Use an accidental-looking mark, such as a scrape on a crate, as a hint, and define in advance what it means. When: designing environmental clues. Why: a mark the player can read consistently becomes a usable lead.
- [rule] Place ambiguous ornamental clues in rooms and let the player decide whether they matter.
- [rule] Pair each clue in an investigation journal with a counter-explanation, and keep it unresolved until a second clue supports the explanation. When: Designing a generated mystery or investigation journal. Why: Players need visible open questions that resolve through corroboration.
- [rule] Include one or two clues that resist every available explanation to serve as the deductive anchor of a generated case. When: Generating a mystery with several explainable clues. Why: A clue no explanation covers gives the case a fixed point for deduction.
- [rule] Chain clues through shops and staff lists, and use a trigger phrase so an NPC can signal the player without alerting a target. When: when designing multi-step investigations.
- [rule] Keep at least one piece of physical evidence ambiguous so the player cannot close every thread. When: Closing a mystery with a late reveal. Why: Leaving one clue unresolved preserves doubt and makes the solution feel less mechanical.
- [heuristic] Leave some props unexplained as later payoffs or a closing hook, and keep a quest log of open anomalies revisited as facts arrive. When: Designing a mystery with layered clues. Why: Open items keep the investigation alive and give the player reason to revisit earlier evidence.
- [heuristic] Choose even vague hints deliberately, since an ambiguous sign should still rest on a definite underlying form. When: writing suggestive clues. Why: vagueness without structure reads as noise.
- [heuristic] Offering two paths, telling the truth or facing a stated penalty, makes silence costly and pushes the suspect toward a choice.
- [heuristic] NPC claims can be designed to conflict on purpose, so the player must cross-check them against earlier dialogue to find the truth. When: Building a mystery plot with dialogue-based clues.
- [heuristic] Place a term with two meanings deliberately and reward the player who learns the specialist sense.
- [heuristic] Design case files so two conclusions both fit the clues, and place a clue that eliminates one only after the player has committed to considering both. When: Designing deduction puzzles with competing answers. Why: Players must weigh consistent evidence instead of spotting a single obvious answer.
- [heuristic] Build crime scenes so each trace supports or undermines a set of hypotheses, leaving some traces ambiguous to reward deduction. When: when designing a scene meant to be solved. Why: ambiguity forces the player to weigh evidence rather than read one clue.
- [heuristic] Pair two clues from one system with a third from a separate system to reward cross-referencing.
- [heuristic] Design clue sets so no single item solves the case, but combinations rule out some suspects, rewarding players who read the set as a whole. When: When designing investigative puzzles with many minor clues. Why: Combination reasoning requires the player to synthesise, not just find, clues.
- [heuristic] Place a locked-door detail mid-case; it can read as fear or as staging, and its meaning changes once the key holder is known. When: a locked room is part of the scene. Why: An ambiguous detail stays open until the key holder is revealed.
- [heuristic] An ambiguous clue can still establish a general fact, such as that a person is probably dead or that one of a small group handled the body. When: A clue does not identify a single culprit. Why: A clue can narrow the field without pointing to one individual.
- [procedure] 1) Give one clue, such as a residue that is poison or medicine, two plausible readings. 2) Place a second test or witness trace later that favours one reading. 3) Let the player resolve the ambiguity by finding it. When: When designing investigative clues in a level. Why: Two readings make the player weigh evidence instead of accepting the first answer; a single reading gives no decision to make.
- [procedure] 1) List every candidate who fits the shared name. 2) Weigh each candidate's place in the list, formal rank and seniority. 3) Weigh which names were left out. 4) Choose the best-supported candidate. When: A document names one person only by a surname shared with others of similar title. Why: A shared name leaves identity open, so context must decide.
- [tradeoff] A flawless public surface can be innocent or concealing; it only reveals the truth when the observer is away from the performer. When: Judging a suspect whose presence seems perfect. Why: Presence itself makes the performance persuasive, so independent observation is needed.
- [pitfall] An ambiguous remark gets fixed to the reading that suits a favored theory, especially when the speaker is absent to explain it, sending the investigator down the wrong path.
- [pitfall] Ambiguous wording can confuse innocent listeners as well as guilty ones, so a double meaning alone cannot show guilt.
- [pitfall] A deliberately incomplete record should not be assumed complete, since removed pages are an absence an investigator must account for.
- [pitfall] Storms, wind and old buildings produce sounds that resemble deliberate signals, so a heard noise should not be read as a signal without checking.
- [pitfall] A flawless offender makes the investigation feel arbitrary; the criminal needs a gap for the solution to feel earned. When: When designing an antagonist's plan. Why: Readers accept a solution only if the offender could have slipped.
- [pitfall] A witness's ambiguous answer can be recorded as a stronger statement than intended, so the transcript may not match what was said.
- [pitfall] Ambiguous phrasing may come from habit or self-deception rather than deliberate deceit, and the speaker may sincerely believe the claim. When: reading a suspicious statement. Why: Deliberate concealment is not the only cause of ambiguity.
- [fact] Doubt about how a legal rule applies can itself create a motive when one party gains if the doubt favours them.
- [fact] Detective fiction often gives a clue only one correct reading, whereas real clues often admit several readings.

## chain of custody
- [model] A trace's meaning depends on its chain of hands, the sequence of people who held it, and any link in that chain can be planted. When: a trace must be tied to a person. Why: Each handoff is an unverified step that may be arranged by someone else.
- [definition] Chain of custody is the recorded sequence of holders and locations of an object or document, which determines whether it can later serve as evidence. When: when a document or object changes hands. Why: Gaps in the record make the evidence doubtful.
- [definition] Provenance is tracing a found object back to its source by matching details such as type and edge wear.
- [mechanism] A written order transfers custody of a prisoner to a bearer and relieves the original keeper of responsibility until the prisoner returns. When: A prisoner is moved between sites. Why: Formal transfer shifts legal responsibility.
- [mechanism] If an object never left its owner, any theft involving it must have occurred before or after certain events, which constrains the order of the timeline. When: Reconstructing when an object could have been taken. Why: Custody limits which actors could have touched the object at each moment.
- [mechanism] A provenance record of past holders lets a player judge how reliable an item's identity and history are.
- [mechanism] An object's provenance can be traced through its chain of custody, from sale to one holder, to resale, to reclaiming, identifying each holder in turn.
- [mechanism] Confessed people kept in custody can be controlled and prevented from withdrawing their statements. When: a confessor is held after making a statement. Why: custody limits access to the confessor and their retraction.
- [mechanism] When a confessed person names associates, each new name can pull more people into the case, so suspects multiply quickly from one informer.
- [mechanism] A fictional witness can sustain a chain of false beliefs: first a lead, then a conspiracy, then a lure, and each stage collapses in turn. Why: Each stage holds the player's attention while exposing the next layer of deception.
- [rule] Record every handler, container and timestamp in an item's custody log, so swaps can be reconstructed; an item leaving custody unrecorded cannot be checked again. When: designing item provenance systems. Why: A full log makes swaps discoverable. (x2)
- [rule] Check a document's provenance, such as its envelope, postmark, prints, filing or handwriting, before relying on its contents or accepting its account of delivery. (x2)
- [rule] Do not treat an inferred chain as established until independent evidence, beyond a single testimony, supports each of its links. When: When judging whether an evidence chain is reliable. Why: Independent verification guards against a single faulty source.
- [rule] Check an object's provenance against the account given, comparing dates and receipts, since the item may turn up somewhere the account says it could not be. When: when an object's history is part of a claim.
- [rule] Test a custody alibi by asking whether the confined person can still communicate with outsiders; confinement alone does not stop messages, accomplices or inside help. When: a jailed or distant suspect seems to rule out involvement. Why: A confined person may still act through others, so the alibi must be tested rather than accepted.
- [rule] Discount evidence whose provenance is unclear, such as an item with no traceable date or a finder who could have placed it.
- [rule] A found object is not automatically the lost one; its chain of custody must be shown before it is treated as the same object. When: A replacement or recovered object is presented as evidence. Why: Objects can be swapped or confused, so provenance must be established.
- [rule] Check who moved or touched a body before attributing stains or marks to the attacker, since helpers can leave marks that look identical. When: Blood or marks are found on a body or its clothing. Why: People who carry a body can transfer blood and leave marks resembling those of an attacker.
- [rule] Run a provenance check when a source's only support is its own assertion, asking where its material came from. When: a source's sole support is its own claim.
- [rule] Collect each sample in its own labelled container tied to its exact location, so later tests remain traceable to where it was found. When: Collecting residue or other trace material.
- [rule] Before accepting an object as evidence, confirm it stayed in a secure place and check who had access to it before the event.
- [heuristic] Trace the chain of hands an item passed through, since each handler may hold the next clue and their traces reveal how many hands it passed through.
- [heuristic] Model bodies as quest items with a recorded chain of custody, so the player must trace each transfer to reconstruct what happened. When: When a body or artefact moves between locations or people in a game. Why: A recorded custody history makes transfers traceable and gives the player a path to follow.
- [heuristic] Use initial-only signatures and recognisable handwriting so players can match a sender across multiple documents. When: Designing anonymous documents for players to link. Why: Recognisable traits let players connect separate clues.
- [heuristic] Assign a provisional name to a set of traces as a hypothesis, and drop the name once the evidence contradicts it. When: Traces point to a person but their identity is not confirmed. Why: A working label organises the evidence while staying open to revision.
- [heuristic] Ask why a source sent a warning at all. Silence might have invited scrutiny that endangered the sender.
- [heuristic] An object's provenance, such as a previous owner's mark, is weak but real evidence linking it to a person, to be weighed with other facts.
- [procedure] 1) List each handoff in order with its holder. 2) At each handoff, ask who had access to it. 3) Mark every span when the object was out of anyone's view. 4) Check each holder's memory of its state. 5) Test each handler's denial against the other handlers' accounts. 6) Identify a plausible reason for each transfer. When: when an object's location, presence or identity changed between points and must be explained. Why: Each handoff is a point where the object could have been swapped, diverted or moved unnoticed.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the printed fragment on the document. 2) Match it to stock taken in a known theft. 3) Link that theft to a place. 4) Trace the route the document took from there. When: Tracing where a document or object came from.
- [procedure] 1) Supply the pen yourself. 2) Have each person who handled the object sign or mark the page bearing the trace, in small writing. 3) Take custody only after signing. 4) Keep the signed page with the object. When: an object with a trace may become evidence. Why: Fixes its state at handover, so later tampering claims can be answered and signing stays under your control.
- [procedure] 1) Ask where the object was kept. 2) Ask who could have taken it. 3) Ask when it was last used. 4) Link the answers into a chain of handovers and mark each gap as a possible access point. When: Establishing who could have used a key, bag or weapon.
- [procedure] 1) Place a small, ordinary-looking mark on an object before it leaves your control. 2) After its return, check the mark to confirm the object was away. 3) Verify that nothing was swapped or missing. When: When evidence can be taken or swapped out of sight and custody must later be proven. Why: A prior mark is the only reliable record that an item was moved, and an obvious mark invites reproduction.
- [pitfall] A seller may recall a purchase but not its purpose; buyer identification is only as good as fading memory, so treat it as probable and ask about appearance and companions. Why: Recall degrades and can be filled in by expectation.
- [pitfall] A custodial condition without a believable reason reads as a convenient delay and undermines the reveal.
- [pitfall] Assuming an object stayed with its owner can build a wrong timeline, and uncertain custody must be verified before it constrains the order of events. When: Reconstructing a timeline from object custody. Why: Unverified custody leads to a wrong order of events.
- [pitfall] Official pressure may tempt a custodian to open sealed evidence early, which defeats the purpose of the delay.
- [pitfall] A chain of custody is unreliable if earlier handlers searched or altered an item before handing it over.
- [pitfall] Taking an object without recording its origin leaves a gap in its chain of custody, so later claims about it cannot be verified. When: When an object is moved or collected during an investigation. Why: Without origin records, the object's history cannot be proven.
- [pitfall] A room kept locked after an event leaves open who entered it while it was shut, weakening the chain of custody. When: A scene is sealed after an incident. Why: Unrecorded access breaks the record of who could have altered the scene.
- [fact] Under the procedure governing accused persons, the investigating magistrate may impose measures such as solitary confinement for the prosecution's interest, within a legal framework of state custody. When: Deciding how to hold a suspect during an investigation.
- [fact] A chemical reagent that reacts only to a blood protein separates blood from look-alike stains such as mud, rust or fruit juice.
- [fact] A suspect's death in custody can close a case without trial, leaving beliefs about earlier crimes unproven.
- [fact] Tracing a chain of strangers depends partly on luck and partly on sustained effort, since the right person must be found at the right moment.
- [fact] A sender's signature, handwriting and wording can identify them across documents, even when the letter comes through an intermediary.

## witness testimony limits
- [definition] A limited witness narrator observes and reports a scene but sees less than the investigator and may misjudge the method, so the account reflects the witness's blind spots.
- [mechanism] The information a public source can report depends on which witnesses are still available; if key witnesses vanish, the account is missing crucial details.
- [mechanism] Revealing later that a damaging testimony came from a witness with limited access rewards players who compare accounts.
- [mechanism] Observers can register details without conscious attention, and replaying a scene later can surface them, but only details that were registered at the time can be recovered. When: when a player or character passed through a scene without focusing on certain objects. Why: Recall depends on whether the detail was encoded at the time, so an unnoticed detail cannot simply be summoned on request.
- [behavior] Crowds, engine noise, screams and cross-talk drown out quiet speakers and key details, so listeners lose track of who said what and clues go unnoticed. When: Dialogue or a scene occurs over ambient, crowd or chaotic sound. Why: Attention is drawn to louder sources, so competing sensory input hides quiet speakers and the important detail.
- [behavior] A witness can report a detail without understanding its significance, so the detail may carry more information than the witness recognises. When: Interpreting a casual remark from a witness. Why: Observers record what they see without knowing what it means.
- [behavior] A witness whose states never share memories can truthfully forget what they knew in the other state, so their accounts conflict. When: a witness's knowledge depends on time or condition. Why: Separate states do not carry recollections across.
- [behavior] Players often see the link between scattered details only after an outside prompt, such as a name appearing in a document. When: after gathering clues but before connecting them. Why: Placing details side by side is what makes a hidden pattern visible.
- [behavior] An unconscious action in response to a cue, such as an instruction spoken without thought, can reveal memory that a conscious answer would conceal. When: A stated memory loss is doubtful. Why: Unthinking acts are harder to control than deliberate answers.
- [behavior] Observers overlook people carrying ordinary objects such as trays or wearing uniforms, treating them as background rather than as possible actors or movers. When: Service or staff figures appear in a scene. Why: Routine objects make a person's role seem unremarkable, so their movements are not recorded.
- [behavior] Under stress, witnesses may forget a detail that returns after hours, days or weeks. When: witness under stress. Why: Memory recall can be delayed, so revisiting a witness pays off.
- [behavior] A creaking floor or other sound reveals a presence before anything is seen, so sound can warn a character or player of danger. When: Sound is audible while vision is limited. Why: Hearing gives early cues when sight cannot.
- [behavior] Under sudden alarm, people make reflexive corrections, like shutting then reopening a door, and these visible actions can later reveal them. When: Under sudden alarm. Why: Panic drives repeated actions before reasoning catches up.
- [behavior] Attacks reported from sleep or half-waking are often nightmares shaped by bodily discomfort, heavy meals, unfamiliar lodging and fear. When: the witness was asleep or half-awake when it began. Why: perception is unreliable in that state.
- [behavior] Observers attend to a person's pleasant manner and miss a mismatch between it and where that person's attention actually goes. When: A friendly character's gaze keeps returning to one place. Why: Admiration for pleasantness hides the discrepancy.
- [rule] A single uncorroborated account is weak support; treat it as a lead and require a second independent clue, such as a physical trace or another witness, before resolving a case. When: A case rests mainly on one person's account of another's conduct. Why: A lone account can be mistaken, motivated or shaped by suggestion. (x2)
- [rule] Read a limited statement at its scope: a witness who could not observe a stretch cannot confirm or deny it, so a servant's 'heard nothing' says little about entry. When: A witness reports no sighting of a key event or route segment. Why: Silence from a witness who could not see the stretch is weak evidence on its own. (x2)
- [rule] Record what each witness can and cannot confirm: a hedge marks a memory limit, and a sincere 'I don't know' is not a denial but stops rumour filling the gap. When: Recording witness testimony, or a witness is unsure about a key point. Why: Admitted uncertainty prevents unsupported claims from filling the gap. (x2)
- [rule] Trust a witness's judgment only within what they could know, and ask what they do not know; certainty beyond that is not evidence. When: A witness offers views on a relationship or situation beyond their direct knowledge. Why: Limited contact limits what a witness can reliably report; someone who never met a partner can say little about the relationship.
- [rule] Reveal only the evidence a witness must answer and keep the key detail from everyone, since full disclosure or spreading word lets the witness shape the account. Why: Word spreads and shapes later answers; showing the whole case lets the witness shape the account.
- [rule] Limit a captive's means of reply, such as a gag, bound hands or only a note, nod or single word, so answers are short and precise. When: An interrogator must extract a single fact. Why: Players must ask precise questions to get useful answers, and answers stay pointed rather than free-ranging.
- [rule] Ask whether a witness read the whole record or only a summary, since a doubt carries weight only if the witness knows the full evidence. When: when the evidence is documentary.
- [rule] Record each witness's knowledge and bias in design data so players can judge how reliable each account is.
- [rule] Limit further arrests to cases of necessity, and restrict printed or public discourse that can feed quarrels. When: When an accusation spreads and detentions multiply. Why: Unchecked arrests and public debate escalate suspicion.
- [rule] Script a witness's sighting of a suspicious figure to stay ambiguous until a later check, such as an autopsy, overturns or confirms it. When: Writing an NPC testimony that the player must weigh. Why: A deferred check keeps the testimony open without making it false by default.
- [heuristic] Treat a witness's account of their route or events as partial, and probe a brief account of significant events with follow-up questions. When: Reconstructing where a person was from their own account, or a witness gives a short account of events they should know well. Why: Lapses of attention leave holes the witness cannot fill; brevity can hide omissions that a fuller account would reveal. (x2)
- [heuristic] Check how well each witness actually knows the person in question, and whether an identification rests on direct contact or only gossip or reputation. When: Weighing testimony about a person's character or identity. Why: Recent or biased acquaintance can distort a witness's account, and inferred identities may come from gossip.
- [heuristic] Too many missing or changed items in one scene drown out the important one, so include only the absences that bear on the question. When: designing a scene with several missing or changed items. Why: crowded clues make the key one hard to notice.
- [heuristic] A suspect who speaks at length gives the examiner more material to check, though a fluent or sincere account can still hide the central fact. When: When a suspect volunteers a long account. Why: Extended speech creates testable details, and sincerity does not confirm truth.
- [heuristic] A witness who guards their own words often still volunteers history about their relatives, lodgers and associates.
- [heuristic] A witness who admits they cannot swear to an identity is more credible than one who insists on it.
- [heuristic] A witness with limited memory can still reliably report an absence, such as that a certain request was never made, which narrows the search. When: A witness cannot recall a specific person but is sure of what did not happen. Why: An absence of action can be remembered even when individuals are not.
- [heuristic] Check what a witness's claim rests on, such as observed behaviour, rather than what the people involved said. When: A witness states a conclusion about a relationship. Why: Conclusions drawn from observation may not match the parties' own accounts.
- [heuristic] Deliver sudden news of a death and watch for an immediate, unguarded outcry; a natural shriek and protest suggests genuine ignorance rather than an act. When: testing whether a witness already knows the truth. Why: unguarded reactions are too natural to be easily staged.
- [procedure] 1) Separate what the witness saw from what they heard or inferred, keeping observed facts apart from inferences. 2) Identify which sense supports each identification. 3) Ask negative questions to find the limits of their knowledge. 4) Cross-check details against independent facts. When: Assessing a witness's identification of a person, or reporting something they could not fully observe. Why: A claim is only as reliable as the sense and circumstances behind it; reasoning from inferences as if observed leads to errors.
- [pitfall] Investigator cues, including naming a topic, can plant ideas or steer a witness toward a choice; record which details came from the witness and which from the investigator. When: An investigator names a topic or guides a witness toward a particular person. Why: A witness may look where directed and confirm the cued choice, so the result may reflect the prompt as much as memory.
- [pitfall] A casual glance misses small anomalies, such as cut or pasted labels, that only close, magnified, methodical inspection reveals; casual viewers take surface appearance at face value. When: Inspecting an object that looks ordinary at a glance but may carry a trace. Why: Key anomalies are small and visible only under close checking.
- [pitfall] A witness can be sincere yet have limited access, such as seeing someone only at work; sincerity does not extend their knowledge beyond that access. Why: honesty does not supply missing observation.
- [pitfall] Witnesses use related words loosely, so a general term may stand for a more specific physical state than they actually saw. Why: Everyday words blur distinct conditions.
- [pitfall] A witness proves an item existed at a time, not where it is now, and does not prevent concealment over a long period. Why: Time allows an item to be moved or hidden.
- [pitfall] A witness kept uninformed about a task's purpose may later repeat what they saw, which weakens secrecy. When: when witnesses are used to hide an operation. Why: Those kept in the dark may talk to others.
- [pitfall] An apparently empty window may still be watched by someone who did not notice, so roles and attention matter as much as presence. When: Judging whether a window was unobserved. Why: People present but inattentive do not register events.
- [pitfall] A corroborating light or witness covers only one household or area, so it does not confirm wakefulness across the whole group. When: when one witness's observation is used to vouch for many people. Why: Corroboration applies only to what that observer could see.
- [fact] A witness with limited hearing may report only that something was noticed, so accounts of sounds carry limited weight.

## coincidence
- [mechanism] A staged death can collapse through a chance discovery by someone who suspects the truth and turns to blackmail. When: a witness or servant notices an inconsistency. Why: a suspicious observer can become a source of pressure on the plotters.
- [mechanism] A repeated chance encounter that sets a suspicion flag lets players treat the coincidence as a clue. When: Repeated meetings with the same NPC occur in a scene. Why: The flag converts an ordinary repetition into a signal the player can act on.
- [mechanism] A chance sighting can supply a lead that patient work had not produced, opening a new line of inquiry.
- [rule] Let a lucky break close the final gap only after sound deduction has narrowed the field, as many solved cases do, so the reveal feels earned.
- [rule] Record small coincidences as possible links to test, not as proof of guilt.
- [rule] Do not reject a lucky break as false merely because it is lucky; examine it on its evidence.
- [heuristic] Before linking suspicious elements or treating a coincidence as meaningful, test whether it is real against independent evidence. When: When two facts line up unexpectedly or two suspicious elements seem linked. Why: Chance alignments are common and can mislead an investigation. (x2)
- [heuristic] Use chance to open a case or turn a plan, but do not let it carry the whole solution. When: Designing how a mystery is solved. Why: Chance supplies openings, while the solution needs deliberate evidence.
- [heuristic] Before accepting a timing as chance, ask who could confirm it was chance, since arranged timing can look accidental.
- [heuristic] Two near-identical crimes by different groups in the same place and time are less likely than one common cause, so a known event can count against a suspected link.
- [heuristic] Build a case from several independent links that point to the same conclusion, since any single coincidence can be explained away. When: Assembling an inference from circumstantial facts. Why: The strength of the inference lies in the series of links, not in one.
- [heuristic] Plant key clues as apparent coincidences, then reread them later as links once the explanation is revealed. When: Clues must not give away the solution early. Why: Readers dismiss a clue as chance, so it only clicks into place after the solution is known.
- [procedure] 1) List every explanation for an event. 2) Count the improbable events each explanation needs at once. 3) Reject explanations requiring several unlikely events together, and keep the rest. When: When several explanations remain and probability can separate them. Why: Explanations that depend on many coincidences are less likely than simpler ones.
- [metric] Finding one specific person by chance in a large city is treated as roughly a thousand-to-one long shot, so it should not be the basis of a plan. When: Weighing a clue that depends on coincidence. Why: Chance encounters are too unlikely to rely on.
- [tradeoff] Added features matching a precedent lower the chance of accident and raise confidence, but an explanation needing more coincidences grows less plausible than alternatives. When: Several independent features match a precedent, or a rational explanation must cover many unrelated clues. Why: Many matches are unlikely to be accidental, yet each added coincidence lowers the explanation's plausibility. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Odd details need traceable causes, yet some unlikely details arise by accident; seeing design behind every coincidence dismisses real chance, so weigh each case. When: An odd detail seems unexplained, or a suspect's knowledge fits a crime too neatly. Why: Unexplained details often hide real causes, but unlikely details can arise by accident. (x2)
- [pitfall] Scattered or single matching dates are not a pattern; a pattern needs several independent matches, since chance alone can produce one matching date. When: When a player or designer infers a connection from dates. Why: Scattered dates can be chance; only multiple independent matches are persuasive. (x2)
- [pitfall] Convenient timing raises suspicion but is not evidence of intent; it may be lucky chance or engineered, so test it before concluding. When: An event coincides with a crime or conveniently helps a suspect. Why: Chance can produce advantageous timing, so timing alone does not show intent; contrived timing may hide a different truth.
- [pitfall] Probability elimination or odds narrow the field but do not prove the answer; a candidate must be verified before the conclusion is accepted. When: When concluding from probability-based elimination or locating an item by odds alone. Why: The remaining explanation may still be wrong; it is only the most likely one left.
- [pitfall] A coincidence feels like a cheat unless the audience can sense how it plausibly happened; when it does all the investigative work, the lead needs systematic follow-up. When: Using chance to advance a plot or puzzle. Why: Unearned luck breaks trust in the fiction.
- [pitfall] Treating a coincidence as a cycle without testing it against a prediction produces false patterns.
- [pitfall] Matching bookings can look planned when they are merely coincidence.
- [pitfall] A misdirection that works only through improbable coincidences makes readers notice the author steering events.
- [pitfall] Misdirection can fail when a chance event exposes the planted trail.
- [pitfall] A perfectly symmetric pair can be coincidence, so test it against physical facts before accepting that it was staged.
- [pitfall] A shared object can link events that only coincide, so test the link against independent evidence before building conclusions on it. Why: Two events may share an object by chance rather than by design.
- [pitfall] A method built on chance means most early leads are probably wrong, so expect many dead ends.
- [pitfall] A clue found only by chance feels like luck; give the player a reason to examine the object before the reveal. Why: players need motivation to inspect ordinary objects.
- [pitfall] A name shared with a character in a source can be coincidence; it counts only when it connects to the people and surrounding facts. Why: a name match alone says little about who is involved.
- [pitfall] Relying on luck to rescue the investigator is weak craft, especially when the offender's own luck can also run out. When: When resolving an investigation. Why: Chance-based resolution feels unearned.
- [pitfall] A reversal that comes from a chance encounter may be luck rather than method, so it needs independent checking. When: A breakthrough that depends on an incidental discovery. Why: Chance finds can feel decisive without a systematic basis.
- [pitfall] Relying on coincidence to delay a reveal can break the audience's trust in the story.
- [pitfall] A remedy that seems to end trouble may be coincidence, so one restoration is not proof of the cause. When: A fix is followed by a stop in the trouble. Why: Trouble can end on its own.
- [pitfall] Treating a run of minor misfortunes as caused by one person without first ruling out natural explanations turns coincidence into false evidence. Why: Witnesses or players often skip checking ordinary causes once a suspect is named.
- [pitfall] A challenge whose result depends on who runs it, rather than on its rules, cannot be trusted by players.
- [pitfall] Two unrelated causes on one night, such as two poisons, can look like a single plot when they are coincidence.
- [pitfall] Several coincidences about a suspect, such as location, purchases, quarrels and silences, can look conclusive together even when each has an innocent cause. When: assembling a case from circumstantial signs. Why: stacked coincidences feel like proof.
- [pitfall] A document can match events by chance, so verify its date and drafting history before reversing the inference. When: A document seems to anticipate events. Why: Coincidence can produce a close fit without any design.
- [pitfall] When the shared element is one of many common features, coincidence is likely and the pattern may not be real.
- [pitfall] A pattern drawn from a small sample can be coincidence, so show the total count so the player can judge how unlikely it is. Why: Without the denominator, a pattern cannot be weighed against chance.
- [pitfall] Isolated incidents can look like a pattern, so check the base rate before concluding a supernatural cause. When: When several similar incidents occur in a place where many people pass through. Why: Frequent exposure makes chance events look connected.
- [fact] A perfect offender also needs luck, since outside circumstances must never cause their downfall. When: When judging whether a crime could go undetected. Why: Chance can undo even careful planning.
- [fact] An alibi can arise by luck, when a suspect's location happens to sit beside another person's activity, rather than by design.

## leading questions and steering
- [definition] A leading question is one whose wording carries content, such as a name or trait, that the witness may then repeat back instead of recalling.
- [mechanism] Pressing an NPC with leading questions lowers the confidence of its testimony, so its later claims should be weighed less. Why: Suggestion weakens the reliability of what is then reported.
- [mechanism] A character can be sent to a location someone else selected by a plausible reason for not going there themselves, so they go alone. When: Directing a character to a place without appearing to control them. Why: A stated constraint on the director makes the redirected character the only one who can go.
- [behavior] A question that presumes an answer, such as guilt, steers replies to follow the premise and the investigator's view before evidence is checked. When: questioning that assumes an answer. Why: The framing of a question supplies the shape of the answer; assumed answers bias what the investigator sees. (x3)
- [behavior] Agreement with a suggested name, event or version is not independent confirmation; the witness may simply follow the question's wording. When: the questioner offers a candidate name or event, or a suggestible witness with uncertain memory is asked a question carrying the expected answer. Why: Suggestible witnesses may adopt the questioner's version rather than recall their own; agreement is easy when the question supplies the answer. (x2)
- [behavior] Witnesses who hear a theory or are shown where to look may report matching features, so findings can reflect suggestion rather than the actual body or event. When: a witness hears a theory or others' guesses first, or observers are directed to a body area or object. Why: Expectation and suggestion shape what people think they saw and how they describe it. (x2)
- [behavior] A witness with a partial view and an unclear memory can be led to a new reading of events by a plausible alternative explanation. When: the witness is unsure of what they saw. Why: A suggestion can replace a vague memory rather than refine it.
- [behavior] Questions put in front of others can shape a witness's answer, and objections from an adult can signal that the account has been influenced. When: A young or suggestible witness is questioned in a group. Why: The witness takes cues from the questioner and the audience.
- [behavior] Questions that presuppose details the witness never observed invite invented answers or collapse under pressure, especially from elderly or eager witnesses. When: Questions assume an unobserved fact such as appearance or clothing. Why: Witnesses feel pressure to answer rather than admit ignorance.
- [behavior] A person with no prior suspicion can settle on a specific neighbor after hearing vague, fated claims from an outside visitor. When: When an anxious person hears general, ominous statements from a stranger. Why: Vague claims invite the listener to fill in a named target.
- [behavior] A witness who is asked a leading question and then agrees with the offered wording tends to adopt that wording as their own recollection. When: An investigator supplies a term before the witness describes what they saw. Why: The sense of being understood makes the witness accept suggested language.
- [rule] Do not embed an assumed answer, desired content or conclusion in a question; ask what the witness saw, since the wording removes innocent or true answers. When: Framing a question to a witness. Why: A leading question tells the witness what to confirm, weakening testimony so the answer reflects the question rather than the events. (x2)
- [rule] Calm a shaken witness by asking a concrete question about a physical object they carry, giving the conversation a fixed point. Why: a physical object anchors attention and restores composure.
- [rule] Stop the interview when a weakened witness becomes agitated; pressing on yields unreliable answers.
- [rule] Give a low-status NPC a plausible motive to steer the player toward them, then supply a clue that clears them. When: designing a suspect for a mystery. Why: A plausible motive makes the detour convincing; the clue makes it fair.
- [heuristic] A witness who insists on a direction, vouches for an associate or volunteers an outside suspect may be steering attention; test the claim before acting on it. When: a witness pushes the investigator toward a place or person. Why: a decoy can send investigators away from the real answer.
- [heuristic] Question a witness step by step, through small concrete questions, to recover precise details that a broad question misses.
- [heuristic] After a refusal, shift to a shared task to keep access to the witness open.
- [heuristic] A dramatic word or familiar outside group that explains a case too neatly should be tested against physical facts before it is accepted. When: an explanation fits the case suspiciously well. Why: suggestive words and known groups can absorb attention and hide the real mechanism.
- [heuristic] When a lead proves false, ask who shaped the search toward it.
- [heuristic] Point a searcher toward an ordinary explanation and withhold the anomaly, so the search appears to confirm the ordinary account. When: A suspect or NPC is conducting a search that could expose the investigator's knowledge. Why: A search that seems to confirm a mundane answer ends further scrutiny.
- [heuristic] Digressions cost time, so steer a witness back to the point when the story wanders.
- [heuristic] Offering a specific detail to investigators can steer them toward a test that leads to a dead end.
- [heuristic] A non-player character who accuses under suggestion can serve as a plot device, letting the player discover who planted the idea. When: When designing an NPC whose accusation should trace back to another character. Why: Revealing the source of a suggestion creates a discovery beat.
- [procedure] 1) Ask open, neutral questions first, since leading questions confirm a client's assumption instead of testing it. 2) Only then put the suggested answer and test whether the witness confirms or rejects it. Why: a leading question can make a witness simply agree.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a formal, neutral request. 2) Press with pointed questions when answers are evasive or minimal. 3) Watch the witness's colour, speech and posture. 4) Use deliberate provocation sparingly to test whether a reaction is genuine, and note any refusal to answer. When: a guarded witness has specific facts to test. Why: escalating in stages reveals genuine reactions before the investigator risks losing control.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a calm, general question and let the witness talk. 2) Narrow to specific points such as visitors or sounds. 3) Test claims against a physical fact. 4) Note changes in posture, tone or repeated lines. 5) Follow any unexpected remark with the next question. When: When questioning a cooperative witness who may hold back or minimise.
- [procedure] 1) Open with easy factual questions that fix a baseline. 2) Re-ask a key point in a different form to test the account. 3) Ask the sensitive question casually. 4) Watch for small changes in expression. 5) Follow brief remarks with narrower questions. When: interviewing a witness about a sensitive matter. Why: routine answers fix a baseline, so deviations stand out.
- [procedure] 1) Ask when the witness last saw a key object. 2) Ask where they went. 3) Ask when they last saw a key person. 4) Ask about background concerns that may explain their actions. When: when a witness's movements and contacts must be reconstructed. Why: staged questions build a fixed sequence of events.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness recall the day's events in order. 2) Anchor the recall with facts already known. 3) Ask the essential question only once the familiar account is secure. 4) If refused, state the consequence of silence. When: witness is weak, fading or emotionally tied to the suspect. Why: familiar material builds recall before the critical question is reached.
- [pitfall] Pressing a witness with suggestion can harden a vague recollection into a firm fact and inflate confidence; a later near-certain claim may reflect the suggestion, not new recall. When: when the witness is uncertain or the interviewer's suggestions are not recorded. Why: Suggestion shapes answers and inflates apparent confidence. (x2)
- [pitfall] Leading questions, such as 'was it right?', can plant answers or conclusions the witness never observed, knew or reached, so replies echo framing even without harmful intent. Why: Suggested content is absorbed into the witness's account and mistaken for knowledge.
- [pitfall] Repeating a suggestion or filling memory gaps about unclear details can produce confident false memories that are reported as observed facts. When: questioning a witness about details they did not clearly see. Why: Suggested details are absorbed into memory and then reported as observed facts.
- [pitfall] Leading questions can make a witness confirm the investigator's theory or identification, so answers must be tested against independent facts before they are accepted. When: when questioning a witness with a fixed theory, or when confirming a witness's identification. Why: Suggested answers can be mistaken for true ones; the questioner's framing can make a weak claim look settled.
- [pitfall] A leading question can plant a detail, so a witness's later report of that detail may reflect the question rather than memory. When: the questioner names a detail before the witness has mentioned it. Why: witnesses may adopt details suggested to them.
- [pitfall] Suggesting a gender, identity, or size to a witness can plant a belief that the witness then adopts as their own memory. When: when asking about a figure the witness only partly saw. Why: witnesses under stress tend to accept supplied details.
- [pitfall] A leading question can plant the answer it seeks, so the phrasing of key questions needs care.
- [pitfall] A numbered list of suggestive items can look stronger than it is, so hedged wording should mark how far each item actually supports the conclusion. When: presenting several weak indications. Why: list formatting implies equal weight.
- [pitfall] Leading questions can plant answers in the witness; keep answers her own rather than shaped by hints, and ask questions whose implication she may not notice.
- [pitfall] Rapid, leading or harsh questioning can produce the answer the questioner wants, or make an honest witness look evasive.
- [pitfall] A sick or sedated witness may agree to whatever is suggested, so confirm key facts with independent records.
- [pitfall] Ignoring that a claimant may be steering the witness toward a desired answer. When: When assessing testimony obtained through a motivated intermediary. Why: A party with a stake can shape what a witness reports.
- [pitfall] Asking a leading question, such as about a specific habit, can shape the answer the subject gives. When: Questioning someone about a possible cause of a physical sign. Why: A suggested answer can steer a subject toward confirming it.

## legal authority and procedure
- [definition] A nuncupative will is a spoken will, declared orally rather than written, offered in place of a written one to show a person's wishes.
- [mechanism] Endorsement by a respected expert or leader gives an unverified claim or accuser's story weight, so audiences accept it without checking the evidence. When: When a respected leader or persuasive expert endorses a claim in front of an audience. Why: Public standing or demonstrated skill substitutes for independent verification. (x2)
- [mechanism] Letting the player examine a corpse for expression, smell and blood, with each observation ruling causes in or out, makes examination a reasoning step. When: Designing a body-examination interaction. Why: Each observable narrows the candidate causes of death.
- [mechanism] An official diagnosis that implies hidden agents nearby sets the frame, so accusers are primed to find suspects matching that premise. Why: The accepted explanation determines which targets seem plausible.
- [mechanism] Confessions take on a common shape when examiners supply it: a yes to a leading question is expanded by the questioner into a full narrative the accused did not originate. When: Questioners ask leading yes-or-no questions and then elaborate the answer. Why: The accused adopts the framing offered, so independent detail is missing.
- [behavior] Officials may protect powerful parties' arrangements, and examiners can be pressured or bribed, so inconvenient findings get stalled, which shapes whose account is accepted; secure the original report. When: An investigation touches a wealthy or powerful party, or findings are inconvenient to them. Why: Institutional incentives favour the influential; examiner methods and records determine how far a finding can be trusted. (x2)
- [behavior] Accepting a satisfying reconstruction or an arrest as the end of inquiry leaves unexplained gaps and alternative explanations unexamined. When: A plausible story is offered in a formal setting, or a suspect has been arrested. Why: A satisfying story or arrest reduces the appetite to question further, creating a false sense the matter is closed.
- [behavior] Pressure from a superior for a quick answer can make an investigator vouch for a suspect and say reassuring things he does not believe. When: a senior figure demands closure. Why: external demands shape statements independent of evidence.
- [behavior] In an interview, a senior person's dismissive remark can end a junior's protest, showing who controls the room. When: a protest is raised during questioning.
- [rule] Do not accept an official's verdict because of rank or claimed competence; check who judged, how, and the evidence; overturn it with harder evidence, not rank. When: When an earlier official judgment about a person is used as settled fact. Why: A self-described authority may be biased or mistaken. (x2)
- [rule] Treat confident claims from authorities or the press as hypotheses to test; confidence resting on someone else's word is not direct evidence. When: A conclusion is supported only by someone else's word. Why: Trust in the source is mistaken for proof.
- [rule] Confirm a rumour with an authority that has standing; a legal check can turn an opinion into a finding or show it has no basis.
- [rule] Confirm the right to search before forcing a locked space, because entry without authority can damage the case. When: evidence may be concealed in a locked room. Why: Improperly obtained evidence can be rejected or weakened.
- [rule] Let authority NPCs turn on the player based on observed actions, requiring new evidence to clear the name. When: when designing a suspicion system. Why: Observed actions drive suspicion.
