- [rule] The evidence required for a capital charge must be as strong as for any other capital crime, with no lower threshold because the crime is unusual. When: when a charge is exceptional, hidden or hard to observe. Why: Lowering the standard lets unusual crimes convict on weaker proof.
- [rule] State the governing legal standard early, then make each later clue a test of that standard. When: Structuring a sequence of accusation-driven scenes. Why: A standard set up front gives the player something concrete to check each piece of evidence against.
- [heuristic] Remind a witness they are under oath before key questions, which changes the stakes of every answer they give. When: when questioning a witness whose answers matter for the case. Why: Awareness of a formal obligation raises the weight of each answer.
- [heuristic] A weaker side in a formal dispute can survive by following each procedural step exactly, leaving the stronger side no valid ground to override it. When: formal rules govern the dispute. Why: strict compliance removes grounds for dismissal.
- [procedure] 1) Brief authorities in advance with names, locations and weapons. 2) On arrival, present suspects and exhibits. 3) Name each exhibit and state each suspect's role. When: when handing a solved case to outside authorities. Why: Prepared handover lets authorities act at once.
- [procedure] 1) Disarm the subject first. 2) Check coat and body for other concealed items. 3) Empty every pocket onto one surface. 4) Examine each item patiently. 5) Open containers to check for hidden compartments. 6) Check the subject's pulse before continuing. When: when a person is subdued and a search is allowed. Why: A fixed order avoids missing items and protects the subject's safety.
- [procedure] 1) Mark sections omitted from the excerpt. 2) Compare the wording with a complete copy to find unmarked edits. 3) Locate a full text. 4) Separate quotation from paraphrase. 5) Date the citing text against the author's changing purpose. When: A retelling is the main surviving version of a document or its author had a stake in it. Why: Excerpts can silently drop, alter or reframe content.
- [tradeoff] Removing a suspect to search can expose the investigator to later legal questions about how the search was conducted. When: An investigator searches while a suspect is removed. Why: Improper searches can have consequences beyond the immediate scene.
- [tradeoff] A fast, thorough physical search finds concealed items quickly but can cause real distress; privacy and consent may matter more than speed. When: when deciding whether to search a person. Why: Speed gains are paid for with the subject's distress.
- [pitfall] Signs from examination may reflect the examiner's assumptions or methods, which subjects echo back; judge each sign by whether the examiner could have caused it. When: When a suspect's behaviour or answers are observed during questioning. Why: Subjects may simply give the examiner what it expects; interrogation methods can produce the reactions they appear to reveal.
- [pitfall] Searches justified as diligence can still reach private property and damage trust, so respect propriety and record every search step carefully.
- [pitfall] Authority does not validate a method; arguments from appeals to authority or principle are only as strong as their sources, and results may depend on facts unrelated to the question. When: When evaluating a written argument or the validity of a test. Why: Status is mistaken for verification.
- [pitfall] A general attack on institutions can replace argument about the evidence, so keep criticism of sources separate from examination of the claim.
- [pitfall] Forcing an unusual exception to a rule draws attention to it, so the request must be prepared in advance to avoid being noticed. When: An exception is needed to bypass a protective rule. Why: Unusual requests stand out to those who watch the routine.
- [pitfall] A stated refusal to use covert methods can weaken under urgency, and self-imposed limits can slow progress. When: A character's principles meet high stakes. Why: Pressure erodes early commitments and restrictions cost time.
- [pitfall] Authority figures who treat a prisoner's silence or repeated denials as proof of guilt will ignore the true explanation unless the player corrects the record. When: An NPC authority interprets a silent or denying suspect. Why: Prisoners' claims of innocence are assumed routine, so their silence gets read as confirmation.
- [pitfall] A sincere-sounding oath of innocence proves nothing about the act it denies, and it can be delivered as a performance. When: A suspect ends a confrontation with a solemn declaration. Why: Staged emotion can persuade listeners without providing evidence.
- [pitfall] Keeping outside authorities out of a scene removes an independent check on the evidence. When: A scene's evidence is interpreted by only the investigating party. Why: Without an outside check, errors and bias go uncorrected.
- [pitfall] A search depends on control of the subject and fails once the subject can act or others may interrupt. When: when planning a search. Why: Control is the precondition for the procedure.
- [pitfall] A respected figure's later account can contradict his own earlier record, so authority does not replace checking statements against the record. When: When a prominent witness gives a revised version years later. Why: Status makes a changed story seem credible without comparison.
- [pitfall] Missing official roles, such as who drew up a warrant or order, cannot be filled in by assumption. Why: Unsupported role attribution produces false conclusions about responsibility.
- [pitfall] A permission granted for one purpose, such as opening an inquiry, is easily stretched to decide the case once a suspect is named. Why: Once a suspect is named, the limit on use is easily forgotten.
- [pitfall] A legal rule explained only once may be forgotten before it matters, so it should be reinforced or planted early and reused. When: A rule the player needs later is taught in passing. Why: Players forget one-time exposition before its payoff.
- [fact] Two situations are recognised exceptions to the need for material proof: a suspect caught in the act, and a suspect who confesses. When: deciding whether an accusation can stand on inference alone. Why: these are the named cases where proof is not required.
- [fact] Without formal authority, investigators may only watch, and the required approval can arrive too late to act.
- [fact] Props signaling authority, such as a card, uniform, sash, or fur coat, can command trust and make a target hand over valuables. When: A con relies on the victim accepting a claimed identity. Why: Visible markers of rank short-circuit careful verification.
- [fact] Authorities may withhold information without giving a reason, so their silence on a lead does not prove the lead is worthless.
- [fact] Objects bearing the searcher's own address show that the other party already knows where to find the searcher. When: when a found item carries the searcher's details. Why: Such items reveal the opponent's knowledge of them.
- [fact] A person can decline a role on a record because signing under their own name would make them legally responsible for it. Why: Legal duties attach to the name written on a document.

## open leads and questions
- [rule] Keep rival explanations, such as illness, natural death, accident, robbery, deliberate act or fled companion, open side by side until evidence settles them. When: when a single neat or official explanation appears early or is pressed. Why: premature acceptance hides contrary evidence; a grudge-to-harm link should stay a hypothesis. (x2)
- [rule] Keep an explicit journal of open questions (who, where, what next), stalled leads and dismissed clues, updated as facts arrive, so players can revisit them. When: when designing investigation interfaces or quests, or when multiple leads and clues accumulate over a long investigation. Why: unrecorded clues are easily forgotten, so players cannot connect new evidence to them. (x2)
- [rule] Track each accepted premise and flag unchecked ones in a to-verify list, plus unrequested tests, unchecked items and secondhand leads, so players see which conclusions rest on assumption. When: when building a player-facing evidence log, or when the player has unconfirmed information. Why: exposes untested reasoning; separating confirmed from unconfirmed facts reduces confusion; visible open leads guide players toward unexplored reasoning.
- [rule] Record each unanswerable question, such as a footmark's direction, with its best candidate answer and what each answer would mean for the case; this separates suspicion from known fact. When: when evidence cannot settle a question but the answer would change other conclusions. Why: keeping open questions visible prevents later reasoning from assuming an answer that was never established.
- [rule] Keep several suspects open rather than committing early, including respectable-seeming people, since dropping them risks clearing a guilty person or losing the chance to prove guilt. When: at the start of an investigation. Why: avoid risks in either direction.
- [rule] Keep an unexplained fragment or phrase, such as an overheard remark or a term a witness never clarifies, as an open lead, not attached to a person until confirmed. When: when collecting partial remarks without context, or when a witness repeats a phrase they do not explain. Why: a fragment attached to the wrong subject produces a false conclusion; unexplained details point toward further evidence.
- [rule] Keep unresolved leads open after an accusation, so the player can still find evidence that points elsewhere.
- [rule] List open conditions in the quest log and mark each one resolved as the player eliminates alternatives. When: when tracking a deduction-based investigation. Why: a visible checklist shows progress toward the answer.
- [rule] Let a summary state what the player has not yet established, so the next step is clear. When: A game summarises the player's investigation progress. Why: Explicit gaps direct the player toward the next action.
- [rule] Do not close an inquiry while contrary traces remain unexplained.
- [rule] Do not discard a witness merely for bias, since a biased witness can still report accurate detail.
- [rule] Keep a person on the suspect list when they have a motive, even a small one, until that motive is ruled out. When: when a suspect has any motive.
- [rule] Before naming a culprit, check whether any question remains open, including how the means of access was achieved. When: when a motive and one link look convincing.
- [rule] Do not demand the source of a suspect's information, since that keeps the suspect cooperative. When: questioning a suspect who has revealed knowledge.
- [rule] Keep the question of guilt open while a suspect is too unwell to be questioned properly, and resume questioning once they recover.
- [rule] Do not drop a weak alibi; mark it unconfirmed and keep it open. Why: weak evidence is still uncertain.
- [rule] When an official verdict closes a quest stage, record the unanswered questions as open journal flags. When: Closing a quest stage with unresolved elements. Why: Players need a trace of what remains open.
- [rule] Keep the open question on the player's journal during light interludes, and reward the player when later evidence supports or undercuts their suspicion. When: When tension is reset between investigation beats. Why: A persistent open question keeps the mystery active after relief.
- [rule] Let an NPC's reaction open a new branch, such as a request to recover the item, rather than settling the question. When: designing dialogue responses to an item reveal. Why: a branch keeps the question open and rewards further investigation.
- [rule] Use locked doors and disposable notices to show a quest-giver's situation has changed, prompting the player to investigate further.
- [heuristic] Keep a thread open after clearance or the main solution, such as an item's chain of custody or why only one character saw a figure, so the world feels larger. When: when designing post-clearance investigation or ending a mystery arc. Why: open threads keep the mystery active and suggest a wider world beyond the story. (x2)
- [heuristic] Explicitly leave specific questions unanswered, such as why someone cannot return, what caused a new bond, or an unknown identity, so the audience keeps tracking them until they pay off. When: when a mystery is in progress, an early scene ends, or a news item or report is left incomplete. Why: unanswered questions stay active in the audience's mind until resolved. (x2)
- [heuristic] Log a half-recognized character or possible identity match as an unresolved lead the player can revisit, inviting them to keep searching. When: when a record or NPC is half-recognized or its identity may match another. Why: an open question gives the player a reason to keep searching. (x2)
- [heuristic] Keep seemingly minor details on file, since they may answer an open question or gain meaning when later facts arrive. When: when gathering evidence over a long investigation. Why: background knowledge can change what an earlier detail means.
- [heuristic] Keep every witness fact, including odd or jumbled ones, until its relevance is tested, since an odd detail may match an earlier planted fact. When: when a witness gives full but jumbled testimony.
- [heuristic] Keep small personal details, such as work hours or pay, because they may connect to the wider matter. When: When recording a witness account. Why: Details that seem trivial can later prove central to the case.
- [heuristic] When a future plan cannot be known, answer with a range of possible options instead of one certain answer. When: when a reveal leaves a question about what comes next. Why: it marks the limits of what could be known.
- [heuristic] Use unexplained items in the world as hooks, since each signals that the player's current theory is missing a piece.
- [heuristic] Let the investigator narrate their reasoning openly, so each conclusion can be traced back to the observations behind it. When: when writing a mystery's deduction scenes. Why: Traceable reasoning lets the audience follow and check the logic.
- [heuristic] Use contact attempts with recorded times that went unanswered as anchors showing when a person was probably not at a location. When: When calls or visits were logged at known times. Why: A logged failed attempt is a dated fact that narrows where someone could have been.
- [heuristic] When a witness says a cry went unanswered, test the claim against who was close enough to hear it, since an explanation for why no one came can be constructed. When: A witness explains why no one responded to a sound.
- [heuristic] A missed-clue marker can show where a suspicious detail was available, making the design visibly fair. When: the player has solved or failed a puzzle. Why: Shows the player the sign they could have caught.
- [heuristic] Mark unresolved points as open rather than forcing a conclusion from incomplete evidence. When: an account leaves gaps. Why: premature conclusions hide what is unknown.
- [heuristic] Introduce the central name or key clue at the opening, so every later clue points back to it. When: starting an investigation plot. Why: A fixed anchor makes later clues cohere.
- [heuristic] Leave one clue deliberately unresolved to add texture without blocking progress. Why: Optional lore enriches a level without gating it.
- [procedure] 1) Let the witness narrate freely at first. 2) Listen closely without interrupting. 3) Steer back to the subject only when the witness drifts too far off track. When: early in an interview when it is unclear which facts matter. Why: A witness may reveal the key fact while wandering.
- [tradeoff] Open narration surfaces unknown facts but takes time; direct questions save time but miss key facts or leave evasive witnesses unchallenged, since witnesses volunteer only what they are asked. When: choosing an interview style or interviewing a witness. Why: key facts stay hidden without a pointed question.
- [pitfall] Failing to ask who could still confirm a key claim leaves that claim untested and the case weaker.
- [pitfall] A reveal that answers a question the audience never asked feels arbitrary, so each explanation should answer a question the story raised. When: Writing explanations at the end of a mystery. Why: Unraised questions make the solution seem contrived.
- [pitfall] Open group discussion can become confused and let the examiner lose control, and accused people present may coordinate their stories.
- [pitfall] If the hidden party never reacts to outside sounds, the listener's inference has nowhere to go.
- [fact] Open questions in a case list typically concern access (who could enter), motive (why someone acted), and identity (who an unseen person was).
- [fact] A practised gatherer of plants usually leaves long stalks, while hurried snatching tends to leave them short. When: judging whether a gathering trace is genuine. Why: different habits and haste leave different marks.

## planted clue setup
- [definition] A plant is an arranged element, such as a false witness, faked death, or planted document, meant to steer investigators toward a wrong conclusion.
- [mechanism] Plant the means of a later reveal early, as setting detail such as a sealed chamber or structural flaw, so the eventual use feels earned. When: the reveal depends on a physical location or object. Why: Details seen first as scenery pay off as the solution.
- [rule] Plant decisive facts such as an injury, a route, or a missing guard, and unexplained clues like predictions, favouritism, or hints, early so the late reveal can recall them. When: Designing a mystery with a late solution. Why: Facts introduced late feel unfair; early seeds and their payoffs make the reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary. (x3)
- [rule] Plant visible physical details or anomalies early that look like mechanics, and resolve them later; left unexplained, they read as authoring error. When: Opening the investigation of a puzzle scenario. Why: Early anomalies read as set dressing and pay off when the solution reframes them, so the later explanation feels earned. (x2)
- [rule] Place a physical tell in plain view early as an unremarkable curiosity, not a clue, so players can notice it and reinterpret it later. When: Designing a hidden clue in a mystery scene. Why: A visible but dismissed clue stays fair and rewards retrospective reasoning without revealing the solution. (x2)
- [rule] Plant a memorable detail or NPC early and return to it later with a sharper cue, since readers may overlook it on first pass. When: Writing a fair-play mystery. Why: A later event makes the player recall the detail and link it to a clue, because distinctive details are recalled and linked when the scene is reconstructed.
- [rule] Plant apparently irrelevant early details, such as a dismissal, an offhand question, a skipped routine, or a secretive habit, so they later pay off as hidden motive or timing. Why: Players forget the detail, then recognise it as the answer when the reveal arrives; ordinary-seeming details gain meaning later, rewarding readers who notice them.
- [rule] Plant the clues a late document will need in the earlier scenes that it later reframes.
- [rule] Plant a seemingly idle line of dialogue about a minor detail that becomes relevant when a timeline is checked. Why: An early casual detail becomes evidence later, rewarding attentive players.
- [rule] Show a culprit's motive, opportunity and access early in the story, so a late reversal reads as deduction rather than accident.
- [rule] Plant hints of concealed knowledge in earlier dialogue or records, and make idle-seeming remarks carry hidden meaning; otherwise the twist feels like a cheat.
- [rule] Plant spatial observations early that seem idle, since they can gain meaning later and reward the audience for noticing them.
- [rule] Plant facts in a villain's journal that the writer does not interpret, so the player can deduce the truth before the character does. When: designing in-game documents. Why: Uninterpreted facts let players reason ahead of the character.
- [rule] Script related events within the same in-game hour when you want players to suspect a hidden connection between them. When: Designing scripted NPC events meant to hint at a hidden plot link. Why: Players read temporal proximity as a sign of connection.
- [rule] Place a clue on the reverse of an item, such as a map fragment or receipt, that players must flip over to discover.
- [rule] Keep a planted item in a secure place until the reveal, since it can be lost or taken before then.
- [rule] Plant one anomaly, such as cargo too small for its stated purpose, that contradicts the obvious story and rewards players who check it.
- [rule] Scatter small anomalies that are each innocently explainable, and reward players who link them into a pattern. When: designing deduction puzzles. Why: linking rewards players while single items stay plausible.
- [rule] Let a planted item point at an NPC who never touched it, and reward players who check the chain of hands. When: designing misleading but fair clues. Why: Checking the chain separates a planted pointer from real involvement.
- [rule] Mark prop-triggered reactions as scripted so careful players can detect that they are staged, and let players introduce their own props to see which NPC responds. When: Designing puzzles or reveal scenes where a prop triggers an NPC reaction. Why: A player's own prop exposes an NPC who responds on cue, revealing the performance.
- [rule] Plant testimony such as a log or note early, so a later revisit makes the missing key deducible. When: Designing mystery clues that pay off later. Why: Early placement lets the player connect the clue when the context returns.
- [rule] Plant the explanation for a character's fear early so that a later use of that fear as a counter feels fair. When: When a later scene depends on a character's weakness. Why: A clue set up before its use lets players recognize the solution as earned.
- [rule] Place a false clue through a non-player character and give it a detectable inconsistency the player can find and link to a second action. When: When designing a mystery with a misleading clue. Why: A detectable inconsistency lets the player expose the staging through the second action.
- [heuristic] When a planted clue points strongly at one suspect, test whether it was placed deliberately before accepting it as evidence against that suspect. When: a single object implicates one suspect.
- [heuristic] Set up a fact early, then reveal it at the moment it explains the present situation, so the reveal feels earned rather than arbitrary.
- [heuristic] Introduce a central object and its delivery rule early, without revealing its importance; the reasons can arrive later. When: a central object must be established before its value is known. Why: setup without explanation builds anticipation for the payoff.
- [heuristic] Give the culprit a planting route that the player can reconstruct afterward from the scene.
- [heuristic] Give a destroyed or lost clue a second trace, such as a slit or worn patch, so a player's mistake does not leave them stranded. When: a clue can be destroyed by player action.
- [heuristic] Plant the absence of an expected detail as a clue, so that its missing trace signals a staged scene.
- [heuristic] Make a moral or occult explanation available early, then reveal the mundane cause, such as a secret, address or key, when the player checks the evidence. When: when designing horror-tinged clues with a human explanation. Why: Early availability sustains the mood, and evidence checking grounds the answer.
- [heuristic] Plant a concrete physical mismatch early, such as a fitting that is too tight or a missing part, and have characters explain it away until it pays off. When: when a clue must survive a long investigation. Why: a concrete detail stays memorable and gains weight when it returns.
- [heuristic] Use several lures from different sources, each presented as genuine, so the target trusts each one and does not suspect a trap. When: designing a trap that depends on the target believing a lure. Why: Independent sources make the lure seem confirmed rather than contrived.
- [heuristic] Introduce a single unexplained detail early and keep it unresolved until the reveal pays it off. Why: An open detail keeps the player checking it.
- [heuristic] Seed suspicion through trivial logistics such as odd equipment requests, so the player's first pass reads them as eccentricity rather than as clues. When: Opening a mystery where the hidden purpose must stay unseen early. Why: Mundane oddities hide their meaning and only gain weight when later facts recontextualise them.
- [heuristic] Plant small concrete tokens such as counts, objects or keys early, so they read as proof of premeditation when they recur later. When: when designing a clue trail for a concealed crime. Why: Early tokens gain weight when the audience recognises them again.
- [heuristic] Plant a mechanism's clue as an ordinary-looking detail, such as a gesture or a reaction to a cue, so players see it before its meaning is clear. When: designing a hidden mechanism. Why: The detail is later recognised as the key clue.
- [procedure] 1) Show the object in everyday use without emphasis. 2) Have a second character comment on it. 3) Link it to a habit. 4) Plant a name or phrase that gains meaning later. When: a later solution depends on an earlier detail. Why: ordinary context lets the detail pass as character, then read as evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Place a minor detail early in a plain scene. 2) Frame it lightly so it does not stand out. 3) Reference it again later, when it connects to other details. When: when a clue must be revealed only in retrospect. Why: A clue dismissed in its own scene must still be retrievable, or the planting fails.
- [procedure] 1) Rebuild the sequence of events step by step. 2) Check that the sequence explains every trace. 3) Test it against what household members know about routines. When: a disguise or a replaced person must be inferred from traces. Why: A sequence that explains every trace is more trustworthy than one that explains some.
- [procedure] 1) Place a cryptic line early in the game. 2) Record it in the player's journal without an answer. 3) Pay it off once the player has the context to interpret it. When: Designing mystery clues that reward later discovery. Why: Delayed resolution lets the clue become meaningful when context arrives.
- [procedure] 1) Place a small, ambiguous tell in a calm scene. 2) Have a second character offer a plausible but wrong reason. 3) Reveal the truth later, pointing back to the earlier moment. When: Foreshadowing a hidden cause.
- [pitfall] An object found along a route may have been planted to mislead, not dropped by the escaper.
- [pitfall] A presupposing question can plant a fact the witness did not know, so any confirmation must be checked against independent sources.

## routine baseline and deviation
- [mechanism] Routine duties reveal who handled an object: its maintained condition shows who managed it, and service routines show who may enter a room or handle it. When: When an object is normally maintained by a particular person. Why: Routines establish a baseline and reveal what must be done with an object.
- [mechanism] A routine task performed by staff, such as laying a table, can arrive at the wrong moment and end a private encounter.
- [mechanism] Discovering a broken assumption triggers a chain of consequences, such as realising another person could have entered, which forces a reassessment of the whole scene.
- [mechanism] Scheduled NPC routines, such as a stop at a friend's before arriving at a location, force the player to reconstruct their movements. When: When designing NPC schedules that feed investigation. Why: Hidden intermediate steps make the timeline something the player must assemble.
- [behavior] A sudden emotional collapse during a public event breaks the scene and lets a quieter bystander speak privately to the investigator. When: a performance or gathering is disrupted by one person's distress. Why: The disruption lifts the social pressure that kept the bystander silent.
- [behavior] A person who normally avoids a certain look may break that habit when news matters to them, so a changed glance can signal concern. When: A character's usual habit of gaze or manner changes during a conversation. Why: Breaking an established habit signals that the subject has become important to the speaker.
- [behavior] A broken arrangement, such as a missed meeting replaced by a message, can signal a shift in intent before the message is read.
- [behavior] Observers judge conduct against shared time norms, so being out past a conventional hour is noticed and read as a breach. When: A social setting with customary hours for rest or departure. Why: Shared expectations give observers a baseline against which deviations stand out.
- [behavior] Players who meet an innocent, mundane scene doubt their working theory, and a well-built red herring rewards those who keep investigating. When: when a scene seems to contradict a theory. Why: ordinary surroundings make a conspiracy look unlikely.
- [behavior] People ignore familiar routine noise, but unusual or prolonged noise can wake sleepers and draw attention. When: when a noise is used to cover movement. Why: Habituation hides expected sounds, while novel sounds break through.
- [behavior] Watchers kept still in a dark, silent room with no activity perceive time as passing slowly, and the wait feels longer than it is. When: Long, quiet waiting periods in a dark space. Why: Little stimulation makes elapsed time feel stretched.
- [behavior] Planners neglect small details they never allowed themselves to consider, so a trivial circumstance can upset the whole plan.
- [behavior] A prejudiced listener can miss a contradiction, treating a detail only one person can perceive as confirmation rather than as a reason for doubt. When: a detail conflicts with the expected conclusion. Why: belief blinds the listener to the conflict.
- [behavior] A fall in a person's visit frequency can signal that the household has changed. When: when a regular visitor notices fewer admissions or contacts. Why: Routine contact breaks down when the household's situation shifts.
- [rule] Note every procedure breach, such as taking an unauthorised visitor into a restricted area or leaving a door unlocked.
- [rule] Log a broken meeting as a game state change, then place a follow-up note from the same person so the player must read it to learn what changed.
- [rule] Let a scheduled NPC movement, such as an arrival at the same hour each night, be watched from a fixed vantage point. When: designing recurring NPC behavior for player observation. Why: a fixed time and place makes the event predictable and watchable.
- [heuristic] A stopped, altered, or suddenly reworded routine is often the first sign of a changed situation, even before the cause is known. Why: Routines are stable, so their interruption or alteration marks a change in circumstances. (x3)
- [heuristic] Treat routines as a baseline: a deviation or intrusion becomes evidence only when it breaks an established pattern, and then stands out at once and often carries meaning. When: When a scene or conduct should follow a known pattern. Why: Regularity makes a missing or changed element noticeable at once. (x2)
- [heuristic] Use a regular habit or witnesses' reports of habitual acts, such as routine orders or nightly pacing, as a dependable time reference for when events or arrivals occurred. When: When estimating when a person arrived or acted, or when witnesses report habitual actions. Why: Routine gives regular observers a dependable reference and anchors when events happened without explanation. (x2)
- [heuristic] A break in routine, such as a skipped meal, late return, or unusual outing by people who never went together, prompts investigation and a timeline check. When: When a regular pattern is interrupted or a character's action departs from their routine. Why: Routine is the baseline against which deviations are noticed, and unusual actions often mark where a hidden event lies.
- [heuristic] When a person known for steady habits breaks one, the break itself is a strong signal that something has changed.
- [heuristic] A departure from a usual schedule, such as an earlier return than normal, is the first signal of a suspicious event and needs explaining. When: comparing a person's movements to their routine.
- [heuristic] Routine observations, such as a change in how much someone eats, can serve as a second line of evidence beside physical traces.
- [heuristic] Establish routines, such as a standing meal or a standing guard, as scripted states that the audience can check against later scenes. Why: a routine sets an expectation that a later scene can confirm or break.
- [heuristic] A scene arranged for an activity at a time when none is expected signals that someone has been there and merits investigation. When: a routine or expected timing is broken in a scene. Why: an out-of-routine arrangement betrays recent or unexpected presence.
- [heuristic] Establish the normal arrangement of keys before judging a deviation, since household routine defines what counts as unusual. When: A locked room is part of the evidence. Why: A deviation is meaningful only against a known baseline.
- [heuristic] A minor detail that breaks an ordinary habit can reveal more than a major fact; ask what a normal person would have done and treat departures as questions. When: when reconstructing a sequence of actions.
- [heuristic] A break from a known routine at the time of a crime signals unease, but it does not prove guilt on its own. When: someone who knows the person's habits notices an odd act. Why: nervousness shows in out-of-character behavior.
- [heuristic] Treat unexplained cancellations, especially two that match in time or place, as possible signs of a concealed link between people. When: A minor schedule change seems to connect two people. Why: Matching gaps can hide a relationship.
- [heuristic] Retained routines such as sleep and appetite can indicate that affliction was less severe than reported. When: Judging the severity of a reported condition. Why: Severe conditions usually disrupt basic routines.
- [heuristic] A person who consistently avoids the main entrance and uses a side or private door suggests a separate relationship with the place. When: when a suspect's movements diverge from the public routine. Why: Habitual use of an unusual entry indicates privileged or hidden access.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the normal routine of a place, household, device or person. 2) Note each break and record when it occurred. 3) Ask what each break signals and compare it to the routine. 4) Confirm the timeline with another source such as access logs or witness entries. When: When a setting follows a known rhythm with no direct evidence, or an event happens at a time that breaks a known pattern. Why: Deviations are meaningful only against an established baseline, and a second source checks the timeline. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) State the suspect's routine claims. 2) Check each against physical features of the scene, such as plants, structures and times. 3) Record contradictions. When: A suspect explains their presence with a routine.
- [tradeoff] A forced entry risks injuring bystanders or the victim, while waiting risks a life; choose by how immediate the threat is.
- [tradeoff] Routine canvass and background checks find witnesses and rule out leads cheaply, but tend to miss inside knowledge when a crime is deliberately designed.
- [pitfall] A single unusual absence from a settled schedule can look more significant than it is; many interruptions are routine and carry no hidden purpose. When: When interpreting one unusual absence or change in a settled schedule. Why: A well-established pattern exaggerates the anomaly. (x2)
- [pitfall] Routine checks can hide a clue, so the investigator must know what a routine check would have revealed before trusting it.
- [pitfall] Overlooking a small observable sign is the usual reason a player or reader fails to solve a case.
- [pitfall] Assuming a disguise hides everything can make an observer miss the habit that identifies the person. Why: Observers focus on the visible disguise and overlook unconscious behaviour.
- [pitfall] A single odd choice may have an innocent cause, such as an obstacle on the shorter path, so verify the alternative route before treating the anomaly as evidence. When: When an unusual route choice is treated as suspicious. Why: Unseen physical obstacles can explain choices that look like deliberate concealment.
- [pitfall] Trapped occupants who ignore small anomalies, such as an unresponsive switch, can miss the hidden mechanism.
- [pitfall] When an audience already knows a performer's habits, a staged joke reads as deliberate. When: the audience has seen the performer's habits before. Why: familiar patterns reveal the act.

## denial and bluffing
- [mechanism] A rival or authority figure who demands proof before acting makes the player trade information for cooperation.
- [mechanism] A character who denies or hides a reaction adds a second layer of ambiguity to the clue.
- [mechanism] Denials count for little when the accused has no counsel and no practice at cross-examination, so the accusation stands unrefuted.
- [mechanism] An unchecked accusation during a panic can escalate from arrests to mass punishment as more people are drawn in. When: during a panic.
- [behavior] A suspect who leaves no proof and has a clean past can resist questioning by denying everything, since investigators must prove what is refused. When: the suspect has covered their tracks. Why: The investigator must establish the facts without the suspect's admission.
- [behavior] Witnesses who deny unfavourable facts, or who refuse to lie even when the truth hurts them, both shape what investigators can prove. When: when a witness is questioned about damaging facts. Why: each choice either removes or preserves evidence.
- [behavior] A denial aimed at one specific claim may show that the rest of a reconstruction is close to the truth. When: a suspect is confronted with a detailed account.
- [behavior] A suspect challenged on an alibi may deny the claim while asserting that no one saw them, keeping the statement literally correct. When: when a suspect's whereabouts are questioned. Why: Literal accuracy lets the suspect avoid stating a falsehood while concealing contact.
- [behavior] A suspect who claims not to recall an act can be contradicted by an official written report from an independent party. When: A suspect's memory is self-serving or convenient. Why: Independent records can establish facts that the suspect's denial does not account for.
- [behavior] Public pressure to name a culprit pushes accusers to name people, and names come out one at a time in an order that favours those wanting them named. When: when a community demands a culprit. Why: accusers respond to pressure by supplying names.
- [rule] Treat an unconfirmed claim, such as a visit or dinner with no witness, as a weak timeline link or weak evidence until a second source corroborates it.
- [rule] Do not make threats or hint at evidence you cannot back up; an unsupported pressure bluff exposes the investigator and weakens the case. When: when using pressure in an interrogation or hinting at evidence not yet secured. Why: Unsupported threats are exposed and damage credibility.
- [rule] Require a verifiable physical token or specific proof before accepting a claim about identity, status or reputation, since repeated talk can be accurate yet unprovable. When: weighing a claim about a person's identity, status or wellbeing, or secondhand reports about a person or group. Why: Checkable proof can be verified; unsupported claims cannot.
- [rule] Ask a pressured suspect for a demonstration of cooperation rather than trusting their word. When: When a suspect offers to cooperate under threat or leverage. Why: Observable action is harder to fake than a verbal promise.
- [rule] Insist that a witness state where each person was and when, since precise times and places are what expose contradictions.
- [rule] Use a feigned state when a character's location or knowledge must stay hidden from those around them. When: a character needs to listen or move unseen. Why: Feigning explains the character's presence without drawing suspicion.
- [rule] Plant a claimed connection, such as a shared acquaintance, that a character uses to gain favor but that is never verified, so the claim's credibility is left open. When: A character's claimed background is used to win trust. Why: Unverified claims can carry tension and invite the player to doubt them.
- [rule] Test any suspect flinch or reaction mechanic against a decoy NPC who triggers the same reaction; otherwise players learn the reaction tells them nothing and ignore it.
- [rule] Give any claimed power a demonstration the player can try to reproduce or disprove. When: when a character claims a supernatural or special ability.
- [rule] Make denial and demands for proof dialogue options, each unlocking or closing off later confessions. When: Designing confrontation dialogue. Why: Branching reactions make the player's pressure choices matter.
- [heuristic] A denial of incriminating items is a fact to weigh, not proof; test it against what others heard or observed, and keep pressure low if the witness may be honest.
- [heuristic] A demonstration does not end a dispute: a suspect may dismiss the evidence, and persuasive demos don't dislodge physical evidence, so keep open questions visible until resolved.
- [heuristic] Focus questioning on what evidence can actually be shown, since a firm denial holds only while investigators lack proof. When: a suspect's story stays fixed.
- [heuristic] A serious question answered with a flippant reply is a probable sign of hidden knowledge, though only a rule of thumb. When: Interpreting a witness's manner under questioning.
- [heuristic] Question a witness further when a firm answer on one point is paired with evasion on a related point. When: When a witness is confident on one matter but reticent on a connected one. Why: Mixed signals suggest the reticence may hide relevant information.
- [heuristic] Use a firm, businesslike tone to bring a flustered witness back to the facts.
- [heuristic] Under emotional appeals, acknowledge the cost to the suspect while holding the factual argument unchanged. When: when a suspect uses affection, tears or appeals during an accusation. Why: Empathy with firmness keeps the case intact.
- [procedure] 1) Set aside the competing theory. 2) List only facts no witness disputes. 3) Build every inference from that list. When: Several accounts compete and a fixed starting point is needed. Why: Disputed starting facts make every later conclusion unreliable.
- [procedure] 1) Check the pulse. 2) Apply smelling salts and brandy. 3) Treat a steady pulse as a sign that the feint is holding. When: judging whether a collapsed person is genuinely unconscious. Why: Each test gives a sign that either supports or exposes the feint.
- [tradeoff] Firm pressure on a key holder can make them surrender the key, but it works best on a reluctant holder who already fears exposure. When: A key holder refuses to hand over a key. Why: Fear of consequences can overcome reluctance, but pressure applied to the wrong person can backfire.
- [tradeoff] Acting on belief alone is fast but risks wrongly punishing the innocent; demanding proof is slower but keeps the outcome grounded in evidence. When: a confrontation after a reveal where the accused denies the secret.
- [pitfall] Silence, denial or refusal to confess can be read as guilt and recorded as evidence, bringing harsher treatment; the accused cannot clear themselves by refusing. Why: denial is treated as defiance rather than an answer.
- [pitfall] Firm or calm delivery is not evidence of truth; practised lies can sound convincing and end questioning early, so test claims against physical evidence. When: when assessing a reply or a claim delivered with strong emphasis. Why: Confidence or calmness of delivery is not reliable evidence of accuracy.
- [pitfall] A witness's denial of seeing a scene or knowing a matter may be honest, defensive, incomplete or concealing, so it cannot clear them; sightline or ignorance alone cannot decide. When: a witness denies seeing a scene or knowing the matter.
- [pitfall] A claim lacking corroboration is not proven false, and an uncontradicted whereabouts is not confirmed; some claims have no possible independent source.
- [pitfall] A suggestion put to an expert and rejected should not be recorded as a finding, even if it was raised in questioning. When: Questioning proposes an explanation that the expert denies. Why: Questions can introduce a theory that the evidence never supported, and treating it as established misleads later reasoning.
- [pitfall] Clearing suspects without new evidence makes the solution feel arbitrary, so each exoneration should rest on a fact. When: a suspect is ruled out. Why: an unsupported clearing looks like authorial convenience.
- [pitfall] A bluff must be sustained across later exchanges, since each new question risks exposing it.
- [pitfall] Demanding certainty that medical evidence cannot give leads to frustration and false confidence in rough estimates. When: An investigator presses an expert for a precise answer. Why: Medical evidence usually gives probabilities, not certainties.
- [pitfall] Accepting that nothing unusual happened, without checking the normal routine, misses the deviations that matter.
- [pitfall] When the questioner already assumes guilt, a denial can be treated as proof of falsehood, especially when witness reactions seem to contradict it.
- [fact] A recantation that denies any source for the accusations removes the claim that they rested on hidden or outside information.

## foreshadowing and narrative hooks
- [mechanism] A suspect escaping through a crowd or train can be a branching point where the player chooses between a new watch and a fresh line of inquiry. When: Designing a pursuit or lost-suspect event. Why: A lost lead forces a choice of next investigative path.
- [mechanism] A status effect that repeats an earlier event works as foreshadowing, which players recognize on second encounter.
- [rule] Mark one unresolved thread as unknown, such as an open-question quest log entry, so players can pursue it in a later session. When: Designing a missing-person mystery. Why: A marked gap gives players a reason to return. (x2)
- [rule] Leave one thread unresolved, such as an object tied to an unknown figure, to seed follow-up and keep the ending believable; many open threads make closure feel missing. When: Designing the end of a case or chapter. Why: One open hook invites continuation; a reveal explaining everything feels mechanical.
- [rule] Close every lead and red herring with a specific checkable fact, not a general impression, showing which parts were false; unresolved red herrings become plot holes.
- [rule] When a search line yields nothing useful, record that it was checked and closed rather than leaving it unstated.
- [rule] Gate reveals with unresolved lines, letting players overhear an alarming statement and learn its context later. When: Pacing a reveal in a quest or scene. Why: Unresolved lines create curiosity that a later reveal satisfies.
- [rule] Keep the release brief after a long build: resolve the climax in a few quick actions. Why: a short release follows the long build.
- [rule] Resolve personal tensions and loose ends in the same closing scene as the case, such as rewards, reconciliations and future plans. When: after the central reveal. Why: unresolved threads leave the outcome unclear.
- [rule] Keep a scene open after an arrest so new evidence can still appear, rather than locking it once a suspect is held. When: an investigation system holds a suspect. Why: late evidence can overturn or confirm the arrest.
- [rule] When a quest branch can fail, keep a path to the truth through other clues so the player can still solve it.
- [rule] Record a failed attempt to reach a character, such as a call with no answer, as a timed event that can change later options.
- [rule] Use strength or stamina feats as puzzle gates, so only a character with the recorded capability can move a heavy object. When: when designing physical obstacles.
- [heuristic] End a scene on an unanswered question, withheld fact, unresolved offer or danger so the audience carries the tension forward. When: Closing a scene, chapter or section before a reveal, decision or next step. Why: Open questions make the following scene feel necessary; uncertainty sustains attention.
- [heuristic] A closing warning aimed at an unnamed party keeps the observer's suspicion alive for the audience without resolving it. When: a scene ends with an unresolved threat. Why: An open warning leaves the audience expecting a further revelation.
- [heuristic] Close a seemingly resolved scene with a single-line threat that reopens tension, shown only after the characters have been reassured. When: Ending a chapter or scene where the party believes the danger has passed.
- [heuristic] Close a confirmed chain while leaving the final outcome open, so a loose thread carries into later play. When: A mystery's middle links are resolved but its ending is not yet reached. Why: An unresolved thread keeps the player engaged and gives a basis for a later part.
- [heuristic] A closing section resolves threads by deciding what evidence is kept or destroyed and what the public learns, once the central question is answered.
- [heuristic] Ask a witness directly whether they saw anything relevant. A clear negative closes that lead quickly and frees effort for others. When: a lead depends on one witness's report.
- [heuristic] End a tense segment on an unexpected encounter that changes the stakes, so the next scene begins from a shifted situation. When: closing a stealth or tension segment. Why: A changed situation at the end pulls the audience forward.
- [heuristic] When doubt is high, show proof openly, since visible documents can establish good faith. When: when the other party is suspicious.
- [heuristic] End a scene with a decisive fact to drive pacing into the next investigation step. When: structuring a sequence of scenes. Why: a strong ending creates a hook for the next scene.
- [heuristic] Use a closing recap to fix the outcome and settle relationships, but skip it when major facts are still uncertain, since it would add confusion.
- [heuristic] Use a timed group decision as a scene's climax only when the audience must feel time running out. When: Choosing a climactic structure for a scene. Why: A decision without time pressure loses its urgency.
- [heuristic] A true-account mechanic can ask the player to fill the missing act of a reconstruction, rewarding correct sequencing. When: designing reconstruction puzzles. Why: the player must order events correctly.
- [heuristic] An inventory screen can mark one out-of-character item to trigger a side quest.
- [heuristic] Store a dialogue line that foreshadows a later event as a quest hook that resolves when the player reaches the matching location. When: Writing NPC dialogue that predicts a future event. Why: Hooks link early dialogue to later payoff and reward attentive listening.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC's dying words give two or three fragments that players must combine with other clues to reach the next lead. When: When designing a quest hint delivered by a dying NPC. Why: Combining fragments makes the hint active rather than passive.
- [heuristic] A mysterious NPC who follows the player and leads toward a location can drive a quest, with the player checking what that NPC could have seen from there.
- [heuristic] Plant a prophetic parting line early that players can recall when stakes rise. When: Setting up a future callback or escalation. Why: A remembered line makes later escalation feel foreshadowed.
- [procedure] 1) State plainly the facts that are known. 2) State what remains unknown. 3) Point to the single clue toward the solution, confirming clues already given rather than introducing new ones. When: Closing a mystery with an open or partly open answer. Why: Lets the audience check the outcome against earlier evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Restate the evidence in chronological order. 2) List each possible conclusion. 3) State what each conclusion must explain to be accepted. When: several explanations remain open. Why: Weighing each option explicitly prevents a premature verdict.
- [procedure] 1) Script each escalation step, such as a knock, a second knock and a forced entry, as a sequential trigger. 2) Let each trigger alert nearby NPCs. 3) Leave a memory of each trigger the player can check later. When: when a reveal should build tension.
- [pitfall] Unpaid planted events, foreshadowed dangers, hooks, teases, flagged motives, cliffhangers and withheld facts feel like a cheat or broken promise, eroding trust; open threads must be answered. Why: A setup without payoff signals a loose thread; a withheld fact also needs an earlier clue to feel fair. (x2)
- [pitfall] A motive or reveal that appears from nowhere or contradicts established evidence without earlier hints feels unfair or cheap to the player.
- [pitfall] A hidden presence introduced only for a jolt, with no later payoff, feels cheap to the audience. Why: a threat that goes nowhere wastes the tension it built.
- [pitfall] A quiet period without new information feels like wasted time and can cause the audience to lose interest. When: a lull is not followed by new facts. Why: Waiting only builds tension if it resolves in new information.
- [pitfall] Withholding evidence without a clear reason or a plan to disclose it later leaves the investigation stalled and unaccountable.
- [pitfall] In an open setting, spotting a stranger proves little, so the method only works where the population is closed. Why: Where many people come and go, an unfamiliar face is normal.
- [pitfall] A reversal or doubted decision made earlier that the final reasoning never justifies erodes the audience's trust in the solution.
- [pitfall] An open threat made during pressure can be used by the suspect against the questioner.
- [pitfall] Letting vague hints accumulate with no later payoff leaves the audience with open threads that never resolve.

## messages and intermediaries
- [mechanism] Each handoff of an object, such as a repair, sale, resale or handover to outside staff, creates a record or witness held outside the owner's control that can trace it. When: an object passes through third parties such as repairers, sellers or staff. Why: Third parties keep their own records, which can reveal movements the owner hoped to hide.
- [mechanism] A go-between who is not the named recipient may refuse to deliver an item, which forces the recipient to come in person. When: An item must reach a specific person who is not reachable through an intermediary. Why: The intermediary is bound by the instruction that the item goes only to its named recipient.
- [mechanism] A warning passed through an intermediary lets a hidden actor act without exposing themselves, adding a second line of action.
- [mechanism] An intermediary can carry an offer while the sender stays hidden, so the terms are delivered plainly and the sender remains out of reach. When: A character wants to negotiate without being seen. Why: Separating sender from message protects the sender and keeps the terms impersonal.
- [mechanism] A report that an official never reads forces the player to follow up through another route. When: designing reporting systems between NPCs.
- [mechanism] Intercepted correspondence can name a meeting or reveal overheard talk, opening new lines of inquiry.
- [mechanism] Intercepted correspondence reveals an address a target is known to use, so that location becomes the first place a pursuer would watch. When: A pursuer reads a target's letters. Why: People tend to return to trusted contacts and known places.
- [mechanism] A clue that is never reinforced may be forgotten entirely, and a clue heard before the wider picture forms may have no context to attach to.
- [mechanism] Media coverage of a lead, such as touched-up photos and features, raises public belief in it and sustains the decoy.
- [mechanism] Subordinates may hush or intercept complaints aimed at powerful people to win favor, so the powerful appear to escape scrutiny without any direct order from them. When: complaints or reports point toward a faction's leaders. Why: Subordinates gain standing by pleasing those above them.
- [behavior] An object can pass during distraction or a routine gesture such as a handshake, so the holder may not notice and bystanders register nothing unusual. When: an exchange happens while attention is elsewhere, or the gesture is familiar and the effect minor and fast. Why: attention is focused elsewhere, or a routine action is not perceived as an event, so the transfer leaves no memory.
- [behavior] A person who restates news shapes it through their manner and wish to calm others, so the official version reflects the speaker's purpose.
- [rule] Do not treat an intermediary's account or advice as neutral; relayed information is weaker than direct observation, and each go-between's stake shapes it. When: a third party or go-between relays information, gives advice, or later describes a dispute they calmed. Why: Calming a scene shapes its outcome and how it is later reported; intermediaries often have stakes in the outcome they recommend. (x2)
- [rule] Make a messenger's motives visible through distress, insistence or evasion, since these signal stakes and whether a delivered lead is real or false. When: a go-between delivers a message with emotional intensity or specific handling demands, or NPC messengers deliver leads. Why: Emotional cues and handling instructions reveal the stakes behind the message; visible motives let players judge a lead's trustworthiness.
- [rule] Do not let a secret channel carry a plot point without showing who could intercept it, since mail routed through others may be opened before arrival.
- [rule] Do not treat press reports as evidence, since parties with a stake in the outcome may have shaped them. When: when weighing published accounts. Why: Stakes give sources reason to distort what is published.
- [rule] Let an intermediary NPC pass along a witness's location and reward players for tracing that relay. Why: Relays turn the search into a chain of discovery.
- [rule] Let a friendly intermediary with standing unlock a locked location or body for the player.
- [rule] Unlock the true version of a document only after the player finds the contradicting physical detail in the decoy. When: designing a document-based reveal. Why: Gating the true version on discovery ties progress to observation.
- [rule] After a briefed handover, let the in-world authority's response confirm the state of the case. When: when designing a case-closing step. Why: The response gives the player clear feedback on the outcome.
- [rule] Have a messenger linked to the target summon the player at a key moment, and let the player decide whether to trust the call.
- [heuristic] Treat an unfinished message as a hypothesis, not proof: the writer may have been interrupted or lost consciousness. When: a found document ends mid-sentence. Why: Readers tend to fill gaps with their own assumptions.
- [heuristic] Track which object passed through which person's hands, since a handover is often the decisive step in a chain of evidence. Why: Transfers between people are the points where an object's link to a person can be established.
- [heuristic] Passing the story from one NPC's testimony to another can reveal different parts of the same event. When: Structuring a story across several narrators. Why: Each narrator sees a different part of the event.
- [heuristic] Examine the medium of a message, such as handwriting, to check whether it matches the named sender, since the writing can reveal who actually produced it. When: A message appears to hide its true author. Why: The physical form of a message can carry evidence that its stated sender did not write it.
- [heuristic] An introducer's endorsement should start a verification check, not replace it. The examiner still tests the claimant before trusting them.
- [heuristic] Uncut pages suggest an owner never read an item, but unread items may be display pieces rather than signs of concealment. When: judging whether a possession was used. Why: Display items are kept without being used.
- [heuristic] Add a mediator NPC trusted by every faction, so the player can end a feud without taking sides. When: designing faction conflict resolution. Why: Universal trust removes the need to choose a side.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the subject's routine from repeated sightings at the same place and hour. 2) Estimate the arrival time with a margin. 3) Check the estimate against every known alternative schedule before committing. When: when planning an intercept, rescue or observation of a routine subject. Why: Repeated sightings separate routine from chance, but a single assumed schedule can fail.
- [procedure] 1) Ask why the messenger came. 2) Identify who sent them. 3) Establish what that sender directs them to do. 4) Note who the messenger reports to. When: Tracing a message passed through several characters. Why: Each link shows who controls whom and whose interests the message serves.
- [pitfall] If the named recipient of a withheld item is unreachable, the clue it carries becomes a dead end.
- [pitfall] A message passed through several paid intermediaries can hide its true sender, and a poor description can send investigators after the wrong person. When: Tracing the origin of a message or action. Why: Each link adds distance and can conceal the origin.
- [pitfall] An introducer's presence can invite confidences that the introducer would rather not hear. When: When an introducer sits in on an interview.
- [pitfall] The trusted go-between may end up exposed to the same risk, so weigh that before setting the bait. When: Planning to use a trusted person as bait. Why: Contact that exposes an enemy can also expose the intermediary.
- [pitfall] A concealment that relies on an unread document can collapse if that document says something different.
- [pitfall] A partial clue that is never completed frustrates the audience unless the gap is explained later. When: Using a cut-off clue. Why: Unresolved gaps feel like errors.
- [pitfall] Every key handoff widens the set of possible suspects, so an owner's habit of sharing keys can multiply the people who could have acted. Why: Each person given access becomes a candidate.
- [pitfall] When one person passes a message or object to another, that link is often the weakest point in the chain. When: Tracing a message or item through several people. Why: Handovers are rarely witnessed or recorded.
- [pitfall] Repeating an account without noting how many people have passed it along hides how far it has drifted from the original event.
- [fact] The person who introduces an outsider may gain the most from the scheme, so control over it is not always obvious. When: a scheme involves an introduction. Why: the introducer can benefit while appearing peripheral.
- [fact] Wording in documents from unfamiliar periods or conventions can mislead modern readers, so the phrasing itself is evidence to be read carefully. Why: Terms can carry meanings that differ from the reader's current usage.
- [fact] An anonymous or private record could never have been publicly checked, so the absence of challenge says nothing about its accuracy. When: assessing an anonymous or private account.

## overlooked clues
- [mechanism] Information delivered in idle talk or ordinary records drops listeners' guard and leaks details; listeners' reactions to a mentioned name become evidence in their own right. When: A character hears a relevant fact unprepared, or should reveal information without knowing it matters. Why: A casual tone signals no test, so listeners do not brace and speakers leak details carelessly.
- [mechanism] A dropped personal item links its owner to a place or another person more strongly than a general impression, once its source and contents are known. When: A dropped item is found by a character who did not own it. Why: The item carries the identity of its sender, connecting otherwise separate parties.
- [mechanism] A witness can give up a clue incidentally, such as mentioning a fought-over object, without realizing its importance. When: When a witness describes a conflict or argument. Why: Witnesses report details of an event without knowing which ones matter to the case.
- [mechanism] An outside observer who reads an incidental clue, such as leftover wine, can reshape suspicion against a whole group, though the culprit never planned that reading.
- [mechanism] A clue remembered only from memory, with no label or markings, can support many different identities, so its identity stays uncertain. When: A physical trace is described from recall without a surviving label. Why: Without recorded features, several objects match the remembered description equally well.
- [mechanism] An object dropped at a measured point lets its owner return to the same spot later, even when conditions have changed. When: a route or site must be revisited. Why: the recorded position persists.
- [rule] Do not dismiss a slight or minor-looking detail, such as an event's day or a witness's remark; it may resolve contradictions or carry the whole case. Why: Neglecting small details can lead to error, and they often decide between conflicting accounts.
- [rule] A dropped item such as a hat or badge can point players to a missing NPC; have several NPCs independently recognise it to build confidence. When: designing a clue that links an item to a missing character. Why: independent recognitions make the link believable.
- [rule] Let a conversation system ask NPCs about incidental details such as seats, light sources or wall objects, marking answers that match or contradict what the player saw. When: designing NPC conversations.
- [rule] Mark an overlooked NPC as a witness on a second visit, so players who return can resolve the clue.
- [rule] Let a minor oddity, such as an offhand remark or a worn object, look trivial until a later reveal gives it meaning. When: Planting clues that must pay off late. Why: Players pass over oddities they do not yet have a reason to question.
- [heuristic] Record even small, seemingly futile or unclear observations, such as timing details or a victim's details, before judging relevance; minor details often prove significant. When: Reviewing evidence during an investigation. Why: Minor-seeming details are dropped from working lists unless deliberately tracked.
- [heuristic] Report small or odd details early, such as a missing weapon, quantity or left-behind object, and return to them later; they can reverse a settled conclusion. When: when a later reveal depends on an earlier detail. Why: Details dismissed as minor can gain meaning once the solution is known.
- [heuristic] Even carefully planned crimes leave incidental difficulties and small traces that chance or overlooked details can expose; these are often the most instructive details. When: when designing how a culprit's plan fails, or building a final reconstruction. Why: Unplanned details and luck create believable exposure without contrivance.
- [heuristic] Minor details gain weight when they match a pattern in other facts, but they may be red herrings; treat them as proof only after corroboration.
- [heuristic] Keep clues at the edge between plausible and supernatural, so each can be explained either way and stays ambiguous. Why: ambiguity keeps the reader uncertain.
- [heuristic] Add a second, overlooked opening such as a skylight to a sealed room to keep the puzzle fair and solvable. When: Designing a locked-room puzzle. Why: A visible alternative route makes the sealing solvable without arbitrary cheating.
- [heuristic] An in-world notice or item description can carry a partial clue that prompts the player to find a second witness.
- [heuristic] The most obvious inference is often the one people overlook. Check it explicitly before reaching for more complex explanations. When: when an investigation stalls on complex theories.
- [heuristic] Let clues reach the player by accident during ordinary activity, such as a small item among a scatter of objects, rather than only at a marked objective. When: when placing evidence or hints.
- [heuristic] Small incidental marks, such as an urgent label, a smudged note or a half-remembered rumour, can carry weight later, so plant them deliberately. When: when planting clues in documents or dialogue. Why: readers treat minor details as significant once suspicion is raised.
- [heuristic] Set aside incidental details such as manner or bearing unless they connect to another fact.
- [heuristic] Seemingly idle personal facts, such as a dentist's name or a physical ability, can serve as connective points that link people or test a claim. When: Routine or physical details might connect to the scene or to records.
- [heuristic] Ask about small unprompted details, such as unanswered calls, to surface witnesses the subject did not plan to mention.
- [heuristic] Minor characters often turn out to matter greatly, so their introduction should be recorded in a way the audience can recall later. Why: Late-revealed relevance of incidental figures can make a solution feel unfair if the earlier appearance was not retained.
- [heuristic] A culprit who cleans carefully often misses one conspicuous object, so check for ordinary items that are out of place in the crime setting. When: The scene looks orderly after the culprit had time to clean. Why: Cleaning targets obvious traces and not familiar belongings.
- [procedure] 1) Turn a small remark into a checkable fact, such as a date, name or cargo. 2) Check it against a reference source. 3) Branch parallel inquiries to each place the subject may be found. Check even minor timing details; a neutral fact confirmed by a third party can fix whereabouts. When: Verifying a suspect's account or a witness's trivial-seeming remark. Why: A checkable fact can confirm or rule out a line of inquiry; trivial details become decisive when tied to a timeline.
- [tradeoff] Repeated ordinary details are often filed as habitual color and missed as evidence, while recurring background noise is overvalued because repetition is mistaken for significance. When: A clue is repeated in an ordinary context (missed) versus recurring incidental chatter (overvalued). Why: Repetition makes details seem habitual to some readers and meaningful to others.
- [pitfall] Observers miss small physical traces, which look like debris from standing height, and fixate on color and fashion; small details, not the general impression, carry key information. When: viewing a scene from a normal standing position. Why: A small link looks like debris from a distance, and attention goes to appearance rather than wear.
- [pitfall] Investigators overlook clues already in view, such as an address on an envelope, which may become meaningful only when a related reference is read.
- [pitfall] A withheld fact that is never hinted at again reads as a dropped thread rather than a deliberate secret. When: A secret is planted without follow-up. Why: Readers lose trust in clues that go nowhere.
- [pitfall] A partial clue invites players to complete it by assumption, which can produce a confident but wrong theory.
- [pitfall] Everyday structures such as pipes or creepers can offer a route that is missed when only obvious entrances are examined. When: Checking how a window or high opening could be reached. Why: Ordinary features can give footholds that are not immediately noticed.
- [pitfall] Investigators often overlook the suspect's own room, where items are moved or destroyed. Search there as well. When: tracing a hidden or stolen item. Why: items are often moved or destroyed at home.
- [pitfall] A closed circle can still hide an outsider who is simply overlooked, so a known population does not prove that no intruder is present. Why: Familiarity can cause people to stop noticing someone who does not belong.
- [pitfall] A trace can be missed even by the person best placed to see it, so being present at a scene does not guarantee a detail was noticed. When: An investigator examines a body or scene they were present at. Why: Attention at the time may be directed elsewhere.
- [pitfall] Identifying someone from voice and symbol without a clear view of the face shows how partial cues can mislead.
- [pitfall] A reporter who judges a detail unimportant may omit it, so a key anomaly can survive only in secondhand talk. When: When information passes through several reporters. Why: Each relay filters details by perceived importance.
- [pitfall] An earlier version of a will can be overlooked, leading the investigator to the wrong beneficiary. When: Identifying who benefits from a will. Why: Only the latest version is often checked, though a change of beneficiary may have occurred.
- [pitfall] Treating a minor inconsistency as proof of lying, when it may reflect confusion or the wording of the question.
- [pitfall] Fixating on a small wound or a fallen object can make the investigator overlook an alternative cause of the same event.
- [pitfall] Investigators who accept a first clue at face value can waste long periods pursuing a false trail. When: When a plausible clue appears early in an investigation. Why: A convincing false clue can mislead even an expert until its true origin is explained.

## timeline anchors
- [mechanism] A daily routine limits when a trace could have been made: writing on a surface that is changed every day dates from the last change. When: a timeline depends on a written or observed routine. Why: routine resets erase earlier traces.
- [mechanism] Varying clothing, names and hair across an NPC's appearances while keeping one small mark constant lets players recognise the NPC by the mark rather than the costume. When: Designing a disguised NPC the player must recognise. Why: Players then learn to look for constant features, which rewards careful observation.
- [mechanism] Two fixed points, such as a clock strike and an estimated later moment, define an interval that can be tested against other evidence. When: Only approximate times are available between anchors. Why: The interval bounds the event, turning a rough estimate into a checkable window.
- [behavior] Fixed routine tasks, such as closing procedures or evening housekeeping, create windows in which an object can change hands or a disturbance goes unseen. When: Tracing when an object was lost or introduced, or when a disturbance occurred during evening routines done at set times. Why: Comparing the object's state before and after a known routine narrows the time frame; no one is scheduled to check after the routine ends.
- [behavior] Access to a secured asset opens during predictable windows, created when key people follow fixed habits and rules have a known exception. When: A guarded asset is protected by a rule with a predictable exception. Why: Fixed routines leave gaps that can be timed.
- [behavior] A character who checks for news at a fixed time each day builds anticipation, since the routine marks when news may arrive. When: Awaiting delayed news. Why: A predictable check point makes arrival predictable.
- [rule] Do not rely on one witness's sequence when it is in doubt; anchor the timeline to surviving records, since timing claims need matching records to be trusted. When: A timeline depends on memory alone with no surviving record.
- [rule] Attach each recorded event to a fixed date so the order and spacing of events can be checked. Why: Fixed dates make sequence and gaps testable.
- [rule] Confirm place and dates early in questioning, because later timelines and conclusions depend on them. When: Reconstructing a sequence of events. Why: Errors in early anchors propagate into everything built on them.
- [rule] Give NPCs fixed routines, such as a guard on a set patrol, so that a change in routine signals an event elsewhere in the world. When: Designing NPC schedules that players should read as clues. Why: A visible baseline lets players notice when something is wrong.
- [rule] Attach dated events to NPC locations so players can test a claimed presence against a timeline. When: building a timeline-based investigation.
- [heuristic] Fixed habits give a baseline for who was available where and when; any departure, such as visiting a usually avoided place, stands out as a clue to purpose or change. When: When the person's habits are known or when reconstructing who could have been in a place at a given hour. Why: Routine sets a baseline, so deviations stand out as meaningful. (x2)
- [heuristic] Keep one solid fact constant across all story versions as the anchor; every competing theory must explain it, and one explaining nothing is kept only as a probe. When: Several theories compete for the same evidence. Why: The anchor separates real explanations from speculation. (x2)
- [heuristic] Anchor timelines first to fixed, independently checkable times, such as scheduled meetings, staff breaks, gates, lamps, clocks or dated newspapers, before placing looser events. When: When the exact order of events matters or the timeline depends on recollection. Why: Routine or recorded events are observed by several people, are harder to dispute than recollection, and give hard reference points for vague memories.
- [heuristic] Establish fixed times early, such as scheduled arrivals, promised visits, clock chimes, meals or outings, so intervals between events can be measured and later claims tested. When: Building a timeline for a mystery in which movements matter. Why: A few fixed points give stable reference marks for checking every movement.
- [heuristic] Anchor a witness's account to a known date or public signal, such as a service, bell or later undisputed public event, so others can confirm it. When: A witness refers to a particular occasion. Why: Public signals are shared and checkable, and recalled dates drift over time.
- [heuristic] Routine activity leaves independent traces, such as objects carried through locked doors, keys left in locks, fuel used, empty bottles and deliveries, that can confirm or contradict a witness's account. When: Reconstructing an evening or journey from ordinary evidence. Why: Each trace is produced without regard to the investigation.
- [heuristic] A timeline anchored to an event that itself shapes what people report is unreliable as a measure of cause and timing. When: when the reference event is controlled or shaped by the investigators. Why: The anchor can distort reports of when things happened.
