- [heuristic] Bind events to a regular cycle such as tides, so gaps and overlaps between events become visible and checkable. When: Reconstructing a sequence or checking an alibi for events bounded by a repeating cycle.
- [heuristic] Anchor the timeline to a household routine, such as when a house was last locked up, to fix times that witnesses can be checked against. When: sightings are loosely timed. Why: fixed routines give reference points.
- [heuristic] Place an object where its target will encounter it during habitual routines, such as near a bedside or a favoured item, so it is likely to be noticed.
- [heuristic] Repeat one constant image that stays steady while everything else moves, giving the audience a fixed point to hold on to.
- [heuristic] Check whether each witness's routine actually places them where they claim to be at the time. When: when verifying a witness's presence during a window. Why: Routines reveal whether a claimed location is plausible.
- [heuristic] Record a person's usual visit schedule to establish when and by whom a resource can be reached.
- [heuristic] Ask witnesses about routine tasks near the event, since routine actions anchor the timeline.
- [heuristic] An action observed in the house, such as a door being locked, can serve as a timestamp that bounds when an intruder could have entered. When: when reconstructing a timeline around a locked room. Why: Known actions give fixed points against which other events can be placed.
- [procedure] 1) Collect fixed anchors such as clock strikes, stopped clocks, recorded calls, signals, nightly habits, dispatch times, weather changes, body state, departures, dawn and light levels. 2) Order events against them. 3) Test each witness claim or alibi, marking claims that do not fit and noting who was absent at each event. When: Witness time accounts are approximate or several people give different times for events. Why: Anchors external to witnesses give a shared, checkable reference, and each account needs one. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Start from fixed transport times such as departures and arrivals. 2) Add the visible acts performed in between. 3) Fill the gaps with what the suspect must have done next. When: When reconstructing a suspect's movements from timed sources. Why: Anchored times make each step checkable against records.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each dated document. 2) Order them by their dates. 3) Link each document to the one it answers or causes. 4) Recover event order even when the narrator reports events late. When: The plot depends on who knew what and when, or on the sequence of a decision. Why: Each document anchors its event by when it was written and what it triggered, so order survives late reporting.
- [procedure] 1) Find a certified or written date as a fixed anchor. 2) Place the certified events first. 3) Fit undated testimony around them using its order of events and references to other people's movements. When: Witnesses disagree or give no dates. Why: A fixed point lets event order be recovered even when calendar dates are lost.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the one event whose date matters. 2) Find a fixed anchor it depends on. 3) Gather several independent sources, each giving a point or range. 4) Calculate from the anchors. 5) If a source fails, move to the next instead of accepting the gap. When: A timeline must be built from patchy records and at least one fixed anchor exists. Why: Several sources narrowing a range are more robust than any single source.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the anchor time from a timed object. 2) Chain inferred events forward and backward from it. 3) Mark each link with how strongly it depends on unstated assumptions. When: Reconstructing when events happened from a single recovered clue. Why: Anchored chains show which links are solid and which are guesswork.
- [procedure] 1) Fix anchor points such as the last transport, the arrival time, the moon's position, first light and any gap of unconsciousness. 2) Place each claim between anchors. 3) Check each claim against the anchors and flag conflicts. When: A witness is the main source of time or place. Why: Fixed events constrain estimates the witness cannot make directly.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the timeline on a few dated events, such as a disappearance, the last recorded message and the night of a death. 2) Order all other observations against those anchors. When: when reconstructing the order of events from several sources. Why: Everything else is placed relative to the anchors, so their accuracy matters most.
- [procedure] 1) Identify each step of a subject's route. 2) Note what ordinary people would normally see or do at each step. 3) Compare the result with witness accounts. When: When rebuilding events from routine behaviour.
- [procedure] 1) Fix anchor times first: meals, messages, arrivals at a site and departures. 2) Note the gap between each pair of anchors, such as time spent at a place. 3) Attach each claim to its nearest anchors. Why: Anchors give a fixed frame for testing every other claim.
- [procedure] 1) Fix a few reliable times as anchors. 2) List every possible exit or route. 3) Check each route's timing against every anchor. 4) Eliminate routes that fall outside the window. When: A locked space must be explained by a route in or out. Why: Hard times rule out routes that seem convenient.
- [procedure] 1) Fix shared, checkable anchors such as a departing vehicle and a station clock. 2) Note each timepiece's known error and correct readings against it. 3) Place each character's claimed movements against those anchors.
- [pitfall] Fixing a time around one striking object, such as a missing item, can hide a more reliable source and lead the whole investigation wrong. Why: a vivid anchor feels decisive, so it is rarely re-checked.
- [pitfall] Making every interrogation a chain of helpful suggestions from one person makes players notice the steering and distrust the scene. When: Writing interrogation scenes with a recurring helper. Why: Players detect a character who always steers, which breaks the sense of a natural exchange.
- [pitfall] A routine event such as a weekend return is ordinary, so a timeline entry for it proves little on its own. Corroborate it with other evidence.
- [pitfall] A timeline fixed by a single later sighting, such as a man reporting a death an hour earlier, can be checked against the suspect's movements. When: Building a timeline for an alibi or suspect movements. Why: A fixed time anchor lets each claimed movement be tested.

## culprit motive and behaviour
- [mechanism] A reversal mechanic can change which NPC is marked as culprit once a hidden item is traced to them.
- [behavior] Culprits often return to the scene of their crime at least once, driven by unease, unfinished business or an unexplained pull. When: Investigating a crime with an unknown perpetrator, or when a scene is revisited after time has passed.
- [behavior] Offenders often break down at the disposal step, even intelligent or careful ones; impulsive offenders rarely plan elaborate disposal, and intelligence does not guarantee clever concealment. When: Modelling or predicting how a culprit conceals a crime or behaves after it. Why: Disposal demands sustained planning and composure, and physical constraints can defeat intelligent offenders.
- [behavior] A guilty party's written account explains, excuses and inflates its author, so it reads as a narrative with a purpose rather than a neutral record. When: a suspect writes their own account of a crime. Why: Self-justification and vanity shape what is told and omitted.
- [behavior] A culprit can predict how investigators will behave and prepare goods to be found at the right place and moment.
- [behavior] Culprits prepare cover answers in advance, such as a partly false letter or a borrowed name, so they have something ready if questioned. When: a culprit expects that an object or act may be questioned. Why: a borrowed name avoids an obvious link to the culprit's own.
- [behavior] A reader who sees a name they associate with a known person reads the message with matching expectations and may not question the sender. When: a letter is signed with a name the reader links to someone. Why: expectation shapes how the message is interpreted.
- [behavior] A culprit may frame a deception as a kindness and recast the accuser's suspicion as spite, turning attention onto the accuser. When: a suspect is challenged about a concealed act. Why: Redirecting motive shifts scrutiny away from the concealed act.
- [behavior] A host may assume a motive, such as debt, that explains a party's secrecy without requiring an explicit lie.
- [behavior] Questioners who assume guilt before a hearing ask leading and trapping questions and read refusal to confess as stubbornness. When: interrogations where the questioner has a stake in the outcome. Why: Assumed guilt makes every answer look like evidence for the charge.
- [behavior] A clever culprit who believes they are safe may make a false move that reveals them, so waiting can expose a guilty party. When: The suspect is active and may act to cover their tracks. Why: Confidence can lead a suspect to act in a way that betrays them.
- [behavior] A person with a motive too weak to convict them may still fear being blamed, and that fear can drive a second, lesser act. When: A suspect is threatened with suspicion but has no decisive motive. Why: Fear of exposure can motivate action that looks more guilty than the underlying motive.
- [rule] Place incriminating items where the culprit did not search, and make the omission traceable to the culprit's assumptions rather than convenient. When: when planting an overlooked clue. Why: A convenient oversight without a reason invites doubt.
- [rule] Establish that a crime occurred before building a motive, since a motive only means something once a death is shown to be a murder.
- [rule] Do not conclude that a witness is lying just because statements conflict; test which version the physical facts support first. Why: Conflicts can arise from honest error as well as deceit.
- [heuristic] A culprit's own retrospective or private written record can reveal motive, self-image and plans directly, without investigators discovering them through others' testimony. When: Telling a story where the reader learns the motive from the culprit.
- [heuristic] Assuming a suspect is lying can be a useful check, but it misleads when the suspect is telling the truth.
- [heuristic] Reason from how a culprit would normally behave; an outsider rarely bothers to tidy a weapon, reload it, and relock a door. When: When no direct witness exists and the case relies on post-event actions. Why: Unusual actions after an event reveal the actor's likely familiarity.
- [heuristic] Let the solution rest on an element the audience has already seen as harmless, so the reveal recasts that element as the cause. Why: A familiar, dismissed detail becomes surprising once its true role is shown.
- [heuristic] Hold a trusted ally back as the final suspect, so the elimination ends on the hardest case.
- [heuristic] Record what a culprit believed about the player character, so the belief can serve as a hook for later confrontations.
- [heuristic] Make the culprit someone the reader and characters rely on, so earlier signs of suspicion become proof once the answer is known.
- [heuristic] Assume everyone involved may have something to hide, and press each witness on what they have not disclosed. When: A witness's account may conflict with another's or contain an omission.
- [heuristic] Use a perpetrator's known care elsewhere as a baseline; a trace that contradicts that pattern is suspect. When: judging a clue against the culprit's established habits. Why: A clue that breaks the pattern of care stands out.
- [heuristic] Show the contradictions in a culprit's inner logic, such as devotion beside anger, because they reveal motive without over-explaining it. When: A culprit's psychology should explain the crime. Why: A rationalization that is too neat reads as a device rather than a person.
- [heuristic] Rotate the culprit archetype across cases, such as insider, outsider or trusted helper, so a familiar structure stays unpredictable. When: Varying a series of mystery cases built on one formula. Why: Repeating the same culprit type makes the answer predictable even when the structure is familiar.
- [heuristic] Give a hidden culprit a sympathetic motive, such as grief, so the reveal reads as a human cover-up rather than a villain's plot.
- [pitfall] Accepting a culprit's stated cause as the whole truth closes the case without further checks and ignores other readings, since a confession can be partial. When: Weighing a confessed motive or writing a reveal that depends on it.
- [pitfall] Assuming the obvious heir is the beneficiary, without tracing each transfer or reading the document's terms, can send an investigation to the wrong person or hide the real motive. When: Following an estate's transfer chain or weighing an heir's apparent benefit. Why: Transfers can pass through several people before reaching the real gainer, and the terms of a document can change who benefits.
- [pitfall] Assuming a second person exists because a threat feels external is a mistake; the source may be one actor wearing two masks.
- [pitfall] Assuming a suspect is responsible because of one damaging act overlooks helpful acts they also performed.
- [pitfall] A culprit who assumes an incriminating document was destroyed may not search for it, so the document survives and exposes the culprit later. When: when a culprit's assumed destruction of evidence is never checked. Why: Assumptions about what was destroyed can be wrong.
- [pitfall] Treating an assumed link between a clue and a trait as proven is a common error that can misdirect the whole case.
- [pitfall] Ruling out a suspect by assumption, without checking, can hide a real motive, so each weak candidate needs an actual check. When: Dismissing candidates during motive enumeration. Why: Unchecked exclusions leave real motives unexamined.
- [pitfall] Asking who benefits from a death is too broad a test, since many people would benefit from almost any death. When: When weighing benefit as evidence. Why: Broad benefit describes many people equally.
- [pitfall] Assuming the culprit took a missing item, without checking the timeline and who had access, is a mistake.
- [pitfall] Assuming a crime follows a known pattern can lead investigators to search for a familiar signature that is absent. When: a crime does not match known habits. Why: The search wastes effort and can mislead.
- [pitfall] Assuming a suspect's gender or social role without evidence can make investigators overlook the real culprit.
- [pitfall] A theory can quietly assume the criminal's knowledge or preferences exactly where the theory needs them.
- [fact] A culprit's motive can combine a belief in his own exceptional ability, contempt for other criminals, and a wish for absolute power outside the law.

## evidence versus inference
- [definition] Observation gathers raw facts from the scene, while deduction chains those facts together into an inference about what happened.
- [mechanism] A dialogue system that separates an NPC's stated opinion from observed fact lets the player test one claim against the other. When: Designing NPC dialogue that carries opinions and facts. Why: Separated claims give the player a basis for checking and contrasting what an NPC says.
- [mechanism] An official finding can stand while an unproven insinuation about it keeps circulating as gossip.
- [rule] Gather complete evidence before forming a theory, since an early unverified claim or theory makes later findings be read through it rather than assessed on their own. When: when analysing a case or playtest result, especially at the start while evidence is new and assumptions untested. Why: Premature conclusions bias judgment; early theories formed on thin evidence bias which facts get noticed and kept. (x2)
- [rule] Record attested observations and actual words separately from the witness's interpretation or claimed cause, and check each on its own terms, since a sincere explanation can mislead. When: when recording testimony or collecting witness statements, or writing NPC dialogue, about an event that comes with an explanation. Why: An attested event does not verify its explanation; mixing what was seen with what was concluded hides the error in the inference and makes evidence look more certain than it is. (x2)
- [rule] Treat a suspicious feeling as a prompt to seek physical evidence, not as proof, and separate it from proven fact before acting. When: When an investigator's suspicion arises from unease or dread. Why: Unverified suspicion can harden into an unjustified accusation; feelings can reflect warning or fixation, and only physical evidence separates them. (x2)
- [rule] Record opinions of people, especially character judgements, separately from observed facts and check each claim about a person against observation, since opinions are weaker evidence and can replace it. Why: Opinions are not observations, and a narrator's opinion colours reports and can stand in for evidence.
- [rule] Sort each witness claim into what was seen, heard, or guessed, weigh each category differently, and mark gaps in overheard speech rather than filling them in. When: when evaluating any witness's testimony, including overheard speech. Why: A witness's opinion can be mistaken for an observation; overheard speech is incomplete.
- [rule] Let some NPCs report only what they saw and others report assumptions, so players learn to separate observation from inference. When: Writing witness dialogue. Why: Players must learn to evaluate claims by their basis.
- [rule] When reviewing a witness account, separate observed facts, such as what was said or where someone went, from interpreted states such as grief, madness or calm.
- [rule] Mark which parts of a witness account are firm observations and which are inferences, since an inference is not an observation.
- [rule] When weighing testimony, separate what a witness observed from what they interpreted, since fear can blur direction and source.
- [rule] Keep observed conduct separate from inferred motive. Do not treat a suspected motive as an established fact. When: Reading a suspect's actions as evidence of intent. Why: Conflating what was seen with what was assumed produces false certainty.
- [rule] State which parts of a joined inference are firm and which are guesses about missing pieces. When: A conclusion rests on partial sources.
- [rule] Keep identification by sight separate from identification by reasoning about motive, since they are different kinds of evidence. When: Weighing a witness's naming of a suspect. Why: Motive narrows suspects but does not show who acted.
- [rule] Separate what is directly observed from what is inferred when stating a cause or time of death. Why: inferences are weaker than observations and must be labelled as such.
- [rule] Do not treat a physical fit between fragments as proof of intent; it shows only what was read or kept. When: when a discarded document is recovered. Why: A match establishes contact with the document, not motive.
- [rule] When questioning a witness who is unsteady, restrict them to answering specific questions rather than volunteering opinions. When: A witness's account is useful but unreliable due to intoxication or emotion. Why: Unprompted opinions from an unsteady witness add noise rather than verifiable facts.
- [rule] A claim that an opinion was widely held at a time, passing through recognized writers, must rest on documents showing that transmission, not on reputation alone.
- [rule] Track evidence as proven or inference-only, and let the player decide when to present a theory, since presenting it changes which NPCs trust them. When: designing player-held deductions.
- [heuristic] Ask a witness for an opinion before asking for facts, so they commit to a position that can be tested later. Why: a stated position can be checked against later evidence.
- [heuristic] Describe a character through precise, observable detail so the audience infers traits from what they see rather than being told them. Why: precise detail makes the audience feel the observer absorbs the scene.
- [heuristic] A witness's opinion about another person's private life is weak evidence, especially when the witness admits it may be imagination. When: a witness judges someone's private conduct. Why: opinion about private matters is seldom observed.
- [heuristic] Keep a witness's opinion separate from observed behavior, since an argument about rights is not a fact about what happened. When: When a witness offers a moral or legal view alongside testimony. Why: Stated opinion can be mistaken for established fact if not separated.
- [heuristic] Hold a conclusion open until later events confirm or refute it, while more evidence can still arrive. When: when a team or investigator is split over an inference.
- [heuristic] Separate what a witness saw, heard, and understood, because a witness may report a vivid visual detail while missing the words or subject of a dispute. When: Evaluating a witness's account of an argument. Why: Visual and emotional detail can make a weak account seem strong.
- [procedure] 1) Separate what the witness observed from the inference drawn from it. 2) Judge each part against known facts, listing facts the inference leaves out. 3) Test the inference against them, keeping the observed core even if rejected. When: when a witness mixes fact with belief.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whether the witness actually looked at the condition. 2) Separate direct observation from assumption. 3) Accept a claim about a physical state only if it was observed. When: Checking a witness claim about a door, lock or similar condition. Why: Assumed conditions are easily reported as observed facts.
- [pitfall] A strong fit to facts does not prove a motive or story; showing no other explanation fits is stronger than showing that one does. Why: A motive that fits many facts can still be wrong.
- [pitfall] A witness can accurately see an act while the explanation the actor gives for it is wrong, so an observation alone is not enough. When: A witness reports what someone did and the actor offers a reason. Why: Actors can reinterpret the same act to suit their own account.
- [pitfall] Strong observation and deduction still fail when specialist knowledge is missing, so both observation and lore are needed. When: when an investigator is skilled at reasoning but lacks domain lore. Why: deduction needs precise facts to act on.
- [pitfall] A witness's opinion of someone's character is not evidence that the person was present at an event.
- [pitfall] A gap in observation is not evidence of an act. The contents of a sealed item remain unknown until it is opened.
- [pitfall] Readers may take a character's reading of another's feelings as proof of that reading, though it is only an observation.
- [pitfall] A confident but unverified opinion, even from a knowledgeable character who admits lacking proof, is a lead to test rather than a fact.
- [pitfall] Attentive observation without empathy can miss what matters most to the people involved.
- [pitfall] Two people can see the same object and read it differently, so record what was observed separately from what it is taken to mean. When: When multiple observers examine the same physical evidence. Why: Noticing a detail does not guarantee understanding its meaning.
- [pitfall] Failure of one theory does not confirm another; a rejected explanation leaves the question open. Why: a rival theory still needs its own evidence.
- [pitfall] Opinions presented as facts mislead an investigation and must be kept apart from verified statements.
- [fact] Finding a hidden item answers where it was kept but does not always establish what it proves or who acted. When: After recovering evidence from a hiding place. Why: Physical location and evidentiary meaning are separate questions.

## overconfidence
- [behavior] A witness's confidence about what they would have seen should be weighed against their vantage point, light and distance. When: A witness's certainty is the main evidence for a claim. Why: Confidence is not reliability; poor light and distance reduce recognition more than witnesses realise.
- [behavior] People recall a promise of secrecy differently, so a confidence shared privately may be remembered and repeated in conflicting ways. When: when a private remark is shared with several people under a promise of secrecy. Why: Memory of a confidence varies with each listener's interest and recall.
- [behavior] Investigators who have had repeated success may treat their conclusions as settled and scrutinize new contrary evidence less. When: An authority figure has a string of earlier successes. Why: Past success builds confidence that can reduce willingness to re-examine a conclusion.
- [rule] Label each conclusion as proven, likely or speculative, keeping levels separate and not presenting a probable answer as settled. When: when recording conclusions before a decisive test. Why: stating a probable answer as fact misleads others and the player.
- [rule] Do not claim certainty for a deduction before independent evidence confirms it; a sense of certainty is no substitute for a test.
- [rule] Suspicious conduct justifies investigation, but confirm identity before acting against a person, since an investigator's sense of certainty can outrun the evidence. When: a suspect looks guilty but identity is not yet confirmed. Why: Suspicion alone can point at the wrong person.
- [rule] Give a sleuth NPC an early, confident accusation that the player can test against later clues.
- [rule] Do not treat a confident statement about another person's reasons as established fact without evidence. Why: Confident claimants often read their own assumptions into another person's act.
- [rule] Store background facts with confidence labels such as first-hand or hearsay, and consider an opt-in personal grudge that changes available dialogue. When: Building a case knowledge system. Why: Labels let players weigh reliability, and grudges make dialogue reflect personal stakes.
- [rule] Let NPC dialogue carry confidence levels, so a guard may recall a night but not the hour, and the player must cross-check the claim. Why: Partial confidence invites verification rather than blind acceptance.
- [heuristic] A witness's certainty and accuracy vary independently, so check emphatic claims against the physical record; treating them as proof is a mistake, especially if the supporting item is gone. When: when a witness speaks firmly about a detail the scene can test. Why: certainty and accuracy vary independently.
- [heuristic] Confident expert opinions and reassurance can fail; probe them with the alternative reading, and verify any claim that everything is accounted for. When: when an expert or authority states a firm conclusion or reassurance. Why: Confidence does not guarantee a conclusion survives scrutiny, and confidence can be wrong.
- [heuristic] Treat strong personal certainty in an investigator as a warning that the inquiry may have closed too early. When: reviewing an arrest or accusation.
- [pitfall] Accepting an accusation or lead because the claimant sounds certain leads investigators to the wrong person; confidence is not evidence. When: when an accuser or claimant is emotional, insistent, or pushes a lead despite doubts about the witness. Why: Strong conviction is easy to mistake for accurate knowledge; it can override the listener's own reservations. (x2)
- [pitfall] A confident delivery can make an unproven claim sound settled and mislead readers or investigators; the most forceful claim is often least supported, since persuasion is not proof. When: when presenting a conclusion in fiction or argument. Why: Strong delivery suppresses alternative explanations. (x2)
- [pitfall] Confident tone, manner, or certainty is not evidence of accuracy; a confident speaker can be wrong even about facts they are sure of, so all claims need checking. Why: Confidence is a delivery trait or belief, not a check on the facts.
- [pitfall] A witness's firm assertion about a disputed detail or identification is not evidence of accuracy and is often immune to proof. When: when a witness holds a contested point or identification firmly under challenge. Why: Certainty and correctness are separate properties of testimony; confidence reflects belief, not the fact.
- [pitfall] A confident witness may be reconstructing the past; a certain-feeling recollection can be shaped by fear, shock, or retelling, so confidence does not prove accuracy.
- [pitfall] Fondness or claimed intimacy can make a witness describe someone favourably; neither confidence nor closeness makes such claims accurate, so check them against behaviour.
- [pitfall] Certainty born of wounded feeling is not knowledge; an emotionally charged detail or character judgment needs evidence, since hurt can yield confident conclusions. When: Weighing a witness's emotional judgments. Why: Hurt can produce confident conclusions without evidence.
- [pitfall] A confident manner or high rank is not evidence a reading is correct; an authoritative speaker can make a guess sound certain and steer the inquiry wrong. When: when an official presents a settled explanation.
- [pitfall] A confidently stated time may be vague, so an approximate time needs a fixed reference, and the more certain the speaker sounds, the more the timeline needs checking. When: when a witness gives an approximate time. Why: Confidence does not make an estimate accurate.
- [pitfall] Confident views from colleagues can pressure an investigator into accepting a rival account before the evidence supports it. Why: Social pressure can substitute for testing.
- [pitfall] A confidently stated theory can be wrong; check it against physical evidence such as the cause of death before accepting it.
- [pitfall] A witness's certainty is not evidence of accuracy; the first explanation that fits their fear is often wrong.
- [pitfall] Confident, detailed claims are not evidence; informants often sound most certain when they know least, and their stories grow as real knowledge shrinks.
- [pitfall] A verdict reached under strong feeling is not more reliable for being certain.
- [pitfall] Confidence in a conclusion tends to grow faster than the evidence supporting it, so each step needs a second check before it is treated as settled. When: Building a conclusion from several inferences. Why: Each inference feels reasonable on its own, and the accumulated certainty is not matched by the grounds underneath.
- [pitfall] An investigator may be sure of a hidden cause yet have no proof, because individually plausible accidents resist proof.
- [pitfall] A confident local theory can close off other lines of inquiry.
- [pitfall] Confidence in spotting lies from demeanour can blind an investigator to a concealed witness, because a steady, plausible speaker may be unreadable.
- [pitfall] A confident inference from character can mislead even when it turns out right, so confidence is not evidence.
- [pitfall] A confident guess about what an anomaly means is an assumption, not a finding, until a source supports it. When: When an investigator or character states a cause with certainty. Why: Confidence can substitute for evidence.
- [pitfall] An accusation can feel certain to its author yet fail to satisfy an audience, because confidence is not the same as evidence. Why: the author's conviction rests on indirect material the audience does not share.
- [pitfall] A confident denial by a servant or participant is not independent confirmation; it is an explanation that can close the question without evidence.
- [pitfall] A confident tone can reflect belief rather than knowledge; the access test shows presence or access, not accuracy. When: using a speaker's confidence as evidence.
- [pitfall] Assuming the person who sounds more confident or expert is correct lets manner decide a disputed detail that evidence should settle. When: two memories of the same event conflict.
- [pitfall] An investigator's confidence that the end justifies the means is itself a bias that can distort judgement.
- [fact] Confidences limit what a witness will offer, so investigators often must work from partial information.
- [fact] Conclusive signs are inconsistent answers under deliberate questioning, a complete set of required causes, a free confession joined to full evidence of the act, and matching gestures among co-accused. When: when classifying evidence in a suspect case. Why: These signs are strong enough to found a conviction when they are documented.

## unreliable and motivated sources
- [mechanism] An NPC with mixed guilt can be shown to have acted on false information, and the player can uncover what they knew through dialogue. When: when designing NPCs with partial responsibility. Why: Revealing knowledge separates deception from complicity.
- [mechanism] A single unnamed mention of an informer can seed mistrust across a group, since any member could be the suspected one.
- [mechanism] A narrator who attributes claims to an unseen authority invites players to find the original source and test the claim themselves.
- [behavior] A person who badly wants a comfortable story dismisses evidence that contradicts it and may never test the one clue that doubts it. When: a character has a strong emotional attachment to the story. Why: attachment crowds out doubt.
- [behavior] A talkative witness may keep speaking to avoid a silence they dread, so the amount of detail volunteered reflects emotional need as much as knowledge. When: an informal witness volunteers claims. Why: the need to fill silence drives speech.
- [behavior] Good and bad qualities can coexist in one person, so a generous character may still cause grave harm.
- [behavior] An informant with a visible grudge, disgrace or envy may mix accurate facts with a damaging conclusion and present both as equally certain. When: An informant brings a damaging, unverified claim about a target. Why: Personal feelings shape both the selection and the certainty of what is reported.
- [rule] Make the player's own journal an unreliable account: record events from memory with drifting dates, so later evidence can correct entries and reinterpret those already read.
- [rule] Do not discard a witness's account merely because its form is unreliable; its content may still point to the lead that matters. When: A child or confused witness gives a rough account. Why: Poor delivery can hide a true observation.
- [rule] Give a reveal a cause inside the scene, such as a visitor's arrival, so the disclosure follows from events rather than appearing arbitrarily.
- [rule] Let an in-world expert draw a wrong conclusion from evidence so the player can outreason that NPC. When: Designing expert characters who give evidence interpretations. Why: Players gain satisfaction by correcting an authoritative but mistaken reading.
- [rule] Mark a source you cannot reach as an explicit gap in the timeline instead of guessing what it would have said. Why: An unmarked gap gets silently filled by assumption, which corrupts later reasoning.
- [rule] Mark a repeating source, such as an idle NPC or caged creature, as unreliable so players learn to weigh its rumours against other evidence. When: a looping chatter source repeats a rumour. Why: a source that cannot understand its words has no credibility.
- [heuristic] NPC claims, especially freely volunteered accounts of others' actions, can be unreliable yet useful; make each cross-checkable against another source so players can verify it. When: when writing NPC backstory, rumours, or a character who speaks freely about others. Why: unreliable tales send players down false paths.
- [heuristic] Treat unprompted mentions, especially of other characters, as data to verify and possibly deliberate concessions; each opens a new line of questioning. When: Designing NPC dialogue, when a witness volunteers a detail. Why: a volunteered detail may be a deliberate concession.
- [heuristic] Flag a narrator's reliability early, such as by admitting doubt about their memory, so readers weigh each claim and later events feel earned. When: a first-person narrator is the source of events and their account rests on possibly compromised memory. Why: readers can then check claims rather than trust them all.
- [heuristic] Notes gathered outside official channels may conflict with the official record, so reconcile them before relying on either.
- [heuristic] A witness's unprompted description carries more weight than a photograph match alone, since the match may be suggested by the photo. When: a witness confirms a photo. Why: a photo can suggest an identity the witness did not form independently.
- [heuristic] Give a grievance-driven NPC a reason to point at a rival, so players can uncover the motive behind the accusation.
- [heuristic] Place a suspect with a real but unrelated motive, so questioning them yields a tempting but false lead. When: Designing misdirection in a mystery. Why: A genuine motive draws suspicion without proving the crime.
- [heuristic] Weigh overheard boasts by the speaker's reliability, since loud or foolish speakers often exaggerate, and do not rely on exact wording. When: deciding how far to trust overheard remarks. Why: boasts and complaints are often inflated.
- [heuristic] Test only the checkable details of an unreliable witness's account, and let claims confirmed by independent sources gain weight while unverified claims remain open. When: A witness is unreliable but may hold a real clue. Why: Independent confirmation supports the verifiable parts without proving the rest.
- [pitfall] A witness or source with a stake, such as an accomplice or a motive to shape the story, can distort what is reported, so its account needs scrutiny. When: relying on a witness with a stake, e.g. to establish an object's origin. Why: Witnesses with a stake can shape what they report. (x2)
- [pitfall] Recalled small details are unreliable unless fixed when observed, and a precise memory, especially under suspicion, is not proof without independent corroboration. When: a witness recalls a minor detail, such as which side of an object was blank, after the fact or under suspicion. Why: minor details are rarely recorded and fade or shift in recall.
- [pitfall] Unlabelled hearsay or rumour is mistaken for first-hand or established fact, so mark each claim's source and uncertainty; a contradicted unmarked rumour feels misleading. When: a story mixes direct observation with secondhand reports or unmarked rumours. Why: Without labels, readers treat secondhand claims as if seen directly, and feel misled when they are later contradicted.
- [pitfall] An excuse that no one confirms or answers remains untested. When: a third party has not responded. Why: Lack of reply leaves the claim open.
- [pitfall] A witness who explains away a contradiction by saying no one could have perceived the detail has made a claim that also needs checking. When: when a witness defends a conflicting account. Why: The defence itself is an unverified assertion about perception.
- [pitfall] A motive estimate can be wrong, and a wrong estimate can clear the guilty person. When: motive is hidden or the suspects' finances are unknown.
- [pitfall] A speaker with a motive to argue can make a true observation serve a false conclusion; audiences may mistake a provocative performance for fact. When: a persuasive character argues a worldview. Why: Entertaining delivery makes provocation sound like fact.
- [pitfall] A narrator's account of a route may be unreliable, especially when the narrator has an involved story to tell. When: when relying on a narrator's description of a journey. Why: a narrator may misstate or omit details.
- [pitfall] Witness reports of direction are unreliable when the event happened in darkness or the witness was intoxicated. When: low visibility or an impaired witness. Why: Poor perception and impairment corrupt the recalled direction.
- [pitfall] If every witness is unreliable, players cannot tell which account to trust, and the investigation loses its footing.
- [pitfall] A narrator who suppresses facts that cast him badly gives an untrustworthy self-account, so it must be checked against other testimony.
- [pitfall] A witness's claim to have been asleep can be false, so it does not settle the timeline on its own.
- [pitfall] When any rumour or gossip that tells against an accused person counts as evidence, its relevance to the charge stops mattering.
- [pitfall] Records kept by an elderly or forgetful keeper should be checked against other sources before being trusted. When: a record's author may be unreliable. Why: Memory lapses can make a single record inaccurate.
- [pitfall] A refusal to grant access or a claim of absence can be false and should be verified directly. When: A witness states that a place or person is unavailable. Why: Witnesses may conceal presence to protect someone.
- [pitfall] Accepting a relayed detail on the word of an unnamed 'reliable' source without checking the original. When: Evaluating a claim attributed to an unnamed source. Why: An unnamed source cannot be checked, and the detail may be garbled.
- [fact] Newspaper accounts and official statements can be inaccurate, incomplete or withheld, so they should not be treated as established fact.
- [fact] A witness can sincerely report vivid experiences, such as dreams or delusions, of events that never happened, so reported experience needs independent checking.

## accepting explanations
- [mechanism] When a person accepts an official order without protest, the usual grounds for later challenge to that order are removed.
- [behavior] Audiences accept a character's plausible innocent explanation for an oddity or illness as settled and stop examining the detail until a crisis contradicts it. When: a character offers a reason or natural explanation for a suspicious detail or strange events. Why: a stated reason closes the question; ordinary-seeming accounts are taken at face value until evidence breaks them.
- [behavior] Explanations that are flattering or spare painful outcomes are readily accepted, and a person with a personal stake builds argument after argument for them. When: the explanation is flattering or removes a painful or threatening outcome. Why: Wishes and social comfort shape what witnesses accept; the wished-for result drives the reasoning.
- [behavior] A witness shielding someone may disclose her situation when asked a general moral or legal question about it, because impersonal framing feels safer. When: the subject discusses her own problem in abstract terms. Why: reasoning about a general problem lowers her guard and exposes her position.
- [behavior] People often accept an accusation against another party because it is easier to believe than a harder truth closer to home. When: A close party is implicated by evidence. Why: Blaming an outsider spares those nearest the crime from a painful conclusion.
- [behavior] A witness's dislike of the accused or loyalty to a friend shapes what they notice and report. When: when a witness has a personal attitude toward a party. Why: Attitude filters attention and memory toward favoured or disfavoured facts.
- [behavior] Once a group holds a belief, ordinary misfortunes such as dead animals, sick children or quarrels are read as signs of the same guilt. When: A community already suspects someone. Why: The belief filters new events so they confirm it.
- [behavior] Prejudice spreads through a household as casual remarks that others repeat, making it feel ordinary. When: A group shares a bias against one member. Why: Repetition normalises the bias.
- [behavior] A trusted insider who is personally harmed by a belief-based system may reverse their stance, recognising the injustice they had helped enforce. When: The insider's own family or close circle is hit by the accusation. Why: Direct personal experience of harm can outweigh an abstract framework they had accepted.
- [behavior] Believers who meet contrary evidence often keep the framework by adding an explanation that absorbs it, such as a hidden deceiver who mimics innocence. When: A held belief is challenged by a case that does not fit it. Why: Adding an exception protects the whole framework instead of revising it.
- [rule] Once impossible options are excluded, accept the remaining explanation even if it seems unlikely, provided it fits every clue.
- [rule] Accept a case with a hidden client only when the apparent motive is honorable and the facts can be checked independently.
- [heuristic] Emotional conviction can override evidence, and intense certainty can rise as evidence worsens, so conviction is not a measure of truth; a player may hold a conclusion physical facts contradict. When: a witness insists they just know. Why: feelings can persuade without proof.
- [heuristic] Let the audience accept an ordinary cause for now, but leave a clue that disagrees with it so the question can return later. When: a mystery needs a temporary explanation. Why: A surviving contradiction keeps the mystery alive.
- [heuristic] Treat a quick, convenient explanation for an object as suspect when that object would be absurd for the use it is given. When: an object is explained as harmless but could serve another purpose.
- [pitfall] Preferring a subtle, vivid, or clever explanation over a plain, tested one lets an impressive theory become fixed belief, since elegance can feel like evidence. When: several explanations fit the facts, or a frame is accepted. Why: Elegance or vividness can feel like evidence even when a plainer account fits better or the frame has not been tested. (x2)
- [pitfall] Accepting the most confident account or accuser without corroboration, or ignoring their stake in the outcome, is a mistake: confidence and motive are not evidence. When: when an account or accusation is delivered with confidence or force. Why: confidence does not establish accuracy; confidence and motive are not evidence.
- [pitfall] Accepting how a scene looks or an official explanation without rechecking the objects it relies on lets investigators miss what actually happened; appearance can hide the real sequence. When: examining a crime scene or when an official account explains a scene. Why: The objects may contradict the explanation; appearance can hide the real sequence of events.
- [pitfall] A neat, confident explanation from an authority, especially one arriving early, can end inquiry; test it against the one fact that could break it, physical evidence and unexplained details. When: A plausible complete account arrives early and seems to close the case. Why: Coherent stories can feel conclusive while leaving key objects or traces unexplained; a neat answer left unchecked stays unverified.
- [pitfall] Accepting neat evidence or the most visible explanation as proof without asking who arranged it falls into the staged-trace trap; repeating the suspect's preferred reading reinforces the staging. When: when an investigator adopts the most visible explanation or neat evidence. Why: Staged evidence is designed to look conclusive and exploits the tendency to accept the reading the culprit wants.
- [pitfall] Accepting a claim because it sounds authoritative or is repeated by many sources is a common error; check its premises first.
- [pitfall] Accepting the official reading of a noise or event without asking what it would have required leads to missed possibilities.
- [pitfall] Accepting a witness's claim that nothing was touched at a scene, without checking the physical evidence, lets the claimant control the investigation. When: The witness reports the scene as undisturbed. Why: Whoever describes the scene first shapes what others see.
- [pitfall] Relying on accepted maxims rather than the facts of the case misleads an investigator, even when the maxim feels reliable. When: reasoning from a rule of thumb about crime. Why: maxims ignore specific case facts.
- [pitfall] A tidy explanation can be accepted before anyone checks where suspects actually were. When: investigators are under pressure to close a case. Why: unchecked whereabouts leave theories untested.
- [pitfall] Taking a victim's stated cause at face value can miss the real cause, which may sit in the victim's past. Why: A general cover story, such as a burglary or vague threat, can hide a personal motive.
- [pitfall] Accepting an agitated witness's out-of-order account leaves the timeline wrong; ask them to put events in sequence.
- [pitfall] Accepting cash or documents on trust, without comparison or recording of identifying details, leaves the receiver exposed to fraud.
- [pitfall] Accepting a helpful offer without asking what it removes from your control can give the helper power over timing, departure, or who stays with you. When: when an ally offers help that separates the group. Why: help can serve the helper's own plan.
- [pitfall] Accepting an in-world curse as the explanation without checking whether any person profits from it can hide a human killer.
- [pitfall] Accepting a confession because it is sincere or emotional ignores whether it fits the evidence.
- [pitfall] Accepting a stated emergency at face value is a mistake when the stated reasons contradict the body's own earlier recorded views. When: A procedure is bypassed citing urgency. Why: Stated urgency can hide a reversal of prior judgment.
- [pitfall] A firm belief is not automatically a motive; it matters only if it actually drives the person's behavior.
- [pitfall] Accepting an explanation by default, because no other has been found, rests on a weak basis. When: An event has an explanation that has not been tested against alternatives. Why: Absence of an alternative is not evidence for the default.
- [pitfall] Accepting a witness's explanation for their silence without testing it against what they do later leads to misjudgment. When: A witness withholds information and gives a reason. Why: The stated reason may be self-serving or incomplete.
- [pitfall] Accepting the first plausible reason leads to false conclusions, and dismissing a witness too quickly can waste a lead. Why: Early explanations are often incomplete and witnesses may hold useful knowledge.
- [pitfall] An official can accept a convenient explanation when the victim's known mood supports it, so the ruling should be tested rather than accepted. When: When a death is ruled quickly on the basis of the victim's mood. Why: Confirmation of an expected story discourages further checking.
- [pitfall] A supernatural explanation can excuse reckless action, such as firing into a dark scene without checking the target. When: when a supernatural belief shapes how people act under threat. Why: Belief in an unseen threat can justify actions that ordinary checking would prevent.
- [pitfall] Accepting a reported theft at face value, without checking delayed inspections or an insurer's silence, lets a staged loss go unexamined. Why: Those gaps are signs that the claim may be fabricated.

## backstory
- [mechanism] Give a character's claimed backstory one checkable contradiction against other NPCs, letters or records, so verifying players discover a slip that unlocks a branch. When: designing character claims the player can verify.
- [mechanism] A character's personal history, such as a grievance or lost prospects, colours how he speaks about others and reads evidence, and others may notice his unguarded remarks. When: When a character's history might affect how he treats witnesses or interprets the scene. Why: Private resentment and sacrifice bias perception and speech, so the character's view is not neutral.
- [mechanism] An object described briefly as background early in a story can later return as evidence, so readers and players who noticed it hold information the offender may have missed. When: Designing mundane props that later matter. Why: Items noticed once and then ignored are recalled as significant when they reappear.
- [mechanism] A background check reveals motive hints only when a real link exists, so routine checks are informative but do not always pay off.
- [behavior] People perform routine acts, such as securing a loose item, almost automatically, so a missing habitual act signals a changed plan or state. When: when a habitual act is absent from an account. Why: routines run without conscious thought.
- [rule] Mark a character's self-reported backstory, single-NPC lore, or claim no one else can confirm as unverified until a second source or physical object confirms it. When: A new character, witness or NPC gives a single-source account or self-explanation. Why: Self-reported details can be false, and recording unconfirmed claims as fact corrupts the case record.
- [rule] Deliver backstory as ordered dialogue beats, each a checkable claim the player can test against the world. When: An NPC explains past events. Why: Checkable claims let players weigh information instead of accepting it passively.
- [rule] Do not rank suspects by background traits such as origin or language skill alone. Why: such traits are weak grounds for suspicion and easily mislead.
- [rule] Treat a trace as meaningful only when it exceeds the natural background level for that substance. Why: Common substances occur naturally in trace amounts.
- [rule] Establish hostility between two characters early, as known background history rather than as a clue.
- [rule] Establish the background fact, such as a known opposition, before inferring belief from a group's choice of advisor. Why: A choice only signals allegiance when the advisor's known stance is established.
- [rule] Tie a natural or elemental threat to a buried, ancient cause rather than a present villain, so the source lies in the past. When: When a supernatural hazard needs a deeper origin. Why: An ancient cause gives players a discoverable backstory that explains the threat.
- [rule] Deliver the motive in a separate backstory block after the present crime is solved, so the past recasts the crime rather than being explained by the investigation. When: a mystery whose present crime is already solved. Why: the investigation stays on who did it, while the past gives the crime its meaning.
- [heuristic] Vivid, uncheckable backstory details reveal a speaker's character and state more than they establish facts; do not read detail as evidence. (x2)
- [heuristic] Check a body against unalterable traits, such as a long-worn ring or scar; an item that cannot be removed from the real person betrays a substituted body. When: A body may have been replaced. Why: A ring worn for years cannot be removed from a substituted body, so its presence or absence reveals the swap.
- [heuristic] Verify a newcomer with a second source; one accepted on a third party's word, without references, may be a plant, since a convincing story can hide a false identity.
- [heuristic] Gather a suspect's background through acquaintances, since relationships, family objections and money controls can supply a possible motive. When: Building a motive profile for a suspect. Why: Personal and financial dependencies often explain why someone acts.
- [heuristic] Treat an unusually polite request from an unlikely source as a warning sign; the length and location of a talk matter more than its content. When: when an unexpected party asks for a private conversation. Why: Such talks can hold a target in place while something else happens nearby.
- [heuristic] Backstory such as lost fortune, family history or wounded pride explains why a threat was so intense. When: A grudge needs to feel strong enough to justify violence.
- [heuristic] Uneven wear on a body, such as one hand larger and more developed than the other, suggests habitual manual work. When: a person's body shows lopsided development. Why: repeated use develops the body unevenly.
- [heuristic] Give look-alike characters one unchanging visible trait, such as eye colour or a crest, so the player can match identities later despite the disguise. When: when several characters share a silhouette or face.
- [heuristic] Trace a suspect's history for past dependence, mistreatment or ties to a criminal family, since these shape their state of mind. When: when a suspect's behavior seems unexplained. Why: Past experience explains why an act felt possible to the person.
- [heuristic] Tie NPC grudges to a concrete asset such as a house, salary or vote, so players uncover allegiances by reading records. When: designing NPC factions for a game. Why: A visible stake makes allegiances traceable through documents.
- [heuristic] Tie a threat to the protagonist's past so the persecution has moral logic.
- [procedure] 1) Learn the victim's identity, origin, habits and known enemies. 2) Only then judge the scene's details against that background. When: beginning an investigation of a death. Why: Background gives the details a frame for judging witnesses.
- [tradeoff] Presenting a long provenance story before naming a value makes the listener accept the high value before bargaining begins, but the story must hold up if tested. When: A seller or persuader sets a price or claim after a narrative. Why: Accepted framing anchors later negotiation; unverified detail risks exposure.
- [pitfall] A disguise never shown or hinted at makes the reveal feel unfair; show the costume early with clear ownership.
- [pitfall] A backstory revealed only at the end feels unearned unless earlier scenes plant the threat. When: Revealing a hidden motive late in a story.
- [pitfall] Accepting a close relative's identification without testing it means the identity rests on emotion as much as on proof. When: an identification comes from someone who wants it to be true. Why: emotional certainty can replace evidence.
- [pitfall] A striking skill, such as recognising faces from eyes alone, must be tested before it is trusted, because prior knowledge or rigging can explain the result. When: when a character's skill is used as evidence. Why: Hidden knowledge can mimic genuine ability.
- [pitfall] A routine known to one character but not another can make the second character misjudge who is present at a given hour, ruining an alibi.
- [pitfall] An unusual request for lodging can be noticed and remembered by staff, which undermines the cover identity. When: A newcomer asks for an odd or inconvenient place to stay. Why: Staff remember out-of-the-ordinary requests.
- [pitfall] A profile built on one unverified trait can mislead, so every attribute needs its own traceable source. When: Building a description of an unknown person. Why: An unsourced trait can send searches to the wrong people.
- [pitfall] Access gained through an assumed name fails once the household checks the claimed background, so the cover depends on no one checking.
- [pitfall] A replacement explanation can rest on an unexamined assumption, such as that a missing person existed, even when its attacks on the first theory are sound. When: building a new theory after refuting an old one. Why: refuting one story does not validate another.
- [pitfall] If no one questions a persona, the audience has no reason to revisit it when contrary evidence arrives. When: When a persona is presented without any doubt raised. Why: Unquestioned surfaces are not reconsidered.
- [pitfall] Accepting other characters' descriptions without testing them lets reputation serve as misdirection.
- [fact] Background facts show that an act was possible for a person, not that they committed it. They must be combined with physical evidence. When: when history is used to support a suspect. Why: Possibility is weaker than proof and can be shared by many people.
- [fact] Background about a person's marriage, finances and reputation can supply a motive and shape how relatives are seen.

## shock and startle reactions
- [mechanism] Shocks temporarily renew a character's energy, and once the stimulus is removed, strength fails quickly.
- [behavior] A witness's visible shock or evasive parrying at news of a death can signal guilt, innocent distress or performance; test it against other facts. When: when a witness reacts strongly to news in an interview. Why: strong emotion can signal guilt or innocent distress.
- [behavior] A sudden accusation or shocking revelation can provoke a physical reaction, such as grabbing at the accuser, standing abruptly or gripping furniture, that shows the stakes. When: when a witness is confronted with an unexpected fact or accusation. Why: strong emotion produces involuntary bodily tension.
- [behavior] Removing the pressure behind a character's choices, through financial relief or learning a feared document is unrelated, can sharply change mood, willingness and attention. When: a debt is eased, a sum is received, or a suspect learns an expected document is unrelated to the crime. Why: the pressure that drove their choices has lifted; fear of a crime link is suddenly removed.
- [behavior] A witness who changes subject, hesitates, asks to be excused or resists details is often holding back a sensitive fact; it shows concealment rather than guilt. When: when a witness avoids a topic or changes the subject abruptly. Why: reluctance signals that testimony touches something sensitive; slips and redirections carry the hidden concern.
- [behavior] A witness who hesitates to swear an oath may have a stake in the answer that they are reluctant to admit.
- [behavior] A person who recognizes someone in an unexpected meeting may cover the reaction with an excuse, and the excuse can reveal the fear beneath it. When: A character unexpectedly meets someone who knows their secret. Why: People reach for a pretext to hide an involuntary fear response.
- [behavior] A witness who fears a hidden person often shows relief when a named candidate is not that person, revealing which names are safe. When: when a witness is shielding an identity. Why: Relief signals elimination, not the target.
- [behavior] A strong, emotionally loaded first impression, such as a recognized costume, can make observers accept an identity before checking details. When: when a body or event is identified under shock. Why: emotional shock slows checking of details.
- [behavior] A character asked to spy on others may feel uneasy about the role, which can shape how willingly they carry out the watch. When: A character must observe someone they would rather not spy on. Why: Covert watching conflicts with personal ethics and trust.
- [behavior] A startling moment can fix overheard words in memory, so a witness may repeat them exactly while misreading what they meant. When: a witness overheard remarks that shocked them. Why: strong emotional arousal strengthens memory of the words.
- [behavior] A frightened or sleeping witness often holds real sensory detail that they cannot recall unprompted, while fear can also add imagined details. When: after a frightening event the witness experienced at close range. Why: shock weakens recall and mixes perception with fear.
- [behavior] A character who reacts sharply to a seemingly harmless remark may have a personal stake in the subject, and the reaction is worth following up. When: a remark touches a character's private concern. Why: strong emotion shows investment beyond the words spoken.
- [behavior] A sudden change in a person's face and eyes at a known figure's arrival reveals fear or guilt before any explanation; most onlookers miss it. When: a known person appears near a suspect. Why: onlookers attend to the arrival, not to the suspect's reaction.
- [behavior] Accusers' distress eased only once the suspect was bound, and the authority recorded this as meaningful. When: when accusers' relief follows the suspect's restraint. Why: the timing was taken as confirmation of the charge.
- [behavior] A target may accept a short delay as a source of hope, which a manipulator can then exploit. When: when a requester offers a brief wait.
- [behavior] People who process shocks alone rather than seeking company are better left unprompted for a while, and pressing them with questions can backfire. When: A witness has just received shocking news and has a known habit of withdrawing. Why: Their stress response is internal, so interruption disrupts processing.
- [behavior] A shocked witness gives approximate intervals and may lose a minute or two, so their sequence of events is blurred. When: a witness recounts an event under horror or fear. Why: shock distorts the sense of time.
- [behavior] Hints that earlier choices mattered produce dread in the audience without revealing answers. When: a retrospective frame signals that events were serious. Why: suggested stakes outrun the facts the audience actually has.
- [behavior] Under shock, people reveal what they know through unguarded reactions such as turning away, pale faces, mutual glances and recoiling from the scene. When: when people are confronted with a body or key clue. Why: shock lowers control over expression.
- [behavior] Observers often attribute unease to external causes such as weather or age rather than to a specific threat. When: A character or player feels unexplained apprehension. Why: People look for a plausible, non-threatening explanation for vague fear.
- [behavior] When nearly everyone believes in an unseen threat, most people accept accusers' claims and only a few distrust them. Why: Shared fear lowers scrutiny of claims.
- [behavior] A casual, offhand remark can revive an unsupported theory, and the listener supplies its meaning, reading hidden intent into tone or look. When: A character holds a wishful theory and hears an ambiguous comment. Why: Listeners project their hopes onto ambiguous signals.
- [behavior] A shaken witness can lose the ability to reason and obey without question.
- [heuristic] A suspect's startled reaction to a pointed question or recognition, such as turning away or urging a companion back, is worth recording; it can reveal what a cover story hides. When: when questioning a suspect with a cover story, or when a suspect is recognised. Why: a sudden reaction can betray what the suspect is trying to conceal. (x2)
- [heuristic] Relief at elimination is ambiguous, not proof: a witness may mislead on purpose, so weigh each relief reaction against other evidence before concluding guilt or concealment. When: interpreting a witness's sudden relief. Why: relief may come from being cleared of suspicion, not from hiding something.
- [heuristic] A reluctant or hesitant answer is a signal to verify, not proof of guilt or falsehood; hesitation can come from loyalty rather than deception.
- [heuristic] A sudden unexpected disclosure can probe a suspect's reaction when the suspect's composure is known to slip under surprise. When: When the shock will not endanger anyone.
- [heuristic] When several observers share the same unease, do not dismiss it just because the lead investigator has not seen it.
- [heuristic] Have other characters notice and comment on a sudden reaction, so it becomes a shared fact in the scene that players can recall later. When: planting a clue through reaction. Why: a witnessed reaction is harder to dismiss.
- [pitfall] A startled reaction can come from fear, surprise, embarrassment, drink or private shame, so innocent causes must be ruled out before reading it as guilt. When: interpreting a reaction to an exposed object. Why: many emotions produce the same response; a visible reaction does not identify its cause.
- [pitfall] Relief that is too long or too complete drains tension, so the next threat reads as repetition instead of escalation.
- [pitfall] Emotional shock can cut a survey short and leave the scene incompletely recorded. When: the investigator or a partner is distressed.
- [pitfall] Victims in shock may not describe what they saw clearly, so their accounts need checking against the scene.
- [pitfall] Relying on shocks without clues that make them meaningful weakens tension, because the audience cannot connect the shock to a question to pursue. When: Designing scares or sudden reveals. Why: Unexplained shocks produce startle without investigative engagement.
- [pitfall] Relief at clearing one suspect can lead a group to drop others too quickly, so earlier assumptions still need rechecking.
- [pitfall] A witness who readily accepts an offered explanation may be relieved rather than truthful, since the offer itself shapes the answer.
- [pitfall] Being accused of fabrication can make investigators doubt their own valid work, even when the evidence is sound.
- [fact] A witness can be sane and honest yet have no recall of events before a certain point, a known pattern that can follow severe shock. When: A witness's account depends on a period that may have been disturbed by trauma. Why: Severe shock can block recall of earlier events without impairing honesty.

## staged scene analysis
- [definition] A staged trail is evidence made to mislead: it serves no purpose except to point suspicion at a convenient person or to hide the real timeline.
- [mechanism] A staged disturbance can make a murder look like a robbery, supplying a false motive and steering investigators toward the wrong suspect. When: when a scene shows apparent theft. Why: Disorder staged for one crime can redirect the whole inquiry.
- [mechanism] Lighting, position and repeated movement control when a viewer notices a familiar figure or object, so a clue can sit in plain view unnoticed. When: a clue depends on comparison. Why: conditions decide whether a viewer registers the detail.
- [mechanism] Investigators accept a staged death scene when its visible evidence matches the explanation they expect, so a false trail can close the case early. When: The staged scene fits a familiar explanation and is not closely examined. Why: Matching expectations ends inquiry before contradictions surface.
- [mechanism] If a staged scene is later shown to be a murder, the evidence it left can point at the person living there, making them the prime suspect. When: Once the real cause of death is discovered. Why: Circumstantial evidence fits the resident and few people can vouch for them.
- [mechanism] A supposed haunting can be produced with sounds, cut lights and a costumed figure, so an apparent supernatural event may be a deliberate staging.
- [behavior] An offender disguising a violent death may clean visible stains, reposition the body and debris, and arrange items to suggest an accident or suicide. Why: to shape the first impression of investigators.
- [behavior] A staged scene can imitate violence with scattered objects, a broken glass, a bare blade and bound restraints, and its arrangement may suggest a struggle that never occurred. When: When a scene shows signs of violence. Why: Arranged debris signals struggle to observers who do not test it.
- [rule] Include contradictions to the obvious story that careful players can detect but a crowd overlooks, letting players decide whether to press. When: when designing a scene for players to read. Why: Detectable contradictions reward attention. (x2)
- [rule] Leave residue such as a forced catch, used bedding or an emptied fuel bin so players can reconstruct what happened. When: Designing a scene that was altered before the player arrives.
- [rule] Treat a deliberate arrangement as evidence of intent, and ask what the arrangement is meant to make observers conclude. Why: a staged scene is built to be read a certain way.
- [rule] Keep a staged scene consistent with what the claimed intruder would have left, so it holds up to a quick look.
- [heuristic] Compare how objects are arranged with the physical struggle the scene claims; items moved during a fight should lie scattered and trampled, not posed or shelved. When: a reported scene includes both violence and a tidy display. Why: a struggle disturbs objects in predictable ways.
- [heuristic] A staged scene shows deliberate signs and overlooks small details; test the staged story against details the planners could not control. When: A scene seems arranged to match a story. Why: Unchangeable or forgotten details resist the disguise and expose the arrangement.
- [heuristic] A posture or grip that had to be forced, such as paper clutched too tightly, suggests the scene was arranged to look like a chosen action.
- [heuristic] Test each element of a staged scene against the purpose it is meant to serve; an element that works against that purpose is a lead, not noise. When: a scene looks coherent but its details seem to conflict with its stated motive. Why: a detail that defeats the plot's own aim shows the staging is not what it claims.
- [heuristic] Examine the craft of a staged scene, not just its appearance, since a tidy-looking arrangement can still show who made it. When: When a staged scene looks convincing at first glance. Why: Technique leaves traces that appearance hides.
- [heuristic] Read a set of traces such as a rope ladder, a chloroform pad, and a syringe placed to suggest suicide as evidence of a staged scene. When: Physical items appear arranged to suggest a particular cause. Why: Items that fit a false narrative are often placed deliberately.
- [heuristic] A staged scene leaves physical traces; test each one against what the suspect could physically do, such as reach, handedness or strength. When: A scene looks staged or a suspect's capacity is in doubt.
- [heuristic] Staged props, such as shoes left before a chair or a crumpled document, imply a sequence of events; check that sequence against the timing. When: props seem to show how an event unfolded. Why: staging can fake a sequence that conflicts with the schedule.
- [procedure] 1) List every object or oddity in the scene, such as clothing swaps, bound witnesses, dug graves, placed weapons. 2) Count instruments of the act against the outcome. 3) Check each action against the claimed actor's plausible behavior. 4) Find one plan explaining every item, and test it against the body's physical positioning; reject accounts that cannot. When: when a tidy explanation is offered for a scene with several unusual details or odd objects. Why: Items that fit no plausible account reveal staging; a consistent plan accounts for every anomaly, while a partial explanation leaves contradictions.
- [procedure] 1) Compare restraints and injuries with their claimed purpose. 2) Check the alleged victim's account against physical traces. 3) Check the route and times against the claimed sequence. 4) Check the alleged victim's finances for hidden gain. When: A claimed abduction or assault seems arranged.
- [procedure] 1) Establish how the person gained access. 2) Trace each action in order. 3) Check whether any disturbance was staged to look like a struggle. When: reconstructing how an event unfolded. Why: Staged evidence can make a sequence look more violent or chaotic than it was.
- [tradeoff] Each added trick in a staged scene weakens credibility and makes the answer feel arbitrary; fewer, checkable arrangements keep the solution believable. When: when designing a locked-room solution. Why: each extra element is another point the reader must accept.
- [tradeoff] An elaborate staged reveal gains drama but can overshadow the reasoning it presents, so keep the display focused on the chain of logic.
- [pitfall] Unusual or staged-looking scenes can be real; test physical logic before concluding arrangement, since one layout may have innocent or staged origin. When: an unusual scene is first examined. Why: Unusual does not mean fabricated.
- [pitfall] An apparent robbery may be staged: valuables gathered and carried off to mask a different aim, such as destroying documents, so a theft must be tested before it is accepted. When: When a theft explanation seems too convenient. Why: Misdirection is designed to pass as the obvious motive.
- [pitfall] A freshly prepared or staged scene can mislead observers about when the events in it actually happened.
- [pitfall] Tampering to hide one fact can draw attention to another, such as an intact mechanism under a smashed device. When: A culprit stages a false time. Why: Staging creates new physical traces that can be examined.
- [pitfall] Staged figures can leave traces such as paint on the hands or clothing, which are easy to miss in dark settings.
- [pitfall] Accepting a trace as meaningful before ruling out a planted or staged explanation risks building a false case. When: A trace appears to confirm a theory. Why: Staged evidence can look exactly like genuine evidence.
- [pitfall] Dramatic staging can give the audience a sense of certainty before the evidence is complete.
- [pitfall] A scene can be arranged so its traces suggest a route that never occurred, so traces must be tested against alternatives.
- [pitfall] Small details betray a staged scene, such as clothes left in an unexpected place for a person of that character. When: when staging a false presence. Why: A detail that breaks the habits of the supposed occupant exposes the deception.
- [pitfall] Details that seem to support an alibi, such as dirty dishes, can be staged, so a fitting detail is not proof.
- [pitfall] Staged traces meant to suggest an outsider may have been made by someone already inside. Ask who gains from the staging before accepting the trace. When: when tracks or signs point to an intruder. Why: The person who benefits from a false outsider theory is often the one who planted it.
- [pitfall] Guards placed for atmosphere can look like real security, so their role and presence must be verified before anyone relies on them. When: When staff appear to control access in a crowded venue. Why: Staged presence can mask the fact that no real control exists.
- [pitfall] Reading a deliberately arranged scene as accidental leads to wrong conclusions about who was present and why.
- [fact] A seemingly impossible sealed room can be the product of the culprit's own arrangements, made before anyone enters.

## movement and track reading
- [mechanism] Ground condition decides which tracks survive: soft, wet soil keeps prints that stone or dry gravel hides, so surface type decides whether tracking can work. When: Tracks are left across varied terrain. Why: Surface material controls whether a print is preserved.
- [mechanism] Dust or residue on an undisturbed floor or closed room accumulates predictably, recording who entered and roughly when; prints and disturbed objects mark recent contact. When: A room has been closed or undisturbed, with fine material covering the floor. Why: Undisturbed surfaces give a baseline, deviation marks recent contact, and fine material retains impressions showing movement and handling.
- [mechanism] Items with generated wear, stains and fittings encode their owner's habits, letting an examining player infer traits without being told. When: items are placed in a world as clues. Why: physical marks record past use that a player can read.
- [mechanism] Dust gaps and disturbed surfaces show that an item was taken, giving players a reason to revisit a room.
- [mechanism] A physics-based trajectory check can give players a clue that they must interpret against the level geometry, rewarding spatial reasoning.
- [mechanism] A trail that stops abruptly away from any obvious exit suggests the person changed footwear or diverted to another route.
