- [rule] Model dried mud, snow, sand or dust floor tiles with timestamped footprint and one-way trail state recording each character's passage, so players read when and which way someone passed. When: Designing terrain or floor surfaces that support tracking or record movement. Why: Timed, directional tracks turn movement into evidence players can order and interpret.
- [rule] Scatter damage or debris in a flooded or collapsed room so the pattern encodes entry order, letting players who compare wreckage deduce which path was used first. When: Designing environmental storytelling in a damaged space. Why: Players can reason from comparative differences to sequence.
- [rule] Give a locked-looking puzzle room a hidden trace, such as a snagged fragment, that reveals an alternate route to players who inspect closely.
- [rule] Give a supernatural-seeming event a discoverable physical cause, and make its appearance change with the player's distance or vantage point so the explanation can be tested. When: Designing a haunting or uncanny event in a generated space. Why: A testable cause lets players reach a fair explanation by reasoning.
- [rule] Let footprints in mud or grass form a trackable trail, but let the trail be lost on paved or trampled ground so the player must search for the next clue. When: When building a tracking mechanic into a game level. Why: Losing the trail at hard ground forces the player to use other clues to continue.
- [rule] After a loss, give players a trail through other NPC reports or map markers, such as sightings, so the search keeps moving. When: when a lost item or suspect is pursued. Why: a cold trail stalls the player.
- [heuristic] A trail that breaks at a surface change or barrier is a clue, not a dead end; keep searching nearby, as it usually resumes on another surface or floor. When: A physical trail ends at a barrier, threshold, or change of surface or level. Why: The stopping point marks where a hidden route or explanation likely lies, and the trail usually resumes nearby. (x2)
- [heuristic] Creature tracks encoding weight, stride and claw marks let players infer whether one or several creatures passed and guide them toward a hidden creature or map region.
- [heuristic] Soft ground that takes clear prints can show direction of travel: prints leading away from a spot with none returning suggest one-way movement. When: Soil is wet or soft enough to hold impressions. Why: Print sequence reveals movement order.
- [heuristic] Follow a trail of marks back to where the event started, since the direction of the marks shows where movement went.
- [heuristic] Make foot size or shoe type a physical identity clue that tools such as a lantern or measuring tape can reveal. When: Designing a suspect identification puzzle. Why: Measurable physical traits let players distinguish individuals.
- [heuristic] Read a visitor's bearing and dress on arrival as clues to their state of mind, before any account is given. When: at the start of a case. Why: manner reveals agitation or composure.
- [heuristic] Rebuild a person's movements through ordinary inquiry, such as walking the area and questioning nearby people about the period. When: when a timeline of movements is missing.
- [heuristic] The most recent sighting, including clothing, narrows where a person may be found now. Why: Recent movements are more likely to still be near the last known point.
- [heuristic] Give physical clues a behavior, such as a stain that spreads or an odor that fades, so players can interpret them rather than merely finding them. When: Placing environmental clues meant to signal past events. Why: A clue that changes over time carries information about when and how an event occurred, not just that it occurred.
- [heuristic] Footprints on carpet let a level designer show who passed through a room and in what order.
- [heuristic] Set weather or room humidity as variables that change how fast clues degrade, and make players account for them when reading timing.
- [heuristic] Scan the sides of a trail as well as its line, since traces that leave or rejoin the path can be missed.
- [heuristic] A single set of tracks crossing an area shows the route actually taken, so counting tracks reveals which path a person followed. When: Reconstructing movement from ground marks.
- [heuristic] Among many similar tracks, isolate the set with a distinctive feature, such as a turn and return, to separate the relevant route. When: A trail contains many similar marks and the target route must be identified. Why: Only a distinctive pattern discriminates the relevant tracks from common ones.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the shapes, sizes and heel patterns of impressions to separate individuals. 2) Use overlaps to determine the order of arrival. 3) Use gaps and changes in stride to infer speed and distress. When: Reconstructing movement from footprints in soft ground. Why: Overlaps show sequence and stride changes show running or carrying.
- [procedure] 1) Separate clear, careful tracks from smudged ones. 2) Read each print's depth, shape and direction. 3) Set aside faint or partial marks until another clue supports them. When: Soft ground holds several overlapping sets of tracks.
- [procedure] 1) Start at the last known point. 2) Ask each witness whether they saw the person at a given place and time. 3) Record each sighting as an observation before drawing conclusions. 4) Work backward along the route. When: When tracing a fleeing person through public places. Why: Backward chaining from a known point links separate witnesses into one route.
- [procedure] 1) Record departure and arrival times with a watch. 2) Use the journey's duration to bound its length. 3) Anchor the timeline at the first recognisable landmark, such as a signal or a station name. 4) Separate what was sensed from what was guessed. When: a captive or blindfolded witness must describe a route.
- [procedure] 1) Name the trace that would have been left. 2) Decide where it would be. 3) Check whether conditions such as mud, water or stone could have erased it. 4) Read a blank as informative only if the trace would have survived. When: an expected trace is missing. Why: blanks can come from erasure.
- [procedure] 1) Look for matching marks on both sides of the barrier. 2) Measure gaps between marks and compare them with the suspected tool's known size; a mismatch rules it out. 3) Compare material from each side for a common source. 4) Test whether a reversed orientation explains anomalies. When: When a barrier was crossed and the question is how, not who.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the known origin and destination. 2) Order each leg by date and time. 3) Check every recorded endpoint against the chronology. 4) Confirm each leg with an independent source.
- [procedure] 1) Mark two known points on a shot's path. 2) Extend the straight line through them back toward the target. 3) Measure the weapon's height where the line passes the origin. 4) Estimate the shooter's height from that weapon height and aiming posture. When: a shot's path is recorded and the shooter's position is in question.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the origin building. 2) Trace the route house by house. 3) Use fixed landmarks, such as passageways beside buildings, to confirm each step. When: explaining how a person traveled between two places.
- [procedure] 1) Photograph the impression before it is disturbed. 2) Make comparison impressions from each candidate source. 3) Discard sets that fail to match. 4) Compare the remaining set with the photograph, checking each mark and each gap. When: A readable pattern is left in a soft surface and candidate sources are available.
- [fact] Broken twigs show recent passage, while hard dry ground leaves no fresh footprints, so ground condition limits which traces remain.
- [fact] Footprints can carry wear signatures such as missing studs or worn heels, letting a player match a suspect's footwear to a track. When: Designing a trace system in a game.

## proof and evidence standards
- [model] Evidence tiers: a rumor opens a lead, corroborated testimony adds weight, physical proof closes a case; block accusation or conviction until physical proof is reached. When: designing investigation gating, or when a suspect is known but evidence is thin. Why: Tiering keeps the player from accusing on inference alone, since a skilled defence can dismantle inferences lacking physical support. (x2)
- [definition] A not-proven verdict means the case was unsupported, not that the accused is innocent; proven innocence is a separate, stronger verdict requiring positive proof. When: Defining the goal or outcome of an investigation. Why: Keeping the two apart stops an inquiry from claiming more than the evidence supports. (x2)
- [mechanism] Once a fact is confirmed, NPC reputation can change their behaviour toward the subject, so the player sees the effect of proof. When: A confirmed fact about a character becomes known to other characters. Why: Confirmed status alters how others treat that character.
- [rule] Secure proof before confronting a suspect; a premature claim exposes the investigator's source and lets the accused recast the dispute as the accuser's fault. When: Preparing an interrogation or accusation. Why: An unprepared accusation gives the accused room to counter-attack. (x2)
- [rule] Gate accusations and arrests behind an evidence checklist, such as a medical or forensic report, so the player can delay action to gather one more item. When: designing a late-stage accusation or arrest.
- [rule] Accept testimony as proof only when detailed and checkable, such as specific meetings, physical marks or objects received, ideally including a detail the witness could not have known. When: when building a clue the player must verify, or when evaluating a witness account. Why: Detailed, checkable claims can be tested against the world; only knowledge outside the accuser's reach proves the account.
- [rule] Judge a suspect's innocence by what the facts show, not by faith in the person.
- [rule] Keep physical conclusions separate from judgments about a suspect's character; doubts about character must not alter what the physical evidence shows. When: a suspect seems unlikely for personal reasons. Why: physical facts and opinions about people are different kinds of evidence.
- [rule] An unmatched trace should not auto-resolve to an unknown intruder. The corpse or the room's own objects should be possible sources. When: A clue system finds a trace that matches no non-player character. Why: Other sources in the scene are plausible and must remain open.
- [rule] Do not spend effort on authorship checks when the authorship of a document is not in doubt. When: Deciding whether a document needs expert comparison. Why: Effort is better spent on questions that affect the case.
- [rule] Include an authority NPC who ignores contradictions, so players learn that proof must be presented in a form that cannot be dismissed. When: designing an antagonistic authority in a mystery.
- [rule] Do not place the burden of disproving a confession on the accused; a confession that cannot be shown false should not by itself settle guilt. When: A confession cannot be checked against independent evidence. Why: Shifting the burden to the accused makes unverifiable claims decisive.
- [rule] Start reasoning from observed facts and test each candidate idea against them, rather than fitting facts to a conclusion reached first. When: Building or evaluating a theory of a case. Why: Preconceived theories lead to searching for evidence that confirms them and to missed contradictions.
- [rule] A defence needs only reasonable doubt about the accused, not proof that the alternative person is guilty. When: when arguing an accused person's innocence. Why: Showing another person could have committed the crime is enough to weaken the case.
- [rule] Prove a hidden cause with a document, a physical object or a sound; use a confession to close the reveal only when no object is available.
- [heuristic] Assemble proof from independent sources, such as a forensic match, lab analyses, a records audit, a physical object and a witness statement, since converging sources are hard to dispute. When: building a final case against a suspect. (x2)
- [heuristic] Record an NPC's explanation as a claim with a verification state, so the player can later test whether the story holds.
- [heuristic] Separate what evidence proves, such as a person's presence, from what it only suggests, such as intent. When: Evidence is used to support a theory about someone's motive. Why: Presence does not establish purpose, so the obvious reading may be wrong.
- [heuristic] Ask for proof of ownership; indirect support offered in its place signals that the claim lacks evidence.
- [heuristic] Give each mystery case one test that separates the true mechanism from the false one, so the answer can be proven rather than asserted. When: Designing the solution of a mystery case. Why: A physical or observable test makes the answer verifiable for the player.
- [procedure] 1) Establish how a statement was obtained, such as whether it was freely given after a caution. 2) Only then weigh what the statement says. When: Evaluating a statement given during an investigation. Why: A statement's content is judged differently depending on how it was obtained.
- [procedure] 1) Record each point that can be proven. 2) Mark each deduction as inference only. 3) Hold the inference until the suspect is linked. 4) Pass the full reasoning to the authorities once the link is established.
- [tradeoff] Aiming to prove a case differs from aiming to find what happened; the two aims can conflict and shape which evidence is pursued. When: Several parties want different results from the same evidence.
- [tradeoff] Setting aside a tight chain of evidence only because it seems improbable, versus accepting an extraordinary conclusion, each carries a cost that must be weighed. When: Evidence forces a choice between a closely fitting chain and a very unlikely conclusion. Why: Rejecting the chain returns the investigator to the start, while accepting the extraordinary conclusion commits to serious consequences.
- [pitfall] A correct motive-based inference is not proof; without a document to show, conclusions from motive and deduction stay unconfirmed until access and knowledge are verified. (x2)
- [pitfall] A timeline built by an enthusiast may carry that person's agenda, and stating specifics that cannot be proven gives the suspect a point to contest. When: When an interrogator recites an unverified timeline. Why: Unsupported details undermine the whole account once one is disproved.
- [pitfall] A supernatural or unprovable explanation cannot support a legal case, however convincing it seems to the people present. When: when the proposed explanation lacks physical or testimonial proof.
- [pitfall] Smell evidence is unreliable when the tester's sense is weak or many odours are present; confirm it with another method.
- [pitfall] An investigator may be unable to prove a denial false, even when suspicious, so denials must be probed rather than accepted.
- [pitfall] A doctor who never treated the deceased may give a cause-of-death verdict that the evidence does not support.
- [pitfall] A proven lie does not automatically discredit a witness when judges already favor the accuser. When: when a court hears contradicting evidence. Why: prior bias can outweigh a new disproof.
- [pitfall] A trace found by one person in a moment others cannot recheck is weak evidence, however clearly that person describes it.
- [pitfall] A verdict without a written record can be changed quietly, leaving no clue that the ruling was altered.
- [pitfall] An impossible claim is only rumour unless the physical object involved has been preserved and can be examined. When: A claim rests on an object that vanished or changed. Why: Without the object, no one can test the claim against physical reality.
- [pitfall] Treating an artistic impression as proof of guilt turns a suspicion into an unsupported accusation.
- [fact] Stillness, absent pulse, pallor, lack of warmth and stiffening are each weak alone, because a living person in deep trance can show the same signs.
- [fact] Investigating judges may accept presumptions, whereas jurors weighing both sides usually require physical, tangible proof. When: a case is presented to different reviewers. Why: reviewers differ in how much they accept inference.
- [fact] Proving a solution is usually harder than explaining it, so the evidence must be arranged to support the explanation.

## statement wording and versions
- [mechanism] Reading a suspect's own recorded words back to him can expose a contradiction he cannot easily deny. When: Recorded remarks conflict with his later account.
- [behavior] A single word or overheard phrase can carry several meanings; keep each reading open, since a first reading may be wrong until a fact or fuller conversation selects one. When: a key remark has no clear referent, or a partial overheard line is interpreted. Why: Meaning depends on the surrounding exchange.
- [behavior] An ambiguous line from a character can carry a harmless reading and a revealing one, and which reading wins depends on what the listener already suspects.
- [behavior] A witness may deny having used a word that the questioner clearly remembers them saying, so disputes over wording are settled only by a written record. When: A witness disputes the exact words used. Why: Memories of specific wording are unreliable on both sides.
- [rule] Check quoted wording and copies against the original; copies hide omissions, misfiled items, copying slips, and a single transcription error in an address. When: Relying on a copy of a record or quoted wording. Why: Treating a copy as the original document can mislead investigators. (x2)
- [rule] Write NPC dialogue so one line reads two ways and signals different things by player knowledge, leading to a different suspect or location. When: designing a clue delivered as dialogue. Why: a second reading rewards returning with new knowledge.
- [rule] Write down small errors that favour the accused, even when none is damaging, and check them. When: a witness's account has minor inaccuracies. Why: Minor errors can hide patterns that matter.
- [rule] Give a suspect two dialogue states: a public face in company and a private one when the player finds them alone.
- [rule] Answer an alternative explanation with new evidence rather than by restating the original conclusion. When: When a suspect or rival disputes an inference. Why: Repetition does not distinguish between the two explanations.
- [rule] Make NPC references such as the usual service or the night watch ambiguous, and let the player ask follow-up questions to resolve contradictions.
- [rule] Track each version of a captured enemy's or NPC's account in dialogue, and let contradictions unlock the next investigation step.
- [rule] Let players confront the source to check exact wording, since a mismatch can unlock a new line of questioning. When: Designing rumour verification mechanics. Why: Verification gameplay rewards players who compare relayed and original words.
- [heuristic] Record transcription corrections separately from original wording and spelling, so originals stay recoverable and readers know what was altered before trusting a word. Why: Altered words can change how a name or claim reads.
- [heuristic] Make overheard, through-wall or phone-call NPC speech ambiguous about who is speaking, so players must question witnesses to resolve the speaker. When: designing speech heard through doors or walls.
- [heuristic] Read a note for what it implies as well as states, since insinuation can alarm more than claims; treat it as a motive source, not settled proof of cause. When: Analyzing a written message whose meaning goes beyond its literal content. Why: Implication carried by phrasing can affect a recipient more than explicit claims do.
- [heuristic] A dying NPC's cryptic line can point at several people; the player's record of who was present and what they knew should decide the reading. When: designing ambiguous last words. Why: knowledge state resolves ambiguity.
- [heuristic] Keep clue wording short and ambiguous enough that players must test it rather than take it at face value.
- [heuristic] Test each ambiguous word in a statement against the speaker's situation and knowledge to decide whether it was meant literally or figuratively.
- [heuristic] Do not rely on a public witness appeal as the main line of inquiry, since the subject may have travelled in a private vehicle unseen.
- [heuristic] When a witness's story is told both impaired and sober, weigh the sober telling more heavily.
- [heuristic] Record who reported each statement and to whom, since the source of a clue is part of the clue itself. When: writing a case where information travels through several people. Why: the chain of reporters determines how much the player trusts it.
- [procedure] 1) Read each statement back and fix it on record. 2) Sort it as lead, background or proof. 3) Treat detailed length as no evidence of proof. 4) Note absences without treating them as proof. When: A large set of statements must be assessed for a case. Why: Statements serve different purposes and must be sorted before weighing.
- [procedure] 1) Put each accuser's claim to the suspect. 2) Record the suspect's answer to each claim. 3) Keep the answers on record so they can be checked against the full examination later. When: when examining a suspect against several accusations. Why: a summary can misreport what was said.
- [procedure] 1) Record each statement in order. 2) Note new names or details that appear. 3) Check whether they arrived after outside information was introduced, which suggests they were supplied, not recalled. When: comparing a suspect's successive statements.
- [procedure] 1) Standardize spelling to one modern form. 2) Leave words and sentence structure unchanged. 3) Adjust punctuation to carry the original sense. 4) Keep archaic forms where the old wording affects meaning. When: Publishing a modernized edition of old records. Why: Consistent edits keep meaning intact while improving readability.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who said what, in what words, and to whom. 2) Ask whether the original speaker used those words. 3) Obtain the original document where possible before reacting. When: A witness repeats another person's disputed words. Why: Summaries and relays can shift meaning, so the source must be tested.
- [pitfall] An ambiguous remark or overheard phrase, even an offer of help heard as a threat, can carry many meanings; reading guilt into it before weighing context is speculation. When: a remark can be read two ways. Why: Meaning depends on context and what the listener knows.
- [pitfall] Quoted speech is only as reliable as a witness's memory and honesty; a single misheard or misremembered word can invert a retold report's meaning. When: a witness repeats another person's words. Why: partial observation distorts recalled dialogue.
- [pitfall] Translated or unrecorded wording can lose nuance, so readings based on it need caution.
- [pitfall] A translation can carry the commissioner's assumptions, and later readers who trust it inherit those assumptions.
- [pitfall] A suspect's own words, quoted out of context, can be used to build a case out of genuine feeling.
- [pitfall] Ambiguous words spoken in anger can mean different things. Read the final words against tone and manner, not the wording alone. When: when a last remark might signal intent. Why: delivery can reverse the apparent meaning of words.
- [pitfall] One incorrect detail in a witness account, such as a wrong station name, can shift the whole sequence. Check each detail against a reference source before building on it. Why: Errors propagate through every later inference.
- [pitfall] Stressing one word in a witness's wording can read as doubt, though it may be only a feeling.
- [pitfall] A refusal to answer can come from shame or from protecting someone else, so it cannot be read as a confession.
- [pitfall] An interviewer who responds only to tearful appeals can be drawn away from the questions that matter. When: when a suspect shifts to pleading. Why: emotion can crowd out the factual line of questioning.
- [pitfall] A statement read back to a witness and sworn to is not the same as an account first taken independently from them. Why: Reading back can shape or harden the first version.
- [pitfall] A pleading voice from behind a barrier can be read in more than one way, so listeners may disagree about what it means.

## estimation and alibi windows
- [model] Model each character's alibi as a time window testable against shared anchors, such as a shared game clock NPC accounts reference; create windows the player must reconcile.
- [mechanism] An alibi holds only within its time window, so a slightly off estimated hour can collapse it; include the estimate's margin when testing routes.
- [mechanism] An alibi covers a time window, and the decisive gap is between the last point where the suspect is accounted for and the critical moment. When: checking whether an alibi excludes a suspect. Why: An alibi can be detailed for one period and still leave the critical moment unaccounted for.
- [mechanism] If a crime's apparent time is moved, an alibi built on a fixed departure can make a suspect look far away at the stated hour. When: a suspect's whereabouts depend on a schedule. Why: a fixed transport time is checkable, so a false crime time makes the alibi look solid.
- [rule] Compute alibi checks from inspectable positions and timers, not hidden flags, and leave checkable traces such as footprints or timestamps, since chance incidents make unreliable systems. When: Generating suspect-tracking and alibi logic. Why: Traces let players test an accuser's claim of unseen means. (x2)
- [rule] Treat rough time estimates and witness clocks as provisional; do not treat a time gap as settled until travel times and clocks are confirmed by independent accounts. When: When an alibi depends on a witness's recorded time. Why: Unverified clocks and travel estimates can make an impossible movement look possible or the reverse. (x2)
- [rule] Any alibi must cover the whole relevant window from when the suspect left onward, with a witness for every stretch; any unwitnessed gap lets the suspect slip away. When: when verifying a suspect's alibi. Why: A gap anywhere in the window lets the suspect slip away unseen; an unwitnessed interval is a gap an alibi cannot close.
- [rule] Require the player to confirm a suspect's whereabouts through a separate source, such as a guard log, servant or timed door, not dialogue alone.
- [rule] Build alibi clues such as a location log, a guard's shift record or a door timestamp that makes a claimed sighting impossible. When: when designing an investigation.
- [rule] Before accepting an alibi, check whether its window is long enough for the act and whether witnesses can confirm it.
- [rule] Verify alibis quietly so suspects do not learn what is being checked. Why: knowing the check lets suspects adjust their stories.
- [rule] Set the standard of proof so that letting several guilty parties escape is preferable to condemning one innocent person on indirect evidence.
- [rule] Let each NPC's alibi be checked by a separate source that is individually true, while one hidden link, such as a mismatched identity, breaks the whole story. Why: Players must test links, not just individual facts.
- [rule] Give suspect NPCs a travel record, such as a ferry log or fare receipt, that lets the player verify their alibi.
- [rule] Show scheduled meetings across a day in an in-game case log so the player can check alibis against the clock.
- [rule] Store each suspect's claimed time intervals with the locations and NPCs who could verify them; if a verifier is removed, another route to that fact must remain. When: designing a solvable alibi system. Why: Removing a verifier must not make the puzzle unsolvable.
- [rule] Give each suspect an anchor-event timeline, and make one alibi depend on an NPC reachable only through a clue such as a hotel or train record. Why: The player must follow the clue to verify the alibi.
- [heuristic] Treat a time-of-death estimate as a range, not a moment; treating it as exact can wrongly exclude innocent people, and a wrong estimate changes the conclusion.
- [heuristic] Narrow the candidates by matching a witness's time window and description against each operator's records.
- [heuristic] An alibi anchored on an arrival time does not cover the earlier window, since the gap may lie before departure or after arrival. When: when a suspect's alibi rests on a known arrival.
- [heuristic] An alibi whose witnesses appear only after the relevant window does not cover that window. When: checking whether an alibi covers the crime period.
- [heuristic] Test witness times against official records, since a time written at the moment of an act can fix when it happened. When: Checking a witness's stated timing against documentary evidence. Why: Contemporaneous records are harder to fabricate than later recollection.
- [procedure] 1) List each suspect's timestamped movements in time order. 2) Match every interval to a landmark or event. 3) Mark windows no one can vouch for, flagging those before the key event. 4) Keep any window long enough for the act, even a short one. When: Testing alibis against a crime, or when a suspect's whereabouts are described only loosely. Why: A quick act needs only a short unobserved interval.
- [procedure] 1) Mark fixed times such as departures and arrivals. 2) Add reliable travel times. 3) Find the gap a suspect could have used. 4) Check whether any decoy's movement fits that gap. When: when a suspect's alibi covers a single known window and travel times are reliable.
- [procedure] 1) List the moments when the suspect's location is already known. 2) Use a schedule to find the earliest departure and latest return that allow presence at both places. 3) Focus checks on that window. When: the main question is whether the suspect could physically have been somewhere and schedules exist. Why: Only the window decides whether the alibi holds.
- [procedure] 1) Measure the spacing and height of handprints on a surface. 2) Compare the reach with a known person's reach. 3) Allow for the posture the person used. When: When marks show where a person's hands rested and a suspect's reach is known. Why: Reach from marks gives an approximate size estimate.
- [procedure] 1) Note the height of the object the person reached. 2) Note the posture used, such as standing on tiptoe and which surfaces were gripped. 3) Apply standard body proportions to estimate height from that reach. When: a visitor left no direct record but the scene shows reach-dependent placement.
- [procedure] 1) Note the origin of the postmark. 2) Record the dates of the message and the event. 3) Subtract the mail transit time from the total gap to estimate the sender's extra travel time. 4) Infer the vessel type from that time. When: the sender's location and speed are unknown and only the postmark is available. Why: the gap measures travel beyond the mail.
- [procedure] 1) Perform the same action yourself. 2) Judge how much strength and practice it demands. 3) Compare that requirement with each suspect's physical capacity. When: A physical attack must be matched against possible suspects. Why: A suspect who looks frail may still have the strength the attack required.
- [procedure] 1) Ask for departure and arrival times. 2) Compare each gap with the expected travel time. 3) For each gap, ask what was done and who could confirm it. 4) Log each unverifiable claim as a task to check independently. Why: Each interval is a separate claim that needs its own support.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the time from a verified timer 2) Look up the external schedule 3) Identify which scheduled event occurred at that minute and location. When: an in-world timestamp must be linked to real-world events. Why: schedules can explain what happened at that moment.
- [pitfall] Travel time and distance estimates from a witness's judgment are ranges, and a travel maximum is an assumption unless it has been measured. When: when timelines depend on witnesses' impressions of journeys. Why: Witnesses judge distance and duration from expectation, not from measurement. (x2)
- [pitfall] Estimated intervals are imprecise, and interested parties may shorten or stretch them, so timelines built from recollection can mislead. When: Times come from witness estimates rather than fixed clocks. Why: Stress degrades time memory and self-interest biases it.
- [pitfall] An alibi placing a suspect at known public venues proves little about the minutes that matter. When: when a suspect's alibi relies on visible public locations. Why: being seen in public does not cover the critical interval.
- [pitfall] A matching time does not prove presence, since a single sighting can be mistaken.
- [pitfall] Phrases such as in a week are estimates, so treating them as exact dates creates false precision in a timeline.
- [fact] Dividing a poison into equal portions lets whoever prepares it control the total dose taken.

## narrative design and scripting
- [model] Short episodic cases share one formula: outside visitor brings odd problem, investigator reads plain clues, wrong culprit pursued, reveal explains all; reusing template makes verdict anticipated. When: Designing a series of self-contained, similar mystery cases. Why: A repeated structure makes each case quick to follow, and the expected outcome becomes part of the pacing rhythm. (x2)
- [model] A detective case runs in order: hook, setup, false solution, pressure, complication, reveal, resolution, with the twist recasting earlier clues. When: structuring a mystery scenario. Why: Each stage shifts suspicion so the player's theory is tested before the final answer.
- [mechanism] Setting up expectations through repeated cues or voiced stakes raises anticipation, so a delayed reveal or scene shift lands harder when it arrives. When: a delayed reveal or scene shift is planned. Why: Expectation raises the stakes the reversal overturns; stated stakes raise expectations.
- [mechanism] Hearing an approach before seeing its source lets the audience anticipate a presence, raising suspense before the reveal.
- [mechanism] A culprit can build an alibi by arranging a respectable third party to be present during the crime window, so the witness can swear the culprit never left.
- [mechanism] A timed chase or rescue between a clue and its reveal keeps pressure on the player and heightens tension before the answer is shown. When: Placing a reveal in a mystery sequence. Why: Pressure makes the eventual answer land with more force.
- [mechanism] A tail mechanic in which the player follows an NPC to discover a hidden meeting place or contact can drive a branching investigation. When: In investigation games with hidden NPC relationships.
- [rule] Write villain dialogue revealing how many plans were exposed, and a consistent action sequence that makes sense only after a reveal, rewarding players who review earlier dialogue and clues.
- [rule] Make ambiguous clues, such as hazards that could be coincidence or attack, or untouched loot on a slain NPC, support both innocent and hidden readings so players judge.
- [rule] Give players a fallback such as a safe room, so that a trap is a tense test rather than a sure death.
- [rule] Design strange quests so their costs, rewards and schedule reveal a hidden function that a player can deduce. When: A quest or job offer has an unexplained purpose. Why: Players solve puzzles from consistent, observable constraints.
- [rule] Build npc dialogue as tone states that escalate with pressure, where tells raise a flag and a softer state unlocks the next clue. When: when designing interrogation or conversation trees.
- [rule] End a play session on a pending offer or choice so the next session opens with the decision already waiting. When: when planning session breaks.
- [rule] Use a restriction, such as a travel limit with arrest as the penalty for leaving, in place of immediate arrest to keep the suspect in play.
- [rule] Make each narrative branch expect a specific event that either occurs or does not. When: Designing branching story logic. Why: Lets player choices produce verifiable outcomes.
- [heuristic] Let an antagonist redirect suspicion onto a witness, and offer the player a dialogue choice to press further or back off.
- [heuristic] Scripted deniable events, such as falling debris, can stay ambiguous until the player aggregates several of them. When: when designing hostile events meant to reveal a pattern later. Why: Single events read as accidents; only the set reveals intent.
- [heuristic] A person's last position relative to a track or road can show which side they approached from, so geography narrows where they came from. When: a person or object moved across unfamiliar ground.
- [heuristic] A step that seems to serve no purpose in early accounts may become the key link once later records reveal its role. Revisit it when new evidence appears.
- [heuristic] A witness who leads someone to a scene may be setting a trap or confessing knowledge; the intent can be left unresolved.
- [heuristic] A map is only as precise as the points it rests on; when its markers are lost, present the resulting line as approximate. When: the reconstruction depends on vanished landmarks.
- [heuristic] Place a second hidden channel only after the first is found, so the discovery itself teaches the method. When: designing a sequence of hidden clues. Why: The first find shows players how to look, making the second clue solvable.
- [procedure] 1) Place yourself where the target is present in public. 2) Speak with a few people, not many. 3) Leave advances to the target, who may dislike overly sociable approaches. 4) Let contact arise naturally. When: a direct approach would alert a wary target or close the door. Why: a fastidious target may respond better to contact they initiate.
- [procedure] 1) Visit the protective witness before the main subject. 2) Gather background on that witness first. 3) Reassure before pressing. 4) Watch reactions to specific questions. 5) Cross-check accounts. When: witness is fragile or protective of a family member. Why: a calmer witness is less alarmed by the visit.
- [procedure] 1) State the basic facts first. 2) Collect small circumstantial details. 3) Group details by suspect. 4) Cross-check each claim against records or timelines before reaching a conclusion. When: Investigating a crime or mystery where suspects must be narrowed down. Why: Early facts are fixed, while details accumulate and need checking before a conclusion is trusted.
- [tradeoff] Reasoning from reported facts avoids visiting the scene but depends on the source being reliable and the facts being complete.
- [pitfall] Events feel arbitrary unless earlier clues or player actions set them up, so prepare sudden turns and interruptions in advance. When: Scheduling events or sudden turns during an investigation. Why: Unmotivated events break trust in cause and effect.
- [pitfall] Over-deferring frustrates the audience, and a reversal that feels arbitrary weakens trust in the narrator. When: Delaying or reversing an expected outcome. Why: Players lose trust when delays or reversals appear unmotivated.
- [pitfall] A figure planted without a reason for the audience to remember them makes their later role feel arbitrary.
- [pitfall] An opening oddity that carries no question the audience can hold is mere strangeness and weakens the hook. When: Choosing a striking opening image. Why: Only questions drive attention forward.
- [pitfall] A plausible local explanation can hide an attack, so test an ambiguous hazard against what is expected before accepting it.
- [pitfall] Character-based crime analysis works only when the analyst knows the candidates well, otherwise it becomes guesswork. When: When applying signature analysis to unfamiliar suspects. Why: Comparison requires knowledge of each person's traits.
- [pitfall] A deadline that is not tied to consequences can feel arbitrary to players.
- [pitfall] An analyst's own sympathies can make some motives look more plausible than the evidence supports.
- [pitfall] An assumption in one annotation can be repeated by later writers until it looks established, even though no source supports it directly.
- [fact] An arranged appointment fixes a person's presence at a place within a set window, which can be used to place them there at that time.
- [fact] Arbitrators who previously sat on the body whose decisions they are judging have a conflict of interest that weakens their impartiality. Why: They are reviewing their own prior decisions.

## repetition as evidence
- [definition] A repeated signature is a feature such as a theme, note or ritual that recurs across acts and suggests a single author rather than coincidence. When: A second act repeats the staging or theme of the first.
- [mechanism] A visual marking raised repeatedly and gaining definition over time signals to the audience that it matters before its meaning is clear. Why: repetition builds salience.
- [mechanism] A predictable reply rhythm (a waiting interval, a reply, then a return delay) lets a planner estimate when a correspondence cycle will close and set a deadline from it. When: When correspondence follows a habitual pattern of delays. Why: Known delays turn a sequence of messages into a countdown the planner can schedule against.
- [mechanism] A character's fidgeting, tapping or pacing signals that their plan is slipping, which raises the audience's sense of stakes.
- [mechanism] Repeating a story, by the witness or by others, can gradually turn a fabrication into a remembered fact. Why: Repetition builds familiarity, which feels like recall.
- [behavior] A phrase repeated by an incidental source gains emotional weight at tense moments and can shape a listener's fear, even though it supplies no evidence. When: a tense scene where the phrase recurs. Why: repetition makes an idle line feel significant.
- [rule] Repeat planted names and clue lines across scenes; a single appearance looks coincidental, while recurrence keeps it in memory so players recall exact words at the link. Why: recall at the moment of connection makes a fair clue solvable.
- [rule] Do not treat a steadily repeated or verbatim statement as true; it shows retention or consistency under questioning, not accuracy. When: assessing a witness's repeated statement, including under cross-examination. Why: a rehearsed or false account can survive repetition and questioning as easily as a true one.
- [rule] Interpret a repeated phrase by its context and tone, not only its literal sense.
- [rule] Do not repeat questions to a witness who can answer fully, since repetition then only confuses or leads the witness. When: The witness is alert and able to give a complete account. Why: Unneeded repetition adds pressure without adding information.
- [rule] Do not rely on a single chance meeting to win trust; use repeated small contacts that each look ordinary. When: an outsider must gain an insider's trust. Why: one encounter is thin, while accumulated contacts build confidence.
- [rule] Track whether an NPC repeats a relayed phrase back, since a follow-up question can serve as a clue.
- [rule] Give repeat-offender culprits learnable habits so players can reward pattern recognition. When: designing culprits with a criminal history. Why: Recurring habits let players match a suspect across scenes.
- [rule] Vary repeated sightings so the player must gather more evidence to resolve them, rather than repeating an identical event. When: designing repeated events that should resolve over time. Why: varied observations add new information instead of repeating ambiguity.
- [heuristic] One incident may be accident, but repeated identical failures or disturbances, at fixed times or nightly, point to a deliberate or stable cause; infer method only from a pattern. When: observing identical failures at one time point or the same disturbance over several nights. Why: repetition suggests a stable cause rather than chance. (x2)
- [heuristic] A culprit who succeeded with a method once tends to reuse it under similar pressure, making the next likely victim or act predictable. When: the suspect's earlier method is known and the situation resembles the earlier one. Why: people fall back on methods that worked before.
- [heuristic] A person who repeats another's words can seem to know more than they do, so check whether they knew the particulars. When: a claim seems to reveal knowledge.
- [heuristic] A speaker who repeats one phrase may hold a fixed idea rather than understand it, so ask what the speaker actually knows. When: a speaker's words seem significant.
- [heuristic] After a prior incident with the same person, a renewed attempt with that person is more likely than a new arrangement with someone else. When: a pattern of prior incidents exists. Why: past behavior with the same partner predicts future behavior.
- [heuristic] Words repeated in fragmented speech usually mark what the speaker cares about most. When: when transcribing broken or partial speech. Why: Speakers return to the ideas that matter most to them.
- [heuristic] Repeat visible time checks across scenes and transitions so the audience keeps feeling how little time remains. When: A story needs urgency within a short window. Why: Repeated reminders keep the deadline present.
- [heuristic] A run of similar objects says more about an occupant than a single stray item, so weigh repeated patterns above isolated ones.
- [heuristic] Treat repetition of a message as information; a word repeated several times usually signals urgency.
- [heuristic] A word a witness repeats that the investigator never used can reveal what they knew before the investigation began. When: Interviewing a witness about an event. Why: Unprompted vocabulary exposes prior knowledge.
- [heuristic] When someone keeps returning to a settled matter, the repetition can reveal their purpose more than the matter itself. When: a suspect's actions look redundant or oddly insistent.
- [procedure] 1) Record when the event ended. 2) Record when responders arrived. 3) Record when any absent witness returned. 4) Compare these intervals against the expected response time. When: a delayed response may be suspicious. Why: Measured intervals separate an abnormal delay from a normal one.
- [pitfall] Repetition is not corroboration: many tellers repeating one rumour, story or source amount to one unverified claim, and several confident accounts can still conflict. Count independent sources with separate access. When: a rumour circulates among many people. Why: repetition creates false confidence and feels like corroboration. (x2)
- [pitfall] Repeated questions can expose inconsistency yet confuse an honest witness, and a yes-or-no prompt may supply its own reply. When: when pressing a witness with repeated questions. Why: honest witnesses may answer differently when the same question is reframed.
- [pitfall] Too many unexplained absences by one character will be noticed, so pace them and vary their reasons.
- [pitfall] Repeating 'trust me' without new information becomes tiresome and drains tension from a withheld secret.
- [pitfall] Repeating words through a tube raises the risk of detection, since repetition is itself audible. When: Sending messages over a shared passage. Why: Repetitive sound draws attention that a single exchange would not.
- [pitfall] A repeated vote may reflect the organizer's wish for display rather than any new information.
- [pitfall] A family repeating the same account is not independent confirmation of it. When: When several members of one household give the same story. Why: Shared origin means shared error, so they count as one source.
- [pitfall] Counting repeated statements as corroboration is an error when witnesses share one source or one dispute, since their agreement may reflect a common motive.
- [pitfall] Repetition of a sighting across places and times does not replace physical verification of it.
- [fact] Repeating a method is the offender's hardest slip because it links crimes; habits like entry method, signature or post-job routine identify repeat offenders as reliably as fingerprints. When: the offender commits several crimes or has a criminal history. Why: recurring signatures and habits give investigators a connection that can be matched across crimes.
- [fact] A repeated remark does not by itself prove guilt, since the same words can express guilt or bravado.

## testing claims
- [mechanism] A false confession that physical evidence can easily disprove works only as a short distraction. When: physical evidence can contradict the confession.
- [rule] Make a witness's theory or an NPC's accusation, including a suspect's motive, disprovable by facts the player can reach. When: Designing NPC accusations or witness theories. Why: Testable accusations let the player reward careful investigation. (x2)
- [rule] Test each claim against the scene, physical record and world facts such as item size or route length, not the witness's status or sympathy. When: Accounts conflict, a witness's motive to lie is plausible, or designing NPC testimony that may contain errors. Why: Physical contradictions give players a checkable way to find lies or mistakes. (x2)
- [rule] Let a companion voice a wrong assumption that the player can disprove with evidence found in the game world. When: when writing companion dialogue about a mystery. Why: the player can test the assumption and overturn it.
- [rule] Plant a believable false lead that a player can disprove by checking it against an anomaly the lead cannot explain.
- [rule] Test an accused person's claim that someone supplied false information against the physical facts before accepting it.
- [heuristic] Test a mundane explanation against time, place, circumstances and physical facts before accepting a supernatural or insane one. When: A clue has a mundane explanation, or an eerie or confusing report comes from a possibly unreliable witness. Why: Ordinary causes often leave traces that a frightened witness cannot see. (x2)
- [heuristic] Test a witness's excuse against the layout and other people's movements before accepting it, especially when it is too convenient. When: A witness explains away their presence somewhere. Why: Excuses that fit perfectly can be constructed to cover a gap.
- [heuristic] Test an alarming label against all observed evidence before acting on it, since a dramatic word can feel decisive while adding no support. When: Judging a suspect's apparent guilt or a witness's odd behaviour.
- [heuristic] Treat an accepted official story as a possible misdirection and test each of its links before relying on it. When: When a prosecution, faction or NPC authority presents a settled account. Why: An accepted narrative may be built to hide the key fact.
- [heuristic] Avoid a lead that is disproved without new information, since that resets the search rather than narrowing it.
- [heuristic] Test a claimed identity by asking staff about routine details a stand-in would need to know, since answers reveal the impersonation. When: a person may have been replaced. Why: A stand-in must know the routine to pass as the real person.
- [heuristic] Store proven facts as case flags, and keep true but unprovable theories out of the official record, or note them separately. When: when designing a mystery's case file.
- [heuristic] Test a witness's claim against physical conditions, such as whether a hat could have stayed on in the wind that day. When: a claim depends on weather, distance, or lighting. Why: physical conditions can make a claim impossible.
- [heuristic] Specific, itemized objections to a record can be tested and answered; a blanket charge that the whole record is false carries little weight. When: A disputed record is challenged. Why: Only itemized claims can be checked against evidence.
- [heuristic] Test a stated reason for an act against the actor's own doubts about it, since those doubts show whether the reason holds up. When: Judging why a character undertook a trip, errand or visit. Why: Stated reasons often fail under the actor's own scrutiny.
- [heuristic] Test a newly offered motive against the objection it was built to answer and against the known facts, not by how neat it sounds. When: A new motive is offered to explain an act. Why: A tidy motive can still fail under scrutiny of the evidence.
- [heuristic] Test whether a method could have been copied by comparing it with a published similar case. When: an outside source describes a method used in the case.
- [heuristic] Test a confession's grand or heroic justification against its practical consequences; self-justifying framing often fails when measured against the facts. When: when a culprit explains an act in idealistic terms. Why: Self-serving framing hides costs and contradictions that the facts reveal.
- [procedure] 1) Identify a claim about a past physical condition or a central case claim, such as wasted muscle. 2) State what traces it predicts: marks on a body, object or place, or follow-up actions such as searches. 3) Check those directly. 4) Record whether they match. When: A witness or suspect makes a claim about a past physical condition or names a physical detail, or a claim is central to a case. Why: A claim that predicts a trace can be confirmed or refuted by a match or absence. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Find the unstated premise the claim needs to hold. 2) Rebuild the physical or causal reasons behind the rule. 3) Check whether the claim ignores a distinction it itself draws. 4) Look for statements that contradict each other. When: judging a report, witness or rule that presents a timing or physical claim as settled.
- [procedure] 1) Search the rooms the person would use. 2) Ask others who might have seen them. 3) Record which places were examined. 4) Treat the claim as unverified until confirmed. When: when a character's absence is central and a claim of departure must be tested.
- [procedure] 1) Take the speaker's full account first. 2) Ask targeted questions about each person involved. 3) Pursue passing details with short confirming questions. 4) End with a next step, not a verdict. When: a story centres on one person who may be disguised or hiding a motive.
- [procedure] 1) Send a short query asking whether a person is at his post. 2) If he is absent, send a message that must be delivered to his own hand and answered. When: Checking whether a person is present at a location. Why: A direct query confirms presence, and a required reply confirms absence.
- [procedure] 1) Record each conflicting claim exactly. 2) Ask what the speaker gains by making it. 3) Compare any revision under re-questioning with the first version. 4) Check which version the physical facts support. When: two statements about one event conflict. Why: Motive and physical evidence together show which claim is more reliable.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who saw the event. 2) Ask how close they were. 3) Ask whether they gained anything. 4) Check whether their statements agree over time. When: Judging a witness's claim.
- [procedure] 1) Describe the claimed method. 2) Compare it with every known natural method. 3) If none fits, flag the claim as unresolved instead of accepting it. When: Assessing a claim that something impossible occurred. Why: Systematic comparison separates claims that fail from those that remain open.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the suspect's character as the source of their opinions. 2) Compare each assertion with established facts. 3) Check whether the claim can be tested or rejects every alternative in advance. When: Evaluating a suspect's denials or explanations. Why: Character explains a stance, but only fact-checking shows whether it holds.
- [procedure] 1) Speak a neutral trigger word near the person. 2) Watch the eyelids and breathing for any sign of awareness. 3) Treat a single brief twitch with caution before concluding unconsciousness. When: When deciding whether an apparently sleeping person can hear. Why: A neutral trigger reveals awareness without tipping off the person.
- [procedure] 1) Repeat the claimed act exactly. 2) Listen or watch from the witness's position and distance. 3) Compare what could be seen or heard with the witness's account. When: A witness's account depends on what could be sensed. Why: Re-enactment shows what the witness could and could not have perceived.
- [procedure] 1) Reproduce the suspicious effect independently 2) compare the same witness's statements over time 3) gather retractions and depositions 4) test whether the original evidence still holds. When: judging a contested trial. Why: Documentary and comparative checks reveal what a single record hides.
- [tradeoff] A test produces a reaction the observer can read and reproduce, while an emotional appeal moves the observer without a checkable result. When: Choosing how to challenge or clear a suspect. Why: Only reproducible results can serve as evidence.
- [pitfall] A theory absorbing every fact, dismissing contrary details as tricks, or unchangeable by any fact is unfalsifiable and halts the search. Reject a detail only with a specific check. When: when evaluating a confident case against a suspect, or when a theory absorbs contrary evidence. Why: the theory explains everything, removing pressure to test it; an unfalsifiable case cannot be corrected by evidence.
- [pitfall] Reading all evidence that favours a suspect as proof of skill lets a theory absorb contrary evidence and stop being testable.
- [pitfall] A claimed partnership with a scapegoat is a lie that the victim can test, and someone who knows the scapegoat may reject it immediately. When: A culprit invents a partner to implicate an innocent person. Why: Personal knowledge of the accused exposes the invented link.
- [pitfall] A reconstruction can be plausible yet unprovable once the physical evidence that would confirm it has been destroyed.
- [pitfall] Presenting a theory without linking each claim to a checkable source lets the audience dismiss it.

## absent traces
- [definition] Absence and residue, meaning what a room has lost, left behind or left untidy, can show how and when someone departed.
- [heuristic] Absences matter: missing expected traces or damage, such as scorch marks, and conflicting traces, such as soot without fire marks, can rule out an assumed cause like fire. When: a hypothesis predicts a visible trace, or when testing a proposed explanation for a scene. (x2)
- [heuristic] A failure to find expected traces, such as footprints, mud, tracks or a body, is itself a finding that can rule out hypotheses and should be reported and reasoned from. When: the ground or surface would normally record traces, or the scene is checked for what should be present. Why: the absence narrows what could have happened.
- [heuristic] Compare what should be present with what is found: an expected object that is missing is evidence, and an absent personal item suggests the actor carried it away. When: an object expected at a scene is missing or no longer where it should be. Why: The actor may have chosen to remove it, which reveals their equipment.
- [heuristic] A negative check, such as an empty search or no calls charged to a room, narrows suspects, leads or explanations and is worth recording. Why: Ruling out a lead removes it from consideration.
- [heuristic] Repeated empty checks or a negative expert report eliminate one line and may mean the target is wrong; re-examine the theory, not just close the case. When: lab results are negative, or repeated checks produce nothing that fits the theory.
- [heuristic] The absence of forced entry does not prove no one entered; the history of keys and access is the relevant trace. When: Investigating how a locked space was accessed. Why: Duplicates leave no visible damage.
- [heuristic] Missing tracks on wet or soft ground can mean deliberate care, so check for their absence before assuming nothing happened there. When: Ground should record prints but shows none. Why: A careful mover leaves no mark.
- [heuristic] When a wound looks suspicious, check for what it lacks, such as bleeding or clothing stains, and what was overlooked, such as foam on the lips. When: Assessing a cause of death. Why: Missing or overlooked signs often point to the real cause more reliably than the obvious injury.
- [heuristic] Missing marks are evidence: someone who never left a room leaves no marks outside it, so test their claimed movements against where tracks are absent. When: A suspect claims to have moved through an area that shows no traces.
- [heuristic] Ask witnesses what they did not see; negative observations can narrow the field of suspects.
- [heuristic] An empty pen or missing writing tool can serve as negative evidence that someone was not writing, but it suggests rather than proves the absence of action. When: Assessing whether a person wrote something around the time of an event. Why: Absence is open to other explanations, so it is only a tentative inference.
- [heuristic] An absence in a record means little unless the routine that would have logged the item was actually checked.
- [heuristic] When every copy or item at a candidate source is accounted for, that source is eliminated, so a negative check is as useful as a positive one. When: Checking a candidate source of an object. Why: Confirming that all items are present rules out the source as the origin.
- [heuristic] Absence of trace is itself informative. When no footprints or witnesses exist, an investigator has neither direct nor circumstantial proof. When: A culprit's entry or exit leaves no physical sign.
- [heuristic] The absence of an item that a person's habits predict can be evidence that the item was never carried. When: When a person's habits imply a predictable set of items. Why: Expected items should be present if the habits held.
- [heuristic] After a failed search, question the search location rather than concluding the object is absent from the building.
- [heuristic] A result that contradicts a long chain of reasoning often has another explanation, so check the test itself before abandoning the chain. When: when a new fact conflicts with an established theory. Why: Tests can fail for reasons unrelated to the theory.
- [heuristic] Record a negative test result as evidence too: if no one reacts to a tested sound, that absence supports the conclusion that it was not heard. When: when a test produces no observable reaction. Why: an absent reaction is informative when the test was properly set up.
- [heuristic] A difference between a reproduction and the evidence is a finding in itself, since it can show who could or could not have caused the result.
- [heuristic] Repeated reports of nothing suspicious narrow suspicion but do not prove innocence. When: When surveillance or search returns no evidence. Why: Absence of evidence lowers some probabilities without ruling everything out.
- [heuristic] A check that yields nothing, such as a witness with no new information, still narrows the field of possible explanations.
- [procedure] 1) Record unexplained marks and defer their interpretation, since premature explanation can fix a wrong reading. 2) Keep a running list of unexplained items. 3) Revisit each item as new facts arrive. 4) Raise open items at the next interview or check. 5) Mark each as fitted, coincidental, or still open. When: A mark is noticed but its cause is unknown. Why: Premature explanation can fix a wrong reading.
- [procedure] 1) Exhaust every lead, including contacts of contacts. 2) If new names stop appearing, reassess the working theory. 3) Consider that the theory may be misdirected before investing more effort. When: Repeated inquiry produces no new name. Why: Continuing a wrong line wastes effort.
- [tradeoff] Absent sightings narrow where observers could have been if their positions are known; a negative canvass across a time window alone proves only that no one was found. When: a search for witnesses or sightings within a time window returns none. Why: Absence of reports is not proof of absence of the event.
- [pitfall] Absence of traces is not proof of innocence or skill on its own; combine it with other findings, since reading it as skill is an assumption without independent support. When: a scene shows no trace of the actor, or a conclusion rests on something that is not there. Why: lack of traces has many possible causes.
- [pitfall] A failed test does not prove a substance or cause was absent; a negative analysis only removes one test, so other possibilities remain open. When: Testing consumed items for a drug, or a negative analysis of a death. Why: Some substances have no taste or odor.
- [pitfall] Not seeing a pursuer does not prove you are unobserved, so keep checking. When: Assessing whether you are still followed.
- [pitfall] Absence of theft does not prove a motive: a thief may be scared off, or may choose to take nothing.
- [pitfall] A negative conclusion must be checked, not assumed; if it rests on one witness's account, that account must be verified. When: Concluding that an item was never acquired. Why: Negatives are easy to assume and hard to prove.
- [pitfall] A trace can be a dead end, so test each trace before building on it, and avoid searching many items when the target is likely elsewhere. When: Many marked items are candidates for a clue. Why: Broad searches of unrelated items waste time.
- [pitfall] Observers may explain away a failed result as success, so decide pass criteria before running the test.
- [fact] An absent sound can be evidence, since a slow, quiet action differs from a slammed one and produces no matching noise.
- [fact] Negative claims are hard to prove, and the same objections can apply to arguments on both sides. When: when a case turns on proving absence.
- [fact] The absence of a smell of anaesthetic at a scene narrows the possible methods, but does not settle who the culprit is. When: Investigating a suspected drugging during a crime. Why: Method evidence narrows options but rarely identifies the person alone.
- [fact] Missing or non-identifying remains are still informative: their absence narrows what can be inferred, but other parts may still support conclusions. When: Evidence includes parts useless for identification. Why: Investigators can still learn from remaining traces even when some parts cannot identify a person.

## crime timeline windows
- [definition] The crime window runs from the last certain sighting or last moment the victim is known alive to the first known death or latest possible time; the event lies between.
- [mechanism] A candle's burn state gives a rough elapsed-time interval rather than an exact clock; a candle that has not guttered shows the open period was short. When: Using a burning candle as evidence of elapsed time. Why: Burn length indicates a rough duration, not a precise time.
- [mechanism] A near-miss event such as a door tried and left closed lets a player feel the threat without being caught. When: When designing tension in a timed sequence. Why: A close call heightens threat while preserving player agency.
- [rule] Build a scene timeline the player reconstructs by questioning NPCs, giving each a different time window so accounts combine to fix when an event happened. When: Designing a generated mystery scene. Why: each partial window is incomplete alone but adds up when combined. (x2)
- [rule] Give each NPC a logged route or timestamped departure and arrival, so players can compare tickets, keys or door logs to find unaccounted gaps. When: Designing a deduction puzzle around NPC movement. Why: Checkable logs turn gaps into discoverable contradictions.
- [rule] Give NPCs daily schedules logged per time slot so players can spot absences and build alibi tables by questioning companions at the right times, checked against statements. When: designing suspect schedules. Why: schedules make absences checkable.
- [rule] Trust a stopped timer as an event time only after cross-checking it against another independent timer. When: multiple timers on the same scene disagree. Why: a single timer may be wrong or altered.
- [rule] Check a suspect's account of intervals against other witnesses, since recalled durations may conflict between sources.
- [rule] Flag NPC alibis that no other character confirms, so players know which accounts need a second source.
- [rule] Design an NPC to behave differently when the player leaves an area, and make the change visible when the player returns. When: When designing state changes that depend on player absence. Why: Visible change after absence rewards players for revisiting and reinforces the sense of a living world.
- [rule] Have NPC dialogue state times and places that the player can check against other NPCs' accounts. When: When designing NPC testimony in a game. Why: Cross-checkable details let players test consistency.
- [rule] Proving an alibi for the wider period does not help if the critical window itself is uncovered.
- [rule] Let NPC alibi witnesses change their dialogue state after the player applies pressure or offers a bribe. When: When designing NPC dialogue that responds to player actions. Why: Dynamic state makes the witness's testimony a result of the player's choices.
- [rule] An NPC scripted to be in a guarded place at the moment a trap fires gives an apparent alibi that the player can break by checking the trap's trigger time. When: designing NPC schedules around a trap or event. Why: Trigger-time checks let players test an apparent alibi against the event.
- [rule] Use NPC dialogue to reveal schedules, such as a guard leaving duty at a set time, that the player can then act on.
- [rule] Give an afflicted state a bounded schedule of days or rests, so testimony follows a checkable calendar the player can compare with other events.
- [rule] Store an NPC's alibi as a time window, and let the player break it by finding a clue that places the NPC elsewhere. When: Designing an NPC with a claimed whereabouts. Why: A time window gives the player a specific claim to test.
- [rule] Build a night timeline puzzle from fixed points, such as a visit, a departure and a dropped item, leaving one unverified interval for the player to resolve. When: when designing a deduction puzzle around a suspect's movements. Why: fixed points give the player anchors and one gap gives a goal.
- [rule] Make each individual incident look like a mishap, so the shared mark is the only way players can see that the incidents are linked.
- [heuristic] Compare device readings with other clocks and testimony, and treat an unexplained discrepancy as an open question, not a minor detail. Why: a small mismatch can hide a hole in the timeline.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs a behavioural timeline so players can build a motive profile by comparing what different observers saw.
- [heuristic] Bound a missing person's possible departure by the period when the place was unobserved; this turns an open question into a limited search window.
- [heuristic] Use a loud, timestamped event as a timer: players compare when they heard it with when they last saw the victim.
- [heuristic] A scripted errand that splits the party creates a timed window for another actor; log the window so the player can reconstruct what happened. When: Scripting events during separation. Why: Recorded timing lets players test alibis against the evidence.
- [heuristic] Make each NPC reaction, such as hiring guards or sending for help, a visible timeline step the player can track. When: designing deadline-driven quests. Why: Visible steps let the player sense progress toward the event.
- [heuristic] Keep an event log of NPC locations, so a watchman NPC's logged visits can contradict a suspect's claim.
- [procedure] 1) Extract any stated date or time from an NPC's offhand remark. 2) Compare it against the in-game calendar or known schedule. 3) Note whether it coincides with the event. Why: turns casual dialogue into a lead.
- [procedure] 1) Estimate a rough time window for the crime. 2) Place each claimed movement inside or outside that window. 3) Check each account against the others. 4) Treat approximate times as ranges rather than exact moments. When: event times are estimates and alibis rest on one person's word. Why: timelines reveal gaps and contradictions.
- [procedure] 1) Record the exact time of each event as witnesses report it. 2) Mark the gaps between events. 3) Use physical states as clocks. 4) List who could have been present during each gap and who was seen leaving. When: reconstructing when a crime occurred and who could have done it. Why: physical evidence and witness reports together bound the window.
- [procedure] 1) Create darkness or stillness so the audience has no other way to pass time. 2) Add recurring time markers. 3) Escalate faint warnings: a glimmer, then a smell, then a hiss. 4) Deliver the climax, then return to quiet. Why: Layered, escalating cues keep the wait meaningful and make the climax feel earned.
- [procedure] 1) List each theft's location and timing. 2) Find the time when the affected places were empty. 3) Use the window and the places to narrow the suspect pool. When: a series of crimes needs a bounded time and place. Why: A shared window of opportunity shows who could have acted.
- [procedure] 1) hook 0-4%: show method, no case yet; 2) inciting case 4-13%: missing person, recurring payment; 3) summons and confession 13-27%: push party, reveal first motive; 4) crisis 27%: a death makes a suspect obvious; 5) false solution 34-42%: arrest, reconstruction names second culprit; 6) pursuit 42-74%: river chase, false lead collapses; 7) reveal 74-98%: empty container, confession, final culprit.
- [metric] A brisk walk can cover a route in about three-quarters of the time a normal-paced walk takes. When: Estimating walking times for a route.
- [pitfall] Duration estimates depend on how the captive experienced time, so verify them against an independent clock when one exists. When: a witness estimates how long a journey took. Why: perceived time under confinement can differ from actual time.
- [pitfall] Confusing not later than with exactly at leads to false precision about when an event happened. When: Stating a time of death from bounds. Why: A bound is a limit, not a measurement.
- [pitfall] Stating a time window too loosely lets every suspect fit, so it stops filtering anyone. When: Witness times are vague. Why: A wide window includes everyone's movements.

## elimination reasoning
- [mechanism] Narrow suspects by asking who could reach the contaminated means at the right moment; positively excluding people from access sharply shrinks the remaining field. When: A poison or substance could have been introduced by a limited set of people. Why: Access removes people who could not have acted.
- [rule] Exclusion yields only a probable answer while unobserved options remain; conclude from it only when the candidate list is complete.
- [rule] Eliminating a suspect on an assumption rather than observed fact invalidates the deduction; record each elimination's premise so it can be reopened if that premise fails. Why: An elimination is only as sound as its underlying assumption.
- [rule] Include one trace that eliminates the most obvious suspect, so players deduce who is present rather than guess.
- [rule] Treat the ease of an explanation as a sign of missing evidence rather than a solution, and test a simple answer before accepting it. When: an obvious explanation comes to mind early in a case. Why: simple answers often fit because important evidence has not yet been found.
- [heuristic] When every alternative fails the evidence and no other path remains, the survivor becomes the working answer, but it must still pass the chain check. When: Several explanations are dismissed one by one, or every rival has been eliminated. Why: Elimination can justify a conclusion when proof is impossible to obtain directly. (x2)
- [heuristic] Make innocent handlers an explicit elimination step so players learn to exclude them before accusing anyone. When: Designing investigation puzzles with shared objects. Why: Excluding innocent handlers prevents false accusation.
- [heuristic] Test an early lead against later clues before trusting it, since first impressions can aim at the wrong suspect.
- [heuristic] Use a partial clue as a filter: rule out candidates that fail each known detail until the remaining set is small. When: Investigating an incomplete description. Why: Known traits reduce the possibilities.
- [heuristic] Exclusion is stronger than matching, since a few samples can miss the actual source, so treat a match as a lead rather than proof.
- [heuristic] Eliminate options by logical exclusion; for example, an exit locked before a certain hour rules out using it after that hour.
- [procedure] 1) List every candidate explanation, such as suicide, accident, justified homicide and murder. 2) Test each against the evidence in turn. 3) Reject contradicted explanations. 4) Accept the remaining one as the working answer. When: Several explanations for one event must be narrowed, or a small known set of explanations exists.
- [procedure] 1) List every possible agent who could have acted. 2) Eliminate each candidate in turn using the evidence, or a denial or changed reaction that behavior contradicts. 3) Repeat until one remains. 4) Accept it only if the list was complete. When: The pool of suspects is small and the scene limits who could act.
- [procedure] 1) Trace the physical means and list every explanation and person who could have acted. 2) Reject those the evidence contradicts. 3) Test the survivor's motive and the facts it rests on against independent evidence. When: A case has a short list of suspects or rival theories. Why: Elimination is only as sound as its starting facts.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the apparent impossibility. 2) List every physically open route or explanation. 3) Remove each option that observation rules out. 4) Hold the remaining option as provisional until it is checked. 5) State each step aloud so others can challenge it. When: the set of routes or explanations is finite and checkable.
- [procedure] 1) List possible ways a fact could have been produced. 2) Judge each by how much risk its perpetrators would have accepted. 3) Discard options that are too risky to be plausible. When: Several explanations fit a fixed fact. Why: Assessing the cost of each option to its perpetrators removes implausible explanations.
- [procedure] 1) List each candidate source of a poison. 2) Test each container. 3) Apply known properties such as taste threshold, onset time and dose to exclude candidates. 4) Reason from the remaining facts.
- [procedure] 1) Clean each person's fingers. 2) Press them onto an inking pad. 3) Roll them onto smooth white paper. 4) Label each impression and file it as an elimination set. When: Traces on an object must be attributed to people with legitimate access. Why: Known prints let remaining prints be assigned to an unknown party.
