- [procedure] 1) Check each person's alibi against the window. 2) Set aside those whose alibis hold. 3) Treat the remaining people inside the window as suspects. When: Access to the scene was controlled. Why: Elimination focuses suspicion on those with access.
- [procedure] 1) List every candidate hiding place for the object. 2) Check and exclude each external place. 3) Search the most likely internal place last. When: Searching for a hidden object when the candidate places form a finite, checkable set. Why: Systematic exclusion narrows the search until the remaining place must hold the object.
- [procedure] 1) Ask closed questions about specific possibilities. 2) Record whether each is denied. 3) Use the pattern of denials to narrow the explanation under test. When: Testing whether a suspicious act or idea was ever raised. Why: Consistent denials of specific possibilities narrow the candidate explanations.
- [procedure] 1) Reduce the account to a short list of fixed premises. 2) Identify the premise that must be false. 3) List everyone who could physically reach the object. 4) Test each suspect against that list. When: When an object seems to vanish from a sealed place. Why: An apparent impossibility means a premise is wrong, and narrowing access finds who acted.
- [procedure] 1) Test ordinary explanations first: records, local history, prior exposure, and the witness's state of mind. 2) Assess only what remains unexplained as supernatural or psychological. When: when a mystery has a supernatural reading not yet ruled in or out. Why: Ordinary causes are checkable and often account for odd details before any unexplained remainder is considered.
- [procedure] 1) List every agent the reports allow. 2) Exclude anyone a witness who knew them would have recognized. 3) Discard candidates who could not have acted in time. 4) Discard candidates who gain nothing from the act. 5) Treat any survivor as provisional until confirmed. When: When one fact requires a single actor and several candidates remain. Why: Systematic elimination narrows candidates using checkable constraints.
- [procedure] 1) List each claimed action of the suspect separately. 2) Test each against the evidence and rule out those it contradicts. 3) Revise the theory around what remains. 4) Confront the suspect with a detail only the guilty party could know. When: A theory is built from many small inferences that can be tested separately. Why: Removing false parts of a theory leaves a narrower case that a guilty detail can break.
- [procedure] 1) List each safeguard such as locks, passwords, signatures, keys and staff checks. 2) State the assumption each safeguard makes. 3) Rule out the crude route first, such as force against a hardened building. 4) Test each remaining route one safeguard at a time. When: Finding how a heavily guarded place could be breached. Why: Listing assumptions narrows the field to the single weak link.
- [tradeoff] Elimination works with a small, known candidate group but weakens when many could reach the means or candidates are open-ended; the answer is only as good as the alternatives considered.
- [tradeoff] Excluding a party from findings protects the investigation, but it can breed resentment and leave the excluded person feeling wronged.
- [pitfall] Eliminating rival explanations or routes shows only what is impossible; it does not explain the act itself, which still needs explanation from further clues. When: Rivals or routes have been ruled out. Why: Removing wrong answers does not supply the right one; impossibility narrows the question rather than answering it.
- [pitfall] The last candidate surviving elimination only fits the description, not proven guilt; treat it as a suspect needing a confirming test, since disguise or later contradicting evidence can defeat it. When: Concluding a suspect from attribute filtering or a shrinking candidate list. Why: Elimination only shows who matches the description, and descriptions based on appearance can be defeated by disguise.
- [pitfall] A false trail or premise that is too easy to disprove wastes time; choose one plausible enough to provoke a reaction and make the player doubt the real clues. When: When designing false leads. Why: A lead that collapses at once gives the player no reason to doubt the real clues.
- [pitfall] An elaborate alibi invites the question of why it was needed, which can make the whole story suspect.
- [pitfall] An alibi covering only the early evening leaves the critical hour open, so it does not exclude the suspect.
- [pitfall] An elimination that ignores unknown motive makes the answer look simpler than the case really is. Why: Missing motive leaves a gap that elimination cannot fill.
- [pitfall] Eliminating a theory point by point risks overlooking an alternative explanation that fits the remaining facts. When: Testing a theory by ruling out its parts one at a time. Why: Each elimination is judged against the current theory, which can hide other explanations.
- [pitfall] An unexplained interval does not prove guilt; treating it as proof assigns opportunity to anyone present. When: A suspect cannot account for a period. Why: A gap shows only that the time is unknown, not what happened in it.

## signs and signals
- [mechanism] Unexplained odd impressions or hints of darker meaning keep the audience curious and speculating without proof, setting up a later payoff.
- [mechanism] Giving each conspirator a partial map marked with a shared sign lets any one of them recover the cache without the others knowing.
- [behavior] A person may call out a community signal to someone they expect, even before seeing them, so the call reveals whom they were expecting. When: a victim uses a signal before seeing the person they expect. Why: the call was intended for a known recipient.
- [behavior] A character's unexplained sense of doom, even when rationally rejected, leaves a lasting impression of threat on the audience. When: when building suspense before a reveal. Why: the feeling stays on record and primes the audience to expect danger.
- [behavior] Witnesses without knowledge of optics or electricity read unusual sights, such as reflections or lightning, through belief rather than natural cause. When: observing a rare phenomenon with no known explanation. Why: the science to explain it was not yet available.
- [behavior] A recognisable idle behaviour that appears at a key moment, especially when repeated across scenes, is noticed as evidence of what the actor was waiting for. When: A character performs a distinctive posture or pause matched to a critical event. Why: A repeated gesture linked to the timing of an event invites the observer to connect it to the actor's intent.
- [rule] Make a symbol or signal readable through in-game sources: a codex, a translating character, or an earlier scene teaching it, such as a swung lantern, before it matters. When: When a symbol or signal must carry meaning for the player later in the game. Why: Meaning must be reachable through in-game sources; learned codes let players interpret the signal when it matters.
- [rule] Withhold a fact from the reader only with some hint; concealment that is never signalled feels like cheating.
- [rule] Build a code on a category the reader can learn; once the scheme is known, every message in that category becomes readable. When: a code must be used by people who need to read it. Why: a learnable scheme lets its readers decode each message.
- [rule] A watcher should respond only to a signal pattern both sides already understand, and may require the signal to be repeated before answering. When: when a signal could be an accident or a trick.
- [rule] Tie each physical sign to a specific plausible cause before using it in a conclusion.
- [rule] Avoid signals that a watcher could also recognise, since the same cue that reaches a contact can alert the enemy. When: Choosing a covert signal in a monitored setting. Why: Any signal visible to a contact is also visible to a watcher.
- [rule] Make a signal simple enough to read but unlikely to occur by chance.
- [rule] Check that a physical sign was read by people with the relevant skill, and that any request for re-examination by skilled examiners was answered. When: when a bodily sign or physical evidence decides a case. Why: untrained or biased readings can mislead.
- [rule] Place a signature block or endorsement at the end of a late document that reassigns credit the title or body implied, so a careful reader sees who acted.
- [heuristic] An anomaly resisting every obvious explanation should stay open as an unresolved clue, not forced into a convenient theory or discarded; meaning may appear when linked to other evidence. When: A trace has no obvious explanation. Why: Its significance may only appear when combined with other evidence.
- [heuristic] Do not abandon a theory at the first detail that cannot be explained at once; test it further with time, patience and research. When: A suspect's account is smooth and one detail resists explanation. Why: An unexplained detail may hide a flaw that more work can find.
- [heuristic] Ruling out a line of inquiry does not resolve an unexplained detail, which may return later and deserve a second look. When: when a discarded line of inquiry leaves a detail unexplained.
- [heuristic] Open with small unexplained events, such as a figure at a window or failing lights, so later events read as a continuation. When: setting up a mystery before the main crime or threat. Why: small anomalies build unease and prepare the audience for escalation.
- [heuristic] Treat a common decorative symbol with no tie to the event as non-evidence; a symbol is clue-worthy only when it connects to the event.
- [procedure] 1) Stage the suspect's routine at a set time. 2) Reproduce the cue yourself. 3) Watch for a response from outside, such as a thrown object. When: A suspected signal needs confirmation. Why: Mirroring the cue draws out the external response.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the reference the speaker relies on. 2) Infer what expectation that reference implies about the speaker. 3) Check whether that expectation explains the speaker's conduct and words. When: A suspect's words seem out of place for their setting.
- [procedure] 1) Log small unexplained incidents as they occur. 2) Revisit the log as new facts arrive. 3) Fit related incidents into a pattern. When: Minor events seem unrelated at first. Why: Small incidents may connect to a larger pattern only once more facts are known.
- [procedure] 1) Guess the language from its letters and grammar. 2) Test whether the message makes sense in that language. 3) If it does not, try another language, since the message may fit a different one. When: a signal is in an unknown language.
- [procedure] 1) Send a controlled signal to the suspects. 2) Record who responds and how. 3) Compare each response with what that person should already know. When: several suspects could be involved in an event. Why: the pattern of responses shows who is informed.
- [procedure] 1) Keep a record of facts that fit no current theory. 2) Ask the person most likely to explain each fact directly. 3) Compare accounts with third-party remarks. 4) Accept an innocent explanation only after it fits all other facts. When: when a working theory leaves facts unexplained.
- [pitfall] Failing to explain why evidence was kept, rather than destroyed, leaves a gap in the theory.
- [pitfall] Mistaking a sign for a firm conclusion: a mended object shows attachment to it, not a trait of character. When: When reading personality from an object's condition. Why: One sign supports a narrow inference, not a broad judgment.
- [pitfall] A conflict between an early stated fact and a later event, left unexplained, reads as a mistake rather than as a clue. Why: without an explanation, the audience cannot tell error from intended misdirection.
- [pitfall] A signal works only if the partner enters the room and notices it, and nothing guarantees either.
- [pitfall] Assuming a deliberate sign was made by the culprit, when the victim could equally have made it.
- [pitfall] Treating strange knowledge, a remark later confirmed by events, or unusual skill as proof of guilt lets suspicion attach to almost any detail.
- [pitfall] A sign with no natural explanation cannot be checked, so it should carry only presumptive weight, never serve as proof.
- [pitfall] An evidence loss that is never explained reads as a cheat; make sure the lost object or person can be found again.
- [fact] Signs of deliberate human arrangement include stones placed along edges, debris-free paths, few straight lines and a repeated curve seen from only one or two viewpoints.
- [fact] Smearing oil or grease on the outside of a lamp's glass cuts its glare, especially on a dusty road, so a dim lamp can be a sign of tampering. When: when a light is unexpectedly dim.

## anomaly investigation
- [definition] An anomaly is a mismatch between an object and its apparent origin or source.
- [behavior] An apparent impossibility, like an unnoticed event or a result in a sealed or controlled situation, is often planned by someone who knows a system's gap, not luck. When: a sealed or controlled situation yields a result that seems impossible. Why: people who know the system's weak point can produce effects that look uncanny to outsiders. (x2)
- [behavior] People sense a deviation as wrong only against an established routine or expected behaviour, often feeling unease before naming the cause; without a baseline, a clue goes unrecognized. When: a sign departs from an established pattern; an ordinary-looking action may be a clue. Why: a deviation needs a baseline to register as meaningful; anomalies are defined relative to expectations, so the observer needs a reference point.
- [behavior] Players who meet a striking physical anomaly with no known purpose often read it as supernatural or careless rather than deliberate. When: a conspicuous trace whose purpose is unclear. Why: unexplained anomalies invite convenient stories that fill the gap.
- [rule] Tie any count anomaly to a known starting figure; an anomaly with no verifiable baseline cannot be used as evidence. When: When a count is the basis for a claim. Why: Without a baseline the discrepancy cannot be confirmed.
- [rule] Resolve every behavioural anomaly in a theory before trusting it; an unexplained refusal or offer is evidence the explanation may be wrong.
- [rule] Test a suspicious record against an independent source, such as another office's totals, before accepting it as a motive. When: Before drawing any conclusion from a financial anomaly. Why: A single record can mislead; a second source confirms or rejects it.
- [rule] Treat an anomaly as a hypothesis with several possible explanations, such as gambling or other spending, until a source confirms one. When: When an anomaly points to a hidden stake. Why: The anomaly shows a stake exists but not which explanation is true.
- [rule] Treat a physical anomaly as a clue and keep it separate from any conclusion about the perpetrator it might support. When: An unexplained physical feature appears in evidence. Why: Separating observation from inference keeps the investigation open to other explanations.
- [heuristic] Acts that contradict expected behaviour or the efficient choice, such as taking originals when copies would suffice, are distinctive clues to flag and treat as questions; unexpected choices reveal intent. When: a single act seems to serve no purpose; a choice departs from the expected efficient option. Why: actions that break expected behaviour can reveal motives or circumstances hidden by routine behaviour; unexpected choices often reveal intent that routine actions conceal.
- [heuristic] Record every anomaly, even one contradicting the working theory without explanation, and test it or compare it with later details; unexplained oddities pay off when revisited. When: a detail breaks the expected pattern and may matter later. Why: an unexplained oddity pays off when it is revisited; filing an anomaly away untested lets it lapse.
- [heuristic] Keep a running list of small anomalies; each may be explicable alone, yet together they can point to a pattern no single item reveals. When: no single clue is decisive. Why: links across items form evidence that individual items do not.
- [heuristic] An odd trace may look like coincidence at first; do not treat every mark as meaningful, but return to an anomaly once its position and cause can be matched. Why: a trace placed wrongly can point the inquiry the wrong way.
- [heuristic] A single small oddity on an object is a lead to test, not proof of wrongdoing, and it may point to a careless handler rather than the sender. When: Interpreting one anomalous detail found during inspection. Why: Small anomalies have many innocent causes, so they must be checked before drawing conclusions.
- [heuristic] Each unusual feature of a scene may be possible alone, but several together weigh against a simple account. When: when judging whether a story fits the scene. Why: Improbabilities accumulate, even when each has an innocent explanation.
- [heuristic] Substitutions are easier to spot when routines are documented and cross-checked, since a deviation then stands out clearly. When: routines are recorded. Why: a baseline makes deviations visible.
- [heuristic] The detail that does not fit the simple account marks where further investigation should focus. When: A case appears settled but one element remains unexplained. Why: Unexplained details are the points where a flawed theory is most likely to break.
- [heuristic] An unusual change in a fixed detail, such as a missing lamp, suggests someone has handled the scene. When: a routine detail differs from usual.
- [heuristic] Dress-based reasoning is weak when the stated circumstance is unusual enough that almost any clothing could be justified. Why: Without a clear norm for the activity, mismatch carries little evidential weight.
- [heuristic] A physical sign that breaks the expected progression carries a trace that needs an explanation, and one asks who or what produced it. When: A body or object state does not match the expected pattern. Why: Deviations from a known pattern indicate interference or a cause to find.
- [heuristic] Read a case through its apparent contradictions: clues that fit too neatly can signal deliberate design rather than chance.
- [procedure] 1) List each puzzling fact as a separate anomaly. 2) Ask which single cause could produce each one. 3) Link the causes into one sequence that explains all the facts. When: when several unrelated facts may share one hidden cause.
- [procedure] 1) Notice an action that breaks the usual pattern. 2) Compare it against what the situation would normally produce. 3) Test the mismatch with a plain challenge and observe the reaction, which then becomes evidence. When: a minor detail looks ordinary but may reveal a hidden intent. Why: A mismatch against the baseline gives a concrete starting point, and the subject's response can confirm or refute it.
- [procedure] 1) Before the interview, list every loose fact tied to the witness. 2) Ask about each fact separately and have the witness explain it in their own words. 3) Cross-check each answer against other witnesses' accounts. When: A guarded witness must explain specific anomalies rather than make a general admission. Why: A separate question per anomaly gives the witness fewer places to hide and makes contradictions visible.
- [procedure] 1) State what a normal sequence would have produced. 2) Note the actual absence. 3) Consider design, necessity or carelessness as causes. 4) Reject theories that call the anomaly an oversight without support. When: An expected detail is missing from a scene. Why: Dismissing an anomaly as carelessness closes the question before the evidence has been used.
- [procedure] 1) Treat the apparent supernatural effect as impossible until tested. 2) Apply graded stimulus to the body while watching its vital signs. 3) Trace the physical chain of causes back to its source. When: A seemingly supernatural death or revival needs explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain the record for the event period. 2) Obtain a control-period record from a comparable time. 3) Check whether the anomaly recurs at the same hour. 4) Test the record with a known load to confirm it responds. When: a record shows an unexplained anomaly. Why: repetition separates a systematic event from a one-off with an innocent cause.
- [procedure] 1) Find a detail the reconstructed story cannot explain. 2) Ask why the object is in its current state. 3) List possible explanations. 4) Test the cheapest, most mundane explanations first. 5) Accept a dramatic explanation only after the simple ones fail. When: A physical object looks too neat or contradicts a known habit. Why: Mundane causes like spare items are often the true answer and must be eliminated before accepting dramatic ones.
- [tradeoff] Seek a mundane mechanism fitting every detail before accepting the supernatural; yet if all anomalies are ordinary, the supernatural never feels real, so keep a few truly unusual. When: a strange sighting has specific reported features. Why: a mechanism that fits all details is stronger than a vague supernatural explanation; uniform natural explanations remove the stakes of the unusual. (x2)
- [tradeoff] A habitually truthful figure's unprompted exact falsehood is read as changed intent, yet observed changes in a person may support either an honest or deceptive reading without inside knowledge. When: a character known for honesty lies. Why: the contrast with a known habit makes the lie stand out.
- [tradeoff] Investigating every odd detail wastes time under pressure; keep pursuing the main objective while logging minor oddities for later. When: a deadline or time limit applies. Why: time spent on minor anomalies can cost the main goal.
- [pitfall] Coincidental resemblances, like a theme recurring across unrelated leads or an object's theme matching the crime, can be chance and create false links; test them independently before accepting them. When: the same pattern recurs across separate leads; an object's theme overlaps the crime. Why: chance repetitions look meaningful but establish nothing on their own; thematic overlap needs independent testing.
- [pitfall] If a deviation gives no explicit signal, players may sense something is off without understanding it, and the anomaly passes unnoticed.
- [pitfall] Anomalies generate puzzles, not answers; a culprit should not be named from theories that still fail to fit the details.
- [pitfall] A theory that explains one anomaly through an assumed sequence of events may misplace another anomaly, so the sequence needs independent confirmation. When: When a theory accounts for an odd detail with an unverified sequence. Why: Assumed sequences can fit one fact while contradicting others.

## clue reinterpretation
- [mechanism] A clue read as trivia or misread early, such as a line, letter, phrase or document, gains meaning only when later facts or a confession supply context. When: clue is introduced before the context or related facts are known. Why: later evidence gives earlier clues new meaning. (x2)
- [mechanism] After a revelation, earlier clues stay unchanged while their meaning shifts; an innocent item can read as suspicious without changing itself. When: A visit, item or action is introduced early without suspicion. Why: New information reframes the same fact, so interpretation evolves.
- [mechanism] Each new fact, such as a hidden relationship, errand or motive, reframes earlier clues, so the player must revise their theory. When: A multi-stage or layered reveal.
- [mechanism] A clue hidden in an ordinary object becomes meaningful only when the viewer changes position, light, time or attention; players can return at a different time to reveal it. When: a clue should be visible but meaningful only after a later reveal, or is hard to see under one condition. Why: changed lighting exposes what was hidden.
- [mechanism] One new clue can recast earlier observations. A signal from outside turns unexplained night movements into possible communication with an accomplice.
- [mechanism] A narrative that is technically accurate can be reframed by a later account, since the teller chose what to report and what to leave out.
- [mechanism] Identifying evidence such as clothing or jewelry can carry a second meaning that the player can later reread, once it proves to belong to someone else. When: When an identifying item is used to establish a victim's identity. Why: Reinterpreting an item after a reveal changes what the identification implies.
- [mechanism] A clue that seems to confirm a time gains a deeper meaning only after a second object is checked against it, prompting players to reinterpret earlier evidence. When: A physical clue fixes a time that the player initially accepts. Why: Cross-checking two objects reveals that the first clue was manipulated.
- [mechanism] Each new death can reverse the meaning of earlier clues, so a lit room and a locked door first fit a burglar and later fit an insider. When: Structuring a multi-victim mystery. Why: Re-reading old evidence after new facts keeps earlier clues active across the whole plot.
- [behavior] A witness who redirects the interview toward another person or demands immediate action may be shifting focus away from themselves; note such redirection.
- [rule] Keep ambiguous or dismissed traces available so players can revisit them, and revisit earlier scenes after a key discovery so details take new meaning. When: a major reveal reframes earlier content, evidence is initially unclear, or an NPC wrongly dismisses a sound or object. Why: Revisiting lets new information change a trace's meaning and rewards attentive players.
- [rule] Ask what has happened that has never happened before, not only what has happened, to focus on the anomaly that breaks the usual pattern.
- [rule] Give each environmental trace a checkable consequence, such as a footprint that confirms a witness claim, so players can test clues against each other.
- [rule] When the intended target changes, re-evaluate the suspect pool, the motive and the meaning of each earlier detail under the new assumption. When: After a reversal of the apparent victim. Why: Every clue was read under the old target, so its significance shifts with the new one.
- [rule] Let NPCs pass an item around and interpret it differently, then leave the player to decide which reading holds.
- [rule] After a reveal, relabel earlier NPC behaviour such as warnings, detours or avoided encounters as clues the player could have noticed. When: A hidden antagonist is revealed late in a story. Why: Retroactive framing rewards attentive players and makes the reveal feel earned.
- [rule] Build a rest or save point where the player can reconsider the collected evidence with fresh eyes. Why: stalled players benefit from a chance to reassess.
- [rule] Reward players who re-examine a room after a triggered event, not only during the first search. When: when a room changes after a triggered event. Why: Revisits are where changed state becomes visible.
- [heuristic] Repeat a question in a different form so the suspect cannot settle on one fixed answer.
- [heuristic] Reveal a clue as a reward after the related backstory is told, so its logic carries more weight. Why: context gives the clue its meaning.
- [heuristic] A second party's practical request can interrupt a digressing speaker and return the talk to the object at hand. When: when a speaker keeps wandering off topic.
- [heuristic] When the surroundings assume a clue's category, test a different grouping against the object itself before accepting the reframed reading.
- [heuristic] A clue noticed early may become meaningful later, so record details without judging their importance yet.
- [heuristic] Reframe the target: a witness may work for a business outside the obvious specialist category, so widen the pool to general employers. When: specialist searches fail. Why: people who used a resource may not work in its usual trade.
- [heuristic] A single clue can implicate either the victim or the culprit. Test each clue against both readings before assigning it to a suspect. When: when a clue seems to point at one person. Why: A clue read in only one direction can mislead the investigation.
- [heuristic] Reframe an early clue read as a sign of a skilled criminal into a trait that only one suspect would find natural. When: When the reveal should recontextualize evidence the reader already saw.
- [heuristic] Recasting an object as a prop can remove its evidential weight, so its presence no longer proves a crime.
- [heuristic] A family-history document listing heirs and their shares gives players a motive map and a reason to return to old locations. When: Designing a mystery whose hidden object sits in a family setting.
- [heuristic] A dropped item can be designed to point to a character's return visit, giving the player a reason to revisit a location.
- [heuristic] Let an item already in view serve a different function, so the player can solve a locked situation by reinterpreting an object rather than finding a missing one.
- [heuristic] Let existing physical clues change meaning instead of adding new ones: a footprint or cord seen early is reread once a later discovery reveals its cause. Why: Rereading known evidence rewards attentive players more than new clues do.
- [procedure] 1) Admit the first theory was wrong and say why. 2) Replay the clues in the order they appeared. 3) Show how each clue fits the mechanism. 4) Link the clues into one chain. When: a solution depends on several earlier clues. Why: a replay lets the audience check the solution against what it already saw.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the fact wanted and the reason behind it. 2) Ask only for the fact, such as a date, letter or object. 3) Use the fact's answer as the basis for the next question. When: A witness refuses a damaging question that is legally or socially protected. Why: A narrower fact-based question is harder to refuse and avoids the protected reason, so it can still produce usable evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Show the object in a routine context. 2) Let the earlier assumption dismiss it. 3) Have the character handle, unfold and read the object. 4) Let the new recognition reorganize the whole theory. When: staging a reveal from an ordinary object.
- [pitfall] A suspect's reframe of a contradiction as misunderstanding is not proof; only counter-evidence that directly contradicts the reframe defeats it. When: when a suspect offers a reframe, or when designing NPC alibis or cover stories. Why: A reframe can only be defeated by evidence that contradicts it directly.

## document verification and forgery checks
- [rule] Test a document's or testimony's claims against independent, checkable facts or records, such as logs, receipts or reports, not its appearance. When: when a document supports a claim.
- [rule] Let a forged-papers mechanic require a past record that a gatekeeper checks against stored files, so a mismatch is caught.
- [rule] Compare a document's paper type, watermark and typing with the stationery of the suspected source before accepting it as genuine. When: when a document seems to come from a specific place. Why: Differences in paper or typing show the document came from elsewhere.
- [rule] Check a tradition about an event's location against records and practical constraints; a plausible tradition still needs reasoning to confirm it.
- [rule] Show documents in a case file with provenance, including who wrote them, who copied them and what was lost, so players can weigh them. When: Designing in-world documents or case files. Why: Provenance lets players judge reliability rather than trust every document equally.
- [heuristic] Physical traits like machine faults or paper watermarks narrow a source but rarely identify it alone; confirm a dating estimate with a second feature, since forgeries copy one period style. When: Judging whether a document is genuine. Why: A single matching feature can be imitated more easily than several.
- [heuristic] Treat a document's physical form, including its handwriting, signature and wear, as evidence in its own right. When: Authorship or authenticity of a document is in question. Why: Physical features can reveal who wrote it and how it was handled.
- [heuristic] A journal that records the player's own assumptions gives later evidence something to test, which rewards careful reading. When: when designing in-world records. Why: Written assumptions can be confirmed or contradicted as the story unfolds.
- [heuristic] Let a later in-game chronicle state an interpretation that players can test against original letters and site clues. When: Designing in-game histories.
- [heuristic] An intact wax seal and undisturbed dust in a document's folds suggest it has not been altered since it was sealed.
- [heuristic] Check authorisations against the signatures they carry, because a repeated forged signature can hide withdrawals from a fund. When: when a fund's withdrawals look approved.
- [heuristic] A genuine document can contain errors, so one failed check does not prove forgery; several failed checks together strongly suggest it. When: when evaluating a suspicious document. Why: Genuine documents can have minor inconsistencies.
- [heuristic] A written document can look damning out of context and harmless with background; establish its context before deciding what it proves. When: Interpreting a letter or record as evidence. Why: Meaning depends on the reader's background and the referenced papers.
- [heuristic] A found letter can carry a watermark or paper type that matches a map region, letting the player link the document to a location through an in-world reference.
- [heuristic] A forgery can copy a known handwriting yet still fail on facts, so check a suspiciously detailed document's facts against the established record. When: a document claims to come from a known person. Why: matching handwriting does not confirm the content is accurate.
- [heuristic] Test a standard of evidence by parallel: if accepting an unverified kind of testimony would also require accepting equally unsupported claims, the standard is shown to be too weak. When: defending a standard of proof for unverified claims.
- [heuristic] Players should compare a found letter or diary with environmental clues before acting on its claims, since documents can be biased. When: Designing found documents as story information. Why: Checking against physical evidence prevents the player from acting on a biased source.
- [heuristic] When a document fits later events too neatly, check whether the events were arranged to fit the document rather than the reverse. When: A document appears to anticipate later events. Why: Reversing the inference can reveal a scheme that exploited the document.
- [heuristic] Let a forged document fail an independent check, such as a date or material compared against a record found elsewhere. Why: A checkable record gives the solver a fair route to expose the forgery.
- [procedure] 1) List each document's date. 2) List the events it describes and the relevant trial dates. 3) Flag any document dated after the moment it could have been used. 4) Pursue every mismatch as a lead. When: when verifying a written record. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Pick a specific detail, such as a letter shape or signature mark. 2) Compare it against known genuine examples. 3) Judge authenticity by any mismatch found. When: a transaction depends on whether money or a document is genuine. Why: comparison with genuine references reveals forged details.
- [procedure] 1) Gather known specimens from the same person. 2) Compare them with the questioned document on distinctive features. 3) Rule out forgery first. 4) Only then have a specialist vouch for authorship. When: When a document's origin matters to the case. Why: Authorship cannot be confirmed while forgery remains possible.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the handwriting with a known sample of the author's hand. 2) Confirm the date. 3) Check named people and places against other facts. 4) Establish where the document was kept. When: Before relying on a written document as evidence. Why: A document's contents count only once its authorship and date are checked.
- [procedure] 1) Keep the document's text unaltered. 2) Obtain endorsement from witnesses who can attest to the facts it records. When: A document must be presented as genuine. Why: Unaltered text and endorsement by knowledgeable witnesses let others judge its authenticity.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the writer from handwriting or other markers. 2) Record postmark, date and signature gaps as facts, not proof. 3) Keep the meaning open until a second source confirms what is referred to. When: Evaluating an unsigned or undated document. Why: Markers establish provenance, but meaning needs independent confirmation.
- [procedure] 1) Request the original from its official source rather than trusting the copy in hand. 2) Compare the copy with the original. 3) Check independent witnesses against both versions. When: when a crucial document is in doubt. Why: The original is the reference point that copies can be tested against.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the paper with the supposed sender's normal stock. 2) Check the form of production, such as typed versus handwritten. 3) Compare signatures and initials with genuine examples. 4) Judge what the writer knew. 5) Trace where the materials came from. When: when a document is central to the case and its authorship is in question.
- [procedure] 1) Collect specimens from each candidate machine and each paper supply. 2) Compare typeface, ink and paper separately against the questioned document. 3) Exclude sources whose specimens differ. When: An anonymous document has no handwriting or signature.
- [procedure] 1) Match specific details between two cases. 2) Check whether independent sources note the same parallels. 3) Infer copying only if they do. When: When a later event closely resembles an earlier published account. Why: Resemblance alone may come from shared conditions.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the document's date with each candidate's recorded whereabouts. 2) Count the actual signatures. 3) Scrutinize undated or untitled items. 4) Check titles against who was acting. 5) Note the addressee. When: Authorship or authority is disputed and candidates' movements are recorded. Why: Dates, signatures, titles and addressees each reveal who really wrote or sanctioned a document.
- [pitfall] Documents capture only their wording, not intentions or later events, so treating one as proof of motive is a mistake. When: Interpreting a letter, contract or memo as evidence. Why: Documents do not record motives or what followed.
- [pitfall] Inferring forgery from format alone, such as a typed letter with a signature, is a mistake; it makes the document suspicious but not proven forged. When: A document lacks handwriting but carries a signature. Why: Typed documents are unusual but can be genuine, so format is only a reason to examine further.
- [pitfall] A suspect who notices a mismatch in a forged message's handwriting or wording may refuse to attend the meeting. When: When a bait message is imitated from a real person's writing. Why: A careful target compares the message to known samples and rejects it on any discrepancy.
- [pitfall] When the original document is never found, a claim resting on a copy or on one person's handwriting cannot be verified and the explanation stays untested.
- [fact] A terse official record can hide how contradictory the facts are, while full notes let an audience later check what was visible from the start.

## false solutions and misdirection
- [model] A mystery can chain false solutions, each more convincing and built on clues later reversed, until a late capture clears the apparent culprit and exposes the true one. When: designing a multi-suspect mystery. Why: Each reversal keeps the answer open, drives the reader through wrong answers, and makes the final reveal surprising.
- [model] The engine of a reveal is the gap between what the audience believes and what an object, body or witness shows. Why: Contradicting evidence is what makes the audience's belief fail.
- [model] A mystery can be structured as a series of plausible solutions, each overturned by new evidence as a deeper secret surfaces, with the reveal arriving late from a previously minor figure. When: designing a multi-layer mystery plot. Why: Each reversal keeps the player revising beliefs, and a late reveal from a minor figure rewards attention to earlier details.
- [model] A detective's own apparent vulnerability can serve as bait, luring a hidden antagonist into revealing a confession. When: designing a trap that exploits the protagonist's apparent weakness. Why: The antagonist expects the victim to be helpless, so they act carelessly and self-incriminate.
- [model] A mystery can run a sequence of false solutions, each with its own motive and alibi, and undo them with one reinterpretation of the victim's last words or timing.
- [mechanism] Overturn each false solution with a physical object tied to a person the reader was told to distrust, so suspicion moves; use one decisive object for a sharp shift. When: Structuring a mystery with several suspects, or when a suspicion needs to be reversed decisively. Why: Physical evidence reattributes guilt more convincingly than argument alone, and a single decisive object gives a clear turn that argument rarely achieves.
- [mechanism] A belief is undone by a hidden physical or staged cause, a cleared suspect or unexpected agent, or the narrator's own misreading acting as the misdirect.
- [mechanism] An official verdict that seems to close a case creates a false floor, so players feel the matter is settled just before evidence reopens it. When: A mystery includes an authority's conclusion that players initially trust. Why: Players lower their guard after an official ruling, making the reopening more effective.
- [mechanism] A sequence of apparent solutions, each supported by distinct evidence, keeps the player's suspicion moving; discrediting one forces re-examination of the others. When: Structuring a long mystery plot with several suspects. Why: Each collapsed suspect invalidates the reasoning that supported it and reopens earlier evidence.
- [mechanism] Each false alarm that turns out harmless lowers tension briefly but keeps the real danger untouched, so later threats feel more urgent. When: when a protagonist fears discovery and gets a harmless scare. Why: The real danger remains unresolved, so the audience stays anxious.
- [rule] Give each false solution a checkable mechanism, such as a timeline or object, and a stated clue proving it false, so players rule it out rather than guess. When: When designing several plausible suspects or explanations, or a false ending or body swap. Why: A checkable mechanism makes a false solution feel solid until contradicted and keeps suspicion moving. Eliminable options make deduction fair; unresolved decoys feel unfair. (x2)
- [rule] Anchor each false solution in a plausible document or witness, so new testimony overturns or reframes it rather than the player changing their mind. When: designing a sequence of mystery answers or a multi-step mystery. Why: Plausible backing keeps each false answer believable until a new source contradicts it. Contradicted theories feel like cheating; reframed ones feel like progress.
- [rule] Open an NPC interrogation with a benign cover action, such as tending a wound, that hides the real question. When: Designing NPC scenes where the player needs information from a fragile character. Why: A benign cover lowers the NPC's guard.
- [heuristic] Make the surface explanation complete enough that the audience builds it themselves, then overturn it with a hidden cause supported by a detail already shown. When: writing the reveal or designing a mystery's false lead. Why: A wrong belief the audience assembled on its own, then broken fairly, makes the surprise land and the correction feel earned.
- [heuristic] Keep a wrong answer credible enough to seem to close the investigation, then overturn it with a stronger clue so the next reveal reads as a correction. When: Opening the first investigation of a mystery. Why: A solution that feels settled makes the next reveal a surprise, and a near-closed case makes the later reversal feel earned.
- [heuristic] A shock the audience expects from a character can be a misdirect that hides the character's real motive.
- [heuristic] A criminal's error may end the contest permanently while an investigator's error can often be recovered, so patience is affordable when the criminal makes a mistake. When: Weighing risk between investigator and criminal. Why: Irreversible errors favour the party who can still correct theirs.
- [heuristic] Seed a later event with an earlier testimony the player hears as belief; the same words gain new meaning once a witness is shown present. When: When designing a reveal that should reinterpret content the player has already seen. Why: Repeating the same words under a witness's presence changes their meaning, so the player re-reads earlier material without new information.
- [heuristic] Use a false solution to shift the player's model without ending the chase; overturn it when evidence contradicts the arrest.
- [heuristic] Let the audience's grief or certainty serve as the false solution, then reverse it with a disclosure that reframes clues already on the page. Why: The reframing rewards attentive readers.
- [heuristic] A plausible but wrong frame, such as madness or occult sacrilege, can hide an ordinary motive like greed, which the player reaches by reading the victim's character. When: the investigation is pulled toward a dramatic explanation. Why: Dramatic frames absorb attention and delay the mundane motive.
- [heuristic] Open with a genre-typical bluff as the first apparent solution, so the audience accepts a harmless confrontation before the real danger appears.
- [heuristic] An apparent victim may have fabricated the scheme, so re-examine a sympathetic party's motives late in the case. When: A late-act reveal could reverse player sympathy. Why: Sympathy shapes trust, and reversing it changes how earlier evidence reads.
- [heuristic] A false solution should be rationally coherent, letting players test it against evidence shown before it is undercut. When: Writing a misdirect for a mystery. Why: Testable false solutions feel fair, so the later reversal feels earned.
- [heuristic] Place a false alarm, such as a wrong identification, before the real signal to test the player's trust and make the true reveal feel earned. Why: A mistaken identification shows that observers can be wrong, lending the real evidence credibility.
- [procedure] 1) Give each accusation a real clue. 2) Let the investigator suspect the next character. 3) Overturn the theory with a new fact. 4) Repeat until the true culprit is reached. When: Structuring a murder mystery built on successive suspects. Why: Each real clue makes a false solution feel earned before it collapses.
- [procedure] 1) Set a code phrase and a demanded price for the exchange. 2) Let the target believe he holds the prize. 3) Show the package was empty only once the target is subdued.
- [pitfall] An accepted explanation, such as calling recurring losses an expected risk, can be partly true yet hide a shared pattern, so test each part. When: When several people agree on how an event happened. Why: Shared assumptions go unexamined.
- [pitfall] An explanation can sound scientific while resting on an assumed mechanism, and dismissing a supernatural claim too quickly can hide a human act. When: evaluating an explanation of a strange event. Why: Unverified mechanisms and hasty dismissal both mislead.
- [pitfall] A friend who wants to protect the investigator may steer her away from a line of inquiry without intending to deceive. When: When an ally offers a benign explanation or changes the topic. Why: Protective intent can still divert attention from the real question.
- [pitfall] A natural explanation can absorb every symptom and hide the real cause, so the investigator must check which symptoms it leaves over. When: when a single mundane cause seems to account for everything. Why: A tidy fit can conceal an unexplained remainder.
- [pitfall] Assuming a culprit is ignorant can lead an investigator to dismiss a skilled actor; weigh the opposite possibility too. When: When judging a culprit's method as clumsy. Why: A deliberate or skilled act can look careless to someone who underestimates it.
- [pitfall] Assuming the obvious executor keeps the role can miss a condition that replaces them. When: A will contains conditional succession of executors. Why: Conditions can transfer control to a different person.
- [pitfall] An absolute safety claim makes people stop checking, so the real danger often lies in what the claim does not cover. When: A system is described as perfect by those who run it. Why: Reassurance lowers vigilance.
- [pitfall] Reading a staged scene at face value sends the investigation to the wrong suspect, because the planted tools were arranged to be believed. When: investigating a scene with planted weapons or tools. Why: Staged evidence is built to match the expected story.

## method and modus operandi
- [definition] Method of exclusion: after ruling out other causes, the remaining candidate gains suspicion even on thin evidence. When: the list of possible causes is complete.
- [behavior] Confidence in one's own method and pride can lead an investigator to dismiss a rival approach, which shows a personal stake in the answer.
- [rule] A slow-acting method is a poor tool for robbery, because the victim cannot be quickly overpowered; filter motives by the method they would require. When: Filtering candidate motives against the chosen method. Why: The method's speed and effect limit which motives it can serve.
- [heuristic] Ask whether a suspect would act this way, not only could; a method clashing with their habits or a tool ill-suited to the task suggests another actor or staging. When: A suspect has a motive but the method, staging or tool seems out of character or ill-suited to the task. Why: Possibility alone does not establish the act; out-of-character details point to a different doer or a staged scene.
- [heuristic] Treat the choice of method as evidence: ask why it was chosen and who would think of it, since the answer reveals needs and narrows the suspect pool. When: A crime or visitor uses an unusual or particular method. Why: Uncommon methods reflect specific knowledge or interest, which narrows the suspect pool.
- [heuristic] Offenders tend to reuse effective methods, so incidents sharing a distinctive method, or a present crime matching a documented earlier one, may link to one actor or an accomplice. When: Several incidents or a present crime share a distinctive method with records of earlier cases. Why: Criminals reuse what has worked before; method fit, not only the target, supports the link.
- [heuristic] Body disposal is hard: bulky, heavy, chemically unstable, emit strong odours, and retain identifying structure; realistic options reduce to burial or dismemberment with dispersal, both tending to lead to discovery. When: Judging whether a concealment or body disposal is plausible. Why: Physical properties of remains make concealment hard, and each option leaves traces investigators can follow.
- [heuristic] A cold, methodical killing can be read as the act of a mind that is mad in a method-driven way, shifting the inquiry toward the killer's mental state.
- [heuristic] Judge a physical detail by what a skilled practitioner would normally use or do; deviations from expected practice suggest a different source. When: Assessing whether an explanation fits the evidence. Why: Professional methods leave characteristic traces.
- [heuristic] An investigator should reconstruct the method of a crime, not only identify the weapon, because the method explains how the act was done unseen.
- [heuristic] Ask how a clue was made. If no tool that could make the marks is found, the method stays open even when the source matches. When: a clue's source is confirmed but its means is not. Why: a clean source match does not explain the method.
- [heuristic] Sound detection rests on a method rather than inspiration, and that method is what checks a gut feeling.
- [heuristic] Reconstruct a hidden method from what is absent, such as smell, supply lines or residue, and from changes that would clear evidence of it. When: Ordinary examination finds no cause. Why: A method that leaves no positive trace is revealed by what is missing.
- [heuristic] Trace each method in the solution to a known precedent so the way the plot was built feels plausible. When: explaining how a plan or trick was executed. Why: Documented precedents make the method credible.
- [heuristic] A cleaned scene still records the cleaning, so reason backward from what a concealer destroyed and what they missed to learn what they feared. When: A scene shows wiping or tidying more elaborate than the crime needed.
- [heuristic] Use cleanup evidence to establish how a concealment was done, not who did it.
- [heuristic] To explain why a community acted on a now-doubtful assumption, reconstruct the shared frame that defined its evidence rather than judging each person's choice alone. When: when analyzing a past group decision. Why: the frame determines what each member could treat as proof.
- [heuristic] An unusual scheme signals unusual means of execution, not that the case is impossible. When: A crime seems impossible under ordinary assumptions. Why: Atypical methods can satisfy conditions that ordinary ones cannot.
- [heuristic] Read the method of dismemberment or damage as a profile of the perpetrator's skill, such as clean joint separation suggesting anatomical or butchery training. When: Physical damage shows a consistent and deliberate method. Why: Technique reveals the skill and training of the person who carried it out.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the physical setting and its constraints. 2) List candidate methods, simplest first. 3) Imagine the act step by step inside it. 4) Test each candidate against evidence and physical possibility; discard failures and keep the fit. 5) Predict where a key object should be and search there. When: Reconstructing how a crime was committed, especially a locked-room attack. Why: Reasoning from mechanism reveals the path that apparent security hides.
- [procedure] 1) Scout the target alone, ideally at night. 2) Brief the team on the layout. 3) Set timing and charges. 4) Withdraw to cover before the effect. When: Planning a direct assault on an isolated building. Why: Solo scouting gives accurate layout detail before committing the team.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the object or means used. 2) Describe how it was delivered through a normal action. 3) Check what bystanders could actually have seen. 4) Trace who had access to the means.
- [procedure] 1) State the observed facts in the order they were gathered. 2) Explain what each fact indicates. 3) Infer the method linking them. 4) Withhold identifying or confidential details. When: explaining a solved case to a listener.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the room's state at two times. 2) Ask why each object is in its current state and whether that state has a plausible reason. 3) Work out which action would produce it. When: After a scene is secured and before it is handled. Why: Backward reasoning from disturbances reconstructs earlier events.
- [procedure] 1) Lay out the offender's actions in order: approach, entry, the act, exit. 2) Add any changes made along the way. 3) Place each physical clue at the step it explains. When: closing a case with a fair-play reveal. Why: A step-by-step replay shows the crime was possible and every clue fits.
- [procedure] 1) Get the medical account of wound path, depth and nearby organs. 2) Reconstruct the victim's posture at firing. 3) Infer attacker position and intent from the angle. 4) Check the scene for facts that contradict an accident. 5) Weigh the physician's alternative readings against those facts. When: wound position can be compared with the room layout. Why: physical evidence reveals how an attack unfolded.
- [procedure] 1) Describe the proposed method. 2) Check how it actually behaves: targeting a moving target, wear on the tool, where objects would land. 3) Check the victim's timing and ability to react. 4) Flag each mismatch as evidence. When: the scene looks too neat or the proposed method looks implausible.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the method and how rare its knowledge, supply, or skill is. 2) Sort possible users by how deliberately they would have acquired that knowledge. 3) Narrow the suspect pool to those in the deliberate tier. 4) Confirm the profile with a separate line of evidence. When: The method is uncommon and its requirements can be checked. Why: Rare methods exclude most people, but the profile is only reliable when independently confirmed.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the culprit's motive. 2) Reason forward through the steps needed to act. 3) Give each link a form a witness or record can confirm. 4) Label unsupported links as guesses. 5) Prefer the reconstruction whose links are each supported. When: a crime seems to need several coordinated steps. Why: each link can then be checked separately.
- [tradeoff] Revealing only the method protects a suspect's identity but leaves the audience unable to judge the full solution; revealing the ending allows judgment but exposes the person. When: closing a case.
- [pitfall] A method copied from a published account may fake an effect or serve as cover, so it can point to the wrong suspect, since a human actor can produce the reported result. When: A documented technique is used to fake an apparent supernatural event or to cover a death. Why: Published accounts are easy to imitate, so the reported result may come from a person rather than the method's author or the claimed cause.
- [pitfall] Treating a similarity of method as proof of an accomplice is a leap; it stays a suspicion until evidence supports it.
- [pitfall] A conclusion about who did it, without an explanation of how it was done, invites ridicule and resistance.
- [pitfall] Explaining how an effect happened does not by itself reveal who caused it; the mechanism still needs a link to a person.
- [fact] Reviewing past cases can show which forensic methods would have changed their outcomes, supporting evaluation of new techniques.

## poison and food effects
- [mechanism] Fast-acting drugs may cause sickness and giddiness; exertion can speed poisoning and trigger fatal collapse at a time unrelated to worst symptoms, making death look like strain. When: When matching a death to the agent's expected effect. Why: Symptoms and collapse can follow different timelines.
- [mechanism] A poison puzzle built on fixed rules, such as detection thresholds and onset delays, lets players deduce which item was tainted.
- [behavior] A witness's disclosure can depend on their state: a sober or pressed witness may reveal more, while an intoxicated witness's account may shift from one telling to the next. When: When interviewing a witness who is drunk or under strain. Why: Impaired memory and changing mood alter what the witness reports.
- [rule] If everyone who shared a dish was unaffected, the substance was likely added to a separate portion set aside afterward. When: when investigating tainted food. Why: A shared dish that was safe for others points to a later addition.
- [rule] Record the exact time of a shared meal, everything eaten and drunk, and who ate and saw each item served, so harm can be traced to one item. When: A poisoning or harm must be traced to one item consumed by one person. Why: Recorded details give each shared item witnesses and let investigators narrow the cause.
- [rule] Give a drugged or possessed NPC a short purposeful routine, then let players reconstruct it from partial evidence. When: Designing an NPC whose actions are later investigated. Why: Purposeful routines leave traces that players can piece together.
- [rule] Place the source of a rare poison in an everyday item in the game world so the player must work out how the culprit obtained it. When: Designing a poison-identification puzzle. Why: A familiar source makes the trace a real deduction step.
- [heuristic] An intoxicated or inattentive witness's account is unreliable: impaired memory yields gaps and errors, so check any timeline built on it before accepting it. When: A witness was drunk, distracted, or admits heavy drinking. Why: Impaired observation and memory produce unreliable detail.
- [heuristic] Drink and flattery loosen a witness's tongue, so an intoxicated speaker says more than intended; treat their relayed gossip and claims as unreliable. When: When a witness is drunk. Why: Drink loosens control over what is revealed.
- [heuristic] A shared dish is cleared only if all co-eaters stayed well; when they did, shift attention to what only one person consumed, but harm to any co-eater implicates the dish. When: Investigating an illness with a possible shared source. Why: Healthy co-diners rule out the common dish; harm to any co-eater implicates it.
- [heuristic] In a poisoning mystery, design symptoms so an expert can rule out some causes, leaving the player to identify the remaining one. When: Writing a death or illness that the player must explain. Why: Ruling out possibilities through expertise narrows the search and guides the player toward the true cause.
- [heuristic] A drink chosen at a scene can reveal the drinker's trade or background, since people tend to pick drinks familiar to their own life.
- [heuristic] A wound alone does not explain a faint; check whether the person fainted or fell and struck their head.
- [heuristic] Before testing an earlier-dosing hypothesis, ask whether an earlier death would change anything relevant, such as an inheritance, to judge whether it matters.
- [heuristic] Make sure every shared dish was eaten by at least two people, ideally about four, so a poison in one dish would affect several witnesses. When: Designing or investigating a shared meal. Why: More eaters means more witnesses to any harm.
- [heuristic] Prepare for poisoning by having medical help and antidotes ready, since prompt treatment can save a victim and reveal how the poison was given. When: a poisoning is expected.
- [heuristic] A poison given in a shared drink suggests someone both victims knew and trusted, which sharply cuts the suspect list. When: The method of death implies inside knowledge or trust.
- [procedure] 1) Ask everyone present what they ate. 2) Record the exact onset of illness. 3) Check the preparation details of each dish. 4) Fix an absent person's whereabouts with a timetable. 5) Compare accounts for consistency on menu and details. When: Investigating a poisoning or illness with a possible source. Why: Onset times and alibis anchor the timeline.
- [procedure] 1) Inspect the injured body and its wounds closely before any formal examination. 2) Use magnification and fine tools. 3) Look for foreign fragments inside and around each wound. When: when a wound may carry evidence of its cause. Why: fragments can reveal the object or environment that caused the injury.
- [procedure] 1) Identify what the victim consumed that others did not. 2) Test common shared sources first. 3) Test the victim's own supply and empty containers. 4) Inspect containers with magnification, handling them minimally. 5) Swab interior surfaces and culture the sample on a nutrient medium at body temperature overnight. When: a cause spreads through a household and the victim's habits set them apart.
- [metric] Swallowed liquid poison symptoms usually appear 1–2 hours after ingestion but range 15 minutes to several hours, depending on whether stomach is empty; hours-late onset suggests later dose. When: Estimating when a poison was taken from when symptoms began. Why: Wide onset variation weakens any single-timeline inference.
- [metric] Strychnine is detectable in solution at about one part in seventy thousand, so only a strongly flavoured drink is likely to hide it.
- [pitfall] A witness who seems drunk or confused may have been drugged, so their recollection is partial and needs medical checking.
- [pitfall] Clearing an item because others ate it unharmed fails when the harmful dose was aimed at one portion. Why: Targeted dosing leaves the others unaffected.
- [pitfall] Audiences assume drugs only stupefy, so explaining purposeful action under a drug must first counter that expectation. When: Presenting a drug-driven act that seems out of character. Why: The common belief makes purposeful drugged behavior seem implausible.
- [pitfall] Accepting intoxication as a stock explanation for conduct skips testing the claim; treat a drunk-state claim as something to verify. When: a character explains an outburst by having been drinking. Why: The excuse is easy to offer and hard to disprove without checking.
- [pitfall] A half-asleep witness can give confident, specific details that are wrong, so the sharpest details deserve the most suspicion. When: the witness was dozing or only half awake during the event. Why: drowsy memory fills gaps with plausible detail.
- [pitfall] Taking an illness at face value before checking the timing of its symptoms can hide a fabrication.
- [pitfall] A body left in a tidal area for days can pick up debris after death, so debris alone may not show when an injury happened. When: when a body was exposed to an environment before examination. Why: debris can be acquired after death.
- [pitfall] A common everyday source can make a rare substance hard to trace, so tracing by source may fail.
- [fact] Some poisons mimic heart failure and leave no characteristic signs, so a routine examination can miss them; test a natural-cause verdict before accepting it. When: A death appears natural. Why: Natural-looking death can hide deliberate harm.
- [fact] Early symptoms of some poisonings are hard to tell apart from common illnesses, so a suspicion needs expert confirmation before it drives action.
- [fact] A water container that a victim asked to have refilled but is found dry suggests someone emptied it, and a staff member's memory of filling it can establish that it was full earlier. When: A missing or emptied container is linked to a poisoning. Why: A discrepancy between a request and the container's state is a lead that points to tampering.
- [fact] A bullet hole in a sash, fired from inside, is physical proof that someone stood outside the window.
- [fact] A drug can cause a person to act in a trance and leave them with no recall of the act afterwards.

## public opinion and appeal
- [model] Case reports pass through a chain of relays: housekeeper, local station, headquarters, duty officer, prosecutor's liaison, then on-scene detectives, each adding detail.
- [mechanism] Public opinion can push an authority to act on a case even when the evidence is incomplete, producing an official outcome that may not match the truth. When: Public attention or outcry is strong while evidence remains thin. Why: Authorities respond to social pressure, so a formal decision can precede or diverge from proof.
- [mechanism] A rallying cry naming a valued item can keep a crowd moving from place to place in search of it.
- [mechanism] Public scandal spreads through rumour and press beyond characters' control, forcing them to respond to a story they cannot shape. When: When a secret is known to several people.
- [mechanism] Public speculation can spread a red herring as effectively as a planted note, because rumour and theory amplify a misleading reading. When: when NPCs or media discuss a case. Why: Repeated interpretations are believed without checking the evidence.
- [mechanism] Public attention can create a false impression: if the public believes the hunt is on the wrong trail, the fugitives relax and stay put. When: when suspects are likely to read news about the search. Why: a public trail changes what fugitives believe and do.
- [mechanism] Information about a community's members moves informally and quickly through the local area, so people often know movements they did not witness. When: A small community where people share news face to face. Why: Gossip circulates faster than any formal record.
- [mechanism] A public channel, such as a newspaper column, can carry messages between parties without direct contact when they have agreed a code in advance.
- [mechanism] Public rewards and subscriptions can turn a search into a shared, visible project.
- [mechanism] Information loses reliability as it passes through intermediaries, since each link adds distance from the original source.
- [mechanism] Authorities who sound the alarm publicly can trigger arrests before any formal proceeding begins.
- [mechanism] News of a ruling reaches allied parties informally before any formal decision, so some allies learn of it before the public does. When: a decision is pending in a faction-based system.
- [mechanism] In a public hearing with spectators, accusers speaking aloud can draw in new accusers after each event, so the proceeding grows on its own. When: a trial or examination is held before a crowd.
- [behavior] A person can keep a steady public manner while private manner changes over the months before an event, so public calm is weak evidence.
- [behavior] During a stall, press attention and official pressure grow, and speculation fills the gap left by missing new facts. When: a case stops progressing in public view. Why: Public interest persists without new evidence.
- [behavior] In a public hearing where each side makes one-sided accusations, the outcome can follow the speeches rather than checked facts. When: A public meeting settles a dispute after speeches. Why: Speeches are persuasive even when unverified.
- [rule] Public mood counts as independent evidence only if formed spontaneously; mood shaped by the reports under review is not confirmation, though a spontaneous judgment may still be sound. When: When judging whether a case is credible from general opinion. Why: Mood reflects the same reports under evaluation. (x2)
- [rule] Present an alibi publicly by naming each independent witness and the distances involved.
- [rule] When reversing a wrong accusation, state the reason for clearing publicly, so the cleared person is not left with lasting doubt. When: An accused person is cleared late in the story. Why: A withdrawn charge without a stated reason leaves public suspicion.
- [heuristic] A rumour gains partial support when an observer independently records the same sign that the rumour describes.
- [heuristic] A crime in a busy public place can seem safer to the culprit, since a quiet exchange there draws no attention.
- [heuristic] Sound out circulating views before committing to a conclusion. When: Forming a conclusion about a public event.
- [procedure] 1) Send an informant to each candidate location. 2) Have them find a talkative local with a memory of the event. 3) Let the account come out through gossip rather than direct questions. 4) Have the informant repeat it back to test retention. When: When local talk is likely to preserve a memory of an event. Why: Repeating the account tests whether the informant kept the facts.
- [tradeoff] A public challenge exposes the target, while a quiet arrangement removes the victim from the situation without public cost to the target.
- [tradeoff] A public appeal can identify a victim quickly but may alert the guilty, so it suits cases where speed matters more than secrecy. When: deciding whether to publish an appeal.
- [pitfall] Public notices reach everyone: naming a target informs anyone who knows the name, and an appeal alerts opponents who may flee or turn against the publisher; plan reactions first. When: When writing a notice or appeal that identifies a person. Why: Public text is readable by people who should not learn of the claim; reactions must be planned before publishing.
- [pitfall] Public opinion shapes what witnesses say, so their conjectures can be mistaken for facts. When: a case is much discussed locally.
- [pitfall] Pressing a suspect in public tends to provoke anger rather than candid answers. When: in front of an audience.
- [pitfall] Public certainty about one suspect directs attention to that suspect and can blind investigators to alternatives.
- [pitfall] Public consensus about a famous event does not mean the matter is settled, because it may rest on a concealment.
- [pitfall] Outbursts from onlookers interrupt proceedings and must be stopped before questioning can continue.
- [pitfall] Financial gains from a death's publicity can be mistaken for gains caused by the death itself. When: Assessing financial motive after a death. Why: Sales or fees may rise after a death without anyone having a motive to cause it.
- [pitfall] Treating a published account as neutral is a mistake when its printer or endorser promoted the case. When: When a printed case includes an endorsing preface or a promoter. Why: Promotion gives the publisher a stake in the account.
- [pitfall] A reputation inherited from a dead relative can make a living person look guilty without any evidence against them.
- [fact] Press or public accounts can mislead on method and outcome, possibly deliberately, and may repeat a false story without revealing full details; weigh them as testimony, not reliable records. When: When using newspaper reports, public bodies, news or rumour as evidence. Why: Sources have purposes and access that shape what they say; public accounts spread the staged narrative rather than the facts.

## reluctant witness disclosure
- [mechanism] A reluctant NPC that gives short answers and changes tone or posture at a sore topic can unlock a hidden fact when the player touches that topic. When: Designing an NPC who withholds information. Why: The emotional reaction gives the player a visible signal that a deeper fact sits behind the topic.
- [behavior] A witness may omit a movement or remark until asked directly about the specific person or subject, which cues recall or a partial admission. When: When an unprompted account omits a movement or remark that is later remembered or partly admitted. Why: A direct question naming the subject cues the memory. (x2)
- [behavior] A reluctant witness may hold back more than they say, and information often emerges only after follow-up pressure. When: a witness refuses at first and later gives way. Why: reluctance can mask knowledge the witness has.
- [behavior] A long, friendly setting, such as a drawn-out bargain over drink, lowers a source's guard and draws out local history. When: Trying to get a reluctant source to talk. Why: Relaxed conversation reduces caution about what is said.
- [behavior] A witness who fears damage to their reputation may refuse at first, then cooperate once they judge they have little left to lose. When: approaching a witness with something to protect. Why: a perceived loss of standing lowers the cost of talking.
- [behavior] A source who privately disagrees with an official line may concede a contrary view under direct questioning, but the same tactic may fail with a source lacking such a view. When: Questioning a source who already holds a doubt about an official position. Why: Existing private disagreement makes concession easier, while a source without it has nothing to reveal.
- [rule] Explain why the information matters and offer a confidentiality promise with stated limits to a witness who fears blame, gossip, reprisal or social cost. When: When a witness fears being blamed for an event, gossip, reprisal or social cost. Why: Fear of blame outweighs the wish to tell; a clear purpose and honest bounds build more trust than an unbounded promise.
- [rule] Give only a partial answer or the action needed now, withhold unconfirmed suspicion even from allies, and promise a full account once decisive evidence is ready. When: When a full answer would reveal a line of inquiry, such as when asked whether someone is suspected.
- [rule] Draw out a defensive witness by alternating pressure with release: press a sore subject, then change topic to lower tension before returning to the point. When: The witness gives minimal answers, repeats refusals, or shifts demeanor on certain topics. Why: Release lowers defensiveness so the witness keeps talking and the point can be revisited.
- [rule] Disclose only what is safe, and frame the aim as holding the guilty to account so the witness shares an interest in the outcome. Why: A shared goal gives the witness a reason to cooperate without full disclosure.
- [rule] Lock a reluctant witness's dialogue branch until the player secures that witness's safety. When: A witness refuses to speak without protection. Why: Fear of retaliation silences the witness, so safety is what should unlock speech.
- [rule] Ask whether a gap was an oversight or a deliberate choice, since the two readings imply different explanations and searches.
- [rule] Do not read a reluctant witness as the culprit; treat their fear as one signal among several.
- [rule] Call witnesses and announce a death at once, since prompt disclosure protects the accused and is itself a sign of good faith.
- [rule] Let an NPC victim refuse to report an incident, and give the player a reason to discover why. When: When designing a victim NPC who conceals an event. Why: A hidden motive creates a quest hook and a reason for further investigation.
- [heuristic] A small incentive and gentle pressure can move a forgetful or reluctant witness from 'cannot remember' to an attempt, narrowing an uncertain time to a clear window. When: A witness is reluctant or forgetful about a time or details. Why: Stakes and invitation lower the perceived cost of trying; incentive and pressure help recall.
- [heuristic] Showing a reluctant witness a written sentence from another source can draw a reaction that shows whether hostility is real or a misunderstanding. When: A witness refuses to explain and the investigator needs to test their stance. Why: The witness's response to a known sentence reveals the feeling behind their silence.
- [heuristic] Write down a witness's account promptly, before it can be disputed or changed. When: Collecting testimony. Why: Early records resist later revision.
- [heuristic] A partial claim works best when a direct question would be refused, because the other party is more likely to correct than confess. When: A guarded party would deny a direct question.
- [procedure] 1) Open with easy, general talk. 2) Narrow toward the sensitive subject in small steps. 3) Watch for physical tells. 4) Ease off as soon as distress appears. When: Questioning a sympathetic witness who has reason to avoid the subject.
- [procedure] 1) Soothe a resisting witness rather than press them. 2) Show interest in visible details of their surroundings. 3) Once they warm, listen and ask occasional questions. 4) Accept refusals and gather the facts by other means. When: the witness guards their words but may know about their circle.
