- [procedure] 1) Give the informant a token of good faith. 2) Promise protection you can keep. 3) Ask them to start from the beginning. 4) Have a second person present to hear the statement. 5) Test the claims against dated facts. When: questioning a frightened or self-interested informant. Why: each step builds trust and keeps the statement on record and checkable.
- [procedure] 1) Ask broad questions about the period before the event 2) Ask whether anything was heard before a fixed time 3) Anchor the question to a known event time. When: a witness may have registered something without noticing it. Why: an anchored clock time lets the witness test memory against a fixed point.
- [procedure] 1) Note what the witness says they cannot recall. 2) Ask a narrower question about what they would normally notice. 3) Request a clear yes or no. When: when a witness gives vague or hedged answers. Why: A witness in a fixed post would likely notice such events, so a narrow question tests whether the memory exists.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the same direct question several times, rejecting vague answers. 2) Stay silent after each answer so the source feels pressure to fill the gap. 3) Reassure the source that the remark stays private. 4) Keep the tone light to avoid making the source retreat. When: A source has already hinted at something and must be turned into a stated opinion. Why: Repeated direct questions, silence, and reassurance lower the cost of speaking and draw out views the source would not give freely.
- [pitfall] Details recalled only after pointed questioning may be genuine or distorted; check them before trusting or rejecting them as evidence. When: A witness recalls a detail only after a specific question. Why: Prompting can both distort and reveal real memories, and may produce a memory never formed earlier.
- [pitfall] Partial answers from a reluctant or frightened witness are incomplete: ask what was omitted and why, and check them against other sources. When: When a witness's account seems complete, or a witness is reluctant or frightened. Why: A frightened witness may reveal only part of a secret.
- [pitfall] A tidy explanation may fit the main event but miss secondary clues; treat any first theory as a working hypothesis and check it against every clue. When: When one tidy theory accounts for the main event but not secondary damage. Why: Ignored clues often point to a different or additional cause, and settling early hides the real route.
- [pitfall] Partial confirmation, whether from a witness or between witnesses, is not full corroboration; witnesses may hold back or share a mistaken assumption. When: Checking an alibi or cross-checking witnesses. Why: Witnesses may hold back information or be uncertain.
- [pitfall] Relying on a collaborator's incomplete facts and mistaking them for a full picture leads an investigator onto the wrong track.
- [pitfall] A single servant's account of a few overheard words can mislead if it is taken as the whole conversation.
- [pitfall] Agreement given grudgingly may later be revoked, so note who consented and under what conditions.
- [pitfall] A threatened or frightened witness may give a reluctant but accurate answer, so reassurance may matter more than pressure.
- [pitfall] Asking whether anyone saw the suspect can prompt a convenient memory of a witness, so that witness must be checked independently. When: a suspect names a witness after being asked.
- [pitfall] Hiding part of the stakes from a partner breeds distrust, and a shrewd partner will test what was left out.

## single witness testimony
- [behavior] A timed account from one witness can hold suspicion on one suspect and leave other candidates unexamined.
- [rule] A single deposition or vivid witness account is not proof or corroboration; the witness's mood and interests can shape what they report. (x2)
- [rule] Do not read one brief or distant observation as proof of motive or purpose; aim and intent are inferred, not confirmed. When: A lone sighting is interpreted. Why: Brief distant views are easily misread; one observation cannot establish intent. (x2)
- [rule] Before accepting a key clue from one witness, weigh their state, fears and expectations; do not treat an agitated witness's unverified sighting as settled. When: When a key clue rests on one witness.
- [rule] Do not establish an unseen act or guilt on one witness's account or on accusers' testimony alone; require a plurality of witnesses and further evidence before conviction. Why: Accusers' accounts can be mistaken or can feed on each other.
- [rule] Do not rely on one partial observer for what was said or who started an exchange; check the sequence against other sources and show what they missed. When: Evaluating an eyewitness report from a distance, behind a barrier, or with partial access. Why: Distance, angle and missed sound limit what one observer can know; partial knowledge misleads.
- [rule] Flag a clue only one character can perceive as unconfirmed and pair it with a player-checkable trace, such as a second witness, physical trace, or unfakeable test. When: When designing a clue that depends on a single witness, trigger or perception such as a vision. Why: No one else can test the detail.
- [rule] Do not treat one witness as decisive or rely on their description when it conflicts with physical evidence; check each account against traces left at the scene.
- [rule] Avoid relying on one costume when the target has reason to suspect outside agents.
- [rule] Never let one sighting be the whole case; a crime must be established on independent grounds in addition to identification. When: when deciding whether an identification is sufficient. Why: A single report, however sincere, can be wrong and needs corroboration.
- [rule] Treat a single anecdote about a physical trait as unconfirmed; verify it through the object itself or a second independent source. When: Using a secondhand report to support an identity claim. Why: One account can be mistaken or incomplete, so corroboration is needed before relying on it.
- [heuristic] A single witness backing a dramatic claim should be treated as unconfirmed until other evidence supports it. When: One testimony supports an extraordinary claim. Why: A lone account, however vivid, lacks independent support.
- [heuristic] A case built on inference can be overturned by one credible first-hand account.
- [heuristic] Before accepting a strange claim from a single witness, check whether an ordinary cause such as intoxication, injury, fear or known capability explains it. When: A supernatural or unusual claim rests on one witness. Why: Witness state and ordinary causes often account for the report.
- [heuristic] A single sight-line from a vantage point supports a claim about what was seen but cannot establish a location on its own.
- [procedure] 1) Record the observer's distance, eyesight, lighting and when they began attention. 2) Identify core facts repeated consistently. 3) Discount details shaped by fear or self-interest. 4) Check core facts against a second independent source. When: When a clue rests on one witness. Why: Viewing conditions limit what a sincere witness can perceive.
- [pitfall] A key fact or alibi resting on one witness stays provisional and unbacked until independent proof arrives, especially if that witness is missing or unreliable. When: When one witness is the only link to an alibi or key identifying fact. Why: Single sources can be wrong, lying, or absent. (x2)
- [pitfall] A timeline resting on one witness for a whole day or time block is unverified and fragile; a second, independently checkable source makes it much harder to break. Why: No second source exists to check the account.
- [pitfall] Treating one matching cue or identification as decisive closes inquiry early; a skilled challenge can undo it unless other evidence supports it. When: An identity question carries significant consequences. Why: Stopping at one matching feature skips checks that could reveal a mismatch.
- [pitfall] Relying on one witness with a stake, such as a grudge or self-protection, distorts the picture even when they supply a useful fact. When: A single witness with a stake supplies the only key detail or key source for understanding events. Why: Self-interest, grudge and self-defense shape what a witness reports and omits.
- [pitfall] When the only witness is the one reporting a private perception, the claim cannot be tested, so its reliability cannot be judged.
- [pitfall] A single visual detail, such as facial hair, is weak identification because it can be false or worn as disguise. Seek more durable marks. When: when identifying a watcher.
- [pitfall] A witness's recall of a single evening may be wrong, however clear it feels to them.
- [pitfall] Taking a judgement of someone's character from a single old memory as settled is a mistake; test it against other evidence.
- [pitfall] When the only witness who could confirm a document disappears, officials may treat the matter as closed, though the claim remains unverified.
- [pitfall] A single watcher in a crowded or complex space can easily lose the subject.
- [pitfall] A detail noticed by one character can have an innocent explanation, so check the object's history before drawing a conclusion.
- [pitfall] A reveal that skips the early impressions leaves the audience unable to see why the earlier theory was wrong.
- [pitfall] Each impression needs a plausible explanation; a deep mark alone does not prove a posture, so check it against other traces.
- [pitfall] A single observation with no baseline proves little on its own. Why: Without an earlier state there is nothing to compare against.
- [pitfall] A plant seen by only one witness depends entirely on that witness's reliability and view, so decide in advance how well they could see it. Why: One observer is a single point of failure for the clue's validity.
- [pitfall] A watch drawn from prominent people can name its own rivals and neighbors as suspects, a bias that the system itself does not correct. When: Watchers are chosen by standing rather than neutrality.
- [pitfall] A last-seen time from one witness is a single data point and may be wrong; confirm it before building on it.
- [pitfall] A clue seen by only one character, and not by the person it concerns, is easy to lose. When: A clue is witnessed by someone other than its subject.
- [fact] A dying or unwell witness may be the only source of a critical fact, so their testimony can be lost before it is checked.

## stain evidence
- [mechanism] A stain on the side of an object that touches a surface shows the object was dropped or moved after the bleeding, which fixes the order of events.
- [mechanism] Environmental wear such as rain, trampling and cleaning acts as noise that makes some clues unreliable.
- [mechanism] A washed object that stays damp can serve as a timed clue whose state changes with the game clock.
- [mechanism] An injury or damage state can be stored as a persistent flag that later dialogue or trial mechanics can reference. When: when a game needs lasting consequences of harm. Why: A stored flag lets later content respond to earlier events.
- [mechanism] Clotting can be stopped by removing fibrin or adding an alkaline salt, leaving blood looking unchanged while it stays liquid.
- [mechanism] Wet blood floods fingerprint ridge valleys and blurs the print; nearly dry blood yields a crisp print showing sweat-gland openings.
- [rule] Store wound, posture, item placement and weapon condition as authored death-state data so investigators can test whether a death fits its claimed cause. When: A game lets players investigate deaths. Why: Stored physical state makes contradictions checkable instead of cosmetic.
- [rule] A positive test shows that a stain is blood but not whose blood it is. Identifying the donor needs a separate step.
- [rule] Place worn items such as a stick, torn map or chewed strap in rooms so players can infer an occupant's profession, route and companion. When: when furnishing a room with personal items.
- [rule] Place worn objects whose clue shows only on close interaction, such as a split seam on a boot that is too small for its owner. When: A clue should reward careful inspection.
- [rule] Give each generated chest or relic a unique wear pattern, so an NPC who saw it can identify it later. When: when generating collectible or container objects that NPCs may recognise.
- [rule] Store trace data per location, so that a matching sample proves where a character has been.
- [rule] Store decals, footprints and blood splatters as timestamped layers so the player can deduce event order from which mark sits on top. When: Building persistent environmental marks in a game. Why: Layer order gives players a readable event history.
- [rule] Track which traces have been cleaned up in a scene so the player can infer what the offender tried to remove. When: A game lets the player clean up or alter traces. Why: Recording removals makes the cover-up itself readable.
- [rule] Store when each communication channel is open in the game world, so puzzles can check whether a message could have passed.
- [rule] Store each mark or wound with its provenance, so the player can tell which marks came from the killer and which from people who moved the body. When: Building a crime-scene data model.
- [heuristic] When blood amount conflicts with wound type, suspect the victim was wounded elsewhere, or that the scene was altered or the account is wrong. When: The amount of blood conflicts with the wound type. Why: A bleeding wound leaves blood where it was inflicted.
- [heuristic] Store how long a fluid has been exposed and change its appearance accordingly, so players can estimate when an event happened and test alibis. When: generating spills or stains. Why: Makes stains carry readable state.
- [heuristic] Estimate a stain's size and origin before accepting a stated cause; a stain too large for that cause suggests a different origin. When: A stated innocent explanation is offered for a mark on a person or object. Why: Size and placement often exceed what the stated cause could produce.
- [heuristic] Trace how a stain reached a hidden surface by following plausible liquid routes, such as running across one surface and soaking into another. When: a stain appears somewhere unexpected. Why: The route can show where the liquid came from and what happened to the object.
- [heuristic] Use wear patterns, such as worn floor tiles near a hidden door or stained clothing on an NPC, as clues the player learns to read. When: designing environmental storytelling. Why: wear reveals history the player can interpret.
- [heuristic] A stain treated with a reagent can be a planted clue that a scene was staged. When: designing a staged scene. Why: Treatment leaves a readable sign.
- [procedure] 1) Inspect the mark with a magnifier. 2) Apply a moisture test to see whether the colour runs. 3) Check whether the stain passes through the fabric. When: assessing a stain as physical evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Dust the impression with a fine dry powder. 2) Pour a liquid mixture onto it drop by drop until it sets into a solid model. 3) Lift the model as the record of the trace. When: A fragile trace such as a footprint will be lost to weather or handling. Why: A cast preserves the trace in a durable form for later examination.
- [metric] Around two hours on, a fresh drop is mostly clear fluid holding a small red clot at its centre. When: estimating how long blood has been exposed.
- [pitfall] Blood can come from many sources, so its path matters more than its mere presence when reconstructing events. When: Interpreting bloodstains at a scene. Why: The route blood takes reveals the sequence of movement, while presence alone is ambiguous.
- [pitfall] An inference about a stain's age fails if the time estimate behind it is wrong.
- [pitfall] Assuming a stain is one kind of material without examining its cells can lead to a wrong identification. When: When judging a stain by appearance alone. Why: Surface appearance can mislead where microscopic structure is distinct.
- [pitfall] Standard body proportions describe typical people, so a height estimate from them can be off for an individual.
- [pitfall] Fragments that crumble when moved cannot be rechecked later, so they should be examined in place before being handled. When: Handling a damaged physical clue. Why: Moving a fragile object can destroy evidence that would otherwise remain available.
- [fact] A trail of blood leading out of a closed room shows that someone left that room after the injury.
- [fact] A stain or hair on the edge of furniture shows where a body struck, which fixes a detail of how the injury happened.
- [fact] A decapitated body does not bleed, so bleeding from a wound on it shows the wound was made while the person was alive. Why: Circulation stops at death, so bleeding requires a living circulatory system.
- [fact] On a non-absorbent surface, fresh blood first gels into jelly, then contracts, splitting into a firm red clot and watery pale fluid.
- [fact] On white paper, blood appears as watery liquid with a solid clot attached, rather than an even clear red liquid.

## time of death and age estimation
- [mechanism] Age, muscular condition, fever and high surrounding temperature change how fast stiffening arrives and how long it lasts, widening or shifting the time estimate. When: when estimating time of death from stiffening. Why: these conditions alter the body's stiffening rate.
- [mechanism] A body that stiffens over a set number of in-game hours gives the player a clock against which to test accounts. When: Designing time-based evidence in a game world. Why: A predictable physical timer lets players check claims.
- [mechanism] A delay before concealing a body lets progressive physical changes, such as stiffening, reveal the true cause of death.
- [mechanism] Organisms that settle on remains, such as snail egg clusters or worm tubes, indicate an approximate submersion duration, giving a rough timeline. When: Estimating how long remains were underwater. Why: These organisms settle and grow over predictable periods, so their presence bounds the exposure time.
- [rule] Report time of death from warmth and stiffness as a probable range; these imprecise signs cannot fix an hour, and the true time may fall before the upper bound. When: when a case relies on an estimate from body signs. Why: signs cannot be pinned to one moment.
- [rule] Represent time of death as a range, and eliminate suspects or test witness accounts whose presence falls outside it. When: when designing or implementing a death-time window for a mystery. Why: A loose window makes an alibi look either fine or broken, so a range keeps elimination fair.
- [rule] Give players a time-of-death range and a known interval between two sightings, so they must work out which characters had opportunity. When: Designing a murder-timeline puzzle.
- [rule] Generate time-of-death windows from the event log, and flag any unexplained event for the player to examine.
- [rule] Label every estimate from remains as approximate and state a range rather than a precise figure, and say what the remains cannot prove. When: when presenting forensic-style estimates to a player. Why: ranges honestly reflect the limits of partial evidence.
- [heuristic] Test a claim with date arithmetic; if the stated ages or birth dates are impossible, the claim is ruled out. When: A story depends on who could have been born or alive at a given time.
- [heuristic] Body warmth and the onset of stiffening bound the time of death, and reasoning from the wound and the missing weapon can rule out suicide. When: Evaluating a death scene from a medical report.
- [heuristic] Estimate a person's present age from a dated image, then work backwards from an observed age to date a past event. When: when a reliable record with a date exists.
- [heuristic] The window in which a substance could have entered the victim can start earlier than the ingestion window, and extends backwards if the substance could sit in a regular supply. When: when the agent could have been placed in a routine item long before use.
- [heuristic] Represent a time of death as a range that narrows as each piece of evidence is found, with documented modifiers shifting it. When: when generating a mystery with a timed death.
- [heuristic] Use an examiner's estimate of time since death to anchor the investigation timeline before testimony is checked. When: When establishing when a death occurred. Why: A medical estimate constrains witness accounts.
- [heuristic] The degree of decay gives a minimum time an object has lain exposed, since heavy decay takes longer than a short exposure.
- [procedure] 1) Estimate the time after which household members would be awake and likely to hear or see the act. 2) Compare the victim's usual routine with that window. 3) Count the movements nobody heard to narrow what was done quietly. Treat the result as a range. When: when a medical time estimate conflicts with other evidence. Why: routine and witness awareness give firmer limits than bodily signs.
- [procedure] 1) Find the last moment the subject was confirmed present. 2) Find the first moment the subject was confirmed absent or found dead. 3) Treat these as the two outer edges of the window. 4) Narrow the window with the most reliable sighting. When: When a body is found long after death and no one saw the event. Why: Confirmed presence and absence form the outer limits of possible time of death.
- [procedure] 1) Note when the victim was last seen with the suspect. 2) Note the first sighting of symptoms. 3) Count the unaccounted minutes between them to bound the time of administration. When: Estimating when a poison or trap could have acted. Why: The gap between last contact and symptoms bounds when the dose was taken.
- [procedure] 1) Get a time-of-death estimate from physical signs. 2) Get the time of any sound a witness heard. 3) Overlap the two to fix a window. 4) Test the window against independent facts. When: When a time of death must be fixed from medical and witness timing.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the ages sworn in depositions. 2) Check each against birth dates in genealogical registers. 3) Reject a candidate whose age is implausible for the event, and leave the question open if evidence is thin. When: testing whether a named person could be the one described. Why: sworn ages are often approximate.
- [metric] Time of death from body signs is a range rarely fixed within an hour or two, and widens when body signs are the only clock. When: when body-based evidence is the only clock available.
- [metric] Muscle stiffness can estimate time of death; a body found stiff about three hours after death suggests a window of that length. When: Estimating time of death from body signs. Why: Rigor mortis progresses in a predictable sequence after death.
- [metric] Stiffening typically begins five to six hours after death and passes by about thirty-six hours, but may start early or late and rarely lasts twenty-one days.
- [tradeoff] Biological clocks are less reliable where water conditions are unknown, since local staining and growth rates vary by site. When: Interpreting traces from an unfamiliar or unrecorded site. Why: Environmental differences change the rate at which traces form.
- [pitfall] Treating the moment an alarm is raised as the moment of the act lets a staged timeline pass unchallenged.
- [pitfall] Age judged from gait or voice can be wrong, and a wig or disguise can make apparent age misleading. When: A witness estimates the age of a disguised person. Why: Disguise and assumption distort apparent age, so estimates should be treated with caution.
- [pitfall] Fixing the time of death from the time of the wound alone ignores that the victim may have survived for a while.
- [pitfall] Time-of-death estimates are approximate, and an error of a few days can change which timeline is plausible. When: using an estimate to fix when an event occurred. Why: estimates carry error ranges.
- [pitfall] A wide time-of-death bracket cannot by itself place a suspect at the scene; the estimate must be tied to the timeline of events. When: When a time estimate is used to implicate someone. Why: A broad range fits many people's movements.
- [fact] Stiffening after death can be almost immediate after violence or strong emotion, particularly after skull injuries, or can be delayed by eight to ten hours. Why: onset is not a fixed clock.
- [fact] A medical estimate of time of death may give only a minimum interval, leaving the death time open at the later end. When: when a doctor estimates time of death. Why: Such estimates often bound death from one side only.
- [fact] Medical examiners can agree on cause of death yet disagree on time of death, since time estimates are approximate and depend on each examiner's reasoning. When: When experts give differing timelines for the same death. Why: Time estimation from the body relies on interpretation rather than a fixed measurement.
- [fact] Time of death from body signs is usually an approximate range, and separating overlapping stiffening phenomena can be difficult. When: An expert is asked for a single exact time. Why: Body signs change at uneven rates, so exact times are rarely supported.
- [fact] A body remains warm for about ten minutes after death, and its vessels still bleed freely during that time. When: When judging whether a wound was inflicted before or after death. Why: Little blood flow suggests the wound was made before death or within minutes of it.

## witness bias
- [behavior] Loyal friends defend a suspect regardless of evidence, citing familiarity as character proof, reluctant to see them as killers; loyalty establishes no fact. When: a witness is attached to or backs the person being questioned. Why: attachment and loyalty outweigh logic and shape how the witness argues.
- [behavior] Personal liking or dislike selects what a witness reports, so favoured people look better and disliked worse, making guilty seem innocent or innocent guilty. When: the witness is partial toward or against someone. Why: Feeling selects which details get told.
- [behavior] A witness's admission that they hoped blame would fall on another person can shift suspicion toward someone new. When: a witness reveals their own motive. Why: Motive statements reframe who appears to benefit.
- [behavior] A witness's view of one person can swing from disparagement to praise to outright hatred within a few entries, shaped by mood and circumstance. When: first-person testimony from a teller close to events and emotionally invested in them. Why: Mood, outside pressure and prior feelings shape what the teller reports about a person.
- [behavior] A witness's stance toward an accused can flip after personal contact, such as a touch or a heartfelt conversation, turning earlier hostility into defense. When: a witness has direct social contact with the accused or a confrontation. Why: personal bonds and contact can outweigh earlier impressions.
- [behavior] Players and characters tend to read a distressed witness as mad, which can cause a true report to be dismissed. When: A character gives an agitated or unusual account of events. Why: Agitation signals unreliability, so accurate content is discounted with the delivery.
- [rule] Set a reviewer's personal assertions, such as claims about what someone saw or read, apart from documented fact when weighing an argument.
- [heuristic] Check each witness's motive, such as reward, loyalty, family tie or self-interest, before weighing their account, since it can bias what is reported in either direction. When: several witnesses have different relationships to the suspects. (x2)
- [heuristic] A grudge lowers trust in a witness's judgement and conclusions but does not prove falsehood; test the account and separate accurate observations from biased interpretation. When: testimony comes from someone with a stake in the outcome; a single informant is the main source. Why: grievance shapes interpretation, so a true observation can come with a biased conclusion. (x2)
- [heuristic] When designing NPC witnesses, give them a reason to lie (self-protection, status, fear), tag motives and biased statements, and show bias in dialogue or reactions so players can judge reliability. When: Designing NPC witnesses for a mystery, or witnesses give conflicting accounts of an event. Why: Reactions expose the witness's stake and perspective. (x2)
- [heuristic] A witness's prior belief about a suspect or household can skew observation, recall and identification, so record their stated opinion alongside testimony. When: witnesses share a household with the suspect or hold prior opinions about them. Why: prior belief can bias observation and reporting. (x2)
- [heuristic] Judge a partisan source's claims on factual merit against the record, not by its aim; a partisan's repetition adds tone but no proof. When: a character defends a claim through a biased or interested source. Why: Conviction and self-interest colour how a chain of testimony is presented. (x2)
- [heuristic] Check a witness's motives and prior stance before weighing their objections; a grudge or prior conflict can let accurate evidence be dismissed as invented. When: a witness has a grudge or prior conflict with the authorities. Why: Objections to a source can reflect the objector's convictions, and bias can discredit accurate observations. (x2)
- [heuristic] Even brief, unreliable or weak-theory accounts usually hold some correct facts; separate reliable details from vague ones rather than dismissing the whole account. Why: partial views usually contain some accurate material.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's dislike, hostility or grief before trusting their praise, blame or description of a person; weigh their opinion apart from facts and check with neutral sources. Why: bias shapes what is noticed and reported.
- [heuristic] A record written by one party, like a losing candidate's diary, is framed: it chose what to include and how to describe opponents, so verify its claims independently. When: relying on a record written by a party to a dispute, especially near a conflict's end. Why: A party controls what it records.
- [heuristic] A person with a stake in a document may be ineligible as a witness. The choice of witnesses can therefore reveal who benefited from the signing. When: judging a disputed document. Why: Eligibility rules exclude interested parties.
- [heuristic] Tag witnesses with motives and prior disclosures so players can judge reliability, and spot a rehearsed story through its inconsistencies.
- [heuristic] Doubt a witness's testimony when the witness has a clear reason to lie, rather than treating the testimony as reliable. When: the witness has a motive to deceive.
- [heuristic] An informant NPC who lied once can still give a true tip, so track trust per claim rather than per character. When: Designing NPCs who have been caught lying. Why: Trust tracked per claim lets a liar remain useful.
- [heuristic] A partisan narrator can leak the truth he meant to hide, because his frankness and blindness to how his words will be read reveal facts against his own side.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's grudge against a party as a source of bias, since resentment can color what they choose to say. When: when a witness has a personal grievance against someone involved. Why: Grievances shape memory and emphasis even when the witness is sincere.
- [pitfall] Witnesses with financial, reputational, family, inheritance or neighbourly/workplace ties can carry a party's interests into their account. When: when witnesses share ties with the parties. Why: stakes and close ties create partisan interests. (x2)
- [pitfall] Witnesses with personal ties, group membership or their own alibi can bend timing claims, since a suspect witness may set discovery time to fit their alibi. When: witness testimony is used to fix a time. Why: The witness controls the discovery and has a stake in the result. (x2)
- [pitfall] Witnesses or rebuttals produced by the accused's allies are partisan, not neutral checks, so the defense must show their knowledge is firsthand. When: when witnesses or rebuttals are chosen or produced by one side's supporters. Why: Allies share the same interest in the outcome.
- [pitfall] Eagerness, tangential motive or agitation can make an honest witness seem unreliable, while dramatic delivery can make a weak or unreliable account sound convincing; judge content, not performance. Why: tone, motive and performance distort how testimony is judged.
- [pitfall] A persuaded witness can appear reliable while only repeating what was suggested to them. When: when a witness repeats a story after being told what to say. Why: consistency can reflect suggestion rather than observation.
- [pitfall] Do not treat a neutral-seeming witness as impartial. Check his links to other parties, such as shared arrival times or initials. Why: Hidden connections can turn an apparently disinterested witness into an accomplice.
- [pitfall] Personal interest, such as attraction to the victim, can colour testimony and should be asked about directly. When: a witness has a personal link to the people involved. Why: undisclosed feelings can shape what a witness reports.
- [pitfall] Reading a source only up to the matching line can hide the context that shows whether the link matters.
- [pitfall] A witness's opinion of others' competence, such as police seeming sleepy, may reflect the witness's own bias rather than real performance.
- [pitfall] Letting a witness's contempt for a rival shape the whole picture of that rival produces a distorted understanding of the case. When: When a single hostile witness is the main source about a person. Why: Hostility biases description and selection of facts.
- [pitfall] A witness close to the suspect may soften the account unconsciously, so test the facts rather than the witness's character.
- [pitfall] A witness who wants to please an authority may name the person they think the questioner expects. When: A witness is questioned by someone whose approval they want. Why: The desire for approval can override accurate observation.
- [pitfall] Trusting a frightened witness's own story can produce a false account, and a confident denial can still be wrong. When: Reconstructing an event from one emotional witness. Why: Strong conviction does not guarantee accuracy.

## family and witness ties
- [mechanism] A shared past with a known person serves as a credential, and the listener tests it against what they remember of that person. When: Characters must recognise each other through history rather than documents. Why: Memory of a mutual acquaintance provides a check the claimant cannot control.
- [mechanism] Relatives who believe the charges may plead with the accused to confess, and turn hostile when refusal continues, which adds social pressure toward a false confession. When: Family members believe the accusation and the accused refuses to confess. Why: Affection turns to anger when the accused refuses, and the family's pleading becomes another source of pressure.
- [mechanism] A punishment directed at one family is felt across its connections, so a warning reaches many people at once. When: A community disciplines a member whose relatives are linked to others. Why: Kinship networks spread the consequences of a single sanction.
- [mechanism] Marriage and family ties link one quarrel to a wide network of allies, so one side's grievance can draw in many households.
- [mechanism] Family or marriage ties among decision-makers can carry advice between them, so a small group's verdicts may reflect a shared network. When: a small group of judges shares social ties.
- [mechanism] Family ties decide who is protected: property passed to relatives can go to those who turned against the accused's household. When: property is transferred during a dispute.
- [mechanism] Neighbors whose homesteads are grouped on shared land develop common interests that bind them into a group.
- [behavior] One relative's prejudice, formed over a family disagreement, can pull the wider family's opinion along with it. When: when a family dispute involves religious or moral practice. Why: family members tend to adopt the views of those close to them.
- [behavior] Under pressure, people may name relatives, implicating family members who had no part in the matter.
- [behavior] Rival leaders often keep personal ties such as family bonds, and factional opposition does not necessarily end those ties.
- [behavior] Suspicion tends to move along household and kinship lines, so related people are accused together. When: Suspicion spreads within a community after a first accusation.
- [rule] Treat a family's account of a past event as untested surmise; compare it with physical evidence first, since consistency with remains does not prove it. When: Reconstructing history from a relative's or household's story or an event surviving in family memory. Why: Details of journeys and arrivals were inferred rather than witnessed or proven. (x2)
- [rule] Treat a shared name as a lead needing a second confirming source, since common names recur across many people and name-only matches are often false. When: When searching records by a common name or matching a name across unrelated sources. Why: Common names recur across many people; coincidences of names are common.
- [rule] Establish the witness's relationship to the victim before the event itself, since it gives the account context and a possible motive.
- [rule] Let family connections decide which NPCs testify and which are spared.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness by how long and how closely they knew the subject; brief or distant contact makes identification weak, while years of shared housing count as direct observation. When: When a witness's identification is central to a timeline. (x2)
- [heuristic] Questioning a witness about family and address history can explain how a misdirected item reached the wrong destination.
- [heuristic] Clusters of related people across roles suggest natural factions or alliances among suspects.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness by how long, where and how closely they observed the subject; a short stay can yield a confident denial that longer observation overturns. When: Witnesses have unequal access to the facts.
- [heuristic] Do not assume every member of an opposing family shares a grudge; separate the parties from the wider community.
- [heuristic] A relative's letter about a person's losses can supply both a motive for an action and the family pressure behind the person's state.
- [heuristic] Tie the true thief to the suspect's family, raising the stakes of a false accusation. When: writing a mystery where an innocent party is wrongly accused. Why: A personal connection makes the wrongful suspicion more costly and the reveal more emotionally charged.
- [procedure] 1) Map who is bound to whom through friendship, shared congregation, family tradition or shared office. 2) Only then weigh each witness's account. When: A witness's account conflicts with others and the witness has a stake. Why: Personal bonds shape how and whether accounts are given.
- [tradeoff] Kinship by blood, marriage and land can form blocs that explain alignment, yet relatives may publicly oppose their group, so family membership alone may not predict alignment. When: Predicting which relatives side with whom in large interrelated families. Why: Such dissent can be dangerous.
- [pitfall] Kinship inferred from a shared surname, a single remark, a marriage or a feature match is weak; present it as belief, and infer close relation only from a strong match. When: When a character's relationship is used to build a motive or a kinship is inferred. Why: One remark or marriage does not confirm the relation; people with the same name may be unrelated. (x3)
- [pitfall] Kinship shows who could mobilize whom, not who is guilty of a given act.
- [pitfall] Treating kinship or character as evidence, such as assuming a relative would take someone in, substitutes assumption for proof.
- [pitfall] A witness who clings to an investigator may later be unable to separate the investigator's word from her own memory.
- [pitfall] A chain of intermediaries can lead to the wrong person if the detail used to identify him is shared by others. Why: a non-unique detail matches several people along the chain.
- [pitfall] Recasting a disagreement between household members as proof of long-running conflict misuses a family quarrel as evidence.
- [pitfall] Family members may conceal or minimize concerns about a relative, which distorts the testimony they give. When: When relying on testimony from a suspect's family. Why: Loyalty biases what witnesses report.
- [fact] Men from one village serving under shared captains are grouped into units, binding neighbors through common military service.
- [fact] Heads of households were addressed as Goodman and Goodwife, and the term Goody was a mark of respect, not a slight.
- [fact] A central role in events does not guarantee trust; the reputation of a witness among people who knew them can overturn it. When: when a key witness's standing is disputed. Why: acquaintances may know prior conduct that the proceedings ignored.

## plant and payoff
- [mechanism] A prediction stated early and specifically, then confirmed later, turns the later event into evidence for the earlier clue, so the audience sees the payoff as earned. When: A lead names a checkable person, place or event that a later event can confirm. Why: Confirmed predictions make the audience trust the storyteller and reread earlier clues.
- [mechanism] A missing non-player character can be explained by a private secret that resolves the quest hook, while a separate hidden event is the real threat. When: Designing a missing-NPC quest with a second, concealed danger. Why: The secret answers the disappearance and diverts attention from the true threat.
- [mechanism] A planted item can be neutralised by the suspect's plausible account of how they found it, so a plant is only as strong as the lack of an alternative explanation. When: A suspect is confronted with a planted item. Why: A believable account offers an innocent route to possession.
- [mechanism] A short hint with a few names, places and circumstances, supplied by someone holding resentment, is enough to steer a whole round of accusations.
- [behavior] A remark that means nothing to listeners can produce a visible reaction, such as a colour change, stare or abrupt departure, that reveals a hidden connection. When: the target knows the reference but the listeners do not. Why: the private meaning shows through the target's body language.
- [rule] Plant a visible emblem or mark, such as a scar, costume detail or symbol, early and let it return at the reveal, rewarding attentive players as proof. (x2)
- [rule] Place clues early while they look trivial, optionally letting a character dismiss them, so a late proof recontextualises clues the audience already saw. When: a late-stage test will explain earlier details. Why: Clues that seem minor are retained, and late reveals feel fair when the audience has already encountered the evidence.
- [rule] Offer dialogue options that hint at a hidden motive and unlock new information when the player returns with evidence. When: designing conversation systems. Why: Evidence-gated hints reward investigation.
- [rule] Plant a false lead, such as a tempting key or suspicious NPC, that players can disprove with a fact found later.
- [rule] Recover a failed plan through a cause planted earlier in the story, not through chance, or the solution feels arbitrary.
- [rule] Give an NPC a vague reason for a hostile act, and reveal the small hidden trigger later through an overheard line or diary entry.
- [rule] Seed the identity clue early, when it looks unimportant, so that it pays off when the pieces are assembled later.
- [rule] Front-load the damning but unexplained objects, such as a key, a will or a payment, in the first scene, so a later explanation recontextualises them. When: Opening a mystery that will reveal a hidden relationship later. Why: Early objects that are later explained feel fair and tie the opening to the resolution.
- [rule] Make planted items visible and specific from the start, so a late payoff feels like deduction rather than a trick. When: Setting up a reveal that depends on earlier objects or details. Why: Arbitrary-seeming items with no clear role make the reveal feel unfair.
- [rule] Make a harmless-seeming request, such as signing a document, the hidden first step toward a later forgery or impersonation. Why: The request supplies the culprit with material such as a sample of handwriting.
- [rule] Plant the decisive word early and leave it unexplained until a late cluster of clues gives it meaning. When: Setting up a late reveal around a single term. Why: A word met early and understood late connects the early and late parts of the story.
- [heuristic] Flag an early hint as important and promise its full answer later, priming the audience to notice it while anticipation builds and the payoff is held back. (x2)
- [heuristic] Plant key clues early as innocent-looking habits or inside ordinary talk, so readers file them as background and accept them at face value, making later significance a surprise. When: A mystery's late proof or harmful hazard must matter later yet stay fair. Why: Mundane framing keeps the detail from drawing early suspicion; quirks accepted at face value make the later significance a surprise, not a cheat.
- [heuristic] Plant a glimpsed clue early, such as an emblem seen in poor light, and pay it off when the player is ready to learn the name.
- [heuristic] Plant an early warning about a danger, such as a health risk, and echo it later so the dramatic event feels both fair and dangerous. Why: A foreshadowed danger gives the later event a cause the audience already knows.
- [heuristic] A hint given before the full explanation must be specific enough to be recognised, or the delay reads as evasion.
- [heuristic] A secret can be conveyed through a glance or line that only one companion understands, and the player then acts on it. When: A hint must pass between characters without being stated to the audience.
- [heuristic] Record a clue while it seems trivial, then leave it untouched for a long stretch, so it pays off late without seeming planned. When: a mystery's proof must be set up well before it is needed. Why: A clue that was ignored for most of the story is remembered as fair when it returns.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC's earlier statement gain meaning once the player finds new evidence, so earlier dialogue can pay off later.
- [heuristic] An unrecognized disguised figure met early can be revealed later as an ally or the investigator, creating an emotional or intellectual payoff. When: Planning a mystery with a disguised investigator. Why: A figure seen but not identified early becomes a satisfying reveal when its identity is finally shown.
- [heuristic] Repeat a distinctive symbol across the early scenes so that it later pays off as a physical key or plate in the climax. When: structuring clues for a late solution. Why: Repetition builds recognition, so the final use feels like a payoff.
- [heuristic] Plant small oddities early, such as contradictions in grooming or minor timing details, and pay them off at the breakthrough. When: setting up clues for a late reveal. Why: Early small anomalies look like noise, but they become decisive evidence when the answer is revealed.
- [heuristic] Hold back the meaning of early foreshadowing until after the crisis breaks, so each hint pays off once the player has the context to read it. Why: Premature meaning removes the surprise, while delayed meaning rewards recall.
- [procedure] 1) Plant an anomaly, such as a warning, unexplained sound or deflected question. 2) Withhold its explanation for now. 3) Answer every planted anomaly later, since an unexplained early remark about the past makes the audience feel misled. When: Building suspense through unexplained details. Why: Unanswered hooks read as broken promises and erode trust; unpaid hints read as cheating. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Plant an unfinished statement early. 2) Keep the hidden fact out of view. 3) Reveal it later through the character's thoughts or an outside observer. 4) Add hints in between so the reticence does not read as a dropped thread. When: Planting a fact for later reveal. Why: Reticence pays off only when the reader can connect the clue to the reveal.
- [procedure] 1) Plant the setting, the attached presence, and the stated immunity early. 2) Keep the final reveal consistent with them. 3) Let the reversal of expectation land last. When: Designing a twist that should feel surprising but fair. Why: Groundwork lets the audience reinterpret the reveal as foreshadowed.
- [tradeoff] A planted instruction builds setup and payoff, but it announces itself to attentive players, so it cannot serve as a surprise hook. When: choosing between a planted setup and a surprise. Why: attentive players recognise planted rules.
- [pitfall] Showing a method only after the fact, with its links hidden, can make the observer look as if they simply knew the answer.
- [pitfall] Hinting at an object's significance can put a subject on guard or plant ideas, so reactions may reflect suggestion rather than knowledge. When: observers want to provoke a reaction. Why: people adopt ideas they are offered.

## unresolved outcomes and verdicts
- [definition] A third verdict, such as Scotland's Not Proven, finds neither enough evidence to convict nor enough to clear, leaving doubt on public record. When: A judgment system allows an inconclusive outcome. Why: The verdict keeps the question open rather than settling guilt.
- [mechanism] A verdict becomes precedent through its printed record, so later cases follow it regardless of whether its reasoning was sound. When: when a past trial is cited in a new case. Why: the written record outlives the evidence and is reused.
- [mechanism] An inconclusive verdict recorded publicly keeps doubt alive for years and can be used by the accused to claim they cannot be cleared. When: A third outcome is recorded in the world state. Why: Public record preserves uncertainty and gives characters a reason to react to it.
- [rule] Mark unexplained anomalies, unsupported doubts and unknown outcomes as unresolved, stating them rather than forcing a verdict or a guess presented as a finding. When: An anomaly goes unexplained, a doubt stays unsupported, or a trail of a person or event goes cold. Why: A guess presented as a finding misleads readers; an open question stays honest until evidence settles it. (x2)
- [rule] Mark unknown outcomes, such as an NPC who vanished without record, as unknown in a case file rather than awarding unsupported resolutions. When: When designing a case file where some records are silent or outcomes are never documented. Why: Invented outcomes make the investigation appear solved; leaving gaps shows the player it is incomplete.
- [rule] Do not accept a quick cause-of-death verdict without an autopsy or asking how it was reached, especially when no post-mortem was done.
- [rule] End a zone with an ambiguous diagnosis rather than a full banishment, leaving the threat intact and the story open. When: When a scenario should leave room for a later encounter. Why: An open ending makes the setting feel alive after the scene ends.
- [heuristic] End a scene on an unresolved cue, such as a discovery before its explanation or a sound beyond a door, to pull attention into the next area. When: When a scene should lead into the next. Why: An unanswered question holds attention and creates pull toward what comes next.
- [heuristic] Ask whether a verdict would survive if its unverifiable evidence were set aside.
- [heuristic] Reasoning that only confirms known facts can miss an unknown factor that changes the conclusion, so look for that factor deliberately.
- [heuristic] Ask who gains from each possible official verdict, since a financial stake in the finding gives someone reason to want a quick answer. When: a party profits from the official finding. Why: Motive shifts the question from how the death happened to who benefits.
- [heuristic] Question an official finding whose timing or convenience is suspicious, even if its explanation sounds sensible in isolation. When: An official finding closes a question too neatly. Why: A planted explanation can look plausible while its timing exposes it.
- [heuristic] Unfinished tidying, such as cigarette ends in a grate, a newspaper across a chair, or a letter left waiting in the hall, suggests a departure on a single day. Why: a sudden departure interrupts ordinary household routines.
- [heuristic] Offer a closing label that is plausible but incomplete, so the audience decides what really happened.
- [heuristic] Leave one charge unprovable so the final verdict does not cover every crime the player uncovered.
- [procedure] 1) Search known reference material for an account matching the observed effect. 2) Compare appearance, mechanism and symptoms. 3) Confirm only if several independent details match. When: A described effect matches no familiar cause and no suspect has an obvious instrument. Why: Multiple independent matches are far stronger than one resemblance.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm the original panel heard the whole case. 2) Confirm any substitution was authorized. 3) Check whether the verdict rests on accepted proof. 4) Reject it if any step fails. When: when reviewing whether a verdict followed proper process. Why: a verdict is valid only if process and proof both hold.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether identity and cause can each be answered from current evidence. 2) If neither can, adjourn the inquiry instead of issuing a verdict. 3) Defer accusation until new evidence arrives. When: When evidence is insufficient to support any conclusion. Why: A verdict the evidence cannot support is an unjustified claim.
- [tradeoff] Letting a culprit escape keeps the question open and unease lingering, moving judgement to the player's sense of justice at the cost of less complete resolution. When: Choosing how a mystery ends, especially when the crime cannot be proven in law.
- [tradeoff] Ending without a confession, or with the investigator stopping reasoning, leaves the criminal question open so the player weighs evidence, but may frustrate players seeking certainty. When: When choosing how a mystery resolves or should end on an open question. Why: An unfinished inference invites the player to reach their own conclusion.
- [tradeoff] Giving an unproven culprit a full ending gives closure but asserts unproven guilt; a case-file note keeps ambiguity but leaves players without closure.
- [tradeoff] Unresolved details build atmosphere, but too many frustrate; not every planted detail needs a payoff.
- [tradeoff] An unresolved ending suits stories where the cause matters less than the mood, but it leaves players without a closing answer. When: when deciding how a mystery concludes. Why: Withholding the answer keeps focus on atmosphere, but risks frustrating players who want resolution.
- [tradeoff] Leaving the official outcome unresolved creates ambiguity, but the player's version must then be marked as an inference, not as established fact. When: the scenario needs ambiguity about who is guilty. Why: Without marking, an unresolved official ending reads as the player's solution being ignored or wrong.
- [pitfall] A verdict does not prove strong evidence; it can rest on mood and health observations rather than proof of how death occurred, so check what corroboration established. Why: Outcomes can hide a weak evidentiary basis. (x2)
- [pitfall] Ending on a verdict or loose end that resolves nothing weakens the payoff and frustrates the audience, unless the open question is a deliberate choice or explicitly labelled uncertain. When: Closing a mystery with a loose end or unresolved verdict. (x2)
- [pitfall] An official verdict can close an inquiry while key questions stay unexplained, so the investigator loses the chance to test a theory later.
- [pitfall] If every clue is ambiguous, readers stop caring, so keep at least one firm anchor clue elsewhere. When: Writing a mystery where many clues admit several readings. Why: Without a fixed point, the reader has nothing to resolve the uncertainty against.
- [pitfall] Judging a person's whole character or guilt from a single emotional episode risks an unfair verdict. Why: One outburst may reflect a passing feeling rather than a settled nature.
- [pitfall] Treating a verdict as final is an error, since a later court or legislature can reopen or overturn it.
- [pitfall] Accepting a supernatural explanation as the answer when it identifies neither motive nor opportunity leaves the mystery unsolved. When: A mystery reaches a supernatural explanation without a culprit. Why: A mechanism without a motive does not answer who committed the act.
- [fact] A verdict does not settle what happened: the guilty can be acquitted, and circumstantial evidence or family connections can reduce a sentence, so a convicted person is not automatically guilty. (x2)
- [fact] The same evidence can yield different verdicts depending on which body hears it, such as a local jury or an appointed committee. When: when a case moves between courts or panels. Why: each body has its own composition and authority.
- [fact] When the criminal escapes or dies abroad, a mystery can close with its uncertainty acknowledged rather than fully resolved. When: Ending a case where the culprit cannot be captured. Why: Acknowledged uncertainty can feel more honest than a forced resolution.

## evidence presentation
- [mechanism] A recorded or timed playback can make a victim seem alive at a later time than the real moment of death, shifting the apparent timeline. When: a voice or sound at a given time appears in an alibi. Why: playback reproduces a voice without the speaker being present.
- [behavior] When damning evidence is presented in full before the standard that invalidates it is named, the audience accepts the apparent guilt until the flaw is revealed. When: a reveal built on a standard of proof that is stated late. Why: the audience can see the flaw without being told what to look for.
- [rule] Record a suspect's statements and the questions asked word for word, since meaning depends on the question and wording can carry unintended meaning. When: A suspect's words are recorded and the question can be reconstructed. Why: So the questioning itself can be checked later.
- [rule] Record off-topic answers and unguarded slips immediately, since they may later connect to alibis, access or other facts. When: A witness gives an answer or remark that seems minor or off-topic. Why: Their meaning often emerges later, so noting them at once preserves evidence.
- [rule] Record what a witness was offered, what they refused and their stated reason, since refusals can reveal the other party's preparation and be tested. When: a refusal is used as evidence. Why: Unrecorded reasons leave the inference untestable; these events can reveal the other party's preparation.
- [rule] Record a suspect's statements as claims and a witness's impressions of appearance or mood as impressions, never as established observations or facts. When: a suspect's account is evidence or a witness gives impressions. Why: A claim is not an observation and should not be treated as one.
- [rule] Make each reveal rest on one physical exhibit the player can reach and inspect, rather than an unexplained expert claim or only deducible evidence. When: Designing the proof of a staged scene or a reveal. Why: A single inspectable proof is more convincing than an unexplained expert claim, and players trust what they can verify by hand.
- [rule] Record every response to a test, including a later loss of response, because the subject's condition can change during observation.
- [rule] Record a witness's earlier admissions word for word, so later denials can be checked against them.
- [rule] Record which witnesses each expert interviewed, so players can see who was overlooked. When: Designing investigation records. Why: Overlooked witnesses expose gaps in an expert's inquiry.
- [rule] Record each agreement made between factions, so a later betrayal can be traced by checking the records. When: when designing faction agreements in a game.
- [rule] Present trivial objects in an opening scene as ordinary, so their significance is recognised only in hindsight and rewards a player who noticed them. When: Designing an opening scene that contains later clues. Why: Ordinary presentation avoids signalling importance, yet preserves the clue for later recognition.
- [rule] End a puzzle chain with a diegetic recap that links each strange event to the object or mechanic that caused it. When: closing a puzzle sequence in-game. Why: the player sees how the clues combine into the answer.
- [rule] Record an expert's unease about a surprising analysis made at a bad moment as a fact in its own right. When: An expert hesitates over a result. Why: Hesitation may reveal a concern not yet stated.
- [rule] Record even a false statement and compare it with other accounts, since a lie can itself be significant.
- [rule] Record each stated duration, source and timeline, because an unchecked claim can later prove false and expose a contradiction. When: when interviewing a witness or suspect. Why: contradictions surface only when claims are kept.
- [rule] Let the player check a claimed injury or substance by touch or with an in-world tool, so the check itself confirms what the thing is.
- [rule] Record ambiguous statements in full, noting every plausible reading, and do not settle on one reading after the fact. When: A suspect's statement could be read as either a confession or a denial. Why: Choosing the reading afterwards lets the interrogator decide the outcome.
- [rule] Present depositions and records without a comparison table, leaving the reader to compare them, so the presentation does not push a view. When: Presenting conflicting testimony or documents to the player. Why: Unguided comparison lets the player form their own conclusion from the evidence.
- [rule] Do not present an ambiguous clue as decisive; show the alternative reading alongside it. When: A clue points to a suspect but also to other explanations. Why: Showing both readings lets the player test the inference.
- [rule] End a mystery by explaining the solution in front of the suspects or authorities, using physical proof rather than confession. When: Staging the resolution of a mystery. Why: Public physical proof makes the answer convincing and leaves the guilty party exposed.
- [heuristic] Build the solution from several kinds of evidence, such as confrontation, documents, testimony and physical proof, rather than one decisive trap. When: presenting a late-stage solution. (x2)
- [heuristic] Open a mystery on a striking image whose cause is withheld, so the audience holds a question while the explanation is delayed. When: Starting a mystery or investigation. Why: A held question pulls attention forward.
- [heuristic] Open an interrogation with a confident claim the suspect cannot easily disprove, and offer a clear reason to be candid.
- [heuristic] A container opened with a key rather than forced suggests the opener had access, and a thief with a professional aim would not usually take papers. When: Judging who opened a container and why. Why: Method of entry reveals access, and professional thieves target valuables rather than documents.
- [heuristic] Displays that recur at moments useful to the accusers, such as new arrests, suggest the display is directed rather than spontaneous.
- [heuristic] Early inquest-style evidence such as a weapon by the body, a quarrel and doubtful timings can make the audience believe the accused is guilty. When: opening a mystery with circumstantial evidence against a suspect. Why: Strong-looking circumstantial evidence sets a convincing false conclusion early.
- [procedure] 1) Give a formal warning that the words will be recorded and may be used. 2) Confirm the medical urgency. 3) Record the words exactly. 4) Question briefly after the continuous account. When: A suspect may die or be unable to speak later. Why: Without urgency, a formal statement would normally wait for a later hearing.
- [procedure] 1) Record every exchange with a hidden stenographer. 2) Establish who was present and their roles. 3) Take the account in sequence, from the start to the final hour. 4) Restate key times and names as questions. 5) Repeat names and hours at the end. 6) Type and copy the record at once.
- [procedure] 1) State the full theory to witnesses in order: method, physical proof, source of the document, access. 2) Hold back one link until the suspect's position weakens. 3) Recite each linked fact when the suspect denies. 4) Make the arrest rest on physical proof. When: The accusation must be made before witnesses. Why: Each link supports the next, and physical proof resists argument.
- [procedure] 1) Show a physical discovery. 2) Add a checkable fact that contradicts the official story. 3) Add a late confession. 4) Add witness accounts. 5) Explain the full mechanism last. When: When a hidden truth must be proven to the reader before the final explanation. Why: Independent layers make the explanation credible and let it arrive after the danger has passed.
- [tradeoff] Showing the full evidence chain lets the reader test the conclusion, but too much detail makes the chain hard to follow. When: designing a mystery that the player must solve from clues. Why: fairness requires visible reasoning, while clarity requires selection.
- [pitfall] A confession that merely restates what the investigator already proved feels like a shortcut and weakens the payoff of the reveal.

## evidence weighting
- [mechanism] Authored NPCs can hold back facts until the player finds corroborating evidence, rewarding investigation over guessing.
- [mechanism] Physical findings such as wounds, bruises and clotting, recorded and examined by a qualified examiner, can contradict rumor or spectral accusation and establish how a death occurred. When: A death must be classified as natural, accidental or murder and a body or wound survives. Why: Concrete bodily traces are checkable facts that outweigh unverified claims.
- [rule] Block a formal accusation based only on witness-only clues until a physical trace or a second independent source confirms them. When: when designing an investigation system with perception-only evidence.
- [rule] Require independent corroboration from a second source before recording a witness claim as a confirmed fact. Why: A single claim should not settle a case.
- [rule] Require physical corroboration before a verdict counts a claim, and track how many accusations rest on a single source.
- [rule] Require independent corroboration before testimony the accused cannot rebut carries weight in a verdict. When: Accusers' testimony is the main evidence. Why: Unrebuttable testimony can decide a case without any outside check.
- [rule] Weigh each account by how closely its source saw the matter, and do not treat gossip as established fact. When: several people describe the same event. Why: distance from events reduces the reliability of testimony.
- [rule] Seek other corroboration for a key fact rather than letting the case stall on one unreachable source. When: When a single source holds a critical fact. Why: Backup sources prevent a blocked investigation.
- [rule] Build a reconstruction on physical traces such as recovered ammunition; treat testimony about a missing weapon as weaker. When: A weapon is missing but its ammunition or mechanism remains. Why: Physical traces are harder to misreport than recollection.
- [rule] Mark which statements need independent corroboration before they are relied on, and do not treat hesitation, evasion or grief as proof of guilt. When: When sorting testimony in a case. Why: Emotional or evasive answers have many causes.
- [rule] Weigh official accounts such as sermons, epitaphs and histories against private talk and domestic testimony, since formal sources often conceal truth that private witnesses reveal. When: Building a character's reputation from multiple in-world sources. Why: Authors of public records know they are on record and tend to flatter.
- [rule] Weigh each claim by its source and checkability, since the fullest account is not necessarily the most reliable. When: When comparing several accounts of one event. Why: Length and detail do not establish accuracy.
- [heuristic] Count matching reports as corroboration only from independent sources; one shared cause, such as one disturbance heard by two people, yields matching reports. When: When checking a witness account against another person's memory. Why: Separate memories reduce the chance of a shared error. (x2)
- [heuristic] Weigh testimony by independent corroboration, not by how vivid, confident or socially respected the witness is; independent confirmation adds weight. When: Evaluating a report, a named suspect or a claim resting on a witness. Why: Vividness, confidence and status do not establish truth.
- [heuristic] When testimony conflicts with physical facts, give physical facts extra weight; facts witnesses cannot explain away should anchor the case. When: When a witness's account contradicts the scene. Why: Physical traces are harder to shape than spoken accounts.
- [heuristic] Require corroboration before naming a suspect when a witness's account is incomplete.
- [heuristic] Ask a suspect for corroboration such as a named person, receipt or document; when none is offered, the account rests on the suspect's word alone. When: Assessing the strength of a suspect's account. Why: Uncorroborated claims cannot be independently confirmed.
- [heuristic] Corroboration through outside accounts matters less when the evidence can be physically examined or independently observed.
- [heuristic] Independent corroboration strengthens a witness account but does not prove it completely; the claim remains partly open.
- [heuristic] Weigh an alternative explanation by its source: an expert offering an implausible theory deserves closer scrutiny than a layman's guess. When: Evaluating a theory offered by a witness or suspect. Why: An expert should know better, so the choice is telling.
- [heuristic] Where no independent check exists, weigh an account for plausibility rather than treat it as proved. When: When no witness or record can confirm a timeline. Why: Unverified accounts support only tentative conclusions.
- [heuristic] A container much heavier than its size suggests may hide contents, a trace that can be noticed before anyone opens it.
- [heuristic] Discount single facts that connect to nothing else, and weigh patterns that recur across many observations. When: when evaluating scattered observations. Why: isolated facts are easily coincidental, while patterns are more reliable.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's own certainty lightly when observation conditions were poor.
- [heuristic] Ask who gains from each version of a secondhand account, and treat the most direct witness as more reliable than retellings. When: several characters report the same hidden event. Why: reporters may have reasons to shade what they say.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the source's vantage point, timing and purpose. 2) Check which quoted figures it could actually have measured. 3) Test its claims against direct observation. When: A mystery presents conflicting reference works, maps or witness statements.
- [pitfall] Confirming a witness was present does not confirm the rest of their account; corroborating one detail is not proof of all of it. When: a witness's location is verified. Why: presence and identity are separate claims.
- [pitfall] Physical evidence has also condemned innocent people, so it must be checked against motive before it is trusted. Why: traces alone do not establish intent.
- [pitfall] Rejecting a whole account over one doubtful detail, or accepting it because of one vivid detail, are both errors.
- [pitfall] A single financial gain does not prove guilt, since several motives can point at the same person.
- [fact] Objects, marks, hiding places and small scene changes reveal who was present, how they moved and what they intended, and can confirm or contradict testimony.
- [fact] Later evidence of the same pressure, such as a broken engagement over money, corroborates a confession's account of that pressure. When: a confession describes financial strain. Why: Independent events matching the motive support the claim.
- [fact] Passers-by can corroborate only what they directly saw, such as a figure in a window, not the identity behind it.

## residue and trace evidence
- [model] Small residues such as consumed fuel, soil, torn fabric and footprints can reconstruct an object's route and reveal who handled it.
- [mechanism] When a scene or object is cleaned or repaired, visible marks may vanish, but outlines, stains, sounds and faint residue survive as evidence of earlier handling. Why: Cleaning does not erase evidence of earlier handling.
- [mechanism] Disturbance by later arrivals overwrites tracks, and repeated trampling by searchers confuses later readings, so disturbed traces become unreliable evidence. When: designing evidence in a level; a scene is repeatedly searched. Why: Disturbance overwrites traces the player may need.
- [mechanism] A physical trace that survives cleaning shows recent use, not merely that the object exists; surfaces a culprit overlooks can reveal what was cleaned elsewhere. When: Reading an object's recent history from a surface that was not cleaned. Why: Cleaning usually targets the surface expected to be examined, leaving other surfaces as evidence.
- [mechanism] Physical residue distributed unevenly across containers can show that a stated number of uses did not happen as described. When: when a witness claims a set of objects was used in a particular way. Why: Each used container should carry a predictable share of residue, so an anomaly exposes an alteration.
- [mechanism] Residue in a pipe builds up with use and is cleared by drying, so a pipe fouled after a day's use was not used first thing in the morning. When: residue condition is used to time a trace. Why: residue accumulates over use and drying resets it.
- [mechanism] Impressions from typed characters can survive on the reverse of a sheet after the ink has been removed, so erased text may remain recoverable. When: A document has been erased or reused. Why: Pressure from typing leaves marks in the paper fibres that outlast the ink.
- [mechanism] A puzzle that asks players to identify a material from its residue rewards careful observation of physical detail over rote lookup. Why: Recognizing a substance by its burn or residue requires attention to visual evidence.
- [mechanism] A prepared surface that holds fingerprints leaves a trace on anyone who handles the object, so handling becomes checkable evidence.
- [behavior] Traces on a person, such as dust or colour transferred to clothing, reveal recent activity and habits.
- [rule] Make physical clues reproducible: a real mark should still be present on re-examination, and one that vanishes signals a flawed search or fabrication. When: designing evidence the player can revisit. Why: Persistent evidence can be verified, while vanishing evidence cannot.
- [rule] Keep uncontrolled visitors out of a scene, since entering with others disturbs fragile traces that evidence depends on. When: Examining a scene with fragile physical evidence. Why: Disturbance from visitors can erase or confuse the traces being examined.
- [rule] Record and photograph traces before any handling, since staff who touch exhibits can destroy evidence. Why: Handling can erase the trace being sought.
- [heuristic] A single remnant or mark may suggest accident or chance, while repeated identical or similar traces, especially along a route and well above chance, suggest systematic failure or a trustworthy pattern. When: several matching marks appear. Why: chance rarely produces many identical marks.
- [heuristic] Residue on a surface records a process; when a stated purpose conflicts with residue, the residue is often the more reliable evidence. When: A verbal account conflicts with the scene. Why: Residue is a physical record that a cover story cannot change.
- [heuristic] An evenly spread residue found inside an object suggests it was deposited from a liquid, which hints at how it was introduced.
- [heuristic] Let residue distinguish one character from others while accepting that common residue is shared by many, so it narrows suspects only partly. When: designing character-linked clues. Why: unique residue singles out a character, while common residue does not.
- [heuristic] Each shape or opening suggests a function. A loose part that moves along one axis shows how it is confined.
- [heuristic] A dust sample can reflect months of accumulation rather than one brief contact, so it reveals long-term habits. When: when a garment has hung or been worn for a long time.
- [heuristic] Mark objects as recently handled, so the game can decide which ones carry usable prints as evidence.
- [heuristic] Compare related objects' dust, cleanliness and finish; a disturbed or recently handled item stands out against its untouched neighbours. When: A suspect may have tidied a scene but missed differences in wear. Why: Handling changes surface condition in ways that differ from undisturbed objects.
- [heuristic] Blood or other stains found on a person's hands, clothing or belongings connect that person to the scene.
- [heuristic] End with a residue the mechanism does not explain, such as a lingering fear or an unexplained sighting, to keep a sequel hook open.
- [procedure] Keep a found trace rather than discarding it: scrape residue into a sealed envelope for later study and comparison once more facts are known. When: a surface holds traces that may matter later; a trace may later be matched to a suspect's possessions. Why: Sealed samples avoid contamination and preserve evidence for later comparison.
- [procedure] 1) Examine the mouth, teeth and clothing with a lens. 2) Remove any tiny object found and mount it on a slide in fluid. 3) Sort crumbs or residue and identify their kind. 4) Use the residue to infer the victim's last food or contacts. When: When a victim's last hours or contacts are unknown and small residues might reveal them. Why: Tiny residues can reveal activities and places without other evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Test each layer or compartment of a sealed object separately. 2) Compare each result with its label and with a clean control. 3) Note whether contaminated items share an identical quantity. 4) Look for a sealed hole that shows the entry point. When: an act happened inside a sealed container and the method is otherwise invisible. Why: comparing layers and controls isolates where and how the tampering occurred.
- [procedure] 1) List each residue and what it could indicate. 2) Form one hypothesis that explains all residues together. 3) Check it against a map and independent records.
