- [pitfall] Do not treat missing residue as conclusive; test innocent causes, such as a tidy or untidy caretaker, and do not assume an item was used up when related surfaces also lack the residue. Why: innocent causes can leave the same traces as the event under inquiry.
- [pitfall] Washing or disposal removes only part of the evidence: scent, handprints and dumped items remain, and searchers can recover them from ditches or vehicles. When: when a character tries to clear traces. Why: traces persist on surfaces and in places items were moved to.
- [fact] Small residues such as tobacco ash can be identified by comparing samples against known varieties, which requires specialist knowledge. When: A residue must be named. Why: Matching depends on reference material.
- [fact] A moist hand leaves residue on cold, smooth surfaces, so an object handled in a tense moment can carry usable latent prints.
- [fact] A weapon that has been cleaned can still carry traces of the act, such as residue in crevices, so physical examination can find what cleaning missed. When: when a weapon was wiped or scraped after use. Why: Cleaning rarely removes material from every surface and seam.
- [fact] Trace material can be recovered from collected dust by dissolving it, recrystallising it and extracting the resulting salts.

## timeline gaps
- [definition] A timeline records where each person was over time, and a brief window when no one can vouch for someone is an opportunity for an act. When: Analysing who could have committed a crime. Why: Gaps in witnessed movement show which suspects had access.
- [mechanism] Once a witness admits the timing was never recorded, a confident identification loses its support, even if the identity is never directly disputed.
- [mechanism] Witness sightings that cover only some time slots, with the uncovered slots shown as unknown, let the player see which intervals remain unresolved. When: When designing witness-based clues in a game. Why: Explicit unknown intervals direct the player's further investigation.
- [behavior] Routine absences, such as a scheduled staff break or a task that draws attention away, leave rooms unobserved, letting an actor move unseen. When: A scheduled break leaves an area without attendants. Why: Routine absences remove the people who would notice an intruder.
- [rule] Mark timeline gaps explicitly as unknown, not blank or guessed, so no one reads absence of record as absence of events. When: a timeline has a stretch with no reliable information, or witnesses cannot place events in time. Why: A blank can be read as nothing having happened.
- [rule] Record each unobserved interval, and any gap a suspect will not explain, as an open unresolved item rather than a settled fact, even if last seen entering a place. When: A witness's account stops at a doorway, staircase or room, or a suspect will not explain a gap. Why: Seeing someone enter does not show they left, so the exit remains unverified.
- [rule] Do not date an event using a process whose rate is unknown. Why: without a rate, the condition shows no elapsed time.
- [rule] For every unobserved interval, ask who can speak for the person during that time; an interval with no witness is a gap. When: Testing an alibi that has unobserved periods. Why: Gaps are where an alibi can hide an opportunity.
- [rule] Treat unexplained intervals in a timeline as the places where further questions belong. When: when no account covers a period between known events.
- [rule] Do not assume guilt from unaccounted time. A person need not account for every minute, though an unwitnessed gap leaves no alibi.
- [rule] Leave a timeline gap that the player can close by visiting a second location.
- [rule] Treat an account of hours you did not witness as testimony to be checked, not as established fact, even when it is told confidently. When: Reconstructing events from a later account. Why: Confident telling does not make unobserved events reliable.
- [heuristic] Unexplained gaps often hide the critical act and matter more than fixed anchors; investigate them first, as closely as anchors, since a gap may hide guilt or an innocent reason. When: a timeline has a period with no accounted events. Why: Investigators overlook missing time, and key actions are concealed where no one is watching. (x2)
- [heuristic] An unaccounted gap matters as much as recorded times but proves neither guilt nor innocence; keep it open and corroborate with a second source before treating it as wrongdoing. When: A person's time cannot be accounted for. Why: Gaps often have ordinary causes, and a gap shows where the investigation should look next. (x2)
- [heuristic] An unaccounted interval near the event carries the most weight in an alibi check: anyone unaccounted for within it stays a possible participant and cannot be cleared. When: when laying a witness timeline against an event. Why: Gaps near the event are where a story can hide an opportunity; an unheard return can keep suspects uncleared and outweigh other links. (x2)
- [heuristic] Note periods a person cannot be found or accounted for, such as alone in a room; they are an alibi's weakest point and must be flagged and accounted for. Why: Unwitnessed spans allow actions no witness can confirm; minutes nobody can confirm are where an act could occur. (x2)
- [heuristic] Store NPC whereabouts with timestamps and explicit gap markers, so the player must rebuild the timeline from partial recollections; a gap gives a concrete question to pursue. When: Designing quest logs, NPC memory, or investigation content with NPC alibis. Why: Overlapping absences that coincide with an event create gaps the player must reason about. (x2)
- [heuristic] An unexplained interval between known times marks a place to look for an encounter, such as a meeting or a stop along the way. When: a timeline has an unexplained interval.
- [heuristic] Treat a pause before access to a building as a lead to investigate, not a conclusion, since it may indicate time needed for someone else to act. When: An access delay or unavailability appears in a timeline. Why: Delays can conceal preparation by another party.
- [heuristic] Keep one timeline variable genuinely indeterminate, so an alibi-style timing argument fails without needing a new witness.
- [procedure] 1) List each unobserved interval the suspect cannot account for. 2) Mark corroborated parts. 3) For each uncorroborated gap, ask what could be done in it and whether the suspected act fits. 4) Treat uncorroborated gaps as the core of the case. When: When a suspect's movements are only partly observed. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Record each person's movements with times. 2) Compare the windows of absence. 3) Find gaps where the act could have happened. 4) Test each candidate gap against independent checks. When: When several people have short, overlapping absences. Why: Gaps not covered by any alibi identify the candidates who had the chance to act.
- [procedure] 1) Log each detail with its source and whether it is first-hand or relayed. 2) Record the witness's awareness window. 3) Flag unexplained details as unresolved, not explained. 4) Check flagged details against primary sources.
- [procedure] 1) Find the last confirmed sighting of the object in place. 2) Find when it was first noticed missing. 3) Treat the interval between them as the custody window. When: Establishing who could have handled an object.
- [pitfall] A complete-looking sequence or silent witness can hide unobserved action between events; silence is not evidence of inactivity, so check those intervals; a gap is itself information. When: Reconstructing a witness's timeline or reviewing a record. Why: Overlooked gaps let hidden action pass unexamined and can conceal movement or events. (x2)
- [pitfall] Recorded or stated times are only as reliable as their clock or memory; guesses, stopped clocks, missing stamps and estimated travel times mislead, so verify against an independent source. When: when building a timeline from recorded or witness-stated times. Why: Individual timekeeping and travel speeds vary, and unchecked times can silently fix the whole timeline on a wrong point.
- [pitfall] Without a recorded time for an event, later reconstructions of the sequence become unreliable, since exact times can only be recovered from readings taken at the moment.
- [pitfall] A gap that no witness or record can fill makes the sequence impossible to fix, and hidden parties can exploit that blur.
- [pitfall] A timetable cannot be fully trusted, since a delay such as fog can break a schedule-based conclusion, so plans built on schedules need margin. When: when a plan relies on published times. Why: real travel is disrupted by weather and other delays.
- [pitfall] An unobserved gap is not proof of tampering. The real question is whether the gap was long enough for the change to occur.
- [pitfall] An unknown anchor time breaks a backward-calculated timeline, because the chain of estimates has nothing fixed to start from.
- [pitfall] Vague timing leaves gaps that a suspect can exploit; the last confirmed sighting must be pinned down. Why: Unpinned timing lets an alibi hide inside an unmeasured span.
- [fact] Gap estimates such as about half an hour carry error, so a timeline should record its tolerance rather than treat them as exact. When: Filling intervals between anchored events. Why: Estimated durations are imprecise, and unrecorded tolerance can make a sequence appear more certain than it is.

## clue gating
- [model] A scene can stay locked to the player until a higher-ranked NPC signs off on the investigation or leaves the area.
- [mechanism] Paid NPC informants can answer with short lines that reveal more when probed, and their dialogue can change when the player shows knowledge.
- [mechanism] Harmful acts are often reached by first moving a target to the edge of what is permitted, then applying a small final push that carries them over.
- [mechanism] An NPC's replies can change as the player presents contradicting evidence, so a confession becomes available only once denial is hopeless. When: designing NPC confrontation dialogue.
- [rule] Confrontation dialogue should require presenting a specific evidence item, offer options stating known facts, and vary NPC tells and bargaining with revealed evidence. When: designing accusation or confrontation scenes. Why: Evidence-dependent responses turn confrontation into a reasoning task and reward careful investigation.
- [rule] Store the exact wording of disputed statements and written messages in the quest log so players can detect contradictions and check paraphrases against the original text. When: two parties give conflicting versions, or written statements are part of the story. Why: Exact lines allow reuse and contradiction detection, and let players compare paraphrases with what was actually written.
- [rule] Give a dying NPC brief lucid moments as a timed dialogue window that the player must use before it closes. When: designing dialogue with a dying character.
- [rule] Let puzzle objects such as coins or phrases in letters carry clues that players read only after gathering a related lore entry. When: when designing lore-linked puzzles. Why: Gated clues reward exploration and link objects to the story.
- [rule] Design puzzles where the player infers the thief's choice from what is absent, narrowed by the victim's known habits. When: Designing a deduction puzzle. Why: Known habits give a baseline that makes absence informative.
- [rule] Let an NPC scholar verify a lore claim, and keep verified facts visibly separate from unverified ones in the player's notes. When: When designing lore-driven investigation in a game. Why: Players need to know which facts are established and which remain open.
- [rule] Give NPCs evasive replies that open new leads, and let players press them with a timer or pressure meter. When: Designing NPC dialogue that resists direct questions. Why: Evasion that yields new leads keeps the player pursuing the case.
- [rule] Let players wear a disguise or take a false role to enter a restricted area, and have NPCs react differently to the persona. When: Designing restricted areas guarded by staff or NPCs. Why: Persona-based access rewards players for role-play choices.
- [rule] Let a former guard or officer who recognises a suspect give that fact more weight than a common villager's claim. When: Designing NPCs who identify a suspect. Why: Authority and past experience make recognition more credible.
- [rule] Use a recognition cue, such as a whistle or silhouette, so an NPC can identify the player without alerting guards. When: Designing stealth encounters with allied NPCs. Why: A cue that only the ally understands lets contact occur without raising the alarm.
- [rule] Let players deliberately decline to investigate a clue, keeping it available as an unresolved thread for later.
- [rule] Let a reveal unlock a true answer only after the player observes evidence in a fixed order with witnesses present; do not harm a companion through delay without the player seeing why. When: Designing a staged reveal with companion characters. Why: A fair order makes the answer earned and avoids unexplained harm to allies.
- [heuristic] Let an informant NPC's dialogue give everything in one visit, or signal that the informant's willingness will fade if the player delays. When: designing a cooperative NPC who holds key information. Why: Players who delay may lose the chance to exhaust the contact's knowledge.
- [heuristic] Design each layer so it can be checked independently, so players can reject a weak link without losing the whole case. When: designing a multi-layer case. Why: independent layers localize failure.
- [heuristic] Lore in a game is spread across journals, NPC dialogue and inscriptions, and the player assembles the truth by cross-checking them. When: Designing a lore-driven story. Why: Distributed sources reward player deduction and make the story feel discovered.
- [heuristic] An NPC informant can reveal information only after the player invests time or money in rapport, with dialogue unlocking as trust rises. When: Designing informant NPCs. Why: Gated trust makes information feel earned.
- [heuristic] Give a deceptive character a brief, honest moment that a player can notice and act on.
- [heuristic] Let NPCs notice details according to their role and interests, so a guard who misses a disturbed tile tells the player something about the guard. When: designing NPC awareness of the environment. Why: what an NPC misses reveals their priorities.
- [heuristic] Puzzles that require connecting an earlier overheard line to a later character reward player attention more than brute-force search. When: When designing clue chains based on conversation. Why: Connecting remembered details feels like insight, while searching exhaustively feels like grinding.
- [heuristic] Show a clue and then remove it, leaving a gap the player can revisit and try to fill.
- [procedure] 1) Front-load setup clues in the opening; 2) release physical evidence and small details steadily mid-case, building suspicion gradually; 3) save the motive-explaining cluster for late. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Present each trace to the suspect one at a time. 2) Ask what it means and let the suspect commit to an explanation. 3) Only then reveal the next item. 4) Compare each trace to its known source. When: Physical evidence and witness accounts are available to test a suspect's statements. Why: Committing to an explanation before revealing more exposes contradictions.
- [procedure] 1) Hold a concrete piece of evidence. 2) Confront the suspect directly with it. 3) Treat the reaction, whether confession or refusal, as data. When: when the suspect is not yet cooperating. Why: A suspect's reaction to evidence is informative even when it does not answer the question.
- [procedure] 1) Block access to a restricted source in the scene. 2) Log the refusal. 3) Let the log point the player toward alternate sources for the same information. When: when an NPC must refuse a question about a restricted source. Why: the player keeps a path forward without the blocked answer.
- [tradeoff] Key evidence gated behind conditions, such as needing a witness present, delays and shapes how the audience learns the truth, at the cost of making the reveal depend on player circumstances. When: A key document should count only under specific conditions, or the expert community is divided. Why: Conditions and disputes control when and how the truth is learned.
- [pitfall] Accepting a mechanism because it is ingenious rather than checking it against the evidence is a common error.
- [pitfall] Explanations for why a building took its shape are inferences and should be labeled as such, not stated as established fact.
- [pitfall] A key clue placed in a scene the audience never revisits, or never clearly shown, makes the final explanation feel unfair. When: Planting clues for a later reveal. Why: The audience cannot connect a clue it has not properly registered.

## confrontation design
- [mechanism] A challenge-and-countersign or knock signal sorts arrivals by demanded replies: a wrong reply marks an outsider, and watching exchanges reveals each member's type. When: A gate or group admits people through a ritual exchange without knowing each visitor personally. Why: Members can perform the ritual correctly, so the exchange tests password knowledge rather than identity.
- [mechanism] In a dialogue system, an NPC statement can be challenged with evidence the player has gathered, and each contradiction unlocks a follow-up question. When: NPC statements conflict with evidence the player has found.
- [mechanism] A half-serious challenge, once accepted, becomes a binding commitment that sets the next investigation steps and the challenger's obligations. When: When a character's pride or dare opens a new investigation path. Why: Acceptance turns a casual claim into an agreement with terms.
- [mechanism] When a conviction transfers property or fees to officials and tradespeople, each conviction gives them a reason to pursue further accusations, so accusing can spread through a system. When: Where confiscation and fees follow a conviction. Why: Each conviction pays the people who profit from the next one.
- [mechanism] A timed confrontation forces the final admission without a conventional proof puzzle, because the guilty party reacts to pressure before evidence is complete. When: Evidence is short but the culprit is known to the player. Why: Pressure at a fixed moment can make the culprit reveal themselves.
- [rule] Make the premise of a case, not only its individual links, something the player can challenge.
- [rule] Include stated assumptions in npc relative dialogue that the player can challenge with other evidence. When: designing witness dialogue. Why: Players engage when a witness's claim can be tested.
- [rule] Press with a pointed question only when independent facts are available to check the answer; without them it signals suspicion but proves nothing.
- [rule] Declare any personal link to a suspect, victim or witness openly, then decide whether to recuse or hand the case to someone else. When: a personal connection to someone in the case exists. Why: disclosure lets others check the investigator's fairness.
- [rule] Confront a witness only with a claim the investigator can show to be false, and have documents ready to prove it. When: the witness is committed to a checkable falsehood. Why: Without documents the witness can simply deny the claim.
- [rule] Design a confrontation where an NPC's flinch or hidden item, prompted by a culprit-only question, produces the next clue. When: Designing a suspect confrontation scene.
- [rule] Stage a reveal in dialogue where an NPC must confirm a physical discovery the player made, turning the solution into a confrontation.
- [rule] When two testimonies directly conflict, hold the conflict open and check other facts before choosing which account to accept.
- [rule] Reward players for reconciling conflicting accounts, and make an unexplained gap the trigger for the next lead. When: Designing progression in a testimony-based investigation. Why: Reconciliation is a skill-based reward and gaps drive exploration.
- [rule] When a complete-looking case feels wrong, name the specific flaw; a gut conviction alone does not settle the question. When: A detective doubts a theory that seems logically complete. Why: A tidy theory can still be wrong, as juries also resist neat cases.
- [rule] Let players choose which accuser to bring forward and which question to ask, with each response revealing a different clue. When: when designing a confrontation scene.
- [rule] Use a trap that tests a suspect's reaction so the culprit exposes themselves through a choice rather than a confession. When: Climax of a mystery where a confession is unlikely or impossible. Why: A reaction under pressure gives proof without requiring the culprit to speak.
- [heuristic] A confrontation option may need to close off the escape route an NPC would otherwise use. When: Designing a confrontation the NPC could dodge. Why: Without closing the exit, an NPC can answer with a technically correct refusal and end the scene.
- [heuristic] Confront a suspect with a direct question about a hidden fact only the culprit would know; this breaks a prepared story. When: The suspect has a rehearsed account. Why: Unexpected knowledge disrupts composure.
- [heuristic] Answer a weak explanation with a specific contradicting observation rather than a vague doubt, because concrete sightings are harder for the speaker to explain away.
- [heuristic] Base each challenge on evidence the suspect cannot be sure the investigator holds, so denials carry risk. When: when confronting a suspect. Why: uncertainty about what the investigator knows makes the suspect hesitate.
- [heuristic] A confrontation scene can draw attention to one character while the real clue remains elsewhere. When: staging a dramatic encounter in a mystery. Why: the emotional focus pulls the player away from the key evidence.
- [heuristic] You can accept an opponent's premises and still mount a sound challenge by showing that their conclusions do not follow from those premises.
- [heuristic] A dialogue system can unlock a confrontation option only after the player presents the matching piece of evidence. When: In dialogue systems tied to an evidence inventory. Why: Gating confrontation on evidence rewards the player for gathering it first.
- [procedure] 1) Claim more knowledge than you hold. 2) Offer terms such as immunity. 3) Set a deadline. 4) Withhold source names. 5) Watch the suspect's reactions. When: A guilty party must be pressed into revealing a position. Why: Pressure and uncertainty make denial harder to sustain.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the suspect's past and who could identify them. 2) Lay out evidence one item at a time, naming each before adding the next. 3) Remind the suspect of any earlier warning. 4) Read their reaction after each item. 5) Press on while stakes rise. When: Confronting a suspect with strong evidence. Why: Sequencing lets each item land and exposes the suspect's responses.
- [procedure] 1) Assess the witness's fitness beforehand. 2) Plan the confrontation with the risk of a breakdown in mind. 3) Bring a companion to take notes so statements can later be verified. When: Preparing to question a witness who may be fragile or under stress. Why: A breakdown can come without warning, and unrecorded statements are hard to prove.
- [procedure] 1) Approach from behind and force a bolted door together. 2) Cover the suspect with a weapon and order them still. 3) Have helpers restrain the arms and move the suspect away from the equipment. 4) Explain the mechanism aloud. 5) Confront the suspect with the physical evidence. 6) Keep the captive away from the apparatus while securing evidence. When: A suspect is caught in the act and may resist, escape or destroy evidence.
- [tradeoff] Confronting a suspect now can close off further information, while waiting keeps information open but lets delay cost something important. When: when a witness is cooperating and the matter is not urgent. Why: a direct challenge may end the cooperation.
- [pitfall] Pressuring or bluffing a suspect can provoke a drawn weapon, so plan bystander safety and account for violent reactions before confronting. When: An interrogation is scripted in a crowded or armed setting, or the suspect may carry a weapon. Why: Pressure can provoke a weapon the investigator has not accounted for. (x2)
- [pitfall] Confronting a character with a claim that has a plausible innocent explanation makes them close up and withdraw.
- [pitfall] Attacking a procedure while leaving its premise intact can let an unverifiable source stay in use for long periods. When: when critics challenge a court's methods. Why: the premise keeps the source credible.

## emotional cues
- [definition] Physiognomy is the practice of judging a person's inner nature from appearance, including face, hands, hair, and movement.
- [behavior] Physical tells in a character's manner, such as sweating or a shaking hand while recounting a story, hint at a hidden history the audience can later connect.
- [behavior] An attentive observer may sense that a polished, friendly surface is deliberately maintained rather than natural.
- [behavior] A change in manner when the questioner speaks can matter as much as the answer itself. When: a witness is questioned directly. Why: tone shifts can reveal discomfort or evasion.
- [behavior] A listener can read withheld information from a speaker's face and manner, treating demeanor as evidence of concealment. When: A speaker gives a shortened account. Why: Nonverbal signs leak what the words omit.
- [behavior] Listeners who hang on a witness's answer reveal what they fear, which can be as informative as the answer itself. When: Observing family or associates during questioning. Why: Anxious reactions expose the stakes people attach to the outcome.
- [rule] Physical reactions and manner shifts like hesitation have many causes; treat them as leads to test against documents or further questioning, not as proof of guilt, lying or supernatural claims. When: reading a witness's body language or manner. Why: Emotion and agitation can arise from many causes besides guilt. (x2)
- [rule] Check prints for missing digits, since a suspect with a missing finger can be excluded when the prints show that finger intact. When: When marks show fingers and a suspect's injury is known. Why: A visible trait can rule a person in or out.
- [rule] Do not treat a relaxed, candid mood as proof of truth, because a witness can be honest on one point and silent on another. When: when assessing a cooperative witness. Why: candor on one topic does not guarantee accuracy on others.
- [rule] After stating an accusation, watch the suspect's physical tells and treat them as further evidence, not as proof.
- [rule] Show distress cues such as hesitation or crying, and open a new dialogue branch when the player presses the right point.
- [heuristic] A mismatch between friendly manner and watchful attention signals a hidden interest, but does not prove guilt on its own.
- [heuristic] Low spirits together with mounting money pressure can point to a motive, though a single observed manner is weak evidence. When: Motive must be inferred rather than proven. Why: Money trouble often shows up as a change in mood.
- [heuristic] Enemies who check written messages and watch for pursuit often miss physical signs left in a room.
- [heuristic] A sudden shift in mood shortly before an event is worth recording as a clue.
- [heuristic] An involuntary physical reaction can reveal a staged performance more clearly than the words that accompany it. When: when a witness's account sounds practised.
- [heuristic] Concrete environmental details such as light, fire and objects set a mood that makes a later shock land harder. When: building the setting for a scare. Why: a grounded setting heightens contrast.
- [heuristic] Frame hints as mood rather than fact, so the audience feels unease while the speaker stays uncommitted to any specific claim. When: the audience needs unease before facts are available.
- [heuristic] Rapid shifts in an informant's mood suggest the report is shaped by their feelings rather than by the facts. When: An informant swings between sympathy, anger and friendliness during a report. Why: Emotional volatility indicates that feelings are steering the account.
- [heuristic] Choose each remark in an interview to produce a specific feeling in the listener, so the emotional beats steer the exchange. When: Scripting an interview or dialogue scene with a strong emotional goal. Why: Deliberate emotional targets make the scene's direction clear.
- [heuristic] When a reaction is far stronger than its stated cause, the stated cause is probably not the real one. Search for a stronger, hidden cause. When: When an outburst seems out of proportion. Why: Intensity points to a deeper motive.
- [pitfall] Mood or atmosphere, such as a funeral's, establishes no fact and cannot replace corroboration; it should support the evidence instead. When: when writing tense scenes meant to drive a mystery. Why: Players need concrete clues, not just tone.
- [pitfall] Inferring motive from mood, such as a cold house, alone misleads, since one manner may have other causes; link the mood to a concrete act first. When: building a motive from the mood of a place or household. Why: Atmosphere is suggestive but not proof, so it needs a concrete link to an act before it supports a conclusion.
- [pitfall] Eliminating a suspect by social standing, manners, size or strength risks error, as such traits prove no innocence; a timed record of presence at the right time is stronger. When: when considering removing or narrowing a suspect. Why: Physical guesses ignore whether the suspect could have been present at the right time.
- [pitfall] A physical trait such as an injury can point at a suspect too early; it may be the answer or a red herring, so wait for other evidence.
- [pitfall] Building suspicion on a single physical resemblance, such as a matching injury, invites a false accusation against whoever seems to fit.
- [pitfall] Prolonged silence or stillness becomes tedious unless the tension source is varied. When: extended tense sequences. Why: Without variation, the audience's attention drifts.
- [pitfall] Reading mood changes as lies can mislead, and an investigator's own view of the suspect can shape that reading, so the reading must be checked.
- [pitfall] A receiver's current mood, rather than the visitor's actual purpose, can drive the first judgment of an unexpected arrival.
- [pitfall] A narrator's emotional distress can distract from factual clues being planted in the same scene. When: Writing a scene that is emotionally intense and contains plot information. Why: Strong emotion draws attention away from details the audience needs.
- [fact] A person under strain can show both careless and careful details in the same scene, so mixed traces do not automatically indicate one state. When: when a scene contains traces pointing in opposite directions. Why: agitation affects some habits while leaving others intact.
- [fact] An ordeal reads a physical outcome as moral judgment, yet the result says nothing about the act being judged.

## pretext for access and interviews
- [mechanism] Framing a dialogue option as a pretext can unlock different NPC responses to the same question, depending on how it is framed. When: dialogue choices that ask about an absent person.
- [behavior] Characters can hide real feelings behind a game or pretend role, and the true feelings tend to surface when the pretence breaks down. When: two characters agree on a pretence about their relationship. Why: the pretence gives safe cover for emotions neither will state.
- [rule] Use a believable pretext, such as a charity collection or survey, to gain access to a restricted building or to ask questions that direct questioning would alert the target to. When: Entry to a restricted building is needed, or direct questioning would alert the target. Why: A plausible purpose opens doors that a plain visitor would not and gives a believable reason for the questions.
- [rule] Keep a pretext consistent and leave on friendly terms, since targets may see through an innocent-seeming cover and exposure ends cooperation. When: When using a pretext to contact a witness. Why: An exposed pretext ends the witness's cooperation and can compromise the investigation.
- [rule] Unlock information through a cover identity the player chooses, so the chosen pretext shapes what is revealed. When: designing dialogue with disguises.
- [rule] Unlock pretext options from a character's background or reputation, with different outcomes for each. When: When designing dialogue or social choices. Why: Background-based options make player choices reflect the character's standing.
- [rule] Let a pretext character grant the player entry, such as posing as a tenant or delivery worker, whose claimed identity the player can check. When: when an NPC gatekeeps a location or a person. Why: a plausible cover opens access without direct confrontation.
- [rule] Without official authority, adopt a plausible outsider identity with a believable reason to ask, so that staff at private firms or front desks will answer. When: the investigator lacks authority and the source is a private or front-desk employee. Why: a plausible customer or client is answered where a direct request is refused.
- [rule] Question people under a false pretext when they would change their answers if they knew the real purpose of the visit.
- [heuristic] Use a small pretext, such as returning a found or dropped item, to conceal the real aim of observing a reaction or checking what is happening inside a room. When: Planning a question that must not reveal its purpose, or checking what is happening inside a room. Why: A plausible reason lowers the suspect's guard and makes their reaction more revealing.
- [heuristic] Check whether a stated reason for entering or acting matches the real situation, especially when the excuse is convenient. When: someone gives an errand to explain their presence. Why: a pretext can conceal the real purpose.
- [heuristic] Ask what pretext would let someone administer the method unnoticed; without a plausible pretext, a candidate is weakened. When: Evaluating whether a suspect could have acted unseen. Why: Access without a believable reason is hard to achieve in practice.
- [heuristic] Choose a pretext whose role fits the interviewee's standing, since a role that does not suit the person's status is likely to be rejected. When: When selecting a cover story for an interview. Why: A mismatch between role and status can lead to refusal or exposure.
- [heuristic] A legitimate task, such as helping finish a job, gives a character reasons to be inside an otherwise closed household or room.
- [heuristic] Use a respectable pretext, a plausible reason for being there, to enter a place or join a group when access is needed. When: Access to a place or group is blocked without a reason.
- [heuristic] A plausible role that matches what the site expects to see can grant limited access, provided it is repeated consistently. When: Entry is needed for a limited time. Why: A role that fits expectations draws little suspicion.
- [procedure] 1) Find a talkative local witness. 2) Invent a plausible reason to speak with them, such as returning an item. 3) Sustain the pretext without exposing yourself. 4) Accept the witness's correction, which often carries more information than the original lead. When: A local witness is talkative and a plausible pretext exists. Why: A plausible reason opens conversation that a direct question would not.
- [procedure] 1) Get an introduction from someone the host trusts. 2) Give a reason for the visit that is partly true. 3) Give a believable reason to stay. 4) Expect the host to scrutinize you. When: when entering a private home or space without arousing suspicion. Why: A trusted introducer and a plausible reason lower the host's guard, though scrutiny continues.
- [procedure] 1) Pick a cover role that supplies a credible pretext for questions. 2) Let a talkative witness run out of words before asking. 3) Ask general questions first. 4) Follow each answer with a narrower question until it is specific. When: interviewing a talkative or digressive witness. Why: a cover role gives a reason to keep asking, while waiting avoids being swamped by talk.
- [procedure] 1) Name a plausible reason why you need the record, such as an omitted detail. 2) Ask to see the copy that would confirm it. 3) Use the record to pursue the next lead. When: When a clerk or official holds a record that would advance an investigation. Why: A believable error or omission makes staff willing to show a record they would otherwise withhold.
- [procedure] 1) Invent a plausible reason for a visit that the target cannot easily refuse. 2) Prepare the cover by learning enough of the target's field to survive questions. 3) Pick a time the target is likely free. 4) Offer bait the target values. 5) Use the occupied target's time to reach the real objective. When: the target is alert but has one weakness a plausible approach can exploit.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a plausible pretext for contact. 2) Deliver it so the suspect must respond. 3) Watch the reaction, since a blocking or fierce response is evidence of temper. When: direct questioning would be refused. Why: a suspect's reaction to a plausible claim reveals character.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a plausible reason to be near the suspect. 2) Observe others present and note what they overhear. 3) Record the suspect's questions and reactions. 4) Adopt a naive manner to draw the suspect out. When: a guarded suspect must be questioned without alerting them. Why: A believable reason and a naive manner lower the suspect's guard.
- [procedure] 1) Adopt a plausible cover role. 2) Offer a small payment or favour. 3) Take a lead, such as an address, from an ordinary object. 4) Follow that lead to the witness. When: a witness must be located without revealing the real purpose. Why: a believable cover and small incentive open doors that direct questions cannot.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a neutral pretext rather than an accusation. 2) Talk on a comfortable subject while observing manner. 3) Move gradually to the sensitive topic. 4) Use hypothetical questions to reveal how firmly the interviewee holds a position. When: when questioning an expert whose claims must be tested without alerting them. Why: A pretext lowers guard and buys time, and the reaction to each probe is evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain a legal or formal reason to search, such as a general warrant. 2) Use that reason to search every room and container, even against refusal. 3) Insist on opening sealed spaces when the suspect objects. When: A suspect refuses direct entry to a closed space. Why: A formal pretext justifies access that would otherwise be refused.
- [procedure] 1) Give the questioning a harmless cover such as a routine check. 2) Pair the cover with a plausible physical action while observing the reaction. 3) Build trust first, then press for facts, leaving the central question for later. When: The witness is fragile and would shut down under a direct accusation. Why: A benign cover lowers the witness's guard so reactions are more open.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a plausible pretext that explains the visit. 2) Ask background questions such as arrival time and reasons for coming. 3) Let each answer shape the next question. 4) Test the suspect with a known name. 5) Change manner if the reaction is unclear. When: The suspect has a reason to hide information and the investigator can reach them through a plausible role. Why: A pretext opens access, and adaptive questioning reveals background step by step.
- [procedure] 1) Lure the suspect to you with a plausible false pretext. 2) Display a physical clue in plain view. 3) Offer an invented but credible account of how the evidence was found. 4) Let the suspect's reaction reveal what cannot yet be proven. When: Physical evidence points to a suspect but cannot yet prove the connection. Why: A guilty suspect's reaction to a visible clue or bluff can disclose knowledge that direct questioning would not.
- [tradeoff] A pretext can open access and draw information that direct questions would not, but it fails once the claim is checked, can taint testimony, and exposes the investigator if discovered. When: A witness is hiding a fact, or direct questioning would alert the suspect or fail. Why: Cover stories depend on claims not being verified, and deception carries ethical and practical risks. (x2)
- [pitfall] A pretext can fail: the witness may distrust the stated reason, and an unlikely lead can waste time at the first address tried. When: When using a pretext or pursuing a long-shot lead. Why: Unverified reasons and unlikely leads carry a real chance of producing nothing.
- [pitfall] A pretext that is out of character for the person offering it is easily recognised, which exposes the plan to the target. When: when a cover offer comes from a character who would not normally make it. Why: Targets notice inconsistencies between an offer and the giver's usual behavior.

## suspense and pacing
- [mechanism] A departure or deadline opens a short window, and the outcome of a scene turns on what happens inside that interval. When: A scene where the result depends on a short window of time.
- [mechanism] Time gaps between events, such as days of fruitless search, increase tension and sharpen a sense of deadline.
- [mechanism] A brief line can cover a long, dull stretch, letting tension be saved for the decisive scene that follows. When: A stretch of waiting, sneaking or other low-event time must be passed. Why: Keeps attention on the moments that matter instead of idle time.
- [mechanism] Interrupting a scene at its peak raises the stakes, and the next scene can open in a different place.
- [mechanism] A remedy that brings brief relief is often taken as proof of a natural cause, so short-term improvement can mislead observers about what caused a condition. When: When a treatment appears to work at first and then fails or changes. Why: Observers attribute the change to the remedy or the cause they already expect.
- [mechanism] A partial, poorly lit view makes an observer react before the nature of the object is shown, so suspense grows from the gap in what is seen. When: A scene must build tension before showing its cause. Why: The observer's reaction signals a discovery while the cause stays hidden.
- [mechanism] When a character lets others feel informed until they discover they were outsiders, the reveal creates suspense and reframes earlier conversations. When: Designing a reveal in a mystery narrative. Why: Characters who believe they know more than they do keep the audience engaged until the gap is exposed.
- [mechanism] Repeating an event with increasing intensity, closer approach or new detail builds suspense and forces the investigator to act. When: A recurring threat is used to build pressure across scenes. Why: Each stronger repetition raises the stakes and narrows the choices.
- [behavior] Observers notice pauses before a subject's answer and read them as meaningful. When: During a staged questioning.
- [behavior] Tension rises during a long wait even without new information, because anticipation itself keeps the stakes high for the audience. When: a long idle wait with no new events. Why: anticipation sustains stakes without new facts.
- [behavior] Small sounds, such as a rustling bush, raise tension so that even careful people hesitate or make mistakes. When: A team is waiting or moving in silence near a target. Why: Heightened alertness makes ordinary noises feel threatening.
- [behavior] Restraint rather than action can drive tension, as a silent observer's held breath and imagined threats build suspense. When: a scene with a hidden observer. Why: an unspoken threat builds suspense.
- [behavior] A sudden change in tone when answering a sensitive question can betray concealment more clearly than the content of the answer. When: a person answers a sensitive question. Why: tone is harder to control than wording.
- [rule] End a tense wait with a clear event that resolves the tension and gives the player or audience its next objective. When: a suspense sequence reaches its climax. Why: A resolved climax releases tension and tells the audience what to do next.
- [rule] Use a late confession to open a timed window in which the player can act before the outcome is fixed.
- [rule] Structure escalating events in tiers, moving from a mild form to obstruction to direct harm, and place a second NPC who witnesses the event as a check on the player's account. When: Designing escalating events with witnesses. Why: Escalation builds stakes, and a second observer corroborates the sequence.
- [heuristic] Each delay in a withheld reveal or waiting period should add a new detail, such as a gesture or sound; repeating the same cue or stalling without new information dulls tension. When: the reveal is held back across several beats, or a waiting period reuses one sound, light or sign. Why: stalling without new information only frustrates, and a cue that brings no new progress stops signalling approach. (x2)
- [heuristic] Pause before a reveal and narrate listener reactions during long explanations, letting the audience form theories and anticipate the twist so tension rises when it lands. When: a reveal is about to happen, or an NPC or narrator delivers a long explanation before a reveal. Why: anticipation primes the audience and lets them form their own theories.
- [heuristic] When outside authorities are approaching, model the time limit in event sequences and demand a rapid account, since the suspect has less time to build a prepared story. When: when outside authorities are close to arriving. Why: little time limits how much a story can be prepared, and time constrains what could have happened.
- [heuristic] Make relief between threats real but partial: the character feels better, yet a lasting problem or required preparation keeps the next threat pressing.
- [heuristic] Use time pressure to raise suspense by showing the cost of delay before the outcome is known. When: when pacing a story or quest with a deadline. Why: Known costs make the player feel the urgency.
- [heuristic] Restate the stakes at each stage of a sequence, such as what the outcome means for a life, so the audience keeps the consequences in view. Why: Repeated reminders keep tension high between events.
- [heuristic] Alternate moments of hope and despair in narration, such as hesitation followed by a decisive sound, to sustain tension. When: Pacing a tense sequence. Why: Shifts between hope and despair keep the audience engaged and anticipating the next outcome.
- [heuristic] Compare restraints with their claimed purpose: a captor who fears escape binds tightly, so loose restraints suggest the bound person could free himself. When: A reported abduction or confinement involves physical restraints. Why: Restraint tightness reflects what the restrainer actually feared.
- [heuristic] Ask the question plainly and then wait; giving the witness time lets them recover details they would otherwise skip. When: A witness hesitates over a detail. Why: Recall takes time.
- [heuristic] Add a timed quest with a fixed reply deadline, where a missing answer changes the story state. When: Designing quests that wait on replies. Why: A fixed deadline creates pressure and a state change on failure.
- [heuristic] Use a dated, timed detail, such as the hour and date of a death, as the hinge that makes a match undeniable. When: Confirming a claim made by an unverifiable source. Why: A precise time is hard to explain away as coincidence.
- [procedure] 1) Alternate slow, rich sensory description with sudden shocks. 2) Let each shock land after a calm passage so it reads as a break. When: Building suspense in a scene. Why: Contrast between calm and abrupt events heightens tension.
- [pitfall] A restrained suspect can still nearly overpower the investigator, so restraint must be complete.
- [pitfall] Resolving every cliffhanger in the next scene removes the suspense that the interruption built.
- [pitfall] A scene built only on sound becomes exhausting if no release or later explanation follows.
- [fact] A crime story can reveal the culprit at the start, shifting suspense from who did it to whether concealment will hold under mounting pressure. When: when the murder occurs early and the audience knows the killer. Why: Suspense then comes from concealment and pressure rather than from a mystery.

## document reading
- [mechanism] Public reports of a grave condition can reinforce an opponent's sense of success, which can change their timetable.
- [behavior] A report that credits work to a group rather than one author can make the work seem more objective and later claims more credible. When: writing reports that will face later scrutiny. Why: Collective credit reads as less self-interested.
- [behavior] Witness reports often comment on the investigator's manner, so interviews reveal witnesses' attitudes as well as case facts. When: During sequenced interviews.
- [behavior] A reporter's prejudice against a group can colour how they weigh a report. Check the source's bias before trusting the account. When: When the reporter dismisses a whole category of evidence.
- [behavior] A first, mechanical reading of a document often misses distinctive traits, which become visible only on a later, deliberate reading. When: reviewing a document for physical clues. Why: Attention goes to content during a first reading.
- [behavior] Readers of an endorsed, reprinted account often treat it as proof, which strengthens the case in later minds. When: When a printed account is reissued in another place. Why: Repetition and endorsement signal authority.
- [rule] When new facts undermine the motive behind a suspicious behaviour, reread the behaviour rather than defending the earlier reading.
- [rule] Place a matching fault that is visible only on a second or third reading, so a puzzle rewards careful rereading of documents. When: designing document puzzles. Why: Clues that need deliberate attention reward careful players.
- [rule] Use periodic report checkpoints that summarise discovered clues for the player, giving a regular review of progress. When: when designing turn-based or daily investigation structure.
- [rule] Deliver the largest reveal as a document within a document, and let each artifact point to the next location or source. When: When placing the climactic clue in a document chain. Why: Embedded documents carry the reveal while directing the player onward.
- [heuristic] Facts a speaker reports without conclusions are often more reliable than conclusions built on them. Keep reporter asides and opinions separate from the evidence. Why: Interpretation adds a layer of error, and mixed asides blur evidence and interpretation.
- [heuristic] Read a written statement or note first for its aim (what it demands, forbids or threatens), then for tone, omissions and rewrites, since wording reveals the writer's intent and stance. When: A letter, note or written statement is a clue, or makes claims about other people. Why: Writers reveal purpose through choices of phrasing and what they leave out.
- [heuristic] Treat a shadowing report only as a lead until other facts confirm it.
- [heuristic] When checking a record for a transaction, start with its most recent entries, since recent payments are most likely to be relevant.
- [heuristic] How an incident is reported indicates its nature; a call that brings in a specialist suggests violence rather than a mere accident. When: Judging the kind of incident from the report that triggered an investigation. Why: Response level reflects what the reporters believed occurred.
- [heuristic] Have a role holder report suspicious outsiders to a nearby liaison who can act immediately. When: when an outsider threatens a covert plan. Why: quick reporting limits exposure.
- [heuristic] Re-examine a clue that everyone reads one way, and ask whether its wording fits live speech or a recorded or read text.
- [heuristic] Ending a report with a prediction or a sign that the next step is near builds anticipation for the next delivery. When: Writing a report that leads to a later event. Why: A forward-looking close creates suspense.
- [heuristic] A report that an object was lost is a claim to test, not a fact to accept. When: A witness says a key, tool, weapon or document is missing. Why: The claim may reflect the witness's belief about where the item was.
- [heuristic] Consider a reporter's physical and mental state, such as fasting, sleep loss or strain, when weighing their account of unusual experiences. When: A report of unusual experience comes from someone under physical or mental stress. Why: Physical strain can distort perception and produce imagined experiences.
- [heuristic] Show the player dated entries such as letters, logs and refused visits so they can build the sequence themselves. When: when presenting clues for player reconstruction. Why: Players who order dated evidence derive the timeline rather than receive it.
- [heuristic] Read a monument or document for what it claims and what it deliberately leaves unclaimed; wording that avoids asserting a fact may be innocent or deliberate. When: Interpreting a grave, plaque, or official document for its assertions. Why: Omissions in a record can be deliberate or innocent, so the reader must weigh which.
- [heuristic] Check a document's date before interpreting its content, since a date lag can reverse a belief that an earlier, undated source encouraged the reader to hold.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the reported facts as a timeline, such as travel, a timed conversation, a visit or a departure. 2) Ask for specific missing details that would confirm or refute each theory. 3) Reason to a solution from those facts. When: case fully described by a source.
- [procedure] 1) Look for recurring visitors or routines. 2) Note entries linking several people. 3) Check for missing days. 4) Flag ambiguous references. 5) Mark names for follow-up rather than treating entries as proof. When: When a victim's private diary or notes may show contacts or changes in routine. Why: Structured reading separates patterns from speculation and keeps follow-up open.
- [procedure] 1) Treat fragments at a torn edge as partial words, not complete ones. 2) Test candidate completions for each gap by checking whether they form coherent words. 3) Compare hypotheses about writing order. 4) Keep the one that predicts the available evidence. When: a damaged document may hold a clue in its missing part.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the grantor and the grantee. 2) Note what was given in exchange. 3) Note any attached condition. 4) Record the date to order the events.
- [procedure] 1) Read the whole passage, including every qualification. 2) Follow each qualifying clause to its end. 3) Compare the passage with the same author's other works. 4) Decide what the source asserts from the full context. When: A testimony or confession seems to say two things at once. Why: Qualifiers can reverse the apparent meaning.
- [pitfall] A summary built from selected entries or a condensed record can mislead, and the selection is open to the same scrutiny. Check it against the original text. When: A document, deposition or transcript is summarized through selected entries or condensed form. Why: A single sample or compression may drop or distort key details and not match the whole. (x2)
- [pitfall] Repeated reading can make an investigator see patterns that are not there, so record what has been checked and how. Why: Expectation shapes what a rereader notices.
- [pitfall] A reviewer who repeats an official stated ground may be reading the document at face value rather than concealing anything. Why: repeating a record is not evidence of deception.

## estate and inheritance motives
- [model] Track changing wills as items in an NPC's file, so players can compare versions and see who benefits. When: Designing an inheritance or quest system where wills change. Why: Versioned records let players reconstruct the beneficiary history.
- [mechanism] A warning that more harm is coming and cannot be stopped makes the threat feel inevitable and raises dread. When: a story needs tension before a climax. Why: Perceived inevitability increases unease.
- [mechanism] A contest over a dead person's estate can absorb a family member's attention and pull them away from their duties.
- [mechanism] A descendant who keeps a family grudge alive can offer a quest hook, and the player can check the story against records.
- [mechanism] Guilt over an unjust inheritance can carry forward to later heirs who keep the property, shaping how they act.
- [behavior] Heirs from an earlier marriage may suspect a later spouse of gaining undue influence over the dying person and judge the resulting will unfair. When: a will favors a later spouse over earlier children.
- [behavior] Family traditions can keep the sentiment of an old grievance accurately while confusing the details of what happened. When: A descendant repeats a story about an ancestor's enemy. Why: Sentiment is passed down more reliably than facts.
- [rule] Present inferred motives as hypotheses marked as such, not as established fact, and leave unproven links visibly open.
- [rule] Run an estate lawsuit alongside the main investigation, so its papers serve as a source of motive clues.
- [rule] Design a character who inherits a feud without sharing its origin, so players can separate the person from the side they were born into. When: when designing a character tied to a feud.
- [heuristic] Inheritance terms create economic motives: state each rule explicitly and check who gains a share from a death, with or without heirs. When: a will or estate division determines who gains from an outcome. Why: Outcomes become checkable when each rule is stated.
- [heuristic] Infer a plot's motive from what it makes possible, not from its stated cover reason, especially when that reason seems odd. When: A plot element seems to serve no purpose beyond its stated reason.
- [heuristic] Map the heirs of an old estate and how much each received, to list people with a stake in a missing object and their possible motives. When: A crime involves an inheritance or a hidden object of family value. Why: Each heir with a share has a reason to find or hide the object.
- [heuristic] A target's indifference to a fact can indicate that they have nothing to hide about it. When: a fact touches the target's own interests.
- [heuristic] Crimes are usually individual acts rather than coordinated group efforts, so look first for a personal motive. When: choosing which suspect to investigate. Why: a single actor's motive is more specific than a vague group assumption.
- [heuristic] A will that passes property to a person on the owner's death or long disappearance gives that person a motive to hurry the outcome, once they know of the will. When: a beneficiary learns of an inheritance tied to death or absence. Why: waiting costs them the gain, so they may act sooner.
- [procedure] 1) Note the suspect's unusual behaviour. 2) Match it to a pattern from earlier cases. 3) Propose a motive that explains several odd facts. 4) Choose the next check that would test it. When: no hard evidence yet.
- [procedure] 1) Identify what silence costs the person. 2) Infer the likely hidden reason and any third party it involves. 3) Test that inference against other evidence before acting on it.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the person's movement from available traces. 2) Judge whether the sequence fits a calm or a panicked state. 3) Infer the fear or expectation behind it. 4) Test each inferred step against other evidence. When: a motive or fear must be inferred to direct an investigation. Why: Each inferred step is a hypothesis, not fact, until other evidence supports it.
- [procedure] 1) Collect facts about the hidden reason from separate locations and conversations. 2) Check the ally's behaviour against them. 3) Accept a motive only if the evidence supports it. When: a withheld personal reason matters to the case.
- [procedure] 1) List every bequest by category: fixed sums, life income, specific gifts, residue. 2) Note who receives each. 3) Set aside charitable gifts as low-interest for motive. When: Reviewing a will or estate during an investigation. Why: Categories show who gains and how much, so motives can be ranked.
- [procedure] 1) List every life that stands between a sum of money and a suspect. 2) Trace each legal link, such as will, life interest or policy, to the suspect. 3) Confirm each link before concluding the motive. When: a suspect's financial gain from a death must be established. Why: Only lives still in the way give the suspect a direct interest, and a missing link leaves coincidences instead of a motive.
- [pitfall] A motive stated by one witness may be incomplete. Ruling out a plausible motive early can be a mistake, since it may return as relevant.
- [pitfall] A motive based on inheritance is valid only when the beneficiaries are confirmed and the facts match.
- [pitfall] Family ties and connections show who had influence, but not that the influence was actually used.
- [fact] When a person leaves no will, inheritance usually follows fixed default rules, so the outcome can be worked out from the family position. When: when a victim left no will.
- [fact] An estate with no eligible heir may pass to the state rather than to any private party.
- [fact] Entailed title and land pass along a fixed line of succession, and the successor may also take the money unless the owner's will redirects it. When: an estate is entailed. Why: Entail limits the owner's control over who inherits.
- [fact] An heir who has not yet made a will leaves the estate's future open, which is itself a question for motive. When: an heir's estate plan is unknown. Why: Without a will the eventual distribution is uncertain.
- [fact] Examining estate and inheritance terms can reveal a motive, but the terms matter only once they are fitted into the wider picture. When: Looking for a financial motive in a case. Why: A single fact gains meaning only when it is placed against the other evidence.
- [fact] Inheritance disputes draw in relatives, creditors and parish bodies, not only the heirs.

## evidence decay
- [mechanism] Weather, drying, sun, trampling, repairs and other visitors erode traces such as blood and footprints, so delayed examination yields less or ambiguous evidence; examine early and carefully. When: A scene is examined after a delay or left exposed. Why: Exposure erodes marks that were clear when fresh. (x2)
- [mechanism] A dropped habit-specific item can fix the moment a person passed, so the sequence of events can be reconstructed from where it lies. Why: The item is left at a specific point in time.
- [mechanism] A trail of blood on plants, stains on the path and a side-slip together record a wound, a stop and a remount, in that order.
- [mechanism] Weather, delay and fading memory destroy evidence that cannot be recovered later, and later questioning of witnesses yields less detail. When: when time passes between a crime and its investigation. Why: Witnesses forget details and deem earlier details unimportant over time.
- [mechanism] Clues tied to perishable landmarks, such as blazed trees or stone heaps, can decay with in-game time, forcing players to triangulate from surviving features. When: landmarks are used as quest clues.
- [mechanism] Physical evidence can decay if not collected quickly, such as items disposed of or moved by an NPC. When: Designing evidence in dungeon or narrative generation. Why: Delayed collection lets NPCs remove traces.
- [rule] Set aside found evidence and keep it sealed, marked and unaltered so it can be preserved intact and examined again later. When: A death may be natural but leaves material that could be retested. Why: A preserved sample keeps its value for a later investigation.
- [rule] Note where a trail stops, such as paved or trampled ground, and treat that point as a place where evidence was lost rather than as the end of the route. When: When tracking a route across mixed ground. Why: Hard or heavily used ground erases tracks without showing where the person went.
- [rule] Keep evidence under watch by combining observers with sight of entrances and windows, an agent with the object, monitoring of communications, and a log of every visitor.
- [rule] Keep objects found on a body away from the suspect until they are used to confront that person. When: when a suspect has not yet been confronted. Why: Early exposure lets the suspect adjust their account.
- [rule] Describe an object by its make and features without handling it, so the object stays intact as evidence.
- [heuristic] Degrade some document clues with faded ink, missing lines or folds, so players must cross-reference them with other sources.
- [heuristic] A physical trace can reveal recent human activity even when no one is seen.
- [heuristic] Assign each trace to the phase that plausibly left it. Blood, objects left behind and uncleaned marks usually belong to the first phase. When: a scene may contain traces from two separate events.
- [heuristic] Concern about disturbing traces matters less when many people have already handled the scene; prioritize tests that can still reveal new information. When: when many people have already entered the scene.
- [heuristic] Date a trace by its time signatures, such as wetness, freshness, colour or smell, which show how long it has been there. When: Estimating when a trace was made. Why: Some properties change predictably with time.
- [heuristic] Date a physical trace by comparing it with daily routines, such as scheduled cleaning or nightly fires, which bound when the trace could have been left. When: the routines of the place are known. Why: a trace can only be made between routine events.
- [procedure] 1) Read the item's current state. 2) Infer how much time that state implies. 3) Check the implied time against a fixed schedule such as deliveries or service times. When: fixing when an event happened.
- [procedure] 1) Note any visual trace, such as a shadow or light patch, that changed during the event. 2) Reconstruct the sequence as it was seen, not as it was expected. 3) Repeat the action under the same conditions. 4) Compare the trace step by step; a mismatch rules out that explanation. When: A witness's visual recall seems to conflict with what they heard. Why: A replay under matched conditions tests whether the recalled trace could have occurred.
- [procedure] 1) Convert the trace's position to an approximate date. 2) Compare that date with dated events such as purchases or illnesses. 3) Reject the story if they conflict. When: a claim depends on when an exposure happened. Why: Dated traces can confirm or break a timeline.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether old traces cross a line of the current text. 2) If they do, the old text was not erased from that sheet. 3) Compare trace length with the expected length of a standard phrase. When: Judging whether a document's text was altered or erased. Why: Erasure removes the upper text but cannot remove marks that were struck through the later line.
- [tradeoff] Keeping evidence on one's person risks a search, and destroying it removes the proof; leaving it among ordinary items can be the least bad option. When: when a culprit holds incriminating evidence.
- [tradeoff] Suppressing records can protect against present accusations but removes the evidence later needed to vindicate the suppressor.
- [pitfall] Reading a fresh trace as old, or the reverse, happens when weather or other events have altered it since it was made.
- [pitfall] Opening windows or doors can dissipate smells and other traces before a later examiner arrives, so the evidence is lost. When: A scene is opened or aired out before it is fully examined. Why: Airflow removes the physical traces that the investigation depends on.
- [pitfall] Brushing, shaking or wiping clothes destroys or moves traces, so untouched items are needed to read where a person has been.
- [pitfall] Erasing a public message destroys evidence of how a rumor spread and who might have passed it on.
- [fact] After a physical trace is erased, only a witness's recollection or a preserved copy remains as evidence of it.
- [fact] Microscopic cell examination becomes useless once stains are a few hours old, while a protein-based test still works on older stains.
- [fact] Disturbed ground and torn vegetation near an edge mark the final stretch of a struggle or flight, and show where movement became most violent. When: Traces cluster near a drop or edge. Why: Concentrated disturbance marks the point of greatest activity.
- [fact] Erasures made after writing carry a different meaning from those made during writing, so the timing of an edit should be established before interpreting it. When: Analyzing deleted text in a document. Why: The meaning of a deletion depends on when it was made.

## physical clue properties
- [definition] A contributory clue points toward a suspect without proving guilt; a decisive clue is timed and exclusive, tying the act to one suspect at a known moment. When: Grading the strength of evidence. Why: Decisive clues are needed before an arrest.
- [mechanism] A physical act done in public, such as removing a false marker, makes the truth visible and hard to undo.
- [mechanism] Measure how far an actor's hand or body falls short of a target and use the gap to estimate how much bigger the actor must be. When: When a physical mark shows how someone reached a high point. Why: The gap between a reachable point and the target gives a measurable size difference.
- [mechanism] A physical detail, such as a damaged item found in an unexpected place, can overturn an accepted story by showing the damage happened earlier than claimed. When: A physical clue conflicts with the accepted timeline. Why: Physical state records a sequence the story did not account for.
- [mechanism] A hidden item can be concealed by swapping its container for a similar empty one, and the empty substitute must then be hidden too. When: When someone wants to hide the contents of a container. Why: The swap keeps the outward appearance intact while moving the contents elsewhere.
- [mechanism] Let an NPC confirm an item with a stated confidence level, so the player must decide how much to trust the identification. When: Designing item identification interactions. Why: Confidence levels create uncertainty that players must weigh.
- [behavior] A physical trace can jog memory, but a speaker may recall where something came from only after being given the specific figures. When: an object or purchase connects to a disputed sum. Why: recall is cued by concrete facts more than by general questions.
- [behavior] The state of a container, such as locked, forced, or empty, can differ from the rest of a scene and suggest a different actor or motive. When: A container's state does not match the rest of the scene. Why: A mismatch between the container and the scene points to a separate person or purpose.
- [rule] Give found items physical features, such as ink colour, paper type, material, wear and craft skill, as leads to the type of person who left them. When: generating items placed in a level.
- [rule] Make the flipping statement reachable through earlier dialogue so the reversal feels earned rather than arbitrary.
- [rule] Publish a physical detail when it could prompt a witness to come forward. When: an investigation needs witnesses. Why: a public detail can reach people who saw the matter.
- [rule] Keep one inspectable physical clue that connects the planner to the method, so the reveal rests on something the audience can examine. Why: the reveal survives if the object is later destroyed.
- [rule] Inspect ordinary containers by opening them and examining contents closely, even when they are messy or dirty. When: a scene contains bins, crates or similar containers. Why: key evidence can sit inside clutter.
- [rule] Do not drop a noticed physical clue because testimony sounds certain. Set the clue aside as unresolved and reopen it when a new question arises. When: When a physical clue conflicts with a firm-sounding testimony. Why: Testimony may be wrong, and physical traces stay available for later questions.
- [rule] Use physical habits such as clothing, seating position or how a weapon is carried as checks that can rule out an otherwise plausible suspect. When: Eliminating suspects after temperament analysis. Why: Physical details are checkable facts that temperament reasoning cannot supply.
- [rule] Ask whether each door was locked or unlocked, since this determines which areas an intruder could reach. When: when reconstructing who could access a room. Why: door state defines the reachable space.
- [rule] Give players a physical clue, such as a reflection, draught or echo, that explains a local legend once they know the period's rules.
- [rule] Let a journal list the possible meanings of an item so the player can test each one.
- [heuristic] Plant physical details, such as sensory specifics or an object's weight or material, in an opening or dialogue so their later meaning or use feels fair and recognisable. When: Writing an opening, dialogue or clue that will return later, such as a late reveal or a lock's key. Why: Early specifics give later scenes something to match; objects read as scenery, so later significance surprises without feeling unfair.
- [heuristic] An act at a scene that does not serve the suspect's apparent purpose suggests a different actor or motive. When: A detail of a crime seems out of character for the suspect. Why: Purpose and character are both evidence, and a mismatch points away from the expected person.
- [heuristic] The quality of consumables an owner buys can hint at their means, especially when a premium item is bought by someone who could economise. When: When assessing an owner's wealth from purchased goods. Why: Choice of quality reflects available money.
- [heuristic] Compare the physical dimensions of a container with what it is meant to hold; an unusual size can reveal a hidden extra item.
- [heuristic] A conspicuous object can betray its holder over a wide area, so it is often the most dangerous trace to keep. Why: it is easily identified across a region.
- [heuristic] Make the physical condition of an in-world document, such as a missing leaf or frayed edge, an observable clue players can examine, not only text to read. When: when designing in-world records. Why: physical state can carry evidence that the text omits.
- [heuristic] Physical details of an object, such as a bend or a fitting, can indicate how it was displaced, supporting a reconstruction of the event.
- [heuristic] A specialized object unsuited to its carrier's apparent purpose can imply planned intent, and item descriptions can hint at that purpose.
- [heuristic] A very small physical trace, such as a torn label or residue, can link an object to a source more strongly than many larger finds. When: Assembling evidence that connects a substance to a purchase. Why: A specific identifying detail can establish a link that bulk cannot.
- [pitfall] An item bearing identifying information, left where it is easy to find, is suspicious and may have been deliberately positioned. Why: easy discovery suggests intent.
- [pitfall] A link that rests on physical description alone, with no name, is weak and needs further corroboration. When: When the identity of a suspect or rival is unknown.
- [fact] Rough contact can transfer fibres from clothing to a surface, revealing the garment's colour and fabric. When: a coat or cloth brushes a wet or rough object.
- [fact] A missing contact mark from a firearm pressed against the head makes close-range self-harm less likely but does not rule it out. When: when judging wound features against a self-inflicted explanation. Why: contact marks are common but not guaranteed.

## planted cues
- [definition] A name or object dropped into ordinary talk can carry a hidden link between people, and its weight comes from how a listener reacts to it.
- [definition] A planted claim is a false or unverified statement offered to test another person's reaction rather than to be believed.
- [mechanism] An antagonist could plant visions through a seer, so the player must track each seer's reliability over time rather than trust them as fixed. When: designing seer or prophet characters in a mystery. Why: reliability can change through hidden manipulation.
- [mechanism] A detail that contradicts an assumption, placed inside emotional material, is registered by the reader as background and stays open for later return. When: Writing a scene where a clue must be noticed but not pursued yet. Why: Emotional focus draws attention away from the detail, so it is noticed without being examined.
- [rule] A reveal feels fair only when every clue it relies on was shown earlier; facts introduced only at the end, unseen by the player, cannot support the solution. When: Structuring a mystery's solution, or when the solution depends on facts outside the shown clues. Why: Unseen information cannot be reasoned about by the player.
- [rule] Build the final reveal only from clues the player already holds, so it reorders known facts and confirms their findings rather than adding new facts. When: Writing a mystery's reveal or ending.
- [rule] Place the reveal at the close of a mystery, after every clue has been planted and shown, and show its reasoning so the audience can recognise the logic and recap the chain. When: structuring the reveal of a puzzle or mystery. Why: the audience can then recap the full chain of clues.
- [rule] A reveal works only when earlier planted details or misdirection build the expectation it overturns, without giving it away; without that setup it feels arbitrary. Why: A reveal without setup feels arbitrary.
- [rule] Let the explanation come from the people involved, drawing only on facts already shown. When: When writing the reveal of a mystery.
- [rule] Plant a witness whose sincere but wrong sighting is later explained by a physical trace, rewarding players who test the claim.
- [rule] Make each step of a reveal yield a new inference that follows from clues already shown, rather than summarizing events. When: when writing a mystery's final explanation. Why: new inferences keep the reveal tense and fair.
- [rule] Stage a confrontation reveal only if the proof is secured and the culprit can be forced into an observable reaction.
- [rule] Plant an unexplained sense of recognition early as a clue, and pay it off later so the audience can carry it forward.
- [rule] Plant an open doubt about a harmless persona early, where the audience can see it, then supply later evidence that contradicts the surface. When: When a reveal depends on a character seeming harmless. Why: Without a visible crack the reveal reads as a cheat.
