- [rule] Plant a witness who saw one suspect at a timed location, letting players break that suspect's stated alibi. Why: a witness gives players a checkable contradiction.
- [rule] Plant an NPC's reaction to an object early, so a later deliberate use of that object exposes a hidden trait and changes the encounter. When: When a later encounter should hinge on an earlier clue. Why: Players who connect an early reaction to a later test find the outcome earned rather than random.
- [heuristic] End each partial reveal on a hook that pulls the player into the next room or chapter before the outcome is settled.
- [heuristic] Plant a remark in an early NPC's dialogue that matters only after another clue is found, and log it in the player's journal.
- [heuristic] Plant an unguarded slip early in dialogue and make a trigger keyword unlock a confession only when used precisely, so the player can recognise its meaning later. When: Designing dialogue that rewards careful questioning. Why: Early plants let the player connect a remark to a later revelation, and precision rewards careful inquiry.
- [heuristic] Designers can plant small repeated habits that reward attention and let players spot inconsistencies.
- [heuristic] Deliver a reversal through outside witnesses or pursuers rather than the protagonist's own account, so the revelation does not depend on the narrator. Why: Independent sources make a reveal more credible.
- [heuristic] Plant a seemingly irrelevant digression, such as a historical tract, that later reveals the key clue to the solution.
- [heuristic] Place the decisive fact in an item or scene the player examines early, so the later reversal is earned rather than merely announced.
- [heuristic] Only unmask someone the audience had reason to suspect of hiding something; otherwise the reveal carries no weight.
- [heuristic] Plant a suspicion early in an incidental line, then repeat it when the audience is most agitated so it returns with added weight. When: structuring foreshadowing or a later reversal. Why: a line primed early is heard differently when it recurs under tension.
- [heuristic] Routine acts such as buying supplies can be planted as clues that look innocent until compared with the stated purpose, when their scale becomes suspicious. When: A character's routine purchase or action is later compared with a stated purpose.
- [heuristic] Flag a physical detail as one to remember, so the reader stores it and recognises it when a later payoff matches it. When: planting a clue early in the story. Why: a flagged detail is kept for later matching.
- [pitfall] A casually left note may be planted to mislead as easily as it reveals the truth. When: A note seems to have been carelessly left. Why: Apparent carelessness can be staged.
- [pitfall] Rumours can be planted deliberately, so a rumour mistaken for independent evidence may actually be a manipulation. Why: A rumour's spread does not show that it is true, and its source may have had a reason to spread it.
- [pitfall] A witness may repeat a false identity the subject supplied, and a repeated name can sound authoritative enough to mislead. Why: Repetition lends an unverified claim false credibility.
- [pitfall] A witness may be a plant sent by the suspect to gather information, so the investigator must watch for this before trusting the answers.

## relationship motives
- [model] Motive can be modelled as a relationship state, such as debt or loyalty, that explains why an NPC protects a secret.
- [mechanism] A desire tied to a visible object or goal, such as a wanted possession or a business, makes a character open to a bargain. When: Designing a character whose cooperation can be bought. Why: A concrete desire gives the other party something specific to offer.
- [behavior] Repeated rejection by family and society can build a believable motive for resentment that observers readily infer. When: a character has been shunned after a long absence.
- [rule] Recognising a document by its outward look is not identification; separate 'it looks the same' from 'I know it is the same' and check which one a witness can actually support. When: A witness claims a disputed paper is authentic. Why: A forger can imitate the feature that a witness compares.
- [rule] Mark an identity as unresolved when the record leaves it open, and do not treat a notice or document as settling it. When: When a person's identity is uncertain despite some supporting documents. Why: A document can exist without answering the question it appears to address.
- [rule] Tie witness testimony to a physical object that can be recognised and produced, so the account can be checked against something tangible. When: several accounts concern one object.
- [rule] When identity is disputed, test features that cannot be altered, such as bone structure or scars, rather than relying on resemblance or personal items that can be swapped. When: An identification rests on clothing, jewellery or a shared appearance. Why: Unalterable features resist substitution in a way items do not.
- [heuristic] Build motive from relationships among the parties; map who gains or suffers from an outcome, asking background questions about relationships, money and reputation. When: A death has several people with ties to the victim. Why: Gain and loss show who had reason to act.
- [heuristic] List relationships such as persistent suitor, rival or heir as possible motives; a recent event such as a rumour of marriage can change who gains or loses. When: Judging who benefits from a character's fate, or designing character motives for a mystery. Why: Recent events alter incentives tied to existing relationships; structured relationships give clear motive candidates that shift with events.
- [heuristic] Motive often lies in a victim's close circle, such as rivalry for one person's affection or for status; gather rivals, family objections and secret ties. When: A crime occurs in a community or close social circle where relationships are dense. Why: Personal ties reveal the reasons people had to harm the victim.
- [heuristic] Motive often hides in a past connection between people, so gather the histories and associations of everyone involved.
- [heuristic] Tie an unexplained feeling to a specific moment so the audience can locate it when the answer arrives.
- [heuristic] A loss that is small for one party but large relative to their income can be a motive for hidden action.
- [heuristic] Imagination can propose methods, but each proposed method must be tied to evidence before it is accepted.
- [heuristic] Build a killer's motive from prior backstory, such as a refused loan or years of resentment, so the act reads as revenge rather than chance. When: when a crime needs a believable reason. Why: A traceable history makes the motive feel earned instead of random.
- [heuristic] Moving a body or weapon and cleaning it implies a motive; if the scene offers none, the relocation itself is suspect.
- [heuristic] When a character needs a plausible motive for hostility or accusation, look first at kin ties, shared property and past disputes between the two parties. When: a motive must be built but none is stated outright. Why: Prior ties and conflicts make hostile acts believable without direct proof of intent.
- [heuristic] When a past dispute is cited as motive, weigh how much time has passed and whether the parties still hold the feeling; old quarrels rarely prove a present motive. When: A past incident is used to explain a later act. Why: Motive needs continuing feeling and a plausible time link.
- [heuristic] Personal ties explain a witness's tone and omissions, but not the facts they report; judge the facts separately from the loyalties. Why: Loyalty bends emphasis, not the underlying events.
- [heuristic] A newly revealed personal relationship can give a previously cleared suspect a motive and send suspicion back to them. When: a late witness exposes a hidden affair or threat. Why: It supplies a motive that earlier evidence did not show.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the point where a matter changed hands. 2) Record the date and the authority involved at that point. 3) Use this as the anchor for judging who decided what. When: When tracing who was responsible for a decision in a multi-step process. Why: Handoffs mark the moment of decision, so they fix responsibility in time.
- [procedure] 1) List the names in an incidental record. 2) Match them to known family members. 3) Check whether the matches imply a relationship. 4) Confirm with a second record naming the same people. When: When establishing a family link from indirect evidence. Why: Matching names across independent documents tests whether a relationship is real rather than coincidental.
- [tradeoff] For a wealthy suspect, money may be an unlikely motive, so ask what standing or reputation they protect; yet wealth and influence can also give rivals reason to act. When: Judging motive for a wealthy or respected, prosperous suspect. Why: People often act to be thought well of; influence and wealth can give rivals reason to act. (x2)
- [pitfall] Reading a relationship as motive is a mistake; a close family or neighbour tie explains interest in the victim but is not evidence of guilt or proof of a reason to harm. (x2)
- [pitfall] A motive offered in a confession may protect someone else, so check whether it covers another person.
- [pitfall] Reading a shared household or kinship as motive is unsafe without evidence of an actual quarrel, since the tie alone does not show conflict. When: Inferring why a person accused another. Why: People who live together may share no grievance, and proximity alone can produce clusters of accusations.
- [pitfall] A witness who refuses to name a person blocks verification unless another source can supply the name. When: A witness protects a companion by withholding identity. Why: Without the name, the claimed person cannot be checked.
- [pitfall] A reputation for brilliance can make a team's own intuition harder to question, so its conclusions need the same verification as anyone else's.
- [fact] Motive is built from a person's history and circumstances, and the same circumstances can point to several suspects.
- [fact] A motive can be assembled from quarrels, money and social rank rather than from any act the accused actually committed.
- [fact] Relationships such as a forbidden courtship or a strong dislike can supply a motive by making one person a threat to another.

## staged scenes
- [definition] A staged death is a killing arranged to look self-inflicted so a pursuer or creditor believes the matter is closed; physical traces in the room can expose it. (x2)
- [definition] A staged death makes a living person appear dead using a substitute body and arranged circumstances, removing them from suspicion; the belief about the body's identity is the load-bearing assumption.
- [mechanism] A deliberate act can be disguised as an ordinary accident performed in plain view, so observers register only a careless mistake while the real preparation stays out of sight. When: an event must look random to observers but was engineered. Why: observers read a visible action at its surface meaning.
- [mechanism] A staged scheme breaks down when its parts contradict one another, such as conflicting reports, an unexplained extra item and a counter-plan that undercuts the cover. When: A cover story involves multiple parts maintained by one planner. Why: Each part must fit the others, and every added complication multiplies the chance of a contradiction.
- [mechanism] A culprit can construct a false sequence of events by placing a body and physical traces so they suggest an outsider's act. Each planted trace should follow from one fact the culprit controls. When: The culprit has the means to move or arrange the body and a clear reason to mislead investigators. Why: Each fabricated trace is anchored to a controllable fact, so the staging stays physically consistent with the faked timeline and route.
- [behavior] A reaction that recurs with the same triggers, such as a gaze starting it and a touch stopping it, suggests staging rather than an uncontrolled event. When: a reaction recurs with consistent triggers. Why: Consistent triggers suggest control.
- [rule] Let a planted false scene, such as a body with a note and weapon, be questioned by the player, with the official verdict open to overturn through contradictions. When: Designing a mystery with a misleading initial verdict. Why: The player can test the scene instead of accepting it.
- [rule] Make every staged event serve a stated purpose so that players can deduce the culprit from what the staging was meant to accomplish. When: Designing a mystery in which events are staged by a culprit. Why: Purpose-driven staging gives players a logical path to the solution.
- [rule] Plant staging clues in the same scene as the apparent crime, so the player can reread them after the reversal.
- [heuristic] To judge whether a scene's disorder is genuine, ask why it exists and who it is meant to convince. When: when examining a disturbed crime scene. Why: Staged disorder is aimed at an audience, so its intended reader reveals its purpose.
- [heuristic] A break made to look natural often differs between its two ends, such as one end frayed and the other cut clean. When: When a broken object appears to have failed under ordinary use. Why: Faking a natural failure on one end is hard to match on the other.
- [heuristic] Test whether a dropped item fell by accident; a staged drop can make a planted item look like a natural loss.
- [heuristic] A deliberate killer may build a false friendship beforehand and disguise the act as an accident, suicide, or another person's doing. When: Testing a premeditated-killing theory.
- [heuristic] A staged scene, such as a suicide with a note, makes players choose between a self-inflicted death and a staged killing, using the room as evidence. When: Designing a death scene the player must interpret.
- [heuristic] A confrontation can present evidence in stages so the audience assembles the chain of reasoning before the final reveal. When: Designing a climactic confrontation. Why: Visible steps make the final accusation feel earned.
- [heuristic] Signs of a staged scene include delayed replies, forged notes, absent witnesses, and items that imply they were prepared in advance. When: a reported theft or loss needs checking. Why: Advance preparation shows the loss was arranged rather than random.
- [heuristic] A scene that looks too neat was probably arranged for discovery; separate the items the planner meant to be found from those that betray the staging. When: A scene looks too neat or several explanations arise at once. Why: Staged evidence is designed to be noticed, so its neatness signals the planner's intent.
- [procedure] Reproduce the physical act yourself to measure how much strength, skill or practice it requires. When: a suspect's account of a physical act is in doubt.
- [procedure] 1) Check the symptoms against physical evidence. 2) Ask when the symptoms occur relative to the routine. 3) Ask who handles the room and when it goes unobserved. 4) Search where that routine creates a chance to hide something. When: a claimed condition conflicts with observations.
- [procedure] 1) Pick a time window tied to an external event. 2) Choose a substitute whose looks partly match the target. 3) Register the substitute's death under the target's name. 4) Time a public notice so the target finds the grave. When: When a culprit fakes a death to stop a search for a missing person. Why: A plausible death and fixed location halt the search.
- [procedure] 1) Present a staged object tied to the crime in front of the suspect. 2) Watch for an involuntary reaction. 3) Press the reaction as a clue rather than showing the object as direct evidence. When: a suspect is withholding a truth. Why: Guilty people often react to a crime-linked object they cannot hide reacting to.
- [pitfall] Stacking staging tricks, repeating a cue, or too many convenient coincidences makes the reveal feel contrived and the staging look authored by the writer, not the culprit. Why: Audiences notice engineered coincidence and stop believing the scene arose from the culprit's actions. (x2)
- [pitfall] Forced-entry signs, such as a torn fastening or scratched lock, can be staged to read as an outside intrusion; do not accept them at face value. When: When a locked space appears to have been forced open. Why: Investigators read damage as proof of entry, and staged marks match what a real break-in would leave.
- [pitfall] Overusing secret interventions makes outcomes seem arbitrary to the player.
- [pitfall] A staged injury or gag can make a victim look innocent, so ask what purpose the staging serves. When: Assessing a victim who appears to have been attacked. Why: Staging can be used to shape how others interpret events.
- [pitfall] A substitute matching only a few traits of the target will be exposed by any detailed description, and a cover tied to one location collapses if other places are checked. When: When a cover story relies on a substitute identity. Why: Detailed scrutiny reveals mismatches and records held in one town are fragile.
- [pitfall] A staged scene can be undone by an unplanned detail that the culprit failed to control. When: A deception relies on a staged scene. Why: Overlooked small facts break the illusion.
- [pitfall] A message-like event may have a convenient reading; do not accept it until it explains all the evidence, not just part of it.
- [fact] A display that seems natural to an unskilled arranger often looks too deliberate to a careful observer. Why: careful inspection exposes the artificiality.
- [fact] Staged darkness and a sedated victim can hide identity and perception, and the staging itself is evidence of intent.
- [fact] A mystery can present an apparent theft as real while the stolen goods are secretly displayed and left behind, reversing the crime's meaning for the reader.

## witness dating
- [behavior] A witness may give an earlier date for a recent transaction to move it away from the crime, reasoning that older matters draw less suspicion. When: A dated transaction is linked to a crime. Why: Older-seeming events are assumed to attract less suspicion.
- [rule] Record uncertain witness times as approximate values or ranges, such as around eleven or about midnight, so the timeline keeps its margin of error rather than false precision. When: When witnesses estimate times from memory, from other events, or give an approximate time. Why: Estimated times carry real margins of error, and false precision misleads later reasoning.
- [rule] Keep an in-world event log with dates and speakers, and let players build timelines from dated letters, rumours and proclamations by checking entries against each other. When: When designing investigation content spread across documents. Why: Players reconstruct the sequence themselves.
- [rule] Date in-world documents with write dates, hedged phrasing, and ink fade or page wear so players can catch backdated entries or later rewrites.
- [rule] Anchor a claimed whereabouts to in-world clocks or events so the claim can be checked. When: Designing timelines for suspect or NPC alibis. Why: Anchored claims can be verified against the world state.
- [rule] Stamp story events with in-game times so the player can assemble a timeline from journal entries or overheard conversations. When: a story unfolds over several in-game days or hours. Why: Timestamps let players order events they discover in different places.
- [heuristic] Dates recalled from memory are weaker than dates tied to a public signal; mark them approximate so a vague recollection is not treated as a precise timeline point. When: a witness gives a date without a public anchor. Why: Memory of when something happened is less reliable than an external marker, so the timeline should carry its own margin of error.
- [heuristic] A timestamped in-world journal lets the player build a timeline, but a self-serving or incomplete journal can mislead, so its entries should be checked against other sources.
- [heuristic] An approximate witness time, such as 'about three', is useful only after it has been tested against other anchors. When: a witness gives a rounded or estimated time. Why: Estimated times can be off, so they gain value only when confirmed.
- [heuristic] Present in-world newspapers or ledgers with timestamps so players can build a timeline of NPC movements and find where a claimed alibi breaks.
- [heuristic] When witness times are approximate, state a reconstructed sequence as a range rather than a single exact point. Why: Imprecise anchors cannot support a precise conclusion.
- [heuristic] Check an in-world letter's date against its supposed author's recorded location; a letter dated while that author is off-map is a clue that the document is false. When: Lore documents carry dates and an NPC has a travel log. Why: Authors cannot write from places they were not.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each witness's account separately. 2) Record only what each person saw and in what order. 3) Merge them into one timeline. 4) Mark the intervals no one witnessed. When: when several witnesses describe the same events. Why: the merged timeline shows where events lack any witness.
- [pitfall] A timeline built from memory is approximate, and a time given from memory can be wrong; verify critical times against dated records, such as a timetable. When: a witness reconstructs durations or dates. Why: Memory of time is imprecise.
- [pitfall] Dates recalled from memory can be wrong and distort the apparent pattern, so take dates from written, dated records.
- [pitfall] Treating approximate witness times as exact creates false certainty and can hide the window that decides an alibi, since small rounding errors erase it. When: a witness gives a rounded or vague time. Why: Small rounding errors can erase the window that matters.
- [pitfall] Approximate times such as 'nearly six' or 'about twenty-five minutes after ten' are estimates; small errors shift the whole sequence, so don't trust them as exact or trust an unknown clock. When: Building a timeline from witness-reported times. Why: Approximate or differently sourced times shift the apparent sequence, and small estimate errors can move every dependent conclusion.
- [pitfall] Treat stated clock times and watch checkpoints as approximate ranges, not exact proof, until a second source confirms them. When: Building a timeline from clocks, rounds, or a witness's recollection of times. Why: Clocks and patrol checks are imprecise, and recalled times are often wrong by a margin, so precise conclusions need corroboration.
- [pitfall] Narrator times and distances are often rough estimates, and second-hand details drift from the original, so they should not be treated as exact.
- [pitfall] Witness dates shift between tellings, so elapsed-time answers should be treated as ranges rather than exact dates. When: a witness gives an approximate time since an event. Why: recollected durations are imprecise and can change.
- [pitfall] An earlier event, weeks or months before, can be essential to a witness's chain, so timing must be checked across the whole span.
- [pitfall] Times estimated from memory can be off by minutes, which can decide whether a suspect could have arrived in time. When: A timeline relies on recalled estimates rather than fixed records.
- [pitfall] Treating an approximate body sign as an exact clock can build an alibi or accusation that collapses under cross-examination.
- [pitfall] A clock wound in haste or misset by an hour gives a systematically wrong time, so any event timed by it is off by that amount. When: When a time reading comes from a personal or hastily set clock. Why: A small setting error can make a timeline appear to contradict or support a theory.
- [pitfall] Recollections of when an activity ended are often wrong, so remembered times need verifying.
- [pitfall] A timeline built from one person's memory may contain wrong dates and invented causes, so it must be checked against other sources.
- [pitfall] Approximate times drift, so accepting one timeline too quickly can hide a gap between claims.
- [pitfall] Later retellings can misdate an order; check dates against records kept at the time. When: reconstructing when a ruling took effect.
- [fact] Times reconstructed from memory are vague, and witnesses often cannot say exactly when someone left. When: A witness is asked to date an event. Why: Human sense of elapsed time is approximate.
- [fact] Timeline reasoning is weak where no time records exist and every account depends on memory. When: no logs or stamped records are available. Why: memory-based accounts drift and cannot be compared precisely.
- [fact] Old records can give dates in ambiguous forms, such as split years, and these must be resolved before events are put in order. When: when placing events from historical documents in sequence. Why: Calendar conventions differed, so one date can have two readings.

## agreements and deals
- [mechanism] A reward offered to a rival in exchange for a hearing secures that rival's cooperation only for as long as the argument lasts.
- [mechanism] An agreeable question that the subject accepts and restates fixes their terms on record, so their commitments can be referred back to later.
- [mechanism] A weak person who finds a secret, is tempted by easy money, and grows greedy will overreach, be exposed, and may commit a desperate act before turning calm. When: designing a blackmail plot or an NPC under pressure. Why: Each demand raises pressure until the person reaches a breaking point.
- [mechanism] Once information leaves one desk, it can spread through connected organisations even without coordination, faster than anyone can recall it. When: A story passes between related outlets or departments. Why: Duplicate channels republish independently, so no single holder controls the spread.
- [mechanism] Release, reward, or a new role after a defection exposes a hidden scheme, because it shows what the switch gained. When: Designing a double agent or turncoat ally. Why: The payoff for the switch is a clue the player can reconstruct.
- [behavior] A recipient with no warning identifies an unexpected visitor from partial cues and prior assumptions, and forms plans about the visit before checking them. When: an unannounced visitor appears. Why: no time or information to verify identity and purpose.
- [rule] Make checks unannounced and at irregular times so the watched person cannot rehearse a false appearance. Why: Predictable visits let a subject prepare.
- [rule] Trust a physical profile only when several traits agree; overcommitting to one trait produces wrong conclusions.
- [rule] Use unequal payouts as a faction clue, pointing to the family or patron that the payment favored.
- [rule] Use an unannounced visit as a surprise only when the audience does not need to know the recipient's prior state.
- [heuristic] Give partner NPCs unequal stashes of compromising letters so an alliance breaks when one side holds more proof than the other. When: Designing a faction or accomplice alliance. Why: Imbalanced leverage makes betrayal a credible and discoverable outcome.
- [heuristic] A blackmailer who waits years before acting is unusual, so the delay can be used to test whether the blackmail claim is plausible. When: Assessing a claim of blackmail that has a long delay before any demand. Why: Blackmail typically follows soon after leverage exists, so long delays suggest the claim may be false.
- [heuristic] A witness who agrees with every party in turn carries no information about the facts. Why: Agreement with all sides is independent of the truth.
- [heuristic] A deal that unlocks a witness's full statement should let the player check it against logs or receipts. When: designing witness deals.
- [heuristic] Heirs who unanimously ask for an estate to be divided by an informal document signal trust and family harmony, though this does not prove fair dealing.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each person's account of the same place and overlapping times. 2) Align all accounts on one timeline. 3) Note disagreements and omissions. 4) Treat each gap as a lead to investigate. When: several people were in the same place at overlapping times. Why: A shared timeline exposes which accounts cannot be true together.
- [procedure] 1) Give a free item on the first visit. 2) On a repeat visit, let the visitor ask for more. 3) Then demand payment, so the player sees the concession and its cost.
- [tradeoff] Agreement between separate witnesses or confessions raises reliability, but shared bias, interest, or pressure can produce matching accounts; check whether sources are truly independent and test core claims apart from details. When: When witnesses or confessions confirm the same claim. Why: Independent sources support shared facts, while shared misconceptions, motives, or pressure can mimic independent confirmation. (x2)
- [pitfall] Threats or promises of penalties or rewards that cannot be enforced or delivered weaken pressure and expose the bluff; penalties deter only when actually enforced. (x2)
- [pitfall] A dealer or witness may not recall a sale, so records should back up memory.
- [pitfall] A reported fact may never reach the official who should act on it, so confirm that a report was followed up.
- [pitfall] A signal with no agreed meaning gives the watcher nothing to act on, and a repeated or missed signal delays the response.
- [pitfall] A deal struck before the witness is secured can be overtaken by events if the witness is interrupted or dies. When: Negotiating with a witness in a dangerous situation. Why: Events can end the witness's ability to deliver before the terms are fulfilled.
- [pitfall] An instruction given without confirmation can let an object slip away, because an ambiguous handoff creates a window for loss. When: when an object changes hands in a hurry.
- [pitfall] Offering a suspect terms in exchange for a confession carries risk to the investigator.
- [pitfall] Assuming an intermediary is the natural choice, such as a lawyer to draw up a will, can mislead; an unusual choice needs an explanation.
- [pitfall] If the player is expected to trace how news or rumour travelled, the transmission channel must be shown clearly, since vague or figurative explanations leave the route impossible to pin down. When: Designing how information moves between NPCs and locations. Why: Players cannot reconstruct a chain of knowledge that the game never shows.
- [pitfall] A confession obtained through a deal may be disputed later, so the terms should be recorded. When: Accepting a confession in exchange for an agreement. Why: Unrecorded terms are easy to contest afterward.
- [fact] Paying a blackmailer cannot end the threat, because the blackmailer keeps the secret and can sell it again.
- [fact] A conditional deal can be a dialogue choice whose consequences depend on whether the item is returned. When: Designing negotiation dialogue in a game.

## framing and planted evidence
- [model] Fabricated accounts gain trust through five devices: a named credible source, an intermediary, exclusivity, admitted editing, and concrete specifics.
- [definition] A frame is a false reconstruction of a past event, built from planted facts and withheld accounts, that shifts blame onto an innocent party.
- [mechanism] Plant evidence giving an innocent character both means and motive, such as revenge against someone with a grievance, so the true actor stays out of view. When: A scene needs a second suspect to draw attention from the real actor. Why: Planted items that fit a plausible motive can redirect suspicion.
- [mechanism] A framer picks a target with suspicious circumstances, such as debts or hidden attachments, and supplies a story that explains the evidence, so the false case is built from partly true pieces. When: Someone wants suspicion to fall on an innocent party. Why: Partly true evidence makes the false conclusion harder to detect.
- [mechanism] A false suspicion that is acted on costs something, such as a lost ally or wasted time, so wrong inferences have consequences.
- [mechanism] Actions an accused person takes after a frame can read as guilt, so the frame strengthens as the person responds. When: A framed character acts to defend themselves. Why: Staged context reinterprets innocent acts.
- [mechanism] Give a character a visible false motive, and place the true motive on a separate trail the player must find to see the real plan. When: A character's known grudge could explain the events. Why: A visible motive absorbs suspicion.
- [mechanism] An expected gain can be tied to a feared future change, such as a new will after a rival relationship forms, which raises the motive.
- [mechanism] A culprit can steer an investigator toward a false suspect by feeding an existing grudge, so the suggestion feels confirmed and attention leaves the real secret. When: The investigator already holds a suspicion about someone. Why: Confirmation of a prior belief makes the false lead feel reliable.
- [rule] Lure an NPC away with a fabricated message or invented story whose real purpose is the absence; give the player a limited window before the NPC returns. When: designing a timed search puzzle. Why: A false pretext removes the NPC from the scene without a hard block.
- [rule] Let an unsigned note in a dungeon push players toward a particular NPC, even when the note is a lie.
- [rule] Before using a false or partly invented accusation, weigh the harm it could do to an innocent person and to bystanders who may take the words as fact. Why: listeners may treat the speaker's words as established fact.
- [rule] Use gossip or rumour items to supply false motives that the player must weigh against physical evidence such as signs of violence or messages at the scene. When: designing red herring story items. Why: players must test motives against proof.
- [rule] A frame needs a stated motive and a believable chain of evidence. Without a motive, planted items look arbitrary. When: when constructing a false implication against someone. Why: motive gives the planted items a reason to exist.
- [rule] Treat a frame-up as a hypothesis to test, not as a default explanation for every case. Why: Most cases with strong evidence are not staged.
- [heuristic] Treat a relative's complaint or serious accusation as a claim with possible private motive, not as proof of intent or truth. When: A relative complains about an estate division or makes a serious accusation. Why: Grievances are often voiced as bluster, and family ties give the accuser access and believability while grudges can drive the claim. (x2)
- [heuristic] Planted evidence may be fabricated if it seems too convenient, sits oddly, or shows fresh scarring or a timing mismatch that a careful examiner finds; check how it got there. When: Evidence seems to point neatly at one person. Why: A framer places items where the blame will land.
- [heuristic] A real object or signal can be turned against an innocent character, so suspicion falls on someone who did not commit the act. When: when designing suspicion among NPCs. Why: Players must weigh competing evidence, which makes the framing a meaningful test.
- [heuristic] A reported sighting that cannot be true may be invented, and the invention itself points toward the fabricator's motive. When: a sighting conflicts with physical or timing facts. Why: a false report is made to serve a purpose.
- [heuristic] Charge an official with deliberately letting offenders escape only on the strongest evidence; hidden shielding by subordinates is usually the more plausible explanation. Why: Deliberate complicity is a heavier charge than suppression by intermediaries.
- [procedure] 1) Leave an incriminating item where the suspect's household will find it. 2) Remove items that point back at the framer or reveal intent. 3) Erase traces that would clear the suspect. 4) Lock the door so the household seems to have sealed it. When: A culprit wants an investigation to target a chosen suspect. Why: Selective traces steer the investigation.
- [procedure] 1) Show the framing threat on the page. 2) Let the player see the plan forming. 3) Spring the trap only after the threat is visible. When: Escalating mid-game tension around a possible frame-up. Why: A visible plan makes the trap feel earned and lets the player act before it closes.
- [procedure] 1) Show the killer buying or preparing the tools early. 2) Place planted evidence where a plausible suspect will find it. 3) Reveal the purpose of the preparations only after the frame takes hold. When: when designing a frame-up plot. Why: Preparations shown early make the later frame legible on reflection, and the planted evidence arises from the game's own logic.
- [pitfall] Claimed visions and unverifiable testimony can be invented, e.g. by a skilled deceiver showing innocent people to halt pursuit; check the gap between claim and source. When: when a source of testimony cannot be checked. Why: Nothing in the report can expose a staged or invented vision.
- [pitfall] Reports can build a false impression of activity or contact even when the sources behind them have no real knowledge of it. When: when press reports are used as evidence. Why: Parties with a stake in an outcome can shape what is published.
- [pitfall] A confident public account that offers a false motive can spread quickly and be taken as true, even when its facts only repeat unverified memory.
- [pitfall] Too much staged noise makes a trail look accidental rather than planned, weakening the misdirection. Why: Excessive disturbance reads as chaos instead of deliberate design.
- [fact] A framed person can appear guilty through motive, testimony and circumstance until a late fact overturns the reading. When: An innocent person is set up to take the blame. Why: Each piece of evidence fits the false story when read alone.
- [fact] A person facing financial crime may fake their death to escape pursuit and later enjoy the proceeds in safety. When: someone is under threat of prosecution for money crimes. Why: a presumed death ends the pursuit.
- [fact] A respectable surface can conceal wrongdoing from observers and from the wrongdoer, so a polished image does not reveal what lies beneath.

## ledger and financial records
- [mechanism] A late annotation added to a document can change how the earlier text reads, producing a twist at the end.
- [mechanism] A player-facing ledger of payments shows which NPCs have been paid, giving clues about who is under pressure and who might talk. When: when the player can track bribes or payments made to NPCs. Why: Visible payment history reveals both pressure points and loyalty risks.
- [rule] Read each receipt item for what it shows about time, place, money and the kind of establishment, not only whether it matches what you searched for.
- [rule] Design unexplained transfers and matching amounts between NPC payment logs to reveal hidden payments and relationships, rewarding players who compare ledgers. When: Designing financial clues in a game. Why: Unexplained entries invite the player to trace hidden flows.
- [rule] A late reveal that clears an earlier suspect should force the player to update their notes and assumptions. When: designing mid to late reversals. Why: revised assumptions keep the reveal meaningful.
- [rule] Use a late document or epilogue to explain the full plot logic and show why earlier red herrings misled, once the audience has the whole picture. Why: hindsight makes earlier misdirection visible.
- [rule] Log each item's handover in a shop or guild ledger so players can reconstruct where an object went.
- [rule] Let a later recorded entry contradict an NPC's earlier statement or action, so players can expose it by laying out the calendar. When: Designing a mystery with contradicted testimony.
- [heuristic] Use this check when a claim rests on a recomputable number, scientific principle or observer viewpoint; it is weak if the checker lacks reference knowledge.
- [heuristic] In a ledger most entries are routine, so an entry whose amount breaks the pattern stands out as a clue.
- [heuristic] Dated merchant or guild ledgers can tie an NPC's employment or payroll to the moment of a theft. When: when designing guild or merchant records for a mystery. Why: Dated records connect people to events in time.
- [heuristic] Treat a mismatch between a shipping receipt and actual arrival as evidence, not clerical error.
- [heuristic] A later document can override an earlier one, so the outcome may depend on which paper a court accepts. When: Two documents with different terms compete. Why: Later transfers or deeds may reflect a more recent or more valid decision.
- [heuristic] A late document that contradicts an earlier court ruling can signal a settled grievance, but that reading is an interpretation, not proof of motive. When: A character's final will or letter defies a legal outcome.
- [heuristic] Ledgers, bills and sudden withdrawals can show who has been paid and when, so check them against other evidence. When: when investigating hush money or a motive tied to finances. Why: Financial trails record transfers that a witness may not reveal.
- [procedure] 1) Ask for a relevant independent record, such as a ledger, catalogue or sale record. 2) Read its entries closely. 3) Note which entries support and which contradict the witness's account. When: when a witness's means or behavior can be documented, or a verbal account can be compared to ledgers, catalogues or sale records. Why: Long-running records are costly to alter consistently; records can confirm or refute claims.
- [procedure] 1) Take the claimed distance or size. 2) Divide it by the stated magnifying power or scale factor. 3) Compare the result with what an observer could actually resolve. When: a claim rests on a number that can be recomputed.
- [procedure] 1) Find the document that sets a financial motive. 2) Recalculate its value under current conditions. 3) Use the recalculated figure, not the original, to judge motive. When: A suspect's motive rests on income or property. Why: Market or price changes can shift a payout far from its nominal figure.
- [metric] The size of a court bond gives a rough measure of how large a person's personal estate was. When: estimating personal wealth from probate records. Why: A bond is set relative to the estate's value.
- [pitfall] Later-written sources can place events at dates the records do not allow, or compress and misplace them, so treat their dates as claims to check even when aligned across sources. Why: Later accounts may compress or misplace events.
- [pitfall] Reading an inheritance only for totals and missing the survivorship clause leads to wrong conclusions about who gains from each death. When: when analyzing a will or contract that shifts shares. Why: the clause that changes shares as people die is easy to overlook.
- [pitfall] A ledger records costs, not causes, so reading it as a complete account of an event overstates what it shows.
- [pitfall] Later additions and repairs change a building's appearance, so separate original fabric from later alterations before dating it.
- [pitfall] A name written later in a different hand reflects a later reader's belief, not the original author.
- [pitfall] A later public repudiation of an earlier role does not erase that role; the earlier participation stays open to judgment. When: a participant later disavows past actions. Why: a late change of stance is not a full cleanup of the record.
- [fact] A torn-out cheque leaves its stub blank, because the amount was written on the removed leaf rather than the stub.
- [fact] A bank account acts as a compressed record of movements, since a payment shows where money went and can identify a connected person. Why: Financial transactions expose relationships and destinations.
- [fact] A pale line added after a finished letter suggests the writer returned to the page later rather than writing in one burst. Why: a second writing session leaves a distinct mark.
- [fact] A bearer instrument is payable to whoever presents it, so possession alone allows money to be collected.
- [fact] Charge-waiver thresholds on absent days turn a per-day billing ledger into a timeline of a guest's absence. When: a hotel or service waives charges after a set number of days away. Why: Billed and waived days record when the guest was not present.

## loose talk and leaks
- [mechanism] A public briefing that discloses only accurate facts and withholds witness testimony can lull a guilty party into false security. When: when investigators want to buy room to work. Why: the guilty party relaxes and acts less carefully.
- [mechanism] A bulletin board or rumor system can expose a player's private actions, and the details in each note can reveal which NPCs were present. When: Designing public rumor or notice systems. Why: Public notes carry details that reveal the observers' positions.
- [behavior] Unguarded speakers who vent, complain or boast while believing no one is listening let slip grievances, money complaints and facts such as times. When: A witness is complaining or boasting, or believes they are alone. Why: Their guard is down, so they say more than they would in company. (x2)
- [behavior] A suspect may reveal guilt through an unprompted remark that shows knowledge only the culprit could have. When: A suspect has partial knowledge and is questioned on a related topic. Why: Knowledge slips out when the suspect is not guarding that detail.
- [behavior] A slip can betray a hidden purpose when the listener is reading the speaker closely and the speaker accepts a question as shared experience. When: a listener probes a character's assumptions. Why: the slip reveals knowledge or feeling the speaker tried to keep back.
- [behavior] A trusted confidant may receive a disclosure and accept it as a plain fact without comment. When: a secret is shared with a trusted person. Why: trust makes disclosure feel ordinary.
- [behavior] Players often accept an odd detail that comes with a brief, offhand explanation and move on without probing its real purpose. When: an unusual item or action is given a dismissive, plausible reason. Why: a casual explanation seems to close the question.
- [behavior] Investigators tend to suspect people whose earlier remarks seem sinister, which makes them easy targets for planted evidence. When: a suspect has made an earlier controversial statement. Why: Prior impressions bias which person is considered suspicious.
- [rule] Record suspect and witness statements word for word, so exact phrasing can be read back or compared later. When: Conducting interviews whose accounts may be checked later. Why: Paraphrase loses the details that reveal contradictions.
- [rule] Introduce a minor character or detail casually early; later show why it mattered when the player revisits that thread. When: Designing clues that seem trivial when first introduced. Why: Delayed significance rewards players who remember and revisit earlier details; significance often depends on corroboration arriving afterward.
- [rule] Let a confidante NPC reveal secrets only after the player earns trust, and mark those secrets as testimony. When: when designing a confidante NPC. Why: Trust gates information and gives it evidential weight.
- [rule] Raise a confidant's rivalry or loyalty once, then let it return when the related character's name draws a suspicious look. When: Writing secondary characters with ties to suspects. Why: Reintroduced loyalties add suspicion without new exposition.
- [rule] Use an NPC's silence in a bulletin or feed to hint at coming events without confirming them. When: Designing news or notice feeds in a game world. Why: Absence hints at change while keeping uncertainty.
- [rule] Give a confidant NPC who supplies an alibi a reason to protect someone, so players must weigh the testimony. When: designing alibi-giving NPCs. Why: motive turns the alibi into a judgment call rather than a plain fact.
- [rule] When a detail appears in public that its owners denied supplying, treat the leak as a question to trace to its source rather than a closed matter. When: Private case details appear in press or public reports. Why: Denials do not rule out leaks from anyone with access elsewhere.
- [heuristic] A belief voiced casually early can later shape how the audience reads a related object or event, when it is recalled at the right moment.
- [heuristic] A chance companion, such as a stranger who knows a family's lawyer, can supply facts about debts, inheritance and heirs.
- [heuristic] Share a sensitive fact only with people who cannot be kept from learning it otherwise, since shared confidences spread beyond the intended circle. When: when deciding whom to tell a secret. Why: Information reaches people who cannot be excluded.
- [heuristic] A plan can advance through a seemingly casual meeting that a natural occasion explains, with trust built across several steps. When: an outsider needs access to a household or group. Why: each contact looks ordinary alone, so the plan goes unnoticed.
- [heuristic] A hint dropped in a careless tone may be deliberate, so the listener must decide whether it was meant.
- [heuristic] A captive who cannot speak openly can leave a sign that means nothing to captors but is meaningful to a partner who knows their habits.
- [heuristic] Place a casual NPC comment or ambient detail naming a location from a document the player has read, so it links two threads of the story. Why: A small, offhand connection can make the player see a link between separate leads.
- [heuristic] Let NPCs repeat dialogue exactly so players can compare versions and catch contradictions. When: Designing NPCs whose statements may later be tested for consistency. Why: Identical wording gives the player a fixed reference for detecting changes or lies.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a witness to repeat a written or spoken statement several times. 2) Compare the versions word for word. 3) Fix the exact wording for analysis once it stays unchanged. When: A written or spoken statement is central evidence and its author is defensive or unknown. Why: Identical repetition shows whether the witness recalls a fixed text or rebuilds a story each time.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness repeat the exact key questions and answers. 2) Record the wording verbatim. 3) Compare it with the relayed summary before accepting it. When: When fixing testimony that passed through intermediaries. Why: A paraphrase can shift meaning.
- [procedure] 1) Have an intermediary raise the topic casually. 2) Watch the listener's face and answer. 3) Follow up gently later on any omission. When: The witness is open to talk, or the questioner wants to avoid signalling interest.
- [pitfall] Letting one's own knowledge spread through casual conversation alerts the culprit to what is known.
- [pitfall] A sympathetic confidant can leak a private plan without meaning to, especially when trying to offer reassurance.
- [pitfall] Treating a casual remark as settled testimony is a common error; asides need checking before they count as facts.
- [fact] A confidante who has long shared a household's private matters can serve as a witness to them. When: when a character has heard household secrets over time.

## reveal design
- [model] A layered misattribution twist runs through a trusted party's setup, a false culprit, a contradiction, an empty reward, a reinterpretation, and a final reversal of the culprit. When: Designing a mystery with several reveals. Why: Each stage explains the previous one, so the player's beliefs about guilt and reward shift together.
- [definition] A two-stage twist first makes the player accept a supernatural explanation, then reveals a mundane living cause beneath it, so each resolved belief opens a second, plainer one.
- [mechanism] Uneven heating reveals some marks before others, so partial clues appear first and invite the investigator to repeat the action.
- [mechanism] Revealing background facts gradually through interviews changes which suspect looks plausible, so each conversation can shift the leading suspect.
- [mechanism] A reversal that re-reads an object the audience has already seen collapses the first solution and makes the final answer feel earned. When: designing a mystery reveal. Why: The audience already holds the evidence, so the new reading feels fair rather than invented.
- [mechanism] Layer reveals so each depends on the previous one: once the alibi trick is known, a second cover-up becomes explicable. Why: Chained dependence makes the later reveal follow from the first.
- [behavior] A culprit careful in one respect may be careless in another, so each category of trace should be judged separately. When: evidence shows mixed care across different traces. Why: Care is rarely uniform across all actions.
- [behavior] Doubt about unverifiable testimony spread slowly and unevenly: some kept a general belief yet refused specific accusations, while others stayed firm.
- [rule] Make reveals fair by planting visible partial clues earlier, even if a mask or role hid the person; show how any framed suspect's trail was built. Why: Audiences can reconsider earlier scenes once the clue is visible, and an unbuilt frame feels unfair. (x2)
- [rule] Let the player's action drive the climax: stage the confrontation with suspects present so the player produces the proof, and trigger the arrest by the player's signal, not a cutscene. When: designing the final confrontation or sequence of a mystery. Why: Player-produced proof and player-triggered arrest make the resolution feel earned.
- [rule] Resolve several earlier unexplained clues in one explanatory scene, such as how the killer entered, why an object was taken and why an innocent suspect looked guilty. When: writing the climax of a mystery with many planted clues or open threads. Why: One explanation tying clues together is more satisfying than piecemeal explanations.
- [rule] Avoid questions that assume the answer or ask about what the witness cannot know, since they may be blocked or struck.
- [rule] Give players two plausible suspects supported by different clues, so the witness they choose to question decides which theory survives. When: designing a choice between leads. Why: the player's choice tests the rival theories.
- [rule] Use a mid-game reveal in which NPCs who accepted an early claim are shown the gap in it. When: an early claim was accepted without verification. Why: Exposing the gap rewards players who questioned the claim and changes NPC standing.
- [rule] Make a mystery's reveal a physical breach or exposure of the mechanism, so the answer is shown directly rather than only described. When: Staging the reveal of a hidden mechanism. Why: Seeing the mechanism makes the answer concrete and self-verifying.
- [rule] Pair a closing theory with concrete events the player witnessed, and end the reveal with a concrete explanation of the main threat. When: Ending a level's reveal. Why: Concrete grounding makes the explanation satisfying.
- [heuristic] Source a second reveal from a witness whose silence was deliberate, withholding the secret until a late account such as a deathbed confession. When: a story needs a late reveal after earlier answers. Why: a motivated silence keeps the secret hidden without breaking credibility.
- [heuristic] Narrow the distance between two suspects in stages, with each clue moving suspicion closer to the real link, without naming the link until the late reveal. When: Structuring a mystery where the answer is one hidden person. Why: Gradual narrowing keeps the audience engaged while the final connection feels earned rather than abrupt.
- [heuristic] Hold an out-of-scheme motive back for a late reveal, so players who reason only from familiar categories are surprised. When: Designing the final twist of a mystery. Why: Players who trust the categories have no box for the true motive.
- [heuristic] Make a large reveal checkable through concrete, verifiable links such as dates or events, so a surprising claim feels fair. When: When delivering a major revelation. Why: Verifiable details lend credibility to claims that would otherwise seem arbitrary.
- [heuristic] Force proof at the reveal through a lure, a staged appearance, or an open admission.
- [procedure] 1) Give the audience the same clues the solver has, showing each before the reveal. 2) Confront the suspect with the clues in order. 3) State the decisive reversal last, once it follows from them. When: building a late or final-act reveal that must feel fair in hindsight. Why: Clues shown in order let the audience recognise the reversal once named and check the solution against facts it already holds.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the accuser's version convincingly. 2) Plant a checkable clue earlier, such as a recalled voice or phrase. 3) Have the investigator name the true culprit with it, exposing the accuser and reframing earlier scenes. 4) Let the physical outcome follow the investigator's word. When: designing a late twist where a character takes credit for or falsely accuses others. Why: A reversal set up by earlier clues feels earned, while an unsupported one feels arbitrary.
- [procedure] 1) Overturn the expected identity through a sworn statement or testimony. 2) Follow with a confession that explains the disguise, substitutions and method in order.
- [procedure] 1) Build each reveal layer on its own proof. 2) Make the first proof a documentary record. 3) Make the second a physical clue, such as a portrait. 4) Make the last a confession.
- [pitfall] A reveal resting on surprise alone, a detail or culprit first shown at revelation, feels cheap or unfair; plant it earlier so the audience can reconsider prior scenes. When: writing identity reversals or any late reveal. Why: The audience cannot reconsider earlier scenes without the clue. (x2)
- [pitfall] Revealing the aim, evidence or culprit early alerts the subject, who can prepare a consistent false account or lose the chance of an unguarded slip; hold details and hints until confrontation. When: planning when to show evidence or hints to a suspect or the audience. Why: A suspect who knows the evidence can prepare a consistent false account, and early hints weaken the reveal.
- [pitfall] A search that appears unfair can turn the group against the investigator and provoke protest. When: Conducting a search of a group. Why: People resist searches they see as unequal or unjust.
- [pitfall] A reveal that jumps to a conclusion without intermediate reasoning feels unfair to the audience or player.
- [pitfall] A private fact that looks minor alone can favour one theory over another, so members tend to underrate what they hold. Why: a fact's bearing often depends on other facts that only show up when combined.

## testimony, claims and memory
- [definition] Unverifiable testimony is a claim about something only the reporter says they perceived, such as a vision or unseen presence, that no one else can confirm.
- [mechanism] A claimant NPC can be introduced as an unverified lead with a registry object the player checks to confirm or rule out the claim. When: Designing NPC identity claims the player must verify. Why: A checkable record turns a rumour into a testable question.
- [behavior] A listener who believes they are unseen reacts more honestly than one who knows they are being watched. When: A hidden listener is within earshot of a staged conversation. Why: A person who thinks they are unobserved drops their guard.
- [behavior] A witness may feel strongly threatened yet be unable to name the threat or any act behind it, so the fear alone is not evidence. When: a witness reports dread with no specifics. Why: Fear can be felt before its cause is understood.
- [rule] Treat a claim that cannot be checked against any other source, with only witnesses' reports as the record, as unverified rather than established. (x2)
- [rule] Treat unverifiable testimony, such as visions seen only by the afflicted, as grounds for suspicion, not proof, especially when the accuser's reactions are read as evidence. When: the vision cannot be physically checked. Why: private perception cannot be confirmed by others.
- [rule] Let an NPC report a sound or sighting the player cannot verify, and provide a timer or event log so the player can judge its reliability. When: designing NPC testimony in a game. Why: A checkable record lets players weigh the report instead of accepting or rejecting it outright.
- [rule] Keep a witness claim open rather than accepting it when the claimed evidence cannot be found on search, however sincere the witness.
- [rule] Do not treat a denial as established until other statements or physical traces have been compared with it. When: a denial is the main claim on a point. Why: A denial alone is only a claim.
- [rule] Keep a speaker's claims about their own name or home marked as statements until independent evidence confirms them.
- [rule] Do not let a list of points against a suspect harden into a verdict before each entry has been tested. When: an investigator compiles a list of accusations. Why: listed claims are only unverified until checked.
- [rule] A claimed blackout is hard to disprove, so treat it as an unverifiable gap rather than as a lie. When: a witness claims to have lost memory of an evening.
- [rule] Give NPCs confident but unverified opinions so the player must decide what to trust. When: designing dialogue for investigation.
- [rule] Treat information from a source that cannot be re-questioned, or that remembers nothing of giving it, as an unverified clue until outside evidence supports it. When: The source is a trance, oracle or other subject with no recall. Why: The source cannot confirm or correct its own account.
- [heuristic] Feelings such as anger or guilt are hard to check directly, so weigh how well each account fits the other facts. When: A testimony rests on a speaker's inner state. Why: Inner states leave few observable traces, so fit with other facts becomes the best test.
- [heuristic] A narrator with no stake in the outcome, whose account is confirmed by other evidence, needs less testing.
- [heuristic] When an official says a message was received but cannot name where a reply should go, flag the gap and treat the claim as unverified.
- [heuristic] Do not plan evidence around a witness's memory returning, since recovery can come suddenly at an unpredictable time. When: A key witness has lost recall. Why: Recovery cannot be timed.
- [heuristic] A sincere but emotionally primed account is weak evidence; treat it as grounds for suspicion rather than as proof.
- [procedure] 1) Treat an unverifiable claim only as a lead. 2) Open an inquiry into the accused's life. 3) Require independent corroboration before any verdict. When: An accusation rests on a private perception.
- [tradeoff] Admitting unverifiable testimony lets a case proceed, but leaves anyone open to accusation without checks. When: a rule-holder decides whether to accept unverifiable testimony.
- [pitfall] Witnesses or evidence holders who cannot testify openly or be questioned again, such as through failing health or dying, cannot be tested; the result rests on agreement or narrator's judgment. Why: Untested evidence cannot be verified, so its effect depends on the agreement around it.
- [pitfall] An unverified claim can shape the questioner's theory even after it has been shown to be false. Why: early assumptions persist after correction.
- [pitfall] A story about a third party who cannot be found is impossible to verify and must be tested before it supports a conclusion.
- [pitfall] Pressing a witness without independent evidence gains little, because repeated denial costs the witness almost nothing. When: the questioner has no independent evidence. Why: denial is cheap for the witness.
- [pitfall] Accepting an account whose supporting records are lost or unverifiable means the account rests on the teller alone.
- [pitfall] Accepting a claim that someone would have noticed an intruder, without asking about line of sight or the noise a person would make, can hide an opportunity. When: when a witness claims they would have noticed. Why: Lack of sight or quiet movement can allow access without detection.
- [pitfall] Acting on an unverified report can alert the suspect or waste time.
- [pitfall] A person claiming to know someone's hours may be bluffing, so the claim should be checked against other sources.
- [pitfall] A statement that is filed but never re-examined shows what was said, not whether it was true. Why: recording a claim does not test it.

## access and opportunity
- [mechanism] Evidence against one suspect is weakened when another party had access to the same spot shortly before. When: Assessing a clue tied to a single location. Why: Another person's presence offers an alternative explanation for the trace.
- [rule] Use a guardian's absence to open a window for an NPC's act, and let players learn its timing from clues, so the act can be anticipated and observation is rewarded. When: designing a scripted act an NPC performs while a guardian or boss is away. Why: Learnable timing lets players and detectives infer the act from the absence and anticipate it in hindsight.
- [rule] Let a later clue challenge the access premise so the suspect shortlist can change. When: the player builds a suspect shortlist from access. Why: A premise that can be overturned keeps the shortlist open to revision.
- [rule] Test whether a person could approach a victim unnoticed by checking the physical evidence against medical testimony. When: When access to a victim is in question. Why: Physical and medical facts constrain what was possible.
- [rule] Eliminating a suspect by access does not prove innocence; it only removes that person from those who could have acted.
- [rule] Use key or access tokens to narrow the suspect list, so only NPCs holding a given key remain in the frame.
- [rule] Encode a site's access limits, such as no vehicle route, in NPC dialogue so players can deduce them and use them in a later puzzle.
- [rule] Keep every access route open until it has been tested, and reject only the routes that are truly impossible. When: When investigating how an event could have happened. Why: Dismissing routes early can exclude the one that actually occurred.
- [heuristic] Test a claimed entry route by checking whether it was visible from the road or locked at the time.
- [heuristic] Tracing where a concealed means came from, such as a social circle, points toward people who had access to it.
- [heuristic] Make the access check a required sub-goal that gates the final accusation. When: designing the endgame of a mystery.
- [heuristic] Rule out a hiding place by checking whether physical access to it is possible, given the observed state of doors and paths. When: when testing whether something could be hidden in a room. Why: Physical access can make a hiding place implausible.
- [heuristic] Narrow an access inquiry by asking where the item was kept, what lay beside it, and which person carried each item, moving from location to handling.
- [heuristic] List everyone who entered a room after an event and narrow the suspect field to that list. When: an event occurred in a room with controlled access. Why: only people who entered could have changed the scene.
- [procedure] 1) Order the events in sequence and mark each window in which an item could have changed hands, such as between the last sighting and a fixed event. 2) List who had access within each window. 3) Test each person against it. When: A crime must have occurred within a narrow time span, or the sequence must be reconstructed before naming a suspect. Why: A bounded window narrows the set of people who could have acted; restricting attention to access windows narrows the field of suspects.
- [procedure] 1) Identify what opening the object without force requires. 2) List every holder of that secret and every route by which it could leak. 3) Cross the list with routine facts. When: A protected object opens with no sign of forced entry and few people could know the secret. Why: Access lists narrow suspects to those who could actually have acted.
- [procedure] 1) Describe the route room by room: connecting rooms, which door opens onto which path, and the target's position. 2) For each candidate, ask whether they could pass unseen. 3) Include furniture as sight blockers. 4) Test every candidate against the same route. When: a crime requires a person to move through a space unseen.
- [procedure] 1) List every lock or barrier guarding the target. 2) Name who holds each key or access item. 3) Check for unrecorded duplicates. 4) Track whether each item left its holder's possession. When: a mystery involves keys or restricted entry. Why: Access chains reduce the suspect pool to those who could physically reach the target.
- [procedure] 1) List each person's absence times, such as days off and return times. 2) Record who holds each key and when it is used. 3) Check each store's position relative to windows and routes. 4) Shortlist those who could reach the item in that window. When: when identifying who could reach a restricted item before naming a suspect. Why: schedules and layout define who had access and when.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm no published or circulated report existed that the speaker could have read. 2) Check whether the speaker's detail exceeds those reports. 3) If so, infer presence or access. When: deciding whether a speaker was present at an event. Why: The inference fails if written reports were available to him.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the time window when an object could be tampered with, between its delivery and its first use. 2) Use routines and watch records to narrow when the target was vulnerable. 3) List everyone with access during that window. When: An object passes through several hands before it is used and suspects must be narrowed. Why: A bounded window with a list of access holders reduces the field of suspects.
- [procedure] 1) List who holds keys or access to the location. 2) Compare access rules with the real routines of those people. 3) Check whether any person with access could act unseen. When: When a closed-access claim seems to rule out human involvement. Why: Stated restrictions often hide a second route or a person who can act.
- [procedure] 1) Take an impression of the key without drawing attention. 2) Have a duplicate made. 3) Enter without changing the keeper's routine. When: Access to a locked space must avoid alerting its keeper. Why: Covert duplication keeps the keeper's routine unchanged.
- [tradeoff] Access narrows suspects when entry is restricted or recorded, since the culprit must have lived in the building or stayed overnight; where a place is open to all visitors with no records, access adds little. When: deciding whether to analyse entry and exit, or building a suspect list. Why: A culprit without access cannot commit the crime; without records or restrictions, access does not narrow the suspects.
- [pitfall] Having the ability or opportunity to reach an object or location does not show that a person acted; keep access separate from motive and evidence of action. When: a suspect had the means to be present but no proven act. Why: Many people can reach the same object, so access alone narrows little; opportunity alone does not establish involvement. (x2)
- [pitfall] Access narrows possible actors but identifies no one; moving from who could handle an object to who took it, without a witness or trail, yields only suspicion.
- [pitfall] Elimination by access rests on the premise that only insiders could act; if that premise is wrong, the whole shortlist is wrong.
- [fact] Close access to events does not guarantee an accurate account, since a well-placed witness can still be wrong or biased. Why: Position gives opportunity to know, not proof that the knowledge is correct.
- [fact] Who holds a key, which door a person uses, and how a household runs all reveal who has access to a place. When: when establishing who could have been present at a scene. Why: Access control and routine define the set of possible actors.

## clue design and reveal
- [mechanism] A clue can sit in plain view as an ordinary detail and become meaningful only once its underlying mechanism is understood. When: A means of harm is carried openly by a person as a tool, item of dress or familiar gesture. Why: The ordinary context makes the object read as décor, so recognition arrives only after the mechanism is revealed.
- [rule] Before a reveal, show the chain of earlier clues and draw only on that evidence in a short reversal, so players can rebuild the solution. Why: The reversal reads as fair deduction rather than invention, and players must be able to rebuild the solution from clues they already saw. (x2)
- [rule] State the decisive clue in plain text within the account before the final explanation, so the player can connect it at reveal. When: Withholding the method of a reveal, or designing a twist that relies on a fact the player already holds. Why: A clue never shown makes the explanation feel like a trick; a twist is fair only if the player had the information needed to work it out. (x2)
- [rule] Make a prior investigator's known conviction and its blind spot visible, so the player knows which question is still open.
- [rule] Show a character's reaction to a sensitive topic without revealing its cause, so the clue stays open for the player to interpret. Why: An unexplained reaction keeps the mystery active and invites the player to test theories.
- [rule] Signal that an answer is near, such as through a changed environment or rising sound, to build suspense before the reveal.
- [rule] Show the consequences of solving a case in the game world, such as factions changing behaviour or rewards being given.
- [rule] Show players which argument moved which NPC, rewarding those who learn each character's reasoning.
- [rule] Show a rationalizing NPC's reasoning alongside the raw observation, so players can see where the explanation goes beyond the evidence.
- [rule] Let a shrine or statue point away from a hidden chamber, with the real entrance placed elsewhere. When: Designing a hidden location tied to a visible landmark. Why: Misdirection rewards players who check the landmark against other clues.
- [rule] A fair-play clue must supply both the reference needed to decode it and the link between them, so the player can solve it with information the story provides. When: when the solution depends on a fact the player can verify within the game. Why: a clue without a decoding path frustrates players rather than rewarding them.
- [rule] Build a confirming check, such as a mirror or second witness, into a discovery so the player tests the clue before acting on it.
- [heuristic] Side plots can pace a mystery and hide the real line of inquiry, provided the true clues remain fair.
- [heuristic] Signpost withheld entries or cut passages so players know a gap exists rather than assuming the record is complete. When: A narrator's account or journal is deliberately incomplete. Why: Visible gaps prevent players from trusting an incomplete record.
- [heuristic] Re-read the same evidence from another suspect's viewpoint, since identical facts can carry a different meaning. When: Investigation has fixed on a single suspect. Why: A single viewpoint can lock the investigator onto one reading.
- [heuristic] When a witness signals a gap, treat the account as incomplete and gather indirect evidence instead of waiting for the witness to disclose. When: a witness starts to speak then stops or avoids a subject.
- [heuristic] Older favourites left on shelves mark earlier stages of interest, while recent titles and a concentration on one subject show current interests.
- [heuristic] Put the final missing link in a place the player has already visited but not searched. When: Placing the last clue of a mystery. Why: Revisiting a known location rewards attention without adding new travel.
- [heuristic] A clue that makes sense only in hindsight must be planted earlier so it can be recognized when later facts arrive. When: When designing clues meant to pay off later. Why: Hindsight recognition requires the earlier clue to have been seen.
- [heuristic] Place the decisive clue in ordinary, early contexts so that a later reveal pays it off without feeling like an afterthought. When: Designing a mystery in which the solution must be fair to the audience. Why: Clues seen early feel earned, whereas late clues feel like cheating.
- [heuristic] A cleaned item can hold a hidden trace, such as a stain in a seam, which the player must find after the obvious cleaning was done. When: when designing a physical-evidence puzzle. Why: A residue the cleaning missed rewards close examination.
- [heuristic] Give each clue an innocent reading when first seen, and only reveal its significance when the pieces are linked. When: writing a mystery whose solution must stay fair. Why: Innocent readings let the audience accept clues without suspecting them, so the reveal feels fair when linked.
- [procedure] 1) Test each side clue. 2) Resolve it or set it aside. 3) Keep focus on clues that bear directly on the central question. When: A case gathers many unrelated secrets or alternatives. Why: Unresolved side clues dilute focus.
- [procedure] 1) Present a witness statement and a ledger side by side. 2) Let the player find the single line that conflicts with the record. 3) Use the conflict as a clue. When: Designing a document puzzle. Why: Players learn to compare testimony to records and spot the decisive discrepancy.
- [procedure] 1) Plant low-weight clues in ordinary talk. 2) Deliver one strong document as a hook. 3) Test that document with a cluster of clues. 4) Close with a late cluster of proof. When: when structuring a mystery's reveal. Why: Ordinary clues build trust and the cluster removes doubt in stages.
- [tradeoff] Place key clues early so the audience can test theories and later material handles aftermath; or use one tight late cluster just before reveal so pieces combine at once. When: Planning the timing of clues for a mystery's reveal. Why: Early clues let the audience test their own theories before the explanation arrives; a compact late cluster lets the mechanism's pieces combine into the explanation at once. (x3)
- [tradeoff] A clue shown to the audience supports an earned reveal; a clue held only in the detective's knowledge leaves the audience unable to check the solution.
- [pitfall] A dramatic side lead, such as a past romance or a missing man, can absorb time without advancing the case.
- [fact] A writer can shape a case by omitting evidence, hedging a claim, or moving a document's context, and comparing the published account with the original reveals these moves.

## deadlines
- [mechanism] A fixed, publicly known deadline gives a countdown that charges each intervening day with worry and shapes every character's plans. When: A fixed, publicly known future moment is announced in advance. Why: A visible countdown turns each day into a reminder, and shared knowledge makes choices urgent and comparable.
- [mechanism] Presenting a report as the first and only source creates urgency.
- [mechanism] An external event that shortens a deadline can force hidden actors to act sooner, driving the plot forward.
