- [mechanism] An unaltered second timer can expose tampering with the first, because its reading reveals when its hands were moved. When: two timers on a scene disagree. Why: the untouched timer keeps honest time.
- [mechanism] An external event that draws a crowd can interrupt a confrontation and delay the decision it was building toward.
- [rule] Treat a reconstructed timeline as unconfirmed until each link has its own cited source, such as verified witness accounts or records; loose estimates do not settle it. When: When a reconstructed or inferred timeline is presented as fact in an investigation. Why: Inferred times can be wrong, and weak sources produce timelines that fall apart. (x2)
- [rule] When decay or ageing acts as a timestamp, expose its rate so players can check the reasoning rather than guess.
- [rule] Do not commit to an action while its timing cannot be checked. When: the window for acting depends on information that cannot be confirmed. Why: Acting on unverified timing risks walking into people who are no longer incapacitated or away.
- [rule] Do not accept a departure time when the only witness admits they did not see the movement; leave the timeline unverified. When: When a timeline depends on an unseen movement.
- [rule] Use the timeline to name the time windows that lack witnesses, and direct questioning at those windows.
- [rule] Track the in-game day explicitly so the player can catch a witness who misstates it. When: Designing a game with witness testimony tied to time. Why: An explicit calendar gives the player a reference to test claims against.
- [rule] Set a deadline for the final act only if it is credible, since an arbitrary deadline weakens suspense. When: Adding urgency to a climactic investigation stage. Why: Audiences discount deadlines that feel contrived.
- [heuristic] Trust a witness's timing detail only after independent verification; a single observer's confident wording carries little weight, and one unchecked time can shift the whole sequence. When: A detail comes from a single source, or a witness's stated times anchor a timeline. Why: Confident wording is not physical evidence; one unchecked statement can make a suspect appear cleared or guilty.
- [heuristic] Use an external deadline, such as a hearing, trial date or approaching authority, to keep the investigation moving, force evidence out and cut off stalling or bargaining. When: Pacing a long investigation, or when authorities or escape threaten to arrive. Why: A fixed external deadline creates pressure, and time pressure limits the suspect's options.
- [heuristic] Reject any proposed explanation for a note whose timing does not fit the time available. Why: a plausible story fails if it cannot happen in the window.
- [heuristic] An externally logged event, such as a recorded phone call, gives a checkable anchor for a timeline. Why: It can be verified independently of anyone's memory.
- [heuristic] An unusual arrival time is significant only once its cause is known; ask the person directly and check their reason against the record.
- [heuristic] A fixed deadline builds expectation toward a set moment, and a story can defeat that expectation when it arrives. When: when a threat is tied to a date. Why: The deadline focuses attention, and its subversion or fulfilment drives the climax.
- [heuristic] Attach a specific consequence to each deadline, so failing a condition triggers a defined outcome. When: Designing timed pressure in a story or quest. Why: Concrete consequences make the deadline meaningful and let players plan around it.
- [heuristic] Withhold the culprit's name until a stated deadline to build anticipation before the naming. When: at the climax of a public reveal. Why: a fixed deadline gives the audience a clear point of anticipation.
- [pitfall] A deadline the audience cannot track, or that never visibly changes the target's behaviour or gets acted on, loses tension and feels arbitrary or like a cheat. When: Setting deadlines in a story. Why: Tension depends on the audience seeing the deadline affect outcomes and follow-through. (x2)
- [pitfall] Verify clocks, timestamps and delivery assumptions before concluding who acted; unverified or unreset clocks, and one person's hour assumed exact for another, can overturn a timeline. Why: Wrong timing assumptions produce a confident but baseless reconstruction.
- [pitfall] One unverified fact, such as an unconfirmed appointment, can undermine an entire timing chain.
- [pitfall] Too much waiting drains tension, so each delay should change the situation or raise the stakes. Why: Repeated waiting without change loses the audience.
- [pitfall] Skipping too much time can leave the audience feeling that something important was missed.
- [pitfall] A trap question built on a wrong timeline can clear a guilty target or expose the questioner, so verify your own dates before relying on the test. Why: A test is only as good as the timeline it is checked against.
- [pitfall] Repeating the deadline too often dulls suspense, because reminders lose their force once they become routine. When: A countdown is restated frequently. Why: Constant repetition makes the date familiar and less alarming.
- [pitfall] A deadline can be defeated by a trick that changes who must attend the scheduled event. When: A character needs to avoid a fixed-time obligation. Why: Changing the participants can invalidate the deadline without changing the time.
- [pitfall] Too many simultaneous deadlines make the sequence of events hard to follow. When: Several time limits run at once. Why: Competing clocks overload the player's tracking of what matters first.

## motive testing and checklists
- [model] A motive can be modeled as a chain: a threat to the character, the options for removing it, why each option fails, and the resulting decision to act. When: when reconstructing or writing a suspect's motive. Why: a stated logical motive can be more convincing than an emotional one.
- [rule] Discount a witness who has reason to shift blame, protect themselves, or fit the story, such as facing a charge or expecting a reward. Why: Their own outcome depends on what the story shows.
- [rule] Design motive clues so players can rule out suspects whose motive does not match an observed behaviour change, and include tests of motive hypotheses that yield nothing. When: Designing suspect sets and motive clues. Why: Elimination by motive gives players a method for narrowing suspects.
- [rule] Use a motive as a basis for a theory only when its supporting evidence cannot be read equally well as innocent.
- [rule] Ask whether a motive exists, not whether it seems adequate.
- [heuristic] Test a candidate motive by asking what the death gained a particular suspect; suspicious conduct alone does not supply motive, and a missing one weakens the case. When: when a suspect looks suspicious, was chosen by elimination, or a candidate motive's credibility is judged. Why: motive separates culpability from suspicious conduct; motive is a standard test of plausibility; a jury would expect one.
- [heuristic] Scale motive to the act: a grave crime needs a reason of comparable weight, and an obvious motive with small gain against violence may be a decoy. When: deciding whether a suspicion is enough to act on, or the apparent motive is simple and obvious. Why: Disproportion suggests the obvious motive is a decoy.
- [heuristic] Test each candidate motive against a physical fact and discard any motive that fact contradicts, keeping the rest open until evidence settles them. When: Several motives are possible and each can be checked against physical evidence. Why: Testing against facts separates plausible motives from impossible ones.
- [heuristic] A motive that cannot account for a violent act cannot carry the case, however plausible it looks on its own.
- [heuristic] Motive is a weak test of guilt because nearly everyone has some motive to harm someone, while a hidden or sudden motive can be more telling. When: When many candidates share an apparent motive. Why: Common motives do not distinguish people.
- [heuristic] Prefer a shared ideological motive when group actions exceed what individual grudges or documented gain can explain; otherwise prefer those simpler motives.
- [procedure] 1) Read the motive from the document. 2) Check what it would have required the person to do. 3) Compare against the person's known character and independent accounts. 4) Keep the motive open only if it fits; a mismatch makes the link doubtful. When: A motive is proposed from a document such as a will. Why: A document can show a grievance without showing the person acted on it.
- [procedure] 1) List every candidate motive. 2) Take each separately and check its evidence support. 3) Check what the suspect would gain from the act. 4) Drop a motive only when evidence is absent; move to motives needing hidden preparation. When: Several explanations for a plot are possible, or a suspect's stated motive is being evaluated. Why: Systematic elimination keeps a plausible motive from being dismissed unchecked; a motive must be supported and offer a plausible gain.
- [procedure] 1) Name the claimed motive. 2) List what was taken and what was left behind. 3) Check whether the left goods fit that motive. 4) Check whether the room's original state is known before reading disorder as proof. When: a single apparent motive rests on timing or on a reading of disorder. Why: a motive is only credible if the outcome matches what the motive would produce.
- [procedure] 1) Build a motive as a chain of links. 2) State each link as a claim. 3) Check each claim against evidence before accepting the whole. When: reasoning about a suspect's motive. Why: a chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
- [procedure] 1) State the suspect's gain from the act. 2) State the risk the act carries for them. 3) Judge the gain against the suspect's means and position. 4) Check whether the accuser holds evidence that could convict. When: An official theory rests on one motive that seems out of proportion. Why: A motive is only credible if the gain is worth the risk for this particular person.
- [procedure] 1) Settle the suspect's identity first. 2) List plausible motives. 3) Test each against the evidence. 4) Set aside unsupported motives while keeping their underlying possibility open. When: when a figure close to the crime may be complicit but evidence is unclear. Why: motives can be tested one at a time without forcing a verdict.
- [procedure] 1) Sort possible motives into a few categories. 2) For each suspect, check whether they gain from the death in each category. 3) Rule out suspects who gain from none. When: when a suspect's motive is proposed or several suspects are possible. Why: Categories let an investigator eliminate suspects systematically rather than by assumption.
- [procedure] 1) List the standard motives: habitual overuse, self-harm, money trouble, romantic involvement. 2) Ask about each. 3) Note which denials are complete. When: Testing whether a denial hides a motive. Why: A fixed list stops the questioner from skipping likely causes.
- [procedure] 1) List broad motive categories such as passion, money, blackmail, suicide and homicidal impulse. 2) Split each into concrete candidates. 3) Filter each candidate by feasibility and timing. When: Early in an investigation when no suspect is favoured. Why: Mapping the full field prevents a plausible motive from being overlooked.
- [procedure] 1) List the relationships among people in the group. 2) Propose each candidate motive. 3) Keep a motive only if it explains every other fact, including the staging, not just the killing. When: Choosing among motives in a small-group crime. Why: A motive that explains the act but not the scene is incomplete.
- [procedure] 1) State the motive as a claim backed by concrete evidence, such as a sum on a document plus testimony. 2) Check whether the pressured party and the killer are one person. 3) Adopt the branch needing fewer unknown people, keeping the other open. 4) Test the motive against behavior. When: When a private transaction involves several people with a possible stake. Why: Branching avoids committing early while favouring the simpler explanation.
- [procedure] 1) List the missing person's finances, debts, routines, vices and other partners. 2) Check each one and rule out motives that do not fit. 3) Read the absence from what remains. When: when someone vanishes and no crime is yet evident. Why: each ruled-out motive narrows whether the absence was voluntary.
- [procedure] 1) List each motive factor separately. 2) Check how the factors interact. 3) Rank the factors that bear directly on the act, and keep the ranked few rather than the full list. When: Explaining why a character acted as they did. Why: Long unranked factor lists dilute the case.
- [procedure] 1) List every suspect. 2) Assign each a motive in the taxonomy. 3) Check that each suspect's motive fits a category, and note any that fit none. When: Building a suspect list for a mystery. Why: Confirms coverage of the cast and exposes motives outside the scheme.
- [tradeoff] Motive pointing away from a fitting explanation: pursue the motive when facts fit, but test the timeline before discarding a theory, since motive can mislead. When: when an explanation fits visible facts but the motive points elsewhere, or a suspect's motive seems to rule out a candidate explanation. Why: Motive can mislead, while timeline facts are more checkable.
- [pitfall] A strong motive can bias reasoning toward a convenient suspect, and competing theories expose that danger.
- [pitfall] Using a motive to dismiss an accusation replaces checking the claim, so true testimony can be discarded, and the bias can run either way.
- [fact] Working out what a crime gained shows how far culprits will go to protect it, since a large gain raises the incentive to protect impunity. When: Estimating a culprit's willingness to act against exposure. Why: Gain indicates what the culprit has to lose.

## physical evidence checks
- [mechanism] Specific physical facts such as injuries, damp clothing and requests for secrecy can overturn an eerie interpretation and reveal a living person. When: When a supernatural reading is challenged by evidence. Why: Concrete details are harder to explain away than atmosphere.
- [rule] Check a suspect's claim, such as a loss, physically against the item instead of debating who is lying or accusing; the check yields evidence without alerting them. When: when a claim can be checked against a physical fact. Why: the check gives evidence without alerting or accusing.
- [rule] Confront a suspect with a physical item linked to the scene and note their reaction; purely theoretical evidence is easily dismissed as invented. Why: it can connect them to the place.
- [rule] Check an individual mark against a physical measure, such as fitting a damage shape to a known hand or dimension.
- [rule] Keep claims of physical acts seen by present witnesses separate from visions, dreams or apparitions reported by one person. When: Evaluating an accusation that rests on supernatural events. Why: A vision cannot be checked against the physical world, while an act observed by several people can.
- [rule] A permanent feature that should appear in a trace but is absent is a clear mismatch. When: when a trace is compared with a reference record. Why: permanent features do not disappear.
- [rule] Confirm a permanent injury through independent records, such as medical files and the treating surgeon's account, before relying on it. When: when a trace depends on a known physical feature. Why: independent records check the reference.
- [rule] Use a height or reach requirement, such as a ceiling-level lever, as a physical constraint that filters suspects. When: When an action requires a particular physical capability. Why: Physical constraints remove candidates in a clear way.
- [rule] Make observation the gate to clues, since a clue the player never notices cannot be used in deduction. When: Designing clue discovery in an investigation game. Why: Deduction depends on the player first perceiving the evidence.
- [rule] Give objects with physical constraints such as catches, hooks or weights a required orientation, so a wrong return reveals an unfamiliar visitor.
- [rule] Mark clues perceived by only one character, such as something seen under a status effect, so players must find a second source before acting. When: Designing clues in a game.
- [rule] Re-search or re-test a physical token before a verdict; a token that vanishes on a second search undermines the case. When: a verdict rests on a found object. Why: The first finding may be an error or a plant.
- [heuristic] Test a theory or unexplained event physically before accepting it, such as firing a shot or checking whether a signal is visible from outside, since physical interaction leaves checkable traces. When: A witnessed event may or may not be physical. Why: Physical interaction produces traces that can be checked.
- [heuristic] Treat a physical mark a witness offers as support as a claim to test, since it may have a cause other than the one claimed.
- [heuristic] Evidence that lacks a matching injury, such as blood with no wound on the person present, shows the injury belonged to someone else. When: testing a theory against physical evidence. Why: traces must correspond to the claimed event.
- [heuristic] Test a presumed culprit against physical traces, such as the method of attack and the physical effort the scene shows, since a contradiction can overturn the theory.
- [heuristic] A guard's account that conflicts with a door's state or a footprint gives the player a lead they discover themselves. When: designing an NPC statement that a world state can contradict. Why: Players who find the contradiction feel they solved it.
- [heuristic] Compare marks on a witness's body with their account; marks showing someone else applied restraint rule out a claim of self-restraint. When: witness claims unassisted restraint.
- [heuristic] Physical findings that conflict with the activity an official account assumes, such as a meal too heavy for a light outing, weaken that account. When: evaluating an accident or activity verdict. Why: the evidence no longer matches the assumed activity.
- [heuristic] Physical details of a captive's state, such as dress, food or restraints, can serve as test clues the player checks against the NPC's story.
- [heuristic] An object still in its original state, such as an item left in a coat pocket, shows it was never handled.
- [heuristic] Do not accept a locked door at face value; ask whether it was really locked or only appeared so, since an incomplete account can make a door seem secure. When: a closed room is reported as sealed.
- [procedure] 1) State a hypothesis about how an event happened. 2) Check it against conditions at that time, such as tide, water depth or access by sea. 3) Discard it if conditions make it impossible.
- [procedure] 1) State a physical hypothesis about the evidence. 2) Obtain an item from the suspect's own belongings that can test it. 3) Compare the item against the traces. 4) Accept the hypothesis only if the item fits exactly. When: A trace such as a track or mark needs a test. Why: Testing with the suspect's own items gives a direct, checkable match.
- [procedure] 1) Open the container. 2) Confirm identity with a marker such as a plate. 3) Post a lookout against interruption. 4) Keep a witness so the act is on record. When: identity depends on physical evidence.
- [pitfall] A setting that looks non-flammable can still hold recent heat, so the appearance of a place is not proof that it is harmless.
- [fact] A physical claim, such as bloodstains on clothing, can be checked directly on the object, turning a vague statement into something testable. When: When a witness describes a physical trace on an object. Why: Objects retain evidence that can confirm or contradict a verbal claim.
- [fact] A physical clue can point toward foul play while forensic findings show no violence or poison, so the clue must be checked against the body.
- [fact] A thorough search can still miss the decisive trace when it skips the most unlikely location, such as a body or the victim's gear. When: After a search is judged complete. Why: Searchers stop at obvious surfaces and never examine objects they assumed were irrelevant.

## speech tells
- [mechanism] An explicit warning not to repeat words confirms that the words touched a real secret. When: When a character responds to an overheard remark. Why: Urgency to suppress information signals its importance.
- [mechanism] Hesitation appears first at ordinary-sounding words, and trigger words then cause a sharp reaction and loss of composure. When: A subject conceals a secret under questioning. Why: Pressure builds gradually until charged content breaks composure.
- [behavior] People who believe no one is listening speak unguarded and may reveal knowledge or motive, with hints whose meaning is unclear at first. When: a person is alone and emotionally shaken, or a character speaks while assuming no listener. Why: the belief of being alone or unheard lowers their guard, and speakers do not guard their words.
- [behavior] A witness may reveal hidden knowledge through an answer given before any question on that subject is asked, such as denying a cause nobody has raised. When: When a shocking announcement is delivered and the witness responds unprompted. Why: Guilty knowledge can surface in reflexive reactions before the witness can guard it.
- [behavior] An unguarded reaction to a mentioned fact, such as a pause, setback or sudden change of topic, can reveal knowledge the speaker would deny if asked directly. When: A key fact is mentioned in conversation with a suspect. Why: Surprise or concern escapes self-control before the speaker can conceal it.
- [behavior] A spoken explanation gives listeners a reason to accept an odd situation, lowering their scrutiny. When: an odd situation is seen only in part. Why: a stated reason satisfies the question before it is asked.
- [behavior] A listener can sense concealment from a manner that seems unnatural, even after the listener has agreed to a plan.
- [behavior] People tend to speak frankly in front of someone they believe is unconscious, so a feigned victim can overhear their plans. When: a character feigns unconsciousness near others who are talking. Why: They assume the person cannot hear, so they reveal what they would otherwise hide.
- [behavior] Investigators may read an unguarded remark as a self-revelation rather than a guess about the external cause. When: when a suspect's words are overheard in a tense situation. Why: Attention shifts from the outside problem to the speaker's own state.
- [heuristic] Speech cues can suggest a suspect's origin or identity, but treat them as partial; corroborate a single slip, such as a foreign phrase, before trusting it. When: identifying a suspect from witness testimony, or identity is uncertain and only casual speech is available. Why: speech cues are informative but incomplete, and one slip can have an innocent explanation.
- [heuristic] A victim who shows no reaction to an approaching person suggests the approach was expected or came from someone known to them. When: when a victim seems undisturbed by an approach. Why: people usually react to unexpected strangers.
- [heuristic] People who cannot be woken and respond unnaturally suggest a drug rather than ordinary sleep. When: Witnesses in a crime scene are unresponsive. Why: Ordinary sleep does not produce that response.
- [heuristic] Give non-player characters a consistent speech habit, then let a single out-of-character statement serve as a detectable tell. Why: a break in an established pattern is easy for players to notice.
- [heuristic] When observed behaviour fits none of the competing explanations neatly, suspect that one of the shared assumptions is wrong.
- [heuristic] Specific, checkable statements count for more than emphatic but vague denials.
- [heuristic] Recurring nursery or idiom references in NPC speech can echo a later signature or code, linking dialogue to a puzzle. When: Writing NPC speech that connects to a puzzle or clue. Why: A familiar register makes a later match feel earned.
- [heuristic] A remark revealing knowledge the speaker could only gain by being present is a trace that exposes their presence. When: when a suspect describes a detail they should not know.
- [pitfall] A reveal that depends only on a character's word feels weak; a visible physical detail gives the audience something to verify.
- [pitfall] A countersign spoken aloud can be learned by anyone within earshot, so the check is compromised once overheard. When: A password is exchanged in public or within earshot of others. Why: Audible passwords spread to listeners.
- [pitfall] Do not treat silence as evidence until the expected reaction is confirmed as normal. A sound sleeper or an unreliable guard can fail to react for unrelated reasons. Why: Without a baseline, a missing reaction can be explained by the observer or the animal rather than the event.
- [pitfall] A confrontation that becomes a speech no one interrupts loses tension and stops feeling like a contest.
- [pitfall] Guarding the obvious communication channels does not mean all channels are closed; a protected plan can still have a gap. When: Securing a plan against leaks. Why: Overlooked routes, such as public news, bypass the controls placed on known routes.
- [pitfall] A hiding place mentioned in conversation reveals the owner's habits to anyone listening.
- [pitfall] Making every character evasive drains their hints of force.
- [pitfall] Evidence that the victim spoke to someone proves they were alive at that moment, not afterward. When: Using a late conversation to set a time of death. Why: Being alive at one time says nothing about later times.
- [pitfall] Assuming an exit is open because it is unguarded is an error; check its timing before accepting the route.
- [pitfall] Spelling and handwriting cannot establish a writer's intelligence or literacy.
- [pitfall] Overlooking how a crowd, a leader or a physical contact shapes what a witness later says leads to misreading their testimony.
- [fact] Harsh words spoken about a person can later support a slander claim and damages, so spoken accusations carry legal weight.

## suspect and villain design
- [model] A hidden director may set accusation order through visible actors; players should check who sets the sequence, which may be older or hidden figures, and be able to expose the director.
- [model] An ideal offender must be meticulous, unseen, without friends or dependents, and quick in mind and body. When: When designing or judging a perfect criminal. Why: These requirements define an ideal that real offenders fail to meet.
- [model] A mystery can run as a ladder of decoy suspects: each is raised to presumptive guilt, then cleared, while the true culprit stays in view from the opening scene. Why: Repeated reversals keep the player's attention moving away from the culprit.
- [mechanism] A key figure hidden among many similar background characters is hard to identify, so investigators can move unnoticed.
- [mechanism] A villain who acts on misinformation creates an opening, because a player who learns the false belief can use it against them.
- [behavior] A witness may hide a visit by someone who had little good feeling toward the victim, because its discovery would make the household seem implicated. When: a visitor had a grudge against the victim. Why: the visit would implicate the household.
- [behavior] A warning given in ordinary conversation can conceal its purpose, which the listener may only understand afterwards. When: A character warns a suspect casually. Why: Ordinary framing lowers the listener's guard.
- [rule] Give every suspect a genuine non-criminal secret or small domestic oddity, set up early, so a wrong suspect is reasonable and suspicion shifts naturally once the mechanism is visible. Why: A plausible wrong suspect keeps the solution fair.
- [rule] Show an NPC's behaviour before revealing the threat behind it, so players must later reconcile the behaviour with the hidden cause.
- [rule] Make a villain's signature, such as a particular lure, drink or device, appear in two earlier incidents so players infer the pattern and expect it again. When: Designing a recurring antagonist.
- [rule] Give each suspect a visible gain from an event, such as a vacancy or a rival's removal, so players can reason about motive. When: Designing suspects in narrative or dungeon generation.
- [rule] Give a suspect NPC a warm dialogue style that conceals motive, and provide a documented record that contradicts the spoken story.
- [rule] Hide opportunistic accusers among genuine witnesses, so the player must separate private gain from honest report.
- [rule] Make an intermediary NPC who quietly suppresses reports to curry favor a hidden mechanic that the player can uncover. When: designing hidden plot mechanics.
- [rule] Make the most convincing suspect a trusted insider, so the reveal reverses a belief the player already holds. When: When choosing the apparent culprit for a mystery. Why: Reversing a strong belief creates a more satisfying reveal.
- [rule] Give a culprit NPC a realistic capability level so the solution is reachable without requiring a flawless plan. When: Designing an antagonist's competence for a mystery puzzle. Why: Realistic capability keeps the puzzle solvable and the culprit credible.
- [rule] Give antagonists a concrete, checkable motive, such as a debt or a rival's gain, that players can discover through documents or NPCs. When: when designing an antagonist's backstory. Why: Discoverable motives reward investigation and make villains credible.
- [rule] Cast doubt on a second trusted figure before the final reveal, so the last unmasking carries higher stakes. When: the hidden antagonist is a late-revealed ally. Why: A prior doubt makes the final suspect feel like a real risk.
- [heuristic] An obvious early motive or visibly angry suspect can pull attention from the real trail; track it for later contradiction instead of chasing it. When: Designing or reading a mystery with an early apparent motive. Why: Players tend to accept a visible motive as the answer before checking other evidence.
- [heuristic] A hidden mastermind is often an unnoticed servant or clerk who stays out of view while others hold the visible roles.
- [heuristic] Leave visible an item whose removal would look odd, such as one the owner was known to possess. When: when a search would notice an absence. Why: removing a known item draws suspicion.
- [heuristic] A visible threat can make one party carry a message to another without alerting them to a concealed plan.
- [heuristic] A villain's written lore or journal can reveal the vanity or fixation that players can exploit, and NPC traits can be tied to predictable mistakes such as returning to a scene. When: Designing antagonists whose weaknesses should be discoverable. Why: Self-revealing writing gives players a way to anticipate the character's errors.
- [heuristic] Make the hidden agent someone close to the protagonist, such as a household member or party member. When: Designing the source of a mystery's threat. Why: Proximity raises stakes and makes suspicion shift inward.
- [pitfall] A planned crime is idealised and leaves out incidental difficulties; real execution introduces errors the plan does not contain.
- [pitfall] A vivid reaction hides the performer's control over it, so observers who do not test it let staging pass as genuine.
- [pitfall] Overplaying a suspect's confidence makes the reveal seem arranged rather than earned. When: Writing a suspect who is certain they will not be caught. Why: Excessive certainty reads as authorial convenience, weakening the reveal.
- [fact] A visible irregularity can belong to a separate, innocent secret rather than to the main event.
- [fact] A detective-style case can hinge on a victim who is secretly the agent, so the reveal reverses who is blamed for the disturbance.

## suspicion shifting
- [model] Suspicion moves in a sequence from one character to another, each shift triggered by the newest witness having a motive the player has just been shown. When: A mystery where the suspect list changes over the course of the story. Why: Each new motive redirects suspicion, keeping the player uncertain about who is responsible.
- [mechanism] Each new fact that clears or incriminates a suspect shifts suspicion to someone else, not only through elimination; no candidate settles while unexplained clues stay open until late confessions. When: when the audience tracks suspects across a story. Why: Repeated invalidation keeps several candidates alive instead of settling on one early. (x2)
- [mechanism] Suspicion lands first on the most visible suspect, then moves to a less likely or unseen party with a motive, driven by new physical or testimonial detail, not confession. When: Pacing suspect changes across a mystery. Why: Visible suspects draw early attention, and new evidence redirects it. (x2)
- [mechanism] Suspicion that moves between human and supernatural causes, with each human suspect failing a test, leads the player to accept a larger explanation. When: When structuring the escalation of a mystery's explanation. Why: Each failed human explanation removes alternatives until only the larger cause remains.
- [mechanism] Suspicion can move from the first accused to a new group when later clues connect a past conflict to a second suspect.
- [mechanism] When suspicion moves from an outside accomplice to the household and then to the disguised agent, each shift reframes earlier evidence. When: structuring suspicion across a mystery. Why: Reframing earlier clues makes the final reveal recontextualize the whole episode.
- [mechanism] When suspicion shifts from a living accomplice to the dead principal, the reader's model of who planned the crime reverses, so the late reveal lands as a reversal. Why: Moving blame to someone the reader thought was out of play overturns the earlier model rather than confirming it.
- [mechanism] Suspicion moves from one suspect to another once a clue establishes who owned a key object, because guilt reassigns to the person that owner was connected with. When: a clue resolves ownership of an object at the scene. Why: Identifying the owner changes which relationships the player treats as suspicious.
- [mechanism] Suspicion moves when the next discovery tests a suspect's motive, so each new clue shifts blame to a different character. Why: A motive is only as strong as the evidence that survives testing.
- [mechanism] Suspicion moves onto a culprit when their motive is tied to a document and their own statements conflict with each other. When: in the middle act of a mystery. Why: A motive plus contradictions gives the player a concrete reason to suspect that person.
- [mechanism] Suspicion shifts in waves, each triggered by a new contradiction or link to the victim, so each suspect receives a full cycle before the next takes over. When: Pacing suspects across a mystery. Why: Short cycles keep any single false solution from lasting too long.
- [behavior] Suspicion falls on whoever a timeline places nearby or last interacted with the scene, the most available culprit by default. When: a group feels threatened by an investigation, or a threatening character is found dead. Why: Blaming the nearest person deflects attention from the group's own exposure, and the nearest actor is blamed by default, so the protagonist can be framed by their own actions. (x2)
- [behavior] Clearing a suspect, including with a search, redirects attention to the remaining candidates, so the final one becomes the focus of the explanation. When: several suspects are eliminated in turn. Why: clearing one suspect redirects attention to the remaining candidates.
- [behavior] When every member of one group seems innocent, investigators tend to shift suspicion to a different group. When: candidates are cleared one by one without a strong suspect. Why: Lacking a clear culprit, attention moves to whoever remains unexamined.
- [behavior] When one suspect is discharged, suspicion often moves to another person named by the same rumor, so the matter returns in another form. When: a first accusation fails or is dismissed. Why: The rumor behind the first accusation outlives its target.
- [behavior] Suspicion settles on the character with the most visible secret, while the true actor is hidden in plain view as a helper, judge, second or servant. When: a scene with several people who have something to hide. Why: Visible secrets draw attention away from quieter, trusted figures.
- [behavior] Suspicion in a case often moves from the most obvious party to an outsider, then to the investigator's own theory. When: a case with several plausible culprits.
- [behavior] Players distrust the first culprit once a midpoint crisis collapses it, so suspicion moves from an outsider to a visibly guilty insider and then to a quieter insider with a hidden motive. When: a mystery shifts suspicion across the cast over its run. Why: Each reversal of a visibly guilty suspect exposes the previous reading as incomplete, pushing attention toward hidden motives.
- [rule] Keep the accused's guilt as the default from the start, and let the reversal come from the witness with the most to lose.
- [rule] Make each new clue shift blame to a different household member, so the audience must keep re-evaluating the whole group rather than one suspect.
- [rule] Let each apparent solution be undone by a verified fact that removes one suspect cleanly. When: when a suspect is cleared. Why: A clean refutation prevents the player from keeping doubt about a cleared suspect.
- [heuristic] Suspicion shifts when a document, disguise, or witness contradiction breaks the current theory, even before proof, and moves to whoever that evidence points at, even a trusted narrator. When: When designing suspicion shifts, or when evidence contradicts a narrator's or a figure's account. Why: Concrete breaking evidence gives the player a reason to revise the theory; a contradicted narrator can become the suspect. (x2)
- [heuristic] After a misdirect has settled, concentrate decisive clues in the middle of the mystery so suspicion moves from the first suspect to the true target. When: when a mystery builds a reputation for one suspect before revealing another. Why: the first half establishes the spectacle, then the middle clues redirect attention.
- [heuristic] Move suspicion between supernatural and living enemies, so the reader is always assigned a human suspect before the story turns again.
- [heuristic] Ask who benefits from each false lead; a suspicion or rumour that serves one party's cover story is likely planted. When: Evaluating suspicions, rumours or accusations. Why: Planted leads serve the planner's interests, so their beneficiary points toward the planner.
- [heuristic] Suspicion should be a tool that shifts from one suspect to another as each new fact arrives, rather than being the subject of the mystery itself. When: Structuring a multi-suspect investigation. Why: Moving suspicion keeps the method and the suspect chain separate, so the method can be revealed while suspicion still moves.
- [heuristic] Suspicion stays diffuse until the deduction names a place, then moves at once to the people tied to that place. When: Designing how a mystery narrows its suspects. Why: Without a location there is no basis for singling out individuals, so the focus shifts only when one is named.
- [heuristic] Once a mechanism is exposed, shift suspicion to those who relied on it rather than to the accused. When: a reveal undermines a group's accusation. Why: The exposed mechanism now implicates its users.
- [tradeoff] Shifting suspicion by reinterpreting existing clues can work without new discovery; otherwise each shift needs a new fact, motive, or contradiction, since unsupported shifts feel arbitrary. When: when rotating suspects across a mystery's cast. Why: Fact-driven shifts feel earned and keep trust; reinterpreting known evidence can overturn a suspect without any new discovery.

## unresolved threads
- [mechanism] Visible unfinished checks before a reveal build tension, because the audience sees how much remains unconfirmed.
- [mechanism] Offering competing explanations for an unexplained event keeps tension open instead of resolving it early. When: an unusual event has occurred. Why: unresolved possibilities sustain uncertainty.
- [behavior] An observer may keep a small unexplained detail in mind, drawing attention back during distraction until later related facts show what it means. When: a detail seems minor, or the observer is distracted while holding it unresolved. Why: an open question keeps attention returning, and its meaning appears only when related facts arrive.
- [behavior] While waiting for an expected threat, a character repeatedly rechecks hiding places and feels a growing urge to act. When: a character waits for a search or arrest that has not yet come. Why: each unconfirmed sound raises fear.
- [behavior] Tension grows when a player must wait with incomplete information while a threat approaches but has not yet been identified. When: approaching sounds reveal a threat before it is seen. Why: uncertainty about who it is and how close it is.
- [behavior] Players may not search an obstacle such as a reed-filled lake when they do not know what they are looking for, so the search seems too hard to attempt. When: A clue points to a large or difficult area to search. Why: Without a target, searching a large area feels costly and players skip it.
- [behavior] A short verification pause in front of an audience builds tension and marks the reveal as serious rather than casual.
- [rule] Fully resolve the central mystery and any cause the main plot depends on; leave only minor clues or side-event causes unexplained so the central logic stays clean. When: designing unresolved events or minor clues. Why: a plot that depends on an open cause cannot resolve.
- [rule] Let one accomplice escape a captured scene, leaving a loose end that keeps the world open for a follow-up.
- [heuristic] Leave some threads unexplained at the end, such as the consequence of the reveal, so an open question sustains mood and engagement after the main reveal. When: at the close of a reversal mystery. Why: an unresolved question keeps the audience engaged after the twist. (x2)
- [heuristic] Close each scene or sequence on an unexplained event or unresolved detail that carries the case forward, leaving the audience waiting for resolution.
- [heuristic] Keep an unexplained detail in play across sections until the reveal, so a later explanation settles it retroactively and reads as the solver's skill rather than a loose end. When: planting questions to resolve later, or a clue has no interim explanation. Why: a detail held open becomes a debt that the later reveal repays.
- [heuristic] End a story with an open central question only when the clues already given are sufficient for the audience to reach the conclusion. When: Choosing an open or unresolved ending.
- [heuristic] Do not close off any direction of approach or escape; keep watch on every direction that presents itself. When: guarding someone who could be reached by several routes. Why: sealing one route invites attack from another.
- [heuristic] An unstated threat can be more frightening than an explicit one, so leave its nature open when it cannot be resolved. When: Writing a threat that the audience cannot yet understand. Why: Open endings let the audience imagine the worst.
- [heuristic] Leaving one gap unresolved after a reversal invites the audience to reconsider the motives of everyone involved.
- [heuristic] Plant household details that the final verdict never explains, such as a servant's remark, so the reader stays unsettled after the case closes.
- [heuristic] Leave some pieces deliberately unresolved, such as a missing witness, so the player must decide what to believe. When: when ambiguity serves the story. Why: Unresolved gaps keep the player's judgment active.
- [heuristic] Leave the last link unconfirmed when the design needs a sequel hook. When: a mystery's final answer is intended to continue. Why: An unconfirmed conclusion keeps the story open for later development.
- [heuristic] Leave one NPC unresolved on purpose to test whether the player notices the thread. When: Adding a red herring or loose end to a mystery. Why: An unresolved detail rewards attentive players and tests observation.
- [tradeoff] Loose ends after the main cause is found leave players unsure the case is over, but one deliberate unexplained thread keeps the mystery feeling real. When: closing a mystery whose main cause is found. Why: a fully tidy answer can make the world feel artificial, while unresolved loose ends leave players unsure the case is over. (x2)
- [pitfall] Unexplained gaps and too many loose ends read as carelessness or an unfinished plot; keep open questions few and minor. Abstract closing theories also frustrate players. When: a hook raises questions, or the final explanation is written. Why: unpaid questions make the writing seem careless, and excess ambiguity reads as incomplete while abstraction disconnects from events. (x2)
- [pitfall] A noticed clue that is raised then dropped, or an unfinished line that never returns, makes players feel cheated; recover the hidden sense in a later scene. When: a clue is raised then dropped, or a character leaves a sentence incomplete as a clue. Why: unresolved hints read as broken writing rather than deliberate foreshadowing, and players expect each noticed clue to resolve.
- [pitfall] A direct, open challenge can give a suspect an exit, since a technically correct refusal can end the question. When: Challenging a suspect who can answer with a narrow refusal. Why: A suspect who disclaims any right to respond closes the question without answering it.
- [pitfall] A precedent may itself have an unsettled verdict, so citing it does not establish guilt in the present case. Why: the precedent's own outcome may have been reversed or left uncertain.
- [pitfall] Disturbing an item and not restoring it alerts the occupant that the room has been searched.
- [pitfall] Tension that never releases wears the audience down, so sustained pressure should be broken by moments of relief. When: Pacing an extended dread sequence. Why: Constant pressure exhausts players and reduces the impact of later peaks.
- [pitfall] A contradiction resolved too quickly kills the thread, and a contradiction never reopened makes the audience feel cheated. When: Planting a clue that the character notices. Why: Players need either a payoff or a later reason to return to the detail.
- [pitfall] Ending on a threat without resolving it can frustrate players if the next step is unclear. When: A scene ends on suspense. Why: Players lose direction when no next step is indicated.

## verifying documents and provenance
- [behavior] Decision-makers who distrust expert evidence on principle may discount technical proof regardless of its strength.
- [rule] Record an object's position, folds, seals and damage when found, since these show whether its owner handled it or it was placed afterward. When: An object's meaning depends on where and how it was found. Why: Marks of handling reveal the sequence of events around the object.
- [rule] Record where each object was found, since the place of discovery matters when the item is later used as evidence. When: Collecting physical items. Why: Provenance decides whether an item can be linked to a scene.
- [rule] Record the source and date of each fact given by a witness, so the record can be checked later. When: When logging testimony or documentary evidence. Why: Sourced facts can be verified and compared when the case develops.
- [rule] Before handling soft, deformable evidence, record its state, for example by photographing it or noting its creases, so the examination does not erase detail. When: the evidence is soft or deformable.
- [rule] Check an inscribed object against an external record; it proves possession, not presence, and does not confirm identity by itself.
- [rule] Record each small physical fact carefully before deciding what it means, since the important one cannot yet be known. When: early in an investigation. Why: Premature interpretation can hide the key detail.
- [rule] When a professional offers prescription books or stock records, ask who independently checked the supply. When: A professional claims everything is accounted for. Why: Self-reported records lack independent verification.
- [rule] Let the player verify a relationship by cross-checking two incidental records that name the same people. When: When designing a relationship puzzle from in-game documents. Why: Two independent records naming the same people make a link checkable.
- [rule] When the suspect controls how a claim is checked, give the player an independent verification route. When: A suspect offers to confirm their own account. Why: A checker controlled by the suspect cannot give a neutral result.
- [heuristic] Verify a suspicious message by asking the people it names or the apparent sender directly; contradictions or denials expose forgery and can reveal the forger. When: a message or call seems to come from someone who did not send it. Why: direct confirmation exposes impersonation.
- [heuristic] A correct key produces readable phrases, which confirms the decoding is right.
- [heuristic] Do not discard official records; instead check precisely what each one attests, since an accurate record may confirm only a narrow fact. Why: Each record has a scope that determines what it proves.
- [heuristic] Record observed emotional cues, such as a worried look on returning home, even when their meaning is unclear. When: During surveillance of a suspect whose reactions may matter later.
- [heuristic] Check whether a reported remark was quoted in full, since a paraphrase or partial quotation can change its meaning.
- [heuristic] Check a document's surface meaning against actual sums, dates and the people who would really gain before accepting it as motive. When: Reading a will, contract or other public document as possible motive. Why: Surface partiality can mislead about who truly benefits.
- [heuristic] Establish a document's chain of custody: who held it, when, and whether the envelope or container is present. Weak provenance lowers how far its contents can be trusted. When: When a letter or paper is offered as evidence. Why: A document's authority depends on its handling history, not only its text.
- [heuristic] Check transaction records against each other, since one book may hold sales the other omits, and treat a date from one book as unsettled until confirmed by the other. When: Sales are recorded in more than one book or register. Why: Separate records can each be incomplete.
- [heuristic] A story packed with dated, named sources and transfers feels documented to listeners, even when they cannot verify any of it. When: A claim must be accepted by someone who cannot easily check it. Why: Specific references create an impression of checkability that discourages scrutiny.
- [heuristic] Check second-hand accounts of a document against the primary record or a certified copy before relying on them. When: When a document's contents are reported by a witness. Why: Witnesses may misremember, frame events in their favour, or omit details.
- [heuristic] Check a reference letter's author, date, and the applicant's previous posts before trusting it. When: Evaluating a written reference.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain known handwriting samples from the suspected author. 2) Compare the disputed note or document against them directly. 3) Accept or reject authenticity on that comparison. When: authorship of a document is in question and a reference sample is obtainable, or a note arrives through an unfamiliar channel before acting on it. Why: A direct comparison with known material is a quick, decisive check, independent of the carrier's account, and guards against forged or misdirected messages.
- [procedure] 1) Identify who could have sent the message. 2) Test its claims against facts the sender could not have known. 3) Confirm the decisive claim through a second independent channel before acting. When: a message is the basis for a serious decision. Why: the sender may be an adversary.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the message's phrasing with the contact's real habits. 2) Note any mismatch in idiom. 3) Check the requested place and deadline. 4) Confirm through a second channel before going. When: an unexpected message claims to come from a trusted contact. Why: impersonators copy tone more easily than habits.
- [procedure] 1) Examine the paper for trimming or cut-away source marks. 2) Compare the handwriting with known samples. 3) Check the content against what the writer could know. 4) Check whether the items could have been placed after death. When: when a confession arrives at a convenient moment or its author cannot be questioned. Why: Each check tests whether the document's physical form and content fit its supposed author.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the issuing source printed on the dated document. 2) Contact that source directly. 3) Ask it to confirm the record and any descriptions or identifiers it holds. When: A document is offered as an alibi.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the document's creation date with the events it seems to anticipate. 2) If the document predates the events, reverse the inference and ask who could have shaped the events. 3) Identify who could control the events and who helped draft or check the document. When: Judging whether a fitting document was written for later events or the events were shaped to match it. Why: A document cannot be written in response to events that occur after it, so the fit must come from the other direction.
- [pitfall] A private record shows intent only if its author and date can be confirmed. When: using a diary or note as evidence.
- [pitfall] Hidden control of cards or seating makes results reflect the controller's design rather than the subjects' character, so results must be judged against that control. When: interpreting behaviour observed in a rigged or scripted social test. Why: The test's own structure shapes what the subjects reveal.

## accidents
- [definition] An apparent accident can be a deliberate act, such as an attack, a distraction, or an attempt to disrupt an investigator.
- [mechanism] An unplanned event can break a long-prepared concealment scheme and make the evidence suggest a different explanation, such as one person killing another.
- [mechanism] An independent record can reveal an unplanned duty that places a suspect elsewhere, removing that suspect from the timeline. When: when a claimed alibi is checked against records.
- [mechanism] Accidental leads arise from unforeseen witnesses, third parties' unplanned acts, and objects carried by chance into new places.
- [behavior] Investigators tend to read a found object as an accidental drop, so well-placed plants are accepted rather than questioned. When: a planted item is found during an ordinary search. Why: people assume items were dropped by accident.
- [behavior] If a community believes an enemy can act at a distance, a missing visible cause is read as proof of guilt rather than as a gap in knowledge. When: when the believed powers are wide and unlimited. Why: the frame explains any unexplained harm as concealed agency.
- [rule] An accidental-looking mark counts as a clue only if the player is shown how it was produced; otherwise reading it is interpretation.
- [rule] When confidential information is accidentally shared with someone outside the circle, acknowledge the breach at once and ask them to keep it secret.
- [rule] When damage looks accidental, examine where the break started and how the edges look before deciding how it happened. When: a platform, floor or object fails. Why: break origin and edges reveal forced or staged damage.
- [rule] Consider an accidental cause, such as a carried light, before assuming deliberate arson when a fire is reported. When: when a fire or damage is attributed to a deliberate act. Why: an accident may be the real cause and must be excluded first.
- [heuristic] The strongest threat to a plan is an accident the planner could not foresee, such as an object carrying an identifying mark the planner cannot remove. When: A culprit has hidden or removed evidence. Why: Some traces sit in things the planner cannot replace.
- [heuristic] When a hired attacker gains nothing from an act, the real motive usually lies with a hidden employer who does gain from it.
- [heuristic] A coincidence may be a mere accident, so leave it marked as unresolved rather than forcing a link.
- [heuristic] An object out of place at a scene that belongs to the victim links the victim to that scene, even if it was left by accident. When: A personal item is found where it should not be. Why: Accidental leftovers are less likely to be staged.
- [heuristic] When a trace should be explained by a source that is missing, the trace may be a deliberate imitation rather than an ordinary result. When: A set of traces looks ordinary but the expected cause is absent. Why: The missing source leaves the trace unexplained.
- [heuristic] A death that looks self-caused or accidental can still be murder if the act and its result are separated by time or by a mechanism. When: a victim's death looks self-caused and the timeline needs testing. Why: A delayed or mechanical link hides the act behind the apparent cause.
- [heuristic] Reconsider the premise: the apparent victim may have authored the staging rather than only being its target. When: A staged death contains details that do not fit an ordinary crime. Why: Staged scenes are often planned by the person who appears to be harmed.
- [heuristic] A pair of changes that both serve the same purpose, such as two windows open where one would be natural, is a stronger anomaly than a single change. When: Reviewing environmental changes at a scene. Why: Redundant changes suggest deliberate clearing of fumes or traces rather than chance.
- [heuristic] Check an apparent accident, such as a dead power source or a missing bulb, at its source before accepting chance as the explanation. Why: Deliberate tampering can look like bad luck.
- [heuristic] Let the killer's own chance accidents expose them, so the final reveal follows from the story's logic rather than luck alone. When: writing how a culprit is caught. Why: Accidents rooted in the killer's own actions feel earned, while random exposure feels contrived.
- [pitfall] Accepting an early benign explanation, such as a natural-cause verdict or a familiar legitimate use, without testing alternatives against the physical pattern can let tampering go unnoticed. When: A death is quickly classed as natural, or an initial explanation fits a known legitimate use. Why: Early verdicts stop further investigation, and a familiar explanation can close inquiry too early.
- [pitfall] A crumpled object can result from accident as easily as concealment, so confirm the sequence of events before concluding that someone tampered with it. Why: Disturbed objects look similar whatever caused the disturbance.
- [pitfall] Accepting each incident as an accident without comparing them lets the attacker continue. When: a series of incidents is explained one at a time.
- [pitfall] A meeting that seems accidental may later be recognised as the first step of a plan, so its timing matters. When: an early encounter is reinterpreted after events unfold. Why: the significance of a first contact only shows in hindsight.
- [pitfall] Treating an estimated time of death as exact is a mistake, because a medical estimate usually gives only an approximate interval. When: When building a timeline around a time of death. Why: Estimates have a range that must be respected.
- [pitfall] Showing an unprepared visitor a corpse may cause them to faint and alter the scene in the process.
- [pitfall] A challenge spoken half-seriously can bind a party to an unplanned path that neither side intended. When: When a casual dare is taken literally.
- [fact] Accident explanations are supported by crossings, roads or paths to the scene, fences with or without gates, and a reason for the person to be there; their absence weighs against accident. When: When assessing whether a death at a location could be accidental. Why: These physical features make an accidental presence plausible.

## eavesdropping and overheard scenes
- [definition] A hidden device can capture what people say when they believe they are unobserved, using a black box, wiring and a receiver to magnify and transmit sound. When: Suspects are likely to talk privately and the setting allows concealment. Why: Speakers lower their guard, and whispers near the device are still captured.
- [mechanism] Echoing architecture garbles speech, so a distant listener receives only isolated words and broken phrases. When: a listener is at an echoing corner or distance. Why: reflections overlap and blur the words.
- [mechanism] A player hears full lines from one speaker and fragments from another, and a noise that interrupts the talk drops lines from what is heard. When: Eavesdropping through a scene with ambient noise or distance. Why: Distance and interruption limit how much speech reaches the listener.
- [mechanism] A hidden watcher who sees a private act and later changes the situation creates dramatic irony, since the target does not know the state has changed. Why: The target acts on outdated assumptions.
- [mechanism] When speakers sense a listener, they lower their voices, so the listener's own noise changes what is said and what can be learned.
- [behavior] A witness who asks eagerly about a particular time usually has a stake in that time. When: a witness presses on the timing of events. Why: they want the time to fall in a way that favours them.
- [behavior] An eager, unsupervised bystander may volunteer details that supply clues without knowing their significance.
- [behavior] Speech overheard through a wall arrives in pieces: muffled sound gives way to sharp, clear words, so a listener catches only parts of the exchange.
- [rule] Give voiced NPC lines readable tells, such as a pause, a changed line, a repeated word or a shift in vocal pitch, that signal concealment or lying. When: Recording dialogue meant to hint at hidden knowledge. Why: Audible tells let players read deception without explicit text.
- [rule] Trigger an NPC's spoken line when the player is hidden nearby, gating it behind a stealth check.
- [rule] Build a hidden informant into the design so the player has a second route to the secret beyond the obvious circle.
- [rule] Make eavesdropping yield a partial line that raises a question without giving the answer. When: Designing an overhearing interaction for players. Why: Partial information keeps the player inquiring rather than solved.
- [rule] Let an NPC who appears dead overhear the player's conversation and reveal what was said later. When: designing a fake death that conceals an NPC. Why: A hidden listener can expose information the player assumed was private.
- [rule] Let an unseen character's voice carry their state, since sound can reveal distress without the player ever seeing the person.
- [rule] Place a hidden listener so gaps in what they hear feel natural. Avoid positions easy to discover, and speakers with no reason to talk freely. When: Staging an eavesdropped scene. Why: Plausible positioning keeps the scene believable.
- [rule] Confirm a secret through overheard dialogue rather than a confession, so the first direct evidence is heard and the accused can still deny it. Why: This keeps the reveal a matter of judgment rather than settled fact.
- [heuristic] An NPC hidden in a room can overhear player dialogue and react later, so a scene should not be treated as private. When: designing dialogue in rooms that may hold unseen characters.
- [heuristic] When a conversation cannot be heard directly, a hidden vantage point, such as a nearby tree, can still reveal the scene to a watcher. When: a private room or talk is out of earshot.
- [heuristic] Sounds through a closed door, such as scuffling, dragging, a heavy crash or a cut-off cry, indicate violence in progress. When: when a person inside may be in danger.
- [procedure] 1) Make the target believe you are incapacitated. 2) Hide a trusted witness where they can hear but not be seen, near the antagonist. 3) Offer a believable pretext that invites gloating. 4) Ask specific leading questions about the means. 5) Reveal the witness and call for help once the admission is made. When: A suspect or antagonist is likely to boast or reveal details if they think no one can use them; staging a confession for a player-triggered scene. Why: An antagonist speaks freely when they believe no one can hear, and a concealed witness makes the confession usable as proof.
- [procedure] 1) Find a concealed opening above or beside the target room. 2) Conceal it from the target's view. 3) Observe and listen from a fixed position over many days. When: A suspect's routine is the best evidence and direct questioning has failed. Why: Repeated observation reveals habits a single visit would miss.
- [procedure] 1) Note when the key talk took place. 2) Note when the suspected listener arrived or came within range. 3) If they arrived after the core of the talk, they could not have heard it. When: testing whether a listener could have heard what they claim.
- [procedure] 1) List every door, bolt and wall between the listener and the sound. 2) Judge whether each one blocks hearing. 3) Accept or reject the claim accordingly. When: when testing a claim that someone could or could not hear something. Why: Unmapped barriers make hearing claims unreliable.
- [procedure] 1) Listen unseen to unguarded talk. 2) Note the grievances, boasts and claims heard. 3) Approach the speaker in person and question them, using the overheard content as the opening. When: the listener can stay out of sight and the speaker is unguarded.
- [pitfall] Listeners who catch only fragments fill the gaps with guesses shaped by their assumptions, so conclusions drawn from overheard talk can be wrong. When: a listener hears speech only partly or uses overheard talk as evidence. Why: Fragments lack full context, so partial hearing invites guessing.
- [pitfall] Revealing surveillance too early lets the suspect change tactics before the trap closes. When: When planning a watch on a suspect. Why: Once a suspect notices watchers, they adjust their behaviour and the advantage is lost.
- [pitfall] Each adjustment raises the chance of discovery by sound or by someone moving nearby, and a partial gain may still miss key words.
- [pitfall] Speakers wrongly assume privacy when they think a listener cannot understand them, so overheard talk can reveal what they hide. When: someone is said not to understand the language. Why: people assume unintelligible listeners are harmless.

## interrupting interviews
- [mechanism] Cutting off a sound, event, or conversation before its explanation or outcome defers the answer, so tension grows while the payoff is postponed, not lost. When: Pacing a scene with a planned confrontation or revelation. Why: Unfinished tension keeps attention and anticipation high, and the audience stays waiting while the story continues.
- [mechanism] A message cut off before its key detail gives partial clues and an open question, which sustains suspense until the gap is resolved. When: Early story hook. Why: The audience needs the missing part.
- [mechanism] A character who enters just before a countdown ends can interrupt it and halt the scripted outcome.
- [mechanism] An outside interruption can cut a probe short before anything is admitted, forcing the questioner to find another opening.
- [mechanism] A small sound, such as a footstep, interrupting a silent scene tests the characters' nerves and raises the stakes of the wait. When: A quiet scene is building toward a decisive moment. Why: An unexpected small sound forces a reaction and reveals how the characters cope under pressure.
- [mechanism] A sound from outside can end a questioning scene and force the characters to drop their plan and hide, reshaping the timeline.
- [mechanism] Interrupting a revelation with a new arrival slows the scene, raises tension, and gives the audience a new character to judge. When: a reveal is in progress. Why: a fresh presence pauses the reveal while adding information.
- [mechanism] An outside interruption such as a guard entering or a bell ringing can pause a revelation, and offering a choice to resume gives the player control over timing. When: Designing dialogue or cutscenes with a key reveal. Why: The pause builds tension and lets the player decide when the scene continues.
- [behavior] A repeated interruption can serve propriety while also monitoring the people present. When: a third party repeatedly enters a private conversation. Why: the visit is socially justified, so it covers the observation.
- [behavior] A suspect who recovers from a break and turns warm signals that control of the conversation has changed hands. When: after an interruption breaks a tense exchange.
- [behavior] A sudden interruption, such as an urgent summons at a tense moment, sharply turns the scene and heightens its tension. When: a scene is building toward a climax. Why: An unexpected interruption resets the audience's expectations.
- [rule] Interrupt an NPC's confession with a scripted event, then resume it later; the secret stays intact while stakes rise, so disclosure is deferred, not lost.
- [rule] Do not treat an interrupted record as a complete account of what followed; the gap is a question to investigate, not a fact to fill in. When: A diary or log stops mid-entry. Why: Filling gaps with assumed detail can mislead the investigation.
- [rule] Interrupt prepared speeches and keep the suspect close, so that pleading or flirtation does not break off the questioning. When: when a suspect tries to steer the conversation with emotion. Why: interruption keeps questions on the sequence of facts.
- [rule] An interruption should not fully replace the lead being followed; the original line of inquiry must stay open. When: a new arrival breaks a scene. Why: dropping the lead wastes the investigation.
- [rule] Players can interrupt rumour escalation by gathering contrary evidence early, before official steps lock in. When: When a rumour has not yet triggered official action. Why: Early counter-evidence stops later steps from gaining credibility.
- [rule] Have an adult NPC interrupt a child NPC who is about to reveal something dangerous, so the interruption itself signals a secret. When: When staging a child informant near a dangerous or hidden fact. Why: The interruption signals the stakes and invites the player to pursue the child later.
- [heuristic] A steady signal that stops suddenly, mid-message, suggests something went wrong, likely a new event interrupting it, rather than a normal ending; the break is evidence. When: when a steady exchange stops at a moment that can be dated. Why: A sudden cut points to a trigger rather than a planned end.
- [heuristic] Remnants of an unfinished activity, such as brushes left clogged in solvent or a tense mid-play board layout, show it was interrupted or recently stopped, not completed.
- [heuristic] Interrupt a long narrative with a specific question, such as asking for the one vital reason, that the speaker must answer, so the key point is not buried in detail.
- [heuristic] Use an interruption within a conversation to pull out key information at the right moment. When: when timing of a revelation matters. Why: interruptions create pressure that releases the fact.
- [heuristic] Cut off a revelation just as it is about to be made; the interruption holds attention and sets up the next scene. When: At a scene break where the answer should come from elsewhere. Why: A withheld payoff pulls the audience forward.
- [heuristic] Interruptions that cut a witness off at a sensitive point signal that the story holds more than is being given, to both witness and examiner. When: A witness is repeatedly stopped just as the account reaches their own whereabouts. Why: The interruption reveals that the examiner suspects a gap in the account.
- [tradeoff] Interruptions build tension, but overuse, or ones that change no order or facts and are just delays, feels arbitrary and contrived; reserve them for key scenes. When: Adding interruptions to scenes. Why: Interruptions without plot effect frustrate audiences.
- [tradeoff] Interrupting a witness early loses their sequence of events, while letting them run on unchecked leaves claims untested. When: Questioning a witness whose account has checkable claims.
- [pitfall] Interrupting a witness too soon breaks a fragile chain of memory and loses the details they would otherwise give. When: a witness is recalling events in sequence.
- [pitfall] An interruption that replaces a needed explanation or revelation without a later payoff frustrates the audience; every cut must lead to an answer they can reach. When: When a revelation is cut off. Why: Unanswered cuts read as evasion.
- [pitfall] Trying to interrupt a talkative witness usually fails, since they swamp the questioner with talk. When: a witness buries answers in digressions.

## red herrings and false trails
- [model] A layered mystery reveal stacks several plausible wrong answers, such as body location, killer route and outside plot, each overturned later by proof of the true scene. When: Structuring a long mystery with several competing theories. Why: Each layer seems to explain the evidence until a later clue contradicts it, sustaining suspense.
- [mechanism] Planted objects and notes can aim suspicion at an innocent rival, away from the planner, so the strongest case hides the real culprit. When: A culprit arranges the scene before investigation, or a suspect is charged on circumstantial evidence resting on one witness. Why: Early suspicion decides where investigators look, so stopping at the first strong case misses the real culprit.
- [mechanism] A planted false trail built from strong scent and blood can redirect a tracker away from the true route, provided the decoy is physically consistent with the scene. When: A plan must mislead trackers or animals that follow scent. Why: Trackers follow scent sources, so a convincing decoy diverts their search.
- [mechanism] A planted, seemingly independent report elsewhere can draw a rival away from a key location, opening a timed window for the investigator. When: The rival must be kept away from a place while the investigator acts. Why: The rival acts on the report as though it were genuine.
- [behavior] Conspirators may seed a plausible innocent explanation before investigators look further, so an official verdict can rest on a planted story. When: A group wants an inquiry closed quickly. Why: Authorities accept a convenient explanation that fits the facts on the surface.
- [rule] Make an incriminating-looking item, one a guilty NPC could also have used innocently, a red herring whose innocent explanation players verify in ledgers or records. When: Designing misleading evidence. Why: Players must test which reading the records support; an item with an innocent use creates real ambiguity rather than an arbitrary decoy. (x2)
- [rule] Plant a plausible false trail, such as footprints or mud, a stolen key, dropped item, letter or visitor, pointing at an innocent NPC; include a discoverable contradiction that clears them. When: Designing clues in a mystery that implicates a false party. Why: Players can reason past the false trail to the truth, and a paired contradiction makes the fake testable.
- [rule] A red herring must be fair: the player must be able to notice the real clue and test the false suspect, clearing them with an available clue or direct question. When: Placing a decoy clue or designing a false suspect. Why: Players accept misdirection only when the real clue was discoverable; an untestable red herring feels arbitrary and blocks progress.
- [rule] Use a physically real item that belongs to another person as a red herring, such as one discarded nearby, so the clue is valid but misleading.
- [rule] Plant a tempting false lead beside the true solution so players must test both leads against the physical evidence. When: Designing a puzzle or investigation. Why: Players need a real choice to test.
- [rule] Plant the facts that support a false story before discovery, so that later clues remain consistent with it. When: Writing a concealed past event for players to uncover.
- [rule] Use a shopkeeper's over-eager pitch as a red herring whose suspicious tone is a habit, not a crime.
- [rule] Let an accusing faction choose between a local magistrate and a higher court with different standards, forcing the player to decide where to press a case. When: designing legal or political plot branches.
- [rule] Release clues in a steady drip, staging the early ones as red herrings that point to rivals before the real suspect.
- [rule] Add dead ends that look like evidence, such as a fake office or wrong address, to build suspicion without revealing the answer.
- [heuristic] Once the pattern of an obstruction is clear, the detention reveals the opponent's real purpose, which is to stop the investigation during the delay. When: when an investigator is detained. Why: The timing of the delay shows what it was meant to achieve.
- [heuristic] A single inconsistency can reveal the whole sequence of an act, so examine small details closely before forming a full account. When: when solving a crime from physical evidence. Why: One clue can constrain the entire reconstruction.
- [heuristic] Plant a visible culprit, such as a fleeing NPC carrying loot, whose actions later prove innocent, so players must revise their first theory. When: designing a misleading early suspect. Why: A decoy whose innocence is later shown forces players to revise their reasoning.
- [heuristic] Before reading an open window as meaningful, check whether the room was normally ventilated. When: Interpreting an environmental change. Why: Ordinary behaviour can explain a change that is not related to the crime.
- [heuristic] A planter's ignorance of a custom shows in a detail the true owner would have avoided.
- [heuristic] Hide a planted clue inside a courteous exchange so the act reads as kindness, not concealment, and the target never notices the object changing hands. When: An NPC secretly places evidence on another character. Why: Courteous moments draw no suspicion, so the physical act passes unnoticed.
- [procedure] 1) Create an NPC or faction that seems guilty through motive. 2) Give the player a physical test, such as strength, reach, or distance, that contradicts the lead. 3) Let the contradiction be checkable so the decoy stays fair. When: designing a misleading suspect in a mystery or dungeon-style investigation. Why: A decoy that a physical check can refute keeps the mystery fair and rewards careful reasoning.
