- [procedure] 1) Stage a loose document with an ambiguous fragment where pursuers will find it. 2) Have an intermediary report their reactions. 3) Use the reactions to see who is involved. When: flushing out a hidden opponent.
- [pitfall] Physical clues, such as footprints made in an innocent person's shoes, thumb-marks or borrowed boots, can be planted to frame someone, so test a clue before treating it as decisive. When: A physical clue seems decisive or points clearly at one person. Why: Anyone with scene access can stage an object, and traces can be borrowed or staged.
- [pitfall] A planted item pointing at an innocent person, or a neatly fitting accusation, can look conclusive, so test it against physical evidence before accepting it as a solution.
- [pitfall] A conspicuous, simple clue can absorb attention or pull investigators toward a grander conspiracy reading that proves wrong, serving as a planted false trail. When: A clue invites a dramatic interpretation.
- [pitfall] A red herring can be built from real facts, so its plausibility can mislead as much as a false claim. When: Judging a motive built on documented events. Why: Real facts lend false motives credibility.
- [pitfall] Two investigators can read the same planted item in opposite ways, so each reading needs its own test rather than agreement.

## dismissing suspects
- [definition] A red herring is a motive that seems believable but is inconsistent with the nature of the act, pointing investigators away from a larger plan.
- [mechanism] A flamboyant conclusion can be a red herring; a contradicting sighting widens the field of suspects and undermines the dramatic theory. When: a witness reports a sighting that does not fit the favoured suspect. Why: an alternative observation reopens the case.
- [mechanism] A plausible rival suspect with a physical match can divert suspicion, and the player can later disprove that match with evidence. When: designing a misdirection in a mystery. Why: a convincing alternative delays the correct conclusion until it is refuted.
- [behavior] Personal dislike and property disputes give suspicion its direction, so an accusation often targets someone already disliked or in conflict over land. When: when analysing why a particular person was accused. Why: Accusers' stakes in property and position shape whom they name.
- [rule] Use a plausible gain-based or financial motive as a deliberate red herring, not the real cause, so the player must test and discard the obvious reason. When: Designing red herrings in narrative or dungeon generation. (x2)
- [rule] Dispute or dismissal events are possible motives that do not automatically point to the culprit; a dislike alone is not a motive, since many disputes are unrelated to crime. When: A witness reports hostility between people. Why: Ordinary quarrels are common.
- [rule] Do not dismiss a suspicion merely because the case looks arranged or its conclusion seems too wicked; wary witnesses may reject correct suspicions for that reason.
- [rule] Show that an accusation is too weak by listing its essential gaps; proving innocence is not required to block an arrest. When: a character proposes arresting someone on a thin case. Why: a case with missing links fails without an alternative culprit.
- [rule] Give an NPC a note naming a powerful figure that the player must check through a direct meeting, while the real connection lies elsewhere. When: Designing a misleading clue. Why: The check resolves the lead and redirects the player.
- [rule] Do not dismiss strange impressions as nonsense merely because no explanation is yet available.
- [heuristic] Make suspicious-looking traits such as accent, job, jealousy or nervousness red herrings, and keep guilt signs ambiguous while placing real clues in the suspect's actions. When: when designing suspects and clues for a mystery. Why: Ambiguous cues keep players from accepting the first answer.
- [heuristic] A sighting that vanishes on approach can work as a deliberate red herring that rewards players who verify before acting on it. When: when designing misleading clues.
- [heuristic] Make a suspect's guilt rest on companions and one published accusation alone, so players must test the claim before accepting it. When: Designing a red herring character. Why: Untested association can look like evidence, which rewards investigation.
- [heuristic] Clear each suspect with a specific test, so suspicion rebounds across suspects without stalling the case. When: a suspect is accused. Why: a concrete clearing keeps the case moving.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a motive or lead without checking its evidence, especially because it conflicts with a favoured theory, can hide the real explanation; recheck the stated reason for rejection. When: An investigator rules out a suspect's apparent motive; a theory conflicts with a character's own explanation. Why: Unchecked elimination removes the correct answer; the theory is preferred over direct testimony. (x2)
- [pitfall] Judge the argument, not its framing or speaker: dismissing a respectable suspect, a modest or disliked witness, or a self-promoting observer mistakes standing or presentation for innocence or accuracy. When: A witness is modest, timid or disliked by peers, or a second observer contradicts an established authority. Why: Social standing and framing do not determine whether an account is accurate; readers and characters discount opinions by how they are framed. (x2)
- [pitfall] Setting aside a suspect's denial leaves the accuser's account unchallenged, letting a weak link stand and tilting the case toward the accuser. When: A motive chain is already built, or a suspect denies a vision reported by an accuser.
- [pitfall] A red herring with a real motive stays convincing until its supporting facts are checked. Why: motive alone can make a false lead look solid.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a belief entirely can miss its influence on the people who hold it.
- [pitfall] Dropping a whole case on one fact can be as hasty as accepting it on many facts; weigh the anomaly against the rest of the evidence.
- [pitfall] Dismissing people as uninvolved causes missed clues; keep everyone present open as a suspect until evidence excludes them.
- [pitfall] A suicide motive can be built on the same facts a murderer would use to disguise a killing, so motive alone should not settle a death.
- [pitfall] Each new plausible claimant pulls attention away from the real question, such as who benefits from the current arrangement.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a hobby as harmless without checking it is a mistake, since it may hold evidence of activity.
- [pitfall] Spreading suspicion over several weakly connected suspects can dilute the case against the one with the strongest motive.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a decades-old grievance as ancient history can brush aside a real motive too quickly.
- [pitfall] A discharged suspect is not thereby innocent in the community's eyes; people may still treat them as under suspicion.

## partial and fragmentary testimony
- [mechanism] A reveal built from successive partial readings, each factually fair and each overturned by the next, makes the final answer feel earned rather than sudden. When: Designing a multi-stage mystery reveal. Why: Every stage is supported by evidence, so overturning it teaches the player that the search was too narrow.
- [behavior] Eavesdropping or glimpsing yields fragments; an observer often cannot see and hear at once, so the pieces must be combined. When: a character learns part of a situation through a keyhole or partial view. Why: A single sensory channel gives only part of the event.
- [behavior] A dying or badly injured witness gives partial, broken words, so the questioner must draw out the rest through short, targeted questions. When: When a dying or incapacitated witness must reveal information. Why: Severe distress limits speech.
- [behavior] An NPC may give partial dialogue, so the player must follow up with specific questions to obtain the key line.
- [behavior] Witnesses are interested and partial, so they can stop short of the most disturbing part of an event. When: a witness is asked to record a distressing detail. Why: self-interest and distress make full disclosure unlikely.
- [rule] Record partial testimony with its gaps and limits visible, and seek another source rather than reading more into the words, so readers can judge how much weight each part bears. (x2)
- [rule] Make NPC dialogue accurate but partial, leaving players to infer what is omitted and cross-check it with other NPCs and environmental evidence. When: When designing clue dialogue or NPC dialogue that withholds information. Why: Accurate partial statements force players to compare sources; selective truth rewards inference and keeps dialogue honest. (x2)
- [rule] Give witness NPCs partial knowledge, such as height and beard but not eye colour, so players must combine fragments from several sources.
- [rule] Have NPCs give partial or biased accounts, and let the player check them against a register, ledger or town record.
- [rule] Trigger a player's public confrontation only when their evidence is ready; if it is premature, nearby NPCs should side with the suspect. When: when generating crowd reactions to an accusation.
- [rule] Mark an NPC's testimony as partial and give a later journal entry or item that reveals the shielded fact. When: When an NPC has reason to hide information. Why: A later reveal rewards careful players.
- [rule] Ask what a witness did not say, since an honest speaker can omit the detail that matters. When: Evaluating a witness account. Why: Sincere testimony is often partial, so omissions can carry the key information.
- [heuristic] Make an NPC's first disclosure partial, such as 'I took it, but it is gone', as a branching clue that points elsewhere, so its fuller account must be verified. When: When designing dialogue branches or NPC lines that reveal incomplete truths. Why: A partial admission signals hidden information without confirming the whole account, which keeps the hidden fact worth pursuing.
- [heuristic] Give witness NPCs in chaotic scenes fragmentary, lower-reliability dialogue so the player must cross-check several accounts. When: Designing NPC dialogue for a fire, collapse or similar scene. Why: Several partial accounts force the player to reason from evidence.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC a partial memory, such as a clear face with a vague name or hair colour, so the player must judge which details to trust. When: when writing NPC recollections. Why: mixed reliability forces the player to weigh evidence.
- [heuristic] Information from a reluctant or captive source usually arrives in fragments the questioner must assemble.
- [heuristic] A dying or broken accusation names a suspect or motive but must be confirmed against evidence before it is accepted as the answer. When: a witness's last words or fragmentary statement point at someone. Why: partial words may have been caught or interpreted wrongly.
- [heuristic] Fragmentary recall from a dazed witness can still identify a key object, though details may be confused.
- [heuristic] A suspect's reaction can change dialogue state, so a pressed NPC may reveal a second route or item. When: designing reactive NPC dialogue. Why: pressure unlocks new information.
- [heuristic] An informant NPC can give part of an answer for a price, unlocking the second half only after the first is delivered. When: Designing staged information from NPCs. Why: Staged payment controls how much information the player gains at each step.
- [heuristic] When an NPC corrects an earlier lie, record which statements are retracted and which remain standing, and open new questions from the admitted detail. When: Writing dialogue that allows an NPC to change its account. Why: Tracking retractions keeps the player's picture of the case accurate and gives new leads.
- [heuristic] Let a test confirm the mechanism while leaving one question unanswered, so the reveal feels proven yet a thread stays open for later. When: Ending a reveal test. Why: A full answer closes the case, while a partial one keeps the player engaged.
- [heuristic] Test a witness's account by checking each detail separately, since a witness may be right on one point and wrong on another, which shows which parts to trust. Why: Mixed accuracy lets the reader judge which parts of a testimony can be relied on.
- [procedure] 1) Record each fragment exactly as spoken, leaving blank gaps between them. 2) Fill each gap with a phrase that fits the words on both sides. 3) Revise until the whole sequence reads naturally in both directions. When: when a speaker's account survives only in broken pieces that context can bridge. Why: Fitting gaps to their neighbours recovers the sense of missing words without inventing unrelated content.
- [procedure] 1) Make NPC dialogue through a door partly audible. 2) Leave the missing words to be pieced together from other sources. 3) Let the player assemble the full statement. When: when designing overheard dialogue.
- [pitfall] A witness who withholds the key point frustrates the audience unless the withholding is justified by the witness's own distress.
- [fact] Overheard speech through a closed door is usually partial, and different listeners may catch different fragments of the same exchange. When: When witnesses hear a conversation without hearing every word. Why: Distance and barriers filter what reaches each listener.

## provocation and reaction
- [mechanism] An NPC who becomes angry after provocation may leave or act, changing the scene, so provocation options should carry a real risk. When: Provocative dialogue options are offered to the player. Why: Reactive NPCs change the state of the scene, which makes the choice consequential.
- [mechanism] Rumours passed through a friend can prompt a target to discuss the matter, provoking a reaction that reveals knowledge or feeling. When: Evidence is circumstantial and the designer controls what the target hears. Why: A reaction to a controlled prompt shows more than an unprompted account.
- [mechanism] A hidden trace can reveal itself when a probing physical action, such as striking a surface, produces a response from the concealed space. When: A hidden fact sits behind a surface that can be tested. Why: The test converts a concealed object into a detectable sound or reaction.
- [mechanism] A casual remark can provoke hidden agitation that sets a flag, unlocking a later accusation. When: a throwaway line touches a sensitive subject. Why: the reaction exposes a concealed motive.
- [behavior] Anger that breaks a guilty person's or witness's composure, such as lashing out at the accuser, can confirm a hidden link or fear more than denial would. When: a hinted accusation hits a real secret, a witness's false claim is exposed, or a witness speaks harshly about the victim. Why: Strong emotion weakens controlled self-presentation and reveals what is feared or hidden.
- [behavior] A guilty person who hears a direct accusation often feels compelled to answer or defend, and may reveal knowledge they meant to hide. When: the accused knows the hidden facts. Why: an unanswered claim seems to damage them, so they respond.
- [behavior] A calm, unexpected question about identity or a charge can provoke a sharp physical reaction, such as a flush, a stagger or a changed voice. When: when a suspect is asked a sudden accusatory question. Why: surprise disrupts composure and can reveal hidden knowledge.
- [behavior] A provocative accusation shows who answers, who avoids the question and who laughs, revealing differences in how people respond to pressure. When: when suspects are not yet alert.
- [behavior] Someone who finds a stranger exploring a sensitive area may act to stop him, which can give a motive for suspicion even when the observer's own motive is unclear. When: a stranger is seen exploring a sensitive area. Why: A protective response to intrusion gives an observer a reason to act.
- [rule] Trigger an NPC confrontation after the player provokes them, so the response itself reveals the link. When: when a player's provocation hits a secret.
- [rule] Do not provoke suspects who are already alert, since the probe may end the investigation.
- [rule] Avoid provoking a suspect when they may turn violent or when the pressure could lead them to destroy evidence. When: A suspect has a volatile temper or access to evidence. Why: Provocation can escalate into harm or loss of evidence.
- [rule] Do not provoke a suspect who has nothing to lose, or push when the questioner has nothing firm to press on.
- [heuristic] A provocative remark about a victim tests a suspect's reaction; a composed suspect answers with a single flat line and shows no fear. When: when physical evidence is incomplete.
- [heuristic] Provoking a witness with a half-truth lets them correct their own story, revealing knowledge they meant to conceal. When: A witness is concealing information and may correct a partial claim. Why: Correcting a claim can expose what the witness actually knows.
- [procedure] 1) Keep your own manner mild and even. 2) Raise a sensitive relationship with a small pointed remark. 3) Judge the reaction: anger, evasion or silence. 4) Use the suspect's own words as the next question. 5) Watch for impulsive movement and stop if danger appears. When: Use when a suspect has a concealed relationship and strong feeling, and a slip is more useful than a direct accusation. Why: Strong emotion can cause a suspect to reveal information that self-control would otherwise keep back.
- [procedure] 1) Keep early questions measured. 2) Wait until the subject believes the exchange is finished. 3) Deliver a prepared pointed remark. 4) Watch for sudden changes in color, speech and posture. When: subject is guarded and a direct accusation would only draw denial. Why: a subject off guard may reveal knowledge that direct questions cannot.
- [procedure] 1) State the suspicion directly. 2) Point out the suspect's slips. 3) Threaten a consequence, such as calling authorities. 4) Watch whether the suspect grows worried. When: a suspect is under pressure and may slip. Why: a confident bluff can draw out a reaction.
- [procedure] 1) Summon the witness with a vague message that hints at evidence without naming its source. 2) Have an official present to take formal notes. 3) Present a partial fact and watch for involuntary reactions. 4) Offer the witness a chance to explain motive, and treat retreat into generalities as information. When: A witness withholds information that a direct question would not get. Why: Involuntary reactions and evasions reveal knowledge that a direct answer would conceal.
- [tradeoff] A cruel provocation tests whether a reaction is genuine, but it also lets the witness take the moral high ground.
- [pitfall] Provocation can trigger flight or fight, ending the conversation before the questioner asks the remaining questions or learns anything.
- [pitfall] Provoking a suspect can endanger a witness or bystander and make the questioner more visible, so plan timing and protection before applying pressure. When: The suspect could harm or flee from a witness or bystander. Why: A provoked suspect may act against the witness or bystander first.
- [pitfall] Strong reaction is not proof of guilt: innocent people react strongly too, and one expression can have several readings, possibly just confirming expectations.
- [pitfall] Flattery, teasing or dramatic, aggressive questioning unsettles a witness, producing protest and defensiveness instead of the facts the interviewer needs. When: Trying to draw out a reluctant or defensive witness. Why: Pressure triggers defensiveness, which hides the facts the interviewer needs.
- [pitfall] Provocation shown in front of others can damage the investigator's standing as much as the witness's, and a hostile reply can reverse the exchange.
- [pitfall] Suspects read probing questions as accusation, so keep the stated purpose clear or the questioner may be seen as acting for an opposing party. When: Questioning a suspect or hostile witness. Why: Unclear intent triggers suspicion and defensiveness.
- [pitfall] Tests that provoke a reaction can also expose the tester's own motives to the other party. When: Probing a suspect with a physical or verbal test. Why: The act of testing can signal what the tester suspects.

## single explanation limits
- [rule] Do not rest a timeline on a single estimate when other evidence is available. When: Building a timeline. Why: One estimate can be off, and corroboration reduces error.
- [rule] Do not treat one estimate, such as rigor timing, as settling the time of death. When: Fixing a time from a single physical sign. Why: Rigor timing varies, so the estimate is a range.
- [rule] Avoid resting the entire plot on one misleading clue; attentive readers who spot the gap will judge the story unfair.
- [rule] Agree on one story and tell it plainly to every audience, adding no embellishment. When: when facing repeated questioning. Why: a consistent, plain account is hard to attack.
- [rule] Do not treat a single disagreement as proof of forgery. Confirm it against the original first. When: when a record conflicts with one account. Why: A single conflict can have other explanations.
- [heuristic] One reproduction or replacement with one person proves little, especially when reactions vary between individuals; repeat tests across several people before confirming a theory about behaviour. When: A re-enactment is used to confirm a theory about a person's behaviour. Why: Individual variation means one run cannot guarantee the same outcome.
- [heuristic] A single stop or departure from routine reveals little; read several small actions together and test it against other evidence before concluding about plans. Why: One act can have innocent causes.
- [heuristic] A single search or empty storage place proves little; absence conclusions need a thorough search, and each new arrival or visitor can change what should be checked. When: When concluding an item is missing from a place. Why: One unchecked location may still hold it.
- [heuristic] A torn or missing page alone is not conclusive, since it may be an ordinary lapse; read it alongside other evidence before concluding. When: when a physical gap is the only clue. Why: gaps can have innocent causes.
- [heuristic] Separate the one checkable fact a rambling witness gives from the remarks around it, and trust that fact more than the rest.
- [heuristic] Eliminating one mechanism does not prove that the whole class of similar explanations is wrong.
- [heuristic] If one observer covers the only route in or out, every movement must pass that point, so the observer's blind spots decide whether an alibi holds. When: When a building or area has one controlled route. Why: A single checkpoint constrains all movement through it.
- [heuristic] Keep a supernatural explanation available but partial, so it excuses events without settling them. When: A curse or supernatural cause is offered within a mystery. Why: Leaving the explanation unsettled keeps the player weighing mundane and supernatural readings.
- [pitfall] Settling on one untested explanation stops the search for alternatives, makes rivals harder to raise and can hide contradictory evidence; keep rivals open, since without them no test separates causes. When: An examiner has chosen a cause before running any tests. Why: Without rival hypotheses, no test can tell the competing causes apart. (x3)
- [pitfall] A chain of plausible inferences can fail at one link, and a plausible alternative can neutralize a clue; test each link against independent evidence before trusting the whole sequence. When: A reconstruction relies on several connected inferences, or a suspect offers a plausible alternative. Why: One wrong step can invalidate later conclusions that depend on it.
- [pitfall] Declaring a case solved on one damning or matching link, such as past record, fingerprint match or sudden departure, skips how the trace came to be where it was found. Why: A single link can make a chain of reasoning feel complete when it is not.
- [pitfall] Acting on a single broken edge without further checks risks a wrong conclusion about how the damage occurred. When: a damage site is used to decide what happened. Why: one feature may be misleading.
- [pitfall] Noticing one error, such as a spelling mistake, can cause the more telling features of a document to be overlooked. When: Reading a document for clues about its origin. Why: A single salient error draws attention away from the full pattern.
- [pitfall] A single wrong detail may be chance; the argument for knowledge rests on several errors pointing in the same direction.
- [pitfall] A route that seems to exclude one candidate may still permit another, so test every candidate rather than only the first.
- [pitfall] A trapped room with only one exit invites physical struggle when the target is cornered, so the confrontation can turn violent. Why: With no other route, a cornered target has little to lose by fighting.
- [pitfall] A single inspection of each route can miss a route built to look sealed. Recheck routes that appear closed. When: When eliminating entry routes in a sealed room. Why: Deliberately disguised openings can pass a quick check.
- [pitfall] Assuming the cover story is the only version in circulation is risky, since other versions may exist. When: when an event has been described to several people. Why: other accounts may contradict the cover story.
- [pitfall] One answer to a control question is a single sample, not proof of candour or guilt. When: interpreting a control question. Why: one response can be coincidence.
- [pitfall] Treating a short gap as the only possible gap can miss other opportunities, such as an act done on an earlier day. When: when a timeline seems to allow only one window. Why: Acts can occur over many days, not only in one short interval.
- [pitfall] Concentrating on one line of enquiry, such as the victim's private life, can produce repeated dead ends while other possibilities stay unexplored.
- [pitfall] Supernatural and human causes can be stacked in one explanation, so each layer must be tested separately. When: An explanation mixes a supernatural cause with a human one.

## stakes and stakeholders
- [mechanism] A stated deadline or end condition that only one event can satisfy puts sharp time pressure on everyone bound by it.
- [mechanism] Parties with financial stakes tend to dominate formal proceedings and steer them toward questions of payment. When: formal inquiries involving insurers or creditors. Why: money interests shape which questions get asked.
- [mechanism] A quest accepted through a dare, with an NPC who must commit to cooperate as a condition, creates an obligation the player can enforce. When: In games where NPCs offer challenges with conditions.
- [behavior] A person more attached to an outcome tends to reject disconfirming evidence, while the observer with less stake can reach the correct inference. When: Observers differ in personal stake in the outcome, or a claim is defended for doctrinal or social reasons. Why: Less stake leaves room for doubt; someone who needs a belief to hold may reject disconfirming accounts. (x2)
- [behavior] A witness with a personal stake may shape their account around protecting it or present it confusedly, so the story can shift under follow-up questions. When: The witness has a personal stake in the property, outcome, or verdict. Why: Their interest in the outcome colours what they report.
- [behavior] Witnesses whose land touches a disputed boundary have reason to defend a particular line, so they may name the same boundary feature. When: A witness has property adjoining a contested boundary. Why: Personal stake in where the line falls shapes what the witness reports.
- [behavior] A stakeholder who answers with hypothetical future doubts instead of facts shifts the question from what happened to how the relationship will fare. When: A character refuses to supply facts and argues instead. Why: Arguing about consequences deflects attention from the disputed events.
- [rule] Do not treat a witness or reporting character with a stake in the outcome as neutral; mark their reports so they are weighed more cautiously. When: A witness or character reporting an event has a stake in the verdict, outcome, or a relationship with the parties, or a motive. Why: Interest and emotion shape what is observed and reported; motive signals potential bias to the player.
- [rule] State a deal's terms in plain figures, including what each side gains or loses and the alternative if it fails, so the other party can confirm or dispute them. When: Presenting terms of an agreement or deal. Why: Explicit terms let both sides agree on consequences and weigh the choice clearly.
- [rule] Before offering terms, state your role and limits so the other party knows what you can and cannot deliver. When: Negotiating for information or a confession. Why: Unclear authority makes the other party doubt whether the terms will be honored.
- [rule] Use stakes to show motive, not action; do not convict on stakes alone.
- [rule] List every party with a stake in a dispute, including advisers who profit from prolonging it, since each may have a different motive.
- [rule] Tag each non-player character's statements with a stake, such as self-protection or protecting another, so contradictions carry meaning for the player. When: designing dialogue with conflicting accounts. Why: Knowing the stake makes contradictions interpretable rather than arbitrary.
- [rule] Give players leverage options, such as threatening a search, that force an NPC to give up an item, with a cost or risk attached.
- [rule] Split an uncertain case into small either-or branches and test each one rather than assuming a single branch.
- [rule] Make the cost of refusing an action explicit in the game so the player can weigh it against the value being protected. When: Designing a choice where the player can refuse to cooperate with a process. Why: A visible cost lets the player make an informed tradeoff rather than a blind one.
- [heuristic] Tie a deadline to a threatened life or scheduled meeting and state it explicitly, so the player can measure remaining time and feel urgency. When: When a witness must be found, a trap or rescue is set, or a countdown is built. Why: Urgency increases tension and drives action; a concrete, stated deadline structures timing. (x2)
- [heuristic] A dispute over an inheritance or title gives each party a stake, and the stake can shift who appears to gain from the result.
- [heuristic] Establish what a wrong judgment has cost before, such as a past failure, so a later challenge or wager carries weight.
- [heuristic] When accusations track property or rank more than their content, the dispute is really over those stakes.
- [heuristic] Give mercy a cost, such as the NPC keeping stolen goods or lying to a later investigator. Why: a free pardon removes the weight of the choice.
- [heuristic] Turn a stakeholder's argument into a personal reason to act, such as making proof of innocence one's own goal, to keep the investigation moving. When: A character responds to challenges with argument rather than facts. Why: Converting the challenge into a goal gives the investigator a direction when the other party deflects.
- [procedure] 1) List the shared resources between each witness and the accused: land, livestock, tools, debts, insults. 2) Mark witnesses who have a live dispute. 3) Weigh each account by that stake before accepting it. When: Before using a witness account as evidence. Why: It shows which accusations a person is likely to make and which claims need outside confirmation.
- [tradeoff] A choice encounter with identical-looking options gives both sides equal odds and avoids open violence, but any visible difference in the options reveals the answer. When: Designing a choice-based confrontation the player should resolve without combat. Why: Equal odds keep the outcome tense, but a cue leaks the correct choice.
- [pitfall] A threat that never visibly advances feels empty, even when its outcome is still deferred.
- [pitfall] Raising the stakes can push a suspect toward a weapon or an alarm, so the investigator must watch for that reaction. When: Pressure is increased during confrontation.
- [pitfall] In a crisis, evidentiary standards tend to drop, and opportunists can hide among honest accusers.

## witness impairment
- [mechanism] A witness under drugs or stress can misreport or fade, so observers' descriptions must be read in light of that condition.
- [mechanism] Giving an NPC witness a reliability value that drops when impaired produces vague or contradictory dialogue. When: designing witness dialogue.
- [mechanism] Perception-altering drugs can dilate pupils, shift heart rate, produce elation and a sense of superiority, and intensify colors and shadows, changing what the user observes. When: An observer has taken a perception-altering substance.
- [behavior] Witnesses often notice details by chance without knowing they matter, so their sightings can be incidental. When: a witness observes an event before its significance is known. Why: attention goes to what seems ordinary at the time.
- [behavior] A witness can be confused in one task yet lucid in other matters on the same day, so reliability should be judged task by task.
- [behavior] A person impaired by drug use can misjudge elapsed days and insist on the wrong day, so their timing should be checked against other sources. When: a witness is intoxicated or otherwise impaired. Why: Intoxication distorts a person's sense of time.
- [behavior] As a witness's physical strength weakens, their recall of old events may become fragmented and out of order, while memory may remain the least damaged faculty. When: Questioning a witness whose health is declining. Why: Memory can persist even as other abilities fail.
- [rule] A sincere but impaired witness, such as one drugged, is unreliable because impairment corrupts perception; weigh their statements against other evidence and give them less weight. When: a witness was drugged or otherwise impaired. Why: impairment corrupts perception even when the witness is honest.
- [rule] Challenge a witness when their motive or earlier statements conflict with what they now claim.
- [rule] Use an in-world witness, such as a ticket seller or guard, as an independent record that confirms or breaks a claim.
- [rule] Deliver an absent NPC's account as a note or recollection, and let the player judge how reliable it is. When: the witness is absent from play.
- [rule] Rest an impeachment on documents and several sources, since a retraction can itself be discounted as unreliable.
- [heuristic] Record passing vehicles and bystanders even when they are mentioned only in passing, since a brief detail can later serve as a witness. When: a scene is being documented. Why: incidental details can become decisive later.
- [heuristic] A witness who faints or cannot tell sleep from unconsciousness is weak on timing and perception, even where a physical detail they report proves true.
- [procedure] 1) Set a sworn statement beside a statement by the same person made earlier or later. 2) Ask whether the witness could have been reliable when the first statement was made. When: a witness has conflicting statements.
- [procedure] 1) List each witness's claims. 2) Check official records for past perjury or punishment for deception. 3) Argue the evidence itself is false, not only the witness's character. When: challenging testimony in a hearing.
- [pitfall] Intoxication or poor sight, such as dim light, makes a witness's identifications and accounts untestable, so they need outside support before being relied on. When: A witness had drink or lacked a clear view. Why: Impaired perception makes claims unverifiable or unreliable.
- [pitfall] Judging what a witness saw without considering intoxication, a fall or fear mistakes a distorted perception for an accurate record.
- [pitfall] Vague time estimates, such as roughly an hour, can shift a timeline's window; verify them before drawing conclusions. Why: Imprecise recollection can place an event on the wrong side of another.
- [pitfall] A witness's inability to describe someone may be real or a dodge, so test it against other evidence.
- [pitfall] An impaired witness may recall vaguely or refuse to describe what they saw.
- [pitfall] An informant who is impaired or self-absorbed may still give useful hints, but their reliability is lower.
- [pitfall] A drowsy or inattentive witness weakens a transfer record, and their later claim to have attended is itself uncertain. When: When the witness is tired or distracted during the exchange. Why: A record only counts if the witness actually observed the exchange.
- [pitfall] Assuming a silent witness has nothing useful to add.
- [pitfall] Relying on a witness with impaired hearing without checking what she could actually perceive can lead to a wrong timeline. When: A witness with hearing loss gives testimony about sounds. Why: Her account of silence may reflect her limits rather than what happened.
- [pitfall] Assuming a pre-existing illness rules out a human cause. The illness may only make the victim vulnerable while a deliberate trigger still acted.
- [pitfall] Altered time perception can make an honest witness seem to have been in two places at once, so a fixed clock is needed before claiming an intruder.

## witness testimony and neutral questioning
- [rule] Keep your reactions neutral when questioning, since visible shock signals the question matters and may silence the witness. When: interviewing an emotionally involved witness. Why: Reactions reveal what is important and change what the witness says.
- [rule] A neutral question with no stated purpose can measure whether a witness answers candidly. When: a truthfulness check is needed without revealing which fact matters. Why: the question hides the purpose of the test.
- [rule] Give watchers narrow orders, such as recording all entries but stopping only exits, so they gather more information.
- [rule] Use neutral wording in public notices, such as saying a person died rather than was murdered, so the culprit is not alerted. Why: loaded wording can warn the person who committed the crime.
- [rule] Flag ambiguous expressions as neutral facts and reveal their meaning only once corroborating evidence is found.
- [heuristic] Phrase questions neutrally and openly, without presuming an answer or revealing how much you know; presumed premises steer witnesses, and visible interest makes them shape or withhold answers. When: When questioning a witness about identity or events. Why: Witnesses tend to accept the premise a question carries, and showing too much interest in one point makes them shape or withhold the answer.
- [heuristic] Give more weight to a neutral witness who had no reason to shape the account, such as someone who only overheard talk. Why: Without a stake, a witness is less likely to bend the account toward a purpose.
- [heuristic] Trust a neutral witness for plain facts such as who was present in a place, even when that witness cannot say what it meant. Why: Neutral testimony can fix a simple fact without requiring an interpretation.
- [heuristic] Introduce a detail in neutral, ordinary description early, so that its later return reads as a payoff the audience could have anticipated. When: when the final reveal depends on a physical detail. Why: the audience accepts the detail without suspicion.
- [heuristic] Even narrow sensory testimony, such as a felt touch of cloth, can support a usable inference about an unseen person's clothing or position.
- [heuristic] Open an interview with neutral everyday topics such as books, hobbies or a meal to lower a guarded witness's defences before the painful subject. When: A distressed or defensive witness is questioned and there is time to build trust. Why: Relaxed talk makes a witness more willing to disclose.
- [heuristic] A witness who has only just taken up a post may not have seen the arrivals they are asked about, so check their tenure before weighing their memory.
- [heuristic] Have more than one observer watch a subject's reaction, so a signal is confirmed by others before it is relied upon.
- [heuristic] When two accounts agree in nearly every detail, their exceptions mark exactly where the later event differed, so examine those points first. When: Two accounts of similar events are compared. Why: Differences are where the accounts' independent content lies.
- [procedure] 1) Ask an open question without proposing an answer. 2) Only if no answer comes, probe for the existence of a memory. 3) Record suggested answers and any hedged acceptance separately from firm recall. When: Judging how much a witness's account can bear. Why: Neutral questions reveal whether a real memory exists before it is shaped.
- [procedure] 1) Collect accounts from everyone present after the event. 2) Compare them for any report of the disputed event. 3) Weigh the absence of reports as evidence of limited confidence, not proof. When: When a disputed event occurred in a crowded setting. Why: Comparing accounts reveals whether anyone else perceived the event.
- [procedure] 1) State your own stake openly, accepting the risk of exposure. 2) Read the witness's reactions as well as their answers. 3) Press on the specific word that produces a strong reaction. 4) Hold ground under threat. When: A witness has a clear reason to conceal and reacts strongly to one subject. Why: Honest stakes and reaction cues reveal where the witness's knowledge lies.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the specific claim a witness makes. 2) Ask a question that tests that claim, not one that repeats the report. 3) Ask about related conditions the report did not cover, such as weather. When: When interviewing a witness whose account fixes a time or place. Why: Repeating the report yields no new information; testing questions expose gaps.
- [procedure] 1) Accept the account as reasonable to keep the witness talking. 2) Raise a plausible alternative that a challenger could argue. 3) Watch whether the witness or others react with new details or defensiveness. When: Questioning a witness whose account may be shaped by motive. Why: Pressure on a plausible story can expose undisclosed disputes or knowledge.
- [pitfall] Observation at night yields less because sight fails; sound may still reveal what sight cannot. When: Covert observation extends into darkness. Why: Vision degrades in low light while hearing does not.
- [pitfall] Overlooking a nearby busy road as a source of witnesses. Even an isolated house may be watched from a highway in view. When: When assuming a location is isolated. Why: A public route in sight of a building can supply observers.
- [pitfall] Giving NPCs biased opinions about one another while the player arrives neutral lets the player assess the scene independently of the group's prejudices. When: When designing a mystery where characters hold opinions about each other. Why: Neutral observation lets the player detect gaps in the group's consensus.
- [pitfall] Treating a suspect's helpful fact as neutral can hide the motive it reveals. When: A suspect offers evidence that seems to help them. Why: Helpful facts often carry an interest that goes unexamined.
- [fact] A witness at a narrow view, such as a keyhole, sees only a fragment and may give a precise-sounding account covering only part of what happened. When: A witness observes through a small or partial opening or gap. Why: The limited vantage restricts what can be seen, so the account covers only a part.
- [fact] Neutral facts such as a denial or an unrelated record can fit either rival explanation, so they settle nothing between them. When: comparing two competing explanations. Why: Consistency with both sides is not discrimination.
- [fact] Two nearby places let each identity gather many witnesses while no one sees both identities at the same time.
- [fact] In disputes with factions, the accused party may choose a council of witnesses, and outside pressure can force additional members onto it. Why: Each side's selection of witnesses shapes who judges the case.

## belief versus proof
- [definition] Suspicion is reasoned doubt justifying keeping someone on a suspect list; proof is specific evidence holding under scrutiny that justifies accusation. These are distinct stages; each claim must be provable.
- [mechanism] A false belief survives after part of it is disproven, because it still explains real clues that the player has already accepted. Why: Each lie accounts for some existing evidence, so the player keeps the belief.
- [rule] Keep belief separate from proof and base decisions on evidence alone: mark proven conclusions versus suspicions; a conviction may be stated openly while admitting it cannot yet be demonstrated. When: A case rests on inference or the decisive evidence is not yet in hand. Why: A strong belief can feel like knowledge; stating the gap keeps the accusation honest.
- [rule] Pressure alone neither proves guilt nor shows the accused knows what the scene reveals; accept a pressured confession only once its statements match what was observed. Why: Pressure can produce false admissions as easily as true ones.
- [rule] Keep an investigator's proof separate from their reputation, so accusations are judged by evidence rather than by standing. When: Rumour attacks the credibility of an accusation. Why: Mixing proof with reputation lets rumour decide what is true.
- [rule] Mark which parts of a speaker's account are confirmed by other sources and which are only that speaker's belief.
- [rule] Separate confirmed case journal entries from rumour entries, so players build the base layer of facts before forming theories. When: Designing a case journal or investigation log. Why: Players who see rumour mixed with confirmed facts may build theories on the wrong base.
- [rule] Keep a witness's belief separate from physical evidence. A physical trace is data, while the claimed nature of a creature is only asserted. When: when a witness describes an unusual cause.
- [rule] Store financial motive and personal motive as separate values, so the player can weigh greed against grudge. When: when modeling NPC motives for a mystery or inheritance plot. Why: separate values let players judge which motive best explains an action.
- [rule] Treat a confirmed difference between matched objects as a lead, then check whether the object was moved or the difference was always present. When: a feature of a matched object does not match its pair. Why: A difference may be innocent and predate the event.
- [rule] Keep the source of each pressure separate from the evidence; record only what the facts support, not the frustration that outside remarks produce.
- [rule] Separate the stated charge from the underlying cause, and check whether the official reason explains the outcome fully. When: Analysing a persecution, expulsion or punishment whose official reason seems incomplete. Why: The stated charge can hide a different motive, such as control of property or office.
- [rule] Present a reconstructed decision as a probable explanation, not proof, when records are missing. Why: Hedged words such as probable mark conjecture, and readers often mistake them for settled fact.
- [rule] Keep the question of whether a harm occurred separate from the question of who caused it, and require independent evidence for the second before resolving an accusation. When: An accuser reports harm and names a specific person. Why: Accepting that harm occurred can quietly stand in for proof of who caused it.
- [rule] Treat a suspect's conviction about an explanation as an argument to weigh, not as proof; the arrangement of objects decides.
- [heuristic] Treat a plausible story as a conjecture, not proof; keep rival explanations open until evidence separates them. When: evidence is partial and one story fits neatly. Why: a neat fit can still be wrong.
- [heuristic] Do not assume a blackmailer and a murderer are the same person without evidence; keep the possibility open.
- [heuristic] Suspicion built from rumour, coincidence and character reading can add up to a strong feeling but does not prove guilt. Why: Each weak cue can have an innocent explanation, and agreement among them does not remove that possibility.
- [heuristic] A character's false belief can reveal their state of mind and motive, especially when the error is explained and connected to the case.
- [pitfall] Eerie atmosphere or emotion, such as imagined apparitions, is not a clue and must not replace checked facts; only verified facts advance the inquiry. When: Interpreting eerie or emotional imagery, or feeling an eerie presence around a case. Why: Mood can feel like proof while carrying no factual weight; feeling is not evidence.
- [pitfall] Threatening consequences alone may not produce a confession; an obstinate suspect can withstand pressure without proof. When: When pressure is the only lever used in questioning. Why: Pressure works best when backed by evidence the suspect knows is real.
- [pitfall] Confirming that an event happened does not confirm what was said during it; only one party may report the content. When: when a call or meeting is confirmed. Why: Confirmation covers the occurrence, not the content.
- [pitfall] Treating a theory about an unwritten document as proof is a pitfall; it needs support from other evidence before it is accepted.
- [pitfall] A surmised motive is not evidence of identity; a theory must be confirmed before it can establish who did the act. When: An investigator builds a case on motive alone. Why: Benefit does not automatically identify the actor.
- [pitfall] A found object can look like it confirms a theory when it only fits the theory loosely, so it should not count as proof on its own. When: Interpreting a single physical find. Why: One object usually establishes only a limited fact.
- [fact] A case record can differ from what investigators believe happened, since unproven crimes stay unrecorded.

## discounting testimony
- [mechanism] Once a listener accepts a general theory that the accuser's mind is disordered, every protest from the accuser can be read as further proof of illness, so the claim cannot be tested in conversation. When: A specific but unverified accusation is answered by questioning the accuser's sanity. Why: An unfalsifiable framing absorbs all counter-argument.
- [rule] Discount testimony from people close to a suspect or quarrelling with the accused unless checked independently; dismissing it outright may discard claims that are true or confirmed elsewhere. (x2)
- [rule] When a watcher is dismissed or caught, trigger a dialogue or event so the failed tail has consequences.
- [rule] Discount accusations offered as personal opinion that no evidence supports, and do not treat them as findings. When: A witness accuses someone without backing. Why: Opinion without evidence is unverified.
- [rule] Do not dismiss a credible expert merely because the investigator dislikes the conclusion.
- [rule] When disputing a published claim, produce the relevant documents in full rather than summaries, so readers can judge the disputed passages themselves.
- [heuristic] Discount embellished accounts, including a witness's self-praise and partisan or dramatic framing, and keep only the bare facts reported. When: A witness's account is wrapped in enthusiasm, self-praise, or strongest-colour framing. Why: Exaggeration and vivid framing can inflate the facts beyond what the evidence supports. (x2)
- [heuristic] Do not dismiss a biased, vague, or unreliable witness outright; their usable facts, leads or event details survive, and dismissing all testimony discards real information. When: A witness has a motive, weak memory, or vague dates but offers concrete information. Why: Bias distorts content, but underlying facts or directions can be correct, and reliable parts are lost when all testimony is dismissed. (x2)
- [heuristic] A dismissed or careless-seeming witness may still be right; re-check sightings conflicting with the official view and minor conflicts with a confident theory before rejecting them. When: A witness's account conflicts with the official view or a confident theory. Why: The witness may be right about a detail the theory missed.
- [heuristic] Weigh a stakeholder narrator's account against his own admissions and against other witnesses before accepting his version of events. When: A narrator has a stake in how events are judged. Why: His self-serving framing and admitted errors make his account partial, so independent checks reveal the facts.
- [heuristic] An NPC who notices a pattern can warn the player while a powerful figure dismisses the warning, creating tension the player can exploit. When: Designing faction conflict around a discovered pattern. Why: The gap between warning and dismissal gives the player a reason to act.
- [heuristic] Set a suspect aside with stated reasons rather than dismissing them outright, so the discount can be checked later. When: A suspect looks guilty because of a convenient role. Why: Explicit reasons make the discount testable and fair.
- [heuristic] Reframing a disputed claim as open questions for decision makers keeps it in play while formally disowning it.
- [tradeoff] Discarding testimony that conflicts with established facts keeps the record clean but may lose real information that the witness did provide. When: witnesses conflict or a suspect's account seems tailored. Why: every rejected account carries a cost as well as a benefit.
- [tradeoff] Discrediting a rival's clue by attacking the rival wins the moment but can cost standing with factions who see the attack as partisan. When: when a dialogue option attacks a source instead of the evidence.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a witness as insane, unwell, or hysterical ends inquiry or lowers their weight without disproving the account; test strange details, since illness alone does not make it false. When: A character or investigator discounts a witness's emotional, ill, or strange testimony. Why: Emotional delivery or illness is not the same as falsehood. (x3)
- [pitfall] Discrediting a witness for questionable conduct or poor moral character can discard accurate testimony, since conduct and character are separate from factual accuracy. When: A witness's own behaviour is questionable or their character is poor. Why: Conduct and character are separate questions from accuracy. (x2)
- [pitfall] Dismissing an early warning or anonymous note as a prank can miss a pattern across later incidents or discard the only insider clue. Why: Notes can carry access information.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a frightened witness as mistaken, or a fear as baseless, before testing the setting can discard a true account or a real hiding place.
- [pitfall] Absurd-sounding explanations may hold the true mechanism, and unlikely second-hand reports may be right; discard an explanation only on direct testimonial contradiction, after checking first-hand sources. When: Choosing between candidate explanations or a theory is dismissed as fanciful. Why: Likelihood is a weaker basis than contradiction; dismissal based on strangeness can discard the explanation that fits the physical facts.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a child's warning too quickly can hide a true clue; weigh it against known facts instead.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a reasonable lead with contempt can shut down a line of inquiry before its value is tested.
- [pitfall] A witness who says they know nothing relevant may still hold the decisive fact. Check what a source contains before treating it as irrelevant. When: when a source seems unhelpful. Why: People often disclaim relevance while holding information they did not think mattered.
- [pitfall] A quick dismissive explanation for a gap may be a deflection; check it rather than accepting it.
- [pitfall] Dismissing the explanations people give as cover for a real motive turns the inference into the observer's assumption rather than evidence. When: a character's stated reason conflicts with the investigator's theory. Why: the investigator stops testing and starts projecting.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a recantation as a lie because the original confession is already on record ignores the conditions the recantation exposes.

## misread clues and signals
- [mechanism] NPC rumours of being watched, with no identified source, create paranoia and ambiguity without resolving anything.
- [mechanism] An official account can absorb an early physical oddity, so a deliberate insider murder passes as a natural death or intruder's work until the oddity is re-examined. When: a death that looks natural or external.
- [rule] Record ambiguous sightings and unexplained odd behaviour as unconfirmed leads, not as proof, and leave them uninterpreted until evidence arrives. When: when a witness reports something that fits no explanation yet. Why: early interpretation of an ambiguous detail can harden into a false conclusion.
- [rule] Plant a misleading reading of a clue that the player can see through only with a later key. When: mystery clue design. Why: the player holds the error until the key arrives.
- [heuristic] Two independent unlikely matches together can exceed what chance allows, though a single common match proves little.
- [heuristic] A common name slows a search; a distinctive detail, such as a religion or a family placement, narrows the candidates quickly. When: a suspect's name matches many people in the records. Why: the detail excludes most candidates at once.
- [heuristic] Let the dialogue system record the cause of a misread, such as a visor or poor lighting, so players can correct the impression. When: When an NPC reads a player's stance or gear as hostile for a visual reason. Why: A recorded cause lets the player understand and fix the misjudgment.
- [heuristic] Use protagonist misreading when key information is held by a group the protagonist does not yet understand; avoid it if the audience must share the blindness throughout.
- [heuristic] A trace is often explained by its most familiar source, but the familiar source can hide a rarer one, so check the material before accepting it. When: a trace resembles a common residue or object. Why: familiar explanations are reached quickly.
- [pitfall] Treating disorder, burning or an incidental item carried from a scene as proof of guilt closes off other explanations; presence alone does not establish the crime. When: Interpreting signs of destruction or incidental items at a crime scene. Why: Disorder has many causes, and presence at a scene does not establish that the person committed the crime. (x2)
- [pitfall] A false lead or decisive fact withheld, never corrected or signalled later, reads as unfair cheating rather than a fair trap; players cannot check what they never had. When: When withholding a decisive fact or leaving a false lead. Why: Players cannot reason toward a fact they never had a chance to check.
- [pitfall] Reading a sound as the event it resembles, such as a blind flapping for a groan, creates false certainty. When: A witness hears an ambiguous noise. Why: Familiar explanations are accepted before alternatives are considered.
- [pitfall] Chasing a detail whose significance is unclear can lead to a false trail.
- [pitfall] A misread letter or signal can send an investigation after the wrong person.
- [pitfall] Hope can read a brief stir from an unconscious patient as meaningful speech or hearing, when it may not be. When: a dying or unconscious witness shows a faint sign.
- [pitfall] An animal's aggression may be aimed at something other than the person it seems to target; revise the reading once the true cause is found.
- [pitfall] Accepting the most common motive, such as silencing a blackmailer, without checking whether it is proportionate to the suspect's position. When: A familiar motive is offered for a crime. Why: Familiar motives are adopted without testing their fit to the suspect.
- [pitfall] Digressions that do not connect back to the main case stall the pace. Why: they delay without adding to the payoff.
- [pitfall] A rumour that is wrong in an unmarked way can mislead the audience permanently if no later passage corrects it. When: when a clue is delivered through gossip. Why: Without correction, the false version stands as accepted fact.
- [pitfall] A hint shared with only one person can leave the audience unsure what was passed, so the later payoff must make it clear. When: A hint is delivered in private.
- [pitfall] If a protagonist's misreading is never corrected, the audience cannot tell the character's mistake apart from the author's intent.
- [pitfall] Errors compound when one unconfirmed guess becomes the basis for the next inference. When: building a chain of deductions.
- [pitfall] A cold or confident manner is not proof of guilt, since it may be affectation or simply temperament. When: Judging a suspect by demeanour alone. Why: Personality traits can look like evidence while meaning nothing about the act.
- [pitfall] A record naming the wrong person may be the only surviving trace of an event, so it can mislead investigators.
- [pitfall] A momentary quiver can be dismissed too quickly, leaving the observer confident in a wrong reading of consciousness. When: When observing a sleeper for signs of awareness. Why: Brief signs are easy to miss or explain away.
- [pitfall] A flushed face may come from embarrassment about an unrelated matter, so a reaction must be interpreted against the topic that caused it. When: Interpreting a witness's visible emotional reaction. Why: The same physical sign can arise from different causes.

## omission as clue
- [mechanism] A frame can survive without outright lies: each planted clue stays consistent with the false story until one withheld account contradicts it. Why: Silence leaves the evidence looking coherent while hiding the decisive fact.
- [behavior] A teller who gives a partial account signals the gap, and a listener who asks directly for the missing part often gets it. When: A speaker's account is incomplete. Why: Partial accounts leave visible seams that careful questioning exposes.
- [rule] Treat excised or omitted passages as evidence: writers' beliefs and compilers' purposes decide what appears, so gaps in an abridged text can say as much as its printed content.
- [rule] Ask which fact a witness has left out, since a conspicuous omission can expose a contradiction with physical facts.
- [rule] Weigh what a writer leaves out as well as what they say, and follow up any gap the writer admits to.
- [rule] Treat an omission from a formal complaint as evidence of a hidden motive only when independent corroboration supports it. When: a complaint leaves out a matter that seems central. Why: silence alone is ambiguous.
- [heuristic] An omitted detail can be the key clue, especially on timing or cause, so probe what a teller did not mention, even if they judged it unimportant. When: a second-hand account lacks a detail the first witness noticed. Why: Tellers often drop facts they judge not worth passing on.
- [heuristic] A name conspicuously absent from a group appeal or petition may show the writer judged that person beyond persuasion, a possible sign of distrust or grudge to confirm elsewhere. When: a person expected in a group appeal or petition is left out, especially in a dispute. Why: Deliberate omission can carry meaning and reflect the relationship.
- [heuristic] If a source never mentions something it would have to know about, the omission suggests it did not know. When: the source would naturally mention the item if aware of it. Why: Silence about an expected detail signals ignorance.
- [heuristic] Omitted exculpatory testimony from a writer who must have known of it signals selective reporting; do not assume omission was innocent without checking what the writer knew. When: A writer covers a case but leaves out defense witnesses. Why: Selective inclusion can shape the case.
- [heuristic] A written account that describes a person in detail but omits the name the writer would know is unnatural and suggests another hand composed it. When: when checking the content of a supposed confession. Why: Writers normally name people they know well.
- [heuristic] A name missing from one witness's list of people present is worth checking against the other accounts.
- [heuristic] A suspect who omits a witness that would support an alibi, even when that witness is named, suggests the witness was not compromised. Why: A compromised witness would normally have been offered as an alibi earlier.
- [heuristic] Failing to sign a corrective statement, when one could help, can indicate the person did not help correct the record.
- [heuristic] Make the omitted passage the clue: the summary says one thing, and the complete text contradicts it. When: designing discovery of hidden lore. Why: Omissions can be checked by a motivated player.
- [heuristic] A document that says little about the writer's life can still be informative through what it omits and through its date and place. When: Reading a sparse personal letter. Why: Absence of detail and the metadata of date and place can carry meaning.
- [heuristic] An omitted statement matters most when it would settle a question, so check whether a key observation was actually recorded. When: Assessing a case file, report or witness account for gaps. Why: A missing observation that would decide a question is a meaningful gap.
- [pitfall] Omission may stem from restraint, fear, protecting the reader, or private reasons, so treat it as a clue to check, not proof of deception. (x2)
- [pitfall] Cutting the part of an answer that addresses the central question, or qualifiers from a quotation, changes its meaning even when the excerpt looks complete. When: Reviewing summaries or excerpts of testimony, advice, confessions or documents. Why: Removed responses or qualifiers change meaning while the excerpt looks complete.
- [pitfall] A witness's summary often skips steps they did not observe, so those steps must be reconstructed from evidence. When: when relying on a secondhand account. Why: unobserved steps are missing from the summary.
- [pitfall] If a withheld fact is too prominent, players dismiss the witness as a liar rather than as a fallible observer.
- [pitfall] A clue left out of the first review may never be tested, so its significance stays hidden. When: Reviewing a set of clues. Why: Unlisted items do not get checked against other evidence.
- [pitfall] A missing clause shows that something was left out, not what it was, so identifying the omission needs a second source.
- [pitfall] Reading an omission in a record as proof of a fact is an error, since careful wording may be innocent. When: Drawing conclusions from what a monument or document does not say. Why: An absent claim does not establish the opposite claim.
- [fact] A suspect's account can leave out a visit that a neutral record, such as a station log or staff memory, would reveal.
- [fact] Omission deceives more quietly than false statement: the listener hears a trimmed version without any claim being false.

## plausible reasoning errors
- [definition] A plausible reconstruction is a coherent account of motive, sequence and character, distinct from evidence that would survive challenge.
- [behavior] A suspicious act or calm, coherent explanation that accounts for odd details is accepted quickly, and inquiry stops, even when it fails to fit all facts. When: when a suspicious act comes with a reasonable explanation, or two readings of an event are both plausible. Why: A plausible reason answers the question, and coherence and comfort make a neat theory easy to accept. (x2)
- [behavior] A suspect may offer an explanation before being asked, which signals the question was anticipated. When: When a suspect volunteers an answer to an unasked question. Why: Anticipating a question suggests the suspect knows the weak point.
- [rule] Make each suspicion rest on a plausible basis in evidence or motive, since misdirection works only when the reason to suspect is credible. When: designing red herrings or rotating suspects. Why: unfounded suspicion reads as arbitrary.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses estimates that are plausible but wrong, so the player must cross-check them against other evidence. When: When designing NPC witness testimony.
- [heuristic] Make the first explanation or suspect plausible, internally logical and partly true or wrong, with real evidence present; then overturn it with one decisive clue the player already saw. When: Designing a mystery with a later reveal. Why: A plausible wrong answer makes the reversal land and feels fair rather than arbitrary. (x2)
- [heuristic] Compare a suspect's reaction to accusation with what a guilty or innocent person would plausibly do in that situation. When: a suspect responds to an accusation. Why: plausibility gives the reaction a reference.
- [heuristic] Judge an account by whether the teller's own behaviour is plausible, such as whether they would destroy the evidence that could check it.
- [heuristic] A plan that would swap one accomplice for a more dangerous one is one a sensible plotter avoids, which can help eliminate a suspect. When: judging whether a suspect would plan a crime through an accomplice. Why: rational plotters avoid added risk.
- [heuristic] Keep 'possible' separate from 'probable': a strained explanation that could be true is not supporting evidence for it.
- [heuristic] Strong positive evidence can outweigh doubts about how strong a motive is.
- [heuristic] Plausible pressure aimed at a witness's specific fear can make a reluctant witness talk. When: When a witness is cooperative in principle but unwilling to confess.
- [heuristic] Odd features of older buildings, such as low ceilings, often had practical reasons like warmth, so judge them by period needs rather than modern expectations.
- [pitfall] Plausible chains of links are not proof: check each link separately, mark inferred links as conjecture, and confirm the theory with a witness or record. Why: Inferred links otherwise look as certain as recorded facts. (x2)
- [pitfall] A story that explains every detail, fits timing, or rests on uncheckable premises can still be false or aim at the wrong object; test each detail independently. (x2)
- [pitfall] Explanations or coincidences fitted after a trace or event is known can match any result, so claims recorded only after confirmation prove nothing.
- [pitfall] A plausible event or assumption about what someone ought to know is not evidence that they acted; linking a named suspect to it needs direct evidence.
- [pitfall] A tidy, plausible premise or theory built on unchecked gaps feels like established fact, spreads unchallenged, and can steer toward a chosen suspect while hiding the real cause. When: when the theory rests on gaps its proponent admits are unchecked. Why: Plausibility is mistaken for verification, so the theory spreads before anyone tests it.
- [pitfall] Plausible routes or methods can fail timing, channel-arithmetic or physical checks, such as groping through a space that would cause a fall; feasibility objections can outweigh theory, so test them. When: when judging a proposed route, method or claim verified only by appearance. Why: Plausible narratives often ignore physical constraints, which may not hold.
- [pitfall] Accepting a story because the teller seems plausible skips verification, and the only vouching party may be the suspect's own partner. When: Weighing testimony from a sympathetic or interested source. Why: Plausible delivery is not evidence, and a partner's vouching has limited independence.
- [pitfall] A plausible explanation that reconciles conflicting accounts is only a hypothesis until a possible actor and a witness check support it. Why: Plausibility is not proof.
- [pitfall] A discrepancy can be explained away by a prepared story chosen to fit it; the story must be tested against evidence before it is accepted.
- [pitfall] A witness's remembered date may be wrong, and a plausible date can hide that mistake. When: a witness's timeline seems consistent with other facts. Why: Consistency with other details can make an error look correct.
- [pitfall] A plausible theory can fail once a single discriminating fact is weighed against it. When: Only one fact contradicts an otherwise coherent story. Why: Fit with most facts does not guarantee the theory is true.
- [pitfall] Treating a plausible timeline as proof of the events inside it is a mistake, since a timeline shows where a person was but not who was present or why. When: a timeline is built from traces. Why: location and time do not establish presence or motive.
- [pitfall] Isolation and personal stake make a chain of links look stronger than it is. When: When an investigator works alone under strain on a case that matters to them. Why: Without outside checks, personal investment inflates confidence in inferences.

## pressure tactics
- [mechanism] Forced inaction raises pressure: when characters cannot act until a signal arrives, restlessness builds and the eventual action feels more urgent. When: when the plot holds characters waiting for a message or event. Why: Frustrated waiting makes the next development land with more force.
- [mechanism] A binary choice with no third option forces a concealed fact into the open, since the suspect must either admit it or accept the test. When: when a rival or witness is holding back an item. Why: Removing an escape option compels a visible answer.
- [behavior] Equal depth in both tracks suggests a rider was forcing the pace, with weight thrown forward onto the handlebars. When: Both tyre tracks show the same depth. Why: Pushing hard shifts weight forward, so the front and rear marks press equally.
- [behavior] Under pressure, a suspect's denial may contradict their own earlier words, a sign that the pressure is working.
- [behavior] Heavy pressure can make a loyal witness shut down completely, and repeated attempts may fail to break her loyalty. When: under repeated questioning. Why: loyalty can outweigh fear of pressure.
- [behavior] Under sharp questioning a witness may show physical tells such as a drained face, a hand pressed to the chest or a sudden flush of anger. When: a witness is pressed on a sensitive fact. Why: pressure produces involuntary physical signs.
- [behavior] A person who has escaped a pressing situation, such as an unwanted engagement, may have a motive to conceal events.
- [rule] Threats and anger are tactics, not evidence; tag each confession with its pressure source, such as threat or despair, and require corroboration before acting on it. When: Logging confessions in a case system. Why: The tag reveals how far the statement can be trusted. (x2)
- [rule] Offer the player a choice between pressing an NPC now and waiting for a better moment, so restraint is a meaningful option. When: when an NPC withholds information. Why: the timing of pressure changes what the player learns.
- [rule] Use pressure tactics only when there is evidence to test the account against.
- [heuristic] Threats and provocation may draw a confession from a volatile suspect, but lose force against a composed, stable one, so pressure alone rarely works. When: Pressing a suspect with no eyewitness and weak physical proof. (x2)
- [heuristic] Use a clue that comes from pressure rather than calm planning when the plot needs a lapse by otherwise composed offenders. When: Writing a mystery where the culprit is usually careful. Why: Pressure-induced mistakes are plausible and differ from the planned behaviour.
- [heuristic] Use pressure rather than proof to draw out a visible reaction; a suspect who feels watched is more likely to make a move the observer can see. When: A suspect can act and the observer needs a visible move. Why: Feeling watched prompts action over silence.
- [heuristic] Silence, sudden accusations and unexpected known facts force reactions that reveal whether a suspect is lying or merely surprised.
- [heuristic] Asking a witness what they mean by not recalling forces a commitment to a claim that can be tested. When: a witness repeatedly answers that they cannot remember.
- [procedure] 1) Control the room so the suspect cannot leave. 2) Show a threat calmly without using it. 3) When fear appears, respond kindly and promise no harm. 4) Signal you already know more than they admitted. When: suspect is frightened and holds only partial knowledge. Why: fear, then reassurance, and visible knowledge lower resistance and remove the option of clever lying.
- [procedure] 1) Recall the two alternatives offered earlier. 2) Set a public challenge against a quiet alternative. 3) Judge the likely response by how much the target fears exposure. 4) Send each contact with a specific purpose. When: the target is sensitive to reputational damage and a legal option exists. Why: the choice is defined by options already raised.
- [tradeoff] Pressure exposes liars and forces clear answers, but also makes honest or reluctant witnesses lie, falter or withdraw; use it when exposure matters more than truth. When: Choosing how hard to question a witness. Why: Pressure cannot tell a nervous truth-teller from a liar, and raises stakes for the subject, who may protect themselves instead of answering. (x2)
- [pitfall] Pressing a defensive, fragile or sensitive-topic witness too hard can make them order you out, withdraw, panic or give guarded replies, ending useful testimony. When: Pressing a defensive witness repeatedly; a witness already holding back; probing a topic they avoid. Why: Excessive pressure turns the exchange hostile and triggers defensiveness, closing the channel and reducing information gained. (x2)
- [pitfall] Pressing a cornered or resistant suspect hard provokes hostility and objection that multiply dangers; calm, persistent questioning often works better.
- [pitfall] Pressure can provoke an outburst that hands control of the room to the suspect.
- [pitfall] Heavy pressure can backfire: a suspect may recast the questioning as persecution, forcing the questioner to soften manner to keep the interview going. When: Interrogation becomes aggressive. Why: Perceived mistreatment gives the suspect sympathy and a reason to disengage.
- [pitfall] Forcing a disguise off can expose the person who forces it to legal liability, such as charges for assault. When: An unmasking is done without consent.
- [pitfall] Using force before establishing the facts shifts moral weight onto the accuser, who can be seen as the aggressor even if they were right.
- [pitfall] A statement made under pressure can be passed on as settled fact by a listener who never witnessed the pressure.
- [fact] Suspects rarely disclose their whole story without sustained pressure, so psychological tactics alone seldom produce a full confession.

## reveal delivery and pacing
- [model] Reveals recast one of three beliefs: that an object is what it seems, that a suspect is guilty, or that the narrator is reliable.
- [model] A reveal arc has six ordered phases: seeding, sightings and lies, reversal and false trail, plan and misfire, reveal through overheard evidence, then denial and confrontation. When: designing a suspicion-driven secret reveal. Why: Each phase builds on the last so the final confirmation feels earned.
