- [definition] A stacked reveal is a sequence in which each reveal overturns the belief set up by the previous one, so the case turns over more than once.
- [mechanism] When the reader already knows a mechanism, a closing line that names its cost recasts the whole scene, so the earlier image reads differently. When: Final beat of a reveal. Why: The reader links the earlier image to the mechanism.
- [mechanism] Showing the hidden truth to the audience at the same moment the narrator learns it creates a shock without withholding information. When: a narrator holds a false belief about the situation. Why: The audience experiences the reveal alongside the narrator, so no fairness is lost.
- [mechanism] A reveal that reclassifies the mystery, such as turning a supernatural curse into a human fraud, gives the player a new frame for reinterpreting the whole investigation. When: The solution changes the nature of the threat, not just its identity. Why: A new frame makes earlier clues mean something different, sustaining interest after the answer.
- [behavior] Let players use the same signal as the detective and reveal whose signal it was later, so the signal's meaning shifts with new information. When: designing a communication signal between hidden characters. Why: Players interpret a signal through their own use of it, and a later reveal reframes it.
- [rule] Do not rely on a reveal's explanation or name link alone; back it with physical evidence, testimony or a confession so it is convincing rather than asserted. When: Revealing a hidden identity or solution. Why: A single link is easy to doubt, while several sources make it convincing. (x2)
- [rule] Do not stage a reveal before its key evidence is set out and the audience is ready; without evidence, the naming feels arbitrary and fails to persuade. When: Planning when to deliver a major or climactic reveal. Why: The reveal depends on its evidence; a naming before the evidence lacks grounds.
- [heuristic] Put early reversals on threats to the protagonist's security, since they attack the audience's sense of safety, and resolve them quickly with documentary proof. When: Structuring the opening act of a mystery. Why: Early security threats hook the audience; quick resolution avoids stalling.
- [heuristic] Hold a key inference back until a later scene, so tension builds and the reveal lands once the player has the evidence to accept it. When: mystery pacing across scenes.
- [heuristic] Weigh several explanations for an alarming claim, such as jealousy, blackmail or misunderstanding, before accepting the most dramatic one. When: when a claim suggests a serious offence. Why: the dramatic reading is often not the only one the facts allow.
- [heuristic] A reveal gains credibility when the most affected person grants permission for it, so the audience trusts the knowledge as coming from a legitimate source. When: A reveal changes the status of people involved and needs acceptance. Why: Sanctioned disclosure makes the account feel authoritative rather than self-serving.
- [heuristic] Pair a reveal with a threat to whoever holds the evidence, so that reading the reveal itself becomes a source of danger. When: When the final reveal should raise stakes rather than end the tension. Why: A threat attached to the evidence makes the act of knowing part of the risk.
- [heuristic] Establish early that the flaw lies in the method, so a later solution reads as a correction rather than a new fact. When: when planning a reversal of the player's assumption. Why: framing makes the solution feel earned.
- [heuristic] Prefer confession or overheard speech over formal explanation as the reveal, since the culprit's own words feel earned.
- [heuristic] End the solution with a reinterpretation of known objects rather than a new fact. When: writing the final reveal. Why: Rereading familiar evidence makes the answer feel earned.
- [heuristic] Expose disguises through a mix of demonstration and confrontation, so each reveal is shown as well as told.
- [procedure] 1) Introduce a plausible suspect backed by evidence. 2) Add a second suspect with a stronger, timed claim. 3) Expose a disguise that breaks that claim. 4) Doubt the witness. 5) Reveal who held the key. 6) Overturn the belief with a document. 7) Expose the motive. When: designing a multi-stage mystery reveal.
- [procedure] 1) Explain the solution to the relevant characters. 2) Back the explanation with a proof arranged in advance, such as a demonstration, a comparison, a physical search or a letter. 3) Show the consequences briefly. When: When resolving a mystery before the affected characters. Why: A prepared proof makes the solution verifiable rather than merely asserted.
- [procedure] 1) Interrupt the scene with a sudden event. 2) Have a trusted figure authorise the reveal. 3) Present evidence in order, dismissing rumours first. 4) Place the decisive fact last. 5) Close with a question that tests the listeners' judgement. When: Structuring a reveal scene where the solution must land with impact. Why: Escalating beats and sanctioned disclosure build tension and make the conclusion feel earned.
- [procedure] 1) Gather the suspects in one room. 2) Explain the false solution. 3) Expose its flaw with a physical proof: a trap, a recovered object, a confession or an on-the-spot experiment. 4) Resolve the culprit's fate. When: Staging the final reveal of a mystery. Why: With suspects present, each reaction is visible and the proof is public.
- [pitfall] Revealing the fallback route can reduce the chance of an honest answer from the witness currently being questioned.
- [pitfall] Repeatedly delaying a payoff without adding new information makes tension feel empty rather than building.
- [pitfall] Showing the source of a threat too early removes the dread, while blurring every detail leaves the audience unable to judge what was actually perceived. Why: suspense depends on partial information that is still clear enough to follow.
- [fact] Reveals often cost the protagonist more than they resolve, leaving them condemned, absolved or troubled at the close.

## suspicious secrecy and behaviour
- [behavior] When a character reacts to an object without a shown cause, the audience tends to blame the person rather than examine the object. When: a reaction is shown without explanation. Why: the reaction has no visible cause to attach it to.
- [behavior] When an act looks inexplicable and the actor cannot or will not give reasons, audiences generate rival motives to fill the gap. When: an act has no stated reason. Why: An unexplained act leaves a gap that people fill with guesses.
- [behavior] A suspect who tries to undo a warning by acting on it often produces the very act that exposes them. When: A suspect reacts to a warning with an outgoing message or move. Why: The reaction itself becomes visible evidence.
- [behavior] Neighbours who cannot explain a rival's sudden large gain tend to suspect envy or wrongdoing, even without evidence of either. When: someone with little visible means acquires a large holding. Why: Unexplained advantage invites suspicion and resentment.
- [rule] An unexplained fact, such as a large purchase, shows only motive. Rule out ordinary explanations like overheard gossip or third-party relay before concluding guilt; physical evidence is needed. When: when a suspect has an unexplained large purchase or resource, or knows something with no recorded route.
- [heuristic] Money that moves in ways the neighbours cannot explain, such as loans, cash payments and large spending, shows a hidden source of funds. When: When a victim's finances do not match her known means. Why: Unexplained income often points to the motive behind a killing.
- [heuristic] An official's anxious interest in a suspect that exceeds the stated reason is a strong clue to a hidden relationship. When: An official shows concern beyond their stated role. Why: Real motive shows in excess concern that the stated reason does not justify.
- [heuristic] Let an unexplained reaction unlock an interview with a third NPC, making it a valid lead the player can follow. When: A reaction points to a relationship the player cannot yet explain. Why: A third character can supply the missing context and move the investigation forward.
- [heuristic] An unexplained change in an NPC's plans, paired with a stated reason that does not fit, can serve as a clue hook for the player to pursue. When: Designing story hooks. Why: A mismatch between action and reason invites investigation.
- [heuristic] A firm ultimatum, such as threatening to inform the authorities, can move a reluctant person to speak. When: a person refuses to cooperate voluntarily.
- [heuristic] Introduce a specific name with no context and watch for abrupt shifts in posture, colour or tone; a quick guard going up is a tell, not proof. When: testing whether a witness's denial holds. Why: a guarded reaction can have many causes beyond knowledge of the subject.
- [heuristic] When a reaction is much stronger than expected, treat the gap between expectation and result as information to study. Why: an unexplained gap may point to knowledge the investigator lacks.
- [heuristic] A large offer with no explanation, especially one promising no questions, warrants scrutiny of the real motive. When: when the reward is out of proportion to the item.
- [procedure] 1) Prepare a question plan in advance. 2) Open calmly and let the suspect commit to a defence. 3) Gauge composure, then pause to reconsider rather than push harder. 4) Ask a pointed question about a specific time, place and detail. 5) Follow with narrow, checkable details. When: when the suspect has given a smooth, prepared account. Why: a specific, unanticipated question tests whether the account holds.
- [pitfall] Withheld information, such as secrecy or a motive, reads as a cheat or misdirection unless the audience later learns why it was held back.
- [pitfall] A sudden change of manner that is not explained can read as an authorial trick rather than as character. When: A character abruptly changes demeanour. Why: Without motivation the change feels contrived to the audience.
- [pitfall] A stranger's unusual interest in an investigation may be either a clue or a red herring, so treat it as ambiguous until tested.
- [pitfall] A pretext that leaves the host uneasy can deepen the very secrecy it was meant to uncover. When: when the host is suspicious after the entry. Why: Unease makes the host more guarded.
- [pitfall] A question whose purpose is unexplained can seem odd, so others may dismiss it before its answer matters.
- [pitfall] Announcing a new arrest without detail can confuse the audience about who is guilty. When: A reversal introduces a new suspect. Why: Vague announcements leave the guilty party unclear.
- [pitfall] A denial with no explanation leaves a suspect exposed, even when the suspect is innocent.
- [pitfall] Underestimating a cool-headed suspect's reaction can lead to injuries to officers.
- [pitfall] A reveal that leaves one action unexplained frustrates the audience, even when the rest of the solution holds.
- [pitfall] Reasoning from constraints assumes behavior that no record confirms, so the conclusion is only as strong as that assumption. When: The act being inferred is undocumented. Why: An unverified behavior may not have happened as assumed.
- [pitfall] A reaction that an innocent person also triggers identifies no one, and explanations offered afterward for that result are not controls.
- [fact] Involuntary tells include a facial spasm, a suspicious glance at passing strangers, and a voice that cannot be steadied.

## timeline and timing
- [mechanism] A time-stamped dialogue record can serve as a timeline that later puzzles check, so events reported in conversation become verifiable facts. Why: Stored timestamps let later game logic test a player's claims against what was recorded.
- [mechanism] Market prices can react to an event before any report appears, so a price series can fix when the event happened. When: Direct witnesses or reports are unavailable. Why: Sharp drops and later recovery mark the event's date.
- [rule] Use separate independent references, such as a stopped device, a celestial position and a tidal state, each to anchor a different part of one sequence.
- [rule] Each new reliable sighting shortens the possible interval and shifts the odds, so an argument that ignores known sightings is weakened.
- [heuristic] Confirm a claimed time against an independent clock or record, such as a call log or relayed signal, not the witness's or suspect's own account or watch alone. When: when a witness or suspect states a time that matters. Why: An outside record does not depend on any one account.
- [heuristic] Anchor a sequence with independent times such as an arrival or a meal hour, which together set the window for each event. When: when witnesses give conflicting or incomplete times.
- [heuristic] Time each step of an alibi with a different witness, so one faulty clock cannot break the whole chain. Why: A failure is contained to one link when sources are independent.
- [heuristic] An independent physical estimate, such as time of death, gives a second window against which a witness's timeline can be tested.
- [heuristic] An independent source fixes a time or place only if it does not depend on the suspect. Uncertain recognition or incomplete records may fail to do so.
- [heuristic] An event that happens at the most inconvenient moment may be more likely staged than accidental.
- [heuristic] When no direct time is recorded, infer one from a related event, such as arrival at a scene, and work from the resulting window. When: an event lacks a recorded time. Why: A bounded window still constrains who could have acted.
- [heuristic] Give each NPC a narrow, sometimes wrong time window so players must merge them into a schedule to find contradictions. When: designing NPC testimony for players to reconcile. Why: Merging partial accounts rewards players who compare them.
- [heuristic] Combine several record types with surviving physical sites, since each source type checks the others. When: documents conflict or are incomplete and sites can still be inspected. Why: Independent sources expose errors that any single source would hide.
- [heuristic] A moving shadow or light patch can act as a slow clock that places an observer in time.
- [heuristic] Use a fixed external schedule, such as a timed power cutoff, as a constraint that explains why an act had to occur at a particular time. When: Building a timeline or motive argument.
- [procedure] 1) Identify a process with a known duration. 2) Get witness-reported start and end times. 3) Compute the earliest completion time. 4) Treat events before that time as possibly having altered the trace. When: A trace such as a stain or mark depends on when a timed process finished. Why: A known duration converts a vague account into a checkable time limit.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the time ranges each witness gives. 2) Intersect them to find the interval all accounts allow. 3) Test that interval against physical evidence. When: several witnesses give overlapping times.
- [procedure] 1) Put each witness's timestamped events in sequence. 2) Check overlaps and gaps between witnesses. 3) Test each claim against physical access limits, such as whether a window could admit a person. 4) Confirm key details directly, not by secondhand report. 5) Mark unknown gaps rather than guessing. When: several people describe one night's events.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the crime's time to a clock reading. 2) Work backward from that time to test each witness's estimate. 3) Record each sound with its time. 4) Turn gaps and overlaps into follow-up questions. When: several witnesses heard or saw events during one night.
- [metric] A gap under about 45 minutes can be too short for a multi-step preparation, making an act in that window implausible. When: judging opportunity inside a narrow window. Why: multi-step tasks need time to complete.
- [metric] A shared window open only about 2.5 hours in each 12-hour cycle leaves every coordinated part needing to finish inside it. When: when a plan depends on a tidal or periodic window. Why: short windows leave little slack for error.
- [pitfall] A timeline built from partial observations can mislead. Gaps in the record can make an innocent explanation look impossible or a guilty one look certain. When: Reconstructing events from scattered observations.
- [pitfall] A very short time window invites improbable escape routes to be proposed, so check each proposed route against the timing. Why: Tight windows tempt people to accept routes that would not fit the clock.
- [pitfall] Assuming dates from a vague or uncertain witness are exact leads to false conclusions. Why: Uncertain recall carries error that must be weighed before comparing.
- [pitfall] Taking the last known sighting as the moment something happened misplaces the event, which may have occurred earlier. When: when placing an event in a timeline. Why: The last observation is only a bound, not the cause.
- [fact] An independent timestamped record, such as a receipt or cloakroom ticket, can contradict a suspect's stated times without relying on anyone's memory.

## withheld reasoning and theories
- [mechanism] Withholding the working conclusion until evidence is complete keeps the question open, so anticipation and tension hold the audience's attention. Why: Unrevealed conclusions create expectation; the unresolved gap holds attention.
- [mechanism] A detective NPC can hint that something is off and reveal the full logic only after the player visits the right location, so the reasoning rests on facts the player has already seen. When: Designing staged reveals of an NPC's deduction. Why: Delayed reveal keeps the reasoning reproducible from what the player has gathered.
- [mechanism] Scattering clues while holding back their connection gives the audience the tools but not the link, sustaining suspense until the reveal. When: the story must delay a reveal.
- [behavior] A witness with a theory but no proof may keep it private, since voicing an unsupported opinion can be dismissed and expose the speaker's own secrets. When: A witness suspects wrongdoing but lacks evidence. Why: Officials dismiss claims that come without support.
- [behavior] A person of rank may give no explanation unless asked, so their silence about a matter is itself a fact to record. When: Someone is questioned about why they were somewhere. Why: People of standing do not volunteer explanations they are not asked for.
- [behavior] When an investigator shares facts but withholds conclusions, the audience reasons toward the answer alongside them, which builds suspense. When: when the audience should reach the conclusion themselves. Why: Hidden reasoning invites the audience to test their own guesses.
- [rule] Explicitly promise that a withheld answer will come later; the promise keeps the question open while an unpromised delay reads as evasion. When: the audience is asked to wait for an answer. Why: The promise gives the audience a reason to keep attention; an unpromised delay frustrates. (x2)
- [rule] Let NPC dialogue withhold a theory or a relevant visit until the player asks the precise question or presents the right evidence, rewarding careful questioning.
- [rule] Keep theories unstated and limit who hears them until evidence tests them; early disclosure lets others interfere or tip off suspects, and untested theories may mislead. When: while an investigation is open and a theory could alert suspects or allies, or affect others if spread early. Why: Untested theories may mislead; unstated theories can be revised without public loss of face.
- [rule] Withhold the culprit's name and the detective's suspicion until the final reveal, so the audience can test the clues before the answer is given. When: the audience has all the clues and the reveal is the payoff. Why: Naming the culprit or revealing suspicion early removes the chance to test clues and turns the reveal into confirmation.
- [rule] Let a magical effect's mechanism stay partly hidden while a plausible natural reading remains; hold back a discriminating clue so the player tests both readings. When: when designing a mystery with competing explanations. Why: Delayed evidence lets the player hold both readings and choose on proof.
- [rule] Keep your strategy and discoveries from the opponent when an early disclosure would let them prepare a counter. When: when the opposing side can adapt.
- [rule] Do not reach a firm conclusion when witnesses disagree or the evidence is only partial.
- [rule] A character may withhold their true purpose, but the withheld information must be present in the story so the reason can be reconstructed later. When: Writing a guide or investigator whose aims are concealed. Why: Concealment is fair only when the player can later reconstruct the hidden reason.
- [rule] Keep a real plan from a helper when telling them would make them interfere, and deflect their questions with a plausible unrelated topic. When: telling the truth would make another person interfere or change behaviour.
- [rule] Declare a clue conclusive without explaining why, so the player must reconstruct the logic behind it.
- [heuristic] Keep suspicions private while questioning, revealing at most that you have an idea; early disclosure lets the source adjust or harden answers to fit your view. When: when questioning a witness or suspect who may adjust to your view. Why: A stated opinion biases the source's responses; early disclosure warns the suspect.
- [procedure] 1) Form the conclusion and write the suspect's name down before any arrest. 2) Delay the arrest until the suspect can be reached. 3) Confirm through an independent report and a verbatim, carefully recorded confession. When: the solver wants certainty before acting on a case. Why: a privately held answer needs confirmation before it is pressed.
- [tradeoff] Leaving a detail or mechanism unexplained keeps the reveal open, but frustrates or reads as evasion unless the unknown is clearly marked as deliberate or its reasons are given. When: the effect or detail is central to the story. Why: Players tolerate a gap they know is deliberate; explaining makes the solution feel fair. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Keeping a plan private prevents leaks to opponents, but leaves allies uninformed and feeling excluded, and exposed to unforeseen danger. When: Deciding whether to share suspicions or a plan during an investigation. Why: Secrecy protects the plan while costing trust and shared reasoning. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Withholding a conclusion until verified guards against premature blame, error and tipping-off, but delays action while an innocent person may suffer or danger continues. When: when a suspicion involves a possibly innocent person or danger may continue. Why: Fairness to hypotheses competes with the cost of delay to the person affected.
- [tradeoff] Withholding reasoning or purpose keeps suspense and dread high, but costs trust as characters and audience feel excluded; fair-play puzzles frustrate without a clear fact to reason with. When: a detective holds back a deduction. Why: Suspense rises while the audience feels shut out.
- [tradeoff] An NPC who withholds a conclusion gives the player a choice of when to act, but risks frustrating players who prefer to move immediately.
- [pitfall] Withholding reasoning too long, or never delivering it, reads as cheating or an unfair reveal even when every fact was given; keep the chain fair, checkable and revealed after testable evidence. When: Structuring a mystery reveal. Why: Audiences need checkable clues to engage with the solution.
- [pitfall] Withholding reasoning too long, or without stated reason, erodes trust, mystifies companions or loses the audience, looks arrogant, and cheats readers who missed early clues. When: when an investigator holds back an inference. Why: Unexplained teasing reads as condescension, not skill.
- [pitfall] A withheld plan feels like cheating when the audience needs it to make a choice before the reveal.

## witness reliability and bystanders
- [mechanism] Bystanders remember exact words, so a slip made in a group becomes testimony that can be used later. When: When a slip occurs in front of other listeners.
- [mechanism] In a crowded setting with many people, no one can reliably confirm another person's movements, so testimony about them becomes unreliable. When: Many people share a location and witnesses are asked about a specific individual. Why: Attention is spread across too many people for any one person's movements to be remembered.
- [behavior] Bystanders' reactions to a question, including who looks to the investigator for cues, reveal who has a stake in the answer. When: several people are present during questioning.
- [behavior] A listener's frown or unease when a gap appears is evidence in its own right and should be recorded alongside the speaker's account. When: someone reacts to a witness's lapse. Why: the other person's reaction can reveal knowledge the speaker is hiding.
- [behavior] A witness who saw a stranger only briefly often gives a generic description, such as height and common clothing, that fits many people. When: The witness had a short or distant view. Why: Brief observation captures only broad features.
- [behavior] Brief visits followed by a quick return are easily overlooked in memory and records. When: a visit was short.
- [behavior] A bystander describing others may shape the account to distance himself from them, so his portrait needs independent checking. When: A peripheral acquaintance describes the people around them. Why: A wish to avoid being linked to those people biases the account.
- [behavior] Workers and passers-by who notice an odd visitor asking strange questions tend to report the visit, making them witnesses.
- [rule] Have each narrator record only events they personally saw or did, and state where their knowledge ends, so gaps stay visible. When: multiple narrators tell parts of one story. Why: clear limits let readers separate seen from heard.
- [rule] Treat a bystander's theory about motive, such as a quarrel, as a suggestion to test rather than as proof.
- [rule] Record the identity of an uninvolved driver used in an evasion and pay them afterwards, so the innocent party is not harmed.
- [rule] Model a busy NPC whose attention is limited by workload, so the player learns that a missing memory is itself information.
- [heuristic] Bystander NPCs who witnessed a public confrontation can confirm or contradict an accuser's account; players must compare their counter-statements against it. When: when designing a scene where a public argument matters later. Why: multiple witnesses let the player check testimony. (x2)
- [heuristic] Brief, poor-light, or unrepeated sightings and identifications are less reliable than prolonged contact; a confident account from a glimpse needs close questioning and confirmation. Why: Fleeting, unconfirmed perceptions are often misreads.
- [heuristic] A witness with a limited view and believable gaps is more credible than one who recalls every detail; check her claims against independent sources. When: A servant or attendant reports events from a narrow position. Why: A limited view should produce a limited account.
- [heuristic] A witness's vantage bounds what they could have known, so sightings of some people alongside disclaimers about others can both be consistent.
- [heuristic] A bounded estimate, such as a range of days, is more useful than a false precise guess from a witness. When: A witness is unsure of an exact date.
- [tradeoff] A bounded-room reveal works only while suspects cannot flee, so a prepared cordon must be in place before the accusation. When: a suspect can escape once accused. Why: exposure gives the suspect a reason to run.
- [pitfall] Witnesses who did not notice are not automatically lying, and a deceptive witness is not merely busy; test any failure to notice against the environment. (x2)
- [pitfall] A brief observer lacking context about someone's history or reasons may judge their sanity or honesty from manner alone and misread intent. When: When forming a lasting impression from a short encounter without context. Why: Odd manner is noticed quickly, while reasoning and context take longer to appear; missing context leads to reading intent or character incorrectly.
- [pitfall] Assuming bystanders saw what happened, when they saw only a normal action, leads to wrong conclusions about the event.
- [pitfall] A brief glance can mislead a watcher who assumes a figure seen in a place is the person who should be there. When: A watcher checks a room or cell briefly. Why: A constructed presence, such as a figure on a bed, looks like the real occupant.
- [pitfall] A timed trick that relies on an unwitting bystander to mask its noise fails if that bystander leaves early.
- [pitfall] Overt bullying can silence a witness and undo progress already made. Pressure works better paired with reassurance. When: Questioning a frightened or threatened witness. Why: Intimidation makes a witness withdraw, while reassurance lets them finish the account.
- [pitfall] A brief explanation offered under challenge should be tested against the full record, not accepted because it sounds plausible.
- [fact] A bystander who seems neutral may be watching for their own reasons, so every observer in a scene can be a possible interested party.

## witness reliability and detail
- [mechanism] Accumulating contradictory details can deepen the sense of mystery, since each new conflict makes the overall case feel less coherent. When: Many clues appear to conflict. Why: Unorganized contradictions raise uncertainty without suggesting an answer.
- [behavior] A detailed message can make its recipient less cautious, because specifics feel like proof of genuineness. When: the message's details fit what the recipient already knows.
- [rule] Do not drop a distinctive detail after introducing it; record it and pay it off when the scene is reconstructed. When: Introducing clues to the player. Why: An unpaid detail leaves the mystery unresolved.
- [rule] Let a field report carry exact details, dates and first impressions, so an absent character can judge progress without visiting the scene. When: A character must follow events they cannot witness. Why: Specific reports let the absent character assess progress.
- [rule] Let a quest-giver NPC answer a fixed set of questions, and have the player's notebook build a suspect profile from the answers. When: When designing investigation quests in a game. Why: A fixed question set makes the profile consistent and easy to match.
- [rule] Attach a reliability marker to a character's account given while poisoned, drunk or frightened, prompting players to corroborate it before acting on it. When: A character's testimony is delivered under impairment or stress. Why: A visible marker tells players the account needs checking.
- [heuristic] A smooth, detailed account is not proof of reliability; test its details against the scene and independent evidence before treating it as settled. When: A witness or suspect gives a vivid, complete, or detailed story. Why: Detail can mask bias, error or invention.
- [heuristic] Check each candidate explanation against every detail; one specific detail that does not fit can rule an explanation out. When: choosing between explanations. Why: the obvious reading may fail on a single detail.
- [heuristic] A witness can be designed to be wrong, such as reporting a struggle that was really a startled gesture.
- [heuristic] A detail that does not fit the official account easily, such as mixed voices heard at one time, is worth treating as significant.
- [heuristic] Minor details gain weight when they explain a mismatch between testimony and the physical record. When: A witness account conflicts with the physical evidence. Why: Small details can resolve the conflict.
- [heuristic] A mismatch between a reported detail and known facts may mean the story changed in retelling or that two items were confused.
- [heuristic] A detail that looks wrong, such as a poorly fitting wig, can be a discoverable clue in dialogue or inspection.
- [heuristic] A repeated detail is strong evidence of common origin only if it is unusual in itself; common details can arise independently. When: judging whether repeated testimony is copied. Why: Only rare details carry enough information to act as a fingerprint.
- [heuristic] A witness distracted during the event recalls little, and a witness with a stake in the outcome may minimize their own role when pressed. When: When weighing how much to trust a witness's account. Why: Distraction weakens memory, and self-interest shapes what a witness admits.
- [procedure] 1) Assess the witness's access to what they observed and the quality of their source. 2) Assess memory of dates and details, including impairment such as drinking. 3) Assess stake, motive and feelings. 4) Weigh facts accordingly before accepting them. When: When several witnesses give accounts of the same events. Why: Each factor limits how far a witness's account can be trusted; interested or impaired witnesses may distort what they report.
- [tradeoff] Examining one detail intensely reveals a few points clearly but loses the whole picture; organized breadth of hypotheses keeps the full situation in view.
- [tradeoff] Strict detachment from people improves clarity of reasoning but can make the investigator seem cold or inhuman to colleagues.
- [pitfall] A detailed itinerary or suspect's story can look credible because of its detail, and detail can cover a false account; detail alone does not verify a claim.
- [pitfall] A large volume of trivial detail can bury the important point in a witness timeline. When: when many small observations are collected.
- [pitfall] Assuming a witness sure of one detail is equally reliable about other details. When: Weighing a witness's full account. Why: Confidence varies across facts, such as a person's condition versus their face.
- [pitfall] A detached observer who believes they can read people completely is often wrong about them.
- [pitfall] Added detail in a retold story does not raise its accuracy, so trace the chain of reporters before trusting extra specifics.
- [pitfall] Trusting the most confident or most detailed witness as the most accurate one is a mistake; detail and certainty do not guarantee accuracy. When: Weighing conflicting testimony. Why: Confidence and detail can be produced by sincere but wrong memory.
- [pitfall] A witness may give a time with apparent precision while only estimating it; check whether the witness could actually see a clock. When: Witness times are used to fix a sequence of events. Why: Precision in speech does not guarantee the observation behind it was exact.
- [fact] Vagueness about what differs between a suspect and the witnessed person is evidence about witness reliability, not proof of innocence. When: A witness cannot explain a difference in a lineup or identification. Why: Vague answers signal weak recall, which neither confirms nor clears the suspect.

## disguise detection and reveal
- [model] A disguise hides a character's identity until it is removed in a reveal, so concealment and reveal are arranged together as one structure. When: identity is central to the plot.
- [mechanism] Disguise items dropped at a scene, such as a wig lost in a struggle, and leftover application or removal materials are evidence that identity was concealed. When: Designing or investigating a disguise. Why: Concealment steps leave physical traces.
- [mechanism] A disguised suspect can produce honest but contradictory reports from different witnesses, since each saw a different partial view. When: a suspect has altered their appearance. Why: each witness completes a different partial glimpse.
- [mechanism] A disguise that changes only conspicuous features can be detected through careful questioning of witnesses about close-up details. When: when designing NPC disguise or impersonation. Why: questioning exposes mismatches the disguise did not cover.
- [mechanism] An NPC who knows a specialty can test a disguise with questions that only real knowledge answers. When: a disguised player speaks to a specialist NPC.
- [rule] Reveal a disguised identity through a physical change, such as a cloak falling away, rather than through speech alone.
- [rule] Stage a disguise reveal for effect by removing a key disguise element in front of the people who failed to recognise you, exposing the whole disguise at once. When: Payoff moment after a disguise has passed scrutiny. Why: A sudden full reveal lands harder than a gradual one.
- [rule] Disguise by changing the cues people use to recognize someone, such as the eyes, rather than costume alone. This applies to dungeon NPCs too. When: a character must pass as someone else. Why: recognition depends more on cues like the eyes than on costume.
- [rule] Let a player hide costume details in a portrait or wanted poster and compare the face underneath, since disguises can conceal identity. When: Designing a disguise puzzle. Why: Covering distinctive costume features can reveal the underlying face.
- [rule] Let a final-act reveal show that a friendly NPC was an investigator in disguise, with earlier clues explaining the change.
- [heuristic] Identify a disguised person by traits a disguise cannot change, such as gait, build, silhouette, voice, dental work, nose, eyes, mouth or a fixed item, not face, clothing or name. When: two people claim different identities, or a disguised character must be recognised. Why: Disguises alter surface features like hair, facial hair and clothing, while body-level traits and underlying proportions persist. (x2)
- [heuristic] A disguised threat that proves empty can serve as a scripted reveal, provided the disguise appears earlier in the story. When: Staging a reveal that changes how a threat is understood. Why: Earlier setup makes the reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [heuristic] A physical match can disambiguate between candidates who share a clue such as an initial.
- [heuristic] A disguise test needs the real person's physical details on record, because without them the investigator cannot spot a mismatch. When: the impersonated person's physical details are unknown to the investigator.
- [heuristic] A found object can be matched to a missing one by comparing its dimensions with an empty frame or container.
- [heuristic] Test an unnatural appearance with a physical action, such as rubbing the face, to reveal whether a disguise is applied rather than grown. When: When a suspect's appearance seems wrong, such as a mismatched mustache or stiff hat. Why: Applied disguises can shift or lift under contact in ways natural features do not.
- [procedure] 1) Write a full description of the suspect. 2) List features a disguise can change, such as hair, beard, age, clothing, glasses, false whiskers or voice. 3) Keep stable features, such as skull shape, height and build, and compare them across sources. When: a suspect's appearance or voice may have been altered. Why: Remaining stable traits are more reliable for identification.
- [tradeoff] A disguise helps avoid recognition but risks being seen both disguised and undisguised by the same people, which invites distrust. When: when deciding whether to change appearance.
- [pitfall] A disguise fails in private: housemates' intimate routines expose it, and a faked tell that vanishes in private conversation reveals the cover. When: the disguised person lives among others, or the disguise includes a faked trait. Why: Intimate routines are hard to keep up in disguise, and inconsistency between public and private behavior reveals the cover.
- [pitfall] A disguise worn in a place where one is known can be discovered and raise suspicion.
- [pitfall] A changed appearance breaks physical description matching, so a disguised person can pass a check that would otherwise expose them.
- [pitfall] Pointing too hard at a disguise makes it obvious; let the detail be half-noticed and then dismissed, so readers can catch it later.
- [pitfall] A disguise tell noticed too late leaves little room to conceal it, so early detection matters.
- [pitfall] A disguise is not reliable under close or repeated scrutiny. When: The cover must survive sustained inspection. Why: Close observation can reveal details that the disguise does not hide.
- [fact] Tinted glasses, an altered voice and false whiskers are typical signs that someone is concealing their identity. When: A witness reports unusual appearance features. Why: Such changes are deliberate and hide who the person is.

## document reconstruction
- [rule] Record damage, wear and destroyed evidence as facts; a burned remnant with no legible fragment is itself information. When: A fragile document is being examined or preserved, or evidence has been destroyed. Why: Fragile originals keep deteriorating, so the record may become the only full view. (x2)
- [rule] Reassemble torn fragments like a puzzle to recover a message that no single piece shows. When: when a clue is a torn document.
- [rule] Let in-world journals or case files carry redacted entries, and let players recover the struck text through a lore or light puzzle. When: Designing in-world written material that hides information. Why: Recovering hidden text rewards the player's attention and reading.
- [rule] Make burned or altered items still identifiable through a test such as flame or solvent, so the player can recover their identity.
- [rule] Let players recover discarded drafts, each with different wording or tone, so they can see the writer's hesitation. When: Designing written clues in a game or puzzle. Why: A draft reveals hesitation only if the player can actually find it.
- [rule] Let a torn note's missing letters be recovered by overlaying a second fragment, and require the player to check the restored words against the scene. When: designing document puzzles.
- [rule] Compare the torn or cut edges of two halves directly; edges that do not coincide rule out a link between them. When: when two halves of an object may come from the same source.
- [heuristic] A tear where an item would be pulled out suggests it was snatched in a rush rather than removed carefully.
- [heuristic] Search the remains of a fire or grate, since partly burned material may survive and carry evidence. Why: Destruction is often incomplete.
- [heuristic] Record the exact fragment, list every possible reading, and test each reading by how well it fits the torn edge rather than by expectation. When: A document is incomplete and its wording is disputed. Why: Strong expectations bias readings, while edge fit is a more objective test.
- [heuristic] A torn edge in a record may be deliberate or accidental, so do not assume significance until the record is compared with an intact copy. When: A record shows damage near relevant content. Why: Damage can be innocent, so comparison is needed before drawing conclusions.
- [heuristic] Make a discarded or burnt document reconstructable from fragments, and match printed fragments to a known source such as a dated publication. When: A document has been destroyed but the player should still be able to recover part of it. Why: Partial recovery gives the player a reason to search and assemble clues.
- [procedure] 1) Gather every related account of the events, including printed reports, confessions and depositions. 2) Note what each includes, omits, agrees on or conflicts with. 3) Date each record and flag undated, incomplete or lost ones. 4) Align dated entries on one timeline. 5) Label conclusions as documented or inferred. 6) Cross-check with surviving physical evidence. When: Reconstructing events from several partial or fragmentary sources.
- [procedure] 1) Collect all fragments, including those found on a second search. 2) Match edges using margins, partial words and machine-cut versus torn edges. 3) Space pieces as a standard sheet to count missing strips. 4) Use partial words and dates to estimate contents. When: Physical evidence is partly destroyed and its layout matters. Why: Edge matching and layout reveal page order, missing pieces and sometimes the writer.
- [procedure] 1) Lay a torn fragment over a complete copy to see what is missing. 2) Turn the fragment over and read its reverse side. 3) Check whether adjoining or reverse text changes the fragment's meaning. When: a torn or partial document is found. Why: Alignment shows the gap, and the reverse can hold text that changes the reading.
- [procedure] 1) Record the document's full state, including worn margins, before any trimming. 2) Note any mounting or treatment that changes its appearance. 3) Record the scale whenever the image is reduced.
- [procedure] 1) Find the written item in the place the person was known to use. 2) Record where it was found. 3) Bring it to the investigator with that account of its location.
- [procedure] 1) List surviving word fragments and note which letters remain and where they break off. 2) Complete each fragment only with words the visible letters allow. 3) Add connecting words the sense requires. 4) Judge the restored whole by its general tenor. When: A torn or partly burned document must be restored to understand its general content. Why: Restoring tone and content avoids overclaiming exact wording that cannot be recovered.
- [procedure] 1) Check the top sheet for impressions. 2) If it is blank, check blotting pads and lower sheets. 3) Tear off a strip and read the reversed impression by turning it over. When: a message may be hidden in lower layers. Why: lower layers often keep a clearer copy.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the surviving words of a lost document or statement. 2) Gather related behaviour and threats. 3) Narrow what the missing content must have said. When: a document or statement has been destroyed or withheld. Why: surrounding words and behaviour constrain the missing content.
- [procedure] 1) Locate the source the fragments came from. 2) Match fragment edges to that source. 3) Mount the fragments on stiff backing so the text can be read and kept. 4) Compare the text with a known sample by the same writer. When: a damaged document is physically present and a reliable comparison sample exists.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether the recovered object is authentic. 2) Test it by weight, appraisal or a second source. 3) Reopen the timeline to see whether the real event came earlier. 4) Only then close the case. When: A recovered item seems to prove a suspect's guilt. Why: Authenticity and timing can overturn an apparently conclusive find.
- [procedure] 1) Search the waste and recover the fragment. 2) Unroll and smooth it. 3) Match its edges precisely to the tear. 4) Measure the blank gap. 5) Check the reverse side. 6) Acquire the same day's original edition from its office. 7) Compare entries by time, origin and destination. 8) Mark the matching entry; keep the fragment as exhibit. When: when a discarded document may hold information about a place or person. Why: Systematic matching identifies the removed text reliably.
- [pitfall] Reconstructing lost words can change a document's meaning, so mark supplied words, since inferred words look identical to original ones. When: Using or completing a partly damaged or fragmentary document. Why: Supplied words can alter the sense of the original text.
- [pitfall] Sentences cut from a real source and reassembled can appear to say something new, as satirical dialogues built from fragments show.

## dying words and deathbed testimony
- [mechanism] A remark made by a cornered or dying speaker can carry meaning only for an audience that shares the reference it relies on, so the clue is unlocked by knowing that reference. When: A dying or cornered character speaks a line that seems out of place for their class or setting. Why: The meaning of a fragmentary remark depends on a shared frame of reference, which the audience must possess to decode it.
- [mechanism] Timing a new revelation just after a sympathetic figure dies can turn that death into a fresh source of fear.
- [behavior] A dying speaker's fragmentary words, possibly partly delirium, can carry motive or knowledge but are inference, not a full statement or literal clue. When: A key witness cannot give a complete statement. Why: Delirium distorts speech, and a fragment can be read to fit many theories. (x2)
- [behavior] A dying person may leave a deliberate sign for the living, or may only repeat a fixed idea without understanding it. When: A victim leaves a final mark or word. Why: A deliberate message and a delirious repetition look alike at first.
- [rule] Have a dying NPC give garbled words that form a partial clue the player must combine and cross-check with other evidence to reach the meaning. When: Designing NPC dying words as clues. Why: Partial clues keep mystery open while requiring player verification. (x2)
- [rule] Let a dying character's words name a suspect, but make the player able to test those words against objects and traces in the scene. When: designing an NPC's final testimony in a mystery. Why: checkable testimony keeps the accusation from deciding the case alone.
- [rule] Use dying words or fragmentary notes as clue text that points to a location or time, to be combined with other evidence. When: Designing clue text.
- [rule] Make an NPC's dying line ambiguous so the player must interpret it against the scene, and let a later NPC correct or contradict an earlier lie. When: Designing dialogue-based clues.
- [rule] Cap the number of exchanges with a dying or injured NPC, offering only a few short hints under a timer.
- [rule] Hold a survivor's testimony back until a dying confession, which resolves a lost-person question and revives the missing character.
- [heuristic] A deathbed statement may be sincere, but fever, drugs, drink, pain, spite or fear can distort it; weigh motive and the speaker's state, and seek corroboration before relying on it. When: when the only witness is dying, feverish or drugged. Why: Impaired state reduces the reliability of memory and perception. (x2)
- [heuristic] Treat a dying person's accusation as hearsay: a lead showing where to look, not proof of identity or intent, to be checked against the physical record. When: investigating a dying person's accusation. Why: Delirious statements lack independent weight and cannot be cross-examined; they may mislead.
- [heuristic] Give a dying word two readings, such as an external cause and the real killer, so the player weighs both; reveal the intended one only at the end. When: Writing a cryptic last utterance that serves as a clue. Why: Ambiguity keeps the decoy plausible while the true meaning stays available to attentive players.
- [heuristic] A dying statement or witness account is only as reliable as the conditions under which it was heard and spoken.
- [heuristic] A dying speaker's words are more reliable when they had no reason to deceive; a faked message would be spoken clearly, so broken speech suggests a genuine one. When: A witness gives a partial utterance near death. Why: A deliberate fake is usually delivered intelligibly.
- [heuristic] Hide a dying clue as a partial string that the player completes against a map or list of locations.
- [heuristic] Use an NPC's dying words as a fair clue to the culprit, such as their gender, even while others dismiss them as delirium.
- [heuristic] Use a dying victim's message as late corroboration of a mechanism the audience has already been shown. When: confirming a hidden method near the climax. Why: A message from the victim confirms the method without adding new explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Record a dying person's exact words, treating them as a partial message. 2) Keep that wording separate from interpretation. 3) List each plausible reading and weigh it against other evidence. When: when a victim speaks final words before dying or losing consciousness and the statement is ambiguous. Why: Interpretations are often accepted as fact before wording is secured; a dying speaker may leave only a few words, easily misremembered if not recorded exactly.
- [procedure] 1) Determine where death happened from room evidence, not where the body lies, since the body may have been moved. 2) Compare the wound's shape and depth with the surface it struck. 3) Use both to test the stated account. When: a scene looks orderly or theatrical. Why: The body's position can differ from the place of death.
- [procedure] 1) Fix a starting time from a reliable record. 2) Fix an end time from a witness who heard the next event. 3) Treat the interval between them as the frame for testing every alibi and sound. When: when a death must be placed within a bounded window. Why: A bounded interval gives a common frame for all accounts.
- [procedure] 1) List each candidate explanation for a death. 2) Gather facts about the deceased's circumstances, the body, and the spot where it was found. 3) Check each explanation against each fact set. 4) Eliminate explanations that conflict with the facts, and test the remaining one. When: At the start of a death inquiry, before findings are settled. Why: Structured elimination shows which facts still need gathering.
- [pitfall] A last-moment confession can seem too convenient, so the audience must trust the source and the timing for it to land. When: when a culprit confesses at the end, especially near death. Why: Convenient timing can look like a device rather than earned revelation.
- [pitfall] Dying speech is short and fragmentary, so plan in advance what information the audience must learn before the speaker dies. When: Writing a dying character who must deliver a clue. Why: A cut-off speech may end before the key information is delivered.
- [fact] A dying statement can be dismissed as delirium, so its weight depends on whether others are willing to credit it.

## false identity
- [model] Many mystery cases hinge on a false identity, such as a body that is not who it seems, a claimant who is the criminal, or a staged witness, with the truth revealed through a disguised confrontation or documentary find. When: When structuring a mystery plot around deception of identity. Why: A false identity misleads the investigator until a reveal exposes the real actor.
- [model] A disappearance that looks romantic or legal can hide a domestic control motive, so the player assumes an outside cause until the real motive is revealed.
- [mechanism] A keyword or behaviour that exposes a disguised player causes the NPC to shut down and refuse cooperation. When: the player uses a false identity.
- [mechanism] A false death can be staged by using the apparent victim's identity as a disguise, so the concealed person's own identity becomes the tool of concealment. When: When a culprit fakes their own death. Why: Assumed identity lets a perpetrator disappear while the case closes on a false conclusion.
- [mechanism] A false belief about a character's identity can persist for a long stretch, letting other plots develop on a false footing until a single mismatch undoes it. When: a story needs a wrong premise to hold while other threads unfold. Why: The false premise shapes every later choice, so its collapse reframes the earlier events.
- [behavior] People talk more freely to a stranger playing a false persona than to a known official, so a disguise can draw out information an officer could not get. When: An investigator needs candid answers from suspects. Why: Suspects who know an official's identity become guarded.
- [rule] Give a cover identity a plausible role whose everyday details others have no easy reason to check. When: A newcomer must blend in among locals without drawing scrutiny. Why: Ordinary, unchecked roles are accepted without questions.
- [rule] Gather information through casual conversation with a cover acquaintance, since a low-status contact may reveal recent events such as an injury. When: Direct questioning of the target would draw suspicion. Why: Ordinary contacts talk freely about what they have witnessed.
- [rule] Treat a witness's report of a false self-identification as evidence of the subject's intent, not as proof of who the subject is.
- [rule] Keep a cover identity consistent across all messages, or the lure will fail.
- [rule] Give a covert agent a plausible cover identity, such as a trade role that explains travel, garage visits and other regular movements. When: an agent's movements need an innocent explanation. Why: a believable role makes unusual trips look routine.
- [rule] A false status must match independent evidence, such as official reports, or the opponent will expose it.
- [rule] A supposedly dead character can be found alive through a witness holding a secret, reachable only after the player earns that witness's trust. When: designing a quest around a character believed dead.
- [heuristic] Give the player a cover role, such as inspector, buyer, insurer or official agent, to open dialogue branches a direct question would not, e.g. a household talking about a lodger.
- [heuristic] Reveal a cover identity only after earlier clues let the audience recheck past scenes and confirm the truth. When: The story has already shown the cover identity. Why: Recasting earlier scenes feels fair only when clues were visible.
- [heuristic] A cover story that is too convenient or inconsistent invites questions from staff. When: Constructing a cover identity to enter a restricted place. Why: Staff notice details that do not fit the role.
- [heuristic] Build a cover persona from expertise or habits you already know well, so routine questions do not expose you. When: you must pose as someone else. Why: familiar language and beliefs are easier to sustain under questioning.
- [heuristic] Back a wrong identity with a genuine witness account so it feels confirmed until a physical contradiction breaks it. When: building a false answer the player should accept for a while. Why: A supported false answer is believed longer than an unsupported one, so the later reversal lands harder.
- [procedure] 1) Pick a private fact about the target that they cannot verify, such as an unknown relative. 2) Create a plausible reason for the stranger's presence. 3) Deliver the document through the most trusted available person. When: Building an impostor cover story. Why: The target lacks knowledge that would expose the lie, and trust carries the claim.
- [procedure] 1) Suspect a false identity when a death lacks independent confirmation. 2) Compare the body with the claimed person's known features. 3) Exhume the grave only when a substitute is strongly suspected. When: a death has been reported but not independently verified. Why: disinterment is decisive but costly, so it is reserved for strong suspicion.
- [tradeoff] A cover role gives a reason to ask questions, but the lie it rests on can later be repeated or exposed by the witness.
- [pitfall] False names and false return addresses defeat direct lookup and can signal that the sender covered their tracks; timing and amounts are harder to fake and remain reliable evidence. When: tracing an anonymous sender. Why: Identity markers are easy to fake while patterns are harder to fake.
- [pitfall] Accepting the first familiar animal that resembles the prints can lead to a false identity.
- [pitfall] Identifying two people as one can explain many facts at once and feel complete, yet it may send the investigation after a false target and hide the real question. When: A single theory accounts for several puzzles by merging identities. Why: A neat explanation reduces the urge to test the merged assumption.
- [fact] A false identity can rest on a document issued in another person's name, and such a document can be questioned. Why: The identity holds only as long as the document is not checked.

## foreshadowing and warnings
- [definition] Foreshadowing hints at a coming disaster while denying specific knowledge of it, building suspense and misdirecting the listener without committing to facts.
- [mechanism] Stating or repeating that harm will come, without disclosing its outcome, builds dread and expectation, so a later return or reveal feels earned rather than arbitrary. When: A story must promise later difficulty or reveal without disclosing it. Why: Anticipation of a known future event heightens tension. (x2)
- [mechanism] Warnings from minor characters that point at a dangerous figure without describing him build suspense about a threat the player cannot yet see. When: opening a story or case. Why: Hinted danger raises tension before the threat is revealed.
- [mechanism] A departure record or forwarding address points to the next destination, letting a trail be followed step by step.
- [behavior] Normally people turn toward a sudden crash; someone who does not may have expected it, so the missing reaction is evidence. When: someone witnesses a sudden event they would ordinarily react to. Why: An expected event draws less surprise, so a muted reaction can signal prior knowledge.
- [rule] Tie each forward hint to evidence the audience already has, and never let foreshadowing replace the evidence that would confirm or refute it. When: Using prophetic or ominous hints in a story. Why: a hint with no visible basis reads as an arbitrary promise. (x2)
- [rule] Use throwaway lines as foreshadowing and record them in the quest log so the player can connect them later; unpaid foreshadowing reads as a loose thread. When: Writing offhand dialogue meant to pay off later. Why: Logged lines let players link early remarks to later events.
- [rule] Foreshadow danger through a remark or an innocent-looking setting, and make sure the foreshadowing pays off later. Why: unpaid foreshadowing leaves the audience with a false warning.
- [rule] Keep forward-looking leads, such as scheduled events, in the case log, and lock past events until new evidence unlocks them.
- [rule] Use retrospective phrasing to flag that a minor event matters, without yet revealing how it will matter.
- [rule] Foreshadow an ending by having a character predict it, then confirm the prediction in the closing section to reward attentive players.
- [rule] Do not use foreshadowing when the audience already knows the threat, since warnings then only repeat what is known. When: deciding whether to foreshadow a danger. Why: foreshadowing adds tension only while the threat is still unknown.
- [rule] Do not let a foreshadowing hint reveal the solution; use it to build anticipation for what follows.
- [rule] Tag foreshadowing lines with the characters who heard them, so players can deduce which character had the knowledge an event required. When: Designing foreshadowing for a mystery.
- [rule] Plant a guiding character's parting line early so players recall it when danger peaks. When: When a mentor or guide leaves before the climax. Why: A remembered line turns a farewell into foreshadowing and raises tension at the climax.
- [rule] Plant anomalies early and resolve them late, so a detail waits for its explanation and rewards the reader who noticed it. When: Seeding physical or circumstantial details in a mystery. Why: Delayed explanations make the reader revisit the detail and trust the eventual solution.
- [heuristic] End a section with a foreshadowed misfortune to create dread and prompt players to reread earlier dialogue for hidden meaning.
- [heuristic] A spontaneous remark counts as foreshadowing only when later suggestion did not shape it. When: a remark seems to predict a later event. Why: suggested remarks may be reconstructed to fit what happened.
- [heuristic] Show an NPC's leverage through dialogue so that a later betrayal feels foreshadowed rather than arbitrary.
- [heuristic] A narrator who points forward to later events signals that the present scene is the start of a longer story.
- [heuristic] A forward hint that later events will be stranger than the present raises pressure on the audience. When: a mystery is approaching a climax. Why: anticipation of something worse keeps the audience engaged.
- [heuristic] A remark about a future event plants a question that the story can answer later, which keeps the reader's attention on that thread. When: A character predicts an event or outcome. Why: An open question prompts the reader to track its answer.
- [procedure] 1) When a past event or disputed item cannot be checked directly, follow it forward through later records such as catalogues or sales rather than retracing the past. 2) Note where the chain breaks. When: Verifying the history of a disputed item or transaction, or a past event that cannot be verified but a future event can be observed. Why: Tracing forward reveals gaps that suggest concealment or loss; retracing the past wastes time and effort.
- [pitfall] Foreboding needs concrete events and a later payoff; without them it reads as filler and drains credibility.
- [pitfall] Overusing death imagery makes warnings feel clichéd, and unfulfilled dread becomes noise that weakens later tension. When: Using repeated death images or warnings for foreshadowing. Why: Repetition without payoff dulls the audience's response to real danger.

## journals and written texts
- [rule] Keep an objective record, such as a message log, shift bell or sensor reading, that can contradict or overturn a witness NPC's claimed account or sequence of events. When: designing witness testimony or verifiable clues. Why: Objective records let players test claims and detect false accounts.
- [rule] Use a journal's dated entries to reveal motive and schedule, and leave its final page unfinished to create a question the player resolves elsewhere. When: Designing a journal item as a story clue. Why: Dated entries give timelines to cross-check, and an unfinished end drives discovery.
- [rule] A quest journal can list unresolved questions alongside candidate answers the player wrote, flagging any candidate a clue has disproven.
- [rule] Store the reasoning behind a puzzle solution in a journal and unlock it at a chosen story moment. When: the player has a puzzle solution that needs explaining. Why: timed unlocks keep the reveal under designer control.
- [rule] Place a key-text code in a library book, and identify the correct edition through a previous owner's marks.
- [rule] Make the correct reading of jargon in codex entries, books, or inscriptions reachable through an NPC expert, a glossary, or a consultable source. When: in-game text uses specialist vocabulary. Why: a literal reading should not be the only one available.
- [rule] Give players a journal they can compare against timestamps, so an unexplained blank period becomes visible and invites investigation. Why: Comparing records exposes gaps the player must explain.
- [rule] Give documents a layered history with erased lines, earlier impressions and traces that a player can inspect with a tool such as a magnifier or lamp. When: Designing readable documents as clues. Why: Layered histories reward careful inspection.
- [rule] Notes, journals, or inscriptions can hide a second layer; compare emphasis and omissions across documents to infer what the author feared.
- [rule] Use a journal or memory fragment to carry a character's rationalization as a clue the player can challenge. When: Revealing a culprit's justification through a document. Why: A written justification gives the player something concrete to test and contradict.
- [rule] Present an observer's log as an in-game journal with unreliable entries, and let the player check it against scene evidence. When: designing diegetic records. Why: checking a flawed record against evidence rewards player deduction.
- [rule] Present facts in a journal and let the player assemble the answer, without the game stating the conclusion outright. When: designing a mystery that rewards deduction. Why: Leaving the inference to the player makes solving it an active achievement.
- [heuristic] Judge a witness's written report by its meaning, separating the message from poor spelling.
- [heuristic] A conclusion drawn from joined partial sources rests on the join itself, so no single fragment needs to be strong for the inference to hold. When: Several weak sources must be combined.
- [heuristic] Enemy or boss cycles can be made discoverable by giving players dated journal entries or logged timestamps, so they can infer the schedule themselves. When: Designing hidden recurring behavior in a game. Why: Players find patterns only when the dates are available to compare.
- [heuristic] A journal entry can flag a case as the start of a longer campaign without revealing its solution.
- [heuristic] A note stating a room and time can direct the player to a meeting spot, with wording understood only by its intended reader. When: a clue must point to a place and moment. Why: specific cues guide the player while staying opaque to others.
- [heuristic] An anonymous note can contain correct details of a real NPC or location that the player can confirm, while its accusations stay unproven until a separate clue supports them. When: Designing written clues that mix verifiable facts with unverified claims.
- [heuristic] A notice or message that gives a specific time and a list of items lets the player plan a response and reveals what the sender knows. When: placing quest messages. Why: Concrete details give the player an actionable plan and a clue to the sender.
- [heuristic] In-game mail can carry disguised handwriting or postmarks as clues that point toward a hidden NPC. When: designing message-based clues. Why: Physical traces in messages give players a route to the sender.
- [procedure] 1) List the terms as numbered items. 2) Cover duration, duties, pay, residence and required references. 3) Compare the list with what was said orally. 4) Confirm ambiguous words. 5) Judge the offer on the written terms, separately from any unease about it. When: Evaluating an offer or agreement presented in writing. Why: Written terms give a fixed basis for judgment.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm who was physically present. 2) Confirm each witness could see the signer write. 3) Confirm witnesses signed in the signer's presence. 4) Judge whether the room and sight lines allow genuineness. When: checking a signing for validity or staging. Why: A formality can look complete on paper yet have been staged.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the exact source text, including its edition. 2) Find each coded word from its page number, line number and word position. 3) Read the located words in order to recover the message. When: a code is built on a known shared book.
- [procedure] 1) Identify who published the record. 2) Check whether its author could be questioned. 3) Measure how widely it circulated. 4) Check whether anyone disputed its specifics at the time. When: weighing a published account from an earlier period. Why: exposure to challenge at the time signals reliability.
- [pitfall] Locations taken from later road or property records may not match the original layout.

## motive-based suspect ranking
- [model] Model character motives as a shared pool where each character holds a stake, and one character can exploit another's stake to frame them. When: when designing suspects with interlocking grievances. Why: Interlocking stakes let false accusations feel plausible.
- [mechanism] When the stakes of a rivalry change, such as a consent being granted, the rival who stands to lose changes, and so does who has reason to act. When: A rivalry's prize or conditions shift during the story.
- [mechanism] When a shared cost, such as paying a minister, falls on sub-groups whose interests differ, the community splits into factions that dispute the terms. When: a community pays for a common institution. Why: Groups with different stakes in the cost push for different outcomes.
- [behavior] Accusations that carry a clear motive, such as inheritance or wealth, seem convincing even when unsupported. When: several characters have plausible reasons to act. Why: a stated motive gives an accusation weight before evidence is checked.
- [behavior] A theory built on psychology and motive, such as hatred toward a rival, can point to a suspect without any physical evidence connecting that suspect to the act. When: an explanation rests on motive rather than physical evidence. Why: Motive is easy to imagine, so it can make a suspect seem guilty even when the act was physically impossible for them.
- [rule] Treat a motive-based conclusion as a suspicion rather than a finding until independent evidence supports it, and ask whether it would survive later developments. When: A theory is driven by motive or judgment about a suspect's character. Why: Motive reasoning can be persuasive without being proven.
- [rule] Give an NPC several motive tags and let the player learn the dominant one through dialogue and history records. When: when designing suspect motives for a mystery. Why: Layered motives make the suspect more believable and reward attention to records.
- [rule] Give each NPC a public reason for an action, such as a debt, fee or permit, plus a separate hidden grievance, and store both so players can connect them. When: designing NPCs whose actions need a plausible surface cause.
- [heuristic] When suspects have comparable, established access, rank them by motive: who gains from the act and whether the gain is worth the risk. When: Several suspects have comparable or established means and opportunity. Why: Motive can separate suspects that opportunity cannot. (x2)
- [heuristic] Actions arise from several interacting drives, such as vanity, ambition, credulity, sincere belief, resentment, desire, jealousy or gain; identify the strongest. When: A suspect's or character's motive or record is mixed, such as admirable and harmful acts together. Why: A single motive explains too little of a mixed record; money is often only one drive. (x2)
- [heuristic] Rank suspects by what each gains from a death, such as an inheritance or debt relief, to see who has a reason to act. When: Early in an investigation with several suspects, especially where a death has financial consequences. Why: Known motive narrows who needs closer examination and shows which facts to check first.
- [heuristic] A victim's known condition can link an object-based clue to a motive, because the condition explains why the clue matters. When: an object clue depends on a person's limitation. Why: Knowing the limitation connects the clue to the person who could exploit it.
- [heuristic] Evidence of heavy physical work at a scene, such as digging, weighs against suspects who could not have done that work alone. Why: Labour requirements limit who could have acted.
- [heuristic] Weigh a motive against medical and legal facts; a motive that could never be acted on, such as through an unmade will, weakens. When: when a motive depends on a document.
- [heuristic] A broad motive that every character shares can hide the one person who had both motive and access. Look for the overlap of motive and opportunity. When: when many characters have the same grievance. Why: Shared motive makes everyone look equally suspicious, which hides the one person who could act.
- [heuristic] Blame in a feud is often shared; when both sides escalate with uncharitable words, assign fault to both rather than one.
- [heuristic] Do not reduce a character's conduct to one explanation: deliberate fraud, self-deception and partial madness can coexist, and cunning does not rule out madness. When: judging a suspect's mixed or changing motives.
- [heuristic] Shared ownership of a plot gives several characters a motive to hide or reveal a crime.
- [procedure] 1) List each suspect's opportunity to overhear plans. 2) List direct gain. 3) List family links. 4) List possession of key objects. 5) Compare the lists to rank suspects. When: Several suspects have overlapping opportunity and motive. Why: Structured comparison exposes which suspects have the most incriminating links.
- [procedure] 1) List everyone with a motive. 2) Ask which of them would take the risk. 3) Link facts such as sightings, quarrels and purchases. 4) Narrow the pool to those whose links reinforce one another. When: Investigating a crime against a widely disliked victim. Why: Many motives exist, so the pool must narrow through linked evidence.
- [pitfall] Motive alone does not identify a culprit; it ranks suspects by possible gain and can wrongly implicate an innocent person. Why: Motive shows possibility, not action, so accusation needs access and evidence.
- [pitfall] Assuming the largest beneficiary or the first motive match is the culprit misleads, since several people may share the same financial stake or strain. When: Multiple suspects have money troubles, claims on the estate, or one motive is found. Why: Financial strain can motivate many people, not only the direct heir.
- [pitfall] Agreeing witnesses with a shared interest, such as protecting the same person, may give coordinated matching accounts; those who saw only part of an episode are also weaker. When: Witnesses or tellers have a common stake in the outcome, or two accounts agree. Why: Agreement from interested parties does not independently confirm the facts.
- [pitfall] Motive reasoning alone can deadlock: each suspect is cleared morally while the physical question of where the object is stays unresolved. When: motive is the only sorting method used. Why: Motive answers who, not where.
- [fact] A belief in a cosmic enemy can be held across learned circles far from the community, making it a shared motive rather than local vanity.

## npc relationship dynamics
- [model] A note or dialogue line can carry two meanings, each pointing toward a different suspect, room or solution. When: Writing a clue with two intended interpretations. Why: Each meaning gives the player a different lead to test.
- [mechanism] When NPC relationships determine who accuses whom, suspicion follows the social graph rather than chance, so relationships drive the outcome. When: A game where NPCs react to each other's behavior. Why: Suspicion travels along existing ties, so changing a relationship changes who is accused.
- [mechanism] When each party withholds information, each suspects the others, creating a deadlock where cooperation becomes awkward.
- [mechanism] An informant NPC can change its dialogue when the player names a suspect, confirming the link and unlocking the next lead.
- [mechanism] Bribery and cover stories offered in dialogue can change how an NPC behaves afterwards. When: the player persuades or pays an NPC.
- [behavior] Each party in a probing exchange may read the other's lack of knowledge as confirmation of its own theory. When: when two parties each hold a partial view of the same matter. Why: silence and ignorance are easily misinterpreted.
- [behavior] Observers without a shared baseline for normal bodies disagree about what counts as an unusual mark, so their findings conflict even when they look at the same body. When: When examiners must judge whether a mark is abnormal. Why: Each observer compares the body against a different private sense of what is normal.
- [rule] Build NPC relationship graphs covering friendships, feuds, inherited grudges, marriages, property claims and financial stakes, so players map motives and predict who testifies, stays silent or slants stories.
