When: Designing characters for a mystery, social dispute or populated world with witnesses and factions. Why: Mapped stakes make motives discoverable; ties drive testimony and silence. (x2)
- [rule] Let small talk on unrelated topics raise a guarded NPC's trust, unlocking deeper dialogue and behavioral clues in later talks instead of direct questions. When: Designing dialogue or open-world social interaction with guarded characters. Why: Rising trust gates access to sensitive information; rapport from casual talk can open disclosure.
- [rule] Let an NPC reputation system weight a character's word by their standing and history. When: designing NPC reputation systems.
- [rule] Do not drop a case while the wronged party is still in danger. When: the victim faces ongoing risk from the offender.
- [rule] Give NPCs emotional bonds in a relationship graph, and design a protective NPC's cover story with a tell the player can expose.
- [rule] Let an NPC who hides a relation be exposed by a name challenge in dialogue, with a reassurance branch that unlocks the confession. When: When designing dialogue for a hidden relationship. Why: Branching dialogue lets the player choose pressure or reassurance.
- [rule] Track NPC relationship values so an NPC's answer about a rival changes with which relationship the NPC chooses to admit. When: A player questions an NPC about another character. Why: Admitted relationships shape what the NPC says.
- [rule] Route a rumour through several NPCs so the player must trace each link back to its source.
- [rule] Track what the player has shared with a companion, and let that companion's stance change when they could act on the secret. When: Designing companion NPCs who receive player secrets. Why: Shared secrets create consequences that make companion relationships meaningful.
- [heuristic] End a resolved story with ordinary everyday talk to show that normal life has resumed.
- [heuristic] How each person sees the other can drive an intrigue, so track both sides' self-regard when reconstructing motive.
- [procedure] 1) Rank each NPC by age, then office, then property. 2) Choose dialogue honorifics that match that rank. 3) Let rank decide whose accusations others credit. When: NPC standing affects whether others listen to them.
- [procedure] 1) State the damage a public case would do. 2) Require the return of stolen goods and receipts. 3) Verify the recovery. 4) Offer the exit only after verification succeeds. When: an investigator considers letting a guilty party go.
- [tradeoff] Keeping allies uninformed protects the plan and makes their behaviour read naturally to watching suspects, but leaves them unable to judge their own risk. When: When allies must stay separate from the real plan, especially if observed by suspects. Why: Uninformed allies cannot give the plan away through their behaviour.
- [tradeoff] A mutual information trade shows what each side will risk, but offering your information reveals your own hand, since the other party learns what you already hold.
- [pitfall] Two statements that agree do not prove either is true, since they may simply share one version of events.
- [pitfall] Recognition can run both ways, so an investigator who is spotted may not be able to rely on staying hidden. When: staging a confrontation with a disguised suspect. Why: The suspect may recognise the investigator in return.
- [fact] Unspoken distrust in a relationship can persist despite a person's will to dismiss it, and explains why earlier warning signs went unacted upon. When: A character ignores warning signs about someone close. Why: Intuition and long-held unease resist deliberate reasoning.

## object traces
- [model] Tag each object with a trace state such as fired, cleaned or handled, so an expert character can report conclusions the player can verify by inspecting the object. When: Designing evidence that depends on an object's history. Why: Explicit states let expert conclusions be checked against the object itself.
- [mechanism] Wear and staining accumulate with repeated use and handling, so wear depth shows how much traffic a surface had, and personal objects record their owner's habits, finances and character. When: when reading an item's history. Why: repeated use and handling leave physical traces.
- [mechanism] Fading ink and worn margins help date a book and show where pages were handled most, since physical wear is evidence of use.
- [mechanism] Objects in a game can record who touched them and when. A clean object can signal a careful culprit, and matching records link suspects to the scene.
- [rule] Show an object's contents and condition to both parties before handing it over, so its state is fixed at the moment of transfer. When: When the object's state may later be disputed. Why: A fixed starting state gives both parties a reference point for later claims.
- [rule] Show object age through wear and dust, so players can tell a fresh disturbance from an older one without reading text. When: When a scene must communicate when something happened. Why: Players read visual wear as a time cue.
- [rule] Do not treat an object as standalone proof; connect it to the timeline and to the people present before drawing a conclusion. When: A single physical item seems to point to a suspect. Why: An object alone can have innocent explanations.
- [heuristic] Heavy folds and faded ink suggest a document was read many times and may have lost legible words. When: Examining a physical document. Why: Repeated handling wears paper and ink.
- [heuristic] Ask whether light objects could have stayed in place through the disturbance described; if not, they were likely placed after it. When: a scene claims heavy traffic or struggle around fragile items. Why: objects cannot persist unmoved through heavy disturbance.
- [heuristic] Worn cuffs and a smooth patch on the elbow suggest long hours of writing at a desk. When: clothing shows wear at the sleeve and elbow. Why: resting the arm on a desk wears those spots.
- [heuristic] Damage concentrated on one side of an object can reveal which hand the owner uses. When: When an object shows one-sided wear or charring. Why: Habitual handling places stress on the dominant side.
- [heuristic] Wear on a personal object, such as tooth marks on a pipe mouthpiece, can reveal its user; compare the wear with the traits the presumed owner should have. When: when the owner of an object is in question. Why: physical wear records how the object was used.
- [heuristic] Compare a print against footwear by its wear, not only its design, since identical shoes can be told apart by wear on their studs. When: A print is matched to a pair of shoes. Why: Wear is individual while design is shared across many owners.
- [heuristic] A physical object's count or arrangement that looks wrong can carry evidence; check it before dismissing it as coincidence.
- [heuristic] A container with no name or route gives no travel trail, so its contents and origin must be established by the owner rather than inferred from where it was found.
- [procedure] 1) Examine the wear marks, which can reveal a previous owner whose build differs from the current holder 2) Compare them with the current holder's body 3) Identify who else in the case has that build. When: an object may have changed hands.
- [procedure] 1) Build a duplicate of the object. 2) Run it under the same conditions as the original. 3) Measure a quantity such as burn time. 4) Compare the result with the observed remains. When: An ordinary object was used and left in a recognisable state. Why: A matched duplicate turns a remaining trace into a measured estimate of past use.
- [procedure] 1) Establish when the area was last cleaned or reset. 2) Check whether the object could predate that point. 3) Test the witness's claim against the object's timing and location. When: When an object's presence conflicts with a claim. Why: Timing determines whether the object contradicts the claim.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the object's source. 2) Find the source's customers. 3) Check which customer could have produced the object's use. 4) Link the customer to a person. When: An object with a known source turns up at a scene. Why: The trace moves from object to supplier to customer to person in order.
- [procedure] 1) Take a sample of the old item. 2) Use it for its intended function under normal conditions. 3) Judge whether it still works from the observed result. When: An found object's age or condition is in doubt.
- [pitfall] Treating a stopped timepiece as exact assumes the owner's winding habits. Without knowing how it was carried and used, the anchor is weaker than it looks. When: Using a timepiece's last set time as proof of when something happened. Why: Unknown carrying and winding habits leave the stop time open to error.
- [pitfall] Inferring an object's type from a tear or a pocket's shape is a hypothesis, not proof, until confirmed by other evidence.
- [pitfall] Old damage can be mistaken for new, and weather or other people may have altered the ground, so the age of a sign must be judged.
- [fact] Objects left in a habitual place, such as a coat on its usual peg or smoked cigarettes, can be linked to a timeline bounding when a person was present. When: No witness saw the person arrive or leave. Why: Objects left behind record that someone was present.
- [fact] A worn seat can show that someone repeatedly stood on it to reach something high. Wear records habits.

## outsider perspective
- [mechanism] When the narrator does not know the plan, the audience shares the surprise and experiences the event as it unfolds. When: surprise matters to the work. Why: the audience has no more knowledge than the narrator.
- [mechanism] Specific detail in questions that outsiders could not have known shows the questioner prepared from prior information, not from the witness.
- [behavior] A narrator who openly admits lapses or skipped parts signals gaps in the record, so the reader should weigh that account less. When: A narrator reports events while admitting inattention. Why: Admitted gaps mean the record is incomplete.
- [behavior] Sounds from outside raise a trapped character's hope, but when their signals go unheard, the failed rescue deepens despair. When: Outside activity is audible but cannot reach the trapped character. Why: Hope raised by sound turns to despair when it is not answered.
- [behavior] A crime can seem incomprehensible from outside yet make sense from the perpetrator's inside perspective, so an outside observer must study it differently from an insider. When: a story presents a crime from the criminal's viewpoint. Why: The perpetrator's logic is hidden from outsiders, so the same act reads differently depending on the viewpoint.
- [behavior] A narrator who frames their own conduct as unavoidable and steers how the listener judges others controls what the listener sees. When: when a witness or suspect tells their own account.
- [behavior] Private talks between a dissenting group and outsiders are often logged as suspicious contact, which casts the group as coordinating against the authority. When: a faction meets outsiders during a dispute. Why: Hidden contact is read as conspiracy.
- [behavior] A newly arrived authority forms first impressions from those who meet him first, and they can steer his movements and decisions. When: an outsider takes up a post. Why: Early contacts control the information the newcomer receives first.
- [behavior] An outsider entering a tight group reads its jokes, ritual phrasing and silence through his own habits, so they can look like insult or evasion. When: a newcomer observes a closed community with its own idioms. Why: the newcomer applies only his own social norms.
- [behavior] An outsider's explanation of a private misfortune can turn it into a public accusation by naming a neighbour as the cause. When: A family illness is attributed to a person outside their household. Why: Naming a culprit gives a private trouble a social target.
- [rule] Ask who else could speak; silence cannot be assumed when others have interests that may align with the accused.
- [rule] Frame a question around how outsiders would judge the matter, so that a private concern feels like a public necessity. When: when a witness resists answering a personal question. Why: a public stake can override reluctance to speak privately.
- [rule] Attach titles or subjects to books and documents so that the content of disturbed items can hint at an NPC's interests. When: populating a room with readable items. Why: Item content gives players a clue to an NPC's identity or habits.
- [heuristic] Reject outsider theories only when access to the means is restricted to a known group; if entrances were open, alibis cannot exclude an outsider. When: Access to the means of a crime is restricted to a known group. Why: Explanations needing an unseen intruder add unverifiable assumptions the evidence does not require.
- [heuristic] Assign narrators by presence at events rather than cleverness or rank, so each account covers what its narrator actually witnessed. When: choosing who tells part of a story. Why: presence determines what a narrator can know.
- [heuristic] A barrier set from outside a sealed door after the intruders left implies an accomplice was on the far side of the door.
- [heuristic] A plot that depends on an outsider acting at a moment they could not have known about is less likely than one that depends on information they had.
- [heuristic] Use an outsider's misreading of a community when the group's rules are not stated openly to the reader. When: the player must read a faction, guild or village with its own idioms.
- [pitfall] Emotional stance or hindsight can colour a narrator's account of people and events, including a victim's private feelings; partisan narrators need extra checking. When: The narrator praises or condemns people involved in the events. Why: Emotional stance colours what is remembered and how it is told.
- [pitfall] Personal narration drifts easily toward the narrator's own life, pulling the account away from the central events. When: a narrator writes a first-person account. Why: self-focus competes with the case.
- [pitfall] Multi-narrator framing breaks down when a narrator relays others' accounts beyond their own knowledge. When: Narrators pass on information they did not witness. Why: Relayed accounts blur the reliability each source is meant to carry.
- [pitfall] Another person may use the same confusion to follow the target, so a pursuer should not assume they are the only one watching. Why: crowds can hide several followers at once.
- [pitfall] A request for a signed or handwritten statement from a newcomer can gather a handwriting sample for forgery, so such requests deserve scrutiny. When: a newcomer claims an identity or role and is asked to write. Why: Forgery needs time to learn a person's handwriting, which a routine-looking request provides.
- [pitfall] With no strong suspect, investigators may fix on whoever is new or unfamiliar, which is a bias rather than evidence.
- [pitfall] An outsider's first impression of a person's role or relationship can be wrong in either direction.

## single trace and mark evidence
- [rule] A single trace, such as a hair, smell, mud or wet boot, has several possible sources; confirm it with reference data or a second independent trace before concluding.
- [rule] Do not build a conclusion or signature from one suggestive detail or sign that several explanations could fit; check each link on its own before relying on it. When: when a small sign could support more than one explanation. Why: Ambiguous signs need corroboration before they support a conclusion.
- [rule] A confident conclusion from one trace can be wrong; when its conditions are disputed and no further evidence is in hand, hedge and promise further proof rather than overclaim. Why: Overclaiming a contested trace invites easy rebuttal.
- [rule] Do not treat a single mark as conclusive without checking it against records.
- [rule] Do not treat a single unusual trace as proof of guilt; a trace with an innocent cause needs corroboration before anyone is accused.
- [rule] A single missing item from a set is a meaningful gap only if it is known that a full set existed.
- [rule] Do not treat a single trace as proof of an absent person's identity or traits. When: concluding about a missing person from a scene. Why: one misread object can mislead the whole profile.
- [rule] Do not infer that a scene was staged from one oddity alone; require other evidence before drawing that conclusion. When: A single detail seems arranged. Why: One unusual detail can have an innocent explanation.
- [rule] Do not treat a single trace as proof; build a case from several pieces of evidence. When: When one object seems to point decisively to a person or event. Why: A single trace may have an ordinary explanation.
- [heuristic] Treat a route inferred from one object as a hypothesis until other traces confirm it.
- [heuristic] A single trace fragment is not proof; it only suggests a place that must be checked.
- [heuristic] Do not treat one unguarded look as proof of a hidden motive; it is only a clue to weigh with others.
- [heuristic] A single mark can support a reconstructed sequence of events, using its size, thickness and border to infer how it was made. When: no witness saw the events.
- [heuristic] Put the decisive proof in a single controllable artifact, such as a negative, a measured photograph or a footprint, so the evidence is clear and checkable.
- [tradeoff] A matching trace can confirm a reconstruction when its position fits the proposed action; an admitted physical trace may reveal a sealed room, while other traces need a second trace.
- [pitfall] Identifying a person or origin from one feature, such as foot size, costume, planted item, dialect or haircut, misleads; confirm only with several independent matching features. When: when identifying a person or confirming a suspect. Why: Matching needs multiple independent features.
- [pitfall] One out-of-character item is not proof on its own; it needs independent confirmation before it is treated as evidence.
- [pitfall] A single trace can support several stories, so test each candidate story against the other traces.
- [pitfall] A single memorable feature can dominate a witness description and mislead searchers who look only for it. When: Using a description to find a suspect. Why: Striking details draw attention away from others.
- [pitfall] Treating one key position as proof ignores exceptions, such as a private room sometimes locked from inside by ordinary choice. Why: Household arrangements vary, and mixed arrangements weaken any general rule.
- [pitfall] An innocent cause can explain mud or a wet boot, so a physical trace needs a second source.
- [pitfall] Building a full profile from one trace overreaches; a single worn surface supports only a probable diagnosis. When: Drawing conclusions from a single physical feature. Why: One feature rarely determines a condition, symptoms, and behavior together.
- [pitfall] A behavioural habit proves nothing on its own; it needs a matching moment in time and a second independent observation to count as evidence. Why: Habits are common, so one match can be coincidence.
- [fact] Singed hair or scorching around a wound indicates firing from close range, which bounds how far away the shooter could have been. When: when a wound shows signs of burning or singeing. Why: residue and heat effects fall off with distance.
- [fact] A partial seal impression may carry no trace of origin, so physical evidence on an anonymous note can lead nowhere. When: When an anonymous note has a seal or stamp that is incomplete. Why: Partial marks often lack the features needed to identify a source.

## suspect pool and framing
- [definition] A scapegoat is a decoy figure placed to absorb suspicion, shielding a hidden organiser who is the real planner.
- [mechanism] Accusations spread outward from a suspect or central source to officials, neighbours, the wealthy and neighbouring places; tracking locations reveals their direction and reach. When: when a process reaches people of every social rank. Why: Suspicion extends along existing relationships, institutions and geography.
- [mechanism] A scapegoat is chosen who has visible access and debts, and the frame needs only their name attached, since the disgrace lands whoever acted. When: The investigators will look no further than the visible suspect. Why: Visible motive and access make the scapegoat plausible without proof.
- [mechanism] Whether an authority accepts a planted scapegoat depends on its incentives, such as preferring a clean record to a doubtful case. When: when a frame is used to close a case. Why: officials act on what they are rewarded for.
- [mechanism] Widening a candidate list overwhelms players unless a second constraint filters it down.
- [behavior] A suggested outside culprit can shield whoever proposes it, drawing attention from the true cause; treat such an excuse, including a recanting witness's outside power, as unproven. When: when someone proposes an intruder. Why: A false external threat shifts blame away from those present. (x2)
- [behavior] Households and police tend to pursue a plausible outside suspect first, which can delay attention to causes inside the household. When: one obvious outside suspect exists. Why: an external culprit explains the event conveniently.
- [rule] A profile fitting many people leaves the pool wide; narrow it with physical evidence such as footprint sizes or footwear, not alibis alone. When: A mystery where alibis are unreliable or easily faked. Why: Physical filters remain checkable when testimony is contested.
- [rule] Point a rumour or dying word at an outside faction while the real mechanism lies inside the locked setting, so the false trail fails under inspection.
- [rule] A scapegoat setup should leave a trail that can be rechecked later.
- [rule] A scapegoat must be an almost certain candidate for the blame, so choosing the patsy is part of designing the frame. When: when planning a frame. Why: a weak candidate lets the frame fail.
- [heuristic] Widen suspects to everyone who knew an item existed, including staff, dealers, visitors and advisers, then to whom those people might have told. When: After an item goes missing, or when the obvious names are checked and the case is still open. Why: Knowledge of an object enables a theft, and the suspect list is often incomplete. (x2)
- [heuristic] Widen the inquiry to surrounding circumstances, including the sources that spread a theory, since seemingly minor details can carry much of the truth.
- [heuristic] An outside danger, such as a hostile fugitive, can serve as a rival threat and alternate suspect that diverts attention from the main mystery. When: when a case needs a second source of menace.
- [heuristic] After a first theory, check whether the figure central to the case could also be involved, instead of stopping at the first suspect. Why: The first theory can be wrong, and a central figure may have both access and interest.
- [heuristic] When a disappearance seems impossible, ask where the missing person would least likely be sought. When: a missing person cannot be found in expected places.
- [heuristic] A stolen or planted object can connect to a larger hidden group, so one clue may point beyond the single suspect it seems to name. When: A clue is linked to a theft or a crime with several possible actors. Why: Objects move through networks, so their origin can reveal more than their immediate owner.
- [heuristic] When an interested party urges dropping an inquiry, weigh their interest in avoiding scandal against the advice. When: a relative or stakeholder discourages investigation. Why: Interest in avoiding exposure can bias advice toward stopping.
- [heuristic] Do not assume every name on an accusation list is guilty, since such lists grow through fear and kinship as well as evidence. When: when evaluating a list of accused people. Why: Accusations spread along family and neighbourhood ties, not only through proof.
- [heuristic] Use a conclusive clue to settle one question, then open a second question about who could reach it, and plant a plausible second suspect near the scene. When: Structuring a mystery's clue sequence. Why: A settled answer shifts the mystery to access, and a second suspect tests the first theory.
- [heuristic] A method that requires specialized knowledge narrows the suspect pool to people with access to that knowledge, either as practitioners or as those who instructed them. When: An identified method demands an uncommon skill or knowledge. Why: The skill requirement limits who could plausibly have executed the method.
- [heuristic] Keep one name recurring through the investigation so it keeps drawing attention even after it is shown to be wrong. When: a suspect has been cleared but may still matter. Why: A persistent name keeps the player's attention on a thread that could still lead to the truth.
- [procedure] 1) Search beyond the scene along the route the actor likely took. 2) Repeat searches at places not yet covered. 3) Read identifying marks on each recovered item to fix its owner. When: Initial searches of the scene fail to turn up key items. Why: Items may be discarded along a route rather than left at the scene.
- [pitfall] Judging a character by profession or outward piety can mislead, since respectability does not rule out violent capacity.
- [pitfall] A framed scapegoat can unravel the plan by generating fresh leads or by confessing. When: when a frame is used to close a case. Why: a questioned fall-guy may point back to the real object.

## theory revision
- [mechanism] Each apparent solution opens a new suspect, and each new trace of a hidden object revises the player's belief, so belief changes several times before the reveal. When: in a multi-stage investigation. Why: Each move of the object along its route creates a new encounter and suspect.
- [behavior] Committing to a test meant to prove a theory can make empty results look like confirmation of that theory. When: observer has publicly committed to a plan. Why: investment in the plan biases interpretation of the outcome.
- [behavior] A pause and a night's rest can let a solver revisit the evidence with fresh eyes and notice the ordinary explanation. When: after an inquiry has stalled. Why: distance from the problem loosens fixed readings.
- [behavior] When a late reveal exposes a feigned role, audiences reread earlier scenes where the character seemed confused to find the missed inconsistencies. When: A character's pretence is exposed late in a story. Why: The reveal gives new meaning to behaviour seen earlier.
- [rule] Recheck each newly raised suspect or strong-looking lead against the original evidence, keeping its explanation open until tested; a match or surface support may have another cause. When: a suspect is newly raised or a lead seems strong on the surface. Why: A match may have another cause, and surface support can mislead.
- [rule] Give players a later clue that contradicts their leading theory so they revise it rather than keep the first explanation. When: players have committed to a single explanation or the first solution is meant to be wrong. Why: Fixation makes contradicting clues easy to overlook; a clear contradiction forces reconsideration.
- [rule] When a new fact or changed evidence source contradicts a theory or working timeline, rebuild it around that fact rather than fitting the fact or patching the theory. When: a new fact conflicts with the current theory or a key evidence source changes. Why: The old theory rested on the original source or fit.
- [rule] Recheck a target's location before acting, and do not commit resources to a fixed position when the target has reason to move. When: Planning an action against a target who may relocate. Why: Trust in an older scout's report can hide a change that happened afterward.
- [rule] After clearing one suspect, reassess the remaining suspects from access and opportunity, not from earlier suspicion.
- [rule] Commit to a witness sighting before confronting the suspect with it, so the suspect's answer is tested rather than shaped by what they already know. When: Questioning a suspect about a witness sighting. Why: Revealing the full evidence first lets the suspect adjust the story.
- [rule] Confirm each party's commitment to a fixed meeting time with follow-up contact, so the schedule is established before the event.
- [heuristic] Hold each hypothesis provisional, since an early theory is useful only until a fact contradicts it; drop a convenient suspect when facts contradict it. When: early in an inquiry, when a theory explains a trace dramatically or information comes from gossip or an official cover story. Why: Fixed early theories cause new facts to be discounted; wanting a culprit shapes which facts seem significant.
- [heuristic] Re-checking a point already examined often confirms the earlier finding rather than overturning it. When: when an earlier investigator's result needs a second check.
- [procedure] 1) List recovered facts in order of occurrence, not report order. 2) Gather entries from movements, routine changes, purchases, nightly habits and stated convictions. 3) Check each entry against a source. 4) Note what was known and what remained unknown. When: an investigator takes over an earlier inquiry that failed to reach a result. Why: lost facts can be recovered and gaps identified before new action.
- [procedure] 1) Show every clue in plain view before the solution. 2) Give each object a new purpose that fits the solution. 3) Reinterpret names and labels the same way. 4) Hold back one clue and reveal it last. When: building a reveal that makes earlier clues consistent. Why: each clue then supports one coherent explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Identify each theory's key assumption. 2) Find a witness or record that can settle it. 3) Drop the theory when a reliable source contradicts the assumption. 4) Move to the next line of inquiry. When: several theories fit the facts and each needs a witness. Why: a reliable source can overturn a key link quickly.
- [pitfall] Investigators committed to a theory, accusation or obsession dismiss, ignore, twist or miss contrary facts and testimony; test each contrary fact instead of discarding it. When: an investigator or decision-maker has settled on a theory or accusation. Why: Expectation and commitment filter out evidence that does not fit. (x3)
- [pitfall] Once committed to a view, people find it hard to back away from a contradicting fact, so a confident wrong theory persists and must be actively revised. When: after a view is committed and a contradicting fact arrives. Why: Commitment to a theory resists correction. (x2)
- [pitfall] Forming or accepting a theory before testing it biases what is sought and how it is read, so only supporting facts get gathered. When: an idea forms before facts are gathered. Why: The theory guides attention before facts do.
- [pitfall] A coherent sequence of events can leave awkward details or the decisive point unexplained, such as why an action occurs at that moment or who the culprit is. When: a chain of events seems to explain the case. Why: Coherence of the main sequence does not explain every awkward detail or the one point that matters most.
- [pitfall] A theory is not established by being believed or by answering every objection; rebuttals resting on guesses about unseen facts can still be wrong. Why: Internal coherence does not confirm the unseen assumptions behind it.
- [pitfall] A tidy motive or confident psychological profile can take hold before physical or medical evidence confirms a crime; keep such theories subordinate to the facts. Why: Confident theories can override plain facts.
- [pitfall] A plausible reinterpretation can slip into the fact base unnoticed; it must be tested against the record before it counts as established.
- [pitfall] Accepting the most comfortable explanation, even with little evidence, is a common error when a motive is unclear. When: an investigator must explain an unclear character. Why: a comfortable explanation reduces uncertainty.
- [pitfall] Repeatedly checking a hiding place reveals to observers where the hidden item is kept. When: a character keeps returning to a stash. Why: the repeated action is visible to others.

## calm and candid interview manner
- [mechanism] When help is traded for candor, later NPC answers can depend on whether the player kept that promise.
- [mechanism] A calm surface over hidden pressure heightens expectation, because the audience senses that something is being held back beneath it.
- [behavior] Calm demeanour, including calm acceptance of an accusation, fits both innocence and guilt, so it does not separate them. When: when a suspect appears composed under detention. Why: Composure can come from many causes, including self-restraint.
- [behavior] People who expect no audience record or state plans, motives, debts, deadlines and who benefits candidly, so private notes or exchanges can reveal intent. When: private records discovered after events, or private exchanges between characters. Why: Writers and speakers do not expect anyone else to read or hear them, so they speak candidly.
- [behavior] A composed denial is unremarkable when the accused has no hidden stake, so on its own it reveals little.
- [behavior] Someone who accepts a refusal without protest, despite claimed urgency, is probably not the genuine need they describe. When: a claimed need is refused. Why: Genuine urgency usually produces resistance or pressure.
- [behavior] A calm reminder from a third party to be gentle can quiet an aggressive questioner, and it also halts the outburst. When: A bystander intervenes during an escalating interrogation. Why: The intervention looks like kindness while redirecting the questioner's momentum.
- [behavior] A suspect who refuses to lie even to protect themselves can see suspicion against them grow. When: the suspect is confronted with incriminating facts. Why: Others may read a candid refusal as a sign of guilt.
- [behavior] A witness who admits being at the scene can become a suspect while their testimony clears others, so frankness can shift suspicion onto them.
- [behavior] Calm refusal and feigned boredom give an interrogator no visible reaction to read. When: when a suspect is pressed without evidence in hand.
- [rule] Calm, cooperative manner or a direct denial of lying is not proof of honesty; observe it as behaviour and treat tone changes as signals to question. When: A witness appears composed during questioning. Why: Composure can be practiced or feigned.
- [heuristic] Alternate calm stretches with sudden shifts or new events, placing calm before an event so it hits harder and keeps the audience pressing forward. When: pacing a tense or long narrative section. Why: Contrast makes the shift more noticeable and keeps attention from settling.
- [heuristic] Question a witness about a reaction only once they are calm enough to answer.
- [heuristic] A promise made by someone who openly admits their limits is more credible than one from someone who denies them. When: evaluating a pledge. Why: honesty about difficulty signals the promise is considered.
- [heuristic] Making candor the condition of help can get a reluctant witness to speak more plainly. When: the witness is guarded about their own role.
- [heuristic] Keep questioning even in tone; a cooperative witness answers more fully without alarm. When: questioning a cooperative but unobservant witness who overheard a conversation. Why: pressure raises alarm and shuts down answers.
- [procedure] 1) Demand a complete, true account, stating that gaps or invented details will be exposed. 2) Confirm each part against known facts. 3) Use the confirmed account to unlock further evidence. When: questioning a suspect whose evidence is already partly known. Why: a checked account anchors the story in fact.
- [tradeoff] Admitting one's own fault without excuse can raise credibility; yet frank admissions of minor faults can hide a central fact, so check what the account leaves out. When: when assessing a witness's or narrator's admission of their own wrongdoing. Why: Unflattering admissions are less likely invented for advantage, but a candid admission can still conceal the central omission.
- [tradeoff] Telling a truthful account protects you when the other side can verify your facts, since hiding checkable facts looks suspicious. It fails when one checkable fact would expose the whole cover story. When: when a questioner can check facts independently. Why: concealment of verifiable facts signals guilt, but one exposed fact can unravel a fabricated story.
- [tradeoff] A candid approach is trusted only when the interviewee will take it seriously, while a pretext can be exposed by a single detail and fail on contact. When: When choosing how to approach an interviewee. Why: Candor depends on the listener's trust, and a pretext depends on being believed in its role.
- [pitfall] Advice that looks like protective care can be a method of controlling a witness's movements and access. When: An investigator directs a witness to hide or wait. Why: Concealed control can pass as concern.
- [pitfall] Trusting a calm or confident witness over a confused one can mislead.
- [pitfall] A candid admission of motive can be a way of appearing above suspicion, so openness is not proof of innocence. Why: A clever suspect may choose which motive investigators find.
- [pitfall] Brevity alone is not evidence of omission, since a short speaker may hide nothing at all.

## cause of death analysis
- [definition] Non-human explanations for a death include self-inflicted harm, an accident, a fall of heavy objects during a struggle, and fate or divine will.
- [mechanism] Cooling after death depends on surroundings: shade and damp grass slow it, so the same body cools at different rates in different places. When: when estimating time of death from body temperature. Why: environment changes heat loss.
- [behavior] A person can insist little time has passed despite evidence otherwise, and that stubbornness can make lost time visible to an audience. When: When a character's perception of time conflicts with a verifiable clock. Why: Confidence in a wrong estimate contrasts with the actual elapsed time.
- [rule] Store each death's posture and wound type so the player can read how an NPC died.
- [rule] Ruling out one cause of death does not establish when the death occurred; treat cause and time as separate questions.
- [rule] When a death could be suicide or murder, keep both readings open until physical evidence or a contradicting note settles which one fits the scene. When: A death scene supports both a self-inflicted and a staged reading.
- [heuristic] When a body shows no visible wound, infer the cause of death from the surrounding situation rather than the body alone. When: Cause of death is unclear from the body. Why: Scene context can reveal causes the body does not show.
- [heuristic] A cause that acted long before a death is a weak explanation for it, because it should have worn off by then. When: When comparing a candidate cause with the time of death.
- [heuristic] If a symptom appears before the suspected cause could have acted, the suspected cause is doubtful. When: checking a claimed cause against a timeline. Why: A cause cannot produce effects that come before it.
- [heuristic] A fast-acting dose suggests a liquid taken by mouth, which narrows the container to look for. When: the speed of an effect is known. Why: Effect speed reveals how a substance was delivered.
- [heuristic] Stupor and a flushed face can indicate that a person was given drink or drugs, which hints that they were deceived.
- [heuristic] A person with no known means who suddenly spends freely is a prime suspect. When: the person's finances are known and the change is observable. Why: a sudden source of money needs an explanation.
- [heuristic] A death ruled self-inflicted rests on absence of struggle, absence of noise and the victim's known low mood, so each premise should be checked. When: When assessing a death that appears self-inflicted. Why: The ruling depends on what is missing as much as what is present, so each absence needs verification.
- [heuristic] Check an apparent cause of death, such as an accident or collapse, against the body; the physical signs can overturn the obvious explanation. When: When a surface cause of death must be verified. Why: Injuries may have been inflicted after death, making the obvious cause misleading.
- [procedure] 1) List every candidate cause. 2) Rule out each cause one at a time with a specific physical check. 3) Check each cause's timing against the death. 4) Read the body for signs. 5) Eliminate causes until a remaining one is supported or unexplained. When: When a death is sudden and the stated cause does not fit the body or timeline.
- [procedure] 1) Start from an observed effect. 2) Establish a normal baseline. 3) Ask about exceptions to the baseline. 4) Pursue a candidate cause with specific questions. 5) Check details that link the cause to the event.
- [procedure] 1) List the candidate causes. 2) Rule out each cause the observed signs contradict. 3) Match the remaining cause against known case records. 4) Confirm with an expert who recognises the pattern. When: A cause of death is unclear and the body still holds traces. Why: Elimination narrows causes, and expert records confirm the match.
- [procedure] 1) Take the time-of-death estimate made at the examination as a range. 2) Subtract the known interval between observations to bound the state at the earlier one. 3) Check the bound against testimony. When: A precise time of death matters and two observations have a known gap.
- [procedure] 1) Find when the victim was last seen well. 2) Find when the victim was first seen unwell. 3) Treat the span between them as the window in which dosing could have occurred.
- [pitfall] A settled cause of death does not name a culprit, so keep cause and culpability as separate questions; players may mistake the answered how for the whole case. When: A key forensic fact has been established. Why: Answering how something happened leaves open who did it.
- [pitfall] A death caused by a sudden movement can look random, which hides the real cause unless its timing is checked against the dose.
- [fact] Some insurance policies forfeit premiums if the insured takes his own life within a set period, such as one year after the policy begins.
- [fact] A suicide can supply a motive for one death without explaining the other killings in the same case.
- [fact] Alkaloid poison can cause asphyxia and failure of the heart and lungs, producing a death that looks supernatural.

## false premises
- [mechanism] Planting a false belief in a suspect, such as a claimed admission or a claimed owner of an object, can make the suspect's reaction reveal what they know. When: When a suspect's account needs to be tested against a fact they may not expect you to know. Why: A person who knows a fact reacts to a false claim about it, exposing that knowledge.
- [mechanism] A false story accepted by the world can become established state, and later events can then prove it wrong. When: a quest system records NPC claims as world facts. Why: Believed claims act as facts until new events contradict them.
- [rule] Make the false culprit plausible early, with a motive and apparently complete theory, so the player accepts them; later evidence must overturn that assumption rather than confirm it. When: Building a mystery with a wrong suspect, around the first quarter. Why: Audiences settle on the most obvious explanation and resist changing it; they accept a suspect when guilt is presented as plausible. (x2)
- [heuristic] Chain false solutions, each stronger than the truth and broken by a different evidence kind (testimony, physical trace, document), so the final answer rests on deduction authorities missed. When: Designing a mystery or chase plot with escalating reveals, or a sequence of wrong solutions before the true one. Why: Each overturned answer keeps the player uncertain and rewards the one who connects facts the authorities missed.
- [heuristic] A false statement repeated to several people may be built to support a later story, so repetition across listeners can signal a plan rather than a slip. When: when the same falsehood is told to more than one person. Why: consistency across listeners suggests preparation.
- [heuristic] Test a guarded witness by offering a tempting or false premise and watching for a change in manner. When: a direct answer from the witness would reveal little.
- [heuristic] Support a false solution with documents that appear to prove it, so the audience's belief stays stable through the middle of the story. When: Maintaining a wrong theory across a long middle act. Why: Apparent proof keeps the audience committed, making the eventual reversal more forceful.
- [heuristic] Author dialogue and documents so they support the wrong theory, placing the true motive only in sources that players must actively check. When: Designing a quest chain with a hidden true motive. Why: Players who check other sources reach the real answer while others accept the decoy.
- [heuristic] Treat a staged intruder story as a false explanation and give the observer a physical test, such as a broken rail, that disproves it. When: a crime is explained by an outside attacker. Why: A fair test lets a careful player reject the cover story.
- [heuristic] Make the official explanation so tidy that the player stops testing it, then let physical evidence contradict it later. When: a scenario where an authority offers a convenient answer to the mystery. Why: A plausible, closed explanation lowers the player's scrutiny, so a later contradiction lands harder.
- [procedure] 1) Pick a convincing false condition. 2) Spread it through a trusted intermediary who repeats it to the target. 3) Keep the closest honest witnesses unaware so their genuine distress sells the scene. 4) Use ordinary materials for fake symptoms and keep distance from close inspection. When: Luring a target who has a reason to approach a supposedly dying person. Why: Trusted channels and genuine reactions make the performance believable.
- [procedure] 1) Offer the player a neat explanation from an NPC. 2) Attach a checkable fact to it, such as a physical measurement or mobility test. 3) Let the fact overturn the explanation. When: Building a mid-plot false solution. Why: A rejection the player verifies themselves is more persuasive than an authorial correction.
- [tradeoff] A false claim can reveal knowledge through the suspect's reaction, but it can also end cooperation; use it only when the falsehood can be checked later. When: When choosing between a bluff and a neutral question. Why: The bluff exposes the suspect but may close off future sources.
- [tradeoff] Weighing a logically complete chain against a suspect's established character risks either accepting a neat but wrong case or dismissing sound circumstantial evidence over an impression. When: When a suspect's known behavior conflicts with the evidence. Why: Both logic and character can mislead when used alone.
- [pitfall] Valid logic cannot rescue false premises. Verify a stated source independently and check the one hard fact is explained; one misidentified detail corrupts every conclusion built on it. Why: The form of an argument does not check whether its starting points are true. (x2)
- [pitfall] Repeated accounts are not independent corroboration when accusers copy or feed each other's stories; repeating a false date across accounts does not make it true. Why: Agreement among accounts can reflect copying rather than independent evidence. (x2)
- [pitfall] A stopped clock or a sleeping person can make a timeline look more precise than the evidence allows.
- [pitfall] A confident witness can give false precision, since an exact time may rest on a faulty reading such as a partly damaged dial. When: a witness gives an exact time. Why: Confidence does not guarantee that the underlying observation was accurate.
- [pitfall] Raising false hopes wrongs the witness and damages later cooperation. Why: Witnesses who feel misled stop trusting the interviewer.
- [pitfall] Specific-looking details in a decoy offer can still be false; the lure only needs to hold while the target wants the reward. Why: the target's interest in the reward, not the accuracy of details, sustains the lure.
- [pitfall] A false-premise trap works only if the investigator has confirmed the underlying facts, such as chain of custody, before relying on the reaction. When: When using a deceptive claim to test a suspect. Why: Without a verified premise, the suspect's reaction carries no reliable meaning.
- [pitfall] An ambitious theory breeds false confidence, and assuming a bait works can walk an investigator into the very trap it was meant to spring. When: Acting on an untested plan against an adversary. Why: Confidence reduces the scrutiny needed to notice that the bait has been turned against its user.
- [pitfall] A clever deduction may still fail to convince a lay audience, so sound reasoning alone does not win a case. When: Presenting a conclusion to a jury or other non-expert panel. Why: Laypeople need more than sound reasoning to be persuaded.
- [pitfall] Telling a suspect falsely that a co-suspect has confessed can produce accusations that are worthless, and the final record may omit the trick.

## sealed and physical evidence handling
- [mechanism] A room can look sealed from outside while one latch or window is left so the culprit has a route out.
- [mechanism] Handling a soft object can restore its original shape, so creases and indentations that carried the record disappear. Why: soft materials spring back and fill the marks left by a record.
- [rule] Restrict a sealed key item to one named recipient or NPC, so opening it requires finding that person; withhold critical facts until a chosen story point. When: designing a restricted sealed item or a critical fact withheld in a story. Why: restricted access controls when information reaches the audience; a single gatekeeper creates a clear, meaningful goal.
- [rule] Seal sensitive evidence and entrust it to a trusted custodian with a fixed opening time, so opponents cannot learn its contents early. When: disclosure could endanger people or alert a suspect. Why: early disclosure would let enemies act first.
- [rule] Track which NPCs handled each item, since a cleared handling record hints at deliberate cleanup, which is a clue in itself. When: designing object histories for NPCs. Why: Missing handling data is itself evidence of concealment.
- [rule] State the release condition for a sealed document plainly so the eventual reveal feels earned rather than arbitrary. When: when a sealed or withheld document gates a reveal. Why: An unstated or unclear condition makes the reveal feel arbitrary.
- [rule] Store sealed, blind-labelled evidence so the player can compare results later without bias. When: Designing evidence checks in a case.
- [rule] Secure empty containers before routine handling or shipping removes them, since they may hold key evidence.
- [heuristic] Prefer bare physical features such as scars, ear shape or facial features over beards, glasses or clothing, since disguises rarely alter them. When: when judging an identification by sight in good light. Why: disguises rarely reproduce or alter the underlying features.
- [heuristic] Re-test a sealed flap after a delay; a seal that opens at once, without sticking or tearing, suggests the letter was handled. When: a document's contents matter and others can reach it. Why: properly sealed gum should hold firm when pressed later.
- [heuristic] A seal impression's shape can point to a specific object, since few common objects share an unusual outline. Why: Distinctive outlines narrow identification.
- [heuristic] Track who holds each key and each handover, since custody determines who could have entered a sealed room. When: An event happens in a room sealed from outside or access depends on one key. Why: Custody history shows who could have entered and when.
- [procedure] 1) Seal the found item in protective material, handing it over unopened if its authenticity may matter later. 2) Mark it with a personal identifier. 3) File it with related documents under a clear label. When: An investigator finds physical evidence and wants to keep it usable. Why: Securing and labelling evidence keeps it usable for later reasoning. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Write a letter naming the suspect, the knowledge source and what the recipient should do. 2) Seal it with a fixed release time unless you return first to cancel. 3) Deliver it and obtain written acknowledgment. 4) Keep the acknowledgment and put your papers in order. When: before confronting a dangerous person alone. Why: Evidence still reaches others if the investigator is harmed.
- [procedure] 1) Record each clue where and how it was found. 2) Keep related finds together. 3) Check the area for further clues before moving any item on. Why: keeps the context of each find intact.
- [procedure] 1) Issue a written instruction for access. 2) Bring the required tradesman. 3) Enter together with witnesses. 4) Record the state of the room before removal. 5) Seal and transport removed objects. When: when evidence integrity may be challenged later. Why: Witnessed, documented access prevents any one person from being accused of private alteration.
- [tradeoff] Sealed evidence prevents leaks but cannot be checked before its deadline, so it risks dismissal or acceptance on faith alone.
- [tradeoff] Holding evidence private until the decisive person has read it lets that person choose, but delays public action. When: Evidence affects a person who must decide how it is used. Why: Early exposure can preempt the decision of the rightful party.
- [pitfall] Absence of tracks is weak evidence no one passed: hard surfaces and short grass hold few marks, so an empty search may have mundane causes. When: checking whether a person took a route or came to a place. Why: hard surfaces hold few marks.
- [pitfall] A sealed-looking scene can hide a path that the witness account does not reveal.
- [pitfall] A trace reads as a clock only if undisturbed; if it was handled or replaced, the reading reflects the handling, not the time.
- [pitfall] Handling an item before it is photographed and recorded contaminates it and can make its traces unusable as evidence.
- [pitfall] Using force on delicate evidence can destroy clues; handle fragile items gently.
- [fact] Hard surfaces such as gravel leave no prints, so the route across them must be inferred from indirect traces. When: a route passes over unmarkable ground. Why: only soft ground records impressions.

## signature clues
- [definition] A signature is a distinctive mark or token repeated at each incident or communication, identifying one author across separate events that look unrelated when judged alone.
- [definition] A deliberate mark left at a scene is a signature: a message that says who acted and why, meant to be read by others. When: A culprit wants to send a message, claim a grievance or identify a group. Why: Marks carry intent beyond the act itself.
- [definition] Signature analysis treats a deliberate act as an expression of the doer's temperament, so a familiar analyst can infer the actor from the act's style. When: When a crime shows a distinctive, planned style and candidates are known. Why: Planned acts reflect personal habits and character.
- [mechanism] A timekeeper that sounds at a fixed interval and halts activity each time builds tension toward the final stroke, because the same pause keeps recurring. When: A recurring sound marks time during an event. Why: A steady rhythm makes the expected moment feel closer with each repetition.
- [mechanism] A recurring in-game cue such as a song or gesture can be a signal; players who trigger it themselves can trace the contact on the other end. When: Designing hidden communication in games. Why: Mirroring the cue exposes the receiving party.
- [mechanism] A recurring event at a similar time each night lets observers learn its pattern and predict when a threat will return. When: an event repeats on a regular schedule. Why: Repetition gives observers a pattern they can anticipate and track.
- [behavior] Players read a sign repeated at a second scene as a deliberate signature, which strengthens a false pattern built from it. When: a clue reappears at a later crime scene. Why: repetition suggests a pattern.
- [rule] Give a recurring thief a signature method, such as a calling card or entry style, that the player learns to recognize across several crimes. When: Designing a recurring antagonist. Why: Recognizable habits let players predict the culprit.
- [rule] Give each location a signature debris set, such as sawdust in a workshop or pile fibres in a carpeted room, so the player can match residue to rooms.
- [heuristic] Treat a deliberate signature as a mindset clue, not confession or proof of literacy or guilt; compare it with a known sample, since it can mislead. When: interpreting a deliberate act left at a crime scene. Why: deliberate acts reflect intent but can be used to mislead. (x2)
- [heuristic] A recurring private phrase that an NPC repeats can signal its weakening mental state when it shifts toward self-accusation. When: Designing NPCs whose psychological state changes over time. Why: Changes in a repeated phrase make inner tension readable.
- [heuristic] A figure who appears at several points in the same events can be a witness, a rival, or a coincidence. Keep that reading open rather than fixing on one early. When: A figure appears at two or more points where each appearance could be innocent or purposeful. Why: Early fixation on one reading can mislead, and several appearances are not yet evidence of a single purpose.
- [heuristic] Repeat a location name or warning across scenes and pay it off with a concrete event later, since repetition without consequence loses force. When: Using motifs to build foreboding. Why: Each recurrence gains weight only when it connects to a new event.
- [heuristic] A known thief's signature technique can recur across a game world, and a found clue such as an old journal or newspaper can tie it to a present crime. When: designing a mystery world with repeat offenders.
- [heuristic] Familiar misdirection tricks recur in different cases, so a known pattern can be recognized from its outline. Why: Methods are reused because they have worked before.
- [heuristic] Track a phrase that repeats across a document even when its meaning is unclear, because repetition marks it as significant and later evidence must explain it. When: a recurring fragment could be a code, location or timing cue. Why: repeated wording signals intent even before its sense is known.
- [heuristic] Before calling a witness's statement contradictory, check whether the wording refers to a recurring service or routine rather than the specific day in question. When: a statement conflicts with a fixed fact and its wording admits two referents. Why: routine references renew daily, so they can point to a different occurrence.
- [heuristic] Use a crime's signature when material evidence is ambiguous or has an innocent explanation, and test the suspect's guilt against the psychology the crime shows. When: material evidence is ambiguous.
- [heuristic] A reused signature can predict the next act, so an investigator can anticipate where the author will strike. When: A signature recurs across more than one act.
- [tradeoff] Physical clues can be manufactured, so a behavioral signature can test them; but the signature is itself interpretive and can be as subjective as intuition. When: when physical evidence is in dispute.
- [pitfall] A signature list shows who was willing to sign, not who agreed with the content, so counting names alone can overstate consensus.
- [fact] Copying a signature is easier than copying a full handwritten text, so a long hand-written passage is harder to forge convincingly. When: Assessing whether a handwritten document is authentic. Why: A signature is short and can be practised, while a whole text reveals many habitual letter forms.
- [fact] A message signed with a name shows only that someone sent it under that name, not who the real sender is.
- [fact] Multiple signers can confirm what was seen, but they do not confirm what caused it.

## verifying physical evidence
- [definition] Some documents are valid only when witnesses see the signer write and sign in the signer's presence and in each other's presence. These formalities are themselves evidence. When: a plot turns on whether a document was validly made. Why: Witnesses who followed the formalities can later testify to them.
- [mechanism] Let players message an off-screen NPC and wait for a reply, so verification takes time and cannot be instant. When: when designing delayed clue checks. Why: Delay makes verification a deliberate act.
- [rule] Do not act on a reading of a partial clue or on a theory until independent facts or a confirming answer verify it. Why: a misheard fragment can mislead.
- [rule] Check a detail recovered through anchored questioning against another source before relying on it. When: When recovered memory is used as evidence. Why: Recall assisted by prompts can carry the questioner's assumptions.
- [rule] Keep a backup observer or written record ready, and bring in replacement observers when the first ones leave during an event. When: A witness may faint or flee during the event. Why: A lost witness otherwise leaves the event unrecorded.
- [rule] Design evidence objects the culprit may try to remove, so an earlier confession or recording can serve as backup proof. When: Physical evidence is at risk of removal. Why: A second record preserves the case if the object disappears.
- [rule] Do not enter a guarded room to check again when a second check would expose you; stay concealed and keep watching. When: A hidden observer is already in position and gathering information. Why: Re-entering a room gives watchers a chance to notice and identify you.
- [rule] Before trusting the apparent time of a voice or sound, ask what could have produced it and whether a device could have played it. When: a time is established by a sound. Why: the sound may not come from a living speaker at that moment.
- [rule] Do not treat a back view or distant glimpse as a positive identification.
- [rule] Verify the layout and physical facts of a place before using them to test a witness, because the method depends on the interviewer knowing the facts. When: Preparing to test a witness's account against a location or object. Why: Checking against wrong facts produces false contradictions.
- [rule] Have a second officer ready to step in when a confronted suspect may attack, and do not provoke a volatile suspect without officers ready.
- [rule] Reproduce a physical trace before drawing a conclusion from it, rather than trusting how the trace looks or what you recall.
- [heuristic] Confirm an item's history by questioning related people without revealing suspicion, so the person does not adjust their account.
- [heuristic] When a primary witness cannot help, keep another route to the same information open, such as a family contact who can provide it. When: A witness's recall is unavailable. Why: A second route preserves progress when the first fails.
- [heuristic] A statement gains weight when respected, named signers are willing to swear to it. When: judging the reliability of a testimony. Why: sworn backing by credible people raises trust.
- [heuristic] Guard shift rosters or access logs can show which character was absent at a critical moment, revealing who could have acted. Why: Attendance data constrains who was present when an event happened.
- [heuristic] Let a test verify a hidden mechanism before it is revealed, so the reveal rests on evidence the player has already seen work. When: Designing a proof step in a mystery that depends on an unusual cause. Why: Demonstrated evidence makes an unusual explanation credible rather than arbitrary.
- [heuristic] Test the evidence itself, not only the suspect, so that trust in the object becomes the lock the story turns on. When: Structuring a mystery whose key clue looks conclusive. Why: Challenging the object exposes flaws the suspect's guilt would otherwise hide.
- [procedure] 1) Make an inference from a physical trace. 2) Check it against a second independent trace. 3) Date the mark with weather or witness timing. 4) Trust it only if it survives both checks. When: Reading marks left at a scene. Why: Single estimates are rules of thumb that can fail.
- [procedure] 1) Note each witness's account of timing and state of the scene. 2) Compare each claim against physical evidence such as doors, windows and marks. 3) Flag claims that the evidence contradicts. When: Several accounts describe one scene. Why: Physical evidence is harder to shade than testimony.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain a verified sample of the suspect's hand. 2) Compare the disputed writing with it. 3) Check whether the claimed action was physically possible. 4) Compare stated figures with physical evidence. When: Testing a planted note or staged scene. Why: Independent samples and physical limits expose staging.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the link a trace suggests. 2) Measure that link against the scene's heights and distances. 3) Accept it only if it fits the geometry.
- [procedure] 1) Record the stated location of hidden goods. 2) Check whether the location is concrete enough to follow. 3) Verify by finding the goods, since a confessor's location may be false or changed. When: A suspect names where stolen goods were concealed. Why: A stated location is a lead, but it must be verified before it is trusted.
- [procedure] 1) Run an untreated control sample alongside the suspect samples. 2) Include a known-positive comparison. 3) Show sensitivity on a tiny divided sample before relying on the test. 4) Seal and label samples blind to their source; a separate person keeps the name list. 5) Test one sample at a time, reading each result before the next. When: A yes-or-no test result will decide a suspect's fate.

## witness reliability and testimony
- [mechanism] A sharp shift in a writer's tone between two statements, from mild concern to accusation, signals that something happened in between that the writer may not describe.
- [mechanism] A character who repeatedly admits earlier statements were false teaches the audience to distrust the next version, so each new account needs checking against evidence. When: a deceptive character gives several accounts in sequence. Why: each retraction shows that stories can be false, which lowers trust in later claims.
- [behavior] When a claim is restated in a form that exposes its weakness, listeners often draw the damaging conclusion themselves rather than accepting it from the speaker. When: When trying to undermine a theory without direct argument. Why: Self-drawn conclusions feel more credible than conclusions handed over.
- [heuristic] Secondhand reports carry the uncertainty of their origin; treat them as leads pointing toward a danger, not proof, and verify before acting. When: When information comes through a relayed or second-hand source. Why: Relayed accounts can be incomplete, altered, or retracted by the original speaker; reconstruction is only as reliable as its sources.
- [heuristic] When a central inference rests on one witness whose evidence is doubtful, treat the case as only as strong as its weakest link. When: When assessing a case built on few witnesses. Why: Partial support from other witnesses does not replace full corroboration.
- [heuristic] Specific personal detail anchored to a witness's own movements or family events gives a statement more weight than general impressions. When: When comparing the detail of several witness accounts. Why: Specific, checkable detail is harder to invent than vague impression.
- [heuristic] Short, identical, unembellished answers can signal a rehearsed or guarded witness. When: Assessing a witness's reliability from the form of their replies. Why: Rehearsal and guardedness reduce spontaneous detail.
- [heuristic] When two sources disagree about one person, weigh each source's familiarity with that person and interest in how they are seen before accepting either account. When: Two witnesses give conflicting accounts of the same individual. Why: Familiarity and self-interest shape what a witness says.
- [heuristic] Trace a story that has passed through several people back to its original source before accepting its time, place, and witness.
- [heuristic] Repeat an identification test with the sample order changed, and require consistent correct matches, since one correct answer may be luck. When: When a single correct identification could be a lucky guess. Why: Changing the order prevents a repeated pattern from reproducing a correct answer by chance.
- [heuristic] Store a witness's observations separately from their beliefs so the player must decide which parts to trust. When: When designing an NPC who gives both facts and interpretations. Why: Separation makes the player evaluate evidence rather than accept or reject the whole account.
- [heuristic] Ask what conditions produced both reports rather than who is lying when two credible witnesses contradict each other. When: Two credible accounts flatly conflict and no direct evidence exists. Why: Shifting the question to conditions can reveal that both witnesses were sincere.
- [heuristic] Use a second witness's testimony to confirm an identity that the first witness could not see clearly, so the reveal rests on two accounts. When: Confirming a disguised identity late in a mystery. Why: Two independent accounts make the identity credible.
- [procedure] 1) Record testimony without interrupting, letting the witness describe impressions freely. 2) Ask for concrete detail. 3) Separate reported incidents from sensations or feelings. 4) Interpret only after the record is complete, and verify only the perceived parts. When: Taking a witness statement that mixes events, sensation, and interpretation. Why: Interrupting or interpreting early blurs fact with feeling, and feelings such as enchantment or being watched cannot be checked directly.
- [procedure] 1) Separate what the witness saw and heard from what the witness concludes. 2) Offer a natural explanation for each perception. 3) Test the supernatural claim against the ordinary explanation. 4) Ask for checkable details before accepting the conclusion. When: A distressed witness claims a supernatural cause without checkable evidence. Why: Separating perception from inference shows which parts of the account can be tested.
- [pitfall] Repetition across many people, or stacking many testimonies, makes a story feel more reliable even though repetition adds no evidence and weak accounts stay weak. When: When a case relies on many witness accounts of varying strength or a story is retold through many people. Why: Familiarity from retelling and sheer volume of accounts are mistaken for confirmation. (x2)
- [pitfall] Sincere and tactical emotion or helpfulness look alike, so trusting apparent sincerity can end questioning too early; judge by checkable inconsistencies with routine or facts. When: Judging whether a suspect's or NPC's distress, surprise, or helpfulness is genuine, including when an NPC may conceal involvement. Why: Strong emotion can be real or used to close off questioning, and visible sincerity is easy to mistake for innocence.
- [pitfall] A timeline built on one witness's times may be entirely that witness's invention. When: Relying on a single source for times. Why: Without independent confirmation, the sequence rests on one account.
- [pitfall] Trusting an account from a source who has a stake in how the subject is seen can distort the picture of that subject. When: A witness benefits from a particular portrayal of someone. Why: Interest pushes testimony toward the witness's purposes.
- [pitfall] A teller losing control may repeat real facts in the wrong order, so comparing sequence as well as content can expose them. When: A suspect's retelling becomes disorganized or rushed. Why: Real memories keep their original order even when the teller loses control of the narrative.
- [pitfall] When a witness repeats another person's words, their own opinion can filter what is passed on. When: when a witness relays what someone else said. Why: Repeated speech carries the reporter's interpretation, which can distort it.
- [pitfall] Accepting a secondhand report as if the object were directly inspected invites error and should be verified. When: Judging an identity claim based on a published account. Why: Reports can misstate details that an examiner would catch on inspection.
- [pitfall] Two witnesses who seem independent may have heard the same false source, so their agreement becomes the trap rather than proof.
- [fact] Events inside a sealed space may have only one witness, the person who was inside, so no eyewitness can check their account.

## npc motive design
- [rule] Leave an NPC's motive real but partly open, so players must test it against evidence and decide how far to trust what the NPC says. When: designing a suspect NPC or writing NPC dialogue with uncertain reliability. Why: A testable motive keeps the investigation open, and partial ambiguity makes trust a player decision rather than a given. (x2)
- [rule] Give two or three suspect NPCs stated motives such as debt, rivalry or inheritance, so the player can rank suspects and check each before accusing. When: designing a mystery with several possible culprits. Why: A ranked suspect list gives the player a starting point, and several plausible motives keep the solution open.
- [rule] Give NPCs motives such as rivalry or family ties that shape their reports and interrogation choices, so hostile accounts visibly differ from neutral ones. When: designing NPC investigators or NPC testimony. Why: Visible bias lets the player learn to discount it.
- [rule] Give an NPC a stated reason and a hidden agenda; let hesitation, evasion, slips, or a cost or quantity mismatch with the stated reason reveal the agenda. When: designing a character with secret motives. Why: Players discover the agenda through play rather than being told, and reward reading small tells.
- [rule] Give NPCs explicit incentives such as debt, pledge or forfeiture, so players can judge whether a witness is self-serving. When: designing NPC witnesses. Why: Visible stakes let players weigh bias.
- [rule] When an NPC reports another character's motives, write the claim so it can be wrong, and let physical evidence confirm or refute it. When: when an NPC explains someone else's reasons. Why: motives are inferences, so the player needs an external check.
- [rule] Give an NPC a changed decision as a motive, paired with an emotional and a material explanation, so the player must weigh both.
- [rule] Tie NPC motives to status and reputation, revealed through dialogue, gifts and gossip rather than through a stated goal. When: designing NPC goals. Why: players piece motives together from behavior.
- [rule] Build a motive board for each NPC listing what each gains from a crime, and seed at least one conflicting statement per suspect. When: designing NPCs for a murder or theft mystery. Why: each suspect then has a reason to act and a testable inconsistency.
- [rule] Tag NPCs with motives such as pride, debt or ambition, so their offers and threats read as motivated rather than arbitrary. When: designing NPC dialogue and behaviour. Why: visible motives make actions legible.
- [rule] List what each NPC gains from a frame or setup; when one gain matches an earlier quarrel, flag it as a lead for the player. When: designing accusations or frames in a story. Why: matching gains and history give players a traceable lead.
- [rule] Tie an NPC's odd behavior or missed appointments to a pending inheritance case, so the player can trace the cause through records. When: designing NPC behavior in a mystery.
- [rule] Track an NPC's motives as a list that can change and grow as the story escalates, such as notoriety followed by fear of consequences.
- [heuristic] Make debt ledgers and inheritance documents discoverable through conversation or records, so players can cite debts, deadlines and inheritances as motives pointing to specific NPCs. When: Designing NPC motives in a narrative game. Why: Visible financial stakes let players build cases from in-world facts. (x2)
- [heuristic] Profit is not the sole possible reason for murder, so each motive category must be tested against evidence rather than assumed.
- [heuristic] Let different NPCs accept or refuse the same bribe, so players learn what each NPC values.
- [heuristic] Seed each motive line with a different NPC so the player's questions lead to separate characters. When: designing a multi-motive mystery.
- [heuristic] Let a final reveal reframe an NPC's motives and attach a choice that rewards mercy or the withholding of punishment.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs backstories that supply motive, and let players uncover them through informants who disagree with each other or have a stake.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC a motive to conceal, so the player must find the reason before the testimony becomes usable.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC's stated fear become a quest hook whose outcome depends on the player's choices. When: Designing a quest triggered by an NPC's worry. Why: A fear the player can act on gives the quest personal stakes.
- [heuristic] Give each non-player character a motive from the categories so the cast includes at least one gain-based and one prevention-based suspect. When: Populating a mystery with suspects. Why: A mixed cast keeps the player's suspicion divided between different kinds of motive.
- [pitfall] A helper whose motives are hidden so thoroughly that their choices seem arbitrary loses credibility. When: Writing an ally who offers help during a pursuit. Why: Players need enough information to interpret an ally's actions.

## public record and publication
- [mechanism] Actions logged in open registries leave readable traces, so an unexpected access can expose a party trying to stay hidden. When: A suspect's action is formally recorded and the record is accessible to others. Why: Anyone able to read the log can connect the access to its source.
- [mechanism] A published physical description of a missing person works as a search tool and turns attention toward that person as a potential witness. When: When a missing person's features are circulated publicly. Why: Public recognition makes the described person a source of information about events.
- [mechanism] Public records created by a culprit, such as anonymous letters or notices, can steer investigators toward a false suspect. When: the culprit has a motive to mislead.
- [mechanism] A false public account carved into monuments, tombs, and tours can outlast the people who knew the facts, keeping the concealed truth buried. When: A group has covered up a crime that is memorialised. Why: Lasting public markers repeat the story without witnesses.
