- [mechanism] A published account of a dramatic case can become a template that later communities copy in their own accusations. When: When a vivid case is printed and widely read. Why: Readers learn the pattern of events and reproduce it.
- [rule] Keep a witness's name and travel out of the public record unless needed, since unnecessary exposure can alert the suspect. When: Information must be presented in an open inquiry. Why: Public disclosure can reach the person being investigated.
- [rule] Keep public information limited. Do not reveal that a solution may lie close to one household or announce key missing evidence. When: An investigation is still open and a suspect pool is narrowing. Why: Public disclosure can alert the culprit and compromise the inquiry.
- [rule] A timed-effect system such as poison, a fuse or a delayed trap should publish exact delay values so players can verify a clue chain.
- [rule] Give in-game courts or councils readable records, so that a rival's protection of a suspect can later be turned into a charge.
- [heuristic] A published account of a past event can serve as a dossier, read by the examiner and used to question the claimant about it directly.
- [heuristic] Test whether a reported event is plausible by asking whether it would be widely known. A famous victim's death would reach national news, so its absence is evidence. When: judging whether a reported serious event actually happened. Why: large events leave a public record.
- [heuristic] Use an official, public setting such as an inquest to force a revelation into a dramatic moment. When: A reveal should happen in front of many people. Why: Public settings raise the stakes of an answer.
- [heuristic] A building's public opening time marks the first moment its exits could be freely used, but it does not show who used them. When: Exit timing is being checked against the crime. Why: Public access makes escape possible for anyone, not only the actor.
- [heuristic] Place each document's publication date against the events, since timing shows what its author could know and say at the time.
- [heuristic] Let the game's official record or town verdict sometimes differ from what the player has deduced, so the player's knowledge drives the next action.
- [heuristic] Let a false story gain institutional force, such as a newspaper report, so the wrong target bears real cost even though the blame is never proven. Why: Consequences attach to the accused regardless of proof.
- [procedure] 1) Enter each timed entry from a public record on its own line. 2) Mark gaps and overlaps between entries. 3) Check absences, such as a missed visit or an unanswered call, against the other entries. When: A case depends on where people were at given times.
- [tradeoff] Publicly exposing evidence can establish justice but can also harm innocent people, so disclosure must weigh the cost to bystanders. When: Deciding whether to publish sensitive evidence. Why: Public exposure reaches people who had no part in the crime.
- [pitfall] A public notice or published discovery can alert its target, since anyone watching the channel or buying the paper sees it. When: Communicating through a channel the target watches; a discovery is reported in a public paper. Why: Anyone who checks the channel or buys the paper will see it, including the target.
- [pitfall] Records that anyone can read may be consulted by the person being traced, so the trail can be disturbed. When: when a trace relies on an open record. Why: Open records give the subject a chance to alter or conceal their trail.
- [pitfall] A published agreement between two authors does not prove they agreed; they may hold different private views. When: Relatives or partners publish together. Why: Joint publication can mask disagreement.
- [fact] Public reports can differ from what happened in the room, so audiences may hold incomplete or distorted facts.
- [fact] A written account can serve to silence dissent, not only to record events, so later readers must untangle its agenda.

## retraction and reversal
- [mechanism] A later retraction by an accuser can undermine their earlier testimony, and later retractions or depositions can crack earlier verdicts that relied on false testimony. When: a witness recants after a verdict, or a later deposition contradicts the testimony a verdict relied on. Why: The retraction revises the reliability of prior statements, and the verdict relied on testimony later shown to be false.
- [mechanism] A reversal works when audience and narrator expect one suspect and the investigator's suspicion shifts to another, turning the story.
- [mechanism] A retraction can lower a tracked suspicion value, while a late confession can open a new line of inquiry. When: When a character withdraws or confesses to an earlier claim. Why: Suspicion state and quest threads respond to changed testimony.
- [mechanism] A retracted accusation can shift the player's attention to a different suspect, so one correction opens a new suspicion thread. When: a minor character withdraws a false accusation.
- [behavior] After a key reveal, players reread and reinterpret earlier scenes, so details that seemed minor gain new meaning as evidence. When: a new idea or discovery changes the context of earlier scenes. Why: Revised understanding reframes previously ignored details as relevant evidence, which rewards attention to them.
- [behavior] A witness who sees the person threatening them may deny earlier admissions, claim to be misunderstood, or say they do not know. When: the intimidating person is present during questioning. Why: Fear of the threat overrides the earlier statement.
- [behavior] Once a late reveal explains a character's earlier conduct, players reinterpret that conduct as planned rather than suspicious.
- [behavior] Revealing a hidden motive can reshape a mystery without resolving it, leaving other open questions for the investigators. When: a motive is disclosed mid-investigation. Why: One answer does not explain every unexplained element.
- [behavior] Revealing a hidden danger can reinterpret the earlier conduct of anyone exposed to it, making innocent-looking actions look significant. When: A hidden cause is discovered after events have been explained. Why: New evidence changes the meaning of past behaviour.
- [behavior] People who lived through a belief-driven prosecution can later question and reject the principles they once accepted. When: After the prosecution has ended and the person reflects on it. Why: Reflection on the process can expose its flaws.
- [rule] Keep retracted or dismissed statements as valid clues: they can still contain real information and read differently once the retraction and truth are known. When: a character admits an earlier lie, or an accusation is withdrawn or proven wrong. Why: Withdrawn claims may still point to the truth, and the reinterpretation makes earlier testimony meaningful on re-reading.
- [rule] A confession mechanic should let a suspect retract, and the game should record the retraction as a new clue.
- [rule] Revise a deduction when another physical test contradicts it rather than forcing the evidence to fit. When: Two physical tests give conflicting conclusions about a person. Why: Forcing a fit hides the error and leads to wrong conclusions.
- [heuristic] Revise an early judgement after watching more behaviour, and let the revision rest on what was observed rather than on the original assumption. When: New behaviour contradicts a first impression. Why: Observed conduct is better evidence than assumptions formed before watching.
- [heuristic] Name a false marker as false when correcting it, so the audience trusts the author more than if the correction were quietly dropped.
- [heuristic] Let a wrong suspicion hold for a stretch, then correct it through a minor character's retraction to reset the player's trust without a full reveal. Why: A retraction reopens the question while the main secret stays hidden.
- [tradeoff] Reversing a belief to its opposite is useful for testing but can also be wrong, so the reversed hypothesis must be checked like any other. When: Applying a reversal test to a plausible account. Why: The opposite of a false belief is not automatically true.
- [pitfall] Repeating the same kind of reversal too often makes audiences or players expect it, so it becomes predictable and loses its effect.
- [pitfall] A witness who changes story may be reinterpreted to fit the accusation instead of being doubted.
- [pitfall] A clause that retracts an earlier claim does not undo the impression the first clause made on the reader. When: Hedged sentences that later qualify a claim. Why: Readers form first impressions and keep them.
- [pitfall] A false confession that is detailed and falsifiable collapses when a physical fact contradicts it, not when a rival suspect appears. When: writing a suspect who confesses falsely. Why: Physical evidence exposes a lie more convincingly than another character's accusation.
- [pitfall] A confession that is retracted in a later beat can be used as a plot turn, but only if the retraction is staged as a separate event after the confession. When: Writing a confession scene that the story must later reverse. Why: Collapsing confession and retraction into one moment leaves the player with no reason to doubt the first statement.
- [fact] A good-faith accusation can name the true culprit by accident and still be withdrawn once its inconsistency is pointed out. When: a character accuses someone and then backs away. Why: Retraction does not make the accusation false.

## selective reporting
- [mechanism] A guarded witness often opens up after the investigator shares something real first, so a partial disclosure invites the other person to reciprocate. When: A witness holds information back and has a reason to guard it. Why: Reciprocity builds trust and makes the witness feel the exchange is fair.
- [mechanism] A quest journal or rumour system presenting accurate but selective information rewards players who compare sources.
- [behavior] A character who knows the full story may omit damaging or decisive parts when retelling it, so the listener hears a partial version that seems whole. When: A detailed account seems full but hides a critical fact. (x2)
- [behavior] A weak witness may respond to only one particular questioner, which limits who can effectively extract testimony. When: Several people try to question a distressed or confused witness.
- [behavior] A witness may notice one striking detail while missing a plainly visible object nearby, so an omission is weak evidence.
- [behavior] A side dispute with no bearing on the main problem can absorb attention so fully that the investigator loses interest in the central question. When: a vivid side quarrel runs alongside the main inquiry. Why: the immediate side issue pulls focus away.
- [behavior] A character who feels safe may later volunteer what they concealed, without being pressed. When: when trust has been built through patience. Why: low pressure lowers the cost of honesty.
- [behavior] A witness who answers a casual question readily may still omit a detail that emerges only under gentle follow-up.
- [behavior] Attention is selective. A fact in full view often goes unnoticed until the frame of inquiry changes and the observer looks at it differently. When: Repeatedly reviewing evidence without finding a solution. Why: A fixed frame filters out facts that do not fit it.
- [behavior] A suspect may offer identity details to seem open while refusing to explain their conduct; openness about facts is not openness about motive.
- [behavior] A culprit who keeps some records but removes others leaves a selective trail that reveals their habits. When: An offender manages receipts or documents. Why: Choosing which records to keep is itself a habit.
- [behavior] Press reports that credit the wrong party for an action can mislead readers about who acted, while the true actor keeps the substance of the gain. When: a public account of a resolved event is printed. Why: Readers trust the printed version, so the misattribution persists and shapes their view of the outcome.
- [rule] Compare an accuser's quotation of a witness with that witness's full dialogue to find any distortion. When: A witness is quoted in an accusation.
- [rule] Let NPC announcements state only true facts while hiding the key ones, so players must work out what was left out. When: when designing NPC public statements.
- [rule] Do not infer bad faith from a selective excerpt alone; test each claim against specific evidence first.
- [heuristic] Ordinary theft takes everything of value, so a selective pattern of removal points to a specific, rule-bound motive. When: when loss follows a consistent pattern.
- [heuristic] A reputation or trust meter can drop when the player withholds findings from a quest-giver. When: When a quest-giver expects shared findings. Why: Withholding information damages the relationship with the one who expects it.
- [heuristic] Assume each character holds something in reserve; no one tells everything, so evasions and gaps are worth reading.
- [procedure] Reveal one finding at a time to a suspect, watch whose reaction it unsettles, and use that reaction to choose the next question.
- [pitfall] Choosing which true facts or readings to present can steer conclusions wrong, making a weak case or ambiguous clue look conclusive by hiding the omitted facts or reverse reading. When: Summarizing for a decision-maker, or presenting or evaluating a case or clue in a persuasive context. Why: Omission shapes the decision as much as falsehood; omission can make a weak link look strong, and ignoring the reverse reading hides the ambiguity. (x2)
- [pitfall] Quoting only part of a source, such as a single line or its cautionary qualifier, can reverse what readers believe the source says. When: Summarizing a source or citing a single line from it. Why: Dropping the qualifiers reverses the impression.
- [pitfall] Selectively reading symptoms or matching precedent features tends to validate the hypothesis favored before evidence accumulated, so readers of one precedent can reach different suspects. When: Interpreting symptoms or matching evidence to a precedent. Why: Each reader emphasises the matches that suit their preferred answer.
- [fact] When one party selects all members of a council, those members owe their seats to the selector, so loyalty shapes their votes. When: a body's members were appointed rather than independently chosen.

## witness interview sequencing
- [mechanism] A test can reveal a different substance from the one suspected, and that single result can redirect the whole investigation.
- [rule] Require a sequence of approaches, such as flattery then payment, before an NPC reveals a simple fact. When: designing NPC dialogue gates.
- [rule] Hold back a sensitive question until the suspect has revealed the relationship that makes it relevant.
- [rule] When one witness's meeting is emotionally heavy, schedule it so that witness is not left upset and then sent away immediately afterwards. When: Multiple witnesses are seen in a fixed order. Why: Order can protect a distressed witness from a harsh exit.
- [rule] Test a witness's sight line before relying on a reconstruction built from it.
- [rule] Pass sensitive material through a trusted person in a sealed note rather than an ordinary messenger. When: when information must stay secret across a team.
- [rule] Run fingerprint checks only after trace analysis, so that handling for prints cannot disturb the trace. When: Trace evidence and prints are both needed. Why: Print handling can disturb or contaminate the trace.
- [heuristic] Test the most obvious motive against the evidence before accepting it; valuables left untouched argue against robbery as the real purpose. When: When a crime scene suggests theft but the evidence does not fit it. Why: A wrong motive sends each later inference in the wrong direction.
- [heuristic] Test an alibi against timed evidence before trusting a theory, because a plausible theory can collapse once the timed evidence is laid out. When: a tidy theory is forming. Why: timelines expose impossibilities that theories hide.
- [heuristic] Delay sensitive findings from people who are not yet ready to hear them, especially when the news may hurt them. When: a finding may distress those affected.
- [heuristic] Start with an easy-to-check fact that narrows the field, rather than the hardest fact, which can waste time before progress is made. When: When several facts remain to be tested. Why: Early narrowing reduces the cost of later checks.
- [heuristic] Test a single anomaly against the other facts before acting on it; resolve to check it first rather than concluding at once. When: a lone fact contradicts an otherwise strong case.
- [heuristic] Test each compartment of a container separately, since scent can concentrate in one small space while the rest is clean.
- [heuristic] When a setting seems too ordinary for the threat described, test the surface with further inquiry rather than accepting the impression. When: the setting contradicts what the investigator was told to expect. Why: a mismatch between expectation and appearance is a warning sign.
- [heuristic] A light teasing remark that touches a sensitive point tends to fail and can damage rapport. When: when a companion has a hidden weakness. Why: the remark exposes what the other person is protecting.
- [heuristic] Ask follow-up questions in an order where each answer points to the next place or person to check. Why: each answer narrows the possibilities.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the time and surroundings of the witness. 2) Walk through events in order, one fact per question. 3) Check what the witness could physically see. 4) Test indirect observation such as reflections. 5) Confirm the end state of objects and doors. 6) Ask whether the witness may have dozed during any gap. When: A witness describes a sequence of actions and her vantage must be judged. Why: A fixed order exposes gaps and tests whether the account fits the physical setup.
- [procedure] 1) Interview witnesses one at a time in a set order, such as by rank. 2) Compare each short report with the others. 3) Check each informal claim against known facts. When: When several witnesses share a household. Why: Patterns and contradictions appear only when reports are compared.
- [procedure] 1) State the known sequence of events one step at a time. 2) Ask the witness to confirm or correct each step. 3) Record confirmed steps as facts and corrections as what the witness knew. When: interviewing a witness who has partial knowledge. Why: Confirmations lock in facts, and corrections reveal the witness's actual knowledge.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a general question about a witness's whereabouts. 2) Narrow it to a time window. 3) Narrow it again to specific places. Each answer sharpens the next question. When: Interviewing a witness about a timed event. Why: Narrowing in steps prevents the witness from answering with vague generalities.
- [procedure] 1) Fix a starting moment, such as when people woke. 2) Walk forward through the day in order. 3) Press vague intervals for a concrete time or last occurrence. 4) Record each person's movements. 5) Mark where accounts disagree for later checking. When: When several people moved through the same space over a day. Why: A sequenced account exposes inconsistencies that a bare timeline hides.
- [procedure] 1) Demand the full account at the outset. 2) Ask about one step at a time: who acted, what was done, in what order, and why. 3) Test each link against facts already held. 4) Get partial admissions on record. 5) Use each admission to check later denials. When: when a suspect's account depends on a chain of decisions. Why: each link can be checked, so weak links surface.
- [procedure] 1) Begin with low-stakes witnesses who give partial testimony. 2) Question the household member whose answers matter most. 3) Question the central suspect. 4) Hold a decisive witness for last. 5) End on an unresolved question. When: Structuring an inquiry where several witnesses each shift the picture. Why: Ordering witnesses by rising stakes builds pressure and makes each answer more consequential.

## anonymous tips and notes
- [definition] An unsigned letter reveals things about its writer through handwriting, wording and knowledge of the subject, but these clues describe the writer and do not prove the letter's claims.
- [mechanism] Discovering a private letter can expose a secret that triggers family conflict and drives the plot forward.
- [behavior] An unsigned accusation plants doubt rather than proof, and the doubt persists after the message is destroyed. When: a recipient receives an anonymous accusation about a trusted person. Why: Suspicion outlasts the paper it was written on.
- [behavior] People who want to be unknown tend to choose large cities, where neighbours rarely know them and newcomers are seldom noticed. When: a person is hiding or disappearing by choice. Why: anonymity is easier where people do not know their neighbours.
- [behavior] An anonymous message that names a recipient's location and time shows that its author has detailed knowledge of the recipient's routine. When: When an unsigned message contains specific information about a target. Why: Specific details about a routine require observation or access.
- [behavior] A message that mixes warning and threat, or signs itself as someone the recipient dreads, blurs its motive and can serve either purpose. When: When an anonymous message's tone is ambiguous. Why: Mixed tone makes intent hard to read and may be a deliberate tactic.
- [rule] Let an anonymous note in a dungeon name a room and a time while leaving the author open, so players must deduce identity from other finds. When: When designing a written clue in a generated dungeon. Why: An unresolved authorship invites inference and connects the note to other clues.
- [heuristic] Identify an anonymous note through phrasing, habits and references only one person would know, since disguising handwriting leaves these traces. When: A note is unsigned and the hand is disguised.
- [heuristic] Attribute an anonymous writing by its initials, style and reasoning, and present the result as the weight of evidence, not certainty. When: no signature identifies the writer. Why: style-based attribution is probabilistic.
- [heuristic] A list of rivals kept in someone's private notes can mark who that person intends to target once power shifts.
- [heuristic] A gift or favour from an unnamed giver can be a clue that the giver wanted influence over the recipient. When: a benefit arrives without a traceable source.
- [heuristic] A message claiming open watching and no wish to hide suggests the sender may be deliberately unconcealed, which warrants checking whether the claim is true. When: When a follow-up message announces ongoing observation. Why: Stated openness can be a bluff or a real intent to intimidate.
- [procedure] 1) Find booking records for private rooms. 2) Ask staff who served the pair whether the pattern recurs. 3) Have staff identify the people from photographs. When: A booking hints at a hidden relationship. Why: Staff can confirm a pattern and identify people.
- [tradeoff] A private record of suspicions helps track evidence as a case develops, but it cannot prove anything and is hard for others to share or check. When: an investigator tracks suspicion without a formal case file. Why: privacy aids tracking and limits verification.
- [pitfall] An unsigned warning lowers the credibility of its information, since the recipient cannot verify or trace the source, so the claims may be dismissed without a fair check. When: Passing on accusations or evidence without attribution. Why: Anonymity removes accountability, so recipients have reason to doubt the claims. (x2)
- [pitfall] An investigator who keeps a theory private risks the household drawing its own conclusions.
- [pitfall] A private record can overstate a feeling, so the written wording may diverge from the writer's own later recollection of it.
- [pitfall] Assuming the apparent sender wrote or posted a message, without checking the chain of handling, misleads the investigation.
- [pitfall] A reveal that depends on the investigator's private knowledge seems unfair unless that knowledge is shown in the dialogue beforehand. When: when a solution rests on unseen knowledge. Why: Unshown premises feel like cheating.
- [pitfall] A private journal entry does not establish that a person wrote a formal report or signed an order. Why: Personal writing and official acts are different kinds of record.
- [pitfall] Judging a message a hoax or a warning merely from its tone is unreliable; the content, delivery and physical evidence must be weighed together. When: When classifying an anonymous message. Why: Tone alone can mislead, since genuine warnings and hoaxes can sound alike.
- [fact] An unnamed tip, such as an anonymous letter, can complete an identity that physical evidence left incomplete. When: a body is unidentified and has no papers.

## authorship and attribution
- [mechanism] Testimony that names who gave an order ties an act to a specific person, making responsibility easier to test. When: when an act's responsibility is disputed. Why: a named authority can be confirmed or denied.
- [rule] Judge disputed authorship by a controlled side-by-side comparison with a known sample from the supposed writer; never link a document to an author on one telling feature alone. When: A document or object can be compared with known samples. Why: One feature can mislead, and confirmation needs a fair comparison. (x2)
- [rule] Do not assume who wrote a typed letter just because someone had access to the machine; test authorship independently.
- [rule] Do not link an anonymous act or document to a named real person without concrete evidence; a guess about authorship is not attribution. Why: tying a real person to an event without evidence can misrepresent that person.
- [rule] Authenticate every document used in a reveal, or the audience may dismiss it as forged. When: when a reveal relies on papers. Why: unverified papers can be waved away.
- [rule] Ask about physical attributes a method requires, since one answer can close an entire line of theory.
- [rule] Author dialogue tells, such as an over-emphatic denial or a question that exposes fear, as signals the player is meant to notice. When: Writing NPC dialogue that hides a truth. Why: Visible tells reward attentive players.
- [rule] Ask who proposed an action and who agreed to it, since attribution of a suggestion can matter more than the action itself.
- [rule] Show each in-game record's author and place of writing, so players can judge the motives behind it.
- [heuristic] When a cry or exclamation could come from several suspects, establish what each could have been doing at that moment before attributing it. When: a sound is linked to multiple candidates. Why: a sound alone rarely names one person.
- [heuristic] When no record names an author or place, combine deeds, handwriting comparison and registers to narrow the candidates.
- [heuristic] Hostile writers may exaggerate and sympathetic writers may excuse, so weigh each account against its author's motive before trusting its details. When: When sources are partisan. Why: Both kinds of bias can distort the same events in opposite directions.
- [heuristic] Let a document's flaws point to whoever handled its drafting, so players can trace responsibility. When: Designing documents that hide a collusion trail. Why: Errors left by a drafter can be followed back to them.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the handwriting with a known sample. 2) Check the signature. 3) Accept a letter that reverses a presumed fact only after both checks pass. When: When a letter contradicts an established fact.
- [procedure] 1) List what the writer must have known. 2) List what access the writer needed. 3) List what materials the writer could obtain. 4) Keep only candidates who meet every condition. When: when an anonymous message reveals what its author must have known. Why: each condition filters the pool of possible writers.
- [pitfall] Accounts naming several people, such as he says or she says, make it easy to lose track of who gave which claim, so record attribution for each claim.
- [pitfall] Long chains of second-hand attribution can hide where a claim first came from, so trace the claim to its origin.
- [pitfall] A message written for an audience can guard its true meaning, so its apparent content may mislead. Why: Coded or public wording is meant to be read by many people, not just the intended recipient.
- [pitfall] A depicted person or artwork is not evidence of a relationship on its own, since it may have an ordinary explanation.
- [pitfall] A genuine-looking report can still be a mistake or a deception, so authenticity is not the same as reliability.
- [pitfall] A letter that only praises its writer invites suspicion; the audience should be able to question it.
- [fact] Physical evidence is only as strong as its attribution, so a genuine trace can still point to the wrong person.

## clock and timing records
- [mechanism] An unreliable clock or a wrong forecast is itself a clue: it undermines trust in the world's timing, and the reader should not assume it is accurate. When: Using time markers or predicted events as narrative tools. Why: A faulty timekeeper can mislead the reader as much as the characters.
- [mechanism] A changed object or unfinished work records when events happened and how long a process took, so it fixes timing for investigators.
- [mechanism] A fixed offset between two clocks, such as a one-hour time-zone difference, shifts every reported time by the same amount and can turn an apparent contradiction into a consistent timeline.
- [mechanism] A pre-recorded voice played after a death makes witnesses hear the victim alive later, shifting the apparent time of death. When: a voice is heard but the speaker is not seen. Why: Listeners cannot tell a recording from a live speaker.
- [behavior] Estimates of when an event happened from physical evidence are approximate, and should be stated as ranges rather than exact times. When: when deriving a time from decay, temperature, or similar physical state. Why: physical clocks vary with conditions and are imprecise.
- [rule] Use one shared clock, such as the in-game clock, to order witness statements and logs; lining them up exposes contradictions among them. When: Several records or accounts describe the same events. Why: A common reference lets players line up accounts. (x2)
- [rule] Do not assume a clock is accurate without knowing whose it is; confirm it still runs and check its drift against a known event before trusting it. When: A timeline depends on a clock, watch or other timer. Why: Damaged or drifting devices can show a time far from the true one, placing events at the wrong times.
- [rule] Collect or record a time-sensitive trace in an exposed scene early, before weather or tide erases it. When: investigation scene exposed to weather or tide where delay is part of the case. Why: Erased traces cannot be re-examined later.
- [rule] Record NPC grudges as explicit, time-stamped threats so that a later death or theft can be traced back to a stated motive. When: Designing NPC rivalries that feed a later crime. Why: A recorded threat gives the player a traceable motive.
- [rule] Correct a clock's reading only when its error is known; a guessed offset adds false precision. When: the source's error is unknown. Why: An invented correction looks exact while being unsupported.
- [heuristic] Do not rely on a witness's sense of time; take the date from a record instead.
- [heuristic] Repeated sounds and clock readings make elapsed time visible, so the audience senses the hours passing.
- [heuristic] Explicit times of day give a timeline fixed points against which other events can be measured.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the witness's clock with a reliable reference at the same moment. 2) Compute the offset. 3) Apply the offset to every time the witness reported, keeping relative order and durations intact. When: Building a timeline from a witness's timestamps, especially when the timing device is known to drift. Why: An uncorrected clock shifts every event it recorded, and a uniform shift keeps order and durations intact.
- [procedure] 1) Note clock times from watches or timestamps. 2) Record how long ago earlier key events occurred. 3) Compare sequences to place events relative to one another. 4) Accept that the timeline shows when events happened, not why. When: ordering several people's movements.
- [procedure] 1) Use regularly repeated sounds, such as bell quarters, as units of time. 2) Count the units between events. 3) Cross-check the total against memory of other landmarks. When: no clock can be trusted.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether the object's winding or power has run out. 2) If stored run remains, treat the stop as possible interference. 3) Test the object directly, which settles whether the stop was natural faster than debate. When: an object has stopped unexpectedly.
- [procedure] 1) Subtract the elapsed time recorded at each checkpoint to get the duration of each session. 2) Compare each player's totals. 3) Estimate the length of a long calculation and place it within a time window. When: An alibi rests on continuous presence and a time-stamped record exists. Why: Timing gaps reveal periods when a player may have been away from the table.
- [metric] A cigarette burns for about twelve minutes in calm weather and about eight minutes in gusty weather. When: estimating how long a cigarette was lit outdoors. Why: wind speeds up burning.
- [pitfall] Treating one witness's time as exact is a mistake when other witnesses differ, since times from different people can vary by several minutes. When: When witnesses give different times for the same events. Why: Each witness's clock or memory carries its own error, so a narrow timeline built on them can mislead.
- [fact] Some people track time through recurring markers, such as a weekly day, and can report events in order without knowing the calendar date. When: a witness cannot read or write. Why: Recurring markers preserve sequence even without dates.
- [fact] An interval between a lightning flash and the following thunder, about a minute and a half, can serve as a readable clock that shows a calm, controlled sequence. When: A storm scene where a flash and thunder are used to mark time. Why: The delay between light and sound lets the observer measure elapsed time and infer deliberate timing.

## clue design and planting
- [mechanism] A foreign or oddly capitalised word can carry a second meaning, such as a place name rather than an object, so solving it requires a lookup. When: When designing word-based puzzles. Why: A surface reading can mislead, and the second meaning rewards map or lookup use.
- [rule] A single marker proves little; rely on several matches that reinforce one another. When: Establishing identity from clues. Why: One match can be coincidence or error.
- [rule] Link recalled sensations and past events into a sequence, rather than treating them as separate anecdotes, to build a usable hypothesis. When: When collecting witness details about a pattern. Why: A sequence of linked details is easier to test than isolated memories.
- [rule] Seed warnings and hesitations from a character whose true role is hidden, so they read as ordinary behaviour until the reveal.
- [rule] Reuse the same kind of clue across cases, such as a sighting, a key item, or a handwriting mismatch, so players learn to read the pattern. When: building a series of mysteries. Why: Repeated clue types let players anticipate where the reversal lies.
- [rule] Plant each part of a trick separately in ordinary-seeming moments, so no single clue reveals the mechanism until the parts are assembled.
- [rule] Seed doubt early with a dismissive remark about a suspicious detail, so the player senses a timing problem without learning its mechanism; hold the proof until the end.
- [heuristic] A physical sign can be shown before its meaning is explained, with its significance depending on later testimony. When: Introducing an unexplained physical clue. Why: Withholding meaning keeps the clue open until corroborating testimony arrives.
- [heuristic] A change in a person's routine, such as moving their work to a different room, is a signal that can reveal a shift in their state or activity. When: Interpreting a character's behavior in a mystery. Why: Deviation from habit is noticeable and carries meaning.
- [heuristic] Retrospective narration that marks a detail as significant before its meaning is known signals to the audience that it will matter. When: Foreshadowing a reveal in first-person or retrospective narration. Why: The framing invites attention without disclosing the answer.
- [heuristic] A single conclusive item can close off a whole group of explanations at once, so one find can rule out many candidates. When: Designing a mystery where clues eliminate branches. Why: Grouping explanations behind one decisive clue lets a single discovery restructure the player's options.
- [heuristic] Words that show knowledge beyond what the suspect should have, such as the names or labels used by the investigation, can reveal inside knowledge of the case. When: A suspect uses terms or refers to people only the investigation would name. Why: Slips of vocabulary expose prior access to information.
- [heuristic] Plant a written clue the player can reread after the reveal, so the earlier text gains meaning once the cause is known.
- [heuristic] Plant a shared identifying detail, such as a birth date or matching item, in a notebook or dialogue that players can check later. When: when a hidden link must be discoverable. Why: checkable clues let attentive players confirm the link.
- [heuristic] Hide the key fact behind a social assumption the audience accepts, such as a character being a bachelor, so the reveal reverses the assumption.
- [heuristic] Let a silent object carry the threat until it is explained, since an unexplained reaction to it builds suspense. When: introducing an ominous prop early in a scenario. Why: Unanswered reactions prompt players to speculate, and a later explanation pays off that tension.
- [heuristic] Leave one or two secondary clues unexplained after the main reveal, so the audience keeps reasoning past the solution. When: Concluding a mystery with a satisfying main answer. Why: Open loops sustain curiosity and reward later investigation.
- [heuristic] Attach small contradictions to ordinary routines so players can catch them without specialised knowledge. When: Designing clues that reward attentive play. Why: Everyday facts are accessible, so the contradiction is noticeable.
- [tradeoff] Recurring a clue keeps it familiar for later reinterpretation, but an unchanged return feels redundant and loses force. When: Repeating a motif or clue across the investigation. Why: Familiarity aids recontextualization, while unchanged repetition gives no new information. (x2)
- [pitfall] One tell, such as a tear or a trembling hand, has many possible causes, including grief, shame, fear, or guilt, so it cannot identify the cause alone.
- [pitfall] Shared geography, such as a find on a suspect's land or near their home, does not establish a connection to them and needs independent support. When: A discovery is located near a suspect. Why: Location alone is coincidence; it does not identify the victim or the culprit.
- [pitfall] A label or sign used by many groups cannot identify one culprit alone; check whether it points to a single group or to many. When: a generic name or sign appears in the case.

## dead ends
- [mechanism] A negative result, such as a shop lacking an item or a negative lab test, can close one branch while pointing the player to where to look next, keeping the mystery moving.
- [mechanism] A dead NPC's belongings in an attic or chest can carry a half-finished plan, which the player reconstructs from the objects and where they were stored.
- [rule] Treat a dead NPC as a possible alternative state, and reveal the true identity only through a grave check or body examination. When: designing a character whose death may be staged. Why: a hidden identity keeps the death ambiguous until tested.
- [rule] When a clue leads to a dead end, offer the player a different route to the same goal so they are not left searching at random. When: Designing a clue chain for a player-driven investigation. Why: A dead end with no alternative pushes players into aimless searching.
- [rule] Do not abandon a lead after one failure; check whether the failure has a cause, and treat it as direction for a new search. When: A lead produces no result. Why: A failure may have an identifiable cause that points to another line of inquiry.
- [heuristic] Place plausible dead ends that a player has a real reason to test, since an unworthy lead will not mislead anyone. When: When designing false leads in an investigation. Why: A lead that nobody pursues cannot misdirect.
- [heuristic] Most leads in an investigation end in dead ends, and only a few prove useful. When: Planning how many clues to follow. Why: Investigation is mostly elimination.
- [heuristic] When a physical trail ends at a dead end, shift weight to other evidence so the case still moves forward. When: a clue matches no known source.
- [heuristic] A dead-end clue still informs: a trace that leads nowhere can reveal that another route into the space exists. When: a physical trace that yields no passage or answer. Why: the failed lead itself narrows the possibilities.
- [tradeoff] Delaying questioning allows a witness to be traced less easily, so each postponed interview can cost time in which evidence is lost. When: When a witness's silence delays the investigation. Why: Trails cool and witnesses become harder to trace over time.
- [pitfall] A timed group decision ending without a verdict feels like a dead end unless it opens a second attempt with a new objective, mirroring a retrial. When: A timed group decision fails to reach a result. Why: Without a new objective the audience has nothing to pursue; a new objective keeps the player engaged after failure.
- [pitfall] A reveal delayed without interim evidence, or with no new clue in the next scene, reads as a stunt and frustrates the audience, who may start to mock the character. When: A reveal is delayed without interim evidence. Why: Without partial evidence the delay reads as vanity rather than method.
- [pitfall] A conclusion formed early can bias how later facts are read, so each confirmation should be checked on its own terms. When: An investigator forms a conclusion before gathering all evidence. Why: Early commitment makes later evidence seem to fit more than it does.
- [pitfall] A wrong early assumption, such as the size of a mark, corrupts every later inference built on it, so each premise should be verified before building on it. When: Reconstructing a process from partial evidence. Why: Downstream deductions inherit the error.
- [pitfall] A trail that ends at a stranger, bookmaker or shop is often a dead end, so plan the next verification step before the interview.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a message because its obvious explanation seems adequate. Why: The obvious explanation can hide the real meaning of the clue.
- [pitfall] Refusing every inference can mislead as much as jumping to one, because caution taken too far blocks inference entirely.
- [pitfall] An owner may dismiss an early count as unimportant, so a loss can be noticed without being acted on until a direct question. When: A count comes up short but seems minor. Why: Small discrepancies are easy to ignore until later evidence gives them weight.
- [pitfall] Reading a document's presence in a place as proof of a person's presence there is an error; the copy may have gone elsewhere. When: Inferring who was somewhere from a found document. Why: Documents travel independently of their handlers.
- [pitfall] A normal test result can end an inquiry prematurely, so a scenario should let a failed test still lead onward. When: when a diagnostic test is the player's main route to the answer. Why: A passing or inconclusive test can close the investigation if it is the only path.
- [fact] Recognising a dead person is weaker than recognising a living face, because appearance changes after death.
- [fact] A rumour of past deaths can be set up early as village memory and dismissed by the protagonist, then overturned by later physical evidence. When: Designing a mystery where the reader should initially accept a false explanation. Why: A dismissed rumour lowers suspicion of the real cause, so later evidence can shift belief sharply.

## delirium and memory testimony
- [mechanism] Planted information stays dormant until a later sighting matches it, at which point the earlier remark is recalled and gains meaning. When: when a later piece of evidence matches the earlier remark.
- [mechanism] Delirium lowers a character's guard, so they drop words that show they knew far more than others assumed. When: a character is in a fever or delirium state. Why: the character no longer filters what they say.
- [mechanism] A widely shared delusion gains strength when a community's gathering network repeats it to many listeners.
- [behavior] In a disordered mental state, dreams can feel more real than ordinary memory and contain details that seem too fitting to have been invented while awake. When: A person is ill, feverish, distressed or intoxicated. Why: A disturbed state heightens the feeling of reality without improving accuracy.
- [behavior] Witnesses often recall distant events only in outline, remembering a general fact such as a resemblance while missing the specifics. When: asked about a childhood or long-past detail. Why: Memory keeps the gist more reliably than particulars over time.
- [behavior] A small public disturbance fixes a person's presence in other people's memory, because disputes and unusual appearances get recalled. When: a minor dispute occurs at a public event. Why: unexpected friction makes witnesses notice and remember details.
- [behavior] Witnesses often recall a distinctive object before a face, so the object can be the more dependable anchor. When: a fleeting sighting. Why: attention fixes on distinctive items first.
- [rule] Do not dismiss dream-framed testimony automatically; it may honestly reflect the witness's state or hide behind uncertainty, so treat details as probable but unproven and test them against other evidence. (x2)
- [rule] Resolve a quest where two NPCs disagree about a past detail only by finding the artifact that matches one of the accounts.
- [heuristic] Statements from a feverish or delirious person are unreliable but informative: they point to leads and concerns, so verify before belief; repeated names show what troubles them, as impressions not testimony. When: When interpreting a feverish or delirious person's speech. Why: Delirium gives hints about concerns without giving reliable statements. (x2)
- [heuristic] Weigh a delirious witness's statements by when they were made, checking them against the speaker's lucid moments. When: a sick or dying witness speaks. Why: reliability varies with mental state.
- [heuristic] Dream or vision fragments can foreshadow a location or event the player will reach later.
- [heuristic] A sale unlike a shop's usual stock is easier for a seller to remember, so it makes a stronger link to the buyer. Why: unusual transactions stand out against routine ones in memory.
- [heuristic] Before dismissing an odd statement from a dying or delirious person, test whether it reflects real knowledge, using questions that separate hallucination from delirium. When: the statement could point to a real fact. Why: delirium and hallucination can both produce similar words.
- [pitfall] Witnesses may present a sleep- or fear-born event as a waking observation; ask whether they mix dreams, belief or superstition with real events before accepting their account. (x2)
- [pitfall] Assuming all of a delirious speaker's words are nonsense, or that all are true, both lead to error.
- [pitfall] Assuming a word spoken in delirium names a specific person is an error, since such words may point at several people.
- [pitfall] A patient's fear of being harmed may be a symptom of illness, so it cannot prove or disprove a plot; treating it as proof or dismissing it outright are both errors.
- [pitfall] A real delusion can mask a real act, so dismissing a confession entirely is also an error.
- [fact] Vivid, disturbing experiences stay long in memory and strongly affect an overwrought nervous system, so their lasting force is not evidence of their truth. When: A recollection feels powerful and persistent. Why: Emotional intensity strengthens memory regardless of whether the event was accurate.
- [fact] A distressed witness's visions are uncertain, because senses can deceive and deception is hard to separate from the witness's own condition.
- [fact] Delirium can make a true statement sound false and a false one sound true, so delirious speech cannot prove a claim alone.

## investigator conduct and exposure
- [behavior] An investigator's manner, such as feigned complacency or a leading question, can mislead others about what is already believed, letting the investigator test a different theory. When: An investigator questions a person whose belief is being tested. Why: Leading questions make a person state a belief that can then be checked against evidence.
- [behavior] An investigator may recognise a disguised person early and keep silent until the moment is right, holding knowledge back from others.
- [behavior] When an investigator hides their real purpose behind a feigned ailment or dismissive talk, the people being watched tend to relax their guard. When: an investigator conceals their purpose. Why: the cover story makes the investigator seem harmless.
- [behavior] An investigator who withholds a solution for a personal aim adds a moral twist, because the player must judge the withholding. When: Writing a detective whose goals diverge from justice. Why: A morally questionable choice by the investigator complicates the player's trust in the solution.
- [rule] Keep the investigator's own name out of a witness's account when it would turn the witness hostile.
- [rule] An investigator may decline covert tactics such as eavesdropping and deception, leaving covert inquiry to a partner. When: Designing investigation roles or a character's code of conduct. Why: Self-imposed limits shape which methods a case can use.
- [rule] Mark explicitly which facts the investigator cannot disclose, so the reveal stays honest about the limits of what is known. When: A story reveal leaves some facts unexplained or privately held. Why: A stated boundary keeps the reveal credible instead of arbitrary.
- [heuristic] An investigator should check their own motives as well as the witness's, since a prior relationship can bias how a witness is trusted. When: when the investigator has a history with someone involved.
- [tradeoff] A disguise may draw more candid answers from wary staff, but a slip reveals the investigator and ends cooperation. When: questioning people who distrust officials.
- [tradeoff] Calling in an investigator fast protects the scene, while publicity around the call can make the household reluctant to consent and changes how much trust the investigator receives.
- [pitfall] Investigators' own footprints can contaminate a scene, so check what they touched before attributing a trace to someone else. When: Investigators walk over the same ground as the suspect. Why: Mixed prints make it impossible to tell whose movements left which marks.
- [pitfall] Harsh or hostile confrontation gives a suspect material for counter-accusations and can shift suspicion onto the investigator, so keep manner measured. When: Confronting a suspect who denies everything. Why: Denial plus perceived hostility turns the accuser into a target, and visible harshness supports claims that the accuser is unstable.
- [pitfall] Chronology errors in the investigator's own file can send a case in the wrong direction.
- [pitfall] An investigator's own first theory can become the suggestion that corrupts a witness's later account.
- [pitfall] Revealing your identity and evidence can make you the target. Sending every investigator into one confrontation risks losing all evidence holders at once. When: When the suspect may retaliate or destroy evidence after a confrontation. Why: Concentrating both knowledge and people in one exposed encounter leaves no one in reserve.
- [pitfall] Investigator overreach or poor procedure can sink a case and bring a reprimand, even when the underlying evidence has some weight.
- [pitfall] An investigator who acts on an unconfirmed report can be misled as much as a suspect, so confirm before acting.
- [pitfall] Expected results depend on the investigator's own knowledge of how an act works, so that knowledge should be checked.
- [pitfall] An investigator linked to the victim, who leaves a scene quickly and withholds a source, can become the prime suspect. When: when the investigator was following the victim. Why: Circumstantial links look like guilt to authorities.
- [pitfall] Withholding information can make the investigator look evasive to the one person whose trust they need. When: An investigator keeps names or facts from a companion. Why: Concealment is read as distrust even when it has a purpose.
- [pitfall] A forbidding entrance can make an investigator more eager to press on, since pride and resistance raise commitment. When: Access to a suspect is made difficult. Why: Obstacles can strengthen the investigator's resolve rather than deter them.
- [pitfall] A test that reveals the investigator's interest can warn the wrong people, so it must appear ordinary to the subject. When: Verifying a suspect's identity or links. Why: Suspicion alerted early lets the subject or their associates adjust.

## mystery design and fairness
- [model] A whodunit or investigation with a hidden culprit runs through a crime hook, opening investigation, obvious false solution, steady clue drip, crisis, strain-and-turn twist, reveal, then aftermath or resolution. When: Designing a whodunit or investigation scenario with a hidden culprit across its full length. Why: Each phase adds information while keeping the answer back.
- [model] A mystery case unfolds in stages: commission, first demonstration, a plausible wrong theory, a hidden clue cluster, a trap or time pressure, a twist, then reveal and resolution. When: designing a self-contained puzzle story. Why: Each stage sets up the next so the reader's belief can be overturned fairly.
- [model] A reusable closed-case mystery has four parts: an arresting death, theft or vanishing; a suspect hiding another secret; an outsider, supernatural or blackmail explanation; then a reversal. When: designing a series of closed-case mysteries. Why: A shared skeleton makes each reversal predictable in shape yet surprising in content.
- [model] A mystery plot can be built as a sequence of premise, misdirect, clue, suspect shift, reveal and resolution, with suspicion passing from one suspect to the next as evidence accumulates. When: designing a investigation-driven scenario. Why: Each new piece of evidence should make the previous suspect less likely, keeping the player moving toward the truth.
- [model] A closed-room murder plot works by making a seemingly impossible entry or exit the central puzzle, then exposing staged evidence and faked alibis to resolve it. Why: The impossibility drives the investigation and the staging supplies the answer.
- [mechanism] A mystery that states its rules early lets the audience reason toward the reveal, so the answer feels earned rather than arbitrary. When: Designing a reveal that should be earned by clues already shown. Why: A rule introduced only after the reveal looks arbitrary.
- [rule] Show every withheld fact and staged clue, including concealed objects or gestures, before the confession; a reveal relying on unseen facts feels like a trick. When: Designing a solution reveal or a reveal that explains earlier events. Why: Players must observe the evidence to accept the conclusion and feel the reveal was earned. (x2)
- [rule] Offer a candidate list, let players rule out each with a specific clue, and require naming motive and method before the final accusation is accepted. When: Designing deduction puzzles or an accusation mechanic. Why: Motive and method checks stop the answer being reached by elimination alone.
- [rule] Introduce the deciding clue early as an ordinary object, keeping it visible but ambiguous, so it gains meaning only once the suspect's role is known. When: When designing a mystery whose solution depends on one decisive clue. Why: Introducing the deciding clue for the first time at the reveal breaks fair play.
- [rule] Do not design a deduction where an NPC's denial or silence counts as proof of guilt; players will sense the unfairness. When: Designing a suspect-based puzzle. Why: Unfalsifiable proof feels unfair to players.
- [rule] Place the record that later changes a verdict, such as a ledger or contract, where the player could have found it earlier. When: Designing an ending that reframes responsibility. Why: Discoverable evidence makes a late verdict change feel earned rather than imposed.
- [heuristic] Reward the player for linking several minor cues, such as mud on a sleeve, a re-tied knot and a wet shoe, into one conclusion, showing cues without the answer. When: Designing deduction rewards in a game world. Why: Combining small cues feels like earned insight rather than handed answers.
- [heuristic] Let the player rebuild a past day from notebook entries in order, with each entry unlocking the next, and use named anchor items to gate the memory. When: When designing a memory or flashback puzzle in a game. Why: Ordered entries and anchors give the player cues and a clear sequence to follow.
- [heuristic] A detective story can follow a repeated formula: a trivial-seeming detail, a plausible wrong suspect, a quiet investigation, and a concrete physical proof that reverses an early belief. When: When structuring a mystery case or scenario. Why: The pattern gives the player a clear path from misdirection to a fair reveal.
- [heuristic] Give each suspect a timeline in a mystery and let players check it against a log, ledger or schedule kept by the game. When: Designing a deduction puzzle with several suspects. Why: Players can only reach contradictions if the timelines can be compared against recorded sources.
- [heuristic] Place the false solution near 50-60% of the runtime, a crisis such as a false confession near 70%, and the true reversal and reveal at 80-100%. When: structuring a whodunit. Why: Spacing the turns keeps each suspect's case distinct before the next one takes over.
- [procedure] 1) Generate all plausible outcomes for a missing NPC. 2) Remove outcomes contradicted by planted clues. 3) Keep the single remaining outcome as the solvable answer. When: Generating a procedural mystery. Why: Elimination ensures one answer stays consistent with all clues.
- [procedure] 1) Hook and setup, 1-7%. 2) Investigation opens, 8-18%. 3) Complication, 19-29%. 4) False solution, 31-39%. 5) Escalation, 42-49%. 6) Confrontation and counterattack, 58-68%. 7) Crisis, 70-79%. 8) Aftermath setup, 81-83%. 9) Reveal, 93-98%. 10) Coda, 100%. When: Pacing a mystery plot across its full length.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a hook that poses a question. 2) Add a complication that makes the easy answer look settled. 3) Investigate with clues. 4) Overturn the official view. 5) Resolve through one deduction and a confrontation. 6) End with an aftermath that holds the cost of delay. When: Structuring a thriller or investigation arc. Why: A fixed sequence of stages keeps pacing controlled and makes each reveal land after the player has been misled.
- [tradeoff] Withholding builds tension in a narrative, but a fair-play puzzle needs every clue visible to the player, so deferred disclosure should not replace clues the player needs to solve it. When: Choosing between suspense and fair-play clue visibility. Why: Suspense serves pacing, while puzzles require the player to have all the information.
- [tradeoff] Gating an NPC with lore questions drawn from in-game codices rewards exploration, but only if the examiner's own knowledge is complete, otherwise the test misleads. When: Designing gates or disguise checks that rely on knowledge. Why: The gate is fair only when the answers exist in the game and the examiner is accurate.
- [fact] A generator can tie an encounter's weapon or method to the culprit's planning level, so an improvised weapon suggests impulse while a prepared trap suggests design. When: Generating culprits and encounters in a game.

## repeated questioning
- [mechanism] Asking the same point in different wording turns any variation in answers into apparent evidence of lying. When: a question returns in new phrasing during an interrogation. Why: Small differences are treated as contradictions.
- [behavior] Re-asking a witness after the investigator gains new information can yield a different answer, as details are recalled or weighed differently. When: after new information is learned. Why: New context changes what the witness recalls.
- [behavior] When an answer changes after a question is repeated, players learn to check consistency and treat first replies with caution. When: An NPC's reply can differ when the same question is asked again. Why: Variation exposes which answers are stable and which depend on wording or state.
- [rule] Repetition alone is not proof: a repeated denial may stem from fear, loyalty or embarrassment, and a claim repeated before an audience or several listeners is not independent corroboration. When: a witness repeats the same denial under questioning, or a culprit repeats one account to several listeners. (x3)
- [rule] Let NPCs give deeper answers when a topic is re-asked, rewarding revisits and precise re-questioning. When: Designing NPC information that changes over time or dialogue that tracks repeated player questions. Why: Revisiting witnesses gives better information; persistence and precision should unlock deeper answers.
- [rule] Re-ask the same point, especially later or after earlier answers, to test whether the account stays consistent under repetition.
- [rule] Repeat the central question and record an identical answer or repeated refusal as a fixed position, not as a non-answer.
- [rule] Implement repeated moments of incomprehension as environmental text or overheard speech, tracked as an open question until resolved. When: The player is meant to lack context early on. Why: Repeated confusion keeps an unresolved question visible.
- [rule] When a witness has held a detail back, question them again and ask why it was withheld. When: a witness is found to have omitted a fact. Why: A second questioning can reveal the reason for the omission.
- [rule] Track which questions an NPC dodges, and let repeated deflection flag a topic for a later confrontation. When: Designing NPC memory for dialogue systems. Why: Recording dodges lets the game return to them at the right moment.
- [rule] Reward a second line of questioning after the first breaks an NPC's resistance. When: designing interrogation scenes. Why: Pressure can reveal further secrets the player did not seek at first.
- [rule] Let a minor accomplice confess and go free, so the player can choose mercy over prosecution. Why: A mercy option gives the player a moral choice without weakening the main culprit's punishment.
- [heuristic] Repeating a question across separate encounters, or asking it from another angle, often reveals a cover story or the true purpose behind a visit.
- [heuristic] When a gatekeeper refuses, try again with a different pretext, name or staff member, since a fresh approach can get a different answer. When: a gatekeeper refuses to answer. Why: different staff may hold different records or be more willing to talk.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the same underlying question again in different forms or from different angles. 2) Compare each answer against earlier ones. 3) Note conflicts, changes, or matches with physical facts. When: When testing a witness's account, especially if answers are evasive or playful. Why: Varied phrasing exposes inconsistency that a single question or answer may hide.
- [procedure] 1) Question a witness once and record what is recalled. 2) Question again on the dismissed or hesitated detail, particularly when alone. 3) Note new details that emerge. When: When a witness dismissed, missed or hesitated over a detail on first questioning. Why: Repeated probing exposes what the witness knows and can recover details first missed.
- [pitfall] Repeating the same questions or demand to a witness who has settled a story or a deflecting reply yields little and does not move them; the discussion stays closed. When: a witness has committed to an account, or a stakeholder refuses to engage. Why: Settled accounts resist pressure on the same points; a deflection that closes the discussion blocks further pressure from the same angle. (x2)
- [pitfall] Repeating a deferral, pause or guess prompt without new information loses the audience and feels mechanical; vary its form or add new interest or pressure each time. When: Several pauses, deferrals or guess prompts occur in one scene or before an admission. Why: Identical stops become predictable; repetition without new input feels like a mechanical trick.
- [pitfall] Repeated false alarms deflate later real threats, which the audience then fails to take seriously. When: When scares recur without consequence. Why: Audiences learn to discount alarms.
- [pitfall] Repeated questioning of a household or group can produce more evasion rather than more truth. When: Questioning the same people several times. Why: Pressure can harden defensiveness and coordinate stories.
- [pitfall] Back-to-back dismissals of clues feel contrived, so space them out.
- [pitfall] A surprise confrontation that unsettles a witness once will not work again, because a prepared witness is harder to catch off guard. When: Planning a second confrontation with a witness who has already been surprised. Why: The witness anticipates the questioner and guards against the tactic.

## account changes and verification
- [mechanism] Shared belief can hold for a long time, then fail quickly once a trusted figure is accused and the accusers' claims are doubted.
- [behavior] As matches accumulate, a suspect's answers may shift from agreement to weak explanations before they stop arguing. When: when a suspect faces a growing set of matching traces. Why: Each match weakens the suspect's denial.
- [behavior] Circumstances can change quickly; a cheerful letter can be followed by a short one reporting a broken engagement, so compare sequential letters. When: reading a series of dated letters. Why: Sequential letters reveal a shift that a single letter hides.
- [rule] A suspect's self-serving account of motive or actions, including a narrator who is also a suspect, should be compared with other sources and treated as a defence to test. When: A suspect explains their actions or motive with a self-serving story. Why: Self-interested accounts can distort facts and shift blame.
- [rule] Test a suspect's explanation against observed facts and secondary claims; plausibility alone does not settle a disputed statement. When: interrogating a suspect or witness who offers a justification or explains a statement. Why: A plausible account can hide a false one.
- [rule] Test each account against independent records, a timeline of who was where, and other witness accounts, so every claim is confirmed by more than one source. When: The suspect's story or a witness account rests on claims others can confirm or contradict.
- [rule] State how an account reached the reader, and mark which details were relayed second-hand rather than taken from firsthand records.
- [rule] When a visible story conflicts with small physical details, trust the details and test the story against them.
- [heuristic] When a condition worsens suddenly, first check what was administered, since an overdose is a common early suspect.
- [heuristic] Every claim should trace to an accountable person who can be questioned, rather than to an unnamed or anonymous report. When: A story relies on many claims about contested events. Why: Accountable speakers can be questioned, so claims can be tested.
- [heuristic] Separate the story people tell about an event from the mechanism that actually produced it. When: A supernatural or hard-to-verify explanation is offered for an event with natural causes.
- [heuristic] A long quiet period followed by abrupt new urgency suggests that something entered the situation recently, and that recent arrival is the likely cause. When: An opponent or character's behavior changes sharply and the change has a visible starting point. Why: The timing of the change narrows which new factor could have caused it.
- [procedure] 1) Split the account into separate checkable claims, setting aside colourful detail and untestable motives. 2) Match each claim to a record that could confirm or refute it. 3) Check every date against a calendar. 4) Trust only what sources confirm. When: when a story mixes checkable facts with motives, or one teller is the only source of a dramatic event, especially if interested or theatrical. Why: each claim can be confirmed or refuted on its own; confident or partisan tellers can embellish claims others can check.
- [procedure] 1) Invite a full account, and offer a stated benefit for it. 2) Test each claim against physical facts such as timing. 3) Hold judgment open until the story is checked. When: when interrogating a captured or cooperative suspect. Why: A full account gives more claims to test, and withheld judgment prevents early acceptance of a self-serving story.
- [procedure] 1) List the expected occupants of each room. 2) Check each room in turn. 3) Note which occupants are absent or unused. 4) Reframe the question from who is hurt to who is unaccounted for. When: first stage of an investigation.
- [procedure] 1) Bring in a second person to confirm or add details. 2) Note any difference between the two accounts. 3) Ask about a related past event to test whether the account holds together. When: when a single account needs testing. Why: contradictions between accounts and related events expose weak claims.
- [tradeoff] A suspect's statements about other people can be unreliable, so they should be checked rather than accepted, even when offered sincerely. When: When a suspect vouches for or describes a third party. Why: A person may misjudge others or have reasons to shade testimony.
- [pitfall] A witness whose detail changes only after challenge, or after a reward or deal, should not be trusted without checks; the change may reflect pressure rather than memory.
- [pitfall] A door's state may look different depending on which account is accepted, so compare several accounts before relying on it.
- [pitfall] Treating a witness's sudden change of account as the truth, without independent checks, is a common and serious mistake.
- [pitfall] Trusting a witness's sudden reversal just because it is emotional or made in public mistakes intensity for reliability. Why: emotion and public display make a changed account feel more certain.

## animal tracks and clues
- [mechanism] Deeper wheel or cart tracks mean more weight on that wheel, so comparing depths reveals which vehicle carried more load or how a rider's weight was distributed. When: Comparing two sets of tracks from vehicles that left the same place. Why: Ground compresses more under greater weight.
- [mechanism] Fresh snow or mud records every track entering and leaving a place, so finding only inbound tracks suggests no one left on foot. When: conditions such as fresh snow have preserved the record. Why: the surface keeps a record of movement.
- [behavior] Animals near a panicking person often react to that panic, so the animal's behaviour can reveal the person's emotional state. When: A companion animal is present during a frightening scene. Why: Animals respond to their owner's emotional state.
- [behavior] Animals and small movements can register as signs of recent presence, prompting unease without establishing a conclusion. When: When a sudden animal flight suggests someone was recently nearby. Why: Disturbed animals signal recent human or other activity.
- [rule] Do not treat an animal's behaviour as proof alone; combine it with other evidence before drawing a conclusion.
- [rule] Test a tracker's conclusion by repeating its behavior under controlled conditions where possible, and accept it as proof only after that test. When: the source's behavior can be repeated.
- [rule] Give non-player animals guarding behavior, such as pacing or staring at a patch of ground, as readable tells instead of map markers. When: designing puzzles around hidden items.
- [rule] Use an animal threat as a visible symptom of a hidden human state, so tracks and sounds make the threat real before its nature is known. When: When an unseen supernatural cause must feel present early. Why: A physical sign gives players concrete evidence to investigate while the underlying cause stays hidden.
- [heuristic] Animals may detect cues such as smell that humans miss, so an abrupt change in a companion animal's behaviour can reveal a hidden change, while people may supply wrong explanations. When: A companion animal's behaviour changes abruptly, or a character has changed in a way others cannot see. Why: Animals react to what people miss, so their behaviour reveals the truth early.
- [heuristic] Bite marks can support a species-level guess about an unseen animal by judging the width of the jaw. When: when an animal is implicated by marks but not observed.
- [heuristic] Animals found inside a sealed space without passing its door suggest another opening exists, which can be searched for.
- [heuristic] If a tracker ignores an object it should have reacted to, doubt any inference drawn from its reaction to a different object. Why: the expected reaction did not occur.
- [heuristic] A dim or partly hidden feature, such as a faded numeral, can turn a passing glimpse into a trackable identifier.
- [heuristic] A biological sample such as blood or hair can match a specific animal location, narrowing the search to one building. When: when a trace points to a place with animals. Why: Animal-specific traces link a suspect to a particular site.
- [procedure] 1) Measure stance spacing, the distance from fore-foot to hind-foot, using prints where the animal stood still. 2) Add neck and head length to estimate body length. 3) Compare stride length to body length to infer leg length. 4) Note toe count and claw marks, and compare print shape against known animal families.
- [tradeoff] Track evidence is strong on wet or soft ground but weak on dry ground or with indistinct prints, where no reliable reference sample can be made. When: Choosing whether to rely on footprint evidence. Why: Surface condition determines whether prints can be compared at all.
- [pitfall] Tracks alone do not prove who made them; reading them well requires knowing what a staged version would look like.
- [pitfall] An animal's fearful reaction is not testimony and should be treated as atmosphere unless other evidence supports it. When: When an animal reacts to a person and the reaction is being used to infer guilt. Why: Animal behavior has many causes and cannot establish a person's intent or actions.
- [fact] Measured tracks can reveal the size, body plan and behavior of a creature no one has seen. When: When tracks are the only record of a creature and can be measured reliably.
- [fact] Footprints on paved or newly surfaced ground often vanish, so a trail may end where the surface changes.
- [fact] A tracking source can find a known individual but cannot identify an unknown one, so its result does not name who it has found.

## clue handling
- [mechanism] An object that fits an entry the characters did not use opens a new line of questions about who had access and when. When: a found item relates to an unexpected location. Why: it implies a route outside the known one.
- [behavior] Ordinary finders who read an item belonging to someone else become interpreters of its meaning, and each may read it differently. When: an item passes from one finder to another. Why: printed names and handwriting invite judgment about importance.
- [rule] Record unverified leads, such as a named person from the past or a timeline gap from an untraced call or unexplained delay, so they can be checked later. When: a lead cannot be confirmed yet.
- [rule] Do not build a conclusion on a remark that cannot be checked against an independent fact; a decisive fragment needs checkable support. When: A clue rests only on a single spoken remark, or the fragment must be decisive. Why: An unverifiable remark can support many readings, and unverifiable decisive information breaks trust.
- [rule] Flavour text or trivial items may hide hints, so signal clearly when a seemingly minor item matters to the game.
- [rule] Let an NPC answer a seemingly trivial question, such as what they drank, and tie that answer to a later check.
- [rule] Let the player choose whether to share a clue with an NPC faction, showing how each choice changes that faction's reading of the case. When: When designing evidence systems with factions. Why: Sharing choices make the player responsible for how each group interprets the case.
- [heuristic] Ask witnesses about trivial details, including names and places, since any detail can prove relevant and may surface facts the witness did not volunteer.
- [heuristic] When a character finds an item missing, treat the absence as a question to answer, and fix the time and position with instruments to build a timeline. When: a disruption leaves a character checking belongings and surroundings. Why: fixed times and places make it possible to reconstruct what happened.
- [heuristic] Start an investigation from a detail that seems trivial, such as shoe wear or a mark on the skin, since small traces can reveal recent history.
- [heuristic] A trivial incident early in the story can prove central later, so plant it in plain view.
- [heuristic] A trivial anecdote can explain a character's reluctance and reveal that a location is a known haunt.
- [heuristic] A trivial topic can fix who was present and what was said, and that fact may later connect to a physical object.
- [heuristic] A hint of hidden knowledge lands harder when the character never states it outright. Why: listeners fill the gap with their own inference.
- [procedure] Clue-naming probe, to observe whether a person reacts and so reveals what they know: 1) Name one element of a known clue, holding back the rest. 2) Watch for flushing, muscle twitches, breath changes or a fixed stare. 3) Follow with a neutral question that draws out the person's own words. 4) If doubt remains, give a related cue. When: Interviewing a suspect who may know the clue.
