- [pitfall] Seemingly trivial objects or details may be the key clue, since planted items are easily overlooked; dismissing them early loses vital evidence, so record them. When: reviewing scene objects during an investigation. Why: Innocent-looking marks can carry meaning once context is added.
- [pitfall] A noticed anomaly, object or recognition that is never revisited or resolved reads as a dead end, loose thread or cheating; give it at least one later check. When: when a clue is introduced. Why: unresolved mentions make the story feel incomplete.
- [pitfall] A planted clue or note found by someone other than its intended target may never arrive or may endanger the whole plan it carries.
- [pitfall] A clue a character relies on privately but never shows the player cannot support the player's reasoning and may be missed entirely. When: a character reaches a conclusion from evidence the player has not seen.
- [pitfall] Assigning significance to a detail without a stated reason is speculation; state the reason and test it.
- [pitfall] A detail that seems trivial can be the only clue that contradicts the official sequence of events.

## costs and trade-offs
- [behavior] People sometimes make small trades to prove to themselves they could do more, so a small trade signals intent without proving motive. When: A small transaction seems out of proportion to its gain. Why: Small trades can serve as tests of capacity.
- [rule] Do not press a witness who is cooperating and has no conflicting facts. When: A witness answers openly and their account matches the evidence. Why: Extra pressure adds risk without new information.
- [rule] Gate a witness behind a social rule, such as a faction that punishes anyone who asks questions, so the player can detect the lock by noticing which NPCs refuse to talk. When: Designing a quest hub or investigation with restricted witnesses. Why: Social refusals and past discipline reveal hidden access controls.
- [rule] Make recovering key evidence a real decision with costs such as an inquest or exposure of an ally, rather than a free pickup. When: Designing a discovery of pivotal evidence. Why: Costly choices give the discovery moral and strategic weight.
- [heuristic] Testimony that costs the speaker standing or safety signals sincerity and is more credible than disinterested testimony. Make speaking for a suspect carry visible risk. When: a witness speaks for another at personal cost. Why: A defence that implicates the speaker is harder to dismiss as self-serving. (x2)
- [heuristic] Lavish payment for a trivial task implies the stakes for the planners are far larger than the task itself. When: A plan's expense is out of proportion to its visible work. Why: Rational planners spend only in proportion to what they stand to gain.
- [heuristic] Compare the effort a suspected plan would need with the value of the goal. If the effort is out of proportion, the motive is probably different from the one assumed. When: Judging whether a suspected plan or motive is plausible. Why: An expensive method for a small prize signals a different underlying reason.
- [heuristic] When someone gives up a benefit they would normally keep, the sacrifice suggests an urgent, time-bound need. When: a choice contradicts the person's stated interests. Why: Giving up a lasting gain only makes sense if a more pressing need outweighs it.
- [heuristic] Weigh what an act costs the actor against its gain; a theft that harms the actor's own prospects is a weak motive for that actor. When: judging whether a suspect would plausibly commit an act. Why: Rational actors avoid acts that undermine their own goals.
- [heuristic] An action that looks costly or unnecessary often reveals an adversary's plan; ask what the action achieves.
- [heuristic] Move from dialogue to the scene in a single transition, so stakes rise without a pause. When: When a conversation should lead directly into the next location or action.
- [tradeoff] Delaying a conclusion, such as slow evidence-gathering, lets evidence surface and guards against error but costs time; when a stakeholder needs a fast result, delay can damage the outcome. When: a stakeholder is waiting for a result. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Sinking or destroying a vehicle removes it from the record, but also removes the means of travel.
- [pitfall] Pursuing a dispute through formal challenge can cost more than available resources, and an unfunded claim can ruin the pursuer before the truth is established. Why: Formal processes have high costs and long delays.
- [pitfall] A false lead that costs the player nothing feels pointless. Make its cost visible, such as an unwatched area or lost time.
- [pitfall] Slow, cautious movement and stops consume the margin in a timed plan, so a plan with little slack can be overrun by ordinary delays. When: When an actor must complete actions within a fixed window. Why: Each delay reduces the time left before the deadline.
- [pitfall] A statement taken without a proper caution or notice of representation may be challenged and excluded, even if it is carefully recorded.
- [pitfall] Long gaps between reports make a story feel slow and build irritation during the wait. When: The protagonist is kept inactive for long periods. Why: Waiting without progress frustrates the audience.
- [pitfall] Too much slow detail stalls a story, so every descriptive passage should serve tension or information.
- [pitfall] Costs can be recorded in detail while the reasons for an arrest go unrecorded, so harm alone does not reveal intent.
- [fact] Cost ledgers for a formal process can reveal how routine and indifferent its handling was, an attitude that witness statements may not show.

## mistaken testimony
- [behavior] A witness can sincerely recall a vivid sound or face at a wrong time; when the recalled time conflicts with fixed evidence, reconcile the two rather than discard either. When: Testimony conflicts with a fixed timing such as time of death. Why: Memory of a vivid event can be confident yet mistimed.
- [behavior] Witnesses often cannot recall the exact words of a brief exchange, so their account of it has gaps that must be filled from other evidence. When: a witness reports a short exchange. Why: brief speech is rarely fixed in memory.
- [rule] Do not build an exact sequence from a witness who admits lost memory. Mark that stretch of time as unknown. When: A witness admits memory loss for part of the events.
- [rule] Build a lost-event mystery from dated letters, a sealed file with a suspicious insertion, and a grave or house whose layout tells part of the story. When: designing a game investigation about past events. Why: each clue type lets the player reconstruct events from different evidence.
- [heuristic] Use a sincere but mistaken witness when the audience should see how an error arose, not when testimony must be fully reliable. When: when designing a witness whose account misleads. Why: Visible error mechanisms teach the audience to test claims.
- [heuristic] Even sincere witnesses misremember or overreach, so questions should aim at specifics rather than general impressions. When: taking any witness account. Why: specifics expose memory errors that general impressions hide.
- [pitfall] Sincerity does not establish accuracy: keep good faith separate from reliability, since a sincere witness can misread reflections, misperceive and discount a sound, or report objects only they perceived. When: when evaluating a witness whose account seems trustworthy. Why: Sincerity and reliability do not guarantee accurate perception. (x2)
- [pitfall] Following too far or in the wrong place, or too closely on open ground, loses the target; in crowds, keep pace with a fast walker to stay in sight.
- [pitfall] Protective advice can be lost when the person it protects judges it unnecessary, leaving that person exposed to the threat. Why: the protected person dismisses the warning.
- [pitfall] Repeated hearsay loses its original source at each retelling, so the chain must be traced back before its claims are trusted. When: when a claim has passed through several people. Why: Each retelling removes the link to the first observer.
- [pitfall] A missed chance to act, taken because of caution or chance, can be judged a failure by others even when caution was reasonable. When: reviewing a confrontation that did not end in capture. Why: Hindsight and outside observers often weigh the missed moment heavily.
- [pitfall] Minor threads, such as an injury noted early, can drop from attention; track each open thread until it is resolved.
- [pitfall] Treating a sincere denial as proof that nobody was present is a mistake when the question was framed around suspicion. When: when a witness denies a presence and the question was narrow. Why: Narrow framing excludes ordinary-looking people.
- [pitfall] Losing confidence just before a tell is confirmed can lead the investigator to apologise and withdraw, letting the suspect escape the trap. When: the reveal is near completion. Why: doubt surfaces at the moment of commitment.
- [pitfall] A sincere witness can still be wrong about times, so vagueness in an account should be treated as a lead to pursue, not a verdict. When: When a witness is honest but imprecise. Why: Honesty does not guarantee accurate memory of time.
- [pitfall] If the culprit dies before further questioning, unresolved threads must be settled in the account already given, since no later questions are possible. When: Culprit is lost before follow-up. Why: Gaps left open cannot be closed later.
- [pitfall] Recording only the answers and not the witness's state of mind loses information about how reliable each answer was.
- [pitfall] A witness can misidentify the day, and without an outside reference the sequence of events cannot be fixed. When: Reconstructing a timeline after an impairment or long sleep. Why: Without an external date, an incorrect day skews the whole sequence.
- [pitfall] A secondhand description of a lost item can miss details that matter, so the clue must be verified through notes or recollection. When: the physical item is no longer available.
- [pitfall] Sincere belief in a flawed standard can produce testimony that is honest but still wrong.
- [pitfall] A lost or delayed notice makes the person receiving a visitor misread the visitor's intent, because they judge without the information the notice would have given.

## motive from behaviour
- [mechanism] Envy shows through comparison with another's rise, such as a former subordinate's new status, and can make a witness hostile to that person. When: A character's envy should shape their statements or actions. Why: Comparison makes the resentment concrete and affects the witness's reliability.
- [behavior] A person may perform an ordinary act for a motive they cannot name, and may then search that act for hidden meaning it does not have. When: Someone acts without being able to state why. Why: Unacknowledged motive leaves the actor uneasy about their own reasons.
- [rule] Let motive emerge from fragments the player finds, such as NPC dialogue or a marriage record and will draft, with each deduction unlocking a new branch of the investigation. When: when designing a mystery's motive. Why: Step-by-step discovery builds a case the player owns.
- [rule] Do not infer motive from one act alone; a violent or clumsy act may still serve a goal, so check what the actors were pursuing first. When: judging why someone acted. Why: clumsiness and motive are independent.
- [rule] Use financial motive to explain an action only once opportunity and a link to the crime are already in view. When: building a case against a suspect. Why: motive is supporting context, not a starting point.
- [rule] Vary each NPC's dialogue response to a search by motive, such as pride, fear or greed, so the reaction gives clues without explicit text. When: when scripting NPC reactions to investigation. Why: motive shapes reaction more than guilt alone.
- [rule] Separate personal motives, such as family ties, from impersonal ones, such as loyalty to a system, because each calls for different pressure.
- [heuristic] Motive is often inferred from changes in conduct, unexplained requests or concealed errands, and these clues also point to the time the suspect is buying. (x2)
- [heuristic] Infer motive by asking what purpose a chain of acts serves; if no purpose is visible, suspect a hidden design behind them. When: a crime's pattern is clear but its reason is not.
- [heuristic] Look beneath the surface of a person's acts for the impulses and motives behind them, rather than accepting visible behavior at face value.
- [heuristic] A sympathetic motive, such as protecting someone from violence, should shape how the investigator chooses to act. When: deciding the outcome for a suspect. Why: motive changes the moral weight of the crime.
- [heuristic] Test a motive against the suspect's known character; a crime that clashes with their habits and temperament weakens the theory. When: A motive points at a suspect whose known behaviour does not match the act. Why: Character fit is evidence, and a mismatch suggests another actor or a cover story.
- [heuristic] Pair an inferred motive with known deadlines; a scheduled visit shows when discovery will come, which explains why the actor acted when they did. When: A fixed arrival or event is known. Why: The deadline shows what the actor had to beat.
- [heuristic] When a character's route does not match their stated purpose, suggest an unspoken motive worth probing, without concluding guilt from that single act. When: A stated errand and the path taken diverge. Why: A mismatch points to a hidden goal but does not prove one.
- [heuristic] A carefully staged, fitting revenge indicates a personal motive rather than a financial one, which points the investigation toward the hidden injury. When: A larger plan is designed to match an earlier wrong. Why: Deliberate fit between act and grievance reveals the emotional source of the plan.
- [procedure] 1) Record each relevant action with its witness or source. 2) Order the actions chronologically. 3) Confront the suspect with the sequence and test their explanation against it. When: motive is not confessed and must be inferred.
- [procedure] 1) Imagine the suspect's inner state with ordinary common sense set aside. 2) Ask which motive that state would act on. 3) Keep only the suspects whose temperament fits the crime. When: when narrowing suspects by motive. Why: a temperament that fits the act is more likely to have committed it.
- [tradeoff] Prefer surfacing motive through personality clashes over announcing it, but state it openly when a suspect will be cleared later or a character announces a framer's motive. Why: Conflict reveals motive more vividly than statement; a candid remark reads as trivial, so its weight is discounted until it matters; announcing lets the reveal land without group deduction.
- [pitfall] A motive reconstructed from a confessor's own reasoning may describe a belief they held, not what actually happened.
- [pitfall] The motive for a denial cannot be read from the denial alone; it may be deliberate concealment or simply lack of nerve.
- [pitfall] A motive does not identify its holder; the same history can support a different actor. When: When a motive is used to name a suspect. Why: Shared history can implicate several people who had the same grievance.

## planted evidence sources
- [definition] Planted evidence is an item placed to point at a convenient suspect, positioned where that suspect will be blamed.
- [mechanism] A note placed in plain view can be a plant, so its apparent authenticity should be tested against physical details of the scene and the purported author's habits. When: A written statement appears to explain an event. Why: Planted evidence can mislead the investigator into accepting a false explanation.
- [mechanism] A returned notice reading 'not known' can be a planted contradiction that makes a documented story look wrong and prompts the player to re-check. When: a documented story has an unexplained conflicting record. Why: contradictions push the player to question records they had accepted.
- [rule] Plant deliberate trace mismatches, e.g. spectacles too old for the body, a wrong fall position, a broken component, or a uniform contradicted by hair or boots, for players to notice. When: when designing clues that reward attention, a scene the player must reconstruct, or a scene with a misleading surface. Why: A mismatch gives the player a concrete lead to test and lets a careful player overturn the obvious reading.
- [rule] Plant a detail that does not fit the decoy's story, such as a document useless to the thieves, so an attentive player can see through the staging. When: When designing a false trail.
- [rule] Plant evidence for every suspect so a favored theory can be tested rather than confirmed by searching only where it predicts clues. When: Designing a mystery with several suspects. Why: Balanced clues stop players from confirming a favored theory.
- [rule] Plant a mismatch, such as a generous gift from an apparently poor character, as a contradiction the player can later uncover. When: building a mystery with NPC wealth or status. Why: contradictions reward attention and drive further investigation.
- [rule] Plant a plausible false culprit with a motive while keeping the real cause available for the player to find. When: designing misdirection in a mystery. Why: the player should be misled by a fair alternative, not by missing clues.
- [heuristic] Ask whether a location was chosen to be found: places already under suspicion or being searched are likely sites for planted evidence, which proves little when found easily. When: when assessing whether evidence was placed, or a clue arrives neatly where the investigator is already looking. Why: Placement is most useful where evidence will be found, so someone wanting a clue found can place it there.
- [heuristic] Ask whether an object at the scene belongs to someone with no link to the crime, since borrowed items may have been planted to connect an innocent person.
- [heuristic] Ask why a convenient discovery, confession or death arrived at that moment, especially when a case has just stalled. When: a convenient discovery arrives as a case stalls. Why: timing reveals whether the event was arranged.
- [heuristic] Ask whether the person a trace points to could have arranged it, since a gift can make the trace a pointer placed by another. When: a trace seems to implicate one person. Why: Items passed between people can be used to misdirect.
- [heuristic] A counterpart may stage a discrepancy as a test of how the other party handles it.
- [heuristic] Plant a distinctive habit early so the audience can judge later inferences, and let a rival imitate it to mislead. When: When designing misdirection around character identity. Why: A planted signature gives the player a basis to test the inference.
- [heuristic] Plant a false trail, such as an incriminating item in a rival's pocket with a route pointing back to the planter, that the player must clear before finding the true culprit. Why: A convincing false answer delays discovery and raises the payoff of the reveal.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the target to state the evidence that would justify an arrest. 2) Plant the object where they will carry it. 3) Keep them talking. 4) Ask them to reach into the pocket holding the object. When: a target has stated a principle that a planted item can test.
- [pitfall] A planted object may implicate an innocent person; treating a discovered item as conclusive proof without questioning whether it was planted is the mistake a frame-up exploits. When: when an object points neatly at a suspect or a recovered item seems to close a case. Why: Planted items can look like genuine evidence and make the wrong person appear guilty.
- [pitfall] Evidence can be planted to point at one person, so the most obvious clue may be the one someone wanted found. Why: A plant aims at the suspect whose access looks most obvious.
- [pitfall] A tidy room may have been arranged to create an impression, so test whether its dust and clutter are real.
- [pitfall] A track that leads nowhere may have been placed deliberately. Compare it with other evidence before accepting it. When: when a trail ends without a clear destination. Why: A false trail can be made to look like a genuine route.
- [fact] A note pointing to a concealed space shows its writer knew of that space before anyone searched for it.

## scene and location evidence
- [mechanism] A place with a known entry point but no recorded exit can serve as the probable site for further investigation, where a missing person may still be. When: A person entered a location and was never seen leaving it. Why: The unrecorded exit makes the location itself the most likely place to search.
- [mechanism] In an open, empty area with no cover or witnesses, an attack leaves few traces, so the investigation depends on the scene's silence and brief sightings. When: When an attack occurs in a location with no cover, witnesses or footprints. Why: Without cover or witnesses, there is little physical or testimonial evidence to collect.
- [heuristic] Positional details such as an open door or a displaced rug can establish when and how a room was used. When: reconstructing a sequence of events in a room. Why: Physical positions record past actions and can fix a timeline.
- [heuristic] Read the body and surroundings for traces of the victim's movements and the attacker's position, since wounds, clothing and objects each record part of the sequence. When: At the scene, before it is moved or cleared. Why: Physical traces are lost or altered once the scene changes.
- [heuristic] The choice of observation position is itself evidence: a watcher who picks a spot facing outward was probably looking for someone. When: An unusual position is chosen. Why: The position reveals the watcher's purpose.
- [heuristic] Test a physical direction given by an examiner, such as which side a wound came from, against the positions of people in the scene. When: A finding implies who could have been where. Why: Positional facts can confirm or exclude a suspect's account.
- [heuristic] Powder development works best on smooth, non-porous surfaces. On rough surfaces the powder cannot hold fine detail, and smeared prints are hard to recover. When: when choosing whether to dust an object.
- [heuristic] A nearly empty place at a set hour limits witnesses, so it defines the opportunity for an act to go unseen.
- [heuristic] Check a place named in records against a map, tying boundaries to landmarks such as bridges or compass lines. When: a record describes a location's bounds. Why: maps can confirm or reveal inconsistencies.
- [heuristic] A location can hold the memory of an event for someone who witnessed it, and that witness may describe or avoid the place accordingly. When: When a character's account is tied to a place where a death or event occurred. Why: Vivid recollection attaches to the setting where the scene was experienced.
- [heuristic] A location with a known history is a strong clue, but the route taken to reach it can tie a suspect to the place. When: Evidence is found at a site connected to past events. Why: The path to the site creates a link between person and place.
- [heuristic] Test a reconstruction across layout, stains and witness account; no single detail should carry it alone, and all must agree. When: testing a reconstruction against a witness account.
- [heuristic] A location where a person's routines and objects were concentrated is a useful place to search for evidence. When: Choosing where investigators should look. Why: Concentrated personal objects and habits make relevant traces more likely to be found there.
- [procedure] 1) List physical traces: lock state, window access, broken foliage and ground firmness. 2) Test each possible route against them. 3) Reject routes the traces contradict and keep those they allow. When: a scene shows evidence of how a person could have entered or left.
- [procedure] 1) List known positions by hour. 2) Mark each as confirmed by a reliable witness or only claimed. 3) Check each leg of movement against a timetable. When: an alibi covers a span of time with some verifiable points. Why: Feasibility depends on both fixed points and the travel between them.
- [procedure] 1) State what the scene claims happened. 2) Work out the disturbance that event would cause. 3) Apply it to the arranged objects. 4) Check whether they react as claimed or whether the arrangement came later. When: a scene includes an arranged object the victim's last acts would not plausibly produce.
- [procedure] 1) Inspect the whole structure, attic to ground floor, not one damaged spot. 2) Check each hole or mark for a matching mark on the opposite side. 3) Note expected traces that are absent. 4) Read how objects are displaced or left intact. When: a dramatic event must be explained from its physical scene. Why: one spot or one testimony can mislead.
- [tradeoff] Named places can anchor timing when confirmed as the event site; a place named in a dying message is not automatically the crime scene or the killer's home. When: When documents name a place whose timing is uncertain. Why: Named places give fixed points witnesses cannot easily alter, but a name alone does not prove where the event occurred. (x2)
- [pitfall] A witness's memory of a place can be reliable in feeling but unreliable in detail, so it is not proof of what happened there. When: When using a recalled scene as evidence. Why: Emotional intensity preserves impressions better than accurate specifics.
- [fact] A postmark from a post office near a venue, within a stated time window, links the sender to that place and time. When: a parcel was posted near the scene.
- [fact] A preserved location, such as a common field kept unbuilt, can carry memory of past events into the present.

## sightings and hearing
- [mechanism] A distant visible sign can convey information that cannot be heard or reached, and a change in its pattern can reveal activity out of sight. When: when a character must learn of a hidden event from afar.
- [mechanism] Each additional locked room between a trapped person and others adds distance and blocks sound, cutting off help.
- [behavior] A hard-of-hearing witness hears only part of what happens and may build their own explanation, which can diverge from the facts. Why: Missing information gets filled by the witness's own interpretation.
- [rule] Treat sounds heard at a distance as support for a timeline, not as identification of a person. Why: distant sound lacks identifying detail.
- [rule] Check a witness who heard nothing for sleep depth and sensitivity; a known light sleeper makes silence informative.
- [rule] A hearing can deliver facts that are new to both protagonist and reader while keeping their true meaning hidden until later. When: Structuring an information reveal in a scene.
- [rule] Follow a suspect at a distance to learn who they meet, where they go, and how long each visit lasts. When: When the suspect's whereabouts are disputed or a meeting may be hidden.
- [rule] Let a hard-of-hearing or distracted suspect mishear a question, creating a branch where the player must clarify.
- [rule] Let players test a witness's claim about what was seen from a window with a line-of-sight check.
- [heuristic] Distance or absence from a room can prove a listener could not have heard the important content, which narrows suspicion.
- [heuristic] A distant or chance witness can confirm a suspect's identity or a location, but only for what he personally saw. When: An identification or location must be confirmed from far away or by accident. Why: A witness's knowledge stops at the edge of his own observation.
- [heuristic] Treat a heard sound as a timed event, and record the listener's delay before acting, since that delay narrows the window for when the event occurred. When: Reconstructing when a shot or similar sound happened.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the witness's exact position. 2) Test what could be seen from it, ideally by re-enacting with a companion. 3) Identify what was unseen and propose a route that explains it. 4) Verify the route. When: A witness's account depends on what they could see from one position.
- [pitfall] A voice heard through a door or from afar is taken as proof of presence, but a brief reply does not confirm location or that the person was alive then. When: A witness hears a familiar voice through a door, from afar or in the dark, or a reply is the only evidence of presence. Why: They cannot compare it with the real voice, and a voice does not confirm location or time. (x2)
- [pitfall] A distant sighting can misidentify the person; discount detailed identification claimed beyond the range the witness could plausibly see, since recognition weakens with range. When: when a witness saw someone from far away.
- [pitfall] Partially heard or recalled speech gets filled with assumptions and associations; mark each detail heard or inferred, and never treat a remembered phrase as exact. When: A witness reports an overheard or recalled exchange. Why: Partial hearing leaves gaps filled by assumption; unmarked inference is later taken as a full transcript.
- [pitfall] Once an accusation drops distance as a limit on the suspect's reach, any location-based alibi can be dismissed.
- [pitfall] Witnesses estimate distance from perceived speed and duration, and these estimates can be badly off, so a confident distance claim still needs checking.
- [pitfall] A distant observer busy with other work cannot reliably say who was seen or fix the time, so such a sighting is weak. Why: Distance and divided attention limit identity and timing.
- [pitfall] A trail that sends the investigation abroad can leave the case unresolved for days, slowing progress.
- [pitfall] A witness who hears poorly may miss part of a question, so a plain yes or no can be misread as a confession or a slip.

## spectral and supernatural clues
- [model] A supernatural-seeming haunting can be resolved by a mechanical illusion, where an apparition is produced by reflections and an operator with access to the staging. When: designing a haunting mystery with a mundane explanation. Why: Players accept the supernatural frame until a mechanism explains each escalating event.
- [definition] Spectral evidence is testimony that an accused person's apparition harmed or appeared to the afflicted, an unseen or supernatural figure no outside observer can independently check.
- [definition] Spectral sight is a claimed ability to perceive a person's spirit rather than their body, used as evidence against them.
- [mechanism] A supernatural-seeming effect that others can reproduce on demand is exposed as mechanical, turning the claim into a demonstrable trick. When: a reported effect appears only when a particular person is present. Why: Reproduction gives an independent, checkable explanation.
- [rule] Pair dream, vision, trance or spirit clues with a checkable anchor, such as an object, time or location the player can physically confirm or rule out. When: Designing supernatural or mystical clues. Why: Independent physical evidence separates true clues from misleading ones. (x2)
- [rule] A supernatural effect in a staged setting may be performance, since skilled performers such as jugglers or ventriloquists can imitate spirit contact. When: A supernatural effect appears in a staged or performed setting, or is claimed by performers. Why: Recognizing the performance mechanism prevents accepting the claim at face value; performance skill can produce the reported effects. (x2)
- [rule] Mark spectral clues the player cannot verify as unverifiable, and give an independent check or second source before any puzzle or case depends on them. When: A clue cannot be checked by the player. Why: Unverifiable clues cannot settle a case alone.
- [rule] Give a supernatural-seeming event a concrete human cause players can uncover through the same records, testimony and traces as other clues. When: Designing an in-world event that looks uncanny, prophesied or magical. Why: Keeps the mystery solvable through fair evidence; players feel satisfied when apparent magic resolves into traceable human action.
- [rule] Unverifiable testimony may justify an inquiry and strengthen other presumptions, but should not convict without further evidence.
- [rule] Being seen as a spectre by the afflicted is not enough to commit or convict someone.
- [rule] Give each supernatural or hidden claim a checkable consequence, such as a time, place, or object that must move, so it can be shown false. When: Designing a supernatural mystery. Why: Claims without consequences make a weak mystery.
- [rule] Design a mystery where the supernatural solution implicates an NPC's inner state, and let the player test whether a human-scale motive fits the clue. When: when designing a supernatural mystery involving NPCs. Why: A testable motive makes the supernatural answer engage with human behaviour.
- [heuristic] Give eerie horror events, like phantom footsteps, spectral sounds or sleeping guards, human causes testable through tracks, dropped keys, disturbed dust, a spent torch or a gas jet. When: Designing supernatural-seeming events in horror content. Why: Players feel the supernatural reading is earned yet false when it can be tested physically; visible traces let players reason to an ordinary cause.
- [heuristic] When a supernatural explanation points at a person, keep the human actor open and check it against motive and knowledge, since the label can conceal an ordinary cause. When: A supernatural claim or diagnosis points at a person or their behaviour. Why: Premature acceptance of the supernatural answer leaves the human cause unexamined.
- [heuristic] Before accepting a supernatural event, check whether a person gained from the fear it caused. When: an event favours one person in a place with a reputation. Why: a staged event serves its beneficiary.
- [heuristic] A dream or vision can echo real events, so separate its supernatural framing from the human elements it reflects and check those elements against evidence. When: A character experiences a dream or vision that seems prophetic. Why: Gothic framing can make ordinary events seem supernatural.
- [heuristic] Check a frightening account against plain physical facts before accepting any supernatural explanation. When: A scene seems uncanny but has no clear source. Why: Most eerie impressions have an ordinary cause once inspected.
- [heuristic] When a mystery calls for dread, let the investigation confirm a human explanation and leave a supernatural remainder unexplained. When: when a horror story must keep an element of mystery after investigation. Why: A remainder keeps the player's model open and sustains tension.
- [procedure] 1) Identify which parts of a scene have ordinary causes. 2) Check the supernatural explanation against a physical or behavioural event. 3) Give it the same corroboration as any other claim. When: when an event seems supernatural but may have ordinary causes. Why: Separating ordinary causes from the supernatural core shows what the explanation actually supports.
- [pitfall] A supernatural explanation can seem to fit a time window; check the window against physical access before accepting it. When: Evaluating an explanation for an event within a time window. Why: Physical access constraints can rule out a seemingly fitting explanation.
- [fact] Spectral sightings are weak evidence because an unseen agent may take the shape of an innocent person, so a face seen in a vision may not match the real one.

## suspicion dynamics
- [model] A suspicion-reversal mystery moves suspicion across several suspects, each shift backed by a clue, so the final answer must survive every earlier false suspect. Why: Each reversal keeps the player's attention on a new candidate until the true culprit is exposed.
- [mechanism] Suspicion rotates among spouses, friends, servants, rivals and outsiders, moving when a physical, routine or official fact contradicts or points elsewhere. When: A mystery with multiple groups of suspects, when a new fact or pressure event appears. Why: A contradicting fact removes the current suspect's credibility; each new candidate gives the audience a different target to test.
- [mechanism] Clear, expose or reclassify each disguised stand-in as the next impostor appears, so suspicion keeps moving instead of settling on one face. When: Structuring who the player suspects across a mystery. Why: A suspect who is cleared quickly leaves the player searching for the next one.
- [mechanism] Suspicion moves to a suspect only after testimony reframes all earlier clues, so the same explained events are reread as evidence against that suspect. When: Late testimony names a hidden identity. Why: A named motive turns previously dismissed oddities into evidence.
- [mechanism] Suspicion shifts from an outsider to a trusted companion after a concrete event such as a corpse, a disappearance, or a physician's letter. When: The story has reached a turning point with a visible event. Why: A concrete event makes the trusted person's involvement harder to dismiss.
- [mechanism] Suspicion cascades through successive suspects, as each reveal implicates a new party until even the victim appears complicit. When: A mystery with several reveals in sequence. Why: Each new revelation resets trust and pushes suspicion onto whoever is next exposed.
- [mechanism] Suspicion moves in waves as gains and clues surface, and the final suspect gathers clues slowly until a late cluster makes the accusation certain. When: when a story has several suspects over time. Why: clues accumulate and shift belief in stages rather than all at once.
- [mechanism] Suspicion cycles: a convenient suspect falls first, then an innocent party is cleared by a specific alibi or test, and the true author emerges from a dismissed clue. Why: Each cleared suspect narrows belief toward the real culprit.
- [mechanism] Suspicion moves from the most visible outsider to the least obvious insider once a physical trace is read; official suspicion follows easy-to-present evidence, while the investigator follows evidence hard to fake or easy to overlook. Why: Easy-to-present evidence like bloodhounds or prints gets acted on, while subtle traces like dust, hairs or pipe bore expose the real culprit.
- [mechanism] Suspicion can widen gradually through successive suspects, each dropped when a new dated document or record removes it, so the investigation grows in scope.
- [mechanism] Suspicion moves to a new suspect whenever the player's current belief breaks, so each reveal inverts the suspect list. When: a chain of false solutions. Why: The player's last belief is what holds the current suspect in place.
- [behavior] Audiences first suspect a conveniently marked outsider, such as a servant, lover, rival or foreigner, then shift toward an overlooked cause. When: during the middle of a mystery. Why: Suspicion follows family, class and reputation lines, so social markers steer blame.
- [behavior] Audience suspicion moves from victim to liar to new suspect when each claim is tested against a physical fact such as a route, a receipt or a search result. When: a story where claims can be verified against objects or places. Why: each check confirms or breaks a claim, reassigning belief.
- [behavior] Accusation spreads from long-troubled, outspoken figures to newcomers and then to respected members, before turning back on the accusers. When: A crisis where accusations multiply through a community. Why: Each accusation widens the circle until it reaches people with standing, which exposes the process.
- [heuristic] Rotate suspicion among plausible suspects with real motives or grounded facts, such as watched, half-explained figures around a missing person, keeping the culprit in plain sight. When: Choosing suspects for a whodunit or keeping a mystery open while the culprit is unknown. Why: Credible motives keep every suspect plausible until the reveal; shifting suspicion keeps players engaged without inventing unsupported guilt.
- [heuristic] A cluster of closely timed coincidences draws suspicion, and concealment of those coincidences adds weight to it. When: Several related events occur within a short span, especially if hidden from parties. Why: Matching timing and concealment are unlikely under innocent explanations.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a misleading observation that suggests an accident or innocent visitor. 2) Reveal murder through a clue. 3) Arrest a suspect justified by real evidence. 4) Introduce a clue that partly contradicts that suspect. 5) Shift to a rival theory. 6) Repeat with a second false solution. 7) End with a partial confession. When: Structuring the reveal sequence of a whodunit or investigation scenario. Why: Each step is justified by evidence yet leaves the next link open, so no suspect is cleanly cleared.
- [pitfall] Suspicion voiced by one witness can shape how others interpret later events. When: A witness publicly suspects a person. Why: Shared suspicion biases interpretation of subsequent evidence.
- [pitfall] Sympathy for an accused person can shape which suspects are considered, and the investigator may conceal that influence from others. When: An investigator is emotionally invested in a suspect's innocence. Why: Emotional bias steers the search without being openly acknowledged.
- [pitfall] Suspicion based on appearance, such as a foreign look or unusual facial hair, is bias, and audiences notice when a story leans on it. When: Building a suspect's characterisation or a suspicion. Why: Appearance is not evidence, and readers reject suspicion that rests on it.
- [pitfall] A suspect's suspicious movement may have been caused by a call or summons from someone else, which the supposed caller later denies. When: a suspect's timing looks incriminating. Why: A misattributed summons can explain the movement and mislead the group.

## trailing and handoffs
- [mechanism] A servant's exclamation can act as a warning signal that alerts a hidden person inside to an approaching visitor. When: servants interact near a concealed person. Why: Audible greetings carry information to anyone who hears them.
- [mechanism] A physical signal line between a trapped person and someone outside can reveal an action without any noise.
- [behavior] Observers often signal one another, so a timed escape should be planned as if it is being watched. When: Watchers are posted near an escape route. Why: Coordinated signals reveal the watch to the escaper.
- [rule] Agree on a physical signal in advance, such as a visible change in light, where its appearance means discovery and its absence means the watch continues. When: observers must communicate across a distance. Why: a physical cue can be read from afar without alerting the target.
- [rule] Coordinate guard movement with a shared signal, such as a called word or a fired shot, so the group acts together. When: multiple agents must move at the same moment. Why: a common trigger keeps timing consistent across guards.
- [rule] Make the player's signal a deliberate in-world action, and let the AI respond by its own route, so the player must plan around the blind spot. When: designing player-triggered guard responses. Why: the AI's independent route creates a planning challenge for the player.
- [rule] Reward players who read a pattern of several signs, not one clue, with a safe way to disarm the threat.
- [heuristic] When a trail ends, search for a new trace such as faint vehicle wheel marks, which can explain the stop. When: a trail stops at a point in slush or mud.
- [heuristic] The point where a track stops suggests where the walker entered cover, so search there.
- [heuristic] Footprints that lead to an edge and stop indicate the direction of travel, so the search should move to that edge. When: Tracks that end abruptly at water, a wall or a drop. Why: A trail that ends points to where the person likely went next.
- [procedure] 1) Follow a track as far as it runs. 2) Search where it ends, looking for where someone stood or waited and examining that spot closely. 3) At a crossing, choose the next route by the following physical clue, not by guess. Why: A pause point often holds more evidence than a passing track.
- [procedure] 1) Identify who is most likely to carry news of an escape to the hidden party. 2) Follow that intermediary discreetly rather than the fugitive. 3) Let the fugitive go once the trail is known. When: A suspect escapes and the accomplice is unknown. Why: The intermediary is more likely than the fugitive to reach the real target.
- [procedure] 1) Follow the clearest prints first, since distinct prints are easy to track. 2) When the trail is lost, mark the last known print. 3) Search the ground around it in widening passes. When: a moving target leaves prints on soft or mixed ground.
- [procedure] 1) Post a second watcher near the exit. 2) When the first follower is seen, the second takes over the watch. 3) The first withdraws without being noticed. When: the target is alert, has several exits, or may flee. Why: a handoff keeps the trail after one follower is spotted.
- [procedure] 1) Work out the method the culprit must have used. 2) List the residue it would leave and where it would sit. 3) Check which surfaces would keep it. 4) Search in a fixed order, including vehicles. 5) Inspect closely under good light. 6) Stop when light fails and resume next day. When: when planning a search for the traces of an act. Why: searching from the method gives the expected traces.
- [procedure] 1) The signaller watches the route and gives the agreed signal when the target appears. 2) The signaller does not act. 3) The second observer approaches and sees the target's face first. When: a watch depends on one observer identifying a target that another observer reports. Why: identification happens before any confrontation.
- [pitfall] A single signal is unreliable: it cannot be repeated once given, and a passing obstruction can hide it, so use more than one cue. Why: the signal is the only channel between observers.
- [pitfall] Thaw, slush and passing traffic erase prints, and weather can remove a trail entirely.
- [pitfall] A trail that returns on itself misleads an investigator who follows only the first leg.
- [pitfall] A tail can be noticed, so the follower must keep distance and avoid losing the subject. When: During active following of a suspect.
- [pitfall] An object's trail can be lost after its first sale; tracing later buyers may depend on someone who knows them.

## witness error
- [rule] Do not discard a biased witness; test each reported fact separately against independent evidence, such as possessions or payments, since observed facts may hold even when interpretation does not. When: The witness was present but has bias, a grievance, hostility to the questioner, or reasons to shade their account. Why: Bias can distort what a witness reports even when sincere; weigh each claim by the speaker's prejudice and state of mind. (x2)
- [rule] Do not treat a confident group account as proof when light was poor or observers were frightened. When: Many observers agree on a crime's details. Why: Agreement among uncertain observers is not independent confirmation.
- [rule] Design an NPC who protects one faction as a source of bias, so their statements can mislead the player toward a rival. When: Writing NPC dialogue and clues. Why: Biased sources add verification work for the player.
- [rule] Do not assume a witness is lying because they are wrong on a detail, since error and deceit are different and must be assessed separately. When: A witness is shown to be wrong on a specific point. Why: A mistaken detail does not by itself prove intent to mislead.
- [rule] Plant a witness's honest mistake, such as hearing one place but being told another, so it reads as innocent first and as a clue later. Why: A clue hidden in an innocent error is recognised only once its meaning is known.
- [heuristic] A witness tied to a suspect or faction by friendship, rivalry, kinship, debt or loyalty has a stake and may point toward a rival, so their account is not neutral. When: The witness has a personal, financial, kinship or factional tie to the suspect, or protects an allied group. Why: Loyalty, interest or a stake in the outcome colours what the witness reports; record the reasons for their stance. (x2)
- [heuristic] A first-person narrator with romance, self-interest or hindsight may give a clean record that omits their own contact with the victim; weigh it against other sources. When: The narrator benefits from how events are recorded. Why: Self-interest shapes which events the record includes.
- [heuristic] Affection, hostility or past history can make a witness minimise, idealise or omit facts; weigh their account against that history and their attachment and defensiveness. When: A companion, relative or another character describes a person they are close to, hostile to, or have history with. Why: Past relations and emotional closeness colour present judgments and what is reported or omitted.
- [heuristic] Watchers blended among ordinary people make a hiding place seem safe to its occupants.
- [heuristic] Minor witnesses may give information grudgingly, so extract it bit by bit and check each piece.
- [tradeoff] A biased witness adds emotional texture and misdirection, but a clean, unbiased witness is needed when the player must learn the event accurately. When: choosing a witness to an event.
- [pitfall] Confidence does not measure accuracy: do not rank a more confident witness as more reliable, and test strong claims, including whether the reported event happened. When: A witness is sure of an identification, especially by conspicuous features when identity matters, or claims they could not be mistaken about someone they know. Why: Sincere, detailed accounts can still be unreliable perception, and confidence reflects assumptions as much as observation; check motive and memory. (x3)
- [pitfall] Even a confident, disciplined witness can be sure of an outcome they never saw; separate what they observed from what they inferred, since reliability does not extend beyond their view.
- [pitfall] Confidence in a face or seal does not confirm dates, timing, settings or names; check those details separately. When: When weighing a witness's confident recognition or seal identification. Why: Confidence reflects the witness's feeling about memory, not the accuracy of its details; they may be certain about the wrong moment.
- [pitfall] Confident tone does not prove direct knowledge or accuracy; emotion, drink, rumour or admitted personal lapses can sound convincing, so separate testimony from actual knowledge. When: Assessing a convinced witness whose knowledge is central to the case. Why: Confidence is a delivery quality, not access to the event; a person can believe they know more than they do.
- [pitfall] Companions who are also suspects or friends may give biased accounts of a suspect's whereabouts.
- [pitfall] Witness descriptions of an object's cost or use may be exaggerated or coloured by the witness's motives and should be checked against other evidence. When: Relying on witness testimony about objects. Why: Witnesses may have reasons to distort what they saw.
- [pitfall] A half-seen listener, such as a glimpse of a coat or a moving door, is not proof of identity and is easily misidentified. When: a listener was only partly seen or heard.
- [pitfall] A forceful lay observer can be right for the wrong reasons, so a reveal should rest on evidence rather than on how confidently someone speaks. When: Weighing competing explanations.
- [pitfall] A confident witness may still misremember a physical detail, so the answer must be asked directly and recorded exactly.
- [pitfall] A detailed, confident statement can still be wrong, because fear can inflate what a witness imagines seeing. When: When a witness under fear gives a vivid, complete account. Why: Fear and imagination can produce confident but mistaken detail.

## crime clocks
- [mechanism] An alibi is judged against the time a crime was believed to occur. When that believed time shifts, an earlier statement can change meaning.
- [mechanism] An object seen before one time and gone at a later check bounds when it was present; the window lies between the two observations. When: A witness reports an object at two observation points. Why: Absence at a later check limits how long the object could have been there.
- [mechanism] A sequence of symptoms that worsens in fixed stages acts as a clock, showing the victim nearing a fatal end and creating a deadline. When: A threat progresses through ordered stages. Why: Each stage signals proximity to the final outcome.
- [behavior] Witnesses usually recall events, sights and sounds, but rarely recall the dates or the intervals between events. When: Eliciting testimony about a sequence of events.
- [behavior] Witnesses of the same event often recall small details differently, so minor disagreements do not by themselves show that one is lying.
- [rule] Anchor each event to one time source shared by all observers and the reader, such as a public clock, a watch set by someone else, or a standing meal time. When: when several observers record events. Why: A shared clock lets every time-stamped event be compared directly; a public clock lets several witnesses check it independently.
- [rule] Map each witness's claim to the exact moment they could have observed it, and discard claims whose timing their position could not allow. When: reconstructing who was where and when. Why: a claim is usable only if the witness was positioned to see it.
- [rule] Ask handlers whether they noticed the individual feature and when; a recollection made before the event is stronger evidence.
- [rule] Ask a witness to tie each event to a clock time rather than a loose period, so the account can be checked against other facts. When: When re-questioning a witness whose account is vague. Why: Exact times can be cross-checked, loose periods cannot.
- [rule] Let a faction's influence shift over time, such as after a vote, to model a weakening hold that opens a window for a new approach. When: designing faction power that changes across the game.
- [heuristic] Ask whether a witness's clock runs true; a known offset from true time lets the investigator correct the time the witness reports. When: A witness's timing depends on a household or public clock, or the witness mentions keeping their clock off true time. Why: Knowing the clock's bias lets the investigator adjust the reported time.
- [heuristic] A survivor who saw companions fall bounds their deaths to a short time window.
- [heuristic] The same timing can support opposing claims, so apply the feasibility check separately to each claim rather than to one favoured story.
- [heuristic] Timing data gathered over a short period may not reflect the subject's full range of behavior. When: when estimating a subject's schedule from limited observation. Why: Short samples miss variants the subject uses at other times.
- [heuristic] Fix the crime to a precise minute so that alibis and the crime can be measured against the same clock. Why: A shared clock makes each alibi's window directly comparable to the event.
- [heuristic] Anchor witness times to events others can confirm, such as a clock striking, a bell, a door closing or a vehicle leaving.
- [procedure] 1) Pick a vivid event both witnesses remember and fix its date. 2) Place other events before or after it. 3) Verify the anchor first, because a misremembered anchor shifts the whole sequence. When: Witnesses give conflicting times and need a common reference point to order events. Why: Without a shared reference, the sequence of events cannot be built reliably.
- [procedure] 1) Lay all accounts side by side on one timeline. 2) Mark which times are fixed by outside events and which are only estimates. 3) Test each alibi and claimed time against the fixed points. Why: Alibis are only as strong as their anchors.
- [procedure] 1) List the scheduled events, such as NPC routines and phone calls. 2) Record each as a checkable time window. 3) Let the player compare windows to find who had the opportunity. When: a game needs a shared timeline of character movements.
- [pitfall] Witnesses may misjudge how long a process takes; check the duration against a second source where possible. Why: A wrong duration shifts the entire computed window.

## culprit identity and motive
- [model] A mystery can open with a visible but dismissed detail, such as a figure seen in the garden, and later pay it off as the true mechanism behind the crime. When: planting clues in a scenario's opening scene. Why: Early dismissed details are remembered and recontextualized once the real mechanism is revealed.
- [mechanism] A trusted helper whose knowledge is precise from the start can be revealed as the true antagonist later, and the reveal feels fair because the early clues were visible. When: Designing a twist where an ally turns out to be the controlling party. Why: Precise early knowledge is a clue the player can later reinterpret, so the unmasking reads as a payoff rather than a cheat.
- [mechanism] A culprit who knows enough to act but not enough to conceal leaves traces that a specialist can read. When: When an offender's method is clumsy, unusual, or uses non-specialist tools. Why: The gap between acting and concealing exposes what the offender did not intend to show.
- [behavior] A narrator who presents as detached may still reveal a personal stake through partly denied motives and minimised admissions, which readers can reread after the reveal. When: when an unreliable narrator hides a motive. Why: Concealment in narration leaves traces that become clear only after the twist.
- [behavior] A contradiction planted early, such as luxury against a claimed poverty, is read as character detail rather than clue, so it works as a later clue. When: when an early detail conflicts with a character's stated situation. Why: Audiences file contradictions as personality until they become relevant.
- [rule] Let the culprit make a mistake that a witness can later recall, so the mistake becomes the trigger for the reveal. When: when a disguised culprit must be exposed. Why: a remembered remark connects the disguise to the person hidden beneath it.
- [rule] Plant the true culprit's motive early in a minor scene so the reveal recontextualizes known material instead of appearing from nowhere.
- [heuristic] Hide the culprit in a familiar, constantly seen role or routine, such as a waiter, postman, servant, or habitual task in the victim's space, so their presence goes unremarked. When: Hiding the culprit among ordinary scenes or choosing a hidden culprit. Why: Routine and familiar presence is seen constantly and rarely examined, so suspicion does not fall on the culprit early.
- [heuristic] A culprit who volunteers unprompted explanations, such as motive asides, leaves a checkable slip in their own dialogue. When: writing an antagonist's dialogue. Why: unrequested explanation can contradict later facts.
- [heuristic] Make an antagonist dangerous through clear internal logic and motive rather than arbitrary irrationality. When: Designing a villain. Why: Consistent motive makes a character both frightening and understandable.
- [heuristic] Trigger a reaction when the player presents a detail that only the culprit could have known. When: Designing a confession or exposure moment. Why: Exact private knowledge is a strong signal that breaks a suspect's composure.
- [heuristic] Reject a culprit theory when physical traces, such as hair or marks, fail to match the proposed agent.
- [heuristic] Turn a character's obsession into a concrete act, so the reveal shows a violation rather than an abstract fixation.
- [heuristic] Let the lure used to trap the culprit be the culprit's own advertisement or message, so the trap feels like a discovery rather than a coincidence. When: designing a trap or lure for a hidden antagonist. Why: A lure drawn from the antagonist's own behavior is more believable to both the antagonist and the player.
- [heuristic] Place the true director among the searchers or helpers, and give him a useful investigative role, so he stays close to the case without drawing suspicion. Why: Proximity to the investigation hides the culprit and gives him access to evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who profits from a death or crime. 2) Check whether that person's stake actually points toward the crime. 3) Map each victim against any payout threshold and the effect of each death on the beneficiary's claim. When: Ranking suspects by gain, especially when rewards depend on conditions. Why: The beneficiary's real stake determines whether the gain supports or undercuts suspicion.
- [procedure] 1) Define the culprit's grievance, fear or passion. 2) Imagine planning the act from that state. 3) Check whether the act is consistent with that state. 4) Read the physical evidence from that viewpoint. When: The puzzle turns on why a person acted or who would act that way. Why: Motive-led reasoning narrows suspects before physical evidence is tested.
- [tradeoff] Keeping an investigator's role hidden stops the other side from adjusting its behaviour, but the advantage ends once the role becomes known early. When: An investigator can act more effectively if the opposing side does not know their involvement. Why: Secrecy removes the chance for the other side to counter; early disclosure removes that advantage.
- [pitfall] Treating a private conviction as if it were evidence can lead an investigation toward the wrong conclusion. When: An investigator is certain of a suspect's guilt or innocence. Why: Certainty substitutes for proof and skews what is pursued.
- [fact] Culprits in mystery resolutions may be punished publicly, escape through social standing, or be handled privately to avoid scandal. When: deciding how a mystery ends. Why: Social position and discretion can change what justice looks like.

## npc dialogue reactions
- [mechanism] Trigger a visible NPC reaction, such as a changed animation or dialogue line, when a contradicting clue is shown. When: Designing confrontation scenes with clues. Why: A visible reaction signals to the player that a contradiction landed.
- [mechanism] Ambient conditions such as room temperature or fuel quality change a slow trigger's timing, so the same puzzle plays out differently across runs.
- [mechanism] Log when an NPC changes its story after speaking with another NPC, giving the player a contradiction to probe.
- [mechanism] An NPC interruption or distraction, such as a drink offer or another character arriving, can change an NPC's willingness to speak and open a window to press a topic.
- [mechanism] A companion NPC can offer a wrong interpretation, with journal entries the player can later correct as new evidence arrives. When: Designing companions who give guidance. Why: Corrections keep the story fair.
- [rule] Give NPCs visible tells, such as a glance, tone change, stammer or flushed face, when they hide information, so players can read deception and record it as a lead. When: When designing dialogue with NPCs who hide information or cut off a topic. Why: A noticeable cue lets players connect the reaction to a hidden room, key or suspect, so deception can be read without a lie detector.
- [rule] Let inspecting a physical object, such as a mirror or a fitting, unlock a new dialogue branch. Why: object inspection rewards exploration with conversation.
- [rule] Let the player show an object to an NPC and return silence, a deflection or a slip; a slip line should appear only after the matching clue is found. When: designing NPC reactions to a found item.
- [rule] Let an NPC hold a hidden fact and give only oblique hints, with the reward scaled to how readily the player catches them.
- [rule] Use a pause or silence in dialogue to prompt the player to speak and reveal something in return. When: Designing a conversation where the NPC wants the player to disclose. Why: Silence creates a turn the player feels compelled to fill.
- [rule] Make a character's reaction differ by topic: calm on neutral subjects and a sudden change on the topic tied to a hidden fact. When: Designing NPC responses that should hint at a hidden fact. Why: Contrast between neutral and sensitive topics makes the sensitive one stand out.
- [heuristic] Use a countdown or ambient cue, such as a striking clock, dim light or a long silence, to build tension before a judgement result. When: A trial or judgement scene. Why: Sensory cues slow the moment and make the wait before the result feel heavier.
- [heuristic] Score a suspect's line in context, so the same line carries different meaning after different preceding events. When: designing interrogation dialogue systems. Why: meaning depends on prior state.
- [heuristic] In an interrogation scene, let players restate a suspect's account; a correction or added detail can open new evidence nodes such as a key or dropped object.
- [heuristic] Track which cues the player has actually observed, so that a later suspect match depends on the cues collected. When: Implementing identification through collected cues. Why: A match based on the player's own observations is fair and traceable.
- [heuristic] Lock NPC memories behind cue items; players unlock a recollection by bringing the right object or person.
- [heuristic] Give NPC dialogue argument-based responses that the player must answer with evidence rather than force, and let a second NPC be brought into the conversation. When: Designing confrontation scenes with NPCs. Why: Evidence and a second voice move an argumentative NPC where repeated pressure does not.
- [heuristic] NPC dialogue can branch on whether the player reveals or conceals what they know, and a frightened NPC can be pressured into luring another character. When: In dialogue systems that track player knowledge. Why: Choices about disclosure change how NPCs respond and what they will do.
- [pitfall] An offhand remark about a suspect's conduct can be taken as an accusation, shifting the witness's stance.
- [fact] A player's confidence in a deduction can be shown by a meter that drops when the player examines a clue closely, so the deduction feels earned. When: Designing investigation feedback in a game.

## physical evidence and objects
- [mechanism] A missing object such as clothing or a collar can stand in for the missing person until a later reveal gives it meaning. When: A body or person is absent or unidentified in a scene. Why: The object carries the question until its meaning is supplied.
- [rule] Keep the central object in motion, changing hands at intervals, so the goal stays open and each new holder redirects the pursuit.
- [heuristic] A route across space that has been occupied for a long time is unlikely to pass unseen, and nearby rooms may show whether a ladder or path was in use. When: When judging whether a route could have gone unnoticed. Why: Sustained occupancy and sightlines make a route visible to observers.
- [heuristic] A missing item can point to a recent action, such as removal shortly before an event, so note what is absent as well as what is present. When: When a person's usual belongings are absent from a scene. Why: Absence can record a deliberate or hurried action.
- [heuristic] Look for an object present at one visit and absent at another; its presence or absence can settle which visit came first. When: Two candidate visit orders exist and one physical item links to only one of them. Why: A dated physical state orders events that testimony alone cannot.
- [heuristic] Let a hidden object be examined for an innocent reason, so the audience files it in the wrong category until the reveal corrects it. When: when an object is central to the eventual reveal. Why: a harmless first impression keeps the true nature hidden.
- [heuristic] Offer a small object tied to a stated habit; if the person's behavior with it contradicts their claim, the claim is weakened without any accusation. When: when a witness asserts a personal habit that can be checked. Why: Actions reveal what claims cannot, and the test stays informal.
- [heuristic] An out-of-place or abandoned object with an unusual feature, such as unusually strong cord, can point to a planned method.
- [heuristic] Let a found item's stains and wear imply its owner's habits and situation, giving the player a profile to search by.
- [heuristic] Pair two pieces of physical evidence so that one explanation, such as a disguise, accounts for both at once. When: Resolving contradictory physical evidence. Why: One explanation that covers both pieces feels more convincing than two separate ones.
- [procedure] 1) Bring the scene object close to a matching item in the suspect's space. 2) Compare the two for an identical mark. 3) Record the match. 4) Combine it with other independent matches before drawing a conclusion. When: Checking whether a scene object links to a suspect or location. Why: Careful comparison yields a record that gains weight only when combined with independent evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Start with the least destructive method, such as feeling, weighing or comparing. 2) Escalate to opening or breaking only if the first methods fail. 3) Keep the evidence intact throughout. When: Evidence might be destroyed or changed by opening or breaking it. Why: Destructive tests can ruin evidence, so they should be a last resort.
- [procedure] 1) Give the stolen item a chain of owners, such as a sale, a club, or a market. 2) Make each owner a separate interview that narrows the search. 3) End the chain at the insider who handled the item last. When: Designing a theft investigation. Why: Each interview eliminates candidates and the chain converges on the true thief.
- [pitfall] An object that carries too many hints at once loses its force, so spread clues across separate objects. When: Designing a clue object. Why: Too many simultaneous hints dilute each one and make the object hard to read.
- [pitfall] A person who destroys evidence in panic often ignores the visible traces left behind, and a surviving duplicate defeats the purpose of destruction. When: A character destroys a document under emotional stress. Why: Strong emotion narrows attention to the act itself rather than the aftermath or copies.
- [pitfall] A missing item is evidence only once someone knows it was present, so witness memory of an item gives its absence weight. When: Judging whether an absence matters. Why: Without knowing the item existed, its absence is not noticed.
- [pitfall] Even skilled readers of remains can reach a wrong answer if they misjudge the decay environment. When: Interpreting remains when the burial or submersion environment is uncertain. Why: Decay signatures depend on environment, so a wrong environment yields wrong conclusions.
- [pitfall] Treating an object's found location as proof of custody without tracing its earlier positions.
- [fact] Paint generally resists water, so a spot that washes off with water is unlikely to be paint.
- [fact] A hazard delivered through a physical object in the room, such as a poisoned lamp, is a stronger mystery element than a hidden attacker. When: designing lethal environments in a closed space. Why: The threat is already present and discoverable, so players investigate the setting rather than search for an intruder.

## physical traces and damage
- [model] A scene's physical record has three trace kinds: damage pattern, residue and marks, which are read together to reconstruct what happened. When: Investigating a room or location.
- [mechanism] A bullet hole with splintering on the room side shows the shot was fired from inside toward the outside, implying a person beyond the room.
- [mechanism] A polished joint surface indicates friction after cartilage loss, which can imply a joint disease, and from it a likely limp or pain. When: Reading wear on a joint surface. Why: Loss of protective cartilage exposes bone to friction, and the resulting disease affects how a person moves.
- [behavior] Damage in a room is often read as a sign of struggle, even when one actor caused it, such as a shot that struck a reflecting surface.
- [rule] Use a physical oddity, such as a mismatched stain or a turned rug, that implies concealment without naming the thief.
- [heuristic] The length left on a partly burnt item shows how long it was used, and a stub's condition can show who could have used it. When: Inspecting partly used items such as matches or cigarette stubs. Why: Burning and wear leave a measurable record of use and of the user.
- [heuristic] An object broken where it fell suggests accident, while one crushed deliberately suggests someone acted on it. When: Judging how a broken object came to its state. Why: The pattern of damage reflects the force applied.
- [heuristic] Make a physical detail falsify an assumed fact, so the reveal comes from the environment rather than new information. When: building a late reversal. Why: a visible detail is checkable by the player.
- [heuristic] An object taken in haste often leaves secondary damage, such as a pulled fastening or a torn tie, that reveals the urgency and purpose of the taking.
- [heuristic] Physical traces such as footprints, damage and marks on a body can connect events and confirm a theory.
- [heuristic] A broken personal item at a site points to a struggle or sudden loss rather than casual dropping, but the damage shows that something happened, not what.
- [heuristic] Compare a damage pattern with what the assumed cause would normally produce; a mismatch suggests a different cause. When: The cause of damage is unclear.
- [heuristic] Physical traces are harder to fake than sounds, so surfaces where a hidden mechanism would leave marks should be inspected directly. When: Investigating a scene where a hidden device could explain sounds. Why: Physical marks persist and are less open to misperception than sounds.
- [procedure] 1) Hold the item by its edge or tip. 2) Breathe gently on a smooth, non-porous surface. 3) Look for a brief ridge pattern as the fog clears. 4) Confirm with powder and photography where it matters. When: checking polished metal for recent handling without equipment. Why: A quick screen reveals likely handling without touching the working surface.
- [pitfall] Calling damage vandalism without examining what was taken and what was left misses the organizing pattern.
- [pitfall] Burnt paper does not prove when an action happened, since a fire may have burned out at another time.
- [pitfall] A sample taken loosely, or one whose label is lost, can be useless or misidentified.
- [pitfall] Leaving the cause of an injury unstated keeps the wound's origin open, but it can frustrate a player who expects an answer by the end. When: A death shows a wound without an explained cause. Why: An unanswered cause can read as an oversight rather than deliberate ambiguity.
- [fact] Blackened, burnt wound edges indicate a close-range shot, while wounds from a greater distance are less severe.
- [fact] Busy entrances are poor sources of footprint evidence because many people have passed through them. When: Searching a heavily used doorway. Why: Heavy traffic overwrites or hides individual traces.

## scripted npc behaviour
- [mechanism] A scripted NPC rebuttal can be answered only by presenting a specific item, so dialogue branches depend on whether the player holds the decisive proof.
- [mechanism] A non-player character running a fake ritual can use scripted effects such as lights out or prepared answers, which the player must uncover by spotting props. When: When designing a deceptive NPC ritual or performance. Why: Scripted effects rely on props and rehearsed responses that a player can detect.
- [mechanism] A character who instructs others what to say fixes their account in advance, so later questioning meets a prepared story rather than spontaneous memory. When: A suspect can influence the people who will be questioned. Why: A pre-set story answers questions before they are asked.
- [rule] Script NPC reactions to probing questions and news as readable tells, such as a changed tone, sudden request, or guilt or relief, so players can test which reading is correct.
- [rule] Script NPC replies to show sharp reactions or topic changes on sensitive subjects, giving the player a clue to follow up. When: A question touches a sensitive subject. Why: Reactions reveal what the NPC is hiding.
- [rule] Script NPC reactions as data, so a changed expression at a specific character's arrival flags a hidden relationship for the player. When: Designing NPCs who hide a relationship with another character. Why: Recorded reactions give the player a readable signal to investigate.
- [rule] Set a scripted reveal for a later event in a specific location, after the player has collected the needed clues. When: designing a scene that resolves a mystery. Why: the reveal then rewards the player's earlier investigation.
- [rule] Trigger an overhearing NPC with a scripted line the player can watch for a reaction to, and make hidden enemies react to the volume and position of player dialogue. When: When designing stealth or eavesdropping encounters. Why: Tying reactions to speech volume and position makes the listener's behaviour legible to the player.
- [rule] Script a series of NPC warnings or rumours to set up a later event, and log who spread each one so the player can trace the motive back. When: When designing a game event that should appear foreshadowed. Why: A traceable chain makes the event feel prepared and lets players reason about motive.
- [rule] Script a suspicious NPC to name a rival when questioned, creating a trust puzzle the player must resolve. When: when the player questions the NPC about a crime. Why: deflection gives players a conflicting source to weigh.
- [rule] Script the order in which information reaches the player, since whichever contact the player meets first can shape how later events are interpreted. When: designing a sequence of NPC encounters.
- [rule] Script a town event in advance and trigger it from earlier clues, so the player arrives into an already charged crowd. When: designing town or community events.
- [rule] Hide a key item with a minor NPC, such as a servant, so the player is surprised when authorities produce it. When: scripting a reveal that depends on a secondary character. Why: a minor NPC holding the clue creates a fair but unexpected turn.
- [heuristic] Give a suspect's scripted excuse, account, or bluff about a character's nature a conflict with facts found later, so players who test it against other evidence are rewarded. When: Designing NPC testimony in a mystery. Why: Rewards players who compare claims with the rest of the evidence.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC a dialogue branch that tests the player's accusation, so a correct accusation produces a telling reaction and an incorrect one produces none. When: Designing NPC dialogue for accusations. Why: Telling reactions reward correct reasoning and give feedback to the player.
- [heuristic] Script a suspect to make a revealing move, such as a visit or moved item, only after apparent inaction, and provide a fallback path for a suspect who does nothing.
