When: Designing investigation triggers for a suspect NPC. Why: A delayed trigger rewards patience while the fallback prevents a stalled case.
- [heuristic] Script an NPC to behave differently when alone or unobserved, giving players a reason to spy on them and watch for tells. When: Designing characters with hidden motives. Why: Players who watch unobserved moments gain evidence the NPC hides in public.
- [procedure] 1) Hold the character in isolation for a period. 2) Stage an emotional meeting with a relative. 3) Branch later dialogue on the player's earlier choices. When: when scripting an interrogation scene.
- [procedure] 1) Script in-world news or NPC hints that push players toward a suspect. 2) Plan a later reveal that corrects the record.
- [fact] A scripted distress display has a fixed sequence: collapse, rigidity, shrieking, then being carried toward the accused, and it can be repeated on cue.

## standing and status
- [mechanism] A sign such as an empty vehicle or an injured person signals violence before the source of the danger is shown.
- [behavior] A family's standing can shelter a member from consequences that others face. When: when an accusation is made against a family member. Why: Influential relations can protect a person from the outcome others face.
- [rule] Let an NPC's testimony depend on a status flag such as drugged or injured, changing how far the player should trust it.
- [rule] When a witness who could confirm a claim is gone, replace that confirmation with a document such as a record or ledger; in games, pair removed testimony with a replacement document.
- [rule] Treat every statement as unverified until it has been checked.
- [rule] Design a status-stake NPC whose later reversal serves as a planted clue. When: designing NPC arcs.
- [rule] Do not treat good standing or a long list of good deeds as proof of innocence.
- [heuristic] A witness who knows damaging details is often removed or sent away before the main action, since they might gossip or testify. When: A plan depends on secrecy. Why: Witnesses who know the context threaten the plan.
- [heuristic] Include a witness who is sure of a detail that the level later contradicts, so the player learns to ask how the witness knew. When: when designing NPC testimony for a mystery level. Why: Players learn to question confident claims by testing them against evidence.
- [heuristic] Ask why a witness was present; a conventional, trustworthy appearance may be the very asset a scheme relies on. When: a witness's presence seems convenient. Why: a witness chosen for usefulness rather than company is suspicious.
- [heuristic] Ask who gained status from a belief, and whether that gain predicts their later support or opposition.
- [pitfall] A witness may be working for the culprit, may be the actor, or may be shielding someone, so their account needs the same checking as anyone else's. When: A witness is close to the event.
- [pitfall] A respected speaker's standing can overshadow the substance of what he said, so the content deserves a separate check.
- [pitfall] A key witness's death can end an inquiry, so its cause should be questioned rather than assumed.
- [pitfall] A witness who names an outside culprit may have their own reasons, so the account must be checked against that witness's history, including unexplained gaps. When: a witness offers an outside suspect. Why: the witness may be steering suspicion away from themselves.
- [pitfall] A witness who also judges the case exceeds their role, and the two roles must stay separate. Why: a witness's stake conflicts with a judge's neutrality.
- [pitfall] A label such as 'in her right mind' does not separate reliable speech from fit speech unless a method for checking that state exists.
- [fact] Witnesses respond to the role the questioner appears to play, so a questioner seen as police changes how a witness speaks. When: A witness perceives the questioner as an official investigator. Why: The perceived role shapes the witness's guardedness and manner of answering.
- [fact] A surviving building can record its owners and visits, and its history can be pieced together by matching it against land records. When: a historic site still stands. Why: Physical places carry traces of ownership that written records can confirm.
- [fact] A later statute raised penalties so that the practice itself, not its harmful result, became the test of guilt. When: when legal tests shift between statutes.

## unlikely suspects
- [rule] If observers would have seen a person on a claimed route, reject that route claim; sightlines and timing decide which paths were possible. When: When a character claims to have escaped or travelled by a particular path. Why: Observed absence on a path makes the claim fail.
- [rule] Do not drop a theory only because its apparent beneficiary looks unlikely, since the real motive may be hidden. Keep the theory open while checking other possibilities.
- [rule] Before treating a missing item as stolen, rule out breakage, discarding, and misplacement. When: An item is missing and theft is suspected. Why: Other causes of absence are common and would change the suspect list.
- [heuristic] An unlikely alternative that fits the facts may still be true, so check whether its requirements can be met before rejecting it, while facts remain unknown.
- [heuristic] Ruling out the obvious owners of a trace shifts attention toward outsiders.
- [heuristic] Check unrelated news items for links to the case, since a report that seems off-topic can connect to a clue. When: Information in a news feed or notice board may bear on an open case. Why: Connections between separate reports are easy to overlook.
- [heuristic] If the victim never acquired a category of item, its absence says nothing about what the culprit took, so that category can be ruled out. When: Purchase or inventory records show no such category. Why: Items never owned cannot have been removed.
- [heuristic] Frivolous or uninformed NPCs can be innocent of the main plot, so the player should not read them as suspects. When: Designing NPCs who seem suspicious through manner alone. Why: A misleading manner can make an innocent character seem guilty.
- [procedure] 1) State dispensing error as an explicit theory. 2) Ask whether it could have happened. 3) Check the figures to rule it in or out. When: A substance may have been mis-supplied. Why: An unchecked error can quietly distort the case.
- [pitfall] A decoy left unresolved, never connecting to anything, frustrates the audience and feels like a cheat; vague uncheckable hints read as teasing, not fair play. When: a clue or hint is planted. Why: an audience needs a way to check a lead.
- [pitfall] Unrelated facts placed near the main claim look like clues and waste investigative time.
- [pitfall] Ruling a person out by assumption or appearance, rather than by a test, invites a wrong conclusion.
- [pitfall] Unresolved facts, such as an unread will that hides who the executors are, can change where a suspect goes next, so the predicted path must be revised.
- [pitfall] Keeping a confidant uninformed creates strain and may lead them to act on false beliefs.
- [pitfall] Hidden accomplices can keep key moments unobserved, so a scene can look innocent even when staging took place.
- [pitfall] A deep print near a tree may be unrelated to the main path, so it must not be read as part of the same sequence. When: When a separate impression lies near the main track. Why: Mixing unrelated marks into one sequence produces a false timeline.
- [pitfall] A decoy can fail when the people acting within it are not told the plan, since they may react in ways that expose it.
- [pitfall] Ruling out a distant sender requires confirmed absence, since an intermediary may have passed the information along.
- [pitfall] A group acting outside official process can be more dangerous than official authority, because its members answer to no one. Why: no formal accountability limits its actions.
- [pitfall] A ruling does not end all pressure; some officials may still argue that the proceeding should continue. When: assuming a ruling settles a dispute.

## alibi reasoning
- [rule] When motive reasoning reaches a deadlock, introduce a new clue that breaks the tie. When: two suspects remain equally plausible after motive tests.
- [rule] Make the real culprit's alibi a witnessed event whose sightline misleads, and make the witness's account something the player can check. Why: A checkable sightline lets a careful player catch the deception.
- [heuristic] One broken link collapses a circumstantial chain however strong the others are, so to break a chain, seek one fact undermining its premise rather than attacking each link.
- [heuristic] An alibi that checks out can overturn the investigator's working theory, so be ready to revise it.
- [heuristic] Where a trail breaks off, reason about how the walker could have avoided leaving marks, such as by wading through water. When: A track ends abruptly at water or hard ground. Why: Knowing how the walker avoided marks helps the investigator predict where to look next.
- [heuristic] Link earlier insults to later misfortunes only with a visible causal trace, or players will read the link as unfair coincidence. When: designing narrative consequences in a game. Why: Unexplained links feel arbitrary to players.
- [heuristic] When an accusation rests on what was seen, catch the suspect in the act, because otherwise the blame falls back on the accusers.
- [heuristic] Disprove each false solution with a physical clue the player has already seen, such as footprints, a count of objects, or a record. When: a suspect is ruled out during an investigation. Why: Physical clues already in view make each correction verifiable and fair.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the event's time window from independent clocks and observers. 2) Record each suspect's time claim and each sighting time. 3) Compute the gap between last sighting and discovery. 4) Check each account fits that gap, cross-checking witnesses covering different parts. 5) Test physical ability to reach the scene. 6) Keep competing causes on record. When: when a suspect must be placed away from a scene at a given hour, or a timeline is contested, such as testing whether a person could have acted within a bounded window. Why: Anchoring the window first keeps suspects' claims from defining it; bounded gaps show which accounts must be explained. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) List everyone with access to the scene, or the means and chance to act. 2) Establish the crime's time window. 3) Confirm each person's alibi against that window. 4) Clear those proven elsewhere; keep the rest for further testing. When: when several people had access to the scene or the means and chance to act.
- [procedure] 1) Establish motive. 2) Establish means, such as how the weapon was acquired. 3) Establish opportunity. 4) Argue each link in turn. When: when no direct witness exists.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the premise the alibi depends on, such as a sealed place or a fixed schedule. 2) Look for a gap in that premise, including unguarded routes. 3) Build a timeline from independent clocks and routines. 4) Place each witness's observation on it. When: Testing an alibi that claims a place was sealed or a schedule was fixed. Why: An alibi is only as strong as its premises, and a timeline shows where a premise fails.
- [procedure] 1) List who had a motive to accuse. 2) Separate harm that followed a quarrel from harm the accused actually caused. When: investigating an accusation built on a sequence of misfortunes. Why: Sequence alone does not establish causation.
- [procedure] 1) List all possible explanations for a result. 2) Drop each explanation that conflicts with the facts. 3) Accept the remaining explanation, after checking the candidate list is complete. When: Several causes could explain a result. Why: Elimination narrows candidates to what the evidence supports.
- [procedure] 1) Attend the scheduled event yourself rather than relying on memory. 2) Record when each suspect is absent from the scene. 3) Compare absences across suspects to find who had an unobserved window. When: A crime occurred during a scheduled event with clear entrances and exits. Why: Direct observation produces reliable absence records that memory cannot.
- [tradeoff] A missing alibi may be neutral (no witness, unwilling silence, or no deliberate cover) or raise suspicion as an unfilled timeline gap; it never proves guilt alone. When: when a suspect's movements cannot be corroborated. Why: The same gap has several causes; many innocent people lack alibis; a missing alibi is a problem of evidence, not innocence, and an unverified claim is not a false one.
- [pitfall] A broken alibi shows only a gap in location, not intent, so it should not be treated as proof of guilt. Why: location and motive are separate questions.
- [pitfall] A tightly bounded set of accepted facts excludes useful evidence that lies outside it, so the boundary should be widened when new credible evidence appears. When: Maintaining a set of established facts during investigation. Why: An overly small set rejects clues that could complete the picture.
- [pitfall] Trusting an alibi because it is detailed is a mistake, since specific detail is cheap to fabricate. When: Evaluating a witness's account of their whereabouts. Why: Invented specifics can be as convincing as true ones, so detail is not evidence.

## blame
- [mechanism] Misfortunes generated by the world can create new suspicion, so the player sees a belief feed itself as events accumulate. When: Designing a village with a suspicion system. Why: Each misfortune is read as evidence, strengthening the belief.
- [mechanism] When a loss follows a recent quarrel, the losing party tends to blame the quarrel partner, turning misfortune into an accusation. When: when an animal, crop or household suffers a loss after a dispute. Why: People look for a cause, and a recent quarrel offers one.
- [mechanism] A plausible explanation that names a convenient culprit with a motive can steer an inquiry away from the real cause. When: a suspect offers an explanation for a crime. Why: a motive that fits the first suspect discourages further search.
- [mechanism] A late reversal can shift blame to a procedural argument, reopening guilt after the culprit is exposed, so long as the argument rests on facts the audience already had. When: Final resolution depends on a detail that reframes responsibility. Why: A reversal consistent with earlier evidence keeps the fair-play promise; one contradicting shown facts breaks it.
- [behavior] A suspect who explains a contradiction by claiming the questioner misunderstood is likely patching the story rather than telling the truth. When: A suspect is confronted with their own earlier words. Why: Reframing as misunderstanding is a common way to defend an inconsistent account.
- [behavior] A partner who senses betrayal may respond with mockery and open threats rather than negotiation. When: a partner believes they will be sacrificed.
- [behavior] Under pressure, a witness may accuse another person to protect themselves, and the accusation often contains a true, checkable fact. When: a frightened witness is pressed by questioning. Why: self-protection pushes suspicion toward someone with a plausible link.
- [behavior] When a belief places an enemy among one's closest circle, the nearest and most prominent people become the most dangerous suspects, because their betrayal feels deepest. When: a fixed belief casts the enemy as hidden inside the community. Why: Betrayal by a close person carries more emotional weight than by a stranger.
- [behavior] When pressed, accusers who blame one another reveal that their account is unstable.
- [behavior] Officials who blame agitators for a dispute may leave the original accusations unexamined. When: When authorities attribute unrest to people who stoke it. Why: Blame moves attention away from whether the claims are valid.
- [behavior] A small, legally pending dispute can serve as the procedural vehicle for a larger grievance, so an action taken over the minor issue may really answer the larger one. When: a formal action cites a minor pending dispute.
- [heuristic] Model blame moving through a town after a disaster as rumour that grows by repetition, and treat individual guilt as a separate matter to show.
- [heuristic] Place a suspect who is blamed for an environmental hazard, such as a trap or creature, while the real cause is visible only in a later test. When: Designing a mystery where a hazard is wrongly attributed to a person. Why: Blaming the wrong agent keeps the real cause hidden until a test exposes it.
- [procedure] 1) List exactly who knows the secret. 2) Confirm that nobody else knows it. 3) Require a secrecy pledge and a conduct pledge together. 4) Attach checkable conditions. 5) Have each party confirm the account aloud. When: a small group shares a sensitive fact. Why: a defined circle makes later suspicion easier to assess.
- [pitfall] Accusing a suspect over misfortunes such as livestock deaths, especially after a quarrel or curse, rests on slender grounds: presumption, not proof, without a separate causal link.
- [pitfall] A confession may shift blame onto others, so every claim in it should be verified before it is accepted.
- [pitfall] Assigning all blame to a hidden party hides the human motives and consents that actually made the harm possible.
- [fact] People often shift blame for a loved one's faults onto outside companions, moving guilt away from the loved one. When: a parent or guardian judges a child's misconduct. Why: protecting the loved one from blame.
- [fact] Someone who acted on false information may be less culpable than the person who deceived them, so blame can shift away from the helper.

## meetings and appointments
- [mechanism] A scheduled meeting that fails to happen shrinks the time left and forces a decision, so suspense rises as waiting or acting becomes urgent. When: A long-awaited revelation is scheduled. Why: Failure removes the expected path and raises the stakes.
- [mechanism] A private reaction noticed by another person can be turned into a public confrontation, making unease a visible event.
- [behavior] A disguised person who fears being watched chooses a private spot off the road to talk, since anyone nearby might be observing. When: A disguised character arranges a meeting in public. Why: Suspicion of watchers moves the meeting to a hidden place.
- [behavior] A character who frames a private matter as a business transaction reveals where their priorities lie.
- [behavior] Observers often miss earlier warning signs and notice only a sudden change in another person's manner. When: tracking changes in someone's behaviour. Why: Gradual signals fade into the background until a sharp shift.
- [rule] Use a signal code only while it stays private to its users, since a code others can read stops protecting them. When: when choosing how to communicate a secret.
- [rule] Agree a regular contact schedule and treat a missed message as a signal to return at once, which can trigger a new event.
- [rule] Verify one witness claim privately, since asking about it in company can alert others involved.
- [rule] Let an NPC privately confirm whether another character was present, and record that answer as a checkable alibi. When: When designing alibi systems for a game. Why: A private confirmation gives the player a source they can verify against other evidence.
- [heuristic] When a person fails to return at the expected time, list other places they could have gone before treating the absence as serious. When: An expected return does not happen. Why: Alternative locations often explain the absence.
- [heuristic] A missed routine is evidence: an unserved breakfast alongside a slept-in bed can point to an early departure.
- [heuristic] A missed meeting can itself be a clue: check whether the witness has left, or whether a shadowing agent has reported on their movements.
- [heuristic] A recurring private act of penance gives a character a visible sign of lasting guilt that players can learn to read over time.
- [heuristic] Sort testimony into what one person reports alone and what several people can check. Sincere witnesses can still be wrong, so this sorting tests evidence, not honesty. When: Evaluating testimony about unseen events.
- [heuristic] Missed appointments can each name someone waiting, which reveals who will notice the absence. When: When a character fails to meet scheduled commitments. Why: Each missed commitment has a dependent who registers the failure.
- [pitfall] A missed promise or appointment can have an innocent explanation, so treat the gap as a point to test; in game design, give the player a discoverable innocent explanation. When: an NPC or person misses a promise, appointment or deadline. Why: The same missed obligation supports both guilt and innocence, and the gap alone is not proof of wrongdoing.
- [pitfall] A witness who turns away during an unmasking can miss the moment of reveal, so the investigator must keep watching the subject closely. When: A distressed or sensitive witness is present during the reveal. Why: Emotional withdrawal can take the witness's attention away from the decisive moment.
- [pitfall] A witness who moves the talk to a private setting narrows who can verify their account, even when the stated reason sounds plausible.
- [pitfall] A staff member who was out of the room may simply have missed an arrival. When: Relying on the absence of a sighting. Why: People cannot see everything in their area.

## patterns and inference
- [mechanism] Regular anonymous sends of money or letters reveal a deliberate schedule, and changes in the amounts over time can signal intent. When: an unknown sender acts repeatedly through indirect channels. Why: Consistent timing and amounts are harder to disguise than names or handwriting.
- [mechanism] Wills, intestate division, inherited judgments and inherited houses constrain the living, so past arrangements shape present action.
- [behavior] Accusers often offer a pattern across many events as proof of a link, even when no single case is shown. When: A group's guilt is argued from a list of incidents without direct evidence for each. Why: Repetition feels persuasive, though it does not establish the link in any one case.
- [rule] Treat repeated unusual details as leads, not proof; do not group incidents into one pattern until each is independently linked, since shared sources or causes can mimic a pattern. When: Incidents share a signature, shared person, or warning but may have different causes. Why: Shared sources or coincidence can make unrelated events look connected; different methods may mean different actors. (x2)
- [rule] A pattern of omissions is not proof on its own; independent evidence is needed before treating the inference as established. Why: The pattern may have an innocent cause.
- [rule] Make a clue's power lie in a pattern across many entries, possibly in the owner's own handwriting, so the player must read the collection in sequence to see it. When: Designing a document-based clue.
- [rule] Repeat a sensory motif, such as recurring imagery, until it forms a pattern players can notice before they understand it. When: When hinting at a hidden nature without stating it. Why: Repetition turns scattered impressions into a recognizable pattern the player can later interpret.
- [heuristic] A single odd action, such as an unusual payment or a stray item, can serve as the hook for an investigation if it is observable and can be reinterpreted later. When: designing the opening clue of an investigation. Why: A small, observable anomaly gives players an entry point and a reason to revisit it.
- [heuristic] Repeated back-and-forth movements can be invisible when each event is examined alone but become clear when events are arranged in time order. When: several similar events occurred at different times. Why: Ordering reveals the rhythm of repetition that single events hide.
- [heuristic] A single disturbed detail is weak evidence. A consistent pattern across several disturbed details, such as arrangement and handling, strengthens the inference about a visitor. When: Interpreting disturbed objects as evidence. Why: Multiple consistent traces are less likely to be coincidence.
- [heuristic] When several cases with different views share the same outcome, the common cause is more likely a policy than separate private quarrels. When: Multiple similar cases are being compared to find the real motive. Why: A shared outcome across unrelated cases points to a systematic cause.
- [heuristic] Pattern matching only singles out one source when the pattern is distinctive; a common pattern shared by many candidates cannot identify one. When: Choosing whether a trace can identify its source.
- [procedure] 1) Gather incidents that look separate. 2) List what they share. 3) Examine how the shared element is meant to work and why it might fail. 4) Note the conditions under which failures occur. 5) Compare against cases lacking the factor. When: several events share a rare feature.
- [procedure] 1) Gather records covering many cases. 2) Filter the cases matching a specific condition. 3) Count and compare the matching cases to reveal a shared pattern. When: A pattern across many records must be assembled from several entries. Why: No single incident shows the pattern, but counting across records does.
- [pitfall] Confirmation bias or a theory built to fit a pattern can make ordinary events look connected, so weigh the chance that parallels are unrelated. (x2)
- [pitfall] A pattern of quarrels preceding a harm is not proof of guilt without a separate link between the accused and the harm. When: when evaluating a case built mainly on prior disputes. Why: Disputes are common and do not establish causation.
- [pitfall] A patient plan can still fail when the target behaves unexpectedly, so it needs contingencies for other behavior.
- [pitfall] A reconciliation vote that passes does not mean reconciliation is complete, since a minority may still dissent.
- [pitfall] Reasoning from patterns across earlier cases to a new case is unreliable, because a pattern is not an infallible rule for an individual case.

## precise statements
- [behavior] A speaker who answers pressure with feigned puzzlement, or over-explains to defend a point, discloses more than planned. When: when questioned under pressure. Why: explaining to defend a point reveals detail.
- [rule] Offer a dialogue option that asks an NPC to be precise, and open a new line of inquiry only when the NPC has a real memory of the event.
- [rule] Do not use relative-position reconstruction when a record gives a precise description that survives unchanged and needs no interpretation. When: when a deed gives exact, stable coordinates or measurements. Why: Interpretation adds error where the record is already unambiguous.
- [heuristic] A precise, confident detail is not proof of truth: the witness may be wrong, exaggerating or repeating hearsay, so check it against independent sources. When: When a witness gives an exact date, name, number or time. Why: Detail and confidence can coexist with error or bias; precision can feel authoritative without being verified. (x2)
- [heuristic] A precise detail, such as an exact timestamp, is easier to check and contradict than a vague claim, so precise alibi claims are more useful to test. When: Evaluating a witness statement or stated alibi for verifiability. Why: A specific claim can be checked and contradicted, while a vague one cannot.
- [heuristic] A specific reference to a place or person provokes visible reaction where broad accusations fail. When: Testing a guarded witness for a hidden connection. Why: Precise references signal knowledge, so the witness's reaction is more revealing than a general question.
- [heuristic] Exact dates, named places and precise times can make an account look reliable while vagueness hides what the author cannot defend. Why: Precision signals reliability to readers.
- [heuristic] NPC witnesses can give timestamped, precise notes, while others give vague accounts that the player must verify against the environment.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs both precise and loose phrasings of the same fact so players can press for the exact detail. When: Writing NPC dialogue that hides a specific fact. Why: Players can pursue the exact fact through follow-up questions.
- [heuristic] An exact description of a missing item narrows the search for it. When: an item has gone missing. Why: Size, calibre or type eliminates candidates.
- [heuristic] Pin down exact wording in a witness's statement, since a single word such as 'only' can change its meaning. When: testing a witness's statement. Why: Small wording differences can hide a changed fact.
- [heuristic] Property settled by deed with precise boundaries reduces later quarrels between heirs.
- [pitfall] A precise clock reading from a busy, distracted or tired witness may come from memory rather than a reliable clock, so precision alone does not make a time trustworthy. Why: Precision does not guarantee accuracy.
- [pitfall] A cover story with extra steps or excess detail, or told too eagerly, invites more scrutiny than a brief, measured one, since each extra detail is another checkable claim. When: when an alibi includes extra steps or errands beyond what was asked. Why: each extra detail creates another checkable claim.
- [pitfall] A well-remembered account is not proof of staging, because honest memory can also be precise. When: when judging whether a witness's detailed account is false. Why: Precision alone does not show deception.
- [pitfall] Precise times can give false confidence if the stretch between two timed anchors is left unexamined.
- [pitfall] A motive that explains everything may explain nothing, and stacked hypotheses leave the case open to attack.
- [pitfall] A witness who describes a suspect too well may reveal that the pursuers have already been briefed. When: a description is unusually precise. Why: precision suggests a prepared source.
- [fact] A witness can recall names, places and dates exactly yet remain unreliable about motive and meaning. When: Evaluating a detailed but sincere testimony. Why: Precise recall of facts does not guarantee an accurate reading of why events happened.

## questioning order and follow-up
- [mechanism] Once a witness begins guessing out of curiosity, they can supply the letter and then the full name, finishing the questioner's chain. When: A witness is drawn into speculating about a hidden name. Why: Curiosity pulls the witness past the questioner's stated aim.
- [behavior] A witness who gives a guarded first answer may add a fuller detail when a mild, repeated prompt asks again. When: questioning a reluctant witness. Why: First answers are often minimal.
- [rule] Agree on the follow-up before the interview, such as which witness to question if the suspect denies a claim, so the denial cannot warn them first.
- [rule] Reward players who ask follow-up questions about details that seem unimportant.
- [rule] Ask every witness the same fixed questions: who knew the hiding place, who overheard talk of it, and whether anything was heard in the night.
- [rule] After an innocent explanation, keep asking who owns or caused the source, since the answer may lead to new people.
- [rule] Let the player question in a fixed order and flag any answer that conflicts with an earlier one.
- [rule] Gate a follow-up question behind a how-do-you-know option, rewarding players who test what they are told. When: Designing dialogue options. Why: Asking for a source is a deliberate act that should unlock deeper information.
- [heuristic] Ask focused, specific follow-up questions; they can draw out details the witness saw only in passing or does not realize they hold, so dialogue should allow them.
- [heuristic] Ask follow-up questions while a shaken witness is being comforted, since the calmer setting tends to draw out more of their account. When: a witness is distressed but willing to talk. Why: Comfort lowers guard and makes further detail easier to share.
- [heuristic] A witness's first unguarded statement is often more reliable than statements given later under pressure.
- [heuristic] Ask what caused a claimed condition and what the person was doing at the time; the answer often leads to the activity behind it. When: when a witness explains an inability with a cause. Why: A cause often connects to an activity relevant to the case.
- [heuristic] Keep questioning of peripheral witnesses short and targeted; identify who was positioned to see or hear something rather than asking everyone broad questions. When: Witnesses are peripheral and their status is unclear. Why: Long, vague interviews generate anxiety rather than useful testimony and waste time.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a fixed opening question. 2) Let each answer unlock the next question. 3) Record physical details that link the informant's account to a suspect. When: designing an informant NPC whose answers reveal clues.
- [procedure] 1) Ask when the person was last seen and in what state. 2) Ask what the witness did afterward. 3) Ask whether entrances were secured. 4) Ask how each claim is known. When: a formal interview must fix a sequence of events. Why: A fixed order makes each answer a checkpoint for the next question.
- [procedure] Ask background questions in a fixed order covering family, foreign languages, clear memory and handwriting, and record each answer as a fact to check. When: when interviewing an unknown person. Why: a consistent order makes answers comparable and easier to test.
- [procedure] 1) Get the witness to commit to a general principle. 2) Name each evasion as evasion. 3) List the unexplained facts in order, each with its motive question. 4) Press on each point until the next admission follows. When: A witness withholds information but gives partial, inconsistent testimony. Why: Stated principles and ordered gaps make the withheld event visible without accusing directly.
- [pitfall] A recipient who confronts the suspect at once can alert the guilty party and lose the chance to verify the accusation.
- [pitfall] A confident, firm questioner is not necessarily a fair one; aggressive questioning can bend the rules of evidence.

## records versus memory and interpretation
- [definition] Reconstructing a past event means rebuilding it from primary records such as depositions, filed documents, town records and physical sites.
- [rule] Let a player verify a claim by finding a matching record entry in a different location.
- [rule] Treat a checkpoint record as evidence only where that checkpoint actually enforces its checks. A lax checkpoint's record proves little. When: Before relying on a logged record.
- [rule] Trust an objective record over a recollection, while still checking the record's own reliability. When: a log conflicts with a witness. Why: records are more stable than memory but can also be wrong.
- [heuristic] Turn records such as arrival logs or vehicle numbers into specific leads that can be checked, rather than accepting them as background. Why: A concrete record can be confirmed or refuted, which strengthens it or removes it from the timeline.
- [heuristic] Records made after an arrest can show whether the debt it claimed to enforce was still outstanding.
- [heuristic] When the person who asked the questions also wrote the minutes, the transcript reflects that person's knowledge and framing rather than an independent account. When: reviewing any recorded interview. Why: The recorder's prior knowledge shapes which answers are kept.
- [pitfall] A recorder's added conclusion can turn an ambiguous report into guilt; dramatic or moralising retellings are interpretations, not records, and distort evidence when treated as such.
- [pitfall] A timed check-in record shows that a punch occurred, not who made it or that the person stayed alert.
- [pitfall] A criminal record for one kind of wrongdoing does not show guilt for a crime with a different method, even when both harm people. When: linking a suspect's past to a new crime. Why: different methods indicate different perpetrators or acts.
- [pitfall] Travel records confirm where a person went, not what they did inside a location. When: Relying on logs such as driver records. Why: Logs record movement, not events inside buildings.
- [pitfall] Comparing physical records proves little unless you know what each record should show for that person and time.
- [pitfall] A dispute settled courteously in the written record can still be remembered as an injury by one party, so the recorded outcome and the remembered outcome can differ. When: when a resolved quarrel resurfaces later. Why: memory keeps the grievance the record closed.
- [pitfall] Records show what happened, not why it happened; separate a stated motive from coincidence before reading a later entry as a cause.
- [pitfall] A dated record and a sighting can both be honest yet still mislead, because the witness works from memory. When: Relying on a dated record or sighting from memory. Why: Memory can misplace dates and details even when the witness is truthful.
- [fact] A personal record can be seized as legal evidence and kept from public view when disclosure would harm a respected institution. When: when the culprit belongs to a respected institution.
- [fact] A private diary is less reliable for events its writer chose not to record, since omissions can be deliberate. When: When relying on a personal record to reconstruct events. Why: Writers select what to record, so the record reflects their choices.
- [fact] Institutional records such as bills, registers, manifests and guest books act as independent witnesses that fix when a person was present or absent. When: a suspect's movements must be reconstructed without a reliable witness. Why: Routine paperwork is recorded independently of the suspect's account.
- [fact] Written court records can outlast the people who heard testimony, so later readers depend entirely on what was written down. When: when no other account survives. Why: spoken testimony is ordinarily lost soon after the event.

## reopened cases
- [mechanism] A closed or resolved case can reopen when new evidence, such as a retrieved document or fresh accusation, contradicts its official verdict or closure. (x2)
- [mechanism] Discovering a missed travel link can reopen a case that seemed closed. When: New timetable or fare evidence turns up after a conclusion was reached. Why: A new fixed point changes which routes are feasible.
- [mechanism] A case closed on one motive can be reopened under a new motive, so a settled matter can return as a live accusation. When: when a previously cleared person is accused of the same event again. Why: a new motive can revive an old event as grounds for prosecution.
- [mechanism] A case that seems closed by a death can reopen when the apparent ending is revealed as false, overturning the belief the culprit relied on. When: When the culprit's plan depends on a belief that can be overturned, such as a victim thought dead. Why: The culprit's security rests entirely on that belief, so overturning it exposes the whole scheme.
- [mechanism] Changing a single key word in the question being asked, such as stolen versus missing, can reopen a case by overturning an assumption the players had accepted. When: A mystery's premise has been settled and needs a new direction. Why: A small wording change alters what the investigators must prove, so an earlier conclusion no longer holds.
- [rule] Recheck a rejected suspect or motive when new facts or testimony arrive, since dismissals relied on incomplete information and a clearing fact can later be reversed. When: When a new source links to an earlier dismissed hypothesis or a cleared suspect. Why: Earlier dismissals were based on incomplete information; a fact that cleared someone can be reversed.
- [rule] Reopen a sealed or formal decision only with fresh evidence and a lawful channel, such as a new application or earned evidence, not the mere passage of time. When: Designing a sealed verdict reopenable through a civil or inquiry quest, or when a prior ruling is believed wrong. Why: Reopening should follow from earned evidence; finality of the record requires new grounds for change.
- [rule] Keep a dismissed clue re-surfaceable so the player can return to it later. When: A clue has been dismissed in play. Why: A dismissed clue that cannot be revisited is lost to the player.
- [rule] Show the player an apparently complete case with one optional link that a diligent player can test to reopen it.
- [rule] When an object's owner is revised, reopen earlier assumptions, such as who a document was meant for, and reread other clues against the revision.
- [rule] Flag an early natural-death ruling as reopenable rather than final, so a later clue can revisit the case. When: A death is ruled natural without full examination. Why: Early closure can hide a cause discovered later.
- [heuristic] Reopen a dismissed lead to test whether an earlier conclusion was wrong, especially when the authority who dismissed it has been wrong before.
- [heuristic] A barrier reopened within an interval suggests people were still present during it, since no later exit would need it reopened.
- [heuristic] A case closed on a single search can be reopened when a chance remark from an outsider reveals a second location missing from the official file. When: the victim lived or worked in more than one place, or the earlier search covered only one. Why: people outside the official record may know about residences it omits.
- [heuristic] Add a checkable physical fact that contradicts a neat solution, so the player can find it and reopen the case. When: a game mystery presents a solution the player may distrust.
- [heuristic] Treat an inconclusive result as an opening for a new investigation rather than an ending for the quest. When: Designing quest outcomes that can end without resolution. Why: Doubt invites the player to pursue the question further.
- [procedure] 1) Identify why the witness is silent 2) Use that reason as the lever to open testimony 3) Check the new account against the known record. When: an earlier statement is shown to be false. Why: the motive for silence explains the lie and makes the truth reachable.
- [tradeoff] Reopening old leads can test earlier conclusions but costs time, so the investigator must choose which dismissed leads are worth following.
- [fact] A person barred from retrial on a criminal charge may still have the same facts examined in a separate civil action, which can produce a new verdict. When: The original judgment blocks one procedure but not another. Why: Different legal routes apply different bars to the same facts.

## testimony and witness reliability
- [mechanism] NPC notes written in terse, guarded language when they hide something let the player learn to read hesitation as a signal. When: Designing a note or journal system for NPCs. Why: Consistent guarded phrasing teaches the player to treat brevity as a clue.
- [rule] Sort each testimony into firsthand observation, secondhand report or rumour, or account shaped by feelings or interests; firsthand carries most weight, and secondhand reports can be excluded. When: Several accounts of one event conflict, come through intermediaries, or a case rests mainly on rumour. Why: Each category deserves a different level of trust.
- [rule] Do not treat folk testimony as verified fact; present it as a story whose truth is uncertain. When: Writing or using oral accounts and legends in a setting. Why: The teller's claims cannot be checked and may be partly wrong.
- [rule] Track whether the player opened a topic or was prompted on it, so later dialogue can reflect what the player volunteered. When: Designing branching NPC conversations. Why: Recording who initiated a topic lets later responses reflect the player's own choices.
- [heuristic] Keep a testimony log that the player can check against inventory items, so statements can be verified against physical objects. When: Designing a game where witness statements matter. Why: Cross-referencing statements with items turns testimony into evidence to be weighed.
- [heuristic] Weigh each testimony by the witness's stake and by whether it fits the physical facts, not by how confident it sounds. When: Several accounts conflict.
- [heuristic] Test a human-error verdict against the physical record, such as a signal's displayed state, since the record may show the operator acted correctly. When: investigating an accident blamed on a person. Why: The mechanical record can overturn testimony that seems self-serving.
- [heuristic] Weigh testimony by who gives it and what that person could plausibly know, since access to information makes some claims more or less credible. When: Assessing witnesses. Why: A claim outside a witness's access is less reliable than one within it.
- [heuristic] Test a witness's account for the sounds or traces it should have produced; a missing shot or a missing stain exposes a false story.
- [procedure] 1) Track which witnesses are present, sober or absent during each event. 2) Let the player discover what each witness saw. 3) Make conflicting testimony discoverable, so a bribed account can be checked against an honest one. When: Designing events with several witnesses. Why: Presence and state decide who can contradict a story.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness indicate the location of a sensation before anyone examines the body. 2) Examine only the area needed. 3) Show the physical sign to observers at the same moment. 4) Match the sign to the witness's earlier description. When: A testimony describes a bodily experience that can be checked directly. Why: Recording the pointed location first fixes the baseline, and a visible sign that matches the account moves the case from words to evidence.
- [procedure] 1) State what the witness would ordinarily do in this situation. 2) Compare the stated excuse with that routine. 3) Check the excuse against verifiable facts such as weather. 4) Note what the witness leaves out. 5) Flag any mismatch as a possible planned departure. When: When a witness's report is the main source of information and can be tested against routine or physical facts. Why: Conflicts with habit, facts or omissions reveal lies that sincere-seeming testimony can hide.
- [procedure] 1) Ask for a plain account of recent events. 2) Collect names, origins and arrival details. 3) Walk through events in order, step by step. 4) Record each concrete detail as a checkable claim. 5) Test every claim against independent sources. When: When a witness is emotional, confused or doubted but holds specific, checkable details. Why: Ordered, concrete recall yields verifiable facts even when the witness's interpretation is unreliable.
- [procedure] 1) Compare each witness's description of clothing or features with the physical evidence. 2) Note any conflict as a clue. 3) Question the witness further before accepting or rejecting the account. When: A witness's claims conflict with physical evidence. Why: Detailed but wrong descriptions can mislead, and conflicts point to a next question.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness to give the full account first. 2) Have them repeat it, and note corrections. 3) Ask pointed follow-up questions on each detail. 4) Let each answer shape the next question. When: Building a sequence of events from one witness. Why: Repetition brings out corrections and new facts, and chained questions test each detail.
- [procedure] 1) Take each second-hand or trance-derived account. 2) Compare it with independent records. 3) Trust only the details that the records confirm. When: A key claim rests on a sensitive's or witness's report. Why: Second-hand testimony is unreliable until checked against independent sources.
- [procedure] 1) Ask for raw symptoms and observed facts first. 2) Keep answers brief and specific. 3) Ask for impressions afterwards and tag them as less certain. 4) Withhold conclusions until the account is complete. When: Interviewing an emotional or vague witness. Why: Raw observation before theory keeps the investigator's ideas from shaping what the witness reports.
- [procedure] 1) Extract the time, place, companions and the witness's reactions from the account. 2) Separate what was perceived from what was felt. 3) Check each part against the environment. When: A player must judge how much to trust a witness report. Why: Breaking the account into checkable parts lets each claim be tested independently.
- [pitfall] A confident or sworn statement may only vouch for a person's character rather than describe events, so it is not proof of what happened. When: When evaluating a deposition. Why: Character testimony and event testimony answer different questions.

## travel and location
- [behavior] People who travel alone, rarely stay in one place, and rarely follow the news are hard to trace, so an alibi resting on them is less likely to be challenged. When: Assessing whether a cover story will be tested. Why: Few independent checks reach such people.
- [rule] Provide a sketch-map tool where players record room layouts, doors, windows and furniture; spatial notes persist as the level is explored and can be compared with later evidence.
- [rule] Do not treat a witness's guess about direction or place as fact until another source corroborates it. When: a witness is unsure where they were. Why: guesses are not observations.
- [rule] Provide a search action that sweeps in lanes and reveals items hidden under cover, rewarding methodical play.
- [rule] Sort matched prints by hand and by room, so the game can show where each character has been. When: when displaying forensic results to players. Why: Location-sorted matches reveal movement patterns.
- [rule] Make each location visit return a clear yes-or-no answer, and show the visited-location list so the player sees progress and what remains. When: the player is canvassing locations. Why: a visible record shows progress and prevents repeat visits.
- [rule] Show confidence levels on a map, such as certain, remembered, traces only, or guessed, so players can judge which locations are reliable.
- [heuristic] Record each sighting of a clue or suspect in the player's map or journal, so later payoffs and movements can be traced back to earlier appearances. When: when a clue recurs across an area. Why: a traceable record makes a payoff feel connected to earlier play.
- [heuristic] An unused ticket or travel item shows intent to make a journey, not that the trip was completed.
- [heuristic] Let quest-givers or hideouts be known only by partial names, so the player must work to link a name to a place or person. When: a mystery requires the player to discover identity. Why: partial names turn identification into a task.
- [heuristic] A suspect who adds an unverifiable stop to fill a gap widens the window, so check whether the total time leaves room for that stop. When: A suspect offers a new stop to explain a gap. Why: Extra stops consume slack that the account already lacks.
- [heuristic] A lettered diagram of where each sample sits on an item gives players a map to reason from. When: when presenting sampled evidence to players.
- [procedure] 1) Record the vehicle's fuel level when it was left. 2) Record the level of spare supplies. 3) Compare consumption with mileage. 4) Fix the travel window by matching the vehicle's location at a known time. When: witness times are unreliable or absent.
- [pitfall] A traveller whose destination no one knows is hard to trace afterward.
- [pitfall] Travel times are estimates, and a wrong figure can clear a guilty party or convict an innocent one, so verify it before relying on the result.
- [pitfall] Assuming where a crime happened without evidence makes every timeline built on that assumption unreliable.
- [pitfall] Building a timeline on checkpoints that cannot be verified gives a false sense of precision. When: sources are unreliable.
- [pitfall] Accepting a witness's story that stops exactly where its claims can no longer be verified leaves the key claim untested.
- [fact] Once a visitor leaves, a lone occupant's movements can go unobserved, so their alibi rests on their own word. When: A character is alone after another has departed. Why: No one else is present to confirm what they did.

## unchecked reasoning
- [mechanism] NPCs who accept a faction leader's stated lineage without checking let players later discover the claim was never verified. When: a faction leader makes an unverified claim of rank or descent. Why: Acceptance without checking leaves a gap the story can later expose.
- [rule] Do not accept an interval, motive or route as settled until independent records confirm it; a record certifying itself does not count as confirmation. Why: Trusting a record because its own source certifies it, without independent checking, can hide errors. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Holding a theory privately lets new facts test it fairly, but it can go unchecked for too long if no new facts arrive. When: when an investigator keeps a theory without publicly committing to it. Why: early public commitment creates pressure to defend the theory rather than test it.
- [pitfall] An explanation that depends on actions no witness saw is weak; mark which links are unconfirmed so the player can judge them.
- [pitfall] A claimed link between a suspect's act and a witness's bodily mark can be accepted without any test of that link.
- [pitfall] Inferred links reflect what the reconstructor expects to find, and without an outside check they can distort the result.
- [pitfall] A single observer's expectation can be wrong, such as assuming a household is sleeping in, yet fit the reasoning without being checked.
- [pitfall] A vague presentiment that is never tested can be left unexamined and forgotten.
- [pitfall] Rejecting an inference only because it is uncomfortable is as biased as accepting it for that reason, so the inference must be tested. When: When an inference points toward a person the investigator would rather not suspect. Why: Emotional preference distorts judgment in both directions.
- [pitfall] Once a deduction is explained it looks simple, which leads people to underrate the method that produced it.
- [pitfall] Accepting a proposed solution before checking it against physical traces, such as an open window, risks a wrong conclusion.
- [pitfall] Without an explicit comparison to the stated source, a mismatch may go unnoticed.
- [pitfall] Odds quoted as evidence are only as sound as the comparison behind them, so they should be checked before being relied on.
- [pitfall] A clever theory can survive simply because nobody checks its assumptions about how the people involved would behave.
- [pitfall] Assuming a required preparation step is impossible for a suspect, without checking how the object is normally used, can wrongly clear that suspect. When: when a suspect is ruled out by a claimed constraint. Why: A constraint may be less strict than assumed, so it needs testing.
- [pitfall] A premise accepted without checking can carry an error through every later step of the deduction.
- [pitfall] Accepting a coincidence without checking it can hide a real pattern, and a speculative theory of fate is not evidence.
- [pitfall] A conclusion preserved without its method looks more authoritative than it is, because the reasoning that produced it cannot be checked.
- [pitfall] Relying on the most recent or most detailed explanation without testing it lets a persuasive but wrong account stand.

## unidentified objects
- [mechanism] An empty pocket search can create an unidentified-victim state that a later clue resolves.
- [mechanism] An unidentified victim blocks motive analysis entirely, because no relations or past exist to connect to a motive.
- [behavior] A character who cannot account for a missing item stays unsettled and keeps returning to the absence instead of dismissing it. When: an item is gone after an event and no explanation is found. Why: an unexplained loss feels unresolved, so it stays in mind.
- [behavior] Witnesses may accept a voice as a particular person and not notice that they are taking that identity for granted. When: when identifying someone by voice on the phone. Why: Assumptions feel like perception, so the witness does not flag them.
- [behavior] A suspect who volunteers another person's name unprompted, and cannot explain why, probably has a real connection to that person. When: Suspect has denied a connection. Why: An unprompted mention suggests overlapping lives.
- [behavior] A private object shown without explanation raises a question that holds attention, and the audience keeps guessing its meaning until it is explained.
- [rule] Announce a reward without naming the investigating authority, so suspects may read it without being warned that they are being hunted. When: The investigator wants to draw out a hidden witness or accomplice. Why: Naming official interest tells suspects to hide or flee.
- [rule] Record what a witness does not know, such as a person's occupation, as a gap rather than guessing it. Why: A guessed value gets treated as fact later.
- [heuristic] Treat an unexplained object in a space, such as food or a vessel left after a sleep, as evidence that someone entered it.
- [heuristic] An unexplained item found on a victim can be a planted red herring or an accident, so it cannot be trusted at face value. When: A victim holds an item with no explanation. Why: Planting and coincidence look the same on the surface.
- [heuristic] A reply showing no recognition of a named person suggests the suspect never met them, which can rule out a claimed acquaintance.
- [heuristic] An unexplained object position, such as a chair turned toward a door, is a valuable clue to explain rather than dismiss. When: An object sits in a position that no ordinary use explains. Why: Odd placement often records a specific recent action.
- [procedure] 1) Collect unidentified remains without guessing their nature. 2) Have a qualified examiner identify them. 3) Act on the identification only after it is confirmed. When: remains or residue are found at a scene. Why: Misidentifying remains can send an investigation the wrong way.
- [metric] Unaccounted items equal items the victim is known to have acquired minus items actually recovered; a positive result marks a gap to explain. When: Purchase records or inventories exist for the victim. Why: The difference between records and finds quantifies the absence.
- [pitfall] A hypothesis explaining most evidence can hide a lone item that does not fit the missing set; a reversal leaving any object unaccounted feels like a trick.
- [pitfall] A servant's confident identification of an unmarked object can be wrong; a person recognised by manner may be correct but unproven without a physical link. When: Ownership or identity depends on recognising an unmarked object or a person by manner. Why: Recognition of similar objects is unreliable without a distinguishing mark.
- [pitfall] A found item shows nothing about presence at a scene until someone identifies it as the suspect's and dates it, since it may belong to anyone.
- [pitfall] An unexplained object, such as a feeding dish with no pet listed, can have many explanations. Connect it to other facts before drawing a conclusion. Why: a single object rarely identifies its own purpose.
- [pitfall] A child's own statements of name and family may not settle identity, so check them against independent records.

## witness demeanor and state
- [behavior] Witness may show pauses, pallor, fidgeting, changed wording or shifts in voice, pace or composure, even when body stays still; these signal concealment or anxiety. When: Pressed on a denied or secret matter. Why: Concern about exposure shows in speech before the body; anxiety alters delivery even when speech stays calm.
- [behavior] Witnesses in a district run by a violent group stay silent out of fear of retaliation, not from lack of knowledge. When: A group threatens anyone who would testify against it. Why: Testifying risks a victim's life, so fear rather than ignorance keeps people quiet.
- [behavior] A witness's sudden strong reaction to a found item signals that the discovery matters to them, but it does not reveal what they are reacting to. When: An NPC shows fright or shock at a discovery. Why: Emotional response indicates significance while leaving its cause open.
- [behavior] A character whose words contradict their facial expression or posture gives the audience a readable cue that something is wrong. When: A character speaks reassuringly while showing a contrary expression. Why: Audiences read nonverbal signals and notice mismatches with speech.
- [behavior] A worried frown after a question about others involved signals that the question has reached a sore point.
- [behavior] Witnesses close to an affair may hold back or bend their statements, and their manner under questioning is itself evidence to weigh. When: when witnesses have a personal stake in the outcome. Why: Loyalty or self-interest pushes people toward favourable or evasive answers.
- [behavior] A sudden change in a witness's demeanour, becoming unusually animated or unusually still, marks a subject of interest worth examining. When: Questioning a witness and noticing shifts in their manner. Why: Abrupt change in behaviour signals that a topic touches something sensitive.
- [behavior] A witness who balances professional secrecy against self-protection often resists publicity and gives minimal answers. When: a witness has a professional or personal reason to avoid exposure. Why: exposure carries a cost to the witness.
- [rule] Record each witness's stake, fear and state at the moment of speaking, and show these as dialogue tags players can weigh.
- [rule] Treat a witness's manner as a reason for follow-up questions rather than as proof of guilt. When: A witness's demeanor seems to conflict with their stated feelings. Why: Grief, shame, or fear can produce the same signs as concealment.
- [heuristic] Testimony loses weight when a witness's motive or state of mind is unclear; strong feeling colours both content and delivery, so separate facts from manner. When: Witness is emotionally charged or visibly shaken. Why: Audience cannot separate report from feeling; fear colours both content and manner.
- [heuristic] Lower a witness's testimony weight when afraid, intoxicated, sleep-deprived, fatigued, feverish or injured; check their perceptions against other sources. When: Witness's condition was impaired at the time, or when weighing their account. Why: Fear, drink and fever can distort sensory memory.
- [heuristic] Read a witness's temperament and frame choices so they have no easy way out, avoiding wording the witness will not tolerate. When: when interviewing a volatile witness.
- [heuristic] Asking what people talked about and how they seemed adds context that a bare timeline lacks.
- [heuristic] Before relying on a witness or confronting them, check whether their mental state and health can bear the strain of testimony. When: A witness's reliability depends on mental state or physical health, or a confrontation is planned. Why: A strained witness may break and reveal more than intended.
- [pitfall] An account from a witness who is drinking heavily or nearly drunk is weakened and needs heavier checking against other evidence. When: the witness was intoxicated when observing or when speaking later. Why: Intoxication impairs attention and memory, so the account may be incomplete or inaccurate.
- [pitfall] Witnesses may describe a fixture's state from a different day or time, so their account of its condition needs a date check.
- [pitfall] A witness who has learned to be impassive gives little to read, so the investigator should watch for the one topic that breaks the pattern. When: Questioning a witness who maintains a controlled manner. Why: A practiced composure hides most signals, so the exception is the informative point.
- [fact] A prior assessment of a witness's condition may not describe their state at the time of testimony, especially when their health is declining. When: Relying on an older medical or mental evaluation of a witness. Why: Health and composure change over time.

## witness testimony and npc statements
- [mechanism] A final explanation built from many converging pieces of testimony and objects, rather than one trap, makes the solution feel proven and complete. When: the case is resolved at the end of a mystery. Why: Convergence of independent sources lets the reveal carry weight without a single dramatic test.
- [behavior] A witness who accuses another character may have a personal motive, so listeners weigh the accusation against the witness's character and affections rather than accepting it at face value. When: A character reports suspicious behavior or madness in another character who is tied to them by family, marriage or inheritance. Why: Personal stakes can bias a witness, and doubting the witness can imply something about the witness's own judgment.
- [behavior] A person who searches the listener's face and asks them to confirm what they know is checking how much the listener already knows.
- [rule] Verify a private exchange reported second-hand against another source, and check the exact wording before building conclusions on it. When: A key fact about a private conversation reaches you through a go-between. Why: Second-hand reports can alter wording, and unconfirmed accounts can mislead.
- [rule] Let an NPC's testimony be checkable against another NPC's recorded position, rather than accepted as given. When: Designing NPC statements about events. Why: Cross-checking against another character's position turns testimony into a verifiable clue.
- [heuristic] A witness's admission explaining one sighting opens a new timeline to test; a careless admission can open a hidden area rather than a direct search. (x2)
- [heuristic] Character and evidential value are independent: poor reputation lowers weight without cancelling it, and respectable witnesses may give weak evidence depending on how obtained; check against internal and external evidence. When: When judging a witness's testimony, especially one with a damaged reputation. Why: A flawed person can still report true facts.
- [heuristic] A witness who confesses a costly lapse or admits doubts tends to be more convincing on other matters and more candid about the admitted points. When: When a witness confesses a personal lapse or admits doubts. Why: Admitting costly faults or doubts signals willingness to report unflattering facts.
- [heuristic] A biased witness may still be substantially true; keep the factual part of their account and test it rather than dismissing it outright. When: When a witness has a motive against the accused. Why: Dismissal discards true information along with the bias.
- [heuristic] When one witness might fail, secure backup testimony in advance so the case does not depend on a single source. When: A case relies on a witness who may change sides or be unreliable. Why: Backup sources keep the case intact if the main witness fails.
- [heuristic] A witness's isolated, sedentary life and craving for excitement can inflate self-regard and colour what they report.
- [heuristic] Check testimony heard through a barrier against what the witness could actually perceive from their position. When: When a key line reaches the investigator secondhand or through a door. Why: Partial perception limits reliability.
- [heuristic] Let objects that undercut the official explanation pile up before anyone states the conclusion, so the player reaches the inference first.
- [procedure] 1) Make a child NPC give rumours and partial truths rather than authoritative hints. 2) Require the player to verify them. 3) Let leaving a child out of an investigation or protecting them change lead availability or NPC trust. When: Designing child NPCs in an investigation game. Why: Unreliable child information keeps verification as the player's task, while choices about the child have consequences.
- [pitfall] Bargained or bribed testimony, such as for immunity, is shaped by the witness's incentive and may hedge or please the payer; payment or protection is not proof of truth. When: When a witness speaks after a promise of protection or after being paid. Why: The incentive shapes the content and certainty of what they say; payment creates an incentive to please the payer.
- [pitfall] Strong emotion, drinking, fear and second-hand hearing each bias a witness's interpretation, even when the witness reports events honestly. When: Assessing witness reports, especially when a witness has a strong emotional stake. Why: Emotion and impairment colour interpretation even when the witness is honest.
- [pitfall] Corroboration from a source sharing the same bias is weaker than it appears. When: Two sources agree but may share a viewpoint or interest. Why: Agreement from a biased source adds little independent support.
- [pitfall] An explanation offered by someone with their own purpose should be weighed alongside that purpose, since the explainer may want a particular outcome. When: Receiving a supernatural debunking from an interested party. Why: The source's motive can shape which explanation they offer and what they want the listener to do.
- [fact] A witness may regain composure and gain new ideas during an interruption, so breaks in questioning can help both the witness and the investigator. When: Questioning is intense and the witness appears distressed. Why: Time away from pressure can restore composure and prompt fresh thinking.

## written letters and statements
- [mechanism] Correspondence between communities can carry suspicion from one place to another, spreading an accusation beyond its origin. When: Leaders in separate communities exchange letters on a shared belief. Why: Letters transmit endorsement and encouragement across distance, making local fears appear more widespread.
- [behavior] A letter's tone can colour how readers take its factual claims. When: reading a personal letter as evidence. Why: Mood and manner shape the reader's trust in the content.
- [rule] Weigh the risk of discovery before opening another person's correspondence, since interception can expose the investigator.
- [rule] A written document placing a suspect elsewhere at the relevant time can serve as an alibi, but it must still be checked against the timeline. When: when a document claims a suspect's location.
- [heuristic] Self-written accounts give times, places and event order as their writer chose; judge them by author, date, and whether complete or selective, asking what they omit. When: when a suspect's or witness's written account is a main source, such as a letter, diary or deposition. Why: Writers can admit some facts while keeping others out of view, so reliability depends on what was included.
- [heuristic] Treat letters written by a person as primary documents that can answer charges about their character, and date them to place them in sequence.
- [heuristic] A letter whose point of view shifts can hint at the writer's bias, giving the player a clue to the writer's identity.
- [heuristic] Check a letter's date and place before deciding whether it is a plea, a fraud or an honest warning. When: A written message is used as evidence. Why: Date and place reveal whether the letter fits the claimed circumstances.
- [heuristic] A suspect's writings reveal where admiration and contempt lie; read them as character evidence.
- [heuristic] Check address books, handwriting samples, and written notes to trace who was told a secret. When: a secret may have spread in writing. Why: written communication leaves a checkable record.
- [heuristic] Treat a written instruction as evidence in its own right, not only as a means of communication. When: a letter directs a hidden action.
- [heuristic] When every witness to an old understanding is dead, the written instrument becomes the only fixed record of it. When: settling a claim based on an old, undocumented understanding. Why: No living person can confirm the original terms.
- [procedure] 1) Write the speaker's account down as they say it. 2) Have the speaker sign it. 3) Have a second person witness the signature, which gives the record standing. When: Recording a confession or testimony that may later be relied on. Why: A signed, witnessed record is a fixed account rather than a memory that can be disputed.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a private, quiet setting. 2) Show the suspect how silence will harm an innocent person. 3) Have the suspect write the account in own words and read it through. 4) Have a respected third party witness the signatures. 5) Pass the document to the proper authority. When: When a suspect's account can clear an innocent person and the core facts are largely known. Why: A witnessed, self-written statement carries weight and cannot easily be disowned.
- [tradeoff] Writing fixes exact terms and settles oral disputes, but later instruments may not match the original oral promise. Trust writing when accounts conflict; doubt it when only later records exist. Why: Writing preserves exact wording, but a later record is a new statement, not a copy of the original understanding. (x2)
- [pitfall] A written approach can be used later, so every phrase must be exact.
- [fact] A written note requesting a small private gathering limits the number of witnesses, so events can happen with few people able to confirm them.
- [fact] A 1666 order required testimony in writing, kept on file by the court clerk, which made later reconstruction possible.
- [fact] Written procedural cautions do not guarantee restraint; authorities can later move quickly to prosecution if the cautions go unenforced.

## alibis and timelines
- [mechanism] A reconstructed sequence exposes hidden steps, such as a message passed to a second party who consults a decision-maker before a plan forms.
- [mechanism] A figure seen performing an ordinary task near a victim can be read as proof the victim was alive, though the figure may be the killer in disguise. When: A witness account is used to fix a victim's last known time alive. Why: Witnesses take an ordinary activity as evidence of the victim, so a disguise is hard to spot.
- [behavior] Close associates such as a spouse or valet can make an absence invisible by repeatedly confirming the story to the household. When: a claimed absence is supported by people close to the person. Why: The household believes the person is at home, so each repeated claim strengthens the story.
- [rule] Store each character's claimed times for players to line up, and let a time stamp or travel record contradict an alibi so players find the gap. When: Designing alibi clues or mysteries where alibis can be contradicted.
- [rule] Hide an NPC's trait behind rumour, but leave a service routine that reveals it to careful players.
- [rule] Give an investigation board a household roster with arrest and location dates, so players can deduce which figure in a sighting was present.
- [rule] Log every event a quest NPC or tracker produces with a timestamp so the game can rebuild the sequence in the player's journal. When: when designing quest tracking or journals.
- [rule] Let players arrange found letters on a timeline, so that contradictory dates can serve as the route to the solution. When: when designing document-based puzzles.
- [rule] Model alibis as sets of observers with explicit positions, so the game can check which claims are consistent with each other. When: Designing alibis or witness systems for a game. Why: Explicit positions let the system test whether testimonies can all be true together.
- [heuristic] Mark an alibi supplied only by a spouse or servant as unverified, and give household witnesses extra scrutiny because shared interests bias what they report. When: when no outside witness confirms whereabouts or when weighing alibi witnesses. Why: that person's reliability is limited, and shared household interests create bias toward the accused. (x2)
- [heuristic] Household talk about a lodger's trade, habits, visitors, odd possessions and payments gives cues for identifying and locating them.
- [heuristic] Scattered events that look unrelated can form one sequence once placed together on a single timeline. When: when several separate events seem disconnected.
- [procedure] 1) Question each household member separately so no account shapes another's. 2) Collect small observations: meals, orders, visits, departures, and changes in mood or health. 3) Combine them into a timeline spanning several days. 4) Record disagreements and resolve each against other evidence. 5) Check the timeline against physical findings and official reports. When: when a suspect's whereabouts must be reconstructed from many observers. Why: independent accounts combined and checked expose gaps.
- [procedure] 1) Start from small traces not yet understood. 2) Order the actions by what each required, such as hiding, entering, unbolting, escaping and covering tracks. 3) Explain which traces were left and which were not. 4) Account for unrelated facts within the same sequence. 5) Ground each step in the actor's motive. 6) Present the theory as a chain where each step causes the next. When: Many small clues point to an unseen act and no single clue explains them. Why: A single ordered chain explains all traces together and exposes gaps.
- [procedure] 1) List each witness's timed sighting. 2) Map each described route. 3) Identify gaps between sightings. 4) Test each account against physical evidence. When: Several witnesses give times and routes that must be reconciled. Why: Ordering the accounts exposes contradictions and the gaps that matter.
- [pitfall] Unstated travel times, vague markers such as 'immediately afterwards', and unaccounted intervals hide gaps; fill them deliberately, since they can make an alibi impossible or conceal the key action. When: when a timeline has unstated travel or unaccounted intervals. Why: the missing time may contain the key action.
- [pitfall] An alibi can be prepared in advance and still be false, so the same fact can support innocence or a planned cover.
- [fact] Survival by less than a minute has decided succession to property, so timing precision in a last-known-life timeline can carry legal weight. When: A timeline determines inheritance or succession. Why: Legal outcomes can turn on very short intervals.

## clue design and distribution
- [model] Clues arrive in three patterns: front-loaded at the premise, a steady drip through each stage, or a late cluster just before the proof. When: pacing clues across a mystery. Why: Each pattern controls when the audience gathers the evidence they need.
- [mechanism] Clues cluster in the first 10-20% of a story, then arrive as a steady drip; late sections bunch them into a single cluster of argument.
- [behavior] Clues often surface by chance, such as a fragment found while searching for something else, and the finder's reaction signals the clue's significance to the audience. When: Introducing a clue through an incidental search. Why: Incidental finds feel natural and the reaction tells the audience what matters.
