- [rule] Front-load clues in the opening scene, deliver the middle as a steady trickle of testimony that shifts suspicion, and hold the decisive proof for a late cluster. Why: Early clues seed every suspect; late proof resolves the case.
- [rule] Anchor a late reversal to a physical clue the audience already saw earlier, so the confession feels earned rather than arbitrary.
- [rule] Build a cluster of physical clues so that no single clue carries the case; the rest survive when one fails. When: Designing evidence for a case that may later be challenged. Why: Redundant evidence keeps the case standing when one item is discredited.
- [heuristic] Drip clues steadily through the story, then cluster the decisive ones late so the final reveal draws on many earlier threads the reader can connect. When: Pacing clue release across a mystery. Why: Early clues need time to be noticed; a steady drip keeps suspicion moving; late clusters make the reveal click and reward accumulated attention. (x2)
- [heuristic] Front-load the earliest clues to set the central question, drip later clues steadily through the middle, and cluster the strongest plants and identity reveals late-middle before the climax. When: Pacing clues across a mystery or concealment plot. Why: Early anchors establish the case, steady dripping sustains interest, and late clustering builds to the reveal.
- [heuristic] Mark clues as corroborated by a second independent source or as memory only, so their reliability is visible. When: Organizing clues or testimony for a case or game. Why: Distinguishing supported clues from unsupported ones guides how much weight each receives.
- [heuristic] Test each apparently meaningful clue as a hypothesis, drop what the evidence does not support, and treat suggestive clues such as initials as possible blinds. When: Several explanations fit the surface facts. Why: A suggestive clue can send the investigation toward the wrong party.
- [heuristic] In a scene arranged with deliberate balance, a single feature that breaks the pattern is likely to be meaningful and points to something hidden, moved or missing. When: The surrounding scene is so ordered that any deviation reads as a deliberate choice by its arranger. Why: A meticulous arranger would not leave one feature lopsided without reason, so the anomaly signals a hidden action.
- [heuristic] Drip clues steadily through the first half, then cluster them at a midpoint trial and before the finale. Why: Clustering raises tension at key turns.
- [heuristic] Place clues in front-loaded, mid and late clusters so suspicion shifts at each stage of the story.
- [heuristic] Cluster the decisive clues into a late public scene, so a reversal of suspicion lands at once rather than drifting. When: when suspicion must move onto a new suspect. Why: a dense cluster of proof makes the reversal feel conclusive.
- [heuristic] Scatter clues across the middle of the story and let them converge just before the reveal, so suspicion builds toward a single payoff. Why: Clues converging at one point make the reveal feel inevitable.
- [pitfall] An event that looks like chance, such as an extinguished candle, may be part of the scene's design. When: when a minor event seems accidental. Why: Coincidence in a staged scene can carry the mechanism of the crime.
- [pitfall] Several apparently independent clues may trace back to one earlier inference, so their agreement can be an illusion. When: When counting clues that seem to support a conclusion. Why: Shared origins make clues look more independent than they are.
- [fact] Key discoveries often depend on small accidents, such as an interruption or a forgotten gesture, that look minor when they happen. When: When explaining how a critical finding came about. Why: Trivial actions can set off the chain of events that leads to the finding.

## dialogue reactions and flags
- [mechanism] A dialogue tree can unlock follow-up questions only after a prior answer is confirmed, so questioning proceeds in steps. When: Designing NPC dialogue for an investigation. Why: Gating follow-ups on confirmed answers enforces a logical order.
- [mechanism] Dialogue can track an NPC's composure so that revealing answers unlock only after its theatrical display drops.
- [mechanism] Reassurance options in branching dialogue can unlock additional detail from a reluctant NPC, so the player must choose the right tone to proceed. When: In dialogue systems where NPCs guard information. Why: Reluctant NPCs release information when they feel safe, so tone choices gate later content.
- [mechanism] An NPC's teasing remark about another character can set a flag that unlocks a later lead once the player records it. When: In games with branching dialogue and flagged world state. Why: Recorded dialogue flags let early conversation gate later content.
- [mechanism] A dialogue tree can present two suspects, with the character's reaction revealing a hidden link to one of them. When: Designing an interrogation dialogue that surfaces hidden information. Why: A reaction to a specific option discloses knowledge the character would not state directly.
- [mechanism] A dialogue option that deflects an NPC's question can carry real consequences for what the NPC does next. When: player chooses a deflecting dialogue option.
- [rule] Keep a running log of every NPC statement, keeping both versions when an NPC changes a statement after new evidence, so players can replay it and detect contradictions. When: Designing NPC dialogue that the player may re-check or that responds to player evidence. Why: A complete record makes inconsistencies detectable, and preserved contradictory versions let the player test the NPC's reliability.
- [rule] Give each suspect NPC a dialogue state that changes after the player says a name or shows an item, with reactions readable in more than one way. When: Designing suspect NPCs in an investigation game. Why: Changing states and ambiguous reactions make the player weigh evidence instead of reading a single signal.
- [rule] Record which of the player's claims an NPC has accepted or challenged, and unlock new answers only when related evidence is shown. When: When building a dialogue system with evidence-gated answers. Why: Tracking claims lets the NPC respond consistently across the conversation.
- [heuristic] Count every response, including a single word, nod or head shake, as an answer to be interpreted. When: When a witness gives minimal or non-verbal replies. Why: Small reactions carry information that an investigator can miss if they listen only for full statements.
- [heuristic] A dialogue system can time player or NPC answers and flag unusual latency on keyword prompts. When: Designing a dialogue or interrogation system that uses response timing. Why: Latency on trigger words can signal that the character is hiding something.
- [heuristic] Let a witness give a hesitant partial answer that the player can later confirm elsewhere, turning the answer into a verifiable dialogue puzzle.
- [heuristic] Redirect a question with a small, unremarkable topic so the change of subject feels natural rather than evasive.
- [heuristic] An NPC's hesitation before naming something signals that the answer lies nearby and can point the player to a hidden inspection action. When: Writing dialogue for an NPC who knows part of the answer. Why: Hesitation draws attention to a topic the player should examine.
- [procedure] 1) Grant the opposing side's central claim where it is strong. 2) Test whether it implies a different motive. 3) Propose a rival explanation and check it against the evidence. When: When the opposing claim is strong and a rival theory is available. Why: Granting a strong claim removes it from dispute and lets the rival theory be tested directly.
- [pitfall] Emotional reactions, such as a defensive remark, indifference or boldness after identification evidence, are clues to weigh with other evidence, not proof of guilt or innocence. When: Interpreting a suspect's or witness's early or emotional reaction to a remark or identification evidence. Why: A defensive reaction alone does not establish guilt, and composure has many causes unrelated to the facts being tested.
- [pitfall] A partial admission or accusation against another party can be a deflection that redirects attention; treat it as a lead to investigate, not a finding. When: When a witness makes a partial admission or points at someone else as the culprit. Why: Apparent admissions and blame can redirect attention or avoid scrutiny of the witness's own conduct.
- [pitfall] Professional courtesy is easy to mistake for personal warmth, so a change in tone needs context before it is read as sincere. When: Reading NPC dialogue tone.

## escape routes
- [mechanism] Repeated near-escapes that reverse at the threshold raise tension, and each failed attempt can make the confined space feel more oppressive.
- [behavior] A subject who suspects being watched may leave by another exit or vehicle, so followers lose them. When: the subject is being tailed. Why: Secrecy avoids observation.
- [rule] Make reaction tells point to more than one possible hider, so players weigh the evidence rather than reading a single guilty face.
- [rule] End a peril segment on an open state, such as a character fainting, so the suspense carries into the next scene. When: transitioning from a dangerous sequence to another scene. Why: An unresolved end keeps the audience's attention on the open question.
- [heuristic] Name each blocked direction in turn, such as foes ahead and behind, with a hazard to one side, to make the narrowing options plain. When: when showing a fugitive's closing options. Why: a clear count makes the shrinking options felt.
- [heuristic] A concealed object in a mundane place, such as a heap of paper or rubbish, is a clue in itself because its location suggests cleverness or intent. When: An object is hidden in an ordinary setting. Why: The choice of hiding place reveals something about who hid it and why.
- [heuristic] An irregular route, such as one used for exit and a different one for return, can indicate that someone else used the route earlier. When: A person's movements do not match the normal pattern. Why: Route irregularities often trace to another actor using the same path.
- [procedure] 1) Trace the object's chain of custody. 2) Find a predictable date, deadline or expiry. 3) Watch the point where the object must be collected in person. 4) Identify who collects it, since that person is the real target.
- [procedure] 1) Keep the target in sight from a distance. 2) When the target turns back, use cover such as a shop window or doorway. 3) Feign a small task. 4) Step aside until the target passes. When: the target may look back or double back. Why: cover and a feigned task avoid face-to-face contact.
- [tradeoff] Sudden flight can signal intent and justify acting immediately; without evidence of plans to leave, do not assume an escape motive. When: a suspect flees. Why: Flight reveals intent.
- [tradeoff] Letting a trapped culprit slip away keeps tension and avoids a contrived ending, but weakens the sense of closure. When: Resolving a confrontation in a thriller after the main threat is caught. Why: A surviving threat keeps tension to the last beat, but a lingering escape weakens closure.
- [tradeoff] Leaving the killer's fate unconfirmed after escape keeps the ending open, at the cost of leaving the official resolution unsatisfying. When: when ending a mystery where the culprit vanishes. Why: An open fate reflects the limits of the investigation but withholds closure.
- [pitfall] Do not accept a claim that nobody came in or out until the watcher's blind spots have been closed. When: When a witness says no one passed the checkpoint. Why: The statement is only meaningful if the watcher could see every route.
- [pitfall] Treating 'no other way in' as settled ignores that an admitted visitor leaves every barrier intact, so elimination does not prove the entry route. When: Concluding an intruder used the only open door in a sealed scene. Why: Admission by the occupant bypasses locks entirely.
- [pitfall] An endpoint watch fails when no predictable event exists or when the target can act well before the date.
- [pitfall] Assuming a culprit fled in the most natural direction can leave the real escape route unexamined.
- [pitfall] A hidden observer on a route someone may use is at risk, since a sharp-eyed member's glance can nearly expose them. When: Choosing a hiding place near traffic or sight lines. Why: Hiding places on frequent routes are often checked by people passing them.
- [fact] Over ten years, thirty escape attempts from prison vans were recorded: twenty-five failed absurdly, four were stopped early, and one man got out and was recaptured within fifty steps. When: Assessing the rarity of escape during transport. Why: Successful escape from transport is very rare.

## forgery and copying
- [mechanism] Once a target's measurements are known, forged physical traces become cheap to make, so a culprit of similar build can copy a rival's footprints and matching footwear. Why: copying measurable features is inexpensive.
- [rule] Make forged NPC messages checkable by giving the real NPC a phrase or habit that an impostor is unlikely to copy.
- [rule] Settle an accusation that one writer copied another by comparing their citation lists rather than by assertion alone. When: a rival accuses one writer of taking cues from another.
- [rule] Make a forged clue imitate a known pattern from elsewhere in the setting, so the decoy is believable within the world. When: designing a false clue.
- [rule] Separate deliberate forgery from honest error by including at least one genuine clerical mistake, so players do not treat every odd detail as evidence of a plot. When: Designing environmental clues in a mystery or puzzle scenario. Why: Otherwise players over-read every inconsistency as deliberate and lose trust in their reasoning.
- [heuristic] Do not drop a shop-based lead just because a careful culprit might have avoided it; such a lead is cheap to check. When: a source inquiry is available at low cost.
- [heuristic] When a detail's importance is unclear, a sidelong check costs less than a confrontation.
- [heuristic] A substitute who copies a target's most distinctive garments can pass for the target to witnesses who see them only at range. When: when an impersonation must deceive a witness. Why: distinctive clothing is the cue witnesses rely on.
- [procedure] 1) Photograph the original printed record. 2) Turn the photograph into a raised relief plate. 3) Ink the relief. 4) Press it onto a new surface to produce a copy. When: When a forger has access to a printed record but not the original object. Why: A faithful copy can be made from the record alone.
- [pitfall] A matching signature does not prove common authorship: marks can be copied or names used as cover, so shared patterns may indicate a shared source; physical evidence must confirm authorship. When: Attributing a document by its signature. Why: Signatures can be copied or falsified. (x2)
- [pitfall] Counting a copy's agreement with its original, or later writers repeating one error, as independent confirmation inflates apparent evidence, since they often copy one original mistake. When: Several secondary accounts agree on an identity or date. Why: Agreement among copies adds no new evidence.
- [pitfall] Identifying a person by easily copied features such as a beard, glasses or distinctive clothing can be mistaken, since anyone willing to copy them can match the description. When: when a witness names a suspect by appearance. Why: conspicuous features are easy to imitate.
- [pitfall] Disguised people may copy a known habit on purpose, so a matching habit does not by itself prove identity.
- [pitfall] A matching description does not prove ownership if the description itself was copied.
- [pitfall] Resemblance to a maker's standard design proves little, because others can copy the design to create a false trail.
- [pitfall] Early disturbances that gain attention are often copied, so the first symptom may not be the real story. When: when investigating the origin of a crisis.
- [pitfall] A surviving copy of a record may not keep its original dates, so dates taken from a copy must be treated with care. Why: The original may be lost, leaving no way to verify the copy.
- [fact] Crimes are sometimes imitated from earlier high-profile cases, so a precedent using the same method can support a copycat theory.

## guesswork and invented details
- [behavior] People facing a visible mark with several plausible readings tend to choose the reading they want, so their guesses reveal their hopes. When: A mark, sign or inscription has no settled meaning. Why: Interpretation is shaped by what the reader wants to believe.
- [rule] Treat a strong intuition as a pointer toward a relevant parallel, and test it against case facts; resemblance alone is never proof. Why: a parallel can feel right yet fail the evidence.
- [heuristic] Use a guess as a probe: the subject's confirming, correcting, or despairing reaction reveals their view or confirms the guess, without a direct accusation.
- [heuristic] Treat a guessed routine or a hider's habits as a question or ranking only; confirm it against physical evidence before trusting it. When: Deducing a hiding place or routine from another's habits. Why: Reasoning about another person's mind is uncertain and can mislead.
- [heuristic] Offer a guessed name and invite correction; people often fix spelling or form, confirming identity without a direct accusation. When: verifying a name tied to an alias. Why: correction is a neutral reaction, not an admission.
- [heuristic] Asking the listener to guess draws them into deduction, so the reveal is earned rather than simply told. When: A secret is about to be disclosed. Why: Active deduction makes the listener a participant in the reveal.
- [heuristic] Speculative reconstruction built on unknown circumstances tends to be wrong; reasoning should rest on known facts rather than imagined scenes. When: Judging how an event probably happened when key circumstances are unknown. Why: Filling gaps with invented detail produces reconstructions that often fail.
- [pitfall] A repeated guess hardens into assumed fact without new evidence; label inferred steps as guesswork and promote a reading only when evidence supports it. When: A character, player or source reuses an uncertain interpretation or conjectured link. Why: Repetition feels like confirmation; labels separate confirmed timeline entries from assumptions. (x2)
- [pitfall] Each unverified link becomes the premise for the next, so a chain drifts beyond evidence; check each link independently before trusting it. When: An investigator builds a conclusion from a partial clue or guess. Why: Unchecked inventive links can drift far from the evidence.
- [pitfall] Keep each hypothesis provisional, whether tidy, plausible or intuitive; a neat story or motive can harden and steer the investigation down a false path. When: Reasoning through competing accounts, a plausible motive, or an intuitive guess. Why: Attachment to a neat story hides contrary facts; an intuitive guess without evidence is only a suspicion.
- [pitfall] Guessing who made an improvised repair from its look, such as assuming a sailor tied it, or acting on a guessed ability rather than a demonstrated one, turns a theory into an unproven accusation.
- [pitfall] An explanation that fits only the headline facts can leave one clear detail unexplained, so accepting it early misleads the investigation.
- [pitfall] Attacking a witness by attributing views they never held is a distraction; the witness can ask which claim is meant and expose the misattribution.
- [pitfall] Invented detail can be disproved later, and one disproved claim discredits everything else the speaker said. Why: a single checkable falsehood undermines the whole account.
- [pitfall] A claimed loss can be invented to explain why someone possesses an item.
- [pitfall] A target under questioning may invent a plausible substitute detail, so a correct-sounding answer does not prove innocence. Why: Stress pushes people to fill gaps in memory with convincing details.
- [pitfall] Headings supplied by guesswork in an earlier transcription can assign a document to the wrong case or date.
- [pitfall] Guessing contents from a partial or abbreviated label can settle on a wrong but common substance. Why: fragments invite the most familiar reading.

## locked-room mysteries
- [model] A locked-room plot runs: method shown, impossible crime, conflicting testimony, false solution on an innocent, mechanism analyzed, then a trap forces a confession.
- [model] A locked-room reveal runs in five beats: sealed-room setup, a staging hint, a competing mechanism, a confession, and corroboration with aftermath.
- [model] A locked-room mystery runs in seven phases: hook, first suspect, open verdict, pivot to new suspects, crisis, trial, reveal.
- [definition] A locked-room impossibility is partly real and partly staged; its solution depends on who controlled the door, window and timing, not on a hidden passage. When: designing a sealed-room mystery.
- [definition] A locked-room mystery presents a crime whose scene seems impossible to enter or leave, and is solved by explaining how that impossibility was produced.
- [rule] Use a key-duplication shop as a location where the player discovers who made a copy and when. When: Designing a location tied to a copied key. Why: A craftsperson's record can reveal who ordered a copy.
- [rule] Verify each lock on every door and identify who held the keys, since access controls determine who could reach the sealed object.
- [rule] Model keys as items with a custody history that logs holders, transfer times and last-seen locations, and let NPC answers be checked against that log. When: Designing locks and keys in a game. Why: A custody log lets the player test NPC claims against recorded facts.
- [heuristic] A locked connecting door whose key is missing limits which rooms could be reached, so note access points when reconstructing movement.
- [heuristic] A locked door whose key sits with one suspect explains why rescue was blocked. Breaking the door in the dark then adds confusion to the scene.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the door, its lock and where the key was. 2) Record who had access to the key and corridor at the time. 3) Note whether the occupant reacted to the lock's sound. 4) Check for any other exit the occupant could have used. When: Solving a locked-room mystery where the key holder is in question. Why: Access records and exit checks narrow the set of people who could have locked the door.
- [procedure] 1) List every exit, key and timed event in the room. 2) Check each exit against the events. 3) Use timed observations to narrow when the person could have left. When: when an impossible exit is the core of a locked-room puzzle. Why: Enumerating exits and timings narrows the possible routes.
- [procedure] 1) Establish whether duplicate keys exist and where they were kept. 2) Establish who held the key on the critical day and when it changed hands. 3) Ask whether the holder had reason for access and whether they asked why the key was wanted. 4) Ask whether the key was returned and whether the holder can identify it. 5) Test the holder's account against the physical record. When: A locked entrance is central and the number of possible key holders is small. Why: A sequenced custody trace links access to people and times, and tests accounts against records.
- [procedure] 1) Show physical traces without explaining them. 2) Build a first route through testimony. 3) Break each route with a new fact. 4) Fail an ambush with a fleeting glimpse. 5) Name the culprit with proof. When: when structuring a locked-room mystery.
- [tradeoff] An intact lock suggests key use and narrows suspects to key holders; but locks don't prove exclusive access, since copies let outsiders enter, so don't assume an insider too quickly. When: A sealed room shows no forced entry or an undamaged lock. Why: Absence of damage points to a legitimate key rather than a break-in; other routes or copies can produce the same undamaged result.
- [pitfall] Assuming a container is secure because it has a lock; check whether it was actually locked and how often it is routinely opened.
- [pitfall] Characters and players often treat a route as impassable because it was checked from one side, missing a concealed mechanism.
- [fact] A locked-room shooting staged with no weapon and no motive gives an investigator an impossible premise to solve.

## narrative framing and twists
- [model] A baffling object, event, or death is shown, a narrator reads it through a pseudo-rational lens, and a late reveal recasts the reader's belief.
- [model] A multi-narrator mystery is a relay of testimonies, with each narrator holding partial knowledge that shapes what the reader can piece together.
- [model] Mystery reveals usually overturn one assumption: an obvious suspect is innocent, a supernatural cause is a disguised living person, an absent rival is an unnoticed insider, or sacrilege hides ordinary greed. When: choosing how a solution overturns expectations. Why: Each reversal recasts a planted assumption rather than adding a new fact.
- [model] A story can hide one identity behind two apparently opposed characters; the reader is led to accept their contrast until a witness sees the change. When: Mystery plots where two rival figures appear to be separate people. Why: Contrast makes readers assume two people, and a visual reveal then overturns that assumption.
- [mechanism] A public report can expose a private investigation, which reduces the investigator's control over timing and forces earlier answers. When: A private inquiry risks being seen by outside observers. Why: Outside observers set the schedule, so the investigator must answer sooner than planned.
- [mechanism] A motif first explained away as a natural effect returns later as evidence, and the audience reads the earlier explanation as a rationalisation. When: a motif is planted and explained within the same story. Why: The later appearance contradicts the earlier explanation.
- [behavior] Players' suspicion moves with their trust in the narrator, and a narrator's bias decides which clues the reader notices. When: Mysteries told through several narrators. Why: Readers see events through a narrator's judgement, so that narrator's biases shape what registers.
- [rule] Keep the antagonist's fate and guilt ambiguous at the end instead of resolving them neatly. When: Closing a story with a morally unclear antagonist. Why: An unresolved fate avoids a tidy ending and leaves the story's threat open.
- [heuristic] Plant small objects and recurring motifs early and repeat them across scenes; a returning object or motif can later serve as evidence and cue the reveal. When: Avoid overloading the opening with habits that never return. Why: Mundane objects that reappear later reward attentive readers. (x2)
- [heuristic] Use an omen only if it has a later payoff, since an omen without one reads as noise. When: Planting early signs of a future event. Why: Unpaid foreshadowing makes the audience distrust later hints.
- [heuristic] Give a potential threat a deferred task or conditional prospect, keeping it occupied and away from the scene until the player is ready. When: when a character might act on a reaction before the player can respond. Why: A pending obligation absorbs the character's attention and delays the threat.
- [heuristic] Plant a name early in a way that provokes a visible emotional reaction, so a later explanation feels earned.
- [heuristic] Label oral tradition as tradition so the audience weighs it as evidence rather than established fact.
- [pitfall] A frame that promises more explanation than it delivers frustrates the audience.
- [pitfall] Overusing dramatic irony removes the pleasure of discovery for the audience. When: Using hidden knowledge across many scenes. Why: Once the audience always knows more, surprise no longer contributes.
- [pitfall] Atmosphere and expectation can produce false sensations, such as believing something touched you, in witnesses. When: Relying on a witness's sensory account in an eerie setting. Why: Mood alters perception.
- [pitfall] An old source may justify a device's existence without showing why it is used now, so current purpose needs separate evidence. Why: Historical lore explains origin, not present motive.
- [fact] A nested frame narrative presents a memoir as the true record of a case, and the frame later reveals the narrator to be the killer. When: when structuring a story with a frame and an inner account. Why: The reader trusts the record until the frame exposes its author.

## over-reading clues
- [rule] A fair-play reveal reorders facts the audience already has and never introduces a new fact; players feel cheated when a reinterpretation relies on information never shown. When: when writing a mystery's final explanation. Why: Fairness requires that every key fact was available to the audience.
- [rule] Plant an ordinary or literal-sounding line in a journal or letter whose meaning changes after a related object or writer's health or history fact is found; resurface it then. When: designing a clue that pays off later. Why: A harmless line can become sinister once new facts are known, so written clues should be reread after each discovery.
- [heuristic] Show the player a sign related to a held-back fact without revealing the fact itself, to create tension. When: a fact must stay hidden for dramatic reasons. Why: the related sign signals that something is unresolved.
- [heuristic] When a search yields nothing, reinterpreting a small physical detail can open a new route of investigation. When: When a line of investigation has stalled. Why: A fresh reading of an overlooked detail can redirect the search toward a productive lead.
- [pitfall] A dramatic or attractive theory, such as romance, must be tested like any other and must not replace evidence or force an interpretation onto an unexplained clue. When: An attractive theory appears early, or an investigator wants closure on an unresolved clue. Why: Its appeal explains every anomaly and discourages testing alternatives; a premature answer replaces the open question with a wrong one. (x2)
- [pitfall] Expecting a decisive clue, or fixing a thesis, makes investigators over-read ambiguous events; the same facts often support the opposite reading. Why: Ambiguous events are easily reread to fit a fixed thesis, and disappointment follows when a clue proves only suggestive. (x2)
- [pitfall] Fragments and gaps invite over-reading; hold each fragment as a hypothesis until other evidence checks it, rather than building an elaborate story from it. When: a document has gaps or a fragment is open to several readings. Why: Incomplete words attract guesses and assumptions; readers project more meaning than the sentence holds, and imagination generates ideas but is a poor judge of conclusions.
- [pitfall] One overheard phrase, a turn of phrase, or tone alone, without context or corroboration, must not build a theory; distress is not guilt unless other clues support it. When: a single line, tone or distressed reaction is read as evidence. Why: Such readings mislead when no other clue supports them.
- [pitfall] Ordinary surprise, a glance, posture or injuries should not be read as guilt, rage or hidden knowledge; such signs support a hypothesis but do not prove it. When: A character reacts strongly, or body language and injuries are used as clues. Why: Gestures and wounds have many ordinary causes, and readers tend to seek dramatic explanations for them.
- [pitfall] Do not conclude a scene is staged, or that a torn item shows struggle, from one oddity or stressed detail; test each detail against physical facts and corroborate first. When: a trace looks suggestive but unusual, or a detail seems staged. Why: Unusual details invite stronger readings than the evidence allows, producing false readings in both directions.
- [pitfall] Ambiguous marks or alterations, such as a highlighted phrase or changed text, may be innocent, like a clerk correcting an error; do not read them as fraud. When: Interpreting an ambiguous mark or document alteration. Why: Ambiguity does not establish intent, so reading it as fraud can produce a false accusation, and a highlighted phrase may mean nothing.
- [pitfall] Trying to connect every detail to the chain of evidence is a sign of inexperience and causes a mystery to explain too much.
- [pitfall] Readers may over-read a passing detail; keep an unexplained bystander as a loose thread, not a confirmed clue.
- [pitfall] Dramatic staging can overshadow the logic if it is not followed by a clear reconstruction. When: Revealing a solution with a flourish. Why: Spectacle without a chain of reasoning leaves the solution unconvincing.
- [pitfall] Resolving every ambiguous glimpse as harmless drains the suspense that earlier sightings built. When: Using ambiguous sightings to build tension. Why: Repeated harmless resolutions teach the audience that tension is not meaningful.
- [pitfall] Over-arguing a case for someone's madness signals steering, and makes the listener more suspicious of the speaker rather than of the accuser. When: Discrediting a witness through a long argument. Why: Excessive persuasion is itself visible as an agenda.
- [pitfall] Dismissing every strange detail as human can blind an investigator to a real anomaly, while a place's reputation can misdirect attention from a human suspect. When: When investigating eerie events. Why: Both blanket dismissal and reliance on reputation distort the investigation.
- [pitfall] Treating a recurring word or mark as significant before its context is known can mislead the investigator, who cannot yet link it to the danger. When: Early in an investigation with partial evidence. Why: A repeated detail feels meaningful, but without context it may not connect to the threat.

## silence
- [mechanism] Extended silence pressures a suspect or opponent to fill the gap, an interrogation or verbal tactic; nervous suspects often reveal more than direct questions draw out. When: when a suspect is being questioned or both parties are trying to learn what the other knows. Why: people tend to fill silence with explanation to end an uncomfortable pause.
- [mechanism] Deliberate silence lets a frightened witness recover composure and gives the interviewer time to organise questions. When: A witness is frightened or overwhelmed during questioning. Why: Pauses reduce the witness's fright and let the interviewer think, so the next question lands better.
- [behavior] Experienced offenders often stay silent, since a defense takes time to build and a careless remark at arrest can hurt them in court. When: at or after arrest. Why: Early statements carry legal risk.
- [behavior] Silence signals that nothing is happening, yet it also prevents intervention, so each choice made during silence carries risk. When: A scene is held quiet while a character waits or observes. Why: Players and audiences read stillness as both safety and danger, which raises stakes.
- [behavior] Prolonged exhaustion can make a person sign a false confession, then deny it once the pressure ends. When: after extended sleep deprivation and forced movement. Why: exhaustion overrides the ability to resist a demanded statement.
- [rule] Record contradictions in signs, sources and behaviour faithfully rather than explaining or smoothing them over early, so careful players can catch them later. When: when comparing accounts or tracking a person's behaviour. Why: early closure can hide evidence that later proves important.
- [rule] Record a witness's silence in response to a question as a fact, without treating it as proof of anything. When: when a witness does not answer a pointed question. Why: silence is observable but ambiguous.
- [rule] Make a target's attendant or associate the vulnerability the player exploits, rather than the target itself. When: designing indirect routes to a protected NPC.
- [rule] Present facts to an investigator committed to a theory, expecting them to be misread in predictable ways, and use that misreading as a lever. When: a detective NPC has committed to an early verdict. Why: the verdict filters what the investigator accepts.
- [rule] Plant a deliberate silence, such as an item no NPC mentions, as a lead rather than a dead end. When: Designing case files or quest logs with gaps. Why: A gap that players can notice and act on gives them a reason to keep investigating.
- [heuristic] A request for silence about specific names or dates signals that the stakes are high.
- [heuristic] A character's earlier silence that looked like evasion can gain a clear motive when a late explanation reveals its reason. When: Writing a reveal that reinterprets a character's behavior. Why: Reinterpreting known behavior makes the reveal feel earned.
- [heuristic] Weigh whether a secret was volunteered or extracted when assigning blame, since an extracted disclosure implicates the person differently. When: assessing a revealed motive. Why: How a secret was obtained affects how much it counts against the person.
- [heuristic] When a targeted appeal for a witness finds nothing, treat the failure as a signal to refine the target rather than as proof the witness is absent. When: a narrow appeal for a witness brings no result. Why: the failure narrows what the witness is likely to be.
- [heuristic] Staying silent when a visitor hesitates gives the observer more time to read them.
- [tradeoff] Silence or a sudden demeanour shift may signal concealed knowledge that raises stakes, or loyalty, fear or private reasons rather than complicity; weigh which before treating it as proof. When: when a witness or suspect withholds information or goes quiet about their own movements. Why: silence depends on feelings, protecting a shameful secret can outweigh telling the truth, and silence has many possible causes, while a shift in behaviour is read as concealed knowledge. (x2)
- [pitfall] A witness's silence can harm the person they are trying to protect, so withholding is not automatically safe.
- [pitfall] Too many secrets can make readers feel manipulated, so limit how many facts are kept back.

## sound cues
- [mechanism] Calls for help, a sudden scream of an animal, and an abrupt silence each raise tension in a scene where sight is limited.
- [mechanism] A fresh coat laid over still-wet oil dries unevenly, leaving dull and glossy patches that expose a recent overpainting. When: a new coat is applied over paint that has not fully dried. Why: parts of the surface set at different rates depending on the wetness beneath.
- [mechanism] A sound with no visible source leads an observer to assume an identity, and the assumption is overturned when the true source is revealed. When: A reveal should reframe a familiar setting. Why: The observer fills the missing source with the most familiar explanation.
- [mechanism] In a silent, dark setting, ordinary small sounds become distinct and ominous, which heightens tension as a central fact approaches. When: At the moment before a major reveal. Why: Isolated sounds stand out when surrounding noise is absent, so each one feels loaded with meaning.
- [mechanism] Actions can differ sharply in noise: seating an object may be almost silent while removing it clangs, so a heard sound can point to the opposite action. When: A witness identifies an action only by sound. Why: Sound depends on the specific movement, not just the object.
- [rule] Keep an uncertain or uninformative physical clue as a possible lead, not proof, and send it for further checking rather than concluding on the spot. When: when a found object might connect to the case. Why: further testing can resolve ambiguity.
- [rule] End a section on an unexplained sound, such as a sob in the night, to close on a question and pull the player forward. When: at a section or session end.
- [rule] Do not treat an uncertain sound as proof that someone entered a place.
- [rule] Plant a fair clue to a hidden source, such as the skill or rhythm of the sound, so a reveal reads as surprise rather than a trick. When: Designing a reveal where the source is hidden at first. Why: A hidden source that is never hinted at feels like cheating.
- [heuristic] Mark elapsed time with everyday sounds such as shutters opening, footsteps and clock strikes, so the countdown feels present. When: when a countdown must feel present.
- [heuristic] Undamaged clothing on a victim suggests they were taken by surprise rather than in a struggle. When: Reading a body's physical condition at a crime scene.
- [heuristic] A witness's account of when an item was left and collected fixes the window in which it was unattended.
- [heuristic] Soft ground that holds only expected marks suggests nobody else used that route. When: when the ground is intact.
- [heuristic] Traces such as dampness, overgrowth, or a dropped item show that time has passed and a place has been unused, but not who passed through. When: When estimating how long a location has been empty. Why: Wear accumulates with time, independent of who visited.
- [pitfall] Physical marks recorded without a stated medical or physical check leave their cause open, so their meaning stays ambiguous.
- [pitfall] A forged substitute keeps its content and goes unnoticed only if the target never inspects it closely or lacks the means to check. When: Replacing a document in front of its owner. Why: Inspection is the only point where the change can be seen.
- [pitfall] Drug behaviour can be uncertain and experts may disagree about dose and effect, so conclusions should allow for that uncertainty. When: Relying on expert pharmacology. Why: Pharmacology has real uncertainty.
- [fact] A volatile poison can leave no trace in the body and carry a smell that is easy to miss, so a death can appear natural. When: Routine examination finds no cause of death. Why: Standard examination does not test for volatile substances, so the method stays hidden.

## time pressure and countdowns
- [mechanism] A visible clock or day-based structure makes each delay feel costly, because the player sees time running out with every setback. Why: elapsed time is made concrete and countable.
- [mechanism] Letting time pass with nothing visible happening raises expectation, and a later shift to a parallel action builds suspense. When: A story has a waiting period the audience must feel. Why: The gap keeps the audience anticipating the next event.
- [mechanism] A visible deadline with stated segment times lets the audience verify the arithmetic themselves, so tension grows as the remaining margin shrinks. When: A timed sequence needs suspense. Why: Checkable arithmetic makes the shrinking margin concrete.
- [mechanism] An unanswered summons, such as a bell, can serve as a timed trigger that creates urgency and reveals an absence window. When: When designing timed events that expose NPC absences. Why: Silence at a call point reveals that someone is away from their post.
- [mechanism] A short time limit, such as twenty-four hours, forces an immediate decision with little room to prepare. When: A character must act on a demand or threat. Why: Limited time removes the option of delay and deliberation.
- [rule] Make elapsed time or a countdown visible or audible, such as a striking clock, chime, timed headline, forecast or daily-updated value, so each update builds pressure toward a withheld outcome. When: A deadline, timed confrontation, or group awaiting a decision. Why: Tension depends on an audience that can follow the time left; repeated visible reminders make the deadline concrete and show the stakes growing.
- [rule] Place world events on a visible calendar so players can order them and spot gaps in what happened. When: when generating or scripting a sequence of world events. Why: Players reason about causes only when the order of events is visible.
- [heuristic] Treat the expected date as an estimate and allow a margin on either side when setting an endpoint watch.
- [heuristic] Do not seize the revealed object at once when a witness is watching; rushing can ruin the whole plan. When: an observer is present at the reveal.
- [heuristic] Common ways to hold back a reveal are refusing to disclose a message's content, promising a later reveal, breaking off for a timed appointment, and ending on an open question.
- [heuristic] A person who keeps distance, watches and feigns a small task while waiting may intend to act once observers leave.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the appointment as a known point. 2) Track the time as it passes without the witness. 3) Set a deadline for waiting. 4) If the deadline passes, escalate, such as by calling in a patrol. When: A witness fails to arrive at a scheduled meeting.
- [tradeoff] Waiting for a predictable event gives certainty about who appears, but costs time the protagonist may not have.
- [tradeoff] Waiting for more pursuit to show itself observes the enemy's next move; anticipating it by forcing contact yields different information at the cost of acting first. When: Deciding how to respond to a suspected pursuer. Why: Each option yields different information and different risks.
- [tradeoff] Enforced waiting builds tension but leaves the player uninformed; provide enough information before a decision that depends on it. When: when the player must choose a course of action. Why: Decisions made without clear information feel arbitrary rather than tense.
- [tradeoff] Waiting keeps the planned sequence intact but risks the witness being harmed or fleeing; going to them at once acts on new insight but abandons the planned meeting. When: A witness misses a scheduled meeting and new insight arrives.
- [pitfall] Waiting for a witness or subject to arrive or return assumes they will, yet the return may be unconfirmed or never happen, and concealment costs time and patience.
- [pitfall] Waiting between interviews lets witnesses compare notes, so limit their contact when the order of accounts matters. When: when accounts must stay independent. Why: shared discussion changes the accounts.

## unrecorded events and traces
- [mechanism] An owner holding two adjoining lots can shift the dividing line without a recorded deed, so the deeds show one lot growing while the other shrinks. When: One owner controls two neighboring holdings for several years. Why: Unrecorded adjustment changes the apparent size of both lots.
- [behavior] People ignore a child or other ordinary-looking observer, so such a watcher can follow a suspect for hours unnoticed.
- [behavior] A person who quietly leaves a house at night may not be missed until morning, so discovery time says little about when they left. When: Someone leaves a home unobserved during the night. Why: Others are asleep and not watching.
- [rule] When a witness claims to hear an event that nearby listeners missed, the asymmetry must be explained, since it signals a hidden cause. When: when witnesses disagree about what was heard. Why: A nearby person would normally have been affected by the same event.
- [heuristic] A regular visitor missing from the log is a lead, but may also be a red herring, so visitor logs should support both readings.
- [procedure] 1) Log a sound event, such as a door slam, without placing it in the sequence. 2) Resolve it later when a second clue fixes its position. When: a sound is heard but its order is unclear.
- [pitfall] A transfer of money or an object without a receipt or signed mark leaves later claims about who paid or held it open to dispute. When: when a transfer happens without documentation.
- [pitfall] Where vehicle use leaves no record, consumption clues are weak and an unmarked vehicle breaks the trail unless traced through another record, such as a registration or rental log. When: vehicle use is not recorded anywhere.
- [pitfall] An object in plain view contributes nothing until noticed, and a record may miss the mark, so matches must rest on other features. When: when placing evidence in a scene.
- [pitfall] Evidence gained by secretly watching a suspect is hard to use later if the watching was not formally recorded.
- [pitfall] An unrecorded change to an object, such as an adjustment its owner was never told about, can mislead anyone unaware of it. When: Reconstructing a timeline that depends on an object's state.
- [pitfall] A privately known solution can be lost if the confession is not recorded carefully.
- [pitfall] A person left alone with an object may act before a timed test ends, so the observer cannot prevent the outcome. When: designing unobserved tests of a suspect. Why: Short unobserved intervals leave room for the suspect to act decisively.
- [pitfall] Comparing items without recording who handled each one weakens the comparison and hides possible tampering.
- [pitfall] A checklist covers only people who were recorded; anyone never entered on the list stays invisible to the matching process. When: when building an expected-person checklist.
- [pitfall] Omissions in a retelling must be recognisable as omissions, or players have no way to notice the gap.
- [pitfall] Evidence produced by an accuser in a moment of distress, with no record of custody, cannot be checked and is weak.
- [fact] Physical traces such as torn cloth, dropped tools or snagged items record movements a person did not intend to leave.

## witness account testing
- [mechanism] Witness NPCs can have shifting memory, stated grudges and partial knowledge, so the player must cross-check their account with a second source. When: when designing witness NPCs for an investigation. Why: Unreliable single accounts force players to compare sources, making the investigation more active.
- [behavior] A witness who first denies that anything happened may later give a detail they did not intend to reveal. When: When a witness's account shifts during questioning. Why: Narrowing questions pulls out specifics the witness had not planned to share.
- [behavior] Witnesses can disagree on a physical detail such as an object being carried. Such conflicts become points of doubt that prompt further checking. When: Witnesses give conflicting accounts of a physical object. Why: Memory of small physical details is often unreliable and contested.
- [rule] Test each witness statement against independent sources and other known facts, such as other statements and timings, before accepting it; update earlier statements when later evidence contradicts them. When: when multiple testimonies or new evidence accumulate. Why: descriptions are strongest when checked against physical facts rather than memory alone.
- [heuristic] Test witness accounts against physical traces, layout, dates and timeline before accepting or building on them, especially when the witness may mislead; memory is often partial. When: taking witness accounts; a story must be checked for consistency; a reader or player must judge whether a story holds up; a witness gives an account that will shape the next step. Why: memory can be partial or wrong; stories can conflict with geography or schedules; partial truths and fabricated details can send an investigation after a wrong target; dated claims and physical checks expose contradictions a bare story hides. (x2)
- [heuristic] Test a timeline and explanations against a neutral record, such as a timetable or staff memory, before accepting them, since smooth answers can be prepared. When: an independent timetable or log exists; a suspect explains suspicious actions, especially involving travel times or movements. Why: smooth, complete answers can be prepared; only checks against independent records expose contradictions.
- [heuristic] Keep the number of people who could contradict a staged timeline low, such as by refusing outside visitors. When: A false timeline must survive official review. Why: Each witness is a chance for the false account to be exposed.
- [heuristic] Ask a witness whether they would swear to a claim when much is at stake, and request concrete specifics, since vague recall is weaker evidence. When: A witness gives a dramatic or important account. Why: Specific, committed detail is harder to invent or drift from than general recall.
- [procedure] 1) Split the account into separate checkable claims (dates, places, names, possessions). 2) Test each against physical traces, public records and other accounts. 3) Accept claims the traces support; set aside and note contradicted claims. 4) Treat a missing object as a clue in its own right. When: a witness reports a physical event that leaves traces; a witness makes factual claims. Why: checkable facts can expose false accounts.
- [procedure] 1) Separate what the witness saw from their conclusions and hedged inference. 2) Check checkable details, such as route, timing and conditions, against reference data and independent accounts. 3) Weigh the witness's motive. 4) Offer innocent alternative readings and test each against precise details and other evidence. 5) Accept only the parts that survive; hold judgement until more evidence arrives. When: a witness's account is emotional or hurried; a single person's memory is the only source for an event; a case depends on what someone saw or heard. Why: the same visible facts can support several stories; a witness with a stake may present events in a favourable light; fluent narration and sincere confidence can hide guesswork or error.
- [procedure] 1) Ask exactly what the witness saw and where they stood. 2) Establish distance, vantage and light, and check whether they allow the reported detail. 3) Test each detail against other facts and normal practice. 4) Check reported injury against surrounding objects and the account. 5) Treat odd details as possible deliberate action. When: when a witness is the only source for a key fact. Why: physical limits and ordinary practice reveal whether a claim is plausible.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the current account with the earlier statement or sworn record. 2) Press one specific point where they conflict; read the earlier statement aloud and ask them to reconcile. 3) Pause in silence. 4) Test recognition with unrelated names. 5) Reassure them their statement is safe. 6) If they refuse to reconcile, treat them as hostile and weigh answers accordingly. When: questioning a witness whose statement can be checked against other sources; a witness's account conflicts with a prior statement. Why: narrow contradictions and silence push a witness to correct or extend a false account; confronting them with their own record forces reconciliation or exposes evasion.
- [procedure] 1) Collect a specific account. 2) Pick its checkable claims. 3) Confront the implicated person with those claims and compare their response.
- [procedure] 1) Record the predicted event and its time. 2) Wait until that time. 3) Observe whether the event happens. 4) Raise the source's reliability if it does, and lower it if not. When: a witness or NPC predicts a future event. Why: A correct prediction is evidence about the source's reliability.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the account with physical objects, fixed times and other statements. 2) Record how it is delivered. 3) Note any revisions made under pressure or confrontation. When: testing a witness's account.
- [procedure] 1) Separate firsthand observation from secondhand talk and rumor. 2) Compare versions of the same event. 3) Test details the speaker volunteers. 4) Check names and wording across records. 5) Ask whether the claimed feat was needed. 6) Mark withdrawn or never-sworn testimony as unsworn. When: A case depends on testimony, reputation, rumor or stories about a person. Why: Each step reveals whether an account is reliable, consistent and checkable.
- [procedure] 1) Record the witness's first, unprompted account. 2) Log each later confirmation separately. 3) Note which terms the investigator supplied before the witness used them. When: Interviewing a witness over several sessions. Why: Separating first accounts from confirmations shows what was observed and what was suggested.
- [pitfall] Assuming a witness who saw a man speaking with a victim also saw the man who committed the crime.

## witness deception and loyalty
- [mechanism] When a criminal group keeps losing members to arrest, survivors ask how the authorities knew, and that question turns into an accusation of a hidden informer. When: a network has suffered repeated losses. Why: Shared loss history makes members doubt one another.
- [mechanism] NPC dialogue branches can depend on affection or loyalty, so a protective lie becomes available only through that relationship.
- [mechanism] Marriage ties across households shape who is protected, because in-law connections can shelter a member from consequences.
- [behavior] Loyalty biases even a sincere NPC's account, including their view of others; weigh statements by the speaker's relationship to the subject and cross-check claims against other sources. When: Assessing a witness close to a suspect. Why: Affection influences what is noticed and reported.
- [behavior] A loyal witness may lie to shield the person they feel loyal to, offering a convincing but false explanation; the motive is personal tie, not self-interest. When: the witness has a personal connection to the suspect. Why: a well-built story can still be untrue.
- [behavior] A loyal witness may refuse to say more, or withhold a name or soften a statement; the account is fair in form, shielded in content, and refusal can signal hidden knowledge. When: when a witness has reason to protect a suspect. Why: loyalty withholds information; loyalty can override full disclosure.
- [behavior] Loyalty can delay suspicion: a witness who withholds another person's history postpones an inquiry line. When: a witness protects someone. Why: protective silence hides relevant background.
- [behavior] Strong loyalty or emotion can make testimony less reliable rather than more, since it pushes the witness toward defense over fact. When: A witness defends a suspect with strong feeling and no proof. Why: Advocacy displaces observation.
- [behavior] A denial to a question about disloyalty confirms loyalty, while hesitation reveals a secret, so loyalty questions can expose hidden contacts. When: when a questioner asks whether a contact spoke against the group. Why: the timing and tone of the answer are read as signals.
- [behavior] A witness with a grudge or lost position may speak frankly and volunteer key objects after receiving only a partial answer from the questioner. When: A witness has a motive to talk and the questioner gives a guarded reply. Why: Resentment and a wish to share information lower the witness's guard.
- [rule] Matching accounts aren't independent proof: they may reflect a true alibi or coordination, weighed against character and motives; shared untestable experience also makes them dependent. When: Two or more accounts match. Why: Matching can result from shared story as well as truth. (x2)
- [rule] Hide the truth behind a loyal character's denial, making the lie checkable: give a visible tell and a motive players can uncover; reward players who spot the mismatch. When: Designing a character who conceals the truth to protect someone. Why: Players can only challenge a cover story if the story contains something checkable.
- [heuristic] Keep the persona by feigning innocence and refusing to explain, so the accusation cannot be pinned on the speaker. When: when the accuser is confronted after a veiled accusation.
- [heuristic] When a witness's confusion appears, test repeatedly to decide whether it is a passing disturbance or a deliberate act, rather than judging early. When: A witness's confusion could be real or feigned. Why: Early judgement can be wrong, so repeated testing separates the two.
- [heuristic] A witness who seems to confirm the theory can be exposed by one test question that only the genuine person could answer. When: a witness or ally is presented as proof. Why: A single decisive check cheaply separates a fraud from a real ally.
- [pitfall] Staying loyal to a theory after its key link has failed wastes time and stalls the investigation. When: a reliable source has contradicted the theory. Why: sunk effort tempts the investigator to keep defending it.
- [fact] A witness who lies about their whereabouts can serve as a plot lever rather than the culprit, which supports branching investigations.
- [fact] A suspect can be held as a material witness to keep them available for questioning without a full arrest.

## witness testimony and credibility
- [mechanism] Split a decisive fact across partial accounts, each adding a piece, to delay the reveal and build suspense, only when the audience need not know the core fact early. When: the answer must feel earned; the audience does not need the core fact early in order to follow the events. Why: each account adds a piece while holding back the decisive fact.
- [mechanism] A suspicious detail with an innocent origin can still shape events, because it is out of character and invites speculation before its cause is known. When: A character performs an uncharacteristic act that others misread. Why: Out-of-character behavior stands out and suggests a hidden plan even when the cause is mundane.
- [mechanism] Incomplete or self-correcting NPC dialogue after a scare makes the player assemble a likely truth from fragments, rather than receive a complete explanation. When: Writing NPC dialogue after a frightening event. Why: Fragments invite the player to reason and feel more involved.
- [mechanism] When the key to a mystery lies in a memory the character cannot access, the player cannot verify it until a staged test makes it observable. When: The reveal depends on a forgotten or drugged action. Why: Neither the character nor the player has the information, so the test is the only route to proof.
- [behavior] A character who cuts off an account at the key moment signals that they already understand it, and the delay itself adds tension. When: A witness's story reaches its central point. Why: The interruption shows the listener's knowledge and withholds the answer.
- [rule] Use the ages and timing of remembered events that players can rebuild from dialogue into a timeline. When: Past events must be reconstructed from character accounts. Why: A consistent timeline lets players test claims against each other.
- [rule] Set up a trusted but limited NPC's limits early, so a later reveal recontextualizes them.
- [rule] Give the final reveal an independent source whose credibility the player can verify through a separate artifact, such as a dated record that matches the reveal's details. When: When the reveal is a claim the player must accept over the investigator's skepticism. Why: A checkable external artifact makes an account credible without requiring the player to trust a single voice.
- [rule] Give an innocent suspect a visible mark of guilt, so the accusation is earned and the later clearing evidence is credible. When: building a list of suspects. Why: Visible marks make the suspicion reasonable, so clearing the suspect feels like a real turn.
- [heuristic] Sudden arrivals, messages or ambient sounds can reset tension in a scene, resolve a confrontation without answers, and give the witness time to recover. When: A scene risks losing momentum or the investigator needs a pause. Why: Breaks change the emotional pace and can help the witness and the player reconsider.
- [heuristic] A second witness or record that describes the same event independently serves as a check on the first account. When: Testing a key claim from one witness. Why: Independent sources reduce the chance that a single account is wrong or invented.
- [heuristic] Choose witnesses that respond in different ways, so that one witness's state is not simply copied by another. When: Using several animal or NPC witnesses to detect a hidden factor. Why: Witnesses that react identically give one signal, not independent evidence.
- [heuristic] Seek an independent witness outside the suspect's household for any claimed whereabouts, rather than accepting the suspect's word. When: when a suspect's alibi relies only on their own account. Why: Independent confirmation is required to test the claim.
- [heuristic] Plant an insider motive, such as a dismissal or grudge, that the player can connect only after the outsider theory fails. When: a crime first blamed on an outsider. Why: A late-connected motive makes the insider reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [heuristic] The length of time between dated exchanges reveals how urgent a matter was and how long parties hesitated. When: when reading a sequence of dated letters or replies.
- [heuristic] When suspicion moves from a client's relatives, it usually lands on insiders such as an employer, family member, or servant who has access to the object. When: Investigation moves beyond the obvious suspects. Why: Insiders have the access the crime requires.
- [pitfall] A witness with no records can be accurate about facts, but that accuracy is harder to prove. When: Evaluating a witness who lacks written support. Why: Without records, accuracy cannot be independently checked.
- [pitfall] A witness who heard but did not see can support only limited claims, and corroboration from a witness who saw an object but not the act does not link a person to the act. When: When weighing witness testimony by sensory channel. Why: Sensory detail limits what a witness can establish about who did what.

## witness testimony weighing
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness by what they directly saw, their perception conditions (distance, lighting, hearing, time precision), stake, prior feelings and past record before accepting. When: when deciding how much to trust any eyewitness, witness or NPC report. Why: Perception quality and motive shape what a witness reports, so raw testimony can mislead. (x2)
- [heuristic] Weigh secondhand reports by what the speaker can know and why they would say it; rank sources by access and motive; intermediaries may sound pessimistic or confident from incomplete information. When: when information comes through an intermediary or several witnesses describe the same person or event. Why: Limited access, incomplete information and motive shape how secondhand claims are framed.
- [heuristic] A witness's past run-in with the law can colour their caution, so weigh their reluctance with that history in mind.
- [heuristic] List the possible sources of a witness's bias, such as outside pressure, prior prejudice and unclear evidence, so the audience can weigh the testimony. When: when a witness's opinions shift sharply. Why: Named sources let the audience discount the testimony accordingly.
- [heuristic] Weigh a single witness against physical traces and other accounts, and discount a witness's identification when they seem stunned. When: Several accounts or physical evidence conflict. Why: Emotional state reduces the reliability of a single account.
- [heuristic] Weigh testimony by how well the witness recalls facts that matter and whether they flag what they do not know; admitted gaps can make a witness more trustworthy. Why: Honest acknowledgement of gaps signals careful reporting.
- [heuristic] Weigh a witness's account by their known temperament and reliability, then check it against independent facts before accepting it. When: When accounts conflict or a claim needs support. Why: Reliability of the witness shapes how plausible a claim is, but independent verification is needed to confirm it.
- [heuristic] Weigh an unconfirmed account by timing and consistency with other facts rather than by the witness's confidence alone. When: a key witness account cannot be corroborated by another witness. Why: Confidence does not measure accuracy, while timing can be checked against records.
- [heuristic] Weigh a sworn account by the time elapsed since the event, the witness's age then, and the witness's stake in the outcome. When: evaluating a deposition taken long after events. Why: Time, age and interest all shape what a witness can reliably recall and report.
- [heuristic] Do not discard a whole account because its teller is unreliable, and do not accept it whole either; separate usable facts from noise by corroboration rather than the witness's manner. When: When evaluating an intoxicated, hostile or hearsay witness. Why: Corroboration is a more dependable test than how the witness behaves.
- [heuristic] When two accounts conflict, a witness with a poor reputation for honesty or sobriety can be discounted in favour of the more credible account. When: when testimonies contradict each other. Why: reputation signals how far a witness's perception can be trusted.
- [procedure] 1) Note who gave the account and any stake. 2) Check whether they observed it directly and under what conditions. 3) Compare with other witnesses' accounts of the same moment. 4) Check any motive to shade the story. 5) Test each version against physical facts. When: evaluating witness accounts of an event, especially when they disagree or an account is the only route to a crime. Why: Testimony is weighed by source, observation, corroboration and physical support.
- [procedure] 1) Ask how each witness recognized the person or object. 2) Note how certain they claim to be. 3) Separate what they saw from what they heard. 4) Combine partial accounts into one timeline. When: several witnesses give partial accounts that must be combined. Why: recognition, certainty and sense channel determine reliability.
- [procedure] 1) Note each speaker's position and length of service. 2) Note their interests and grudges. 3) Discount remarks those interests would shape. 4) Keep hearsay as evidence of motive, not of fact. When: collecting staff or bystander gossip. Why: each speaker's status and grudges bias what they say.
- [procedure] 1) Record the remembered remark exactly as spoken. 2) Note what context is missing. 3) Consider the witness's position and stake. 4) Note when the remark was first disclosed. 5) Check secondhand reports against the original source. When: using a witness's memory of someone's words.
- [procedure] 1) Decide whether the statement proves the claim or was introduced for effect. 2) Read the circumstances that produced it. 3) Offer innocent explanations for each reported fact. 4) Assess the speaker's stake and bias. 5) Cross-check against independent sources. When: A sworn statement is central to a dispute or accusation. Why: Separating proof from effect and testing each fact prevents a biased account from deciding the outcome.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a witness as mad can hide a real crime, so their account should be tested before being discounted. When: A witness's account seems implausible. Why: A real event may be mistaken for delusion.
- [pitfall] Accepting a witness's conclusion instead of the observed facts beneath it skips the evidence that actually supports or undermines it. When: when a witness states a verdict such as 'it was murder'. Why: The conclusion carries the witness's bias and may not follow from the observations.

## alibi verification
- [mechanism] Tracking alibis as sworn records makes a disproved alibi visibly collapse a suspect's standing. When: A suspect's alibi is contradicted by new evidence. Why: Visible state change lets the player see how evidence reshapes suspicion.
- [mechanism] A single credible alibi can overturn a chain of suspicion built on physical clues, shifting the player's belief to another suspect. When: a suspect has been built up by circumstantial evidence. Why: Testimony that breaks a theory forces the player to abandon a chain of reasoning, reopening the case.
- [mechanism] A trusted narrator's alibi for a suspect leads the audience to assume the narrator is protecting that suspect. When: a narrator vouches for someone. Why: Trust in the narrator transfers suspicion onto the vouched-for person.
- [rule] An alibi holds only if its timing and location can be checked against independent evidence, such as travel records or a message timed to the event. When: A suspect's account depends on travel times or a single witness, or when checking whether the suspect could have committed an event at a given time. Why: Unverifiable timing and place leave the alibi open to challenge; a timed message or independent travel record makes the claim checkable.
- [rule] An alibi is only as strong as the time window it covers; check for unaccounted intervals before accepting it. When: Evaluating an alibi. Why: A gap in coverage leaves room for the act.
- [heuristic] A stated alibi can be tested by checking it at a second location, such as an office or inn, which shows whether the claim holds. When: A suspect's whereabouts matter to the case. Why: A second location provides independent confirmation.
- [heuristic] Every detail a witness repeats becomes a claim that can be checked, so alibis hold only while stories stay consistent and timing holds. When: when assessing or building an alibi. Why: Repeated details create a trail that others can test.
- [heuristic] Make every acquittal or alibi reveal a new secret instead of ending the case. When: when a witness clears a suspect. Why: Clearing a suspect should move the investigation forward, not end it.
- [heuristic] Make the alibi that clears the primary suspect and the disguised witness the same event, so clearing one exposes the other. When: Writing an alibi that must also reveal the true culprit. Why: A shared event means the alibi cannot be accepted without re-examining the witness.
- [procedure] 1) Send the one witness who could see you away on a plausible errand. 2) Wait for a quiet interval after their movements fade. 3) Choose the exit least likely to be watched. 4) Leave the way back in unbarred. When: A suspect must leave a house unseen and knows the household's routines. Why: Removing observers and timing the exit lowers the chance of being noticed.
- [procedure] 1) State each witness's vantage point. 2) Record the time each witness reports. 3) Compare the accounts side by side. 4) Mark where they agree and where they conflict. When: Testing a suspect's alibi against several witnesses. Why: Conflicts between witnesses and vantage points become timeline clues.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the suspect where they were. 2) Ask whether anyone can confirm it. 3) Mark any period without an outside witness as unverified. When: when testing a suspect's account of their movements. Why: A suspect's word alone cannot establish an alibi.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the suspect's known location at the time of the crime. 2) Check whether that location could be reached and returned from in the available time. 3) Clear the suspect if the trip is impossible. When: a suspect is accused and has a claimed whereabouts. Why: a verified alibi removes a suspect from consideration.
- [procedure] 1) List each character's expected location for each hour from their routine. 2) Confirm each routine with observation. 3) Identify which characters could have acted at each hour. When: A crime is assumed to have happened at night. Why: Schedules turn alibis into positions in time that can be tested.
- [procedure] 1) Write down the suspect's claimed whereabouts and time. 2) Find a record kept by someone the suspect did not control. 3) Compare the record with the claim. 4) Compare the timeline with arrival and departure moments of others. When: A suspect's account of where they were can be tested against records kept by others. Why: A planned alibi can be built to match the suspect's own story, but independent sources are harder to shape.
- [tradeoff] A confirmed alibi shows only absence from the scene, not non-involvement, yet it can end a suspect theory; a missing motive should first prompt checking for an unfound form. When: When a confirmed alibi or a missing motive challenges a suspect theory. Why: Premature dismissal and stubborn defence both distort the investigation, and involvement can occur without physical presence at the scene.
- [pitfall] An alibi supported by family and servants may be sincere yet shaped by loyalty, so it is not fully independent. When: An alibi rests on witnesses bound to the suspect. Why: Social ties can bias testimony even without intent to deceive.

## associations
- [mechanism] Accusations spread along kin and neighbour networks: accusers and accused, often rivals, are neighbours bound by marriage, debt or local disputes, and harm to one household reaches connected ones.
- [mechanism] When one partner's self-image clashes with the other's wish to leave, the conflict can escalate toward violence and supply a motive.
- [mechanism] An NPC may remember a fact only after the relationship with the player changes, which can trigger new dialogue.
- [rule] Do not treat a grudge, an unrelated absence, a misplaced source or a person seen with money as proof that a document is a hoax. Why: these connections are loose and establish nothing.
- [rule] Use association results to choose a line of questioning and check them against facts, since reading the answers depends on interpretation.
- [rule] Store relationship events such as quarrels, letters and insults so the game can show the player the chain of hostility behind a frame. When: building NPC relationship state. Why: recorded history lets the game surface motives for players.
- [rule] Use relationship data between NPCs to narrow suspects, but require physical or testimonial evidence before an accusation counts. When: when designing suspect logic based on NPC relationships. Why: Relationships suggest motives but do not prove them.
- [heuristic] Accusations follow kinship, neighbourhood and rivalry lines rather than spreading at random; tracing who accuses whom reveals grudges that testimony hides. When: when accusations centre on one household, faction or a group facing suspicion. Why: People act through their closest ties, which shape who is noticed and blamed.
- [heuristic] Let dialogue puzzles present trigger words to NPCs and time replies; quick ordinary replies show nothing hidden, while delayed or unexpected replies, flagged as clues, point to a hidden association.
- [heuristic] Scan a register or guest list for names linked to a known person, revealing who else is present and possibly why.
- [heuristic] When motive is possible, ask personal questions about the witness's relationships to the victim, since a relationship can become the central line of inquiry.
- [heuristic] Before first contact, identify the target's known associates and avoid them, since they could expose the cover. When: a persona must be introduced to a new target.
- [heuristic] A judge's citation of a writer's work as authority can link that writer to the proceedings, but establishes association rather than responsibility. Why: Citation shows reliance on a source, not endorsement of every action taken.
- [procedure] 1) Ask for the relationship in fixed categories, such as friendly, strained or hostile. 2) Make the witness choose one. 3) Note vague words used for events. 4) Ask follow-ups on those words. When: A family or business dispute must be assessed for motive. Why: Fixed categories force a concrete answer that can be compared.
