- [pitfall] Once an item traces to a household, family and friends become suspects by association alone. Spread accusations via relationships and rumour; separate true suspects from those caught only by association. (x2)
- [pitfall] Accusing a stranger without knowledge invites conflict that can overshadow the real problem and leave the accusation unresolved. When: a confrontation starts from a misidentification. Why: the dispute draws attention away from the actual issue.
- [fact] Relatives can be on opposite sides of the same long dispute, such as a contested land claim.

## body size and footsteps
- [mechanism] Footstep rhythm and range reveal agitation: stride changes across a room or back-and-forth pacing within a few yards signal a rising-mood occupant. When: footprints or footsteps are readable across a space or audible from a hidden position. Why: Agitation alters gait; rhythm and range reveal emotional state.
- [mechanism] The delay between dropping an object and hearing it land or splash grows with pit depth, so a listener can estimate a hidden drop without seeing it.
- [rule] Use an outside sound such as distant music as a timer, since its rhythm marks time passing and makes silence around the action more oppressive. When: When a scene needs a sense of passing time. Why: A regular rhythm makes waiting felt.
- [rule] Use footstep sounds of differing weight and count to signal how many people are present and whether they are advancing or retreating. When: designing audio cues for groups moving nearby. Why: Mixed step sounds reveal multiple presences.
- [heuristic] Stride length on soft ground gives an estimate of a walker's height, which can be checked against another trace such as writing height on a wall. When: Estimating a walker from footprints. Why: Writing height is a second independent trace.
- [heuristic] A long, unhurried step over an obstacle suggests a walker's age and fitness. When: Reading a footprint pattern. Why: Stride style reflects physical condition.
- [heuristic] A strong corrective measurement suggests a long-standing condition, which should leave matching physical signs on the body.
- [heuristic] An enemy patrol can be identified by its footstep cadence, and changing that cadence when alarmed, such as from walking to running, gives the player a readable signal. When: Designing patrol detection and alert states. Why: Audio cues let players detect threats without line of sight.
- [heuristic] Footstep cadence conveys distance: steps that grow louder and more distinct signal a closer threat. When: a threat approaches on foot. Why: the player reads closeness from the sound.
- [heuristic] Shared audible timers, such as hourly chimes, give every character a common timeline and can give a level a rhythm players learn to read.
- [procedure] 1) Listen first to locate the occupant. 2) Interpret sound cues such as footsteps and locks. 3) Look only after the cues establish position. When: a hidden observer must gather information. Why: sound gives position before risky sight.
- [procedure] 1) Map each distinct sound, such as a pause, a door, a switch or a crash, to a stage 2) Listen from concealment 3) Track the sequence stage by stage. When: observing an event without line of sight. Why: sounds give reliable stage markers.
- [procedure] 1) Pick an observable act the witness will notice. 2) Calibrate the recording's replies to its pauses. 3) Start playback at the act so the cue lands at the right moment. When: A timed audio trick must match a visible action.
- [fact] Measuring the spacing between footprints gives stride length and direction of travel. When: a sequence of prints is visible. Why: regular spacing reflects gait and heading.
- [fact] Mechanical noises such as a click or grinding reveal how a device works, but a device designed to be silent removes that clue.
- [fact] An object sized to one original can fit two people differently: too loose on one, too tight on the other, which reveals a difference in hand size between the two. When: A worn object's fit is used to infer a physical trait. Why: Object fit is set by the original's dimensions, so a mismatch between wearers exposes bodily asymmetry.
- [fact] The entry angle of a gunshot wound can estimate the shooter's height range, which can exclude suspects who are too short or too tall. When: a forensic clue is used to narrow suspects. Why: Trajectory geometry links the angle to the shooter's position.

## certainty
- [mechanism] Tagging witness claims with confidence levels lets hostile or flustered NPCs lose confidence under repeated questioning. When: Designing NPC testimony that the player can probe. Why: Repeated pressure reduces stated certainty, which the player can exploit.
- [behavior] A witness who claims to report only facts often mixes in opinion, praise and moral judgement. When: a witness states a principle of giving pure facts. Why: Judgement slips in through selection and interpretation.
- [rule] When a speaker or narrator claims to know an absent person's mind or feelings, ask what that claim rests on; confidence alone is a claim to test, not evidence. When: someone speaks for another person who is not present. Why: Confidence about another's thoughts can exist without any basis.
- [rule] Ask whether a witness could have known a claim directly, not from rumor or feeling; confidence doesn't prove vantage, and trusting it over observation conditions makes poor placement look reliable. When: a witness reports something they did not see. Why: Confidence does not show the witness could actually see the event.
- [rule] Do not convict on stacked presumptions; a verdict requires sufficient proof, and certainty is easy when unverifiable evidence counts as proof, so presumptions only justify further examination. When: deciding whether a case warrants a formal finding.
- [rule] Give a witness NPC's description confidence levels tied to lighting and distance, so the player learns which parts to trust. When: designing a witness description for a mystery. Why: the player can weigh clues by how well the witness could see.
- [rule] A staged death must convince the opponent, since the opponent is the audience whose behaviour the deception needs to change. When: Staging a death to mislead enemies.
- [heuristic] A witness may report a sound without knowing its cause; state how sure the witness is before reasoning from the report. When: Taking a witness's account as evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the question. 2) Note any hesitation or hedge, separating firm details from half-recalled ones and recording each hedge. 3) Ask again, pressing on qualifiers such as 'appears' until their meaning is clear. When: a witness hedges or gives a single-word answer. Why: Qualifiers often hide the answer the witness is least sure of; hedges mark which details are firm and which are shaky.
- [pitfall] Certainty, whether a witness's, accuser's or defender's, does not establish what happened; sincere witnesses can be wrong, so confident claims must be tested against other facts. When: a witness or party states a claim with strong conviction. Why: Conviction and accuracy are independent; confidence reflects how sure someone feels, not whether perception was accurate.
- [pitfall] A claim presented as certain, or an explanation that smooths over odd facts, can close inquiry early; test it rather than accepting it. When: an expert presents an identification as certain, or several explanations are offered for an anomaly. Why: Smoothness and confidence are not evidence; authorities tend to accept confident claims without testing them.
- [pitfall] A conclusive-seeming trace or physically plausible act can mislead; check its timing, context and third-party records before treating it as final. Why: Records can contradict a plausible performance; physical plausibility does not settle a timeline.
- [pitfall] Treating a witness's confidence about small details as evidence can hide an unverified assumption.
- [pitfall] When police efficiency is judged by convictions, effort can narrow onto one suspect and neglect alternatives.
- [pitfall] A conviction formed from feeling can outlast the evidence, and an investigator may avoid the subject while half expecting to be wrong.
- [pitfall] A claim that matches information the witness already had, such as where they were hurt, is weak evidence because it may simply repeat what was known.
- [fact] A trial held in default, without the accused present, can still yield a sentence, so absence itself can produce a legal outcome. When: The accused cannot appear for trial. Why: Legal systems may proceed without the defendant, so the result rests on the defendant's absence rather than on a direct test of guilt.

## clue confirmation and correction
- [rule] When a clue is revised, show the cause of the revision, such as cleaning or new evidence, or the change will seem like a cheat. When: Correcting an earlier clue's reading. Why: A visible cause makes the change credible.
- [rule] Having a suspect repeat a statement aloud and confirm it under oath fixes the wording, so it can be checked against later statements. When: A suspect's account must be locked in for later comparison. Why: A fixed wording gives a stable reference point for detecting contradictions.
- [rule] When a key source is unreachable, wait for confirmation rather than assuming the answer.
- [rule] Do not repeat an event at the same level; each repetition should change something the player can detect. When: Repeating a threat or event across scenes. Why: Identical repetition becomes predictable and stops producing tension.
- [rule] Give an unexplained clue in a verbatim form the player can record and check later. When: Writing a cryptic clue meant to be solved later. Why: A recorded exact wording lets the player test it when new information arrives.
- [rule] Leave some clues unexplained and mark them for later, so the audience senses that the system is wrong. When: Writing an investigation whose resolution is institutional rather than a revealed culprit. Why: Unresolved details make a later reversal feel more credible.
- [heuristic] Show an unresolved clue, such as a missing companion, early with its meaning withheld, so attentive players can notice it and accept the later reveal as fair. When: Planting a clue that contradicts the main theory, or showing a clue early with its meaning withheld. Why: Early visibility rewards attentive players, and the player already had all the evidence needed to reach the answer. (x2)
- [heuristic] Raise a question about a visible fact that does not match the stated account, and leave it unanswered for now. When: A character's appearance, wealth or circumstances conflict with the official story. Why: An open anomaly invites the reader to investigate and keeps a lead alive.
- [heuristic] A visible detail, such as an object in a photograph, can overturn an explanation that seemed settled.
- [heuristic] A single reaction or calm response is one signal among others, not proof, so keep the reading open until more evidence comes in. When: Interpreting a suspect's expression or demeanor. Why: Innocent reactions and calm can look like tells or cover when read alone.
- [heuristic] Give the player a visible, wrong answer that the evidence supports, so that a later reversal feels earned rather than arbitrary. When: planning a mystery's false solution. Why: A wrong answer grounded in visible evidence makes the eventual correction read as deduction, not invention.
- [heuristic] Leave a loose thread, such as an unexplained name, as an optional lead even if the story does not pursue it. When: when a narrative has spare detail. Why: An open lead adds texture and invites player curiosity without needing resolution.
- [tradeoff] A minor anomaly kept open across many scenes can gain weight and recast the story, but if left too long unresolved it reads as an authoring error. When: A minor clue, such as a missing object or early planted detail, stays unresolved across many scenes. Why: Sustained open questions keep readers tracking the detail until it resolves, while long gaps make the detail look forgotten. (x2)
- [pitfall] Having the investigator stumble on a key fact that was never mentioned earlier breaks fair play, because the audience had no chance to connect it. When: Resolving a mystery through a sudden discovery. Why: The audience cannot make the link without a prior mention of the fact.
- [pitfall] An anomaly that is never explained undermines trust in the whole story, because the audience feels the clue was a cheat. Why: audiences stop investing in clues they expect to be ignored.
- [pitfall] Players feel cheated when a clue seems to point at a culprit and is never confirmed, so state whether the ambiguity is intended. When: a clue points toward a culprit without resolution. Why: unmet expectations from a pointing clue.
- [pitfall] If the audience sees a removed clue vanish, a shifted charge can look contrived. When: A case changes its charge after a clue is discredited. Why: The visible disappearance makes the substitution feel arbitrary.

## confession motives
- [mechanism] Offering leniency only in exchange for a full confession gives a withholding witness a reason to speak. When: the witness faces consequences and holds back details. Why: a conditional path to forgiveness makes disclosure worth the risk.
- [mechanism] A motive stated through confession, such as past poverty or humiliation, makes a character's later concealment plausible. When: A character's later action should follow from an earlier stated desire. Why: A motive disclosed early gives the reader a reason to understand later behaviour.
- [behavior] A person facing hardship worse than the charge may confess to escape it; the confession signals despair more than guilt and gives a reason to reopen the case. When: the accused faces hardship worse than the charge. Why: Confessing offers a way out of unbearable circumstances.
- [behavior] A speaker who gives shifting, contradictory reasons signals that an unstated cause is being avoided, and listeners will compare the reasons and press for one. When: A confession or explanation is meant to feel partial. Why: Each shift reveals a motive the speaker keeps circling without naming.
- [behavior] Admitting guilt is a separate choice from the facts of a case, so a suspect can know the evidence yet refuse to confess.
- [behavior] A suspect may confess fully when she believes the listener cannot act on the account or when the consequences seem limited to herself or her family. When: A suspect is cornered but feels protected by circumstance. Why: Perceived safety lowers the cost of speaking.
- [rule] Make an NPC confession's stated motive visible and self-interested, and let story actions reveal the real motive, so players can test the admission against other evidence. When: Designing NPC confessions players should evaluate, including ones that reveal a hidden location or action. Why: Matching actions against claims and a visible motive let players weigh the admission; self-interested reasons require testing the story. (x2)
- [rule] Let a confession mechanic offer escape from danger, with the cost of the confession visible to the player. When: designing confession mechanics.
- [heuristic] A confession may serve the speaker's own interests by controlling disclosure or naming others, so check it against physical evidence and whether the speaker gains. When: A confession explains reconstructed events, names others, or gives a detailed account that benefits the speaker. Why: The confessor chooses what to reveal and may withhold names or shape views of others; detail can make a self-serving account more convincing. (x3)
- [heuristic] A written confession works best when it states motive as well as method, so the audience learns why from the culprit rather than by inference.
- [heuristic] A confession at the close can tie off loose threads and fill in the timeline, from the early waiting period through to the final act.
- [heuristic] Give a confessing witness a reason to speak, such as relieving guilt or protecting someone, so the account gains credibility.
- [heuristic] A confession can gate the next quest stage, but the emotional weight of such a scene needs careful handling. When: Scripting a confession that unlocks progress. Why: Heavy scenes can feel exploitative if treated only as a progression step.
- [heuristic] A refusal often reveals more about the refuser's self-image than an admission does. When: A suspect rejects an offer or request in a formal or grand manner. Why: How someone declines exposes their values and self-perception.
- [heuristic] Give a false confession a motive that points to a real secondary character, so the player has a reason to believe it. Why: A plausible motive makes the confession credible.
- [pitfall] Do not treat a confession as a neat ending: it does not resolve victims' suffering and may shield a larger secret, so the investigation continues. Why: Victims' suffering remains after the admission, and an admission can cover a larger secret. (x2)
- [fact] People confess for many reasons beyond guilt, including fear, duress, expediency, protecting a loved one, chivalry, duty and vanity.

## crime scene and disappearance deduction
- [model] The detective story formula: the reader sees the crime or its setup early, then watches the investigator read physical traces that overturn an official belief about who did it or how. Why: Each story turns on a wrong suspect or wrong explanation, with the solution coming from forensic detail that authorities dismissed or missed.
- [definition] A controlled press notice is a deliberately vague public statement that hints at a breakthrough, planted to provoke a reaction from a target.
- [mechanism] A custody record such as a pawnbroker's duplicate names an owner and a value, and can conflict with a story told about the object, exposing a second account. When: An object's history is recorded by a third party. Why: Independent records often contradict the account given by the person holding the object.
- [mechanism] Describing a family's desperation makes an unusual source acceptable, because the audience understands why people turn to it. When: An unconventional source or remedy is accepted by characters. Why: Desperation provides the motivation that makes the source credible within the story.
- [mechanism] A brief cross-examination of a witness can be read as weakness by observers, even when the examiner has little to gain from a longer one. When: When a party chooses to question a witness briefly. Why: Observers judge the length of questioning as a signal of strength.
- [mechanism] A hidden mark on a key item, tracked across scenes, lets a game detect whether an NPC or player moved the item and confirm its later return. When: In games where key items may be moved or stolen. Why: Persistent state on the item records its movement history without relying on player memory.
- [mechanism] A deadline reversal, where relief such as a pardon arrives already overtaken by events, resets the stakes and changes the whole situation.
- [rule] Be wary of a guide who advises avoiding other acquaintances and trusting no one unknown, since this keeps you dependent on that guide. When: when a source advises restricting your contacts. Why: Limiting access to other sources makes the guide the only channel of information.
- [rule] Stage the final reveal as a demonstration with physical evidence rather than a verbal accusation alone. When: resolving a mystery with a hidden culprit. Why: Physical proof makes the reconstruction verifiable within the fiction and harder to dispute.
- [heuristic] Stories in this formula close on the protagonist's death rather than an arrest or trap, using a note, letter or editor's statement to end the frame.
- [heuristic] To link a fragment to its source, recognising its design or pattern matters more than knowing its value, age or maker.
- [heuristic] Use a sudden personal crisis that forces intervention, so the truth comes out before the suspect can escape. When: a suspect is about to flee or conceal the truth. Why: Intervention compels disclosure within the scene.
- [heuristic] Make the act of discovering a hidden space hazardous, so the reveal becomes a survival scene and not only an explanation. Why: Physical danger turns exposition into action and raises stakes at the reveal.
- [procedure] 1) Identify what should have remained at the scene if the object or body was moved. 2) Inspect the route between the scene and exit for those traces. 3) Ask household witnesses whether any item is missing. 4) Infer whether the subject left under its own power. When: A body or object appears to have vanished. Why: Systematic checks separate forced removal from voluntary departure.
- [procedure] 1) List each strange effect separately. 2) For each, ask which ordinary act could produce it. 3) Identify the device or mechanism behind it. 4) Trace where any concealed route leads. When: When a reported phenomenon has several distinct effects. Why: Breaking effects into ordinary causes exposes the mechanism behind each.
- [fact] Persuasive weight and formal proof are separate standards; corroboration may convince yet fail formal acceptance, and stricter standards reject evidence lower ones accept. When: Judging whether supporting evidence will convince an authority or be weighed by different people. Why: Lower standards accept a neat conclusion that stricter ones reject.
- [fact] Proof is either direct, such as an eyewitness to the act, or circumstantial, a chain of linked facts pointing to the act. Direct proof is often unavailable. When: Deciding how a case can be established. Why: Many crimes leave no witness, so inference from linked facts is the usual route.

## hypothetical questioning
- [behavior] A guilty speaker may test a confidant by describing a crime as a general or hypothetical method, then watch the listener's reaction before committing. When: A suspect is likely to test a confidant before revealing guilt. Why: A hypothetical frame lowers the risk of exposure while still gauging the listener.
- [rule] Offer players hypothetical or suppose-style dialogue options so the NPC's committed answers reveal its beliefs without committing the player. When: when designing dialogue trees for information gathering or for NPCs holding views. Why: hypotheticals invite estimates without commitment.
- [rule] Offer a hypothetical dialogue prompt whose reply sets NPC flags that change later lines. When: designing branching dialogue.
- [rule] Ask a witness a hypothetical about what they would do in the same situation, and press for an answer, to draw out their stance.
- [heuristic] Avoid hypothetical probing with hostile or guarded subjects, who will simply refuse to commit. When: when the subject is hostile or guarded.
- [heuristic] Frame a sensitive topic as a hypothetical so the witness can consider it without committing to an answer. When: A witness must be drawn toward a painful subject. Why: A hypothetical lowers the stakes of answering.
- [heuristic] Ask one precise question that a reliable source can answer and that would confirm or refute a specific theory. When: when a theory depends on one hidden fact.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the person to suppose a condition that bears on their view. 2) Get them to commit to their position under that supposition. 3) Reveal a verifiable fact that contradicts the commitment. 4) Observe whether they shift. When: when a person holds a fixed belief you need to test and is willing to talk.
- [procedure] 1) Describe a general case rather than accuse. 2) Ask the subject to judge it. 3) Watch colour changes and pauses. 4) Note verbal slips. 5) Ask a neutral question about a third party and see if the slip repeats. When: a direct question would be refused. Why: A judgement on a general case touches the subject's own stake.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a hypothetical case that mirrors the suspect's secret. 2) Tell it while watching the suspect's face. 3) Record each change in reaction and what was said at that moment. When: a suspect's guilt is likely and direct questions yield nothing. Why: A mirrored story can prompt a reaction the suspect cannot easily hide.
- [procedure] 1) Frame a fictional scheme that mirrors the case, so the listener can discuss it without feeling accused. 2) Ask them to suggest methods, alibis or ways to shift blame. 3) Watch hesitation, quick dismissals and topic avoidance. 4) Note any legal obstacle they raise and whether they propose a workaround. 5) Probe the scheme's weak points. When: A suspect will talk but would refuse or rehearse a direct question.
- [procedure] 1) Ask an insider a general hypothetical about how an object could be hidden. 2) Record the negative facts in the answer, such as absent structures. 3) Verify each negative claim with a second specialist. 4) Keep the question general so the subject does not feel accused. When: after a search fails and location depends on building construction. Why: Insider answers rule out whole categories of hiding places without alerting the subject.
- [procedure] 1) Pose a hypothetical about a third party in a similar situation. 2) Ask what that person would do. 3) Ask why, to draw out motive without a direct accusation. When: A witness knows a sensitive relationship or fact they will not state. Why: Opinions about someone else's behavior can reveal motive without a formal accusation.
- [pitfall] A hypothetical question put to a witness, such as asking whether someone was named, is a probe; its answer is not a finding.
- [pitfall] A theory built on a hypothetical event, such as a document that was never made, fails once a reliable source denies that the event happened. When: a theory assumes an unverified action. Why: the theory's foundation depends on an event that may not have occurred.
- [pitfall] A joke or hypothetical can harden into a suspect in others' minds. When: A speculative idea is repeated in a group. Why: Repetition turns speculation into perceived fact.
- [pitfall] A hypothetical that is too specific can reveal your own suspicions, and a sharp listener may read it as a test.

## intimidation and pressure
- [mechanism] In a dialogue state where a visible weapon is shown and then reassurance follows, an NPC's trust and offered options can shift, opening more answers. Why: threat followed by a promise of safety changes how the NPC weighs cooperation.
- [mechanism] A reprieve followed by a fresh threat keeps stakes rising, because relief that is immediately undercut sustains tension. When: When a tense scene resolves with temporary relief. Why: New threats prevent the tension from ending.
- [behavior] Harsh labels a witness applies to others reveal the speaker's own values and prejudices as much as they describe the people labelled.
- [behavior] Showing insight into a source's identity makes them more forthcoming, though they may also become unsettled.
- [behavior] Accusers who blame a loss on a particular person may attack that person's house and body, for example with stones. When: A loss is blamed on a named suspect.
- [rule] Harsh pressure or forced confession can close a witness off for good; note what a refusal implies, not a false answer, and press with restraint, keeping the topic open. When: when a witness declines to discuss a subject or is fragile or protective. Why: Forcing a confession can close the topic for good.
- [rule] Do not discard a theory because of one gap, but do not accept it while unexplained gaps remain. When: A theory has one or more clues it does not explain. Why: One gap may be a detail, but unresolved gaps indicate the theory may be wrong.
- [rule] Holding a suspect against their will carries legal risk, and the suspect may sue for unlawful restraint. When: An investigator locks a suspect in a room. Why: Restraint without lawful authority is a civil or criminal wrong.
- [heuristic] A defeated adversary who keeps leverage, such as an insurance copy of the evidence, can still threaten the protagonist after losing the object.
- [heuristic] Keep a visible formal consequence in reserve while speaking calmly, so pressure toward candour stays credible without overt threats. When: interrogating a suspect. Why: a visible option makes refusal costly.
- [procedure] 1) Note the slip and its exact words. 2) Ask the suspect to justify it, such as by asking why they mentioned the name. 3) Compare the forced explanation against other facts. When: Suspect has let slip a name or detail. Why: A forced explanation often deepens the slip rather than covering it.
- [procedure] 1) Note the specific avoidance. 2) Name it openly and calmly. 3) Ask the witness to explain their reluctance before revealing your inference. 4) Separate firsthand knowledge from assumption. 5) Check the answer against physical facts.
- [pitfall] Sympathy that is not sincere is a manipulation the subject may later recognise, which undermines the cooperation it was meant to win.
- [pitfall] Pressing a denial harder without new evidence gets the same unchanged answers. When: questioning a suspect who holds a fixed story.
- [pitfall] A repeated line can carry the weight of first-hand knowledge in the listener's mind, alarming a target who assumes the speaker knows details.
- [pitfall] Severe penalties for witnesses can deter honest testimony as well as false testimony, so witnesses may stay silent. Why: Fear of punishment affects every witness, not only liars.
- [pitfall] Statements obtained through coercion may be incomplete or shaped by fear, so they need checking.

## object clue meaning
- [mechanism] An object kept apart from memory cannot be reshaped by recollection, which makes it a more reliable check than another person's memory.
- [mechanism] An object found later, such as a veil under a seat, can connect separate witnesses and the places where they saw people. When: A physical item is discovered after witness accounts are taken. Why: Shared physical traces tie separate observations to the same people or vehicle.
- [behavior] Characters can express tension through an object handled during a scene, letting mood show without direct speech. When: a tense exchange where direct speech is avoided. Why: the object carries emotion the characters will not state.
- [behavior] An object that fails on first use reads as dead to the player, so its later working surprises them. When: a device appears broken before it is used. Why: The early failure sets the expectation that the object is inert.
- [rule] Judge a witness's account by checking its specific claims against independent objects, not by how confidently or vividly it is told.
- [rule] When a physical object found away from the scene contradicts a witness's account, reopen the timeline and explain both the object and the testimony rather than dismissing either. When: A physical clue conflicts with a witness's account of a locked or sealed place. Why: A contradiction forces reconsideration of what was possible.
- [rule] Do not treat an object as significant until its location and history in the scene are established. When: an object is found in an unexpected place. Why: Where an object lay can matter as much as what it is.
- [rule] Reveal motive through a found object such as an inscription rather than a confession. When: Explaining the cause of a haunting or threat. Why: An object carries history and identity without requiring a character to admit guilt.
- [heuristic] An object bearing a victim's name, such as a carved door or ship, prompts the audience to ask why that name is there.
- [heuristic] Give book and letter items inscriptions and loose notes that the player finds by inspecting each one, grouping the most relevant ones together. When: Designing collectible items that carry story information. Why: Inspection rewards thoroughness, and grouping directs attention to the important items.
- [heuristic] A short, quickly extinguished burn on an item usually indicates a secondary use rather than its intended one. When: When an item shows a burn far shorter than its normal use would produce. Why: Its brief burn does not match its primary function.
- [pitfall] A found object proves its owner was present at one point, not that they committed the act or what happened afterward. When: when interpreting an object found at a scene. Why: presence at one moment does not establish later events.
- [pitfall] An object found in a corridor cannot by itself show who put it there.
- [pitfall] An object that implicates an innocent person can mislead the investigator about who was present at the scene.
- [fact] An object's meaning depends on who finds it and how they read it; the same object can be a red herring for one investigator and a clue for another.
- [fact] An object tying a suspect to public news of a crime can serve as a link between them and the crime. When: when a found item relates to reports of a crime.
- [fact] One physical trace can carry a message and a memorial together, so an object may serve emotional and evidential roles at once.

## object placement movement
- [mechanism] Tracking where a small physical item moves between places can reveal who was present at each point and what they did. When: the item passes through a household or routine. Why: each location and handover leaves a trace in the item's path.
- [behavior] An object found in a place where its ordinary use would not occur, with no sign of that use, suggests it was carried in rather than used there. When: When a used item lies in a room where it was not likely used. Why: The absence of the expected context, such as a missing holder or unheard action, points to transport.
- [rule] Deliver a sealed account directly to the people best placed to open it, where it cannot be missed.
- [rule] Model stains and wounds as a placement puzzle where the player positions victim and attacker so that the marks are consistent with their positions. When: building a deduction puzzle from physical marks. Why: A consistency check gives the player a verifiable solution.
- [rule] Hide the item in containers tied to the NPC's habits, so searching them reveals something about that NPC. When: An item is hidden by or for a character. Why: Habit-linked places make the search itself informative.
- [heuristic] Work out an object's original position before it was found; an item placed to block a route was positioned there, not dropped by chance. When: an object found in a route may have been moved.
- [heuristic] The placement of objects around a room, such as bottles, glasses or clocks, can reveal who handled the room.
- [heuristic] Treat a prominently placed object as likely important, since its position signals its significance to the occupants. When: interpreting items in a room.
- [heuristic] Forcing damage placed where it defeats a mechanism with least force suggests professional knowledge, while crude, misplaced damage suggests amateur use. When: Judging the skill behind a forced entry.
- [heuristic] Brackets and placement can signal that a passage was never presented as evidence; check these marks in every edition, since later editions may drop them. When: Reading a printed transcript or deposition. Why: Readers lose the signal when cues are dropped.
- [heuristic] An object found out of its usual place points to the person who moved it, and its label or appearance can mislead until it is examined. When: an object is found away from its normal location. Why: Displacement is a trace, and misleading labels hide its meaning until examination.
- [procedure] 1) Read the date on the found document. 2) Match it against the event date. 3) Place the document on the timeline only if the match holds up under checking. When: When a found document must be dated to fit a timeline. Why: A matching date can be coincidental or misleading.
- [procedure] 1) List every step needed to prepare the object. 2) Identify the physical ability each step requires. 3) Check which suspects can meet every requirement. When: when an object must be prepared before use. Why: Required steps narrow the set of people who could have prepared it.
- [procedure] 1) Count what each person left with. 2) Identify what the taker must have left behind in exchange. 3) Check which exits were unguarded, and when. When: A missing item must be traced to a taker and a route. Why: Counting constrains who could have carried the item out.
- [procedure] 1) Check whether the object could have reached its position by its own motion given the layout. 2) Compare dust cover on the surface beneath it. 3) Test clean and dirty contrast with similar material. 4) Check the suspected placer against who had access to the room. When: judging whether an object was placed or moved. Why: layout, dust and access together test a placement claim.
- [pitfall] An object's location near a possible route does not prove the route was used; the testimony that contradicts that route must still be explained. Why: Location shows where an object lay, not how it got there.
- [pitfall] An object left behind after a scheme can be found by accident and become key evidence.

## removed evidence and traces
- [mechanism] A source object removed and secretly replaced reveals that someone could reach it, so the replacement can serve as an opportunity clue. Why: Tampering with a source proves access, which can be tracked as a state change.
- [mechanism] A second cue, such as a disfigured face on the body, can remove the check that would otherwise reveal a substitution. When: when an impersonation depends on a body being viewed. Why: the one cue that would reveal the swap becomes unavailable.
- [behavior] A culprit who removes or discards an item may leave a trace attached or nearby, or create new links, so a retained fragment can undo the cover. When: A culprit tries to eliminate evidence or clear a trail by disposing of items. Why: Items are linked to other items and surroundings; each disposal step creates a new place or item that can carry evidence. (x2)
- [behavior] After a suspect is removed, the accusers' outward disturbance may stop, so observers read the removal as the end of the trouble.
- [rule] Explain why a decisive object was removed, not only that it is missing, and withhold the reason until late so the absence stays noticed. When: A key item disappears from the scene before the reveal. Why: A missing item draws attention, but its unexplained absence is only resolved by the stated motive.
- [heuristic] Missing identifiers, such as removed labels, papers or laundry marks, are a fact to explain and may signal deliberate concealment of identity, so ask who wanted it hidden. When: when a person's clothing or belongings lack expected identifiers. Why: removal of identifiers can be intentional; players read missing identifiers as evidence of intent, not just absence.
- [heuristic] Removed evidence can signal deliberate blocking of a comparison, suggesting its content matters, but the motive to hide it must be confirmed separately. When: A second source disappears. Why: Blocking suggests the content matters.
- [heuristic] A person may remove an item that bears identifying marks, such as a name written inside, because the marks link it to the owner. When: When an object could be traced back to someone. Why: Identifying marks are the easiest way to connect an object to its owner.
- [heuristic] Removing one person from a case rarely removes its evidence, since the work is reassigned and records persist. When: An NPC leaves or is removed from an investigation.
- [heuristic] Repeated repairs to an object, weighed against its original price, suggest the owner valued it. When: When an object shows multiple repairs. Why: Owners spend effort on objects they value more than their cost.
- [heuristic] A door found locked from the inside suggests that someone inside turned the key.
- [procedure] 1) Notice the slip that revealed a sensitive fact. 2) Judge whether silence is riskier than correction. 3) If so, volunteer the correct fact yourself before the questioner finds it. When: when a small slip has revealed something. Why: self-disclosure can be safer than being caught concealing.
- [pitfall] Removing an object can itself become evidence of the removal, because the act is visible to anyone who notices it.
- [pitfall] Missing traces someone removed, such as torn papers or emptied drawers, hides what actually happened in the scene.
- [pitfall] Forgetting that arrests and departures remove people from a location alters who could physically have been there at a given time.
- [fact] A repaired item with a newer replacement part can serve as a timestamp showing when its owner last visited a particular shop.
- [fact] Removing an object after a confession removes physical proof but does not undo what was said. When: A suspect tries to take away evidence after admitting a crime. Why: A spoken admission remains a record independent of the object.

## rival characters and disclosure
- [mechanism] A boastful rival leaks information: what they brag about reaches the source, who repeats details and reveals how the rival learns things. When: When a rival is in a competitive relationship with a source. Why: Competitive boasting and flattered sources spread details between parties.
- [mechanism] Pitting two rivals against each other lets one death remove a threat while the surviving rival absorbs the blame. When: Scheming to eliminate someone and frame another. Why: The survivor has motive and is visibly connected to the fight.
- [behavior] Rivalry over the same person or prize is itself a motive; rivals readily suspect each other, and quarrels and insults in the record reveal it. When: two characters compete for the same prize, person or resource.
- [behavior] A rival who wants to protect their own share may reveal what others were hiding. When: conflict exists among people involved in a plot.
- [behavior] People tend to overstate a rival's motive when the rival is already disliked. When: a rival is already disliked by the observer. Why: prior dislike biases how ambiguous evidence is read.
- [behavior] Rivals tend to correct or contradict each other when pressed, which reveals facts that either would conceal alone.
- [behavior] Rival authorities may resent outsiders and hold back facts, and their cooperation depends on who receives credit. When: A rival agency shares a case. Why: Credit and status shape what rivals are willing to reveal.
- [rule] Include a rival character who challenges the player's neat theory aloud or holds a confident solution that may be wrong, so the player must test it. When: designing investigator characters or when a theory is presented as the answer. Why: it rewards checking rather than trusting boldness; spoken objections expose gaps a player may otherwise accept.
- [rule] Rivals working the same case can agree explicit rules: one may not publish what it learned only from an official source, and each may keep back a vital discovery. When: Two agents hold different sources and agendas. Why: Agreed limits let them cooperate without giving up all advantage.
- [rule] A rival faction can plant decoy evidence whose lie becomes visible to players who cross-check it.
- [rule] Let rival factions respond to earlier reveals by moving or hiding evidence, so the player's timing changes what the rival can do. When: designing a game with rival factions and clue reveals. Why: Timing changes how opponents respond and builds tension.
- [rule] A rival's sworn claim is an accusation to be tested, not an established fact.
- [heuristic] Weigh a rival's claims, denials or accusations for envy and self-interest; they do not settle which theory is right. When: a rival disparages another investigator or theory; rivalry shapes what officials and witnesses say. Why: rivalry can distort warnings and statements.
- [heuristic] A rival NPC who attacks witnesses by inventing their views should reward a player who asks them to name the claim they are answering.
- [heuristic] Old social rivalries, such as competition over a marriage, can supply a motive for a present crime and should be recorded. When: Reconstructing a family's social history during an investigation.
- [heuristic] Test a rival suspect separately, even at some cost, to remove doubt about a psychological reading.
- [pitfall] A rival pursuing the same goal may watch the same endpoint, complicating the operation; a second character's inquiry about the same target can reveal such a rival tracker.

## rumour source tracing
- [mechanism] Once a secret leaks to an enemy, it becomes a time-limited danger, since the enemy must act before the advantage is gone. When: Information about a plan reaches the opposing side. Why: The enemy's knowledge creates urgency that forces an earlier response.
- [rule] Let players trace a rumor back along the NPCs who passed it on to its first witness, to judge whether later reports are independent. (x2)
- [rule] Track the source of each lead, because a cover story may later conflict with testimony and expose itself.
- [rule] Check each informal detail against a dated source before accepting it.
- [rule] Let a rumor-spreading NPC repeat an authority's framing, and plant a clue that reveals the influence behind it. When: An NPC's gossip echoes an official explanation. Why: Players can detect where a story was shaped.
- [rule] Let false in-world claims spread through a rumour system, and require the player to trace who started a story and check it against evidence. When: when a game world carries false reports. Why: Tracing sources teaches the player to weigh claims rather than accept them.
- [rule] Track who asserted what about whom, so that a second rumour can be flagged as hearsay rather than treated as fact.
- [rule] Give each rumor an NPC source with a recorded grudge, so players can weigh the speaker's motive against the accusation. When: Designing rumors players must evaluate.
- [rule] Design rumors to be checkable: a player who gathers an alibi or witness should be able to lower a rumor's credibility.
- [rule] Use a rumour that contains a true lead even when its tone is unreliable. When: Designing rumours that guide player action. Why: A mix of accurate lead and biased framing rewards careful evaluation.
- [heuristic] Facts restated, questioned and challenged between speakers arrive in a form the listener can check.
- [heuristic] Check whether the person spreading a rumour was also a source of it, and whether their own impairment shaped what they said.
- [heuristic] Let a rumor spread through several NPCs while keeping one originating source discoverable, so players learn to trace apparent agreement back to a single origin. When: designing a rumor that appears to be confirmed.
- [procedure] Before treating a rumour as a finding, 1) ask who first observed or made the claim. 2) Note each person who relayed it, including you, and check each link. 3) Note any link whose source cannot be named. 4) Rate by how close the first teller was to the event. When: a claim arrived through other people. Why: Each relay can add, drop or shift details, or add embellishment or bias, distorting the original facts. (x3)
- [procedure] 1) List everyone who knew of a planned event and which facts each was given. 2) Identify what the culprit wanted. 3) Compare what each person could have passed on. 4) Check the list rather than trusting it. When: a secret plan has leaked or an NPC reveals an undisclosed fact.
- [procedure] 1) List every route by which a detained person could have learned outside information, such as insiders or visitors. 2) For each route, identify the record it leaves, such as a permit or logbook. 3) Check each record against an independent source. When: A detained person seems to know things they should not. Why: Each route leaves a checkable trail, and independent checks reduce reliance on any single account.
- [procedure] 1) Note each claim about movements or timing. 2) Compare it with an external record such as a schedule or programme. 3) Ask an unrelated question to shift the topic and test attention. When: an informal witness gives timing or motive claims. Why: external records expose contradictions and an abrupt topic change tests attention.

## securing and preserving scenes
- [mechanism] Seizing one person's property can extend to spouse and relatives, who may be jailed or stripped of provisions.
- [rule] Examine a scene before anyone handles it, and leave it unchanged until its traces are recorded or a full search is made, so the search starts from the original state. When: A scene has just been discovered or is being investigated and may hold evidence not yet examined. Why: Handling erases or alters traces; disturbed objects destroy clues, mislead later searchers, and prevent later accounts from being checked against the original state. (x2)
- [rule] Secure physical evidence or hard-to-replace identifying sources as soon as their value is recognised, before they are altered, consumed or lost, and protect them. When: Evidence may be destroyed or used before collection, or a source provides hard-to-replace identification. Why: Acting late can allow a second harm; an unprotected source may be lost or damaged. (x2)
- [rule] Keep a sample from any test item and keep an item consumed by only one person intact for analysis, since an unpreserved item cannot clear anyone. When: For test items, or when only one person consumed the item. Why: Analysis confirms the reaction reading; no other eater can vouch for a solitary item, so only its own evidence can clear it.
- [rule] Collect small residues, such as dust, that routine cleaning would otherwise erase, so the trace survives for later analysis.
- [rule] Secure a distressed witness's help by acknowledging their courage and framing the request as painful but necessary. When: asking a witness to face a distressing task. Why: Recognition and framing make cooperation more likely.
- [rule] When a key item is still missing, keep the suspect or area under watch so the item cannot be disposed of. When: When a suspect may destroy or hide a key item. Why: Watching the suspect keeps the missing link recoverable.
- [rule] Keep the original form when the exact wording is itself evidence. When: Presenting old records as evidence. Why: Modernizing can erase the detail that matters.
- [rule] Reward the player for preserving a trace before it is disturbed by player or NPC actions. When: a scene's evidence can be contaminated. Why: preservation rewards careful play.
- [rule] Avoid searching methods that destroy the only evidence of a secret; restore the scene where possible so it can be checked again. When: a fragile or single clue must be inspected. Why: destroyed evidence cannot be used later.
- [heuristic] When a suspect owns only one book, that volume is likely the key and can be requested for inspection. When: Numeric correspondence exists and the candidate key book can be identified and seized.
- [heuristic] Store sealed evidence in a secure vault rather than close at hand, so an adversary cannot track where it is.
- [procedure] 1) Close the door and keep others away from the scene. 2) Send for the qualified examiner. 3) Clear the room of everyone not required to stay. 4) Leave the scene unaltered until the examiner views the body and surroundings. 5) Search only after that viewing. When: At the discovery of a body or crime scene, before evidence is moved, examined or cleaned. Why: Early visitors and disturbance can alter the scene, and a search from a disturbed state finds less.
- [procedure] 1) Count and record the prisoner's money and personal effects against him in the register. 2) Measure height and note removed items such as boots. 3) Keep scene clothing as evidence and issue standard garments. When: A prisoner is booked into custody. Why: Written inventory fixes what can later be disputed or altered.
- [procedure] 1) Photograph the item. 2) Request any fingerprints on it. 3) Alert the institution holding the funds to stop payment to the suspect.
- [pitfall] A preserved scene can still hide evidence, so preservation does not replace a thorough search. When: Investigating a locked-down scene. Why: Freezing the room protects evidence from disturbance but does not reveal what is hidden in it.
- [fact] Seizures took livestock, crops, household goods and tools from estates, reaching several households at once.

## sensory and sound testimony
- [mechanism] Binding and blindfolding remove visual cues, so the candidate must rely on the group's spoken signals. When: group initiation trials. Why: Removing one channel forces reliance on another.
- [mechanism] A familiar scent or object can trigger partial recall of associated past events, giving access to memory without direct questioning. When: A character has lost or partly lost access to a memory. Why: Sensory input links to memories through association, so a cue can reactivate them.
- [behavior] A witness who learns she was overheard may change her tone, so impressions formed before and after that point cannot be compared directly. When: A witness discovers that her words were heard by someone who is investigating. Why: Awareness of being observed changes how she presents herself.
- [behavior] A single distinctive sensory cue, such as a scent or a fragment of a voice, can anchor a witness's memory of a person they never saw clearly. When: a witness recalls someone seen only briefly or poorly. Why: A vivid partial cue gives memory a fixed point, so the recognition feels firm despite weak sight.
- [rule] Log timed in-game events and have NPC witnesses report them with sensory cues, such as a clock striking or a hinge creaking.
- [rule] Judge sound testimony by the listener's position, distance from the source and any barriers between them. When: a witness reports hearing something rather than seeing it. Why: Hearing depends on position and obstruction.
- [rule] Do not treat a smell or other sensory impression as identifying contents; confirm the contents with a test. When: a sensory clue points to a substance. Why: smell alone does not establish what something is.
- [rule] Pair each twist with a proof the player can check through an in-world sense such as touch, smell or taste, not sight alone. Why: The player can verify the answer by the same means the investigator uses.
- [heuristic] Odd smells and similar easily dismissed sensory cues can identify a cause that visual evidence misses. When: Investigating an event with limited visibility.
- [heuristic] Present a vivid sensory image before explaining what it means, so the audience experiences it first and interprets it second.
- [heuristic] Ask precise, seemingly trivial sensory questions, since a fabricated account rarely anticipates concrete detail.
- [procedure] 1) Ask targeted questions about sound, smell, light and handwriting. 2) Ask about physical state, such as dust or disturbed objects. 3) Check each answer against what the scene should show. When: reconstructing an account after a frightening or confused event. Why: Targeted questions recover details the witness did not consciously record.
- [tradeoff] A perceived detail contradicting an easy explanation keeps the question open, but an unverified sound under fear is not evidence even when reasoning says it is unlikely. When: an offered explanation conflicts with what was perceived: keep the question open if the perception is verified; discount it if unverified under stress. Why: Direct perception is harder to dismiss than a general theory, but unverified perception under stress is unreliable because fear shapes what is heard. (x2)
- [pitfall] Smell or sound rarely marks when an event began or ended, and a witness may mistake a sound for another event, so verify a sound-based time before fixing the timeline. When: a witness relies on smell or sound to place someone or anchor a timeline. Why: Sensory impressions persist without marking when they began or ended.
- [pitfall] A missing trace proves little when the observer was too far away or lacked the sensing range needed to detect it.
- [fact] Witnesses usually hear more than they see, so a sound from a room confirms presence there but not the identity of whoever made it.
- [fact] A witness can attest only what their senses reported; a sighting may be false through a deluded sense, a deceiving appearance, or a real figure mistaken for its likeness. When: when a claim rests on a sighting. Why: perception can be deceived in several distinct ways.

## silent suspect behavior
- [model] Model a silent suspect as a game state that only other evidence can break.
- [behavior] In a tense silent exchange where both characters privately think of the same thing, the one who looks away first is read as conceding the point. When: Two characters share a secret and hold a steady look. Why: Breaking eye contact signals that the holder has lost nerve, so the moment is decided by it.
- [behavior] A suspect who shows no visible reaction to an incriminating object may still recognise it, so an absence of emotion is worth noting but is not proof. When: a suspect is shown an object linked to a crime.
- [behavior] A suspect who refuses to account for their whereabouts leaves the investigator to supply the answer. When: when the suspect stays silent under direct questioning.
- [behavior] A suspect who refuses to defend himself or who admits damaging facts to shield another can look guilty even when innocent. When: A suspect withholds a fact that protects someone else. Why: Authorities read silence and self-damaging answers as guilt, unless the hidden reason is discovered.
- [behavior] Questioners can halt a colleague with a slight gesture, such as a head shake, without any spoken order.
- [rule] At official premises, observe and collect information without commenting, since comments can reveal your hypotheses.
- [heuristic] Judge a silent or absent party by their own written words, which can show whether they knew the secret being kept. When: A witness has said nothing directly about a secret.
- [heuristic] A dog that does not react to a visitor suggests the visitor was someone the dog knew. When: when an intrusion occurs and a guard animal is present. Why: Animals usually bark at strangers.
- [heuristic] A witness who heard nothing carries little weight if their room lay far from the event, since distance limits what can be heard. When: the witness claims to have heard nothing. Why: distance limits what can be heard.
- [heuristic] A door that opens without noise suggests its hinges were oiled beforehand, so silence can indicate preparation rather than normal use.
- [tradeoff] Silent listening draws more from a witness with a motive to talk, but direct questioning is faster when a fact is needed now from a hostile witness.
- [tradeoff] A silent witness builds suspense but delays the clue, while a witness who speaks plainly delivers information quickly but offers less mystery. When: When deciding how fast a story must deliver a clue.
- [pitfall] Strongly shared beliefs can treat disagreement as heresy, silencing sceptics; unvoiced doubt lets rumours grow unchallenged, so early voiced doubt can stop an escalating accusation. When: when a community strongly holds a belief or an accusation starts to spread. Why: social pressure discourages doubters, and silent doubt leaves rumours unchecked.
- [pitfall] Assuming a silent room holds an empty or sleeping occupant, without a timed check, can mislead the investigation.
- [pitfall] A silent cross-examination does not concede that the evidence is sound.
- [fact] If the accused and the only witness who can confirm the timing both stay silent, neither is fully cleared and the case reduces to one person's word against the other's.

## suspect and lead selection
- [model] A mystery can be built as a chain of hunts, where a dismissed explanation gives way to a secret investigator who follows successive suspects, each overturned by the next. When: structuring a detective investigation. Why: A chain of overturned theories keeps the player moving forward while the true explanation stays hidden.
- [rule] Give each suspect its own evidence trail: one clue that makes them seem the answer, then a new fact that clears or rebalances them, so the player revises the theory. When: writing a rotation of suspects in a mystery. Why: Each specific new fact keeps shifts in suspicion grounded and believable, and testing each suspect keeps the search alive.
- [rule] Test an unfashionable line of inquiry before deciding it is wrong; dropping it merely for being unpopular is an error.
- [rule] Give suspects access and daily routines that conflict with a supernatural story, so the player must check the human explanation. When: When designing suspects in a mystery. Why: Conflicting routines make the human explanation testable.
- [rule] Give each secondary suspect a full cycle of spotlight so no single false solution lasts too long. When: Balancing a cast of suspects. Why: Rotating focus keeps the mystery moving and prevents fatigue.
- [heuristic] Rank suspects by access and relationship to the victim, not equally; ranking narrows the field but establishes neither motive nor a deed. When: a timeline is partly fixed, or when designing a suspect list the player can investigate.
- [heuristic] When several characters have motives, test each one's claims against facts before accepting any accusation. When: more than one suspect has a plausible motive. Why: shared motives do not identify the actor.
- [heuristic] Let a rational authority supply a human suspect, then let that suspect fade, so the player must decide who the real threat is. When: when the mystery should move from a mundane explanation to an open question. Why: A discarded suspect shifts the player's suspicion and keeps the threat ambiguous.
- [heuristic] At the start of a theft mystery, map the inheritance chain and rank suspects by who gains, not by who is loudest. When: Beginning a theft investigation with family or estate ties. Why: Gain from the object is a stronger signal than noise.
- [heuristic] Make each named suspect a separate branch the player checks in turn, so the investigation has a clear order of tests. When: Designing a mystery with several named suspects. Why: Separate branches give the player a manageable sequence rather than one tangled question.
- [heuristic] Make an innocent suspect a plausible false solution by tying them to one incriminating fact, and let the player see the gap.
- [heuristic] Let the investigator catch the suspect before the motive is known, so the final act concerns meaning rather than who did it. When: a mystery whose motive lies in a hidden past. Why: a solved whodunit leaves the late story to explain why.
- [procedure] 1) Weigh each suspect's motive, means and access separately. 2) Check whether the suspect could have known the terms that make the motive work. 3) Ask who was present when each physical clue was recovered. 4) Treat background pressures as context only. When: narrowing a list of suspects with overlapping access where the evidence must be weighed fairly. Why: Motive, access and evidence reliability are distinct, and mixing them produces unfair accusations; a suspect may fit one factor strongly and fail the others.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who could physically reach the victims. 2) Ask who knew and trusted them. 3) Ask who had a reason to harm them, using background history to answer. When: Physical traces are thin and suspects must be narrowed.
- [procedure] 1) List everyone who could have placed the cause. 2) List who could obtain the means. 3) List who gained from the result. 4) Tie each list to a record that can be checked independently. When: several people had access and the case turns on who could both obtain and benefit from the means.
- [pitfall] If no human suspect is raised before a supernatural reveal, the eventual ghost explanation has no alternative to test against and feels arbitrary. When: Building a mystery that ends in an occult explanation. Why: A human alternative that the player can consider and reject makes the final explanation feel earned.
- [fact] In closed-case mysteries the culprit is usually someone already present in the scene, so the question is which person in the room could have acted.

## timeline and sightings
- [mechanism] A known countdown raises tension because each passing moment is a loss, and tension grows as the count approaches zero. When: when a timed reveal or discovery threat is set. Why: each passing moment reduces the remaining time.
- [mechanism] A new incident can connect earlier unlinked incidents when it shares a location, person or record with them. When: A later event shares an element with earlier separate events. Why: The shared element makes the earlier events visible together.
- [rule] Record each person's last certain sighting and anything heard afterwards, since these set the boundary of what is known.
- [rule] Do not use photographs taken long after an event to answer questions about its timing. When: Using recorded images as evidence. Why: Later images may show a changed scene.
- [rule] Tie each sighting to a clock reference such as a departure, a sound, or the moment of sleep, so its timing can be checked even when identity is uncertain. When: when recording testimony about a sequence of events. Why: Timing anchors make a witness's account usable as evidence even when identity is weak.
- [heuristic] The largest unknown interval in a timeline is the most important gap to investigate, because it hides the most about when the event occurred.
- [heuristic] A later independent sighting of someone who left an event bounds when that event could have ended, which helps order events.
- [heuristic] A journey broken at an intermediate stop, such as a port, gives the traveller opportunity to make calls or send messages.
- [heuristic] A witness pressed in one meeting may give less than on a later, unpressured visit, so revisit witnesses once pressure is removed. When: When a witness was cautious or evasive in an earlier meeting.
- [procedure] 1) Identify who last saw the person. 2) Record exactly what each witness saw. 3) Note what the person carried or did just before being seen. When: when a person has vanished. Why: the last moments narrow where to look next.
- [procedure] 1) List each successive moment after the event. 2) Count who was present to observe at each. 3) Rank moments by fewest observers. 4) Treat the lowest-count moment as the most likely escape window, after stating assumptions. When: a crowded timeline in which witnesses change position. Why: An escape is most explainable when the fewest people could have seen it.
- [procedure] 1) List each recorded departure and arrival time. 2) Compute the gaps between connections. 3) Sum the gaps to estimate how far ahead the adversary is. When: Working out who could have acted before whom. Why: Summing known travel and waiting intervals gives a lead estimate from records.
- [procedure] 1) Date the event the witness describes. 2) Ask who in the witness's life could have told them. 3) Check whether that source existed and was in contact with the witness in time. When: A witness claims knowledge they could not have witnessed. Why: The check shows whether the knowledge could have been obtained through ordinary means.
- [pitfall] Equating the last witnessed moment with time of death or event time is a mistake; death or the event may have occurred later, and later changes can hide it. When: Timing an event from witness sightings. Why: The last sighting only bounds the event from one side; the scene may have been changed afterwards.
- [pitfall] Do not treat a late return as guilt without checking the gap it leaves, weighing weather, route and stated reasons first.
- [fact] A witness's last sighting of a person alive sets the earliest possible time of death and the latest moment known alive, anchoring the timeline and bounding what happened afterward. When: Reconstructing a timeline. Why: The victim cannot have died before being seen alive; a last-known time anchors the sequence.
- [fact] Laudanum acts in three phases: a stimulating phase, then a sedative phase, then deep sleep.

## timeline overlap and time windows
- [rule] Test whether an act could fit the entire interval at any hour, not only the hour a favored theory prefers. When: when a theory depends on when something happened.
- [rule] Record witness claims with explicit time windows, so players can check whether each claim covers the events they care about. When: authoring witness statements in a game. Why: Undated claims cannot be tested against the timeline.
- [rule] Check whether the official time window is established or only assumed before judging any alibi against it.
- [rule] Turn a short time window into a puzzle where the player must confirm each suspect's location during that interval.
- [rule] Do not present a time-of-death window as an exact time; it records only what can be shown. When: Reporting a reconstructed time of death. Why: Bounds from sightings are limits, not precise measurements.
- [heuristic] Where traces cross or overlap, the mark laid over or partly erasing another was made later, so overlap order fixes the sequence of passage. When: Several traces cross or overlap on one surface. Why: Later passes disturb earlier impressions; reading overlap backwards reverses apparent direction of travel.
- [heuristic] Express an event's time as a window built from several approximate estimates; overlapping independent estimates narrow it, and other evidence can test the band. When: Evidence is approximate or witness times are estimates. Why: Overlapping estimates give a band that other evidence can test.
- [heuristic] Ask witnesses for a bounded time window, such as the last few minutes, because a window narrows the search for a passer-by.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the earliest and latest moments the act could have occurred, using reliable witness times. 2) Exclude any time outside the window. 3) Weigh times inside the window by the actor's incentive. When: when an act must be placed in time from several clock-based accounts. Why: A bounded window narrows the search, and incentive points toward likely timing.
- [procedure] 1) State the inference, such as a recent arrival. 2) Ask a direct question that would confirm or deny it. 3) Accept or revise the inference by the answer. When: A timing-based inference needs a quick check before it guides further reasoning. Why: A direct question turns a plausible story into a testable claim.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the last moment the item was known to be present. 2) Fix the first moment someone needed it. 3) State the window between them explicitly. 4) Test each witness against that window. When: A small or personal object disappears and the question is who had opportunity. Why: A bounded window limits which people and times remain possible.
- [tradeoff] Frequent time checks sustain tension but slow the pace, so they must be balanced with action. When: Writing a timed sequence.
- [pitfall] Time overlap shows opportunity, not action, and can be arranged; treat timing and reaction inferences as hypotheses to check. Why: Such inferences are probable, not proven, and reading too much into them misleads. (x2)
- [pitfall] A claim or denial covers only the period it names; events outside that window remain unexamined, so check the timing of each claim. When: A witness denies involvement or makes a claim. Why: The denial is bounded in time.
- [pitfall] Long gaps between dated events, such as a weekend, can hide movements that a timeline cannot show. When: a timeline has large unrecorded intervals. Why: Unrecorded time can conceal what happened.
- [pitfall] A timeline with many unverifiable steps makes readers lose track of who can confirm what, weakening the whole deduction. When: Constructing a long sequence of movements. Why: Each unverifiable step adds doubt that spreads to the steps that could be verified.
- [fact] Boundary disputes and releases between neighboring towns appear as entries in an ownership chain, marking where claims overlapped.

## withheld information and disclosure
- [mechanism] Stating a stark fact while withholding its outcome keeps tension high, because the audience waits for the next update. When: Between revelations in a story. Why: Unresolved outcomes keep attention on what comes next.
- [mechanism] An investigator who claims to hold decisive proof but refuses to reveal it keeps fear alive after a trap has failed. When: when a trap or interrogation has not produced a confession. Why: Unnamed proof leaves the suspect uncertain how much is known.
- [behavior] Precautions shown without a stated purpose invite the audience to keep a question open until it is answered. When: characters take protective steps without explanation. Why: unexplained action creates curiosity.
- [rule] Let NPCs withhold a key fact until the player presents evidence, then release it in stages that depend on the player's choices. When: Designing NPC disclosure in a game. Why: Staged release rewards evidence-building and keeps information meaningful.
- [rule] Do not hold back facts that the other person needs in order to act. When: when deciding what to withhold from a listener.
- [heuristic] Hold back an investigator's reason or a fact the player lacks, so the later reveal reframes earlier scenes and makes the action look suspicious first, then sensible. When: When an action would look odd before the reveal, or when planning reveals in a mystery. Why: Delayed explanation keeps the player's reading open and rewards them when the reason is shown; withheld knowledge makes earlier events look different once disclosed. (x2)
- [heuristic] Open the story with a threat whose purpose is withheld, so the audience senses danger before it knows the reason behind it. When: Opening a mystery with a sinister event. Why: An unexplained purpose keeps the audience reading later events for meaning.
- [heuristic] Avoid pursuing a sensitive area when each question could start a chain of disclosure that the questioner cannot control.
- [heuristic] Leave one method of the solution unexplained at the end to keep an element of mystery and room for a merciful resolution. When: closing a mystery in which the guilty party has repented. Why: A partial answer keeps the ending open while still resolving the main question.
- [heuristic] A detective who privately holds a conclusion while sharing only part of it creates tension rather than a plot hole. When: The investigator has identified the truth but not yet revealed it. Why: Withheld knowledge keeps the audience anticipating the reveal.
- [tradeoff] Withholding outcomes holds tension, but it blocks a reader who needs a clear answer before taking the next step. When: The audience must understand the situation to follow what comes next. Why: Withholding trades clarity for suspense.
- [tradeoff] Keeping a trap's method secret preserves its effect, but frustrates helpers who cannot follow the reasoning. When: Investigators hold a plan that would be weakened if revealed. Why: Disclosure would warn the target, while silence costs the team understanding and cooperation.
- [pitfall] Withheld information can be read as evasion or concealment, eroding trust, so the reason for the delay must be clear to the audience and to allies. When: Withholding information from allies or witnesses, or when a character or reveal delays information. Why: Withheld information can be read as concealment, eroding trust.
- [pitfall] Withheld knowledge needs a concrete, satisfying payoff; unpaid secrets make the audience feel cheated, and vague threats left unresolved read as filler. When: Designing secrets, hidden knowledge, or delayed reveals. Why: Audiences need a resolution to feel the withholding was purposeful; suspense without resolution loses trust and interest.
- [pitfall] Withheld or forgotten testimony still matters, and the investigator should note the gap rather than ignore it. When: A witness cannot or will not give an account.
- [pitfall] Clues shown early but left uninterpreted keep tension, yet a clue that is never explained leaves the player with nothing to act on. When: when designing a mystery reveal. Why: Withholding meaning sustains suspense only until the reveal makes the clue's purpose legible.
- [fact] A story can hold back the protagonist's past guilt until late, so the threat's logic becomes readable only in hindsight. When: when the threat is tied to the protagonist's history. Why: A late disclosure reframes earlier clues and sustains suspense without an early explanation.

## baseline conduct
- [behavior] Ordinary routine, such as sport, polite drinks and a tidy house, reads as innocent and makes investigators drop lines of inquiry they should keep open. When: investigating a setting that outwardly looks domestic. Why: familiar signs of harmless life lower expectations of threat.
- [behavior] People with an orderly view of the world find it hard to accept that rank does not guarantee virtue, so they resist accusations against office holders. Why: they expect judges and clergy to be upright.
- [rule] Do not treat ordinary conduct, such as a lively household or a lost temper, as proof of a crime.
- [rule] A witness whose conviction-supporting account rests on seeing or hearing must rely on ordinary human faculties, not on claimed perceptions only they have. When: when judging whether a witness account can support a verdict.
- [rule] Investigators should use the same lawful methods for every crime, instead of special tests or procedures for one kind of offence. When: when investigating a crime that seems to need special handling. Why: Ordinary methods can be checked, while special tests are easier to bend toward a predetermined result.
- [heuristic] Ordinary crimes with many plausible motives and methods are harder to solve than unusual ones, since they lack distinguishing features and each explanation seems equally possible. When: a case looks routine and several explanations seem to fit. Why: no single explanation is favoured by the evidence, and nothing focuses the investigation.
- [heuristic] Before accepting apparently supernatural knowledge or a spectacle as supernatural, check ordinary channels first: gossip, a relative, an earlier record, or whether a skilled performer could produce it by ordinary means. When: a witness reveals something they could not have observed directly, or a spectacle seems supernatural. Why: ordinary sources can account for knowledge or feats that appear impossible.
- [heuristic] Ordinary states such as a mount's freshness or dry boots can test an NPC's account of travel, so use them as checkable clues. When: an NPC describes a journey. Why: everyday conditions reflect the effort of travel.
- [heuristic] Describing a culprit as unremarkable is typical of hidden masterminds, so blandness can itself be a clue. When: a witness describes the suspect as ordinary. Why: hidden masterminds are deliberately forgettable.
- [heuristic] When a key object disappears from its last recorded location, check ordinary explanations such as cleaning or routine disposal before assuming tampering. When: A recorded object is missing from where it was last seen. Why: Mundane causes are more common than deliberate removal.
- [procedure] 1) List the usual practice for each actor in the story. 2) Compare each reported action against that practice. 3) Treat each mismatch, a departure from common practice that suggests a hidden purpose, as a lead to test against the explanation.
