When: a witness account must be checked for plausibility. Why: practice is predictable, so a departure from it signals a motive.
- [procedure] 1) Observe and record the scene before the event. 2) Compare the scene afterwards against that baseline. 3) Treat any change as evidence that someone handled it.
- [pitfall] The most ordinary reading may be right in one respect yet miss the case, so each reading must be tested against the other facts. When: an event has a mundane explanation. Why: partial truths can hide the real cause.
- [pitfall] Assuming that because an ordinary person cannot do something, nobody could, overlooks routes that exceptional abilities open. When: Judging whether a suspect could reach a sealed place. Why: Ability differences are ignored when the route is judged by normal capability.
- [pitfall] The norm departure method depends on the investigator's knowledge of normal practice, which can itself be wrong. Why: A mistaken idea of normal practice makes ordinary behavior look suspicious.
- [pitfall] Assuming a nominal ruler acts independently is a mistake when advisers and early contacts shape his views and decisions. When: a figurehead holds formal power.

## cultural and supernatural beliefs
- [mechanism] A long-repeated folk belief passed through many speakers gains a false air of truth and shapes what people perceive without their noticing.
- [behavior] Unfamiliar customs such as tipping, seating, greetings and dress are read by outsiders as insults, threats or signs of character.
- [rule] Cursed-relic lore or a seer's hint serves as misdirection: players blame a curse or monster; a human NPC culprit is revealed by a rational check such as the operator's influence.
- [rule] Give staff NPCs a reference or record with flaws the player must weigh, rather than ignore or accept outright.
- [rule] Plant a folk saying early that later proves literal, so a casual phrase becomes a key to a later puzzle.
- [rule] Make a cursed-object clue that names a suspect contradict the timeline or physical evidence, so careful players can detect the mismatch.
- [rule] Give a cursed location a sound clue with a mundane source, and let its lore shape interpretation while allowing a rational check.
- [heuristic] A custom only carries weight if it is widely shared; where habits vary across people, a broken habit proves little. When: Habits vary widely across the people involved.
- [heuristic] Treat an NPC's ward or talisman as a clue to their belief and fear, not as proof that magic exists. When: Designing an NPC who carries a protective object. Why: The object reveals psychology while leaving the cause of events open.
- [heuristic] Some strangeness is real but lies in human choices, such as the obstinate retention of a damaging wording, rather than in hidden forces. When: when an odd document or motive resists easy explanation. Why: human choices often produce oddities that look uncanny.
- [procedure] 1) Collect the incidents from the relevant period. 2) Filter for ones of the same kind. 3) Check each pair for a shared location, person or record. When: Starting a search for links between incidents. Why: Builds a candidate set of events that might connect.
- [pitfall] Folk beliefs about guilt, such as a murderer unable to bear the victim's blood, and links between hair or build and temperament are superstition, not proof of guilt or character.
- [pitfall] Choosing the most dramatic, mystical reading of a foreseen event over a mundane explanation such as coincidence leads investigators astray.
- [pitfall] A family prophecy can be reused to explain every later sudden death, turning separate events into a supposed pattern.
- [pitfall] A folk rule about reading faces, such as distrusting direct eye contact, can confirm the observer's existing suspicion rather than reveal anything about the person. Why: The rule supplies a reason to believe what the observer already expects.
- [pitfall] A folk saying can recast a frightened person's flight as superstition, so the real cause of their fear is never examined.

## decoys and props
- [mechanism] A character with a harmless surface lowers the audience's guard, so their testimony and importance are discounted until the surface is pressed. When: When a character's apparent simplicity would make readers dismiss them. Why: Readers judge by first impression.
- [behavior] Players who classify items by their surroundings will misread a key item placed among decor that suggests another use. When: a key item is placed among decor. Why: surroundings set the expected category of an object.
- [rule] Give props two readings, one misleading and one a careful player can overturn by inspection, e.g. a token as clue or decoy, a tool whose innocent use explains a stain. Why: Objects with two readings keep players uncertain until they test both.
- [rule] Plant a memorable but harmless NPC, then reveal its true role through a visible change.
- [rule] Let an apparently harmless prop on a character be a verifiable trace that contradicts a witness's account. When: Designing witness testimony that can be checked. Why: A mundane object can expose a false account without seeming significant at first.
- [rule] Place an object whose ordinary use hides its clue value in a room, and flag it as a clue only after the player examines it. When: designing clue placement in a room.
- [rule] Keep a small budget of decorative detail that can be dismissed without breaking the puzzle logic.
- [rule] Stage a pair of suspects who look like victims, so the culprit hides among the people who found the body.
- [rule] Hide a fake-alibi device, such as a recording or timed trigger, inside an ordinary room object the player has already seen and dismissed. When: Designing an alibi that the player must later break. Why: A dismissed object is overlooked, so the trick survives until the reveal.
- [heuristic] Replacing real evidence with a convincing decoy lets a suspect return to check it, revealing their interest without losing the real proof. When: when a suspect will recheck hidden evidence. Why: The decoy keeps the suspect's behaviour observable while the original is secured.
- [heuristic] Plant a second suspect in plain view, with a role that gives access to the site, and let the player connect them through a tool or trace. When: when a mystery needs a hidden culprit. Why: A suspect whose access is visible but unexamined can be exposed by a single trace.
- [heuristic] Place a decoy that resembles the real object so players who misread it are corrected only at the reveal. When: The true clue object could be mistaken for ordinary stock or property. Why: A convincing substitute keeps the real object's meaning hidden until the reveal reframes it.
- [heuristic] Give the audience a plausible wrong answer that they believe at first, so the later correction feels earned. When: a mystery with one hidden answer. Why: A surprise lands harder when the wrong belief was reasonable.
- [pitfall] Ornament used to hide a seam can itself draw attention to the spot it covers. When: When camouflaging a secret with rosettes, carvings or similar detail. Why: Unusual or clumsy decoration invites a closer look at the area.
- [pitfall] Reading a decorative fixture or prop as functional; props can look operational without working.
- [pitfall] Ignoring a mark because it looks decorative can hide a clue; visible marks should be checked for possible meaning. When: A setting includes signs, initials or dates. Why: Decorative-seeming details can carry meaning.

## layered reveals and misdirection
- [model] A layered reveal moves through setup clues, disguise hints, a false trail, a false conclusion, a documentary link, a confession and a late reveal. When: designing a multi-stage twist in a story or investigation. Why: each stage builds on clues the audience already holds.
- [model] A layered reveal stacks false solutions so each reveal reframes the one before, moving blame between suspects and finally to whether a crime happened at all.
- [model] A layered identity reveal peels back a hidden antagonist in steps, each exposing a more trusted figure, so the final reveal lands on the character the audience trusted most. When: designing a mystery with a hidden antagonist who may be a trusted ally. Why: Each layer reuses audience trust as cover for the next.
- [model] A layered mystery runs in phases: fixed evidence, several false solutions each undone by a counter-source, a late reversal cluster, then reconciliation of partly true solutions.
- [definition] A layered misdirection presents one clue under successive readings, each backed by a different authority, before its true origin is revealed.
- [mechanism] Two linked misdirections can be undone together when one second witness and one physical object reframe both at the same time.
- [mechanism] When a captured thief's identity reveals a worse crime than the initial theft, the stakes of the chase rise and the quest moves from theft to murder. When: a pursuit follows a robbery and the captive's past is revealed. Why: The reframed crime raises the threat level and the reader's investment after the apparent resolution.
- [mechanism] Stacking a reconstructed impostor, a false alibi and a later confession keeps a reveal fair when each explanation is physically grounded and overturns the last.
- [mechanism] Reversing the roles of investigator and criminal, so trusted detectives are exposed as culprits, recasts every earlier scene once the masked leader is unmasked. When: Designing a late twist that overturns the reader's trust in the investigators. Why: Earlier scenes are re-read with the new identities, so their evidence seems to have pointed to the truth all along.
- [rule] Place the decisive reversal near the end so a sudden late event breaks the closing belief; guilt reassignment surprises once each earlier correction is accepted as truth. When: planning the climax of a mystery. Why: A late shock overturns the audience's settled conclusion, and the reversal works only when earlier corrections were accepted as truth.
- [heuristic] Place the central fact late, and let it turn a distant threat into a present one, so the stronger fact changes the reader's sense of danger. When: A mystery needs a climax that raises stakes. Why: Late, close-to-home facts carry more weight than early, abstract ones.
- [heuristic] Layer two plots: a small, quickly solved crime, and a larger planned one that the solution exposes, with the minor culprit as a frightened accomplice whose weak motive leaves the mastermind open. When: Designing a mystery with more than one crime. Why: The second layer gives players a reason to keep investigating after the first is solved.
- [procedure] 1) Clear the innocent suspects first. 2) Confirm the evidence matches. 3) Explain the mechanism of the crime. 4) Name the culprit last. When: Building a climactic accusation after the evidence is laid out. Why: Ordered layering lets the audience accept each step before the final naming.
- [procedure] 1) Let one character confess a lesser crime. 2) Use the confession to reopen a solved case. 3) Reveal a second culprit whose role reframes the earlier map. When: Designing a climax that should change the player's understanding of the whole level. Why: Layered revelations keep the player re-evaluating after apparent closure.
- [procedure] 1) Introduce a plausible but wrong culprit with physical links. 2) Let investigators build a case, then have them admit it is weak. 3) Replace it with a second suspect whose evidence seems stronger. 4) Break that reading with a physical test. When: Mystery plots that need suspicion to move several times before the real answer. Why: Each false solution that is disproved raises confidence in the eventual solution.
- [procedure] 1) Confront the culprit with witness testimony. 2) Put physical evidence on the table. 3) Let the culprit confess. 4) Have the investigators explain how they reached the answer. Why: Several independent confirmations make the reveal feel complete.

## logging clues and events
- [rule] Log each NPC or interrogation question and suggestion with its presumptions, so players can reconstruct a hidden goal or spot when a question assumes guilt. (x2)
- [rule] Log suspicious NPC dialogue and behaviour early as clearly recallable world events, so a later reveal about a trusted NPC can recontextualize them via moments already seen. Why: Hindsight reinterpretation only works if the detail can be recalled; a late reveal is backed by moments the player already saw.
- [rule] A dialogue system should log each suspect's exact words so the player can later confront him with his own recorded statements.
- [rule] Offer a humorous deflection and record it in the dialogue log, so the player can return to the question later. When: An NPC avoids a sensitive question with humour. Why: A logged deflection keeps the question open rather than letting it disappear.
- [rule] Record incidental bystanders even when their role is unexplained, since they may matter later as witnesses or alibis. When: when observing a scene. Why: Unexplained figures can become important once the picture changes.
- [rule] In a questioning system, log contradictions between an NPC's answers and show them when the player presents a conflicting fact.
- [rule] Log NPC threats and public quarrels so they can be reused as motive evidence when the player later confronts that suspect. When: Designing NPC interactions that may matter to a later accusation.
- [rule] Log the timing of events the player witnesses, so a character's spoken timeline can be checked against the game's own record.
- [rule] Log only facts the player has actually seen, so the final explanation reinterprets earlier events rather than introducing new facts. When: designing a quest log.
- [rule] Check a death or trap-triggered event in a game against logged evidence such as inventory counts, timers and wounds, and record each failed check. When: When designing game events that must be explainable. Why: Recorded checks let the player and designer trace the cause.
- [rule] When accounts conflict, let a fixed sequence of logged events, such as calls and sightings, decide which account to trust rather than memory. Why: memory of time is unreliable.
- [rule] Script NPC reactions to specific words or items and log them as clues the player can review later.
- [heuristic] Let dialogue or interrogation systems express hidden thoughts through glances, pauses and dropped objects, and log these cues so players can reconstruct the link. When: designing NPC systems that conceal intent. Why: logged cues give players anchors to reason from.
- [heuristic] A timestamped log of each character's location lets a player reconstruct a timeline, and any gap becomes a lead. When: when designing an in-game event log for mystery play. Why: Missing entries show the player where to look next.
- [procedure] 1) Record each witness clue separately. 2) Note what was volunteered versus asked; log volunteered statements as unverified and reserve judgement until checks confirm or contradict them. 3) Mark each open thread as a task to investigate. When: Interviewing a witness who gives partial or evasive answers, or offers history, motive or character unprompted. Why: Separating clues keeps unverified impressions distinct from checkable leads; unprompted material often shows what the speaker wants believed.
- [procedure] 1) Log each fragment the player hears. 2) Record where it was heard. 3) Revisit the log when the wider picture arrives so the player can weigh each fragment. When: when a game delivers clues as partial overheard speech. Why: Source and context let the player reassess earlier fragments.

## message tracing and handling
- [mechanism] A message or call arriving at the peak of expectation can give a new lead and send the protagonist away.
- [mechanism] A notice left in plain view can force a culprit to change the staging of a crime.
- [rule] Use a message's content as a clue only when its tone or wording differs from the sender's usual style. When: Reading a short or unusual note.
- [rule] Printed appeals reach only people who can read, so an illiterate person must be reached by word of mouth instead.
- [rule] Track each message's writer, poster and reader, so the player can rebuild the prompt behind an NPC's action.
- [rule] Deliver a faction's story through in-world documents such as notes or newspapers, released as the player progresses.
- [rule] Date a received message and check what it prompted afterward, since that link can explain later actions that otherwise look odd. When: when a later action has no obvious cause.
- [heuristic] Use in-world dialect or code words as signals that identify a faction or origin.
- [heuristic] The height of a wall message shows the writer's posture; a message low to the floor suggests the writer was lying or sitting there.
- [heuristic] A message that points to a specific object, with no prior agreement, implies its sender saw that object up close, making the message evidence of that knowledge.
- [procedure] 1) List every person a message passes through. 2) Note whether each actually saw the next. 3) Confirm the final recipient received it. When: when a claim depends on a message passing through several hands. Why: Anyone who handled a message had a chance to read or change it.
- [procedure] 1) Examine typeface and paper to exclude source categories. 2) Detach fragments and check their reverse side for printed text. 3) Match the printed source to a physical object. When: a composed message made of printed fragments.
- [procedure] 1) Note the initials and pickup address in the notice. 2) Ask the holding clerk who claimed the item and when. 3) Question each claimant. 4) Link the claimants to the notice. When: a message is held for pickup at a post office or register. Why: Claim records turn an anonymous address into a chain of people.
- [pitfall] A hired hand may not know who hired them, so an investigation can stop at the middleman.
- [fact] A message left in a hidden cache may describe an observer and warn of future meetings.
- [fact] When an adversary passes intelligence in person, a mail channel is unlikely to be their route for the secret.

## name matching and lookalikes
- [rule] Treat a claimed or alias name as a lead only; confirm it against a second, independent record before trusting an identity or accusing anyone. When: A character, player, witness or suspect gives a name that cannot yet be confirmed. Why: A stated name can be false or unverified, inviting misidentification. (x2)
- [rule] Use an index of names with page references to follow one person through a whole account. When: when a person appears across many parts of a long record. Why: Scattered mentions are easy to miss without a cross-reference.
- [heuristic] If a person may have changed their name, search by description and circumstance rather than by name, since name searches will fail.
- [heuristic] A person whose recorded name changes between documents may be concealing an identity.
- [heuristic] An NPC's real name can hide behind a nickname or alternate spelling, found by asking neutral questions.
- [heuristic] A name's spelling can reveal its origin, so confirm the spelling before drawing conclusions from the name.
- [heuristic] Match a person across variant spellings of their name by context, not by spelling alone. When: when the same person appears under several spellings in different records. Why: Spelling of names varies between records and writers.
- [procedure] 1) Ask whether anyone entered or left close to a key time. 2) Check the names of late entries against the expected name. 3) Consider an alias if the expected name is missing. When: When a sought person does not appear on a list under their own name. Why: People traveling or hiding may register under a different name at the last moment.
- [pitfall] Similar names or spellings can merge two people into one, showing one person acting in two places if both lived in one town; missing sex or date details invite misreading.
- [pitfall] A name variant can make one person look like two people, or two people look like one, when matching identities across documents. When: matching identities across documents.
- [pitfall] Historical records can mislead when two families share similar names; confirm which family each record concerns.
- [pitfall] Working from original figures can hide a motive when the value of an asset has changed. When: A contract's terms were set before a major change in prices. Why: The nominal sum no longer matches its real worth.
- [pitfall] Similarity between two crimes does not prove the same person is responsible.
- [pitfall] Renamed streets and varied spellings of a surname can hide an unbroken chain of ownership from a casual reader. When: Comparing records written in different periods. Why: Surface differences make one continuous chain look like separate properties.
- [pitfall] A name matched by context may still refer to two different people, so the match needs a separate check. When: when two records share a name and a rough context. Why: Similar names and situations can belong to different individuals.
- [fact] One person may appear under several spellings, nicknames, titles, a mark or a full signature, and places carry several spellings; spelling was unsettled even among educated writers. When: When comparing records from different scribes or periods. Why: Scribes wrote names as they heard them, and no standard spelling existed.

## npc knowledge and loyalty
- [mechanism] A rival or official NPC holding private information can release it through conversation, a permit or a favour, giving the player a reason to pursue relationships. When: Designing information access for an NPC faction. Why: Gated information turns social actions into progress.
- [mechanism] An NPC's willingness to disclose responds to the player's tone, so reassuring dialogue can draw a fuller answer than pressure does. When: player chooses reassuring or pressuring dialogue.
- [behavior] Readers trust a quiet, harmless-seeming companion, so ordinary actions by that companion are read as innocent even when they are preparation for a crime. When: a companion's ordinary action is visible early in the story. Why: The surface reading of harmlessness hides the planning, so the reader misses the clue until a deduction.
- [rule] Track a hidden trust or fear value per NPC; let it change how much they reveal and how reliable their information is. When: Designing NPC interrogation scenes or information-giving NPCs. Why: Trust and fear determine willingness to disclose and reliability, so the player must judge trust in context.
- [rule] Give each NPC a stated stake in what they say, so players can judge when a witness is protecting someone. When: When designing NPC testimony. Why: Knowing the stake lets players discount biased claims.
- [rule] Build NPC dialogue so each NPC reveals only part of the truth, with each holding a different slice and a different stake. When: When designing a mystery with several informants. Why: Partial, self-interested accounts require players to combine sources.
- [rule] Post a notice or bounty naming a ship, guild or location tied to an NPC's past, so the player can deduce the connection. When: Designing world notices that link to NPC backstory. Why: Known connections let players infer ties without being told.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses a loyalty or price value, and change their statements when the player bribes, threatens or befriends them. When: Designing NPCs who witness a crime. Why: Witness statements then depend on the player's actions.
- [rule] Model servants and gossips as relays that pass information with noise, so a rumor may name the wrong amount or culprit. When: Designing an NPC gossip or rumor network. Why: Noise in relays makes the player verify before trusting.
- [rule] Give each NPC a hidden secret that offers a second motive, so the player must test which motive explains an act.
- [rule] Let an NPC withhold information from another NPC so the player must choose whom to tell. When: when designing NPC knowledge systems.
- [heuristic] A nominal intermediary can be named on paper to protect a real investigator's role, even if the intermediary does little of the work. When: A hidden party must be formally represented without revealing their involvement. Why: A formal name can shield the true actor from being identified.
- [heuristic] Model each character's knowledge and their contacts, so the player can trace where a secret leaked through the network. When: Designing secrets that spread among NPCs. Why: Explicit knowledge and contact links make leaks traceable and fair.
- [pitfall] Withholding too long leaves the audience feeling cheated and without footing; each reveal needs enough earlier facts understood to land. When: Planning how long to delay key information. Why: Without context, a reveal feels arbitrary rather than meaningful.
- [pitfall] Promising more than you can deliver, such as absolute discretion, creates risk when your obligations to others limit what you can keep private.
- [pitfall] Leaving a client waiting while attending to another matter can cost goodwill, so manage the client's perception of attention. When: When an investigator must juggle several threads at once. Why: Visible neglect of the client's concerns damages the relationship.

## npc leads and referrals
- [mechanism] A shop ledger in the game world can confirm or contradict an NPC's account of a sale; a matching entry builds trust, a missing line opens a new branch. When: Designing NPC sale claims verifiable through in-world records. Why: Records give players a way to test NPC statements.
- [mechanism] A shop NPC who recognises a mark can offer a lead, so a dialogue check becomes a clue source. When: designing dialogue-based clues.
- [mechanism] In town, neighbours' indignation and nearby justice let a single complaint set an investigation in motion quickly. Why: Close neighbours and authorities are able to act on a report almost immediately.
- [behavior] Observers classify an object by the nearest group it appears with, so grouping steers interpretation before any deduction begins. When: an object is displayed among other items. Why: people assign a category from their neighbours.
- [rule] Let related NPCs be referred together, but require the player to separate each person's individual evidence from the shared reputation, since grouping lends each case unearned weight. When: Designing or referring linked suspects in one document. Why: Shared grouping makes each case look stronger than its individual evidence supports; shared reputation can hide weak evidence.
- [rule] Treat ordinary conversation with side characters as an information-gathering action.
- [rule] Make contact NPCs return nothing useful for a culprit with no history, so the player cannot solve the case by asking the wrong source. When: designing informant characters. Why: Otherwise a wrong source would give a shortcut.
- [rule] A ghost NPC that names a culprit should give the player a lead to check, not a verdict, and the game should tag such claims as unverified. When: designing ghost or spirit witnesses.
- [heuristic] Let a local answer questions with the subject's name and occupation, then add a second question that tests the player's interest. When: Designing NPC information exchanges.
- [heuristic] Judge a tip by its source's motive and track record as well as its content. When: a tip comes from a source with a known motive or fallibility. Why: A source's history shapes how far its content can be trusted.
- [heuristic] Do not press a contact on topics they steer away from. Their redirection signals a line they will not cross.
- [heuristic] Mark which characters stay silent at a key moment, since silence in a timeline can point to a later confrontation. When: When designing a timeline of NPC statements. Why: Absence can foreshadow conflict.
- [heuristic] Use a town-scale investigation when rumour spreads and many suspects appear at once; a closed circle of suspects suits a single-scene mystery better.
- [heuristic] End a scene on an NPC's departure to create a new objective to find him. When: Closing a confrontation scene. Why: A sudden exit converts the scene's tension into a search goal.
- [procedure] 1) State a limited aim honestly. 2) Show the object. 3) Invoke shared history. 4) Let the contact choose what to share. 5) Follow up discreetly. When: When approaching a contact who knows a specialised market.
- [pitfall] A matching print shows someone touched an object, not that they used it to commit a crime; pair it with other evidence before concluding intent.

## object examination inference
- [mechanism] Physical state such as dampness, wear or age records how long an object was kept and where, so the object itself carries a timeline.
- [rule] Inventory every object and its position against the expected count; a shortfall is evidence, identified by its markings, and an item found elsewhere can complete the count. When: Checking the contents of a scene or examining a scene. Why: A missing item signals removal or displacement, and objects and gaps both reveal who was present.
- [rule] Sketch a suspected object with accurate dimensions so the design can be compared with later finds.
- [heuristic] Examine ordinary objects such as books, music, handwork, clothing and marks on glass for signs of their owner's habits and for signs that a hidden person is present. When: A suspect is absent or another person's presence must be inferred from a scene. Why: Objects carry traces of character and history that reveal concealed presence.
- [heuristic] Note an object's shape as well as its location, since a trace that looks wrong for its owner's usual habits can point to a deliberate act. When: an object shows a cut, wear, or form that seems atypical. Why: Mismatch between a trace and its owner's habits suggests another person or intent.
- [heuristic] Read inscriptions, dates, and object placement in a room to infer relationships and history. When: searching a room for background information.
- [heuristic] Make an object's state, such as a window left open a set distance, a fact the player can verify by asking an NPC who observed it.
- [heuristic] Ask what purpose a small object served and how it was handled; its wear, placement and marks can reveal how it was used and sometimes by whom. When: When an object turns up where it has no obvious reason to be, or its state does not fit normal use. Why: Use leaves characteristic marks that differ from ordinary handling.
- [heuristic] Wear and condition show how a possession was used; compare wear across items, since a lightly used item may show more wear than expected elsewhere. When: When reading an object's history from its condition. Why: Differential wear reveals how each item was handled.
- [heuristic] Note how an item was found, such as turned inside out, since the condition at discovery can show how it was removed. When: When recording an item's state at the scene. Why: Physical state records the manner of handling.
- [heuristic] An object that was never modified keeps its original dimensions, so its fit is a reliable physical record of the body it was made for. When: Using an object's fit as evidence of identity or physique. Why: Alterations change fit, so only unmodified objects preserve the original measurement.
- [procedure] 1) Read physical wear first. 2) Treat engravings or dates as a working hypothesis. 3) Check the hypothesis, including any personal trait, against an outside record before treating it as proof. 4) Chain related inferences, such as an item tied to a career change suggesting a junior rather than senior role. When: when deducing facts about a person from objects.
- [procedure] 1) Examine the object by eye for overall wear. 2) Use magnification to inspect fine marks. 3) Compare marks across the object for repetition. 4) State inferences as balances of probability. When: when reading an item for backstory. Why: layered examination recovers evidence that a glance misses.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the object with its stated source or origin. 2) Read accompanying documents such as labels or leaflets. 3) Inspect the object's form and surfaces for signs of concealment. 4) Examine it closely with a lens. 5) Only then consider destructive examination.
- [procedure] 1) Note an object that suggests a relationship, such as a figurine of a person. 2) Form a hypothesis about the relationship it implies. 3) Confirm it by asking, and watch how the person reacts. When: When a personal space holds objects hinting at relationships. Why: An object may have an ordinary explanation, so inference needs confirmation by questioning.
- [fact] An everyday item's properties can reveal its user's habits and conditions; matches that light easily and are hard to put out suit lighting a pipe in bad weather.

## physical traces
- [definition] A physical trace is a small disturbance in a scene, such as a moved object, a dent, a torn fastening or a faint odour, that shows who was present and what they did.
- [mechanism] Tying a twist to where a document was physically kept lets the player see the forgery only after learning the item's last location from witness statements. When: Designing a mystery whose reversal depends on a document or object's location. Why: The location detail is needed to expose the substitution, so it must be learned before the reveal.
- [behavior] A physical impossibility, such as a body with no bleeding at the scene, prompts players to infer a hidden act such as the body having been moved. When: a crime-scene puzzle where the evidence contradicts the apparent cause of death. Why: The mismatch between the scene and the stated explanation signals that something was hidden from view.
- [rule] Stage a reveal through physical evidence players can connect, such as a line of burnt marks or a missing item, so the solution feels earned. When: When a twist depends on a hidden action by a character. Why: Concrete clues let players reason to the answer rather than receive it as an arbitrary disclosure.
- [rule] Watch a suspect in custody for sudden changes in colour, posture or responsiveness, and treat them as a signal of a crisis to be read rather than ignored. When: A suspect's condition changes abruptly during questioning. Why: A sudden physical change can end the session and may indicate a means of escape or harm.
- [heuristic] Use a checkable physical detail, such as handedness, the side an object lies on, or blow force against a frail build, that the suspected character cannot match, reversing the suspicion. When: A player has been led to suspect a character, or early evidence has set up a false suspect. Why: A physical, verifiable fact overturns suspicion without relying on the narrator's word; a capability mismatch lets players reverse suspicion through deduction. (x2)
- [heuristic] Treat physical traces such as containers, labels, residue and lab results as evidence that narrows possibilities, and note what each one cannot establish. When: investigating an object-based clue. Why: each trace supports only part of a conclusion.
- [heuristic] Physical signs on a person, such as a change in colour, can point to a likely source before the suspected object is examined. When: A bodily sign hints at a hidden cause. Why: A visible symptom narrows the search to a plausible origin.
- [heuristic] Reuse one physical sign across several scenes, so its meaning becomes clear only when the secret is revealed.
- [heuristic] Use physical evidence that changes which suspect fits, so each new artifact shifts suspicion to a different character. When: Mid-to-late mystery where suspicion must move between candidates. Why: Each artifact reframes the evidence, keeping the suspect field active.
- [heuristic] A physical trace that points to the victim rather than the suspect can clear the suspect and link the death to the dead person.
- [procedure] 1) Map every trail: which marks lead in, which lead out, and where they stop. 2) Compare footwear with the surface. 3) Test whether the implied route is physically possible. 4) Check companions' prints and disturbed ground. 5) Date prints by their condition. When: When a person seems to vanish and the ground or floor can hold impressions. Why: Traces record movement, and each check removes a possible explanation.
- [procedure] 1) State the established physical facts, such as blood loss and body temperature. 2) Infer when the injury occurred from those facts. 3) Check whether the conclusion follows before moving on. When: When physical signs are used to reorder events. Why: Each step rests on a checkable fact, so the conclusion can be tested rather than trusted on authority.
- [procedure] 1) State in advance that an injury to one entity will appear on a linked body 2) inspect that body 3) compare the marks with the injury.
- [pitfall] A physical trace, such as a flat mat or a trail under a door, outranks a witness's confident report; accounts backed by physical traces are more credible than bare sightings. When: A witness's account conflicts with physical evidence or is weighed against evidence. Why: Physical traces are harder to mistake than memory.
- [fact] Buildings and objects such as doors, bars, bells, rooms and lamps can reveal and hide information, so a setting can serve as both a clue and a trap for its occupant.

## plan feasibility and failure
- [rule] Check each claimed plan against schedules and travel durations to confirm it was physically possible in the time available. When: a suspect's route or trip is part of the claim. Why: Plans that fail the clock are leads to test.
- [heuristic] An apparent timing contradiction may come from a planned delay, such as a letter mailed in advance. Check for one before assuming an error. When: when a date or timing conflicts with other facts.
- [heuristic] Plans can slip, so compare the planned date with the date actually used; a one-day delay can explain why an act came late. When: when an act appears later than the schedule predicts.
- [heuristic] A character's wrong assumption that is later corrected can serve as a planned reversal.
- [heuristic] Check whether a planned arrangement matches the timeline, and ask why a plan changed at short notice. When: A promised arrangement does not happen as expected. Why: A sudden change can mean someone wanted a person out of the way.
- [heuristic] Ask whether a culprit could foresee every condition a plan relied on; a plan needing both precise foresight and favourable chance is improbable. When: testing an explanation that depends on uncontrollable conditions. Why: each dependence on luck or unforeseeable events lowers its likelihood.
- [heuristic] A deliberately planned alibi keeps to public places and normal behaviour among others, so test an alibi by checking the suspect's public activity. When: verifying a suspect's alibi. Why: careless alibis are a common failure to watch for.
- [heuristic] Tie the culprit's hidden planning to an unforeseen weak point, so the reveal shows the plan had a flaw all along. When: when writing a mystery's final reveal.
- [heuristic] Check whether a change in venue or procedure was arranged before the hearing began; prior arrangement is evidence of planning. When: a proceeding changes mid-stream.
- [heuristic] Comparing a written plan with what actually happened shows where a person's intentions failed, letting the reader judge the gap.
- [heuristic] Ask what an explanation requires of the actor; a method that does not fit the claimed intent counts against that explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Count the time left before the deadline. 2) Treat the interval before it as the window to act. 3) Schedule the key step inside that window. When: A plan must be completed before a fixed date. Why: A counted interval turns an open deadline into a concrete plan.
- [pitfall] A carefully planned act most often fails at points the planner cannot control, such as a witness assumed absent who turns out present or another person's unplanned action. When: Designing or evaluating a plan that must stay hidden. Why: Other people's memories and choices are outside the planner's control.
- [pitfall] Carefully built plans often fail through one unforeseen witness and through panic afterwards, which can undo the preparation.
- [fact] In a disguise scheme, the difficult part is the planning and nerve required, not the physical execution of the disguise. When: Designing how difficult an impersonation should feel to the player. Why: Execution is easy; the challenge lies in timing and daring.
- [fact] A crime's overall plan may be made in advance while its details are improvised on the spot.

## player-driven inquiry choices
- [mechanism] When a player's advice changes an NPC's next action, the dialogue forks into a branching path that the player's words caused.
- [mechanism] A noise or struggle just before an accusation raises tension and lets the audience anticipate the reveal before anything is said.
- [mechanism] In a confrontation, the player's reconstruction can trigger a visible reaction from the suspect. Why: The reaction confirms the player's deduction on screen.
- [rule] Let players choose when to share a clue with an ally or withhold it, and show later dialogue consequences of that choice.
- [rule] Let an NPC ask the player to keep a request secret, and track whether the player honours it.
- [rule] Let the player's dialogue choices reveal what the player already knows, so an NPC can react to prior discoveries. When: when designing reactive dialogue. Why: Reactions to known facts make the conversation feel responsive.
- [rule] Let the player become the prime suspect of a scene they did not create, so they must clear themselves by finding contradictions in the evidence. Why: Tests whether the player can reason their way out of a false accusation.
- [rule] Record what the player did not check or was not asked, since an omission can serve as a clue.
- [rule] Let the player state a deduction in a journal or companion dialogue and have an NPC challenge each step, showing whether the chain holds. When: when designing a deduction system for players. Why: Challenge exposes weak links in the player's reasoning.
- [rule] Track which facts the player has established and which are merely assumed, so a wrong premise produces a plausible dead end. When: When designing a puzzle with branching deductions.
- [rule] When a game depicts an old event, let players reconstruct it from archives and physical remains while in-world characters hold only their own beliefs.
- [rule] Have players reach the conclusion themselves by combining evidence they already possess, rather than receiving it directly.
- [heuristic] Show the player the exact question an NPC was asked, so they can judge what was actually confirmed rather than assuming the answer proves more. When: An NPC vouches for another character in a generated scene. Why: Players can only weigh a confirmation if they see its scope.
- [heuristic] Let players test a theory by performing an action and watching an NPC's reaction, as a way to reveal what the NPC knows.
- [heuristic] Let players check a character's stated route against a map overlay or a journal of timestamps. When: Designing NPC alibis.
- [fact] Before an official inquiry, those on site decide who holds the evidence, whether to summon an outside investigator, and how public the matter becomes.

## reversal and twist structure
- [model] A reversal-driven plot has seven stages: premise, false solution, investigation pressure, escape and misdirection, crisis, complication and reversal, and reveal with aftermath.
- [model] A reversal-driven mystery runs: hook, opening misdirections, suspicion on the household, false solution, reconstruction crisis, second false solution, climax, aftermath. When: outlining a mystery built on reversals. Why: Each segment tests and overturns a belief about the culprit.
- [mechanism] When a vanished person reappears in the same sealed room, the puzzle is reframed, and the audience needs a cause for the return as well as the disappearance. When: A missing person returns to the room they vanished from. Why: The return adds a second question that the story must answer.
- [mechanism] A later event such as a light change can reverse an earlier reading of a scene, forcing the player to reinterpret what they saw. When: Designing a scene whose meaning changes with conditions. Why: New information recasts earlier observations and rewards attention.
- [behavior] An audience expecting danger from outside is changed when a character in the room confesses, reversing their view of who is trustworthy and who is the threat. When: A confession reveals the culprit is among those trusted. Why: The reversal overturns expectations the audience built from earlier cues.
- [rule] At the final proof, show a physical object that contradicts a common belief, such as a corpse that looks lifelike, to overturn the audience's assumption. When: Climax proof of a supernatural identity. Why: A reversal makes the proof memorable and undermines the expected sign.
- [rule] Resolve the legal or material consequence of a reversal, such as acquittal and inheritance, to show who benefits from the new truth. When: Closing a mystery whose solution changes ownership or guilt. Why: Showing the consequence makes the reversal concrete rather than only a changed suspicion.
- [rule] Show the physical result of a trick before its cause, so the audience registers the effect first and the explanation later confirms it.
- [heuristic] Reverse the victim's role late: reveal the victim's own action, like paying for an arrangement, aided the plot, or a seeming loss is a gain for protagonist or hidden party. When: Choosing the strongest late twist for a victim-centred plot or a late-stage twist in a heist story. Why: Revealing the victim as complicit or as gaining reverses the audience's assumption about who is harmed and recasts the whole scheme. (x2)
- [heuristic] Revise a first impression of an NPC, whether composed or quick to agree, with a later second encounter or scripted check that corrects the player's initial reaction. When: Designing NPCs whose early demeanor or responses should be doubted later. Why: A delayed check or second encounter corrects a false first impression that later evidence would overturn.
- [heuristic] Stage a reversal by returning to the scene while the threat is still alive and visible, rather than explaining it in retrospect. When: Revealing that the apparent threat was a human mechanism. Why: A live reveal keeps tension and lets the player witness the exposure directly.
- [heuristic] When a target looks unbreakable, seek the single assumption that fails rather than attacking every safeguard at once. When: Facing a system that appears airtight. Why: A plan must defeat every check together, so one failing assumption can open the whole route.
- [heuristic] Undo a theory with a source the player did not weigh earlier, such as a witness's motive to please or a financial record. When: revealing that a planted solution was wrong. Why: A new kind of source reverses the conclusion without introducing a new suspect.
- [procedure] 1) Disprove the identification of the suspect. 2) Show that the witness never existed. 3) Expose the purpose of the lure. Each stage removes one layer of the false belief while keeping the player engaged. When: breaking a false belief in a mystery. Why: Breaking the belief in stages keeps the player from losing the whole case at once.
- [metric] Place the late counter-proof cluster at roughly 80-86% of the way through, and the final reconciliation at roughly 92-97%. When: pacing a multi-solution mystery.
- [pitfall] An informant can be right about the outcome and wrong about the cause, so hearsay is unreliable for mechanisms or amounts. When: A rumor reports a result and an explanation for it. Why: Partial reporting can get the result right while the explanation is wrong.

## suspect reactions and tells
- [mechanism] Tagging dialogue lines with the emotional reaction they cause lets a game check whether a rivalry was actually touched. When: In dialogue systems that track NPC relationships. Why: Reaction tags turn a line into a checkable state change rather than mere flavor.
- [mechanism] A suspect who expected the visit, after seeing the investigator with a known associate, will have prepared responses, so early contact can reveal that the investigator's approach is already known. When: A suspect has seen the investigator's movements before the formal visit. Why: Prior observation lets the suspect prepare for the inquiry.
- [behavior] A pause and fixed stare when a witness requests secrecy show that this one demand matters more to them than the rest of what they said. When: a witness reacts strongly to one request. Why: a strong reaction exposes which concern is central.
- [behavior] A suspect's flicker, pause, sudden return to a subject, or overly quick denial can reveal knowledge they would not state directly. When: An interviewer probes a subject the suspect knows about. Why: Concealing knowledge produces involuntary tells in reaction to a probe.
- [rule] Use a planned denial as a clue: have a later witness who saw the connection contradict the denial, revealing the hidden relationship. When: Designing an NPC who must deny knowing a contact. Why: The contradiction lets the player discover the concealed link.
- [heuristic] Show a character's reaction before explaining its cause, and explain the cause only afterward. Why: Delaying the reason keeps the reader curious and invites them to read the trace.
- [heuristic] A speaker can reduce disbelief by admitting they once held the listener's view and changed their mind under evidence. When: The claim is extraordinary. Why: Shared past skepticism shows the speaker reasoned their way to the claim.
- [heuristic] Attach predicted reactions to a suspect's dialogue, such as a denial or a shock, and let the player test the prediction by choosing what to say. When: Designing a dialogue-driven accusation or interrogation system. Why: Letting the player check a prediction makes interrogation an active test rather than passive reading.
- [heuristic] Use a visible character reaction, such as a flustered remark, to signal that a recalled fact now matters. When: Revealing that a previously mentioned detail is significant. Why: A visible reaction draws attention to the detail without stating its importance outright.
- [heuristic] Reread excessive praise as possible mockery or a hidden motive once the group's real purpose becomes clear. When: Praise is later revealed to serve another goal.
- [heuristic] Answer a blanket accusation with specific, checkable items rather than a general denial, since each defeated item weakens the sweeping claim.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a gesture or phrase the disguised character cannot easily drop. 2) Use it at each appearance. 3) Let players connect it to the earlier profile, even when faces differ. Why: A recurring tell lets players recognize a disguised suspect. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Post-crime conduct is evidence: leaving openly before witnesses is hard to reconcile with a hidden body, yet such behavior has many explanations and proves neither guilt nor innocence. When: Weighing a suspect's flight, abandonment of an accomplice, or conduct after an alleged act. Why: Post-crime conduct has many explanations and does not establish guilt or innocence.
- [tradeoff] A suspect who keeps refusing stays plausible but risks a dead end; players need some clear answers soon to stay engaged. When: a suspect must hide a motive. Why: repeated refusals with no progress frustrate.
- [pitfall] A tell or flinch may reflect nervousness or distress rather than guilt or a specific mark, so test it against other evidence before concluding. When: Interpreting a suspect's glances, manner changes, or physical reaction as evidence of guilt or identity. Why: Agitation and distress have many causes unrelated to the crime or the identity being tested.
- [pitfall] Treating a stranger's unusual attention as hostile without checking the pattern of movements, or missing that perfect indifference is itself the clue. When: Interpreting a group's unnatural calm toward an outsider.

## trap and ambush design
- [definition] A staged trigger raises a relevant subject unexpectedly while a person is off guard, to prompt a slip or a confession.
- [behavior] A trap that protects a decoy can fail to protect the true target, so the audience's belief about where danger lies can be turned against them. When: a protective trap is set around a decoy. Why: the trap assumes the threat comes from outside, which the twist overturns.
- [rule] Use a staged trap, such as a feigned illness or bait advertisement, so the culprit acts on his own assumption and exposes himself before the investigator.
- [rule] Tie the protagonist's want, such as escape or romance, to the lever the trap uses against them.
- [rule] Before treating a discovery's timing as evidence, identify who controlled its trigger, such as who ordered the works that exposed it. Why: Coincidence stays a suspicion until control of the event is shown.
- [heuristic] Make a trap a welcoming space, with warm hosts and a locked exit appearing only after the player has relaxed, so the reversal hits harder. When: Designing a sanctuary that turns hostile. Why: Contrast between comfort and threat intensifies the reversal.
- [procedure] 1) Make a false clue or forged message. 2) Deliver it to the suspect. 3) Watch the suspect's reaction to reveal their guilt.
- [procedure] 1) Adopt a false identity that unsettles the suspect's expectations. 2) Invent a plausible consequence, such as a prosecution by a named authority. 3) Place the suspect in a room with a route to act. 4) Station a backup outside, ready to enter when the suspect acts. When: A suspect is guilty of a lesser crime and can be made to fear exposure. Why: Control of setting and timing lets the investigator intervene at the moment of action.
- [procedure] 1) Learn the suspect's hiding place. 2) Inform the authorities of the location. 3) Schedule their arrival to control the timing of capture. When: A pursuit has a clear location and a timed final moment. Why: Controlling arrival timing turns an apparent escape into a controlled capture.
- [procedure] 1) Let the suspect proceed so the act incriminates him fully. 2) Fix a time window from his stated conditions. 3) Place watchers out of sight and conceal the potential victim. 4) Signal the suspect to the decisive point. 5) Close the trap as he enters. When: the suspect's plan is known in outline and timing can be controlled. Why: intervening at commitment yields evidence from the suspect's own act.
- [tradeoff] Watching a suspect rather than confronting them lets them reveal more over time, at the cost of delaying resolution and sustaining tension. When: An investigator can gather more by observation than by direct questioning. Why: Patient observation can surface clues that a confrontation would end early.
- [pitfall] A sudden visible change of mood can make a careful target suspicious, so the shift should be gradual or plausible. When: Using a quarrel to steer a target who is alert. Why: Abrupt emotional change reads as staged to a watchful person.
- [pitfall] Naming an unseen agent can satisfy an audience while leaving unanswered how the agent acts; the mechanism must still be explained.
- [pitfall] A bluff can drive a frightened person to self-harm, so a sting should not be used on fragile suspects and medical care must be planned in advance. When: Planning a confrontation that relies on fear of exposure. Why: Acute fear can push a vulnerable person to a dangerous act.
- [pitfall] Taking a tidy-looking room for innocence is a mistake, because a closed drawer may hide a search.
- [pitfall] A late threat with no earlier planted cause feels like a cheat, and over-neat resolution removes the suspense built by escalation. When: Resolving a multi-stage threat. Why: Unearned threats and tidy endings both undercut tension.

## victim timeline and movement
- [mechanism] Mud that is dried or freshly made after rain tells marks left on entry apart from marks left on exit, so the order can be fixed by the mud's state. When: after rain falls between two visits. Why: rain changes how marks look over time.
- [behavior] Key witnesses move, travel or settle abroad, so an investigator can arrive a day too late and find the witness gone. When: witnesses are not fixed in one place during an inquiry.
- [behavior] A trapped victim who expects a search may write a message where the attacker is unlikely to look, since paper is easy to find or destroy. When: A victim is trapped and wants to name an attacker. Why: Paper can be found or destroyed.
- [behavior] A target hurrying to answer a lure leaves traces such as transport use and timetable inquiries, which investigators can follow to the destination. When: The target acts quickly on a forged request. Why: Haste forces unplanned actions that reveal the route taken.
- [rule] Log the player's movements after a discovery so witness NPCs report flight and calm differently, letting one action read as guilt or innocence.
- [rule] Make a suspect's death close one thread while opening another, so the case moves forward rather than stalling. When: Killing a suspect in the middle of a mystery. Why: A death removes a false lead and creates a new question about who was responsible.
- [heuristic] A victim's remarks about a past marriage or hidden means, along with unusual visitors, hint at a concealed history that may explain the crime. When: When reconstructing a victim's secrets from scene evidence. Why: Offhand statements and callers reveal connections the victim did not disclose.
- [heuristic] A missing key witness who holds the proof gives the story a clock, keeping the case open and driving the search. When: the story depends on the witness's return.
- [heuristic] Check a suspect's movements over a long period, and weigh a record of unexplained absences as evidence. When: assessing a suspect's opportunity. Why: Patterns of absence reveal opportunity over time.
- [heuristic] Ask a suspect to describe a claimed experience in detail, such as a game move by move, to test whether they actually know it. When: A suspect claims familiarity with an activity.
- [heuristic] Work backward from a victim's schedule to plant questions about unexpectedly early actions that players must solve from the evidence.
- [heuristic] Trace the victim's last movements as well as the suspects' movements; the route can reveal who followed the victim and why. When: The suspect list is wide and the victim's route is unexplained. Why: A victim's path often points to an unlisted pursuer.
- [heuristic] Lights or traces showing where a victim was fix the victim's position and so the likely place of attack. When: Establishing where a crime occurred. Why: A victim's position is evidence of the attack location.
- [procedure] 1) Lay out each person's movements against a clock, sequencing departures, arrivals and destinations. 2) Mark intervals when no one saw them. 3) Test whether those intervals let each person reach the scene. 4) Shared destinations or meetings then stand out. When: several parties' movements fall within a short window, or when locating opportunity in a case. Why: Ordering movements in time exposes shared destinations and meetings; unobserved intervals are where opportunity hides.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the victim's known behaviour and dates, not the suspects. 2) Check each stated time against independent physical facts such as distance and travel time. 3) Test the date of any message against when it was used. When: a suspect's account of when something was known conflicts with independent timing.
- [pitfall] Overlooking that the victim could keep moving after dosing changes the timeline and can make a suspect look impossible when they are not.

## wealth cues
- [behavior] People who spread large payments across many institutions often want to hide their total wealth from others. When: Transactions are split across several banks. Why: Spreading funds keeps anyone from seeing the full amount.
- [behavior] Physical wear such as dirt, tears or crumpling makes an object read as worthless, so players dismiss it even when it matters. When: An important item is shown in a damaged state. Why: Players judge value from appearance and condition.
- [behavior] Visible valuables draw the eye and hold attention even when a viewer tries to look away from them. When: A valuable object is displayed in a shared scene. Why: Conspicuous objects capture visual attention.
- [behavior] A wealthy person who holds no office and is not old is seated with ordinary members, so money alone does not earn deference. When: community ranks by age and office. Why: age and office set rank, and property does not.
- [rule] Make false leads resolvable: reveal missing support, such as an accuser without proof, or the motive behind a false tip, so players can dismiss it. When: Designing red herrings or misleading NPC information. Why: Players gain confidence in their reasoning when a false lead can be ruled out by evidence or an understood motive. (x2)
- [rule] Give a merchant or lord NPC a visible debt record, and use a shop or bank event that reveals financial trouble to trigger a quest offer. When: designing NPC bargains in a town or dungeon. Why: the player can see why the character accepts or refuses a deal.
- [rule] Make a debt discoverable through social systems, and give a second NPC an unexplained gap that complicates the motive.
- [heuristic] Spending beyond known income is a lead, not proof of hidden funds: trace where the surplus came from and verify it, since a second money source may exist. When: when a visible lifestyle or expensive possession exceeds a suspect's known income or declared means. Why: Spending beyond declared means points to a second source of money that must be verified.
- [heuristic] A merchant or quest-giver who displays wealth can be marked as a suspect, and an item left in view can be made inspectable as a clue. When: Designing NPCs and scene objects for a mystery.
- [heuristic] Worn footwear combined with carefully kept nails suggests a person whose appearance does not match their apparent occupation. When: Judging a disguised or misrepresented social station. Why: Physical upkeep reflects daily habits that disguise rarely covers completely.
- [heuristic] An item worn in one specific way points to habitual, repeated use by one person, which can identify an owner. When: reading personal items for routine. Why: repeated handling leaves a consistent pattern.
- [procedure] 1) List the suspect's visible possessions, clothing and receipts. 2) Compare them against a baseline, such as a comparable household. 3) Check each stated income source before concluding that spending exceeds means. When: When testing whether a suspect's lifestyle is supported by known income. Why: A baseline makes the contrast visible, and checking sources prevents conclusions from unverified assumptions.
- [pitfall] A comfortable display of wealth can hide private ruin, so surroundings do not reliably show a person's finances. When: when judging a character's financial state from appearances. Why: Comfort and exhausted funds can coexist.
- [pitfall] Spending alone does not prove theft, because the suspect may have legitimate sources such as a pension, salary, loan or sold assets. When: When treating lavish spending as evidence of a crime. Why: Lifestyle shows spending, not the source of the money or who acted.
- [pitfall] Showing only a suspect's wealth hides the motive; the debt and its urgency are what give a reason to act.
- [fact] An estate can be split so one party holds life use while another inherits the remainder after that party's death. When: dividing property between a surviving spouse and heirs. Why: Splitting interests in time lets each party's claim be honoured.

## witness account revision
- [mechanism] A witness who revises a story under pressure undergoes a state change that the player can detect and use to test other statements. When: a character is questioned repeatedly. Why: Revision is a visible signal that the earlier account is open to challenge.
- [mechanism] A witness may omit a fact another witness reports, and their silence about it becomes evidence when they are asked directly. When: Two witness accounts cover the same event and one leaves out a detail. Why: Omission may reflect forgetfulness, embarrassment, or concealment, so it is a lead rather than proof.
- [mechanism] Let a witness revise her account when she recognises a companion, so the player must cross-check testimony against physical evidence.
- [mechanism] Recalling a suspect after a break can produce a more guarded second account, which observers notice and which can alter the picture. When: Re-interviewing a central suspect after an adjournment or new evidence. Why: A suspect who knows more evidence exists becomes more careful.
- [behavior] A witness who blurts a name and then quickly tries to take it back may be shielding a person the group is concealing. When: a witness shows fear or over-protectiveness. Why: Fear of exposing someone can make a witness hurry to retract a name.
- [behavior] One witness report can be valued differently by one audience as a lead and by another as material for publicity, shaping how it is presented. When: A witness report is passed to officials or the press. Why: Audiences with different goals select which parts of an account to use.
- [behavior] Under emergency pressure, first impressions may be wrong, and details recalled later can reverse an earlier judgment. When: a witness or responder made a quick judgment during a crisis. Why: hurried observation misses cues that reflection later surfaces.
- [rule] Log each revision of a witness's story as a discrepancy instead of overwriting the earlier version. When: when a witness changes their account under questioning. Why: The sequence of revisions is itself evidence of inconsistency.
- [rule] Make witness NPCs repeat their statements under pressure, and keep those statements stable unless new evidence changes them. When: designing dialogue for witness characters. Why: stable statements let players test them against other evidence.
- [rule] Model witness statements as partial records with gaps, and let players compare accounts to find where they agree and conflict. When: designing testimony in a game.
- [heuristic] A witness may retract or change an account under questioning; compare each revision with the first account, since changes can signal honest correction or a shift toward concealment. When: A witness retracts or revises a statement during an interview. (x2)
- [heuristic] One testimony can support two opposite inferences, so note what each detail rules out before using it as proof. When: a single witness statement is used to argue both guilt and innocence. Why: Details that seem to help one side often cut against it when read closely.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness a question in plain terms. 2) Compare the answer against any earlier written statement. 3) Press loose phrasing with repeated, plainer questions until the precise fact emerges. When: A witness's phrasing may hide a fact. Why: Loose wording often conceals a specific detail that surfaces under repeated plain questioning.
- [procedure] 1) Check the account's claims against contemporary documents. 2) Check its physical claims against the landscape, such as sight-lines. 3) Judge whether the independent evidence converges on the claim. When: evaluating a legend or memoir written long after events. Why: convergence strengthens a claim without proving it.
- [pitfall] When the accuser who makes a charge also confirms it, testimony stands in for evidence and nothing independent is checked.
- [fact] Testimony can be shaped by fear, strong emotion, other people's input and written preparation, so it is not a pure record of what a witness experienced.

## witness account verification
- [mechanism] A witness-reliability system can check an NPC's statement against world state such as weather, time or location before accepting it. When: When designing dialogue whose claims can be contradicted by the game world. Why: Checking claims against state makes testimony a puzzle rather than a fixed fact.
- [rule] Treat an alibi from a single second-hand source as a claim to verify, not as settled fact.
- [rule] Ask a reluctant witness directly for their own suspicions, and explicitly allow them to answer honestly without fear of blame. When: questioning a reluctant witness.
- [rule] Do not rank a witness's reliability by status alone; weigh sobriety, fear and whether the account is first-hand. When: Ranking witnesses in an investigation. Why: Status does not guarantee accurate observation.
- [heuristic] Check whether a witness's statements stay consistent after their emotion settles; content that holds when the performance fades is more reliable. When: judging how much of a witness's account to trust.
- [heuristic] Separate what a witness reports from how the witness wants to be seen, since self-protective framing can shape an otherwise frank account. When: A witness gives a key fact while defending their own reputation. Why: Self-interest colors testimony even when the witness seems trustworthy.
- [heuristic] Check whether a witness could distinguish direction before trusting a precise location they report. When: when a witness places a sound or figure at a specific spot. Why: A witness who cannot separate one side from the other gives a location that is not reliable.
- [heuristic] Test a witness's condition, such as intoxication, before accepting their account. When: A witness may be impaired by drink, drugs or distress. Why: Impairment changes how reliable the report is.
- [heuristic] A witness who has forgotten or is unavailable can still offer clues that the player must confirm through other means. When: A key witness cannot give a full account.
- [procedure] 1) Read exactly what the report states. 2) Compare its specific items with the case facts. 3) Go to the source holding the specifics before treating the link as confirmed. When: when a news item, report or rumor seems connected to an investigation. Why: A dramatic report can seem conclusive while its specifics do not match; the best source for specifics gives reliable confirmation.
- [procedure] 1) Ask what each witness could actually see from their position, given distance, speed of movement and posture. 2) Ask about physical details noticed and how sure they are of each. 3) Ask whether the observed figure matches the suspect and weigh the match against those observer conditions. When: when testing a witness's identification or describing a person they only partly saw. Why: Partial sightings often produce confident but limited descriptions; perception conditions determine how much the match can bear.
- [procedure] 1) Identify concrete, checkable details such as time, place and object. 2) Check each against independent facts or sources; independent confirmation adds weight. 3) Accept general impressions only as hypotheses. When: when weighing a witness account or assessing testimony in an investigation. Why: Precise details can be verified, while vivid impressions can mislead; a specific detail confirmed by another source is harder to dismiss.
- [procedure] 1) Record the witness's account in detail. 2) Identify a physical check the account implies. 3) Perform that check on the relevant people or objects. 4) Compare the result with the account. When: When a witness account makes a claim that can be physically verified. Why: Physical checks tie testimony to evidence that can confirm or contradict it.
- [procedure] 1) Ask narrow questions about how the witness came to act. 2) Compare the answer against the facts of the situation. 3) Ask for a yes or no to remove qualification and expose evasion. When: When a witness's account depends on a claim that can be tested. Why: Narrow questions reveal what a broad account hides.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness act out their positions and movements in sequence. 2) Check what could have been seen from the suspect's spot through doorways and angles. 3) Anchor each step to physical objects the witness confirms. When: testimony is reluctant or the sequence of events is unclear. Why: physical reconstruction shows what was possible from each position.
- [pitfall] Assuming a witness could see from a spot without checking light, distance and obstruction produces false conclusions. When: Accepting a claimed observation at face value. Why: Visibility depends on physical conditions that are easy to overlook.

## witness protection and safety
- [mechanism] A sole-check witness who can confirm or break an alibi becomes dangerous to its beneficiary and may be removed; protect them before relying on their testimony. When: A witness is the sole independent check on a suspect's whereabouts. Why: Their testimony threatens the person whose alibi is at stake. Loss of the witness removes the only check.
- [mechanism] Delay and interrogation intensify a witness's fear, and that fear lowers the reliability of their later statements. When: A witness is kept waiting or questioned at length. Why: Fear compounds with each delay, degrading the accuracy of what the witness reports.
- [behavior] People who fear future interference with their papers or affairs often take protective legal steps in advance. When: a person worries that others will tamper with their records. Why: advance protection guards against later meddling.
- [rule] When a document may have been tampered with, copy its contents and destroy the original to limit what a watcher can later use. When: a document is exposed to others. Why: the original is the most useful evidence.
- [rule] Check that a suspected protector had access or power to act, since emotional motive alone does not establish opportunity.
- [rule] When a witness's safety is threatened because of what they know, assign watchers to follow and guard them.
- [rule] Gate a protected informant or leave-alone order behind more than one clue, so its reveal rests on accumulated evidence. When: designing quest branches involving a protected character. Why: Multiple clues make the branch depend on evidence rather than a single lucky find.
- [rule] Do not reveal which witness supplied a clue during questioning, so the source stays protected.
- [rule] Do not dismiss a witness's fear entirely when it inflates an ordinary sign, since the reaction may still reflect something real about the listener. When: a witness's fear may be inflating an ordinary sign.
- [heuristic] A witness's protective actions, like moving valuables or defending a source, reveal what they stand to lose; note when defending someone tells you something. When: A witness takes protective action after an event. Why: Protective actions show what the person stands to lose.
- [heuristic] A witness who protects another may be shielding them or exposing their own involvement; test this, and treat any revealed exposure as a new line of questioning. When: A witness's conduct seems evasive, or a witness defends another character. Why: Protective conduct can hide another person's involvement. The risk they accept makes their own involvement a new lead.
- [heuristic] Set up protection before a threat acts, since an enemy who senses danger may move quickly.
- [heuristic] Protect a child witness by placing them somewhere safe and limiting visitors to those with written authorization. When: A child witness may be exposed to a sensitive investigation. Why: Controlled access reduces exposure and pressure on the child.
- [procedure] 1) Move a threatened witness out of reach immediately. 2) Expect the opposition to target them next, since they are the remaining witness. When: A witness is endangered by an opponent.
- [pitfall] Guards can be defeated, so protection lowers risk but does not guarantee a witness's safety.
- [pitfall] A promise of protection can make a witness's cooperation depend on what they want kept hidden. When: A witness is promised anonymity in exchange for information.

## witness rapport
- [mechanism] When a character is re-read after the player learns more, the meaning of that character's earlier lines can shift.
- [mechanism] Track rapport as a state value: blunt questions lower it, and a well-judged approach raises it and unlocks deeper answers. When: Designing dialogue systems for guarded NPCs. Why: Rapport gates which information an NPC will reveal.
- [behavior] A witness who sees the listener as an ally, or who feels flattered and at ease, may reveal hidden motives or say more than intended. When: when the witness sees the listener as an ally or the interview is relaxed or flattering. Why: Comfort or perceived shared sides lower the guard that normally limits disclosure. (x2)
- [behavior] A witness who feels their account is taken seriously volunteers background and gossip freely, even without prompting. When: when the interviewer shows mild familiarity with the subject. Why: the witness does not feel their story is being dismissed.
- [rule] Let a lost memory return by placing the character back in the same state or location where it was formed. When: Designing a memory-recovery moment in a story. Why: Returning to the original context can trigger recall.
- [rule] Offer small, concrete rewards to a child or servant, then negotiate upward if needed, since a loosened tongue can open talk among the adults around them. When: A household is guarded. Why: Small rewards build rapport cheaply.
- [rule] Design dialogue for rambling NPCs so off-topic answers still hold hints that players can recover by asking the right follow-up. When: when writing long conversations with talkative characters.
- [heuristic] Asking several witnesses or searching old papers can help recover details, though it may still leave questions open. When: a key memory is vague. Why: Second sources add partial recovery without guaranteeing answers.
- [heuristic] When a witness closes up, switch to a narrower question that secures the one fact still needed, rather than pressing on the broader topic.
- [heuristic] Build rapport with a witness before raising a point that threatens their account, so they relax and are less guarded when the point is made. When: Before confronting a witness with a timing or consistency problem.
- [procedure] 1) Calm a witness who breaks down. 2) Return to the question asked. 3) Recover the sequence of events in order. When: when a witness becomes too distressed to answer. Why: Distress blocks recall until the witness is steadied.
- [procedure] 1) Build rapport with hospitality and compliments. 2) Ask for a physical description. 3) Ask for independent identifiers such as handwriting or a photograph. When: a witness is needed to identify a person.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the group most likely to have seen the subject. 2) Frame each request as a specific question with a time window and location. 3) Use separate requests for separate sightings. 4) Name one contact point. 5) Run the notice for a fixed period unless cancelled. When: when the witness is unknown and the event was public enough that someone may have noticed.
