- [tradeoff] Indirect rapport-building yields more disclosure but needs time; a deadline forces a direct question that usually gets less. When: Choosing how to question a guarded witness under time pressure. Why: Trust-building takes time that a deadline may not allow.
- [pitfall] Rapport can make a witness protect the suspect, so the questioner hears mainly what is comforting. Why: Sympathy for the suspect filters what the witness chooses to say.
- [pitfall] A remark that someone is improving is not a statement that travel or activity is safe; reading it as one is a common reasoning error. When: Interpreting a witness's comment on a person's condition.

## witness separation
- [mechanism] Isolation, such as a long drive from help and servants who keep leaving, removes easy assistance and raises the stakes. When: a setting is placed far from outside help. Why: distance and loss of staff make the situation harder to escape.
- [mechanism] Advice can be framed so that following it cuts the listener off from their allies, binding them more closely to the speaker. When: When a powerful speaker offers counsel that seems neutral. Why: Acting on the advice removes the listener's other sources of support.
- [rule] Cut off detained suspects from outside contact so they cannot coordinate a story; isolation also removes witnesses who could corroborate them. When: after arrest. Why: Limits coordination with accomplices or witnesses and removes sources of corroboration. (x2)
- [rule] Question witnesses away from anyone who intimidates them, and note who briefed them first, since a present threat or prior briefing can undo or steer testimony. Why: A prior briefing can filter or steer testimony without the investigator knowing. (x2)
- [rule] Keep witnesses or NPCs describing the same event separated so agreement or contradiction stays testable; compare details like menu and preparation, since contradictions point to a liar. When: several witnesses or NPCs describe the same event. Why: Coordinated stories hide contradictions.
- [rule] Define each NPC's knowledge and guilt separately, so an NPC can be innocent of the main crime yet still hold a clue. Why: separate axes prevent innocence from erasing useful knowledge.
- [rule] Track living and dead NPCs separately in game state, so a corpse can still be counted by an observer who does not know its status. When: NPCs can die while remaining in view. Why: A count based on presence alone will include the dead and mislead the player.
- [rule] Separate characters so that one faces the danger alone while the others can only hear it or help from a distance. When: building a peril scene. Why: Isolation heightens fear and makes the rescue depend on indirect information.
- [heuristic] Separate mutually suspicious accomplices so they cannot coordinate, since their distrust makes them easier to isolate and their coordination is the main threat. When: When several participants are mutually suspicious and their coordination is the threat. Why: Accomplices who distrust each other gain little from contact and are easier to pick apart.
- [heuristic] Few nearby residents limit the number of possible witnesses, which narrows the set of people who could have seen events. When: when assessing a remote scene.
- [heuristic] When two witnesses might coordinate their accounts, check whether they can meet, since shared time allows alignment of stories. When: Two witnesses may be sharing a location. Why: Coordination is possible when they can communicate before speaking to the investigator.
- [procedure] 1) Summon each suspect separately under a pretext so neither knows the other is coming. 2) Place each in a position where their reaction to the accusation can be observed. 3) Voice the accusation and watch for reactions an innocent person would not show. When: Two or more suspects could have committed a crime and a reaction to an accusation may separate them. Why: Separation and concealed observation prevent coordinated responses and expose unusual reactions.
- [procedure] 1) Interview each person in a chain of action separately. 2) Ask the same routine questions. 3) Note each time marker. 4) Line the markers up against one another. 5) Separate first-hand sight from assumption. 6) Map the exact sequence of handovers. When: When several people were involved in a chain of actions. Why: Separate, comparable accounts reveal disagreements about who was where and when.
- [procedure] Keep a frightened witness's account private and away from household talk, so the testimony stays uncontaminated.
- [pitfall] A pattern can go unnoticed when each event is recalled separately; comparing event dates side by side reveals it.
- [pitfall] Separating witnesses stops them coordinating, but a suggestion all of them received can still shape their matching accounts.

## accomplice behaviour
- [model] Separate who committed an act from who assisted it, since a person may have had a hand in an event without being its author. When: Investigating a crime with possible helpers. Why: Assistance and authorship imply different suspects and different questions.
- [definition] An accomplice alibi is a cover in which a partner builds a timeline so the crime appears to happen while the suspect is elsewhere.
- [mechanism] An accomplice's written confession that shifts blame can make the accused drop a defence and admit earlier lies.
- [behavior] Accomplices expect quarrels over shared gains and fear counter-plots, so they read each other's disguises and moves as possible traps. When: A criminal partnership with a pending division of spoils. Why: Each partner knows the other could betray them for a larger share.
- [behavior] A new or slow helper may fail to raise an alarm, letting a brief absence of the guard go unnoticed. When: A guard is absent for a short time and a less experienced helper is present. Why: Unfamiliar or slow responders may not recognise a problem.
- [rule] Split investigation tasks among non-player helpers by region or suspect, so partner characters cover different ground.
- [heuristic] Model accomplice NPC loyalty as tied to leverage, so the player can turn, threaten, or expose their partner. When: designing accomplice NPCs.
- [heuristic] Accomplices tend to hide their valuables before fleeing, so valuables left behind suggest a person who left in haste without preparing. When: When a vanished person's behavior must be inferred from what they left. Why: Preparing to flee is a deliberate act that an unprepared departure would skip.
- [heuristic] When a theory needs two or more people to coordinate, check what each would gain or lose by joining. Discard the theory if a partner would lose money or standing by taking part. When: a plot requires coordination between characters. Why: People rarely cooperate against their own interest, so such a theory is unlikely.
- [procedure] 1) Have a frightened suspect write a note to an accomplice setting a time and place. 2) Use the threat of police as the lever. 3) Let the accomplice walk into the trap at that time and place. When: When a suspect has a reason to cooperate and an accomplice is still outside. Why: The suspect's own note draws the accomplice into a controlled meeting.
- [pitfall] Accomplices who are paid, threatened, or sustainedly pressured may crack and expose the plot or turn on the one applying pressure; expect them to give the game away eventually. When: A conspiracy or false death depends on reluctant, paid, threatened, or several silent partners. Why: Cruelty, sustained pressure, or loyalty bought by money or fear is unstable.
- [pitfall] Accepting an accomplice explanation too easily is a mistake when the physical evidence does not fit that explanation.
- [fact] Mutually distrustful accomplices often keep letters or other records against each other, and those records can later be recovered and used. When: When accomplices have quarrelled or do not trust each other. Why: Distrust leads partners to hoard evidence that can be turned against them.
- [fact] Judging a disguised person's physical capability can reveal that a different, more active person is involved, suggesting an accomplice. When: when a disguise's physical demands do not match its wearer. Why: Physical actions expose the true actor behind a disguise.
- [fact] A staged death usually needs an accomplice, and the accomplice is often bound to the plan through a personal interest. When: a false death requires help from outside the subject. Why: the plan cannot run without someone to handle the arrangements.

## accusation and suspects
- [mechanism] A mystery can clear each suspect in turn through a test or witness, shifting blame back toward whoever controlled the key objects, so the handler of the evidence becomes the final suspect. When: Designing a whodunit where several characters are plausibly suspected in sequence. Why: Each cleared suspect removes an alternative, and the person with exclusive access to the instruments of the crime is left standing.
- [mechanism] Each accepted accusation hardens the official story, so the next suspect is judged against a settled account. When: a sequence of wrong suspects. Why: each arrest makes the official account harder to challenge.
- [behavior] When a central clue collapses, the authority may shift the charge to a different offence rather than drop the verdict. When: A case built on one piece of evidence loses that evidence. Why: The institution needs a conviction, so it substitutes another charge.
- [rule] Give each false culprit a checkable detail, such as a timeline, letter or object, that a clue already on the table can break, so the reversal feels earned.
- [rule] Do not treat a witness's anger or grief as proof of error; keep open both that they are right and that their judgment is disturbed.
- [rule] Unlock an accusation only after the player has collected convergent clues from a minimum number of different categories. When: When designing an accusation mechanic in a mystery game. Why: Requiring varied convergent clues prevents accusations from resting on a single source of evidence.
- [heuristic] Let a captured antagonist falsely accuse an ally, forcing the player to produce proof before the scene resolves. When: Designing a late-scene twist with a captured enemy. Why: A desperate false accusation creates a misdirect that only evidence can clear.
- [heuristic] Build an accusation where players must disprove each false claim against physical evidence before a final confrontation with a culprit-only detail. When: Designing a deduction climax. Why: Stepwise disproof makes the final reveal a result of the player's own reasoning.
- [heuristic] Make the most aggressive accuser a suspect, since visible exposure behavior draws attention away from their own act.
- [heuristic] Make an absent rival the default suspect, so suspicion flows outward toward them and the insider in plain view is overlooked. When: building a red herring for a closed-setting mystery. Why: A visible threat from an absent figure absorbs suspicion that would otherwise fall on those present.
- [procedure] 1) Place several cheap minor clues, such as an object, a dropped word and a timing. 2) Require the player to link them before an accusation is possible. 3) Let an NPC voice the chain as a dialogue trigger that reveals a reaction. When: Designing an accusation mechanic built on several minor clues. Why: Minor clues that combine make the accusation a reasoned act rather than a guess.
- [procedure] 1) Keep a written tally of each clue and whom it implicates. 2) Note when several clues from different sources point unanimously to one person. 3) Confirm the pattern before acting on it. When: When no single clue is conclusive but several point the same way. Why: Converging weak points can form a pattern that a single clue cannot.
- [procedure] 1) Give the player a suspect with a motive and a visible alibi. 2) Add a physical or timed clue that disproves that suspect. 3) Repeat with the next suspect until the remaining one seems guilty. 4) Overturn that final answer with a late clue. When: Designing a whodunit whose suspects are removed one at a time. Why: Each elimination feels like progress, and the last overturn delivers the surprise.
- [procedure] 1) Accuse the culprit procedurally by listing faults in the earlier investigation. 2) Press the culprit until a confession behind a closed door. When: when staging the reveal of a hidden culprit. Why: Procedural faults build the case before the culprit cracks.
- [pitfall] Equating the ability to act with the likelihood of having acted leads to accusations on weak grounds.

## contradiction checking and tests
- [mechanism] One sighting that conflicts with a stated schedule can break an alibi and force the whole movement record to be reexamined. When: A witness places a suspect somewhere the schedule says they were not. Why: Once the stated timeline is shown false, every other claim in the record becomes suspect.
- [mechanism] Repeated questioning from several angles, with each answer checked against earlier ones, can expose a false account, since one noticed slip may unravel the whole story. When: A suspect's account has already changed once and can be compared against known facts. Why: Each answer becomes a commitment that later questions can test for conflict.
- [mechanism] A visibly loaded threat can be secretly harmless; revealing this afterwards keeps tension high while the outcome stays under designer control. When: A confrontation where a weapon or danger is shown. Why: Players feel real tension, and the later revelation resolves the threat safely.
- [rule] Allow a player to pin one NPC statement against an item or another NPC's testimony to expose contradictions. When: designing investigation interfaces for testimony. Why: direct comparison lets players test claims against evidence.
- [rule] Control who can hear a sensitive exchange by lowering the voice or speaking aside, so the subject misses remarks not meant for them. When: A conversation contains information meant for only one listener. Why: Deliberate audience control lets the questioner speak freely without alerting the subject.
- [rule] Control what each character learns. Let them hear only what serves the scene, so the player can later discover the gap between what is known and what is hidden. When: Writing dialogue where some characters should remain uninformed. Why: Selective knowledge creates tension and a fair later twist.
- [rule] Let a witness see something that contradicts their own belief, such as a supernatural explanation, so the belief fails fairly.
- [heuristic] Design NPC lies to contradict known routine or world-state traces, so attentive players can detect them and advance the case. When: When designing NPC lines that may be false and can be checked against the environment. Why: Exposing a lie rewards the player and moves the case forward, and a lie that conflicts with known habit gives attentive players a fair way to detect it.
- [heuristic] Keep a supernatural agent's behavior consistent, such as blocking prayer, speaking and urging harm, so the reader can track its escalation.
- [heuristic] When a statement from an impaired state also appears in the character's lucid speech, treat it as a stronger indication of the character's true motive, though not of fact. When: Judging a character's motive from statements made in different mental states. Why: Agreement across states shows a stable belief, but the belief can still be wrong about what happened.
- [heuristic] Stage a conversation the player overhears to control what the player believes while hiding the true facts. When: A scripted scene must mislead the player on purpose. Why: Overheard talk is trusted as context and shapes belief.
- [heuristic] A character who provokes conflict while appearing calm and detached draws less suspicion than the people who react to them. When: when designing a manipulator who must stay hidden. Why: Visible emotion draws scrutiny, so the calm instigator is overlooked.
- [heuristic] Track a match in the player's journal as a separate state from confirmed and ruled out, so consistent but unverified matches remain visible. When: Designing a journal or record for mystery clues. Why: A third state preserves partial progress without implying certainty.
- [procedure] 1) Limit the scene to a known set of usable rooms and access points, locking the rest. 2) Research the place's history before the test. 3) Run a fixed routine of checking every room and lock. 4) Observe covertly and keep notes. When: Testing a suspected place for an unseen factor. Why: A known set of access points and a fixed routine make later changes stand out.
- [procedure] 1) Give the hidden agent a material form by a lure with known properties. 2) Ensure the lure meets its stated conditions, such as freshness and strength. 3) Observe the response so the agent becomes visible. When: when a hidden agent cannot be observed directly. Why: A controlled lure forces the agent to act within a condition the investigator set.

## cover exposure and breakdown
- [mechanism] A cover story fabricated for one crime can later be exposed by facts, and its details can reveal a repeated pattern.
- [behavior] Cover-up efforts leave their own evidence; an altered or replaced object and its materials can reveal what it was meant to hide. Doing nothing afterward is hardest to catch. When: after a crime has been committed. Why: Cover-up actions leave traces of their own.
- [behavior] Demands for silence and checks for eavesdroppers signal that a cover protects something real.
- [heuristic] When a visitor's behaviour is out of proportion to the stated goal, suspect the request is cover for another aim. When: a visitor's request and reactions do not match.
- [heuristic] Concealing one fact often leaves a second, small contradiction in an unrelated object, such as a note written on the back of a paper. Why: people who hide one item seldom clean up every item they handled.
- [heuristic] Cover is weakest where routine observers see both identities, and staff familiar with the second identity can react to it at an unusual hour and expose the arrangement. When: when a hidden identity is exposed to people who know both roles. Why: Familiarity with one identity lets observers connect it to the other under unusual conditions.
- [heuristic] End a case with an aftermath that shows the consequence of the concealed act, closing the loop the reversal opened.
- [tradeoff] A cover role may hold up against ordinary staff but fail if checked by someone with authority over the site. When: Choosing a pretext for entry. Why: Authority figures are more likely to verify credentials.
- [pitfall] A cover that depends on distraction or on not being examined becomes a clue under careful, repeated inspection, and the staging fails. When: a disguise or deception depends on preventing close examination. Why: Careful attention exposes the mismatch; a cover that relies on not being inspected fails once inspection is repeated with comparison. (x2)
- [pitfall] A cover identity or story collapses if one relative, mutual contact, or independent check can confirm or deny it, so the victim must be isolated from people who could check it. When: Maintaining a false identity. Why: One independent check can expose the entire lie.
- [pitfall] If a slip exposes the questioner's real role, witnesses change what they say, so the cover must be maintained throughout.
- [pitfall] A cover can break through a single slip, or through a suspect who notices a stranger's unusual interest.
- [pitfall] Half-truths tend to be found out, and the discovery of concealment can do more damage than the truth would have. When: When a character's partial account is likely to be checked later. Why: Hidden information that surfaces later erodes trust in the whole account.
- [pitfall] A cover persona that slips in its slang or details can expose the investigator. When: Maintaining an undercover identity over time. Why: Inconsistent details invite suspicion from those who know the group.
- [pitfall] Sharing a cover identity with an ally adds risk, because the ally's questioning can expose the cover. When: Two or more people operate under a shared cover. Why: An ally who is questioned may reveal the shared story.

## discarded evidence
- [mechanism] Everyday refuse such as wrappers and discarded letters often survives destruction by chance, and can carry more useful information than deliberate evidence. When: Physical trail is thin and suspects have tried to destroy items. Why: People tend to destroy deliberate evidence but overlook packaging and scraps.
- [mechanism] Discarded documents survive when layered under later refuse and ash, since each layer adds protection from decay and disturbance. When: When designing hidden or buried clues in a level. Why: Successive covering layers shield fragile material from being destroyed.
- [behavior] A culprit may discard an item they would be exposed by carrying farther, showing awareness of what the item reveals.
- [heuristic] Keep a record of facts set aside during early sorting, and do not discard facts that disagree with the working theory, since the discarded fact may be the decisive one. When: Facts are being filtered before they are tested, or when they disagree with the working theory. Why: Early selection or theory-driven discarding can throw away the fact that matters and hide evidence that could overturn the theory.
- [heuristic] Discarded clothing can show that a suspect changed appearance after leaving the place where they were seen. When: Searching for someone who may have changed their look. Why: Changed clothing reveals a deliberate change of appearance.
- [heuristic] Discarding the only escape vehicle a fugitive needs looks like a diversion rather than a real act of flight, and should be treated as suspicious.
- [heuristic] A passage a writer deliberately removed may reveal a revision made after reflection, so note what was left out. Why: Deletions can show how a position changed.
- [pitfall] Declaring evidence worthless without testing it can lose the key clue, since an item that seems meaningless may solve the case. When: Assessing a seemingly trivial or suspicious item. Why: Apparent worthlessness is not verified until the item is examined.
- [pitfall] Discarded items can be recovered, and items hidden in water still give investigators reason to search.
- [pitfall] A discarded forged message can be recovered later, so the forger leaves a paper trail that investigators can use to reconstruct the lure. Why: Discarded paper is rarely destroyed completely.
- [pitfall] Discarding packaging removes the only independent test of an account of how an item arrived.
- [pitfall] Disposing of items in several places multiplies the locations an investigator must search, and each location can yield a trace. When: A culprit spreads discarded items across different places. Why: More disposal sites mean more chances for evidence to be found.
- [pitfall] A narrator's rational dismissal of a witnessed anomaly can keep the clue from being examined, and it may be lost. When: An observer notices an anomaly and another character explains it away. Why: Explaining away prevents further examination.
- [fact] Physical evidence discarded before inspection cannot be rechecked later, so its state must be recorded when it is found.
- [fact] Discarded objects often end up in nearby concealed spots such as gardens or bushes, where they can remain for a long time.

## frame design and checks
- [model] A frame is a set of planted items that all support one false story, such as a booking, cash, a disguise and a stated motive. When: when a culprit wants blame to fall on a specific person. Why: each item reinforces the others and makes the story believable.
- [mechanism] NPC responses that change with how the player frames a question let a tone choice unlock different information.
- [mechanism] Extra steps taken to shift blame create additional traces that a player or investigator can find, so they can serve as deliberate detection points. When: Designing a scripted cover-up or frame-up. Why: Each added action leaves a further record or inconsistency.
- [behavior] Who is present in a house decides who would be framed, so the obvious suspect shifts with the people who were there.
- [rule] Let an NPC copy another character's outfit or tracks to frame them, and give the player a visible mismatch to detect.
- [rule] Frame a witness interview as voluntary and private, asking for help rather than making a charge, so the witness feels free to cooperate. When: questioning a witness without formal authority.
- [rule] Place a planted item pointing at an NPC with a test, such as an alibi or time record, that players can run to discover the frame. When: Designing a false lead in a quest.
- [rule] Keep the framing questions alongside recorded answers, since answers alone hide the premise that shaped them. When: recording interrogations.
- [heuristic] A scapegoat with a verifiable alibi or clean record is unlikely to be framed successfully, since others will check those facts. When: Assessing whether a frame will hold. Why: Verifiable records let investigators disprove the accusation.
- [heuristic] A frame feels arbitrary unless the framed character has a real tie to the scene, so give the accused a believable link to it. When: Choosing who to frame. Why: Unconnected frames look contrived.
- [heuristic] Compare planted evidence with the habits of the person it implicates; physical traces can be planted, but personal habits are harder to fake. When: When evidence looks too neat or too consistent with one suspect. Why: Staged items often contradict the routine of the framed person.
- [heuristic] A mistaken shared frame tends to survive argument and gives way mainly when events contradict it. When: when a community clings to a doubtful belief despite critique. Why: people revise frames under observed failure more than under reasoning.
- [procedure] 1) List everyone who could have entered the place. 2) For each document, ask who could have written it or swapped a page. 3) Note when each access could have happened. When: items may have been planted.
- [pitfall] Framing a question or presentation can change how a statement reads or how an expert's estimate is answered, with no new facts. Tie each reading to the facts. When: when an estimate is questioned under pressure or a statement is interpreted. Why: framing changes the answer or reading given, not the evidence.
- [pitfall] A frame with gaps invites questions, and an unexplained key or exit route gives the defence its strongest arguments. When: A planted frame is built. Why: Unexplained details become points of attack.

## hidden clues and threats
- [mechanism] A message released on a condition lets knowledge and instructions outlive the person who wrote them.
- [mechanism] A suspect who knows a detail no one disclosed to them can be flagged, so the knowledge itself becomes a clue the player tracks.
- [behavior] A person may reveal knowledge of a secret through an offhand remark rather than a direct confession. When: questioning a witness about a hidden item. Why: Casual speech often exposes what a person heard or saw.
- [rule] Invisible threats seen by only one NPC need corroboration from another NPC, an environmental trace, or a logged event.
- [rule] Hide the true mechanism in an ordinary object that the player has no reason to test until a sample is taken. When: when designing a concealed method of harm or deception. Why: Players test objects they find suspicious, so an everyday object stays unexamined.
- [rule] Hide a person in the room and reveal them through a mechanism, such as a swinging panel, rather than through testimony.
- [heuristic] A character's fear of interception may be well founded or mistaken, so make clear which one it is.
- [heuristic] A visitor who taps a window instead of using the bell suggests the visitor knew the household well enough to skip the formal signal. When: A visitor's method of announcing arrival differs from the normal one. Why: Skipping the usual signal implies familiarity with the occupants.
- [heuristic] Hide the decisive trait behind a missing or damaged component so that identification requires a second discovery. When: Designing a body identification puzzle. Why: Withholding the confirming detail turns a partial match into a reason to keep searching.
- [heuristic] Hide a clue in a detail visible only under magnification or an overlay, so the player must inspect closely to find the inconsistency. When: designing a clue meant to reward careful inspection. Why: Requiring a deliberate inspection action turns discovery into an active choice rather than a passive reveal.
- [tradeoff] A dialogue clue can be kept fair yet unobvious by letting the protagonist's bias hide it until a later reveal recovers the sense. When: A clue must be fair but must not look like one. Why: A bias-driven misreading hides the clue, and the reveal rewards a second reading.
- [pitfall] Clues or anomalies the player cannot see or hear feel unfair, so reveal incidental clues to both sides and make character dismissals follow visible clues. When: Hiding a clue in casual conversation or an object, or having a character dismiss an anomaly. Why: Players cannot reason from information they never perceived.
- [pitfall] A covert change the player cannot notice or learn about removes their agency over the outcome. When: the player is meant to act on the outcome.
- [pitfall] A joking answer to a noticed reaction can bury the clue, leading the observer to dismiss the reaction along with the joke. When: A character deflects a question about a revealing reaction with humour. Why: Humour ends the question without answering it, so the reaction is easily forgotten.
- [pitfall] Recording failure at an unrelated test, such as reciting a prayer, as evidence of guilt substitutes an irrelevant test for proof.

## impossible events and access
- [mechanism] Open with a stated physical impossibility, then supply a mechanism that explains it, so the audience gets a fair puzzle to attempt before the solution is revealed. When: A mystery should feel impossible yet remain fair. Why: Stating the impossibility first gives the audience a puzzle to attempt before the reveal.
- [mechanism] A planted clue fails when its staged action is physically impossible, so a wound angle or grip can serve as a checkable puzzle condition. When: Designing a staged clue the player must test. Why: A physical check exposes staging that a story alone would hide.
- [rule] Treat a sealed-room claim as a method question, not proof of impossibility: keep asking how anyone could enter or leave and whether the space was truly empty at the event. When: A room or crime appears sealed or impossible given its enclosure. Why: Sealed-room claims often hide an overlooked route or timing gap. (x2)
- [rule] When testimony or an answer seems impossible, ask which further facts would make it possible instead of discarding or rejecting it outright.
- [rule] Do not accept a claim that no one could have done something until it is checked against every other handler's account.
- [heuristic] When a sighting or normal explanation seems impossible, examine the means of access and test it; uncanny explanations are premature because the gap usually lies in a checkable route. When: A sighting seems impossible on its face, or a normal explanation appears closed off. Why: Apparent impossibility often reflects an unexamined assumption about the system. (x2)
- [heuristic] An item in a place it should not be is itself evidence, because its presence shows that someone had access to it.
- [heuristic] When a room seems unreachable, look for a route that a person with an unusual ability could use, once that ability is known. When: A locked or sealed room appears impossible to enter. Why: Known abilities can make an apparently impossible route plausible.
- [heuristic] If a perishable still shows a state that heat or elapsed time would have destroyed, it must have arrived after that period. When: checking a delivery's timing.
- [procedure] 1) List every access point, including doors, windows, side entries and overhead openings. 2) Verify each lock's state independently and rule out exits that fail established facts. 3) Set the physical facts against the anomaly and keep the route that fits all of them as the method. 4) Ask what that route hides. 5) Identify the author only after the method is determined. When: A scene seems sealed and every obvious exit has been checked, or someone's entry or exit from a secured space must be worked out. Why: Elimination against fixed facts exposes overlooked routes that a first look misses.
- [procedure] 1) List the physical traces each proposed explanation must leave. 2) Check each trace against the scene. 3) Discard any explanation with a missing trace. When: a scene seems sealed and several explanations compete. Why: Traces make explanations testable.
- [procedure] 1) Open with an impossibility, such as a death with no heard shot, smoke or weapon. 2) Let the player investigate it with specific tools. 3) Resolve it through a chain of physical clues. When: when designing an opening mystery built on an impossible scene. Why: A concrete impossibility gives the player a question that physical evidence can answer.
- [procedure] 1) Count everyone who had access to the place. 2) List the access methods such as keys, passwords and signatures. 3) Test each human explanation against those methods to find who could act. When: An apparently impossible event occurs in a controlled place. Why: A finite set of access holders converts a supernatural-seeming event into a checkable human mechanism.
- [pitfall] A report of something impossible can distract from the practical facts that can be tested. When: a witness reports a supernatural or impossible event. Why: Focusing on the impossible claim leaves the checkable details unexamined.
- [fact] A citation pointing to a location that does not exist signals an error, and the surrounding context often reveals the intended reference.

## investigator method and bias
- [model] A common mystery structure makes the apparent investigator the hidden criminal, so the solver's own tools and actions steer belief away from the truth.
- [model] A case file that is also the culprit's confession reframes each entry as evidence, so the investigator is the culprit recording his own crime. When: when the narrator of an investigation is the killer. Why: Each recorded detail becomes evidence once the frame is revealed.
- [rule] Keep evidence of intent or a plan separate from evidence the act occurred; a reasoned motive account does not prove the act was done. When: A mystery turns on whether a scheme happened, or a character's plan or reasoning sounds like a confession. Why: Documents of intent alone do not prove the act; players should notice the gap before proof of action arrives. (x2)
- [rule] An immobile witness who perceives everything needs a clear in-world reason for stillness, or the scene looks contrived. When: Placing a helpless character who overhears or sees the whole scene. Why: Without a reason, the convenient vantage point breaks believability.
- [rule] An investigator who reveals too much to a witness cannot later tell what the witness saw from what the witness was told. When: Deciding how much theory to share during questioning. Why: Shared theory becomes indistinguishable from independent observation.
- [rule] Keep one secret in the investigator's hand, such as a hidden family link, and reveal it late through the investigator's own knowledge. When: a mystery depends on a concealed link between characters. Why: Investigator knowledge makes the late reveal feel earned.
- [heuristic] Let the investigator's first reading of people be partly wrong, so a private suspicion becomes a usable lead. Why: A mistaken but plausible suspicion drives investigation and later correction.
- [heuristic] Establish an investigator's idle habits early so that a later change in behavior reads as meaningful rather than convenient. When: The story depends on the protagonist's later close attention to ordinary things. Why: A established baseline makes a shift in attentiveness feel earned.
- [heuristic] Widen the investigation timeline by requesting records from well before the crime, since the relevant date may be earlier than the event itself. When: When a crime's origin is unclear. Why: Motive and setup can predate the act by years.
- [heuristic] The player's expectation of a monster can be inverted by making the threat a person in a disguised state. When: Designing a reveal that subverts a monster expectation.
- [heuristic] Insert a pressure event, such as an attack or threat, during the investigation to test the protagonist's resolve. When: the investigation is gathering clues. Why: Pressure forces the protagonist to act, which exposes character and advances the plot.
- [tradeoff] Casting the investigator as culprit gives a stronger twist; it works fairly only when each trusted tool appears as ordinary detail before its meaning is revealed. When: Deciding whether the solver is the culprit, or the investigator is also a suspect. Why: A hidden tool that appears only at the reveal feels like a cheat; the reversal reuses the trust already placed in those tools.
- [pitfall] An investigator's personal bias, such as jealousy or dislike, can make a red herring against a suspect look convincing; a biased guide adds doubt beyond the evidence. When: The investigator has a personal bias toward a suspect, or a detective guide leads the player's reasoning. Why: Emotion distorts how plausible a misleading lead appears, and a biased guide makes the player question conclusions rather than accept them unexamined. (x2)
- [pitfall] Dismissing a tight evidence chain merely for being improbable returns the investigator to where they started. When: Evaluating a convergent body of evidence. Why: Improbability alone does not refute a chain that fits the facts.
- [pitfall] Assuming the intended victim from a poisoned item's delivery route can mislead, because the route may be set up to point at the wrong target. When: a poisoned item was delivered to one person. Why: A staged delivery route can make the wrong person look like the target.

## misdirection techniques
- [model] A mystery can be built as a chain of misdirections, each stage shifting suspicion to a new suspect before a final reveal exposes a schemer hiding in plain sight. When: designing a multi-stage whodunit. Why: Each shift delays the true answer and keeps the audience guessing.
- [model] Misdirection by allegiance keeps the reader focused on foreign figures and outsiders while the real answer sits among the investigators and their trusted friends. When: Designing a mystery with a hidden culprit who is part of the investigating group. Why: Readers assign suspicion by social distance, so the closest allies stay unsuspected while outsiders absorb blame.
- [model] A reveal can plant a wrong attribution in a source the reader trusts, then replace that identity with a second holder that independent dates settle.
- [mechanism] A rational false explanation placed early, then corrected through the protagonist's own reported observations, makes the correction feel earned and punishes the player's skepticism. When: When designing a mystery's first misdirect. Why: The player commits to the plausible explanation, so the later evidence carries weight. (x2)
- [mechanism] A plausible outside suspect or public explanation, such as a feud, draws attention away from insiders while the true evidence builds inside the location. When: an identity or staged-death mystery. Why: Searching for an outsider keeps the player from testing the insider's account.
- [mechanism] A motif repeated across many sources steers interpretation toward one frame, acting as misdirection that pushes the audience toward a supernatural reading.
- [mechanism] A frame-up stays hidden from the characters but not the audience when the sleight is shown openly, because the audience sees the setup while the group believes the accusation.
- [rule] Let the most obvious helper carry the central action without drawing attention, since errands look like ordinary service.
- [rule] Keep an outside-intruder theory alive through an official voice, so the player is misled by apparent authority.
- [heuristic] Use the strongest official theory to hide the true cause, such as blaming an arrested suspect or a convenient group. When: Building a misdirect in a mystery. Why: A well-supported wrong theory keeps the player from looking at the real cause until late.
- [heuristic] Offer mundane explanations, such as mental or financial motives, to hold back a supernatural or hidden cause until late. When: the true cause would be surprising if stated early. Why: Plausible everyday explanations keep the audience's expectations grounded until the reveal.
- [procedure] 1) Ask what the disturbing act actually changes. 2) List who benefits from those changes. 3) Test motives such as theft against the valuables present. 4) Discard theories that do not fit the facts. When: when a strange act seems pointless. Why: The effects of an act reveal its purpose more reliably than its appearance.
- [procedure] 1) plant an early misleading reading of a clue; 2) correct one reading in the same scene; 3) repeat the clue at a later point to make the false pattern look stronger; 4) confirm the author in a late confession.
- [pitfall] Planted doubt can point an investigator in the wrong direction without changing their core belief, so the investigator may still hold the wrong conclusion. When: When a misdirection is used against a skeptical investigator. Why: Doubt redirects attention but does not necessarily overturn an existing conviction.
- [pitfall] A decoy that is too obvious leads the player to dismiss the real clue along with it. When: when placing a distraction near a real clue.

## npc testimony and reliability
- [mechanism] Gaps across several NPC accounts signal either a lie or a missing witness, giving the player a lead to follow.
- [mechanism] An authority NPC holding a biased theory can be challenged by letting the player's alternative theory be tested against evidence, rewarding players who question the official line. When: Designing an investigation where an NPC authority is wrong. Why: Testing an alternative gives the player a meaningful way to overturn the wrong conclusion.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses a reliability value and a motive or bias tag; low-character or intoxicated witnesses give partial information that players must cross-check. When: When designing NPC testimony for a game. Why: Explicit tags make contradictory accounts a reasoning task, and partial, biased information rewards player verification.
- [rule] Give witnesses a reliability score; tag claims as facts or impressions, testing facts and discounting impressions; fearful witnesses may change details under pressure. When: When designing NPC testimony or interview dialogue. Why: Impressions carry less certainty than observed facts, and opinions cannot be verified the way facts can.
- [rule] Give an expert NPC a plausible but misleading lecture that sends the player toward the wrong district or faction; the player must decide whether to act on it or verify it. When: When designing misdirection through an expert character or any NPC who gives information. Why: Plausible misdirection tests whether players verify claims, which makes information gathering a decision.
- [rule] Let NPC explanations be testable against the scene, such as a mundane source like wind or a draft, or whether a burial site holds the remains claimed. When: When designing NPC accounts of strange events or on-the-spot explanations. Why: A testable explanation makes the player's investigation determine the outcome.
- [rule] Give NPC testimony a stated vantage point and confidence level so players can judge its reliability. When: When designing NPC dialogue that reveals information. Why: Players can weigh statements only when they know how the speaker knows them.
- [rule] Let a second NPC partly confirm or contradict the first and leave the gap for the player to resolve. When: When designing linked NPC testimony. Why: Partial overlap creates a puzzle the player must reason through.
- [rule] Give two NPCs opposed opinions about the same figure, so the player must decide whom to believe and why. When: Designing a conflict of testimony for the player to resolve. Why: Opposed accounts force the player to weigh reliability.
- [rule] Let NPC witnesses report partial observations with gaps, leaving the player to fill in the rest and check each claim. When: designing witness dialogue for a mystery. Why: Partial and interpreted reports keep the player an active evaluator rather than a recipient of settled facts.
- [rule] Do not treat a suspect's outburst as proof on its own; link it to physical evidence or a previously established clue. Why: Outbursts are ambiguous and gain weight only when tied to other facts.
- [heuristic] Denials by people who would have received or seen something can work as negative evidence that undermines a stated purpose. When: A claimed reason for an action is contradicted by those who should know. Why: The absence of the claimed item or event among those expected to have it weakens the claim.
- [heuristic] Let NPC dialogue contradict scene data so the player can catch a lie or confusion, and let vantage rules limit what each NPC can report. When: Designing NPC dialogue that interacts with world state. Why: Contradictions and vantage limits make testimony a puzzle the player must solve.
- [heuristic] Each consultation with a non-specialist creates a record of what the culprit attempted, which can later be used to reconstruct the method. When: When a culprit sought outside help or information. Why: Outside contacts can remember or document the offender's intentions.
- [heuristic] Make an NPC's account detailed about the wrong moment, so the player notices what the account skips. When: Writing an NPC who gives a testimony about a scene. Why: Detail in the wrong place draws attention to the gap.

## planted clues
- [mechanism] A planted inscription in a game room can name the wrong culprit; players should be able to test it against a second source to discover the plant. When: When designing misleading written clues in a level. Why: A checkable second source rewards careful players without making the clue unfair.
- [mechanism] A deliberately placed object can carry a hint, and the person most likely to find it is often the one who placed it. When: Evaluating whether an object was planted. Why: A planter tends to know where the object will be discovered and by whom.
- [rule] Overheard references to unexplained things can be planted as clues that stay uninterpreted until a later payoff. Why: Unexplained fragments keep a thread open and reward recall.
- [rule] Plant every fact used in a reveal earlier in the story, tying each to an earlier mention. When: Writing a reveal built on hidden information. Why: A reveal resting on unseen facts feels like cheating and loses credibility.
- [rule] Place a key somewhere unexpected as a discrepancy that sends the player back to question its holder. When: Designing investigation clues around keys. Why: A mismatch between an account and the item's location prompts renewed questioning.
- [heuristic] Set up the decisive detail in plain sight early, before its meaning is known, then return to it as proof, so the evidence was visible from the start. When: Setting up a clue that will prove a key link later. Why: Early visibility lets the player connect the object once its meaning is revealed. (x2)
- [heuristic] Plant the unexplained object early and hold back its cause until mid-story, so the later explanation answers the question the audience holds.
- [heuristic] Present oddities or identity-revealing details as ordinary background early, so they are accepted without scrutiny and recalled or reread when a later line changes their meaning. When: Seeding clues in a bargain or introduction scene, or setting up a disguised-character reveal. Why: Early oddities feel mundane, so they are remembered when they become significant; ordinary details are accepted without scrutiny and later read differently.
- [heuristic] A clue planted in plain view should be explained by a later event, since an unpaid hint reads as a loose thread and erodes trust. When: Planting a hint the story will later resolve. Why: Unresolved hints make the story feel careless and reduce reader trust.
- [heuristic] Leave an unexplained detail, such as mismatched handwriting or a minor figure, as a hook that a later reveal turns into a clue. When: Building clues for a twist that reframes earlier evidence. Why: A hook already in the report becomes meaningful when the reveal explains it, rather than seeming like an error.
- [heuristic] Plant an object that looks like an odd detail, then use it to carry the reconstruction of the reveal, so the reader can recheck it against what they already saw. When: Setting up a physical clue meant to be reinterpreted later. Why: Objects seen early can be re-read once their meaning changes, making the reveal checkable.
- [heuristic] Use one physical object that passes between suspects, since it carries the player from one false lead to the next.
- [procedure] 1) Show a small, odd detail early without explanation. 2) Mention it again briefly with no comment. 3) Give it enough narrative weight that it returns in memory. 4) Reveal its meaning later. When: Setting up a mystery clue the audience should notice but not yet understand. Why: A detail the audience dismisses early will not register when it later matters.
- [pitfall] A clue that fits the theory or neatly names the culprit may be planted; check it against physical setting, materials and the writer's known habits before trusting it. When: A physical clue appears to confirm a theory; a clue arrives neatly and matches a suspect's visible grudge. Why: Planted evidence can imitate genuine evidence and is designed to end inquiry early; fit alone does not establish authenticity.
- [pitfall] A matching item found in a room proves only that the item was there, not who placed it or when. When: Interpreting an object found at a location. Why: Presence of an object does not establish its owner or time of placement.

## public and private conduct
- [behavior] A celebrated public figure may act awkward or sulky in private, so public reputation can differ from private conduct. When: A suspect is widely admired in public.
- [behavior] Once an actor's stance is entered on the record, retreating from it costs standing, so the actor may give up the contest rather than defend the stance. When: an actor has publicly committed to a position that a record now exposes. Why: Reversing a recorded position looks like admitting fault, which damages reputation.
- [behavior] People who believe they are unobserved can drop a composed public face, showing strain such as tears or anger that contrasts with their calm in company. When: A suspect is alone after appearing calm before others. Why: Public composure is kept for observers and relaxes when no one watches.
- [behavior] Targets tend to volunteer their own beliefs and practices when the person they face appears receptive and sensitive. When: an investigator adopts a listening, sympathetic persona. Why: people speak more when they feel understood.
- [behavior] A visible public record of offices, charity, and manners can stand in for character, discouraging observers from scrutinizing the person. When: when judging someone of high standing. Why: visible virtue substitutes for inspection.
- [behavior] A soft, sincere manner combined with ready explanations can make a false account persuasive to someone seeing the speaker for the first time. When: a suspect's story fits a convenient narrative. Why: tone is read as honesty.
- [behavior] A rough manner and quick temper can make ordinary disputes look like motive, so a person's quarrels are read as a reason to suspect them of harm. When: when a character has a known temper and a dispute precedes a loss.
- [behavior] Observers read pallor, trembling and agitation as signs of guilt or illness, and their suspicion rises or falls with the suspect's visible manner. When: A person is questioned in a conversation or interrogation.
- [heuristic] Substantive questioning often shifts to a private setting after a public exchange, once an adviser asks others to withdraw. When: after a public confrontation.
- [procedure] 1) Collect a figure's public and private statements on the same matter. 2) Check whether private tone matches a claimed moderation or distance. 3) Treat any gap as a test of sincerity, since gaps often reveal the real picture. When: A figure's public stance and private conduct may diverge. Why: Gaps can reveal a stance that public statements disguise. (x2)
- [tradeoff] A dramatic public account serves the investigator's interests without commitment, but misleading others risks the truth coming out later. When: An investigator shares a story they do not fully believe.
- [tradeoff] A quiet early interview avoids exposing a suspect too soon but gathers less public pressure, while a public accusation carries real risk. When: choosing how openly to confront a suspect.
- [pitfall] Over-reading meekness, blushing or embarrassment as proof of wrongdoing is a mistake, since these have innocent causes.
- [pitfall] Escalating a matter a private talk could settle into a public hearing adds little to the case while spreading fear through the group. When: a private conversation would settle the matter.
- [pitfall] Public actions such as visible travel or landmark visits create a timeline that others can reconstruct, exposing an alibi. When: when a character tries to hide movements. Why: Witnessed actions give investigators points to check.

## quest logs and case files
- [mechanism] An NPC-posted job can draw the true target into a set room, where a trigger fires once they arrive.
- [rule] Date each hostile event in a quest log, and let case files hold dated documents with editorial notes, so players compare them to rebuild the rival's timeline. (x2)
- [rule] Attach a named source to each piece of evidence and each accusation, since players weigh first-hand reports and an unnamed accusation cannot be tested and stays unverified. When: Designing a case file or evidence system. Why: Named sources let players compare reports and judge reliability; a withheld name stops the listener from checking the claim. (x2)
- [rule] When a quest or faction requires corroboration, check that the witnesses are truly independent, since players can challenge a list that shares one loyalty. Why: Players spot shared allegiance and dismiss the verification.
- [rule] Ask narrow questions about a specific object or document, because vague claims of never having read something may hide selective memory.
- [rule] Give each guard, servant or NPC a logged sighting so players bound a victim's time of death using the earliest and latest entries. When: Designing a murder puzzle with logged witnesses. Why: Combining log entries gives players a checkable window.
- [rule] Give each quest thread concrete next steps and avoid leads that only produce atmosphere. When: Designing investigation quests. Why: Concrete steps keep players moving toward a resolution.
- [rule] Document each NPC action as a question paired with a motive answer, so a player can rebuild the chain of reasons from a dossier. When: Designing NPC behavior for a mystery. Why: A written chain lets the player reconstruct intent from the evidence.
- [heuristic] Quest log entries that record NPC statements may exaggerate, so the player should be given a way to test them.
- [heuristic] Teach players to ask what a fake quest makes possible, since that question tends to lead them to the real target.
- [heuristic] Build a mystery quest log as explicit motive lines, such as revenge, rivalry and access, each with its own checklist. When: designing a mystery with several possible motives. Why: the player's question list drives discovery.
- [heuristic] Design a quest from its final state: define the endpoint first, then place each earlier objective to serve it. When: when authoring a multi-step quest. Why: a fixed end state gives each objective a purpose.
- [heuristic] Include near-identical documents so players must read exact wording before drawing a conclusion.
- [heuristic] Quests can log item transfers through NPC records and handwritten routes, with dead-end addresses that the player must visit to verify. When: designing a traceable item chase. Why: verification in person makes records meaningful rather than just readable.
- [fact] A missing-person quest can require following records across several locations, each with its own registry.

## reconstruction hypothesis testing
- [definition] A reductio applies an accepted rule to its own proponent; if the proponent fails the rule, the rule's authority is undermined without being proven false.
- [rule] Present a reconstructed motive as a possibility rather than fact when evidence is incomplete. When: evidence is incomplete. Why: gaps in evidence make the reconstruction uncertain.
- [rule] Treat a reconstructed sequence as testable claims, each pointing to a line of inquiry, and do not present imagined steps as established fact. When: presenting an investigator's reconstruction of events. Why: untested steps can mislead if taken as fact.
- [rule] Keep a reconstructed document separate from the surviving fragments and do not present the restoration as the original text. When: Using a reconstructed document as evidence. Why: A reconstruction is a provisional inference, and treating it as original overstates what is known.
- [rule] Treat a reconstruction as a working hypothesis, and mark unresolved routes as open while doors, keys or exits remain unaccounted for. Why: Claiming certainty over unexplained exits invites error.
- [heuristic] A reconstruction of unseen movement must fit what was seen and explain what was missing.
- [heuristic] Test any reconstructed sequence of events against the recorded positions of physical objects; a reconstruction that conflicts with an object's location is wrong.
- [heuristic] Reconstruction works only while the location and marks remain intact; disturbed ground or objects make it unreliable.
- [procedure] 1) State the theory as a specific action the suspect should repeat. 2) Match the original conditions: place, objects, dose and companions. 3) Time each stage with a watch. 4) Record results and have witnesses sign them on the spot. When: Testing a theory about what a suspect did under specific conditions. Why: Matching conditions and timing makes the repeat test a checkable comparison.
- [procedure] 1) Build a full account that explains motive, accomplice and sequence. 2) Identify the one fact the account must explain, such as a door's state. 3) Check whether the account truly addresses that fact. 4) Mark each step as resting on evidence or on assumption. When: A reconstruction is complete and needs testing. Why: A consistent account can still be wrong if it does not explain the hardest fact.
- [procedure] 1) List small facts that do not fit the working theory. 2) Propose a sequence of events that explains them. 3) Test the sequence against each anomaly. 4) Rewrite the whole line of reasoning if the premise fails. When: A theory explains some facts but leaves a cluster of contradictions. Why: Anomalies that cannot be explained by the premise expose its failure, and a corrected sequence accounts for them.
- [procedure] 1) Hold back the full explanation. 2) In the closing reconstruction, cite only physical objects the player already holds. 3) Link the objects into one account of the act. When: Ending a mystery with a proof rather than a confession. Why: The reveal becomes a recap of earned evidence, not a new lecture.
- [pitfall] A reconstruction that fits the evidence remains a hypothesis, not proof; test it against independent evidence, such as a confession, before relying on it.
- [pitfall] A reconstruction can contain errors, so the method must allow revision when a claim is only partly right.
- [pitfall] A timeline reconstruction is only as reliable as its map distances and the accuracy of each witness's stated time.

## stolen property
- [model] A stolen-object chase follows an item through successive owners, and the thief is often a trusted insider rather than the most suspected person. When: Designing a theft mystery. Why: The item's chain of custody gives the player a path, and the insider's position hides the thief.
- [mechanism] A stolen item that needs the owner's personal authorisation is useless to thieves, so taking it reveals that they misjudged their target. When: When evaluating a theft.
- [behavior] A thief may take a single unit and keep it in reserve, so a one-item shortage can be deliberate rather than accidental. When: A small, single item is missing from a controlled store. Why: One unit may be enough for a purpose that the thief plans to use later.
- [rule] Stolen goods carry provenance, so a found item matching a known loot list can link to a specific theft and to its hideout. When: Designing items taken from a crime and placed in the world.
- [rule] Give stolen items an engraved name or crest that points the player to the owner or to an NPC linked to that owner. When: Designing a stolen item clue. Why: A readable mark links an item to a person.
- [rule] Plant a tempting motive, such as a valuable item whose value or purpose does not match the crime, so players must look for the larger plan. When: In mystery design.
- [heuristic] Information that raises the value of an object makes theft a more plausible motive for targeting it.
- [heuristic] Known valuables carried by a person weigh against suicide and in favour of homicide, suggesting a motive. When: When a death involves a person known to carry valuable property. Why: Valuables give a plausible reason for an attack.
- [heuristic] When a theft ignores obvious valuables and takes one item, treat that item as the target rather than general loot. When: a theft skips valuables.
- [heuristic] Small, portable losses narrow the likely type of thief. When: a series of thefts takes only easily carried items. Why: The kind of goods taken points toward a kind of thief.
- [procedure] 1) Offer a promise of no prosecution in exchange for information. 2) Name a price for the stolen items. 3) Use the agreement to learn where the goods are held. When: Stolen property is held by a third party such as a receiver. Why: A deal gives a holder of stolen goods reason to disclose their location.
- [procedure] 1) List everyone told the object existed. 2) Add household members deliberately kept ignorant, since they are still inside the house. 3) Add anyone who could have received the knowledge through an informant.
- [procedure] 1) Establish what was valuable and where it was kept. 2) Identify who knew of the hiding place. 3) Check the financial picture. 4) Note the victim's routines and who watched them. When: A theft is assumed to be the motive but has not been tested.
- [tradeoff] A direct seizure from a dangerous, guarded target risks the taker's life, while a covert swap avoids confrontation but depends on a controlled diversion.
- [pitfall] An unsold stolen item does not prove the theft was pointless; the thief may be waiting for a safe moment to sell. When: When stolen goods have not yet surfaced. Why: Delayed resale is a normal pattern.

## timed reveal design
- [mechanism] A concealed crime seems complete while the witness is gone; a timed visit by authorities can disprove that and force the hidden truth into view. When: a character believes a secret is safe. Why: The visit creates a deadline that the concealment cannot survive.
- [rule] Post a timed notice on a noticeboard or in a newspaper that the player must find on a specific day, linking a name to an identifier found on a body.
- [rule] Let clues degrade or be cleaned up if the player delays too long, so that urgency drives the investigation. When: Designing investigation gameplay with evidence. Why: Time pressure rewards prompt action and makes preservation a meaningful choice.
- [rule] Front-load several unexplained details in the setup, then resolve them together in one explanatory reveal so the payoff recontextualises all of them at once. When: Writing a mystery with multiple clues that must pay off at the climax. Why: A single reveal that explains many earlier clues feels fair and satisfying, while scattered explanations weaken the payoff.
- [heuristic] Anchor a timeline players can verify with time-stamped sounds, device events or timed notes left at the scene, so events can be dated fairly. When: When building event sequences or when an event's timing is central to a mystery. Why: Anchored times let players check claims against one another and reason from a fair chronology.
- [heuristic] Contradictions between witnesses' timing claims, or between stated times and game logs, can fix when an event occurred, so an earlier false report changes meaning.
- [heuristic] Use mail, notes or messengers as timed clue carriers with fixed travel delays, so players can plan around each arrival. When: When designing clue delivery in a narrative or quest. Why: Predictable delivery times let players anticipate and act before the next event.
- [heuristic] Give the player a later event that answers the open question, so time itself becomes part of the reveal. When: an answer cannot come from argument alone. Why: later events can settle what reasoning cannot.
- [heuristic] Hold a key accusation or reveal until a set trigger, such as a scripted hearing scene, instead of disclosing it early.
- [procedure] 1) Show a status cue first, such as an empty vehicle arriving. 2) Follow with an audio cue. 3) Reveal the location last.
- [procedure] 1) Log each action in a separate record in the order it happened. 2) Present the full sequence afterwards from that record. 3) Keep every clue in the record so the reveal can be checked. When: A complex sequence of events must be revealed clearly and fairly. Why: A time-ordered record lets the audience verify the reasoning against the clues.
- [metric] In one layered structure, the identity reveal falls near 60 percent through the story, the confession near 80 percent and the final reveal near 95 percent. When: placing reveals in a long narrative with two late twists.
- [metric] A tale's sections roughly fall at: hook 2-11%, testimony 11-24%, planted anomaly 24-37%, false solution 37-54%, crisis 54-71%, reveal 71-89%, aftermath 89-98%. When: pacing a mystery of single-narrator length.
- [pitfall] A timing claim placed just before a critical hour carries extra weight, so a staged statement is easy to build around the moment that matters. When: When a witness's timing claim falls directly before a decisive event. Why: The claim is positioned to cover the critical moment rather than to record it.
- [pitfall] A reveal that depends on staging, such as darkness hiding reactions, fails if the explanation does not follow promptly, because the audience sees only the result. When: Designing a dramatic reveal. Why: Audiences need the reasoning to accompany the spectacle.

## trace-based reasoning
- [model] An unknown culprit can be identified from small objects and habits, with each trace weighed for what it implies about the person who left it. When: The culprit is unknown and several small objects at the scene may share one source. Why: Converging minor traces can narrow a large suspect pool to one person.
- [rule] Let a clue carry a traceable source, such as a page number or printed text, that players can match to a specific book in the world.
- [rule] Give a missing NPC or closed door at least two plausible causes so players must choose which to test.
- [rule] Judge a trace against its setting: a smear that fits the wrong context is itself a clue. When: a residue or mark appears in an unexpected place. Why: context mismatch signals a different source.
- [heuristic] A physical trace becomes evidence only after it is checked against weather, measurements, and timing; an unchecked trace is only a suggestion. When: when interpreting prints, marks, or other residue at a scene. Why: environmental conditions determine whether a trace could have formed when claimed.
- [procedure] 1) List each small trace and witness report. 2) Assign each one checkable cause. 3) Chain the causes into a candidate sequence of events. 4) Test each link against independent evidence, including the subject's own account. 5) Keep untested links labelled as hypotheses. When: a stranger arrives with several small traces, or events must be reconstructed from physical traces and witness reports. Why: each cause can be checked, and the subject's account tests the whole chain. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Ask the same question of each record. 2) Collect the answers into one list. 3) Look for a common beneficiary across entries. 4) Treat the result as direction, not proof of who ordered each action. When: Evidence is many small records. Why: Consistent questions make entries comparable, and the list reveals where value flows.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the household where an accident victim was taken. 2) Ask about the time, the vehicle and any visitors. When: A person is involved in a roadside accident.
- [procedure] 1) List each odd sensation a witness reports. 2) Assign each a mundane cause, such as a hidden person or a moved object. 3) Treat anything resisting mundane explanation as a possible real anomaly, not as dismissed. When: a witness's account contains an apparent anomaly.
- [pitfall] A pronoun slip or a missing stop may have an innocent cause, so each should be treated as a lead to test, not as proof.
- [pitfall] Treating a trace only as a record of position misses what it implies about sequence and events. When: Interpreting physical evidence. Why: A single mark can carry more than one fact.
- [fact] Changes after an event mark where things happened but do not show what happened; a place can look trivial once ordinary life has moved in. When: revisiting a disturbed scene.
- [fact] A trace consistent with poisoning can coexist with death from natural causes, so the trace alone may settle nothing about the cause. When: When a trace suggests a harmful substance. Why: Presence of a substance does not establish it caused the death.
- [fact] Ordinary crimes leave traces in rough edges and small inconsistencies; a botched act leaves them everywhere.
- [fact] Dropped objects, witness sightings and the physical state of a body can each serve as a link in a chain of traces that reconstructs events.

## witness testimony scope
- [mechanism] Witnesses at stations and on trains notice more than they intend, and their partial accounts combine into a picture of a pursuer's movements. When: a pursuer moves through public places. Why: incidental observers record details without knowing they matter.
- [rule] Count a witness's observations as evidence only after separating them from inferences, labeling theories as opinion, and checking them against other accounts and tests. When: Recording or weighing a witness statement. Why: Sincere witnesses can be wrong about cause, and keeping observation apart from opinion keeps testimony credible.
- [rule] Keep a witness to what they actually witnessed, and do not let them draw others into the account or do the work of proof for the listener.
- [rule] Treat a witness-only account as a lead to investigate, not as proof of guilt. When: when the only evidence is a claim perceived by one person.
- [heuristic] Give each NPC witness a different partial slice, such as a gesture, cloak color, or carried item, so players combine fragments and weigh them against physical traces. When: Designing NPC testimony in a game. Why: Combining fragments makes the player reason toward identity rather than receive it; partial, conflicting knowledge makes players investigate instead of accepting one account.
- [heuristic] A witness's independence depends on their actual views and conditions for taking part, not on the role they nominally hold. Why: Position alone does not show whether a witness holds a separate opinion.
- [heuristic] A witness may report who gave an instruction without knowing the identity of the instruction's author, so do not assume the witness saw the culprit. When: relying on a witness account to identify a culprit. Why: Witnesses often hear instructions without seeing the person behind them.
- [heuristic] A witness is usually more reliable about her own actions and thoughts than about other people's motives or characters. When: Weighing a witness's account.
- [heuristic] Record a witness's own limits, such as absences, scruples and reliance on others, when weighing how much of their account to trust.
- [heuristic] Give witnesses two kinds of testimony: precise, cross-checkable facts and vague impressions that fit several suspects. When: when designing NPC testimony for deduction. Why: Precise facts allow verification, while vague impressions create ambiguity.
- [procedure] 1) Ask each witness what they remember exactly. 2) Ask whether they remember the gist or the exact words. 3) Record which parts they can vouch for and which they cannot. When: when taking testimony about a conversation. Why: a witness may vouch for only part of an account, and the gaps must be recorded.
- [procedure] 1) Plant early a detail about the key object that reads as routine. 2) Present witness accounts that contradict each other on where a character went. 3) Make each account checkable against physical evidence. 4) Reveal the culprit when the contradictions are stacked. When: Building a late-stage reveal in a mystery. Why: Checkable contradictions let the player reconstruct the truth themselves, and routine early details become meaningful in hindsight.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness to state their own position at the time of the event. 2) Ask who else was nearby and where objects were left. 3) Reconstruct the scene from the answers and check it against the evidence. When: Building a reconstruction of an event from a witness's account. Why: A witness's own position and surroundings constrain what they could have seen or done.
- [pitfall] A sincere, accurate witness can still mislead, because a sighting records what happened in one moment and not why it happened. When: A single confident witness anchors the case. Why: A sighting captures the event but not the motive or context behind it.
- [fact] Witnesses present during a fit can attest only to the words and convulsions they saw, not to the unseen apparition the speaker described.

## world lore and folklore
- [behavior] Local tradition tends to lose details such as who owned a place while keeping the story of the place itself, which survives longer within a family. When: when an account has been passed down for more than a century. Why: Stories tied to emotional or family memory are retained better than administrative facts.
- [rule] Treat oral tradition as useful but uncertain; never use it as sole proof, and corroborate it with other clues or later documents. When: when designing local lore or NPC testimony in a game, or when tradition is the main basis for a claim about a place or event. Why: players weigh unverified sources instead of accepting them outright; retold accounts drift and need corroboration.
- [rule] Seed generated lore with legends of old feuds that are partly false, and let the player find the true origin through records. When: when generating background lore.
- [rule] Plant a previous unsolved incident in a world's history that shares a trap signature with a current one, so players who research it can infer a copycat or red herring. When: Building backstory for a mystery in a generated world. Why: Historical parallels give players a line of inference.
- [heuristic] Give one partial clue, such as a disturbed chair or a fragment with partial details, and leave its cause or the remaining details for the player to infer or find elsewhere. When: when designing unsettling rooms, or message and note clues. Why: the player completes the picture; exploration completes the clue.
- [heuristic] Place rare lore needed to use a trap, lock, or potion in one book or with one NPC, so the method becomes a clue to who set it. When: Designing a dungeon element whose use requires specialised knowledge. Why: Limiting the lore's source makes the method's user traceable.
- [heuristic] Leave some cache contents unknown so the player must decide whether the cache matters to the plot. When: Designing caches tied to plot decisions. Why: Uncertainty about contents creates a choice about the cache's importance.
- [heuristic] Keep tradition and rumor shaped by local pride or jealousy separate from records written at the time. When: Local stories are used as evidence. Why: Interest can color oral accounts.
- [heuristic] Explain an odd custom in human terms, such as burial rites or inheritance rules, so that an uncanny location feels grounded. When: when writing lore for an unusual place or custom. Why: a human basis makes a strange custom credible and understandable.
- [heuristic] Establish the world's governing explanation before the case clues, so later evidence feels pre-explained. When: scripting a mystery or trial. Why: Players then interpret each clue within the frame the designer chose.
- [procedure] 1) List each uncanny claim. 2) Test whether a human motive, such as grief, withdrawal or devotion, explains it. 3) Keep only the claims no human motive covers. When: when a rumour mixes ordinary and supernatural claims. Why: most claims often have a mundane cause, leaving few that need the uncanny.
- [pitfall] Long-lived oral tradition can be persistent yet unverifiable; record it as tradition rather than established fact. Why: persistence across generations does not confirm an event.
- [pitfall] Oral tradition about a celebration is less reliable than recorded acts, so do not build conclusions on it alone.
- [fact] Oral tradition mixes fact with rumour and fable, and dates or causes shift on each retelling; sifting them is slow and may not begin until after the account is written. (x2)
- [fact] A feud that was never written down survives only in oral tradition, so its motive rests on retelling rather than documents.

## admissions and reassurance
- [mechanism] Withdrawing a confession can bring renewed or harsher custody, since a court may respond to a retraction by tightening custody, risking liberty and life. When: a confessor is already in custody or retracts after pressure. Why: the retraction exposes the person to harsher punishment, so withdrawing a confession takes great resolve.
- [mechanism] Reassuring text placed beside an unexplained threat makes the threat more unsettling, not less.
- [rule] Offer a reason to cooperate, such as a warning of consequences or a favourable word, but never promise protection the questioner cannot provide. When: a witness must be persuaded to speak. Why: The method works only if the witness believes the offer.
