- [rule] When a suspicion is shown to a witness, reassure them that the disclosure stays private, or they may stop talking. When: A witness has been confronted with a suspicion they fear. Why: Fear of exposure can make the witness withdraw the moment their secret is named.
- [rule] In dialogue puzzles with two-reading lines, let players re-ask the NPC with the exact line to hear the speaker's explanation. When: when a line can be read two ways.
- [rule] Let a later recantation reopen a closed case by exposing the pressure behind the original confession.
- [rule] Let a witness recant when confronted with a prior statement, and reward players who keep records of what each NPC said. When: designing witness confrontations in a mystery.
- [rule] Use a recording or hidden device to turn suspicion into an admission the accused cannot deny. When: when a suspect must be confronted with evidence of a plot. Why: A recorded admission removes the accused's ability to dispute the accusation.
- [heuristic] Do not judge denials by manner: calm, reassuring answers can make a question seem settled, and stout or sharp denials are easily misread as guilt. When: when assessing a suspect's denial during questioning. Why: composure can substitute for evidence; tone and demeanor are weak indicators, and treating them as evidence of guilt tends to convict the innocent. (x2)
- [heuristic] Reassurance after pressure draws out admissions more reliably than pressure alone. When: When a witness has become guarded or distressed. Why: Pressure alone can shut down cooperation.
- [heuristic] Repeated reassurance and claims of acting without counsel often signal what the writer is anxious about.
- [procedure] 1) Record the speaker's exact words. 2) Note what question or pressure prompted them. 3) Note who heard them. 4) Check whether the speaker later repeated or denied them. When: Interpreting a recorded statement that may count as an admission. Why: The same words can mean guilt, bravado or distress depending on context and listener.
- [pitfall] Taking a reassuring first sentence as the author's position while the operative clauses say otherwise. Why: Readers stop at the opening and miss the clauses that decide the outcome.
- [pitfall] Accepting a general claim of good health or a clarifying story without particulars or confirmation can mislead an investigation. When: When a witness offers reassurance rather than specifics. Why: General claims cannot be tested.

## bribery and bought testimony
- [mechanism] Payment can buy only partial information from an informant, so the player may need several sources to complete the picture. When: A game NPC sells information. Why: Paid information is limited in scope.
- [mechanism] A confirmed bribe shows that an alibi was false, but it does not establish that the alibi-holder committed the crime. When: When an alibi is revealed to have been bought or coerced. Why: A false alibi proves a lie, not the identity of the culprit.
- [mechanism] A witness who was paid to keep quiet may feel insulted by the payment, and that resentment can turn the bargain into a threat that loosens the silence. When: When a witness has been bribed to stay silent and feels underpaid or demeaned. Why: Wounded pride and grievance over the payment can drive the witness to confess.
- [mechanism] A secret held by one person can leak to another under pressure, but the leak alone does not prove the source is guilty. When: A character is confronted and reveals information. Why: The disclosure may be coerced rather than voluntary.
- [mechanism] A suspect who pays or befriends a witness before questioning can shape what that witness later says, so the account reflects the people who will be asked about it. When: A witness's testimony will decide the outcome and the witness has an incentive to be unhelpful. Why: Goodwill and payment give the witness a reason to confirm the suspect's version.
- [behavior] A witness who wants a deal shows it through physical cues, such as touching an object and a change in facial expression, that signal the offer has landed. When: An offer is made during an interrogation. Why: A tempting offer produces involuntary reactions before words are spoken.
- [behavior] A suspect who moves from defiance to requesting specific terms reveals exactly what he is trying to protect. When: during confrontation. Why: concrete demands expose priorities.
- [behavior] Bribery fails with witnesses whose loyalty to a leader outweighs money, so offers work better on those with weaker loyalty.
- [behavior] A bribe offered to a suspect signals how much the offerer values the matter and hints at what they know; the size of the offer is evidence. When: A character offers money to keep a matter quiet. Why: No one pays heavily over a trivial matter, so a large offer implies high stakes.
- [rule] Use a friendly or bribed non-player character as a plot lever that the player must find and test. When: Designing hidden allies or informants. Why: A compromised witness creates a discoverable but risky source.
- [rule] Give NPC bribes or deals an unusually broad clause so that a player who notices it gains a motive clue without a confession. When: Designing NPC offers in investigation games. Why: Lets motive be inferred from wording rather than stated outright.
- [heuristic] An offered bribe during questioning signals the witness's fear and motive. When: A witness offers money to avoid questioning. Why: Attempts to buy silence reveal that the witness has something to hide.
- [procedure] 1) Offer a reward for a specific identifying detail. 2) Gather testimony from many sources. 3) Cross-check the accounts against each other before acting. When: Searching for an unidentified person. Why: A targeted reward drives collection of usable testimony.
- [pitfall] Testimony obtained through money or favour needs caution; a suspect's assurance that a witness will stay quiet proves nothing, and purchased silence can be bought again.

## confession as proof
- [mechanism] A suspect who retells events as fiction often leaks real facts, since invented details draw on memory and real names, objects and sequences slip into the story. When: A suspect talks freely about a fictional or hypothetical case while avoiding direct questions. Why: Storytelling draws on actual memory, so true details surface even when the teller intends to conceal them.
- [behavior] A suspect may change an answer after being reminded of a prior warning or pressed by a steady look, so a sudden confession can follow pressure. When: an interrogation scene where a suspect first denies a charge. Why: reminders and pressure can shift a stated answer.
- [behavior] Confessions made under torment are read as proof of guilt by the system, though they may later be retracted. When: A coercive investigation relies on confessions to close cases. Why: The system values confession as closure and does not weigh how it was obtained.
- [rule] Design an NPC confession so the player's assumptions about allies and threats are tested, and let a suspect seen as a threat clear the others. When: Designing a reveal that changes trust. Why: Reversing suspicion makes the reveal a mechanic that changes how the player reads the cast.
- [rule] Let a captured antagonist's confession explain the past, but keep at least one present-tense fact the player must verify.
- [rule] Treat a confession as a fact that can be reinterpreted, not as the end of the mystery.
- [heuristic] Have the culprit or a substitute confirm the twist, backed by physical proof; a confession with proof lands harder than a late deduction alone and leaves no room to deny. When: when resolving a case with a suspect who might dispute the evidence. Why: An object cannot be disputed, so the reveal feels settled and the suspect has nothing to contest. (x2)
- [heuristic] Let an NPC's confession unlock the next layer of a reveal rather than the player's deduction alone.
- [heuristic] Check when a confession arrives; one timed just after a disruption subsides suggests management of the scene rather than spontaneous truth. When: a confession follows a disturbance. Why: Timing reveals who controlled the scene.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a harmless official pretext that avoids the central subject. 2) Have the relevant person present. 3) Raise the subject while they are there. 4) Arrange backup in advance. 5) Once they are cornered, secure a full confession. When: No eyewitness exists and physical proof is weak. Why: Surprise and a prepared setting make a slip more likely, and backup secures the result.
- [procedure] 1) Have a hidden character explain their motive and history. 2) Use that explanation as the proof that closes the case. 3) Keep the confession tied to the earlier clues. When: resolving a mystery that depends on a hidden character's past. Why: A single confession can carry motive, history and proof together, making the resolution feel earned.
- [tradeoff] A culprit's self-confession can close the case and deliver a reversal when no decisive proof or checkable location exists, but the reader must trust the speaker's word. When: when the investigation has no decisive physical proof or the hidden location cannot be checked. Why: The culprit's own words close the case.
- [pitfall] A confession carries its own motive, so the confessor may frame events to appear driven or justified, and the account cannot be taken as neutral. When: Evaluating a confessor's account. Why: Confessors shape their story to protect themselves or justify actions.
- [pitfall] A promise extracted under pressure may later be used to control the person who made it. When: when a character has given a promise under pressure. Why: The promise becomes a lever over the promisor.

## confirming before acting
- [mechanism] A message arriving mid-scene that confirms a player's hunch rewards inference, because the player reached the conclusion first and the message only verifies it. When: when a scene is designed to reward deduction. Why: confirmation feels earned when the player has already guessed.
- [rule] Confirm a heard or recalled remark before relying on it by asking the speaker to verify the exact wording, since remarks are often misremembered. When: a key word was heard in a stressful or chaotic moment, or a remark is recalled.
- [rule] Confirm a fact only with two or more independent observers or sources, especially one deciding whether an item was consumed; revise the working theory only after such confirmation. When: a new fact rests on a single secondhand claim. Why: A single memory is fragile and easy to distort.
- [rule] Treat stated plans and claimed errands as claims to be confirmed, not as established movements. Why: A stated plan shows intent, not what was actually done.
- [rule] Confirm a physical match before confronting a suspect, because a confirmed match turns a theory into a checked fact.
- [rule] Agree a signal in advance, such as a lit match, so that a watcher can confirm the target has acted. When: Covert observers must report a hidden party's action without contact. Why: A prearranged signal conveys a specific result without requiring communication.
- [rule] Confirm a reading of habit-based traces with witnesses who know the routines, since interpretation depends on that knowledge.
- [rule] Do not assume a path without evidence; confirm the traces before they settle the question of where the crime occurred. When: A route seems plausible but is unverified. Why: Plausible routes can be wrong when the traces are not checked.
- [rule] Confirm the final solution with a witnessed document and a private confrontation, not a public accusation. Why: A witnessed statement is hard to dispute, and a private setting lets the culprit admit the truth.
- [heuristic] Hold action until one decisive confirming fact is found when evidence points one way but lacks confirmation, since acting early risks exposing the plan or failing. When: a case rests on circumstantial points and a conclusive fact may still emerge, or a suspicion exists but acting early would warn an opponent. Why: A decisive fact resolves uncertainty that the tally cannot.
- [heuristic] Confirm a surprising observation by looking again under the same conditions before relying on it as evidence.
- [heuristic] Before drawing conclusions from two similar sets of tracks, confirm the direction of each set. When: Track sets look alike. Why: Similar marks can belong to different movements.
- [tradeoff] Acting now on partial evidence risks a wrong move; waiting risks losing the window in which evidence stays available. When: Deciding whether to act on partial evidence or gather more. Why: Some evidence decays over time while some errors can be corrected later.
- [pitfall] A witness may confirm a fact just to end an interview, so the answer may reflect a reaction to pressure rather than a real recollection. When: a witness is pressed or wants to leave. Why: agreement is a quick way out of an uncomfortable exchange.

## crime scene staging
- [mechanism] A grave may hold a planted corpse standing in for the intended victim, so exhuming it can expose the substitution and the plot behind it. When: A burial or funeral appears to mark a known death. Why: A body in a grave is usually taken as proof of death.
- [mechanism] Each added precaution taken to hide an act adds a trace someone can later examine, so extra care can itself cause detection.
- [behavior] A person may remove labels or empty bottles to keep others from blame, which alters the physical record of a death before anyone examines it.
- [rule] Leave objects in place so the scene can be read as it was, and do not disturb evidence before it is examined.
- [rule] Stage the final proof so it is performed in front of the culprit, not only described afterward. When: writing the climax of a mystery. Why: A proof the audience watches happen is more convincing than a proof reported after the fact.
- [rule] Give the first theory a physical prop that later reads as staged, so the obvious suspect seems guilty until the prop is reinterpreted. When: building an early false suspicion. Why: A prop that seems to prove guilt is later shown to have been placed.
- [heuristic] Use a plausible, harmless role or pretext when direct questions would alert a suspect or make staff guarded. When: When an investigator needs information from people who would refuse formal questioning. Why: A non-threatening cover gets people talking and opens doors that stay shut under direct questioning.
- [heuristic] Preparatory acts made before a delayed event, such as protective measures taken shortly before, can reveal that the act was planned. When: Investigating a delayed or planned harmful act. Why: Advance preparation shows the agent anticipated the outcome.
- [heuristic] Keep physical proof separate from early assertions, so players must search the world for it rather than accept the claims. When: when a claim needs verification. Why: found evidence feels more authoritative than stated claims.
- [heuristic] Stage a reveal as a sequence of partial proofs, each confirming one suspicion without giving the full truth. When: Building a multi-step mystery. Why: Each partial proof keeps tension while the complete picture is held back.
- [heuristic] Keep the detective's private preparation visible but unexplained so that its later use feels earned. When: Introducing a protagonist's hidden work early in a story. Why: Visible but unexplained preparation rewards the player when it pays off.
- [heuristic] Build the opposing case complete on paper, so the protagonist's doubt, not a hole in the evidence, drives the story. Why: A convincing case forces the solver to find a deeper flaw.
- [procedure] 1) Move the obstacle without disturbing the trace. 2) Lift the trace with careful fingers and avoid crushing it. 3) Unfold it gently so that surface residue such as dust stays in place. When: Recovering a small fragile piece of evidence. Why: Handling that preserves residue keeps the trace a record of where it lay.
- [fact] Excess precaution is often cited as a cause of detection, but the claim is drawn only from detected cases and cannot estimate how often precautions succeed.

## deferred and delayed reveals
- [model] A delayed frame reveals an arrival's identity and motive first, and only later reveals the true direction or mechanics of the events that brought it.
- [mechanism] Withholding what is seen, and letting light or argument change over time, builds suspense before the reveal arrives. When: Designing a scene that builds toward a reveal. Why: Uncertainty about what is present keeps the audience engaged until the reveal pays off.
- [mechanism] A lost interval that the protagonist explains away as a dream can hide a deed, so the reader treats the gap as harmless until physical traces contradict the explanation.
- [mechanism] A device left under a door latch after the culprit exits can make a room look sealed from inside, creating a false alibi for the moment of death.
- [behavior] A visible change in manner tends to fade over time as the person's habitual pattern returns. When: When a suspect's unusual behavior is observed across an extended period. Why: Sustaining a concealing manner is effortful, so habits gradually reassert themselves.
- [heuristic] Let players trust a document for a long stretch before undercutting it, so the reversal changes meaning rather than just adding information. When: when planning a late reversal of a settled belief. Why: a belief held long enough makes its overturning a shift in understanding.
- [heuristic] Show a premise clue early as trivial; it can later become a key piece of evidence once its context is revealed.
- [heuristic] Let the investigator defer accusation and let the staging show itself, so the proof is visible rather than asserted. When: writing the final confrontation. Why: Visible proof persuades more than a direct charge.
- [tradeoff] A deferred offer buys time, but if the target takes it seriously it creates an obligation that is hard to withdraw; use it only when the offer can be cancelled. When: when using a fake or conditional offer to delay someone. Why: Accepted offers create commitments that the offering side cannot easily undo.
- [pitfall] A confident, detailed witness is not necessarily accurate; detail can coexist with inference, bias, or repeated hearsay. When: When judging a witness's reliability. Why: Confidence and detail do not establish that the observation was firsthand.
- [pitfall] Labelling a strange event as a trick can dismiss a real unexplained detail that the trick does not account for. When: Explaining away an event as a prank. Why: A single explanation may cover only part of the evidence, leaving some details unresolved.
- [pitfall] Delaying an explanation too long confuses the audience when the scene depends on its logic to follow. When: The climax needs the logic to be understood.
- [pitfall] When a narrator labels a character's remark as superstition, readers may discount the remark entirely, even if it later proves meaningful. When: An omen is voiced by a character marked as superstitious. Why: The label signals the remark is unreliable, so the audience ignores it.
- [pitfall] Accepting a deferred meeting wastes time and may let the witness be warned or prepared, while social settings add people who shape the answers. When: A witness can only be reached at a later scheduled event. Why: Delay gives the witness time to prepare and brings in other voices.

## document delivery and access
- [rule] Record and honour a party's request about who receives a copy of a document, rather than routing it by default. When: Handling copies of agreements for interested parties.
- [rule] Record the bait announcement in writing and have it signed, so the bait itself becomes a documented step.
- [rule] Ask how a document reached its holder; the delivery route can be as informative as the document's content.
- [rule] Give an in-game note checkable requirements, such as knowledge of a password, access to a machine or a specific material, so the player can deduce the author by elimination. When: when designing a letter or note that identifies its author.
- [rule] When a lock must be forced, do it in front of witnesses so the opening is observed and documented.
- [rule] Give each in-game document its own gaps and bias, so cross-checking produces a different picture than any single file.
- [rule] Require the player to gain permission or a ruling before a sensitive document can be used as evidence. When: Designing a document that is contested or private. Why: A gate adds a step that delays the reveal and raises stakes.
- [heuristic] Confront a suspect with documents or objects from their possession so they must account for each, and watch for manner shifts revealing knowledge of contents they claimed not to know. When: When a suspect holds case-linked items or may recognise a document they claim not to know.
- [heuristic] An NPC who offers a written statement can carry false information, which the player must verify against objects in the scene. When: Designing NPC-provided documents. Why: Written testimony should be checkable against the world.
- [heuristic] Use official notices, letters or bounty bills that look like they concern the main case but resolve into a side quest.
- [heuristic] When the audience cannot judge written documents, handle letters and records carefully and rely on clearer forms of evidence. When: Presenting written evidence to readers or listeners with limited literacy or expertise. Why: Audiences that cannot evaluate documents may misjudge their weight.
- [pitfall] A search of documents may fail to answer the question at all, so plan a second line of inquiry rather than relying on one archive.
- [fact] A document kept by one party can threaten another if a single accident puts it in the wrong hands. When: when a secret record is kept by someone with a conflicting interest. Why: Exposure risk depends on who can reach the record.
- [fact] A document can be presented to a court long after it was written, so its writing date and its filing date must be tracked separately.

## gifts and favours
- [mechanism] Routing a gift through an intermediary while keeping the giver unnamed lets the giver gain hidden influence over the recipients. When: Modelling patronage or faction influence through gifts. Why: The recipient does not know the source, so gratitude and control are not directed to the giver.
- [behavior] Hospitality, gifts and favours from a powerful host can be an attempt to buy goodwill, revealing what standing the host wants to secure. When: a host offers gifts or advice to a visitor. Why: goodwill can serve as a bid for influence.
- [rule] Let an NPC's offer of gifts, safe passage or shelter carry a hidden condition the player can discover later.
- [rule] Use a generous-seeming offer as a red herring, and let the player test it against another NPC's warnings.
- [rule] Record a favour given to an informant as a cost that affects later dialogue with that informant. When: Designing information trades with NPCs. Why: Recorded costs make reciprocity have lasting consequences on relationships.
- [heuristic] A courier chosen for discretion, and unable to read, keeps message contents hidden even under questioning, though she still knows where she went. When: when a message must be carried without revealing its content. Why: Inability to read removes the content from her knowledge.
- [heuristic] A gift that the recipient is unlikely to use can be a plant, so an unusual gift is worth reading as a clue. When: when a crime seems prepared in advance. Why: an odd choice of gift can serve a hidden purpose.
- [pitfall] Generous or friendly behaviour, especially when given publicly, does not establish innocence; it can frame self-interest as disinterest and lower others' guard. When: a character offers gifts or favours, especially publicly while holding a private aim. Why: kindness can be a tool for pursuing a hidden aim, and visible kindness lowers others' guard.
- [pitfall] A favoured reading may fail to explain parts of the evidence, so check the preferred reading against the facts it cannot explain.
- [pitfall] A will favoring one person can be read as motive while another real beneficiary of other arrangements goes unnoticed.
- [pitfall] Allowing a generous margin for travel time can hide how early a suspect could have left, so estimates should use realistic speeds. Why: padding travel time shifts the apparent earliest departure.
- [pitfall] A favour granted to a contact can be remembered as a debt that may cost the investigator later.
- [pitfall] Treating a gift as proof of guilt is an error, because a gift can explain a trace without implicating the giver. When: a trace came from a gift. Why: The giver may have had no part in the act.
- [pitfall] A promise of reciprocity makes an informant's account look more useful than it is. When: An informant offers information in exchange for a favour. Why: The expectation of return inflates the perceived value of the information.

## hedged testimony and phrasing
- [mechanism] Track hedging words such as 'maybe' or 'appears' as dialogue flags or branches; hesitant or hedged replies unlock follow-up lines or leads the player can later expose. When: designing dialogue systems.
- [behavior] Witnesses leak views via hedges, qualifiers, tone and indirect phrasing even when content sounds innocent, such as implying someone else disagrees; treat it as a clue. When: Listening to a witness who gives a qualified, unusually framed or indirect statement. Why: Speakers often leak implications through hedges and manner; restraint leaves a trace in phrasing that reveals a view they would not state outright. (x2)
- [behavior] A listener who hears a speaker hedge after a promise may read the hedge as concealment and suspect that something is being held back.
- [rule] Mark interpretations as guesses with hedges such as 'probably' or 'seems'; read hedged claims as impressions, not verified facts, until other evidence confirms them. When: reasoning from partial evidence. Why: an inference can look like fact once stated.
- [rule] Let a forensic NPC give a hedged diagnosis that the player can firm up only by asking the right follow-up questions. When: Designing a forensic-style NPC. Why: Follow-up questions reveal how much the expert actually knows.
- [rule] Let players notice hedged or indirect dialogue as a clue, and reward them for weighing it against the speaker's position. When: Designing dialogue that hides information. Why: Rewarding inference makes indirect speech a playable clue rather than noise.
- [heuristic] Record a witness's hedged identification, such as 'might have been', or sighting as uncertainty: weak alone, neither discarded nor firm, but usable as a lead to pursue. When: when a witness is unsure of an identity or sighting. Why: uncertainty limits evidential value.
- [heuristic] Weigh hedged witness claims such as 'almost sure' or 'not certain' lower than firm ones, judging them by specificity and agreement with other evidence. When: recording witness claims. Why: hedges reflect the witness's own confidence.
- [heuristic] Hedged or vague answers, such as a 'figure of speech', are weak and mark where to press with specific follow-up; make NPC hedging a visible cue to the next answer. Why: Visible hesitation tells players where to continue questioning.
- [heuristic] State conclusions from physical traces or traits, such as a profile, as hypotheses or likelihoods, since one trace rarely settles a question; say plainly what cannot be known. When: Physical evidence supports an inference. Why: Traces support probability more than proof.
- [heuristic] Give NPC witnesses a mix of hedged and flatly contradicted statements, so the player must check each against logs and other sources. When: Designing testimony in a game investigation.
- [heuristic] Give NPC witnesses confidence levels tied to how much they observed, so a partial glimpse yields a hedged statement. When: designing witness dialogue. Why: Confidence should track the quality of the observation.
- [heuristic] Treat a physician's guarded readings as limited evidence, since experts may hedge to avoid committing to a conclusion. When: when a medical opinion is non-committal. Why: hedging avoids overclaiming.
- [pitfall] Turning a hedged statement such as 'probably right' into a fixed fact about a faulty source corrupts any timeline built on it.

## hidden identity
- [model] A mystery built on two swapped identities, where the victim and the person present are both misidentified, so the solution reverses who died and who was there. When: designing a murder whose key error is identity. Why: Reversing both identities at once doubles the reframing of the evidence.
- [model] A mystery can separate the letter-writer, the intruder, the disguised ally and the killer as distinct identities, so the expected controlling figure can be absent from the scene. When: designing a mystery with a planner or threat figure. Why: Keeping roles separate lets the reader's assumption about who is in control fail when the planner never appears.
- [mechanism] A disguised ally's true identity can be revealed fairly if the physical proof, such as a planted card or plate, has been set up early and recurs. When: a late reveal depends on an object the reader has already seen. Why: Planted and repeated clues make the reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [rule] In an infiltration plot, hide the protagonist's real allegiance in dialogue until the trap room, then drop the disguise and disarm enemies.
- [heuristic] If two apparent people are never seen together and one appears only when the other is away, suspect they are the same person in disguise. When: Witness sightings show a pattern of alternation. Why: Mutually exclusive appearances suggest one person changing appearance.
- [heuristic] Hide a late motive in a document the player can read, so the final reveal feels earned rather than invented. When: planning a mystery's final motive. Why: A motive the player could have read earlier makes the reveal a recognition.
- [heuristic] A harmless-seeming character can be a hidden protagonist; show the disguise on the page, then disclose the identity in dialogue afterward. Why: A disguise visible on the page makes the later disclosure fair.
- [heuristic] Keep the accuser's grudge off-page until late; a credible witness whose motive is hidden can become the real suspect. When: designing a witness twist. Why: The revealed motive reframes the witness.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the formal record that the hidden party touched. 2) Find the clerk or official who handled it. 3) Trace the people connected to that official. 4) Follow an intermediary link to the party who made the request. When: A hidden actor's identity must be recovered from a logged action. Why: Indirect ties often reveal a name the direct record hides.
- [procedure] 1) Search records for the person's past under any false name. 2) Identify associates who recognise the person. 3) Link past events, such as old thefts or sentences, to the attackers. When: A person is attacked and the real identity or motive is unknown. Why: Records and associates reveal a real identity that a false name conceals, and link it to the motive.
- [procedure] 1) Link incidents that share a thread. 2) Follow each link upward through its agents. 3) Stop when the chain reaches one controlling figure. When: When tracing a conspiracy to its planner.
- [procedure] 1) Examine every possession of an unidentified person, including inside and both sides of objects. 2) Review papers for any name. 3) If no name appears, ask whether anyone came looking for the person. When: An unidentified person is connected to a scene. Why: Belongings and visitor questions can narrow the search even without a name.
- [pitfall] Two names do not prove two people, since a fictitious identity can be made to look real.
- [fact] Twins share a resemblance that makes a swap of identity easier to believe. When: A plot involves a substitution between related people. Why: Close family likeness lowers observers' suspicion.

## information control
- [mechanism] Control over who knows a death, when they learn it, and what is opened shapes how others read the death and the people connected to it.
- [mechanism] Staging who learns what and when keeps each person calm and cooperative, and withholds what would make them act rashly. When: An investigator controls what each character knows. Why: Partial or premature knowledge can trigger reactions that damage the investigation.
- [rule] Keep assistants and allies uninformed of covert plans or extra insight, since they may reveal it by look or act. When: Running a covert operation with a helper, or writing an investigator with more insight than the cast. Why: A helper may give the plan away unintentionally; keeping the player ahead sustains suspense. (x2)
- [rule] Agree a visible cue and tell allies to stay quiet, so you control what the public, press and suspects learn and when. When: A trap or investigative plan depends on secrecy. Why: Each leak can warn the culprit or ruin a planned trap.
- [rule] Set a fixed reporting schedule and forbidden zones, and route urgent messages through one channel, so contact stays controlled.
- [rule] Use one instructed spokesperson to relay the false status, since controlled bulletins shape what rivals believe.
- [rule] Let players compare an item against a control set of similar items, so the clue carries meaning only through contrast.
- [rule] Check the answer to a neutral dialogue question against logs or other testimony to measure consistency. When: designing a dialogue-based truthfulness check. Why: a checkable answer lets players judge consistency.
- [rule] Track what has been disclosed in dialogue so later questions and answers stay consistent with earlier ones. When: Designing a dialogue system with ongoing questioning. Why: Inconsistent disclosure breaks the player's trust in the record.
- [heuristic] A written approach to a suspect can confirm that findings exist and who holds them, while keeping the conclusions and reasoning private. When: when a suspect may be warned or may shape a story. Why: Revealing possession of evidence prompts a response without giving the suspect the investigator's reasoning.
- [heuristic] In a feud with several parties and shared assets, who controls a committee or fund often matters more than the stated complaint.
- [procedure] 1) Run the in-world test on a character known to be innocent. 2) If it returns the same guilty result, treat the test as unreliable. 3) Use that failure as a mystery beat or reversal scene. When: designing lie detectors or trap tests in a game. Why: A control exposes tests that cannot distinguish guilt from innocence.
- [pitfall] A staged departure only works if the suspect hears the news through a channel the investigator controls; if that route fails, the deception collapses. When: planning a feint. Why: The false belief depends on the suspect receiving it.
- [pitfall] When the witness starts asking questions, the questioner may be forced to disclose information before intending to, such as confirming a detail under direct questioning. When: A witness turns the questioning around. Why: A direct question can compel an answer the questioner had not planned to give.

## linking clues and incidents
- [behavior] Separate incidents that share an unusual detail, such as a method, object or location, can be seen as unrelated for a long time until a chance remark links them. When: When several incidents occur with a recurring unusual detail. Why: People judge each incident in isolation, so a shared trait stays hidden until someone compares them directly.
- [rule] Do not conclude from one trace alone; connect it with other traces, such as a bracket mark and a rope break, before deciding what happened. When: When a single physical clue seems to explain the whole event. Why: Linked traces support each other, while an isolated trace can mislead.
- [heuristic] Connect separate records or sources sharing people or places; overlaps reveal links no single one states, building a sequence of events, such as a trip abroad before a death. When: when multiple documents or sources mention related people or places. Why: Overlaps between separate accounts expose links no single source states. (x2)
- [heuristic] A chain of linked documents, such as a petition followed by an order to an officer, shows how a decision moved through a chain of command.
- [heuristic] An object in one location that matches the material or style of an object elsewhere can tie their owners together.
- [heuristic] A found object gains evidential weight when it matches a known item from the event; an object with no established link should stay unresolved. When: a button or wrapper is found at a scene. Why: matching evidence to a known source separates relevant items from coincidental debris.
- [heuristic] Recurring signatures across unrelated incidents can reveal a single organizer behind them.
- [heuristic] Repeated incidents that look accidental can be linked through the victim's fixed habits. Compare each incident against the routine rather than accepting it as chance. When: a series of similar incidents keeps being explained as accidents. Why: a fixed routine can be exploited each time.
- [heuristic] Link each trace to a specific owner or item so the player can verify the match directly. When: when designing clues that point to a suspect. Why: a clue tied to a checkable owner can be confirmed or refuted.
- [heuristic] Test a working theory that links several incidents into one plan, but judge each incident on its own evidence. When: when several incidents seem related.
- [heuristic] Link an unfulfilled intention to a suspect by asking who would lose or gain if the planned change had happened.
- [heuristic] A connection between a person and an object shows where to ask next, not who is responsible. When: Before drawing conclusions from a link. Why: Links are leads that need corroboration.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who else could have known the information, to trace how it spread. 2) Collect odd details from each source. 3) Place the details side by side and look for a shared pattern. When: a hidden agent is suspected from scattered traces.
- [pitfall] Two events, such as a dismissal and a missing sum, can look connected when they are not; an unknown detail leaves the link unproven.

## location and exit observation
- [definition] A room with one exit watched by a trusted observer works as a human substitute for a locked room.
- [rule] Do not search a location where physical evidence already excludes the object being sought. Why: Effort is better spent on places still open.
- [rule] Let the decisive evidence come from a location the characters have not yet searched, so the player feels the discovery is earned through exploration. When: Revealing the culprit in a mystery. Why: Discovery in an unsearched place rewards exploration and keeps the reveal plausible.
- [heuristic] Use independent indicators of location, such as lights lit elsewhere, to test a theory that places someone in a particular spot. When: A theory depends on where a person was. Why: Outside evidence can undercut a theory built on the scene alone.
- [heuristic] Use a location that shows the crime's path: objects there connect the body to the scene and to the person who was present.
- [procedure] 1) List the physical traces the visitor left. 2) Estimate height from marks at a reach height. 3) Estimate age and agility from the feats the traces imply. 4) Infer habits from residue left behind. When: An unseen visitor left several small traces. Why: Each trace narrows one trait, so a sketch can be built from many small clues.
- [procedure] 1) Examine the outer boundary first. 2) Record the traces there before entering. 3) Enter afterward, so the traces are recorded before anyone is alerted.
- [procedure] 1) Describe the setting as named places with clear edges. 2) For each place, record who was inside, who passed through, and who would have noticed a stranger. 3) Treat the boundaries as hard limits. 4) Check each witness against the boundaries. When: A person vanishes inside a small, bounded place. Why: Fixed boundaries turn an open-ended disappearance into a finite list of places and people to check.
- [pitfall] A slow entry method can hide an extended presence, so the time it requires must be considered when reconstructing events. When: Reconstructing how long an intruder was active. Why: Slow methods imply the intruder stayed unnoticed for a long period.
- [pitfall] A witness's account of a door is weak until a second source confirms it. When: A door's state is reported by one person. Why: One account can be mistaken or incomplete.
- [pitfall] A surviving cellar or foundation proves a site existed but not who lived there at a given time; pair physical remains with dated documents.
- [pitfall] Matching a real location to a story creates false certainty; several sites may each seem to fit, and none may be the actual model. When: Linking a historical event to a physical place. Why: Partial resemblance is easy to find, so a fit can be coincidental.
- [pitfall] Players who accept a staged location at face value stop reconsidering the premise and miss that the event happened somewhere else.
- [fact] A small craft with few hiding spaces makes concealment hard, so a thorough search is harder to resist. When: when hiding items in a confined space. Why: few hiding places leave little room for concealment.

## movement and route clues
- [mechanism] Suspense builds when a fugitive's escape options are removed one at a time, so each closed route raises the stakes until the last open chance is dangerous. When: when pacing a chase or narrowing sequence. Why: the outcome stays uncertain until the final moment.
- [rule] Rule out a location when required travel and meeting time exceeds the available gap; a short gap of an hour or two can still hide a return trip, so check distances first. Why: Travel time must be compared with the gap, since it can fit inside an apparently small window.
- [rule] When an independent record already fixes a suspect's location at the relevant time, witness-based alibi testing is not needed for that moment.
- [heuristic] Ask indirect questions about spatial facts, since a witness may answer before realising the answer's significance.
- [heuristic] The route a victim chose against a warning is itself a fact to weigh, since it shows the victim's risk tolerance or intent. When: When a victim goes somewhere they were warned against. Why: Choosing a risky route reveals what the victim knew or wanted.
- [procedure] 1) Notice an observable sign that should not be where it is. 2) Ask where it must have come from. 3) Search for the implied route and test it with a second, independent check. When: A route cannot be seen but its traces or carriers can be examined. Why: Tracing a sign back to its source can reveal an unseen passage.
- [pitfall] A signal such as a patterned knock can also be used by others, so it may identify the wrong arrival.
- [pitfall] Assuming a person took the shortest route can miss a less obvious path they actually used.
- [pitfall] Records often lack the later fates of many participants, so a motive trail built from surviving documents may be incomplete.
- [fact] Events driven by a shared tide can occur at nearly the same time across distant sites, differing by minutes rather than hours. When: when sites share one environmental trigger. Why: the trigger is common to all locations.
- [fact] Two sightings placed on a map form a line of travel, which narrows where a party probably went.
- [fact] A hidden route previously used by two characters can be known to both, making a trap through it plausible and letting the player learn the route from history. When: when characters share past use of a concealed passage. Why: prior knowledge of a route makes it available for later use.
- [fact] An index can also link people to places and events, such as a meeting-house or prison, to show where each role occurred.
- [fact] Road and boundary directions change over time, so a deed's compass direction may not match the modern map. When: Reading old deeds against current geography. Why: Landmarks and roads move, altering the meaning of directional descriptions.

## mystery pacing and structure
- [model] Self-contained mystery cases follow a fixed skeleton: puzzling premise or commission with surface story, clues and misdirects, belief-to-truth twist or partial reveal, nested subcase, proof demonstration or trap, resolution. When: Building a series of self-contained mystery cases or short mystery stories. Why: A repeated shape lets players learn the rhythm and predict where misdirects fall, while each case still feels fresh and the audience tracks where the story is heading. (x2)
- [model] Mystery pacing runs in seven bands: hook 0-13%, setup 13-40%, investigation 40-49%, complication 49-68%, false solution 68-86%, crisis and reveal 86-95%, aftermath 95%+. When: structuring a long investigation story. Why: each band has a distinct job in the reveal.
- [model] A mystery plot can be organized as a sequence of gates in which the protagonist is repeatedly denied knowledge, and each refusal turns into a new lead rather than ending the search. When: Designing investigation-driven narratives where the protagonist's access to truth is restricted. Why: Each denial forces a reversal and a new objective, keeping momentum while withholding the answer.
- [model] A mystery can follow a sequence: a hook with conclusive-seeming identifiers, an investigation with a decoy suspect, a complication with a second case, a false public solution, a reveal from a small detail, a crisis where an innocent is committed, and a staged confession. When: When pacing a multi-act mystery with a steered reader. Why: Staged stages move the player from a convenient false theory to the real culprit.
- [model] Mystery plots run in phases: hook, investigation, false solution and reveal, crisis by argument, then a closing twist that reverses the reader's frame. When: Approximate story positions: hook 11-34%, investigation 34-48%, reveal 48-65%, argument crisis 70-89%, twist 98%.
- [model] A mystery's acts run: premise, commission, search, pressure, false solution, complication, crisis and reveal, aftermath. When: outlining an investigation-driven plot. Why: Each act has a distinct job in escalating the search.
- [heuristic] Nest a subcase inside the main investigation so that its resolution overturns the initial solution. When: a mystery needs a second turn after the first answer. Why: A nested case gives the audience a reason to doubt the solution they already accepted.
- [procedure] 1) State the plan's outline and purpose. 2) Keep its method back. 3) Reveal the method only at the payoff. When: A character is explaining a plan to others who need only part of it. Why: Partial disclosure keeps the audience curious while staying honest about the plan.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a hook that links two unexplained scenes. 2) Set up watched figures and fixations. 3) Add a complication that inflates a rivalry. 4) Build pressure toward a crime. 5) Stage a crisis with a missing victim. 6) Lead to a false solution. 7) Shift attention to new investigators. 8) End with a late cluster and an unresolved act. When: Structuring the beats of a mystery plot across its length. Why: Spreading hook, pressure, false solution and open ending across the run keeps suspicion moving.
- [procedure] 1) hook 0-11%: introduce lead and puzzling habits; 2) investigation 11-32%: read clues, set traps; 3) complication 32-47%: wrongful arrest, wider conspiracy; 4) suspect caught 47-55%, motive unknown; 5) backstory 55-67%: past timeline opens; 6) crisis 67-81%: escalation, loss, pursuit; 7) confession 81-97%: full account; 8) aftermath 97-100%: diminished credit.
- [metric] A mystery's beats can be paced by percentage: hook at 2-7%, midpoint crisis at 50-68%, false solution at 75-81%, reveal and aftermath at 88-96%. When: planning a full-length mystery. Why: Spacing beats this way keeps tension rising and places the false solution before the final reveal.
- [metric] Typical mystery timing: setup by 10%, first false solution around 29-42%, reversal 65-79%, trap 79-94%, unmasking in the final 6%.
- [pitfall] Delaying an explanation too long deflates the audience, especially if they have already guessed the cause; a long delay needs a payoff matching the build-up.
- [pitfall] Too many waits or long gaps with no new information drain momentum, and a clue that is teased but never explained feels like a broken promise. When: Pacing a sequence of staged revelations. Why: Tension goes slack without new information, and unpaid teasers erode trust.

## npc dialogue and access
- [behavior] Guarded speech and suspicion of the questioner reveal whom a witness is protecting, such as a debtor or a person they fear to implicate. When: When a witness is reluctant or hostile to a questioner. Why: People shield those they depend on or feel loyalty toward.
- [behavior] Gatekeepers decide who enters, and a silent gatekeeper who asks no questions leaves the visitor unsettled and uninformed. When: A visitor is admitted by staff who do not explain or converse. Why: Silence withholds reassurance and information, increasing the visitor's unease.
- [rule] Gate accusations and confrontation options on facts confirmed through indirect questions or new evidence, or an official pressure event, so suspicion never rests long on one character. When: Designing dialogue branches that depend on prior investigation, or when several characters could plausibly be suspected. Why: Confirmed inferences give the player a justified basis to confront, and gating spreads suspicion across characters. (x2)
- [rule] Speakers should have a reason to ignore a witness who hears everything, or eavesdropping will feel convenient. When: Characters discuss plans in front of a witness. Why: Believing the witness is insensible justifies frank talk and keeps the scene credible.
- [rule] Gate a key revelation behind a sequence of conversations or discoveries, each supplying one piece. When: when designing story reveals.
- [rule] Gate fuller NPC information behind the NPC's emotional state, unlocking the complete account after the NPC calms, and reward patient listening over interruption. When: when an upset NPC holds key information. Why: Timing the reveal to the character's state makes the scene feel earned.
- [heuristic] Coded group slang hides meaning from outsiders; decode it with the right key, such as a translation earned in earlier dialogue, since terms may mean jewels, payments or gang membership. When: Investigating a group that speaks in codes, or designing faction dialogue with jargon. Why: Coded terms are decodable with the right key, and earned translations reward attention and make speech a puzzle.
- [heuristic] A hasty agreement made during distraction can itself be a planted opening that later becomes significant. When: Writing a moment where a character accepts a request quickly. Why: The quick acceptance is later seen as the way a plot entered the household.
- [heuristic] A dialogue branch can reveal more information as the player asks mechanical questions, unlocking fear-driven admissions step by step. When: when designing an NPC who conceals a motive. Why: Gradual unlocking rewards precise questioning over broad accusation.
- [procedure] 1) Claim prior knowledge of the listener's aim. 2) Name a suspected target. 3) Obtain a promise to confirm or deny the guess. 4) Use that commitment to press for more. When: when a source must be persuaded to disclose something. Why: A commitment made before the answer is hard to retract.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the intermediaries who control access. 2) Request an introduction through them. 3) If refused, accept a social setting where the witness is one guest among several. When: A key witness is gated by intermediaries or social rules. Why: Indirect routes can be the only available path to a protected witness.
- [procedure] 1) Identify a legitimate right to information, such as a family's entitlement to verify statements. 2) State that right openly to the gatekeeper. 3) Use it to request permission to stay or observe. When: An outsider needs access to a restricted investigation. Why: A recognized right is harder to refuse than a personal request.
- [tradeoff] Give NPCs timed reactions or micro-expressions that change when a sensitive topic is raised, so attentive players gain hints without the NPC stating the secret. When: Designing NPCs who conceal information. Why: Attentive players can use subtle cues as clues, rewarding observation.
- [pitfall] A trusted confidant may be the character controlling what others learn, so their account should be checked against what others were told. When: A character appears to share openly with the investigator. Why: Withholding and selective framing can hide a motive to protect someone.

## npc social manipulation
- [mechanism] Gathering all suspects in one enclosed place creates social pressure and lets their reactions be observed.
- [mechanism] Gate some answers behind an NPC's trust rather than evidence, so the player unlocks them through relationship instead of investigation. When: Designing case files with confidant NPCs. Why: Trust is a separate unlock path.
- [mechanism] Excessive praise can lower a guest's guard and keep him in place, and its real purpose may be hidden behind its warmth. When: A character's praise is out of proportion to the act praised. Why: Flattery softens targets and binds them to a group.
- [behavior] A person who tidies clothes or hair before an authority figure is often trying to appear composed, not showing vanity. When: when a suspect prepares to face an authority. Why: Presenting oneself well is a common response to a formal meeting.
- [rule] Gather documents that show contact with a relative or other leverage before confronting an adversary.
- [rule] When an NPC reports fear without detail, prompt the player to gather specifics before the report counts as evidence. When: an NPC voices vague dread about another character. Why: Unspecific fear cannot support a conclusion until its basis is found.
- [heuristic] An impossible or grotesque form of a myth can discourage close questioning, since witnesses are reluctant to examine something so strange. When: a hoax needs to avoid scrutiny. Why: Strangeness makes witnesses reluctant to test the details.
- [heuristic] Make a gentle-seeming NPC the antagonist, with earlier hints that players can recognize in hindsight.
- [heuristic] Gentle prodding, such as offering help or asking whether more time would help, raises stakes without pushing a stalled group too hard. When: A group is stalled in a timed decision. Why: Mild pressure keeps the group moving without forcing an outcome.
- [heuristic] Appearing weak or unthreatening can lower a suspect's guard, leading them to speak more freely and reveal hidden intent. When: Interrogating a suspect who may be on guard. Why: A suspect who believes the investigator is harmless may disclose information or intent.
- [heuristic] Keep praise plausible and in character, since heavy-handed flattery telegraphs the trap. When: Writing a character who lures through praise.
- [heuristic] Script an NPC's courtesy to escalate as the player is pulled deeper, so warmth reveals intent over time. When: Designing an NPC who may be setting a trap.
- [procedure] 1) Estimate the likely emotional cause of the witness's distress. 2) Name it gently. 3) Let the witness confirm or correct it instead of accusing them. When: A witness shows distress or defensiveness about a sensitive subject. Why: A witness who confirms a point discloses more reliably than one who is accused.
- [pitfall] Grisly detail can overshadow the investigative point, so the physical clue should stay the focus.

## npc state signals
- [mechanism] In an interrogation system, emotional reactions can change an NPC's state without unlocking a confession, so the player must still gather proof. Why: Separating reaction state from proof prevents emotional responses from acting as a shortcut to admission.
- [behavior] An unguarded flash of surprise can reveal that an opponent's assumption about your motive was wrong, and they lower their estimate of you. When: Watching an opponent during a bargaining exchange. Why: Unguarded reactions expose assumptions the opponent did not mean to show.
- [rule] Record treatments in a chart the player can read, so the question of what was given and when becomes a deduction. When: medical or poisoning mysteries.
- [rule] Record an NPC's debts or prior dealings in a log the player can read, giving motive before the event.
- [rule] Give NPCs readable wear, such as boot type, sunburn, or mourning colors, so players can infer backstory from them. When: when designing NPC appearance. Why: Visible details let players reason about a character's past.
- [rule] Build a retreat state where a guarded NPC withdraws and returns later with different dialogue options. When: Designing NPCs who react to pressure. Why: A retreat state makes pressure have lasting consequences on dialogue.
- [rule] Script confrontations between an NPC and two possible culprits, showing a reaction cue that can be misread by the player. When: designing a confrontation with ambiguous culprits. Why: a readable but misleading cue creates productive uncertainty.
- [rule] Build physical tells such as a tremor or limp into NPCs as observable clues that change with stress. When: Designing NPC appearance and behaviour that conveys condition or history. Why: Changing physical signs give players observable evidence to interpret.
- [heuristic] Give NPCs observable tells such as glancing away, hesitating, or shifting posture and expression, so players can read their state when sensitive subjects come up. When: designing NPC dialogue. Why: Visible state changes give players a readable channel for information not stated in dialogue. (x2)
- [heuristic] Make an NPC's reaction a readable signal so players learn whether a hidden line landed.
- [heuristic] Give a rival a backstory, such as a lost inheritance or a fallen family, so the player can read the grudge as motivated. When: Presenting an NPC's grudge to the player. Why: Backstory makes the reason for the grudge clear.
- [heuristic] An NPC who believes the player holds proof can be made to reveal a hiding place or act on it, so bluffing about knowledge can change NPC behavior. When: In dialogue systems where NPCs track what the player appears to know. Why: Actions taken on false beliefs expose hidden information.
- [tradeoff] Small signs like face, hesitation and manner can leak inner state, but the same reaction is often read in opposite ways, so treat it as interpretation, not evidence. When: Observing suspects or people hiding emotion in conversation. Why: Involuntary signs can leak state even when words do not, yet expressions carry no fixed meaning.
- [pitfall] A readable mark is also a clue for whoever holds the object, and may expose the owner as well. When: A marked item is in a thief's possession. Why: The mark can be read by anyone holding it.

## reaction-driven dialogue
- [mechanism] Revealing a fact that contradicts an NPC's earlier commitment can unlock a new dialogue branch. When: in dialogue trees with commitment-based answers.
- [mechanism] A reaction system can unlock new dialogue options when a named location or object enters the conversation. When: A named location or object is mentioned during dialogue. Why: The mention triggers a linked response, extending the conversation along the relevant topic.
- [mechanism] Confronting one NPC with another's statement can open a branch in which the contradiction unlocks new evidence.
- [behavior] A sharp reaction to a particular name, item or keyword can reveal a hidden trait before the character speaks. When: When a character is confronted with a specific keyword in play. Why: Involuntary reactions expose what the character would rather conceal.
- [rule] Let player-found items or witnesses expose contradictions in suspect statements; contradictions unlock dialogue options, a consistent cover story opens other options, and polished rhetoric is a red herring, not proof. When: Designing interrogation dialogue with testable claims. (x2)
- [rule] Let the player show an item to an NPC or stage a planted item in a location; a dialogue or animation reaction reveals whether the NPC recognises it. When: Designing item clues or item-reveal interactions with an NPC. Why: A reaction confirms the item's significance and gives the player a result; prior description makes the reaction a readable signal. (x2)
- [rule] Track suspects' visible reactions, such as paling, flinching, withdrawal or topic change, as dialogue state; contradicting clues or accusations trigger them and flags accumulate toward a later reveal. When: Designing suspect reactions in interrogation dialogue that build toward a confession. Why: A contradiction that cannot be explained produces visible stress; accumulated reaction flags make a later reveal feel earned.
- [rule] Make NPC reactions to presented facts open new investigation paths and reveal hidden states rather than trigger automatic confessions or direct answers. When: Designing NPC responses to accusations, cryptic clues or held-back information. Why: Players then act on evidence instead of receiving answers for free; a reaction reveals a hidden state without requiring confession.
- [rule] Use separate summons and hidden positions for NPC suspects so the player can overhear reactions to an accusation as a clue. When: Scripting a confrontation scene between NPC suspects. Why: Overheard reactions give the player evidence without a direct confession.
- [rule] Show the player a contradiction in an interrogation, then offer a demonstration, such as opening a container, as the next step.
- [rule] Let the player propose theories that NPCs accept or dispute, and resolve disputes by requiring the player to find corroboration. When: designing conjecture dialogue.
- [rule] Separate 'considering' from 'committed' flags in quest state, so an NPC's musing about a plan does not count as an agreed outcome. When: designing NPC plans and quest outcomes. Why: Speculation should not trigger outcomes that only a firm decision should.
- [rule] Give NPC dialogue branches that change depending on whether the player probes a sensitive topic, so probing opens or closes answers. When: when designing conversation with a guarded character. Why: Responsive branches reward careful questioning and make the NPC feel reactive.
- [procedure] 1) Log facts the NPC knows. 2) Compare each suspect answer with logged facts. 3) Unlock the confession only after enough mismatches; small inconsistencies can yield confession without decisive physical proof. When: Designing an NPC interrogation dialogue that branches on contradictions, with thin physical evidence and measurable gaps in the account. Why: Tying the confession to accumulated mismatches makes questioning matter; each contradiction narrows the account until the suspect cannot hold every claim.

## reader bias and assumptions
- [model] A reader first takes an obsessive protagonist's behavior as madness, then as rational deduction, and finally learns that a key moment was a deliberate staged trick.
- [behavior] Readers stay engaged when the puzzle lies in the reasoning path and the chain of consequences, not in the offender's identity, so revealing the culprit early can still hold interest. When: Choosing whether to hide the culprit's identity. Why: Interest shifts from who did it to how the discovery is made when all facts are shown.
- [behavior] Audiences keep a wrong theory alive by assuming the rich never want more and that blackmail is always about money. When: A cast includes wealthy characters and a payment-based threat. Why: These two illusions remove the alternative motives from consideration.
- [rule] Let a character's silence leave a gap that a careful player can notice and later fill, rather than leaving the gap invisible. When: When a character's silence matters to the plot. Why: Players reward noticing gaps and feel satisfied when they fill them.
- [rule] Give the audience the same clues the investigator had, with key details recorded, so the solution can be followed and checked. When: When revealing a mystery's solution. Why: Unverifiable solutions feel arbitrary.
- [heuristic] Treat a stranger's background read from dress and bearing as a hunch, and weigh it against later behavior or an independent record before accepting it. When: Outward signs are the main evidence available. Why: Appearance is a first impression that later behavior can confirm or overturn. (x2)
- [heuristic] Clothing cut, footwear, worn hands, poor teeth or recent manual work can reveal background, occupation, modest means or a recent change in fortune, and can contradict a claimed journey. When: Judging a person's background or claimed origin from physical appearance or bodily condition. Why: Appearance and bodily condition reflect habits and history.
- [heuristic] Plant an anomaly where the audience can see it before the character does, so the character's dismissal creates dramatic irony. When: The audience should notice a discrepancy first.
- [procedure] 1) Note visible cues such as tan pattern, posture, wear and carried items. 2) Tie each cue to one conclusion about background. 3) Check the conclusions against an independent record. When: Judging a stranger's past before they speak. Why: Explicit cue-to-conclusion links make inference checkable and less like luck.
- [pitfall] If a clue depends on the audience's unstated assumptions, the author has offloaded work that the clue itself should do.
- [pitfall] A reading of a reaction depends on assumptions about how guilty or fraudulent people behave, and respected readers can agree on it and still be wrong.
- [pitfall] One reported detail often fits several readings, and choosing the reading that suits the accusation rather than independent evidence is a common error.
- [pitfall] A reader's inherited reverence or an old grudge can color how they read a stranger's face and bearing. Why: Prior feelings supply the interpretation the observer expects to find.
- [pitfall] Polished or redundant prose can hide thin evidence, so writing quality should not be taken as a sign of reliability. When: Judging a written account. Why: Fluent or elaborate wording can make weak evidence look stronger.

## solution and proof structure
- [model] Model a solution as required links, such as each party's location, whether they met, and whether there was time to act, which the player must supply before the case closes. When: When designing or analyzing a mystery's answer or win condition. Why: Breaking the answer into facts makes its gaps visible; explicit links give the player a checklist and make the final step feel earned. (x2)
- [rule] Reveals not backed by clues the player has already met read as tricks, so make every solution path rest on seen clues and replay key evidence in a final sequence. (x2)
- [rule] Outline the solution's skeleton before placing decoys, so the hidden answer stays consistent as red herrings are added.
- [rule] Check the inner edge of a sole separately from the rest of the shoe, since that area carries different wear and residue.
- [rule] Give each case an official solution complete enough that a single hidden detail reframes the existing evidence. When: authoring a mystery whose twist must recontextualize clues. Why: A reversal only lands if the first reading was coherent and the new detail explains what it had left unresolved.
- [heuristic] Solutions are usually explained after the fact, often by a detective to a witness, using available proof: a document, a physical trap, a reconstruction, or a confession. Why: A clear explanation tied to available proof resolves the case for the player.
- [heuristic] Resolve mysteries by inference from physical objects rather than by confession; a confession may follow, but the proof should not depend on it.
- [procedure] 1) Walk the listener through the reasoning in order. 2) Tie each step to a fact the listener has already seen. 3) Let the listener check each step. 4) Hand over results to those who must act. When: an official team must act on the reasoning.
- [procedure] 1) Gather the group at a set place and time. 2) State the frame of the problem. 3) Present reasoning in a clear sequence. 4) Test each item with a pause before its result. 5) Stop before the final step to show the outcome, then name the culprit. When: The verdict depends on checks the audience can follow. Why: Visible steps and pauses make the accusation feel earned.
- [procedure] 1) State the stumbling block that rules out the obvious suspect. 2) Name the anomaly in the evidence. 3) Infer the hidden actor from the anomaly. 4) Explain the motive and means. When: when delivering a final reveal. Why: ordered steps let the audience follow and verify each inference.
- [tradeoff] A bluff finale closes the case quickly by provoking a confession but leaves no legal proof; a proof-based finale is slower but gives players a verifiable solution. When: Choosing how a mystery resolves when evidence is incomplete. Why: Forcing a reaction ends the case quickly, but players may feel the solution is unverified.
- [pitfall] Layers that rest on one contested fact all fall when that fact fails, so the whole case collapses with a single weak link. When: a case is built from stacked inferences. Why: the layers share one foundation.
- [pitfall] Treating one small detail as proof of a conclusion overreaches, since trifles support other conclusions rather than standing alone. When: Drawing conclusions from minor physical details. Why: A single small detail can have innocent explanations and needs corroboration.
- [pitfall] Presenting a solution as a list of conclusions, without the steps that led to it, leaves the audience unable to check it. When: when writing a reveal. Why: unverifiable conclusions cannot be trusted or tested.

## staged crimes and deaths
- [definition] A staged corpse is a substitute body placed so the apparent victim escapes, hiding who actually died; close associates may be complicit. When: A mystery where a death is reported and the identity of the dead is in doubt. Why: Readers assume a body is the person named, so the substitution hides the true actor.
- [definition] A self-staged crime is one where the apparent victim arranges their own abduction to pressure another person, so it reads as a third-party crime.
- [mechanism] A staged death, sham funeral, or natural-seeming illness can hide a deliberate, targeted plot, so an ordinary cause may turn out to be malice. When: An apparent misfortune is staged or convenient for someone. Why: Audiences accept an ordinary cause until a concrete event contradicts it.
- [mechanism] A second body found mid-story reverses suspicion when it contradicts the first theory, forcing the player to rebuild the whole reading. When: midpoint of a mystery. Why: A new fact that undoes the current explanation resets the player's suspicions.
- [mechanism] When a danger is revealed as a performance, earlier sounds and details that matched the act become evidence the player can reread. Why: The performance leaves traces that fit the staged frame.
- [mechanism] Evidence that a death was staged, such as a wound inflicted after death, overturns earlier theories about who killed the victim and why. When: a reconstruction shows a scene was arranged. Why: Killer theories depend on the assumed sequence of events.
- [heuristic] An apparent disappearance can be explained by the missing person's own choices, such as relocating without notice, rather than by an external cause. When: Resolving why a character seemed lost.
- [heuristic] A staged element traced back to its original owner shows that its removal served a purpose other than the one it appeared to serve.
- [heuristic] Let the player reconstruct a faked crime from clues such as a dropped object or a thrown item, proving the scene was staged by someone the player trusted. When: Revealing that a crime scene was fabricated. Why: Physical evidence that the player can verify makes the staging believable.
- [procedure] 1) Release findings first where they touch the other side's theory. 2) Hold the most damaging facts back until later. 3) Hear the other side's account before revealing inferences. When: Presenting evidence to a party who holds information you need. Why: Ordering disclosure for effect tests the other side's theory and protects your advantage.
- [procedure] 1) Appear in public in one guise at a known place. 2) Change identity out of sight. 3) Appear again in the second guise, so staff sightings cover the gap. When: Designing or analysing a staged alibi. Why: Public sightings in each guise make the switch invisible to witnesses.
- [procedure] 1) Hold back a central fact until the listener is ready to receive it. 2) Watch the listener's hesitation and reaction. 3) Reveal the hidden matter in small steps, each adding one piece. 4) Let the listener supply facts where possible. When: when a hidden fact would harm a third party if revealed too early or the listener must be prepared. Why: Gradual disclosure prevents shock and keeps the listener engaged in reasoning.
- [procedure] 1) Circulate a false report that implicates one suspect. 2) Summon each suspect separately. 3) Watch each reaction for the one that exposes the guilty party. When: when logic alone cannot separate suspects. Why: The guilty party may react to the bait where innocent suspects do not.
- [procedure] 1) Let a character be identified as dead early. 2) Present a sighting of that character alive later. 3) Have the solver reconstruct the disguise from details already reported. When: Building a twist where a presumed victim turns out to be the killer. Why: Reusing reported details makes the reversal feel deduced rather than invented.

## stopped clocks and timing
- [mechanism] Fixed clocks, watches and calculated doses fix a timeline and can expose what someone knew or intended. When: A timeline must be proven or a suspect's account of time must be checked. Why: Objective time records are harder to dispute than recollection.
- [behavior] Shock or unconsciousness leaves a witness's sense of time imprecise, so their timing becomes approximate. When: a witness has fainted or been in distress. Why: Unconsciousness and distress disrupt how the witness judges elapsed time.
- [rule] Record each change to a fixture with its time and origin, then test any official explanation for it against what witnesses saw.
- [rule] Pair each fixture state change with a plausible in-world excuse, and let players find that the excuse conflicts with the recorded facts.
- [heuristic] Record when a found watch or mechanical timer stopped and compare that moment with the event timeline, since a stopped mechanism freezes a datable time. When: a watch or mechanical timer is found halted. Why: A stopped mechanism freezes a moment that can be dated against the schedule. (x2)
- [heuristic] A lamp still burning in daylight shows someone was active in the room recently. When: A light source is found running at an unexpected time. Why: Fuel burns only while someone keeps it lit or leaves it on.
- [heuristic] Compare a suspect's stated plan with the reconstructed timing; a mismatch in the stated hour can expose an alibi.
- [heuristic] A stated wish, such as a request to be woken early, fixes when others expected a person to be active.
- [heuristic] An object that should be running but has stopped may carry a false time or a deliberate sign, so its reading must be examined before it is accepted. When: an object's state contradicts its expected state. Why: a stopped object can mislead about when an event happened.
- [pitfall] A stopped timer fixes an event time only if it was running then and stopped because of that event, not from an unrelated cause such as running down. When: a stopped clock is used as a timestamp. Why: A clock not running at the event cannot record its time, and coincidental stops mislead. (x2)
- [pitfall] Do not accept a stopped or moved clock as event-time proof unless checking whether it stopped by accident or was set by hand; mechanisms fail or are manipulated. When: a stopped or moved clock is used to fix when an event happened. Why: Clocks can be set or stopped by hand or fail mechanically, so they can suggest a false hour.
- [fact] A stopped clock shows only the moment it stopped, so any later time must be inferred from other references.
- [fact] A steamship arrives almost as fast as its letter, while a sailing ship is slow. A long gap between letter and event suggests sailing travel. Why: steam removes most of the delay.
- [fact] Mechanical timers often stop when physically shocked, so a stopped timer may mark the moment of an impact. When: a timer was on a body during a violent event. Why: shock can disrupt the mechanism.

## supernatural and anomaly explanation
- [model] Cases can be sorted into three classes: subjective, external, or mixed, which helps judge how far each explanation can be trusted.
- [mechanism] A dream sequence that leaves a physical state change on waking, such as an injury or status effect, makes the illusion checkable, so the deception is fair. When: when a story or game stages apparent events, such as dreams or hallucinations, that are later undercut. Why: The physical sign gives the audience a checkable clue, converting an apparent event into evidence they can verify.
- [mechanism] Dreams often borrow imagery from recent experience, with places and people reappearing in altered form, so strange content can have a rational origin. When: An uncanny image appears that may trace back to the character's recent experience. Why: Dream content recombines what the mind recently encountered, so the source is often ordinary.
- [mechanism] Revealing that a feared threat was a dream or delusion recasts earlier encounters as possibly imagined, reframing the story after the fact.
- [mechanism] A reasonable false explanation keeps the audience calm; when the true cause appears, it reads as a correction rather than a cheat. When: a reveal overturns an explanation the audience accepted. Why: The audience had a plausible account they can now see was wrong.
- [behavior] Ordinary human behavior, such as imaginative play, can explain strange conduct and make it less alarming, but this does not make the person's account trustworthy. When: a witness's odd conduct has a harmless-looking explanation.
- [rule] Use a dream or vision as a foreshadowing cue whose details map to real NPCs and places, so the player can check them. When: Designing a foreshadowing sequence. Why: Checkable details turn foreshadowing into a clue the player can verify.
- [rule] If the story should remain supernatural, rule out the human explanation explicitly. When: Writing a genuinely supernatural mystery. Why: Without explicit elimination, readers assume a grounded cause and the supernatural claim loses force.
