- [heuristic] Early small signs, such as a repeated wish to visit a location, can point to the real human cause before the reveal. When: Planting a hidden human cause behind a supernatural event. Why: Prevents the reveal feeling arbitrary.
- [heuristic] Offer a supernatural or official explanation early to absorb the first theory of an impossible event, so the audience sets it aside once evidence appears. When: at the opening of an impossible-event mystery. Why: an easy answer satisfies the first question until evidence contradicts it.
- [heuristic] Give a stated cause for a missing marker, such as forced sale or seizure, so its absence feels explained rather than arbitrary.
- [procedure] 1) Split each strange event into its component sensations. 2) Assign each sensation a candidate ordinary cause. 3) Test each cause against the physical scene. 4) Keep the explanation provisional until physical evidence supports it. When: A sequence of odd events seems supernatural but each piece might share a common cause. Why: Separating components exposes which parts a rational cause fails to cover.
- [pitfall] A clue shown to the reader and later explained away must still match the physical facts, or the reader will notice the gap. When: Writing a clue that is dismissed by an in-story explanation. Why: Mismatch between explanation and physical facts breaks reader trust.
- [pitfall] Explaining away an odd detail, such as an unusual voice or mask, without asking what it rules out lets a flawed theory survive. When: when an anomaly fits a convenient explanation. Why: Dismissing anomalies removes the evidence that would expose the error.

## theory building and testing
- [mechanism] Each suspect theory feels strongest just before a test breaks it, so the player's confidence peaks and then reverses sharply. When: pacing suspicion toward a reversal. Why: Confidence peaking before a test makes the disproof a sharp turn.
- [rule] Make at least one death testable, such as through records or an autopsy, so the player can confirm foul play rather than merely suspect it. When: When a conspiracy depends on suspicious deaths. Why: A checkable death lets the player move from suspicion to proof.
- [heuristic] When a lead seems to answer the main question but carries signs of a separate motive, test whether it explains the facts or belongs to a different crime. When: When an official-looking or politically charged clue appears. Why: A dramatic lead can be a side effect of an unrelated crime, not the activity under investigation.
- [heuristic] Test a proposed cause by comparing it with when the person was last observed well; a theory that fails the timing is weakened.
- [heuristic] Offer a false solution the player can test and fail; the closed trail teaches the player which evidence to doubt.
- [procedure] 1) List every fact the suspect or explanation must account for. 2) Check whether it explains each one. 3) Reject it if a central contradiction remains, since a convenient explanation may be a decoy. When: A single suspect or explanation appears to explain everything, or fits only part of the evidence. Why: A theory that fails on some details is likely incomplete, wrong, or a decoy.
- [procedure] 1) Accept a surprising claim or supernatural frame as unverified. 2) List other explanations that fit the same facts, testing ordinary ones first. 3) Test each directly, including the original claim, before acting on any of them. When: A single surprising fact seems to settle a question, or a supernatural frame is proposed.
- [procedure] 1) Record the witness's explanation for a physical mark. 2) Judge the mark's apparent age against the stated date. 3) Examine its pattern against the explanation. 4) Have a second observer confirm the reading. When: A witness explains a bruise, wound or other physical trace. Why: Mismatches in age, pattern or cause expose a story that does not fit the evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Assume the most ordinary cause, such as an echo. 2) Reproduce the conditions by stamping or walking briskly. 3) Check whether the sound returns each time. 4) Search the area for a source. 5) Repeat the test rather than accepting one result. When: An unexplained sound or sign has a possible mundane source that can be tested on the spot. Why: Repeatable tests separate natural causes from the unexplained without relying on a single observation.
- [procedure] 1) Take hold of the first loose clue. 2) Follow it step by step in every direction it leads. 3) Continue until the whole connected clue is gathered. When: A single clue opens onto several connected leads. Why: Following each thread in turn builds a complete picture from a small start.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the favoured suspect. 2) Check the suspect's location at the relevant time against the alibi. 3) Check whether a motive exists. 4) Drop or revise the theory if the alibi holds and motive is absent. When: Before building an accusation on a suspect theory. Why: A plausible theory that lacks motive and has a confirmed alibi fails regardless of its appeal.
- [procedure] 1) Build motive from relationships among characters. 2) Record the facts that contradict the theory. 3) List questions the theory cannot answer. 4) Test the alibi against its supporting witnesses. 5) Keep open questions alive until resolved. When: Laying out suspects and a working theory. Why: A theory is useful only if it explains known facts and the facts that cut against it.
- [procedure] 1) Propose the apparent purpose behind how remains were handled. 2) Check the purpose against the physical traces. 3) If it does not fit, propose another purpose and check again. When: Judging whether a proposed explanation for remains matches the evidence. Why: Traces constrain purpose; a mismatch signals the explanation is wrong.
- [pitfall] A theory defended from pride or attachment can outlast its evidence, causing investigators to ignore disconfirming facts. When: An investigator has committed to an early theory. Why: Personal investment in a first theory resists revision.

## witness observation and reports
- [mechanism] Overhearing part of a private exchange reveals a forming decision and can shift a listener's view; in design, holding back the remainder creates curiosity and a later payoff. When: When a character waits where a conversation about her can be heard, or when designing restricted-access eavesdropping scenes. Why: The overheard decision is raw information about how she will be judged; partial information creates curiosity and gives the full meaning a later payoff.
- [behavior] Reasoning about an ambiguous clue tends to swing between readings until a fact decisive enough to separate them is found. When: no decisive fact is yet available. Why: each reading stays plausible until it is tested.
- [rule] Separate what a witness saw from what they assumed, since confident witnesses often present assumptions as observations.
- [rule] Have different characters report different phenomena at the same event, so the mismatch becomes a deduction puzzle for the player. When: Designing conflicting NPC testimony. Why: Mismatched reports invite the player to reason about who saw what.
- [rule] Let an NPC witness a suspicious act and report it, but have others dismiss the report because of that NPC's reputation, so the player must recover it from rumour. When: when designing NPC testimony and rumour systems.
- [heuristic] An observer's intoxication, excitement or emotional state can distort their sensory reports and their reading of others' tells, so check it before accepting the account. When: When a witness reports a sensory impression under poor conditions, or when reading another person's tells. Why: Impaired or agitated observers give weaker accounts, and their impressions may be imagined.
- [heuristic] Several independent identifications of an object, especially one located near a body, strengthen a case; a second witness repeating a shared source adds no confirmation. When: When linking a weapon or item to an event, or when two witnesses agree. Why: Independent identifications reduce the chance one mistaken witness drives the conclusion; repeated information looks like corroboration but adds no independent evidence.
- [heuristic] Let an observant character register what others miss, and give a dismissive remark that acts as a hint for a careful player. When: Writing dialogue where a character dismisses a clue. Why: Careful players can separate the dismissal from the truth.
- [heuristic] An observer who admits limits on their own judgment makes a physical description read as objective observation rather than flattery.
- [heuristic] An NPC witness can give accurate information whose reliability depends on conditions the player can verify, such as light, distance and line of sight. When: when designing NPC testimony in a game. Why: Making reliability depend on checkable conditions lets players weigh what they are told.
- [heuristic] Reveal a disguise through a witness directly observing the change rather than through a confession. When: Staging the exposure of a disguised character. Why: Seeing the transformation is more convincing than a spoken explanation.
- [pitfall] Overlooking sound is a mistake, since a creak can reveal a hidden watcher as surely as a glimpse. When: Assessing whether a hidden observer could have been detected. Why: Sound can betray presence even when sight is blocked.
- [pitfall] An observer's excitement can pass to witnesses and spoil their independent behaviour, so the observer should stay calm and passive during a test. When: Running a test in which witnesses react to the scene. Why: Witnesses pick up the observer's cues, which contaminates their reactions.
- [fact] A witness's failure to see a person clearly, due to poor lighting at meetings, is itself a fact to record. When: when a witness could not identify someone they met. Why: The limit on observation shapes what the testimony can establish.

## wound direction analysis
- [heuristic] A projectile entering high and leaving lower, or an oblique downward path, suggests the shooter stood above the victim, such as on a staircase, especially at close range. When: reconstructing a shot from wound geometry. Why: The trajectory angle reflects the shooter's height.
- [heuristic] A wound's side, angle and extent indicate roughly the hand used; a blow from behind favours the attacker's likely handedness. Record direction and extent when describing an injury. When: reading an injury to infer how it was inflicted, or a wound is inflicted from behind. Why: Stance and reach favour one hand; angle and extent constrain who could have made the wound.
- [heuristic] Judge wound state (fresh, clotted or dried) to set order against a fatal injury; a bloodless wound may be post-mortem, added to suggest a cause that did not kill. When: a surface injury could come from a fatal event or earlier violence, or a murder method seems excessive or senseless. Why: Bleeding and drying change over time; a heart that has stopped produces no bleeding.
- [heuristic] A fatal wound matching no weapon found on the scene suggests the victim struck a broad surface, such as a wall, during a struggle.
- [heuristic] A wound and its dressing can serve as independent proof that contradicts a verbal account. When: A person's story about an injury is questioned. Why: Physical injuries are hard to fabricate convincingly.
- [heuristic] Check whether a wound's position fits the claimed act; a wound in an unexpected place may indicate a staged scene. When: a scene suggests a particular cause. Why: Physical injury must match the method claimed.
- [heuristic] A shot placed in a victim's back suggests the attacker stood close behind them. Why: a rear wound implies close following.
- [heuristic] Two wounds with suspiciously similar angles suggest the victim was not in the position the shooter's account requires. When: Reconstructing shooter position from wounds.
- [procedure] 1) Sort wounds by type, such as blunt or sharp. 2) Separate injuries by depth and location. 3) Identify which wound could have caused a fatal injury. When: Examining a body after a violent death. Why: Wound types point to different weapons and causes.
- [pitfall] A wound-order argument fails if its assumed direction of impact is wrong, so verify the assumed source of the injury first. Why: The conclusion depends on the relative position of the injury and the cause.
- [pitfall] Estimates of height or distance from a wound angle are rough, and a small error in distance can distort them considerably. When: inferring a shooter's position from an entry angle. Why: Angle-based estimates are sensitive to small measurement errors.
- [fact] A wound's entry point and angle constrain both the victim's posture at the time of the shot and the shooter's position relative to them. When: when interpreting a gunshot or stab wound. Why: geometry links the wound to body position and direction of force.
- [fact] A wound's depth and outline can indicate the kind of object that made it.
- [fact] A wound below the heart bleeds before the victim falls, while a later wound leaks as the victim lies across a surface, so bleeding order helps reconstruct positions. When: reconstructing a victim's position from wounds. Why: Bleeding depends on the body's posture at the time each wound was made.

## allegiance and loyalty
- [mechanism] Paying bail or legal defence for captured agents keeps the chain loyal. When: When captured agents can be supported by the organization.
- [mechanism] NPCs speak differently depending on their perceived allegiance to the player, so the same question can yield a different answer.
- [mechanism] Tying the consequences of how much truth a player tells an ally to that ally's loyalty and discretion makes disclosure a meaningful choice.
- [behavior] Accusers may avoid a respected figure directly and strike at his daughters, grandchildren, in-laws and servants, reaching him through his household. When: when a prominent person is protected by standing. Why: attacking close relations pressures the person without a direct confrontation.
- [behavior] People bound by friendship or shared membership often act from a common stance, so their parallel choices reflect the bond. When: Two allied figures make parallel decisions about the same matter. Why: Shared ties create shared expectations.
- [behavior] A witness publicly tied to a party may disapprove of its course yet record the outcome indirectly, so the disapproval shows in the wording. When: A witness associated with someone whose conduct they disagree with. Why: Public ties discourage open dissent.
- [rule] Let an ally share the quest goal while keeping back the personal reason, and hint at it through a locked or partial dialogue topic.
- [rule] Reveal alliances in council scenes through seating and past favours rather than explicit statements. When: Designing a council or vote scene.
- [heuristic] When a crime is a secret faction or inner allegiance with hidden members, infer it from indirect marks such as missing persons and rifled stores. When: An investigation relies on indirect evidence, such as when the crime is defined by belief or a secret pact. Why: proof must be sought in indirect marks. (x2)
- [heuristic] Make a mentor-style character sharp but incomplete, so the player must check claims independently.
- [tradeoff] An ally who promises to keep a visitor's presence quiet protects them, but may repeat the story and spread the cover beyond control.
- [pitfall] Association alone, such as faction membership, alliance, or loyal service, does not prove conspiracy or innocence, since a faction may be one side of a dispute and sincere devotion can be mistaken. When: Judging someone by their faction, allies, or the loyalty of those who serve them. (x2)
- [fact] Group initiations can test nerve and pain tolerance as part of admitting a new member.

## clue density and balance
- [mechanism] Placing a dense cluster of clues at the start of each case, followed by one or two misdirects and a sharp late cluster before the reveal, gives players early useful information. When: Structuring the clue pacing of a mystery case. Why: Early density orients the player, and the late cluster sets up the reveal.
- [rule] Make a clue appear only when the player chooses a specific dialogue topic, so exploring the conversation tree reveals it.
- [heuristic] Evidence that is too complete or points neatly at one person may be staged or planted to frame a scapegoat; check it before trusting it. When: evidence or a clue seems to point too clearly or unusually well to one suspect. Why: real events rarely produce a perfectly consistent trail; planting can aim evidence at a scapegoat; over-convenient evidence reads as contrivance.
- [heuristic] A suspect's account or a theory that fits every fact with no leftover detail may be constructed; persuasiveness is not proof of truth. When: choosing between candidate explanations, or a suspect's account matches all the evidence. Why: a perfect fit can indicate a constructed account; tidy stories can fit visible facts without being true.
- [heuristic] A pair that differs in every visible trait suggests a staged arrangement, since real rivals usually share some point of contact that makes them clash. When: A set of people or objects looks suspiciously symmetrical. Why: A complete reversal leaves nothing pushing against anything, which natural contrasts rarely do.
- [heuristic] When events seem too well timed to be spontaneous, check who benefits from each development and look for a pattern across several events. Why: A single coincidence is weak evidence, but a repeated pattern of benefit is stronger.
- [pitfall] Too many red herrings or false leads dilute the real danger and make the mystery feel arbitrary; each false lead should be knocked down by a visible fact.
- [pitfall] Planting many minor details without distinguishing the useful ones dilutes the important clue, so players cannot tell which detail matters. When: planting several small clues. Why: too many trifles compete for the player's attention.
- [pitfall] Repeated false alarms without progress make the audience lose patience, so the suspense collapses rather than grows. When: Staging delays before a reveal. Why: Setbacks without advancement stop feeling meaningful and the audience stops caring.
- [pitfall] Trying too few patterns can lead the solver to give up or settle on a false reading.
- [pitfall] Assuming a clear-looking set of facts is complete is a mistake; distrust tidy facts and ask for the detail that would test the theory.
- [pitfall] Too many unresolved questions at once frustrate the audience, so close some threads as new ones open.
- [pitfall] Asking a dying speaker too many questions is unrealistic and can break the scene's credibility. When: When a dying witness is being questioned. Why: Excessive questioning strains plausibility.

## concealment and cover stories
- [model] Hidden-cause stories often run: plant a clue, offer a comfortable explanation, escalate into crisis, then reveal the true cause through physical proof or confession. When: designing a mystery or reveal sequence. Why: The audience must hold a plausible wrong belief before the reveal can correct it.
- [mechanism] A patron who says not to be told can gate endings, and a secret kept from them can carry a visible consequence, such as an unburied victim. When: when designing endings that depend on what the player reveals to allies. Why: Linking concealment to visible consequences makes the choice to hide information matter.
- [behavior] A culprit who controls access to the scene can remove evidence by locking doors, removing keys, changing clothes, cleaning marks, and disposing of objects, so a search of their room may find nothing. When: When the culprit can act in the scene before others arrive and time is available. Why: Removing traces before inspection leaves investigators without physical links.
- [rule] Leave a character's cover story unverified at first, then flag it as a gap the player may return to. When: Introducing an NPC whose account may be false. Why: A deferred check rewards attentive players.
- [rule] If a staged event hides a real one, reconstruct the real action later, or the concealment stays unexplained. When: Using a staged cover event in the story. Why: Unresolved concealment leaves the reader without an explanation for the cover.
- [rule] Mislead only someone with no independent reason to check, since a cover story fails once the person verifies it. When: using a cover story with an ally.
- [rule] Check whether an on-the-spot explanation fits the physical evidence, since a plausible story can absorb a real clue. When: when evaluating an explanation given for an observed act.
- [rule] Keep the culprit's concealment in the narration's omissions, such as delayed visits, skipped guests and interrupted interviews, so readers can recheck them after the reveal. When: when a narrator-culprit investigates the case. Why: Omissions are only recognisable as clues once the truth is known.
- [heuristic] A cover identity such as a relation or acquaintance lets an investigator question a person without drawing public notice. When: when direct questioning would draw attention or produce guarded answers. Why: A familiar role lowers the target's guard and reduces public scrutiny.
- [heuristic] Give a culprit an innocent-seeming habit that also masks evidence, so the cover reads as eccentricity rather than deception. When: designing a culprit's daily routine. Why: A habit that hides a clue passes as harmless to the audience.
- [heuristic] A false name can be chosen to lure a pursuer toward the wrong person, which a late reveal can explain as a deliberate misdirect. When: A pursuer tracks a false identity. Why: A deliberate choice of name explains why a trap is set where it is.
- [pitfall] Concealment can fail through burning clothes, which looks suspicious if discovered, and through abandoning a weapon, which gives investigators the object most likely to link the crime to a person. When: When a culprit disposes of evidence. Why: Some disposal acts are themselves noticeable, and a left-behind weapon can identify the culprit.
- [fact] Crimes can happen in ordinary, hospitable surroundings and leave no visible sign, so ordinary surroundings do not indicate a supernatural cause. When: When judging whether a setting implies a supernatural explanation. Why: Human acts can go unseen in everyday places.

## conditional cooperation and leverage
- [mechanism] A withheld statement works as leverage only while its agreed release condition holds. If the outcome changes, the secret may lose its power. When: A secret is kept in reserve and released only if a condition is met. Why: Leverage depends entirely on the terms agreed for its release.
- [mechanism] One official who holds legislative, judicial, executive and military roles at once leaves no independent check on decisions. Why: Each role that would normally review another is held by the same person.
- [behavior] A lone investigator may be right against an official consensus, yet rank, experience and force of personality decide which theory gets acted upon. When: Two explanations of the same evidence compete and one is held by superiors.
- [behavior] Audiences read a hidden document as likely concealing a cost, so secrecy around terms itself raises suspicion. When: A character withholds the written terms. Why: Concealment suggests the terms are unfavourable.
- [rule] Give a threat a concrete form only if the player can ever learn it. When: Deciding how much to reveal about an unseen threat. Why: An unresolvable concrete threat loses credibility.
- [rule] Write NPC dialogue with conditional lines that expose a detail only the killer could know, and let players trigger them by asking the right question. When: Designing interrogation dialogue for a culprit NPC.
- [rule] Make a suspect's help conditional on frank answers, then press each evasive reply rather than accepting it. When: questioning a subject who hides facts that bear on motive. Why: Evasive replies mark what the subject most wants hidden.
- [heuristic] When a person without independent means stays in a shameful situation, ask who holds leverage over them; that controller is often the one supplying their money. When: someone acts against their own interest and cannot leave. Why: Control of resources is a likely source of compulsion.
- [heuristic] Give one NPC both secret witness knowledge and control over arrests, so players have a concentrated power they can investigate, expose or overthrow. Why: A single holder of hidden power gives players a clear target.
- [procedure] 1) Let the suspect set terms before giving an account. 2) Caution the suspect that statements may be used as evidence. 3) Decide whether to accept the terms, noting any promise you cannot legally keep. When: A suspect is willing to talk but will surrender only on negotiated conditions. Why: Terms agreed in advance can constrain later actions, and an unauthorized promise can bind the investigators.
- [pitfall] Official confirmation can rest on a conditional motive, such as silence granted only while the person behaves, so it may not be neutral. When: An authority confirms a person's past but agrees to stay silent. Why: The confirmer's incentive shapes what they report.
- [pitfall] A confidence shared with a relative or ally can later be used to press the confider toward a decision. When: Personal information is shared with someone who has their own interests. Why: Confided information becomes leverage when the listener's aims diverge from the confider's.
- [fact] A chain of inferences weakens with each added conditional link, so a motive built on many assumptions is probable at best, not proven. When: When reasoning from a motive to a suspect through several steps. Why: Each uncertain link multiplies the chance that the whole conclusion is wrong.

## confessions and endings
- [mechanism] A confession that protects someone else can misdirect an investigation until physical evidence contradicts the confessor's account. When: a character confesses to a crime. Why: A confessor may lie to shield another person, and the physical record exposes the lie.
- [rule] Deliver the explanation after the player survives the climax, through a cutscene, journal entries or found documents such as letters. When: A mystery's full logic is revealed late. Why: The reveal rewards survival and fills gaps the player has already noticed.
- [rule] When copies of evidence can multiply, secure it at its source first, since recovery takes priority over slow legal remedies. When: When legal processes are slow and evidence can be lost or copied. Why: Each delay gives copies time to spread.
- [rule] Use a quiet resolution as a reward, such as an NPC who leaves or an open escape route the player may choose to take. When: ending a dangerous sequence. Why: Choice in the aftermath gives the player agency after the peak of danger.
- [rule] Stage the final confession as a conversation in which the protagonist's reasoning, not a newly introduced item, reveals the truth.
- [heuristic] An observer can keep a polite public stance while privately doubting the explanation, and the stated account stays on record. When: Questioning a witness in a social setting. Why: Keeping the two separate preserves the conversation and the evidence.
- [heuristic] End with a public misattribution of credit, which shows that the protagonist's private knowledge exceeds what the official record states. When: closing a mystery with an official outcome. Why: The gap between public credit and private knowledge gives the ending a closing irony.
- [heuristic] Keep the final consequence private, so the ending closes with restraint rather than public punishment. When: resolving a scandal that would damage those involved. Why: Discretion can end the story quietly while still resolving the threat.
- [heuristic] Introduce a late threat after the main solution to keep the story open and give the player a new objective. When: The main mystery has been solved but the world still needs a forward hook. Why: A new danger after resolution prevents the story from ending and prompts further play.
- [heuristic] Use a public crisis, such as a riot, to force a wrong resolution and raise stakes before the reveal.
- [heuristic] Let the proof be a physical trap or detail rather than a confession, so the culprit is exposed by what they did. When: resolving a mystery's proof. Why: Physical evidence cannot be withdrawn the way a confession can.
- [tradeoff] A partial confession that admits presence but not the link to the main suspect keeps the last link open, at the cost of leaving the resolution unresolved. When: Ending a reveal act that should set up a further act. Why: It preserves suspense for the next stage while still delivering a major reveal.
- [tradeoff] Closed endings with a confession or arrest give clear closure, while letting villains escape or die offscreen keeps the world open but leaves justice incomplete. When: Choosing how a case ends.

## defence and defenders
- [behavior] A witness who insists a person is honest and did nothing wrong can make that defense itself look suspicious. When: a witness defends someone unprompted.
- [behavior] Defending an accused person in public can cost a witness socially, so pressure to apologize or retract tends to silence the defense. When: a witness speaks for an accused during a public panic. Why: The social cost of testimony can outweigh its benefit to the witness.
- [rule] Let a player's defence be answerable by specific clues, so the verdict depends on the case the player has built. When: when designing a trial where players argue their case.
- [rule] A defense can name people who knew the accused longest and were of good report, and ask that they testify under oath. When: an accused person cannot plead their own case.
- [heuristic] A plausible defence can reframe an account, so a statement must be tied to what the physical record shows.
- [heuristic] A heated defence signals the defender's feelings more than the facts, so weigh its force separately from its evidence.
- [procedure] 1) State the theory outright early so that questions can be aimed at it. 2) Identify the links the theory needs, such as possession, knowledge and intent. 3) Prove each link. 4) Test the theory against the link that is weakest. When: Building a defense or accusation that must hold up under questioning. Why: A stated theory directs questions and lets listeners judge the purpose of seemingly odd questions.
- [tradeoff] When the physical facts are settled, the defense can shift the contest from what happened to who and why by reshaping the motive and character of the parties. When: Forensic or physical evidence is overwhelming and hard to challenge. Why: Challenging settled facts is futile, so the contest moves to motive and character.
- [pitfall] Even defensive answers can reveal more than intended, so each reply should be checked for what it implies.
- [pitfall] Pressure can make a witness defend the person being asked about, which hides the information the questioner needs.
- [pitfall] A defender may have their own reasons to protect a suspect, so their endorsement must be read with that stake in mind.
- [pitfall] A defence that reasons toward another source of harm can be recorded as an accusation against a third party.
- [fact] A surviving defence document does not prove that decision-makers read or considered it. When: Evaluating whether a defence was heard in a tribunal. Why: A document can exist without reaching the people who decide the case.

## dialogue and social cues
- [mechanism] Flag sore-point cues such as hesitations or stressed keywords; a question touching one unlocks a new line, and a changed line or animation marks the reaction. When: Designing dialogue that rewards careful questioning. Why: Signalling cues in speech lets players discover new lines of inquiry from how an NPC answers. (x2)
- [mechanism] A furious NPC line can hint at a different target; players uncover the true object of anger through a second dialogue or a written document. When: Designing NPC dialogue with hidden motives. Why: Second sources confirm or correct the first.
- [behavior] Requests for small commitments made during an emotional appeal are attempts to extract agreement the speaker can later use. When: when a speaker pleads for a quick favour or meeting.
- [behavior] A speaker's cut-off or pointed remark can carry a warning that a listener, bound by his own assumptions, reads as rudeness or small talk. When: A character's dialogue hides information the listener lacks. Why: The listener interprets words through his own assumptions, so the hidden sense appears only on a second reading.
- [behavior] Secondary characters often reveal knowledge or shared feeling through unguarded interjections that the main account omits. When: Several people give accounts of the same event. Why: People are less guarded when they are not the primary speaker, so their remarks can contradict the main story.
- [rule] Run NPC interrogations on small talk with branching remarks, letting the player infer what the NPC knows from shifts in tone and pauses.
- [rule] Allow players to skip optional rambling dialogue, but never skip dialogue that carries a critical clue, and keep a direct route to the lead. When: Designing a rambling quest-giver who delays a clue. Why: Characterful digression should not block progress or hide essential information.
- [rule] Use a plausible social pretext, such as a small delivery, to give a reason to visit and to carry messages.
- [heuristic] A sudden shift in a witness's mood or topic usually marks a sore point worth pursuing. When: During an indirect interview.
- [heuristic] In social scenes with several NPCs, let body language and glances between characters hint at who is hiding what.
- [heuristic] Scatter casual dialogue from several sources, such as a guard's mention of a flooded drain, so that it pays off later when matching evidence appears. Why: small talk from several sources can combine into a pattern in hindsight.
- [procedure] Question a reticent witness one fact at a time, using narrow questions, so each answer narrows what can be inferred.
- [fact] Offering a drink is a social move that both sides use to signal they are not hostile. When: at the start of a tense meeting.

## documents and claim checks
- [model] A death-investigation plot can be built as a chain of corrections: each reveal overturns the current belief and reassigns suspicion until a final confession closes the case. When: designing a mystery with several suspects. Why: Each reversal makes the player re-evaluate who is responsible.
- [rule] Check claimed explanations, such as no fire or no recent use, against the object's physical state; separate the room as it is from the room as felt. When: Evaluating an account in a mystery. Why: Perception and physical record can diverge, especially under altered mental states.
- [rule] Check specific facts in personal documents, such as appearance, dates and places, rather than judging only by the tone or praise. When: Reading a personal letter as evidence. Why: Warm tone can hide concrete details that matter to the case.
- [rule] Compare a reading of a writer's state with what the writer later says before treating the reading as reliable. When: Interpreting a document before meeting its author. Why: Only a later statement can confirm or correct the reader's impression.
- [heuristic] A witness's stated reason, such as money, is a claim that can be checked against records like bills. When: A witness gives a motive for an action. Why: Records provide independent confirmation or contradiction.
- [heuristic] Reviewing back issues of a public notice column for repeated signatures can reveal a hidden channel linking a victim to a secret party. When: A private arrangement may run through published messages.
- [heuristic] Place the cause of a visible effect in an inset text, so the reader learns the mechanism at the same moment the protagonist sees the effect.
- [procedure] 1) For each object, ask who had access to it. 2) Check whether it fits the rest of the scene. 3) Treat it as possibly planted if it does not. When: An investigator must weigh clues against the chance they were placed. Why: Planted evidence can look convincing in isolation.
- [procedure] 1) List each detail in the retold story. 2) Check each against known facts. 3) Treat matches as real knowledge and unmatched details as possible cover. 4) Wait for a pattern before concluding. When: A suspect recounts a fictional case while avoiding direct questions. Why: Matches reveal what the teller actually knows, while a single invented detail is weak evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Quote each condition in the will exactly. 2) Check each part literally against the facts. 3) Name the beneficiary or executor only after every condition is confirmed. When: A motive or control of property depends on the wording of a will. Why: A paraphrase or assumption can yield a different beneficiary than the literal clause.
- [tradeoff] Separate the truth of a claim from its source: a claim can prove accurate while its origin stays unresolved. When: Designing a mystery where the supernatural origin of information is left open. Why: Confirmed accuracy can settle the claim without settling how it was obtained.
- [pitfall] A found document that explains everything removes the need for deduction; let it raise questions as well as answer them.
- [pitfall] A suspect who claims powers or behaves sinisterly is not thereby guilty of the act in question; the claim and the deed must be assessed separately. Why: Showmanship and claimed power are not evidence of a specific crime.

## eliciting accounts and duty
- [behavior] Targets find a request framed as a moral duty hard to refuse, even when the request arrives on forged letterhead. When: When a lure can use real letterhead and an appeal to duty.
- [rule] Frame a suspect's obligation to speak as a duty to free someone wrongly accused, separate from any blame for the crime. When: suspect is not culpable but holds knowledge. Why: people cooperate more readily when their silence would harm an innocent party.
- [rule] Plant an odd question from an NPC early, such as one about rare poisons, so the player can recall it when a related clue appears. When: designing NPC dialogue for a mystery. Why: a planted question becomes meaningful when a later clue connects to it.
- [heuristic] Move a guarded witness onto familiar local topics to get fluent talk and lower their guard, then return to the question that matters. When: a witness resists the key question. Why: Comfortable topics relax people, making them easier to draw out.
- [heuristic] A talkative witness reveals more when the listener seems sympathetic and responds with short encouraging remarks rather than direct questions. When: when interviewing a motivated witness. Why: Feeling heard keeps the witness talking about what they believe.
- [heuristic] Check deeds, wills and estate records before accepting a person's social status from earlier accounts, which may understate it. Why: property records can overturn accounts based on reputation.
- [procedure] 1) Ask questions that let each party state their own account. 2) Note exactly where the accounts disagree. 3) Weigh each account against checkable facts. When: gathering testimony about one event.
- [procedure] 1) Promise confidentiality to the suspect. 2) Ask for a complete written account. 3) Check the account for gaps against known facts. When: A talkative suspect may withhold details that matter to the timeline. Why: A confidentiality promise encourages fuller disclosure, but does not guarantee completeness.
- [procedure] 1) Let suspects talk freely about the topic. 2) Introduce a remark that invites a reaction. 3) Listen for repeated phrases or details only the culprit could know. When: Interrogating a suspect without a full accusation.
- [procedure] 1) Let the witness narrate freely first. 2) Return to specific senses: darkness, sounds, touch, smell. 3) Offer concrete cue prompts for impressions not yet verbalized. 4) Ask whether the presence felt familiar or unknown. 5) Test each detail from another angle. When: when questioning a witness who was frightened or asleep during an event. Why: fear and shock blur memory, but accurate sensory detail often survives if prompted gently.
- [pitfall] Releasing a witness before the whole truth is known risks losing cooperation; release only once the remaining stakes are minor.
- [pitfall] An earlier statement is only as reliable as the note-taking that recorded it. When: Relying on a prior written record to test a witness. Why: Transcription errors can make a record disagree with what was actually said.
- [fact] In the first half hour after a drug taken by mouth, its symptoms closely resemble feigned illness, so an early diagnosis cannot easily expose faking. Why: symptoms have not yet diverged.

## episodic structure and pacing
- [model] Episodic mysteries can share one investigator while each case is self-contained, opening with a crime that looks impossible or motiveless and solved from physical clues.
- [model] A linked episode story opens with a theft that is announced, staged or impossible-looking, shown from the victim's side, with misdirection from a visible suspect or sealed scene and a solution that reverses who controls the situation. When: designing a run of linked mystery episodes with a recurring thief protagonist. Why: The repeated shape gives readers a predictable frame in which the surprise lies in who is really in control.
- [mechanism] Delays such as travel, illness or waiting periods stretch the interval between news items and raise tension. When: Pacing the release of information through in-world events. Why: Each wait holds the next revelation back and gives the audience more time to anticipate it.
- [mechanism] When exits close step by step, each small refusal or delay tightens the situation, so the character's way out narrows as the hour grows late. When: A night-long or timed scene that should grow more threatening.
- [mechanism] A cold or similar environment can keep a body undiscovered until the victim dies, so a staged activity that delays discovery can shift the apparent time of death. When: A death depends on environmental conditions and the timing of discovery. Why: The environment finishes the killing while the staged activity keeps the body hidden.
- [rule] Use the final beat only when no unanswered questions remain, since an ending cannot resolve them.
- [heuristic] Set a fixed deadline for replies to inquiries and decide beforehand what a missing answer would mean. When: Waiting for responses that will test a theory. Why: A deadline turns open waiting into a test that can be passed or failed, and prevents rationalizing silence.
- [heuristic] Separate a mystery's force from its director so the source can be a distinct, findable actor with its own history.
- [tradeoff] Stopping a plan early frees the suspect to try again, while letting it proceed risks the victim's safety and timing errors. When: deciding when to intervene against a known plan. Why: early intervention preserves safety but leaves the threat active.
- [pitfall] Over-explaining the outcome of a mystery's ending can flatten it; tying up every thread leaves the reader with nothing to think about. When: Writing the closing section after a case is solved. Why: Full explanation removes the reader's reason to keep reflecting on the case.
- [pitfall] Escalation without a planned payoff exhausts the audience, so the climax should be planned before the first repetition. Why: Rising tension needs a resolution or it wears out the player.
- [pitfall] Ruling out a route because it seems hard can hide the one that is merely tedious. When: Eliminating options in a theft or breach analysis. Why: Difficulty and effort are different, and a tedious route may still be viable.
- [fact] In an episodic mystery collection, each case closes quickly, so the collection's pacing relies on the repetition of one story arc.

## forgery and forged evidence
- [mechanism] A deception holds when a forged document and a conversation the victim overhears agree with each other, since the paper gains believability from the context and the context gains weight from the paper. When: A deceiver wants a victim to accept a false situation without outside checks. Why: Both channels must agree, or the victim may notice a contradiction.
- [mechanism] A document that looked authentic, once shown to be forged from trimmed or mismatched stock, flips belief from the apparent author to the forger. When: A key document is revealed to be fake. Why: Physical traces of forgery overturn trust in the document's apparent source.
- [rule] Plant a forgery's contradiction in a checkable property, such as paper, ink, handwriting or a machine's purchase date, and name that property before the player needs it. When: Designing a document that may later prove to be false. Why: A checkable contradiction lets the player expose the frame by their own deduction, and a fair reversal needs a way to test the document. (x2)
- [rule] Present a forged or altered document that the player must check against a second source, such as a ledger or witness. When: Designing a puzzle built on a document that may be false. Why: Requiring a second source makes the deception discoverable by fair play.
- [heuristic] Confirm a hidden-name link only on an exact letter match; loose resemblance or shared sounds are weaker evidence and easily overread. When: Testing whether an alias hides a known name.
- [heuristic] Give the true culprit a motive that appears early, such as a quarrel or absence, but leave it unremarked until the reversal. When: Writing a mystery where a secondary character hides the real crime. Why: An early but unemphasized motive is fair play that the player can recall once the twist lands.
- [heuristic] Split trusted allies with a forged message, and plant a small detail, such as a misspelled signature, that exposes the forgery. When: creating a false belief between protagonists. Why: A detectable flaw lets the audience and characters recover the truth.
- [heuristic] Forged or conspicuously intact evidence may be a planted misdirection, so check whether its presence looks deliberate before accepting it. When: a forged letter or wrapper survives the investigation unchanged. Why: Evidence that is too convenient may have been placed to mislead.
- [tradeoff] A forged invitation can pull suspects into one room, but it also means the expected threat may never show, so the lure must be paid off by another event. When: gathering suspects for a confrontation. Why: The lure creates pressure and a single setting, at the cost of a possibly empty payoff.
- [pitfall] A forged document can be found later, and a staged story can be exposed by a single contradiction. When: A deception relies on one convincing scene and a document. Why: Overconfidence in one scene can make the deceiver careless about the rest.
- [pitfall] A seal that delays the answer too long can make the reader forget its release instruction. When: when the gap between seal and release is long. Why: The instruction fades from memory before the release arrives.
- [pitfall] A document can be false, and a list of names proves contact rather than guilt. When: Relying on written records as evidence.
- [fact] Records and staff accounts that use false names confuse the official trail as well as the people searching it.

## investigation partners and staff
- [mechanism] When the player's chosen companion changes who is present, the observations the player receives also change, because an absent character can reveal different clue text. When: The game lets the player choose which NPC accompanies them. Why: Each present character filters what is noticed and reported.
- [behavior] Partners in a crime may cooperate while each suspects the other would abandon them in danger. When: two accomplices must work together. Why: Each partner's cooperation is also a reason they might betray the other.
- [behavior] Two investigators can exchange meaning through a glance, conveying understanding that a third party only partly grasps. When: Multiple investigators question a witness together. Why: Shared context lets a brief look carry meaning without words.
- [rule] Keep an observing companion uninformed of your theory so their impressions form independently and can be compared with your own conclusions. Why: An observer's impressions lose their independent value once they have heard the investigator's theory.
- [rule] Split investigation between the player and an NPC partner, with the partner handling covert actions. When: Designing cooperative investigation gameplay. Why: Division of methods lets each role fit its character.
- [rule] Agree on signals with a companion before questioning, and have them keep a record ready even while appearing inattentive. When: Two people question one subject together. Why: Signals coordinate action, and a ready record preserves evidence without alerting the subject.
- [rule] Give a companion NPC the role of recording a suspect's statements so the player's journal can log them for later reference. When: Designing dialogue scenes where statements may later be disputed. Why: A recorded statement can be shown as fact.
- [heuristic] Have two staff members give partial accounts of one event, so players must compare them to find the contradiction.
- [heuristic] Let a rival or mentor supply the final synthesis from documents, so the last step is deduction rather than combat. When: resolving a mystery's final step. Why: Deduction from documents resolves the case without requiring a confrontation.
- [heuristic] Give a trusted ally a useful role in the investigation, so his presence in the case keeps him plausible as a helper and his later exposure reads as a betrayal. Why: An active role inside the case makes the ally appear trustworthy and gives him reasons to be present.
- [tradeoff] Leaving a suspect unattended to fetch another opinion or ally gives the suspect the chance to leave, so the investigator trades control for outside help. When: An investigator considers bringing in a second party while a suspect is present. Why: An unattended suspect can depart, creating a sudden loss of the subject.
- [pitfall] A witness who is also a party to the dispute can appear neutral when they are not.
- [fact] Investigators pool information, so an officer may already know a person's background from records rather than needing to deduce it. When: A mystery where investigators have access to records. Why: Shared records can supply facts a detective would otherwise have to infer.

## knowledge and belief
- [behavior] A contact who knows a market reacts to a shown object with detached knowledge rather than surprise. Their reaction reveals what they know. When: When an expert examines an object linked to a case. Why: Genuine expertise shows as recognition, not astonishment.
- [behavior] A community leader's public statements can change how townsfolk treat a suspect. When: When a respected leader speaks publicly about the accused or related beliefs. Why: People follow the stance of trusted leaders.
- [rule] Separate what a witness actually knows from what they hope or have persuaded themselves to believe, since protective bias and feelings are not evidence. Why: Protective bias can distort testimony, and feelings are not evidence.
- [rule] Tag each NPC's knowledge by how it was obtained, such as seen directly, overheard or heard secondhand, and show that tag to the player. When: Writing NPC dialogue that carries information. Why: Players can then weigh claims by their source.
- [rule] Present confirmed facts separately from working theories, and keep unresolved questions open rather than auto-solving them. When: Designing summary screens or case journals. Why: Keeps the player's model of the case accurate about what is established.
- [heuristic] Give the player a knowledgeable NPC who can confirm or reject a hypothesis, turning a guess into a quest step. When: designing investigation quests. Why: verification gives the guess a consequence.
- [heuristic] Reveal a fact the suspect believes you lack; a denial that conflicts with it shows their knowledge exceeds what they admit.
- [heuristic] Knowledge of a test is itself a clue, because it narrows who could have planned a substitution. When: when a scenario hinges on who knew about a test. Why: Only people aware of the test could have prepared to defeat it.
- [procedure] 1) Ask what the other side already knows before stating your own facts. 2) Withhold your own information while they speak. 3) Compare their claims with what you know. When: when you need facts from a party without revealing your hand. Why: the exchange becomes a comparison of two fact sets.
- [pitfall] Inferring knowledge from a method does not show where that knowledge came from. When: Using a method to infer a suspect's expertise. Why: Knowing that someone had specialised knowledge does not reveal how they acquired it.
- [fact] Showing that a writer knew the true facts does not settle guilt or innocence; competing readings of the same document can remain.
- [fact] Legitimate sources of a fact include the victim, interviewed staff, the police and the press; each must be checked against the suspect's contacts.
- [fact] Leading thinkers of an era can reject ideas that later became accepted, so great minds share the blind spots of their period.

## late evidence discovery
- [rule] Plan a late independent confirmation, such as a confession or confirmed record, that tests the player's deduction from public sources, rewarding fair reasoning.
- [rule] Converge decisive documents and physical proof into one tight late cluster, supported by everything already seen, so each remaining alternative falls at once. When: at a mystery's climax, once the player has accepted a different culprit. Why: Clustered failed claims change belief at once, giving the strongest reversal and leaving no open threads.
- [rule] A sudden noise or fearful NPC reaction can trigger a search task whose outcome stays uncertain until it is checked. When: when designing reactive events for players. Why: Uncertain outcomes keep players investigating rather than assuming.
- [rule] Reveal a detail the suspect did not expect to open a new line of questioning, rewarding players for collecting clues.
- [rule] Introduce a final, decisive clue without comment so it is noticed only when the explanation arrives. Why: an uncommented clue invites the audience to reread it after the reveal.
- [heuristic] Search where the sought item is least expected and in less-searched, out-of-the-way places, since evidence often turns up where it was not anticipated; treat such finds as serious leads. When: a case hinges on one item whose origin is still open. Why: out-of-the-way locations are less searched and may hold overlooked evidence.
- [heuristic] A visitor arriving at an unexpected hour can shift the scene without warning.
- [heuristic] Recover physical proof late from the suspect's own belongings, so the confirmation comes from evidence that is hard to explain away. Why: Evidence found among the suspect's possessions is difficult to dismiss and rewards late investigation.
- [pitfall] Investigations fail from missing the moment evidence is available, not from lacking it; traces degrade or become unreadable, so late discovery may arrive too late. When: An investigation stalls despite evidence existing. Why: Traces can be lost or cease to be readable after a limited time; hidden evidence may lose value before it is found. (x2)
- [pitfall] Introducing a critical fact, decisive clue or new person only at the reveal or climax feels arbitrary and cheats, since the audience cannot check it against earlier clues. Why: The audience cannot check it against anything shown earlier and could not have reached the answer from what it saw.
- [pitfall] A count taken after an item has left its owner's control cannot establish a baseline for a dispute.
- [pitfall] Narrative pressure from a locked room feels unfair when the key's whereabouts are unclear.
- [pitfall] Evidence gathered late and in poor light is partial, and once disposed of by others it cannot be recovered.

## means and motive
- [mechanism] Several suspects can each satisfy every apparent requirement of guilt while being innocent, because weak individual links can look persuasive when accumulated. When: A case has many suspects with circumstantial evidence. Why: Each thin link appears stronger in combination than it is alone.
- [mechanism] A strong motive combined with no provable alibi can build a convincing case against a person who is innocent. When: when a suspect has a clear motive but cannot confirm their whereabouts. Why: Motive and unverifiable alibi together create an apparently complete case.
- [heuristic] Pair the method of the act with its motive when disclosing the solution, so the audience understands both. When: at the final reveal.
- [heuristic] Matching amounts between two people's payments can reveal a hidden link, such as dependence or a secret deal. When: when two people's finances show regular, matching flows.
- [heuristic] Ask how the suspect came to hold the agent at that moment; a proposed mechanism without a means of access remains unsupported.
- [heuristic] Reason about means from the victim's surroundings, since an alternative tool is likely to exist nearby and the suspect may know of it. When: When the primary means is unrecovered or unclear. Why: Familiar environments supply tools that people can use.
- [heuristic] Link a poison to a workplace or to the suspect's training, such as a firm that uses the substance or a chemistry background, to establish means.
- [heuristic] Give each suspect a motive and an opportunity, and let a new witness reframe a relationship so the player reconsiders motive. When: Designing suspects for a mystery. Why: Opportunity plus motive gives the player grounds to test each suspect.
- [heuristic] In a suspicion analysis, weigh motive, knowledge of the setting, and opportunity separately; a suspect who has all three is the strongest candidate even without proof. When: A case has a sincere-seeming ally who knows much about the victim and setting. Why: Combining the three factors narrows suspicion.
- [procedure] 1) State what the act was meant to achieve. 2) Identify the outcome that serves that purpose. 3) Look for the person who needed that outcome. 4) Match the motive to the actor who carried the act out, which may differ from the beneficiary. When: An act's purpose is clear but its doer is not. Why: Narrowing suspects by purpose targets the person who needed the result.
- [pitfall] Naming a hidden mastermind without evidence can send an investigation after the wrong person. When: Suspecting a concealed controlling figure. Why: A suspicion without support diverts attention from the people actually involved.
- [pitfall] The most visible motive can still be false, so a motive alone should not settle the question. When: A suspect has an obvious motive. Why: Visibility of a motive does not establish that it caused the event.
- [pitfall] Opportunity alone does not show motive, and motive alone does not show access. Each category must be established as a separate deduction.

## physical evidence and containers
- [mechanism] A place where used containers accumulate in order works as a log that can be checked later, preserving a history of use. When: used containers are kept in sequence. Why: stock order records what was used and when.
- [behavior] Burning a document removes its content but leaves residue such as cinders, and an observer can read that residue as proof the document was burned. When: A character destroys evidence in a visible place. Why: Destruction by fire leaves physical traces that can be inspected after the act.
- [rule] Check every container and packet at a scene for names, since an overlooked one can implicate a third party.
- [heuristic] Pair an object that seems to confirm a theory with one that contradicts it, so neither evidence settles the question alone.
- [heuristic] Among a set of similar items, compare appearances to find the one that differs, and test that one first. When: Several near-identical items may hide something. Why: A difference in appearance flags the item most likely to hold a hidden property.
- [heuristic] Make the container itself the evidence: a labelled item shown early can hold the key document, teaching players to inspect objects rather than only their contents. When: Designing a document-based clue. Why: Players focus on what they see, and inspecting the container reveals the hidden evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Read a vehement or self-contradictory document twice. 2) Compare it with the writer's earlier statements. 3) Note any change in tone or claim. 4) Ask what happened between the two statements.
- [tradeoff] Destroyed documents can still be recovered through the leads they name, but when a destroyed physical artifact cannot be examined, only the destroyer's account remains. When: Key evidence is destroyed: recovery works if other sources name leads; if no other record survives, verification depends on the destroyer. Why: Leads named in a document exist independently of it, but without the physical record, claims cannot be verified.
- [pitfall] Do not assume a debris pile holds evidence; examine it before claiming any clue from it.
- [pitfall] Accepting a recurring correlation as a cause before running a test risks a wrong conclusion. When: When a pattern matches a trigger but the mechanism is unknown. Why: Matching timing does not prove that the trigger produces the effect.
- [pitfall] Sweeping every surface evenly can dilute the one spot that matters, so a general sample reads clean even when the trace is present.
- [fact] A match between identical common items is consistent with a theory but not conclusive, because such items are widespread. When: Weighing a match between two common objects. Why: Widespread items appear in many places, so a match alone does not identify an owner.
- [fact] Who finds an item, and when, is itself part of the evidentiary record and can carry meaning. When: Interpreting the discovery of a clue. Why: The finder's identity and timing can reveal access, intent or opportunity.

## plan intent inference
- [mechanism] A scheme that sets two enemies against each other works by predicting each one's habits, so each motive and habit becomes a link in the plan. When: when a planner manipulates several targets.
- [behavior] A persistent fixed idea can reverse a settled plan, so a character's stated intention is a weak predictor of what they will actually do. When: A character has decided on an act but is preoccupied with a thought. Why: An obsessive thought can take over the decision that was already made.
- [rule] Investigate toward a defined goal with a plan rather than reacting to whatever detail or action comes next.
- [rule] Test a circumstantial case against physical facts before acting on it, such as planning a confrontation with a suspect. When: A plan depends on a theory built from indirect evidence. Why: Acting on an untested theory risks losing the chance to confirm it.
- [rule] Place a survey plan or diagram where a player can find it, so it can confirm a place's identity when a label conflicts. When: A location has conflicting labels. Why: Documentary layout resolves naming conflicts.
- [rule] Separate a suspect's plan from its outcome, so that a correct suspicion of intent can still be wrong about what actually happened. When: a suspect is correctly suspected of a plan. Why: the plan and its result may differ, creating a late surprise.
- [heuristic] A mismatch between stated plans and actual whereabouts, such as a missed engagement, is a warning sign worth investigating. Why: People who skip planned events may have been doing something else.
- [heuristic] A planned schedule, such as a pre-booked transport or a set meeting, shows what each person expected to happen, which is evidence of intent.
- [heuristic] Separate the planner of a crime from the actor who carries it out; each role has its own route, motive and distaste for violence. When: when a crime involves more than one person. Why: roles differ in knowledge, exposure and willingness to harm.
- [heuristic] An appointment made for a time when a house is empty suggests planning and a known visitor. When: When a visit occurs at a time chosen to avoid witnesses. Why: Choosing an empty time indicates prior knowledge and intent.
- [pitfall] Careless details, such as a payment left with a victim, can link the planner to the scene; one forgotten item can undo an elaborate deception.
- [pitfall] A planner's own account can itself be part of the plant, and exposure of that account would expose the planner. Why: self-reports are shaped by the planner's aims.
- [fact] Skill at planning a crime does not guarantee care with money, so careless spending can betray even a clever offender.

## private confrontation and motive
- [behavior] A character who distrusts ordinary communication may send messages by a private route, and that choice reveals what the sender fears. When: A character suspects the household post is monitored. Why: Fear of interception drives use of a private route.
- [behavior] Individuals may use a public crisis to settle a private score, so a public accusation can hide a personal motive. When: A community is in a time of accusation or fear. Why: Crisis lowers the cost of accusing and gives private hostility a public outlet.
- [rule] Tie a private appeal to a concrete request, so its flattery has a visible motive the player can exploit or expose.
- [heuristic] Question a subject alone, or send witnesses away before a confrontation, to get an unguarded, candid account, since others' presence can shape or distort the response. When: When a subject's account or reaction may be shaped or distorted by the presence of others. Why: Without an audience, the subject speaks and reacts more freely.
- [heuristic] When a culprit's motive is personal and emotional rather than criminal, let that motive explain the act and keep the resolution private and lenient. When: When the culprit's motive is personal rather than criminal.
- [heuristic] A witness's account of how she learned a non-public fact can reveal a private channel between people and show that she treated the information as secret.
- [heuristic] A suspect who names a private detail that no one told them is stronger evidence than a vision alone; grade such a clue above unverifiable sightings.
- [heuristic] When the culprit has social standing, end with a private confrontation rather than a public arrest, to keep the resolution contained. When: When the guilty party is a respected or socially prominent figure. Why: A private resolution avoids a public trial while still closing the case.
- [procedure] 1) Put a precise accusation to the suspect in private. 2) Describe the suspect's actions step by step until the suspect believes he was observed. 3) Set terms and a deadline. When: When a suspect has a hidden motive and strong interest in keeping it secret. Why: A precise account of observed actions makes denial less credible and pressures the suspect to bargain.
- [procedure] 1) Call the suspect in alone. 2) Promise that nothing said will be repeated. 3) Walk through the reasoning. 4) Give a clear chance to confess. When: a confession is needed without public scandal.
- [pitfall] A motive that depends on a suspect's private history may be hard to prove.
- [pitfall] Giving accusers private communication with the examiner before and during hearings lets their views shape the outcome out of sight.
- [fact] A private diary listing grievances reveals its writer's temperament as much as the claims it makes.

## recorded observations and times
- [mechanism] A dialogue challenge that cites an observation the player has recorded can change the NPC's reaction, so earlier discovery alters the conversation.
- [rule] Record event times and durations as they occur, and record each witness's answer to time questions; precise logged times, like a call time, beat general recollection. When: Collecting times or durations during an investigation. Why: Recorded times can be compared and checked, while recalled times drift. (x2)
- [rule] Record witnessed exits in world state so later NPCs can confirm or deny that the player left through the door. When: When tracking movement through a guarded exit.
- [rule] Record which NPCs name an event before it is announced, and let the player notice the slip. When: When designing scenes where news breaks.
- [rule] A dialogue system should record an NPC's stated basis for a claim so that later questions can contradict it.
- [rule] Record gaps about a companion the witness saw poorly instead of filling them in. When: a witness saw a companion only partly. Why: filling gaps creates false detail.
- [rule] Store each household's ties and known quarrels in game data so the player can deduce motive from the network of relationships. When: Building a community with accusations or conflicts. Why: A visible network lets the player reason about motive without a stated confession.
- [heuristic] Record a visitor's habitual pattern, such as using only one hand or keeping a limb in a pocket, as evidence to compare later.
- [heuristic] A fact nobody recorded or observed cannot carry evidential weight, so verify whether a key fact was actually witnessed. When: Judging whether a key fact can support a conclusion. Why: Unobserved facts give no basis for inference.
- [procedure] 1) Stay hidden where the speakers cannot see you. 2) Hold their exact words in mind. 3) Write them down as soon as possible while memory is fresh. When: when a concealed listener needs overheard talk to count as evidence. Why: Exact, prompt recall keeps overheard talk usable later.
- [pitfall] Trying to record every detail overloads the investigator; keep only details that answer an open question.
- [pitfall] A concealed witness who adds no new information makes the surprise read as a cheat.
- [fact] Recorded descriptions of people seen at a location, such as an inn, let players identify a forger later.

## reveal consistency and logic
- [behavior] A reveal hits hardest when the hidden figure has been an object of dread, because the fear is reversed when the mask falls. When: a masked figure has been presented as threatening.
- [rule] Do not introduce facts at the final explanation that earlier material never showed; confirm only clues already shown. When: Writing the final explanation of a mystery, including a late reveal that closes a sequence of partial accounts. Why: New facts feel arbitrary and break fair play; the player should feel the answer was earned from evidence already seen. (x2)
- [rule] Follow an empty reveal with a brief, flat line from a character that confirms the reversal without extra explanation. When: After a reversal has been shown. Why: Restraint lets the image carry the meaning.
- [rule] Explain the purpose of a concealed action only afterwards, once the moment has passed.
- [rule] Drive each correction of the audience's belief with a new witness or document rather than with the protagonist's reasoning alone.
- [rule] Do not reverse established roles without showing evidence for the new reading; the reversal must be earned by what the audience has already seen. When: Revealing that an apparent aggressor is the one being manipulated. Why: An unsupported reversal reads as a cheat rather than a surprise.
- [heuristic] End a reveal by returning to a wider setting, moving the resolution from the single case to a larger situation.
- [heuristic] An unmasked person may be the genuine identity rather than an impostor, so check the legal status before treating the reveal as fraud. When: A disguise is removed and the person is revealed.
- [heuristic] Plant small mechanical contrivances early, such as a cord, a lamp or a locked door, so they can be re-read and explained in one chain at the reveal. When: Planning clues that will be explained later. Why: Earlier small details that pay off in one explanation make the reveal feel complete and fair.
- [pitfall] A reveal that contradicts earlier scenes breaks reader trust in the whole structure, so it must match what was already shown.
- [pitfall] A delayed reveal fails unless the audience already has enough information to imagine what lies behind the door. When: when withholding a reveal. Why: Without context the wait reads as confusion rather than suspense.
- [pitfall] Omitting the step from a planted object to the suspect it points to leaves the solution feeling arbitrary. Why: The audience cannot follow the link that justifies the conclusion.
- [pitfall] A reversal without earlier planted evidence feels arbitrary, and accusing the wrong person in a crowd can let the real culprit escape.

## role labels and knowledge
- [definition] A role index pairs each person with the pages where they appear and a role label, such as arrest, examination, trial, execution, or excommunication.
- [behavior] Someone playing a role often betrays it through actions that depart from a real resident's routine, such as entering a familiar place without the expected ease. When: When observing someone claiming a familiar place or identity. Why: Real routines are habitual, while a role must be consciously performed.
- [rule] Group characters by role topics such as afflicted or confessors, and use those groupings to decide which characters the player is told to watch.
- [rule] Compare a character's claimed role with observed behavior; if the role implies one conduct and the observed conduct differs, treat the mismatch as a contradiction to pursue. Why: Conduct inconsistent with a stated role exposes a false claim or hidden motive.
- [heuristic] Keep speech and conduct consistent with the assumed role, since outward plausibility often does more than detailed questioning. When: Maintaining a cover during an investigation. Why: Plausible conduct keeps the cover intact without constant probing.
- [heuristic] Give a character only the knowledge that serves their role, because irrelevant facts blur their profile and crowd out useful ones. Why: A focused knowledge set makes the character's purpose legible.
- [heuristic] Read trace features such as print size, stride and boldness of movement together to infer who assisted and who acted. When: Several people left traces at one scene. Why: Combined movement features indicate roles.
- [heuristic] Count the roles a plot requires separately from the people visible in it; a threat that seems to need several parties may need only one. When: a threat appears to need several outside parties. Why: one person can fill more than one role.
- [heuristic] A person's seat or role determines which stage he could have witnessed, so check who sat where before judging whether he was present. When: inferring whether an official saw a particular stage.
- [heuristic] Judge an official or witness by their practical role in proceedings, not only by public reputation, which can hide real influence. When: assessing how much an official shaped a proceeding.
- [pitfall] Treating a partial participant as the main offender, or the reverse, leads to wrong expectations about who will respond and what they know. Why: a character's role determines their likely behavior and knowledge.
- [pitfall] Eliminating a suspect because their role seems to rule them out, without checking the timing, can wrongly clear the guilty.
- [fact] A role label records what happened to a person but not why it happened.

## route reconstruction
- [rule] Test a witness's described route against physical evidence, such as the state of a door or wall, before accepting the route. When: A witness describes how someone entered or left. Why: A route that conflicts with the scene signals an inaccurate or false account.
- [rule] Provide a physical route that fits the thief's size, so the solution can be checked against the environment. When: designing the entry solution of a locked-room mystery. Why: A checkable physical route makes the solution verifiable in play.
- [heuristic] A fugitive who avoids busy lit streets, cuts through gaps and goes around obstacles likely knows the area. Why: Route choices reveal familiarity with the local layout.
- [heuristic] Reconstruct a substitution method by asking what each participant had to do at each step of the route. When: Investigating a staged route or alibi. Why: Stepwise reconstruction exposes the required actions and the people who performed them.
- [heuristic] Check the stops along a suspect's route for places where an object could be left, collected or handed over. When: A suspect's movements are tracked and an object may have moved with them. Why: A stop on a route can serve as a hidden drop point for moving an object.
- [heuristic] Infer a movement route from the street layout and from the only direction a site can be reached. When: reconstructing how a prisoner or cart travelled. Why: terrain and street plans constrain possible paths.
- [heuristic] Judge each entry route by how easy it is, how noisy it would be, and who could have observed it, rather than accepting the first plausible one.
- [procedure] 1) Find objects away from the body. 2) Confirm each object's owner, for example through servants or records. 3) Order the finds along a plausible route. 4) Check the route against the layout, such as tunnels, gates and roads. When: a trace is found away from the body.
- [procedure] 1) Mark a trail by blazing trees or cutting bark. 2) Clear brush so horses can pass; where roots or stones block the way, the track is a bridle-path. 3) Widen it for ox-carts, making it a road. 4) Add gates or bars where it crosses fenced land. 5) Fence both sides to make a public highway. When: describing how a route matured over time.
- [procedure] 1) Collect dated, checkable events: asset sales, cash withdrawals, transport changes, and last sightings. 2) Order them by time. 3) Mark the point where the record stops as the place to begin the search. When: A person has vanished and the record ends at a known point. Why: A chain of dated events shows where the trail goes cold and where to look next.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the final resting place. 2) Follow the water route upstream toward the likely starting point. 3) Confirm the route against the layout of the surroundings. When: A body or object was moved by water. Why: Backward reasoning from the endpoint narrows the starting location.
- [fact] Traces such as remains, ruts and debris accumulate over time. Read in sequence, they reveal a route and what happened along it, even without a witness.
- [fact] A multi-stop route limits where an item could first have been sent, so the posting port narrows where to search. When: tracing an item through a multi-stop route.

## stalled investigations
- [mechanism] A stop order from a higher authority can end a case even while lower officials are still scheduled to sit. When: a higher authority rules on the admissibility of a case's evidence.
