- [behavior] A person who knows a secret but cannot prove it is stuck: plans of exposure fail and the accuser fears punishment for an unsupported claim. When: an accuser has knowledge but no corroboration. Why: Anger has no outlet without evidence, and an unsupported accusation can backfire.
- [rule] An investigator who recognises their own strong emotion should step back or hand the case to someone else.
- [rule] Stop pressing a witness once they refuse to say more.
- [rule] Stop widening the candidate list once a candidate is confirmed, since further widening only adds noise.
- [rule] Show the investigation failing to find evidence before staging the trap, so the trap feels necessary and believable. When: Building toward a sting or lure in a mystery. Why: A visible lack of physical proof justifies a staged approach.
- [heuristic] When a case stalls, identify which element is missing (motive, method or victim identity) and pursue that gap first. When: when a case seems stuck.
- [pitfall] An approach can stall for days if the target keeps avoiding the same room, and a spoiled first impression may need repair before contact works.
- [pitfall] Stopping at the first objection misses later flaws in the same theory, so keep testing after one failure.
- [pitfall] Delaying a reveal too long can cost the audience's attention. When: building suspense before a reveal. Why: Excess waiting breaks the momentum that suspense depends on.
- [pitfall] Too many time gaps without new evidence make an investigation feel stalled.
- [pitfall] A hint repeated without development becomes a stalled thread rather than a motive.
- [pitfall] A plan that relies on the culprit's error fails if the culprit stays quiet, so the investigation needs another route. When: Designing a trap that depends on a suspect acting. Why: A careful suspect may simply do nothing, leaving the case stalled.

## surveillance and records
- [definition] A surveillance log is a day-by-day timeline of a suspect's visits, meetings, meals, calls and money movements, with times, places, companions and contacts, read as a sequence.
- [definition] Surveillance means posting a watcher at a fixed point, such as a house opposite, to record a suspect's movements and contacts over time.
- [mechanism] A photographer's studio records can identify a portrait's sitter and supply the sitter's address. When: an unknown person appears in a photograph. Why: studios keep sitter details.
- [mechanism] Store each claimed detail, such as place, time and companion, so the player can later compare an NPC's statements against other evidence. When: designing NPC dialogue and quest state.
- [heuristic] Surveillance shows behavior but rarely proves contact; use it to test what a suspect does next, not to confirm a link.
- [heuristic] Organise case notes into one record per person plus one for loose facts, so contradictions between accounts become visible. When: from the first day of an investigation, when facts arrive unsorted. Why: Separate records make conflicting statements easy to compare.
- [procedure] Trace the chain of succession by asking who inherits if the present heir dies, since title and land may pass along a fixed line. When: an heir stands to gain from a death. Why: A successor beyond the heir can also be a motive holder.
- [procedure] 1) Watch the target over a long period from a hidden vantage. 2) Wait for a single window of opportunity. 3) Act in that window and remove traces afterward.
- [procedure] 1) Identify each beneficiary's share. 2) When one beneficiary dies, check whether their share passes equally to the others. 3) Recalculate what each survivor would receive if only one remains. When: when a series of deaths might be linked to inheritance. Why: survivorship clauses shift shares as beneficiaries die.
- [pitfall] Cases that left a documentary trail may not represent the rest; surviving records can give a distorted picture of how common an event was.
- [pitfall] A watch that begins after an event will miss an entry that happened before it started. When: Relying on surveillance to bound a time window. Why: Coverage gaps before the watch leave the earlier window unobserved.
- [fact] Documented facts such as sworn statements, a medical certificate, a funeral and recognition by family outweigh interpretations of a witness's mental state. When: a claim is judged on the record. Why: checkable records resist psychological explanation.
- [fact] Partial physical records can survive destruction, and a fragment such as an unburned edge can still carry a date or detail that anchors a reconstruction.

## timing of action
- [rule] Let an informant's stated fatigue limit how many questions can be asked in one session. When: When designing an informant scene.
- [heuristic] Establish the order in which people were woken and where they went first, since that sequence reveals who was alerted. When: reconstructing a night's events.
- [heuristic] When a witness cannot supply key timing facts, question the people who handled transport or logistics, since they may give more direct evidence. When: Timing facts are needed and the peripheral witnesses are unhelpful. Why: People directly involved in logistics tend to know schedules and timings more precisely.
- [heuristic] Payment for a shady arrangement is typically made in advance, before the outcome, when the payer can no longer back out. When: Assessing when a covert payment is likely to occur. Why: Paying early locks in the agreement and reduces the payer's option to withdraw.
- [heuristic] Being woken abruptly can be a timing clue suggesting that another party acted at a specific moment. When: when a character's sleep is interrupted during an event. Why: The interruption fixes when outside action occurred.
- [heuristic] Estimate how long a cause needs to act, using a comparable test, and count that delay when placing events; an apparently late event may have begun earlier. When: an event's timing depends on how long a cause takes to take effect. Why: a cause may act slowly, so the observed time is not the start time.
- [tradeoff] A surprise arrest while the suspect is off-guard leaves no time for a prepared defence, but acting on presumption alone risks a wrongful arrest that cannot be undone. When: when deciding whether to arrest before evidence is complete. Why: Speed favours the investigator only when the evidence is already sound.
- [tradeoff] Acting at once keeps momentum but risks rushed conclusions; a reflective pause yields clearer reasoning but can invite wild guesses while it lasts. When: choosing between immediate action and reconsidering an open case.
- [pitfall] A locked door explained too quickly loses its tension, so an unexplained cause should stay open for a while. Why: Premature explanation removes the uncertainty that drives the scene.
- [pitfall] Acting early against a small agent lets the larger figure escape.
- [pitfall] Reading a room too quickly causes obvious traces in plain sight to be missed.
- [pitfall] Delivering news in a way that signals its significance can alert the suspect before the planned moment.
- [fact] An accusation, warrant, arrest and examination can all occur within a single night, so a false accusation can escalate very quickly.

## trust and deception
- [behavior] Witnesses are more likely to share sensitive information after the questioner states a clear purpose and offers a verifiable identity. When: When a witness is initially reluctant to disclose a location or private fact. Why: Trust depends on the questioner appearing legitimate and transparent.
- [behavior] Nonverbal reactions from an expert, such as a dismissive gesture, signal doubt and let the audience gauge how far each expert is trusted. When: Experts disagree and their reactions are shown. Why: Reactions reveal trust levels without explicit statements.
- [behavior] A victim who trusts the person delivering a claim and cannot easily verify it is likely to accept the staged story. When: The victim cannot check the document or destination directly. Why: Trust removes the motive to question the claim.
- [heuristic] Build a character's sympathy in plain sight, such as sincere principles stated in a calm scene, then invert it as hidden facts surface so the exposure lands with force. Why: The reader accepts the virtue at face value, so the reversal contradicts a belief the reader actually held. (x2)
- [heuristic] Let the hired protector become part of the trap, so the character the reader trusts is the means of the theft. When: writing a mystery where the victim hires help. Why: Betraying trust reverses the reader's expectation of safety.
- [tradeoff] A trusted NPC's result can be correct only if the player verifies the process, so reliance on the NPC's reputation trades speed for risk of error. When: When designing a puzzle where an NPC provides a test result. Why: Trust can hide a gap in the procedure, and verification costs time.
- [tradeoff] Sympathy can open information to the player while lowering their guard, a tradeoff that a trust or composure meter on an NPC can model.
- [pitfall] Trusting a sales pitch, staff assurance or credible source's attributed claim stops checking; omitted parts or wrong attribution carry forward unless tested. Why: Trust in the source stops the reader from testing the claim. (x2)
- [pitfall] Looking only at total gain and ignoring the order of events misses how a sequence can shift a claim. When: Analyzing a motive tied to multiple events. Why: Gain depends on sequence as well as amount.
- [pitfall] Accepting the appearance of a natural cause without checking the mechanism behind it allows a planned act to pass as fate. When: Judging whether an event was accidental. Why: Appearances can be arranged to match a natural cause, so only the mechanism reveals the truth.
- [pitfall] Asking a helpful witness for favours spends their trust; abusing it can end their cooperation and damage later investigation. When: when relying on a sympathetic character to deliver a favour. Why: Cooperation depends on trust, which is finite and easily lost.
- [pitfall] Judging a witness's reliability by appearance or social status, rather than by checkable position, leads to accepting false testimony. When: Assessing whether a witness can be trusted. Why: Appearance and status do not establish where a witness actually was or what they saw.
- [pitfall] An unusually good offer can be a lure: its oddities may hide a fabricated identity or a trap, so such offers should be treated as clues rather than luck. When: A character offers an unusually favourable deal. Why: The offer conceals a motive, and its oddities expose it.

## verdicts and endings
- [mechanism] A closing clinical verdict can reframe an unexplained supernatural cause as a symptom, leaving the reader unable to tell whether the cause was real.
- [behavior] Once a guilty verdict is on record, later testimony is read as confirming it, even when that testimony is ambiguous. When: a mystery where the accusation is settled before the investigation is shown. Why: a prior conclusion changes how every later clue is interpreted.
- [rule] End a threat's resolution with an unresolved personal cost, so the aftermath keeps weight after the danger is removed. When: When closing a scenario whose threat is banished. Why: A lingering consequence gives the ending emotional weight beyond the defeat of the threat.
- [rule] When a loud player or NPC action draws no response, make its cause checkable: alert systems off, sound masked, or NPCs complicit. A second test action can reveal which. When: Designing a game reaction to a noisy action that no character notices. Why: Unexplained silence confuses players, while a testable cause lets them reason to an answer.
- [rule] Let the final accuser reason to a conclusion they cannot prove, so the player's uncertainty carries into the next scene. When: closing a mystery arc. Why: An unproven ending keeps the central question open.
- [heuristic] End with the underlying mystery unexplained so the player's own reasoning completes the story; the formal question may be settled while the final deed stays unnamed. (x2)
- [heuristic] Unmasking a human source does not have to end the threat. A continuing effect after exposure keeps tension and resists a clean ending.
- [heuristic] Treat a suspect's wish to commit a crime and their resolve to carry it out as separate elements; a wish alone does not show a plan. When: Testimony gives a motive but no physical proof.
- [heuristic] Hold a question open with a small unexplained act, so investigators keep playing after the main mystery seems answered. When: Closing a mystery without a full reveal. Why: A lingering unexplained detail sustains curiosity and motivates continued play.
- [heuristic] Vary outcomes across a series of similar cases, such as acquittal, release on bond, reprieve, and execution, so the pattern does not become predictable. When: Several encounters share one formula and the same resolution would repeat. Why: Predictable endings let the player stop investigating and simply expect the same result.
- [tradeoff] A verdict of Not Proven leaves the player with doubt and a new objective, whereas a clear explanation closes the question; the first sustains investigation, the second ends it. When: Choosing how an investigation's formal outcome should end. Why: An ambiguous outcome keeps the question open and motivates further play.
- [tradeoff] Leaving some guilty parties unpunished makes the ending feel earned rather than tidy, but it can frustrate players who expect justice. When: writing the aftermath. Why: Partial justice reads as realistic, at the cost of satisfaction.
- [pitfall] A verdict resting on an accusation with no independent corroboration is fragile; a lie can stay hidden until after an irreversible act. When: a trial relies on one witness. Why: Nothing tests the testimony before action is taken.

## witness cooperation and courtesy
- [behavior] A witness eager to help grows less forthcoming over time, and may hold back facts they shared freely at first. When: the cooperative witness is interviewed later rather than immediately. Why: Their zeal cools, so later interviews yield less than the first meeting.
- [behavior] A witness can steer conversation toward general reflections to keep it away from the case itself.
- [rule] Do not count two accounts as corroboration if the witnesses might have coordinated their stories.
- [rule] Give a reluctant witness a graceful exit, such as a pause or withdrawal to another room, so they can regroup and return on their own terms. When: A witness is distressed mid-interview. Why: Space lets the witness recover and makes their return more candid.
- [heuristic] Blunt demands make reluctant witnesses and suspects evasive; courteous, apologetic questioning in their own language lowers guard, so they share more detail even while pressing for facts. When: Witness or suspect is hostile, evasive, or defensive. Why: Disarmed people are less guarded and cooperate more; manner and rapport affect how readily a witness speaks.
- [heuristic] Open an interview with a courteous, non-threatening tone, since a comfortable witness talks more; a severe manner can soften into a kind one once rapport forms. When: a witness is cooperative but reserved. Why: comfort makes the witness talkative and willing to volunteer detail.
- [heuristic] A courteous request for a handover signature may still be taken as an accusation, but the procedure should be followed anyway. When: requesting custody marks from people who handled an item.
- [heuristic] Frame a question as shared interest in stopping a wrongdoer, since suggesting the suspect's name is being misused can win cooperation. When: A witness is initially hostile or defensive. Why: Appealing to a shared interest lowers the witness's resistance.
- [heuristic] Remarks let fall in casual conversation can support belief without proof, which pushes the audience to look for a physical or documentary link. When: the solution rests on offhand remarks. Why: hints create belief but not demonstration.
- [heuristic] Several messages that all point to the same suspect group suggest coordinated misdirection rather than independent reports.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the holder of records for permission to examine them rather than demanding access. 2) Frame the request around a third party's transactions, not a named suspect. 3) Let the holder reach the suspicion himself. 4) Share only the case detail the auditor needs. When: A records holder is willing but reluctant to speak about a suspect. Why: Framing protects the holder from appearing to inform and keeps the request neutral.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a trusted intermediary who understands the witness to explain the real aim. 2) Wait a day. 3) Let the witness speak freely without interruption. 4) Do not laugh at trifling details. When: Interviewing a witness who is ashamed, distrustful, or unable to recall on direct questions. Why: A trusted intermediary lowers the witness's guard, and the witness will share small details only if they are not mocked.
- [fact] A courteous verdict can still be a strong condemnation in substance, so judge the content rather than the tone.

## witness observation versus interpretation
- [mechanism] A brief obstruction that pauses a moving person can give a watcher time to see an object dropped and picked up by someone else.
- [behavior] Real witnesses blend what they saw with what they concluded, so testimony mixes observation and inference rather than giving exact, formal descriptions. When: taking testimony from a witness.
- [behavior] Witnesses can report the same observed symptoms yet reach different interpretations, and a confident wrong explanation can shape what they do next. When: Several characters describe one shared observation. Why: People attach their own assumptions to observations, so identical facts yield divergent conclusions.
- [behavior] Witnesses of an impossible event may stay unsure whether to believe their own senses when no mechanism is given to settle the doubt. When: after witnessing an impossible event. Why: no explanation is available to resolve what was seen.
- [rule] Separate a witness's observations (saw, heard) from inferences and feelings, and check each against what they could actually know; feelings are not evidence. When: when a witness reports an event, states a conclusion, or is emotional. Why: Each kind of perception has different reliability; conclusions and emotions can outrun what was perceived. (x2)
- [rule] Separate a witness's assumptions and general impressions from firm observations; treat recall under brief, faint, or poor views cautiously, recording them as tentative impressions, not identifications. When: Taking testimony about events or appearances; when a sighting rests on a brief or poor view. Why: Assumptions often enter memory and get reported as observations; confident testimony can exceed what was perceived.
- [rule] Ask witnesses for their impressions as well as their facts, since interpretation is part of testimony.
- [rule] Give each witness a stated vantage point so the reader can judge what they could and could not have observed. When: Presenting witness testimony in a mystery. Why: Knowing the vantage point lets the reader weigh silence and conflicts correctly.
- [heuristic] A witness's report of nothing unusual, or a vivid detailed account, reflects only their view and attention; ask what lay outside their frame. When: When a witness's report is taken as proof nothing happened, or a detailed account is taken as the whole story. Why: Observation is limited to the witness's position and attention; a detailed account can still omit the decisive moment.
- [heuristic] Letting the player stand where a witness stood and view what was visible from there teaches sightline reasoning and tests the witness's account.
- [procedure] 1) Identify what the witness directly observed. 2) Verify that observation against physical facts. 3) Evaluate the witness's explanation separately, since interpretation can change on later reflection; apply extra scrutiny if the witness has a grievance. When: Weighing testimony that mixes observed facts with explanations or identifications. Why: An observation can be accurate while the interpretation built on it is wrong; sensory facts are firmer than the cause assigned to them.
- [procedure] 1) Present the plain observed facts first. 2) Present the writer's analysis separately. 3) Let the reader check one against the other. When: when a found text mixes events and interpretation. Why: Separating the two lets the reader test the interpretation against what was actually seen.
- [fact] A witness may report speech or actions they could not see directly, such as through thin walls or a shared space, so their knowledge is limited by vantage point. When: Assessing what a witness could have perceived. Why: Sound and sightline limits restrict what a witness can know firsthand.

## absent witnesses and testimony
- [behavior] A missing person leaves no physical trace in a busy room, so a failed search there tells little about whether the person was present. When: When a search fails in a crowded or busy location. Why: Many people and movements erase traces, and a search can miss a person who left.
- [rule] A key witness who vanishes, especially after handling a key object, is a central lead; do not accept a theory relying on them without asking why they are absent. When: A key witness cannot be found, does not testify, or vanishes after contact with a key object. Why: Disappearance removes the chance to verify the account, and a central witness's absence may itself be evidence.
- [rule] The absence of people who could have been witnesses, by chance, does not clear a suspect.
- [rule] In a case file or quest log, leave a key witness statement absent so a player who notices the gap can go find the missing testimony. When: Designing investigation content with missing evidence. Why: Noticing a gap prompts the player to seek the missing information.
- [heuristic] Give a clear reason for why witnesses are absent, so the audience does not question why no one checks the scene. When: Staging a scene where bystanders are removed. Why: Unexplained absence breaks plausibility.
- [heuristic] If nearby helpers would have come had they been allowed, their absence is informative and suggests they were prevented. When: A request for help or a visit went unfulfilled. Why: Expected presence gives a testable baseline.
- [heuristic] A witness who passed the location and did not notice an item suggests the item may not have been there when they passed. When: Checking whether a found item was present at a given time. Why: A person who walked the spot would ordinarily have seen a conspicuous object.
- [heuristic] A fixed-position witness who saw no one enter or leave during an interval bounds when access was possible. When: checking who could have reached the scene. Why: Absence of sightings closes windows of possible access.
- [heuristic] A vanished witness with no record on file can be the pressure point that forces the player to reconsider earlier testimony.
- [pitfall] A witness who was not watching a spot, or failed to describe someone, cannot prove nothing happened or nobody was there; the gap stays open. When: A witness claims nothing could have passed unseen or nobody was seen. Why: Witnesses cannot observe places they were not positioned to watch, and crowded places can hide people.
- [pitfall] When the official holding the warrant is absent, accusations can spread largely unchecked. When: When the authority who signs detentions is away from proceedings. Why: No one with power over warrants reviews the accusations.
- [pitfall] A witness who is awake but paralysed can report only what happens around them, so gaps in their knowledge remain. When: A narrator is incapacitated and relies on their account. Why: Limited perception leaves events outside view unknown.

## body position and movement
- [mechanism] Moving a body or item toward a door versus a hiding spot can encode whether the actor sought help or concealment, giving a readable choice to interpret. When: Designing a scene where a body or item is moved. Why: Direction of movement carries an interpretable intent.
- [mechanism] Moving a body away from the scene can delay its discovery rather than hide where the crime happened, so the timing of discovery is itself a clue.
- [mechanism] A victim's physical state at discovery, such as warm body temperature, bounds how recently the act happened and narrows the window of the crime. When: a body is found and examined. Why: physical cooling rates give a measurable elapsed-time estimate.
- [rule] Check the body's position against the wound; a posture that prevents the hand reaching the wound argues against self-infliction. When: when deciding between suicide and homicide from an injury. Why: Posture can make a self-inflicted wound physically impossible.
- [heuristic] Body position and orientation relative to doors and objects can show how an event happened and the direction the victim was moving. When: When reading a body at a scene. Why: Position records movement and force that the scene itself may not show.
- [heuristic] Body position after an injury can show the sequence of a struggle, such as a blow from behind that catches a crouching person. When: A body is found at a scene with signs of violence. Why: Posture at impact reflects the victim's stance and the attacker's direction.
- [heuristic] Follow a trail in both directions; prints that lead in but none that lead out point to where the subject stopped or stayed.
- [heuristic] Compare the body's location with the wound and the scene; a lack of blood at the site suggests the killing happened somewhere else. When: The body's location seems inconsistent with the wound. Why: Blood at a death site reflects where the fatal event occurred.
- [procedure] 1) Watch institutional intake for a body of similar build. 2) Swap it for the victim's body at the point of storage. 3) Move the victim's body to where the substitute would be found. 4) Alter the features others will check. When: When a concealment plan relies on a body already held by an institution. Why: Each step removes a link between the killer and the body while placing the substitute where expected.
- [tradeoff] A route that stays on open ground leaves traces, while a route over roofs in rain is screened. Route choice trades physical exposure against difficulty. When: When moving a body without being seen. Why: Concealment cover reduces observation but may make the route harder or riskier.
- [pitfall] A body may be in a state that contradicts the scene's story, such as being alive under a drug, so check its condition against the timeline. When: when a body is assumed to be dead. Why: appearances can mislead about condition.
- [fact] A body found at a set time gives the latest possible time of death, while the last confirmed sighting alive gives the earliest.

## conditional inheritance and bequests
- [mechanism] A conditional bequest triggered by a later event reveals testator intent and who benefits if the condition is met or broken, serving as a puzzle clue. When: designing an inheritance mystery. Why: The condition points toward a beneficiary.
- [mechanism] A legacy tied to a condition links the inheritance to a task or theme, so the heir's gain depends on acting within it.
- [mechanism] Conditions on residence, marriage, or absence restrict what a beneficiary can receive, and a penalty such as disinheritance adds a second layer of motive. When: when an inheritance includes conditions or penalties. Why: conditions and penalties change who gains and how much is at stake.
- [mechanism] A will that ties an inheritance to a physical condition gives a beneficiary a stake in that condition never being met, so the uncertainty itself can be the motive. When: When a disappearance or unconfirmed death changes who inherits or controls property. Why: If the condition fails, a different party gains, so that party benefits from the missing body staying missing.
- [rule] Tie a reveal to a specific recipient, such as one person alone, so the clue is delayed until that listener is present. When: A clue should be earned rather than handed over at once.
- [rule] Give protected documents conditional access terms, such as release only on joint demand of two parties, so custody itself becomes a point of dispute. When: when designing a secret that must be shared under conditions. Why: Conditions create negotiation and conflict between holders.
- [rule] Attach a condition to a meeting, such as forbidding a companion, so that the choice becomes a test of loyalty.
- [heuristic] A conditional gift can read as a burden or as proof of forgiveness; examine its wording and recipient to see which reading the evidence supports.
- [heuristic] When a grant carries a condition, later ownership suggests whether the condition was kept. When: a grant requires a specific use such as building a works.
- [heuristic] A conditional inheritance can make a relative the chief beneficiary and create a motive that was not visible at first. When: when investigating financial motive after a death. Why: Hidden terms of a will can reveal a beneficiary who gained by the death.
- [heuristic] A conditional-inheritance clue can create a second motive that becomes visible only after the player finds a missing draft. When: when designing a hidden motive revealed by a found item. Why: Gating a motive behind a found item rewards thorough investigation.
- [fact] Release from custody can be made conditional on paying the jailer's fees and the costs of arrest and transport.

## diaries and written accounts
- [mechanism] A diary written by an NPC who misreads events gives the player information the NPC lacks, letting the player act on the gap. When: a found journal is placed in a game world. Why: the player's knowledge exceeds the writer's.
- [rule] Let written diaries or notes act as items that anchor NPC testimony to specific dates.
- [rule] Check a diary's dates and wording against other accounts before using it as a timeline or as a record of events.
- [rule] Do not promise a reduced penalty that cannot be delivered; state any lighter outcome only as a possibility. When: offering incentives for a confession. Why: unkept promises damage trust in the exchange.
- [heuristic] A dated diary can give a checkable timeline and show its writer's state of mind, but it does not prove the events it reports; leave the author's bias for others to weigh. When: Designing found-document clues or assessing a diary as evidence. Why: Timestamps can be checked against other events, and motive remains open to judgment. (x2)
- [heuristic] Misspellings corrected by another hand suggest a text was written from dictation rather than composed freely. When: A draft shows corrections by a different hand. Why: A dictated text carries errors that a free composer would not make.
- [heuristic] Journal entries about other characters show where a culprit's plan was exposed and where he misjudged people, so they can serve as evidence.
- [heuristic] Use a culprit's written record to prove the reveal after identification; it does not help identify him beforehand.
- [heuristic] Diary entries reveal motive as well as mood, so read recorded prayers, requests and remarks for the interests they serve. Why: Personal records expose priorities that formal statements conceal.
- [heuristic] Separate what a source knows from what it hopes or fears, since wishes shape what a letter or warning emphasises. When: Evaluating a letter, warning or advice from a third party. Why: Motive and emotion can make a source's claims unreliable even when sincere.
- [fact] A written account left by someone who has departed can answer a mystery, supply a motive and fix a timeline.
- [fact] A personal record with side remarks is vivid but may reflect the keeper's feelings and grievances.

## discovery and suspicion
- [mechanism] A system that controls which characters learn a discovery, and in what order, changes how each character reacts.
- [rule] Present a timeline in true order even when the investigator discovered the events in another sequence. When: Giving the player a case-file or recap of a solved mystery. Why: Reversed order confuses the audience; the true order makes causes clear.
- [rule] Do not treat where a body or object is found as where the crime happened; separate the discovery site, the killing site and any site where remains were moved. Why: remains and objects can be placed or moved after the act.
- [rule] Make a hidden errand discoverable by letting players ask the right question of the right NPC.
- [rule] Test a claimed discovery for physical plausibility, since an item in a pocket is unlikely to fall out without rough handling. When: an item is said to be found on a body. Why: ordinary positions do not dislodge items.
- [heuristic] A discovery that follows closely after public accusations deserves scrutiny, since it may have been arranged to fit them.
- [heuristic] Objects left a long time in a busy public spot would likely have been noticed, so their remaining undiscovered suggests a shorter placement. When: judging how long objects were left unseen. Why: busy places make discovery likely.
- [heuristic] Direct attention to the part of a person or object that takes repeated contact, such as trouser knees or sleeves, where traces accumulate. When: examining a suspect's clothing or belongings. Why: repeated contact concentrates wear.
- [heuristic] Finding a body does not itself implicate the person who finds it, because someone must discover every crime.
- [pitfall] Discovery order reflects the search, not true sequence; ordering events or traces by it can falsely link independent things or separate connected ones, and misreads a depositor's route. (x2)
- [pitfall] Being discovered while hiding or tailing can end the investigation.
- [pitfall] A discovered covert placement can end all cooperation with the household. Why: Discovery makes the target distrust every future approach.

## documents and diaries
- [behavior] When a reader holds facts a diarist lacks, the reader feels suspense while watching the diarist's entries misread events. When: a character's diary is shown to the player alongside knowledge the character does not have. Why: the reader can see the gap between what the writer knows and what is true.
- [rule] Treat a personal diary as a partial record, since the writer's feelings and incomplete knowledge shape what is recorded. When: using a diary as a source of information. Why: its author's affection and fear filter every entry.
- [rule] Give players a document that contradicts an earlier one, so they must compare the two to find the lie or the change.
- [rule] Use the route-elimination method when a crime seems to have no entrance or when door and window evidence contradicts.
- [rule] Dialogue can mark which statements are confirmed and which remain open, so the player decides what to trust. When: Designing witness dialogue in a deduction game. Why: Explicit status markers make verification visible and keep judgment with the player.
- [rule] Check dates retold in secondhand accounts against original records, because dates drift as they are passed along. When: when a timeline relies on recounted information.
- [rule] Use a second, independent source, such as an old letter or deed paper, to show that a suspect misled the investigator about a genuine record. Why: An independent source can overturn a suspect's claim the suspect controls.
- [rule] Make a supernatural claim concrete and checkable before asking the audience to doubt it, so they have specific details to test. When: Introducing a spectral or otherwise unverifiable source of information. Why: Specific details such as a wound, a description or a name change give the audience something to test.
- [rule] Delay verification of a supernatural claim until the end of the case, so the claim stays in play throughout. When: Structuring a mystery whose central claim comes from an unverifiable source. Why: Early confirmation would close the question before the audience has been held by it.
- [procedure] 1) Gather dates from separate sources that do not know about each other. 2) Compare them on a shared date. 3) Measure the gap between them. 4) Treat a tight gap as a link, not proof. 5) Record each source and speaker so dates can be weighed later. When: Two people or records claim to describe the same event or identity. Why: Independent sources give a measurable constraint without a single verdict.
- [pitfall] Readers can project meaning onto ordinary diary entries when the dramatic tone is strong, and missing days may hide what matters. When: interpreting an incomplete or emotionally charged diary. Why: tone and gaps both invite over-reading.
- [fact] A letter can instruct its recipient to keep an identity hidden for a set period, writing the concealment into the document itself.

## ethics, mercy and institutions
- [definition] Legal proof, which must persuade a court and the public, is distinct from a privately held conviction, which can be firm without evidence to support it. When: Deciding whether a conclusion can be acted on publicly. Why: A conviction felt strongly is not admissible support for an accusation.
- [mechanism] An investigation can close through an institutional reversal, such as an authority withdrawing its charges, without any single culprit being unmasked. When: A mass accusation is wrong and no clear culprit is found. Why: The authority's withdrawal ends the case even though the underlying mysteries stay unexplained.
- [mechanism] A cluster of accusations can collapse together when an authority reverses, so the acquittal of many at once makes earlier false confidence visible. When: A case has accused many people on the same testimony. Why: A group reversal exposes the shared weakness behind the earlier accusations.
- [behavior] Institutions may hide identities by recording people only by location or role rather than by name, which limits what staff can later reveal. When: when an institution is a source of records about visitors. Why: Routine practices deliberately or habitually obscure identity.
- [heuristic] Revealing a sympathetic character as the true instigator can invert the audience's earlier sympathy.
- [heuristic] Granting mercy after a confession tends to buy gratitude and silence rather than the truth. When: When a confession is followed by a lenient outcome. Why: The confessor's incentive shifts from accuracy to keeping the benefit.
- [heuristic] Raise dread by making the danger seem intelligent and aware of the characters watching it. When: Designing an antagonist or hidden threat. Why: A watching, thinking enemy feels more menacing than a mindless one.
- [heuristic] Individual deaths or events may each have ordinary explanations, yet the record as a whole can make those explanations less convincing. When: Several incidents share a condition and each has a separate natural cause. Why: A common pattern across many cases is harder to attribute to chance.
- [heuristic] Close a solved mystery with mercy or restitution where it fits, so the solution changes the situation rather than only ending a fight. When: choosing an ending for a solved mystery. Why: Restitution gives the solution consequences beyond punishment.
- [tradeoff] Ending by leaving the official inquiry to others gives moral closure but leaves the legal outcome unresolved. When: choosing how a mystery ends. Why: The investigator's judgement is settled while the formal verdict stays open.
- [pitfall] Treating a formal legal finding as established fact misleads investigators, since a court may declare someone dead who is alive; rulings reflect admitted evidence, not necessarily reality. When: When interpreting an official ruling about a person or event. Why: Legal records decide on admitted evidence, not necessarily on what is physically true.
- [pitfall] A character whose indifference is too complete makes later sharp deduction feel unearned. Why: Readers cannot believe a sudden turn to acuity without earlier signs of capacity.

## fair-play clue design
- [rule] Show every clue a reveal depends on in earlier scenes, objects or testimony, before the protagonist assembles them, so the audience can check the conclusion. When: Designing a mystery or late reveal whose solution must be deducible by the player. Why: A reveal resting on withheld facts feels unfair; players accept only conclusions they could assemble themselves.
- [rule] Show identifying details, such as a face, mark or earlier name, before the character's identity is named, so the reveal feels fair. When: Planning a late identity reveal. Why: A reveal the audience could have seen earlier feels earned rather than arbitrary.
- [rule] Make the clue behind a reversal visible earlier in the story, held by a minor character, so the reveal does not feel like an unfair surprise. When: designing a twist that overturns the player's conclusion. Why: players can only be surprised fairly if the information was available to them.
- [rule] Give players a reason to suspect the victim before the reveal, by planting mood cues and physical evidence that later explain the twist. When: When a twist recasts a character's role. Why: A reveal feels fair when each clue is shown before it is explained, so players can recognize the pattern afterward.
- [rule] Plant signals, staged sounds and timing early so that a later reversal can be reinterpreted fairly by the player. When: Designing a twist or reversal. Why: Planted clues make the reversal feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [rule] Place the final culprit's decisive clue, such as a remaining count of an item, inside an apparently closed early exchange, so a later confession makes it feel earned. Why: The clue is seen once as small and recalled as decisive.
- [heuristic] Show the physical mechanism or system earlier, ideally in the protagonist's own observations, before the crime or reversal is named, so the reveal re-reads known evidence. When: The reveal relies on physical logic or a method the audience must identify. Why: The audience can reconstruct the cause from a system already seen, making the explanation fair and satisfying.
- [heuristic] Deal the contradicting clues early, so the reader holds the mismatch before the reveal and the late twist feels prepared rather than sprung. When: a mystery with a late reveal. Why: Evidence held early makes a late answer feel fair.
- [heuristic] Set each fair physical clue against a misdirect, so the true mechanism can be checked while the obvious reading stays plausible.
- [heuristic] State the logical principle behind a twist, such as that the contrast is too neat, before showing the proof, so the audience can guess early. When: Designing a reveal that should be fair to the audience. Why: A stated principle lets attentive players reason to the answer before the confirmation arrives.
- [heuristic] Scatter early clues across the story so the late reveal requires players to recall several of them together. When: Planning clue placement for a late reveal. Why: Dispersed clues accumulate in memory and combine at the reveal, rewarding attention over time.
- [procedure] 1) Show a specific physical detail early in plain view, placed without emphasis in an unrelated scene, and let a character dismiss it. 2) Withhold its meaning. 3) Later pose a question giving it weight. 4) Supply the explanation so the holder recalls it with a visible reaction. When: Designing a clue that pays off later in a mystery. Why: An incidental-seeming detail made relevant later rewards attentive recall without feeling unfair. (x2)

## fragile evidence and witnesses
- [rule] Do not use a staged reveal as a trap on someone already fragile; let them recover before the conversation continues.
- [rule] Make physical clue items fragile or losable, so players must protect and memorise them.
- [rule] Handle evidence through a clean cloth and hold it by its edges to preserve surface marks for later examination. When: When collecting objects that may carry fingerprints or surfaces to examine. Why: Bare-handed handling can disturb marks needed later.
- [heuristic] Use pressure on an emotionally fragile witness with care, since it can produce a statement shaped by the questioner. When: interviewing a vulnerable witness. Why: Pressure can distort what the witness says.
- [pitfall] A single observer or witness can be mistaken, lying, or forgetful, so an alibi or clue resting on one memory is fragile; long night watches also make observers drowsy. Why: A single unverified recollection can be wrong or forgotten.
- [pitfall] A voice-imitation cover rests on luck about distance and light; a single close observer can break it.
- [pitfall] A password taken on trust from a doorkeeper can pass a first checkpoint, but it is fragile because the group may change it. When: Relying on a borrowed password to enter a group's space. Why: Passwords are shared and can be rotated, so they expire as cover.
- [pitfall] Small traces are easy to overlook, and handling them can destroy them, such as brushing residue off a sleeve.
- [pitfall] Physical evidence is easily lost, and heavy handling by many people makes it hard to establish who touched an item. When: Investigating an object that passed through many hands. Why: Each handler is a possible source of contamination or misattribution.
- [pitfall] A planted witness relies on events the planner cannot control, so the whole chain breaks if an ordinary arrangement changes. Why: the witness's presence depends on routines that can shift.
- [pitfall] A concealment that depends on one unlucky lighting moment feels arbitrary if the reveal is only bad luck; give the player a way to find the truth beforehand. When: Designing a reveal that depends on timing. Why: Chance-only reveals feel unfair without earlier discoverable evidence.
- [fact] Physical evidence such as torn paper degrades over time, so some traces may not survive long enough to be recovered. When: Evidence is old when investigated. Why: Time erodes materials and removes traces.

## harm and hazards
- [model] Unseen harm is assumed to have a human agent, so the investigative question becomes who is responsible. When: illness or injury has no visible cause. Why: an agent is sought for every harm.
- [rule] Separate proof that harm occurred from proof that a specific person caused it; with no one observing the act, harm is not evidence of cause; guilt must be shown, not inferred. Why: a victim's suffering does not identify the agent.
- [rule] Let environmental hazards act as the mechanism of an apparent accident, and reveal tampering through small inconsistencies such as neatly folded clothing.
- [rule] Avoid tests that harm people, even when the method is effective. When: when designing an investigation or trial that might injure someone. Why: A harmful method is unacceptable even when it would produce a clear result.
- [rule] Do not use force near live equipment until its safety has been explained.
- [rule] Do not use planted bait when it could reach innocent people or cause them harm.
- [heuristic] A hazard that strikes just when its apparent targets are elsewhere suggests the planner knew their movements. When: A hazard hits a place its likely victims have left.
- [tradeoff] Forcing a locked door saves time to open but damages property and can delay or spoil what the investigator needs, so forced entry carries real costs. When: when choosing between forcing a lock and waiting for a proper key or tradesman. Why: Force is fast but destructive and may compromise evidence.
- [pitfall] Assuming a cause without testing it closes off alternative questions, such as whether the victim's identity is confirmed, and can be overturned by a replica or reenactment. When: A cause appears obvious early in an investigation. Why: Assumed links stop the investigator from checking alternatives.
- [pitfall] A reversal caused by a rule the audience never saw feels arbitrary and cheats them, so state the rule early.
- [pitfall] Recorded losses are not proof of cause; a grudge can be mistaken for motive when the link between threat and loss is never shown.
- [fact] Environmental hazards such as cold can cause death without visible struggle, so a staged accident may leave no sign of violence.

## hidden identity and impostors
- [definition] An identifying trait is a physical detail, such as a limp, cane or face shape, described early as characterization and later used to recognise the person.
- [mechanism] A document that reveals a hidden identity can open a new route, letting the player use the disclosed identity to progress. When: Quest items that disclose a secret.
- [mechanism] A single character's identity can be revised several times by successive clues, moving between honest, impostor, accomplice, target and noble, so the player must keep re-evaluating. When: a mystery centres on who a character really is. Why: Each new clue changes which category the character fits, keeping belief unstable longer than the case's main answer.
- [mechanism] A victim is killed before a checkpoint, and a disguised impersonator boards there, so a witness's sighting creates a false alibi for another suspect. When: Building a false timeline where a disguise covers a death. Why: The impersonator's appearance replaces the victim's, so the timeline appears intact.
- [heuristic] Personal items such as rings, pins or clothing can be carried by someone other than the owner, so make them the clue players trust, letting their failure become the main twist. When: A body or person is identified by belongings and the identity is central to the plot. Why: Players rarely question items accepted as proof of identity, and matching possessions does not prove who the person is. (x2)
- [heuristic] A body or character presented as one identity can be re-matched to another when a later item, such as a name, clothing mark or sample, is found.
- [heuristic] Use a single recurring phrase or inscription to link a dead NPC to a past wrong and a hidden enemy. When: Designing a thread that connects a victim to an unseen antagonist. Why: A repeated phrase gives the player a concrete lead that points to the past.
- [heuristic] Establish an impostor through physical evidence such as footwear, fingerprints or mismatched belongings before naming any human suspect. When: when a character's identity is in doubt. Why: Physical traces are harder to explain away than testimony.
- [procedure] 1) Collect several independent physical markers from the subject. 2) Compare each marker against a separate record. 3) Confirm the identity only when the matches reinforce each other. When: Identity is in question and the body or subject is too decayed to recognise. Why: Several independent matches are much stronger than a single marker.
- [procedure] 1) Use the posting location and any first name as partial identifiers. 2) Link the writer to a person through later references in other documents. When: A letter is unsigned or signed only with a first name. Why: Partial clues combine into an identification that a later clue can complete.
- [procedure] 1) Have the witness produce a sketch of a face or figure. 2) Find a historical record that matches it. 3) Ask the witness to confirm the match. When: Identifying an unseen figure from a witness's description. Why: A witness's recognition of a match identifies the figure more reliably than a description alone.
- [pitfall] Reassurance grounded in a person's standing rather than facts can stop a listener from checking the actual claim. When: A listener is told a report is false because of who is involved. Why: A reputation argument is not verification and can end the search for facts.

## layout and landmarks
- [behavior] Open layouts with little room to conceal a person narrow the hiding places available in a small setting. When: A bounded setting has open sightlines and few enclosed spaces. Why: Visibility limits where a person can stay unseen, making remaining hiding spots finite and checkable.
- [rule] Before an overhearing scene, establish the layout constraint that keeps the listener in place, such as a single exit through the room. When: a character must overhear a secret. Why: otherwise the audience asks why the listener did not leave.
- [heuristic] Question a suspect about the layout a crime required, so the answers test whether they could have acted. When: checking a suspect's plausibility. Why: Describing the scene reveals whether the suspect knows its details.
- [heuristic] Map a scene's layout for access routes, such as balconies, windows and drops, to see how someone could reach a room. When: A crime method depends on reaching a particular room.
- [procedure] 1) Locate the scene on a large-scale map. 2) Mark neighbouring sites and points of interest within a set radius. 3) Note distances to the nearest dwellings and how isolated the site is. When: when a site is remote and a map is available before any visit. Why: Study can happen before a visit and shows which people could have witnessed events.
- [procedure] 1) Collect every reference to the person. 2) Order them by date. 3) State what each shows and what it does not show. 4) Mark where the trail ends. When: A person vanishes and leaves no final record. Why: Scattered fragments reveal a last likely sighting only when ordered and bounded explicitly.
- [pitfall] Boundaries described by landmarks such as trees, stumps, pens, bridges, roads or lines drift or become disputed when a landmark moves or the description is vague, becoming hard to relocate. When: when a boundary is defined by physical markers. Why: landmarks are not permanent and their positions drift.
- [pitfall] A room arranged to attract paying guests may reflect the landlord's intent rather than the occupant's own taste.
- [pitfall] A rearrangement that explains the layout can still hide the true cause, so keep testing after it fits.
- [pitfall] Assuming a building's later appearance matches its use at the time of the events can mislead a location check.
- [fact] Layout shows only what was possible, not what happened, so it cannot replace witness testimony.
- [fact] The layout of doors, gardens, alleys and rooms holds evidence about how a person could be reached, watched or taken.

## misreading and false conclusions
- [heuristic] Give each misreading a factual alternative that fits both the honest and the deliberate interpretation until a decisive clue arrives. When: A player is led to a wrong conclusion about an incident. Why: Players accept a misreading only when the evidence genuinely supports both readings, so they do not feel cheated when corrected.
- [pitfall] Anomalous clues or mismatched records get dismissed as untidiness or process error and recognised only later; plant mismatches so a second-event reading stays available. When: An anomalous detail is seen on arrival, or two records or entries fail to agree. Why: Observers do not interpret a clue until it connects to a broader pattern, and a plausible administrative explanation hides it until wider evidence supports another reading. (x2)
- [pitfall] A satisfying solution can still be wrong, so the investigator must keep looking for the fact it fails to explain. When: A theory feels complete and resolves most of the case. Why: Satisfaction is not proof, and an unexplained fact may reveal the real cause.
- [pitfall] A flattering or romantic reading of an object can lead an investigation away from the plausible explanation. When: when interpreting an object with emotional appeal.
- [pitfall] A social scandal is not automatically a motive for murder; check whether it actually connects to the death. When: A witness reveals an embarrassing private matter. Why: Scandal is common and often unrelated to crime.
- [pitfall] Pressing ordinary acts for hidden meaning produces false significance, and a character's agitation can grow beyond what the facts support. When: A character or investigator is anxious or suspicious. Why: Anxiety reads ordinary actions as signs of a concealed purpose.
- [pitfall] Investigators can be misled more by implication than by direct statement, so a sincere-seeming hint can shape judgment without being proven. When: weighing an observer's impression of a suspect's hesitation or remark. Why: implied suggestions carry emotional weight beyond their evidence.
- [pitfall] An emotionally charged reading of document fragments can impose a false sense, such as threats where none are intended. When: Interpreting partial text with strong expectations about its content. Why: Preconceptions about the writer or situation shape how fragments are read.
- [pitfall] Avoiding the front of a house can mean concealment or simple convenience, so routine behaviour needs a second explanation before it is read as hiding. When: when interpreting an unusual movement pattern. Why: The same behaviour has more than one plausible cause.
- [pitfall] A moral or spiritual explanation can stand in for a concrete human cause and feel more satisfying than the evidence supports. When: when an investigator interprets an unusual appearance or event. Why: Moral framing offers a clean answer that avoids checking the mundane facts.
- [pitfall] Vivid supernatural imagery can make an investigator see the supernatural where only a human pattern exists. When: when a mystery is described in intense or unusual terms. Why: Striking imagery shapes perception before the evidence is weighed.
- [pitfall] Assuming an angry remark targets the person it names can mislead; the anger may be aimed at a third party. When: When interpreting heated statements. Why: Named targets can be stand-ins.

## motives and public suspicion
- [mechanism] A quarrel overheard by others seems decisive because its emotional heat is taken as evidence of intent, even when it serves a different plan. When: when a public or overheard argument precedes an event. Why: Observers weight emotional intensity more heavily than context.
- [rule] Treat an offhand remark by an official about someone withholding information as a signal of private knowledge, not as proof. When: An official hints that another party is hiding something. Why: A hint indicates private information but does not confirm its content.
- [heuristic] Create a moment where a character must publicly admit or deny a relationship, and let the response change the player's standing with that character. When: Designing social consequences in a narrative game. Why: A public choice with lasting effect makes relationships feel consequential.
- [heuristic] Keep some motives private, stated as the character's own matter, to create a hook the audience wants resolved. When: Revealing a character's reasons. Why: Withheld motives create curiosity.
- [heuristic] Stage an identity reveal in a public setting where witnesses can confirm it, using a physical item as proof. When: when a hidden identity must be made undeniable. Why: witnesses and proof remove the chance of explaining the anomaly away.
- [heuristic] Show a suspect's temper in public before the crime, so later evidence against them feels earned rather than invented. When: Planting a suspect who will later be framed or accused. Why: Prior visible behavior makes later accusation credible to the player.
- [procedure] 1) Give the observer a clear sightline on the staged place. 2) Build a hush by fixing attention on one door or approach. 3) Let the intruder seize control with a gesture, so the official loses command. 4) Tie the climax to an external marker such as a clock striking. When: Staging a dramatic reveal before a group of witnesses. Why: Shared attention and a fixed external moment make the shock land for everyone at once.
- [pitfall] Heavy publicity of a lure, notice or reward warns the target as well as intended audiences; weigh wide reach against tipping off the wrong people. When: Publicising a lure, notice or reward. Why: Wide exposure reaches unintended audiences along with the target; the same announcement that attracts informants also tells the thief what is being done.
- [pitfall] An official's loaded characterization of a crime can prejudice listeners against the one suspect; a neutral, clear question is safer. When: When an authority figure addresses a public audience during an investigation. Why: Charged wording shapes judgment before the facts are established.
- [pitfall] Jumping to a motive before the mechanism is clear invites unsupported answers; settle the motive by a test rather than assumption.
- [pitfall] Taking a publicly stated motive at face value can hide the real stake; check it against the legal facts. Why: Stated motives may be incomplete or convenient for the person giving them.
- [pitfall] Prejudice against outsiders can make the solver overlook an insider who has the means, opportunity and routine to commit the act. When: A closed cast includes both insiders and outsiders. Why: Bias directs attention away from people who already fit the profile of the culprit.

## npc bias and credibility
- [mechanism] Give a dangerous-quest NPC a credibility rating built from demeanour and from whether their claim can be tested in the world. When: designing NPC quest givers.
- [mechanism] An NPC witness can carry an assumption tag, so investigation can reveal both the truth and the NPC's error, such as a sound taken for a dream.
- [rule] Attach a visible motive tag such as grudge, fear, or loyalty to each NPC witness or informant, so the player can discount testimony by that stake. When: When designing NPC testimony or clue-giving dialogue. Why: Players can weigh claims against the witness's motive, and a visible motive builds investigative skill. (x2)
- [rule] Give NPCs motives that bias their reports, and let other NPCs contradict them so the player must weigh each claim rather than accept it as given.
- [rule] Give NPC witnesses personal states such as fear, pride or bias that colour their conclusions while stated facts stay true, so players separate what was seen from what was felt. When: when designing unreliable NPC testimony. Why: Players can separate the trustworthy facts from the biased judgment.
- [rule] Require an NPC to initiate contact before trust grows, and track the player's first impression as a value that affects whether the NPC approaches. When: designing NPC trust mechanics.
- [rule] Store each NPC's record of past offenses, such as a conviction for lying, and reveal it when the player confronts that witness. When: designing NPC witnesses for an investigation.
- [heuristic] An NPC who blames a common culprit for an incident may conceal a second plot, which a questioning player can uncover to open a new thread.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC's grudge or loyalty colour their report, so players learn to cross-check what that NPC says. When: when an NPC has a personal stake in the event. Why: Biased reports teach players to verify before acting.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC's confident theory conflict with a physical clue, forcing players to weigh whose account to trust. When: Designing NPC dialogue that offers explanations.
- [heuristic] Read a suspect through the manner of a subordinate companion, since that person's behavior can be more honest than the suspect's own statements. When: when a suspect's account must be weighed against others. Why: subordinates have less reason to perform for the suspect.
- [pitfall] A source already discredited by another character colors how a listener weighs what that source says, even when the claim is plausible. When: Testimony comes from a character a third party has warned against. Why: Prior distrust shifts the credibility the listener assigns to the new claim.

## npc statement logging
- [mechanism] A dialogue system can have an NPC demand a decision after a player's report and log which names the player withheld, so later reactions reflect that choice. When: when the player reports a suspicion to an NPC with authority. Why: Recording withheld information lets later dialogue respond to what the player chose to conceal.
- [rule] Log every NPC statement verbatim with a timestamp so later contradictions, including denials of words used, can be flagged and shown to the player as clues. When: Building an NPC dialogue system or player journal for a mystery. Why: Timestamped, verbatim records let the game and player detect contradictions across time. (x3)
- [rule] Have an NPC write a word or sign a line through a plausible request, unlocking a later comparison puzzle. When: Designing handwriting or signature matching puzzles. Why: The player gets comparison material without the NPC knowing it matters.
- [rule] Give NPCs a verification step, such as asking a clerk, so a player's cover story can be confirmed or exposed in play. When: a player invents a story to approach an NPC. Why: verification makes the player's choices consequential.
- [rule] Log NPC state changes with their triggering events, so the player can see each sudden change and its known cause. When: Designing NPC behaviour that shifts over time. Why: Linked logs let players reason from behaviour changes to motives.
- [rule] Record each NPC's witness state as saw, heard or assumed, and let contradictions between states unlock an accusation. When: Designing investigation mechanics with multiple witnesses. Why: Distinguishing knowledge types makes contradictions detectable.
- [rule] Store an NPC's scripted line separately from its true memory, so repeated or rephrased questions can expose the difference. When: Designing NPC dialogue that can be coached or concealed. Why: Separating the two lets the game reveal the real answer under pressure.
- [rule] Flag an NPC who readily accepts a suggested story for further checks when the player offers an explanation for a found item.
- [rule] Give each NPC statement a checkable part and an uncheckable part, so the player can choose which claims to press. When: Designing NPC testimony.
- [rule] Let the player check an NPC's record: who they vouched for, who they accused, and what they did afterward.
- [heuristic] Attach a source to each NPC accusation, such as the room the speaker was in, so the player can judge how far the claim reaches. When: Designing NPC accusations in a game. Why: A stated source lets the player weigh a claim's reliability.
- [procedure] 1) Record every claim a witness NPC makes. 2) Log the relevant game-state facts, such as door locks or light sources. 3) Flag any claim that conflicts with the logged state. When: Designing an NPC whose story the player can test. Why: Later contradictions can then be surfaced in dialogue.

## opposing sides and counter-moves
- [mechanism] When a hidden leader is removed, the organization collapses: its members flee and leave incriminating papers that authorities can act on.
- [behavior] A single act can support opposing readings, such as vengeance or reconciliation, so an interpreter should not present only one. Why: The same act can carry two meanings depending on the intent assumed for it.
- [behavior] In a public calamity, some people exploit the disorder for private gain, including by making false accusations. When: a disaster or crisis disrupts normal order. Why: Disorder gives cover for private gain.
- [heuristic] Test an opposing timeline for its weakest point; one decisive witness can reverse a window that looked settled.
- [heuristic] Repeated private meetings and passed messages between dissenters are a sign of organized opposition, and authorities tend to treat them as a threat. When: a divided group with rival camps. Why: Coordinated contact points to a shared aim rather than scattered complaints.
- [heuristic] Frame a conflict as a contest between opposed systems to absorb local disputes into one larger story.
- [heuristic] An opponent's own account of a quarrel's origin can contradict the motive claim, so check the accuser's records before accepting the accusation.
- [procedure] 1) List the clues. 2) Group them by the motive and action they imply, not by object. 3) Look for the grouping that explains the most clues. 4) Test that grouping against remaining evidence. When: Many clues appear to conflict and the investigator is stuck. Why: Grouping by motive reveals the overall pattern that individual objects hide.
- [metric] Give opponents a fixed decision window, about two hours, before moving on; this creates suspense and forces them to reveal their position.
- [pitfall] Setting one witness's opinion against another can make a disagreement look settled when it is only two opinions. When: Presenting conflicting witness views. Why: Opinions carry no more weight than their reasons.
- [pitfall] Accounts that agree in outline can still disagree on times or on who was present, so agreement in general shape is not corroboration.
- [fact] An opponent's reply to a lead can reveal how much the opponent knows. When: A lead ends in a direct contest with a suspect. Why: A counter-move depends on what the opponent has learned.

## promises and offers
- [behavior] A promise can bind a witness to silence, explaining why they refuse to talk without revealing what they are hiding. When: A witness stays silent despite having relevant knowledge. Why: Loyalty or a vow can outweigh the urge to speak.
- [rule] Deliver every promised reveal or payment; track NPC promises, such as allowances or inheritances, as state variables and test each is fulfilled. When: a character promises to explain something later, or an NPC promises an allowance or inheritance. Why: unfulfilled promises turn anticipation into frustration.
- [rule] Do not offer leniency without authority to deliver it. Promise only that the matter will be considered. When: a suspect asks for mercy. Why: unauthorized promises create false expectations.
- [rule] A witness may limit an oath to the parts they can vouch for, and the unsworn remainder must not be treated as established. When: when a witness can swear to only part of an account. Why: an oath covers only what the witness swears to, so the rest stays unproven.
- [heuristic] Check whether a confession was offered in exchange for a promised outcome such as a reprieve, since that promise is itself a source of pressure. When: reviewing a confession made during custody or accusation. Why: the promised benefit can push a person to confess regardless of guilt.
- [heuristic] Propose payment in advance to test how far the other side will go in revealing information.
- [heuristic] Let a council in the game be pressured to act on unverifiable claims, and let players trace the consequences afterward.
- [heuristic] An offer whose conditions reach beyond its stated purpose, such as holding even when the expected event does not occur, can hint at motive or private knowledge. When: When an offer's terms are unusually broad. Why: Such reach serves the proposer's interest in the outcome, though greed can also explain it.
- [tradeoff] Agreeing to a promise of no molestation until statements are finished buys cooperation and a calm interview, at the cost of limiting the investigators' freedom of action. When: A suspect will talk only if the investigators promise not to act during the interview. Why: Promises bind the police and restrict what they may do later.
- [pitfall] A witness promised protection may tell the questioner what protects them rather than what happened. When: a witness gains from a promise of immunity. Why: self-interest shapes what the witness chooses to say.
- [pitfall] A promise made under pressure may not hold, so an appointment set through a channel needs a fallback plan. Why: Someone pressed into a commitment may not keep it.
- [pitfall] A demonstration offered only after pressure was prompted by the questioning and is not freely given, so weigh it accordingly.

## resemblance and identity
- [heuristic] A resemblance alone does not settle identity, and shared appearance does not show shared guilt; only a specific, checkable mark can confirm identity. When: A look-alike exists in the records or the cast. (x2)
- [heuristic] Do not dismiss a witness who saw real features; use clothing-only identifications only as weak support and seek a second cue such as a voice or mark. When: When weighing a witness's identification of a suspect. Why: Distinctive features are stronger evidence than a shared outfit.
- [heuristic] A family resemblance between a living person and an old portrait is a lead to examine, not proof that the same conduct continued.
- [heuristic] A trait shared by many people, such as hair colour or build, cannot prove identity on its own. When: When judging whether a shared trait confirms a match. Why: Many candidates share generic features.
- [heuristic] Matching the same finger placement and pressure marks is a stronger identity test than matching general appearance. When: When comparing hands or rings on a body. Why: Specific physical traces are harder to share by chance.
- [tradeoff] A public reputation and a visual likeness can contradict each other, and the investigator must weigh which account to trust. When: When an official or social image of a person conflicts with a portrait or photograph. Why: Two accounts of the same person may disagree, and neither is automatically correct.
- [pitfall] Resemblance judged from appearance or photographs is weak evidence that cannot be fully trusted, yet should be treated as a lead to test, not a match. When: identifying a person by appearance, or a bystander comparing a face to a known offender. Why: Photos and general impressions can be similar across different people.
- [pitfall] Resemblance between a suspect object and a predicted trace is not proof, since copies can mimic traces; inspect and test the object itself rather than assuming a match. Why: Copies can mimic a trace.
- [pitfall] A description matching a suspect in every respect shows only resemblance; treating it as identification without independent proof confuses the two. When: a lookalike description points at a suspect. Why: Many people can fit one description, so a close fit does not prove who was present.
- [pitfall] Treating a resemblance or a convenient fact as identity lets a red herring drive the whole investigation.
- [pitfall] Treating a figure that merely resembles someone seen in a crowd as proof of presence is a mistake; a clear view of a face is far stronger.
- [pitfall] Identifying a person by what the witness expects them to be, rather than by what was seen, produces confident but unreliable identifications. When: when a dim or distant sighting fits a witness's existing belief. Why: Expectation substitutes for observed detail.

## reveal and twist structure
- [model] A two-stage reveal first seals a suspect's guilt with physical evidence and an eyewitness, then reopens it by reconstructing the suspect's own forgotten actions. When: Mysteries where the suspect cannot remember the act. Why: The second stage supplies a hidden cause that reverses the first stage's conclusion.
- [model] A two-movement mystery frames a solved present crime around a past backstory that explains its motive, which arrives late in a separate block.
- [mechanism] A disguised identity can be exposed in two stages: a visible disguise item falls first, then a written record confirms the link, revising the reader's belief twice. When: A mystery hides one person behind a disguise or double identity. Why: A visible clue creates doubt, and a document settles it, so the reader accepts the reversal.
- [rule] Vary the mechanism of each case in a series, such as document decoding, disguise, or reinterpreting a death, to keep a recurring formula fresh. When: Designing a series of mysteries that share a structure. Why: Repeating the same solution type makes the formula predictable and erodes suspense.
- [heuristic] Hold back the full meaning of a dramatic reveal and supply a later written account, so the audience can grasp what they saw. When: A public reveal is shocking but its significance is not immediately clear. Why: A shock without follow-up explanation leaves the audience confused.
- [heuristic] Common twists overturn one assumption: an apparent crime hides another motive, a helpless victim proves capable, or apparent intruders turn out to be the authorities. Why: Each assumption is one the player is likely to hold.
- [heuristic] Make the twist turn on a remembered concrete detail, such as a material drawn from a person, that recasts the present scene.
- [procedure] 1) Let sensation such as touch, sound or smell arrive before the visual identity of a threat. 2) Show the character's reaction rather than a full description. 3) Raise pressure through a decision the character cannot make. 4) Track changes in habits as signs of rising fear. When: a reveal should build gradually. Why: sensation before sight preserves dread while readers still sense the stakes.
- [procedure] 1) Share a partial reconstruction with an ally. 2) Deliver the full proof as a document, such as a confession letter. 3) Give the complete deduction after the proof lands. When: Closing a mystery where the investigator held back the answer. Why: Staging the reveal in steps keeps the payoff gradual and documented.
- [pitfall] A withheld explanation feels like a trick when its clue was never planted earlier in the story.
- [pitfall] A reveal that a character is someone else fails when no earlier clue exists; presenting the false identity as fact until the reveal leaves the player unable to check it. When: Writing a disguise or double-identity reveal. Why: Without earlier setup the reveal feels arbitrary rather than fair.
- [fact] Stretched wire can show as thin lines of light under lanterns, exposing rigged devices. When: When looking for concealed trigger mechanisms in a lit space. Why: Thin wire catches light that reveals its path.

## reveal deadlines and threats
- [rule] Delay revealing a hidden observer's identity if the audience should share the observer's uncertainty. When: When the audience's uncertainty is part of the scene. Why: Early identity removes the shared suspense.
- [rule] If a reaction appears only when staged, reveal the staging to the player so the test can be detected. When: when a game test can be prepared in advance.
- [rule] Add new accuser NPCs after each event in a town hearing, revealing their names one at a time to build pressure.
- [heuristic] Reveal a hidden manipulation through witness testimony about how it was done, not only through the document itself.
- [tradeoff] Bringing in a late witness can strengthen a case but may expose a secret motive to the opposing side; weigh the testimony's value against that cost before disclosing. When: The late witness's value depends on disclosing a damaging secret. Why: Disclosure can hand the opponent a new line of attack.
- [pitfall] Stating a deadline to an opponent gives time to plan around it, weakening the pressure it was meant to create; reveal it only when necessary. When: Negotiating while holding a time-limited advantage. Why: The deadline tells the opponent how long they have.
- [pitfall] Revealing a lead or decoy to a suspect tells them what the investigator knows, letting them adjust their account. When: Staging a deception that later unravels. Why: The suspect can adjust their account once they learn what is known.
