- [pitfall] Showing a suspect they are watched, or revealing a hidden listening method, changes their behaviour and exposes the listener to counter-moves, weakening later questioning. When: Investigators plan surveillance or confrontation. Why: Awareness of observation makes the suspect more guarded or more performative.
- [pitfall] Revealing a full blockade all at once loses the gradual build of tension that closing routes one by one creates.
- [pitfall] Showing the threat clearly before the climax removes the uncertainty that drives the wait, so the tension collapses. When: the event is meant to be anticipated. Why: Suspense depends on not knowing exactly what is coming and when.
- [pitfall] Asking questions that reveal what the investigator already knows exposes the investigation.
- [pitfall] Interrupting a witness can reveal the examiner's own hidden knowledge and warn the witness to be more careful in later answers.

## scene search and layout
- [rule] Let an NPC fetch an item as a quest step, since the retrieved item can reveal the next clue.
- [rule] Ask what an object held when it left its origin, to fix its contents before any later change can be claimed. When: an object's contents are disputed. Why: the origin record sets the baseline against which later changes are judged.
- [heuristic] Compare records with fixed entry positions, so a missing entry appears as a blank gap too narrow for the next group of entries. When: Entries sit in set positions on the page. Why: Position-based layout turns absence into a visible space.
- [heuristic] Check floors and furniture edges, since small items can lie out of sight and be missed on a casual first pass.
- [heuristic] Start an investigation at a fixed scene fact, such as a body or sealed room, and have the player work back to the method, then test whether a suspect's motive fits. When: Designing deduction puzzles. Why: A fixed fact anchors reasoning and gives a checkable endpoint.
- [heuristic] A gap in a fitting, such as shutters that barely meet, can permit a view into a room from outside. Why: Small gaps can admit sight even when they block passage.
- [heuristic] A food or drink item can carry quality or origin data that signals a second character was present.
- [heuristic] Make a missing object the focal clue, since locating it can lead to the culprit.
- [procedure] 1) Hold a position with line of sight to the target. 2) When the target moves, go at once to the exit they are likely to use. 3) Intercept there. When: a target may escape through a crowded space. Why: a route to the exit is faster when planned in advance.
- [procedure] 1) Fit the found fragment against its supposed source, such as the torn edges of a garment. 2) Compare the material and weave. 3) Record whether the fit confirms the claimed origin. When: a clue's source is known and must be matched. Why: a successful fit confirms the claimed origin.
- [procedure] 1) List each room's visitors. 2) Note the times each room is cleaned or prepared. 3) Find rooms left unvisited at night. 4) Ask where you would hide an object from the offender's side. When: Locating where a concealed object could survive. Why: Routine leaves some rooms unobserved for long periods.
- [procedure] 1) Note the changed conduct of the creature that hid the item. 2) Infer its motive, such as protecting a precious object. 3) Search the sites that motive would choose, not the usual storage place. When: a hidden item was placed by a creature or agent with predictable habits. Why: A creature's motive predicts a hiding place that differs from its normal one.

## search targets and technique
- [definition] A search inventory is a numbered record of found objects, each with its location and condition, so that traces can be read together rather than alone.
- [mechanism] Searching right after an ambush, or after any long delay, lets the attacker flee or let suspects move or remove hidden traces, weakening what the search finds. When: When an attacker has fled before the search starts, or a long time passes before searching. Why: Each extra hour gives a suspect time to alter or remove evidence, and delay gives the attacker time to escape and remove traces. (x2)
- [behavior] A room ransacked in a targeted way, with containers forced and bedding emptied while valuables remain, suggests the culprit sought documents rather than goods. When: When reading a crime scene for the intruder's real goal. Why: Searchers look for what they want and ignore what has no use to them.
- [behavior] Searchers check the nearest plausible hiding spots to a crime scene or findspot first, before examining places farther away. When: when a hidden item is linked to a known location. Why: spots nearest the object are the most likely hiding places.
- [rule] Allow an NPC to destroy evidence before the player searches their quarters, so a failed search is a meaningful outcome. When: when designing searchable NPC spaces.
- [rule] Keep local incident history as a searchable log that the player can check against recent events.
- [rule] Give different NPCs different search results depending on what each one expects to find. When: Designing a search mechanic with multiple searchers. Why: Expectation-driven results create believable, varied clues.
- [heuristic] Hand marks on a fence or rail show someone searching by touch, while a direct path to a target suggests the person already knew the way. When: Judging whether someone was searching or knew the location. Why: Searching requires groping; prior knowledge allows a direct route.
- [procedure] 1) State the object a claim predicts must exist. 2) Search behind and under furniture with a light source. 3) Leave any find undisturbed until it is recorded. When: A claim predicts a particular small object is present in a room. Why: A clear target and careful handling prevent overlooking or destroying evidence.
- [pitfall] Searching only the prominent objects misses traces, which often sit in gaps, containers, and corners.
- [pitfall] Assuming a hidden item is kept where things are normally stored leads to a failed search. Why: Agents hiding something valuable often avoid their usual place.
- [fact] The person directing a search chooses which places are checked, so the findings reflect what that guide chose to show.

## single culprit and motive theories
- [model] A single-killer mystery pins the death first on an outside rival, then on a trusted suspect, and surfaces the real killer only in the final stretch.
- [rule] Do not treat one suspicious act as proof of intent or guilt; require a sequence of acts pointing the same way, since one act can misdirect an investigation. When: When deciding whether a suspect's behavior justifies action.
- [heuristic] A single shared habit is weak evidence easily dismissed as coincidence; treat it as a lead to test, since many people share the same habit. When: Only one habit links a suspect to a witness's description.
- [heuristic] Do not assume motive from one relationship without checking the others, since a single tie may mislead. When: A motive appears to rest on one relationship. Why: Other ties may explain the act better or rule the suspect out.
- [heuristic] If one perpetrator is assumed for linked events, a suspect with a sound alibi for one event may be eliminated from the others as well. When: Several crimes are assumed to share a culprit. Why: Presence elsewhere during one event excludes the same person from the other.
- [heuristic] If re-entry needed a key and only one person could open the door, a missing key suggests a single actor did the act.
- [pitfall] Attributing the whole plot or event sequence to one suspect hides other participants' roles and distorts the account; check each participant's part separately.
- [pitfall] Relying on a single watcher, or on the guardian's own presence alone, creates one point of failure.
- [pitfall] A theory that explains every fact through one motive can fit many people, so it may point confidently at the wrong one.
- [pitfall] Assuming one beneficiary behind every accusation misses the wider pattern in which many officials and tradespeople each profited.
- [pitfall] Treating greed as the only motive misses feuds and gossip. Accusations often have mixed motives that must be weighed together.
- [fact] A theory built on one person's movements stays unverified until independent evidence supports it.

## supernatural and folklore frames
- [model] Build an apparent supernatural event around a hidden or disguised human actor; give the human cause the same visible traces, so investigators check arrangement, not label, weighing both explanations. When: A story offers a supernatural explanation for a frightening event.
- [mechanism] A local legend regarded as a tale becomes credible when physical evidence in place ties it to a specific site and a written account confirms it.
- [mechanism] A local legend can serve as a false frame that a human plot exploits, so the belief in the fable becomes part of the crime's power. When: Building a locale with folklore that hides a real antagonist. Why: The antagonist gains influence from the community's acceptance of the myth.
- [rule] Plant a lore fact early, then pay it off with a physical injury or mark on a character, turning an abstract myth into verifiable proof. When: Designing a reveal the player can check. Why: A matching physical sign ties a myth to a specific character.
- [rule] Scatter a torn lore document across rooms with straight edges and overlapping words as solvable constraints, and let later pieces resolve ambiguous text. When: Designing a document-assembly puzzle for a player. Why: Physical fit and later context give the player a checkable way to reconstruct the text.
- [rule] Use an in-world reference such as a note or book to point to deeper lore, so an unresolved detail becomes an optional follow-up. When: Leaving a minor detail unexplained in a level. Why: A referenced source turns an open question into an invitation rather than a defect.
- [rule] Let the player suspect a legend exists before revealing its link to a place, so the discovery answers a question they already hold.
- [heuristic] Many apparent hauntings are solved by thorough search and an open mind, and human devices such as wire, hidden bells or ceiling gaps often explain them. When: Unexplained events occur and a human agent is plausible. Why: Ordinary mechanisms are more common than supernatural ones.
- [heuristic] A previous in-world incident can reveal the hidden mechanic that explains a present contradiction. When: Designing lore that supports a present-day puzzle. Why: Players connect the past record to the current puzzle and infer the mechanic.
- [tradeoff] Item-by-item human explanations suit cases where most events have ordinary mechanisms. Forcing a human frame onto thin evidence overreaches. When: When deciding whether to explain an anomaly through a concealed human action.
- [pitfall] If every character dismisses a legend, players have no reason to take it seriously; give at least one character a reason to believe it.
- [fact] In a place with almost no animal life, a fresh animal sign is conspicuous and carries more weight than it would in a crowded setting. When: when an isolated setting has few animals. Why: The rarity of animal activity makes any sign stand out.

## suspect elimination and lists
- [rule] Question suspects apart from one another so their accounts cannot be aligned or reconciled with each other. When: When more than one suspect is linked to the same act. Why: Separate accounts reveal contradictions that shared accounts conceal.
- [rule] Make each new piece of evidence reframe the suspect list rather than only add to it, so the player feels the culprit has changed.
- [heuristic] Spread suspicion across several characters who each have a motive and an alibi, so attention does not settle on one suspect or location. When: Multiple incidents occur in different places. Why: Diffused evidence weakens the pull toward any one suspect. (x2)
- [heuristic] Use the skill a task requires to filter suspects: work that can be done from memory needs no physical copy, while copying requires the physical materials and training. When: When the object's theft depended on a specialized skill. Why: Only some suspects could have produced the result with their abilities.
- [heuristic] A single fast answer is only a lead until corroborated, so it should be noted and checked rather than pressed immediately. When: Receiving a quick answer from a witness. Why: Fast answers can be managed and are unverified.
- [heuristic] Keep separate leads apart, such as a record, a deal and a named person, until evidence connects them. When: A case has several unrelated threads.
- [heuristic] Most cases are explained by the simplest account; the real difficulty is proving it rather than finding it.
- [heuristic] Let the wrong suspect be a sincere actor who believes what they see, which makes the false solution convincing. When: designing a false solution. Why: A sincere mistake reads as credible, unlike a clear liar.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the uncanny event. 2) List plausible human or mundane sources. 3) Check each against available evidence. 4) Mark the event open if no source is confirmed. When: An unexplained event could have an ordinary cause that has not yet been tested. Why: Assuming the supernatural before testing ordinary causes leads to unfounded conclusions, while assuming ordinary causes without evidence hides real unknowns.
- [pitfall] A single alternative explanation can be as unsupported as the claim it challenges, so it must be tested like any other.
- [pitfall] Treating every incident as the work of one person can hide a second actor, so test whether the events truly share a single perpetrator. When: When a series of events is attributed to one suspect. Why: Assuming a single source overlooks a second party with separate goals.
- [pitfall] A detective's first argument can be wrong and reversed by a later confession, so mysteries should allow the leading theory to be overturned. When: structuring suspicion across a scenario. Why: Players who commit to one theory feel cheated if the reversal is unsupported.

## timeline and timing tests
- [behavior] Testimony gains value when the person it implicates can no longer deny it, so a planted link is set to matter only after that person is dead or silenced. When: a witness's account will decide an accusation. Why: an accusation cannot be contested by someone who is gone.
- [rule] Check stiffening against the stated time of death, adjusting for temperature, and corroborate before relying on it. When: Comparing a body's state with an account of death time. Why: Temperature shifts rigor timing.
- [heuristic] Small mismatches between witnesses, such as times or appearance details, often mark the weak point of a case and should be tested rather than dismissed as sloppiness. When: When two sworn accounts disagree on time or description. Why: Discrepancies can expose a false alibi or a misidentification.
- [heuristic] Test a stated routine, such as where valuables are kept each night, against the physical evidence before accepting it, since the scene may contradict it.
- [heuristic] Cases become more testable when events are fixed in order and each crucial moment has several independent observers.
- [heuristic] Be cautious when testimony seems to fix a time that physical evidence does not firmly support, since the apparent fixed point may be an assumption. When: Physical or medical evidence gives only a loose time range. Why: Witness timing can be assumed rather than observed.
- [heuristic] Record when and before whom each statement was given, so its timing relative to the event can be placed and weighed.
- [heuristic] Build fair-play deductions from timestamps, schedules and time-zone differences that the reader can check, so the timeline itself carries the solution. Why: A checkable timeline lets the reader test the detective's reasoning against stated facts.
- [procedure] 1) Record the date of each incident from written entries. 2) Compute the intervals between them. 3) Form a provisional schedule theory. 4) Predict the next incident date. 5) Check the prediction against new records.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain the exact sequence of events after the first sound or event. 2) Check whether each step is physically possible in the time allowed. 3) Reenact the sequence while timing it. 4) Reject any account that cannot be performed in the time. When: when a witness's account depends on how long actions took. Why: a story that cannot be performed in the available time is false, however plausible it sounds.
- [procedure] 1) Mark checkpoints such as first contact, key handover, observation period and discovery. 2) Place each suspect's movements against those checkpoints. 3) Mark which movements conflict.
- [procedure] 1) Fix times using observable landmarks such as the moon's position or a lit window. 2) Use each landmark as a checkpoint in the timeline. 3) Check which accounts each landmark corroborates. When: when reconstructing a night timeline. Why: Environmental markers give checkable reference points independent of memory.

## timing and durations
- [model] A fair-play timing twist misreads trusted witnesses and a visible object until a late reinterpretation reverses the apparent timeline.
- [rule] Mark vague times as soft and precise times from reliable sources as firm, and keep the two categories separate in the record.
- [rule] Check how long a sound lasted and how far it could carry before accepting a timing claim. When: a witness gives an exact time for a sound. Why: Duration and range limit when a sound could be placed.
- [rule] Measure an interval from a clearly defined start event to a clearly defined end event. When: Timing an action for a rule check.
- [rule] Compare a measured duration with the rule's limit; any interval beyond the limit is a breach of that rule. When: Checking a time-limited rule.
- [heuristic] Times resting on one witness's watch or memory are weak; check them against a second independent device or record that could corroborate or contradict them. When: A timeline rests on one witness's account. Why: A second independent source can confirm or break the claim.
- [pitfall] Approximate witness times and stated durations are soft and may be wrong or deliberately low; walking or travel estimates often underestimate, so carry a margin of uncertainty unless measured. When: A timeline depends on approximate witness times or stated durations. Why: Poor measurement conditions and approximate recollections vary widely and can hide gaps that matter to an alibi. (x2)
- [pitfall] A small error in one witness's time spreads through every timeline built on it, shifting the whole sequence enough to clear or implicate someone.
- [pitfall] If no event follows the deadline, the countdown goes slack and tension collapses.
- [pitfall] Presenting a time of death as a single point rather than a range overstates the precision of the estimate.
- [pitfall] One small detail, such as who knocked at a door or who set down an object, can carry the timing of a whole episode. When: Reconstructing a sequence of events. Why: Minor actions often serve as the hinges of a timeline.
- [fact] Precise timing turns vague claims into checkable facts, because a measured duration can be tested against a known limit. When: A claim depends on how long something lasted.

## undated and unattributed records
- [rule] Undated documents or facts give no anchor for when events occurred; do not place them in a timeline, since that invents precision the evidence does not support.
- [rule] Treat a paper lacking the usual attestation and oath as unfinished and unofficial, and never present it as evidence that was offered. When: reviewing loose records. Why: missing formal attestation shows it was never presented.
- [heuristic] Treat claims citing unnamed authority, or undated letters bearing only a bare name, as unverified; a name alone does not show who made the claim or request. When: when assessing reported claims. Why: Nothing ties the text to a checkable author or moment. (x2)
- [heuristic] Record an odd observation, such as a missing object or strange visitor, in a journal with no explanation so it can be linked later. When: a game has a log or journal system. Why: unexplained entries become clues when later facts arrive.
- [heuristic] An unexplained name in a guest or access record flags a possible uninvited person; trace the record's source before dismissing it.
- [heuristic] Use an object that is known to exist but unavailable at the critical moment; avoid this device if the audience must examine the object itself. When: the plot needs evidence that cannot be inspected at the key point. Why: examination requires the object to remain intact.
- [heuristic] A withheld letter or a message with no return address can serve as a quest flag that the player must chase down. When: When designing quests around communication.
- [pitfall] Undocumented transfers of an item between holders open room for tampering or doubt, making the evidence unreliable. When: when evidence changes hands informally. Why: Without a record, no one can confirm the item's condition.
- [pitfall] Without dates, an order inferred from message content may be wrong. When: Reconstructing a sequence of messages that lack timestamps. Why: Content-based order depends on assumptions about what each message presupposes.
- [pitfall] A notice or sign can be placed or removed by someone with an interest, and the official record may not show who did it.
- [pitfall] Evidence obtained without authority may be inadmissible, so how a document was obtained matters as much as what it shows.
- [pitfall] Treating an undated, uncited journal line as authoritative only because it is old. When: A document is used as the only authority for an event. Why: Age does not establish accuracy or a date.

## witness timeline testimony
- [definition] A timeline from testimony orders the times witnesses give, anchors them to events all sides can confirm, and marks gaps, showing who was where and when. When: when the case depends on who could have been where at a given hour.
- [rule] Deliver testimony as dated facts that the player assembles into a timeline.
- [heuristic] A suspect's day is usually reconstructed from witnesses who each saw only part of it, not from one complete account.
- [procedure] 1) Extract every duration, date and time of day each witness mentions. 2) Order the times into one sequence, linking separate movements into one route. 3) Mark conflicts and gaps. 4) Note each witness's limits before trusting the times. When: reconstructing event order or alibis from several witnesses. Why: combining accounts exposes the full sequence of movements.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor the timeline on independent, verifiable points such as departures and arrivals, before relying on memory. 2) Place each witnessed event at its stated time, in sequence. 3) Check each claim against what that witness could physically perceive. 4) Mark agreements, conflicts and gaps; leave gaps unfilled by guesswork. When: several witnesses give times for overlapping events, accounts disagree, or a person's possible movements must be located. Why: Independent records are less error-prone than recollection, shared fixed points let contradictions surface, and an unexplained gap is evidence in itself.
- [procedure] 1) Collect each witness's time window. 2) Overlay the windows on one timeline. 3) Mark overlaps, conflicts and gaps. 4) Ask precise questions about exact wording to expose weak points. When: reconstructing an event sequence from several accounts.
- [procedure] 1) List each witness's location at each time. 2) Compare these with the times of key events. 3) Mark accounts that place a witness where they could not have been. When: testimony conflicts or relies on a witness's own position. Why: timing shows which accounts can be true.
- [procedure] 1) List each reported step in the order given, with any time marker the speaker supplies. 2) Separate firm anchors from soft ones. 3) Test the sequence against fixed points such as appointments or deadlines. 4) Check claimed rest periods against other witnesses. When: When several accounts must be fitted together.
- [procedure] 1) Assemble a timeline from transport records and places. 2) State it as established fact. 3) Let the suspect confirm, deny or stay silent. Each fixed point removes a place to hide. When: When confronting a suspect with precise movement records. Why: Specific, proven details leave the suspect fewer ways to evade.
- [procedure] 1) Convert each stop in the account into a timestamp. 2) Lay the timestamps against known event times. 3) Mark which intervals are unaccounted for. 4) Ask for times and places, setting aside remarks about character. 5) Note where the relayer hedges. When: when checking a relayed alibi against physical facts. Why: Testable detail can be checked, unlike character remarks.
- [procedure] 1) Build the timeline from the witness's own stated times. 2) Compare subjective durations against an objective clock. 3) Mark gaps and sudden changes to show when an effect began. When: when a witness's account of time conflicts with records or a room seems sealed. Why: A fixed reference settles disputes that memory cannot.
- [pitfall] A witness's timing depends on when they woke, which is itself uncertain, so their account is weakened. When: when a witness's testimony depends on waking or sleeping times. Why: The reference point they use for timing is unreliable.

## accusation spread and chains
- [model] Model an accusation as a chain: a first suspect, a failed hearing, and a second suspect pulled in by the same rumor, so suspicion visibly moves. When: designing investigation plots. Why: A moving target keeps suspicion visible rather than letting it vanish.
- [mechanism] Each newly named suspect prompts further warrants and examinations, so a household accusation widens across the community with every round of names. When: people in a close community know one another.
- [mechanism] Warrants can spread across neighbouring settlements within weeks, naming people far from the original case.
- [mechanism] Accusers meeting privately can hand new targets to one another, so accusations grow through peer suggestion. When: when a group of accusers meets without outsiders. Why: each suggestion is accepted within the group.
- [mechanism] An accusation can grow from a household episode into a crowd and then a formal hearing, as each new group accepts it as more credible. When: When a private claim is repeated and publicized. Why: Each audience's acceptance raises the claim's apparent weight for the next.
- [mechanism] A physical clue used to accuse can be turned back on the accuser, and once the same mark is shared it becomes a general claim, not a single finding. When: an accusation supported by a physical sign. Why: the accused can show the sign exists elsewhere.
- [behavior] When accusers are questioned together, each may blame the other for who first named a suspect, deflecting responsibility. When: when multiple accusers give joint accounts. Why: shifting blame protects each accuser's own position.
- [behavior] Accusations travel by word of mouth, and a public outcry can lead others to avoid the accused household. When: when a claim is voiced in a public gathering. Why: Social avoidance spreads quickly once a claim is shared.
- [rule] Make a mocking or false accusation cost the player rather than being free of consequence.
- [heuristic] Raise the chance of formal accusation as disputes accumulate between factions in a closed community. When: designing a closed community with rival factions. Why: Each unresolved dispute adds grievance that can turn into a formal charge.
- [pitfall] Accepting a volunteered culprit at face value, or ignoring the speaker's past connections to the crime's pattern, can lead to a wrong conclusion. When: When evaluating a suspect's offered explanation. Why: Diversions can be false, and connections to the crime's pattern reveal the speaker's involvement.

## alibi and timeline reasoning
- [definition] A fabricated alibi is a witness account that places a suspect elsewhere, where the witness is the suspect in disguise, so the account is planted to mislead.
- [mechanism] Dust accumulates on undisturbed surfaces, so clean and dusty patches show when an object last covered or left a surface. When: a surface is under or around an object. Why: covered areas stay clean while uncovered areas collect dust.
- [rule] Explain why a scripted delay happens so players feel uncertainty rather than confusion. When: A planned moment is postponed to build suspense. Why: An unexplained wait reads as a bug or confusion, not as tension.
- [heuristic] A household member's habitual heavy sleep, especially after illness, creates a predictable window when an unseen exit is most likely. When: A suspect plans a movement through a house at night. Why: People who sleep heavily early in the night are less likely to notice movement.
- [heuristic] Fix each step of a sequence to a clock, a dated record, or a published schedule rather than to memory alone. When: A timeline must be checked against independent evidence. Why: Anchored steps can be tested, while memory-only steps can drift.
- [heuristic] A group alibi is strong only if the timeline covers the exact moment in question, since a continuous routine gives general but weaker corroboration than a specific witness. When: Evaluating a group account of where people were. Why: A routine running without interruption does not prove each member was in view at the critical moment.
- [heuristic] Store events on a global clock with local time offsets so the player can line up records from several locations. When: When a game spans several locations with separate records. Why: A shared clock lets the player match events across places and find meaningful overlaps.
- [procedure] 1) Pick fixed landmarks such as floor pattern or wall marks. 2) Measure each movement against them. 3) Count steps or turns against the reference. When: Recording a moving target's path in poor visibility. Why: Fixed reference points make movement records measurable and comparable.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the latest moment a missing person is certainly known to be alive. 2) List every place they may have gone and the possible order of visits. 3) If an unobserved visit may have come later, add the shortest travel time between the two places to the last sighting. When: A person has vanished and a timeline has unknown visit order. Why: The last certain moment of life governs legal questions such as inheritance and succession.
- [procedure] 1) List everyone who could have acted, including performers, staff, guards and investigators. 2) Eliminate each person by a specific placement, such as a sound or presence they can be heard or seen from. 3) Identify the independent witnesses. 4) Ask whether each witness could have left their position. When: Several people give a shared alibi covering the same moment. Why: A group account can hide individual gaps, so each member's position must be checked separately.
- [pitfall] A cover story that a witness can verify and find false damages trust, so keep any pretext simple enough to hold up under checking. When: When an investigator adopts a cover identity or story. Why: A discovered pretext makes the investigator's other statements suspect.

## altered records and documents
- [rule] Plant a faint, later-looking note in a document as a clue that the record was altered after the fact. When: when designing in-game clues.
- [rule] Place an edited archive copy whose key word points to one suspect, with the original as the evidence that unlocks the truth.
- [rule] Treat a discrepancy between an official document and a rumored version as a clue about who may have altered the text. When: When a document exists in more than one version. Why: Differences between versions point to the party who changed them.
- [heuristic] A label or form written in an unfamiliar hand suggests someone else has altered the object, which is a lead worth following. Why: A second writer means the object was touched after its creation.
- [heuristic] Check the seam of a cut-and-patched label or document, since altered papers often show an uneven edge where the edit was joined. When: a document or label may have been changed. Why: joins are hard to make invisibly.
- [heuristic] When a document seems altered, ask which change would be easiest for a forger. Changes between similar-looking characters, such as one day name for another, are the most likely. When: A date or figure looks changed. Why: Easy substitutions require minimal effort and avoid detection.
- [pitfall] Claims by a party, such as petitions or records by those who acted, are advocacy that softens or omits their own role; check them against the other side's account.
- [pitfall] A cover-up that alters dates on records can reveal the true day, because the altered date conflicts with the real schedule.
- [pitfall] Dates can be wrong or added in later copies, so check the original record where possible. When: when working from copies of documents.
- [pitfall] The same parcel's size can be recorded differently across successive documents, so area figures alone cannot identify a lot. When: when matching a parcel across several records. Why: Measurements were often re-estimated at each transfer.
- [pitfall] Trusting the top layer because it is most visible can hide the true record beneath an overlay. When: An object carries multiple labels or markings. Why: Newer surfaces are designed or accidentally placed to overwrite older information.

## atmosphere and audience
- [mechanism] Atmosphere such as darkness, silence, oppression, and matching weather sets the pacing and mood, reinforcing the protagonists' gloom.
- [behavior] When a decisive fact is disclosed to a hushed room, the audience's attention turns to the implicated person, who is watched closely for a reaction. When: a decisive fact is disclosed in front of a group. Why: people look for signs of guilt in the accused.
- [behavior] Audience sympathy can override evidence, so a case may turn more on who seems wronged than on the facts. When: A trial or judgement is made before an audience with emotional stakes. Why: People favour the party they sympathise with over what the evidence shows.
- [behavior] Public appeals address an audience, while private praise addresses an ally whose support is needed. When: A writer sends a flattering private letter to someone whose backing they need. Why: The recipient's support is the real target.
- [rule] Describe the setting's mood as part of the mystery, showing danger and violence as ordinary, so the place itself signals threat.
- [heuristic] Atmosphere frames a mystery but is not proof: test each eerie cue against physical evidence, like a hidden chest or drawer, since mood can color ordinary facts. When: When evaluating eerie details in an investigation or a scene relying heavily on tone. Why: Physical evidence distinguishes human work from supernatural causes; mood alone cannot establish facts or let players make progress. (x2)
- [heuristic] Words spoken for an audience, including denials, may mislead anyone who takes them at face value, so separate what is said for watchers from what is meant. When: Interpreting dialogue in a monitored or hostile setting. Why: Speakers shape words to deceive listeners who may be watching.
- [tradeoff] Explaining away every eerie detail drains dread and dismissing all atmosphere leaves the world flat, while explaining nothing loses the audience's trust. When: When resolving a horror mystery or designing an investigation with an eerie setting. Why: Full explanation removes the unknown and removing all atmosphere drains mood, while no explanation makes the story seem arbitrary.
- [pitfall] Ornament untied to plot dilutes attention when evidence is needed, and overused cues without payoffs lose force, so tie each cue to a following event. When: Repeating mood imagery across a story, or when the reader needs evidence. Why: Cues without payoffs become empty and reduce trust in future warnings. (x2)
- [pitfall] A narrator kept in the dark can make the audience feel excluded from the solution.
- [pitfall] Too much staging, such as dramatic arrivals or shouting, can pull attention away from the real clues. When: A confrontation is heavily dramatized. Why: Spectacle captures attention that should go to factual evidence.

## blunt and bold tactics
- [behavior] Observers tend to read a blunt, businesslike manner as a sign of honesty. When: Judging a witness's trustworthiness. Why: Plain style signals sincerity to many readers.
- [behavior] A culprit who believes pressure falls on someone else, and that proof is thin, may make a bold move that exposes themselves. When: an investigator openly admits weak proof. Why: The culprit's perceived risk drops, so caution gives way to action.
- [heuristic] Do not discount a bold reconstruction merely for being bold; check it against the facts, since such stories can be right or wrong. When: an amateur builds a dramatic account from a single clue. Why: boldness does not indicate accuracy.
- [heuristic] A bold, direct act at a dangerous spot suggests nerve and planning rather than impulse. When: Inferring temperament from a crime's method. Why: Acting with composure in a risky position requires control that impulsive acts lack.
- [heuristic] A blunt weapon implies that great force was needed to use it.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a sudden, blunt question about a specific fact. 2) Watch physical reactions such as breathing, standing up or tears. 3) Follow up on what the reaction reveals. When: when a witness's spoken answer seems incomplete.
- [tradeoff] Blunt pressure or interruptions can yield a quick admission, but they wound the speaker, reduce cooperation, and may push them to withhold more.
- [tradeoff] A motive stated openly risks being dismissed as melodrama, while one stated as a whim or joke stays visible but can be missed. When: Deciding how directly to reveal a character's motive early on. Why: Directness aids comprehension but can reduce believability.
- [pitfall] A blunt guess can read as an insult, so the investigator must let the subject supply the answer rather than state it. When: Confronting a suspect with an inference. Why: Direct accusation damages rapport and can end the exchange.
- [pitfall] A bold bluff is risky and costs credibility if exposed; it works only when the reconstruction matches what the suspect knows. When: Using an unverified reconstruction to pressure a suspect.
- [pitfall] An investigator who acts impulsively under pressure, such as physically grabbing the suspect, can undermine the scene and the credibility of the case. When: During a confrontation with a cornered suspect. Why: Adrenaline and urgency override deliberate judgment.

## child and vulnerable witnesses
- [behavior] Vulnerable witnesses such as children may be pressed to testify against relatives, so their testimony reflects that pressure. When: authority figures question a child about family members. Why: pressure from authority shapes what a child says.
- [rule] Treat a child's account as a lead to check against other evidence, not as direct proof; it may serve as an unreliable witness whose statement conflicts with others. When: A child witness provides information about a case, or a story needs unreliable witnesses. Why: Unverified child testimony can be mistaken or exaggerated. (x2)
- [rule] Do not press or question a child to the point of pressure, since it can cause distress and harm the child. When: An investigator interviews a child about a sensitive matter. Why: Pressure can distress the child and upset the adults caring for them.
- [rule] Do not rely on a child's recall of events the child slept through, though details the child remembers may still be useful. When: When a child is offered as a witness to an event. Why: A child who did not witness an event cannot testify to it, but repeated details can still point somewhere.
- [heuristic] When an adult interrupts or repeatedly tries to hush or remove a child witness, treat it as evidence that the adult is controlling the account and protecting a secret. When: When a child witness is questioned in the presence of adults or an adult tries to remove a child from an interview. Why: Adults who silence a child may be shaping what the child reveals, since controlling a child's speech is a way to protect a secret.
- [heuristic] Claims of illness, delirium or unusual lucidity made under suspicion deserve scrutiny, since they are a common way to deflect questions. When: A suspect volunteers a claim about their own mental state while under suspicion.
- [tradeoff] Use a child NPC as unreliable testimony through fear or repeated prompting, leaving prompting clues in dialogue; or as a reliable observer the player must verify against environmental evidence. When: Designing child NPC testimony or an NPC who reports a sighting. (x2)
- [pitfall] A child or paid witness may hide part of the truth, so a figure they give can be understated. When: a witness has been paid or wants to please. Why: Payment or a wish to please shades what is said.
- [pitfall] A child's memory of an outing can fix the scene accurately while blurring the details. When: when testimony comes from a witness who was young at the event. Why: Children retain vivid scenes but not precise particulars.
- [pitfall] Adults may overrule a child's account to avoid a disturbing conclusion, which can cause an important observation to be lost. When: When an adult dismisses a child's report because the conclusion is unsettling. Why: Avoidance of a disturbing conclusion can override the evidence.
- [fact] A child's testimony can be valuable for vivid, unfiltered detail, but the same account mixes real events with gossip, games and invented material. When: An investigator takes testimony from a child witness. Why: Children mishear, exaggerate and repeat adult talk, so their accounts need filtering.

## consequences and timing
- [model] Contingency plans for a crime can include four parts: an escape route, a cover story, a reserve of money, and a disguise.
- [mechanism] A partly consumed object, such as a half-full glass or burned-down candle, can be read as a clock to estimate when an event occurred. When: An object burns, melts or accumulates at a known rate. Why: Its state works as a clock only while nobody has handled it.
- [mechanism] A small early action with a dangerous side effect, such as a dropped light source, can set up a later disaster that it explains. When: Planting a cause that pays off later in the plot. Why: A seeded consequence makes the later event feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [mechanism] Stating the legal or personal consequences of an act, and showing how much is already known, adds pressure on a suspect.
- [behavior] The amount each person consumed from a shared object reveals who handled it and in what order, which can point back to the intended target. When: Several people shared a poisoned or trapped object. Why: Consumption differences trace the object's path and show who was meant to be harmed.
- [rule] Give ultimatum choices explicit consequences, so that a confession branch has a visible and meaningful effect on the outcome. When: when designing a confession or refusal option. Why: Vague consequences make the choice feel empty and weaken the branch.
- [heuristic] Show the consequence of a disclosure in the next scene rather than in the reveal itself.
- [heuristic] A holder's account of keeping an object continuously in sight shrinks the window of possible access to the time it was out of their sight.
- [heuristic] A bait the player sets, such as an advertisement, can cause a later death, and the resulting guilt steers the player's next choices.
- [tradeoff] A continuous timeline keeps simultaneous threads and builds tension but may feel long; discrete sections isolate units but repeat shared background and fragment the thread. When: Several threads run at once. Why: Structure choice trades felt simultaneity against standalone readability.
- [tradeoff] A tragic outcome deepens the aftermath but removes any trial, while an arrest allows a trial but gives a plainer close. When: when choosing how the culprit's fate closes the case.

## damaged evidence
- [rule] Flag erased or worn words as unreadable, not filled with assumed content; never read a gap as containing the answer it lacks; record a missing final answer as a gap. When: transcribing damaged records. Why: assumed content can pass as evidence.
- [rule] Make a wound or damage pattern readable: its angle and location should reveal the attacker's position and the victim's posture to the player. When: when designing environmental or body damage as clues. Why: readable damage lets players deduce the event.
- [rule] Treat weather or wear as lowering a clue's legibility rather than erasing it; partly readable evidence still carries information.
- [heuristic] A body with an unrecognisable face is often accepted, because examiners cannot swear to who the face belongs to.
- [heuristic] Make one timestamp deliberately damaged so the player must infer the missing digit from other clues. Why: Inference from other clues turns the gap into a puzzle rather than a dead end.
- [heuristic] Let a damaged or burned object support an inference about its material, and have players record that inference as uncertain.
- [procedure] 1) Test the altered residue with a flame. 2) Dissolve the residue in alcohol. 3) Examine it under a microscope for fibres and binder, then compare with a known sample. When: the original material is burned or altered.
- [pitfall] Destroying an item does not destroy what is attached to it, and burning materials such as felt can produce smell that draws attention. When: Attempting to destroy evidence by fire. Why: Fire leaves fragments, fittings and odours that persist and can be noticed.
- [pitfall] A report cut short leaves the key fact unknown, so the investigator must return to the source to confirm it.
- [pitfall] Broken edges and other damage on the object do not reflect tooth marks, so exclude them from the comparison.
- [pitfall] Partly destroyed or broken evidence can mislead when the surviving fragment is read on its own.

## decisive evidence
- [rule] Present the decisive clue as a mundane detail, such as a count or smell, stating its key detail only at the later payoff, so it is overlooked until then. When: Hiding the solution's key evidence in a mystery. Why: A familiar, minimized object is overlooked until its hidden detail is explained.
- [rule] Do not require a group of clues when one trace is decisive on its own. Use grouping only for evidence that is individually weak. When: When evaluating a piece of evidence that is conclusive by itself. Why: Forcing a group analysis on a decisive trace wastes effort and can dilute a clear result.
- [heuristic] A single checkable discrepancy, such as a date conflict between two records, can be the decisive proof where broader argument fails. When: building a case. Why: verifiable contradictions are hard to dismiss.
- [heuristic] A single well-chosen clue can settle a case, and later evidence then only confirms the first inference. When: when designing the key clue of a mystery. Why: One decisive observation can anchor the solution.
- [heuristic] Look for one decisive contemporaneous document, such as a letter written at the time, that can clear a suspect when other facts cannot. When: Most evidence for a suspect also implicates them. Why: A single record made at the time can outweigh inferred motive.
- [heuristic] The most useful check is whether a particular observer saw a particular person pass, since that fixes the timing.
- [heuristic] Seek one concrete, physical fact tied to the crime that fixes a clue's meaning, since a tangible object resolves ambiguity better than a psychological reading. Why: A physical object can be checked, while a reading of behaviour depends on the reader.
- [heuristic] Weigh evidence that looks decisive against the rest of the case, since it may be coincidence rather than cause.
- [heuristic] Hold a favoured natural explanation until an event it cannot cover arrives, then treat that event as the decisive test. When: when a natural explanation has been kept for comfort despite conflicting evidence. Why: A single event that breaks the explanation shows its limit more clearly than repeated argument.
- [procedure] 1) Explain how the crime was done with a mechanism the player can see. 2) Confirm who did it with an independent outside check, such as a physical match. Why: a method alone does not identify the people.
- [pitfall] A dramatic weapon can look decisive while a broken part or misplaced item quietly contradicts the claimed use.

## dialogue and exposition
- [rule] Set explicit terms before work begins: agree expenses plus a fee and lawful scope; for challenges needing the challenger's help, require full cooperation and dropped objections. When: When accepting a job or a challenge.
- [rule] Explain your purpose to a witness in plain, conversational terms; an overly formal explanation can lose their attention entirely.
- [rule] Ask witnesses for facts rather than verdicts, so they do not steer the account toward a conclusion.
- [rule] Stage the full explanation as a scene where the detective already knows the answer, so tension comes from how the room reacts rather than the solution.
- [heuristic] A failed appointment, where the expected person had already left, changes what the suspect does next, so record it as an event that branches the timeline.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC's protective excuse appear in dialogue so players learn to test excuses against physical evidence.
- [heuristic] Tagging each account with its speaker's stake lets a designer plant motive early without a direct exposition dump. When: Delivering backstory through dialogue. Why: Speaker motive carries information that a flat recital would lack.
- [heuristic] Quote sources at length so readers can see gradual shifts in wording that a stripped excerpt would hide.
- [heuristic] Deliver the missing steps of a reconstructed sequence through a short dialogue that closes the gap. When: When the player needs a brief explanation to complete a timeline. Why: A concise spoken account closes gaps without a lengthy info dump.
- [procedure] 1) Keep the exchange going by asking one follow-up question after another. 2) When the witness mentions something unexpected, ask an open follow-up rather than a closed one. 3) Invite their opinion, then test it against what else is known. When: a witness is willing to talk. Why: Open follow-ups surface leads that closed questions would end.
- [pitfall] A long backstory monologue delivered after the climax can drag and undo the tension built by the discovery. When: Delivering exposition following a major reveal. Why: Extended explanation after the peak of tension lowers momentum and pacing.

## direct versus relayed knowledge
- [definition] A direct indication shows presence outright, while a circumstantial indication only suggests it; clues differ in strength and should be sorted by this.
- [behavior] A key fact that reaches the player only through a second character is held with less certainty, and players tend to test it rather than accept it. When: a reveal delivered by an intermediary. Why: the source is one step removed from the event.
- [rule] Separate what a source directly observed from what it was told, and note where each source's knowledge stops. Why: Secondhand accounts can sound as firm as eyewitness accounts while hiding how little the source actually knows.
- [rule] Separate what a witness saw and heard firsthand from what another person told them afterwards, and flag any parts they cannot repeat accurately. When: A witness reports a private exchange or a later account. Why: Relayed or remembered speech is easier to distort than direct perception.
- [rule] Examine the physical evidence directly rather than accepting a lead offered by someone else. When: when a colleague or witness offers a ready explanation. Why: direct reading keeps the investigation honest.
- [rule] Require character testimony to come from people with direct, long-term contact with the subject.
- [rule] When data reaches you through a trusted intermediary who reads figures aloud, record that person as the source of the timeline. Why: The source's reliability shapes how far the timeline can be trusted.
- [heuristic] A plausible route by which a witness could have absorbed relevant history unknowingly can explain knowledge they claim to have gained elsewhere.
- [procedure] 1) Tag each report by source. 2) Mark whether the speaker saw the event or repeated what others said. 3) Weigh firsthand reports above relayed ones. When: When a case rests on many small reports, some of them relaying speech. Why: Relayed speech adds a link where error or bias can enter.
- [tradeoff] Demanding direct proof for obscure matters may leave no verdict possible, while accepting circumstantial proof lowers the bar in practice. When: when the crime is hidden and direct evidence is scarce. Why: Circumstantial proof can fill the gap but makes wrongful conviction more likely.
- [pitfall] Traces the investigator did not see personally rest on other people's descriptions and should be treated as less certain.

## document provenance and reliability
- [model] A frame-narrative investigation moves through linked documents, each pointing to the next source, so understanding widens in time and place while the explanation keeps shifting. When: When structuring a mystery told through found documents. Why: Each document narrows or expands the protagonist's belief, sustaining the investigation.
- [rule] Let a threat exist only in documents, so the player must verify its existence before accepting the accused as guilty.
- [rule] Use a physical proof that is hard to fake and easy to test, such as prints on an object, as the decisive reveal. When: when the solution must convince an official audience. Why: A testable proof resists counterclaims and makes the conclusion checkable.
- [rule] Make a document, not a character's speech, deliver the final reveal, so the reader can check it against earlier scenes. When: Choosing how to deliver a major plot revelation. Why: A document can be examined and compared with earlier evidence, which makes the reveal verifiable.
- [heuristic] Use a reconstructed document, like a letter or sealed declaration from within the affected family or group, as final proof where testimony cannot settle the case, not a new witness. When: resolving a mystery's central secret. Why: Documents from within the story carry authority and keep the resolution tied to material the player already knows about. (x2)
- [heuristic] Check a document's addressee before acting on its contents, since a shared name can make a letter belong to someone else. When: Items that identify or introduce a character by name. Why: Similar names let an item reach the wrong person unnoticed.
- [heuristic] Check how a document arrived, including postmark, envelope and delivery record, since a note from a private route changes its meaning. When: when a document's route to the investigator is unclear. Why: Delivery route is evidence about who sent it and how.
- [heuristic] A harmless message can still prove a link, because the sender's knowledge of the hidden party is the valuable part.
- [procedure] 1) Write the letter, journal or contract with deliberate gaps, such as a missing name. 2) Let each gap reveal an author's blind spot. 3) Place the document where the player can find and examine the gap. 4) Place a second source so that finding it opens the gap as a quest hook. When: Designing written clues in a level. Why: Gaps the player can interpret give a specific place to look and an inference to make; a missing detail motivates the player to search for the corroborating source.
- [pitfall] A grieving or angry writer may exaggerate or contradict themselves, so vivid accusations need corroboration before they are believed.
- [fact] A written statement is evidence, but its reliability depends on the writer's state of mind, its internal consistency, and how it compares with the writer's earlier statements.

## emotional npc scenes
- [rule] Track NPC emotional state to gate dialogue: open with ambient topics, unlock sensitive ones only after tells show readiness, so player care or refusal changes what is revealed. When: Designing NPC or companion dialogue, especially with sensitive subjects. Why: Premature sensitive topics cause the NPC to shut down.
- [rule] Change NPC dialogue with the player's discoveries, so asking the same question again yields a new answer.
- [rule] Let NPCs respond to player actions with emotional displays, and make the player judge whether each display is genuine or aimed at a goal. When: when designing NPC dialogue that reacts emotionally. Why: it makes the player weigh NPC motives.
- [heuristic] Stage an early, seemingly trivial encounter whose meaning becomes clear later, rewarding attentive audiences. Why: hindsight rewards attention.
- [heuristic] Conflict between allies adds pressure without adding plot facts, so it can sustain tension between discoveries.
- [heuristic] Place a revealing, emotional line that the player only hears if they keep talking to an NPC, since unguarded moments tell more than refusals. When: Designing NPC dialogue that hides information. Why: Emotional slips leak information that a guarded refusal does not.
- [heuristic] Convey an NPC's reliability through emotional tone in dialogue, such as panic or bravado, rather than through a stated reliability value. When: Scripting NPC reports whose weight should vary. Why: Tone signals credibility implicitly and keeps the report diegetic.
- [heuristic] Let the accused's shame carry the scene, so pressure on the victim drives the drama until the reveal.
- [pitfall] An emotional scene can move the witness toward belief in the suspect's innocence, which can defeat the planned pressure.
- [pitfall] A pointed remark made before enough is known can alert the subject before the investigator can use the reaction.
- [pitfall] Emotional confrontations can stall pacing; keep exchanges short and return to the facts. When: when an accusation scene grows emotional. Why: Long emotional beats delay resolution.

## gatekeeper npc design
- [mechanism] Trust built in an earlier encounter lets a gatekeeper listen before any request is made, which changes how they respond. When: character has met the gatekeeper in a previous scene. Why: past favorable contact lowers guardedness.
- [behavior] A gatekeeper may hint at a next source or character without naming it, or at a condition pointing to a second location or later quest trigger, admitting nothing outright. When: gatekeeper will not confess directly; designing gatekeeper NPC dialogue. Why: hints move the story forward while protecting the gatekeeper; the refusal's stated reason and conditions give the player a path to hidden material. (x2)
- [behavior] A gatekeeper may yield a partial answer, useful only with another fact, after appeals to honesty or a credible claim of skill, even while doubting it will help. When: requester argues an amateur can succeed where professionals cannot; or when building an interrogation scene.
- [behavior] A gatekeeper's report about a visitor's appearance can decide whether she is admitted, and the gatekeeper's own opinion filters that report. When: A visitor must pass a reporter before meeting the person in charge. Why: The reporter's words reveal their own taste and bias as much as the visitor's qualities.
- [rule] When a gatekeeper bound by client constraints blocks access to a witness or location, plan a second route to the same facts. When: a formal channel refuses access to a witness or location. Why: Formal gatekeepers follow their client's constraints, which limits what they will share. (x2)
- [rule] Let a gatekeeper NPC ask a fixed set of questions drawn from lore the player may have found. Answers matching the world state open the way.
- [rule] Let gatekeeper NPCs be persuaded by a cover story or small bribe that opens a locked location or reveals a contact. When: designing NPC access checks. Why: cheap persuasion gives players a route that avoids combat.
- [rule] A gatekeeper NPC answers with true but general statements until the player shows a specific clue, then gives a partial fact. When: When designing an NPC that guards information. Why: Specific evidence unlocks specific answers, which rewards investigation.
- [heuristic] Getting information from a gatekeeper depends on how the request is framed, on showing the requester can handle risk, and on accepting a partial answer. When: player must extract information from an official through dialogue.
- [heuristic] Dialogue extraction suits an official who holds needed information; a gatekeeper with no reason to share will not be moved. When: choosing whether an official can be used as a source.
- [heuristic] A gatekeeper NPC can refuse access to a witness until the player builds trust or gives a reason, and the refusal can be framed as protection. When: When designing access restrictions to an information source. Why: Access gated by trust creates a meaningful progression.

## identification and suspects
- [mechanism] A guest or servant who seems harmless can be revealed late as a disguised criminal or supernatural being, overturning the audience's expectation of an outsider. When: Late reveal of a trusted or ordinary-looking character. Why: Audiences assume the threat comes from outside the household.
- [heuristic] A person may mistake an intruder for someone else and freeze in surprise until a voice reveals the truth. When: explaining a delayed or absent reaction to an intruder. Why: misperceived identity delays response.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC misidentify a character under certain question orders, and let the player re-ask with different phrasing to get a more reliable answer. When: Designing NPC witness dialogue that can err. Why: Misidentification becomes a puzzle when the player can test it.
- [heuristic] Read a character's odd conduct against their occupation and habits before treating it as guilty; the same act may be routine for them. When: A suspect's behaviour looks suspicious. Why: Habits give innocent explanations that an outsider's standards overlook.
- [heuristic] Keep the cast minimal: a companion should supply context for the scene, not take part in the investigation. When: Single-scene mystery with few characters. Why: Extra investigators dilute the reveal.
- [heuristic] Pair each identity clue with a second independent clue so the eventual explanation has more than one support. When: Building toward a disguise reveal. Why: Two independent supports make the final explanation more convincing and fair.
- [procedure] 1) List the conditions: length of absence, expected inquiries, and whether a sealed place would hide a body. 2) Ask whether those conditions favour concealment. 3) Separate possible from probable. 4) Find the plan's weak point. When: a suspect's motive or access is known but the act is unproven. Why: Judging opportunity by conditions gives a structured test rather than a guess.
- [procedure] 1) Offer a plausible identity for the victim. 2) Back it with a witness. 3) Test it against physical marks. 4) Discard it with a contradiction. 5) Move suspicion to the next candidate. When: structuring a whodunit where the victim's identity is disputed. Why: Repeated test-and-discard cycles keep the reader's belief moving and build toward the real answer.
- [tradeoff] Leaving the final identity open when the enemy's body is unrecognisable keeps the threat alive for a sequel but withholds closure; confirming identity gives satisfaction and ends the thread. Why: Each option trades lingering tension against a clean resolution; an open identity keeps the disguise chain available for later encounters.
- [fact] Overconfidence in a safeguard becomes a serious risk mainly when it causes lax habits.
- [fact] A mystery can open on an unidentified corpse and be driven by the question of who the dead person is, with identity itself as the central puzzle. When: designing a detective plot built around a body. Why: Identity uncertainty gives the investigation a question that drives every scene.

## missing physical evidence
- [rule] A missing-item puzzle can show the player the gap first, letting them infer the owner, the weapon type and the time it vanished. When: designing a missing-item puzzle. Why: Inference from a visible gap rewards attention.
- [rule] Treat a missing page or item in a record as a clue, since the gap may show someone wanted a particular entry hidden. When: A record is incomplete. Why: Deliberate removal often signals a concealed entry.
- [heuristic] When an expected item is missing from an inventory, point the player toward the owner's most likely confidant. When: designing an item-tracing clue.
- [heuristic] Build a missing-person quest where each trace, such as a messenger, ticket or carriage, is a node that the player follows to find the failed link. When: Designing a search quest. Why: Sequential traces give the player steps that can each be checked.
- [heuristic] A conspicuously missing trace where others should appear may show that the area was deliberately cleaned. When: a trace is absent from a place where it is expected. Why: A deliberate act can remove evidence.
- [heuristic] When expected traces are missing, propose alternative causes, such as another means of transport or wind dispersal, and test each with a targeted check. When: when the traces a method should leave are absent.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the original count of a set of similar objects. 2) Count the members present. 3) Count the separated pieces. 4) If a piece is unaccounted for, estimate what it held from its size. When: a set of standard objects such as cut sheets or tickets has a discrepancy. Why: A count mismatch shows that a member is missing, and its size limits what it could have contained.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm the display's contents with someone who knew it well. 2) Confirm which item is missing. 3) List everyone who had access to it. When: A weapon is missing from a known display. Why: Confirmed absence and access narrow who could have taken it.
- [tradeoff] Absence of an expected trace rules out its cause only if removal is unlikely; if cleaning or purging could erase it, absence is inconclusive; search for the trace. When: A suspected cause should leave a physical trace, such as a residue, stain, marker or footprint. Why: Cleaning, purging or vomiting can remove residue, making absence inconclusive.
- [pitfall] A writing tool may be missing from the body, so its absence must be checked rather than assumed.
- [pitfall] A claimed trace that cannot be found later neither confirms nor refutes the claim, since its absence has many causes. When: when a witness reports a feature that has since vanished. Why: evidence that is gone cannot be checked.

## narrative structure and twists
- [model] A recurring mystery shape runs: client hook, test at site, mundane explanation, escalation, rite or confrontation, trap and reversal, then partial unmasking that leaves something unresolved. When: Structuring a horror or mystery scenario with a supernatural agent. Why: The repeated arc lets players anticipate beats while the specifics surprise them.
- [model] A grievance plot has eight phases: setup, harassment, complication, triangle clues, false solution and reversal, crisis, reveal, aftermath.
- [mechanism] When the audience holds every clue before the connection is made, their own inference becomes the source of the surprise. When: designing a reveal. Why: the surprise feels earned because the pieces were already available.
- [mechanism] When the reader knows the killer's plan from the start, suspense shifts from who did it to whether the frame will hold and the innocent will be caught. When: when the audience sees the crime's preparation. Why: Dramatic tension comes from the outcome for the framed party, not from identity.
- [heuristic] Let the protagonist's doubt justify the player's disbelief, then pay it off with physical evidence that the anomaly is real. When: when staging the reveal of a hidden rival. Why: physical proof that contradicts a justified doubt lands with force.
- [heuristic] Leave the final layer of a reveal presumed rather than proved when a lingering question is wanted.
- [procedure] 1) Establish a fixed idea or intent. 2) Turn it into an act. 3) Feed a series of false alarms and provocations. 4) Close in with interrogations until a confession. When: when building a concealment-driven plot. Why: Escalating pressure steadily tightens the story toward a confession.
- [tradeoff] Keeping a self-staged crime hidden from the public preserves the twist, but leaves in-world characters without full closure. When: Ending a mystery where the culprit's identity should stay unknown to the world.
- [pitfall] Persisting along a closed line of inquiry out of stubbornness wastes time that a second anchor could recover. When: An investigator keeps retracing a dead end. Why: Sunk effort makes the blocked path feel more promising than it is.
- [fact] A closed-room domestic mystery can be built as a chain of suspect shifts, where each apparent solution is overturned by a physical clue the investigator had already seen but misread. When: Designing a mystery with several suspects and a fixed set of clues. Why: Each shift keeps suspicion moving while the reader's trust in each answer is repeatedly undercut.
- [fact] A story can present an official verdict on a death alongside contrary rumours, so that the reader holds both without resolution. When: Writing an opening death scene in a mystery. Why: Holding incompatible truths creates suspense that persists into later chapters.

## over-caution and suspicion
- [mechanism] A writer who runs characters together to hide a message often leaves unusual crowding at the points where a natural pause would fall, and these gaps reveal the message's structure. When: A message is deliberately run together to conceal it. Why: Writers tend to over-correct for concealment, leaving irregular spacing at phrase boundaries.
- [mechanism] Guarding hard against a small risk can create a visible sign, and that sign can expose an otherwise careful plan.
- [behavior] A setup built to block every suspicion can look rehearsed, so observers may read the safeguards as evidence of foreknowledge. When: A suspect's safeguards are elaborate and cover every route. Why: An innocent person rarely guards against an accusation not yet made.
- [rule] Hold a question open when the most forceful speaker is certain, rather than letting confidence settle the matter.
- [heuristic] Treat unusual over-precaution as a lead toward a concealed act, not proof of it; attributing motive to over-caution without other supporting evidence is unwarranted.
- [pitfall] Seeing a frame-up in every odd object makes an investigator dismiss real evidence; some are innocent oversights. Keep the other possibility open until evidence settles it. When: a real clue looks suspicious. Why: Premature doubt blocks the true explanation.
- [pitfall] Making the framed party's innocence too obvious removes the doubt that misdirection needs. When: Writing a mystery with a red herring. Why: Doubt must persist for misdirection to work.
- [pitfall] A watcher so careful not to be seen can lose the subject, which defeats the watch.
- [pitfall] Treating every setback as staged wastes time chasing a genuine loss.
- [pitfall] A witness who seems unusual may still be right; dismissing an unlikely account without testing it against records can discard the truth. Why: Over-correction treats oddness as falsehood.
- [pitfall] A routine assumed too strictly can be broken by an unscheduled visit, so schedules must allow for exceptions. When: Relying on a fixed schedule to rule out visitors. Why: Unplanned visits fall outside the expected pattern.

## photographs and images
- [rule] Show a photograph to witnesses to test identification rather than assuming a suspect is recognised.
- [heuristic] Circulate a photograph widely when a face is the only link to a claimed past identity.
- [heuristic] Read a photograph closely for distinctive features, such as hair, beard, moustache and eyebrows, to build a description to test against later reports.
- [procedure] 1) Present a set of photographs to each witness. 2) Record which faces each witness recognises. 3) Confirm any identification later with independent evidence. When: Identifying a person from memory of their appearance. Why: Structured recognition gives checkable identifications.
- [procedure] 1) Show a photograph of the suspected stand-in to people who knew the real person. 2) Record whether they recognise the face. 3) Treat recognition as identity evidence only if the witnesses are independent. When: Testing whether a documented person was actually present. Why: Recognition by people who knew the real person links the face to the identity.
- [procedure] 1) Anchor the witness to a narrow time window and a specific location. 2) Check both directions of a route. 3) Show the photo to several witnesses separately. 4) Record each negative answer as information. When: Testing whether a suspect was at a place and time. Why: Narrow anchors make recall specific, and several separate witnesses cross-check each other.
- [pitfall] A photograph shows one instant and fixes a face and date but not relationships, so confirm what it shows and interpret it with surrounding evidence. Why: One instant can mislead without context. (x2)
- [pitfall] A photo-based identification may reflect politeness, suggestion or the shown image rather than memory of the original encounter, so it is weaker than it seems. When: Using a photo identification as evidence, or showing witnesses a photo before or during identification. Why: The shown image shapes what the witness reports; recognition can be driven by the image rather than memory.
- [fact] Staff who saw published photographs can recognise a person, so a face on record can expose a false identity.
- [fact] A photograph records fine physical features, such as the shape of a person's ears, that witnesses cannot reliably describe in words or memory. When: Identification depends on subtle physical features. Why: A photograph keeps exact visual detail that memory loses.
- [fact] Labelled old photographs can identify who appears in an image and when it was taken, where written records are absent.

## physical constraints and plausibility
- [mechanism] Physical constraints, such as wound logic, the need to conceal traces, or measurable facts like water depth, can exclude whole classes of explanation or a suspect's actions.
- [mechanism] A locked-room theft that seems impossible for an adult can be solved by a small intruder through a route that only fits a child, reversing the assumed size of the thief. When: designing an impossible-theft solution. Why: The size assumption is the unstated premise, so overturning it resolves the paradox.
- [rule] Check the rules of the scene before using a physical test on a suspect, since some tests may be unlawful or unfair. When: planning a physical test on a suspect. Why: Tests that break rules can invalidate the result or harm the investigator's standing.
- [rule] Do not treat a physical match as identification until a detail such as clothing or jewellery agrees.
- [rule] Make the reveal turn on a physical constraint the audience can check, such as a jump distance or a locked gate, so the solution is fair. When: when a reveal rules out a suspect. Why: a physical fact the audience can verify makes the deduction feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [heuristic] Test whether a trace's position or a claimed action is physically possible; an impossible arrangement, such as an awkward grip for the claimed blow, exposes staging. When: A trace's position or claimed action conflicts with the account. Why: Physical limits cannot be faked; an impossible arrangement points to staging after the event.
- [heuristic] A matching mark can still prove the wrong thing. Check whether it could physically have been made in the recorded pose, not only whether it matches. When: when a single match carries the case. Why: a match shows similarity, not who made the mark.
- [heuristic] Logical checks on physical states, such as a window closed at one time and open later, bound what must have happened in between. When: when a physical state changes across the timeline. Why: A state change implies an event occurred in the interval.
- [heuristic] Rule out a suspect by a physical capability only after establishing the limit that applies, such as whether the person could make a given jump. When: Ruling out a person by physical ability. Why: An unestablished limit can wrongly exclude the real culprit or wrongly accept a disguise.
- [procedure] 1) Identify what the event requires physically. 2) Compare the pattern of the event with the limits of a candidate agent. 3) Narrow candidates to those that fit. 4) Test each step against the evidence before accepting it. When: When an event seems supernatural or impossible. Why: Physical constraints can rule out candidates and turn an uncanny event into a solvable cause.
- [procedure] 1) List the fixed physical conditions of the scene. 2) Determine what a normal actor would have had to disturb to create them. 3) Identify which unusual agents could satisfy every detail. 4) Test each candidate against the whole arrangement. When: The usual suspect is excluded by the scene's fixed details. Why: Working backward from the arrangement isolates explanations consistent with all evidence.

## physical marks and possessions
- [definition] A distinguishing mark, such as a secret sign on an envelope, lets a recipient identify which correspondent wrote a given letter. When: when several secret senders use the same channel. Why: The mark identifies the author without opening the letter.
- [mechanism] A distinctive damage mark, such as a burnt corner, lets an investigator recognize the same object across different scenes when no paperwork exists.
- [rule] Give suspects and clue objects distinctive visible marks; unlabelled items, such as clothing without maker's marks, block identification and stall the investigation. When: when writing suspect descriptions for a mystery or designing objects meant to identify their owner. Why: Distinctive details narrow identity and let players link witness accounts or items to one individual; unmarked items cannot be traced.
- [heuristic] Distinctive marks such as a crest, initials or brand tie an item to one person; record small finds, and count a physical match only if its feature is rare.
- [heuristic] Distinctive prints, such as very high narrow heel impressions, tiptoe marks or squared-toed boot prints, separate one walker's track from others at a scene.
- [heuristic] A specific distinctive mark, such as a scar, is a stronger identifier than general appearance and can be checked directly. When: appearance is ambiguous and a mark can be checked. Why: a distinctive mark is rarer than shared features.
