- [heuristic] A repeated individual defect, such as a bent character or a chipped type face, is unlikely on other machines and can distinguish one device from many similar ones. When: a document's origin is disputed and a machine is suspected. Why: individual wear is rarer than shared model features.
- [procedure] 1) Inspect the victim's injuries directly and deliberately. 2) Note each mark's location and appearance. 3) Record them in a form that can be used as evidence later. When: when injuries may be needed in a formal complaint or testimony. Why: Records made at the time carry more weight than later recollection.
- [pitfall] An unusually distinctive landmark marking a hiding place can also be remembered and found by an adversary. When: Choosing a marker for a concealed cache. Why: Memorable features are easy for anyone to recall.
- [fact] A trail of blood or drag marks along a path shows that a body was moved from one place to another. Why: Dragging leaves continuous marks that reveal the route and direction.
- [fact] A worn or odd object stands out and can become a trace that others remember, so it can later link a person to a place or time.

## prediction of suspect moves
- [mechanism] If a witness claims a patient is near death and that claim is later disproved, a later real death will seem expected and draw less suspicion. When: When a death follows earlier statements about the victim's condition. Why: The earlier claim sets expectations that the death appears to fulfil.
- [heuristic] If an offender used a vehicle or tool and abandoned it, the object should be findable, and any removed part should be traceable. When: reasoning about what an offender must have left behind. Why: the act of using and discarding an object leaves a physical record.
- [heuristic] Predict a suspect's next step from the delay, such as complaining to the bank and then approaching the executors, and state it as an expectation to be confirmed. Why: A stated expectation keeps the inference open to correction.
- [heuristic] A tip's prediction that comes true soon after raises trust in the source's other claims.
- [heuristic] An explanation that accounts for any outcome has no predictive value; test a theory by whether it rules out some possible observations. When: evaluating a proposed explanation. Why: an explanation that fits every result cannot be checked by evidence.
- [heuristic] Predict where traces should appear from what the act produces, such as bleeding from a stab wound, then search that spot.
- [heuristic] Use a stakeout only when the target's route is predictable and a direct approach would warn them.
- [procedure] 1) Infer the actor's need from the costly act or the logic of the crime. 2) Predict what else must be done to meet it, such as ordering a second container after returning an empty one. 3) Check whether those actions leave traces. When: A motive is suggested but not yet confirmed, or a movement record has a gap. Why: Predicted actions give testable consequences; the culprit's motive dictates the action taken.
- [procedure] 1) Read the partial change as evidence of recent activity. 2) Combine it with testimony. 3) Predict where the actor will return and choose where to wait.
- [pitfall] A predicted notice date is only an estimate, so the search should also cover nearby days.
- [pitfall] Letting a suspect go free depends on predicting his next move accurately, so a wrong prediction can ruin the trap.

## reveal reframing of facts
- [mechanism] A final reveal supplies the missing link, recasting earlier facts so events that seemed puzzling or misleading fall into place and fit the solution. When: a central fact is disclosed. Why: A new frame changes how earlier details connect, and earlier facts gain meaning from the solution.
- [mechanism] A reveal can reframe an earlier ambiguous image: a scene first read as threatening can be recast once the explanation supplies its true cause. When: When an early image was left open to more than one reading. Why: The explanation gives the image a new meaning without changing what was shown.
- [mechanism] A game that tracks the player's working theory can reveal facts that do not fit once the theory is pursued too far, turning a wrong conclusion into a discovery. When: Designing mystery systems where players form and pursue theories. Why: Contradictions that surface after commitment make the player reassess, which deepens the twist.
- [mechanism] A control device such as an oath, shown early as romantic flavour, reads as harmless until revealed as the mechanism of the crime, reframing earlier scenes.
- [mechanism] A route assumption that looks like the killer's path can be reversed late by a timing clue, forcing players to reread earlier evidence with the corrected timeline. When: An entry or exit path seems to explain the event. Why: A timing clue that contradicts the path changes how all earlier evidence is interpreted.
- [rule] Overturn a confidently wrong conclusion with a new fact instead of erasing it, so earlier evidence gains a second meaning and the twist feels earned. Why: Earlier clues stay meaningful and connect to the twist, which the player already partly knows. (x2)
- [rule] Let a reveal reclassify a map element, such as a patrol that proves to be a shelter, while another unexplained element keeps tension alive. When: designing reveals in a level. Why: Partial resolution maintains tension.
- [rule] Hint a hidden motive early and let the reveal reframe earlier suspicion, so the twist does not feel arbitrary.
- [rule] In the reveal, explain point by point why the misleading emphasis was wrong, so the player sees exactly where attention went astray.
- [heuristic] In the solution, replay collected clues and reinterpret evidence already shown, showing each item's place in the solution; the final speech only ties facts together. When: when writing a solution. Why: Audiences accept reveals grounded in earlier evidence.
- [heuristic] A reveal can invert who is victim and who is manipulator, provided the earlier facts support both readings and the apparent target is shown to be the trap's designer.

## sealed room investigation
- [rule] A puzzle room sealed by several locks should track which key is missing and where it was last seen, so the player can rebuild the route. When: Designing a locked-room puzzle. Why: The player needs traceable state to deduce the route.
- [rule] Show the physical facts of a sealed room early, but leave the method and timing for the confession to explain. When: sealed-room mystery design. Why: players hold early facts and reinterpret them at the reveal.
- [heuristic] Test every door, servant entrance and connecting passage of a sealed room, not only the occupant's route, since an overlooked exit may remain. When: when a sealed-room claim must be checked or a room is fastened from the inside. Why: A sealed door shows only that one route is blocked; looking only at obvious exits leads to a wrong conclusion.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm room sealed and object missing. 2) Rule out occupants as takers, testing them and what they consumed. 3) Check windows, locks, ceiling, floor, sills and outside ground for traces. 4) Sound walls and cellars for hidden passages. 5) If insiders are cleared and routes fail, conclude a third party used another route and reason from the culprit's known style. When: a room is sealed and an object is missing, or a theft seems impossible given the locks and seals. Why: Eliminating insiders and ruling out routes shifts attention to an unexpected entry path that traces can confirm.
- [procedure] 1) Estimate time of death from bodily signs. 2) Compare that estimate with the last confirmed contact. 3) Log every entry, with items left and the lock state on leaving. 4) Test each entrant's claim against what they could actually have seen. When: a sealed room or impossible-access case.
- [procedure] 1) Establish the seal: confirm entries and windows were closed and nothing was disturbed. 2) Take the last-seen timeline from the final person to leave. 3) Record the scene as found. 4) Note what witnesses could not perceive. 5) Only then seek an explanation. When: when a scene looks closed and an account of the last hours exists. Why: Ordering the evidence before theorising keeps the explanation tied to facts.
- [procedure] 1) Check traces at the edges of a closed door, such as odor through a crack. 2) Read ambient smells as clues to the hazard inside. 3) Force the entry from a position out of the line of any rush. 4) Vent the room before treating anyone inside. When: A closed space may hide a hazard that outweighs the cost of forcing it. Why: A closed door can hide lingering fumes that become deadly in small spaces.
- [procedure] 1) List every opening on each floor, including basement doors, kitchen windows, dining-room windows and living-room windows. 2) Record each opening's state: bolted, boarded, barred or sash-locked. 3) Note what each opening leads to, since some open only onto an inner court. 4) Eliminate secured openings. 5) Test the remaining route against the premise that the victim may have admitted the visitor. When: A scene looks sealed and the choice is between an outside intruder and a visitor admitted from inside. Why: A complete survey shows which routes were open, but an admitted visitor leaves barriers intact.
- [procedure] 1) List every entrance to the room. 2) Note when each was last checked or used. 3) Record any inconsistency, such as a lock on one side and an open window. 4) Use each recorded action as a timestamp to bracket possible entry. When: when a room appears sealed. Why: Each constraint narrows when an intruder could have acted.
- [pitfall] Treating a sealed room as a complete alibi is an error, because anyone inside could have left before the seal began.
- [pitfall] Apparent proof that a room is impossible to enter or leave can be false, since an overlooked exit may remain, and abandoning the method for a convenient conclusion closes the case wrongly. When: Investigating a seemingly sealed scene. Why: Looking only at obvious exits leads to a wrong conclusion.

## section endings and pacing
- [rule] End each scene or chapter on an open question that reopens the case rather than resolving it, making the next objective urgent because unresolved curiosity pulls the audience forward. When: Structuring a sequence of scenes or chapters in a mystery or investigation narrative. Why: Unresolved curiosity carries momentum into the next section.
- [rule] End a section on a concrete visible action whose purpose is not yet stated, rather than on a summary of mood. When: closing a chapter or scene that hands off to the next. Why: an unexplained action pulls the audience forward.
- [rule] Close a section on a new shock to push the audience into the next part. When: ending a section mid-tension. Why: An unresolved shock creates pull toward what follows.
- [rule] End a section on the accusation so the next section opens with its consequence. When: Structuring chapters or scenes around a reveal. Why: A closing accusation creates a hook that carries into the next scene.
- [rule] End each case with a short aftermath that closes the loop, such as arrests, rescues, a confession, or an escape that cannot be traced. When: When concluding a mystery case. Why: Closing consequences give the player a sense of resolution.
- [heuristic] End sections on a turning point: a changed state such as a found object, new name, new body, physical clue, message, or hidden visitor, that raises a question.
- [heuristic] End a section on anticipation, deferring the answer so the audience waits for the result.
- [heuristic] Each section should advance the story through a new discovery, setback, or deadline, keeping the audience's attention active.
- [heuristic] Set up a consequential action as a small, concrete step, then close the segment on its consequence. When: Ending a chapter or scene on a decisive choice.
- [heuristic] End a section on a reversal of the expected outcome, such as apparent safety followed by a sudden loss, to shift pacing and sharpen suspense. When: the audience or player expects safety or resolution.
- [procedure] 1) Scan the text for places where characters are unusually close together. 2) Use those spots as division points. 3) Read the resulting phrases. 4) Test the phrases against meaning before trusting them. When: Recovering a message whose words are run together. Why: Unusual crowding marks likely phrase boundaries, but any split is only a hypothesis until checked.

## stacked evidence and inferences
- [mechanism] Stacked pressures such as raids, debt, lost leaders and a feared enemy make hostility and suspicion feel earned to those living through them. When: A region is under several strains at once. Why: Accumulated hardship and fear normalize extreme responses.
- [mechanism] Player confidence in a hidden truth rises as several weak, partly contradictory clues accumulate, even when no single clue proves it. When: a reveal built from a sighting, a lie, a courtesy and an unexplained habit. Why: Each clue is ambiguous alone, but together they point one way.
- [heuristic] Check several independent facts: one failure can be explained away, but several converging facts raise the overall case and are hard to dismiss. When: A verdict rests on accumulated circumstantial facts. Why: Converging independent-looking facts raise the overall probability of guilt. (x2)
- [heuristic] Stacking weak indicators or coincidences before verifying each builds conclusions on untested links; check each for an innocent explanation before weighing the total. When: the player must weigh minor indicators rather than one decisive proof. Why: A large pile of items can feel conclusive even when each item is ambiguous.
- [heuristic] Stacking several pressures in quick succession, each adding to the last, keeps tension rising through a sequence. When: building a run of setbacks or threats.
- [heuristic] Following one misdirection with a second unrelated disturbance pulls attention further from the main case.
- [tradeoff] Several independent motives strengthen a case more than one alone, but unchecked stacked motives can make a weak case look strong; check each separately.
- [tradeoff] Stacking evidence toward one reading sets a firm conclusion that later review can overturn, but too much leaves no alternative reading for the audience. When: presenting a case whose evidence seems to point one way.
- [pitfall] Repeated evasions read as filler and stall an investigation unless each one narrows the question or points somewhere new. When: Several witnesses refuse or deflect without adding new evidence. Why: Refusals that yield no new direction leave the player with no progress.
- [pitfall] Each inference built on the last compounds uncertainty, such as moving from 'she went out' to 'someone locked up after her'; test each link separately. Why: Chained conclusions can seem solid while each step rests on assumption.
- [pitfall] Stacking inferences until they form a full person can build a convincing but false character, since each guess may be wrong. When: multiple weak traces are combined into one profile. Why: each added guess compounds the error.

## suspect interrogation and reactions
- [mechanism] A suspect who believes the investigator knows where hidden evidence lies may act on that belief, such as fetching the item, and expose themselves. When: When the hidden item is outside the suspect's knowledge. Why: If the suspect knew the item's location, they could deny everything instead of acting.
- [behavior] Under questioning, a suspect's voice, posture, gaze or pallor can reveal knowledge, but observers can misread these signs, so they are leads rather than proof. When: When questioning a suspect or a person about a sensitive matter. Why: Pressure weakens control over the body and voice, but reactions are informative yet ambiguous and should not be treated as proof.
- [behavior] A suspect confronted with a specific claim may show pallor, sweating or an outburst, signalling a reaction to the claim. When: When a specific hidden fact is put to the suspect. Why: The claim touches something concealed, and the body betrays the strain.
- [behavior] A suspect who recognises a displayed object may start and try to seize it, which confirms a connection the investigator could not yet prove. When: A physical clue is shown during a confrontation. Why: Guilty knowledge produces an involuntary reaction when the object is recognised.
- [behavior] Noting an accused person's reaction to evidence gives suspicion a human basis that a later reveal can redirect to another character. When: Early suspicion falls on one character and must later shift to another. Why: A visible reaction makes the initial suspicion feel earned, so the redirect feels like a correction.
- [rule] Make a suspect's recognition tell subtle so careful observers catch it while those who only read dialogue miss it. When: designing a suspect's reaction to a trigger. Why: subtle tells reward attentive play without giving the answer away.
- [heuristic] Give each suspect a real but explainable lie; suspicion stays high even though the suspect is innocent. Why: An evasive but explicable lie keeps the audience suspicious without proving guilt.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a follow-up that invites a checkable detail. 2) Identify who or what could confirm it. 3) Verify or contradict the claim before committing to a theory. When: A suspect gives a vague excuse for their movements. Why: A vague answer can hide an invented story that a specific question exposes.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the stated purpose of an action with independent records, such as travel times. 2) Note any mismatch between purpose and conduct. 3) Record changes in the suspect's manner as timeline details. When: A suspect's explanation is plausible but unverified. Why: Independent records can confirm or refute a plausible account.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the witness's own account of the problem. 2) Ask targeted follow-up questions about why key actions did not happen. 3) Ask about mechanics: when, where and how payments or meetings occurred. 4) Ask what was feared. When: when a witness is hiding a motive. Why: Moving from the stated problem to its mechanics reveals concealed motives.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the key question without lead-in, just after a disorienting moment. 2) Record the immediate answer as a lead. 3) Watch the speaker's follow-up hedges and whom they glance at. 4) Check the answer against other witnesses and the timeline before relying on it. When: A suspect is among others who may coordinate their stories and is off guard. Why: A fast answer shows less managed content, and a glance can reveal coordination.

## testimony as evidence
- [model] Witness testimony has three layers: first-hand observation, reported speech, and inference. Each layer must be separated before a single claim is trusted. When: when a witness is the only source for a key fact. Why: the layers differ in reliability.
- [model] Store each witness testimony as separate claims for identity, time and place, so the player can press on the weakest claim. When: a witness-NPC system is designed.
- [rule] Treat witness statements as evidence, not proof; weigh them by the speaker's position, firsthand access, motive, and whether the physical scene supports them. When: Weighing a witness statement or several accounts of the same events. Why: Each witness has different access and motives; the physical scene can confirm or undercut an account. (x2)
- [rule] Treat testimony from any witness, official or doctor as a claim to test before accepting it as fact, even when the speaker is sincere.
- [rule] Test a symbol's proposed meaning against testimony about the events it claims to explain, since a witness's account can rule out a reading. When: a symbol has a rival reading tied to an event. Why: Factual testimony can eliminate an interpretation that the physical evidence allows.
- [rule] Judge testimony by the cost the speaker accepts, and weigh it against available proof before accepting the account.
- [rule] Separate what a statement proves from what it cannot prove. Estimate both before deciding how much weight the statement carries in a case. When: Evaluating any witness statement. Why: A statement may prove one fact while leaving the link to the main charge unproven.
- [rule] Record your own state while observing, since your account is also testimony that others may test. When: Reporting what you saw during a tense event. Why: Your condition affects your reliability as a witness.
- [heuristic] Testimony lacking legal weight can still direct a search or confirm a line of inquiry, so judge it for investigative use as well as proof. When: A statement is too weak to convict but points somewhere useful. Why: Leads and confirmations drive investigation even when evidence is not decisive.
- [heuristic] A later witness can supply the mechanism linking a financial oddity to a motive, turning an unexplained anomaly into a usable explanation. When: When an anomaly has no explanation yet. Why: Testimony about actual payments or dealings gives the anomaly a cause.
- [heuristic] Compare testimony from people who knew the land during the original owner's lifetime to settle how a boundary was drawn. When: a boundary is disputed decades after it was set. Why: Those who knew the land at the time have direct knowledge of its layout.

## tests and trial mechanics
- [definition] A water ordeal is a trial where the accused is cast into a river and the result is read as the verdict: drowning means guilt, surviving means innocence.
- [mechanism] A quest can require the player to secure a vow from an NPC, tracked in state so the vow can be broken later with consequences. Why: tracked promises create consequences that can trigger later.
- [mechanism] A community decision later declared void can still drive later conflict, because the record shows what the parties were fighting over.
- [behavior] A suspect who reacts with sudden violence to a harmless-looking test item shows the item was meant to harm the tester. When: when a test item is offered to a suspect.
- [rule] Make a warning line produce a branch so that non-response leads to a forced entry with its own consequences. When: Scripting an NPC warning before a forced entry. Why: Branching gives silence a meaningful consequence rather than a dead end.
- [heuristic] A merchant NPC can offer a side wager that grants access to his records, rewarding players who check the odds.
- [procedure] 1) Offer a small wager on a checkable fact. 2) Let the informant consult his own records to prove his point. 3) Check the records he reads aloud against other sources. When: an informant holds records but refuses direct questions.
- [procedure] 1) Form a theory. 2) Send a warning based on it. 3) Observe the recipient's reaction. 4) Compare the reaction and later news with the reasoning. When: when a theory predicts how someone will respond. Why: the response confirms or refutes the reasoning.
- [procedure] 1) Place a candidate object into the dent and check for an exact fit. 2) Set it on a smooth surface and look for a second impression. 3) If both match, conclude it lay there earlier.
- [pitfall] A visibly staged test can alert the guilty party, who may then become careful or start investigating the test itself. When: when the test is noticed by the people being investigated. Why: the suspect gains time to react before the result is read.
- [pitfall] A test with a visible result can look honest while its operator controls the outcome, so a convincing demonstration is not proof of accuracy. When: when the operator of a test also benefits from its result. Why: The person administering the test can shape what appears to happen.

## tidy scene and story suspicion
- [mechanism] Tidying erases some evidence but leaves signs like a swept corner or disturbed dust; a tidy arrangement implies no later touch, so a later disturbance reveals a visit.
- [rule] Use tidy paths and arranged objects to tell players someone maintains an area, a clue to an unseen NPC or hidden faction.
- [heuristic] A tidy case or solution explaining every clue and matching the player's hopes may be staged or a planted decoy; scrutinize it. When: A case looks clear and tidy, each explanation fits too easily, or a theory arrives quickly and fits the evidence too well. Why: The visible surface may be arranged.
- [heuristic] A shared theme among restored words can narrow a document's origin, but it is suggestive, not proof, so do not pick the most attractive reading. When: restored words are used to infer where a document came from.
- [pitfall] A tidy, coherent story can be invented or fit any set of facts, so a neat fit shows only possibility; truth requires evidence for each part. When: Judging a reconstructed account that fits neatly together. Why: Coherence can be constructed, while truth requires evidence for each part.
- [pitfall] A neat, dovetailing reconstruction is not proof: its logic can hide a weak link or alternative explanation, and unflagged guesses look established; test each link separately.
- [pitfall] A tidy reconstruction or fact list can be wrong or give false confidence while omitting the decisive question, such as how the death came about; check for missing questions.
- [pitfall] A tidy theory can absorb contradictory evidence and make the remaining details seem irrelevant.
- [pitfall] A tidy-looking ledger can hide money held under another name, so tidiness does not prove a record is complete. When: when reviewing financial records. Why: Presentation can disguise concealed holdings.
- [pitfall] A neat sequence of events can imply causation that the documents do not establish; each link in a causal chain needs documentary support.
- [pitfall] A tidy space shows that someone worked there, not who that person is; elimination works only when each suspect's habits are known.

## timeline and inference building
- [heuristic] Infer event order from traces: if an organism can only settle after soft tissue is gone, the exposure must have preceded its settling. When: Reconstructing the order of events from physical traces. Why: Each trace requires a prior condition, so its presence implies that condition came earlier.
- [procedure] 1) List each witness's timed claims in order, such as hearing a sound, coming downstairs, calling, and help arriving. 2) Place them on one shared clock. 3) Use events shared by two or more accounts as anchors. 4) Flag times resting only on one person's memory. 5) Mark remaining gaps no account explains. When: several witnesses give overlapping accounts or had windows of opportunity. Why: fixing times across accounts bounds where each person could have been, and shared anchors keep the timeline reliable.
- [procedure] 1) Record each stated time, such as a planned meeting, a death or an arrival. 2) Add durations and travel distances. 3) Check each account against the resulting sequence.
- [procedure] 1) Start recounting events from a fixed date. 2) Anchor each event to a date taken from a written record. 3) Cross-check time-stamped entries against each other to expose contradictions.
- [procedure] 1) State the account a suspicion would require to be true. 2) List every fact that must hold for it. 3) Choose a test for each fact. 4) Begin with the most accessible fact. When: When a suspicion is broad and needs a plan of attack. Why: Separate checkable facts make progress measurable.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the simplest fact whose purpose is clear. 2) State each next inference. 3) Attach each inference to its source clue. 4) Check that every link holds before revealing. When: explaining a solution at the end of a mystery. Why: tracing each link to a clue keeps the reveal verifiable.
- [procedure] 1) Create a false paper trail, such as a fabricated report supporting a plausible story. 2) Place an object belonging to another person where it points to that person. When: a culprit needs suspicion moved to someone else. Why: Documents and objects make the false story feel supported.
- [procedure] 1) List the known facts. 2) Join them into a step-by-step sequence of who was where, what was done and what was hidden. 3) Check each step against the evidence. 4) Mark the sequence as provisional. When: When forming a theory from evidence.
- [procedure] 1) List every dated event, such as meetings, purchases and illness episodes. 2) Order them chronologically. 3) Scan for near-matches that cluster together. When: a chain of events may connect a person to a result. Why: ordering makes near-coincidences visible.
- [procedure] 1) Fix times that independent observers can confirm, such as routine arrivals. 2) Fill gaps between fixed points with stated durations. 3) Record the tolerance of each interval. 4) Separate the onset of an event from the moment help is summoned. When: Reconstructing the order of events from testimony and routines. Why: Anchored times and explicit tolerances prevent estimates from distorting the sequence, and separating onset from discovery avoids misplacing events.
- [fact] Physical capacity and criminal skill answer different questions, so a suspect unable to do the physical work may still be involved through an accomplice.

## unfalsifiable explanations
- [definition] An unfalsifiable accusation is one whose theory reads every answer, denial, or silence as confirmation, so no outcome can refute it.
- [rule] Do not build a conclusion or accusation on an anomaly or account that cannot be checked against an independent source; record it for later.
- [heuristic] Unnamed corroborators carry little weight until they can be identified and verified.
- [pitfall] An explanation that fits or absorbs any observation or misfortune is unfalsifiable, gives no way to test it, and should be distrusted. When: A hidden cause or explanation is assumed to cover every anomaly or event without specifics. Why: Explanations that cannot fail give no information. (x2)
- [pitfall] Adding a new accomplice or ad hoc patch to explain each contrary fact makes a theory unfalsifiable and weakens it. When: A suspect explanation is revised repeatedly to fit contradicting evidence. Why: Ad hoc patches remove the theory's ability to be proven wrong, so it no longer guides the investigation. (x2)
- [pitfall] Dismissing contrary evidence as the culprit's cleverness or a planted fake makes a theory impossible to disprove or test.
- [pitfall] A test that cannot fail, like a cure following contact, a check any reply passes, or an unanswerable display, confirms any accusation and leaves no defence.
- [pitfall] A red herring, or a solution dismissing an impossibility by a trick the player cannot check, feels unfair and breaks fair play.
- [pitfall] An untested delay mechanism that can absorb any timing contradiction makes the theory unfalsifiable and should not be accepted.
- [pitfall] A missing trace explained by an uncheckable account is erased without any test, so the explanation cannot be verified.
- [pitfall] A claim that rejects every alternative in advance cannot be tested, so it should raise doubt rather than settle the question. When: A suspect or witness answers every challenge with a fixed explanation. Why: A claim immune to disproof gives no evidence either way.

## urgency and pressure cues
- [mechanism] Visible progress toward a destination while time runs down, with a reward for speed, heightens urgency. When: A timed journey or final approach.
- [mechanism] A conditional clause can imply consequences without stating them, creating a veiled threat that the recipient must interpret. When: A writer wants to pressure a recipient without an explicit demand. Why: Leaving the consequence unstated forces the recipient to fill it in, which increases its force.
- [rule] Make an NPC's urgent request to leave double as a plot beat and as evidence of when the character must have acted.
- [rule] Vary the questioning tone deliberately, moving from firm to soft reassurance to sharp again, to find which register opens the witness up. When: when a witness stays closed under one tone. Why: different witnesses respond to different registers.
- [rule] Use an urgent-seeming request from a character as the entry point to a crime, so the player's compliance becomes the harmful act.
- [heuristic] An observer should note any urge to strike out or seize evidence, since it shows how strong a reaction is. When: when observing a strong reaction to evidence.
- [heuristic] Avoid repeating the same near-rescue pattern, since the suspense effect fades when each near-miss follows an identical beat. When: When a sequence contains several near-rescue moments. Why: Repetition makes the pattern predictable and dulls tension.
- [heuristic] Do not press an upset witness; pressure tends to produce hysterics rather than usable answers, so wait for a calmer moment. When: A witness is distressed after a discovery. Why: Pressure under distress yields emotional outbursts instead of information.
- [heuristic] A costly act usually signals a pressing need; the more risk an actor accepted, the more urgent the need probably was. When: An actor takes a significant risk. Why: Risk is accepted when the need seems to demand it.
- [pitfall] Wounds and urgency during an arrest can overshadow the reveal, so pacing must give the reveal room. When: A reveal happens during a tense capture. Why: Physical urgency competes for attention with the story information.
- [pitfall] Reading urgency into the words alone misses the physical sequence, which can show the wording was chosen deliberately. Why: an emotional reading may be overturned by physical evidence.

## victim motive and reactions
- [mechanism] A victim who trusts a public name and a published notice can be steered to seek a specific figure, without verifying that figure's identity. When: The victim has a reason to seek help and a trusted information channel that can be influenced. Why: Trust in a public source replaces independent verification of the person it advertises.
- [mechanism] A motive can reverse the apparent victim: the dead man was planning harm against the killer, making the death the outcome of a plot rather than a random attack.
- [behavior] A threatened target's reactions, such as contacting authorities, hiring protection or seeking help, can each move them closer to a planned trap. When: a threat has been issued to a target. Why: Each protective action is a step the threat-maker can anticipate and exploit.
- [behavior] A victim who does not report an attack and waits a long time before disclosing it limits what can be checked and may conceal the attack's cause. When: When an attack victim stays silent or delays disclosure. Why: Delay erodes physical evidence and gives the victim time to control the story.
- [rule] Victim's fits or reaction to a look or touch is no infallible proof of guilt; it may be a red herring for an innocent character, so test against other evidence. When: designing mystery clues.
- [heuristic] When the manner of death is unclear, examine the victim's recent activities and relationships for motive, enemies, or offences. When: the cause of death is ambiguous.
- [heuristic] Examine the dead person's finances, debts and obligations, since they can reveal a motive that points to a different culprit.
- [heuristic] A victim's diary naming incidents and wrongs gives a list of people with cause for revenge, widening the field of suspects. When: reviewing a victim's records.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the victim's preparations. 2) Infer the criminal enterprise they imply. 3) Identify who that enterprise targets. 4) Treat that target as a likely suspect. 5) Test the theory against the facts. When: a victim's arrangements suggest a hidden plan. Why: A victim's plan can point to the person it was aimed against.
- [pitfall] Victims may downplay harm out of loyalty or fear, so the record can understate events; a victim's minimizing account is not the full measure of harm.
- [fact] When a charge names specific victims, its proof rests on the victims' accounts of their injuries.

## voice identification
- [rule] A voice heard without sight is hearsay about who was present; it establishes presence, not identity, so ask how the witness excludes another speaker. When: when a witness names someone from a voice heard without seeing them, or reports a second person they did not see. Why: A voice may belong to more than one person; hearing a voice does not confirm who spoke.
- [heuristic] A sound few other sources could make, such as a known door creak, can pin a witness's timing to one event or show who moved when. When: the sound is distinctive and witnesses know it well. Why: A sound only one source can produce pins the listener's timing to one event.
- [heuristic] A shift in narrative voice can suggest the writer's identification or bias; treat it as a lead to test, not as proof.
- [heuristic] A strong, distinctive voice suits imitation: listeners remember its traits, and the copy need not be perfect.
- [heuristic] Use a voice imitation as cover only when witnesses hear it at a distance, not when a witness can see the face clearly or handle the body.
- [heuristic] Voice recognition is untested until the witness hears the voice again; ask whether they would know it, and then test it. When: A witness claims to recognise a voice from an earlier event. Why: A recognition claim made from memory alone may not hold up when the voice is heard again.
- [heuristic] A disguised voice can sound unnatural to someone who knows the speaker, so familiarity can expose a disguise. When: A witness heard a voice through a door or at a distance. Why: Known speakers have characteristic pitch and cadence that a disguise alters.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a line the victim said earlier. 2) Practise it aloud until delivery feels natural. 3) Build the cover story around that line.
- [pitfall] Accepting a voice on the telephone without a second check lets an impersonator pass as a trusted contact.
- [pitfall] Assume a voice heard through a barrier may belong to someone other than the expected person until sight or a second clue confirms it. When: When identifying a speaker by voice alone. Why: Voices are easy to mistake behind a door.
- [fact] A voice heard through a closed door is weak identification. The listener may be unable to name the speaker and may only believe it matches a voice heard earlier. When: identifying a speaker by sound through a barrier. Why: muffled, indistinct sound carries little identifying detail.

## weapon and object traces
- [mechanism] Linking a weapon to a specific item of the victim's clothing, such as a hat with a matching hole, ties the object to the victim. When: Establishing ownership of a weapon through a matching item. Why: A physical correspondence between two items connects them.
- [mechanism] A soft bullet fired through woven cloth usually picks up an impression of the weave, so a recovered bullet can link to the garment it passed through.
- [rule] Striking bone can flatten one side of a bullet, erasing its fabric marks there; the unflattened side may keep them, so match only if some surface stays intact. When: A bullet is recovered for comparison.
- [rule] Track who has handled a weapon or item, since each handling can change what it can prove and an unknown chain makes it unreliable. When: an item is moved, grabbed or struggled over. Why: handling can add or remove traces.
- [rule] Do not identify a person from the visible hilt of a weapon alone. When: A weapon is found at a scene. Why: A weapon's visible part is shared and does not establish who held it.
- [heuristic] Treat an item-fit clue as weak when the item could have been worn on either hand or its owner is unknown. When: an item-fit clue is used to narrow suspects. Why: Without a fixed hand or known owner, the fit says little about the wearer.
- [heuristic] A weapon that belonged to a known household links the crime to that household, so tracing an object's owner gives a lead.
- [heuristic] Check whether a weapon was actually fired; undischarged chambers can weaken an explanation that assumes it was.
- [pitfall] Reading a cut or tear as a weapon mark without checking the garment's style or whether the weapon was drawn is a common error.
- [fact] A weapon's owner, loaded count and physical condition are checkable facts, so each can confirm or dispute a claim about the weapon. When: A weapon's history is part of the investigation.
- [fact] Where a projectile lodges in an object constrains the shooter's position relative to the victim's body.

## witness descriptions
- [behavior] Some witnesses who never saw faces say they would not recognize the people involved, because such people do not stand out in memory. When: Asking witnesses whether they would recognize a disguised culprit. Why: Unremarkable appearance leaves weak memory traces.
- [rule] Use a verbal description only as a lead, never as firm evidence; recognition from a description alone does not confirm identity, and vague sightings mislead if treated as proof. When: When a suspect is known only through description. Why: Descriptions are indirect and cannot establish that the person met is the one described. (x2)
- [rule] Name the exact target item so searchers can flag near-matches, such as a similar but wrong object, for closer checking.
- [heuristic] Do not identify a suspect from a vague witness description alone; require a second clue such as a distinctive item or scar. Give NPC witnesses vague sightings by default. When: Identifying a suspect from a witness, or designing identification in a mystery. Why: Generic traits match too many candidates; vague descriptions should not resolve a case alone.
- [procedure] 1) Record the witness's account exactly as given. 2) Ask specific questions about clothing, features or details to narrow a vague description. 3) Ask follow-ups that eliminate candidates one at a time. When: When a witness recalls a person only vaguely or describes a group of possible suspects. Why: Specific questions turn a vague memory into a usable description and separate candidates.
- [pitfall] Confident or vivid delivery of a vague description is mistaken for accuracy, though broad categories or a strong impression without specifics cannot single out one person. When: A witness describes a person only in broad categories or gives a strong impression without specifics. Why: Confidence and vividness are mistaken for accuracy; a clear mental picture may still lack the detail that identifies its subject. (x2)
- [pitfall] Vague or inconsistent descriptions of an object weaken any timing inference drawn from it, so compare accounts across sources first.
- [pitfall] Vague or generic features make a reveal feel arbitrary rather than earned.
- [pitfall] A description too vague to single out a person identifies no one, so a disguise that defeats recognition also defeats the evidence.
- [pitfall] A frightened witness may describe a human being as a monstrous or unnatural thing, so the description should be checked before it is believed. When: A witness reports a terrifying sight. Why: Fear distorts perception and description.
- [fact] Loose descriptions of age, clothing, vehicles or manner narrow the field slightly, fit many people, and cannot separate the person seen from similar people; a partial fit is not proof.

## accusation and alibi weighing
- [behavior] Observers weigh a culprit's stated motive by its frankness and justification; a blunt, unjustified motive can count against him. When: a court or community judges a confessed act. Why: an unjustified reason reads as crude and less forgivable.
- [rule] Do not accept an alibi or accusation from an interested party without independent physical or documentary corroboration, rather than judging by standing or temper. When: A witness has a stake or motive to accuse or protect. Why: An interested witness can shape a story to protect themselves. (x2)
- [rule] Do not test an alibi where no one can confirm times, because the timeline then has nothing to anchor it. Why: Unanchored times cannot be compared against a claimed schedule.
- [rule] Weigh a source's family ties, reputation and institutional links before accepting its account, but do not discard the source solely because it has a motive.
- [rule] Check the accused party's own records, such as treatment dates and counts, against the timing of the complaint. When: Assessing a complaint against a professional.
- [heuristic] Weigh claims from a party with a personal stake or plausible motive to mislead, such as a grudge or rejected deal, and limit that party's authority until checked. When: A complaint or claim comes from someone who gains from the outcome or has a clear reason to lie. Why: Personal feeling or motive can distort judgement and what a source reports. (x2)
- [heuristic] A withheld alibi may protect someone else's reputation, and outsiders often read that silence as guilt, so find the reason for refusal before judging. When: A suspect has a verifiable alibi but declines to disclose it.
- [heuristic] Weigh a suspect's rebuttal on its argument as well as on the emotion it shows, since a reasoned defence can still be evaluated.
- [heuristic] Close a final accusation on motive reasoning rather than physical proof, and deliberately leave one loose thread unresolved. When: Writing the resolution of a deduction-based mystery. Why: Motive reasoning fits a deduction ending, and an open thread keeps the mystery memorable.
- [procedure] Accusation case template: 1) the afflicted accuse a person 2) neighbours' misfortunes and quarrels accumulate as suspicion 3) a confession or claimed sight serves as proof 4) a verdict closes the case. When: designing a trial or accusation sequence. Why: A repeated template makes the outcome predictable and builds suspicion step by step.

## ambiguous readings
- [mechanism] A cryptic hint delivered before a crowd leaves listeners puzzled rather than persuaded, and the hint gains meaning only when a later event confirms it. When: The speaker has a reason to conceal what they know. Why: The audience cannot yet connect the hint to any fact, so it stays open until the event.
- [behavior] Players hold two interpretations at once when a physical clue carrying the suspect's mark has a second plausible reading. When: An accusation rests on evidence with an alternative explanation. Why: Neither reading is ruled out, so the question stays open and the player keeps reconsidering.
- [behavior] An antagonist whose candour fits both innocent and guilty readings cannot be dismissed by the player, so suspicion stays alive. When: Writing an antagonist who gives open, plausible answers. Why: Openness that serves two readings keeps the player weighing the character rather than discarding them.
- [rule] Ambiguous clues should be resolved by later facts; ambiguity that is never resolved leaves the player with no way to choose a reading. When: Planting an unclear clue or figure. Why: Unresolved ambiguity frustrates players who cannot test their interpretation.
- [heuristic] Hold several readings of an ambiguous clue open and revise them as facts arrive; early commitment can yield a plausible but false reconstruction. When: A scene raises a question before its answer is available, or few fragments remain and a partial word or name has several plausible completions. Why: Partial sight supports several plausible readings until further evidence settles one; early commitment can produce a plausible but false reconstruction.
- [heuristic] An NPC that swings between theatrical and lucid gives players two readings, eccentric or conspiratorial, and later evidence should settle which one holds. When: designing a suspect whose behavior is unclear.
- [heuristic] A clue can be written so its meaning changes once a second clue is found, rewarding players who keep it. When: when placing a written clue on a body or in an item. Why: Two-stage meaning makes early findings pay off later.
- [procedure] 1) List every explanation the clue allows. 2) Test each against independent facts already known. 3) Eliminate explanations the facts contradict. 4) Accept that the question may remain open. When: a clue supports several readings.
- [pitfall] A single observed sign often has several innocent explanations, so a conclusion built on trivial signs can seem unconvincing. When: When building a case from minor details such as appearance or a changed habit. Why: Each sign can result from many causes, so only the combination carries weight.
- [pitfall] Vague, ominous lines from a witness can be read as either threat or admission until follow-up questions settle the meaning.

## antagonist and ally roles
- [mechanism] When the antagonist's own failed plan or rash letter triggers the crisis, the conflict arises from the character's choices rather than external chance. When: Building the climax of a plot where the villain's plan must unravel. Why: Self-caused crises feel earned and keep the outcome tied to character action.
- [mechanism] When an announced antagonist never appears, the reader's assumption that the author of the threat is in the room is overturned, and the threat becomes a phantom. When: a threat figure is announced early but withheld from the scene. Why: The expected confrontation is replaced by an unresolved relationship, which raises tension and surprise.
- [rule] Plant the true culprit early as a bystander with a motive and a noted presence, expressed in passing, so the reader trusts them as harmless. When: Hiding the real antagonist in plain sight. Why: A character seen as a witness is rarely suspected, so a later admission surprises the player.
- [heuristic] Make a charming ally the disguised threat, withholding the reveal until the final confrontation backed by an earlier planted clue, so trust lands on the wrong person. When: designing a companion or helper character, or when the antagonist hides behind a trusted name. Why: A trusted figure's secret identity gives a reversal, and a planted clue makes the reveal fair and earned.
- [heuristic] Show an ally's habits early so a later clue can be checked against earlier scenes; a new fact then reframes those already-shown traits as evidence without changing their scenes. When: Revealing or planning a twist where a trusted character is the hidden culprit. Why: Habits and traits seen earlier make the late reveal fair and checkable rather than arbitrary.
- [heuristic] Keep bystanders present during a reveal, since their reactions and whispers add pressure and show who is afraid. When: Running a group reveal. Why: Observers amplify tension and expose hidden anxiety.
- [heuristic] A plan stated in advance gives a fixed expected schedule that later actions can be tested against. When: A character announces a plan before an event. Why: A recorded expectation makes departures from it visible.
- [heuristic] Let the antagonist's death end the threat, which keeps the reveal in an emotional register and avoids a trial. When: Closing a mystery where the culprit is exposed. Why: A death resolves the threat quickly and shifts focus to the emotional fallout.
- [procedure] 1) Hold a working hypothesis that someone is shielding another. 2) Ask which person and how much help was given. 3) Keep the theory open until a planned test is run. When: Evidence suggests a suspect had outside help. Why: A confident theory can narrow the search before it is tested.
- [pitfall] The person who gains from a missing item is not thereby guilty; the benefit is a motive to test, not proof.

## authority and institutional cover
- [mechanism] A trusted authority figure who seems to have closed a case may have concealed the truth, so a late confession can reveal complicity and reverse trust in official accounts. When: An official account has been accepted without question. Why: Audiences trust officials, so their concealment is a strong late reversal.
- [mechanism] When the false explanation is offered by a credible authority figure, the player must defeat a trusted voice rather than a rumour, which raises the difficulty of the reveal. When: Designing the misleading explanation in a mystery. Why: Authority makes the false answer more persuasive, so disproving it requires stronger proof.
- [mechanism] When an authority figure closes a line of inquiry too early, players trust the decision and only later notice the gap it left behind. When: a trusted investigator dismisses a suspect's alibi. Why: Players defer to the authority's judgment.
- [behavior] A disturbance reported by a judge or authority figure can damage that figure's composure, and others may read the shaken state as evidence. When: When an authority figure reports a disturbing event and shows distress. Why: Visible distress by a figure of authority changes how others interpret the event.
- [behavior] When an authority figure misjudges publicly, players can see the error and doubt the conclusion, which invites them to question the official theory. When: A respected character publicly names the wrong suspect. Why: Visible error on the authority's part lets players discount the stated verdict.
- [rule] Test a respected authority's theory against an alternative explanation when new evidence arrives, rather than treating the theory as settled. When: A respected expert holds a theory that new evidence may not support. Why: Settled conclusions receive less scrutiny, which lets errors persist.
- [rule] Place the true antagonist in an authority role the player has no easy reason to suspect, and let that role supply the information they need. When: Designing a hidden culprit who holds an official position. Why: Trust in an official's role masks the influence they exert on the case.
- [heuristic] Make an authority figure's wrong theory plausible at each stage so the player's correction must be earned by evidence and the real culprit stays hidden until a final logic check. When: Writing an official investigator whose conclusions the player must challenge, or the real culprit must stay hidden late in the story. Why: A weak wrong theory makes the correction trivial and removes tension; the audience accepts an official theory and stops testing alternatives. (x2)
- [heuristic] Let a recurring authority figure dismiss the protagonist's theory, so the protagonist's later correction feels earned. When: a protagonist must prove a theory against official opinion. Why: The dismissal sets up a visible contrast that the correction then resolves.
- [pitfall] Assuming a judge will always give an untrained party full consideration is a mistake, since judges may carry biases from their background or dislike certain witnesses. When: Planning a formal hearing where one party is untrained. Why: Personal bias and prior experience can shape how fairly a judge weighs a party.

## clothing as evidence
- [mechanism] Disguising a person with another's clothing can make observers misidentify them, especially in poor light when observers expect to see a familiar figure. When: poor light and familiar expectation. Why: clothing cues dominate quick recognition.
- [behavior] A witness who identifies a person by clothing or outline, especially at a distance or in poor light, can be wrong, because common outfits are shared by many people. When: When a witness describes a suspect only by outfit, hat or silhouette. Why: Shared clothing gives many people the same outline, so the match can be coincidence.
- [rule] Do not convict on a clothing description alone, and give little identifying weight to common garments, since many people wear them and they narrow the field very little. When: The only evidence against a person is a description of their clothing, or identification rests on clothing alone. Why: Common clothing matches many people, so it cannot single out one individual.
- [heuristic] Clothing worn in an unusual combination can signal haste or deliberate intent, especially when it departs from the person's established habits. When: when a person's dress differs from their normal routine. Why: people rarely break habitual dress without a reason.
- [pitfall] Relying on common clothing descriptions to pick out a person in a crowd often fails, since many travellers wear the same outfit. When: Searching for a person in a crowded place. Why: Common clothing matches many people and identifies none.
- [pitfall] A cut-out label on a garment can suggest deliberate removal of identity, but it may also mislead investigators. When: Interpreting a removed tag or mark on discarded clothing. Why: The removal can be read as a clue when it has another cause.
- [fact] Several simple changes together, such as shaving, a false hair frame and tinted lenses, can alter a person's appearance completely.
- [fact] Clothing and footwear record recent movements, such as mud on shoes or wet trim that points to rain.
- [fact] A detached fragment of clothing can link a wearer to a scene and may leave no fingerprints. When: prints are absent but a fragment is found. Why: Fragments can identify a wearer where other traces fail.
- [fact] Finer fabrics still leave marks, and each layer of a garment can leave its own impression on the bullet.

## clue identification and filler
- [rule] Let the player find the planted setup somewhere in the story, so the reveal feels fair rather than arbitrary. When: a hidden trigger is revealed later. Why: an undiscoverable setup makes the reveal feel unfair.
- [rule] Keep several suspects plausible and reveal a focusing clue only after the player has ruled out one branch. When: designing a multi-suspect mystery. Why: Gradual narrowing keeps the choice meaningful.
- [heuristic] Mark a trivial detail as important by having a character state that it matters or will return later, so players remember it.
- [heuristic] Follow leads through the smallest detail, since a trivial object mentioned by a witness can open a new line of inquiry. When: a witness mentions a minor object or remark. Why: small details can link to larger events.
- [heuristic] When the solution depends on a repeated name, date or amount, scan long repetitive documents for that repeated detail rather than reading each entry for meaning. When: A solution is buried in many entries. Why: The one entry that matters is easy to miss in long, repetitive material.
- [heuristic] Trivial dialogue lines can hold timeline facts, so designers should not mark routine chatter as filler. When: Writing NPC dialogue that carries clue information. Why: Ordinary chatter can contain the cues needed to reconstruct events.
- [heuristic] Plant the decisive clue as a bland detail the investigator dismisses at first and later recognises as important.
- [pitfall] A comic frame can make a clue look like filler, so the payoff must be clear enough to reward recall.
- [pitfall] Formal inquiries can fixate on minor details, so decide in advance which details could change the conclusion. When: gathering exhaustive evidence. Why: detail volume hides what matters.
- [pitfall] A character's fixation on minor details may reflect anxiety rather than real risk, so readers may take the worry as character rather than evidence.

## clue seeding and reveal order
- [rule] Pair two clues that only make sense together, such as a used object at each theft site and a bite test in the study.
- [rule] Let players discover that a nuisance is a cover by examining what it changes. When: when designing puzzles around ambient disturbances.
- [heuristic] Place a physical object early, tagged as minor, that later proves a connection, such as an item at a scene identifying the true person. When: Foreshadowing a reveal; setting up a solving detail for a late reveal. Why: The object becomes proof once its owner is established; a clue that looks trivial is remembered as ordinary and then reread.
- [heuristic] Let a paid NPC give a true but narrow answer that points the player toward the next location. When: when designing clues delivered by a paid or bribed NPC. Why: A narrow truthful answer advances the player without revealing too much.
- [heuristic] Require the player to preserve evidence before a later confrontation, so the order of actions changes the outcome. When: In games where evidence can degrade or be lost. Why: Ordering makes preservation a meaningful choice.
- [heuristic] Seed a hidden mechanism with three or four minor environmental details that each look trivial, so the player notices them but has no reason to link them until a test. When: when a reveal depends on several small clues. Why: each detail looks harmless alone but gains meaning when combined.
- [heuristic] Open a mystery with a small object the investigator can read; deducing its owner builds trust in the investigator's method before the stakes are stated.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the force behind the phenomenon 2) identify the agent directing it 3) determine its motive, testing each step before moving on. When: when a phenomenon defies known causes.
- [procedure] 1) Explain each case in turn. 2) Base each explanation on that case's own evidence, such as papers, a confrontation or a confession. When: When a story contains several linked cases. Why: Ordering keeps each solution clear.
- [procedure] 1) Plant a staging clue in the opening scene that supports a wrong cause of death. 2) Add one small anomaly that contradicts it. 3) Leave the anomaly unexplained for a long stretch. When: Opening a mystery where the reader should accept an early false explanation. Why: The reader accepts the wrong cause early, and the lingering anomaly later recasts the whole case.

## confession and interrogation
- [model] In a self-accusation frame the protagonist is both suspect and investigator, so the reader's suspicion moves from the protagonist's mind to the protagonist's actions. When: A concealed deed committed by the narrator. Why: No outside investigator is needed.
- [mechanism] A second conversation with an NPC can change based on evidence the player has gathered since the first one. When: Designing repeat NPC dialogue. Why: Responsive dialogue rewards investigation and makes the player's progress visible.
- [rule] Let the culprit's exit be self-inflicted and triggered by discovery, closing the thread without a combat or arrest sequence. When: the culprit cannot be brought to trial or the player should not fight them. Why: The culprit's own action ends the case and avoids a forced final confrontation.
- [rule] Let a second confession complicate the first, so the final solution rests on two accounts that do not fully agree.
- [heuristic] A small slip or a name read aloud during a test can turn it into a confession, prompting the suspect to act and be restrained. When: A test is running in front of the group. Why: Public tests push guilty parties to react.
- [heuristic] Give a suspect space in silence, since the explanation offered unprompted is often fuller than answers to direct questions. When: Interviewing a suspect who may reveal more when not pressed. Why: Unprompted speech tends to contain more detail than responses to focused questions.
- [heuristic] One trivial routine fact, such as a service worker's count of residence months, can overturn a fabricated identity in a single line. When: A newcomer's account conflicts with a background witness's knowledge. Why: Background staff observe routines, so their everyday facts often contradict a cover story.
- [procedure] 1) Stage a confrontation with the suspects. 2) Attach a timed threat, such as a warned ambush. 3) Let the guilty party react under pressure and confess. Why: A deadline forces the guilty party to act, exposing them.
- [tradeoff] Keeping a confession in reserve preserves its power to free an innocent person; revealing it early spends that power and may leave the accusation standing. When: a secret document could clear a wrongly accused character.
- [pitfall] A confession staged only for shock wears thin, so a reveal must change how the audience understands the characters. When: Designing a confession or reveal scene. Why: Without changing understanding of characters, the reveal feels like an isolated twist rather than meaningful.

## confession unlocked leads
- [mechanism] One person's confession can prompt another to confess, so a confession seen by others may become a model that pulls in further confessions. When: Accused people are held together and can see one another's statements. Why: Witnessing a confession makes it seem safe or expected, which weakens resistance in others.
- [behavior] An informant or suspect who confesses past actions reveals his motive and names other people, places, meetings, roles or methods, creating new leads and widening the suspect set. When: an informant or suspect admits past actions or names other people, places or methods. Why: the confession exposes motives and connections; named details create new leads to pursue. (x2)
- [behavior] A witness caught concealing something may volunteer a small hidden motive together with a ready alibi, presenting the matter as minor. When: a witness is accused of concealment. Why: A voluntary admission looks honest.
- [rule] Repeat a suspect's own slipped phrase back in dialogue and invite him to continue, which can open a confession branch. Why: Hearing one's own words returned can provoke a revealing reaction.
- [rule] Let a confession unlock the motive and open a new area or quest step.
- [rule] Give a suspect NPC a confession branch triggered by the player's reconstruction of events, making the reconstruction itself a playable event.
- [rule] A confession that names others should unlock each named accomplice as a new suspect the player can question.
- [pitfall] A confession that fits a prior suspicion can act as a red herring, and certainty about an early suspect shows tunnel vision. When: An investigator is confident about a suspect before evidence confirms it. Why: Early certainty filters out evidence that points elsewhere.
- [pitfall] A case closed on a false confession has no path to the truth unless an independent clue survives outside the confession.
- [pitfall] A confession that repeats details already in circulation may reflect what the confessor heard, not what happened.

## consequences of failed inquiry
- [mechanism] One illicit act often forces the next, as each step taken to conceal or cover an earlier wrong creates a new one. When: when a character commits an initial wrong under pressure. Why: Covering an initial act requires more acts, each harder to undo.
- [mechanism] A case built on one kind of evidence collapses once it reaches a respected person, since the accusers' credibility is then exposed. When: An accusation based on a single evidence type extends to a figure the community trusts. Why: Accusing a respected person makes the weakness of the evidence visible.
- [rule] End the falsely accused thread with a visible cost or profit to the accused, so the consequences of the frame are shown.
- [rule] Close an investigation by making the evidence inaccessible, so that the player's final knowledge is what they carry rather than what they can check. When: When ending a mystery on an unresolved, uncertain note. Why: Removing the ability to verify leaves the player with belief instead of proof, sustaining the sense of unease.
- [heuristic] An investigator who notices a tell and moves on without pursuing it lets the subject recover, which keeps them talking. When: when questioning a reluctant suspect. Why: Pressing an embarrassing reaction tends to end the conversation, while sparing it keeps information flowing.
- [heuristic] The evidence required for a conclusion should rise with its seriousness: a grave conclusion needs stronger proof than a provisional one, and an early accusation must not be treated as settled. When: Deciding whether evidence supports an accusation or a formal finding. Why: Serious consequences require stronger certainty, while preliminary steps need less.
- [heuristic] Keep evidence intact and warn suspects against destroying it, since suspects may try to destroy proof. When: Confronting a suspect with evidence.
- [pitfall] Returning evidence to a suspect can alert them, so the timing of returning or showing an object matters. When: Deciding when to show an item to a suspect. Why: Showing evidence gives the suspect information to react to and adapt.
- [pitfall] A lead that fits one clue but fails a later test leaves the investigation stuck; the false account is exposed once the search turns up nothing. When: when the suspected cause is searched for and never found. Why: The explanation covers the original evidence but not the absence of the predicted result.
- [pitfall] Accepting visible damage at face value is a common error, because crash damage can conceal the real cause.

## deduction and player hints
- [model] An argument-driven mystery uses timeline and identity challenges to move suspicion between suspects, ending on a physical lead rather than a full on-page reveal.
- [model] A mystery format where a stationary solver reasons from reported facts, an official solution forms and an innocent suspect is arrested, then a hidden detail reverses the case and the solver reconstructs the truth by argument. When: designing reasoning-driven mystery cases told through reports. Why: The reversal reframes existing evidence, so the player experiences the solution as an inference rather than a discovery.
- [mechanism] A crime-scene mode with a numbered checklist turns each step into a recorded observation that feeds a final deduction, and negative results still move the player forward. When: Designing investigation gameplay. Why: Recorded observations accumulate into a conclusion, and eliminations keep progress visible.
- [rule] Make NPC claims checkable, such as warnings or a guide's walk duration tested against a timer or map, so their words gain meaning and the guide's fairness can be tested. When: An NPC gives a warning the player might dismiss, or a trusted guide gives a timing claim. Why: A later confirmation rewards attention, and a checkable claim lets apparent fairness be tested. (x2)
- [heuristic] Ask for one precise fact from a source rather than a general account, so the query is fast and the answer narrows the search. When: An investigator needs a specific detail to move forward. Why: A narrow question gets a usable answer without long delay.
- [procedure] 1) Set out every plausible explanation, including accidental ones. 2) Test each against the evidence. 3) Only then conclude the most likely cause. When: Forming a conclusion about a cause or culprit. Why: A rival explanation left untested can overturn a theory built on a single suspect.
- [pitfall] A single check does not establish truth: cheap surface answers mislead, and a cover story passing one known test can still fail another, since planners rarely anticipate every method. When: Investigating a case with planted misdirection, or assessing whether a cover story will hold. Why: Surface answers are easy to produce and planners rarely anticipate every verification method.
- [pitfall] Advice that sounds protective, such as destroying a dangerous item in a way that keeps it in use, can shift the risk onto the target. When: an NPC gives the player safety advice. Why: The safe-sounding action actually increases danger, so it can serve as a trap.
- [pitfall] Building a larger conspiracy around a foreign or official-looking detail without checking its purpose leads to false theories. When: When a single striking clue suggests espionage or a big plot. Why: Dramatic details invite elaborate explanations that the actual facts may not support.
- [fact] A checklist of case elements orders what must be tested; it is not proof of guilt.

## disguise and physical marks
- [mechanism] Loose garments, veils and large hats hide height, shape, dress and face, so witnesses describe only partial features that do not narrow identity. When: A culprit disguises appearance with loose clothing or a veil, or witnesses saw the person briefly. Why: Covering the body or face removes cues witnesses use to recognize people, and partial concealment is enough to block recognition.
- [behavior] A disguise made from a wig, false beard and costume can conceal a younger person's identity, especially when family portraits show a strong resemblance. When: A character is seen in a costume that imitates an older person. Why: Costume pieces hide surface features, while shared family features remain visible to those who compare portraits.
- [rule] Give a disguised character a fixed bodily tell, such as a burn, missing finger, hand or gait, visible only on close inspection so players can unmask them by looking closely. When: Designing disguised characters. (x2)
- [rule] Build scenes where authorities accept a cover story while the player notices anomalies, and reward players who test the staged plot against its flaws. When: When designing an investigation with an official explanation. Why: Players who spot flaws the authorities missed gain a sense of insight.
- [heuristic] Disguises usually change clothing, hair and manner, so look past targeted features; fixed marks like scars or moles in unexpected places are hard to disguise and can confirm identity. When: A disguise is suspected and the person controls the features others normally check. Why: Clothing, hair and manner can change, while permanent marks usually cannot.
- [heuristic] Tie one fixed, verifiable mark to a schedule others know, such as tides, bells or shift changes, to anchor a timeline when witnesses are unreliable. When: Witness memory is clouded or witnesses disagree about when events happened.
- [heuristic] Prove a disguise with several independent physical traces, such as smell, sweat and stray hair, rather than one observation. When: a suspect's identity is hidden by disguise. Why: multiple corroborating traces make the deduction hard to dismiss.
- [pitfall] A flamboyant cover can make the real secret look ordinary, pulling the investigator toward the wrong question.
- [pitfall] A disguise such as a veil or mourning dress hides exactly the features investigators need to match a suspect.
- [fact] A disguise can survive a search when it is hidden under a covering such as a glove, so a refusal to uncover a body part is worth noting.

## disguise mechanics
- [rule] Give a disguised NPC a sensory clue such as a scent, sound or visible seam so players who check non-visual cues can expose the impostor. When: when designing disguised characters.
- [heuristic] Hint at a concealed identity with small cues, such as changed appearance or banter, and introduce the disguise's physical features early, so the reveal is surprising yet fair. When: Early chapters of a disguise plot, or when planting a costume that will be revealed later. Why: Naming the disguise before it is shown makes the reveal fair and memorable. (x2)
- [heuristic] Conspicuous features like hair, beard and nose are easiest to counterfeit, so witness memory of them is unreliable; eye markings, fingernail shape and ear set are hard to fake. When: when checking whether a person is who they appear to be, or identifying a person from witness descriptions. Why: Eye-catching features are chosen for disguise because they draw attention, while hard-to-change features are rarely altered.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC wear another character's cloak to fake a presence, and let a written note serve as a false alibi that the player can test against other evidence. When: Designing disguise or alibi mechanics. Why: Visible tokens create apparent presence, and the player can expose them through timing or witnesses.
- [heuristic] A test can be hidden behind a harmless request, such as fetching an item, so the subject's behavior is judged without their awareness. When: Checking whether a person resembles someone or matches a clue. Why: A concealed purpose yields more natural reactions than a stated test.
- [heuristic] A disguise is easiest to expose through non-visual traces, such as smell, skin warmth or the way hair is set, which the wearer cannot easily hide. When: when a witness's visual description may be unreliable because of disguise. Why: Disguise materials and construction leave traces outside what the eye checks.
- [heuristic] Let a disguise pass on sight by matching a shared dress code, but fail on sound or behaviour, so an observant player can still catch it. When: hiding a living intruder among staff or a uniformed group. Why: Visual checks are easy to satisfy, while sound and movement are harder to fake.
- [procedure] 1) Note conspicuous visual features. 2) Check hard-to-fake features. 3) Check sensory traces such as smell and skin. 4) Treat each trace as weak alone and suspicious only when several agree. When: when judging whether a person is in disguise. Why: Single traces have ordinary explanations, but agreement among small details builds real suspicion.
- [pitfall] Assuming a witness who saw someone in unusual clothing is mistaken, rather than checking whether that clothing was worn by someone else, is a mistake. When: A witness reports a person in atypical attire. Why: The clothing may be a disguise worn by a different person.
- [fact] A disguise usually covers the face and clothing but not body proportions such as height, or the hands, which can betray a hidden identity.

## empty room and container clues
- [mechanism] An empty container built up as a reward can carry more narrative weight than its treasure, because its absence becomes a question the plot must answer. When: A sealed reward is promised and built up, so the audience over-values it. Why: Removing the expected prize removes the obstacle driving conduct; disappointment makes the player seek the reason for its absence.
- [mechanism] A missing key item from a known place tells the player that someone has been there, so it works as a trigger.
- [heuristic] Empty pockets are evidence in themselves: they leave the victim unidentified and should be recorded as a finding.
- [heuristic] Check which items are missing from a container; an emptied box opened on the night of a crime is a physical trace linking the object to the timeline.
- [heuristic] Treat unexpected empty positions in a crowd as deliberate features to explain, not as details to ignore.
- [heuristic] When a container is found empty, its maker, markings and history can carry the clue in place of its contents. When: the container is found empty.
- [heuristic] Before searching a place a clue points to, confirm it is occupied; a location that has stood empty for weeks is likely a dead end. When: when a clue points to a vacant building. Why: searching a deserted site wastes effort.
- [pitfall] An empty room or container can mislead searchers into thinking the search is finished while other rooms or leads remain. When: Clearing a building room by room. Why: Searchers can mistake one clear room for a clear building.
- [fact] An empty room shows only that the person is not there, not where they went; their location needs other evidence.
- [fact] An empty container that was opened with a key suggests papers were removed, which can be checked against the dates of those papers. When: A container is found empty after being opened without force. Why: Removed papers may contradict a claimed purchase or timeline if their dates fall later.

## gesture and body language
- [mechanism] Posture and nervous gestures let the player read a character's state without dialogue.
