- [behavior] A symbolic gesture passed around a social table is read at once by those present, so its meaning must be clear in context.
- [heuristic] A gesture or body position is not proof of guilt or a particular cause; first ask what innocent or injury-driven explanation exists. Why: Pacing is common when people are memorising material or under stress, and the same posture can result from different causes.
- [heuristic] Victims found with open hands and extended limbs, showing no struggle, were probably taken by surprise.
- [heuristic] Impressions implying a posture no one would choose freely suggest the subject was placed there, or could not move, which points toward restraint. When: Measured distances between marks and the body suggest an unnatural pose. Why: Free movement leaves a different pattern.
- [heuristic] A person still in the position they held at a known earlier moment probably has not moved since then. When: Checking whether someone has left a place since a known moment.
- [heuristic] A body position that contradicts a stated account, such as a victim who supposedly ducked and fell forward, is a strong test of that account.
- [heuristic] A character's habitual gesture, such as a handshake or toast, can carry a hidden function that the player recognises later. When: Designing an NPC interaction with a concealed mechanism. Why: Routine acts are unlikely to be questioned, so the means of harm blends into normal behavior.
- [pitfall] Comparing one's own reach with a handprint is only approximate, since the result depends on the posture the person used. Why: Different postures change the reach without changing height.
- [pitfall] A crouch or stoop widens the shooter height range, so the posture assumption must be stated and checked.

## group consensus and experts
- [mechanism] Visitors who seek out accusers for help carry the accusations home, so the accusations reach communities far from their origin. When: when accusers offer consultations to outsiders. Why: each visitor becomes a new channel for the claim.
- [behavior] A confident account from one character can set the group's expectation, so the audience adopts the wrong motive and stops checking it against the physical evidence. When: a suspect or witness offers an early theory. Why: People accept a shared explanation before testing it.
- [rule] Do not dismiss a consensus merely because it is consensus, since experience counts and officials are not always wrong.
- [rule] Offer a compare-notes action that lets players collect contradicting accounts, and use the group's silence as a clue. When: When designing a player action to gather witness accounts. Why: Comparing accounts tests reliability and surfaces what no one saw.
- [heuristic] A confident group consensus about cause of death can be wrong. Check the wound directly rather than trusting the earlier assumption.
- [heuristic] Consult several experts on an ambiguous rule, since conflicting readings show how uncertain the motive really is.
- [procedure] 1) Identify each source that supports a belief. 2) Trace where each source's authority came from. 3) Merge sources that share an origin. 4) Count the remaining independent sources. When: Judging whether apparent agreement is independent evidence. Why: Consolidating shared origins reveals how much real support exists.
- [pitfall] Public consensus shifts with attention and can be wrong, so it is weak proof of what happened. When: When an event is accepted because many people believe it. Why: Shared belief spreads without independent evidence. (x2)
- [pitfall] Group consensus among officials can outweigh a correct minority view, so a lone investigator may be overruled. When: officials disagree about a suspect's identity.
- [pitfall] Agreement among authorities can hide a shared error, because later sources often repeat the same premise rather than test it.

## hidden antagonists and bosses
- [model] A hidden antagonist's harm can follow a chain of roles: an accuser presents charges, an authority grants permission, and an executor carries out the harm. When: explaining harm that has no visible perpetrator. Why: A staged chain of roles makes unseen causation legible and reconstructable.
- [mechanism] A faction's hidden boss can issue orders through agents, so catching and replacing agents reveals the boss's presence without exposing them.
- [rule] Build a hidden antagonist whose agents act openly, with each action benefiting the antagonist and traceable to a shared location. When: designing a conspiracy in a game.
- [rule] Give a hidden antagonist a concrete motive, such as envy or a grudge, so its choice of targets makes sense to players. When: designing a hidden or unseen antagonist.
- [rule] Build a helper who doubles as the trap by offering visibly too-precise knowledge, then unmasking them as the source of danger.
- [heuristic] A hired party may stay hidden, even from the investigator, so the case must be judged on its own facts.
- [heuristic] A game handler can know a masked NPC's true identity while the player does not, with the reveal triggered by a specific player action.
- [heuristic] Formal office can hide who actually decides; trace who selected each officer and who had their ear. When: judging who controls a government or council.
- [heuristic] Hide a rescuer NPC in plain sight by marking their gaze early, so players recall the figure when the rescue happens. When: Designing a later-revealed ally. Why: An early marked detail makes the late identity feel earned.
- [tradeoff] Early naming of a hidden antagonist and goal gives audiences a question to pursue, but a fixed early identity removes reason to investigate; keep identity as rumour until direct evidence. When: an unseen boss drives the plot. Why: A named target gives the audience a question to pursue; a fixed early identity removes the reason to investigate.

## identity and engineered staging
- [mechanism] An antagonist can remove an investigator from the scene using a formal, legitimate-looking process timed to a window of opportunity. When: when an opponent has a plausible legal or social means to stop the protagonist. Why: The process looks lawful, so it is hard to resist directly.
- [mechanism] A plotter can make a location predictably empty at a known hour by arranging a servant's leave, travel times and a planned outing. When: When a plan requires a location to be unobserved at a specific time. Why: Scheduled absences remove witnesses at a chosen moment.
- [mechanism] A stopping point that depends on a person's inability to sense a condition suggests the conditions were engineered rather than arising by chance. When: an incomplete action coincides with a sensory limitation of the actor. Why: A limitation the actor cannot sense explains why the stop occurred only if someone arranged the situation.
- [mechanism] A suspect can secure an alibi by being in a witnessed place when the crime happens, while the crime itself runs without them. When: a non-present suspect needs confirmed innocence. Why: Independent witnesses confirm the suspect's location at the critical moment.
- [mechanism] A staged death can invert identity: the body may be someone else, or the man presumed dead or living may be the impostor.
- [heuristic] A convenient coincidence may be a deliberate arrangement, and a case that fits too neatly is suspicious since a shrewd culprit can plant misleading loopholes. When: A coincidence fits the timing and people involved, or a circumstantial case fits together too cleanly. Why: A shrewd culprit can leave misleading loopholes that look like a tidy theory.
- [heuristic] Objects with a hidden second layer, such as a label revealed by scraping or a seal, can reveal a second identity. When: Designing an item that hides a second identity. Why: Revealing an underlying layer rewards players for careful inspection.
- [heuristic] Attach the identity clue to a shared physical object that only a few named characters touched, so the suspect list stays small and the clue is fair. When: a reveal depends on one physical trace. Why: A short named suspect list lets the audience test the clue.
- [heuristic] A physical identifier such as a scar or a fingerprint is useless until it is matched against a second independent record, such as a witness description.
- [pitfall] Identifying marks can be altered after death to create a false identity, so a match holds only if the body has not been modified.

## identity reveal structure
- [model] An identity-swap reveal hides that one person has taken another's place, and is built from partial exposures, each confirming a suspicion but not the full truth.
- [mechanism] A twist that a character is a second self can be built by planting two separate facts early, such as a key and a will, which the audience reads as unrelated until a later reveal links them. When: Designing a reveal where two apparently different characters are the same person. Why: Separate early facts let the audience hold both pieces before knowing they connect, so the reveal reframes rather than contradicts them.
- [rule] Plant the key identity clue, such as a portrait, record, object, or gesture, in the first act in plain sight, so the answer is visible before the reveal. When: Writing a hidden-identity twist. (x2)
- [rule] Break one identity into stages, such as stranger, performer, former lover, and parent, each revealed in a separate scene so understanding changes in steps.
- [heuristic] Deliver an identity reversal through a document or incidental aside rather than a dramatic accusation, so it reads as a discovery.
- [heuristic] Plant identity clues early and feed later evidence in a steady trickle, so the question stays open until the late reveal.
- [heuristic] Reveal a stranger NPC's identity through an in-world log or record after the player leaves a zone, enabling a late callback. When: Designing a delayed identity reveal. Why: Records let identity be disclosed without interrupting play.
- [heuristic] Hold back the culprit's full identity until a late reveal that proves it, rather than disclosing it piece by piece in private. When: when the culprit has been hidden behind a trusted role.
- [procedure] 1) Let an authority figure gather physical proof, such as a grave, tomb, or working object. 2) Stage the reveal as a public or semi-public act. 3) Close with a brief aftermath where the narrator leaves, carrying lasting unease. When: Designing the climax where a hidden identity is exposed. Why: Physical proof lets the audience verify the solution rather than accept a claim.
- [procedure] 1) Exchange roles so the suspect and staff see the wrong person in the wrong role. 2) Arrange the scene the suspect will enter. 3) Keep the people who know the truth apart. When: The suspect has never seen the real person. Why: A swap works only while those who know the truth stay separated.

## implausible claims and explanations
- [rule] Accept an improbable explanation only after the likelier explanations have been tested and failed, or closed off by physical constraints. When: Several explanations remain, one of them improbable. Why: Eliminating the easier options leaves the improbable one as the only consistent answer.
- [heuristic] If a claimed result needs many separate unlikely accidents, treat the claim as suspicious and examine it more closely.
- [heuristic] An explanation is weakened when the action it implies is unlikely for the actors involved, such as a family hiding a dangerous person at home instead of sending them away.
- [heuristic] A theory can be improbable and still a serious candidate if every rival explanation is also improbable.
- [heuristic] When a method seems implausible for ordinary people, check whether it really excludes them rather than accepting the obvious suspect. When: a method appears to require an unusually strong or skilled person. Why: Implausibility can clear some suspects while leaving the true culprit's capacity unexamined.
- [heuristic] A claimed duration far longer than the expected travel time for a short journey is a point to probe.
- [heuristic] When a stated reason looks too minor to explain the outcome it produced, look for a larger pressure that the complaining party chose not to mention. When: an official ground seems out of proportion to an action.
- [heuristic] Quest hooks that promise improbable rescues can tempt players into investing in the wrong lead; give players a way to recognize that mistake later. When: Designing tempting but false leads. Why: Players need a discoverable signal to correct a misreading.
- [pitfall] Confusing an improbable truth with a planned lie is an error; a self-serving or unlikely account may still be true. When: when judging a witness whose account seems too convenient.
- [pitfall] Improvised detail added under pressure creates new checkable claims that can be exposed later.

## lost item and theft
- [mechanism] When a hidden item is sold within an undifferentiated lot, its trail ends with the buyer unless the seller recorded where each unit went.
- [mechanism] A lost item that is later stolen creates a loss-then-theft sequence, so the order of events itself becomes a timeline clue.
- [behavior] Items are rarely truly lost; people more often believe they have lost something, so a loss report often reflects their habits of storing things. When: A person reports losing an item. Why: People tend to misremember where they last used or put an item.
- [behavior] A stored item's absence is often discovered only when someone needs it, so the loss is revealed at the moment of use. When: A small or personal object is kept out of sight. Why: Nobody checks for an item until it is required.
- [rule] Use a lost-item hook to start dialogue with an NPC who would otherwise refuse to talk.
- [heuristic] Place dropped or lost-and-found items in a level as trace evidence that players can link to an NPC.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the owner to list what is missing. 2) Compare the list with the scene. 3) Infer the likely culprit's kind or purpose from which items were taken. When: a reported loss can be checked against the scene. Why: the set of missing items is itself evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Determine the quantity taken. 2) Compare it to a known harmful or significant threshold. 3) Judge the theft's seriousness from that comparison. When: when a missing object could be a weapon, clue, or means of harm. Why: the same loss matters differently depending on how it relates to a threshold.
- [pitfall] A list of losses alone does not identify a culprit; it needs surrounding context before it can point to anyone.
- [fact] The person who carried an object may notice its loss quickly, which can expose a theft sooner than the thief expects. When: when an object is regularly carried by one person. Why: the carrier is most likely to notice missing items.

## moral judgment
- [definition] Moral or circumstantial evidence, such as motive, presence or manner, supports likely guilt; legal proof needs direct evidence, like witnessing an act or a physical link. Why: the two standards differ in what they require.
- [definition] Moral certainty is a strong belief in guilt, whereas legal certainty requires evidence that can be shown and sustained.
- [definition] A moral impossibility is an act a person would refuse because it clashes with their instinctive manner, even though they could physically commit it.
- [mechanism] A mission frame can justify a group's general policy as well as its individual prosecutions, so suspicion gains a purpose beyond each case.
- [behavior] A confession can resolve a moral question rather than a legal one, leaving the culprit unpunished by law. When: ending a mystery where justice and law diverge. Why: Motive and remorse can close the story without a formal arrest.
- [heuristic] Judge a document by what it can actually establish; a short later letter may give only moral support, not decisive proof. When: Weighing how much a document settles a question.
- [tradeoff] Letting an offender go spares them punishment but removes accountability and may let them wrong others later. When: dropping a case against a remorseful offender.
- [pitfall] Moral disapproval, such as of a suspect's luxury or unsavoury past, can replace evidence; it is opinion, not proof, and skips motive, opportunity and reliable clues. When: When a judgement about lifestyle or past is used to infer guilt. Why: Disapproval feels like proof but is an opinion, not a fact. (x2)
- [pitfall] Praise for those who refuse to confess is moral judgment and does not prove innocence.
- [pitfall] Offering moral judgement on a witness's personal relationships can end their cooperation and lose the detail the investigator still needs.

## mystery structure and serial arcs
- [model] A single-scene frame stages one isolated location, a confined protagonist, and a reading that reverses the meaning of an object in the final beat. When: Designing a short tale set in one location. Why: One place and one object keep attention on the reveal.
- [model] Detective stories in this formula follow six stages: premise, apparent simple answer, misdirection and pressure, forensic reversal, reconstruction and confession, then aftermath.
- [model] A serial mystery is a chain of duels against one enemy: each investigation ends in a new trap, so the story is a sequence of confrontations rather than a single puzzle. When: Designing a multi-stage mystery or campaign with a recurring antagonist. Why: Each stage gives the player a new problem and a new reason to continue.
- [definition] A single-investigation plot chains complications where each new death or suspect reframes the case, keeping the audience's picture of who is lying shifting until the confessions.
- [mechanism] A slow investigation by an amateur can reconstruct a faked event piece by piece from scattered documents, testimony and gaps the investigator must fill.
- [mechanism] Unmasking an apparent culprit does not end the threat when a second, unrelated presence continues after the exposure. When: Designing a threat that seems resolved after the culprit is revealed. Why: A continuing threat after the reveal undercuts closure and keeps tension high.
- [heuristic] Leave one symbol or account unresolved as a deliberate hook for a later story. When: Ending a story that may continue. Why: An open thread gives the player a reason to return.
- [heuristic] Let the reasoning character stand outside the action, receiving information as reports, so the solver's argument itself becomes the reveal. When: the scenario's solver should not witness events directly. Why: Information filtered through reports keeps the solver's inference as the main act of discovery.
- [procedure] 1) hook at 0-4%; 2) first investigation with a false solution, 4-18%; 3) second front that widens the enemy, 18-33%; 4) decoy and betrayal, 33-47%; 5) mid-story murder that raises stakes, 47-62%; 6) escalation with traps, 62-84%; 7) faked death and assembly, 84-97%; 8) crisis and close, 97-100%. When: Pacing a long mystery or campaign arc of roughly 100 percent of its length.
- [pitfall] Once a topic has been changed by distress, returning to the original question by repetition tends to fail; a fresh approach is needed. When: Trying to resume questioning after a witness recovers. Why: The witness has already reframed the matter and repetition sounds like pressure.

## narrative pacing and rhythm
- [model] A mystery can be staged in five stages: premise, hidden clues, origin reveal, escalating pressure, and collapse.
- [model] A mystery can be staged in seven parts in order: hook, misdirected investigation, pressure and crisis, complication, false solution, doubt, and trap. When: Structuring a mystery plot by escalation.
- [model] A plot can be planned as percentage-bounded stages: hook, voyage and suspicion, accusation, survey and pressure, detention, rival-location and overhearing, separation, climax and epilogue, each carrying its own clues and reveals. When: Designing a mystery or espionage story with a long investigative middle. Why: Staged percentage bounds let the designer pace reveals and check that suspicion shifts follow new facts.
- [model] A reversal-driven story runs in phases: premise, background grievances, rising strife, context, outbreak, trials, then collapse and reckoning, with suspicion escalating before it reverses.
- [definition] Pumping means raising a name or topic as if idly, so the other party's reaction reveals what they already know.
- [heuristic] A quiet closing image can resolve an emotional thread without further dialogue.
- [heuristic] Track each re-vote as a state change in the group's disposition. When: a group must approve several steps in turn.
- [heuristic] Stating in advance that events will be told in their true sequence builds trust that a later reveal will be coherent and worth waiting for. When: a reveal will come after a long or indirect account. Why: a promised order signals that the reveal is structured.
- [pitfall] An explanation that closes an inquiry quickly may have been designed to close it, so speed of acceptance is not evidence of truth.
- [fact] In a quiet room a listener can hear another's breathing, so stillness does not guarantee that a person has left.

## npc roles and loyalty
- [definition] Social invisibility is a culprit hidden by an everyday role that people stop noticing, so the culprit is present in the scene yet never seen as a suspect.
- [mechanism] An NPC who claims neutrality can be scored by their gain from each outcome, so the player must infer their real loyalty from incentives. When: Designing NPC allegiance that is not stated outright. Why: Incentives reveal loyalty more reliably than declared positions.
- [behavior] A protagonist's confident conclusion is overturned when the authorities already hold the key evidence, obtained through a minor character she had overlooked. When: a reveal must overturn the protagonist's theory. Why: the decisive clue sat with a character the protagonist never considered.
- [rule] A returned character's explanation for missing time should match physical marks such as injuries or damp clothing.
- [rule] Tag each piece of NPC information with its source, such as seen directly, heard from someone, or told by a dead person, so players can judge trust. When: Designing an interrogation or information system. Why: Source tags let players weigh reliability instead of accepting all claims equally.
- [heuristic] A quest where one NPC is sent by another lets the player trace the original instruction and discover who controls whom. When: Designing NPC quest chains. Why: Tracing the chain of command reveals hidden power relations.
- [heuristic] Delay a scripted arrival with dialogue beats that build toward the reveal of a masked contact. When: Scripting the appearance of a key contact. Why: Dialogue during the wait keeps the anticipation active until the arrival.
- [heuristic] Give the player an NPC who can confirm a clue, with a second source available if that NPC is removed or lies. When: A clue depends on one character's testimony. Why: A backup source keeps progress possible.
- [heuristic] A restrained or injured NPC can be the conspirator rather than the victim, so do not assume a bound character's role until evidence confirms it.
- [pitfall] A misdelivered item that shares a surname can look like a deliberate link between two characters and mislead the reader. Why: Overlapping names make coincidence seem like intent.

## outside experts and records
- [mechanism] Outside evidence such as a departure notice can reveal an opponent's escape plan and shift the investigation's deadline.
- [mechanism] Information from outside, such as a newspaper's description of valuables, can prompt an outsider to form a plan. When: a scheme targets a valued possession. Why: public descriptions reveal targets and their worth.
- [mechanism] Leaving a locked room whose key is outside requires reopening the door, which exposes the leaver to anyone nearby. Why: Reopening the door takes time and makes the leaver visible.
- [rule] Engage an outside examiner who receives only the case detail the task requires, and cross-check their findings with interviews. When: Financial or transactional records must be read. Why: Limited information keeps the examiner's reading unbiased, and interviews check what records alone show.
- [rule] Have an independent specialist classify a physical material so the conclusion does not rest only on the investigator's judgment. When: identifying material from a trace. Why: Outside classification adds an independent check.
- [heuristic] If a person acts against their own interest, look for an outside influence that prompted the act.
- [heuristic] Use a third sample from a new location to redirect the investigation from the scene to the outside world.
- [procedure] Do not accept a stated account, such as an itinerary, until an outside witness confirms it: identify someone in a position to know, send a written question, and compare the reply with the account. When: when the account rests on the teller's word, especially when the teller benefits from it. Why: An outside reply is an independent check.
- [procedure] 1) Negotiate which bodies may sit, excluding any whose members pushed for the council. 2) Add neutral members at trusted advice to reduce the initiating party's control.
- [pitfall] A reveal resting on a single outside insight feels unearned if the supporting clues were never shown. Why: The audience has no way to check the insight against evidence.

## plain statements and rules
- [rule] Present an estate's inheritance rules to the player in plain terms so that outcomes and their motives can be checked. When: Designing inheritance or settlement systems for players. Why: Visible rules let players test claims about motive.
- [rule] Keep background plain and checkable when the investigation needs facts, rather than dressing the setting in atmosphere. When: Presenting setting information that will be used as evidence. Why: Checkable facts can be tested, while atmosphere cannot.
- [rule] State a charge plainly in front of those present, and restate it when the suspect asks what it means.
- [rule] Keep the reveal itself short and plain, stating the act and its consequences in flat words without elaboration. When: Delivering a confession or admission. Why: Plain statement carries more weight after a long build-up.
- [rule] State an inference plainly so the listener can test it. When: Presenting a circumstantial conclusion to others. Why: A stated inference can be checked, challenged or confirmed.
- [heuristic] A large, plain, obvious clue is revealed at once by direct examination, so peripheral search is needed mainly for faint clues. When: choosing how to search a scene. Why: obvious evidence does not depend on how it is viewed.
- [heuristic] State legal, technical or rule-based limits in ordinary words so a non-specialist can follow the constraint without expert knowledge. When: A limit matters to later events and the audience is not expected to be a specialist. Why: Jargon hides the constraint and weakens the later deduction.
- [heuristic] A plain cover identity, such as a common trade and modest occupations, that explains the party's behaviour invites fewer questions.
- [heuristic] Concealment often happens in plain sight among other discarded items, so a second searcher may find evidence the first one missed. When: evidence is hidden among other objects. Why: clutter hides items from a quick search.
- [heuristic] Clues can sit in plain sight as ordinary objects or gestures whose meaning becomes clear only later, so the reader can notice them before understanding them. When: Planting clues for a mystery. Why: Early visibility rewards attentive readers without giving away the answer.

## plausible false solutions
- [mechanism] A plausible everyday explanation that fits some of the facts can close inquiry and divert attention from the true cause; weigh it against the full scene. When: A misleading explanation is offered for an event and covers part of the evidence. Why: A simple, familiar story is easy to accept before evidence is checked; partial fit makes it feel complete, so searchers stop testing it against remaining clues.
- [behavior] A witness adopts a wrong theory of an investigator's motives when it fits visible facts such as age, relationships and an odd request. When: An outsider hears an unusual request about a person in their circle. Why: Visible facts make the wrong theory feel plausible, so the witness treats the request as improper.
- [rule] Make an NPC's explanation partly true without being a plain lie, and require players to test it against physical evidence. When: Designing misleading NPC gossip or rumor. Why: Confirmed detail lends credibility to the unconfirmed remainder, so a partly true story is more believable and forces players to verify rather than dismiss it.
- [rule] Make each suspect's guilt, including a wrong one, plausible on the evidence the player holds at that moment, so an arrest or blame is accepted. When: A suspect is arrested, named or led to be blamed. Why: A weak false suspect is dismissed quickly, which removes the trap; the player must be able to accept the arrest on what they know.
- [heuristic] Make the official theory coherent and wrong only in its motive or cause, then let the true solution emerge from rereading the same evidence. When: Writing a false solution for a mystery. Why: An internally logical wrong answer is more convincing than an absurd one, so the eventual correction carries weight.
- [heuristic] Chain false solutions that each use real evidence read in a different frame, assigning the same shared facts to a different suspect each time, until a final inversion. When: Structuring a mystery with several suspect theories. Why: Each theory is consistent with real evidence, so the wrong frame is hard to spot; a reading that fits real evidence is hard to dismiss without a new source.
- [heuristic] Include decoy suspects who are real enemies with their own goals, so they feel plausible without being the answer. When: When building false leads for a mystery. Why: Decoys with real motives remain credible and therefore hold the player's attention.
- [heuristic] Give the audience a plausible political or conspiratorial explanation that is wrong, so attention goes to the wrong motive. When: Building misdirection into a mystery. Why: A believable alternative explanation absorbs suspicion that would otherwise fall on the real answer.
- [pitfall] A plausible, true-seeming reason does not clear a suspect, since an account can be true and still misleading. When: Evaluating a suspect's stated reason. Why: Plausibility is not the same as full disclosure.
- [pitfall] A tidy rational explanation offered early can mislead as much as a supernatural one, especially when it was built to make the event look like a delusion. Why: A rational cover story can be engineered to hide the real act.

## private documents and knowledge
- [rule] Keep a character's private knowledge hidden from others so that what they know and what they say differ, creating a gap for the audience to notice. When: Writing characters who withhold information from each other. Why: A knowledge gap creates tension and invites the audience to question motives.
- [rule] Do not accept a supernatural or unusual explanation for private knowledge until you check how the knowledge could have been obtained. When: when a witness knows what was said privately.
- [rule] Use private marginalia or personal notes as collectible clues that reveal inner state, while letting the investigator respect their privacy. When: when placing personal documents in a mystery. Why: Private material exposes hidden feelings and can be used as evidence without public exposure.
- [heuristic] When public behavior or agreement looks too neat, check private settings or records, since public unity can hide private disagreement. When: Public behavior or agreement appears flawless. Why: The contrast between public and private faces reveals the hidden side; people display unity publicly while differing in private records. (x2)
- [tradeoff] Investigating privately before informing authorities can save time when they are busy, but leaves the investigator to carry the risk alone. When: official help is occupied elsewhere.
- [pitfall] Private letters can reveal plans, but some passages are not meant for public ears, so ask who holds a document and why.
- [pitfall] Using a private document raises questions of consent and of what may be used afterward, so its contents deserve care.
- [pitfall] A decision to withhold evidence based on belief in someone's innocence rests on an unproven judgement and can be wrong. When: When an investigator decides what to disclose based on a belief about a suspect. Why: Belief in innocence is not evidence, so withholding on that basis can protect the wrong person.
- [fact] Evidence convincing to an investigator may still fall short of the proof a formal proceeding requires.
- [fact] Omissions made for privacy may be innocent, but they still change what the reader can infer from the evidence.

## proof and deduction method
- [rule] Do not treat a theory as settled while its key proof is missing, even if it explains most of the facts. When: A theory rests on a decisive item that has not been found. Why: Without the decisive item the theory stays unconfirmed and can be wrong.
- [heuristic] Separate an apparently natural or supernatural cause from a human act by asking who would benefit and what mechanism was available. When: An event looks accidental or uncanny and the cause is unclear. Why: Motive and means reveal whether a natural-seeming event was in fact engineered.
- [heuristic] Confirm a mystery's answer with both documentary proof and physical proof, so players can verify it in two independent ways. When: when designing the final confirmation of a mystery. Why: two independent kinds of proof reduce remaining doubt.
- [heuristic] Use a checkable, concrete inconsistency, such as a wrong face in a grave, as the mid-level clue that proves a death was faked or a person substituted. Why: A concrete fact the reader can check undercuts the official story more convincingly than an assertion.
- [pitfall] Treating an unexplained behavior as proof of guilt or innocence before testing it can mislead an investigation. When: When a suspect's action lacks an obvious explanation. Why: The behavior may have an innocent or unrelated cause that testing would reveal.
- [pitfall] Trusting stated constraints or a thorough search without testing them can let a false premise stand, and a search that reassures everyone may still miss the object.
- [pitfall] A weakly supported theory is easy to dismantle, and once the witness exposes it the questioner loses ground. When: When pressing a witness with an unverified theory. Why: A theory that fails under one question leaves the questioner with no further lines of pressure.
- [pitfall] Players who expect a supernatural reveal may dismiss ordinary clues, so ordinary clues must be specific enough to test. Why: Vague mundane clues cannot be checked and invite dismissal.
- [pitfall] Assuming a mechanism is silent or loud without testing it leads to false conclusions about who acted and when. When: Reasoning about a witness's sounds. Why: Mechanisms vary in noise and are easily misjudged from memory.
- [pitfall] An invented forensic method can serve as a story's internal logic, but it is not established science. Do not present it to players as real-world fact. When: writing in-world forensic or pseudoscientific methods. Why: Presenting fiction as fact misleads players and weakens the story's credibility when they check it.

## prop clues and usage
- [mechanism] A small flaw on a common object, such as a hole, can change meaning once the player knows an event occurred, turning damage into a trace of that event. When: the object is a familiar domestic item. Why: the event explains the flaw.
- [rule] Record a few concrete facts about a prop, such as its number, appearance, or price, so a later scene can check it. Why: Vague props cannot be tested or compared later.
- [rule] Give props a usage pattern such as wear, length or scent that players can compare across rooms to link items to NPCs.
- [rule] Place a mundane source such as an echo, draft or loose board in a room, so players can test it by acting with a clear result each time. When: Designing environmental sounds in a level. Why: Testable sources let players reason about the environment rather than accept a supernatural answer.
- [rule] Use props in a room to hint at a character's history, such as a poor room holding one rare object, giving the player a question to pursue. When: Designing environmental storytelling that implies a character's past. Why: A contradiction between setting and possessions prompts the player to investigate.
- [heuristic] Props in mid-use (half-finished meal, paused game) or moved/torn signal recent or past activity and who used the room, so players read them as evidence. When: Environmental storytelling. Why: Players read changed props as evidence of past events. (x2)
- [heuristic] A staged scene is unlikely to leave its props in full view, so ask why each object was arranged as it is.
- [pitfall] In a scene full of props, the important item is easily overlooked, so keep it visible but unremarkable. When: a key item sits among many objects. Why: crowding dilutes attention to any single item.
- [pitfall] A prop that copies a visible trait can itself expose the impostor, because the substituted detail may contradict the real person's record.
- [pitfall] A physical object offered as corroboration shows only that someone held it, not when or where the holder was. When: When a suspect offers an object to prove a claim.

## quest-giver and npc design
- [mechanism] Ending each segment at a point of interest postpones the outcome, because curiosity about the next part outweighs the urge to see the threat resolved.
- [rule] Require a second independent source before a strong quest-giver claim is accepted as fact, especially when the giver has an emotional stake. When: a biased NPC reacts strongly to a clue. Why: a single emotionally charged source may be wrong.
- [rule] A quest-giver who insists the player meet a victim elsewhere can serve as a timed lure that creates a witnessed alibi for them. When: designing quest-giver meeting places. Why: A fixed meeting place ties both locations and timing together.
- [rule] Let an errand NPC carry a note the player can follow or intercept, turning the delivery into a small investigation.
- [rule] Tie a rival's payout to a missing NPC's status staying unconfirmed so that the player learns the rival wants the body never found. When: When designing a quest where a rival's reward depends on an NPC's fate. Why: The conditional payout reveals the rival's preferred outcome to the player.
- [heuristic] A quest-giver can have the player held by a plausible official process, with a time limit and consequences for the investigation if the player does not act. When: when designing a timed quest. Why: A believable obstacle creates pressure without arbitrary rules.
- [heuristic] A quest-giver's body language can signal the quest type, letting a player calibrate expectations before the dialogue begins.
- [heuristic] Let a quest-giver's identity be revealed later, offering partial information at first and deferring the name until the player is ready.
- [heuristic] A quest giver who claims poverty while displaying wealth gives players a lead, discoverable through inventory, clothing or dialogue. When: Designing a quest giver whose stated situation can be checked.
- [heuristic] A secret request from an NPC can start a quest where the real stakes are found in a new location, even when the stated danger is minor. When: Starting a quest from an NPC summons. Why: The gap between stated and real stakes gives the player a reason to investigate.

## questioner bias
- [mechanism] A questioner who controls a subject's responses can shape what the subject appears to reveal, so the answers mirror the questioner's wishes. When: The subject is under suggestion or command. Why: A passive, compliant subject adopts the framing it is given.
- [behavior] An interviewee infers what an investigator suspects from the framing of the questions and uses that inference to judge how much danger they face. When: during an interrogation or interview. Why: Questions expose what the questioner already believes.
- [pitfall] Questions naming the accused and act before a witness speaks make answers echo the wording; a questioner's bias can steer questions so commitments reflect framing, not real views. (x2)
- [pitfall] A questioner's assumptions shape how an ambiguous phrase is read and every follow-up; a single phrase can be misread as proof of a hidden relationship. When: a witness's wording is open to more than one reading. Why: the listener's expectation selects one reading.
- [pitfall] An interrogator's curiosity can override caution, leading them to push a reluctant witness too hard.
- [pitfall] A questioner's dislike of a witness can colour the questions, so the interviewer should set aside personal distaste.
- [pitfall] A motive drawn from an earlier question can be an artifact of how the question was asked, not evidence of intent.
- [pitfall] A questioner's own uncertainty can leak through in remarks and tone, signalling the gap in their knowledge to the target.
- [pitfall] A witness can assume an investigator's questions come from a personal motive, such as romantic interest, and answer according to that assumption rather than the stated purpose. When: An investigator's visible feelings or relationships are plausible grounds for a wrong theory. Why: A plausible alternative motive closes off the true line of questioning.
- [pitfall] An interrogator who has already settled on an answer hears only what confirms it, missing contrary details. When: Questioning a witness with a fixed view. Why: Prior conclusions filter what the questioner notices.

## reasoning and proof weighing
- [behavior] A remark implying that someone lacks full knowledge hints at a hidden fact without stating it.
- [rule] Have an in-world listener voice disbelief at implausible claims, so the player is alerted to doubt without the designer stating it outright. When: A claim in the story is meant to be questioned. Why: A character's reaction signals doubt more naturally than narration does.
- [rule] When an in-world authority judges a player's case, weight dated, signed records above the player's inferred reasoning. When: designing judgement scenes. Why: authorities trust records over inference.
- [rule] Weigh an explanation honestly to decide which way the probabilities fall, rather than building a case against the speaker.
- [rule] Separate what is implied from what is proven, and do not rely on implied warnings where a mystery's fairness requires the fact to be stated plainly. When: when writing clues for a mystery. Why: implication alone cannot support a fair solution.
- [rule] Let one suspect's confession implicate another only when a second, independent clue confirms it. When: Designing multi-suspect accusation systems. Why: A second clue stops a single claim from carrying two people to judgment.
- [heuristic] When every route to a conclusion is closed, re-examine the witness accounts behind the eliminations rather than accept an impossible result. When: Every possible explanation has been eliminated.
- [heuristic] If an argument would prove too much in either direction, the inference has been stretched beyond what the fact supports. When: Evaluating whether a clue supports a conclusion. Why: A reasoning pattern that supports any outcome carries no discriminating weight.
- [procedure] 1) List every claim each proposed solution makes. 2) Check each claim against fixed facts and later sources. 3) Credit the true claims. 4) Build one account that keeps all true claims and drops the false ones. When: ending a mystery where players have proposed competing solutions. Why: Partly correct theories reward attention across the whole session, not just one decisive clue.
- [pitfall] Benefit to one party does not prove that party arranged the scheme; the beneficiary and the arranger can be different people. When: Assigning responsibility for an arranged outcome. Why: Gain and control over events are separate facts that must each be shown.

## recurring characters and motifs
- [model] A recurring formula pursues a respectable protagonist with a threat visible only to them, presented as a case file carrying an editor's disclaimer.
- [model] A sequence of self-contained cases can share one engine: a premise, a set of unexplained clues, a plausible official theory, and a late reveal that reframes those clues. When: Designing an episodic mystery collection with closed cases. Why: A repeated structure gives players a predictable rhythm while each case uses a different mechanism for its solution.
- [mechanism] A recurring signature, such as a repeated mark or item, can connect separate quest events and reward a player who notices it. When: In quest design with multiple related events. Why: Players who spot a repeated detail gain a connection that makes later events meaningful.
- [behavior] Readers infer romance or grief from surface cues; when a hidden identity is revealed, these inferred feelings reverse and earlier scenes are reinterpreted. When: A character's apparent emotional bond is shown to belong to a disguised or concealed identity. Why: Readers take emotional cues at face value until a reveal reframes them.
- [rule] Give recurring characters and suspects a distinctive trait, such as a habit or vanity, stated early and repeated, so it persists through disguise and players can recognise them later. When: Designing a recurring character, suspect, or disguised character that players must recognise later. Why: Persistent traits give players a way to recognize the character.
- [rule] Repeat an NPC's song or phrase later as a cue that links back to the earlier encounter.
- [heuristic] Fragments that repeat unchanged across different mental states can signal a true motive, making them a useful hook for a designed secret. When: Scripting an NPC's recurring words across dialogue states. Why: A repeated fragment reads as a stable underlying motive rather than a random slip.
- [heuristic] Give a recurring NPC a stated reason and an observable tell, so the player can test the reason with a question and presence itself becomes a clue. When: Designing an NPC who appears repeatedly. Why: Repeated appearances invite suspicion, and a testable reason turns that suspicion into play.
- [heuristic] Make the protagonist a pawn: reversing who profits at the end recasts the earlier success as a trap. When: in a twist ending where the gain turns out to be worthless.
- [pitfall] Assuming every missed chance is permanent can cause panic and rash action, while assuming a criminal's error is always final overlooks evidence lost to time or to the criminal's own care. When: Judging whether a missed opportunity can be recovered. Why: Most missed moments are not final, but evidence can still disappear.

## refusal and rejection of claims
- [behavior] When a learned person produces unexplained results, the public may treat them as magic and refuse natural explanations. When: when a skilled person's results lack a familiar explanation. Why: The accepted framework offers no natural account the public will accept.
- [rule] If a suspect refuses to talk, move to a formal step such as seeking a warrant rather than continuing to press. When: a suspect declines to answer. Why: Pressing a refusing suspect yields no account; formal authority is the next source of evidence.
- [rule] Give a rejected NPC a reason to act against the winning faction, and reveal that grievance through diaries or letters. When: designing an NPC who lost a contest.
- [heuristic] A pointed reply can reject an excuse without refuting it, which keeps the claim open for later testing. When: a character offers an explanation that cannot yet be checked. Why: Doubt can be voiced while the evidence remains incomplete.
- [heuristic] A rejected account may still preserve useful details, so keep it separate from the findings that were accepted.
- [tradeoff] Refusing inspection or a decoy reads as concealment, a cost in itself, to those expecting examination, but as principled skepticism when the stated stance explains it; prepare a plausible reason. When: A staged condition invites inspection. Why: Audiences read refusals through the character's stated stance; those expecting examination read them as concealment. (x2)
- [tradeoff] A defendant who refuses to plead can stop a trial and freeze its legal effects, but the refusal may be read as defiance or confession and bring harsher treatment. When: A character must choose between entering a broken process and protecting something of value by refusing to enter it. Why: Refusal blocks the process but invites punishment, since the authority may read silence as guilt or defiance.
- [pitfall] Dismissing a supernatural or folk reading shows only that it is doubtful, not that a mundane origin is true; an early hunch still needs testing. When: Evaluating a hunch that seems to solve a mystery. Why: Rejecting one story does not confirm another.
- [pitfall] Rejecting a conclusion because it seems improbable can lead a detective to dismiss the correct answer.
- [pitfall] Treating a refusal to explain conduct as proof of conspiracy can convict an innocent person. When: A suspect withholds an explanation. Why: Secrecy has many innocent causes and does not establish guilt.

## release of suspects
- [mechanism] A key set on a table with the holder's back turned releases a captive without any spoken permission.
- [mechanism] A suspect discharged for lack of proof can be arrested again while public spite against them remains unsatisfied. When: when a discharged suspect is still widely disliked. Why: the community's grievance outlasts the lack of evidence.
- [rule] Track the consequences of a release, such as the thief reappearing or the origin of the stolen items, so the choice has lasting effects.
- [rule] When an alibi holds, release the suspect and reconsider the case rather than continuing to pursue a person who has been cleared.
- [heuristic] Releasing a suspect while secretly tracking their movements and searching their rooms can expose associates, since the freed suspect may report success to the group. When: A suspect is believed to belong to a network and is released under surveillance. Why: Relief and perceived freedom lead to contact with associates.
- [heuristic] A confessor who is later released hints at a real role the player can investigate.
- [tradeoff] A clever suspect may recognise release as bait and refuse to act, leaving the investigation without leverage, whereas hardship may still push him to act. When: Planning a controlled release. Why: Awareness of the trap weighs against the pressure of need.
- [tradeoff] Releasing a weakly supported suspect and tailing them may expose guilt, but the plan depends on the suspect becoming careless, which may not happen. When: Deciding whether to release and surveil a suspect. Why: Surveillance gains depend on the suspect's behavior.
- [pitfall] Release may need a stated payoff to be approved; without one it is hard to justify.
- [pitfall] A release can look as if the investigator is shielding the guilty party, which makes the outcome seem unjust to observers.

## returning to scenes and witnesses
- [mechanism] Having the culprit return to the death site can trigger a clue when the player is nearby, rewarding a revisit. When: A culprit may revisit the crime location in a game. Why: A returning culprit exposes evidence to a player who is present.
- [rule] When a player re-enters a level after a failed encounter, present earlier events as a chronological journal so they can reconstruct what happened. When: player returns after a failed encounter. Why: an ordered record lets the player understand the failure and plan the next action.
- [rule] Give players a reason to return to a location or person to receive a withheld item, which can drive a second visit. When: Designing a story that needs players to return to a place. Why: A deferred reward gives players a purpose for returning.
- [rule] State any return condition aloud during the transfer so both parties can later be held to it. When: When an object is lent or passed on with conditions. Why: Spoken terms heard by a witness gain a status that can be cited later.
- [rule] A returning NPC whose face is familiar from an earlier scene can prompt the player to recall the link. When: designing recurring characters. Why: familiar appearance triggers recall of earlier context.
- [rule] Revisit a planted casual detail later, because a detail never returned to leaves the player no way to recover its importance. When: Planting a clue that should matter later. Why: Players can only connect a clue when it is raised again.
- [rule] Give a returning NPC partial amnesia and an old cloak or emblem that matches a portrait found elsewhere, so the player can recognize them. When: Designing a character the player meets again after an earlier encounter. Why: A matching visual clue lets players connect the NPC to lore they have already discovered.
- [heuristic] A returning absent witness can test earlier accounts of who was where, turning their return into a check on other testimony. Why: Their location during the event can contradict or confirm what others said.
- [procedure] 1) Note the exact date of the event. 2) Revisit places linked to it, such as graves or memorials. 3) Check who is present there and why. When: when an investigator revisits a place connected to a crime. Why: Places tied to an event can draw the people connected to it.
- [pitfall] A visit to the scene is not proof of guilt, since a curious visitor may simply be trying to make sense of their own feelings.

## rivalry
- [definition] Common fame is general reputation used as grounds for an accusation, alongside sworn testimony.
- [behavior] Factions may choose committee members precisely so the opposing party's influence cannot sway decisions. When: a committee is contested between factions. Why: Control of decisions is the goal of the selection.
- [behavior] A refused favour or trade between neighbours can later be recorded as part of a grievance and used in a serious charge against the refuser. When: when a community has small quarrels before a serious accusation. Why: Earlier friction gives later suspicion a ready motive.
- [behavior] Illness or harm striking several neighbors at once can be blamed on one invisible agent. When: Several people in a community fall ill or suffer harm together.
- [behavior] Accusers are often neighbors with a stake in the accused's land, livestock, debts or reputation, so accusations cluster around existing local disputes. When: In small communities where resources are shared or contested. Why: Shared boundaries, animals and insults create quarrels that witnesses then act on.
- [rule] Do not confront a watcher in public, because a public scene gives the opposing side a legal or social pretext. When: Discovering a tail.
- [heuristic] Rivalry often runs along several axes at once, such as romance and status, so separate the axes to learn which one drove an action.
- [heuristic] Households beside a dispute's origin are often where an affair begins, so check neighbour proximity when tracing a charge. When: when tracing where an accusation started. Why: nearby households share the dispute and its witnesses.
- [pitfall] Common everyday goods, such as a widely sold brand, do not identify anyone, so they should not be used to name a person.
- [fact] Committee and seating assignments can reveal rivals linked by family, marriage and land.

## safe confession and questioning
- [mechanism] When confession promises safety, accused people may confess to many crimes to secure it. When: confession is offered as a way out. Why: the promised safety outweighs the cost of false admissions.
- [behavior] A person may falsely confess to a killing to protect another, and the confession can be exposed by checking the objects the confessor claims to have used. When: A confession seems to close a case too easily. Why: The confessor's claimed actions may not match the physical evidence.
- [rule] When a suspect is about to harm themselves, switch from questioning to protecting life.
- [rule] Design suspect tests so they cannot harm innocent people.
- [rule] Grant a reprieve where a judge doubts a verdict, and grant bail to anyone accused only through unverifiable testimony.
- [heuristic] Design a lure so that a wrong guess about the target only leads them to think the notice rested on a misleading detail, without exposing the investigation. When: the investigator is unsure of the target's knowledge. Why: a failed lure should cost the investigator nothing.
- [heuristic] Check which party a proposed safeguard disadvantages; a restraint that removes the subject's means of escape serves the proposer, not the safety it claims. When: A test or condition is proposed as a precaution. Why: Precautions can hide an attack on the person they supposedly protect.
- [heuristic] A vague but plausible official statement can reassure the public while committing the source to very little. When: when an authority must say something before facts are settled. Why: Limited commitment keeps the source flexible as the facts develop.
- [procedure] 1) Control the suspect's hands and pin the arms before any search. 2) Withdraw the arm from a pocket slowly. 3) Check the outside of the pocket before reaching in. When: Searching a suspect who may be armed or may struggle. Why: A restrained suspect cannot strike quickly, and checking the exterior first reduces the risk of a hidden weapon.
- [pitfall] Sarcasm can invite a witness to explain in full, leaving the questioner embarrassed.

## search and record checks
- [model] A search-driven reveal has four parts: a question, a misleading visible marker, a convincing inference, and a closing record that restores trust in the conclusion.
- [rule] A search should cover everyone equally, including the most senior people, and should not begin unless it can be completed for all. When: An inquiry requires checking the belongings or rooms of many people. Why: A partial search is perceived as unfair and invites suspicion.
- [heuristic] Record dates precisely so that intervals between events can be calculated. Why: interval arithmetic depends on exact dates.
- [heuristic] Track which open questions lack supporting evidence, so players know to search new areas rather than rereading old notes.
- [heuristic] Before treating a physical search as proof, ask who searched, when, and what they expected to find. When: A physical search is offered as proof of guilt or identity. Why: Expectations and timing shape what searchers report.
- [pitfall] An empty search does not prove a fact never existed or that someone is innocent, since records or evidence may have been destroyed or removed beforehand. When: when records may have been disturbed or a suspect's premises are searched and find nothing. Why: Destroyed or removed evidence leaves nothing to find, so negative results are weak evidence.
- [pitfall] Searching an exposed scene later may find nothing, which wrongly suggests nothing happened there. Why: Erasure removes the physical trace, not the event that caused it.
- [pitfall] Skimming an object misses hidden evidence, which is found only by checking every leaf or surface. When: An investigator searches a book or similar object. Why: Evidence hidden inside an object is only reached by a complete search.
- [fact] An empty search can still confirm the hypothesis being tested when that hypothesis predicted the location would be empty.
- [fact] Court files covering wills, contracts, boundaries and slander show ordinary relations between neighbors, not only crimes. When: when reconstructing a community from records. Why: daily disputes were recorded alongside serious offenses.

## second witness and observer
- [mechanism] A second person who holds a damaging secret becomes as dangerous to the culprit as the first holder, so the culprit may act against them too. When: Someone else besides the culprit knows the hidden past. Why: Exposure threatens the culprit whoever reveals it.
- [mechanism] A second character entering a stalemate can produce a confession the first refused to give, especially when they claim responsibility to shield the other. When: when two characters are protecting each other.
- [mechanism] A perpetrator who joins a crowd in a public place after an act can be seen there, creating a second alibi for the same night.
- [rule] Keep questioning while a second observer watches the subject, since the questioner alone can miss tells that the observer catches.
- [heuristic] Treat objects arranged too neatly as a sign of staging by a non-thief, and give players reason to suspect it as a second deduction layer. When: items look placed rather than dropped, or a scene's evidence is suspiciously complete. Why: Orderly placement signals a different cause from the obvious one, and noticing the staging is a deduction in its own right.
- [heuristic] A grammatical slip, such as a plural written in singular form, can reveal that a second person wrote the note.
- [heuristic] Have a second independent witness inspect the same mark, because a witness may confirm a mark simply because they expect to.
- [heuristic] A second questioner can ask about a topic nobody covered, such as clothing, and surface details the first pass missed. When: A first round of questioning has finished without a full description. Why: Different questions open different lines of recall.
- [pitfall] A second round of questioning can make a witness look guilty through tone and position rather than through evidence.
- [pitfall] A satisfying explanation for one anomaly can hide a second, more serious one that the first does not account for. When: Resolving an apparent puzzle with a plausible answer. Why: Closure on the first anomaly reduces scrutiny of the rest.

## secrets and withheld knowledge
- [mechanism] When a character reads part of a secret decision, such as a document, they may draw a plausible but wrong conclusion about its motive, creating suspense for an audience who knows more. When: A hidden decision is partly visible to a character. Why: Partial information yields a guess shaped by the character's own interests.
- [mechanism] A group that agrees on a shared fiction can hide real beliefs from one another, with both sides knowing the fiction without either stating it. When: Members of a group maintain a comforting pretence about a loss or uncertain event. Why: Unspoken agreement lets a fiction persist while private beliefs diverge from it.
- [behavior] A character may withhold evidence when delivering it would cancel an advantage they hope to gain, treating silence as a tradable good. When: Evidence would undo a benefit the holder is pursuing. Why: Holders weigh disclosure against the value they expect from keeping it hidden.
- [rule] Resolve every withheld matter eventually, since unanswered gaps frustrate rather than engage the audience.
- [heuristic] Ask what a suspect knew about a key fact, and treat a silence on that point as a meaningful clue. When: A suspect avoids a topic central to the case. Why: Omission on a relevant point can indicate knowledge or concealment.
- [heuristic] Make the protagonist's self-deception the obstacle, and let the reveal rest on contradictory physical evidence the protagonist must confront.
- [procedure] 1) Give the hidden stash or secret room a backstory. 2) Link an NPC's personal loss to the device guarding it. 3) Let the player discover the backstory through the old lore and a newer private use. When: Designing a secret room or stash in a level. Why: Lore-based discovery makes the guarded object meaningful and the mechanism believable.
- [pitfall] Telling a witness too much about the investigation can cause a leak, so keep the real plan from anyone who might blurt it out. When: When a witness is connected to the suspect or the crime. Why: Careless talk alerts the culprit and destroys the element of surprise.
- [pitfall] A routine can also hide things, because an actor who blends into the pattern is harder to notice. When: when a character's behaviour fits the expected pattern. Why: Expected activity draws less scrutiny than unusual activity.
- [pitfall] An official who refuses to disclose a source should be treated as information in itself. When: When an official withholds the origin of a fact. Why: The refusal narrows what can be known and signals that a source exists.

## servant witnesses
- [mechanism] Routine tidying by household staff carries a dropped item through the household toward its intended reader.
- [behavior] Servants or others who share a secret tend to look away and give short answers, and their silence is itself a signal to investigate. When: When a group of witnesses is questioned about a shared secret. Why: Shared secrets create coordinated reticence.
- [rule] Have household NPCs remark on a suspect's changed behaviour or routine, giving timed clues and early unease before the cause is known. When: designing household NPC dialogue or seeding early unease in a setting.
- [rule] Question household members separately, since slightly different accounts of an absence can expose a false alibi. When: checking an alibi through servants.
- [rule] Treat staff who served throughout as witnesses and assess how reliable each one is. When: Staff handled or served the food. Why: Their accounts are evidence, but only as trustworthy as their observation.
- [rule] Place low-status NPCs as witnesses who saw more than the powerful suspected, rewarding players who talk to them.
- [heuristic] Remarks from people who serve the occupant, such as a landlady on payment and meals, add a second layer of testimony on their habits.
- [heuristic] Question the servants of a likely recipient, since a servant who sees an object can recognise it or react, confirming the link.
- [heuristic] A household servant's memory of who called and when gives an independent check on residents' accounts of their visitors. When: A household has its own record of visitors.
- [fact] Gossip from servants or doormen can reveal a hidden routine, such as a secret exit used at night. When: checking a suspect's movements. Why: staff observe habits the investigator cannot see.

## staged crime design
- [model] A staged-crime mystery moves through disappearance, a charge against a suspect, misdirection, a confession that splits suspect from threat, and a reversal.
- [mechanism] A culprit can arrange a scene, with a false identity, disguised body and fake records, so inspection finds nothing damning or points at someone else. When: A scene must be read as a false story. Why: Each prepared element is built to survive examination.
- [mechanism] A cause of death or harm that matches a recognised natural pattern can pass examination, because examiners compare signs against known natural causes. When: The apparent cause is strong and the physical signs match a natural event. Why: Examiners read the body against familiar patterns, so a plausible match can hide a planned act.
- [behavior] A thief may rely on the owner not needing a taken item for a short while, so the absence goes unnoticed for a time. When: When an item is taken from a place where the owner is unlikely to check soon. Why: Delayed need for an item delays discovery of its theft.
- [rule] Display stolen items in an odd arrangement and have a note mark the arrangement as meaningful so the player must decode it. When: when designing staged-scene puzzles.
- [heuristic] Give the first suspect a plausible prop, such as a weapon or piece of jewelry, that later reads as staged, so the framing becomes visible in hindsight. When: designing a red-herring suspect. Why: A prop that seems incriminating early can later show the scene was arranged.
- [heuristic] Test an outsider-thief theory against insiders' gains, since a theft can be staged by beneficiaries using a fake loss. When: A theft appears to be committed by an outsider. Why: Staged crimes benefit someone inside the circle, which outsider theories ignore.
- [procedure] 1) Announce the newcomer through a letter or rumour. 2) Delay the arrival with weather or a timed event. 3) Let the wait build tension. 4) Reveal the character at the arrival. When: a new character should be surrounded by expectation before being seen. Why: Alternating waiting and arrival makes tension rise before the meeting.
- [procedure] 1) Keep the suspect engaged in conversation to hold their attention. 2) Have a second person search their belongings. 3) Accept that a failed search costs the investigator standing. When: Circumstantial evidence points to hidden papers and the suspect can be kept occupied. Why: Divided attention prevents the suspect from interfering while the search proceeds.
- [procedure] 1) List every strange occurrence from the outcome. 2) For each, ask who could have produced it. 3) Check the means, opportunity and access for that person. 4) Keep items that resist every explanation separate and state them plainly. When: When an event looks supernatural and a concealed human action is suspected. Why: Testing each anomaly item by item shows which ones have ordinary mechanisms.

## staged story reveals
- [model] Many closed-world mysteries build a sensational frame, let a false solution hold, then reread one visible detail to show the frame was a staged performance. Why: The frame looks real until a known object is reinterpreted.
- [definition] A staged haunting is an apparently supernatural event that a living person produces using hidden passages, dummies, sound and misdirection, usually revealed late in the scenario.
- [mechanism] Revelations released in staged installments, each holding back its meaning, build suspense and make the audience wait for the payoff. When: Structuring clue delivery over time. Why: Partial information creates anticipation that a single reveal would not.
- [mechanism] Presenting the outcome before the mechanism, and letting the audience ask how it works, keeps curiosity alive and makes the eventual explanation feel like an answer. When: A story or puzzle where the audience should share uncertainty before the answer. Why: Delaying the explanation sustains interest while the audience is still wondering how the outcome happened.
- [mechanism] A staged death of a protected character exploits the player's assumption of safety, creating false tension until the false face is exposed.
- [heuristic] Use a staged rescue as an entry ticket: a role that places the protagonist inside the target works better than a direct approach. When: when the protagonist must reach a guarded target. Why: an insider role provides access the protagonist could not gain directly.
- [procedure] 1) Describe general character. 2) Name past events the subject confirms. 3) Reveal a sensitive event written privately rather than spoken aloud. When: Staging an apparently uncanny reading. Why: Building trust with confirmed facts before the sensitive reveal makes the final claim persuasive.
- [procedure] 1) Deliver the reversal first by a written message. 2) Follow with an in-person meeting that expands it. Staging the shock softens its impact and prolongs it. When: a major reveal overturns the protagonist's understanding. Why: sequencing the news in stages makes the shock register in layers.
- [procedure] 1) Show a recurring vision or dream early. 2) Repeat it with one new detail each time. 3) Continue until the player understands the threat. When: when a threat should be revealed gradually through recurrence. Why: Incremental detail builds understanding without an upfront explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Give a general principle first. 2) Only then apply it to a specific target. 3) Share only what each listener needs to stay calm and cooperative. When: Presenting a theory to a listener who must act on it. Why: A general principle builds understanding before specific accusations, reducing reactive mistakes.

## suspense and speculation
- [behavior] An unread document can be given any meaning readers want, so its unknown contents fuel speculation. When: A sealed document's contents are withheld from everyone. Why: Without the actual content, imagination fills the gap.
- [behavior] Audiences guess at causes when the true reason is hidden; offering two or three plausible wrong explanations before the true one sustains speculation. When: a key cause is withheld. Why: each wrong guess is tested and keeps the true answer open.
- [heuristic] Treat motive inferred from relationships and circumstances as speculative until it is tested against known facts.
- [heuristic] Treat a theory that needs a special exception, such as a surname used as a first name, with suspicion.
- [heuristic] Warn the audience that the outcome may differ from expectation, so the eventual reveal is read as deduction rather than trickery.
- [pitfall] Public speculation can outrun proof: a seemingly settled case may rest on one unverified lead, and early conclusions spread by public reports harden before evidence is checked. When: When public opinion has formed around a suspect. Why: Repetition and sensational framing create confidence that outpaces the evidence.
- [pitfall] Presenting a theory as idle speculation when it is a direct accusation leaves the audience unsure what it means.
- [pitfall] Speculation that a death was an accident or a plan is often wishful or spiteful; treat it as a lead to test, not a fact. When: when a third party raises a suspicion about a death.
- [pitfall] Speculating about side details without evidence, such as rumoured honours or status, adds noise and weakens the main inference. When: building a motive from gossip or hearsay. Why: unsupported details can crowd out the evidence that matters.
- [fact] Suspense can come from clocks, departures and late arrivals, each of which sets a window in which a scene's outcome is decided.

## time and alibi recall
- [mechanism] Routine activities anchor memory, so each small remembered event prompts the next and the sequence of a day can be rebuilt from them. When: Reconstructing a timeline from an ordinary witness's account. Why: Each routine task serves as a cue for the following event.
- [behavior] A character recalling a triggered memory may be unsure whether it is distant or recent and may doubt being awake, so content returns without a reliable date. When: A character with a confused sense of time recalls an event through a cue. Why: Impaired orientation in time weakens the sense of when an event occurred.
- [behavior] A person who wakes instantly from deep sleep may misjudge how long they slept, leaving an unaccounted gap in their timeline. When: when a witness recounts waking from deep sleep. Why: Deep sleep erases time awareness, so the sleeper's estimate is uncertain.
- [heuristic] Durations and approximate times recalled from memory are estimates; use ranges with a margin for error and do not treat exact ordering as certain when building a timeline. When: Building a timeline from remembered durations or approximate witness times. Why: Memory of elapsed time is imprecise; loose times can reverse or blur the order of events. (x2)
- [heuristic] A family's recollection of an object's age gives only a rough date, so treat it as an approximate dating clue. When: An object's age is estimated from memory. Why: Memories are imprecise and cannot fix an exact date.
- [heuristic] When a blackout or cutscene hides time, let players rebuild the gap from light, clocks or sounds.
- [procedure] 1) Find when the material was applied. 2) Add its drying time to find when it set. 3) Note when the mark was first seen. 4) Limit the mark to the interval when the material was still wet. When: a small mark might fix when someone was present.
- [procedure] 1) Pick the moment the alibis depend on. 2) Re-establish each suspect's location from that moment forward. 3) Measure each suspect's distance to the scene. 4) Compare realistic travel time against the available window. When: earlier alibis are vague or one event fixes the time of the crime. Why: a shared anchor makes every suspect's timeline comparable.
- [pitfall] A witness's memory may be anchored to a routine that changed that day, misleading the timeline. Why: Recalled routines are assumed normal and may not match the actual day.
- [pitfall] Times reconstructed from memory can shift under stress, so exact times need an independent source. When: Building a timeline from witness recollections. Why: Stress distorts recall of durations and sequences.

## weak link analysis
- [mechanism] A defence can discredit a whole inference chain by finding its one thin or unexplained point and casting doubt on everything built on it. When: a case relies on a chain of reasoning. Why: sceptics judge the chain by its weakest link.
- [rule] Give a faked death a visible weak point, such as a body mismatch or a witness, so a careful player can expose it. When: designing a staged death in a story or world. Why: a fair weak point rewards careful players without making the fake obvious.
- [heuristic] Every concealment plan has a weak point, often a post-event step that invites suspicion; without direct evidence, look there for the culprit's gap. Why: plans have logical gaps. (x2)
- [heuristic] Test a reconstruction against its weakest point, meaning the single detail it explains worst. If that point fails, the account is incomplete. When: A reconstruction fits most facts but leaves one contradiction. Why: One unexplained detail can overturn an otherwise tidy story.
- [heuristic] Focus on the moment a victim becomes vulnerable, such as during exhaustion, rather than on the device used, because that moment reveals the real opening. When: analyzing how a defended target was reached. Why: focusing on the device hides the opening.
- [heuristic] A case checklist is only as strong as its weakest entry, so a missing element such as an unrecovered weapon leaves a visible gap. When: When assessing an accusation against a checklist. Why: One unfilled element can invalidate the whole case.
- [heuristic] Label a hypothesis that rests only on one interested party's suspicion as weak, even while still pursuing it. Why: Honest labelling prevents a thin lead from being treated as established.
- [pitfall] A reconstructed chain is only as strong as its weakest link, so check each link; a step without an observed cue is a guess that breaks the inference. Why: a plausible whole can hide one unanchored step.
- [pitfall] A chain that reads as complete can hide a weak link, so each step needs independent checking rather than repeated reading of one document. When: when a single written source supports several steps. Why: Re-reading one source confirms its claims, not their independent truth.
- [pitfall] Weak links accumulated together do not automatically form a strong chain. When: When many small pieces of evidence point to one suspect. Why: Quantity of weak evidence does not raise its quality.

## witness interviews and evasion
