- [behavior] A questioner who is emotionally attached to a distressed witness often drops a pressing question and turns to comfort, so the witness's distress can end the questioning. When: The questioner cares about the witness and the answer matters to the case. Why: Affection pulls the questioner's attention from the question to the witness's well-being.
- [behavior] A suspect who turns suddenly polite and guarded is often sensing pressure, so a sharp change in courtesy signals that scrutiny is building. When: A suspect becomes aware of an investigation. Why: Guarded courtesy often masks awareness of pressure.
- [behavior] Distressed, grieving or dazed witnesses often have trouble with time and sequence, so a single account from them may be unreliable. When: A witness is emotionally shaken or confused. Why: Strong emotion disrupts memory of order and timing.
- [heuristic] Appearing inattentive lets an observer take in more than those around them. When: Visual evidence is blocked or the observer wants to stay unnoticed.
- [procedure] 1) Ask permission before raising a delicate matter. 2) Start with a neutral past fact the suspect can confirm. 3) Get a clear answer before linking it to the present event. 4) Corroborate the fact with a third-party source. 5) Present the theory in steps, checking each with a short question. 6) Watch the suspect's expression throughout. 7) Rule out frightening alternatives to calm the suspect. When: Questioning a vulnerable or sympathetic suspect when information matters more than confrontation. Why: Gentle, step-by-step questioning gathers information without alarming the suspect.
- [procedure] 1) Start with indirect or harmless questions. 2) Raise a specific claim as a test. 3) Note whether the witness accepts, rejects, or challenges it. 4) Escalate to pointed questions only as the witness reveals defensive moves. When: When questioning a reluctant witness who will not volunteer facts. Why: Staged pressure reveals defensive reactions, which yield partial admissions rather than full confessions.
- [procedure] 1) Let the witness finish without interrupting. 2) Tell them their account is what is needed. 3) Once they calm, ask practical questions about location and expenses. 4) Only then ask harder questions, promising they will be believed. When: when a witness is angry, grieving or frightened but key facts are needed. Why: Letting emotion pass keeps the account coherent and encourages a fuller telling.
- [tradeoff] Gentle questioning gathers information with less alarm but may yield only partial agreement, while confrontation risks defensiveness. When: Choosing an approach for a suspect. Why: Each approach has costs in what it reveals and how the suspect reacts.
- [pitfall] Emotional display, such as distress or appeals to feeling, can hide the truth or serve to avoid answering, so emotion must be separated from content. When: A witness becomes emotional during questioning. Why: Emotional display can obscure what is actually said.
- [fact] A witness can give many words and promises yet reveal very little, so an investigator should judge what is actually disclosed, not how much is said.

## witness pressure response
- [mechanism] A witness glimpsed just before a reveal adds pressure without new information, reminding the audience that someone is watching. When: A reveal is about to happen with an observer nearby. Why: Visible observation raises stakes without adding facts.
- [behavior] Rapid, sustained questions on specific checkable details can break a witness's composure faster than attacks on the witness's character. When: a witness is questioned in quick succession on narrow points. Why: specific gaps are harder to defend than general credibility.
- [behavior] Emotional distress can cause an evasive witness to end questioning, leaving a contradiction unresolved. When: A witness is pressed on a weak point. Why: Distress shifts the witness's response from answering to withdrawing.
- [rule] Make intimidating a witness in a pending case a serious offense, with the most severe penalty when the case involves a life. When: when designing a court or witness system. Why: Threats against witnesses corrupt testimony before a verdict.
- [heuristic] A witness who suddenly goes quiet or looks frightened after a conversation may be under pressure rather than simply reticent. When: interviewing a witness who has just spoken with another party. Why: A sudden change in manner often follows an intimidating exchange.
- [procedure] 1) Use a direct light or controlled setting to unsettle the witness. 2) Ask a sudden, pointed question. 3) Watch the mouth and hands rather than the eyes for reactions. When: Questioning an evasive witness. Why: Mouth and hand movements are harder to control than gaze.
- [tradeoff] Pressing an evasive witness can open up partial knowledge, but pressing one with nothing to give tends to harden them. When: when deciding how hard to press a witness. Why: pressure only helps when the witness is holding something back.
- [pitfall] Even a witness of good character may be pressured into silence or changed testimony by fear. When: When a witness has reason to fear consequences. Why: Fear overrides character in shaping what is reported.
- [pitfall] Pressing a volatile witness at close range raises the interviewer's fear sharply and can turn the interview hostile. When: A witness reacts strongly and is physically close. Why: Close proximity to an agitated person escalates threat and fear.
- [fact] A legal hold on a witness can be challenged within about forty-eight hours, so investigators cannot keep a witness held indefinitely. When: the legal system allows a rapid challenge to a material-witness hold.

## accused responses
- [behavior] Pressured suspects discredit the accuser: framing the accusation as mental illness, turning the accuser's intellect against them, or calling the investigator mad and threatening confinement. When: when a plain accusation lacks a prepared answer to a rival explanation, or when the suspect is confronted with strong evidence. Why: Discrediting the accuser contests the case without answering it; a prepared alternative frame can move the conversation even if not fully accepted; the threat can visibly unsettle the investigator.
- [behavior] A suspect's visible reaction, such as a drained colour, is read before any dialogue, so it works as a clue in its own right. When: the accused is named in front of others.
- [behavior] An accused person under pressure may name others, sometimes out of concern for the other's soul, and such accusations can seal a co-accused's conviction. When: when a confession includes accusations against family or associates. Why: the confession's accusatory content carries weight in the proceedings even when its origin is pressure.
- [behavior] Accused people may answer with lawsuits, and a counter-suit can be read as proof of innocence or as a way to hide guilt. When: when an accused person sues an accuser or a witness. Why: the same act can signal either innocence or an attempt to shift suspicion.
- [behavior] Under confrontation, a suspect typically denies the facts, appeals to the investigator's right to question, or breaks down emotionally, rather than confessing. When: when shown evidence that contradicts their account. Why: Pressure first produces defensiveness and distress; admission is not the usual immediate response.
- [behavior] An accused person's own defensive or self-damaging remarks, such as a wish to be tested, are recorded and read as evidence against them. When: an accused character speaks during an investigation. Why: the listener interprets speech through the existing accusation.
- [heuristic] An accused person who refuses a verdict can be read by the deciding authority as more guilty, so defiance adds pressure while damaging her own case. When: a character is pressed to accept a judgment. Why: refusal is taken as a sign of guilt by those deciding the case.
- [pitfall] Every response from an accused person, including denial, calm, eye movement or head shaking, can be read as guilt, so no response can exonerate.
- [pitfall] An accused person who names others may be trading accusations for a reprieve, so every name carries its own motive.

## baseline and basic checks
- [mechanism] A control sample gives a baseline, so a reaction in a test sample means something and false exoneration or false accusation becomes less likely.
- [rule] Check a suspect's basic facts, such as finances, shared profits, spending and character, before accepting their guilt. When: A suspect is under pursuit. Why: Neglected basic facts let a wrong explanation survive.
- [rule] Record a starting count of a small countable item before it changes hands, so later disputes about it can be tested. When: A countable item is central to a suspicion. Why: A fixed agreed number turns a claim of loss into a checkable fact.
- [heuristic] Ask concrete questions about food and drink; the answers show how long a captive was held and whether the account fits the known facts.
- [heuristic] Judge whether a behaviour was unusual only against a baseline of the person's normal habits, such as usual drinking or seating.
- [heuristic] Compare an object's current state with its known earlier state. The difference between two observations can be the clue. When: when a scene's objects have a known or recalled earlier state. Why: A change is only visible against a baseline.
- [heuristic] Compare a found object with the victim's own belongings; a mismatch lets that object be excluded as theirs.
- [procedure] 1) Speak close to the patient's ear. 2) Press the patient's hand. 3) Lift an eyelid. If there is no reaction, the patient cannot yet give testimony. When: before relying on a bedside statement. Why: Testimony needs a responsive witness.
- [procedure] 1) Find the sign that looks like evidence. 2) Survey how often the same sign occurs naturally in the area. 3) Treat the sign as meaningful only if it is unusual compared with that baseline. When: a sign such as a broken twig or disturbed foliage appears. Why: the environment can produce the same sign without any crime.

## case collapse
- [mechanism] Once one piece of a constructed case is shown to be false, the rest of the planted evidence tends to fail with it. When: when a single fact is disproved. Why: Planted evidence depends on each piece supporting the others.
- [mechanism] A coerced confession can open leads that look strong but collapse when the player finds no physical support. When: A player follows a lead from a forced confession. Why: Physical evidence decides whether the lead holds.
- [mechanism] A character's refusal to learn the truth can fix the outcome, leaving a crime unresolved and the authority figure permanently uninformed. When: when an authority figure chooses not to receive information. Why: Withholding knowledge closes off paths that would have led to resolution.
- [mechanism] A case collapses when a confession separates the real threat from the accused and the victim disowns the accused as the attacker.
- [mechanism] A late ruling that invalidates a whole category of evidence can overturn a case without any new discovery or witness. When: a case resting on one kind of proof. Why: the change is in the rule, not in the facts.
- [behavior] Under close questioning, apparent knowledge of a secret tends to collapse, and the speaker becomes confused and vacant. When: a witness is pressed for specifics.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a stated claim or puzzle. 2) Log concrete physical details without explaining them. 3) Settle on a plausible wrong explanation. 4) Add a crisis that rejects it. 5) Reconstruct the case from the logged details with physical proof. When: structuring a single investigation scenario. Why: Logged details that later return as proof make the final reconstruction feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [tradeoff] A lenient or private outcome keeps focus on the puzzle, while a full legal aftermath pulls focus away from the mystery itself. When: closing a case.
- [fact] An investigation can close without legal proof: circumstantial evidence and an outside event, or a procedural step such as a charge dropped without trial, ends the case without a positive finding of innocence. (x2)

## certified and written records
- [mechanism] A signed register entry that records buyer, purchase and date turns a packet into a documented transaction that can be checked. When: Linking a physical item to a sale. Why: A written record gives an independent point of verification.
- [rule] When a document is reported to have changed, ask who gains or loses from that change. When: a will or contract was reportedly altered. Why: Gain and loss expose motive.
- [heuristic] A written account that names people, times and objects can be checked against physical clues, which makes it more useful than general impressions.
- [heuristic] Keep a message or call log that players can check against the timeline they build, so records can confirm or expose claims. Why: independent records make claims testable.
- [heuristic] An official's private judgment about acceptable methods can be checked against other records from the same period before being taken as fact.
- [procedure] 1) List each step of the verdict or claim. 2) Locate each cited source and confirm it exists with the stated details. 3) Check that the source applies to these facts, not only the general field, and judge the claim by what it says. When: a decision or record is justified by citing earlier sources.
- [pitfall] Changing signatures between sends breaks a simple link between letters, so linking requires other shared traits. When: linking anonymous messages. Why: Surface identifiers can be varied on purpose.
- [pitfall] Photographs of a scene that has since changed can mislead about what the scene looked like at the time. When: Comparing old records with the present state of a place. Why: Later records reflect later conditions.
- [fact] A copied record certified by its owner's signature can be used as formal evidence.

## closed setting and access
- [model] A closed-room death accepted as accident can be a murder by a visitor, proven by a second person's trace left inside the sealed room.
- [model] A typical mystery sets an apparently impossible or sinister act inside a closed setting, puts forward a plausible suspect, clears that suspect, and explains the act through an overlooked detail. When: structuring a closed-setting or locked-room mystery. Why: Clearing the first suspect and exposing a small detail drives the solution.
- [mechanism] A forced waiting period with no available action builds frustration and tension, since the investigator cannot advance the case. When: Access to a key witness is postponed by a scheduled event. Why: Lack of agency during a wait increases the pressure to act.
- [mechanism] Keeping the player close to each suspect makes later reversals feel earned rather than arbitrary, because the player has seen each suspect's behavior first-hand.
- [rule] Treat an apparent impossibility as evidence that a stated premise is false; a claim that no one could enter often hides a second route, so conclude someone moved the object. When: When evaluating whether a space was sealed or an act was impossible. Why: Unverified access claims can conceal entry paths.
- [heuristic] List everyone with access to a closed space to narrow suspects, and check whether each control was real. When: Investigating who could have entered a restricted room. Why: Access controls differ in strength, so the real list may differ from the apparent one.
- [heuristic] Access rules limit which NPCs could have taken an item, so the player can eliminate suspects by location and skill. When: In games where NPCs have locations and abilities. Why: Restricted access makes elimination a fair deduction method.
- [heuristic] A chain of mundane causes can explain how and why a discovery happened, but it does not substitute for evidence that identifies what was found. When: Presenting a discovery whose circumstances are plausible but unidentified. Why: Explaining access is distinct from establishing identity.
- [heuristic] Hint at the final hiding place through an architectural feature early in the setting, then open it only late, so the solution is anchored in the location. When: planning a concealed room or route that resolves the case. Why: A feature seen early but used late makes the reveal feel grounded rather than invented.

## clue pacing and release
- [model] Early clues establish household, appearance, habits and objects; mid-case clues scatter the scheme and clear suspects one by one; late clues cluster to confirm one culprit. When: pacing clues in a multi-suspect mystery. Why: Gradual elimination narrows the field so the final clues point to one person. (x2)
- [mechanism] Clustering clues in the opening section and releasing them together as one passage delays the player's realisation until the decoding scene.
- [mechanism] When clues arrive steadily and each is tied to a suspect, suspicion shifts every time a clue is interpreted differently. When: releasing clues across a long mystery. Why: Each new interpretation reassigns a shared clue to another suspect.
- [heuristic] Front-load strongest clues (impossibility, solution-dissolving) in first quarter to fifth; drip identity, alibi, motive clues through middle; cluster evidence against each suspect late. When: pacing clue delivery across a long mystery. Why: Early strong clues hook the audience; steady later release keeps interest and lets them test theories before evidence concentrates. (x2)
- [heuristic] Keep confessions brief, since a long, complete account slows pace. When: When writing a culprit's confession after a deduction. Why: Full confessions with every detail drag once the audience has already reasoned to the answer.
- [heuristic] Front-load clues in the first case, then release fewer each time a chapter closes so the player keeps an active set of leads. When: Pacing clue delivery across a long mystery. Why: Early clues build the frame, and sparse later clues keep the player connecting dots.
- [heuristic] Deal clues steadily through the first half of a mystery, then cluster the decisive ones in the final third. When: a mystery of standard length.
- [tradeoff] Spreading clues evenly across the middle delays suspicion of the real threat, while front-loaded clues fix suspicion early on a suspect who may be wrong. When: Pacing a mystery's clue delivery. Why: Early clues anchor the audience's suspect before later evidence can redirect it.
- [pitfall] A long digression stalls the story's momentum. When: Inserting a backstory or explanatory section into an ongoing plot. Why: Readers lose the thread of the active scene during extended exposition.

## clue placement and timing
- [rule] Place all clues for a twist before the reveal, and keep suspicion focused on a more obvious threat so the real danger goes unexamined. When: Structuring a plot twist. Why: Front-loaded clues can be recalled after the reveal, while a decoy suspect absorbs the player's attention.
- [rule] Place the decisive clue in a location or detail the player has already passed, so the solution feels earned rather than arbitrary. When: placing the final proof. Why: Players connect a revealed clue more readily when they saw it earlier.
- [rule] Place a contradicting clue early and let characters explain it away, so players can recall it when the picture changes later. When: Structuring clues in a mystery with a false initial solution. Why: An early anomaly rationalized at the time becomes a retrievable clue once the solution shifts.
- [heuristic] Plant the decisive clue in the first third of the case as an ordinary, incidental object, and explain its meaning only late in the story. When: Planting clues for a later payoff or twist reveal. Why: Mundane placement avoids drawing suspicion. An early ordinary clue gains meaning only when the solution explains it, reads as setting rather than a cheat, and feels clever to those who saw it. (x2)
- [heuristic] Show the key clue early as a throwaway moment without comment, so its meaning stays unknown until a later test confirms it. When: Planting clues for a late proof or later reveal. Why: Hidden early clues reward attentive audiences without announcing importance, and the later test makes the reveal feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [heuristic] Put a seemingly trivial document in a dated or labeled place to signal that it will return. Why: A labeled storage spot tells attentive readers the item matters without naming its role.
- [heuristic] Place the most dangerous warning at the end of a message or briefing, where it has the most impact. When: Ending a message that carries a critical warning. Why: The final line is remembered most and raises stakes before the next step.
- [heuristic] Give the active suspect the heavy middle-section clues, and present decisive late clues as minor points, so they are noticed only after the reinterpretation. Why: Clues presented as minor are discounted when seen and recalled later.
- [tradeoff] Introduce premise, suspect pool and principles early; then either hold physical clues for a late cluster that carries the solution, or front-load clues and deal a steady drip of contradictions. When: Structuring a reveal or a mystery's clue pacing. Why: A late cluster lets players reconstruct the answer quickly; a steady drip lets them test theories as the case unfolds.

## counting and tallies
- [rule] Give a game's council or jury seat rules that exclude parties with a stake, so the player can check the body for bias.
- [heuristic] Count independent sources or matching details, not repeats: shared-loyalty witnesses add nothing new; several independent matches point to one author, a single match may be chance. Why: Shared loyalty makes their views a single source.
- [heuristic] A small mismatch between an expected count and an observed count is often the first sign that someone acted outside the stated story. When: When a known starting figure exists to compare against. Why: Mismatches reveal actions the account omits.
- [heuristic] Report a tally built on a range estimate as a range, not a single exact figure, since the width of the range shows how far the total may be off. When: Some recalled payments are uncertain and given as alternative amounts. Why: A single number hides the uncertainty carried by the estimate.
- [procedure] 1) Count accusations within a small area. 2) Note how many accused had blameless lives. 3) Track growth in accusers over time. 4) Count outcomes for accused who denied guilt. When: a body of testimony looks suspicious as a whole.
- [pitfall] Counting accusers or incriminating items is a pitfall; each item must be weighed, since volume of accusation is not proof and merely counting misranks suspects. When: Weighing suspicion against a person. Why: Volume of accusation is not the same as proof.
- [pitfall] A single counting slip shifts every later word, so the decoder must recount.
- [pitfall] Changing the count of items is a detectable error, so a swap must keep the number the same.
- [fact] A count of missing items can rule out a simple explanation; a partial count can fit neither an accidental nor a deliberate single-dose cause. When: Physical evidence includes a countable quantity.

## dialogue interpretation
- [mechanism] A dialogue line that slips out unintentionally can be stored and revisited later, so a hint of hidden knowledge pays off when the player returns. When: Designing NPC dialogue that may hide knowledge. Why: A remembered slip rewards attentive players and links later scenes.
- [mechanism] Overheard or relayed dialogue delivered with uncertain accuracy prompts the player to verify it with a second source. When: Designing dialogue delivered through an intermediary. Why: Uncertain accuracy makes cross-checking a meaningful action.
- [rule] Tag dialogue lines that have two readings so that a suspicious listener selects the damaging literal reading. When: Writing dialogue that can be misread by a skeptical NPC. Why: Ambiguity becomes a mechanism when listener bias chooses between readings.
- [heuristic] When a suspect offers to waive or dismiss a source as unimportant, check that source, since it may be something they want hidden. When: A suspect offers to let the investigator skip a document or area. Why: Volunteering to drop a source can keep the investigator from examining it.
- [heuristic] Unguarded behaviour is often more reliable than deliberate statements, so witnesses to such moments deserve extra weight. When: Weighing a character's words against their actions. Why: People control what they say more than what they do unseen.
- [pitfall] A volunteered denial draws attention to the denied topic and can make an innocent witness look guilty, since audiences read unprompted denials as signs the denied thing is real. When: a witness offers a denial unprompted. Why: the denial signals that the topic matters to them.
- [pitfall] Vague answers such as 'some business' should be followed up before committing to a theory. When: A suspect gives an unspecific reason. Why: Unexamined vagueness can hide the truth.
- [pitfall] A callback must point to an accessible scene, since a vague reference cannot be checked and the reveal then feels arbitrary. When: Referring back to earlier material in a reveal. Why: A reference the audience cannot locate gives no means of verification.
- [pitfall] An obscure remark reads as a random outburst unless it is tied to a visible motive. When: Writing a cryptic line for a character. Why: Without a visible motive, the audience cannot see why the speaker would hint at all.

## discreet investigation and discretion
- [behavior] A witness who learns the investigator must share information with colleagues may immediately ask how discreet those colleagues are. When: When an investigator states that information will be passed on to others. Why: The witness's concern shifts from the facts to who else will learn them.
- [rule] Keep surveillance discreet and avoid alarming people close to the trail, because visible pursuit ends the chance of learning more. When: Shadowing a contact who may lead to an accomplice. Why: Visible approaches cause the contact to notice the watch and change their behaviour.
- [rule] When a questioner who stands to gain presses for information, give answers that are true but reveal nothing new. When: A friendly-seeming questioner asks about sensitive matters. Why: True but unhelpful answers protect what is known without deception.
- [heuristic] Offer the player a discreet way to end a blackmail threat, such as a trusted authority figure, so it resolves without public exposure. When: Designing a blackmail quest. Why: Victims often avoid authorities who might expose their secret, so a trusted channel must exist.
- [heuristic] Recruit agents from people whose circumstances make them easily employed and discreet, drawing on a prepared register of such people. When: A network of covert agents is needed quickly. Why: Ready candidates shorten placement and reduce the risk of indiscretion.
- [heuristic] Request comparison material without revealing the aim of the examination. When: comparison material is held by others.
- [procedure] 1) Split the investigation into discrete tasks. 2) Give each task a named place, a time and a target object. 3) Ask for a report on every result, including negative ones. When: an outsider without official powers wants to steer an existing inquiry. Why: Narrow, checkable tasks are easier for the official team to act on.
- [tradeoff] Offering discretion is cheap and can draw out fuller detail from a witness, but it trades away pressure and may protect a guilty party. When: Choosing how to press a reluctant witness who fears exposure. Why: The assurance costs the questioner little and removes the main risk to the witness, but it costs leverage and risks protecting the culprit.
- [pitfall] Promising discretion in return for a disclosure can stop the investigator from checking the disclosed account with others. When: When a witness offers a private account in exchange for confidentiality. Why: A promise of secrecy creates a social obligation that discourages verification.

## displacement and disputed objects
- [mechanism] Fear directed at a red-herring legend draws attention away from the real threat, which can then be held back until it is revealed. When: a larger threat is hidden behind a more visible one. Why: the audience's attention follows the legend.
- [mechanism] An item moved from inside to an unexpected outside location raises a second question about who moved it and why. When: When a missing object is found somewhere it should not be. Why: Displacement implies a further action.
- [mechanism] A harmful object aimed at one person can strike another when it passes between hands, so the actual victim may differ from the intended target. When: A poison or trap sits on an object that is handed on. Why: Each handover moves the object to a new holder, changing who is exposed.
- [rule] Note objects out of usual place and ask occupants what normally sits where; displacement means little without that baseline, or once the scene is cleared or no routine exists. When: when the household's routine can be learned. Why: A displacement only means something relative to the usual arrangement; without a baseline no comparison remains.
- [heuristic] An object lying far from a body on a still day suggests it was thrown or placed afterward, which contradicts a simple accident account. When: reconstructing an accident scene. Why: no wind or ordinary motion explains the distance.
- [tradeoff] Removing a disputed fence at once concedes the ground immediately, while letting it stand until the bounds are fixed keeps the claim open. When: when a neighbor disputes the line of a structure. Why: each option trades an immediate concession against an unresolved claim.
- [pitfall] A recorded item can be disputed later, so sealing evidence in the suspect's presence protects its integrity.
- [pitfall] A displaced target can make a crime look random, hiding the real intent for too long, so the intended victim should be stated clearly at some point. When: Writing a crime whose surface victim differs from its intent. Why: Without a clear statement of intent, readers lose track of who was meant to be harmed.
- [pitfall] An object found far from its owner may have been planted or moved, so its route must be explained before it is used as proof.

## evidence contamination
- [mechanism] A spilled substance on a floor leaves a footprint outline that can be followed, so the contaminant works as a tracking marker across a space. When: when a character or route must be traced through an area. Why: the spill transfers to footsteps and marks the path.
- [mechanism] A crime-scene system can log who entered each room and what each person touched, so evidence contamination can be modeled.
- [mechanism] Blood added to a weapon after handling cannot show whether it was present before the struggle, so the question may become permanently unanswerable. When: a weapon was handled or injured someone after the event. Why: the timeline of traces is lost.
- [mechanism] A second event that removes or moves key evidence overnight signals that someone active in the setting is managing the scene. When: Plotting a mystery where the culprit must hide evidence. Why: The removal itself is a clue about who is acting and shifts suspicion toward the actor.
- [heuristic] Physical evidence found on ground a suspect crossed shortly before is weak proof against that suspect, since their presence may have moved or deposited it.
- [pitfall] Moving or searching a body or objects before investigators secure the scene, even by the first entrant, destroys or contaminates evidence and makes later accounts describe an altered scene. When: a scene is accessed before investigators secure it. Why: disturbance changes the original configuration. (x2)
- [pitfall] Once a theory has been revealed to a witness, that witness can no longer serve as an independent check on the theory. Why: Their later account may echo what they were told.
- [pitfall] If the central witness is heard first, peripheral witnesses may be shaped by what has already been said.
- [pitfall] Testing an object can change its state, so record what is found before any further handling.

## false solutions and wrong suspects
- [behavior] A comforting explanation voiced by a character with a motive to want it makes players doubt it and test it against physical evidence. When: A character proposes an innocent explanation that benefits them. Why: Players notice the motive behind the explanation and check it.
- [rule] Offer a plausible false explanation, then overturn it with a physical fact, such as an object proving an earlier claim wrong, which points to a different cause. When: Designing a mystery with a plausible false explanation, or when a false solution needs overturning. Why: Physical evidence is harder to dismiss than testimony, and it rewards players who test the theory. (x2)
- [rule] Give the player two or three competing explanations for an event, each with its own evidence, and let the evidence decide which holds. When: Designing a mystery with a supernatural surface. Why: Competing accounts keep the player weighing evidence rather than accepting the first explanation offered.
- [rule] Give the investigator a theory that is wrong and gets dismissed, so the player can be wrong alongside them.
- [heuristic] Give the wrong suspect a complete motive chain and an accepted evidence pile, so the false solution feels finished to the audience. When: when designing a false solution in a mystery. Why: A finished-looking wrong answer makes the late reveal more surprising.
- [procedure] 1) State the natural explanation first and check it against all evidence. 2) Keep it in play until the evidence clearly rules it out. 3) Introduce the supernatural explanation only after the natural one fails. When: A mystery could have a human or supernatural cause and both must be weighed fairly. Why: Testing the mundane option first makes the eventual supernatural answer feel earned and keeps the reader's reasoning active.
- [procedure] 1) List every candidate explanation, such as suicide, murder, natural death, or a mixture. 2) Test each against the physical facts. 3) Commit to none until a test is made. When: Several explanations fit the surface facts.
- [pitfall] Choosing an explanation for emotional comfort, such as hoping for a natural cause, delays recognition of the truth. When: when the explanation is preferred because it is reassuring. Why: Attachment to the comforting answer lowers the scrutiny applied to it.
- [pitfall] A plausible, rational-sounding theory offered early can close the case and redirect the search away from the real mechanics of an event. When: An explanation is proposed before the event's physical details are tested. Why: A satisfying theory ends further questioning, so searches follow the theory instead of the evidence.

## generalisation and bias fallacies
- [mechanism] Each observer group sees only the role it expects, so assumptions about role let a person pass unnoticed among them. When: A character crosses between social groups. Why: Expectations filter what observers perceive.
- [heuristic] State what you know only in general terms, and let the suspect make the next move, rather than naming the culprit outright. When: Questioning a suspect during an investigation. Why: A general statement invites a response without warning the culprit.
- [pitfall] A general principle or belief, even when an authority endorses it, does not prove a specific accusation or claim drawn from it. (x2)
- [pitfall] Stereotypes or motives assigned to a whole group, such as clergy or a nationality, lack case evidence and do not prove any individual's intent or conduct. Why: Group-level attribution unfairly implicates individuals who acted otherwise. (x2)
- [pitfall] A genuine victim can look staged, and a staged scene can still include real harm, so neither appearance settles the question. When: Judging whether a scene was arranged. Why: Appearances mix real and arranged elements in the same event.
- [pitfall] Assuming a culprit's identity from a general theory about who commits subtle crimes biases the search. Treat such theories as questions to test. When: a general theory about offenders is offered.
- [pitfall] A grand motive can justify action against any suspect, so it does not prove that a particular person is guilty.
- [pitfall] Generalizing about a whole group from a few incidents makes the observer blind to individuals who differ from the group.
- [pitfall] Over-reading a common scent or paper type leads to false matches, so weigh how widely the material is available.

## hidden culprit and reveal
- [model] A protective device that seems strange may conceal a private motive; tracing its origin and what it currently guards can reveal the real purpose behind it. When: A protective device or ritual seems inexplicable and needs a personal or material explanation. Why: Origin and current use together often explain behavior that looks mad on the surface.
- [model] A jailed mastermind who still directs the scheme is a twist whose misdirection is the belief that imprisonment ends the threat. When: designing a captive antagonist reveal. Why: Confidence in containment makes the reader accept the threat as ended.
- [mechanism] A witness found in a place they should not be can be more credible, since their presence exposes them to risk. When: When assessing a witness discovered in an unexpected location. Why: Accepting risk to be present is costly, which makes the account more believable.
- [mechanism] A culprit's signature clues can stay in plain view while being attached to harmless explanations, so readers attribute them to an innocent suspect until a late search exposes the true author. When: Designing a mystery whose solution is hidden behind a frame on another character. Why: Readers accept an explanation that fits the planted clue, so suspicion runs opposite to the truth until new evidence appears.
- [rule] Keep a hidden leader masked and offstage until the reveal, appearing only in group meetings and unmasking late. When: A secret organisation whose leader is also a suspect or friend. Why: Limited exposure protects the identity and keeps the reveal dramatic.
- [heuristic] Plant a culprit's or second culprit's presence in ordinary acts, like an everyday request, noted time, limp, case or repeated check, so it reads as background until reveal. When: When hiding a culprit present throughout the story, or a second culprit. Why: Unremarkable details are passed over on first reading and gain meaning when the reveal recontextualizes them, so the reveal reads as fair.
- [heuristic] Do not fix on the most visible grudge; a suspect with no obvious grudge can still hold the motive that explains the crime. When: When a single obvious suspect is emerging early in an investigation. Why: Visible motives can distract from concealed ones.
- [heuristic] Unexplained personal spending can be the root of a debt that drives later crime, so note private obligations even when they are not fully explored. When: when a financial problem has no clear origin. Why: Private expenses often start the chain of pressure that leads to misconduct.
- [heuristic] Give an alibi witness a motive hidden in plain sight, so a neutral-seeming account becomes damning once the witness's identity is exposed.

## investigation records and estimates
- [rule] Store in-world lore fragments and documents in full so a lone fragment cannot mislead; let players find partial excerpts in rival reports, so comparing them exposes omissions. When: Designing in-world records and rival accounts. Why: Players can detect what a partial copy hides.
- [rule] Do not accept a mechanism that explains the main sight but leaves a smaller detail unexplained.
- [rule] Record even a fruitless search, noting what was absent and where you looked, because an empty result still carries information.
- [heuristic] Anomalies are often in the fringes of a scene rather than the central event, so peripheral oddities deserve close scrutiny.
- [procedure] 1) State a proposed explanation. 2) List every later event it must account for. 3) Reject the explanation if any later event contradicts it. When: an explanation fits only one moment. Why: A cause must hold across the whole sequence.
- [metric] Distance travelled can be estimated as fuel used divided by consumption rate, giving a check on a claimed round trip. When: a journey claim is checked against fuel consumed. Why: the estimate depends on the assumed consumption rate.
- [pitfall] A forecast can be far off; when the predicted time passes with no change, the state may persist for much longer than expected.
- [pitfall] If the investigator learns the content of a destroyed message by accident, the cost of destroying it disappears.
- [pitfall] Information given freely may be harmless, while a gatekeeper's hint may steer the player into danger; weigh each before acting.

## locating a witness
- [heuristic] When one witness is the only link, shift the work from questioning to tracking them down, and plan concrete steps such as visiting a set location. When: When the key witness is absent or unreachable.
- [heuristic] In a small community with few civilians, a distinctive appearance is easy to notice, so a description narrows the search. When: the target is local and must be found within a bounded area. Why: few people means a distinctive look stands out.
- [heuristic] Use a precedent's motive to identify who would have been harmed by the event, then search among those people for the hidden party. When: the precedent involves a motive that blocks someone's goal. Why: the motive narrows the field of possible culprits.
- [heuristic] When a contact has moved, follow the record of the move rather than ending the line of inquiry. When: Investigating through a chain of contacts. Why: The move record can lead to new sources and reveal hidden links.
- [procedure] 1) Ask acquaintances, such as club members or servants, for the witness's address. 2) Get their travel route and a rough return date. 3) If the witness is still absent, leave a written message to keep contact open.
- [procedure] 1) Write to an intermediary who may have been in contact with the witness. 2) Ask that replies be forwarded or sent to a distant post office to protect the search. When: a witness's location is unknown and the search must stay discreet. Why: Intermediaries relay addresses, and distance hides the searcher.
- [procedure] 1) Check registries for the target vessel. 2) Cross-check its name against origin records. 3) Confirm the crew's whereabouts with a contact at the dock. When: tracking a target that is travelling.
- [procedure] 1) List the places a hidden person could have been placed. 2) Check the most likely places one by one until the person is found. When: when a person's location is concealed. Why: Ordered checks of likely places are efficient.
- [procedure] 1) List every household member. 2) Record each member's location and any marriage, move or arrest with its date. 3) For the sighting date, remove those who were absent. 4) Weigh the remaining candidates. When: an unexplained figure appears at a known household. Why: physical presence follows documented movements.

## natural explanations and anomalies
- [definition] A supernatural-seeming phenomenon can be treated as a force with a natural, knowable cause; the open question is how much is known and admitted.
- [mechanism] A discovery becomes believable when an ordinary, routine cause brought someone to the spot, such as a scheduled inspection, a repair or a flood. When: A finding needs a plausible reason for being made at that time and place. Why: A visible, mundane cause explains access without needing contrivance.
- [rule] Test every proposed human explanation against specific recorded observations and conditions; one that ignores the evidence or is invented to fit a preferred conclusion will not hold. When: Presenting or proposing a human explanation for a supernatural-seeming event or reconciling conflicting accounts. Why: Explanations that fail to account for observed facts lose credibility with the player, and a tidy explanation may fit the desired answer rather than the facts.
- [heuristic] Give each threat one natural and one supernatural explanation and keep both live until the final scene.
- [heuristic] A natural explanation that fits the sightings but leaves one key problem unsolved should be treated as provisional, not accepted outright. When: Evaluating an explanation for a mystery. Why: A partial fit can seem convincing while hiding a contradiction that the evidence later exposes.
- [heuristic] A victim's silence can have ordinary causes such as a dying light source, a person woken from sleep, or shock. When: explaining why a person did not react or call out. Why: physical and psychological circumstances often explain apparent passivity.
- [heuristic] Most apparent anomalies turn out to have nothing abnormal in them, so a feeling of wrongness should prompt further checks rather than serve as proof. When: An investigator is tempted to treat a vague sense of unease as evidence. Why: Most odd events have mundane causes once examined.
- [heuristic] Explain early odd events with mundane causes, then let them recur. Accumulated dismissals make a later supernatural reading feel plausible.
- [pitfall] Explaining away every strange event as a human act can make the solution feel rigged, so some anomaly should be left open or supported by evidence. Why: Readers distrust a mystery that dismisses every uncanny element without grounds.

## ordeal and outcome reasoning
- [mechanism] Revealing an outcome early, paired with an open question about how it came about, sustains suspense. When: Structuring a mystery's reveals. Why: The open question holds attention after the answer is known.
- [rule] Ordeals such as heated iron, water, or swimming tests should not be accepted as evidence of guilt, as they are superstitious. When: when considering physical tests as a basis for proof. Why: they do not reliably establish the facts of an accusation.
- [heuristic] A claim that an event already produced a result is false if the event had not yet occurred at the claimed time. When: when an account reports the outcome of a dated event. Why: an outcome cannot exist before its event.
- [heuristic] When no direct record of an outcome survives, infer it from later documents, such as evidence that a person was alive years after a sentence.
- [heuristic] When an impossible event occurs, begin with an ordinary explanation such as illness, and proceed cautiously while testing it. When: an impossible event is witnessed. Why: ordinary causes are more likely than the impossible.
- [pitfall] Discovering a culprit can do more harm than the crime itself, so weigh the outcome of action, not only the fact of guilt. When: deciding whether to pursue formal action. Why: exposure has its own consequences.
- [pitfall] A conviction can persist after the evidence behind it has been repudiated, so a verdict's continued existence does not confirm its truth. Why: Courts may keep enforcing a judgment long after the evidence supporting it is discredited.
- [pitfall] A procedure that declares an accused person innocent can still kill them, so its verdict does not prove the test was sound.
- [pitfall] Claims about how something was done need evidence of the mechanism, not just the outcome; the number found in a result cannot settle the method used. Why: Several methods can produce the same observed result.

## personal marks and initials
- [definition] Personal objects link a person to places, times and actions. Tracing an object's path and condition can connect an unidentified body or missing person to a known life.
- [rule] Identify a specific object by an accidental, individual flaw such as a crack, damage or repair, rather than by its general type. When: when several identical objects could be the one in question.
- [rule] Plant identifying marks such as a brand, a ring or a card in the opening scene so the player can later check them against the twist. When: a body or character is presented as a known person. Why: Early checkable marks let the player verify the reveal instead of accepting it on trust.
- [heuristic] Initialed items on fallen adventurers or NPCs can serve as identifiers that unlock dialogue or quests. When: designing dead or injured characters in a game.
- [heuristic] Let a small personal object carry the identity question, and test it against each candidate owner using a physical feature such as wear, residue or damage. When: designing an identification puzzle or whodunit. Why: A concrete object can be matched to several suspects, so the answer becomes checkable rather than asserted.
- [procedure] 1) Check where ownership is usually written, such as the flyleaf or cover. 2) Check the rest of the item. 3) Compare names, initials, and handwriting against the known owner. 4) Check the leaves for loose scraps of paper. 5) Note what each item reveals and set aside those that might help. When: Examining a set of personal items for names, dates, or hidden notes. Why: A systematic order ensures ownership and concealed notes are not overlooked.
- [pitfall] Initials, a monogram, or a name entry is not proof of identity, since many people share the same initials or names. When: Using a marked object or record entry to identify a suspect or identity. Why: Shared names and initials can point to several people. (x2)
- [pitfall] Initials on an object may not match its owner. Check that they belong to the owner before reading them as the culprit's mark. Why: A coincidental match can send the investigation after the wrong person.
- [fact] Some physical features vary enough between people to serve as individual markers.

## physical evidence analysis
- [mechanism] An obstacle found exactly where it was left in a gap shows the gap was not used, because a person could not easily restore it. When: When an entry point is blocked by an object that could be moved. Why: Restoring an obstacle precisely is hard, so its unchanged position is evidence.
- [rule] Plant an odd, unexplained object early and pay it off in the final scene without explaining it. When: when building an eerie or ambiguous story. Why: The object keeps the reader attentive while leaving the cause open.
- [rule] Confirm an environmental fact such as weather from an independent source rather than from the suspect's own account. When: When a conclusion depends on a weather or condition claim. Why: A suspect has a motive to misstate conditions that affect their alibi.
- [heuristic] Build distinct damage signatures into objects so players can match one wreck to another and find shared causes.
- [heuristic] Showing that a wound was inflicted after death reframes the case: the assumed murder becomes a staging, and the apparent victim's identity becomes uncertain. When: A murder is solved by a physical finding that contradicts the first account. Why: A changed cause of injury alters what the reader believes happened and who is dead.
- [procedure] 1) Examine every part, not only the most obvious damage. 2) Look for signatures a crash alone would not produce, such as burned insulation and fused wires. 3) Use intact parts to exclude causes. 4) Compare separate wrecks for shared damage. 5) Lock wreckage away unchanged after inspection. When: a failure is blamed on ordinary causes but the damage looks unusual.
- [pitfall] A place left unchanged for years can be misread if the investigator does not know what has already been removed.
- [pitfall] Do not assume a stain is the suspected substance before testing it.
- [pitfall] Testing only the full containers can clear the real route, since the wrong sample can rule out the true source.

## physical tests and proof
- [mechanism] A chemical interaction that the player can test, such as precipitation, can serve as the final proof, turning an earlier trivial container into the key clue. When: Building a poisoning or mechanism-based reveal. Why: A testable reaction makes the proof checkable, and the container was seen earlier as trivia.
- [rule] Place a physical contradiction shortly before the trap springs, giving players a last chance to notice what the story hides.
- [rule] Pay off a hidden test with a physical effect that repeats an earlier event, so the reveal is proven by something the player has already seen. When: Resolving a trap that was set up by an earlier test. Why: A repeated physical cue makes the reveal concrete and memorable.
- [rule] Use a physical test to settle a hidden state, such as a working device on an apparently dead body, so the audience can verify the truth. When: A character's condition is uncertain and cannot be seen directly. Why: A working object gives the audience concrete evidence rather than a claim.
- [heuristic] A confession gains weight when a physical consequence confirms it, such as a body returning or an object appearing. When: a character confesses to a hidden act.
- [heuristic] Keep the decisive proof physical and inspectable, such as a ballistic trace, so the accusation rests on an object the player can examine.
- [procedure] 1) Run a private physical test on the suspect, such as a touch, measurement, or staged trip that exposes a lie. 2) Observe the reaction. 3) Reveal the answer to the group only after the test confirms it. When: Confirming a suspect before a public reveal, without tipping off the suspect. Why: A physical test gives proof that does not depend on confession, and a covert test confirms the theory while keeping the suspect unaware.
- [procedure] 1) Ask precise questions about physical evidence first. 2) Ask for general impressions only after the facts are laid out. When: Interviewing a witness about a death or incident. Why: Facts anchor the witness's later feelings and keep interpretation from running ahead of evidence.
- [tradeoff] Demanding a high proof standard prevents wrongful accusation but can leave an investigator stuck when the needed evidence is hard to find. When: Setting how much evidence is needed before naming a culprit. Why: A strict threshold protects against error at the cost of progress.

## physical trace geometry
- [mechanism] Stalled threads compete with active ones for an investigator's attention, so unresolved leads can crowd out new work when many run at once. When: When an investigation has many open leads at the same time. Why: Limited attention must be divided between pending and active threads.
- [behavior] A fleeing person throws an item to be rid of it, so its landing spot reveals who was actually targeted. When: An object is thrown during an escape. Why: Escape aims to shed the item, not to deliver it.
- [rule] Measure distances from a suspected heat source and inspect nearby surfaces for effects, since both can rule that source in or out. When: A heat source is suspected.
- [heuristic] Read floor coverings and stains as a map: where a covering is missing or a stain pools shows where an event happened and how far it spread. When: investigating a scene's layout.
- [heuristic] Use footprints that lead beneath a closed door as physical evidence that rules out a simple supernatural explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Compare paired parts on opposite sides for length and shape. 2) Match worn joint surfaces across separate finds. 3) Confirm with several independent features before concluding the parts belong together. When: Deciding whether scattered remains come from one individual. Why: Several independent matches are much harder to produce by chance than a single feature.
- [procedure] 1) Record where each trace lies on the object. 2) Map the trace pattern onto the anatomy or structure to find which surfaces faced where. 3) Test each explanation for the arrangement against the physical state of joints or connections. When: A minor physical trace follows a regular pattern and suggests how an object lay. Why: Placement of small traces can reveal orientation and whether parts were separated before deposit.
- [fact] A thumb meets a flat surface through its side, not its palm, so a print showing all five palm-side surfaces together cannot come from a hand pressed flat. When: when judging whether a print's pose is possible. Why: the contact geometry of the digits limits possible arrangements.
- [fact] Dragged bleeding differs from arterial tracks left by a victim who could still move, so compare a mark with wound evidence before interpreting it.

## presence as evidence
- [mechanism] A per-event presence list narrows suspects by showing who could have been present, excluding anyone absent from each event.
- [rule] Do not treat a suspect's silence about his movements as proof of guilt; the real question is whether he was at the scene. When: a suspect will not account for his time. Why: silence alone does not place him at the crime.
- [rule] Confirmed presence in a place does not verify what the person did there or during an unexplained gap. Treat those parts as unverified. When: when a confirmed alibi covers only part of a period.
- [heuristic] A person who admits being at the scene while denying the act can remain a suspect if the timeline leaves them alone with the victim's belongings. When: when a suspect admits presence but denies the crime. Why: opportunity with the victim's possessions is still incriminating.
- [heuristic] A suspect seen in company when an event happens gets an alibi that witnesses tend to accept without question. Why: A companion's presence is taken as proof of where the suspect was.
- [heuristic] A person's presence in a place can be established by others who were there the same day, which places that person within reach of the scene. Why: Shared presence with other occupants gives an independent link to the location.
- [procedure] 1) Test a claimed presence against a dated schedule of events. 2) Check the wording of any denial. 3) Check the witness's role. 4) Conclude only if all three agree. When: judging whether a witness attended a stage of a proceeding. Why: A narrow denial alone is not proof of presence elsewhere.
- [pitfall] Overlap with events or confirmed presence shows only proximity, not connection; the case must also link the suspect to the crime itself. Why: Linking a figure only because movements overlap can send the investigation the wrong way.
- [pitfall] A verified document can be a weak alibi if it proves presence in a place without proving who was there.

## provisional theories
- [rule] A reading of a partly heard clue should remain provisional until a later action or source confirms it. When: A clue is given as a fragment with missing words. Why: Filling gaps with expectation can produce a confident but wrong meaning.
- [rule] Make each reveal change the threat's identity, so the player must rebuild their model of the enemy rather than confirm it.
- [heuristic] Keep a diagnosis or working hypothesis provisional when proof is missing, even if one explanation seems most likely. When: when the investigator has a strong guess but no confirmation. Why: Holding the explanation open allows later evidence to revise it.
- [heuristic] A suspect may have been able to act yet still be unlikely to have done so, given the risk, lack of positive evidence and open conduct afterward.
- [heuristic] A provisional theory that is partly right keeps the audience engaged while the full mechanism stays hidden. When: the true cause is still unknown. Why: A partly correct explanation sustains interest without revealing the answer.
- [heuristic] Treat every solution as provisional until physical evidence and a witnessed statement independently confirm it. Why: A belief resting only on inference breaks easily and undermines trust in the case.
- [pitfall] A theory tied to a location requires a search that may find nothing, and a place shows only where to look, not proof of a crime. When: Reasoning about a crime from a location. Why: A location can suggest a theory without confirming it.
- [pitfall] A clue that looks meaningless alone can mislead if its significance is assumed too early, before it is connected to other evidence.
- [pitfall] A note that reveals method can answer a question too early unless it is framed as a boast or taunt. When: when writing confession or taunting notes.

## quarrels and resentment motive
- [behavior] A heated argument absorbs a group's attention and can collapse the mood of the whole gathering until a host intervenes.
- [behavior] Suspicion tends to follow existing quarrels, land disputes and group allegiances rather than evidence of specific acts.
- [behavior] People closest to a secret decision-maker attract the most resentment, whatever role they actually played. Why: Proximity to power is taken as a sign of complicity.
- [rule] Do not treat a quarrel held in the heat of the moment as proof of intent. Weigh the witness's own anger alongside the words. When: when a public quarrel precedes a death. Why: anger distorts both speech and its interpretation.
- [rule] Do not treat a family quarrel as proof of wrongdoing; a dispute can be real without any criminal act behind it.
- [rule] Let a quarrel in one village create suspects in neighbouring households, so the player can trace who had motive. When: modelling faction and grudge networks.
- [pitfall] A witness who resents others, or has a prior quarrel with a party such as a rival or neighbour, describes them non-neutrally; moral judgements are not factual testimony. When: when a witness describes people they feel strongly about, or when a neighbor or rival testifies. Why: Feeling colours perception and judgement; past hostility shapes how events are interpreted. (x2)
- [pitfall] Private anger can push an investigator toward plans outside procedure, even plans to harm a suspect. When: an investigator's hurt turns into a wish for revenge. Why: strong negative emotion can override procedural restraint.
- [fact] A law may punish malicious intent to kill even when the means used could never cause death. When: judging offences defined by intent. Why: The wrong lies in the intention, so an ineffective method still counts.

## reference collections and lookup
- [rule] Treat a reference entry, even a written or polished one, as an incomplete hypothesis to test, not as confirmed; check whether its giver can be reached to verify it.
- [rule] Collect reference prints from the right people, since a comparison built on the wrong group proves nothing.
- [rule] Place solution hints in reference items the player carries, such as notes, codices or a bestiary, so a quiet review reveals the answer. When: A game needs a fair, self-contained solution path. Why: Reference items are already in the player's possession and are reread.
- [rule] Store the day or event each NPC statement refers to, so the game can check whether a line fits the timeline.
- [heuristic] Keep a broad reference collection including dusts, muds, fibres and food products, since any of them may later become evidence. When: When building a forensic reference library. Why: Unexpected materials can become relevant to a case.
- [heuristic] Decode unfamiliar clues with a reliable reference such as timetables or maps rather than guesses, because the hearer's own background knowledge may be lacking.
- [pitfall] A reference can supply the name behind initials, but the link between that name and the case still has to be shown. When: initials or a name are identified from an outside source. Why: a source supplies a name, not proof of relevance.
- [pitfall] Without reference patterns, two sets of footprints can only be counted as separate sets, not attributed to particular people.
- [fact] A witness may describe a document they no longer possess, so such claims stay unverified until the document or a copy is produced. When: when a witness refers to a letter or record they say is lost. Why: Missing evidence cannot confirm the content described.

## reveal timing and endings
- [definition] A chance confirmation verifies a suspicion by accident rather than by deduction, so the player confirms a belief instead of solving a mystery.
- [rule] Make the final explanation use only clues already seen, and account for every flagged gap, such as a stray item or an empty container. When: when writing the solution of a mystery. Why: New facts at the reveal feel unfair and leave flagged gaps unexplained.
- [rule] Close a mystery with an external report, such as a newspaper, so the player learns the outcome without further investigation.
- [heuristic] Keep the aftermath brief and often ironic, ending soon after the culprit is exposed or handed to an authority; the final word usually goes to the editorial or narrating voice.
- [heuristic] Deliver a climax before its full explanation when the scene works without context, and fill in the context afterwards. When: The climax is effective without full context. Why: Later explanation adds meaning after the fact.
- [heuristic] After the main reveal, close a minor side thread, such as a valuable revealed as worthless, to tie off loose ends. When: A subplot remains open after the climax. Why: Settling small threads quickly lets the main reveal carry the story's weight.
- [heuristic] End on a short, clean line the reader will quote, since a memorable final phrase carries the reveal in memory.
- [pitfall] Hiding a purpose so completely that the later reveal feels arbitrary makes the reveal unsatisfying. When: Planning when and how a hidden purpose is revealed. Why: Players cannot connect a reveal to earlier clues they never saw.
- [pitfall] A human agent introduced only at the reveal, with no earlier signs, feels arbitrary, and an inconsistent supernatural frame makes the solution look like a cheat. When: Revealing a human cause behind a supernatural frame.

## rewards for questioning
- [mechanism] Offering a reward to anyone who brings help quickly enlists passers-by as a summoned guard. When: a protected person needs help during the night. Why: the reward makes passers-by an extra layer of protection.
- [mechanism] A reward or wanted notice can rise in value as the player learns more, reversing the sense of a small task into a serious one. When: A minor task is linked to a larger plot thread. Why: New information changes the stakes of an apparently small task.
- [rule] Design NPCs who reveal a detail or change a confession under mild pressure, and reward patient questioning and noticing the shift. When: When designing NPC dialogue.
- [rule] Reward the dialogue choice that brings a rambling NPC back on topic, since patience and a good pretext unlock the key facts. When: when a conversation has many digressions.
- [rule] Reward the player for finding the lone dissenting witness, whose testimony costs them something to give. When: Designing a mystery or investigation where dissent is risky. Why: Testimony given at personal cost carries more weight and rewards careful searching.
- [heuristic] Reward players who exhaust a cooperative contact's knowledge before that contact becomes unavailable.
- [heuristic] Let players notice a mismatch between an NPC's energy and the subject at hand, and reward that attention with a new lead.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC offer a small aside that opens a new line of questioning, so attentive players are rewarded. When: Designing dialogue that should reward careful listening. Why: A passing remark that opens a lead makes attentiveness pay off in the game's progression.
- [pitfall] Anyone who responds to a payment offer may be after the reward, so verify each claim independently.

## rumour spread and sources
- [mechanism] A witness's account can change after they consult another source, so a second source can correct an earlier report. When: When a witness's story changes between statements. Why: The witness's view follows the influence of whoever they last spoke to.
- [mechanism] Rumour grows as it travels, and each new teller can add embellishments. When: A story passes through many people. Why: Each retelling adds invented detail.
- [behavior] After an incident, rumour splits into rival camps, such as political insult, prank or supernatural explanation, each favouring the reading that suits it. When: Gossip circulates about a disputed event. Why: Each group has its own reason to prefer its explanation.
- [rule] Design rumour chains passed among NPCs, each adding, dropping or slanting detail, so players can trace them to a primary source and weigh each link's reliability. When: Designing rumours or legends spread through characters. Why: Distortion turns information gathering into verification, and layered retelling makes the source a discovery task.
- [rule] Make the messenger's motive visible, and trust a hostile or gossiping source less than a neutral witness. When: Designing rumor delivery in a narrative or NPC system. Why: The motive shapes how reliable the report is.
- [heuristic] Let a town rumor or newspaper announce the player's actions so an NPC demands answers before the player is ready. When: Designing pressure from a game world on the player's investigation. Why: Public exposure forces the player to act on the timeline the world sets.
- [procedure] 1) Ask a direct question first. 2) Ask how the witness knows the answer. 3) If the witness changes subject or becomes distressed, return to the question with a firm demand for a direct answer. 4) Ask whether that is all they know. When: Interviewing a witness whose claims may rest on hearsay. Why: Asking for the source shows whether the claim is observed or repeated.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the person directly implicated in the rumor. 2) Note whether the answer confirms or denies the claim. 3) Treat silence or admission as evidence only the involved person can supply. Why: Only the person concerned can resolve the gap in a secondhand report.
- [fact] A published item about an investigation is a sign that someone outside is watching, not evidence of the underlying crime. When: Interpreting a public mention of an ongoing inquiry. Why: The item reveals observation, not what was found.

## setting and social context
- [mechanism] Barriers, nearby listeners and watching staff reduce what a witness will say, so statements recorded in such places are incomplete. When: Interviews held in shared, noisy or monitored spaces. Why: People guard their speech when they expect to be overheard.
- [mechanism] Memory of a stranger is likely in quiet places and unlikely in busy hubs, so failed checks in crowded places do not prove a lie. When: Judging whether a witness should remember a person. Why: Quiet settings make a visitor stand out and be recalled.
- [behavior] A striking outside theory that fits public fears of danger attracts wide attention and can push quieter, more mundane facts into the background. When: A dramatic rival explanation is publicised. Why: Vivid stories compete more strongly for attention than intimate detail.
- [behavior] Public sermons that picture accused people as servants of the devil can intensify popular fear. When: Religious or political speech during accusations.
- [heuristic] Use a series of minor cases to set expectations of harmlessness, then place a serious item within one of them. When: Structuring a sequence of investigations for a reveal. Why: Established expectations make the later reversal land with surprise.
- [heuristic] A crime can be fitted to the season and landscape where it occurs, so the setting shapes what the audience sees first. When: designing a crime scenario tied to a specific place and time. Why: Setting determines the visible surface of an event and the expectations the audience brings to it.
- [heuristic] Test whether a decoy motive fits its setting; a financial dispute rarely escalates to violence, so a more serious motive may explain the same facts better.
- [pitfall] A sensational setting does not make a case remarkable, and ordinary conduct can be misread as strange, so surface oddness is weak evidence.
- [fact] A location's layout, sounds and decay can reveal its history, hint at what happened there, and suggest who may be present. When: a place should function as a clue. Why: the present state of a place records its past.

## sightlines and vantage
- [behavior] An observer who arrives just after destruction and says nothing directly can still send a signal that the destroyer feels read. When: A witness discovers someone has just destroyed something. Why: Silence and timing convey knowledge without confrontation, which the destroyer interprets.
- [rule] Before accepting that no one passed unseen, list the doorways, check whether an open door or a standing person blocks view of both entrances. When: When a room has several openings and people may have moved through them. Why: Sightlines decide whether an action could have gone unnoticed.
- [heuristic] Check a witness's vantage point: light, distance, obstruction, windows, glass partitions and floor surfaces determine what they could see or hear from where they stood. When: Evaluating an eyewitness account or whether a witness could have observed an event from their position. Why: Each factor can enable or block sight and sound; a witness cannot report what their position hides from view.
- [heuristic] Use a separate observer who sees the figure from another angle to expose a disguise, since that witness may mistake the stand-in for the person. When: Testing a disguise or false alibi. Why: A separate sighting can reveal the substitution that the household accepted.
- [heuristic] A second reading taken from a different position narrows where a hidden source can be, because the two bearings intersect at a single point. When: a source's direction is known from one spot. Why: intersecting bearings fix a point that one bearing cannot.
- [heuristic] Use a sighting of the supposed dead as the hinge of the twist, with the deduction following from it rather than replacing it. When: Constructing the moment a presumed death is overturned. Why: A concrete sighting gives the player a fixed point to test the deduction against.
- [procedure] 1) Map windows, glass partitions, lamps and surfaces on a plan. 2) Mark the witness's position. 3) Check whether light, distance and obstruction allowed the claimed observation. When: Testing a witness claim of seeing or hearing something. Why: A plan lets each claimed observation be checked against physical constraints.
- [pitfall] A single sighting can be explained in many ways, so it cannot identify anyone on its own. When: Drawing conclusions from one partial observation. Why: One data point leaves too many explanations open.
- [pitfall] Treating one directional reading as proof of a source is a mistake; the nearest structure on the bearing is not necessarily the source and must be checked.

## silhouette identification
- [mechanism] Partial clues, such as build, clothing, or a witness's silhouette-only sighting, narrow suspects without naming one; the player must combine them to identify a person. When: Designing witness clues with limited detail. Why: Partial clues reward combining them with other evidence.
- [behavior] Observers viewing a shadow or silhouette at distance see only outline and profile, so a similar figure can be mistaken for another person. When: The observer sees shape through a screen, blind, or at distance. Why: Silhouettes convey shape and profile but not facial features.
- [rule] Treat a silhouette, shadow, or single sighting as evidence of presence, not identity; name the person only after a clearer view or a second check. When: when a figure is seen only as a shadow or outline, or briefly in poor light. Why: A shape alone cannot distinguish one person from another; a resembling silhouette can belong to someone else. (x2)
- [rule] Let an item or NPC leave a recognizable scent, and add masking scents as deliberate cover-ups the player must see through. When: Designing scent-based clues in a generated dungeon.
- [rule] Give each scent profile to only a few NPCs, so each scent test is a real narrowing step rather than a dead end. When: Designing scent-based deduction in a dungeon.
- [rule] A stealth or deduction game can use scent as a clue type, where the player sniffs NPCs or objects and the game matches the profile against a list. When: Designing a deduction mechanic.
- [rule] Make a figure seen only as a silhouette identifiable by matching its outline to a known character, so the player must recognise the shape. When: When designing identification challenges in level content. Why: Outline recognition turns observation into a puzzle.
- [heuristic] Make NPCs identifiable by silhouette at range, such as a distinctive cloak or gait, while close-up verification of the face remains needed.
- [pitfall] A single sighting is a weak basis for a long watch, and a watch that one message can break is fragile.

## single revelation and reaction cues
- [behavior] A single incident can lead an observer to revise their reading of a person's feelings, so one event can reshape the whole picture of their character.
- [behavior] One past incident can become decisive character evidence, and a reputation built on it spreads through gossip and hints rather than fresh observation. When: a community forms a verdict on a person. Why: rumour repeats the incident without new observation.
- [heuristic] Do not treat one involuntary reaction (flinch, startle, probe response) as proof of guilt or future conduct; fear, grief, embarrassment, or innocence can cause it. Seek corroboration. When: the reaction or behaviour is the only evidence available. Why: the reaction does not identify its own cause.
- [heuristic] Do not confirm one striking clue or test result, such as an animal's response, until other facts corroborate it; a lone observation may be incomplete or mistaken. When: one dramatic clue points to a named culprit, or an identity test yields one striking result. Why: one observation can mislead, so corroboration is needed.
- [heuristic] Give the player one pointed question with clear options to an NPC that confirms a hidden state, such as a key holder or changed routine, not a long dialogue tree. When: designing dialogue where the player must pursue a line of inquiry. Why: clear options keep the questioning moving.
- [heuristic] A single recalled phrase is weak evidence, so use it as a lead that directs inquiry rather than as proof of motive.
- [pitfall] Depending on a single person to carry a reveal is fragile, because a delay or absence can make the reveal fail. When: Planning how a reveal will reach its audience. Why: One point of failure can stop the reveal from happening.
- [pitfall] A quiet reaction has many causes, so infer hiding only from a surrounding pattern of behavior, not from one silence.
- [pitfall] Do not treat one emotional moment as proof of inner life; it is a hint to be weighed with other evidence.

## social standing and pressure
- [mechanism] An NPC's social network can reveal relationships, debts or grudges that the player can use as motives. When: Designing NPC relationship systems that feed investigation. Why: Relationship data becomes actionable motive information.
- [mechanism] A spreading accusation cascade halts trade, drives people to flee, and can reach respected members of the community, since no one feels safe.
