- [rule] Make an honest skeptic's doubts partly correct; a skeptic written as plainly foolish makes the misdirection unfair. When: Writing an expert who doubts a suspect. Why: Players need a fair chance to side with the skeptic.
- [heuristic] Personal or social details may or may not bear on the crime, so check their relevance before acting on them.
- [pitfall] Investigators may hesitate before powerful suspects, letting high-status culprits escape while smaller suspects are caught. When: when a suspect's rank is high. Why: Social pressure can weaken the willingness to act on the same evidence.
- [pitfall] Trusting a witness because of social standing rather than checking the times they give.
- [pitfall] Social standing can push investigators toward hasty conclusions.
- [fact] In a small community, hostility often has several sources, so one visible grudge does not settle a case.
- [fact] An organisation that depends on one hidden leader may collapse if that leader is removed. When: Analyzing a group structured around a central figure. Why: Centralized control means the group has few functioning substitutes for its leader.

## specialist knowledge clues
- [definition] Specialist knowledge is the lore that lets a distinctive trace be matched to a small set of possible sources, such as a tobacco ash type, a footprint or a trade-shaped hand. When: when a trace is distinctive. Why: lore converts a trace into a narrow set of candidates.
- [mechanism] A specialist NPC giving a skill-based verdict, such as amateur or professional, can narrow the suspect list for the player.
- [rule] Do not claim a species identity without a matching reference; leave the name open until the evidence fits.
- [heuristic] Test a claimed expert by asking specific questions about names, dates and context in their field, and judge the answers rather than their confidence. When: Identity or expertise matters and a real expert's knowledge is available as reference. Why: A real practitioner answers specific questions easily while a pretender cannot.
- [heuristic] Extend appeals to specialist trade journals, where a sale record of a distinctive garment may be traced.
- [heuristic] Specialist analysis of physical traces can narrow a search, for example by showing that original documents exist rather than copies. When: When a search is unfocused and a specialist can examine traces. Why: Analysis tells the searcher what kind of object to look for and where it may be.
- [tradeoff] An unusual technique may narrow culprits to skilled people, but if applying the method needs little know-how, don't assume a specialist background. When: A rare technique suggests specialist skill; when the know-how required is small, the method implies nothing about background. Why: Specialist skill is rarer than general ability, yet the know-how needed to apply a substance may be small.
- [fact] A physical sign reads as clue only with the specialist knowledge behind it; without that lore, residues such as ash read as noise, so the lore must be learned first. When: a sign depends on specialist knowledge. Why: a sign has meaning only within the knowledge that interprets it; meaning depends on recognising the material.
- [fact] An animal's species indicates its habitat, so a creature found in a place can show where it has been living.

## staff witnesses and routines
- [behavior] Household staff reveal routines and private habits when sympathetic people comment on events, but deflect pointed questions; unlock their gossip through friendly conversation, not direct questioning. When: Investigating through servants or other staff. Why: Direct questioning signals a motive and gets refused, while sympathy invites talk.
- [behavior] Service staff who distrust police give guarded answers, so cooperation from them is limited. When: questioning hotel or service staff as an official. Why: Distrust of authority makes witnesses withhold information.
- [heuristic] Shop staff can act as witnesses who confirm buyers and say whether they recognize a suspect. When: when a trade record must be verified against people who handled it. Why: Staff can confirm records that documents alone cannot establish.
- [heuristic] Track staff changes before a death, since a replacement may be the person present at the critical moment. When: When staff were replaced shortly before a death.
- [heuristic] Ask household staff who recently left and whether the victim had recent guests, since answers can point to a specific person. When: Investigating a household crime.
- [metric] A high number of special formal meetings within a short period signals that a dispute has been pushed into formal procedure. When: tracking a conflict through community records. Why: Frequency of formal meetings reveals how far a conflict has been formalized.
- [fact] Staff who change employers can carry knowledge of a household to outside places, opening new routes for information.
- [fact] A staff member's recollection can supply a vehicle type and a departure time that written records do not contain.
- [fact] A long-serving household member can supply reliable knowledge of routine and local history that cannot be observed directly. When: Gathering background information from a servant or local resident. Why: Long familiarity gives access to patterns and history that a visitor would not know.

## stress and strain signs
- [mechanism] An NPC's stress threshold can trigger a volatile outburst that mixes true clues with false accusations. When: an NPC is under sustained questioning. Why: pressure lowers control over what is said.
- [behavior] Emotional strain can distort an investigator's judgement and push them to abandon investigation altogether.
- [behavior] Stress and confusion reduce recall, so a witness's silence on details may reflect the circumstances rather than concealment. When: a witness is questioned about a frightening period. Why: Stressful events impair memory of the details.
- [behavior] A person under strain may brood, lash out at work and neglect routine duties, all of which are visible to colleagues.
- [behavior] Sudden physical changes such as draining color, averted gaze, dry lips, or repeated mouth wiping often appear when a witness hears a sensitive name or fact. When: When a questioner raises a topic the witness wants to avoid. Why: Stress produces involuntary bodily reactions that betray concealed knowledge.
- [rule] Give a character a composure or stress meter so players notice holding back through behavior rather than through statements.
- [pitfall] A declaration signed in haste under emotional strain may read as hysteria rather than remorse, so it is unreliable as an account of facts. When: When a statement is written under pressure.
- [pitfall] A tester who holds the wrong reading explains away contrary facts with increasingly strained inferences rather than abandoning the reading. When: When a favored hypothesis faces growing contradictions. Why: Commitment to a reading makes each contradiction seem explainable.
- [pitfall] Financial strain can look like motive even when the accused is not personally responsible for the loss that caused it.

## suspect elimination logic
- [rule] Do not accept a door as an exit merely because it is near a trail's end; its direction and distance must match the prints.
- [rule] Keep the question of how someone entered separate from why they entered, since a thief who left an item behind poses a different problem.
- [rule] Make the character who controls entry to a sealed space the culprit or hazard, with that control shown on the page from the start. Why: players trust that character, so the lock is the trust placed in them.
- [heuristic] When a crime is suspected, check whether the body could practically be disposed of; if disposal would be implausible, doubt the crime explanation. When: Testing a murder theory against physical evidence. Why: Murder requires removing the body, so the logistics constrain which explanations are credible.
- [heuristic] A fact the investigator already holds can rule out a hypothesis that a clue seems to support.
- [heuristic] Give the public a false culprit with physical evidence, so the player must test that evidence rather than accept it. When: the public has already named a suspect. Why: Testing the evidence forces the player to reason about it instead of following the crowd.
- [heuristic] Treat only facts that agree across several independent accounts of the same event as firm; conflicting versions are not reliable. When: when sources disagree about an event.
- [pitfall] A system that looks airtight may depend on a human habit, such as forms relaxing over time, that becomes the real weak point. When: Assessing the security of a procedure-bound system. Why: Human routines can bypass formal safeguards.
- [fact] Elimination reaches a sound conclusion only when all of its premises are true; one false premise undermines the whole deduction. When: Concluding the culprit by eliminating other suspects. Why: The conclusion inherits any weakness in its premises.

## thin evidence and tiers
- [model] Rank evidence into three tiers: unwarrantable signs rejected outright, probable signs suggesting guilt or opening a path, and certain signs that alone can found a conviction. When: when ranking signs before relying on them for a verdict, or designing progression gated by evidence. Why: Ranking signs by reliability prevents weak signs from supporting strong conclusions; presumption and proof carry different weight.
- [model] A case against a suspect is commonly built on three elements: means, opportunity and motive. Each suspect can be scored against all three. When: Structuring a deduction or an investigation board. Why: Separating the elements shows which part of the case is strong and which is missing.
- [heuristic] Give an NPC a small set of questions, each unlocking a different clue, so the player's choice of what to reveal has a visible cost. When: Designing a dialogue puzzle with an information-controlling NPC. Why: Each reveal shifts the NPC's valuation of the player.
- [heuristic] When a suspect's matching item is unavailable, look for a third matching item, since a print may have come from a different pair. When: A suspect's own pair is elsewhere at the time. Why: An unexplained match implies another matching item exists.
- [heuristic] Give different levels of detail to different people, so that each information channel is controlled and a leak reveals only part of the plan. When: Protecting a trap with several people involved.
- [procedure] 1) Treat gossip as a lead only. 2) Trace it to a firm secondhand source. 3) Confirm it with physical proof before treating it as established.
- [pitfall] A thin first result can look like an excuse yet still hold valid evidence after more study. When: when an early examination yields little. Why: a first pass may miss detail that deeper study reveals.
- [pitfall] Handwriting comparison is inconclusive when the document is undated or the comparison material is thin.
- [fact] Thin staffing limits observation: a house with few servants has few people watching who comes and goes. When: Estimating what witnesses could have seen. Why: Fewer observers means fewer sightings.

## threat and danger
- [mechanism] An antagonist's threats or insanity claim, modeled as a dialogue system, can change what the player is able to prove.
- [behavior] A suspect who is threatened with exposure may attack the witness's character and sanity instead of answering the evidence, and dismiss the witness so she cannot continue. When: A witness has a fear or accusation but no proof. Why: Personal attacks shift the discussion away from facts that the suspect cannot rebut.
- [rule] A dialogue option that threatens escalation to a higher NPC should change the witness's answer and be logged as a consequence. When: Designing dialogue options that threaten escalation.
- [heuristic] Build a threat as a sequence of reversals, each showing that the danger is more deliberate than it first appeared. When: Structuring a story around a single victim and a hidden plot. Why: Each reversal raises stakes and recasts earlier events.
- [heuristic] An anonymous written threat with its stated demands is documentary evidence whose wording and form can be checked. When: when a letter with demands is found. Why: Written demands and their form can link a letter to its sender or purpose.
- [procedure] 1) Give a cold, firm demand to step back when a witness lunges. 2) Expect a shift to flattery or apology once the demand is obeyed. When: A witness becomes physically threatening during questioning. Why: A firm boundary restores control and often produces a mood swing.
- [procedure] 1) After a sudden death in custody, examine the body for the means as well as the cause. 2) Examine the surroundings for objects that could have supplied the means. When: A suspect dies suddenly during or after questioning. Why: The means of death often points to how the suspect obtained it and whether others were involved.
- [pitfall] A mocking suspect who attends the investigation gives a natural chance to leave unseen traces. When: A suspect is present during an investigation. Why: Physical presence and contact with objects create opportunities for unintended evidence.
- [pitfall] A provoking test that endangers the investigator or alerts the suspect before completion ruins the evidence and may cause harm. When: When designing an in-scene test of a suspect. Why: A premature or dangerous test removes the chance to observe the true reaction.

## trait and habit evidence
- [behavior] A single revealed trait can recast earlier events for the player, changing how they read facts already known.
- [rule] Add a character trait that rules out an action, so players can clear a suspect by reasoning from who that person is. When: a suspect is wrongly implicated. Why: trait-based reasoning gives players a legitimate way to eliminate suspects.
- [heuristic] A trait matching a clue can be a decoy; corroborate it with independent evidence, such as other candidates' possessions or recalled habits, like which hand they use for cards. When: a trait points to one suspect and needs support. Why: Independent observations test whether the trait is distinctive.
- [heuristic] A trait introduced as a light joke or teasing point can later become a key identifying clue, if it is recalled when it matters.
- [heuristic] Compare a suspect's visible trait, such as an injury or gait, with records kept by those who treated them. A surprising trait may be staged. When: When a visible trait is central to a suspect's identity. Why: Records made by people with no stake in the case are harder to fake.
- [heuristic] A small personal trait can change how a motive reads and can explain an action that physical evidence leaves unclear.
- [pitfall] Treating a physical trait as proof of identity, without checking when the trait first appears in the record, is an error.
- [fact] A trade shapes the hand, so hand form can reveal a person's occupation, including slaters, sailors, compositors and diamond-polishers, and can help identify unclaimed bodies. When: when examining a hand or body for occupation. Why: repetitive trade work leaves lasting physical marks.
- [fact] A body, its belongings and its surroundings carry evidence about habits, wealth and recent history that an expert can read as clues.

## unfounded accusations and suspicion
- [model] An accusation from an afflicted person has three possible explanations: the accused did the harm, a deceiver wore their likeness, or the accuser's perception was deceived. When: weighing an accusation from an afflicted person.
- [rule] Do not present an unproven suggestion as established fact or bluff without firm grounds; a bluff can collapse when a composed suspect denies it. Any admission must come from the suspect.
- [rule] Do not accuse publicly on moral conviction alone; without direct proof, an accusation risks the accuser's standing and can backfire as leverage.
- [rule] Do not press a suspect who is clearly unwell or not fit to make a statement. When: Before pressuring any suspect for a confession. Why: A statement from someone unfit is unreliable and the pressure can cause serious harm.
- [pitfall] A trait shown in an unrelated activity, or a past offense unrelated to honesty, does not reliably show anything about the crime or a present claim's falsity. (x2)
- [pitfall] Reading criminal intent into an arrangement may be wrong, since an alibi or precaution can have an innocent reason; the inference is a hypothesis to test. Why: Behaviour resembling crime has innocent explanations.
- [pitfall] A secret unconnected to the crime may still cast an innocent witness as a suspect once it comes out.
- [pitfall] Accusing someone of an unfounded private motive, such as an affair, can do serious damage; rumor-based motives should be treated as weak.
- [pitfall] An accusation that no one else can observe is hard to refute, which makes it dangerous as a basis for judgment.

## vague location and directions
- [mechanism] Vague landmark phrases fit several locations, so players reason over candidates and corroborate evidence until the place is narrowed. When: when NPCs or testimony describe a hidden place by a common feature or imprecise direction. Why: Common features appear in many places, so multiple candidates let evidence narrow the answer.
- [mechanism] Each round of accusations after an execution tends to reach people of higher social standing, so suspicion widens upward through the ranks. Why: Rank and rivalry decide who is named next.
- [rule] Do not locate an object from one sightline, because a single bearing gives only a direction, not a position.
- [rule] Pin down vague locations in witness accounts, such as near a window, with follow-up questions to narrow the search.
- [rule] Store guard patrol timings and sleep states as data so an alibi claim can be checked against the schedule. When: when implementing guard alibis in a game. Why: Stored schedules let the game and players verify claims objectively.
- [procedure] 1) Choose two fixed observation points. 2) Draw a sightline from each point to the splash or object. 3) Read where each sightline meets a fixed scale marker, counting from the same start. 4) The object lies where the two lines cross. When: An object was dropped into open water or a similar open area with a fixed reference line. Why: Two bearings fix a position where a single bearing gives only a direction.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the landmarks that still exist, using remnants like stumps to mark removed ones. 2) Recover missing measurements from another source. 3) Project the unknown position by proportion from a reference of known size. 4) Observe at the moment the instruction specifies. When: when directions are relative and some anchors may be missing. Why: Anchors and proportion turn vague instructions into a physical location.
- [pitfall] Vague labels such as eccentricity can explain almost anything, so they hide the premises instead of testing them.
- [pitfall] Vague time references such as past three or some hours later cannot be fixed without corroboration. When: When a witness gives loose time estimates. Why: Imprecise times need independent anchors.

## victim and remains identification
- [rule] Establish the victim's identity first, since every later deduction depends on it.
- [rule] Give an NPC's corpse a distinguishing mark, such as a scar or a missing item, that players can compare with the NPC's known description. When: Designing an identifiable body in a mystery.
- [heuristic] Burned remains can still identify what was destroyed; compare how the residue burns and look for less-charred fragments that reveal the original item. When: An object was partly or fully burned. Why: Burn patterns and surviving fragments preserve enough of the original to be recognized.
- [heuristic] When a face is too damaged to recognize, identify a person through lasting features: build, carriage, hair colour and small distinctive marks. When: identity must be fixed from disfigured remains or partial evidence. Why: Such features persist when the face is unusable.
- [heuristic] Let a victim refuse to name an attacker early, as a visible anomaly that hints the scene was staged. When: staged-crime design. Why: a supposed victim's silence signals that the scene was arranged.
- [procedure] 1) Find a specific, idiosyncratic physical mark on the remains. 2) Compare it with the known record of the candidate. 3) Accept identity only if the mark matches. When: Confirming identity from remains. Why: A specific mark is harder to fake than a general resemblance.
- [procedure] 1) Publish a reward notice describing the body, clothing and jewellery in detail. 2) Place it where the victim's circle or trade will read it. 3) Follow each lead that comes back. When: the victim is unknown and ordinary inquiry has failed.
- [procedure] 1) Recover the object and link it to the body part or fragment. 2) Document the discovery process and location. 3) Check whether the identifying item is unique before accepting an identity. When: Establishing identity from items found separately from remains. Why: An object is only as strong as its uniqueness and the chain of discovery that connects it to the person.
- [fact] Human remains keep permanent identifiable structures over long periods, and identification has been possible from remains recovered from furnace ashes. When: Assessing whether remains can later be identified after attempted destruction. Why: Bone and structure persist through many destructive processes.

## victim identity and claims
- [mechanism] Subverting the expected victim: make the apparent target the one drawn toward the threat, so the reveal reverses the audience's assumption about who is in danger. When: When designing a stray-animal or monster mystery with a companion NPC. Why: Players who expect the victim to be passive are surprised when the victim is the agent, which strengthens the reveal.
- [mechanism] When a victim's own information, such as a schedule, is used by an opponent, that information becomes the means to predict and intercept the opponent later. When: a character's ordinary information is visible to a threat. Why: Turning the victim's knowledge against the thief lets the pursuer anticipate a waypoint.
- [mechanism] A document the victim left behind can reverse an accusation, showing the death was self-inflicted and clearing the suspect. When: a suspect is blamed for a death that the victim may have caused. Why: the victim's own record reframes the motive and removes the apparent killer.
- [behavior] A victim of high social standing may refuse to prosecute and resolve matters privately, so the investigator's findings may never reach the courts. When: when the victim has social influence. Why: Social standing gives the victim leverage to avoid public process.
- [rule] Make the victim's identity the hidden variable, and keep a checkable description such as hair color or a physical feature that players can compare against the body. When: authoring a murder mystery with an identity twist, or designing a body discovery scene. Why: A checkable description lets the player detect the mismatch, so the reversal is fair; a recognition or hesitation turns a passive body into an active lead.
- [heuristic] Let the injured party be a possible culprit, so the investigation tests the player's trust in the victim. When: A crime is staged or the victim has a hidden stake. Why: A victim who may have caused the crime turns the investigation into a question of trust.
- [heuristic] Let the victim's own belongings become the evidence that moves suspicion, so an ordinary object shifts the theory. When: Introducing a physical clue in a mystery. Why: A personal item ties the crime to the victim and redirects suspicion.
- [heuristic] Keep the victim's identity uncertain, with conflicting accounts, until the reveal, since confusion over who died can be a deliberate design tool. When: the reveal depends on who the victim was. Why: Uncertainty holds attention and makes the eventual identification a payoff.
- [pitfall] Do not treat a victim's movements as proof of identity until other traces confirm the path. When: Tracing a victim's route. Why: An unconfirmed route can lead to the wrong suspect.

## visitor identification
- [mechanism] When an expected visitor enters, a trigger can change an NPC's behavior, with preset detention or dialogue outcomes. Why: a scripted state change responds to the arrival of a specific character.
- [mechanism] Visits to an isolated person can serve as channels that carry names and claims out to outsiders. When: when a confined or isolated person receives regular visitors. Why: Visitors pass on what they hear to others.
- [rule] Do not treat a glimpse made under stress or at night as proof of identity.
- [rule] Ask what an unauthorized visitor came to obtain, since the purpose points to something overlooked in the scene. When: Someone entered a place without authorization. Why: Purpose reveals targets the scene may still hide.
- [heuristic] A visitor who leaves visibly shaken signals that the news they carried was grave. When: a visitor leaves visibly upset after a conversation.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the name a visitor gives with what the employer and other witnesses reported. 2) Check whether the visit matches the normal official process. 3) Count independent sources supporting the claim. When: A visitor gives a name, acts eccentric and refuses to wait, or an authority figure asks for something valuable that cannot be checked directly. Why: A mismatch in name, process or sources can expose impersonation.
- [procedure] 1) Collect visit accounts from several witnesses. 2) Build a combined visit history with dates and entry points. 3) Check each entry against at least one other source. 4) Look for a repeated pattern. When: a timeline depends on entries that a single checkpoint does not record. Why: cross-checked sources reveal patterns that one record would miss.
- [pitfall] A person who visits a crime scene is not necessarily the culprit; a later intruder may be a different party. When: Interpreting a stakeout's results. Why: Assuming a single identity for everyone who returns leads to wrong conclusions.
- [pitfall] A shared description such as approximate age or poor clothing is a weak link on its own and should not be treated as proof of identity. When: Matching an unidentified body or person to a known individual. Why: Many people share such general traits.

## witness availability and access
- [behavior] In settings where most people are indoors or unwell, fewer people move about, so a suspect is less likely to be seen. When: crowded or sparse settings such as a rough crossing. Why: Fewer people are present to notice the suspect.
- [rule] Keep witnesses in the area until a scripted later event and require attendance at further questioning unless prevented; highest-stakes claims also need physical presence. When: when a statement must be tested in person, or a scripted investigation has a later hearing. Why: a filed statement alone cannot answer new questions; witnesses who leave the scene cannot be used in later stages. (x2)
- [rule] Test a witness's account against known facts only if the witness had access to the events in question. Why: a witness without access cannot confirm or refute the record.
- [rule] Separate the witness pool so an NPC linked to the accuser's faction cannot vouch for the accused. When: designing NPC testimony systems.
- [heuristic] Order witness lists by urgency so the most perishable leads come first. When: designing a timed investigation.
- [heuristic] When a witness did not report something she would probably have seen, such as paper in a person's hand, that absence can count against a theory. When: A witness was positioned to observe a detail that the theory requires. Why: A predicted observation that never appears weakens the theory.
- [heuristic] Witnesses who cover different segments of the same night can jointly support an alibi that no single witness could, since each fills gaps the others leave open. When: when several household members or associates account for one period. Why: combined coverage closes gaps left by any one account.
- [heuristic] When a witness's account is the only account, ask who was prevented from speaking with that witness. When: Assessing a single-source account. Why: Restricted access signals that the account has not been checked.
- [pitfall] A large number of witnesses is not proof when they may share a single source, so count independent sources rather than people.

## witness echo and repetition
- [behavior] A witness who has already heard others' stories can repeat them convincingly.
- [behavior] A witness who merely echoes another's claims is likely coached, and comparing their statements exposes the echo. When: two witnesses give similar accounts. Why: Coaching produces repetition rather than independent recall.
- [rule] Treat an embedded narrator's account as testimony to check against outside facts, since the narrator's claim of truth confirms nothing. When: when a narrator swears the account is true. Why: A narrator who has a stake in the outcome can shape what is remembered.
- [heuristic] Treat a retold account as partial when the intermediary admits omitting or altering details; infer what was left out from the marked gaps. When: evidence reaches the investigator through an intermediary. Why: Marked omissions show where the record is incomplete.
- [heuristic] Repeat a single word a witness has used, which can prompt them to name a person or place they had kept back.
- [heuristic] A pattern that explains one clue but not the rest is a candidate, not an answer; test it against every other detail first. When: a scene's details echo a known story or name.
- [pitfall] A witness who repeats the investigator's exact wording may be echoing an earlier answer or the investigator, so the claim needs testing.
- [pitfall] Accepting an account because a second agrees confuses agreement with independent proof; accusers who drew on the same suggestions count as one source, not many.
- [pitfall] A witness's account can be shaped by what they have already heard, including the investigator's own words, so later agreement is weak evidence. When: Questioning a witness after the investigator has named a theory. Why: A witness who adopts a term offered to them may not have observed the thing described.

## witness role and leverage
- [behavior] A non-suspect who has seen a hidden act may use that knowledge as leverage, offering mutual silence in exchange for silence. When: A minor character witnessed the protagonist's secret. Why: Knowing a secret gives the witness a bargaining position.
- [behavior] A person who turns away from the observer while reading or speaking hides the face the observer would otherwise read for tells. When: someone reads or answers with their back turned.
- [behavior] A witness loyal to a suspect is more likely to speak when told honest answers are safe and the matter can be handled discreetly. When: witness is fond of or loyal to the suspect. Why: fear of exposure or public scandal keeps witnesses silent.
- [rule] Plant the sleight in plain view with a detail that seems minor to the characters but is noticed by one witness.
- [heuristic] Let a witness be both source and suspect, so the person who reports a sighting is later investigated in turn.
- [heuristic] Give a torn witness a constructive step, such as speaking to the suspect themselves, so they feel involved rather than accused. When: witness is split between loyalty and suspicion. Why: feeling accused makes witnesses defensive.
- [heuristic] Use a witness report, such as a description of an unusual person, to locate the real figure behind an apparent attack. When: Designing how a detective finds the true culprit. Why: A witness's description narrows the search and leads to a confession or proof.
- [tradeoff] Witnesses giving sympathetic but vague accounts work as red herrings, while witnesses giving precise, verifiable details work as reliable clue sources. When: Designing NPC testimony for a mystery. Why: Vague testimony misleads without contradiction, while precise testimony can be cross-checked by the player.
- [pitfall] A witness who switches sides may be deliberately staging the turn; treating it as mere delusion misses the deception. When: a witness changes allegiance mid-case. Why: The turn itself can be the tactic.

## assumption tracking and revision
- [mechanism] Revising a single assumption about a witness's knowledge can overturn the whole reading of an event.
- [rule] Challenge the shared assumptions of witnesses and officials about who acted and how they escaped, and test each assumption rather than accepting it.
- [rule] Record which assumption the player accepts during a leading interrogation, so later evidence can reveal the assumption as wrong.
- [pitfall] A wrong assumed dimension, tool, or any unchecked assumption propagates its error into every dependent deduction and plan, so confident conclusions and plans fail.
- [pitfall] Explanations of a plotter's hesitation rest on assumptions about their reasoning, which cannot be tested directly. Why: Motives and judgments are not observable, so the explanation remains provisional.
- [pitfall] Assuming a reconstruction is complete can mislead, because a single overlooked small object can change how an event actually happened.
- [pitfall] Mixing a witness's assumptions with their observations leads to false identifications.
- [pitfall] Accepting the first explanation that matches an assumption, such as a belief that a given person would never commit a crime, closes off the real line of inquiry.

## body traits evidence
- [mechanism] Incomplete remains can still indicate age, build and health, so a partial body can narrow identity even without identifying parts. When: Only some remains are available for analysis. Why: Size, bone structure and wear reflect a person's physical characteristics.
- [rule] Heritable physical traits, such as build, ear shape, face shape, and pigment, can support a hypothesis of kinship but are not confirmation alone. When: When suspecting a family link from appearance. Why: Resemblance suggests a relation but does not prove it.
- [heuristic] To infer a hidden person's height, start from an object of known size and the height at which they touched it. When: the person is unseen but has leaned on or handled an object.
- [heuristic] Height from marks is not conclusive on its own, so combine it with other evidence such as a physical trait before identifying a person. When: When identifying a person from marks. Why: Many people share similar reach.
- [heuristic] Hand condition, such as broken nails or hard skin, can contradict a person's apparent class or occupation.
- [heuristic] Record a victim's normal daily routine and health, so a sudden decline is judged against a known baseline. When: Harm appears suddenly after a day of ordinary activity. Why: Without a baseline, normal and abnormal condition cannot be told apart.
- [pitfall] An injury pattern may suggest a left-handed attacker, but treating that suggestion as proof of who acted confuses a narrowed possibility with identity.
- [fact] Human hair grows about six inches a year, a rate that lets traces along a strand be dated.

## case structure and chaining
- [model] A chain-of-investigations mystery widens the case: each new client, body or suspect opens a fresh question, growing from a small missing-person case into a larger conspiracy.
- [rule] Structure a quest as a chain in which each clue leads to the next, so each new clue becomes a further thread to pull. When: Designing a multi-step investigation. Why: A chain of linked clues sustains progression.
- [rule] Give a closed set of NPCs shared routines and let community gossip supply partial, biased clues that players can verify or discard. When: Designing a village-based cast of characters. Why: Shared routines make each character's movements checkable, and biased gossip rewards verification.
- [heuristic] Release quest information through a chain of messages, with each step revealing more than the last, and gate the next revelation behind a timed event. When: Designing message-based quest progression. Why: A chain with timed gates gives the player a real reason to wait and a growing picture.
- [procedure] 1) Stage a crime that looks impossible, motiveless, or misread, within a plausible premise. 2) Make a plausible or convenient suspect or official explanation the first accusation. 3) Reverse it with a planted physical trace, changing culprit or events late. 4) Expose the culprit with a trap or confession. When: Designing a series or a set of self-contained mysteries. Why: A repeated structure makes each case recognisable and testable.
- [procedure] 1) Deliver a found item as the first link. 2) Send the player to a destination that the item points to. 3) Reveal a dead witness's record as the final link. Each link unlocks the next. When: When a reveal should build dread through delay and partial evidence. Why: A chain of partial items controls what the player learns and when, and holds back the most disturbing detail until late.
- [pitfall] Letting the client set investigation priority can push the investigation away from authorities who may be needed later. When: A reluctant client avoids official channels and sets the agenda. Why: Client priorities may exclude help that becomes necessary later.
- [fact] A collection of case studies can be built on one repeated formula: an accusation, a build-up of testimony, a turn that reframes the evidence, and an outcome set by a formal authority. When: Designing a series of similar encounters rather than one continuous plot. Why: A stable cycle lets each case feel distinct while the player learns one pattern to test against.

## clue discriminating power
- [rule] Do not treat every clue as planted; decide whether the offender could have placed it before accepting or rejecting it. When: Evaluating a clue that may be staged. Why: Some clues are genuine, so blanket suspicion discards real evidence.
- [rule] Give each major clue at least two plausible readings so a later discovery can flip the player's conclusion. When: designing key evidence in a mystery. Why: ambiguity lets new facts reverse the player's interpretation.
- [rule] Give every false solution a real, checkable clue, so each wrong suspect is supported by evidence the player can test. Why: Each suspect survives until its own clue is disproved.
- [heuristic] A clue that fits both an explanation and a rival cannot discriminate between them and settles nothing alone; check whether a match actually discriminates. When: Two readings fit one piece of evidence. Why: Matching patterns can arise whether an item is genuine or forged; a clue that supports more than one account cannot settle the question alone.
- [heuristic] An expected action that never happens can count as evidence of what is not occurring.
- [pitfall] Treating a physical test as conclusive is a mistake when the tester's strength or skill differs from the suspect's. When: a test is run by someone with different physical capability. Why: The result shows what that tester could do, not what the suspect could do.
- [pitfall] A reveal that depends on a clue the audience has never seen leaves the audience unconvinced. When: Planning the final reveal of a mystery. Why: Audiences cannot verify a solution built on evidence they never encountered.
- [fact] Throwing with the non-dominant hand reaches much less far, so a thrown object's landing distance can expose the thrower's handedness.

## clue-driven narrowing and hypotheses
- [model] Several separate clues, such as a note, a sighting and a mismatched grave, can converge on one hidden space and one faked death, making the reveal one payoff. Why: Converging clues make the final explanation feel earned rather than arbitrary.
- [mechanism] Tracking which candidate explanations each discovered clue eliminates lets the player's notes narrow gradually instead of jumping to a single answer. When: A mystery encounter offers a fixed set of candidate causes tied to clues. Why: Incremental elimination rewards investigation and keeps the answer earned rather than guessed.
- [behavior] A physical clue gains meaning for players only when a social fact is attached to it, such as who knew a word or who had access. When: Revealing a mechanism through environmental evidence. Why: Without the social link, a physical trace reads as an object rather than a solvable puzzle.
- [rule] Build a reversal in which an ally turns out to be the antagonist, supported by clues planted earlier such as signals, timing and explanations. When: Designing a twist in a narrative. Why: Planted clues make the reversal fair and satisfying.
- [rule] Let a time clue and an identity clue combine, so the player can narrow the suspect pool to one person.
- [heuristic] A quest chain where a clue such as a changed NPC habit unlocks a search sub-goal makes investigation feel earned. When: Designing investigation chains in a game. Why: Gating the search behind a clue ties the action to earned evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Show a detail that appears to confirm a suspect's account. 2) Later reveal a physical detail that undermines it. 3) Let the player re-read the earlier confirmation as false. When: designing a suspect whose story should collapse. Why: The player's belief reverses only after they have accepted the first confirmation.
- [tradeoff] Establish identity cumulatively from several small matching details, or via one decisive identifier in a small visible mark seen earlier; the single mark suits identity twists. When: Designing how a character's identity is revealed. Why: Cumulative details reward attention; a mark seen earlier keeps the reveal fair and recognisable.

## confidentiality constraints
- [behavior] A promise of confidentiality given before testimony shapes what the witness discloses, so the assurance itself affects the evidence. When: when eliciting an account from a stakeholder. Why: A witness who expects protection tends to speak more freely.
- [rule] Information given in confidence limits how it can be used and blocks the checks needed to test it, so verify a damaging claim before relying on it; a relative may be shielding someone. When: An informant or relative gives information in confidence, or asks that a damaging claim be kept secret. Why: Confidentiality blocks the very check the investigator needs to test the claim.
- [rule] Ask a person for discretion rather than silence: name what they may keep to and what they should avoid saying. When: Enlisting a bystander who must not spread sensitive information. Why: A specific request is easier to follow than a general demand for secrecy.
- [rule] Block a question about a protected source or an unhelpful opinion only after checking whether the answer would change the outcome, not merely because it is uncomfortable. When: when a question touches a sensitive source or is uncomfortable to answer. Why: uncomfortable questions can still bear on the outcome.
- [procedure] 1) Tell each person only what their role requires. 2) Withhold the cause when it would harm them or the case. 3) Give each listener a clear, limited role. 4) Ask them for discretion about what they learn. When: An investigator must inform or enlist people during a sensitive case. Why: Narrow disclosure protects the case and gives each person a defined part to play.
- [pitfall] A suspect who asks for confidentiality under questioning may be showing pressure rather than innocence. When: a suspect requests privacy during questioning.
- [pitfall] A confidentiality promise is only as strong as the channels it passes through; a public hearing can expose what was promised to stay private.
- [pitfall] An assurance of secrecy may not hold, and other people may still face consequences after a confession. When: Offering protection to a suspect in exchange for a confession.

## conflicting documents records
- [mechanism] In-world maps that describe the same landmark differently across versions force the player to compare sources and decide which is right. When: when designing map artefacts for a mystery or exploration puzzle. Why: Differing descriptions create a comparison task that rewards careful reading.
- [rule] When two dated instructions conflict, the later one, especially if marked urgent, supersedes the earlier; the date sequence decides which instruction stands.
- [rule] Include in-world documents that conflict with a later NPC's legend, and let players verify the claim by visiting the site.
- [heuristic] Present conflicting in-world sources, like a witness annotation correcting an earlier one or two side-by-side documents, so players judge which account to believe and why, weighing author motives. (x2)
- [heuristic] When an owner's belongings point to a different origin than their stated identity, keep both readings open rather than trusting either. Why: Objects and people can point in different directions, so one clue alone does not settle origin.
- [heuristic] Conflicting facts are a starting point for ordering a case, not a sign that the investigation has failed.
- [pitfall] Two conflicting times often describe two separate events rather than a contradiction, so check what each time measures before ruling one account false. When: a clock time and an event time disagree. Why: different clocks and different events are easily confused.
- [pitfall] Ignoring conflicting dates across a source chain hides errors; the reader must decide which source to trust and note why. When: Sources give different dates for one event.

## dialogue and lecture reveals
- [rule] Script a confrontation so a line of dialogue reveals a language or ability the player can notice and act on. When: when an NPC has been described as lacking a skill. Why: contradictions between description and speech reward attention.
- [heuristic] Design an NPC offer whose meaning shifts with the player's knowledge, so a player who recalls a fact hears the same line as a threat. When: writing dialogue with hidden meaning. Why: the same words carry different weight given what the listener knows.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC withhold a fact until the player has combined the contradictions or gaps they noticed, and present the dialogue as a sequence of inconsistencies the player can point out. When: Designing dialogue that reveals a secret through player reasoning. Why: Each point the player raises unlocks the next admission, which rewards collecting evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Withhold the conclusion while planting the clues. 2) Reveal the conclusion at a chosen moment. 3) Walk through the reasoning in order, linking each early clue to the answer. When: Closing a mystery where the solution depends on earlier clues. Why: Ordered recaps let the audience see how seemingly minor details form the solution.
- [tradeoff] Layered presentation makes each link checkable but can make the combined case look stronger than its foundations, since stacked inferences add apparent weight. When: a case rests on inference rather than physical proof. Why: each added layer can seem to confirm the last.
- [tradeoff] Layered testimony makes an account partly unreliable without making it false, but stacking too many filters leaves the audience unable to tell what happened. When: Designing how much intermediation a story uses. Why: Each filter adds doubt, and too many erase the core facts.
- [pitfall] Delivering the full explanation at once reads as a lecture and drains the reveal's impact; spread it out so the audience can confirm it from earlier clues. When: the full solution is delivered at once. Why: Too much exposition at once overwhelms the audience.
- [pitfall] Leaving an overheard scene early can miss the rest of the statement, which may change its meaning.

## discrepancy analysis
- [rule] Treat witness discrepancies as contradictions to resolve and clues to observer state, not noise; call them evidence, not proof, until you know what each witness could perceive. When: when accounts of one event conflict. Why: Differences reveal each observer's state and vantage, and a witness may have inferred rather than observed. (x2)
- [rule] Question a witness about discrepancies only when you hold independent evidence to test any admission against.
- [rule] Design a puzzle event so some hypotheses are clearly ruled out, and avoid events that every theory explains since they give the player no information. When: When scripting a deduction event for the player. Why: Only outcomes that discriminate between hypotheses advance the player's reasoning.
- [heuristic] Decide between rival readings of a trace by naming and applying a test whose outcome differs between them, such as whether enough material remains to analyze. When: When a trace fits more than one explanation. Why: A named test turns an open question into a checkable one.
- [heuristic] Test a theory by asking for something it predicts a guilty party would refuse, so the answer discriminates between the theory and innocence. When: a theory predicts a specific reaction. Why: A yes or no then carries information.
- [heuristic] A detail that fails to match the expected fact, such as a house number differing from the given address, signals a deliberate misdirect. Why: Checking small inconsistencies exposes a planted lure.
- [procedure] 1) List each point where the witness's account conflicts with the evidence. 2) Order the points from least to most dangerous. 3) Put each point to the witness in turn. 4) Record each answer exactly as it is spoken. When: a witness has already given a checkable statement. Why: Ordered questioning builds pressure gradually and keeps answers reliable.
- [procedure] 1) Establish a known inventory of the container or space. 2) Compare its present state against that inventory. 3) Treat a missing item as evidence only if it was known to be present before. When: When a space or container may have been entered or disturbed. Why: Comparison against a known baseline is what makes an absence meaningful.

## disguised speech and writing
- [mechanism] Model disguised speech or hidden faces as partial information with a reveal condition, so identity is only confirmed once the condition is met. When: when designing concealed identities. Why: Gating reveals keeps uncertainty meaningful.
- [heuristic] Disguised handwriting suggests concealment; study strokes, capitals and spacing, but a single known-sample comparison is weak evidence since disguise can match by chance. When: When analyzing an anonymous or unusual handwriting. Why: Disguise can match or mismatch a sample by chance. (x2)
- [heuristic] When disguise hides common letters, a single recurring habit carries much more weight as evidence of a shared author. When: Samples are deliberately disguised. Why: Disguise removes most ordinary letter cues.
- [heuristic] Speech that sounds unnaturally exaggerated may indicate a deliberately disguised voice, suggesting concealment of identity. When: when a speaker's manner seems artificial. Why: Disguise is a common way to hide who is speaking.
- [heuristic] Include lines of questioning that seem irrelevant to hide the real purpose and avoid alerting other witnesses. When: a group shares one story and one member could warn the others.
- [heuristic] A disguised NPC can be identified by a voice line, distinctive gesture or uncovered feature rather than appearance, and a player's disguise can fail on a fixed detail a guard remembers. When: designing disguise mechanics for characters. Why: fixed details give players and NPCs a way to detect disguises.
- [pitfall] Word-based conclusions mislead when the writer chose words deliberately for disguise, and others may reasonably contest them.
- [fact] A disguised handwriting does not hide the writer from a physical trace such as a thumbprint, which can identify them. Why: physical traces are independent of how the writing looks.

## documents and written evidence
- [behavior] A written notice can act as a barrier, setting the terms of contact and shaping expectations before any dialogue occurs. When: A suspect communicates access terms through a written warning. Why: A written warning frames the encounter and raises stakes without direct confrontation.
- [heuristic] Writing a sensitive reveal instead of saying it aloud makes the claim seem discreet and gives the reader a reason to hide the method. When: Delivering a private reveal in a performance. Why: Written delivery frames the claim as confidential, which lends it credibility.
- [heuristic] A single document that explains several earlier anomalies at once makes the proof feel satisfying and complete. When: confirming a hidden cause near the climax. Why: One source accounting for many clues ties the investigation together.
- [heuristic] Introduce an unexplained document early, so a later reveal can reclassify it, such as proving it a forgery.
- [tradeoff] Wide distribution helps a hidden clue survive but also lets other readers find it, so the designer must accept that others may discover it. When: when choosing how many copies of a clue-bearing document exist. Why: Every copy that aids survival is also a copy that the wrong person can read.
- [pitfall] If an observer's accurate work is never shown, the audience will also discount them, so the device has no payoff. When: Using a discredited character as a clue source. Why: The audience judges the character by the same label the group uses.
- [fact] A written statement of cause, shown to the examining doctor, records the cause in writing and can prevent others being suspected of poisoning.
- [fact] Naming independent witnesses to a document's signing gives a revealed document standing as valid once its hidden text is exposed. When: Resolving a dispute over a document's validity. Why: Witnesses to the signing support the document's claim to be genuine.

## doubles and impostors
- [model] A blackmailer who seems to be an outside stranger can be a second agent of the victim's own family, hidden by costume. When: Blackmail or extortion plots with an apparently external threat. Why: Costume hides the family link, so the outsider assumption survives until the disguise is exposed.
- [model] One antagonist can appear under two personas, each carrying a different clue; the player must notice that the clues belong to the same person.
- [mechanism] A character who shares the protagonist's name, appearance or birthday produces unease that grows as each shared trait accumulates. When: when introducing a doppelgänger rival. Why: each matching trait is noticeable and adds to the suspicion.
- [mechanism] A character's repeated habits, such as nightly checks or fixed watching, create standing unease and suspicion before any proof exists. When: A character is suspicious but has no hard evidence yet. Why: Recurring behavior signals menace that players read as a threat without proof.
- [heuristic] Plant early, checkable clues about a doubling or disguised character, such as matching name, birthday or appearance, or an odd stare, and leave them unexplained until the reveal. When: when planning a rival, mirror or disguised character. Why: early, checkable traits or oddities give players a fair thread to verify and pull later.
- [heuristic] Reveal each disguise as an impostor so the antagonist resets to a new face while the same enemy persists, letting the player meet it again in a new form. When: Designing a recurring antagonist who keeps hiding. Why: A new face gives a fresh reveal without changing the threat.
- [heuristic] Give the enemy a repeated signature, such as a number or a trace, that appears across different suspects so the player can link the crimes. When: Tying together crimes by a disguised or hidden enemy. Why: A recurring mark lets the player trace the enemy even when the face changes.
- [heuristic] Stage the protagonist's apparent death at the midpoint, then let the player's assumption of safety become the trap for the next scene. When: Planning a midpoint pivot in a suspense story. Why: The false death resets the stakes and makes the player doubt their sense of safety.

## dropped theories and hypotheses
- [rule] An investigator may drop a case when the key witness will not testify and the offender has shown real remorse, rather than prosecute a case that would collapse. When: the case depends on an unwilling witness and the offender is remorseful. Why: a prosecution that would collapse gains nothing, and punishment may prevent reform.
- [rule] Drop a candidate explanation when no motive can be found for it, even if it was briefly considered earlier. When: evaluating a candidate explanation.
- [rule] Drop a theory when a verified timeline places the suspect elsewhere at the critical time. Reopen the question if the alibi witnesses are themselves involved.
- [tradeoff] Drop a hypothesis once a test or confirmed fact refutes it, since clinging hides the true answer; yet treat rejected explanations as branch points, not dead ends. When: A tentative theory or candidate explanation is refuted by a test or confirmed fact. Why: Holding onto refuted theories wastes effort and misleads the inquiry. (x2)
- [pitfall] Dropping a dissenting conclusion from the record hides an unresolved possibility that later evidence may need. When: when a participant holds a different verdict.
- [pitfall] Dropping explanations too early can hide the true cause, so keep alternatives under consideration until testing rules them out. When: When reasoning toward a single explanation. Why: A premature conclusion can close off the correct account.
- [pitfall] Dropping a planted contradiction without a later answer leaves the player with an unresolved and frustrating loose end. When: a statement conflicts with another. Why: each contradiction needs a later resolution.
- [pitfall] A reconstruction can drift away from its purpose; once the reason for the tally is lost, the arithmetic answers no question. When: A person starts a sum and forgets why they began it. Why: A tally is only useful for the question it was meant to answer.

## evidence chain overturning
- [definition] A reasoned reversal is a mystery where deduction from a physical detail overturns the lead suspect, rather than a new witness or confession alone.
- [rule] Frame a visible suspect with overwhelming evidence and one contradicting clue; reinterpreting a dismissed clue can clear the suspect and redirect the case. When: designing mystery plots.
- [rule] A general rule is overturned only by a competing general rule, not by a few counterexamples.
- [rule] Reject an explanation whose key act would simply be overridden by a later event that could happen, since that act cannot explain the puzzle. When: an explanation relies on an action that a later action would reverse. Why: a reversed action does not account for the observed result.
- [heuristic] Set up a plausible early impression, then overturn it with a hidden clue players can verify independently; reward those who find it over those picking the expected answer. When: designing clue sequences or pacing a mystery's early scenes. Why: Unsettled expectations keep attention engaged.
- [heuristic] A witness who saw only the end of a chain can confirm the outcome but cannot explain how the object reached that point. When: A witness joins the story late or from a distance. Why: Without the earlier events, the witness has no basis for the earlier links.
- [pitfall] A baseline built from partial records, such as one person's memory, can produce false gaps that do not reflect real absence. When: Records are incomplete or come from a single source. Why: Missing records look like missing objects.
- [pitfall] If a verification method is later ruled unlawful or unusable, every result it produced loses standing, even results that were presented as proof at the time. When: a trial or check whose method is later judged invalid. Why: its outcomes depended on the method's legitimacy.

## low-value and weak clues
- [mechanism] When available valuables are small, a theft motive looks implausible, which pushes players toward other explanations.
- [behavior] Rooms holding items of little resale value are unlikely to be disturbed by thieves, so their hidden contents tend to stay undisturbed. Why: Thieves seek goods they can sell.
- [behavior] A small payment paired with a claim that the evidence is worth little can prompt a source to offer more to prove its value. Why: Sources may want to defend their worth.
- [rule] Treat overheard rumours as low-reliability clues or log entries, upgrading them only when an independent second source confirms them. When: When designing rumour clues or building a witness log for an investigation. (x2)
- [rule] Use magnification and raking, low-angle light to reveal small traces that plain lighting hides. When: When a scene is weathered or handled and remaining evidence is faint or small. Why: Low-angle light casts shadows that bring out surface relief.
- [rule] Use small, low-stakes probes when proof is lacking or a direct accusation would cause scandal.
- [heuristic] Low-status workers such as stable-hands or servants often know routines, visitors and habits, see more than the powerful suppose, and share for small rewards, but are unreliable by default. When: Seeking routine information about a target. Why: Routine contact gives them observations others lack.
- [heuristic] Several facts pointing the same way do not prove guilt when none shows timing or exclusivity; they remain circumstantial. When: Building a case from circumstantial evidence. Why: Coincidence can explain several weak facts together.

## misleading clues and false evidence
- [mechanism] An object that looks like a plain fact can actually be a message; its meaning stays hidden until later evidence reframes it as a route or identity clue. When: Designing a mystery where an item is found early but interpreted late. Why: Players reread a mundane item differently once it gains a new meaning, which rewards careful attention.
- [rule] Let a confession mislead the audience by seeming to resolve the case, then show it is false through later evidence. When: a false confession is used as a reversal. Why: A believed confession makes its overturning feel stronger.
- [rule] Give each false solution one fact that is true and one interpretation that is wrong, so the suspect stays damning until a later fact reframes it. Why: A true fact makes the wrong inference feel reliable.
- [heuristic] A clue traced back to the victim can mislead the player into thinking the victim controlled events, when another person did. When: a purchase or record leads to the victim. Why: Tracing a clue to its owner feels like progress even when it points the wrong way.
- [heuristic] Physical traces such as footprints can belong to a visitor who frightened the victim, not to a killer, so their meaning should be reinterpreted late. When: Writing evidence that initially suggests an attack. Why: Reinterpreting an early clue changes the case without new physical evidence.
- [heuristic] Mislead with a gendered or appearance-based description and let the reveal correct it, so players form a wrong picture of the hidden character. When: describing an unseen or hidden character early in a scenario. Why: Players accept the first description and only revise it when a later reveal contradicts it.
- [pitfall] Negative test results can mislead players into trusting the source they were told to ignore; the one unverified source is often the true culprit's domain. When: Lab tests or analyses clear the obvious suspects early in a mystery. Why: Clean results appear to close the question, so the unexamined source stays hidden.
- [pitfall] A planted clue that is too neat, pointing obviously at the wrong person, can betray the staging. When: Designing or judging planted evidence. Why: Conspicuous pointing reads as artificial.

## misread motives and emotions
- [mechanism] An observer can misread a face or expression as hostile when a mundane cause, such as poor eyesight or effort to focus, produces the look. When: When judging mood or intent from a person's facial expression. Why: Physical strain or impairment can mimic anger or ill will.
- [behavior] A concealed motive can make a sincere act look suspicious, because observers see only the act and not its hidden cause. When: a hidden reason explains behaviour that observers misread. Why: the real explanation stays hidden from observers.
- [behavior] An observer who misreads another's fear or attachment may admit the error later in the same scene, correcting the misjudgment.
- [behavior] A single odd remark can show that the subject assumed a different visit, so a pretext can be read wrongly.
- [rule] Do not treat a missing motive as proof of innocence; keep alternative explanations open until each one is checked. When: when no motive has been found for a suspect. Why: an unfound motive may simply be unrecorded.
- [pitfall] A concealed motive misread as guilt can send an investigation after the wrong person.
- [pitfall] A reaction read as guilt may be interest, embarrassment or irritation, so the observer's hopes can bias the reading.
- [pitfall] Letting an offender go rests on the investigator's judgement of remorse, which can be wrong.

## missing documents and omissions
- [mechanism] A missing record can freeze a legal or administrative process, such as an estate, even when it does not prove the underlying fact. When: a process requires proof that a record provides. Why: Institutions act on documents, so a gap halts action regardless of what it implies.
- [rule] Note what a fragment is missing, such as the sender or date, and do not treat it as proof of authorship or fill the gaps with assumptions. When: Using an incomplete record as evidence. Why: Missing parts limit what the record can prove.
- [rule] Before reading deliberate intent into a gap in a document, check whether the gap is actually significant; many omissions are blind spots rather than planned outcomes. When: Interpreting an apparently strategic omission. Why: Treating every gap as malice leads to false conclusions.
- [heuristic] A missing document can supply motive, but its existence must be proved from another source such as a copy elsewhere. When: when a document is missing but its contents matter to motive. Why: An absent document cannot be assumed to have existed without corroboration.
- [heuristic] Examine what a document leaves out, such as a missing fallback for failure, because gaps can show the writer's assumptions as clearly as the terms do. When: Reading a document whose wording looks absurd or one-sided. Why: An omitted contingency often shows the writer never considered it.
- [procedure] 1) Compare the account against the expected facts. 2) Note any omitted item. 3) Ask about the omitted item directly. 4) Ask for small details, since they often give the best clues. When: A witness's account skips a key fact. Why: Gaps in testimony often point to the most important evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Work out the legal consequence of the document's absence for each party. 2) Identify who would lose or gain. 3) Establish when it was last seen and who could reach it. 4) Check for duplicates or records elsewhere. When: a missing item has financial or legal consequences.
- [pitfall] Missing one document, such as an unsigned will, can change who benefits from a death and invalidate the apparent motive. When: When an inheritance seems fixed. Why: Unfinalized documents leave benefits open.

## motive and causation
- [definition] A prevention motive is killing to stop someone from acting, such as a blackmailer, a political rival, or an inconvenient spouse. When: Classifying a suspect's prudential motive.
- [rule] Give an NPC a will or contract that creates motive, and let the player decide whether it is genuine or a lure toward the wrong suspect.
- [rule] A suspect gains from an outcome only if they knew its terms. Establish that knowledge before counting the outcome as a motive. Why: Benefit without awareness of the arrangement gives no reason to act.
- [heuristic] Treat an apparently simple death as a claim to test, and check facts that would contradict the obvious explanation before accepting it. When: a death or loss looks ordinary. Why: A simple-looking case can hide a different cause.
- [heuristic] When a dispute is framed as principle but a specific office is at stake, control of the appointment may be the strongest motive. When: a dispute involves a contested post or succession.
- [pitfall] Building a conspiracy from anecdotes that share a single source produces a pattern that depends on one unreliable account. When: Several reports seem to confirm one another. Why: Reports from a common source are not independent confirmation.
- [pitfall] Explaining a conflict only by one party's personal ambition overlooks long-standing feuds that divide the community.
- [pitfall] Treating a neighbor's anecdote about a different case as proof about this one; an analogy from another situation is not evidence here. When: When a prediction or verdict rests on a story from a different context. Why: Different circumstances can make the comparison invalid.

## motive and theft
- [definition] A gain motive is killing to obtain what another person holds, by theft or inheritance. When: Classifying a suspect's prudential motive.
- [mechanism] Revealing that apparent victims staged the affair turns the thief from actor into pawn, reversing his role in the story.
- [behavior] What a thief takes and what they miss reveals what they expected to find, which is evidence for analysing a theft. When: when analysing the pattern of a theft. Why: a thief's choices follow their information about the target.
- [behavior] The party who gains from a missing item is most likely to press a theory that it was stolen. When: Several parties have competing claims on the item. Why: They have a direct stake in the outcome.
- [rule] In a theft mystery, offer a cheap supernatural rumor alongside a plain thief, and let the return of the item separate them. When: Designing a theft quest with competing explanations. Why: Returning the item gives the player a test that favours one explanation.
- [heuristic] If goods were taken, a paid job becomes likelier; if nothing was taken, a financial motive weakens and a non-financial one such as punishment gains ground. When: Deciding between a paid crime and a revenge crime. Why: Robbery marks profit as the aim, so its presence or absence separates the two motives.
- [heuristic] When a stated motive seems too slight for the action taken, search for a hidden trigger in a passing detail or overheard remark. When: a narrator's reason does not match the consequences. Why: A small trigger can sit behind a casual explanation.
- [tradeoff] Suspicion resting only on a weak or unflattering motive should not be acted on alone; but real murders often have thin motives among cohabitants, so thinness alone need not refute. When: Judging whether a weak motive justifies acting on, or dismissing, a suspect. Why: Close relationships produce frequent conflict, and violence often follows trivial triggers.

## motive and valuables
- [rule] Treat a rumoured motive as unverified until a record, such as a will, confirms it; do not upgrade gossip to fact. When: A motive comes only from gossip or staff suspicion. Why: Gossip can point to a motive without proving it.
- [heuristic] Untouched valuables or unspent proceeds make robbery less likely as the whole aim; theft stays possible, so keep rival motives open and ask what else the act was for. When: When valuables are left untouched or stolen goods are unspent. Why: A thief who keeps the money untouched suggests a different underlying purpose.
- [heuristic] A person who accepts far less than normal pay for a post may have a hidden reason for wanting that position. When: A character's terms are unusually favourable to the other side. Why: Unusual willingness usually points to an unstated gain.
- [heuristic] A literal-minded thief values an object at its market price, while an abstract-minded person does not steal a physical object they see as trivial. When: when matching a theft to a suspect's temperament. Why: a literal mind reads value in market terms, an abstract one does not.
- [pitfall] Assuming deliberate intent without evidence is as misleading as dismissing it.
- [pitfall] Assuming a will or inheritance without evidence builds a false motive; verify the document before using it to accuse a suspect.
- [fact] An unsigned promised gift generally does not pass property after the giver dies, and an estate with no will passes to legal heirs.
- [fact] Goods bought for cash without a maker's mark or sales record leave no trace, so tradesmen checks on them may fail. When: When an item must be traced through its seller or maker. Why: Cash transactions often generate no record for the investigator to follow.

## npc tells and reactions
- [behavior] A remark that provokes a visible flush or resentment indicates it has struck a nerve, which other listeners can read. When: A casual or teasing remark draws an unusually strong reaction. Why: Visible embarrassment or resentment signals that the remark touched a sensitive point.
- [rule] Give NPCs strong reactions to specific news, objects, or ordinary-looking figures to direct investigation; give the NPC a weak excuse a companion can question. When: Designing NPC reactions that prompt player investigation. Why: Strong topic-specific reactions make a subject stand out, and the mismatch creates a reason to revisit the NPC later.
- [rule] Script subtle tells, such as brief animations, dialogue pauses, or feigned ignorance or disdain, that attentive players catch on a second conversation but careless ones miss. When: Designing NPCs who hint at or conceal hidden knowledge. Why: Subtle tells reward observation and repeated play without giving away the answer.
- [rule] Use suspect tells sparingly, since too many make every character look guilty. When: when writing character reactions in a mystery. Why: Constant tells dilute their meaning and remove the signal that marks a real secret.
- [rule] Key NPC tell animations to specific player questions, and offer a face-saving dialogue option that lets the NPC continue. When: when designing interrogation or dialogue in a game. Why: Matched tells make the NPC's reaction legible, and an exit keeps the dialogue from stalling.
- [rule] Show a character's dramatic outburst as a reaction rather than the solution, so the player does not mistake the reaction for the answer. When: A character reacts strongly during a mystery scene. Why: A vivid reaction can look like the key clue when it is only a response.
- [heuristic] Let NPCs react differently to a bluff, and let a guard who seems told the truth betray knowledge through a pause, glance, or quick denial. When: Designing NPC dialogue that responds to player probing. Why: Reactions carry information the player must read and interpret.
- [pitfall] Pressing a suspect hard or probing overtly makes them conceal everything, including unrelated truths, since they sense interrogation and stop speaking freely. When: Interrogating a suspect who is already defensive or may hold back knowledge. Why: Heavy pressure shifts the suspect from correcting a story to withholding all information.

## npc tells and testimony
- [mechanism] A rare trait that appears in only one character's description can let the player identify a body, while a second character confirms a fact but declines to explain it. When: Designing a mystery where a found body must be matched to an NPC. Why: Rare traits act as unique keys, and partial knowledge from different NPCs keeps the player reasoning rather than receiving a direct answer.
- [rule] Give NPC tells, like nervousness or sudden topic changes, a test players can run, such as a follow-up question or second look, so manner is never the verdict. When: Designing NPCs with a hidden stake in an outcome. Why: Observable tells invite investigation without giving away the answer. (x2)
- [rule] Give NPC testimony a way for players to test it; testimony players cannot check should count only as presumption. When: designing NPC testimony in an investigation.
- [rule] NPC dialogue can contain a plausible lie that the player tests against a known constraint, such as when an item could have been changed.
- [rule] Track which NPCs are drawn in by testimony and keep their personal attitudes separate from their family's.
- [heuristic] Build non-player character theories as specific, checkable claims, so the player can disprove them and learn from the failure. Why: vague claims cannot be tested or refuted.
- [heuristic] A confused NPC may retain one clear memory; let that fragment serve as the clue rather than the whole speech. When: Designing an NPC whose memory is declining or fragmented. Why: A single clear fragment can carry a clue without making the NPC seem fully lucid.
- [heuristic] Author physical details on NPCs, such as a bandage or a missing shave, as small tells that connect to the mystery's solution. When: Writing characters who hide a connection to the crime. Why: Visible details reward attention and can be explained only by the solution.

## object comparison limits
- [rule] Keep both the first reading and the revised reading of a clue in view, so you can see how its meaning changed.
- [rule] Do not judge divergence between a figure's public and private stance from a single surviving document; comparison needs at least two. When: Only one document survives. Why: Divergence cannot be seen from one statement.
- [heuristic] Compare two similar objects, such as identical steps at two houses, to find which one saw more use from a difference in wear.
- [heuristic] Comparing parts of one object helps: a worn, discoloured part beside a new one suggests a replacement, and the wear estimates its age.
- [heuristic] Compare a physical trace with how the normal version of the act would leave it; a mismatch can expose a staged reason for someone's presence. When: a person gives a routine reason for being somewhere. Why: staged routines often leave traces that differ from genuine ones.
- [procedure] 1) Judge the suspect object against the similar objects beside it. 2) If something differs, inspect every comparable object. 3) Treat the trace as meaningful only if it is unusual across the set.
- [metric] Beyond obvious defects, check fourteen further machine characteristics; a match across many independent traits is stronger than one shared defect.
- [pitfall] A sample or fabric impression match shows only what material a projectile or object touched; it does not show who held, fired, or is responsible. When: using physical comparison as evidence. Why: A match describes material, not the person who handled it. (x2)

## questioning and answers
- [mechanism] A vague answer from the questioner can prompt a witness to volunteer the object the questioner was seeking, sometimes without the questioner having to reveal the purpose. When: A witness is eager to share and the questioner withholds intent. Why: The witness fills the gap with information they hold.
