- [behavior] A delayed answer to a sensitive question, especially with belated emphasis or a long silence on money or shared events, usually signals concealment or an unwelcome truth, not ignorance. When: A direct sensitive question is asked, or a character hesitates on a sensitive topic such as money or a shared event. Why: Delay and emphasis signal effort to conceal; the speaker may be weighing how to avoid or soften the truth.
- [behavior] A statement is only as reliable as the questions it answers; gaps in what a witness was asked are themselves a source of uncertainty. When: When evaluating whether an account rules out a suspect or event. Why: Unasked areas remain unverified regardless of how confident the witness sounds.
- [behavior] A witness may admit a possibility only when asked directly about a specific detail, so precise follow-up questions reveal what broad questions miss. When: a witness's account is partial. Why: broad questions let witnesses avoid committing.
- [rule] Ask about marginal figures and peripheral details in a testimony, since questions there reveal what the witness did not attend to. When: Interviewing a witness about a central event. Why: Peripheral questions reach details the witness never focused on.
- [heuristic] Confirm only what is asked with a bare yes or no, which makes the other party supply details and reveals less to them. When: Answering questions about a secret. Why: Withholding unrequested detail keeps the questioner's work visible to the other party.
- [tradeoff] Delaying a revelation builds suspense but blocks audience action; give it a payoff, since long delays frustrate, and avoid delay when the audience must act on the answer.
- [pitfall] Delaying a confrontation gives a suspect time to entrench behind an account that cannot be traced.

## reputation and motive
- [mechanism] Once a speaker is labeled foolish, listeners interpret their later statements with suspicion or ignore them, regardless of accuracy. When: A character's clue or testimony must be dismissed by others for reasons inside the story. Why: The established label colors every later interpretation, so accurate work goes unnoticed.
- [behavior] A reputation for indolence leads readers and other characters to discount what the man notices, so his later attention becomes a turning point. Why: Low expectations make the protagonist's later perception surprising and dramatic.
- [rule] Let a threat begin as a seduction or relationship before it becomes frightening, so the eventual danger feels personal. When: When a monster or supernatural force targets a single character. Why: A slow build through a relationship makes the later threat intimate rather than abstract.
- [heuristic] Treat the order of events as part of a motive, since a death before another can change a claim more than the total amount does. When: Several deaths or events determine a reward. Why: The timing of each event changes who receives what.
- [heuristic] A report that contradicts a person's stable reputation is itself a lead worth following up. When: when a witness account seems at odds with known character.
- [procedure] 1) Gather accounts from many observers, especially people who know the character. 2) Note who is included or omitted. 3) Compare praise or labels with actual conduct. 4) Treat uniform praise as a claim to test. Do not accept a reputation such as madness or shrewdness unchecked. When: Judging a character whose reputation matters to the mystery, or who is labelled by reputation without verification. Why: Reputation can follow charm rather than conduct, omission can reveal bias, and unverified labels can mislead the investigator.
- [pitfall] Explaining a character or feud by one motive, such as grief or one person's enmity, hides contradicting details and others who gain from the same event. Why: A single cause flattens the character or feud and hides contradicting facts or other beneficiaries.
- [pitfall] A respected person can still have a motive, so a good reputation should not be treated as a reason to rule them out. When: When eliminating suspects by character. Why: Reputation is not evidence about what a person did or wanted.

## resolution and aftermath
- [rule] Do not let a retrospective explanation contradict details the audience has already seen; keep earlier details unchanged. When: Recasting earlier scenes after a reveal. Why: A contradiction breaks trust in the reveal.
- [rule] End an investigation on a sealed or destroyed artifact, so the player cannot re-verify the conclusion. When: When closing a mystery whose evidence should stay unexamined. Why: Removing access to the evidence ends the investigation without a final human antagonist.
- [heuristic] Keep the aftermath short and let a single beat carry the character's lasting emotional cost. When: Closing a story after the climax. Why: A long resolution dilutes the emotional impact of the reveal.
- [heuristic] Explain a hidden cause after the danger has passed, so the audience reinterprets earlier details as their meaning becomes clear. When: the reveal can reframe earlier scenes. Why: retrospect gives earlier details new meaning.
- [heuristic] Offer a restitution or confession branch as an alternative to combat once the act has been reconstructed and the evidence is shown to the culprit. When: The culprit is identified and the stakes allow a non-violent resolution. Why: Showing evidence can lead the culprit to return what was taken without a fight.
- [heuristic] Leave one unresolved element after the main answer is revealed, such as a hidden object or an unidentified figure, to serve as a sequel hook. When: Closing a mystery whose main answer has been revealed. Why: A residual question keeps the world open and invites continued play.
- [tradeoff] Proof gathered through witnesses and records makes a case convincing without confession, but leaves the outcome open if the evidence cannot be legally secured. When: Choosing how a mystery is resolved at its end. Why: Witness and document proof avoids a staged confession, though it may not settle whether a crime can be proven.
- [pitfall] A summary of outcomes can feel rushed, so decide which resolutions to show directly and which to compress. When: Compressing the final events.

## reveal and twist timing
- [mechanism] A late family-secret reveal reframes earlier scenes, explaining a character's earlier role and motive for silence.
- [mechanism] Linking an ordinary-seeming character to a hidden identity can recast a domestic story as espionage, raising the stakes and changing the genre. When: A mystery whose domestic setting hides a larger plot. Why: A new identity reinterprets every earlier domestic detail as part of the larger scheme.
- [mechanism] Revealing late that the sought object is a duplicate reframes all earlier pursuit as misdirected.
- [rule] Offer a mundane cause alongside the supernatural explanation, such as a drug that made a witness susceptible, and let evidence decide between them. When: Presenting a reveal that could have a mundane or supernatural cause. Why: Keeping both explanations open makes the player weigh evidence rather than accept a single answer.
- [heuristic] Domestic problems that look romantic or criminal often resolve into a family member's control of money, a secret marriage, or a betrayal, so the first motive is usually the wrong one.
- [heuristic] Put the most important identity clue in plain sight early, while the reader is not yet looking for it. When: Hiding a key identity in an opening scene. Why: Unnoticed early clues are accepted as background and then reread once the reveal arrives.
- [pitfall] Revealing a trap early removes the suspense of the approach. When: Planning the reveal of a trap in a pursuit. Why: Suspense depends on uncertainty about the outcome.
- [pitfall] Letting a hidden role become known early removes the advantage of secrecy. When: A concealed identity or role is in play. Why: Once the other side knows, it can respond, so secrecy no longer protects the actor.

## rumours and public reports
- [mechanism] A hidden party acting on a false belief about one person can form a second false belief about another. Both errors can then be exploited. When: A culprit suspects a witness knows more than they do. Why: An error in one belief carries into later judgments about other people.
- [mechanism] A false alarm draws attention to a harmless cue before the real threat arrives, misdirecting the audience's focus.
- [mechanism] A false public solution, such as an announced arrest, can make the audience doubt the investigator too early, so it must be resolved in the reveal. Why: Competing accounts create doubt that the true reveal must answer.
- [rule] Let some rumour clues be false in the level data, and reward players who trace the chain back to its origin.
- [heuristic] Treat a report delivered in secret, rather than confronted openly, as less reliable. When: Judging a damaging claim whose source avoided direct confrontation. Why: Whispered accusations avoid the scrutiny that an open claim would face, which weakens their credibility.
- [heuristic] A prosperous NPC can become the target of a whispered accusation; let the rumor change as it passes between NPCs. When: designing social pressure on a character. Why: Mutating rumor makes the source harder to trace.
- [pitfall] Overusing false alarms or rumours teaches the audience to disregard later cues and flattens suspense; each false lead should have a real consequence.
- [pitfall] A false report can alarm people who did nothing, and they may act on it. When: A planted story reaches innocent people. Why: Believed falsehoods cause real action by those who had no part in events.

## sealed answer verification
- [mechanism] A subject writes a private event before a reading and seals it, so the reader later names it and the subject confirms, creating the appearance of insight from hidden knowledge. When: Staging a reading or interrogation where the subject should feel the reader knows something private. Why: The subject cannot check the reveal before it lands, and the sealed slip hides the source of the insight.
- [rule] Record a signed, sealed verdict in writing so that any later change can be detected by comparing it with the original. When: when a judge's ruling could be altered. Why: Written records outlast spoken rulings and leave a fixed trace.
- [rule] Log each NPC claim with its in-game timestamp and seal it before the player learns the outcome, then compare it with the event time.
- [heuristic] Record a provisional conclusion in sealed form, to be opened only once the truth is established, as a check on one's own earlier error.
- [heuristic] A sealed or delayed disclosure keeps the audience waiting for its contents, so the reaction to it carries suspense. When: When a key fact should arrive at a later moment. Why: Waiting for contents sustains attention.
- [procedure] 1) Write the expected identity and seal it before the reveal. 2) Record the solution in sealed form and set an opening condition, such as a deadline or trial event. 3) Perform the reveal. 4) Have a third party open the sealed note only when that condition is met and compare it with what was revealed. When: An investigator or game must show that a reveal was fixed in advance and not improvised. Why: A prediction or sealed record fixed before evidence is seen cannot be shaped by later observation or altered after the fact.
- [procedure] 1) Privately write one suspect's name. 2) Have the hidden answer checked against it. 3) Confirm or deny the name, showing whether the reasoning matches the evidence without revealing the rest of the deduction. When: The game has a hidden identity or fact the player must deduce, and a theory must be checked without giving the answer away to the group. Why: A fixed answer written in advance gives an unambiguous way to judge the player's reasoning.
- [tradeoff] A sealed, unread reply prevents the sender from editing it, but the checker still depends on the questions asked; a neutral source tied to the claimant offers no real check. When: Deciding whether a third-party reply can be trusted. Why: Sealing protects the answer, while independence protects the source.

## secondary injury and reactions
- [mechanism] A second, unrelated story can absorb attention and offer a rival explanation, pulling the audience toward a wrong motive. When: A false trail is needed to hold interest until a turn.
- [behavior] Bystanders and staff may recognise a visitor and report the encounter to the suspect, which can expose a covert visit. When: When an investigator visits a suspect's household or workplace unannounced. Why: Staff who notice a visitor tend to pass on what they saw to the people they serve.
- [rule] Collect secondary descriptors such as height, build, complexion, facial hair, and clothing, and separate clear observations from uncertain ones. When: interviewing a witness about a person. Why: secondary details test whether the primary identification holds.
- [heuristic] A minor cut on the hand opposite the main wound can indicate that the blade's path continued beyond the main injury. When: when an injury has additional small marks. Why: Secondary marks show the motion behind the main wound.
- [heuristic] Run a secondary character's hidden history beside the main plot, so the audience knows more than the protagonist does. When: when the protagonist is unaware of an important backstory. Why: the audience's extra knowledge sustains tension in scenes with that character.
- [heuristic] An injury that does not match the claimed fall, such as one on the back of the head, may have a separate cause and should not be assumed to come from the fall. When: A medical report lists an injury inconsistent with the stated event. Why: A single event rarely explains injuries in several places on the body.
- [heuristic] Treat a later reference's claims, such as a named relative or description, as unverified until an independent source confirms them.
- [pitfall] A secondary source's judgment of a person can shape later readers' view of the event, so their character assessment must be checked against the documents.

## selection bias and framing
- [behavior] Investigators tend to draw the deduction that matches their own method, so contradictory conclusions can look equally convincing. When: when several investigators reach different conclusions from the same evidence.
- [rule] Record only the dates that bear on the case, and pass quickly over idle intervals. When: Building a chronological record of a case or quest. Why: Irrelevant entries dilute the sequence that matters.
- [heuristic] Do not treat every object as a clue. Check whether each one would actually be needed for something before reading it as evidence.
- [heuristic] When a claimed harm would hit everyone who meets its source equally, not only a chosen target, treat the claimed mechanism with suspicion. When: when evaluating a claimed curse or gaze-based power.
- [procedure] 1) Release one fact to a witness. 2) Observe the reaction, such as surprise or relief. 3) Use that reaction to judge what the witness already knew or feared. When: A reaction is more useful than the fact itself.
- [pitfall] A selected, non-random set of documents or examples shows a pattern but not its frequency; conclusions drawn from it need caution and may misstate how common an event was. (x2)
- [pitfall] Reading witness details in one direction distorts a case, since emphasising only incriminating points produces a biased conclusion. When: Presenting evidence against a suspect. Why: Omitted exculpatory details leave the conclusion unbalanced.
- [pitfall] A framing built on chosen conditions is an argument rather than a neutral survey, so the selection of conditions should not be taken as the full picture. When: Reading an account that presents context to support a conclusion. Why: The author's choice of pressures shapes which causes appear important.

## simple explanation preference
- [behavior] Speakers often give a brief account of an event that closes the topic, leaving out motive and detail. When: a speaker wants to avoid further questions. Why: A short version discourages follow-up.
- [behavior] Observers tend to accept a simple remaining explanation once every alternative has been closed off. When: all other routes of an apparent impossibility have been ruled out.
- [heuristic] One theory holds that simple, concrete details catch a cunning person more often than complex traps do, because the person prepares for complexity.
- [heuristic] When an unexplained figure appears at a place, the simplest candidate consistent with the records usually beats the most dramatic identity.
- [heuristic] Ruling out the simplest explanation first, such as an agency allocation, makes the remaining anomaly stronger evidence of deliberate action.
- [procedure] 1) Start from the most probable explanation. 2) Question everyone who knows the event most closely. 3) Compare their accounts. 4) Consider supernatural causes only after human causes are tested. When: An event could be human or supernatural. Why: The probable explanation is tested before rarer ones.
- [tradeoff] Prefer the simpler explanation when it fits evidence, not rejecting it merely for being neat; yet a crime looking simple and above-board deserves suspicion, since culprits betray themselves covering tracks. When: Prefer simple when a complex explanation is being built around scene details; suspect simple-looking crimes when they appear above-board. Why: Clever reasoning invents elaborate accounts when a plain one is available; culprits usually betray themselves while covering their tracks.
- [pitfall] Treating the simplest explanation as proven is an error; simplicity is a guide to likelihood, not certainty.

## source interest and motive
- [model] Criminal records of fingerprints, measurements and photographs, plus underworld informers, together identify offenders who have a past. When: the culprit is a known offender. Why: Records and contacts supply a background to match against.
- [rule] Make threats specific and plausible; concrete consequences create more tension than vague general warnings. When: A character or antagonist warns of consequences.
- [rule] Reveal a witness's financial stake through dialogue so that players can judge how far to trust them. When: Writing witness characters.
- [heuristic] Read each source or relayed account for what its author or relayer had reason to say, given their stake in the outcome; loyalty and social wishes shape what is told. Why: Authors and relayers emphasize what serves their own interests. (x2)
- [heuristic] Weigh each informant's interest before trusting them: a lender who profits from ruin may exaggerate, and a paid informant may shape what they report. When: receiving an account from a financially or commercially involved person. Why: incentives distort reports.
- [heuristic] A reported harm whose outcome benefits the alleged victim, or a victim who refuses to prosecute, warrants a check for staging. When: A claimed victim gains financially or socially from the event. Why: Gain from the event gives the claimed victim a reason to arrange it.
- [heuristic] Warnings about a witness from people with their own stakes do not prove the witness is unreliable; a speaker's character does not disprove what they said. When: Hearing negative opinions about a witness from interested parties. Why: Interested warners may be motivated by loyalty or dislike.
- [pitfall] If a suspect asks who told the investigator a fact, the investigator needs a believable answer, or the bluff collapses. When: when a challenge reveals knowledge the suspect did not expect. Why: the suspect will test the source of the claim.

## speaker behaviour and guilt
- [behavior] A speaker who asks not to learn the investigator's findings keeps his own involvement vague and gains a reason to say nothing more. When: the speaker has a stake in the matter. Why: Staying ignorant limits what he must reveal.
- [behavior] A speaker's eagerness to pass on a story can colour what they repeat, so their enthusiasm is part of what the listener must weigh.
- [heuristic] A long, documented stretch of unchanged state makes a single later change stand out clearly. Why: Contrast with a stable baseline reveals the deviation.
- [heuristic] Limit each speaker's authority to what they personally observed, so a long-serving NPC is reliable about one matter and only guessing about another. When: when writing testimony from several characters. Why: A witness's claim covers only their direct experience.
- [heuristic] Have a speaker pull back at the last moment and change course, which keeps tension alive without resolving it.
- [heuristic] A speaker's agitation and sudden exclamations can be as telling as the answers they give.
- [heuristic] Use hallucination or guilt effects sparingly so the player is never sure whether a figure is real.
- [heuristic] Attempts to interrupt or steer a conversation may suggest the speaker wants something kept back. When: A witness tries to stop another person from answering. Why: Interruption can be an effort to control what is revealed.

## supernatural claims testing
- [mechanism] A fake supernatural effect exposed by a single captured frame lets the reveal rest on one controllable piece of evidence that the eye missed. When: Designing a hidden mechanism meant to look occult. Why: A photograph can record a detail that observation during the event did not register, so one artifact can overturn the supernatural reading.
- [heuristic] When a game offers a curse or ghost explanation, check whether each event has a human motive, planning and a beneficiary; if so, make the human explanation discoverable. When: Designing a supernatural mystery with a hidden human cause. Why: Players reward a mystery whose rational answer is findable.
- [heuristic] Check the source of a supernatural claim before accepting or dismissing it; approach the sound and identify its origin. When: Evaluating a local legend or eerie report in a mystery setting. Why: Rumours can mask ordinary causes that direct observation exposes.
- [procedure] 1) Separate the claimed cause, such as madness, curse or inherited taint, from observable conduct. 2) Ask whether a physical agent with a motive could have acted. 3) Trace who could reach the object or location, and check planning and beneficiary. 4) Prefer the human explanation with clear motive and execution that fits these physical and motive constraints. When: An unusual or uncanny event is explained as irrational or supernatural. Why: Most apparent supernatural acts reduce to a physical mover with a reason to act; physical and motive constraints separate plausible explanations from implausible ones.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the mundane mechanism a legend could hide, such as a concealed key or passage. 2) Search the fabric of the place, including ground and fixtures, for it. 3) Accept the explanation only after the physical search confirms it; skipping this hides human action. When: A legend or seemingly impossible event explains a disappearance or anomaly and the place may hide a mechanism. Why: Acting on the hypothesis verifies it rather than relying on testimony; physical records often explain apparent impossibilities.
- [procedure] 1) Name each non-human explanation offered, such as a curse or accident. 2) Check each against where every object lies. 3) Compare when an injury occurred with when the damage happened. 4) Set aside explanations that cannot be tested. When: In a game with supernatural elements, when a curse or accident story is offered.
- [procedure] 1) For each claimed effect, list the physical conditions it requires, such as sound, movement, or a hidden body. 2) Identify who could produce those conditions. 3) Test the candidate mechanisms until one separates from the others. When: An unverified effect is offered as proof of an unseen cause. Why: Specifying requirements turns a claim into checkable conditions.
- [pitfall] Not every superstition or false belief signals guilt; treating a characterisation device as evidence against someone is a mistake.

## suspect guilt signals
- [model] Separate two questions in a mystery: whether events form a deliberate pattern, and whether that pattern can be proved and punished. When: designing or analysing a case where the culprit may be known without proof. Why: knowing the answer and being able to prove it are distinct states.
- [behavior] A source who turns pale, refuses to discuss a matter, or gives only a limited assurance signals concealment, even though the reaction reveals no fact directly. When: the source is questioned about a sensitive matter. Why: distress and evasion show that the source is hiding something.
- [behavior] A guilty suspect confronted with a precise question about the victims can panic and act in ways that expose their guilt. When: an interrogation scene near the climax. Why: Direct questions about a hidden act can overwhelm a guilty person's composure.
- [behavior] A guilty character's fear of discovery can make innocent events look like threats, because the fear is built on their own guilt. When: when a concealing character hears a summons, noise or questions. Why: Guilt primes the character to read ordinary events as danger.
- [heuristic] Flag a protagonist's reticence early, so that a later disclosure of guilt feels earned rather than sudden.
- [heuristic] A supernatural excuse offered for failure can signal that a method is being concealed rather than that the effect is genuine. When: An interested party explains a failed effect with an unseen cause. Why: Excuses often protect the mechanism behind an effect.
- [pitfall] Reading fear as proof of guilt in the main crime is a mistake when it may only reflect the false news; check it against what the bait said.
- [fact] A character can be guilty of a lesser wrong, such as sending a note, while innocent of the central crime, such as the killing. Why: Involvement in a plot and guilt for the act are separate questions.

## suspect identification
- [behavior] A visible personal motive such as rivalry or jealousy draws suspicion onto anyone it connects to, even when the real scheme lies elsewhere. When: when several characters have openly stated conflicts with a victim or each other. Why: Conspicuous motives attract attention and are assumed to be decisive.
- [rule] Let self-interested NPC admissions unlock dialogue branches, but let players verify them. Unverified remarks from interested sources are not independent evidence and lead to false motive conclusions. When: when an NPC volunteers a motive, or a motive rests only on a single informant's remarks. Why: Verification keeps performed candor from being taken as proof; interested sources are not independent evidence.
- [rule] Give a wanted description several specific traits, such as eye colour, hair and a distinctive habit, and unlock identification only when a combination of them matches. When: a player must identify an NPC from a description. Why: a single common trait would otherwise trigger a false match.
- [rule] Show players the letters needed to verify a name clue, since a clue they cannot check feels unfair. When: A character hides behind a new name. Why: Verifiable evidence lets the player earn the connection.
- [rule] Give each suspect a plausible motive and a clue that is weak alone, so the group must weigh the evidence rather than accept it. When: designing a set of suspects. Why: Weak individual clues require comparison, which keeps the group deliberating.
- [heuristic] When unlikely failures cluster, ask whether they were arranged and who benefited, rather than only what bad luck occurred. When: Several unrelated failures occur together. Why: Coincidences can be produced by someone who knows the weak points.
- [tradeoff] Treating offenders as types, such as a stock criminal profile, is quick but skips the individual motive; reasoning from inside the culprit's motive reveals who would act. When: Choosing how to reason about a suspect. Why: Types describe categories, while motive explains one person's choice.
- [pitfall] A weak identification can still drive an arrest when motive and missing alibi are strong. When: An arrest rests on an identification plus other circumstantial evidence. Why: Strong motive and alibi gaps can make a weak identification seem sufficient.

## suspect identity and links
- [rule] Before naming a suspect, check a matching description against measurable features such as height, and never rely on a single report.
- [heuristic] Check whether the accused had direct contact with the people in the accusation, since a missing contact leaves a gap in the story. When: an accusation depends on a relationship between two people. Why: Without contact, the claimed motive or plan has no route to act on.
- [heuristic] Require a claimant to describe the item's wear or contents before receiving it, which filters out impostors. When: When designing a lost-item quest. Why: Details known only to the true owner are hard for impostors to fake.
- [heuristic] A contact close to a victim, such as a teacher or companion, can reveal attention, gifts or routines that suggest a relationship. When: Investigating a person's private relationships.
- [heuristic] Test a claim of regular access against the normal pattern of contact; if that contact would be unusual, the claim of constant presence is weak. When: Someone says they were always in touch with a person or place. Why: Routine patterns show whether frequent access is plausible.
- [procedure] 1) Identify a person with sole access to something that could be altered. 2) Check it at uneven intervals over several days. 3) Enter without warning. 4) Inspect the item, the person's contacts, and their handling of the subject. When: The subject is medicine, food, a locked object or similar. Why: Surprise checks catch what scheduled visits miss.
- [procedure] 1) Obtain the earlier case's records, such as press reports. 2) Identify the earlier offender's accomplices. 3) Check whether those accomplices connect to the present crime. When: a present method has been matched to an earlier case. Why: the earlier network may reveal the present culprit.
- [pitfall] Building cases against several suspects without verifying the connections between them lets red herrings accumulate unchallenged. When: Multiple suspects each appear guilty. Why: Unverified links make innocent suspects look connected.

## suspense through waiting
- [mechanism] Delaying a known, unavoidable event extends the wait and danger, sustaining tension as each delay heightens stakes and the audience stays alert. When: When a known outcome is awaited and cannot be avoided; when pacing an approaching threat. Why: Each delay heightens stakes while the character imagines worse outcomes; extended anticipation keeps the audience alert.
- [mechanism] Suspense grows when the audience waits with uncertain timing while small sensory cues each bring the expected event closer without yet delivering it. When: an event's timing is uncertain and must be waited for. Why: Each cue shows time passing and the threat approaching, which raises anticipation.
- [mechanism] A timed wait with no contact builds suspense, so a later message that changes the plan lands with more force. When: when a story needs a turn after a quiet period. Why: the absence of contact raises expectation before the message arrives.
- [heuristic] Stretch perceived time through repetition, such as a character pacing the same path or a clock hand that does not move. When: When building suspense during a wait. Why: Repeated actions make waiting feel longer to the reader.
- [heuristic] Distracted or absorbed companions can heighten a character's solitude during a wait. When: When a character must wait alone in a tense scene. Why: Inattentive others leave the character alone with their fear.
- [heuristic] Pace the waiting between repeated tests with other events, which separates the tests and raises pressure. When: structuring time between repeated observations. Why: interleaved events make waiting feel longer and more tense.
- [tradeoff] A reassurance that the threat is over buys time before the next pressure point, but it risks deflating tension if held too long. When: Pacing a mystery's middle section. Why: The promise lowers alertness briefly, so the next pressure point hits harder, at the cost of lost momentum if the pause runs long.
- [pitfall] Repeated waiting without new information or change erodes patience, letting impatience replace tension, so delays should be used sparingly. When: Designing an anticipation scene such as a delayed arrival. Why: Players tolerate delay when it is rewarded, but repeated empty waiting erodes patience.

## timeline and window checks
- [mechanism] Known departure and return times of household members bracket the period in which an intruder could have acted. When: when several people's movements are known. Why: Absence periods define the window when the house was unwatched.
- [rule] Do not build a timeline from a window too wide to mean anything, or from events whose times were never recorded. Why: Without a meaningful window or recorded times, any overlap is arbitrary.
- [rule] Do not use process-time arithmetic when the duration is unknown or witnesses disagree about when the process started. Why: Without agreed start and duration values, the computed window is unreliable.
- [heuristic] A time window is only as firm as its endpoints, so verify each endpoint before relying on it, especially when it comes from memory rather than records. When: when a window is built from several witness times or its endpoints come from memory. Why: One unchecked or misremembered endpoint can wrongly open or close the span and change who fits.
- [heuristic] A window of possible times is not the act itself; the exact moment stays open until other evidence fixes it. When: when a time window has been established but not narrowed further. Why: Confusing a possibility range with a fixed time leads to premature conclusions.
- [heuristic] Ask why someone with a fixed schedule changed it, because the change may reveal the reason behind the unusual act. When: a regular routine is broken.
- [procedure] 1) Use an early document to fix a time or place 2) search the physical scene at that target 3) confirm the finding with traces. When: when the answer must be proven by something checkable.
- [procedure] 1) Find an upper bound: a known event that would have removed or altered the deposit. 2) Find a lower bound from its physical state. 3) Check whether the bounded window fits a known disappearance date. When: judging when an object or body was deposited. Why: Two bounds from independent evidence narrow the timing.

## timelines and timing checks
- [rule] Store an event timeline the player can check against NPC statements, so a shifting date becomes a detectable contradiction.
- [rule] Use dates and relationships as checkable facts, so the player can test a confession against the timeline. When: A story reveal depends on a past connection between characters. Why: Testable facts let players verify a confession and feel the reveal is earned.
- [rule] Give a late return a route and reason that players can check, so the return can clear a suspect as well as condemn them.
- [heuristic] Anchor the timeline to fixed, objective times where available, such as a stated departure or arrival, and check witness accounts and other evidence against them, since memory shifts more easily. When: When a person's timeline is central to the case. Why: Fixed times are harder to shift than memory, so a precise anchor makes contradictions in other evidence visible. (x2)
- [heuristic] Tie a witness's own movements to checkable details such as clocks, bells or purchases, so staff can confirm them and the reveal is fair.
- [heuristic] Chain timed events in order, so each confirmed time anchors the next claim.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the date of the last confirmed sighting. 2) Place later events such as deliveries, sales and visits against it. 3) Check each claimed later sighting for travel time and physical feasibility. 4) Note who benefits if the date is moved. When: When a disappearance or death depends on a date. Why: Exposes sightings that are impossible or staged to shift suspicion.
- [procedure] 1) List each witness's claimed times for one event. 2) Place all claims on one shared clock. 3) Mark the gaps and conflicts between them; these are the first leads to pursue. When: Several accounts of one event must be reconciled.

## vanity and pride motives
- [behavior] Praising an assistant's skill while denying him leadership keeps him compliant. When: the subordinate is vain about his abilities. Why: Recognition of skill satisfies the need for status.
- [behavior] A person who wants to prove a point will reveal facts they would withhold under direct questioning, because pride outweighs caution when stakes are low. When: a low-stakes wager is offered.
- [behavior] A proud person may conceal marital unhappiness so well that they appear unmoved by a spouse's death, and may later admit the unhappiness only reluctantly. When: A witness describes a relationship as steady but seems emotionally flat. Why: Pride and reluctance to admit failure suppress open displays of feeling.
- [behavior] Vanity or grievance can make a witness either eager to help or eager to deny involvement, so their stance must be read alongside their content.
- [behavior] A witness who enjoys being treated as an authority may shape what they report to appear competent, not simply to report what happened. When: when a witness's status depends on being seen as expert. Why: self-image colours what they choose to say.
- [heuristic] Gate an NPC's secret information behind a pride or reputation value so flattering options or deference unlock it, and reward players who let the talker lead with guessing questions.
- [heuristic] Tying an outcome to pride as well as to fact builds tension, since the result matters to a character's standing. When: When designing a confrontation where a character's reputation is at stake.
- [pitfall] A later statement that a principle was wrong does not repair harm if it offers no specific reparation. Why: General acknowledgment does not address the people harmed.

## verdicts and official records
- [rule] Let an official in-world verdict, such as a coroner's finding, close a thread after the true cause is known, so the investigation ends without a culprit. When: Closing a mystery where the threat is removed by a finding rather than capture. Why: An official ruling gives a formal ending when no punishment is needed.
- [rule] Reveal a hidden relation through an outside record rather than a false statement from the character, so the reveal stays fair. Why: Players accept a record they can check but resent an outright lie.
- [rule] Let the official line be wrong for a reason the player can see, so the error is visible rather than arbitrary. When: Writing an authority figure who dismisses a warning. Why: Visible reasons make the dismissal a fair part of the puzzle instead of a cheat.
- [rule] Let an official explanation stand until a specific physical contradiction breaks it, rather than dismissing it early. When: Presenting a public or authority-held theory of a crime. Why: A theory the player watches collapse under evidence is more convincing than one simply rejected.
- [heuristic] When an official record such as a death certificate seems unassailable, look for an independent dated record of an event it depends on. When: A false document anchors a character's supposed fate. Why: A dated external record can show that the document covered a different person.
- [heuristic] Pair an official verdict with private rumour so the player holds two incompatible truths at the same time. When: An in-world authority closes a death with a conclusion the player doubts. Why: The conflict between verdict and rumour keeps the question open without contradicting the authority outright.
- [tradeoff] Leaving a question open avoids a premature decision but leaves the player without resolution; deciding early risks an unsupported conclusion. When: Evidence is insufficient to settle a question. Why: Each option has a cost: an open question frustrates, a premature answer misleads.
- [fact] A Not Proven verdict is not a finding of innocence; it means the evidence did not reach a positive conclusion either way. When: Interpreting a three-outcome verdict. Why: The verdict reports insufficient proof, not a determination of what happened.

## victim habits and background
- [rule] Use the victims' appearance and condition as a clue to what they experienced.
- [heuristic] A person who arranges an alibi is probably engaged in something criminal, so the arrangement is a clue to hidden intent. When: the victim's own preparations reveal intent investigators did not see. Why: Precautions reveal behaviour that ordinary explanations would not produce.
- [heuristic] To reason about a victim's message, imagine their confinement, remaining time and options, then infer what they would most likely choose to do. When: A victim may have left a record in a confined space.
- [heuristic] Profile a victim's habits, wealth display, impressionability and superstitions to identify who could exploit them.
- [heuristic] Rebuild a victim's history from prior investigations, old partnerships and rumours; a background gathered over years yields the strongest list of possible motives. When: When many past associations could explain a motive. Why: Each past association can be checked against records.
- [heuristic] A theory requiring a victim to act against their known habits or the scene's layout is weak and should be tested first. When: when evaluating a crime theory. Why: Known behavior constrains what the victim could have done.
- [procedure] 1) Ask who the victim was and where she came from. 2) Ask what she did, how she lived, her habits and morals. 3) Ask her company, her enemies and whether she was thought rich. When: When a victim's past is unknown and a motive must be found. Why: These questions cover the places where motives and secrets usually sit.
- [fact] A victim's described symptoms, such as numbness, tingling, drowsiness, and warmth, can help identify the drug involved. When: A poisoning is suspected and the victim can describe symptoms. Why: Symptom patterns are specific enough to narrow the possible drugs.

## witness account drift
- [mechanism] A source's account of events can shift over time as its author's stake in how those events look changes, so one person may tell different stories at different dates. When: the source has a personal stake in the outcome. Why: later reputational or political pressure changes what the author wants to emphasize.
- [behavior] Under a suggested theory, a witness can move from certainty about one account to tentative agreement and then to belief in the suggested account within a short exchange. When: a theory is put to a witness repeatedly. Why: Social suggestion can reshape recall.
- [behavior] A witness who first claims to have heard nothing may recall a specific detail after hearing another account repeated. When: after exposure to other testimony or a repeated prompt. Why: new information reshapes memory.
- [behavior] A witness's account is shaped both by how questions are asked and by what the witness wants to hide. When: interviewing a person who has a reason to be guarded. Why: both the question framing and concealment change what is reported.
- [behavior] A witness who later realises a threat stood close by may overturn their own earlier account, so earlier statements need re-checking.
- [procedure] 1) Record the order of each witness's statement. 2) Check whether that witness heard earlier accounts. 3) Compare statements to see whether they echo one another. When: several witnesses give accounts of the same event. Why: echoed accounts can look like independent corroboration.
- [pitfall] Witnesses who compare notes or discuss the event blend what they heard with what they were told and may recall incidents that never happened; warn them not to discuss it. When: when witnesses have compared notes, discuss the matter with friends, or want to seem important. Why: Gossip, conversation and emotion reshape what people report and recall.
- [pitfall] Changes in minor details across retellings can be ordinary memory drift, not deliberate lies. Treating every change as deception misjudges the witness. When: Comparing successive accounts from one witness. Why: Memory reconstructs events each time it is recalled.

## witness glimpse and gesture tells
- [behavior] A fixed gaze at an object can silently prompt a speaker to mention that object, even without a question being asked. When: during conversation about a relevant object.
- [behavior] A witness who repeatedly glances at a scene element and looks away quickly shows awareness of it.
- [behavior] A gesture toward something the observer cannot see is clear in intent but unexplained, so it can read as madness or as a hint. When: A character points at a hidden object. Why: Missing context leaves the gesture open to interpretation.
- [rule] A single glimpse rarely identifies a person; pair it with a physical item such as a uniform or emblem. Why: the item links the partial description to a known source.
- [heuristic] A witness who only glimpsed an event and cannot describe it or agree with others provides little more than a witness who saw nothing. When: Several witnesses report the same event. Why: Unidentifiable or conflicting sightings cannot be matched to a suspect.
- [heuristic] Watching a hidden person take a delivered object can briefly reveal their condition through their face. When: a hidden person is observed at a handover.
- [procedure] 1) Record the accused's movements. 2) Check whether an accuser shows a reaction or marks at that moment. 3) Repeat the movement deliberately. 4) Record whether the reaction matches each time, and include a control. When: Physical traces are claimed to follow a suspect's movements. Why: Repetition with a control separates a real link from a chosen pattern.
- [pitfall] Reading a witness's hesitation or glance toward a person as confirmation of identity is a mistake. When: A witness hesitates or looks at someone during an identification. Why: A glance is ambiguous and can be shaped by the room's expectations rather than by recognition.

## written document ambiguity
- [behavior] The same document can support opposite readings, such as a warning sign or a sign of trust, so decide between them using independent evidence. When: A will or record drawn shortly before a death. Why: Its meaning depends on the reading chosen, not on the text alone.
- [rule] Before acting on ambiguous wording, shorthand, or an unexplained name such as a place or person, confirm its meaning with the issuer. When: A written term has two plausible senses, is shorthand, or names an unexplained place or person. Why: Readers can misread a word in good faith.
- [rule] Make a payment or ledger support more than one NPC's story, so dialogue lets players argue for either reading. When: Designing ambiguous documents in dialogue-driven investigations. Why: Ambiguity makes players weigh evidence instead of accepting the first reading.
- [rule] Give ambiguous in-world signatures a disambiguating context the player can gather, such as rank, location and who was present, rather than leaving the identity unresolvable. When: An NPC signs with a name shared by several characters. Why: Players must be able to solve the ambiguity from clues.
- [pitfall] An ambiguous item, such as a blank stub or emotionally loaded note, fits several explanations and gains meaning only when combined with other facts.
- [pitfall] A witness may answer from a prepared document rather than memory without noticing, and may repeat another person's claims as their own. When: when the witness was coached or shown papers. Why: Written scripts blend memory with other people's assertions.
- [pitfall] Ambiguous legal wording, such as an unclear term, can be read in opposing ways, making a motive look stronger or weaker than it is.
- [pitfall] A route described as mostly shut may be open at set times; ask what the phrase actually means before dismissing it.

## abandonment and interruption signals
- [mechanism] A route that travelers abandon loses its legal use and can be plowed back into fields, so it disappears from the landscape and survives only in records, stones and fences.
- [behavior] A sudden, unexplained departure from a gathering can signal a quarrel with someone in the victim's circle. When: A character leaves a social setting abruptly. Why: Abrupt exits often follow a confrontation.
- [rule] Abandon a conspicuous object rather than keep it when pursuers could identify it quickly once found. Why: a found object alerts pursuers rapidly.
- [heuristic] Work left mid-process, such as paint on a palette or brushes standing in solvent, suggests sudden abandonment that needs explaining.
- [pitfall] Abandoning the past entirely can miss clues that only past testimony or records can supply. When: past records or witnesses can still be checked.
- [pitfall] A major event reported in a brief passage with little reaction can feel abrupt, so it needs a short emotional beat.
- [pitfall] An abrupt interruption ends an exchange before more is learned, so keep the questioning at a steady rhythm.

## admitted gaps and errors
- [rule] Treat a witness's admitted missed details as weak evidence, and fill those gaps from other sources. Why: A witness who lost track of events cannot vouch for them.
- [rule] Disclose known defects before a deal is made; a flaw named in advance cannot later be claimed as concealed. When: parties commit to a space or agreement with hidden drawbacks. Why: prior disclosure removes grounds for later complaint.
- [rule] State plainly when data is missing, and do not reach a conclusion without it. Why: Conclusions without supporting data are guesses.
- [heuristic] A witness who records what they cannot explain, such as the source of a feeling, is more credible than one who hides the gap. When: when assessing a narrator's reliability. Why: Acknowledged uncertainty signals honest reporting rather than a tidy but unsupported story.
- [heuristic] End a reveal by admitting what remains uncertain rather than claiming total certainty. When: Closing a mystery's explanation. Why: Acknowledged loose ends seem more credible.
- [heuristic] A reveal in which the solver openly names their own earlier mistake feels earned rather than lucky. When: Writing the moment of solution. Why: Acknowledging error places the lesson on reasoning rather than chance.
- [pitfall] An investigator's admitted errors must match the clues actually shown, or the reveal loses its fairness. When: the investigator confesses missed signs. Why: Mismatched admissions break the fair-play contract.

## alibi and timeline checks
- [mechanism] Someone who handles a mechanical object can leave it in a changed state, such as running, that occupants have not noticed.
- [heuristic] Leave an unverified cover story with a visible gap so the audience can notice it and return to it later. When: A character's alibi or account is accepted without check. Why: A noticed gap can be used by later sections.
- [procedure] 1) Note the visitor's route and who knows it. 2) Overlay the claimed visit on each occupant's movements. 3) Check arrivals that overlap the visit. 4) Phrase the claim conditionally and keep belief separate from reported appearance. When: a death or disappearance is linked to a claimed visit with no witnesses. Why: Access routes and occupants' movements bound what could have happened.
- [pitfall] An account resting only on one person's word, such as an alibi or a claim of being alone, cannot be checked and should be treated as unverified, leaving a gap filled by guesswork. When: A suspect's alibi or a witness says they spent time somewhere without anyone else present. Why: Without independent confirmation, the claim cannot be cross-checked.
- [pitfall] Absence of sightings neither proves nor disproves a visit; an unseen visit that was never searched stays unconfirmed, supporting suspicion but not proving it happened. When: A timeline is built from witness sightings. Why: Absence of observation is not evidence of absence.
- [pitfall] Travel plans announced in advance can change without any record of the change, making the announced plan unreliable. When: A stated schedule is used as the baseline for checking a suspect's movements. Why: Unlogged changes make the announced plan look valid when it no longer applies.
- [pitfall] Trusting a witness's stated time without checking it against an independent event leads to false timelines. When: A witness gives a precise time for an event. Why: Independent events are needed to verify a witness's clock.

## ally and captive responses
- [behavior] A suspect who sees a formal search coming and has no time to destroy the object is likely to hand it over. Why: Resistance no longer helps and the evidence is at risk.
- [behavior] Acting on a coerced confession can alert the other side, who may respond with a quick ambush. When: A suspect yields information that is then acted on. Why: The opposing party learns of the investigation through the action taken.
- [behavior] An ally who holds a wrong belief creates a gap between their conclusion and the evidence, which a player can exploit to reach the truth first. When: investigations with an official NPC ally. Why: the ally's conclusion is visible but not supported.
- [rule] Ask an ally of the adversary for a written account, stating that it will be demanded if refused, so a record exists.
- [rule] Secure pledges of silence from witnesses and from anyone with an interest in the case, since a witness not properly bound may speak to others. Why: Information flows only where the designer or investigator intends.
- [heuristic] Give a trusted ally a visible heroic act, since that act becomes the strongest cover for revealing them later as the real antagonist. When: planning a hidden-boss twist. Why: Heroism raises trust, which hides the true identity.
- [procedure] 1) Give the captive paper and a pencil for a written reply. 2) Read the answer. 3) Judge whether the written answer is likely to be true. When: a captive cannot speak.

## body and death evidence
- [mechanism] A victim-may-be-alive state lets a missing body later be found moving under its own power, so disappearance does not always mean death. When: When designing encounters where a body disappears. Why: Keeping the victim's status open creates a reversal the player can discover.
- [rule] Make some deaths clearly accidental so that suspicious deaths stand out and players can separate conspiracy from chance. When: When designing a set of witness deaths. Why: Contrast with clearly natural deaths makes the suspicious ones meaningful.
- [heuristic] Stage an accident via an early quarrel and push, letting one noticed but unpursued flaw slip by, so a later murder reveal turns earlier details into proof. When: Writing an accident that will later be revealed as a planned killing. Why: A noticed but dismissed flaw signals the cover story to attentive players and makes the confession feel earned; the reversal gives incidental earlier details new meaning.
- [heuristic] A killer can leave no visible injury, so a lack of marks does not settle whether a death was natural or staged.
- [heuristic] Make the proof a trait of a person's body that the player could have checked, such as an arm or hand, so an impostor is exposed by something visible.
- [fact] A missing blood trail and a missing outer garment suggest the person left under their own power rather than being carried away by another. When: a body is missing and the case is open.
- [fact] Adipocere, a waxy residue formed by wet decay, is absent in dry environments or when most flesh is removed before bones enter water. When: Reading decay residue on remains to infer environment or prior handling. Why: Adipocere forms only under wet, anaerobic decay conditions.

## buried clues and leads
- [rule] Use a word from one scene to unlock a clue in a later scene, so the player feels the click of recall.
- [rule] Leave disposal traces that a player can find when designing a hidden-body or cover-up puzzle, since concealment is hard under physical constraints. When: Designing a hidden-body or cover-up puzzle. Why: Physical constraints make concealment leave findable traces.
- [rule] Leave one physical seal or marker unexplained, so the player carries an open detail into the climax and can revisit it later. When: Structuring clues in a mystery. Why: An unresolved detail keeps the player engaged and rewards revisiting after the main reveal.
- [heuristic] Restate a key clue plainly, without revealing its meaning, near the reveal and more than once; a single mention among jokes or details is easily missed. When: A key clue appears early in a long text, among jokes, or among other descriptive detail. Why: Players forget or skim clues, and a single, one-time description reads as an afterthought. (x2)
- [heuristic] A final word naming a category, such as a type of enemy, may point to a group rather than a single attacker. When: A dying speaker names an enemy type. Why: A category describes many possible perpetrators, not one person.
- [tradeoff] Burying a clue in NPC asides lets players catch it, but within fact lists or long digressions it looks like background and gets skipped; bury only where still catchable. When: Designing NPC dialogue or long texts that hide clues. Why: Clues buried in asides or lists can be found, but clues inside lists or digressions look like background and are skipped.
- [tradeoff] Searching for hidden remains exposes the crime and its participants, while leaving them buried keeps the truth concealed; each choice carries social or legal cost. When: Physical evidence is hidden at a place with a known history. Why: Recovery produces proof but also public consequences.

## caution and restraint
- [mechanism] An interrogation system that tracks whether a caution was given can mark later statements inadmissible when the caution was skipped.
- [behavior] A contact may first deny knowledge, then offer a cautious hint while noting that it has passed through many hands. When: When a contact is asked about a sensitive matter. Why: Denial protects the contact, and a hint lets them help without full exposure.
- [heuristic] Do not treat a later, more cautious retraction as the truth just because it came later.
- [heuristic] Use a cooperative approach with reachable witnesses, and be cautious with frightened ones, for whom any warning can feel like coercion. When: choosing an interview approach.
- [heuristic] Read a witness's claim in light of its qualifications and circumstances rather than discarding it outright. When: Assessing a witness who has real knowledge but a conflict of interest. Why: Charity means interpreting the claim fairly, not rejecting it by default.
- [pitfall] A cautionary phrase can mislead a careless reader into thinking the source opposed a practice it endorsed in other clauses. Why: Endorsing clauses can outweigh qualifying words.
- [pitfall] Treating caution as guilt in itself is a mistake, since a sensible person also takes precautions. When: interpreting a character's defensive behavior. Why: Precaution alone is not evidence of wrongdoing.

## clue fairness and recoverability
- [mechanism] A clue hidden inside a widely distributed document survives the loss of its author or memory, because many copies keep the information available. When: when a secret must outlast its keeper or a long time gap. Why: Redundancy across many copies preserves the key even if the original holder is gone.
- [behavior] A clue can be planted in an ordinary object that the investigator rejects at first, then retrieves later so the reader sees it existed before its importance was clear. When: A later revelation depends on a document or fact the reader has already seen. Why: Early dismissal hides the trace in plain sight, and retrieval later makes the reader feel the clue was fair.
- [rule] A fair-play clue must stay readable: include enough detail for the audience to recover it, and never withhold it entirely, since total concealment removes the payoff. When: Designing a hidden clue meant to be solved by the player, or concealing information in a scene. Why: Withholding all details makes the solution impossible to reach fairly; a clue must remain legible to be recognised when the key appears.
- [rule] Make a planted detail memorable enough that the audience can recall it when it matters; a detail too minor to recall breaks fair play. When: Planting a clue meant to be recalled later. Why: A clue the player cannot recall cannot be connected to the later question.
- [rule] Show each misleading clue openly and note its oddity in the text, so the eventual reveal is fair. When: Planting a clue that points to a false suspect. Why: Readers can only reinterpret evidence they actually saw and had reason to notice.
- [heuristic] Track which clues the player has witnessed and which were dismissed, so later reveals can point back to earlier moments. When: Designing a mystery with delayed reveals.
- [procedure] 1) Show the object early as ordinary, with a reading that seems to confirm a simple story. 2) Reveal a new source or cleaning that corrects the reading. 3) Let the corrected reading change the object's meaning. When: A detail must look innocent at first and gain meaning later. Why: A visible correction makes the revised meaning feel earned rather than arbitrary.

## clue overload and dilution
- [mechanism] A gossiping NPC can carry one real, verifiable clue inside a large amount of unreliable talk, rewarding players who filter for it. When: Designing talkative NPCs who hold useful information. Why: Filtering noise to find the checkable detail is the skill the scene rewards.
- [pitfall] Presenting too many odd details or minor clues at once dilutes each one, so the decisive clue loses its pull; avoid marking every trace as decisive. When: Designing a set of clues, or when many odd details appear together. Why: Attention is spread across too many hooks, and a flood of minor clues weakens the key one.
- [pitfall] Side secrets, digressions, or chasing every object can bury decisive facts and draw the investigator away from the key evidence and main line of inquiry. When: Many unrelated secrets or objects surround a central question. Why: Attention spent on side clues delays the decisive one.
- [pitfall] Describing a planted object too often makes the audience suspect it, so mention it once and move on. When: Planting a clue that should stay unnoticed until the reveal. Why: Repetition signals importance and gives away the twist.
- [pitfall] A recap that introduces new facts feels like cheating, and over-explaining drains suspense. When: Writing the solution reveal of a mystery.
- [pitfall] A trace that is found but never connected to an explanation adds noise instead of meaning.
- [pitfall] Presenting too much evidence at once gives the suspect time to rationalise each link. When: Confronting a suspect.

## confinement pacing tension
- [definition] Confinement suspense holds a character in a murky, airless place, building tension through worsening physical danger, unseen threats, and false hopes of rescue.
- [behavior] Confining a suspect does not limit an accusation that claims unnatural powers, since such powers are assumed to exceed ordinary restraints. When: A jailed suspect is blamed for harm elsewhere. Why: Belief in unnatural agency is assumed to defeat physical containment.
- [rule] Open a confinement scene with an unexpected closure, such as a door that locks itself with no visible means of opening it. When: Starting a scene where a character becomes trapped.
- [heuristic] A secret confided to only a few people stays contained and limits who can reveal the truth.
- [heuristic] Use confinement to slow the pace and build dread before a reveal, and sustain engagement with a sequence of rising hopes and failures. When: Before a reveal that needs build-up.
- [procedure] 1) Let the barrier begin to yield, showing light through a crack. 2) Let the threat escape through another opening, so the rescue turns into a new danger. When: Building the climax of a confinement sequence.
- [pitfall] Confining suspects can breed resentment that colors their testimony.

## constrained interviews
- [behavior] A witness who cannot speak freely gives an account shaped by fear or emotion, so the statement needs checking before it is trusted. When: a witness is afraid or cannot speak openly. Why: fear or emotion shapes what is said.
- [heuristic] A costly or distance-constrained action taken before a claimed time is strong evidence that the actor knew something earlier than they admitted. When: an independent action conflicts with a stated knowledge time. Why: the action required prior knowledge to be taken.
- [procedure] 1) Clear bystanders from the room, or restrict who may speak, before a sensitive exchange so a fragile witness is not confused or steered. 2) Restate the demand plainly. 3) Repeat it without following tangents, mockery or changes of subject until answered. When: Interviewing a witness who may speak more freely alone, a fragile witness with several people present, or a suspect dodging a plain question. Why: Removing bystanders and limiting speech reduces evasion and steering, and repetition blocks topic changes that would otherwise deflect the question.
- [procedure] 1) Set the money visible on the table. 2) Seat the witness facing the light. 3) Sit the interviewer apart. 4) Keep the manner gentle, so the witness stays at ease while the interviewer keeps control. When: Interviewing a nervous witness who must be kept calm. Why: A comfortable witness speaks more freely, and the interviewer's position keeps the exchange under control.
- [procedure] 1) Open with a low-stakes question to build rapport. 2) Ask about the relationship with the subject. 3) Ask about their habits and character. 4) Ask direct questions on dependence and grievance. 5) Check their account against other sources. When: The subject is the only source for a relationship and cannot be questioned freely. Why: Answers can supply or rule out motive and need corroboration.
- [procedure] 1) Wait for a natural opening in the conversation. 2) Ask the sensitive question as it arises rather than opening with it. 3) Add an explicit exit so refusal is easy. 4) Let the subject narrate. When: A direct question would make the subject defensive or end the conversation. Why: Easy refusal and a narrated answer lower defensiveness and invite fuller disclosure.
- [tradeoff] Limiting replies keeps questions pointed, but long written exchanges slow the pace and become tiresome, so keep the constrained exchange short. When: choosing how long the captive's replies should run.

## cross-referenced records
- [behavior] Offering a detail another witness reported can revive a memory, but the recall may then reflect the prompt rather than perception. Why: suggestion can blend with genuine perception.
- [rule] Give diaries, accounts and case files dated, cross-referenced entries that players check against other clues, such as receipts or patrol schedules, to place events on a timeline and spot conflicts. When: When designing a document-based investigation. Why: Cross-references turn separate records into a checkable sequence.
- [rule] Give each in-world document a known author and known bias, and let the player cross-check documents against each other and against related dates to rebuild an event. When: When designing in-game ledgers, letters or court notes as clues. Why: Known bias lets the player weigh each document rather than accept it as neutral truth.
- [rule] Do not rely on one document alone, since a register or log can be incomplete, and cross-check it with other records where possible.
- [heuristic] Cross-check independent records, such as chemists' receipts and nurse-kept books, against one another. When: Several records cover the same supply. Why: Agreement between separate records is stronger than one record alone.
- [procedure] 1) Identify a lead from an object. 2) Send inquiries to each possible source. 3) Compare replies against each other. 4) Re-check any conflict before drawing a conclusion. When: When tracing an unknown person through objects and records. Why: Independent sources reduce the risk of acting on a single incorrect record.
- [procedure] 1) Keep a private notebook of names, initials and facts. 2) Record every name or alias seen in each source. 3) Look for matches across unrelated sources and link threads through them.

## culprit deliberate actions
- [mechanism] Each incident can be waved off as accident, so a campaign built from single deniable events stays hard to prove even when its cause is certain. When: when a rival uses small, plausible-looking hostile acts. Why: Deniability protects the planner, since each event has a harmless explanation on its own.
- [behavior] Offenders do slightly more than the crime requires; concealment steps, especially those needing fine control, can leave traces the actor would otherwise avoid. When: When a crime was staged or concealed by the offender. Why: Concealment adds steps, and each extra step can leave evidence of intent. (x2)
- [heuristic] Suspect a deliberate act only when some detail resists the accidental explanation; evidence of intent rules out explanations that require chance. When: When weighing a natural versus a deliberate cause. Why: Otherwise every mishap looks suspicious.
- [heuristic] A deliberate act is unlikely when it would defeat the culprit's own aim, such as burning a scene when concealment was the goal. Why: A culprit normally avoids actions that expose the plan.
- [heuristic] A character designed to be flawless removes the weak point an investigator needs; leaving a plausible overlooked detail gives the story a way to be discovered. When: Writing an antagonist or planner whose plan must be discoverable. Why: Without any overlooked point, there is no hook for detection.
- [heuristic] Hide the key document with the culprit, and let its later appearance prove the fraud the culprit committed. When: a document is central to the motive. Why: A document the culprit controls exposes the fraud when it surfaces, rather than being found by chance.
- [pitfall] A suspect who believes they were seen may act to correct the timeline, which can create new evidence. When: A suspect fears a sighting has exposed them. Why: Corrective actions leave traces that can be followed.

## decision and adjudication
- [rule] Decline a hidden-client case when the unknown interest could compromise the investigation or when uncertainty builds on several sides at once.
- [rule] Decline an offered test when accepting it would expose the cover, and keep reading the suspect's reaction to the offer. When: a cover identity is at risk. Why: Declining protects the cover while the reaction still gives information.
- [heuristic] When two experts disagree, find the single question whose answer separates their readings, and put it to the witnesses. When: A cause or diagnosis is disputed. Why: One decisive answer can settle a disagreement.
- [heuristic] Treat the reliability of the decision-maker as a separate question from the reliability of the testimony. When: when a verdict is contested. Why: a flawed judge can reject sound evidence, and a sound judge can accept weak evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Reduce the case to one decisive question. 2) List each explanation. 3) Record the facts each explains and the facts each leaves unexplained. 4) Prefer the explanation that accounts for most facts. When: A case rests on one contested item. Why: Separating explanations by the facts they cover shows which one is best supported.
- [procedure] 1) Give the full timeline of events. 2) State the conclusion. 3) Ask the listener to judge whether the evidence holds. 4) Offer a conditional exit, such as dropping the matter if told to. 5) Record the reply. When: when a listener's decision determines whether the investigation continues. Why: Making the listener's choice explicit turns the briefing into a decision point with a recorded outcome.
- [fact] An official verdict can be reasonable given the information it received, even when a better-informed party holds facts that were never disclosed.

## decoys and misdirection
- [model] An antagonist's identity can be a sequence of impostors and disguised allies, where each reveal replaces the previous threat identity.
- [mechanism] A supernatural explanation accepted early, or a setting's ghost reputation, absorbs strange sightings and noises, so players discount them and the living culprit hides inside the frame. When: A setting has a superstitious reputation, or a supernatural explanation is accepted early. Why: Attributing anomalies to ghosts diverts attention from real human activity, and the frame gives strange events a ready cause so players stop questioning them.
- [mechanism] A supernatural explanation kept alive as a misdirection, then rejected by rational deduction, makes the audience test the rule before the true answer arrives. When: a legend or myth is introduced early. Why: The audience weighs the legend against the investigator's reasoning.
- [mechanism] A mystery keeps the reader's belief moving by passing guilt along a chain of suspects, each cleared or reframed by a later clue, so the true culprit sits in plain view among the investigators. When: Designing a whodunit with several suspects and a hidden killer. Why: Each overturned clue shifts suspicion to the next candidate, and the reader keeps reinterpreting earlier evidence.
- [heuristic] A false fact can be fixed by a trusted witness, so the player's trust in that witness becomes the misdirection itself.
- [pitfall] A trail may be built deliberately to point toward a false exit, placed where a searcher would naturally look.
- [pitfall] A clue can be true in one sense and misleading in another, such as a moved body that was moved by someone other than the killer. When: When interpreting a physical clue that appears to confirm the main theory. Why: Accurate facts can support a false inference about who caused them.

## document analysis and verification
- [mechanism] A reliable-seeming third-party manuscript can override earlier rational explanations and convert a prior belief into an eyewitness event, closing the investigation. When: Late in an investigation, when the reveal is delivered as a document from a witness the player trusts more than the investigator. Why: A first-hand account from a separate source carries more weight than the investigator's theories, so it reframes all earlier clues.
- [mechanism] When each later document overturns the one before it, the believed answer keeps flipping until the final sealed proof settles it. When: when building a lore-document mystery. Why: the chain sustains uncertainty while preserving a single final truth.
- [rule] When an NPC presents a conclusion, offer at least one other reading of the same clue and let the player choose which to pursue.
- [heuristic] A question of whether a claim was ever true can require checking several sources, such as records, witnesses and physical traces, before accepting the conclusion. When: Designing a puzzle where the player must verify a historical claim. Why: No single source is sufficient, so cross-checking builds confidence in the conclusion.
- [pitfall] A clean result from a physical check is not conclusive, because its reliability depends on when and how the check was made. When: When a physical check finds no trace. Why: Traces may have been removed or may not have been present at the time of checking.
- [fact] A document addressed to someone else can misidentify its bearer, so an introduction may point to the wrong person.
- [fact] Confessions reported after a story ends can confirm a deduction, giving closure without a full on-page reveal.

## essential clues and information flow
- [definition] Essential circumstances are causally tied to how a mystery resolves; incidental circumstances merely accompany the event by chance and do not determine the outcome.
- [rule] Do not withhold facts the audience needs in order to follow the present action. Why: Hidden information needed now leaves the audience unable to follow events.
- [rule] End a level with a debrief that recaps each misleading clue and its real cause, leaving one optional thread players can follow.
- [rule] Do not leave open any point the player needs to finish the case; only minor or background details should remain unsettled. When: Deciding which details stay unresolved. Why: Unresolved essentials block progress and frustrate players.
- [rule] Front-load the core questions in the opening so that mid-game clues can make them concrete. When: a multi-stage investigation. Why: later clues then have questions to resolve.
- [heuristic] At case end, replay the clues the player collected and link each to the conclusion, so the reasoning can be checked.
- [heuristic] Mark one essential clue as must-remember so it is not lost among many weaker leads.

## flight and guilt
- [behavior] Observers who did not see why someone fled read the flight as guilt, while the person may have acted from shock. When: a witness reports that a household left during a crisis. Why: the same act reads as guilt or shock depending on what the observer knows.
- [behavior] A person who flees on seeing a stranger often warns others, which indicates the household expects visitors who mean harm. When: When a witness runs or alerts someone upon meeting an unknown visitor. Why: Prior threats or expectations make strangers feel dangerous.
- [rule] Let a suspect's flight or dismissal open new paths, such as a changed location or a new hiding place.
- [rule] Do not treat flight as proof of guilt when a verifiable, independent cause for it exists.
- [metric] To test whether a person could have fled, add each leg of the journey, including wait, transit and walk, and check whether the total fits the gap. When: a sequence of alibis or an escape must fit a time window.
- [pitfall] Reading a hurried exit or flight as guilt without other evidence is a mistake, since innocent people sometimes flee in panic.
- [pitfall] Treating a servant's flight as proof of guilt, without the victim's plan in view, can mislead the investigation. Why: Flight may follow orders or fear, not complicity.

## foreshadowing and early clues
- [mechanism] A small ritual error or superstitious remark can plant unease that pays off later, since readers recall half-noticed details when the reveal arrives. When: The eventual reveal depends on the audience remembering an early detail. Why: A trivial detail becomes a sign only in hindsight, once a later event gives it meaning.
- [rule] Place decisive clues early in testimony, scenes, or passing mentions (e.g., a culprit's errands) so the solution is fair yet easy to overlook and reveals read as recognition. When: a mystery's answer depends on a clue the player has seen. Why: The solution stays fair yet easy to overlook, and players accept late reveals more readily when they can recall information already on screen. (x2)
