- [rule] Foreshadow that an ordinary document will form part of later evidence without naming what it proves. Why: Naming the evidence too directly spoils the reveal and removes suspense.
- [rule] Plant an unexplained timer, count, or question early, and let only the climax reveal its purpose. When: Opening a mystery whose answer comes late. Why: An unresolved detail keeps the audience reading later events for its meaning.
- [rule] Plant a sound anomaly early, before its meaning is known, so the player hears it and can connect it to the answer later. When: designing a mystery whose solution is hidden in the scene. Why: A heard cue that is explained later rewards attention without giving the answer away.
- [heuristic] Mention a hidden room in an early document, before it is physically visible, so an attentive reader can anticipate it when the room is later reached. Why: Early hints let the reveal confirm a suspicion instead of arriving from nowhere.
- [heuristic] Plant the mechanism of a later reveal in an innocent-looking early scene, then pay it off with a repeat appearance when the stakes rise.

## found and planted objects
- [model] Planted evidence takes five forms: a placed trace, a motive document, staged props, removed belongings and a substitute item.
- [rule] Let a single found object seed deduction about a larger faction when its features point to that faction's history. When: a found object carries faction-specific features. Why: a clue with faction-specific features opens a larger line of inquiry.
- [rule] A journal found in a hidden place can carry a location's backstory; describe its discovery place and seal first. When: when designing story documents for players to find. Why: The discovery context shapes how players weigh the contents.
- [rule] Give found in-game documents deliberate gaps, guessed labels, or misspellings that players must detect, and flag which entries are verified originals versus uncertain copies. When: Designing player-found documents. Why: Source reliability becomes a playable skill.
- [heuristic] Judge an explanation for a found object against the likely intent of the act; an explanation that contradicts that intent is weaker.
- [heuristic] A freshly placed object in a disturbed scene may be a deliberate signal left by the searcher for investigators. When: when a new object appears in a disturbed scene. Why: Searchers sometimes leave messages.
- [pitfall] Treating a found object as proof that an event occurred at its location, or that someone intended the act, is a pitfall when you do not know where it lay and for how long.

## game crime and legal design
- [behavior] A witness who fears punishment may stop contesting a false statement, believing a retraction will not be credited over a confession. When: a witness wants to take back testimony under threat. Why: examiners credit confessions over denials.
- [rule] Insist on guarantees that do not depend on the suspect's word before accepting a restitution offer. Why: A verbal promise cannot protect the victim.
- [rule] A guarantee answers only the fear it addresses; other fears the witness holds remain, and should not be assumed gone.
- [rule] Define a game crime by intent or allegiance, so players prove guilt through plot evidence such as letters, meetings or pledges rather than a physical act. When: when designing crimes in a game world.
- [rule] In a setting where a law criminalizes an act, require players to prove the act happened, not the magical effect the law assumes. When: Designing in-world law for a game.
- [heuristic] Read each article of a multi-part verdict separately, since one ruling can condemn one act, clear another, and make a sanction conditional.
- [fact] A grand jury can return a no true bill, ending the case before trial; the accused may then be released on paying costs.

## gothic atmosphere and setting
- [mechanism] Fog and smoke reduce visibility, leaving distant objects indistinct and sometimes losing moving animals from view. When: An observer looks across a foggy or smoky space. Why: Reduced visibility blurs distant detail and hides moving targets.
- [rule] Let a repeated test change a sound's rhythm so players can tell an echo from a second source. When: Designing responsive audio in a level. Why: Changed timing gives players evidence that separates an echo from an independent source.
- [heuristic] Use moved furniture, open doors and changed room use as clues that a presence is active in a space. When: Designing environmental storytelling for a haunted or occupied location. Why: Physical rearrangement implies recent activity without dialogue.
- [heuristic] Furnishings and marks in a room reveal what its usual occupants do there, letting an observer infer routines and hidden purposes without dialogue. When: A setting must signal a social routine, habit, or hidden purpose without explicit exposition. Why: Objects are physical residue of repeated activity, so they carry evidence of who uses a space and how.
- [heuristic] A witness's fear can make an ordinary event seem supernatural, but the fear may be real even when its supposed cause is not. When: A witness reports an uncanny event while frightened. Why: Fear shapes perception and turns a crime into a legend, yet the emotion itself is genuine.
- [pitfall] Gothic atmosphere can make an ordinary human explanation seem supernatural, so do not accept a supernatural reading while a human one remains available. When: A scene is staged with dark or eerie atmosphere. Why: Atmosphere raises the sense of mystery and lowers scrutiny.
- [pitfall] A bounded setting can create false comfort, since the obvious suspects nearest the scene may be the only ones examined while others go unchecked. When: Investigating within a small, enclosed location. Why: Proximity to the scene draws attention, and an apparently complete list can still miss people further away.

## helpers and guides
- [mechanism] A guide's familiarity with a route makes an outsider dependent on them and signals local knowledge. When: When a player or character enters an unfamiliar, dangerous area with a local guide. Why: Outsiders cannot navigate safely without local knowledge.
- [mechanism] An NPC led through a sequence of stops to a chosen place can be reconstructed by the player if each stop is shown. When: Designing an NPC movement sequence. Why: Visible stops let players trace the route.
- [rule] Give a mastermind or witness NPC a helpful-sounding suggestion that quietly steers the inquiry toward an innocent target or convenient theory.
- [rule] Let a helper NPC's letter or codex supply a motive chain that players must verify against in-world facts. When: when delivering lore that bears on a mystery.
- [heuristic] A helpful character who volunteers information and then arranges privacy can look supportive while isolating the accused. When: writing a character who seems allied with the player. Why: Helpfulness can disguise control, so players should not trust helpfulness alone.
- [pitfall] Reading each action against the person who performed it turns helpful acts, such as urging a meeting, into evidence for the opposing side. When: analysing the conduct of a suspect or a go-between. Why: Interpretation is tilted toward the frame of the accusation.
- [pitfall] A helper's own doubts about the errand can disrupt the collection, so a plausible cover story is needed. When: a helper must carry out a task without knowing its full purpose.

## hidden clue placement
- [mechanism] Hide a decisive item inside ordinary-looking set dressing or a mundane container so it becomes a key only when combined with a later clue or its revealed purpose. When: When placing a valuable clue in a scene or designing item-based progression in a level. Why: A mundane container avoids suspicion; ordinary-looking items reward attention and tie earlier and later discoveries together. (x2)
- [rule] Let a boastful NPC's exaggerated claims contain a real clue hidden among the exaggerations. When: Designing a boastful NPC who carries information. Why: Players who sift the boasts can find the genuine lead.
- [rule] Hide the explanatory key in a memory or record the protagonist cannot reach, then give the player a way to reconstruct it. When: Designing a reveal that reverses an accusation. Why: The character's ignorance keeps the explanation hidden from the reader until the reconstruction.
- [rule] Plant the real killer's tells in plain view, such as a distinctive ring, a missing coat, or a night visitor, so the reveal feels inevitable in hindsight.
- [rule] Recover a hidden original record late in the story to confirm that a suspect's written account was false. Why: A late physical proof settles what earlier documents only suggested.
- [procedure] 1) Take a directional reading while the suspect source is active. 2) Repeat it after conditions change to check the bearing stays fixed. 3) Confirm with a second, independent observation before naming the source. When: a signal or cause cannot be seen directly. Why: one bearing gives direction only, not distance or identity.
- [pitfall] A key left on a wall can seem to clear a suspect, but a spare or second key may exist, so the key's presence does not rule out another route. When: when a key appears to rule out a suspect. Why: Visible keys do not exclude duplicates.

## identity and recognition
- [definition] A recognition signal is a spoken phrase that must receive a set reply before any message or item is handed over.
- [mechanism] A distinctive mark recorded in a list can be spotted by the player in a crowd or portrait, so the player can confirm a dead or missing character's identity. When: Designing missing or dead character clues. Why: A specific, recordable feature gives a checkable link between a character and a clue.
- [heuristic] A person who knows someone well can recognise them by gait or posture even when a disguise hides the face, since habitual movement is harder to disguise than appearance. When: Identifying a person through a recurring trait, or a disguised figure near someone familiar with them. Why: Movement is harder to disguise than appearance and can link identities. (x2)
- [heuristic] Specific details of a victim's flight, such as clothing or a weapon seen with a pursuer, can point to an unlisted suspect. When: A pursuer is glimpsed but unidentified. Why: Distinctive details narrow the search to someone not yet considered.
- [pitfall] Assuming a recognition phrase stays secret once the carrier knows it is a mistake.
- [fact] Fingerprints are permanent and unique, unlike face, hair, height or build, which can change or be duplicated, so they serve as a more reliable identifier. When: When identifying a person from physical evidence. Why: Permanence and uniqueness make the mark a stable identifier.
- [fact] Displaced sheets, fresh work or rotted boards on surfaces and fittings can mark recent work and where something was hidden.

## inscriptions and objects
- [rule] Give crafters or merchants production records the player can inspect to uncover a missing copy. When: designing a clue chain around crafted items. Why: records turn a count discrepancy into a discoverable lead.
- [rule] Make dated photographs or portraits in an inn interactable, so they identify characters and confirm when those characters lived. When: when placing environmental lore clues.
- [rule] Leave an inspectable flag behind any in-world excuse for a failed testimony.
- [rule] Use environmental text such as tombstones, plaques or ledgers to imply a fact without confirming it, so players must weigh what is stated against what is left out. When: Designing in-world text that players must interpret. Why: Implied facts invite players to reason rather than simply read a confirmed answer.
- [rule] Write an antiquarian document, such as a ritual or inscription, as a set of instructions that point to a physical place. When: designing a clue hidden in an old object or text. Why: An ordinary-looking relic then works as a map the player can follow.
- [heuristic] Give a key item an inscription with a name, date and place tying it to a character and occasion, so finding the item links it to that character. When: designing a clue item tied to an NPC.
- [heuristic] Give a scene an inspectable fake forced-entry mark so players can judge whether it is staged or real. When: Designing a mystery scene with a staged clue. Why: Players who examine closely can catch the fake.

## investigation stage progression
- [rule] Define a separate evidence threshold for each escalation stage, such as suspicion, detention and accusation, so the player must earn each step; skipping stages lets suspicion jump straight to conviction.
- [heuristic] Use searches and accusations that clear suspects as steps in the investigation rather than dead ends. When: When a search yields nothing and the investigation must keep moving. Why: A negative result still narrows the field and advances understanding.
- [heuristic] Recovery of a victim can take priority over capture of culprits, so the client's stated goal can set the investigation's order of action. When: A client's goal conflicts with pursuing the culprits. Why: Immediate harm to a victim usually outweighs later capture.
- [procedure] 1) Split the event into ordered stages. 2) For each stage, ask when a harmful agent could realistically have been added. 3) Discard stages the victim was never alone for. 4) Discard items others consumed unharmed, unless dosed separately. 5) Test each stage against how fast symptoms appear. When: several people could have acted and the method is known or suspected. Why: Stage-by-stage checks narrow the list using access and timing.
- [procedure] 1) State the first question the case must answer. 2) Settle it with evidence. 3) Pose the next question only after that answer is known. When: Working through a large, multi-part mystery. Why: Later questions often depend on earlier answers.
- [pitfall] Merging the evidence-gathering stage with the later trial in memory hides where the evidence was actually built. When: reconstructing how a case was assembled.
- [fact] Common known methods of exposing a stage trick include cabinets, dark clothing, soft-soled shoes and dimmed lights.

## legal process and fairness
- [model] A vigil case has the investigator stay in a haunted place, watch an apparently supernatural presence act, then find a physical or human mechanism behind it.
- [mechanism] A reveal lands when the wrong suspect was shown every incriminating fact but no exonerating one, so the player never had grounds to clear them.
- [behavior] An unrepresented party in a formal process may be out-manoeuvred by opposing counsel, who knows procedure and can respond to surprises. When: A party acts alone in a formal or procedural setting. Why: Unfamiliarity with procedure leaves the party exposed to a more practised opponent.
- [behavior] A suspect's explanation that cannot be checked is read by the system as evasion and as proof of guilt, keeping the case closed. When: A suspect offers an explanation the investigation does not pursue. Why: Without checking the source, the system has no reason to accept the explanation.
- [heuristic] Compare the terms offered to two people, such as pay, since a difference between them can hint at differing motives worth investigating. When: when two people with a shared link receive different terms. Why: Unequal terms can reflect different interests or stakes.
- [pitfall] Using unlawful methods carries a cost to the investigator that must be weighed before acting.
- [pitfall] Vague answers such as 'usually' or 'I did not look' leave gaps that independent evidence must fill. When: A key holder gives non-specific answers about custody. Why: Vague statements cannot establish access on their own.

## machine and mechanical evidence
- [rule] A machine-based match identifies the device, not the user, so a machine trace should only narrow suspects and a second independent source is needed to name the person. When: Designing clues that narrow but do not name a suspect. Why: Two independent sources are needed to pin down an identity; the link is to the device, not to the person.
- [rule] Use a mechanism-driven reveal only when the timing of the reveal is itself a clue; crimes without a performance need only discovery.
- [heuristic] A hidden item can be found through a physical snag that the searcher recognizes from earlier experience, making the snag the moment of discovery. When: When evidence is concealed inside furniture or containers. Why: Earlier experience links the jam to its cause.
- [heuristic] Independent machine records, such as utility load curves, fix event times without depending on witness memory, so they are preferred when witness times are unreliable. When: witness times conflict or are doubtful and a machine record exists. Why: instrument timestamps do not depend on recall.
- [procedure] 1) Collect a sample from the suspect's device. 2) Compare its defective characters with a known sample under magnification. 3) Count how many defects match across the sample. When: A suspect's device could have produced a written or printed document. Why: Shared, distinctive wear indicates a common source.
- [procedure] 1) Match the suspected object's weight and position to the original. 2) Set up a substitute that holds it at a fixed distance. 3) Release it and check whether it leaves the same trace. When: A trace has a plausible cause but the mechanism has not been shown to work. Why: A reproduction that matches the original turns a theory into repeatable evidence.
- [fact] Typewriters develop individual wear over time, so characters degrade in distinctive ways and two machines rarely produce identical output.

## maker and manufacturing
- [rule] Keep a current table of symbol-to-letter pairs once several are known, so mappings do not get confused.
- [heuristic] A manufacturer's stamp on an object can point to a retailer, opening a separate line of inquiry. When: an object carries a maker's name. Why: a traceable source links the item to a shop and its customers.
- [heuristic] An honest maker's account can contradict a suspect's version, so the discrepancy needs explaining rather than dismissing. When: a maker's records conflict with a suspect's statement. Why: either account may be wrong, and the conflict often hides the key fact.
- [procedure] 1) List distinctive faults or traits, such as machine, paper or handwriting, in each document. 2) Compare the lists across documents. 3) Link documents only when several matching traits agree, not on a single shared fault, to expose a shared author or source. When: two documents might share a source, or a document's origin is disputed. Why: Several matches give a stronger link than one.
- [procedure] 1) Read the item's labels and marks. 2) Contact the retailer or maker. 3) Check its staff or customer records to narrow the candidates. When: when a clue is a manufactured object such as clothing or paper.
- [procedure] Compare a trace item against the local stock or household supply to identify its type and narrow where it came from. When: When an item is common enough that its origin is in question. Why: Matching to local stock reveals which source it likely belongs to.
- [fact] A maker can identify its own product from construction features such as material, reinforcement, fittings, and standard sizes. When: an object carries a maker's mark or has distinctive build features.

## marked objects and mail
- [mechanism] A marked object given to one of two look-alikes ties suspicion to that person, so its theft or disposal can shift who looks guilty. Why: the object links identity to a physical trace.
- [rule] Examine every item of correspondence, not only the expected ones, since a witness's written account can arrive after that witness has died.
- [heuristic] Make mail and notes into items, since the address on a letter reveals who knows where the player stays and interception creates risk. When: Designing in-game correspondence.
- [heuristic] Marked correspondence can separate secret items from ordinary mail and fix a timeline when dated records note the marking. When: Letters carry a distinctive mark or handling instruction. Why: The marking signals restricted content and can be matched against dated notes.
- [heuristic] Design a marked item so each handoff leaves a record, letting players trace its path through the world. When: when building clue trails for a mystery.
- [pitfall] A stamped mark or initials can identify an object's owner and link it to a named person, but shows ownership, not action; someone else may have placed or altered it.
- [fact] Old luggage labels can reveal a person's earlier ships and hotels, giving a traceable past.

## misdirection and red herrings
- [definition] A red herring is a plausible, dramatic explanation that lacks supporting evidence and draws attention away from the true lead.
- [definition] A planted-evidence twist has a character frame an innocent person in public with a planted object, then a witness who saw the sleight exposes the frame.
- [mechanism] Casting doubt on whether a central object or claim ever existed shifts investigators from asking where it went to asking whether they were deceived. When: When a theory depends on one unverified object or claim. Why: Questioning existence undermines the premise, so attention moves from the object's location to the reliability of the observers.
- [rule] Plant a false lead, such as a rumoured affair or motive, that players can check and dismiss to test their reasoning. When: Designing clue sets for a mystery.
- [heuristic] Let the protagonist's concealed plan turn out to be a decoy, so the player's trust in the ally's secrecy becomes the trap. When: Writing a twist that uses the player's trust in an ally. Why: The player feels pleased to be surprised by someone they already trusted.
- [pitfall] A culprit-planted object chosen to be noticed and point at the obvious suspect can mislead investigators; it feels solid until revealed as staged in final reconciliation. When: A scene contains an object that seems to explain the crime. Why: Objects placed deliberately to be noticed steer interpretation; obvious planted evidence feels solid until the reasoning shows it was staged. (x2)
- [pitfall] A red herring can look like the main event, so always test what the act actually changes. When: when evaluating a distracting event.

## npc dialogue and routines
- [behavior] People with little to occupy them tend to fill their time in disruptive ways, so routines during idle periods are easily disturbed. When: Characters or groups have long stretches with nothing to do. Why: Boredom drives activity that interrupts settled routines.
- [rule] Let gossiping or routine-chatter NPCs mention quest-relevant facts in passing, since casual delivery lowers discovery friction and surfaces details direct questions suppress. When: Designing NPC dialogue for clue discovery. Why: Casual delivery lowers the friction of discovering the fact; routine recall surfaces details that direct questions suppress. (x2)
- [rule] Let a passing NPC the player ignores be flagged later as a key figure, rewarding attention to minor characters.
- [rule] Give NPCs dialogue options that offer help in exchange for information, and let their reactions signal guilt without giving the answer away. When: an NPC holds information the player must earn.
- [heuristic] Record idle-seeming answers as facts to test later rather than acting on them at once.
- [heuristic] Second-hand NPC reports can be designed as warnings the player may choose to ignore, with consequences that follow.
- [pitfall] An idle-seeming question can lead nowhere, so the time spent on it can be wasted.

## numbered clue lists
- [rule] Present an accusation as separate numbered grounds, so the suspect cannot dismiss one point without facing the rest. When: when cornering a suspect with a multi-part case. Why: Separate points resist piecemeal rebuttal.
- [heuristic] Items that carry serial numbers, makers' marks or issue records can be traced to a single source, such as a shop, bank or issuer. When: When a subject carries an object with identifying numbers or marks. Why: Issue records link an object back to its origin and possibly to a person.
- [heuristic] A written list rearranges existing knowledge and cannot replace new information.
- [procedure] 1) Write each open issue as a separate numbered question. 2) Mark which questions depend on others. 3) Reason through each item separately. 4) Test a dependent question only after the questions it rests on hold. 5) Join items once new evidence links them. 6) Restate what remains as practical questions. Why: Separate threads stay clear until evidence connects them.
- [procedure] 1) List each detail as a numbered point. 2) Read the list as a whole rather than item by item. 3) Test whether the details form one consistent picture. 4) Note any mismatch between parts. When: When several minor clues must be assessed together. Why: Numbering forces the investigator to consider the set instead of isolated items.
- [pitfall] Numbered or anonymous labels can make people seem like abstract roles, causing investigators to overlook their real identities.
- [fact] Numbered official messages that reply to earlier ones let an investigator trace a chain of communications between parties. Why: each reference links a message to its predecessor.

## numeric and tally misreading
- [rule] Check an explanation against the actual amounts involved, and reject it if the quantity is too small to produce the claimed effect. When: an explanation depends on a substance or dose. Why: Amounts can make a proposed cause impossible.
- [heuristic] Compare a claim's ratios with established values; a basic ratio error exposes a fabrication even when the surrounding detail is vivid.
- [heuristic] Do not let a rare exception stand in to explain every outcome; if it can cover any result, it explains nothing.
- [pitfall] A small tally mark can understate or overstate evidence, so a single entry may feel more decisive than it is. When: evidence is recorded as simple counts. Why: a simple count can hide how strong each item is.
- [pitfall] Rarity does not prove ownership unless the true sales area of the item is known. When: judging whether an item points to one person. Why: Items may be common in areas the investigator has not considered.
- [pitfall] A complete copy of a document may be rare, so an apparently verified excerpt may rest on a single surviving text that is hard to check.
- [pitfall] A miscounted start or end point changes the measured interval, so confirm both points before comparing with a limit.

## observed behaviour and reaction
- [behavior] A witness's physical reaction can exceed the question asked, such as a shudder or grip tightening once a suspect is described, and this signals recognition. When: A description of a suspect provokes a reaction in the witness. Why: The reaction reveals recognition the witness may not state.
- [behavior] A person who keeps busy with a task without looking up may be listening closely while concealing their attention. When: Someone appears absorbed in an unrelated activity during conversation. Why: Apparent distraction can mask focused listening.
- [rule] Record observable behaviour as plain facts, kept separate from both the meaning assigned to it and the observer's likes or fears about the person. When: when a character's behaviour or demeanour is used as evidence about their state or character. Why: Feelings and interpretations distort reports, while recorded observations remain checkable and can be reinterpreted later.
- [heuristic] Show a character's reaction in front of the whole group, giving the audience observed behaviour rather than the narrator's interpretation.
- [heuristic] Small behavioral anomalies, such as an unexpectedly muted emotional response, can direct attention without proving guilt. When: Setting up suspicion around a character. Why: They prompt the audience to look closer while remaining inconclusive evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Position yourself to see the subject's face and hands during evidence. 2) Track changes over time: colour, sweat, repeated gestures, eye focus. 3) Note silence and absent gestures. 4) Record minor details for later use. When: when watching a suspect receive damning evidence. Why: Physical reactions can reveal shock where speech stays controlled.
- [pitfall] Recording every physical movement of a suspect aloud turns demeanour into evidence, so ordinary movements can be read as guilt.

## physical state timing
- [mechanism] Physical changes that accumulate over time, such as growth of stubble or wilting, indicate how long ago an event happened. When: when estimating elapsed time without a timestamp. Why: Such changes progress at roughly steady rates, so their extent measures duration.
- [behavior] An unusually rigid or deep sleep state is a strange observation to record, not proof of innocence. When: when a suspect is found in an unusual sleep state. Why: An anomalous state invites suspicion but does not establish alibi.
- [heuristic] Physical details, such as an object's location or a person's dress and appearance, can fix when an action or disturbance began and test the accounts given of it. When: when timing an event is uncertain.
- [heuristic] A visible physical change in a character can appear before its explanation, serving as foreshadowing of what is to come.
- [heuristic] Real illness is hard to fake, so when a suspect's symptoms appear at a time that conflicts with a faked story, treat the timing as a test of that story. When: A suspect is too ill or silent to speak and the cover story depends on the timing. Why: Genuine physical symptoms follow biology, not the timing a guilty person would choose.
- [heuristic] Ask why an item appeared in its exact place and at that time; the placement often reveals whom the item was meant to implicate.
- [fact] Physical states such as wet ink or fresh adhesive reveal how recently a message was made or placed.

## physical traces and falls
- [mechanism] A body shot through the chest tends to crumple forward or down, while a body falling straight back stays extended, with items displaced behind it. When: Judging whether a body's posture fits a claimed fall. Why: Gravity and the direction of impact determine how the limbs and loose items settle.
- [rule] Test each fastening on its own rather than assuming a seal is complete.
- [heuristic] Hand prints with fingers pointing up a slope, plus rounded knee marks, suggest repeated falls while climbing.
- [heuristic] Treat a witness's statement that a door was bolted as testimony from the person who tried it, not as established fact. Why: the witness may be mistaken or lying.
- [heuristic] An object found partway down a slope suggests a fall was not unbroken, so something may have caught the falling person.
- [pitfall] A single trace can be faked, since a cunning person can swap tyres to leave unfamiliar tracks. Check each trace against the others.
- [pitfall] In a cluttered scene, many objects look irrelevant, so a meaningful trace can be dismissed at first.

## priming perception and audiences
- [mechanism] A manipulator can prime an intermediary with a false suspicion so that the intermediary carries out the plan willingly. When: a plan requires a go-between. Why: a believed grievance turns the intermediary into a willing tool.
- [mechanism] A prepared public address, delivered to an assembled and already moved audience, can turn vague fears into fixed doctrine and retroactively justify earlier actions. When: a gathering follows a day of accusations and examinations. Why: Listeners already primed by events accept the speech's framing of them.
- [behavior] A witness primed by earlier talk of a threat may perceive a figure that a calm companion does not. When: a witness heard rumors before a shared event. Why: Prior expectation shapes perception, especially under fear.
- [rule] Present rival theories before the solution so the audience is primed to question conclusions and test them against the clues.
- [rule] Use an NPC's sightings that match a claimed cause as a clue to that NPC's bias.
- [heuristic] Have a character warn that the antagonist is cunning, so the audience expects a trap. When: a scene is building toward a surprise or ambush. Why: a stated warning sets an expectation that later events can play on.
- [procedure] 1) Brief a witness about a newcomer before the meeting. 2) Expect the witness to form a favorable view. 3) Treat that prepared view as a bias to discount, and check it against later evidence before trusting it. When: an investigator or character needs a witness to hold a prepared view, or a character or player holds an impression set up by someone else. Why: A briefed impression shapes judgment, so it is not independent evidence about the person. A prepared impression can be false, and trusting it leads to conclusions the evidence does not support.

## probabilistic inference from facts
- [rule] State inferences drawn from appearance as probabilities rather than certainties, and keep the basis for each stated. When: when reasoning from observed appearance.
- [procedure] 1) State the chain-of-evidence idea aloud to the suspect. 2) Watch the listener's reaction while speaking. 3) Treat the reaction as a signal, not as proof. When: An investigator wants to test a suspect without presenting firm evidence. Why: Speaking a theory can expose a reaction that a plain argument would not.
- [pitfall] Probability depends on context, so a dramatic theory is not automatically the probable one.
- [pitfall] A probable circumstance can be accidental, so treating it as proof of guilt or innocence confuses likelihood with certainty. When: Reasoning from a single circumstance that seems to point toward a conclusion. Why: Accidents and coincidences can produce a probable-looking circumstance without any link to the outcome.
- [pitfall] A motive can be invented to fit the facts, so answers should be labelled as probabilities rather than settled conclusions. When: Reconstructing an actor's motive from incomplete facts. Why: Fitting a story to the facts after the fact can mislead.
- [fact] Matching two facts, such as a witness's answer and a name, creates a strong probability of a link, not proof of identity.
- [fact] Probable signs include strong suspicion, bad reputation, habitual hostile remarks, unusual physical marks, testimony of victims, and suspected family ties, each suggesting guilt without establishing it. When: when classifying evidence in a suspect case. Why: Each of these fits a suspect but could also arise innocently.

## purchase and seller evidence
- [rule] Log NPC purchases of tools that imply a plan, so players can deduce intent from what was bought and where it was taken. When: Designing an NPC inventory or shop record that carries story clues. Why: Players can reconstruct hidden plans from visible purchasing behaviour.
- [heuristic] Physical objects bought or moved during a timeline suggest a purpose, even when no one states it, and should be weighed as evidence. Why: purchases reveal intent that a witness may not admit.
- [heuristic] Plain, undecorated goods suggest a practical buyer, such as a servant, rather than a wealthy one. When: when a purchase is used to narrow down suspects.
- [heuristic] Small purchases and instructions to a driver can reveal a planned future appointment or destination. When: observing a target's errands. Why: preparations hint at what is coming.
- [heuristic] A purchase made shortly before an event is more likely relevant than an older one, since a substance is carried only for a limited time.
- [heuristic] Verify who actually made a purchase or visit, because a lookalike's action can be attributed to a rival and turned into evidence against them.
- [procedure] 1) Interview the sellers of an item. 2) Record the buyer's measurements and the item's description. 3) Ask each seller the same questions. When: tracing a purchased item to its buyer. Why: Identical questions let answers be compared across sellers.

## question design and framing
- [rule] Let an NPC's answer name a different person than the player expects, so the player must check their assumption against the answer. When: Designing NPC answers about who was present.
- [rule] Let player questions be closed prompts that can rule out a suspect's explanation, so a witness's answers narrow the possibilities. When: Designing player dialogue for deduction. Why: Closed prompts make denials informative.
- [heuristic] Ask what has happened that has never happened before, since an unusual event gives a sharper question than a routine one. When: framing the central question of an investigation. Why: a novel event narrows the field of possible explanations.
- [heuristic] A note can answer one question while leaving others open, so check which questions remain unresolved after reading it.
- [heuristic] The wording and order of a question shape what a witness reports, so re-ask with different phrasing to check an answer. When: Eliciting identification from a witness. Why: Question framing can lead a witness to an unreliable answer.
- [procedure] 1) Ask about structure first, such as the first letter's range in the alphabet. 2) Narrow to a single letter. 3) Then ask for the full name. Use only yes or no answers. When: Identifying a concealed name through questioning. Why: Each yes or no answer eliminates candidates, so the name is reached without revealing more than needed.
- [pitfall] A question whose answer would fit every competing theory cannot test any of them.

## quiet investigation and monitoring
- [rule] Keep sensitive leads and record requests quiet, made through a neutral intermediary, and monitor quietly to catch the culprit in the act. When: Public or official alarm, an accusation, or a sensitive lead would warn the watched party. Why: A warned suspect destroys or alters evidence, removes it, and confesses nothing.
- [heuristic] Walk along the quietest available streets, looking back often, so a follower is easier to spot. When: Suspecting a tail on an urban walk. Why: Few other people make pursuers stand out.
- [heuristic] A death that seems to occur in a quiet place may have happened during a busy event; check whether a crowd timing explains the traces better. When: reading a scene that appears to suit a lone culprit. Why: a loud event can mask an act that looks isolated.
- [heuristic] Keep investigating quietly during a lull, and signal that work continues so the calm reads as preparation rather than lost time. When: public progress has paused. Why: Visible ongoing work prevents the lull feeling wasted.
- [heuristic] Ask about the quiet interval before an event and about the witness's views of others, noting hostility as possible bias.
- [procedure] 1) Begin the first questioning with few observers and little publicity. 2) Avoid exposing suspects before the evidence is in.
- [pitfall] Keeping a suspect under watch at home only works if the watch can follow them when they leave. When: Surveilling a suspect to catch a meeting. Why: Losing the subject at departure defeats the surveillance.

## scene testimony comparison
- [model] A crime scene is a set of competing claims: who has authority, who touched what, and who says what happened.
- [rule] Separate who committed an act from how the scene was staged; identifying the perpetrator matters more than correcting a misdirected scene.
- [rule] Keep what a scene shows separate from what the people in it claim until both have been compared.
- [heuristic] Objects found at a scene can be tested against witness claims about a product, place or time. When: When a witness makes a checkable claim. Why: Objects are physical facts that can contradict testimony.
- [procedure] 1) Inspect the scene before interviewing household members. 2) Keep witnesses apart from the scene and each other while they wait. 3) Interview each witness in a chosen order. 4) Compare each account with those already taken. When: when several witnesses may influence one another. Why: keeping witnesses apart stops their accounts from contaminating each other.
- [procedure] 1) State what the crime would have required at the location. 2) List the physical signs that act would leave. 3) Compare the observed signs with those expected. 4) Treat a mismatch as evidence the body or crime was moved. When: When a body or object's placement does not fit the act. Why: A set of agreeing traces is needed; a single odd detail is weak.
- [pitfall] Do not treat saw nothing as nothing happened until you have checked the observer's coverage of the route.

## sealed rooms and access
- [mechanism] A social barrier, such as an assertion that no one goes somewhere, restricts access less than a physical barrier, and open access can still allow tampering. When: A space is guarded by a stated rule rather than a lock. Why: People respect verbal restrictions unevenly, and unlocked spaces remain open to anyone who chooses to enter.
- [heuristic] Give the culprit a delivery or service role, which justifies movement across the setting while drawing no scrutiny from others. When: the culprit must move through a restricted setting. Why: An ordinary messenger is seen everywhere and so is rarely questioned.
- [procedure] 1) Call the missing person's name and search hiding places. 2) Test each exit in turn and confirm whether it is still locked. 3) Rule out ordinary routes before considering unusual ones. 4) Widen the search across the house and grounds. When: A person vanishes from a sealed room. Why: Checking exits in order closes ordinary routes and keeps the impossibility open.
- [procedure] 1) List every possible way into or out of the room. 2) Test each route against the physical facts. 3) Test each against the people present and their sightlines. 4) Eliminate failed routes; the remainder is the answer. When: When a room seems closed or unreachable. Why: Elimination against facts and witnesses narrows the routes to the plausible one.
- [procedure] 1) Map every route out of the room. 2) Map what each witness could see from where they stood. 3) Time the blind intervals between sightlines. 4) Test the story against physical evidence such as noise from a latch. 5) Accept the sealed-room claim only after all routes are checked. When: A person appears to have vanished from a sealed space. Why: Apparently impossible disappearances usually depend on what observers could not see.
- [pitfall] A simple barrier such as a weight or spring can be passed by anyone who knows it is there. When: A space is guarded only by a lightweight mechanism. Why: Knowledge of the mechanism is enough to defeat it.
- [pitfall] A room used by several groups can mislead an observer who assumes it serves a single purpose; objects may reflect multiple overlapping routines. When: Inferring a room's use from its objects. Why: A single room can host the habits of several distinct groups, each leaving different traces.

## settlement and closure
- [rule] When rival readings clash, settle the dispute by returning to a fixed written record rather than continuing to argue.
- [rule] Settle who is present before questioning, because a witness may refuse to dismiss others and an investigator without authority cannot force it.
- [rule] A single reliable, independent positive identification can settle an open clue question, after which the result can be acted on. When: a specific check can confirm a clue. Why: One trustworthy confirmation may be enough to proceed.
- [heuristic] Frame a timing question as a yes-or-no matter first, since it settles quickly, and defer longer questions until timing is fixed. When: several questions compete during an investigation.
- [heuristic] A dated record of an agreed settlement can show that a later arrest for the same debt breached it.
- [heuristic] End a mystery by hushing the matter up through a settlement or offer rather than justice, leaving the social situation closed. When: When the culprit has a strong motive to conceal the truth.
- [tradeoff] Settlement closes disputes fast but leaves truth and culprit unestablished; investigation costs time but finds liars. Quiet settlement after confession suits cases where public trial would harm innocents. When: when a dispute can be bought off, or when a culprit confesses and public trial would harm innocents. Why: A public trial can harm innocent parties, so mercy can be the stronger choice. (x2)

## single clue overreliance
- [rule] Do not rely on a single found object or shared detail; treat the link as provisional until other evidence confirms it. When: A lone object or shared detail appears to implicate or link a person. Why: One matching detail can coincide without a real connection. (x2)
- [rule] Let a clue depend on one assumption the player must test, rather than stating the conclusion outright. When: designing a clue that points toward a suspect. Why: A testable assumption lets the player reach the conclusion through their own reasoning.
- [pitfall] A single physical clue, such as powder, can fit several explanations or event sequences; do not read too much into it alone.
- [pitfall] No single clue should carry the case: it can mislead, and another trace may exonerate its suspect, so test each clue and treat it as one of several. When: Building the evidence chain for a mystery. Why: If one clue fails to land, the solution collapses.
- [pitfall] Fixating on one vivid clue blocks other lines of thought.
- [pitfall] Making one sealed document the only clue makes the story depend on a single object, so losing or missing it stalls the whole mystery. When: when designing a withheld-information reveal. Why: All progress rests on one item.
- [pitfall] Treating one reaction as proof of a hidden trait leads to a wrong conclusion; independent confirmation is still needed. When: When interpreting a suspect's response to a test. Why: A single reaction can have several causes, so it is only a lead until corroborated.

## social cues and address
- [behavior] A forced laugh after a calm answer can betray fear of discovery that the spoken answer hides. When: the investigator is caught observing the witness's surroundings.
- [rule] Give a friendly NPC a brief tell, such as a hard glance after a warm greeting, and let the player decide whether to trust it.
- [rule] Let a friendly NPC's gaze repeatedly settle on one object or door, a small tell hinting at a second motive that a later check can reveal. When: Writing a helpful character who has an undisclosed agenda. Why: Players who noticed the tell gain an advantage when the motive surfaces.
- [heuristic] Track forms of address in dialogue as a clue-bearing record of relationships; a formal title in place of a given name usually signals emotional distance. When: Reading personal correspondence or dialogue. Why: Forms of address encode the speaker's relationship to the person named.
- [heuristic] Use an unexpected foreign word spoken by a character as a flag that something in the scene is not what it seems.
- [pitfall] Friendliness or goodwill can conceal hidden opinions or intent to harm, so don't take a friendly witness's account at face value or treat goodwill as proof of innocence. When: Assessing testimony from a sympathetic witness. Why: Friendliness can conceal a shared opinion that colours the account; flattery can conceal intent to harm. (x2)
- [pitfall] A rule forbidding the accused to look at accusers makes any glance an offence, so ordinary behavior becomes apparent proof of guilt.

## sourced logs and timelines
- [rule] Send a messenger immediately and press on before the opponent can react; speed is the counter to a timed obstruction. When: when an obstruction is timed to an opportunity. Why: Delay gives the opponent free rein.
- [rule] Split a quest log into separate threads, and let a player test a theory against evidence before committing, so a red herring can fit one thread but not the others. When: designing a mystery with multiple parallel leads. Why: separate threads reveal inconsistencies that a single thread hides.
- [rule] Ask how a witness knows a time: direct observation, a personal watch, or a chime heard while distracted. Each carries different reliability. When: when a witness gives a time.
- [rule] Mark a source's claim as the source's claim, not an established fact, when footnotes or testimony describe an unverified trait. When: A document asserts a trait that cannot be checked. Why: Separating asserted claims from established facts prevents false certainty.
- [rule] Do not rely on memory for a recurring pattern when a written schedule can confirm it, and leave unconfirmed points open until a source settles them. When: A witness claims a pattern but cannot confirm details about other events. Why: Confident recollection of a pattern can be wrong without a source.
- [heuristic] A case file in a game can record each clue with its source, so the player can weigh who observed it. When: Clues come from multiple characters or observations. Why: Recorded sources let the player judge reliability.
- [procedure] 1) Arrange facts in dated order. 2) Log each timed fact with its source, separating testimony from independently confirmed facts; a plausible story is not a source. 3) Set entries against the crime's time window. 4) Mark gaps: undated periods and claims resting on one source. When: establishing whether a person could have been present, or whether a movement claim can be checked. Why: Mixing unverified claims with confirmed facts hides which parts of the timeline are reliable. (x2)

## speaker identity and voice
- [rule] Give overheard speakers distinct pitch, tone, phrasing or a repeated rhyme, so listeners can tell them apart and match a recited phrase to a known event without seeing them. When: speakers are heard through a wall or door. Why: voice traits remain distinct without visual contact.
- [rule] Let a character appear to be in conversation while being silent or dead, so the player notices the gap between what they see and hear. When: Designing a scene with multiple characters. Why: Mismatches between visual and audio cues prompt the player to re-examine the scene.
- [heuristic] Match a witness's detail to the exact placement of an item, such as the finger a ring is worn on, rather than to the item alone. When: A witness recalls a specific, unusual detail about someone's appearance. Why: Exact placement is more distinctive than the item.
- [procedure] 1) Have a watcher confirm that no one entered or left, fixing the sequence of arrivals. 2) Give each watcher a position and a signal. 3) Tell the witness to speak only if certain. 4) Reveal the face suddenly under light. 5) Accept a one-word confirmation. When: when a suspect was seen briefly in poor light and must be identified. Why: fixed sequence and separate roles prevent leading the witness.
- [pitfall] A fast response shows speed, not identity. A timeline narrows the field of possible leakers but cannot by itself name the one responsible.
- [pitfall] Counting two spellings of one name as two witnesses or two accused people inflates the cast and corrupts the timeline.
- [pitfall] Assuming an attacker's identity from a whispered phrase alone is unsafe; the phrase must be tied to other evidence. When: When a single overheard phrase links to a suspect. Why: Words can be reused, coincidental, or misheard.

## specific checkable details
- [rule] When interviewing a reluctant witness, keep questioning on specific facts such as threats and motive rather than general impressions, since witnesses often don't know which details matter. When: when interviewing a reluctant witness. Why: Witnesses often don't know which details matter, so ask the specific question instead of waiting for them to volunteer it.
- [heuristic] Make claims specific by naming the act, victim, place, slope, or time, since specific details can be checked against other evidence while vague claims cannot be tested. When: when writing or evaluating witness accounts, appearance details, or quest accusations. Why: Specific details can be verified unlike general impressions; precise claims are falsifiable and let players act on evidence. (x2)
- [heuristic] Judge witness claims by small specific details, such as build, age, accent, overheard speech fragments, or observations tied to a known routine, rather than by general impressions.
- [heuristic] A detail a witness insists on can be more stable than the identity they claim, so test each detail separately.
- [heuristic] A capability claim gains weight when several witnesses describe specific acts, such as lifting heavy objects. When: when assessing whether someone could have moved something.
- [heuristic] Press a witness with narrow questions about details that a true account would have to get right, so each answer can be checked. When: When a witness's account touches a physical or medical point. Why: Specific claims expose inaccuracies that vague claims hide.
- [pitfall] Specific details feel like proof and raise credibility but are not corroboration; detailed names, dates and measurements are often chosen to persuade, not to make an account true. When: A vision names objects that match people or events in the world. Why: Specificity raises perceived credibility, though it is not independent corroboration. (x2)

## staged tests and proof
- [mechanism] A dialogue test that asks the player to choose answers can decide whether a later trap triggers, so the player's responses determine the outcome. When: Designing a dialogue-gated trap. Why: Branching answers tie the trap's activation to the player's own choices.
- [rule] Make the reveal a physical demonstration: a staged test such as a fake collapse or a dropped object exposes the suspect rather than only a verbal explanation. When: Designing the climax of a mystery where a suspect must be exposed. Why: A test the player can watch gives the reveal proof and makes the solution feel earned.
- [heuristic] Evidence that looks most conclusive should be checked against the suspected person's habits and character before it is trusted. When: A staged scene offers a strong, tidy explanation. Why: The most polished false evidence is designed to read as conclusive, so only comparison with established behaviour exposes it.
- [procedure] 1) Reproduce the original conditions: timing, dose and deprivation. 2) Place sceptical or hostile observers where they can watch. 3) Record each action against the original account. 4) Declare which parts reproduced and which did not. When: Proving a reconstructed past event, especially when the final proof must convince people who previously doubted the answer. Why: Matching conditions and watched results make the reproduction credible, and witnesses who doubted the theory and then observe the outcome cannot dispute it.
- [procedure] 1) Have the trusted helper request a task from the player. 2) Make the task a test of the player's trustworthiness. 3) Reveal the test's true purpose only after the player has accepted it. When: Designing a quest whose hidden purpose is a trap. Why: Players accept a request framed as help, so the test feels like part of the quest rather than a hostile act.
- [procedure] 1) Put a name or face in a public or accidental encounter. 2) Watch whether the stranger reacts. 3) Note both recognition and absence of reaction as possible signals. When: Identity is in doubt and a name can be tested in public. Why: A staged encounter reveals recognition or concealment without direct accusation.
- [procedure] 1) Seat suspects together in a formal setting. 2) Present physical evidence one item at a time, raising pressure at each stage. 3) Observe and record reactions against the statement being made. 4) Confront with the record only after the reactions are reviewed. When: Physical evidence is in hand and admission is sought through pressure. Why: Escalating stages let reactions be matched to specific claims.

## suspect list and alibis
- [mechanism] Seed two or three suspects per level, each with a plausible alibi that a single physical test breaks, such as a mold, a reflection or a trapped demonstration. When: When populating a level with suspects. Why: Each alibi that one test can break gives the player a discrete, fair check.
- [mechanism] Each identity reveal re-sorts the suspect list, so suspicion passes from one character to the next in sequence. When: A mystery with several identity reveals. Why: A new identity changes who had motive, access and opportunity.
- [behavior] Repeated glances toward a hidden spot and watching through a gap in a door show a suspect is monitoring the investigator. When: A suspect's attention keeps returning to the investigator's activity. Why: Monitoring reveals concern about what the investigator might find.
- [rule] When laying out suspects, write motive, opportunity and counter-evidence side by side. When: Comparing several suspects in a mystery. Why: Side-by-side layout exposes which suspect has the strongest combined case.
- [heuristic] Give each suspect a plausible guilt pattern, then clear them with a new fact rather than a twist, testing and dropping each false solution before raising the next. When: building a mystery with multiple suspects. Why: Repeated testing keeps the audience engaged and uncertain. (x2)
- [heuristic] Keep a shortlist of suspects with plausible motives open until direct physical evidence narrows the field. When: several suspects have plausible motives. Why: Early conclusions drawn from one reading can send the investigation down a false path.
- [procedure] Move a suspect out of earshot before discussing the threat, so the group can speak freely while the suspect is watched without being alerted. When: A suspect is present while the group plans. Why: Speaking openly in front of a suspect may alert them and disrupt observation.

## suspect reasoning and linkage
- [model] A linked mystery collection repeats a shape: a bold claim or impossible event, small physical clues logged without explanation, a plausible wrong solution, a crisis, then a reconstruction that reruns the clues. When: designing a series of mystery cases with a shared solver. Why: The shared shape lets players learn to distrust the first explanation while the mechanisms vary.
- [mechanism] A leaked detail such as a map or description can trace back to one NPC, creating an optional investigation into who leaked it. When: Designing optional side content around information leaks. Why: Tracing a leak gives the player a self-contained goal with a specific culprit.
- [heuristic] Keep the proof incomplete until a late clue arrives, so the first theory has to be argued rather than simply confirmed. When: A mystery's first theory is pivotal. Why: Argument keeps the theory contested and the player engaged.
- [heuristic] The most helpful character is often the one who casually dismisses clues, so treat such dismissal as a warning sign. When: evaluating an NPC who guides the investigation. Why: Dismissing evidence can hide its authorship.
- [procedure] 1) Note the remark and who was present. 2) Note the target's reaction. 3) Infer a personal sensitivity from the reaction. 4) Ask who could most easily exploit that sensitivity. 5) Seek that person and confirm with later evidence. When: When a social remark might point toward a person connected to an event. Why: Each step is a small inference, and later evidence is needed before the lead is trusted.
- [pitfall] Ignorance by request can look like a plot convenience. Make it costly by showing a visible consequence, such as an unresolved crime. When: when a character asks not to be told the truth. Why: Without a cost, the choice reads as a shortcut rather than a meaningful decision.
- [pitfall] Letting the audience assume an investigator knows more than the narrator without signalling the gap. When: Writing a mystery from a limited viewpoint. Why: Unsignalled differences in knowledge mislead the audience about who knows what.

## suspense through anticipation
- [mechanism] Visible anticipation, such as every eye turning to a door or a stir at a small gesture, builds tension before a key reveal. When: A scripted reveal is about to happen and the audience must wait. Why: Repeated expectant cues keep attention fixed on the coming event.
- [mechanism] A summons demanding immediate action and secrecy makes the recipient fear more than the stated facts, so unnamed dread grows. When: A message calls a character to act quickly and keep it quiet. Why: The request for secrecy and haste suggests a hidden threat larger than the message states.
- [mechanism] Building expectation around an unseen arrival, then delaying it, raises tension and turns the eventual appearance into a reveal. When: introducing a new character who should be anticipated. Why: A withheld payoff keeps curiosity active until the character appears.
- [mechanism] Repeating a test at a fixed time while withholding its result builds suspense, since the audience expects the next occurrence. When: evidence is incomplete and the answer depends on a later observation. Why: a fixed schedule creates anticipation while the outcome stays hidden.
- [behavior] A threat left undefined in a character's mind often feels worse than a known one. When: A character receives vague warning of danger. Why: Without a definite shape, the imagination fills the gap with greater fears.
- [heuristic] Delay the full explanation and give partial hints. Suspense comes from anticipation and open questions more than from the answer itself. When: The audience must gather evidence before the reveal. Why: Unresolved questions keep the audience moving toward the next event.
- [procedure] 1) Start with a distant sound. 2) Move to a closer sound. 3) Insert a pause in which the threat seems near. 4) Release the tension with a sharp event. When: Building suspense as a threat approaches slowly. Why: Escalation in steps keeps tension rising until release.

## suspicion shifted to third party
- [mechanism] Suspicion that moves outward to an external group and then back inward to staff can hide an insider until tool evidence lines up. When: Shifting suspicion across factions during a mystery. Why: An external suspect absorbs early attention, so the return to insiders feels like a fresh discovery.
- [behavior] Once evidence exposes a substitution, cover-up or frame (a proof, or a witness's described physical act even without the object shown), suspicion shifts to whoever arranged it. When: A substitution or cover-up is exposed. Why: The party who arranged the concealment becomes the logical source of the deception.
- [behavior] Under public accusation, suspicion is shifted onto a third party through rumour, and the accuser's own honesty may be attacked. When: When characters face a public accusation. Why: Pointing at someone else deflects attention from the accused.
- [rule] Make the external threat believable before revealing the internal one; a credible outside culprit gives an insider cover to act unseen. When: Designing a mystery where the culprit is a trusted insider. Why: Players accept the outside suspect first, so the insider's real motive stays hidden.
- [heuristic] Make an innocent suspect's flight a turning point in the middle of the case, not the ending. When: a suspect runs or disappears before being cleared. Why: A midpoint flight keeps suspicion high while the investigation continues.
- [heuristic] Let a trusted helper who guards, searches or assists the player be a suspect in plain sight, with clues that look procedural rather than suspicious. When: Placing a culprit among the investigators. Why: Routine actions look like normal duty, so their suspicious meaning is missed until late.
- [pitfall] When an outsider or supernatural suspect is introduced early, a visible insider detail gets dismissed and household members holding the inside plot go unchecked. When: an outsider or supernatural suspect is presented early or set up as the obvious culprit. Why: The outsider explanation absorbs attention, leaving the detail unweighed. (x2)

## timing as proof
- [mechanism] A dated, repeating pattern gives the audience a clock, so they can predict the next event and feel the timing of the threat. When: a recurring threat appears on a schedule. Why: Predictable intervals make the audience anticipate the next event and feel tension.
- [heuristic] Timing evidence alone rarely proves an alibi or route: it sets limits other facts must fit, so corroborate any timed result before trusting it. When: A timing result is used as evidence. Why: Time windows constrain without establishing presence or absence, and one measurement can mislead without corroborating evidence.
- [heuristic] Time each arrest after enough evidence and suspicion have built, so the group's distrust matures before it is used.
- [procedure] 1) Fix the event time from objects still in place, such as cards on a table or unmoved chairs. 2) Use a suspect's departure as the boundary after which he could not have acted. 3) Narrow the window to the interval between these markers. When: An event must be timed from a scene. Why: Unchanged objects record the moment the scene was last left alone.
- [pitfall] A timing link or match alone is weak evidence: it suggests a connection without proving one, and witness uncertainty and reporting-chain time reckoning limit its value.
- [pitfall] Timing logic can point suspicion at a witness; a sworn denial must be checked against evidence rather than dismissed or accepted by default. Why: A plausible sequence can be wrong even when it singles out someone.
- [pitfall] A timing estimate is only as reliable as its assumed burn rates and the weather conditions it assumes. Why: wrong rates or conditions shift the estimated duration.

## tone shift as clue
- [behavior] A disguised speaker's ironic or mocking remark can betray their identity to someone who knows their manner of speech. When: a disguised character speaks. Why: Habitual tone and wit persist beneath a disguise.
- [heuristic] Alternate light and grim scenes; abrupt contrast, such as a calm domestic scene followed by violent news or banter followed by grim news, heightens tension and keeps the audience unsettled. When: When pacing a sequence of scenes or moving a scene from relaxed to ominous. Why: Contrast with the prior mood sharpens the impact of the next discovery or news, and abrupt tonal change keeps the audience uneasy.
- [heuristic] Letters or journal entries can change wording with an NPC's mood, so players learn to read tone and omission as clues. When: Designing written NPC communication.
- [heuristic] Use a change in dialogue tone as a tell the player tracks over time, not as a fixed verdict. When: Designing NPC reactions as clues. Why: A tell suggests a question without settling it.
- [heuristic] Following a grave scene with a light one sets expectations for tone and hints at character stakes such as financial strain.
- [tradeoff] Firmness draws out evasive answers but can close a witness down; a friendlier tone and questions about the past draw out a holding-back suspect's background. Use firmness only for evasion. When: A witness refuses to answer or talks around a matter; a suspect is holding back on a topic. Why: Firmness signals that evasion will be noticed, but it can also end cooperation.
- [pitfall] Witness tone, confidence, stammer or attitude is not evidence: a stiff or evasive manner is not proof of guilt, and sincere protest can sway listeners even after gaps are exposed. Why: Attitude changes reflect feeling, not facts; a reader's judgment of tone can stand in for evidence, so conclusions about people can outrun what was observed. (x2)

## trace collection
- [rule] Record and document each mark in place before interpreting what it means. When: Examining a scene.
- [heuristic] Collect each small physical trace separately, marking its origin, even before its meaning is known, since it may connect to another source later. When: Gathering physical evidence at a scene. Why: Mixed or unlabeled samples cannot be linked back to their source, and an unexplained trace can gain meaning once another clue is found.
- [heuristic] Let a merchant NPC sell a suspect's discarded item, so the player can test a physical clue before making an accusation. When: Designing clue-testing in a game.
- [procedure] 1) Cut a small sample from inside a seam. 2) Seal it. 3) Label it with owner, item and date before sending it to a specialist. When: a stain or residue must be tested by a lab. Why: keeps the sample's identity and custody clear.
- [procedure] 1) Record each trace in a numbered list. 2) Test each one by smell, taste or fresh examination. 3) Keep samples sealed so they can be re-examined. When: Investigating a scene disturbed by many people. Why: Systematic records keep traces comparable and reliable.
- [fact] Mud, dust and wet ground preserve physical marks such as ruts and footprints, which can later be read as evidence. When: A scene holds marks that witnesses cannot supply. Why: Soft surfaces retain marks for later inference.
- [fact] Physical traces include fingerprints, footprints, cigarette ash, mud and handwriting, each supplying facts rather than final answers. Why: raw traces need interpretation before they explain an event.

## two-part evidence design
- [model] Evidence falls into two tiers: grounds that justify examination, and proofs that can sustain a verdict, namely a voluntary confession or two credible witnesses to a specific act. When: when grading evidence before an accusation. Why: separating leads from conclusive proof prevents weak indicators from becoming a conviction.
- [rule] Give clues two plausible readings, one harmless and one damning, and let context, a second item, or later confirmation settle which holds, so the player weighs and chooses. When: Designing evidence documents or visual clues for players. Why: A clue with one obvious reading gives no reason to deliberate, and players who read context reach different conclusions.
- [heuristic] Check both sides of a document, since one object can carry several kinds of information that a single glance would miss. When: The object has writing or information on more than one face.
- [heuristic] A scroll that quotes a second character's report gives the player two sources, each with its own bias, to weigh against each other. When: when writing in-world documents. Why: Competing sources make players judge reliability.
- [heuristic] Divide the explanation between an outside witness account and an insider confession, so the second part adds new information instead of repeating the first. When: Delivering a late reveal that needs both an external view and internal motive. Why: Two sources cover different ground, so the audience gets both how and why.
- [procedure] 1) Plant the link as two separate facts in the first scene. 2) Keep a plausible separate-person explanation in place. 3) Have an outside witness show the transformation. 4) Follow with a confession that gives motive and mechanism. When: Revealing that a surprising figure is a transformed or hidden version of another character. Why: A witnessed demonstration makes the reveal believable, and the confession adds history the witness could not provide.
- [fact] A single short note can be written in alternating words by two people, and their differing stroke strength and letterforms reveal who wrote which words.

## uncertainty and assumptions
- [rule] Treat a document's emotional tone as a sign of possible bias, not as proof of its claims.
- [rule] Suppress theorizing while observing, because speculation shapes the imagination and distorts what is seen. When: Recording events as they happen. Why: Speculation fills gaps in perception with imagined content.
- [rule] Treat an inferred belief drawn from another person's reading of behaviour as a lead to pursue, not a settled fact. When: A belief is inferred second-hand from observed behaviour. Why: The inference is itself an interpretation and may be wrong.
- [rule] When evidence supports several explanations, state the uncertainty openly rather than forcing one answer. When: evidence is genuinely ambiguous on a side matter. Why: openly stated ambiguity reads as realism rather than carelessness.
- [heuristic] A ready explanation, such as having a reason, can end inquiry too early, so the investigator should ask what that reason actually is. When: A person offers a justification for an unusual request. Why: Accepting a stated reason without probing leaves the real purpose hidden.
- [procedure] 1) List each symptom. 2) Assign it to the proposed cause if that cause explains it. 3) Collect the symptoms left over as the unexplained residue. When: when a witness offers a natural explanation for a strange condition. Why: Separating explained effects from the remainder shows whether the cause is complete.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the claim the whole inquiry depends on. 2) Ask whether anyone verified it. 3) Propose a rival explanation, such as impersonation, that would explain the facts. 4) Work out who the alternative actor is and why they would act that way. When: An investigation or deduction rests on a claim that no one has checked. Why: Testing a foundational assumption can reopen the full set of explanations, even though it proves nothing by itself.

## victims and past connections
- [behavior] People who do not know a colleague's hidden past judge them only by present conduct, while a few confidants know the history. When: a person's past is known to only a few. Why: secrets are shared selectively, so few people can explain later reactions.
- [rule] Place a key fact with a side character who may disclaim its relevance. Its significance should become clear only when it fills a gap in the player's notes. When: when designing clues delivered through dialogue. Why: Delayed meaning rewards players who keep and compare information.
- [heuristic] A gentle or friendly appearance is no guide to guilt; a suspect's history and background give better evidence.
- [heuristic] Check a suspect's past dealings with the victim, such as an earlier charge, as a possible hidden tie that explains the link. When: Reviewing motive and connections. Why: Prior contact can reveal motive or a concealed relationship.
- [procedure] 1) Keep a central figure's past out of the main action. 2) Have an outside witness reveal one fragment of it in passing. 3) Give the witness a reason to be reluctant or a personal stake. 4) Add a contrasting view from another character. When: A victim's past must matter later but cannot be stated outright without spoiling the reveal. Why: A witness with a stake makes the fact feel earned and lets readers weigh sources.
- [pitfall] Agreement among several writers can hide a single origin when all of them draw on the same source, so they should count as one witness. When: multiple accounts appear to confirm one another. Why: shared sourcing is easy to miss.
- [fact] Internal bleeding can hide a serious wound from bystanders, so an apparently unhurt person may be badly injured.

## weather and wetness clues
- [heuristic] Weather changes falling between two traces bound when an intrusion or event could have occurred, so its timing can be read without a witness.
- [heuristic] Wheel ruts and hoof marks in wet ground can show that a vehicle was present during a period of rain, dating the marks when the rain's timing is known. When: Dating a mark against weather. Why: Rain timing bounds when the mark could have formed.
- [heuristic] Wet or muddy clothing can contradict a claimed alibi, especially when the weather or location says the person should have stayed dry. When: a witness claims to have stayed indoors.
- [heuristic] Deliberate dusting or wiping of surfaces suggests the actor knew their own traces were already on those objects.
- [tradeoff] A clean surface suggests deliberate wiping by a careful culprit, but when a surface shows no traces, first check whether it could hold one, since the material may explain the absence. When: A surface shows no prints or traces. Why: Absence can come from the surface rather than from deliberate action.
- [pitfall] Weathering dates an object only when its starting age is known; with an uncertain origin, decay evidence misleads.
- [pitfall] Wet ground and busy footpaths can multiply or erase tracks, so sorting them can defeat the whole approach. When: Tracks are collected from a site with heavy use or wet conditions. Why: Overlapping and washed-out prints are hard to attribute.

## world-state consistency checks
- [mechanism] A changed plan, such as a canceled departure, can be a visible world-state flag whose timing is itself informative. When: When designing world-state changes that follow a revealing event. Why: A reversal right after a slip shows the event's effect on the character.
- [rule] Avoid plot links that the world's own rules cannot support, since players will reject contrived connections. When: Designing story links and reveals. Why: Connections that violate established rules break trust in the deduction.
- [rule] Flag recurring locations or names across quests in a world-state log to prompt players to connect a chain of events.
- [rule] Check a witness's statement against world facts only a present character could know, and flag statements that contradict the current state of the scene.
- [rule] Separate what the game world records as true, such as quest state or faction status, from what is physically true, so NPCs can act on recorded facts the player knows are false. When: Designing world state in narrative games. Why: Creates believable NPC behavior and dramatic irony.
- [heuristic] Log death and event dates in world state so players can rule out candidate NPCs by timeline.
- [heuristic] When a character argues that a harmful act is justified, ask whether the speaker would perform it personally; a retreat to 'just arguing' exposes a hollow justification. When: a character defends a deed in dialogue. Why: unwillingness to act suggests the argument lacks conviction.

## accusation scene design
- [rule] Write accusations as templates with slots for accused, act, harm and consequence, each mapped to a clue the player can check; let the accused's story shift under follow-up. When: Designing accusation-based quests or NPC-to-NPC accusation dialogue. Why: Verifiable accusations let players test claims, since each slot becomes something they can verify or disprove. (x2)
- [rule] An accusation test should show a reaction the player can read and state its limit, rather than automatically clearing the suspect. When: Designing an accusation or ordeal scene. Why: Stated limits keep the test from being mistaken for proof.
- [heuristic] A final accusation scene that walks through the crime step by step lets the player see the full logic before choosing a confession or a fight. When: Designing the climax of a mystery. Why: Showing the full reasoning makes the player's final choice informed.
- [procedure] 1) Place the culprit in a constrained position. 2) Name the method step by step. 3) Name the motive. 4) Force the culprit to surrender the stolen items. When: when the solution must be explained directly to the culprit. Why: the culprit's presence adds tension to the explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the crime step by step: motive, background pressures, method and cover story. 2) Deliver the reconstruction calmly. 3) Offer a way out, such as a confession in exchange for a settlement.
