When: A case is circumstantial and a confession would settle it. Why: A calm, complete account convinces the suspect the case is solved and makes confession the easiest option.
- [pitfall] Pushing a witness past her composure with an accusation rather than reassurance can shut down cooperation. When: When a witness is close to an admission. Why: Accusation raises defensiveness and ends the exchange.

## alibi and timelines
- [rule] Give a single object a second reading that becomes available only after the first suspect has been cleared. Why: The new reading then has no earlier answer to conflict with.
- [rule] Anchor a case on one exact physical match, precise enough to carry weight beyond testimony. When: Building a case against a suspect alongside witness accounts. Why: A precise physical match gives the case a fixed point that testimony alone lacks.
- [heuristic] Let a false solution's own evidence cut against it later, such as an alibi that fails under a second check.
- [heuristic] Make a false alibi depend on one unverified fact, such as a timing, so that a single independent record can break it. When: Designing a suspect's alibi that the player must test. Why: A single hinge fact is easy to check once the player knows to look.
- [pitfall] Do not build a timeline on one witness's clock or memory, especially when the witness was asleep or emotionally shaken; one faulty time marker can shift every dependent event. When: The timeline depends on a single time source, such as a witness who reports a time while impaired or distressed. Why: Sleep and strong emotion distort time perception and recall.
- [pitfall] An alibi resting on one document can collapse if its timing was faked or the message was sent in advance or by someone else. When: When an alibi depends on a single message or record. Why: A document proves only what its timestamp and sender actually establish.

## anomaly and supernatural
- [heuristic] Tie a mystery flag to a specific premise so the system can check whether a claimed anomaly depends on an unstated assumption. When: Implementing a mystery or anomaly flag in a game. Why: Explicit premises make a flagged anomaly verifiable rather than vague.
- [heuristic] Introduce small unexplained anomalies sparingly and plan their payoff before planting them, so the player carries them forward as live questions. When: when seeding details the audience will track across the story. Why: planted questions give the audience a reason to keep reading.
- [heuristic] Treat a character's apparent madness as a possible deliberate test, so the reader's suspicion becomes the setup for a later reveal that recasts earlier dialogue.
- [heuristic] A set of strange clues may all be one motive seen from different angles, so the player should look for a shared cause rather than separate explanations. When: many odd clues point in different directions. Why: A single motive can unify anomalies that look like unrelated sacrilege, madness or intrusion.
- [procedure] 1) Treat the frightening appearance as a surface. 2) Check what behaviour or motive it could hide. 3) Look for a human cause behind it. When: Investigating an apparent supernatural event.
- [pitfall] Interpreting an animal's internal state is uncertain; an observer cannot fully gauge what an animal feels. When: Drawing conclusions from animal reactions. Why: Animal reactions are observable, but their inner states are not directly accessible.

## appearance and character cues
- [heuristic] Have the suffering character reveal the origin of their affliction; this makes the reveal personal and removes the need for a detective figure.
- [heuristic] Use witnesses with a known history together to establish a baseline of normal behaviour against which unusual reactions can be compared. When: Assessing whether a witness's reaction is abnormal. Why: A known baseline gives a reference for judging deviations.
- [pitfall] Appearance unreliably signals guilt: a calm culprit may seem innocent, and a suspect who looks guilty from appearance or record may be innocent. When: When judging suspects by demeanor, appearance, or past record. Why: Composure can mask guilt, and appearance or record can mislead.
- [pitfall] A trait presented with affection can read as romance rather than information, so the audience may fail to register it as a marker.
- [pitfall] A visible behavioral change is a clue only against a known baseline, and it is not proof of guilt because many causes can produce it. When: When interpreting a suspect's changed manner as evidence. Why: Without a baseline and alternative explanations, a change can mislead.
- [pitfall] Excluding a suspect because their character seems unfit for the crime ignores that character is often misjudged and that self-interest can be hidden. When: When ruling out suspects by judging their personality. Why: Personality impressions are unreliable, and concealed incentives can override them.

## biased npc information
- [rule] Give self-interested NPCs biased accounts with visible motives so players can test which claims hold up; never discard a biased account, since it may still contain a true fact. When: designing NPC testimony. Why: Visible motive lets players discount bias without losing the true details.
- [rule] Give some NPCs biased opinions about others, so players must weigh the source of a claim as well as the claim itself. When: Designing NPC dialogue that expresses judgements about other characters. Why: Players then evaluate testimony by its source, which deepens investigation.
- [rule] Treat an NPC's claims of certainty as biased, and let the player verify each factual claim against the world.
- [rule] Give a powerful NPC advice that seems neutral but binds the player to one faction, and let reporting it to rivals change faction standing. When: When designing faction-based choices. Why: Reporting gives the player a lever over allegiance.
- [rule] Let a biased NPC withhold an exculpatory document, so the player must find it elsewhere to reach the truth.
- [rule] Give an NPC a briefing about another character before they meet, and make the briefing's bias discoverable, so the player can check the NPC's view against the world state. When: designing NPC dialogue where one character's opinion of another is shaped in advance. Why: Players can then detect where an NPC's view is wrong and reason about why.

## booking and record logs
- [mechanism] A game can model booking as a logged inventory where any missing or changed item becomes a clue. When: Designing item tracking in a custody or inventory system. Why: Logged items make discrepancies detectable.
- [rule] A booking alone does not place anyone at a scene, so corroborate it with other evidence.
- [rule] Include a clerk's name error that players can catch by cross-checking names, and reward the catch with a corrected timeline.
- [rule] Give shopkeepers, clerks or ledgers records that players can cross-check, and let a contradiction trigger new questions. When: When designing record-keeping NPCs or objects in a game world. Why: Checkable records let players test testimony and generate follow-up investigation.
- [fact] A booking made at a travel office creates a dated, witnessed record that fixes a planned movement. Why: The clerk who takes the details becomes a witness.
- [fact] Left-luggage staff may log a deposit time yet be unable to describe the depositor, so a stored object can preserve traces that human memory loses.

## borrowed identity and credibility
- [behavior] A witness's account that sounds too much like a familiar story may be borrowed from something heard or read rather than remembered.
- [tradeoff] Copied descriptions suggest fabrication and warrant tracing; repeated phrasing across speakers may just reflect a shared source, so note it without concluding. When: Copied descriptions in one source suggest fabrication; a phrase reappearing in another speaker's account is only noted. Why: Reuse can indicate a shared source or an adopted framing.
- [pitfall] A matching permit or real person's documents does not confirm identity: permits can be used by others, and false identities can be built on real people's papers. When: When verifying a visitor against an access record. Why: Permits can be obtained under a pretext and used by an impostor.
- [pitfall] Endorsement by a higher authority or respected figure can lend legitimacy to weak evidence or accusations without testing them.
- [pitfall] A helper who presents a planted conclusion as their own discovery may come to believe it is theirs, which weakens their credibility under questioning.
- [pitfall] Dismissing an object on another person's authority, without testing it, can lose a real clue.

## charm and charisma bias
- [mechanism] A charming character who occupies a host with questions about a building can divert attention from the real interest in that building.
- [rule] Let a charming suspect leave a visible gap that the player finds only by asking targeted questions. When: designing suspect characters.
- [heuristic] A character discredited by a listener's existing low opinion of them is accepted more easily, because the listener already has a prior assumption that fits the explanation. When: The listener already trusts the speaker more than the accuser. Why: Prior assumptions make a dismissive explanation feel like an answer.
- [pitfall] A charming person can earn trust while contradicting evidence accumulates, or carry out a flawed plan; charm proves neither innocence nor competence, so check claims against behaviour. (x2)
- [pitfall] A pleasing appearance can hide a serious character; an observer's interest in a witness, face-value reading of a suspect's self-presentation, or admirers' framing clouds judgement and misleads the investigation. When: when interviewing witnesses who are loyal to the suspect. Why: admiration and shared sympathy repeat the suspect's framing. (x2)
- [pitfall] A warm word from an employer is not proof of influence; influence is indicated by a promise tied to a specific act. When: Inferring bribery or loyalty from an authority figure's manner. Why: Kindness is common and does not establish a bargain.

## cognitive bias in deduction
- [rule] Let the protagonist's expertise rule out the obvious cause early, so the player's contradiction does the work of misdirection. When: when an expert character's domain makes a common cause look impossible. Why: A plausible exclusion pushes the player toward a false culprit until the real mechanism appears.
- [heuristic] Place a suspect's expertise, such as a chemistry hobby, in the same scene as their arrival so it reads as background but can later become the means. When: Introducing a suspect who may later supply the method of a crime. Why: Background detail seems harmless at first, so it is less likely to be suspected early.
- [pitfall] Accepting a theory early hides the true sequence of events, because prior belief makes each new clue read as confirmation of the favored suspect and stops the search for contradicting evidence. When: when an investigation has settled on a plausible suspect or answer early. Why: Prior belief filters how new evidence is read; early acceptance stops the search for contradicting evidence.
- [pitfall] A witness may describe the effect of a problem without naming its cause, and a guessed cause from outward signs is not the same as a confided one. When: Interviewing someone who observed another person's distress. Why: Observers infer causes from behaviour that the subject never discussed.
- [pitfall] Witnesses who expect an effect often perceive it, so expectation can distort what observers believe they felt or heard. When: Observers are primed by a dramatic or eerie setting. Why: Expectation shapes perception and memory.
- [pitfall] Searching only for the expected kind of mechanism can miss the real one, which may be a body rather than a device. When: Investigating a staged or hidden effect. Why: Assumptions about method narrow the search.

## complaints and communication
- [mechanism] A communication network that spreads alerts across distant zones can drive a pursuit, with suspects fleeing across the map as information travels. When: When designing a chase or manhunt across a game world. Why: Rapid signaling lets pursuers respond to a suspect's location at a distance.
- [behavior] A person who is asked about their hardships may disclose mood and daily routines through complaints, revealing habits without direct questions. When: when questioning someone about their condition or routine. Why: people describe their state freely when invited to talk about it.
- [heuristic] Aim a complaint at one individual rather than an institution, and avoid written statements that could be recast as libel. When: raising a grievance inside a formal institution.
- [heuristic] Read a compiled collection through its editor's framing, publication details and dates, since these shape which claims a reader sees.
- [heuristic] Give the player or client the next step to keep confidence, while withholding the answer itself.
- [metric] A complainant had to post a twenty-pound bond to pursue a case, so a complaint carried a financial risk to the accuser. When: a legal system requires a bond to pursue a complaint. Why: A bond makes accusers bear part of the cost if the charge fails.

## concealed relationships and cover
- [behavior] Subjects may leave out relationships they did not volunteer; pointed follow-up questions tend to bring them out and they must be explored. When: when a subject's account omits a known connection. Why: concealment protects the subject.
- [behavior] People hiding a relationship often arrive separately and are seen together only in private rooms, so the link goes unnoticed. When: A relationship is officially unknown. Why: Separate arrivals and private meetings avoid notice.
- [heuristic] Complicated cover stories, such as an alibi backed by planted trails, fail more often than simple ones because each extra detail adds a chance to slip.
- [heuristic] Give the killer a benevolent public image and a professional alibi, which makes suspicion of them feel unlikely. When: designing a culprit who should be hidden in plain sight. Why: A trusted public role lowers the audience's suspicion until the late reveal.
- [tradeoff] Concealing inquiry purpose from a suspect's associates prevents them preparing a cover, but hiding it from record keepers or witnesses can reduce what they volunteer. When: when questioning people connected to a suspect, or when questioning record keepers or witnesses. Why: A revealed purpose lets the suspect prepare a cover; a candid request may draw out more volunteered information.
- [pitfall] A suspect's apparent absence may conceal their presence and may have been used to set up earlier events.

## connection mapping and followers
- [rule] Follow at a distance and on the same side of the street, planning position so the target does not easily recognise the follower. When: tailing on foot. Why: a suspect may still recognise a follower.
- [heuristic] When incidents seem unrelated, check which location, person or record recurs across them. When: Reviewing a set of seemingly separate incidents. Why: Recurring elements are the associations that connect events.
- [heuristic] A secretive person usually confides in someone close, so a close associate of the subject is the most likely source of hidden facts. When: someone holds key facts but keeps them guarded. Why: people tend to share concealed matters with a trusted intimate.
- [heuristic] An object found at a scene is weaker evidence when its finder had other chances to move or plant it. When: The finder had access to the scene before the discovery. Why: Access gives the finder a plausible route to placing the item.
- [procedure] 1) Identify the next link, such as an agent or trade house. 2) Contact that link in the next location. 3) Give instructions and repeat until the suspect is reached. When: a suspect has moved across several locations and must be followed through contacts. Why: each intermediary holds the lead to the next.
- [pitfall] A sudden rush of connections feels like proof but must be checked link by link, since it can still be wrong.

## context and interpretation
- [mechanism] Supplying missing background can change the meaning of earlier clues, so the audience must reassess events it already witnessed. When: a reveal supplies context not previously available. Why: meaning depends on context the audience lacked.
- [rule] Log each stray remark or NPC line with its trigger, listener and whether the speaker confirmed it, then link it to later facts it may explain. When: Recording stray remarks or NPC dialogue that may serve as evidence. Why: A remark's meaning depends on the situation or question it answers. (x2)
- [rule] Set out the conditions a community lived under before judging its conduct, so the reader can weigh its actions against the pressures it faced. When: Evaluating a community's cruelty, suspicion or decisions. Why: Pressures such as hardship, fear and loss explain conduct that looks inexplicable in isolation.
- [heuristic] Judge a found object by the conditions under which it likely reached its position, not only by what the object is. When: Evaluating an object as evidence.
- [pitfall] Context explains why people believed or acted but does not prove a factual claim or what a specific person did; using it to excuse unsupported conduct replaces evidence. When: Context is used to soften judgment of a person's actions or to support a factual claim. Why: Broad conditions do not establish what a particular person did or knew.
- [pitfall] A single overheard exchange taken without context can suggest a motive that is not really there, since ambiguous phrases mislead.

## contradiction and convenient events
- [mechanism] A dialogue option to withhold news can set a flag that later changes an NPC's trust or what that NPC will reveal.
- [rule] When witness accounts cannot fit one sequence, store each version and flag the mismatch for questioning, not silent resolution; the player exposes it by presenting conflicting statements. Why: Lets the player discover contradictions through play.
- [rule] A quest system could flag when a convenient event lines up with the player's stated goal, prompting a check before action.
- [rule] Flag unverifiable events as unverifiable rather than folding them into the record as fact.
- [heuristic] Flag a claim that a person's situation contradicts, such as claiming independence while others clearly control them.
- [heuristic] Give NPC testimonies overlapping details that contradict one another, so the player must find physical evidence to decide which account is true. When: Designing a mystery where player judgment depends on evidence. Why: Contradictions that only physical evidence can resolve reward investigation over trust in dialogue.

## documents and written proof
- [rule] Update a game journal after a reveal so earlier conversations gain new, clearer meaning. When: A reveal changes the meaning of past dialogue. Why: Re-reading earlier entries lets the player see the new meaning.
- [rule] Mark journals and letters with a reliability level so the player must judge how far to trust them. When: Designing in-world documents. Why: Varying trust makes documents a reasoning challenge rather than a fixed answer.
- [heuristic] When a source makes a claim the narrator distrusts, frame it with explicit doubt while still following its instructions, so the audience sees both caution and compliance. When: An unlikely document or source must still be acted on. Why: Explicit doubt keeps credibility in question without rejecting the source outright.
- [heuristic] A signed record listing every attending witness makes a summary feel authoritative. When: Presenting an account the audience may find hard to believe. Why: Official sign-off signals verification.
- [tradeoff] Deliver the climax as a found document that reframes prior scenes, but a single hidden document feels contrived unless foreshadowed early; alternatively corroborate with several documents and confessions. When: Designing the climax reveal of a mystery. Why: A found document reinterprets prior events and lets the audience deduce the answer; late, unforeshadowed documents read as contrivance. (x2)
- [pitfall] Letting a vivid report shape the hypothesis before its specifics are confirmed makes a general report seem to identify a specific person. Why: the jump from a general finding to a specific identity is unsupported until details match.

## duplicate evidence and names
- [heuristic] One matching item may be ordinary, but a second matching item turns an apparent accident into a suspicious duplicate.
- [pitfall] A stolen valuable replaced by a convincing copy hides the theft, so a witness who examined the object may have confirmed only the copy. When: an item's identity or value matters to the mystery. Why: A good duplicate is hard to distinguish from the original without expert inspection.
- [pitfall] Removing one copy of evidence does not erase it if duplicates exist elsewhere. Investigators should look for copies before assuming the evidence is gone. When: Someone attempts to destroy an identifying item. Why: Copies made earlier can survive the removal.
- [pitfall] Identical names can belong to different people, so check each index entry against its source before merging them.
- [pitfall] Assuming a river or road keeps the same name across periods leads to misreading older documents, since one physical feature may carry several names over time. When: reading records from different periods. Why: names change while the feature stays in place.
- [fact] When two identical items exist, a matching trace implicates whoever held either one, so the evidence stays ambiguous until ownership is checked.

## evidence destruction and cleanup
- [behavior] Players who see evidence apparently destroyed often stop searching, so a convincing destruction can misdirect them away from the real item. When: An investigation where a key document appears burned or lost. Why: Apparent closure signals that the trail is exhausted, which ends further inspection.
- [rule] Make a destroyed or withheld item a meaningful clue, and let the NPC's account of it be checkable. When: an item is removed or destroyed in a mystery. Why: a checkable account lets the player test the explanation.
- [heuristic] Brush or cleaning marks on a surface are a trace to check against the account of who cleaned there and when. When: a surface shows signs of recent sweeping. Why: cleaning marks can contradict or support a witness account.
- [heuristic] Check hearths and grates for partly burned papers, since ashes and fragments show that records were destroyed. When: a suspect may have destroyed documents.
- [pitfall] Clean-up by a bystander can destroy the one clue that separates an accident or suicide from murder. When: a death could be read as homicide. Why: loose papers and labels can be lost among ordinary clutter.
- [fact] Water washes off visible traces, but only thorough cleaning defeats a sensitive biological test.

## hindsight reasoning
- [behavior] After a reveal, earlier insignificant details are recognized as clues, and spontaneous events are re-read as deliberate arrangements, with details recast as planted lures without contradicting earlier scenes. When: when a reveal recontextualizes earlier scenes. Why: Hindsight reframes earlier details as evidence; retrospective meaning changes how innocent details are understood. (x2)
- [heuristic] Praise for a dead person that carries implied fault can reveal a speaker's blame, so such remarks can be treated as possible evidence of motive. When: a witness speaks warmly of someone who has died. Why: blame often surfaces disguised as praise.
- [pitfall] Hindsight makes a clue reading seem obvious though it was unclear when first observed; presenting the solution as obvious hides that earlier uncertainty, making the reasoning look unearned.
- [pitfall] Hindsight makes a plant look obvious; a real decoy should be checkable from the evidence available at the time.
- [pitfall] Hindsight can make a whole period look careless; a fair account first reconstructs what the period knew before judging its conduct.
- [pitfall] Motives that look clear in hindsight may not have existed when the act was committed. When: Reconstructing why someone acted in the past. Why: Later knowledge projects a motive backward onto earlier choices.

## label and naming claims
- [mechanism] Once a suspect is given a label, the powers associated with that label, such as affliction or apparition, become the evidence expected and accepted. When: A suspect is labelled and then examined in an investigation. Why: The label sets the frame in which testimony is interpreted and accepted.
- [rule] Label conclusions that go beyond the evidence as guesses, and do not present an untested hypothesis as established fact. When: presenting a theory drawn from a physical trace. Why: unverified reasoning can look certain if not labelled.
- [rule] Use labels that match the names used in the explanation, so the audience can follow each item the argument mentions.
- [rule] Treat a label or brand name as a claim and check it against the contents before relying on it. Why: Labels can be wrong or shared across different products.
- [rule] Use an accusation's chosen label as a clue, since a different label would have pointed to different evidence and a mislabelled suspect can reveal investigative bias. When: Designing wanted posters, accusations or clue ledgers that name suspects. Why: The label shapes which evidence is sought, so the choice of label exposes the investigator's assumptions.
- [pitfall] Treating a label, such as 'maniac' or a charged term like 'spy', as an explanation of behavior adds no evidence and leads to unfounded conclusions. When: when a testimony or observation offers a charged term. Why: the label feels like an answer but adds no evidence.

## limits of physical tests
- [rule] Do not use physical tests to judge intent or motive; they show only what an action could physically achieve. When: a claim concerns why someone acted. Why: Physical evidence cannot reveal what a person intended.
- [rule] When a test cannot separate two relevant sources, such as the blood of two similar animals, use a different test for that question.
- [pitfall] A negative test on the wrong sample proves nothing about the item that matters; check whether the suspect item was included in the tests. When: a lab test clears a case. Why: a negative result only rules out what was tested.
- [pitfall] A test that fails to detect a substance may reflect the limits of the tools rather than the absence of the substance. When: A search or chemical test returns nothing and is taken as proof of absence. Why: Detection methods have thresholds and blind spots, so a negative result is weaker than it appears.
- [fact] A specific test can separate human blood from animal blood, so a claimed animal-accident explanation can be checked.
- [fact] A demonstration shows that a mechanism works as described, not that it caused the harm in question. When: A defence rests on a device test.

## motive versus proof
- [model] Mystery proof takes one of four kinds: a reconstructive test, a document, a trap, or a confession. When: choosing how to confirm a hidden mechanism. Why: Each kind gives the audience a different form of certainty.
- [rule] Keep the final proof narrow and personal; a confession can carry the reveal when the physical chain is thin. When: when the reveal lacks a full physical evidence chain. Why: A personal admission gives the reveal weight without a complete case file.
- [heuristic] Combine a culprit's psychological profile with physical facts, since motive alone rarely settles who committed an act. When: Solving a mystery. Why: Physical evidence confirms or rules out what the motive suggests.
- [heuristic] Rank suspects by motive, such as desire for credit or reputation, as well as by access; motive can point to a different suspect than access alone. When: Several suspects could have performed an act. Why: A suspect's desire may point to a different kind of act than the one committed.
- [pitfall] Motive and suspicion are far weaker than proof of an act; a stated motive can explain a relationship without any crime, so motive alone does not establish that an act occurred. When: Building a case on motive; evaluating a suspect's stated reason. Why: A plausible reason for an act does not confirm it occurred; a motive describes intent or interest, not the action itself.
- [pitfall] Romance and money motives are easy to over-weight, so check them against evidence before building a story around them. When: Assigning motive to suspects.

## npc corroboration design
- [mechanism] Letting players verify an NPC's presence claim by checking other NPCs' positions builds a web of mutual corroboration. When: NPCs make claims about where they were.
- [rule] Players should cross-check an NPC's claim against world state, since informants may be accurate or corrupted, and reward players who do.
- [rule] Give a second independent NPC who can corroborate or contradict any clue an agreeable NPC confirms after an item is shown, so informant claims stay open to challenge. When: Designing NPC clue confirmation. Why: Agreeable NPCs may confirm without being reliable.
- [rule] Let players gain reward by cross-checking a rumour-spreading NPC against one who saw an event directly. When: designing conflicting npc accounts.
- [rule] Require corroboration from independent sources before accepting an NPC's accusation, instead of relying on how many NPCs agree. When: an accusation rests on several NPC witnesses. Why: Agreement among NPCs that share an assumption is not independent confirmation.
- [heuristic] Design NPC event accounts so two independent witnesses' agreement confirms a fact, while mismatches, checkable against a timeline, become leads or puzzles. When: Designing NPC testimony about events or writing witness dialogue for a mystery. Why: Agreement confirms; disagreement prompts further checking.

## npc dialogue design
- [mechanism] A witness or frightened NPC may require an oath, reassurance, or payment before revealing key or sensitive information, so the player's social choices shape what they learn. When: Designing NPC dialogue for an investigation or questioning a witness who guards information. Why: Gating information behind a social action makes player choices matter; openly raising a sensitive topic shifts the exchange's terms toward the witness.
- [mechanism] Dialogue that flags a skipped question can trigger an NPC follow-up line, making the player's omissions meaningful to the story. When: Designing NPC dialogue trees with tracked questions. Why: A reactive follow-up rewards thorough questioning and makes gaps visible.
- [heuristic] Give NPC answers that are literally true but misleading, and let body language or conflicting data expose the gap for players who compare them. When: Writing NPC dialogue meant to be questioned by the player. Why: Players reward careful comparison of words and evidence, which deepens investigation.
- [heuristic] Build NPC dialogue trees with follow-up questions that test answers, recording corrections and cross-checking them against earlier lines. When: Designing NPC interviews in a dialogue system. Why: Layered follow-ups let the player test and refine what an NPC says.
- [heuristic] An NPC's talk about a false pattern or lucky streak can show desperation, and the player can test the claim against the game's rules. When: designing NPC dialogue.
- [heuristic] Open with a gentle question, since a blunt one can make a frightened witness shut down completely. When: first question to a nervous witness. Why: abrupt pressure triggers fear and withdrawal.

## observation conditions
- [rule] Check every sense when searching a scene, including smell, because a scent can identify a visitor who leaves no visible mark. When: A search focuses on visible traces. Why: Scent and residue persist where visual evidence does not, and they are missed unless someone checks for them.
- [rule] Check the witness's state at the moment of observation, since drugging or drunkenness can cloud what they remember.
- [rule] Before accepting a witness's claimed observation, check the light, distance and alertness under which it was made.
- [pitfall] Witness perception in darkness or poor light is uncertain and may be admitted; a witness may still report a detail with false certainty, since poor conditions limit what is seen. When: Evaluating a witness's visual claim, especially in poor lighting or at distance. Why: Poor viewing conditions limit what can actually be seen, and the witness may admit the uncertainty.
- [pitfall] Staging a chance encounter to watch someone can reveal the observer's intent to the person being watched.
- [pitfall] Artificial light can hide or distort fine marks, so examine them under suitable light before judging them. When: Examining a scene at night or indoors.

## optional and branching content
- [mechanism] Optional small-talk dialogue branches that look unrelated can record an NPC's attitudes or knowledge for later use.
- [heuristic] Let an NPC give a long, ordered account, with optional branches for each detail so players can ask for everything. When: Designing NPC dialogue for clue delivery.
- [heuristic] Add neglected checks, such as a will, a partner's share or a lock's key holder, as optional tasks that let the player reopen a closed case. When: Designing a case that can be closed too early. Why: Overlooked basic facts give the player a route back to the truth.
- [heuristic] A small practical explanation for an observed state, such as opening a window to clear smoke, can change what that state means.
- [heuristic] Read the operative sentences of an argument, which show what is actually recommended, rather than only the cautious qualifiers around them.
- [tradeoff] Red herrings trade off: optional innocent-resolving clues reward exploration without false solutions, while hidden NPC side-secrets consume player effort without advancing the answer. When: Designing false leads or red herrings. Why: Clues that resolve innocently reward exploration; side secrets generate real leads that cost effort.

## parallel cases and leads
- [rule] Cut between parallel locations with rising stakes to keep several threads running at once.
- [heuristic] A hint can take the form of a parallel case whose structure mirrors the answer without stating it. When: the answer must stay hidden but should be recognisable. Why: the audience can map the parallel onto the answer.
- [heuristic] A parallel case can guide reasoning about an undocumented act, but it is not proof that the same act occurred here. When: A similar recorded case exists for comparison. Why: Similarity suggests a pattern without establishing the specific event.
- [procedure] 1) Pursue a promising lead briefly. 2) If it leads nowhere, park it. 3) Revisit it when new facts arrive. When: A lead looks promising but produces no results. Why: Parking keeps effort focused while preserving the lead for later.
- [tradeoff] Juggling several cases or leads spreads effort thin and invents false links; focusing deepens analysis but delays others. Test each lead, including self-offered experts, as a possible distraction. When: when multiple open cases or leads compete for attention.
- [pitfall] A detailed parallel between two cases tempts reasoners to treat them as identical, though small differences can send the cases in very different directions. When: a previous case seems to explain a new one. Why: the match feels convincing even when key details differ.

## possession and ownership
- [heuristic] An item that cannot slip off once fitted, if missing from remains, was most likely removed on purpose, so its absence implies intent. When: an item that could not come off by accident. Why: Physical fit limits accidental loss.
- [heuristic] A mismatch between a room's surroundings and its occupant's apparent means invites questions about who the occupant is and why they live that way. When: A room's contents seem inconsistent with the apparent wealth or status of its occupant. Why: Contradictions between setting and status prompt the observer to seek an explanation.
- [pitfall] A sale record shows who bought an object, not who holds it now, so records alone cannot locate it. When: when using trade records to find a current holder. Why: Ownership can change after sale.
- [pitfall] A forger who copies a known sample can pass a single comparison, so check the writing against several independent samples. Why: One sample can be duplicated.
- [pitfall] A key holder's exclusive control may be an illusion because keys can be copied, so every copy must be counted before ruling anyone out. When: Ruling suspects in or out based on key possession. Why: Duplicate keys give access to people who appear to have none.
- [fact] Lawsuits over rent or lease reveal who occupied land, even where the question of ownership remains unclear. When: Ownership is uncertain but occupation matters. Why: Court actions record who was in possession of a place.

## proximity and proxy effects
- [mechanism] A threat carried out by a proxy with a disarmed weapon looks dangerous at the scene while the planner stays away from it. When: a plot must threaten a victim while concealing the person who arranged it. Why: the proxy performs the act and the planner keeps distance.
- [rule] When a suspected source is ruled out, consider that the visible effect may be a reflection or proxy of another source. When: when an observed effect has no matching source.
- [heuristic] Being near a passage does not guarantee perceiving someone who passes; assuming a witness saw an event because they were nearby accepts claims they were not positioned to observe. When: when a witness's claim rests on being near a route. Why: perception also depends on attention, noise and barriers.
- [pitfall] Treating proximity to a scene, or a convenient departure, as evidence of guilt. Why: Innocent people near a scene can look guilty.
- [pitfall] Being close to a witness, or being told a story by them, does not make the account reliable.
- [pitfall] A figure who is merely near both events may be coincidence rather than a true connection.

## replacement and substitution
- [mechanism] A stand-in resembling a public figure covers a crime's timing; a bandage or hooded cloak limits close inspection, and those who know the person best notice substitutions. When: A crime relies on a person being seen but not closely examined, or a substitution plot is being designed. Why: A visible cue justifies the lack of close examination; those who know the person best are most likely to notice a substitution.
- [mechanism] An imitation can replace an unchangeable fact, such as a person's death, with a new apparent fact of presence that the cover story rests on.
- [mechanism] A stand-in can be recruited through a hidden incentive, such as a payment that avoids a financial liability, which explains why they cooperated.
- [mechanism] A killer can stage a death by substituting a different corpse, so the police identify a body that matches no suspect and the true victim stays hidden. When: designing a cover-up that hides a murder as a different death. Why: A stand-in body gives investigators a plausible name, so the substitution stays concealed.
- [heuristic] Rejecting a popular explanation does not establish a replacement; the new diagnosis still needs evidence. When: an expert offers a rival explanation.
- [heuristic] A replaced covering often hides a damaging trace, such as blood that soaked into the original, so a replacement suggests something to conceal.

## reused names and identities
- [rule] Let one title or name cover two people, and resolve which one is meant only when a second source identifies the referent.
- [procedure] 1) Note the alias and any contact address the suspect uses. 2) Confirm the alias through someone who dealt with the user, such as a landlord. 3) Plant a false but plausible story in a channel the suspect reads, so that they are drawn to act. When: A suspect hides behind an alias and reads the press.
- [pitfall] A cover name used by several agents becomes easy to trace, because repeated use links otherwise separate people.
- [pitfall] Reusing a signature name in an unrelated context can mislead the audience into connecting things that have no real link.
- [fact] Clothing worn during a crime and reused afterwards can become a traceable physical clue.
- [fact] Text on a reused page may belong to an earlier writer, so settling the order of writing settles who owns that text. When: a sheet carries writing from two different hands.

## room object and trace reading
- [rule] Treat an interpretation of a room's objects as a hypothesis, not as proof of a person's motive.
- [heuristic] Read a private room's furnishings, decoration and collected objects as evidence of the occupant's profession, wealth, spending, taste and associates. When: a character's personal life must be inferred from the environment, or players need a profile before speaking to the character. Why: private spaces reflect habits without the occupant speaking.
- [heuristic] Room condition, such as dust or ash, gives a time window: a spotless room with no dust suggests that a document was written and torn recently.
- [heuristic] Read a room's books and unfinished work as a record of what its occupant studied, feared or was preoccupied with.
- [heuristic] Disorder confined to one spot marks a localized event; rooms beyond that look orderly suggest the struggle did not spread. When: When assessing the extent of a disturbance at a scene. Why: The spread of disorder shows where an event occurred.
- [fact] Physical traces reported after each visit to a booked room, such as disturbed bedding, can show what occurred there.

## rumor and source checking
- [rule] Do not rely on a sighting or rumour that cannot be traced to a source; check single-source rumours against records before treating them as fact. When: When a sighting or rumour is used as evidence. Why: A single source can mislead. (x2)
- [rule] Separate claims based on sight from claims based on rumor, and do not accept fearful claims at face value. Why: Accepting them unchecked spreads error.
- [heuristic] When several separate accounts repeat the same odd detail, suspect one earlier source, such as coaching or rumor, rather than independent observation. When: reports seem independent but share an unusual specific detail. Why: An unusual detail recurring independently is improbable, so a common channel is the likelier explanation.
- [heuristic] Rumours or in-world articles can be fallible sources that players learn to cross-check against physical clues. When: Designing information the player receives from in-world media. Why: Cross-checking teaches players to weigh sources by evidence.
- [pitfall] Witnesses, even if interviewed apart, that agree may share one source, rumour or leading questions; count origins, not voices, since one error can appear as several confirmations. When: A set of accounts seems to corroborate each other. Why: Repeated accounts may trace back to a single origin. (x2)
- [fact] A matching document shows a shared source for two pieces of evidence but does not identify who wrote or handled it.

## self-created evidence
- [mechanism] An item that degrades or burns when exposed makes its own loss a clue, pointing toward whoever had access to it at the critical moment. When: a document must be known to exist yet be unavailable when it matters. Why: its destruction is traceable to the people present.
- [behavior] An investigator's own carelessness, such as leaving belongings in plain view, can become evidence that others read.
- [rule] Document each of your own actions, since they may later have to be described as testimony.
- [heuristic] Check a postmark against the sender's whereabouts, since a sender who posts an item personally takes a risk and may gain an alibi from the timing. When: the sender posted the item personally. Why: posting in person is a risk taken in exchange for an alibi.
- [pitfall] A copy you make yourself carries little formal weight; a certified copy from the official keeper may be needed to prove a record's contents. When: The finding must hold up in a formal proceeding. Why: Self-made copies can be disputed.
- [pitfall] A suspect's explanations introduce new claims others can check, so each explanation adds a new point where the account can be contradicted. When: a suspect explains away evidence. Why: every stated detail becomes testable.

## separate incidents and events
- [mechanism] A crime stays hidden while its related events remain separate, because unconnected incidents form no visible pattern. When: Several incidents occur without a visible link. Why: Only a shared element can join events into a pattern.
- [rule] Give a hidden household its own entrance so it never passes through a shared business below.
- [rule] Keep the fabricated lead clearly separated from genuine evidence so the decoy does not contaminate later findings. When: A false lead has been planted to provoke a reaction. Why: Mixing fabricated and real traces makes later conclusions unreliable.
- [rule] Model identification and cause-of-death examination as separate steps from discovery, each with its own person and time.
- [rule] Track a remorse value separately from guilt so that the player's choice of confession or defiance changes how other characters treat them. When: implementing reputation or social systems. Why: guilt and remorse are different signals that others read differently.
- [heuristic] Separate incidents before combining them, since one explanation for two different attacks may be wrong. When: Several attacks or incidents are being explained together. Why: Different incidents may have different causes.

## source contact and access
- [rule] Discard a dubious clue source without discarding the questions it raised, which may still be meaningful.
- [heuristic] Reliability of a source depends on its purpose and its access to events, not on how exact or official its facts seem. When: Comparing conflicting accounts. Why: Precise-sounding statements can still serve a motive.
- [heuristic] Asking who initiated a message or meeting can reverse the apparent motive behind an event. When: an arranged meeting or message is central to a case.
- [heuristic] Record the source of each piece of quest information; a rumour from a third NPC should carry less certainty than a fact the player witnessed. When: when designing quest information in a game. Why: Players weigh information by how it reached them.
- [procedure] 1) Stage an early favor by arranging a threat the target can be rescued from, which builds trust. 2) Accept the grateful target's invitation. 3) Use the new access, including restricted rooms, to observe the target's household. Why: Trust and access to restricted rooms come from the staged rescue.
- [procedure] 1) Restate the claim as a question about its source. 2) Wait for the witness to commit to a name, place or circumstance. 3) Check that detail against a second source before building a theory on it.

## stalling and escape tactics
- [mechanism] A sudden accusation followed by an apology puts a target on the defensive and keeps them engaged, making them easier to move. When: Needing a character to stay connected or to accept a suggestion. Why: Being put on the back foot reduces resistance and makes the target eager to repair the relationship.
- [behavior] A witness may use sentiment, such as a song or a sudden sleep, strategically, so the investigator must judge whether it is sincere, vain, or controlling. When: a witness's emotional display seems aimed at the investigator.
- [behavior] A suspect under scrutiny may offer hospitality, announce a departure or raise unrelated topics to keep the investigator occupied. When: A suspect is being examined closely. Why: Distraction diverts the investigator's attention from the object of the search.
- [behavior] An uncooperative suspect adds detail to delay the end of an interview, and the detail often reveals the sequence of events and the gaps investigators can fill. When: A suspect is stalling against a deadline. Why: Stalling buys time, and the extra detail is an unintended disclosure.
- [heuristic] A sudden shift from accusation to tears can look like a tactic, so investigators who notice the timing tend to keep pressing. When: A witness becomes distressed in the middle of questioning. Why: Suspicious timing signals deliberate deflection.
- [pitfall] A stalling suspect may be using the delay to prepare an escape, so the investigator should not treat the stall as harmless. When: A suspect is extending the interview beyond what seems necessary. Why: Time spent stalling can be used to prepare an exit or a means of harm.

## stock phrasing and stereotypes
- [behavior] A witness who repeats one stock explanation yields little, while a talkative witness can offer useful facts when followed up. When: questioning a witness. Why: A stock answer closes the topic, whereas open talk exposes details.
- [rule] Give a stock explanation for a missing ally that contains a contradiction the player can find.
- [heuristic] A stereotype-based inference can be built as a trap that rewards players who test the assumption.
- [pitfall] Accounts forced into stock phrases or matching a familiar stock figure are shaped by expectations, stripping atmosphere and motive; treat them as interpretation, not raw observation, and distrust them. Why: Witness expectations shape such accounts, and stock phrasing strips atmosphere and motive, so retold accounts are interpreted rather than raw observation.
- [pitfall] Judging who could be harmed or who is the culprit by assumed traits (reputation, cheerfulness, gender or other stereotypes) is weak; test such assumptions against evidence before narrowing suspects. When: judging who could be a target or culprit, or building a profile from assumed traits. Why: Reputation and temperament do not determine who is harmed or who did it; stereotypes can exclude or include suspects for the wrong reasons.
- [pitfall] Inferring a person's appearance from national stereotype treats an assumption as evidence and can send the investigation the wrong way. Why: Stereotypes are not observations of the individual.

## style and document analysis
- [rule] Store document contents as structured text so the game can show exactly what was promised and to whom. When: Building letters, contracts or notes that carry promises. Why: Structured records let the game check and display exact terms.
- [heuristic] Hairstyle and dress reveal an item's period, so stylistic features can date a photograph to an earlier time. Why: fashions change in recognizable ways.
- [heuristic] When a writer's style is more formal than their education supports, the statement's aim becomes too visible to hide.
- [heuristic] A stray original document can be decisive, but it can also be wrong, so it must be tested like any other source. Why: Originals carry authority but can contain errors or be superseded.
- [tradeoff] A weaker final act may point to a different perpetrator, but style alone can mislead since one person may behave differently at a case's end. When: Comparing a case's final act with its earlier acts to judge whether the same perpetrator committed them. Why: A perpetrator's style can differ from earlier acts, yet one person may also behave differently at the end of a case.
- [pitfall] Doubt based on style or precision is evidence about the text, not proof of falsehood; the core claim may still be true and should be weighed separately. Why: Stylistic oddity and factual error are different things.

## supply and stock counting
- [rule] Count a remaining supply against its recorded amount to rule out or confirm an extra dose or missing item. When: When a substance or item may explain a death or event.
- [heuristic] Bulk stored raw materials found without their finished form indicate what was being made or prepared. When: A scene holds large quantities of unfinished material. Why: Stock reveals the activity that consumes it.
- [heuristic] Regular movement of food or supplies toward a location implies someone is being fed there, even if no one is seen.
- [heuristic] Total a person's transactions over a period, since repeated sales or payments can add up to a large, deliberate sum that single entries hide.
- [pitfall] A store lead can yield several candidates; a label narrows the field without naming the person.
- [fact] Surplus stock sold at auction often carries markings, such as on collars or waistbands, that identify it as condemned stock.

## suspense through withholding
- [mechanism] Withholding a key fact or name until late, while slowing the scene with close physical detail, keeps the audience waiting and builds suspense. When: A reveal can be delayed for effect and the audience needs to anticipate it. Why: Expectation and suspicion grow while the answer is held back. (x2)
- [mechanism] Suspense grows when characters who know more refuse to explain, so the gap between audience knowledge and character knowledge becomes the source of tension. When: some characters know the truth and the audience does not. Why: an open question keeps attention fixed on the hidden fact.
- [mechanism] Suspense builds when a sealed document's contents are withheld and the decision to open it is delayed to a later moment. When: A reveal must be postponed or handed to a character's choice. Why: The unknown outcome keeps the audience uncertain and attentive.
- [rule] Use a locked gate or refusing NPC whose reason is held back to create suspense, and resolve the reason later. When: designing an obstacle that should keep the player curious. Why: An unexplained barrier keeps the question open until the reason is revealed.
- [heuristic] Keep repeated observations ambiguous so no firm answer comes, sustaining tension until more evidence arrives. When: designing repeated sightings or tests. Why: unresolved ambiguity holds attention without resolving the mystery.
- [pitfall] A deferred reveal frustrates the audience if the eventual choice carries no new information. When: Withholding a reveal behind a decision. Why: A delay without payoff reads as stalling.

## suspense versus frustration
- [tradeoff] Withholding a reveal builds suspense, but holding it too long reads as evasion and frustrates the audience. Balance the delay against the payoff of the reveal. When: when deciding how long to hold back an explanation. Why: Delay that is too long reads as unfair withholding. (x2)
- [pitfall] Stillness or a long delay reads as padding and drains tension unless a reveal follows or a clear threat is approaching. When: Using quiet or ambient tension scenes, or delaying without a clear sense of approach. Why: Tension with no resolution or direction loses its effect.
- [pitfall] Repeating a false alarm without a payoff weakens later suspense. When: Building tension with recurring warnings. Why: The audience learns that warnings do not lead to real danger.
- [pitfall] Withholding that the player can see through quickly loses tension. When: When a character conceals information with obvious tells. Why: Predictable concealment removes the suspense of the reveal.
- [pitfall] Ambiguous repeated tests frustrate an audience if no other route to the answer is offered. When: designing repeated ambiguous tests. Why: players need an alternative path to resolve repeated uncertainty.
- [pitfall] If the reveal disappoints after a long build, the accumulated tension is wasted, so the payoff must match the anticipation.

## suspicion grounds
- [rule] Hold every suspect open until each person's whereabouts are known, rather than fixing suspicion on a favourite. When: When assessing suspects during an investigation. Why: Premature fixation on one suspect causes the investigator to overlook evidence against others.
- [rule] Keep the frame on an innocent suspect active until the final act so the player continues guessing. When: Pacing the suspect arc of a mystery. Why: An unresolved suspicion sustains tension and delays the reader's conclusion.
- [heuristic] Every suspicion rests on some base, even when appearances mislead. Find that base and test it before acting on the suspicion. When: when a character or player forms a conclusion from observation. Why: a conclusion can feel certain while its foundation is an unchecked assumption.
- [heuristic] Let suspicion of a protagonist's guilt rise gradually across the story rather than all at once.
- [heuristic] Estrangement or old feuds are reasons to look closer, not proof of guilt. When: When a suspect has a motive-related history. Why: A grievance explains a motive but does not establish action.
- [heuristic] Let each false suspect explain one clue and leave one contradiction unexplained, so that suspicion shifts while the final answer stays open. When: Designing a chain of suspects before the true culprit is revealed. Why: Partial explanations make each suspect plausible, and the leftover contradiction points toward the real answer.

## temperament and motive
- [rule] Let a villain's stated reason for an action be a claim the player can test against other evidence in the level. When: A game antagonist explains his actions. Why: Testable motives turn the player into an investigator.
- [rule] Give each enemy or NPC a temperament that governs how it carries out a deed, so a scene that breaks the temperament signals a different actor. When: Designing cast behaviour for a mystery. Why: Consistent temperament lets players spot staged or mismatched scenes.
- [heuristic] A passionate motive is unlikely for a suspect whose calm, profit-seeking conduct contradicts anger; temperament can rule a motive out. When: a passion-based motive is proposed for a suspect. Why: Motives show in how a person acts under pressure.
- [heuristic] Infer a culprit's temperament from their method: a crime copied from earlier patterns suggests an imitative rather than inventive mind. When: The method of a crime seems to point to a type of mind. Why: Method reflects habits of mind.
- [pitfall] Treating a character's rudeness or temper as evidence of crime confuses temperament with motive; a motive built from temperament alone fits many people and needs physical or situational support.
- [pitfall] Judging a person's character by temperament is open to bias, and assumptions about how people behave can mislead an investigation. When: An investigator concludes that a suspect would or would not act a certain way. Why: Character assumptions are subjective and can exclude a real culprit.

## threat and motive link
- [mechanism] Threats of prosecution carry little weight while stolen goods remain with the victim; leverage comes from the suspect's false belief.
- [rule] Tie an angry threat to the crime through time and place before treating it as proof of motive. When: A threat is the main evidence of a suspect's motive. Why: A threat shows feeling, not action.
- [rule] Pair a visible threat with a hidden benefactor so the obvious target draws attention away from the real danger.
- [rule] Pair an earlier threat with a later misfortune as a clue to motive, leaving the player to judge if the connection is real.
- [heuristic] Use motive to estimate how aggressively a culprit will pursue exposure, and expect ongoing threats to those who expose them. When: Assessing danger to investigators or victims. Why: A conspirator with much to lose will pursue those who threaten it.
- [heuristic] A threatening stranger may seem the culprit, yet his behaviour can have an emotional cause unrelated to the crime. When: when a suspect appears guilty early.

## timeline and movement
- [rule] When a witness cannot give a precise time, record the account as a range or estimate rather than an exact time. When: A witness is unsure of the exact time of an event. Why: Treating an approximate time as exact creates false precision in the sequence.
- [rule] Require each timeline clue's date to be confirmed by two unrelated in-world events, such as a festival, delivery, or death, before the player can rely on it. When: When designing a timeline system for player-discovered clues. Why: A single anchor can be wrong, so independent confirmation makes the timeline trustworthy.
- [heuristic] Record bearings and distances between locations, since a scene's position and layout determine what can be reached from where.
- [procedure] 1) List every time stamp with its source. 2) Mark each as measured (clock, bell) or estimated (guess, duration). 3) Chain the intervals between anchors and note gaps with no witness. 4) Check estimates against the chain; where they disagree, the gap is where the account can be bent. When: Investigators rebuild who was where and when from many time readings. Why: Chaining measured anchors exposes estimates and unwitnessed gaps that hide movement.
- [pitfall] Accepting a conventional start date for a disappearance without checking the last certain sighting can mislead the whole inquiry. When: An investigation adopts a start date from common assumption. Why: The question asked then concerns the wrong period.
- [fact] Sounds of arrivals by different routes, such as a lift and a stairway, reveal the order in which people came. When: Visual evidence is unavailable.

## timestamped physical clues
- [mechanism] Tying a mismatch to a timestamp lets players date the clean-up against other events.
- [rule] Give each timestamp a source, such as a watch or chime, so the reader can test it. When: Presenting times as evidence in a mystery. Why: A time with no stated source cannot be checked, so it cannot support a deduction.
- [rule] Pair a clue with a timeline stamp, such as an arrival date, so players combine two weak facts into a reliable inference.
- [rule] Give notes and letters in the game world timestamps and copy counts so players can build a timeline from paperwork. When: Designing in-world documents for a mystery. Why: Paperwork then becomes a checkable timeline source.
- [heuristic] A time written in a message gives a fixed point for ordering the events around it.
- [heuristic] A sudden physical sign with a timestamp, such as an animal's paralysis, can narrow a timeline and confirm an earlier suspicion. When: A health change in a person or animal is observed. Why: A dated onset places an event within a known window.

## timing as motive and coincidence
- [heuristic] Timing of actions close to a key or scheduled event can suggest a motive linked to that event, such as acts on the eve of a planned departure. When: when a sequence of actions follows a key occurrence or a behaviour coincides with a scheduled event. Why: Timing links the actions to the event or expectation that prompted them.
- [heuristic] Keep the timeline separate from the question of motive. An opportunity window alone does not identify who acted. When: when a suspect has access but no clear reason to act. Why: Access and motive must both be established to point at one person.
- [heuristic] Check the timing of a lawful act: a legitimate duty performed at the wrong moment can displace a more important one and hide a harmful purpose. When: judging a suspect's alibi or errand.
- [heuristic] When a death falls on a date the victim had feared or announced, check the coincidence against the rest of the evidence rather than treating it as confirmation. When: When a death matches a previously stated fear or prediction. Why: A matching date is striking but does not establish cause.
- [pitfall] Coincidences occur by chance, so a single timing match does not prove deception or intent; treat it as suggestive until tested, keeping a deadline-created motive separate from proof. Why: Chance produces many matches, so one match is expected by chance.
- [pitfall] Timing alone does not prove intent; a replacement or change can be innocent even when it coincides with a suspicious event.

## vehicles and vessel traces
- [mechanism] Vehicle-type clues, such as wheel marks, can resolve a trail dead end and point the player to the next location. When: designing tracking clues.
- [mechanism] Mud spatter on one side of a person can identify a vehicle and seat position, since each vehicle throws mud in a characteristic direction. When: a person's clothing shows spatter from travel. Why: the spray pattern depends on the vehicle and where the passenger sat.
- [heuristic] Used vessels and consumed supplies in a room indicate how many people were present and how long they stayed.
- [procedure] 1) Record the impression precisely. 2) Compare it with a reference pattern from a checkable source. 3) Have an independent expert confirm the reference before accepting the match. When: A vehicle must be linked to a track. Why: A shared, verifiable reference keeps the match from resting on one person's memory.
- [metric] Elapsed time multiplied by a vehicle's speed gives the farthest it could have travelled since it left a point. When: Checking whether a car could have reached a spot after a separation.
- [tradeoff] Shadowing by vehicle gains speed and flexibility, but the watcher's secrecy depends on the driver, who may talk. When: when choosing a method of surveillance.

## villain motive and culprit reveal
- [mechanism] A villain who explains the plan while the captive is still active can leak information the captive uses to reverse the trap. Why: Explanation scenes give the trapped party facts they can act on.
- [rule] A villain who makes lethal attacks should have a motive the player can discover in proportion to the threat.
- [rule] Allow a character the player likes to be a suspect, and provide clues that test that affection against the evidence. When: Designing a suspect the player is fond of. Why: Affection otherwise replaces evidence in the player's judgment.
- [rule] Let the villain die by the same means used on the victims; the matching end gives strong closure without a separate trial. When: Resolving a story whose antagonist used a hazard or tool against others. Why: A poetic mirror satisfies the player's sense of justice more directly than an off-screen resolution.
- [rule] Make the obvious suspects plausible, then reveal the culprit as a trusted insider.
- [pitfall] Assuming a lone actor without checking for others can misdirect the whole timeline and the suspect list.

## witness evidence sources
- [rule] Give witness NPCs a source field of saw, heard or inferred, and let players ask how each claim is known, since a claim's reliability depends on its source. When: when writing NPC testimony or when a witness's account is central and its basis is unclear. Why: Explicit sources let players test claims.
- [rule] Let NPC-signed in-world records serve as fixed reference points for disputed events, so players have a trustworthy anchor to weigh conflicting testimony against. When: Multiple NPCs have sworn to an event. Why: Witnessed records anchor contested accounts.
- [heuristic] A heated quarrel witnessed by bystanders establishes both a motive and a checkable record, since others can corroborate or contradict the account. When: when a public disagreement may bear on a death. Why: witnesses give independent confirmation of what was said.
- [heuristic] A witness at a fixed vantage point gives specific sightings, and an item missing from one person later found elsewhere can corroborate a link.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness to fetch the physical evidence. 2) Accompany the witness to where it is kept. 3) Observe the item in its original place. When: a physical record is needed to test a claim.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness to sketch the scene roughly. 2) Mark where key objects stood. 3) Check those positions against the real layout. Why: a sketch turns vague memory into testable positions.

## witness record keeping
- [rule] Record each witness answer with its source, who saw what and when, and a firsthand flag, so players can cross-check contradictions, overlaps and single-source gaps. When: Witness testimony matters to the solution or players must investigate it. Why: A player can only check contradictions if observations are recorded; structured metadata makes corroboration and single-source gaps visible. (x2)
- [rule] Order the case file so the player reads one witness's record before another's, mirroring a court's sequence. When: Presenting multiple witness records in a case file. Why: A deliberate sequence helps players assemble the account as a court would.
- [rule] A witness's own report is not enough to establish an impossible event when no physical trace supports it. When: Evaluating an account of an impossible appearance or disappearance. Why: Without physical evidence, the claim rests only on the witness's perception or memory.
- [heuristic] Track each witness's lighting, distance and fear level, and let these determine how many details they report, so the player can probe for gaps. When: Designing witness NPCs. Why: A perception record makes testimony consistent and gives the player something to test.
- [heuristic] Store each claim a player hears from a witness and check it against world state, such as a hole present or an object absent.
- [procedure] 1) Note whether the witness perceived the event directly. 2) Check whether the witness might have been noticed. 3) Estimate how strong the witness's emotion was. 4) Record the witness's stated uncertainty with the report. When: A witness's report is primary evidence for an event. Why: Direct perception, exposure and emotional state each shape how far the report can be trusted.

## writing style and register
- [heuristic] A distinctive mark tied to one region points to a homeland, and the inference strengthens when a second item from that region agrees. When: a person carries a regional mark or item. Why: specialist knowledge links the mark to a place and a second item corroborates it.
- [heuristic] A call or signal used within one community reveals a person's background, so a single cry can indicate where the speaker has lived. When: an everyday call is heard. Why: the call belongs to a particular community.
- [heuristic] Compare a document's spelling, vocabulary and products against its claimed origin, since regional wording can reveal a false source. When: A document claims an origin that may be false. Why: Language habits are hard to disguise consistently.
- [heuristic] Use a formal register when a message must signal authority, distance or the seriousness of an accusation; avoid it when warmth or plain clarity is needed. When: when choosing the tone of a written message. Why: Register sets the reader's sense of the author's stance.
- [procedure] 1) Inspect the register entry for the claimed alibi. 2) Compare its handwriting with other entries known to be written by the same person. When: a suspect's account names a guest or visitor register.
- [pitfall] Regularised spelling hides the original form of a name, which may be needed to identify the person. When: when a modernised edition is the only source used. Why: Original spellings can carry clues that normalisation removes.

## absence and missing evidence
- [mechanism] A presumption of death after a short absence requires evidence that makes death highly probable, and the shorter the absence, the stronger the evidence must be. When: Deciding whether to presume a person dead after they disappear. Why: A short absence leaves many innocent explanations open, so stronger evidence is needed to rule them out.
- [behavior] A missing expected entry, such as an unpaid fuel charge, is evidence only once the expected pattern is known. When: reading a ledger or account book. Why: Absence means something only against a known norm.
- [pitfall] Absence of a visible sign or of anyone hearing an event does not prove nothing happened; check whether the setting could mask it. When: An examination finds no marks but the witness reports an injury, or nobody heard the event. Why: Some effects leave no visible residue, and the setting may mask the event.
- [pitfall] Having no other candidate is an argument from absence, not proof that the chosen suspect is guilty.
- [fact] A forensic finding that no poison was swallowed contradicts a suicide-by-ingestion reading and suggests the drug was administered by another person. When: A death first read as self-administered poisoning. Why: A missing trace in the body is a physical fact that can overturn a method-based assumption.

## ambush and traps
- [model] A thief who has taken a valuable must find a buyer; a public reward notice makes the usual market hostile, so the thief must either stay hidden with unsellable goods or come forward. When: A thief must eventually move stolen goods and the item is identifiable. Why: Notices alert sellers, closing the usual channels for disposing of the item.
- [heuristic] Choose a bait that fits the culprit's psychology, such as an offer the culprit expects to accept. When: designing a trap that lures a culprit into the open. Why: A bait the target expects to take draws them in without suspicion.
- [heuristic] Let a set ambush produce an unexpected arrival, so watchers witness a false suspect's innocent action and clear that suspect. When: during a watch on a disturbed object.
- [heuristic] Let an ambush fail with a fleeting glimpse rather than a clean capture, so the culprit stays at large and tension carries forward. When: when a trap is set for the culprit. Why: a glimpse keeps the threat alive and gives a clue for later.
- [procedure] 1) Let the culprit act while the detective watches from concealment. 2) Recover the stolen item at the moment of the act. 3) Confront the culprit with the item and the route taken.

## anger and hostility
- [behavior] Accusations voiced in anger reveal suspicion between speakers, often in both directions, but they are charges made in heat, not findings.
- [pitfall] Animosity or jealousy can push an investigator to conclude before facts are in, so they stop verifying, read later facts through that conclusion, and may make unfounded accusations. When: The investigator is emotionally invested in the outcome. Why: Emotion replaces verification as the basis for acting.
- [pitfall] Statements made under anger, including confessions, mix truth with overstatement and spite, so a calm admission carries more weight; record exact wording and check each slip against other evidence. When: A suspect speaks under emotional pressure. Why: Emotional speech mixes truth with overstatement and spite.
- [pitfall] Antagonism with an official team reduces its cooperation, so an outside investigator's requests lose effect when the tone turns hostile. When: an outsider works alongside an official inquiry. Why: Officials act less on requests from people they resent.
- [pitfall] Anger can reveal the questioner's own weak position as well as the other party's.

## case reconstruction
- [mechanism] A clue given as a partial phrase, with the missing part recoverable only through a later action, makes the player reconstruct its meaning and invest in the discovery. When: Designing a clue delivered in fragments. Why: The player must act to complete the sentence, so the answer feels earned.
- [mechanism] A reconstruction that is only partly right can be overturned by one further clue, so the solution is revised rather than discarded.
- [procedure] 1) Group questions by source document. 2) For each question, offer a motive and test it against the actor's known behavior. 3) Set a greater motive against a lesser one to explain a single act. 4) Label answers as probabilities, not certainties. When: A case has many separate actions that must each be explained. Why: A chain of reasons makes an otherwise arbitrary actor's conduct discoverable.
- [procedure] 1) Reconstruct the disputed event step by step in front of witnesses. 2) Present the identifying object as proof. 3) Let witnesses accept the account, turning a private admission into a public verdict. When: ending a mystery with a confrontation. Why: A public account with witnesses fixes the outcome in a way a private confession does not.
- [procedure] 1) Name the hidden actor behind the disguise; 2) link them to a witness's testimony that explains the sighting; 3) confirm with an independent record that breaks the alibi. When: Delivering a reveal that exposes a disguised actor and a false alibi. Why: Naming, linking and confirming makes the reveal clear and checkable.

## cell and physical traces
- [rule] Separate prisoners into different cells to prevent exchange of information between them. When: Multiple prisoners are held in custody. Why: Co-location allows communication and collusion.
- [rule] Prefer checkable physical facts such as eye colour, facial marks and clothing over impressions of character when describing a person. Why: Physical facts can be matched against later sightings, while impressions cannot.
- [heuristic] Use a precise physical detail, such as a wound's location or a scar on a specific limb, as a checkable trait; a suspect cannot easily hide it, and it can be verified against evidence. When: A description or witness claim needs verification against physical evidence. Why: A physical mark can be tested directly, unlike a general description; precise details can be confirmed or refuted.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm the comparison list is complete. 2) Include the victim and the scene as possible sources. 3) Check whether the trace could have been placed after the fact. 4) Only then trust the match or non-match. When: A trace matches nobody on a suspect list, or matches someone strongly. Why: An incomplete list or a planted trace can make a match or non-match misleading.
- [fact] Blood cell shape distinguishes sources: mammal corpuscles are round, while camel-family corpuscles are oval, separating some stains from bird or human blood. When: When identifying the animal origin of a blood stain. Why: Cell morphology differs between animal groups.

## ceremony and closure
- [rule] Close a quest beat on a message or NPC reaction that starts the next objective.
- [heuristic] End a chapter on a reversal when the reframing will carry the player into the next chapter. When: end of a chapter or act. Why: Reversals create suspense and invite continuation.
- [heuristic] A public ceremony that acknowledges past errors gives a divided community a shared end point. When: a conflict has ended and trust must be rebuilt. Why: Shared ritual marks a common transition.
- [heuristic] End a mystery with a light, closing gesture after the reveal to release tension, especially when the cause is unusual or the resolution informal. When: Writing the final scene after a dramatic reveal. Why: A lighter ending releases the tension built by the reveal and softens an informal outcome.
- [pitfall] A public ceremony of confession can be read as proof that the wrong was real, when it may only show that the authority could enforce silence. When: A public confession or rebuke is offered as evidence. Why: Compelled public acts reflect the power of the enforcing authority, not the truth of the charge.

## conduct and physical evidence
- [mechanism] Rain, darkness and moonlight limit what an observer can see, and can also expose the observer's own position.
