- [heuristic] Test a witness's claimed conditions, such as weather, against physical traces like wet floors or shoes to estimate when events happened. When: a claimed condition can leave physical marks.
- [heuristic] Behaviour such as agitation or evasive answers is weak evidence, because it may have an innocent cause that the person's own stated reason can reveal. When: interpreting a suspect's behaviour. Why: distress and guilt look alike, so a stated cause must be tested before it is discounted.
- [heuristic] Favoritism or later actions by a person can support one claim of intent over another. When: Intent is disputed and conduct is documented. Why: Behavior around the time of a document reveals what the person likely wanted.
- [fact] Confinement and guards posted outside a door are actions an outside party can later evaluate as evidence.

## corroboration requirements
- [rule] Check that accounts are independent before treating their agreement as corroboration; copied accounts or sources who have spoken to each other may agree from a shared origin or bias. When: Two accounts agree on a point, or two witness statements are being compared. Why: Copied accounts repeat a single source and so do not confirm each other; shared conversation can produce agreement that reflects shared bias rather than truth.
- [rule] Require two credible, independent witnesses who each attest firsthand to the act before accepting an accusation, or require a confession that is matched to the physical fact it describes. When: Formal accusation or conviction is being decided. Why: A single or uncorroborated account can be mistaken, shaped by pressure or motivated.
- [rule] Require two separate witness NPCs before a quest accuses a character of magic, and distinguish those who saw an event from those who only heard of it. When: Scripting an accusation that changes the quest state. Why: Direct sight and a second witness reduce false triggers caused by rumour.
- [procedure] 1) Find a second source for the claim. 2) Compare the two. 3) Treat agreement between an official and an informal source as strong support.
- [pitfall] A case that moves from an unverifiable accusation to conviction on loose supporting evidence has no real corroboration standard. Why: Any trifle is accepted as confirmation once the accusation is heard.

## crime signature and style
- [model] A case built on an old crime and a family inheritance combines three elements: a motive, a hidden object, and people with a stake in finding it.
- [model] A crime's style can be analyzed along seven dimensions: approach, conception, technique, imagination, attack, method, and organization. When: When comparing a crime's style with candidate suspects. Why: Separate dimensions allow a structured comparison of personality.
- [rule] Let players match a crime's style against NPC personalities, not only against physical clues, so character reading becomes a route to the answer.
- [heuristic] Judge a crime by its conception and execution, which reveal its psychological signature (personality and method), not only its physical traces.
- [tradeoff] A recurring signature can signal one responsible person, so compare incidents for it; yet it may also mislead, inviting a single-author assumption while the real link lies elsewhere. When: When several incidents may share a responsible person; when linking several crimes in one investigation. Why: Shared patterns suggest common responsibility; but a shared pattern invites assuming one author when the real connection lies elsewhere.

## cryptic remarks and cues
- [heuristic] Let a specific word, item or place presented to a character trigger a reaction that unlocks a dialogue branch. When: Designing character interviews. Why: Cues make dialogue respond to what the player actually shows.
- [heuristic] Design each reading of a cryptic clue to lead to a distinct, checkable location, so each reading can be tested. When: Writing an ambiguous inscription or message that points to several targets. Why: Distinct, checkable targets let players test readings instead of guessing.
- [procedure] 1) Deliver a short, cryptic message to one suspect with no explanation. 2) Observe the reaction on the spot. 3) Note any follow-up question or request to repeat. When: when testing whether a suspect knows a specific fact.
- [pitfall] A cryptic remark spoken in front of others can warn the target and let them prepare. Why: the target learns that the speaker knows more than they should.
- [pitfall] An interpretation built on a few visible cues can be overturned by fuller observation that the witness did not weigh.

## death and remains
- [mechanism] A body altered after death to imitate another victim leaves a physical detail, such as a removed item, that reveals the true sequence of events. When: when a false scene is staged to hide the real crime. Why: the alteration requires an action that leaves physical evidence.
- [mechanism] A death can be caused by a psychological event, such as a sudden shock from seeing a person, so the apparent murder is not a physical attack. When: Designing a death scene where the cause is not a physical attack. Why: Reinterpreting the cause removes the crime and dissolves the investigation without a culprit.
- [heuristic] A poisoning scene can hold a label or packet that a player matches to a shop, and a tidying NPC can erase it unless the player acts first.
- [heuristic] Ligaments outlast muscle, so bones still joined by ligament suggest most soft tissue was gone before separation. When: Judging how a skeleton was handled or how far decay had progressed before it was separated. Why: Ligament persists longer than muscle through decay, so joined bones indicate soft tissue loss before separation.
- [pitfall] Remains evidence requires knowledge of decay and handling; without it, the same marks carry no meaning. When: Interpreting physical traces on skeletal remains. Why: Trace meaning depends on understanding how decay and handling produce them.

## decoy suspects and evidence
- [rule] Give a decoy suspect a real alibi and let the player clear that suspect before the true reveal. Why: A cleared decoy shifts suspicion, so the next answer feels like a correction.
- [heuristic] Make the decoy suspect's evidence convincing: give the decoy motive a real physical trace, such as dated notes, strong enough to convict on paper so players stop seeking alternatives. When: building a mystery with a decoy suspect and a misleading but plausible motive. Why: Players who accept a convincing case stop looking for alternatives, and a real trace makes the wrong theory feel supported rather than invented.
- [heuristic] Plant contradictory clues on purpose so a wrong premise becomes visible when enough anomalies pile up. When: Designing a mystery whose initial theory should eventually fail. Why: Accumulated anomalies let the player discover the error without the designer stating it.
- [pitfall] A decoy that is too loud is dismissed early, and one that is too weak is never noticed; both fail to misdirect. When: when tuning the prominence of a red herring. Why: Misdirection depends on the decoy being noticed but not immediately discounted.
- [pitfall] A recovered object that seems to prove the crime can be a planted decoy, making the real crime appear to have happened earlier or elsewhere. When: A mystery where a key item is recovered and treated as proof. Why: Players trust physical proof, and a decoy exploits that trust.

## delayed recall effects
- [mechanism] Once a name is spoken, forgotten remarks and small incidents return with new meaning, as memory reorganises around the revealed identity. When: A key identity or fact is revealed late. Why: The revealed fact reframes previously ignored details.
- [behavior] Witnesses questioned right after an event may offer nothing, while a later, calmer round can recover recollections the first round did not trigger. When: witnesses are excited or busy immediately after an event. Why: Immediate stress and duties crowd out recall that returns with time and different questioning.
- [behavior] Long-delayed testimony can contain vivid, precise detail that is still inaccurate, especially if the witness only began to suspect something during the event. When: testimony given long after the event. Why: memory is reconstructed and shaped by later suspicion.
- [rule] When several people have motives and opportunities, delay settling on the most convenient suspect until each suspect's evidence has been weighed. When: multiple suspects look plausible. Why: early settling on the convenient suspect can hide the real answer.
- [pitfall] A delayed check lets a suspect's situation change before you verify it, so verify claims as early as possible.

## deposit and deposition records
- [definition] A deposition is sworn testimony taken to fix a witness's memory on record, so it can be used later. When: A witness is old or a dispute may return to court. Why: Recording testimony early preserves it against the loss of memory or the death of the witness.
- [mechanism] A sealed deposit ties the suspect's safety to the investigator's, because any harm to the investigator would expose the suspect. Why: Release is triggered by the investigator's absence.
- [pitfall] A sealed deposit is useless if the recipient is untrustworthy, late or absent when the release time arrives. Why: The method depends on the recipient acting as instructed.
- [pitfall] A suspect who learns of a sealed deposit may demand its destruction, so the plan must allow for that demand.
- [pitfall] Enmity recorded in a deposition is a motive to examine, not proof of guilt.

## disorder interpretation
- [mechanism] Sudden disorder pulls everyone's attention away, leaving an object unwatched for a moment.
- [heuristic] Disorder shows what searchers wanted, but it can also point away from where the object really is, so test it against the physical scene. When: a room shows signs of a violent or unexplained search.
- [heuristic] A search that restores objects to their original order is hard to do perfectly, and a neatly rearranged space can itself be a sign of tampering. When: A character searches a room or belongings and tries to leave no trace. Why: Perfect restoration is difficult, so small irregularities or unusual neatness reveal the search.
- [pitfall] Treating disorder as proof of theft is a guess: it can be staged or have other causes, and it shows a search only if the undisturbed baseline is known. Why: a messy scene has several possible causes; without a baseline, disorder proves little.
- [pitfall] Do not assume one person caused the disorder; check who else had access before attributing it to a single intruder.

## dissent and npc behavior
- [behavior] Open disapproval of an accusation can make the dissenter a target, so doubt becomes risky to voice.
- [behavior] A single insulting label applied to critics can make them seem odious and end their objections. When: A faction names those who doubt its proceedings. Why: The label shifts attention from the objection to the critic.
- [rule] Give objecting characters the ability to restrict rooms or postpone the investigator, so their dissent changes the player's options.
- [rule] Give each NPC a distinctive script so the player can match a forged note to its writer.
- [pitfall] Allies may resist an unfamiliar method, so the investigator must explain the procedure clearly. When: when proposing an untested investigative method to a group. Why: Unclear procedure breeds doubt even when the method is sound.

## faint marks and fading text
- [rule] Make faint audio cues clearly distinct from background sound so the listener can tell a clue from noise.
- [pitfall] A long-healed scar can be faint and missed unless the investigator looks closely.
- [pitfall] Blotter impressions are faint and easily misread; record each reading as tentative rather than certain. Why: Uncertain readings can mislead later reasoning if treated as firm.
- [pitfall] Faint or straggling handwriting may reflect illness or fatigue rather than intent, so meaning should be read into it only with other evidence. When: Interpreting irregular writing as evidence. Why: Physical condition can change handwriting without any change in meaning.
- [pitfall] Fading ink and worn margins can erase the strokes that a handwriting comparison depends on.

## guard and security clues
- [rule] Give a guard NPC an entry log so players reconstruct a sequence by asking about count, order and appearance, not by receiving a single name. When: Designing an NPC witness in a dungeon or level. Why: Partial sequences make players reason rather than look up an answer.
- [rule] Let a guard stationed at one door act as a witness, and use line-of-sight and audio cues so players can check what the guard could see or hear. When: designing guard NPCs near key chokepoints. Why: limits on sight and sound make the guard's report testable.
- [rule] Give a guard a motive, such as a personal attachment to a prisoner, so players have a reason to question the guard's report. When: designing guard NPCs who report events. Why: a bias gives players grounds to doubt the report.
- [heuristic] An extra or missing guard in a count signals a disguised or dead character, making headcount discrepancies usable as clues. When: a count of guards or NPCs is shown to the player. Why: Discrepancies between expected and observed numbers point to hidden status changes.
- [pitfall] A guard animal's silence is evidence of no intrusion only if its reliability is known.

## hedged and inferred claims
- [definition] Induction is reasoning from many particular observations to a general likelihood, producing a provisional conclusion that ranks possibilities rather than proving them. When: When an investigator must reach a conclusion from incomplete evidence. Why: Induction yields probable readings, which remain open to challenge.
- [rule] Treat an inference from partial information, like a completed witness story, as a hedged hypothesis, not settled fact, especially when evidence is a single or trance-derived account. When: Stating a theory from limited evidence. Why: Hedged claims signal uncertainty and prevent a weak theory from being taken as fact.
- [rule] Present a rival hypothesis as a guess to be tested, and acknowledge that guesses may miss, since a wrong guess costs little. When: When proposing a theory that lacks full evidence. Why: Openness that a guess is a guess keeps the reasoning honest and the cost of error low.
- [heuristic] Present sensory readings as inference with visible confidence, not as verified fact. Why: Sound-based inferences can be wrong.
- [tradeoff] A vague standard for accepting inferences lets decision-makers split the difference, while a strict standard risks rejecting a true conclusion built from linked facts. When: Setting how much evidence a final judgment requires. Why: Without a clear threshold, the verdict depends on how each judge reads what counts as a just inference.

## hidden clue searching
- [mechanism] Overheard but unseen voices narrow possibilities: their number, kind, and voice quality can suggest who was involved without identifying them. When: when the people present were heard but not seen. Why: Partial sensory evidence narrows possibilities even without identification.
- [rule] Do not rely on an unexplained secret passage as the answer to a locked-room puzzle; use it only as a passing guess. When: Resolving a sealed-room mystery. Why: An unexplained passage feels like a cheat and leaves the puzzle unresolved.
- [pitfall] Treating an unlocked space as closed to everyone, or a locked space as safe from insiders, leads to wrong access conclusions. When: Judging whether a space was accessible. Why: Locks indicate physical control, not who holds keys or has permission.
- [pitfall] Searching unrelated events, such as birthdays or weddings, for a link produces false patterns and wastes effort.
- [fact] An unseen investigator can gather fragments of speech and visual reflections that point toward hidden matters.

## hints, optional content, and rewards
- [rule] Offer optional backstory only when the player's conversation reaches a matching point, not from a menu, and include an explicit option to decline. When: Designing NPC backstory delivery. Why: Contextual timing and a safe exit make players more willing to reveal and engage.
- [heuristic] Release hints in a fixed order, starting with a general rule and then the specific target, so the player builds the theory step by step. When: Designing how a mystery's clues are revealed to the player. Why: A general-to-specific sequence lets the player construct the explanation incrementally.
- [tradeoff] An optional explanation of how an item was taken rewards curious players, but it removes the mystery that a fully unexplained default preserves. When: choosing how much of a mystery to resolve by default. Why: Explaining everything satisfies some players and deflates the mood for others.
- [pitfall] Open rewards for information draw many unreliable claimants, who waste investigative effort. Why: Anyone seeking the reward will offer an answer, true or not.
- [pitfall] Hints that never connect to a later event read as padding. Each hint should link to a later test or escalation. When: Scattering clues through a mystery. Why: Unconnected hints waste the audience's attention and erode trust.

## historical tombs and monuments
- [rule] Test a monument's name against documents and tradition before accepting it as evidence of a location, since the name carries unearned authority. When: A memorial is presented as marking where something happened. Why: A name on a marker can make a claim seem established without support.
- [heuristic] With no clue, move through oddities the pursued target would also have noticed, since what caught the pursuer's eye may have caught theirs. When: no solid lead exists.
- [heuristic] Finding a modern cause for one sighting does not prove every other claim about the event false.
- [pitfall] A moving farewell can bind the reader's emotions to one reading of events, so the reader accepts the explanation it suggests.
- [pitfall] Modern tombs can look old, so check the date of construction before treating a monument as historically original. When: Judging a monument's age from its appearance. Why: Weathering and style can make recent structures seem to date from earlier periods.

## identity and alias reveals
- [definition] An anagram alias rearranges every letter of a true name, hiding identity in plain sight until the letters are compared.
- [mechanism] A notice that names a person fails silently when the person travels under a false name, even if they are alive and nearby. When: The sought person is known to use an alias. Why: Recipients cannot link the notice to the person without recognising the name.
- [behavior] Players accept an identity introduced by a character they trust, and do not question it when witnesses agree with that identity. When: A character is introduced with an identity that others confirm. Why: Shared acceptance by multiple witnesses removes the impulse to test the identity.
- [rule] Give an NPC an almost-recognition moment that stops short of naming someone, and use it to unlock a later identification. When: planting a future identity reveal. Why: A hesitation the player notices makes the later identification feel earned.
- [procedure] 1) Show the character under one name. 2) Show a related name earlier in a separate context, sharing letters or sound. 3) Deliver the link at the moment of exposure. 4) Confirm the identity through a second independent witness. When: A hidden identity must be revealed at a climax without a separate explanation. Why: The reader already holds every fact and needs only the recognition, and two sources make the reveal feel earned.

## information gaps
- [mechanism] A short message that omits size, comfort and crew, and asks for odd items, invites the reader to guess a hidden purpose and keep reading. When: when a message should promise more than it tells. Why: missing details invite the reader to supply suspicion.
- [mechanism] A missing address or name can stop a message from reaching its recipient, delaying the truth as effectively as deliberate concealment. When: A clue or message depends on a recipient's location or identity. Why: Without the correct information the delivery fails, regardless of intent.
- [heuristic] Do not dismiss an unexplained phenomenon; admit the gap and keep it open for later weighing. When: an event resists explanation. Why: Honest uncertainty keeps the player weighing both explanations.
- [pitfall] Too much information can bury the one vital fact among many irrelevant ones, so the decisive clue goes unnoticed.
- [pitfall] Partially briefed allies can act independently and change the situation, so withholding information from people who must act together can backfire. When: Coordinating a group that must act quickly. Why: Partial knowledge leaves allies unprepared and prone to uncoordinated action.

## isolated trace reading
- [mechanism] Distance from neighbours and authority makes a crime less likely to be noticed or reported, so a remote location gives a perpetrator more room to act unseen. When: When judging how easily a crime could go unnoticed in a location. Why: Few people are nearby to witness events and few authorities are close enough to respond.
- [behavior] People in lonely houses who know little of the law may never complain about mistreatment, so abuse can continue unreported. When: When residents are isolated and have little legal knowledge. Why: They lack nearby neighbours to notice and little knowledge of how to seek help.
- [heuristic] A single trace read in isolation can mislead; check normal behaviour and test each alternative explanation against other evidence before concluding. When: When interpreting a trace or physical evidence with several possible explanations. Why: Ordinary sequences can produce changes that look suspicious, and alternatives can fit one reading but fail under other checks. (x2)
- [pitfall] Individual records or facts look harmless or confused alone; their connections and meaning emerge only when compared against each other. When: Reviewing individual transactions or facts in isolation. Why: Single entries lack the context that a comparison supplies.
- [pitfall] Suspicion gathered around an isolated group can make it look guilty of later events without direct evidence.

## late clue clustering
- [mechanism] A late witness account that contradicts the accepted suspect cracks a wrong solution and reopens the case. When: when a false solution holds the story. Why: A contradiction from a witness exposes the gap in the accepted explanation.
- [rule] Stage a confession letter as a late cluster that rewards the player for solving the room before an NPC confirms it.
- [rule] A later stop or cancellation order can reverse an earlier assumed sponsorship, revealing that the party the reader trusted quietly halted the plot.
- [heuristic] Cluster the decisive clues late as several small facts, so suspicion cycles through earlier suspects and the final deduction gains weight. When: structuring the final act or climax of a deduction-based mystery. Why: Late clues keep earlier suspects plausible, and a dense late cluster lets the player assemble the answer.
- [heuristic] Place a late cluster of clues that fit several theories at once, so the reader must choose between them. When: Entering the final act of a mystery with competing theories. Why: Ambiguous evidence forces the reader to weigh each candidate explanation.

## look-alike misidentification
- [behavior] Observers can mistake a closely resembling person for the target without any lie, and trusting a witness's sense that someone looked right lets an impostor pass unnoticed. When: two people closely resemble each other.
- [behavior] Witnesses often misidentify a person in a group when individuals arrive together, linger, or enter in quick succession. When: Several people arrive or move through a space close together. Why: Brief, grouped movement makes individuals hard to separate in memory.
- [rule] Use a look-alike relative in a character dossier as a red herring, so players must check a physical detail before accepting an identity. When: Designing a misidentification in a mystery.
- [pitfall] Identifying someone by one common trait can mislead, because many people share it, so a single match should not be treated as proof. Why: common traits occur by coincidence across many people.
- [fact] Two people who look alike in daylight can be mistaken for each other in dim light, so a brief sighting in low light is unreliable for identification. When: Witness accounts of a figure seen briefly in low light. Why: Poor light blurs distinguishing features.

## medical findings scope
- [definition] A medical cause of death explains how the body failed, not who or what set that failure in motion.
- [rule] Let a medical NPC give a range rather than a single time, and let players combine that range with other NPCs' sightings. When: When writing medical or forensic dialogue for a mystery. Why: Ranges invite cross-referencing, which makes the player's deduction active.
- [heuristic] Treat a condition confirmed by medical evidence as an observed fact rather than a claim.
- [heuristic] Read medical findings as consistent with several scenarios rather than as proof of one specific cause. Why: Many different events can produce the same physical result.
- [fact] Medical time-of-death estimates rest on signs like stiffening and wound angle; they are judgments with wide margins, such as a seven-to-ten-hour window, not a fixed hour. When: Using a medical estimate in a timeline. Why: Medical evidence narrows time only within its margin.

## motive and gossip
- [procedure] 1) Give an NPC's claim about another NPC a stake the player can discover, such as marriage or inheritance. 2) Let the player judge the claim against that motive. 3) Offer a rival NPC reading the player can choose to trust. When: Designing NPC dialogue that the player must evaluate. Why: Discoverable motive makes accusations something the player weighs, not just receives.
- [tradeoff] A line of testimony drawn from gossip can seem to implicate a suspect, but its unreliable origin reduces its weight until stronger evidence removes it. When: A witness repeats hearsay that points at a suspect. Why: Unverified origin lowers credibility, so the hearsay can be discarded once proof arrives.
- [pitfall] Secondhand or relayed accounts can be unreliable: each retelling may add or drop details, and gossip bends stories to fit expectations, so informants must be corroborated. When: When a motive or claim rests on secondhand or relayed sources. Why: Informants may be biased, and every retelling can alter specifics the original source held accurately.
- [pitfall] Rumours from people with a grudge can spread without any firsthand basis. When: When rumours circulate about a person's origins or conduct. Why: Grudges motivate spreading claims that no one has witnessed.
- [pitfall] If the full motive is revealed too early, a character's misreading loses its tension. When: Structuring a secret the character misjudges. Why: The gap between the character's guess and the truth creates the suspense.

## npc rivalry protection
- [rule] If a player provokes an NPC into violence, let the consequences fall on the player and the NPC's situation, after a clear prior warning.
- [rule] Have an NPC press a rival explanation, so players must test it against evidence rather than accept it. When: when designing misleading NPC pressure.
- [rule] Let a family's social connections, not only guilt, decide whether an NPC is protected or exposed. When: when designing NPC consequences in a game.
- [rule] Let an NPC hint at a coming threat without specifics, record the hint as a flag, and let a later event confirm or contradict it.
- [heuristic] Model NPC rivalries with grudges, and let rivals leak information to one another so the player can overhear and act on it. When: When designing NPC relationships that carry story information.

## over-pressing witnesses
- [pitfall] Pressing a witness too hard can make them close off, stop cooperating, and turn a neutral party into a defender of the person questioned. (x2)
- [pitfall] Pushing a suspect too far can cause them to object and withdraw, and a question refused early may be impossible to ask again in the same form. When: Interrogating a suspect who may deny everything under pressure. Why: Excessive pressure damages trust and closes the line of questioning.
- [pitfall] Pressing a witness too hard can look like badgering, and the other side may argue the loose phrasing was innocent. When: Repeatedly questioning a witness about a loose answer. Why: Persistence without restraint can damage the questioner's credibility.
- [pitfall] Pressing too hard can end the conversation before the visitor reveals the motive.
- [pitfall] Pressing a reluctant witness too hard makes them close up, so stop once they have given a checkable fact. When: Questioning a reluctant witness. Why: Excessive pressure triggers withdrawal and ends the flow of information.

## pattern shifts
- [mechanism] A rival who keeps reappearing across different locations turns single surprises into a recognisable pattern the player can follow. When: when a rival must be tracked over a long campaign. Why: repetition across places makes the rival's presence a pattern, not a one-off.
- [heuristic] Make a suspect's conduct suspicious through a pattern of individually defensible actions rather than one damning act. When: writing a suspect whose guilt should be inferred. Why: Each step keeps an innocent reading, so the pattern carries the suspicion.
- [heuristic] Track how a pattern, such as call frequency, changes over time, since a shift can mark an event worth checking. When: Reviewing a record of repeated contacts.
- [heuristic] Reveal a pattern in observable responses to changing conditions to overturn a false explanation without naming the true cause.
- [procedure] 1) Note events that recur on a schedule or share a trigger. 2) Check the pattern against an independent record. 3) Treat the match as a lead, then run a test before accepting a cause. When: When scattered events seem random but may share a hidden trigger. Why: An independent record can confirm a schedule, but only a test can establish the cause.

## precedent-based inference
- [mechanism] A crime that shares distinctive features with an earlier unsolved case suggests the culprit studied that case, though the parallel may also be coincidence. When: Comparing a new crime to an earlier unsolved one. Why: Shared method signatures imply knowledge of the precedent or deliberate imitation.
- [rule] Treat precedent as a hint directing the search, not proof; a single similar case cannot establish a general rule and only supports a specific mechanism. Complex cases still need on-site examination. (x2)
- [heuristic] Compare a new crime with recorded earlier cases to test for a shared method, not just a shared story, since repeated methods leave recognizable patterns. When: a new crime resembles an earlier one, or its scene's method is unusual but has possible precedents. Why: Known methods leave known traces.
- [heuristic] A past case using a similar trick makes a human cause more plausible, though it does not prove the same method was used now. When: Weighing a human explanation for a strange event. Why: Similar prior events show a method exists, but each case still needs its own evidence.
- [procedure] 1) Choose a known precedent whose method, victim, physical trace and motive resemble the current case. 2) List each matching feature. 3) Use the stacked matches to form a working hypothesis. When: a recognised pattern exists but hard evidence is not yet available. Why: stacked resemblances make a shared pattern more likely than chance.

## protagonist and professional roles
- [heuristic] Give the protagonist an inner resolve with a set deadline, such as a day to test a suspicion, to pace the story and raise stakes. Why: a deadline gives the investigation a clock.
- [heuristic] Give the protagonist a motive for concealment, so withholding information becomes a source of tension in its own right.
- [pitfall] A feature shared by a whole product line narrows the field but does not single out one person.
- [pitfall] A professional may stay silent about an irregularity to avoid consequences, so a physical trace can be hidden by discretion. When: A witness with expertise notices an anomaly. Why: Self-protection can suppress reporting.
- [fact] Professional registers let an investigator find everyone who held a given job, so a past occupation can be used to locate a person. When: A suspect's past profession is known. Why: Occupational records list people by role rather than by current name.

## public communication
- [behavior] Frightened onlookers calm when a device's harmless mechanism is explained aloud, but only accurately; a wrong reassurance endangers the people it was meant to calm. When: A frightening display is active in the room.
- [rule] Release a story in stages: hold unverified detail back until the report is ready, and limit what staff say before then. When: when facts must reach the public or a suspect at a chosen moment. Why: Early release can tip off parties or spread incomplete facts.
- [rule] Attach a reward and a reply route to a public appeal, so any witness who can act has a way to respond. When: Publishing an appeal for information.
- [heuristic] Stagger contacts across a day, such as an early visit, a midday meeting and an afternoon report, so the sequence shows what was known and when. When: when alibis depend on exact hours.
- [heuristic] Compare a publication's described purpose with its real aim; a work presented as a report may aim to stop opposition. When: A document presents itself as neutral reporting. Why: A stated genre can disguise advocacy.

## reconstruction purpose and use
- [heuristic] Reconstruction from context is unreliable where the source can be re-interviewed or checked against independent evidence; check directly in those cases. When: when deciding whether to reconstruct a gap or verify it.
- [heuristic] Reconstruct a damaged document for its general character and meaning rather than its exact words when the question is what kind of document it is. When: Deciding how precisely to reconstruct a damaged document. Why: General meaning often suffices for present needs even when some words stay uncertain.
- [heuristic] Reconstruct a sequence of events when a sealed or confusing scene needs explaining; it is less useful when no physical evidence survives.
- [fact] Reconstructed speech recovers the thought underneath a speaker's words, not their exact wording.
- [fact] A detective's full model of a crime can be held back and released in a closing reconstruction that cites objects the player has already seen. When: Ending a puzzle or mystery with a complete explanation. Why: Connecting known objects makes the answer feel composed rather than announced.

## reconstruction sources and limits
- [heuristic] When a primary record is lost, reconstruct the event from side records such as lawsuits, letters or ledgers, and label the result as indirect evidence. When: When the primary record of an event does not survive. Why: Side records preserve fragments of testimony but are not the original account.
- [procedure] 1) Collect dated in-game ledgers, gravestones and burial sites. 2) Order the dated items. 3) Cross-check them against one another. 4) Derive the town's timeline from the agreed order. When: When designing a town's history for the player to rebuild. Why: Physical and written items together give the player a checkable timeline.
- [procedure] 1) Recognize when a line of inquiry is blocked. 2) Pick a different known fixed point, such as a death or a departure. 3) Reconstruct the unknown interval forward or backward from that anchor. 4) Ask targeted questions to the right source. When: A suspect's background cannot be traced past a certain point, or a chain of evidence has a missing middle. Why: A second anchor bypasses a dead end without needing the blocked path.
- [pitfall] A motive reconstructed from another person's intentions is persuasive but not established by documents, and should not be presented as proof. When: presenting a theory of hidden intent. Why: intentions are inferred, not observed.
- [fact] Sources for reconstructing a past community include court files, church books, wills, inventories, parish reports, colonial records and letters.

## records and faithful copies
- [rule] Give the same words in a faithful version and a misleading version, so the player must weigh the speaker's reliability.
- [rule] Disclose how a found record was edited, including any translation, cuts and name changes, so readers can judge how far to trust it. When: when presenting a found document as a source. Why: Undisclosed edits make readers suspect hidden clues, undermining the whole frame.
- [tradeoff] An exact reprint keeps every error and can hinder understanding, while a modernized copy reads clearly but loses original form. When: Choosing how to present an old record. Why: Faithfulness and clarity pull in opposite directions.
- [fact] Recorded measurements can be falsified by an insider with records access, so their values are not reliable proof. When: Relying on official measurements. Why: Access allows editing.
- [fact] A printed transcript may be reworded for presentation, so it can differ from what was actually spoken and heard live. When: Relying on a written record of spoken testimony. Why: Editors smooth language, which can alter the meaning or delivery.

## relative timing and measures
- [heuristic] Express timing relative to a known anchor or other events, such as 'ten days later' or 'two months earlier', letting readers sequence events without exact dates and spot contradictions.
- [heuristic] Judge a sum by the holder's situation, not its face value; an amount that seems trivial can be enough to break one person. When: weighing a motive for a character. Why: Money has relative value to each person.
- [heuristic] Ask a witness to judge height relative to a known person, such as the investigator, to give a comparison point. Why: A relative comparison is easier to judge than an absolute height estimate.
- [pitfall] Accepting a time because it is repeated or gossiped locally is risky, since local talk is partly true and partly untrue.
- [fact] A message dated only relatively, such as 'tomorrow', cannot fix when it was written; a postmark or envelope is needed.

## removing witnesses and suspects
- [mechanism] Sending a person who could check a claim away from the setting protects an impostor's position while the claim stays unverified. Why: A false claim can only be disproved by someone present who knows the truth.
- [behavior] A person who wants to control a situation may dismiss staff, send a trusted witness away on a pretext and cut off medical or outside help, narrowing who can see or report events. When: A controlling figure wants observers absent at a decisive moment. Why: Each removal narrows the witnesses, and the sum of mundane reasons can look sinister.
- [rule] Remove a suspect only when a verified alibi or a clear, stated reason excludes them. When: when narrowing a suspect list.
- [procedure] 1) Create a believable errand that draws the witness away. 2) Choose a destination that is hard to return from at the chosen time. 3) Confirm the errand's source can be checked. 4) Prepare a signal in case the witness returns early. When: An investigator must search a location while a witness is present. Why: A plausible errand clears the scene for a set period and the signal protects the plan.
- [fact] Removing one suspect, even by death, does not clear the remaining suspects while the central question stays unresolved.

## revisiting refused or dismissed items
- [rule] Revisit a dismissed open item when new reasoning reframes its absence as evidence. When: When an item was earlier judged unrecoverable. Why: A reframed absence can carry more information than the item itself.
- [heuristic] Let the player revisit a refused topic after gaining another clue, so the refusal pays off later. When: when designing dialogue branches. Why: Later context changes what the refusal means.
- [heuristic] Return to an earlier hesitation the witness did not volunteer, since pressing it can expose an uncertainty they had concealed.
- [heuristic] A witness who was advised to omit something may reveal it later, once the reason for silence no longer binds them, so re-question them after their protection changes. When: A witness withheld facts on someone else's advice or to protect themselves. Why: The motive for silence weakens when the witness's risk or obligation changes.
- [procedure] 1) Let a questioner leave after a first answer. 2) Return after a short delay. 3) Compare the new answer with the first to test consistency. When: When an answer may not be final. Why: A returning questioner tests whether the story holds.

## rushed action and risk
- [mechanism] A court created quickly, by reversing an earlier decision under claimed emergency, can move from trial to execution within about a week, leaving outside bodies no time to intervene. Why: Compressed timelines remove the window for review.
- [tradeoff] Gaps caused by a rushed event, such as a hurried levy or a fire, can explain why a town's archive is incomplete, giving the world a believable reason for missing records. When: When designing why a town's archive lacks certain documents. Why: A cause for the gap makes missing records feel plausible rather than arbitrary.
- [pitfall] Rushing a frightened witness, or pressing them about their own wrongdoing, can make them shut down and stop volunteering information. When: When a witness fears blame for what they overheard or did. Why: Fear of punishment makes witnesses guarded.
- [pitfall] A rushed entry can injure bystanders or the victim, so speed must be balanced against the risk inside.
- [pitfall] Rushing an arrest because a witness may slip away risks acting on incomplete evidence.

## same-act and same-victim ambiguity
- [heuristic] Hide a clue among objects of the same kind rather than in a secret place, where no one expects to look. When: when concealing evidence in a scene.
- [pitfall] The same act, such as a suicide attempt, can be read as a danger to manage or as a clue, depending on who observes it. When: When interpreting a suspect's self-harm. Why: Observers with different roles weigh the same act differently.
- [pitfall] Confusing 'same victim' with 'same culprit' is a central error, since a shared victim does not identify a shared culprit. When: Two cases involve the same person. Why: Shared circumstances are treated as proof of identity without support.
- [pitfall] Assuming all traces at a scene come from the same moment blocks the two-phase explanation and hides the real sequence of events.
- [pitfall] A letter may refer to an event that happened the day before it was written, so do not assume the event and the document share a date.

## scouting and surveillance
- [mechanism] A planner who scouts a location in advance creates evidence of intent, so reconnaissance can expose the planner as well as inform the act.
- [heuristic] Confused or scuffed prints suggest deliberate concealment, but the observer must judge whether the disturbance is careless or intended. When: Tracks are disordered or partly erased. Why: Disturbance can come from haste or from a deliberate attempt to hide movement.
- [procedure] 1) Send one observer forward to look through a window. 2) Keep the rest of the group waiting. 3) Have the observer report back to the group. When: when the group needs a close look without exposing everyone.
- [pitfall] A suspicious employer's penetrating gaze can unsettle an impostor and lower their confidence, breaking a prepared cover. When: An impostor faces direct questioning or inspection. Why: Nerves reduce the composure needed to keep a rehearsed story consistent.
- [fact] Scorching on fabric indicates that a shot was fired at close range.

## sound and sensory cues
- [heuristic] Build dread with repeated sensory cues such as heat, smell, pale light, and silence, so the player senses a threat before it is shown. When: Preparing a player for a danger that has not yet appeared. Why: Recurring sensations accumulate into an expectation of threat.
- [heuristic] Symptoms that ease when a subject is away and return on exposure point to a source inside the environment they left. When: Locating a recurring cause in a known environment.
- [pitfall] Relying on one sense can miss cues from another; combine what is heard, smelled and seen where possible.
- [fact] A hidden person can produce rapping or knocking sounds with a body part, such as a foot, from behind a concealing screen.
- [fact] Sound-based inference is unreliable when sounds are masked or many people arrive at once.

## story structure and summaries
- [model] Clue flow has three phases: front-loaded opening clues, a steady trickle during the main action, and a late cluster that turns the reader toward the resolution. When: Planning clue placement across a story. Why: Each phase serves a different job.
- [model] A trial-then-investigation mystery opens with the prosecution's case, then an amateur inquiry reverses it through a chain of false solutions, each supported by a real clue.
- [procedure] 1) Hook and premise, 0-3% of length. 2) False frame, 3-8%. 3) Complication, 8-25%. 4) False solution, 25-42%. 5) Reveal, 48-59%. 6) Crisis, 65-82%. 7) Aftermath, 88-98%. When: pacing a mystery across its full length. Why: Fixed phases keep the reveal in the middle third and the peak of danger late.
- [fact] This structure map divides a mystery story into setup, clues, suspicion, misdirect, pressure, oddities, reveal and resolution, with percentages marking their positions in the text.
- [fact] A mystery story can use a convenient suspect and a false theory, with the decisive clues placed in environmental details rather than human motives.

## surveillance and observation
- [rule] Keep findings quiet, especially from associates of a suspect, so no one is warned. When: When an investigation is still active. Why: Warning a suspect or their friends lets evidence be hidden or altered.
- [heuristic] Show planted clues, such as hidden messages, weapons or objects, openly before the reveal, so the later explanation feels fair in hindsight. When: Planting a hidden message, weapon or object that will matter later. Why: Visible but unremarked evidence makes the reveal feel fair and rewards attentive players when its role is revealed.
- [heuristic] Surfaces in prolonged contact with a person, such as a bed, are likely places for residue, so sample them most carefully. Why: Long contact transfers more material to the surface.
- [heuristic] Plant a decisive marker, such as a name marked on an item, in plain sight, where it reads as meaningless until the interpretation changes. When: Designing clues for a substitution reveal. Why: The clue is visible from the start, so its meaning comes from a later change in framework.
- [pitfall] A prolonged waiting period strains watchers, and small noises can mislead them. When: a trap requires a long wait. Why: fatigue and noise degrade observation.

## suspect motive
- [behavior] A suspect's private monologue can state motive directly, giving the player dramatic irony that the other characters do not share. When: A suspect is alone and reacting to a threat. Why: Private thought shows what the suspect hides from others.
- [behavior] When a suspect attacks a witness's reliability, the attack can expose a personal motive that the player can use later. When: A suspect responds to an accusation with personal insults. Why: Emotional attacks often reveal the attached stake behind the suspect's fear.
- [heuristic] A stated motive that seems too slight to explain the outcome suggests a deeper cause, such as an older grievance.
- [heuristic] Stack several suspects who each carry a real motive so that each accusation carries weight and the player keeps reconsidering. When: designing a mystery's suspect set. Why: Suspects with credible motives sustain doubt, while a single weak suspect is dismissed quickly.
- [heuristic] Give the reader a suspect's reasons and emotional state early, so a later reversal of the suspicion feels earned rather than arbitrary. Why: Established motive makes the reader's earlier judgment visible, so reversing it reads as a correction.

## suspicion and clustered deaths
- [mechanism] A crowd's prior expectation determines whether a genuine call for help is believed, so a real plea can be dismissed as a prank. When: A character signals real danger to a group that expects them to joke. Why: Expectations filter incoming evidence, so the group discounts what it has already categorized.
- [behavior] When witnesses die one after another, each death may look natural, but their accumulation makes players suspect a link. When: When several people who hold knowledge die in a short span. Why: A cluster of deaths tied to shared knowledge suggests deliberate silencing even if each death alone is explained.
- [rule] Concentrate plan-revealing details in a single cluster, with a late burst of specifics, so the audience can assemble the mechanism at once. When: a hidden method must be revealed. Why: a clustered set of clues makes the method legible.
- [heuristic] Stage a crowd moment such as a scream or alarm to force an identity into the open, rather than resolving it through private dialogue. When: The reveal needs to land at a set moment with several witnesses present. Why: A shared reaction makes the revelation public and hard to dismiss.
- [pitfall] Witness agreement supports an explanation but does not prove it; a group sharing one viewpoint can agree on a wrong account, adding little independent evidence. When: Presenting testimony as evidence, or several witnesses report the same event together. Why: Consensus can be shared error; shared conviction feels like verified fact.

## tentative conclusions and identification
- [rule] Treat a witness's hedged recognition as no identification, including when an identification weakens once the witness is asked whether they are certain. When: A witness hedges a recognition claim. Why: Hedged recognition gives no basis for singling out a person.
- [rule] Hold a theory tentatively and accept that partial correctness is possible; competing views may each capture part of the truth. When: Two explanations for the evidence conflict. Why: Each view may account for different clues, so both can be partly right.
- [rule] Label a reconstruction of events as a tentative hypothesis until evidence confirms it. When: Proposing how a crime was committed before proof exists. Why: Presenting a guess as a finding can mislead the investigation.
- [heuristic] State the limits of an expert's tentative opinion explicitly, such as being unable to tell which wound came first. Why: Unstated limits leave room for false certainty.
- [pitfall] Giving a precise date from a rough biological clue overstates what the evidence supports; state a range instead. When: Reporting exposure time from biological traces. Why: Such traces only bound the time approximately, and local conditions vary.

## terms and definitions
- [rule] Let a character state the terms of a bargain themselves, so the motive shows through the offer rather than through narration.
- [heuristic] Define abstract terms early in a dialogue and hold them fixed, since loosely used words drift in meaning over time. When: A conversation relies on abstract concepts that the answers depend on. Why: Drift in meaning makes replies from different points in the exchange hard to compare.
- [heuristic] A repeated numeral written larger each time suggests a code, but treat that reading as a hypothesis to test against other evidence. When: A repeated symbol appears in a final message. Why: Repetition invites a code reading that may be coincidence.
- [procedure] 1) Draw each boundary the grant describes, such as rivers, lines and widths. 2) Compare the drawn lines with each claim. 3) Locate where the claims overlap or conflict. When: a boundary dispute depends on grant wording. Why: Plotting the description shows where a conflict actually arises.
- [procedure] 1) Identify a phrase with more than one plausible sense. 2) Check each sense against verifiable facts such as membership and dated events. 3) Accept only the sense the facts support. When: An ambiguous claim about relationships or affiliations matters to the case. Why: Reading an ambiguous phrase only in the favoured sense leads to false conclusions.

## timestamped witness claims
- [rule] Store NPC and witness claims as timestamped statements so players can line up accounts, assemble a timeline, and spot agreements, contradictions, or unverifiable claims. When: Designing testimony or witness data for a game or timeline puzzle. Why: Timestamps let statements be compared automatically or by the player, and make contradictions findable.
- [rule] Anchor an account with precise clock times and durations between events, so readers can rebuild the order and pace of what happened. When: when readers must trust the sequence of events.
- [rule] Store NPC alibis as timestamped events that the player checks against a shared time window. When: designing suspect alibis.
- [rule] Provide a timestamped log or journal so the player can catch a false claim about when something happened. When: Designing clues that test a player's reasoning about timing. Why: Recorded times give the player a fixed reference to contradict claims.
- [fact] A timestamped check-in or arrival record brackets where a person must have been after a given event.

## trial and justice
- [heuristic] Track whether ordered official actions were carried out, since a later petition can reveal that a committee was never convened.
- [procedure] 1) Indict, naming the accused, charge and alleged harm. 2) Take the plea. 3) Swear a jury to decide on the evidence. 4) Adjourn if no agreement, keeping the accused in custody. 5) Seek written legal opinions on contested questions. 6) Reach a verdict. 7) Let a later court refuse to enforce it. 8) Allow appeal to a higher authority.
- [procedure] 1) Read the formal charge and take the accused's plea. 2) Hear the accusers' evidence. 3) Introduce related prior acts. 4) Hear the defence. 5) Deliver the verdict. When: when building a courtroom or case-file sequence.
- [procedure] 1) Identify who had authority to order each action. 2) Identify who only relayed or filtered complaints. 3) Check whether the record supports the favoritism charge. 4) Assign blame to the actor who actually shielded the suspect. When: a suspect seems exempt from scrutiny while others are pursued on the same grounds. Why: Blame lands on the wrong actor when intermediaries, not the senior figure, did the shielding.
- [tradeoff] Offering a suspect a trial with a not-guilty plea or a full confession with mercy trades a contested outcome for a surer, lighter one.

## unlocated threats and locations
- [rule] Do not treat a sound whose source cannot be located as proof of a route through a space.
- [heuristic] Keep a threat's source hard to pin down, for example a sound that seems to move from wall to floor, so the threat stays unlocated. When: At a moment of peril where the source should stay uncertain.
- [heuristic] Do not assume a hiding place when it is unknown, because the thief may have had more information than the investigator does. When: when reasoning about where stolen goods were hidden.
- [pitfall] Withholding a danger that the player cannot later perceive in some form makes the threat feel arbitrary. When: when a threat is hidden from the player. Why: A threat the player never gets evidence of cannot be felt as real.
- [fact] When the means of an apparent self-inflicted death cannot be found, that explanation is hard to prove, so the missing object decides between self-harm and murder. Why: The method must be located to support either explanation.

## will and inheritance clues
- [rule] Do not use a will as direct evidence of guilt or of what happened after death; it shows the testator's intent, circumstances and allies, not what a person did.
- [rule] Model a will or entail as a quest rule that the player learns through documents or conversation, revealing the heir and succession chain. When: designing inheritance mysteries. Why: Gradual discovery sustains the investigation.
- [pitfall] A will's pious wording can conceal the testator's real aims. Compare its stated intentions with the arrangements it actually makes. When: when reading a will as evidence. Why: Stated intentions may hide self-serving aims.
- [fact] A testator can redirect property by changing a will, so both the current heir's plans and the existing will determine who gains. When: assessing who will inherit. Why: A will can override the default succession.
- [fact] A will's detailed provisions reveal relationships and who was expected to provide what within a household.

## accusation thresholds
- [mechanism] A wrongful arrest of a bystander raises pressure without ending the investigation, because the real question stays open. When: mid-case, when an innocent suspect is detained. Why: the arrest raises the stakes while the actual culprit is still unknown.
- [rule] Accuse only after two or more independent verified clues converge, stating openly what remains unproven; one suggestive clue cannot close a case. When: designing a mystery quest; no single clue settles the matter. (x3)
- [rule] Accusing a respected figure without firm proof provokes outright rejection and may get the accuser dismissed as unbalanced; withhold until evidence can be shown. When: culprit is socially protected and early accusation would fail. Why: Without proof the accuser has no standing and the accusation is discredited. (x2)
- [rule] Do not act on or name a suspect before proof is secure; with a wary suspect and costly false move, early action warns them, and early naming risks false accusation. When: investigator has a theory but insufficient proof, or a match is still being tested. Why: premature action warns the suspect and loses the case. (x2)

## ancient lore and sorcery
- [rule] Apparition cannot prove guilt, since a deceiving agent may take an innocent person's shape; treat its accusation as a reason to investigate, e.g. questioning or examining the accused.
- [rule] Make an oracle's apparently impossible insight trace back to a visible human source, such as a note, a witness, or an observed tell, that the player can reconstruct. When: Designing a supernatural-versus-human puzzle or fortune-teller NPC. Why: A traceable source lets the player separate apparent magic from ordinary information.
- [pitfall] Authority drawn from ancient texts can stop officials from asking whether the alleged crime was possible at all.
- [fact] Ancient sorcery was not originally classed as morally evil; the devil-based interpretation developed later.

## biased written records
- [rule] Include a biased character's document with a note of its writer's involvement, so players can weigh its claims themselves. When: designing in-game documents.
- [heuristic] An official with a standing grudge, or who arrested the witness and wrote the record, can steer players toward the wrong suspect; test their conclusions against evidence. (x2)
- [procedure] 1) Write the journal entry from the author's stake and mood. 2) Tag it with the writer's stake. 3) Provide a second source the player can cross-check against it. When: An NPC with a grudge or personal interest writes a journal or quest log. Why: Tagging the stake teaches the player to discount the entry, and a second source lets them test it.
- [pitfall] Stakeholder records (diaries, published case records, accounts clearing or shielding others) shape what is included and omitted; confirm them independently. When: Relying on a diary, published case record, or witness record as evidence. Why: Self-regard, bias, or a held conclusion can shape even a detailed record toward its writer's aims. (x3)

## citation and paraphrase
- [rule] Check the reverse of a scrap, since printed or blank forms on it can reveal the paper's source. When: when a clue is a loose paper.
- [pitfall] A party's paraphrase of a document may not match what was written, and without the original text, disputes over wording stay unresolved. When: A written claim is being used as evidence. Why: Memory of a document's exact wording is often unreliable.
- [pitfall] Later writers who paraphrase a source without citing it hide their dependence, so check the texts themselves, not only the citation lists.
- [fact] Restating a document's import in one's own words is paraphrase, not quotation, and its fairness must be judged separately from the text's accuracy.

## clue coverage gaps
- [mechanism] A later disturbance of a covering can expose an earlier one, so the sequence of disturbances shows how an object was hidden and then found.
- [rule] Leave deliberate gaps in a route record for players to fill through observation and deduction, rather than supplying a complete log. When: Designing a character's movement or whereabouts as a clue. Why: Gaps invite players to reason about the missing parts.
- [heuristic] A gap in observer coverage at the critical moment is a place to investigate, not proof of guilt. Why: Gaps can arise from fog, cover or weak sightlines as well as wrongdoing.
- [pitfall] A covering can hide the moment an object was dropped, so track when the object was last seen.

## complete explanation traps
- [rule] A replacement explanation must account for every detail, including unexpected ones, not just reject the original supernatural reading. When: Replacing an improbable explanation with an ordinary one. Why: A rejection without a full alternative leaves unexplained facts open.
- [heuristic] Prefer the explanation that accounts for every clue, and check what a compelling theory fails to explain, since unexplained facts mislead investigators.
- [tradeoff] An explanation that answers every question can drain suspense, so leaving one question open can carry the story forward if more is needed. When: Writing the final reveal of a mystery. Why: Complete closure removes remaining tension.
- [pitfall] A neat chain of links can look complete while resting on an untested premise, and a hypothesis that fits every visible fact can still be wrong; distrust explanations that come too easily.

## convenient suspect traps
- [heuristic] The suspects that an accusing theory names are often the most convenient to blame, so they should be tested as possible decoys.
- [heuristic] A witness who switches sides at a convenient moment may be running a cover story, so check the timing and what they gain. When: A witness changes position and is then released or rewarded. Why: Benefits from a switch can reveal coordinated intent.
- [pitfall] Fixating on the most convenient culprit can absorb the whole investigation, hiding the real mechanism or skipping the real method behind the event.
- [pitfall] Accepting a convenient answer too early closes the question and loses the lead. When: a witness offers a neat explanation. Why: Neat answers often end inquiry before it is tested.

## convenient timing and tools
- [heuristic] Evidence or messages arriving exactly when they help may be staged; scrutinize undated or unstamped documents as possible plants and ask who benefits from each arrival. Why: documents that conveniently surface are unusual; timing that is too convenient may be staged.
- [heuristic] Ask whether the scene conveniently supplied tools used or tracks sit in a convenient spot, such as a lone damp patch; convenient setup can point to planning or staging.
- [pitfall] A convenient delay in calling outside authorities can serve investigators as much as a suspect, so weigh who gains from it.
- [pitfall] A convenient coincidence in timing invites scrutiny, so an alibi built on it must hold up against independent records. When: An alibi depends on an alarm or event arriving at a convenient moment. Why: Timing that suits the suspect too well draws suspicion.

## criminal networks and status
- [mechanism] Disputes across several arenas at once, such as records, shared grounds, land and boundaries, feed each other, so each challenge or reversal draws in more of the community.
- [heuristic] Treat a crime as a network: the person caught is often one link, and the one who ordered the act lies further along the chain.
- [heuristic] Compare testimony from witnesses of different status, so each account can be weighed against the others.
- [fact] Money obtained through a crime may be paid out if no crime has been formally charged.

## debris and location traces
- [heuristic] Loose debris lying beside a damaged spot shows that the damage is recent, because nobody has yet cleaned it away. When: When a damaged surface may have been made just before the scene was examined. Why: Debris is removed by dusting or handling, so its presence indicates little time has passed.
- [heuristic] Look for debris, such as mould knocked from soles, on hard surfaces where prints stop to find evidence of the route. When: prints end at a hard surface. Why: loose material is shed where the walker crossed.
- [heuristic] Debris landing on a high surface suggests the hand that caused it belonged to a taller person than the expected suspect. When: broken items scatter across a scene. Why: landing height depends on where the breaker stood.
- [heuristic] Debris type suggests a location: sawdust points to a carpenter's workshop, a dead leaf to a garden or common, a cobweb to a wine cellar or potting shed.

## disguise and hiding places
- [mechanism] A regular, unremarkable scene that hides a death suggests the killers disguised the cause, because a visible murder would have required a hidden grave. When: A death appears natural or routine. Why: Concealing a violent cause is more likely than hiding a normal one.
- [behavior] Matching voice and manner reinforce a costume-based disguise, making a substitute harder to detect in brief contact. When: when an impersonator speaks to a witness. Why: voice and manner add cues to the outfit.
- [heuristic] The relationship between a subject and a visitor, such as client, friend or lover, implies different likely places for a hidden object, so identify it early.
- [pitfall] A cover story repeated without any variation can seem rehearsed to a careful observer.

## disguise and undercover tracing
- [mechanism] A change of clothes in an empty place leaves no witnesses, so the change itself is hard to detect. When: A disguise is put on or removed where no one is present. Why: Without observers, nothing records the change.
- [heuristic] Plant a suspect's evasion or visible lie early to keep a spouse or associate under suspicion while the real suspect is developed. When: Writing a mystery where an obvious suspect must stay under suspicion for a time. Why: A visible lie gives the wrong suspect a reason to be watched, which buys time for the real suspect.
- [procedure] 1) Adopt a disguise that fits a community whose members talk freely among themselves. 2) Ask about a relevant subject that leads to the person who witnessed the target. 3) Gather the witness's description of the target's movements and appearance. When: Local knowledge is needed and the community speaks to outsiders on its own terms. Why: Insiders share information with those who appear to belong, while strangers are noticed.
- [pitfall] A disguise can be very small, such as a veil, a hat or a coat, and still be enough to fool witnesses. When: Assessing whether a suspect could have disguised themselves. Why: Minor changes often suffice because observers focus on whole appearance.

## disordered appearance
- [heuristic] Disordered or unfastened clothing supports a sudden change of purpose rather than a planned sequence.
- [heuristic] Check whether a person's clothing and equipment fit the stated purpose; a mismatch contradicts the account and becomes evidence. When: A stated motive or activity implies particular clothing or equipment. Why: People dressed for an activity usually match their attire to it.
- [heuristic] Clothing that is torn or badly fastened can show that someone else dressed or disturbed the wearer, possibly with clumsy hands.
- [tradeoff] Disordered rooms (clothes on floor, pockets out, open drawers) may show a hurried occupant search or panic, or a search by someone else; do not assume the occupant caused it.

## endorsement and reliability
- [behavior] Endorsement by respected authorities can lend a spreading belief credibility and remove remaining doubt, since people defer to authority when judging unfamiliar claims. When: when respected figures publicly support a claim or a crowd still has reservations. Why: people defer to the judgement of respected figures when judging unfamiliar charges.
- [rule] Trace each endorsement to its source and ask what the endorser actually saw; a secondhand vouch may say nothing about the conduct in question. When: A suspect's character is argued from third-party endorsements.
- [pitfall] Endorsement, approval or praise reflects an authority's standing, not verified accuracy; judge the claim itself rather than treating endorsement as evidence. When: when a reference text or source is trusted because of endorsements or praise. Why: approval reflects status and authority rather than checked facts.
- [pitfall] Accepting a single reference without seeing the referee or the institution makes the whole judgment depend on one unverified source. Why: A single source can be wrong, biased, or unavailable.

## explanation acceptance and overreach
- [mechanism] Offering a rational explanation, then letting the protagonist's past or the final scene unsettle it, keeps the reader from ever fully settling on one account.
- [heuristic] Treat a witness's proposed explanation as partly true, accepting it for the symptoms it covers and rejecting it for the rest. When: when a witness blames a mundane cause for a whole set of symptoms. Why: Most explanations cover some effects but not all.
- [pitfall] Explaining most anomalies or one mechanical event does not solve the whole case. Leftover unexplained items must be stated plainly, not hidden.
- [pitfall] A hoax can explain some effects while others remain unexplained, so one solution does not close the whole mystery. When: When one trick is found in a multi-effect haunting. Why: Some effects can have independent causes.

## false confessions and accusations
- [behavior] When an accusation and its retraction are separated by long time gaps, players tend to forget the first claim by the time the retraction arrives. When: events spread over years within a story. Why: the early claim fades before the correction is shown.
- [heuristic] A cleared suspect's false confession can give readers a brief false resolution; reveal a second layer that undercuts it so the mystery stays open. When: A late-act confession seems to close the case. Why: Players readily accept confessions, so a later reveal can exploit that trust.
- [tradeoff] A false confession by a proxy suspect tests the protagonist's nerve, but a doubting investigator must keep the threat alive or the pressure dissolves. When: when an innocent person confesses to the crime. Why: The doubt keeps the protagonist in danger; without it the false solution ends the pressure.
- [pitfall] A group confession made together under pressure is not proof of group guilt, and a confession that matches the threat exactly is a warning sign. When: When evaluating a confession obtained under pressure. Why: Pressure can produce false, uniform admissions that fit the threat rather than the facts.

## investigation loops and rhythm
- [heuristic] An apparent delay or hesitation by a plotter often has a risk-based cause, so ask what the actor would find safest. When: A gap in a plotter's behavior looks odd. Why: Careful actors avoid unnecessary risk, so waiting usually has a reason.
- [heuristic] Repeated passes of a figure across the same frame build rhythm; place the clue on the final pass. When: staging a recognition. Why: the rhythm primes attention for the reveal.
- [pitfall] A road's course may have changed, so deeds written for the old course can mislead a reader using the current route. When: Interpreting a deed that refers to a road. Why: Old descriptions no longer fit a road that has been rerouted.
- [pitfall] Ritual acts that look like investigation, such as burning animal parts, produce no evidence. When: A ritual is used to identify a culprit. Why: The act looks rigorous but tests nothing.

## investigator referrals and recusal
- [behavior] Official investigators often withhold information from outside parties, treating them as interlopers, so outsiders have limited access to the case. When: A non-official character seeks details of an ongoing investigation. Why: Authorities control who learns what to protect their process.
- [heuristic] Let each interview name the next source, so one witness leads to another who holds further evidence. When: Tracing a trail of witnesses.
- [heuristic] A local body unsure of its authority over a serious case should refer it to a higher court rather than decide it alone.
- [tradeoff] Stepping away from a conflicted case protects fairness but may look like avoidance; staying on is defensible only after honest self-examination and external checks. When: a conflicted investigator is deciding whether to continue. Why: each option trades perceived integrity against risk of bias.

## late testimony and tests
- [mechanism] A targeted lab analysis for an unconsidered substance can overturn a settled explanation and change the meaning of the whole case. When: A natural cause is accepted but circumstances remain unexplained. Why: A specific test can reveal a hidden cause that earlier evidence missed.
- [rule] Let a non-player character remember new details after a trigger, but only if the detail is consistent with recorded events the player can check. When: Designing NPC memory reveals. Why: Checkable consistency keeps new recollections fair and meaningful.
- [heuristic] Scrutinize testimony given long after events, especially under custody or mainly to sway an audience, by checking independent corroboration before using it as proof. When: A witness's account changes, first appears after a long delay, or is admitted mainly to persuade. Why: Late recall can be sincere yet unreliable; time and persuasive intent distort memory, and corroboration separates reliable accounts from distorted ones. (x2)
- [pitfall] Key test questions are often asked too late; ask questions that could eliminate hypotheses early.

## legal records and citations
- [rule] Present a will as a readable in-world document so players can compare each beneficiary's stake themselves. When: Designing estate or inheritance story content. Why: Players then reason about motive from the terms rather than from a summary.
- [rule] Let players present evidence to an in-game council whose verdict depends on the quality of the rebuttal they offer. Why: the outcome then rewards argument and evidence.
- [rule] Let an NPC justify a decision by citing in-world laws, and let the player check whether each cited law actually applies to the case.
- [rule] Let a faction publish its own ledger or proclamation that shifts reputation, and let players find a rival's contradicting entry.

## local source advantage
- [rule] When a case depends on local memory, ask who worked longest alongside the people involved, since long-serving locals often hold the best history. When: when reconstructing a community's past.
- [heuristic] Let a local character who knows the terrain supply a fact about hidden features, which can rule out routes or explain how an event happened.
- [heuristic] Local sources such as a tavern or village often yield more useful detail than distant inquiries made elsewhere. When: gathering information about a community. Why: local talk gathers what the whole neighbourhood knows.
- [pitfall] Local sources often misremember names and histories, and a claim repeated many times is not thereby confirmed. When: when relying on community gossip for identities or backgrounds. Why: Repetition spreads errors just as easily as it spreads truth.

## missing npc knowledge
- [rule] Let a note left by a missing NPC, delivered to the right faction, explain a disappearance and give players a motive thread. When: designing NPC disappearances.
- [rule] Scatter fragments such as a letter, a debt entry, or a later reference so players can reconstruct a missing character's last known location. When: Designing a missing-person mystery. Why: Players can only deduce a location from clues they can assemble themselves.
- [heuristic] Missing knowledge is evidence: a forger often knows a name but not internal details, so gaps in a writer's knowledge can expose a fake.
- [pitfall] A missing acknowledgment of receipt leaves a gap in the paper trail that a careful checker will notice and question. Why: Gaps in a chain of custody invite doubt about the whole transfer.

## motive and secrets
- [behavior] A person may frankly state a self-interested motive, and this candor can be a performance that must be checked against what the person actually does. When: When a witness volunteers reasons for their actions. Why: Frankness about motive does not guarantee honesty, so behavior is the test.
- [procedure] 1) Date each diary entry and letter. 2) Reveal them in date order. 3) Let the player see motive build from a long gap, a sudden change, then a shift in feeling. When: Presenting a sequence of documents to the player. Why: Chronological order shows cause and effect in the subject's own voice.
- [pitfall] A secret that depends on a holder's false belief collapses once that belief is corrected, and delay from missing information can look like deliberate withholding. When: Designing secrets supported by a character's mistaken belief or an information gap. Why: Correction removes the secret's basis, and unclear causes make players misread intent.
- [fact] A motive a suspect openly admits, such as a planned legal action, should be recorded even when the suspect denies intent to harm. When: when a suspect admits a grievance but denies violence. Why: An admitted motive is evidence regardless of the denial.

## over-length and fragmentation
- [pitfall] Logging every day produces a record so long that the important signal is buried.
- [pitfall] Interrupting a narrative too often can drop the context that later explains the key point.
- [pitfall] A withheld disclosure that stretches too long reads as evasion, especially when the audience needs the information to follow the scene. When: When a disclosure is delayed across several scenes. Why: Extended withholding feels manipulative.
- [pitfall] Excessive subdivision fragments tension and hides links between parallel events, and can overwhelm readers the way endless numbered headings do.

## perishable evidence and timelines
