- [mechanism] A disturbed scene that persists, such as a pulled drawer or a displaced book, signals a prior intruder and can tie an object's state to a character's habits. When: Designing rooms that record past visits. Why: Lasting disturbance gives players evidence of who was present.
- [rule] Model perishable evidence, such as a briefly speaking witness or an item whose condition records time since placement or delivery, to create time pressure and serve as a clock.
- [procedure] 1) Find the interval when the key person was away from the victim. 2) Find when the victim was next seen or re-entered. 3) Test which phase fits inside those bounds.
- [fact] Early boundary points were often removable or perishable objects, such as marked trees and heaps of stones, so original surveys of such boundaries frequently do not survive.

## premeditation evidence
- [rule] Make a prepared replacement or tool a visible sign of premeditation, so the player can read a planned act from the scene. When: Designing a planned crime or action. Why: Players reason from visible preparation.
- [heuristic] Judge whether a crime was planned by gathering several arrangements, such as a watched target, a waiting substitute or a carried tool; they strengthen the case when they point the same way. When: a crime shows signs of setup. Why: several independent preparations are harder to explain innocently than one.
- [heuristic] Premeditation shows as purchases that each serve one purpose; ordinary items look harmless alone but become suspicious when combined, so check each item's probable use. When: when a suspect bought items before an act.
- [procedure] 1) Confirm the item was present and is now absent with no substitute left. 2) If the culprit planned the removal, expect a replacement or altered contents. 3) If neither is found, infer improvisation. When: An unexplained gap is found at a scene. Why: Planning usually leaves preparations behind.

## premise reasoning checks
- [mechanism] Overturning a story's central premise, such as a belief about a death, changes the whole motive, so earlier accounts built on that premise must be re-examined in full. When: a twist reverses the premise behind a character's account. Why: the earlier account rested on the false premise.
- [heuristic] Check a theory's premises against relevant records and physical facts before building on it; one contradicting record or medical or positional detail can collapse the whole theory. Why: Records can contradict the premise outright.
- [procedure] 1) Name each assumption the conclusion depends on; mark observed premises and label the rest provisional, granted only for the argument. 2) Test every unmarked premise before accepting it by asking what evidence or what follows if it is false. 3) Use conclusions as premises for the next step, keeping the chain visible to expose the weakest step. When: When several facts point in different directions or a case has closed on untested assumptions. Why: Unverified premises can carry a wrong conclusion.
- [pitfall] A neat argument built on a mistaken premise weakens once the premise is corrected, however sound its logic seems. Why: the conclusion depends on the premise, not on the reasoning alone.

## public trial and verdicts
- [mechanism] A repeated public hearing can turn a private lapse into a judgment the whole group must witness and vote on, so the procedure itself becomes pressure.
- [heuristic] A public hearing can settle its verdict through who speaks to whom and who pressures whom, not only through the evidence presented. When: designing a public meeting or trial scene.
- [tradeoff] A public trial may expose innocent people and their names, while a negotiated release trades punishment for recovered goods and certainty that the matter ends. When: a public case would harm innocent people.
- [fact] A mystery can open with an arrest for murder and then run a long investigation in which confessions, suspects and documents keep shifting. When: structuring a mystery that begins with an accused suspect. Why: Opening on an arrest sets a clear stake that the investigation must resolve.

## remote checks and orders
- [mechanism] A trap triggered through an instruction given to a third party leaves the culprit without control over the outcome, so suspense rises while the result is reported only from outside. When: A scene needs a delayed payoff where the outcome is uncertain to the schemer. Why: Reliance on others' compliance and delayed news keeps the schemer waiting without knowing the result.
- [mechanism] Issuing arrest orders from a distant authority, rather than the local one, prevents the target from being warned in advance.
- [rule] Test a claimed identity through a distant office, which confirms it without alerting locals. When: a story needs checking discreetly. Why: Remote confirmation avoids warning the people involved.
- [fact] A query naming one person to a remote contact can return a background report covering family, travel, correspondence and property.

## search null results
- [behavior] When a thorough search of a closed area finds nothing, but contrary evidence remains, the missing intruder becomes a puzzle in its own right. When: A locked-room style search returns no results despite signs of a presence. Why: A failed search contradicts the evidence, so the premise itself is questioned.
- [rule] Record null results, such as searches or background checks that find nothing, as information rather than ignoring them. Why: A null result is still information and can be reconsidered later.
- [rule] When no candidate's marks match, widen the search, since a negative result only excludes those already checked. When: A comparison yields no match against the current suspect pool. Why: Exclusion does not identify the culprit.
- [pitfall] A failed match or identification does not prove innocence or guilt, since the person may be absent from the collection or unseen by witnesses. When: Interpreting a lineup, witness check, or database comparison where no match is found. Why: Witnesses may not have seen the person or the timing may be wrong; absence from a database is not non-involvement. (x2)

## shooter and shot reconstruction
- [procedure] 1) Fix the victim's posture and facing from observed facts. 2) Work out the single spot from which the attack could have been made. 3) Mark that spot on the scene. 4) Test each route and exit against the facts. 5) Note items that are missing. When: a body's posture or furniture constrains where an attacker could stand.
- [procedure] 1) Count the empty chambers or missing cartridges in a dropped weapon. 2) Treat the count as the number of shots fired. 3) Do not treat the count as proof that any shot hit. When: A weapon is recovered at a scene with some cartridges missing. Why: Missing cartridges show the weapon was discharged, but not whether the discharges struck anything.
- [metric] Natural shooting posture bounds estimated shooter height, producing a range rather than a single figure.
- [fact] Missing powder marks on clothing suggest a shot was fired from a distance. When: examining a gunshot victim's clothing. Why: Powder residue travels only a short distance from the muzzle.

## silence in records
- [rule] Silently log harmless-seeming dialogue questions so a later clue can be checked against what the NPC said.
- [heuristic] A routine register that is brief and never mentions an event can itself be evidence, when compared with its coverage of other events.
- [pitfall] Silence in an official record does not prove that nothing happened.
- [fact] Silence in a legal record, such as an unanswered petition, shows that the request was not weighed by the court. When: when reviewing how a court handled requests. Why: omissions in the record reveal gaps in the process.

## site map and scene
- [rule] Meet where observers' sightlines do not reach, such as a third party's rooms reached by a separate route. When: a covert meeting must avoid being observed. Why: A watcher can only report what falls within their line of sight.
- [procedure] 1) Check the whole space, including books, cupboards, boxes and clothing pockets. 2) Note which places were disturbed. 3) Use the pattern to map how far the search went.
- [pitfall] Maps show layout but not ground traces, may be outdated or incomplete, and modern ones may misrepresent period routes. A map cannot replace a site inspection. When: when relying on a map, especially to infer a historical route. (x2)
- [fact] A memorial is placed for visibility or convenience, so it can stand near an event without marking its exact location. When: A marker is offered as the site of a death or burial. Why: Placement follows practical factors, not necessarily the precise spot.

## skill mechanics
- [rule] Let a skilled culprit leave a few traces for the investigator to find, since a flawless act removes the tension of the investigation. When: when writing a clever antagonist's crime. Why: Players need something to test in order to feel the challenge.
- [heuristic] A skill that few people can perform narrows the set of likely owners of a trace to a small group.
- [heuristic] A person's abilities, such as speaking a language, can reveal where they have lived or traveled. When: Deciding who came from where in a story. Why: Acquired skills reflect past experience.
- [pitfall] A list of skills, even deep ones, rarely reveals a single unifying role. The designer must supply the purpose that ties the skills together. When: when a character's skills seem to have no common calling. Why: Skills alone do not imply one role.

## stale information
- [mechanism] An attacker acting on stale information may strike the wrong person after a substitution, revealing that the change went unnoticed.
- [rule] Use an old dispute as a red herring that looks like a motive but is cleared by a later timeline. When: Designing suspects and clues. Why: Players test motives against when events actually happened.
- [pitfall] A plan built on out-of-date information can fail even when executed flawlessly, because the target may have moved. When: An attack depends on a target's location or routine. Why: Execution quality cannot compensate for a premise that is no longer true.
- [pitfall] Letting a theory that has been cleared keep its place in the case distorts later reasoning.

## stated knowledge
- [rule] State a plausible wrong theory openly, so attentive players can later compare it with the true account and find where it failed. Why: a visible wrong theory rewards careful reasoning rather than surprising the player.
- [rule] Have characters state the limits of what they know, such as having a strong idea but no proof. This keeps their reasoning credible. When: A character offers a theory without full evidence. Why: Acknowledged uncertainty makes a character more believable.
- [heuristic] Ask by stating what you already know, rather than a yes-or-no question, so the suspect must answer or reveal a lie, even if the claim cannot be checked. When: When a suspect is likely to deny being present or involved, and the investigator can afford to be wrong about the stated knowledge. Why: A direct yes-or-no question invites an easy denial, while a stated claim presses the suspect to respond.
- [heuristic] Weigh a suspect's spoken accounts of their inner state against their observed behavior, since self-reports are often unreliable. When: when a character describes their own feelings or condition. Why: Spoken claims about one's state can be false, while behavior is observed directly.

## suspense
- [mechanism] Suspense grows as repeated setbacks, partial results and small disturbances delay a payoff, including a pursuer's repeated failures and a long gap between a wrong and its revenge. When: A reveal must carry weight and the audience needs to feel the wait. Why: Each false alarm or partial find keeps the expected payoff pending while anticipation builds.
- [mechanism] Suspense grows when a stretch of uncertain waiting is followed by a sudden escalation, so the next event lands harder. When: pacing a sequence of events. Why: The wait raises expectation, and the escalation then feels sharper against it.
- [behavior] Delaying the moment of looking, by hiding the face and fixing attention elsewhere first, builds suspense before a reveal.
- [rule] Each stretch of waiting must include new signals, such as a sound or movement, so the build does not stall. When: a sequence built on patience. Why: a wait without change stalls the build.

## suspense from withheld answers
- [mechanism] Withholding the nature of a crime while showing its effects on people builds suspense, because the audience knows something terrible happened and waits for the reveal. When: The reveal would be spoiled by early disclosure but the consequences are already visible. Why: Unresolved consequences create pressure that drives attention toward the hidden act.
- [mechanism] A decision the character cannot make, such as whether to leave, raises tension, and changes in habits such as sneaking or hesitating signal rising fear. When: building suspense through a constrained choice. Why: an unresolved choice keeps pressure rising without a visible threat.
- [heuristic] Withholding information a character holds sustains suspense when the audience already has the clues needed for the reveal or the hidden purpose is disclosed in time. When: A character withholds a known solution or knows more than the audience while building toward a reveal. Why: Visible groundwork lets the audience anticipate the reveal; withheld knowledge sustains tension while the eventual disclosure rewards attention. (x2)
- [heuristic] Withholding a threatening figure's face keeps the audience's curiosity alive until the reveal. When: when a threat is shown before its identity is known. Why: The unresolved feature invites the audience to speculate.

## suspicion follows ties
- [behavior] Suspicion in a community tends to follow family ties, shared land and old quarrels more than any act the accused was shown to have done. When: a community decides who to blame or distrust. Why: Existing ties supply ready explanations for blame.
- [behavior] When a person has open quarrels and threats and unrelated misfortune follows, observers tend to read the misfortune as malice caused by that person. When: a community linking a person to local losses. Why: recent hostility is taken as the cause of later harm.
- [heuristic] When the threat is inside a trusted household, suspicion usually moves from outsiders to family members after a physical test exposes the insider. When: Designing the progression of suspicion in a closed-circle mystery. Why: Outsiders are the default suspects, so the insider is revealed only after a test shows them to be the actual threat.
- [pitfall] Suspicion by association assigns guilt because of a relative's guilt, but kinship alone is weak evidence of accomplice intent: relatives share household access, not necessarily intent.

## suspicion meter
- [model] Give each suspect a gain tied to a fixed event, such as an inheritance or a deadline, so suspicion shifts along each gain line as the story unfolds. When: when several characters could plausibly be guilty. Why: a clear motive makes a character a plausible suspect at each stage.
- [mechanism] A suspicion value can rise with each clue or rumour and fall when the player supplies an innocent reading of an item. When: building a system that tracks how suspicious a suspect appears. Why: Letting players reduce suspicion through explanation keeps evidence open to interpretation.
- [mechanism] An NPC suspicion meter rises when the player reveals knowledge the NPC believes was private, so exposing hidden information makes the NPC defensive.
- [pitfall] Too many false alarms make the audience stop reacting to real threats.

## suspicion versus proof
- [behavior] A character can hold suspicions without confirmed knowledge, and the two should be kept distinct when tracking what each person knows. When: Tracking characters' beliefs about a hidden event. Why: Suspicion is not proof, so treating it as fact misstates what the character can act on.
- [rule] Distinguish suspicion from proof; do not charge or accuse on suspicion, opportunity, or motive alone. When: When a convergence of clues points to a suspect but no decisive fact exists. Why: Accusing too early risks losing the case if the suspicion is wrong.
- [heuristic] A witness who agrees too quickly may be performing rather than telling the truth, so the agreement should be re-examined. When: A witness immediately accepts a claim that favours them. Why: Immediate, convenient agreement can hide a motive.
- [heuristic] A clue that seems to implicate someone too neatly may instead be the strongest evidence of their innocence, so check the mechanism's constraints first. When: Evaluating a clue whose timing or content looks incriminating. Why: Convenient fit can be a sign of staging or of a flawed inference rather than guilt.

## sympathy distorting testimony
- [heuristic] Balance a witness's emotional account against what the witness actually saw, because sympathy can distort reporting. When: Evaluating testimony from a biased or attached witness.
- [procedure] 1) Have a colleague watch for loss of focus in the sympathetic investigator. 2) Warn when personal engagement starts to affect judgment. 3) Keep the team's distance from the witness. When: A witness is vulnerable and the team risks losing objectivity. Why: An outside observer can notice bias that the involved person cannot see.
- [pitfall] Audience sympathy and appealing stories can settle a verdict over complex evidence, because audiences fill gaps with the most natural story. When: A case is presented with emotional framing or an emotionally appealing explanation. Why: Emotionally satisfying stories are accepted over complex evidence.
- [pitfall] Sympathy from listeners, including for a grieving witness, can make a witness's account seem more credible than the evidence supports. When: Evaluating testimony that reveals a hidden personal matter. Why: Emotional reaction can make a witness seem more credible than the evidence supports.

## tell cross-checking
- [behavior] Overly casual indifference that follows a reaction can be a cover for the first response and is worth noting. When: A suspect's calm seems forced right after a visible reaction. Why: Overacting calm is an attempt to conceal the earlier reaction.
- [rule] Record each answer and each reaction in a journal so the player can use the accumulated pattern to narrow a secret. When: Designing a dialogue puzzle that uses yes or no questioning. Why: A written record lets the player follow the pattern of answers and tells.
- [heuristic] Cross-check guarded speech against involuntary signs, since a mismatch between calm words and a flushed or fidgeting body is a usable clue. When: A suspect's words and physical cues disagree. Why: The contradiction points to agitation the words conceal.
- [pitfall] A single bodily tell is weak evidence, since fear, shame or privacy can cause it; confirm it with a second source, such as a mirror or another witness, before acting. When: When a witness's nervousness or a suspicious tell is interpreted as guilt. Why: Fear, shame or privacy can produce the same signs as concealment.

## typewriter and typed evidence
- [heuristic] Each typewriter has individual defects such as a chipped letter, misaligned character or uneven shape; compare typed letters for matching defects, which point to one machine. Why: Wear and damage are unique to each machine.
- [procedure] 1) Classify each NPC answer as denial, partial admission or reframed admission. 2) Weight the type by the NPC's experience. 3) Use the weighting as one signal, not as proof. When: Designing NPC interrogation responses.
- [pitfall] Assuming who physically produced a document can hide the person who supplied the knowledge or tools used to make it.
- [fact] A typeface identifies a machine model, but many machines share that model, so a typeface match alone is weak evidence about who used the machine. Why: the model is widely used across offices.

## uncanny event explanation
- [mechanism] A supernatural claim that gives concrete, checkable details and is later confirmed by independent news makes the audience carry the claim forward on trust until the match arrives. When: A story presents an unverifiable supernatural source whose details can be tested later. Why: Withholding verification keeps the claim in play, and a dated, timed match then resolves the doubt.
- [rule] Let supernatural language describe a character's mind while actions are explained by ordinary means. When: writing horror-tinged narration or dialogue. Why: it keeps the atmosphere while grounding events in plausible causes.
- [heuristic] Before accepting an uncanny explanation, list ordinary causes, including a non-human creature used by a person, and check which fit every physical trace. When: When an event seems supernatural or impossible. Why: Most apparent uncanny events have ordinary causes visible in the physical traces.
- [tradeoff] Keep an unexplained event open rather than assuming it is ordinary; but when resolving a supernatural mystery, leaving the uncanny unexplained or explaining it without trace support frustrates players. When: A sound or event has no confirmed source; or when resolving a supernatural mystery. Why: Presenting an open question as settled removes its tension and misinforms the reader; players need answers the evidence can support.

## unexplained absences
- [mechanism] Suspicion grows with each day that passes without a sighting of the missing person after their last confirmed appearance. When: When a person disappears and no further sightings occur. Why: The absence of reports becomes more significant as time passes.
- [rule] Keep an unexplained absence, such as a missing item or witness, as an open thread and return to it; unresolved absences frustrate rather than engage the audience. When: a story or investigation introduces an unexplained absence. Why: unresolved clues that vanish make a mystery feel careless.
- [heuristic] An unexplained absence, such as a character with no stated destination or a trip during an evening, creates a gap the timeline must account for and check before accepting. When: Tracking character positions across a timeline. Why: Unexplained absence leaves a window where events can be hidden.
- [pitfall] An unexplained absence invites suspicion toward whoever could have used it, so every gap should be accounted for or revisited. When: Scenes contain time gaps between suspects. Why: Readers and players assume unaccounted time hides something.

## weather mood and setting
- [mechanism] Bad weather moves a crowd into fewer indoor venues, concentrating listeners and changing who hears what.
- [mechanism] Weather cues such as still air or unexplained movement in leaves warn that a storm or turning point is coming before it arrives. When: Building suspense before a reveal or turning point. Why: Audiences read environmental signs as predictions and feel tension while waiting.
- [rule] A windowless room with one thick door cuts off outside help and muffles violence, so it suits a final confrontation. When: Staging a climactic confrontation. Why: Isolation removes rescue and hides noise, raising the stakes of the scene.
- [heuristic] Let weather echo a character's emotional state, so storms and debris outside mirror disorder inside.

## young and worried witnesses
- [behavior] An adult may dismiss a child's detailed report at first, then reconsider when pressed to check the scene herself. When: When an adult hears an unusual report from a child. Why: Adults may resist disturbing claims until they test them directly.
- [heuristic] A young or frightened witness's identification can be challenged easily, so it should be corroborated by other evidence before it carries weight. When: The sole identifying witness is a child or highly distressed. Why: Fear and limited understanding make recall vulnerable to challenge.
- [pitfall] Companions' waiting or worry does not independently confirm where a person was, since it reflects expectation rather than observation.
- [pitfall] Assuming a claim is supernatural because the witness was too young to remember the event hides the likelier channel, such as someone who passed it on.

## canvassing and witness sourcing
- [procedure] 1) Obtain names and addresses of every operator in the stated area. 2) Visit each establishment in turn. 3) Note closed yards and refusals to show records. When: Records of several operators must be checked for one event.
- [pitfall] Wide canvassing or paid rewards draw in suggestible witnesses who describe whatever resembles the picture they were shown. When: circulating a picture to find witnesses. Why: Witnesses want to match what the investigator seeks.
- [pitfall] Checking addresses by pretext is slow; wrong names and moved households waste many checks.

## clue setup and payoff
- [heuristic] Defer a choice's outcome by hinting that events would have gone differently had another choice been made. When: A choice's consequences should stay open for now. Why: Hinting at alternatives keeps the audience uncertain.
- [heuristic] Plant identity and staged-death clues across the middle of the case, then pay them off together in a short cluster so players can reassemble them. When: A mystery whose solution depends on several earlier clues. Why: Scattered payoffs are easily missed, while a clustered reveal lets earlier clues connect.
- [heuristic] Plant an object the player dismisses early, then reveal its link to the victim at the climax, so it reads as something the dead person already knew.

## complete accounting checks
- [rule] A two-phase explanation must account for every injury, including injuries the victim concealed, before it is accepted.
- [heuristic] Exit elimination is only sound when the list of openings is complete; an unrecorded opening can break the reasoning. When: The building has openings that may not be in the records. Why: Ruling out only recorded exits leaves the unrecorded one open.
- [procedure] 1) Ask the witness for a complete account of who was present. 2) Press on each gap. 3) Follow each partial answer with a targeted question.

## descriptive imagery and style
- [heuristic] Specific details such as colour, texture and shape are more useful for identification than general terms, since general terms cannot be checked against a suspect. When: writing or reading a physical description used for identification.
- [pitfall] Overusing a symbol such as weather, or heavily emphasising a plant, reads as a signal to the audience and removes the surprise of the later payoff. Why: Obvious emphasis tells the audience what matters too early.
- [pitfall] Heavy vocabulary can bury the point a message must make, so the formal tone may obscure the accusation. When: when writing an accusatory document. Why: Stiff phrasing competes with the content for the reader's attention.

## distributed knowledge
- [behavior] Parties to one incident often describe it differently, so an event one side calls rough play may be read by the other as an attack. When: when two people describe the same event. Why: each party frames the event by its own stake in it.
- [behavior] Characters given different versions of a secret can each reveal only their own partial account, so an investigator must track who was told what. When: A secret is held by several characters and each is told a different version. Why: Each character's knowledge limits what they can reveal, and selective accounts can be mistaken for the whole truth.
- [heuristic] Spread facts across NPC witnesses or objects, each holding a different timeline part with recognition cues, so players must reconcile accounts; empty containers count as independent evidence. When: designing witness testimony and clues in a mystery. Why: partial knowledge requires cross-checking, which rewards deduction and makes objects carry testimony. (x2)

## dramatic irony
- [mechanism] When the audience knows what a character does not, suspense comes from the gap between knowledge and power: the character acts in ignorance or cannot respond. When: The audience must learn information the protagonist cannot share or act on; the reveal should drive tension rather than surprise. Why: Knowledge without power drives suspense; knowledge gaps convert the character's ordinary actions into tense ones.
- [mechanism] A clue that characters dismiss, such as a report called a joke, stays available to the audience and creates dramatic irony that rewards attentive players.
- [heuristic] When the audience knows more than an authority figure, dramatic irony builds, but its emotional payoff depends on showing the cost of the gap. When: when the player knows a truth that an ally does not. Why: Tension from the gap lands only when its consequences are shown.

## fallback arrangements
- [rule] When a witness will not volunteer more, turn to other sources and physical evidence instead of pressing harder.
- [heuristic] Confederates may be given backup instructions, such as fleeing to a prearranged spot if the main party fails to return by a set time, which reveals a planned contingency. Why: Contingency arrangements indicate that the plan anticipated its own failure.
- [heuristic] Keep rejected candidates as fallback objectives, since a rejected option may still matter later.

## hereditary and inherited clues
- [mechanism] An inherited grievance deepens when one side blocks a shared resource while the other side grows poorer and keeps asking. When: A feud spans generations over a shared asset. Why: Repeated refusal and worsening hardship keep the dispute alive.
- [pitfall] When an investigator's reasoning rests on a mistaken identity, every later inference inherits the error and must be rechecked. When: An early identification shapes later deductions. Why: Errors in a foundational premise propagate through the whole chain of reasoning.
- [fact] Family history or hereditary risk is not proof of any act; an inherited tendency may or may not appear and cannot establish what a person has done or is doing. When: Using inheritance to explain or prove behavior. Why: Inherited traits do not establish present or past conduct; a tendency is a possibility, not a demonstration.

## lesser criminal and suspect routes
- [heuristic] Seek admission of a lesser offence before a greater one, since a suspect who denies the serious crime may still admit the smaller one. When: a suspect is accused of several crimes. Why: smaller admissions are easier to obtain.
- [heuristic] Pressure a lesser informant with arrest threats and reminders of past offences, then offer a choice of cooperation. When: a witness has partial knowledge and something to lose.
- [tradeoff] Pursue a minor culprit for a small provable offence to unlock the main investigation, or leave them unpursued to reach the figure behind them; choose by whether they lead upward. When: a small-time accomplice is involved in a larger scheme. Why: Detaining or exposing the lesser culprit opens the main case, while leaving them free may lead to the figure at the top.

## limited viewpoint suspense
- [mechanism] Restricting what a character can see keeps destination and outcome hidden, so the character must infer the situation from sound, motion and fragments of sight. When: a sequence where the reveal of place or identity matters. Why: inference from partial cues builds suspense.
- [rule] Use a limited viewpoint when the reveal depends on facts the observer could not know, but never hide clues the observer would reasonably have seen. When: Writing a narrator with restricted knowledge. Why: Hidden obvious clues make the reveal feel cheated.
- [pitfall] A witness reports only what they could see from their position; looking up a stairwell gives a limited view, so coverage must be checked.

## long-running secret
- [mechanism] Anonymous summons and recurring symbols keep a hidden history alive until a confession explains it.
- [rule] Plant an old feud or past crime that the present suspect inherits, adding a second story layer behind the immediate case.
- [heuristic] Use a delayed-disclosure secret when it must stay hidden across many scenes while the character's inner conflict builds.

## midpoint reversals and false solutions
- [mechanism] A midpoint false solution, in which the apparent threat dies or flees, convinces the audience the case is closed and raises the impact of the later reversal. When: pacing a mystery's middle act. Why: Relief from a false ending makes the later reversal hit harder.
- [rule] Let the investigator's own theory be confidently wrong at the midpoint, sending the story in a new direction.
- [heuristic] Use an attack on the investigator at the midpoint to raise stakes without resolving the central mystery. When: Planning the middle act of a mystery. Why: A threat to the protagonist raises tension and keeps the mystery moving.

## money trail tracing
- [heuristic] Trace unexplained withdrawals and large payments to infer a motive and who was being paid, then rank suspects by their ability to pay or need for money. When: investigating who had a motive for a crime. Why: Money movements often reveal who received payments and why.
- [procedure] 1) List every inflow and outflow over the period. 2) Total the holdings at the end. 3) Compare that total with the figures in the account. When: A money movement must be checked over a period.
- [procedure] 1) Find withdrawals from a known account shortly before the death. 2) Follow the cash to where notes are spent or cashed. 3) Check wills and contracts for a motive. 4) Check whether money is missing from the scene. When: a financial record gives a timeline, a sum or a beneficiary.

## npc routines and behavior
- [mechanism] After an event, NPC behaviour drifts back toward its baseline over time, which creates a window for detection. When: An NPC has changed behaviour after a major event. Why: Old patterns return gradually, revealing the change.
- [rule] Let an NPC remove clues on a schedule, so the player must reach the scene before cleanup or question the NPC about what was removed. When: Designing an NPC who tidies a room in a game. Why: Time pressure and questioning turn cleanup into a playable challenge.
- [rule] Give NPCs routines so that a change in schedule or a hidden item becomes a readable tell for the player. When: designing NPC behavior for player observation. Why: a stable routine lets deviations signal meaning.

## npc testimony and sacrifice
- [behavior] Some accused people choose death over coercive interrogation, so refusal can be extreme when every outcome seems unsurvivable. When: torture is threatened. Why: they see no survivable path through the process.
- [rule] Let the player check NPC claims against evidence: stated sacrifices against observed actions, item handovers against the receiver's log or inventory, stated conditions against symptoms and schedule.
- [rule] Build NPC testimony about another NPC's feelings as a claim the player must check against logged actions or other characters' statements. When: an NPC describes what another NPC thinks or feels. Why: Testimony about inner states is only useful when cross-checked.

## physical record comparison
- [heuristic] Compare a message's physical details, such as an earlier firm envelope and a later shaky letter, to infer the writer's state of mind.
- [heuristic] Compare physical records side by side without the suspect present, rather than accepting their word or letting them adjust their account. When: Checking a claimed presence against a token or log. Why: Hiding the comparison keeps the suspect from adapting their story to it.
- [fact] Objects, marks and the state of a room record past actions and can testify as clearly as people. Why: Traces persist after the event and reveal what was done.

## piecemeal reasoning
- [pitfall] Each point or explanation can seem sound alone, hiding a contradiction or pattern visible only when judged together with specific testimony or other clues. When: When a theory rests on several separate points or a series of plausible explanations is offered for clues. Why: The conflict lies between points, not inside any one; each explanation looks sufficient alone, hiding the pattern across them.
- [pitfall] A plausible account, including a psychologically plausible confession, is not thereby true; plausibility is not verification and must be followed by confirmation. When: When an account is judged credible on its face. Why: Plausibility only makes a claim worth checking.
- [pitfall] Confirming each detail of a story separately can create false confidence when the records confirm parts but not the whole claim. Why: Individually accurate records can jointly support a false conclusion.

## planning and surveillance
- [rule] Arrange an unobtrusive exit so the watch can end at any hour without drawing attention.
- [pitfall] Shadowing without method produces noisy, unreliable reports.
- [fact] A premeditated plan is argued to stay hidden unless the planner is pressed for time or hit by an unforeseeable coincidence. When: Assessing whether a deliberate plan can be detected. Why: Pressure and chance are the two main sources of error.

## puzzle failure states
- [heuristic] Do not expect the tipping point of a collapsing belief to be predictable; opinion often shifts unseen for a long time before it becomes visible. Why: The exact trigger is often unknown even to observers.
- [pitfall] Letting one reversal reset every earlier conclusion without leftover clues leaves the player nothing to reinterpret. When: a reversal is introduced. Why: earlier clues should remain visible and meaningful.
- [pitfall] A test is only as good as its preparation, so a lure that misses its required conditions will fail to reveal anything. When: when a controlled test depends on specific conditions. Why: Missing conditions break the causal link the test relies on.

## registry records and searches
- [heuristic] When witnesses are gone or silent, registry deeds, gifts and probated wills can establish who owned, owed or inherited something. When: the question is ownership, debt or inheritance and witnesses are unavailable. Why: Formal instruments survive their makers.
- [procedure] 1) Visit lodgings in the area where the suspect may have stayed. 2) Check each register for the sought name or a known alias. 3) If the name never appears, consider that it may be an invented alias and check it against lists of real names. When: The suspect's real name is unknown but a surname or alias is known. Why: Registers capture even short stays, and a missing name suggests an alias.
- [tradeoff] A register search is simple and often effective, but its cost grows with each establishment visited. When: Choosing whether to search lodging registers. Why: Each additional lodging adds travel and checking time.

## returned objects as clues
- [mechanism] Returning an item in good faith removes the accuser's motive and ends the pressure; an intact return of an entrusted valuable carries trust itself as physical evidence of honesty.
- [heuristic] An object found back in its usual place can be a clue, since its return rather than its removal may show that someone acted.
- [pitfall] A gun found near a body may have rolled there, so its position can mislead the reconstruction.

## riddles and puzzle solving
- [procedure] 1) Map each riddle phrase to an instrument, direction or landmark. 2) Find the single vantage point from which the clue becomes visible. 3) Take bearings on the spot. When: a riddle encodes a physical location.
- [procedure] 1) Record the unexplained phrase verbatim. 2) Turn it into a list of constraints such as count, time and landmark. 3) Test each candidate against every constraint. 4) Keep the candidate that meets all of them. When: Solving a clue whose meaning is initially hidden. Why: Checking constraints one at a time narrows the answer to a single fit.
- [pitfall] A riddle with no reachable key gives players nothing to act on, so the key must exist somewhere in the game. When: Designing riddles. Why: Unsolvable clues stall play.

## round numbers and approximation
- [procedure] 1) Count the rounds in the weapon. 2) Account for each empty chamber and each wound. 3) Check that the remaining count matches the expected total. When: A shooting must be reconciled with the weapon's ammunition. Why: Each shot is then either accounted for or shown to be missing.
- [pitfall] Round numbers are only suspicious in context; treating every round figure as a clue produces false motives. When: When reviewing ordinary records such as receipts or ledgers. Why: Round sums are often ordinary, so context must decide their meaning.
- [pitfall] A timeline is only as precise as its times, so a rough interval leaves the gap it covers uncertain. Why: Precision cannot exceed the precision of the recorded times.

## scene inference and layout
- [procedure] 1) Note checkable signs such as bearing, dress, footwear, and carried items. 2) Tie each inference to one specific sign. 3) Chain the signs into a working hypothesis. 4) Test the hypothesis against later evidence. When: when a person is seen only briefly. Why: Each inference stays checkable and can be revised.
- [procedure] 1) Derive lot dimensions and a building's position from land descriptions. 2) Compare the present structure with that footprint. 3) Note which parts are original and which were altered. When: testing where a building stood at an earlier time. Why: later appearance may not match the original.
- [pitfall] Assuming a place is deserted from a quick look at the ground floor can miss evidence of a hurried departure or recent presence. When: When a location appears empty after a brief survey. Why: Partial surveys miss traces of recent occupation.

## social standing and address
- [rule] When a document names an office instead of a person, find the holder from dates and circumstances rather than from the title alone.
- [heuristic] A shared office's push to gain its house and land may be read as a bid for influence as a landholder, not simple greed.
- [fact] Offices that conferred standing included minister, deacons, parish clerk, constable, magistrates and military officers.

## source tagging in dialogue
- [rule] Let an NPC's wording reveal its source, so players can infer who told them and where to look next.
- [heuristic] Tag each NPC or witness claim with source and access level, such as witnessed, heard, believed, eyewitness, rumour or second-hand, so players weigh claims by how directly they were known. When: NPC testimony or a case rests on several accounts, such as frightened, drunk, or secondhand witnesses. Why: Explicit source tags let claims be weighed by how directly the source knew the event.
- [heuristic] Tag each record with its source type so documents, witness testimony and inference can be told apart.

## stranger identity clues
- [mechanism] A stranger cannot be released on his own word; without a known local guarantor, detention lasts longer. When: when a protagonist lacks local standing. Why: Release depends on someone vouching for the detainee.
- [procedure] 1) Ask for a general physical description first. 2) Ask about height relative to the witness, build, face, skin and marked features. 3) Follow with a direct recognition question. When: A witness's memory of a brief encounter with a stranger is the main lead. Why: Staged questioning moves from general to specific features, which improves recall.
- [pitfall] Claims from a stranger, including a reveal resting on his word alone, may be wrong or guessed and are treated as suspicious until checked before believing or acting.

## supernatural and phenomena
- [rule] Resolve a supernatural threat through a relationship or social act rather than a kill, so the climax carries emotional resolution. When: When the threat stems from a hidden personal desire or conflict. Why: Ending the threat through a human change gives the climax emotional weight instead of only combat payoff.
- [heuristic] Renaming an impossible feat with a different label, such as telepathy or levitation, does not change what the act physically requires; the label is not an explanation. When: A rational or mystic label is offered for a strange event. Why: Labels describe an effect without showing its mechanism.
- [procedure] 1) Trace each link in the chain of testimony back to whoever witnessed the event. 2) Check whether each witness was present. 3) Accept the supernatural claim only if every link holds. When: when a supernatural explanation is offered for an event. Why: Testing each link exposes the mundane explanation hidden in the chain.

## suspense devices
- [model] Suspense before a revelation can be built with five devices: a vague stranger's warning, a disguised figure, a reassuring authority, fear displaced onto a legend, and a held-back threat. When: a story or level needs tension before the real danger is revealed.
- [mechanism] Suspense arises from urgency, reversals, time gaps, unexplained anomalies, and watcher presences; staged reveals plant clues for later payoff. (x2)
- [mechanism] A recurring image that returns with small new details gathers force each time, so the threat becomes clearer and more alarming. When: when a dream, vision or motif recurs. Why: Each return adds information and reinforces the association.

## suspense from glimpsed secrets
- [mechanism] A character rehearsing a deception in front of the audience tells the reader the secret while the other characters remain ignorant, creating dramatic irony. When: a secret plan is carried out by a character the audience can observe. Why: The audience holds information the cast lacks, so tension builds from waiting for it to be discovered.
- [mechanism] The gap between what a character sees and what they understand drives suspense, and hindsight makes missed patterns clear. When: Structuring a mystery's reveal. Why: Readers track the difference.
- [heuristic] Suspense needs the audience to glimpse that a secret exists; a secret never hinted at creates no tension.

## suspense sources
- [model] Suspense can be built from three sources: anticipated horror that still lands hard, reversals at section endings, and a sense of an unseen observer who anticipates the player's moves.
- [mechanism] Suspense is built from three combined sources: prolonged waiting, small physical signs of agitation, and an abrupt sound that breaks the silence.
- [mechanism] Suspense grows when repeated episodes escalate in intensity, moving from small signs to physical blows to violent confrontation. When: Structuring a multi-stage threat. Why: Rising intensity keeps tension building across episodes.

## suspense through interruption
- [rule] Let a staged crisis escalate in steps so each event looks more supernatural, while each step still has a mundane mechanism. When: authoring a sequence of staged events in a haunting. Why: Escalation sustains the illusion of the supernatural, while each mechanism remains recoverable.
- [heuristic] Interrupting an account at a moment of tension creates immediate suspense that holds attention until the next revelation. Why: Unfinished tension keeps the audience engaged.
- [pitfall] Repeated interruptions frustrate the audience without adding tension, so limit them and keep each one moving toward the answer. When: Delaying a reveal. Why: Delays that repeat the same hint feel like padding.

## suspicion along social lines
- [behavior] Suspicion travels along property lines, family ties, quarrels and self-appointed groups, so accusations often follow existing social connections. When: when a community begins naming suspects. Why: existing ties and shared interests decide whom people believe and blame.
- [behavior] In a small, isolated community, residents judge newcomers and people of unfamiliar appearance as suspects, so prejudice can point at the wrong people. When: A closed group with shared routines has a crime to explain. Why: Limited contact and visible differences make outsiders stand out and invite suspicion regardless of evidence.
- [heuristic] A new face in a household can raise a careful suspect's suspicion, so a stand-in should be used with care. When: when substituting household staff to create cover. Why: Unfamiliar people are noticed and questioned by those who know the routine.

## suspicion biases reading
- [behavior] An authority figure who pushes a confident theory and dismisses motive is trusted, so the audience does not suspect them until a reversal.
- [pitfall] A panel with a prior suspicion or fixation on one suspect reads the same ambiguous sign differently from a neutral examiner and accepts or rejects evidence too quickly. When: when an examination panel has a prior suspicion. Why: prior belief shapes how ambiguous evidence is interpreted. (x2)
- [pitfall] Judging guilt from appearance, such as disliking a face, or from strong emotional reaction is prejudice, not a finding; it favours some suspects and closes off others. When: when an investigator forms early judgments. Why: Premature judgment on looks removes alternatives from consideration.

## suspiciously clean evidence
- [heuristic] An unusually clean or pristine surface or impression suggests deliberate preparation; check how the mark was produced instead of accepting it as ordinary. When: when evidence looks too perfect. Why: a surface can be polished before a mark is placed on it.
- [heuristic] When a clue seems fabricated, look for the extra step the staging required, since that step is where the fabrication shows. When: When an investigator suspects a clue was placed to mislead. Why: Staging needs actions beyond the crime itself, and those actions leave traces.
- [pitfall] A planted clue that looks too convenient is suspect; test how well it fits the scene before trusting it. When: a clue arrives exactly when it resolves a question. Why: convenient finds are often planted.

## sworn testimony
- [rule] Where the accused requests it, testimony should be sworn rather than given in writing before the account is accepted. When: when a party asks for sworn evidence instead of a written attestation. Why: an oath binds the witness more firmly to the account than a written attestation.
- [heuristic] Weigh a sworn witness's account against other evidence, since a sworn witness can be mistaken and dismissing their word needs justification.
- [fact] Sworn testimony written down before a hearing creates a durable evidence trail that fixes a witness's version for later comparison. When: when a claim must be checked after the event. Why: a written commitment resists drift in memory.

## symbol interpretation
- [rule] Compare a specialist's identification of a symbol with other sources before acting on it, and record which reading the evidence supports. When: a symbol has been identified by a single source.
- [pitfall] Symbols can carry unrelated readings from different traditions; treating one meaning as certain when the evidence allows others produces false attributions, so an identification must be weighed first.
- [fact] A drawn sign can look meaningless until a specialist recognizes its source, and its meaning depends on the tradition it comes from and who reads it. When: a symbol appears at a scene and its origin is unknown.

## symptom pattern matching
- [heuristic] Symptoms gain evidential value once they fit a recognized pattern, so compare observations with a reference description of each candidate cause.
- [heuristic] Give several ambiguous physical signs of death in one scene so they form a conclusion only when read together. When: Revealing a death through indirect evidence. Why: Individually weak signs are easy to dismiss, but together they point clearly to one conclusion.
- [fact] A shaking hand, irritability and poor sleep are physical signs that can point to a cause, though one sign alone does not establish a diagnosis. When: Observing a person's physical signs as possible evidence of a condition. Why: Several causes can produce the same set of signs.

## tagging npc statements
- [rule] Tag each non-player statement as seen, heard or assumed, and let players weigh each tag differently. When: when writing NPC dialogue that reports events. Why: Players can cross-check claims only when they can classify them.
- [rule] Log an NPC's reaction as a flag the player can later weigh against other statements. When: tracking NPC responses to evidence. Why: stored reactions allow later comparison with other testimony.
- [heuristic] Write NPC rumours as partly true clues with a known source and bias, so the player must weigh them. When: When designing tavern tales or rumours in a game world. Why: Known bias gives the player a way to judge reliability.

## tenancy and title
- [behavior] People who hold land only as tenants, without legal title, are unlikely to bury someone permanently on that land. When: Judging where a person without title might have acted. Why: Lack of title removes both the right and the security needed for such an act.
- [fact] A tenant's legal standing to claim land depends on the owner's title, so possession and title can belong to different people. When: A tenant and an owner both have some connection to the same land. Why: The tenant's right to act for the land derives from the owner's legal claim.
- [fact] Without a valid will, an estate typically passes to blood relatives. When: under typical inheritance rules.

## timeline and schedule logs
- [rule] Log NPC positions, transit times and arrivals with minute-level timestamps so players can test alibis, check travel at walking speed, and find schedule gaps. When: When designing NPC schedules, alibi checks, or puzzles that depend on where a character was at a given time. Why: Ordered, precise timestamps make movement claims checkable against one another and reveal where an NPC could have acted. (x2)
- [heuristic] An unreliable sense of time, such as an NPC's distorted perception, can be used deliberately to create confusion that the player must work through. When: a story needs the player to doubt a character's timing. Why: Players must cross-check conflicting times, which adds challenge and mystery.
- [procedure] 1) Record each dated event, such as visits, refusals and deliveries. 2) Order them by date. 3) Look for the point where the pattern changes. When: when several dated events must be ordered to locate a change. Why: A sorted sequence exposes when a shift began.

## touch and surface evidence
- [behavior] A hidden physical tell can be found by touch or close contact after a visible disguise has passed, since gloves and coats can conceal it.
- [procedure] Ask about each surface a person could have touched, testing every route by which the evidence could have been handled or entered. When: tracing who handled an object or entered a space. Why: Covering every route prevents a missed contact from being overlooked.
- [fact] Prints on an object show that a particular person handled it, which can point to a second person when the expected handlers are excluded. When: When physical traces on an object conflict with the stated account. Why: Traces record contact, so unexpected prints reveal additional involvement.

## unlocked access and entry
- [mechanism] A system's security can be defeated through information gathered by an insider rather than through force, so a claimed impregnable system is still vulnerable. When: a guarded system is assumed impregnable. Why: procedural security checks do not protect against copied records.
- [pitfall] Leaving an opening unlocked gives the suspect a real chance to flee, so the risk must be accepted and the authorities must agree.
- [fact] A window that can be pushed open from outside gives access to anyone who knows it is unlocked.

## weighing impaired testimony
- [mechanism] When a suspect pleads a mental defence, the central question moves from who committed the act to whether the suspect's mind can be judged responsible, which a specialist must assess. When: A suspect's confession is paired with a claim of madness. Why: A plea of insanity changes what must be proven and who is competent to prove it.
- [pitfall] Vivid, certain impressions and feelings of insight from someone impaired, distressed, or under a perception-altering drug are not evidence of accuracy; verify them independently. When: Receiving testimony or observations from someone impaired, distressed, or under a perception-altering effect. Why: Impairment can produce confident, detailed recollections, and elation or sensory intensity can feel like insight while being inaccurate. (x2)
- [pitfall] A witness's senses can be confused by fear, fatigue, or outside influence, so a striking perception must be checked against a second observer. When: when a witness reports a frightening sight. Why: Strong emotion and tiredness distort perception, and a second observer can confirm or refute it.

## witchcraft charges
- [definition] Witch is the only term among overlapping labels for suspected magical practitioners that carries a compact with the Devil; the other terms do not convey that idea. When: Interpreting the label applied to a suspect in a record. Why: The label determines which alleged allegiance and offence is presumed.
- [fact] Early statutes made witchcraft a capital offence only when the practice had caused a death, so the harmful result was the test of guilt.
- [fact] A 17th-century charging formula defined witchcraft as keeping familiarity with Satan and doing works beyond the course of nature.

## 'may have' statements
- [pitfall] A witness who says a detail 'may have' been present has not confirmed it, so the detail must not be recorded as fact.
- [pitfall] Hedged, vague predictions cannot be disproved, so trust rests on the performer's claimed past accuracy rather than on the forecast itself. When: A reader offers forecasts with limited stated expertise. Why: Unfalsifiable statements make audiences trust reputation instead of testing claims.

## bizarre crimes and creatures
- [rule] Provide a bestiary of reference descriptions so players can match a physical trace to a creature entry. When: designing traces that point to a creature. Why: a reference lets players compare traces with documented features.
- [heuristic] Bizarre crimes often prove less mysterious than they look, and the bigger the crime, the more obvious its motive tends to be. When: A plot seems inexplicable. Why: Large schemes need large motives, which are easier to identify.

## call records and location
- [behavior] Body language during a call, such as a flushed face, rigid posture, or turning away, can reveal an emotional bond the speaker hides. When: Observing a person during a phone call or interview. Why: Involuntary cues leak feelings the speaker does not state.
- [heuristic] A telephone call or booking can fix the caller's location when only one reachable point could have sent it.

## creator and creature facts
- [rule] Weigh a creator's own denial or claim about their sources alongside the physical evidence rather than dismissing it. When: Judging whether a work was modeled on a specific real place or event. Why: A creator's statement is itself a source about how the work was made.
- [heuristic] A creature that needs food and shelter is unlikely to persist for years in an unoccupied place, so its presence there is doubtful. When: when a sound or sign suggests an animal in an abandoned place. Why: food and shelter are needed for long-term survival.

## delayed reveal structure
- [model] A delayed-reveal mystery moves through six phases: frame, arrival, accumulating clues, escalation, testimony, and exposure with aftermath. When: Designing a story where a hidden identity is revealed late.
- [procedure] 1) Suspend the detective's thread. 2) Supply the hidden answer in a digression using facts shown earlier. 3) Return to the detective at the point of confusion. When: Structuring a mystery so the audience outpaces the investigator. Why: Reveal through digression keeps the reader ahead while the investigator's uncertainty creates suspense.

## digestion and diet clues
- [behavior] Observed behavior near food, such as climbing toward caged prey, can reveal an unseen animal's diet. When: When an animal's actions near food can be observed or inferred. Why: Actions near food indicate what the animal eats.
- [heuristic] Digestion timing is an estimate, so test results must be read with care about expected timing. When: Interpreting stomach contents for time of ingestion. Why: Digestion varies, so timing carries uncertainty.

## displayed stance
- [rule] Give characters a displayed face or bearing that can differ from their hidden stance, so a player can notice a mismatch. When: designing NPC tells.
- [heuristic] An ostentatious, ugly cover can signal that the wearer wants it noticed, so display suggests pride rather than shame.

## investigation scope
- [mechanism] After an inquiry escalates, the scope tends to widen quickly, with more warrants issued and more people accused. When: an inquiry has just moved to a higher body.
- [rule] Keep only details tied to the central purpose of the story and leave out domestic events that do not advance it. Why: Off-purpose detail dilutes the main line.

## last testimony weight
- [behavior] Observers tend to treat the last testimony heard as decisive, so the order of evidence can shape a verdict without any new fact.
- [rule] Give the victim a partial dying message that a tool or map can complete into a place name outside the scene, rewarding attention to what was left behind.

## legend masks concealment
- [mechanism] A rumour of a supernatural or monstrous secret can keep people from looking closely at a mundane concealment.
- [procedure] 1) Hide a key or code between pages stuck together in a lore book. 2) Let the player reveal it by cutting or parting the pages. 3) Place an inscription chain across several NPC hands for the player to read in order. When: Designing hidden clues in in-game lore items. Why: Physical concealment rewards thorough player inspection and sequence reading.

## limits of reductio
- [rule] A reductio against an accuser shows inconsistency in the accuser's standards but does not establish the innocence of the accused.
- [pitfall] A complete-looking taxonomy does not prove every case is covered, and the most interesting crime may sit outside every category. When: Relying on a classification scheme to solve a case. Why: Schemes are built from known motives and can miss unfamiliar ones.

## lineup identification procedure
- [procedure] 1) Present several candidates who partly fit the description. 2) Have the witness signal rejection of each under an agreed sign. 3) Log each candidate as seen. When: a witness must identify a suspect from several people. Why: an agreed procedure keeps the identification controlled and recorded.
- [procedure] 1) Assemble a parade of similar decoys with the suspect. 2) Have the witness pick a person. 3) Check whether the witness repeatedly picks one person or simply agrees with the suggested suspect. When: Testing whether an identification is genuine. Why: Decoys reveal whether the witness discriminates or is merely confirming a suggestion.

## lingering unexplained unease
- [behavior] An unexplained sense of dread with no traceable cause stays with the audience as a mood to recall when later events give it meaning.
- [rule] Leave some final signal unexplained so the audience remains uncertain after the reveal. When: Closing a multi-stage mystery. Why: Residual doubt preserves suspense beyond the apparent resolution.

## listening through digression
- [heuristic] Digressions can contain useful names or objects, so listen for them within irrelevant talk.
- [heuristic] Pay close attention to details a witness offers unprompted, since small asides can point to important leads worth pursuing. When: A witness volunteers a passing remark during questioning. Why: Unsolicited comments often reveal knowledge the witness did not intend to share.

## live suspect status
- [rule] Keep NPCs who have access to a crime as live suspects with testable evidence, not fixed red herrings that the story dismisses in advance. When: Designing mysteries where several characters could have acted. Why: Players can only reason fairly if each suspect stays open until evidence rules it out.
- [pitfall] Assuming every trace belongs to a living suspect overlooks the victim and the scene as possible sources. When: Interpreting an unmatched physical trace. Why: Traces can come from the body or the environment itself.

## location trace limits
- [heuristic] If the seals on other doors stay whole while only one room's seal breaks, the disturbance stayed within that room. When: Comparing physical markers across a building. Why: Intact markers elsewhere localize the cause.
- [pitfall] A trace that places a caller at a public location narrows the search but does not identify the person if no one saw them. When: Relying on a telephone or location trace. Why: A place gives direction of travel, not identity.

## loot carries clues
- [mechanism] A loot pattern that takes only one kind of material from a shrine suggests a particular taker and reason, so the player can infer an NPC's motive.
- [rule] Let a defeated NPC's inventory carry letters, tickets and other items that point to other places or people, so loot doubles as investigation. When: when designing NPC inventories. Why: Clue-bearing loot links the investigation forward.

## narrative tone and style
- [behavior] Delivering a trivial result with grave solemnity creates bathos, a deflating contrast that heightens the letdown. When: Revealing that a promising clue is harmless. Why: The mismatch between tone and result produces the letdown.
- [heuristic] Shift the narrative mode within a scene, such as from a dramatic version to a first-person account, to change how the listener hears it. When: Presenting an account that must be reinterpreted. Why: A change of voice alters the weight and trust the audience gives the same events.

## perception under stress
- [behavior] Under fear, surprise, or fatigue, observers misperceive details, such as doubled figures, changed room size, or a living person taken for a spirit in poor light, and recall of event order breaks down. When: An observer is frightened, surprised, or fatigued during an event. Why: Stress and poor light distort perception; stress affects both perception and memory, not only later recall.
- [heuristic] Let a stressed NPC misremember a detail that the player can later confirm with a record, which gives the player a reason to revisit evidence. When: Writing NPC testimony that the player must verify. Why: Confirmable errors motivate investigation and reward checking.

## quest information
- [rule] Give a quest-giver partial information and hold the rest back until the player earns it by visiting other NPCs; flag hedged dialogue as a possible hidden agenda. When: Designing quest dialogue. Why: Withheld information rewards exploration and tests the player's judgement.
- [heuristic] An NPC's half-finished remark can serve as a quest marker that resolves only when the player finds its subject. When: Designing unresolved hints in dialogue. Why: The open question sustains interest until the subject is found.

## responsibility and punishment spread
- [mechanism] Spreading punishments over several months prolongs a crisis and keeps public pressure high.
- [heuristic] Distribute oddities across several NPCs so that they form a pattern only when the player gathers and compares them. When: when building a multi-step mystery. Why: Distribution forces the player to visit and connect sources.

## room recall and questioning
- [procedure] 1) Ask where the witness sat and where light sources and the sun fell. 2) Rebuild the scene from their own vantage point. 3) Ask about peripheral objects such as wall pictures. When: a witness has been in a location and gives an account of it. Why: Peripheral details show whether the room was really observed.
- [procedure] Ask where a meeting happened as well as who attended, since the room shows who else was nearby.

## scattered objects puzzle
- [heuristic] A container that breaks and releases several small items gives the player a set of objects to sort and connect into a sequence.
- [heuristic] Place the parts of a mechanism in ordinary containers early so they read as trivia, and combine them only at a final puzzle. When: Setting up a multi-part solution to be assembled late. Why: Separated, innocuous parts do not signal the solution, and combining them at the end makes the climax a deduction.

## scent and clue linking
- [definition] A smell can be planted deliberately to mislead, or tested to show which object carried it, so scent works both as a decoy and as a link between objects.
- [fact] A distinctive scent or brand choice on an object can link it to the person who handled it, while a strong masking odour can indicate an attempt to hide a trace. (x2)

## setting and scene context
- [mechanism] When newspapers and outside contact are scarce, a regular gathering becomes the main place to hear and retell news. When: few other news sources exist. Why: Scarcity makes the gathering the only dependable channel.
- [pitfall] Assuming that a beautiful rural landscape means safety. A pleasant appearance can conceal a hidden history of cruelty. Why: Appearance says nothing about what has happened inside a place.

## suspense from lost sight
- [mechanism] Removing sight forces characters to rely on sound, touch and guesses about direction, which raises tension. When: a dangerous scene where visibility is cut off. Why: Uncertainty about the environment and each other's position sustains dread.
- [mechanism] Blocking sight of a threat at the critical moment withholds its appearance, so tension builds and the eventual reveal lands with more force. When: at the climax of an investigation or encounter. Why: Delayed sight keeps the audience anticipating the answer.

## suspense from silent witness
- [mechanism] Delaying a reveal while a listener risks discovery raises tension, because the listener's fear is felt by the audience. When: When a hidden listener is present. Why: Discovery risk increases anticipation.
- [heuristic] A mysterious witness who confronts without revealing information builds suspense before any clue is delivered.

## suspense structure
- [model] Suspense rests on three parts: escalating threats, brief relief between them, and early setups that are paid off later.
- [model] A mystery can delay its answer by stacking false solutions, then shift the central question from who the culprit is to what the culprit is to the protagonist. When: Designing a mystery with a late reveal of a hidden relationship. Why: Changing the question late gives the audience a fresh frame, so the reveal adds meaning rather than only a name.

## suspicion as hypothesis
- [heuristic] Treat a suspicion about a rival's supposed discovery as a hypothesis to test, not as established fact.
- [heuristic] Plant suspects and grievances through ordinary business such as land, debts and lawsuits long before the crisis, so later accusations read as continuations of known feuds. When: Opening the first fifth of a mystery or conflict-driven story. Why: Familiar disputes make a sudden crisis feel like an escalation the player already understood.

## suspicion basis check
- [heuristic] Do not dismiss a suspect because his apparent interest runs against the crime; check whether the benefit depends on conditions or sequence. When: A suspect seems to have reason to keep the victim alive. Why: A reward that depends on conditions or order can reverse an apparent interest.
- [procedure] 1) Ask what a stated suspicion rests on. 2) Check that basis against observed facts. 3) Weigh the suspicion according to how well its basis holds. When: someone states a suspicion about another person. Why: Suspicions often rest on impressions rather than evidence.

## suspicion checkability
- [rule] Attach each suspicion to a checkable observation, so players eliminate theories by consulting witnesses rather than guessing. When: designing a suspicion system. Why: Checkable observations make elimination fair.
- [rule] Let the player test whether an NPC's hint served the NPC, by comparing it with later evidence. When: designing dialogue hints that may be red herrings. Why: comparison separates a true clue from a self-serving one.

## suspicion reads odd behaviour
- [behavior] An observer who already suspects a target reads odd behaviour, such as feigned drunkenness or lingering, as purposeful rather than accidental. When: When an observer already suspects the target. Why: Suspicion gives ordinary acts a hidden purpose.
- [heuristic] Treat a suspect's self-description of impulsiveness as a claim to check against their conduct, not as a verdict on intent. When: When judging whether a suspect's account of intent is credible or reconstructing whether an act was spontaneous or prepared. Why: A self-description can hide a planned act, and it carries the same uncertainty as any other claim.

## suspicion spread outward
- [mechanism] Suspicion can pass along a chain of suspects and return to an earlier one when new evidence appears, so the culprit is not fixed early. When: in a mystery with several plausible suspects. Why: New evidence re-weights earlier suspects, keeping the question open.
- [fact] Suspicion can radiate out from a few households to neighbours, relatives and distant people, until neighbours turn on one another.

## suspicion spreads too far
- [behavior] After a main suspect is cleared, the player's suspicion does not move cleanly to one new person but splits across several candidates before narrowing. When: A main suspect's alibi collapses mid-story. Why: Suspicion is anchored to the old theory, so it scatters before a new target forms.
- [pitfall] Suspicion can spread so widely that the group collapses before the investigator can exploit it.

## suspicion versus identity
- [heuristic] Pair a sympathetic detail with a suspicious one in the same scene so that neither settles the question and the player stays torn. When: designing an ambiguous accused character. Why: the two details pull the player's judgment in opposite directions.
- [pitfall] Treating a complainant's suspicion as proof of the culprit's identity confuses accusation with evidence. When: A complainant names or suspects a person without direct evidence. Why: Suspicion is a belief and does not establish identity.

## suspicious conduct ambiguity
- [behavior] Hiding or fleeing from authorities fits guilt, but also fits an innocent person afraid of being wrongly charged. Such conduct is weak evidence alone. When: Evaluating a suspect's evasive behavior. Why: Fear of false accusation produces the same visible actions as guilt.
- [behavior] A person who takes precautions more elaborate than the situation needs draws attention, even though each precaution alone looks ordinary. When: a suspect's conduct is examined. Why: The pattern across the steps, not any one step, reveals design.

## suspiciously smooth account
- [heuristic] An account that is too complete and convenient deserves scrutiny; its ease can hide weak points.
- [pitfall] A culprit whose rationalization is too neat reads as a plot device, so the contradictions in their reasoning must stay visible. When: Writing a culprit's motive. Why: Overly tidy justification removes the human texture that makes motive believable.

## sympathetic suspect design
- [rule] Give a suspect a sympathetic motive and a lawful errand whose timing contradicts the stated purpose, so the player can catch the mismatch.
- [heuristic] Make the most sympathetic claimant the actual danger, so a player who trusts the wronged party is led into the reveal. When: designing a mystery with a claimant or heir. Why: Sympathy lowers the player's guard against the true threat.

## sympathetic witness supports story
- [behavior] A sympathetic witness chosen to observe an act is likely to support the story rather than question it. Why: Sympathy makes the witness less inclined to scrutinise the framing.
- [heuristic] Let a sympathetic witness hold the final key, so the reveal is pulled from them rather than discovered alone.

## sympathy and trust
- [rule] Let the player explain a device to frightened characters during a confrontation so that they earn the characters' trust. When: Designing an arrest or boss-confrontation sequence.
- [pitfall] A sympathetic backstory can lead the audience to trust a character's conclusions too quickly, even when his grudges may bias them. When: When a character is both sympathetic and the source of key interpretations. Why: Sympathy is read as reliability, so biased claims go unchecked.

## sympathy as proof
- [pitfall] Trusting a sympathetic witness or dismissing one who confesses dislike skips the corroboration step.
- [pitfall] Clues that cut against a sympathetic reading can feel unfair to the audience until the confession that explains them arrives.

## sympathy bias
- [pitfall] Sympathy for a distressed witness lowers an investigator's scrutiny, leading them to accept the witness's framing and trust sincerity over the facts. When: when the witness is distressed or vulnerable and the investigator is moved or grows attached to them. Why: Empathy and emotional engagement reduce distance from the evidence and lower scrutiny of the witness's account. (x2)
- [pitfall] A confident, sympathetic witness can seem more reliable than a better-evidenced one, and readiness to name a culprit can outpace what they actually saw. When: when comparing witnesses of differing status or warmth. Why: social appeal can substitute for evidence.

## symptom-to-cause branching
- [mechanism] A chain of branching questions moving from a symptom toward its cause lets players follow a logical path to the hidden explanation.
- [procedure] 1) Read a physical trace as a condition. 2) Infer the likely diagnosis from it. 3) Infer symptoms, then the way of moving. 4) Present each step as probable, not certain. When: Building a profile from skeletal or bodily evidence. Why: Each layer depends on expert knowledge and is less certain than the one before.

## tagging npc claims
- [rule] Record each NPC hint or testable claim with a confidence level so a later check against evidence can flag weak claims or red herrings. When: NPCs or a dialogue system deliver hints or statements the player must evaluate later. Why: Logged claims allow later comparison against evidence. (x2)
- [heuristic] Tag each NPC claim with its stated premises so players can find the hidden assumption that fails.

## tampering clue design
- [mechanism] A signal that fails to ring when touched suggests its mechanism was disturbed, which can indicate tampering by someone with access. When: A tripwire or bell cord does not respond as expected. Why: Failure of a signal is itself evidence that someone interfered.
- [heuristic] Use a dim light or odd object as a tampering clue that careful players notice and impatient players miss.

## targeted test choice
- [rule] Choose a stimulus that bears directly on the hypothesis being tested, since an unrelated trigger produces a result that proves nothing. When: When provoking a suspect to reveal a hidden trait. Why: Only a stimulus linked to the hypothesis produces evidence that bears on it.
