- [heuristic] Order a lab test for a specific hypothesis rather than a general scan, since a question-driven analysis is easier to interpret. When: Choosing an analysis for an unexplained death. Why: Results from a vague test are hard to interpret.

## targets cluster by community
- [behavior] When accusers choose targets from rumor, the targets often cluster in one community or congregation that accusers already hear spoken of with hostility. Why: Shared hostility in one group makes its members easy to name.
- [heuristic] The choice of victim can suggest a targeted attack when the victim's vulnerability matches the mechanism's effect. When: A harmful act appears to affect a particular person. Why: Matching vulnerability to the method implies deliberate selection.

## technically true concealment
- [behavior] A technically true but incomplete answer can conceal a key fact and serve as the planted clue to that concealment; the listener must judge what was omitted and why. When: When a character has a motive to hide part of a truth. Why: Accurate but selective statements can mislead without a lie. (x2)
- [rule] Include true but selective statements in NPC dialogue so the player can catch the omission later. When: When writing dialogue that conceals part of a truth. Why: A later-caught omission rewards attention to what was left unsaid.

## tell baseline
- [behavior] A person who appears impassive on blunt questions may brighten sharply on a topic where they feel at ease, revealing their comfort zone. When: A reserved person is asked about varied subjects. Why: Comfort and discomfort show in changes of expression and energy.
- [heuristic] Establish each character's normal manner before reading a tell, since a tell gains weight only when it contrasts with that baseline. When: Interpreting a reaction as evidence of knowledge or guilt. Why: Without a baseline, ordinary behaviour is easily mistaken for a meaningful signal.

## tells as hypotheses
- [rule] Treat observed tells as questions to test against evidence, never as conclusions; demeanour alone cannot support a case.
- [rule] Present the culprit's method as a proposal the player can test, not as a settled fact, so the solution stays open to checking. When: when the culprit has not confessed. Why: A testable claim lets the player verify the method.

## tells of inner state
- [rule] Plant a behavioural tell on an antagonist early, so that its later recognition feels earned rather than sudden. When: Building a reveal in which a character is identified by appearance or gesture. Why: A tell seen earlier lets the player recognise the antagonist before the protagonist states it, which makes the payoff satisfying.
- [tradeoff] Tells such as flushing, paling, nail-biting, sudden silence, averted eyes or folded hands can signal concealed distress, yet also stem from illness, anger or embarrassment. When: when a suspect's inner state shows only through visible behaviour, particularly when an investigator probes a hidden secret. Why: Involuntary reactions reveal distress the subject would not state, but the same signs are ambiguous across causes. (x2)

## tension through contrast
- [mechanism] A calm baseline sharpens tension through contrast: a composed character or calm social scene makes an unresolved problem or threat feel more pressing. When: a character works through confusing evidence while others remain calm; calm social scenes are mixed with threatening ones. Why: Contrast with the calm makes the difficulty or threat stand out more strongly.
- [heuristic] Compare where each party leaves marks. One person's traces together with another's absence of traces can show who moved and how.

## witness dismissal of evidence
- [behavior] A witness with fixed expectations may dismiss real evidence as useless before examining it, such as marks the authorities have already disturbed. When: when a witness has preconceptions about a scene. Why: expectations filter what the witness considers worth attention.
- [behavior] A witness who hears a clue-bearing remark often does not recognise its importance and treats the words as trivial. When: the remark is heard before its context is known. Why: the witness lacks the later fact that links the words to the event.

## witness record comparison
- [heuristic] A witness's memory is weak evidence on its own; it becomes strong when an independent record fixes the same facts.
- [heuristic] A witness with a criminal record may give a vivid account, but the record makes the account suspect until confirmed independently.

## 'looks like' identifications
- [pitfall] A witness who says a person 'looks like' someone is weaker than one who is sure, so do not treat the two as equal.

## body marks as occupation clues
- [heuristic] Physical marks such as thickened ears, hand calluses or partly erased tattoos hint at a person's past trade, habits or attachments.

## combined reveal scene
- [rule] Explain the impossibility and name the culprit in the same scene, so the solution of the method and the identity land together.

## companion bias warnings
- [rule] Let a companion NPC warn the player when personal feelings may be affecting a judgment, and offer a hint to correct it.

## companion conversation trigger
- [mechanism] A harmless companion or animal can draw a person into conversation, producing informal information that a direct question might not. When: When an NPC is guarded and needs an easy opening for talk. Why: A shared, low-stakes topic lowers defenses and lets information surface naturally.

## concrete over feelings
- [heuristic] Matching physical details between independent accounts is stronger evidence than matching emotions or vague impressions. Why: Specific details can be verified; feelings cannot.

## confidant vs public reveal
- [tradeoff] Revealing a solution to a trusted confidant keeps it private but leaves the public record incomplete, inviting criticism of the investigator's competence. When: When deciding who learns a solved case's truth. Why: Private resolution protects people at the cost of public credit.

## conflicting readings of a person
- [behavior] Two characters in the same household can give opposite readings of one person's behavior, and each reading reflects the observer's assumptions. When: Characters with different relationships to the same person describe that person's mood or conduct. Why: Observers interpret behavior through their own expectations, such as gratitude or dullness, so their readings diverge.

## contested inquest findings
- [behavior] The same evidence can support opposing verdicts, so an examination can be adjourned for closer testing before a finding is fixed. When: a physical finding is disputed. Why: Incomplete or contested evidence can be read both ways.

## context-matched recognition in games
- [heuristic] Weight NPC recognition by context match, so a face seen at a matching location is more reliable than one seen elsewhere. When: Designing NPC recognition rules in a game. Why: Recognition should depend on the viewing conditions, as in real witnessing.

## correcting garbled terms
- [procedure] 1) Compare a second-hand technical term with its likely meaning in context. 2) Check the term against the original wording where possible. 3) Correct the term if the context shows it was garbled. When: A relayed report uses a technical term that seems wrong. Why: Relayed terms are often misquoted, and context reveals the intended meaning.

## correcting protagonist impression
- [heuristic] Let the protagonist's early impression be wrong, then correct it with an objective artifact such as a photograph, teaching players to trust evidence over impressions.

## corroborating expert opinion
- [heuristic] Have a second expert examine the evidence before removal, so a surprising conclusion rests on more than one opinion. When: When an expert conclusion overturns the obvious explanation. Why: Corroboration guards against a single opinion sounding settled too early.

## cross-checking accounts
- [procedure] 1) Collect each witness's independent account of one event. 2) List the concrete physical details in each. 3) Compare the details for exact matches. 4) Treat matches as links and mismatches as leads. When: Two witnesses must be tied together by a shared event. Why: Checkable details separate real connections from coincidence.

## decisive clue dissolution
- [mechanism] A decisive clue that is re-tested can dissolve after it has done its work, removing the basis for the verdict while other evidence remains. When: A case rests heavily on one physical token and the token can be examined again. Why: A second examination can undo the first without any new evidence entering the case.

## disguised confrontation
- [rule] Use a disguised confrontation to force a confession when the culprit has no witness. When: No witness exists and the culprit can be reached in person.

## hailing transport away from stands
- [heuristic] Hail a fast vehicle from a point away from the usual stand, so foot pursuers cannot keep up. When: Needing to break a pursuit in a city. Why: Foot pursuers cannot match a fast vehicle.

## hidden accomplice fallacy
- [pitfall] A hidden-accomplice explanation can seem rational but fails once every exit is still secured.

## hidden investigator method
- [rule] Keep the investigator's method partly hidden until the reveal, and withhold conclusions until the proof is in place. When: When designing the reveal of a mystery. Why: Concealed method preserves surprise and makes the proof land.

## hidden surveillance reveal
- [rule] Hide the investigator's own surveillance from the player until a late turn, so the sense of who is watching shifts at the reveal.

## hidden weapon reveal
- [mechanism] A murder weapon that is a common object already present in the scene is accepted more readily once revealed, because it was in plain view and was misread as ordinary. When: Planning a concealed-cause twist such as an accident that turns out to be murder. Why: Players recognize the object in hindsight and feel the clue was fair rather than arbitrary.

## inconclusive medical evidence
- [fact] Medical examination can fail to establish a cause of death when injuries obscure the mechanism of harm. When: when injuries are severe to the relevant body region. Why: Heavy damage can hide the evidence the examination needs.

## indirect confirmation
- [procedure] 1) Build a theory from second-hand information gathered in casual conversation. 2) Ask the informant small, relevant questions that each check one point. 3) Avoid stating the accusation. 4) Let the subject volunteer the answer. When: The subject is guarded and a direct accusation would end the conversation. Why: Single-point questions confirm a theory without revealing it, keeping the subject cooperative.

## inferred description cues
- [heuristic] Age, build and dress can be inferred from small cues heard without sight, such as a walking stick.

## inferring occupant routines
- [procedure] 1) Note the objects and marks in a space. 2) Infer the routines that would produce them. 3) Hold the inference provisionally. 4) Test it against observed behaviour of people in the space. When: Judging who uses a room and for what, from physical evidence alone. Why: Objects suggest routines but cannot prove a particular person's presence or conduct.

## inspect joins for traces
- [heuristic] Inspect seams and joints where grime gathers, rather than only the visible outer surface. When: Looking for traces on an object.

## invented motive
- [pitfall] A confident motive can be invented to fit the facts, and destroying evidence can look like concern or privacy. When: evaluating a suspect's explanation or removal of an item. Why: both can hide the real cause while appearing innocent.

## killer's error as trail
- [mechanism] When a culprit's own mistake, such as taking the wrong coat, leaves a material trail, the investigation can proceed without a confession or lucky break. When: when a thief or killer escapes a crime scene. Why: The physical error gives the investigator something recoverable to trace.

## last-minute plan changes
- [pitfall] Last-minute changes to a plan, such as a missed transport, can break an alibi or create one, so schedules must account for disruptions. When: when an alibi depends on a planned route or meeting. Why: Unplanned events alter who was where and when.

## later admission cancels disclaimer
- [heuristic] Check whether a later clause cancels an earlier disclaimer, such as admitting that evidence could still be received and acted on. When: A passage opens with a disclaimer. Why: Later admissions can override the disclaimer.

## layered cover stories
- [procedure] 1) Give each listener a cover story shaped to their role. 2) Keep the stories consistent with each other. 3) Set timing so no one can check the absence before the window closes. When: when a character must be unaccounted for during a window of time. Why: Each witness confirms only part of the picture, so the whole story holds.

## layered disguise checks
- [rule] Separate eye-catching disguise features from hard-to-fake features so that players checking only obvious traits are fooled while careful players can catch the lie. When: when designing disguise detection challenges.

## lifelong military titles
- [fact] Militia titles were kept for life, so a former junior officer might still be styled by a higher title.

## likely appeal readers
- [heuristic] Household servants, shop assistants and others in a victim's circle are the likeliest readers of an appeal to identify them.

## likely explanation testing
- [procedure] Test even the most probable explanation against evidence: 1) State the proposed mundane cause. 2) Check it against every observation, including timing and the person's reaction. 3) Accept it only if it fits the whole pattern. When: When an eerie event is given a natural explanation. Why: A cause that fits only some observations is a red herring, not an answer. (x2)

## limit reveals per beat
- [rule] Do not stack many revelations at once, or the audience loses track of which claim is being tested. When: during a multi-claim reveal.

## limited period science
- [fact] Astronomy, chemistry, optics, pneumatics and geography were largely undeveloped in the period, so ordinary events lacked natural explanations for those who saw them.

## limited writer knowledge
- [rule] Make a note writer's knowledge visibly limited, so the document itself reveals how much the writer knew. When: when designing npc-written documents.

## limits of consistency checks
- [fact] Consistency checks on motive and conduct do not always settle a suspicion, because a guilty mind can be hard to read.

## limp from prints
- [heuristic] A weaker print from one foot suggests less weight was placed on it, which points to a limp. When: Prints from the same shoe differ in depth. Why: Reduced weight shows as a shallower impression.

## lingering anxiety signal
- [heuristic] Lingering anxiety after a detail resurfaces suggests the detail matters to the witness.

## lingering at door
- [heuristic] A person who lingers at a door before knocking, looking pale and shaking, may have been listening.

## lingering memory in replies
- [behavior] A suspect whose thoughts still dwell on an earlier story may link a trigger word to that story rather than its usual meaning. When: a suspect recently heard a story tied to a key object. Why: Recent attention primes an unrelated association.

## lingering official disclaimers
- [pitfall] A formal disclaimer does not stop a vivid theory from shaping how people interpret later facts.

## linking traces to unknown person
- [procedure] 1) Find a physical detail shared by separate incidents, such as a maker's mark or description. 2) Trace the mark to a source that can identify the person. 3) Treat the link as provisional until proven. When: Two unrelated reports may concern the same unidentified person. Why: A shared physical detail gives a lead, but proof is still needed.

## linking witness facts
- [heuristic] One account can join unrelated facts into a single sequence and point to where to look next.

## list clue readings
- [rule] List every reading a single clue supports before accepting any one, since one physical fact can support several contradictory deductions. When: when a single clue is treated as proof of one identity.

## list order as rank
- [heuristic] In lists of officials, the first-named of several same-surname people is usually the one with the presiding office or longest service. When: Ordering follows local convention and the reader accepts that convention. Why: Writers tend to list by office and seniority of settlement.

## list order assumptions
- [pitfall] Ordering conventions vary between writers and places, so an inference from list order holds only if the reader accepts the convention in use.

## listener doubt
- [behavior] A listener checks a relayed account against what they already know and reacts openly where it strains belief, showing the audience where to doubt. When: An in-world listener hears a claim that seems implausible. Why: Prior knowledge gives a basis for judging how credible a claim is.

## listener-shaped testimony
- [behavior] Witness accounts are shaped by who is listening and when they are recorded, so alibis offered late are often recorded and then set aside. When: When an alibi or account is first offered after an accusation. Why: Late statements look self-serving and are harder to check.

## listener-tailored retelling
- [behavior] Each teller tends to supply the detail that suits the listener, so repeated retellings shift emphasis away from what was originally known. When: A story is passed on to different listeners. Why: Tellers adapt content to the audience.

## listening to an intruder
- [procedure] 1) Listen before acting. 2) Stay silent so the intruder does not learn you are present. 3) Avoid sudden movement that could reveal your position. When: an unseen visitor is moving nearby in the dark. Why: Sounds reveal what the intruder is doing, and silence keeps the observer hidden.

## listing apparent impossibilities
- [procedure] 1) List every apparent impossibility as a separate question. 2) Target a different assumption in each: weapon, silence, access, exit, sequence. 3) Answer each in order. 4) Require each answer to fit all constraints. When: A scene has several inconsistencies that no single theory explains. Why: Each question narrows the explanation, and an answer must satisfy every constraint, not just one.

## listing possible knowers
- [procedure] 1) List everyone who could have learned the secret or hidden object's location, such as visitors and staff, before concluding no outsider knew it. 2) Test each person for access, presence at the key time, and a provable alibi. 3) Count each person once. When: a secret or object's location is believed known only to few people or insiders. Why: access to the secret is the central question.

## local dissent weighing
- [heuristic] Record a local informant's rejection of a common explanation and weigh it seriously rather than dismissing it.

## local motive assumption
- [pitfall] Assuming a motive must lie locally can send the search the wrong way when the cause lies far from the scene.

## local origin deadline
- [mechanism] A local postmark removes the travel delay, so the time available before the event is short. When: the sender's origin is near the event. Why: no transit time is needed.

## locating a turning point
- [procedure] 1) Compare the outward relationship with later changes in behaviour. 2) Find the point where the attitude turned. 3) Look for a trigger, such as a disclosure. 4) Check whether the hostility was concealed. When: A private grievance is not visible in the public record.

## locating key secret
- [heuristic] An NPC's most important secret is often the subject it works hardest to close off, so players can spot it by watching deflections.

## location by incongruity
- [procedure] 1) Name the place where the body was found. 2) List every fact that conflicts with a crime happening there. 3) Test each conflict on its own. 4) Reject the place if several conflicts hold. When: A body is found somewhere that does not fit how the death occurred. Why: Each conflict may be weak, but together they can rule out the obvious location.

## location from written note
- [heuristic] A note written from a post the author could not leave places the author there on that date. When: A dated note mentions the writer's duty or location.

## location reveals needs
- [heuristic] The place where an act occurs can reveal what the actor needed, such as light, so consider why that location was chosen. When: an act happened somewhere odd.

## lodging register records
- [fact] Hotels and furnished lodgings must record every guest's name, even for a single night, so their registers cover a wide range of people. When: Tracing a person through lodging records. Why: Legal record-keeping obligations apply to all tenants.

## long relief scene
- [pitfall] A relief scene that runs long drains the tension that the misdirection depends on.

## long-missing owner significance
- [heuristic] An item belonging to someone missing for years, with no word since, is especially significant, since it may be the first sign of their fate. When: a found object connects to a long-missing person. Why: the absence of news makes any trace of the person unusually valuable.

## loose caution wording
- [pitfall] A caution given loosely may fail to protect the statement that follows it. When: Cautioning a witness informally or hastily. Why: The caution must clearly convey the statement's risk.

## loose clue widens search
- [behavior] A partial or vague clue supporting many readings widens the search, because a reading flexible enough to fit every hiding place rules none out. When: A clue is partial and admits many interpretations. Why: Generous readings match many locations, so the search spreads without narrowing.

## loose description match
- [pitfall] A loose match between a description and a record needs a second independent check before it is relied on.

## loose detail retention
- [heuristic] Do not reject a theory merely because one detail is unexplained; check whether that detail really falls outside the theory. When: a theory explains most evidence but leaves one detail open.

## loose joint multiple causes
- [pitfall] A loose joint can have more than one cause, such as deliberate handling in care settings, so it must be interpreted carefully. When: Interpreting a loosened limb. Why: Innocent handling can mimic tampering.

## loose labels
- [pitfall] Inconsistently applied or loosely used labels can mislead, so a term's meaning should not be treated as fixed; records show motive only when clearly linked to the outcome. When: Reading case records or historical/in-world labels for suspects where terms or records are used inconsistently. Why: Vague or overlapping terms shift meaning between accusers and courts, and weakly linked records can imply a motive the evidence does not support.

## loose point
- [rule] Do not reject a theory only for one loose point; that point may be a detail the theorist has not yet explained.

## loose timeline motive
- [pitfall] A motive inferred from a loose timeline can be wrong even when it fits the people involved.

## loose-thread claims
- [heuristic] Leave an unverifiable claim as a loose thread that players can test later, paying off only if a living witness confirms it.

## marking unreliable flashbacks
- [rule] Show dream or flashback scenes in rich detail while marking them as unreliable, so players must test them against other clues. When: Presenting a character's memory or dream in a game journal or cutscene. Why: Rich detail with an unreliability marker invites verification rather than blind trust.

## matching clue design
- [rule] Hide matching objects in two locations and require several matched objects before a quest state changes, so single common items act as hints rather than proof. When: Designing evidence checks in a game. Why: Multiple independent matches give more reliable confirmation than one common item.

## missing bodies and victims
- [model] A missing-body mystery can resolve as self-removal: the supposed victim was alive, moved away alone, and planted a forged note to frame another person.

## near-synonym conditions
- [rule] Treat near-synonymous descriptions of a physical state, such as locked and bolted, as possibly different, since they imply different access. When: Interpreting witness descriptions of a barrier. Why: Each condition permits different actions.

## npc errand mismatch as hook
- [rule] Give a visible oddity, such as an NPC errand whose path mismatches its purpose or a strange pay schedule, a hidden purpose so curiosity leads players into the plot. When: Designing a character behavior or system rule that should raise questions. Why: A visible mismatch invites players to investigate without stating the secret; the detail becomes the quest hook.

## scattered culprit clues
- [heuristic] Scatter a culprit's neutral-looking actions across separate scenes so players must reassemble them to see the pattern.

## separate eager witness
- [rule] Ask an eager witness to separate what they actually observed from what they assume, since a helpful witness may add assumed detail.

## suspect story as designed clue
- [mechanism] A suspect's tidy story can be designed to convince, so the player must test it for a flaw rather than accept or reject it on first sight.

## suspect-chosen witnesses
- [pitfall] Witnesses named by the suspect may have been arranged to be absent or unable to confirm, so their corroboration carries limited weight. When: the suspect supplies the witnesses. Why: the suspect controls who can be checked.

## suspense from unexplained action
- [mechanism] Showing an ominous action without its purpose builds suspense, because the audience senses danger without knowing the full picture. When: Story needs tension before the reveal.

## suspense in custody
- [heuristic] Waiting carries no risk when the witness is already in custody, so an appointment-based suspense device loses most of its force. When: Witness is in custody.

## suspense through case order
- [heuristic] Lay out the full case against a character before showing the defence, and hold back the decisive answer. This keeps the audience waiting. When: when the audience needs suspense before a counter-argument.

## suspense through sensory limits
- [mechanism] Limiting the character's perception, through darkness, silence and brief light, creates dread because the character's limited awareness is itself the source of tension. When: stealth or tense scenes. Why: Restricted sensing forces the audience to imagine threats the character cannot yet see.

## suspicion before arrest
- [fact] Suspicion of a person can already exist among some people well before any formal charge or arrest is made. When: When tracing when an accusation first began. Why: Informal talk precedes official action.

## suspicion cuts access
- [mechanism] Suspicion directed at the investigator can cut off access to the information needed to clear them. When: when authorities suspect the investigator. Why: Blocked sources prevent exoneration.

## suspicion from era fears
- [behavior] Observers guess at hidden wrongdoing using the fears fashionable in their era, so their suspicions reflect general anxieties more than anything they have seen. When: An observer knows little about the person being suspected. Why: Familiar fears supply ready explanations when direct observation is absent.

## suspicion from rumour
- [rule] Do not settle on a suspect's guilt from rumour or ambiguous gestures alone; wait for corroborated evidence before committing. When: a suspect's behaviour could be read two ways. Why: ambiguous signs can mislead when read without corroboration.

## suspicion meter from gossip
- [mechanism] Gossip can drive a suspicion value that changes townsfolk reactions independent of what a character actually did. When: when designing NPC reputation systems.

## suspicion of neat evidence
- [behavior] An investigator may doubt a case because its evidence looks too neat, even before the reason for that doubt is shown.

## suspicion shaping sightings
- [pitfall] Suspecting a particular person can lead a witness to report seeing that person, so check any such sighting against other evidence.

## suspicion social factors
- [pitfall] Suspicion driven by grudges, property claims, rank, class or kinship rather than factual evidence misleads investigations; accusations need a factual basis. When: Investigating a death with several possible culprits, or when a suspect is chosen because of rank, class or kinship. Why: Social motives can outweigh the available evidence, and status-based suspicion has no factual grounding. (x2)

## suspicion state journal
- [heuristic] Keep suspicions tentative until a test or corroboration confirms them, on case boards or clue journals, so the suspicion-to-proof gap becomes a playable mechanic and theories aren't treated as facts. When: designing a clue journal or tracking multiple suspicions during an investigation. Why: Unconfirmed theories should not be treated as established facts. (x2)

## suspicion use
- [rule] Use suspicion to decide where to look and whom to watch, not as the sole basis for an accusation or arrest. Why: Suspicion guides investigation, but accusation requires proof.

## suspicion without anchor
- [pitfall] Suspicion that shifts without an anchoring clue reads as indecision rather than misdirection. When: suspects change with no new clue. Why: the audience sees no reason for the change.

## suspicious attention to belongings
- [pitfall] Close attention to a speaker's belongings may be read as suspicion.

## suspicious claimant reaction
- [behavior] A brief change in a claimant's expression while a document is identified can reveal more than their testimony. When: A person is questioned about a document they stand to benefit from. Why: Involuntary reactions can betray knowledge the testimony hides.

## suspicious member betrays leader
- [mechanism] A member who suspects a leader may sell that leader out to the authorities to protect themselves.

## suspicious noise explanation
- [pitfall] A quick, ready explanation for a suspicious noise should be checked rather than accepted, since cover stories can be offered at once. When: someone explains away a noise connected to an event. Why: An immediate explanation may be prepared in advance, so it is not evidence that the noise was harmless.

## suspicious pretext
- [pitfall] An invented errand used to clear the room can later be noticed as suspicious.

## suspicious scouting questions
- [behavior] Overly curious questions alert the person being investigated, so a scout's questions must look ordinary to avoid suspicion. When: a visitor gathers information from an occupant. Why: unusual questions signal intent.

## suspicious tip as bait
- [heuristic] A tip that arrives at a convenient moment may be bait, so ask whether the suspect could have written it and would gain from the timing. When: a tip arrives just when the suspect benefits. Why: a convenient tip may serve the suspect's own plan.

## suspiciously complete evidence
- [heuristic] Damaging finds that each look incriminating, and together look overwhelming, may have been selected rather than found; question how the set came together. When: several damaging items point the same way at once.

## suspiciously exact tracks
- [heuristic] Measurements that agree too closely across several tracks are more likely staged than coincidental, so judge how tight the agreement is. When: when judging whether tracks are genuine. Why: real walkers rarely match exactly.

## suspiciously surviving clues
- [heuristic] A clue that survives when it could easily have been destroyed may have been left on purpose, and such deliberate clues can backfire on their authors. When: A key item survives in a place where destruction was easy. Why: Culprits who leave clues to mislead take the risk that the clue exposes them.

## suspiciously tidy clue
- [heuristic] A trace that is too neat, or that leads exactly where investigators will look, may have been placed deliberately and should be tested. When: a clue seems conveniently placed. Why: Staged evidence often points directly at the investigation.

## sustained feigned illness risk
- [pitfall] Keeping a feigned condition convincing over many days is hard and carries real risk to the person faking it. When: A staged incapacity must last a long time. Why: Each day of performance adds a chance of exposure and personal danger.

## sustained secrecy signal
- [heuristic] If a secret has held among several people who had reason to talk, the secret is probably real. When: several people share a secret and each had incentive to reveal it. Why: pressure to betray would usually have broken the silence.

## sweep causes panic
- [pitfall] Sweeping a whole group can cause panic and rumour that bury the facts the investigator needs.

## sweeping hypothesis test
- [procedure] 1) Assume every witness statement is false. 2) List which physical facts fit that assumption. 3) Note which physical facts contradict it.

## switch angle on failure
- [rule] When one line of questioning fails, change angle, such as asking about access to a room, rather than repeating the same question.

## switch evasive source
- [rule] With an evasive witness, switch to another source instead of pressing the same person again.

## switch operator suspicion
- [pitfall] A single controllable switch makes its operator a suspect once the lights return and the scene is reviewed.

## switchable suspicion
- [rule] Track motive for both sides of a conflict, so the player can shift suspicion when a new record changes the picture.

## sworn body examination
- [procedure] 1) Appoint named examiners and swear them. 2) Have them search for the sought sign. 3) Write their findings, sign them and attest them before an official. 4) File the report as a formal record. When: When physical evidence needs an expert eye and a formal record. Why: The oath and attestation give the report weight, which is why its content must still be checked.

## sworn detail trap
- [pitfall] Treating an account as firm evidence simply because it is sworn and detailed.

## sworn form as proof
- [pitfall] Do not treat an oath as proof: sworn form records what was said, not that it was true. Why: an oath fixes the statement but not its accuracy.

## sworn statement cross-check
- [procedure] 1) Identify the sworn account's source, date and signatories. 2) Check its account against the written record line by line. 3) Locate the points of disagreement. 4) Judge whether each difference changes substance. When: Verifying a witness account against documents. Why: Structured comparison separates real contradictions from minor wording variation.

## sworn statement raises weight
- [mechanism] A sworn or formal statement can raise a witness's weight in the eyes of listeners even when their general standing is low. Why: Formal commitment signals accountability.

## symbol alone as motive
- [pitfall] A motive built from a symbol alone is speculation; a symbolic grievance needs independent corroboration before it implies intent.

## symbol group attribution
- [heuristic] A symbol with a known meaning, found on victims, can reveal which group carried out an act.

## sympathetic npc biased tips
- [mechanism] A sympathetic NPC can give the player a biased tip; rewarding cross-checking of that tip against the scene encourages evidence-based reasoning over trust. Why: Affection for an NPC can shape how much the player believes that NPC's information.

## sympathy and harm
- [heuristic] A sympathetic profile should not excuse a harm; weigh the harm itself separately from the character's good qualities. When: Assessing a character who did both good and serious wrong. Why: Sympathy can hide the cost to victims.

## sympathy factions
- [heuristic] Sympathy factions that defend or shield a suspect can act as allies or obstacles to the player, independent of the clues.

## sympathy over completeness
- [pitfall] Gentleness can make an interviewer drop a point they needed, so sympathy trades completeness for the witness's comfort.

## sympathy turning to prejudice
- [behavior] Sympathy for a victim can turn into prejudice against a suspect, shaping public belief and possibly how a jury reacts. When: A victim is widely pitied and a suspect is publicly known. Why: Feelings about one person spread to judgments about another.

## symptom as proof
- [pitfall] Physical symptoms a confessor reports after speaking can be read as proof of sincerity, though they say nothing about the claim itself.

## symptom mismatch
- [heuristic] Check whether observed symptoms fit the claimed cause; symptoms that the claimed cause would not produce make that cause doubtful.

## systematic person examination
- [procedure] 1) Examine the hair. 2) Examine the jaw. 3) Examine the arms. 4) Examine the hands, using magnification for small signs. Record what each part reveals about occupation. When: at the start of an interview when the person's background is unknown. Why: a fixed order ensures no part is missed and small signs are caught.

## tacky adhesive dating
- [fact] Adhesive that is still tacky indicates a very recent application, so it can date a replacement to the most recent period.

## tag incapacitated admissions
- [rule] Record admissions made while an NPC is incapacitated as evidence but tag them less reliable, so trust can vary.

## tag npc claims for retraction
- [rule] Tag each NPC claim as true or false in the game data, so that a later retraction can resurface the earlier line as a clue. When: when NPCs make statements the player may later revisit. Why: Stored truth values let the game connect retractions to earlier dialogue.

## tagged npc rumours
- [rule] Have gossip NPCs spread rumours about each other, tagging each with the speaker's status, grudge, source and bias, so players judge how far to trust partly accurate claims. When: Designing gossip systems or gossip NPCs whose information is partly true. Why: Source bias makes players weigh claims, and explicit bias lets players calibrate trust in partly accurate rumours. (x2)

## tagged testimony storage
- [rule] Tag NPC testimony and relayed rumours with their source, confidence or self-interest, and hop count, so players can weigh reliability and cross-check claims against map or item data. When: when a game records what characters say about events or passes information along through dialogue. Why: tags let players judge reliability; visible hop counts show how far a claim is from its source. (x2)

## tagging claims by source
- [procedure] 1) Record each claim's source and basis as seen, heard, or assumed. 2) Mark hearsay as unconfirmed. 3) Upgrade a claim to confirmed only after a direct witness or independent record supports it. When: players collect multiple statements or a journal or rumor system presents hidden events. Why: knowing how a claim was obtained changes how much weight it deserves, and players need to know which information is provisional. (x2)

## tagging clue reliability
- [rule] Tag each NPC clue fragment with the observer's distance or conditions so players can judge how reliable it is.

## tail record and read
- [procedure] 1) Record every stop the target makes. 2) Note each small deliberate act. 3) Read the acts together to infer the target's plans. When: shadowing a suspect's routine. Why: habits and plans show in small acts.

## tail use condition
- [heuristic] Use a tail when a target's movements are the only way to find a contact or hiding place.

## tailed npc faction reveal
- [mechanism] A captive NPC released under tail can reveal a hidden faction through where he goes, letting the player learn the group's location. When: Designing quests around captive NPCs. Why: The NPC's movements expose associates.

## tailing and timed confrontation
- [procedure] 1) Post a tail to follow the target. 2) Learn where the target is at a set time. 3) Plan the confrontation for that time, expecting the target to be present. When: the target must be found again after a gap.

## tailor clothing labels
- [fact] Tailor-made clothing normally carries sewn strips naming the maker and client, and often the date, so missing strips are unusual.

## talkative npc clue filtering
- [heuristic] A talkative NPC can hold useful clues among filler dialogue, so the game should give players a way to filter for them. When: Designing an NPC with a lot of chatter. Why: Players need a way to separate the usable clues from the noise.

## talkative witness handling
- [heuristic] Let a talkative witness run on rather than cutting them off, then sift the talk for the few usable facts it contains. When: A witness gives long, rambling answers. Why: Useful clues can sit among filler dialogue, so interrupting may lose them.

## talkative witness pacing
- [rule] Let a talkative or elderly witness speak at their own pace, and steer back to the subject in small steps rather than with sharp, direct questions. When: when the witness digresses and the needed facts are scattered through background talk. Why: sharp questions make digressive witnesses lose the thread.

## tamper check order
- [procedure] 1) Check innocent causes first, such as too little moisture or defective gum. 2) Rule each one out. 3) Only then consider deliberate tampering. When: a seal fails. Why: simpler causes are more probable.

## targeted npc questions
- [rule] Give players targeted questions for NPCs, and let each answer unlock the next deduction.

## teasing exhausts audience
- [pitfall] A pattern of teasing without new information exhausts the audience, and interruptions that feel arbitrary weaken the scene.

## technical phrasing hides doubt
- [pitfall] Complicated technical terms can make an uncertain cause seem settled when it is not.

## technical term sense check
- [rule] Check a technical term's professional sense and the sources it cites before relying on it, rather than accepting the everyday reading.

## tell use limit
- [rule] Use a behavioral tell, such as a physical reaction, only to choose the next line of questioning, never as sole ground for an accusation or proof of guilt or knowledge. When: When a tell appears during questioning. Why: Tells signal where to look but prove nothing alone; fear and discomfort have many sources. (x2)

## telling-answer test
- [heuristic] Ask the suspect a question whose answer would be telling if they were guilty, such as asking about symptoms that would appear after poisoning. When: Testing a suspect's guilt without decisive evidence. Why: A guilty suspect's answer or reaction can betray knowledge they should not have.

## tells point to items
- [rule] Let tells point to hidden items, so the player connects an NPC's reaction to a location.

## telltale document features
- [rule] Give in-game documents telltale features, such as inconsistent detail, odd phrasing or broken sentences, so close readers can judge whether a note is finished or a rough draft. When: Writing notes, journals or ledgers for players to read. Why: Careful readers use textual signs to judge authenticity.

## telltale trap
- [mechanism] A small object left on a surface can transfer to a visitor's clothing and later reveal that they were present. When: a hidden visitor must be exposed later. Why: objects pick up material from whatever touches them.

## temper under warning
- [heuristic] A sharp reply to a warning is evidence of how a person may react under pressure, so record it.

## timeline from spending
- [definition] Timeline reconstruction from spending means recalling small payments, summing them, and checking the total against cash still held to rebuild a sequence of events.
